Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Majjhimanikāye

The Middle-Length Discourses

Mūlapaṇṇāsa-ṭīkā

The Subcommentary to the Root Fifty

(Paṭhamo bhāgo)

(First Part)

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Introduction

1. Saṃvaṇṇanārambhe [V 1.0001][M 1.0001] ratanattayavandanā saṃvaṇṇetabbassa dhammassa pabhavanissayavisuddhipaṭivedanatthaṃ, taṃ pana dhammasaṃvaṇṇanāsu viññūnaṃ bahumānuppādanatthaṃ, taṃ sammadeva tesaṃ uggahadhāraṇādikkamaladdhabbāya sammāpaṭipattiyā sabbahitasukhanipphādanatthaṃ. Atha vā maṅgalabhāvato, sabbakiriyāsu pubbakiccabhāvato, paṇḍitehi samācaritabhāvato, āyatiṃ paresaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjanato ca saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ ratanattayapaṇāmakiriyā. Atha vā ratanattayapaṇāmakaraṇaṃ pūjanīyapūjāpuññavisesanibbattanatthaṃ. Taṃ attano yathāladdhasampattinimittakassa kammassa balānuppadānatthaṃ. Antarā ca tassa asaṅkocanatthaṃ. Tadubhayaṃ anantarāyena aṭṭhakathāya parisamāpanatthaṃ. Idameva ca payojanaṃ ācariyena idhādhippetaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati “iti me pasannamatino…pe… tassānubhāvenā”ti. Vatthuttayapūjāhi niratisayapuññakkhettasaṃbuddhiyā aparimeyyapabhāvo puññātisayoti bahuvidhantarāyepi lokasannivāse [V 1.0002] antarāyanibandhanasakalasaṃkilesaviddhaṃsanāya pahoti. Bhayādiupaddavañca nivāreti. Yathāha –

1. At the commencement of this exposition, homage is paid to the Triple Gem in order to disclose the origin, basis, and purity of the Dhamma to be expounded. Further, this homage is for the purpose of producing great respect in the wise for these expositions of the Dhamma, and for the purpose of their correctly grasping, retaining, and practicing it, which leads to the accomplishment of all welfare and happiness. Alternatively, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem is included in this exposition because it is auspicious, because it is a preliminary duty for all undertakings, because it is practiced by the wise, and because it leads to others following their example in the future. Or again, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of generating the special merit of venerating what is worthy of veneration. This serves to strengthen the power of one's own kamma, which is the cause of the fortune one has obtained, and to prevent its diminution in the meantime. Both these serve for the unhindered completion of the commentary. This is indeed the purpose intended by the teacher here, for he will say: “Thus, with a confident mind … by its power….” Through veneration of the Triple Gem, an abundance of merit of immeasurable power arises from the Perfectly Enlightened One, who is an unsurpassed field of merit. Even amidst the many kinds of obstacles in the world, this is capable of dispelling all defilements bound up with hindrances. It also wards off fear and other calamities, as it is said:

“Pūjārahe pūjayato. Buddhe yadi va sāvake”tiādi (dha. pa. 195; apa. 1.10.1), tathā [M 1.0002] –

“One who venerates those worthy of veneration, whether Buddhas or disciples…” and so on (Dhp 195; Ap 1.10.1); likewise:

“Ye, bhikkhave, buddhe pasannā, agge te pasannā, agge kho pana pasannānaṃ aggo vipāko hotī”tiādi (itivu. 90, 91),

“Bhikkhus, those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the supreme. For those with confidence in the supreme, the result is supreme,” and so on (It 90, 91).

“Buddhoti kittayantassa, kāye bhavati yā pīti;

Varameva hi sā pīti, kasiṇenapi jambudīpassa.

“When proclaiming ‘Buddha,’ the joy that arises in the body—that joy is truly excellent, surpassing even a kasina that covers all of Jambudīpa.

Dhammoti kittayantassa…pe… kasiṇenapi jambudīpassa;

Saṅghoti kittayantassa…pe… kasiṇenapi jambudīpassā”ti. (itivu. aṭṭha. 90),

When proclaiming ‘Dhamma,’ … surpassing even a kasina that covers all of Jambudīpa; when proclaiming ‘Sangha,’ … surpassing even a kasina that covers all of Jambudīpa.” (It-a on It 90).

Tathā –

Likewise:

“Yasmiṃ mahānāma samaye ariyasāvako tathāgataṃ anussarati, nevassa tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na dosa…pe… na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hotī”tiādi (a. ni. 6.10; 11.11),

“Mahānāma, at a time when a noble disciple is recollecting the Tathāgata, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, not obsessed by hatred ... not obsessed by delusion,” and so on (AN 6.10; 11.11).

“Araññe rukkhamūle vā…pe…

Bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā,

Lomahaṃso na hessatī”ti ca. (saṃ. ni. 2.249);

“In the forest, at the foot of a tree… fear or dread or horripilation will not arise.” And: (Cf. SN 11.3).

Tattha yassa vatthuttayassa vandanaṃ kattukāmo, tassa guṇātisayayogasandassanatthaṃ “karuṇāsītalahadaya”ntiādinā gāthāttayamāha. Guṇātisayayogena hi vandanārahabhāvo, vandanārahe ca katā vandanā yathādhippetaṃ payojanaṃ sādhetīti. Tattha yassā desanāya saṃvaṇṇanaṃ kattukāmo. Sā na vinayadesanā viya karuṇāppadhānā, nāpi abhidhammadesanā viya paññāppadhānā[V 1.0003], atha kho karuṇāpaññāppadhānāti tadubhayappadhānameva tāva sammāsambuddhassa thomanaṃ kātuṃ tammūlakattā sesaratanānaṃ “karuṇāsītalahadaya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kiratīti karuṇā, paradukkhaṃ vikkhipati apanetīti attho. Atha vā kiṇātīti karuṇā, paradukkhe sati kāruṇikaṃ hiṃsati vibādhatīti attho. Paradukkhe sati sādhūnaṃ kampanaṃ hadayakhedaṃ karotīti vā karuṇā. Atha vā kamiti sukhaṃ, taṃ rundhatīti karuṇā. Esā hi paradukkhāpanayanakāmatālakkhaṇā attasukhanirapekkhatāya kāruṇikānaṃ sukhaṃ rundhati vibandhatīti attho[M 1.0003]. Karuṇāya sītalaṃ karuṇāsītalaṃ, karuṇāsītalaṃ hadayaṃ assāti karuṇāsītalahadayo, taṃ karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ.

Here, as he wishes to pay homage to the Triple Gem, he utters three verses beginning with “whose heart is cooled by compassion” in order to demonstrate its connection with supreme qualities. For it is through connection with supreme qualities that one becomes worthy of homage, and homage paid to one who is worthy accomplishes the intended purpose. Here, as he wishes to expound on this teaching: it is not, like the Vinaya teaching, chiefly concerned with compassion, nor, like the Abhidhamma teaching, chiefly concerned with wisdom; rather, it is chiefly concerned with both compassion and wisdom. Therefore, to praise the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who is preeminent in both—and because these are the root of the other two Gems—the passage beginning “whose heart is cooled by compassion” was stated. Herein, karuṇā is so called because “it scatters” (kirati); the meaning is that it dispels and removes the suffering of others. Or, karuṇā is so called because “it injures” (kiṇāti); the meaning is that when others suffer, it injures and torments the compassionate person. Or, karuṇā is so called because when others suffer, it “causes” (karoti) the good to tremble and feel heartache. Or, kam means happiness, and karuṇā is so called because “it obstructs” (rundhati) that. For this compassion, characterized by the desire to remove the suffering of others, disregards one's own happiness and thus obstructs the happiness of the compassionate; this is the meaning. “Cooled by compassion” is karuṇāsītalaṃ. “One whose heart is cooled by compassion” is karuṇāsītalahadayo. That is karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ.

Tattha kiñcāpi paresaṃ hitopasaṃhārasukhādiaparihānicchanasabhāvatāya, byāpādāratīnaṃ ujuvipaccanīkatāya ca parasattasantānagatasantāpavicchedanākārappavattiyā mettāmuditānampi cittasītalabhāvakāraṇatā upalabbhati, tathāpi paradukkhāpanayanākārappavattiyā parūpatāpāsahanarasā avihiṃsābhūtā karuṇāva visesena bhagavato cittassa cittapassaddhi viya sītibhāvanimittanti vuttaṃ “karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti. Karuṇāmukhena vā mettāmuditānampi hadayasītalabhāvakāraṇatā vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā asādhāraṇañāṇavisesanibandhanabhūtā sātisayaṃ niravasesañca sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ viya savisayabyāpitāya mahākaruṇābhāvaṃ upagatā karuṇāva bhagavato atisayena hadayasītalabhāvahetūti āha “karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti. Atha vā satipi mettāmuditānaṃ sātisaye hadayasītibhāvanibandhanatte sakalabuddhaguṇavisesakāraṇatāya tāsampi kāraṇanti karuṇāva bhagavato “hadayasītalabhāvakāraṇa”nti vuttā. Karuṇānidānā hi sabbepi buddhaguṇā. Karuṇānubhāvanibbāpiyamānasaṃsāradukkhasantāpassa hi bhagavato paradukkhāpanayanakāmatāya anekānipi asaṅkhyeyyāni kappānaṃ akilantarūpasseva niravasesabuddhakaradhammasambharaṇaniratassa samadhigatadhammādhipateyyassa ca sannihitesupi sattasaṅkhārasamupanītahadayūpatāpanimittesu na īsakampi cittasītibhāvassa aññathattamahosīti. Etasmiñca atthavikappe tīsupi avatthāsu bhagavato karuṇā saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, although it is found that loving-kindness and sympathetic joy are also causes for the cooling of the heart—due to their nature of wishing for others' welfare and happiness and not for the loss of it, and because they proceed in a way that cuts off the affliction in the mental continuums of other beings, being the direct opponents of ill will and discontent—nevertheless, it is compassion that is the special cause for the cooling of the Blessed One's heart, like tranquility of mind itself. For compassion has the nature of non-harming, the function of not tolerating the torment of others, and it proceeds in the manner of removing others' suffering. Thus it is said, “whose heart is cooled by compassion.” Or it should be seen that loving-kindness and sympathetic joy are said to be causes for the cooling of the heart by way of compassion. Or, just as the omniscient knowledge—which is the basis for the distinction of extraordinary knowledge, is supreme, and is exhaustive—pervades its entire domain, so too compassion, having attained the state of great compassion by pervading its domain, is the preeminent cause for the cooling of the Blessed One's heart. Thus he says, “whose heart is cooled by compassion.” Or, although loving-kindness and sympathetic joy are an excellent basis for the cooling of the heart, since compassion is the cause of all the Buddha's special qualities, it is also the cause of those two, and thus compassion alone is said to be the “cause for the cooling of the heart” of the Blessed One. For all the qualities of a Buddha are rooted in compassion. Indeed, for the Blessed One—whose compassion extinguished the fever of suffering in saṃsāra, who for countless incalculable eons was tirelessly devoted to accumulating all the qualities that make a Buddha, solely out of a desire to remove the suffering of others, thereby gaining mastery of the Dhamma, and who was untiring in this—even when signs of affliction arose in his heart on account of the conditioned existence of beings, there was not the slightest alteration in the coolness of his mind. And in this interpretation, it should be understood that the Blessed One's compassion is included in all three stages.

Pajānātīti paññā, yathāsabhāvaṃ pakārehi paṭivijjhatīti attho. Paññāva ñeyyāvaraṇappahānato pakārehi dhammasabhāvajotanaṭṭhena pajjototi paññāpajjoto. Savāsanappahānato visesena hataṃ samugghātitaṃ vihataṃ, paññāpajjotena vihataṃ paññāpajjotavihataṃ. Muyhanti tena, sayaṃ vā muyhati, mohanamattameva vā tanti moho, avijjā, sveva visayasabhāvapaṭicchādanato andhakārasarikkhatāya tamo viyāti tamo, paññāpajjotavihato [V 1.0004] mohatamo etassāti paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo, taṃ paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ. Sabbesampi [M 1.0004] hi khīṇāsavānaṃ satipi paññāpajjotena avijjandhakārassa vihatabhāve saddhāvimuttehi viya diṭṭhippattānaṃ sāvakehi paccekasambuddhehi ca savāsanappahānena sammāsambuddhānaṃ kilesappahānassa viseso vijjatīti sātisayena avijjāpahānena bhagavantaṃ thomento āha “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti.

“It understands” (pajānāti), thus it is wisdom (paññā); the meaning is that it penetrates their true nature in various ways. Wisdom itself is a lamp (pajjoto), thus “lamp of wisdom” (paññāpajjoto), because by abandoning the obstruction to the knowable, it illuminates the nature of phenomena in various ways. Because of the abandonment of the latent tendencies, it is especially struck, eradicated, dispelled; dispelled by the lamp of wisdom is paññāpajjotavihataṃ. “One is deluded by it, or it is deluded itself, or it is mere delusion,” thus it is delusion (moho), that is, ignorance (avijjā). Because it conceals the true nature of its object, it is like darkness (andhakāra), thus it is darkness (tamo). “He for whom the darkness of delusion is dispelled by the lamp of wisdom” is paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo. That is paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ. For although the darkness of ignorance has been dispelled by the lamp of wisdom for all whose taints are destroyed, there is still a distinction in the abandoning of defilements between the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas and the disciples—those liberated by faith and those who are attainers-of-view—and the Paccekabuddhas, namely, the abandoning of the latent tendencies. Thus, praising the Blessed One for his supreme abandonment of ignorance, he says, “the one whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the lamp of wisdom.”

Atha vā antarena paropadesaṃ attano santāne accantaṃ avijjandhakāravigamassa nibbattitattā, tathā sabbaññutāya balesu ca vasībhāvassa samadhigatattā, parasantatiyañca dhammadesanātisayānubhāvena sammadeva tassa pavattitattā bhagavāva visesato mohatamavigamena thometabboti āha “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti. Imasmiñca atthavikappe “paññāpajjoto”ti padena bhagavato paṭivedhapaññā viya desanāpaññāpi sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesanayena vā saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Alternatively, because the complete removal of the darkness of ignorance was produced in his own mental continuum without the instruction of another, because he had attained mastery over the powers and omniscience, and because that removal rightly occurred in the mental continuums of others through the mighty power of his sublime Dhamma teaching, the Blessed One is especially to be praised for the removal of the darkness of delusion. Thus he says, “the one whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the lamp of wisdom.” In this interpretation, it should be understood that by the term “lamp of wisdom,” the Blessed One's wisdom of teaching is included along with his wisdom of penetration, either by general designation or by the method of elliptical reference.

Atha vā bhagavato ñāṇassa ñeyyapariyantikattā sakalañeyyadhammasabhāvāvabodhanasamatthena anāvaraṇañāṇasaṅkhātena paññāpajjotena sabbañeyyadhammasabhāvacchādakassa mohandhakārassa vidhamitattā anaññasādhāraṇo bhagavato mohatamavināsoti katvā vuttaṃ “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti. Ettha ca mohatamavidhamanante adhigatattā anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ kāraṇūpacārena sasantāne mohatamavidhamananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Abhinīhārasampattiyā savāsanappahānameva hi kilesānaṃ ñeyyāvaraṇappahānanti, parasantāne pana mohatamavidhamanassa kāraṇabhāvato anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ “mohatamavidhamana”nti vuccatīti.

Alternatively, because the Blessed One's knowledge encompasses all that can be known, the darkness of delusion, which conceals the true nature of all knowable phenomena, has been dispelled by the lamp of his wisdom, which is designated “unobstructed knowledge” because it is capable of awakening to the true nature of all knowable phenomena. Therefore, the Blessed One's destruction of the darkness of delusion is unique, and so it is said, “the one whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the lamp of wisdom.” Here it should be understood that since the unobstructed knowledge is attained after the darkness of delusion has been dispelled, it is called “the dispeller of the darkness of delusion” in one's own continuum by a metaphorical usage of the cause. For the abandoning of the obstruction to the knowable is precisely the abandoning of the defilements together with their latent tendencies, through the accomplishment of the original aspiration. In the mental continuums of others, however, the unobstructed knowledge is called “the dispeller of the darkness of delusion” because it is the cause for dispelling it.

Kiṃ pana kāraṇaṃ avijjāsamugghātoyeveko pahānasampattivasena bhagavato thomanānimittaṃ gayhati, na pana sātisayaṃ niravasesakilesappahānanti? Tappahānavacaneneva tadekaṭṭhatāya sakalasaṃkilesagaṇasamugghātassa jotitabhāvato. Na hi so tādiso kileso atthi, yo niravasesaavijjāppahānena na pahīyatīti.

But what is the reason that the uprooting of ignorance alone is taken as the sign of praise for the Blessed One, as the attainment of abandonment, and not the surpassing, complete abandonment of all defilements? Because by the very statement of its abandonment, the uprooting of the entire mass of defilements is illuminated, owing to its having the same meaning. For there is no defilement that is not abandoned by the complete abandonment of ignorance.

Atha vā vijjā viya sakalakusaladhammasamuppattiyā niravasesākusaladhammanibbattiyā saṃsārappavattiyā ca avijjā padhānakāraṇanti tabbighātavacanena [M 1.0005] sakalasaṃkilesagaṇasamugghāto vuttoyeva hotīti vuttaṃ “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti.

Alternatively, just as wisdom is for the arising of all wholesome states, so ignorance is the principal cause for the production of all unwholesome states and for the continuation of saṃsāra. Thus, by the statement of its destruction, the uprooting of the entire mass of defilements is indeed stated. Hence it is said: “the one whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the lamp of wisdom.”

Narā [V 1.0005] ca amarā ca narāmarā, saha narāmarehīti sanarāmaro, sanarāmaro ca so loko cāti sanarāmaraloko. Tassa garūti sanarāmaralokagaru, taṃ sanarāmaralokagaruṃ. Etena devamanussānaṃ viya tadavasiṭṭhasattānampi yathārahaṃ guṇavisesāvahatāya bhagavato upakāritaṃ dasseti. Na cettha padhānāppadhānabhāvo codetabbo. Añño hi saddakkamo, añño atthakkamo. Edisesu hi samāsapadesu padhānampi appadhānaṃ viya niddisīyati yathā “sarājikāya parisāyā”ti (cūḷava. 336). Kāmañcettha sattasaṅkhārokāsavasena tividho loko, garubhāvassa pana adhippetattā garukaraṇasamatthasseva yujjanato sattalokassa vasena attho gahetabbo. So hi lokīyanti ettha puññapāpāni tabbipāko cāti “loko”ti vuccati. Amaraggahaṇena cettha upapattidevā adhippetā.

Humans and devas are `narāmarā`. 'With humans and devas' is `sanarāmaro`. A world that is with humans and devas is `sanarāmaraloko`. The revered one of that is `sanarāmaralokagaru`. To that `sanarāmaralokagaruṃ`. By this is shown the Blessed One’s helpfulness to devas and humans, and also to the remaining beings according to their capacity, by his bringing them special qualities. Here the distinction between primary and secondary should not be raised, for the order of words is one thing, the order of meaning another. For in such compound expressions the primary term is sometimes stated as if it were secondary, as in ‘the assembly with its king.’ Although here the world is threefold—as beings, formations, and space—since reverence is what is meant, the meaning should be taken as the world of beings, since it is only this that is capable of showing reverence. For it is that wherein merit, demerit, and their fruit are experienced (lokīyati), thus it is called ‘world’ (loko). By the term ‘immortals’ here, devas by rebirth are intended.

Atha vā samūhattho lokasaddo samudāyavasena lokīyati paññāpīyatīti. Saha narehīti sanarā, sanarā ca te amarā cāti sanarāmarā, tesaṃ lokoti sanarāmaralokoti purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Amarasaddena cettha visuddhidevāpi saṅgayhanti. Te hi maraṇābhāvato paramatthato amarā. Narāmarānaṃyeva ca gahaṇaṃ ukkaṭṭhaniddesavasena yathā “satthā devamanussāna”nti (dī. ni. 1.157). Tathā hi sabbānatthaparihārapubbaṅgamāya niravasesahitasukhavidhānatapparāya niratisayāya payogasampattiyā sadevamanussāya pajāya accantūpakāritāya aparimitanirupamappabhāvaguṇavisesasamaṅgitāya ca sabbasattuttamo bhagavā aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ uttamagāravaṭṭhānaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “sanarāmaralokagaru”nti.

Alternatively, the word ‘loka’ has the meaning of a collection, since it is regarded and designated as a multitude. ‘With humans’ is `sanarā`; those `sanarā` and the immortals are `sanarāmarā`; their world is `sanarāmaraloka`. This should be construed according to the previous method. Here, the term ‘immortals’ also includes the pure devas, for they are truly immortal in the ultimate sense due to the absence of death. The mention of only humans and immortals is by way of an excellent designation, as in ‘the Teacher of devas and humans.’ For indeed, the Blessed One, the highest of all beings, is the supreme object of reverence for limitless beings in limitless world-systems, on account of his accomplishment of effort, which is preceded by the removal of all that is harmful, is intent on establishing complete welfare and happiness, is unsurpassed, is of extreme benefit to the populace with its devas and humans, and is endowed with special qualities of immeasurable, incomparable power. Thus it is said: ‘the revered one of the world with its humans and devas.’

Sobhanaṃ gataṃ gamanaṃ etassāti sugato. Bhagavato hi veneyyajanupasaṅkamanaṃ ekantena tesaṃ hitasukhanipphādanato sobhanaṃ, tathā [M 1.0006] lakkhaṇānubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍitarūpakāyatāya dutavilambita-khalitānukaḍḍhana-nippīḷanukkuṭika-kuṭilākulatādi-dosarahita-mavahasita-rājahaṃsa- vasabhavāraṇa-migarājagamanaṃ kāyagamanaṃ ñāṇagamanañca vipulanimmalakaruṇā-sativīriyādi-guṇavisesasahitamabhinīhārato yāva mahābodhiṃ anavajjatāya sobhanamevāti. Atha vā sayambhuñāṇena sakalamapi lokaṃ pariññābhisamayavasena parijānanto ñāṇena sammā gato avagatoti sugato. Tathā lokasamudayaṃ pahānābhisamayavasena pajahanto anuppattidhammataṃ āpādento sammā gato atītoti sugato, lokanirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena sammā gato adhigatoti sugato, lokanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ bhāvanābhisamayavasena sammā gato paṭipannoti sugato. “Sotāpattimaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti na pacceti na paccāgacchatīti sugato”tiādinā (mahāni. 38; cūḷani. 27) nayena ayamattho [V 1.0006] vibhāvetabbo. Atha vā sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ sammāsambodhiṃ, nibbānameva vā gato adhigatoti sugato. Yasmā vā bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ veneyyānaṃ yathārahaṃ kālayuttameva ca dhammaṃ bhāsati, tasmā sammā gadati vadatīti sugato da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā. Iti sobhanagamanatādīhi sugato, taṃ sugataṃ.

His going is beautiful (sobhanaṃ), thus he is the Well-Gone One (Sugata). For the Blessed One's approach to those who can be trained is entirely beautiful because it brings about their welfare and happiness. Likewise, his bodily gait—adorned with the major and minor marks—is free from such faults as being too fast or too slow, stumbling, dragging the feet, pressing down too hard, stooping, or being crooked or agitated; it resembles the gait of a royal swan, a noble bull, a lordly elephant, or a lion king. His going is both bodily and mental, and his mental going, accompanied by the special qualities of vast, immaculate compassion, mindfulness, energy, and so on, from his initial aspiration up to great enlightenment, is beautiful because of its faultlessness. Alternatively, he is the Well-Gone One because with his self-originated knowledge he has rightly gone to and understood the entire world through the full understanding of comprehension. Similarly, he is the Well-Gone One because he has rightly gone beyond and abandoned the origin of the world through the full understanding of abandonment, having rendered it incapable of arising again. He is the Well-Gone One because he has rightly gone to and realized the cessation of the world, Nibbāna, through the full understanding of realization. He is the Well-Gone One because he has rightly gone along and developed the path leading to the cessation of the world through the full understanding of development. This meaning should be elaborated according to the method beginning: “The defilements that are abandoned by the path of stream-entry—to those defilements he does not go again, does not return to, does not come back to; thus he is the Well-Gone One.” Or, he is the Well-Gone One because he has gone to the beautiful place, that is, to perfect self-enlightenment or to Nibbāna itself. Or, because he speaks what is true, factual, beneficial, and timely and appropriate for those to be trained, he speaks rightly (sammā gadati); thus he is the Well-Gone One (Sugata), by changing the letter ‘d’ to ‘t’. Thus, because of his beautiful going and so on, he is the Well-Gone One; to that Well-Gone One.

Puññapāpakammehi upapajjanavasena gantabbato gatiyo, upapattibhavavisesā. Tā pana nirayādivasena pañcavidhā. Tāhi sakalassapi bhavagāmikammassa ariyamaggādhigamena avipākārahabhāvakaraṇena nivattitattā bhagavā pañcahipi gatīhi suṭṭhu mutto visaṃyuttoti āha “gativimutta”nti. Etena bhagavato katthacipi gatiyā apariyāpannataṃ dasseti, yato bhagavā “devātidevo”ti vuccati. Tenevāha –

Destinations (gati) are particular kinds of rebirth-existence, so called because one goes to them by way of rebirth as a result of meritorious and demeritorious actions. These are fivefold, beginning with the hells. Because all kamma that leads to existence has been turned back by the attainment of the noble path, having been rendered incapable of producing a result, the Blessed One is well freed and dissociated from all five destinations. Thus he is called ‘freed from destinations.’ This shows that the Blessed One is not included in any destination whatsoever, for which reason he is called the ‘Deva above devas.’ Thus it is said:

“Yena devūpapatyassa, gandhabbo vā vihaṅgamo;

Yakkhattaṃ yena gaccheyyaṃ, manussattañca abbaje;

Te mayhaṃ āsavā khīṇā, viddhastā vinaḷīkatā”ti. (a. ni. 4.36);

“That kamma by which I might be reborn as a deva, or become a gandhabba or a sky-farer; by which I might reach the state of a yakkha, or attain the human state—those taints of mine are destroyed, shattered, and annihilated.” (AN 4.36)

Taṃtaṃgatisaṃvattanakānañhi kammakilesānaṃ aggamaggena bodhimūleyeva suppahīnattā natthi bhagavato gatipariyāpannatāti accantameva bhagavā sabbabhavayonigati-viññāṇaṭṭhiti-sattāvāsa-sattanikāyehi parimutto, taṃ gativimuttaṃ. Vandeti namāmi, thomemīti vā attho.

Because the kamma and defilements that lead to this or that destination have been thoroughly abandoned by the supreme path at the very root of enlightenment, the Blessed One is not included in any destination. Therefore, the Blessed One is completely liberated from all forms of existence, wombs, destinations, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, and classes of beings; to him, the one freed from destinations. ‘I pay homage’ means ‘I salute’ or ‘I praise.’

Atha [M 1.0007] vā gativimuttanti anupādisesanibbānadhātuppattiyā bhagavantaṃ thometi. Ettha hi dvīhi ākārehi bhagavato thomanā veditabbā attahitasampattito parahitapaṭipattito ca. Tesu attahitasampatti anāvaraṇañāṇādhigamato savāsanānaṃ sabbesaṃ kilesānaṃ accantappahānato anupādisesanibbānappattito ca veditabbā, parahitapaṭipatti lābhasakkārādinirapekkhacittassa sabbadukkhaniyyānikadhammadesanato viruddhesupi niccaṃ hitajjhāsayato ñāṇaparipākakālāgamanato ca. Sā panettha āsayato payogato ca duvidhā parahitapaṭipatti, tividhā ca attahitasampatti pakāsitā hoti. Kathaṃ? “Karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti etena āsayato parahitapaṭipatti, sammāgadanatthena sugatasaddena payogato parahitapaṭipatti, “paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ gativimutta”nti etehi catusaccapaṭivedhatthena ca sugatasaddena tividhāpi attahitasampatti, avasiṭṭhaṭṭhena [V 1.0007] tena “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti etena cāpi sabbāpi attahitasampattiparahitapaṭipatti pakāsitā hotīti.

Alternatively, ‘freed from destinations’ praises the Blessed One for his attainment of the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. Here, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood in two ways: through the accomplishment of his own welfare and through his practice for the welfare of others. Among these, the accomplishment of his own welfare is to be understood from his attainment of unobstructed knowledge, his utter abandonment of all defilements with their latent tendencies, and his attainment of the Nibbāna-element without residue. His practice for the welfare of others is to be understood from his teaching the Dhamma that leads out from all suffering with a mind unconcerned with gain and honor, from his constant disposition of welfare even toward the hostile, and from his awaiting the time for the ripening of knowledge in his disciples. Here, that practice for the welfare of others is shown to be twofold, by disposition and by application, while the accomplishment of his own welfare is shown to be threefold. How so? By ‘with a heart cooled by compassion,’ the practice for others’ welfare by disposition is shown. By the word ‘Sugata’ in the sense of speaking rightly, the practice for others’ welfare by application is shown. By the phrases ‘who has dispelled the darkness of delusion with the light of wisdom’ and ‘freed from destinations,’ and by the word ‘Sugata’ in its sense of penetrating the Four Truths, the threefold accomplishment of his own welfare is shown. And by the remaining meaning of the phrase ‘who has dispelled the darkness of delusion with the light of wisdom,’ all aspects of both the accomplishment of his own welfare and the practice for the welfare of others are revealed.

Atha vā tīhi ākārehi bhagavato thomanā veditabbā – hetuto phalato upakārato ca. Tattha hetu mahākaruṇā, sā paṭhamapadena dassitā. Phalaṃ catubbidhaṃ ñāṇasampadā pahānasampadā ānubhāvasampadā rūpakāyasampadā cāti. Tāsu ñāṇapahānasampadā dutiyapadena saccapaṭivedhatthena ca sugatasaddena pakāsitā honti, ānubhāvasampadā pana tatiyapadena, rūpakāyasampadā yathāvuttakāyagamanasobhanatthena sugatasaddena lakkhaṇānubyañjanapāripūriyā vinā tadabhāvato. Upakāro anantaraṃ abāhiraṃ karitvā tividhayānamukhena vimuttidhammadesanā. So sammāgadanatthena sugatasaddena pakāsito hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Alternatively, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood in three ways: by cause, by fruit, and by benefit. Here, the cause is great compassion, shown by the first phrase. The fruit is fourfold: the perfection of knowledge, the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of power, and the perfection of the physical form. Among these, the perfections of knowledge and abandonment are revealed by the second phrase, and by the word ‘Sugata’ in its sense of penetrating the truths. The perfection of power is shown by the third phrase. The perfection of the physical form is indicated by the word ‘Sugata’ in the sense of the beauty of his bodily gait as described above, since this would not exist without the fulfillment of the major and minor marks. The benefit is the teaching of the Dhamma of liberation through the gateway of the three vehicles, without making an inside and an outside. This is revealed by the word ‘Sugata’ in its sense of speaking rightly. Thus it should be understood.

Tattha “karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti etena sammāsambodhiyā mūlaṃ dasseti. Mahākaruṇāsañcoditamānaso hi bhagavā saṃsārapaṅkato sattānaṃ samuddharaṇatthaṃ katābhinīhāro anupubbena pāramiyo pūretvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ adhigatoti karuṇā sammāsambodhiyā mūlaṃ. “Paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti etena sammāsambodhiṃ dasseti[M 1.0008]. Anāvaraṇañāṇapadaṭṭhānañhi maggañāṇaṃ, maggañāṇapadaṭṭhānañca anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ “sammāsambodhī”ti vuccatīti. Sammāgamanatthena sugatasaddena sammāsambodhiyā paṭipattiṃ dasseti līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhanakāmasukhallikattakilamathānuyogasassatucchedābhinivesādi antadvayarahitāya karuṇāpaññāpariggahitāya majjhimāya paṭipattiyā pakāsanato sugatasaddassa. Itarehi sammāsambodhiyā padhānāppadhānabhedaṃ payojanaṃ dasseti. Saṃsāramahoghato sattasantāraṇañhettha padhānaṃ payojanaṃ, tadaññamappadhānaṃ. Tesu padhānena parahitapaṭipattiṃ dasseti, itarena attahitasampattiṃ, tadubhayena attahitāya paṭipannādīsu catūsu puggalesu bhagavato catutthapuggalabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tena ca anuttaradakkhiṇeyyabhāvaṃ uttamavandanīyabhāvaṃ attano ca vandanakiriyāya khettaṅgatabhāvaṃ dasseti.

Here, by the phrase 'with a heart cooled by compassion,' the root of perfect self-enlightenment is shown. For the Blessed One, whose mind was impelled by great compassion, having made the aspiration to lift beings out of the swamp of saṃsāra, fulfilled the perfections in gradual succession and attained unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment. Thus compassion is the root of perfect self-enlightenment. By the phrase 'with the light of wisdom that has dispelled the darkness of delusion,' perfect self-enlightenment is shown. For path knowledge has unobstructed knowledge as its proximate cause, and unobstructed knowledge has path knowledge as its proximate cause; this is called 'perfect self-enlightenment.' By the term 'Sugata,' because it signifies 'one who has gone well,' the practice for perfect self-enlightenment is shown, since the term 'Sugata' proclaims the middle way, which is embraced by compassion and wisdom and is free from the two extremes such as being established in sloth and restlessness, the application of sensual pleasures and self-mortification, and the adherence to eternalism and annihilationism. By the other terms, the distinction between the principal and subordinate purpose of perfect self-enlightenment is indicated. Here, ferrying beings across the great flood of saṃsāra is the principal purpose; the other is subordinate. Through the principal one, the practice for the welfare of others is shown; through the other, the attainment of one's own welfare. By both, the Blessed One's status as the fourth person among the four persons beginning with one who practices for his own welfare is indicated. And thereby, his state as the unsurpassed recipient of offerings, his supreme venerability, and his being a field for one's own act of veneration are shown.

Ettha ca karuṇāgahaṇena lokiyesu mahaggatabhāvappattāsādhāraṇaguṇadīpanato bhagavato sabbalokiyaguṇasampatti dassitā hoti, paññāgahaṇena sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānamaggañāṇadīpanato sabbalokuttaraguṇasampatti. Tadubhayaggahaṇasiddho hi attho “sanarāmaralokagaru”ntiādinā vipañcīyatīti. Karuṇāgahaṇena ca upagamanaṃ nirupakkilesaṃ dasseti, paññāgahaṇena apagamanaṃ. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena lokasamaññānurūpaṃ bhagavato pavattiṃ dasseti lokavohāravisayattā [V 1.0008] karuṇāya, paññāgahaṇena samaññāya anatidhāvanaṃ sabhāvānavabodhena hi dhammānaṃ samaññaṃ atidhāvitvā sattādiparāmasanaṃ hotīti. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena mahākaruṇāsamāpattivihāraṃ dasseti, paññāgahaṇena tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇaṃ catusaccañāṇaṃ catupaṭisambhidāñāṇaṃ catuvesārajjañāṇaṃ.

Here, by mentioning compassion, the Blessed One's accomplishment in all mundane qualities is shown, through the illumination of the extraordinary virtues attained in exalted worldly states. By mentioning wisdom, his accomplishment in all supramundane qualities is shown, through the illumination of path knowledge, which is the proximate cause of the knowledge of omniscience. The meaning established by mentioning both is indeed elaborated by such phrases as 'the teacher of the world with its devas and human beings.' Further, by mentioning compassion, it shows his engagement as being undefiled; by mentioning wisdom, his disengagement. Likewise, by mentioning compassion, it shows the Blessed One's conduct in conformity with worldly convention, because compassion is the domain of worldly discourse; by mentioning wisdom, it shows his not transgressing convention, for it is by not understanding the intrinsic nature of phenomena that one transgresses convention and grasps at 'a being,' etc. Furthermore, by mentioning compassion, it shows his abiding in the attainment of great compassion; by mentioning wisdom, it shows the knowledge unimpeded in the three periods of time, the knowledge of the four noble truths, the knowledge of the four analytical knowledges, and the knowledge of the four kinds of fearlessness.

Karuṇāgahaṇena mahākaruṇāsamāpattiñāṇassa gahitattā sesāsādhāraṇañāṇāni, cha abhiññā, aṭṭhasu parisāsu akampanañāṇāni, dasa balāni, cuddasa buddhañāṇāni, soḷasa ñāṇacariyā, aṭṭhārasa buddhadhammā, catucattālīsa ñāṇavatthūni, sattasattatiñāṇavatthūnīti evamādīnaṃ anekesaṃ paññāpabhedānaṃ vasena ñāṇacāraṃ dasseti. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena caraṇasampattiṃ, paññāgahaṇena vijjāsampattiṃ. Karuṇāgahaṇena attādhipatitā, paññāgahaṇena dhammādhipatitā. Karuṇāgahaṇena lokanāthabhāvo, paññāgahaṇena [M 1.0009] attanāthabhāvo. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena pubbakāribhāvo, paññāgahaṇena kataññutā. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena aparantapatā, paññāgahaṇena anattantapatā. Karuṇāgahaṇena vā buddhakaradhammasiddhi, paññāgahaṇena buddhabhāvasiddhi. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena paresaṃ tāraṇaṃ, paññāgahaṇena sayaṃ taraṇaṃ. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena sabbasattesu anuggahacittatā, paññāgahaṇena sabbadhammesu virattacittatā dassitā hoti.

Since the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion is included by mentioning compassion, the range of knowledge is shown by way of the numerous divisions of wisdom, such as: the remaining unique knowledges, the six higher knowledges, the knowledges of being unshaken in the eight assemblies, the ten powers, the fourteen Buddha-knowledges, the sixteen modes of knowledge-conduct, the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, the forty-four bases of knowledge, and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge. Likewise, by mentioning compassion, the accomplishment in conduct is shown; by mentioning wisdom, the accomplishment in true knowledge. By mentioning compassion, sovereignty over oneself; by mentioning wisdom, sovereignty of the Dhamma. By mentioning compassion, his status as protector of the world; by mentioning wisdom, his status as his own protector. Likewise, by mentioning compassion, his being one who has formerly done a service; by mentioning wisdom, his gratitude. Likewise, by mentioning compassion, his not afflicting others; by mentioning wisdom, his not afflicting himself. Or, by mentioning compassion, the accomplishment of the qualities that make a Buddha; by mentioning wisdom, the accomplishment of the state of a Buddha. Likewise, by mentioning compassion, the ferrying across of others; by mentioning wisdom, the ferrying across of oneself. Likewise, by mentioning compassion, a mind of helpfulness towards all beings is shown; by mentioning wisdom, a mind dispassionate towards all phenomena is shown.

Sabbesañca buddhaguṇānaṃ karuṇā ādi tannidānabhāvato, paññā pariyosānaṃ tato uttari karaṇīyābhāvato. Iti ādipariyosānadassanena sabbe buddhaguṇā dassitā honti. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena sīlakkhandhapubbaṅgamo samādhikkhandho dassito hoti. Karuṇānidānañhi sīlaṃ tato pāṇātipātādiviratippavattito, sā ca jhānattayasampayoginīti. Paññāvacanena paññākkhandho. Sīlañca sabbabuddhaguṇānaṃ ādi, samādhi majjhe, paññā pariyosānanti evampi ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇadassanena sabbe buddhaguṇā dassitā honti nayato dassitattā. Eso eva hi niravasesato buddhaguṇānaṃ dassanupāyo, yadidaṃ nayaggāhaṇaṃ. Aññathā ko nāma samattho bhagavato guṇe anupadaṃ niravasesato dassetuṃ. Tenevāha –

And of all the Buddha's qualities, compassion is the beginning because it is their source, and wisdom is the conclusion because there is nothing further to be done beyond it. Thus, by showing the beginning and the conclusion, all the Buddha's qualities are shown. Similarly, by mentioning compassion, the aggregate of concentration, which is preceded by the aggregate of virtuous behavior, is shown. For virtuous behavior has compassion as its source, since it proceeds from abstinence from the destruction of life, etc.; and that compassion is associated with the three jhānas. By the word 'wisdom,' the aggregate of wisdom is shown. And virtuous behavior is the beginning of all the Buddha's qualities, concentration is the middle, and wisdom is the conclusion. In this way too, by showing what is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the conclusion, all the Buddha's qualities are shown, since they are shown by way of a method. This indeed is the means for showing the Buddha's qualities without remainder, that is, the grasping of a method. Otherwise, who indeed would be able to show the Blessed One's qualities without remainder, foot by foot? Therefore it is said:

“Buddhopi buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ;

Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno.

A Buddha himself might speak the praise of a Buddha, though speaking for an eon on nothing else;

Khīyetha [V 1.0009] kappo ciradīghamantare;

Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassā”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.305; 3.141; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.425; udā. aṭṭha. 53; apa. aṭṭha. 2.7.20; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 4.4; cariyā. aṭṭha. 3.122 pakiṇṇakakathā);

The eon would be exhausted in that long stretch of time, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.

Teneva ca āyasmatā sāriputtattherenapi buddhaguṇaparicchedanaṃ pati anuyuttena “no hetaṃ, bhante”ti paṭikkhipitvā “apica me, bhante, dhammanvayo vidito”ti (dī. ni. 2.146) vuttaṃ.

For this very reason, when the Venerable Elder Sāriputta was pressed concerning the delimitation of the Buddha's qualities, he rejected it, saying, 'Not so, venerable sir,' and said, 'However, venerable sir, the sequence of the Dhamma is known to me.'

2. Evaṃ saṅkhepena sakalasabbaññuguṇehi bhagavantaṃ abhitthavitvā idāni saddhammaṃ thometuṃ “buddhopī”tiādimāha. Tattha buddhoti kattuniddeso. Buddhabhāvanti kammaniddeso. Bhāvetvā sacchikatvāti ca pubbakālakiriyāniddeso[M 1.0010]. Yanti aniyamato kammaniddeso. Upagatoti aparakālakiriyāniddeso. Vandeti kiriyāniddeso. Tanti niyamanaṃ. Dhammanti vandanakiriyāya kammaniddeso. Gatamalaṃ anuttaranti ca tabbisesanaṃ.

2. Having thus praised the Blessed One in brief with all the qualities of an omniscient one, he now says 'A Buddha himself…' etc., in order to praise the good Dhamma. Therein, 'Buddha' is a designation of the agent. 'The state of a Buddha' is a designation of the object. 'Having developed and realized' is a designation of a prior action. 'Which' is an indefinite designation of the object. 'Has attained' is a designation of a subsequent action. 'I pay homage' is a designation of action. 'That' is a specification. 'Dhamma' is a designation of the object of the action of paying homage. 'Stain-free' and 'unsurpassed' are its qualifiers.

Tattha buddhasaddassa tāva “bujjhitā saccānīti buddho, bodhetā pajāyāti buddho”tiādinā niddesanayena (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. 97) attho veditabbo. Atha vā savāsanāya aññāṇaniddāya accantavigamato, buddhiyā vā vikasitabhāvato buddhavāti buddho jāgaraṇavikasanatthavasena. Atha vā kassacipi ñeyyadhammassa anavabuddhassa abhāvena ñeyyavisesassa kammabhāvena aggahaṇato kammavacanicchāya abhāvena avagamanatthavaseneva kattuniddeso labbhatīti buddhavāti buddho yathā “dikkhito na dadātī”ti. Atthato pana pāramitāparibhāvito sayambhuñāṇena saha vāsanāya vihataviddhastaniravasesakileso mahākaruṇāsabbaññutaññāṇādiaparimeyyaguṇagaṇādhāro khandhasantāno buddho. Yathāha –

Therein, first, the meaning of the word 'Buddha' should be understood by way of the exposition: 'He has understood the truths, thus he is a Buddha; he is an enlightener of the generation, thus he is a Buddha.' Alternatively, because of the final departure of the sleep of ignorance together with its latent dispositions, or because his intelligence has blossomed, he is a Buddha, in the sense of being awake and blossoming. Or, because there is no knowable phenomenon whatsoever that has not been understood by him, since he does not grasp any specific knowable as an object, and since there is no desire for a word in the objective case, the designation of the agent is obtained simply in the sense of understanding, thus he is a Buddha, as in the expression 'the consecrated one does not give.' But in terms of meaning, a Buddha is a continuity of aggregates that has been imbued by the perfections, who with self-originating knowledge has struck down and demolished all defilements without remainder together with their latent dispositions, and is a repository for the host of immeasurable qualities such as great compassion, the knowledge of omniscience, etc. As it is said:

“Buddhoti yo so bhagavā sayambhū. Anācariyako pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃ saccāni abhisambujjhi, tattha ca sabbaññutaṃ patto balesu ca vasībhāva”nti (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. 97; paṭi. ma. 3.161).

'He is the Buddha, that Blessed One, the Self-become. Without a teacher, in regard to phenomena unheard before, he fully awakened to the truths by himself, and in that respect he attained omniscience and mastery over the powers.'

Api-saddo [V 1.0010] sambhāvane. Tena “evaṃ guṇavisesayutto sopi nāma bhagavā”ti vakkhamānaguṇe dhamme sambhāvanaṃ dīpeti. Buddhabhāvanti sammāsambodhiṃ. Bhāvetvāti uppādetvā vaḍḍhetvā ca. Sacchikatvāti paccakkhaṃ katvā. Upagatoti patto, adhigatoti attho. Etassa “buddhabhāva”nti etena sambandho. Gatamalanti vigatamalaṃ, niddosanti attho. Vandeti paṇamāmi, thomemi vā. Anuttaranti uttararahitaṃ, lokuttaranti attho. Dhammanti yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne apāyato ca saṃsārato ca apatamāne katvā dhāretīti dhammo. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – evaṃ vividhaguṇagaṇasamannāgato buddhopi bhagavā yaṃ ariyamaggasaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā, phalanibbānasaṅkhātaṃ pana sacchikatvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ adhigato, tametaṃ buddhānampi buddhabhāvahetubhūtaṃ sabbadosamalarahitaṃ attano uttaritarābhāvena anuttaraṃ paṭivedhasaddhammaṃ namāmīti. Pariyattisaddhammassāpi tappakāsanattā idha saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

The word api is in the sense of affirmation. Thereby it shows the affirmation of the Dhamma with its qualities about to be mentioned, with the thought: 'Even that Blessed One, endowed with such special qualities…' 'The state of a Buddha' means perfect self-enlightenment. 'Having developed' means having generated and augmented it. 'Having realized' means having made it manifest. 'Has attained' means has reached, has acquired. This is connected with 'the state of a Buddha.' 'Stain-free' means with stains gone, that is, faultless. 'I pay homage' means I bow down to, or I praise. 'Unsurpassed' means without a superior, that is, supramundane. 'Dhamma' is so called because it supports those who practice in accordance with what has been taught by making them not fall into the plane of misery and into saṃsāra. Herein this is the concise meaning: Even the Buddha, the Blessed One, endowed with such a host of diverse qualities, attained unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment by having developed the Dhamma designated as the noble path and having realized the Dhamma designated as fruition and Nibbāna. I bow to that good Dhamma of penetration, which is the cause for the state of a Buddha even for Buddhas, which is free from all faults and stains, and which is unsurpassed because there is nothing superior to it. The inclusion here of the good Dhamma of learning should also be understood, since it proclaims that Dhamma of penetration.

Atha [M 1.0011] vā “abhidhammanayasamuddaṃ adhigacchi, tīṇi piṭakāni sammasī”ti ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā pariyattidhammassapi sacchikiriyāsammasanapariyāyo labbhatīti sopi idha vutto evāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā “yaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā saccikatvā”ti ca vuttattā buddhakaradhammabhūtāhi pāramitāhi saha pubbabhāge adhisīlasikkhādayopi idha dhammasaddena saṅgahitāti veditabbaṃ. Tāpi hi malapaṭipakkhatāya gatamalā anaññasādhāraṇatāya anuttarā cāti. Tathā hi sattānaṃ sakalavaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇatthāya katamahābhinīhāro mahākaruṇādhivāsapesalajjhāsayo paññāvisesaparidhotanimmalānaṃ dānadamasaṃyamādīnaṃ uttamadhammānaṃ satasahassādhikāni kappānaṃ cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni sakkaccaṃ nirantaraṃ niravasesānaṃ bhāvanāpaccakkhakaraṇehi kammādīsu adhigatavasībhāvo acchariyācinteyyamahānubhāvo adhisīlādhicittānaṃ paramukkaṃsapāramippatto bhagavā paccayākāre catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassamukhena mahāvajirañāṇaṃ pesetvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddhoti.

Alternatively, since it is said in the commentary, “He reached the ocean of the Abhidhamma method and comprehended the three Piṭakas,” it should be understood that the mode of realization and comprehension pertaining to the Dhamma of learning is also included here. Likewise, since it is stated, “Having developed and realized that Dhamma,” it should be understood that the preliminary practices such as the higher training in virtue, along with the perfections that constitute the qualities that make a Buddha, are also encompassed here by the term “Dhamma.” For they are stain-free, being the antidote to defilements, and they are unsurpassed, being unique. Indeed, for the sake of the liberation of beings from all the suffering of the round of existence, having made the great aspiration, with a disposition amiable and sustained by great compassion, the Blessed One—having for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more diligently and uninterruptedly cultivated to direct experience, without remainder, the supreme qualities of giving, self-control, restraint, and so on, which are stainless, being thoroughly cleansed by special wisdom; having attained mastery over actions and so on; possessing wonderful, inconceivable, and great power; having reached the ultimate peak of perfection in the higher virtue and the higher mind—sent forth the great diamond-like knowledge through the twenty-four hundred thousand crores of openings in the conditional relations and fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment.

Ettha ca “bhāvetvā”ti etena vijjāsampadāya dhammaṃ thometi, “sacchikatvā”ti etena vimuttisampadāya. Tathā paṭhamena jhānasampadāya, dutiyena vimokkhasampadāya. Paṭhamena vā samādhisampadāya, dutiyena samāpattisampadāya. Atha vā paṭhamena khayeñāṇabhāvena, dutiyena anuppādeñāṇabhāvena. Purimena vā vijjūpamatāya, dutiyena vajirūpamatāya. Purimena vā virāgasampattiyā, dutiyena nirodhasampattiyā. Tathā paṭhamena niyyānabhāvena, dutiyena nisssaraṇabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā hetubhāvena, dutiyena asaṅkhatabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā dassanabhāvena, dutiyena vivekabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā adhipatibhāvena, dutiyena amatabhāvena dhammaṃ [V 1.0011] thometi. Atha vā “yaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā buddhabhāvaṃ upagato”ti etena svākkhātatāya dhammaṃ thometi. “Sacchikatvā”ti etena sandiṭṭhikatāya. Tathā purimena akālikatāya, pacchimena ehipassikatāya. Purimena vā opaneyyikatāya, pacchimena paccattaṃ veditabbatāya dhammaṃ thometi. “Gatamala”nti iminā saṃkilesābhāvadīpanena dhammassa parisuddhataṃ dasseti, “anuttara”nti etena aññassa visiṭṭhassa abhāvadīpanena vipulaparipuṇṇataṃ. Paṭhamena vā pahānasampadaṃ dhammassa dasseti, dutiyena sabhāvasampadaṃ. Bhāvetabbatāya vā dhammassa gatamalabhāvo yojetabbo[M 1.0012]. Bhāvanāguṇena hi so dosānaṃ samugghātako hotīti. Sacchikātabbabhāvena anuttarabhāvo yojetabbo. Sacchikiriyānibbattito hi taduttarikaraṇīyābhāvato anaññasādhāraṇatāya anuttaroti. Tathā “bhāvetvā”ti etena saha pubbabhāgasīlādīhi sekkhā sīlasamādhipaññākkhandhā dassitā honti, “sacchikatvā”ti etena saha asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā asekkhā sīlasamādhipaññākkhandhā dassitā hontīti.

Here, by ‘having developed’ he praises the Dhamma in terms of the accomplishment in knowledge, and by ‘having realized’ he praises it in terms of the accomplishment in liberation. Similarly, by the first he praises it in terms of the accomplishment in jhāna, and by the second in terms of the accomplishment in deliverance. Or by the first in terms of the accomplishment in concentration, and by the second in terms of the accomplishment in attainment. Alternatively, by the first in terms of the state of the knowledge of destruction, and by the second in terms of the state of the knowledge of non-arising. Or by the first through its likeness to lightning, and by the second through its likeness to a diamond. By the first in terms of the attainment of dispassion, and by the second in terms of the attainment of cessation. Similarly, by the first in terms of being a means of escape, and by the second in terms of being a way of release. Or by the first in terms of being a cause, and by the second in terms of being the unconditioned. Or by the first in terms of being a vision, and by the second in terms of being seclusion. Or by the first in terms of being a dominant factor, and by the second in terms of being the deathless, he praises the Dhamma. Alternatively, by the words ‘the Dhamma which he developed and thereby attained Buddhahood,’ he praises the Dhamma for being well-proclaimed. By ‘having realized,’ he praises it for being directly visible. Similarly, by the former for being timeless, and by the latter for being ‘come and see.’ Or by the former for being leading onward, and by the latter for being personally knowable by the wise, he praises the Dhamma. By ‘free from defilement,’ he shows the purity of the Dhamma by indicating the absence of defilements; by ‘unsurpassed,’ he shows its vastness and completeness by indicating the absence of anything more distinguished. Or by the first he shows the Dhamma’s accomplishment in abandoning, and by the second its accomplishment in its intrinsic nature. Or the state of being free from defilement should be connected with the Dhamma’s quality of being fit to be developed; for by the virtue of development it becomes the uprooter of faults. The state of being unsurpassed should be connected with its quality of being fit to be realized; for having been brought to realization, it is unsurpassed because there is nothing further to be done and because it is not shared by others. Similarly, by ‘having developed,’ together with the preliminary virtues and so on, the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom of a trainee are shown; by ‘having realized,’ together with the unconditioned element, the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom of one beyond training are shown.

3. Evaṃ saṅkhepeneva sabbadhammaguṇehi saddhammaṃ abhitthavitvā idāni ariyasaṅghaṃ thometuṃ “sugatassā”tiādimāha. Tattha sugatassāti sambandhaniddeso, tassa “puttāna”nti etena sambandho. Orasānanti puttavisesanaṃ. Mārasenamathanānanti orasaputtabhāve kāraṇaniddeso. Tena kilesappahānameva bhagavato orasaputtabhāve kāraṇaṃ anujānātīti dasseti. Aṭṭhannanti gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso. Tena satipi tesaṃ sattavisesabhāvena anekasahassasaṅkhābhāve imaṃ gaṇanaparicchedaṃ nātivattantīti dasseti maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhabhāvānātivattanato. Samūhanti samudāyaniddeso. Ariyasaṅghanti guṇavisiṭṭhasaṅghāṭabhāvaniddeso. Tena asabhipi ariyapuggalānaṃ kāyasāmaggiyaṃ ariyasaṅghabhāvaṃ dasseti diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhatabhāvato.

3. Having thus briefly praised the good Dhamma with all its qualities, now, in order to praise the noble Saṅgha, he says, ‘Of the Well-Gone One,’ and so on. Herein, ‘of the Well-Gone One’ is an indication of connection; its connection is with ‘sons.’ ‘Legitimate’ is a qualification of the sons. ‘Who crush Māra’s army’ is an indication of the reason for their being legitimate sons. By this he shows that the abandoning of the defilements is acknowledged as the very reason for being the Blessed One’s legitimate sons. ‘Eight’ is an indication of numerical definition. By this he shows that although they are many thousands in number on account of their individual distinctions as beings, they do not transgress this numerical definition because they do not go beyond the states of those on the path and those in the fruit. ‘A community’ is an indication of a collection. ‘The noble Saṅgha’ is an indication of its nature as a community distinguished by quality. By this he shows the state of being the noble Saṅgha for a physical gathering of noble persons, who are not worldlings, because of their being united by a commonality of view and virtue.

Tattha urasi bhavā jātā saṃvaddhā ca orasā. Yathā hi sattānaṃ orasaputtā attajātatāya pitu santakassa dāyajjassa visesena bhāgino honti, evameva tepi ariyapuggalā sammāsambuddhassa dhammassavanante ariyāya jātiyā jātatāya bhagavato santakassa vimuttisukhassa ariyadhammaratanassa ca ekantabhāginoti orasā viya orasā. Atha vā bhagavato dhammadesanānubhāvena ariyabhūmiṃ okkamamānā okkantā ca ariyasāvakā bhagavato urena vāyāmajanitābhijātitāya nippariyāyena “orasaputtā”ti vattabbataṃ arahanti. Sāvakehi pavattiyamānāpi hi dhammadesanā “bhagavato dhammadesanā”icceva vuccati taṃmūlikattā lakkhaṇādivisesābhāvato ca.

Herein, ‘legitimate’ (orasā) means born, sprung from, and nurtured at the breast (urasi). For just as the legitimate sons of beings, being born from their own father, are special heirs to their father’s property, so too these noble persons, having been born with the noble birth at the conclusion of hearing the Dhamma from the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, are the exclusive heirs to the Blessed One’s property, the happiness of liberation and the jewel of the noble Dhamma. Thus they are legitimate like legitimate sons. Alternatively, the noble disciples who are entering and have entered the noble plane through the power of the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma deserve to be called ‘legitimate sons’ in a direct sense, because they are of noble birth, generated by the effort from the Blessed One’s breast. For even a Dhamma teaching set forth by the disciples is called ‘the Blessed One’s Dhamma teaching’ because it is rooted in him and because there is no difference in its characteristics and so on.

Yadipi [V 1.0012][M 1.0013] ariyasāvakānaṃ ariyamaggādhigamasamaye bhagavato viya tadantarāya karaṇatthaṃ devaputtamāro, māravāhinī vā na ekantena apasādeti, tehi pana apasādetabbatāya kāraṇe vimathite tepi vimathitā eva nāma hontīti āha – “mārasenamathanāna”nti. Imasmiṃ panatthe “māramārasenamathanāna”nti vattabbe “mārasenamathanāna”nti ekadesasarūpekaseso katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā khandhābhisaṅkhāramārānaṃ viya devaputtamārassapi guṇamāraṇe sahāyabhāvūpagamanato kilesabalakāyo “senā”ti vuccati. Yathāha “kāmā te paṭhamā senā”tiādi (su. ni. 438; mahāni. 28, 68, 149). Sā ca tehi diyaḍḍhasahassabhedā anantabhedā vā kilesavāhinī satidhammavicayavīriyasamathādiguṇapaharaṇehi odhiso vimathitā vihatā viddhastā cāti mārasenamathanā, ariyasāvakā. Etena tesaṃ bhagavato anujātaputtataṃ dasseti.

Although at the time the noble disciples attain the noble path, Māra the devaputta or Māra’s army does not necessarily assail them to create an obstacle, as they did for the Blessed One, yet when the cause that is to be repelled by them is crushed, they too are indeed crushed. Hence it is said: ‘who crush Māra’s army.’ In this sense, it should be understood that when ‘crushers of Māra and Māra’s army’ should have been said, a haplology of a single part has been made, resulting in ‘crushers of Māra’s army.’ Alternatively, just as there are the Māras of the aggregates and of formations, the host of defilements is called an ‘army’ (senā) because it becomes an ally of Māra the devaputta in destroying virtues. As it is said: ‘Sensual pleasures are your first army,’ etc. (Snp 436). And that army of defilements, with its one thousand five hundred divisions or its infinite divisions, is specifically crushed, struck down, and demolished by them with the weapons of such qualities as mindfulness, investigation of states, energy, and serenity. Thus the noble disciples are crushers of Māra’s army. By this he shows their status as the Blessed One’s faithful sons.

Ārakattā kilesehi, anaye na iriyanato, aye ca iriyanato ariyā niruttinayena. Atha vā sadevakena lokena “saraṇa”nti araṇīyato upagantabbato upagatānañca tadatthasiddhito ariyā, ariyānaṃ saṅghoti ariyasaṅgho, ariyo ca so saṅgho cāti vā ariyasaṅgho, taṃ ariyasaṅghaṃ. Bhagavato aparabhāge buddhadhammaratanānampi samadhigamo saṅgharatanādhīnoti ariyasaṅghassa bahūpakārataṃ dassetuṃ idheva “sirasā vande”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

By way of etymology, they are ‘noble’ (ariyā) because they are far (ārakā) from the defilements, because they do not fare (na iriyanti) wrongly, and because they fare (iriyanti) rightly. Or, they are noble because they should be gone to (araṇīyato) as a refuge by the world with its gods, and because those who have gone to them achieve their aim. The Saṅgha of the noble ones is the noble Saṅgha; or, it is a Saṅgha that is noble, thus the noble Saṅgha. To show the great helpfulness of the noble Saṅgha—since in the period after the Blessed One the attainment of the Buddha-jewel and the Dhamma-jewel is also dependent on the Saṅgha-jewel—it should be understood that it is right here that the words ‘I revere with my head’ are stated.

Ettha ca “sugatassa orasānaṃ puttāna”nti etena ariyasaṅghassa pabhavasampadaṃ dasseti, “mārasenamathanāna”nti etena pahānasampadaṃ sakalasaṃkilesappahānadīpanato. “Aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti etena ñāṇasampadaṃ maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhabhāvadīpanato. “Ariyasaṅgha”nti etena pabhāvasampadaṃ dasseti sabbasaṅghānaṃ aggabhāvadīpanato. Atha vā “sugatassa orasānaṃ puttāna”nti ariyasaṅghassa visuddhanissayabhāvadīpanaṃ, “mārasenamathanāna”nti sammāujuñāyasāmīcippaṭipannabhāvadīpanaṃ, “aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti āhuneyyādibhāvadīpanaṃ, “ariyasaṅgha”nti anuttarapuññakkhettabhāvadīpanaṃ. Tathā “sugatassa orasānaṃ puttāna”nti etena ariyasaṅghassa lokuttarasaraṇagamanasabbhāvaṃ dīpeti. Lokuttarasaraṇagamanena hi te bhagavato orasaputtā jātā. “Mārasenamathanāna”nti etena abhinīhārasampadāsiddhaṃ [M 1.0014] pubbabhāge sammāpaṭipattiṃ dasseti. Katābhinīhārā hi sammāpaṭipannā māraṃ māraparisaṃ vā abhivijinanti. “Aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti etena paṭividdhastavipakkhe sekkhāsekkhadhamme dasseti puggalādhiṭṭhānena maggaphaladhammānaṃ pakāsitattā. “Ariyasaṅgha”nti aggadakkhiṇeyyabhāvaṃ dasseti. Saraṇagamanañca sāvakānaṃ sabbaguṇānaṃ ādi, sapubbabhāgapaṭipadā sekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo majjhe, asekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo [V 1.0013] pariyosānanti ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇā saṅkhepato sabbe ariyasaṅghaguṇā pakāsitā honti.

Here, the phrase 'the Sugata’s true-born sons' shows the noble Sangha’s accomplishment in origin. The phrase 'the crushers of Māra’s army' shows their accomplishment in abandonment, by illuminating the abandonment of all defilements. The phrase 'the assembly of the eight' shows their accomplishment in knowledge, by illuminating the state of those established in the path and the fruit. The phrase 'the noble Sangha' shows their accomplishment in eminence, by illuminating their supreme status among all Sanghas. Alternatively, 'the Sugata’s true-born sons' illuminates the noble Sangha’s pure basis of reliance. 'The crushers of Māra’s army' illuminates their practice, which is right, direct, and proper. 'The assembly of the eight' illuminates their being worthy of offerings and so on. 'The noble Sangha' illuminates their being an unsurpassed field of merit. So too, 'the Sugata’s true-born sons' illuminates the noble Sangha’s essential nature of having gone for refuge to the supramundane. For it is by going for refuge to the supramundane that they are born as the Blessed One’s true-born sons. 'The crushers of Māra’s army' shows the right practice in the preliminary stage, accomplished through the fulfillment of their aspiration. For those who have made their aspiration and practice rightly conquer Māra and his retinue. 'The assembly of the eight' shows the qualities of the trainee and the adept, whose opposing states have been penetrated, because the path and fruit states are explained with individuals as their basis. 'The noble Sangha' shows their state as the foremost of those worthy of offerings. The going for refuge is the beginning of all the disciples’ virtues; the aggregates of virtue, etc., of the trainee, along with the preliminary practice, are the middle; the aggregates of virtue, etc., of the adept are the conclusion. Thus, in brief, all the virtues of the noble Sangha—excellent in the beginning, the middle, and the end—are proclaimed.

4. Evaṃ gāthāttayena saṅkhepato sakalaguṇasaṃkittanamukhena ratanattayassa paṇāmaṃ katvā idāni taṃnipaccakāraṃ yathādhippete payojane pariṇāmento “iti me”tiādimāha. Tattha ratijananaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, buddhadhammasaṅghā. Tesañhi “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinā yathābhūtaguṇe āvajjentassa amatādhigamahetubhūtaṃ anappakaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ uppajjati. Yathāha –

4. Thus, having paid homage to the Three Jewels with three stanzas by way of a brief extolling of all their virtues, now, dedicating that reverence to its intended purpose, he says, 'iti me,' etc. Here, 'jewel' (ratana) has the meaning of generating delight—that is, the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. For when one adverts to their qualities as they really are, beginning 'Iti’pi so bhagavā…,' abundant joy and gladness arise, which becomes a cause for the attainment of the Deathless. As it is said:

“Yasmiṃ mahānāma, samaye ariyasāvako tathāgataṃ anussarati, nevassa tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na dosa…pe… na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti…pe… ujugatacitto kho mahānāma, ariyasāvako labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammavedaṃ, labhati dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ, pamuditassa pīti jāyatī”tiādi (a. ni. 6.10; 11.11).

“Mahānāma, on an occasion when a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor by hatred… nor by delusion…. On that occasion, Mahānāma, the noble disciple’s mind is rightly directed. He gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. When he is gladdened, rapture is born in him,” and so on.

Cittīkatādibhāvo vā ratanaṭṭho. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Alternatively, the meaning of 'jewel' is the state of being prized, and so on. For this has been said:

“Cittīkataṃ mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccatī”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.33; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.223; khu. pā. aṭṭha. 6.3; su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.226; mahāni. aṭṭha. 50);

“Prized and of great price, matchless, and rarely seen; an exquisite possession for the noblest beings, therefore it is called a jewel.”

Cittikatabhāvādayo ca anaññasādhāraṇā buddhādīsu eva labbhantīti.

And these qualities, such as being prized, are unique, found only in the Buddhas and the like.

Vandanāva vandanāmayaṃ yathā “dānamayaṃ sīlamaya”nti (dī. ni. 3.305; itivu. 60). Vandanā cettha kāyavācācittehi tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇaninnatā, thomanā vā. Pujjabhavaphalanibbattanato [M 1.0015] puññaṃ, attano santānaṃ punātīti vā. Suvihatantarāyoti suṭṭhu vihatantarāyo. Etena attano pasādasampattiyā ratanattayassa ca khettabhāvasampattiyā taṃ puññaṃ atthappakāsanassa upaghātakaupaddavānaṃ vihanane samatthanti dasseti. Hutvāti pubbakālakiriyā. Tassa “atthaṃ pakāsayissāmī”ti etena sambandho. Tassāti yaṃ ratanattayavandanāmayaṃ puññaṃ, tassa. Ānubhāvenāti balena.

Veneration itself is 'consisting of veneration' (vandanāmayaṃ), just as there is 'consisting of giving' (dānamayaṃ) and 'consisting of virtue' (sīlamayaṃ). Here, veneration is the inclination of body, speech, and mind toward the qualities of the Three Jewels, or it is praise. It is 'merit' (puñña) because it generates the fruit of a worshipful state, or because it purifies one’s own mental continuum. 'With obstacles well removed' (suvihatantarāyo) means one whose obstacles are thoroughly removed. This shows that by means of one’s own accomplishment in faith and the Three Jewels’ accomplishment as a field of merit, that merit is capable of destroying the detrimental dangers that obstruct the explanation of the meaning. Hutvā is a verb of prior action; it is connected with 'I will explain the meaning.' Tassa refers to that merit consisting of veneration of the Three Jewels. Ānubhāvena means 'by the power.'

5. Evaṃ [V 1.0014] ratanattayassa nipaccakāre payojanaṃ dassetvā idāni yassā dhammadesanāya atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇetukāmo, tassā tāva guṇābhitthavanavasena upaññāpanatthaṃ “majjhimapamāṇasuttaṅkitassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha majjhimapamāṇasuttaṅkitassāti nātidīghanātikhuddakapamāṇehi suttantehi lakkhitassa. Yathā hi dīghāgame dīghapamāṇāni suttāni, yathā ca saṃyuttaṅguttarāgamesu dvīsu khuddakapamāṇāni, na evaṃ idha. Idha pana pamāṇato majjhimāni suttāni. Tena vuttaṃ “majjhimapamāṇasuttaṅkitassāti nātidīghanātikhuddakapamāṇehi suttantehi lakkhitassati attho”ti. Etena “majjhimo”ti ayaṃ imassa atthānugatasamaññāti dasseti. Nanu ca suttāni eva āgamo, kassa pana suttehi aṅkananti? Saccametaṃ paramatthato, suttāni pana upādāya paññatto āgamo. Yatheva hi atthabyañjanasamudāye “sutta”nti vohāro, evaṃ suttasamudāye ayaṃ “āgamo”ti vohāro. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Āgamissanti ettha, etena etasmā vā attatthaparatthādayoti āgamo, ādikalyāṇādiguṇasampattiyā uttamaṭṭhena taṃtaṃabhipatthitasamiddhihetutāya paṇḍitehi varitabbato varo, āgamo ca so varo cāti āgamavaro. Āgamasammatehi vā varoti āgamavaro, majjhimo ca so āgamavaro cāti majjhimāgamavaro, tassa.

5. Having thus shown the purpose of revering the Three Jewels, now, as he wishes to comment on the meaning of a certain Dhamma teaching, in order to introduce it by way of praising its qualities, he first says, 'of that which is marked by suttas of middle length,' etc. Here, 'marked by suttas of middle length' means distinguished by discourses that are neither too long nor too short. For just as in the Long Discourses there are long suttas, and in the Connected and Numerical Discourses there are short suttas, it is not so here. Here, the suttas are of a middle length. Therefore it is said: '“marked by suttas of middle length” means distinguished by discourses that are neither too long nor too short.' This shows that 'middle' is a designation that accords with its meaning. But are not the suttas themselves the Collection (āgama)? So what is this 'marking by suttas'? In the ultimate sense this is true, but the Collection is a designation based upon the suttas. For just as the term 'sutta' is used for a collection of meaning and phrasing, so the term 'Collection' is used for a collection of suttas. 'Here' means in this Dispensation. One's own welfare, the welfare of others, etc., come (āgamissanti) to it, by it, or from it; therefore it is a 'Collection' (āgama). Because it possesses the quality of being good in the beginning, etc., it is supreme; and because it is the cause for the accomplishment of various wished-for things, it should be chosen (varitabbato) by the wise; therefore it is 'excellent' (varo). It is a Collection and it is excellent, thus 'excellent Collection' (āgamavaro). Or, it is excellent because it is approved by the Collections, thus 'excellent Collection.' It is middle and it is that excellent Collection, thus 'middle excellent Collection'; 'of that' refers to this.

Buddhānaṃ anubuddhānaṃ buddhānubuddhā, buddhānaṃ saccapaṭivedhaṃ anugamma paṭividdhasaccā aggasāvakādayo ariyā. Tehi atthasaṃvaṇṇanāguṇasaṃvaṇṇanānaṃ vasena saṃvaṇṇitassa. Atha vā buddhā ca anubuddhā ca buddhānubuddhāti yojetabbaṃ. Sammāsambuddheneva hi vinayasuttābhidhammānaṃ pakiṇṇakadesanādivasena yo paṭhamaṃ attho vibhatto, so eva pacchā tassa tassa saṃvaṇṇanāvasena saṅgītikārehi saṅgahaṃ āropitoti. Paravādamathanassāti aññatitthiyānaṃ vādanimmathanassa, tesaṃ diṭṭhigatabhañjanassāti attho. Ayañhi [M 1.0016] āgamo mūlapariyāyasuttasabbāsavasuttādīsu diṭṭhigatikānaṃ diṭṭhigatadosavibhāvanato saccakasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 1.353) upālisuttādīsu (ma. ni. 2.56) saccakādīnaṃ micchāvādanimmathanadīpanato visesato “paravādamathano”ti thomitoti. Saṃvaṇṇanāsu cāyaṃ ācariyassa pakati, yā taṃtaṃsaṃvaṇṇanāsu ādito tassa tassa saṃvaṇṇetabbassa dhammassa visesaguṇakittanena thomanā. Tathā hi sumaṅgalavilāsinīsāratthapakāsinīmanorathapūraṇīsu aṭṭhasālinīādīsu ca yathākkamaṃ “saddhāvahaguṇassa, ñāṇappabhedajananassa, dhammakathikapuṅgavānaṃ vicittapaṭibhānajananassa, tassa gambhīrañāṇehi ogāḷhassa abhiṇhaso nānānayavicittassa abhidhammassā”tiādinā thomanā katā.

Of that which was commented upon by the Buddhas’ followers (`buddhānubuddha`)—that is, by the noble ones such as the chief disciples, who have penetrated the truths by following the Buddhas’ penetration of the truths—by way of commenting on its meaning and commenting on its qualities. Alternatively, `buddhānubuddha` should be construed as 'the Buddhas and the Anubuddhas.' For the meaning that was first analyzed by the Perfectly Enlightened One himself through the Vinaya, Suttas, Abhidhamma, miscellaneous teachings, etc., was later compiled by the Reciters at the Councils by way of commenting on each point. 'Of the crusher of others' doctrines' means of the subduer of the doctrines of other sectarians; that is, the breaker of their wrong views. For this Collection is especially praised as 'the crusher of others' doctrines' because in the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, the Sabbāsava Sutta, and others, it analyzes the faults of those holding wrong views, and in the Saccaka Sutta, the Upāli Sutta, and others, it shows the subduing of the false doctrines of Saccaka and others. Moreover, this is the teacher’s customary practice in the commentaries: at the start of each commentary, to praise the particular Dhamma to be commented upon by extolling its special qualities. Thus, in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, Sāratthapakāsinī, Manorathapūraṇī, Aṭṭhasālinī, etc., praise is given respectively, thus: 'of that which has the quality of inspiring faith'; 'of that which generates the various kinds of knowledge'; 'of that which generates the diverse brilliance of the bull-like Dhamma-speakers'; 'of the Abhidhamma, which is profound, penetrated by deep knowledge, and constantly variegated with numerous methods,' and so on.

6. Attho [V 1.0015] kathīyati etāyāti atthakathā, sā eva aṭṭhakathā ttha-kārassa ṭṭha-kāraṃ katvā yathā “dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.17; 2.8) āditotiādimhi paṭhamasaṅgītiyaṃ. Chaḷabhiññatāya paramena cittissariyabhāvena samannāgatattā jhānādīsu pañcavidhavasitāsabbhāvato ca vasino, therā mahākassapādayo. Tesaṃ satehi pañcahi. Yāti yā aṭṭhakathā. Saṅgītāti atthaṃ pakāsetuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne “ayaṃ etassa attho, ayaṃ etassa attho”ti saṅgahetvā vuttā. Anusaṅgītā ca yasattherādīhi pacchāpi dutiyatatiyasaṅgītīsu. Iminā attano saṃvaṇṇanāya āgamanasuddhiṃ dasseti.

6. Meaning (`attho`) is explained (`kathīyati`) by this (`etāya`), thus `atthakathā`. This very thing becomes `aṭṭhakathā` by changing the `ttha` to `ṭṭha`, as in the example 'the meaning of oppression for suffering' (`dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho`), and so on. This commentary was recited at the First Council. The elders, Mahākassapa and others, were masters (`vasino`), because they possessed the six higher knowledges, were endowed with supreme sovereignty of mind, and had the fivefold mastery over the meditative attainments and so forth. By five hundred of them. `Yā` means 'which commentary.' `Saṅgītā` means it was recited in concert, having collected and stated in the appropriate places, 'This is the meaning of this, this is the meaning of that,' in order to explain the meaning. And it was subsequently recited (`anusaṅgītā`) by the Elder Yasa and others at the Second and Third Councils. By this, he shows the purity of the tradition for his own commentary.

7. Sīhassa lānato gahaṇato sīhaḷo, sīhakumāro. Taṃvaṃsajātatāya tambapaṇṇidīpe khattiyānaṃ, tesaṃ nivāsatāya tambapaṇṇidīpassa ca sīhaḷabhāvo veditabbo. Ābhatāti jambudīpato ānītā. Athāti pacchā. Aparabhāge hi nikāyantaraladdhīhi asaṅkaratthaṃ sīhaḷabhāsāya aṭṭhakathā ṭhapitāti. Tena mūlaṭṭhakathā sabbasādhāraṇā na hotīti idaṃ atthappakāsanaṃ ekantena karaṇīyanti dasseti. Tenevāha “dīpavāsīnamatthāyā”ti. Tattha dīpavāsīnanti jambudīpavāsīnaṃ, sīhaḷadīpavāsīnaṃ vā atthāya sīhaḷabhāsāya ṭhapitāti yojanā.

7. Sīhaḷa, the lion-prince, is so called from taking and capturing the lion. Because the khattiyas on the island of Tambapaṇṇi were born of his lineage and because they reside there, the island of Tambapaṇṇi is to be understood as Sīhaḷa. 'Brought' means brought from Jambudīpa. 'Then' means afterwards. For in a later period, to avoid confusion with the tenets of other schools, the commentary was established in the Sinhala language. This shows, therefore, that the original commentary is not common to all and that this exposition of the meaning must definitely be made. For that reason he said, 'for the benefit of the island-dwellers.' Here, the construction of 'for the benefit of the island-dwellers' is that it was established in the Sinhala language for the benefit of the inhabitants of Jambudīpa or of the island of Sīhaḷa.

8. Apanetvānāti [M 1.0017] kañcukasadisaṃ sīhaḷabhāsaṃ apanetvā. Tatoti aṭṭhakathāto. Ahanti attānaṃ niddisati, manoramaṃ bhāsanti māgadhabhāsaṃ. Sā hi sabhāvaniruttibhūtā paṇḍitānaṃ manaṃ ramayatīti. Tenevāha “tantinayānucchavika”nti, pāḷigatiyā anulomikaṃ pāḷibhāsāyānuvidhāyininti attho. Vigatadosanti asabhāvaniruttibhāsantararahitaṃ.

8. 'Having removed' means having removed the Sinhala language, which is like a sheath. 'From that' means from the commentary. 'I' indicates himself; 'a delightful language' means the Māgadhī language. For it, being the natural mode of expression, delights the minds of the wise. For that reason he said, 'suitable to the textual method,' which means conforming to the style of the Pāli, following the Pāli language. 'Free from faults' means devoid of other languages that are not the natural mode of expression.

9. Samayaṃ avilomentoti siddhantaṃ avirodhento. Etena atthadosābhāvamāha. Aviruddhattā eva hi theravādāpi idha pakāsīyissanti. Theravaṃsadīpānanti thirehi sīlakkhandhādīhi samannāgatattā therā, mahākassapādayo. Tehi āgatā ācariyaparamparā theravaṃso, tappariyāpannā hutvā āgamādhigamasampannattā paññāpajjotena tassa samujjalanato theravaṃsadīpā, mahāvihāravāsino, tesaṃ. Vividhehi ākārehi nicchīyatīti vinicchayo, gaṇṭhiṭṭhānesu khīlamaddanākārena pavattā vimaticchedanī kathā. Suṭṭhu nipuṇo saṇho vinicchayo etesanti sunipuṇavinicchayā. Atha vā vinicchinotīti vinicchayo, yathāvuttatthavisayaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Suṭṭhu nipuṇo cheko vinicchayo etesanti yojetabbaṃ. Etena mahākassapāditheraparamparābhato, tato eva ca aviparīto saṇho sukhumo mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ vinicchayoti tassa pamāṇabhūtataṃ dasseti.

9. 'Not transgressing the doctrine' means not contradicting the established teaching. By this, he states the absence of faults in meaning. Indeed, because it is not contradictory, the tenets of the Theravāda will also be explained here. 'Of the illuminators of the Theravaṃsa': The elders (theras), such as Mahākassapa and others, are so called because they are endowed with stable qualities such as the aggregate of virtue. The lineage of teachers that has come down from them is the Theravaṃsa. Because, being included in that, they are accomplished in the scriptures and realization, and because they illuminate that lineage with the light of wisdom, they are 'illuminators of the Theravaṃsa' (theravaṃsadīpā), the residents of the Mahāvihāra. 'A decision' (vinicchaya) is so called because it is determined in various ways; it is a discussion that cuts through doubt, proceeding in the manner of driving out a peg in knotty points. They are 'of very skillful decision' because their decision is very skillful and subtle. Or, 'a decision' is so called because it decides; it is the knowledge concerning the subject matter as stated. It should be construed as: 'their decision is very skillful and expert.' By this he shows that the decision of the Mahāvihāra residents—which is subtle, refined, unerring, and brought down from the lineage of elders beginning with Mahākassapa—is authoritative.

10. Sujanassa [V 1.0016] cāti ca-saddo sampiṇḍanattho. Tena “na kevalaṃ jambudīpavāsīnameva atthāya, atha kho sādhujanatosanatthañcā”ti dasseti. Tena ca “tambapaṇṇidīpavāsīnampi atthāyā”ti ayamattho siddho hoti uggahaṇādisukaratāya tesampi bahukārattā. Ciraṭṭhitatthanti ciraṭṭhitiatthaṃ, cirakālaṭṭhitiyāti attho. Idañhi atthappakāsanaṃ aviparītapadabyañjanasunikkhepassa atthasunayassa ca upāyabhāvato saddhammassa ciraṭṭhitiyā saṃvattati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “dveme, bhikkhave, dhammā saddhammassa ṭhitiyā asammosāya anantaradhānāya saṃvattanti. Katame dve? Sunnikkhittañca padabyañjanaṃ attho ca sunīto”ti (a. ni. 2.20).

10. In 'and of good people,' the word 'and' has the sense of inclusion. Thereby he shows: 'Not only for the benefit of the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, but also for the delight of good people.' And by this the meaning 'also for the benefit of the inhabitants of Tambapaṇṇidīpa' is established, since it is of great service to them too because of the ease of learning and so on. 'For the sake of long duration' means for the purpose of long duration, that is, for the purpose of lasting for a long time.
