For this exposition of the meaning, being a means for the correct placement of unerring words and phrases and for the good derivation of the meaning, conduces to the long duration of the good Dhamma. This has been said by the Blessed One: 'Bhikkhus, these two things conduce to the stability, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the good Dhamma. What two? Well-laid-down words and phrases and a well-inferred meaning' (A. 2.20).

11. Yaṃ [M 1.0018] atthavaṇṇanaṃ kattukāmo, tassā mahattaṃ pariharituṃ “sīlakathā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “na taṃ idha vicārayissāmī”ti. Atha vā yaṃ aṭṭhakathaṃ kattukāmo, tadekadesabhāvena visuddhimaggo gahetabboti kathikānaṃ upadesaṃ karonto tattha vicāritadhamme uddesavasena dasseti “sīlakathā”tiādinā. Tattha sīlakathāti cārittavārittādivasena sīlassa vitthārakathā. Dhutadhammāti piṇḍapātikaṅgādayo terasa kilesadhunanakadhammā. Kammaṭṭhānāni sabbānīti pāḷiyaṃ āgatāni aṭṭhatiṃsa, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dveti niravasesāni yogakammassa bhāvanāya pavattiṭṭhānāni. Cariyāvidhānasahitoti rāgacaritādīnaṃ sabhāvādividhānena sahito. Jhānāni cattāri rūpāvacarajjhānāni, samāpattiyo catasso arūpasamāpattiyo. Aṭṭhapi vā paṭiladdhamattāni jhānāni, samāpajjanavasībhāvappattiyā samāpattiyo. Jhānāni vā rūpārūpāvacarajjhānāni, samāpattiyo phalasamāpattinirodhasamāpattiyo.

11. To indicate the greatness of the exposition of the meaning he wishes to make, 'the talk on virtue,' etc., is stated. For that reason he says: 'I will not examine that here.' Or, giving instruction to those who would compose a commentary that the Visuddhimagga should be taken as a part of it, he indicates by way of a summary the matters examined there with 'the talk on virtue,' etc. Herein, 'the talk on virtue' is the detailed discourse on virtue by way of what should be practiced and what should be avoided. 'The ascetic qualities' are the thirteen qualities that shake off the defilements, such as the alms-food-eater's practice. 'All meditation subjects' means the thirty-eight that have come down in the Pāli and two in the commentary; that is, without remainder, the grounds for the practice of the yogi's work of development. 'Accompanied by the classification of temperaments' means accompanied by the classification of the greedy temperament, etc., by way of their nature. The four jhānas are the fine-material sphere jhānas; the four attainments are the immaterial sphere attainments. Or, the eight are jhānas in so far as they are merely attained, but they are attainments through reaching the state of mastery in entering them. Or, the jhānas are the fine-material and immaterial sphere jhānas; the attainments are the attainment of fruition and the attainment of cessation.

12. Lokiyalokuttarabhedā cha abhiññāyo sabbā abhiññāyo. Ñāṇavibhaṅgādīsu (vibha. 751) āgatanayena ekavidhādinā paññāya saṃkaletvā sampiṇḍetvā nicchayo paññāsaṅkalananicchayo.

12. The six direct knowledges, divided into mundane and supramundane, are all the direct knowledges. The decision that collects and summarizes them by wisdom in one way and so on, according to the method that has come down in the Ñāṇavibhaṅga and other texts (Vibh 751), is the 'decision by collection through wisdom.'

13. Paccayadhammānaṃ hetādīnaṃ paccayuppannadhammānaṃ hetupaccayādibhāvo paccayākāro, tassa desanā paccayākāradesanā, paṭiccasamuppādakathāti attho. Sā pana nikāyantaraladdhisaṅkararahitatāya suṭṭhu parisuddhā, ghanavinibbhogassa sudukkaratāya nipuṇā saṇhasukhumā, ekattanayādisahitā ca tattha vicāritāti āha “suparisuddhanipuṇanayā”ti. Paṭisambhidādīsu āgatanayaṃ avissajjetvāva vicāritattā avimuttatantimaggā.

13. The mode of conditionality is the state of conditioning phenomena, such as the root-condition, being a condition for conditionally arisen phenomena. The exposition of that is the 'exposition of the mode of conditionality,' which means the discourse on dependent origination. Moreover, because it is free from confusion with the tenets of other schools, it is thoroughly pure; because the analysis of its dense structure is very difficult, it is skillful, subtle, and refined; and because it is examined there together with the method of unity, etc., he says it is 'of a thoroughly pure and skillful method.' Because it is examined without abandoning the method that has come down in the Paṭisambhidāmagga and other texts, it is 'a path with an unabandoned textual lineage.'

14. Iti [V 1.0017] pana sabbanti iti-saddo parisamāpane, pana-saddo vacanālaṅkāre, etaṃ sabbanti attho. Idhāti imissā aṭṭhakathāya. Na taṃ vicārayissāmi punaruttibhāvatoti adhippāyo.

14. In 'Thus all this,' the word 'thus' is for conclusion, the word 'now' is a mere particle, and the meaning is 'all this.' 'Here' means in this commentary. The intention is: 'I will not examine that, as it would be a repetition.'

15. Idāni tasseva avicāraṇassa ekantakāraṇaṃ niddhārento “majjhe visuddhimaggo”tiādimāha. Tattha “majjhe ṭhatvā”ti etena majjhaṭṭhabhāvadīpanena [M 1.0019] visesato catunnaṃ āgamānaṃ sādhāraṇaṭṭhakathā visuddhimaggo, na sumaṅgalavilāsinīādayo viya asādhāraṇaṭṭhakathāti dasseti. “Visesato”ti ca idaṃ vinayābhidhammānampi visuddhimaggo yathārahaṃ atthavaṇṇanā hoti evāti katvā vuttaṃ.

15. Now, determining the definite reason for not examining just that, he says, 'The Visuddhimagga in the middle,' etc. Herein, by 'standing in the middle,' by this indication of its central position, he shows that the Visuddhimagga is a commentary common to the four Nikāyas in particular, not an uncommon commentary like the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī and others. And the word 'in particular' is stated because the Visuddhimagga is indeed an exposition of the meaning for the Vinaya and Abhidhamma as well, as is appropriate.

16. Iccevāti iti eva. Tampīti visuddhimaggampi. Etāyāti papañcasūdaniyā. Ettha ca “sīhaḷadīpaṃ ābhatā”tiādinā aṭṭhakathākaraṇassa nimittaṃ dasseti, “dīpavāsīnamatthāya, sujanassa ca tuṭṭhatthaṃ, ciraṭṭhitatthañca dhammassā”ti etena payojanaṃ, “majjhimāgamavarassa atthaṃ pakāsayissāmī”ti etena piṇḍatthaṃ, “apanetvāna tatohaṃ sīhaḷabhāsa”ntiādinā, “sīlakathā”tiādinā ca karaṇappakāraṃ. Sīlakathādīnaṃ avicāraṇampi hi idha karaṇappakāro evāti.

16. 'Thus' means thus indeed. 'That too' means the Visuddhimagga too. 'By this' means by the Papañcasūdanī. And herein, with 'brought to the island of Sīhaḷa,' etc., he shows the occasion for writing the commentary; with 'for the benefit of the island-dwellers,' 'for the delight of good people,' and 'for the long duration of the Dhamma,' he shows the purpose; with 'I will explain the meaning of the excellent Majjhima Nikāya,' he shows the summary meaning; and with 'having removed from that the Sinhala language,' etc., and 'the talk on virtue,' etc., he shows the mode of composition. For here the non-examination of the talk on virtue, etc., is itself a mode of composition.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the introductory discourse to the book is finished.

Nidānakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Introductory Discourse

1. Vibhāgavantānaṃ [V 1.0018] sabhāvavibhāvanaṃ vibhāgadassanamukheneva hotīti paṭhamaṃ tāva paṇṇāsavaggasuttādivasena majjhimāgamassa vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha majjhimasaṅgīti nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti yaṃ vuttaṃ “majjhimāgamavarassa atthaṃ pakāsayissāmī”ti, tasmiṃ vacane. Yā majjhimāgamapariyāyena majjhimasaṅgīti vuttā, sā paṇṇāsādito edisāti dasseti “majjhimasaṅgīti nāmā”tiādinā. Tatthāti vā “etāya aṭṭhakathāya vijānātha majjhimasaṅgītiyā attha”nti ettha yassā majjhimasaṅgītiyā atthaṃ vijānāthāti vuttaṃ, sā majjhimasaṅgīti nāma paṇṇāsādito edisāti dasseti. Pañca dasakā paṇṇāsā, mūle ādimhi paṇṇāsā, mūlabhūtā vā paṇṇāsā mūlapaṇṇāsā. Majjhe bhavā majjhimā, majjhimā ca sā paṇṇāsā cāti majjhimapaṇṇāsā. Upari uddhaṃ paṇṇāsā uparipaṇṇāsā. Paṇṇāsattayasaṅgahāti paṇṇāsattayaparigaṇanā.

1. Since the elucidation of the intrinsic nature of things that have divisions occurs precisely through showing the divisions, first, in order to show the division of the Majjhima Nikāya by way of the Fifties, Vaggas, Suttas, and so on, he says, 'Therein, the Majjhima Saṅgīti by name,' etc. 'Therein' refers to that statement where it was said, 'I will explain the meaning of the excellent Majjhima Nikāya.' With 'the Majjhima Saṅgīti by name,' etc., he shows that the Majjhima Saṅgīti, which is spoken of by the term Majjhima Nikāya, is of such a kind, beginning with the Fifties. Or, 'therein' refers to the passage, 'By this commentary understand the meaning of the Majjhima Saṅgīti.' Here he shows that the Majjhima Saṅgīti whose meaning, it was said, you should understand, is of such a kind, beginning with the Fifties. Five tens are a fifty. The fifty at the beginning is the Root Fifty, or the foundational fifty is the Root Fifty. That which is in the middle is the middle one; and that is the fifty, thus the Middle Fifty. The fifty that is above is the Upper Fifty. 'The collection of the three fifties' is the enumeration of the three Fifties.

Ayaṃ saṅgaho nāma jātisañjātikiriyāgaṇanavasena catubbidho. Tattha “yā cāvuso visākha, sammāvācā, yo ca sammākammanto, yo ca sammāājīvo[M 1.0020], ime dhammā sīlakkhandhe saṅgahitā”ti (ma. ni. 1.462) ayaṃ jātisaṅgaho. “Yo cāvuso visākha, sammāvāyāmo. Yā ca sammāsati, yo ca sammāsamādhi, ime dhammā samādhikkhandhe saṅgahitā”ti ayaṃ sañjātisaṅgaho. “Yā cāvuso visākha, sammādiṭṭhi, yo ca sammāsaṅkappo, ime dhammā paññākkhandhe saṅgahitā”ti ayaṃ kiriyāsaṅgaho. “Hañci cakkhāyatanaṃ rūpakkhandhagaṇanaṃ gacchati, tena vata re vattabbe cakkhāyatanaṃ rūpakkhandhena saṅgahita”nti (kathā. 471) ayaṃ gaṇanasaṅgaho. Ayameva ca idhādhippeto. Tena vuttaṃ “paṇṇāsattayasaṅgahāti paṇṇāsattayaparigaṇanā”ti.

This grouping is fourfold by way of class, association, function, and reckoning. Herein: “Friend Visākha, right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these phenomena are included in the aggregate of virtue” (MN 44)—this is the class grouping. “Friend Visākha, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these phenomena are included in the aggregate of concentration”—this is the association grouping. “Friend Visākha, right view, and right intention—these phenomena are included in the aggregate of wisdom”—this is the function grouping. “If the eye base comes under the reckoning of the form aggregate, then it must be said that the eye base is included by the form aggregate” (Kv 471)—this is the reckoning grouping. And this is what is intended here. Therefore it is said: “The grouping of the three fifties means the enumeration of the three fifties.”

Vaggatoti samūhato, so panettha dasakavasena veditabbo. Yebhuyyena hi sāsane dasake vaggavohāro. Tenevāha “ekekāya paṇṇāsāya pañca pañca vagge katvā”ti. Pannarasavaggasamāyogāti pannarasavaggasaṃyogāti attho. Keci pana samāyogasaddaṃ samudāyatthaṃ vadanti. Padatoti ettha aṭṭhakkharo gāthāpādo “pada”nti adhippeto, tasmā “akkharato cha akkharasatasahassāni caturāsītuttarasatādhikāni catucattālīsa sahassāni ca akkharānī”ti pāṭhena [V 1.0019] bhavitabbanti vadanti. Yasmā pana navakkharo yāva dvādasakkharo ca gāthāpādo saṃvijjati, tasmā tādisānampi gāthānaṃ vasena aḍḍhateyyagāthāsataṃ bhāṇavāro hotīti katvā “akkharato satta akkharasatasahassāni cattālīsañca sahassāni tepaññāsañca akkharānī”ti vuttaṃ. Evañhi padabhāṇavāragaṇanāhi akkharagaṇanā saṃsandati, netarathā. Bhāṇavāroti ca dvattiṃsakkharānaṃ gāthānaṃ vasena aḍḍhateyyagāthāsataṃ, ayañca akkharagaṇanā bhāṇavāragaṇanā ca padagaṇanānusārena laddhāti veditabbā. Imameva hi atthaṃ ñāpetuṃ suttagaṇanānantaraṃ bhāṇavāre agaṇetvā padāni gaṇitāni. Tatridaṃ vuccati –

“By vagga” means “by collection,” and here it should be understood as being by way of tens. For in the Dispensation, the term “vagga” is mostly used for a group of ten. Hence it is said: “Having made five vaggas for each fifty.” “The combination of fifteen vaggas” means the conjunction of fifteen vaggas. Some, however, say the word “samāyoga” means “a collection.” Regarding “by pada,” here an eight-syllable verse line is intended by the term “pada.” Therefore, some say the reading should be: “In terms of syllables, there are 644,184 syllables.” But since verse lines of nine up to twelve syllables also exist, by taking such verses into account, a recitation section (bhāṇavāra) consists of two hundred and fifty verses. Thus it is said: “In terms of syllables, there are 740,053 syllables.” For only in this way does the syllable count correspond with the counts of lines and recitation sections; not otherwise. A recitation section (bhāṇavāra) consists of two hundred and fifty verses of thirty-two syllables, and it should be understood that this syllable count and recitation section count are obtained in accordance with the line count. Indeed, to make this very meaning known, after counting the suttas, the lines (padas) were counted without counting the recitation sections. Herein, this is said:

“Bhāṇavārā yathāpi hi, majjhimassa pakāsitā;

Upaḍḍhabhāṇavāro ca, tevīsatipadādhiko.

“Just as the recitation sections for the Majjhima have been declared, so too a half-recitation section exceeds by twenty-three lines.

Satta satasahassāni, akkharānaṃ vibhāvaye;

Cattālīsa sahassāni, tepaññāsañca akkhara”nti.

One should discern seven hundred thousand syllables, and forty thousand and fifty-three syllables.”

Anusandhitoti [M 1.0021] desanānusandhito. Ekasmiṃ eva hi sutte purimapacchimānaṃ desanābhāgānaṃ sambandho anusandhānato anusandhi. Ettha ca attajjhāsayānusandhi parajjhāsayānusandhīti duvidho ajjhāsayānusandhi. So pana katthaci desanāya vippakatāya dhammaṃ suṇantānaṃ pucchāvasena, katthaci desentassa satthu sāvakassa dhammapaṭiggāhakānañca ajjhāsayavasena, katthaci desetabbassa dhammassa vasena hotīti samāsato tippakāro. Tena vuttaṃ “pucchānusandhiajjhāsayānusandhiyathānusandhivasena saṅkhepato tividho anusandhī”ti. Saṅkhepeneva ca catubbidho anusandhi veditabbo. Tattha “evaṃ vutte aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca ‘kiṃ nu kho, bhante, orimaṃ tīraṃ, kiṃ pārimaṃ tīraṃ, ko majjhe saṃsīdo, ko thale ussādo, ko manussaggāho, ko amanussaggāho, ko āvattaggāho, ko antopūtibhāvo’ti” (saṃ. ni. 4.241)? Evaṃ pucchantānaṃ vissajjentena bhagavatā pavattitadesanāvasena pucchānusandhī veditabbo. “Atha kho aññatarassa bhikkhuno evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi ‘iti kira bho rūpaṃ anattā… vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ anattā, anattakatāni kammāni kamattānaṃ phusissantī’ti. Atha kho bhagavā tassa bhikkhuno cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya bhikkhū āmantesi ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, vijjati, yaṃ idhekacco moghapuriso avidvā avijjāgato taṇhādhipateyyena cetasā satthusāsanaṃ atidhāvitabbaṃ maññeyya ‘iti kira bho rūpaṃ anattā…pe… phusissantī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha[V 1.0020], bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti (ma. ni. 3.90) evaṃ paresaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā bhagavatā pavattitadesanāvasena parajjhāsayānusandhi veditabbo.

“By connection” means by the connection of the discourse. For in a single sutta, the connection is the relation between the earlier and later parts of the discourse, established by linking them. Here, the connection by inclination is twofold: connection by one's own inclination and connection by another's inclination. This, however, is of three kinds in brief: it occurs sometimes by way of questions from those listening to a disjointed teaching; sometimes by way of the inclination of the Teacher who is teaching, or of a disciple, and of the recipients of the Dhamma; and sometimes by way of the Dhamma to be taught. Therefore it is said: “In brief, the connection is threefold: by way of connection through questioning, connection through inclination, and sequential connection.” And in brief, the connection is to be understood as fourfold. Here, when it was said thus, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the near shore? What is the far shore? Who sinks in the middle? Who is stranded on high ground? Who is seized by humans? Who is seized by nonhumans? Who is seized by a whirlpool? Who is inwardly putrid?” (SN 35.241). The connection through questioning should be understood by way of the teaching given by the Blessed One in response to their questioning. “Then a certain monk had this thought: ‘So indeed, form is nonself… feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness is nonself. How can deeds done by what is nonself touch a self?’ Then the Blessed One, knowing with his mind the thought in that monk's mind, addressed the monks: ‘It is possible, monks, that some senseless man here, unknowing and ignorant, his mind dominated by craving, might think to outstrip the Teacher's instruction thus: “So indeed, form is nonself… touch a self.” What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent?’” (MN 109). The connection through another's inclination should be understood by way of the teaching given by the Blessed One after discerning the inclination of others.

“Tassa mayhaṃ brāhmaṇa etadahosi ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ yā tā rattiyo abhiññātā abhilakkhitā cātuddasī pañcadasī aṭṭhamī ca pakkhassa, tathārūpāsu rattīsu yāni tāni ārāmacetiyāni vanacetiyāni rukkhacetiyāni bhiṃsanakāni salomahaṃsāni, tathārūpesu senāsanesu vihareyyaṃ appeva nāmāhaṃ bhayabheravaṃ passeyya’nti” (ma. ni. 1.49) evaṃ bhagavatā, “tatrāvuso lobho ca pāpako doso ca pāpako lobhassa ca pahānāya dosassa ca pahānāya atthi majjhimā paṭipadā, cakkhukaraṇī [M 1.0022] ñāṇakaraṇī upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.33) evaṃ dhammasenāpatinā ca attano ajjhāsayeneva pavattitadesanāvasena attajjhāsayānusandhi veditabbo. Yena pana dhammena ādimhi desanā uṭṭhitā, tassa anurūpadhammavasena vā paṭipakkhadhammavasena vā yesu suttesu upari desanā āgacchati, tesaṃ vasena yathānusandhi veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ ākaṅkheyyasutte (ma. ni. 1.65) heṭṭhā sīlena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari abhiññā āgatā. Vatthusutte (ma. ni. 1.70) heṭṭhā kilesena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari brahmavihārā āgatā. Kosambakasutte (ma. ni. 1.491) heṭṭhā bhaṇḍanena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari sāraṇīyadhammā āgatā. Kakacūpame (ma. ni. 1.222) heṭṭhā akkhantiyā vasena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari kakacūpamā āgatāti.

The connection by one's own inclination should be understood by way of a discourse set forth from one's own inclination. For instance, by the Blessed One: “Then, brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Suppose I were to dwell in such fearful and terrifying places—shrines in parks, forest shrines, and tree shrines—on those renowned and specially marked nights, the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight. Perhaps I might encounter that same fear and dread.’” (MN 4). And by the General of the Dhamma: “Here, friend, greed is unwholesome, and hatred is unwholesome. For the abandoning of greed and hatred there is a middle way that gives rise to vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.” (MN 8). The sequential connection should be understood by way of those suttas where the teaching later on follows from the principle with which the discourse began, either as a concordant principle or as an opposing one. For example: In the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta (MN 6), the teaching begins below with virtue, and higher knowledge comes above. In the Vatthu Sutta (MN 7), the teaching begins below with defilement, and the divine abodes come above. In the Kosambaka Sutta (MN 48), the teaching begins below with quarrels, and the principles conducive to cordiality come above. In the Kakacūpama Sutta (MN 21), the teaching begins below with impatience, and the simile of the saw comes above.

Vitthārato panetthāti evaṃ saṅkhepato tividho catubbidho ca anusandhi ettha etasmiṃ majjhimanikāye tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sutte yathārahaṃ vitthārato vibhajitvā viññāyamānā navasatādhikāni tīṇi anusandhisahassāni honti. Yathā cetaṃ paṇṇāsādivibhāgavacanaṃ majjhimasaṅgītiyā sarūpadassanatthaṃ hoti, evaṃ pakkhepadosapariharaṇatthañca hoti. Evañhi paṇṇāsādīsu vavatthitesu tabbinimuttaṃ kiñci suttaṃ yāva ekaṃ padampi ānetvā imaṃ majjhimasaṅgītiyāti kassaci vattuṃ okāso na siyāti.

But when these connections, threefold and fourfold in brief, are analyzed in detail as is fitting in each sutta of this Majjhima Nikāya, they are found to be three thousand nine hundred. And just as this statement about the divisions into fifties serves to show the true form of the Majjhima Collection, so too it serves to avoid the fault of interpolation. For when the divisions into fifties are established, no one has the opportunity to introduce any sutta or even a single word extraneous to them and say, “This belongs to the Majjhima Collection.”

Evaṃ paṇṇāsavaggasuttabhāṇavārānusandhibyañjanato majjhimasaṅgītiṃ vavatthapetvā idāni naṃ ādito paṭṭhāya saṃvaṇṇetukāmo attano saṃvaṇṇanāya tassā paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiyaṃ nikkhittānukkameneva pavattabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha paṇṇāsāsu mūlapaṇṇāsā ādī”tiādimāha. Tattha yathāpaccayaṃ tattha tattha desitattā paññattattā ca vippakiṇṇānaṃ dhammavinayānaṃ saṅgahetvā gāyanaṃ [V 1.0021] kathanaṃ saṅgīti, mahāvisayattā pūjanīyattā ca mahatī saṅgītīti mahāsaṅgīti, paṭhamā mahāsaṅgīti paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti, tassā pavattitakālo paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikālo, tasmiṃ paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle. Nidadāti desanaṃ desakālādivasena aviditaṃ viditaṃ katvā nidassetīti nidānaṃ, yo lokiyehi “upogghāto”ti [M 1.0023] vuccati, svāyamettha “evaṃ me suta”ntiādiko gantho veditabbo, na pana “sanidānāhaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desemī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.126) viya ajjhāsayādidesanuppattihetu. Tenevāha “evaṃ me sutantiādikaṃ āyasmatā ānandena paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle vuttaṃ nidānamādī”ti. Kāmañcettha yassaṃ paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiyaṃ nikkhittānukkamena saṃvaṇṇanaṃ kattukāmo, sā vitthārato vattabbā. Sumaṅgalavilāsiniyaṃ (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.nidānakathāvaṇṇanā) pana attanā vitthāritattā tattheva gahetabbāti imissā saṃvaṇṇanāya mahantataṃ pariharanto “sā panesā”tiādimāha.

Having thus established the Middle Collection by means of its fifties, chapters, suttas, recitation sections, connections, and phrasing, now, wishing to comment on it from the beginning, in order to show by his own commentary that it proceeded exactly according to the sequence laid down in the First Great Council, he says, beginning with: 'Therein, among the fifty, the Root Fifty is first.' Herein, a 'chanting together' (saṅgīti) is the collecting, reciting, and rehearsing of the scattered Dhamma and Vinaya, which were taught and laid down here and there according to the appropriate conditions. Because of its great scope and its venerability, a great chanting together is a 'Great Council' (mahāsaṅgīti). The first Great Council is the First Great Council; the time it occurred is the time of the First Great Council. At that time of the First Great Council. An 'introduction' (nidāna) is so called because it lays down and points out the teaching, making known what was unknown regarding the circumstances of the teaching, the time, etc., which is called a 'prologue' (upogghāta) by worldly people. Here, this should be understood as the text beginning 'Thus have I heard,' not as the cause for the arising of the teaching, such as the disposition of the audience, as in passages like 'Monks, I teach the Dhamma with its cause' (AN 3.126). Therefore he said: 'The introduction beginning "Thus have I heard," spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council, is the beginning.' And although here, if one wishes to comment on it according to the sequence laid down in the First Great Council, that Council should be described in detail, since it has been explained in detail by himself in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī (Dīgha Nikāya Ṭīkā 1, Commentary on the Introduction), it should be understood from there. Thus, avoiding the great length of this commentary, he says, beginning with 'But this...'

Nidānakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Introductory Story is concluded.

1. Mūlapariyāyavaggo

1. The Chapter on the Root Sequence

1. Mūlapariyāyasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Root Sequence

Abbhantaranidānavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Internal Introduction

1. Evaṃ [V 1.0022][M 1.0024] bāhiranidāne vattabbaṃ atidisitvā idāni abhantaranidānaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya saṃvaṇṇetuṃ “yaṃ paneta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yasmā saṃvaṇṇanaṃ karontena saṃvaṇṇetabbe dhamme padavibhāgaṃ padatthañca dassetvā tato paraṃ piṇḍattādidassanavasena saṃvaṇṇanā kātabbā, tasmā padāni tāva dassento “evanti nipātapada”ntiādimāha. Tattha padavibhāgoti padānaṃ viseso, na padaviggaho. Atha vā padāni ca padavibhāgo ca padavibhāgo, padaviggaho ca padavibhāgo ca padavibhāgoti vā ekasesavasena padapadaviggahā padavibhāgasaddena vuttāti veditabbaṃ. Tattha padaviggaho “subhagañca taṃ vanañcāti subhagavanaṃ, sālānaṃ rājā, sālo ca so rājā ca itipi sālarājā”tiādivasena samāsapadesu daṭṭhabbo.

1. Having thus dealt by extension with what was to be said on the external introduction, now, in order to comment on the internal introduction from the beginning, the passage beginning 'But this...' has been stated. Therein, since one who is making a commentary should do so by first showing the word-division and the word-meaning of the teaching to be commented on, and thereafter by way of showing the collective meaning and so on, therefore, first showing the words, he says, beginning with: 'evaṃ is a particle-word.' Therein, 'word-division' (padavibhāgo) means the distinction of words, not the analysis of words (padaviggaho). Alternatively, it should be understood that 'words and word-division' is 'word-division'; or 'word-analysis and word-division' is 'word-division'; or that by way of ellipsis (ekasesa), 'words' and 'word-analysis' are expressed by the term 'word-division.' Therein, word-analysis should be seen in compound words by way of examples such as: 'a lovely wood' (subhagavanaṃ) is 'it is lovely and it is a wood'; 'king of sāla trees' (sālarājā) is 'king of sāla trees' or 'he is a sāla tree and he is a king'.

Atthatoti padatthato. Taṃ pana padatthaṃ atthuddhārakkamena paṭhamaṃ evaṃsaddassa dassento “evaṃ-saddo tāvā”tiādimāha. Avadhāraṇādīti ettha ādi-saddena idamatthapucchāparimāṇādiatthānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hi “evaṃgatāni puthusippāyatanāni (dī. ni. 1.163), evavidho evamākāro”ti ca ādīsu idaṃ-saddassa atthe evaṃ-saddo. Gata-saddo hi pakārapariyāyo, tathā vidhākāra-saddā ca. Tathā hi vidhayuttagata-sadde lokiyā pakāratthe vadanti. “Evaṃ su te sunhātā suvilittā kappitakesamassū āmukkamaṇikuṇḍalābharaṇā odātavatthavasanā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitā samaṅgībhūtā paricārenti, seyyathāpi tvaṃ etarahi sācariyakoti. No hidaṃ, bho gotamā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.286) pucchāyaṃ. “Evaṃlahuparivattaṃ (a. ni. 1.48) evamāyupariyanto”ti (pārā. 12) ca ādīsu parimāṇe.

'By meaning' (atthato) means by the meaning of the word (padatthato). Showing that word-meaning first for the word 'evaṃ' by the method of extracting the meaning, he says, beginning with: 'First, the word evaṃ...' In 'emphasis, etc.' (avadhāraṇādi), the word 'etc.' (ādi) should be seen as an inclusion of the meanings of 'this matter,' 'question,' 'measure,' and so on. For in passages such as 'the numerous crafts are of this kind' (evaṃgatāni puthusippāyatanāni, DN 1.163), 'of this sort' (evavidho), and 'of this manner' (evamākāro), the word 'evaṃ' is in the sense of the word 'this' (idaṃ). For the word 'gata' is a synonym for 'manner' (pakāra), and so too are the words 'vidha' and 'ākāra'. For worldly people use the word 'gata' when joined with 'vidha' in the sense of 'manner'. In passages such as 'Are your disciples, well-bathed, well-anointed, with trimmed hair and beards, adorned with jeweled earrings and ornaments, dressed in white clothes, furnished and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure, enjoying themselves, just as you yourself are now with your teacher? — This is not so, Master Gotama' (DN 1.286), it is used in a question. And in passages such as 'so quick to change' (evaṃlahuparivattaṃ, AN 1.48) and 'this is the limit of the lifespan' (evamāyupariyanto, Pārā. 12), it is used in the sense of measure.

Nanu [V 1.0023] ca “evaṃ su te sunhātā suvilittā, evamāyupariyanto”ti ettha evaṃ-saddena pucchanākāraparimāṇākārānaṃ vuttattā ākārattho eva [M 1.0025] evaṃ-saddoti? Na, visesasabbhāvato. Ākāramattavācako hi evaṃ-saddo ākāratthoti adhippeto yathā “evaṃ byā kho”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.234, 396), na pana ākāravisesavācako. Evañca katvā “evaṃ jātena maccenā”tiādīni upamādiudāharaṇāni upapannāni honti. Tathā hi “yathāpi…pe… bahu”nti (dha. pa. 53) ettha puppharāsiṭṭhāniyato manussūpapatti-sappurisūpanissaya-saddhammassavana-yonisomanasikāra- bhogasampatti-ādidānādi-puññakiriyahetusamudāyato sobhā-sugandhatādiguṇayogato mālāguṇasadisiyo pahūtā puññakiriyā maritabbasabhāvatāya maccena sattena kattabbāti jotitattā puppharāsimālāguṇāva upamā, tesaṃ upamākāro yathā-saddena aniyamato vuttoti “evaṃ-saddo upamākāranigamanattho”ti vattuṃ yuttaṃ. So pana upamākāro niyamiyamāno atthato upamāva hotīti āha “upamāyaṃ āgato”ti. Tathā “evaṃ iminā ākārena abhikkamitabba”ntiādinā upadisiyamānāya samaṇasāruppāya ākappasampattiyā yo tattha upadisanākāro, so atthato upadeso evāti vuttaṃ “evaṃ te…pe… upadese”ti. Tathā “evametaṃ bhagavā, evametaṃ sugatā”ti ettha ca bhagavatā yathāvuttamatthaṃ aviparītato jānantehi kataṃ tattha saṃvijjamānaguṇānaṃ pakārehi haṃsanaṃ udaggatākaraṇaṃ sampahaṃsanaṃ. Yo tattha sampahaṃsanākāroti yojetabbaṃ.

But is it not so that in the phrases 'evaṃ su te...' and 'evamāyupariyanto,' since the manner of questioning and the manner of measure are stated by the word 'evaṃ,' the word 'evaṃ' just has the meaning of 'manner'? No, because a specific sense exists. The word 'evaṃ' is intended to have the meaning of 'manner' when it expresses just manner in general, as in phrases like 'evaṃ byā kho' (MN 1.234, 396), but not when it expresses a specific manner. This being so, examples of simile, etc., like 'Thus by a mortal who is born...' (Dhp 53) become appropriate. For instance, in the passage 'Just as... many...' (Dhp 53), the simile is the qualities of a garland from a heap of flowers, because it is illuminated that abundant meritorious actions—similar to the qualities of a garland due to their connection with qualities like beauty and fragrance, arising from a collection of causes for meritorious action such as human rebirth, reliance on good persons, hearing the good Dhamma, wise attention, attainment of wealth, giving, etc.—should be done by a mortal being who is subject to death. The manner of their simile is expressed indefinitely by the word 'yathā' (just as), so it is right to say that 'the word "evaṃ" has the purpose of concluding the manner of the simile.' But when that manner of the simile is determined, in meaning it becomes the simile itself; thus he said, 'it has come in a simile.' Similarly, with regard to the accomplishment of deportment suitable for a recluse, which is being instructed by 'one should go forward in this manner,' etc., the manner of instruction there is, in meaning, the instruction itself. Thus it was said, 'evaṃ te... in instruction.' Likewise, in 'It is so, Blessed One; it is so, Fortunate One,' there is gladdening, elation, and rejoicing done by those who know without distortion the meaning spoken by the Blessed One, by way of the qualities existing there. The manner of rejoicing there should be connected.

Evamevaṃ panāyanti ettha garahaṇākāroti yojetabbaṃ, so ca garahaṇākāro “vasalī”tiādikhuṃsanasaddasannidhānato idha evaṃ-saddena pakāsitoti viññāyati. Yathā cettha, evaṃ upamākārādayopi upamādivasena vuttānaṃ puppharāsiādisaddānaṃ sannidhānato daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ, bhanteti pana dhammassa sādhukaṃ savanamanasikāre sanniyojitehi bhikkhūhi attano tattha ṭhitabhāvassa paṭijānanavasena vuttattā ettha evaṃ-saddo vacanasampaṭicchanattho vutto. Tena evaṃ, bhante sādhu, bhante, suṭṭhu, bhanteti vuttaṃ hoti. Evañca vadehīti “yathāhaṃ vadāmi, evaṃ samaṇaṃ ānandaṃ vadehī”ti yo evaṃ vadanākāro idāni vattabbo. So evaṃsaddena nidassīyatīti “nidassane”ti vuttoti. Evaṃ noti etthāpi tesaṃ yathāvuttadhammānaṃ ahitadukkhāvahabhāve sanniṭṭhānajananatthaṃ anumatigahaṇavasena [M 1.0026] “saṃvattanti vā no vā, kathaṃ vo ettha hotī”ti pucchāya katāya “evaṃ no ettha hotī”ti vuttattā tadākārasanniṭṭhānaṃ evaṃ-saddena vibhāvitanti viññāyati. So pana tesaṃ dhammānaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanākāro niyamiyamāno avadhāraṇattho hotīti āha “evaṃ no ettha hotītiādīsu avadhāraṇe”ti.

In 'Thus indeed they come,' the 'manner of reproach' should be connected. And it is understood that this manner of reproach is revealed here by the word 'evaṃ' because of its proximity to abusive words like 'outcaste' (vasalī). Just as here, so too the manner of simile and so on should be understood from the proximity of words like 'heap of flowers,' etc., which are spoken by way of simile and the like. But 'Yes, venerable sir' (Evaṃ, bhante) is said by monks who have been enjoined to listen to and carefully attend to the Dhamma, as a way of acknowledging their state of being established therein. Here the word 'evaṃ' is said to have the meaning of assenting to what was said. By this is meant, 'Yes, venerable sir; good, venerable sir; excellent, venerable sir.' And in 'Speak thus' (Evañca vadehī), the manner of speaking which is now to be spoken, 'As I speak, so should you speak to the recluse Ānanda,' is indicated by the word 'evaṃ.' Thus it is said to be 'in indication.' Similarly, in 'Thus for us' (Evaṃ no), here too, in order to generate a conclusion about the unbeneficial and painful nature of those things that were mentioned, by way of gaining consent, when the question was asked, 'Do they conduce to what is unbeneficial and painful, or not? What is your opinion on this?', and the reply was given, 'For us, it is thus,' the conclusion in that manner is clarified by the word 'evaṃ.' But that manner of those things conducing to what is unbeneficial and painful, being determined, has the meaning of emphasis. Thus it is said: 'in emphasis, in passages such as "For us, it is thus."

Nānānayanipuṇanti [V 1.0024] ekattanānattaabyāpāraevaṃdhammatāsaṅkhātā, nandiyāvattatipukkhalasīhavikkīḷitaaṅkusadisālocanasaṅkhātā vā ādhārādibhedavasena nānāvidhā nayā nānānayā, nayā vā pāḷigatiyo, tā ca paññattianupaññattiādivasena saṃkilesabhāgiyādilokiyāditadubhayavomissakādivasena kusalādivasena khandhādivasena saṅgahādivasena samayavimuttādivasena ṭhapanādivasena kusalamūlādivasena tikappaṭṭhānādivasena ca nānappakārāti nānānayā. Tehi nipuṇaṃ saṇhaṃ sukhumanti nānānayanipuṇaṃ. Āsayova ajjhāsayo, te ca sassatādibhedena, tattha ca apparajakkhatādibhedena aneke, attajjhāsayādayo eva vā samuṭṭhānaṃ uppattihetu etassāti anekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Atthabyañjanasampannanti atthabyañjanaparipuṇṇaṃ upanetabbābhāvato, saṅkāsanapakāsana-vivaraṇa-vibhajana-uttānīkaraṇa-paññattivasena chahi atthapadehi, akkhara-padabyañjanākāraniruttiniddesavasena chahi byañjanapadehi ca samannāgatanti vā attho daṭṭhabbo.

Regarding ‘skilled in various methods,’ the ‘various methods’ are those designated as the unity and diversity of non-operation and the nature of things thus. Or, the various methods are of different kinds based on distinctions such as the basis, designated as nandiyāvatta, tipukkhala, sīhavikkīḷita, and aṅkusadisālocana. Or, the methods are the ways of the Pāli, and these are of many kinds: by way of designation and subsequent designation, etc.; by way of what is connected with defilements, what is worldly, etc., and what is a mixture of both; by way of what is wholesome, etc.; by way of the aggregates, etc.; by way of inclusion, etc.; by way of the temporally liberated, etc.; by way of establishment, etc.; by way of wholesome roots, etc.; and by way of the threefold framework, etc. Thus they are ‘various methods.’ ‘Skilled in various methods’ means subtle and refined through these methods. ‘Disposition’ (āsaya) is inclination (ajjhāsayo), and these are numerous, distinguished by eternalism, etc., and among them, by having little dust, etc. Or, one's own inclinations and so on are the origin, the cause of its arising; hence, ‘arising from many dispositions.’ ‘Endowed with meaning and phrasing’ means complete in meaning and phrasing because there is nothing to be added. Or, the meaning should be seen as being endowed with the six aspects of meaning—namely, indication, manifestation, exposition, analysis, making plain, and designation—and with the six aspects of phrasing—namely, letters, words, phrases, form, etymology, and exposition.

Vividhapāṭihāriyanti ettha pāṭihāriyapadassa vacanatthaṃ (udā. aṭṭha. 1; itivu. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.1 devatāsaṃyutta) “paṭipakkhaharaṇato, rāgādikilesāpanayanato ca pāṭihāriya”nti vadanti, bhagavato pana paṭipakkhā rāgādayo na santi, ye haritabbā. Puthujjanānampi vigatūpakkilese aṭṭhaguṇasamannāgate citte hatapaṭipakkhe iddhividhaṃ pavattati, tasmā tattha pavattavohārena ca na sakkā idha “pāṭihāriya”nti vattuṃ. Sace pana mahākāruṇikassa bhagavato veneyyagatā ca kilesā paṭipakkhā, tesaṃ haraṇato “pāṭihāriya”nti vuttaṃ, evaṃ sati yuttametaṃ. Atha vā bhagavato ca sāsanassa ca paṭipakkhā titthiyā, tesaṃ haraṇato pāṭihāriyaṃ. Te hi diṭṭhiharaṇavasena diṭṭhipakāsane asamatthabhāvena ca iddhiādesanānusāsanīhi haritā apanītā hontīti[M 1.0027]. “Paṭī”ti vā ayaṃ saddo “pacchā”ti etassa atthaṃ bodheti “tasmiṃ paṭipaviṭṭhamhi, añño āgañchi brāhmaṇo”tiādīsu (su. ni. 985; cūḷani. 4) viya, tasmā samāhite citte vigatūpakkilese ca katakiccena pacchā haritabbaṃ pavattetabbanti pāṭihāriyaṃ, attano vā upakkilesesu catutthajjhānamaggehi haritesu pacchā haraṇaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ, iddhiādesanānusāsaniyo ca vigatūpakkilesena katakiccena ca sattahitatthaṃ puna pavattetabbā, haritesu ca attano upakkilesesu parasattānaṃ upakilesaharaṇāni hontīti pāṭihāriyāni bhavanti. Pāṭihāriyameva pāṭihāriyaṃ, pāṭihāriye vā iddhiādesanānusāsanisamudāye bhavaṃ ekamekaṃ pāṭihāriyanti vuccati. Pāṭihāriyaṃ vā catutthajjhānaṃ maggo ca paṭipakkhaharaṇato, tattha jātaṃ, tasmiṃ vā nimittabhūte, tato vā āgatanti [V 1.0025] pāṭihāriyaṃ. Tassa pana iddhiādibhedena visayabhedena ca bahuvidhassa bhagavato desanāyaṃ labbhamānattā āha “vividhapāṭihāriya”nti.

Regarding ‘manifold miracles’: Here, they state the verbal meaning of the word ‘miracle’ (pāṭihāriya) as: ‘It is a miracle because it removes the opponent and because it removes defilements such as greed.’ However, the Blessed One has no opponents such as greed and other defilements that are to be removed. Even for worldlings, the kinds of psychic power operate when the mind is free from imperfections, endowed with the eight qualities, and has its opponents destroyed; therefore, based on the usage prevalent there, one cannot say ‘miracle’ here. But if the defilements found in those to be trained are the opponents for the greatly compassionate Blessed One, and it is called a ‘miracle’ because of their removal, then this is proper. Or else, the opponents of the Blessed One and his Dispensation are the adherents of other sects, and it is a ‘miracle’ because of their removal. For they are removed and dispelled by the miracles of psychic power, revelation, and instruction, by way of removing their views and by their inability to proclaim their views. Or, the word ‘paṭi’ conveys the meaning ‘afterwards,’ as in such passages as: ‘After he had entered, another brahmin came.’ Therefore, what is to be brought forth and manifested afterwards in a concentrated mind that is free from imperfections and has completed its task is a ‘miracle.’ Or, when one's own imperfections have been removed by the fourth jhāna and the path, the subsequent removal is a ‘miracle.’ The miracles of psychic power, revelation, and instruction are to be manifested again for the welfare of beings by one who is free from imperfections and has completed his task. And when one's own imperfections are removed, the removal of the imperfections of other beings occurs; thus these are miracles. A miracle is just a miracle. Or, each single thing that occurs in the collection of miracles—psychic power, revelation, and instruction—is called a miracle. Or, the fourth jhāna and the path are a miracle because they remove the opponent; what is born in them, or has them as its condition, or comes from them is a miracle. Since this is found in the Blessed One's teaching in many forms, distinguished by psychic power, etc., and by its domain, he said ‘manifold miracles’.

Na aññathāti bhagavato sammukhā sutākārato na aññathāti attho, na pana bhagavato desitākārato. Acinteyyānubhāvā hi bhagavato desanā. Evañca katvā “sabbappakārena ko samattho viññātu”nti idaṃ vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ bhavati, dhāraṇabaladassanañca na virujjhati sutākārāvirajjhanassa adhippetattā. Na hettha atthantaratāparihāro dvinnampi atthānaṃ ekavisayattā. Itarathā thero bhagavato desanāya sabbathā paṭiggahaṇe samattho asamattho cāti āpajjeyyāti.

‘Not otherwise’: The meaning is: not otherwise than the way it was heard in the Blessed One's presence, but not that it was not otherwise than the way the Blessed One taught it. For the Blessed One's teaching has inconceivable power. This being so, the statement, ‘Who is capable of understanding it in every way?’ is supported, and the demonstration of the power of retention is not contradicted, since what is intended is non-deviation from the way it was heard. Here there is no abandonment of a different meaning, since both meanings have the same subject. Otherwise, it would follow that the Elder was both capable and incapable of grasping the Blessed One's teaching in every way.

“Yo paro na hoti, so attā”ti evaṃ vuttāya niyakajjhattasaṅkhātāya sasantatiyā vattanato tividhopi me-saddo kiñcāpi ekasmiṃyeva atthe dissati, karaṇasampadānasāminiddesavasena pana vijjamānaṃ bhedaṃ sandhāyāha “me-saddo tīsu atthesu dissatī”ti.

Because it refers to one's own continuity, designated as one's own and personal in the statement, ‘What is not other is self,’ the word ‘me,’ though seen in only one sense, is threefold. But with reference to the existing distinction by way of indicating the instrument, the recipient, and the owner, he says: ‘The word “me” is seen in three senses.’

Kiñcāpi upasaggo kiriyaṃ viseseti, jotakabhāvato pana satipi tasmiṃ sutasaddo eva taṃ tamatthaṃ vadatīti anupasaggassa sutasaddassa atthuddhāre saupasaggassa gahaṇaṃ na virujjhatīti dassento “saupasaggo ca anupasaggo cā”tiādimāha. Assāti sutasaddassa. Kammabhāvasādhanāni idha sutasadde sambhavantīti vuttaṃ “upadhāritanti vā upadhāraṇanti vā [M 1.0028] attho”ti. Mayāti atthe satīti yadā me-saddassa kattuvasena karaṇaniddeso, tadāti attho. Mamāti atthe satīti yadā sambandhavasena sāminiddeso, tadā.

To show that, although a prefix qualifies the verb, because it is an indicator, even when it is present it is the word ‘suta’ itself that expresses this or that meaning, and thus in extracting the meaning of the unprefixed word ‘suta,’ the taking of the prefixed word is not contradicted, he said: ‘both with a prefix and without a prefix,’ etc. ‘Of it’ means of the word ‘suta.’ It is said that here in the word ‘suta,’ derivations in the sense of object and state are possible, thus: ‘the meaning is “was held” or “the holding”.’ ‘When the meaning is “by me”’: the meaning is, when the word ‘me’ is an indication of the instrument in the sense of the agent, then... ‘When the meaning is “of me”’: when it is an indication of the owner by way of relation, then...

Suta-saddasannidhāne payuttena evaṃ-saddena savanakiriyājotakena bhavitabbanti vuttaṃ “evanti sotaviññāṇādiviññāṇakiccanidassana”nti. Ādi-saddena sampaṭicchanādīnaṃ pañcadvārikaviññāṇānaṃ tadabhinīhaṭānañca manodvārikaviññāṇānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sabbesampi vākyānaṃ eva-kāratthasahitattā “suta”nti etassa sutamevāti ayamattho labbhatīti āha “assavanabhāvapaṭikkhepato”ti. Etena avadhāraṇena nirāsaṅkataṃ dasseti. Yathā ca sutaṃ sutamevāti niyametabbaṃ, taṃ sammā sutaṃ hotīti āha “anūnānadhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassana”nti. Atha vā saddantaratthāpohanavasena saddo atthaṃ vadatīti sutanti asutaṃ na hotīti ayametassa atthoti vuttaṃ “assavanabhāvapaṭikkhepato”ti[V 1.0026]. Iminā diṭṭhādivinivattanaṃ karoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “na idaṃ mayā diṭṭhaṃ, na sayambhuñāṇena sacchikataṃ, atha kho sutaṃ, tañca kho sammadevā”ti. Tenevāha – “anūnānadhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassana”nti. Avadhāraṇatthe vā evaṃ-sadde ayamatthayojanā karīyatīti tadapekkhassa suta-saddassa ayamattho vutto “assavanabhāvapaṭikkhepato”ti. Tenevāha “anūnānadhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassana”nti. Savanasaddo cettha kammattho veditabbo “suyyatī”ti.

It is said that the word ‘evaṃ,’ being used in proximity to the word ‘suta,’ must be an indicator of the act of hearing; thus: ‘“evaṃ” is an indication of the function of ear-consciousness and other consciousnesses.’ By the word ‘etc.,’ the inclusion of the five-door consciousnesses such as receiving, and the mind-door consciousnesses brought forth by them, should be understood. Since all the sentences are accompanied by the meaning of ‘eva’ (only), this meaning is obtained for ‘suta’: ‘heard only.’ Thus he says: ‘by the rejection of the state of not-hearing.’ By this emphasis, he shows freedom from doubt. And just as what is heard must be determined as ‘heard only,’ so it is well heard. Thus he says: ‘an indication of grasping without deficiency, excess, or distortion.’ Or, since a word expresses its meaning by way of excluding the meaning of other words, the meaning of ‘suta’ is ‘it is not unheard.’ Thus it is said: ‘by the rejection of the state of not-hearing.’ By this, he effects the exclusion of ‘seen,’ etc. This is what is said: ‘This was not seen by me, nor realized by self-originated knowledge, but it was heard, and that too, quite rightly.’ Therefore he says: ‘an indication of grasping without deficiency, excess, or distortion.’ Or, when the word ‘evaṃ’ has the sense of emphasis, this application of meaning is made. Hence, for the word ‘suta,’ which is dependent on it, this meaning is stated: ‘by the rejection of the state of not-hearing.’ Therefore he says: ‘an indication of grasping without deficiency, excess, or distortion.’ Here the word ‘savana’ (hearing) should be understood in the objective sense, as ‘what is heard.’

Evaṃ savanahetusuṇantapuggalasavanavisesavasena padattayassa ekena pakārena atthayojanaṃ dassetvā idāni pakārantarehipi taṃ dassetuṃ “tathā eva”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tassāti yā sā bhagavato sammukhā dhammassavanākārena pavattā manodvāraviññāṇavīthi, tassā. Sā hi nānappakārena ārammaṇe pavattituṃ samatthā. Tathā ca vuttaṃ “sotadvārānusārenā”ti. Nānappakārenāti vakkhamānānaṃ anekavihitānaṃ byañjanatthaggahaṇānaṃ nānākārena. Etena imissā yojanāya ākārattho evaṃ-saddo gahitoti dīpeti. Pavattibhāvappakāsananti pavattiyā atthibhāvappakāsanaṃ. Sutanti dhammappakāsananti yasmiṃ ārammaṇe [M 1.0029] vuttappakārā viññāṇavīthi nānappakārena pavattā, tassa dhammattā vuttaṃ, na sutasaddassa dhammatthattā. Vuttassevatthassa pākaṭīkaraṇaṃ “ayañhetthā”tiādi. Tattha viññāṇavīthiyāti karaṇatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Mayāti kattuatthe.

Having thus shown in one way the application of meaning to the triad of words by way of the cause of hearing, the person hearing, and the distinction of hearing, now, to show it in other ways too, it is said, ‘just so,’ etc. Therein, ‘of that’ means: of that cognitive series of mind-door consciousness which proceeded in the manner of hearing the Dhamma in the Blessed One's presence. For it is capable of proceeding towards its object in various ways. And so it is said: ‘in accordance with the ear-door.’ ‘In various ways’ means: in the various manners of grasping the meaning and phrasing of the many things to be explained. By this he indicates that in this application, the word ‘evaṃ’ is taken in the sense of ‘manner.’ ‘Manifestation of the state of occurrence’ means the manifestation of the existence of the occurrence. ‘Heard’ is a manifestation of the Dhamma. It is so called because the object in which the aforesaid cognitive series proceeded in various ways is the Dhamma, not because the word ‘suta’ means Dhamma. The making plain of what has just been said is ‘for here,’ etc. Therein, ‘by the cognitive series’ is the instrumental case in the instrumental sense. ‘By me’ is in the sense of the agent.

Evanti niddisitabbappakāsananti nidassanatthaṃ evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ nidassetabbassa niddisitabbattābhāvābhāvato. Tena evaṃ-saddena sakalampi suttaṃ paccāmaṭṭhanti dasseti. Suta-saddassa kiriyāsaddattā savanakiriyāya ca sādhāraṇaviññāṇapabandhapaṭibaddhattā tattha ca puggalavohāroti vuttaṃ “sutanti puggalakiccappakāsana”nti. Na hi puggalavohārarahite dhammapabandhe savanakiriyā labbhatīti.

The word 'evaṃ' is taken for the purpose of illustration, that is, for indicating what is to be pointed out, since what is to be demonstrated is indeed what is to be pointed out. By this word 'evaṃ,' it shows that the entire sutta is recalled. Because the word 'suta' is a verbal noun, and because the act of hearing is connected with the common stream of consciousness where there is personal convention, it is said: '"Suta" is the disclosure of a person's function.' For the act of hearing is not found in a sequence of phenomena devoid of personal convention.

Yassa cittasantānassātiādipi ākāratthameva evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā purimayojanāya aññathā atthayojanaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha ākārapaññattīti upādāpaññatti eva dhammānaṃ pavattiākārūpādānavasena tathā vuttā. Sutanti visayaniddesoti sotabbabhūto dhammo savanakiriyākattupuggalassa savanakiriyāvasena pavattiṭṭhānanti katvā vuttaṃ. Cittasantānavinimuttassa paramatthato kassaci kattu abhāvepi saddavohārena buddhiparikappitabhedavacanicchāya cittasantānato aññaṃ viya taṃsamaṅgiṃ katvā vuttaṃ “cittasantānena [V 1.0027] taṃsamaṅgino”ti. Savanakiriyāvisayopi sotabbadhammo savanakiriyāvasena pavattacittasantānassa idha paramatthato kattubhāvato, savanavasena cittappavattiyā eva vā savanakiriyābhāvato taṃkiriyākattu ca visayo hotīti vuttaṃ “taṃsamaṅgino kattuvisaye”ti. Sutākārassa ca therassa sammānicchitabhāvato āha “gahaṇasanniṭṭhāna”nti. Etena vā avadhāraṇatthaṃ evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā ayamatthayojanā katāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The phrase 'of which mental continuum,' etc., is also stated to show a different application of meaning from the previous construction, by taking the word 'evaṃ' in the sense of 'mode.' Therein, 'designation by mode' is a derivative designation, so called because it is based on the mode of occurrence of phenomena. 'Suta' is a specification of the object: this is said on the grounds that the Dhamma to be heard is the basis for the occurrence of the act of hearing for the person who is the agent of that act. Although in an ultimate sense there is no agent apart from the mental continuum, by way of verbal convention and with the wish to express a conceptually fabricated distinction, it is spoken of as if the one endowed with it is different from the mental continuum. Hence it is said, 'by the mental continuum of the one endowed with it.' The object of the act of hearing, the Dhamma to be heard, is also the object for the agent endowed with that action. This is said because here, in an ultimate sense, the mental continuum occurring by way of hearing is the agent, or because the act of hearing is simply the occurrence of consciousness by way of hearing. Hence it is said, 'in the object of the agent endowed with it.' And because the Elder's mode of hearing was rightly ascertained, he says, 'the ascertainment of the grasping.' Alternatively, it should be understood that this application of meaning is made by taking the word 'evaṃ' for the purpose of emphasis.

Pubbe sutānaṃ nānāvihitānaṃ suttasaṅkhātānaṃ atthabyañjanānaṃ upadhāritarūpassa ākārassa nidassanassa, avadhāraṇassa vā pakāsanasabhāvo evaṃ-saddoti tadākārādiupadhāraṇassa puggalapaññattiyā upādānabhūtadhammapabandhabyāpāratāya vuttaṃ – “evanti puggalakiccaniddeso”ti. Savanakiriyā pana puggalavādinopi viññāṇanirapekkhā natthīti visesato viññāṇabyāpāroti āha “sutanti viññāṇakiccaniddeso”ti. “Me”ti saddappavattiyā ekanteneva sattavisayattā viññāṇakiccassa ca tattheva samodahitabbato [M 1.0030] “meti ubhayakiccayuttapuggalaniddeso”ti vuttaṃ. Avijjamānapaññattivijjamānapaññattisabhāvā yathākkamaṃ evaṃ-sadda – suta-saddānaṃ atthāti te tathārūpa-paññatti-upādānabhūta-dhammapabandhabyāpārabhāvena dassento āha – “evanti puggalakiccaniddeso, sutanti viññāṇakiccaniddeso”ti. Ettha ca karaṇakiriyākattukammavisesappakāsanavasena puggalabyāpāravisayapuggalabyāpāranidassanavasena gahaṇākāragāhakatabbisayavisesaniddesavasena kattukaraṇabyāpārakattuniddesavasena ca dutiyādayo catasso atthayojanā dassitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The word 'evaṃ' has the nature of clarifying the mode, illustration, or emphasis of the ascertained form of the meaning and phrasing of the various kinds of previously heard teachings designated as suttas. This is said because the ascertainment of that mode, etc., is an operation of the sequence of phenomena that is the basis for personal designation. Thus it is said: '"Evaṃ" is a specification of a person's function.' But since the act of hearing, even for the Personalists, is not independent of consciousness, it is especially an operation of consciousness. Thus he says: '"Suta" is a specification of consciousness's function.' Because the word 'me,' in its occurrence, is exclusively concerned with the sphere of a being, and because the function of consciousness is to be included right there, it is said: '"Me" is a specification of the person connected with both functions.' The meanings of the words 'evaṃ' and 'suta' are, respectively, of the nature of a non-existent designation and an existent designation. Showing that they are so by being an operation of the sequence of phenomena that is the basis for such a designation, he says: '"Evaṃ" is a specification of a person's function; "suta" is a specification of consciousness's function.' And here it should be understood that the second and subsequent four applications of meaning are shown: by way of clarifying the distinctions of instrument, action, agent, and object; by way of indicating the sphere of a person's operation and the person's operation; by way of specifying the distinctions of the mode of grasping, the grasper, and the object to be grasped; and by way of specifying the agent, instrument, and operation.

Sabbassapi saddādhigamanīyassa atthassa paññattimukheneva paṭipajjitabbattā sabbapaññattīnañca vijjamānādivasena chasu paññattibhedesu antogadhattā tesu “eva”ntiādīnaṃ paññattīnaṃ sarūpaṃ niddhārento āha – “evanti ca meti cā”tiādi. Tattha “eva”nti ca “me”ti ca vuccamānassatthassa ākārādino dhammānaṃ asallakkhaṇabhāvato avijjamānapaññattibhāvoti āha – “saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena avijjamānapaññattī”ti. Tattha saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasenāti bhūtatthauttamatthavasena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo māyāmarīciādayo viya abhūtattho, anussavādīhi gahetabbo viya anuttamattho ca na hoti, so rūpasaddādisabhāvo, ruppanānubhavanādisabhāvo vā attho saccikaṭṭho paramattho cāti vuccati, na tathā “evaṃ me”ti padānaṃ atthoti. Etamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “kiñhettha ta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Sutanti pana saddāyatanaṃ sandhāyāha “vijjamānapaññattī”ti. Teneva hi “yañhi taṃ ettha sotena upaladdha”nti vuttaṃ, “sotadvārānusārena upaladdha”nti pana vutte atthabyañjanādisabbaṃ labbhati.

Since every meaning comprehensible through words must be accessed only through the gate of designation, and since all designations are included in the six kinds of designation based on being existent, etc., determining the nature of such designations as 'evaṃ' and so on, he says: '"Evaṃ" and "me"...' etc. Therein, because the meaning referred to by 'evaṃ' and 'me'—the mode, etc.—is not a characteristic of phenomena, it is a non-existent designation. Thus he says: 'In terms of real and ultimate meaning, it is a non-existent designation.' Here, 'in terms of real and ultimate meaning' means in terms of true meaning and highest meaning. This is what is said: That meaning which is not unreal like a magical illusion or a mirage, and not a non-ultimate meaning like what is to be learned from oral tradition—that is, the nature of form, sound, etc., or the nature of being afflicted, of experiencing, etc.—is called 'real meaning' and 'ultimate meaning.' The meaning of the words 'evaṃ me' is not like that. To make this very meaning clearer, the passage beginning 'What here...?' is stated. But with reference to the sound base, he says of 'suta' that it is an 'existent designation.' For that reason it is said: 'For that which is apprehended here by the ear...' But if it were said, 'apprehended in accordance with the ear-door,' then all meaning, phrasing, etc., would be obtained.

Taṃ [V 1.0028] taṃ upādāya vattabbatoti sotapathamāgate dhamme upādāya tesaṃ upadhāritākārādino paccāmasanavasena “eva”nti, sasantatipariyāpanne khandhe upādāya “me”ti vattabbattāti attho. Diṭṭhādisabhāvarahite saddāyatane pavattamānopi sutavohāro “dutiyaṃ tatiya”ntiādiko viya paṭhamādīni diṭṭhamutaviññāte apekkhitvāva pavattoti āha “diṭṭhādīni upanidhāya vattabbato”ti asutaṃ na hotīti hi sutanti pakāsitoyamatthoti. Attanā paṭividdhā suttassa pakāravisesā “eva”nti therena paccāmaṭṭhāti āha “asammohaṃ dīpetī”ti. Nānappakārapaṭivedhasamattho hotīti etena [M 1.0031] vakkhamānassa suttassa nānappakārataṃ duppaṭivijjhatañca dasseti. Sutassa asammosaṃ dīpetīti sutākārassa yāthāvato dassiyamānattā vuttaṃ. Asammohenāti sammohābhāvena, paññāya eva vā savanakālasambhūtāya taduttarakālapaññāsiddhi. Evaṃ asammosenāti etthāpi vattabbaṃ. Byañjanānaṃ paṭivijjhitabbo ākāro nātigambhīro, yathāsutadhāraṇameva tattha karaṇīyanti satiyā byāpāro adhiko, paññā tattha guṇībhūtāti vuttaṃ “paññāpubbaṅgamāyā”tiādi “paññāya pubbaṅgamā”ti katvā. Pubbaṅgamatā cettha padhānatā “manopubbaṅgamā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 1, 2) viya. Pubbaṅgamatāya vā cakkhuviññāṇādīsu āvajjanādīnaṃ viya appadhānatte paññā pubbaṅgamā etissāti ayampi attho yujjati. Evaṃ satipubbaṅgamāyāti etthāpi vuttanayānusārena yathāsambhavamattho veditabbo. Atthabyañjanasampannassāti atthabyañjanaparipuṇṇassa, saṅkāsanapakāsanavivaraṇavibhajanauttānīkaraṇapaññattivasena chahi atthapadehi, akkharapadabyañjanākāraniruttiniddesavasena chahi byañjanapadehi ca samannāgatassāti vā attho daṭṭhabbo.

The meaning is that 'evaṃ' is to be said by way of reviewing the ascertained mode, etc., of the phenomena that have come into the range of hearing, depending on them; and 'me' is to be said depending on the aggregates included in one's own continuity. Although occurring in the sound base, which is devoid of the nature of the seen, etc., the convention 'suta' (heard), like 'second,' 'third,' etc., proceeds only by depending on what is first seen, sensed, and cognized. Thus he says: 'because it is to be spoken by referring to the seen, etc.' For this meaning is disclosed: 'suta' is so called because it is not 'asuta' (unheard). The Elder recalled with 'evaṃ' the special kinds of things in the sutta that he himself had penetrated. Thus he says: 'He reveals non-delusion.' By this is shown the diversity and difficulty of penetration of the sutta to be explained, in that he is capable of penetration in various ways. 'He reveals the non-confusion of what was heard' is said because the mode of what was heard is shown as it really is. 'Without confusion' means by the absence of delusion, or by the wisdom that arose at the time of hearing, which is the accomplishment of wisdom at a later time. The same should be said for 'with non-confusion.' The mode of the phrasing to be penetrated is not very profound; what should be done there is just to retain what was heard. Thus the operation of mindfulness is predominant, and wisdom is secondary. Hence it is said, 'by that which has wisdom as its forerunner,' etc., construing it as 'forerunner by wisdom.' Here, 'forerunner' can mean 'predominant,' as in 'mind is the forerunner,' etc. Or, just as attention, etc., precedes eye-consciousness, etc., in a non-primary role, this meaning is also fitting: 'wisdom is its forerunner.' Similarly, in the case of 'that which has mindfulness as its forerunner,' the meaning should be understood according to what is appropriate, following the method stated. 'Endowed with meaning and phrasing' means complete in meaning and phrasing; or, the meaning should be seen as: endowed with the six items of meaning—concise statement, elucidation, exposition, analysis, making plain, and designation—and with the six items of phrasing—letters, words, phrases, mode, etymology, and specification.

Yonisomanasikāraṃ dīpeti evaṃ-saddena vuccamānānaṃ ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇatthānaṃ aviparītasaddhammavisayattāti adhippāyo. Avikkhepaṃ dīpetīti “mūlapariyāyaṃ kattha bhāsita”ntiādipucchāvasena pakaraṇappattassa vakkhamānassa suttassa savanaṃ samādhānamantarena na sambhavatīti katvā vuttaṃ. Vikkhittacittassātiādi tassevatthassa samatthanavasena vuttaṃ. Sabbasampattiyāti atthabyañjanadesakapayojanādisampattiyā. Aviparītasaddhammavisayehi viya ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇatthehi yonisomanasikārassa, saddhammassavanena viya ca avikkhepassa yathā yonisomanasikārena phalabhūtena attasammāpaṇidhipubbekatapuññatānaṃ siddhi vuttā tadavinābhāvato, evaṃ avikkhepena phalabhūtena kāraṇabhūtānaṃ saddhammassavanasappurisūpanissayānaṃ siddhi dassetabbā siyā assutavato sappurisūpanissayarahitassa ca tadabhāvato. Na hi vikkhittacittotiādinā samatthanavacanena pana avikkhepena kāraṇabhūtena sappurisūpanissayena ca phalabhūtassa saddhammassavanassa siddhi dassitā. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo yutto siyā – saddhammassavanasappurisūpanissayā [V 1.0029] na [M 1.0032] ekantena avikkhepassa kāraṇaṃ bāhiraṅgattā, avikkhepo pana sappurisūpanissayo viya saddhammassavanassa ekantakāraṇanti. Evampi avikkhepena sappurisūpanissayasiddhijotanā na samatthitāva, no na samatthitā vikkhittacittānaṃ sappurisapayirupāsanābhāvassa atthasiddhattā. Ettha ca purimaṃ phalena kāraṇassa siddhidassanaṃ nadīpūrena viya upari vuṭṭhisabbhāvassa, dutiyaṃ kāraṇena phalassa siddhidassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ ekantavassinā viya meghavuṭṭhānena vuṭṭhippavattiyā.

It illuminates wise attention by the word 'thus,' which has the meanings of mode, indication, and ascertainment, because its subject is the undeviating good Dhamma—this is the intention. It illuminates non-distraction thus: because listening to the sutta that is about to be spoken—the subject of the treatise—by way of questions such as, 'Where was the Root Discourse spoken?', is not possible without concentration, it is stated in this way. The phrase 'for one with a distracted mind,' etc., is stated to support this very point. By 'all accomplishment' is meant the accomplishment of meaning, phrasing, teaching, purpose, and so on. Just as the success of right application of oneself and previous merit is stated by means of wise attention, which is the result—because they are inseparable from it—so too, the success of listening to the good Dhamma and reliance on superior persons, which are the causes, should be shown by means of non-distraction, which is the result; for this is absent in one who has not heard the Dhamma and who lacks reliance on superior persons. Indeed, by the supporting statement beginning 'for a distracted mind,' the success of listening to the good Dhamma, which is the result, is shown by means of non-distraction, which is the cause, and by reliance on superior persons. Herein, this might be the proper intention: listening to the good Dhamma and reliance on superior persons are not the exclusive causes of non-distraction, as they are external factors; but non-distraction, like reliance on superior persons, is an exclusive cause of listening to the good Dhamma. Even so, the illumination of the success of reliance on superior persons by means of non-distraction is not fully supported. Yet it is not unsupported, since for those with distracted minds the absence of association with superior persons is established by implication. Herein, the first—the showing of the success of the cause by the result—should be seen like the existence of rain upstream from the flooding of a river. The second—the showing of the success of the result by the cause—should be seen like the occurrence of rain from the rising of a cloud that will definitely rain.

Bhagavato vacanassa atthabyañjanapabhedaparicchedavasena sakalasāsanasampattiogāhanākāro niravasesaparahitapāripūrikāraṇanti vuttaṃ “evaṃ bhaddako ākāro”ti. Yasmā na hotīti sambandho. Pacchimacakkadvayasampattinti attasammāpaṇidhipubbekatapuññatāsaṅkhātaṃ guṇadvayaṃ. Aparāparavuttiyā cettha cakkabhāvo, caranti etehi sattā sampattibhavesūti vā. Ye sandhāya vuttaṃ “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, cakkāni, yehi samannāgatānaṃ devamanussānaṃ catucakkaṃ vattatī”tiādi (a. ni. 4.31). Purimapacchimabhāvo cettha desanākkamavasena daṭṭhabbo. Pacchimacakkadvayasiddhiyāti pacchimacakkadvayassa atthitāya. Sammāpaṇihitatto pubbe ca katapuñño suddhāsayo hoti tadasuddhihetūnaṃ kilesānaṃ dūrībhāvatoti āha – “āsayasuddhi siddhā hotī”ti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “sammāpaṇihitaṃ cittaṃ, seyyaso naṃ tato kare”ti (dha. pa. 43), “katapuññosi tvaṃ ānanda, padhānamanuyuñja, khippaṃ hohisi anāsavo”ti (dī. ni. 2.207) ca. Tenevāha “āsayasuddhiyā adhigamabyattisiddhī”ti. Payogasuddhiyāti yonisomanasikārapubbaṅgamassa dhammassavanapayogassa visadabhāvena. Tathā cāha “āgamabyattisiddhī”ti. Sabbassa vā kāyavacīpayogassa niddosabhāvena. Parisuddhakāyavacīpayogo hi vippaṭisārābhāvato avikkhittacitto pariyattiyaṃ visārado hotīti.

The mode of comprehending the entire accomplishment of the teaching by way of classifying the divisions of meaning and phrasing of the Blessed One’s word is said to be 'thus, a goodly mode,' because it is a cause for the complete fulfillment of others' welfare without remainder. The connection is: 'because it is not.' The accomplishment of the two later wheels means the pair of qualities called right application of oneself and previous merit. Here, their wheel-like nature is due to their successive operation, or because beings fare on to prosperous existences by means of them. In reference to which it is said: 'Monks, there are these four wheels, endowed with which gods and humans cause the four-wheeled vehicle to roll onward,' and so on (AN 4.31). Here, the distinction between earlier and later should be seen according to the sequence of the teaching. By 'the success of the two later wheels' is meant the existence of the two later wheels. One with a rightly directed self and who has previously made merit has a pure disposition, because the defilements that are the cause of its impurity have been removed; thus he says: 'Purity of disposition is accomplished.' For it has been said: 'A rightly directed mind can do one better than that' (Dhp 43), and: 'You have made merit, Ānanda. Apply yourself to striving; you will soon be without taints' (DN 16). Therefore he says: 'Through purity of disposition, the success of proficiency in attainment is achieved.' By 'purity of application' is meant the clarity of the application to listening to the Dhamma, which is preceded by wise attention. And so he says: 'The success of proficiency in the scriptures is achieved.' Or, by the faultlessness of all bodily and verbal application. For one whose bodily and verbal application is pure, being without remorse, has an undistracted mind and becomes skilled in the scriptural learning.

Nānappakārapaṭivedhadīpakenātiādinā atthabyañjanesu therassa evaṃsaddasuta-saddānaṃ asammohāsammosadīpanato catupaṭisambhidāvasena atthayojanaṃ dasseti. Tattha sotabbabhedapaṭivedhadīpakenāti etena ayaṃ suta-saddo evaṃ-saddasannidhānato, vakkhamānāpekkhāya vā sāmaññeneva [M 1.0033] sotabbadhammavisesaṃ āmasatīti dasseti. Manodiṭṭhikaraṇā pariyattidhammānaṃ anupekkhanasuppaṭivedhā visesato manasikārapaṭibaddhāti te vuttanayena yonisomanasikāradīpakena evaṃsaddena yojetvā, savanadhāraṇavacīparicayā pariyattidhammānaṃ visesena sotāvadhānapaṭibaddhāti te avikkhepadīpakena suta-saddena yojetvā dassento sāsanasampattiyā [V 1.0030] dhammassavane ussāhaṃ janeti. Tattha dhammāti pariyattidhammā. Manasānupekkhitāti “idha sīlaṃ kathitaṃ, idha samādhi, idha paññā, ettakā ettha anusandhiyo”tiādinā nayena manasā anu anu pekkhitā. Diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhāti nijjhānakkhantibhūtāya, ñātapariññāsaṅkhātāya vā diṭṭhiyā tattha tattha vuttarūpārūpadhamme “iti rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpa”ntiādinā suṭṭhu vavatthapetvā paṭividdhā.

By the phrase beginning 'by illuminating the various kinds of penetration,' he shows the Elder's application of the meaning of the words 'thus' and 'heard' in terms of the four analytical knowledges, by illuminating non-delusion and non-confusion regarding the meanings and phrasings. Herein, by 'illuminating the penetration of the different things to be heard,' he shows that this word 'heard,' due to its proximity to the word 'thus,' or in expectation of what is to be said, generally refers to the specific qualities of the Dhamma to be heard. Since mental review and thorough penetration by view of the scriptural Dhamma are especially connected with mental application, he connects them with the word 'thus,' which illuminates wise attention in the way stated; and since hearing, retaining, and verbal familiarity with the scriptural Dhamma are especially connected with attentiveness of the ear, he connects them with the word 'heard,' which illuminates non-distraction, thereby generating enthusiasm for listening to the Dhamma for the sake of the accomplishment of the Dispensation. Herein, 'Dhamma' means the scriptural Dhamma. 'Reviewed by the mind' means repeatedly reviewed by the mind in such ways as: 'Here virtue is spoken of, here concentration, here wisdom; so many are the connections here.' 'Thoroughly penetrated by view' means thoroughly penetrated by defining them, by means of a view that is reflective acceptance or that is knowledge as full understanding, with respect to the material and immaterial phenomena spoken of in the various places, in such ways as: 'This is material form, this much is material form.'

Sakalena vacanenāti pubbe tīhi padehi visuṃ visuṃ yojitattā vuttaṃ. Attano adahantoti “mameda”nti attani aṭṭhapento. Asappurisabhūminti akataññutaṃ “idhekacco pāpabhikkhu tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammavinayaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā attano dahatī”ti (pārā. 195) evaṃ vuttaṃ anariyavohārāvatthaṃ, sā eva anariyavohārāvatthā asaddhammo. Nanu ca ānandattherassa “mamedaṃ vacana”nti adhimānassa, mahākassapattherādīnañca tadāsaṅkāya abhāvato asappurisabhūmisamatikkamādivacanaṃ niratthakanti? Nayidamevaṃ “evaṃ me suta”nti vadantena ayampi attho vibhāvitoti dassanato. Keci pana “devatānaṃ parivitakkāpekkhaṃ tathāvacananti edisī codanā anavakāsāvā”ti vadanti. Tasmiṃ kira khaṇe ekaccānaṃ devatānaṃ evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi “bhagavā ca parinibbuto, ayañca āyasmā desanākusalo, idāni dhammaṃ deseti sakyakulappasuto tathāgatassa bhātā cūḷapituputto, kiṃ nu kho sayaṃ sacchikataṃ dhammaṃ deseti, udāhu bhagavatoyeva vacanaṃ yathāsuta”nti. Evaṃ tadāsaṅkitappakārato asappurisabhūmisamokkamādito atikkamādi vibhāvitanti. Appetīti nidasseti. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthesu yathārahaṃ satte netīti netti, dhammoyeva netti dhammanetti.

'By the entire utterance' is said because it was previously connected separately with the three phrases. 'Not attributing it to oneself' means not placing it in oneself as 'this is mine.' 'The plane of the inferior person' means ingratitude, the state of ignoble behavior, as stated thus: 'Here, some evil bhikkhu, having mastered the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, attributes it to himself' (Pārā. 195). That very state of ignoble behavior is the bad Dhamma. But is not the statement about transcending the plane of the inferior person, etc., meaningless, since the Elder Ānanda had no conceit, 'This is my utterance,' and the Elder Mahākassapa and others had no such suspicion? This is not so, because by one who says, 'Thus have I heard,' this meaning too is clarified—this is the explanation. But some say: 'Since the statement was made in consideration of the thoughts of the devas, such a charge is baseless.' For at that moment, it is said, a thought arose in the minds of certain devas thus: 'The Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, and this venerable one is skilled in exposition. Now he teaches the Dhamma—he who was born in the Sakyan clan, the Tathāgata's kinsman, the son of his paternal uncle. Is he teaching a Dhamma he has realized himself, or is it the Blessed One's word just as he heard it?' Thus, the transcending, etc., of the descent into the plane of the inferior person, etc., is clarified in the manner of what was suspected then. 'Applies' means 'shows.' Because it leads beings according to their due in matters concerning the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal, it is a guide (netti). The Dhamma itself is the guide, the Dhamma-guide.

Daḷhataraniviṭṭhā vicikicchā kaṅkhā. Nātisaṃsappanā matibhedamattā vimati. Assaddhiyaṃ vināseti bhagavatā desitattā, sammukhāvassa paṭiggahitattā, khalitaduruttādigahaṇadosābhāvato [M 1.0034] ca. Ettha ca paṭhamādayo tisso atthayojanā ākārādiatthesu aggahitavisesameva evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā dassitā, tato parā catasso ākāratthameva evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā vibhāvitā, pacchimā pana tisso yathākkamaṃ ākāratthaṃ nidassanatthaṃ avadhāraṇatthañca evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā yojitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Doubt (vicikicchā) that is more firmly established is wavering (kaṅkhā). Perplexity (vimati) is not excessive vacillation but a mere difference of opinion. It destroys lack of faith because it was taught by the Blessed One, because it was received in his presence, and because of the absence of the fault of taking up stumbles, misstatements, and so on. Herein, it should be seen that the first three applications of meaning are shown by taking the word 'thus' as referring to the unspecified meanings of mode, etc.; the next four are explained by taking the word 'thus' as having only the meaning of mode; but the last three are connected by taking the word 'thus' as having, respectively, the meaning of mode, the meaning of indication, and the meaning of ascertainment.

Eka-saddo aññaseṭṭhāsahāyasaṅkhyādīsu dissati. Tathā hesa “sassato attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti ittheke abhivadantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.27) aññatthe dissati[V 1.0031], “cetaso ekodibhāva”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.228) seṭṭhatthe, “eko vūpakaṭṭho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.405) asahāye, “ekova kho, bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”tiādīsu saṅkhyāyaṃ. Idhāpi saṅkhyāyanti dassento āha “ekanti gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso”ti. Kālañca samayañcāti yuttakālañca paccayasāmaggiñca khaṇoti okāso. Tathāgatuppādādiko hi maggabrahmacariyassa okāso tappaccayapaṭilābhahetuttā. Khaṇo eva ca samayo. Yo “khaṇo”ti ca “samayo”ti ca vuccati, so ekovāti hi attho mahāsamayoti mahāsamūho. Samayopi khoti sikkhāpadapūraṇassa hetupi. Samayappavādaketi diṭṭhippavādake. Tattha hi nisinnā titthiyā attano attano samayaṃ pavadantīti. Atthābhisamayāti hitapaṭilābhā. Abhisametabboti abhisamayo, abhisamayo attho abhisamayaṭṭhoti pīḷanādīni abhisametabbabhāvena ekībhāvaṃ upanetvā vuttāni. Abhisamayassa vā paṭivedhassa visayabhūto attho abhisamayaṭṭhoti. Tāneva tathā ekattena vuttāni. Tattha pīḷanaṃ dukkhasaccassa taṃsamaṅgino hiṃsanaṃ avipphārikatākaraṇaṃ. Santāpo dukkhadukkhatādivasena santāpanaṃ paridahanaṃ.

The word eka is seen in such senses as other, supreme, without a companion, and number. Thus, it is seen in the sense of 'other' in passages such as: 'The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, anything else is foolish,' some assert thus' (MN 3:27); in the sense of 'supreme' in 'unification of mind' (DN 1:228); in the sense of 'without a companion' in 'alone and secluded' (DN 1:405); and in the sense of 'number' in 'There is, bhikkhus, only one moment and occasion for living the holy life.' Here too, showing that it is in the sense of number, it is said: 'Ekaṃ is an indication of delimitation by counting.' 'Time and occasion' means the right time and the congruence of conditions. 'Moment' (khaṇa) means opportunity. For the arising of the Tathāgata is an opportunity for the path of the holy life because it is a cause for obtaining its conditions. Indeed, a moment (khaṇa) is also an occasion (samaya). What is called both 'moment' and 'occasion' is one and the same—this is the meaning. 'A great occasion' (mahāsamayo) means a great assembly. 'An occasion also' (samayo pi kho) is also a cause for fulfilling the training rules. 'Proclaimers of doctrines' (samayappavādake) refers to proclaimers of views. There, seated, the sectarians proclaim their own respective doctrines. 'Penetration of the goal' (atthābhisamayā) means the attainment of benefit. 'What is to be penetrated' (abhisametabbo) is penetration (abhisamayo); penetration is the meaning; 'the meaning of penetration' (abhisamayaṭṭho)—thus, terms like 'oppression' are used by bringing them together under the single nature of what is to be penetrated. Alternatively, the meaning that is the object of penetration or realization is 'the meaning of penetration.' Those very terms are thus spoken of as unified. Therein, 'oppression' (pīḷana) is the affliction of one who possesses the truth of suffering, the state of being unable to get free. 'Torment' (santāpo) is the scorching, the burning, by way of suffering due to pain, etc.

Tattha sahakārīkāraṇaṃ sannijjhaṃ sameti samavetīti samayo, samavāyo. Sameti samāgacchati maggabrahmacariyaṃ ettha tadādhārapuggalehīti samayo, khaṇo. Sameti ettha, etena vā saṃgacchati satto, sabhāvadhammo vā sahajātādīhi uppādādīhi vāti samayo, kālo. Dhammappavattimattatāya atthato abhūtopi hi kālo dhammappavattiyā adhikaraṇaṃ karaṇaṃ [M 1.0035] viya ca kappanāmattasiddhena rūpena voharīyatīti. Samaṃ, saha vā avayavānaṃ ayanaṃ pavatti avaṭṭhānanti samayo, samūho yathā “samudāyo”ti. Avayavasahāvaṭṭhānameva hi samūhoti. Avasesapaccayānaṃ samāgame eti phalaṃ etasmā uppajjati pavattati cāti samayo, hetu yathā “samudayo”ti. Sameti saṃyojanabhāvato sambandho eti attano visaye pavattati, daḷhaggahaṇabhāvato vā saṃyuttā ayanti pavattanti sattā yathābhinivesaṃ etenāti samayo, diṭṭhi; diṭṭhisaññojanena hi sattā ativiya bajjhantīti. Samiti saṅgati samodhānanti samayo, paṭilābho. Samayanaṃ, sammā vā ayanaṃ apagamoti samayo, pahānaṃ. Abhimukhaṃ ñāṇena sammā etabbo abhisametabboti abhisamayo, dhammānaṃ aviparīto sabhāvo. Abhimukhabhāvena sammā eti gacchati bujjhatīti abhisamayo, dhammānaṃ aviparītasabhāvāvabodho. Evaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ atthe samaya-saddassa pavatti veditabbā. Samayasaddassa atthuddhāre abhisamayasaddassa udāharaṇaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Assāti samayasaddassa[V 1.0032]. Kālo attho samavāyādīnaṃ atthānaṃ idha asambhavato, desadesakaparisānaṃ viya suttassa nidānabhāvena kālassa apadisitabbato ca.

Herein, samaya means concurrence or conglomeration, because a cooperative cause or a conjunction comes together or coincides. It means an occasion or a moment, because the path and the holy life come together here through the persons who are their support. It means time, because a being or a natural phenomenon comes together or coincides here or by this with its co-nascent factors, arising, etc. For although time is in reality non-existent, being merely the occurrence of phenomena, it is spoken of as a basis and an instrument for the occurrence of phenomena, like something established by mere conceptual designation. It means a group, as in 'aggregate,' because there is a balanced or simultaneous going, occurrence, or state of the parts. For a group is just the simultaneous state of the parts. It means a cause, as in 'origin,' because when the remaining conditions come together, the fruit comes, arises, and proceeds from this. It means a view, because a connection comes together in the sense of a fetter, or because it proceeds in its own domain, or because beings, being yoked, go and proceed according to their adherence due to firm grasping. For by the fetter of views, beings are very strongly bound. It means attainment, as it is a coming together, a meeting, a combination. It means abandonment, as it is a quieting, or a right going away, a removal.
