Abhisamayo means penetration, the unperverted true nature of phenomena, because it is to be rightly approached and penetrated face-to-face with knowledge. Abhisamayo also means penetration, the understanding of the unperverted true nature of phenomena, because one rightly goes and understands by way of facing it. Thus the usage of the word samaya should be understood in each respective meaning. In extracting the meaning of the word samaya, the example of the word abhisamaya should be understood in the way already stated. Of this word samaya, the meaning here is 'time,' because the meanings of concurrence, etc., are not possible, and because time must be indicated as the basis of the sutta, like the place, the speaker, and the assembly.

Kasmā panettha aniyamitavaseneva kālo niddiṭṭho, na utusaṃvaccharādivasena niyametvāti? Āha – “tattha kiñcāpī”tiādi. Utusaṃvaccharādivasena niyamaṃ akatvā samayasaddassa vacanena ayampi guṇo laddho hotīti dassento “ye vā ime”tiādimāha. Sāmaññajotanā hi visese avatiṭṭhatīti. Tattha diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo devasikaṃ jhānaphalasamāpattīhi vītināmanakālo, visesato sattasattāhāni. Suppakāsāti dasasahassilokadhātusaṃkampanaobhāsapātubhāvādīhi pākaṭā. Yathāvuttabhedesu eva samayesu ekadesaṃ pakārantarehi saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ “yo cāya”ntiādimāha. Tathā hi ñāṇakiccasamayo attahitapaṭipattisamayo ca abhisambodhisamayo, ariyatuṇhībhāvasamayo diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo, karuṇākiccaparahitapaṭipattidhammikathāsamayo desanāsamayo eva.

Why here is time indicated indefinitely, and not defined by way of seasons, years, and so forth? He says: 'There, although...' etc. Showing that by not making a definition by way of seasons, years, etc., but by using the word 'occasion,' this advantage is also obtained, he says: 'Or these...' etc. For a general indication comes to rest on the particular. Therein, the occasion for blissful abiding in the present life is the time of passing the days with daily attainments of jhāna and fruition, especially the seven weeks. 'Well-manifested' means made evident by the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world-system, the appearance of a radiance, and so on. To show how one part of the aforesaid kinds of occasions can be included under other modes, he says: 'And this...' etc. Thus, the occasion of the task of knowledge and the occasion of practice for one's own welfare is the occasion of full enlightenment. The occasion of noble silence is the occasion of blissful abiding in the present life. The occasion of the task of compassion, of practice for the welfare of others, and of Dhamma talk is the occasion of teaching.

Karaṇavacanena [M 1.0036] niddeso katoti sambandho. Tatthāti abhidhammatadaññasuttapadavinayesu. Tathāti bhummakaraṇehi. Adhikaraṇattho ādhārattho. Bhāvo nāma kiriyā, tāya kiriyantaralakkhaṇaṃ bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ. Tattha yathā kālo sabhāvadhammaparicchinno sayaṃ paramatthato avijjamānopi ādhārabhāvena paññāto taṅkhaṇappavattānaṃ tato pubbe parato ca abhāvato “pubbaṇhe jāto, sāyanhe gacchatī”ti ca ādīsu, samūho ca avayavavinimutto avijjamānopi kappanāmattasiddho avayavānaṃ ādhārabhāvena paññāpīyati “rukkhe sākhā, yavarāsiyaṃ sambhūto”tiādīsu, evaṃ idhāpīti dassento āha “adhikaraṇañhi…pe… dhammāna”nti. Yasmiṃ kāle dhammapuñje vā kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ eva kāle dhammapuñje ca phassādayopi hontīti ayañhi tattha attho. Yathā ca “gāvīsu duyhamānāsu gato, duddhāsu āgato”ti dohanakiriyāya gamanakiriyā lakkhīyati, evaṃ idhāpi “yasmiṃ samaye, tasmiṃ samaye”ti ca vutte “satī”ti ayamattho viññāyamāno eva hoti padatthassa sattāvirahābhāvatoti samayassa sattākiriyāya cittassa uppādakiriyā phassādīnaṃ bhavanakiriyā ca lakkhīyati. Yasmiṃ samayeti yasmiṃ navame khaṇe, yasmiṃ yonisomanasikārādihetumhi, paccayasamavāye vā sati kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃyeva khaṇe, hetumhi, paccayasamavāye vā phassādayopi hontīti ubhayattha samayasadde bhummaniddeso kato lakkhaṇabhūtabhāvayuttoti dassento āha “khaṇa…pe… lakkhīyatī”ti.

The connection is that the indication is made with the instrumental expression. 'Therein' means in the Abhidhamma, the other Sutta texts, and the Vinaya. 'Likewise' means with the locative and instrumental cases. The meaning of 'basis' (adhikaraṇa) is the meaning of 'locus' (ādhāra). 'State' (bhāva) means action; the marking of one action by another is the locative absolute construction. Therein, just as time—which is delimited by natural phenomena and is itself ultimately non-existent—is designated as a basis because of the non-existence of things that occur at that moment before or after it, as in 'he was born in the morning, he goes in the evening'; and just as a collection—which is non-existent apart from its components and is established by mere convention—is designated as a basis for its components, as in 'a branch on a tree,' 'produced in a heap of barley'; so too here, it is shown by saying: 'For the basis... of phenomena.' For this is the meaning there: at whatever time or in whatever collection of phenomena a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, at that very time and in that very collection of phenomena contact and the other mental factors also occur. And just as in 'he went while the cows were being milked; he came after they were milked,' the action of going is marked by the action of milking, so too here, when it is said, 'At what time... at that time...,' the meaning 'when... exists' is understood, because there is no absence of existence in the meaning of the word. Thus, by the action of the occasion's existence, the action of the arising of consciousness and the action of the occurrence of contact and so on are marked. 'At what time' means: when, at the ninth moment, or when there is a cause such as wise attention, or a congruence of conditions, a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, at that very moment, or when that cause or congruence of conditions is present, contact and so on also occur. Showing that in both places the word samaya is indicated in the locative case, being connected with the state that serves as a mark, he says: 'moment... etc. ... is marked.'

Hetuattho [V 1.0033] karaṇattho ca sambhavati “annena vasati, ajjhenena vasati, pharasunā chindati, kudālena khaṇatī”tiādīsu viya. Vītikkamañhi sutvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā otiṇṇavatthukaṃ puggalaṃ paṭipucchitvā vigarahitvā ca taṃ taṃ vatthuṃ otiṇṇakālaṃ anatikkamitvā teneva kālena sikkhāpadāni paññapento bhagavā viharati sikkhāpadapaññattihetuñca apekkhamāno tatiyapārājikādīsu viya.

The meaning of cause and the meaning of instrument are possible, as in such examples as 'he lives by means of food,' 'he lives by means of study,' 'he cuts with an axe,' 'he digs with a spade.' For having heard of a transgression, having had the Saṅgha of bhikkhus assemble, having questioned the person concerning the matter that had occurred, and having rebuked him, the Blessed One lays down the training rules at that very time, without letting the time when that matter occurred pass, and having regard for the reason for laying down the training rule, as in the case of the third pārājika offense and so on.

Accantameva ārambhato paṭṭhāya yāva desanāniṭṭhānaṃ parahitapaṭipattisaṅkhātena karuṇāvihārena. Tadatthajotanatthanti accantasaṃyogatthajotanatthaṃ. Upayogavacananiddeso kato yathā “māsaṃ ajjhetī”ti.

Continuously from the very beginning right up to the conclusion of the discourse, with the abiding in compassion designated as the practice for the welfare of others. 'For the purpose of clarifying that meaning' means for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of continuous connection. The indication is made with an expression of duration, as in 'he studies for a month.'

Porāṇāti [M 1.0037] aṭṭhakathācariyā. Abhilāpamattabhedoti vacanamattena viseso. Tena suttavinayesu vibhattibyattayo katoti dasseti.

'The ancients' means the commentary teachers. 'A difference in mere expression' means a distinction in wording only. By this, he shows that in the Suttas and the Vinaya an interchange of case endings has been made.

Seṭṭhanti seṭṭhavācakaṃ vacanaṃ “seṭṭha”nti vuttaṃ seṭṭhaguṇasahacaraṇato. Tathā uttamanti etthāpi. Gāravayuttoti garubhāvayutto garuguṇayogato, garukaraṇārahatāya vā gāravayutto. Vuttoyeva, na pana idha vattabbo visuddhimaggassa imissā aṭṭhakathāya ekadesabhāvatoti adhippāyo.

'Supreme' (seṭṭhaṃ): a word expressive of supremacy is called 'supreme' because it accompanies the quality of supremacy. Similarly here also with 'highest' (uttamaṃ). 'Connected with gravity' (gāravayutto) means connected with the state of gravity due to its connection with the quality of gravity, or connected with gravity because it is worthy of being respected. The meaning is: it has already been stated and need not be repeated here, since the Visuddhimagga is a part of this commentary.

Aparo nayo (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.1; sārattha. ṭī. 1.vinayānisaṃsakathāvaṇṇanā; visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.144; itivu. aṭṭha. ganthārambhakathā) – bhāgavāti bhagavā, bhatavāti bhagavā, bhāge vanīti bhagavā, bhage vanīti bhagavā, bhattavāti bhagavā, bhage vamīti bhagavā, bhāge vamīti bhagavā.

Another method (as in Saṃyutta Nikāya Ṭīkā 1.1.1; Sārattha Ṭīkā, Vinayānisaṃsa Kathāvaṇṇanā; Visuddhimahāṭīkā 1.144; Itivuttaka Aṭṭhakathā, Ganthārambhakathā): He is Bhagavā because he possessed shares (bhāga). He is Bhagavā because he attended upon (bhatavā). He is Bhagavā because he had desire for shares (bhāge vanī). He is Bhagavā because he had desire for shares (bhāge vanī). He is Bhagavā because he analyzed (bhattavā). He is Bhagavā because he vomited out shares (bhage vamī). He is Bhagavā because he vomited out shares (bhage vamī).

Bhagavā bhatavā bhāge, bhage ca vani bhattavā;

Bhage vami tathā bhāge, vamīti bhagavā jino.

The Victorious One is the Blessed One (Bhagavā) because he possessed shares (bhāga), cultivated (bhatavā), frequented shares (bhāge vani), and broke (bhattavā); and because he rejected shares (bhage vami), therefore the Victorious One is the Blessed One.

Tattha kathaṃ bhāgavāti bhagavā? Ye te sīlādayo dhammakkhandhā guṇabhāgā guṇakoṭṭhāsā, te anaññasādhāraṇā niratisayā tathāgatassa atthi upalabbhanti. Tathā hissa sīlaṃ, samādhi, paññā, vimutti, vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ, hirī, ottappaṃ, saddhā, vīriyaṃ, sati sampajaññaṃ, sīlavisuddhi, diṭṭhivisuddhi, samatho, vipassanā, tīṇi kusalamūlāni, tīṇi sucaritāni, tayo [V 1.0034] sammāvitakkā, tisso anavajjasaññā, tisso dhātuyo, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāro sammappadhānā, cattāro iddhipādā, cattāro ariyamaggā, cattāri ariyaphalāni, catasso paṭisambhidā, catuyonipaṭicchedakañāṇaṃ, cattāro ariyavaṃsā, cattāri vesārajjañāṇāni, pañca padhāniyaṅgāni, pañcaṅgiko sammāsamādhi, pañcañāṇiko sammāsamādhi, pañcindriyāni, pañca balāni, pañca nissāraṇīyā dhātuyo, pañca vimuttāyatanañāṇāni, pañca vimuttiparipācanīyā saññā, cha anussatiṭṭhānāni, cha gāravā, cha nissāraṇīyā dhātuyo, cha satatavihārā, cha anuttariyāni, cha nibbedhabhāgiyā saññā, cha abhiññā, cha asādhāraṇañāṇāni, satta aparihāniyā dhammā, satta ariyadhammā, satta ariyadhanāni, satta bojjhaṅgā, satta sappurisadhammā, satta nijjaravatthūni, satta [M 1.0038] saññā, satta dakkhiṇeyyapuggaladesanā, satta khīṇāsavabaladesanā, aṭṭha paññāpaṭilābhahetudesanā, aṭṭha sammattāni, aṭṭha lokadhammātikkamā, aṭṭha ārambhavatthūni, aṭṭha akkhaṇadesanā, aṭṭha mahāpurisavitakkā, aṭṭha abhibhāyatanadesanā, aṭṭha vimokkhā, nava yonisomanasikāramūlakā dhammā, nava pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgāni, nava sattāvāsadesanā, nava āghātapaṭivinayā, nava saññā, nava nānattā, nava anupubbavihārā, dasa nāthakaraṇā dhammā, dasa kasiṇāyatanāni, dasa kusalakammapathā, dasa sammattāni, dasa ariyavāsā, dasa asekkhadhammā, dasa tathāgatabalāni, ekādasa mettānisaṃsā, dvādasa dhammacakkākārā, terasa dhutaguṇā, cuddasa buddhañāṇāni, pañcadasa vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā, soḷasavidhā ānāpānassati, soḷasa aparantapanīyā dhammā, aṭṭhārasa buddhadhammā, ekūnavīsati paccavekkhaṇañāṇāni, catucattālīsa ñāṇavatthūni, paññāsa udayabbayañāṇāni, paropaṇṇāsa kusaladhammā, sattasattati ñāṇavatthūni, catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhāsamāpattisañcārimahāvajirañāṇaṃ, anantanayasamantapaṭṭhānapavicayapaccavekkhaṇadesanāñāṇāni tathā anantāsu lokadhātūsu anantānaṃ sattānaṃ āsayādivibhāvanañāṇāni cāti evamādayo anantāparimāṇabhedā anaññasādhāraṇā niratisayā guṇabhāgā guṇakoṭṭhāsā saṃvijjanti upalabbhanti, tasmā yathāvuttavibhāgā guṇabhāgā assa atthīti “bhāgavā”ti vattabbe ā-kārassa rassattaṃ katvā “bhagavā”ti vutto. Evaṃ tāva bhāgavāti bhagavā.

Herein, how is the Blessed One 'Bhagavā' because he possesses shares? Those aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue, the portions of excellence, the divisions of excellence—these are unique, unsurpassed, and found in the Tathāgata. For indeed, his virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, knowledge and vision of liberation, moral shame, moral dread, faith, energy, mindfulness, clear comprehension, purity of virtue, purity of view, serenity, insight, the three wholesome roots, the three good conducts, the three right thoughts, the three blameless perceptions, the three elements, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases of spiritual power, the four noble paths, the four noble fruits, the four analytical knowledges, the knowledge that severs the four kinds of birth, the four noble lineages, the four kinds of confidence, the five factors of striving, the five-factored right concentration, the five-knowledge right concentration, the five faculties, the five powers, the five elements of escape, the five knowledges of the bases of liberation, the five perceptions that ripen for liberation, the six objects of recollection, the six respects, the six elements of escape, the six constant abidings, the six unsurpassable things, the six perceptions pertaining to penetration, the six direct knowledges, the six kinds of uncommon knowledge, the seven factors of non-decline, the seven noble qualities, the seven noble treasures, the seven factors of enlightenment, the seven qualities of a superior person, the seven grounds for wearing away, the seven perceptions, the seven teachings on persons worthy of offerings, the seven teachings on the powers of one whose taints are destroyed, the eight teachings on the causes for acquiring wisdom, the eight rightnesses, the eight transcendences of worldly conditions, the eight grounds for exertion, the eight teachings on inopportune moments, the eight thoughts of a great man, the eight teachings on the bases of mastery, the eight liberations, the nine states rooted in wise attention, the nine factors of striving for purity, the nine teachings on the abodes of beings, the nine methods for dispelling resentment, the nine perceptions, the nine diversities, the nine successive abidings, the ten qualities that give protection, the ten kasiṇa bases, the ten wholesome courses of action, the ten rightnesses, the ten noble abodes, the ten qualities of one beyond training, the ten powers of the Tathāgata, the eleven benefits of loving-kindness, the twelve aspects of the Wheel of Dhamma, the thirteen ascetic qualities, the fourteen knowledges of a Buddha, the fifteen qualities that ripen for liberation, the sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing, the sixteen qualities that do not lead to later remorse, the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, the nineteen reviewing knowledges, the forty-four bases of knowledge, the fifty knowledges of arising and passing away, the fifty-nine wholesome qualities, the seventy-seven bases of knowledge, the great diamond-like knowledge that traverses the attainments numbering twenty-four hundred thousand koṭis, the knowledges for teaching involving the reviewing and investigation of the Conditional Relations with its infinite methods, and the knowledges for discerning the dispositions and so forth of infinite beings in infinite world-systems—thus, these and other countless, immeasurable, unique, unsurpassed portions and divisions of excellence exist and are found in him. Therefore, because he possesses these portions of excellence as described, though it should be said 'Bhāgavā,' by shortening the long vowel 'ā' to 'a,' he is called 'Bhagavā.' Thus, indeed, the Blessed One is 'Bhagavā' because he possesses shares.

Yasmā sīlādayo sabbe, guṇabhāgā asesato;

Vijjanti sugate tasmā, bhagavāti pavuccatīti.

Since all the portions of excellence, such as virtue, exist completely in the Well-Gone One, therefore he is called the Blessed One.

Kathaṃ bhatavāti bhagavā? Ye te sabbalokahitāya ussukkamāpannehi manussattādike aṭṭha dhamme [V 1.0035] samodhānetvā sammāsambodhiyā katamahābhinīhārehi mahābodhisattehi paripūritabbā dānapāramī, sīla, nekkhamma, paññā, vīriya, khanti, sacca, adhiṭṭhāna, mettā, upekkhāpāramīti dasa pāramiyo dasa upapāramiyo dasa paramatthapāramiyoti samatiṃsa pāramiyo, dānādīni cattāri saṅgahavatthūni, saccādīni cattāri adhiṭṭhānāni, aṅgapariccāgo nayanadhanarajjaputtadārapariccāgoti pañca mahāparicāgā, pubbayogo, pubbacariyā, dhammakkhānaṃ, ñātatthacariyā, lokatthacariyā, buddhicariyāti [M 1.0039] evamādayo, saṅkhepato vā sabbe puññañāṇasambhārā buddhakaradhammā, te mahābhinīhārato paṭṭhāya kappānaṃ satasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkheyyāni yathā hānabhāgiyā saṃkilesabhāgiyā ṭhitibhāgiyā vā na honti, atha kho uttaruttari visesabhāgiyāva honti, evaṃ sakkaccaṃ nirantaraṃ anavasesato bhatā sambhatā assa atthīti “bhatavā”ti vattabbe “bhagavā”ti vutto niruttinayena ta-kārassa ga-kāraṃ katvā. Atha vā bhatavāti teyeva yathāvutte buddhakaradhamme vuttanayeneva bhari sambhari, paripūresīti attho. Evampi bhatavāti bhagavā.

How is the Blessed One 'Bhatavā'? There are qualities that make one a Buddha to be fulfilled by great bodhisattvas who, striving for the welfare of all the world and having combined the eight factors beginning with the human state, have made the great aspiration for perfect enlightenment. These qualities are: the ten perfections—generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity—which become thirty as the ten perfections, ten subsidiary perfections, and ten ultimate perfections; the four bases of beneficence such as giving; the four resolutions such as truthfulness; the five great sacrifices—the sacrifice of limbs, eyes, wealth, kingdom, and children and wife; previous application, previous conduct, teaching the Dhamma, conduct for the welfare of kinsmen, conduct for the welfare of the world, and conduct for the sake of awakening; in brief, all the accumulations of merit and knowledge. From the time of the great aspiration, for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more, these qualities were not of a kind that leads to decline, defilement, or stagnation, but rather to ever higher distinction. Thus, they were borne (bhatā) and accumulated (sambhatā) by him diligently, continuously, and completely. Therefore, while it should be said 'Bhatavā,' by a rule of etymology the 't' is changed to 'g,' making it 'Bhagavā.' Alternatively, 'bhatavā' means that he bore (bhari), accumulated (sambhari), and fulfilled (paripūresi) those very Buddha-making qualities in the way described. In this way too, 'Bhatavā' is 'Bhagavā'.

Sammāsambodhiyā sabbe, dānapāramiādike;

Sambhāre bhatavā nātho, tenāpi bhagavā matoti.

For the sake of perfect enlightenment, the Lord accumulated all the requisites, beginning with the perfection of giving; for that reason too he is considered the Blessed One.

Kathaṃ bhāge vanīti bhagavā? Ye te catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhā devasikaṃ vaḷañjanakasamāpattibhāgā, te anavasesato lokahitatthaṃ attano ca diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāratthaṃ niccakappaṃ vani bhaji sevi bahulamakāsīti bhāge vanīti bhagavā. Atha vā abhiññeyyadhammesu kusalādīsu khandhādīsu ca ye te pariññeyyādivasena saṅkhepato vā catubbidhā abhisamayabhāgā, vitthārato pana “cakkhu pariññeyyaṃ sotaṃ…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ pariññeyya”ntiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.21) aneke pariññeyyabhāgā, “cakkhussa samudayo pahātabbo…pe… jarāmaraṇassa samudayo pahātabbo”tiādinā pahātabbabhāgā, “cakkhussa nirodho…pe… jarāmaraṇassa nirodho sacchikātabbo”tiādinā sacchikātabbabhāgā, “cakkhussa nirodhagāminī paṭipadā”tiādinā, “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādinā ca anekabhedā bhāvetabbabhāgā ca dhammā, te sabbe vani bhaji yathārahaṃ gocarabhāvanāsevanānaṃ vasena sevi. Evampi bhāge vanīti bhagavā. Atha vā “ye ime sīlādayo dhammakkhandhā sāvakehi sādhāraṇā guṇabhāgā guṇakoṭṭhāsā, kinti nu kho te vineyyasantānesu patiṭṭhapeyya”nti mahākaruṇāya vani abhipatthayi, sā cassa abhipatthanā yathādhippetaphalāvahā ahosi. Evampi bhāge vanīti bhagavā.

How is the Blessed One one who 'frequented shares' (bhāge vani)? For the welfare of the world and for his own blissful abiding in this very life, he constantly and completely frequented, served, and made much of the shares of attainment for daily use, which number twenty-four hundred thousand koṭis. Thus he is one who 'frequented shares.' Or, concerning the things to be directly known, such as wholesome states and the aggregates, there are the shares of realization, which are briefly fourfold. In detail, there are many shares to be fully understood, such as: "The eye is to be fully understood, the ear… aging-and-death is to be fully understood," etc.; many shares to be abandoned, such as: "The origin of the eye is to be abandoned… the origin of aging-and-death is to be abandoned," etc.; many shares to be realized, such as: "The cessation of the eye… the cessation of aging-and-death is to be realized," etc.; and many shares to be developed, such as: "The path leading to the cessation of the eye," etc., and "the four foundations of mindfulness," etc. All these he frequented (vani, bhaji, sevi) as appropriate, by way of resort, development, and service. In this way too, he is one who 'frequented shares.' Or, with great compassion, he desired (vani, abhipatthayi): "How might I establish these qualities—the aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue, the shared portions of excellence—in the mental continuities of those to be trained?" And that aspiration of his bore the fruit he had intended. In this way too, he is one who 'frequented shares.'

Yasmā [V 1.0036] ñeyyasamāpattiguṇabhāge asesato;

Bhaji patthayi sattānaṃ, hitāya bhagavā tatoti.

Because the Blessed One completely partook of the shares of things to be known, of attainments, and of qualities, and desired the welfare of beings, therefore he is the Blessed One.

Kathaṃ [M 1.0040] bhage vanīti bhagavā? Samāsato tāva katapuññehi payogasampannehi yathāvibhavaṃ bhajīyantīti bhagā, lokiyalokuttarā sampattiyo. Tattha lokiye tāva tathāgato sambodhito pubbe bodhisattabhūto paramukkaṃsagate vani bhaji sevi, yattha patiṭṭhāya niravasesato buddhakaradhamme samannānento buddhadhamme paripācesi, buddhabhūto pana te niravajjasukhūpasaṃhite anaññasādhāraṇe lokuttarepi vani bhaji sevi, vitthārato pana padesarajjaissariyacakkavattisampatti-devarajjasampattiādivasena- jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattiñāṇadassana-maggabhāvanāphalasacchi- kiriyādi-uttarimanussadhammavasena ca anekavihite anaññasādhāraṇe bhage vani bhaji sevi. Evampi bhage vanīti bhagavā.

How is the Blessed One one who 'partook of portions' (bhage vani)? In brief, worldly and supramundane attainments are called 'portions' (bhagā) because they are partaken of (bhajīyanti) by those who have made merit and are endowed with diligence, according to their ability. Therein, in the worldly sphere, the Tathāgata, before his enlightenment while still a bodhisattva, partook of and cultivated the most excellent portions. Established in these, while bringing the Buddha-making qualities to perfection without remainder, he matured them. Having become a Buddha, he partook of and cultivated the faultless, blissful, and incomparable supramundane portions. In detail, he partook of and cultivated many kinds of incomparable portions: worldly portions such as regional kingship, universal sovereignty, and divine kingship; and supramundane portions, which are higher human states, such as jhāna, liberation, concentration, attainments, knowledge and vision, development of the path, and realization of the fruit. Thus, he is one who 'partook of portions.'

Yā tā sampattiyo loke, yā ca lokuttarā puthu;

Sabbā tā bhaji sambuddho, tasmāpi bhagavā matoti.

Whatever attainments exist in the world, and the many that are supramundane, the Perfectly Enlightened One partook of them all; therefore he is also considered the Blessed One.

Kathaṃ bhattavāti bhagavā? Bhattā daḷhabhattikā assa bahū atthīti bhattavā. Tathāgato hi mahākaruṇāsabbaññutaññāṇādiaparimitanirupamapabhāvaguṇavisesasamaṅgibhāvato sabbasattuttamo, sabbānatthaparihārapubbaṅgamāya niravasesahitasukhavidhānatapparāya niratisayāya payogasampattiyā sadevamanussāya pajāya accantūpakāritāya dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇa-asītianubyañjana-byāmappabhādianaññasādhāraṇa- visesapaṭimaṇḍita-rūpakāyatāya yathābhucca-guṇādhigatena “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinayappavattena lokattayabyāpinā suvipulena suvisuddhena ca thutighosena samannāgatattā ukkaṃsapāramippattāsu appicchatāsantuṭṭhiādīsu suppatiṭṭhitabhāvato dasabalacatuvesārajjādiniratisayaguṇavisesa-samaṅgibhāvato ca rūpappamāṇo rūpappasanno, ghosappamāṇo ghosappasanno, lūkhappamāṇo lūkhappasanno, dhammappamāṇo dhammappasannoti evaṃ catuppamāṇike lokasannivāse sabbathāpi pasādāvahabhāvena samantapāsādikattā aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ sadevamanussānaṃ ādarabahumānagāravāyatanatāya paramapemasambhattiṭṭhānaṃ. Ye tassa ovāde patiṭṭhitā aveccappasādena samannāgatā honti, kenaci asaṃhāriyā tesaṃ pasādabhatti samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā. Tathā hi te attano jīvitapariccāgepi tattha pasādaṃ na pariccajanti, tassa vā āṇaṃ daḷhabhattibhāvato. Tenevāha –

How is Bhagavā derived from bhattavā (one who has devotees)? He is called bhattavā because he has many devotees (bhattā) with firm devotion. For the Tathāgata is the foremost of all beings because he possesses great compassion, omniscience, and other immeasurable, incomparable, and supreme qualities; because through his unsurpassed accomplishment in practice he is ever intent on providing complete welfare and happiness, preceded by the removal of all that is unbeneficial, and is thus an utmost benefactor to the world with its gods and humans; because his physical body is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-long aura, and other unique special features; because he is endowed with a very extensive and pure sound of praise, pervading the three worlds, which proceeds in the manner of “Thus is the Blessed One…” and which is acquired through his qualities as they really are; because he is well established in qualities that have reached the peak of perfection, such as fewness of wishes and contentment; and because he possesses the ten powers, the four kinds of confidence, and other unsurpassed special qualities. Thus, in the fourfold measure of the world, he is one who is measured by form and pleases by form, who is measured by voice and pleases by voice, who is measured by austerity and pleases by austerity, and who is measured by the Dhamma and pleases by the Dhamma. Being in every way confidence-inspiring and lovely to behold, he is a basis for the reverence, high esteem, respect, and supreme love and devotion of countless beings, gods, and humans. The faith and devotion of those who are established in his instruction and endowed with confirmed confidence is unshakeable by any ascetic or brahmin, by any deva, Māra, or Brahmā. For they would not abandon their confidence in him even at the cost of their own lives, nor his command, because of their firm devotion. Therefore it is said:

“Yo [V 1.0037][M 1.0041] ve kataññū katavedi dhīro;

Kalyāṇamitto daḷhabhatti ca hotī”ti. (jā. 2.17.78);

“One who is grateful and acknowledges what is done, the wise one, a good friend, and one of firm devotion.” (Jā 2.17.78)

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahāsamuddo ṭhitadhammo velaṃ nātivattati, evameva kho, bhikkhave, yaṃ mayā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, taṃ mama sāvakā jīvitahetupi nātikkamantī”ti (a. ni. 8.20; udā. 45; cūḷava. 385) ca.

“Just as, bhikkhus, the great ocean is of a stable nature and does not transgress its boundary, so too, bhikkhus, whatever training rule has been laid down by me for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their lives.” (AN 8.20; Ud 5.5; Cv V.3.2)

Evaṃ bhattavāti bhagavā niruttinayena ekassa ta-kārassa lopaṃ katvā itarassa ga-kāraṃ katvā.

Thus, by the etymological method, Bhagavā is formed from bhattavā by eliding one letter ‘t’ and changing the other to a ‘g’.

Guṇātisayayuttassa, yasmā lokahitesino;

Sambhattā bahavo satthu, bhagavā tena vuccatīti.

Because he is endowed with surpassing virtues, and because he seeks the world’s welfare, many are the Teacher’s devotees; therefore he is called Bhagavā.

Kathaṃ bhage vamīti bhagavā? Yasmā tathāgato bodhisattabhūtopi purimāsu jātīsu pāramiyo pūrento bhagasaṅkhātaṃ siriṃ issariyaṃ yasañca vami, uggiri, kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya anapekkho chaḍḍayi; pacchimattabhāvepi hatthāgataṃ cakkavattisiriṃ devalokādhipaccasadisaṃ catudīpissariyaṃ cakkavattisampattisannissayaṃ sattaratanasamujjalaṃ yasañca tiṇāyapi amaññamāno nirapekkho pahāya abhinikkhamitvā sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho, tasmā ime siriādike bhage vamīti bhagavā. Atha vā bhāni nāma nakkhattāni, tehi samaṃ gacchanti pavattantīti bhagā, sineruyugandharauttarakuruhimavantādibhājanalokavisesasannissayā sobhā kappaṭṭhiyabhāvato, tepi bhage vami tannivāsisattāvāsasamatikkamanato, tappaṭibaddhachandarāgapahānena pajahīti. Evampi bhage vamīti bhagavā.

How is Bhagavā derived from ‘he abandoned fortunes’? Because the Tathāgata, even when he was a bodhisatta in previous births fulfilling the perfections, vomited out, spat out, and abandoned without attachment—like a lump of phlegm—the glory, sovereignty, and fame designated as ‘fortunes’ (bhaga). And in his final existence, not esteeming it even as much as a blade of grass, he relinquished without attachment the glory of a wheel-turning monarch that had come into his hands—a sovereignty over the four continents comparable to the lordship of the deva world, radiant with the seven treasures and fame—and went forth, having awakened to perfect self-awakening. Therefore, because he abandoned these fortunes such as glory, he is Bhagavā. Alternatively, bhāni are the constellations. Things that proceed along with them are called bhagā (portions), that is, the splendor dependent on the special receptacle worlds such as Sineru, Yugandhara, Uttarakuru, and the Himālaya, which last for an eon. He abandoned those portions too by transcending the abodes of the beings who dwell there; he forsook them by abandoning the desire and lust connected with them. In this way too, he is Bhagavā because he abandoned the portions.

Cakkavattisiriṃ yasmā, yasaṃ issariyaṃ sukhaṃ;

Pahāsi lokacittañca, sugato bhagavā tatoti.

Since the Well-farer abandoned the glory of a wheel-turning monarch, fame, sovereignty, happiness, and the worldly mind, therefore he is the Bhagavā.

Kathaṃ bhāge vamīti bhagavā? Bhāgā nāma sabhāgadhammakoṭṭhāsā, te khandhāyatanadhātādivasena, tatthāpi rūpavedanādivasena, pathaviyādiatītādivasena ca anekavidhā. Te bhagavā sabbaṃ papañcaṃ sabbaṃ yogaṃ sabbaṃ ganthaṃ sabbaṃ saṃyojanaṃ samucchinditvā amataṃ dhātuṃ samadhigacchanto vami uggiri, anapekkho chaḍḍayi na paccāgami. Tathā hesa “sabbatthameva pathaviṃ [V 1.0038] āpaṃ [M 1.0042] tejaṃ vāyaṃ, cakkhuṃ sotaṃ ghānaṃ jivhaṃ kāyaṃ manaṃ, rūpe sadde gandhe rase phoṭṭhabbe dhamme, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ…pe… manoviññāṇaṃ, cakkhusamphassaṃ…pe… manosamphassaṃ, cakkhusamphassajaṃ vedanaṃ…pe… manosamphassajaṃ vedanaṃ, cakkhusamphassajaṃ saññaṃ…pe… manosamphassajaṃ saññaṃ, cakkhusamphassajaṃ cetanaṃ…pe… manosamphassajaṃ cetanaṃ, rūpataṇhaṃ…pe… dhammataṇhaṃ, rūpavitakkaṃ…pe… dhammavitakkaṃ, rūpavicāraṃ…pe… dhammavicāra”ntiādinā anupadadhammavibhāgavasenapi sabbeva dhammakoṭṭhāse anavasesato vami uggiri, anapekkhapariccāgena chaḍḍayi. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ “yaṃ taṃ, ānanda, cattaṃ vantaṃ muttaṃ pahīnaṃ paṭinissaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ tathāgato puna paccāgamissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.183). Evampi bhāge vamīti bhagavā. Atha vā bhāge vamīti sabbepi kusalākusale sāvajjānavajje hīnapaṇīte kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāge dhamme ariyamaggañāṇamukhena vami uggiri anapekkho pariccaji pajahi, paresañca tathattāya dhammaṃ desesi. Vuttampi cetaṃ “dhammāpi vo, bhikkhave, pahātabbā, pageva adhammā (ma. ni. 1.240), kullūpamaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desessāmi nittharaṇatthāya, no gahaṇatthāyā”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.240). Evampi bhāge vamīti bhagavā.

How is Bhagavā derived from ‘he vomited out the portions’? ‘Portions’ means the divisions of related phenomena, which are of many kinds by way of the aggregates, sense bases, elements, etc., and also by way of form, feeling, etc., and by way of earth, etc., past, etc. Having cut off all proliferation, all yokes, all bonds, and all fetters, while attaining the deathless element, the Blessed One vomited them out, spat them out, abandoned them without attachment, and did not return to them. Thus, by way of the detailed analysis of phenomena step by step, he vomited out and spat out without remainder all the divisions of phenomena—earth, water, fire, air; eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind; forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, mental phenomena; eye-consciousness… mind-consciousness; eye-contact… mind-contact; feeling born of eye-contact… feeling born of mind-contact; perception born of eye-contact… perception born of mind-contact; volition born of eye-contact… volition born of mind-contact; craving for forms… craving for mental phenomena; thought on forms… thought on mental phenomena; examination of forms… examination of mental phenomena. He abandoned them by way of relinquishment without attachment. For it is said: “Ānanda, that the Tathāgata would return to what has been given up, vomited out, released, abandoned, and relinquished—this is impossible” (DN 16). In this way too, he is Bhagavā because he vomited out the portions. Alternatively, ‘he vomited out the portions’ means that by means of the knowledge of the noble path, he vomited out, spat out, relinquished without attachment, and forsook all dhammas—wholesome and unwholesome, blameable and blameless, inferior and superior, the dark and the bright with their counterparts. And he taught the Dhamma to others so that they too could become thus. For this too is said: “Bhikkhus, you should abandon even dhammas, how much more so non-dhammas” (MN 22); and “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma compared to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping” (MN 22). In this way too, he is Bhagavā because he vomited out the portions.

Khandhāyatanadhātādi-dhammabhāgāmahesinā;

Kaṇhasukkā yato vantā, tatopi bhagavā matoti.

Since the dark and the bright portions of phenomena—the aggregates, bases, elements, and so on—have been vomited up by the Great Sage, for that reason too he is considered Bhagavā.

Tena vuttaṃ –

Thus it is said:

“Bhāgavā bhatavā bhāge, bhage ca vani bhattavā;

Bhage vami tathā bhāge, vamīti bhagavā jino”ti.

“He analyzed the portions; he partook of fortunes and had devotees; he vomited forth fortunes, and likewise the portions he vomited; thus the Conqueror is Bhagavā.”

Dhammasarīraṃ paccakkhaṃ karotīti “yo vo, ānanda, mayā dhammo ca vinayo ca desito paññatto, so vo mamaccayena satthā”ti (dī. ni. 2.216) vacanato dhammassa satthubhāvapariyāyo vijjatīti katvā vuttaṃ. Vajirasaṅghātasamānakāyo parehi abhejjasarīrattā. Na hi bhagavato rūpakāye kenaci sakkā antarāyo kātunti.

Because he directly realizes the Dhamma-body, it is said: “Ānanda, the Dhamma and the Vinaya that I have taught and laid down for you will be your teacher after I am gone” (DN 16). It is said thus because there is a sense in which the Dhamma is the Teacher. His body is like a mass of diamond because his body is unbreakable by others. For no one is able to cause harm to the Blessed One’s physical body.

Desanāsampattiṃ niddisati vakkhamānassa sakalassa suttassa “eva”nti nidassanato. Sāvakasampattiṃ niddisati paṭisambhidāppattena pañcasu ṭhānesu bhagavatā etadagge ṭhapitena mayā mahāsāvakena [V 1.0039] sutaṃ, tañca kho mayāva [M 1.0043] sutaṃ, na anussutikaṃ, na paramparābhatanti imassa atthassa dīpanato. Kālasampattiṃ niddisati bhagavā-saddasannidhāne payuttassa samaya-saddassa kālassa buddhuppādapaṭimaṇḍitabhāvadīpanato. Buddhuppādaparamā hi kālasampadā. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

The accomplishment of the teaching is indicated by the word “thus,” which points to the entire sutta that is about to be spoken. The accomplishment of the audience is indicated by its showing that “it was heard by me,” a great disciple who had attained the analytical knowledges and had been placed by the Blessed One as the foremost in five respects; and that “it was heard by me myself,” not as a report, not as a tradition. The accomplishment of time is indicated by the word “time,” used in connection with the word “Blessed One,” because this shows that the time was adorned by the arising of a Buddha. For the supreme accomplishment of time is the arising of a Buddha. Therefore it is said:

“Kappakasāye kaliyuge, buddhuppādo aho mahacchariyaṃ;

Hutāvahamajjhe jātaṃ, samuditamakarandamaravinda”nti. (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.1; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.1; a. ni. ṭī. 1.1.1 rūpādivaggavaṇṇanā);

“In the dregs of the eon, in the age of strife, the arising of a Buddha is a great wonder! It is like a lotus with abundant nectar born in the midst of a sacrificial fire.”

Bhagavāti desakasampattiṃ niddisati guṇavisiṭṭhasattuttamagarugāravādhivacanabhāvato.

The word “Bhagavā” indicates the accomplishment of the teacher, because it is an epithet for the foremost being, who is distinguished by virtue, venerable, and worthy of respect.

Maṅgaladivaso sukhaṇo sunakkhattanti ajja maṅgaladivaso, tasmā sunakkhattaṃ, tatthāpi ayaṃ sukhaṇo. Mā atikkamīti mā rattivibhāyanaṃ anudikkhantānaṃ ratti atikkamīti evaṃ sambandho veditabbo. Ukkāsu ṭhitāsu ṭhitāti ukkaṭṭhā (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.255; a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.36). Ukkāsu vijjotalantīsu ṭhitā patiṭṭhitāti mūlavibhūjādipakkhepena (pāṇini 3.2.5) saddasiddhi veditabbā. Niruttinayena vā ukkāsu ṭhitāsu ṭhitā āsīti ukkaṭṭhā. Apare pana bhaṇanti “bhūmibhāgasampattiyā manussasampattiyā upakaraṇasampattiyā ca sā nagarī ukkaṭṭhaguṇayogato ‘ukkaṭṭhā’ti nāmaṃ labhī”ti.

“An auspicious day, a fortunate moment, a good constellation” means: today is an auspicious day, therefore it is a good constellation, and within that this is a fortunate moment. “Let it not pass by” means: let not the night pass by for those who are looking towards the dawn; this is how the connection should be understood. Ukkaṭṭhā means “established (ṭhitā) while torches (ukkāsu) are held up (ṭhitāsu)” (DN-ṭ 1.255; AN-ṭ 2.4.36). The word formation should be understood by the affixation of the mūlavibhujādi group (Pāṇini 3.2.5) to mean ‘established while torches are blazing.’ Or, by the etymological method, ‘it was established while torches were held up,’ hence Ukkaṭṭhā. But others say: “That city obtained the name ‘Ukkaṭṭhā’ from its connection with superior qualities (ukkaṭṭhaguṇa), due to the excellence of its land, its people, and its provisions.”

Avisesenāti na visesena, vihārabhāvasāmaññenāti attho. Iriyāpatha…pe… vihāresūti iriyāpathavihāro dibbavihāro brahmavihāro ariyavihāroti etesu catūsu vihāresu. Samaṅgiparidīpananti samaṅgībhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Etanti “viharatī”ti etaṃ padaṃ. Tathā hi taṃ “idhekacco gihīhi saṃsaṭṭho viharati sahanandī sahasokī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.241) iriyāpathavihāre āgataṃ; “yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 160; vibha. 624) dibbavihāre; “so mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.556; 3.308; ma. ni. 1.77; 2.309; 3.230) brahmavihāre; “so kho ahaṃ aggivessana tassāyeva kathāya pariyosāne tasmiṃ eva purimasmiṃ samādhinimitte ajjhattameva [V 1.0040][M 1.0044] cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi sannisādemi ekodiṃ karomi samādahāmi, yena sudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.387) ariyavihāre.

Not by a distinction: that is, not in a special way; the meaning is by the commonality of the state of dwelling. Postures... in dwellings: in these four dwellings, namely, the dwelling of posture, the divine dwelling, the brahma-dwelling, and the noble dwelling. The explanation of being endowed: this is the explanation of the state of being endowed. This: this is the word 'dwells.' For it is found in the dwelling of posture in such passages as: 'Here, some person dwells associating with householders, sharing their joys and sorrows'; in the divine dwelling in such passages as: 'At the time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures... having entered the first jhāna, dwells therein'; in the brahma-dwelling in such passages as: 'He dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness'; and in the noble dwelling in such passages as: 'Then, Aggivessana, at the conclusion of that very talk, I steadied my mind internally on that very same preliminary sign of concentration, settled it, unified it, and concentrated it, by which I dwell for the most part.'

Tattha iriyanaṃ vattanaṃ iriyā, kāyappayogo. Tassā pavattanupāyabhāvato ṭhānādi iriyāpatho. Ṭhānasamaṅgī vā hi kāyena kiñci kareyya gamanādīsu aññatarasamaṅgī vā. Atha vā iriyati pavattati etena attabhāvo, kāyakiccaṃ vāti iriyā, tassā pavattiyā upāyabhāvato pathoti iriyāpatho, ṭhānādi eva. So ca atthato gatinivattiādiākārena pavatto catusantatirūpapabandho eva. Viharaṇaṃ, viharati etenāti vā vihāro, iriyāpatho eva vihāro iriyāpathavihāro. Divi bhavoti dibbo. Tattha bahulappavattiyā brahmapārisajjādidevaloke bhavoti attho. Tattha yo dibbānubhāvo, tadatthāya saṃvattatīti vā dibbo, abhiññābhinīhāravasena mahāgatikattā vā dibbo, dibbo ca so vihāro cāti dibbavihāro, catasso rūpāvacarasamāpattiyo. Āruppasamāpattiyopi ettheva saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Brahmūnaṃ, brahmāno vā vihārā brahmavihārā, catasso appamaññāyo. Ariyānaṃ, ariyā vā vihārā ariyavihārā, cattāri sāmaññaphalāni. So hi bhagavā ekaṃ iriyāpathabādhanantiādi yadipi bhagavā ekenapi iriyāpathena cirataraṃ kālaṃ attabhāvaṃ pavattetuṃ sakkoti, tathāpi “upādinnakasarīrassa nāma ayaṃ sabhāvo”ti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā vā bhagavā yattha katthaci vasanto veneyyānaṃ dhammaṃ desento, nānāsamāpattīhi ca kālaṃ vītināmento vasatīti veneyyasattānaṃ attano ca vividhaṃ hitasukhaṃ harati upaneti uppādeti, tasmā vividhaṃ haratīti evamettha attho veditabbo.

Herein, the act of moving or functioning is called iriyā, which is the application of the body. Because it is the means for movement to occur, standing and other postures are called iriyāpatha. One endowed with standing might perform some action with the body, or be endowed with one of the other movements such as walking. Alternatively, iriyā is that by which the individual existence moves or functions, or it is bodily activity; because it is the means (patha) for its occurrence, it is iriyāpatha, that is, standing, etc. In essence, this is the continuous series of the fourfold material continuity, proceeding in modes such as moving and stopping. Dwelling (viharaṇaṃ), or 'one dwells by this,' is a dwelling (vihāro); the posture itself is a dwelling, hence iriyāpathavihāro, the dwelling of posture. 'Divine' (dibba) means 'being in heaven' (divi bhava). Here, the meaning is 'being in the divine world of Brahmā’s retinue, etc.,' because of its frequent occurrence there. Alternatively, it is 'divine' because it conduces to divine power, or because it is a great going attained through direct knowledge and aspiration. Thus, the divine dwelling (dibbavihāro) refers to the four attainments of the form sphere. The formless attainments are also included here. The dwellings of the brahmās, or the brahma-dwellings (brahmavihārā), are the four illimitables. The dwellings of the noble ones, or the noble dwellings (ariyavihārā), are the four fruits of recluseship. Indeed, the Blessed One, even if afflicted by a single posture, could sustain his bodily existence for a very long time; yet, it is said to illustrate that 'this is the nature of a body sustained by clinging.' Alternatively, because the Blessed One, dwelling anywhere, teaching the Dhamma to those who can be trained and spending time in various meditative attainments, brings and generates various kinds of welfare and happiness for both himself and those who can be trained, the meaning here should be understood as 'he brings in various ways' (vividhaṃ harati).

Subhagattāti sirīkāmānavasena sobhanattā. Tenevāha “sundarasirikattā sundarakāmattā cā”ti. Chaṇasamajjaussaveti ettha chaṇaṃ nāma phaggunamāsādīsu uttaraphaggunādi-abhilakkhitadivasesu saparijanānaṃ manussānaṃ maṅgalakaraṇaṃ. Samajjaṃ nāma naṭasamajjādi. Ussavo nakkhattaṃ. Yattha gāmanigamavāsino tayo satta vā divase nakkhattaghosanaṃ katvā yathāvibhavaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattā bhoge paribhuñjantā nakkhattakīḷanaṃ [M 1.0045] kīḷanti. Tesaṃ taṃ tatheva hotīti tesaṃ manussānaṃ taṃ patthanaṃ tannivāsidevatānubhāvena yebhuyyena tatheva hoti, patthanā samijjhatīti attho. Bahujanakantatāyāti iminā “sundarakāmattā”ti etasseva padassa pakārantarena atthaṃ vibhāveti. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – kamanīyaṭṭhena suṭṭhu bhajīyatīti subhagaṃ, subhā agā rukkhā etthāti vā subhagaṃ, sundarakittiyogato vā “subhaga”nti evampettha atthaṃ vaṇṇenti. Keci pana “subhāgavane”ti paṭhanti, “sundarabhūmibhāge [V 1.0041] vane”ti cassa atthaṃ vadanti. Subhagassa nāma yakkhassa vanaṃ tena pariggahitattāti “subhagavana”nti aññe. Vananaṃ bhattītiatthe taṃ vananaṃ kāretīti etasmiṃ atthe vanayatīti padasiddhi veditabbā. Tenevāha “attani sinehaṃ uppādetī”ti. Yācanatthe vanute iti vananti upacārakappanāvasena vana-saddo veditabbo.

Because it is fortunate (subhagattā): because it is beautiful (sobhanattā) by way of splendor (sirī) and desirability (kāmana). Hence it is said: 'because of beautiful splendor and beautiful desirability.' In the phrase 'festivals, fairs, and celebrations' (chaṇasamajjaussave): here, a 'festival' (chaṇa) is the performance of auspicious rites by people with their families on days marked by the Uttaraphaggunī asterism and others in the month of Phagguna and so on. A 'fair' (samajja) is a theatrical show and the like. A 'celebration' (ussavo) is a holiday related to an asterism (nakkhattaṃ). It is where the inhabitants of villages and towns, having announced the holiday for three or seven days, enjoy their wealth according to their means, adorned and prepared, and engage in holiday games. For them, it is just so: the meaning is that the aspiration of those people is for the most part fulfilled just so by the power of the deities dwelling there; their aspiration succeeds. Because it is dear to many people (bahujanakantatāya): by this, he clarifies the meaning of the phrase 'because of beautiful desirability' in another way. Here, this is the word-meaning: it is 'fortunate' (subhagaṃ) because it is well-frequented, being desirable; or it is 'fortunate' because there are beautiful houses or trees here; or it is called 'fortunate' from its connection with beautiful fame. Thus the meaning is explained here. Some, however, read it as subhāgavane and state its meaning as 'in a beautiful region of the forest.' Others say it is 'Subhaga's Grove' (subhagavana) because it is the grove possessed by a yakkha named Subhaga. The derivation of the word vanayati should be understood in the sense of 'he causes that desiring,' where desiring (vananaṃ) is in the sense of devotion. Hence it is said: 'It generates affection in oneself.' The word vana should be understood as a metaphorical application in the sense of requesting, from vanute, 'he requests.'

Ujuvaṃsāti ujubhūtaviṭapā. Mahāsālāti mahārukkhā. Aññatarasmiṃ sālamūleti aññatarassa rukkhassa mūle. Vanappatijeṭṭhakarukkhoti vanappatibhūto jeṭṭhakarukkho. Tameva jeṭṭhakabhāvanti vanappatibhāvenāgataṃ seṭṭhabhāvaṃ padhānabhāvaṃ. Tena hi so “sālarājā”ti vutto. Upagatānaṃ rañjanaṭṭhena rājā, aññasmimpi tādise rukkhe rājavohāraṃ dassetuṃ “supatiṭṭhitassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha brāhmaṇa dhammikāti ālapanaṃ. Nippariyāyena sākhādimato saṅghātassa suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhane avayavavisese pavattamāno mūla-saddo. Yasmā taṃsadisesu tannissaye padese ca ruḷhīvasena pariyāyato pavattati, tasmā “mūlāni uddhareyyā”ti ettha nippariyāyamūlaṃ adhippetanti ekena mūla-saddena visesetvā āha “mūlamūle dissatī”ti yathā “dukkhadukkhaṃ (saṃ. ni. 4.327), rūparūpa”nti (visuddhi. 2.449) ca. Asādhāraṇahetumhīti asādhāraṇakāraṇe. Lobhasahagatacittuppādānaṃ eva āveṇike nesaṃ suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanato mūlaṭṭhena upakārake paccayadhamme dissatīti attho.

Upright bamboos: those with upright branches. Great sāla trees: great trees. At the root of a certain sāla tree: at the root of a certain tree. The chief tree, a lord of the forest: the chief tree that is a lord of the forest. That very state of being chief: the state of being best, the state of being principal, that comes with being a lord of the forest. Therefore it is called the 'king of sāla trees.' It is a king (rājā) in the sense of delighting (rañjana) those who approach it. To show the royal designation for another such tree as well, 'well-established,' etc., is said. Herein, 'Brahmin, righteous one' is a term of address. The word 'root' occurs in its primary sense for a specific part that establishes the well-established nature of the aggregate possessing branches and so on. Because it also occurs by extension through convention in reference to things similar to it and to the region dependent on it, therefore, to indicate that 'one should uproot the roots' here refers to the root in the primary sense, he specifies it with the single word 'root' and says, 'it is seen in the root of the root,' just as in 'the suffering in suffering' and 'the form in form.' Because of an uncommon cause: because of an uncommon reason. The meaning is: it is seen in a supporting condition that has the sense of a root because it establishes the well-established nature peculiar to the arisings of mind accompanied by greed.

Tatthāti “ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ viharati subhagavane sālarājamūle”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ vākyaṃ, tatta. Siyāti kassaci evaṃ parivitakko siyā, vakkhamānākārena kadāci codeyya vāti attho. Atha tattha viharatīti yadi subhagavane sālarājamūle viharati. Na vattabbanti nānāṭhānabhūtattā [M 1.0046] ukkaṭṭhāsubhagavanānaṃ, ekaṃ samayanti ca vuttattāti adhippāyo. Idāni codako tameva attano adhippāyaṃ “na hi sakkā”tiādinā vivarati. Itaro sabbametaṃ aviparītaṃ atthaṃ ajānantena vuttanti dassento “na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabba”nti āha. Tattha etanti “ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ viharati subhagavane sālarājamūle”ti etaṃ vacanaṃ. Evanti “yadi tāva bhagavā”tiādinā yaṃ taṃ bhavatā coditaṃ, taṃ atthato evaṃ na kho pana daṭṭhabbaṃ, na ubhayattha apubbaacarimaṃ vihāradassanatthanti attho.

Herein refers to the statement, 'At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhaga Grove at the root of the king of sāla trees.' There might be: someone might think thus; the meaning is that one might occasionally raise an objection in the manner to be described. Then, 'if he dwells there' means if he dwells at the root of the king of sāla trees in the Subhaga Grove. It should not be said: the intention is that this should not be said because Ukkaṭṭhā and the Subhaga Grove are different locations, and because 'at one time' is stated. Now, the objector explains his own intention with 'for it is not possible,' etc. The other, showing that all this has been said by one who does not know the undistorted meaning, says, 'But this should not be seen thus.' Here, 'this' refers to the statement, 'dwelling at Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhaga Grove at the root of the king of sāla trees.' 'Thus' means: that which was objected to by you with 'if indeed the Blessed One,' etc., should not be seen thus in meaning; it is not for the purpose of showing a dwelling in both places without precedence or sequence. That is the meaning.

Idāni attano yathādhippetaṃ aviparītaṃ atthaṃ, tassa ca paṭikacceva vuttabhāvaṃ, tena ca appaṭividdhattaṃ pakāsento “nanu avocumha…pe… sālarājamūle”ti āha. Evampi “subhagavane [V 1.0042] sālarājamūle viharatī”cceva vattabbaṃ, na “ukkaṭṭhāya”nti codanaṃ manasi katvā vuttaṃ “gocaragāmanidassanattha”ntiādi.

Now, clarifying his own intended, undistorted meaning, and showing that it had been stated in advance but not understood by the objector, he said: 'Did we not say... up to 'at the root of the king of sāla trees'?' Bearing in mind the objection that even so, one should say only, 'He dwells in the Subhaga Grove at the root of the king of sāla trees,' and not 'at Ukkaṭṭhā,' it was said: 'for the purpose of indicating the resort village,' and so on.

Avassaṃ cettha gocaragāmakittanaṃ kātabbaṃ. Tathā hi taṃ yathā subhagavanādikittanaṃ pabbajitānuggahakaraṇādianekappayojanaṃ, evaṃ gahaṭṭhānuggahakaraṇādivividhappayojananti dassento “ukkaṭṭhākittanenā”tiādimāha. Tattha paccayaggahaṇena upasaṅkamanapayirupāsanānaṃ okāsadānena dhammadesanāya saraṇesu sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāpanena yathūpanissayaṃ uparivisesādhigamāvahanena ca gahaṭṭhānaggahakaraṇaṃ, uggahaparipucchānaṃ kammaṭṭhānānuyogassa ca anurūpavasanaṭṭhānapariggahenettha pabbajitānuggahakaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Karuṇāya upagamanaṃ, na lābhādinimittaṃ, paññāya apagamanaṃ, na virodhādinimittanti upagamanāpagamanānaṃ nirupakkilesataṃ vibhāveti. Dhammikasukhaṃ nāma anavajjasukhaṃ. Devānaṃ upakārabahulatā janavivittatāya. Pacurajanavivittaṃ hi ṭhānaṃ devā upasaṅkamitabbaṃ maññanti. Tadatthaparinipphādananti lokatthanipphādanaṃ, buddhakiccasampādananti attho. Evamādināti ādi-saddena ukkaṭṭhākittanato rūpakāyassa anuggaṇhanaṃ dasseti, subhagavanādikittanato dhammakāyassa. Tathā purimena parādhīnakiriyākaraṇaṃ, dutiyena attādhīnakiriyākaraṇaṃ. Purimena vā karuṇākiccaṃ, itarena paññākiccaṃ. Purimena cassa paramāya anukampāya samannāgamaṃ, pacchimena paramāya upekkhāya samannāgamaṃ [M 1.0047] dīpeti. Bhagavā hi sabbasatte paramāya anukampāya anukampati, na ca tattha sinehadosānupatito paramupekkhakabhāvato, upekkhako ca na ca parahitasukhakaraṇe apposukko mahākāruṇikabhāvato.

Here, the praise of the village for alms-resort must certainly be made. For just as the praise of the Subhaga Grove and so on has many purposes, such as the support of the renunciants, so too, it serves various purposes such as the support of householders. To show this, he said, 'by the praise of Ukkaṭṭhā,' and so on. Herein, the support of householders is to be understood as giving them the opportunity to approach, attend, and serve by the acceptance of requisites, by the teaching of the Dhamma, by establishing them in the refuges and precepts, and by leading them to the attainment of higher distinctions according to their supporting conditions. The support of the renunciants is to be understood as the acceptance of a suitable dwelling for study, inquiry, and application to a meditation subject. Approaching out of compassion, not for the sake of gain, and departing through wisdom, not on account of conflict—this clarifies the purity of his coming and going. 'Righteous happiness' is blameless happiness. The great helpfulness of the deities is due to seclusion from the populace, for deities consider a place secluded from many people as worthy of approach. 'Fulfilling that purpose' means fulfilling the world's welfare; the meaning is fulfilling the Buddha's duty. By 'and so on,' with the word 'ādi,' it shows the support of the form-body through the praise of Ukkaṭṭhā, and of the Dhamma-body through the praise of the Subhaga Grove and so on. Thus, the former shows the performance of actions dependent on others, the latter the performance of actions dependent on oneself. Or, the former is the work of compassion, the latter the work of wisdom. The former reveals his possession of supreme compassion, the latter his possession of supreme equanimity. For the Blessed One has compassion for all beings with supreme compassion, yet he is not attached by the flaw of affection because of his state of supreme equanimity; and he is equanimous, yet not indolent in bringing about the welfare and happiness of others because of his state of great compassion.

Tassa mahākāruṇikatāya lokanāthatā, upekkhakatāya attanāthatā. Tathā hesa bodhisattabhūto mahākaruṇāya sañcoditamānaso sakalalokahitāya ussukkamāpanno mahābhinīhārato paṭṭhāya tadatthanipphādanatthaṃ puññañāṇasambhāre sampādento aparimitaṃ kālaṃ anappakaṃ dukkhamanubhosi, upekkhakatāya sammā patitehi dukkhehi na vikampi. Tathā mahākāruṇikatāya saṃsārābhimukhatā, upekkhakatāya tato nibbindanā. Tathā upekkhakatāya nibbānābhimukhatā, mahākāruṇikatāya tadadhigamo. Tathā mahākāruṇikatāya paresaṃ abhiṃsāpanaṃ, upekkhakatāya sayaṃ parehi abhāyanaṃ. Mahākāruṇikatāya paraṃ rakkhato attano rakkhaṇaṃ, upekkhakatāya attānaṃ rakkhato paresaṃ rakkhaṇaṃ. Tenassa attahitāya paṭipannādīsu catutthapuggalabhāvo siddho hoti. Tathā mahākāruṇikatāya saccādhiṭṭhānassa cāgādhiṭṭhānassa ca pāripūri, upekkhakatāya upasamādhiṭṭhānassa paññādhiṭṭhānassa ca pāripūri. Evaṃ parisuddhāsayapayogassa [V 1.0043] mahākāruṇikatāya lokahitatthameva rajjasampadādibhavasampattiyā upagamanaṃ, upekkhakatāya tiṇāyapi amaññamānassa tato apagamanaṃ. Iti suvisuddhaupagamāpagamassa mahākāruṇikatāya lokahitatthameva dānavasena sampattīnaṃ pariccajanā, upekkhakatāya cassa phalassa attano apaccāsīsanā. Evaṃ samudāgamanato paṭṭhāya acchariyabbhutaguṇasamannāgatassa mahākāruṇikatāya paresaṃ hitasukhatthaṃ atidukkarakāritā, upekkhakatāya kāyampi analaṃkāritā.

Through his great compassion he is the protector of the world; through his equanimity he is his own protector. For as a bodhisatta, with his mind stirred by great compassion, he strove for the welfare of the entire world. From his great aspiration onwards, in order to fulfill that purpose, he accumulated the stores of merit and wisdom and experienced no little suffering for an immeasurable period of time, yet through his equanimity he was not shaken by the suffering that befell him in due course. Thus, through great compassion there was an inclination towards saṃsāra; through equanimity, revulsion towards it. Thus, through equanimity there was an inclination towards Nibbāna; through great compassion, its attainment. Thus, through great compassion he does not cause injury to others; through equanimity he himself does not fear others. Through great compassion, in protecting others he protects himself; through equanimity, in protecting himself he protects others. Thereby the state of the fourth person—one who is practicing for his own welfare and for the welfare of others—is established for him. Thus, through great compassion there is the fulfillment of the determination of truth and the determination of generosity; through equanimity, the fulfillment of the determination of tranquility and the determination of wisdom. Thus, for one of pure intention and application, through great compassion he takes up sovereignty and other worldly prosperity only for the welfare of the world; through equanimity, not considering them even as a blade of grass, he departs from them. Thus, for one of utterly pure approach and departure, through great compassion he relinquishes his possessions by way of giving for the welfare of the world; through equanimity, he does not expect the fruit for himself. Thus, from its very arising, being endowed with marvelous and astonishing qualities, through great compassion he performs extremely difficult deeds for the welfare and happiness of others; through equanimity, he does not even adorn his body.

Tathā mahākāruṇikatāya carimattabhāve jiṇṇāturamatadassanena sañjātasaṃvego, upekkhakatāya uḷāresu devabhogasadisesu bhogesu nirapekkho mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhami. Tathā mahākāruṇikatāya “kicchaṃ vatāyaṃ loko āpanno”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.57; saṃ. ni. 2.4, 10) karuṇāmukheneva vipassanārambho[M 1.0048], upekkhakatāya buddhabhūtassa satta sattāhāni vivekasukheneva vītināmanaṃ. Mahākāruṇikatāya dhammagambhīrataṃ paccavekkhitvā dhammadesanāya apposukkataṃ āpajjitvāpi mahābrahmuno ajjhesanāpadesena okāsakaraṇaṃ, upekkhakatāya pañcavaggiyādi veneyyānaṃ ananurūpasamudācārepi anaññathābhāvo. Mahākāruṇikatāya katthaci paṭighātābhāvenassa sabbattha amittasaññāya abhāvo, upekkhakatāya katthacipi anurodhābhāvena sabbattha sinehasanthavābhāvo. Mahākāruṇikatāya gāmādīnaṃ āsannaṭṭhāne vasantassapi upekkhakatāya araññaṭṭhāne eva viharaṇaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “purimena cassa paramāya annukampāya samannāgamaṃ, pacchimena paramāya upekkhāya samannāgamaṃ dīpetī”ti.

Thus, through great compassion, in his final existence, a sense of urgency arose in him at the sight of the old, the sick, and the dead; through equanimity, indifferent to magnificent enjoyments similar to those of the devas, he went forth in the Great Renunciation. Thus, through great compassion, the beginning of his insight meditation was by way of compassion, with the thought, 'Alas, this world has fallen into trouble!' and so on; through equanimity, having become a Buddha, he spent seven weeks solely in the bliss of seclusion. Through great compassion, having reflected on the profundity of the Dhamma, although he became disinclined to teach, he made an opportunity on the pretext of the great Brahmā's request; through equanimity, there was no alteration in him even at the unsuitable conduct of the group of five and other disciples to be trained. Through great compassion, because he had no aversion towards anything, he had no perception of an enemy anywhere; through equanimity, because he had no partiality towards anything, he had no affection or intimacy anywhere. Through great compassion, though he dwelt in a place near villages and so on, through equanimity, he dwelt only in the forest. Therefore it was said: 'The former reveals his possession of supreme compassion, the latter his possession of supreme equanimity.'

Tanti “tatrā”ti padaṃ. Desakālaparidīpananti ye desakālā idha viharaṇakiriyāvisesanabhāvena vuttā, tesaṃ paridīpananti dassento “yaṃ samayaṃ…pe… dīpetī”ti āha. Taṃ-saddo hi vuttassa atthassa paṭiniddeso, tasmā idha kālassa, desassa vā paṭiniddeso bhavituṃ arahati, na aññassa. Ayaṃ tāva tatra-saddassa paṭiniddesabhāve atthavibhāvanā. Yasmā pana īdisesu ṭhānesu tatra-saddo dhammadesanāvisiṭṭhaṃ desaṃ kālañca vibhāveti, tasmā vuttaṃ “bhāsitabbayutte vā desakāle dīpetī”ti. Tena tatrāti yattha bhagavā dhammadesanatthaṃ bhikkhū ālapi abhāsi, tādise dese, kāle vāti attho. Na hītiādinā tamevatthaṃ samattheti. Nanu ca yattha ṭhito bhagavā “akālo kho tāvā”tiādinā bāhiyassa dhammadesanaṃ paṭikkhipi, tattheva antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhito tassa dhammaṃ desetīti? Saccametaṃ, adesetabbakāle adesanāya idaṃ udāharaṇaṃ. Tenevāha “akālo kho tāvā”ti. Yaṃ pana tattha vuttaṃ [V 1.0044] “antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhamhā”ti (udā. 10), tampi tassa akālabhāvasseva pariyāyena dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tassa hi tadā addhānaparissamena rūpakāye akammaññatā ahosi, balavapītivegena nāmakāye, tadubhayassa vūpasamaṃ āgamento papañcaparihāratthaṃ bhagavā “akālo kho”ti pariyāyena paṭikkhipi. Adesetabbadese adesanāya pana udāharaṇaṃ “atha kho bhagavā maggā okkamma aññatarasmiṃ [M 1.0049] rukkhamūle nisīdi (saṃ. ni. 2.154), vihārato nikkhamitvā vihārapacchāyāyaṃ paññatte āsane nisīdī”ti (dī. ni. 1.363) ca evamādikaṃ idha ādi-saddena saṅgahitaṃ.

The word is 'tatra.' To show that 'indicating the place and time' means indicating those places and times that are stated here as a qualification of the act of dwelling, he said, 'at what time... he indicates.' The word 'taṃ' indeed is a reference to what has been said. Therefore, here it can be a reference to the time or the place, not to anything else. This, firstly, is the explanation of the meaning of the word 'tatra' in its referential sense. But since in such instances the word 'tatra' clarifies the place and time qualified by the Dhamma teaching, it was said, 'or he indicates the place and time suitable for speaking.' Thus 'tatra' means: in such a place, or at such a time, where the Blessed One addressed and spoke to the bhikkhus for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. By 'For not...' etc., he supports this very meaning. But is it not the case that where the Blessed One was standing when he rejected Bāhiya's request for a Dhamma teaching, saying, 'It is not the time now,' he taught him the Dhamma while standing right there in the middle of the street? This is true. This is an example of not teaching at an unsuitable time. That is why he said, 'It is not the time now.' And what was said there, 'We have entered among the houses,' was also said to show indirectly that it was an unsuitable time. For at that time, due to the fatigue of the journey, his physical body was unwieldy, and his mental body was so due to the strong impulse of joy. Awaiting the subsiding of both, the Blessed One rejected him indirectly with the words, 'It is not the time,' in order to avoid proliferation. But an example of not teaching in an unsuitable place is included here by the word 'ādi' (etc.), such as: 'Then the Blessed One, having left the road, sat down at the foot of a certain tree,' and 'having left the monastery, he sat down on a prepared seat in the shade of the monastery.'

“Atha kho so, bhikkhave, bālo idha pubbe rasādo idha pāpāni kammāni karitvā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.251) padapūraṇamatte kho-saddo, “dukkhaṃ kho agāravo viharati appatisso”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.21) avadhāraṇe, “kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso, satthu pavivittassa viharato sāvakā vivekaṃ nānusikkhantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.31) ādikālatthe. Vākyārambheti attho. Tattha padapūraṇena vacanālaṅkāramattaṃ kataṃ hoti, ādikālatthena vākyassa upaññāsamattaṃ, avadhāratthena pana niyamadassanaṃ, tasmā āmantesi evāti āmantane niyamo dassito hotīti.

In such passages as, 'Then, bhikkhus, that fool, having formerly been a glutton here, having done evil deeds here…,' the word 'kho' is a mere expletive. In such passages as, 'Indeed, one dwells in suffering without reverence, without deference…,' it is for emphasis. In such passages as, 'To what extent, friends, when the Teacher is dwelling in seclusion, do the disciples not train in conformity with that seclusion?...' it has the sense of 'at the beginning.' The meaning is the start of a sentence. Therein, by being an expletive, it serves merely as a verbal ornament; by having the sense of 'at the beginning,' it is a mere introduction to the sentence; but by being emphatic, it shows a restriction. Therefore, by 'he addressed,' a restriction is shown in the addressing, which implies, 'he certainly addressed them.'

“Bhagavāti lokagarudīpana”nti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu pubbepi bhagavā-saddassa attho vuttoti? Yadipi pubbe vutto, taṃ panassa yathāvutte ṭhāne viharaṇakiriyāya kattuvisesadassanatthaṃ kataṃ, na āmantanakiriyāya, idha pana āmantanakiriyāya, tasmā tadatthaṃ puna “bhagavā”ti pāḷiyaṃ vuttanti tassatthaṃ dassetuṃ “bhagavāti lokagarudīpana”nti āha. Kathāsavanayuttapuggalavacananti vakkhamānāya mūlapariyāyadesanāya savanayogyapuggalavacanaṃ. Catūsupi parisāsu bhikkhū eva edisānaṃ desanānaṃ visesena bhājanabhūtā, iti sātisayasāsanasampaṭiggāhakabhāvadassanatthaṃ idha bhikkhugahaṇanti dassetvā idāni saddatthaṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādimāha.

Why is it said, 'The word "Blessed One" indicates the Teacher of the world'? Was not the meaning of the word 'Blessed One' already explained before? Although it was explained before, that was to show the distinction of the agent in the act of dwelling in the described state, not for the purpose of address. Here, however, it is for the purpose of address. Therefore, to show that meaning, the word 'Bhagavā' is used again in the Pāli, and to clarify its meaning, it is said, 'The word "Blessed One" indicates the Teacher of the world.' 'A statement for a person fit to hear the talk'—this refers to a statement for a person suitable to hear the forthcoming Discourse on the Root of All Things. Among the four assemblies, monks are the special recipients of such teachings. Thus, to show their superior status as receivers of the Teaching, the word 'monks' is used here. Now, to explain the meaning of the word, it begins with 'Moreover,' etc.

Tattha bhikkhakoti bhikkhūti bhikkhanadhammatāya bhikkhūti attho. Bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti buddhādīhipi ajjhupagataṃ bhikkhācariyaṃ uñchācariyaṃ ajjhupagatattā anuṭṭhitattā bhikkhū. Yo hi koci appaṃ vā mahantaṃ vā bhogakkhandhaṃ pahāya agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito, so kasigorakkhādīhi jīvikākappanaṃ hitvā liṅgasampaṭicchaneneva bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatattā bhikkhu, parapaṭibaddhajīvikattā vā vihāramajjhe kājabhattaṃ bhuñjamānopi bhikkhācariyaṃ [V 1.0045] ajjhupagatoti bhikkhu, piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ nissāya pabbajjāya ussāhajātattā vā bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti bhikkhūti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Ādinā nayenāti “bhinnapaṭadharoti bhikkhu, bhindati pāpake akusale dhammeti bhikkhu, bhinnattā [M 1.0050] pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhikkhū”tiādinā vibhaṅge (vibha. 510) āgatanayena. Ñāpaneti avabodhane, paṭivedaneti attho.

Herein, 'bhikkhu' means one who begs; he is a bhikkhu because of the nature of begging. 'One who has undertaken the practice of alms-seeking': he is a bhikkhu because he has undertaken and practices the alms-round and gleaning, a practice undertaken even by the Buddha and others. For whoever, having abandoned a small or great mass of wealth, has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, and having given up making a living by such means as agriculture and cattle-herding, is a bhikkhu simply by having accepted the insignia and undertaken the practice of alms-seeking. Or, because his livelihood is dependent on others, even one who eats food provided in the monastery is a bhikkhu because he has undertaken the practice of alms-seeking. Or, because enthusiasm for the going forth arises in dependence on alms-food, he is a bhikkhu because he has undertaken the practice of alms-seeking. Thus the meaning here should be understood. 'By the method beginning with...' refers to the method that comes in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh 510), beginning: 'A bhikkhu is one who wears a torn robe,' 'a bhikkhu is one who breaks down evil, unwholesome qualities,' 'because of the breaking down of evil, unwholesome qualities, he is a bhikkhu,' and so on. 'Making known' (ñāpana) means causing to understand, that is, penetration (paṭivedana).

Bhikkhanasīlatātiādīsu bhikkhanasīlatā bhikkhanena ājīvanasīlatā, na kasivaṇijjādīhi ājīvanasīlatā. Bhikkhanadhammatā “uddissa ariyā tiṭṭhantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 153; mi. pa. 4.5.9) evaṃ vuttabhikkhanasabhāvatā, na sambhāvanākohaññasabhāvatā. Bhikkhane sādhukāritā “uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyyā”ti (dha. pa. 168) vacanaṃ anussaritvā tattha appamajjanā. Atha vā sīlaṃ nāma pakatisabhāvo, idha pana tadadhiṭṭhānaṃ. Dhammoti vataṃ. Apare pana “sīlaṃ nāma vatasamādānaṃ, dhammo nāma paveṇīāgataṃ cārittaṃ, sādhukāritāti sakkaccakāritā ādarakiriyā”ti vaṇṇenti. Hīnādhikajanasevitanti ye bhikkhubhāve ṭhitāpi jātimadādivasena uddhatā unnaḷā. Ye ca gihibhāve paresu atthikabhāvampi anupagatatāya bhikkhācariyaṃ paramakāpaññataṃ maññanti, tesaṃ ubhayesampi yathākkamaṃ “bhikkhavo”ti vacanena hīnajanehi daliddehi paramakāpaññataṃ pattehi parakulesu bhikkhācariyāya jīvikaṃ kappentehi sevitaṃ vuttiṃ pakāsento uddhatabhāvaniggahaṃ karoti, adhikajanehi uḷārabhogakhattiyakulādito pabbajitehi buddhādīhi ājīvavisodhanatthaṃ sevitaṃ vuttiṃ pakāsento dīnabhāvaniggahaṃ karotīti yojetabbaṃ. Yasmā “bhikkhavo”ti vacanaṃ āmantanabhāvato abhimukhīkaraṇaṃ, pakaraṇato sāmatthiyato ca sussūsājananaṃ sakkaccasavanamanasikāraniyojanañca hoti. Tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “bhikkhavoti iminā”tiādimāha.

In such phrases as 'the habit of begging' (bhikkhanasīlatā), this term means the habit of living by begging, not the habit of living by agriculture, trade, and so on. 'The nature of begging' (bhikkhanadhammatā) is the nature of begging as spoken of thus: 'The noble ones stand with a purpose' (Paṭis I 153; Mil 4.5.9), not the nature of expectation and hypocrisy. 'Acting well in begging' (bhikkhane sādhukāritā) is non-negligence in it, remembering the saying, 'One should rise up and not be negligent' (Dhp 168). Alternatively, sīla is natural disposition, but here it is the resolve for it. Dhamma is the observance. Others, however, explain: 'Sīla is the undertaking of an observance, dhamma is traditional conduct, and sādhukāritā is acting carefully, an act of respect.' 'Practiced by lowly and superior people': This should be construed as follows. With the word 'bhikkhus,' in regard to those who, though established in the state of a bhikkhu, are arrogant and proud on account of birth and so on, he restrains their arrogance by pointing to a practice followed by lowly people—the poor, those reduced to extreme destitution, who make their living by the alms-round among other families. And in regard to those who, in the lay state, did not even have to ask others for anything and thus consider the alms-round to be the utmost misery, he restrains their dejection by pointing to a practice followed by superior people for the purification of livelihood—those gone forth from eminent, wealthy khattiya families, such as the Buddha and others. Because the word 'bhikkhus,' being an address, brings them face to face, and by the power of the context, it generates a desire to listen and enjoins careful listening and attention, he stated 'By this word "bhikkhus"...' and so on, to show this meaning.

Tattha sādhukasavanamanasikāreti sādhukasavane sādhukamanasikāre ca. Kathaṃ pana pavattitā savanādayo sādhukaṃ pavattitā hontīti? “Addhā imāya sammāpaṭipattiyā sakalasāsanasampatti hatthagatā bhavissatī”ti ādaragāravayogena, kathādīsu aparibhavanādinā ca. Vuttaṃ hi “pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato suṇanto saddhammaṃ bhabbo niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattaṃ. Katamehi pañcahi? Na kathaṃ paribhoti, na kathikaṃ paribhoti, na attānaṃ paribhoti, avikkhittacitto dhammaṃ suṇāti ekaggacitto, yoniso ca manasi karoti. Imehi kho, bhikkhave[M 1.0051], pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato suṇanto saddhammaṃ bhabbo niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ [V 1.0046] kusalesu dhammesu sammatta”nti (a. ni. 5.151). Tenevāha “sādhukasavanamanasikārāyattā hi sāsanasampattī”ti. Sāsanasampatti nāma sīlādinipphatti.

Therein, 'proper listening and attention' means in proper listening and in proper attention. And how do listening and so on proceed properly? Through the application of respect and reverence, with the thought, 'Surely, through this right practice, the complete accomplishment of the Dispensation will be attained,' and by not disparaging the discourse and so on. For it is said: 'Bhikkhus, endowed with five qualities, one who listens to the good Dhamma is capable of entering upon the fixed course, the rightness in wholesome states. What five? One does not disparage the discourse, does not disparage the speaker, does not disparage oneself; one listens to the Dhamma with an undistracted mind, with a concentrated mind, and attends wisely. Bhikkhus, endowed with these five qualities, one who listens to the good Dhamma is capable of entering upon the fixed course, the rightness in wholesome states' (AN 5.151). Therefore it is said: 'For accomplishment in the Dispensation depends on proper listening and attention.' Accomplishment in the Dispensation is the perfection of virtue and so on.

Paṭhamaṃ uppannattā adhigamavasena. Satthucariyānuvidhāyakattā sīlādiguṇānuṭṭhānena. Tiṇṇaṃ yānānaṃ vasena anudhammapaṭipattisabbhāvato sakalasāsanapaṭiggāhakattā. Santikattāti samīpabhāvato. Santikāvacarattāti sabbakālaṃ sampayuttabhāvato. Yathānusiṭṭhanti anusāsanianurūpaṃ, anusāsaniṃ anavasesato paṭiggahetvāti attho. Ekacce bhikkhūyeva sandhāyāti ye suttapariyosāne “te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandu”nti vuttā pañcasatā brāhmaṇapabbajitā, te sandhāya.

Because they arose first by way of attainment. Because they follow the Teacher's conduct by practicing the qualities of virtue and so on. Because they are receivers of the entire teaching, since there exists for them the practice in conformity with the Dhamma by way of the three vehicles. Because of nearness, that is, due to proximity. Because of moving in his presence, that is, due to being constantly associated. 'As instructed' means in conformity with the instruction; that is, having accepted the instruction without remainder. 'With reference to certain bhikkhus only': this refers to the five hundred brahmin ascetics who are mentioned at the end of the sutta: 'Those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One's words.'

Pubbe sabbaparisasādhāraṇattepi bhagavato dhammadesanāya “jeṭṭhaseṭṭhā”tiādinā bhikkhūnaṃ eva āmantane kāraṇaṃ dassetvā idāni bhikkhū āmantetvāva dhammadesanāya payojanaṃ dassetuṃ “kimatthaṃ pana bhagavā”ti codanaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Tattha aññaṃ cintentāti aññavihitā. Vikkhittacittāti asamāhitacittā. Dhammaṃ paccavekkhantāti tadā hiyyo tato paradivasesu vā sutadhammaṃ pati pati manasā avekkhantā. Bhikkhū āmantetvā dhamme desiyamāne ādito paṭṭhāya desanaṃ sallakkhetuṃ sakkontīti imamevatthaṃ byatirekamukhena dassetuṃ “te anāmantetvā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Although the Blessed One's teaching of the Dhamma was previously common to all assemblies, having shown with such words as 'chief and best' the reason for addressing the bhikkhus in particular, the commentator now raises a question in order to show the purpose of teaching the Dhamma only after having addressed the bhikkhus: 'For what reason, then, did the Blessed One do this?' Here, 'thinking of something else' means their minds are directed elsewhere. 'With scattered minds' means with unconcentrated minds. 'Reflecting on the Dhamma' means they are repeatedly reviewing in their minds the Dhamma they heard on that day, or yesterday, or on the days before that. When the Dhamma is taught after the bhikkhus have been addressed, they are able to pay attention to the teaching from the very beginning. To show this very meaning by way of contrast, it was said, 'Without addressing them...'

Bhikkhavotīti ca sandhivasena i-kāralopo daṭṭhabbo “bhikkhavo itī”ti. Ayaṃ hi iti-saddo hetu-parisamāpanādipadatthavipariyāya-pakārāvadhāraṇanidassanādianekatthappabhedo. Tathā hesa “ruppatīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā ‘rūpa’nti vuccatī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.79) hetuatthe dissati; “tasmā tiha me, bhikkhave, dhammadāyādā bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā, atthi me tumhesu anukampā ‘kinti me sāvakā dhammadāyādā bhaveyyuṃ, no āmisadāyādā’ti”ādīsu parisamāpane; “iti vā, iti evarūpā naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā [M 1.0052] paṭivirato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.13) ādiatthe; “māgaṇṭhiyoti tassa brāhmaṇassa saṅkhā samaññā paññatti vohāro nāmaṃ nāmakammaṃ nāmadheyyaṃ nirutti byañjanamabhilāpo”tiādīsu (mahāni. 73) padatthavipariyāye; “iti kho, bhikkhave, sappaṭibhayo bālo, appaṭibhayo paṇḍito, saupaddavo bālo, anupaddavo paṇḍito, saupasaggo bālo, anupasaggo paṇḍito”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.124) pakāre; “atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ, kiṃ paccayā jarāmaraṇanti [V 1.0047] iti ce vadeyya, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iccassa vacanīya”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.96) avadhāraṇe; “sabbamatthīti kho, kaccāna, ayameko anto, sabbaṃ natthīti kho, kaccāna, ayaṃ dutiyo anto”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.15) nidassane. Idhāpi nidassaneva daṭṭhabbo. Bhikkhavoti hi āmantitākāro, tamesa iti-saddo nidasseti “bhikkhavoti āmantesī”ti. Iminā nayena “bhaddante”tiādīsupi yathārahaṃ iti-saddassa attho veditabbo. Pubbe “bhagavā āmantesī”ti vuttattā “bhagavato paccassosu”nti idha “bhagavato”ti sāmivacanaṃ āmantanameva sambandhīantaraṃ apekkhatīti iminā adhippāyena “bhagavato āmantanaṃ paṭiassosu”nti vuttaṃ. “Bhagavato”ti pana idaṃ paṭissavasambandhanena sampadānavacanaṃ yathā “devadattassa paṭissuṇotī”ti.

In 'bhikkhavotīti,' the elision of the letter 'i' should be understood as due to sandhi, so that it means 'bhikkhavo iti' ('O bhikkhus'). This particle 'iti' has many different meanings, such as cause, conclusion, 'and so on,' reversal of a word's meaning, manner, delimitation, and illustration.
