For example, it is seen in the sense of cause in passages like: 'Because it is afflicted (ruppati), bhikkhus, it is therefore called 'form' (rūpa).' In the sense of conclusion, as in: 'Therefore, bhikkhus, be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things. I have compassion for you and think: 'How can my disciples become my heirs in the Dhamma and not my heirs in material things?'' In the sense of 'and so on,' as in: '...or thus, he abstains from such things as visiting shows of dancing, singing, and music.' In the sense of reversal of a word's meaning, as in: 'Māgaṇḍiya—this is the designation, term, concept, convention, name, nomenclature, appellation, expression, and verbal token for that brahmin.' In the sense of manner, as in: 'Thus, bhikkhus, the fool is subject to fear, the wise one is not subject to fear; the fool is subject to calamity, the wise one is not subject to calamity; the fool is subject to adversity, the wise one is not subject to adversity.' In the sense of delimitation, as in: 'When asked, Ānanda, 'Does aging-and-death have this as its condition?' one should say, 'It does.' If one should say, 'What is the condition for aging-and-death?' one should reply, 'Birth is the condition for aging-and-death.'' In the sense of illustration, as in: 'That everything exists, Kaccāna, is one extreme. That everything does not exist, Kaccāna, is the second extreme.' Here too, it should be understood as illustration. For 'bhikkhavo' is a form of address, and this particle 'iti' illustrates it, meaning: 'He addressed them as 'bhikkhavo'.' In the same way, the meaning of the particle 'iti' in such cases as 'bhaddante' should be understood as appropriate. Since it was said earlier, 'The Blessed One addressed them,' in the phrase 'they responded to the Blessed One,' the genitive 'bhagavato' ('of the Blessed One') refers to the address itself, which requires another related term. With this intention it is said, 'they responded to the address of the Blessed One.' But this word 'bhagavato' is a dative in connection with the response, as in 'he responds to Devadatta.'

Yaṃ nidānaṃ bhāsitanti sambandho. Etthāha – kimatthaṃ pana dhammavinayasaṅgahe kariyamāne nidānavacanaṃ, nanu bhagavatā bhāsitavacanasseva saṅgaho kātabboti? Vuccate – desanāya ṭhitiasammosasaddheyyabhāvasampādanatthaṃ. Kāladesadesakanimittaparisāpadesehi upanibandhitvā ṭhapitā hi desanā ciraṭṭhitikā hoti asammosadhammā saddheyyā ca, desakālakattusotunimittehi upanibaddho viya vohāravinicchayo. Teneva ca āyasmatā mahākassapena “mūlapariyāyasuttaṃ āvuso, ānanda, kattha bhāsita”ntiādinā desādipucchāsu katāsu tāsaṃ vissajjanaṃ karontena dhammabhaṇḍāgārikena “evaṃ me suta”ntiādinā imassa suttassa nidānaṃ bhāsitaṃ. Apica satthusampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ. Tathāgatassa hi bhagavato pubbaracanānumānāgamatakkābhāvato sammāsambuddhabhāvasiddhi[M 1.0053]. Na hi sammāsambuddhassa pubbaracanādīhi attho atthi sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇacāratāya ekappamāṇattā ca ñeyyadhammesu. Tathā ācariyamuṭṭhidhammamacchariyasāsanasāvakānurodhābhāvato khīṇāsavabhāvasiddhi. Na hi sabbaso khīṇāsavassa te sambhavantīti suvisuddhassa parānuggahappavatti. Evaṃ desakasaṃkilesabhūtānaṃ diṭṭhisīlasampadādūsakānaṃ avijjātaṇhānaṃ accantābhāvasaṃsūcakehi ñāṇasampadāpahānasampadābhibyañjakehi ca sambuddhavisuddhabhāvehi purimavesārajjadvayasiddhi, tato eva ca antarāyikaniyyānikadhammesu sammohābhāvasiddhito pacchimavesārajjadvayasiddhīti bhagavato catuvesārajjasamannāgamo attahitaparahitapaṭipatti ca nidānavacanena pakāsitā hoti tattha tattha sampattapariyāya ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhānena dhammadesanādīpanato, idha pana pathavīādīsu vatthūsu puthujjanānaṃ paṭipattivibhāgavavatthāpakadesanādīpanatoti yojetabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “satthusampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacana”nti.

The connection is: 'Why was the introduction spoken?' Here it is said: But why is the introduction stated when a compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya is being made? Should not only the words spoken by the Blessed One be compiled? It is said: For the sake of establishing the stability of the teaching, its freedom from confusion, and its credibility. For a teaching that is established by being linked to the time, place, speaker, occasion, and assembly is long-lasting, not liable to be confused, and credible, like a legal decision that is linked to the speaker, time, agent, listener, and occasion. It was for this reason that when the Venerable Mahākassapa asked questions about the place, etc., beginning, 'Friend Ānanda, where was the Mūlapariyāya Sutta spoken?' the treasurer of the Dhamma, in answering those questions, stated the introduction to this sutta beginning, 'Thus have I heard.' Moreover, the statement of the introduction is for the purpose of revealing the Teacher's attainments. For the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, the attainment of the state of a Perfectly Enlightened One is established by the absence of prior composition, inference, tradition, and reasoning. For a Perfectly Enlightened One has no need for prior composition and so on, because his knowledge moves without impediment everywhere and is of a single measure in regard to all knowable things. Similarly, the attainment of the state of one whose taints are destroyed is established by the absence of a 'teacher's fist,' of stinginess with the Dhamma, and of favoritism toward disciples. For these do not exist at all for one whose taints are completely destroyed, whose conduct is for the benefit of others, being utterly pure. Thus, the attainment of the first two grounds of self-confidence is due to the purity of the Enlightened One, which indicates the utter absence of ignorance and craving—the defilements of the speaker that corrupt right view and virtuous conduct—and which manifests the accomplishment in knowledge and the accomplishment in abandonment. And from that very fact, the attainment of the latter two grounds of self-confidence is due to the established absence of confusion regarding obstructive and emancipating dhammas. Thus the Blessed One's possession of the four grounds of self-confidence and his practice for his own welfare and the welfare of others are revealed by the statement of the introduction, by illuminating the teaching of the Dhamma with a ready wit that arises on the spot, in accordance with the disposition and the particular attainment on each occasion. Here, however, this should be connected by its illuminating the teaching that establishes the division in the practice of worldlings in regard to things such as the earth element. Therefore it is said: 'The statement of the introduction is for the purpose of revealing the Teacher's attainments.'

Tathā [V 1.0048] sāsanasampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ. Ñāṇakaruṇāpariggahitasabbakiriyassa hi bhagavato natthi niratthikā paṭipatti, attahitatthā vā. Tasmā paresaṃ eva atthāya pavattasabbakiriyassa sammāsambuddhassa sakalampi kāyavacīmanokammaṃ yathāpavattaṃ vuccamānaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi yathārahaṃ sattānaṃ anusāsanaṭṭhena sāsanaṃ, na kabyaracanā, tayidaṃ satthucaritaṃ kāladesadesakaparisāpadesehi saddhiṃ tattha tattha nidānavacanehi yathārahaṃ pakāsīyati, idha pana “pathaviyādīsu vatthūsū”ti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva. Tena vuttaṃ “sāsanasampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacana”nti. Apica satthuno pamāṇabhāvappakāsanena sāsanassa pamāṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ, tañca desakappamāṇabhāvadassanaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena “bhagavā”ti ca iminā padena vibhāvitanti veditabbaṃ. “Bhagavā”ti iminā tathāgatassa rāgadosamohādisabbakilesamaladuccaritādidosappahānadīpanena vacanena anaññasādhāraṇasuparisuddhañāṇakaruṇādiguṇavisesayogaparidīpanena tato eva sabbasattuttamabhāvadīpanena ayamattho sabbathā pakāsito hotīti idamettha nidānavacanappayojanassa mukhamattadassanaṃ.

Similarly, the statement of the introduction is for the purpose of revealing the attainment of the Teaching. For the Blessed One, all of whose actions are encompassed by knowledge and compassion, has no practice that is purposeless or for his own benefit. Therefore, all the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the Perfectly Enlightened One—all of whose actions proceed only for the welfare of others—when recounted as they occurred, constitute the Teaching by way of instructing beings appropriately in regard to their welfare in the present life, in future lives, and in the ultimate sense; it is not a poetic composition. This conduct of the Teacher, together with the time, place, speaker, and assembly, is revealed as appropriate here and there by the introductory statements. Here, however, the phrase 'in regard to things such as the earth element' is entirely similar to what was stated before. Therefore it is said: 'The statement of the introduction is for the purpose of revealing the attainment of the Teaching.' Moreover, the statement of the introduction is for the purpose of showing that the Teaching is the standard by revealing that the Teacher is the standard. And that showing that the speaker is the standard should be understood as being clarified by this word 'Bhagavā' (Blessed One), in accordance with the method stated previously. By this word 'Bhagavā,' this meaning is fully revealed: by indicating the Tathāgata's abandonment of all defilements, stains, and misconduct such as greed, hatred, and delusion; by disclosing his possession of the special qualities of supremely pure knowledge and compassion, which are shared by no one else; and thereby by showing his state as the highest of all beings. This here is just a brief indication of the purpose of the statement of the introduction.

Abbhantaranidānavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Internal Introduction is finished.

Suttanikkhepavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Sutta

Nikkhittassāti [M 1.0054] desitassa. Desanāpi hi desetabbassa sīlādiatthassa vineyyasantānesu nikkhipanato “nikkhepo”ti vuccati. Suttanikkhepaṃ vicāretvā vuccamānā pākaṭā hotīti sāmaññato bhagavato desanāsamuṭṭhānassa vibhāgaṃ dassetvā “etthāyaṃ desanā evaṃsamuṭṭhānā”ti desanāya samuṭṭhāne dassite suttassa sammadeva nidānaparijānanena vaṇṇanāya suviññeyyattā vuttaṃ. Evañhi “assutavā bhikkhave puthujjano”tiādinā, “yopi so, bhikkhave, bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.8), “tathāgatopi kho, bhikkhave, arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.12) ca pavattadesanā anusandhidassanasukhatāya suviññeyyā hoti. Tattha yathā anekasataanekasahassabhedānipi suttantāni saṃkilesabhāgiyādipadhānanayavasena soḷasavidhataṃ nātivattanti, evaṃ attajjhāsayādisuttanikkhepavasena catubbidhabhāvanti āha “cattāro hi suttanikkhepā”ti.

“Of what is laid down” means of what is taught. For teaching is also called an “exposition” because it lays down the meaning of virtue and so forth in the mental continuities of those to be trained. It is said that by investigating the exposition of the sutta, what is spoken becomes clear. For when the origin of a teaching has been pointed out by saying, “Here, this teaching arises in such a way”—after having first shown in general the classification of the origins of the Blessed One’s teaching—the commentary becomes easily understood through a correct understanding of the sutta’s causal occasion. For in this way, teachings that begin with “Bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling,” and so on, or “Bhikkhus, that bhikkhu who is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed,” and so on, or “Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, too, is an arahant, a perfectly self-enlightened one,” and so on, are easily understood because of the ease of seeing their connection. There, just as the suttas, though divided into many hundreds and thousands, do not go beyond the sixteenfold classification based on the primary method of what partakes of defilement and so on, so too they are fourfold when classified by way of the exposition of suttas based on one’s own inclination and so on. Hence it is said: “For there are four expositions of the suttas.”

Ettha ca yathā attajjhāsayassa aṭṭhuppattiyā ca parajjhāsayapucchāhi saddhiṃ saṃsaggabhedo sambhavati [V 1.0049] “attajjhāsayo ca parajjhāsayo ca, attajjhāsayo ca pucchāvasiko ca, aṭṭhuppattiko ca parajjhāsayo ca, aṭṭhuppattiko ca pucchāvasiko cā”ti ajjhāsayapucchānusandhisabbhāvato, evaṃ yadipi aṭṭhuppattiyā attajjhāsayenapi saṃsaggabhedo sambhavati, attajjhāsayādīhi pana purato ṭhitehi aṭṭhuppattiyā saṃsaggo natthīti nayidha niravaseso vitthāranayo sambhavatīti “cattāro suttanikkhepā”ti vuttaṃ, tadantogadhattā vā sambhavantānaṃ sesanikkhepānaṃ mūlanikkhepavasena cattārova dassitā. Tathādassanañcettha ayaṃ saṃsaggabhedo gahetabboti.

Here, just as a distinction of combination is possible for one’s own inclination and for the arising of an occasion with another’s inclination and with questions—thus: “one’s own inclination and another’s inclination; one’s own inclination and being dependent on a question; the arising of an occasion and another’s inclination; the arising of an occasion and being dependent on a question”—due to the existence of a connection between inclination and question; so too, although a distinction of combination is possible between the arising of an occasion and one’s own inclination, since one’s own inclination and the others are established beforehand, there is no combination with the arising of an occasion. Therefore an exhaustive method of detailed explanation is not possible here. Thus it is said, “four expositions of the suttas.” Or, because the remaining possible expositions are included within these, only four are shown as the root expositions. And here this distinction of combination should be understood as shown.

Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – nikkhipīyatīti nikkhepo, suttaṃ eva nikkhepo suttanikkhepo. Atha vā nikkhipanaṃ nikkhepo, suttassa nikkhepo suttanikkhepo, suttadesanāti attho. Attano ajjhāsayo attajjhāsayo, so assa atthi kāraṇabhūtoti attajjhāsayo. Attano ajjhāsayo etassāti vā attajjhāsayo. Parajjhāsayepi eseva nayo. Pucchāya vaso pucchāvaso, so etassa atthīti [M 1.0055] pucchāvasiko. Suttadesanāvatthubhūtassa atthassa uppatti atthuppatti, atthuppattiyeva aṭṭhuppatti ttha-kārassa ṭṭha-kāraṃ katvā. Sā etassa atthīti aṭṭhuppattiko. Atha vā nikkhipīyati suttaṃ etenāti suttanikkhepo, attajjhāsayādi eva. Etasmiṃ pana attavikappe attano ajjhāsayo attajjhāsayo. Paresaṃ ajjhāsayo parajjhāsayo. Pucchīyatīti pucchā, pucchitabbo attho. Pucchanavasena pavattaṃ dhammapaṭiggāhakānaṃ vacanaṃ pucchāvasikaṃ, tadeva nikkhepa-saddāpekkhāya pulliṅgavasena “pucchāvasiko”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā aṭṭhuppatti eva aṭṭhuppattikoti evampettha attho veditabbo.

Here is the verbal explanation. “It is expounded,” thus it is an “exposition” (nikkhepo); the sutta itself is an exposition, hence suttanikkhepo. Or, the expounding is an “exposition”; the exposition of the sutta is suttanikkhepo, which means the teaching of the sutta. “One’s own inclination” is attajjhāsayo; it exists for one as a cause, hence it is called attajjhāsayo (an exposition based on one’s own inclination). Or, “one’s own inclination is its basis,” hence attajjhāsayo. The same method applies to parajjhāsayo (another’s inclination). “Being dependent on a question” is pucchāvaso; this is its basis, hence it is called pucchāvasiko. The arising (uppatti) of a matter (attha) that is the basis for the teaching of a sutta is atthuppatti; aṭṭhuppatti is simply atthuppatti with the sound ttha changed to ṭṭha. This is its basis, hence it is called aṭṭhuppattiko. Or, “a sutta is expounded by means of this,” thus it is a suttanikkhepo; this refers to one’s own inclination, etc. In this alternative explanation, “one’s own inclination” is attajjhāsayo. “Another’s inclination” is parajjhāsayo. “It is asked,” thus it is a “question” (pucchā), that is, a matter to be asked about. The speech of the receivers of the Dhamma that proceeds by way of questioning is pucchāvasikaṃ; with reference to the masculine noun nikkhepa, this is called pucchāvasiko. Similarly, aṭṭhuppatti itself becomes aṭṭhuppattiko. Thus the meaning here should be understood.

Apicettha paresaṃ indriyaparipākādikāraṇanirapekkhattā attajjhāsayassa visuṃ suttanikkhepabhāvo yutto kevalaṃ attano ajjhāsayeneva dhammatantiṭhapanatthaṃ pavattitadesanattā. Parajjhāsayapucchāvasikānaṃ pana paresaṃ ajjhāsayapucchānaṃ desanāpavattihetubhūtānaṃ uppattiyaṃ pavattitānaṃ kathamaṭṭhuppattiyaṃ anavarodho, pucchāvasikaaṭṭhuppattikānaṃ vā parajjhāsayānurodhena pavattikānaṃ kathaṃ parajjhāsaye anavarodhoti? Na codetabbametaṃ. Paresañhi abhinīhāraparipucchādivinimuttasseva suttadesanākāraṇuppādassa aṭṭhuppattibhāvena gahitattā parajjhāsayapucchāvasikānaṃ visuṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tathā hi brahmajāla (dī. ni. 1.1) dhammadāyādasuttādīnaṃ (ma. ni. 1.29) vaṇṇāvaṇṇaāmisuppādādidesanānimittaṃ “aṭṭhuppattī”ti vuccati. Paresaṃ pucchaṃ vinā ajjhāsayaṃ eva nimittaṃ katvā desito parajjhāsayo, pucchāvasena desito pucchāvasikoti pākaṭoyamatthoti.

Moreover, here, because it is independent of such causes as the maturation of others’ faculties, it is proper for “one’s own inclination” to be a separate type of sutta exposition, since it is a teaching set forth solely from one’s own inclination for the purpose of establishing the continuity of the Dhamma. But then, in the case of expositions based on another’s inclination and on questions—which are set forth when their causes, namely, the inclinations and questions of others, have arisen—how are they not included under “arising of an occasion”? Or in the case of expositions dependent on questions and the arising of an occasion, which proceed in accordance with another’s inclination, how are they not included under “another’s inclination”? This objection should not be raised. For “arising of an occasion” is taken to be the arising of a reason for teaching a sutta that is free from others’ instigation, inquiry, and so on; therefore, “another’s inclination” and “dependent on a question” are taken as separate categories. Thus, for example, in the Brahmajāla Sutta, the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, and others, the occasion for the teaching—such as the arising of praise and blame, or of a material offering—is called an “arising of an occasion.” An exposition taught by taking another’s inclination as the occasion, without their asking a question, is “based on another’s inclination.” An exposition taught by way of a question is “dependent on a question.” This meaning is clear.

Attano [V 1.0050] ajjhāsayeneva kathesi dhammatantiṭhapanatthanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sammappadhānasuttantahārakoti anupubbena nikkhittānaṃ saṃyuttake sammappadhānapaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ suttānaṃ āvaḷi. Tathā iddhipādahārakādayo.

It should be understood that he spoke from his own inclination for the purpose of establishing the continuity of the Dhamma. The Sammappadhānasuttantahāraka is the series of suttas on the right strivings in the Saṃyutta Nikāya that were expounded sequentially. Similarly for the collections on the bases for spiritual power, and so on.

Vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā saddhindriyādayo. Ajjhāsayanti adhimuttiṃ. Khantinti diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiṃ. Mananti cittaṃ. Abhinihāranti paṇidhānaṃ. Bujjhanabhāvanti bujjhanasabhāvaṃ, paṭivijjhanākāraṃ vā.

Qualities that lead to the maturing of liberation are the faculties such as faith and so on. “Inclination” (ajjhāsaya) means resolution (adhimutti). “Forbearance” (khanti) means the acceptance that comes from scrutinizing views. “Mind” (mano) means the mind (citta). “Aspiration” (abhinīhāra) means resolve (paṇidhāna). “The state of understanding” (bujjhanabhāva) means the nature of understanding, or the mode of penetration.

Uppanne māne nikkhittanti sambandho. Itthiliṅgādīni tīṇi liṅgāni. Nāmādīni cattāri padāni. Paṭhamādayo satta vibhattiyo. Muñcitvā na kiñci katheti sabhāvaniruttiyā [M 1.0056] tatheva pavattanato. Gaṇṭhibhūtaṃ padaṃ. Yathā hi rukkhassa gaṇṭhiṭṭhānaṃ dubbinibbedhaṃ duttacchitañca hoti, evamevaṃ yaṃ padaṃ atthato vivarituṃ na sakkā, taṃ “gaṇṭhipada”nti vuccati. Anupahaccāti anuddharitvā.

“When pride has arisen, it is laid down”—this is the connection. The three genders are the feminine and so on. The four kinds of words are the noun and so on. The seven cases are the first and so on. “Having released, he says nothing,” because it proceeds just so by way of natural expression. A word that has become a knot. Just as a knot in a tree is difficult to split and hard to shape, so too a word that cannot be explained as to its meaning is called a “knot-word.” “Without harming” means without extracting.

Yena yena sambandhaṃ gacchati, tassa tassa anavasesataṃ dīpetīti iminā imassa sabba-saddassa sappadesataṃ dasseti. Sabba-saddo hi sabbasabbaṃ padesasabbaṃ āyatanasabbaṃ sakkāyasabbanti catūsu visayesu diṭṭhappayogo. Tathā hesa “sabbe dhammā sabbākārena buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇamukhe āpāthamāgacchantī”tiādīsu (mahāni. 156; cūḷani. 85; paṭi. ma. 3.6) sabbasabbasmiṃ āgato. “Sabbesaṃ vo, sāriputta, subhāsitaṃ pariyāyenā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.345) padesasabbasmiṃ. “Sabbaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi…pe… cakkhuñceva rūpā ca…pe… mano ceva dhammā cā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.23) ettha āyatanasabbasmiṃ. “Sabbaṃ sabbato sañjānātī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.5) sakkāyasabbasmiṃ. Tattha sabbasabbasmiṃ āgato nippadeso, itaresu tīsupi āgato sappadeso, idha pana sakkāyasabbasmiṃ veditabbo. Tathā hi vakkhati “sakkāyapariyāpannā pana tebhūmakadhammāva anavasesato veditabbā”ti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1 suttanikkhepavaṇṇanā).

By this phrase, “it illuminates the completeness of whatever it is connected with,” he shows that this word “all” is qualified. For the word “all” is seen used in four domains: the universal all, the partial all, the all of the sense bases, and the all of identity. Thus, in such passages as, “All phenomena in every way come into the range of the Blessed One’s knowledge,” it occurs as the universal all. In such statements as, “All of what you have said, Sāriputta, is well-spoken in its own way,” it occurs as the partial all. In the passage, “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the all… the eye and forms… the mind and mental objects,” it occurs as the all of the sense bases. In such phrases as, “He perceives all from the all,” it occurs as the all of identity. Among these, when it occurs as the universal all, it is unqualified; when it occurs in the other three cases, it is qualified. Here, however, it is to be understood as the all of identity. For it will be said: “The phenomena of the three planes included in identity are to be known completely, without remainder.”

Saccesūti ariyasaccesu. Ete caturo dhammāti idāni vuccamāne saccādike cattāro dhamme sandhāya vadati. Tattha saccanti vacīsaccaṃ. Ṭhitīti vīriyaṃ, “dhitī”ti vā pāṭho, so evattho. Cāgoti alobho. Diṭṭhaṃ so ativattatīti yasmiṃ ete saccādayo dhammā upalabbhanti, so diṭṭhaṃ attano amittaṃ atikkamati, na tassa hatthataṃ gacchati, atha kho naṃ [V 1.0051] abhibhavati evāti attho. Sabhāve vattati asabhāvadhammassa kāraṇāsambhavato. Na hi nissabhāvā dhammā kenaci nibbattīyanti. Attano lakkhaṇaṃ dhārentīti yadipi lakkhaṇavinimuttā dhammā nāma natthi, tathāpi yathā diṭṭhitaṇhāparikappitākāramattā attasubhasukhasassatādayo, pakatiyādayo, dabbādayo, jīvādayo, kāyādayo lokavohāramattasiddhā gagaṇakusumādayova saccikaṭṭhaparamatthato na upalabbhanti, na evamete, ete pana saccikaṭṭhaparamatthabhūtā upalabbhanti, tato eva sattādivisesavirahato dhammamattā sabhāvavantoti dassanatthaṃ “attano lakkhaṇaṃ dhārentī”ti vuttaṃ[M 1.0057]. Bhavati hi bhedābhāvepi sukhāvabodhanatthaṃ upacāramattasiddhena bhedena niddeso yathā “silāputtakassa sarīra”nti. Dhārīyanti vā yathāsabhāvato avadhārīyanti ñāyantīti dhammā, kakkhaḷaphusanādayo.

“‘In truths’ means in the noble truths. When it is said, ‘These four things,’ this refers to the four things beginning with truth that are now being discussed. Therein, ‘truth’ means truthfulness of speech. ‘Steadfastness’ is energy; or the reading is ‘fortitude,’ which has the same meaning. ‘Generosity’ is non-greed. ‘He surpasses his enemy’: he in whom these qualities—truth and so forth—are found, transcends his enemy; he does not fall into his grasp, but rather overcomes him—this is the meaning. It exists by its own nature, because a phenomenon without intrinsic nature cannot arise, as a cause is impossible for it. For phenomena without intrinsic nature cannot be produced by anything. ‘They bear their own characteristics’: although there are no phenomena devoid of characteristics, yet, unlike the conceptions born of craving for views—such as self, beauty, pleasure, permanence, etc., or primal nature, substance, soul, body, etc.—which are merely established by worldly convention and, like flowers in the sky, do not exist in an ultimate sense, these phenomena, however, exist as ultimate realities. Thus, to show that they are mere phenomena devoid of distinctions like ‘a being,’ etc., but possessing intrinsic nature, it is said, ‘They bear their own characteristics.’ For even in the absence of division, for the sake of easy understanding, descriptions may use figurative divisions, such as ‘the body of a stone doll.’ Or, they are called ‘phenomena’ (dhammā) because ‘they are borne’ (dhāriyanti), that is, they are determined or known according to their intrinsic nature, such as hardness, contact, etc.

Asādhāraṇahetumhīti asādhāraṇakāraṇe, sakkāyadhammesu tassa tassa āveṇikapaccayeti attho. Kiṃ pana tanti? Taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiyo, avijjādayopi vā. Yatheva hi pathavīādīsu maññanāvatthūsu uppajjamānā taṇhādayo maññanā tesaṃ pavattiyā mūlakāraṇaṃ, evaṃ avijjādayopi. Tathā hi “assutavā puthujjano”tiādinā “apariññātaṃ tassāti vadāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.2) “nandī dukkhassa mūla”nti (ma. ni. 1.13) ca anvayato, “khayā rāgassa…pe… vītamohattā”ti byatirekato ca tesaṃ mūlakāraṇabhāvo vibhāvito.

“‘In the uncommon cause’ means in the uncommon reason; that is, the specific condition for each of the phenomena of personal identity. But what is that? Craving, conceit, and views, or also ignorance and so on. For just as craving, conceit, etc., which are forms of conceiving that arise in regard to the bases for conceiving such as earth, etc., are the root cause of their occurrence, so too are ignorance and so on. Indeed, their status as the root cause is demonstrated affirmatively by such passages as ‘the uninstructed worldling…’ and ‘…I say, is due to not having fully understood it,’ and ‘delight is the root of suffering’; and negatively by ‘with the destruction of lust… with the removal of delusion.’”

Pariyāyeti desetabbamatthaṃ avagameti bodhayatīti pariyāyo, desanā. Pariyāyati attano phalaṃ pariggahetvā vattati tassa vā kāraṇabhāvaṃ gacchatīti pariyāyo, kāraṇaṃ. Pariyāyati aparāparaṃ parivattatīti pariyāyo, vāro. Evaṃ pariyāyasaddassa desanākāraṇavāresu pavatti veditabbā. Yathārutavasena aggahetvā niddhāretvā gahetabbatthaṃ neyyatthaṃ. Tebhūmakā dhammāva anavasesato veditabbā maññanāvatthubhūtānaṃ sabbesaṃ pathavīādidhammānaṃ adhippetattā.

“A ‘discourse’ (pariyāya) is so called because it teaches, makes one understand, and awakens one to the meaning that should be taught; it is a teaching (desanā). A ‘discourse’ is so called because it proceeds having encompassed its own fruit, or because it becomes a cause for it; it is a cause (kāraṇa). A ‘discourse’ is so called because it revolves again and again; it is a turn (vāra). Thus the usage of the word ‘pariyāya’ should be understood in the senses of teaching, cause, and turn. A meaning that requires drawing out (neyyattha) is one that should be grasped after having ascertained it, not by taking it literally as it is stated. All phenomena of the three planes should be understood without remainder, since all the phenomena, such as earth and so forth, that are the bases for conceiving are intended.”

Kāraṇadesananti kāraṇañāpanaṃ desanaṃ. Taṃ atthanti taṃ sabbadhammānaṃ mūlakāraṇasaṅkhātaṃ, kāraṇadesanāsaṅkhātaṃ vā atthaṃ. Tenevāha “taṃ kāraṇaṃ taṃ desana”nti. Ekatthametanti etaṃ padadvayaṃ ekatthaṃ. Sādhu-saddo eva hi ka-kārena vaḍḍhetvā “sādhuka”nti vutto. Teneva hi sādhusaddassa atthaṃ vadantena atthuddhāravasena sādhukasaddo udāhaṭo. Dhammarucīti puññakāmo. Paññāṇavāti paññavā. Addubbhoti adūsako, anupaghātakoti attho. Idhāpīti imasmiṃ mūlapariyāyasuttepi. Ayanti sādhukasaddo. Ettheva daḷhīkammeti sakkaccakiriyāyaṃ. Āṇattiyanti [V 1.0052] āṇāpane. “Suṇātha sādhukaṃ manasi karothā”ti hi vutte sādhukasaddena savanamanasikārānaṃ sakkaccakiriyā viya tadāṇāpanampi vuttaṃ hoti. Āyācanatthatā viya cassa āṇāpanatthatā veditabbā.

“‘The teaching of the cause’ is a teaching that makes known the cause. ‘That meaning’ means that which is designated as the root cause of all phenomena, or the meaning designated as the teaching of the cause. Hence he said, ‘That is the cause, that is the teaching.’ ‘These have one meaning’: these two words have one meaning. For the word ‘sādhu’ itself, when augmented with the ‘ka’ suffix, is spoken as ‘sādhuka.’ For that very reason, when stating the meaning of the word ‘sādhu,’ the word ‘sādhuka’ was cited by way of clarifying the meaning. ‘One with a taste for the Dhamma’ means one who desires merit. ‘One possessing wisdom’ means one who is wise. ‘Not treacherous’ means not corrupting, not harming—this is the meaning. ‘Here too’ means also in this Discourse on the Root of All Things. ‘This’ means the word ‘sādhuka.’ ‘Herein, for confirmation’ is in the sense of careful action. ‘In the sense of a command’ means in enjoining. For when it is said, ‘Listen well and attend carefully,’ by the word ‘sādhukaṃ’ (well), the careful performance of listening and attending is expressed, as is the enjoining of it. And its meaning as an injunction should be understood as being like its meaning as a request.”

Idānettha [M 1.0058] evaṃ yojanā veditabbāti sambandho. Sotindriyavikkhepavāraṇaṃ savane niyojanavasena kiriyantarapaṭisedhanabhāvato, sotaṃ odahathāti attho. Manindriyavikkhepanivāraṇaṃ aññacintāpaṭisedhanato. Purimanti “suṇāthā”ti padaṃ. Etthāti suṇātha, manasi karothā”ti padadvaye, etasmiṃ vā adhikāre. Byañjanavipallāsaggāhavāraṇaṃ sotadvāre vikkhepapaṭibāhakattā. Na hi yāthāvato suṇantassa saddato vipallāsaggāho hoti. Atthavipallāsaggāhavāraṇaṃ manindriyavikkhepapaṭibāhakattā. Na hi sakkaccaṃ dhammaṃ upadhārentassa atthato vipallāsaggāho hoti. Dhammassavane niyojeti suṇāthāti vidahanato. Dhāraṇūpaparikkhāsūti upaparikkhaggahaṇena tulanatīraṇādike diṭṭhiyā ca suppaṭivedhaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

“Now the construction here should be understood thus—this is the connection. The prevention of distraction of the ear-faculty is by way of enjoining one to listen, in that it prohibits other activities; the meaning is ‘lend an ear.’ The prevention of distraction of the mind-faculty is by prohibiting other thoughts. ‘The former’ is the word ‘Listen.’ ‘Here’ refers to the two words ‘Listen’ and ‘attend carefully,’ or to this section. The prevention of grasping a perversion of the phrasing is because it obstructs distraction at the ear-door. For one who listens properly, there is no perverse grasping of the sound. The prevention of grasping a perversion of the meaning is because it obstructs distraction of the mind-faculty. For one who carefully reflects on the Dhamma, there is no perverse grasping of the meaning. He enjoins one to listen to the Dhamma by the instruction, ‘Listen.’ ‘In retention and examination’: by the word ‘examination,’ it includes weighing, judging, etc., and also thorough penetration by view.”

Sabyañjanoti ettha yathādhippetamatthaṃ byañjayatīti byañjanaṃ, sabhāvanirutti. Saha byañjanenāti sabyañjano, byañjanasampannoti attho. Araṇīyato upagandhabbato anuṭṭhātabbato attho, catupārisuddhisīlādiko. Saha atthenāti sāttho, atthasampannoti attho. Dhammagambhīrotiādīsu dhammo nāma tanti. Desanā nāma tassā manasā vavatthāpitāya tantiyā desanā. Attho nāma tantiyā attho. Paṭivedho nāma tantiyā tantiatthassa ca yathābhūtāvabodho. Yasmā cete dhammadesanāatthapaṭivedhā sasādīhi viya mahāsamuddo mandabuddhīhi dukkhogāḷhā alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā ca, tasmā gambhīrā. Tena vuttaṃ “yasmā ayaṃ dhammo…pe… sādhukaṃ manasi karothā”ti. Ettha ca paṭivedhassa dukkarabhāvato dhammatthānaṃ desanāñāṇassa dukkarabhāvato desanāya dukkhogāhatā, paṭivedhassa pana uppādetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā tabbisayañāṇuppattiyā ca dukkarabhāvato dukkhogāhatā veditabbā.

“Herein, ‘with its phrasing’: ‘phrasing’ (byañjana) is so called because it expresses (byañjayati) the intended meaning; it is the natural expression. ‘With its phrasing’ (saha byañjanena) means ‘sabyanjano’; that is, endowed with phrasing—this is the meaning. The ‘meaning’ or goal (attha) is so called because it should be gone to (araṇīya), approached (upagandhabba), and undertaken (anuṭṭhātabba); it refers to the fourfold purity of virtue and so on. ‘With its meaning’ (saha atthena) means ‘sāttho’; that is, endowed with meaning—this is the meaning. In such phrases as ‘profound in the Dhamma,’ ‘Dhamma’ is the scriptural text. ‘Teaching’ is the exposition of that scriptural text which has been mentally determined. ‘Meaning’ is the meaning of the scriptural text. ‘Penetration’ is the correct understanding of both the scriptural text and its meaning. And because these—the Dhamma, the teaching, the meaning, and the penetration—are, like the great ocean for hares and other animals, hard to fathom for those of dull wisdom and their bottom is unattainable, they are therefore profound. Hence it was said: ‘Because this Dhamma… attend carefully.’ Herein, the teaching is hard to fathom due to the difficulty of the knowledge of exposition concerning the meaning of the Dhamma and due to the difficulty of penetration. Penetration, in turn, should be understood to be hard to fathom because it is impossible to generate and because of the difficulty of the arising of the knowledge concerning its domain.”

Desanaṃ nāma uddisanaṃ. Tassa niddisanaṃ bhāsananti idhādhippetanti āha “vitthāratopi naṃ bhāsissāmīti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Paribyattaṃ kathanaṃ vā bhāsanaṃ. Sāḷikāyiva nigghosoti sāḷikāya ālāpo viya madhuro kaṇṇasukho pemanīyo. Paṭibhānanti saddo. Udīrayīti uccārīyati, vuccati vā.

“‘Teaching’ (desanā) means a summary statement. Its detailed explanation is called ‘expounding’ (bhāsana), which is intended here, as it is said: ‘I will expound it in detail.’ Or, ‘expounding’ is articulate speech. ‘A voice like a myna bird's’ means like the call of a myna bird—sweet, pleasant to the ear, and lovely. ‘Eloquence’ (paṭibhāna) means the sound. ‘He utters’ means he brings forth or speaks.”

Evaṃ [M 1.0059] vutte ussāhajātāti evaṃ “suṇātha sādhukaṃ manasi karotha bhāsissāmī”ti vutte na [V 1.0053] kira satthā saṅkhepeneva desessati, vitthārenapi bhāsissatīti sañjātussāhā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā hutvā. Idhāti iminā vuccamānaadhikaraṇaṃ tassa puggalassa uppattiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ adhippetanti āha “desāpadese nipāto”ti. Lokanti okāsalokaṃ. Idha tathāgato loketi hi jātikhettaṃ, tatthāpi ayaṃ cakkavāḷo adhippeto. Samaṇoti sotāpanno. Dutiyo samaṇoti sakadāgāmī. Vuttañhetaṃ “katamo ca, bhikkhave, samaṇo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno hotī”ti (a. ni. 4.241) “katamo ca, bhikkhave, dutiyo samaṇo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā sakadāgāmī hotī”ti ca (a. ni. 4.241). Idheva tiṭṭhamānassāti imissā eva indasālaguhāyaṃ tiṭṭhamānassa.

“‘When this was said, they became enthusiastic’: when it was said, ‘Listen well, attend carefully, I will speak,’ they became enthusiastic, joyful, and delighted, thinking: ‘It seems the Teacher will not teach only in brief, but will also expound in detail.’ ‘Here’: by this is intended the subject under discussion, which is the place of origin of that person; thus it is said, ‘a particle indicating place.’ ‘World’ means the world as location. For ‘a Tathāgata here in the world’ refers to the field of his birth; and even there, this world-sphere is intended. ‘An ascetic’ means a stream-enterer. ‘The second ascetic’ means a once-returner. For it was said: ‘And what, bhikkhus, is an ascetic? Here, bhikkhus, with the destruction of the three fetters, a bhikkhu is a stream-enterer.’ And: ‘And what, bhikkhus, is the second ascetic? Here, bhikkhus, with the destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, a bhikkhu is a once-returner.’ ‘While standing right here’ means while standing right in this Indasāla Cave.”

2. Assutavāti ettha (a. ni. ṭī. 1.1.51) sutanti sotadvārānusārena upadhāritaṃ, upadhāraṇaṃ vā, sutaṃ assatthīti sutavā. Vā-saddassa hi attho atthitāmattādivasena anekavidho. Tathā hi “antavā ayaṃ loko parivaṭumo”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.54; paṭi. ma. 1.140) atthitāmattaṃ attho. “Dhanavā bhogavā, lābhī annassā”ti ca ādīsu bahubhāvo. “Rogavā hoti rogābhibhūto”tiādīsu kāyābādho. “Kuṭṭhī kuṭṭhacīvarenā”tiādīsu nindā, “issukī maccharī saṭho māyāvino keṭubhino”tiādīsu abhiṇhayogo. “Daṇḍī chattī alambarī”tiādīsu (visuddhi. 1.142) saṃsaggo. “Paṇḍito vāpi tena so”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 63) upamānaṃ, sadisabhāvoti attho. “Taṃ vāpi dhīrā muniṃ vedayantī”tiādīsu (su. ni. 213) samuccayo. “Ke vā ime kassa vā”tiādīsu (pārā. 296) saṃsayo. “Ayaṃ vā imesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sabbabālo sabbamūḷho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.181) vibhāvano. “Na vāyaṃ kumāro mattamaññāsī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.154) padapūraṇaṃ. “Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.170) vikappo. “Sakyaputtassa sirīmato [M 1.0060] (dī. ni. 3.277), sīlavato sīlasampattiyā kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggacchatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.150; 3.316; a. ni. 5.213; mahāva. 285) ca ādīsu pasaṃsā. “Paññavā hoti udayatthagāminiyā paññāya samannāgato ariyāya nibbedhikāya sammā dukkhakkhayagāminiyā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.317, 355) atisayo. Idhāpi atisayo, pasaṃsā vā attho, tasmā yassa pasaṃsitaṃ, atisayena vā sutaṃ atthi, so sutavāti saṃkilesaviddhaṃsanasamatthaṃ pariyattidhammassavanaṃ, taṃ sutvā [V 1.0054] tathattāya paṭipatti ca “sutavā”ti iminā saddena pakāsitā. Atha vā sotabbayuttaṃ sutvā kattabbanipphattivasena suṇīti sutavā, tappaṭikkhepena na sutavāti assutavā.

2. Herein, regarding ‘assutavā’: ‘Suta’ is what has been ascertained through the ear-door, or it is the act of ascertaining. One who possesses what has been heard is a ‘sutavā.’ The meaning of the suffix ‘-vā’ is indeed manifold, in senses such as mere existence. For example: in phrases like ‘this world is finite…’ (Dī. Ni. 1.54; Paṭi. Ma. 1.140), it denotes mere existence; in ‘wealthy, possessing enjoyments…,’ it signifies abundance; in ‘he is sickly…,’ it refers to bodily affliction; in ‘a leper with a leper’s robe…,’ it conveys censure; in ‘envious, avaricious…,’ it indicates frequent practice; in ‘one with a staff, one with an umbrella…’ (Visuddhi. 1.142), it denotes connection; in ‘by that he is also wise’ (Dha. Pa. 63), it is a simile, meaning similarity; in ‘the wise also know him as a sage’ (Su. Ni. 213), it is conjunction; in ‘who are these, or whose are they?’ (Pārā. 296), it is doubt; in ‘this one is the most foolish…’ (Dī. Ni. 1.181), it is specification; in ‘this boy is not intoxicated…’ (Saṃ. Ni. 2.154), it is an expletive; in ‘whatever ascetics or brahmins…’ (Ma. Ni. 1.170), it is an alternative; in ‘of the glorious son of the Sakyans’ (Dī. Ni. 3.277) and ‘a good report concerning a virtuous one…’ (Dī. Ni. 2.150; etc.), it is praise; in ‘he is endowed with wisdom…’ (Dī. Ni. 3.317, 355), it is excellence. Here too, the meaning is excellence or praise. Therefore, one who possesses what has been heard in a praised or excellent way is a ‘sutavā.’ Thus, the hearing of the Dhamma of the scriptures, which is capable of shattering defilements, and the practice for its realization after having heard it, are indicated by the word ‘sutavā.’ Alternatively, one who, having heard what ought to be heard, accomplishes what ought to be done is a ‘sutavā.’ Its negation is ‘assutavā,’ one who has not heard.

Ayañhi a-kāro “ahetukā dhammā (dha. sa. 2.dukamātikā), abhikkhuko āvāso”tiādīsu (pāci. 1046, 1047) taṃsahayoganivattiyaṃ icchito. “Apaccayā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 7.dukamātikā) taṃsambandhībhāvanivattiyaṃ. Paccayuppannañhi paccayasambandhīti appaccayuppannattā ataṃsambandhitā ettha jotitā. “Anidassanā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 9.dukamātikā) taṃsabhāvanivattiyaṃ. Nidassanañhi daṭṭhabbatā. Atha vā passatīti nidassanaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, taggahetabbabhāvanivattiyaṃ yathā “anāsavā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 15.dukamātikā), “appaṭighā dhammā (dha. sa. 10.dukamātikā), anārammaṇā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 55.dukamātikā) taṃkiccanivattiyaṃ, “arūpino dhammā (dha. sa. 11.dukamātikā) acetasikā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 57.dukamātikā) tabbhāvanivattiyaṃ. Tadaññathā hi ettha pakāsitā. “Amanusso”ti tabbhāvamattanivattiyaṃ. Manussamattaṃ natthi, aññaṃ samānanti. Sadisatā hi ettha sūcitā. “Assamaṇo samaṇapaṭiñño, anariyo”ti (a. ni. 3.13) ca taṃsambhāvanīyaguṇanivattiyaṃ. Garahā hi idha ñāyati. “Kacci bhoto anāmayaṃ, anudarā kaññā”ti (jā. 2.20.129) tadanappabhāvanivattiyaṃ, “anuppannā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 17.tikamātikā) taṃsadisabhāvanivattiyaṃ. Atītānañhi uppannapubbattā uppādidhammānañca paccayekadesanipphattiyā āraddhuppādibhāvato kālavimuttassa ca vijjamānattā uppannānukūlatā pageva paccuppannānanti tabbidūratāva ettha viññāyati “asekkhā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 11.tikamātikā) tadapariyosānanivattiyaṃ. Tanniṭṭhānañhi ettha pakāsitanti. Evamanekesaṃ atthānaṃ jotako. Idha pana “arūpino dhammā acetasikā dhammā”tiādīsu viya tabbhāvanivattiyaṃ [M 1.0061] daṭṭhabbo, aññattheti attho. Etenassa sutādiñāṇavirahataṃ dasseti. Tena vuttaṃ “āgamādhigamābhāvā ñeyyo assutavā itī”ti.

Indeed, this letter ‘a-’ is intended in the sense of removal of association with that, as in ‘causeless dhammas’ (Dhs. 2.dukamātikā) and ‘an abode without a bhikkhu’ (Pāc. 1046, 1047). In ‘unconditioned dhammas’ (Dhs. 7.dukamātikā), it is in the sense of removal of the state of being related to that. For what has arisen from a condition is related to a condition; since these are unconditioned, their unrelatedness is indicated. In ‘non-manifest dhammas’ (Dhs. 9.dukamātikā), it is in the sense of removal of that nature. For ‘manifestation’ (nidassana) is visibility. Or ‘that which sees’ (passati) is ‘manifestation’ (nidassana), i.e., eye-consciousness; it is in the sense of removal of the state of being graspable by that. Just as in ‘taintless dhammas’ (Dhs. 15.dukamātikā), ‘unimpacted dhammas’ (Dhs. 10.dukamātikā), and ‘objectless dhammas’ (Dhs. 55.dukamātikā), it is in the sense of removal of that function. In ‘formless dhammas’ (Dhs. 11.dukamātikā) and ‘non-mental dhammas’ (Dhs. 57.dukamātikā), it is in the sense of removal of that state, for here something different from that is indicated. In ‘a non-human’ (amanusso), it is in the sense of removal of just that state. It means there is not the mere state of a human, but something else similar; for similarity is indicated here. In ‘a non-ascetic who claims to be an ascetic, a non-noble one’ (AN 3.13), it is in the sense of removal of the qualities to be expected of that; for censure is understood here. In ‘Are you well, sir? A slim-waisted girl’ (Jā. 2.20.129), it is in the sense of negation of an undesirable state. In ‘unarisen dhammas’ (Dhs. 17.tikamātikā), it is in the sense of removal of a state similar to that. For since past dhammas have arisen before, and since dhammas that are arising have begun to arise through the partial fulfillment of their conditions, and since that which is timeless exists, their conformity to the arisen is even more so than that of present dhammas; thus their remoteness from that is to be understood here. In ‘dhammas of one beyond training’ (Dhs. 11.tikamātikā), it is in the sense of removal of its non-completion; for their finality is indicated here. Thus it illuminates many meanings. Here, however, as in ‘formless dhammas, non-mental dhammas,’ etc., it should be seen in the sense of removal of that state; the meaning is ‘otherness.’ By this, it shows his lack of knowledge from learning and so on. Therefore it is said: ‘Due to the absence of learning and realization, he should be known as an unlearned person.’

Idāni tassa atthaṃ vivaranto yasmā khandhadhātvādikosallenapi maññanāpaṭisedhanasamatthaṃ bāhusaccaṃ hoti. Yathāha “kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, bahussuto hoti? Yato kho bhikkhu khandhakusalo hoti dhātu, āyatana, paṭiccasamuppādakusalo hoti, ettāvatā kho bhikkhu bahussuto hotī”ti, tasmā “yassa hi khandhadhātuāyatanasaccapaccayākārasatipaṭṭhānādīsūtiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha vācuggatakaraṇaṃ uggaho. Atthaparipucchanaṃ paripucchā. Kusalehi saha codanāpariharaṇavasena vinicchayakaraṇaṃ vinicchayo. Maggaphalanibbānāni adhigamo.

Now, explaining its meaning: since great learning, through skill in the aggregates, elements, etc., is capable of rejecting conceit. As it is said: ‘To what extent, venerable sir, is one greatly learned? When, bhikkhu, one is skilled in the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination, to that extent one is greatly learned.’ Therefore it was said: ‘…in regard to the aggregates, elements, sense bases, truths, conditionality, foundations of mindfulness, etc.’ Therein, making it come forth from the mouth is learning by heart. Questioning about the meaning is inquiry. Making a decision by way of examining and refuting along with the skillful is judgment. The paths, fruits, and Nibbāna are realization.

Bahūnaṃ [V 1.0055] (dha. sa. mūlaṭī. 1007) nānappakārānaṃ kilesasakkāyadiṭṭhīnaṃ avihatattā tā janenti, tāhi vā janitāti puthujjanā. Avighātameva vā jana-saddo vadati. Puthu satthārānaṃ mukhamullokikāti ettha puthu janā satthupaṭiññā etesanti puthujjanāti vacanattho. Puthu sabbagatīhi avuṭṭhitāti ettha janetabbā, jāyanti vā ettha sattāti janā, nānāgatiyo, tā puthū etesanti puthujjanā. Ito pare jāyanti etehīti janā, abhisaṅkhārādayo, te etesaṃ puthū vijjantīti puthujjanā. Abhisaṅkharaṇādiattho eva vā jana-saddo daṭṭhabbo. Oghā kāmoghādayo. Rāgaggiādayo santāpā. Te eva, sabbepi vā kilesā pariḷāhā. Puthu pañcasu kāmaguṇesu rattāti ettha jāyatīti jano, rāgo gedhoti evamādiko, puthu jano etesanti puthujjanā. Puthūsu vā janā jātā rattāti evaṃ rāgādiattho eva vā janasaddo daṭṭhabbo. Rattāti vatthaṃ viya raṅgajātena cittassa vipariṇāmakarena chandarāgena rattā sārattā. Giddhāti abhikaṅkhanasabhāvena abhijjhānena giddhā gedhaṃ āpannā. Gadhitāti ganthitā viya dummocanīyabhāvena tattha paṭibaddhā. Mucchitāti kilesavasena visaññībhūtā viya anaññakiccā mucchaṃ mohamāpannā. Ajjhosannāti anaññasādhāraṇe viya katvā gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā ṭhitā. Laggāti vaṅkadaṇḍake viya āsattā mahāpalipe vā yāva nāsikaggā palipannapuriso viya uddharituṃ asakkuṇeyyabhāvena nimuggā[M 1.0062], lagitāti makkaṭālepe ālaggabhāvena paccuḍḍito viya makkaṭo pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ vasena ālaggitā. Palibuddhāti baddhā, upaddutā vā. Āvuṭāti āvunitā, nivutāti nivāritā. Ovutāti paliguṇṭhitā, pariyonaddhā vā. Pihitāti pidahitā, paṭicchannāti paṭicchāditā. Paṭikujjitāti heṭṭhāmukhajātā. Puthūnaṃ vā gaṇanapathamatītānantiādinā puthu jano puthujjanoti dasseti.

Because they generate many kinds of unabandoned defilements and identity view, or because they are generated by them, they are 'puthujjanas' (ordinary people). Or the word 'jana' simply means non-destruction. In the phrase 'they look up to the faces of many teachers,' the meaning is: 'puthu' (many) are the 'janā' (people) who take them as teachers; hence 'puthujjanas.' In the phrase 'they have not emerged from all destinations,' 'janā' means the various destinations, because beings are to be born or are born there. 'Puthu' (many) are the 'janā' (destinations) for them; hence 'puthujjanas.' Further, 'janā' are that by which they are born, i.e., volitional formations, etc. For them, these 'janā' exist in 'puthu' (many) ways; hence 'puthujjanas.' Or the word 'jana' should be seen as having the meaning of forming volitions, etc. The floods are the flood of sensuality, etc. The fevers are the fire of lust, etc. These themselves, or all defilements, are torments. In the phrase 'they are attached to the five strands of sensual pleasure in many ways,' 'jano' is what is born, i.e., lust, greed, and so on. 'Puthu' (many) is the 'jano' for them; hence 'puthujjanas.' Or the word 'jana' should be seen as meaning lust, etc.—they are born and attached in many ways. 'Infatuated' (rattā) means they are impassioned, their minds altered by desire and lust like a cloth by dye. 'Greedy' (giddhā) means they are avaricious, having fallen into greed with a nature of intense longing. 'Ensnared' (gadhitā) means they are bound to them, hard to be freed, as if tied in a knot. 'Stupefied' (mucchitā) means they have fallen into a stupor, a delusion, as if they have become senseless through the defilements, with no other concern. 'Devoured' (ajjhosannā) means they have, as it were, made them their own, swallowed them, and settled down having consumed them. 'Stuck' (laggā) means they are submerged, as if in a great swamp, unable to pull themselves out, like a person sunk up to the tip of his nose; or 'clinging' (lagitā), like a monkey stuck fast to monkey-lime, they are stuck fast by way of the five sense faculties. 'Obstructed' (palibuddhā) means they are bound, or oppressed. 'Enveloped' (āvuṭā) means they are wrapped up, 'screened' (nivutā) means they are obstructed. 'Overspread' (ovutā) means they are cloaked, or veiled. 'Closed off' (pihitā) means they are shut, 'covered' (paṭicchannā) means they are concealed. 'Overturned' (paṭikujjitā) means they have become face-down. Or, it shows 'puthujjana' as 'a multitude of people' (puthu jano) by the phrase 'they have gone beyond the path of calculation,' etc.

“Assutavā”ti etena avijjandhatā vuttāti āha “andhaputhujjano vutto hotī”ti. Ārakattā (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.3.1) kilesehi maggena samucchinnattā. Anayeti avaḍḍhiyaṃ, anattheti attho. Anaye vā anupāye. Nairiyanato avattanato. Ayeti vaḍḍhiyaṃ, atthe, upāye vā. Araṇīyatoti payirupāsitabbato. Niruttinayena padasiddhi veditabbā purimesu atthavikappesu. Pacchime pana saddasatthavasenapi. Yadipi ariya-saddo “ye hi vo ariyā parisuddhakāyakammantā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.35) visuddhāsayapayogesu puthujjanesupi vattati. Idha pana ariyamaggādhigamena sabbalokuttarabhāvena ca ariyabhāvo adhippetoti dassento āha “buddhā”tiādi. Tattha “paccekabuddhā tathāgatasāvakā ca sappurisā”ti idaṃ ariyā sappurisāti idha vuttapadānaṃ atthaṃ asaṅkarato dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana nippariyāyato ariyasappurisabhāvā abhinnasabhāvā. Tasmā “sabbeva vā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

By ‘uninstructed one,’ the blindness of ignorance is stated; thus he says: ‘the blind worldling is spoken of.’ Because of remoteness from the defilements, since they have been cut off by the path. ‘In decline’ means in non-growth; the meaning is in what is unbeneficial. Or, ‘in decline’ means on a wrong course. From ‘not proceeding,’ from ‘not occurring.’ ‘In growth’ means in increase, in what is beneficial, or on the right course. From being ‘fit to be associated with,’ from being ‘fit to be attended upon.’ The derivation of the word should be understood by way of etymology in the former alternative meanings, but in the latter also by way of phonology. Although the word ‘noble’ is also used for worldlings in contexts of pure intention and practice, such as ‘those of you who are noble, of purified bodily conduct,’ etc., here, however, the noble state is intended by way of the attainment of the noble path and the state of being entirely supramundane. To show this, he says: ‘Buddhas,’ etc. Here, the phrase ‘Paccekabuddhas, disciples of the Tathāgata, and good persons’ is stated to show without confusion the meaning of the terms ‘noble ones’ and ‘good persons’ as used here. But since, in the definitive sense, the state of a noble one and the state of a good person are not different in nature, therefore it is said: ‘Or all indeed,’ etc.

Ettāvatā [V 1.0056] hi buddhasāvako vutto. Tassa hi ekantena kalyāṇamitto icchitabbo paratoghosamantarena paṭhamamaggassa anuppajjanato. Visesato cassa bhagavāva kalyāṇamitto adhippeto. Vuttañhetaṃ “mamañhi, ānanda, kalyāṇamittaṃ āgamma jātidhammā sattā jātiyā parimuccantī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.2). So eva ca aveccapasādādhigamena daḷhabhatti nāma. Vuttampi cetaṃ “yaṃ mayā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, taṃ mama sāvakā jīvitahetupi nātikkamantī”ti (udā. 45). Kataññutādīhi paccekabuddhā buddhāti ettha kataṃ jānātīti kataññū. Kataṃ viditaṃ pākaṭaṃ karotīti katavedī. Anekesupi hi kappasatasahassesu kataṃ upakāraṃ jānanti paccekabuddhā pākaṭañca karonti satijananaāmisapaṭiggahaṇādinā[M 1.0063], tathā saṃsāradukkhadukkhitassa sakkaccaṃ karonti kiccaṃ, yaṃ attanā kātuṃ sakkā. Sammāsambuddho pana kappānaṃ asaṅkhyeyyasahassesupi kataṃ upakāraṃ maggaphalānaṃ upanissayañca jānāti, pākaṭañca karoti, sīho viya ca evaṃ sabbattha sakkaccameva dhammadesanaṃ karonto buddhakiccaṃ karoti. Yāya paṭipattiyā diṭṭhā nāma honti, tassā appaṭipajjanabhāvo, tattha ca ādarābhāvo ariyānaṃ adassanasīlatā ca, na ca dassane sādhukāritā ca veditabbā. Cakkhunā adassāvīti etta cakkhu nāma na maṃsacakkhu eva, atha kho dibbacakkhupīti āha “dibbacakkhunā vā”ti. Ariyabhāvoti yehi yogato “ariyā”ti vuccanti. Te maggaphaladhammā daṭṭhabbā.

Thus far the disciple of the Buddha has been spoken of. For him, a spiritual friend should definitely be sought, because without the voice of another the first path does not arise. And in particular, the Blessed One himself is intended as the spiritual friend. For it has been said: ‘Indeed, Ānanda, it is by relying on me as a spiritual friend that beings subject to birth are freed from birth,’ and so on. And he it is who, through the attainment of confirmed confidence, is one of firm devotion. And it has been stated: ‘Whatever training rule I have laid down for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their lives.’ Because of gratitude and so on, Paccekabuddhas are called 'buddhas' (awakened ones). Here, one who knows what has been done is ‘grateful’ (kataññū). One who makes known what has been done is ‘one who shows gratitude’ (katavedī). For Paccekabuddhas know a help that was done even over many hundreds of thousands of eons and they make it manifest by such means as arousing mindfulness and accepting material offerings; similarly, for one afflicted with the suffering of saṃsāra, they respectfully do what needs to be done, whatever they are able to do themselves. The Perfectly Enlightened One, however, knows a help that was done even over incalculable thousands of eons, and its function as a supporting condition for the paths and fruits, and he makes it manifest; and like a lion, he performs the Buddha’s duty by teaching the Dhamma respectfully on all occasions. The fact of not undertaking the practice by which noble ones are seen, the lack of respect for it, the habit of not seeing the noble ones, and not acting rightly on seeing them—this should be understood. Herein, regarding ‘not seeing with the eye,’ the eye is not just the fleshly eye, but also the divine eye; thus he says ‘or with the divine eye.’ The noble state: those things because of connection with which they are called ‘noble ones.’ These path and fruit Dhammas are to be seen.

Tatrāti ñāṇadassanasseva dassanabhāve. Vatthūti adhippetatthañāpanakāraṇaṃ. Evaṃ vuttepīti evaṃ aññāpadesena attūpanāyikaṃ katvā vuttepi. Dhammanti lokuttaradhammaṃ, catusaccadhammaṃ vā. Ariyakaradhammā aniccānupassanādayo vipassiyamānā aniccādayo, cattāri vā ariyasaccāni.

‘Therein’: that is, in the state of seeing, which is precisely knowledge and vision. ‘The basis’: the reason for making known the intended meaning. ‘Even when it is said thus’: even when it is said having made it personally applicable by way of indirect reference. ‘The Dhamma’: the supramundane Dhamma, or the Dhamma of the Four Truths. ‘The noble-making Dhammas’: the contemplation of impermanence and so on; or impermanence and so on, being contemplated; or the Four Noble Truths.

Avinītoti na vinīto, adhisīlasikkhādivasena na sikkhito. Yesaṃ saṃvaravinayādīnaṃ abhāvena ayaṃ avinītoti vuccati, te tāva dassetuṃ “duvidho vinayo nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha sīlasaṃvaroti pātimokkhasaṃvaro veditabbo, so ca atthato kāyikavācasiko avītikkamo. Satisaṃvaroti indriyarakkhā, sā ca tathāpavattā sati eva. Ñāṇasaṃvaroti “sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmī”ti (su. ni. 1040) vatvā “paññāyete pidhīyare”ti vacanato sotasaṅkhātānaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhiduccaritaavijjāavasiṭṭhakilesānaṃ saṃvaro pidahanaṃ samucchedañāṇanti veditabbaṃ. Khantisaṃvaroti adhivāsanā, sā ca tathāpavattā khandhā, adoso vā. Paññāti eke, taṃ aṭṭhakathāya virujjhati. Vīriyasaṃvaro kāmavitakkādīnaṃ vinodanavasena [V 1.0057] pavattaṃ vīriyameva. Tena tena guṇaṅgena tassa tassa aguṇaṅgassa pahānaṃ tadaṅgapahānaṃ. Vikkhambhanena pahānaṃ vikkhambhanapahānaṃ. Sesapadatthayepi eseva nayo.

‘Undisciplined’ means not disciplined, not trained by way of the training in the higher virtue and so on. To show first those things—restraint, discipline, etc.—due to the absence of which one is called ‘undisciplined,’ he says: ‘Discipline is twofold,’ etc. Herein, ‘restraint by virtue’ should be understood as the Pātimokkha restraint, and that, in essence, is non-transgression by way of body and speech. ‘Restraint by mindfulness’ is the guarding of the sense faculties, and that is simply mindfulness so occurring. ‘Restraint by wisdom’ should be understood as the restraint, the closing off, the eradicating wisdom regarding the things called ‘streams’—namely, craving, wrong views, misconduct, ignorance, and the remaining defilements—in accordance with the words, ‘I speak of the restraint of the streams’ and ‘they are shut off by wisdom.’ ‘Restraint by patience’ is endurance, and that is patience so occurring, or non-hatred. Some say it is wisdom, but that contradicts the commentary. ‘Restraint by energy’ is simply the energy that proceeds by way of dispelling sensual thoughts and so on. The abandoning of this or that unwholesome quality by means of this or that wholesome quality is abandoning by substitution of opposites. Abandoning by suppression is abandoning by suppression. This same method applies to the meaning of the remaining terms.

Iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarenātiādi sīlasaṃvarādīnaṃ vivaraṇaṃ. Tattha samupetoti ettha iti-saddo ādisattho. Tena “sahagato samupagato”tiādinā [M 1.0064] vibhaṅge (vibha. 511) āgataṃ saṃvaravibhaṅgaṃ dasseti. Esa nayo sesesupi. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ anantarasutte āvi bhavissati.

‘By this Pātimokkha restraint,’ etc., is an explanation of restraint by virtue and so on. Herein, regarding ‘endowed’ (samupeto), the word ‘iti’ has the sense of ‘and so on.’ Thereby he indicates the analysis of restraint found in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh 511) with such phrases as ‘accompanied by, endowed with.’ This is the method in the other cases as well. Whatever should be said on this point will become clear in the next sutta.

Kāyaduccaritādīnanti dussīlyasaṅkhātānaṃ kāyavacīduccaritādīnaṃ muṭṭhassaccasaṅkhātassa pamādassa abhijjhādīnaṃ vā akkhantiaññāṇakosajjānañca. Saṃvaraṇatoti pidahanato thakanato. Vinayanatoti kāyavācācittānaṃ virūpappavattiyā vinayanato apanayanato, kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ vā vinayanato, kāyādīnaṃ vā jimhappavattiṃ vicchinditvā ujukaṃ nayanatoti attho. Paccayasamavāye uppajjanārahānaṃ kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ tathā tathā anuppādanameva saṃvaraṇaṃ vinayanañca veditabbaṃ.

‘Of bodily misconduct, etc.’: of bodily and verbal misconduct, etc., which are designated as immorality; of negligence, designated as forgetfulness; or of covetousness, etc., and of impatience, ignorance, and laziness. Because it restrains (saṃvaraṇato): because it closes off, because it obstructs. Because it disciplines (vinayanato): because it removes, it gets rid of, the improper activity of body, speech, and mind; or because it disciplines bodily misconduct, etc.; or the meaning is that it cuts off the crooked activity of the body, etc., and leads them straight. Restraint and discipline should be understood as precisely the non-arising, in such and such a way, of bodily misconduct, etc., which are liable to arise when there is a conjunction of conditions.

Yaṃ pahānanti sambandho. “Nāmarūpaparicchedādīsu vipassanāñāṇesū”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu nāmarūpaparicchedapaccayapariggahakaṅkhāvitaraṇāni na vipassanāñāṇāni sammasanākārena appavattanato? Saccametaṃ. Vipassanāñāṇassa pana adhiṭṭhānabhāvato evaṃ vuttaṃ. “Nāmarūpamattamidaṃ, natthi ettha attā vā attaniyaṃ vā”ti evaṃ pavattañāṇaṃ nāmarūpavavatthānaṃ. Sati vijjamāne khandhapañcakasaṅkhāte kāye, sayaṃ vā satī tasmiṃ kāye diṭṭhīti sakkāyadiṭṭhi. “Rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.81; 4.345) evaṃ pavattā micchādiṭṭhi. Tasseva rūpārūpassa kammāvijjādipaccayapariggaṇhanañāṇaṃ paccayapariggaho. “Natthi hetu natthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāyā”ti (dī. ni. 1.168) ādinayappavattā ahetukadiṭṭhi. “Issarapurisapajāpatipakatiaṇukālādīhi loko pavattati nivattati cā”ti pavattā visamahetudiṭṭhi. Tassevāti paccayapariggahasseva. Kaṅkhāvitaraṇenāti yathā etarahi nāmarūpassa kammādipaccayato uppatti, evaṃ atītānāgatesupīti tīsupi kālesu vicikicchāpanayanañāṇena. Kathaṃkathībhāvassāti “ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) ādinayappavattāya saṃsayappavattiyā. Kalāpasammasanenāti “yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppanna”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 1.361; 2.113; 3.86, 89) khandhapañcakaṃ ekādasasu okāsesu pakkhipitvā sammasanavasena pavattena nayavipassanāñāṇena[V 1.0058]. Ahaṃ mamāti gāhassāti attattaniyagahaṇassa. Maggāmaggavavatthānenāti maggāmaggañāṇavisuddhiyā. Amagge maggasaññāyāti obhāsādike amagge “maggo”ti uppannasaññāya.

The connection is with ‘what is abandoning.’ Why is it said, ‘in the insight knowledges such as the determination of mentality-materiality’? Is it not that the determination of mentality-materiality, the discerning of conditions, and the overcoming of doubt are not insight knowledges because they do not proceed in the mode of comprehension? This is true. However, it is said thus because they are the foundation for insight knowledge. The knowledge that proceeds thus, ‘This is merely mentality-materiality; there is no self or what belongs to a self here,’ is the determination of mentality-materiality. When the body designated as the five aggregates exists, the view that ‘I am’ in that body is identity view. The wrong view that proceeds thus, ‘One regards form as self’ (SN 3:81; 4:345). The knowledge that discerns the conditions—kamma, ignorance, etc.—of that same materiality and immateriality is the discerning of conditions. The view of causelessness, which proceeds in the manner of ‘There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings’ (DN 1:168), etc. The view of uneven cause, which proceeds thus: ‘The world proceeds and ceases due to a lord, a person, Prajāpati, nature, atoms, time, etc.’ ‘Of that same’: of that same discerning of conditions. ‘By overcoming of doubt’: by the knowledge that dispels doubt concerning the three periods of time, thinking: ‘Just as mentality-materiality now arises from kamma and other conditions, so it was in the past and so it will be in the future.’ ‘Of the state of uncertainty’: of the occurrence of doubt that proceeds in the manner of ‘Was I indeed in the past?’ (MN 1:18; SN 2:20), etc. ‘By comprehension of groups’: by the insight knowledge of the method that proceeds by way of comprehending the five aggregates after having placed them in the eleven instances with the words, ‘Whatever kind of materiality, whether past, future, or present,’ etc. (MN 1:361, etc.). ‘Of the grasp “I” and “mine”’: of the grasping of self and what belongs to a self. ‘By the determination of path and non-path’: by the purification of knowledge and vision of what is path and what is not path. ‘Of the perception of the path in the non-path’: of the perception that arises in regard to the non-path, such as the illumination, etc., thinking: ‘This is the path.’

Yasmā [M 1.0065] sammadeva saṅkhārānaṃ udayaṃ passanto “evameva saṅkhārā anurūpakāraṇato uppajjanti, na pana ucchijjantī”ti gaṇhāti, tasmā vuttaṃ “udayadassanena ucchedadiṭṭhiyā”ti. Yasmā pana saṅkhārānaṃ vayaṃ passanto “yadipime saṅkhārā avicchinnā vattanti, uppannuppannā pana appaṭisandhikā nirujjhante vā”ti passati, tassevaṃ passato kuto sassataggāho, tasmā vuttaṃ “vayadassanena sassatadiṭṭhiyā”ti. Bhayadassanenāti bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇena. Sabhayeti sabbabhayānaṃ ākarabhāvato sakaladukkhavūpasamasaṅkhātassa paramassāsassa paṭipakkhabhāvato ca sabhaye khandhapañcake. Abhayasaññāyāti “abhayaṃ khema”nti uppannasaññāya. Assādasaññā nāma pañcupādānakkhandhesu assādavasena pavattasaññā, yā “ālayābhiniveso”tipi vuccati. Abhiratisaññā tattheva abhirativasena pavattasaññā, yā “nandī”tipi vuccati. Amuccitukamyatā ādānaṃ. Anupekkhā saṅkhārehi anibbindanaṃ, sālayatāti attho. Dhammaṭṭhitiyaṃ paṭiccasamuppāde paṭilomabhāvo sassatucchedaggāho, paccayākārapaṭicchādakamoho vā, nibbāne paṭilomabhāvo saṅkhāresu rati, nibbānapaṭicchādakamoho vā. Saṅkhāranimittaggāhoti yādisassa kilesassa appahīnattā vipassanā saṅkhāranimittaṃ na muñcati, so kileso, yo “saṃyogābhiniveso”tipi vuccati. Saṅkhāranimittaggahaṇassa atikkamanameva vā pahānaṃ.

Because one who rightly sees the arising of formations understands, 'Formations arise from a corresponding cause, they are not annihilated,' therefore it is said: 'by seeing arising, [one abandons] the view of annihilation.' And because one who sees the passing away of formations understands, 'Although these formations continue without interruption, having arisen again and again they cease without any subsequent connection,' how could there be any grasping at eternalism for one who sees thus? Therefore it is said: 'by seeing passing away, [one abandons] the view of eternalism.' 'By seeing what is fearful' means by the knowledge of the appearance of what is fearful. 'In what is fearful' refers to the five aggregates, which are fearful because they are a source of all fears and the opposite of the ultimate solace, which is described as the appeasement of all suffering. 'The perception of safety' is the perception that arises as 'safety, security.' 'The perception of gratification' is the perception that occurs by way of gratification in the five aggregates subject to clinging, which is also called 'adherence to attachment.' 'The perception of delight' is the perception that occurs by way of delight in those same things, which is also called 'delight.' 'Unwillingness to be released' is grasping. 'Indifference' is not becoming disenchanted with formations; the meaning is being attached. 'Opposition to the stability of the Dhamma': in regard to dependent origination, this is the grasping at eternalism and annihilation, or the delusion that conceals the conditional structure; in regard to Nibbāna, this is delight in formations, or the delusion that conceals Nibbāna. 'Grasping at the sign of formations': this is the defilement which, because it is not abandoned, prevents insight from releasing the sign of formations; this defilement is also called 'adherence to the fetters.' Or, the overcoming of grasping at the sign of formations is itself the abandonment.

Pavatti eva pavattibhāvo, pariyuṭṭhānanti attho. Nīvaraṇādidhammānanti ettha ādi-saddena nīvaraṇapakkhiyā kilesā vitakkavicārādayo ca gayhanti.

'Occurrence' is the state of occurring; the meaning is manifestation. In the phrase 'of hindrances and other things,' the word 'other' includes the defilements allied with the hindrances, and also thought, examination, and so on.

Catunnaṃ ariyamaggānaṃ bhāvitattā accantaṃ appavattibhāvena yaṃ pahānanti sambandho. Kena pahānanti? Ariyamaggehevāti viññāyamānoyamattho tesaṃ bhāvitattā appavattivacanato. Samudayapakkhikassāti ettha cattāropi maggā catusaccābhisamayāti katvā tehi pahātabbena tena tena samudayena saha pahātabbattā samudayasabhāgattā, saccavibhaṅge ca sabbakilesānaṃ samudayabhāvassa vuttattā “samudayapakkhikā”ti diṭṭhiādayo vuccanti. Paṭippassaddhattaṃ vupasantatā. Saṅkhatanissaṭatā saṅkhārasabhāvābhāvo. Pahīnasabbasaṅkhatanti virahitasabbasaṅkhataṃ, visaṅkhāranti [V 1.0059] attho. Pahānañca taṃ vinayo cāti pahānavinayo purimena atthena, dutiyena pana pahīyatīti pahānaṃ, tassa vinayoti yojetabbaṃ.

The connection is: 'That which is abandonment through complete non-occurrence because the four noble paths have been developed.' By what is it abandoned? By the noble paths. This meaning is understood from the statement of non-occurrence due to their having been developed. 'Of what is on the side of origin': Here, since the four paths are the direct realization of the four truths, and since [the defilements] must be abandoned along with that particular origin which is to be abandoned by them, and since they share the nature of the origin, and since in the Analysis of the Truths it is said that all defilements have the nature of origin, views and so on are called 'on the side of origin.' 'Tranquility' is being pacified. 'Escape from the conditioned' is the absence of the nature of formations. 'That which has abandoned all that is conditioned' means devoid of all that is conditioned; the meaning is 'the unconditioned.' 'Abandonment-and-discipline' (pahānavinayo): according to the first meaning, it is a compound. But according to the second, it should be construed as: 'that which is abandoned is abandonment, and the discipline thereof.'

Bhinnasaṃvarattāti [M 1.0066] naṭṭhasaṃvarattā, saṃvarābhāvatoti attho. Tena asamādinnasaṃvaropi saṅgahito hoti. Samādānena hi sampādetabbo saṃvaro tadabhāve na hotīti. Evañhi loke vattāro honti “mahā vata no bhogo, so naṭṭho tathā akatattā”ti. Ariyeti ariyo. Paccattavacanañhetaṃ. Eseseti eso so eva, atthato anaññoti attho. Tajjāteti atthato taṃsabhāvo, sappuriso ariyasabhāvo, ariyo ca sappurisasabhāvoti attho.

'Because his restraint is broken' means because his restraint is destroyed, that is, because of the absence of restraint. By this, one who has not undertaken restraint is also included. For restraint is to be accomplished by undertaking it; in its absence, it does not exist. For people in the world are wont to say: 'Great, indeed, was our wealth, but it is lost because we did not act in such a way.' 'Noble' (ariye) means a noble one. This is a term for an individual. 'This very one' (es'eso) means 'this is that very one'; the meaning is that in essence he is not other. 'Of such a nature' (tajjāte) means that in essence he has that nature; the meaning is that a good person has a noble nature, and a noble one has the nature of a good person.

Taṃ atthanti “sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”nti evaṃ vuttamatthaṃ. Kasmā panettha puggalādhiṭṭhānā desanā katāti? Yadettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ “yasmā puthujjano apariññātavatthuko”tiādinā (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.2) sayameva vakkhati. Dhammo adhiṭṭhānaṃ etissāti dhammādhiṭṭhānā, sabhāvadhamme nissāya pavattitadesanā. Dhammavaseneva pavattā paṭhamā, puggalavasena uṭṭhahitvā puggalavaseneva gatā tatiyā, itarā dhammapuggalānaṃ vomissakavasena. Kasmā pana bhagavā evaṃ vibhāgena dhammaṃ desetīti? Veneyyajjhāsayena desanāvilāsena ca. Ye hi veneyyā dhammādhiṭṭhānāya dhammadesanāya sukhena atthaṃ paṭivijjhanti, tesaṃ tathā dhammaṃ deseti. Esa nayo sabbattha. Yassā ca dhammadhātuyā suppaṭividdhattā desanāvilāsappatto hoti, sāyaṃ suppaṭividdhā, tasmā desanāvilāsappatto dhammissaro dhammarājā yathā yathā icchati, tathā tathā dhammaṃ desetīti evaṃ iminā veneyyajjhāsayena desanāvilāsena ca evaṃ vibhāgena dhammaṃ desetīti veditabbo.

‘That meaning’ means the meaning stated as ‘the Discourse on the Root of All Things.’ Why was the teaching here given with a person as its basis? Whatever should be said on this, he himself will state with the words beginning: ‘Because a worldling has not fully comprehended the object….’ The Dhamma is its basis, thus it is ‘based on the Dhamma’; it is a teaching that proceeds by relying on intrinsic natures. The first proceeds solely by way of the Dhamma; the third, having arisen by way of a person, proceeds by way of a person; the other proceeds by way of a mixture of the Dhamma and persons. But why does the Blessed One teach the Dhamma with such a division? Because of the dispositions of those to be trained and because of the grace of his teaching. For he teaches the Dhamma in such a way to those to be trained who easily penetrate the meaning through a discourse on the Dhamma that is based on the Dhamma. This is the method everywhere. And because he has thoroughly penetrated the Dhamma element, he has attained the grace of teaching. Since it is thoroughly penetrated, he who has attained the grace of teaching, the lord of the Dhamma, the king of the Dhamma, teaches the Dhamma in whatever way he wishes. Thus it should be understood that he teaches the Dhamma with such a division because of the dispositions of those to be trained and because of the grace of his teaching.

Chadhāturoti pathavidhātu āpo-tejo-vāyo-ākāsadhātu viññāṇadhātūti imesaṃ channaṃ dhātūnaṃ vasena chadhāturo. “Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā somanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ rūpaṃ upavicaratī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 3.324) vuttānaṃ channaṃ somanassūpavicārānaṃ, channaṃ domanassaupekkhūpavicārānañca vasena aṭṭhārasamanopavicāro. Saccādhiṭṭhānādivasena caturādhiṭṭhāno. Paññācakkhunā diṭṭhadhammikassa samparāyikassa ca atthassa adassanato andho, diṭṭhadhammikasseva dassanato ekacakkhu, dvinnampi dassanato dvicakkhu, veditabbo.

‘A person of six elements’: this is by way of the six elements: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element. ‘Having eighteen mental explorations’: this is by way of the six mental explorations connected with gladness, and the six connected with sadness and with equanimity, spoken of in the text beginning: ‘Having seen a form with the eye, one explores a form that is a basis for gladness.’ ‘Having four determinations’: this is by way of the four determinations, beginning with the determination of truth. One who does not see with the eye of wisdom the good pertaining both to the present life and to the future life is blind; one who sees only the good pertaining to the present life is one-eyed; one who sees the good of both is two-eyed—this should be understood.

Svāyaṃ [M 1.0067] niddisīti sambandho. Svāyanti ca so ayaṃ, yathāvuttadesanāvibhāgakusalo bhagavāti attho. Apariññātavatthukoti tīhi pariññāhi apariññātakkhandho. Khandhā hi pariññātavatthu. Apariññāmūlikāti parijānanābhāvanimittā tasmiṃ sati bhāvato. Pariññānañhi [V 1.0060] avijjādayo kilesā paṭipakkhā tammūlikā ca sabbamaññanāti. Ariyānaṃ adassāvīti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho. Tena “ariyadhammassa akovido”tiādikaṃ puthujanassa visesanabhāvena pavattaṃ pāḷisesaṃ gaṇhāti puthujjananiddesabhāvato. Tenāha “evaṃ puthujjanaṃ niddisī”ti.

The connection is: ‘This one designated.’ And ‘this one’ (svāyaṃ) means ‘he, this one’; the meaning is the Blessed One, who is skilled in the divisions of the teaching as stated above. ‘One for whom the subject matter is uncomprehended’ means one whose aggregates are uncomprehended by the three kinds of full understanding (pariññā). For the aggregates are the subject matter to be fully understood. ‘Rooted in non-comprehension’ means that because of the absence of full understanding, it is the cause of its existence. For ignorance and the other defilements are the opponents of full understanding, and all conceiving is rooted in them. ‘Not a seer of the noble ones’: here the word iti has the sense of ‘and so on.’ Thereby it includes the rest of the Pāli text that occurs as a qualification of the worldling, beginning ‘unskilled in the noble Dhamma,’ because this is an exposition of the worldling. Therefore he said: ‘Thus he designated the worldling.’

Suttanikkhepavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of the Sutta is finished.

Pathavīvāravaṇṇanā

An Exposition of the Earth Section

Tassāti puthujjanassa. Vasati ettha ārammaṇakaraṇavasenāti ārammaṇampi vatthūti vuccati pavattiṭṭhānabhāvatoti āha “pathavīādīsu vatthūsū”ti. Sakkāyadhammānampi ārammaṇādinā satipi maññanāhetubhāve maññanāhetukatteneva tesaṃ nibbattitoti vuttaṃ “sabbasakkāyadhammajanitaṃ maññana”nti. Ettha ca pathavīdhātu sesadhātūnaṃ sasambhārāsambhārabhāvā satipi pamāṇato samabhāve sāmatthiyato adhikānadhikabhāvena veditabbā. Sambhārantīti sambhārā, parivārā. Taṃtaṃkalāpehi lakkhaṇapathaviyā sesadhammā yathārahaṃ paccayabhāvena parivārabhāvena ca pavattanti. Tenāha “sā hi vaṇṇādīhi sambhārehi saddhiṃ pathavīti sasambhārapathavī”ti. Pathavitoti ettha puthulaṭṭhena puthuvī, puthuvī eva pathavī. Sā hi satipi paricchinnavuttiyaṃ sabbesaṃ sakalāpabhāvānaṃ ādhārabhāvena pavattamānā puthulā patthaṭā vitthiṇṇāti vattabbataṃ arahati, na pana taṃ anupavisitvā pavattamānā āpādayo. Sasambhārapathaviyā pana puthulabhāve vattabbameva natthi. Ārammaṇapathaviyaṃ vaḍḍhanapharaṇaṭṭhehi puthulaṭṭho, itarasmiṃ ruḷhiyāva daṭṭhabbo. Ārammaṇapathavīti jhānassa ārammaṇabhūtaṃ pathavīsaṅkhātaṃ paṭibhāganimittaṃ. Tenāha “nimittapathavītipi vuccatī”ti. Āgamanavasenāti pathavīkasiṇabhāvanāgamanavasena. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “āpo ca devā pathavī, tejo vāyo tadāgamu”nti (dī. ni. 2.340).

Of that: of the worldling. Because it serves as an object, the object is also called a ‘basis’ since it is a place of occurrence; thus he said: ‘in bases such as earth, etc.’ Although the phenomena of identity are a cause for conceiving by way of being an object, etc., their production is due to their being a cause for conceiving; thus it is said: ‘all conceiving is generated by the phenomena of identity.’ Here, the earth element, in relation to the other elements, should be understood as being superior or inferior in terms of capacity, although it is equal in measure, whether it is with or without its constituents. Constituents (sambhārā) are so called because they constitute; they are the retinue (parivārā). In the respective material groups, the other phenomena occur in dependence on the earth-as-characteristic, appropriately as conditions and as a retinue. Therefore he said: ‘For it is earth together with its constituents such as color, etc.; this is earth-with-its-constituents.’ Here, pathavī is puthuvī in the sense of being extensive (puthula); puthuvī is just pathavī. For although it has a limited function, since it occurs as the support for all things existing in groups, it deserves to be called extensive, spread out, and wide; but not so water and the other elements, which occur by pervading it. As for earth-with-its-constituents, however, there is no need to speak of its extensiveness. In the case of the object-earth, the sense of ‘extensive’ is due to its meaning of expansion and pervasion; in the other case, it should be understood simply by convention. The object-earth is the counterpart sign called ‘earth,’ which is the object of jhāna. Therefore he said: ‘It is also called the sign-earth.’ By way of the text: by way of the text on the development of the earth kasiṇa. For thus it is said: ‘And the devas of water, earth, fire, and air came there.’

Sabbāpīti catubbidhā pathavīpi. Anussavādimattaladdhā maññanā vatthu hotiyeva. Tathā hi “kakkhaḷaṃ kharigata”ntiādinā (vibha. 173) lakkhaṇapathavīpi uddharīyati. Yaṃ [M 1.0068] paneke vadanti “lakkhaṇe diṭṭhe maññanā natthi, sañjānātīti vuttasaññā ca diṭṭhiggāhassa mūlabhūtā piṇḍaggāhitā, sā lakkhaṇe nakkhamati, tasmā lakkhaṇapathavī na gahetabbā”ti, tadayuttaṃ lakkhaṇapaṭivedhassa idha anadhippetattā. Tenāha “lokavohāraṃ gahetvā”ti. Na ca sabbasaññā piṇḍaggāhikā[V 1.0061], nāpi diṭṭhiggāhasseva mūlabhūtā, tasmā lakkhaṇapathaviyāpi kāyadvārānusārena aññathā ca upaṭṭhitāya maññanā pavattateva. Teneva ca “anussavādimattaladdhā”ti vuttaṃ. Pathavitoti paccate nissakkavacananti dassento “pathavīti sañjānātī”ti āha. Yasmā catubbidhampi pathaviṃ “pathavī’ti sañjānanto tena tena nayena pathavīkoṭṭhāseneva sañjānātīti vuccati, na āpādikoṭṭhāsena, tasmā vuttaṃ “pathavibhāgena sañjānātī”ti. Lokavohāraṃ gahetvāti lokasamaññaṃ avijahitvā. Etena lakkhaṇapathaviyampi vohāramukhenevassā pavattīti dasseti.

All: even the four kinds of earth. Conceiving based merely on what is obtained through hearsay and so on is indeed a basis. For thus even the earth-as-characteristic is adduced by way of such phrases as ‘the hard, the harsh.’ But what some say—‘When the characteristic is seen, there is no conceiving.
