The perception spoken of as “he perceives” is a grasping of the mass, the root of the grasp of views; this is not fit for the characteristic. Therefore the earth-as-characteristic should not be taken’—that is incorrect, because penetration of the characteristic is not intended here. Therefore he said: ‘having taken worldly convention.’ For not all perception is a grasping of the mass, nor is it only the root of the grasp of views. Therefore, conceiving does indeed occur in regard to the earth-as-characteristic when it has arisen in accordance with the body-door and otherwise. And for that reason it was said: ‘obtained merely through hearsay, etc.’ Showing that the word ‘earth’ is a specific, unambiguous term, he said: ‘he perceives as “earth.”’ Since one who perceives the fourfold earth as ‘earth’ is said to perceive it in this or that way as a part of earth, not as a part of water, etc., therefore it was said: ‘he perceives by way of the earth part.’ ‘Having taken worldly convention’ means not having abandoned the worldly designation. By this he shows that its occurrence, even in the case of the earth-as-characteristic, is only through the door of convention.

Yadi lokavohārena tattha pavatti, ko ettha doso, nanu ariyāpi “ayañhi bhante mahāpathavī”tiādinā lokavohārena pavattantīti? Na ettha vohāramatte avaṭṭhānaṃ adhippetaṃ, atha kho vohāramukhena micchābhinivesoti dassento “saññāvipallāsena sañjānātī”ti āha. Tassattho – ayonisomanasikārasambhūtāya “subha”ntiādinayappavattāya viparītasaññāya sañjānātīti. Etena dubbalā taṇhāmānadiṭṭhimaññanā dassitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kasmā saññā gahitāti? Pākaṭabhāvato. Yathā nāma aggimhi mathiyamāne yadā dhūmo upalabbhati, kiñcāpi tadā vijjateva pāvako avinābhāvato, pākaṭabhāvato pana dhūmo jātoti vuccati, na aggi jātoti, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yadipi tattha maññanākiccaṃ atthi, na pana vibhūtaṃ apākaṭabhāvato saññākiccameva vibhūtaṃ, taṃ pana maññanānukūlaṃ maññanāsahitaṃ cāti āha “saññāvipallāsena sañjānātī”ti. Evaṃ pathavībhāgaṃ amuñcantoyeva vā sañjānātīti sambandho. Yo hi vuttappabhedāya pathaviyā pathavibhāgaṃ amuñcantoyeva avijahantoyeva sīsapiṇḍe suvaṇṇasaññī viya anattādisabhāvaṃyeva taṃ attādivasena sañjānāti, tassa vasena vuttaṃ “pathavī”tiādi. Na vattabbaṃ puthujjanaggāhassa yuttimaggananivāraṇatoti dassento āha “ummattako viya…pe… gaṇhātī”ti[M 1.0069]. Ariyānaṃ adassāvitādibhedanti ariyānaṃ adassāvitādivisesaṃ vadantena bhagavatāva ettha yathāvuttasañjānane kāraṇaṃ vuttanti yojanā.

If its occurrence is by way of worldly convention, what is the fault in that? Do not the noble ones too proceed by worldly convention, saying, 'Venerable sir, this great earth,' etc.? It is not mere reliance on convention that is intended here, but rather wrong adherence by way of convention. To show this, he said: 'he perceives with distortion of perception.' The meaning of this is: he perceives with a perverted perception that has arisen from unwise attention and proceeds in the manner of 'beautiful,' etc. It should be understood that by this the subtle conceivings of craving, conceit, and views are indicated. If so, why is perception taken up? Because of its manifestness. For example, when fire is being kindled by friction, smoke is found. Although fire is also present then due to their inseparability, because of its manifestness it is said, 'smoke has arisen,' not 'fire has arisen.' This should be understood in the same way. Although the function of conceiving is present there, it is not manifest, being unapparent. The function of perception, however, is manifest. Since it is favorable to conceiving and accompanied by conceiving, he said: 'he perceives with distortion of perception.' Or the connection is as follows: 'Thus he perceives while not abandoning the earth part.' For in reference to one who, not abandoning the earth part of the aforesaid kinds, perceives that very thing—which has the nature of non-self, etc.—as self, etc., like one who perceives gold in a lump of lead, it was said: 'earth,' etc. He said, 'like a madman... he grasps,' to show that the worldling's grasp is not something to be discussed, as it obstructs the path of reasoning. The connection is that the reason for perceiving in the aforesaid way has been stated here by the Blessed One himself when he speaks of the special quality of the noble ones, namely, that it is not shown to them, etc.

Evanti “pathavibhāgena sañjānātī”tiādinā vuttappakārena. Sañjānitvāti pubbakālakiriyāniddesoti āha “aparabhāge…pe… gaṇhātī”ti. Papañcasaṅkhāti papañcakoṭṭhāsā. Papañcanti sattā saṃsāre cirāyanti etehīti papañcā, maññanti “etaṃ mamā”tiādinā parikappenti etāhīti maññanāti dvīhipi pariyāyehi taṇhādayova vuttāti āha “taṇhāmānadiṭṭhipapañcehi idha maññanānāmena vuttehī”ti. Ajaññassa jaññato, aseyyādikassa [V 1.0062] seyyādito gahaṇato diṭṭhimaññanā viya taṇhāmānamaññanāpi aññathā gāho evāti āha “aññathā gaṇhātī”ti. Ārammaṇābhiniropanādinā bhinnasabhāvānampi vitakkādīnaṃ sādhāraṇo upanijjhāyanasabhāvo viya anugijjhanuṇṇatiparāmasanasabhāvānampi taṇhādīnaṃ sādhāraṇena ārammaṇaparikappanākārena pavatti maññanāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha “tīhi maññanāhi maññatī”tiādi. Assāti puthujjanassa, udayabbayānupassanādīsu viya sukhumanayenapi maññanāpavatti atthīti vibhāvanasukhatāya thūlaṃyeva taṃ dassetukāmo “oḷārikanayenā”tiāha. Oḷārike hi vibhāge dassite sukhumavibhāvanā sukarāti dassetuṃ ayamatthayojanā vuccatīti sambandho. Ajjhattikāti indriyabaddhā sattasantānapariyāpannā niyakajjhattā vuttā vibhaṅge paṭisambhidāmagge ca.

Thus: in the manner stated, 'he perceives by way of the earth part,' etc. 'Having perceived' is a statement of a prior action; thus he said: 'at a later time... he grasps.' The parts of proliferation. Proliferations (papañca): beings are delayed in saṃsāra by these, thus they are proliferations. Conceivings (maññanā): they conceive, they imagine by means of these with 'this is mine,' etc., thus they are conceivings. In both ways, craving, etc., are meant; thus he said: 'by the proliferations of craving, conceit, and views, which are here called by the name "conceiving."' Just as the conceiving of views is a wrong grasp because one grasps what is not known as known, what is not a bed, etc., as a bed, etc., so too the conceivings of craving and conceit are a wrong grasp; thus he said: 'he grasps otherwise.' Just as thought, etc., though having different natures by way of directing the mind toward an object, etc., have the common nature of close examination, so too it should be understood that for craving, etc., which have the natures of coveting, elation, and misapprehending, their occurrence in the common mode of fashioning an object is 'conceiving.' Therefore he said: 'he conceives with the three conceivings,' etc. Of this one: of the worldling. Just as in the contemplation of rise and fall, etc., there is an occurrence of conceiving even in a subtle way, wishing to show it only in a gross way for the sake of easy explanation, he said: 'by the gross method.' The connection is that this connection of meaning is stated to show that when the gross division is shown, the subtle explanation is easy. Internal: connected with the faculties, included in the continuity of a being, one's own internal, as stated in the Vibhaṅga and the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

Vibhaṅgeti dhātuvibhaṅge (vibha. 173). Bāhirāti anindriyabaddhā saṅkhārasantānapariyāpannā. Kakkhaḷanti thaddhaṃ. Kharigatanti pharusaṃ. Kakkhaḷabhāvo kakkhaḷattaṃ. Kakkhaḷabhāvoti kakkhaḷasabhāvo. Bahiddhāti indriyabaddhato bahiddhābhūtaṃ. Anupādinnanti na upādinnaṃ. Ayoti kāḷalohaṃ. Lohanti jātilohaṃ vijātilohaṃ kittimalohaṃ pisācalohanti catubbidhaṃ. Tattha ayo sajjhu suvaṇṇaṃ tipu sīsaṃ tambalohaṃ vekantakalohanti imāni satta jātilohāni nāma. Nāganāsikālohaṃ vijātilohaṃ nāma. Kaṃsalohaṃ vaṭṭalohaṃ ārakuṭanti tīṇi kittimalohāni nāma. Morakkhakaṃ puthukaṃ malinakaṃ capalakaṃ salakaṃ āṭalaṃ bhattakaṃ [M 1.0070] dusilohanti aṭṭha pisācalohāni nāma. Tesu vekantakalohaṃ nāma sabbalohacchedanasamatthā ekā lohajāti. Tathā hi taṃ vikantati chindatīti vikantakanti vuccati. Vikantakameva vekantakaṃ. Nāganāsikālohaṃ lohasadisaṃ lohavijāti haliddādivijāti viya. Tathā hi taṃ lohākāraṃ lohamalaṃ viya ghanasaṃhataṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati, tāpetvā tāḷitaṃ pana bhinnaṃ bhinnaṃ hutvā visarati mudu maṭṭhaṃ kammaniyaṃ vā na hoti. Tiputambe missetvā kataṃ kaṃsalohaṃ. Sīsatambe missetvā kataṃ vaṭṭalohaṃ. Jasatambe missetvā kataṃ ārakuṭaṃ. Teneva taṃ karaṇena nibbattattā kittimalohanti vuccati. Yaṃ pana kevalaṃ rasakadhātu viniggataṃ, taṃ “pittala”ntipi vadanti. Taṃ idha nādhippetaṃ, yathāvuttaṃ missakameva katvā yojitaṃ kittimanti vuttaṃ. Morakkhakādīni evaṃnāmānevetāni. Tesu yasmā pañca jātilohāni pāḷiyaṃ visuṃ vuttāneva, tasmā vekantakalohena saddhiṃ vuttāvasesaṃ sabbaṃ idha lohanti veditabbaṃ.

In the Vibhaṅga means in the Analysis of Elements (Vibh. 173). “External” means not bound to the sense faculties but included in the continuum of formations. “Hard” means stiff. “Coarse” means rough. The state of hardness is hardness. The nature of hardness is the intrinsic quality of hardness. “External” means what exists outside of being bound to the sense faculties. “Unappropriated” means not appropriated. “Iron” means black iron. “Metal” is of four kinds: natural metal, processed metal, artificial metal, and base metal. Among these, iron, silver, gold, tin, lead, copper, and vekantaka metal—these seven are called natural metals. Nāganāsikā metal is called processed metal. Bronze, vaṭṭa metal, and brass—these three are called artificial metals. Morakkhaka, puthuka, malinaka, capalaka, salaka, āṭala, bhattaka, and dusiloha—these eight are called base metals. Among these, vekantaka metal is a type of metal capable of cutting all other metals. For this reason, it is called “vikantaka” because it cuts and severs. Vikantaka is simply vekantaka. Nāganāsikā metal resembles metal but is a different species of it, just as there are different species of turmeric. Indeed, it takes the form of metal and remains solid like metal dross, but when heated and hammered, it shatters into pieces and does not become soft, smooth, or workable. Bronze is made by mixing tin and copper. Vaṭṭa metal is made by mixing lead and copper. Brass is made by mixing zinc and copper. Because they are produced by such a process, they are called artificial metals. What is produced solely from the element of mercury is also called “pittala,” but that is not intended here. Only what is mixed as described and used is called “artificial.” Morakkhaka and the others are simply known by these names. Among these, since five natural metals are separately mentioned in the Pāli text, the rest, along with vekantaka metal, should be understood here as “metal.”

Tipūti setatipu. Sīsanti kāḷatipu. Sajjhanti rajataṃ. Muttāti hatthikumbhajādikā aṭṭhavidhāpi muttā. Tathā hi hatthikumbhaṃ varāhadāṭhā bhūjaṅgasīsaṃ valāhakūṭaṃ veḷū macchasīro saṅkho [V 1.0063] sippīti aṭṭha muttāyoniyo. Tattha hatthikumbhajā pītavaṇṇā pabhāhīnā. Varāhadāṭhā varāhadāṭhavaṇṇāva. Bhujaṅgasīsajā nīlādivaṇṇā suvisuddhā vaṭṭalā ca. Valāhakajā bhāsurā dubbibhāgarūpā rattibhāge andhakāraṃ vidhamantiyo tiṭṭhanti, devūpabhogā eva ca honti. Veḷujā karakupalasamānavaṇṇā na bhāsurā, te ca veḷū amanussagocare eva padese jāyanti. Macchasīrajā pāṭhīnapiṭṭhisamānavaṇṇā vaṭṭalā laghavo ca honti pabhāvihīnā, te ca macchā samuddamajjhe eva jāyanti. Saṅkhajā saṅkhodaracchavivaṇṇā kolappamāṇāpi honti pabhāvihīnāva. Sippijā pabhāvisesayuttā honti nānāsaṇṭhānā. Evaṃ jātito aṭṭhavidhāsupi muttāsu yā macchasaṅkhasippijā, tā sāmuddikā honti, bhujaṅgajāpi kāci sāmuddikā honti, itarā asāmuddikā. Yasmā bahulaṃ sāmuddikāva muttā loke dissanti, tatthāpi sippijāva, itarā kādācikā. Tasmā sammohavinodaniyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 173) “muttāti sāmuddikā muttā”ti vuttaṃ.

“Tin” (tipu) is white tin; “lead” (sīsa) is black tin. “Silver” (sajjha) is rajata. Pearls are of eight kinds, those born from an elephant’s frontal globes and so on. For there are eight sources of pearls: an elephant’s frontal globes, a boar’s tusks, a serpent’s head, a thundercloud, a bamboo stem, a fish’s head, a conch, and an oyster. Among these, those born from an elephant’s frontal globes are yellowish and lack luster. Those from a boar’s tusks are the color of a boar’s tusk. Those born from a serpent’s head are of various colors such as blue, are very pure, and are round. Those born from a thundercloud are radiant, their form is hard to discern, they dispel darkness at night, and they are only for the enjoyment of devas. Those born from bamboo are the color of a water-pot sherd and are not radiant; and those bamboos grow only in a region frequented by non-humans. Those born from a fish’s head are the color of a pāṭhīna fish’s back, are round and light, and lack luster; and those fish are born only in the middle of the ocean. Those born from a conch are the color of the inner surface of a conch, can be the size of a jujube fruit, and also lack luster. Those born from an oyster possess a special radiance and have various shapes. Thus, among the eight kinds of pearls by origin, those from fish, conch, and oyster are marine. Some born from serpents are also marine; the others are non-marine. Since it is mostly marine pearls that are seen in the world, and among those, mostly pearls from oysters—the others being occasional—it is therefore said in the Sammohavinodanī (Vibh-a 173): “A pearl is a marine pearl.”

Maṇīti [M 1.0071] ṭhapetvā pāḷiāgate veḷuriyādike seso jotirasādibhedo sabbopi maṇi. Veḷuriyanti vaṃsavaṇṇamaṇi. Saṅkhoti sāmuddikasaṅkho. Silāti kāḷasilā paṇḍusilā setasilādibhedā aṭṭhapi silā. Rajatanti kahāpaṇādikaṃ vuttāvasesaṃ rajatasammataṃ. Jātarūpanti suvaṇṇaṃ. Lohitaṅgoti rattamaṇi. Masāragallanti kabaramaṇi tiṇādīsu bahibhārā tālanāḷikerādayopi tiṇaṃ nāma. Antosāraṃ khadirādi antamaso dārukhaṇḍampi kaṭṭhaṃ nāma. Muggamattato yāva muṭṭhippamāṇā marumbā sakkharā nāma. Muggamattato paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā vālikā nāma. Kaṭhalanti kapālakhaṇḍaṃ. Bhūmīti sasambhārapathavī. Pāsāṇoti antomuṭṭhiyaṃ asaṇṭhahanato paṭṭhāya yāva hatthippamāṇaṃ pāsāṇaṃ, hatthippamāṇato pana paṭṭhāya upari pabbatoti. Ayaṃ ayoādīsu vibhāganiddeso. Nimittapathavīti paṭibhāganimittabhūtaṃ pathavikasiṇaṃ. Tampi hi “rūpāvacaratikacatukkajjhānaṃ kusalato ca vipākato ca kiriyato ca catutthassa jhānassa vipāko ime dhammā bahiddhārammaṇā”ti vacanato “bāhirā pathavī”ti vuccati. Tena vuttaṃ “yā ca ajjhattārammaṇattike nimittapathavī, taṃ gahetvā”ti. Uggahanimittañcettha taṃgatikameva daṭṭhabbaṃ, nimittuppattito pana pubbe bhūmiggahaṇeneva gahitanti.

“Gem” (maṇi): Setting aside those mentioned in the Pāli canon such as beryl (veḷuriya), all the rest, distinguished by their luster and so on, are gems. “Beryl” (veḷuriya) is a gem the color of bamboo. “Conch” (saṅkha) is a sea conch. “Stone” (silā): There are eight kinds of stone, such as black stone, pale-yellow stone, and white stone. “Silver” (rajata) is what is considered silver, such as coins (kahāpaṇa), and the rest of what has been mentioned. “Gold” (jātarūpa) is suvaṇṇa. “Ruby” (lohitaṅga) is a red gem. “Cat’s eye” (masāragalla) is a variegated gem. Among things like grass, those with an external core such as palm and coconut trees are also called “grass” (tiṇa). Those with an internal core, such as the khadira tree, down to a piece of timber, are called “wood” (kaṭṭha). Coarse sand (marumbā) from the size of a mung bean up to the size of a fist is called “gravel” (sakkharā). What is smaller than a mung bean is called “sand” (vālikā). “Potsherd” (kaṭhala) is a fragment of a pot. “Earth” (bhūmi) is the earth element with its constituents. “Rock” (pāsāṇa) is from a size that cannot be held in the fist up to the size of an elephant; from the size of an elephant upwards it is called a “mountain” (pabbata). This is the detailed classification of iron, etc. The “sign of earth” (nimittapathavī) is the earth kasiṇa that has become the counterpart sign. For this too is called “external earth” in accordance with the statement: “The four jhānas of the form sphere—wholesome, resultant, and functional—and the resultant of the fourth jhāna: these states have an external object.” Thus it is said: “…taking the sign of earth, which is in the triad of internal objects.” And here the learning sign should be seen as having the same destination, for before the arising of the sign, it is grasped simply by the taking up of the earth.

Tīhi maññanāhīti vuttaṃ maññanāttayaṃ saparasantānesu saṅkhepato yojetvā dassetuṃ “ahaṃ pathavī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ahaṃ pathavītiādīnā ajjhattavisayaṃ diṭṭhimaññanaṃ mānamaññanañca dasseti attābhinivesāhaṃkāradīpanato. Mama pathavīti iminā taṇhāmaññanaṃ mānamaññanampi vā pariggahabhūtāyapi pathaviyā seyyādito mānajappanato. Sesapadadvayepi iminānayena maññanāvibhāgo [V 1.0064] veditabbo. Tattha pathavikasiṇajjhānalābhī jhānacakkhunā gahitajhānārammaṇaṃ “attā”ti abhinivisanto tañca seyyādito dahanto atthato “ahaṃ pathavī”ti maññati nāma, tameva “ayaṃ mayhaṃ attā”ti gahaṇe pana “mama pathavī”ti maññati nāma. Tathā taṃ “parapuriso”ti vā “devo”ti vā vādavasena “ayameva paresaṃ attā”ti vā abhinivisanto “paro pathavī, parassa pathavī”ti maññati nāma. Iminā nayena sesapathavīsupi yathārahaṃ catukkaṃ niddhāretabbaṃ.

To show how the triad of conceivings mentioned in the phrase “by three conceivings” is to be briefly applied to one’s own and others’ continuities, the passage beginning “I am earth” was stated. Here, the phrases beginning “I am earth” show, in regard to the internal, conceiving through view and conceiving through conceit, because they reveal adherence to a self and I-making. By the phrase “my earth,” conceiving through craving and also conceiving through conceit are shown, because of conceited muttering based on superiority, etc., even in regard to the earth that has become one’s possession. The division of conceivings in the remaining two phrases should be understood in the same way. Here, one who has attained the earth-kasiṇa jhāna, adhering to the jhāna object grasped with the jhāna-eye as “self” and considering it as superior, etc., in effect conceives, “I am earth.” But when one grasps it as “this is my self,” one conceives, “my earth.” Similarly, on the basis of the assertion “this is another person” or “this is a deva,” or by adhering to it as “this is another’s self,” one conceives, “another is earth, another’s is earth.” In this way, the tetrad should be determined as appropriate for the remaining instances of earth.

Evaṃ “pathaviṃ maññatī”ti ettha catukkavasena maññanaṃ dassetvā idāni maññanāvatthuṃ maññanāyo ca vibhajitvā anekavihitaṃ tassa maññanākāraṃ [M 1.0072] dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādimāha. Tattha ayanti yathāvutto puthujjano. Chandarāganti bahalarāgaṃ. Assādetīti nikāmeti, “ime kesā mudusiniddhakuñcitanīlobhāsā”tiādinā tattha rasaṃ vindati. Abhinandatīti sappītikāya taṇhāya abhimukho nandati pamodati. Abhivadatīti uppannaṃ taṇhābhinandanāvegaṃ hadayena sandhāretuṃ asakkonto “aho me kesā”ti vācaṃ nicchāreti. Ajjhosāya tiṭṭhatīti balavataṇhābhinivesena gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpetvā tiṭṭhati. Aññataraṃ vā pana rajjanīyavatthunti kesādito aññataraṃ vā karacaraṇādippabhedaṃ niyakajjhattapariyāpannaṃ rāguppattihetubhūtaṃ vatthuṃ. Itīti iminā siniddhādippakārenāti patthayitabbākāraṃ parāmasati. Tattha nandiṃ samannānetīti tesu bhāvīsu kesādīsu siddhaṃ viya katvā nandiṃ taṇhaṃ samannāharati samupacāreti. Paṇidahatīti patthanaṃ ṭhapeti.

Thus, in the phrase “he conceives earth,” having shown conceiving by way of a tetrad, now, to show the various modes of that conceiving by analyzing the object of conceiving and the conceivings themselves, the passage beginning “Or else…” is stated. Herein, “this one” refers to the aforementioned ordinary person. “Lustful desire” means intense lust. “He delights in it” means he desires it; he finds a taste in it, thinking, “These hairs are soft, smooth, curly, and dark blue,” etc. “He rejoices in it” means he faces it with craving accompanied by joy, he delights and exults. “He speaks in praise of it” means, being unable to contain in his heart the force of the craving and rejoicing that has arisen, he utters the words, “Oh, my hair!” “He remains clinging to it” means he remains, having been engulfed and consumed by the strong adherence of craving. “Or some other alluring object” means some other object, such as the various parts of one’s own body like hands and feet, which is a cause for the arising of lust. “Thus” refers to the longed-for mode, grasping it in the manner of smoothness, etc. Herein, “he arouses delight” means that, treating those future hairs, etc., as if they were already accomplished, he brings to bear and applies delight, that is, craving. “He makes an aspiration” means he establishes a wish.

Sampattiṃ nissāya “seyyohamasmī”ti, vipattiṃ nissāya “hīnohamasmī”ti mānaṃ janetīti yojanā. Pathavīkoṭṭhāsabhūtānaṃ kesādīnaṃ sampattivipattīhi mānajappanā pathaviyā maññanā hotīti āha “evaṃ ajjhattikaṃ pathaviṃ mānamaññanāya maññatī”ti. Avayavabyatirekena samudāyassa abhāvato samudāyo jīvābhiniveso avayavepi hotīti dassento “taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīranti āgatanayena pana kesaṃ ‘jīvo’ti abhinivisatī”ti āha. “Kesā nāmete issaravihitā pajāpatinissitā aṇusañcayo pakatipariṇāmo”tiādinā nayenapettha diṭṭhimaññanā veditabbā.

The connection is: “Depending on success, he generates the conceit, ‘I am superior’; depending on failure, he generates the conceit, ‘I am inferior.’” The conceited muttering about the success and failure of the hairs, etc., which are parts of the earth element, is a conceiving of earth. Thus it is said: “In this way he conceives the internal earth with the conceiving through conceit.” To show that since the aggregate does not exist apart from its components, the adherence to a “living being” occurs even in regard to the components, it is said: “Then, in accordance with the traditional expression ‘that is the living being, that is the body,’ he adheres to a hair as ‘the living being.’” Here, the conceiving through view should be understood by way of such theories as: “These hairs are created by a Lord, they originate from a Progenitor, they are an accumulation of atoms, a transformation of primordial nature.”

Imissā pavattiyāti nikantimānadiṭṭhīnaṃ pariyādānasamugghāṭappavattiyā. “Etaṃ mamā”tiādinā yadipi tissannampi maññanānaṃ sambhavo dassito. Taṇhāmānamaññanānaṃ pana heṭṭhā [V 1.0065] dassitattā diṭṭhimaññanā evettha visesato uddhaṭāti veditabbaṃ. Tenāha “evampi ajjhattikaṃ pathaviṃ diṭṭhimaññanāya maññatī”ti.

“By this course” means by the course of the exhaustion and uprooting of craving, conceit, and views. Although by means of “This is mine,” etc., the possibility of all three kinds of conceiving has been shown, since conceiving through craving and conceiving through conceit have been shown below, it should be understood that it is conceiving through view that is specifically extracted here. Therefore he said: “In this way too, he conceives the internal earth with conceiving through view.”

Bāhirampi pathaviṃ tīhi maññanāhi maññatīti yojanā. Taṃ pana maññanāvidhiṃ dassetuṃ “katha”nti āha. Tassattho heṭṭhā vuttanayena veditabbo.

“He also conceives the external earth with three kinds of conceiving”—this is the connection. To show the method of that conceiving, he said, “How?” Its meaning should be understood in the way stated above.

Ayaṃ [M 1.0073] jīvoti ayaṃ kāḷalohaṃ “jīvo attā”ti abhinivisati ekacce nigaṇṭhā viya. Evaṃ bāhiraṃ pathaviṃ diṭṭhimaññanāya maññatīti etthāpi “yā ceva kho pana ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu, yā ca bāhirā pathavīdhātū”tiādinā nayena ānetvā vattabbo.

He adheres to this black iron as 'the life-principle, the self,' like some Nigaṇṭhas. In the same way, regarding “he conceives the external earth with conceiving through view,” here too it should be explained by bringing in the method beginning: “Whatever is the internal earth element, and whatever is the external earth element,” and so on.

Pathavīkasiṇaṃ attato samanupassatītiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Ayampi ca nayo “rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī”ti ettheva antogadhoti daṭṭhabbo kasiṇānampi rūpasamaññāsambhāvato. Pathaviṃ maññatīti ettha yādiso maññanāvatthumaññanānaṃ vitthāranayo vutto, tādiso ito paraṃ vuttanayovāti āha “ito paraṃ saṅkhepeneva kathayissāmā”ti, atādiso pana vitthāratopi kathayissatīti attho.

Whatever should be said regarding such phrases as “one regards the earth kasina as self” has already been stated above. This method should be understood as included right here in “one regards form as self,” because kasinas too can be designated as “form.” Regarding “conceives earth,” a detailed method concerning the object of conceiving and the conceivings has been stated. He says that from here on, where the method is the same as what has been stated, he will explain it concisely, but where it is not the same, he will explain it in detail.

Tasmāti yasmā “pathaviyā”ti idaṃ bhummavacanaṃ, tasmā, so attaparattadupakaraṇānaṃ ādhārabhāvena taṃ maññanāvatthuṃ kappetīti attho. Tenāha “ahaṃ pathaviyā”tiādi. Nanu ca indriyabaddhānindriyabaddhapabhedassa dhammappabandhassa sasambhārapathavī ca ādhāranissayo, itarā ārammaṇanissayo tadārammaṇassāti ettha nibbirodhoti? Na, maññanāvatthuṃ nissayabhāvena parikappanato. Ayañhi “aha”nti diṭṭhimaññanāya mānamaññanāya ca vatthubhūtassa attano pathavisannissayaṃ katvā “ahaṃ pathaviyā”ti maññati, taṇhāmaññanāya vatthubhūtassa upakaraṇassa pathaviṃ sannissayaṃ katvā “mayhaṃ kiñcanaṃ palibodho pathaviyā”ti maññati. Parotiādīsupi iminā nayena attho veditabbo.

Therefore: since “of the earth” (pathaviyā) is a locative expression, he therefore construes that object of conceiving as a basis for the requisites of himself and others—this is the meaning. Therefore he said, “I am of the earth,” etc. Is it not so that the earth with its components is a support by way of basis for the continuity of phenomena, which is divided into that bound to the faculties and that not bound to the faculties, while the other is a support by way of object for that which has it as an object? Thus there is no contradiction. No, because one construes the object of conceiving as a support. For this person, having made the earth a support for the self which is the object of view-conceiving and conceit-conceiving, conceives, “I am of the earth.” Having made the earth a support for his possessions which are the object of craving-conceiving, he conceives, “My possession and impediment are of the earth.” The meaning should be understood in this way also for “another,” etc.

Yvāyaṃ atthanayoti sambandho. Vutto paṭisambhidāmagge. Eteneva nayenāti yvāyaṃ “so kho pana me attā imasmiṃ rūpe”ti samudāyassa ādhārabhāvadīpano atthanayo vutto, eteneva nayena. Na hi avayavabyatirekena samudāyo labbhati, tasmā samudāye vuttavidhi avayavepi labbhatīti adhippāyo. Tenāha so kho pana me ayaṃ attā imissā pathaviyāti maññantoti. Tasmiṃyeva panassa attanīti ettha assāti puthujjanassa. Tasmiṃyeva attanīti ajjhattikabāhirapathavīsannissaye [V 1.0066] attani. “Pathaviyā maññatī”ti padassāyaṃ vaṇṇanā. Evaṃ “pathaviyā maññatī”ti ettha attavasena diṭṭhimānataṇhāmaññanaṃ dassetvā idāni paravasena dassetuṃ “yadā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha assāti [M 1.0074] parassa. Tadāti paravasena maññanāyaṃ. Diṭṭhimaññanā eva yujjati tattha niccābhinivesādayo sambhavantīti katvā. Avadhāraṇena mānataṇhāmaññanā nivatteti. Na hi “seyyohamasmī”tiādinā, “mayha”nti ca pavattalakkhaṇā mānataṇhā parasmiṃ parassa santakabhāvena gahite ca pavattantīti adhippāyo. Itarāyopīti mānataṇhāmaññanāyopi. Icchanti aṭṭhakathācariyā. Parassapi hi pathavīsannissayena sampattiissariyādikassa vasena attani seyyādibhāvaṃ dahato paṇidahato ca cittaṃ tathābhāvāya mānataṇhāmaññanā sambhavantīti ācariyānaṃ adhippāyo. “Paro pathavī parassa pathavī”ti etthāpi ime dve pakārā sādhippāyā niddhāretabbā.

“This is the method of meaning” is the connection. It is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. “By this very method” means: by this very method of meaning which was stated—the one that illuminates the state of being a basis for the aggregate in the phrase “This self of mine is in this form.” For an aggregate is not found apart from its components; therefore, the procedure stated for the aggregate is also applicable to the component—this is the intention. Therefore he said: “he conceives, ‘This self of mine is in this earth.’” In “in that very self of his,” “of his” refers to the worldling. “In that very self” means in the self that is supported by the internal and external earth. This is the explanation of the phrase “conceives in the earth.” Thus, having shown the view-, conceit-, and craving-conceivings by way of the self in “conceives in the earth,” now in order to show them by way of another, “But when…” etc., was said. Therein, “of his” refers to another. “Then” refers to conceiving by way of another. Only view-conceiving is appropriate there, because adherence to permanence, etc., is possible. By the emphasis, it excludes conceit-conceiving and craving-conceiving. The intention is that conceit and craving, which are characterized by proceeding as “I am better,” etc., and “mine,” do not proceed in regard to another or what is grasped as belonging to another. “The others too” means conceit- and craving-conceivings too. The commentators hold this. For the teachers’ intention is that conceit- and craving-conceivings can arise for one who, by way of another’s wealth, lordship, etc., which are supported by the earth, places or directs his mind toward a state of superiority, etc., in himself for that state. In “another is earth, the earth is of another,” these two modes should also be determined along with their intention.

“Pathavito sañjānātī”ti, “ādito”ti ca ādīsu anissakkavacanepi to-saddo diṭṭhoti āha “pathavitoti nissakkavacana”nti. Saupakaraṇassāti hiraññasuvaṇṇagatassa dāsaporisādinā vittupakaraṇena saupakaraṇassa, attano vā parassa vā tesaṃ upakaraṇassa vāti attho. Yathāvuttappabhedatoti lakkhaṇādiajjhattikādivuttappakāravibhāgato. Uppattiṃ vā niggamanaṃ vāti “taṃ aṇḍaṃ ahosi hemamayaṃ, tasmiṃ sayaṃ brahmā uppanno”ti brahmaṇḍavādavasena vā “dvīhi aṇūhi dviaṇuka”nti evaṃ pavattaaṇukavādavasena vā pathavito uppattiṃ vā “sabboyaṃ loko issarato viniggato”ti issaravādavasena issarakuttato pathavito niggamanaṃ vā maññamānoti yojanā. Pathavito vā añño āpādiko attāti adhippāyo. Ettha ca purimasmiṃ atthavikappe kārakalakkhaṇaṃ nissakkavacanaṃ, dutiyasmiṃ upapadalakkhaṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Attano pariggahabhūtapathavito sukhappattiṃ tato eva ca parehi seyyādibhāvaṃ kappentassa vasenapettha taṇhāmānamaññanā veditabbā. Apareti sārasamāsācariyā. Tato aññaṃ appamāṇaṃ attānaṃ gahetvāti pubbe bhāvitaāpādiappamāṇakasiṇavasena vā kāpilakāṇādadiṭṭhivasena vā appamāṇaṃ byāpinaṃ attānaṃ gahetvā. Pathavitoti pacchā abhāvitaavaḍḍhitapathavīkasiṇasaṅkhātapathavito. Bahiddhāpi me attāti ito pathavito bahipi me attāti adhippāyo.

Regarding “perceives from earth” (pathavito sañjānāti): since the suffix -to is seen even in non-ablative expressions such as “from the beginning” (ādito), he says, “`pathavito` is an ablative expression.” “Of one with requisites” means: of one who has requisites in the form of wealth such as gold and silver, slaves and workers, etc.; or the meaning is, for the requisites of oneself or another. “According to the stated classification” means: from the division into types stated as characteristics, internal, etc. “Either origin or emergence”: the connection is “conceiving either an origin from earth… or an emergence from earth.” This is either by way of the doctrine of Brahmā’s egg—“That egg was golden; in it Brahmā arose by himself”—or by way of the atomic theory that proceeds thus, “a dyad is from two atoms”; or, by way of the doctrine of a creator—“This whole world has emerged from a creator”—conceiving an emergence from earth due to the creator’s making. The intention is: or a self related to water, different from earth. And here it should be understood that in the first alternative meaning, the ablative expression has the characteristic of an agent, while in the second it has the characteristic of a prepositional term. Herein, craving- and conceit-conceivings should be understood by way of one who construes the attainment of happiness from the earth that has become his possession, and from that very thing a state of superiority to others. Others, the Sārasamāsa teachers, say as follows. “Having taken another, immeasurable self” means: having taken an immeasurable, all-pervading self either by way of a previously developed infinite water kasina, or by way of the views of Kapila, Kaṇāda, etc. “From earth” means: from the earth reckoned as the earth kasina that is subsequently undeveloped and unexpanded. “My self is also outside” means: my self is also outside of this earth.

Kevalanti [M 1.0075] anavasesaṃ. Mahāpathaviṃ taṇhāvasena mamāyati, ayañca nayo catudīpissariye ṭhitassa dīpacakkavattino ca labbheyya, maṇḍalikarājamahāmattakuṭumbikānampi vasena labbhateva tesampi yathāpariggahaṃ anavasesetvā maññanāya sambhavato. “Evaṃ mamā”ti gāhassa “esohamasmiṃ, eso me attā”ti gāhavidhūratāya vuttaṃ “ekā taṇhāmaññanā eva labbhatī”ti[V 1.0067]. Iminā nayenāti vuttamatidesaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “sā cāya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sā cāyanti sā ca ayaṃ taṇhāmaññanā yojetabbāti sambandho. Yathā pana diṭṭhimaññanāmaññite vatthusmiṃ sinehaṃ mānañca uppādayato taṇhāmānamaññanā sambhavanti, evaṃ taṇhāmaññanāmaññitena vatthunā attānaṃ seyyādito dahato tañca attaniyaṃ niccaṃ tathā taṃsāmibhūtaṃ attānañca parikappentassa itaramaññanāpi sambhavantīti sakkā viññātuṃ. “Me”ti hi iminā atthaggahaṇamukheneva attaniyasambandho pakāsīyatīti.

“Entirely” (kevalaṃ) means without remainder (anavasesaṃ). One regards the great earth as “mine” by way of craving. This method may be found in the case of a ruler of the four continents and a universal monarch, and it is certainly found in the case of regional kings, great ministers, and householders, because it is possible for them too to conceive of their possessions without remainder, according to how they are possessed. Because the grasping “Thus, this is mine” is remote from the grasping “This I am, this is my self,” it is said, “only one, craving-conceiving, is obtained.” To explain the stated extension “by this method,” “and this…” etc., was said. Therein, “and this…” is the connection: “and this craving-conceiving should be connected.” Just as for one who generates affection and conceit for an object conceived with view-conceiving, craving- and conceit-conceivings arise, so it can be understood that for one who, by means of an object conceived with craving-conceiving, considers oneself superior, etc., and who construes that possession as permanent and likewise the self as its owner, the other conceivings also arise. For by this “my,” the relationship with what is one’s own is revealed precisely through the grasping of the meaning.

Abhinandatīti iminā taṇhādiṭṭhābhinivesānaṃ saṅgahitattā te dassento “assādeti parāmasati cā”ti āha. Diṭṭhivippayuttacittuppādavasena cetassa dvayassa asaṅkarato pavatti veditabbā, ekacittuppādepi vā adhipatidhammānaṃ viya pubbābhisaṅkhāravasena tassa tassa balavabhāvena pavatti. Etasmiṃ attheti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena abhinandanatthe. Etanti “pathaviṃ abhinandatī”ti etaṃ padaṃ. Yesaṃ vineyyānaṃ yehi pakāravisesehi dhammānaṃ vibhāvane kate visesādhigamo hoti, tesaṃ tehi pakāravisesehi dhammavibhāvanaṃ. Yesaṃ pana yena ekeneva pakārena dhammavibhāvane kate visesādhigamo hoti, tesampi taṃ vatvā dhammissaratāya tadaññaniravasesappakāravibhāvanañca desanāvilāso. Tenāha “pubbe maññanāvasena kilesuppattiṃ dassetvā idāni abhinandanāvasena dassento”ti. Dhammadhātuyāti sammāsambodhiyā. Sā hi sabbañeyyadhammaṃ yathāsabhāvato dhāreti upadhāreti, sakalañca vineyyasattasaṅkhātadhammappabandhaṃ apāyadukkhasaṃsāradukkhapatanato dhāreti, sayañca aviparītapavattiākārā dhātūti dhammadhātūti idhādhippetā. Sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānañhi maggañāṇaṃ, maggañāṇapadaṭṭhānañca sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ sammāsambodhīti. Suppaṭividdhattāti [M 1.0076] suṭṭhu paṭividdhabhāvato, sammā adhigatattāti attho. Abhikaṅkhanasampaggahaparāmasanānaṃ vasena ārammaṇe parikappanāpavatti maññanā. Tattha “mamaṃ, aha”nti ca abhinivesanaṃ parikappanaṃ. Yena ajjhosānaṃ hoti, ayaṃ abhinandanāti ayametesaṃ viseso. Suttādiaviruddhāyeva attanomati icchitabbā, na itarāti suttena tassā saṅgahaṃ dassetuṃ “vuttañceta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Desanāvilāsavibhāvanassa pana sahetukahetusampayuttadukādidesanāya nibaddhatā niddhāretabbā.

"He delights in it": by this, showing that adherences to craving and views are included, it is said, "he relishes and adheres to it." The occurrence of these two should be understood as unmixed by way of the arising of a mind-moment dissociated from views; or, even in a single mind-moment, their occurrence is by the force of previous volitional formations, like dominant factors, through the strength of one or the other. In this, it has the meaning of delighting by way of craving and views. "This" refers to the phrase "he delights in the earth." For those to be trained for whom a special attainment occurs when the distinctions of phenomena are analyzed in particular ways, the phenomena are analyzed for them in those particular ways. But for those for whom a special attainment occurs when phenomena are analyzed in just one way, even for them, after stating that one way, the exposition unfolds by analyzing all other aspects without remainder for the sake of mastery over the Dhamma; this is the elegance of the teaching. Therefore, it is said: "Having first shown the arising of defilements by way of conceiving, he now shows it by way of delighting." "By the Dhamma-element" refers to perfect self-enlightenment. For it holds and sustains all knowable phenomena according to their true nature, and it holds the entire continuity of phenomena designated as beings to be trained, preventing them from falling into the suffering of the plane of misery and the suffering of saṃsāra. And since it is itself an element whose mode of occurrence is unperverted, it is here intended as the "Dhamma-element." The knowledge of the path is the proximate cause for the knowledge of omniscience, and the knowledge of omniscience is the proximate cause for the knowledge of the path—this is perfect self-enlightenment. "Being well penetrated" means because of being thoroughly penetrated, that is, because of being rightly attained. Conceiving is the process of constructing in regard to an object by way of longing, grasping, and adherence. Here, the adherence "mine, I" is the constructing. That by which there is attachment is delighting; this is the distinction between them. One's own opinion should be accepted only when it does not contradict the Suttas, etc., not otherwise. To show its inclusion in the Sutta, it is said, "And this was said," etc. However, it should be determined that the analysis of the elegance of the exposition is connected with the teaching of dyads, etc., such as those that are "with a cause" and "associated with a cause."

Tassāti tena. Ñātasaddasambandhena hetaṃ kattari sāmivacanaṃ. Tasmāti apariññātattā. “Apariññāta”nti paṭikkhepamukhena yaṃ parijānanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ atthato tividhā pariññā hotīti taṃ sarūpato pavattiākārato ca vibhāvento “yo hī”tiādimāha.

"Tassa" means "tena" (by him). For this is a genitive in the sense of the agent, by connection with the word "ñāta" (known). "Tasmā" means "because of not being fully understood." The full understanding that was stated by way of negation as "not fully understood" is, in meaning, threefold full understanding. Explaining this according to its nature and its mode of occurrence, he says, "For one who…" and so on.

Tattha [V 1.0068] yāya paññāya vipassanābhūmiṃ parijānāti paricchindati, sā parijānanapaññā ñātapariññā. Sā hi tebhūmakadhammajātaṃ “ayaṃ vipassanābhūmī”ti ñātaṃ viditaṃ pākaṭaṃ karontīyeva lakkhaṇarasādito ajjhattikādivibhāgato ca paricchijja jānāti. Idha pana pathavīdhātuvasena veditabbāti vuttaṃ “pathavīdhātuṃ parijānātī”tiādi. Tīraṇapariññāti kīraṇavasena parijānanakapaññā. Sā hi parivārehi aniccatādiākārehi aniccatādisabhāvassa upādānakkhandhapañcakassa tīraṇavasena sammasanavasena taṃ paricchijja jānāti. Aggamaggenāti arahattamaggena. So hi anavasesato chandarāgaṃ pajahati. Aggamaggenāti vā aggabhūtena maggena, lokuttaramaggenāti attho. Ubhayathāpi hi samucchedapahānakārī eva paññā nippariyāyena pahānapariññāti dasseti.

Herein, the wisdom by which one fully understands and delimits the ground for insight is ñātapariññā, the full understanding of the known. For, making the collection of phenomena of the three planes known, understood, and manifest as "this is the ground for insight," it knows them by defining them according to characteristic, function, etc., and by way of the division into internal, etc. Here, however, it is said that this should be understood in terms of the earth element, thus: "one fully understands the earth element," etc. Tīraṇapariññā, full understanding by scrutiny, is the wisdom that fully understands by way of scrutinizing. For it knows the five aggregates subject to clinging—which have the nature of impermanence, etc.—by defining them through scrutinizing and comprehending them with their adjuncts in the modes of impermanence, etc. "By the foremost path" means by the path of arahantship, for that path abandons sensual desire without remainder. Or, "by the foremost path" means by the path that has become foremost, that is, by the supramundane path. For in both ways it shows that it is the wisdom that effects abandonment by eradication which is, in the primary sense, pahānapariññā, full understanding as abandonment.

Nāmarūpavavatthānanti etena paccayapariggahopi saṅgahitoti daṭṭhabbo nāmarūpassa hetuvavatthānabhāvato. Sopi hi hetupaccayamukhena nāmarūpassa vavatthānamevāti. Kalāpasammasanādivasena tīraṇapariññā aniccādivasena sammasanabhāvato. Tasmāti yasmā tā pariññāyo natthi, tasmā. Atha vā tasmā apariññātattāti yasmā apariññātā pathavī, tasmā apariññātattā pathaviyā taṃ pathaviṃ maññati ca abhinandati cāti.

By "the determination of mentality-materiality," it should be seen that the comprehension of conditions is also included, because this is the determination of the cause of mentality-materiality. For that too is the very determination of mentality-materiality by way of cause and condition. Full understanding by scrutiny is by way of comprehending groups, etc., because it is comprehension by way of impermanence, etc. "Tasmā" (therefore) means: because those full understandings are absent, therefore... Or alternatively, "tasmā apariññātattā" (therefore, because of not being fully understood) means: because the earth is not fully understood, therefore, because of the earth's not being fully understood, one conceives and delights in that earth.

Pathavīvāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Earth is finished.

Āpovārādivaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Sections on Water, etc.

Āpaṃ [M 1.0077] āpatoti ettha appoti, appāyatīti vā āpo, yasmiṃ saṅghāte sayaṃ atthi, taṃ ābandhanavasena byāpetvā tiṭṭhati, paribrūhetīti vā attho. Atthānaṃ adhi ajjhattaṃ. Pati pati attānanti paccattaṃ. Ubhayenapi sattasantānapariyāpannameva vadati. Āpo āpogatantiādīsu ābandhanameva āpo, tadeva āposabhāvaṃ gatattā āpogataṃ, sabhāveneva āpabhāvaṃ pattanti attho. Sinehanavasena sineho, soyeva sinehanasabhāvaṃ gatattā sinehagataṃ. Bandhanattaṃ rūpassāti avinibbhogarūpassa bandhanabhāvo, avippakiraṇavasena sampiṇḍananti attho. Uggaṇhantoti yathāparicchinne āpomaṇḍale yathā uggahanimittaṃ upalabbhati, tathā nimittaṃ gaṇhanto. Vuttoti “āpasmi”nti ettha vuttaāpo. So hi sasambhāraāpo, na “āpokasiṇa”nti ettha vuttaāpo. Sesanti ārammaṇasammutiāpānaṃ sarūpavibhāvanaṃ. “Āpaṃ [V 1.0069] āpato pajānātī”tiādipāḷiyā atthavibhāvanañceva tattha tattha maññanāvibhāgadassanañca pathaviyaṃ vuttasadisamevāti. Tattha “pathavīkasiṇameko sañjānātī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 3.360; a. ni. 10.25) vuttaṃ, idha “āpokasiṇameko sañjānātī”tiādinā vattabbaṃ. Tattha ca “pathavīti sañjānātī”ti vuttaṃ, idha pana “āpoti sañjānātī”tiādinā vattabbanti evamādi eva viseso. Sesaṃ tādisameva. Tena vuttaṃ “pathaviyaṃ vuttasadisamevā”ti. Yo panettha viseso, taṃ dassetuṃ “kevala”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha mūlarasoti mūlaṃ paṭicca nibbattaraso. Khandharasādīsupi eseva nayo. Khīrādīni pākaṭāneva. Yathā pana bhesajjasikkhāpade (pārā. 618-625), na evamidha niyamo atthi. Yaṃ kiñci khīraṃ khīrameva. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Bhummānīti āvāṭādīsu ṭhitaudakāni. Antalikkhānīti pathaviṃ appattāni vassodakāni, pattāni pana bhummāneva. Evaṃ vuttā cāti ca-saddena himodakakappavināsakaudakapathaviyāantoudakapathavīsandhārakaudakādiṃ pubbe avuttampi samuccinoti.

In the phrase "āpaṃ āpato" (water as water), "āpo" (water) is so called because it pervades ("āpnoti") or because it swells ("āpyāyati"); the meaning is that in whatever conglomerate it exists, it remains pervading it by way of binding, or it causes it to grow. "Ajjhattaṃ" (internal) is "adhi-attānaṃ" (concerning the self). "Paccattaṃ" (individual) is "pati-attānaṃ" (to each self). By both terms, what is included in the continuity of a being is spoken of. In phrases such as "āpo āpogataṃ" (water that has become water-natured), water is cohesion itself. That very thing, because it has gone to the state of water, is "āpogataṃ," meaning it has attained the nature of water. "Sineha" (cohesion) is so called because of its moistening nature; that very thing, having gone to the state of cohesion, is "sinehagataṃ." "The binding nature of matter" means the state of binding for inseparable matter; the meaning is cohesion by way of non-scattering. "Grasping" means grasping the sign in the way that a sign for grasping is obtained in a defined water-circle. "Stated" refers to the water stated here in the phrase "in water." This is water with its constituents, not the water spoken of in the phrase "water kasiṇa." The rest is the analysis of the nature of water as a conceptual object. The analysis of the meaning of the Pāli phrase "one understands water as water," etc., and the explanation of the division of conceiving in each case, is similar to what was said for earth. There it is said, "One perceives the earth kasiṇa" (D iii 274; A v 46), etc.; here it should be said, "One perceives the water kasiṇa," etc. And there it is said, "one perceives as earth"; here it should be said, "one perceives as water," etc. This is the only kind of difference. The rest is similar. Therefore it is said: "is similar to what was said for earth." To show what is different here, it is said, "only," etc. Therein, "root-sap" is the sap that arises depending on a root. This same method applies to "stem-sap," etc. Milk, etc., are obvious. But here there is no restriction as in the training rule on medicines (Vin iv 89ff). Any kind of milk is just milk. This same method applies to the others. "Terrestrial waters" are waters standing in wells, etc. "Atmospheric waters" are raindrops that have not reached the earth; once they have reached it, they are terrestrial. And by the word "and" in "thus stated, and...," he includes what was not stated before, such as snow-water, the water at the end of a world-cycle, water within the earth, the water that holds up the earth, etc.

Tejaṃ tejatoti ettha tejanaṭṭhena tejo, tejanaṃ nāma dahanapacanādisamatthaṃ nisānaṃ, yaṃ uṇhattanti vuccati. Yena cāti yena tejogatena [M 1.0078] kupitena. Santappatīti ayaṃ kāyo samantato tappati ekāhikajarādibhāvena usumajāto hoti. Yena ca jīrīyatīti yena ayaṃ kāyo jīrīyati, indriyavekallataṃ balaparikkhayaṃ valitādibhāvañca pāpuṇāti. Yena ca pariḍayhatīti yena kupitena ayaṃ kāyo parito ḍayhati, so ca puggalo ḍayhāmīti satadhotasappigosītacandanādilepañceva tālavaṇṭavātañca paccāsīsati. Yena ca asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchatīti yena asitaṃ vā odanādi, pītaṃ vā pānakādi, khāyitaṃ vā piṭhakhajjakādi, sāyitaṃ vā ambapakkamadhuphāṇitādi sammadeva paripākaṃ gacchati, rasādibhāvena vivekaṃ gacchatīti attho. Ettha ca sarīrassa pakatiusumaṃ atikkamitvā uṇhabhāvo santāpo, sarīradahanavasena pavatto mahādāho paridāho, satavāraṃ tāpetvā udake pakkhipitvā uddhaṭasappi satadhotasappi, rasarudhiramaṃsamedaaṭṭhiaṭṭhimiñjasukkā rasādayo. Tattha purimā tayo tejā catusamuṭṭhānā, pacchimo kammasamuṭṭhānova.

In the phrase `tejaṃ tejato` (fire as fire), `tejo` (the fire element) is so called because of its meaning of maturing. 'Maturing' is the capacity to burn, cook, etc., which is called heat. 'And by which': by which aggravated fire element. 'One is scorched': this body is heated all over, becoming feverish with a one-day fever, etc. 'And by which one ages': by which this body ages, it reaches impairment of the faculties, decline of strength, a wrinkled state, etc. 'And by which one is consumed by fever': by which aggravated fire element this body is burnt all over, and that person, feeling 'I am burning,' longs for applications of ghee washed a hundred times, cool sandalwood, etc., and for the breeze from a palm-leaf fan. 'And by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted undergoes proper digestion': by which what is eaten, such as boiled rice; or drunk, such as beverages; or chewed, such as flour-cakes and sweets; or tasted, such as ripe mangoes, honey, and molasses, goes to proper digestion, meaning it becomes separated into nutritive essence, etc. And here, the state of heat that exceeds the body's natural warmth is 'scorching' (`santāpo`). The great fever that occurs by way of burning the body is 'consumption' (`paridāho`). Ghee that has been heated a hundred times, thrown into water, and taken out is `satadhotasappi` (ghee washed a hundred times). 'Nutritive essence, etc.' (`rasādayo`) are nutritive essence, blood, flesh, fat, bone, bone-marrow, and semen. Among these four functions of the fire element, the first three have four origins, while the last (digestion) has only kamma as its origin.

Tejobhāvaṃ gatattā tejogataṃ. Usmāti uṇhākāro. Usmāva usmābhāvaṃ gatattā usmāgataṃ. Usumanti caṇḍausumaṃ. Tadeva usumagataṃ, sabhāveneva usumabhāvaṃ pattanti attho. Kaṭṭhaggīti kaṭṭhupādāno aggi. Sakalikaggīādīsupi eseva nayo. Saṅkāraggīti kacavaraṃ paṭicca uppannaaggi. Indaggīti asaniaggi. Santāpoti jālāya vā vītaccitaṅgārānaṃ vā santāpo[V 1.0070]. Sūriyasantāpoti ātapo. Kaṭṭhasannicayasantāpoti kaṭṭharāsiṃ paṭicca uppannasantāpo. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ vuttā cāti. Ca-saddena petaggikappavināsakagginirayaggiādike avuttepi samuccinoti.

Because it has gone to the state of radiance, it is 'gone to radiance.' 'Heat' is the characteristic of heat. Because it has gone to the state of heat, it is 'gone to heat.' 'Intense heat' is fierce heat. That itself is 'gone to intense heat'; the meaning is that it has attained the state of intense heat by its own nature. 'Wood-fire' is fire with wood as its fuel. The same method applies to 'splinter-fire' and the like. 'Rubbish-fire' is fire that has arisen in dependence on rubbish. 'Indra's fire' is lightning-fire. 'Heat' is the heat of a flame or of embers that have passed beyond flame. 'Sun-heat' is sunshine. 'Heat from a pile of wood' is heat that has arisen in dependence on a heap of wood. The same method applies to the rest. Thus what has been stated, and... By the word 'and,' it also includes what has not been stated, such as the fire of the departed, the fire that destroys the aeon, the hell-fire, and so on.

Vāyaṃ vāyatoti ettha vāyanaṭṭhena vāyo. Kimidaṃ vāyanaṃ nāma? Vitthambhanaṃ, samudīraṇaṃ vā, vāyanaṃ gamananti eke. Uddhaṅgamā vātāti uggārahikkādipavattakā uddhaṃ ārohanavātā. Adhogamā vātāti uccārapassāvādinīharaṇatā adho orohanavātā. Kucchisayā vātāti antānaṃ bahivātā. Koṭṭhāsayā vātāti antānaṃ antovātā. Aṅgamaṅgānusārino vātāti dhamanījālānusārena sakalasarīre aṅgamaṅgāni anusaṭā samiñjanapasāraṇādinibbattakā vātā[M 1.0079]. Satthakavātāti sandhibandhanāni kattariyā chindantā viya pavattavātā. Khurakavātāti khurena viya hadayamaṃsachedanaphālanakavātā. Uppalakavātāti hadayamaṃsassa samuppāṭanakavātā. Assāsoti antopavisanakanāsikāvāto. Passāsoti bahinikkhamananāsikāvāto. Ettha ca purimā sabbe catusamuṭṭhānā, assāsapassāsā cittasamuṭṭhānāva.

In the phrase `vāyaṃ vāyati` (the wind blows), `vāyo` (wind) is so called because of its meaning of blowing. What is this blowing? Distension, stimulation, or movement, some say. Upward-going winds are winds that rise upward, causing belching, hiccupping, and so on. Downward-going winds are winds that descend downward, for the expulsion of feces, urine, and so on. Winds in the belly are the winds outside the intestines. Winds in the bowels are the winds inside the intestines. Winds that course through the limbs are winds that, following the network of vessels, are diffused through all the major and minor limbs in the entire body, producing bending and stretching, and so on. Knife-like winds are winds that operate as if cutting the ligaments of the joints with scissors. Razor-like winds are winds that cut and split the heart-muscle as if with a razor. Uprooting winds are winds that uproot the heart-muscle. In-breath is the nasal wind that enters. Out-breath is the nasal wind that exits. Here, all the former winds are of fourfold origin, but the in-breaths and out-breaths are of mind-origin only.

Vāyogatanti vāyova vāyogataṃ, sabhāveneva vāyobhāvaṃ pattanti attho. Thambhitattaṃ rūpassāti avinibbhogarūpassa thambhitabhāvo. Puratthimā vātāti puratthimadisato āgatā vātā. Pacchimādīsupi eseva nayo. Sarajādīsu saha rajena sarajā, rajavirahitā suddhā arajā. Sītautusamuṭṭhānā, sītavalāhakantare vā jātā sītā. Uṇhautusamuṭṭhānā, uṇhavalāhakantare vā jātā uṇhā. Parittāti mandā tanukavātā. Adhimattāti balavavātā. Kāḷāti kāḷavalāhakantare samuṭṭhitā. Yehi abbhāhato chavivaṇṇo kāḷako hoti, tesaṃ etaṃ adhivacanantipi eke. Verambhavātāti yojanato upari vāyanavātā. Pakkhavātāti antamaso makkhikāyapi pakkhāyūhanavātā. Supaṇṇavātāti garuḷavātā. Kāmaṃ cetepi pakkhavātāva, ussadavasena pana visuṃ gahitā. Tālavaṇṭavātāti tālavaṇṇehi katena, aññehi vā katena kenaci maṇḍalasaṇṭhānena samuṭṭhāpitavātā. Vidhūpanavātāti bījanapattakena samuṭṭhāpitavātā. Imāni ca tālavaṇṭavidhūpanāni anuppannampi vātaṃ uppādenti, uppannampi parivattenti. Idhāpi ca-saddo udakasandhārakavātakappavināsakavātajālāpellanakavātādike avuttepi samuccinoti. Ettha ca “āpaṃ maññatī”tiādīsu yasmā tīhi maññanāhi – “ahaṃ āpoti maññati, mama āpoti maññatī”tiādinā pathavīvāre vuttanayena sakkā maññanāvibhāgo vibhāvetunti vuttaṃ “sesaṃ vuttanayamevā”ti. Tasmā tattha vuttanayānusārena imesu tīsu vāresu yathārahaṃ maññanāvibhāgo vibhāvetabbo.

'Gone to wind' is the wind itself, which has become wind; the meaning is that it attains the state of wind by its very nature. 'The rigidity of form' refers to the rigid nature of inseparable matter. The 'eastern winds' are winds that come from the eastern direction. The same applies to the western and other directions. Among the 'dusty winds,' those mixed with dust are called dusty, while those free from dust are called pure and dustless. 'Cold winds' arise from the cold season or are born in cold cloud regions. 'Hot winds' arise from the hot season or are born in hot cloud regions. 'Minor winds' are weak and thin. 'Excessive winds' are powerful. 'Black winds' arise from dark cloud regions. Some say this term also refers to those winds by which the skin’s color turns black when struck. The 'Verambha winds' are winds that blow above a yojana. 'Wing-winds' are winds from the flapping of wings, even of a fly. The 'Supaṇṇa-winds' are Garuḷa-winds. Though these too are wing-winds, they are separately mentioned due to their force. 'Palm-leaf-fan winds' are winds raised by a palm-leaf fan, or by anything else made in a circular shape. 'Fanning winds' are winds produced by a fan or a leaf. These palm-leaf-fan and fanning winds can generate wind where there was none or alter existing winds. Here too, the word 'and' also includes unmentioned winds like water-bearing winds, the aeon-destroying wind, winds that shake trellises, and so on. In passages like 'he conceives water,' because the threefold conceiving—'I am water,' 'water is mine,' etc.—can be distinguished as explained in the section on the earth element, it is said, 'the rest is in the way stated.' Therefore, in these three sections, the analysis of conceiving should be made appropriately according to the method explained there.

Ettāvatāti [V 1.0071] ettakena iminā catuvāraparimāṇena desanāvisesena. Ca-saddo byatireko. Tena vakkhamānaṃyeva visesaṃ joteti. Yvāyanti yo ayaṃ lakkhaṇo nāma hāro vuttoti sambandho. So pana lakkhaṇahāro yaṃlakkhaṇo tattha vutto, taṃ dassetuṃ [M 1.0080] “vuttamhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha vuttamhi ekadhammeti kusalādīsu khandhādīsu vā yasmiṃ kasmiñci ekadhamme sutte sarūpato niddhāraṇavasena vā kathite. Ye dhammā ekalakkhaṇā tenāti ye keci dhammā kusalādibhāvena, rūpakkhandhādibhāvena vā tena vuttadhammena samānalakkhaṇā. Vuttā bhavanti sabbeti sabbepi kusalādisabhāvā, khandhādisabhāvā vā dhammā sutte avuttāpi tāya samānalakkhaṇatāya vuttā bhavanti, ānetvā saṃvaṇṇanavasenāti adhippāyo.

'To this extent' means by this much, by this measure of four sections, by this specific teaching. The word 'and' is exclusive; by that, it illuminates the very distinction that will be explained. 'That which' connects to what was stated as 'the method called Characteristic.' To show the characteristic of that Characteristic Method spoken of there, the phrase beginning 'in what has been said' was stated. Therein, 'in what has been said, one thing' refers to any single phenomenon—among wholesome states, etc., or the aggregates, etc.—that is discussed in a sutta, whether by its form or by way of determination. 'Those phenomena that have a single characteristic with it' means any phenomena that have the same characteristic as that stated phenomenon, whether by being wholesome, etc., or by being the aggregate of form, etc. 'All are stated' means that all phenomena—whether of a wholesome nature, etc., or of the nature of the aggregates, etc.—even if unstated in the sutta, are considered stated because of that sameness of characteristic. The intention is that this is by way of bringing them in for exposition.

Ettha ca ekalakkhaṇāti samānalakkhaṇā vuttā. Tena sahacaritā samānakiccatā samānahetutā samānaphalatā samānārammaṇatāti evamādīhipi avuttānaṃ vuttānaṃ viya niddhāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Itīti iminā pakārena. Tenāha “evaṃ nettiyaṃ lakkhaṇo nāma hāro vutto”ti, nettipāḷiyaṃ (netti. 23) pana “ye dhammā ekalakkhaṇā keci so hāro lakkhaṇo nāmā”ti pāṭho āgato. Tassa vasenāti tassa lakkhaṇahārassa vasena. Rūpalakkhaṇaṃ anatītattāti ruppanasabhāvena samānasabhāvattā. Vadantena bhagavatā. Etāti “rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī”ti evaṃ vuttadiṭṭhī. Ettha ca sakkāyadiṭṭhimaññanādassaneneva sakalarūpavatthukā taṇhāmānamaññanāpi dassitā evāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “tasmiṃyeva panassa diṭṭhimaññanāya maññite vatthusmiṃ sinehaṃ mānañca uppādayato taṇhāmānamaññanāpi veditabbā”ti. Atha vā pathaviṃ āpaṃ tejaṃ vāyaṃ meti maññati abhinandatīti ca vadantena vuttanayeneva sakalarūpavatthukā taṇhāmaññanā tadanusārena mānamaññanāpi vuttāva hotīti evampettha itaramaññanāpi niddhāretabbā.

And here, 'having a single characteristic' means having a common characteristic. Therefore, the determination of unstated things from stated ones should be understood also by way of things that are concomitant, have a common function, a common cause, a common result, a common object, and so on. 'Thus' means in this way. Therefore he said: 'Thus in the Netti the method called Characteristic is stated.' But in the Netti scripture the reading is found: 'Whatever phenomena have a single characteristic, that is the method called Characteristic.' 'By means of that' means by means of that Characteristic Method. 'Because the characteristic of form is not transcended' means because of having the same nature, the nature of being afflicted. Spoken by the Blessed One. 'This' refers to the view stated thus: 'one regards form as self.' And here it should be understood that by the mere conceiving and seeing of identity view, the conceivings of craving and conceit regarding all material objects are also shown. For it is said: 'Moreover, when one generates affection and conceit for that very object conceived through the conceiving of view, the conceivings of craving and conceit should also be understood.' Alternatively, when he says, 'one conceives and delights in earth, water, fire, and air as "mine,"' in the way stated, the conceiving of craving regarding all material objects is stated, and in accordance with that, the conceiving of conceit is also stated. Thus in this way the other conceivings should also be determined.

Āpovārādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on water, etc., is concluded.

Bhūtavārādivaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Bhūtavāra, etc.

3. “Pathaviṃ maññati, pathaviyā maññatī”tiādīhi padehi “rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, rūpasmiṃ attānaṃ samanupassatī”tiādīnaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhīnaṃ niddhāritattā vuttaṃ “evaṃ rūpamukhena saṅkhāravatthukaṃ maññanaṃ vatvā”ti[M 1.0081]. Tesu saṅkhāresu sattesupīti tadupādānesupi sattesu[V 1.0072]. Dhātūsūti pathavīādīsu catūsu dhātūsu. “Jātaṃ bhūtaṃ saṅkhata”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.207; saṃ. ni. 5.379) bhūta-saddo uppāde dissati, saupasaggo pana “pabhūtamariyo pakaroti puñña”ntiādīsu vipule, “yebhuyyena bhikkhūnaṃ paribhūtarūpo”tiādīsu hiṃsane, “sambhūto sāṇavāsī”tiādīsu (cūḷava. 450) paññattiyaṃ, “abhibhūto māro vijito saṅgāmo”tiādīsu vimathane, “parābhūtarūpo kho ayaṃ acelo pāthikaputto”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.23, 25, 31, 32) parājaye, “anubhūtaṃ sukhadukkha”ntiādīsu vediyane, “vibhūtaṃ vibhāvitaṃ paññāyā”tiādīsu pākaṭīkaraṇe dissati. Te sabbe rukkhādīsūti. Ādi-saddena saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā. “Kālo ghasati bhūtānīti (jā. 1.2.190), bhūtā loke samussaya”nti (dī. ni. 2.220; saṃ. ni. 1.186) ca ādīsu avisesena sattavācakopi bhūtasaddo, upari devādipadehi sattavisesānaṃ gahitattā idha tadavasiṭṭhā bhūtasaddena gayhantīti āha “no ca kho avisesenā”ti. Tenevāha – “cātumahārājikānañhi heṭṭhā sattā idha bhūtāti adhippetā”ti. Yo hi sattanikāyo paripuṇṇayoniko catūhipi yonīhi nibbattanāraho, tatthāyaṃ bhūtasamaññā aṇḍajādivasena bhavanato.

3. By phrases such as “he conceives earth, he conceives in earth,” because the identity views, such as “he regards form as self, he regards self in form,” etc., are defined, it is said, “thus, having spoken of conceiving based on formations through the doorway of form.” Among those formations, even among beings—that is, among beings clinging to them. In the elements—that is, in the four elements beginning with earth. In phrases like “born, become, conditioned,” etc., the term “bhūta” is seen in the sense of arising, while with prefixes, as in “the noble one produces abundant merit,” etc., it denotes abundance; in “mostly despised by the monks,” etc., it conveys harm; in “Sambhūta, the ascetic of hemp-cloth,” etc., it refers to designation; in “Māra is vanquished, the battle is won,” etc., it signifies crushing; in “this naked ascetic Pāthikaputta is utterly defeated,” etc., it denotes defeat; in “experienced pleasure and pain,” etc., it refers to feeling; in “manifested, made evident through wisdom,” etc., it indicates making clear. All these are seen in trees, etc. It should be understood that other things are included by the word 'etc.'. In phrases like “time devours beings” and “beings in the world are aggregates,” etc., the term “bhūta” is also used generically to denote beings. Since specific beings like devas are mentioned later, here the remaining beings are referred to by the term “bhūta,” hence it is said, “but not generically.” Therefore, it is stated: “For the beings below the Four Great Kings are intended here by ‘bhūta.’” Indeed, any group of beings complete in their origin, capable of being born through all four modes of birth, is designated by the term “bhūta” due to their coming into being, whether egg-born, etc.

Bhūteti vuttadesaādesite bhūte. Bhūtato sañjānātīti iminā “bhūtā”ti lokavohāraṃ gahetvā yathā tattha taṇhādimaññanā sambhavanti, evaṃ viparītasaññāya sañjānanaṃ pakāsīyati. Svāyamattho heṭṭhā “pathavito sañjānātī”ti ettha vuttanayānusārena sakkā jānitunti āha “vuttanayamevā”ti. Yathā suddhāvāsā sabbadā abhāvato imaṃ desanaṃ nāruḷhā, evaṃ nerayikāpi sabbamaññanānadhiṭṭhānato. Eteneva ekaccapetānampettha asaṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Apare pana “diṭṭhimaññanādhiṭṭhānato tesampettha saṅgaho icchitoyevā”ti vadanti. “Samaṅgibhūtaṃ paricārenta”ntiādinā sutte vuttanayena. Rajjatīti “subhā sukhitā”ti vipallāsaggāhena tattha rāgaṃ janeti. Evamettha rajjanto ca na kevalaṃ dassanavaseneva, savanādivasenapi rajjatevāti dassento “disvāpi…pe… utvāpī”ti āha. Tattha ghāyanādivasena rajjanaṃ tehi anubhūtagandhamālādivasena ceva visabhāgavatthubhūtānaṃ tesaṃ [M 1.0082] paribhogavasena ca yathānubhavaṃ anussaraṇavasena ca veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ bhūte taṇhāmaññanāya maññatīti vuttanayena bhūte paṭicca chandarāgaṃ janento tesaṃ paṭipattiṃ assādento abhinandanto abhivadanto ajjhosāya tiṭṭhanto “īdisī avatthā mama anāgatamaddhānaṃ siyā”tiādinā vā pana nayena tattha nandiṃ samannānento bhūte taṇhāmaññanāya maññatīti attho. Appaṭiladdhassa khattiyamahāsālādibhāvassa, sampattiṃ vipattinti jātivasena ukkaṭṭanihīnataṃ. Dahatīti ṭhapeti. Yo [V 1.0073] evarūpo mānoti yo eso “ayaṃ pubbe mayā sadiso, idāni ayaṃ seṭṭho ayaṃ hīnataro”ti uppanno māno. Ayaṃ vuccati mānātimānoti ayaṃ bhārātibhāro viya purimaṃ sadisamānaṃ upādāya mānātimāno nāmāti attho.

`Bhūte` means in the being indicated in the passage stated. By “he perceives from bhūta,” taking the conventional usage “bhūta,” it is explained how conceivings of craving, etc., arise there, and how perception occurs through distorted perception. This meaning can be known by following the method stated below regarding “he perceives from earth”; thus, it is said, “it is just the method stated before.” Just as the Suddhāvāsa devas, due to their complete absence from these states, are not included in this teaching, so too the hell-beings, because they are not a basis for any conceiving. By this, it should be seen that some petas are also not included here. Others, however, say, “Because they are a basis for the conceiving of views, their inclusion here is indeed intended.” This is by the method stated in the sutta, beginning with “attending to one who is endowed…,” etc. ‘He is impassioned’ means that by grasping through distortion as ‘beautiful’ and ‘happy,’ he generates lust there. Thus, here, one is impassioned not only through seeing, but also through hearing and so on; this is shown when it says, “having seen… having heard…” There, being impassioned through smelling, etc., should be understood as arising from experiencing scents, garlands, etc., from using those things which are of an unsuitable nature, and also from recollecting according to one’s experience. Thus, ‘he conceives through the conceiving of craving regarding beings’ means, following the stated method, that by generating desire and lust towards beings, relishing their conduct, delighting in them, praising them, and clinging to them, or by fostering longing there, thinking, “May such a state be mine in the future,” etc., he conceives through the conceiving of craving regarding beings. Regarding what is unattained—such as the status of a wealthy khattiya, etc.—prosperity and decline are distinctions based on high and low birth. ‘He places’ means ‘he establishes.’ ‘Such conceit’ is the conceit that arises, thinking, “This one was once equal to me, now he is superior, now he is inferior.” This is called ‘conceit beyond conceit’; this means that, like ‘burden beyond burden,’ ‘conceit beyond conceit’ is so named by taking the former conceit of equality as its basis.

Niccātiādīsu uppādābhāvato niccā, maraṇābhāvato dhuvā, sabbadā bhāvato sassatā. Aniccapaṭipakkhato vā niccā, thirabhāvato dhuvā, sassatisamatāya sassatā, jarādivasena vipariṇāmassa abhāvato avipariṇāmadhammāti maññati. Sabbe sattāti oṭṭhagoṇagadrabhādayo anavasesā sañjanaṭṭhena sattā. Sabbe pāṇāti “ekindriyo pāṇo dvindriyo pāṇo”tiādivasena vuttā anavasesā pāṇanaṭṭhena pāṇā. Sabbe bhūtāti anavasesā aṇḍakosādīsu bhūtā sañjātāti bhūtā. Sabbe jīvāti sāliyavagodhūmādayo anavasesā jīvanaṭṭhena jīvā. Tesu hi so virūhabhāvena jīvasaññī. Avasā abalā avīriyāti tesaṃ attano vaso vā balaṃ vā vīriyaṃ vā natthīti dasseti. Niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatāti ettha niyatīti. Niyatatā, acchejjasuttāvutaabhejjamaṇi viya avijahitapakatitā. Saṅgatīti channaṃ abhijātīnaṃ tattha saṅgamo. Bhāvoti sabhāvoyeva, kaṇḍakānaṃ tikhiṇatā, kapiṭṭhaphalādīnaṃ parimaṇḍalāditā, migapakkhīnaṃ vicittavaṇṇāditāti evamādiko. Evaṃ niyatiyā ca saṅgatiyā ca bhāve ca pariṇatā nānappakārataṃ pattā. Yena hi yathā bhavitabbaṃ, so tatheva bhavati. Yena na bhavitabbaṃ, so na bhavatīti dasseti. Chasvevābhijātīsūti kaṇhābhijātiādīsu chasu eva abhijātīsu ṭhatvā sukhañca dukkhañca paṭisaṃvedenti, aññā sukhadukkhabhūmi natthīti dasseti. Vā-saddena antādibhede diṭṭhābhinivese saṅgaṇhāti.

In the terms “permanent,” etc.: they are permanent due to the absence of arising; stable due to the absence of death; eternal due to their perpetual existence. Or, they are permanent as the opposite of impermanence; stable due to their firm nature; eternal due to their similarity to eternity; and one conceives them to be of an unchanging nature due to the absence of change through aging, etc. “All beings”—this includes all without exception, such as camels, cattle, donkeys, etc., in the sense of being attached (sañjanaṭṭhena sattā). “All living creatures”—this refers to all without exception, such as those spoken of as “one-sensed living creature, two-sensed living creature,” etc., in the sense of breathing (pāṇanaṭṭhena pāṇā). “All creatures”—this includes all without exception, those that have come into being (bhūtā) or been born (sañjātā) in eggs, wombs, etc. “All life”—this refers to all without exception, such as rice, barley, wheat, etc., in the sense of sustaining life. For in these, due to their state of sprouting, one perceives the designation of life. “Without power, without strength, without energy”—this shows that they have no control, strength, or energy of their own. “Transformed by destiny, association, and inherent state”—here, “destiny” (niyati) means fixedness, unalterability, like an unbreakable gem strung on an unbreakable thread, not abandoning its inherent nature. “Association” (saṅgati) refers to the coming together of the six classes of birth therein. “Inherent state” (bhāva) is their very nature—such as the sharpness of thorns, the roundness of fruits like the wood-apple, the varied colors of animals and birds, and so on. Thus, having been transformed by destiny, association, and inherent state, they have attained various forms. For whatever must be so, it is so; whatever must not be, it is not—this is shown. “Only in the six classes of birth”—this means they experience pleasure and pain only while existing in these six classes of birth, such as the dark class, etc., and there is no other plane of pleasure and pain. By the word 'or', it includes attachments to views in their various divisions, beginning with the extreme views.

Upapattinti [M 1.0083] iminā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sattanikāye bhūtānaṃ sahabyataṃ ākaṅkhatīti dasseti. Sukhuppattinti iminā pana tattha tattha uppannassa sukhuppattiṃ. Ekacce bhūte niccātiādinā ekaccasassatikadiṭṭhiṃ dasseti. Ahampi bhūtesu aññatarosmīti iminā pana catutthaṃ ekaccasassatikavādaṃ dasseti.

By “birth” (upapatti), it is shown that one longs for fellowship with beings in each particular group of beings. By “happy birth” (sukhuppatti), however, it indicates the arising of happiness for one born in each particular place. By “some beings are eternal,” etc., it indicates the partial eternalist view. By “I too am one among beings,” however, it indicates the fourth kind of partial eternalist doctrine.

Yato kutocīti issarapurisādibhedato yato kutoci. Ekā taṇhāmaññanāva labbhatīti idhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayena itaramaññanānampi sambhavo niddhāretabbo. Vuttappakāreyeva bhūte taṇhādiṭṭhīhi abhinandatītiādinā vattabbattā āha “vuttanayamevā”ti. Yojanā kātabbāti “yo bhūtapaññattiyā upādānabhūte khandhe parijānāti, so tīhi pariññāhi parijānātī”tiādinā yojanā kātabbā. Apare panettha bhūtagāmopi bhūta-saddena saṅgahitoti rukkhādivasenapi [V 1.0074] maññanāvibhāgaṃ yojetvā dassenti, tathā mahābhūtavasenapi, taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ natthi.

“From whatever source”—from whatever source, such as distinctions of lords, individuals, etc. “Only the conceit of craving is found”—thus, even here, the possibility of other conceits should be determined in the manner previously stated. Because it is to be said, “one delights in beings in the manner described through craving, views, etc.,” it is stated, “it is just the method described.” “The connection should be made”—thus, the connection should be made by saying, “one who fully understands the aggregates, which are the basis for clinging underlying the concept of ‘being,’ understands them through the three kinds of full understanding,” etc. Others, however, here include even the plant kingdom under the term “bhūta,” and they explain the distinctions of conceit in terms of trees, etc., as well as in terms of the great elements. But this is not found in the commentary.

Bhūmivisesādinā bhedenāti bhūmivisesaupapattivisesādivibhāgena. Iddhiyāti puññavisesanibbattena ānubhāvena. Kiñcāpi deva-saddo “viddhe vigatavalāhake deve”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.110; 3.102; 5.146-148; ma. ni. 1.486; a. ni. 10.15; itivu. 27) ajaṭākāse āgato, “devo ca thokaṃ thokaṃ phusāyatī”tiādīsu meghe, “ayañhi deva kumāro”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.34, 35, 36) khattiye āgato, “pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgibhūto paricāreti devo maññe”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.183; ma. ni. 2.211) viya idha upapattidevesu āgato, deva-saddena pana vattabbasatte anavasesato uddharitvā tato idhādhippete dassetuṃ “te tividhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sesā cha kāmāvacarā idha devāti adhippetā itaresaṃ padantarehi nivattitattāti adhippāyo. Bhūtā devāti gahitesu sattesu taṇhādimaññanānaṃ pavattākārenapi tividhalakkhaṇanti āha “bhūtavāre vuttanayena veditabbā”ti.

“By distinctions such as types of realms”—that is, by divisions such as distinctions of realms, distinctions of birth, etc. “By psychic power”—by the extraordinary influence produced by a distinction of merit. Although the term “deva” appears in contexts such as “in a clear sky free from clouds,” etc. (Saṃ. Ni. 1.110; 3.102; 5.146–148; Ma. Ni. 1.486; A. Ni. 10.15; Itivu. 27), referring to the open sky; in phrases like “the deva rains lightly,” etc., referring to clouds; in expressions like “this deva-prince,” etc. (Dī. Ni. 2.34, 35, 36), referring to a noble; or in statements like “he enjoys himself, endowed and furnished with the five strands of sensual pleasure, like a deva, one would think,” etc. (Dī. Ni. 1.183; Ma. Ni. 2.211), here it refers to devas by rebirth. However, in order to extract completely what is meant by the word “deva” with respect to beings, and then to point out the intended meaning here, it is stated, “they are of three kinds,” etc. The remaining six sense-sphere devas are intended here as “devas,” as the others are excluded by other terms; this is the idea. Regarding the beings taken as ‘conventional devas’ (bhūtā devā), their threefold characteristic is also present in the way that the conceits of craving, etc., occur. Thus, it is said, “they should be understood in the manner explained in the section on beings.”

“Aññatarassa upāsakassa pajāpati abhirūpā hotī”tiādīsu (pārā. 168) pajāpati-saddo gharaṇiyaṃ āgato, “pajāpati kāmadāyī suvaṇṇavaṇṇā me pajā hotū”tiādīsu diṭṭhigatikaparikappite, “pajāpatissa devarājassa [M 1.0084] dhajaggaṃ ullokeyyāthā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.249) devajeṭṭhake, idha pana adhipatīti vadanti, taṃ upari brahmuno gayhamānattā tesaṃ matimattaṃ. Devānanti cātumahārājikādidevānaṃ. Mahārājādīnanti ādi-saddena sakkasuyāmasantussitasunimmitavasavattino gahitā. Tesanti mahārājādīnaṃ. Sattasaṅkhātāyāti kāmabhūmiyaṃ sattasaṅkhātāya. Pajāpatinti pajāpatibhāvaṃ. Pajāpatibhāvena hi mānaṃ jappento pajāpatiṃ mānamaññanāya maññatīti vutto.

In passages such as, “A certain lay follower’s wife was beautiful” (Pārā. 168), the word ‘pajāpati’ is used in the sense of ‘wife.’ In passages such as, “May my wife be a giver of pleasures, golden in complexion,” it refers to one conceived through speculative views. In passages such as, “You should look up at the banner of King Pajāpati, the lord of devas” (Saṃ. Ni. 1.249), it refers to the chief of the devas. Here, however, they say it means ‘lord,’ but since this is taken as referring to Brahmā who is above, that is merely their opinion. By ‘of the devas’ is meant the devas of the Four Great Kings and so forth. By ‘the Great Kings and so forth,’ the word ‘so forth’ includes Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Sunimmita, and Vasavatti. By ‘of them’ is meant the Great Kings and so forth. By ‘counted as seven’ (sattasaṅkhātāya) is meant what is counted as seven in the sensual realm. By ‘Pajāpati’ (pajāpatiṃ) is meant the state of being a pajāpati. For one who boasts with pride about the state of being a pajāpati is said to conceive of himself as Pajāpati through the conceit of pride.

Ekā diṭṭhimaññanāva yujjatīti vuttaṃ, pajāpatino pana samipataṃ salokataṃ vā ākaṅkhato, tathābhāvāya cittaṃ paṇidahato, tathāladdhabbāya sampattiyā attano seyyādibhāvaṃ dahato ca taṇhāmānamaññanāpi sambhavantīti sakkā viññātuṃ. Ye ca dhammāti āyuvaṇṇādike vadati. Pajāpatinti etthāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayena itaramaññanānampi sambhavo veditabbo.

It is said that only the conceit of views is applicable. However, it can be understood that for one who desires closeness to or co-existence with Pajāpati, or who directs the mind towards such a state, or who establishes his own superiority and so forth in the attainment to be gained in that way, the conceits of craving and pride can also arise. By ‘and those qualities’ (ye ca dhammā), he speaks of life span, beauty, and so forth. In ‘Pajāpati’ (pajāpatiṃ) too, the possibility of other conceits should be understood in the manner explained above.

Brūhitoti [V 1.0075] parivuddho. Guṇavisesehīti jhānādīhi visiṭṭhehi guṇehi uttarimanussadhammatāya. Brahma-saddassa satipi avisesato visiṭṭhavācakatte yattha yattha panassa guṇavisesayuttādirūpā pavatti, taṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sahassoti sahassiyā lokadhātuyā adhipatibhūto. Paṭhamābhinibbattoti paṇītena paṭhamajhānena nibbatto, paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ vā paṭhamaṃ abhinibbatto. Gahitāti veditabbā padhānaggahaṇena appadhānānampi kenaci sambandhena gahitabhāvasiddhito. Ettha ca brahmāti mahābrahmā adhippeto. So hi vaṇṇavantatāya ceva dīghāyukatāya ca brahmapārisajjādīhi mahanto brahmāti mahābrahmā, tassa pana purohitaṭṭhāne ṭhitāti brahmapurohitā, parisāyaṃ bhavā paricārakāti brahmapārisajjāti veditabbā. Ukkaṭṭhekapuggalabhāvato pajāpatismiṃ viya brahmani maññanā vattatīti vuttaṃ “pajāpativāre vuttanayeneva veditabbā”ti. Tathā hi bahupuggalabhāvasāmaññato ābhassaravārādīnaṃ bhūtavārasadisatā vuttā.

By 'brūhito' is meant 'grown' or 'developed'. By 'by distinguished qualities' (guṇavisesehi) is meant qualities distinguished by jhānas and so forth, due to their nature as superior human states. Although the word 'Brahma' (brahma-saddassa) generally denotes excellence without distinction, the phrase 'apicā' and so forth is stated to show where its occurrence is associated with distinguished attributes and so forth. By 'of a thousand' (sahasso) is meant being the overlord of a thousandfold world-system. By 'first-born' (paṭhamābhinibbattoti) is meant born through the excellent first jhāna, or first arisen in the plane of the first jhāna. By 'grasped' (gahitā) should be understood 'included,' since the inclusion of the principal implies the inclusion of the non-principal due to some connection. Here, by 'Brahmā' is meant Mahābrahmā.
