For he is Mahābrahmā because of his beauty and long life, and because he is great compared to the Brahma's attendants and so forth. Those who stand in the position of his chief priest are called 'Brahma's chief priests' (brahmapurohitā), and those who are his servants in the assembly are called 'Brahma's attendants' (brahmapārisajjā)—so it should be understood. It is said that because of being a pre-eminent individual, conceit (maññanā) occurs regarding Brahmā, just as it does regarding Pajāpati, and this should be understood in the manner explained in the section on Pajāpati. Similarly, due to the commonality of a multitude of beings, the Ābhassara section and so forth are said to be similar to the Bhūta section.

Yathāvuttapabhāya ābhāsanasīlā vā ābhassarā. Ekatalavāsinoti idaṃ jhānantarabhūmīnaṃ viya heṭṭhuparibhāvābhāvato vuttaṃ, ṭhānāni [M 1.0085] pana nesaṃ paricchinnāneva. Ābhassarehi parittā ābhā etesanti parittābhā. Appamāṇā ābhā etesanti appamāṇābhā.

They are Ābhassara because they are of a luminous nature with the radiance as described. The phrase 'dwellers on a single plane' (ekatalavāsino) is stated because there is no higher or lower division among them, unlike other jhāna realms; however, their locations are indeed distinct. Those whose radiance is limited are called 'of limited radiance' (parittābhā). Those whose radiance is immeasurable are called 'of immeasurable radiance' (appamāṇābhā).

Subhāti sobhanā pabhā. Kañcanapiṇḍo viya sassirikā kañcanapiṇḍasassirikā. Tattha sobhanāya pabhāya kiṇṇā subhākiṇṇāti vattabbe bhā-saddassa rassattaṃ, antima-ṇa-kārassa ha-kārañca katvā “subhakiṇhā”ti vuttā. Subhāti ca ekagghanā niccalā pabhā vuccati, parittā subhā etesanti parittasubhā. Appamāṇā subhā etesanti appamāṇasubhā.

By 'subhā' is meant beautiful radiance. 'Radiant like a mass of gold' (kañcanapiṇḍasassirikā) means having the splendor of a mass of gold. There, though it should be said 'subhākiṇṇā' (filled with beautiful radiance), by shortening the 'bhā' sound and changing the final 'ṇa' to 'ha,' it is stated as 'subhakiṇhā'. By 'subhā' is also meant concentrated, unwavering radiance. Those whose radiance is limited are called 'of limited radiance' (parittasubhā). Those whose radiance is immeasurable are called 'of immeasurable radiance' (appamāṇasubhā).

Vipulaphalāti vipulasantasukhāyuvaṇṇādiphalā.

By 'abundant fruits' (vipulaphalā) is meant fruits abundant in peace, happiness, longevity, beauty, and so forth.

Satipi devabrahmādīnaṃ puññaphalena jhānaphalena ca paṭipakkhābhibhave yesaṃ pana puthujjanaasaññasattesu abhibhūvohāro pākaṭo niruḷho ca, tesaṃ vasenāyaṃ desanā pavattāti dassento āha “asaññabhavassetaṃ adhivacana”nti. Yathā pajāpativāre “idhekacco pajāpatismiṃyevā”tiādinā maññanāpavatti dassitā, tathā idhāpi taṃ dassetuṃ sakkāti āha “sesaṃ pajāpativāre vuttanayamevā”ti.

Even though there is overcoming of opponents by the fruit of merit and the fruit of jhāna for devas, Brahmās, and so forth, yet for those ordinary people and non-percipient beings for whom the usage of 'overcoming' (abhibhūvohāro) is manifest and established, showing that this teaching proceeds on account of them, he said: 'This is a designation for the non-percipient realm' (asaññabhavassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ). Just as in the Pajāpati section the occurrence of conceiving (maññanāpavatti) is shown with phrases like 'here, someone is conceited regarding Pajāpati' (idhekacco pajāpatismiṃyevā) and so forth, so too here it can be shown in the same way. Hence, it is said: 'The rest should be understood in the manner explained in the Pajāpati section' (sesaṃ pajāpativāre vuttanayamevā).

Bhūtavārādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Bhūta section and so forth is concluded.

Ākāsānañcāyatanavārādivaṇṇanā

The commentary on the section on the base of infinite space and so forth.

4. Evaṃ [V 1.0076] sattavasena bhūmikkamadassane suddhāvāsānaṃ aggahaṇe kāraṇaṃ niddhārento “evaṃ bhagavā”tiādimāha. Tattha anāgāmikhīṇāsavāti anāgāmino ca khīṇāsavā ca. Kiñcāpi suddhāvāsā attheva anekakappasahassāyukā, ukkaṃsaparicchedato pana soḷasakappasahassāyukāva, na tato paranti āha “katipayakappasahassāyukā”ti. Kāmarūpabhavesu pavattamānāpi ākāsānañcāyatanādidhammā arūpāvacarabhāvato taṃbhūmikavohāraṃ na labhantīti “tatrūpapannāyevā”ti avadhāretvā vuttaṃ. Abhibhūvāre vuttanayena veditabbā yathārahanti adhippāyo. Na hettha vaṇṇavantatādi sambhavatīti. Pajāpativāre vuttanayenāti [M 1.0086] ettha “ahamasmi arūpo pahīnarūpapaṭighasañño”tiādinā mānamaññanā veditabbā.

4. Thus, in showing the sequence of planes by way of beings, while determining the reason for the non-inclusion of the Pure Abodes, he said: 'Thus, the Blessed One' and so forth. Here, by 'non-returners and those with destroyed taints' (anāgāmikhīṇāsavā) are meant non-returners and those whose taints are destroyed. Although the beings in the Pure Abodes do exist and live for many thousands of eons, yet because their highest limit is sixteen thousand eons, not beyond that, it is said: 'for some thousands of eons' (katipayakappasahassāyukā). Even though the phenomena of the base of infinite space and so forth occur in the realms of sensual desire and form, they do not obtain the designation of that realm because of being formless-sphere states; therefore, it is stated definitively: 'only those reborn there' (tatrūpapannāyevā). The meaning is that it should be understood as appropriate in the manner explained in the Abhibhū section. For qualities like possessing beauty and so forth are not possible here. By 'in the manner explained in the Pajāpati section' (pajāpativāre vuttanayena) is meant that conceiving through pride (mānamaññanā) should be understood here with phrases like 'I am formless, with perception of form and resistance abandoned' (ahamasmi arūpo pahīnarūpapaṭighasañño) and so forth.

Ākāsānañcāyatanavārādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the section on the base of infinite space and so forth is concluded.

Diṭṭhasutavārādivaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section on the Seen, Heard, and So On

5. Rūpamukhena maññanāvatthudassanaṃ saṅkhepoti katvā vuttaṃ “vitthāratopī”ti. Tampi hi “yattha neva pathavī, na āpo, na tejo, na vāyo, na ākāsānañcāyatana”ntiādiggahaṇaṃ viya saṅkhepato pañcavokārabhavadassanaṃ hotīti.

5. It is said, 'even in detail,' because the presentation of the basis for conceiving by way of form is brief. For that too, like the inclusion of 'where there is neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air, nor the base of infinite space,' etc., is a brief presentation of the five-constituent existence.

Diṭṭhanti yaṃ cakkhudvārena katadassanakiriyāsamāpanaṃ, yañca cakkhu dvayaṃ passati passissati sati sambhave passeyya, taṃ sabbakālanti visesavacanicchāya abhāvato diṭṭhanteva vuttaṃ yathā “duddha”nti. Tenāha “rūpāyatanassetaṃ adhivacana”nti. Ayañca nayo sutādīsupi yojetabbo. Sattāti rūpādīsu sattā visattāti sattā. Sañjanaṭṭhena sāmaññasaddopi cesa satta-saddo “itthirūpe”ti visayavisesitattā idha purisavācako daṭṭhabbo. Rattāti vatthaṃ viya raṅgajātena cittassa vipariṇāmakārakena chandarāgena rattā sārattā. Giddhāti abhikaṅkhanasabhāvena abhigijjhanena giddhā gedhaṃ āpannā. Gadhitāti ganthitā viya lobhena dummocanīyabhāvena ārammaṇe paṭibaddhā. Mucchitāti kilesavasena visaññībhūtā viya anaññakiccā mucchaṃ mohaṃ āpannā. Ajjhosannāti visaye aññasādhāraṇe viya katvā gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpetvā viya ṭhitā. Imināti suvaṇṇavaṇṇādiākārena. Maṅgalaṃ amaṅgalanti īdisaṃ diṭṭhaṃ maṅgalaṃ, īdisaṃ amaṅgalanti[V 1.0077]. Rūpasmiṃ attānaṃ samanupassananayenāti idaṃ vedanādiarūpadhamme, rūpāyatanavinimuttasabbadhamme vā attato gahetvā tato ajjhattikaṃ, bāhiraṃ vā rūpāyatanaṃ tassokāsabhāvena parikappetvā “so kho pana me ayaṃ attā imasmiṃ rūpāyatane”ti maññanto diṭṭhasmiṃ maññatīti imaṃ nayaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Pathavito maññatī”tiādīsu yathā “saupakaraṇassa attano vā parassa [M 1.0087] vā”tiādimaññanāpavatti dassitā, evaṃ “diṭṭhato maññatī”tiādīsu sakkā taṃ dassetunti āha “tesaṃ pathavīvāre vuttanayeneva veditabba”nti.

'Seen' refers to what is accomplished through the eye-door as the act of seeing is completed, and whatever the eye sees, will see, or might see when conditions are present—all this is called 'seen' without any temporal specification, just as the word 'milk' (duddha) is used. Hence it is said, 'This is a designation for the form base.' This same method should be applied to the heard and so forth. 'Beings' (sattā) are those attached to forms and so forth; they are clung (visattā). Though the word 'being' is a common term in the sense of attachment, here, due to the specification of the object as 'female form,' this word 'being' should be understood as referring to a male. 'Infatuated' (rattā): They are dyed, like cloth, by the color generated by lust, which alters the mind; they are thoroughly infatuated. 'Greedy' (giddhā): They are greedy, having fallen into greed through the nature of desiring and intense craving. 'Bound' (gadhitā): They are bound, as if tied by a knot, fastened to the object due to greed, being difficult to release. 'Bewildered' (mucchitā): They are bewildered, as if senseless due to defilements, having lost awareness of other tasks, overcome by bewilderment and delusion. 'Grasping' (ajjhosannā): They are fixed, as if having seized, swallowed, and consumed the object, making it as if it were not for common use. 'By this' (iminā) refers to forms like golden color and so forth. 'Auspicious, inauspicious': 'This seen thing is auspicious, this is inauspicious'—thus. 'By the method of regarding self in form' (rūpasmiṃ attānaṃ samanupassananayena): This refers to taking feeling and other immaterial phenomena, or all phenomena apart from the form base, as self. Then, conceiving the internal or external form base as its location, and thinking, 'This self of mine is in this form base,' one thus conceives in the seen. This method is intended here. Just as in 'conceives from earth,' etc., the arising of conceiving is shown in terms of 'one's own or another's with its accessories,' etc., so too in 'conceives from the seen,' etc., it is possible to show that. Therefore, it is said, 'It should be understood in the same way as explained in the section on earth.'

Āhaccāti visayaṃ anvāya, patvāti attho. Tenāha “upagantvā”ti. Aññamaññasaṃsileseti cakkhurūpasotasaddā viya dure ahutvā aññamaññaṃ alliyane.

'Having reached' (āhacca) means having attained the object. Therefore, it is said, 'having approached.' 'In mutual contact' (aññamaññasaṃsilese) refers to mutually clinging, like the eye and form, or the ear and sound, not being distant from each other.

Manasā viññātaṃ kevalanti attho. Itarānipi hi manasā viññāyantīti. Sesehi sattahi āyatanehi paññattiyā asaṅgahitattā tampi saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ “dhammārammaṇassa vā”ti vuttaṃ. Dvīsupi vikappesu lokuttarānampi saṅgaho āpannoti āha “idha pana sakkāyapariyāpannameva labbhatī”ti. Vitthāroti maññanānaṃ pavattanākāravitthāro. Etthāti etesu sutavārādīsu.

The meaning is that only what is cognized by mind is meant, for other things are also cognized by mind. Since concepts are not included by the remaining seven bases, to include them also, it is said, 'or of a mental object.' In both alternatives, the inclusion of the supramundane is implied, hence it is stated, 'but here only what is connected with the aggregates is obtained.' 'Elaboration' (vitthāro) means the detailed manner of occurrence for conceiving. 'Here' (ettha) refers to these, such as the sections on the heard and so forth.

Diṭṭhasutavārādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Section on the Seen, Heard, and So On is concluded.

Ekattavārādivaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section on Unity and So On

6. Samāpannakavārenāti samāpannakappavattiyā, rūpāvacarārūpāvacarajhānappavattiyāti attho. Sā hi ekasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe ekākārena pavattatīti katvā “ekatta”nti vuccati, evañca katvā vipākajjhānappavattipi idha samāpannakavāraggahaṇeneva gahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Asamāpannakavārenāti kāmāvacaradhammappavattiyā. Upacārajjhānenapi hi cittaṃ na sammā ekattaṃ gatanti vuccatīti.

6. By 'the section on one who has attained' (samāpannakavārena) is meant by the occurrence of attainments, that is, the occurrence of form-sphere and formless-sphere jhānas. For it arises with a single characteristic on a single object, hence it is called 'unity.' And so, the occurrence of resultant jhāna should also be understood to be included here by the inclusion of the section on attainment. By 'the section on one who has not attained' (asamāpannakavārena) is meant by the occurrence of sense-sphere phenomena. For even with access concentration, the mind is not said to have properly reached unity.

Yojanāti maññanāyojanā. Bhinditvāti vibhajitvā. Sāsananayenāti pāḷinayena. Tattha “ekattaṃ maññatī”tiādīsu “vedanaṃ attato samanupassatī”tiādinā nayena, “nānattaṃ maññatī”tiādīsu [V 1.0078] pana “rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī”tiādinā nayena vuttavidhiṃ anugantvā maññanā veditabbā.

'Yoking' (yojanā) means the yoking of conceiving. 'Having broken apart' (bhinditvā) means dividing. 'According to the method of the Teaching' (sāsananayena) means according to the method of the Pāli text. There, in phrases like 'he conceives unity,' conceiving should be understood to follow the method stated in phrases like 'he regards feeling as self,' while in phrases like 'he conceives diversity,' conceiving should be understood to follow the method stated in phrases like 'he regards form as self.'

Pathavīvārādīsu vuttena ca aṭṭhakathānayenāti “ahaṃ vedanāti maññati, mama vedanāti maññatī”tiādinā, “ahaṃ rūpanti maññati, mama rūpanti maññatī”tiādinā cāti attho. Tenāha “yathānurūpaṃ [M 1.0088] vīmaṃsitvā”ti, ekattanānattabhāvesu yo yojanānayo sambhavati, tadanurūpaṃ vicāretvāti attho. Kecīti abhayagirivāsino. Apareti sārasamāsācariyā. Diṭṭhābhinivesaṃ vadantīti sambandho. Puthujjanassa maññanā nāma sakkāyaṃ bhinditvāva yathāupaṭṭhitavisayavaseneva pavattatīti na tattha ayamekattanayo ayaṃ nānattanayoti vibhāgavaseneva, ekattasaññī attā hotītiādīsu ca attano ekattanānattasaññitā vuttā, na pana ekattaṃ nānattanti evaṃ pavattassa diṭṭhābhinivesassa ekattanānattabhāvoti evamettha tadubhayassa idha anadhippetabhāvo daṭṭhabbo.

And according to the method of the commentary stated in the sections on earth and so forth, it means, 'he conceives "I am feeling," he conceives "feeling is mine,"' etc., and 'he conceives "I am form," he conceives "form is mine,"' etc. Hence it is said, 'having investigated appropriately,' meaning having investigated according to the method of application that is possible in the case of unity and diversity. 'Some' (kecī) refers to the Abhayagiri residents. 'Others' (apare) refers to the teachers of the Sārasamāsa. The connection is with the statement, 'they speak of adherence to views.' The conceiving of an ordinary person occurs only by analyzing the personality, arising dependent on the presented object. Thus there is no division there as 'this is the method of unity, this is the method of diversity.' And in phrases like 'the self is a perceiver of unity,' etc., one's own state of perceiving unity and diversity is stated, but not the state of unity and diversity of an adherence to a view that proceeds as 'unity is diversity'; thus, it should be understood that both are not intended here.

Yaṃ yathāvuttaputhujjano anavasesato gaṇhanto gahetuṃ sakkoti, taṃ tassa anavasesato gahetabbataṃ upādāya “sabba”nti vuccatīti dassento “tamevā”ti āha, sakkāyasabbanti attho. Sabbasmimpi tebhūmakadhamme ādīnavadassane asati nibbidābhāvato assādānupassanāya taṇhā vaḍḍhatevāti āha “sabbaṃ assādento sabbaṃ taṇhāmaññanāya maññatī”ti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “saṃyojaniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.53, 57). “Sabbamidaṃ mayā nimmita”nti tena nimmitamaññanāya attānaṃ seyyādito dahanto tena mānena nimmitaṃ maññatiyeva nāma nimmitamaññanāya vinā tathāmānuppattiyā abhāvatoti āha “attanā nimmitaṃ maññanto sabbaṃ mānamaññanāya maññatī”ti. Sabbaṃ natthītiādinā nayenāti ādi-saddena niyativādādike saṅgaṇhāti. Mahā me attāti iminā sabbato attano vibhūtipavattivādaṃ dasseti. “Sabbaṃ sabbatthaka”nti diṭṭhivasena – “ahaṃ sabbasmiṃ mayhaṃ kiñcanaṃ palibodho sabbasmiṃ, paro sabbasmiṃ parassa kiñcanaṃ palibodho sabbasmi”ntiādinā nayenapettha maññanā sambhavatīti dassento āha “sesaṃ pathavīvāre vuttanayena veditabba”nti. Apica “sabboyaṃ loko purisamayo”ti evaṃdiṭṭhiko purisasaṅkhātato sabbato, attano uppattiṃ vā niggamanaṃ vā maññanto diṭṭhimaññanāya sabbato maññati, tasmiṃyeva pana diṭṭhimaññanāya maññite vatthusmiṃ sinehaṃ mānañca uppādayato taṇhāmaññanā mānamaññanā ca veditabbā. Taṃyeva pana sabbaṃ mayhaṃ attā kattā [V 1.0079] sāmīti vā maññanto “sabbaṃ [M 1.0089] me”ti maññati, tathāyaṃ diṭṭhitaṇhābhinandanāhi abhinandanto sabbaṃ abhinandatīti evampettha maññanānaṃ pavatti veditabbā.

Showing that what the ordinary person, as described, can grasp entirely without omission is called 'all' because it is to be taken entirely, he says 'that very thing' (tameva), meaning the all of personality. When one does not see the danger in all phenomena of the three realms, there is no disenchantment, and through contemplating gratification, craving only increases. Thus, it is said: 'Delighting in all, one conceives of everything through conceiving by way of craving.' For this has been declared by the Blessed One: 'Bhikkhus, when one dwells contemplating gratification in things that fetter, craving grows.' 'All this has been created by me'—thus, by considering oneself as superior and so on through that conceit, one indeed conceives it as created, for without such a conceiving of it as created, there is no arising of such a conceit. Therefore, it is said: 'Conceiving all as created by oneself, one conceives of everything through conceiving by way of conceit.' By the method of 'all is nothing,' etc.—here, by the word 'etc.' he includes determinism and so forth. By 'My self is great,' he shows the doctrine of one's own power proceeding in all respects. By way of the view 'All is everywhere'—'I am in all; whatever is mine is an obstacle in all; another is in all; whatever is another's is an obstacle in all'—showing that conceiving is possible here too by this method, he says, 'The rest should be understood in the manner explained in the earth exposition.' Furthermore, one who holds the view 'This entire world consists of man,' conceiving one's own origin or departure from everything reckoned as 'person', thus conceives of everything through conceiving by way of views. But when one generates affection and conceit regarding that very object conceived by way of views, conceiving by way of craving and conceiving by way of conceit should be understood. Furthermore, conceiving that very all as 'my self, the doer, the master,' one conceives 'all is mine.' Similarly, by delighting in views and craving, one delights in all. In this way, the occurrence of conceiving here should be understood.

Tanti sakkāyaṃ. Ukkaṃsagatasukhasahitañhi khandhapañcakaṃ diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādī nibbānanti maññati, taṃ panatthato sakkāyoyevāti. Ekadhāti pañcavidhampi nibbānabhāvena ekajjhaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Yatoti yasmā. Pañcahi kāmaguṇehīti manāpiyarūpādīhi pañcahi kāmakoṭṭhāsehi, bandhanehi vā. Samappito suṭṭhu appito allīno hutvā ṭhito. Samaṅgibhūtoti samannāgato. Paricāretīti tesu kāmaguṇesu kāmakoṭṭhāsesu yathāsukhaṃ indriyāni cāreti sañcāreti ito cito ca upaneti. Atha vā laḷati ramati kīḷati. Ettha dvidhā kāmaguṇā mānusakā ceva dibbā ca. Mānusakā ca mandhātukāmaguṇasadisā, dibbā paranimmitavasavattidevarājassa kāmaguṇasadisā. Evarūpe kāme upagatānañhi te diṭṭhadhammanibbānasampattiṃ paññapenti. Tenāha “ettāvatā kho…pe… hotī”ti. Diṭṭhadhammoti paccakkhadhammo vuccati, tattha tattha paṭiladdhattabhāvassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, diṭṭhadhamme nibbānaṃ imasmiṃyeva attabhāve dukkhavūpasamanaṃ diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ. Paramaṃ uttamaṃ diṭṭhadhammanibbānanti paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ, taṃ patto hotīti attho. Pañcadhā āgatanti yathāvuttakāmaguṇasukhassa ceva catubbidharūpāvacarajjhānasukhassa ca vasena pāḷiyaṃ pañcappakārena āgataṃ. Nibbānaṃ assādentoti paramaṃ sukhaṃ nissaraṇanti maññanāya assādento.

That is the personality. For those who hold the view of Nibbāna in this very life, they imagine the five aggregates—associated with exalted happiness—as Nibbāna, but in reality, it is merely the personality. ‘In one way’ (ekadhā) means that the fivefold aggregates are spoken of as combined into one as Nibbāna. ‘Because’ (yato) means ‘since’ (yasmā). ‘By means of the five strands of sensual pleasures’ (pañcahi kāmaguṇehi) means by means of the five delightful forms, etc., the five divisions of sensual pleasures, or bonds. ‘Thoroughly attached’ (samappito) means having become well-attached, clinging, and remaining. ‘Endowed’ (samaṅgibhūto) means ‘possessed of’ (samannāgato). ‘He indulges’ (paricāreti) means he directs and moves his faculties as he pleases among those sensual pleasures, those divisions of sensual pleasures, bringing them here and there. Or alternatively, he sports, delights, and plays. Here, sensual pleasures are twofold: human and divine. Human sensual pleasures are like those of King Mandhātu, while divine ones resemble the pleasures of the king of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas. For those who have attained such sensual pleasures, they declare the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life. Hence it is said, “To this extent… it is so.” ‘This very life’ (diṭṭhadhammo) is called directly experienced reality; this is a designation for the state attained here and there. Nibbāna in this very life is the cessation of suffering in this very existence. ‘The supreme Nibbāna in this very life’ (paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ) means the supreme Nibbāna in this very life; the meaning is that one has attained it. ‘Arrived in five ways’ (pañcadhā āgataṃ) means that it has come in the Pali in five aspects, by way of the happiness of the aforementioned sensual pleasures and the happiness of the fourfold form-sphere jhānas. ‘Relishing Nibbāna’ (nibbānaṃ assādento) means relishing, conceiving supreme happiness to be liberation.

“Imasmiṃ nibbāne patte na jāyati, na jīrati, na mīyatī”ti evampi nibbānasmiṃ maññati. “Ito paraṃ paramassāsabhūtaṃ natthī”ti gaṇhanto nibbānato maññati. Tayidaṃ nibbānaṃ mayā adhigataṃ, tasmā “nibbānaṃ me”ti maññati. Tatoyeva taṃ nibbānaṃ diṭṭhābhinandanāya abhinandati. Ayaṃ tāvettha diṭṭhimaññanā. Tasmiṃyeva pana diṭṭhimaññanāya maññite vatthusmiṃ sinehaṃ mānañca uppādayato taṇhāmānamaññanāpi niddhāretabbā.

“In this Nibbāna that has been attained, there is no birth, no aging, no death,” thus, too, does one conceive in Nibbāna. “Beyond this, there is no higher state of relief,” grasping thus, one conceives from Nibbāna. “This Nibbāna has been attained by me, therefore Nibbāna is mine,” thus one conceives. Therefore, one rejoices in that Nibbāna with delight in views. This, for the present, is conceiving by way of views. But in that very thing that is conceived by conceiving by way of views, when affection and conceit arise, conceiving by way of craving and conceit must also be determined.

Yādisoti yathārūpo, yehi jegucchādisabhāvehi passitabboti attho. Esāti ayaṃ. Tenassa attano suṇantānañca paccakkhasiddhatamāha. Asubhādisabhāvena saha vijjamānānaṃ rūpādidhammānaṃ kāyo samūhoti sakkāyo, upādānakkhandhā. Tathāti tassa bhāvabhūtena paṭikūlatādippakārena. Sabbamaññanāti pathavīādike sarūpāvadhāraṇādivibhāgabhinne [M 1.0090] visaye pavattiyā anekavihitā sabbā taṇhāmaññanā.

‘Of what kind’ (yādiso) means ‘of such a form’ (yathārūpo); the meaning is that it should be seen by means of such qualities as loathsomeness, etc. ‘This’ (esā) means ‘this’ (ayaṃ). Thus, he states that it is directly evident to himself and to those who hear him. ‘Personality’ (sakkāyo) means a collection, a group of phenomena such as form, etc., which exist together with qualities such as the repulsive; that is, the aggregates of clinging. ‘In such a way’ (tathā) means by its inherent characteristic of repulsiveness, etc. ‘All conceiving’ (sabbamaññanā) means all manifold conceiving by way of craving that arises in the sphere of objects such as earth, etc., differentiated by such divisions as the ascertainment of own nature.

Jegucchoti [V 1.0080] jigucchanīyo. Tenassa asubhājaññaduggandhapaṭikūlabhāvaṃ dasseti. Siduroti khaṇe khaṇe bhijjanasabhāvo. Tenassa aniccaaddhuvakhayavayapabhaṅgurasabhāvaṃ dasseti. Ayanti sakkāyo. Dukkhoti na sukho. Tenassa kicchakasirābādhadukkhavuttitaṃ dasseti. Apariṇāyakoti pariṇāyakarahito. Tenassa attasuññaasāravuttitaṃ dasseti. Tanti sakkāyaṃ. Paccanīkatoti sabhāvapaṭipakkhato, subhaniccasukhaattāditoti attho. Gaṇhanti gaṇhanto, tattha subhādigāhavasena abhinivisantoti attho.

‘Loathsome’ (jeguccho) means ‘to be loathed’ (jigucchanīyo). By this, he shows its nature of being unlovely, impure, ill-smelling, and repulsive. ‘Fragile’ (siduro) means having a nature of breaking at every moment. By this, he shows its nature of being impermanent, unstable, decaying, perishing, and perishable. ‘This’ (ayaṃ) refers to the personality. ‘Suffering’ (dukkho) means ‘not pleasant’ (na sukho). By this, he shows its nature of being troublesome, wretched, afflicted, and characterized by suffering. ‘Without a leader’ (apariṇāyako) means ‘devoid of a leader’ (pariṇāyakarahito). By this, he shows its nature of being empty of self and devoid of essence. ‘That’ (taṃ) refers to the personality. ‘Opposed’ (paccanīkato) means ‘by nature opposed’; the meaning is ‘contrary to beauty, permanence, pleasure, self, etc.’ ‘Grasping’ (gaṇhanti) means ‘grasping’; the meaning is ‘clinging there by way of grasping at beauty, etc.’

Idāni tissopi maññanā upamāhi vibhāvetuṃ “subhato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yathā mahāpariḷāhe vipulānatthāvahe ca aggimhi salabhassa patanaṃ subhasukhasaññāya, evaṃ tādise sakkāye salabhassa taṇhāmaññanāti imamatthaṃ dasseti “subhato…pe… taṇhāya maññanā”ti iminā.

Now, in order to illustrate the three kinds of conceiving with similes, the passage beginning with ‘as beautiful,’ etc., was stated. Herein, just as a moth falls into a great, vast, and destructive fire, perceiving it as beautiful and pleasant, so too, in such a personality, is the conceiving by way of craving like the moth—this meaning is shown by the phrase: “as beautiful… the conceiving by way of craving.”

Gūthādī kīṭako gūtharāsiṃ laddhā asampannepi tasmiṃ sampannākāraṃ pavattayamāno attānaṃ ukkaṃseti, evamanekādīnave ekantabhedini sakkāye niccasaññaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā sampattimadena tattha bālo mānaṃ jappetīti imamatthamāha “niccasaññaṃ…pe… mānena maññanā”ti.

Just as a dung-eating insect, having obtained a pile of dung, even though it is incomplete, exalts itself by behaving as if it were complete, so too, a fool, intoxicated by attainment, establishes the perception of permanence in the personality, which has many dangers and is utterly subject to dissolution, and there utters pride. This meaning is stated by the phrase ‘the perception of permanence… the conceiving by way of conceit’.

Yathā bālo muddhadhātuko sammūḷho koci ādāse attano paṭibimbaṃ disvā “ayaṃ maññe ādāsasāmiko, yadi ahamimaṃ gahetvā tiṭṭheyyaṃ, anatthampi me kareyyā”ti chaḍḍetvā palāyanto tattha avijjamānameva kiñci vijjamānaṃ katvā gaṇhi, tathūpamo ayaṃ bālo sakkāye attattaniyagāhaṃ gaṇhantoti imamatthaṃ dīpeti “attā…pe… diṭṭhiyā hoti maññanā”ti iminā.

Just as a foolish person, of a confused disposition, bewildered, sees his own reflection in a mirror and thinks, “This, I think, is the owner of the mirror. If I were to take and keep him, he might even do me harm,” and so he throws it away and flees, grasping something nonexistent as if it were existent – in the same way, this fool grasps at self and what belongs to self in the personality. This meaning is illuminated by the phrase ‘self… there is conceiving by way of views’.

Sukhumaṃ mārabandhanaṃ vepacittibandhanatopi sukhumatarattā. Tenāha bhagavā “aho sukhumataraṃ kho, bhikkhave, mārabandhana”nti.

The bond of Māra is subtle because it is even more subtle than the bond of Vepacitti. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Indeed, bhikkhus, the bond of Māra is extremely subtle.”

Bahunti ativiya, anekakkhattuṃ vā. Vipphandamānopi sakkāyaṃ nātivattati saṃsāraṃ nātivattanato. Yathāha “ye te, bhikkhave, samaṇā sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti, te, sakkāyaṃyeva anuparidhāvanti seyyathāpi sā gaddulabandhano”tiādi. Yathā hi sattasupi [M 1.0091] ucchedavikappesu saṃsāranāyikānaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhīnaṃ pahānaṃ sambhavati, evaṃ sassatavikappesupīti [V 1.0081] kathañci pana diṭṭhigatikassa bhavavippamokkho. Tena vuttaṃ “sakkāyaṃ nātivattatī”ti.

‘Much’ (bahuṃ) means ‘exceedingly’ (ativiya), or ‘many times’ (anekakkhattuṃ). Even though struggling, one does not transcend the personality, since one does not transcend saṃsāra. As it was said: ‘Bhikkhus, those ascetics who propound the cutting off, destruction, and annihilation of an existent being, they only run around the personality, just like a dog tied to a tether,’ and so on. Just as the abandoning of craving and views, which lead in saṃsāra, is possible in the seven annihilationist conceptions, so also in the eternalist conceptions, yet how can there be liberation from existence for one who is given to views? Therefore, it was said: ‘One does not transcend the personality.’

Sasoti so eso puthujjano. Niccanti sabbakālaṃ.

‘He’ (saso) means ‘that ordinary person’ (so eso puthujjano). ‘Always’ (niccaṃ) means ‘at all times’ (sabbakālaṃ).

Tanti tasmā sakkāyamalīnassa jātiyādīnamanativattanato. Asātatoti dukkhato.

‘That’ (taṃ) means ‘therefore,’ because one who is defiled by the personality does not transcend birth and so on. ‘From the unpleasant’ (asātato) means ‘from suffering’ (dukkhato).

Passaṃ evamimanti asubhāniccadukkhānattasabhāvaṃ taṃ sakkāyaṃ vuttappakārena yathābhūtavipassanāpaññāsahitāya maggapaññāya passanto. Pahāyāti samucchedavasena sabbā maññanāyo pajahitvā. Sabbadukkhā pamuccatīti sakalasmāpi vaṭṭadukkhato pamuccatīti.

‘Seeing thus this’ (passaṃ evaṃ imaṃ) means seeing that personality, which has the nature of being unlovely, impermanent, suffering, and not-self, with path-wisdom accompanied by insight-wisdom as it really is, in the manner described above. ‘Abandoning’ (pahāya) means having abandoned all conceivings by way of complete eradication. ‘He is freed from all suffering’ (sabbadukkhā pamuccati) means he is freed from all the suffering of the round.

Ekattavārādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the section beginning with ‘in one way’ is concluded.

Paṭhamanayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first method is concluded.

Sekkhavāradutiyanayavaṇṇanā

The Second Exposition on the Trainee's Method

7. Adhippetassa atthassa aniyametvā vacanaṃ uddeso, niyametvā vacanaṃ niddesoti āha “yoti uddesavacanaṃ, soti niddesavacana”nti. Sampiṇḍanatthoti samuccayattho. Sampiṇḍanañca sabhāgatāvasena hotīti āha – “ārammaṇasabhāgenā”ti, ārammaṇassa sabhāgatāya sadisatāyāti attho. Sekkhaṃ dasseti sāmaññajotanāya visese avaṭṭhānato, sekkhavisayattā ca tassa vacanassa.

7. Without determining the intended meaning, a statement is called an uddesa; having determined the intended meaning, a statement is called a niddesa. Thus it is said, "'Yo' is a word of uddesa, 'so' is a word of niddesa." The meaning of sampiṇḍana is the meaning of samuccaya (collection). And sampiṇḍana occurs by way of similarity of nature. Thus it is said, "by similarity of the object," meaning by the similarity or likeness of the object. It indicates the trainee by manifesting the general characteristic, since it does not remain fixed on particulars, and because that statement pertains to the domain of the trainee.

Kenaṭṭhenāti yasmā ñāṇena araṇīyato attho sabhāvo, tasmā kenaṭṭhena kena sabhāvena kena lakkhaṇena sekkho nāma hotīti attho. Yasmā pana sekkhadhammādhigamena puggale sekkhavohārappavatti, tasmā “sekkhadhammapaṭilābhato sekkho”ti vuttaṃ. Sekkhadhammā nāma catūsu maggesu, heṭṭhimesu ca tīsu phalesu sammādiṭṭhiādayo. Tenāha “sekkhāya sammādiṭṭhiyā…pe… ettāvatā kho bhikkhu sekkho hotī”ti. Evaṃ abhidhammapariyāyena sekkhalakkhaṇaṃ dassetvā [M 1.0092] idāni suttantikapariyāyenapi taṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sikkhatīti iminā sikkhāttayasamaṅgī apariniṭṭhitasikkho sekkhoti dasseti. Tenāha “sikkhatī”tiādi[V 1.0082]. Sikkhāhi niccasamāyogadīpanatthañcettha “sikkhati sikkhatī”ti āmeḍitavacanaṃ. Atha vā sikkhanaṃ sikkhā, sā etassa sīlanti sekkho. So hi apariyositasikkhattā tadadhimuttattā ca ekantena sikkhanasīlo, na asekkho viya pariniṭṭhitasikkho tattha paṭippassaddhussukko, nāpi vissaṭṭhasikkho pacurajano viya tattha anadhimutto. Atha vā ariyāya jātiyā tīsu sikkhāsu jāto, tattha vā bhavoti sekkho. Atha vā ikkhati etāyāti ikkhā, maggaphalasammādiṭṭhi. Saha ikkhāyāti sekkho.

By what meaning? Since the meaning, the nature, is to be known by knowledge, therefore, by what meaning, by what nature, by what characteristic is one called a trainee? This is the meaning. Moreover, because the designation 'trainee' applies to a person through the attainment of the qualities of a trainee, it is said: "A trainee is one who has obtained the qualities of a trainee." The qualities of a trainee are right view and so forth in the four paths and the lower three fruits. Therefore, it is said: "With the trainee's right view... to this extent, bhikkhu, one is a trainee." Having thus shown the characteristic of a trainee according to the Abhidhamma method, now to show it also according to the Sutta method, it is said: "Moreover..." Herein, "one trains" indicates that a trainee is one who is endowed with the threefold training but whose training is not complete. Hence it is said: "one trains" and so on. The repetition of "trains, trains" here is to indicate constant association with the trainings. Alternatively, sikkhā (training) is the act of training; one who has that as his virtue is a trainee. For he, being incomplete in training and devoted to it, is continually inclined toward training—unlike a non-trainee, who has completed training and whose effort is calmed therein, or unlike an ordinary person, who has abandoned training and is indifferent to it. Or, one is born into the noble lineage in the three trainings, or exists therein—thus, a trainee. Or, that by which one sees is ikkhā, which is right view of path and fruit. One who is with ikkhā is a sekkha.

Anulomapaṭipadāya paripūrakārīti yā sā sīlādikā vipassanantā dukkhanirodhagāminiyā lokuttarāya paṭipadāya anulomanato anulomapaṭipadā, tassā sampādanena paripūrakārīti. Idāni taṃ paṭipadaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānena dassetuṃ “sīlasampanno”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sīlasampannoti pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlena samannāgato, paripuṇṇapātimokkhasīlo vā. Pātimokkhasīlañhi idha “sīla”nti adhippetaṃ padhānabhāvato. Rūpādiārammaṇesu abhijjhādīnaṃ pavattinivāraṇasaṅkhātena manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ pidhānena indriyesu guttadvāro. Pariyesanādivasena bhojane pamāṇajānanena bhojane mattaññū. Vigatathinamiddho hutvā rattindivaṃ kammaṭṭhānamanasikāre yuttatāya jāgariyānuyogamanuyutto. Kathaṃ pana jāgariyānuyogo hotīti taṃ dassetuṃ “pubbarattā…pe… viharatī”ti vuttaṃ. Yathāha “kathañca pubbarattāpararattaṃ jāgariyānuyogamanuyutto hoti? Idha bhikkhu divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi cittaṃ parisodheti, rattiyā paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ caṅkamena…pe… sodheti, evaṃ kho bhikkhu pubbarattāpararattaṃ jāgariyānuyogamanuyutto hotī”ti (vibha. 519). Imasmiṃ panattheti “maññati, na maññatī”ti ca vattabbabhāvasaṅkhāte atthe. No puthujjano adhippeto “appattamānaso, anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ patthayamāno”ti ca vuttattā.

"He is one who fulfills the conforming practice" means that practice which, beginning with virtue and ending with insight, conforms to the supramundane path leading to the cessation of suffering; by accomplishing that, he is one who fulfills it. Now, to illustrate this practice through the individual's standpoint, it is said, "endowed with virtue," etc. Herein, "endowed with virtue" means possessing the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha or being complete in the Pātimokkha virtue. For here, "virtue" refers specifically to the Pātimokkha virtue because of its primary importance. "Guarded in the sense faculties" means guarding the doors of the senses by restraining the arising of covetousness and other defilements regarding objects such as forms, by means of the mind, which is the sixth sense faculty. "Knowing moderation in eating" means knowing the proper measure in food with regards to seeking, etc. "Devoted to wakefulness" means being free from sloth and torpor and being diligent in applying himself to the meditation subject day and night. To explain how one is devoted to wakefulness, it is said, "he dwells during the first part of the night..." As it is said: "And how, bhikkhus, is one devoted to wakefulness during the early part and the latter part of the night? Here, a bhikkhu purifies his mind from obstructive states during the day by walking and sitting meditation. In the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind by walking... and so on. Thus, bhikkhus, one is devoted to wakefulness during the early part and the latter part of the night." (Vibh. 519) In this context, "he conceives, he does not conceive" refers to the meaning characterized by the state of being expressible. An ordinary person is not intended here, because it is said, "one who has not attained his mind's aim, aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage."

Sampayuttattā manasi bhavoti rāgo mānaso, mano eva mānasanti katvā cittaṃ mānasaṃ, anavasesato mānaṃ sīyati samucchindatīti aggamaggo [M 1.0093] mānasaṃ, tannibbattattā pana arahattassa mānasatā daṭṭhabbā. Janesutāti jane sakalasattaloke vissutā, patthaṭayasāti attho.

Because it is associated with the mind, lust is mental; considering the mind itself as mental, the mind is mental. Because it completely cuts off conceit, the supreme path is mental. But the state of being mental should be seen as arising from it for arahantship. "Renowned among people" means famous among people, throughout the entire world of beings; the meaning is widespread fame.

Natthi ito uttaranti anuttaraṃ. Taṃ pana sabbaseṭṭhaṃ hontaṃ ekantato sadisarahitameva hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “anuttaranti seṭṭhaṃ, asadisanti attho”ti. Patthayamānassāti taṇhāyantassa. Pajappitānīti mānajappanāni. Yasmiñhi vatthusmiṃ taṇhāyanā patthayamānamaññanā sambhavati, tasmiṃyeva “seyyohamasmī”tiādīni pajappitāni sambhavantīti adhippāyo. Pavedhītanti parivāsitaṃ. Pakappitesūti taṇhādiṭṭhikappehi parikappitesu ārammaṇesu. Sotanti kilesasotaṃ[V 1.0083]. Tasmiñhi chinne itarasotaṃ chinnamevāti. Viddhastanti vināsitaṃ. Tañca kho lomahaṃsamattampi asesetvāti dassento āha “vinaḷīkata”nti, vigatāvasesaṃ katanti attho. Adhimuttiyā idhādhippetapatthanā pākaṭā hotīti “tanninno”tiādi vuttaṃ, na pana kusalacchandassa adhimuttibhāvato. Adhimuccantoti okappento.

There is nothing beyond this; therefore, it is unsurpassed. That which is the best of all is utterly incomparable; therefore, it is said, 'The unsurpassed is the best; the meaning is incomparable.' For one who desires—that is, for one who is craving. The murmurings—these are the murmurings of conceit. Indeed, in whatever object craving and the conceiving of desiring arise, in that very object the murmurings of 'I am better' and so forth arise—such is the meaning. Agitated—that is, imbued. In what is contrived—that is, in objects contrived by craving and views. The stream—this is the stream of defilements. When this is cut off, the other stream is also cut off. Destroyed—that is, annihilated. And showing that not even a hair's breadth remains, it is said, 'completely eradicated,' meaning made without any remainder. By resolve, the aspiration intended here becomes evident, as stated in 'inclined toward that,' and so on, but not because of the nature of resolve as wholesome desire. Resolving—that is, deciding.

Sabbākāraviparītāyāti “subhaṃ sukhaṃ nicca”ntiādīnaṃ sabbesaṃ attanā gahetabbākārānaṃ vasena tabbiparītatāya, anavasesato dhammasabhāvaviparītākāragāhiniyāti attho. Abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇenāti asampajānanamicchājānanāni viya na dhammasabhāvaṃ appatvā nāpi atikkamitvā, atha kho avirajjhitvā dhammasabhāvassa abhimukhabhāvappattiyā abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena, ñātapariññādhiṭṭhānāya tīraṇapariññāya pahānapariññekadesena cāti attho. Tenāha “pathavīti…pe… vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Pathavībhāvanti pathaviyaṃ abhiññeyyabhāvaṃ. Lakkhaṇapathavī hi idhādhippetā, pariññeyyabhāvo panassā “aniccātipī”tiādinā gahitoti. Abhiññatvāti ñātatīraṇapahānapariññāhi heṭṭhimamaggañāṇehi ca abhijānitvā. Māmaññīti appahīnānaṃ maññanānaṃ vasena māti maññatīti mā, pahīnānaṃ pana vasena na maññatīti amaññī, mā ca so amaññī ca māmaññīti evamettha padavibhāgato attho veditabbo. Tattha yena bhāgena amaññī, tena maññīti na vattabbo. Yena pana bhāgena maññī, tena amaññīti na vattabboti. Evaṃ paṭikkhepappadhānaṃ atthaṃ dassetuṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “maññī ca na maññī ca na vattabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Paṭikkhepappadhānatā cettha [M 1.0094] labbhamānānampi maññanānaṃ dubbalabhāvato veditabbā. Tenevāha – “itarā pana tanubhāvaṃ gatā”ti. Māti ca nipātapadametaṃ, anekatthā ca nipātāti adhippāyena “etasmiñhi atthe imaṃ padaṃ nipātetvā vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Nipātetvāti ca pakatiādivibhāganiddhāraṇe anumānanayaṃ muñcitvā yathāvutte atthe paccakkhatova dassetvāti attho. Puthujjano viyāti etenassa uparimaggavajjhataṇhāmānavasena maññanā na paṭikkhittāti dīpeti.

'By being contrary in all aspects' means: because it is contrary to all the aspects to be grasped by oneself, such as 'beautiful, pleasant, permanent,' and so on, it grasps without remainder the aspects contrary to the true nature of phenomena—this is the meaning. 'With distinguished knowledge' means knowledge that is not like non-comprehension or wrong knowing, which neither reaches nor surpasses the true nature of phenomena. Rather, it is knowledge that has fully developed by directly facing the true nature, without deviation, due to the attainment of facing the true nature, serving as the basis for full understanding as the known, full understanding by investigation, and a part of full understanding by abandoning. Hence it is said, 'earth... as stated.' 'The nature of earth' refers to the aspect of earth that should be directly known. Here, earth as a characteristic is intended, but its nature of being fully understood is grasped by statements like 'impermanent,' and so on. 'Having directly known' means having known directly through full understanding as the known, full understanding by investigation, and full understanding by abandoning, and also through the lower path-knowledges. The term māmaññī is explained thus: by way of unabandoned conceivings, mā means 'he conceives'; but by way of abandoned conceivings, amaññī means 'he does not conceive.' Thus, the meaning here should be understood by dividing the words as mā and amaññī. In this context, it should not be said that 'he conceives' by the part by which he does not conceive. And it should not be said that 'he does not conceive' by the part by which he conceives. Thus, to emphasize the sense of negation, the commentary states, 'He should not be called a conceiver, nor should he be called a non-conceiver.' And here, the predominance of negation should be understood from the weakened state of even the conceivings that are found. Therefore, it is said, 'the others, however, have become diminished.' The word mā is a particle, and particles have many meanings. With this in mind, it is said, 'In this sense, this word is stated as a particle.' And 'stated as a particle' means setting aside the method of inference in determining the division of root words and so forth, and directly showing the meaning as stated. By 'like an ordinary person,' it is indicated that his conceiving by way of craving and conceit, which are to be abandoned by the higher paths, is not rejected.

Atha vā mā maññīti parikappakiriyāpaṭikkhepavacanametaṃ “mā randhayuṃ, mā jīrī”tiādīsu viya, na maññeyyāti vuttañhoti. Yathā hi puthujjano sabbaso appahīnamaññanattā “maññati”cceva vattabbo, yathā ca khīṇāsavo sabbaso pahīnamaññanattā na maññati eva, na evaṃ sekkho. Tassa hi ekaccā maññanā pahīnā, ekaccā appahīnā, tasmā ubhayabhāvato ubhayathāpi na vattabbo. Nanu ca ubhayabhāvato ubhayathāpi vattabboti? Na. Yā hi appahīnā, tāpissa tanubhāvaṃ gatāti tāhipi so na maññeyya vibhūtatarāya [V 1.0084] maññanāya abhāvato, pageva itarāhi. Tenāha bhagavā “mā maññī”ti. Tena vuttaṃ “mā maññīti parikappakiriyāpaṭikkhepavacanametaṃ ‘mā randhayuṃ, mā jīrī’tiādīsu viya, na maññeyyāti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Ayañcassa amaññanā vatthuno pariññeyyattā, na asekkhassa viya pariññātattā. Yañhi ekantato parijānitabbaṃ parijānituṃ sakkā, na tattha tabbidhure viya puthujjanassa maññanā sambhavanti. Tenāha “pariññeyyaṃ tassāti vadāmī”ti.

Alternatively, the phrase 'do not conceive' is a statement rejecting the activity of conceiving, as in 'do not cook, do not grow old,' and so on; it means 'one should not conceive.' For just as an ordinary person, due to not having abandoned conceiving entirely, must be said to 'conceive,' and just as one with taints destroyed, due to having abandoned conceiving entirely, does not conceive at all, it is not so for a trainee. For them, some conceivings have been abandoned, while some have not. Therefore, due to this dual nature, they cannot be described in either way. But shouldn’t they be described in both ways due to this dual nature? No. For those conceivings that have not been abandoned have become attenuated for them, so they would not conceive even through these, due to the absence of a more manifest conceiving—how much more so through the others. Hence, the Blessed One said, 'Do not conceive.' Therefore, it is said: 'The phrase "do not conceive" is a statement rejecting the activity of conceiving, as in "do not cook, do not grow old," and so on—it means "one should not conceive."' And this non-conceiving of theirs is because the object is to be fully understood, not because it has been fully understood as in the case of one beyond training. For what is to be fully understood can indeed be fully understood; therein, conceivings do not arise as they do for an ordinary person who is destitute of that understanding. Hence, it is said: 'I say that it is to be fully understood by him.'

Okkantaniyāmattāti anupaviṭṭhasammattaniyāmattā, otiṇṇamaggasotattāti attho. Sambodhiparāyaṇattāti uparimaggasambodhipaṭisaraṇattā, tadadhigamāya ninnapoṇapabbhārabhāvatoti attho. Ubhayenapi tassa avassaṃbhāvinī sesapariññāti dasseti. Pariññeyyanti parijānitabbabhāvena ṭhitaṃ, pariññātuṃ vā sakkuṇeyyaṃ. Tappaṭipakkhato apariññeyyaṃ. Puthujjanassa viyāti etena idhādhippetaputhujjanassa pariññeyyabhāvāsaṅkā eva natthi anadhikāratoti dasseti. “Mābhinandī”ti etthāpi imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

‘Having entered the fixed course’ means having entered the fixed course of rightness, meaning having entered the stream of the path. ‘Having enlightenment as one’s destination’ means having the higher path’s enlightenment as one’s refuge, meaning being inclined, tending, and gravitating towards its attainment. By both, it shows that the remaining full understanding is inevitable for him. ‘To be fully understood’ refers to what stands in the state of being fully understood, or what can be fully understood. From the opposite perspective, it is ‘not to be fully understood.’ By ‘like an ordinary person,’ it shows that for the ordinary person intended here, there is no possibility of the state of being fully understood, as they are not entitled to it. Here too, in ‘do not delight,’ the meaning should be understood in the same way.

Sekkhavāradutiyanayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the second method concerning the section on the trainee is concluded.

Khīṇāsavavāratatiyādinayavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Method for the Third and Subsequent Sections: On the One Whose Taints Are Destroyed.

8. Sabhāgo [M 1.0095] diṭṭhasaccatādisāmaññena. Ārakā kilesehi arahanti padassa niruttinayena atthaṃ vatvā taṃ pāḷiyā samānento “vuttañceta”ntiādimāha. Tattha pāpakāti lāmakaṭṭhena duggatisampāpanaṭṭhena ca pāpakā. Sāvajjaṭṭhena akosallasambhūtaṭṭhena ca akusalā. Saṃkilesaṃ arahanti, tattha vā niyuttāti saṃkilesikā. Punabbhavassa karaṇasīlā, punabbhavaphalaṃ arahantīti vā ponobhavikā. Saha darathena pariḷāhena pavattantīti sadarā. Dukkho kaṭuko, dukkhamo vā vipāko etesanti dukkhavipākā. Anāgate jātiyā ceva jarāmaraṇānañca vaḍḍhanena jātijarāmaraṇiyāti. Evametesaṃ padānaṃ attho veditabbo. Kāmañcāyaṃ suttantavaṇṇanā, abhidhammanayo pana nippariyāyoti tena dassento “cattāro āsavā”tiādimāha. Samucchinnā paṭippassaddhāti na kevalaṃ samucchinnā eva, atha kho paṭippassaddhāpīti maggakiccena sadisaṃ phalakiccampi niddhāreti.

8. It is shared by the commonality of having seen the truth, and so on. Having stated the meaning of the word 'arahant' according to the etymological method—that one is an 'arahant' because one is far from the defilements—he then aligns it with the Pāli text, saying, 'And this was stated,' and so on. Herein, evil means both base and leading to a bad destination. Unwholesome means blameworthy and arising from unskillfulness. Defiling means they are fit for defilement, or are appointed to it. Productive of renewed existence means they are by nature the cause of renewed existence, or are fit for the fruit of renewed existence. With anguish means they proceed together with anguish and torment. Painful in result means their result is suffering or bitter. Productive of birth, aging, and death means they increase future birth, aging, and death. Thus, the meaning of these terms should be understood. And although this is a Suttanta commentary, the Abhidhamma method is definitive, so to show that, it says, “the four taints,” and so on. “Cut off and calmed” means not only cut off but also calmed—thus, it establishes that the function of the fruit is similar to the function of the path.

Sīlavisodhanādinā [V 1.0085] garūnaṃ paṭipattiyā anukaraṇaṃ garusaṃvāso. Ariyamaggapaṭipatti eva ariyamaggasaṃvāso. Dasa ariyāvāsā nāma pañcaṅgavippahīnatādayo. Ye sandhāya vuttaṃ –

The emulation of the conduct of the teachers, beginning with the purification of virtue, is living with the teachers. The practice of the Noble Path is indeed living with the Noble Path. The ten noble abodes are the abandonment of the five factors and so on. This is what was meant by the statement—

“Dasayime, bhikkhave, ariyāvāsā, ye ariyā āvasiṃsu vā āvasanti vā āvasissanti vā. Katame dasa? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti chaḷaṅgasamannāgato, ekārakkho, caturāpasseno, panuṇṇapaccekasacco, samavayasaṭṭhesano, anāvilasaṅkappo, passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro, suvimuttacitto, suvimuttapañño. Ime kho, bhikkhave, dasa ariyāvāsā”ti (a. ni. 10.19).

“These, bhikkhus, are the ten noble dwellings in which the noble ones dwelt, dwell, or will dwell. What are the ten? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors, possesses six factors, has a single protection, is supported by four things, has dispelled individual truths, has his seeking fully subsided, has intentions that are unclouded, has bodily formations that are tranquilized, is well liberated in mind, and is well liberated in wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the ten noble dwellings.”

Vussatīti vā vusitaṃ, ariyamaggo, ariyaphalañca, taṃ etassa atthīti atisayavacanicchāvasena arahā “vusitavā”ti vutto. Karaṇīyanti pariññāpahānabhāvanāsacchikiriyamāha. Taṃ pana yasmā catūhi maggehi catūsu saccesu kattabbattā soḷasavidhanti veditabbaṃ. Tenāha “catūhi maggehi [M 1.0096] karaṇīya”nti. Sammāvimuttassāti aggamaggaphalapaññāhi samucchedapaṭippassaddhīnaṃ vasena suṭṭhu vimuttassa. Santacittassāti tato eva sabbakilesadarathapariḷāhānaṃ vūpasantacittassa. Bhinnakilesassa khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno. Katassa pariññādikiccassa paṭicayo puna karaṇaṃ natthi, tato eva karaṇīyaṃ na vijjati na upalabbhati.

‘He has lived the life’ or ‘the noble path and the noble fruit have been lived’; meaning he possesses this accomplishment—thus, due to the desire to express excellence, the Arahant is called ‘one who has lived the life.’ ‘To be done’ refers to full understanding, abandoning, developing, and realizing. And that, since it is to be done in the four truths by the four paths, should be understood as sixteenfold. Hence, it is said, ‘to be done by the four paths.’ ‘Of one rightly liberated’—well-liberated by means of cutting off and tranquillizing through the wisdom of the supreme path and fruit. ‘With peaceful mind’—because of that, the mind is calmed from all defilements, anguish, and torment. For a bhikkhu whose defilements are destroyed, whose taints are extinguished, there is no further accumulation of the task of full understanding and so on that has been done; therefore, nothing further to be done is found or exists.

Bhārāti osīdāpanaṭṭhena bhārā viyāti bhārā. Vuttañhi “bhārā have pañcakkhandhā”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 3.22). Attano yonisomanasikārāyattanti attupanibandhaṃ, sasantānapariyāpannattā attānaṃ avijahanaṃ. Tayidaṃ yadipi sabbasmiṃ anavajjadhamme sambhavati, akuppasabhāvāparihānadhammesu pana aggabhūte arahatte sātisayaṃ, netaresūti dassento āha “attano paramatthaṭṭhena vā”ti, uttamaṭṭhabhāvenāti attho.

Burdens are so called because they cause sinking; thus, ‘bhārā.’ As it is stated, “Indeed, the five aggregates are a burden” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.22). It is bound to oneself because it depends on one’s own wise attention, being included in one’s own continuum and not abandoning oneself. Though this applies to all blameless states, it is especially so in the highest state of Arahantship, which is unshakeable and free from decline, and not so in other states—thus, indicating this, it is said, ‘or in the ultimate sense of oneself,’ meaning the state of being the highest.

Suttantanayo nāma pariyāyanayoti nippariyāyanayena saṃyojanāni dassento “bhavarāgaissāmacchariyasaṃyojana”nti āha, na pana “rūparāgo”tiādinā. Bhavesu saṃyojantīti kilesakammavipākavaṭṭānaṃ paccayo hutvā nissarituṃ appadānavasena bandhanti. Satipi hi aññesaṃ tappaccayabhāve na vinā saṃyojanāni tesaṃ tappaccayabhāvo atthi, orambhāgiyauddhambhāgiyasaṅgahitehi ca tehi taṃtaṃbhavanibbattakakammaniyamo bhavaniyamo ca hoti[V 1.0086], na ca upacchinnasaṃyojanassa katānipi kammāni bhavaṃ nibbattentīti tesaṃyeva saṃyojanaṭṭho daṭṭhabbo.

The Suttanta method is the discursive method. Showing the fetters by the non-discursive method, it says, ‘the fetter of desire for existence, envy, and stinginess,’ and not by way of ‘desire for form,’ etc. They bind by becoming the condition for the round of defilements, kamma, and results, not allowing for escape. For even though other things may be conditions for them, their being conditions does not exist without the fetters; and through those fetters, which are included among the lower and the higher, the fixed order of kamma that produces this or that existence and the fixed order of becoming occur. And for one whose fetters are cut off, even kamma that has been performed does not produce existence. Thus, the meaning of ‘fetter’ should be understood as belonging to them alone.

Sammā aññāyāti ājānanabhūtāya aggamaggapaññāya sammā yathābhūtaṃ dukkhādīsu yo yathā jānitabbo, taṃ tathā jānitvā. Cittavimutti sabbassa cittasaṃkilesassa vissaggo. Nibbānādhimutti nibbāne adhimuccanaṃ tattha ninnapoṇapabbhāratā. Tanti pathavīādikaṃ. Pariññātaṃ, na puthujjanassa viya apariññātaṃ, sekkhassa viya pariññeyyaṃ vā. Tasmāti pariññātattā.

‘Rightly knowing’ means knowing with the wisdom of the supreme path, which is true knowing; rightly knowing suffering and so forth as they truly should be known. ‘Liberation of mind’ is the relinquishing of all mental defilements. ‘Resolution toward Nibbāna’ is being resolved on Nibbāna, being inclined, sloping, and tending towards it. ‘This’ refers to earth and so forth. ‘Fully understood’—not un-understood, like an ordinary person, nor to be fully understood, like a trainee. ‘Therefore’ means because it has been fully understood.

Catutthapañcamachaṭṭhavārā tattha tattha kilesanibbānakittanavasena pavattattā nibbānavārā nāma. Tattha pathavīādīnaṃ pariññātattā amaññanā, sā pana pariññā rāgādīnaṃ khayena siddhāti imassa atthassa dīpanavasena pāḷi pavattāti dassento “pariññātaṃ tassāti sabbapadehi yojetvā puna [M 1.0097] khayā rāgassa vītarāgattāti yojetabbaṃ. Esa nayo itaresū”ti āha. Tattha itaresūti pañcamachaṭṭhavāresu. Yadi evaṃ kasmā pāḷi evaṃ na dissatīti āha “desanā pana ekattha vuttaṃ sabbattha vuttameva hotīti saṃkhittā”ti.

The fourth, fifth, and sixth sections are called ‘Nibbāna sections’ because they proceed by way of proclaiming the extinguishing of defilements in each case. Therein, because the earth element, etc., have been fully understood, there is no conceiving. This full understanding, however, is accomplished through the destruction of lust, etc. To clarify this meaning, the Pāli text proceeds by showing that one should connect ‘to him who has fully understood’ with all the terms, and then connect ‘due to being free from lust through the destruction of lust.’ This, it is said, is the method for the others—meaning, in the fifth and sixth sections. If so, why does the Pāli not appear this way? It is said, ‘The teaching, however, is concise; what is stated in one place is as if stated everywhere.’”

Na khayā rāgassa vītarāgo sabbaso appahīnarāgattā. Vikkhambhitarāgo hi soti. Bāhirakaggahaṇañcettha tathābhāvasseva tesu labbhanato, na tesu eva tathābhāvassa labbhanato. Idāni yā sā “pariññātaṃ tassā”ti sabbapadehi yojanā vuttā, taṃ vināpi nibbānavāraatthayojanaṃ dassetuṃ “yathā cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha maññanaṃ na maññatīti maññanā nappavattatīti attho. Maññanāya maññitabbattepi tassā vatthuantogadhattāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

He is not free from lust through the destruction of lust, for lust has not been entirely abandoned. For he is one whose lust is merely suppressed. And the grasping of external objects here occurs because such a state is found in them (i.e., in the person), not because such a state is found in the objects themselves. Now, that connection with all terms, ‘to him who has fully understood,’ has been stated. In order to show the meaning of the Nibbāna section even without that connection, ‘and just as,’ etc., has been said. Here, ‘he does not conceive conceiving’ means that conceiving does not occur. Even though there is conceivability by means of conceiving, because it is included within the object, the meaning should be understood thus.

Yadipi pariññātapadaṃ aggahetvā nibbānavāradesanā pavattā, evampi “khayā”tiādipadehi pariññāsiddhi eva pakāsīyatīti ko tesaṃ visesoti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “ettha cā”tiādi. Maggabhāvanāpāripūridassanatthaṃ vutto, maggakiccantā hi pariññāyoti adhippāyo. Itare…pe… veditabbā vītarāgādikittanatoti. Dvīhi vā kāraṇehīti yathāvuttakāraṇadvayena. Assāti khīṇāsavassa. Ayaṃ visesoti idāni vuccamāno viseso. Yadipi khīṇāsavo ekantena vītarāgo vītadoso vītamoho eva ca hoti, yāya pana pubbabhāgapaṭipadāya vītarāgatādayo savisesāti vattabbataṃ labhanti, taṃ dassento “tīsu hī”tiādimāha[V 1.0087]. “Ratto atthaṃ na jānātī”tiādinā (netti. 11) rāge ādīnavaṃ passato “rāgo ca nāma sukhābhisaṅgena uppajjati, sukhañca vipariṇāmato dukkhaṃ. Pageva itara”nti sahetuke rāge ādīnavadassanaṃ dukkhānupassanāya nimittaṃ, dukkhānupassanā ca paṇidhiyā paṭipakkhabhāvato appaṇihitavimokkhaṃ paripuretīti āha “rāge…pe… vītarāgo hotī”ti. Tathā “duṭṭho atthaṃ na jānātī”tiādinā (itivu. 88) dose ādīnavaṃ passato “doso ca nāma dukkhaṃ paṭicca uppajjati, tañca ubhayaṃ anavaṭṭhitaṃ ittaraṃ pabhaṅgū”ti sahetuke dose ādīnavadassanaṃ aniccānupassanāya nimittaṃ, aniccānupassanā ca niccanimittādīnaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvato animittavimokkhaṃ paripūretīti āha “dose…pe… hotī”ti. Tathā “mūḷho [M 1.0098] atthaṃ na jānātī”tiādinā (itivu. 88) mohe ādīnavaṃ passato “moho nāma yathāsabhāvaggahaṇassa paribbhamanto”ti mohassa vikkhambhanaṃ anattānupassanāya nimittaṃ, anattānupassanāya ca attābhinivesassa paṭipakkhabhāvato suññataṃ vimokkhaṃ paripūretīti āha “mohe…pe… vītamoho hotī”ti.

Even if the teaching on the Nibbāna section proceeds without taking the term ‘fully understood,’ still, the accomplishment of full understanding is clearly demonstrated through terms like ‘destruction,’ etc. So, with reference to the objection, ‘What is the distinction between them?’ he says, ‘Here also,’ etc. It is stated for the purpose of showing the complete fulfillment of path development, for the culmination of the path’s function is full understanding—this is the meaning. The others… should be understood as praise for being free from lust, etc. Or by two reasons—that is, by the pair of reasons as previously stated. ‘Of him’—of the one whose taints are destroyed. ‘This is the distinction’—the distinction now being stated. Even though one whose taints are destroyed is entirely free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion, yet, to show that through the preliminary practice they attain a state where they can be described as free from lust, etc., with distinctions, he says, ‘In three ways,’ etc. By the passage, ‘One who is lustful does not understand the meaning’ (Netti. 11), when one sees the danger in lust—‘Lust arises through attachment to pleasure, and pleasure, due to change, is suffering—how much more so the rest’—the seeing of danger in lust, which has a cause, is a condition for the contemplation of suffering. And the contemplation of suffering, being the opposite of aspiration, fulfills the desireless liberation. Thus it is said, ‘Through lust… one becomes free from lust.’ Similarly, by the passage, ‘One who is hateful does not understand the meaning’ (Itiv. 88), when one sees the danger in hatred—‘Hatred arises dependent on suffering, and both are unstable, fleeting, and perishable’—the seeing of danger in hatred, which has a cause, is a condition for the contemplation of impermanence. And the contemplation of impermanence, being the opposite of the sign of permanence, etc., fulfills the signless liberation. Thus it is said, ‘Through hatred… one becomes free from hatred.’ Likewise, by the passage, ‘One who is deluded does not understand the meaning’ (Itiv. 88), when one sees the danger in delusion—‘Delusion is the wandering from grasping things as they truly are’—the overcoming of delusion is a condition for the contemplation of non-self. And the contemplation of non-self, being the opposite of clinging to self, fulfills the emptiness liberation. Thus it is said, ‘Through delusion… one becomes free from delusion.’”

Evaṃ santeti yadi vītarāgatādayo vimokkhavibhāgena vuttā, evaṃ sante. Tasmāti yasmā vimokkhamukhavimokkhānaṃ vasena niyametvā na vuttaṃ, tasmā. Yaṃ kiñci arahato sambhavantaṃ vibhajitvā vuccatīti vārattayadesanā katāti imamatthaṃ dasseti “yaṃ arahato”tiādinā.

‘This being so’ means: if freedom from lust and so forth are spoken of by way of the division of liberations, then it is so. ‘Therefore’ means: because it was not stated by specifying them according to the doors to liberation and the liberations. The phrase ‘whatever for the Arahant,’ etc., indicates this meaning: that the teaching was given in three sections because whatever arises in an Arahant is analyzed and spoken of.

Evaṃ vimuttivibhāgena khīṇāsavassa vibhāgaṃ vārattayadesanānibandhanaṃ dassetvā idāni avibhāgenapi tattha pariññāvisayassa anusayavisayassa ca vibhāgaṃ tassa nibandhanaṃ dassento “avisesenā”tiādimāha. Tattha upekkhāvedanā visesato saṅkhāradukkhaṃ sammohādhiṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ “saṅkhāra…pe… moho”ti. Sesaṃ vuttanayattā suviññeyyameva.

Having thus shown the classification of one whose taints are destroyed by means of the classification of liberation, which is connected to the threefold teaching, now, even without classification, showing the distinction there between the sphere of full understanding and the sphere of latent tendencies and its basis, he says, "without distinction," and so on. Therein, equanimous feeling is specifically the suffering of formations, the basis of delusion, as stated: "formations... and delusion." The rest is easily understood according to the method explained.

Khīṇāsavavāratatiyādinayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the method concerning the third section, and so on, on the one whose taints are destroyed is concluded.

Tathāgatavārasattamanayavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Method of the Seventh Section Concerning the Tathāgata

12. Yehi (dī. ni. abhi. ṭī. 1.7.cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā; a. ni. ṭī. 1.1.170) guṇavisesehi nimittabhūtehi bhagavati “tathāgato”ti ayaṃ samaññā pavattā, taṃ dassanatthaṃ [V 1.0088] “aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā tathāgato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Guṇanemittakāneva hi bhagavato sabbāni nāmāni. Yathāha –

12. To show by which special qualities, serving as characteristics, the designation "Tathāgata" is applied to the Blessed One, it is said: "The Blessed One is the Tathāgata for eight reasons," and so on. For all the Blessed One's names are indeed based on qualities as their cause. As it is said:

“Asaṅkhyeyyāni nāmāni, saguṇena mahesino;

Guṇena nāmamuddheyyaṃ, api nāmasahassato”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1313; udā. aṭṭha. 53; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.76; dī. ni. abhi. ṭī. 1.7.cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā; a. ni. ṭī. 1.1.170) –

"Innumerable are the names of the Great Sage, possessed of virtues; a name is to be derived from a quality, even from a thousand names."

Tathā āgatoti ettha ākāraniyamanavasena opammasampaṭipādanattho tathā-saddo. Sāmaññajotanā hi visese avatiṭṭhatīti paṭipādagamanattho āgata-saddo, na ñāṇagamanattho “tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato”tiādīsu [M 1.0099] (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.12; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.3.78; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.170; udā. aṭṭha. 18; itivu. aṭṭha. 38; theragā. aṭṭha. 1.1.3; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 2.bāhiranidāna; mahāni. aṭṭha. 14) viya, nāpi kāyagamanādiattho “āgato kho mahāsamaṇo, māgadhānaṃ giribbaja”ntiādīsu (mahāva. 63) viya. Tattha yadākāraniyamanavasena opammasampaṭipādanattho tathā-saddo, taṃ karuṇāppadhānattā mahākaruṇāmukhena purimabuddhānaṃ āgamanapaṭipadaṃ udāharaṇavasena sāmaññato dassento yaṃtaṃsaddānaṃ ekantasambandhabhāvato “yathā sabbaloka…pe… āgatā”ti sādhāraṇato vatvā puna taṃ paṭipadaṃ mahāpadānasuttādīsu (dī. ni. 2.4) sambahulaniddesena supākaṭānaṃ āsannānañca vipassīādīnaṃ channaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ vasena dassento “yathā vipassī bhagavā”tiādimāha. Tattha yena abhinīhārenāti manussatta-liṅgasampatti-hetu-satthāradassana-pabbajjā-abhiññādiguṇasampatti-adhikāra-chandānaṃ vasena aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatena kāyapaṇidhānamahāpaṇidhānena. Sabbesañhi sammāsambuddhānaṃ kāyapaṇidhānaṃ imināva nīhārena samijjhatīti.

In 'tathā āgata,' the word 'tathā' here conveys the meaning of illustrating a simile by way of determining the mode. The word 'āgata' signifies proceeding along a path, since the illumination of the general rests on the particular—not in the sense of attaining knowledge, as in such phrases as 'he has come to the characteristic of suchness,' nor in the sense of bodily movement, as in 'the great ascetic has come to the Magadhans’ mountain stronghold.' Therein, when the word 'tathā' conveys the meaning of illustrating a simile by way of determining the mode, it demonstrates in a general sense, as an example, the path of arrival of previous Buddhas by way of great compassion, since compassion is primary. Due to the inseparable connection of the words 'yaṃ' and 'taṃ,' it is stated universally, 'just as all the world... have come,' and then, further illustrating that path by means of the six Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones such as Vipassī, who are recent and well-known through the extensive explanations in suttas like the Mahāpadāna, it says, 'just as the Blessed One Vipassī...' and so on. Therein, 'by which aspiration' refers to the great aspiration, the bodily aspiration, which is endowed with eight factors: the human state, the perfection of gender, the supporting cause, seeing the Teacher, the going forth, the attainment of qualities such as the higher knowledges, the act of service, and zeal. For the bodily aspiration of all Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones succeeds by this very method.

Evaṃ mahābhinīhāravasena “tathāgato”ti padassa atthaṃ vatvā idāni pāramīpūraṇavasena dassetuṃ “atha vā yathā vipassī bhagavā…pe… yathā kassapo bhagavā dānapāramiṃ pūretvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne suttantikānaṃ mahābodhiyānapaṭipadāya kosallajananatthaṃ pāramīkathā vattabbā, sā pana sabbākārasampannā cariyāpiṭakavaṇṇanāya (cariyā. pakiṇṇakakathā) vitthārato niddiṭṭhā, tasmā atthikehi tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Yathā [V 1.0089] pana pubbe vipassīādayo sammāsambuddhā abhinīhārasampattiyaṃ patiṭṭhāya suvisuddhāya paṭipadāya anavasesato sammadeva sabbā pāramiyo paripūresuṃ, evaṃ amhākampi bhagavā paripūresīti imamatthaṃ sandhāyāha “samattiṃ sapāramiyo pūretvā”ti. Satipi aṅgapariccāgādīnaṃ dānapāramibhāve pariccāgavisesabhāvadassanatthañceva sudukkarabhāvadassanatthañca “pañca mahāpariccāge”ti visuṃ gahaṇaṃ, tatoyeva ca aṅgapariccāgato visuṃ nayanapariccāgaggahaṇampi kataṃ, pariggahapariccāgabhāvasāmaññepi dhanarajjapariccāgato puttadārapariccāgaggahaṇañca kataṃ.

Having thus explained the meaning of the word "Tathāgata" by way of the great aspiration, now, to illustrate it by way of the fulfillment of the perfections, it is said: "Or just as the Blessed One Vipassī… up to… just as the Blessed One Kassapa fulfilled the perfection of generosity," and so on. In this context, for the sake of generating skill in the path of the great enlightenment vehicle for the Suttantikas, the discussion of the perfections should be given. However, that, complete in every aspect, is explained in detail in the commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka. Therefore, those who are interested should understand it according to the method explained there. Just as in the past, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones like Vipassī, having established themselves in the attainment of aspiration, fulfilled all the perfections completely and rightly through a supremely purified practice, so too did our Blessed One fulfill them. With this meaning in mind, it is said: "Having fulfilled the thirty perfections." Moreover, even though the perfection of generosity includes the relinquishment of limbs and so on, the separate mention of the "five great relinquishments" is made both to show the distinction in the nature of the relinquishment and to highlight its extreme difficulty. For that very reason, the relinquishment of eyes is mentioned separately from the relinquishment of limbs, and the relinquishment of wife and children is distinguished from the relinquishment of wealth and kingdom, even though they share the general characteristic of relinquishing possessions.

Gatapaccāgatikavattapūraṇādikāya pubbabhāgapaṭipadāya saddhiṃ abhiññāsamāpattinipphādanaṃ pubbayogo, dānādīsuyeva sātisayapaṭipattinipphādanaṃ pubbacariyā[M 1.0100], sā cariyāpiṭakasaṅgahitā. Abhinīhāro pubbayogo, dānādipaṭipatti, kāyavivekavasena ekacariyā vā pubbacariyāti keci. Dānādīnañceva appicchatādīnañca saṃsāranibbānesu ādīnavānisaṃsānañca vibhāvanavasena sattānaṃ bodhittaye patiṭṭhāpanaparipācanavasena ca pavattā kathā dhammakkhānaṃ, ñātīnaṃ atthacariyā ñātatthacariyā, sāpi karuṇāya vaseneva. Ādi-saddena lokatthacariyādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Kammassakatañāṇavasena, anavajjakammāyatanasippāyatanavijjāṭṭhānaparicayavasena khandhāyatanādiparicayavasena, lakkhaṇattayatīraṇavasena ca ñāṇacāro buddhicariyā, sā pana atthato paññāpāramīyeva, ñāṇasambhāradassanatthaṃ visuṃ gahaṇaṃ. Koṭīti pariyanto, ukkaṃsoti attho.

The prior effort is the accomplishment of higher knowledges and meditative attainments together with the preliminary practice consisting of fulfilling the duties of coming and going, and so on. The prior conduct is the accomplishment of an excellent practice in giving and so forth, and that conduct is included in the Cariyāpiṭaka. Some say the aspiration is the prior effort, and the practice of giving and so forth, or solitary conduct by way of physical seclusion, is the prior conduct. The teaching of the Dhamma is discourse that proceeds by way of distinguishing the dangers and benefits in saṃsāra and Nibbāna, of generosity and other virtues, and of qualities like contentment, and by establishing and maturing beings in the threefold enlightenment. Conduct for the welfare of relatives is conduct for the sake of relatives, and that too is by way of compassion. By the word "and so forth," he includes conduct for the welfare of the world and other such deeds. The exercise of knowledge—by way of the knowledge of ownership of kamma, by way of familiarity with blameless fields of action, crafts, and branches of knowledge, by way of familiarity with the aggregates, sense bases, and so forth, and by way of discerning the three characteristics—is the conduct of wisdom. In essence, it is the perfection of wisdom itself, but it is mentioned separately to show the accumulation of knowledge. "Koṭi" means limit; the meaning is "excellence."

Cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāvetvā brūhetvāti sambandho. Tattha bhāvetvāti uppādetvā. Brūhetvāti vaḍḍhetvā. Satipaṭṭhānādiggahaṇena āgamanapaṭipadaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dasseti. Vipassanāsahagatā eva vā satipaṭṭhānādayo daṭṭhabbā. Ettha ca “yena abhinīhārenā”tiādinā āgamanapaṭipadāya ādiṃ dasseti, “dānapāramī”tiādinā majjhaṃ, “cattāro satipaṭṭhāne”tiādinā pariyosānanti veditabbaṃ.

The connection is: "Having developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness." Here, “having developed” means having produced. “Having cultivated” means having increased. By the inclusion of the foundations of mindfulness and so on, he shows the path of arrival brought to its culmination. Alternatively, the foundations of mindfulness and so on should be regarded as accompanied by insight. And here, it should be understood that with “by which aspiration,” and so on, he shows the beginning of the path of arrival; with “the perfection of giving,” and so on, the middle; and with “the four foundations of mindfulness,” and so on, the conclusion.

Sampatijātoti muhuttajāto manussānaṃ hatthato muttamatto, na mātukucchito nikkhantamatto. Nikkhantamattañhi mahāsattaṃ paṭhamaṃ brahmāno suvaṇṇajālena paṭiggaṇhiṃsu, tesaṃ hatthato cattāro mahārājāno ajinappaveṇiyā, tesaṃ hatthato manussā dukūlacumbaṭakena paṭiggaṇhiṃsu, manussānaṃ hatthato muccitvā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhitoti. Yathāha bhagavā mahāpadānadesanāyaṃ. Setamhi chatteti dibbasetacchatte. Anudhārīyamāneti dhārīyamāne. Ettha ca chattaggahaṇeneva khaggādīni pañca kakudhabhaṇṭānipi vuttānevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Khaggatālavaṇṭamorahatthakavālabījanīuṇhīsapaṭṭāpi [V 1.0090] hi chattena saha tadā upaṭṭhitā ahesuṃ, chattādīniyeva ca tadā paññāyiṃsu, na chattādiggāhakā. Sabbā ca disāti dasapi disā. Nayidaṃ sabbadisāvilokanaṃ sattapadavītihāruttarakālaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mahāsatto hi manussānaṃ hatthato muccitvā puratthimadisaṃ [M 1.0101] olokesi. Tattha devamanussā gandhamālādīhi pūjayamānā “mahāpurisa idha tumhehi sadisopi natthi, kuto uttaritaro”ti āhaṃsu. Evaṃ catasso disā, catasso anudisā; heṭṭhā, uparīti sabbā disā anuviloketvā sabbattha attanā sadisaṃ adisvā “ayaṃ uttarā disā”ti tattha sattapadavītihārena agamāsi. Āsabhinti uttamaṃ. Aggoti sabbapaṭhamo. Jeṭṭho seṭṭhoti ca tasseva vevacanaṃ. Ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavoti imasmiṃ attabhāve pattabbaṃ arahattaṃ byākāsi.

“Just born” means born for a moment, just released from the hands of humans, not just emerged from the mother’s womb. For when the Great Being first emerged, the Brahmās received him with a golden net; from their hands the four great kings received him with antelope skins; from their hands humans received him with a fine cloth, and having been released from the hands of humans, he stood firm on the ground, as the Blessed One said in the Great Discourse on the Lineage. “A white parasol” refers to a divine white parasol. “Being held over” means being carried. Here, by the mention of the parasol alone, the five royal emblems—the sword and so on—are also implied and should be seen as included. For at that time, the sword, the palm-leaf fan, the peacock-feather fan, the yak-tail fan, and the turban-band were present along with the parasol, and only the parasol and so on appeared, not the bearers of the parasol and so on. “All directions” means the ten directions. This looking around in all directions should not be understood as occurring after the seven steps. For the Great Being, having been released from the hands of humans, looked towards the eastern direction. There, gods and humans honoring him with perfumes and garlands said, “O great man, here there is none equal to you, how much less superior?” Thus, having looked around in all directions—the four directions, the four intermediate directions, below, and above—and seeing no one equal to himself anywhere, he declared, “This is the northern direction,” and there he went with seven steps. “The bull” means the supreme. “The chief” means the foremost of all. “The eldest, the best” are synonyms for the same. “This is my last birth; now there is no more becoming”—thus he proclaimed the attainability of arahantship in this very life.

Anekesaṃ visesādhigamānaṃ pubbanimittabhāvenāti saṃkhittena vuttamatthaṃ “yañhī”tiādinā vitthārato dasseti. Tattha etthāti –

“As the preliminary sign for the attainment of many distinctions,” the meaning stated concisely is explained in detail by the passage beginning “for indeed.” Herein, it is as follows:

“Anekasākhañca sahassamaṇḍalaṃ,

Chattaṃ marū dhārayumantalikkhe;

Suvaṇṇadaṇḍā vītipatanti cāmarā,

Na dissare cāmarachattagāhakā”ti. (su. ni. 693);

“Many-branched and thousand-circled, The parasol was held by the devas in the sky; Golden-handled chowries fluttered, The bearers of the chowries and parasol were not seen.”

Imissā gāthāya. Sabbaññutaññāṇameva sabbattha appaṭihatacāratāya anāvaraṇañāṇanti āha “sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇapaṭilābhassā”ti. Tathā ayaṃ bhagavāpi gato…pe… pubbanimittabhāvenāti etena abhijātiyaṃ dhammatāvasena uppajjanakavisesā sabbabodhisattānaṃ sādhāraṇāti dasseti. Pāramitānissandā hi teti.

In this verse, it is said that the knowledge of omniscience is unobstructed knowledge because of its unimpeded range everywhere, hence the phrase “of the attainment of omniscient and unobstructed knowledge.” Similarly, this Blessed One also went...pe... in the manner of a preliminary sign. By this it is shown that the special occurrences at a noble birth, by way of natural law, are common to all Bodhisattas. For they are the outflow of the perfections.

Vikkamīti agamāsi. Marūti devā. Samāti vilokanasamatāya samā sadisiyo. Mahāpuriso hi yathā ekaṃ disaṃ vilokesi, evaṃ sesadisāpi, na katthaci vilokane vibandho tassa ahosīti. Samāti vā viloketuṃ yuttā, visamarahitāti attho. Na hi tadā bodhisattassa virūpabībhacchavisamarūpāni viloketuṃ ayuttāni disāsu upaṭṭhahantīti.

“He strode forth” means he went. “Marū” means devas. “Equal” means equal in the faculty of looking around, similar. For just as the Great Being looked in one direction, so too in the other directions; there was no obstruction to his looking anywhere. Or, “equal” means fit to be looked at, devoid of unevenness—this is the meaning. For at that time, unpleasant, repulsive, or uneven forms unfit to be seen did not appear to the Bodhisatta in any direction.

Evaṃ “tathā gato”ti kāyagamanaṭṭhena gata-saddena tathāgata-saddaṃ niddisitvā idāni ñāṇagamanaṭṭhena taṃ dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādimāha. Tattha nekkhammenāti alobhappadhānena kusalacittuppādena[V 1.0091]. Kusalā hi [M 1.0102] dhammā idha nekkhammaṃ, na pabbajjādayo, “paṭhamajjhāna”nti (dī. ni. abhi. ṭī. 1.7.cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā; a. ni. ṭī. 1.1.170) ca vadanti. Pahāyāti pajahitvā. Gato adhigato, paṭipanno uttarivisesanti attho. Pahāyāti vā pahānahetu, pahānalakkhaṇaṃ vā. Hetulakkhaṇattho hi ayaṃ pahāya-saddo. Kāmacchandādippahānahetukaṃ “gato”ti hettha vuttaṃ gamanaṃ avabodho, paṭipatti eva vā kāmacchandādippahānena ca lakkhīyatīti. Esa nayo padāletvātiādīsupi. Abyāpādenāti mettāya. Ālokasaññāyāti vibhūtaṃ katvā manasikaraṇena (dī. ni. abhi. ṭī. 1.7.cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā) upaṭṭhitaālokasañcānanena. Avikkhepenāti samādhinā.
