Dhammavavatthānenāti kusalādidhammānaṃ yāthāvanicchayena. “Sappaccayanāmarūpavavatthānenā”tipi vadanti.

Thus, having explained the word 'Tathāgata' with the word 'gata' in the sense of physical going, as in 'thus gone,' he now says 'Or else,' etc., to show it in the sense of going by knowledge. Herein, 'by renunciation' means by the arising of wholesome consciousness predominated by non-greed. For here, wholesome states are 'renunciation,' not the going forth and so on; and they also say 'the first jhāna.' 'Having abandoned' means having relinquished. 'Gone' means attained, or having practiced for a higher distinction—this is the meaning. Or, 'having abandoned' means for the sake of abandoning, or as a characteristic of abandoning. For this word 'pahāya' has the meaning of cause and characteristic. The 'going' spoken of here as 'gone' is understanding, which has the abandoning of sensual desire and so on as its cause; or it is the practice itself, which is characterized by the abandoning of sensual desire and so on. This same method applies to 'having broken down,' etc. 'By non-ill will' means by loving-kindness. 'By the perception of light' means by attending to the perception of light and making it clear, through the manifestation of light-perception. 'By non-distraction' means by concentration. 'By the discernment of phenomena' means by the correct determination of wholesome states and so on. Some also say, 'by the discernment of name-and-form with its conditions.'

Evaṃ kāmacchandādinīvaraṇappahānena “abhijjhaṃ loke pahāyā”tiādinā (vibha. 508) vuttāya paṭhamajjhānassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadāya bhagavato tathāgatabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni saha upāyena aṭṭhahi samāpattīhi aṭṭhārasahi ca mahāvipassanāhi taṃ dassetuṃ “ñāṇenā”tiādimāha. Nāmarūpapariggahakaṅkhāvitaraṇānañhi vinibandhabhūtassa mohassa dūrīkaraṇena ñātapariññāyaṃ ṭhitassa aniccasaññādayo sijjhanti, tathā jhānasamāpattīsu abhiratinimittena pāmojjena. Tattha “anabhiratiyā vinoditāya jhānādīnaṃ samadhigamo”ti samāpattivipassanānaṃ arativinodanaavijjāpadālanādīni upāyo, uppaṭipāṭiniddeso pana nīvaraṇasabhāvāya avijjāya heṭṭhā nivaraṇesupi saṅgahadassanatthanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Samāpattivihārappavesavibandhanena nīvaraṇāni kavāṭasadisānīti āha “nīvaraṇakavāṭaṃ ugghāṭetvā”ti. “Rattiṃ anuvitakketvā anuvicāretvā divā kammante payojetī”ti (ma. ni. 1.251) vuttaṭṭhāne vitakkavicārā dhūmāyanāti adhippetāti āha “vitakkavicāradhūma”nti. Kiñcāpi paṭhamajjhānupacāreyeva dukkhaṃ, catutthajjhānupacāre ca sukhaṃ pahīyati, atisayappahānaṃ pana sandhāyāha “catutthajjhānena sukhadukkhaṃ pahāyā”ti.

Thus, having shown the Blessed One’s state as a Tathāgata by the preliminary practice for the first jhāna, which is the abandoning of the hindrances such as sensual desire, as stated in the phrase “having abandoned covetousness for the world” (Vibh. 508), he now begins with “with knowledge,” etc., to demonstrate that along with the means—through the eight attainments and the eighteen great insights. For one who stands in full understanding through comprehension, perceptions of impermanence and so on succeed by removing delusion, which is a fetter to the discernment of name-and-form and the overcoming of doubt. Similarly, joy arises in the jhāna attainments through the sign of delight. Here, “the attainment of jhānas etc. by the dispelling of discontent” means that the dispelling of discontent, the breaking down of ignorance, and so on, are the means for attainments and insights. The reverse-order explanation, however, should be understood as for the purpose of showing the inclusion of the hindrances below, which share the nature of ignorance. The hindrances are like closed doors, obstructing entry into the attainments and meditative abidings—hence it is said, “having opened the door of the hindrances.” Regarding the passage, “by night, reflecting and examining, by day, applying oneself to work” (MN 1.251), the terms “reflection and examination” are intended to mean “smoke-like”—thus it is said, “the smoke of reflection and examination.” Although suffering is abandoned even in the access to the first jhāna, and pleasure is abandoned in the access to the fourth jhāna, the emphasis here is on the surpassing abandonment—hence it is said, “by the fourth jhāna, having abandoned pleasure and pain.”

Aniccassa, aniccanti ca anupassanā aniccānupassanā, tebhūmakadhammānaṃ aniccataṃ gahetvā pavattāya vipassanāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Niccasaññanti saṅkhatadhammesu “niccā sassatā”ti evaṃpavattamicchāsaññaṃ. Saññāsīsena diṭṭhicittānampi [M 1.0103] gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Esa nayo ito paresupi. Nibbidānupassanāyāti saṅkhāresu nibbijjanākārena pavattāya anupassanāya. Nandinti sappītikataṇhaṃ. Virāgānupassanāyāti saṅkhāresu virajjanākārena pavattāya anupassanāya. Nirodhānupassanāyāti [V 1.0092] saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhassa anupassanāya. Yathā vā saṅkhārā nirujjhantiyeva, āyatiṃ punabbhavavasena na uppajjanti, evaṃ anupassanā nirodhānupassanā. Tenevāha “nirodhānupassanāya nirodheti, no samudetī”ti. Muccitukamyatā hi ayaṃ balappattāti. Paṭinissajjanākārena pavattā anupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanā, paṭisaṅkhāsantiṭṭhanā hi ayaṃ. Ādānanti niccādivasena gahaṇaṃ. Santatisamūhakiccārammaṇānaṃ vasena ekattaggahaṇaṃ ghanasaññā. Āyūhanaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ. Avatthāvisesāpatti vipariṇāmo. Dhuvasaññanti thirabhāvaggahaṇaṃ. Nimittanti samūhādighanavasena sakiccaparicchedatāya ca saṅkhārānaṃ saviggahaggahaṇaṃ. Paṇidhinti rāgādipaṇidhiṃ. Sā panatthato taṇhāvasena saṅkhāresu ninnatā. Abhinivesanti attānudiṭṭhiṃ.

The contemplation of the impermanent as 'impermanent' is the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā); this is the name for the insight that arises by grasping the impermanence of phenomena in the three realms. The perception of permanence (niccasaññā) is the wrong perception that arises regarding conditioned phenomena as 'permanent, eternal.' By the term 'perception,' the inclusion of views and thoughts should also be understood. This principle applies to the subsequent terms as well. The contemplation of disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā) is the contemplation that proceeds in the mode of weariness toward formations. 'Delight' (nandi) refers to craving accompanied by joy. The contemplation of dispassion (virāgānupassanā) is the contemplation that proceeds in the mode of detachment toward formations. The contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā) is the contemplation of the cessation of formations. Alternatively, just as formations cease and do not arise again in the future by way of renewed existence, so the contemplation of this is the contemplation of cessation. Hence it is said: 'Through the contemplation of cessation, one brings them to cessation; they do not arise.' For this is the desire for liberation that has attained strength. The contemplation that proceeds in the mode of relinquishment is the contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā), for this is a firm stance based on reflection. 'Grasping' (ādāna) is the holding onto things as permanent and so forth. The perception of compactness (ghanasaññā) is the grasping of unity by way of continuity, collection, function, and object. 'Accumulation' (āyūhanaṃ) is the act of forming (abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ). 'Change' (vipariṇāmo) is the attainment of a different state. The perception of stability (dhuvasaññā) is the grasping of a stable state. 'The sign' (nimitta) is the grasping of formations as a substantial mass, by way of their being a collection and so forth, and by the limitation of their own function. 'Longing' (paṇidhi) is the longing rooted in lust and so forth. In essence, this is the inclination toward formations due to craving. 'Adherence' (abhinivesa) is the view of self.

Aniccadukkhādivasena sabbadhammatīraṇaṃ adhipaññādhammavipassanā. Sārādānābhinivesanti asāresu sāraggahaṇavipallāsaṃ. Issarakuttādivasena loko samuppannoti abhiniveso sammohābhiniveso. Keci pana “ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhānantiādinā (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) pavattasaṃsayāpatti sammohābhiniveso”ti vadanti. Saṅkhāresu leṇatāṇabhāvaggahaṇaṃ ālayābhiniveso. “Ālayaratā ālayasammuditā”ti (dī. ni. 2.64, 67; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 7, 8) vacanato ālayo taṇhā, sāyeva cakkhādīsu rūpādīsu ca abhinivisanavasena pavattiyā ālayābhinivesoti keci. “Evaṃvidhā saṅkhārā paṭinissajjīyantī”ti pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhānupassanā. Vaṭṭato vigatattā vivaṭṭaṃ, nibbānaṃ, tattha ārammaṇakaraṇasaṅkhātena anupassanena pavattiyā vivaṭṭānupassanā, gotrabhū. Saṃyogābhinivesanti saṃyujjanavasena saṅkhāresu nivisanaṃ. Diṭṭhekaṭṭheti diṭṭhiyā sahajātekaṭṭhe pahānekaṭṭhe ca. Oḷāriketi uparimaggavajjhakilese apekkhitvā vuttaṃ, aññathā dassanena pahātabbāpi dutiyamaggavajjhehi oḷārikāti. Aṇusahagateti aṇubhūte. Idaṃ heṭṭhimamaggavajjhe apekkhitvā [M 1.0104] vuttaṃ. Sabbakileseti avasiṭṭhasabbakilese. Na hi paṭhamādimaggehi pahīnā kilesā puna pahīyantīti.

Examining all phenomena by way of impermanence, suffering, and so forth is insight into phenomena as higher wisdom (adhipaññā-dhammavipassanā). Adherence to grasping the essential is the perversion of grasping the essential in what is non-essential. The adherence that the world arises through the work of a creator, etc., is adherence rooted in delusion. Some, however, say that adherence rooted in delusion is the falling into doubt that arises, such as, 'Did I exist in the past?' and so forth. The grasping of a state of shelter and refuge in formations is adherence rooted in clinging. From the statement, 'Delighting in clinging, rejoicing in clinging,' clinging is craving. Some say that adherence rooted in clinging is that which proceeds by way of settling upon forms, etc., in the eye, etc. The knowledge that proceeds thus, 'Such formations are to be relinquished,' is the contemplation by reflection. Because it has departed from the round of existence, it is the un-round (vivaṭṭaṃ), Nibbāna. The contemplation of the un-round proceeds by way of the contemplation that takes that [Nibbāna] as its object; this is the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū). Adherence to fetters is the settling upon formations by way of binding. 'In one aspect with the view' means in one aspect co-arisen with the view, and in one aspect with its abandoning. 'Coarse'—this is said with reference to the defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths; otherwise, even those to be abandoned by seeing are coarse in relation to those to be abandoned by the second path. 'Accompanied by the subtle' means the subtle ones. This is said with reference to the defilements to be abandoned by the lower path. 'All defilements' means all the remaining defilements. For defilements abandoned by the first path and so on are not abandoned again.

Kakkhaḷattaṃ kathinabhāvo. Paggharaṇaṃ dravabhāvo. Lokiyavāyunā bhastassa viya yena vāyunā taṃtaṃkalāpassa uddhumāyanaṃ, thaddhabhāvo vā, taṃ vitthambhanaṃ. Vijjamānepi kalāpantarabhūtānaṃ kalāpantarabhūtehi samphuṭṭhabhāve taṃtaṃbhūtavivittatā rūpapariyanto ākāsoti yesaṃ yo paricchedo, tehi so asamphuṭṭhova, aññathā bhūtānaṃ paricchedasabhāvo na siyā byāpībhāvāpattito, abyāpitāva [V 1.0093] asamphuṭṭhatāti yasmiṃ kalāpe bhūtānaṃ paricchedo, tehi asamphuṭṭhabhāvo asamphuṭṭhalakkhaṇaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā ākāsadhātuniddese (dha. sa. 637) “asamphuṭṭhaṃ catūhi mahābhūtehī”ti.

Hardness is the state of being rigid. Flowing is the state of being liquid. Just as bellows are inflated by worldly wind, so too the inflation of each group of matter by the wind, or its rigidity, is called expansion. Even though there is contact among the elements of one group with the elements of another group, the distinctness of each element—space, which is the limit of form—is such that it is untouched by them. Otherwise, there would be no characteristic of delimitation among the elements, because they would become all-pervasive. Their non-pervasiveness is, indeed, their state of being untouched. In whatever group of matter the delimitation of the elements exists, their state of being untouched is the characteristic of being untouched. Therefore, the Blessed One said in the explanation of the space element (Dhs. 637): 'It is untouched by the four great elements.'

Virodhipaccayasannipāte visadisuppatti ruppanaṃ. Cetanāpadhānattā saṅkhārakkhandhadhammānaṃ cetanāvasenetaṃ vuttaṃ “saṅkhārānaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇa”nti. Tathā hi suttantabhājanīye saṅkhārakkhandhavibhaṅge (vibha. 92) “cakkhusamphassajā cetanā”tiādinā cetanāva vibhattā. Abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇā ca cetanā. Yathāha “tattha katamo puññābhisaṅkhāro? Kusalā cetanā kāmāvacarā”tiādi. Pharaṇaṃ savipphārikatā. Assaddhiyeti asaddhiyahetu. Nimittatthe bhummaṃ. Esa nayo kosajjetiādīsu. Upasamalakkhaṇanti kāyacittapariḷāhūpasamalakkhaṇaṃ. Līnuddhaccarahite adhicitte pavattamāne paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu abyāvaṭatāya ajjhupekkhanaṃ paṭisaṅkhānaṃ pakkhapātupacchedato.

In the presence of opposing conditions, dissimilar production is 'ruppanaṃ' (vexation). Due to the prominence of volition among the phenomena of the formations aggregate, it is said by way of volition that 'the characteristic of formations is the act of forming.' Indeed, in the analysis of the formations aggregate in the Suttanta classification (Vibh. 92), volition itself is analyzed with phrases such as 'volition born of eye-contact,' and so on. And volition has the characteristic of forming, as stated: 'Here, what is the meritorious formation? It is wholesome volition pertaining to the sensuous sphere,' and so forth. 'Pharaṇaṃ' (pervading) means thorough pervasion. 'Assaddhiyeti' means 'due to lack of faith.' 'Nimittatthe bhummaṃ' means the locative case is used in the sense of cause. This is the method in cases like 'kosajjeti,' etc. 'The characteristic of tranquility' refers to the characteristic of calming the fever of body and mind. When the higher mind proceeds free from sluggishness and restlessness, equanimity is reflection, due to its non-engagement in uplifting, restraining, and gladdening, and due to the cutting off of partiality.

Musāvādādīnaṃ visaṃvādanādikiccatāya lūkhānaṃ apariggāhakānaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvato pariggāhakasabhāvā sammāvācā siniddhabhāvato sampayuttadhamme sammāvācāpaccayasubhāsitānaṃ sotārañca puggalaṃ pariggaṇhātīti tassā pariggāhalakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Kāyikakiriyā kiñci kattabbaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, sayañca samuṭṭhahanaṃ ghaṭanaṃ hotīti sammākammanta saṅkhātāya viratiyā samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā ukkhipanaṃ samuṭṭhāpanaṃ kāyikakiriyāya bhārukkhipanaṃ viya. Jīvamānassa sattassa, sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā jīvitindriyappavattiyā, ājīvasseva vā suddhi vodānaṃ. Sasampayuttadhammassa cittassa saṃkilesapakkhe patituṃ adatvā sammadeva paggaṇhanaṃ paggaho.

Because it is the opposite of coarse and non-embracing things, which have the function of deception regarding false speech and the like, right speech has an embracing nature due to its agreeable quality. And because it embraces the associated states, well-spoken words conditioned by right speech, and the person who listens, its characteristic of embracing is stated. Bodily action initiates something to be done, and its own arising is an exertion; thus, the characteristic of initiating should be seen in the abstinence designated as right action. Or, it is the lifting up, the initiating, of associated states, like the lifting of a burden by bodily action. For a living being, purification and cleansing occur for the associated states through the operation of the life faculty, or for the livelihood itself. It is the right upholding of the mind together with its associated states, not allowing it to fall to the side of defilement; this is exertion.

“Saṅkhārā”ti [M 1.0105] idha cetanā adhippetāti vuttaṃ “saṅkhārānaṃ cetanālakkhaṇa”nti. Namanaṃ ārammaṇābhimukhabhāvo. Āyatanaṃ pavattanaṃ. Āyatanānaṃ vasena hi āyasaṅkhātānaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ pavatti. Taṇhāya hetulakkhaṇanti vaṭṭassa janakahetubhāvo, maggassa pana nibbānasampāpakattanti ayametesaṃ viseso.

'Formations' here means volition; thus it is said, 'the characteristic of formations is volition.' Bending is the state of being turned towards an object. The sphere is that which causes to proceed. For indeed, the proceeding of mind and mental factors, which are designated as 'income' (āya), occurs by way of the spheres (āyatana). The characteristic of craving as a cause is its being the generative cause of the round of existence; but the characteristic of the path is its bringing about the attainment of Nibbāna—this is their distinction.

Tathalakkhaṇaṃ aviparītasabhāvo. Ekaraso aññamaññānativattanaṃ anūnānadhikabhāvo. Yuganaddhā samathavipassanāva. Saddhāpaññā paggahāvikkhepātipi vadanti.

The characteristic of suchness is its unperverted nature. It has a single essence: not transgressing one another, being neither deficient nor excessive. Yoked together are tranquility and insight. They also say it is faith and wisdom, or exertion and non-distraction.

Khīṇoti [V 1.0094] kilese khepatīti khayo, maggo. Anuppādapariyosānatāya anuppādo, phalaṃ. Passaddhi kilesavūpasamo. Chandassāti kattukāmatāchandassa. Mūlalakkhaṇaṃ patiṭṭhābhāvo. Samuṭṭhānabhāvo samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ ārammaṇapaṭipādakatāya sampayuttadhammānaṃ uppattihetutā. Samodhānaṃ visayādisannipātena gahetabbākāro, yā saṅgatīti vuccati. Samaṃ saha odahanti anena sampayuttadhammāti vā samodhānaṃ, phasso. Samosaranti sannipatanti etthāti samosaraṇaṃ. Vedanāya vinā appavattamānā sampayuttadhammā vedanānubhavananimittaṃ samosaṭā viya hontīti evaṃ vuttaṃ. Gopānasīnaṃ kūṭaṃ viya sampayuttānaṃ pāmokkhabhāvo pamukhalakkhaṇaṃ. Tato, tesaṃ vā sampayuttadhammānaṃ uttari padhānanti tatuttari, paññuttarā hi kusalā dhammā. Vimuttiyāti phalassa. Tañhi sīlādiguṇasārassa paramukkaṃsabhāvena sāraṃ. Ayañca lakkhaṇavibhāgo chadhātupañcajhānaṅgādivasena taṃtaṃsuttapadānusārena porāṇaṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatanayena ca katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi pubbe vuttopi koci dhammo pariyāyantarapakāsanatthaṃ puna dassito. Tato eva ca “chandamūlakā kusalā dhammā manasikārasamuṭṭhānā phassasamodhānā vedanāsamosaraṇā”ti, “paññuttarā kusalā dhammā”ti, “vimuttisāramidaṃ brahmacariya”nti, “nibbānogadhañhi āvuso brahmacariyaṃ nibbānapariyosāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.466) ca suttapadānaṃ vasena “chandassa mūlalakkhaṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

It destroys, it casts out defilements, thus it is 'destruction' (khaya); this is the path. Because it culminates in non-arising, it is 'non-arising' (anuppāda); this is the fruit. Tranquility is the calming of defilements. 'Of desire' (chandassa) means of the desire to act. The root characteristic is the state of being a foundation. The characteristic of arising is the state of arising, which is the cause for the arising of associated states by presenting the object. 'Meeting' (samodhāna) is the mode to be grasped through the conjunction of the object and so on, which is called 'connection.' Or, associated states place themselves together with this, thus it is 'meeting' (samodhāna); this is contact. 'They converge, they come together here,' thus it is 'convergence' (samosaraṇa). It is said thus because associated states, which do not occur without feeling, are as if converged for the sake of experiencing feeling. Like the peak of gabled rafters, the state of being foremost among associated states is the characteristic of leadership. Beyond that, or further pre-eminent among those associated states, is 'tatuttari'; for wholesome states are indeed led by wisdom. 'Of liberation' (vimuttiyā) refers to the fruit. For it is the essence, being the supreme excellence of the essence of such virtues as morality. And this distinction of characteristics should be understood as made according to the six elements, the five jhāna factors, and so on, following the wording of the respective suttas and the method found in the ancient commentaries. Thus, even a previously mentioned teaching may be shown again to explain it from another angle. Therefore, based on the sutta passages—'Wholesome states are rooted in desire, arise from attention, are brought together by contact, and converge upon feeling,' 'Wholesome states are led by wisdom,' 'The essence of this holy life is liberation,' and 'Friends, the holy life is grounded in Nibbāna and culminates in Nibbāna' (MN 1.466)—it is said: 'The root characteristic is of desire,' and so on.

Tathadhammā nāma cattāri ariyasaccāni aviparītasabhāvattā. Tathāni taṃsabhāvattā. Avitathāni amusāsabhāvattā. Anaññathāni aññākārarahitattā. Jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭhoti jātipaccayā sambhūtaṃ [M 1.0106] hutvā sahitassa attano paccayānurūpassa uddhaṃ āgatabhāvo, anupavattanaṭṭhoti attho. Atha vā sambhūtaṭṭho ca samudāgataṭṭho ca sambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho, na jātito jarāmaraṇaṃ na hoti, na ca jātiṃ vinā aññato hotīti jātipaccayasambhūtaṭṭho. Itthañca jātito samudāgacchatīti jātipaccayasamudāgataṭṭho, yā yā jāti yathā yathā paccayo hoti, tadanurūpaṃ pātubhāvoti attho. Avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭhoti etthāpi na avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo na hoti, na ca avijjaṃ vinā saṅkhārā uppajjanti, yā yā avijjā yesaṃ yesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ yathā yathā paccayo hoti, ayaṃ avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭho paccayabhāvoti attho.

The four Noble Truths are called 'true things' (tathadhammā) because their nature is not distorted. They are 'true' (tathāni) because that is their nature. They are 'not unreal' (avitathāni) because their nature is not deceptive. They are 'not otherwise' (anaññathāni) because they are devoid of any other mode. 'The meaning of being produced and arisen from birth as condition' is: having been produced from birth as condition, it is the state of having come forth in accordance with its own accompanying condition; the meaning is that of continuation. Or, the meaning of 'produced' and the meaning of 'arisen' is 'the meaning of being produced and arisen.' 'The meaning of being produced from birth as condition' is that it is not the case that aging and death do not come from birth, nor do they come from anything else without birth. And thus, 'it arises from birth' is 'the meaning of arising from birth as condition'; the meaning is that whatever birth is a condition in whatever way, the manifestation is in accordance with that. Here too, 'the meaning of ignorance as condition for formations' is: it is not the case that ignorance is not a condition for formations, and formations do not arise without ignorance. Whatever ignorance is a condition for whichever formations in whatever way, this is 'the meaning of ignorance as condition for formations'; the meaning is the state of being a condition.

Bhagavā taṃ sabbākārato jānāti passatīti sambandho. Tenāti bhagavatā. Taṃ vibhajjamānanti yojetabbaṃ. Tanti rupāyatanaṃ. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhādīti ādi-saddena majjhattaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, tathā atītānāgatapaccuppannaparittaajjhattabahiddhātadubhayādibhedaṃ. Labbhamānakapadavasenāti “rūpāyatanaṃ [V 1.0095] diṭṭhaṃ, saddāyatanaṃ sutaṃ, gandhāyatanaṃ rasāyatanaṃ phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ mutaṃ, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ manasā viññāta”nti (dha. sa. 966) vacanato diṭṭhapadañca viññātapadañca rūpārammaṇe labbhati, rūpārammaṇaṃ iṭṭhaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ majjhattaṃ parittaṃ atītaṃ anāgataṃ paccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā diṭṭhaṃ viññātaṃ rūpaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ rūpadhātu vaṇṇanibhā sanidassanaṃ sappaṭighaṃ nīlaṃ pītakanti evamādīhi anekehi nāmehi.

The Blessed One knows and sees it in all aspects—this is the connection. 'By him' means by the Blessed One. 'Analyzing it' should be connected. 'That' refers to the form base. 'Pleasant, unpleasant, etc.'—by the word 'etc.' the neutral is included, as well as distinctions such as past, future, present, limited, internal, external, and both. By way of the terms that can be obtained, from the statement: 'The form base is seen, the sound base is heard, the odor base, the taste base, the tangible base is touched, all form is cognized by the mind' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī §966), the terms 'seen' and 'cognized' are obtained in relation to form objects. A form object is pleasant, unpleasant, neutral, limited, past, future, present, internal, external, seen, cognized, form, the form base, the form element, appearance, visible form, with impact, blue, yellow, and so on, by these and many other names.

Terasahi vārehīti rūpakaṇḍe (dha. sa. 616) āgate terasa niddesavāre sandhāyāha. Ekekasmiñca vāre catunnaṃ catunnaṃ vavatthāpananayānaṃ vasena “dvepaññāsāya nayehī”ti āha. Tathameva aviparītadassitāya appaṭivattiyadesanatāya ca. “Jānāmi abhiññāsi”nti vattamānātītakālesu ñāṇappavattidassanena anāgatepi ñāṇappavatti vuttāyevāti daṭṭhabbā. Vidita-saddo anāmaṭṭhakālaviseso veditabbo “diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ muta”ntiādīsu (dha. sa. 966) viya. Na upaṭṭhāsīti attattaniyavasena na upagacchi. Yathā rūpārammaṇādayo dhammā yaṃsabhāvā yaṃpakārā ca, tathā ne passati jānāti gacchatīti tathāgatoti evaṃ padasambhavo veditabbo. Keci pana “niruttinayena pisodarādipakkhepena (pāṇini 6.3.109) vā dassi-saddassa lopaṃ, āgata-saddassa cāgamaṃ katvā tathāgato”ti vaṇṇenti.

The phrase 'by thirteen series' refers to the thirteen exposition series that come in the Form Section (Dhammasaṅgaṇī §616). And for each series, by way of four establishing methods each, it is said, 'by fifty-two methods.' Likewise, because of the teaching that shows without distortion and is irreversible. By showing the occurrence of knowledge in the present and past times with 'I know, I have directly known,' it should be understood that the occurrence of knowledge in the future is also stated. The word 'vidita' should be understood as not specifying a particular time, as in 'seen, heard, cognized,' and so on (Dhammasaṅgaṇī §966). 'He did not attend to it' means he did not take it up in terms of self or what belongs to self. The arising of the word 'Tathāgata' should be understood thus: just as form-objects and other phenomena are of a certain nature and a certain kind, so (tathā) he sees, knows, and goes (gacchati) to them. Some, however, explain it by way of etymology, applying the rule for irregular compounds like 'pisodara' (cf. Pāṇini 6.3.109), by eliding the word 'dassi' and making an augment of the word 'āgata', thus forming 'Tathāgata'.

Niddosatāya [M 1.0107] anupavajjaṃ. Pakkhipitabbābhāvena anūnaṃ. Apanetabbābhāvena anadhikaṃ. Atthabyañjanādisampattiyā sabbākāraparipuṇṇaṃ. No aññathāti “tathevā”ti vuttamevatthaṃ byatirekena sampādeti. Tena yadatthaṃ bhāsitaṃ, ekantena tadatthanipphādanato yathā bhāsitaṃ bhagavatā, tathevāti aviparītadesanataṃ dasseti. Gadaatthoti etena tathaṃ gadatīti tathāgatoti da-kārassa ta-kāro kato niruttinayenāti dasseti.

By being free from fault, it is blameless. By having nothing to add, it is not deficient. By having nothing to remove, it is not excessive. Through excellence in meaning and phrasing, it is perfectly complete in every way. 'Not otherwise'—thus, it confirms the meaning stated as 'just so' by way of exclusion. Therefore, whatever meaning was spoken, because it unfailingly fulfills that meaning, it shows the teaching is not contrary, being just as it was spoken by the Blessed One. By 'gada' (speaking), it indicates that because he speaks what is true (tathaṃ gadatī), he is called the Tathāgata, with the 'da' changed to 'ta' according to the method of etymology.

Tathā gatamassāti tathāgato. Gatanti ca kāyavācāpavattīti attho. Tathāti ca vutte yaṃtaṃsaddānaṃ abyabhicārisambandhitāya yathāti ayamattho upaṭṭhitoyeva hoti, kāyavacīkiriyānañca aññamaññānulomena vacanicchāyaṃ kāyassa vācā, vācāya ca kāyo sambandhībhāvena upatiṭṭhatīti imamatthaṃ dassento āha “bhagavato hī”tiādi. Imasmiṃ pana atthe tathāvādītāya tathāgatoti ayampi attho siddho hoti. So pana pubbe pakārantarena dassitoti āha “evaṃ tathākāritāya tathāgato”ti.

'His going is thus,' thus he is the Tathāgata. 'Going' here means the activity of body and speech. And when 'thus' is said, the meaning 'as' is already present due to the invariable connection between the relative and demonstrative pronouns. And showing this meaning—that the actions of body and speech are in mutual accordance, and that when there is a wish to speak, speech is related to the body and the body to speech—he says, 'For the Blessed One...' and so on. Moreover, in this sense, the meaning of 'Tathāgata' as 'one who speaks thus' is also established. But since this was previously shown in another way, he says, 'Thus, by acting thus, he is the Tathāgata.'

Tiriyaṃ aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsūti etena yadeke “tiriyaṃ viya upari adho ca santi lokadhātuyo”ti [V 1.0096] vadanti, taṃ paṭisedheti. Desanāvilāsoyeva desanāvilāsamayo yathā “puññamayaṃ, dānamaya”ntiādīsu.

By 'in the immeasurable world-systems across,' he refutes what some say: 'World-systems exist above and below just as they do across.' The word `desanāvilāsamayo` means 'consisting of the splendor of teaching' (desanāvilāsa), just as in the cases of `puññamayaṃ` ('consisting of merit') and `dānamayaṃ` ('consisting of generosity').

Nipātānaṃ vācakasaddasannidhāne tadatthajotanabhāvena pavattanato gata-saddoyeva avagatatthaṃ atītatthañca vadatīti āha “gatoti avagato atīto”ti.

Because particles function by illuminating their meaning when in proximity to an expressive word, he says that the word 'gata' itself expresses the meaning 'understood' and 'past'. Hence it is said, 'Gata means understood and past.'

Atha vā abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya yāva sammāsambodhi, etthantare mahābodhiyānapaṭipattiyā hānaṭṭhānasaṃkilesanivattīnaṃ abhāvato yathā paṇidhānaṃ, tathā gato abhinīhārānurūpaṃ paṭipannoti tathāgato. Atha vā mahiddhikatāya paṭisambhidānaṃ ukkaṃsādhigamena anāvaraṇañāṇatāya ca katthacipi paṭighātābhāvato yathā ruci, tathā kāyavacīcittānaṃ gatāni gamanāni pavattiyo etassāti tathāgato. Yasmā ca loke vidha-yutta-gata-ppakāra-saddā samānatthā dissanti. Tasmā yathāvidhā vipassīādayo bhagavanto, ayampi bhagavā tathāvidhoti tathāgato[M 1.0108], yathāyuttā ca te bhagavanto, ayampi bhagavā tathāyuttoti tathāgato. Atha vā yasmā saccaṃ tacchaṃ tathanti ñāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tasmā tathena ñāṇena āgatoti tathāgato. Evampi tathāgata-saddassa attho veditabbo.

Alternatively, starting from his aspiration up to perfect enlightenment, in this entire period, due to the absence of turning back from decline, stagnation, or defilement in the practice of the great vehicle of enlightenment, he proceeded in accordance with his aspiration, having practiced in conformity with his resolve; thus, he is the Tathāgata. Or, due to his great power, the attainment of excellence in the analytical knowledges, and unobstructed knowledge, there being no obstruction anywhere, the movements and proceedings of his body, speech, and mind are just as he wishes; thus, he is the Tathāgata. Moreover, since in the world, words like 'vidha,' 'yutta,' 'gata,' and 'ppakāra' are seen to have similar meanings, just as the Blessed Ones such as Vipassī were of such a kind, this Blessed One is also of such a kind; thus, he is the Tathāgata. And just as those Blessed Ones were rightly endowed, this Blessed One is also rightly endowed; thus, he is the Tathāgata. Alternatively, because 'truth,' 'the real,' and 'thus' are designations for knowledge, he has arrived by means of that true knowledge; thus, he is the Tathāgata. In this way also, the meaning of the term 'Tathāgata' should be understood.

Pahāya kāmādimale yathā gatā,

Samādhiñāṇehi vipassiādayo;

Mahesino sakyamunī jutindharo,

Tathā gato tena mato tathāgato.

Just as the great seers, Vipassī and others, went by means of concentration and wisdom, having abandoned the stains of sensual desires and the like; so too has the Sakyan sage, the resplendent one, gone. For that reason, he is considered the Tathāgata.

Tathañca dhātāyatanādilakkhaṇaṃ,

Sabhāvasāmaññavibhāgabhedato;

Sayambhuñāṇena jino samāgato,

Tathāgato vuccati sakyapuṅgavo.

And because the Conqueror, with self-born wisdom, has fully understood the characteristics of elements, sense bases, and so on, as they truly are, according to the distinctions of their individual nature, general nature, and specific divisions, the bull of the Sakyans is called the Tathāgata.

Tathāni saccāni samantacakkhunā,

Tathā idappaccayatā ca sabbaso;

Anaññaneyyena yato vibhāvitā,

Yāthāvato tena jino tathāgato.

Since the truths as they are, and this-conditionality in every way as it is, have been made manifest as they truly are by the All-Seeing One, who is not led by another, therefore the Victor is the Tathāgata.

Anekabhedāsupi [V 1.0097] lokadhātusu,

Jinassa rūpāyatanādigocare;

Vicitrabhedaṃ tathameva dassanaṃ,

Tathāgato tena samantalocano.

Even in many diverse world-systems, within the Conqueror's sphere of the form-base and so on, his vision is truly varied and diverse; therefore, the Tathāgata is the one with vision on all sides.

Yato ca dhammaṃ tathameva bhāsati,

Karoti vācāyanulomamattano;

Guṇehi lokaṃ abhibhuyyirīyati,

Tathāgato tenapi lokanāyako.

And since he speaks the Dhamma just as it is, acts in accordance with his own words, and conducts himself having surpassed the world with his virtues, therefore the Tathāgata is also the leader of the world.

Yathābhinīhāramato yathāruci,

Pavattavācā tanucittabhāvato;

Yathāvidhā yena purā mahesino,

Tathāvidho tena jino tathāgatoti. (itivu. aṭṭha. 38; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.7 cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā);

Because his speech, body, and mind proceed according to his aspiration and according to his wish; and because he is of such a kind as were the great seers of old, for that reason the Victor is the Tathāgata. (Itivuttaka Aṭṭhakathā 38; Dīgha Nikāya Ṭīkā 1.7 Cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā).

Ārakattātiādīnaṃ [M 1.0109] padānaṃ attho visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.125) buddhānussatisaṃvaṇṇanāya vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattāti imināssa paropadesarahitassa sabbākārena sabbadhammāvabodhanasamatthassa ākaṅkhāpaṭibaddhavuttino anāvaraṇañāṇasaṅkhātassa sabbaññutaññāṇassa adhigamo dassito.

The meaning of the terms beginning with 'because of being distant,' etc., should be understood in the way explained in the description of the recollection of the Buddha in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. 1.125). By the phrase 'because of having rightly and by himself understood all things,' is shown his attainment of the knowledge of omniscience—designated as unobstructed knowledge—which is capable of comprehending all things in every way without the instruction of another, and whose operation is dependent on his wish.

Nanu ca (itivu. aṭṭha. 38) sabbaññutaññāṇato aññaṃ anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ, aññathā cha asādhāraṇañāṇāni buddhañāṇānīti vacanaṃ virujjheyyāti? Na virujjhati visayappavattibhedavasena aññehi asādhāraṇañāṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ ekasseva ñāṇassa dvidhā vuttattā. Ekameva hi taṃ ñāṇaṃ anavasesasaṅkhatāsaṅkhatasammutidhammavisayatāya sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, tattha ca āvaraṇābhāvato nissaṅgacāramupādāya anāvaraṇañāṇanti vuttaṃ. Yathāha paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.119) “sabbaṃ saṅkhatāsaṅkhatamanavasesaṃ jānātīti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, tatthāvaraṇaṃ natthīti anāvaraṇañāṇa”ntiādi, tasmā natthi nesaṃ atthato bhedo, ekantena cetaṃ evamicchitabbaṃ, aññathā sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇānaṃ sāvaraṇatā asabbadhammārammaṇatā ca āpajjeyya. Na hi bhagavato ñāṇassa aṇumatampi āvaraṇaṃ atthi, anāvaraṇañāṇassa ca asabbadhammārammaṇabhāve [V 1.0098] yattha taṃ nappavattati, tatthāvaraṇasabbhāvato anāvaraṇabhāvoyeva na siyā. Atha vā pana hotu aññameva anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇato, idha pana sabbattha appaṭihatavuttitāya anāvaraṇañāṇanti sabbaññutaññāṇameva adhippetaṃ, tassa cādhigamena bhagavā sabbaññū sabbavidū sammāsambuddhoti ca vuccati, na sakimeva sabbadhammāvabodhato. Tathā ca vuttaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.162) “vimokkhantikametaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ bodhiyā mūle saha sabbaññutaññāṇassa paṭilābhā sacchikā paññatti yadidaṃ buddho”ti. Sabbadhammāvabodhanasamatthañāṇasamadhigamena hi bhagavato santāne anavasesadhamme paṭivijjhituṃ samatthatā ahosīti.

But is it not said (in Itivuttaka Aṭṭhakathā 38) that unobstructed knowledge is distinct from omniscient knowledge? Otherwise, the statement that 'the six unique knowledges are the Buddha's knowledges' would be contradicted. There is no contradiction, because a single knowledge is described in two ways to show its unique nature, distinct from others, by way of the difference in its domain and operation. For that very knowledge, because its domain is all conditioned, unconditioned, and conventional phenomena without exception, is called 'omniscient knowledge.' And because there is no obstruction in it, it is also called 'unobstructed knowledge' on account of its unimpeded proceeding. As is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 1.119): 'He knows all conditioned and unconditioned things without remainder—this is omniscient knowledge. There is no obstruction in it—this is unobstructed knowledge,' and so on. Therefore, there is no difference in meaning between them. And this should be accepted as certain, for otherwise, it would follow that omniscient knowledge has obstructions and that unobstructed knowledge does not have all phenomena as its object. Indeed, there is not even the slightest obstruction to the Blessed One's knowledge. And if unobstructed knowledge did not have all phenomena as its object, then wherever it does not operate, due to the presence of an obstruction there, its very nature as unobstructed would not exist. Or, alternatively, let unobstructed knowledge be distinct from omniscient knowledge. Here, however, by 'unobstructed knowledge' is meant precisely omniscient knowledge, because of its unimpeded operation everywhere. Through the attainment of this, the Blessed One is called omniscient, all-knowing, and perfectly enlightened—not because he comprehends all phenomena at once. And so it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 1.162): 'This is the finality of liberation for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones: the direct realization and designation 'Buddha' at the root of the Bodhi tree, together with the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience.' For it was through the attainment of knowledge capable of comprehending all phenomena that the capacity to fully penetrate all phenomena without remainder arose in the Blessed One’s mental continuum.

Etthāha – kiṃ panidaṃ ñāṇaṃ pavattamānaṃ sakiṃyeva sabbasmiṃ visaye pavattati, udāhu kamenāti. Kiñcettha – yadi tāva sakiṃyeva sabbasmiṃ visaye pavattati, atītānāgatapaccuppannaajjhattabahiddhādibhedena bhinnānaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ [M 1.0110] asaṅkhatasammutidhammānañca ekajjhaṃ upaṭṭhāne dūrato cittapaṭaṃ avekkhantassa viya paṭivibhāgenāvabodho na siyā, tathā ca sati “sabbe dhammā anattā”ti vipassantānaṃ anattākārena viya sabbe dhammā anirūpitarūpena bhagavato ñāṇassa visayā hontīti āpajjati. Yepi “sabbañeyyadhammānaṃ ṭhitalakkhaṇavisayaṃ vikapparahitaṃ sabbakālaṃ buddhānaṃ ñāṇaṃ pavattati, tena te sabbavidūti vuccanti. Evañca katvā ‘caraṃ samāhito nāgo, tiṭṭhantopi samāhito’ti idampi vacanaṃ suvuttaṃ hotī”ti vadanti, tesampi vuttadosānativatti. Ṭhitalakkhaṇārammaṇatāya hi atītānāgatasammutidhammānaṃ tadabhāvato ekadesavisayameva bhagavato ñāṇaṃ siyā, tasmā sakiṃyeva ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti na yujjati.

Here it is asked: Does this knowledge, as it proceeds, operate all at once in every object, or does it operate sequentially? What is the issue here? If it operates all at once in every object, then when conditioned, unconditioned, and conventional phenomena—distinguished as past, future, present, internal, external, and so on—are present all together, a distinct understanding of them would not be possible, just as for one looking at a painted cloth from a distance. And if that were so, it would follow that all phenomena would become objects of the Blessed One’s knowledge in an uninvestigated form, just as for those practicing insight meditation on 'all phenomena are not-self,' they appear under the aspect of not-self. Even those who say, 'The knowledge of the Buddhas operates at all times, free from conceptualization, having the static characteristic of all knowable phenomena as its object, and for this reason they are called 'all-knowing.' And by this, the statement, 'Walking, the great being is concentrated; standing, too, he is concentrated,' is well-spoken,'—even they do not escape the stated fault. For if its object were the static characteristic, then since past, future, and conventional phenomena lack that, the Blessed One's knowledge would have only a partial domain. Therefore, it is not tenable that the knowledge operates all at once.

Atha kamena sabbasmiṃ visaye ñāṇaṃ pavattati, evampi na yujjati. Na hi jātibhūmisabhāvādivasena disādesakālādivasena ca anekabhedabhinne neyye kamena gayhamāne tassa anavasesapaṭivedho sambhavati apariyantabhāvato ñeyyassa. Ye pana “atthassa avisaṃvādanato ñeyyassa ekadesaṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā sesepi evanti adhimuccitvā vavatthāpanena sabbaññū bhagavā, tañca ñāṇaṃ ananumānikaṃ saṃsayābhāvato. Saṃsayānubandhañhi loke anumānañāṇa”nti vadanti, tesampi taṃ na yuttaṃ. Sabbassa hi appaccakkhabhāve atthassa avisaṃvādanena ñeyyassa ekadesaṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā sesepi evanti adhimuccitvā vavatthāpanassa asambhavato. Yañhi taṃ sesaṃ, taṃ appaccakkhanti. Atha tampi paccakkhaṃ, tassa sesabhāvo eva na siyāti? Sabbametaṃ akāraṇaṃ. Kasmā? Avisayavicāraṇabhāvato. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā [V 1.0099] “buddhavisayo bhikkhave, acinteyyo na cintetabbo, yo cinteyya, ummādassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti (a. ni. 4.77). Idaṃ panettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ – yaṃ kiñci bhagavatā ñātuṃ icchitaṃ sakalamekadeso vā, tattha appaṭihatavuttitāya paccakkhato ñāṇaṃ pavattati, niccasamādhānañca vikkhepābhāvato, ñātuṃ icchitassa ca sakalassa avisayabhāve tassa ākaṅkhāpaṭibaddhavuttitā na siyā, ekanteneva ca sā icchitabbā “sabbe dhammā buddhassa bhagavato āvajjanapaṭibaddhā ākaṅkhapaṭibaddhā manasikārapaṭibaddhā cittuppādapaṭibaddhā”ti (mahāni. 69, 156; cūḷani. 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5) vacanato. Atītānāgatavisayampi bhagavato ñāṇaṃ anumānāgamatakkagahaṇavirahitattā paccakkhameva.

Then, if knowledge operates gradually in every object, even this is not fitting. For when the knowable, divided into many distinctions by way of birth, plane, inherent nature, etc., and by way of direction, location, time, etc., is grasped gradually, its complete penetration is impossible due to the limitless nature of the knowable. But as for those who say: 'The Blessed One is all-knowing by directly perceiving one part of the knowable and, through the non-discrepancy of the meaning, confidently determining that the rest is also thus; and that knowledge is not inferential due to the absence of doubt—for in the world, inferential knowledge is accompanied by doubt'—this is not correct for them either. For if the whole is not directly perceived, it is impossible to confidently determine the rest to be the same after directly perceiving one part of the knowable through the non-discrepancy of the meaning. For that which is the remainder is not directly perceived. If that too were directly perceived, it would simply not be a remainder. All this is unfounded. Why? Because it is a matter beyond the scope of investigation. This was indeed stated by the Blessed One: 'Monks, the sphere of a Buddha is inconceivable and should not be pondered. Whoever ponders it would partake of madness and vexation' (A. 4.77). Here, the conclusion is this: Whatever the Blessed One wishes to know—whether in whole or in part—knowledge operates there directly due to its unobstructed functioning, and his concentration is constant due to the absence of distraction. If the entirety of what he wishes to know were beyond his scope, its functioning, which is bound to his aspiration, would not occur. Indeed, it should be understood as exclusively bound by that wish, according to the text: 'All phenomena are bound to the Blessed Buddha’s attention, aspiration, mental engagement, and arising of mind' (Mahāni. 69, 156; Cūḷani. 85; Paṭi. Ma. 3.5). Even the Blessed One’s knowledge of the past and future is direct, being devoid of grasping through inference, tradition, or logical reasoning.

Nanu [M 1.0111] ca etasmimpi pakkhe yadā sakalaṃ ñātuṃ icchitaṃ, tadā sakiṃyeva sakalavisayatāya anirūpitarūpena bhagavato ñāṇaṃ pavatteyyāti vuttadosānativattiyevāti? Na, tassa visodhitattā. Visodhito hi so buddhavisayo acinteyyoti. Aññathā pacurajanañāṇasamānavuttitāya buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ ñāṇassa acinteyyatā na siyā, tasmā sakaladhammārammaṇampi taṃ ekadhammārammaṇaṃ viya suvavatthāpiteyeva te dhamme katvā pavattatīti idamettha acinteyyaṃ, anantañca ñāṇaṃ ñeyyaṃ viya. Vuttañhetaṃ “yāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Yāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ. Ñeyyapariyantikaṃ ñāṇaṃ, ñāṇapariyantikaṃ ñeyya”nti (mahāni. 69, 156; cūḷani. 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5). Evamekajjhaṃ, visuṃ sakiṃ, kamena vā icchānurūpaṃ sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddho.

Is it not then the case that even in this view, when the whole is wished to be known, the Blessed One’s knowledge would operate all at once, encompassing all objects in an undifferentiated form, thus not overcoming the stated flaw? No, because it has been purified. For that sphere of the Buddhas is indeed purified and inconceivable. Otherwise, the knowledge of the Blessed Ones, the Buddhas, would not be inconceivable, as its operation would be similar to the knowledge of ordinary people. Therefore, even though it has all phenomena as its object, it operates by having established those phenomena very well, as if it had a single phenomenon as its object. This is what is inconceivable here, and the infinite knowledge is like the knowable. For it is said: 'As far as the knowable extends, so far extends the knowledge. As far as the knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable. Knowledge has the knowable as its limit, and the knowable has knowledge as its limit' (Mahāni. 69, 156; Cūḷani. 85; Paṭi. Ma. 3.5). Thus, all at once, separately, or gradually, according to his wish—because he has rightly and by himself awakened to all phenomena, he is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Tanti yathāvuttaṃ pathavīādibhedaṃ. Pariññātanti parito samantato sabbākārato ñātaṃ, taṃ parijānitabbabhāvaṃ kiñci asesetvā ñātanti attho. Ayameva hi attho “pariññātanta”nti imināpi padena pakāsitoti dassento “pariññātantaṃ nāmā”tiādimāha. Tena tena maggena kilesappahānena viseso natthīti idaṃ taṃtaṃmaggavajjhakilesānaṃ buddhānaṃ sāvakānañca tena tena maggeneva pahātabbabhāvasāmaññaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na sāvakehi buddhānaṃ kilesappahānavisesābhāvato. Tathā hi sammāsambuddhā eva savāsanakilese jahanti, na sāvakā. Ekadesamevāti attano santānagatameva. Sasantatipariyāpannadhammapariññāmattenapi hi catusaccakammaṭṭhānabhāvanā samijjhati. Tenevāha – “imasmiṃyeva byāmamatte kaḷevare sasaññimhi samanake lokañca paññapemi lokasamudayañca paññapemī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 1.107; a. ni. 4.45). Aṇuppamāṇampi [V 1.0100] …pe… natthi, yato chattiṃsakoṭisatasahassamukhena buddhānaṃ mahāvajirañāṇaṃ pavattatīti vadanti.

The treatise is as stated, distinguished by earth and so forth. 'Fully understood' means known completely, in all aspects, without leaving anything of its nature to be fully comprehended. This very meaning is also indicated by the word 'pariññātantaṃ,' as shown by the phrase 'what is called "pariññātantaṃ," ' etc. The statement 'there is no difference in the abandonment of defilements by this or that path' is said with reference to the commonality that defilements to be abandoned by their respective paths must be abandoned by those respective paths, both by the Buddhas and their disciples; it is not said because there is no difference in the abandonment of defilements between the Buddhas and their disciples. For the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones alone abandon defilements along with their latent tendencies, whereas the disciples do not. 'Only a part' means only what pertains to one’s own continuum. For even the cultivation of the meditation subject of the four truths is accomplished merely by comprehending phenomena included in one’s own continuum. Hence it is said: 'In this very fathom-long body, endowed with perception and mind, I proclaim the world, the origin of the world,' etc. (S. 1.107; A. 4.45). Even a minute amount... there is none, since they say the great diamond knowledge of the Buddhas operates through thirty-six trillion doorways.

Tathāgatavārasattamanayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the seventh method in the section concerning the Tathāgata is finished.

Tathāgatavāraaṭṭhamanayavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Eighth Method in the Tathāgata Section

13. Purimataṇhāti [M 1.0112] purimataresu bhavesu nibbattā paccuppannattabhāvahetubhūtā taṇhā. Taggahaṇeneva ca atītaddhasaṅgahā avijjāsaṅkhārā saddhiṃ upādānena saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Etthāti “bhavā jātī”ti etasmiṃ pade. Tena upapattibhavenāti “bhavā jātī”ti jātisīsena vuttaupapattibhavena. Bhūtassāti nibbattassa. So pana yasmā satto nāma hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “sattassā”ti. Evañca jānitvāti iminā “bhūtassa jarāmaraṇa”nti etthāpi “iti viditvā”ti idaṃ padaṃ ānetvā yojetabbanti dasseti.

13. 'Prior craving' means craving that arose in earlier existences and is the cause of the present state of existence. It should be understood that by its inclusion, ignorance and volitional formations along with clinging are encompassed as a collection from the past. 'Here' refers to this phrase 'from becoming, birth'. 'Through that rebirth-becoming' means through the rebirth-becoming indicated by 'birth' as the heading in the phrase 'from becoming, birth'. 'Of what has come to be' refers to what has been born. Since that is called a being, it is therefore stated as 'of a being'. 'And having known thus' indicates that in 'of what has come to be, aging and death,' the words 'having thus understood' should be brought in and connected there as well.

Yadipi tebhūmakā upādānakkhandhā “yaṃ kiñci rūpa”ntiādinā (vibha. 2; ma. ni. 1.244) ekādasasu okāsesu pakkhipitabbā sammasitabbā ca, te pana yasmā bhagavatā “kimhi nu kho sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hoti, kiṃpaccayā jarāmaraṇa”ntiādinā (dī. ni. 2.57; saṃ. ni. 2.4, 10) paṭiccasamuppādamukhena sammasitā, paṭiccasamuppādo ca pavattipavattihetubhāvato purimasaccadvayameva hoti, tasmā tadabhisamayaṃ “maññanābhāvahetu paccayākārapaṭivedho”ti vibhāvento “yaṃ bodhirukkhamūle…pe… dassento”ti āha. Saṃkhippanti ettha avijjādayo viññāṇādayo cāti saṅkhepā, atīte hetuādayo “hetu, phala”nti evaṃ saṃkhippantīti vā saṅkhepā, avijjādayo viññāṇādayo ca. Saṅkhepa-saddo bhāgādhivacananti daṭṭhabbo. Tenāha “koṭṭhāsāti attho”ti. Te pana atīte hetusaṅkhepo, etarahi phalasaṅkhepo, etarahi hetusaṅkhepo, āyatiṃ phalasaṅkhepoti cattāro saṅkhepā etassāti catusaṅkhepo, taṃ catusaṅkhepaṃ. Hetuphalasandhi, phalahetusandhi, puna hetuphalasandhīti evaṃ tayo sandhī etassāti tisandhi, taṃ tisandhiṃ. Atītapaccuppannānāgatabhedā tayo addhā etassāti tiyaddho, taṃ tiyaddhaṃ. Sarūpato avuttāpi tasmiṃ tasmiṃ saṅkhepe ākirīyanti avijjāsaṅkhārādiggahaṇehi pakāsīyantīti ākārā, atītahetuādīnaṃ vā pakārā ākārā, te ekekasaṅkhepe pañca pañca katvā vīsati ākārā etassāti vīsatākāro, taṃ vīsatākāraṃ.

Even though the aggregates of clinging of the three realms should be included and contemplated upon in the eleven instances beginning with 'whatever form' (Vibh. 2; M. 1.244), yet because they were contemplated by the Blessed One through the perspective of dependent origination, as in 'When what exists does aging-and-death occur? What is the condition for aging-and-death?' (D. 2.57; S. 2.4, 10), and because dependent origination, due to being the cause of the continuity of existence, is essentially the two former truths, therefore, explaining that realization as 'the penetration of the conditional structure, the cause for the absence of conceiving,' he said, 'showing what... at the foot of the Bodhi tree...'. 'Summaries' (saṅkhepā) are so called because ignorance and so forth, and consciousness and so forth, are summarized herein; or, because past causes and so forth are summarized as 'cause, result,' they are summaries—that is, ignorance and so forth, and consciousness and so forth. The word 'summary' should be understood as a term denoting a part. Therefore, it is said, 'the meaning is "sections".' Now, the summary of past causes, the summary of present results, the summary of present causes, and the summary of future results—these are the four summaries, hence it has four summaries (catusaṅkhepo); that which has four summaries. The connection of cause and result, the connection of result and cause, and again the connection of cause and result—these are the three connections, hence it has three connections (tisandhi); that which has three connections. Divided into past, present, and future, these are the three periods, hence it has three periods (tiyaddho); that which has three periods. 'Modes' (ākārā) are so called because, though not stated in their own nature, they are scattered in each summary and are revealed by the inclusion of ignorance, formations, etc.; or, the modes (ākārā) are the ways (pakārā) of the past causes, etc. Since there are twenty modes for it, five in each summary, it has twenty modes (vīsatākāro); that which has twenty modes.

Esa [V 1.0101][M 1.0113] sabboti esa catusaṅkhepādipabhedo anavaseso paccayo. Paccayalakkhaṇenāti paccayabhāvena attano phalassa paṭisandhiviññāṇassa paccayabhāvena, avinābhāvalakkhaṇenāti attho. Yathā hi taṇhaṃ vinā avijjādayo viññāṇassa paccayā na honti, evaṃ taṇhāpi avijjādike vināti. Ettha dukkhaggahaṇena viññāṇanāmarūpasaḷāyatanaphassavedanānaṃ, bhavaggahaṇena ca taṇhāsaṅkhārupādānānaṃ gahitatā vuttanayā evāti na uddhaṭā.

This is the whole. This is the condition, without remainder, in its fourfold summary and so forth. ‘By the characteristic of a condition’ means by the nature of being a condition for its own resultant rebirth-linking consciousness, by the characteristic of inseparability—this is the meaning. For just as ignorance and so forth are not conditions for consciousness without craving, so too craving is not without ignorance and so forth. Here, by the inclusion of ‘suffering,’ consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are included; and by the inclusion of ‘becoming,’ craving, volitional formations, and clinging are included—as stated above, thus they are not extracted.

Idāni te vīsati ākāre paṭisambhidāmaggapāḷiyā vibhāvetuṃ “evamete”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha (paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.47) purimakammabhavasminti purime kammabhave, atītajātiyaṃ kammabhave kayiramāneti attho. Moho avijjāti yo tadā dukkhādīsu moho, yena mūḷho kammaṃ karoti, sā avijjā. Āyūhanā saṅkhārāti taṃ taṃ kammaṃ karonto dānupakaraṇādi sajjanādivasena yā purimacetanāyo, te saṅkhārā. Paṭiggāhakānaṃ pana hatthe deyyadhammaṃ patiṭṭhāpayato cetanā bhavo. Ekāvajjanajavanesu vā purimā cetanā āyūhanā saṅkhārā, sattamā bhavo. Yā kāci vā pana cetanā bhavo, sampayuttā āyūhanā saṅkhārā. Nikanti taṇhāti yaṃ kammaṃ karontassa upapattibhave tassa phalassa nikāmanā patthanā, sā taṇhā nāma. Upagamanaṃ upādānanti yaṃ kammabhavassa paccayabhūtaṃ “idaṃ kammaṃ katvā asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne kāme sevissāmi ucchijjissāmī”tiādinā nayena pavattaṃ upagamanaṃ gahaṇaṃ parāmasanaṃ, idaṃ upādānaṃ nāma. Cetanā bhavoti dvīsu atthavikappesu vuttassa āyūhanassa avasāne vuttacetanā, tatiye pana āyūhanasampayuttacetanā bhavo. Iti ime pañca dhammā purimakammabhavasmiṃ idha paṭisandhiyā paccayāti ime yathāvuttā mohādayo pañca dhammā atītakammabhavasiddhā etarahi paṭisandhiyā paccayabhūtāti attho.

Now, to explain those twenty modes from the Pāḷi of the Path of Discrimination, “Thus these” and so forth is said. Therein (Patisambhidamagga Atthakatha 1.47), “in the previous kamma-existence” means in the past life, in the kamma-existence being performed—this is the meaning. Delusion is ignorance: that delusion at that time regarding suffering and so forth, by which one, being deluded, performs kamma, that is ignorance. Accumulation is volitional formations: those preceding volitions by which one performs that kamma, such as by way of preparing requisites for giving. But for the recipients, the volition that establishes the gift in their hands is becoming. Or in a single process of adverting and impulsions, the preceding volitions are accumulation, the seventh is becoming. Or any volition is becoming, and the associated accumulation is volitional formations. Delight is craving: the longing and aspiration for the result of that kamma being performed in the rebirth-existence, that is called craving. Approaching is clinging: that which, being a condition for the kamma-existence, proceeds in such ways as, “Having done this kamma, I will enjoy pleasures in such a place, I will be annihilated,” and so forth—this approaching, grasping, and misapprehension is called clinging. Volition is becoming: in the two interpretations of meaning, the volition stated at the end of the accumulation is becoming; in the third, the volition associated with the accumulation is becoming. Thus, these five phenomena in the previous kamma-existence are conditions for rebirth-linking here—these five phenomena, delusion and so forth, as stated, accomplished in the past kamma-existence, are now conditions for rebirth-linking—this is the meaning.

Idha paṭisandhiviññāṇanti yaṃ bhavantarapaṭisandhānavasena uppannattā paṭisandhīti vuccati, taṃ viññāṇaṃ. Okkanti nāmarūpanti yā gabbhe rūpārūpadhammānaṃ okkanti āgantvā pavisantī viya, idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ. Pasādo āyatananti idaṃ cakkhādipañcāyatanavasena vuttaṃ. Phuṭṭho phassoti yo ārammaṇaṃ phuṭṭho phusanto uppanno, ayaṃ phasso. Vedayitaṃ [M 1.0114] vedanāti yaṃ paṭisandhiviññāṇena vā saḷāyatanapaccayena vā phassena sahuppannaṃ vipākavedayitaṃ, sā vedanā. Iti ime…pe… paccayāti ime viññāṇādayo pañca koṭṭhāsikā dhammā purimabhave katassa kammassa kammavaṭṭassa paccayā, paccayabhāvato taṃ paṭicca idha etarahi upapattibhavasmiṃ upapattibhavabhāvena vā hontīti attho.

Here, rebirth-linking consciousness is the consciousness that arises by way of linking one existence to another, hence it is called rebirth-linking. The descent of name-and-form refers to the entry of material and immaterial phenomena into the womb, as if arriving and entering. The sensitivity of the sense bases is what is spoken of in terms of the five sense bases such as the eye and so forth. ‘Touched’ is contact: that which arises when an object is touched, making contact. ‘What is felt’ is feeling: the resultant feeling that arises together with rebirth-linking consciousness or with contact conditioned by the six sense bases. Thus, these... conditions—these five categories of phenomena, beginning with consciousness, are conditioned by the kamma of a previous existence, by the round of kamma. Because of their nature as conditioned things, they arise here and now in this rebirth-existence as the state of rebirth-existence. This is the meaning.

Idha [V 1.0102] paripakkattā āyatanānaṃ mohoti paripakkāyatanassa kammakaraṇakāle asammohaṃ dasseti. Daharassa hi cittappavatti bhavaṅgabahulā yebhuyyena bhavantarajanakakammāyūhanasamatthā na hotīti. Kammakaraṇakāleti ca iminā sabbo kammassa paccayabhūto sammoho gahito, na sampayuttova. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Here, the phrase ‘delusion due to the maturity of the sense bases’ indicates non-delusion at the time of performing kamma on the part of one with mature sense bases. For in the young, the mental process consists mostly of the life-continuum and is generally incapable of accumulating kamma capable of generating another existence. And by the phrase ‘at the time of performing kamma,’ all delusion that serves as a condition for kamma is included, not just the associated delusion. The rest is as previously explained.

Padayojanāyāti “tasmā”tiādīnaṃ padānaṃ sambandhena saha. Atthanigamananti imasmiṃ aṭṭhamavāre desanatthanigamanaṃ. Nandīti evaṃ vuttānaṃ sabbataṇhānanti “nandī dukkhassa mūla”nti evaṃ nandanatthasāmaññato ekavacanena vuttānaṃ sabbataṇhānaṃ santānārammaṇasampayuttadhammappavattiākārādibhedena anekabhedānaṃ sabbāsaṃ taṇhānaṃ. Khayavevacanānevāti samucchedapahānavevacanāneva. “Accantakkhayā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Catumaggakiccasādhāraṇametanti catunnaṃ ariyamaggānaṃ pahānakiccassa sādhāraṇaṃ sāmaññato gahaṇaṃ etaṃ khayādivacananti attho. Tesaṃ pana maggānaṃ kamena pavattanaṃ kiccakameneva dassetuṃ “virāgā”tiādi vuttanti dassento “tato…pe… yojetabba”nti āha. Tathā satipi khayādisaddānaṃ pahānapariyāyabhāve pahātabbāya pana visayabhedabhinnāya taṇhāya anavasesato pahīnabhāvadīpanatthaṃ khayādipariyāyantaraggahaṇaṃ katanti dassento “yāhī”tiādimāha. Yathāvuttasañjananādihetubhūtāya taṇhāya pahīnattā tappahānadīpanaṃ katvā vuccamānaṃ khayādivacanaṃ na kathañci dhammataṃ vilometīti vuttaṃ “na kiñci virujjhatī”ti.

Regarding the word-connection: This is with the connection of the words 'therefore' and so forth. Regarding the conclusion of meaning: This is the conclusion of the meaning of the discourse in this eighth section. Regarding 'delight': This refers to all cravings thus stated, 'Delight is the root of suffering.' Thus, all cravings are spoken of in the singular due to the common meaning of delight, though they are of many kinds due to distinctions such as their mode of occurrence as phenomena associated with the stream and objects, and so forth. Regarding 'terms synonymous with destruction': These are indeed terms synonymous with complete eradication. For it is said: 'utter destruction.' Regarding 'this is common to the function of the four paths': This means that the inclusion of these terms such as 'destruction' is, in general, common to the function of abandoning by the four Noble Paths. To show the sequential operation of these paths according to their respective functions, he said, explaining that 'through dispassion' and so forth was stated: 'from that... should be connected.' Even so, although the words 'destruction' and so forth are synonyms for abandoning, he said, indicating that other synonyms for destruction and so forth were included to illustrate the complete abandonment of craving, which is to be abandoned and is distinguished by distinctions in its objects: 'yāhī' and so forth. Since craving—the cause of generation and so forth, as previously described—has been abandoned, the utterance of terms such as 'destruction,' having explained that abandonment, does not in any way contradict the nature of things, as stated: 'nothing is contradicted.'

Uttaravirahitanti attānaṃ uttarituṃ samatthattā uttarena adhikena virahitaṃ. Ayañcassa uttaravirahatā attano seṭṭhabhāvenāti āha “sabbaseṭṭha”nti. Yathā sammā-saṃ-saddā “aviparītaṃ, sāma”nti imesaṃ padānaṃ atthaṃ vadanti, evaṃ pāsaṃsasobhanatthepīti āha “sammā sāmañca bodhiṃ pasatthaṃ sundarañca bodhi”nti. Bujjhi ettha paṭivijjhi cattāri ariyasaccāni, sabbampi vā neyyanti rukkho bodhi, bujjhati etenāti pana maggo bodhi, tathā [M 1.0115] sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, nibbānaṃ pana bujjhitabbato bodhīti ayamettha sādhanavibhāgo daṭṭhabbo. Paṇṇattiyampi attheva bodhi-saddo “bodhirājakumāro”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.324; cūḷava. 268). Apareti sārasamāsācariyā. Ettha ca saupasaggassa bodhi-saddassa atthuddhāre anupasaggānaṃ udāharaṇe kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

“Uttaravirahita” means lacking anything superior because of its capacity to surpass. And this lack of anything superior, due to its own supreme nature, is why it is called “foremost of all.” Just as the words “sammā” and “saṃ” convey the meaning “not inverted” and “by oneself,” so too, in the sense of praise and beauty, it is said: “awakening rightly and by oneself” and “praised and beautiful awakening.” Here, “bujjhi” means realized—he realized the four noble truths, or all that is to be understood. The tree is called “Bodhi” because one awakened there. The path is called “Bodhi” because one awakens through it. Similarly, omniscient knowledge is Bodhi, and Nibbāna is Bodhi because it is to be realized. This distinction of instrumentality is to be seen here. Even in conventional usage, the word “Bodhi” has meaning, as in “Bodhirājakumāro” and similar instances (Majjhima Nikāya 2.324; Cūḷavagga 268). Other teachers, those who summarize the essence, explain it. Here, in determining the meaning of the word “Bodhi” with a prefix, the reason for giving examples of the form without a prefix has already been stated below.

Lokuttarabhāvato vā tatthāpi heṭṭhimamaggānaṃ viya tatuttarimaggābhāvato ca “siyā nu kho anuttarā bodhī”ti āsaṅkaṃ sandhāya taṃ vidhamituṃ “sāvakāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Abhinīhārasampattiyā phalavisesabhūtehi ñāṇavisesehi ekaccehi sakalehi saddhiṃ samijjhamāno [V 1.0103] maggo ariyānaṃ taṃ taṃ ñāṇavisesādiṃ dento viya hotīti tassa asabbaguṇadāyakattaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena anaññasādhāraṇābhinīhārasampadāsiddhassa niratisaya-guṇānubandhassa vasena arahattamaggo anuttarā bodhi nāma hotīti dasseti. Sāvakapāramiñāṇaṃ aññehi sāvakehi asādhāraṇaṃ mahāsāvakānaṃyeva āveṇikaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Paccekaṃ saccāni buddhavantoti paccekabuddhā. Nanu ca sabbepi ariyā paccekameva saccāni paṭivijjhanti dhammassa paccattaṃ vedanīyabhāvatoti? Saccaṃ, nayidamīdisaṃ paṭivedhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, yathā pana sāvakā aññasannissayena saccāni paṭivijjhanti paratoghosena vinā tesaṃ dassanamaggassa anuppajjanato, yathā ca sammāsambuddho aññesaṃ nissayabhāvena saccāni abhisambujjhanti, na evamete, ete pana aparaneyyā hutvā apariṇāyakabhāvena saccāni paṭivijjhanti. Tena vuttaṃ “paccekaṃ saccāni buddhavantoti paccekabuddhā”ti.

Or, from the standpoint of its supramundane nature, and also because there is no higher path beyond it, just as with the lower paths, the words 'for the disciples,' and so forth, are stated in reference to and to dispel the doubt, 'Could there be an unsurpassed enlightenment?' The path, being accomplished through the fulfillment of aspiration and associated with certain or all special knowledges that are the special fruits, appears as if bestowing those special knowledges upon the noble ones; thus, its nature of not bestowing all qualities is stated. Thereby, it is shown that the path of arahantship, achieved through the fulfillment of an aspiration not shared by others and endowed with unsurpassable qualities, is called 'unsurpassed enlightenment.' The knowledge of the disciples' perfection is not common to other disciples; it is the exclusive knowledge of the great disciples. 'They awaken to the truths individually'—thus they are Paccekabuddhas. But do not all noble ones realize the truths individually, since the Dhamma is to be experienced personally? True, but this is not said with reference to such a realization. For just as disciples realize the truths with dependence on another, since their path of vision does not arise without a voice from another, and while a Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha awakens to the truths as a basis of reliance for others, these are not so; for they, being unteachable by another and without a guide, realize the truths. Therefore, it is said, 'They awaken to the truths individually—thus they are Paccekabuddhas.'

Itīti karīyati uccārīyatīti itikāro, iti-saddo. Kāraṇattho aniyamarūpenāti adhippāyo, tasmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “yasmā cā”ti. Pubbe pana iti-saddaṃ pakāratthaṃ katvā “evaṃ jānitvā”ti vuttaṃ, idhāpi taṃ pakāratthameva katvā atho yujjati. Kathaṃ? Viditvāti hi padaṃ hetuatthe daṭṭhabbaṃ “paññāya cassa disvā”ti (ma. ni. 1.271), “ghataṃ pivitvā balaṃ hotī”ti ca evamādīsu viya, tasmā pakāratthepi iti-sadde paṭiccasamuppādassa viditattāti ayaṃ attho labbhateva. Paṭiccasamuppādaṃ viditvāti etthāpi hetuatthe viditvā-sadde yathāvuttā atthayojanā yujjateva. Ettha ca paṭhamavikappe paṭiccasamupādassa viditatthaṃ maññanābhāvassa kāraṇaṃ [M 1.0116] vatvā taṇhāmūlakassa paṭiccasamuppādassa dassitattā ettha taṇhāppahānaṃ sammāsambodhiyā adhigamanakāraṇaṃ uddhatanti dassitaṃ, tasmā “pathaviṃ na maññatī”tiādi nigamanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dutiyavikappe pana paṭiccasamuppādavedanaṃ taṇhāppahānassa kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ abhisambodhiyā abhisambodhimaññanābhāvassāti ayamattho dassitoti ayametesaṃ dvinnaṃ atthavikappānaṃ viseso, tasmā “nandī dukkhassa mūla”nti vuttaṃ.

The word 'iti' is called 'itikāra' because it is done or uttered. The intention is that it signifies a reason in an indeterminate way; therefore, it means 'therefore.' Thus, it is said, 'and because.' Previously, however, having taken the word 'iti' to signify manner, it was said 'having known thus'; here too, it is fitting to take it as signifying manner. How so? The word 'having known' should indeed be regarded as having the meaning of a reason, as in 'having seen with wisdom' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.271), or 'having drunk ghee, there is strength,' and so forth. Therefore, even when the word 'iti' has the meaning of manner, the meaning 'because dependent origination is understood' is indeed obtained. Even in 'having known dependent origination,' the connection of meaning as stated is indeed fitting for the word 'having known' in the sense of a reason. And here, in the first alternative, having stated that the understanding of dependent origination is the cause for the absence of conceiving, and because dependent origination rooted in craving is shown here, the abandoning of craving is highlighted as the cause for attaining complete enlightenment. Therefore, the conclusion 'he does not conceive earth' and so on should be seen. In the second alternative, however, the knowing of dependent origination is stated as the cause for abandoning craving, and this is shown to be the cause for the absence of conceiving of enlightenment. This is the difference between these two alternatives of meaning. Therefore, it is said, 'delight is the root of suffering.'

Taṃ kuto labbhatīti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “yattha yattha hī”tiādi. Sāsanayutti ayaṃ sāsanepi evaṃ sambandho dissatīti katvā. Lokepi hi yaṃ-taṃ-saddānaṃ abyabhicārisambandhatā siddhā.

'From where is that obtained?' In reference to this question, it is said, 'Wherever, wherever indeed,' and so forth. This is a logical principle of the Teaching, because such a connection is seen even in the Teaching. Indeed, in the world too, the invariable connection of the words 'yaṃ' and 'taṃ' is established.

Evaṃ abhisambuddhoti vadāmīti abhisambuddhabhāvassa gahitattā, asabbaññunā evaṃ desetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā ca “sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ dassento”tiādimāha.

Because he says, 'I declare thus as one fully enlightened,' the state of full enlightenment has been grasped, and because one who is not omniscient would be unable to teach thus, he says, 'Showing the knowledge of omniscience,' and so forth.

Vicitranayadesanāvilāsayuttanti [V 1.0104] puthujjanavārādivibhāgabhinnehi vicittehi tanti nayehi, lakkhaṇakammataṇhāmaññanādivibhāgabhinnehi vicittehi atthanayehi, abhinandanapaccayākārādivisesāpadesasiddhena desanāvilāsena ca yuttaṃ. Yathā te na jānanti, tathā desesīti imināpi bhagavato desanāvilāsaṃyeva vibhāveti. Taṃyeva kira pathavinti ettha pathavīgahaṇaṃ upalakkhaṇamattaṃ āpādivasenapi, tathā “kīdisā nu kho idha pathavī adhippetā, kasmā ca bhūtarūpāniyeva gahitāni, na sesarūpānī”tiādināpi tesaṃ saṃsayuppatti niddhāretabbā. Atha vā kathaṃ nāmidanti ettha iti-saddo pakārattho. Tena imasmiṃ sutte sabbāyapi tesaṃ saṃsayuppattiyā pariggahitattā daṭṭhabbā. Antanti mariyādaṃ, desanāya antaṃ paricchedanti attho, yo anusandhīti vuccati. Koṭinti pariyantaṃ, desanāya pariyosānanti attho. Ubhayena sutte ajjhāsayānusandhi yathānusandhīti vadati.

It is connected with diverse methods and a display of teaching: with various textual methods distinguished by divisions such as the section on the worldling; with various methods of meaning distinguished by divisions such as characteristics, functions, craving, and conceiving; and also with a display of teaching established through special designations such as the mode of conditionality of delight. 'Just as they do not know, so he taught'—by this too, he reveals the Blessed One's display of teaching. 'Indeed, that very earth'—here, the mention of earth is merely illustrative, even by way of water, etc. Likewise, the arising of their doubts should be determined, such as 'What kind of earth is intended here? Why are only the primary material elements taken, and not the other forms of matter?' Or else, in 'how indeed is this?', the word 'iti' has the meaning of manner. Therefore, it should be seen that in this discourse, all their arising doubts are encompassed. 'End' means the limit, the boundary of the teaching; the meaning is what is called the connection. 'Culmination' means the final end, the completion of the teaching. By both, he speaks of the connection of intention and the connection as it is in the sutta.

Antarākathāti kammaṭṭhānamanasikārauddesaparipucchādīnaṃ antarā aññā ekā tathā. Vippakathāti aniṭṭhitā sikhaṃ appattā. Kaṅkhaṇānurūpenāti tasmiṃ khaṇe dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ajjhāsayānurūpena. Idanti idāni vuccamānaṃ mūlapariyāyajātakaṃ.

An intermediate talk is another single talk occurring between meditation subjects, reflection, recitation, questioning, and so forth. Interrupted talk means unfinished, not having reached the peak. 'In accordance with the occasion' means in accordance with the inclination of the monks gathered at that moment in the Dhamma assembly. 'This' means the Mūlapariyāya Sutta that is now being spoken.

Disāpāmokkhoti [M 1.0117] paṇḍitabhāvena sabbadisāsu pamukhabhūto. Brāhmaṇoti brahmaṃ aṇatīti brāhmaṇo, mante sajjhāyatīti attho. Tiṇṇaṃ vedānanti iruveda-yajuveda-sāmavedānaṃ. Pāragūti atthaso byañjanaso ca pāraṃ pariyantaṃ gato. Saha nighaṇḍunā ca keṭubhena cāti sanighaṇḍukeṭubhā, tesaṃ. Nighaṇḍūti rukkhādīnaṃ vevacanappakāsakaṃ satthaṃ. Keṭubhanti kiriyākappavikappo, kavīnaṃ upakārāvahaṃ satthaṃ. Saha akkharappabhedenāti sākkharappabhedā, tesaṃ, sikkhāniruttisahitānanti attho. Itihāsapañcamānanti āthabbaṇavedaṃ catutthaṃ katvā “itiha asa, itiha asā”ti īdisavacanapaṭisaṃyutto purāṇakathāsaṅkhāto itihāso pañcamo etesanti itihāsapañcamā, tesaṃ. Padaṃ tadavasesañca byākaraṇaṃ kāyati ajjheti vedeti cāti padako, veyyākaraṇo. Lokāyataṃ vuccati vitaṇḍasatthaṃ. Mahāpurisānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ lakkhaṇadīpanagantho mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ. Tesu anūno paripūrakārīti anavayo.

Disāpāmokkha means having become foremost in all directions due to his wisdom. A Brahmin is so-called because he utters Brahma; this means he recites the sacred texts. Of the three Vedas—the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda. He is a master, having reached the farthest shore in both meaning and expression. 'With Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha' refers to their Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha. Nighaṇḍu is a treatise that explains synonyms for trees and other things. Keṭubha refers to the arrangement and modification of poetic composition, a text beneficial to poets. 'With the analysis of syllables' means accompanied by phonetics and etymology. 'Having Itihāsa as the fifth' means making the Atharvaveda the fourth, and Itihāsa, which consists of ancient narratives connected with sayings like 'Thus it was, thus it was,' as the fifth of these Vedas. A 'padaka' or grammarian is one who composes, studies, and knows words and the remaining grammar. Lokāyata is called the art of sophistry. The Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa is a text that illuminates the marks of great beings like the Buddhas. 'Anavaya' means he is complete and without deficiency in these.

Manteti vede. Yadipi vedo “manto, brahmaṃ, kappo”ti tividho, manto eva pana mūlavedo, tadatthavivaraṇaṃ brahmaṃ, tattha vuttanayena yaññakiriyāvidhānaṃ kappo. Tena vuttaṃ “manteti vede”ti. Paṇḍitāti paññāvanto. Tathā hi te puthupaññātāya bahuṃ sahassadvisahassādiparimāṇaṃ ganthaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā gaṇhanti uggaṇhanti, javanapaññatāya lahuṃ sīghaṃ gaṇhanti, tikkhapaññatāya [V 1.0105] suṭṭhu avirajjhantā upadhārenti, satinepakkasampattiyā gahitañca nesaṃ na vinassati na sammussatīti. Sabbampi sippanti aṭṭhārasavijjāṭṭhānādibhedaṃ sikkhitabbaṭṭhena sippanti saṅkhyaṃ gataṃ sabbaṃ bāhirakasatthaṃ mokkhāvahasammatampi na mokkhaṃ āvahatīti āha “diṭṭhadhammasamparāyahita”nti. Sampiṇḍitā hutvāti yathā mittā, tathā piṇḍitavasena sannipatitā hutvā. “Evaṃ gayhamāne ādinā virujjheyya, evaṃ antenā”ti cintentā ñātuṃ icchitassa atthassa pubbenāparaṃ aviruddhaṃ nicchayaṃ gahetuṃ asakkontā na ādiṃ, na antaṃ addasaṃsu.

They recite the Vedas. Although the Vedas are threefold—"mantra, brāhmaṇa, kappa"—the mantra is indeed the root Veda. The brāhmaṇa is the explanation of its meaning, and the kappa is the prescribed method of performing sacrifices as stated therein. Hence it is said, "They recite the Vedas." The learned are those endowed with wisdom. Indeed, due to their broad wisdom, they take up and study a vast number of texts, such as thousands or twice thousands in extent, making them well-known. With swift wisdom, they quickly grasp them; with sharp wisdom, they thoroughly retain them without erring; and due to their accomplishment of mindfulness and intelligence, what they have learned does not perish or become confused. All arts—classified as the eighteen branches of knowledge and the like—are designated as skills because they must be mastered. But even all the external scriptures, though deemed conducive to liberation, do not lead to liberation; therefore, it is said that they are for the benefit of this life and the next. "Having gathered together" means having assembled in a group, just as friends do. Thinking, "If it is grasped in this way, it might be contradicted by the beginning; if in that way, by the end," and desiring to understand the meaning, they were unable to grasp a conclusion where the latter part was not contradicted by the former; they did not see the beginning or the end.

Lomasānīti lomavantāni, ghanakesamassuvānīti attho. Kesāpi hi lomaggahaṇena gayhanti yathā “lomanakhaṃ phusitvā suddhi kātabbā”ti. Kaṇṇaṃ viyāti kaṇṇaṃ, paññā, tāya sutvā kātabbakiccasādhanato vuttaṃ “kaṇṇavāti paññavā”ti.

Lomasāni means 'hairy,' that is, 'with thick hair and beards.' For head-hairs are also included under the term 'body-hair' (loma), as in the phrase 'having touched body-hair and nails, purification should be done.' Kaṇṇaṃ viya means 'like an ear.' Kaṇṇaṃ here means wisdom. It is said 'one with an ear' (kaṇṇavā) for one who has wisdom (paññavā), because by hearing with it, what should be done is accomplished.

Yasmā [M 1.0118] sattānaṃ gacchante gacchante kāle āyuvaṇṇādiparikkhayo hoti, tasmā taṃ kālena kataṃ viya katvā vuttaṃ “nesaṃ āyu…pe… khādatīti vuccatī”ti.

Because as time passes for beings, there is a decline in their lifespan, beauty, and so forth, therefore, speaking as if time itself does this, it is said, "Time devours their life..." and so on.

Abhiññāyāti kusalādibhedaṃ khandhādibhedañca desetabbaṃ dhammaṃ, veneyyānañca āsayānusayacariyāvimuttiādibhedaṃ, tassa ca nesaṃ desetabbappakāraṃ yāthāvato abhijānitvā. Dhammaṃ desemīti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikanibbānahitāvahaṃ saddhammaṃ kathayāmi. No anabhiññāyāti yathā bāhirakā asammāsambuddhattā vuttavidhiṃ ajānantāyaṃ kiñci takkapariyāhataṃ vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ kathenti, evaṃ na desemīti attho. Sanidānanti sakāraṇaṃ, veneyyānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena vā pucchāya vā aṭṭhuppattiyā vā sanimittaṃ hetuudāharaṇasahitañcāti attho. Sappāṭihāriyanti sanissaraṇaṃ sappaṭiharaṇaṃ, paccanīkapaṭiharaṇena sappāṭihāriyameva katvā desemīti attho. Apare pana “yathārahaṃ iddhiādesanānusāsanipāṭihāriyasahita”nti vadanti, anusāsanipāṭihāriyahitā pana desanā natthīti. Hitūpadesanā ovādo, sā eva anusāsanī. Anotiṇṇavatthuvisayo vā ovādo, otiṇṇavatthuvisayā anusāsanī. Paṭhamūpadeso vā ovādo, itarā anusāsanī. Alañca panāti yuttameva. Niṭṭhamagamāsīti atthasiddhiṃ gatā.

Abhiññāya means having directly known in accordance with reality the Dhamma to be taught, including its distinctions of skillful and so forth, and its divisions into aggregates and so forth; and having directly known the inclinations, latent tendencies, conduct, liberation, and other distinctions of those to be taught, as well as the appropriate way to teach them. Dhammaṃ desemi means 'I proclaim the true Dhamma, which brings benefit in this life, the next, and leads to Nibbāna.' No anabhiññāya means 'not teaching like outsiders, who, not being Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas and not knowing the method stated, speak whatever is based on reasoning, follows from speculation, or arises from their own ingenuity; I do not teach in such a way.'
