Sanidānaṃ means 'with a cause,' that is, with a reason, whether due to the inclinations of those to be taught, their questions, or the circumstances that have arisen; and accompanied by signs, reasons, and examples. Sappāṭihāriyaṃ means 'with an escape' and 'with a counter-action,' meaning 'I teach having made it miraculous by countering what is inimical.' Others, however, say it means 'accompanied by the appropriate miracles of psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction,' but a teaching is not something accompanied by the miracle of instruction. Instruction in what is beneficial (hitūpadesanā) is advice (ovādo); that itself is admonition (anusāsanī). Or, advice pertains to matters not yet entered upon, while admonition pertains to matters already entered upon. Alternatively, the initial instruction is advice, while the other is admonition. Alañca pana means 'and indeed, it is fitting.' Niṭṭhamagamāsi means 'it has reached the accomplishment of its purpose.'

Tathāgatavāraaṭṭhamanayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the eighth method in the section on the Tathāgata is completed.

Ayaṃ tāvettha aṭṭhakathāya līnatthavaṇṇanā.

This much here is the explanation of the hidden meaning in the commentary.

Nettinayavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Method of the Nettī

Idāni [V 1.0106] (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.149; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.nettinayavaṇṇanā; a. ni. ṭī. nettinayavaṇṇanā) pakaraṇanayena pāḷiyā atthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāma. Sā panāyaṃ atthavaṇṇanā yasmā desanāya samuṭṭhānapayojanabhājanesu piṇḍatthesu ca niddhāritesu sutarā hoti suviññeyyā ca, tasmā suttadesanāya samuṭṭhānādīni paṭhamaṃ niddhārayissāma. Tattha samuṭṭhānaṃ tāva pariyattiṃ nissāya mānuppādo, payojanaṃmānamaddanaṃ. Vuttañhi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sutapariyattiṃ…pe… ārabhī”ti. Apica veneyyānaṃ pathavīādibhūtādibhedabhinne sakkāye puthujjanassa sekkhādiariyassa ca saddhiṃ hetunā maññanāmaññanavasena [M 1.0119] pavattivibhāgānavabodho samuṭṭhānaṃ, yathāvuttavibhāgāvabodho payojanaṃ, veneyyānañhi vuttappakāre visaye yathāvuttānaṃ puggalānaṃ saddhiṃ hetunā maññanāmaññanavasena pavattivibhāgāvabodho payojanaṃ.

Now, we shall explain the meaning of the Pāli text according to the method of the treatise. Since this explanation of meaning becomes clearer and more easily understood when the origins, purposes, divisions, and condensed meanings of the teaching have been determined, we will first determine the origins and so forth of the sutta's teaching. Here, the origin is the arising of conceit based on the scriptural teaching. The purpose is the crushing of conceit. For it is said in the commentary: "Regarding the scriptural teaching... he began." Furthermore, the origin is the lack of understanding, for those to be trained, of the divisions of behavior—by way of conceiving and not conceiving, together with the cause—regarding the existing body (sakkāya), which is differentiated into earth and other elements, in the case of an ordinary person and a noble one such as a trainee. The purpose is the understanding of the divisions as stated. Indeed, for those to be trained, the purpose is the understanding of the divisions of behavior—by way of conceiving and not conceiving, together with the cause—regarding the individuals as stated in the described sphere.

Apica samuṭṭhānaṃ nāma desanānidānaṃ. Taṃ sādhāraṇaṃ asādhāraṇanti duvidhaṃ. Tattha sādhāraṇampi ajjhattikabāhirabhedato duvidhaṃ. Tattha sādhāraṇaṃ ajjhattikasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma lokanāthassa mahākaruṇā. Tāya hi samussāhitassa bhagavato veneyyānaṃ dhammadesanāya cittaṃ udapādi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “sattesu ca kāruññataṃ paṭicca buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokesī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.283; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 9). Ettha ca hetāvatthāyapi mahākaruṇāya saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo yāvadeva saṃsāramahoghato saddhammadesanāhatthadānehi sattasantāraṇatthaṃ taduppattito. Yathā ca mahākaruṇā, evaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ dasabalañāṇādīni ca desanāya abbhantarasamuṭṭhānabhāve vattabbāni. Sabbampi hi ñeyyadhammaṃ, tesaṃ desetabbappakāraṃ, sattānañca āsayānusayādiṃ yāthāvato jānanto bhagavā ṭhānāṭṭhānādīsu kosallena veneyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ vicittanayadesanaṃ pavattesīti. Bāhiraṃ pana sādhāraṇaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ dasasahassabrahmaparivāritassa sahampatimahābrahmuno ajjhesanaṃ. Tadajjhesanuttarakālañhi dhammagambhīratāpaccavekkhaṇājanitaṃ appossukkataṃ paṭippassambhetvā dhammassāmī dhammadesanāya ussāhajāto ahosi. Asādhāraṇampi ambhantarabāhirabhedato duvidhameva. Tattha abbhantaraṃ yāya mahākaruṇāya yena ca desanāñāṇena idaṃ suttaṃ pavattitaṃ, tadubhayaṃ veditabbaṃ. Bāhiraṃ pana pañcasatānaṃ brāhmaṇajātikānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pariyattiṃ nissāya mānuppādanaṃ, vuttameva taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ.

Furthermore, the origin is called the cause of the teaching. It is twofold: common and uncommon. Among these, the common is also twofold: internal and external. Here, the internal common origin is the great compassion of the Lord of the World. For it was, having been stirred by this compassion, that the Blessed One's mind arose to teach the Dhamma to those capable of being trained. Referring to this, it is said, "And out of compassion for beings, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye," and so on (Majjhima Nikāya 1.283; Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.172; Mahāvagga 9). And here, the scope of great compassion should be understood as extending even to the causal state, right from its arising, for the purpose of rescuing beings from the great flood of saṃsāra by the gift of the hand that is the teaching of the true Dhamma. Just as with great compassion, so too omniscience, the ten powers of knowledge, and other knowledges should be stated as being internal origins for the teaching. For the Blessed One, knowing in accordance with reality all knowable phenomena, the manner in which they should be taught, and the inclinations, latent tendencies, and so forth of beings, skillfully delivered a teaching of diverse methods suited to the dispositions of those capable of being trained, with skill regarding what is possible and impossible, and so forth. The external common origin, however, is the entreaty of the great Brahmā Sahampati, surrounded by ten thousand Brahmās. For in the time after that entreaty, the Master of the Dhamma, having allayed the reluctance generated by reflection on the profundity of the Dhamma, became energetic for teaching the Dhamma. The uncommon origin is also twofold: internal and external. Here, the internal should be understood as both the great compassion and the knowledge of teaching by which this discourse was delivered. The external, however, is the arising of conceit in five hundred brahmin-born monks, based on their scriptural learning; this has already been stated in the commentary.

Payojanampi sādhāraṇaṃ asādhāraṇanti duvidhaṃ. Tattha sādhāraṇaṃ anukkamena yāva anupādāparinibbānaṃ [V 1.0107] vimuttirasattā bhagavato desanāya. Tenevāha “etadatthā tathā, etadatthā mantanā”tiādi (pari. 366). Eteneva ca saṃsāracakkanivatti saddhammacakkappavatti sassatādimicchāvādanirākaraṇaṃ sammāvādapurekkhāro akusalamūlasamūhananaṃ kusalamūlasaṃropanaṃ apāyadvārapidahanaṃ saggamokkhadvāravivaraṇaṃ pariyuṭṭhānavūpasamanaṃ anusayasamugghātanaṃ [M 1.0120] “mutto mocessāmī”ti (udā. aṭṭha. 18; itivu. aṭṭha. 38) purimapaṭiññāavisaṃvādanaṃ tappaṭipakkhamāramanorathavisaṃvādanaṃ titthiyadhammanimmathanaṃ buddhadhammapatiṭṭhāpananti evamādīnampi payojanānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Asādhāraṇaṃ pana tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ mānamaddanaṃ. Vuttañcetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1) “desanākusalo bhagavā mānabhañjanatthaṃ ‘sabbadhammamūlapariyāya’nti desanaṃ ārabhī”ti. Ubhayampetaṃ bāhiyameva. Sace pana veneyyasantānagatampi desanābalasiddhisaṅkhātaṃ payojanaṃ adhippāyasamijjhanabhāvato yathādhippetatthasiddhiyā yathākāruṇikassa bhagavatopi payojanamevāti gaṇheyya, iminā pariyāyenassa abbhantaratāpi veditabbā.

The purpose is also twofold: common and uncommon. Herein, the common purpose is the essence of liberation in the Blessed One's teaching, in sequence up to final Nibbāna without clinging. Hence it is said, “For this purpose is the teaching, for this purpose is the counsel,” and so on (Pari. 366). By this very means, it should be understood that the following purposes are also included: the cessation of the wheel of saṃsāra, the turning of the wheel of the true Dhamma, the refutation of wrong views such as eternalism, the prioritization of right view, the eradication of unwholesome roots, the planting of wholesome roots, the closing of the doors to the lower realms, the opening of the doors to heaven and liberation, the calming of obsessions, the uprooting of latent tendencies, the non-contradiction of the former promise, “Freed, I shall free others” (Udā. Aṭṭha. 18; Itivu. Aṭṭha. 38), the thwarting of the aspirations of Māra, its opponent, the crushing of the doctrines of sectarians, and the establishment of the Buddha’s Dhamma. The uncommon purpose, however, was the subduing of the pride of those monks. This is stated in the commentary (Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.1): “The Blessed One, skilled in teaching, began the discourse on ‘The Root of All Phenomena’ for the purpose of crushing pride.” Both of these are external. But if one were to consider the purpose that reaches the mental continuum of the disciples—a purpose designated as the accomplishment through the power of the teaching, due to the fulfillment of the intention and the achievement of the desired goal—as a purpose for the compassionate Blessed One himself, then by this method, its internal aspect should also be understood.

Apica veneyyānaṃ pathavīādibhūtādivibhāgabhinne sakkāye puthujjanassa sekkhādiariyassa ca saddhiṃ hetunā maññanāmaññanavasena pavattivibhāgānavabodho samuṭṭhānaṃ, imassa suttassa yathāvuttavibhāgāvabodho payojananti vuttovāyamattho. Veneyyānañhi vuttappakāre visaye yathāvuttānaṃ puggalānaṃ saddhiṃ hetunā maññanāmaññanānaṃ vasena pavattivibhāgāvabodho imaṃ desanaṃ payojeti “tannipphādanaparāyaṃ desanā”ti katvā. Yañhi desanāya sādhetabbaṃ phalaṃ, taṃ ākaṅkhitabbattā desakaṃ desanāya payojetīti payojananti vuccati. Tathā veneyyānaṃ sabbaso ekadesato ca maññanānaṃ appahānaṃ, tattha ca ādīnavādassanaṃ, niraṅkusānaṃ maññanānaṃ anekākāravohārassa sakkāye pavattivisesassa ajānanaṃ, tattha ca pahīnamaññanānaṃ paṭipattiyā ajānanaṃ, taṇhāmukhena paccayākārassa ca anavabodhoti evamādīni ca payojanāni idha veditabbāni.

Furthermore, for those amenable to guidance, the non-comprehension of the division of activity—based on conceiving and not-conceiving, along with its cause, in the existing body which is differentiated by the divisions of elements beginning with earth, for both the ordinary person and the noble ones such as the trainee—is the cause; the comprehension of the aforesaid division is the purpose of this sutta. This is the meaning that has been stated. Indeed, for those amenable to guidance, the comprehension of the division of activity in the aforesaid subject, regarding the aforesaid persons, based on conceiving and not-conceiving along with its cause, motivates this teaching, it being ‘a teaching aimed at accomplishing that.’ For whatever fruit is to be accomplished by the teaching, that, being desired, impels the teacher to the teaching; thus it is called the purpose. Similarly, the following should be understood here as purposes for those amenable to guidance: the non-abandonment of conceivings, either completely or partially; the failure to see the danger therein; the ignorance of the specific modes of activity in the existing body and of the manifold expressions of unrestrained conceivings; the ignorance of the practice of those for whom conceiving is abandoned; and the non-comprehension of the causal process through the gateway of craving.

Bhūmittayapariyāpannesu asaṅkhātadhammavippakatapariññādikiccasaṅkhātadhammānaṃ sammāsambuddhassa ca paṭipattiṃ ajānantā asaddhammassavanadhāraṇaparicayamanasikāraparā saddhammassavana-dhāraṇaparicayapaṭivedhavimukhā ca veneyyā imissā desanāya bhājanaṃ. Piṇḍatthā pana “assutavā”tiādinā ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro akusalamūla-samāyogo olīyanātidhāvanāpariggaho upāyavinibaddhānubrūhanā micchābhinivesasamannāgamo avijjātaṇhā-parisuddhi [M 1.0121] vaṭṭattayānuparamo āsavoghayogaganthāgatitaṇhuppādupādānāviyogo cetokhila-cetovinibaddhaabhinandana-nīvaraṇasaṅgānatikkamo [V 1.0108] vivādamūlāpariccāgo anusayānupacchedo micchattānativattanaṃ taṇhāmūladhammasannissayatā akusalakammapathānuyogo sabbakilesa-pariḷāhasāraddhakāyacittatāti evamādayo dīpitā honti. “Pathaviṃ pathavito sañjānātī”tiādinā taṇhāvicaritaniddeso mānajappanā vipariyesābhiniveso saṃkileso sakkāyapariggaho bālalakkhaṇāpadeso vaṅkattayavibhāvanānuyogo bahukārapaṭipakkhadīpanā tividhanissayasaṃsūcanā āsavakkhayakathananti evamādayo dīpitā honti.

Those disciples who are the recipients of this teaching are those who do not know the practice of the Perfectly Enlightened One concerning the conditioned phenomena—designated as the duties of full understanding and so on, which are incomplete with respect to the unconditioned—and the unconditioned phenomena themselves, all included in the three planes of existence; who are devoted to hearing, retaining, practicing, and attending to the false Dhamma; and who are averse to hearing, retaining, practicing, and penetrating the true Dhamma. In summary, however, by the words 'an uninstructed person' and so on, the following are indicated: the cultivation of unwise attention, association with unwholesome roots, being gripped by slackness and over-exertion, the proliferation of bondage to expedients, being endowed with wrong adherence, impurity regarding ignorance and craving, the non-cessation of the threefold cycle, non-separation from taints, floods, yokes, bonds, destinations, the arising of craving, and clinging, the non-transcendence of mental barrenness, mental bondage, delight, hindrances, and attachments, the non-abandonment of the roots of disputes, the non-cutting off of latent tendencies, the non-overcoming of wrongness, dependence on craving-rooted phenomena, the pursuit of unwholesome courses of action, and the state of having a body and mind agitated and inflamed by the fever of all defilements. By the words 'One perceives earth as earth' and so on, the following are indicated: the exposition of the roaming of craving, the muttering of conceit, adherence to perversions, defilement, grasping at the existing body, the indication of the characteristics of a fool, the pursuit of manifesting the three crookednesses, the showing of the many opposing factors, the indication of the threefold dependence, and the discourse on the destruction of the taints.

Soḷasahāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Sixteen Modes of Discourse

1. Desanāhāravaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Mode of Discourse

Tattha ye upādānakkhandhadhamme upādāya pathavīādibhūtādibhedā paññatti, te paññattipaṭipādanabhāvena jātijarāmaraṇavisesanadukkhapariyāyena ca vuttā taṇhāvajjā tebhūmakadhammā dukkhasaccaṃ. Maññanābhinandananandīpariyāyehi vuttā taṇhā samudayasaccaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva suttantanayo. Abhidhammanaye pana yathāvuttataṇhāya saddhiṃ “assutavā”tiādinā dīpitā avijjādayo, maññanāpariyāyena gahitā mānadiṭṭhiyo, bhavapadena gahito kammabhavo cāti sabbepi kilesābhisaṅkhārā samudayasaccaṃ. Ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ. Ariyadhammaggahaṇena, pariññābhikkhusekkhābhiññāgahaṇehi, rāgādikhayavacanehi, sammāsambodhigahaṇena ca maggasaccaṃ. Keci pana taṇhākkhayādivacanehi nirodhasaccaṃ uddharanti, taṃ aṭṭhakathāya virujjhati tattha taṇhākkhayādīnaṃ maggakiccabhāvassa uddhaṭattā.

Herein, the designations, such as the distinctions of the earth element and so on, which are dependent on the phenomena of the aggregates of clinging; and the phenomena of the three planes, with the exception of craving, which are spoken of by way of establishing designation and by the term ‘suffering’ characterized by birth, aging, and death—these are the truth of suffering. Craving, spoken of by way of conceiving, delighting, and enjoying, is the truth of the origin. This, for a start, is the Sutta method. In the Abhidhamma method, however, along with craving as aforesaid, ignorance and so on, indicated by ‘an uninstructed person,’ etc.; conceit and views, taken by way of ‘conceiving’; and kamma-becoming, taken by the word ‘becoming’—all these defilements and formations are the truth of the origin. The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation. By the grasping of the noble Dhamma, by the graspings of full understanding, of the monk, of the trainee, and of higher knowledge, by the words on the destruction of lust and so on, and by the grasping of perfect enlightenment, the truth of the path is indicated. Some, however, extract the truth of cessation from the words ‘destruction of craving’ and so on, but this contradicts the commentary, wherein it is pointed out that the destruction of craving and so forth is a function of the path.

Tattha samudayena assādo, dukkhena ādīnavo, magganirodhehi nissaraṇaṃ, tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ mānabhañjanaṃ phalaṃ, tathā “yathāvuttavibhāgāvabodho”tiādinā vuttaṃ payojanañca. Tassa nipphattikāraṇattā desanāya vicittatā catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ yāthāvato sabhāvūpadhāraṇañca upāyo[M 1.0122], pathavīādīsu puthujjanādīnaṃ pavattidassanāpadesena pathavīādayo ekantato parijānitabbā, maññanā ca pahātabbāti ayamettha bhagavato āṇattīti. Ayaṃ desanāhāro.

Herein, gratification is through the origin, danger is through suffering, and escape is through the path and cessation. For those monks, the breaking of conceit is the fruit, and likewise, the purpose is as stated by 'the comprehension of the divisions as explained' and so forth. Because it is the cause of the accomplishment of that, the variety of the teaching and the accurate observation of the true nature of the four types of individuals is the method. By way of showing the conduct of ordinary people and so forth in regard to earth and so on, the instruction of the Blessed One here is this: ‘Earth and so on must be thoroughly understood, and conceiving must be abandoned.’ This is the mode of discourse.

2. Vicayahāravaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Mode of Investigation

Maññanānaṃ [V 1.0109] sakkāyassa avisesahetubhāvato, kassacipi tattha asesitabbato ca sabbagahaṇaṃ, sabhāvadhāraṇato nissattanijjīvato ca dhammaggahaṇaṃ, patiṭṭhābhāvato āveṇikahetubhāvato ca mūlaggahaṇaṃ, kāraṇabhāvato desanatthasambhavato ca pariyāyaggahaṇaṃ, sammukhabhāvato sampadānatthasambhavato ca “vo”ti vacanaṃ, tathārūpaguṇayogato abhimukhīkaraṇato ca “bhikkhave”ti ālapanaṃ. Desetuṃ samatthabhāvato tesaṃ satuppādanatthañca “desessāmī”ti paṭijānanaṃ, desetabbatāya paṭiññātabhāvato, yathāpaṭiññañca desanato “ta”nti paccāmasanaṃ, sotabbabhāvato, savanatthassa ca ekantena nipphādanato “suṇāthā”ti vuttaṃ. Sakkātabbato, sakkaccakiriyāya eva ca tadatthasiddhito “sādhuka”nti vuttaṃ. Dhammassa manasikaraṇīyato tadadhīnattā ca sabbasampattīnaṃ “manasi karothā”ti vuttaṃ yathāpariññātāya desanāya paribyattabhāvato vitthāratthasambhavato ca “bhāsissāmī”ti vuttaṃ. Bhagavato sadevakena lokena sirasā sampaṭicchitabbavacanattā, tassa ca yathādhippetatthasādhanato “eva”nti vuttaṃ. Satthu uttamagāravaṭṭhānabhāvato, tattha ca gāravassa uḷārapuññabhāvato “bhante”ti vuttaṃ. Bhikkhūnaṃ tathākiriyāya nicchitabhāvato vacanālaṅkārato ca “kho”ti vuttaṃ. Savanassa paṭijānitabbato, tathā tehi paṭipannattā ca “paccassosu”nti vuttaṃ paccakkhabhāvato, sakalassapi ekajjhaṃ karaṇato “eta”nti vuttaṃ.

Because conceiving is the non-differentiating cause of identity view, and because it must be entirely abandoned by anyone, the word 'all' (sabba) is used. Due to determining the inherent nature, and due to being without substance or life, the word 'phenomena' (dhamma) is used. Because there is no basis, and because it is a unique cause, the word 'root' (mūla) is used. Due to being a cause and the possibility of the teaching's meaning, the word 'method' (pariyāya) is used. Because of direct presence and the possibility of the dative sense, the word 'vo' is used. Due to possessing such qualities and for turning them towards it, the address 'bhikkhave' is used. Because of the ability to teach and for the arising of mindfulness in them, the declaration 'I will teach' is made. Because it must be taught and it is acknowledged, and because the teaching is as declared, 'that' (taṃ) is used to refer back to it. Because it must be heard, and because the purpose of hearing is entirely accomplished, 'listen' is said. Because it must be honored, and because the purpose is achieved only through careful action, 'well' is said. Because the Dhamma must be attended to, and because all attainments depend on it, 'pay attention' is said. Because the teaching is expressed as it is fully known, and because of the possibility of an extensive meaning, 'I will explain' is said. Because the Blessed One's words are to be accepted with the head by the world with its gods, and because they accomplish the intended purpose, 'thus' is said. Because the Teacher holds the highest position of reverence, and because reverence for him brings great merit, 'Venerable sir' is said. Because the monks are certain in acting thus, and because it is an embellishment of speech, 'indeed' is said. Because hearing must be acknowledged, and because they have acted accordingly, 'they assented' (paccassosuṃ) is said. Because it is directly perceptible, and because the whole is done at once, 'this' is said.

Vuccamānassa puggalassa lokapariyāpannattā lokādhārattā ca lokaṃ upādāya “idhā”ti vuttaṃ. Paṭivedhabāhusaccābhāvato pariyattibāhusaccābhāvato ca “assutavā”ti vuttaṃ. Puthūsu, puthu vā janabhāvato “puthujjano”ti vuttaṃ. Anariyadhammavirahato ariyadhammasamannāgamato ca “ariyāna”nti vuttaṃ. Ariyabhāvakarāya paṭipattiyā abhāvato, tattha kosalladamathābhāvato “ariyānaṃ adassāvī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Asantadhammassavanato santadhammasamannāgamato sabbhi pāsaṃsiyato [M 1.0123] ca “sappurisāna”nti vuttaṃ. Sappurisabhāvakarāya paṭipattiyā abhāvato, tattha ca kosalladamathābhāvato “sappurisānaṃ adassāvī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pathavīvatthukānaṃ maññanānaṃ, upari vuccamānānañcamaññanānaṃ mūlakattā papañcasaṅkhānaṃ “pathaviṃ pathavito sañjānātī”ti vuttaṃ. Andhaputhujjanassa ahaṃkāra-mamaṃkārānaṃ katthacipi appahīnattā “pathaviṃ maññatī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Regarding the person being spoken of, because they are included in the world and supported by the world, with reference to the world the word 'here' (idha) is used. Due to the absence of great learning through penetration and the absence of great learning through study, the word 'uninstructed' (assutavā) is used. Because they exist among the many, or due to their common nature, the word 'ordinary person' (puthujjano) is used. Because they are devoid of ignoble qualities and endowed with noble qualities, the word 'of the noble ones' (ariyānaṃ) is used. Due to the absence of the practice that makes one noble, and the lack of skill and self-control therein, 'does not see the noble ones' (ariyānaṃ adassāvī) and so on, is said. Because they hear the true Dhamma, are endowed with the qualities of true persons, and are praised by the good, the word 'of true persons' (sappurisānaṃ) is used. Due to the absence of the practice that makes one a true person, and the lack of skill and self-control therein, 'does not see the true persons' (sappurisānaṃ adassāvī) and so on, is said. Because it is the root of conceivings based on earth and of the conceivings mentioned hereafter, which are termed proliferation, 'one perceives earth as earth' (pathaviṃ pathavito sañjānāti) is said. Due to the blind ordinary person not having abandoned I-making and mine-making anywhere, 'they conceive earth' (pathaviṃ maññati) and so on, is said.

Pubbe [V 1.0110] aggahitattā, sāmaññato ca gayhamānattā, puggalassa pathavīādiārammaṇasabhāgatāya labbhamānattā ca “yopī”ti vuttaṃ. “Yo”ti aniyamena gahitassa niyametabbato paṭiniddisitabbato ca; “so”ti vuttaṃ sātisayaṃ saṃsāre bhayassa ikkhanato kilesabhedanasambhavato ca “bhikkhū”ti vuttaṃ. Sikkhāhi samannāgamato sekkhadhammapaṭilābhato ca “sekkho”ti vuttaṃ. Manasā laddhabbassa arahattassa anadhigatattā adhigamanīyato ca “appattamānaso”ti vuttaṃ. Aparena anuttaraṇīyato, paraṃ anucchavikabhāvena uttaritvā ṭhitattā ca “anuttara”nti vuttaṃ. Yogena bhāvanāya kāmayogādito ca khemaṃ sivaṃ anupaddavanti “yogakkhema”nti vuttaṃ. Chandappavattiyā ussukkāpattiyā ca “patthayamāno”ti vuttaṃ. Tadatthassa sabbaso sabbairiyāpathavihārassa samathavipassanāvihārassa dibbavihārassa ca vasena “viharatī”ti vuttaṃ. Sekkhassa sabbaso abhiññeyyabhāvañceva pariññeyyabhāvañca ñāṇena abhibhavitvā jānanato “abhijānātī”ti vuttaṃ. Sekkhassa sabbaso appahīnamaññanatāya abhāvato “mā maññī”ti vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ. Iminā nayena ito paraṃ sabbapadesu vinicchayo kātabbo. Sakkā hi aṭṭhakathaṃ tassā līnatthavaṇṇanañca anugantvā ayamattho viññūhi vibhāvetunti ativitthārabhayena na vitthārayimha. Iti anupadavicayato vicayo hāro.

Because it was not grasped before, and because it is taken in a general sense, and because it is obtained by the individual through having the object of earth, etc., in common, the word 'whosoever' (yopi) is used. Because what is taken indefinitely as 'who' (yo) must be defined and specified, the word 'he' (so) is used. Because of seeing exceeding fear in the cycle of existence and because of the possibility of destroying the defilements, the word 'bhikkhu' is used. Because of being endowed with the trainings and because of attaining the qualities of a learner, the word 'learner' (sekkho) is used. Because the state of Arahantship, to be attained by the mind, has not been attained and is yet to be attained, the word 'one whose mind has not attained the goal' (appattamānaso) is used. Because it is not to be surpassed by another, and because it stands having surpassed what is inferior, the word 'unsurpassed' (anuttara) is used. Because it is security (khema) from the yokes (yoga) of sensuality and so on, through meditative development, and is safe, peaceful, and free from calamity, it is called 'security from the yokes' (yogakkhema). Because of the arising of desire and the occurrence of eagerness, the word 'aspiring' (patthayamāno) is used. Because of dwelling for that purpose in every way, in all postures, in the dwelling of serenity and insight, and in the divine dwelling, the word 'he dwells' (viharati) is used. Because the learner knows by overcoming through knowledge all that is to be directly known and all that is to be fully understood, the word 'he directly knows' (abhijānāti) is used. Because for the learner conceiving is entirely unabandoned, the phrase 'let him not conceive' (mā maññī) is used. The rest should be understood according to the method stated. By this method, the analysis of all the following passages should be done. For it is possible for the wise to discern this meaning by following the commentary and its explanation of the hidden meaning; for fear of excessive elaboration, we have not elaborated. Thus, from the word-by-word examination, this is the mode of investigation.

3. Yuttihāravaṇṇanā

3. Exposition of the Mode of Justification

Sakkāyassa sabbamaññanānaṃ mūlabhāvo yujjati parikappamattakattā lokavicittassa. Byāhusaccadvayarahitassa andhaputhujjanabhāvo yujjati puthukilesābhisaṅkhārajananādisabhāvattā. Yathāvuttaputhujjanassa vā vuttappakārabāhusaccābhāvo yujjati tasmiṃ sati sabbhāvato. Tattha assutavato [M 1.0124] puthujjanassa ariyānaṃ sappurisānañca adassāvitādi yujjati ariyakaradhammānaṃ ariyabhāvassa ca tena adiṭṭhattā appaṭipannattā ca tathā tassa pathaviyā “ahaṃ pathavī, mama pathavī, paro pathavī”ti sañjānanaṃ yujjati ahaṃkāramamaṃkārānaṃ sabbena sabbaṃ appahīnattā. Tathā sañjānato cassa pathaviṃ kammādikaraṇādivasena gahetvā nānappakārato maññanāpavatti yujjati saññānidānattā papañcasaṅkhānaṃ. Yo maññati, tassa apariññātavatthukatā yujjati pariññāya vinā maññanāpahānābhāvato. “Āpaṃ āpato sañjānātī”tiādīsupi eseva nayo. Apariyositasikkhassa appattamānasatā yujjati katakiccatābhāvato. Sekkhassa sato yogakkhemapatthanā yujjati tadadhimuttabhāvato. Tathā tassa pathaviyā abhijānanā yujjati pariññāpahānesu mattaso kāribhāvato. Tato eva cassa “mā maññī”ti vattabbatā yujjati vatthupariññāya [V 1.0111] viya maññanāpahānassapi vippakatabhāvato. Sekkhassa pathaviyā pariññeyyatā yujjati pariññātuṃ sakkuṇeyyattā sabbaso apariññātattā ca. “Āpaṃ āpato”tiādīsupi eseva nayo. Arahattādiyuttassa pathaviyādīnaṃ abhijānanā maññanābhāvo ca yujjati saṅkhātadhammattā, sabbaso kilesānaṃ pahīnattā, tato eva cassa vītarāgādibhāvo tato sammadeva ca paṭiccasamuppādassa paṭividdhatāti. Ayaṃ yuttihāro.

That identity is the root of all conceivings is justified, because the world's diversity is merely a conceptual construction. The state of being a blind ordinary person for one devoid of the two kinds of great learning is justified, because their nature involves producing abundant defilements, volitional formations, and so on. Or, for such an ordinary person as described, the absence of the aforementioned great learning is justified, because of its absence in that state. In this case, for the uninstructed ordinary person, not seeing the noble ones and true persons, and so on, is justified, because the qualities that make one noble and the noble state have not been seen or practiced by them. Thus, for them, perceiving the earth as 'I am the earth, the earth is mine, earth is other' is justified, since I-making and mine-making have not been fully abandoned in every way. Likewise, for one who perceives thus, the arising of various conceivings—grasping the earth by way of action, instrument, and so on—is justified, because conceptual proliferation has perception as its source. For one who conceives, the state of not having fully understood the object is justified, because without full understanding, the abandonment of conceiving is not possible. The same method applies to instances such as 'he perceives water as water', and so on. For one whose training is not finished, the state of a mind that has not attained the goal is justified, due to the incompleteness of their task. For one who is a trainee, the aspiration for security from the yokes is justified, because they are intent upon it. Similarly, their direct knowledge of the earth is justified, as they are engaged to some extent in full understanding and abandoning. Hence, it is fitting to say to them, 'Do not conceive,' because, like the full understanding of the object, the abandonment of conceiving is also incomplete. For a trainee, the earth is a thing to be fully understood, as they are able to understand it, yet it has not been fully comprehended in every way. The same method applies to instances such as 'water', and so on. For one who possesses Arahantship and so on, the direct knowledge of earth and the like, as well as the absence of conceiving, is justified, because phenomena have been comprehended and all defilements have been abandoned; and for that very reason they are free from lust and the like, and thus dependent origination has been rightly penetrated. This is the mode of justification.

4. Padaṭṭhānahāravaṇṇanā

4. Exposition of the Mode of Proximate Cause

Kissopi maññanā sakkāyassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, maññanānaṃ ayonisomanasikāro padaṭṭhānaṃ, sutadvayaviraho andhaputhujjanabhāvassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, so ariyānaṃ adassāvitāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, sā ariyadhammassa akovidatāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, sā ariyadhamme avinītatāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. “Sappurisānaṃ adassāvī”ti etthāpi eseva nayo. Saññāvipallāso maññanānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ. Saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhāti. Maññanāsu ca taṇhāmaññanā itaramaññanānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ “taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphandita”nti, (dī. ni. 1.105-109) “taṇhāpaccayā upādāna”nti (ma. ni. 3.126; mahāva. 1) ca vacanato, taṇhāgatasseva ca “seyyohamasmi”ntiādinā mānajappanāsabbhāvatā. Sabbāpi vā maññanā sabbāsaṃ maññanānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ[M 1.0125]. “Upādānapaccayā taṇhā”ti hi vacanato diṭṭhipi taṇhāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. “Ahamasmi brahmā mahābrahmā”ti (dī. ni. 1.42; 3.39) ādivacanato mānopi diṭṭhiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tathā “asmīti sati itthaṃsmīti hoti, evaṃsmīti hoti, aññathāsmīti hotī”tiādivacanato mānassapi taṇhāya padaṭṭhānatā labbhateva. Sekkhā dhammā sappadesato maññanāpahānassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Asekkhā nippadesato maññanāpahānassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Kammabhavo ca jātiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Jāti jarāmaraṇassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Paccayākārassa yathābhūtāvabodho sammāsambodhiyā padaṭṭhānanti. Ayaṃ padaṭṭhāno hāro.

Any conceiving is the proximate cause for identity. Unwise attention is the proximate cause for conceivings. The absence of hearing the twofold teaching is the proximate cause for the state of a blind ordinary person. That is the proximate cause for not seeing the noble ones. That is the proximate cause for not being skilled in the noble Dhamma. That is the proximate cause for not being trained in the noble Dhamma. 'Not seeing good persons'—here too the same method applies. Perceptual distortion is the proximate cause for conceivings. For conceptual proliferation originates from perception. And among conceivings, craving-conceiving is the proximate cause for other conceivings, as it is said: 'Those obsessed with craving tremble and flounder,' and 'From craving as condition, clinging arises.' Moreover, the very nature of pride and boasting, such as 'I am better,' arises in one obsessed with craving. Or all conceiving is the proximate cause for all conceivings. For according to the statement 'From clinging as condition, craving arises,' even view is a proximate cause for craving. From statements like 'I am Brahmā, the Great Brahmā,' pride too is a proximate cause for view. Similarly, from statements like 'When there is “I am,” there comes to be “I am thus,” “I am like this,” “I am otherwise,”' it is indeed found that pride is a proximate cause for craving. The qualities of a trainee are the proximate cause, in part, for the abandoning of conceiving. The qualities of a non-trainee are the proximate cause, in full, for the abandoning of conceiving. Kamma-becoming is the proximate cause for birth. Birth is the proximate cause for aging and death. The comprehension of the mode of conditionality as it really is is the proximate cause for perfect enlightenment. This is the method of proximate cause.

5. Lakkhaṇahāravaṇṇanā

5. Exposition on the Method of Characteristics

“Sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”nti ettha mūlaggahaṇena mūlapariyāyaggahaṇena vā yathā taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiyo gayhanti, evaṃ dosamohādīnampi sakkāyamūladhammānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo sakkāyassa mūlabhāvena ekalakkhaṇattā. “Assutavā”ti iminā yathā tassa puggalassa pariyattipaṭivedhasaddhammānaṃ abhāvo gayhati, evaṃ paṭipattisaddhammassapi abhāvo gayhati saddhammabhāvena ekalakkhaṇattā. Ariyānaṃ adassanakāmatādilakkhaṇā. “Ariyadhammassa akovido”ti [V 1.0112] iminā ariyadhammādhigamassa vibandhabhūtaṃ aññāṇaṃ. “Ariyadhamme avinīto”ti iminā ariyavinayābhāvo. So panatthato ariyavinaye appaṭipatti eva vāti tīhipi padehi yathāvuttavisayā micchādiṭṭhi vicikicchā ca gahitāva honti. Taggahaṇena ca sabbepi akusalā dhammā saṅgahitāva honti saṃkilesalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. “Sappurisānaṃ adassāvī”ti etthāpi eseva nayo.

In 'The Discourse on the Root of All Phenomena,' by grasping the root or by grasping the discourse on the root, just as craving, conceit, and views are included, so too should the inclusion of hatred, delusion, and other phenomena rooted in identity be understood, due to their having the single characteristic of being the root of identity. By 'uninstructed,' just as the absence of the true Dhamma of learning and penetration in that person is included, so too is the absence of the true Dhamma of practice included, due to their having the single characteristic of being the true Dhamma. They are characterized by not wanting to see the noble ones, and so on. By 'unskilled in the noble Dhamma' is meant ignorance, which is an impediment to the attainment of the noble Dhamma. By 'undisciplined in the noble Dhamma' is meant the absence of noble discipline. But in meaning, this is simply non-practice in the noble discipline. Thus, by these three terms, wrong view and doubt concerning the aforementioned subjects are indeed included. And by their inclusion, all unwholesome states are indeed included, due to their having the single characteristic of defilement. 'Not seeing good persons'—here too, the same method applies.

“Pathaviṃ pathavito sañjānātī”ti idaṃ diṭṭhimaññanādīnaṃ saññāya kāraṇabhāvadassanaṃ. Tattha yathā saññā, evaṃ vitakkaphassāvijjāayonisomanasikārādayopi tāsaṃ kāraṇanti atthato tesampettha saṅgaho vutto hoti maññanānaṃ kāraṇabhāvena ekalakkhaṇattā. “Maññatī”ti iminā maññanākiccena taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiyo gahitā [M 1.0126] tāsaṃ kilesasabhāvattā. Taggahaṇeneva vicikicchādinampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo kilesalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. Tathā taṇhāya hetusabhāvattā taggahaṇeneva avasiṭṭhākusalahetūnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo hetulakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. Tathā taṇhādiṭṭhīnaṃ āsavādisabhāvattā taggahaṇeneva avasiṭṭhāsavoghayogaganthanīvaraṇādīnampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo āsavādisabhāvattā ekalakkhaṇattā. Tathā “pathaviṃ maññatī”tiādinā pathavīādīnaṃ rūpasabhāvattā tabbisayānañca maññanānaṃ rūpavisayattā taggahaṇeneva sakalarūpakkhandhavisayāpi maññanā dassitā honti rūpavisayalakkhaṇena āsaṃ ekalakkhaṇattā. Evaṃ cakkhāyatanādivisayāpi maññanā niddhāretabbā. “Apariññāta”nti pariññāpaṭikkhepena tappaṭibaddhakilesānaṃ pahānapaṭikkhepoti daṭṭhabbo maggakiccabhāvena pariññāpahānānaṃ ekalakkhaṇattā. Iminā nayena sesesupi yathārahaṃ ekalakkhaṇā niddhāretabbāti. Ayaṃ lakkhaṇo hāro.

"He perceives earth as earth"—this shows perception as the cause of views, conceiving, and so on. Here, just as perception is a cause, so too are thought, contact, ignorance, unwise attention, and others causes for them; thus, by implication, they are also stated to be included here because they share the common characteristic of being causes of conceiving. By "he conceives," craving, pride, and views are included by the act of conceiving, due to their nature as defilements. And by their inclusion, doubt and other defilements should also be seen as included, since they share the common characteristic of being defilements. Similarly, because craving has the nature of being a root, by its inclusion, the remaining unwholesome roots should also be seen as included, since they share the common characteristic of being roots. Likewise, because craving and views have the nature of taints and so on, by their inclusion, the remaining taints, floods, yokes, bonds, hindrances, and so on, should also be seen as included, since they share the common characteristic of being taints and so on. Further, by "he conceives earth," and so on, since earth and so on have the nature of form, and the conceivings regarding them have form as their object, by their inclusion, all conceivings pertaining to the entire form aggregate are shown, since they share the common characteristic of having form as their object. In the same way, conceivings regarding the eye-base and other objects should also be deduced. "Not fully understood"—by the rejection of full understanding, the rejection of abandoning the defilements bound to it should be seen, because full understanding and abandoning share the common characteristic of being functions of the path. In this way, the remaining cases should also be deduced according to their respective common characteristics. This is the method of characteristics.

6. Catubyūhahāravaṇṇanā

6. Exposition on the Method of the Fourfold Array

Pathavīādīsu vatthūsu byañjanacchāyāya atthaṃ gahetvā dhammagambhīrataṃ asallakkhetvā asaddhammassavanādinā vañcitā hutvā saddhammassavanadhāraṇaparicayamanasikāravimukhā pathavīādīsu vatthūsu puthujjanasekkhāsekkhatathāgatānaṃ paṭipattivisesaṃ ajānantā ca veneyyā imissā desanāya nidānaṃ. Te “kathaṃ nu kho yathāvuttadosavinimuttā yathāvuttañca visesaṃ jānantā sammāpaṭipattiyā ubhayahitaparāyaṇā saveyyu”nti ayamettha bhagavato adhippāyo. Padanibbacanaṃ niruttaṃ, taṃ “eva”ntiādinidānapadānaṃ, “sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”ntiādipāḷipadānañca [V 1.0113] aṭṭhakathāyaṃ, tassā līnatthavaṇṇanāyañceva vuttanayena suviññeyyattā ativitthārabhayena na vitthārayimha.

Regarding the bases such as earth, grasping the meaning through the letters and appearances, not discerning the profound depth of the Dhamma, deceived by listening to false teachings and the like, turning away from listening to, retaining, familiarizing themselves with, and attending to the true Dhamma, and not knowing the distinctions in the practices of ordinary persons, trainees, non-trainees, and Tathāgatas regarding the bases such as earth, the educable ones are the occasion for this discourse. The Blessed One’s intention here is: “How might they, free from the faults as described, and knowing the distinctions as described, rightly practice, intent on the benefit of both?” The explanation of words is etymology; this refers to the introductory words such as “eva” and the Pali words such as “the Discourse on the Root of All Phenomena” in the commentary and in the explanation of its hidden meaning. Since they are easily understood in the manner stated, we have not elaborated them here for fear of excessive detail.

Padapadatthadesanānikkhepasuttasandhivasena pañcavidhā sandhi. Tattha padassa padantarena sambandho padasandhi, tathā padatthassa padatthantarena sambandho padatthasandhi, yo “kiriyākārakasambandho”ti vuccati. Nānānusandhikassa suttassa taṃtaṃanusandhīhi sambandho, ekānusandhikassa pana pubbāparasambandho desanāsandhi. Yā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “pucchānusandhi ajjhāsayānusandhi yathānusandhī”ti [M 1.0127] tidhā vibhattā. Ajjhāsayo cettha attajjhāsayo parajjhāsayoti dvidhā veditabbo. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā nidānavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttameva. Nikkhepasandhi catunnaṃ suttanikkhepānaṃ vasena veditabbo. Suttasandhi idha paṭhamanikkhepavaseneva veditabbo. Kasmā panettha mūlapariyāyasuttameva paṭhamaṃ nikkhittanti? Nāyamanuyogo katthaci nappavattati, apica yasmā maññanāmūlakaṃ sakkāyaṃ, sabbamaññanā ca tattha eva anekabhedabhinnā pavattati, na tassā savisayāya lesamattampi sāraṃ atthīti pathavīādivibhāgabhinnesu maññanāsu ca sātisayaṃ nibbedhavirāgasañjananī upari sekkhāsekkhatathāgataguṇavibhāvanī ca ayaṃ desanā. Suttantadesanā ca visesato diṭṭhiviniveṭhanakathā, tasmā sanissayassa diṭṭhiggāhassa ādito asārabhāvadīpanaṃ upari ca sabbesaṃ ariyānaṃ guṇavisesavibhāvanamidaṃ suttaṃ paṭhamaṃ nikkhittaṃ. Kiñca sakkāye maññanāmaññanāmukhena pavattinivattīsu ādīnavānisaṃsavibhāvanato sabbesaṃ puggalānaṃ paṭipattivibhāgato ca idameva suttaṃ paṭhamaṃ nikkhittaṃ.

Connection (sandhi) is fivefold by way of word-connection, meaning-connection, teaching-connection, summary-connection, and sutta-connection. Herein, the connection of a word with another word is word-connection; similarly, the connection of a meaning with another meaning is meaning-connection, which is called “the connection of action and agent.” For a sutta with multiple continuities, its connection is with those respective continuities; but for a sutta with a single continuity, its connection with what precedes and follows is the teaching-connection. In the commentaries, this is classified threefold as “question-continuity, intention-continuity, and natural continuity.” Here, intention should be understood as twofold: one’s own intention and another’s intention. What should be stated here has already been stated in the introductory commentary below. The summary-connection should be understood in terms of the four summaries of the sutta. The sutta-connection here should be understood by way of the first summary. Why then is the Mūlapariyāya Sutta placed first here? This is not an invalid question. Rather, because self-identity (sakkāya) is rooted in conceit, and all forms of conceit, fragmented into many divisions, manifest in relation to it—yet there is not even the slightest essence in that which has an object—this teaching is exceedingly effective in generating disenchantment and dispassion toward the conceits regarding classifications like earth, etc. Furthermore, it reveals the qualities of trainees, non-trainees, and Tathāgatas. And the teaching of the suttas is particularly a discourse on the uprooting of views. Therefore, this sutta is placed first to illuminate the lack of essence in the clinging to views that has a basis, and furthermore, to reveal the special qualities of all noble ones. Moreover, because this sutta demonstrates the dangers and benefits through the arising and ceasing of conceit and conceiving in self-identity, and because it distinguishes the practices of all individuals, this sutta is placed first.

Yaṃ pana ekissā desanāya desanantarena saddhiṃ saṃsandanaṃ, ayampi desanāsandhi, sā evaṃ veditabbā. “Assutavā puthujjano…pe… nibbānaṃ abhinandatī”ti ayaṃ desanā. “Idha, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano…pe… sappurisadhamme avinīto manasikaraṇīye dhamme nappajānāti, amanasikaraṇīye ca dhamme nappajānāti, so manasikaraṇīye dhamme appajānanto amanasikaraṇīye ca dhamme appajānanto ye dhammā na manasikaraṇīyā, te dhamme manasi karoti…pe… anuppanno vā kāmāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā kāmāsavo pavaḍḍhati. Anuppanno vā bhavāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā bhavāsavo pavaḍḍhati, anuppanno vā avijjāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā avijjāsavo pavaḍḍhatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.17) imāya desanāya saṃsandati. Tathā “tassetaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ subhanimittaṃ manasi karissati, tassa subhanimittassa manasikārā rāgo cittaṃ anuddhaṃsessati, so sarāgo sadoso samoho sāṅgaṇo saṃkiliṭṭhacitto kālaṃ karissatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.59) imāya desanāya saṃsandati. Tathā “cakkhuñcāvuso [V 1.0114] paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā [M 1.0128] vedanā. Yaṃ vedeti taṃ sañjānāti, yaṃ sañjānāti taṃ vitakketi, yaṃ vitakketi taṃ papañceti, yaṃ papañceti tatonidānaṃ purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācarantī”ti (ma. ni. 1.204) imāya desanāya saṃsandati. Tathā “idha, bhikkhave, asutavā puthujjano…pe… sappurisadhamme avinīto rūpaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassati. Vedanaṃ…pe…, saññaṃ…pe…, saṅkhāre…pe…, viññāṇaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassati. Yampi taṃ diṭṭhaṃ…pe… yampi taṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ, so loko so attā so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassāmīti, tampi ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.241) imāya desanāya saṃsandati.

Furthermore, the connection of one teaching with another is also a teaching-connection, and it should be understood as follows: “The uninstructed ordinary person… delights in Nibbāna”—this is one teaching. This connects with the teaching: “Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person… untrained in the Dhamma of the noble ones, does not understand what things should be attended to and what things should not be attended to. Not understanding what should be attended to and what should not be attended to, he attends to things that should not be attended to… the unarisen influx of sensuality arises in him, and the arisen influx of sensuality increases; the unarisen influx of existence arises, and the arisen influx of existence increases; the unarisen influx of ignorance arises, and the arisen influx of ignorance increases.” (MN 1.17) Similarly, this connects with the teaching: “It is to be expected of him that he will attend to an attractive sign. Because he attends to an attractive sign, lust will overwhelm his mind. With lust, hate, and delusion, stained with defilements, with a corrupted mind, he will die.” (MN 1.59) Likewise, this connects with the teaching: “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling; what one feels, one perceives; what one perceives, one thinks about; what one thinks about, one proliferates; what one proliferates, because of that, perceptions and notions born of proliferation assail a person.” (MN 1.204) Similarly, this connects with the teaching: “Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person… untrained in the Dhamma of the noble ones, regards form thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ He regards feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ And whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—that too he regards thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ And even that standpoint of views: ‘This world is the self; after death I shall be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, I shall remain the same for ever and ever’—that too he regards thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’” (MN 1.241)

“Yopi so, bhikkhave, bhikkhu…pe… nibbānaṃ mābhinandī”ti ayaṃ desanā. “Idha, devānaminda, bhikkhuno sutaṃ hoti ‘sabbe dhammā nālaṃ abhinivesāyā’ti, evañcetaṃ, devānaminda, bhikkhuno sutaṃ hoti ‘sabbe dhammā nālaṃ abhinivesāyā’ti, so sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhijānāti, sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhiññāya sabbaṃ dhammaṃ parijānāti, sabbaṃ dhammaṃ pariññāya yaṃ kiñci vedanaṃ vedeti sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā, so tāsu vedanāsu aniccānupassī viharati, virāgānupassī viharati, nirodhānupassī viharati, paṭinissaggānupassī viharatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.390) imāya desanāya saṃsandati. “Yopi so, bhikkhave, bhikkhu arahaṃ…pe… abhisambuddhoti vadāmī”ti ayaṃ desanā “sutavā ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako…pe… sappurisadhamme suvinīto rūpaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassati, vedanaṃ…pe…, saññaṃ…pe…, saṅkhāre…pe…, viññāṇaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassati. Yampi taṃ diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ viññātaṃ pattaṃ pariyesitaṃ anuvicaritaṃ manasā, tampi ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassati. Yampi taṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ, so loko so attā so pecca bhavissāmi ‘nicco dhuvo sassato api pariṇāmadhammo sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassāmī’ti, tampi ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassati. So evaṃ samanupassanto na paritassatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.241) evamādidesanāhi saṃsandatīti, ayaṃ catubyūho hāro.

“Even that bhikkhu, O bhikkhus… should not delight in Nibbāna,” this is the teaching. This connects with the teaching: “Here, O lord of devas, a bhikkhu has heard: ‘All things are not fit for clinging.’ When a bhikkhu has heard thus, ‘All things are not fit for clinging,’ he directly knows all things. Having directly known all things, he fully understands all things. Having fully understood all things, whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he dwells contemplating impermanence in those feelings, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment.” (MN 1.390) “Even that bhikkhu, O bhikkhus, who is an arahant… I declare him fully enlightened,” this is the teaching. This connects with such teachings as: “But the instructed noble disciple, O bhikkhus… well-trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones, regards form thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ He regards feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ And whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—that too he regards thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ And even that standpoint of views: ‘This world is the self; after death I shall be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, I shall remain the same for ever and ever’—that too he regards thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Thus regarding, he is not agitated.” (MN 1.241) This is the fourfold guide.

7. Āvattahāravaṇṇanā

7. The Exposition of the Mode of Recurrence.

“Assutavā [V 1.0115][M 1.0129] puthujjano”ti iminā yonisomanasikārapaṭikkhepamukhena ayonisomanasikārapariggaho dīpito. “Ariyānaṃ adassāvī”tiādinā sappurisūpanissayādipaṭikkhepamukhena asappurisūpanissayādipariggaho dīpito. Tesu purimanayena āsayavipatti kittitā, dutiyena payogavipatti. Purimena cassa kilesavaṭṭaṃ, tañca yato vipākavaṭṭanti sakalaṃ saṃsāracakkamāvattati. “Pathaviṃ maññatī”tiādinā tattha tisso maññanā vuttā. Tāsu taṇhāmaññanā “etaṃ mamā”ti taṇhāggāho, mānamaññanā “esohamasmī”ti mānaggāho, diṭṭhimaññanā “eso me attā”ti diṭṭhiggāho. Tattha taṇhāggāhena “taṇhaṃ paṭiccapariyesanā”tiādikā (dī. ni. 2.103; dī. ni. 3.359; a. ni. 3.23; vibha. 963) nava taṇhāmūlakā dhammā āvattanti. Mānaggāhena “seyyohamasmī”tiādikā nava mānavidhā āvattanti. Diṭṭhiggāhena “rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī”tiādikā (saṃ. ni. 4.345) vīsativatthukā sakkāyadiṭṭhi āvattati. Tīsu ca gāhesu yāya saññāya taṇhāggāhassa vikkhambhanā, sā dukkhasaññā dukkhānupassanā. Yāya saññāya mānaggāhassa vikkhambhanā, sā aniccasaññā aniccānupassanā. Yāya pana saññāya diṭṭhiggāhassa vikkhambhanā, sā anattasaññā anattānupassanā. Tattha paṭhamaggāhavisabhāgato appaṇihitavimokkhamukhaṃ āvattati, dutiyaggāhavisabhāgato animittavimokkhamukhaṃ āvattati, tatiyaggāhavisabhāgato suññatavimokkhamukhaṃ āvattati.

“An uninstructed ordinary person”—through this, by way of rejecting wise attention, the adoption of unwise attention is shown. “Not seeing the noble ones,” and so on—through this, by way of rejecting reliance on good people, and so on, the adoption of reliance on bad people, and so on, is shown. Of these, by the first way the failure of disposition is stated, by the second the failure of effort. Through the former, the round of defilements revolves, and from that, the round of results; thus the entire wheel of saṃsāra revolves. “He conceives earth,” and so on—here, three kinds of conceiving are mentioned. Among these, craving-conceiving is the grasping of craving: “This is mine.” Conceit-conceiving is the grasping of conceit: “I am this.” View-conceiving is the grasping of views: “This is my self.” Here, through the grasping of craving, nine craving-rooted things revolve, such as “conditioned by craving, seeking” (Dīgha Nikāya 2.103; Dīgha Nikāya 3.359; Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.23; Vibhaṅga 963). Through the grasping of conceit, nine kinds of conceit revolve, such as “I am better.” Through the grasping of views, the twenty-based personality belief revolves, such as “seeing form as self” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.345). And among these three graspings, the perception by which the grasping of craving is suppressed is the perception of suffering, the contemplation of suffering. The perception by which the grasping of conceit is suppressed is the perception of impermanence, the contemplation of impermanence. But the perception by which the grasping of views is suppressed is the perception of non-self, the contemplation of non-self. Here, from opposition to the first grasping, the entrance to the undirected deliverance revolves; from opposition to the second grasping, the entrance to the signless deliverance revolves; from opposition to the third grasping, the entrance to the emptiness deliverance revolves.

Sekkhaggahaṇena ariyāya sammādiṭṭhiyā saṅgaho, tato ca paratoghosayonisomanasikārā dīpitā honti. Paratoghosena ca sutavā ariyasāvakoti āvattati, yonisomanasikārena nava yonisomanasikāramūlakā dhammā āvattanti, catubbidhañca sampatticakkaṃ. “Mā maññī”ti maññanānaṃ vippakatappahānatāgahaṇena ekaccāsavaparikkhayo dīpito hoti, tena ca saddhāvimuttadiṭṭhippattakāyasakkhibhāvā āvattanti. “Arahaṃ khīṇāsavo”tiādinā asekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo dassitā honti, sīlakkhandhādipāripūriyā ca dasa nāthakaraṇā dhammā āvattanti. “Na maññatī”ti maññanāpaṭikkhepena pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu “netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā”ti sammāpaṭipatti dassitā, tāya ca sātisayā nikantipariyādānamānasamugghāṭanadiṭṭhiugghāṭanāni [M 1.0130] pakāsitānīti appaṇihitānimitta-suññatavimokkhā āvattanti.

By the inclusion of the trainee, noble right view is comprehended, and from that, the voice of another and wise attention are shown. Through the voice of another, one revolves as a learned noble disciple; through wise attention, nine states rooted in wise attention revolve, and the fourfold wheel of success revolves. “Let him not conceive”—by grasping the state of incomplete abandonment of conceivings, the partial destruction of the taints is shown, and by that, the states of being one liberated by faith, one who has attained the view, and a bodily witness revolve. “The Arahant with taints destroyed,” and so on—by this, the aggregates of virtue, and so on, of one beyond training are shown, and by the fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue, and so on, the ten protective qualities revolve. “He does not conceive”—by the rejection of conceiving, right practice is shown in the five aggregates subject to clinging as “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self,” and by that, the excellent eradication of delight, uprooting of conceit, and uprooting of views are made clear—thus the undirected, the signless, and the emptiness liberations revolve.

“Tathāgato”tiādinā [V 1.0116] sabbaññuguṇā vibhāvitāti tadavinābhāvato dasabala-catuvesārajjaasādhāraṇañāṇaāveṇikabuddhadhammā āvattanti. “Nandī dukkhassa mūla”ntiādinā saddhiṃ hetunā vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitanti pavattinivattitadubhayahetuvibhāvanena cattāri ariyasaccāni āvattanti. “Taṇhānaṃ khayā”tiādinā taṇhappahānāpadesena tadekaṭṭhabhāvato diyaḍḍhassa kilesasahassassa pahānaṃ āvattati. “Sabbaso taṇhānaṃ khayā sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho”ti ca vuttattā “nandī dukkhassa mūla”nti, “iti viditvā”tiādinā vuttassa maññanābhāvahetubhūtassa paccayākāravedanassa sāvakehi asādhāraṇañāṇacārabhāvo dassito, tena catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasamāpattisañcāri bhagavato mahāvajirañāṇaṃ āvattatīti. Ayaṃ āvatto hāro.

By “The Tathāgata,” and so on, the qualities of omniscience are explained; and due to their inseparability, the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, the unshared knowledge, and the exclusive qualities of a Buddha revolve. By “Delight is the root of suffering,” and so on, along with the cause, the round of existence and its cessation is explained; and through the analysis of the causes for both continuation and cessation, the Four Noble Truths revolve. By “With the destruction of craving,” and so on, by indicating the abandonment of craving, due to its being of one meaning with that, the destruction of the one-and-a-half thousand defilements revolves. And because it is said, “Having fully understood the destruction of all craving, he attained supreme enlightenment,” and also, “Delight is the root of suffering,” and “having known this,” and so on—the state of having knowledge and conduct not common to disciples regarding the understanding of dependent origination, which is the cause of the absence of conceiving, is shown; thereby, the great diamond-like knowledge of the Blessed One, which ranges throughout twenty-four trillion concentrations, revolves. This is the mode of recurrence.

8. Vibhattihāravaṇṇanā

8. The Exposition of the Mode of Differentiation

“Sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”nti ettha sabbadhammā nāma tebhūmakā dhammā sakkāyassa adhippetattā. Tesaṃ maññanā padaṭṭhānaṃ papañcasaṅkhānimittattā lokavicittassa. Tayime kusalā akusalā abyākatāti tividhā. Tesu kusalānaṃ yonisomanasikārādi padaṭṭhānaṃ, akusalānaṃ ayonisomanasikārādi, abyākatānaṃ kammabhavaāvajjanabhūtarūpādi padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tattha kusalā kāmāvacarādivasena bhūmito tividhā, tathā abyākatā cittuppādasabhāvā, acittuppādasabhāvā pana kāmāvacarāva tathā akusalā. Pariyattipaṭipattipaṭivedhasutakiccābhāvena tividho assutavā. Andhakalyāṇavibhāgena duvidho puthujjano. Sammāsambuddhapaccekabuddhasāvakabhedena tividhā ariyā. Maṃsacakkhudibbacakkhupaññācakkhūhi dassanābhāvena tividho adassāvī. Maggaphalanibbānabhedena tividho, navavidho vā ariyadhammo. Savanadhāraṇaparicayamanasikārapaṭivedhavasena pañcavidhā ariyadhammassa kovidatā. Tadabhāvato akovido. Saṃvarapahānabhedena duvidho, dasavidho vā ariyadhammavinayo, tadabhāvato ariyadhamme avinīto. Ettha padaṭṭhānavibhāgo heṭṭhā dassitoyeva. “Sappurisānaṃ adassāvī”tiādīsupi eseva nayo. “Pathaviṃ maññatī”tiādīsu maññanāvatthuvibhāgo pāḷiyaṃ āgatova, tathā ajjhattikabāhirādiko ca antaravibhāgo.

In “The Discourse on the Root of All Things,” here “all things” refers to phenomena of the three realms, since personality is intended. Their conceiving is the proximate cause, being the sign of conceptual proliferation, for the diversity of the world. These are threefold: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. Among them, the proximate cause of wholesome states is wise attention and so forth; of unwholesome states, unwise attention and so forth; and of indeterminate states, the proximate cause is kamma-becoming, adverting, primary material elements, and so on. Among these, wholesome states are threefold in terms of plane: sense-sphere and so on. Similarly, indeterminate states are of the nature of mind-arisings, but those that are not of the nature of mind-arisings are only of the sense-sphere, as are unwholesome states. Due to the absence of the function of learning, practice, and penetration, the uninstructed person is threefold. By the distinction between the blind and the virtuous, the ordinary person is twofold. By the distinction between Perfectly Enlightened Ones, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples, the noble ones are threefold. Due to the absence of vision through the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the eye of wisdom, the one who does not see is threefold. The noble Dhamma is threefold, or ninefold, by division into path, fruit, and Nibbāna. Skill in the noble Dhamma is fivefold by way of hearing, retention, familiarity, attention, and penetration. Its absence makes one unskilled. The noble discipline is twofold, or tenfold, by division into restraint and abandoning. Its absence means one is undisciplined in the noble Dhamma. Here, the division of proximate causes has already been shown above. The same method applies in passages like “not seeing good people,” and so on. In “he conceives earth,” and so on, the division of the objects of conceiving is already given in the Pāli text, as is the internal division into internal, external, and so on.

Maññanā [M 1.0131] pana taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena saṅkhepato tividhā, vitthārato pana taṇhāmaññanā tāva kāmataṇhādivasena aṭṭhasatavidhā, tathā “asmīti sati itthaṃsmīti hotī”tiādinā. Evaṃ mānamaññanāpi. “Asmīti sati itthaṃsmīti hotī”tiādinā papañcattayaṃ uddiṭṭhaṃ niddiṭṭhañcāti[V 1.0117]. Etena diṭṭhimaññanāyapi aṭṭhasatavidhatā vuttāti veditabbā. Apica seyyassa “seyyohamasmī”tiādinā mānamaññanāya navavidhatā tadantarabhedena anekavidhatā ca veditabbā. Ayañca attho hīnattikatthavaṇṇanāya vibhāvetabbo. Diṭṭhimaññanāya pana brahmajāle āgatanayena dvāsaṭṭhividhatā tadantarabhedena anekavidhatā ca veditabbā. “Apariññāta”nti ettha ñātapariññādivasena ceva rūpamukhādiabhinivesabhedādivasena ca pariññānaṃ anekavidhatā veditabbā. Tathā aṭṭhamakādivasena sekkhavibhāgo paññāvimuttādivasena asekkhavibhāgo ca. Ayamettha dhammavibhāgo. Padaṭṭhānavibhāgo ca bhūmivibhāgo ca vuttanayānusārena veditabbāti. Ayaṃ vibhattihāro.

Conceiving, however, is briefly threefold by way of craving, conceit, and views; but in detail, craving-conceiving is first of one hundred and eight kinds through sensual craving and so on, and through such as, “When there is ‘I am,’ there is ‘I am thus.’” Similarly for conceit-conceiving. By such as, “When there is ‘I am,’ there is ‘I am thus,’” the threefold proliferation is stated and explained. By this, it should be understood that view-conceiving is also of one hundred and eight kinds. Furthermore, through expressions like “I am better,” and so on, conceit-conceiving is to be known as ninefold, and by its internal subdivisions, as manifold. This meaning should be clarified in the explanation of the meaning of the triad of inferiorities. As for view-conceiving, according to the method that comes in the Brahmajāla Sutta, it is to be known as sixty-twofold, and by its internal subdivisions, as manifold. In the term “uncomprehended” (apariññāta), the manifold nature of comprehension should be known through comprehension by knowing, and so on, and through the distinctions of attachment to form, appearance, and so on. Similarly, there is the division of trainees by way of the eight individuals, and so on, and the division of those beyond training by way of the one liberated by wisdom, and so on. This is the division of phenomena here. The division of proximate causes and the division of planes should be understood according to the method stated. This is the mode of differentiation.

9. Parivattahāravaṇṇanā

9. The Exposition of the Mode of Application

“Sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”nti ettha “sabbadhammā”ti pañcupādānakkhandhā gahitā, tesaṃ mūlakāraṇanti ca taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiyo. Tathā assutavā puthujjano…pe… sappurisadhamme avinītoti. Yāvakīvañca pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu subhato sukhato niccato attato samanupassanavasena “etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā”ti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhigāhā na samucchijjanti, tāva nesaṃ pabandhūparamo supinantepi na kenaci laddhapubbo. Yadā pana nesaṃ asubhato dukkhato aniccato anattato samanupassanavasena “netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā”ti pavattamānā appaṇihitānimittasuññatānupassanā ussakkitvā ariyamaggādhigamāya saṃvattanti, atha nesaṃ pabandhūparamo hoti accantaappaññattikabhāvūpagamanato. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbadhammāti pañcupādānakkhandhā gahitā, tesaṃ mūlakāraṇanti ca taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiyo”ti. Tathā assutavā puthujjano…pe… sappurisadhamme avinīto tīhipi maññanāhi pathaviṃ maññati yāva nibbānaṃ abhinandati, tīhipi pariññāhi tassa taṃ vatthu apariññātanti katvā. Yassa pana taṃ vatthu tīhi pariññāhi pariññātaṃ, na so itaro viya taṃ maññati. Tenāha [M 1.0132] bhagavā “sutavā ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako…pe… sappurisadhamme suvinīto rūpaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassati, vedanaṃ…pe… asati na paritassatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.241). Sekkho pathaviṃ mā maññi, yāva nibbānaṃ mābhinandi, arahā sammāsambuddho ca pathaviṃ na maññati, yāva nibbānaṃ nābhinandati, maññanāmaññitesu vatthūsu mattaso sabbaso ca pariññābhisamayasaṃsiddhiyā pahānābhisamayanibbattito. Yassa pana tesu vatthūsu sabbaso mattaso vā pariññā eva natthi, kuto pahānaṃ, so yathāparikappaṃ niraṅkusāhi maññanāhi “etaṃ mamā”tiādinā [V 1.0118] maññateva. Tenāha bhagavā “idha, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano…pe… sappurisadhamme avinīto rūpaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassati, vedanaṃ…pe…, sañña…pe…”ntiādi (ma. ni. 1.241). Ayaṃ parivatto hāro.

“The Exposition of the Root of All Things.” Here, “all things” are taken as the five aggregates subject to clinging, and their root causes are craving, conceit, and views. Thus, the uninstructed ordinary person… untrained in the True Person's Dhamma. For as long as the grasp of craving, conceit, and views is not uprooted through perceiving the five aggregates subject to clinging as beautiful, pleasant, permanent, and self—thinking, “This is mine, this I am, this is my self”—the cessation of their continuity has never been attained by anyone, even in a dream. But when the contemplations of the desireless, the signless, and emptiness, proceeding by way of perceiving them as unattractive, suffering, impermanent, and not-self—thinking, “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self”—are cultivated and lead to the attainment of the noble path, then the cessation of their continuity occurs, due to reaching the state of being utterly uncharacterizable. Therefore, it is said: “All things are taken as the five aggregates subject to clinging, and their root causes are craving, conceit, and views.” Thus, the uninstructed ordinary person… untrained in the True Person's Dhamma conceives earth by means of the three conceivings, all the way to delighting in Nibbāna, because for them that object is not fully understood by the three kinds of full understanding. But one for whom that object is fully understood through the three kinds of full understanding does not conceive it as the other does. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “But the instructed noble disciple, bhikkhus… well-trained in the True Person's Dhamma perceives form as ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self,’ perceives feeling… when it is not, he is not agitated” (MN 1.241). A trainee should not conceive earth, nor should they delight in Nibbāna. The Arahant and the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One do not conceive earth, nor do they delight in Nibbāna, because of the accomplishment of the realization of full understanding and the production of the realization of abandonment in regard to the conceivings and the objects conceived, both partially and completely. But for one who has no full understanding of these objects whatsoever, either partially or completely, whence could there be abandonment? They conceive according to their own imaginings with unrestrained conceivings, thinking, “This is mine,” and so on. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person… untrained in the True Person's Dhamma perceives form as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self,’ perceives feeling… perception…” and so on (MN 1.241). This is the method of conversion.

10. Vevacanahāravaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Method of Synonyms

“Sabbadhammā sakaladhammā anavasesadhammā”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ, “mūlapariyāyaṃ mūlakāraṇaṃ asādhāraṇahetu”nti pariyāyavacanaṃ, “mūlapariyāyanti vā mūladesanaṃ kāraṇatathana”nti pariyāyavacanaṃ, “vo tumhākaṃ tumha”nti pariyāyavacanaṃ, “bhikkhave, samaṇā tapassino”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ, “desessāmī kathessāmī paññapessāmī”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ, “suṇātha sotaṃ odahatha sotadvārānusārena upadhārethā”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ, “sādhukaṃ sammā sakkacca”nti pariyāyavacanaṃ, “manasi karotha citte ṭhapetha samannāharathā”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ, “bhāsissāmi byattaṃ kathessāmi vibhajissāmī”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ, “evaṃ, bhante, sādhu suṭṭhu bhante”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ, “paccassosuṃ sampaṭicchiṃsu sampaṭiggahesu”nti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu vevacanaṃ vattabbanti. Ayaṃ vevacano hāro.

“All phenomena, the totality of phenomena, phenomena without residue” is a synonymous expression; “the root exposition, the root cause, the uncommon cause” is a synonymous expression; “the root exposition or the root teaching, the stating of the cause as it is” is a synonymous expression; “for you, of you, your” is a synonymous expression; “bhikkhus, recluses, ascetics” is a synonymous expression; “I will teach, I will relate, I will make known” is a synonymous expression; “listen, lend an ear, attend in accordance with the ear-door” is a synonymous expression; “well, rightly, respectfully” is a synonymous expression; “apply your minds, place it in your hearts, direct your attention” is a synonymous expression; “I will speak, I will make it clear, I will analyze” is a synonymous expression; “yes, venerable sir, good, very good, venerable sir” is a synonymous expression; “they responded, they accepted, they received” is a synonymous expression. In this way, synonyms should be spoken in all passages. This is the method of synonyms.

11. Paññattihāravaṇṇanā

11. Explanation of the Method of Designations

“Sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”nti ettha sabbadhammā nāma sakkāyadhammā, te khandhavasena pañcadhā paññattā, āyatanavasena dvādasadhā, dhātuvasena aṭṭhārasadhā [M 1.0133] paññattā. “Mūla”nti vā “mūlapariyāya”nti vā maññanā vuttā, tā taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena tidhā antarabhedena anekadhā ca paññattā. Atha vā “sabbadhammā”ti tebhūmakadhammānaṃ saṅgahapaññatti, “mūlapariyāya”nti tesaṃ pabhavapaññatti, “vo”ti sampadānapaññati, “desessāmi bhāsissāmī”ti paṭiññāpaññatti, “suṇātha sādhukaṃ manasi karothā”ti ca āṇāpanapaññatti, “assutavā”ti paṭivedhavimukhatāpaññatti ceva pariyattivimukhatāpaññatti ca, “puthujjano”ti anariyapaññatti, sā ariyadhammapaṭikkhepapaññatti ceva ariyadhammavirahapaññatti ca, “ariyāna”nti asamapaññatti ceva samapaññatti ca. Tattha asamapaññatti tathāgatapaññatti, samapaññatti paccekabuddhānañceva ubhatobhāgavimuttādīnañca vasena aṭṭhavidhā veditabbā. “Ariyānaṃ adassāvī”tiādi dassanabhāvanāpaṭikkhepapaññatti, “pathaviṃ maññatī”tiādi pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ dvādasannaṃ āyatanānaṃ aṭṭhārasannaṃ dhātūnaṃ sammasanupagānaṃ indriyānaṃ nikkhepapaññatti [V 1.0119] ceva pabhavapaññatti ca, tathā vipallāsānaṃ kiccapaññatti pariyuṭṭhānaṃ dassanapaññatti kilesānaṃ phalapaññatti abhisaṅkhārānaṃ virūhanapaññatti taṇhāya assādanapaññatti diṭṭhiyā vipphandanapaññatti, “sekkhā”ti saddhānusārīsaddhāvimuttadiṭṭhippattakāyasakkhīnaṃ dassanapaññatti ceva bhāvanāpaññatti ca “appattamānaso”ti sekkhadhammānaṃ ṭhitipaññatti, “anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ patthayamāno”ti paññāya abhinibbidāpaññatti, “abhijānātī”ti abhiññeyyadhammānaṃ abhiññāpaññatti, dukkhassa pariññāpaññatti, samudayassa pahānapaññatti, nirodhassa sacchikiriyāpaññatti, maggassa bhāvanāpaññatti, “mā maññī”ti maññanānaṃ paṭikkhepapaññatti, samudayassa pahānapaññatti. Iminā nayena sesapadesupi vitthāretabbaṃ. Ayaṃ paññatti hāro.

In “The Exposition of the Root of All Things,” “all things” are the phenomena of personal identity; they are designated in five ways by way of the aggregates, in twelve ways by way of the sense bases, and in eighteen ways by way of the elements. “Root” or “exposition of the root” is said to be conceiving; this is designated in three ways by way of craving, conceit, and views, and in many ways through internal division. Alternatively, “all things” is a collective designation for the phenomena of the three realms; “exposition of the root” is a designation of their origin; “to you” is a designation of the recipient; “I will teach, I will speak” is a designation of a declaration; and “listen, attend carefully” is a designation of a command. “Uninstructed” is a designation of being devoid of penetration and devoid of learning. “Ordinary person” is a designation for a non-noble one; it is a designation of the rejection of the noble Dhamma and a designation of the absence of the noble Dhamma. “Of the noble ones” is a designation of the unequal and a designation of the equal. Therein, the designation of the unequal is the designation of the Tathāgata; the designation of the equal should be understood as eightfold by way of the Paccekabuddhas, those liberated in both ways, and so on. “One who has not seen the noble ones,” and so on, is a designation of the rejection of seeing and development. “Conceives earth,” and so on, is a designation of the laying down and a designation of the origin of the five aggregates subject to clinging, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, and of the faculties that are means for comprehension. Likewise, it is a designation of the function of distortions, a designation of the manifestation of obsessions, a designation of the fruit of defilements, a designation of the sprouting of volitional formations, a designation of the gratification of craving, and a designation of the agitation of views. “Trainee” is a designation of seeing and development for faith-followers, those liberated by faith, those who have attained to view, and body-witnesses. “One whose mind has not attained” is a designation of the stability of a trainee’s qualities. “Aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage” is a designation of disenchantment by means of wisdom. “Directly knows” is a designation of the direct knowledge of things to be directly known, a designation of the full understanding of suffering, a designation of the abandoning of the origin, a designation of the realization of cessation, and a designation of the development of the path. “Should not conceive” is a designation of the rejection of conceiving and a designation of the abandoning of the origin. In this way, it should be elaborated in the remaining passages as well. This is the method of designation.

12. Otaraṇahāravaṇṇanā

12. Explanation of the Method of Entry

“Sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”nti ettha sabbadhammā nāma lokiyā pañcakkhandhā dvādasāyatanāni aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo dve saccāni ekūnavisati indriyāni dvādasapadiko paccayākāroti, ayaṃ sabbadhammaggahaṇena khandhādimukhena desanāya otaraṇaṃ. “Mūla”nti vā “mūlapariyāya”nti vā maññanā vuttā, tā atthato taṇhā māno diṭṭhi cāti tesaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgahoti ayaṃ khandhamukhena otaraṇaṃ. Tathā “dhammāyatanadhammadhātūhi saṅgaho”ti ayaṃ āyatanamukhena dhātumukhena ca otaraṇaṃ. “Assutavā”ti iminā sutassa [M 1.0134] vibandhabhūtā avijjādayo gahitā, “puthujjano”ti iminā yesaṃ kilesābhisaṅkhārānaṃ jananādinā puthujjanoti vuccati, te kilesābhisaṅkhārādayo gahitā, “ariyānaṃ adassāvī”tiādinā yesaṃ kilesadhammānaṃ vasena ariyānaṃ adassāviādibhāvo hoti, te diṭṭhimānāvijjādayo gahitāti sabbehi tehi saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgahoti pubbe vuttanayeneva otaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Sañjānāti maññati abhijānāti na maññatī”ti etthāpi sañjānanamaññanāabhijānanānupassanānaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannattā vuttanayeneva otaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tathā sekkhaggahaṇena sekkhā, “araha”ntiādinā asekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo gahitāti evampi khandhamukhena otaraṇaṃ, āyatanadhātādimukhena ca otaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tathā “na maññatī”ti taṇhāgāhādipaṭikkhepena dukkhānupassanādayo gahitā, tesaṃ vasena appaṇihitavimokkhamukhādīhi otaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Pariññāta”nti iminā parijānanakiccena pavattamānā bodhipakkhiyadhammā gayhantīti satipaṭṭhānādimukhena otaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Nandiggahaṇena bhavaggahaṇena taṇhāgahaṇena ca samudayasaccaṃ, dukkhaggahaṇena jātijarāmaraṇaggahaṇena ca dukkhasaccaṃ, “taṇhānaṃ khayā”tiādinā [V 1.0120] nirodhasaccaṃ, abhisambodhiyā gahaṇena maggasaccaṃ gahitanti ariyasaccehi otaraṇanti. Ayaṃ otaraṇo hāro.

Here, in 'The Root of All Things,' 'all things' refers to the five mundane aggregates, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the two truths, the nineteen faculties, and the twelve-linked dependent origination. This inclusion through the aspect of all things is an entry into the teaching by way of the aggregates and so on. The terms 'root' or 'root discourse' refer to conceiving; in meaning, these are craving, conceit, and views, which are included in the aggregate of volitional formations. This is the entry by way of the aggregates. Similarly, 'inclusion through the sense base of phenomena and the element of phenomena' is the entry by way of the sense bases and elements. By 'uninstructed,' ignorance and the like, which are impediments to instruction, are included. By 'ordinary person,' those defilements and volitional formations are included by which one is called an ordinary person due to their generation and so on. By 'one who does not see the noble ones' and so on, those defilements are included by virtue of which one is a non-seer of the noble ones and so on; these are views, conceit, ignorance, and so on. All these are included in the aggregate of volitional formations. The entry should be understood in the manner stated previously. Here too, in 'perceives, conceives, directly knows, does not conceive'—since perceiving, conceiving, direct knowing, and contemplation are included in the aggregate of volitional formations, the entry should be understood in the manner stated previously. Similarly, by the inclusion of 'trainee,' trainees are included; by 'arahant' and so on, non-trainees, the aggregate of virtue, and so on, are included. Thus, the entry is by way of the aggregates, and also by way of the sense bases, elements, and so on. Similarly, by 'does not conceive'—through the rejection of grasping such as craving—contemplation of suffering and so on are included. By means of these, the entry should be understood through the door of the desireless liberation and so on. By 'fully understood,' the factors of enlightenment that arise through the function of full understanding are included. Thus, the entry should be understood by way of the foundations of mindfulness and so on. By the inclusion of delight, the inclusion of existence, and the inclusion of craving, the truth of origin is included. By the inclusion of suffering, the inclusion of birth, aging, and death, the truth of suffering is included. By 'the destruction of craving' and so on, the truth of cessation is included. By the inclusion of perfect awakening, the truth of the path is included. Thus, the entry is through the Noble Truths. This is the mode of entry.

13. Sodhanahāravaṇṇanā

13. Explanation of the Mode of Analysis
