“Sabbadhammamūlapariyāyaṃ vo, bhikkhave…pe… idha, bhikkhave, assutavā…pe… pathaviṃ pathavito sañjānātī”ti ārambho. “Pathaviṃ pathaviyā saññatvā pathaviṃ maññatī”ti padasuddhi, no ārambhasuddhi. Tathā “pathaviyā maññati pathavito maññati pathaviṃ meti maññati pathaviṃ abhinandatī”ti padasuddhi, no ārambhasuddhi. “Taṃ kissa hetu apariññātaṃ tassāti vadāmī”ti padasuddhi ceva ārambhasuddhi ca. Sesavāresupi eseva nayoti. Ayaṃ sodhano hāro.

The opening passage is: 'Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Root of All Things... Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person... perceives earth as earth.' 'Having perceived earth as earth, he conceives earth'—this is a correction of the phrase, not a correction of the opening. Similarly, 'he conceives in earth, he conceives from earth, he conceives "earth is mine," he delights in earth'—this is a correction of the phrase, not a correction of the opening. 'Why is that? Because it is not fully understood by him, I say'—this is a correction of both the phrase and the opening. The same method applies to the remaining instances. This is the mode of analysis.

14. Adhiṭṭhānahāravaṇṇanā

14. Explanation of the Mode of Designation

“Sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”nti ettha sabbadhammaggahaṇaṃ sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ. “Pathaviṃ āpa”ntiādi pana taṃ avikappetvā visesavacanaṃ. Tathā “mūlapariyāya”nti [M 1.0135] sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ avikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “pathaviṃ maññati…pe… abhinandatī”ti. “Pathaviṃ maññatī”ti ca sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ taṇhādiggāhānaṃ sādhāraṇattā maññanāya, taṃ avikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā”ti, evaṃ suttantarapadānipi ānetvā visesavacanaṃ niddhāretabbaṃ. Sesavāresupi eseva nayo. “Sekkho”ti sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ avikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “kāyasakkhī diṭṭhippatto saddhāvimutto saddhānusārī dhammānusārī”ti. Tathā “sekkho”ti sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ avikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sekkhāya sammādiṭṭhiyā samannāgato hoti…pe… sekkhena sammāsamādhinā samannāgato hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.13). “Araha”nti sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ avikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “ubhatobhāgavimutto paññāvimutto (pu. pa. 13.2; 15.1 mātikā), tevijjo chaḷabhiñño”ti (pu. pa. 7.26, 27 mātikā) ca. “Khīṇāsavo”ti sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ avikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, bhavāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccitthā”tiādi (pārā. 14). Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. “Abhijānātī”ti sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ avikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “maññatī”ti. Maññanābhāvo hissa pahānapaṭivedhasiddho, pahānapaṭivedho [V 1.0121] ca pariññāsacchikiriyābhāvanāpaṭivedhehi na vināti sabbepi abhiññāvisesā maññanāpaṭikkhepena atthato gahitāva hontīti. Tathā “araha”nti sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ avikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “vītarāgattā vītadosattā vītamohattā”ti. Iminā nayena sesapadesupi sāmaññavisesaniddhāraṇā veditabbā. Ayaṃ adhiṭṭhāno hāro.

Here, in 'The Root of All Things,' the inclusion of 'all things' is a general designation. But 'earth, water,' and so on, are specific expressions without differentiating that. Similarly, 'root discourse' is a general designation, and without differentiating it, the specific expressions are 'he conceives earth... delights in it.' And 'he conceives earth' is a general designation, since conceiving is common to grasping such as craving. Without differentiating it, the specific expressions are 'this is mine, this I am, this is my self.' In this way, the specific expressions should be determined by bringing in terms even from other suttas. The same method applies to the remaining instances. 'A trainee' is a general designation, and without differentiating it, the specific expressions are 'a body-witness, one attained to view, one liberated by faith, a faith-follower, a Dhamma-follower.' Similarly, 'a trainee' is a general designation, and without differentiating it, the specific expressions are 'Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with a trainee’s right view... endowed with a trainee’s right concentration' (SN 5.13). 'An arahant' is a general designation, and without differentiating it, the specific expressions are 'one liberated in both ways, one liberated by wisdom' (Pug. 13.2; 15.1 mātikā), and 'one possessing the three knowledges, one possessing the six supernormal powers' (Pug. 7.26, 27 mātikā). 'One whose taints are destroyed' is a general designation, and without differentiating it, the specific expressions are 'his mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, his mind was liberated from the taint of existence,' and so on (Pārā. 14). The same method applies to the remaining terms. 'He directly knows' is a general designation, and without differentiating it, the specific expression is 'he conceives.' For him, the absence of conceiving is established by abandoning and penetration; and abandoning and penetration are not without penetration by full understanding, realization, and development. Therefore, all special direct knowledges are indeed grasped in meaning by the rejection of conceiving. Similarly, 'an arahant' is a general designation, and without differentiating it, the specific expressions are 'due to being free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion.' In this way, the determination of general and specific should be understood in the remaining terms as well. This is the mode of designation.

14. Parikkhārahāravaṇṇanā

14. Explanation of the Requisites Mode

“Sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”nti ettha sabbadhammā nāma pariyāpannadhammā, te kusalākusalābyākatabhedena tividhā. Tesu kusalānaṃ yonisomanasikāro alobhādayo ca hetū, akusalānaṃ ayonisomanasikāro lobhādayo ca hetū, abyākatesu vipākānaṃ yathāsakaṃ kammaṃ, itaresaṃ bhavaṅgamāvajjanasamannāhārādi ca hetū. Ettha ca sappurisūpanissayādiko paccayo hetumhi eva samavaruḷho, so tattha [M 1.0136] ādi-saddena saṅgahitoti daṭṭhabbo. “Mūla”nti vuttānaṃ maññanānaṃ hetubhāvo pāḷiyaṃ vutto eva. Maññanāsu pana taṇhāmaññanāya assādānupassanā hetu. “Saññojaniyesu dhammesu assādānupassino taṇhā pavaḍḍhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.52) hi vuttaṃ. Mānamaññanāya diṭṭhivippayuttalobho hetu kevalaṃ saṃsaggavasena “ahamasmī”ti pavattanato. Diṭṭhimaññanāya ekattanayādīnaṃ ayāthāvaggāho hetu, assutabhāvo puthujjanabhāvassa hetu, so ariyānaṃ adassanasīlatāya, sā ariyadhammassa akovidatāya, sā ariyadhamme avinītatāya hetu, sabbā cāyaṃ hetuparamparā pathavīādīsu “etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā”ti tissannaṃ maññanānaṃ hetu, sekkhārahādibhāvā pana mattaso sabbaso ca maññanābhāvassa hetūti. Ayaṃ parikkhāro hāro.

Here, in 'The Root of All Things,' 'all things' means included phenomena, which are threefold by division into wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. For the wholesome among them, wise attention and non-greed, etc., are the causes. For the unwholesome, unwise attention and greed, etc., are the causes. For the indeterminate, the respective kamma is the cause for resultant states; for the others, life-continuum, adverting, preparing, etc., are the causes. And here, the condition of reliance on good persons, etc., is included within the cause itself; it should be understood as included there by the word 'etc.' The fact that the conceivings called 'root' are a cause is stated in the Pāli text itself. Among the conceivings, the contemplation of gratification is the cause for the conceiving of craving. For it is said: 'For one who contemplates gratification in things that are fetters, craving increases' (SN 2.52). For the conceiving of conceit, greed dissociated from views is the cause, because it arises as 'I am' merely by way of association. For the conceiving of view, the incorrect grasping of the method of oneness, etc., is the cause. Not having heard is the cause of being an ordinary person; that is due to the habit of not seeing the noble ones, which is due to not being skilled in the noble Dhamma, which is due to not being trained in the noble Dhamma. This entire chain of causes is the cause for the three conceivings regarding earth, etc.: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.' The states of being a trainee, an arahant, etc., however, are the causes for the partial and complete absence of conceiving. This is the requisites mode.

16. Samāropanahāravaṇṇanā

16. Explanation of the Samāropaṇa Mode

“Sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”ntiādīsu mūlapariyāyaggahaṇena assutavāgahaṇena sañjānanamaññanāpariññāgahaṇehi ca saṃkilesadhammā dassitā, te ca saṅkhepato tividhā taṇhāsaṃkileso diṭṭhisaṃkileso duccaritasaṃkilesoti. Tattha taṇhāsaṃkileso taṇhāsaṃkilesassa, diṭṭhisaṃkilesassa, duccaritasaṃkilesassa ca padaṭṭhānaṃ, tathā diṭṭhisaṃkileso diṭṭhisaṃkilesassa, taṇhāsaṃkilesassa, duccaritasaṃkilesassa ca padaṭṭhānaṃ, duccaritasaṃkilesopi duccaritasaṃkilesassa, taṇhāsaṃkilesassa, diṭṭhisaṃkilesassa ca padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tesu taṇhāsaṃkileso atthato lobhova, yo “lobho lubbhanā lubbhitattaṃ sārāgo sārajjanā sārajjitatta”ntiādinā [V 1.0122] (dha. sa. 389) anekehi pariyāyehi vibhatto. Tathā diṭṭhiyeva diṭṭhisaṃkileso, yo “diṭṭhigataṃ diṭṭhigahanaṃ diṭṭhikantāro diṭṭhivisūkaṃ diṭṭhivipphandita”ntiādinā (dha. sa. 1105) anekehi pariyāyehi, “santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.30) dvāsaṭṭhiyā pabhedehi ca vibhatto. Duccaritasaṃkileso pana atthato dussīlyacetanā ceva cetanāsampayuttadhammā ca, yā “kāyaduccaritaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ kāyavisamaṃ vacīvisama”nti (vibha. 913, 924), “pāṇātipāto adinnādāna”nti (vibha. 913) ca ādinā anekehi pariyāyehi, anekehi pabhedehi ca vibhattā.

In the 'Discourse on the Root of All Things' and so on, the defilements are shown by the grasping of the Root Discourse, by the grasping of the uninstructed person, and by the grasping of perceiving, conceiving, and full understanding. These are briefly threefold: the defilement of craving, the defilement of views, and the defilement of misconduct. Among these, the defilement of craving serves as the proximate cause for the defilement of craving itself, the defilement of views, and the defilement of misconduct. Similarly, the defilement of views serves as the proximate cause for the defilement of views itself, the defilement of craving, and the defilement of misconduct. Likewise, the defilement of misconduct also serves as the proximate cause for the defilement of misconduct itself, the defilement of craving, and the defilement of views. Herein, the defilement of craving is, in essence, greed, which is analyzed in many ways, such as 'greed, greediness, the state of being greedy, passion, passionateness, the state of being passionate,' and so on (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 389). Similarly, the defilement of views is simply view, which is analyzed in many ways, such as 'a resort to views, a jungle of views, a wilderness of views, a contortion of views, a vacillation of views,' and so on (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1105), and also by its sixty-two kinds, as in 'There are, monks, some ascetics and brahmins...' (Dīgha Nikāya 1.30). The defilement of misconduct, however, is essentially immoral volition and the mental states associated with that volition, which are analyzed in many ways, such as 'bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, bodily crookedness, verbal crookedness' (Vibhaṅga 913, 924), and 'the destruction of living beings, taking what is not given,' and so on (Vibhaṅga 913), as well as in many kinds.

Tesu [M 1.0137] taṇhāsaṃkilesassa samatho paṭipakkho, diṭṭhisaṃkilesassa vipassanā, duccaritasaṃkilesassa sīlaṃ paṭipakkho. Te pana sīlādayo dhammā idha pariññāgahaṇena sekkhaggahaṇena “araha”ntiādinā ariyatādiggahaṇena ca gahitā. Tattha sīlena duccaritasaṃkilesappahānaṃ sijjhati, tathā tadaṅgappahānaṃ vītikkamappahānañca, samathena taṇhāsaṃkilesappahānaṃ sijjhati, tathā vikkhambhanappahānaṃ pariyuṭṭhānappahānañca. Vipassanāya diṭṭhisaṃkilesappahānaṃ sijjhati, tathā samucchedappahānaṃ anusayappahānañca. Tattha pubbabhāge sīle patiṭṭhitassa samatho, samathe patiṭṭhitassa vipassanā, maggakkhaṇe pana samakālameva bhavanti. Pubbeyeva hi suparisuddhakāyavacīkammassa suparisuddhājīvassa ca samathavipassanā āraddhā gabbhaṃ gaṇhantiyo paripākaṃ gacchantiyo vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanaṃ paribrūhenti, vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchantī maggena ghaṭenti maggakkhaṇe samathavipassanā paripūreti. Atha maggakkhaṇe samathavipassanābhāvanāpāripūriyā anavasesasaṃkilesadhammaṃ samucchindantiyo nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikarontīti. Ayaṃ samāropano hāro.

Among these, for the defilement of craving, serenity is the counterpart; for the defilement of views, insight is the counterpart; for the defilement of misconduct, virtue is the counterpart. These qualities—virtue and so on—are here grasped through the grasping of full understanding, through the grasping of the trainee, and through the grasping of nobility and so on, as in the term 'arahant.' Therein, through virtue, the abandoning of the defilement of misconduct is accomplished, as well as abandoning by substitution and abandoning by transgression. Through serenity, the abandoning of the defilement of craving is accomplished, as well as abandoning by suppression and abandoning of obsession. Through insight, the abandoning of the defilement of views is accomplished, as well as abandoning by eradication and abandoning of latent tendencies. In the preliminary stage, for one established in virtue, there is serenity; for one established in serenity, there is insight. But at the moment of the path, they occur simultaneously. For even beforehand, serenity and insight, when undertaken by one whose bodily and verbal actions are thoroughly purified and whose livelihood is thoroughly purified, take hold, mature, and develop insight that leads to emergence. Insight that leads to emergence, reaching the culmination of development, connects with the path. At the moment of the path, serenity and insight reach fulfillment. Then, at the moment of the path, through the fulfilled development of serenity and insight, they eradicate all defiled states without remainder and realize cessation, Nibbāna. This is the Samāropana mode.

Soḷasahāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Sixteen Modes is concluded.

Pañcavidhanayavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Fivefold Method

1. Nandiyāvaṭṭanayavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Method of the Auspicious Swastika

“Sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”ntiādīsu [V 1.0123] sabbadhammamūlaggahaṇena maññanāgahaṇena ca taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiyo gahitā. Maññanānampi hi maññanā kāraṇanti dassitoyamattho. “Assutavā”tiādinā avijjāmānadiṭṭhiyo gahitā, sabbepi vā saṃkilesadhammā, tathā saññāapariññātaggahaṇena. “Khīṇāsavo parikkhīṇabhavasaññojano”ti ettha pana āsavā saññojanāni ca sarūpato gahitāni, tathā nandiggahaṇena taṇhāgahaṇena ca taṇhā, evampettha sarūpato pariyāyato ca taṇhā avijjā tappakkhiyadhammā ca gahitā. Tattha taṇhāya visesato rūpadhammā adhiṭṭhānaṃ, avijjāya arūpadhammā, te pana sabbadhammaggahaṇena pathavīādiggahaṇena ca dassitā eva. Tāsaṃ samatho vipassanā ca paṭipakkho, tesamettha gahetabbākāro heṭṭhā dassito eva. Samathassa cetovimutti phalaṃ[M 1.0138], vipassanāya paññāvimutti. Tathā hi tā “rāgavirāgā”tiādinā visesetvā vuccanti, imāsamettha gahaṇaṃ sammadaññāvimuttavītarāgādivacanehi veditabbaṃ. Tattha taṇhāvijjā samudayasaccaṃ, tappakkhiyadhammā pana taggahaṇeneva gahitāti veditabbā. Tesaṃ adhiṭṭhānabhūtā vuttappabhedā rūpārūpadhammā dukkhasaccaṃ, tesaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhapajānanā paṭipadā maggasaccaṃ. Taṇhāgahaṇena cettha māyā-sāṭheyya-mānātimāna-madappamāda-pāpicchatā-pāpamittatā-ahirikānottappādivasena akusalapakkho netabbo, avijjāgahaṇena viparītamanasikāra-kodhūpanāha-makkha-paḷāsa-issā-macchariya- sārambhadovacassatā-bhavadiṭṭhi-vibhavadiṭṭhiādivasena akusalapakkho netabbo, vuttavipariyāyena amāyāasāṭheyyādiaviparītamanasikārādivasena, tathā samathapakkhiyānaṃ saddhindriyādīnaṃ vipassanāpakkhiyānaṃ aniccasaññādīnañca vasena vodānapakkho netabboti. Ayaṃ nandiyāvaṭṭassa na yassa bhūmi.

In the 'Discourse on the Root of All Things' and so on, craving, conceit, and views are grasped through the grasping of 'the root of all things' and through the grasping of conceiving. For it is shown that the cause of conceivings is conceiving. Through 'the uninstructed person' and so on, ignorance, conceit, and views are grasped, or indeed all defiled states, and likewise through the grasping of uncomprehended perception. In the phrase 'one whose taints are destroyed, whose fetters of existence are exhausted,' the taints and fetters are grasped according to their own nature. Similarly, through the grasping of delight and the grasping of craving, craving is grasped. Thus, here craving, ignorance, and their associated states are grasped both in their own nature and by way of method. Among these, material phenomena are the particular basis for craving, while immaterial phenomena are the basis for ignorance. These, however, are shown by the grasping of 'all phenomena' and by the grasping of 'earth,' etc. Their counterparts are serenity and insight, and the manner of grasping them here has already been shown below. The fruit of serenity is liberation of mind, while that of insight is liberation by wisdom. For they are specified by such phrases as 'through dispassion for lust,' and their grasping here should be understood through terms like 'rightly knowing and liberated, free from lust,' etc. Here, craving and ignorance are the truth of the origin, and their associated states should be understood as grasped by the grasping of them. The material and immaterial phenomena of the kinds mentioned, which are their basis, are the truth of suffering. Their non-occurrence is the truth of cessation, and the path is the full understanding of cessation. Through the grasping of craving, the unwholesome side should be inferred by way of deceit, fraud, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, negligence, evil wishes, bad friendship, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread, etc. Through the grasping of ignorance, the unwholesome side should be inferred by way of wrong attention, anger, hostility, contempt, insolence, envy, stinginess, contention, difficulty in being admonished, the view of existence, and the view of non-existence, etc. Conversely, by way of the absence of deceit, fraud, etc., and by way of right attention, etc., and also by way of the factors on the side of serenity—such as the faculty of faith—and the factors on the side of insight—such as the perception of impermanence—the side of purification should be inferred. This is the domain of the method of the auspicious swastika.

2. Tipukkhalanayavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Method of the Triad

Tathā vuttanayena sarūpato pariyāyato ca gahitesu taṇhāvijjātappakkhiyadhammesu taṇhā lobho, avijjā moho, avijjāya sampayutto lohite sati pubbo viya taṇhāya sati sijjhamāno āghāto doso, iti tīhi akusalamūlehi gahitehi, tappaṭipakkhato maññanāpaṭikkhepapariññāgahaṇādīhi ca kusalamūlāni siddhāniyeva honti. Idhāpi “lobho sabbāni [V 1.0124] vā sāsavakusalākusalamūlāni samudayasaccaṃ, tehi nibbattā, tesaṃ adhiṭṭhānagocarabhūtā ca upādānakkhandhā dukkhasacca”ntiādinā saccayojanā veditabbā. Phalaṃ panettha tayo vimokkhā, tīhi pana akusalamūlehi tividhaduccarita-saṃkilesamala-visamaakusala-saññā-vitakkādivasena akusalapakkho netabbo. Tathā tīhi kusalamūlehi tividhasucarita-samakusala-saññā-vitakka-saddhamma-samādhi-vimokkhamukha-vimokkhā-divasena kusalapakkho netabboti. Ayaṃ tipukkhalassa nayassa bhūmi.

Among the states of craving, ignorance, and their associates, grasped in their own nature and by way of method in the manner thus stated, craving is greed, ignorance is delusion, and hatred is aversion, which, being associated with ignorance, is accomplished in the presence of craving, like pus in the presence of blood. Thus, when the three unwholesome roots are grasped, the wholesome roots are indeed established by their counterparts, such as the rejection of conceiving, the grasping of full understanding, and so on. Here too, the application of the truths should be understood thus: 'Greed and all the wholesome and unwholesome roots accompanied by taints are the truth of the origin; the aggregates of clinging, which are produced by them and which are their basis and object, are the truth of suffering,' and so on. Here the fruit is the three liberations. The unwholesome side should be inferred by way of the three unwholesome roots in terms of threefold misconduct, defilement, impurity, improper unwholesome perceptions and thoughts, etc. Similarly, the wholesome side should be inferred by way of the three wholesome roots in terms of threefold good conduct, proper wholesome perceptions and thoughts, the true Dhamma, concentration, the entrances to liberation, liberation, etc. This is the domain of the method of the triad.

3. Sīhavikkīḷitanayavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Method of the Lion's Sport

Tathā vuttanayena sarūpato pariyāyato ca gahitesu taṇhāvijjātappakkhiyadhammesu visesato taṇhādiṭṭhīnaṃ vasena asubhe “subha”nti[M 1.0139], dukkhe “sukha”nti ca vipallāsā, avijjādiṭṭhīnaṃ vasena anicce “nicca”nti, anattani “attā”ti ca vipallāsā veditabbā. Tesaṃ paṭipakkhato maññanāpaṭikkhepapariññāgahaṇādisiddhehi sativīriyasamādhipaññindriyehi cattāri satipaṭṭhānāni siddhāneva honti. Tattha catūhi indriyehi cattāro puggalā niddisitabbā. Kathaṃ? Duvidho hi taṇhācarito mudindriyo tikkhindriyoti, tathā diṭṭhicarito. Tesaṃ paṭhamo asubhe “subha”nti vipariyāsaggāhī satibalena yathābhūtaṃ kāyasabhāvaṃ sallakkhento taṃ vipallāsaṃ samugghāṭetvā sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamati. Dutiyo asukhe “sukha”nti vipariyāsaggāhī “uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 3.310; ma. ni. 1.26; a. ni. 4.14, 114; a. ni. 6.58) vuttena vīriyasaṃvarabhūtena vīriyabalena taṃ vipallāsaṃ vidhamento sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamati. Tatiyo anicce “nicca”nti ayāthāvaggāhī samādhibalena samāhitacitto saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇikabhāvasallakkhaṇena taṃ vipallāsaṃ samugghāṭento ariyabhūmiṃ okkamati. Catuttho santatisamūhakiccārammaṇaghanavañcitatāya phassādidhammapuñjamatte anattani “attā”ti micchābhinivesī catukoṭikasuññatāmanasikārena taṃ micchābhinivesaṃ viddhaṃsento sāmaññaphalaṃ sacchikaroti.

In the manner stated, when craving, ignorance, and their associated states are grasped in their own nature and by way of method, it should be understood that, specifically due to craving and views, there are distortions—perceiving the foul as 'beautiful' and suffering as 'pleasurable.' Due to ignorance and views, there are distortions—perceiving the impermanent as 'permanent' and non-self as 'self.' As their opposites, the four foundations of mindfulness are indeed established through the faculties of mindfulness, energy, concentration, and wisdom, which are perfected by means of rejecting conceiving, grasping full understanding, and so forth. Herein, four types of individuals are to be distinguished by these four faculties. How? The one of craving-temperament is twofold: one with dull faculties and one with sharp faculties; likewise for the one of speculative-temperament. The first, who grasps the distortion of perceiving the foul as 'beautiful,' discerns the true nature of the body with the power of mindfulness, uproots that distortion, and enters the fixed course of rightness. The second, who grasps the distortion of perceiving the unpleasant as 'pleasurable,' dispels that distortion with the power of energy—which is restraint through energy, as stated: 'He does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual pleasure,' and so on—and enters the fixed course of rightness. The third, who wrongly grasps the impermanent as 'permanent,' with a mind concentrated through the power of concentration, uproots that distortion by discerning the momentary nature of formations and enters the noble stage. The fourth, deceived by the compactness of continuity, collection, function, and object, wrongly adheres to non-self as 'self' in what is merely a mass of phenomena such as contact. By shattering that wrong adherence through the contemplation of emptiness in four aspects, he realizes the fruit of recluseship.

Idhāpi subhasaññāsukhasaññāhi catūhipi vā vipallāsehi samudayasaccaṃ, tesaṃ adhiṭṭhānārammaṇabhūtā pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhasaccantiādinā saccayojanā veditabbā. Phalaṃ panettha cattāri sāmaññaphalāni, catūhi cittavipallāsehi caturāsavogha-yoga-kāyagantha-agati-taṇhuppāda-sallupādāna-viññāṇaṭṭhiti-apariññādivasena akusalapakkho netabbo. Tathā catūhi satipaṭṭhānehi [V 1.0125] catubbidhajhāna-vihārādhiṭṭhāna-sukhabhāgiyadhamma-appamaññā-sammappadhāna-iddhipādā- divasena vodānapakkho netabboti. Ayaṃ sīhavikkīḷitassa nayassa bhūmi.

Here too, the application of the truths should be understood thus: the truth of the origin is through the perceptions of beauty and pleasure, or through all four distortions; and the five aggregates subject to clinging, which serve as their basis and object, are the truth of suffering. The result here is the four fruits of recluseship. The unwholesome side is to be understood through the four mental distortions, in terms of the four taints, floods, yokes, bodily knots, wrong courses, arising of craving, darts, clinging, stations of consciousness, non-full-understanding, and so on. Likewise, the side of purification is to be understood through the four foundations of mindfulness, in terms of the four kinds of jhānic abidings, determinations, states partaking of happiness, illimitables, right strivings, bases of spiritual power, and so on. This is the ground for the method of the lion’s sport.

4-5. Disālocana-aṅkusanayadvayavaṇṇanā

4-5. Explanation of the Two Methods: Directional Analysis and the Goad.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇaṃ atthanayānaṃ siddhiyā vohārena nayadvayaṃ siddhameva hoti. Tathā hi atthanayānaṃ disābhūtadhammānaṃ samālocanaṃ disālocanaṃ, tesaṃ samānayanaṃ aṅkusoti pañcapi nayā niyuttāti veditabbā.

Now, for the accomplishment of these three methods of meaning, two methods of expression are indeed established. For, regarding the methods of meaning, the thorough consideration of phenomena that are directions is Directional Analysis, and the bringing together of those phenomena is the Goad. Thus, the five methods should be understood as being employed.

Pañcavidhanayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Fivefold Method is concluded.

Sāsanapaṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Establishment of the Dispensation

Idañca [M 1.0140] suttaṃ soḷasavidhe suttantapaṭṭhāne saṃkilesanibbedhāsekkhabhāgiyaṃ, sabbabhāgiyameva vā “sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”nti ettha sabbadhammaggahaṇena lokiyakusalānampi saṅgahitattā. Aṭṭhavīsatividhena pana suttantapaṭṭhāne lokiyalokuttarasabbadhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ ñāṇañeyyaṃ dassanabhāvanaṃ sakavacanaṃ vissajjanīyaṃ kusalākusalaṃ anuññātaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ cāti veditabbaṃ.

This sutta is included in the sixteenfold classification of suttas as pertaining to defilement, penetration, and the non-trainee's portion. Alternatively, it is entirely comprehensive, as indicated by the phrase 'the discourse on the root of all phenomena,' since the term 'all phenomena' here includes even worldly wholesome states. In the twenty-eightfold classification of suttas, it should be understood as establishing all phenomena, both worldly and supramundane: knowledge and the knowable, seeing and cultivation, one's own utterance, exposition, the wholesome and unwholesome, the permitted and the prohibited.

Nettinayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Netti Method is concluded.

Mūlapariyāyasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Exposition of the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, the Clarification of its Hidden Meanings, is completed.

2. Sabbāsavasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Discourse on All Taints

14. Apubbapadavaṇṇanāti [V 1.0126] atthasaṃvaṇṇanāvasena heṭṭhā aggahitatāya apubbassa abhinavassa padassa vaṇṇanā atthavibhajanā. “Hitvā punappunāgatamattha”nti hi vuttaṃ. Nivāsaṭṭhānabhūtā bhūtapubbanivāsaṭṭhānabhūtā, nivāsaṭṭhāne vā bhūtā nibbattā nivāsaṭṭhānabhūtā, tattha māpitāti attho. Yathā kākandī mākandī kosambīti yathā kākandassa isino nivāsaṭṭhāne māpitā nagarī kākandī, mākandassa nivāsaṭṭhāne māpitā mākandī, kusambassanivāsaṭṭhāne māpitā kosambīti vuccati, evaṃ sāvatthīti dasseti. Upanetvā samīpe katvā bhuñjitabbato upabhogo, saviññāṇakavatthu. Parito sabbadā bhuñjitabbato paribhogo, nivāsanapārupanādi aviññāṇakavatthu. Sabbamettha atthīti niruttinayena sāvatthī-saddasiddhimāha. Satthasamāyogeti satthassa nagariyā samāgame, satthe taṃ nagaraṃ upagateti attho. Pucchite satthikajanehi.

14. Explanation of an unprecedented word: This is the explanation, the analysis of meaning, of a new, unprecedented word whose meaning was not previously grasped, by way of explaining its meaning. For it is said: 'Having abandoned the meaning that has come up again and again.' The term 'nivāsaṭṭhānabhūtā' means a place that served as a dwelling in the past, or a place that came into existence in a dwelling place, or a place established as a dwelling; the meaning is that it was built there. Just as the cities Kākandī, Mākandī, and Kosambī are said to be named after the dwelling places of the sages Kākanda, Mākanda, and Kusamba, respectively—so too, he shows, is Sāvatthī. Because it is to be enjoyed after bringing it near, it is 'upabhoga' (use); this refers to animate things. Because it is to be enjoyed all around at all times, it is 'paribhoga' (enjoyment); this refers to inanimate things such as dwellings and clothing. He states the derivation of the word Sāvatthī by the etymological method as 'Everything exists here.' 'Satthasamāyoge' means: at the meeting of the caravan with the city; the meaning is, when the caravan arrived at that city. When asked by the people of the caravan.

Samohitanti sannicitaṃ. Rammanti anto bahi ca bhūmibhāgasampattiyā ceva ārāmuyyānasampattiyā ca ramaṇīyaṃ. Dassaneyyanti visikhāsannivesasampattiyā ceva pāsādakūṭāgārādisampattiyā ca dassanīyaṃ passitabbayuttaṃ. Upabhogaparibhogavatthusampattiyā ceva nivāsasukhatāya ca nibaddhavāsaṃ vasantānaṃ itaresañca sattānaṃ manaṃ rametīti manoramaṃ. Dasahi saddehīti hatthisaddo, assa-ratha-bheri-saṅkha-mudiṅga-vīṇā-gīta sammatāḷasaddo, asnātha-pivatha-khādathāti-saddoti [M 1.0141] imehi dasahi saddehi. Avivittanti na vivittaṃ, sabbakālaṃ ghositanti attho.

'Samohitaṃ' means 'well-gathered' (sannicitaṃ). 'Rammaṃ' means 'delightful' (ramaṇīyaṃ) both inside and outside due to the excellence of the land and the excellence of its parks and gardens. 'Dassaneyyaṃ' means 'worth seeing' (dassanīyaṃ), 'fit to be seen' (passitabbayuttaṃ), due to the excellence of its street layout and the excellence of its palaces, gabled houses, and other buildings. It is called 'manoramaṃ' because it delights the minds of those who dwell there permanently and of other beings, through the excellence of goods for use and enjoyment and the comfort of residence. 'Dasahi saddehi' refers to ten sounds: the sound of elephants, horses, chariots, kettledrums, conch shells, mudiṅga drums, lutes, singing, cymbals, and the sounds of 'eat, drink, consume.' 'Avivittaṃ' means 'not secluded' (na vivittaṃ); the meaning is 'always resounding' (sabbakālaṃ ghositaṃ).

Vuddhiṃ vepullataṃ pattanti tannivāsī sattavuddhiyā vuddhiṃ, tāya parivuddhitāyeva vipulabhāvaṃ pattaṃ, bahujanaṃ ākiṇṇamanussanti attho. Vittūpakaraṇasamiddhiyā iddhaṃ. Sabbakālaṃ subhikkhabhāvena phītaṃ. Antamaso vighāsāde upādāya sabbesaṃ kapaṇaddhikavanibbakayācakānampi icchi tatthanipphattiyā manuññaṃ jātaṃ, pageva issariye ṭhitānanti dassanatthaṃ puna “manorama”nti vuttaṃ. Aḷakamandāvāti āṭānāṭādīsu dasasu vessavaṇamahārājassa nagarīsu aḷakamandā nāma ekā nagarī, yā loke aḷākā eva vuccati[V 1.0127]. Sā yathā puññakammīnaṃ āvāsabhūtā ārāmarāmaṇeyyakādinā sobhaggappattā, evaṃ sāvatthīpīti vuttaṃ “aḷakamandāvā”ti. Devānanti vessavaṇapakkhiyānaṃ cātumahārājikadevānaṃ.

'Vuddhiṃ vepullataṃ pattaṃ' (it has reached growth and abundance) means that through the growth of the beings dwelling there, it has attained growth, and through that very growth, it has attained an expansive state, meaning it is crowded with many people. It is 'iddhaṃ' (prosperous) with wealth and resources. It is 'phītaṃ' (flourishing) at all times with plentiful food. Even for all the poor, travelers, merchants, and beggars, down to eaters of leftovers, their desires are fulfilled there, making it agreeable; how much more so for those in positions of power. To illustrate this, it is again called 'manoramaṃ' (delightful). 'Aḷakamandāvā' (like Alakamandā) refers to Alakamandā, one of the ten cities of the great King Vessavaṇa, among Āṭānāṭā and others; in the world it is simply called Alakā. Just as that city serves as a dwelling place for those who have done meritorious deeds and is beautiful with delightful parks and groves, so too is Sāvatthī—hence it is called 'like Alakamandā.' 'Devānaṃ' (of the gods) refers to the Cātumahārājika deities, those belonging to Vessavaṇa’s party.

Jinātīti iminā sota-saddo viya kattusādhano jeta-saddoti dasseti. Raññāti pasenadikosalarājena. Rājagataṃ jayaṃ āropetvā kumāro jitavāti jetoti vutto. Maṅgalakabyatāyātiādinā “jeyyo”ti etasmiṃ atthe “jeto”ti vuttanti dasseti. Sabbakāmasamiddhitāyāti sabbehi upabhogaparibhogavatthūhi phītabhāvena vibhavasampannatāyāti attho. Samiddhāpi maccharino kiñci na dentīti āha “vigatamalamaccheratāyā”ti, rāgadosādimalānañceva macchariyassa ca abhāvenāti attho. Samiddhā amaccharinopi ca karuṇāsaddhādiguṇavirahitā attano santakaṃ paresaṃ na dadeyyunti āha “karuṇādiguṇasamaṅgitāya cā”ti. Tenāti anāthānaṃ piṇḍadānena. Saddatthato pana dātabbabhāvena sabbakālaṃ upaṭṭhapito anāthānaṃ piṇḍo etassa atthīti anāthapiṇḍiko. Pañcavidhasenāsanaṅgasampattiyāti “nātidūraṃ naccāsannaṃ gamanāgamanasampanna”nti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, “divā appākiṇṇaṃ rattiṃ appasaddaṃ appanigghosa”nti ekaṃ, “appaḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassa”nti ekaṃ, “tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane viharantassa appakasirena uppajjanti cīvara…pe… parikkhārā”ti ekaṃ, “tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane therā bhikkhū viharanti bahussutā”ti ekaṃ, evametehi pañcavidhasenāsanaṅgehi sampannatāya. Yadi jetavanaṃ tathaṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmoti āha “so hī”tiādi.

"Jināti" (he conquers): by this, it shows that the word 'jeta' is an agentive formation (kattusādhana), like the word 'sota'. "Raññā" (by the king): meaning by King Pasenadi of Kosala. Having attributed the victory belonging to the king to the prince, he was called 'Jeta' because he was victorious. By way of auspicious poetic convention, etc., it shows that 'jeto' is used in the sense of 'jeyyo'. "Sabbakāmasamiddhitāya" (by the fulfillment of all wishes): meaning abundance due to being filled with all objects of enjoyment and use, that is, endowed with prosperity. Since even the wealthy who are miserly give nothing, he says, "vigatamalamaccheratāya" (free from the taint of stinginess), meaning the absence of the taints of greed, hatred, etc., as well as stinginess. And since even the wealthy who are not miserly but lack qualities like compassion and faith would not give their possessions to others, he says, "karuṇādiguṇasamaṅgitāya ca" (and endowed with qualities like compassion). "Tena" (by this): meaning by giving alms to the unprotected. But according to the meaning of the word, he is Anāthapiṇḍika because the alms for the unprotected are always supplied, being fit to be given. "Pañcavidhasenāsanaṅgasampattiyā" (by possession of the five aspects of a suitable dwelling), meaning: 1. "Not too far, not too near, convenient for coming and going," this is one aspect. 2. "During the day, uncrowded; at night, quiet and without noise," this is one aspect. 3. "Free from the touch of gnats, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping things," this is one aspect. 4. "For one dwelling in that dwelling, robes... and other requisites arise with little difficulty," this is one aspect. 5. "In that dwelling, elder monks dwell, learned," this is one aspect. Thus, by being endowed with these five aspects of a suitable dwelling. If Jetavana is such, then it is Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery; thus it is said, "so indeed," etc.

Kītakālato [M 1.0142] paṭṭhāya anāthapiṇḍikasseva taṃ vanaṃ, atha kasmā ubhinnaṃ parikittananti āha “jetavane”tiādi. “Yadipi so bhūmibhāgo koṭisantharena mahāseṭṭhinā kīto, rukkhā pana jetena na vikkītāti jetavananti vattabbataṃ labhī”ti vadanti.

From the time of its purchase, that grove belonged to Anāthapiṇḍika alone. So why is it celebrated under both names? He said, "Jetavana," etc. They say: "Even though that piece of land was bought by the great merchant by spreading crores, the trees were not sold by Jeta, therefore it came to be called Jetavana."

Kasmā idaṃ suttamabhāsīti kathetukamyatāya suttanikkhepaṃ pucchati. Sāmaññato hi bhagavato desanākāraṇaṃ pākaṭamevāti. Ko panāyaṃ suttanikkhepoti? Attajjhāsayo. Parehi anajjhiṭṭho eva hi bhagavā attano ajjhāsayena imaṃ suttaṃ desetīti ācariyā. Yasmā panesa bhikkhūnaṃ upakkiliṭṭhacittataṃ viditvā “ime bhikkhū imāya desanāya upakkilesavisodhanaṃ katvā āsavakkhayāya paṭipajjissantī”ti ayaṃ desanā āraddhā, tasmā parajjhāsayoti apare. Ubhayampi pana yuttaṃ. Attajjhāsayādīnañhi saṃsaggabhedassa sambhavo heṭṭhā dassitovāti. Tesaṃ bhikkhūnanti tadā dhammapaṭiggāhatabhikkhūnaṃ. Upakkilesavisodhananti samathavipassanupakkilesato [V 1.0128] cittassa visodhanaṃ. Paṭhamañhi bhagavā anupubbikathādinā paṭipattiyā saṃkilesaṃ nīharitvā pacchā sāmukkaṃsikaṃ desanaṃ deseti khette khāṇukaṇṭakagumbādike avaharitvā kasanaṃ viya, tasmā kammaṭṭhānameva avatvā imāya anupubbiyā desanā pavattāti adhippāyo.

Why was this discourse spoken? He asks about the introduction of the discourse out of a desire to speak. Indeed, in general, the reason for the Blessed One’s teaching is quite evident. But what is this introduction of the discourse? It is the inclination of the self (attajjhāsayo). For the Blessed One, unasked by others, teaches this discourse out of his own inclination—so say the teachers. Moreover, knowing the defiled minds of the monks, thinking, "These monks, having purified their defilements through this teaching, will practice for the destruction of the taints," this teaching was undertaken—therefore, it is the inclination of others (parajjhāsayo), say others. Both, however, are fitting. For the possibility of combination and distinction of self-inclination and the like has been shown below. "Tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ" (of those monks): meaning the monks who were receptive to the Dhamma at that time. "Upakkilesavisodhanaṃ" (purification from defilements): meaning the cleansing of the mind from the defilements relating to serenity and insight. First, the Blessed One removes the defilements related to practice through gradual instruction and the like, and afterward teaches the exalted teaching—just as plowing is done after removing stumps, thorns, and bushes from the field. Therefore, without even mentioning the meditation subject, the teaching proceeds through this gradual method—this is the meaning.

Saṃvarabhūtanti sīlasaṃvarādisaṃvarabhūtaṃ saṃvaraṇasabhāvaṃ kāraṇaṃ, taṃ pana atthato dassanādi evāti veditabbaṃ. Saṃvaritāti pavattituṃ appadānavasena sammā, sabbathā vā vāritā. Evaṃbhūtā ca yasmā pavattidvārapidhānena pihitā nāma honti, tasmā vuttaṃ “vidahitā hutvā”ti. Evaṃ accantikassa saṃvarassa kāraṇabhūtaṃ anaccantikaṃ saṃvaraṃ dassetvā idāni accantikameva saṃvaraṃ dassento yasmiṃ dassanādimhi sati uppajjanārahā āsavā na uppajjanti, so tesaṃ anuppādo nirodho khayo pahānanti ca vuccamāno atthato appavattimattanti tassa ca dassanādi kāraṇanti āha “yena kāraṇena anuppādanirodhasaṅkhātaṃ khayaṃ gacchanti pahīyanti nappavattanti, taṃ kāraṇanti attho”ti.

"Saṃvarabhūtaṃ" (being a restraint) means the cause that is by nature restraining, that which constitutes the restraint of virtue and other restraints. That, in meaning, should be understood as vision and so on. "Saṃvaritā" (restrained) means rightly prevented from arising by not giving way, or completely prevented in every way. And because such states are said to be "closed" by the shutting of the doors of arising, therefore it is said "vidahitā hutvā" (having been closed). Having thus shown the non-ultimate restraint as the cause of the ultimate restraint, now, showing the ultimate restraint itself, he says that when vision and so on are present, the taints liable to arise do not arise; that non-arising of them, being called cessation, destruction, and abandonment, is in meaning merely non-occurrence, and vision and so on is its cause. Thus, he says: "By which cause they go to destruction, called non-arising cessation, are abandoned, do not arise—that is the meaning of 'cause.'"

Cakkhutopi…pe… manatopīti (dha. sa. mūlaṭī. 14-19) cakkhuviññāṇādivīthīsu tadanugatamanoviññāṇavīthīsu ca kiñcāpi kusalādīnampi pavatti atthi, kāmāsavādayo [M 1.0143] eva pana vaṇato yūsaṃ viya paggharaṇakaasucibhāvena sandanti, tasmā te eva “āsavā”ti vuccanti. Tattha hi paggharaṇaasucimhi niruḷho āsava-saddoti. Dhammato yāva gotrabhunti tato paraṃ maggaphalesu appavattanato vuttaṃ. Ete hi ārammaṇavasena dhamme gacchantā tato paraṃ na gacchanti. Nanu tato paraṃ bhavaṅgādīnipi gacchantīti ce? Na, tesampi pubbe ālambitesu lokiyadhammesu sāsavabhāvena antogadhattā tato paratābhāvato. Ettha ca gotrabhuvacanena gotrabhuvodānaphalasamāpattipurecārikaparikammāni vuttānīti veditabbāni. Paṭhamamaggapurecārikameva vā gotrabhu avadhinidassanabhāvena gahitaṃ, tato paraṃ pana maggaphalasamānatāya aññesu maggesu maggavīthiyaṃ samāpattivīthiyaṃ nirodhānantarañca pavattamānesu phalesu nibbāne ca āsavānaṃ pavatti nivāritāti veditabbaṃ. Savantīti gacchanti, ārammaṇakaraṇavasena pavattantīti attho. Avadhiattho ā-kāro, avadhi ca mariyādābhividhibhedato duvidho. Tattha mariyādaṃ kiriyaṃ bahi katvā pavattati yathā “āpāṭaliputtā vuṭṭho devo”ti. Abhividhi pana kiriyaṃ byāpetvā pavattati yathā “ābhavaggā bhagavato yaso pavattatī”ti. Abhividhiattho cāyaṃ ā-kāro idha gahitoti vuttaṃ “antokaraṇattho”ti.

"Even from the eye... up to the mind" (Dhs. Mūlaṭī. 14-19)—though in the cognitive processes of eye-consciousness and so on, and in the subsequent mind-consciousness processes, there may arise wholesome and other states, yet the taints of sensual desire and so on flow forth like pus from a wound due to their oozing, impure nature. Therefore, they are called "āsavas." Herein, the term "āsava" is rooted in the meaning of oozing impurity. It is said that with respect to phenomena, they continue up to the change-of-lineage moment (gotrabhū) because they do not arise beyond that in the path and fruition states. For these taints, while they proceed in regard to phenomena by way of an object, do not go beyond that. But do they not proceed beyond that into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and so on? No, because even those are included within the tainted nature of the mundane states previously taken as objects, there is no going beyond. Here, by the word "gotrabhū" should be understood the change-of-lineage, purification, fruition attainment, and the preceding preliminary works. Alternatively, the change-of-lineage moment preceding the first path alone is taken as indicating the limit. Beyond that, however, due to the similarity of path and fruition, in the other paths, in the path cognitive process, in the attainment process, in the fruition states arising immediately after cessation, and in Nibbāna, the arising of taints is understood to be prevented. "They flow" (savantī) means they proceed, that is, they occur by making something an object. The prefix "ā-" signifies a limit (avadhi), and "limit" is of two kinds: boundary (mariyādā) and inclusiveness (abhividhi). Here, a boundary excludes the action, as in "the rain has ceased outside Pāṭaliputta." Inclusiveness, however, encompasses the action, as in "the glory of the Blessed One spreads up to the highest state of existence." In this context, the prefix "ā-" is taken in the sense of inclusiveness, hence it is said to mean "including."

Madirādayoti [V 1.0129] ādi-saddena sindhavakādambarikāpotikādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Cirapārivāsiyaṭṭho viraparivutthatā purāṇabhāvo. Avijjā nāhosītiādīti ettha ādi-saddena “purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi na paññāyati bhavataṇhāyā”ti (a. ni. 10.62) idaṃ suttaṃ saṅgahitaṃ. Avijjāsavabhavāsavānaṃ ciraparivutthatāya dassitāya tabbhāvabhāvino kāmāsavassa ciraparivutthatā dassitāva hoti. Aññesu ca yathāvutte dhamme okāsañca ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattamānesu mānādīsu vijjamānesu attattaniyādiggāhavasena abhibyāpanaṃ madakaraṇavasena āsavasadisatā ca etesaṃyeva, na aññesanti etesveva āsava-saddo niruḷhoti daṭṭhabbo. Na cettha diṭṭhāsavo nāgatoti gahetabbaṃ bhavataṇhāya viya bhavadiṭṭhiyāpi bhavāsavaggahaṇeneva gahitattā. Āyataṃ anādikālikattā. Pasavantīti phalanti. Na hi taṃ kiñci saṃsāradukkhaṃ [M 1.0144] atthi, yaṃ āsavehi vinā uppajjeyya. Purimāni cetthāti ettha etesu catūsu atthavitappesu purimāni tīṇi. Yatthāti yesu suttābhidhammapadesesu. Tattha yujjanti kilesesuyeva yathāvuttassa atthattayassa sambhavato. Pacchimaṃ “āyataṃ vā saṃsāradukkhaṃ savantī”ti vuttanibbacanaṃ. Kammepi yujjati dukkhappasavanassa kilesakammasādhāraṇattā.

Regarding 'madirādayo,' by the word 'ādi' the inclusion of sindhavaka, kādambarika, āpotika, and others should be understood. The meaning of 'long-established' is long-residing, ancientness. Regarding 'Avijjā nāhosītiādi,' here by the word 'ādi' this sutta is included: 'Monks, a first point of craving for existence is not discerned' (AN 10.62). Since the long-residing nature of the influxes of ignorance and existence has been shown, the long-residing nature of the influx of sensuality, which partakes of that same nature, is thereby also shown. And with regard to other states, such as conceit and so on, which arise by taking the aforementioned things as their opportunity and object, the pervasion by way of grasping at self and what is mine, and the similarity to influxes by way of causing intoxication, belong to these alone, not to others. Thus, it should be understood that the term 'āsava' is conventionally applied only to these. And here, it should not be taken that the influx of views is not included, because the view of existence is also included by the inclusion of the influx of existence, just as craving for existence is. It is extensive because it is beginningless. 'Pasavanti' means they bear fruit. For there is no suffering of saṃsāra whatsoever that could arise without the influxes. Regarding 'Purimāni cettha,' here, among these four alternative meanings, the first three are meant. 'Yattha' means in which passages of the Suttas and Abhidhamma. There, they apply only to the defilements, because of the possibility of the three meanings as stated before. The last is the explanation stated as: 'or they flow forth as the extensive suffering of saṃsāra.' It also applies to kamma, because the production of suffering is common to both defilements and kamma.

Diṭṭhadhammā vuccanti paccakkhabhūtā khandhā, diṭṭhadhamme bhavā diṭṭhadhammikā. Vivādamūlabhūtāti vivādassa mūlakāraṇabhūtā kodhūpanāha-makkha-paḷāsa-issā-macchariya-māyā-sāṭheyya-thambha-sārambha-mānātimānā.

'Things seen' are called the directly experienced aggregates; things that exist in the seen are 'things pertaining to the present life.' 'Being the root of dispute' means being the root cause of dispute: anger, resentment, contempt, denigration, envy, avarice, deceit, dishonesty, stubbornness, competitiveness, conceit, and arrogance.

Yena devūpapatyassāti yena kammakilesappakārena āsavena devesu upapatti nibbatti assa mayhanti sambandho. Gandhabbo vā vihaṅgamo ākāsacārī assanti vibhattiṃ pariṇāmetvā yojetabbaṃ. Ettha ca yakkhagandhabbatāya vinimuttā sabbā devagati devaggahaṇena gahitā. Avasesā ca akusalā dhammāti akusalakammato avasesā akusalā dhammā āsavāti āgatāti sambandho.

‘By which there would be rebirth among devas’ means: by which kind of kamma, defilement, or influx would rebirth, an arising, among the devas be for me? This is the connection. Or ‘a gandhabba, a bird, a sky-goer I would be’—it should be connected by changing the grammatical case. And here, all deva-destinies, apart from the state of yakkhas and gandhabbas, are included by the term ‘deva’. ‘And the remaining unwholesome states’—the connection is that the unwholesome states remaining from unwholesome kamma are what is meant by ‘influxes’.

Paṭighātāyāti paṭisedhanāya. Parūpavā…pe… upaddavāti idaṃ yadi bhagavā sikkhāpadaṃ na paññapeyya, tato asaddhammappaṭisevanaadinnādānapāṇātipātādihetu ye uppajjeyyuṃ parūpavādādayo diṭṭhadhammikā nānappakārā anatthā, ye ca tannimittā eva nirayādīsu nibbattassa pañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇādivasena mahādukkhānubhavādippakārā anatthā, te sandhāya vuttaṃ. Te paneteti ete kāmarāgādikilesa-tebhūmakakammaparūpavādādiupaddavappakārā āsavā. Yatthāti [V 1.0130] yasmiṃ vinayādipāḷipadese. Yathāti yena duvidhādippakārena aññesu ca suttantesu āgatāti sambandho.

‘For warding off’ means for preventing. ‘Criticism from others… and so on… distress’—this is said with reference to the various kinds of immediate harms, such as criticism from others, that would arise if the Blessed One did not lay down the training rule, due to causes such as engaging in wrong conduct, taking what is not given, killing living beings, and so forth; and also with reference to the harms for one reborn in hell and other realms, caused by just that, such as the experience of great suffering in the manner of the fivefold bondage, the causes of kamma, and so on. But these are those influxes, which are the kinds of defilements such as sensual lust, kamma pertaining to the three realms, and distress such as criticism from others. ‘Where’ means in which passage of the Pāli texts such as the Vinaya. ‘How’ means in what twofold manner and other ways it is found also in other suttas—this is the connection.

Nirayaṃ gamentīti nirayagāminiyā. Chakkanipāte āhuneyyasutte. Tattha hi āsavā chadhā āgatā āsava-saddābhidheyyassa atthassa pabhedopacārena āsava-pade pabhedoti vutto, koṭṭhāsattho vā pada-saddoti āsavapadeti āsavappakāre saddakoṭṭhāse atthakoṭṭhāse vāti attho.

‘Because they lead to hell,’ it is called ‘leading to hell.’ In the Book of the Sixes, in the Āhuneyya Sutta. For there the influxes are presented in six ways. By a figurative division of the meaning denoted by the word ‘āsava,’ it is called a ‘division’ in the term ‘āsava-pada.’ Or, the word ‘pada’ means ‘portion.’ Thus, ‘in the āsava-pada’ means in the kinds of influxes, in the portion of the word, or in the portion of the meaning.

Tathā [M 1.0145] hīti tasmā saṃvaraṇaṃ pidahanaṃ pavattituṃ appadānaṃ, teneva kāraṇenāti attho. Sīlādisaṃvare adhippete pavattituṃ appadānavasena thakanabhāvasāmaññato dvāraṃ saṃvaritvāti gehadvārasaṃvaraṇampi udāhaṭaṃ. Sīlasaṃvarotiādi heṭṭhā mūlapariyāyavaṇṇanāya vuttampi imassa suttassa atthavaṇṇanaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā vattukāmo puna vadati. Yuttaṃ tāva sīlasatiñāṇānaṃ saṃvarattho pāḷiyaṃ tathā āgatattā, khantivīriyānaṃ pana kathanti āha “tesañcā”tiādi. Tassattho – yadipi “khamo hoti…pe… sītassa uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”tiādiniddese khantivīriyānaṃ saṃvarapariyāyo nāgato, uddese pana sabbāsavasaṃvarapariyāyanti saṃvarapariyāyena gahitattā attheva tesaṃ saṃvarabhāvoti.

‘Thus’ means: therefore restraint is a closing off, a not-giving-way for them to proceed; for that very reason—this is the meaning. When restraint such as virtue is intended, because of the similarity to the state of blocking by way of not allowing to proceed, ‘having restrained the door’—the restraining of a house-door—is also cited as an example. ‘The restraint of virtue,’ etc.—although this was stated below in the commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, wishing to give a complete commentary on the meaning of this sutta, he says it again. It is fitting, first, that the meaning of restraint applies to virtue, mindfulness, and wisdom, because it is found thus in the Pāli. But how does it apply to patience and energy? He says, ‘And of them,’ etc. The meaning of this is: although in the explanation beginning ‘He is patient… of cold… he does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire,’ the method of restraint is not mentioned for patience and energy, yet in the summary, because they are included by the method of restraint as ‘the method of restraining all influxes,’ their nature as restraint does indeed exist.

Pubbe sīlasatiñāṇānaṃ pāṭhantarena saṃvarabhāvo dassitoti idāni taṃ imināpi suttena gahitabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Khantivīriyasaṃvarā vuttāyeva “khamo hoti sītassā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.14) pāḷiyā dassanavasena. “Tañca anāsanaṃ, tañca agocara”nti ayaṃ panettha sīlasaṃvaroti tañca “yathārūpe”tiādinā vuttaṃ ayuttaṃ aniyatavatthukaṃ raho paṭicchannāsanaṃ, tañca yathāvuttaṃ ayuttaṃ vesiyādigocaraṃ, “paṭisaṅkhāyoniso parivajjetī”ti āgataṃ yaṃ parivajjanaṃ, ayaṃ pana ettha etasmiṃ sutte āgato sīlasaṃvaroti attho. Anāsanaparivajjanena hi anācāraparivajjanaṃ vuttaṃ, anācārāgocaraparivajjanaṃ cārittasīlatāyasīlasaṃvaro. Tathā hi bhagavatā “pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharatī”ti (vibha. 508) sīlasaṃvaravibhajane ācāragocarasampattiṃ dassentena “atthi anācāro, atthi agocaro”tiādinā (vibha. 513, 514) anācārāgocarā vibhajitvā dassitā. Idañca ekadesena samudāyanidassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ samuddapabbatanidassanaṃ viya.

Previously, the nature of restraint for virtue, mindfulness, and wisdom was shown through a different passage. Now, to show that this is also included in this sutta, ‘Moreover,’ etc., is said. The restraints of patience and energy have already been mentioned by way of demonstration from the Pāli text beginning ‘He is patient with cold,’ etc. (MN 2). ‘And that improper seat, and that improper resort’—this here is the restraint of virtue. This means: that improper, object-unspecified, secluded, and hidden seat mentioned in the passage beginning ‘such as’; and that aforementioned improper resort, such as to courtesans; the avoidance of these which is mentioned as ‘reflecting wisely, he avoids’—this is the restraint of virtue mentioned here in this sutta. For by the avoidance of improper seats, the avoidance of improper conduct is stated. And the avoidance of improper conduct and resort is the restraint of virtue in terms of conduct-virtue. Indeed, the Blessed One, when explaining the accomplishment of conduct and resort in his analysis of the restraint of virtue with ‘He dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint’ (Vibh 508), showed improper conduct and resort by analyzing them with the passage beginning ‘There is improper conduct, there is improper resort’ (Vibh 513, 514). And this should be seen as an indication of the whole by way of a part, like the indication of the ocean by a mountain.

Sabbattha paṭisaṅkhā ñāṇasaṃvaroti ettha “yonisomanasikāro, paṭisaṅkhā ñāṇasaṃvaro”ti vattabbaṃ[V 1.0131]. Na hi dassanapahātabbaniddese paṭisaṅkhāgahaṇaṃ atthi, “yoniso manasi karotī”ti pana vuttaṃ. Yonisomanasikaraṇampi atthato paṭisaṅkhā ñāṇasaṃvaramevāti evaṃ pana atthe gayhamāne yuttametaṃ siyā. Keci pana “yattha yattha ‘idha paṭisaṅkhā yoniso’ti āgataṃ[M 1.0146], taṃ sabbaṃ sandhāya ‘sabbattha paṭisaṅkhā ñāṇasaṃvaro’ti vutta”nti vadanti. Tesaṃ matena “idaṃ dukkhanti yoniso manasi karotī”tiādikassa ñāṇasaṃvarena ca asaṅgaho siyā, “dassanaṃ paṭisevanā bhāvanā ca ñāṇasaṃvaro”ti ca vacanaṃ virujjheyya, tasmā vuttanayenevettha attho veditabbo. “Sabbattha paṭisaṅkhā ñāṇasaṃvaro”ti iminā sattasupi ṭhānesu yaṃ ñāṇaṃ, so ñāṇasaṃvaroti parivajjanādivasena vuttā sīlādayo sīlasaṃvarādayoti ayamattho dassito. Evaṃ sati saṃvarānaṃ saṅkaro viya hotīti te asaṅkarato dassetuṃ “aggahitaggahaṇenā”ti vuttaṃ parivajjanavisesasaṃvarādhivāsanavinodanānaṃ sīlasaṃvarādibhāvena gahitattā, tathā aggahitānaṃ gahaṇenāti attho. Te pana aggahite sarūpato dassento “dassanaṃ paṭisevanā bhāvanā”ti āha.

"Everywhere, restraint by knowledge through reflection"—here, it should be said: "wise attention, restraint by knowledge through reflection." For in the exposition of what is to be abandoned by seeing, there is no mention of reflection; rather, it is said: "one attends wisely." Since wise attention, in terms of meaning, is indeed restraint by knowledge through reflection, if the meaning is taken in this way, it would be appropriate. Some, however, say: "Wherever 'here, reflection is wise' occurs, all of that is referred to by 'everywhere, restraint by knowledge through reflection.'" According to their view, statements like "one attends wisely to 'this is suffering,'" etc., would not be included under restraint by knowledge, and the statement "seeing, using, and developing are restraint by knowledge" would be contradicted. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood according to the method stated. By "Everywhere, restraint by knowledge through reflection," it is shown that in all seven instances, that which is knowledge is restraint by knowledge; and that virtue, etc., spoken of by way of avoidance, etc., are virtue-restraint, etc. This being so, it would be like a confusion of the restraints. To show them as unconfused, it is said: "by taking what has not been taken." This means that because avoidance, endurance, and removal have been taken as virtue-restraint, etc., it is by taking what has not been so taken. Then, to show in their own nature what has not been taken, he says: "seeing, using, and developing."

Etena sīlasaṃvarādinā karaṇabhūtena, kāraṇabhūtena vā. Dhammāti kusalākusaladhammā. Sīlasaṃvarādinā hi sahajātakoṭiyā, upanissayakoṭiyā vā paccayabhūtena anuppannā kusalā dhammā uppattiṃ gacchanti uppajjanti, tathā aniruddhā akusalā dhammā nirodhaṃ gacchanti nirujjhantīti attho. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “anuppannā ceva āsavā na uppajjanti, uppannā ca āsavā pahīyantī”ti akusaladhammānaṃ anuppādapahānāni eva vuttāni, na kusaladhammānaṃ uppādādayoti? Nayidamevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, “yoniso ca kho, bhikkhave, manasikaroto”tiādinā kusaladhammānampi uppatti pakāsitāva āsavasaṃvaraṇassa padhānabhāvena gahitattā. Tathā hi pariyosānepi “ye āsavā dassanā pahātabbā, te dassanā pahīnā hontī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.28) āsavappahānameva padhānaṃ katvā nigamitaṃ.

By this, as an instrument or a cause, namely, restraint through virtue, etc. By 'states' (dhammā) are meant wholesome and unwholesome states. For through restraint by virtue, etc., as a conascent condition or as a strong supporting condition, unarisen wholesome states arise and come into being, and unceased unwholesome states cease and are destroyed—this is the meaning. But in the canonical text, it is said: 'The unarisen taints do not arise, and the arisen taints are abandoned'—thus only the non-arising and abandoning of unwholesome states are mentioned, not the arising, etc., of wholesome states. Is it to be seen only in this way? No, it should not be seen thus, for in the passage, 'When, monks, one attends wisely,' etc., the arising of wholesome states is also clearly shown, since the restraint of the taints is taken as the primary factor. Similarly, even at the conclusion, it is concluded by making the abandoning of the taints primary, as in 'Those taints that are to be abandoned by seeing are abandoned by seeing,' etc. (MN 1.28).

15. Jānato passatoti ettha dassanampi paññācakkhunāva dassanaṃ adhippetaṃ, na maṃsacakkhunā dibbacakkhunā vāti āha “dvepi padāni ekatthānī”ti. Evaṃ santepīti padadvayassa ekatthatthepi. Ñāṇalakkhaṇanti ñāṇassa sabhāvaṃ, visayassa yathāsabhāvāvabodhananti attho. Tenāha “jānanalakkhaṇañhi ñāṇa”nti. Ñāṇappabhāvanti ñāṇānubhāvaṃ, ñāṇakiccaṃ visayobhāsananti [M 1.0147] attho. Tenevāha “ñāṇena vivaṭe dhamme”ti. “Jānato passato”ti ca jānanadassanamukhena puggalādhiṭṭhānā desanā pavattāti āha “ñāṇalakkhaṇaṃ ñāṇappabhāvaṃ upādāya puggalaṃ niddisatī”ti. Jānato passatoti “yoniso ca manasikāraṃ ayoniso ca manasikāra”nti [V 1.0132] vakkhamānattā yonisomanasikāravisayajānanaṃ, ayonisomanasikāravisayadassanaṃ. Tañca kho pana nesaṃ āsavānaṃ khayūpāyasabhāvassa adhippetattā uppādanānuppādanavasena na ārammaṇamattenāti ayamattho yuttoti āha “yonisomanasikāraṃ…pe… ayamettha sāro”ti.

15. In 'for one who knows and sees' (jānato passato), seeing too is intended as seeing with the eye of wisdom, not with the fleshly eye or the divine eye. Therefore, he says: 'Both words have the same meaning.' 'Even so' (evaṃ santepi) means even though the two words have the same meaning. 'The characteristic of knowledge' (ñāṇalakkhaṇaṃ) means the intrinsic nature of knowledge, which is the comprehension of an object according to its true nature. Therefore, he says: 'For knowledge has the characteristic of knowing.' 'The power of knowledge' (ñāṇappabhāvaṃ) means the influence of knowledge, its task of illuminating the object. Therefore, he says: 'By knowledge, phenomena are revealed.' And 'for one who knows and sees'—the teaching proceeds with the person as its basis, through knowing and seeing. Therefore, he says: 'With reference to the characteristic and power of knowledge, the person is indicated.' In 'for one who knows and sees'—because 'wise attention and unwise attention' will be stated, the knowing pertains to the object of wise attention, and the seeing pertains to the object of unwise attention. However, since the nature of the means for the destruction of the taints is intended for them, it is not merely a matter of the object but of arising and non-arising. This meaning is appropriate here. Therefore, he says: 'Wise attention... this is the essence here.'

“Jānato”ti vatvā jānanañca anussavākārapaṭivitakkamattavasena na idhādhippetaṃ, atha kho rūpādi viya cakkhuviññāṇena yonisomanasikārāyonisomanasikāre paccakkhe katvā tesaṃ uppādavasena dassananti imamatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “passato”ti vuttanti evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Aññatthāpi hi “evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato (itivu. 102), jānaṃ jānāti passaṃ passati (ma. ni. 1.203), evaṃ jānantā evaṃ passantā (ma. ni. 1.407), ajānataṃ apassata”nti ca ādīsu ñāṇakiccassa sāmaññavisesadīpanavasenetaṃ padadvayaṃ āgatanti. Kecīti abhayagirivāsisārasamāsācariyā. Te hi “samādhinā jānato vipassanāya passato jānaṃ jānāti passaṃ passati, evaṃ jānanā samatho, passanā vipassanā”ti ca ādinā papañcenti. Teti papañcā. Imasmiṃ attheti “jānato”tiādinayappavatte imasmiṃ suttapadaatthe niddhāriyamāne. Na yujjanti jānanadassanānaṃ yonisomanasikārāyonisomanasikāravisayabhāvassa pāḷiyaṃ vuttattā.

Having stated 'knowing' (jānato), knowing here is not intended as by way of mere hearsay and reflection. Rather, to clarify this meaning—that just as forms are seen by eye-consciousness, so too, by directly experiencing wise attention and unwise attention through their arising—'seeing' (passato) is stated. Or, the meaning here should be understood in this way. Elsewhere, too, this pair of words appears to illustrate the general and specific functions of the act of knowing, as in 'thus knowing, thus seeing' (Itivuttaka 102), 'knowing, he knows; seeing, he sees' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.203), 'thus knowing, thus seeing' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.407), and 'not knowing, not seeing.' 'Some' (kecīti) refers to the teachers of the Abhayagiri monastery, the Sārasamāsācariyas. They elaborate thus: 'Through concentration, one knows; through insight, one sees. Knowing, he knows; seeing, he sees. Thus, knowing is serenity, seeing is insight,' and so on. These are their elaborations. In this context—when the meaning of this sutta passage, proceeding by way of 'knowing' etc., is determined—their explanation does not hold, because in the canonical text the sphere of knowing and seeing is stated to pertain to wise and unwise attention.

Āsavappahānaṃ āsavānaṃ accantappahānaṃ. So pana nesaṃ anuppādo sabbena sabbaṃ khīṇatā abhāvo evāti āha “āsavānaṃ accantakhayamasamuppādaṃ khīṇākāraṃ natthibhāva”nti. Ujumaggānusārinoti kilesavaṅkassa kāyavaṅkādīnañca pahānena ujubhūte savipassane heṭṭhimamagge anussarantassa. Tadeva hissa sikkhanaṃ. Khayasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Tato aññā anantarāti khayasaṅkhāte aggamagge tappariyāpannameva ñāṇaṃ paṭhamaṃ uppajjati[M 1.0148], tadanantaraṃ pana aññaṃ arahattanti. Yadipi gāthāyaṃ “khayasmiṃ”icceva vuttaṃ, samucchedavasena pana āsavehi khīṇotīti maggo khayoti vuccatīti āha “maggo āsavakkhayoti vutto”ti. Samaṇoti samitapāpo adhippeto. So pana khīṇāsavo hotīti “āsavānaṃ khayā”ti imassa phalapariyāyatā vuttā, nippariyāyena pana āsavakkhayo maggo, tena pattabbato phalaṃ. Eteneva nibbānassapi āsavakkhayabhāvo vuttoti veditabbo.

The abandonment of taints (āsavappahānaṃ) is the complete abandonment of taints. That non-arising of them is their complete destruction and absence. Thus he says: 'the complete destruction of taints, their non-arising, the state of cessation, and non-existence.' 'One who follows the straight path' (ujumaggānusārino) means one who, by abandoning the crookedness of defilements and of the body, etc., recollects the lower path, which is made straight and is accompanied by insight. For that is his training. 'The first knowledge is in destruction' (khayasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ ñāṇaṃ). 'Then, immediately after, comes another' (tato aññā anantarā) means that in the supreme path called destruction, the knowledge associated with it arises first, and immediately after that comes the other, which is arahantship. Although in the verse it is said 'in destruction,' he says that the path is called 'destruction' (khayo) because it destroys (khīṇoti) the taints by way of eradication: 'The path is called the destruction of taints.' A recluse (samaṇo) is intended as one who has pacified evil. He is one whose taints are destroyed—thus, 'by the destruction of taints' (āsavānaṃ khayā) is stated as a synonym for the fruit. In a direct sense, however, the destruction of taints is the path, and the fruit is what is to be attained by it. By this, it should be understood that Nibbāna is also stated as the destruction of taints.

“Jānato passato”ti jānato eva passato evāti evamettha niyamo icchito, na aññathā visesābhāvato aniṭṭhasādhanato cāti tassa niyamassa phalaṃ dassetuṃ “no ajānato no [V 1.0133] apassato”ti vuttanti āha “yo pana na jānāti na passati, tassa neva vadāmīti attho”ti. Iminā dūrīkatāyonisomanasikāro idhādhippeto, yonisomanasikāro ca āsavakkhayassa ekantikakāraṇanti dasseti. Etenāti “no ajānato no apassato”ti vacanena. Te paṭikkhittāti ke pana teti? “Bāle ca paṇḍite ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karissanti (dī. ni. 1.168; ma. ni. 2.228), ahetū apaccayā sattā visujjhantī”ti (dī. ni. 1.168; ma. ni. 2.227) evamādivādā. Tesu hi keci abhijātisaṅkantimattena bhavasaṅkantimattena ca saṃsārasuddhiṃ paṭijānanti, aññe issarapajāpatikālādivasena, tayidaṃ sabbaṃ “saṃsārādīhī”ti ettheva saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In 'knowing and seeing' (jānato passato), the rule intended here is that one truly knows and truly sees, and not otherwise, due to the absence of distinction and because it would not achieve the desired outcome. To demonstrate the result of that rule, it is said that 'not unknowing, not unseeing' (no ajānato no apassato) is stated, meaning: 'I do not speak of one who neither knows nor sees.' By this, improper attention is intended to be rejected here, and proper attention is shown to be the sole cause for the destruction of the taints. By this (etena) is meant the statement 'not unknowing, not unseeing.' 'But who are those rejected?' (te paṭikkhittā) They are those who hold such views as: 'Both the foolish and the wise, having wandered and transmigrated, will make an end of suffering' (Dī. Ni. 1.168; Ma. Ni. 2.228), or 'Beings are purified without cause or condition' (Dī. Ni. 1.168; Ma. Ni. 2.227). Among these, some assert purification through mere transmission of birth or mere transmission of existence, while others attribute it to a lordly god, a creator, time, or similar causes. All such views should be understood as included here under 'transmigration and so on' (saṃsārādīhi).

Purimena vā padadvayenāti “jānato, passato”ti iminā padadvayena. Upāyo vutto “āsavakkhayassā”ti adhikārato viññāyati. Imināti “no ajānato, no apassato”ti iminā padadvayena. Anupāyo eva hi āsavānaṃ khayassa yadidaṃ yoniso ca ayoniso ca manasikārassa ajānanaṃ adassanañca, tena tathattāya appaṭipattito micchāpaṭipattito ca. Nanu “passato”ti iminā ayonisomanasikāro yathā na uppajjati, evaṃ dassane adhippete purimeneva anupāyapaṭisedho vutto hotīti? Na hoti, ayonisomanasikārānuppādanassapi upāyabhāvato satibalena saṃvutacakkhundriyāditā viya sampajaññabaleneva niccādivasena abhūtajānanābhāvo [M 1.0149] hotīti. Tenāha “saṅkhepena…pe… hotī”ti. Tattha saṅkhepenāti samāsena, anvayato byatirekato ca vitthāraṃ akatvāti attho. Ñāṇaṃ…pe… dassitaṃ hoti “jānato”tiādinā ñāṇasseva gahitattā. Yadi evaṃ “svāyaṃ saṃvaro”tiādi kathaṃ nīyatīti? Ñāṇassa padhānabhāvadassanatthaṃ evamayaṃ desanā katāti nāyaṃ doso, tathā aññatthāpi “ariyaṃ vo bhikkhave sammāsamādhiṃ desessāmi saupanisaṃ saparikkhāra”nti (ma. ni. 3.136) vitthāro.

"By the former pair of words" means by the pair of words "knowing, seeing." The means is stated as "for the destruction of the taints," and it is understood from the context of the subject. "By this" means by the pair of words "not knowing, not seeing." Indeed, a non-means for the destruction of the taints is the non-knowing and non-seeing of attention, both wise and unwise, due to non-practice and wrong practice in that regard. Now, does the word "seeing" not imply that unwise attention does not arise, and thus, if seeing is intended, is the rejection of the non-means not already stated by the former pair? It is not so, for even the non-arising of unwise attention is a means, just as the restraint of the eye faculty and so on by the power of mindfulness is a means; similarly, the absence of knowing what is unreal, such as permanence, by the power of clear comprehension, is also a means. Therefore, it is said, "In brief... it is." Here, "in brief" means concisely, without elaborating on the positive and negative aspects. Knowledge... is shown by "knowing," etc., because knowledge itself is taken. If so, how is "this very restraint" and so on to be understood? This teaching is given to show the primacy of knowledge, so there is no fault here. Similarly, elsewhere there is the elaboration: "Monks, I will teach you noble right concentration with its supports and requisites" (MN 3.136).

Dabbajātikoti dabbarūpo. So hi drabyoti vuccati “drabyaṃ vinassati nādrabya”ntiādīsu. Dabbajātiko vā sārasabhāvo, sāruppasīlācāroti attho. Yathāha “na kho dabba dabbā evaṃ nibbeṭhentī”ti (pārā. 384, 391; cūḷava. 193). Vattasīse ṭhatvāti vattaṃ uttamaṅgaṃ, dhuraṃ vā katvā. Yo hi parisuddhājīvo kātuṃ ajānantānaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ, attano vā vātātapādipaṭibāhanatthaṃ chattādīni karoti, so vattasīse ṭhatvā karoti nāma. Padaṭṭhānaṃ na hotīti na vattabbā nāthakaraṇadhammabhāvena upanissayabhāvato. Vuttañhi [V 1.0134] “yāni tāni sabrahmacārīnaṃ uccāvacāni kiccakaraṇīyāni, tattha dakkho hotī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.497).

"Of the nature of Dabba" means having the form of Dabba. For he is called 'drabya,' as in the sayings, "The perishable perishes, not the imperishable," and so on. Or, "of the nature of Dabba" means having an essential nature, one of proper conduct and behavior. As it is said, "Not indeed, Dabba, do the Dabbas explain thus" (Pārā. 384, 391; Cūḷava. 193). "Standing at the head of the duties" means making the duties the foremost part, or the main responsibility. For one who, with a purified livelihood, performs tasks like making umbrellas for fellow monastics who do not know how, or for his own protection against wind and sun, is said to be one who stands at the head of the duties. It should not be said that this is not a proximate cause, for it is a supporting condition by nature of being a quality that brings help. As it is stated, "He is skilled in whatever duties, high or low, are to be done for his fellow monastics," and so on (Ma. Ni. 1.497).

Upāyamanasikāroti kusaladhammappavattiyā kāraṇabhūto manasikāro. Pathamanasikāroti tassā eva maggabhūto manasikāro. Aniccādīsu aniccantiādināti aniccadukkhaasubhaanattasabhāvesu dhammesu “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ asubhaṃ anattā”tiādinā eva nayena, aviparītasabhāvenāti attho. Saccānulomikena vāti saccābhisamayassa anulomavasena. Cittassa āvaṭṭanātiādinā āvaṭṭanāya paccayabhūtā tato purimuppannā manodvārikā kusalajavanappavatti phalavohārena tathā vuttā. Tassā hi vasena sā kusaluppattiyā upanissayo hoti. Āvajjanā hi bhavaṅgacittaṃ āvaṭṭayatīti āvaṭṭanā. Anu anu āvaṭṭetīti anvāvaṭṭanā. Bhavaṅgārammaṇato aññaṃ ābhujatīti ābhogo. Samannāharatīti samannāhāro. Tadevārammaṇaṃ attānaṃ anubandhitvā uppajjamānaṃ manasi karoti ṭhapetīti manasikāro. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ upāyapathamanasikāralakkhaṇo yonisomanasikāro nāma vuccati, yassa vasena puggalo dukkhādīni saccāni āvajjituṃ sakkoti[M 1.0150]. Ayonisomanasikāre saccapaṭikūlenāti saccābhisamayassa ananulomavasena. Sesaṃ yonisomanasikāre vuttavipariyāyena veditabbaṃ.

"Attention to the means" is the mental attention that serves as a cause for the arising of wholesome states. "Attention of the path" is the mental attention that constitutes the path for that very arising. Regarding impermanence and so on, it means contemplating phenomena with the nature of impermanence, suffering, unattractiveness, and non-self—in the manner of "impermanent, suffering, unattractive, non-self"—that is, in a way that is not contrary to their true nature. Or, "in accordance with the truths" means in a way that aligns with the realization of the truths. By "the turning of the mind," etc., is meant the mind-door wholesome impulsion that arose previously, which is a condition for turning, and is thus spoken of by way of its result. For by means of that, it becomes a supporting condition for the arising of wholesomeness. Indeed, adverting turns the life-continuum—thus it is called turning. Repeatedly turning is called repeated turning. Bending towards an object other than that of the life-continuum is called bending. Bringing together is called gathering. Arising while pursuing that very object, it places it in the mind—this is called mental attention. This, characterized by attention to the means and the path, is called wise attention, by which a person is able to advert to truths such as suffering. In unwise attention, "contrary to the truths" means in a way that does not align with the realization of the truths. The rest should be understood in a way opposite to what was said about wise attention.

Yuttinti upapattisādhanayuttiṃ, hetunti attho. Tenevāha “yasmā”tiādi. Etthāti “ayoniso bhikkhave…pe… pahīyantī”ti etasmiṃ pāṭhe. Tatthāti vākyopaññāsanaṃ. Kasmā panettha ayamuddesaniddeso parivattoti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “yoniso”tiādi. Tattha manasikārapadaṃ dvinnaṃ sādhāraṇanti adhippāyena “yoniso ayonisoti imehi tāva dvīhi padehī”ti vuttaṃ. Yonisoti hi yonisomanasikāro, ayonisoti ca ayonisomanasikāro tattha anuvattanato vakkhamānattā ca. Satipi anatthuppattisāmaññe bhavādīsu puggalassa bahulisāmaññaṃ dassetvā taṃ parivattitvā visesadassanattaṃ nāvādi upamāttayaggahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Cakkayantaṃ āhaṭaghaṭīyantanti vadanti.

'Yutti' means reasoning that establishes suitability; it means cause. Therefore, it is said, 'Because,' and so on. 'Here' refers to this passage: 'Unwise attention, monks... are abandoned.' 'There' refers to the statement. In reference to the question, 'Why is this summary and exposition reversed here?', it is said, 'Wise,' and so on. In that context, the word 'attention' is common to both, hence it is said, 'Firstly, by these two terms, 'wise' and 'unwise'.' For 'wise' means wise attention, and 'unwise' means unwise attention, because of their recurrence there and what will be stated. Even though there is a general principle of the arising of what is unbeneficial, having shown the frequent generality of a person in regards to becoming and so on, and then having reversed it to show the distinction, the taking of the three similes beginning with a boat should be understood. They call the wheel-machine a water-drawing machine with pots attached.

Anuppannāti anibbattā. Ārammaṇavisesavasena tassa anuppatti veditabbā, na rūpārammaṇādiārammaṇasāmaññena, nāpi āsavavasena. Tenāha “ananubhūtapubbaṃ ārammaṇaṃ…pe… aññathā hi anamatagge saṃsāre anuppannā nāma āsavā na santī”ti. Vatthunti saviññāṇakāviññāṇakappabhedaṃ āsavuppattikāraṇaṃ. Ārammaṇaṃ ārammaṇapaccayabhūtarūpādīni[V 1.0135]. Idāni āsavavasenapi anuppannapariyāyo labbhatīti dassetuṃ “anubhūtapubbepī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pakatisuddhiyāti pubbacariyato kilesadūrībhāvasiddhāya suddhipakatitāya. Pāḷiyā uddisanaṃ uddeso, atthakathanaṃ paripucchā. Ajjhayanaṃ pariyatti, cīvarasibbādi navakammaṃ, samathavipassanānuyogo yonisomanasikāro. Tādisenāti yādisena “manuññavatthū”timanasikārādinā kāmāsavādayo sambhaveyyuṃ, tādisena. Āsavānaṃ vaḍḍhi nāma pariyuṭṭhānatibbatāya veditabbā, sā ca abhiṇhuppattiyā bahulīkāratoti te laddhāsevanā bahulabhāvaṃ pattā maddantā pharantā chādentā andhākāraṃ karontā aparāparaṃ uppajjamānā ekasantānanayena “uppannā pavaḍḍhantī”ti vuccanti. Tena vuttaṃ “punappunaṃ uppajjamānā uppannā pavaḍḍhantīti vuccantī”ti. Ito aññathāti ito [M 1.0151] aparāparuppannānaṃ ekattaggahaṇato aññathā vaḍḍhi nāma natthi khaṇikabhāvato.

'Unarisen' means not yet produced. Their non-arising should be understood by way of a specific object, not by the generality of objects such as form-objects, nor by way of the taints. Therefore, it is said: 'An object not previously experienced... For otherwise, in the beginningless cycle of existence, there would be no taints that were unarisen.' The basis refers to the cause for the arising of taints, distinguished as that which is with consciousness and that which is without consciousness. The object refers to things such as form, which serve as the object-condition. Now, to show that the category of the unarisen can also be obtained by way of the taints, it is said: 'Even in the case of what was previously experienced...' 'By natural purity' means by a nature of purity established through the distancing of defilements from previous practice. The recitation of the Pāḷi is the lesson; the explanation is the questioning. Study is the scriptural learning; new work is sewing robes and so on; the practice of serenity and insight is wise attention. 'By such means' refers to those means by which, through attention to 'a pleasant object,' etc., the taints of sensual desire and so on could arise. The increase of taints should be understood as the intensity of obsession, and that is due to frequent arising and habitual practice. Thus, having gained repeated practice, they reach a state of abundance, crushing, pervading, covering, creating darkness, arising again and again in a single continuity—they are called 'arisen and increasing.' Therefore, it is said: 'Arising again and again, they are called arisen and increasing.' 'Otherwise than this' means that apart from taking this successive arising as a unity, there is no such thing as increase, due to their momentary nature.

So ca jānātīti dhammuddhaccaviggahābhāvamāha. Kārakassevāti yuttayogasseva. Yassa panātiādinā anuddesikaṃ katvā vuttamatthaṃ purātanassa purisātisayassa paṭipattidassanena pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “maṇḍalārāmavāsīmahātissabhūtattherassa viyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tañhi sabrahmacārīnaṃ āyatiṃ tathāpaṭipattikāraṇaṃ hoti, yato edisaṃ vatthu vuccati. Tasmiṃ yevāti maṇḍalārāmeyeva. Ācariyaṃ āpucchitvāti attano uddesācariyaṃ kammaṭṭhānaggahaṇatthaṃ gantuṃ āpucchitvā. Ācariyaṃ vanditvāti kammaṭṭhānadāyakaṃ mahārakkhitattheraṃ vanditvā. Uddesamagganti yathāāraddhaṃ uddesapabandhaṃ. Tadā kira mukhapāṭheneva bahū ekajjhaṃ uddisāpetvā manosajjhāyavasena dhammaṃ sajjhāyanti. Tatthāyaṃ thero paññavantatāya uddesaṃ gaṇhantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhorayho, so “idānāhaṃ anāgāmī, kiṃ mayhaṃ uddesenā”ti saṅkocaṃ anāpajjitvā dutiyadivase uddesakāle ācariyaṃ upasaṅkami. “Uppannā pahīyantī”ti ettha uppannasadisā “uppannā”ti vuttā, na paccuppannā. Na hi paccuppannesu āsavesu maggena pahānaṃ sambhavatīti āha “ye pana…pe… natthī”ti. Vattamānuppannā khaṇattayasamaṅgino. Tesaṃ paṭipattiyā pahānaṃ natthi uppajjanārahānaṃ paccayaghātena anuppādanameva tāya pahānanti.

He knows it, thus he speaks of the absence of agitation and contention regarding the Dhamma. It is just like that of the doer, meaning it is just like that of one who is properly engaged.
