But as for that which begins with 'yassa pana,' having made it a general statement, the meaning already stated is made clearer by showing the practice of the ancient extraordinary person, as in the case of the Elder Mahātissa who lived in the Maṇḍalārāma. For that indeed becomes a reason for fellow practitioners to practice in the same way in the future, since such an account is told. In that very place—meaning in the Maṇḍalārāma itself. Having taken leave of the teacher—having asked permission from his own recitation teacher to go for the purpose of receiving a meditation subject. Having paid respects to the teacher—having paid respects to the Elder Mahārakkhita, the giver of the meditation subject. The lesson sequence—the continuous lesson sequence as begun. At that time, it is said, many would have the text recited together orally and then contemplate the Dhamma through mental repetition. There, this elder, due to his great wisdom, was a leader for the monks who took up recitation. Thinking, 'Now I am a non-returner; what need have I for recitation?' he did not shrink back, but on the second day at the time of recitation, he approached the teacher. 'Those arisen are abandoned'—here, 'arisen' refers to those liable to arise, not the presently arisen. For it is not possible to abandon presently arisen taints by the path, thus it is said, 'but as for those... there are none.' Presently arisen taints possess the three moments. For them, there is no abandoning by practice; the non-production of those liable to arise by the destruction of their conditions is itself the abandoning by that practice.

16. Yadi evaṃ dutiyapadaṃ kimatthiyanti? Padadvayaggahaṇaṃ āsavānaṃ uppannānuppannabhāvasambhavadassanatthañceva pahāyakavibhāgena pahātabbavibhāgadassanatthañca. Tenāha “idameva padaṃ gahetvā”ti. Aññampīti ñāṇato aññampi satisaṃvarādiṃ. Dassanāti idaṃ hetumhi nissakkavacananti dassanenāti hetumhi karaṇavacanena tadatthaṃ vivarati. Esa nayoti tamevatthaṃ atidisati. Dassanenāti sotāpattimaggena. So hi paṭhamaṃ nibbānadassanato “dassana”nti [V 1.0136] vuccati. Yadipi taṃ gotrabhu paṭhamataraṃ passati, disvā pana kattabbakiccassa kilesappahānassa akaraṇato na taṃ dassananti vuccati. Āvajjanaṭṭhāniyañhi taṃ ñāṇaṃ maggassa, nibbānārammaṇattasāmaññena cetaṃ vuttaṃ, na nibbānapaṭivijjhanena, tasmā dhammacakkhu punappunaṃ nibbattanena bhāvanaṃ appattaṃ dassanaṃ nāma, dhammacakkhuñca pariññādikiccakaraṇavasena catusaccadhammadassanaṃ tadabhisamayoti nutthettha gotrabhussa dassanabhāvappatti[M 1.0152]. Ayañca vicāro parato aṭṭhakathāyameva (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.22) āgamissati. Sabbatthāti “saṃvarā pahātabbā”tiādīsu. Saṃvarāti saṃvarena, “saṃvaro”ti cettha satisaṃvaro veditabbo. Paṭisevati etenāti paṭisevanaṃ, paccayesu idamatthikatāñāṇaṃ. Adhivāseti khamati etāyāti adhivāsanā, sītādīnaṃ khamanākārena pavatto adoso, tappadhānā vā cattāro kusalakkhandhā. Parivajjeti etenāti parivajjanaṃ, vāḷamigādīnaṃ pariharaṇavasena pavattā cetanā, tathāpavattā vā cattāro kusalakkhandhā. Kāmavitakkādike vinodeti vitudati etenāti vinodanaṃ, kusalavīriyaṃ. Paṭhamamaggena diṭṭhe catusaccadhamme bhāvanāvasena uppajjanato bhāvanā, sesamaggattayaṃ. Na hi taṃ adiṭṭhapubbaṃ kiñci passati, evaṃ dassanādīnaṃ vacanattho veditabbo.

16. If so, what is the purpose of the second term? The purpose of taking both terms is to show the possibility of the taints having arisen and not yet arisen, and also to show the division of things to be abandoned according to the division of the abandoning agent. Therefore it is said, "taking just this term." "And others": 'other' means other things besides knowledge, such as restraint by mindfulness, etc. "By seeing" (dassanā): This is an ablative of cause. He explains its meaning with the instrumental 'by seeing' (dassanena) as an instrumental of cause. This is the method: He extends that very meaning. "By seeing" refers to the path of stream-entry. For it is called "seeing" because it first sees Nibbāna. Even though the change-of-lineage consciousness sees it earlier, since it does not perform the task of abandoning defilements after seeing, it is not called "seeing." That knowledge is indeed in the position of a preliminary attention for the path, and this is said by way of its common characteristic of having Nibbāna as its object, not by way of its penetrating Nibbāna. Therefore, the Dhamma-eye, which has not yet attained development through repeated arising, is called "seeing." And the Dhamma-eye is the seeing of the four noble truths by way of performing the task of full understanding, etc., which is their penetration. Thus, here, the change-of-lineage consciousness does not attain the state of seeing. And this discussion will come up later in the commentary itself (Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 1.22). "Everywhere" refers to contexts like "(taints) to be abandoned by restraint," etc. "By restraint" (saṃvarā): by means of restraint. Here, "restraint" should be understood as restraint by mindfulness. "One uses this" (paṭisevati etenā): this is using (paṭisevanaṃ), which is the knowledge of the purposefulness in requisites. "One endures with this" (adhivāseti etāya): this is endurance (adhivāsanā), which is the non-aversion that arises by way of enduring cold, etc., or the four wholesome aggregates with that as primary. "One avoids with this" (parivajjeti etenā): this is avoiding (parivajjanaṃ), which is the intention that arises by way of avoiding wild beasts, etc., or the four wholesome aggregates arising in that way. "One dispels with this" (vinodeti etenā): this is dispelling (vinodanaṃ), which is wholesome effort that dispels sensual thoughts, etc. "Development" (bhāvanā): this is the remaining three paths, arising by way of developing the four noble truths seen by the first path. For it does not see anything previously unseen. Thus, the meaning of terms like "seeing," etc., should be understood in this way.

Dassanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Taints to be Abandoned by Seeing

17. Kusalākusaladhammehi ālambiyamānāpi ārammaṇadhammā āvajjanamukheneva tabbhāvaṃ gacchantīti dassento “manasikaraṇīye”ti padassa “āvajjitabbe”ti atthamāha. Hitasukhāvahabhāvena manasikaraṇaṃ arahantīti manasikaraṇīyā, tappaṭipakkhato amanasikaraṇīyāti āha “amanasikaraṇīyeti tabbiparīte”ti. Sesapadesūti “manasikaraṇīye dhamme appajānanto”tiādīsu. Yasmā kusaladhammesupi subhasukhaniccādivasena manasikāro assādanādihetutāya sāvajjo ahitadukkhāvaho akusaladhammesupi aniccādivasena manasikāro nibbidādihetutāya anavajjo hitasukhāvaho, tasmā “dhammato niyamo natthī”ti vatvā “ākārato pana atthī”ti āha.

17. To show that object-states, even when taken as an object by wholesome and unwholesome states, attain that status only through the gateway of attention, he says that the meaning of the term 'manasikaraṇīye' (to be attended to) is 'āvajjitabbe' (to be adverted to). Because they are worthy of attention due to bringing benefit and happiness, they are called 'manasikaraṇīyā' (to be attended to). And because they are the opposite of that, they are 'amanasikaraṇīyā' (not to be attended to), as he says, 'amanasikaraṇīye means the opposite of that.' 'In the remaining terms' refers to phrases like 'not fully understanding the states to be attended to,' etc. Since even in wholesome states, attention as beautiful, pleasant, permanent, etc., is blameworthy because it is the cause of relish, etc., and brings harm and suffering; and even in unwholesome states, attention as impermanent, etc., is blameless because it is the cause of disenchantment, etc., and brings benefit and happiness; therefore, having said, 'there is no rule according to the nature of the states,' he says, 'but there is according to the mode.'

Vā-saddo yebhuyyena “mamaṃ vā hi bhikkhave (dī. ni. 1.5, 6), devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.186; ma. ni. 2.79, 80) vikappattho diṭṭho, na samuccayatthoti tattha samuccayatthe payogaṃ dassetuṃ “yathā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evañca katvā samuccayatthadīpakaṃ panetaṃ suttapadaṃ samudāhaṭaṃ.

The word "vā" is mostly seen with a sense of option or alternative, as in "mamaṃ vā hi bhikkhave" (Dī. Ni. 1.5, 6), "devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā" (Ma. Ni. 1.186; Ma. Ni. 2.79, 80), and not with a cumulative sense. Therefore, to show its usage in a cumulative sense, "yathā" and so on is stated. And having done so, this sutta passage is cited as an example clarifying the cumulative meaning.

Kāmāsavoti [V 1.0137] pañcakāmaguṇasaṅkhāte kāme āsavo kāmāsavo. Tenāha “pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo”ti. Bhavāsavaṃ pana ṭhapetvā sabbo [M 1.0153] lobho kāmāsavoti yuttaṃ siyā. Rūpārūpabhaveti kammupapattibhedato duvidhepi rūpārūpabhave chandarāgo. Jhānanikantīti jhānassādo. “Sundaramidaṃ ṭhānaṃ niccaṃ dhuva”ntiādinā assādentassa uppajjamāno sassatucchedadiṭṭhisahagato rāgo bhave āsavoti bhavāsavo. Evanti sabbadiṭṭhīnaṃ sassatucchedadiṭṭhisaṅgahato bhavāsaveneva diṭṭhāsavo gahito taṃsahagatarāgatāyāti adhippāyo. Apare pana “diṭṭhāsavo avijjāsavena ca saṅgahito”ti vadanti. Ettha ca “bhavāsavo catūsu diṭṭhigatavippayuttalobhasahagatacittuppādesu uppajjatī”ti (dha. sa. 1465) vacanato diṭṭhisampayuttarāgassa bhavāsavabhāvo vicāretabbo, atha “kāmasahagatā saññāmanasikārā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.332) viya ārammaṇakaraṇattho sahagatattho, evaṃ sati bhavāsave diṭṭhāsavassa samodhānagamanaṃ kataṃ na siyā. Na hi tampayogatabbhāvādike asati taṃsaṅgaho yutto, tasmā yathāvuttapāḷiṃ anusārena diṭṭhigatasampayuttalobhopi kāmāsavoti yuttaṃ siyā. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikadukkhānañhi kāraṇabhūtā kāmāsavādayopi dvidhā vuttā.

'Taint of sensuality' (kāmāsavo): the taint concerning sensual pleasures designated as the five strands of sensuality. Therefore it is said, 'lust connected with the five strands of sensuality.' However, setting aside the taint of existence, all greed could reasonably be considered the taint of sensuality. In the realms of form and formlessness: desire and lust for existence in both types of form and formless existence, distinguished by kamma and rebirth. 'Delight in jhāna' (jhānanikantī): the savoring of jhāna. For one who savors it with thoughts like 'This state is beautiful, permanent, and eternal,' the lust that arises, accompanied by the view of eternalism or annihilationism, is the taint of existence concerning existence. Thus, because all wrong views are included under the categories of eternalism or annihilationism, the taint of views is encompassed by the taint of existence due to the lust associated with it. This is the intended meaning. Others, however, say, 'The taint of views is included along with the taint of ignorance.' Here, considering the statement, 'The taint of existence arises in four types of consciousness accompanied by greed dissociated from wrong view' (Dhs. 1465), the status of lust associated with wrong view as the taint of existence should be examined. Alternatively, just as in passages like 'Perception and attention accompanied by sensuality' (SN 4.332), the term 'accompanied' signifies that it takes that as its object; in this way, the inclusion of the taint of views within the taint of existence would not be established. For in the absence of its being connected with that, its inclusion is not justified. Therefore, in accordance with the aforementioned Pāli text, even greed associated with wrong view should reasonably be considered part of the taint of sensuality. Indeed, the taints of sensuality and so on, which are the cause of suffering both in this present life and in future lives, are also spoken of as twofold.

Abhidhamme (dha. sa. 1103) ca kāmāsavaniddese “kāmesūti kāmarāgadiṭṭhirāgādīnaṃ ārammaṇabhūtesu tebhūmakesu vatthukāmesū”ti attho sambhavati. Tattha hi uppajjamānā sā taṇhā sabbāpi na kāmacchandādināmaṃ na labhatīti. Yadi pana lobho kāmāsavabhavāsavavinimuttopi siyā, so yadā diṭṭhigatavippayuttesu cittesu uppajjati, tadā tena sampayutto avijjāsavo āsavavippayuttoti domanassavicikicchuddhaccasampayuttassa viya tassapi āsavavippayuttatā vattabbā siyā “catūsu diṭṭhigatavippayuttalobhasahagatacittuppādesu uppanno moho siyā āsavasampayutto, siyā āsavavippayutto”ti. “Kāmāsavo aṭṭhasu lobhasahagatacittuppādesu uppajjatī’ti (dha. sa. 1465), “kāmāsavaṃ paṭicca diṭṭhāsavo avijjāsavo”ti (paṭṭhā. 3.3.109) ca vacanato diṭṭhisahagatarāgo kāmāsavo na hotīti na sakkā vattuṃ. Kiñca abhijjhākāmarāgānaṃ viseso āsavadvayaekāsavabhāvo siyā, na abhijjhāya ca noāsavabhāvoti noāsavalobhassa sabbhāvo vicāretabbo. Na hi atthi abhidhamme “āsavo ca [M 1.0154] noāsavo ca dhammā āsavassa dhammassa āsavassa ca noāsavassa ca dhammassa hetupaccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 3.3.16-17) sattamo navamo ca pañho. Gaṇanāyañca “hetuyā sattā”ti (paṭṭhā. 3.3.40) vuttaṃ, no “navā”ti. Diṭṭhisampayutte pana lobhe noāsave vijjamāne sattamanavamāpi pañhā vissajjanaṃ labheyyuṃ, gaṇanāya ca “hetuyā navā”ti vattabbaṃ siyā, na pana vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhivippayutte ca lobhe noāsave vijjamāne vattabbaṃ [V 1.0138] vuttameva. Yasmā pana suttantadesanā nāma pariyāyakathā, na abhidhammadesanā viya nippariyāyakathā, tasmā balavakāmarāgasseva kāmāsavaṃ dassetuṃ “kāmāsavoti pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo”ti vuttaṃ, tathā bhavābhinandananti.

In the Abhidhamma (Dhs. 1103), in the exposition on the taint of sensuality, the meaning 'in sensual pleasures' is possible, that is, in the objective sensual pleasures of the three realms that serve as the object for sensual lust, lust associated with views, etc. For there, all craving that arises does not fail to receive the name 'sensual desire,' etc. However, if greed could also be free from the taints of sensuality and existence, then when it arises in consciousness dissociated from views, the taint of ignorance associated with it would have to be said to be dissociated from the taints, just as for that which is associated with grief, doubt, and restlessness, its dissociation from the taints would have to be stated: 'The delusion that arises in the four types of consciousness accompanied by greed dissociated from views may be associated with the taints or may be dissociated from the taints.' From the statements, 'The taint of sensuality arises in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed' (Dhs. 1465), and 'Conditioned by the taint of sensuality, the taint of views and the taint of ignorance arise' (Paṭṭh. 3.3.109), it cannot be said that lust accompanied by views is not the taint of sensuality. Moreover, regarding the distinction between covetousness and sensual lust, it might be that the latter is the state of being two taints or one taint, and not that covetousness has the nature of being no-taint; thus the existence of greed that is 'no-taint' should be examined. Indeed, in the Abhidhamma, there is no seventh or ninth question such as: 'A taint-phenomenon and a no-taint-phenomenon are related by root condition to a taint-phenomenon' or '...to a taint-phenomenon and a no-taint-phenomenon.' And in the enumeration, it is said, 'In the root condition, seven,' (Paṭṭh. 3.3.40) not 'nine.' However, if there were a 'no-taint' greed associated with views, the seventh and ninth questions would receive answers, and in the enumeration, it would have to be said, 'In the root condition, nine,' but this is not stated. And if there is a 'no-taint' greed dissociated from views, what should be said has been said. Because the Suttanta teaching is a teaching by way of implication, not a teaching without implication like the Abhidhamma teaching, it is said, 'The taint of sensuality is the lust for the five strands of sensuality,' to indicate only strong sensual lust; similarly, 'delighting in existence.'

Sāmaññena bhavāsavo diṭṭhāsavaṃ antogadhaṃ katvā idha tayo eva āsavā vuttāti tassa tadantogadhataṃ dassetuṃ “evaṃ diṭṭhāsavo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati bhavāsavassa animittavimokkhapaṭipakkhataṃ. Catūsu saccesu aññāṇanti idaṃ suttantanayaṃ nissāya vuttaṃ. Suttantasaṃvaṇṇanā hesāti, tadantogadhattā vā pubbantādīnaṃ. Yathā atthato kāmāsavādayo vavatthāpitā, tathā nesaṃ uppādavaḍḍhiyo dassento “kāmaguṇe”tiādimāha. Assādato manasikarototi “subhasukhā”tiādinā assādanavasena manasi karontassa. Catuvipallāsapadaṭṭhānabhāvenāti subhasaññādīnaṃ vatthubhāvena. Vuttanayapaccanīkatoti “kāmā nāmete aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā”tiādinā kāmaguṇesu ādīnavadassanapubbakanekkhammapaṭipattiyā chandarāgaṃ vikkhambhayato samucchindantassa ca anuppanno ca kāmāsavo na uppajjati, uppanno ca pahīyati. Tathā mahaggatadhammesu ceva sakalatebhūmakadhammesu ca ādīnavadassanapubbakaaniccādimanasikāravasena nissaraṇapaṭipattiyā anuppannā ca bhavāsavaavijjāsavā na uppajjanti, uppannā ca pahīyantīti evaṃ taṇhāpakkhe vuttassa nayassa paṭipakkhato sukkapakkhe vitthāro veditabbo.

Generally, the taint of existence includes the taint of wrong view, and so here only three taints are mentioned. To show this inclusion, 'thus the taint of wrong view' and so on is stated. Indeed, it will be said that the taint of existence is the counterpart to signless liberation. 'Ignorance of the four truths'—this is stated based on the suttanta method. For this is a commentary on the Suttas, or because of their inclusion in the past and so on. Just as the taints of sensuality and so on are distinguished according to their meaning, so too their arising and increase are shown by stating 'sensual qualities' and so on. 'Paying attention through gratification'—by focusing on 'beautiful and pleasant' and so on through the aspect of gratification. 'Because they are the basis for the four perversions'—by being the objects of perceptions of beauty and so on. 'Opposed to the stated method'—by first seeing the danger in sensual qualities, as in 'these sensual qualities are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,' one suppresses and eradicates desire and lust through the practice of renunciation. Thus, the unarisen taint of sensuality does not arise, and the arisen one is abandoned. Similarly, by first seeing the danger in exalted states and all mundane phenomena, and through the practice of escape by contemplating impermanence and so on, the unarisen taints of existence and ignorance do not arise, and the arisen ones are abandoned. In this way, the detailed explanation of the bright side should be understood as the opposite of the method stated on the side of craving.

Tayo evāti abhidhamme viya “cattāro”ti avatvā kasmā tayo eva āsavā idha imissaṃ dassanāpahātabbakathāyaṃ vuttā? Tattha kāmāsavassa taṇhāpaṇidhibhāvato appaṇihitavimokkhapaṭipakkhatā veditabbā. Bhavesu niccaggāhānusārato yebhuyyato bhavarāgasampattito bhavāsavassa animittavimokkhapaṭipakkhatā, bhavadiṭṭhiyā pana [M 1.0155] bhavāsavabhāve vattabbameva natthi, anattasaññāya ñāṇānubhāvasiddhito avijjāsavassa suññatavimokkhapaṭipakkhatā. Etthāti etissaṃ āsavakathāyaṃ. Vaṇṇitanti kathitaṃ. Abhedatoti sāmaññato.

Why are only three taints mentioned here in this discussion on what is to be abandoned by seeing, instead of saying 'four' as in the Abhidhamma? Here, the taint of sensuality should be understood as being the counterpart to the desireless liberation, due to its nature as the aspiration of craving. The taint of existence is the counterpart to the signless liberation, due to following the grasping at permanence in existences and generally occurring as lust for existence. As for the view of existence, there is nothing to be said about its being the taint of existence. The taint of ignorance is the counterpart to the emptiness liberation, due to the accomplishment of the power of knowledge by means of the perception of non-self. 'Here' means in this discourse on the taints. 'Explained' means spoken. 'Without distinction' means in a general sense.

18. Kāmāsavādīnanti manussalokadevalokagamanīyānaṃ kāmāsavādīnaṃ. Nirayādigamanīyā pana kāmāsavādayo “dassanā pahātabbe āsave”ti ettheva samāruḷhā. Atha vā yadaggena so puggalodassanāpahātabbānaṃ āsavānaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ, tadaggena kāmāsavādīnampi adhiṭṭhānaṃ. Na hi samaññābhedena vatthubhedo atthīti dassetuṃ “ettāvatā”tiādi [V 1.0139] vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “sāmaññato vuttāna”nti. Kasmā panettha dassanāpahātabbesu āsavesu dassetabbesu “ahosiṃ nu kho aha”ntiādinā vicikicchā dassitāti āha “vicikicchāsīsena cetthā”tiādi. Evanti yathā soḷasavatthukā vicikicchā uppajjati, evaṃ ayonisomanasikāroti.

18. 'Of the taints of sensuality and so on' means of those taints of sensuality and so on that lead to the human world and the deva world. However, the taints of sensuality and so on that lead to hell and other such destinations are included right here under 'the taints to be abandoned by seeing.' Alternatively, to show that insofar as that person is the basis for the taints to be abandoned by seeing, to that same extent he is also the basis for the taints of sensuality and so on, and that there is no difference in substance due to a mere difference in designation, it is said, 'to this extent,' and so on. For that reason, he said, 'of those spoken of generally.' Why is it that here, when the taints to be abandoned by seeing are to be shown, doubt is indicated by phrases like 'Was I indeed in the past?' and so on? He says: 'here with doubt at the head,' and so on. Thus, just as doubt with its sixteen grounds arises, so too does unwise attention.

Vijjamānataṃ avijjamānatañcāti (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.2.20) sassatāsaṅkaṃ nissāya “ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhāna”nti atīte attano vijjamānataṃ, adhiccasamuppattiāsaṅkaṃ nissāya “yato pabhuti ahaṃ, tato pubbe na nu kho ahosi”nti atīte attano avijjamānatañca kaṅkhati. Kasmā? Vicikicchāya ākāradvayāvalambanato. Tassā pana atītavatthutāya gahitattā sassatādhiccasamuppattiākāranissayatā dassitā. Evaṃ āsappanaparisappanāpavattikaṃ katthacipi appaṭivattihetubhūtaṃ vicikicchaṃ kasmā uppādetīti na codetabbametanti dassento āha “kiṃ kāraṇanti na vattabba”nti. Sveva puthujjanabhāvo eva. Yadi evaṃ tassa ayonisomanasikāreneva bhavitabbanti āpannanti āha “nanu ca puthujjanopi yoniso manasi karotī”ti. Tatthāti yonisomanasikaraṇe.

“Existence and non-existence” (Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 2.2.20). Relying on the apprehension of eternalism, one doubts, “Did I exist in the past?”—thus doubting one’s existence in the past. Relying on the apprehension of spontaneous origination, one doubts, “Before that from which I came to be, did I not exist?”—thus doubting one’s non-existence in the past. Why? Because doubt relies on two aspects. However, since it is grasped as a past object, its dependence on the aspects of eternalism and spontaneous origination is shown. Thus, to show that one should not raise the question, “Why does one produce such doubt, which is characterized by wavering and agitation and is a cause for not progressing anywhere?”, it is said, “The question, ‘What is the reason?’ should not be asked.” It is simply the state of an ordinary person. If so, it follows that this must be due to unwise attention. To this, it is said, “But does not even an ordinary person attend wisely?” There, meaning in the case of wise attention.

Jātiliṅgūpapattiyoti khattiyabrāhmaṇādijātiṃ gahaṭṭhapabbajitādiliṅgaṃ devamanussādiupapattiñca. Nissāyāti upādāya.

“By birth, characteristics, and rebirth”: birth as a khattiya, brahmin, and so on; characteristics as a householder, renunciant, and so on; and rebirth as a deva, human, and so on. “Nissāya” means “based upon”.

Tasmiṃ kāle sattānaṃ majjhimappamāṇaṃ, tena yutto pamāṇiko, tadabhāvato, tato atītabhāvato vā appamāṇiko veditabbo. Kecīti sārasamāsācariyā. Te hi “kathaṃ nu khoti issarena [M 1.0156] vā brahmunā vā pubbakatena vā ahetuto vā nibbattoti cintetī”ti āhu. Tena vuttaṃ “hetuto kaṅkhatīti vadantī”ti. Ahetuto nibbattikaṅkhāpi hi hetuparāmasanamevāti.

At that time, beings were of medium size; therefore, one endowed with that size was considered of standard size. Due to the absence of that size, or because of exceeding it, one should be understood as being of non-standard size. Some—the teachers of the Sārasamāsa—say: “They speculate: ‘How, indeed, is one produced? Is it by Īśvara, or Brahmā, or a prior act, or without a cause?’” Therefore, it is said: “They speak of doubting about a cause.” For even doubt about arising without a cause is simply grasping at a cause.

Paramparanti pubbāparappavattiṃ. Addhānanti kālādhivacanaṃ, tañca bhummatthe upayogavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

“Succession” means the continuous occurrence of what precedes and follows. “Duration” is a term for time, and that should be regarded as a term used in the sense of abundance.

Vijjamānataṃ avijjamānatañcāti sassatāsaṅkaṃ nissāya “bhavissāmi nu kho ahamanāgatamaddhāna”nti anāgate attano vijjamānataṃ, ucchedāsaṅkaṃ nissāya “yasmiñca attabhāve ahaṃ, tato paraṃ na nu kho bhavissāmī”ti anāgate attano avijjamānatañca kaṅkhatīti heṭṭhā vuttanayena yojetabbaṃ.

“Existence and non-existence”: this should be construed according to the method stated before, that is, doubting, based on the apprehension of eternalism, “Will I exist in the future?” regarding one’s own existence in the future; and doubting, based on the apprehension of annihilationism, “After this individual existence in which I am, will I not exist?” regarding one’s own non-existence in the future.

Paccuppannamaddhānanti [V 1.0140] addhāpaccuppannassa idhādhippetattā “paṭisandhiṃ ādiṃ katvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Idaṃ kathaṃ idaṃ katha”nti pavattanato kathaṃkathā, vicikicchā, sā assa atthīti kathaṃkathīti āha “vicikiccho hotī”ti. Kā ettha cintā, ummattako viya hi bālaputhujjanoti paṭikacceva vuttanti adhippāyo. Taṃ mahāmātāya puttaṃ. Muṇḍesunti muṇḍena anicchantaṃ jāgaraṇakāle na sakkāti suttaṃ muṇḍesuṃ kuladhammatāya yathā taṃ ekacce kulatāpasā, rājabhayenāti ca vadanti.

Regarding “the present duration” (paccuppannamaddhāna), because the present time is intended here, it is said, “taking rebirth-linking as the beginning,” and so on. Because it proceeds as “How is this? How is that?” there is perplexity (kathaṃkathā), which is doubt (vicikicchā). Because he has this, he is called “one who is perplexed” (kathaṃkathī); hence it is said, “he is doubtful.” What consideration is there here? The meaning is that it has already been said that a foolish ordinary person is like a madman. That refers to the son of the great queen. “They shaved him” (Muṇḍesuṃ): because he was unwilling to be shaved and it was not possible to do so while he was awake, they shaved him while he slept, in accordance with the family custom, as do some family ascetics; some also say it was due to fear of the king.

Sītibhūtanti idaṃ madhurakabhāvappattiyā kāraṇavacanaṃ. “Setibhūta”ntipi pāṭho, udake ciraṭṭhānena setabhāvaṃ pattanti attho.

“Become cool” is a term indicating the reason for attaining a state of sweetness. The reading “become white” is also found, meaning having attained a white state by long standing in water.

Attano khattiyabhāvaṃ kaṅkhati kaṇṇo viya sūtaputtasaññī. Jātiyā vibhāviyamānāya “aha”nti tassa attano parāmasanaṃ sandhāyāha “evañhi siyā kaṅkhā”ti. Manussāpi ca rājāno viyāti manussāpi keci ekacce rājāno viyāti adhippāyo.

He doubts his own khattiya status like Kaṇṇa, who was known as the son of a charioteer. Referring to his own grasping of the notion of “I am” when his birth is being clarified, he said, “Thus indeed there might be doubt.” And “even men like kings” means that some men, certain ones, are like kings.

Vuttanayameva “saṇṭhānākāraṃ nissāyā”tiādinā. Etthāti “kathaṃ nu khosmī”ti pade. Abbhantare jīvoti paraparikappitaṃ antarattānaṃ vadati. Soḷasaṃsādīnanti ādi-saddena sarīra-parimāṇa-parimaṇḍala-aṅguṭṭhayavaparamāṇu-parimāṇatādike saṅgaṇhāti.

The method is as stated: “depending on shape and form,” and so on. Here, this refers to the phrase “how indeed am I.” “Life within” (abbhantare jīvo) refers to the inner self imagined by others. “Of the sixteen parts and so on”—with the word “and so on,” it includes body measurements, roundness, the size of a thumb, a barleycorn, an ultimate particle, and similar things.

“Sattapaññatti [M 1.0157] jīvavisayā”ti diṭṭhigatikānaṃ matimattaṃ, paramatthato pana sā attabhāvavisayāvāti āha “attabhāvassa āgatigatiṭṭhāna”nti, yatāyaṃ āgato, yattha ca gamissati, taṃ ṭhānanti attho.

“The designation of a being pertains to a soul” is merely the opinion of those holding wrong views; but in the ultimate sense, it pertains to individual existence. Hence, it is said, “the coming, going, and station of individual existence,” the meaning of which is: the place from which one has come and to which one will go, that is the station.

19. Yathā ayaṃ vicikicchā uppajjatīti ayaṃ vuttappabhedā vicikicchā yathā uppajjati, evaṃ ayoniso manasikaroto. Etena vicikicchāya attābhinivesasannissayatamāha. Yathā hi vicikicchā attābhinivesaṃ nissāya pavattati, yato sā sassatādhiccasamuppattisassatucchedākārāvalambinī vuttā, evaṃ attābhinivesopi taṃ nissāya pavattati “ahosiṃ nu kho aha”ntiādinā antogadhāhaṃkārassa kathaṃkathibhāvassa attaggāhasannissayabhāvato. Tenevāha “savicikicchassa ayonisomanasikārassa thāmagatattā”ti. Vikappatthoti aniyamattho. “Aññatarā diṭṭhi uppajjatī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Suṭṭhu daḷhabhāvenāti abhinivesassa ativiya thāmagatabhāvena. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ bhave. Paccuppannamevāti avadhāraṇena [V 1.0141] anāgate atthibhāvaṃ nivatteti, na atīte tatthapi sati atthitāya ucchedaggāhassa sabbhāvato. Atīte eva natthi, na anāgatepīti adhippāyo.

19. “Just as this doubt arises”: this doubt of the kinds described arises for one who attends unwisely. By this, the dependence of doubt on clinging to self is stated. For just as doubt proceeds depending on clinging to self—since it is described as relying on the aspects of eternalism, spontaneous origination, eternalism, and annihilation—so too does clinging to self proceed depending on it, because the state of being perplexed about an ego that is included within, as in “Was I in the past?”, is dependent on grasping at self. Therefore, it is said, “because of the strengthening of unwise attention in one who is doubtful.” “In the sense of an alternative” (Vikappattho) means in the sense of being indefinite (aniyamattho). For it is said, “One or another view arises.” “Thoroughly and firmly” (Suṭṭhu daḷhabhāvena) means due to the extreme strengthening of clinging. “Here and there” (Tattha tatthāti) means in that existence. By the emphasis in “only in the present,” it negates existence in the future, but not in the past, because even there, if there is existence, the grasp of annihilationism is present. The meaning is: “It does not exist in the past at all, nor in the future either.”

Saññākkhandhasīsenāti saññākkhandhapamukhena, saññākkhandhaṃ pamukhaṃ katvāti attho. Khandheti pañcapi khandhe. Attāti gahetvāti “sañjānanasabhāvo me attā”ti abhinivissa. Pakāsetabbaṃ vatthuṃ viya, attānampi pakāsento padīpo viya, sañjānitabbaṃ nīlādiārammaṇaṃ viya attānampi sañjānātīti evaṃdiṭṭhitopi diṭṭhigatito hotīti vuttaṃ “attanāva attānaṃ sañjānāmī”ti. Svāyamattho saññaṃ tadaññataradhamme ca “attā anattā”ti ca gahaṇavasena hotīti vuttaṃ “saññākkhandhasīsenā”tiādi. Ettha ca khandhavinimutto attāti gaṇhato sassatadiṭṭhi, khandhaṃ pana “attā”ti gaṇhato ucchedadiṭṭhīti āha “sabbāpi sassatucchedadiṭṭhiyovā”ti.

By “with the aggregate of perception as the chief” (saññākkhandhasīsena) is meant “with the aggregate of perception at the forefront,” the meaning being “having made the aggregate of perception the principal.” Regarding “the aggregates” (khandhe), this means all five aggregates. By “having taken as self” is meant, having fixated on the notion, “My self is of the nature of perceiving.” One with such a view—that just as a lamp illuminates an object to be illuminated and also itself, or just as one perceives a blue or other object, so too one perceives oneself—is said to hold a wrong view, as in the statement “By oneself, one perceives oneself.” This meaning, that perception and other such phenomena are grasped as “self” or “not-self,” is what is meant by “with the aggregate of perception as the chief,” etc. Here, one who grasps a self as distinct from the aggregates holds the eternalist view, while one who grasps an aggregate as self holds the annihilationist view. Thus it is said, “All are indeed eternalist or annihilationist views.”

Abhinivesākārāti vipariyesākārā. Vadatīti iminā kārakavedakasattānaṃ hitasukhāvabodhanasamatthataṃ attano dīpeti. Tenāha “vacīkammassa kārako”ti. Vedetīti vediyo, vediyova vedeyyo. Īdisānañhi padānaṃ bahulā kattusādhanataṃ saddasatthavidū maññanti. Uppādavato ekanteneva vayo icchitabbo, sati ca udayabbayatte neva [M 1.0158] niccatāti “nicco”ti vadantassa adhippāyaṃ vivaranto āha “uppādavayarahito”ti. Sārabhūtoti niccatāya eva sārabhāvo. Sabbakālikoti sabbasmiṃ kāle vijjamāno. Pakatibhāvanti sabhāvabhūtaṃ pakatiṃ, “vado”tiādinā vā vuttaṃ pakatisaṅkhātaṃ sabhāvaṃ. Sassatisamanti sassatiyā samaṃ sassatisamaṃ, thāvaraṃ niccakālanti attho. Tatheva ṭhassatīti yenākārena pubbe aṭṭhāsi, etarahi tiṭṭhati, tatheva tenākārena anāgatepi ṭhassatīti attho.

By 'the form of clinging' (abhinivesākāra) is meant 'the form of perversion.' By 'speaks' (vadati), it indicates its own ability to enlighten beings who act and experience regarding their welfare and happiness. Therefore, it is said, 'the doer of verbal action.' By 'he experiences' (vedeti) is meant 'the experiencer' (vediya); the experiencer is indeed 'that which is to be experienced' (vedeyya). Indeed, scholars of grammar consider that such words frequently denote the agent's role. For what has an origin, passing away must be absolutely expected; and when arising and passing away are present, there is no permanence. Thus, to clarify the intention of one who says 'permanent,' it is stated, 'devoid of arising and passing away.' By 'essential' (sārabhūta) is meant 'the state of being essential by way of permanence.' By 'at all times' (sabbakālika) is meant 'existing at all times.' By 'natural state' (pakatibhāva) is meant 'the inherent nature,' 'the natural condition,' or 'the intrinsic state designated by terms like "speaker" (vada) or similar.' By 'like what is eternal' (sassatisama) is meant 'equal to eternity,' that is, 'stable' and 'for all time.' By 'will remain just so' (tatheva ṭhassati) is meant that 'in the future, it will remain in the same way it existed before and exists now.'

Paccakkhanidassanaṃ idaṃ-saddassa āsannapaccakkhabhāvaṃ katvā. Diṭṭhiyeva diṭṭhigatanti gata-saddassa padavaḍḍhanamattataṃ āha. Diṭṭhīsugatanti micchādiṭṭhīsu pariyāpannanti attho. Tenevāha “dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiantogadhattā”ti. Diṭṭhiyā gamanamattanti diṭṭhiyā gahaṇamattaṃ. Yathā pana pabbatajalaviduggāni dunniggamanāni, evaṃ diṭṭhiggāhopīti āha “dunniggamanaṭṭhena gahana”nti. Taṃ nāma udakaṃ, taṃ gahetvā taṃ atikkamitabbato kantāro, nirudakavanaṃ, taṃ pavanantipi vuccati. Añño pana araññapadeso duratikkamanaṭṭhena kantāro viyāti, evaṃ diṭṭhipīti āha “duratikkamanaṭṭhenā”tiādi. Vinivijjhanaṃ vitudanaṃ. Vilomanaṃ vipariṇāmabhāvo. Anavaṭṭhitasabhāvatāya vicalitaṃ vipphanditanti āha “kadācī”tiādi. Andubandhanādi viya nissarituṃ [V 1.0142] appadānavasena aseribhāvakaraṇaṃ bandhanaṭṭho, kilesakammavipākavaṭṭānaṃ paccayabhāvena dūragatampi ākaḍḍhitvā saṃyojanaṃ saṃyojanaṭṭho, diṭṭhipi tathārūpāti vuttaṃ “diṭṭhisaṃyojana”nti. Bandhanatthaṃ dassento kiccasiddhiyāti adhippāyo. Tenevāha “diṭṭhisaṃyojanena…pe… muccatī”ti. Tattha etehīti iminā jātiādidukkhassa paccayabhāvamāha. Jātiādike dukkhadhamme sarūpato dassetvāpi “na parimuccati dukkhasmā”ti vadantena bhagavatā diṭṭhisaṃyojanaṃ nāma sabbānatthakaraṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ sabbassapi dukkhassa mūlabhūtanti ayamattho vibhāvitoti dassetuṃ “kiṃ vā bahunā, sakalavaṭṭadukkhatopi na muccatī”ti vuttaṃ.

This is a direct demonstration, taking the word 'idaṃ' to mean what is immediately present. By 'a view is indeed a view-adherence' (diṭṭhiyeva diṭṭhigataṃ) is meant that the word 'gata' is merely a verbal suffix. By 'adherence to a view' (diṭṭhigata) is meant 'included in wrong views.' Therefore he said, 'because it is included within the sixty-two views.' By 'the mere going of a view' (diṭṭhiyā gamanamattaṃ) is meant 'the mere grasping of a view.' Just as mountains, water, and impassable places are difficult to escape, so too is the grasping of views. Therefore he said, 'a thicket in the sense of being difficult to escape.' That which is called a 'wilderness' (kantāra) is a waterless forest, also called a 'pavanam,' because one must cross it after having taken water. Or else, another forest region is like a wilderness in the sense of being difficult to cross; so too is a view. Therefore he said, 'in the sense of being difficult to cross,' etc. 'Piercing' (vinivijjhanaṃ) is 'stabbing' (vitudanaṃ). 'Opposition' (vilomanaṃ) is the state of being overturned. Due to its unstable nature, 'wavering' (vicalitaṃ) is 'throbbing' (vipphanditaṃ). Therefore he said, 'sometimes,' etc. Like a leg-fetter and so on, the meaning of 'bondage' is making one unfree by not providing an escape. The meaning of 'fetter' (saṃyojana) is that which yokes by drawing in even what is far away, due to being a condition for the round of defilements, action, and result. A view is also of such a nature, thus it is said, 'view-fetter.' The intention is the accomplishment of its function by showing the meaning of bondage. Therefore he said, 'by the view-fetter... one is not freed.' There, by 'by these' (etehi) is indicated the conditionality for suffering beginning with birth. Having shown the phenomena of suffering, beginning with birth, in their own nature, the Blessed One, by saying, 'one is not freed from suffering,' has clarified this meaning: that the view-fetter causes all misfortune, is greatly blameworthy, and is the root of all suffering. To show this, it was said, 'What more is there to say? One is not freed even from the suffering of the entire round.'

20. Nanu cettha diṭṭhisaṃyojanadassanena sīlabbataparāmāsopi dassetabbo, evañhi dassanena pahātabbā āsavā anavasesato dassitā hontīti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “yasmā”tiādi. Sīlabbataparāmāso kāmāsavādiggahaṇeneva gahito hoti kāmāsavādihetukattā tassa. Appahīnakāmarāgādiko hi kāmasukhatthaṃ vā bhavasuddhatthaṃ [M 1.0159] vā evaṃ bhavavisuddhi hotīti sīlabbatāni parāmasanti, “imināhaṃ sīlena vā vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā”ti (ma. ni. 1.186; ma. ni. 2.79), “tattha nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.19), “sīlena suddhi vatena suddhi sīlabbatena suddhī”ti (dha. sa. 1222) ca suttevuttaṃ sīlabbataṃ parāmasanti. Tattha bhavasukhabhavavisuddhiatthanti bhavasukhatthañca bhavavisuddhiatthañca. Tassa gahitattāti sīlabbataparāmāsassa diṭṭhiggahaṇena gahitattā yathā “diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāyā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 277). Tesanti dassanapahātabbānaṃ. Dassetuṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya. Tabbiparītassāti yonisomanasikaroto kalyāṇaputhujjanassa.

20. Now, should not clinging to rites and rituals also be shown here by the showing of the view-fetter? For in this way, the taints to be abandoned by seeing are shown completely. With reference to this objection, he said, 'Because,' etc. Clinging to rites and rituals is included by the inclusion of the taint of sensual desire and so on, since it has the taint of sensual desire and the like as its cause. For one who has not abandoned sensual lust and so on clings to rites and rituals for the sake of sensual pleasure or for the sake of the purification of existence, thinking, 'By this morality or observance or austerity or holy life, I shall become a god or some other god' (MN 1.186; MN 2.79), and 'Therein I shall remain permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, eternally the same' (MN 1.19). And they cling to the rites and rituals mentioned in the suttas, such as, 'Purity comes through morality, purity comes through observance, purity comes through rites and rituals' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1222). Therein, 'for the sake of the pleasure of existence and the purification of existence' means both for the sake of the pleasure of existence and for the sake of the purification of existence. By 'because it is included' (tassa gahitattā) is meant 'because clinging to rites and rituals is included in the grasping of a view,' as in passages like 'for the abandonment of view-adherences' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 277). By 'of those' (tesaṃ) is meant 'of what is to be abandoned by seeing.' 'To show' refers to the teaching based on the standpoint of the individual. By 'to one who is the opposite of that' (tabbiparītassa) is meant 'to a virtuous ordinary person who attends wisely.'

Tassāti “sutavā”tiādipāṭhassa. Tāvāti “sutavā”ti ito paṭṭhāya yāva “so idaṃ dukkha”nti padaṃ, tāva imaṃ padaṃ avadhiṃ katvāti attho. Heṭṭhā vuttanayenāti ariyasappurisa-ariyadhamma-sappurisadhamma-manasikaraṇīya-amanasikaraṇīyapadānaṃ yathākkamaṃ mūlapariyāye idha gahetvā vuttanayena attho veditabboti sambandho. Vuttapaccanīkatoti “sutavā ariyasāvako, ariyānaṃ dassāvī, sappurisānaṃ dassāvī”ti etesaṃ padānaṃ sabbākārena vuttaviparītato attho veditabbo, kovidavinītapadānaṃ pana na sabbappakārena vuttaviparītato. Arahā hi nippariyāyena ariyadhamme kovido ariyadhamme suvinīto ca nāma. Tenāha “paccanīkato ca sabbākārena…pe… ariyasāvakoti veditabbo”ti. Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ sikhāppattavipassanā. Keci pana “bhaṅgañāṇato paṭṭhāya sikhāpattavipassanā”ti vadanti, tadayuttaṃ[V 1.0143]. Tadanurūpena atthenāti tassa puggalassa anurūpena ariyaṭṭhena, na paṭivedhavasenāti adhippāyo. Kalyāṇaputhujjano hi ayaṃ. Yathā cassa “yopi kalyāṇaputhujjano”ti ārabhitvā “sopi vuccati sikkhatīti sekkho”ti pariyāyena sekkhasutte (saṃ. ni. 5.13) sekkhabhāvo vutto, evaṃ idha ariyasāvakabhāvo vutto. Vuṭṭhānagāminīvipassanālakkhaṇehi ye ariyasappurisadhammavinayasaṅkhātā bodhipakkhiyadhammā tisso sikkhā eva vā sambhavanti, tesaṃ vasena imassa ariyasāvakādibhāvo vutto[M 1.0160]. Tenāha “tadanurūpena atthenā”ti. Ariyassa sāvakoti vā ariyasāvakatthena eva vutto yathā “agamā rājagahaṃ buddho”ti (su. ni. 410). Sikhāppattavipassanāggahaṇañcettha vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā anivattipaṭipadāyaṃ ṭhitassa gahaṇatthanti yathāvuttā atthasaṃvaṇṇanā suṭṭhutaraṃ yujjateva.

By 'of that' (tassa) is meant 'of the passage beginning with "sutavā" (learned).' By 'up to' (tāva) is meant 'from "sutavā" up to the word "so idaṃ dukkhaṃ" (he... this is suffering),' taking this word as the limit. By 'according to the method stated previously' (heṭṭhā vuttanayena) is meant that the meaning should be understood according to the method stated by taking the terms noble and virtuous person, noble teaching, teaching of the virtuous, to be attended to, and not to be attended to, in order, from the root exposition here. By 'the opposite of what is stated' (vuttapaccanīkato) is meant that the meaning of the phrases 'a learned noble disciple,' 'one who sees the noble ones,' and 'one who sees the virtuous' should be understood as being in every way the opposite of what was stated. However, for the terms 'skilled' (kovida) and 'trained' (vinīta), the meaning is not in every way the opposite of what was stated. For an arahat is indeed, without qualification, skilled in the noble teaching and well-trained in the noble teaching. Hence it is said, 'the opposite in every way... should be understood as a noble disciple.' Insight at its peak (sikhāppattavipassanā) is the knowledge of equanimity toward formations (saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa). Some, however, say that insight at its peak begins with the knowledge of dissolution (bhaṅgañāṇa), but that is incorrect. By 'according to a meaning suitable to that' (tadanurūpena atthena) is meant 'in a way fitting for that person in a noble sense, not by way of actual realization.' This refers to a virtuous ordinary person. Just as in the Discourse on the Learner (sekkhasutta, Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.13), the state of being a learner is spoken of figuratively for a virtuous ordinary person, starting with 'even a virtuous ordinary person,' and concluding with 'he too is called a learner because he trains (sikkhatīti sekkho),' so too here, the state of a noble disciple is spoken of. The state of being a noble disciple and so on is described for this person by means of those factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammā) or the three trainings that arise, which are characterized by insight leading to emergence and are designated as the teaching and discipline of a noble and virtuous person. Hence it is said, 'according to a meaning suitable to that.' Or, 'disciple of a noble one' (ariyassa sāvako) is said with the meaning of 'noble disciple' as a designation, just as it is said, 'The Buddha went to Rājagaha' (Sutta Nipāta 410). Here, the inclusion of insight at its peak is for the purpose of including one who, having striven in insight, is established on the irreversible path. Therefore, the explanation of meaning as stated is indeed more appropriate.

21. Yathā dhātumukhena vipassanaṃ abhiniviṭṭho dhātukammaṭṭhāniko āyatanādimukhena abhiniviṭṭho āyatanādikammaṭṭhāniko, evaṃ saccamukhena abhiniviṭṭhoti vuttaṃ “catusaccakammaṭṭhāniko”ti. Caturoghanittharaṇatthikehi kātabbato kammaṃ, bhāvanā. Kammameva visesādhigamassa ṭhānaṃ kāraṇanti, kamme vā yathāvuttanaṭṭhena ṭhānaṃ avaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvanārambhokammaṭṭhānaṃ, tadeva catusaccamukhena pavattaṃ etassa atthīti catusaccakammaṭṭhāniko. Ubhayaṃ nappavattati etthāti appavatti. Uggahitacatusaccakammaṭṭhānoti ca catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ pāḷito atthato ca uggahetvā manasikārayoggaṃ katvā ṭhito. Vipassanāmaggaṃ samāruḷhoti sappaccayanāmarūpadassane patiṭṭhāya tadeva nāmarūpaṃ aniccādito sammasanto. Samannāharatīti vipassanāvajjanaṃ sandhāyāha, tasmā yathā “idaṃ dukkha”nti vipassanāñāṇaṃ pavattati, evaṃ samannāharati āvajjatīti attho. Kathaṃ panettha “manasi karotī”ti iminā “vipassatī”ti ayamattho vutto hotīti āha “ettha…pe… vuttā”ti. Etthāti ca imasmiṃ sutteti attho. Vipassatīti ca yathā upari visesādhigamo hoti, evaṃ ñāṇacakkhunā vipassati, oloketīti attho. Maggopi vattabbo. Purimañhi saccadvayaṃ gambhīrattā duddasaṃ, itaraṃ duddasattā gambhīraṃ.

21. Just as one who is engaged in insight through the element-door is an element-meditator, and one engaged through the sense-base-door is a sense-base-meditator, so it is said that one engaged through the truth-door is a 'four-truth meditator.' The work (kamma) is to be done by those who desire to cross over the four floods; it is development (bhāvanā). The work itself is the basis and cause for special attainment. Or, the work, in the sense explained, is the foundation, the establishment, the commencement of development, which is the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). And because this proceeds by way of the four truths for him, he is called a four-truth meditator. 'Appavatti' means that neither of the two occurs here. 'One who has grasped the four-truth meditation subject' means one who, having learned the four-truth meditation subject from the Pāli text and its meaning, and having made it suitable for mental application, is established therein. 'Has embarked on the path of insight' means, having established oneself in the discernment of name-and-form with its conditions, one contemplates that very name-and-form as impermanent, and so on. 'He directs his mind' is said with reference to the adverting of insight. Therefore, just as insight-knowledge proceeds with the thought, 'This is suffering,' so he directs his mind, he adverts—that is the meaning. How, here, is the meaning 'he sees with insight' expressed by the phrase 'he applies his mind'? It is said, 'Here... it is said.' 'Here' means in this sutta. 'He sees with insight' means that just as higher realization occurs, so one sees with the eye of wisdom, one observes—that is the meaning. The path, too, is designated. For the first two truths are difficult to see due to their profundity, while the other is profound because it is difficult to see.

Abhinivesoti vipassanābhiniveso vipassanāpaṭipatti. Tadārammaṇeti taṃ rūpakkhandhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavatte. Yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ vavatthapetvāti aviparītaṃ attano ārammaṇaṃ sabhāvacchedanādikiccañceva aññāṇādilakkhaṇañca asaṅkarato hadaye ṭhapetvā. Iminā pubbe nāmarūpaparicchede katepi dhammānaṃ salakkhaṇavavatthāpanaṃ paccayapariggahena suvavatthāpitaṃ nāma hotīti dasseti yathā “dvikkhattuṃ baddhaṃ subaddha”nti. Evañhi ñātapariññāya kiccaṃ siddhaṃ nāma [V 1.0144] hoti. Paccayato paccayuppannato ca vavatthāpitattā pākaṭabhāvena siddhenapi siddhabhāvo pākaṭo hotīti vuttaṃ “ahutvā hontī”ti. Aniccalakkhaṇaṃ āropetīti asato hi [M 1.0161] uppādena bhavitabbaṃ, na sato, uppādavantato ca nesaṃ ekantena icchitabbā paccayāyattavuttibhāvato, sati uppāde avassaṃbhāvī nirodhoti nattheva niccatāvakāsoti. Sūpaṭṭhitāniccatāya ca udayabbayadhammehi abhiṇhapaṭipīḷanato dukkhamanaṭṭhena dukkhaṃ. Tenāha “udayabbayapaṭipīḷitattā dukkhāti dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ āropetī”ti. Katthacipi saṅkhāragate “mā jīri mā byādhiyī”ti alabbhanato natthi vasavattananti āha “avasavattanato anattāti anattalakkhaṇaṃ āropetī”ti. Paṭipāṭiyāti udayabbayañāṇādiparamparāya.

'Abhinivesa' refers to engagement, namely, engagement in insight meditation, the practice of insight. 'Taking that as object' means proceeding by making the form aggregate the object. 'Determining the characteristic as it truly is' means establishing in the heart without confusion the undistorted nature of one's object, its function of defining its own nature, etc., and its characteristic of non-knowledge, etc. By this, it is shown that even though name-and-form discrimination was done before, the determination of the characteristics of phenomena through the grasping of conditions is called well-determined, as it is said, 'twice bound, well-bound.' Thus, the task of full understanding by knowing is accomplished. Because it is determined by conditions and the conditioned, and because its accomplished nature is evident, its state of accomplishment is evident, as stated, 'they become, having not been.' 'It imposes the characteristic of impermanence' because what does not exist must come into being, not what exists. And since they have an arising, their existence is entirely dependent on conditions; when there is arising, cessation is inevitable—there is no room for permanence. Due to well-established impermanence and the constant oppression by the phenomena of arising and passing away, there is suffering. Hence it is said, 'because oppressed by arising and passing away, it is suffering—thus the characteristic of suffering is imposed.' Since in any case regarding formations, one cannot obtain the wish, 'may it not age, may it not sicken,' there is no mastery over them. Thus it is said, 'because of non-mastery, it is not-self—thus the characteristic of not-self is imposed.' 'In sequence' refers to the succession of the knowledge of arising and passing away, etc.

Tasmiṃ khaṇeti sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe. Ekapaṭivedhenevāti ekañāṇeneva paṭivijjhanena. Paṭivedho paṭighātābhāvena visaye nissaṅgacārasaṅkhātaṃ nibbijjhanaṃ. Abhisamayo avirajjhitvā visayassa adhigamasaṅkhāto avabodho. “Idaṃ dukkhaṃ, ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito bhiyyo”ti paricchinditvā jānanameva vuttanayena paṭivedhoti pariññāpaṭivedho. Ayaṃ yathā ñāṇe pavatte pacchā dukkhassa sarūpādiparicchede sammoho na hoti, tathā pavattiṃ gahetvā vutto, na pana maggañāṇassa “idaṃ dukkha”ntiādināpi vattanato. Tenāha “na hissa tasmiṃ samaye”tiādi. Pahīnassa puna appahātabbatāya pakaṭṭhaṃ hānaṃ cajanaṃ samucchindanaṃ pahānaṃ, pahānameva vuttanayena paṭivedhoti pahānapaṭivedho. Ayampi yena kilesena appahīyamānena maggabhāvanāya na bhavitabbaṃ, asati ca maggabhāvanāya yo uppajjeyya, tassa kilesassa padaghātaṃ karontassa anuppattidhammataṃ āpādentassa ñāṇassa tathāpavattiyā paṭighātābhāvena nissaṅgacāraṃ upādāya evaṃ vutto. Sacchikiriyā paccakkhakaraṇaṃ, anussavākāraparivitakkādike muñcitvā sarūpato ārammaṇakaraṇaṃ idaṃ tanti yathāsabhāvato gahaṇaṃ, sā eva vuttanayena paṭivedhoti sacchikiriyāpaṭivedho. Ayaṃ pana yassa āvaraṇassa asamucchindanato ñāṇaṃ nirodhaṃ ālambituṃ na sakkoti, tassa samucchindanato taṃ sarūpato vibhāvitameva pavattatīti evaṃ vutto.

At that moment—in the moment of the path of stream-entry. 'By a single penetration'—by means of a single act of knowing, by piercing through. Penetration is a piercing, characterized by unimpeded movement in the object due to the absence of resistance. Direct realization is understanding, characterized by the attainment of the object without failing. Having delimited and known, 'This is suffering, this much is suffering, nothing beyond this'—this, in the stated manner, is the penetration of full understanding. This is stated in such a way that, when the knowledge has occurred, there is no delusion afterward regarding the defining characteristics of suffering, etc., not that the path-knowledge itself operates by stating, 'This is suffering,' etc. Hence it is said, 'For at that time, for him...' and so on. Abandoning is the excellent forsaking, giving up, and eradicating, because what has been abandoned is not to be abandoned again; this is the penetration of abandoning. This too is stated thus with reference to the unimpeded movement of the knowledge that strikes at the root of a defilement—which would arise if the path were not developed—and brings it to a state of non-arising, for without abandoning that defilement, the development of the path cannot occur. Realization is the act of making directly present, relinquishing reliance on hearsay, speculation, etc., and taking the object as it truly is, according to its own nature—this is the penetration of realization. This is stated in such a way that, because knowledge cannot take cessation as its object without eradicating a particular obstruction, when that obstruction is eradicated, it proceeds having made cessation manifest in its own nature.

Bhāvanā uppādanā vaḍḍhanā ca, tattha paṭhamamagge uppādanaṭṭhena, dutiyādīsu vaḍḍhanaṭṭhena, ubhayatthāpi vā ubhayathāpi veditabbaṃ. Paṭhamamaggopi hi yathārahaṃ vuṭṭhānagāminiyaṃ pavattaṃ parijānanādiṃ vaḍḍhento pavattoti tatthāpi vaḍḍhanaṭṭhena bhāvanā [M 1.0162] sakkā viññātuṃ. Dutiyādīsupi appahīnakilesappahānato puggalantarasādhanato uppādanaṭṭhena bhāvanā, sā eva vuttanayena paṭivedhoti bhāvanā paṭivedho. Ayampi hi yathā ñāṇe pavatte pacchā maggadhammānaṃ sarūpaparicchede [V 1.0145] sammoho na hoti, tathā pavattimeva gahetvā vutto, tiṭṭhatu tāva yathādhigatamaggadhammaṃ yathāpavattesu phaladhammesupi ayaṃ yathādhigatasaccadhammesu viya vigatasammohova hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “diṭṭhadhammo pattadhammo viditadhammo pariyogāḷhadhammo”ti (dī. ni. 1.299, 356; mahāva. 27, 57). Yato cassa dhammatāsañcoditā yathādhigatasaccadhammāvalambiniyo maggavīthito parato maggaphalapahīnāvasiṭṭhakilesanibbānānaṃ paccavekkhaṇā pavattanti. Dukkhasaccadhammā hi sakkāyadiṭṭhiādayo. Ayañca atthavaṇṇanā “pariññābhisamayenā”tiādīsupi vibhāvetabbā. Ekābhisamayena abhisametīti vuttamevatthaṃ vibhūtataraṃ katvā dassetuṃ “no ca kho aññamaññena ñāṇenā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Development (bhāvanā) is both arising (uppādanā) and growth (vaḍḍhanā). In the first path, it is to be understood in the sense of arising; in the second and subsequent paths, in the sense of growth. Or, it should be understood in both ways in both cases. For even the first path proceeds by increasing the comprehension, etc., that occurs in the practice leading to emergence; thus, there too, development can be understood in the sense of growth. In the second and subsequent paths, development is in the sense of arising due to the abandonment of unabandoned defilements and the accomplishment of a higher type of individual. This very development, in the manner stated, is the penetration of development. This too is stated with reference to its very occurrence, so that when the knowledge has occurred, there is subsequently no delusion regarding the delimitation of the nature of the path-factors. Not to mention the path-factors as attained, he is without delusion even regarding the fruit-factors that occur, just as he is regarding the truth-factors as attained. Therefore, it is said: 'one who has seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, understood the Dhamma, thoroughly penetrated the Dhamma.' And since for him, impelled by the nature of things, after the path-process, reviewing-knowledges arise which have as their support the truth-factors as attained, concerning the path, the fruit, the abandoned and remaining defilements, and Nibbāna. For the phenomena of the truth of suffering are personality-view, etc. This explanation of the meaning should also be applied in passages like 'through the direct realization of full understanding' and so forth. To show the meaning already stated, 'one directly realizes by a single direct realization,' in a more evident way, it was said, 'but not, indeed, by separate knowledges' and so on.

Vitaṇḍavādī panāha “ariyamaggañāṇaṃ catūsu saccesu nānābhisamayavasena kiccakaraṇaṃ, na ekābhisamayavasena. Tañhi kālena dukkhaṃ pajānāti, kālena samudayaṃ pajahati, kālena nirodhaṃ sacchikaroti, kālena maggaṃ bhāveti, aññathā ekassa ñāṇassa ekasmiṃ khaṇe catukiccakaraṇaṃ na yujjati. Na hidaṃ katthaci diṭṭhampi suttaṃ atthī”ti. So vattabbo – yadi ariyamaggañāṇaṃ nānābhisamayavasena saccāni abhisameti, na ekābhisamayavasena, evaṃ sante paccekampi saccesu nānakkhaṇeneva pavatteyya, na ekakkhaṇena, tathā sati dukkhādīnaṃ ekadesekadesameva parijānāti pajahatīti āpajjatīti nānābhisamaye paṭhamamaggādīhi pahātabbānaṃ saññojanattayādīnaṃ ekadesekadesappahānaṃ siyāti ekadesasotāpattimaggaṭṭhāditā, tato eva ekadesasotāpannāditā ca āpajjati anantaraphalattā lokuttarakusalānaṃ, na ca taṃ yuttaṃ. Na hi kālabhedena vinā so eva sotāpanno ca asotāpanno cāti sakkā viññātuṃ.

The caviller then says: 'The knowledge of the noble path performs its function regarding the four truths through various realizations, not through a single realization. For at one time it fully understands suffering, at another time it abandons the origin, at another time it realizes cessation, and at another time it develops the path. Otherwise, it would not be fitting for a single knowledge to perform four functions in a single moment. For this is neither seen nor heard of anywhere in a sutta.' He should be told: 'If the knowledge of the noble path realizes the truths through various realizations, not through a single realization, then it would proceed regarding each of the truths in separate moments, not in a single moment. If so, it would follow that only parts of suffering and so forth are fully understood and abandoned. Consequently, with various realizations, there would be a partial abandoning of the three fetters and so forth, which are to be abandoned by the first path and so on, leading to the state of being on a partial stream-entry path, and so on. From this, it would result in being a partial stream-enterer, and so on, due to the immediate fruition of supramundane wholesome states. But this is not proper. For without a distinction in time, it is not possible to know the same person as both a stream-enterer and a non-stream-enterer.'

Apicāyaṃ nānābhisamayavādī evaṃ pucchitabbo “maggañāṇaṃ saccāni paṭivijjhantaṃ kiṃ ārammaṇato paṭivijjhati, udāhu kiccato”ti? Jānamāno “kiccato”ti vadeyya, “kiccato paṭivijjhantassa kiṃ nānābhisamayenā”ti vatvā paṭipāṭiyānidassanena [M 1.0163] saññāpetabbo. Atha “ārammaṇato”ti vadeyya, evaṃ sante tassa ñāṇassa vipassanāñāṇassa viya dukkhasamudayānaṃ accantapariññāsamucchedā na yuttā anissaṭattā. Tathā maggadassanaṃ. Na hi maggo sayameva attānaṃ ārabbha pavattatīti yuttaṃ, maggantaraparikappanāya pana anavaṭṭhānaṃ āpajjati, tasmā tīṇi saccāni kiccato, nirodhaṃ kiccato ca ārammaṇato ca paṭivijjhatīti evaṃ asammohato paṭivijjhantassa maggañāṇassa nattheva nānābhisamayo. Vuttañhetaṃ “yo bhikkhave dukkhaṃ passati, dukkhasamudayampi so passatī”tiādi. Na cetaṃ kālantaradassanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “yo nu kho, āvuso, dukkhaṃ passati, dukkhasamudayampi [V 1.0146] …pe… dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadampi so passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1100) ekaccadassanasamaṅgino aññasaccadassanasamaṅgibhāvavicāraṇāyaṃ tadatthasādhanatthaṃ āyasmatā gavampatittherena ābhatattā, paccekañca saccattayadassanassa yojitattā, aññathā purimadiṭṭhassa puna adassanato samudayādidassanamayojaniyaṃ siyā. Na hi lokuttaramaggo lokiyamaggo viya katakārībhāvena pavattati samucchedakattā, tathā yojanena ca sabbadassanaṃ dassanantaraparamanti dassanānuparamo siyāti evaṃ āgamato yuttito ca nānābhisamayo na yujjatīti saññāpetabbo. Evaṃ ce saññattiṃ gacchati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce gacchati, abhidhamme (kathā. 274) odhisokathāya saññāpetabboti.

Moreover, this proponent of various realizations should be asked thus: 'When path-knowledge penetrates the truths, does it penetrate them by way of object or by way of function?' If he knows, he would say, 'By way of function.' Then, having said, 'For one who penetrates by way of function, what need is there for various realizations?' he should be made to understand by showing the sequence. But if he says, 'By way of object,' then in that case, for that knowledge, like insight-knowledge, the complete full-understanding and cutting off of suffering and its origin would not be fitting, since they are not relinquished. Likewise for the seeing of the path. For it is not fitting that the path occurs by taking itself as an object. Furthermore, by imagining another path, one would fall into an infinite regress. Therefore, it penetrates three truths by way of function, and cessation by way of function and by way of object. Thus, for the path-knowledge that penetrates without confusion, there are no various realizations. For this has been said: 'Monks, one who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering,' and so on. And this was not said with reference to seeing at different times, since it was cited by the Venerable Gavampati Thera to establish that meaning in his examination of whether one endowed with seeing one truth is also endowed with seeing the other truths, as in: 'Friend, does one who sees suffering also see... the path leading to the cessation of suffering?' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1100). And because the seeing of the triad of truths is applied to each. Otherwise, since what was previously seen is not seen again, the seeing of the origin and so on would be inapplicable. For the supramundane path, because it cuts off, does not proceed like the mundane path in the manner of having completed its task. And by such an application, all seeing would have a subsequent seeing as its successor, and there would be no end to seeing. Thus, he should be made to understand that, according to scripture and reason, various realizations are not fitting. If he accepts this explanation, it is good. If he does not, he should be made to understand through the discussion on limited grief in the Abhidhamma (Kathāvatthu 274).

Nirodhaṃ ārammaṇatoti nirodhameva ārammaṇatoti niyamo gahetabbo, na ārammaṇatovāti. Tena nirodhe kiccatopi paṭivedho siddho hoti. Tasmiṃ samayeti saccānaṃ abhisamaye. Vīsativatthukātiādi “tīṇi saññojanānī”ti vuttānaṃ sarūpadassanaṃ. Catūsu āsavesūti idaṃ abhidhammanayena vuttaṃ, na suttantanayena. Na hi sutte katthaci cattāro āsavā āgatā atthi. Yadi vicikicchā na āsavo, atha kasmā “sakkāyadiṭṭhi vicikicchā sīlabbataparāmāso, ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, āsavā dassanā pahātabbā”ti vuttanti āha “dassanā pahātabbā”tiādi. Ettha pariyāpannattāti etena sammāsaṅkappassa viya paññākkhandhe kiccasabhāgatāya idha vicikicchāya āsavasaṅgaho katoti dasseti.

By 'cessation as its object,' the rule should be understood that cessation itself is the object, not merely that it is by way of object. Through this, the penetration of cessation by way of function is also established. 'At that time' means at the time of the realization of the truths. The phrase 'having twenty bases,' etc., is a showing of the nature of what was stated as 'the three fetters.' 'Regarding the four taints'—this is stated according to the Abhidhamma method, not according to the Suttanta method. For nowhere in the Suttas have the four taints appeared. If doubt is not a taint, then why was it said: 'Identity-view, doubt, and adherence to rites and observances—these, monks, are called taints to be abandoned by seeing'? To this, it is replied: 'to be abandoned by seeing,' etc. Here, by the words 'because it is included,' it is shown that doubt is included among the taints, just as right intention is included in the aggregate of wisdom due to sharing a common function.

Sabbo [M 1.0164] attaggāho sakkāyadiṭṭhivinimutto natthīti vuttaṃ “channaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ…pe… vibhattā”ti. Sā hi diṭṭhi ekasmiṃ cittuppāde santāne ca ṭhitaṃ ekaṭṭhaṃ, tattha paṭhamaṃ sahajātekaṭṭhaṃ, itaraṃ pahānekaṭṭhaṃ, tadubhayampi niddhāretvā dassetuṃ “diṭṭhāsavehī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sabbathāpīti sabbappakārena, sahajātekaṭṭhapahānekaṭṭhappakārehīti attho. Avasesāti diṭṭhāsavato avasiṭṭhā. Tayopi āsavāti kāmāsavabhavāsavaavijjāsavā. Tathā hi pubbe “catūsu āsavesū”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā bahū evettha āsavā pahātabbā, tasmā bahuvacananiddeso kato “ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, āsavā dassanā pahātabbā”ti. Porāṇānanti aṭṭhakathācariyānaṃ, “purātanānaṃ majjhimabhāṇakāna”nti ca vadanti.

There is no self-grasping that is free from identity view; it is said, "Of the six views… they are analyzed." For that view stands as one in a single thought-moment and in a continuity. There, the first is co-arisen as one, and the other is abandoned as one. Having ascertained both, it is said 'by the view-taints,' etc., to show them. "In every way" means in all aspects—through the aspects of co-arising as one and abandoning as one. "The remainder" refers to those remaining after the taint of views. "Those three taints" are the taints of sensual desire, existence, and ignorance. For earlier it was said, "In the four taints." Therefore, because many taints are to be abandoned here, the plural description is made: "These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by seeing." "The ancients" refers to the teachers of the commentaries, and some say, "the ancient Middle Reciters."

Dassanā pahātabbātiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

What needs to be said regarding 'to be abandoned by seeing,' etc., has already been stated earlier.

Dassanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the taints to be abandoned by seeing is completed.

Saṃvarāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Taints to be Abandoned by Restraint

22. Saṃvarādīhīti [V 1.0147] saṃvarapaṭisevanaadhivāsanaparivajjanavinodanehi. Sabbesampīti catunnampi ariyamaggānaṃ. Ayanti saṃvarāpahātabbādikathā pubbabhāgapaṭipadāti veditabbā. Tathā hi heṭṭhā “upakkilesavisodhanaṃ ādiṃ katvā āsavakkhayapaṭipattidassanattha”nti suttantadesanāya payojanaṃ vuttaṃ. Na hi sakkā ādito eva ariyamaggaṃ bhāvetuṃ, atha kho samādinnasīlo indriyesu guttadvāro “saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati, saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāseti, saṅkhāyekaṃ parivajjeti, saṅkhāyekaṃ vinodetī”ti (dī. ni. 3.348; ma. ni. 2.168) evaṃ vuttaṃ caturāpassenapaṭipattiṃ paṭipajjamāno sammasanavidhiṃ otaritvā anukkamena vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā āsave khepeti. Tenāha bhagavā “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahāsamuddo anupubbaninno anupubbapoṇo anupubbapabbhāro, na āyatakeneva papāto, evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye anupubbasikkhā anupubbakiriyā anupubbapaṭipadā, na āyatakeneva aññāpaṭivedho”ti (a. ni. 8.20; udā. 45; cūḷava. 385).

22. 'By restraint, etc.' means by restraint, using, enduring, avoiding, and removing. 'For all' refers to all four noble paths. This discussion on what is to be abandoned by restraint, etc., should be understood as the preliminary part of the practice. For it was stated earlier that the purpose of the Suttanta teaching was 'to show the practice for the destruction of the taints, beginning with the purification of the defilements.' For it is not possible to develop the noble path from the very beginning. Rather, one who has undertaken the virtue, is guarded in the sense-faculties, and undertakes the practice based on the four supports as stated—'One uses something after wise reflection, one endures something after wise reflection, one avoids something after wise reflection, one removes something after wise reflection' (Dī. Ni. 3.348; Ma. Ni. 2.168)—descends into the method of comprehension, gradually develops insight with diligence, and by the sequence of the path, destroys the taints. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'Just as, monks, the great ocean slopes away gradually, inclines gradually, shelves gradually, not with an abrupt precipice, so too, monks, in this Dhamma and Discipline, there is a gradual training, a gradual practice, a gradual path, not an abrupt penetration to final knowledge' (A. Ni. 8.20; Udā. 45; Cūḷava. 385).

Idhāti [M 1.0165] ayaṃ idha-saddo sabbākārato indriyasaṃvarasaṃvutassa puggalassa sannissayabhūtasāsanaparidīpano, aññasāsanassa tathābhāvapaṭisedhano cāti vuttaṃ “imasmiṃ sāsane”ti. Ādīnavapaṭisaṅkhāti ādīnavapaccavekkhaṇā. Sampalimaṭṭhanti (a. ni. ṭī. 3.6.58) ghaṃsitaṃ. Anubyañjanasoti hatthapādahasitakathitavilokitādippakārabhāgaso. Tañhi ayoniso manasikaroto kilesānaṃ anu anu byañjanato “anubyañjana”nti vuccati. Nimittaggāhoti itthipurisanimittādikassa vā kilesavatthubhūtassa vā nimittassa gāho. Ādittapariyāyanayenāti ādittapariyāye (saṃ. ni. 4.28; mahāva. 54) āgatanayena veditabbā ādīnavapaṭisaṅkhāti yojanā. Yathā itthiyā indriyanti itthindriyaṃ, na evamidaṃ, idaṃ pana cakkhumeva indriyanti cakkhundriyanti. Titthakāko viyāti titthe kāko titthakāko, nadiyā samatikkamanatitthe niyataṭṭhitiko. Āvāṭakacchapotiādīsupi eseva nayo.

"Here" — this word "here" illuminates the Teaching as the foundation for a person restrained in all respects by sense restraint, and it denies that same status to other teachings. Thus, it is said: "in this Dispensation." "Reflecting on the dangers" means the reviewing of drawbacks. "Touched" (A. Ni. Ṭī. 3.6.58) means rubbed. "Secondary characteristics" refers to the various aspects such as the hands, feet, laughter, speech, and glances. For one who attends to these unskillfully, it is because defilements manifest again and again (anu anu byañjanato) through them that they are called "secondary characteristics" (anubyañjana). "Grasping at signs" means seizing upon signs such as those of women or men, or any object that serves as a basis for defilements. The phrase "in the manner of the Discourse on the Burning" is a connection indicating that the reflection on dangers should be understood according to the method found in the Discourse on the Burning (Saṃ. Ni. 4.28; Mahāva. 54). The phrase "the female faculty" (itthindriyaṃ) means "the faculty of a woman" (itthiyā indriyaṃ), but this is not so here; rather, this is simply the eye which is the faculty, hence "the eye faculty" (cakkhundriyaṃ). "Like a crow at a ford" means a crow at a landing place, one that remains fixed at a river’s crossing point. The same method applies to "a turtle in a hole," and so on.

Evaṃ tappaṭibaddhavuttitāya cakkhundriye niyataṭṭhāno saṃvaro cakkhundriyasaṃvaro. Muṭṭhassaccaṃ satipaṭipakkhā akusaladhammā. Yadipi aññattha asaṅkheyyampi bhavaṅgacittaṃ nirantaraṃ uppajjati, pasādaghaṭṭanāvajjanuppādānaṃ pana antare dve eva bhavaṅgacittāni uppajjantīti ayaṃ cittaniyāmoti āha bhavaṅge “dvikkhattuṃ uppajjitvā niruddhe”ti.

Thus, because its mode of operation is bound to it, the restraint established in the eye faculty is 'restraint of the eye faculty.' Lapsed mindfulness refers to unwholesome states that are the counterpart to mindfulness. Although elsewhere countless life-continuum consciousnesses may arise uninterruptedly, in the interval between the striking of the sensitive matter and the arising of adverting, only two life-continuum consciousnesses arise—this is the fixed order of consciousness. Thus it is said of the life-continuum: 'when it has arisen twice and ceased...'

Javanakkhaṇe [V 1.0148] pana sace dussīlyaṃ vātiādi (visuddhi. ṭī. 1.15; dha. sa. mūlaṭī. 1352) puna avacanatthaṃ idheva sabbaṃ vuttanti chasu dvāresu yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Na hi pañcadvāre kāyavacīduccaritasaṅkhāto dussīlyasaṃvaro atthīti so manodvāravasena, itaro channampi dvārānaṃ vasena yojetabbo. Muṭṭhassaccādīnañhi satipaṭipakkhādilakkhaṇānaṃ akusaladhammānaṃ siyā pañcadvāre uppatti, na tveva kāyikavācasikavītikkamabhūtassa dussīlyassa tattha uppatti pañcadvārikajavanānaṃ aviññattijanakattāti.

However, regarding the moment of impulsion, if there is misconduct or the like (as mentioned in Visuddhimagga Ṭīkā 1.15; Dhammasaṅgaṇī Mūlaṭīkā 1352), to avoid repetition, everything said here should be connected with the six doors as is appropriate. For misconduct consisting of bodily and verbal misdeeds does not occur in the five doors; therefore, it should be connected by way of the mind door. The other forms of unrestraint, however, should be connected by way of all six doors. For unwholesome states, such as lapsed mindfulness, which have the characteristic of opposing mindfulness, may arise in the five doors, but misconduct that is an actual bodily or verbal transgression does not arise there, because the impulsions of the five doors do not generate intimations.

Yathā kinti yena pakārena javane uppajjamāno asaṃvaro “cakkhudvāre asaṃvaro”ti vuccati, taṃ nidassanaṃ kinti attho. Yathātiādinā nagaradvāre asaṃvare sati taṃsambandhānaṃ gharādīnaṃ asaṃvutatā [M 1.0166] viya javane asaṃvare sati taṃsambandhānaṃ dvārādīnaṃ asaṃvutatāti aññāsaṃvare aññāsaṃvutatāsāmaññameva nidasseti, na pubbāparasāmaññaṃ, antobahisāmaññaṃ vā. Sambandho ca javanena dvārādīnaṃ ekasantatipariyāpannatāya eva daṭṭhabbo. Paccayabhāvena purimanipphannaṃ javanakāle asantampi bhavaṅgādi phalanipphattiyā cakkhādi viya santaṃyeva nāma. Na hi dharamānaṃyeva “santa”nti vuccati, tasmā sati dvārabhavaṅgādike pacchā uppajjamānaṃ javanaṃ bāhiraṃ viya katvā nagaradvārasamānaṃ vuttaṃ. Itarañca antonagaragharādisamānaṃ. Javanassa hi paramatthato asatipi bāhirabhāve itarassa ca abbhantarabhāve “pabhassaramidaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, tañca kho āgantukehi upakkilesehi upakkiliṭṭha”nti (a. ni. 1.49) ādivacanato āgantukabhūtassa kadāci kadāci uppajjamānassa javanassa bāhirabhāvo, tabbidhurasabhāvassa itarassa abbhantarabhāvo ca pariyāyato veditabbo. Javane vā asaṃvare uppanne tato paraṃ dvārabhavaṅgādīnaṃ asaṃvarahetubhāvāpattito nagaradvārasadisena javanena pavisitvā dussīlyādicorānaṃ dvārabhavaṅgādīsu musanaṃ kusalabhaṇḍavināsanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Uppanne hi asaṃvare dvārādīnaṃ tassa hetubhāvo paññāyati, so ca uppajjamānoyeva dvārādīnaṃ saṃvarūpanissayabhāvaṃ paṭibāhentoyeva pavattatīti ayañhettha asaṃvarādīnaṃ pavattinayo. Pañcadvāre rūpādiārammaṇe āpāthagate yathāpaccayaṃ akusalajavane uppajjitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otiṇṇe manodvārikajavanaṃ taṃyeva ārammaṇaṃ katvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati, puna tasmiṃyeva dvāre “itthī puriso”tiādinā visayaṃ vavatthapetvā javanaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ otarati, puna vāre rajjanādivasena javanaṃ javati, punapi yadi tādisaṃ ārammaṇaṃ āpāthamāgacchati, taṃsadisameva pañcadvāre rūpādīsu javanaṃ uppajjati. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “evameva javane dussīlyādīsu uppannesu tasmiṃ asaṃvare sati dvārampi agutta”ntiādi. Ayaṃ tāva asaṃvarapakkhe atthavaṇṇanā.

The question is, 'In what way is unrestraint arising at the impulsion called "unrestraint at the eye-door"?' What is the illustration for this? By the words 'just as,' and so on, it illustrates merely the general similarity of unrestraint in one case to unrestraint in another, not a sequential or internal-external similarity. Just as when there is unrestraint at the city gate, the connected houses and so on are unrestrained, so too when there is unrestraint in the impulsion, the connected doors and so on are unrestrained. The connection of the doors and so on with the impulsion should be seen as their inclusion in a single continuum. The bhavaṅga and so on, though produced previously and not existing at the time of the impulsion, are still called 'existing' because they are a condition for the production of a result, just like the eye, etc. For it is not only what is currently existing that is called 'present.' Therefore, with the door, bhavaṅga, and so on being present, the impulsion that arises later is treated as external and is said to be like the city gate. And the other (the door, bhavaṅga, etc.) is like the houses inside the city. For although in an ultimate sense the impulsion is not external nor is the other internal, from statements such as, 'Luminous, monks, is this mind, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements' (A.N. 1.49), the externality of the impulsion, which arises only from time to time like an adventitious thing, and the internality of the other, which is of a different nature, should be understood figuratively. Alternatively, when unrestraint has arisen in the impulsion, it should be seen that thereafter, because the door, bhavaṅga, and so on become a cause for that unrestraint, thieves of immorality and so on enter by way of the impulsion, which is like the city gate, and plunder the door, bhavaṅga, and so on, destroying the treasure of wholesome states. For when unrestraint has arisen, the role of the door and so on as its cause becomes apparent. And as it arises, it proceeds by obstructing the state of the door and so on from being a support for restraint. This is the mode of operation of unrestraint and related states. When a form or other object comes into the range of the five doors, an unwholesome impulsion arises according to conditions and then subsides into the life-continuum. Then a mind-door impulsion takes that very object and subsides into the life-continuum. Again, at that same door, having determined the object as 'a woman,' 'a man,' etc., the impulsion subsides into the life-continuum. Again, at the door, the impulsion impels by way of lust and so on. And if a similar object comes into range again, a similar impulsion arises at the five doors regarding forms and so on. It is with reference to this that it is said: 'In the same way, when misconduct and so on arise in the impulsion, with that unrestraint, the door too is unguarded,' and so on. This, for now, is the explanation of the meaning on the side of unrestraint.

Saṃvarapakkhepi [V 1.0149] imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Saṃvarena samannāgato puggalo saṃvutoti vuttoti āha “upetoti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Ekajjhaṃ katvāti “pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto”ti padañca atthato abhinnaṃ samānaṃ katvā. Ayameva cettha attho sundarataro [M 1.0167] uparipāḷiyā saṃsandanato. Tenāha “tathāhī”tiādi. Yanti ādesoti iminā liṅgavipallāsena saddhiṃ vacanavipallāso katoti dasseti, nipātapadaṃ vā etaṃ paccattaputhuvacanatthaṃ. Vighātakarāti cittavighātakaraṇā cittadukkhanibbattakā ca. Yathāvuttakilesahetukā dāhānubandhā vipākā eva vipākapariḷāhā. Yathā panettha āsavā aññe ca vighātakarā kilesavipākapariḷāhā sambhavanti, taṃ dassetuṃ “cakkhudvārehī”tiādi vuttaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva. Ettha ca saṃvaraṇūpāyo, saṃvaritabbaṃ, saṃvaro, yato so saṃvaro, yattha saṃvaro, yañca saṃvaraphalanti ayaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo. Kathaṃ? Paṭisaṅkhā yonisoti hi saṃvaraṇūpāyo. Cakkhundriyaṃ saṃvaritabbaṃ. Saṃvaraggahaṇena gahitā sati saṃvaro. Asaṃvutassāti saṃvaraṇāvadhi. Asaṃvarato hi saṃvaraṇaṃ. Saṃvaritabbaggahaṇena siddho idha saṃvaravisayo. Cakkhundriyañhi saṃvarañāṇaṃ rūpārammaṇe saṃvarīyatīti avuttasiddhoyamattho. Āsavatannimittakilesādipariḷāhābhāvo phalaṃ. Evaṃ sotadvārādīsupi yojetabbaṃ. Sabbatthevāti manodvāre pañcadvāre cāti sabbasmiṃ dvāre.

On the side of restraint, too, the meaning should be understood in this same way. A person endowed with restraint is called 'restrained'; thus it says, 'is said to be possessed.' The phrase 'having made it one' means having made the term 'restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha' identical in meaning. This is indeed the more beautiful meaning here, as it corresponds with the Pāli text above. Therefore, it is said: 'For thus...' and so on. The word 'yanti' (they go) is a substitution; this shows that along with the change of gender, a change of number has also been made. Or else it is a particle, meaning an independent plural. 'Distressing' means causing mental distress and producing mental suffering. The results, caused by the aforementioned defilements and followed by burning, are themselves the 'burning of results.'
