To show how taints and other distressing things—defilements and the burning of results—can arise here, it is said, 'through the eye-doors,' etc. That is easily understood. Here, this division should be understood: the means of restraint, what is to be restrained, restraint itself, that from which there is restraint, that wherein there is restraint, and the fruit of restraint. How? Wise reflection is the means of restraint. The eye faculty is what is to be restrained. By the term 'restraint,' mindfulness is meant. 'Of one who is unrestrained' indicates the boundary for restraining, for restraining is from unrestraint. By the mention of 'what is to be restrained,' the object of restraint is established here. For that the eye faculty is restrained by the knowledge of restraint in regard to a form-object is a meaning established without being stated. The fruit is the absence of the taints and the burning of defilements and so on caused by them. This should be applied to the ear-door and so on as well. 'In every case' means in the mind-door and in the five doors, thus in all doors.

Saṃvarāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the taints to be abandoned by restraint is concluded.

Paṭisevanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Taints to be Abandoned by Proper Use

23. Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvarantiādīsu “sītassa paṭighātāyā”tiādinā vuttaṃ paccavekkhaṇameva yoniso paṭisaṅkhā. Īdisanti evarūpaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ. Bhavapatthanāya assādayatoti bhavapatthanāmukhena bhāvitaṃ ārammaṇaṃ assādentassa. Cīvaranti nivāsanādi yaṃ kiñci cīvaraṃ. Paṭisevatīti nivāsanādivasena paribhuñjati. Yāvadevāti payojanaparimāṇaniyamanaṃ. Sītapaṭighātādiyeva hi yogino cīvarapaṭisevane payojanaṃ. Sītassāti dhātukkhobhato vā utupariṇāmato vā uppannasītassa. Paṭighātāyāti paṭibāhanatthaṃ tappaccayassa vikārassa vinodanatthaṃ. Uṇhassāti aggisantāpato uppannassa uṇhassa. Ḍaṃsādayo pākaṭāyeva. Puna yāvadevāti niyatapayojanaparimāṇaniyamanaṃ. Niyatañhi payojanaṃ cīvarapaṭisevanassa hirikopīnapaṭicchādanaṃ, itaraṃ kadāci kadāci[M 1.0168]. Hirikopīnanti sambādhaṭṭhānaṃ[V 1.0150]. Yasmiñhi aṅge vivaṭe hirīkuppati vinassati, taṃ hiriyā kopanato hirikopīnaṃ, tassa paṭicchādanatthaṃ cīvaraṃ paṭisevati.

23. In 'reflecting wisely on the robe' and so on, the consideration mentioned in 'for protection from cold' and so on is precisely wise reflection. 'Such' means a desirable object of this kind. 'Delighting in it with longing for existence' means for one who savors an object cultivated through the means of longing for existence. 'The robe' means any robe, such as a lower garment. 'Uses it' means one partakes of it by way of wearing it and so on. 'Only to this extent' is a limitation of the extent of the purpose. For a yogi, the purpose of using the robe is solely to ward off cold and so on. 'From cold' means cold arising from a disturbance of the elements or from a change in the weather. 'For protection' means for the sake of repelling it, for eliminating the affliction caused by that condition. 'From heat' means heat arising from the burning heat of fire. Gadflies and so on are self-evident. Again, 'only to this extent' is a limitation of the extent of the definite purpose. For the definite purpose of using the robe is to cover the private parts; other uses are occasional. 'Private parts' means the shameful area. For when that part of the body is exposed, shame is agitated and lost. Hence, it is called 'hirikopīna' because it agitates shame. The robe is used to cover it.

Piṇḍapātanti yaṃ kiñci āhāraṃ. So hi piṇḍolyena bhikkhanāya patte patanato tattha tattha laddhabhikkhāpiṇḍānaṃ pāto sannipātoti “piṇḍapāto”ti vuccati. Neva davāyāti na kīḷanāya. Na madāyāti na balamadamānamadapurisamadatthaṃ. Na maṇḍanāyāti na aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ pīṇanabhāvatthaṃ. Na vibhūsanāyāti na tesaṃyeva sobhanatthaṃ, chavisampatiatthanti attho. Imāni ca padāni yathākkamaṃ moha-dosa-saṇṭhāna-vaṇṇa-rāgūpanissaya-pahānatthāni veditabbāni. Purimaṃ vā dvayaṃ attano attano saṃkilesuppattinisedhanatthaṃ, itaraṃ parassapi. Cattāripi kāmasukhallikānuyogassa pahānatthaṃ vuttānīti veditabbāni. Kāyassāti rūpakāyassa. Ṭhitiyā yāpanāyāti pabandhaṭṭhitatthañceva pavattiyā avicchedanatthañca cirakālaṭṭhitatthaṃ jīvitindriyassa pavattāpanatthaṃ. Vihiṃsūparatiyāti jighacchādukkhassa uparamaṇatthaṃ. Brahmacariyānuggahāyāti sāsanamaggabrahmacariyānaṃ anuggahatthaṃ. Itīti evaṃ iminā upāyena. Purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmīti purāṇaṃ abhuttapaccayā uppajjanakavedanaṃ paṭihanissāmi. Navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmīti navaṃ bhuttapaccayā uppajjanakavedanaṃ na uppādessāmīti. Tassā hi anuppannāya anuppajjanatthameva āhāraṃ paribhuñjati. Ettha ca abhuttapaccayā uppajjanakavedanā nāma yathāpavattā jighacchānimittā vedanā. Sā hi abhuñjantassa bhiyyo bhiyyo pavaḍḍhanavasena uppajjati, bhuttapaccayā uppajjanakavedanāpi khudānimittāva aṅgadāhasūlādivedanā appavattā. Sā hi bhuttapaccayā anuppannāva na uppajjissatīti. Vihiṃsānimittatā cetāsaṃ vihiṃsāya viseso.

'Almsfood' means any food. It is called 'almsfood' (piṇḍapāta) because it is the gathering (pāta) of lumps (piṇḍa) of alms obtained here and there as they fall into the bowl during the alms-round. 'Not for amusement' means not for play. 'Not for intoxication' means not for the sake of the intoxication of strength, the intoxication of pride, or the intoxication of manliness. 'Not for beautification' means not for the sake of plumping the limbs and minor limbs. 'Not for adornment' means not for the sake of their beauty, that is, for the sake of perfecting the complexion. And these terms should be understood as being, in respective order, for the abandoning of delusion, hatred, lust for form, lust for color, and the basis of lust. The first two are for preventing the arising of one's own defilements, while the others are for preventing those of others as well. All four are said to be for abandoning indulgence in sensual pleasure. 'Of the body' means of the physical body. 'For its endurance, for its sustenance' means for the sake of its continuous existence, for the sake of the non-interruption of its continuity, for its long-term existence, and for the maintenance of the life faculty. 'For the cessation of affliction' means for the sake of ending the suffering of hunger. 'For supporting the holy life' means for the sake of supporting the holy life of the Dispensation and the Path. 'Thus' means in this way, by this means. 'I will ward off old feeling' means I will ward off the old feeling that arises from not having eaten. 'And I will not arouse new feeling' means I will not arouse the new feeling that arises from having eaten. For one consumes food solely for the non-arising of that which has not yet arisen. Here, the feeling arising from not having eaten is the feeling with hunger as its sign, which occurs naturally. For one who does not eat, this feeling arises by way of growing ever stronger. The feeling arising from having eaten is also a feeling with hunger as its sign, namely, the unarisen feeling of burning in the limbs, stabbing pains, and so on. For, conditioned by having eaten properly, that which has not yet arisen will not arise. And their nature as a cause of affliction is a specific kind of affliction.

Yātrā ca me bhavissatīti yāpanā ca me catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ bhavissati. Yāpanāyāti iminā jīvitindriyayāpanā vuttā, idha catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ avicchedasaṅkhātā yāpanāti ayametāsaṃ viseso. Anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro cāti ayuttapariyesanapaṭiggahaṇaparibhogaparivajjanena anavajjatā, parimitaparibhogena phāsuvihāro. Asappāyāparimitabhojanapaccayā aratitandīvijambhitāviññugarahādidosābhāvena vā anavajjatā, sappāyaparimitabhojanapaccayā kāyabalasambhavena [M 1.0169] phāsuvihāro. Yāvadatthaudarāvadehakabhojanaparivajjanena seyyasukhapassasukhamiddhasukhādīnaṃ abhāvato anavajjatā, catupañcālopamattaññīnabhojanena catuiriyāpathayogyatāpādanato phāsuvihāro. Vuttañhetaṃ –

'And my journey will be maintained' means the sustenance of my four postures will be maintained. By 'for its sustenance' in the previous reflection, the sustenance of the life faculty was stated; here, 'sustenance' is described as the non-interruption of the four postures. This is the distinction between them. 'And blamelessness and a comfortable living': blamelessness is by avoiding improper seeking, receiving, and consuming; comfortable living is by moderate consumption. Or, blamelessness is through the absence of faults such as discontent, sloth, drowsiness, yawning, and blame from the wise, which are due to unsuitable and excessive food; comfortable living is through the arising of bodily strength due to suitable and moderate food. By avoiding eating to the full extent of the stomach’s capacity, blamelessness arises from the absence of the pleasures of lying down, leaning, and sleeping; by eating with the knowledge of the right amount, leaving four or five mouthfuls, comfortable living arises from becoming fit for the four postures. For it has been said:

“Cattāro [V 1.0151] pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno”ti. (theragā. 983);

"Leaving four or five mouthfuls uneaten, one should drink water; this is enough for the comfortable living of a resolute bhikkhu."

Ettāvatā payojanapariggaho, majjhimā ca paṭipadā dīpitā hoti.

By this much, the comprehension of the purpose has been shown, and the middle way has been explained.

Senāsananti sayanañca āsanañca. Yattha hi vihārādike seti nipajjati, āsati nisīdati, taṃ senāsanaṃ. Utuparissayavinodanapaṭisallānārāmatthanti utuyeva parisahanaṭṭhena parissayo, sarīrābādhacittavikkhepakaro, atha vā yathāvutto utu ca sīhabyagghādipākaṭaparissayo ca rāgadosādipaṭicchannaparissayo ca utuparissayo, tassa vinodanatthañceva ekībhāvasukhatthañca. Idañca cīvarapaṭisevane hirikopīnapaṭicchādanaṃ viya tassa niyatapayojananti puna “yāvadevā”ti vuttaṃ.

'Lodging' (senāsana) means both a place for lying down (sayana) and a place for sitting (āsana). For in whatever dwelling one lies down or reclines, or sits, that is lodging. 'For warding off the dangers of the weather and for the delight of seclusion': 'dangers of the weather' (utuparissaya) refers to the affliction from the weather itself, which harms the body and distracts the mind. Or, it refers to the weather, obvious dangers such as lions and tigers, and hidden dangers such as lust and hatred. The purpose is to dispel these and for the happiness of solitude. And this is its definite purpose, just as covering one's private parts is in the case of using the robe; thus, it is again said, 'only to this extent'.

Gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāranti rogassa paccanīkappavattiyā gilānapaccayo, tato eva bhisakkassa anuññātavatthutāya bhesajjaṃ, jīvitassa parivārasambhārabhāvehi parikkhāro cāti gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāro, taṃ. Uppannānanti jātānaṃ nibbattānaṃ. Veyyābādhikānanti byābādhato dhātukkhobhato ca tannibbattarogato ca jātānaṃ. Vedanānanti dukkhavedanānaṃ. Abyābajjhaparamatāyāti niddukkhaparamabhāvāya paṭisevāmīti yojanā. Evamettha saṅkhepeneva pāḷivaṇṇanā veditabbā. Navavedanuppādanatopīti na kevalaṃ āyatiṃ eva vipākapariḷāhā, atha kho atibhojanapaccayā alaṃsāṭakādīnaṃ viya navavedanuppādanatopi veditabbāti attho.

'The requisite of medicine as a support for the sick' (gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāra): it is a support for the sick (gilānapaccaya) because it counteracts the onset of illness; it is medicine (bhesajja) because it is a thing permitted by a physician; and it is a requisite (parikkhāra) because it is an accessory for the maintenance of life. This is the requisite of medicine as a support for the sick. 'That have arisen' means that are born, that have come into being. 'Afflictive' means born from affliction, from a disturbance of the elements, and from the disease resulting from that. 'Feelings' means painful feelings. 'For the sake of utmost freedom from affliction' is to be connected with 'I make use of it for the sake of the ultimate state free from suffering'. Thus, here, the explanation of the Pāli should be understood in brief. Regarding 'the production of new feelings': it should be understood that this refers not only to future karmic results and torment, but also to the production of new feelings from overeating, similar to the discomfort from a tight garment. This is the meaning.

Paṭisevanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the taints to be abandoned by use is concluded.

Adhivāsanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Taints to be Abandoned by Endurance

24. Khamoti [M 1.0170] khamanako. Kammaṭṭhānikassa calanaṃ nāma kammaṭṭhānapariccāgoti āha “calati kampati kammaṭṭhānaṃ vijahatī”ti. Adhimattampi uṇhaṃ sahati, sahanto ca na naggasamaṇādayo viya sahati, atha kho kammaṭṭhānāvijahanenāti āha “sveva thero viyā”ti. Bahicaṅkameti leṇato bahi caṅkame. Uṇhabhayenevāti narakaggiuṇhabhayeneva. Tenāha “avīcimahānirayaṃ paccavekkhitvā”ti, tampi “mayā anekakkhattuṃ anubhūtaṃ, idaṃ pana tato mudutara”nti [V 1.0152] evaṃ paccavekkhitvā. Etthāti etasmiṃ ṭhāne. Aggisantāpova veditabbo sūriyasantāpassa parato vuccamānattā.

24. 'Patient' means one who endures. For a meditator, 'moving' means abandoning the meditation subject, as it is said: 'He moves, he shakes, he abandons the meditation subject.' He endures even extreme heat, but he does not endure like naked ascetics and others; rather, he endures by not abandoning the meditation subject, as it is said: 'Just like that elder.' 'On the walking path outside' means on the walking path outside the cave. 'By the fear of heat' means by the fear of the heat of the fires of hell. Therefore it is said: 'Having reflected on the Avīci great hell,' and also reflecting thus: 'I have experienced that many times, but this is milder than that.' 'Here' means in this place. The heat of fire should be understood, because the heat of the sun is mentioned further on.

Parisuddhasīlohamasmīti sabbathāpi “visuddhasīlohamasmī”ti maraṇaṃ aggahetvā avippaṭisāramūlikaṃ pītiṃ uppādesi. Saha pītuppādāti pharaṇapītiyā uppādena saheva. Visaṃ nivattitvāti pītivegena ajjhotthataṃ daṭṭhamukheneva bhassitvā. Tatthevāti sappena daṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva. Cittekaggataṃ labhitvāti “pītimanassa kāyo passambhatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.466; 3.359; saṃ. ni. 5.376; a. ni. 3.96; 11.12) nayena samādhānaṃ pāpuṇitvā.

'I am one of purified virtue' means in every way, 'I am one of purified virtue'—without taking death into consideration, he generated joy rooted in non-remorse. 'With the arising of joy' means simultaneously with the arising of pervasive joy. 'Having expelled the poison' means that, overwhelmed by the force of joy, it fell from the very mouth that was bitten. 'Right there' means in the very place where he was bitten by the snake. 'Having obtained one-pointedness of mind' means having attained concentration according to the method beginning with 'For one with a joyful mind, the body becomes tranquil,' and so on.

Paccayesu santoso bhāvanāya ca āramitabbaṭṭhānatāya ārāmo assāti paccayasantosabhāvanārāmo, tassa bhāvo paccaya…pe… rāmatā, tāya. Mahātheroti vuḍḍhataro thero. Vacanameva tadatthaṃ ñāpetukāmānaṃ pathoti vacanapatho.

Contentment with requisites and delight in development (paccayasantosabhāvanārāma): because it is a place for establishing development, it is called 'delight in contentment with requisites and development'; its state is 'delight in contentment with requisites and development', by that. 'Great elder' means a more senior elder. 'The path of speech' (vacanapatha) is the way of speaking for those wishing to make known that meaning.

Asukhaṭṭhena vā tibbā. Yañhi na sukhaṃ, taṃ aniṭṭhaṃ “tibba”nti vuccati. Evaṃsabhāvoti “adhivāsanajātiyo”ti padassa atthamāha. Muhuttena khaṇeva vāte hadayaṃ phāletuṃ āraddheyeva. Anāgāmī hutvā parinibbāyīti arahattaṃ patvā parinibbāyi.

Or, it is intense by the characteristic of suffering. For what is not pleasant, that which is undesirable, is called 'intense'. 'Such is its nature' explains the meaning of the phrase 'of the nature of endurance'. In a moment, in an instant, the wind was just about to split the heart. 'Having become a Non-returner, he attained final Nibbāna' means having reached Arahantship, he attained final Nibbāna.

Evaṃ sabbatthāti “uṇhena phuṭṭhassa sītaṃ patthayato”tiādinā sabbattha uṇhādinimittaṃ kāmāsavuppatti veditabbā, sītaṃ vā uṇhaṃ vā aniṭṭhanti adhippāyo. Attaggāhe sati attaniyaggāhoti āha “mayhaṃ sītaṃ uṇhanti gāho diṭṭhāsavo”ti. Sītādike upagate sahantī khamantī te attano upari vāsentī viya hotīti vuttaṃ “āropetvā vāsetiyevā”ti[M 1.0171]. Na nirassatīti na vidhunati. Yo hi sītādike na sahati, so te nirassanto vidhunanto viya hotīti.

'Thus, in all cases' means that in all cases, the arising of the taint of sensual desire should be understood from the sign of heat, etc., as in 'one touched by heat longs for coolness,' and so on. The intention is that cold or heat is undesirable. When there is clinging to self, there is clinging to what belongs to self, as he says: 'The clinging "mine is cold, mine is heat" is the taint of wrong view'. When cold and so on are encountered, enduring and tolerating them is like making them dwell upon oneself, hence it is said: 'as if causing them to dwell, having placed them upon oneself'. 'He does not cast them away' means he does not shake them off. For one who does not endure cold and so on is like one casting them away, shaking them off.

Adhivāsanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the taints to be abandoned by endurance is concluded.

Parivajjanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā

The Elucidation of the Taints to be Abandoned by Avoidance.

25. Ahaṃ [V 1.0153] samaṇoti (a. ni. ṭī. 3.6.58) “ahaṃ samaṇo, kiṃ mama jīvitena vā maraṇena vā”ti evaṃ acintetvāti adhippāyo. Paccavekkhitvāti gāmappadesaṃ payojanādiñca paccavekkhitvā. Paṭikkamatīti hatthiādīnaṃ samīpagamanato apakkamati. Kaṇṭakā yattha tiṭṭhanti, taṃ kaṇṭakaṭṭhānaṃ. Amanussaduṭṭhānīti amanussasañcārena dūsitāni, saparissayānīti attho. Samānanti samaṃ, avisamanti attho. Akāsi vā tādisaṃ anācāraṃ.

25. “I am a monk” (A.N.Ṭī. 3.6.58) means that one should not think, “What is life or death to me?” “Having reflected” means having reflected on the village area and its purposes. “He retreats” means he withdraws from approaching elephants and the like. Where thorns stand, that is a thorny place. “Places troubled by non-human beings” means those corrupted by the movement of non-human beings, that is, they are fraught with peril. “Samāna” means equal, that is, not unequal. Or he committed such misconduct.

Sīlasaṃvarasaṅkhātenāti “kathaṃ parivajjanaṃ sīla”nti yadettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Apica “caṇḍaṃ hatthiṃ parivajjetī”ti vacanato hatthiādiparivajjanampi bhagavato vacanānuṭṭhānanti katvā ācārasīlamevāti veditabbaṃ.

Regarding what is called restraint of virtue, what should be said here about how avoidance constitutes virtue has already been stated below. Moreover, since it is said, “One should avoid a fierce elephant,” avoiding elephants and the like, being the carrying out of the Blessed One’s instruction, should also be understood as virtuous conduct.

Parivajjanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Taints to be Abandoned by Avoidance is completed.

Vinodanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā

The Elucidation of the Taints to be Abandoned by Dispelling.

26. Itipīti iminā kāraṇena, ayonisomanasikārasamuṭṭhitattāpi lobhādisahagatattāpi kusalapaṭipakkhatopītiādīhi kāraṇehi ayaṃ vitakko akusaloti attho. Iminā nayena sāvajjotiādīsupi attho veditabbo. Ettha ca akusalotiādinā diṭṭhadhammikaṃ kāmavitakkassa ādīnavaṃ dasseti, dukkhavipākoti iminā samparāyikaṃ. Attabyābādhāya saṃvattatītiādīsupi imināva nayena ādīnavavibhāvanā veditabbā. Uppannassa kāmavitakkassa anadhivāsanaṃ nāma puna tādisassa anuppādanaṃ, taṃ panassa pahānaṃ vinodanaṃ byantikaraṇaṃ anabhāvagamananti [M 1.0172] ca vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti pāḷiyaṃ “uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”ti vatvā “pajahatī”tiādi vuttanti tamatthaṃ dassento “anadhivāsento kiṃ karotīti pajahatī”tiādimāha. Pahānañcettha vikkhambhanameva, na samucchedoti dassetuṃ “vinodetī”tiādi vuttanti vikkhambhanavaseneva attho dassito.

26. “Thus” (it is said) for this reason: because it arises from unwise attention, because it is accompanied by greed and the like, and because it opposes wholesome states—for these reasons, this thought is unwholesome—this is the meaning. In this way, the meaning should be understood in “blameworthy” and the like as well. Here, “unwholesome” and the like show the immediate danger of sensual thought, while “painful result” shows the future danger. “Leads to self-affliction” and so on should similarly be understood as elaborating the dangers. Not tolerating an arisen sensual thought means not generating such again; its abandonment, removal, destruction, and disappearance can also be expressed. Thus, in the Pāḷi, having stated, “One does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought,” it says, “abandons it,” etc., to indicate this meaning. To show this meaning, it said, “Not tolerating, what does one do? One abandons it,” etc. And here, abandonment is only suppression, not eradication; thus, “removes” and the like are said, and the meaning is shown only in terms of suppression.

Kāmavitakkoti sampayogato ārammaṇato ca kāmasahagato vitakko. Tenāha “kāmapaṭisaṃyutto [V 1.0154] takko”tiādi. Kāmapaṭisaṃyuttoti hi kāmarāgasaṅkhātena kāmena sampayutto vatthukāmasaṅkhātena paṭibaddho ca. Uppannuppanneti tesaṃ pāpavitakkānaṃ uppādāvatthāgahaṇaṃ vā kataṃ siyā anavasesaggahaṇaṃ vā. Tesu paṭhamaṃ sandhāyāha “upannamatte”ti, sampatijāteti attho. Anavasesaggahaṇaṃ byāpanicchāya hotīti dassetuṃ “satakkhattumpi uppanne”ti vuttaṃ. Ñātivitakkoti “amhākaṃ ñātayo sukhajīvino sampattiyuttā”tiādinā gehassitapemavasena ñātake ārabbha uppannavitakko. Janapadavitakkoti “amhākaṃ janapado subhikkho sampannasasso ramaṇīyo”tiādinā gehassitapemavaseneva janapadaṃ ārabbha uppannavitakko. Ukkuṭikappadhānādīhi dukkhe nijjiṇṇe samparāye attā sukhī hoti amaroti dukkarakārikāya paṭisaṃyutto amaratthāya vitakko, taṃ vā ārabbha amarāvikkhepadiṭṭhisahagato amaro ca so vitakko cāti amaravitakko. Parānuddayatāpaṭisaṃyuttoti paresu upaṭṭhākādīsu sahanandikādivasena pavatto anuddayatāpatirūpako gehassitapemena paṭisaṃyutto vitakko. Lābhasakkārasilokapaṭisaṃyuttoti cīvarādilābhena ceva sakkārena ca kittisaddena ca ārammaṇakaraṇavasena paṭisaṃyutto. Anavaññattipaṭisaṃyuttoti “aho vata maṃ pare na avajāneyyuṃ, na heṭṭhā katvā maññeyyuṃ, pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garuṃ kareyyu”nti uppannavitakko.

“The thought of sensuality” is a thought accompanied by sensuality both by way of association and by way of object. Hence it is said, “thought connected with sensuality,” and so on. “Connected with sensuality” means associated with sensuality, which is designated as sensual lust, and bound to what is designated as the object of sensuality. “Having arisen again and again” refers either to taking up the state of the repeated arising of those evil thoughts or to taking up their objects without remainder. With regard to the first, it is said, “just arisen,” meaning newly arisen. To indicate the grasping without remainder, it is said, “even if it has arisen a hundred times.” “The thought of relatives” is a thought that arises concerning relatives, based on affection for one’s home, such as, “Our relatives live happily, endowed with prosperity,” and so on. “The thought of the country” is a thought that arises concerning the country, based on affection for one’s home, such as, “Our country is prosperous, abundant in crops, and delightful,” and so on. The thought of immortality is a thought connected with difficult practices, arising from the idea that after enduring suffering through practices like squatting and so forth, the self will be happy and immortal in the next life. Alternatively, it is a thought connected with the view of eternalism, which is distracted regarding immortality, or it is that thought itself which is called “immortal thought.” “The thought connected with seeming sympathy for others” is a thought that arises concerning others, such as attendants, with a semblance of compassion, appearing as shared joy and so on, but is actually connected with affection for one’s home. “The thought connected with gain, honor, and fame” is a thought connected with gain, such as robes, etc., as well as honor and the sound of praise, by way of making them its object. “The thought connected with not being disrespected” is a thought that arises, such as, “Oh, may others not despise me, may they not regard me as inferior, may they respect me like a stone parasol!”

Kāmavitakko kāmasaṅkappanasabhāvattā kāmasaṅkappapavattiyā sātisayattā ca kāmanākāroti āha “kāmavitakko panettha kāmāsavo”ti. Tabbisesoti kāmāsavaviseso, rāgasahavuttīti adhippāyo. Kāmavitakkādike vinodeti attano santānato [M 1.0173] nīharati etenāti vinodanaṃ, vīriyanti āha “vīriyasaṃvarasaṅkhātena vinodanenā”ti.

The thought of sensuality is of the nature of sensual desire because it has the characteristic of sensual intention, proceeds from the activity of sensual intention, and is excessive. Hence, it is said: 'Here, the thought of sensuality is the taint of sensual desire.' 'Its specific form' means a specific form of the taint of sensual desire; the implied meaning is that it is accompanied by lust. 'Dispelling' is so called because by that one dispels and expels thoughts of sensuality and the like from one’s own mind-stream. It is energy, hence it is said: 'by dispelling, which is reckoned as the restraint of energy'.

Vinodanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Taints to be Abandoned by Dispelling is completed.

Bhāvanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Taints to be Abandoned by Development.

27. “Satta bojjhaṅgā bhāvitā bahulīkatā vijjāvimuttiyo paripūrentī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.187) vacanato vijjāvimuttīnaṃ anadhigamo tato ca sakalavaṭṭadukkhānativatti abhāvanāya ādīnavo, vuttavipariyāyena bhagavato orasaputtabhāvādivasena ca bhāvanāya ānisaṃso veditabbo. Uparimaggattayasamayasambhūtāti dutiyādimaggakkhaṇe jātā, bhāvanādhikārato dutiyamaggādipariyāpannāti attho. Nanu ca te lokuttarā eva, kasmā visesanaṃ [V 1.0155] katanti? Nayidaṃ visesanaṃ, visesitabbaṃ panetaṃ, lokuttarabojjhaṅgā eva adhippetā, te ca kho uparimaggattayasamayasambhūtāti. Bojjhaṅgesu asammohatthanti vipassanājhānamaggaphalabojjhaṅgesu sammohābhāvatthaṃ. Missakanayena hi bojjhaṅgesu vuccamānesu tadaṅgādivivekadassanavasena vipassanābojjhaṅgādayo vibhajitvā vuccanti, na nibbattitalokuttarabojjhaṅgā evāti bojjhaṅgesu sammoho na hoti bojjhaṅgabhāvanāpaṭipattiyā ca sammadeva pakāsitattā. Idha panāti imasmiṃ sutte, imasmiṃ vā adhikāre. Lokuttaranayo eva gahetabbo bhāvanāmaggassa adhikatattā.

27. "The seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill knowledge and liberation" (SN 5.187). From this, the danger of not developing them is the non-attainment of knowledge and liberation, and consequently the failure to transcend all the suffering of the cycle of existence. Conversely, the benefit of developing them should be understood through the opposite, such as becoming the Buddha's own son, and so on. 'Those arising at the time of the three higher paths' means they are born at the moment of the second path and so on, and are included in the second path and so on, because this is the section on development. But are these not supramundane? Why is a qualification made? This is not a qualification but a specification: only the supramundane factors of enlightenment are intended, and these arise at the time of the three higher paths. 'For the purpose of non-delusion regarding the factors of enlightenment' means for the absence of delusion regarding the insight, jhāna, path, and fruition factors of enlightenment. For when the factors of enlightenment are spoken of in a mixed way, the insight factors of enlightenment and so on are distinguished and spoken of by way of seeing the distinction of their components, etc.; it is not that they are only the produced supramundane factors of enlightenment. Thus, there is no delusion regarding the factors of enlightenment, because the practice of developing the factors of enlightenment is correctly explained. But here—in this sutta or in this section—only the supramundane method should be taken, because the path of development is the topic.

Ādipadānanti (a. ni. ṭī. 1.1.418) “satisambojjhaṅga”nti evamādīnaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ vākye ādibhūtānaṃ padānaṃ. Atthatoti visesavasena sāmaññavasena ca padatthato. Lakkhaṇādīhīti lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānato. Kamatoti anupubbito. Anūnādhikatoti tāvattakato. Vibhāvināti viññunā.

'Of the initial words' (AN-ṭīkā 1.1.418) refers to the initial words in each respective sentence, such as 'the mindfulness factor of enlightenment,' and so forth. 'In terms of meaning' means in terms of the meaning of the words, both specifically and generally. 'By characteristics and so on' means by characteristic, function, and manifestation. 'In order' means sequentially. 'Neither deficient nor excessive' means just so much. 'By one who understands' means by an intelligent person.

Satisambojjhaṅgeti satisambojjhaṅgapade. Saraṇaṭṭhenāti anussaraṇaṭṭhena. Cirakatādibhedaṃ ārammaṇaṃ upagantvā ṭhānaṃ, anissajjanaṃ vā upaṭṭhānaṃ. Udake alābu viya pilavitvā gantuṃ adatvā pāsāṇassa viya niccalassa ārammaṇassa ṭhapanaṃ sāraṇaṃ asammuṭṭhatākaraṇaṃ apilāpanaṃ. Vuttampi [M 1.0174] hetaṃ milindapañhe. Bhaṇḍāgārikoti bhaṇḍagopako. Apilāpe karoti apilāpeti. Therenāti nāgasenattherena. Sammosapaccanīkaṃ kiccaṃ asammoso, na sammosābhāvamattaṃ. Gocarābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānāti kāyādiārammaṇābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā.

In the phrase 'the mindfulness factor of enlightenment.' 'In the sense of remembering' means in the sense of recollecting. Having approached an object of various kinds, such as something done long ago, the establishment, or the non-abandonment, is presence. Like a gourd in water, not allowing it to float away, or like a stone, motionless, the placing of the object is remembering, the causing of non-forgetfulness, the prevention of floating away. This has also been stated in the Questions of Milinda. 'A treasurer' is a keeper of goods. 'He makes it not float away' means he prevents it from floating away. 'By the Elder' means by the Elder Nāgasena. The function opposed to confusion is non-confusion, not merely the absence of confusion. 'Its manifestation is the state of facing the domain' means its manifestation is the state of facing an object such as the body.

Bodhiyā dhammasāmaggiyā, aṅgo avayavo, bodhissa vā ariyasāvakassa aṅgo kāraṇaṃ. Patiṭṭhānāyūhanā oghataraṇasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.1) –

A factor or constituent of the collection of phenomena that is enlightenment; or a factor, a cause, for the enlightened one or the noble disciple. In the commentary on the Discourse on Crossing the Flood (SN-a 1.1.1), 'establishment and accumulation' are explained:

“Kilesavasena patiṭṭhānaṃ, abhisaṅkhāravasena āyūhanā. Taṇhādiṭṭhīhi patiṭṭhānaṃ, avasesakilesābhisaṅkhārehi āyūhanā. Taṇhāvasena patiṭṭhānaṃ, diṭṭhivasena āyūhanā. Sassatadiṭṭhiyā patiṭṭhānaṃ, ucchedadiṭṭhiyā āyūhanā. Līnavasena patiṭṭhānaṃ, uddhaccavasena āyūhanā. Kāmasukhānuyogavasena patiṭṭhānaṃ, attakilamathānuyogavasena āyūhanā. Sabbākusalābhisaṅkhāravasena patiṭṭhānaṃ, sabbalokiyakusalābhisaṅkhāravasena āyūhanā”ti –

"By way of defilements, there is establishment; by way of formations, there is accumulation. By craving and views, there is establishment; by the remaining defilements and formations, there is accumulation. By way of craving, there is establishment; by way of views, there is accumulation. By the view of eternalism, there is establishment; by the view of annihilationism, there is accumulation. By way of sluggishness, there is establishment; by way of restlessness, there is accumulation. By way of devotion to sensual pleasure, there is establishment; by way of devotion to self-mortification, there is accumulation. By way of all unwholesome formations, there is establishment; by way of all worldly wholesome formations, there is accumulation."

Vuttesu pakāresu idha avuttānaṃ vasena veditabbā. Yā hi ayaṃ bodhīti vuccatīti yojetabbaṃ[V 1.0156]. “Bujjhatī”ti padassa paṭibujjhatīti atthoti āha “kilesasantānaniddāya uṭṭhahatī”ti. Taṃ pana paṭibujjhanaṃ atthato catunnaṃ saccānaṃ paṭivedho, nibbānasseva vā sacchikiriyāti āha “cattārī”tiādi. Jhānaṅgamaggaṅgādayo viyāti yathā aṅgāni eva jhānamaggā, na aṅgavinimuttā, evamidhāpīti attho. Senaṅgarathaṅgādayo viyāti etena puggalapaññattiyā avijjamānapaññattibhāvaṃ dasseti.

What is not mentioned here should be understood by way of the modes that have been stated. The phrase 'That which is called enlightenment' should be connected. He said the meaning of the word 'awakens' is 'to awaken,' that is, 'one arises from the sleep of the continuity of defilements.' But that awakening, in terms of its meaning, is the penetration of the four truths or the realization of Nibbāna; thus he said 'the four,' and so on. 'Like the factors of jhāna, path factors, and so on' means: just as jhāna and the path are themselves factors, not separate from their factors, so too is it here. 'Like the components of an army, the parts of a chariot, and so on': by this he shows that the designation of a 'person' is a designation for what does not ultimately exist.

Bodhāya saṃvattantīti bojjhaṅgāti idaṃ kāraṇattho aṅga-saddoti katvā vuttaṃ. Bujjhantīti bodhiyo, bodhiyo eva aṅgāti bojjhaṅgāti vuttaṃ “bujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā”ti. Anubujjhantīti vipassanādīnaṃ kāraṇānaṃ bujjhitabbānañca saccānaṃ anurūpaṃ bujjhanti. Paṭibujjhantīti kilesaniddāya uṭṭhahanato paccakkhabhāvena vā paṭimukhaṃ bujjhanti. Sambujjhantīti aviparītabhāvena sammā ca bujjhanti. Evaṃ upasaggānaṃ atthavisesadīpanatā daṭṭhabbā. Bodhi-saddo hi sabbavisesayuttaṃ bujjhanaṃ sāmaññena gahetvā ṭhito.

'They conduce to awakening, therefore they are factors of enlightenment': this is said taking the word 'factor' in the sense of a cause. 'They awaken, therefore they are awakenings; the awakenings themselves are the factors, therefore they are factors of enlightenment' is said as 'they awaken, therefore they are factors of enlightenment.' 'They awaken accordingly' means they awaken in a way that is suitable to the causes, such as insight, and to the truths to be awakened to. 'They awaken to' means they awaken by rising from the sleep of defilements, or they awaken face-to-face, in the manner of direct experience. 'They fully awaken' means they awaken correctly and without perversion. In this way, the illustration of the specific meanings of the prefixes should be seen. For the word 'awakening' stands, having grasped awakening in general, together with all its specific features.

Vicinātīti [M 1.0175] “tayidaṃ dukkha”ntiādinā vīmaṃsati. Obhāsanaṃ dhammānaṃ yathābhūtasabhāvapaṭicchādakassa sammohassa viddhaṃsanaṃ yathā āloko andhakārassa. Yasmiṃ dhamme sati vīro nāma hoti, so dhammo vīrabhāvo. Īrayitabbatoti pavattetabbato. Kosajjapakkhato patituṃ appadānavasena sampayuttānaṃ paggaṇhanaṃ paggaho. Upatthambhanaṃ anubalappadānaṃ. Osīdanaṃ layāpatti, tappaṭipakkhato anosīdanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pīṇayatīti tappeti vaḍḍheti vā. Pharaṇaṃ paṇītarūpehi kāyassa byāpanaṃ. Tuṭṭhi nāma pīti. Udaggabhāvo odagyaṃ, kāyacittānaṃ ukkhipananti attho. Kāyacittadarathapassambhanatoti kāyadarathassa cittadarathassa ca passambhanato vūpasamanato. Kāyoti cettha vedanādayo tayo khandhā. Daratho sārambho, dukkhadomanassapaccayānaṃ uddhaccādikilesānaṃ, tappadhānānaṃ vā catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Uddhaccādikilesapaṭipakkhabhāvo daṭṭhabbo, evañcettha passaddhiyā aparipphandanasītibhāvo daṭṭhabbo asāraddhabhāvato. Tenāha bhagavā “passaddho kāyo asāraddho”ti (ma. ni. 1.52).

'It investigates' (`vicināti`) means it scrutinizes (`vīmaṃsati`) thus: 'This is suffering,' and so on. The illumination of phenomena is the destruction of delusion, which conceals their true nature, just as light dispels darkness. When that quality exists, one is called a hero; that quality is heroism. 'It should be set in motion' means it should be made to occur. Exertion (`paggaho`) is the upholding of associated states by not allowing them to fall into the side of laziness. Support is the giving of further strength. Sinking is falling into lethargy; its opposite, non-sinking, should be seen. 'It gladdens' (`pīṇayati`) means it satisfies or increases. Suffusion (`pharaṇa`) is the pervasion of the body with sublime material qualities. Contentment (`tuṭṭhi`) is a name for rapture (`pīti`). Elevation is exaltation; the meaning is the uplifting of body and mind. 'The calming of bodily and mental distress' means the pacification and subsiding of bodily distress and mental distress. Here, 'body' refers to the three aggregates: feeling and the others. 'Distress' (`daratho`) means agitation (`sārambho`), a designation for restlessness and other defilements which are a condition for suffering and displeasure, or for the four aggregates in which these are predominant. It should be seen as the state opposing restlessness and other defilements. And thus, the non-trembling and cooled state of tranquility should be seen as the absence of agitation. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'The body is tranquil, not agitated' (MN 1.52).

Samādhānatoti sammā cittassa ādhānato ṭhapanato. Avikkhepo sampayuttānaṃ avikkhittatā, yena sasampayuttā dhammā avikkhittā honti, so dhammo avikkhepoti. Avisāro attano eva avisaraṇasabhāvo. Sampiṇḍanaṃ sampayuttānaṃ avippakiṇṇabhāvāpādanaṃ nhānīyacuṇṇānaṃ udakaṃ viya. Cittaṭṭhitipaccupaṭṭhānoti “cittassa ṭhitī”ti (dha. sa. 11) vacanato cittassa pabandhaṭhitipaccupaṭṭhāno. Ajjhupekkhanatoti udāsīnabhāvato. Sāti bojjhaṅgaupekkhā[V 1.0157]. Samappavatte dhamme paṭisañcikkhati upapattito ikkhati tadākārā hutvā pavattatīti paṭisaṅkhānalakkhaṇā, evañca katvā “paṭisaṅkhā santiṭṭhanā gahaṇe majjhattatā”ti upekkhākiccādhimattatāya saṅkhārupekkhā vuttā. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ yathāsakakiccakaraṇavasena samaṃ pavattanapaccayatā samavāhitā. Alīnānuddhatappavattipaccayatā ūnādhikatānivāraṇaṃ. Sampayuttānaṃ asamappavattihetukapakkhapātaṃ upacchindantī viya hotīti vuttaṃ “pakkhapātupacchedarasā”ti. Ajjhupekkhanameva majjhattabhāvo.

Concentration is the right placing and settling of the mind. Non-distraction is the state of non-distractedness of associated states, whereby the associated states remain undistracted—this is non-distraction. Non-scattering is its own nature of not dispersing. Cohesion is the bringing about of the non-scattered state of associated states, like water for bathing powder. Its manifestation as the steadiness of mind is the appearance of the mind’s sustained stability, as stated: “the steadiness of the mind.” Looking on with equanimity is due to a state of neutrality. That is the equanimity enlightenment factor. It reflects on phenomena as they proceed evenly, observes them from their arising, and proceeds by taking on their characteristics—thus, it has the characteristic of reflection. And so, because of the preponderance of the function of equanimity, it is called equanimity toward formations: “reflection, settling, neutrality in grasping.” Balanced progression is the condition for associated states to proceed evenly according to the performance of their respective functions. It is the condition for proceeding without sluggishness or restlessness, preventing deficiency and excess. It is as if it cuts off the partiality that is the cause of the uneven progression of associated states—thus it is said, “its function is to cut off partiality.” Looking on with equanimity is itself the state of neutrality.

Sabbasmiṃ līnapakkhe uddhaccapakkhe ca atthikā patthanīyā icchitabbāti sabbatthikā, taṃ sabbatthikaṃ. Samānakkhaṇapavattīsu sattasupi sambojjhaṅgesu vācāya [M 1.0176] kamappavattito paṭipāṭiyā vattabbesu yaṃ kiñci paṭhamaṃ avatvā satisambojjhaṅgasseva paṭhamaṃ vacanassa kāraṇaṃ sabbesaṃ upakārakattanti vuttaṃ “sabbesa”ntiādi. Sabbesanti ca līnuddhaccapakkhikānaṃ, aññathā sabbepi sabbesaṃ paccayāti.

Because it is needed, wished for, and desired in every case of sluggishness and restlessness, it is 'needed in all cases' (sabbatthikā). That is what is meant by 'universally needed' (sabbatthikaṃ). Among the seven enlightenment factors that proceed at the same moment, or that are to be spoken of in sequence according to the progression of speech, the reason for stating the mindfulness enlightenment factor first, without stating any other first, is that it is helpful to all of them. Hence, it is said, “for all,” etc. And “for all” refers to those on the side of sluggishness and restlessness; otherwise, all factors would be conditions for all.

“Kasmā satteva bojjhaṅgā vuttā”ti codako saddhālobhādīnampi bojjhaṅgabhāvaṃ āsaṅkati, itaro satiādīnaṃyeva bhāvanāya upakārataṃ dassento “līnuddhaccapaṭipakkhato sabbatthikato cā”tiādimāha. Tattha līnassāti atisithilavīriyatādīhi bhāvanāvīthiṃ anotaritvā saṃkuṭitassa cittassa. Tadā hi passaddhisamādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgā na bhāvetabbā. Tañhi etehi allatiṇādīhi viya paritto aggi dussamuṭṭhāpiyaṃ hotīti. Tenāha bhagavā “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjāletukāmo assa, so tattha allāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyyā”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.234). Dhammavicayavīriyapītisambojjhaṅgā pana bhāvetabbā, sukkhatiṇādīhi viya paritto aggi līnaṃ cittaṃ etehi susamuṭṭhāpiyaṃ hotīti. Tena vuttaṃ “yasmiñca kho”tiādi. Tattha yathāsakaṃ āhāravasena dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādīnaṃ bhāvanā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ “atthi, bhikkhave, kusalākusalā dhammā…pe… pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya…pe… saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232). Tattha sabhāvasāmaññalakkhaṇapaṭivedhavasena pavattamanasikāro…pe… dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādayo bhāveti nāma.

“Why are only seven enlightenment factors mentioned?” The questioner suspects that faith, covetousness, and so forth, also have the nature of enlightenment factors. The other speaker, showing that only mindfulness and so forth are beneficial for development, says, “as an antidote to sluggishness and restlessness, and as universally applicable,” and so forth. Herein, “for the sluggish” (līnassa) refers to a mind that has not entered the path of development due to excessive laxity of energy and so forth, and is contracted. At that time, the enlightenment factors of tranquillity, concentration, and equanimity should not be developed. For then, like a small fire with damp grass and so forth, it would be difficult to ignite. Therefore, the Blessed One said, “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man wants to kindle a small fire, and he places damp grass on it,” and so forth (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.234). However, the enlightenment factors of investigation of states, energy, and rapture should be developed, for a sluggish mind, like a small fire with dry grass and so forth, can be easily ignited by these. Hence, it is said, “whereby,” and so forth. Herein, the development of the enlightenment factors of investigation of states and so forth should be understood according to their respective nutriment. For it is said, “There are, bhikkhus, wholesome and unwholesome states… conduces to the further growth of the rapture enlightenment factor,” and so forth (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232). Herein, attention applied towards the penetration of the specific and general characteristics… develops the enlightenment factors of investigation of states and so forth.

Uddhaccassāti cittassa accāraddhavīriyatādīhi sītibhāvapatiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ anotiṇṇatāya, tadā dhammavicayavīriyapītisambojjhaṅgā na bhāvetabbā. Tañhi etehi sukkhatiṇādīhi viya aggikkhandho duvūpasamayaṃ hoti. Tenāha bhagavā “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ [V 1.0158] nibbāpetukāmo assa, so tattha sukkhāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyyā”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.234). Passaddhisamādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgā pana bhāvetabbā, allatiṇādīhi viya aggikkhandho uddhataṃ cittaṃ etehi suvūpasamayaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “yasmiñca kho”tiādi. Etthāpi yathāsakaṃ āhāravasena passaddhisambojjhaṅgādīnaṃ bhāvanā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ “atthi, bhikkhave, kāyapassaddhi [M 1.0177] cittapassaddhi…pe… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232). Tattha yathāssa passaddhiādayo uppannapubbā, taṃ ākāraṃ sallakkhetvā tesaṃ uppādanavasena tathā manasikarontova passaddhisambojjhaṅgādayo bhāveti nāma. Satisambojjhaṅgo pana sabbattha bahūpakāro. So hi cittaṃ līnapakkhikānaṃ passaddhiādīnaṃ vasena layāpattito, uddhaccapakkhikānañca dhammavicayādīnaṃ vasena uddhaccapātato rakkhati, tasmā so loṇadhūpanaṃ viya sabbabyañjanesu sabbakammikaamacco viya ca rājakiccesu sabbattha icchitabbo. Tenāha “satiñca khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbatthikaṃ vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234).

As for restlessness (uddhaccassa), it is the mind’s failure to settle into a state of calm due to excessive energy and so forth. At such times, the enlightenment factors of investigation of states, energy, and rapture should not be developed. For then, like a great mass of fire with dry grass and so forth, it would be difficult to subdue. Therefore, the Blessed One said, “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire, and he were to throw dry grass into it,” and so forth (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.234). However, the enlightenment factors of tranquillity, concentration, and equanimity should be developed, for a restless mind, like a great mass of fire with damp grass and so forth, can be easily subdued by these. Hence, it is said, “whereby,” and so forth. Here too, the development of the enlightenment factors of tranquillity and so forth should be understood according to their respective nutriment. For it is said, “There is, bhikkhus, bodily tranquillity, mental tranquillity… conduces to the further growth of the equanimity enlightenment factor” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232). Herein, by discerning the manner in which tranquillity and so forth have previously arisen for him, and by attending in that way for their production, one develops the enlightenment factors of tranquillity and so forth. The mindfulness enlightenment factor, however, is universally beneficial. It protects the mind from sinking into sluggishness due to tranquillity and so forth, and from falling into restlessness due to investigation of states and so forth. Therefore, like salt seasoning in all dishes, or like a versatile minister in all royal affairs, mindfulness is always desirable. Thus the Blessed One said, “Mindfulness, bhikkhus, I declare to be useful everywhere” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.234).

Ñatvā ñātabbāti (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.129) sambandho. Vaḍḍhi nāma vepullaṃ bhiyyobhāvo punappunaṃ uppādo evāti āha “punappunaṃ janetī”ti. Abhivuddhiṃ pāpento nibbatteti. Vivittatāti vivittabhāvo. Yo hi vivecanīyato viviccati, yaṃ viviccitvā ṭhitaṃ, tadubhayaṃ idha vivittabhāvasāmaññena “vivittatā”ti vuttaṃ. Tesu purimo vivecanīyato viviccamānatāya vivekasaṅkhātāya viviccanakiriyāya samaṅgī dhammasamūho tāya eva viviccanakiriyāya vasena vivekoti gahito. Itaro sabbaso tato tato vivittasabhāvatāya. Tattha yasmiṃ dhammapuñje satisambojjhaṅgo viviccanakiriyāya pavattati, taṃ yathāvuttāya viviccamānatāya vivekasaṅkhātaṃ nissāyeva pavattati, itaraṃ pana tanninnatātadārammaṇatāhīti vuttaṃ “viveke nissita”nti. Yathā vā vivekavasena pavattaṃ jhānaṃ “vivekaja”nti vuttaṃ, evaṃ vivekavasena pavatto bojjhaṅgo “vivekanissito”ti daṭṭhabbo. Nissayaṭṭho ca vipassanāmaggānaṃ vasena maggaphalānaṃ veditabbo. Asatipi pubbāparabhāve “paṭiccasamuppādā”ti ettha paccayānaṃ samuppādanaṃ viya abhinnadhammādhārā nissayanabhāvanā sambhavantīti. Ayamevāti viveko eva. Viveko hi pahānavinayavirāganirodhā ca samānatthā.

The connection is “knowing what should be known” (Ñatvā ñātabbāti, Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 1.1.129). Growth (vaḍḍhi) means expansion, increase, and repeated arising; thus it is said, “produces again and again.” It brings about development and generates. Vivittatā means the state of being secluded. That which separates from what is to be separated, and that which stands separated—both are here called “seclusion” (vivittatā) in the general sense of the state of being secluded. Among these, the former is a group of states endowed with the act of separating; it is understood as 'seclusion' (viveka) by means of that very act of separating, which is called 'seclusion' because it is the process of separating from what is to be separated. The latter is so called because of its nature of being entirely secluded from this and that. Therein, in that mass of states where the mindfulness enlightenment factor proceeds through the act of separating, it proceeds depending only on that which is called 'seclusion', namely, the process of separating as described above. The other factors, however, are said to be “dependent on seclusion” because of their inclination towards it and having it as their object. Just as a jhāna that proceeds by way of seclusion is called “born of seclusion,” so too should the enlightenment factor that proceeds by way of seclusion be regarded as “dependent on seclusion.” And the meaning of dependence for the paths and fruits should be understood by way of the insight-paths. Even in the absence of a prior-subsequent relationship, just as in 'dependent origination' there is a co-arising of conditions, so the development of dependence is possible, having inseparable states as its support. “This itself” means seclusion alone. For seclusion, abandoning, removal, dispassion, and cessation share the same meaning.

Tadaṅgasamucchedanissaraṇavivekanissitataṃ vatvā paṭipassaddhivivekanissitatāya avacanaṃ “satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvetī”tiādinā bhāvetabbānaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ idha vuttattā. Bhāvitabbojjhaṅgassa hi ye sacchikātabbā phalabojjhaṅgā, tesaṃ kiccaṃ paṭipassaddhiviveko. Ajjhāsayatoti [V 1.0159] “nibbānaṃ sacchikarissāmī”ti mahantaajjhāsayato. Yadipi vipassanākkhaṇe saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ [M 1.0178] cittaṃ, saṅkhāresu pana ādīnavaṃ suṭṭhu disvā tappaṭipakkhe nibbāne adhimuttatāya ajjhāsayato nissaraṇavivekanissitatā dāhābhibhūtassa puggalassa sītaninnacitattā viya. Na paṭisiddhā vipassanāpādakesu kasiṇārammaṇādijhānesu satiādīnaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyattā. Anuddharantā pana vipassanā viya bodhiyā maggassa āsannakāraṇaṃ jhānaṃ na hoti, nāpi tathā ekantikaṃ kāraṇaṃ, na ca vipassanākiccassa viya jhānakiccassa niṭṭhānaṃ maggoti katvā na uddharanti. Ettha ca kasiṇaggahaṇena tadāyattāni āruppānipi gahitānīti daṭṭhabbāni. Tānipi hi vipassanāpādakāni nibbedhabhāgiyāni ca hontīti vattuṃ vaṭṭati tanninnabhāvasabbhāvato. Yadaggena hi nibbānaninnatā, tadaggena phalaninnatāpi siyā. “Kudāssu nāmāhaṃ tadāyatanaṃ upasampajja vihareyya”nti (ma. ni. 1.465) ādivacanampetassa atthassa sādhakaṃ.

Having stated the dependence on the seclusion of escape through substitution and eradication, the non-mention of dependence on seclusion through tranquillization is because the enlightenment factors to be developed are mentioned here by “one develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor” and so forth. For the enlightenment factors to be developed, the function of the resultant enlightenment factors that are to be realized is seclusion by way of tranquillization. By resolve (ajjhāsayato) means with the great resolve, “I will realize Nibbāna.” Even though at the moment of insight the mind takes formations as its object, yet having clearly seen the danger in formations, it is inclined towards Nibbāna as their opposite; thus, the dependence on the seclusion of escape is by resolve. This is like a person overwhelmed by heat whose mind is inclined toward coolness. The jhānas based on kasiṇa objects and so forth, which are the basis for insight, are not rejected, since mindfulness and so forth within them are conducive to penetration. However, they are not mentioned because, unlike insight, jhāna is not the proximate cause of the path to awakening, nor is it such an exclusive cause, nor does the function of jhāna culminate in the path as does the function of insight. Here, it should be understood that by the grasping of a kasiṇa, the formless attainments dependent on it are also included. For these too can be said to serve as a basis for insight and be conducive to penetration, given their inherent nature of inclining towards it. For in whatever way there is an inclination towards Nibbāna, in that way there may also be an inclination towards the fruit. The statement, “When indeed shall I enter and dwell in that base?” (M.N. 1.465), also supports this meaning.

Vossagga-saddo pariccāgattho pakkhandanattho cāti vossaggassa duvidhatā vuttā. Vossajjanañhi pahānaṃ, vissaṭṭhabhāvena nirāsaṅkapavati ca, tasmā vipassanākkhaṇe tadaṅgavasena, maggakkhaṇe samucchedavasena paṭipakkhassa pahānaṃ vossaggo, tathā vipassanākkhaṇe tanninnabhāvena, maggakkhaṇe ārammaṇakaraṇena vissaṭṭhasabhāvato vossaggoti veditabbaṃ. Yathāvuttena pakārenāti tadaṅgasamucchedapakārena tanninnatadārammaṇakaraṇapakārena ca. Pubbe vossagga-padasseva atthassa vuttattā āha “sakalena vacanenā”ti. Pariṇamantaṃ vipassanākkhaṇe, pariṇataṃ maggakkhaṇe. Pariṇāmo nāma paripākoti āha “paripaccantaṃ paripakkañcā”ti. Paripāko ca āsevanalābhena āhitasāmatthiyassa kilesassa pariccajituṃ nibbānañca pakkhandituṃ tikkhavisadasabhāvo. Tenāha “ayañhī”tiādi. Esa nayoti yvāyaṃ “tadaṅgavivekanissita”ntiādinā satisambojjhaṅge vutto, sesesu dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādīsupi esa nayoti evaṃ tattha netabbanti attho.

The word 'vossagga' has the meaning of abandonment (pariccāga) and the meaning of plunging into (pakkhandana); thus the twofold nature of vossagga is stated. For relinquishment (vossajjana) is abandonment, and by the state of being released, it proceeds without hesitation. Therefore, at the moment of insight, the abandonment of the opposing factor by way of substitution (tadaṅga) is vossagga; and at the moment of the path, by way of eradication (samuccheda) is vossagga. Similarly, at the moment of insight, it is vossagga by way of being inclined towards that (Nibbāna); and at the moment of the path, it is vossagga by way of making that (Nibbāna) the object, due to its nature of being released. It should be understood in the manner described, that is, by the mode of abandonment by substitution and by eradication, and by the mode of being inclined towards that and making that the object. Since the meaning of the word 'vossagga' itself was stated earlier, it is said, 'with the entire expression.' It is maturing (pariṇamantaṃ) at the moment of insight, and matured (pariṇataṃ) at the moment of the path. Maturation (pariṇāma) means ripening (paripāka); thus it is said, 'ripening and ripened.' And ripening is the sharp and clear nature, with the capacity acquired through repeated practice, to abandon defilements and to plunge into Nibbāna. Thus it is said, 'for this is indeed,' and so forth. This is the method—just as it was explained concerning the mindfulness enlightenment factor with the phrase 'dependent on seclusion by substitution' and so forth, so too should this method be applied to the remaining enlightenment factors, beginning with the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor. This is the meaning.

Evaṃ ādikammikānaṃ bojjhaṅgesu asammohatthaṃ missakanayaṃ vatvā idāni nibbattitalokuttarabojjhaṅgavasena atthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “idha panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idha panāti imasmiṃ sabbāsavasuttante. Maggo eva vossaggavipariṇāmī bhāvanāmaggassa idha adhippetattā. Tañca khoti satisambojjhaṅgaṃ. Samucchedatoti samucchindanato.

Thus, having stated the mixed method to prevent confusion regarding the enlightenment factors for beginners, now, to clarify the meaning in terms of the arisen supramundane enlightenment factors, “But here” (idha pana) and so forth is stated. “But here” (idha pana) refers to this Discourse on All the Āsavas. The path itself is relinquishment-transformed, because the path of development is intended here. “And that indeed” (tañca kho) refers to the mindfulness enlightenment factor. “By cutting off” (samucchedato) means by way of eradication.

Diṭṭhāsavassa[M 1.0179] paṭhamamaggavajjhattā “tayo āsavā”ti vuttaṃ. Tepi anapāyagamanīyā eva veditabbā [V 1.0160] apāyagamanīyānaṃ dassaneneva pahīnattā. Satipi sambojjhaṅgānaṃ yebhuyyena maggabhāve tattha tattha sambojjhaṅgasabhāvānaṃ maggadhammānaṃ vasena vuttamaggattayasampayuttā bojjhaṅgāti paccekabojjhaṅge “bojjhaṅgabhāvanāyā”ti iminā gaṇhanto “maggattayasampayuttāyā”ti āha.

Since the taint of views is abandoned by the first path, it is said, ‘three taints.’ These too should be understood as not leading to the lower realms, since those that lead to the lower realms are abandoned by seeing alone. Even though the factors of enlightenment are mostly path-states, the factors of enlightenment associated with the threefold path are spoken of in each instance by way of the path-factors that are of the nature of enlightenment factors. Thus, taking ‘by the development of the factors of enlightenment’ in regard to each individual factor of enlightenment, he says, ‘associated with the threefold path.’

Bhāvanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the taints to be abandoned by development is concluded.

28. Thomentoti āsavappahānassa sudukkarattā tāya eva dukkarakiriyāya taṃ abhitthavanto. Assāti pahīnāsavabhikkhuno. Ānisaṃsanti taṇhācchedādidukkhakkhayapariyosānaṃ udrayaṃ. Etehi pahānādisaṃkittanehi. Ussukkaṃ janentoti evaṃ dhammassāmināpi abhitthavanīyaṃ mahānisaṃsañca āsavappahānanti tattha ādarasahitaṃ ussāhaṃ uppādento. Dassaneneva pahīnāti dassanena pahīnā eva. Tena vuttaṃ “na appahīnesuyeva pahīnasaññī”ti.

28. ‘They praise’ (thomento) means praising him for that very difficult practice, because the abandoning of the taints is very difficult. ‘His’ (assa) refers to the bhikkhu whose taints are abandoned. ‘Benefit’ (ānisaṃsa) means the outcome culminating in the cessation of suffering, beginning with the cutting off of craving. By these summaries of abandonment and so on. ‘Generating diligent effort’ (ussukkaṃ janento) means generating zealous effort accompanied by respect towards the abandoning of the taints, thinking: ‘The abandoning of the taints is praiseworthy even by the Lord of the Dhamma, and it has great benefit.’ ‘Abandoned by seeing alone’ (dassaneneva pahīnāti) means they are indeed abandoned by seeing. Therefore it was said: ‘One should not be conscious of abandonment regarding what has not been abandoned.’

Sabba-saddena āsavānaṃ, āsavasaṃvarānañca sambandhavasena dutiyapaṭhamavikappānaṃ bhedo daṭṭhabbo. Dassanābhisamayāti pariññābhisamayā pariññākiccasiddhiyā. Tenāha “kiccavasenā”ti, asammohapaṭivedhenāti attho. Samussayo kāyo, attabhāvo vā.

By the word ‘all’ (sabba), the distinction between the second and first alternatives regarding the taints and the restraint of the taints should be understood in terms of their connection. ‘Realization by seeing’ (dassanābhisamaya) means realization by full understanding, by the accomplishment of the task of full understanding. Therefore he says, ‘by way of function’ (kiccavasena), meaning by penetration without confusion. ‘Samussaya’ means the body, or individual existence.

Anavajjapītisomanassasahitaṃ cittaṃ “attano”ti vattabbataṃ arahati atthāvahattā, na tabbiparītaṃ anatthāvahattāti pītisampayuttacittataṃ sandhāyāha “attamanāti sakamanā”ti. Tenāha “tuṭṭhamanā”ti. Attamanāti vā pītisomanassehi gahitamanā. Yasmā pana tehi gahitatā sampayuttatāva, tasmā vuttaṃ “pītisomanassehi vā sampayuttamanā”ti. Yadettha atthato na vibhattaṃ, taṃ vuttanayattā suviññeyyattā cāti veditabbaṃ.

A mind accompanied by blameless joy and happiness deserves to be called ‘one’s own’ (attano) because it brings benefit, and not the opposite, which brings harm. Thus, referring to a mind associated with joy, he says, ‘delighted’ (attamana) means ‘having one’s own mind’ (sakamanā). Therefore he says, ‘contented-minded’ (tuṭṭhamanā). Alternatively, ‘delighted’ (attamana) means a mind seized by joy and happiness. But since being seized by them is precisely association, therefore it is said, ‘or a mind associated with joy and happiness’ (pītisomanassehi vā sampayuttamanā). Whatever is not differentiated here in meaning should be understood because of the method stated and because of its easy intelligibility.

Sabbāsavasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The exposition of the Sabbāsava Sutta, clarifying its hidden meaning, is concluded.

3. Dhammadāyādasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Exposition of the Dhammadāyāda Sutta.

29. Tasmā [V 1.0161][M 1.0180] taṃ dassetvāti yasmā suttantavaṇṇanā suttanikkhepaṃ dassetvā vuccamānā pākaṭā hoti, yasmā cassa dhammadāyādasuttassa aṭṭhuppattiko nikkhepo, tasmā taṃ nikkhepaṃ dassetvā, kathetvāti attho. Lābhasakkāreti (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.2.63) lābhasakkārasaṅkhātāya aṭṭhuppattiyāti keci, lābhasakkāre vā aṭṭhuppattiyāti apare. Yā hi lābhasakkāranimittaṃ tadā bhikkhūsu paccayabāhullikatā jātā, taṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā bhagavā imaṃ desesīti. Yamakamahāmeghoti heṭṭhāolambanaupariuggamanavasena satapaṭalo sahassapaṭalo yugaḷamahāmegho. Tiṭṭhanti ceva bhagavati katthaci nibaddhavāsaṃ vasante, cārikaṃ pana gacchante anubandhanti ca. Bhikkhūnampi yebhuyyena kappasatasahassaṃ tato bhiyyopi pūritadānapāramisañcayattā tadā mahālābhasakkāro uppajjīti vuttaṃ “evaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassapī”ti.

29. ‘Therefore, having shown that’ (tasmā taṃ dassetvā) means, since the exposition of a Sutta becomes clear when it is spoken after showing the Sutta’s introduction, and since the introduction to this Dhammadāyāda Sutta is based on its occasion of arising (aṭṭhuppattiko nikkhepo), therefore, having shown that introduction, it is explained. ‘In gain and honor’ (lābhasakkāre) (Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 2.2.63): some say this refers to the occasion of arising designated as gain and honor; others say it refers to gain and honor as the occasion of arising. For when an abundance of requisites arose among the bhikkhus at that time on account of gain and honor, the Blessed One taught this Sutta, taking that as the occasion of arising. ‘A pair of great clouds’ (yamakamahāmegho) means a pair of great clouds, layered a hundredfold or a thousandfold, hanging low below and rising high above. They remain when the Blessed One dwells in a fixed residence somewhere, and they follow when he goes wandering. For most of the bhikkhus, due to the accumulation of the perfection of generosity fulfilled over a hundred thousand eons or more, great gain and honor arose at that time; thus it is said, ‘so too for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.’

Sakkatoti sakkārappato. Garukatoti garukārappatto. Mānitoti bahumato manasā piyāyito ca. Pūjitoti mālādipūjāya ceva catupaccayābhipūjāya ca pūjito. Apacitoti apacāyanappatto. Yassa hi cattāro paccaye sakkatvāpi abhisaṅkhate paṇītapaṇīte upanenti, so sakkato. Yasmiṃ garubhāvaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā te denti, so garukato. Yaṃ manasā piyāyanti bahumaññanti ca, so bahumato. Yassa sabbametaṃ pūjāvasena karonti, so pūjito. Yassa abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānañjalikammādivasena paramanipaccakāraṃ karonti, so apacito. Bhagavati bhikkhusaṅghe ca loko evaṃ paṭipanno. Tena vuttaṃ “tena kho pana…pe… parikkhārāna”nti. Lābhaggayasaggapattanti lābhassa ca yasassa ca aggaṃ ukkaṃsaṃ pattaṃ.

‘Honored’ (sakkato) means one who obtains respect. ‘Revered’ (garukato) means one who obtains reverence. ‘Esteemed’ (mānito) means highly regarded and cherished in the mind. ‘Worshipped’ (pūjito) means one who is worshipped with offerings such as garlands and with the four requisites. ‘Venerated’ (apacito) means one who obtains veneration. For one to whom they present the four requisites, having respectfully prepared them to be exquisite and choice, that one is ‘honored’. One to whom they give, having established a sense of deep reverence, that one is ‘revered’. One whom they cherish in the mind and highly regard, that one is ‘esteemed’. One for whom they perform all these acts in the manner of worship, that one is ‘worshipped’. One for whom they perform the utmost respectful acts, such as bowing, rising, and joining the palms, that one is ‘venerated’. The world conducts itself thus toward the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Therefore it is said: ‘For this reason… up to… the requisites.’ ‘Attained the highest gain and glory’ (lābhaggayasaggapatta) means having attained the peak, the summit of gain and glory.

Paccayā cīvarādayo garukātabbā etesanti paccayagarukā, āmisacakkhukāti attho. Paccayesu giddhā gadhitā paccayānaṃ bahulabhāvāya paṭipannāti paccayabāhulikā. Bhagavatopi pākaṭā ahosi pakaticārittavasenāti adhippāyo aññathā apākaṭasseva abhāvato. Dhammasabhāvacintāvasena pavattaṃ sahottappañāṇaṃ dhammasaṃvego, idha [M 1.0181] pana so bhikkhūnaṃ lābhagarutādhammavasena [V 1.0162] veditabbo. Samaṇadhammavuttīti samaṇadhammakaraṇaṃ. Sāti dhammadāyādadesanā. Paṭibimbadassanavasena sabbakāyassa dassanayoggo ādāsoti sabbakāyikaādāso.

‘Those who regard requisites as important’ (paccayagarukā) means that requisites such as robes should be regarded as important by them; the meaning is ‘those whose eye is on material things’ (āmisacakkhukā). ‘Those who pursue an abundance of requisites’ (paccayabāhulikā) means those who are greedy for requisites, attached to them, and committed to the increase of requisites. The meaning is that the Blessed One, too, became renowned through his natural conduct; otherwise, there would be no one who is not renowned. The knowledge accompanied by moral dread that arises through reflection on the nature of phenomena is ‘spiritual urgency’ (dhammasaṃvego); here, however, it should be understood in the sense of the bhikkhus' high regard for gains. ‘Living by the ascetic’s duty’ (samaṇadhammavuttī) means the performance of ascetic duties. ‘That’ (sā) refers to the teaching on inheriting the Dhamma. ‘A mirror for the whole body’ (sabbakāyikaādāso) means a mirror suitable for seeing the entire body by way of reflection.

Pitu-dāyaṃ, tena dātabbaṃ, tato laddhabbaṃ arahabhāvena ādiyantīti dāyādā, puttā. Tañca loke āmisameva, sāsane pana dhammopīti tattha yaṃ sāvajjaṃ aniyyānikañca, taṃ paṭikkhipitvā, yaṃ niyyānikaṃ anavajjañca, tattha bhikkhū niyojento bhagavā avoca “dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā”ti. Dhammassa me dāyādāti mama dhammassa ogāhino, dhammabhāgabhāginoti attho. Tathā hi vakkhati “dhammakoṭṭhāsasseva sāmino”ti (ma. ni. aṭṭha.1.29). Nibbattitadhammoti asaṃkilesikānuttarādibhāvena dhammasāmaññato niddhāritadhammo. Pariyāyeti sabhāvato parivattetvā ñāpeti etenāti pariyāyo, leso, lesakāraṇaṃ vā. Tadabhāvato nippariyāyadhammo maggappattiyā apāyapatanādito accantameva vāraṇato. Itaro vuttavipariyāyato pariyāyadhammo accantaṃ apāyadukkhavaṭṭadukkhapātanato paramparāya vāraṇato. Yathā hi lokiyaṃ kusalaṃ dānasīlādi vivaṭṭaṃ uddissa nibbattitaṃ, ayaṃ taṃ asampādentampi taṃ sampāpakassa dhammassa nibbattakāraṇabhāvapariyāyena pariyāyadhammo nāma hoti, evaṃ taṃ vaṭṭaṃ uddissa nibbattitaṃ, yaṃ taṇhādīhi savisesaṃ āmasitabbato āmisanti loke pākaṭaṃ acchādanabhojanādi, tassa, taṃsadisassa ca phalavisesassa nimittabhāvapariyāyena pariyāyāmisanti vuccatīti dassento āha “yaṃ panidaṃ…pe… idaṃ pariyāyāmisaṃ nāmā”ti.

‘Heirs’ (dāyādā) means sons, those who take an inheritance from the father, which is to be given by him and received from him by right of being an heir. And that inheritance is merely material in the world, but in the Dispensation, it is also the Dhamma. Therein, rejecting what is blameworthy and not leading out, and engaging the bhikkhus in what is leading out and blameless, the Blessed One said: ‘Be my heirs in the Dhamma, bhikkhus, not heirs in material things.’ ‘Heirs of my Dhamma’ (dhammassa me dāyādā) means those who immerse themselves in my Dhamma, partaking of the share of Dhamma—this is the meaning. For thus it will be said: ‘of the master of the portion of Dhamma’ (dhammakoṭṭhāsasseva sāmino). ‘Generated Dhamma’ (nibbattitadhammo) refers to the Dhamma distinguished from the general meaning of ‘dhamma’ by its nature as the unsurpassed state free from defilements, and so on. ‘Indirectly’ (pariyāyeti) means that by which one makes known by transforming according to its nature; thus, it is an indirect way, a hint, or a cause of hinting. Due to the absence of that, the ‘non-indirect Dhamma’ (nippariyāyadhammo) is the path attainment, because it absolutely prevents falling into the lower realms, etc. The other, in contrast to what was stated, is the ‘indirect Dhamma’ (pariyāyadhammo), because it prevents falling into the suffering of the lower realms and the suffering of the cycle of existence only in succession. For just as worldly wholesome kamma—such as giving and virtue—generated aiming at liberation, even if it does not fully accomplish that, is called ‘indirect Dhamma’ (pariyāyadhammo) because it serves as a means for generating the Dhamma that accomplishes it, so too, what is generated aiming at the cycle—namely, what is tangible through craving, etc., and thus evident in the world as clothing, food, etc.—and what serves as a sign for such special results, is called ‘indirect material’ (pariyāyāmisa). Illustrating this, he says: ‘But this... this is called indirect material.’

“Sakalameva hidaṃ, ānanda, brahmacariyassa yadidaṃ kalyāṇamittatā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.2, 3) ādivacanato sāvakehi adhigatopi lokuttaradhammo satthuyevāti vattabbataṃ arahatīti vuttaṃ “nippariyāyadhammopi bhagavatoyeva santako”ti. Sāvakānañhi dhammadiṭṭhipaccayassapi yonisomanasikārassa visesapaccayo paratoghoso ca tathāgatādhīnoti tehi paṭividdhopi dhammo dhammassāminoyevāti vattuṃ yuttaṃ. Tenāha “bhagavatā hī”tiādi. Tattha anuppannassa maggassāti kassapassa bhagavato sāsanantaradhānato pabhuti yāva imasmā buddhuppādā asambodhavasena na uppannassa ariyamaggassa. Uppādetāti nibbattetā. Taṃ panetaṃ maggassa [M 1.0182] bhagavato nibbattanaṃ, na paccekabuddhānaṃ viya sasantāneyeva, atha kho parasantānepīti dassetuṃ “asañjātassa maggassa sañjanetā, anakkhātassa maggassa akkhātā”ti vuttaṃ. Tayidaṃ maggassa uppādanaṃ sañjānanañca atthato jānanaññeva asammohapaṭivedhabhāvatoti vuttaṃ “maggaññū maggavidū”ti. Akkhānaṃ panassa sukusalabhāvenāti vuttaṃ “maggakovido”ti. Satthārā [V 1.0163] yathāgataṃ maggaṃ anugacchantīti maggānugā bhagavato eva taṃ maggaṃ suṭṭhu adhigamanato. Pacchā parato sammā anu anu āgatā paṭipannāti pacchā samannāgatā.

From the initial statement, ‘Indeed, Ānanda, the entire holy life is this: good friendship’ (Saṃ. Ni. 5.2, 3), even the supramundane Dhamma attained by disciples deserves to be called the Teacher’s. Thus it is said, ‘Even the non-indirect Dhamma belongs to the Blessed One alone.’ For the special condition for the disciples' wise attention—which is a condition for right view of the Dhamma—and the voice of another are dependent on the Tathāgata. Therefore, even though the Dhamma is penetrated by them, it is fitting to say that the Dhamma belongs to its Master. Therefore he says, ‘by the Blessed One,’ and so forth. Here, ‘of the unarisen path’ (anuppannassa maggassa) refers to the Noble Path that had not arisen from the time of the disappearance of the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa until the arising of this Buddha, due to the absence of full awakening. ‘The producer’ (uppādetā) means the one who brings it forth. This production of the path by the Blessed One is not like that of the Paccekabuddhas, who generate it only within their own continuum, but also in the continuums of others. To indicate this, it is said: ‘the generator of the ungenerated path, the expounder of the unexpounded path.’ This generation and recognition of the path is, in essence, the very state of knowing and penetrating without delusion, thus it is said: ‘the knower of the path, the understander of the path.’ Its exposition, moreover, is due to his great skill, thus it is said: ‘skilled in the path.’ ‘Followers of the path’ (maggānugā) are those who follow the path as it came from the Teacher, following after the Blessed One who has thoroughly attained that path. Those who have come later and practiced accordingly are ‘later endowed’ (pacchā samannāgatā).

Jānaṃ jānātīti jānitabbameva abhiññeyyādibhedaṃ jānāti ekantahitapaṭipattito. Passaṃ passatīti tathā passitabbameva passati. Atha vā jānaṃ jānātīti sabbaññutaññāṇena jānitabbaṃ jānātiyeva. Na hi padesañāṇena jānitabbaṃ sabbaṃ ekantato jānāti. Passaṃ passatīti dibbacakkhu paññācakkhu dhammacakkhu buddhacakkhu samantacakkhusaṅkhātehi pañcahi cakkhūhi passitabbaṃ passatiyeva. Atha vā jānaṃ jānātīti yathā aññe savipallāsā kāmarūpapariññāvādino jānantāpi vipallāsavasena jānanti, na evaṃ bhagavā. Bhagavā pana pahīnavipallāsattā jānanto jānātiyeva, diṭṭhidassanassa ca abhāvā passanto passatiyevāti attho. Cakkhubhūtoti paññācakkhumayattā tassa ca pattattā sattesu ca taduppādanato dassanapariṇāyakaṭṭhena lokassa cakkhu viya bhūto. Ñāṇabhūtoti etassa ca evameva attho daṭṭhabbo. Dhammā bodhipakkhiyā, brahmā maggo, tehi uppannattā, tesaṃvā pattattā adhigatattā, lokassa ca taduppādanato “dhammabhūto, brahmabhūto”ti ca veditabbo. Vattāti catusaccadhammaṃ vadatīti vattā. Ciraṃ saccappaṭivedhaṃ pavattento vadatīti pavattā. Atthassa ninnetāti dhammatāsaṅkhātaṃ paramatthaṃ nibbānañca niddhāretvā dassetā, pāpayitā vā. Amatassa dātāti amataṃ sacchikiriyaṃ sattesu uppādento amataṃ dadātīti amatassa dātā. Bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ tadāyattabhāvato dhammassāmī.

“Knowing, he knows” means he knows what should be known, differentiated as that which is to be directly known and so forth, through the practice that is solely beneficial. “Seeing, he sees” means he sees in such a way what should be seen. Or alternatively, “knowing, he knows” means he truly knows what is to be known by means of omniscient knowledge. For one with partial knowledge does not know completely all that should be known. “Seeing, he sees” means he truly sees what is to be seen with the five kinds of eyes, namely, the divine eye, the eye of wisdom, the Dhamma-eye, the Buddha-eye, and the all-seeing eye. Or alternatively, “knowing, he knows” means that unlike others who, being deluded, claim to know the full understanding of the sensual and form realms, but know only through delusion, the Blessed One is not like that. The Blessed One, having abandoned delusion, truly knows as one who knows; and because of the absence of seeing through views, he truly sees as one who sees—this is the meaning. “He has become the eye” means he has become like the eye of the world because he is composed of the eye of wisdom, has attained it, and arouses it in beings, thus serving as the guide to vision. “He has become knowledge” should be understood in the very same way. The Dhamma consists of the factors of enlightenment, and the sublime (brahmā) is the path. Because he has arisen through them, or because he has attained and realized them, and because he arouses them in the world, he is to be known as “one who has become Dhamma” and “one who has become sublime.” “He is the speaker” because he speaks the Dhamma of the four noble truths. “He is the proclaimer” because he speaks while setting in motion for a long time the penetration of the truth. “He is the guide to the meaning” because he determines and shows the ultimate meaning, which is called the nature of things, and Nibbāna, or because he leads others to attain it. “He is the giver of the deathless” because he generates the realization of the deathless in beings, thus giving the deathless. “He is the lord of the Dhamma” because the factors of enlightenment are dependent on him.

“Yā ca nibbānasampatti, sabbametena labbhati;

Sukho vipāko puññānaṃ, adhippāyo samijjhati. (peṭako. 23);

“And the attainment of Nibbāna, all this is gained through this; pleasant is the fruition of merit, one's intention is fulfilled.

Nibbānapaṭisaṃyutto, sabbasampattidāyako”ti –

Connected with Nibbāna, bestowing all accomplishments.”

Evamādiṃ [M 1.0183] bhagavato vacanaṃ sutvā eva bhikkhū dānādipuññānaṃ vivaṭṭasannissayataṃ jānanti, na aññathāti vuttaṃ “pariyāyadhammopi…pe… paṭilabhatī”ti. “Edisaṃ paribhuñcitabba”nti kappiyassa ca cīvarādipaccayassa bhagavato vacanena vinā paṭiggahopi bhikkhūnaṃ na sambhavati, kuto paribhogoti āha “nippariyāyāmisampī”tiādi.

Only by having heard such words of the Blessed One do the monks understand that merit from giving and so on is a basis for liberation, and not otherwise—as it is said: 'Even the Dhamma taught indirectly... one attains.' 'It is to be used in this way'—without the Blessed One's word, even the acceptance of suitable requisites such as robes would not be possible for monks, how much less their use. Hence it is said: 'Even direct material things...' and so on.

Pariyāyāmisassa bhagavato santakabhāvo pariyāyadhammassa tabbhāveneva dīpito. Tadeva sāmibhāvaṃ [V 1.0164] dassentoti sambandho. Tasmāti attādhīnapaṭilābhapaṭiggahatāya attano santakattā ca. Tatthāti tasmiṃ dhammāmise.

The Blessed One's ownership of the indirect material gain is explained by the very nature of the indirect teaching. This itself shows the state of being the master—this is the connection. The word 'therefore' (tasmā) means because of acquisition and acceptance being dependent on oneself, and because of it being one's own possession. The word 'therein' (tatthā) means in that material gain of the Dhamma.

Paccayā cīvarādayo paramā pāpuṇitabbabhāvena uttamamariyādā etassa na uttarimanussadhammā appicchatādayo cāti paccayaparamo, lābhagarūti attho. Taṇhuppādesūti “cīvarahetu vā, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, piṇḍapātasenāsanaitibhavābhavahetu vā, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.311; a. ni. 4.9; itivu. 105) evaṃ vuttesu catūsu taṇhuppattikoṭṭhāsesu. Appicchatāsantuṭṭhisallekhapavivekādayo appicchatādayo.

Requisites such as robes are the highest boundary for him in the sense of being the ultimate to be attained; there is nothing superior to them, such as the qualities beyond the human state of fewness of wishes, etc. Thus, he is 'foremost in requisites' (paccayaparamo)—this is the meaning of being 'heavy with gains' (lābhagarū). The phrase 'as for the arising of craving' (taṇhuppādesu) refers to the four instances of the arising of craving stated thus: "Monks, when craving arises in a monk, it arises concerning robes, or concerning almsfood, lodgings, or existence and non-existence" (Dī. Ni. 3.311; A. Ni. 4.9; Itivu. 105). Fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, seclusion, etc., are the qualities of fewness of wishes and so on.

Tatthāti tasmiṃ ovāde, tesu vā dhammapaṭiggāhakesu bhikkhūsu. Bhavissati vā yesaṃ tatthāti yojanā. Imasmiṃ pakkhe tatthāti tasmiṃ ovāde icceva attho daṭṭhabbo. Adhippāyo āmisadāyādatāya uppajjanakaanatthānuppādassa dhammadāyādatāya uppajjanakaaṭṭhuppattiyā ca ākaṅkhā. Tenāha “passatī”tiādi. Tattha āmise upakkhalitānanti āmisahetu vippaṭipannānaṃ. Atītakāleti kassapasammāsambuddhakāle. Kapilassa bhikkhuno vatthu kapilasuttena, “saṅghāṭipiādittā hotī”tiādinā lakkhaṇasuttena (saṃ. ni. 2.218) ca vibhāvetabbaṃ. Āmisagaruko appagghabhāvena kūṭakahāpaṇo viya nittejo samaṇatejena anujjalato nibbutaṅgāro viya nippabho ca hotīti yojanā. Tatoti paccayagarukabhāvato. Vivattitacittoti vinivattitamānaso, sallekhavuttīti attho.

The word 'therein' (tatthā) means in that advice, or among those monks who are receivers of the Dhamma. Or alternatively, the construction is 'for whom there will be therein' (yesaṃ tatthā bhavissati). In this latter case, the meaning of 'therein' (tatthā) should be understood as simply 'in that advice'. The intention (adhippāyo) is the aspiration for the non-arising of what is unbeneficial that arises from being an heir to material things, and for the arising of what is beneficial that arises from being an heir to the Dhamma. Therefore it is said, 'he sees,' etc. Here, 'those who have stumbled in regard to material gains' (āmise upakkhalitānaṃ) refers to those who have practiced wrongly on account of material things. The phrase 'in the past' (atītakāle) means in the time of Kassapa, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha. The story of the monk Kapila should be clarified through the Kapila Sutta, and the Lakkhaṇa Sutta (Saṃ.
