Ni. 2.218), where it is said, 'even his outer robe was burning,' etc. One who is 'heavy with material things' (āmisagaruko), being of little value like a counterfeit coin, becomes without spiritual power, not shining with the radiance of an ascetic, and without lustre like an extinguished ember—such is the connection. The word 'from that' (tato) refers to the state of being heavy with requisites. The phrase 'one whose mind has turned away' (vivattitacitto) means one whose mind has turned back, meaning one who has a practice of effacement (sallekha).

Dhammadāyādāti [M 1.0184] ettāvatā antogadhāvadhāraṇaṃ vacananti tena avadhāraṇena nivattitamatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “mā āmisadāyādā”ti paṭikkhepo dassito. Tatheva ca vibhāvetuṃ adhippāyānisaṃsavibhāvanesupi dassito, tathā ādīnavavibhāvanena dhammadāyādatāpaṭikkhepo. Apadisitabbāti heṭṭhā katvā vattabbāti. Ādiyāti ettha yasmā ā-kāro mariyādattho, tasmā dhammadāyādatāvidhurena āmisadāyādabhāvena hetubhūtena, karaṇabhūtena vā ādiyaṃ vivecanaṃ viññūhi visuṃ karaṇaṃ vavatthānassa hotīti āha “visuṃ kātabbā”ti. Tenāha “viññūhi gārayhā bhaveyyāthāti vuttaṃ hotī”ti.

The statement 'heirs to the Dhamma' is a phrase with an implicit emphasis. By means of that emphasis, the negation 'Do not be heirs to material things' is shown in order to clarify the meaning that is excluded. Likewise, to clarify, it is also shown in the explanations of the intention and benefits, and similarly, through the explanation of drawbacks, the rejection of being heirs to material things is shown. 'To be pointed out' means 'to be stated after having subordinated it'. Here, regarding the word 'ādiya' (to be taken up), since the prefix 'ā-' has the meaning of a limit, therefore, by means of the state of being an heir to material things—which is devoid of being an heir to the Dhamma and serves as the cause or instrument—the discrimination to be undertaken becomes, for the wise, a distinct making of a separation. Thus he says, 'it is to be made distinct'. Therefore he says, 'This means it is said: "You would be censurable by the wise."

“Atthi me tumhesu anukampā…pe… no āmisadāyādā”ti bhikkhūsu attano karuṇāyanākittanaṃ [V 1.0165] tesaṃ mudukaraṇaṃ, “ahampi tenā”tiādi pana tatopi savisesaṃ mudukaraṇanti āha “atīva mudukaraṇattha”nti.

The proclaiming of one's own compassion among the monks, 'I have compassion for you... not heirs to material things,' is a way of making them pliant. But 'I too...' etc., is an even more exceptional way of making them pliant. Thus it is said, 'for the purpose of exceedingly making them pliant'.

Nāḷakapaṭipadādayo nāḷakasuttādīsu (su. ni. 684-728) āgatapaṭipattiyo. Tā pana yasmā nāḷakattherādīhi paṭipannā paramasallekhavuttibhūtā atiukkaṭṭhapaṭipattiyo, tasmā idha dhammadāyādapaṭipadāya udāharaṇabhāvena uddhaṭā. Sakkhibhūtāti tāya paṭipattiyā vuccamānāya “kiṃ me vinā paṭipajjanako atthī”ti asaddahantānaṃ paccakkhakaraṇena sakkhibhūtā. Imasminti “tumhe ca me bhikkhave dhammadāyādā”tiādike vākye. Sesanti “tumhe ca me”tiādikaṃ sukkapakkhe āgataṃ pāḷipadaṃ. Vuttanayapaccanīkenāti “tena dhammadāyādabhāvena no āmisadāyādabhāvenā”ti evaṃ kaṇhapakkhe vuttanayassa paṭipakkhena.

The practices of Nāḷaka and so on are the practices that appear in the Nāḷaka Sutta and others (Su. Ni. 684-728). But since these were practiced by the Elder Nāḷaka and others, are of the nature of supreme effacement, and are extremely excellent practices, therefore, they are cited here as examples for the practice of being heirs to the Dhamma. They are 'witnesses' (sakkhibhūtā) in that they serve as direct evidence for those who do not believe when that practice is being spoken of, by making it directly perceptible, as if to ask, 'Is there a practitioner apart from me?' The word 'in this' (imasmiṃ) refers to the statement 'And you, monks, are my heirs to the Dhamma,' etc. The word 'the rest' (sesaṃ) refers to the Pāli phrase 'And you are mine...' etc., which appears in the bright side. The phrase 'by the opposite of the stated method' (vuttanayapaccanīkena) means by the opposite of the method stated in the dark side, as in, 'Through that state of being heirs to the Dhamma, not through being heirs to material things.'

30. Thomanaṃ sutvāti paṭipajjanakassa puggalassa pasaṃsanaṃ sutvā yathā taṃ saparisassa āyasmato upasenassa paṭipattiyā sīlathomanaṃ sutvā. Nipātapadanti iminā idha-saddassa anatthakatamāha. Pavāritoti paṭikkhepito. Yo hi bhuñjanto bhojanena titto parivesakena upanītabhojanaṃ paṭikkhipati, so tena pavāritena paṭikkhepito nāma hoti. Tenāha “pavāritoti…pe… vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Pakārehi diṭṭhādīhi vāreti saṅghādike yācāpeti bhatte [M 1.0185] karoti etāyāti pavāraṇā, āpattivisodhanāya attavossaggo okāsadānaṃ. Sā pana yasmā yebhuyyena vassaṃvutthehi kātabbā vuttā, tasmā “vassaṃvutthapavāraṇā”ti vuttaṃ. Pavāreti paccaye icchāpeti etāyāti pavāraṇā, cīvarādīhi upanimantanā. Pakārayuttā vāraṇāti pavāraṇā, vippakatabhojanatādicaturaṅgasahito bhojanapaṭikkhepo. Sā pana yasmā anatirittabhojananimittāya āpattiyā kāraṇaṃ hoti, tasmā “anatirittapavāraṇā”ti vuttā. Yāvadatthabhojanassa pavāraṇā yāvadatthapavāraṇā, pariyositabhojanassa upanītāhārapaṭikkhepoti attho.

30. The phrase 'having heard the praise' (thomaṇaṃ sutvā) means having heard the praise of a person who practices rightly, just as the Venerable Upasena, with his assembly, heard praise of his virtuous conduct. By the term 'particle' (nipātapada), he indicates that the word 'idha' (here) is without a specific meaning. The word 'refused' (pavārito) means rejected. For one who, while eating, is satisfied with the food and rejects additional food offered by the server, is said to have rejected it by that refusal. Hence it is said, 'refused... as stated.' It is called 'invitation' (pavāraṇā) because by it one invites correction regarding things seen, etc.; it is the relinquishment of oneself for the purpose of clearing offenses, the granting of an opportunity. Since it is mostly stated to be done by those who have completed the rains residence, it is called 'the rains-residence invitation' (vassaṃvutthapavāraṇā). It is called 'invitation' (pavāraṇā) because by it one causes a desire for requisites to be expressed; it is an invitation with robes, etc. It is called 'invitation' (pavāraṇā) because it is a rejection (vāraṇā) connected with a reason, a rejection of food accompanied by the four factors, such as the food being interfered with. Since it is the cause for an offense on account of un-left-over food, it is called 'the invitation regarding un-left-over food' (anatirittapavāraṇā). The 'invitation of eating to satisfaction' (yāvadatthapavāraṇā) is the rejection of food brought when one has finished eating—this is the meaning.

“Bhuttāvī”ti vacanato bhojanapāripūritā idhādhippetāti āha “paripuṇṇoti bhojanena paripuṇṇo”ti. Pariyositoti etthāpi eseva nayo “bhojanena bhojanakiriyāya pariyosito”ti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana adhippetatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetuṃ bhojana-saddassa lopo vutto. Dhātoti titto. Sādhakānīti ñāpakāni. Pariyositabhojanaṃ suhitayāvadatthatāgahaṇehi bhuttāvitādayo, bhuttāvitādiggahaṇehi vā itare bodhitā hontīti aññamaññaṃ nesaṃ ñāpakañāpetabbataṃ dassetuṃ “yo hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ chahipi padehi udarāvadehakaṃ bhojanaṃ dassitaṃ[V 1.0166], tañca kho parikappanāvasena. Na hi bhagavā evaṃ bhuñjati. Tenāha “sabbañcetaṃ parikappetvā vutta”nti.

From the word 'Bhuttāvī,' fullness with food is intended here, as stated: '`Paripuṇṇo` means full with food.' In 'Pariyosito' too, the same method applies: '`Pariyosito` means completed with food, finished with the act of eating.' In the commentary, however, to show the intended meaning clearly, the elision of the word 'bhojana' is stated. 'Dhāto' means satiated. 'Sādhakāni' means indicative. To show their mutual nature of being indicator and indicated—that by the inclusion of 'finished eating,' 'satisfied,' and 'as much as one needs,' 'Bhuttāvī' etc. are indicated, or by the inclusion of 'Bhuttāvī' etc., the others are understood—'for whoever...' etc. is stated. In this way, all six terms indicate eating that smears the stomach, but this is only by way of supposition. For the Blessed One does not eat in such a manner. Therefore, it is said: 'All this is stated by way of supposition.'

“Siyā eva, nāpi siyā”ti ca idaṃ atthadvayampi idha sambhavatīti vuttaṃ “idha ubhayampi vaṭṭatī”ti. Athāti anantaraṃ, mama bhojanasamanantaramevāti attho. Taṃ pana yasmā yathāvuttakālapaccāmasanaṃ hoti, tasmā “tamhi kāle”ti vuttaṃ. Apparuḷhahariteti ruhamānatiṇādiharitarahite. Abhāvattho ca ayaṃ appa-saddo “appiccho”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.252, 336; saṃ. ni. 2.148) viya.

And this twofold meaning, 'It might be so, and it might not be so,' is possible here, hence it is said: 'Here both are valid.' Atha means immediately after, that is, right after my meal. But because this is a reviewing at the aforementioned time, it is therefore said, 'at that time.' Apparuḷhaharite means devoid of sprouting grass and other greenery. And this word appa has the meaning of absence, as in appiccho (with few wishes) and so on.

Kathitepīti pi-saddo avuttasamuccayattho. Tena vāpasamīkaraṇādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tathā hesa vutta-saddo “no ca kho paṭivutta”ntiādīsu (pārā. 289) vāpasamīkaraṇe dissati, “pannalomo paradattavutto”tiādīsu (cūḷava. 332) jīvitavuttiyaṃ, “paṇḍupalāso bandhanā pavutto”tiādīsu (pārā. 92; pāci. 666; mahāva. 129; ma. ni. 3.59) apagame, “gītaṃ pavuttaṃ [M 1.0186] samihita”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.285) pāvacanabhāvena pavattite, loke pana “vuttaṃ parāyaṇa”ntiādīsu (mahābhāsa 7.2.26) ajjhene dissatīti.

The particle pi in kathitepi has the meaning of gathering together what is unsaid. Thereby, it includes repetition and so on. Similarly, this word vutta is seen in the sense of repetition in contexts like no ca kho paṭivutta (Pārā. 289); in the sense of livelihood in pannalomo paradattavutto (Cūḷava. 332); in the sense of departure in paṇḍupalāso bandhanā pavutto (Pārā. 92; Pāci. 666; Mahāva. 129; Ma. Ni. 3.59); in the sense of being uttered as a teaching in gītaṃ pavuttaṃ samihitaṃ (Dī. Ni. 1.285); and in the world, it is seen in the sense of study in vuttaṃ parāyaṇaṃ (Mahābhāṣya 7.2.26).

Na ettha piṇḍapātabhojanena dhammadāyādatā nivāritā, piṇḍapātabhojanaṃ pana anādaritvā dhammānudhammapaṭipattīti ettha kāraṇaṃ dassento āha “piṇḍapātaṃ…pe… vītināmeyyā”ti. Tattha vītināmeyyāti kammaṭṭhānānuyogena khepeyya. Tenāha “ādittasīsūpamaṃ paccavekkhitvā”ti. Ādittasīsūpamantiādittasīsūpamasuttaṃ.

Here, the inheritance of the Dhamma is not prevented by the eating of almsfood. Rather, to explain the reason for practicing in accordance with the Dhamma while disregarding the eating of almsfood, he said: 'almsfood... and so on... one should pass the time.' Herein, 'one should pass the time' means one should spend it engaged in meditation subjects. Therefore, he said: 'having reflected on the simile of one's head being on fire.' Ādittasīsūpamaṃ refers to the Ādittasīsūpama Sutta.

Kiñcāpīti ayaṃ “yadipī”ti iminā samānattho nipāto. Nipāto ca nāma yattha yattha vākye payujjati, tena tena vattabbatthajotako hotīti idha “piṇḍapāta”ntiādinā anuññāpasaṃsāvasena vuccamānassa atthassa jotakoti adhippāyena “anujānanapasaṃsanatthe nipāto”ti vuttaṃ, anuññāpasaṃsārambhe pana “asambhāvanatthe”ti vuttaṃ siyā purimeyeva sambhāvanāvibhāvanato adhikattānulomato ca.

Kiñcāpi is a particle with the same meaning as yadipi. A particle, wherever it is used in a sentence, serves to illuminate the meaning to be expressed in that context. Thus here, in connection with 'almsfood' and so on, it is said, 'the particle is in the sense of permission and praise,' with the intention of illuminating the meaning being expressed by way of permission and praise. However, at the start of the permission and praise, it might be said to be 'in the sense of improbability' because of the preceding clarification of possibility and because it is in accordance with what is additional.

Ekavāraṃ pavattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkhipanaṃ kathaṃ dīgharattaṃ appicchatādīnaṃ kāraṇaṃ hotīti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “tassa hī”tiādi. Tattha atricchatāti atra icchatīti atriccho, tassa bhāvo atricchatā, atthato paralābhapatthanā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “purimeyeva sakalābhena asantuṭṭhi, paralābhe [V 1.0167] ca patthanā, etaṃ atricchatālakkhaṇa”nti (vibha. aṭṭha. 849). Pāpicchatāti asantaguṇasambhāvanādhippāyatā. Pāpā icchā etassāti pāpiccho, tassa bhāvo pāpicchatā. Yathāha “asantaguṇasambhāvanatā paṭiggahaṇe ca amattaññutā, etaṃ pāpicchalakkhaṇa”nti (vibha. aṭṭha. 851). Mahantāni vatthūni icchati, mahatī vā tassa icchāti mahiccho, tassa bhāvo mahicchatā. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “santaguṇasambhāvanatā paṭiggahaṇe ca amattaññutā, etaṃ mahicchalakkhaṇa”nti. Paccavekkhamāno nivāressatīti yojanā. Assa bhikkhuno saṃvattissati piṇḍapātapaṭikkhepo.

Addressing the question, 'How can the rejection of almsfood, even if it occurs just once, be a cause for fewness of wishes and so on in the long term?', he said: 'for him indeed,' and so on. Herein, atricchatā (excessive desire): one who desires excessively is an atriccha; the state of that person is atricchatā, which in essence is the longing for others' gain. For thus it is said: 'Dissatisfaction with one's own gain already obtained, and longing for others' gain—this is the characteristic of excessive desire' (VibhA. 849). Pāpicchatā (evil desire) means the intention of making known non-existent virtues. One whose desire is evil is a pāpiccha; the state of that person is pāpicchatā. As it is said: 'The making known of non-existent virtues and immoderation in receiving—this is the characteristic of evil desire' (VibhA. 851). One who desires great things, or great is their desire, is a mahiccha (one with great desire); the state of that person is mahicchatā (great desire). Regarding which it was said: 'The making known of existent virtues and immoderation in receiving—this is the characteristic of great desire.' The connection is that by reflecting, one will restrain these qualities. For that monk, the rejection of almsfood will conduce to this.

Mahiccho puggalo yathā paccayadānavasena paccayadāyakehi bharituṃ asakkuṇeyyo, evaṃ paccayapariyesanavasena attanāpīti vuttaṃ “attanopi [M 1.0187] upaṭṭhākānampi dubbharo hotī”ti. Saddhādeyyassa vinipātavasena pavattiyā aññassa ghare chaḍḍento. Rittapattovāti yesu kulesu paṭipiṇḍavasena pavattati, tesaṃ sabbapacchimaṃ attano yathāladdhaṃ datvā tattha kiñci aladdhā rittapatto vihāraṃ pavisitvā nipajjati jighacchādubbalyenāti adhippāyo. Yathāladdhapaccayaparibhogena, puna pariyesanānāpajjanena attano subharatā, yathāladdhapaccayena avaññaṃ akatvā santosāpattiyā upaṭṭhākānaṃ subharatā veditabbā.

Just as a person with great desires cannot be supported by donors by way of their giving of requisites, so too is he unable to support himself by way of seeking requisites—thus it is said: 'He becomes hard to support for himself and for his supporters.' This occurs by his wasting the gifts of faith, throwing them away in another's house. Rittapatto ('with an empty bowl') means that in whatever families he regularly goes for alms, having given away the last of what he himself had received, and then having received nothing there, he enters the monastery with an empty bowl and lies down, weak from hunger—this is the intention. One's own ease of support should be understood as coming from consuming requisites as they are received and not setting out to seek more again; the ease of support for one's supporters should be understood as coming from contentment and not showing contempt for requisites as they are received.

Kathāvatthūnīti appicchatādipaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ kathānaṃ vatthūnīti kathāvatthūni, appicchatādayo eva. Tīṇīti tīṇi kathāvatthūni. Abhisallekhikāti ativiya kilese sallikhatīti abhisallekho, appiccha tādiguṇasamudāyo, so etissā atthīti abhisallekhikā, mahicchatādīnaṃ tanubhāvāya yuttarūpā appicchatādipaṭisaṃyuttatā. Cetovinīvaraṇasappāyāti kusalacittuppattiyā nivārakānaṃ nīvaraṇānaṃ dūrībhāvakaraṇena cetovinīvaraṇasaṅkhātānaṃ samathavipassanānaṃ sappāyā. Samathavipassanācittasseva vā vibhūtibhāvakaraṇāya sappāyā upakārikāti cetovinīvaraṇasappāyā. Ekantanibbidāyātiādi yena nibbidādiānisaṃsena ayaṃ kathā abhisallekhikā cetovinīvaraṇasappāyā ca nāma hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha ekantanibbidāyāti ekaṃsena vaṭṭadukkhato nibbindanatthāya. Virāgāya nirodhāyāti tasseva virajjanatthañca nirujjhanatthañca. Upasamāyāti sabbakilesavūpasamāya. Abhiññāyāti sabbassapi abhiññeyyassa abhijānanāya. Sambodhāyāti catumaggasambodhāya. Nibbānāyāti anupādisesanibbānāya. Etesu hi ādito tīhi vipassanā vuttā, puna tīhi maggo, itarena nibbānaṃ. Tena samathavipassanā ādiṃ katvā nibbānapariyosāno ayaṃ sabbo uttarimanussadhammo dasakathāvatthulābhino sambhavatīti dasseti. Paripūressantīti taṃsabhāvato upakārato [V 1.0168] ca saṃvattissanti. Appicchatādayo hi ekavārauppannā upari tadatthāya saṃvattissanti. Kathāvatthuparipūraṇaṃ sikkhāparipūraṇañca vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Kathāvatthūni (topics of discussion) are the grounds (vatthūni) for talks connected with fewness of wishes and so on; indeed, fewness of wishes and so on are themselves the topics. Tīṇi means three topics of discussion. Abhisallekhikā (conducive to effacement): abhisallekho (effacement) is so called because it thoroughly scrapes away (sallikhati) the defilements; it is the collection of qualities such as fewness of wishes. A talk has this, thus it is abhisallekhikā, being suitable for the attenuation of great desire and so on, and connected with fewness of wishes. Cetovinīvaraṇasappāyā (conducive to the removal of mental hindrances) means it is conducive to serenity and insight—which are called 'the removal of mental hindrances'—by causing the removal of the hindrances that obstruct the arising of wholesome consciousness. Or, it is conducive and helpful for making the mind of serenity and insight itself manifest, hence cetovinīvaraṇasappāyā. Ekantanibbidāya (for complete disenchantment) and so on are stated to show the benefits, such as disenchantment, by which this talk is called abhisallekhikā and cetovinīvaraṇasappāyā. Herein, ekantanibbidāya means for the purpose of becoming completely disenchanted with the suffering of the cycle of existence. Virāgāya (for dispassion) and nirodhāya (for cessation) mean for the purpose of its fading away and ceasing. Upasamāya (for pacification) means for the pacification of all defilements. Abhiññāya (for direct knowledge) means for directly knowing all that is to be directly known. Sambodhāya (for awakening) means for the awakening of the four paths. Nibbānāya (for Nibbāna) means for Nibbāna without residue remaining. Among these, insight is expressed by the first three, the path by the next three, and Nibbāna by the last. Thus it is shown that this entire supramundane state, beginning with serenity and insight and culminating in Nibbāna, is possible for one who obtains the ten topics of discussion. 'They will fulfill' means they will conduce to that state by their own nature and by being helpful. For qualities like fewness of wishes, once they have arisen, will conduce to that goal in the future. The fulfillment of the topics of discussion and the fulfillment of the training should be understood in the manner already explained.

Amataṃ nibbānanti anupādisesanibbānadhātuṃ. Itarā pana sekkhāsekkhadhammapāripūriyā paripuṇṇā. Nibbānapāripūri cettha tadāvahadhammapāripūrivasena pariyāyato [M 1.0188] vuttāti veditabbā. Idāni yāyaṃ appicchatādīnaṃ anukkamaparivuddhiyā guṇapāripūritā, taṃ upamāya sādhento “seyyathāpī”tiādimāha. Tattha pāvussakoti vassānamāse uṭṭhito. So hi cirānuppavatti hoti. Pabbatakandarā pabbatesu upaccakādhiccakāpabhavanijjharādinadiyo. Sarasākhāti yattha upariunnatapadesato udakaṃ āgantvā tiṭṭhati ceva sandati ca, te. Kusobbhā khuddakataḷākā. Kunnadiyoti pabbatapādato nikkhantā khuddakanadiyo. Tā hi mahānadiyo otarantiyo paripūrenti. Paramadhammadāyādanti paramaṃ uttamaṃ dhammadāyādabhāvaṃ, paramaṃ dhammadāyajjaṃ vā. Te bhikkhūti te dhammapaṭiggāhake bhikkhū. Sanniyojentoti mūlaguṇehi appicchatādīhi yojento.

'The deathless' means the Nibbāna-element without residue. But the other perfection is complete through the perfection of the qualities of trainees and those beyond training. And here, the perfection of Nibbāna should be understood as being spoken of figuratively through the perfection of the qualities that lead to it. Now, establishing by simile this perfection of qualities through the gradual increase of fewness of wishes and so on, he said: 'just as,' etc. Herein, 'pāvussaka' means arisen in the rainy season months, for it occurs after a long interval. 'Pabbatakandarā' refers to the rivers that arise from mountain slopes, plateaus, springs, and waterfalls in the mountains. 'Sarasākhā' refers to those places where water comes from elevated regions above and both stands and flows. 'Kusobbhā' are small lakes. 'Kunnadiyo' are small rivers emerging from the foot of mountains. For these, descending into the great rivers, fill them. 'Paramadhammadāyāda' means the supreme, excellent state of being an inheritor of the Dhamma, or the supreme inheritance of the Dhamma. 'Those bhikkhus' refers to those bhikkhus who receive the Dhamma. 'Sanniyojento' means yoking them with the root qualities, such as fewness of wishes and so on.

Uggahetvāti atthato byañjanato ca upadhāraṇavasena gahetvā aviparītaṃ gahetvā. Saṃsandetvāti mama desanānusārena mamajjhāsayaṃ avirajjhitvā. Yathā idheva cintesīti yathā imissā dhammadāyādadesanāya cintesi, evaṃ aññatthāpi dhammathomanatthaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ pavisanto cintesi. Ekajjhāsayāyāti samānādhippāyāya. Matiyāti paññāya. Ayaṃ desanā aggātiādi bhagavā dhammasenāpatiṃ guṇato eva paggaṇhātīti katvā vuttaṃ.

'Uggahetvā' means having grasped it correctly in meaning and wording, having taken it up without error through retention. 'Saṃsandetvā' means without deviating from my teaching, in accordance with my intention. 'Yathā idheva cintesi' means just as he reflected on this teaching of the Dhamma inheritance, so too elsewhere, when entering the fragrant hut, he reflected for the sake of praising the Dhamma. 'Ekajjhāsayāya' means with a similar intention. 'Matiyā' means with wisdom. 'Ayaṃ desanā aggā' and so on—this was said because the Blessed One praises the general of the Dhamma precisely for his virtues.

Cittagatiyāti cittavasena kāyassa pariṇāmanena “ayaṃ kāyo idaṃ cittaṃ viya hotū”ti kāyassa cittena samānagatikatādhiṭṭhānena. Kathaṃ pana kāyo dandhappavattiko lahuparivattanacittena samānagatiko hotīti? Na sabbathā samānagatiko. Yatheva hi kāyavasena cittapariṇāmane cittaṃ sabbathā kāyena samānagatikaṃ na hoti. Na hi tadā cittaṃ sabhāvasiddhena attano khaṇena avattitvā dandhavuttikassa rūpadhammassa khaṇena vattituṃ sakkoti, “idaṃ cittaṃ ayaṃ kāyo viya hotū”ti pana adhiṭṭhānena dandhagatikassa kāyassa anuvattanato yāva icchitaṭṭhānappatti, tāva kāyagatiṃ anulomentameva hutvā santānavasena pavattamānaṃ cittaṃ kāyagatikaṃ katvā pariṇāmitaṃ nāma hoti, evaṃ “ayaṃ kāyo idaṃ cittaṃ viya hotū”ti adhiṭṭhānena pageva lahusaññāya sukhumasaññāya ca sampāditattā abhāvitiddhipādānaṃ viya dandhaṃ avattitvā yathā lahuṃ katipayacittavāreheva icchitaṭṭhānappatti hoti[M 1.0189], evaṃ pavattamāno kāyo cittagatikabhāveneva pariṇāmito nāma hoti, na ekacittakkhaṇeneva pavattiyā. Evañca katvā [V 1.0169] bāhusamiñjanappasāraṇūpamāpi upacārena vinā suṭṭhutaraṃ yuttā hoti, aññathā dhammatāvilomitā siyā. Na hi dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇaññathattaṃ iddhibalena kātuṃ sakkā, bhāvaññathattameva pana sakkāti.

'The movement of the mind' means by transforming the body according to the mind, with the determination, "May this body become like this mind," so that the body has a movement similar to that of the mind. But how can the body, which moves slowly, become synchronized with the swiftly changing mind? It is not entirely synchronized. Just as when the mind is transformed according to the body, the mind does not fully move in unison with the body. For at that time, the mind, without deviating from its own naturally established moment, cannot function in the moment of the slow-moving material phenomenon. However, by the determination, "May this mind become like this body," the mind follows the slow movement of the body until the desired place is reached. Thus, the mind, flowing in a continuous stream while conforming to the body’s movement, is said to be transformed by making its movement similar to that of the body. Similarly, by the determination, "May this body become like this mind," because the perception of swiftness and subtlety has been accomplished beforehand, the body—not moving slowly like that of those whose bases of psychic power are undeveloped—reaches the desired place swiftly in just a few mind-cycles. In this way, the body, moving in such a manner, is said to be transformed by having the movement of the mind, not by functioning in a single mind-moment. And so, even the analogy of bending and stretching the arm becomes more fitting without being figurative. Otherwise, it would contradict the natural order of things. For it is impossible to alter the defining characteristics of phenomena through psychic power; only their condition can be changed.

31. Bhagavato adhippāyānurūpaṃ bhikkhūnañca ajjhāsayaṃ ñatvāti vacanaseso. Desakāle viya bhājanampi oloketvā eva mahāthero dhammaṃ katheti. Pakkantassāti idaṃ anādare sāmivacananti dassento “pakkantassa sato”tiādimāha. Kittakenāti kena parimāṇena. Taṃ pana parimāṇaṃ yasmā parimeyyassa atthassa paricchindanaṃ hoti, tasmā “kittāvatāti paricchedavacana”nti āha. Nukāro pucchāyanti ayaṃ nu-saddo idheva pucchāyaṃ āgatoti katvā vuttaṃ. Nu-saddena hettha jotiyamāno attho kiṃ-saddena parimāṇo attho parimeyyattho ca. Ettha saṃkilesapakkho vivekassa ananusikkhanaṃ āmisadāyādatā, vodānapakkho tassa anusikkhanaṃ dhammadāyādatāti. Tīhi vivekehīti vivekattayaggahaṇaṃ tadantogadhattā vivekapañcakassa. Vivekapañcakaggahaṇe panassa sarūpena kāyaviveko gahito na siyā, tadāyattattā vā satthārā tadā payujjamānavivekadassanavasena “tīhi vivekehī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aññatarampīti kasmā vuttaṃ. Na hi kāyavivekamattena dhammadāyādabhāvo sijjhatīti? Na, vivekadvayasannissayasseva kāyavivekassa idhādhippetattā. Evañca katvā cittavivekaggahaṇampi samatthitaṃ hoti. Na hi lokiyajjhānādhigamamattena nippariyāyato satthudhammadāyādabhāvo icchito, nibbānādhigamena pana so icchito, tasmā sabbāpi sāsane vivekānusikkhanā nibbānapoṇā nibbānapabbhārā nibbānogadhā cāti vuttaṃ “tiṇṇaṃ vivekānaṃ aññatarampī”ti. Asati āloke andhakāro viya asati dhammadāyādatāya ekaṃsiyā āmisadāyādatāti āha “āmisadāyādāva hontī”ti. Esa nayo sukkapakkhepīti kaṇhapakkhato sādhāraṇavasena labbhamānaṃ atthasāmaññaṃ atidisati, na atthavisesaṃ tassa visadisattā, atthavisesameva vā atidisati visadisūdāharaṇūpāyañāyena. “Tiṇṇaṃ vivekānaṃ aññatara”nti idaṃ idha na labbhati. Tayopi [M 1.0190] hi vivekā, tesu eko vā itaradvayasannissayo idha labbhati.

31. The remainder of the statement is "knowing the intention of the Blessed One and the inclination of the monks." The great elder teaches the Dhamma only after examining the vessel, just as one considers the time and place. "Of one who has departed"—showing that this is a genitive of disregard, he said, "of one who has departed," and so on. "By how much" means by what measure. Since that measure defines the extent of the meaning to be measured, he said it is "a term of limitation." The particle "nu" indicates a question—this was said because the word "nu" is used here in the sense of an inquiry. By the word "nu," the meaning being illuminated is, by the word "kiṃ," the measure and the thing to be measured. Here, the side of defilement is the non-training in seclusion, which is the inheritance of material things; the side of purification is the training in it, which is the inheritance of the Dhamma. "By three kinds of seclusion"—the triad of seclusion is grasped because the fivefold seclusion is included within it. But if the fivefold seclusion were grasped, bodily seclusion, in its own form, would not be included; or, because the others are dependent on it, the Teacher on that occasion said "by three kinds of seclusion" and so on, in order to show the seclusion that was being practiced. "Any one of them"—why is this said? Is the state of being an inheritor of the Dhamma not achieved merely by bodily seclusion? No, because here bodily seclusion is intended only as dependent on the other two kinds of seclusion. And by this, the grasping of mental seclusion is also justified. For the inheritance of the Teacher’s Dhamma in the primary sense is not desired merely by attaining mundane jhāna, but it is desired through the attainment of Nibbāna. Therefore, all training in seclusion within the Dispensation is directed toward Nibbāna, inclined toward Nibbāna, and immersed in Nibbāna—hence it is said, "any one of the three kinds of seclusion." Just as in the absence of light there is darkness, so in the absence of the inheritance of the Dhamma, there is exclusively the inheritance of material things. Thus he says, "they are indeed heirs in material things." "This is the method in the bright side as well"—this extends the common meaning obtained from the dark side, not the particular meaning, due to its dissimilarity. Or, it extends the particular meaning itself by means of a dissimilar example. "Any one of the three kinds of seclusion"—this is not obtained here. For here, all three kinds of seclusion are obtained, or one dependent on the other two.

Dūratopīti dūraṭṭhānatopi. Tenāha “tiroraṭṭhatopī”tiādi. Kāmaṃ “paṭibhātū”ti ettha paṭi-saddāpekkhāya “sāriputta”nti upayogavacanaṃ, attho pana sāmivacanavaseneva veditabboti dassento āha “āyasmatoyeva sāriputtassā”ti. Bhāgo hotūti iminābhāgattho paṭi-saddoti dasseti lakkhaṇādiatthānaṃ idha ayujjanato. Tenāha “evaṃ saddalakkhaṇena sametī”ti. Dissatūti ñāṇena dissatu, passatūti vā attho. Upaṭṭhātūti ñāṇassa paccupatiṭṭhatu. Uggahessantīti [V 1.0170] vācuggataṃ karissanti. Vācuggatakaraṇañhi uggaho. Pariyāpuṇissantīti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Puripucchanādinā vā atthassa citte āpādanaṃ paṭṭhapanaṃ pariyāpuṇanaṃ. Kāraṇavacananti yathāvuttassa kāraṇabhāvena vacanaṃ “hetumhi karaṇavacana”nti katvā. Vuttatthapaccāmasanaṃ taṃ-saddena karīyatīti. Tenāha “yasmā”tiādi.

'From afar' means even from a distant place. Hence he said, "from beyond the country," and so on. Although in the phrase "let it appear," the word "Sāriputta" is a vocative in relation to the particle "paṭi," to show that the meaning should be understood in the sense of a genitive, he said, "of the Venerable Sāriputta himself." By "let there be a share," he shows that the particle "paṭi" has the meaning of "a share," because meanings such as 'characteristic' are not applicable here. Hence he said, "thus it accords with the characteristic of the word." "Let it be seen" means let it be seen by knowledge, or let him see. "Let it be present" means let it be present to knowledge. "They will learn" means they will learn it by heart. For learning by heart is learning. "They will master" is a synonym for the same. Or, mastering is implanting and establishing the meaning in the mind through prior questioning and so on. 'A causal expression' is a word that expresses the reason for what has been said, in accordance with the grammatical principle, "the instrumental case is used for a cause." The referring back to the stated meaning is done with the word "taṃ." Hence he said, "because," and so on.

Ekenevākārenāti āmisadāyādatāsiddhena ādiyatāsaṅkhātena ekeneva pakārena. Tameva hi ākāraṃ sandhāyāha “bhagavatā vuttamattha”nti. Aññathā “satthu pavivittassa viharato sāvakā vivekaṃ nānusikkhantī’ti ekeneva ākārena so attho therenapi vutto. Tīhi ākārehīti āmisadāyādapaṭipadābhūtehi tiṇṇaṃ vivekānaṃ ananusikkhanākārehi. Ettāvatāti “idhāvuso…pe… nānusikkhantī”ti ettakena kaṇhapakkhe uddesapāṭhena.

'In one way only' means in one way only, that is, by the mode called 'taking,' established through being an heir to material things. It is with reference to this very mode that it is said, 'the meaning spoken by the Blessed One.' Otherwise, the meaning 'while the Teacher dwells secluded, the disciples do not train in imitation of seclusion' is also stated by the Elder in just one way. 'By three ways' means by the ways of not training in imitation of the three kinds of seclusion, which constitute the practice of being heirs to material things. 'Up to this point' means with this much of the recitation of the summary concerning the dark side: 'Here, friends... they do not train in imitation of.'

Vitthārato suvibhatto hoti anavasesato sammadeva niddiṭṭhattā. Nanu ca uddese satthunopi ādiyatā bhagavatā gahitā, sā na niddiṭṭhāti anuyogaṃ sandhāyāha “so ca kho”tiādi. Sāvake anuggaṇhantassāti “āmisadāyādā satthu sāvakā”ti satthu parappavādapariharaṇatthampi “tumhehi dhammadāyādehi bhavitabba”nti evaṃ sāvake anukampamānassa. Sāvakānaṃ taṃ na yuttaṃ sāmīciabhāvatoti yojanā. Esa nayoti yadidaṃ “ettāvatāyaṃ bhagavā”tiādinā kaṇhapakkhe uddesassa atthavibhāgadassanamukhena sambandhadassanaṃ, esa nayo sukkapakkhepi sambandhadassaneti adhippāyo. Tenāha “ayaṃ tāvettha anusandhikkamayojanā”ti, satthārā desitāya uddesadesanāya mahātherena [M 1.0191] desitāya ca anusandhikkamena sambandhoti attho. Yathānusandhi eva cettha anusandhi veditabbo.

It is well-divided in detail, without omission, because it is rightly indicated. With reference to the objection, 'But surely, in the summary, the taking up by the Teacher, the Blessed One, was also grasped, yet it was not indicated,' he says, 'But that...' and so on. Of the one who supports the disciples: for the sake of warding off the criticisms of others that 'the Teacher's disciples are heirs to material things,' and out of compassion for the disciples, he said, 'You should become heirs in the Dhamma.' The connection is that this was not proper for the disciples, as it was not fitting. This is the method: this showing of the connection in the dark side by means of showing the explanation of the meaning of the summary with the words 'to this extent the Blessed One,' etc.—this same method applies to showing the connection in the bright side as well; this is the intention. Therefore, he says, 'This, indeed, is the application of the sequential connection here.' The meaning is that there is a connection, by way of a sequential method, between the exposition of the summary taught by the Teacher and that taught by the great Elder. And here the connection should be understood just as it is sequentially connected.

Accantapavivittassāti ekantaupadhiviveko viya itarepi viveko satthu ekantikāvāti. Anusikkhanaṃ nāma anu anu pūraṇanti tappaṭikkhepena āha “na paripūrentī”ti, na paribrūhentīti attho, na paripūrentīti vā na paripālentīti attho. Yadaggena hi vivekaṃ nānusikkhanti, tadaggena na paribrūhenti, na paripālentīti vā vattabbataṃ labhantīti. Kasmā panettha “vivekaṃ nānusikkhantī”ti uddese viya avisesavacane kāyavivekasseva gahaṇaṃ katanti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “yadi panā”tiādi. Pucchāyāti pucchāto aviseso siyā vibhāgassa alabbhamānattā vissajjanassa. Nanu ca “vivekaṃ nānusikkhantī”ti avisesavacanato pāḷiyaṃ vibhāgo na labbhatevāti? Na, padantarena vibhāvitattā. Tenāha “yesañca dhammāna”ntiādi. Byākaraṇapakkhoti vissajjanapakkho. Vissajjanañca na pucchā viya avisesajotanā[V 1.0171], atha kho yathādhippetatthavibhajananti adhippāyo. Iminā padenāti “vivekaṃ nānusikkhantī”ti iminā padena kāyavivekaṃ aparipūriyamānaṃ dassetīti adhippāyo. Cittavivekaṃ upadhivivekanti etthāpi eseva nayo.

'Of one utterly secluded' means that just as seclusion from the substrates of existence is absolute, so too are the other kinds of seclusion for the Teacher ultimate. 'Training in imitation of' means repeatedly fulfilling; by way of negating that, it is said, 'they do not fulfill,' meaning they do not develop. Or, 'they do not fulfill' means they do not maintain. For in whatever respect they do not train in imitation of seclusion, in that respect they come to be called 'not developing' or 'not maintaining.' With reference to the charge, 'Why here, in the general statement "they do not train in imitation of seclusion," as in the summary, is only bodily seclusion taken?' he says, 'But if...' and so on. Regarding the question: the answer would be without distinction from the question, since no division would be obtained for the answer. 'But surely, from the general statement in the Pāli, "they do not train in imitation of seclusion," no division is obtained, is it not?' No, because it is made clear by another phrase. Therefore, he says, 'And of which things...' and so on. 'The side of the explanation' means the side of the answer. And the answer, unlike the question, does not indicate a lack of distinction, but rather divides the meaning as intended; this is the intention. 'By this phrase' means that by this phrase, 'they do not train in imitation of seclusion,' he shows that bodily seclusion is not being fulfilled; this is the intention. The same method applies here also for mental seclusion and seclusion from the substrates of existence.

Ettha ca nappajahantīti pahātabbadhammānaṃ pahānābhāvavacanaṃ pahānalakkhaṇavivekābhāvadīpanaṃ, taṃ vatvā puna “viveke nikkhittadhurā”ti vacanaṃ tato sātisayavivekābhāvadīpananti tadubhayavivekābhāvadassanena “yesañca dhammāna”ntiādināva pārisesañāyena “vivekaṃ nānusikkhantī”ti iminā vivekadvayamūlabhūtakāyavivekābhāvadassanaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Avigatataṇhatāya taṃ taṃ parikkhārajātaṃ bahuṃ lanti ādiyantīti bahulā, bahulā eva bāhulikā yathā “venayiko”ti (ma. ni. 1.246; a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 8). Te pana yasmā paccayabahulabhāvāya yuttappayuttā nāma honti, tasmā āha “cīvarādibāhullāya paṭipannā”ti. Sikkhāya ādarabhāvābhāvato sithilaṃ adaḷhaṃ gaṇhantīti “sāthalikā”ti vuttaṃ. Sithilanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, sithila-saddena vā samānatthassa sāthala-saddassa vasena “sāthalikā”ti padasiddhi veditabbā. Avagamanaṭṭhenāti adhogamanaṭṭhena[M 1.0192], orambhāgiyabhāvenāti attho. Upadhiviveketi sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggatāya upadhīhi vivitte. Oropitadhurāti ujjhitussāhā.

And here, 'they do not abandon' is a statement about the non-abandonment of things that should be abandoned, indicating the absence of seclusion characterized by abandoning. Having said that, the statement 'having laid down the burden in seclusion' further indicates the absence of a more excellent seclusion. Thus, by showing the absence of both these kinds of seclusion, it should be understood that by the phrase 'And of which things...' etc., through the method of elimination, the absence of bodily seclusion—which is the root of the two kinds of seclusion—is shown by this phrase 'they do not train in imitation of seclusion.' Because their craving has not departed, they take (lanti)—that is, they accept—many kinds of requisites; hence they are 'excessive' (bahulā). Those who are excessive are 'indulgent' (bāhulikā), as in 'one devoted to the Vinaya' (venayiko). And since they are indeed engaged in acquiring an abundance of requisites, he says, 'practicing for an abundance of robes, etc.' Because they lack reverence for the training, they take it up loosely, not firmly; hence they are called 'lax' (sāthalikā). 'Loosely' (sithilaṃ) is a neuter designation of a state; or the formation of the word sāthalikā should be understood as based on the word sāthala, which has the same meaning as the word sithila. 'Leading downwards' means going downwards; the meaning is being in the state of the lower fetters. 'In seclusion from the substrates of existence' means secluded from the substrates of existence through the complete relinquishment of all substrates of existence. 'Having laid down the burden' means having given up striving.

Aniyamenevāti kiñci visesaṃ anāmasitvā “sāvakā”ti aviseseneva. Niyamento“therā”tiādinā. Dasavasse upādāyāti dasavassato paṭṭhāya. Issariyeti “seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ senāpatiṭṭhāna”ntiādīsu viya. Acirakkhaṇobhāsena lakkhavedhako akkhaṇavedhi. Ṭhitiyanti avaṭṭhāne. Ṭhānasoti taṅkhaṇeyeva. Tiṭṭhatīti ādhārādheyyabhāvenāti āha “tadāyattavuttibhāvenā”ti. Upekkhānubrūhanā sattasaṅkhāresu udāsīnatāpi asaṅkhatādhigamassa upāyoti tabbipariyāyato cīvarādimaṇḍanā na upadhivivekapāripūriyā saṃvattatīti āha “cīvarapatta…pe… apūrayamānā”ti. Tatthāti theravāre. Idhāti majjhimanavakavāresu. Tathā hi “majjhimatherakāle”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'Without specification' means without touching upon any particular distinction, with the general term 'disciples.' 'Specifying' is by means of 'elders,' and so on. 'Having taken the ten years' means starting from ten years. 'In sovereignty' is like in 'the position of a treasurer, the position of a general,' and so on. An akkhaṇavedhi is an archer who pierces the target with a momentary flash. 'In the state' means in the position. 'Instantly' means at that very moment. 'It stands' means through the relationship of support and supported; hence, he says, 'through the state of having its existence dependent on that.' The development of equanimity, that is, indifference towards beings and formations, is also a means for attaining the unconditioned. Therefore, since adorning oneself with robes, bowls, and so on is the opposite of that, it does not lead to the fulfillment of seclusion from the substrates of existence; hence he says, 'robes, bowls... not fulfilling.' 'There' means in the section on the elders. 'Here' means in the sections on the middle-aged and the newly ordained. For it is said, 'at the time of the middle-aged elders,' and so on.

32. Imasmiñca kaṇhapakkheti imasmiñca niddesavāre kaṇhapakkhe, na uddesavāre kaṇhapakkhe. Uddesavāre pana kaṇhapakkhe vuttavipariyāyena gahetabbattho “esa nayo sukkapakkhepī”ti atidesena dassito. Vuttapaccanīkanayenāti “kāyavivekaṃ nānusikkhanti na paripūrentī”tiādinā vuttassa atthassa paccanīkanayena, “kāyavivekaṃ anusikkhanti paripūrentī”tiādinā [V 1.0172] nayena. Etthāti etasmiṃ sukkapakkhe. Saṅkhepoti atthasaṅkhepo. Yojanaparamparāyāti gāmantato dūrabhāvena ekaṃ dve tīṇīti evaṃ yojanānaṃ paṭipāṭiyā. Araññavanapatthānīti araññesu vanasaṇḍabhūtāni. Pantānīti pariyantāni. Upagantuṃ yuttakālo jarājiṇṇakālo gocaragāme dūre gamanāgamanasamatthatābhāvato. “Evaṃ guṇavantesu dinnaṃ aho sudinna”nti paccayadāyakānaṃ pasādaṃ janenti. Pāsaṃsāti pasaṃsitabbā. Ayampi mahātherotiādi ekaṃ appamādavihārinaṃ vuddhataraṃ niddisitvā vadantānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Paviṭṭho vivekaṭṭhānaṃ. Sāyaṃ nikkhamati yonisomanasikāraṃ upabrūhetvāti adhippāyo. Kasiṇaparikammaṃ karoti, na yaṃ kiñci kiccantaraṃ. Samāpattiyo nibbatteti, na moghamanasikāraṃ. Sabbathātiādito tāva tadaṅgavasena kilesehi cittaṃ vivecento tato vikkhambhanavasena samucchedavasena paṭipassaddhivasenāti sabbappakārena cittavivekaṃ pūreti. Paṃsukūlāni dhāretīti iminā bāhulikatābhāvaṃ dasseti, asithilaṃ sāsanaṃ [M 1.0193] gahetvāti iminā sāthalikatābhāvaṃ, vigatanīvaraṇoti iminā okkamane nikkhittadhurataṃ, phalasamāpattintiādinā pavivekapubbaṅgamataṃ dasseti.

32. In this dark fortnight section, the dark fortnight is mentioned in this exposition section, not in the enunciation section. However, in the enunciation section concerning the dark fortnight, the meaning should be understood in the reverse manner as stated; 'this method applies to the bright fortnight as well,' thus shown by extension. By the method of stating the opposite—meaning by the method opposite to the meaning stated as 'they do not train in bodily seclusion, they do not perfect it,' and so on—it is explained by 'they train in bodily seclusion, they perfect it,' and so on. Here—in this bright fortnight. Briefly—a summary of the meaning. By the sequence of leagues—meaning by the order of leagues, such as one, two, or three leagues in sequence away from the village. Forest groves—meaning forested areas in the wilderness. Remote—meaning border regions. The suitable time to approach—the time of aging, when one is old and unable to travel to and from the alms village. 'They give thus to those endowed with virtues—ah, well given!'—they inspire faith in the donors. Praiseworthy—meaning deserving praise. This great elder, etc.—spoken by those who, having pointed out one older and more advanced in heedful living, speak thus. He entered a secluded place. In the evening, he emerges after strengthening wise attention—this is the intended meaning. He performs kasiṇa preliminaries, not any other task. He attains meditative states, not engaging in useless attention. From the beginning—first, by temporarily making the mind secluded from defilements, then by suppression, eradication, and pacification—he fulfills mental seclusion in every way. He wears rag-robes—this shows his lack of acquisitiveness. He maintains the training without slackness—this shows his lack of slackness. Free from hindrances—this shows his putting down the burden when entering. With fruition attainments, etc.—this shows his inclination toward seclusion as the foremost.

33. Tatrāvusoti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho. Tena “lobho ca pāpako”tiādinayappavattaṃ uparidesanaṃ anavasesato pariyādiyati. Ko anusandhīti yā sā bhagavatā saṃkilesapakkhena saha dhammadāyādapaṭipattibhāvinī “dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā”tiādinā desanā uddiṭṭhā, taṃ “satthu pavivittassa viharato”tiādinā ārabhitvā aṭṭhārasavārapaṭimaṇḍitāya niddesadesanāya vibhajitvā tato paraṃ “tatrāvuso lobho ca pāpako”tiādinayāya uparidesanāya sambandhaṃ pucchati. Evanti saṃkilesapakkhe “nappajahantī”ti pahānābhāvadassanavasena, vodānapakkhe “pajahantī”ti pahānasabbhāvadassanavasenāti evaṃ. Aniddhāritasarūpā yaṃ-taṃ-saddehi dhamma-saddena sāmaññato ye pahātabbadhammā vuttā, te sarūpato dassetunti yojanā. Ime teti ettha kasmā lobhādayo eva pahātabbadhammā vuttā, nanu ito aññepi mohadiṭṭhivicikicchādayo pahātabbadhammā santīti? Saccaṃ santi, te pana lobhādīhi tadekaṭṭhatā gahitā eva hontīti vuttā. Atha vā imesaṃyevettha gahaṇe kāraṇaṃ parato āvi bhavissati.

33. Here, in 'tatrāvusoti' (there, friends), the particle 'iti' has the sense of 'and so on'. By this, the subsequent teaching that proceeds in the manner of 'greed is unwholesome,' etc., is fully encompassed without omission. What is the connection? It refers to the teaching given by the Blessed One regarding the side of defilements, along with the practice of being heirs to the Dhamma—such as, 'Be my heirs in the Dhamma, monks, not heirs in material things.' This teaching was introduced beginning with 'when the Teacher dwells in seclusion' and was elaborated through an exposition adorned with eighteen sections. After that, the connection is questioned through the subsequent teaching, starting with 'here, friends, greed is unwholesome.' 'Thus'—by showing the absence of abandoning on the side of defilements with 'they do not abandon,' and by showing the existence of abandoning on the side of purification with 'they abandon'—in this way. The construction is that those things to be abandoned, whose specific nature was not determined and which were mentioned generally with the word 'dhamma' using the pronouns 'whatever' and 'that', are now shown specifically. Here, why are only greed and the like mentioned as things to be abandoned? Are there not others, such as delusion, wrong view, doubt, and so on? It is true they exist, but they are included under greed and the like because they are taken as having the same basis. Alternatively, the reason for mentioning only these here will become clear later.

Idāni upacayena anusandhiṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sāvakānaṃ yassa dhammassa dāyādabhāvo satthu abhirucito, so “cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāvetī”tiādinā akatthetvā “vivekaṃ anusikkhanti, te ca dhamme pajahanti, na ca bāhulikā”tiādinā kathitattā [V 1.0173] heṭṭhā pariyāyeneva dhammo kathitoti vuttaṃ. “Te ca dhamme nappajahanti, okkamane pubbaṅgamā”tiādinā āmisaṃ pariyāyenapi kathitaṃ. “Siyā ca me piṇḍapāto”tiādinā, “bāhulikā ca hontī”tiādinā ca āmisaṃ nippariyāyenapi kathitaṃ. Atha vā yāyaṃ bhagavatā āmisadāyādapaṭikkhepanā dhammadāyādatā vuttā, yañca tadatthaṃ vibhajantena mahātherena attanā vivekānusikkhanādi vuttaṃ, tadubhayaṃ hetuvasena vibhāvetuṃ “tatrāvuso, lobho cā”tiādi vuttaṃ[M 1.0194]. Hetunirodhena hi saṃkilesapakkhassa, nirodhahetusampādanena ca vodānapakkhassa tappāpakatā.

Now, to show a further connection, 'moreover' and so on was said. Therein, that inheritance of the Dhamma which is pleasing to the Teacher for the disciples is not stated as 'one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness' and so on. But because it was stated previously as 'they train in seclusion, abandon those things, and are not excessive,' and so on, it is said that the Dhamma was spoken of previously only indirectly. And material gain was spoken about indirectly in 'They do not abandon those things, and they take the lead in indulgence' and so on. And material gain was spoken about directly in 'Perhaps there will be almsfood for me' and so on, and 'they are excessive' and so on. Or else, to explain in terms of causes both the Blessed One's rejection of the inheritance of material gain and statement of the inheritance of the Dhamma, and what the great elder said when differentiating its meaning—namely, training oneself in seclusion and so on—therefore 'Here, friends, greed is...' and so on was said. For by the cessation of the cause, there is the rejection of the side of defilement, and by the production of the cause of cessation, there is the accomplishment of the side of purification.

Atītadesanānidassananti atītāya therena yathādesitāya desanāya ca paccāmasanaṃ. Tenevāha “satthu pavivittassa…pe… desanāyanti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Tatthāti yaṃ vuttaṃ visesato “yesaṃ dhammānaṃ satthā pahānamāhā”ti, etasmiṃ pade. Tattha hi pahātabbadhammā lobhādayo sāmaññato vuttā. Lāmakāti nihīnā. Lobhadosā hi hetuto paccayato sabhāvato phalato nissandato saṃkiliṭṭhapakatikā, āyatiṃ dukkhassa pāpanaṭṭhena vā pāpakā. Lubbhanalakkhaṇoti ārammaṇassa abhigijjhanalakkhaṇo. Tathā hi so lubbhanti tena, sayaṃ vā lubbhati, lubbhanamattameva vā tanti “lobho”ti vuccati. Rasādīsu abhisaṅgaraso, apariccāgapaccupaṭṭhāno, saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu assādadassanapadaṭṭhāno. Dussanalakkhaṇoti ārammaṇe byāpajjanalakkhaṇo. Tathā hi so dussanti tena, sayaṃ vā dussati, dussanamattameva vā tanti “doso”ti vuccati. Rasādīsu visappanaraso, sanissayadahanaraso vā, dussanapaccupaṭṭhāno, āghātavatthupadaṭṭhāno.

'Indication of the past teaching' means a reflection on the teaching as it was taught in the past by the Elder. Hence, it was said, 'The Teacher, secluded… the teaching is said.' Here, that which was said specifically, 'Of those things the Teacher proclaimed abandonment,' refers to this passage. In this passage, the things to be abandoned—such as greed and so on—are mentioned generally. 'Lowly' means base. For greed and hatred, due to cause, condition, nature, result, and outflow, are by nature defiling, or are evil in that they lead to suffering in the future. The characteristic of greed is the characteristic of clinging intensely to an object. For one is greedy through it, or one is greedy oneself, or it is merely a state of greed, therefore it is called 'greed.' Its function is clinging to flavors, etc., its manifestation is non-relinquishing, and its proximate cause is seeing satisfaction in things that bind. The characteristic of hatred is the characteristic of being hostile towards an object. For one is hostile through it, or one is hostile oneself, or it is merely a state of hostility, therefore it is called 'hatred.' Its function is to spread like poison, or the function of burning with dependence, its manifestation is hostility, and its proximate cause is a basis for aversion.

Tesūtiādinā dassanena lobhadosānaṃ ekantato pahātabbatādassanaṃ. Āmisadāyādassa paccayānaṃ lābhe hotīti idaṃ lobhassa ārammaṇaggahaṇasabhāvataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, taṇhāya vasena pana anugijjhanaṃ sandhāya “aladdhaṃ patthetī”ti āha. Alābhe paccayānaṃ āmisadāyādassa hotīti ānetvā yojanā. Alabhantoti ettha “paccaye”ti vibhattiṃ pariṇāmetvā yojetabbaṃ. Vighātavāti “yampicchaṃ na labhati, tampi dukkha”nti (ma. ni. 1.120; vibha. 190) vacanato icchāvighātavā. Lobho ca deyyadhamme hoti āmisadāyādassāti sambandho. Esa nayo anantarapadepi. Deyyadhammeti ca idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ sattakelāyanādivasenapi tassa lobhuppattisabbhāvato. “Taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā, pariyesanaṃ paṭicca lābho”ti evamādayo nava taṇhāmūlakā. Paripūreti āmisadāyādoti vibhattivipariṇāmo veditabbo. Āvāsamacchariyādīni pañca macchariyāni.

By the demonstration beginning with 'among them,' it is shown that greed and hatred should be completely abandoned. The statement, 'For an heir of material things, it arises upon the gain of requisites,' was said with reference to the nature of greed to grasp at objects. But with reference to coveting through craving, he said, 'He desires what he has not obtained.' The phrase 'When there is no gain in requisites for an heir of material things, it arises' should be supplied and connected. Here, in 'alabhanto' (not obtaining), the word 'paccaye' (requisites) should be connected by changing its case ending. 'Having frustration' means having frustration due to not getting what one wants, because of the saying, 'Whatever one desires and does not get, that too is suffering.' And the connection is: greed arises in a gift for one who is an heir to material things. This method applies to the next word too. And 'in a gift' is merely an illustration, since there is the possibility of the arising of greed even through the seven kinds of play and amusement, etc. 'Dependent on craving, there is seeking; dependent on seeking, there is gain'—these are the nine rooted in craving. In 'paripūreti āmisadāyādo', a change of case ending should be understood. The five kinds of stinginess are stinginess regarding dwellings, etc.

Magganti [V 1.0174][M 1.0195] ariyamaggaṃ. So hi kilese mārento gacchati, nibbānatthikehi ca maggīyati, sayaṃ vā sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena nibbānaṃ maggatīti nippariyāyena “maggo”ti vuccati. Eko antoti itarena asammisso eko koṭṭhāso, hīnatāya vā lāmakaṭṭhena eko anto. Kāmaṃ aññepi kusaladhammā ete ante asampayogato na upenti, tehi vimuttā eva, ayaṃ pana accantavimuttiyā na upetīti āha “vimutto etehi antehī”ti. Tasmāti antadvayavimuttattā. Etesaṃ majjhe bhavattāti idaṃ maggassa ubhayantavimuttatāya eva vuttaṃ, na tappariyāpannatāya, vaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇatthikehi paṭipajjitabbato ca. Tathāti yathā itarena asammissaṭṭhena lāmakaṭṭhena ca lobho eko anto, tathā kāmasukhallikānuyogoti attho. Esa nayo sesesupi. Maggassa anupagamanañca nesaṃ antānaṃ sabbaso appavattikaraṇeneva daṭṭhabbaṃ. Purimanayenāti “ete dve ante na upetī”tiādinā pubbe vuttanayena.

The path is the noble path. For it destroys the defilements as it goes, is sought by those seeking Nibbāna, and itself seeks Nibbāna through realization—thus it is called 'path' in the primary sense. One extreme means a single portion, unmixed with the other, or one extreme due to its inferiority and baseness. Although other wholesome states, by virtue of non-association, do not approach these extremes and are indeed free from them, this path, however, is absolutely liberated from them and thus does not approach them; hence it is said, 'liberated from these extremes.' Therefore means because it is liberated from both extremes. Being in the middle of these is said with reference to the path's liberation from both extremes, not to its being included within them, and because it is to be practiced by those seeking escape from the suffering of the round. Likewise means just as greed, by being unmixed with the other and by its baseness, is one extreme, so too is the practice of indulgence in sensual pleasure. This same method applies to the remaining cases. And the path’s non-approach to these extremes should be understood as its causing them to cease completely. By the previous method means by the method stated before, beginning with 'it does not approach these two extremes.'

Saccānanti catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ. Dassanapariṇāyakaṭṭhenāti dassanassa pariññābhisamayādibhedassa parito sabbathā nayanaṭṭhena pavattanaṭṭhena. Cakkhukaraṇīti dhammacakkhussa karaṇī nipphādikā. Tayidaṃ satipi paṭipadāya dhammacakkhuto anaññatte avayavavasena sijjhamāno attho samudāyena kato nāma hotīti upacāravasena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati “maggoyeva hi maggatthāya saṃvattati maggena kātabbakiccakaraṇato”ti. Ñāṇāyāti yāthāvato jānanāya. Tenāha “viditakaraṇaṭṭhenā”ti. Visesañātabhāvāpādanañhi viditakaraṇaṃ. Vūpasamanatoti samucchindanavasena vūpasamanato. Dukkhādīnaṃ pariññeyyādibhāvo viya abhiññeyyabhāvopi maggavaseneva pākaṭo hotīti āha “catunnampi saccānaṃ abhiññeyyabhāvadassanato”ti, vibhāvanatoti attho. Sambodhoti maggo “sambujjhati etenā”ti katvā. Tassatthāyāti maggakiccatthāya. Na hi maggato añño maggakiccakaro atthi. Tenāha “maggoyeva hī”tiādi. Atha vā sammādiṭṭhi uppajjamānā sahajātādipaccayabhāvena itare uppādeti, evaṃ sesamaggadhammāpīti evampi maggatthāya saṃvattanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sacchikiriyāya paccakkhakammāyāti sacchikaraṇasaṅkhātapaccakkhakammāya. Nibbānāyāti vā anupādisesanibbānāya. Upasamāyāti [M 1.0196] iminā saupādisesanibbānaṃ gahitanti. Ayanti “sā hi saccāna”ntiādinā yathāvutto atthanayo. Etthāti “cakkhukaraṇī”tiādīsu padesu. Sāro sundaro anapanīto. Ito aññathāti “dukkhassa pariññāya diṭṭhivisuddhiṃ karotīti cakkhukaraṇī”tiādinā atthavaṇṇanāpapañco kevalaṃ vitthāratthāya.

'Of the truths' means of the four noble truths. 'Leading to vision' means by way of guiding, that is, by causing the vision—which is differentiated as full understanding, direct knowledge, and so on—to occur in every way. 'Making the eye' means producing the Dhamma-eye. This should be understood as spoken figuratively, for although the path is not different from the Dhamma-eye, the meaning accomplished by way of the parts is said to be accomplished by the whole. For it will be said: 'The path itself leads to the purpose of the path, by accomplishing the task that is to be done by the path.' 'For knowledge' means for knowing things as they really are. Hence it is said: 'by the meaning of making known.' For making known is to bring about the state of being distinctly known. 'For calming' means for calming by way of eradication. Just as the state of suffering and so on as something to be fully understood becomes manifest through the path, so too their state as something to be directly known becomes manifest. Hence it is said: 'by showing the state of the four truths as something to be directly known,' which means by clarifying them. 'For enlightenment' refers to the path, because 'one is enlightened by this.' 'For its purpose' means for the purpose of the path's function. For there is no other agent of the path's function than the path itself. Hence it is said: 'For the path itself,' and so on. Alternatively, this leading to the purpose of the path should be understood in this way: when right view arises, it produces the other factors by being a co-nascent condition, and so too with the other path-factors. 'For realization' means for the direct experience called realization. 'For Nibbāna' means for Nibbāna without remainder of aggregates. By 'for calming,' Nibbāna with remainder of aggregates is included. 'This' refers to the method of meaning stated above, beginning with 'for it is of the truths.' 'Here' refers to the passages such as 'making the eye.' The essence is excellent, not to be set aside. 'Otherwise than this' refers to the proliferation of commentary, such as '“making the eye” means it produces purity of view for the full understanding of suffering,' which is merely for the sake of detail.

Ayamevāti ettha ayanti iminā attano aññesañca tassaṃ parisāyaṃ ariyānaṃ maggassa [V 1.0175] paccakkhabhāvaṃ dasseti. Āsannapaccakkhavācī hi ayaṃ-saddo. Aññamaggapaṭisedhanatthanti aññassa nibbānagāmimaggassa atthibhāvapaṭisedhanatthaṃ. Sattāpaṭikkhepo hi idha paṭisedhanaṃ alabbhamānattā aññassa maggassa. Buddhādīnaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvo anaññatā. Tenāha brahmā sahampati –

In the phrase 'this very,' the word 'this' (ayaṃ) indicates the direct experience of the path for oneself and for the other noble ones in that assembly. For the word 'ayaṃ' expresses nearness and direct perception. 'For the purpose of precluding another path' means for the purpose of precluding the existence of any other path leading to Nibbāna. For here the preclusion is an absolute rejection, because no other path is to be found. The non-otherness is the commonality for the Buddhas and others. Thus said Brahmā Sahampati:

“Ekāyanaṃ jātikhayantadassī,

Maggaṃ pajānāti hitānukampī;

Etena maggena tariṃsu pubbe,

Tarissanti ye ca taranti ogha”nti. (saṃ. ni. 5.384, 409; mahāni. 191; cūḷani. 107, 121; netti. 170);

"Seeing the destruction of birth, the one compassionate for the welfare of others knows the path, the sole way. By this path they crossed over in the past, and by it they will cross and are crossing the flood."

Ārakattāti iminā niruttinayena ariya-saddasiddhimāha. Aripahānāyāti atthavacanamattaṃ. Arayo pāpadhammā yanti apagamanti etenāti ariyo. Ariyena desitoti ettha ariyassa bhagavato ayanti ariyo. Ariyabhāvappaṭilābhāyāti ettha ariyakaro ariyoti uttarapadalopena ariya-saddasiddhi veditabbā. Yasmā maggaṅgasamudāye maggavohāro hoti, samudāyo ca samudāyīhi samannāgato nāma hotīti āha “aṭṭhahi aṅgehi upetattā”ti, tasmā attano avayavabhūtāni aṭṭha aṅgāni etassa santīti aṭṭhaṅgiko. Yasmā pana paramatthato aṅgāniyeva maggo, tasmā vuttaṃ “na ca aṅgavinimutto”ti yathā “chaḷaṅgo vedo”ti. Sadisūdāharaṇaṃ pana dassento “pañcaṅgikatūriyādīni viyā”ti āha. Ādi-saddena caturaṅginī senāti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Mārento gacchatīti niruttinayena saddasiddhimāha. Maggatīti gavesati. Ariyamaggo hi nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karonto taṃ gavesanto viya hotīti. Maggīyati nibbānatthikehi vivaṭṭūpanissayapuññakaraṇato [M 1.0197] paṭṭhāya tadatthaṃ paṭipattito. Gammatīti etena ādiantavipariyāyena saddasiddhimāha yathā “kakū”ti. “Seyyathidanti nipāto”ti vatvā tassa sabbaliṅgavibhattivacanasādhāraṇatāya “katamāni tāni aṭṭhaṅgānī”ti vuttaṃ. Nanu ca aṅgāni samuditāni maggo antamaso sattaṅgavikalassa ariyamaggassa abhāvatoti? Saccametaṃ saccapaṭivedhena, maggapaccayatāya pana yathāsakaṃ kiccakaraṇena paccekampi tāni maggoyevāti āha “ekamekañhi aṅgaṃ maggoyevā”ti, aññathā samuditānampi nesaṃ maggakiccaṃ na sambhaveyyāti. Idāni tamevatthaṃ pāḷiyā samatthetuṃ “sammādiṭṭhimaggo ceva hetu cā”ti vuttaṃ.

By 'from being far off,' he states the derivation of the word 'ariya' (noble) by this etymological method. 'For abandoning the adversaries' is merely an explanation of the meaning. An 'ariya' is one by whom the adversaries (arayo), that is, evil states, go away (yanti). In the phrase 'taught by the Noble One,' 'ariya' is derived as 'this belongs to the Noble One (ariyassa ayaṃ), the Blessed One.' In the phrase 'for the attainment of the noble state,' the derivation of the word 'ariya' should be understood by the elision of the final member of 'ariyakaro' (maker of the noble). Because the term 'path' is used for the collection of path-factors, and a collection is said to be endowed with its constituents, it is said: 'because it is endowed with eight factors.' Therefore, it is 'eight-factored' (aṭṭhaṅgiko) because it has eight factors which are its own components. But since, in the ultimate sense, the factors themselves are the path, it is said, 'it is not devoid of factors,' just as one says 'the Veda has six limbs.' Showing a similar example, he says, 'like a five-limbed musical instrument, etc.' By the word 'etc.,' such things as a four-limbed army are included. By the etymological method 'destroying, it goes' (mārento gacchati), he shows the derivation of the word 'magga' (path). 'It seeks' (maggati) means it searches. For the noble path, by taking Nibbāna as its object, is as if it were searching for it. 'It is sought' (maggīyati) by those intent on Nibbāna, from the practice for that purpose, beginning with the performance of merit that is a decisive support for turning away from the round. By 'it is gone to' (gammati), he shows the derivation of the word by metathesis, as in 'kakū.' Having said, 'seyyathidaṃ is a particle,' it is said, 'what are those eight factors?' because that particle is common to all genders, cases, and numbers. Is it not the case that the combined factors are the path, since there is no noble path deficient in even one factor? That is true regarding the penetration of the truths, but with respect to being a condition for the path, since each performs its own function, each one individually is also the path. Thus it is said: 'for each single factor is the path.' Otherwise, even when combined, their function as a path would not be possible. Now, to support this same meaning with the Pāli, it is said: 'right view is the path and also the cause.'

Sammā aviparītaṃ pariññābhisamayādivasena catunnaṃ saccānaṃ dassanaṃ paṭivijjhanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ [V 1.0176] etissāti sammādassanalakkhaṇā. Sammā aviparītaṃ sampayuttadhamme nibbānārammaṇe abhiniropanaṃ appanālakkhaṇaṃ etassāti sammāabhiniropanalakkhaṇo musāvādādīnaṃ visaṃvādanādikiccatāya lūkhānaṃ apariggāhakānaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvato siniddhasabhāvattā sampayuttadhamme, sammāvācappaccayasubhāsitasotārañca janaṃ sammadeva pariggaṇhātīti sammāvācā sammāpariggaho lakkhaṇaṃ etissāti sammāpariggahalakkhaṇā. Yathā kāyikā kiriyā kiñci kattabbaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, sayañca samuṭṭhahanaṃ ghaṭanaṃ hoti, tathā sammākammantasaṅkhātā viratipīti sammāsamuṭṭhānalakkhaṇo sammākammanto. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā ukkhipanaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ kāyikakiriyāya bhārukkhipanaṃ viya. Jīvamānassa sattassa, sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā suddhi vodānaṃ, ājīvasseva vā jīvitappavattiyā suddhi vodānaṃ etenāti sammāvodānalakkhaṇo sammāājīvo. Kosajjapakkhe patituṃ adatvā sampayuttadhammānaṃ paggaṇhanaṃ anubalappadānaṃ paggaho. Ārammaṇaṃ upagantvā ṭhānaṃ, tassa vā anissajjanaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ. Ārammaṇe sampayuttadhammānaṃ sammā, samaṃ vā ādhānaṃ samādhānaṃ. Sammā saṅkappeti sampayuttadhamme ārammaṇe abhiniropetīti sammāsaṅkappo. Sammā vadati etāyāti sammāvācā. Sammā karoti etenāti sammākammaṃ, tadeva sammākammanto. Sammā ājīvati etenāti sammāājīvo. Sammā vāyamati ussahati etenāti sammāvāyāmo. Sammā sarati anussaratīti sammāsati[M 1.0198]. Sammā samādhiyati cittaṃ etenāti sammāsamādhīti evaṃ sammāsaṅkappādīnaṃ nibbacanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Right view has right seeing as its characteristic, being the correct and undistorted seeing and penetration of the four truths by way of full comprehension, realization, and so on. Right intention has right directing as its characteristic, being the correct and undistorted directing and applying of associated states onto the object, Nibbāna. Right speech has right embracing as its characteristic; for, being of a gentle nature, it is opposed to what is harsh and unaccommodating—such as the deceptive function of false speech and the like—and it rightly embraces associated states and those people who hear what is well-spoken on account of it. Just as a physical action initiates something to be done and is itself an initiating and accomplishing, so too, right action, which is an abstention, has right initiating as its characteristic. Or, the raising up or initiating of associated states is like lifting a burden by physical action. Right livelihood has right cleansing as its characteristic, being the purification and cleansing of a living being, or of associated states, or the purification through this of the continuation of life itself. Right effort is exertion, the grasping and strengthening of associated states, giving them support, without giving way to the side of laziness. Right mindfulness is presence, being the approaching and remaining with the object, or the non-abandonment of it. Right concentration is collectedness, being the correct or balanced placing of associated states upon the object. Right intention is so called because it rightly intends, that is, it directs associated states toward an object. Right speech is so called because one speaks rightly through it. Right action is so called because one acts rightly through it; this itself is right action. Right livelihood is so called because one lives rightly through it. Right effort is so called because one exerts rightly through it. Right mindfulness is so called because one recollects rightly. Right concentration is so called because the mind is rightly concentrated through it. In this way, the derivation of terms like right intention and the others should be understood.

Micchādiṭṭhinti sabbampi micchādassanaṃ. Tappaccanīyakileseti ettha taṃ-saddena sammādiṭṭhi. Na hi micchādiṭṭhiyā kilesā paccanīyā, atha kho sammādiṭṭhiyā. Avijjañcāti avijjāggahaṇaṃ tassā saṃkilesadhammānaṃ pamukhabhāvato. Tenāha “avijjā, bhikkhave, pubbaṅgamā akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samāpattiyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1). Dassananivārakassa sammohassa samugghātena asammohato. Ettha ca micchādiṭṭhiṃ…pe… pajahatīti etena pahānābhisamayaṃ, nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karotīti etena sacchikiriyābhisamayaṃ, sampayuttadhammetiādinā bhāvanābhisamayaṃ sammādiṭṭhikiccaṃ dasseti. Pariññābhisamayo pana nānantariyatāya atthato vutto eva hotīti daṭṭhabbo.

"Wrong view" refers to all forms of wrong seeing. In the phrase "the defilements opposed to that," the word "that" refers to right view. For the defilements are not opposed to wrong view, but rather to right view. "And ignorance" refers to the inclusion of ignorance, because it is pre-eminent among defiling states. Hence it is said: "Ignorance, monks, is the forerunner in the attainment of unwholesome states" (SN 5.1). By the eradication of delusion, which obstructs seeing, one becomes undeluded. Here, "abandoning wrong view..." and so on indicates the breakthrough of abandonment; "making Nibbāna the object" indicates the breakthrough of realization; and "associated states," and so on shows the function of right view in the breakthrough of development. However, the breakthrough of full understanding should be understood as implicitly stated due to its inseparability.

Kathaṃ pana ekameva ñāṇaṃ ekasmiṃ khaṇe cattāri kiccāni sādhentaṃ pavattati. Na hi tādisaṃ loke diṭṭhaṃ, na āgamo vā tādiso atthīti na vattabbaṃ. Yathā hi padīpo ekasmiṃyeva khaṇe vaṭṭiṃ dahati, snehaṃ pariyādiyati, andhakāraṃ vidhamati, ālokañca vidaṃseti, evametaṃ ñāṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Maggasamaṅgissa ñāṇaṃ dukkhepetaṃ ñāṇaṃ, dukkhasamudayepetaṃ ñāṇaṃ[V 1.0177], dukkhanirodhepetaṃ ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāyapetaṃ ñāṇanti suttapadaṃ (vibha. 754) ettha udāharitabbaṃ. Yathā ca sammādiṭṭhi pubbabhāge dukkhādīsu visuṃ visuṃ pavattitvā maggakkhaṇe ekāva catunnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ kiccaṃ sādhentī pavattati, evaṃ sammāsaṅkappādayo pubbabhāge nekkhammasaṅkappādināmakā hutvā kāmasaṅkappādīnaṃ pajahanavasena visuṃ visuṃ pavattitvā maggakkhaṇe tiṇṇaṃ catunnañca kiccaṃ sādhentā pavattanti. Sammāsamādhi pana pubbabhāgepi maggakkhaṇepi nānāyeva hutvā pavattatīti kāmañcettha sammādiṭṭhiyā sabbepi pāpadhammā paṭipakkhā, ujuvipaccanīkatādassanavasena pana sammādiṭṭhiyā kiccaniddese micchādiṭṭhiggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Teneva ca “tappaccanīyakilese cā”ti vuttaṃ.

But how does a single knowledge, in a single moment, accomplish four functions while it occurs? It should not be said that nothing like this is seen in the world or that there is no scriptural authority for such a thing. For just as a lamp, in a single moment, burns the wick, consumes the oil, dispels the darkness, and produces light, so too should this knowledge be understood. The knowledge of one endowed with the path is knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of suffering—this scriptural passage (Vibh 754) should be cited here. And just as right view, in the preliminary stage, operates separately regarding suffering and so on, but at the moment of the path, it operates as one, accomplishing the function of the four knowledges, so too right intention and the others, in the preliminary stage, operate separately under the names of renunciation intention and so on, by way of abandoning sensual intentions and so on, but at the moment of the path, they operate accomplishing the function of three or four. Right concentration, however, operates distinctly both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path. And here, though all evil states are opposed to right view, the mention of wrong view in the explanation of right view's function is made from the perspective of seeing direct opposition. Therefore, it is said: "And the defilements opposed to that."

Yesaṃ kilesānaṃ anupacchindane sammādiṭṭhi na uppajjeyya, te micchādiṭṭhiyā sahajekaṭṭhatāya tadekaṭṭhāva tappaccanīyakilesā daṭṭhabbā. Sammāsaṅkappādīnaṃ kiccaniddesepi eseva nayo. Sotāpattimaggādivasena cattāro lokuttaramaggabhāvasāmaññena ekato katvā. Lobhadosā samudayasaccaṃ, yassa pana so samudayo taṃ dukkhasaccaṃ, pahānabhāvo maggasaccaṃ, yattha taṃ [M 1.0199] pahānaṃ, taṃ nirodhasaccanti imāni cattāri saccāni. Kasmā panettha lobhadosānaṃ visuṃ ādito ca gahaṇaṃ? Visuṃ gahaṇaṃ tāva tathābujjhanakānaṃ puggalānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena, imehi lobhadosehi āmisadāyādatā, tappahānena ca dhammadāyādatāti dassanatthaṃ, tadanusārena catusaccayojanāya evaṃ ekekassa niyyānamukhaṃ hotīti dassanatthañca. Sesavāresupi eseva nayo. Ādito gahaṇaṃ pana ativiya oḷārikatāya supākaṭabhāvato vakkhamānānaṃ aññesañca pāpadhammānaṃ mūlabhāvato tadekaṭṭhatāya ca veditabbaṃ.

When certain defilements are not cut off, right view does not arise; those defilements opposed to it should be seen as being one with wrong view due to having a common state with it. The same method applies in specifying the functions of right intention and the others. The four [paths] are grouped together by way of the common characteristic of being supramundane paths, such as the path of stream-entry. Greed and hatred are the truth of origin; that of which this is the origin is the truth of suffering; the state of abandoning is the truth of the path; and where that abandoning occurs is the truth of cessation—these are the four truths. But why, in this context, are greed and hatred mentioned separately and at the beginning? The separate mention is, firstly, in accordance with the inclinations of those persons who are capable of understanding in that way, in order to show that through this greed and hatred there is inheritance of material things, and through their abandoning, there is inheritance of the Dhamma; and furthermore, following this, to show that for each, the application of the four truths is a way of escape. The same method applies in the remaining instances. The initial mention, moreover, is to be understood because of their extreme coarseness, their very manifest nature, their being the root of the other evil states to be discussed, and their being of one state with them.

Kujjhanalakkhaṇoti kuppanasabhāvo, cittassa byāpajjanāti attho. Caṇḍikkaṃ luddatā, kururabhāvoti attho. Āghātakaraṇarasoti “anatthaṃ me acarī”tiādinā citte āghātassa karaṇaraso. Dussanapaccupaṭṭhānoti saparasantānassa vināsanapaccupaṭṭhāno laddhokāso viya sapatto. Upanandhanaṃ nānappakārassa uparūpari nandhanaṃ viya hotīti katvā. Tathā hesa “veraappaṭinissajjanaraso, kodhānupabandhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno”ti ca vutto. Aparakāle upanāhotiādīti ādi-saddena “upanayhanā upanayhitattaṃ āṭhapanā ṭhapanā saṇṭhapanā anusaṃsandanā anuppabandhanā daḷhīkamma”ntiādīnaṃ (vibha. 891) niddesapadānaṃ atthavaṇṇanaṃ saṅgayhati. Upanāhasamaṅgī hi puggalo verassa anissajjanato ādittapūtialātaṃ viya jalati eva, cittañcassa dhoviyamānaṃ acchacammaṃ viya, masimakkhitapilotikā viya ca na sujjhateva.

The characteristic of anger is its nature of agitation; its meaning is hostility of mind. Harshness is cruelty; its meaning is a state of ferocity. Its function is causing resentment; its taste is producing resentment in the mind with thoughts like, "They have wronged me." Its manifestation is destruction; it appears as the ruin of one's own and others' continuums, like an enemy who has found an opportunity. Upanandhana (binding) is so called because it is like repeatedly binding in various ways. Thus, it is also said, "Its function is not abandoning enmity, and its manifestation is the state of being continuously bound by anger." At a later time, 'harboring resentment' and so on—here, the word 'etc.' includes the collected explanations of terms like 'binding, being bound, heating up, fixing, establishing, persistence, continuous binding, and hardening' (Vibh 891). Indeed, a person endowed with resentment burns like a blazing, rotten torch due to not abandoning enmity. And their mind, even when washed, does not become clean, like a bear's hide or a rag smeared with soot.

Paraguṇamakkhanalakkhaṇoti [V 1.0178] udakapuñchaniyā udakaṃ viya paresaṃ guṇānaṃ makkhanasabhāvo. Tathābhūto cāyaṃ attano kārakaṃ gūthena paharantaṃ gūtho viya paṭhamataraṃ makkheti evāti daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hessa saparasantānesu guṇaṃ makkhetīti makkhoti vuccati. Yugaggāho samadhuraggahaṇaṃ asamānassapi abhūtassa samāropanaṃ. Samabhāvakaraṇaṃ samīkaraṇaṃ. Paresaṃ guṇappamāṇena attano guṇānaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetīti āha “paresaṃ guṇappamāṇena upaṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhāno”ti. Tathā hesa paresaṃ guṇe ḍaṃsitvā viya attano guṇehi same karotīti paḷāsoti vuccati.

The characteristic of denigration is the nature of smearing the virtues of others, like a water-wiper obliterates with water. It should be seen that such a person, like dung that first soils the one who throws it, first soils himself. Thus, because he smears virtue in his own and others' continuums, he is called a denigrator. Rivalry is grasping the yoke equally, imposing equality on what is unequal and non-existent. Making things equal is equalizing. He presents his own virtues according to the measure of others' virtues, and makes them manifest; thus it is said, 'its manifestation is presenting and making manifest by the measure of others' virtues.' Thus, as if having bitten into others' virtues, he makes his own virtues equal to them; therefore, he is called one who engages in rivalry.

Parasampattikhīyanaṃ [M 1.0200] parasampattiyā usūyanaṃ. Issati parasampattiṃ na sahatīti issā. Tathā hesā “parasampattiyā akkhamanalakkhaṇā”ti vuccati. Tatthāti parasampattiyaṃ. Anabhiratirasā abhiratipaṭipakkhakiccā. Vimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā parasampattiṃ passitumpi appadānato. Nigūhanalakkhaṇaṃ attano sampattiyā parehi sādhāraṇabhāvāsahanato. Asukhāyanaṃ na sukhanaṃ dukkhanaṃ, arocananti adhippāyo.

Being vexed at others' success is being envious of others' prosperity. One is envious of another's prosperity and cannot bear it, thus it is envy. Thus, it is said to have the characteristic of not tolerating others' prosperity. 'Therein' means in others' prosperity. Its function is displeasure, the opposite of delight. Its manifestation is turning away, from not allowing oneself even to see the prosperity of others. Stinginess has the characteristic of concealment, from being unable to bear one's own prosperity being shared with others. Its function is causing unhappiness, not happiness, but suffering; the meaning is displeasure.

Katassa kāyaduccaritādipāpassa paṭicchādanaṃ katapāpapaṭicchādanaṃ. Tassa pāpassa āvaraṇabhāvena paccupatiṭṭhatīti tadāvaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānā, māyā, yāya samannāgato puggalo bhasmachanno viya aṅgāro, udakachanno viya khāṇu, pilotikapaṭicchāditaṃ viya ca satthaṃ hoti. Avijjamānaguṇappakāsanaṃ attani avijjamānasīlādiguṇavibhāvanaṃ, yena sāṭheyyena samannāgatassa puggalassa asantaguṇasambhāvanena cittānurūpakiriyāviharato “evaṃcitto, evaṃkiriyo”ti dubbiññeyyattā kucchiṃ vā piṭṭhiṃ vā jānituṃ na sakkā. Yato –

The concealment of a committed evil deed, such as bodily misconduct, is the concealment of committed evil. Deceit has as its manifestation the covering of that evil, and a person endowed with it is like embers covered with ashes, a stump concealed by water, or a sword wrapped in rags. The display of non-existent virtues is the making known in oneself of qualities, such as virtue, that do not exist.
