Through such craftiness, with a person endowed with it who dwells acting in accordance with their mind by esteeming non-existent virtues, it is not possible to know their 'belly or back,' due to the difficulty of discerning them as 'of such a mind, of such action.' Whence:

“Vāmena sūkaro hoti, dakkhiṇena ajāmigo;

Sarena nelako hoti, visāṇena jaraggavo”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.296; vibha. aṭṭha. 894; mahāni. aṭṭha. 166) –

"On the left, he is a pig; on the right, a goat-deer. By voice, he is a mongoose; by horn, an old ox."

Evaṃ vuttayakkasūkarasadiso hoti.

Thus, he is like the aforementioned yaksha-pig.

Cittassa uddhumātabhāvo thaddhalūkhabhāvo. Appatissayavuttīti anivātavutti. Amaddavākārena paccupatiṭṭhati, amaddavataṃ vā paccupaṭṭhapetīti amaddavatāpaccupaṭṭhāno, thambho, yena samannāgato puggalo gilitanaṅgalasīso viya ajagaro, vātabharitabhastā viya ca thaddho hutvā garuṭṭhāniye ca [V 1.0179] disvā onamitumpi na icchati, pariyanteneva carati. Karaṇassa uttarakiriyā karaṇuttariyaṃ. Visesato paccanīkabhāvo vipaccanīkatā. Parena hi kismiñci kate taddiguṇaṃ karaṇavasena sārambho pavattati.

The mind's state of being puffed up is stiffness and roughness. 'A non-deferential way of life' means a non-humble way of life. It manifests in an ungentle manner, or it makes ungentleness manifest—thus, its manifestation is ungentleness, which is obstinacy. A person endowed with this is like a python that has swallowed a ploughshare or like a bellows filled with wind, remaining rigid and unwilling to bend even when seeing one worthy of reverence, moving only at the periphery. The surpassing action of doing is overdoing. Specifically, the state of being an opponent is opposition. For when something is done by another, contention arises by way of doing twice as much.

Seyyādiākārehi unnamanaṃ unnati. Omānopi hi evaṃ karaṇamukhena sampaggahavaseneva pavattati. “Ahamasmi seyyo”tiādinā ahaṃkaraṇaṃ sampaggaho ahaṅkāro. Pare abhibhavitvā adhikaṃ unnamanaṃ abbhunnati[M 1.0201]. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “pubbakāle attānaṃ hīnato dahati aparakāle seyyato”ti (vibha. 877).

Elevating oneself through modes such as 'superior' is elevation. Contempt also proceeds in this way, by means of grasping through the avenue of action. The 'I-making' and grasping, such as 'I am superior,' is egoism. Overcoming others and elevating oneself further is exaltation. This is in reference to what was said: 'Formerly, one places oneself as inferior; later, as superior.'

Mattabhāvo jātiādiṃ paṭicca cittassa majjanākāro, yassa vā dhammassa vasena puggalo matto nāma hoti, so dhammo mattabhāvo. Madaggāhaṇaraso madassa gāhaṇakicco. Mado hi attano majjanākāraṃ sampayuttadhamme gāhento viya pavattamāno taṃsamaṅgiṃ puggalampi tathā karonto viya hoti. Ahaṅkāravasena puggalaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ karonto cittassa ummādabhāvo viya hotīti ummādapaccupaṭṭhāno. Satiyā aniggaṇhitvā cittassa vossajjanaṃ cittavossaggo, sativirahitoti attho. Yathāvuttassa vossaggassa anuppadānaṃ punappunaṃ vissajjanaṃ vossaggānuppadānaṃ. Imesaṃ kodhādīnaṃ lobhādīnampi vā. Lakkhaṇādīnīti lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānāni. Padaṭṭhānaṃ pana dhammantaratāya na gahitaṃ. Nibbacanaṃ “kujjhatīti kodho, upanayhatīti upanāho”tiādinā suviññeyyamevāti na vuttaṃ, atthato pana kodho doso eva, tathā upanāho. Pavattiākāramattato hi kato nesaṃ bhedo, makkhapaḷāsasārambhā tadākārappavattā paṭighasahagatacittuppādadhammā, māyāsāṭheyyathambhamadappamādā tadākārappavattā lobhasahagatacittuppādadhammā. Thambho vā mānaviseso cittassa thaddhabhāvena gahetabbato, tathā mado. Tathā hi so “māno maññanā”tiādinā vibhaṅge (vibha. 878) niddiṭṭho. Idha pana mānātimānānaṃ visuṃ gahitattā majjanākārena pavattadhammā eva “mado”ti gahetabbā. Sesānaṃ dhammantarabhāvo pākaṭo eva.

The state of intoxication is the mode of the mind's drunkenness on account of birth and so on; or it is that state by means of which a person is called intoxicated. Its function is the grasping of intoxication; its duty is grasping. For intoxication, while occurring, is as if it makes its associated states grasp its own nature of drunkenness, and it is as if it makes the person endowed with it do likewise. By means of egoism, it makes a person undesirable; it is like a state of the mind's madness, thus its manifestation is madness. Letting go of the mind without restraining it by mindfulness is 'letting go of the mind'; the meaning is being devoid of mindfulness. The repeated indulgence in the aforesaid letting go is 'repeatedly letting go.' Of these states, such as anger, or those such as greed, their characteristics, etc., are their characteristics, functions, and manifestations. The proximate cause, however, is not taken up due to the diversity of states. The etymology is not stated as it is easily understood from 'one is angry, thus anger; one is hostile, thus hostility,' and so on. But in meaning, anger is simply hatred, and likewise hostility. Their distinction is made merely from the mode of occurrence. Denigration, rivalry, and contention are states arising with consciousness accompanied by aversion, occurring in such modes. Deceit, craftiness, obstinacy, intoxication, and heedlessness are states arising with consciousness accompanied by greed, occurring in such modes. Or, obstinacy is a specific kind of conceit, to be understood as the rigidity of the mind; and so too is intoxication. For it is explained in the Vibhaṅga as 'conceit is the act of conceiving,' etc. Here, however, because conceit and excessive conceit are taken up separately, those states occurring with the mode of drunkenness are to be understood as 'intoxication.' The fact that the remaining states are distinct is quite evident.

Kasmā panettha ete eva aṭṭha dukā gahitā, kimito aññepi kilesadhammā natthīti? No natthi, ime pana āmisadāyādassa savisesaṃ kilesāya saṃvattantīti taṃ visesaṃ vibhāventena āmisadāyādassa lobhādīnaṃ pavattanākāraṃ dassetuṃ “visesato”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha etthāti etesu lobhādīsu. Alabhanto āmisanti adhippāyo. Tatuttari uppanno kodhoti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Santepīti vijjamānepi. Issatīti issaṃ janeti. Padussatīti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Tathā hi sā “issati dussati padussatī”tiādinā niddiṭṭhā. Yasmā vā issaṃ [V 1.0180][M 1.0202] janento ekaṃsato paduṭṭhacitto eva hoti, tasmā “padussatī”ti vuttaṃ. Assāti āmisadāyādassa. Evaṃ paṭipannoti evaṃ asantaguṇappakāsanaṃ paṭipadaṃ paṭipanno. Ovadituṃ asakkuṇeyyoti etena thambho nāma dovacassakaraṇo dhammoti dasseti. Kiñci vadati ovādadānavasena. Thambhena…pe… maññantoti iminā ca thambhassa mānavisesabhāvaṃ dasseti, thambhena vā hetunāti attho. Matto samānoti matto honto. Kāma…pe… pamajjatīti etena madavasena ekaṃsato pamādamāpajjatīti dasseti.

Why are just these eight pairs taken up here? Are there no other defiling states? It is not that there are none, but these especially conduce to the defilement of an heir to material things. Therefore, to clarify that distinction, the passage beginning 'especially' was started in order to show the mode of occurrence of greed and so on for an heir to material things. Therein, 'in these' means in these states such as greed. 'Not obtaining material gain' is the meaning. 'Further, anger arises' should be supplied and connected. 'Even when present' means 'even when existing.' 'Is envious' means generates envy. 'Is malevolent' is a synonym for that. For so it is pointed out: 'is envious, is resentful, is malevolent,' and so on. Or, because one who generates envy is certainly one of a corrupted mind, therefore it is said 'is malevolent.' 'Of him' means of the heir to material things. 'Having undertaken thus' means having undertaken the practice of displaying non-existent virtues. By 'they would be unable to admonish him,' it shows that obstinacy is a state that makes one difficult to admonish. 'He says something' means by way of giving an admonition. By 'through obstinacy... he conceives,' it shows that obstinacy is a specific kind of conceit, or the meaning is 'because of obstinacy.' 'Being intoxicated' means becoming intoxicated. By 'sensual pleasures... becomes heedless,' it shows that by means of intoxication one certainly falls into heedlessness.

Evanti iminā āmisadāyādassa lobhādīnaṃ uppattikkamadassaneneva idha pāḷiyaṃ nesaṃ desanākkamopi dassitoti daṭṭhabbo. Na kevalaṃ imeheva, atha kho aññehi ca evarūpehi pāpakehi dhammehi aparimutto hotīti sambandho. Ke pana teti? Atricchatāmahicchatādayoti. Evaṃ mahādīnavā āmisadāyādatāti tato balavataro saṃvego janetabboti ayamettha ovādo veditabbo. Etthāti etasmiṃ sutte. Sabbatthāti sabbesu vāresu. Nibbisesoyevāti eteneva paṭhamataraṃ idha dassitasaccayojanānayena sabbavāresu yojetabboti veditabbo.

Thus, by this very showing of the sequence of the arising of greed and the like for an heir to material things, the sequence of their teaching in the Pāli text is also shown here; this should be understood. Not only by these, but also by other such evil states, one is not freed—this is the connection. 'What are they?' They are excessive desire, great desire, and so on. Thus, being an heir to material things is of great danger; therefore, a stronger sense of spiritual urgency should be aroused—this is the advice to be understood here. 'Here' means in this sutta. 'In all cases' means in all instances. 'Without distinction' means that by this very method of connecting the reasons shown here earlier, it should be applied to all instances—this is how it should be understood.

Ñāṇaparicayapāṭavatthanti maggassa aṭṭhaṅgasattaṅgatādivisesavibhāvanāya ñāṇassa āsevanaṭṭhena paricayo ñāṇaparicayo, tassa paṭubhāvatthaṃ kosallatthaṃ. Etthāti ariyamagge. Bhedoti viseso. Kamoti aṅgānaṃ desanānupubbī. Bhāvanānayoti bhāvanāvidhi. “Kadāci aṭṭhaṅgiko, kadāci sattaṅgiko”ti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivaranto puna “ayaṃ hī”tiādimāha. Tattha lokuttarapaṭhamajjhānavasenāti lokuttarassa paṭhamajjhānassa vasena. Ettha ca keci jhānadhammā maggasabhāvāti ekantato jhānaṃ maggato visuṃ katvā vattuṃ na sakkāti “lokuttarapaṭhamajjhānasahito”ti avatvā “lokuttarapaṭhamajjhānavasena”icceva vuttaṃ. Atha vā lokuttarapaṭhamajjhānavasenāti lokuttarā hutvā paṭhamajjhānassa vasenāti evamettha attho veditabbo. Ariyamaggo hi vipassanāya pādakabhūtassa, sammasitassa vā paṭhamajjhānassa vasena aṭṭhaṅgiko hoti. Atha vā ajhānalābhino sukkhavipassakassa, jhānalābhino vā pādakamakatvā paṭhamajjhānassa, pakiṇṇakasaṅkhārānaṃ vā sammasane [M 1.0203] uppanno ariyamaggo aṭṭhaṅgiko hoti, svāssa aṭṭhaṅgikabhāvo paṭhamajjhānikabhāvenāti dassento “paṭhamajjhānavasenā”ti āha. Evaṃ “avasesajjhānavasenā”ti etthāti yathārahaṃ attho veditabbo.

'For skill in familiarity with knowledge' means: for manifesting the distinctions such as the eightfold and sevenfold nature of the path. Familiarity with knowledge (ñāṇaparicayo) is familiarity in the sense of cultivating knowledge, for the purpose of its sharpness and skill. 'Here' means in the Noble Path. 'Distinction' means a specific aspect. 'Order' refers to the sequence of the factors in the teaching. 'Method of development' means the procedure of cultivation. Elaborating on the meaning briefly stated as 'sometimes eightfold, sometimes sevenfold,' he says again 'this is indeed,' and so on. Therein, 'by means of the first supramundane jhāna' means by the power of the first supramundane jhāna. And here, some say that since the jhāna factors are of the nature of the path, it is not possible to speak of jhāna as entirely separate from the path. Therefore, instead of saying 'accompanied by the first supramundane jhāna,' it is said 'by means of the first supramundane jhāna.' Alternatively, 'by means of the first supramundane jhāna' means 'having become supramundane, by means of the first jhāna'—this is how the meaning should be understood here. For the noble path becomes eightfold by means of the first jhāna which has become the basis for insight, or which has been contemplated. Alternatively, for a dry-insight meditator who has not attained jhāna, or for one who has attained jhāna but has not made the first jhāna the basis, the noble path that has arisen during the contemplation of miscellaneous formations becomes eightfold. To show that its eightfold nature is due to its state of being related to the first jhāna, it is said 'by means of the first jhāna.' Similarly, 'by means of the remaining jhānas' should be understood here according to what is appropriate.

Yadi ariyamaggo sattaṅgikopi hoti, atha kasmā pāḷiyaṃ “aṭṭhaṅgiko”icceva vuttanti āha “ukkaṭṭhaniddesato”tiādi. Yathā cettha paṭipadāya maggavasena aṭṭhaṅgikasattaṅgikabhedo[V 1.0181], evaṃ bojjhaṅgavasena sattaṅgikachaḷaṅgikabhedo veditabbo appītikajjhānavasena chaḷaṅgikattā, maggavasena pana desanā āgatāti svāyaṃ bhedo aṭṭhakathāyaṃ na uddhaṭo. Ito paranti ito aṭṭhaṅgato paraṃ ukkaṃsato, avakaṃsato pana sattaṅgato paraṃ maggaṅgaṃ nāma natthīti. Nanu maggavibhaṅge (vibha. 493-502) pañcaṅgikavāre pañceva maggaṅgāni uddhaṭāni, mahāsaḷāyatane (ma. ni. 3.431) ca “yā tathābhūtassa diṭṭhi, yo tathābhūtassa saṅkappo, yo tathābhūtassa vāyāmo, yā tathābhūtassa sati, yo tathābhūtassa samādhi, svāssa hoti sammāsamādhī”ti vatvā pubbabhāgavasena pana “pubbeva kho panassa kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ ājīvo suparisuddho hotī”ti sammāvācādayo āgatāti? Saccametaṃ, taṃ pana sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ kārāpakaṅgānaṃ atirekakiccadassanavasena vuttaṃ, tasmā na ariyamaggo sammāvācādivirahito atthīti “ito parañhi maggaṅgaṃ natthī”ti suvuttametanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

If the Noble Path is also seven-factored, then why is it said in the Pāli only as 'eight-factored'? He says, 'due to the exposition of the excellent,' and so on. Just as here there is a distinction between the eight-factored and seven-factored by way of the path of practice, so too a distinction between the seven-factored and six-factored by way of the enlightenment factors should be understood, due to its being six-factored by means of the jhāna without rapture. But since the teaching comes by way of the path, this distinction is not brought up in the commentary. 'From here onwards' means that beyond the eight factors at the highest, and beyond the seven factors at the lowest, there is no such thing as a path factor. 'Is it not so that in the Analysis of the Path (Vibhaṅga 493–502), only five path factors are mentioned in the five-factored section, and in the Great Sixfold Sense Base Sutta (MN 149) it is said: "For one thus constituted, there is right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—this is his right concentration." And furthermore, in the preliminary section, it is stated: "But beforehand, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood are thoroughly purified," thus including right speech, etc.?' This is true. But that was said by way of showing the additional function of the five causative factors, namely right view and so on. Therefore, since the noble path does not exist devoid of right speech and so on, 'beyond this, there is no path factor' is well said; this should be understood.

Sabbakusalānanti sabbesaṃ kusaladhammānaṃ. Niddhāraṇe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Kāmāvacarādivasena taṃtaṃkusaladhammesu sā sammādiṭṭhi seṭṭhā. Tassā seṭṭhabhāvena hi “paññājīviṃ jīvitamāhu seṭṭha”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 184) vuttaṃ, maggasammādiṭṭhiyā pana sabbaseṭṭhabhāve vattabbameva natthi. Kusalavāreti kusaluppattisamaye. Pubbaṅgamā kusalādidhammānaṃ yāthāvasabhāvabodhena sampayuttadhammānaṃ pariṇāyakabhāvato. Tenevāha “sammādiṭṭhiṃ sammādiṭṭhīti pajānātī”tiādi. Sā sammādiṭṭhi pabhavo etassāti tappabhavo, sammāsaṅkappo. Sammādassanavasena hi sammāsaṅkappo hoti. Tato abhinibbattānīti tappabhavābhinibbattāni. Tappabhavābhinibbattānipi “tadabhinibbattānī”ti vuccanti kāraṇakāraṇepi kāraṇūpacāratoti āha “tappabhavābhinibbattāni sesaṅgānī”ti. Tenāha “sammādiṭṭhissā”tiādi. Yathā hi sammādassanaṃ [M 1.0204] sammāvitakkanassa visesapaccayo, evaṃ sammāvitakkanaṃ sammāpariggahassa sammāpariggaho sammāsamuṭṭhānassa, sammāsamuṭṭhānaṃ sammāvodānassa, sammāvodānaṃ sammāvāyāmassa, sammāvāyāmo sammāupaṭṭhānassa, sammāupaṭṭhānaṃ sammādhānassa visesapaccayo, tasmā “purimaṃ purimaṃ pacchimassa pacchimassa visesapaccayo hotī”ti iminā visesapaccayabhāvadassanatthena kamena etāni sammādiṭṭhiādīni aṅgāni vuttānīti dassitāni.

'Of all wholesome states' refers to all wholesome qualities. This is a genitive case of specification. Among the various wholesome qualities pertaining to the sense-sphere and so on, that right view is the best. Because of its excellence, it is said, 'They declare the life led by wisdom as the best' (SN 1.246; Snp 184). However, regarding the path right view, there is nothing at all to be said about its being the very best. 'In the instance of the wholesome' means at the time of the arising of wholesome states. It is a forerunner because it leads the associated states by means of understanding the true nature of wholesome and other states. Therefore, it is said, 'One understands right view as right view,' and so on. That right view is the source of this—thus, right intention is 'born from that source.' For right intention arises through right seeing. The phrase 'produced from that' means 'produced from that source.' Even those produced from that source are called 'produced from it' due to the metaphorical extension of 'cause' even to the cause of the cause. Hence, it is said, 'The remaining factors are produced from that source.' Therefore, it is said, 'For one with right view...' and so on. Just as right seeing is the specific condition for right thought, so too right thought is for right speech, right speech for right action, right action for right livelihood, right livelihood for right effort, right effort for right mindfulness, and right mindfulness for right concentration. Therefore, by showing the nature of this specific condition with the words, 'Each preceding factor is the specific condition for each succeeding one,' it is shown that these factors—beginning with right view—are explained in sequence.

Bhāvanānayoti samathavipassanānaṃ yuganaddhabhāvena pavatto bhāvanāvidhi. Ayañhi ariyamaggakkhaṇe bhāvanāvidhi. Tassa pana pubbabhāge bhāvanānayo kassaci samathapubbaṅgamo hoti[V 1.0182], kassaci vipassanāpubbaṅgamoti. Taṃ vidhiṃ dassetuṃ “kocī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha paṭhamo samathayānikassa vasena vutto, dutiyo vipassanāyānikassa. Tenāha “idhekacco”tiādi. Tanti samathaṃ samādhiṃ, jhānadhammeti vā attho. Taṃsampayutteti samādhisampayutte, jhānasampayutte vā dhamme. Ayañca nayo yebhuyyena samathayānikā arūpamukhena, tatthāpi jhānamukhena vipassanābhinivesaṃ karontīti katvā vutto. Vipassanaṃ bhāvayatoti paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiṃ ārabhitvā yathādhigataṃ taruṇavipassanaṃ vaḍḍhentassa. Maggo sañjāyatīti pubbabhāgiyo lokiyamaggo uppajjati. Āsevati nibbidānupassanāvasena. Bhāveti muñcitukamyatāvasena. Bahulīkaroti paṭisaṅkhānupassanāvasena. Āsevati vā bhayatūpaṭṭhānañāṇavasena. Bahulīkaroti vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāvasena. Saṃyojanāni pahīyanti, anusayā byantī honti maggapaṭipāṭiyā.

"The method of development" is the process of meditation that occurs through the union of serenity and insight. This is the method of meditation at the moment of the noble path. In its preliminary stage, the approach to development may be serenity-led for some and insight-led for others. To explain this method, the text begins with "someone." Here, the first case is stated for one who follows the serenity vehicle, and the second for one who follows the insight vehicle. Hence, it is said, "Here, someone..." The word "that" (taṃ) means tranquility, or concentration, or the jhana factors. "Associated with it" refers to states connected with concentration or absorption. This approach is mostly for those who follow the serenity vehicle, largely through the formless attainments, and even through the jhanas, as they apply themselves to insight. "One develops insight" means for one who, starting from the purification of knowledge and vision of the way, develops the immature insight as attained. "The path arises" refers to the preliminary mundane path arising. One cultivates through the contemplation of disenchantment. One develops through the desire for deliverance. One makes much of through the contemplation of reflection. Alternatively, one cultivates through the knowledge of the appearance of danger, and one makes much of through insight leading to emergence. The fetters are abandoned, and the underlying tendencies are destroyed in the sequence of the path.

Samathaṃ anuppādetvāvāti avadhāraṇena upacārasamādhiṃ nivatteti, na khaṇikasamādhiṃ. Na hi khaṇikasamādhiṃ vinā vipassanā sambhavati. Vipassanāpāripūriyāti vipassanāya paripuṇṇatāya vuṭṭhānagāminibhāvappattiyā. Tatthajātānanti tasmiṃ ariyamaggakkhaṇe uppannānaṃ sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ. Niddhāraṇe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Vavassaggārammaṇatoti vavassaggassa ārammaṇatāya. Vavassaggo vossaggo paṭinissaggoti ca apavaggoti ca atthato ekaṃ, nibbānanti vuttaṃ hoti, tasmā nibbānassa ārammaṇakaraṇenāti attho. Cittassa ekaggatāti maggasammāsamādhimāha. Ariyamaggo hi ekanta samāhito asamādhānahetūnaṃ kilesānaṃ samucchedanato. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

"Without developing tranquility"—this emphatic statement excludes access concentration, not momentary concentration. For without momentary concentration, insight is not possible. "The fulfillment of insight"—this refers to the perfection of insight, having reached the state leading to emergence. "Those arisen therein"—this is a genitive of specification for the states, such as right view, that arise in that moment of the noble path. "Having relinquishment as its object" means having relinquishment as its object. Relinquishment, letting go, renunciation, and abandonment are the same in meaning—it is said to be Nibbāna. Therefore, the meaning is: by making Nibbāna its object. "Unification of mind"—this refers to right concentration on the path. For the noble path is exclusively concentrated, because of its cutting off the defilements that are the cause of non-concentration. The rest is as previously explained.

Yuganaddhāva [M 1.0205] honti tadā samādhipaññānaṃ samarasatāya icchitabbato. Maggakkhaṇe hi na samathabhāvanāyaṃ viya samādhi, vipassanābhāvanāyaṃ viya ca paññā kiccato adhikā icchitabbā, samarasatāya pana aññamaññassa anativattanaṭṭhena dvepi yuganaddhā viya pavattanti. Tena vuttaṃ “samathavipassanā yuganaddhāva hontī”ti.

At that time, concentration and wisdom should be desired to occur in unison due to their equal savor. For at the moment of the path, neither concentration, as in serenity meditation, nor wisdom, as in insight meditation, should be desired as having a superior function. Rather, due to their equal savor, both proceed in unison like a yoke, without surpassing each other. Hence it is said: "Serenity and insight occur in unison."

Dhammadāyādasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The exposition of the hidden meaning of the commentary on the Dhammadāyāda Sutta is complete.

4. Bhayabheravasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Bhayabherava Sutta

34. Evaṃ [V 1.0183] me sutanti bhayabheravasuttaṃ. Ko nikkhepo? Keci tāva evamāhu “pucchāvasiko nikkhepo”ti. Duvidhā hi pucchā pākaṭāpākaṭabhedato. Tattha yassā desanāya nimittabhūto ñātuṃ icchito attho kiṃ-saddapubbakena pakāsīyati, sā pākaṭā pucchā yathā “kiṃsūdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭha”nti evamādi (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 183). Yassā pana desanāya nimittabhūto ñātuṃ icchito attho kiṃ-saddarahitena kevaleneva saddapayogena pakāsīyati, sā apākaṭā pucchā. Ñātuṃ icchito hi attho “pañhā, pucchā”ti vuccati, tasmāyeva idha “ye me bho gotamā”tiādikā apākaṭāti “pucchāvasiko nikkhepo”ti. Tayidaṃ akāraṇaṃ, yasmā so brāhmaṇo “yeme bho gotamā”tiādīni vadanto na tattha kaṅkhī vicikicchī saṃsayamāpanno avoca, atha kho attanā yathānicchitamatthaṃ bhagavati pasādabhāvabahumānaṃ pavedento kathesi. Tenāha “bhagavati pasādaṃ alatthā”tiādi (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.34). Vihāreti vihārake nivāse. Avicchinneyevāti pavattamāneyeva. Padadvayassapi vasante evāti attho. Etaṃ purohitaṭṭhānaṃ uṇhīsādikakudhabhaṇḍehi saddhiṃ laddhaṃ, tathā ca “assa raññā dinna”nti vadanti. Tenāha “taṃ tassa raññā dinna”nti. Brahmanti vedaṃ. So pana mantabrahmakappavasena tividho. Tattha mantā padhānaṃ mūlabhāvato, ye aṭṭhakādīhi pavuttā, itare tannissayena jātā, tena tesaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ “mante sajjhāyatī”ti[M 1.0206]. Te hi guttabhāsitabbatāya “mantā”ti vuccanti. Idameva hīti avadhāraṇena “brahmato jātā”tiādikaṃ niruttiṃ paṭikkhipati.

34. The Bhayabherava Sutta [begins with the phrase] “Thus have I heard.” What is its exposition? Some indeed say, “The exposition is based on the question.” For questions are of two kinds: evident and non-evident. Herein, a question is evident when the meaning intended to be understood, which is the basis for the teaching, is expressed by a word preceded by “what,” as in “What is the best wealth for a man?” and so on (Saṃ. Ni. 1.246; Su. Ni. 183). But a question is non-evident when the meaning intended to be understood, which is the basis for the teaching, is expressed without a word like “what,” but solely by the use of words. The meaning intended to be understood is called a “question” or “inquiry.” Therefore, here, the non-evident question is “Venerable Gotama, those who…” and so on; hence [they say] “the exposition is based on the question.” But this is without reason, because that brahmin, while saying “Venerable Gotama, those who…” and so on, did not speak with doubt, perplexity, or uncertainty about it. Rather, he spoke expressing the meaning he himself had ascertained, manifesting his faith and high regard for the Blessed One. Therefore it is said, “He gained faith in the Blessed One,” and so on (Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.34). “He dwells” means he resides in a dwelling. “Uninterruptedly” means continuously. The meaning is that both words mean “constantly.” This position of chaplain was obtained along with the royal insignia such as the turban and other articles of royal honour, and thus they say, “It was given by the king.” Therefore it is said, “It was given to him by the king.” “Brahma” means the Veda. But it is threefold by way of mantra, brahma, and ritual rules. Among these, the mantras are primary, being the root, as stated by the Aṭṭhakas and others; the others are born dependent on them. Therefore, it is these that are meant by 'he recites the mantras.' They are called “mantras” because they must be spoken guardedly. By the emphasizing particle “indeed” (hi) in “this indeed” (idameva hi), it rejects the etymology “born from Brahma” and so on.

Yena vā kāraṇenāti (sārattha. ṭī. verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ 2; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.1; a. ni. ṭī. 2.2.16) hetumhi idaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Hetuattho hi kiriyākāraṇaṃ, na karaṇaṃ viya kiriyattho, tasmā nānappakāraguṇavisesādhigamatthā idha upasaṅkamanakiriyāti “annena vasatī”tiādīsu viya hetuatthamevetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ yuttaṃ, na karaṇatthaṃ tassa ayujjamānattāti vuttaṃ “yena vā kāraṇenā”tiādi. Bhagavato satatappavattaniratisayasāduvipulāmatarasasaddhammaphalatāya sāduphalaniccaphalitamahārukkhena bhagavā upamito, sāduphalūpabhogādhippāyaggahaṇeneva hi mahārukkhassa sāduphalatā gahitāti.

“By whatever reason” (Sārattha. Ṭī. Verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ 2; Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 1.1.1; A. Ni. Ṭī. 2.2.16) — this instrumental word is in the sense of cause. For the meaning of 'cause' is the reason for an action, not, like an instrument, the means for an action. Therefore, since the act of approaching here is for the purpose of attaining various kinds of excellent and distinct qualities, this instrumental word is fitting only in the sense of cause, as in “he lives by food” and so on, and not in the sense of instrument, because the latter is inapplicable. Thus it is stated “by whatever reason” and so on. The Blessed One is compared to a great tree constantly bearing sweet fruits, due to the ceaseless, unsurpassed, sweet, abundant, deathless essence of the true Dhamma’s fruits. For the great tree’s sweetness is understood by grasping the intention of enjoying sweet fruit.

Upasaṅkamīti [V 1.0184] upasaṅkanto. Sampattukāmatāya hi kiñci ṭhānaṃ gacchanto taṃtaṃpadesātikkamanena upasaṅkami, upasaṅkantoti vā vattabbataṃ labhati. Tenāha “gatoti vuttaṃ hotī”ti, upagatoti attho. Upasaṅkamitvāti pubbakālakiriyāniddesoti āha “upasaṅkamanapariyosānadīpana”nti. Tatoti yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patto “upasaṅkamī”ti vutto, tato upagataṭṭhānato. Yathā khamanīyādīni pucchantoti (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.112) yathā bhagavā “kacci te brāhmaṇa khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīya”ntiādinā khamanīyādīni pucchanto tena brāhmaṇena saddhiṃ samappavattamodo ahosi pubbabhāsitāya, tadanukaraṇena evaṃ sopi brāhmaṇo bhagavatā saddhiṃ samappavattamodo ahosīti yojanā. Taṃ pana samappavattamodataṃ upamāya dassetuṃ “sītodakaṃ viyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sammoditanti saṃsanditaṃ. Ekībhāvanti sammodanakiriyāya samānataṃ ekarūpataṃ. Khamanīyanti “idaṃ catucakkaṃ navadvāraṃ sarīrayantaṃ khaṇabhaṅguratāya sabhāvato dussahaṃ, kacci khamituṃ sakkuṇeyya”nti pucchati. Yāpanīyanti paccayāyattavuttikaṃ cirappabandhasaṅkhātāya yāpanāya kacci yāpetuṃ sakkuṇeyyaṃ. Sīsarogādiābādhābhāvena kacci appābādhaṃ. Dukkhajīvikābhāvena kacci appātaṅkaṃ. Taṃtaṃkiccakaraṇe uṭṭhānasukhatāya kacci lahuṭṭhānaṃ. Tadanarūpabalayogato kacci balaṃ. Sukhavihārasabbhāvena kacci phāsuvihāro atthīti tattha tattha kacci-saddaṃ yojetvā attho veditabbo.

“Upasaṅkami” (he approached) means “upasaṅkanto” (having approached). For one who goes to some place out of a desire to reach it, by passing through various regions, he “approached” (upasaṅkami) or attains the state of being called “having approached” (upasaṅkanto). Therefore it is said, “it means ‘gone’”; the meaning is “arrived.” “Upasaṅkamitvā” (having approached) is a designation of a prior action, thus he says, “it indicates the completion of the act of approaching.” “Tato” (from there) means “from that place of arrival, the place which was reached and referred to as ‘he approached’.” Just as when asking about well-being and so on (Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 1.1.112), just as the Blessed One, asking about well-being and so on with “I hope, brahmin, you are well? I hope you are managing?” and so on, had a mutually flowing joy with that brahmin due to prior conversation, so too, by imitating that, this brahmin also had a mutually flowing joy with the Blessed One—this is the connection. To illustrate that mutually flowing joy, it is said, “like cool water” and so on. There, “sammodita” (having rejoiced together) means “saṃsandita” (mingled). “Ekībhāva” (being of one mind) means “equality, oneness in the act of rejoicing.” “Khamanīya” (well-being)? He asks, “Can one endure this body-machine with its four wheels and nine gates, which is naturally hard to bear due to its momentary breaking up?” “Yāpanīya” (managing)? “Can one sustain oneself, whose existence is dependent on requisites, by means of a sustenance reckoned as long-term continuity?” “Kacci appābādhaṃ” (I hope you are free from illness)? “Is one free from ailments such as headaches?” “Kacci appātaṅkaṃ” (I hope you are free from affliction)? “Is one free from affliction due to the absence of a difficult livelihood?” “Kacci lahuṭṭhānaṃ” (I hope you are energetic)? “Is one quick to rise for various tasks due to the ease of exertion?” “Kacci balaṃ” (I hope you are strong)? “Is one strong due to possessing appropriate power?” “Kacci phāsuvihāro atthīti” (I hope you are living comfortably)? “Is there comfortable abiding due to the presence of pleasant dwelling?” The meaning should be understood by connecting the word “kacci” (I hope) in each instance.

Balavappattā [M 1.0207] pīti pītiyeva. Taruṇapīti pāmojjaṃ. Sammodanaṃ janeti karotīti sammodanikaṃ, tadeva sammodanīyanti āha “sammodajananato”ti. Sammoditabbato sammodanīyanti imaṃ pana atthaṃ dassento “sammodituṃ yuttabhāvato”ti āha. Saritabbabhāvatoti anussaritabbabhāvato. “Saraṇīya”nti vattabbe dīghaṃ katvā “sāraṇīya”nti vuttaṃ. Suyyamānasukhatoti āpāthamadhurataṃ āha, anussariyamānasukhatoti vimaddaramaṇīyataṃ. Byañjanaparisuddhatāyāti sabhāvaniruttibhāvena tassā kathāya vacanacāturiyamāha, atthaparisuddhatāyāti atthassa nirupakkilesataṃ. Anekehi pariyāyehīti anekehi kāraṇehi.

“Balavappattā pīti” (joy that has attained strength) is simply “pīti” (joy). “Taruṇapīti” (young joy) is “pāmojja” (gladness). It generates or makes rejoicing, hence it is “sammodanika”; the same is “sammodanīya”, thus he says, “from generating rejoicing.” However, showing this meaning “sammodanīya” (fit to be rejoiced over) from “sammoditabbato” (because it should be rejoiced over), he says, “because of being fit to be rejoiced over.” “Saritabbabhāvato” (by reason of being remembered) means “anussaritabbabhāvato” (by reason of being recollected). Though it should have been said “saraṇīya”, it is said “sāraṇīya” by lengthening [the vowel]. “Suyyamānasukhata” (delightfulness when heard) means “sweetness to the ear,” he says. “Anussariyamānasukhata” (delightfulness when recollected) means “delightfulness of careful consideration.” “Byañjanaparisuddhatāya” (by purity of expression) means “the eloquence of speech of that talk by way of its natural and flawless diction,” he says. “Atthaparisuddhatāya” (by purity of meaning) means “the meaning’s freedom from defilement.” “Anekehi pariyāyehi” (by many methods) means “by many reasons.”

Abhidūraaccāsannapaṭikkhepena nātidūranāccāsannaṃ nāma gahitaṃ, taṃ pana avakaṃsato ubhinnaṃ pasāritahatthasaṅghaṭṭanena daṭṭhabbaṃ. Gīvaṃ pasāretvāti gīvaṃ parivattanavasena pasāretvā.

By the rejection of “too far” and “too near,” the term “not too far, not too near” is understood. This should be observed by the lowering of the body and the touching of the outstretched hands of both parties. “Gīvaṃ pasāretvā” (having extended the neck) means “having extended the neck by turning it.”

Yemeti ettha sandhivasena ikāralopoti dassento “ye ime”tiādimāha. Uccākulīnatāya jātivasena abhijātā jātikulaputtā. Tenāha “uccākulappasutā”ti. Ācārasampattiyā [V 1.0185] abhijātā ācārakulaputtā. Tenāha “ācārasampannā”ti. Yattha katthaci apākaṭepi kule. Tena brāhmaṇena adhippetā bhikkhūsu duvidhāpi saṃvijjantīti āha “idha pana dvīhipi kāraṇehi kulaputtāyevā”ti.

Here, showing that the elision of the ‘i’ vowel in “yeme” is due to sandhi, he begins with “ye ime” and so on. Those who are well-born (abhijātā) by way of birth, due to being of high family, are “kulaputtas by birth.” Therefore it is said, “born into high families.” Those who are well-born (abhijātā) by way of accomplishment of conduct are “kulaputtas by conduct.” Therefore it is said, “endowed with good conduct.” Even in an obscure family, wherever it may be. Since both types intended by that brahmin exist among the bhikkhus, he says, “but here, they are indeed kulaputtas for both reasons.”

Saddhāti idaṃ karaṇatthe paccattavacananti āha “saddhāyā”ti, saddhāti vā saddahitvāti attho. Imasmiṃ pakkhe pāḷiyaṃ ya-kāralopena niddesoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Agāratoti agāravāsato, uttarapadalopena, nissayūpacārena vā ayaṃ niddesoti. Bhikkhanasīlatādilakkhaṇo bhikkhubhāvo pabbajjāsahacaritāya saddhiṃ bhikkhubhāvaṃ anvācinantoti āha “pabbajjaṃ bhikkhubhāvañcā”ti. Kammavācālakkhaṇe pana bhikkhubhāve adhippete samuccayattho ca-saddo daṭṭhabbo. Anagārassa bhāvoti etena pabbajjānissito suvisuddho sīlācāraguṇaviseso gahito, kasigorakkhādikammapaṭikkhepo idha anuppādādīhi veditabbo. Sesaggahaṇe pana saraṇagamanādivasena pabbajjāya, saraṇagamanādivasena upasampadāya ca anekabhedattā āha “sabbathāpī”ti, tena tena pakārenāti attho. Puratogāmitā paṭipattigamanena, na kāyagamanenāti āha “nāyako”ti[M 1.0208], sammāpaṭipattiyā nibbānasampāpakoti attho. Hitakiriyāyāti diṭṭhadhammikādihitacariyāya. Gāhaṇaṃ adhisīlādīsu accantāya niyojanaṃ, na kathanamattanti dassento “gāhetā”ti vatvā “sikkhāpetā”ti āha. Diṭṭhānugatinti diṭṭhiyā anugamananti dassento “dassanānugati”nti vatvā sikkhāttayasaṅgahaṃ bhagavato sāsanaṃ tena diṭṭhattā diṭṭhi, tassa tasseva khamanavasena khanti, ruccanavasena ruci, taṃdiṭṭhikhantirucikāva bhagavato sāvakāti āha “yaṃdiṭṭhiko”tiādi.

“Saddhā” (faith): he says this is a word in the instrumental case in the sense of instrument, thus “saddhāya” (by faith), or the meaning is “saddhā” (faith) or “saddahitvā” (having believed). In this case, it should be understood that the designation in the Pāli is by the elision of the ‘ya’ sound. “Agārato” (from the household) means “from household life” (agāravāsato), by elision of the latter word, or this designation is by metonymy based on dependence. The state of being a bhikkhu, characterized by the habit of alms-seeking and so on, implies the state of being a bhikkhu along with the going forth, thus he says, “the going forth and the state of being a bhikkhu.” However, when the state of being a bhikkhu characterized by the formal act is intended, the conjunction ‘ca’ should be understood as having a collective meaning. By “the state of being homeless” (anagārassa bhāvo) is taken the very pure special quality of virtue and conduct dependent on the going forth. Here, the rejection of activities like farming and cattle-tending should be understood by non-arising and so on. However, in the remaining cases, due to the many distinctions of the going forth by way of taking refuge and so on, and of full ordination by way of taking refuge and so on, he says “sabbathāpi” (in every way), meaning “by each respective method.” “Puratogāmitā” (going in front) is by way of going in practice, not by physical going, thus he says “nāyako” (leader), meaning “one who brings about the attainment of Nibbāna through right practice.” “Hitakiriyāya” (for the welfare) means “for conduct beneficial in this life and so on.” “Gāhaṇaṃ” (grasping) is complete commitment in higher virtue and so on, not mere verbal instruction; showing this, having said “gāhetā” (one who instructs), he says “sikkhāpetā” (one who trains). “Diṭṭhānugati” (following what is seen): showing that this is following by means of view, having said “dassanānugati” (following by seeing), he says “yaṃdiṭṭhiko” and so on, because the Blessed One’s teaching, which comprises the threefold training, is “view” (diṭṭhi) because it is seen by him; “patience” (khanti) by way of enduring it; “liking” (ruci) by way of approving it. Thus, the Blessed One’s disciples are those of such view, patience, and liking.

Esa kira alatthāti sambandho. Devaputte viyātiādi kassaci pārijuññassa abhāvadīpanato “saddhāyā”tiādinā vuttassa pabbajitabhāvassa pākaṭīkaraṇaṃ. Saddhāya gharā nikkhamma pabbajitvāti idaṃ haṭṭhapahaṭṭhādibhāvassa kāraṇavacanaṃ. Ghāsacchādanaparamatāya santuṭṭheti idaṃ anussaṅkitāparisaṅkitatāya kāraṇavacananti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The connection is to 'he, it seems, obtained.' By stating 'like a deva-son,' etc., by revealing the absence of any decay, it clarifies the state of having gone forth, as mentioned by 'through faith,' etc. 'Having left home through faith and gone forth'—this is a statement of the reason for his state of joy and delight. 'Being content with mere food and robes'—this should be seen as a statement of the reason for his being free from anxiety and apprehension.

Evametantiādinā āmeḍitavacanaṃ sampahaṃsanavasena, pasādavasena vā katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi evaṃ-saddo sampaṭicchanattho abbhanumodanattho ca vutto. Mamanti upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ, nipātapadaṃ vā etaṃ “ma”nti iminā samānatthanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ādīnīti ādi-saddena najīvikāpakatādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti īdisānaṃyevāti saddhāpabbajjāya vibhāvitaanabhijjhāluādisabhāvānaṃyeva, na itaresaṃ abhijjhālusabhāvānaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

By “Evam etaṃ” and so on, it should be understood that this emphatic statement is made in the manner of rejoicing or appreciation. For the word 'evaṃ' is said to convey the meanings of acceptance and agreement. 'Maṃ ti' is a possessive word in the sense of utility, or it may be regarded as a particle, being synonymous with 'ma.' 'Ādīni ti' includes, through the word 'ādi,' things like not making a living by wrong means, etc., referring only to those of such a nature—namely, those whose nature of non-greed and so on has been made clear by the going forth in faith, and not to others who are by nature greedy. For this has been said—

“Saṅghāṭikaṇṇe [V 1.0186] cepi me, bhikkhave, bhikkhu gahetvā piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandho assa pade padaṃ nikkhipanto, so ca hoti abhijjhālu kāmesu tibbasārāgo byāpannacitto paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappo muṭṭhassati asampajāno asamāhito vibbhantacitto pākaṭindriyo, atha kho ārakāva mama ahañca tassā”ti (itivu. 92).

“Even if, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu were to take hold of the hem of my outer robe and follow closely behind me, placing his foot in my footsteps, yet if he is covetous, with intense passion for sensual pleasures, with a mind full of ill will, with corrupt intentions, unmindful, without clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a deranged mind, and with unrestrained faculties—then he is far from me and I am far from him.”

Ajjhogāhetvā adhippetatthaṃ sambhavituṃ sādhetuṃ dukkhānīti durabhisambhavāni. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana tattha nivāsoyeva dukkhoti dassetuṃ “sambhavituṃ dukkhāni dussahānī”ti vuttaṃ. Araññavanapatthānīti araññalakkhaṇappattāni vanasaṇḍāni. Vanapattha-saddo hi saṇḍabhūte rukkhasamūhepi vattatīti [M 1.0209] araññaggahaṇaṃ. Kiñcāpīti anujānanasambhāvanatthe nipāto. Kiṃ anujānāti? Nippariyāyato araññābhāvaṃ “gāmato bahi arañña”nti. Tenāha “nippariyāyenā”tiādi. Kiṃ sambhāveti? Āraññakaṅganipphādakattaṃ. Yañhi āraññakaṅganipphādakaṃ, taṃ visesato “arañña”nti vuttanti. Tenevāha “yaṃ taṃ pañcadhanusatika”ntiādi. Nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlāti indakhīlato bahi nikkhamitvā, tato bahi paṭṭhāyāti attho. Bahi indakhīlāti yattha dve tīṇi indakhīlāni, tattha bahiddhā indakhīlato paṭṭhāya, yattha taṃ natthi, tattha tadarahaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāyāti vadanti. Yasmā bahi indakhīlato paṭṭhāya manussūpacāre bhayabheravaṃ natthi, tasmā idha nādhippetanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Having plunged into the intended meaning, 'sufferings' means 'difficult to endure.' In the commentary, however, to show that dwelling there itself is suffering, it is said, 'sufferings are unbearable to endure.' 'Forest groves' means forest thickets that possess the characteristics of a wilderness. The term 'vanapattha' applies even to a dense cluster of trees, hence the inclusion of 'wilderness.' 'Kiñcāpi' is a particle in the sense of permission or possibility. What does it permit? The state of being a wilderness without qualification—'outside the village is wilderness.' Therefore, it is said, 'without qualification,' etc. What does it make possible? The fulfilling of the forest-dweller's ascetic practice. For that which fulfills the forest-dweller's ascetic practice is specifically called 'wilderness.' Hence it is said, 'that which is five hundred bow-lengths,' etc. 'Having gone out beyond the boundary post' means having gone outside the boundary post, starting from there outward. 'Beyond the boundary post'—where there are two or three boundary posts, it means starting from outside the outermost boundary post; where there is none, it means starting from a place suitable for that, they say. Since, starting from beyond the boundary post, in the area frequented by humans, there is no fear or terror, it should be understood that this is not intended here.

Gāmantanti gāmasamīpaṃ. Anupacāraṭṭhānanti niccakiccavasena nupacaritabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Tenāha “yattha na kasīyati na vapīyatī”ti. Pantānīti iminā “pariyantāna”nti imassa pariyāyassa idha pāḷiyaṃ gahitattā vuttaṃ “pariyantānanti imamekaṃ pariyāyaṃ ṭhapetvā”ti. Dūrānanti pana ayaṃ pariyāyo ṭhapetabbo siyā tassāpi “pantānī”ti imināva atthato gahitattā, tathā sati “na manussūpacārāna”nti edisānampi ṭhapetabbatā āpajjati, tasmā saddato eva ṭhapanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pavivekanti pakārato, pakārehi vā vivecanaṃ, rūpādiputhuttārammaṇe pakārato gamanādiiriyāpathappakārehi attano kāyassa vivecanaṃ gacchatopi tiṭṭhatopi nisajjatopi ekasseva pavattati. Teneva hi vivecetabbānaṃ vivecanākārassa ca bhedato bahuvidhattā te ekattena gahetvā “paviveka”nti ekavacanena vuttaṃ. Dukkaraṃ pavivekanti vā pavivekaṃ kattuṃ na sukhanti attho. Ekībhāveti ekikabhāve. Dvayaṃdvayārāmoti dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ bhāvābhirato. Haranti viyāti saṃharanti viya vighātuppādanena. Tenāha “ghasanti viyā”ti, bhayasantāsuppādanena khādituṃ āgatā yakkharakkhasapisācādayo viyāti adhippāyo. Īdisassāti aladdhasamādhino. Tiṇapaṇṇamigādisaddehīti vāteritānaṃ tiṇapaṇṇādīnaṃ migapakkhiādīnañca [V 1.0187] bhiṃsanakehi bheravehi saddehi vividhehi ca aññehi khāṇuādīhi yakkhādiākārehi upaṭṭhitehi bhiṃsanakehi. Evaṃ dukkaraṃ durabhisambhavaṃ nāma karonto aho acchariyā eteti vimhito.

'Gāmanta' means the vicinity of a village. 'Anupacāraṭṭhāna' refers to a place that should not be frequented for daily duties. Hence it is said, 'where there is no plowing or sowing.' Regarding 'Pantāni': by this, since its synonym 'pariyantāna' is taken here in the Pāli, it is said, 'having excluded this one synonym, "pariyantāna".' Furthermore, this synonym 'Dūrāna' should be excluded, as its meaning is already conveyed by 'pantāni.' If this were so, the exclusion of such phrases as 'not frequented by people' would also follow. Therefore, the exclusion should be understood as being by word alone. 'Seclusion' means separation by way of mode, or by means of modes: the separation of one's own body from various sensory objects like forms, etc., through modes of posture such as walking. This occurs for one who is alone, whether walking, standing, or sitting. Indeed, because the things to be secluded from and the ways of seclusion are manifold due to their differences, they are taken as one and referred to with the singular term 'seclusion.' Alternatively, 'seclusion is difficult' means it is not easy to achieve seclusion. 'Ekībhāve' means in the state of being alone. 'Dvayaṃdvayārāmo' means one who delights in the state of being in pairs. 'As if they carry away' means as if they destroy by causing trouble. Hence it is said, 'as if they devour'; the intention is: like yakkhas, rākkhasas, pisācas, and so on, who have come to devour by causing fear and terror. 'Of such a one' means of one who has not attained concentration. 'By the sounds of grass, leaves, animals, etc.' means by the frightening and terrifying sounds of grass, leaves, and so on, stirred by the wind, and of animals, birds, and so on, and by various other frightening things that appear, such as stumps in the form of yakkhas. Thus, performing what is difficult and hard to accomplish, he was amazed, thinking, 'Oh, how astonishing this is!'

Kāyakammantavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Section of Bodily Action

35. Soḷasasu [M 1.0210] ṭhānesūti “ye kho kecī”tiādinā pāḷiyaṃ vakkhamānesu soḷasasu kāraṇesu. Aparisuddhakāyakammantatādayo araññe viharantānaṃ cittutrāsanimittatāya visesato vikkhepāvahā, parisuddhakāyakammantatādayo pana tadabhāvato tesaṃ avikkhepāvahā. Tenāha “aparisuddhakāyakammantasandosahetū”tiādi. Soḷasasūti ca vodānapakkhaṃyeva gahetvā vuttaṃ. Saṃkilesaggahaṇampi yāvadeva vodānadassanatthanti. Ārammaṇapariggaharahitānanti aparisuddhakāyakammantādikassa araññe diṭṭhassa tassa ārammaṇassa “ye kho kecī”tiādinā pāḷiyaṃ āgatanayena pariggaṇhanañāṇarahitānaṃ. Ārammaṇapariggahayuttānanti ettha vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo. Attanāti bhagavantaṃ sandhāya vadati, sayanti attho. Tādisoti ārammaṇapariggahayutto.

35. 'In sixteen places,' refers to the sixteen causes to be spoken of in the Pāli passage beginning with 'ye kho keci.' Impure bodily conduct and the like are especially conducive to distraction for those dwelling in the forest, as they are a sign of mental agitation, while pure bodily conduct and the like, due to the absence of that, are conducive to non-distraction for them. Hence it is said, 'due to the cause of the fault of impure bodily conduct,' and so on. The phrase 'in sixteen' is stated taking only the side of purification into account. The inclusion of defilements is merely for the purpose of showing purification. 'Devoid of apprehending the object' means of those who lack the knowledge to apprehend that object seen in the forest—such as impure bodily conduct and the like—in the manner that has come in the Pāli passage beginning with 'ye kho keci.' 'Connected with apprehending the object' should be understood here with the opposite meaning of what was stated. 'By himself' is said referring to the Blessed One; the meaning is 'oneself.' 'Such a one' means one connected with apprehending the object.

Sambujjhati etenāti sambodho, ariyamaggoti āha “ariyamaggappattito”ti. Aggamaggādhigamādhīno buddhānaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇādhigamoti āha “anabhisambuddhassāti appaṭividdhacatusaccassā”ti. Anavasesato ñeyyaṃ, bujjhituṃ arahatīti bodhi, mahāvīriyatādinā tattha visesayogato sattoti āha “bujjhanakasattassā”ti. Tenāha “sammāsambodhi”ntiādi. Niyatabhāvappattito paṭṭhāya mahāsattā yathā mahābodhiyānapaṭipadā hānabhāgiyā, ṭhitibhāgiyā vā na hoti, atha kho visesabhāgiyā nibbedhabhāgiyā ca hoti, tathā paṭipajjanato bodhiyaṃ ninnagoṇapabbhārā evāti āha “bodhiyā vā sattasseva laggassevā”ti. Tenāha “dīpaṅkarassa hī”tiādi. Aṭṭhadhammasamodhānenāti –

One fully awakens by this, thus it is 'full awakening' (sambodho); this is the noble path, he says, 'because of the attainment of the noble path.' The attainment of the omniscient knowledge of the Buddhas is dependent on the attainment of the supreme path; therefore, he says, 'of one who is not fully awakened' means 'of one who has not penetrated the four truths.' 'Enlightenment' (bodhi) is that which is worthy of being understood, the knowable without remainder. A 'being' (satta) is so called because of a special connection to that through great effort and so on; therefore, he says, 'of a being capable of understanding.' Hence he says, 'perfect full awakening,' and so on. Beginning from the attainment of a fixed state, because great beings practice in such a way that the great practice of the vehicle to enlightenment is not subject to decline or stagnation, but is rather conducive to progress and penetration, they are indeed inclined, sloping, and bent towards enlightenment. Therefore, he says, 'or of a being attached, clinging to enlightenment.' Hence he says, 'Indeed, of Dīpaṅkara,' and so on. 'By the combination of eight qualities' means—

“Manussattaṃ liṅgasampatti, hetu satthāradassanaṃ;

Pabbajjā guṇasampatti, adhikāro ca chandatā”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.59) –

“Human existence, perfection of gender, the cause, seeing the Teacher; going forth, perfection of qualities, meritorious service, and aspiration.” (Bu. Va. 2.59)

Imesaṃ abhinīhārassa aṅgabhūtānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ dhammānaṃ samodhānena samavadhānena.

By the combination and conjunction of these eight qualities, which are constituent parts of the great aspiration.

Pabbajjūpagatāti [V 1.0188][M 1.0211] pabbajjaṃ upagatā. Tena pabbajjāmattena samaṇā, na samitapāpatāyāti dasseti. Jātimattena idha brāhmaṇāti adhippetāti āha “bhovādino vā”ti. Te hi “bho bho”ti vadanasīlā, tenāha “bhovādī nāma so hoti, sace hoti sakiñcano”ti (dha. pa. 396; su. ni. 625). Pāṇātipātādināti ādi-saddena adinnādānaṃ abrahmacariyañca saṅgaṇhāti. Aparisuddhenāti ca visesanaṃ kāyakammantāpekkhāya, na pāṇātipātādiapekkhāya. Na hi pāṇātipātādiko tassa pubbabhāgapayogo ca koci parisuddho nāma atthi. Bhāyanaṭṭhena bhayaṃ, bhīrutāvahaṭṭhena bheravaṃ. Sandosahetūti sadosahetu. Sa-saddo hi idha sānusāro vutto. Tenāha “attano dosassa hetū”ti. Ekantena cittutrāsalakkhaṇassa bhayassa vasena “sāvajja”nti vuttaṃ. Cittutrāso hi ekantasāvajjo bhāyanaṭṭhena bhayañcāti. Akkhemanti idaṃ ubhayavasena. Cittutrāsopi hi sarīracittānaṃ anatthāvahato akkhema, tathā bhayānakārammaṇampīti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana atthadvayaṃ yathāsaṅkhyaṃ yojitaṃ. Sayaṃ parikappitabhayānakārammaṇanimittaṃ cittutrāsasamuppādanavasena ānentā bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti viya hontīti vuttaṃ “avhāyantīti pakkosantī”ti. Teti māritamanussānaṃ ñātimittādayo. Gacchaṃ gahanabhūtaṃ mahantaṃ kaṇṭakasaṇḍaṃ, gumbaṃ nātimahantanti vadanti. Gacchanti pana tiṇavanaṃ veditabbaṃ, “gacche ruḷhatiṇe”ti vuttaṃ, gumbaṃ kaṇṭakalatādibharitāviruḷhaṃ. Baddhā vadhitā viyāti baddhā hutvā tāḷiyamānā viya.

'Pabbajjūpagatā' means those who have gone forth. This shows that they are ascetics merely by having gone forth, not because they have quelled evil. Here, 'brahmins' is intended to mean those who are so by mere birth; thus it is said, 'or those who say "bho".' For they are accustomed to saying 'bho, bho'; hence it is said, 'He is called a "bhovādī" if he has defilements.' By 'killing, etc.' (pāṇātipātādinā), the word 'etc.' includes taking what is not given and unchastity. The qualification 'unpurified' (aparisuddhena) is with reference to bodily action, not to killing, etc. For no killing, etc., nor any preliminary act for it, is ever called purified. 'Fear' (bhaya) is so in the sense of frightening; 'terror' (bherava) is so in the sense of bringing cowardice. 'A cause with fault' (sandosahetu) means a cause that has a fault (sadosahetu). Here, the word 'sa' is spoken with an anusvāra. Hence it is said, 'a cause of one's own fault.' It is called 'blameworthy' (sāvajja) because of fear, which is characterized entirely by mental agitation. For mental agitation is entirely blameworthy, and it is fear in the sense of frightening. 'Unsafe' (akkhema) applies in a twofold way: mental agitation is unsafe because it brings harm to body and mind, and so too is a terrifying object. In the commentary, however, the two meanings are applied respectively. By bringing on mental agitation through a self-conceived sign of a terrifying object, they are as if summoning fear and terror; thus it is said, 'they summon' means 'they call forth.' 'They' (te) refers to the relatives, friends, and so on, of the people who were killed. They say that a 'thicket' (gaccha) is a large, dense thorn-thicket, and a 'bush' (gumba) is not very large. However, a 'gaccha' should be understood as a grass-wood, as it is said, 'in a thicket of grown grass,' and a 'gumba' as overgrown and filled with thorns, creepers, and so on. 'As if bound and struck' (baddhā vadhitā viya) means as if, having been bound, they were being beaten.

“Na kho panāti ettha khoti avadhāraṇatthe nipāto, panā”ti visesatthe. Tenetaṃ dasseti “aññe samaṇabrāhmaṇā viya ahaṃ aparisuddhakāyakammanto hutvā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni na kho pana paṭisevāmi, parisuddhakāyakammantoyeva pana hutvā tāni paṭisevāmī”ti. Evaṃ vā ettha atthayojanā veditabbā. “Parisuddhakāyakammantohamasmī”ti hi tena avadhāraṇena vibhāvitatthadassanaṃ. Tesamahaṃ aññataroti tāya parisuddhakāyakammatāya tesaṃ ariyānaṃ ahaṃ aññataroti kāyakammapārisuddhiyā mahāsatto attānaṃ ariyesu pakkhipati. Paramasallekhabhāvappattā hi tadā bodhisattassa kāyakammapārisuddhi[M 1.0212], tathā vacīkammādipārisuddhi, yato māro randhagavesī hutvā chabbassāni nirantaraṃ anubandho antaraṃ na labhati. Tenāha –

In 'Na kho pana,' the particle 'kho' is used in the sense of emphasis, and 'pana' in the sense of distinction. Thus, this shows: 'Unlike other ascetics and brahmins, I do not (kho) frequent remote forest and woodland thickets and secluded lodgings with unpurified bodily conduct; but (pana) with purified bodily conduct, I do frequent them.' Or, the connection of meaning here should be understood in this way. For by that emphasis, the meaning is shown to be clearly: 'I am one whose bodily conduct is purified.' 'Among them, I am one': by that purity of bodily conduct, the Great Being includes himself among those Noble Ones. At that time, the Bodhisatta’s purity of bodily action had reached the highest state of effacement, as had the purity of verbal action and so on, to the extent that Māra, seeking a vulnerability, followed him continuously for six years without finding an opportunity. Therefore, it is said:

“Satta vassāni bhagavantaṃ, anubandhiṃ padāpadaṃ;

Otāraṃ nādhigacchissaṃ, sambuddhassa satīmato”ti. (su. ni. 448);

“For seven years I followed the Blessed One, step by step; yet I could not find an opening in the mindful, Fully Awakened One.”

Bhiyyoti [V 1.0189] adhikaṃ savisesaṃ, uparūpari vā. Bhītatasitā bhayūpaddavena chambhitasarīrā haṭṭhalomā honti, abhītātasitā pana bhayūpaddavābhāvato ahaṭṭhalomā khemena sotthinā tiṭṭhantīti tesaṃ khemappatti sotthibhāvo vā pannalomatāya pākaṭo hotīti pāḷiyaṃ “palloma”nti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “pannalomata”ntiādi. Ettha ca bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāyāti paṭiññāniddeso. Parisuddhakāyakammantohamasmīti hetudassanaṃ. “Ye hi vo ariyā”ti sadisūdāharaṇadassanaṃ. Ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vāti visadisūdāharaṇadassanaṃ. Sesāni anvayabyatirekavibhāvanānīti daṭṭhabbanti ayamettha yuttivibhāvanā. Iminā nayena sesavāresupi yuttivibhāvanā veditabbā.

“Bhiyyo” means exceeding, superior, or further and further. Those who are frightened and terrified, their bodies stiffened by fear and danger, have their hair standing on end; but those who are fearless and unafraid, because of the absence of fear and danger, have their hair lying flat and remain safe and secure. Thus, their attainment of safety and well-being is evident through their hair lying flat—this is called “palloma” in the Pāli text. Hence, it is said, “pannalomata,” and so on. Here, “bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya” is the declaration of the undertaking to dwell in the forest. The statement, “I am one whose bodily conduct is perfectly pure,” shows the reason. The phrase, “Ye hi vo ariyā,” shows a similar example. The phrase, “Ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā,” shows a dissimilar example. The rest should be regarded as illustrating presence and absence; this is the analysis of the method here. In this way, the analysis of the method should be understood in the remaining instances as well.

Kāyakammantavārakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on bodily conduct is completed.

Vacīkammantavārādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discussion on the Section on Verbal Conduct and So Forth

36. Aparisuddhena musāvādādināti ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Ādi-saddena pana saṅgahitaṃ tesañca musāvādādīnaṃ pavattibhedaṃ bhayabheravāvhānamukhena dassetuṃ “katha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

36. Regarding the phrase 'by impure false speech and so forth' (aparisuddhena musāvādādinā), what is to be said here is in the same manner as stated previously. However, to show the various modes of occurrence of that false speech and so forth, which are included by the word 'and so forth,' by way of invoking fear and terror, the phrase 'how' (kathaṃ) and so forth is stated. What is to be said in that connection has already been stated previously.

Bhaṇḍesūti saviññāṇakāviññāṇakesu bhaṇḍesu. Uppādetvāti attano pariṇāmavasena abhijjhāsaṅkhātaṃ visamalobhaṃ uppādetvā. Kujjhitvāti vināsacintāvasena parassa kujjhitvā. Evañhi nesaṃ “yesaṃ aparajjhimhā, te idāni anubandhitvā”tiādinā pacchā āsaṅkuppatti siyā. “Ete amhākaṃ pariggahavatthuṃ gahetukāmā maññe, vināsaṃ kātukāmā maññe”ti yathā pare parato tesaṃ abhijjhābyāpādappavattiṃ pariggaṇhanti, tādisaṃ [M 1.0213] manokammantaṃ sandhāya “te paresa”ntiādi vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kāmaṃ akusalakāyakammavacīkammapavattikālepi abhijjhādayo pavattantiyeva, tadā pana te cetanāpakkhikā vā abbohārikā vāti manokammantavāre eva abhijjhādivasena yojanā katā. Atha vā dvārantare pavattānampi pāṇātipātādīnaṃ vacīkammādibhāvābhāvo viya dvārantare pavattānampi abhijjhādīnaṃ kāyakammādibhāvābhāvo, manokammabhāvo eva pana siddhoti katvā manokammantavāre eva abhijjhādayo uddhaṭā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

The phrase 'in goods' (bhaṇḍesu) refers to goods with consciousness and without consciousness. The phrase 'having aroused' (uppādetvā) means having aroused unrighteous greed, which is called covetousness, through one's own disposition. The phrase 'having become angry' (kujjhitvā) means having become angry with another through thoughts of destruction. For thus, their subsequent anxiety might arise with thoughts like, 'Those whom we wronged, now they pursue us,' and so on. 'These, it seems, wish to take what belongs to us; it seems they wish to destroy us'—it should be understood that the phrase 'they... of others' (te paresaṃ) and so forth is stated with reference to such a mental action that others perceive in them the arising of covetousness and ill will. Although during the arising of unwholesome bodily and verbal actions, covetousness and the like still arise, at that time they are either secondary to volition or are not conventionally designated as such; thus, the classification by way of covetousness and so on is made specifically in the section on mental action. Alternatively, just as killing living beings and so forth, which occur through other doors, are not verbal actions and so forth, so too covetousness and so forth, which occur through other doors, are not bodily actions and so forth—but their nature as mental action is indeed established. Therefore, covetousness and the like are set forth specifically in the section on mental action. For thus it is said—

“Dvāre [V 1.0190] caranti kammāni, na dvārā dvāracārino;

Tasmā dvārehi kammāni, aññamaññaṃ vavatthitā”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1.kāyakammadvāra);

“Actions proceed at the doors, the doors are not the agents; therefore, actions are distinguished from each other by means of the doors.”

Kiñcāpi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ sāsane pabbajitavasena ājīvavāre bhayabheravāvhānaṃ yojitaṃ, “ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā”ti pana vacanato bāhirakavasena gahaṭṭhavasena ca yojanā veditabbā. Gahaṭṭhānampi hi jātidhammakuladhammadesadhammavilomanavasena aññathāpi micchājīvo labbhateva, tāya eva ca ājīvavipattiyā aññathā vā nesaṃ araññavāso sambhaveyyāti.

Although in the commentary, the invoking of fear and terror is applied in the section on livelihood with reference to those who have gone forth into the Dispensation, from the statement 'whatever recluses or brahmins,' it should be understood that the application is also to outsiders and to householders. For even householders can indeed engage in wrong livelihood by contravening the customs of birth, family, or region; and because of just such failure in livelihood, or for other reasons, their dwelling in the forest might become possible.

37. Evaṃ ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlavasena bhayabheravaṃ dassetvā tato paraṃ nīvaraṇappahānādivasena taṃ dassetuṃ desanā vaḍḍhitāti tadatthaṃ vivaranto “ito para”ntiādimāha. Tattha nīvaraṇavasena puna vuttāti ayamadhippāyo – evaṃ sīlavisuddhimattampi araññe viharato bhayabheravābhāvaṃ āvahati, kimaṅgaṃ pana nīvaraṇāni pahāya appanāsamādhiṃ, upacārasamādhimeva vā sampādayatoti samādhisampadāya bhayabheravābhāvahetukaṃ dassetuṃ upari desanā vaḍḍhitāti akusalamanokammantabhāvena gahitāpi abhijjhābyāpādā nīvaraṇavasena puna vuttāti adhippāyo. Abhi-pubbo jhā-saddo abhijjhāyanatthoti āha “parabhaṇḍādiabhijjhāyanasīlā”ti. Vatthukāmesūti rūpādīsu kilesakāmassa vatthubhūtesu kāmesu. Bahalakilesarāgāti thiramūladummocanīyatāhi ajjhosāne pabhūtakilesakāmā. Abhijjhā cettha appattavisayapatthanā, tibbasārāgo sampattivisayābhiniveso. Te [M 1.0214] hi lobhābhibhūtā puggalā attani tibbasāpekkhatāya eva lobhābhibhūtatāya avavatthitārammaṇā avinicchitavisayā araññe taṃ taṃ visayaṃ anupadhāritvā viharanti, rajjuādīni yāthāvato na sallakkhenti. Tenāha “tesa”ntiādi. Upaṭṭhāti santacittatāya. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “ākulacittā”ti. “Idānimha naṭṭhā”ti tasanti vitasanti, āgantvā bādhiyamānā viya honti, evaṃ taṃ bhayabheravaṃ attani samāropanaṭṭhena avhāyanti pakkosantīti yojanaṃ sandhāyāha “sesaṃ tādisamevā”ti. “Anabhijjhāluhamasmī”ti pāḷipade ciraparicitaalobhajjhāsayatāya kamaladale jalabindu viya alaggamānasattā sabbattha anapekkhohamasmīti attho.

37. Having thus shown fear and terror by way of the virtue with livelihood as the eighth, the teaching is then expanded to show it by way of the abandonment of hindrances and so forth. Explaining that meaning, he says 'from here onwards' (ito paraṃ) and so forth. Here, the intention is that they are repeated by way of the hindrances: even mere purity of virtue brings about the absence of fear and terror for one dwelling in the forest; how much more so, then, for one who has abandoned the hindrances and accomplished absorption concentration or even access concentration? Thus, to show that the absence of fear and terror is caused by the accomplishment of concentration, the teaching is expanded further on. This is the intention: even though covetousness and ill will are included as unwholesome mental actions, they are repeated by way of the hindrances. He says that the word 'jhā' preceded by 'abhi-' has the meaning of 'coveting,' hence it is said, 'those whose nature is to covet others' possessions and so forth' (parabhaṇḍādiabhijjhāyanasīlā). The phrase 'in sensual objects' (vatthukāmesu) refers to sensual objects such as forms, which are the basis of defilement-sensuality. The phrase 'with abundant defilement-lust' (bahalakilesarāgā) refers to those with profuse defilement-sensuality due to an attachment that is firm-rooted and difficult to release. Here, covetousness is the longing for what is not attained, while intense greed is the fixation on what is attained. For such individuals, overwhelmed by greed, dwell in the forest with unsettled objects and undetermined aims, due to their intense attachment to themselves and their being overwhelmed by greed; they do not investigate this or that object, nor do they perceive things like ropes as they truly are. Hence he says 'for them' (tesaṃ) and so forth. The phrase 'arises' (upaṭṭhāti) is due to an unpeaceful mind. As it is said, 'with agitated minds' (ākulacittā). 'Now we are lost'—they tremble and panic, feeling as if they are being attacked upon arrival. Thus, they summon and call forth that fear and terror by imposing it upon themselves. With reference to this application, he says, 'the rest is similar' (sesaṃ tādisameva). The meaning of the Pāli phrase 'I am not covetous' (anabhijjhāluhamasmi) is that, due to a long-familiar disposition of non-greed, one's mind does not cling anywhere, like a water drop on a lotus leaf, and thus 'I am unattached everywhere.'

38. Pakatibhāvavijahanenāti parisuddhabhāvasaṅkhātassa ca pakatibhāvassa vijahanena. Sāvajjadhammasamuppattiyā hi cittassa anavajjabhāvo jahito hotīti. Vipannacittāti kilesāsucidūsitatāya [V 1.0191] kuthitacittā. Tenāha “kilesānugataṃ…pe… pūtikaṃ hotī”ti. Paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappāti visasaṃsaṭṭhamuttaṃ viya dosena padūsitacittasaṅkappā. Vuttanayenevāti “te avavatthitārammaṇā hontī”tiādinā abhijjhāluvāre vuttanayeneva. Yathā hi lobhavasena, evaṃ dosādivasenapi avavatthitārammaṇā hontīti. Sabbatthāti heṭṭhā upari cāti sabbattha ṭhānesu vaṇṇetabbā.

38. The phrase 'by abandoning the natural state' (pakatibhāvavijahanena) means by abandoning the natural state, which is designated as the pure state. For with the arising of blameworthy states, the mind's blameless nature is indeed lost. The phrase 'with a corrupted mind' (vipannacittā) refers to a mind festering and tainted by the impurity of defilements. Hence he says, 'overcome by defilements... it becomes putrid' (kilesānugataṃ...pe... pūtikaṃ hoti). The phrase 'with corrupt mental intentions' (paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappā) refers to mental intentions corrupted by aversion, like urine mixed with poison. The phrase 'in the way previously stated' (vuttanayeneva) refers to the way stated in the section on the covetous one, with 'they are unsteady in their objects' (te avavatthitārammaṇā honti) and so forth. For just as it is through the power of greed, so too through the power of aversion and other states—they are unsteady in their objects. The phrase 'everywhere' (sabbattha) means below and above—thus it should be described in all places.

39. “Yā cittassa akallatā akammaññatā”ti vacanato thinaṃ cittassa gelaññabhāvena gahaṇaṃ gacchatīti āha “cittagelaññabhūtena thinenā”ti. Tathā “yā kāyassa akallatā akammaññatā”ti (dha. sa. 1163) vacanato middhaṃ visesato nāmakāyassa gelaññabhāvena gahaṇaṃ gacchatīti āha “sesanāmakāyagelaññabhūtena middhenā”ti. Sesaggahaṇañcettha cittanivattanatthaṃ. Idañca middhaṃ rūpakāyassapi gelaññāvahanti daṭṭhabbaṃ niddāya hetubhāvato. Tathā hi taṃ “niddā capalāyikā”ti niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tenāha “te niddābahulā hontī”ti.

39. From the statement 'the unfitness and unworkability of the mind' (yā cittassa akallatā akammaññatā), it is understood that sloth is taken as the sickness of the mind; hence he says, 'with sloth, which is the sickness of the mind' (cittagelaññabhūtena thinena). Similarly, from the statement 'the unfitness and unworkability of the body' (yā kāyassa akallatā akammaññatā), it is understood that torpor is taken as particularly the sickness of the mental body; hence he says, 'with torpor, which is the sickness of the remaining mental body' (sesanāmakāyagelaññabhūtena middhena). Here, the inclusion of 'remaining' is to exclude the mind. And this torpor should also be seen as bringing about sickness in the physical body because it is a condition for sleep. For thus it is indicated as 'sleep, the fickle one' (niddā capalāyikā). Therefore, he says, 'they are full of sleep' (te niddābahulā honti).

40. Uddhaccapakatikāti uddhaccasīlā anavaṭṭhitasabhāvā. Anavaṭṭhānarasañhi uddhaccaṃ. Tenāha “vipphandamānacittā”tiādi. Idhāti “avūpasantacittā”ti imasmiṃ [M 1.0215] pade. Kukkuccaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭati saṃvaṇṇanāvasena pacchānutāpassapi cittassa avūpasamakarattā. Uddhaccaṃ pana sarūpeneva gahitanti adhippāyo.

40. The phrase 'prone to restlessness' (uddhaccapakatikā) refers to those who are habitually restless, unstable in nature. For restlessness has the characteristic of instability. Hence he says, 'with agitated minds' (vipphandamānacittā) and so forth. Here, in this phrase 'with uncalmed minds' (avūpasantacittā), it is fitting to include remorse by way of description, since regret also causes the mind to be uncalmed. But the intention is that restlessness is taken here in its own specific sense.

41. Ekamevidaṃ pañcamaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ kaṅkhā vicikicchāti ca. Yadi evaṃ kasmā dvidhā katvā vuttanti āha “kiṃ nu kho”tiādi. Kaṅkhanatoti saṃsayanato. Vicikicchāti vuccati “dhammasabhāvaṃ vicinanto etāya kicchati, vigatā tikicchā vā”ti katvā.

41. This fifth hindrance, namely doubt (kaṅkhā) and uncertainty (vicikicchā), is a single thing. If so, why is it stated as two? He says, 'What now?' (kiṃ nu kho) and so forth. The phrase 'from doubting' (kaṅkhanato) means from being in suspense. Uncertainty (vicikicchā) is so called because 'one struggles with it while investigating the nature of phenomena,' or because 'a cure is lacking' (vigatā tikicchā).

42. Evaṃ nīvaraṇābhāvakittanamukhena samādhisampadāya bhayabheravābhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni attukkaṃsanādiabhāvakittanamukhena paññāsampadāya bhayabheravābhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “ye kho kecī”tiādinā upari desanā vaḍḍhitā, tadatthaṃ vivarituṃ “attukkaṃsanakā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ukkaṃsenti mānavasena paggaṇhanena. Tenāha “ucce ṭhāne ṭhapentī”ti. Thinamiddhauddhaccakukkuccavicikicchāvāresu gayhamānaṃ abhijjhāluvārasadisanti tattha taṃ anāmasitvā attukkaṃsakavāre kiñci visadisaṃ atthīti taṃ dassetuṃ “te katha”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

42. Having thus shown the absence of fear and terror through the perfection of concentration by praising the absence of the hindrances, now, to show the absence of fear and terror through the perfection of wisdom by praising the absence of self-exaltation and so forth, the teaching above is expanded with 'whatever recluses or brahmins' (ye kho keci) and so forth. To explain its meaning, the phrase 'self-exalting' (attukkaṃsanakā) and so forth is stated. They exalt themselves by grasping through conceit. Hence he says, 'they place themselves in a high position' (ucce ṭhāne ṭhapenti). What is grasped in the chapters on sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt, is similar to the chapter on covetousness. Without mentioning that, to show that there is something somewhat different in the chapter on self-exaltation, the phrase 'how then' (te kathaṃ) and so forth is stated.

43. Chambhanaṃ [V 1.0192] chambho, kāyassa chambhitattahetubhūto balavacittutrāso. So etesaṃ atthīti chambhī. Tenāha “kāyathambhanā”tiādi. Bhīrukajātikāti bhāyanakasīlā. Ekameva cetaṃ sāvajjabhayaṃ kāye chambhitattassa, citte ca kāye ca thaddhabhāvassa uppādanavasena “chambho bhīrutā”ti ca vuccatīti taṃsamaṅgino samaṇabrāhmaṇā “chambhī bhīrukajātikā”ti vuttā, idha bhayabheravaṃ sarūpeneva gahitaṃ.

43. Trembling (chambhanaṃ) is terror (chambho), a strong mental fear that is the cause of the body's trembling. Those who have this are called 'terrified' (chambhī). Hence he says, 'bodily paralysis' (kāyathambhanā) and so forth. The phrase 'timid by nature' (bhīrukajātikā) refers to those whose nature is to be fearful. And this single blameworthy fear is called both 'terror' (chambho) and 'timidity' (bhīrutā) because it causes trembling in the body and rigidity in both mind and body. Thus, those recluses and brahmins who possess this are called 'terrified and timid by nature' (chambhī bhīrukajātikā). Here, fear and terror are taken in their own form.

44. Labbhati pāpuṇīyatīti lābhasaddassa kammasādhanattamāha. Sakkaccaṃ kātabbo dātabboti sakkāro. Tadatthadīpakanti lābhādiṃ pahāya araññe vasato bhayabheravāvhāyanaṃ natthīti dīpakaṃ. So kira lābhagarutāyeva piyo gāmo etassāti “piyagāmiko”ti nāmaṃ labhati. Kammamuttoti jarājiṇṇattā kammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkotīti sāmikehi vissaṭṭho.

44. He states that the word 'gain' (lābha) is derived in the objective sense, because it is what is obtained (labbhati) or attained (pāpuṇīyati). The word 'respect' (sakkāro) means what should be done or given respectfully. The phrase 'elucidating that meaning' (tadatthadīpakaṃ) is an elucidation that for one dwelling in the forest, having abandoned gains and so forth, there is no instigation of fear or terror. Indeed, he obtains the name 'one who loves the village' (piyagāmiko) because the village is dear to him due to his attachment to gain. The phrase 'released from work' (kammamutto) means released by his owners because, being old and frail, he is unable to do work.

45. Alasabhāvena [M 1.0216] sammāvāyāmassa akaraṇato kucchitaṃ sīdantīti kusītā. Vīrassa bhāvo, kammaṃ vā vīriyaṃ, vidhinā vā īretabbaṃ pavattetabbanti vīriyaṃ, sammāvāyāmo. Tena hīnā hīnavīriyā. Kāyaviññattiyā samuṭṭhānavasena pavattavīriyaṃ kāyikavīriyaṃ, vattakaraṇacaṅkamanādīsu daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nisajja sayitvā ca kammaṭṭhānamanasikāravasena pavattavīriyaṃ cetasikavīriyaṃ. Tattha purimaṃ visesato kosajjapaṭipakkhatāvasena, dutiyaṃ vīriyārambhatāvasena pākaṭaṃ hotīti dassento “kusītā”tiādimāha. Te hi hīnavīriyā alasatāyeva ārammaṇavavatthānamattampi kātuṃ na sakkonti.

45. ‘Lazy’ (kusītā) refers to those who sink into wretchedness due to laziness, from not making right effort. ‘Energy’ (vīriya) means the state of a hero or the act of exertion, or what should be stirred up and set in motion according to method; it is right effort. Those deficient in that are ‘of low energy’ (hīnavīriyā). Bodily energy (kāyikavīriya) is the energy that arises through physical manifestation, to be seen in the performance of duties, walking, and so forth. Mental energy (cetasikavīriya) is the energy that arises by way of attending to meditation subjects while sitting or lying down. Here, showing that the former is particularly evident as the opponent to laziness, while the latter is evident as the initiation of effort, he says ‘lazy’ (kusītā) and so forth. For those of low energy, due to laziness, cannot even undertake the mere defining of an object.

46. Naṭṭhassatīti alabbhamānassati, paccayavekallena vijjamānāyapi satiyā satikiccaṃ kātuṃ asamatthatāya evaṃ vuttaṃ. Na sampajānāti asampajānā. Taṃyoganivattiyañcāyaṃ a-kāro “ahetukā dhammā (dha. sa. 2.dukamātikā), abhikkhuko āvāso”tiādīsu (cūḷava. 76) viyāti āha “paññārahitā”ti. Nanu soḷasamo paññāvāro, ayaṃ sativāro, tattha kasmā saṃkilesapakkhe paññā gahitāti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “imassa cā”tiādi. Satibhājanīyamevetaṃ, yadidaṃ cuddasamo vāro, paññā panettha cuddasame vāre kevalā sati dubbalāti satidubbalyadīpanatthaṃ “asampajānā”ti paṭikkhepamukhena vuttā. Idāni vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “duvidhā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

46. ‘With lost mindfulness’ (naṭṭhassati) means with mindfulness not being obtained—even when mindfulness is present, due to a lack of requisites, one is unable to perform the function of mindfulness; hence, it is said thus. ‘Not clearly comprehending’ (asampajānā) means one who does not clearly comprehend. The ‘a-’ here negates the association, as in ‘rootless phenomena’ (ahetukā dhammā) or ‘a dwelling without monks’ (abhikkhuko āvāso), etc. Hence, he says, ‘devoid of wisdom’ (paññārahitā). Now, the sixteenth section is on wisdom, while this is the section on mindfulness—why then is wisdom included on the side of defilements? To address this objection, it is said, ‘And of this…’ (imassa cā) etc. This, namely the fourteenth section, pertains to mindfulness. Here in this fourteenth section, wisdom is mentioned by way of negation as ‘not clearly comprehending’ (asampajānā) to highlight the weakness of mindfulness, for mere mindfulness is weak. Now, to make the stated meaning clearer, it is said, ‘For there are two kinds…’ (duvidhā hī) etc.

47. Appanāsamādhinā, upacārasamādhinā vā cittaṃ ārammaṇe samaṃ, sammā vā āhitaṃ nāma hoti, nāññathāti dassento “asamāhitāti upacārappanāsamādhivirahitā”ti āha[V 1.0193]. Vibbhantacittāti anavaṭṭhitacittā. Pubbe nīvaraṇabhāvasāmaññena uddhaccaṃ gahitaṃ “uddhatā avūpasantacittā”ti, idha samādhānābhāvena uddhaccahetuko cittavibbhamo vutto “asamāhitā vibbhantacittā”ti, ayametesaṃ viseso. Pubbe vuttanayenāti pubbe “uddhaccena hi ekārammaṇe cittaṃ vipphandati dhajayaṭṭhiyaṃ vātena paṭākā viyā”ti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.40) vuttanayena. Sabbaṃ pubbasadisamevāti bhayabheravāvhāyanassa abhijjhāluvāre vuttasadisataṃ sandhāya vadati.

47. To show that the mind is properly fixed on its object only when it is either in absorption concentration or access concentration, and not otherwise, it is said: ‘unconcentrated’ (asamāhitā) means devoid of access and absorption concentration. ‘With wandering mind’ (vibbhantacittā) means with an unsteady mind. Previously, restlessness was taken as a general type of hindrance as ‘agitated, with uncalmed minds’ (uddhatā avūpasantacittā). Here, the wavering of mind caused by restlessness due to the absence of concentration is stated as ‘unconcentrated, with wandering mind’ (asamāhitā vibbhantacittā). This is the distinction between them. ‘In the way stated before’ refers to the way previously stated: ‘For through restlessness, the mind wavers over a single object, like a banner on a flagstaff in the wind’ (MN-a 1.169). ‘All is similar to the previous’ refers to the similarity with what was stated in the section on covetousness concerning the arising of fear and terror.

48. Duppaññāti [M 1.0217] ettha du-saddo “dussīlo”tiādīsu viya abhāvattho, na “duggati, duppaṭipanno”tiādīsu viya garahatthoti dassetuṃ “nippaññānametaṃ adhivacana”nti vatvā “paññā pana duṭṭhā nāma natthī”ti vuttaṃ. Teti duppaññā. Sabbatthāti catūsupi pāṭhavikappesu. Elanti vā doso vuccati. Tenāha “yā sā vācā nelā kaṇṇasukhā”ti. Tathā hi sīlaṃ “nelaṅga”nti vuttaṃ. Duppaññā ca kathentā sadosameva kathaṃ kathenti apaṇḍitabhāvato. Tenevāha “dubbhāsitabhāsī”ti. Tasmā elasabbhāvato elaṃ mukhaṃ etesanti elamūgāti vuttāti evampi vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yāya paññāya vasena “paññāsampanno”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ byatirekamukhena dassetuṃ “no ca kho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nanu ca bodhisattā bahulavipassanāpaññāya samannāgatā hontīti? Honti, tadā pana bodhisattena na vipassanārambho kato, no ca vipassanāpaññā adhippetāti vuttaṃ “no ca kho vipassanāpaññāyā”ti.

48. In ‘unwise’ (duppaññā), the prefix ‘du-’ conveys the sense of absence, as in ‘unvirtuous’ (dussīlo), etc., and not the sense of blame, as in ‘unfortunate destiny’ (duggati), ‘practicing wrongly’ (duppaṭipanno), etc. To indicate this, it is said: ‘This is a term for the absence of wisdom,’ and further, ‘but there is no such thing as corrupted wisdom.’ ‘These’ (te) means the unwise. ‘In every way’ (sabbatthā) means in all four earth kasinas. ‘Ela’ is said to be a fault or defect.
