Hence it is said: ‘That speech which is not faulty (nelā) is pleasant to the ear.’ Similarly, virtue is called ‘unblemished’ (nelaṅga). And the unwise, when speaking, speak only faulty words due to their lack of wisdom. Therefore, it is said: ‘a speaker of ill-spoken speech’ (dubbhāsitabhāsī). Thus, because their nature is faulty (ela), their mouths are faulty (ela)—hence they are called ‘faulty-mouthed’ (elamūgā). Even this meaning should be seen here. To show, by way of exclusion, the wisdom by which one is called ‘endowed with wisdom,’ it is said: ‘but not…’ (no ca kho) etc. Now, are not bodhisattas endowed with abundant insight wisdom? They are, but at that time the Bodhisatta had not yet undertaken insight meditation, nor was insight wisdom intended—hence it is said: ‘but not with insight wisdom.’

Keci panettha “saddhāvirahitā aparisuddhakāyakammantādayo viya bhayabheravāvhāyanassa visesakāraṇaṃ, nāpi saddhālutā pallomatāyāti saddhāvāro anuddhaṭo”ti vadanti, taṃ akāraṇaṃ. Kammaphale hi saddahanto kammapaṭisaraṇataṃyeva nissāya bhayabheravaṃ tiṇāyapi amaññamāno pallomatamāpajjeyya. Yasmā pana vīriyādayo saddhāya vinā nappavattantīti tesaṃ upanissayabhūtā sahajātā ca sā taggahaṇeneva gahitā hotīti visuṃ na uddhaṭā. Tathā hi sā jhānassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadāyampi na uddhaṭā, kiṃ vā etāya saddhāya, addhā sā imasmiṃ ārammaṇapariggahaṭṭhāne na gahetabbāva, tato dhammassāminā idha na uddhaṭā, evaṃ aññesupi edisesu ṭhānesu nicchayo kātabbo. Yathānulomadesanā hi suttantakathāti.

Some here say that the section on faith is not mentioned because faith is not a specific cause for the arising of fear and terror—unlike lack of faith, impure bodily action, and so on—nor is faith a cause of faint-heartedness. This reasoning is unfounded. For one who has faith in the fruit of kamma, relying solely on kamma as their refuge, might regard fear and terror as insignificant and thus fall into faint-heartedness. However, since energy and other factors do not arise without faith, it, being their supporting condition and co-arisen with them, is included by their mention and thus not stated separately. Indeed, it is not separately mentioned even in the preliminary practice for jhāna. What need is there for this faith? Surely, in this context of grasping an object, it should not be taken up; therefore, the Master of the Dhamma did not mention it here. A conclusion should be drawn in this way in other similar instances as well. For the Sutta discourse is a teaching that follows the natural order.

Vacīkammantavārādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section beginning with verbal action is concluded.

Soḷasaṭṭhānārammaṇapariggaho niṭṭhito.

The comprehension of the sixteen bases as objects is concluded.

Bhayabheravasenāsanādivaṇṇanā

The Description of Dwellings of Fear and Dread, etc.

49. Soḷasārammaṇānīti [V 1.0194] soḷasaṭṭhānāni ārammaṇāni. Evarūpāsu rattīsūti cātuddasīādikā upari vakkhamānā rattiyo sandhāya vadati[M 1.0218]. Evarūpe senāsaneti etthāpi eseva nayo. Yāti aniyamato uddiṭṭhānaṃ puna “tā”ti vacanaṃ niddeso viya hotīti vuttaṃ “yā tāti ubhayametaṃ rattīnaṃyeva uddesaniddesavacana”nti. Abhīti lakkhaṇatthe “aññe ca abhiññātā brāhmaṇamahāsālā”tiādīsu viya. Kathaṃ panettha lakkhaṇatthatā veditabbā? Lakkhīyati etenāti lakkhaṇanti āha “candapāripūriyā”tiādi. Puṇṇamāsiyaṃ candapāripūriyā amāvāsiyaṃ candaparikkhayena. Ādi-saddena candassa upaḍḍhamaṇḍalatārāhuggahatādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Upasaggamattameva abhi-saddo lakkhitasaddeneva lakkhaṇatthassa viññāyamānattāti adhippāyo.

49. 'Sixteen objects' means the sixteen bases that are objects. 'In such nights' refers to nights such as the fourteenth, which will be mentioned later. 'In such a dwelling': here too the same method applies. The word 'yā' refers to what is indefinitely indicated; the word 'tā' then acts as a specification. Thus it is said: 'Both yā and tā are words of indication and specification for the nights.' 'Abhi-' is in the sense of a characteristic, as in 'other well-known (abhiññātā) wealthy brahmins' and so on. How, then, is the sense of a characteristic to be understood here? He says, 'A characteristic is that by which something is marked,' as in 'by the fullness of the moon,' etc., meaning by the moon's fullness on the full-moon day, and by the moon's waning on the new-moon day. By the word 'etc.' should be understood the inclusion of the moon's half-disc, the rising of stars, and so forth. The word 'abhi' is merely a prefix; the sense of a characteristic is understood from the very word that is characterized. This is the intended meaning.

Paṭhamadivasato pabhutīti paṭhamapāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya. Yasmā codako bhagavato kāle anabhilakkhitāpi aparabhāge abhilakkhitā jātā, tasmā taṃ abhilakkhaṇīyataṃ upādāya “sabbadassinā bhagavatā pañcamī kasmā na gahitā”ti codeti, itaro sabbakālikāsu cātuddasīādīsu gayhamānāsu asabbakālikāya kathaṃ gahaṇanti adhippāyena “asabbakālikattā”ti pariharati.

'From the first day onwards' means starting from the first day of the lunar fortnight. Since the fifth day, although not marked during the Blessed One's time, became marked later, the questioner, taking that mark-worthiness into account, asks, 'Why was the fifth not taken by the All-Seeing Blessed One?' The other, with the thought, 'How could one that is not for all times be taken, when the fourteenth and so on, which are for all times, are taken?' replies, 'Because it is not for all times.'

Tathāvidhāsūti “abhiññātā”tiādinā yathā vuttā, tathāvidhāsu. Devatādhiṭṭhitabhāvena ārāmādīnaṃ lokassa cetiyabhāvoti āha “pūjanīyaṭṭhenā”ti. Manussā yebhuyyena gāmādīnaṃ dvāresu tathārūpe rukkhe cetiyaṭṭhāniye katvā voharantīti āha “gāmanigamādidvāresū”tiādi. Dassanamattenapi savanamattenapi bhayuppādanena pākatikasatte bhiṃsentīti bhiṃsanakāni. Tenāha “bhayajanakānī”tiādi. Bhāyati etasmāti bhayaṃ, ativiya sappaṭibhayaṃ bheravaṃ.

'Of such kinds' means of such kinds as were stated with 'well-known,' etc. Because parks and so on are established by deities, they become shrines for the world; thus he says, 'in the sense of being worthy of veneration.' People generally, having made such trees at the gates of villages and the like into places of worship, use that designation; thus he says, 'at the gates of villages, towns, etc.' Because they frighten ordinary beings by producing fear merely by being seen or heard, they are 'frightening.' Therefore, he says, 'fear-inducing,' etc. 'Fear' is that from which one fears; 'dread' is that which is extremely and particularly fearful.

Āyācanaupahārakaraṇārahanti taṃtaṃbalikammapaṇidhikammakaraṇayoggaṃ. Pupphadhūpa…pe… dharaṇitalanti idaṃ yathāpaṭisūtena suppādinā upahārakaraṇadassanaṃ. Koṭṭentoti paharanto, siṅgappahārakhurappahārehi saddaṃ karontoti adhippāyo. Sabbacatuppadānaṃ idha magoti nāmaṃ, na “acchacammaṃ migacammaṃ eḷakacamma”ntiādīsu (mahāva. 259) viya, rohitotiādi migavisesānanti [M 1.0219] adhippāyo. Cāletvāti aggamaddanena cāletvā. Moraggahaṇañcettha upalakkhaṇanti dassento āha “idha sabbapakkhigahaṇaṃ adhippeta”nti. Esa nayoti idaṃ yathā “moro vā”ti [V 1.0195] ettha vā-saddo avuttavikappanattho, evaṃ “migo vā”ti etthāpīti migasaddassa visesatthavuttitaṃ sandhāyāha. Ito pabhūtīti “yaṃnūnāhaṃ yā tā rattiyo”tiādinā bhayabheravassa gavesanacintanato pabhuti, na gavesanārambhato pabhuti. “Appeva nāmāhaṃ bhayabheravaṃ passeyya”nti etthāpi hi ārammaṇameva bhayabheravaṃ. Sukhārammaṇaṃ rūpaṃ sukhamiva “rūpaṃ sukhaṃ sukhānupatitaṃ sukhāvakkanta”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.60). Kathaṃ bhayaggahaṇena ca rūpārammaṇaggahaṇanti āha “parittassa cā”tiādi. “Āgacchatī”ti vacanato gavesanārambhato pabhuti “etaṃ bhaya”nti ārammaṇaṃ adhippetanti keci “taṃ na passeyya”nti cakkhunā dassanassa adhippetattā, tasmā vuttanayeneva attho gahetabbo. Bhayaṃ ākaṅkhamānoti upaparikkhanavasena ahaṃ bhayavatthuṃ ākaṅkhanto viharāmi, taṃ kimatthiyaṃ, ettakopi bhayasamannāhāro mayhaṃ ayuttoti adhippāyo.

'Worthy of making requests and offerings' means suitable for performing various sacrificial acts and acts of resolution. 'Flowers, incense... ground': this shows the making of an offering as clearly indicated according to the Sutta. 'Striking' means hitting; the meaning is making a sound with strikes of the horn and strikes of the hoof. Here, 'miga' is a name for all quadrupeds, not as in 'bear hide, deer hide, sheep hide,' etc. (Mahāva. 259); the meaning is specific kinds of deer such as the rohita. 'Shaking' means shaking by trampling the top part. And showing that the mention of the peacock here is an illustration, he says, 'here the taking of all birds is intended.' This is the method: just as the word 'or' in 'or a peacock' has the sense of an unstated alternative, so too in 'or a deer'; he says this referring to the word 'deer' being used in a specific sense. 'From this point on' means from the thought of searching for fear and terror, starting with 'What if I... those nights...,' not from the start of the search. Even in 'Perhaps I might see fear and terror,' the object is indeed fear and terror, just as a pleasant object, a form, is pleasant, as in 'form is pleasant, associated with pleasure, inclined toward pleasure' (Saṃ. Ni. 3.60). How is there a grasping of a form-object by the grasping of fear? He says, 'of the limited,' etc. Because of the word 'comes,' some intend the object 'this is fear' from the start of the search. But since 'might not see it' implies seeing with the eye, the meaning should be taken as stated. 'Desiring fear' means: 'I am dwelling, investigating and desiring an object of fear. For what purpose? Even this much mental application to fear is unsuitable for me.' This is the intended meaning.

Yaṃ pakāraṃ bhūto yathābhūto, so panettha pakāro iriyāpathavasena yutto pāḷiyaṃ tathā āgatattāti āha “yena yena iriyāpathena bhūtassā”ti. Bhavitassāti idaṃ “bhūtassā”ti iminā samānatthaṃ padanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Samaṅgībhūtassā”ti padaṃ purimapadalopena bhūtassāti vuttanti dassento “samaṅgībhūtassa vā”ti āha. Bhayabheravārammaṇeti bhayabheravābhimate ārammaṇe. Neva mahāsatto tiṭṭhatītiādi “tathābhūto ca taṃ paṭivineyya”nti yathā cintitaṃ, tathā paṭipannabhāvadassanaṃ. Iriyāpathapaṭipāṭi nāma ṭhānagamananisajjānipajjāti vadanti, uppaṭipāṭi pana paṭhamaṃ nipajjā, puna nisajjā, puna ṭhānaṃ, pacchā gamananti evaṃ veditabbā. Āsannapaṭipāṭiyāti gamanassa tāva ṭhānaṃ āsannaṃ, ṭhānassa nisajjā gamanañca, nisajjāya nipajjā ṭhānañca, nipajjāya nisajjā āsannā. Idha pana gamanassa ṭhānaṃ, ṭhānassa ca gamanaṃ, nisajjāya ca nipajjā, nipajjāya ca nisajjā āsannabhāvena gahitā, itare paramparāvasenāti veditabbā. Bhikkhussa pana iriyāpathā sampattapaṭipāṭiyā viya aparāparuppattivasena vuccanti.

'Yathābhūto' means in whatever manner one is. Here that manner is connected with the postures, because it appears that way in the Pāli; thus he says, 'by whatever posture of the being.' The word 'bhavitassa' should be understood as a word with the same meaning as 'bhūtassa.' Showing that the word 'samaṅgībhūtassa' is stated as 'bhūtassa' through the elision of the preceding part, he says, 'or of one endowed with (samaṅgībhūtassa).' 'In an object of fear and dread' means in an object desired as fear and dread. 'The great being does not stand,' etc., shows the state of having practiced in accordance with what was thought: 'being thus, he should dispel it.' The sequence of postures, they say, is standing, walking, sitting, and lying down. The reverse sequence, however, should be understood as first lying down, then sitting, then standing, and finally walking. As to the adjacent sequence: to walking, standing is adjacent; to standing, sitting and walking; to sitting, lying down and standing; to lying down, sitting is adjacent. Here, however, standing is taken as adjacent to walking, and walking to standing; lying down to sitting, and sitting to lying down, while the others should be understood as being in succession. For a bhikkhu, however, the postures are spoken of in terms of their successive arising, as if in the order of attainment.

Bhayabheravasenāsanādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The description of dwellings of fear and dread, etc., is concluded.

Asammohavihāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Dwelling in Non-delusion

50. Ayañca [M 1.0220] me sabbaso bhayabheravābhāvo visesato asammohadhammattāti dassetuṃ “santi [V 1.0196] kho panā”tiādinā upari desanā vaḍḍhitāti ayaṃ vā ettha anusandhi. Jhāyīnaṃ sammohaṭṭhānesūti iminā ajjhāyīnaṃ sammohaṭṭhānesu vattabbameva natthīti dasseti. Atthīti idaṃ nipātapadaṃ puthuvacanampi hoti “atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.373-374; ma. ni. 1.110; 3.154; saṃ. ni. 4.127; khu. pā. 3.dvatiṃsākāra) viyāti “santī”ti padassa atthadassanavasena vuttaṃ. Kiṃ khaṇattayasamaṅgitāya te atthi, noti āha “saṃvijjanti upalabbhantī”ti, mahati lokasannivāse edisāpi saṃvijjanti ñāṇena gahetabbatāya upalabbhantīti. Odātakasiṇalābhīti appamāṇaodātakasiṇalābhī. Evaṃ hissa samantato āloko viya upaṭṭhāti. Parikammanti samāpattipubbabhāgamāha. Ettakaṃ sūriye gate vuṭṭhahāmīti, no ca kho addhānaparicchede kusalo hoti, kevalaṃ “divā eva vuṭṭhahāmī”ti manasikāraṃ uppādesi. Visadaṃ hoti sabbaṃ ārammaṇajātaṃ, dibbacakkhunā passantassa viya vibhūtaṃ. Avisadanti ettha vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo. Evaṃsaññinoti rattiṃ “divā”ti, divā ca “rattī”ti evaṃsaññino.

50. And to show that for me there is absolutely no fear or terror, especially due to the nature of non-delusion, the teaching above has been expanded with the phrase, 'There are indeed...' Thus, this is the connection here. 'For meditators, in places of delusion'—this indicates that for non-meditators in places of delusion, there is nothing to be said. The particle 'atthi' can also be a plural word, as in 'atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā' (There are hairs on this body), and so on; thus, the word 'santi' (there are) is stated in the sense of showing the meaning. Are they existent, endowed with the three moments, or not? He says, 'They exist, they are found'—in this vast world, such things do exist and are found, fit to be grasped by knowledge. 'An attainee of the white kasiṇa' refers to one who has attained the boundless white kasiṇa. For such a person, it appears all around like light. 'Preparation' refers to the preliminary part of attainment. He resolves, 'I will emerge when the sun has gone this far,' but he is not skilled in measuring time—he simply gives rise to the thought, 'I will emerge during the day.' The entire field of objects becomes clear, distinct, as if seen by the divine eye. 'Unclear'—here, the meaning should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated. 'Thus perceiving'—perceiving 'day' at night, and 'night' during the day—such are those who perceive thus.

Antosenāsane rattiṃ nisinno hotīti ratti-saddo ajjhāharitabbo. Parittāsanādīhi, aññehi vā kāraṇehi. Gambhīrāya bhūmigabbhasadisāya ghanavanapaṭicchannāya bahalatarajālavanapaṭalapaṭicchannāya. Antarahitasūriyāloke kāleti eteneva divāti avuttasiddho. Sammohavihāro nāma bahuvidhoti āha “sammohavihārānaṃ aññatara”nti.

At night, seated in a secluded dwelling—the word 'night' should be supplied. Due to slight fear or other reasons. Like a deep, cave-like place, covered by dense forest, concealed by a very thick network of creepers. Spending time where the sunlight is obscured—by this, it is implicitly understood that it is day. The state of bewilderment is of many kinds—thus it is said, 'one of the states of bewilderment.'

Pākaṭo bodhisattassa rattindivaparicchedo antamaso lavatuṭikhaṇassapi upādāya suvavatthitattā, tathā rattidivasakoṭṭhāsaparicchedo attanā kātabbakiccavasena kālañāṇavasena ca.

The division of day and night for the Bodhisatta was clearly established, even taking into account the smallest moment such as a snap of the fingers, because of his well-established nature. Likewise, the division of portions of day and night was determined by himself in accordance with the tasks to be done and according to his knowledge of time.

Kālathambhe [M 1.0221] laddhabbachāyāvasena dvaṅgulakāle. Yāmaghaṇṭikaṃ paharati saṅghassa taṃtaṃvattakaraṇatthaṃ. Muggaranti ghaṇṭikappaharaṇamuggaraṃ. Yāmayantaṃ patati aññehi bhikkhūhi yojitanti adhippāyo. Yāva aññe bhikkhū bhojanasālaṃ upagacchanti, tāva divāvihāraṭṭhānaṃ gantvā samaṇadhammaṃ karoti.

At the time when the shadow is two fingers long against the Kāla post, the meal bell is struck for the Sangha to signal the time for their respective duties. The mallet for striking the bell is called 'muggara.' The time-measuring device falls, meaning it is set by other monks. While other monks go to the dining hall, he goes to his daytime dwelling and practices the duties of a contemplative.

Yaṃ kho tanti ettha yanti aniyamuddeso, khoti avadhāraṇe, yameva puggalanti attho. Tanti vuccamānākāravacanaṃ. Mamevāti maṃ eva. Asammohasabhāvoti sabhāvabhūtaasammoho. “Uppanno”ti vuttattā “manussaloke”ti vuttaṃ. Paññāsampattiyāti yāthāvato hitassa jānanasamatthena attano paññāguṇena, na kevalaṃ ajjhāsayeneva hitesitā, atha kho payogenāti [V 1.0197] dassento “hitūpadesako”ti āha. Ajjhāsayena pana hitesitā “lokānukampāyā”ti iminā dassitā. Upakaraṇehi vinā na kadāci bhogasukhaṃ upakaraṇadānañca cāgasampattihetukanti āha “cāgasampattiyā…pe… dāyako”ti. Mettāsampattiyā hitūpasaṃhārena rakkhitā. Karuṇāsampattiyā dukkhāpanayanena gopāyitā. Nanu ca pubbepi vuttaṃ “hitāya sukhāyā”ti, atha kasmā puna taṃ gahitanti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “idha devamanussaggahaṇenā”tiādi. Tena pubbe avisesato hitādīni dassitāni, idāni visesato saha payojanena tāni dassitānīti dīpeti. Nibbānato paro paramo attho nāma natthīti āha “paramatthattāyā”ti. Hinoti nibbānaṃ gacchatīti hitaṃ, maggo. Ukkaṃsato sukhatthaṃ ariyaphalanti āha “tato uttari sukhābhāvato”ti.

Here, 'yaṃ' is an indeterminate designation, 'kho' is for emphasis, and the meaning is 'that very person'. The word 'taṃ' denotes the form of speech. 'Mameva' means 'me alone'. 'Asammohasabhāvo' signifies the natural state of non-delusion. Since it is said 'uppanno' (arisen), 'manussaloke' (in the human world) is stated. 'Paññāsampattiyā' refers to the perfection of wisdom, by truly knowing what is beneficial through the excellence of one's own wisdom—not merely by intention alone, but also by effort—thus it is said, 'hitūpadesako' (the advisor of benefit). The desire for benefit by intention, however, is shown by 'lokānukampāya' (out of compassion for the world). Without the means of support, worldly pleasures are never attained, and the giving of such means is the cause of generosity's perfection—hence it is said, 'cāgasampattiyā…pe… dāyako' (by the perfection of generosity… the giver). Protected by the perfection of loving-kindness through the promotion of welfare, guarded by the perfection of compassion through the removal of suffering. But was it not previously stated, 'for welfare and happiness'? Why then is it repeated? Addressing this objection, it is said, 'here, by including devas and humans,' and so on. Thus, previously, welfare and the like were shown generally, but now they are shown specifically along with their purpose. It is said, 'paramatthattāya' (because it is for the ultimate goal), meaning there is no goal beyond Nibbāna. 'Hitaṃ' means that which goes to Nibbāna, that is, the path. 'Ukkaṃsato' (from the standpoint of excellence), the noble fruit is for the sake of happiness—hence it is said, 'tato uttari sukhābhāvato' (because there is no happiness beyond that).

Asammohavihāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Dwelling Without Delusion is concluded.

Pubbabhāgapaṭipadādivaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Preliminary Practice and So On.

51. Asammohavihāranti asammohavuttiṃ, asammohasambodhinti vā attho. Tanti samathavipassanābhāvanāsaṅkhātaṃ paṭipadaṃ. Pubbabhāgato pabhutīti bhāvanāya pubbabhāgavīriyārambhādito paṭṭhāya. Kecīti uttaravihāravāsino.

51. 'Dwelling without delusion' means conduct without delusion, or the meaning is 'awakening without delusion.' 'That' refers to the practice consisting of the development of serenity and insight. 'From the preliminary part onwards' means starting from the initial exertion of energy in the preliminary part of the development. 'Some' refers to those dwelling in the northern monasteries.

Bodhimaṇḍeti [M 1.0222] (sārattha. ṭī. 1.11.verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā; a. ni. ṭī. 3.8.11) bodhisaṅkhātassa ñāṇassa maṇḍabhāvappatte ṭhāne. Caturaṅganti “kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca, aṭṭhi ca avasissatū”tiādinā (ma. ni. 2.184; saṃ. ni. 2.237; a. ni. 2.5; 8.13; mahāni. 17, 196) vuttacaturaṅgasamannāgataṃ. Paggahitanti ārambhaṃ sithilaṃ akatvā daḷhaparakkamasaṅkhātussahanabhāvena gahitaṃ. Tenāha “asithilappavattitanti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Asallīnanti asaṅkucitaṃ kosajjavasena saṅkocaṃ anāpannaṃ.

'At the Bodhimaṇḍa' means the place where the knowledge designated as enlightenment (bodhi) attains the state of being the essence (maṇḍa). 'Four-limbed' refers to being endowed with the four limbs as stated in the phrase, 'Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain,' etc. (Majjhima Nikāya 2.184; Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.237; Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.5; 8.13; Mahāniddesa 17, 196). 'Exerted' means taken up with firm effort, not slackening in endeavor, characterized by the state of strong endurance. Hence it is said, 'It is called “unslackening in progress.”' 'Unshrinking' means not contracted, not succumbing to contraction due to laziness.

Upaṭṭhitāti ogāhanasaṅkhātena apilāpanabhāvena ārammaṇaṃ upagantvā ṭhitā. Tenāha “ārammaṇābhimukhībhāvenā”ti. Sammosassa viddhaṃsanavasena pavattiyā na sammuṭṭhāti asammuṭṭhā. Kiñcāpi cittamiva cittapassaddhivasena kāyapassaddhivaseneva kāyo passaddho hoti, tathāpi yasmā kāyapassaddhi uppajjamānā cittapassaddhiyā saheva uppajjati, na vinā, tasmā vuttaṃ “kāyacittapassaddhisambhavenā”ti[V 1.0198]. Rūpakāyopi passaddhoyeva hoti kāyapassaddhiyā ubhayesampi kāyānaṃ passambhanāvahattā. So ca kho kāyo. Vigatadarathoti vigatakilesadaratho. Nāmakāye hi vigatadarathe rūpakāyopi vūpasantadarathapariḷāho hoti. Sammā āhitanti nānārammaṇesu vidhāvanasaṅkhātavikkhepaṃ vicchinditvā ekasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe avikkhittabhāvāpādānena sammadeva āhitaṃ. Tenāha “suṭṭhu ṭhapita”ntiādi. Cittassa anekaggabhāvo vikkhepavasena cañcalatā, sā sati ekaggatāya na hotīti āha “ekaggaṃ acalaṃ nipphandana”nti. Ettāvatāti “āraddhaṃ kho panā”tiādinā vīriyasatipassaddhisamādhīnaṃ kiccasiddhidassanena. Nanu ca saddhāpaññānampi kiccasiddhi jhānassa pubbapaṭipadāya icchitabbāti? Saccaṃ icchitabbā, sā pana nānantariyabhāvena avuttasiddhāti na gahitā. Asati hi saddhāya vīriyārambhādīnaṃ asambhavoyeva, paññāpariggahe ca nesaṃ asati paññāyārambhādibhāvo na siyā. Tathā asallīnāsammosatādayo vīriyādīnanti asallīnatādiggahaṇenevettha paññākiccasiddhi gahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Jhānabhāvanāyaṃ vā samādhikiccaṃ adhikaṃ icchitabbanti dassetuṃ samādhipariyosānāva jhānassa pubbapaṭipadā kathitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

"It is established" means it remains having approached the object without floundering, which is the characteristic of immersion. Hence it is said, "by facing the object." It is not deluded, due to its arising through the destruction of delusion; thus, it is non-deluded. Although the body becomes tranquil through mental tranquility, just as the mind does, as well as through bodily tranquility, nevertheless, because bodily tranquility arises together with mental tranquility and not without it, it is therefore said, "through the arising of bodily and mental tranquility." The material body also becomes tranquil due to bodily tranquility, because it brings about the calming of both bodies. And that body is indeed free from distress—free from the distress of defilements. For when the mental body is free from distress, the material body also has its fever of distress calmed. "Rightly directed" means cutting off distraction, which is characterized as wandering among various objects, and properly directing the mind by placing it undistractedly on a single object. Hence it is said, "well-established," etc. The mind’s lack of one-pointedness is its restlessness due to distraction, but this does not occur when there is one-pointedness. Therefore, it is said, "one-pointed, unwavering, without agitation." Up to this point, by showing the accomplishment of the functions of energy, mindfulness, tranquility, and concentration through the phrase "now, it is begun," etc. But should not the accomplishment of faith and wisdom also be desired as the preliminary practice for jhāna? Indeed, it should be desired, but since it is accomplished without being explicitly stated as an immediate factor, it is not mentioned here. For without faith, the undertaking of energy and the like would not be possible, and without their being grasped by wisdom, their initiation by wisdom would not occur. Similarly, non-sloth, non-delusion, etc., pertain to energy and the rest. Thus, it should be understood that by mentioning non-sloth and the like, the accomplishment of wisdom’s function is thereby included. Alternatively, to show that in the development of jhāna, the function of concentration is primarily to be desired, it should be understood that the preliminary practice for jhāna is discussed as culminating in concentration.

Vuttaṃ, tasmā idha na vattabbaṃ. Visuddhimaggo hi imissā saṃvaṇṇanāya ekadesabhūtoti vuttovāyamatthoti. Viharatīti āgataṃ paruddesikattā [M 1.0223] vihārassa. Idha vihāsinti āgataṃ atthuddesikattā. Idaṃ kira sabbabuddhānaṃ avijahitanti āha “ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhāna”nti. Rūpavirāgabhāvanāvasena (sārattha. ṭī. 1.12.nerañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā) pavatto catubbidhopi arūpajjhānaviseso catutthajjhānasaṅgaho evāti āha “cattāri jhānānī”ti. Yuttaṃ tāva cittekaggatā bhavokkamanatthatā viya vipassanāpādakatāpi catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ sādhāraṇāti tesaṃ vasena “cattāri jhānānī”ti vacanaṃ, abhiññāpādakatā pana nirodhapādakatā ca catutthasseva jhānassa āveṇikā, sā kathaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ sādhāraṇā vuttāti? Paramparādhiṭṭhānabhāvato. Padaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānampi hi padaṭṭhānanteva vuccati, kāraṇakāraṇampi kāraṇanti yathā “tiṇehi sattaṃ siddha”nti, evañca katvā payojananiddese aṭṭhasamāpattiggahaṇaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. Cittekaggatatthānīti cittasamādhānatthāni, diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāratthānīti attho. Cittekaggatāsīsena hi diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāro vutto, sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tenāha “ekaggacittā sukhaṃ divasaṃ viharissāmā”ti. Bhavokkamanatthānīti bhavesu nibbattiatthāni.

It has been said, therefore it should not be stated here. For the Visuddhimagga is indeed a part of this commentary, and thus this meaning has already been stated. The word 'viharatīti' (dwells) is used because it refers to the monastery. Here, 'vihāsinti' (we will dwell) is used because it refers to the meaning. This, it is said, is not abandoned by all Buddhas, as stated: 'the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing.' The fourfold distinction of the formless attainments, which arises through the development of dispassion toward form, is indeed included within the fourth jhāna. Therefore, it is said: 'the four jhānas.' It is indeed fitting to use the phrase 'the four jhānas' in reference to them, since unification of mind, being a basis for insight, and serving the purpose of arising in new existence are all common to the four jhānas. However, the ability to lead to direct knowledge and cessation is unique to the fourth jhāna alone. How, then, is it said to be common to the four jhānas? Due to its nature as a foundation by succession. For even what is a foundation for a foundation is simply called 'foundation,' just as the cause of a cause is called 'cause,' as in the phrase: 'a binding is made with grass.' And by this reasoning, the inclusion of the eight attainments in the explanation of purpose is justified. 'For the purpose of unification of mind' means for the purpose of mental concentration, that is, for the purpose of dwelling happily in this very life. For dwelling happily in this very life is stated under the heading of unification of mind, and this is said with reference to dry-insight practitioners and arahants. Therefore, it is said: 'With a unified mind, we will dwell happily for the day.' 'For the purpose of arising in existence' means for the purpose of being reborn in realms of existence.

Yasmā (sārattha. ṭī. 1.12.nerañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā) bodhisattena bodhimaṇḍūpasaṅkamanato pubbepi carimabhave catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattitapubbaṃ, tadā pana taṃ nibbattitamattameva ahosi, na vipassanādipādakaṃ[V 1.0199], tasmā “bodhirukkhamūle nibbattita”nti tato visesetvā vuttaṃ. Vipassanāpādakanti vipassanārambhe vipassanāya pādakaṃ. Abhiññāpādakanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Buddhānañhi paṭhamārambhe eva pādakajjhānena payojanaṃ ahosi, na tato paraṃ uparimaggādhigamaphalasamāpattiabhiññāvaḷañjanādiatthaṃ. Abhisambodhisamadhigamato paṭṭhāya hi sabbaṃ ñāṇasamādhikiccaṃ ākaṅkhamattapaṭibaddhamevāti. Sabbakiccasādhakanti anupubbavihārādisabbakiccasādhakaṃ. Sabbalokiyalokuttaraguṇadāyakanti ettha vipassanābhiññāpādakattā eva catutthassa jhānassa bhagavato sabbalokiyalokuttaraguṇadāyakatā veditabbā. Sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānañhi maggañāṇaṃ, maggañāṇapadaṭṭhānañca sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ abhisambodhi, tadadhigamasamakālameva bhagavato sabbe buddhaguṇā hatthagatā ahesuṃ, catutthajjhānasannissayo ca maggādhigamoti.

Because the Bodhisatta had previously generated the fourth jhāna even before approaching the Bodhi seat in his final existence, but at that time it was merely generated and not yet a basis for insight and other such states, it is therefore distinguished and stated as 'generated at the foot of the Bodhi tree.' 'Basis for insight' means a foundation for the commencement of insight. The same principle applies to 'basis for higher knowledge.' For Buddhas, a jhāna serving as a foundation was necessary only at the initial commencement; beyond that, it was not required for attaining higher paths, fruitions, the use of higher knowledges, and so on. From the moment of supreme enlightenment onward, all functions of knowledge and concentration were bound solely by wish. 'Accomplisher of all tasks' refers to accomplishing all tasks, including progressive abidings. 'Bestower of all worldly and transcendent qualities'—here, it should be understood that the fourth jhāna bestowed all worldly and transcendent qualities upon the Blessed One precisely because it served as the basis for insight and higher knowledges. For path-knowledge is the foundation for the knowledge of omniscience, and supreme enlightenment, the knowledge of omniscience, is the foundation for path-knowledge. At the very moment of its attainment, all the Buddha-qualities came into the Blessed One's possession, and the attainment of the path was dependent on the fourth jhāna.

Pubbabhāgapaṭipadādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the preliminary practice and so forth is completed.

Pubbenivāsakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Past Lives

52. Dvinnaṃ [M 1.0224] vijjānanti pubbenivāsañāṇadibbacakkhuñāṇasaṅkhātānaṃ dvinnaṃ vijjānaṃ. Anupadavaṇṇanāti tāsaṃ vijjānaṃ niddesapāḷiyā anupadavaṇṇanā. Bhāvanānayoti uppādanavidhi. “So”ti paccattavacanassa ahaṃ-saddena sambandhane kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “abhininnāmesi”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ vā “abhininnāmesi”nti uttamapurisassa yogoti ahaṃ-saddena ānetvā vuccamāne tadattho pākaṭo hotīti “so aha”nti vuttaṃ. Abhinīharinti cittaṃ jhānārammaṇato apanetvā pubbenivāsābhimukhaṃ pesesiṃ, pubbenivāsaninnaṃ pubbenivāsapoṇaṃ pubbenivāsapabbhāraṃ akāsinti attho.

52. 'Of the two knowledges' refers to the two knowledges, namely, the knowledge of past lives and the divine eye knowledge. 'The word-by-word explanation' is the word-by-word explanation of those knowledges according to the exposition text. 'The method of development' is the method of generation. To show the reason for connecting the word 'so' (he) with the word 'ahaṃ' (I), it is stated: 'abhininnāmesi' (I directed) and so on. Or, in the Pali text, 'abhininnāmesi' is in the first person; thus, when it is brought into connection with the word 'ahaṃ' and stated, its meaning becomes clear, hence 'so ahaṃ' (so I) is stated. 'Abhinīhariṃ' (I directed) means: I turned the mind away from the object of jhāna and directed it towards past lives, making it inclined towards past lives, tending towards past lives, predisposed towards past lives—this is the meaning.

Pubbeatītajātīsu nivutthakkhandhā pubbenivāso. Nivutthāti ca ajjhāvutthā anubhūtā attano santāne uppajjitvā niruddhā, gocaranivāsena nivutthadhammā vā attano viññāṇenaviññātā, paraviññāṇaviññātāpi vā chinnavaṭumakānussaraṇādīsu, taṃ pubbenivāsaṃ yāya satiyā anussarati, tāya sampayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiññāṇaṃ. Paṭinivattantassāti pubbenivāsaṃ anussaraṇavasena yāvadicchakaṃ gantvā paccāgacchantassa. Tasmāti vuttassevatthassa kāraṇabhāvena paccāmasanaṃ, paṭinivattantassa paccavekkhaṇabhāvatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Idhūpapattiyāti idha [V 1.0200] carimabhave upapattiyā. Anantaranti atītānantaramāha. Amutrāti amukasmiṃ bhaveti attho. Udapādinti uppajjiṃ. Tāhi devatāhīti tusitādevatāhi. Ekagottoti tusitagottena ekagotto. Mahābodhisattānaṃ santānassa pariyosānāvatthāya devalokūpapattijanakaṃ nāma akusalena kammunā anupaddutameva hotīti adhippāyena “dukkhaṃ pana saṅkhāradukkhamevā”ti vuttaṃ. Mahāpuññānampi pana devaputtānaṃ pubbanimittuppattikālādīsu aniṭṭhārammaṇasamāyogo hotiyevāti “kadāci dukkhadukkhassapi sambhavo natthī”ti na sakkā vattuṃ. Sattapaññāsa…pe… pariyantoti idaṃ manussānaṃ vassagaṇanāvasena vuttaṃ. Tattha devānaṃ vassagaṇanāya pana catusahassameva.

The aggregates that have been dwelt in during past existences constitute 'past dwelling' (pubbenivāsa). 'Dwelt in' (nivutthā) means they were lived in, experienced, and then ceased after arising in one's own continuity; or they are phenomena that were dwelt in by way of their range of dwelling, known either by one's own consciousness or by another's consciousness, as in recalling interrupted paths, and so forth. The knowledge associated with the mindfulness by which one recollects that past dwelling is the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiññāṇa). 'Of one who turns back' (paṭinivattantassa) refers to one who, by way of recollecting past dwelling, goes as far as desired and then returns. 'Therefore' (tasmā) is a reflection upon the stated matter as a cause; this is said because it is the state of reviewing for one who is turning back. 'By birth here' (idhūpapattiyā) means by birth in this final existence. 'Immediately after' (anantaraṃ) refers to the immediately preceding past. 'There' (amutrā) means in such-and-such an existence. 'I arose' (udapādiṃ) means I was born. 'By those deities' (tāhi devatāhi) refers to the Tusita deities. 'Of one lineage' (ekagotto) means of the Tusita lineage. With the intention that for great Bodhisattas, in the final state of their continuity, the kamma that generates rebirth in a devaloka is indeed unafflicted by unwholesome kamma, it is said, 'But suffering is only the suffering of formations.' However, even for devaputtas of great merit, the conjunction with undesirable objects does occur at times, such as when the preliminary signs of death appear. Thus, it cannot be said that 'there is never any occurrence of the suffering of suffering.' 'Fifty-seven... up to ... the limit' refers to the counting of years by humans. For the devas, however, it is only four thousand.

Atītabhave (sārattha. ṭī. 1.12.pubbenivāsakathāyaṃ) khandhā tappaṭibaddhanāmagottāni ca sabbaṃ pubbenivāsanteva saṅgahitanti āha “kiṃ viditaṃ karoti? Pubbenivāsa”nti. Moho paṭicchādakaṭṭhena “tamo”ti vuccati “tamo viyā”ti katvā. Obhāsakaraṇaṭṭhenāti [M 1.0225] kātabbato karaṇaṃ, obhāsova karaṇaṃ, attano paccayena obhāsabhāvena nibbattetabbaṭṭhenāti attho. Sesaṃ pasaṃsāvacananti paṭipakkhavidhamanapavattivisesānaṃ bodhanato vuttaṃ. Avijjā vihatāti etena vijjanaṭṭhena vijjāti ayampi attho dīpitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yasmā vijjā uppannāti etena vijjāpaṭipakkhā avijjā, paṭipakkhatā cassā pahātabbabhāvena vijjāya ca pahāyakabhāvenāti dasseti. Esa nayo itarasmimpi padadvayeti iminā tamo vihato vinaṭṭho. Kasmā? Yasmā āloko uppannoti imamatthaṃ atidisati. Pesitattassāti yathādhippetatthasiddhiṃ pati vissaṭṭhacittassa. Yathā appamattassāti aññassapi kassaci mādisassāti adhippāyo.

In a past existence (Sāratthaṭīkā 1.12, in the discourse on past dwelling), the aggregates, and the names and clans connected to them—all are included in 'past dwelling' (pubbenivāsa). Hence, it is said: 'What does one know? Past dwelling.' Delusion, due to its nature of concealing, is called 'darkness' (tamo), thus 'like darkness.' 'By the meaning of producing light' means that the making is of what is to be made; light itself is the making. The meaning is: because it has to be produced by its own condition as the state of light. The rest are words of praise; this is said because it makes known the particulars of the occurrence of the destruction of the opponent. By 'Ignorance is destroyed,' it should be seen that this meaning of 'knowledge' (vijjā) as 'knowing' is also illuminated. By 'Because knowledge has arisen,' it shows that ignorance is the opposite of knowledge, and its opposition is by way of its being what is to be abandoned and knowledge being the abandoner. This is the method in the other pair of words as well; by this, it applies by extension the meaning: 'darkness is destroyed, annihilated.' Why? 'Because light has arisen.' 'Of one whose mind is sent forth' (pesitattassa) means of one whose mind is released towards the achievement of the intended purpose. 'Like one who is heedful' (yathā appamattassa) means the intention is 'like any other heedful person such as myself.'

Pubbenivāsakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the discourse on past dwelling is concluded.

Dibbacakkhuñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Divine Eye

53. Idhāti bhayabheravasutte vuttaṃ. Idha ayaṃ visesoti yojanā. Vuttasadisameva “meti mayā”tiādinā. Parikammakiccanti “abhiññāpādakacatutthajjhānato vuṭṭhāya sabbapacchimā nisajjā āvajjitabbā”tiādinā, kasiṇārammaṇaṃ abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ sabbākārena abhinīhārakkhamaṃ katvā”tiādinā ca vuttena parikammena kiccaṃ payojanaṃ natthi. Na [V 1.0201] tena idha atthoti tena bhāvanānayena idha pāḷiyā atthavaṇṇanāyaṃ attho natthi tathābhāvanāya idha anadhippetattāti adhippāyo.

53. 'Here' means as stated in the Bhayabherava Sutta. The connection is: 'Here, this is the distinction.' It is just as was stated in 'by me,' and so on. Regarding the preparatory function, there is no need for or purpose in the preparatory work stated as: 'after emerging from the fourth jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge, the very last sitting should be adverted to,' and so on, and 'having made the kasiṇa object, the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge, capable of being directed in every way,' and so on. 'There is no purpose in that here' means: by that method of development, there is no purpose here in the explanation of the meaning of the Pāli text, because such a development is not intended here. This is the intention.

Dibbacakkhuñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the discourse on the knowledge of the divine eye is concluded.

Āsavakkhayañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints

54. Vipassanāpādakanti (sārattha. ṭī. 1.14.āsavakkhayañāṇakathāyaṃ; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.248; a. ni. ṭī. 2.3.59) vipassanāya padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ. Vipassanā ca tividhā vipassanakapuggalabhedena. Mahābodhisattānañhi paccekabodhisattānañca vipassanā cintāmayañāṇasaṃvaddhitattā sayambhuñāṇabhūtā, itaresaṃ [M 1.0226] sutamayañāṇasaṃvaddhitattā paropadesasambhūtā, sā “ṭhapetvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ avasesarūpārūpajjhānānaṃ aññatarato vuṭṭhāyā”tiādinā anekadhā arūpamukhavasena catudhātuvavatthāne vuttānaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ dhātupariggahamukhānaṃ aññataramukhavasena anekadhāva visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.306) nānānayato vibhāvitā. Mahābodhisattānaṃ pana catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassamukhena pabhedagamanato nānānayaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇasannissayassa ariyamaggañāṇassa adhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ pubbabhāgañāṇagabbhaṃ gaṇhāpentaṃ paripākaṃ gacchantaṃ paramagambhīrasaṇhasukhumataraṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ hoti, yaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu mahāvajirañāṇanti vuccati. Yassa ca pavattivibhāgena catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassappabhedassa pādakabhāvena samāpajjiyamānā catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhā devasikaṃ satthu vaḷañjanakasamāpattiyo vuccanti, svāyaṃ buddhānaṃ vipassanācāro paramatthamañjūsāya visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāya (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.144) uddesato dassito, atthikehi tato gahetabboti.

54. 'Basis for insight' (vipassanāpādakaṃ) means that which is the proximate cause for insight. And insight is threefold, according to the division of individuals who practice insight. For the great Bodhisattas and for Paccekabodhisattas, insight is self-originated knowledge, as it is developed by wisdom born of reflection. For others, it is produced from the instruction of another, as it is developed by wisdom born of learning. That insight is analyzed in various ways in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 1.306) according to various methods, by way of any of those modes of apprehending the elements mentioned in the classification of the four elements—such as 'having arisen from any of the remaining form or formless jhānas apart from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,' and so on, by way of the formless. But for the great Bodhisattas, as it proceeds by way of twenty-four hundred thousand crore methods, the insight-knowledge is extremely profound, subtle, and more refined, unique to themselves, which, as it matures, causes the grasping of the embryonic preliminary knowledge that is the foundation for the noble path knowledge which relies on omniscience. This is called 'the great diamond knowledge' (mahāvajirañāṇa) in the commentaries. And the twenty-four hundred thousand crore concentrations which are entered into as the basis for the twenty-four hundred thousand crore divisions of its occurrence are called the Master's daily 'concentrations for use' (vaḷañjanakasamāpattiyo). This course of insight of the Buddhas is shown summarily in the Paramatthamañjūsā, the commentary on the Visuddhimagga (Vism-mhṭ. 1.144). It should be understood from there by those who are interested.

Āsavānaṃ khepanato samucchindanato āsavakkhayo, ariyamaggo, ukkaṭṭhaniddesavasena arahattamaggaggahaṇaṃ. Āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇaṃ āsavakkhayañāṇanti dassento “tatra cetaṃ ñāṇa”nti vatvā khayeti ca ādhāre bhummaṃ, na visayeti dassento “tappariyā pannattā”ti āha. Idaṃ dukkhanti dukkhassa ariyasaccassa tadā paccakkhato gahitabhāvadassanaṃ. Ettakaṃ dukkhanti dukkhassa ariyasaccassa tadā paccakkhato gahitabhāvadassanaṃ. Ettakaṃ dukkhanti tassa paricchijja gahitabhāvadassanaṃ. Na ito bhiyyoti anavasesetvā gahitabhāvadassanaṃ. Tenāha “sabbampi [V 1.0202] dukkhasacca”ntiādi. Sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhenāti sabhāvasaṅkhātassa lakkhaṇassa asammohato paṭivijjhanena. Asammohapaṭivedhoti ca yathā tasmiṃ ñāṇe pavatte pacchā dukkhassa sarūpādiparicchede sammoho na hoti, tathā pavatti. Tenāha “yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsi”nti. Yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvāti yaṃ nibbānaṃ maggassa ārammaṇapaccayaṭṭhena kāraṇabhūtaṃ āgamma. Tadubhayavato hi puggalassa patti tadubhayassa pattīti vuttaṃ. Patvāti vā pāpuṇanahetu. Appavattinti appavattinimittaṃ. Te vā nappavattanti etthāti appavatti, nibbānaṃ. Tassāti dukkhanirodhassa. Sampāpakanti sacchikiriyāvasena sammadeva pāpakaṃ.

The destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya) is so called from their being wasted away and uprooted; it is the noble path, and by way of the highest designation, the path of arahantship is meant. To show that 'the knowledge in the destruction of the taints is the knowledge of the destruction of the taints,' having said 'therein, this knowledge,' and to show that the word 'khaye' (in destruction) is a locative of location, not of object, he says 'it is included therein.' 'This is suffering' shows the state of the noble truth of suffering having been grasped directly at that time. 'This much is suffering' shows the state of its having been grasped by delimiting it. 'Nothing beyond this' shows the state of its having been grasped completely, without remainder. Therefore, he says, 'all is the truth of suffering,' and so on. 'By penetration of the essential characteristic' means by the non-deluded penetration of the characteristic known as own-nature. And 'non-deluded penetration' is an occurrence such that, when that knowledge has occurred, there is subsequently no delusion in the defining of suffering, its nature, and so on. Therefore, he says, 'he fully understood it as it really is.' 'Having reached that state' means having come to Nibbāna, which is the cause by way of being the object-condition for the path. For the attainment of a person possessing both the path and its object is said to be the attainment of both. Or, 'having reached' (patvā) is the cause of reaching (pāpuṇanahetu). 'Non-occurrence' (appavatti) means the sign of non-occurrence. Or, 'they do not occur here' (te vā nappavattanti ettha), thus it is 'non-occurrence' (appavatti), which is Nibbāna. 'Of that' means of the cessation of suffering. 'That which brings to' (sampāpakaṃ) means that which brings to attainment perfectly by way of realization.

Kilesavasenāti [M 1.0227] āsavasaṅkhātakilesavasena. Yasmā āsavānaṃ dukkhasaccapariyāyo tappariyāpannattā, sesasaccānañca taṃsamudayādipariyāyo atthi, tasmā vuttaṃ. “Pariyāyato”ti. Dassento saccānīti yojanā. Āsavānaṃyeva cettha gahaṇaṃ “āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāyā”ti āraddhattā. Tathā hi āsavavimutti sīseneva sabbasaṃkilesavimutti vuttā. “Idaṃ dukkhanti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsi”ntiādinā missakamaggo idha kathitoti “saha vipassanāya koṭippattaṃ maggaṃ kathetī”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha ca saccapaṭivedhassa tadā atītakālikattā “yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsi”nti vatvāpi abhisamayakāle tassa paccuppannataṃ upādāya “evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato”ti vattamānakālena niddeso kato. So ca kāmaṃ maggakkhaṇato paraṃ yāvajjatanā atītakāliko eva, sabbapaṭhamaṃ panassa atītakālikattaṃ phalakkhaṇena veditabbanti āha “vimuccitthāti iminā phalakkhaṇaṃ dassetī”ti. Jānato passatoti vā hetuniddesoyaṃ. Jānanahetu dassanahetu kāmāsavā cittaṃ vimuccitthāti yojanā. Bhavāsavaggahaṇeneva cettha bhavarāgassa viya bhavadiṭṭhiyāpi samavarodhoti diṭṭhāsavassapi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

By way of defilements means by way of the defilements designated as taints. Because the taints are included under the aspect of the truth of suffering, and the other truths also have their aspects, such as origin and so on, therefore it is said, 'By way of aspect.' The construction is: 'showing the truths.' Here, only the taints are taken up, because it was begun with 'for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.' For indeed, liberation from the taints is described as the foremost of all liberations from defilements. The mixed path is explained here by such phrases as 'He fully understood as it really is, “This is suffering,”' and so on; therefore it is said, 'he teaches the path that has reached its culmination together with insight.' And here, since the penetration of the truths was past at that time, even though it is said, 'he fully understood as it really is,' the description is made in the present tense—'for one who knows thus, who sees thus'—by taking into account its presentness at the time of realization. And although that is indeed past from the moment of the path up until today, its being past in the very first instance is to be understood by the moment of fruition; therefore, it is said, '“he was liberated”—by this he shows the moment of fruition.' Alternatively, 'for one who knows, who sees' is an indication of the cause. The construction is: because of knowing, because of seeing, the mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire. And here, it should be seen that by the grasping of the taint of existence, just as craving for existence is included, so too is the view of existence; thus the taint of views is also included.

Khīṇājātītiādīhi padehi. Tassāti paccavekkhaṇañāṇassa. Bhūmīnti pavattiṭṭhānaṃ. Na tāvassa atītā jāti khīṇā maggabhāvanāyāti adhippāyo. Tattha kāraṇamāha “pubbeva khīṇattā”ti. Na anāgatā assajāti khīṇāti yojanā. Na anāgatāti ca anāgatattasāmaññaṃ gahetvā lesena codeti. Tenāha “anāgate vāyāmābhāvato”ti, anāgataviseso panettha adhippeto, tassa ca khepane vāyāmopi labbhateva. Tenāha “yā pana maggassā”tiādi. Ekacatupañcavokārabhavesūti bhavattayaggahaṇaṃ vuttanayena anavasesato jātiyā khīṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Tanti yathāvuttaṃ jātiṃ. Soti bhagavā.

By the words 'birth is destroyed,' and so on. Of that means of the knowledge of reviewing. Ground means the place of occurrence. The intention is that his past birth is not destroyed by the development of the path. There, he states the reason: 'because it was destroyed before.' The connection is: 'his future birth is not destroyed.' And by 'not future,' taking the general nature of the future, he subtly questions. Therefore, he says, 'due to the absence of effort in the future.' However, a specific future is intended here, and effort can indeed be applied to eliminate it. Therefore, he says, 'but that which is of the path,' and so on. 'In one, four, or five-constituent existences' means the grasping of the three states of existence, stated to show the complete destruction of birth in the manner explained. That means birth as previously described. He means the Blessed One.

Brahmacariyavāso nāma idha maggabrahmacariyassa nibbattanamevāti āha “niṭṭhita”nti. Sammādiṭṭhiyā [V 1.0203] catūsu saccesu pariññādikiccasādhanavasena pavattamānāya sammā saṅkappādīnampi dukkhasacce pariññābhisamayānuguṇā pavatti, itarasaccesu ca nesaṃ pahānābhisamayādivasena pavatti pākaṭā eva. Tena vuttaṃ “catūhi maggehi pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanāvasenā”ti. Itthattāyāti ime pakārā itthaṃ, tabbhāvo itthattaṃ, tadatthanti vuttaṃ [M 1.0228] hoti. Te pana pakārā ariyamaggabyāpārabhūtā pariññādayo idhādhippetāti āha “evaṃsoḷasakiccabhāvāyā”ti. Te hi maggaṃ paccavekkhato maggānubhāvena pākaṭā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, pariññādīsu ca pahānameva padhānaṃ tadatthattā itaresanti āha “kilesakkhayāyavā”ti. Pahīnakilesapaccavekkhaṇavasena vā etaṃ vuttaṃ. Itthattāyāti nissakke sampadānavacananti āha “itthabhāvato”ti. Aparaṃ anāgataṃ. Ime pana carimattabhāvasaṅkhātā pañcakkhandhā. Pariññātā tiṭṭhantīti etena tesaṃ appatiṭṭhataṃ dasseti. Apariññāmūlakā hi patiṭṭhā. Yathāha “kabaḷīkāre ce, bhikkhave, āhāre atthi rāgo atthi nandī atthi taṇhā, patiṭṭhitaṃ tattha viññāṇaṃ virūḷha”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.64; mahāni. 7; kathā. 296). Tenevāha “chinnamūlakā rukkhā viyā”tiādi.

The holy life here means the production of the path of the holy life; thus he says, 'it is accomplished.' When right view is functioning in the four truths by way of accomplishing duties such as full understanding, then the operation of right thought and so on is also in accordance with the realization of the truth of suffering through full understanding, and their operation in the other truths by way of abandonment, realization, and so on, is evident. Therefore, it is said, 'through the four paths, by means of full understanding, abandonment, realization, and development.' 'For this state' (itthattāya) means 'these modes are thus,' and their being thus is 'this state'; for that purpose, it is said. But these modes, which are the activities of the noble path, such as full understanding, are intended here; thus he says, 'for the state of having sixteen functions.' For when one reflects on the path, these become evident through the power of the path and appear. And among full understanding and the rest, abandonment is primary, as the others are for that purpose; thus he says, 'or for the destruction of defilements.' Or this is said by way of reflecting on the abandoned defilements. The word 'itthattāya' is a dative of purpose indicating finality; thus he says 'itthabhāvato' ('from the state of being thus'). 'Aparaṃ' means 'future'. But these five aggregates are what is designated as the final existence. By 'they remain fully understood,' he shows their non-establishment. For establishment is indeed rooted in non-full-understanding. As it is said: 'Monks, if there is lust, delight, or craving for edible food, consciousness becomes established there and grows,' and so on (SN 12.63; Mahāni. 7; Kathā. 296). Therefore, he says, 'like trees with their roots cut off,' and so on.

Paccavekkhaṇañāṇapariggahitaṃ, na paṭhamadutiyañāṇadvayādhigamaṃ viya kevalanti adhippāyo. Dassento nigamanavasenāti adhippāyo. Sarūpato hi taṃ pubbe dassitamevāti. Pubbenivāsañāṇena atītārammaṇasabhāgatāya tabbhāvībhāvato ca atītaṃsañāṇaṃ saṅgahetvāti yojanā. Tattha atītaṃsañāṇanti atītakhandhāyatanadhātusaṅkhāte atītakoṭṭhāse appaṭihataṃ ñāṇaṃ. Dibbacakkhunāti saparibhaṇḍena dibbacakkhuñāṇena. Paccuppannaṃso ca anāgataṃso ca paccuppannānāgataṃsaṃ, tattha ñāṇaṃ paccuppannānāgataṃsañāṇaṃ. Sakalalokiyalokuttaraguṇanti etena sabbaṃ lokaṃ uttaritvā abhibhuyya ṭhitattā sabbaññutaññāṇassa viya sesāsādhāraṇañāṇassa balañāṇaāveṇikabuddhadhammādīnampi anaññasādhāraṇānaṃ buddhaguṇānaṃ saṅgaho veditabbo. Tenāha “sabbepi sabbaññuguṇe saṅgahetvā”ti.

It is encompassed by reviewing knowledge, not merely like the attainment of the first two knowledges—this is the meaning. Showing by way of conclusion—this is the meaning. For it has already been shown in its own nature. By the knowledge of past existences, due to having the past as its object and because of its connection to that state, it includes the knowledge of the past dimension—this is the construction. Here, 'knowledge of the past dimension' refers to unimpeded knowledge regarding the past portion, designated as the past aggregates, sense bases, and elements. 'With the divine eye' means with the divine eye knowledge with its accompanying factors. The present dimension and the future dimension are the present-and-future dimension; the knowledge therein is the knowledge of the present-and-future dimension. By 'all mundane and supramundane qualities,' it should be understood that, since it stands having transcended and overcome the entire world, like omniscience, this includes other knowledges not shared by others, such as the knowledge of the powers, the unique qualities of a Buddha, and other unequalled Buddha-qualities. Therefore, it is said: 'Having included all the qualities of the Omniscient One.'

Āsavakkhayañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints is concluded.

Araññavāsakāraṇavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Reasons for Dwelling in the Forest

55. Siyā kho pana te brāhmaṇāti ettha siyāti “appevā”ti iminā samānattho nipāto[V 1.0204], tasmā ‘brāhmaṇa, appeva kho pana te evamassā’ti [M 1.0229] attho. Yaṃ pana aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “kadācī”ti vuttaṃ, tampi imamevatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ akāraṇaṃ brāhmaṇena parikappitamatthaṃ paṭipakkhipitvā attano adhippetaṃ kāraṇaṃ dassento. Atthova phalaṃ tadadhīnavuttitāya vaso etassāti atthavaso, hetūti evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Attano ca diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāranti etena satthā attano vivekābhiratiṃ pakāsetīti dassento “diṭṭhadhammo nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha iriyāpathavihārānanti iriyāpathapavattīnaṃ. Tappavattiyo hi ekasmiṃ iriyāpathe uppannadukkhaṃ aññena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā haraṇato vihārāti vuccanti. Pacchimañca janataṃ anukampamānoti etena yo ādito brāhmaṇena “bhavaṃ tesaṃ gotamo pubbaṅgamo…pe… diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjatī”ti vutto, yo ca tathā “evametaṃ brāhmaṇā”tiādinā attanā sampaṭicchito, tameva atthaṃ nigamanavasena dassento yathānusandhināva satthā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

55. "It might be, brahmin"—here, 'siyā' is a particle with the same meaning as 'appeva'; therefore the meaning is: "Brahmin, perhaps it might be thus for you." What is stated in the commentary as 'sometimes' (kadācī) is also said with this very meaning in mind, rejecting the brahmin's baseless assumption and presenting his own intended reason. The meaning ('attho') itself is the fruit; its dependence ('vaso') is so called because its occurrence is dependent on that; hence 'atthavaso' (dependent on meaning). Or, the meaning here should be understood as 'cause' ('hetu'). By "And for my own pleasant abiding in this very life," the Teacher reveals his own delight in seclusion, showing it by saying, "what is called the seen dhamma," and so on. Here, 'abidings in postures' refers to 'the occurrences of the postures.' For these occurrences are called 'abidings' because they remove the suffering that has arisen in one posture by cutting it off with another posture. By "And out of compassion for the future generation," the Teacher concluded the teaching in accordance with the sequence, showing by way of conclusion the very meaning that was initially stated by the brahmin ("The Venerable Gotama is their forerunner... follows their example") and later accepted by him ("So it is, brahmin," etc.).

Araññavāsakāraṇavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Reasons for Dwelling in the Forest is concluded.

Desanānumodanāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Appreciation of the Teaching

56. Evaṃ niṭṭhāpitāya desanāya brāhmaṇo tattha bhagavati pasādaṃ pavedento “abhikkanta”ntiādimāha. Abhikkantāti (sārattha. ṭī. 1.15.desanānumodanakathā; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.250; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.1; a. ni. ṭī. 2.2.16) atikkantā, vigatāti atthoti āha “khaye dissatī”ti. Teneva hi “nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo”ti vuttaṃ. Abhikkantataroti ativiya kantataro manoramo. Tādiso ca sundaro bhaddako nāma hotīti āha “sundare dissatī”ti.

56. When the teaching was thus concluded, the brahmin, expressing his faith in the Blessed One, said, "Excellent," and so on. 'Abhikkanta' means 'surpassed,' 'gone beyond'—this is the meaning; thus it is said, "it is seen in the sense of destruction." For this reason, it is said, "The first watch has departed." 'Abhikkantatara' means 'exceedingly pleasing,' 'most delightful.' And such a thing is called beautiful and auspicious; thus it is said, "it is seen in the sense of the beautiful."

Koti devanāgayakkhagandhabbādīsu ko katamo. Meti mama. Pādānīti pāde. Iddhiyāti imāya evarūpāya deviddhiyā. Yasasāti iminā edisena parivārena parijanena. Jalanti vijjotamāno. Abhikkantenāti ativiya kantena kamanīyena abhirūpena. Vaṇṇenāti chavivaṇṇena sarīravaṇṇanibhāya. Sabbā obhāsayaṃ disāti dasapi disā obhāsento pabhāsento, cando viya sūriyo viya ca ekobhāsaṃ ekālokaṃ [M 1.0230] karontoti gāthāya attho. Abhirūpeti uḷārarūpe sampannarūpe.

Among gods, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and so on, who is this? Which one? "Me" means "mine." "Pādāni" means "feet." "By power" (iddhiyā) means "by this kind of divine power." "By glory" (yasasā) means "by this kind of retinue and following." "Shining" (jalanti) means "shining forth." "Most excellent" (abhikkantena) means "exceedingly pleasing, lovely, and beautiful." "By complexion" (vaṇṇena) refers to "by skin color, by the radiance of the body's complexion." "Illuminating all directions" (sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā) means "illuminating and shining in all ten directions, making a single radiance and light like the moon and the sun"—this is the meaning of the verse. "Beautiful" (abhirūpe) means "in magnificent form, in perfect form."

“Coro [V 1.0205] coro, sappo sappo”tiādīsu bhaye āmeḍitaṃ. “Vijjha vijjha, pahara paharā”tiādīsu kodhe, “sādhu sādhūtiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.327; saṃ. ni. 2.127; 3.35; 5.1085) pasaṃsāyaṃ, “gaccha gaccha, lunāhi lunāhī”tiādīsu turite, “āgaccha āgacchā”tiādīsu kotūhale, “buddho buddhoti cintento”tiādīsu (bu. vaṃ. 2.44) acchare, “abhikkamathāyasmanto, abhikkamathāyasmanto”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.20; a. ni. 9.11) hāse, “kahaṃ ekaputtaka, kahaṃ ekaputtakā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.353; saṃ. ni. 2.63) soke, “aho sukhaṃ aho sukha”ntiādīsu (udā. 20; dī. ni. 3.305; cūḷava. 332) pasāde. Ca-saddo avuttasamuccayattho. Tena garahāasammānādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tattha “pāpo pāpo”tiādīsu garahāyaṃ. “Abhirūpaka abhirūpakā”tiādīsu asammāne daṭṭhabbaṃ.

"Thief, thief! Snake, snake!" and so on, is repetition in fear. "Shoot, shoot! Strike, strike!" and so on, is in anger. "Good, good!" and so on, is in praise. "Go, go! Cut, cut!" and so on, is in urgency. "Come, come!" and so on, is in eagerness. "Thinking 'Buddha, Buddha!'" and so on, is in astonishment. "Come forth, venerables, come forth, venerables!" and so on, is in laughter. "Where is my only child? Where is my only child?" and so on, is in sorrow. "Ah, happiness! Ah, happiness!" and so on, is in faith. The word "ca" (and) is for including what is unstated. Therefore, the inclusion of censure, disrespect, and so on should be understood. Here, "Wicked, wicked!" and so on, is in censure. "Handsome, handsome!" and so on, should be understood as disrespect.

Nayidaṃ āmeḍitavasena dvikkhattuṃ vuttaṃ, atha kho atthadvayavasenāti dassento “atha vā”tiādimāha. Abhikkantanti vacanaṃ apekkhitvā napuṃsakaliṅgavasena vuttaṃ, taṃ pana bhagavato vacanaṃ dhammassa desanāti katvā tathā vuttaṃ. Atthamattadassanaṃ vā etaṃ, tasmā atthavasena liṅgavibhattivipariṇāmo veditabbo. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Dosanāsanatoti rāgādikilesadosavidhamanato, guṇādhigamanatoti sīlādiguṇānaṃ sampāpanato. Ye guṇe desanā adhigameti, tesu padhānabhūtā dassetabbāti te padhānabhūte tāva dassetuṃ “saddhājananato paññājananato”ti vuttaṃ. Saddhāpamukhā hi lokiyā guṇā, paññāpamukhā lokuttarā. Sīlādiatthasampattiyā sātthato, sabhāvaniruttisampattiyā sabyañjanato. Suviññeyyasaddapayogatāya uttānapadato, saṇhasukhumabhāvena dubbiññeyyatthatāya gambhīratthato. Siniddhamudumadhurasaddapayogatāya kaṇṇasukhato, vipulavisuddhapemanīyatthatāya hadayaṅgamato. Mānātimānavidhamanena anattukkaṃsanato, thambhasārambhamaddanena aparavambhanato. Hitādhippāyapavattiyā paresaṃ rāgapariḷāhādivūpasamanena ca karuṇāsītalato, kilesandhakāravidhamanena [M 1.0231] paññāvadātato. Karavīkarutamañjutāya āpātharamaṇīyato, pubbāparāviruddhasuvisuddhatthatāya vimaddakkhamato. Āpātharamaṇīyatāya eva suyyamānasukhato, vimaddakkhamatāya hitajjhāsayappavattitatāya ca vīmaṃsiyamānahitato. Evamādīhīti ādisaddena saṃsāracakkanivattanato, saddhammacakkappavattanato, micchāvādavidhamanato, sammāvādapatiṭṭhāpanato, akusalamūlasamuddharaṇato, kusalamūlasaṃropanato, apāyadvārapidhānato, saggamaggadvāravivaraṇato, pariyuṭṭhānavūpasamanato, anusayasamugghātanatoti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

This was not stated twice by way of repetition, but to show the twofold meaning; therefore, he said "or else" and so on. The word "excellent" (abhikkantaṃ) is used in the neuter gender with reference to the statement; it is said thus because the Blessed One's statement is the teaching of the Dhamma. Or, this is merely a showing of the meaning; therefore, the change in gender and inflection should be understood according to the meaning. The same method applies to the second phrase. "Removing faults" means dispelling the defilement-faults such as lust; "attaining virtues" means achieving qualities such as virtue. Those qualities that the teaching leads to attainment—among them, the principal ones should be shown. Therefore, to show those principal ones, it is said: "by generating faith, by generating wisdom." For mundane qualities are headed by faith, while supramundane qualities are headed by wisdom. "Meaningful" (sāttha) refers to the attainment of meaning such as virtue; "with good expression" (sabyañjana) refers to the attainment of natural expression. "With clear phrasing" (uttānapada) means easy to understand due to the use of easily comprehensible words; "with profound meaning" (gambhīrattha) means difficult to grasp due to its subtle nature. "Pleasing to the ear" (kaṇṇasukha) means delightful due to the use of smooth, soft, and sweet words; "captivating the heart" (hadayaṅgama) means inspiring profound and pure affection. "Without self-praise" (anattukkaṃsana) means dispelling conceit and excessive pride; "without disparaging others" (aparavambhana) means crushing stubbornness and contention. "Cool with compassion" (karuṇāsītala) means acting with a wish for others' welfare and calming their fever of lust and so on; "radiant with wisdom" (paññāvadāta) means dispelling the darkness of defilements. "Beautiful as a karavīka bird's call" (karavīkarutamañjuta) means delightful at first hearing; "capable of analysis" (vimaddakkhama) means perfectly pure and without contradictions. "Delightful to hear" (suyyamānasukha) means pleasant when heard due to its immediate charm; "beneficial when examined" (vīmaṃsiyamānahita) means beneficial when examined, arising from a wish for welfare. "And so on" (evamādīhi) —by this word "and so on," the following should be understood: stopping the wheel of saṃsāra, turning the wheel of the true Dhamma, dispelling wrong views, establishing right doctrine, uprooting unwholesome roots, planting wholesome roots, closing the doors to the lower realms, opening the doors to the heavenly path, calming the obsessions, and eradicating the underlying tendencies.

Adhomukhaṭṭhapitanti [V 1.0206] kenaci adhomukhaṃ ṭhapitaṃ. Heṭṭhāmukhajātanti sabhāveneva heṭṭhāmukhajātaṃ. Ugghāṭeyyāti vivaṭaṃ kareyya. Hatthe gahetvāti “puratthābhimukho, uttarābhimukho vā gacchā”tiādīni avatvā hatthe gahetvā “nissandehaṃ esa maggo, evaṃ gacchā”ti vadeyya. Kāḷapakkhacātuddasīti kāḷapakkhe cātuddasī.

"Placed face down" (adhomukhaṭṭhapita) means placed face down by someone. "Naturally facing downward" (heṭṭhāmukhajāta) means naturally arisen facing downward. "Should open" (ugghāṭeyya) means should make it open. "Having taken by the hand" (hatthe gahetvā) means without saying things like, "Go facing east or north," but having taken them by the hand, one should say, "This is the certain path, go thus." "The fourteenth of the dark fortnight" (kāḷapakkhacātuddasī) means the fourteenth day in the dark fortnight.

Nikujjitaṃ ādheyyassa anādhārabhūtaṃ bhājanaṃ ādhārabhāvāpādanavasena ukkujjeyya. Heṭṭhāmukhajātatāya saddhammavimukhaṃ, adhomukhaṭṭhapitatāya asaddhamme patitanti evaṃ padadvayaṃ yathārahaṃ yojetabbaṃ, na yathāsaṅkhyaṃ. Kāmaṃ kāmacchandādayopi paṭicchādakā, micchādiṭṭhi pana savisesaṃ paṭicchādikāti āha “micchādiṭṭhigahanapaṭicchanna”nti. Tenāha bhagavā “micchādiṭṭhiparamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, vajjaṃ vadāmī”ti (a. ni. 1.310). Sabbo apāyagāmimaggo kummaggo “kucchito maggo”ti katvā. Sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ ujupaṭipakkhatāya micchādiṭṭhiādayo aṭṭha micchattadhammā micchāmaggo. Teneva hi tadubhayapaṭipakkhataṃ sandhāya “saggamokkhamaggaṃ ācikkhantenā”ti vuttaṃ. Sappiādisannissayo padīpo na tathā ujjalo, yathā telasannissayoti telapajjotaggahaṇaṃ. Etehi pariyāyehīti etehi nikujjitukkujjanapaṭicchannavivaraṇādiupamopamitabbapakārehi, etehi vā yathāvuttehi soḷasārammaṇapariggahaasammohavihāradibbavihāravibhāvanapariyāyehi vijjāttayavibhāvanāpadesena attano sabbaññuguṇavibhāvanapariyāyehi ca. Tenāha “anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito”ti.

One should set upright an overturned vessel, which is not a support for what is to be placed in it, in order to make it a support. Due to being born with a downward-facing mouth, one turns away from the true Dhamma; due to being placed upside down, one falls into false teachings—these two phrases should be applied appropriately, not according to numerical order. Indeed, sensual desire and similar things are concealers, but wrong view is especially a concealer—hence it is said, "concealed by the thicket of wrong view." Therefore, the Blessed One declared, "Monks, I say that wrong view is the most reprehensible fault." All paths leading to the lower realms are wrong paths, hence called "the despicable path." Because right view and the like are direct opposites, the eight wrong qualities—beginning with wrong view—constitute the wrong path. For this very reason, referring to the opposition between the two, it is said, "by one pointing out the path to heaven and liberation." A lamp dependent on ghee and such does not shine as brightly as one dependent on oil—hence the choice of an oil lamp. "By these methods"—by these methods of overturning, setting upright, concealing, revealing, and other illustrative comparisons; or by these aforementioned methods for the exposition of grasping the sixteen objects, abiding in non-delusion, and divine abiding; by means of the exposition of the threefold knowledge, and by methods of expounding the qualities of his own omniscience. Thus it is said, "the Dhamma has been illuminated in many ways."

Desanānumodanāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The description of rejoicing in the teaching is completed.

Pasannakāravaṇṇanā

The Description of the Cause of Faith.

Pasannakāranti [M 1.0232] pasannehi kātabbaṃ sakkāraṃ. Saraṇanti paṭisaraṇaṃ. Tenāha “parāyaṇa”nti. Parāyaṇabhāvo ca anatthanisedhanena atthasampaṭipādanena ca hotīti āha “aghassa tātā hitassa ca vidhātā”ti. Aghassāti dukkhatoti vadanti, pāpatoti pana yuttaṃ. Nissakke cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Ettha ca nāyaṃ gami-saddo nī-saddādayo viya dvikammako, tasmā yathā “ajaṃ gāmaṃ netī”ti vuccati, evaṃ “gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti vattuṃ na sakkā, “saraṇanti gacchāmī”ti pana vattabbaṃ. Iti-saddo cettha luttaniddiṭṭho, tassa cāyamattho – gamanañca tadadhippāyena bhajanaṃ, tathā jānanaṃ vāti dassento “iti iminā adhippāyenā”tiādimāha[V 1.0207]. Tattha bhajāmītiādīsu purimassa purimassa pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ atthavacanaṃ. Bhajanaṃ vā saraṇādhippāyena upasaṅkamanaṃ, sevanaṃ santikāvacaratā, payirupāsanaṃ vattapaṭivattakaraṇena upaṭṭhānanti evaṃ sabbathāpi anaññasaraṇataṃyeva dīpeti. “Gacchāmī”ti padassa kathaṃ “bujjhāmī”ti ayamattho labbhatīti āha “yesañhī”tiādi.

“Pasannakāranti” means the respect that should be shown by the faithful. “Saraṇa” means refuge. Therefore, it is said, “parāyaṇa” (ultimate resort). And the state of being an ultimate resort arises by preventing what is harmful and providing what is beneficial, as stated: “the protector from evil and the provider of welfare.” “Aghassa” is said to mean “of suffering”; however, “of evil” is more fitting. This is the genitive case in an objective sense. Here, the verb “gam” is not a verb taking two objects, like the verb “nī” and so on. Therefore, just as one says, “He leads a goat to the village,” one cannot say, “I go to Gotama for refuge.” Instead, one should say, “I go to refuge,” where the word “iti” is elided. And its meaning is this: going, associating with that intention, or knowing it as such. This is shown when he says, “with this intention,” etc. Therein, in phrases like “bhajāmi,” and so on, each latter word is an explanation of the meaning of each preceding one. “Bhajana” (associating) is approaching with the intention of taking refuge; “sevana” (serving) is staying near; “payirupāsana” (attending) is waiting upon by performing duties and counter-duties. Thus, in every way, it indicates having no other refuge. How is the meaning “I understand” obtained from the word “gacchāmi”? This is explained when he says, “for those who…” etc.

Adhigatamagge, sacchikatanirodheti padadvayenapi phalaṭṭhā eva dassitā, na maggaṭṭhāti te dassento “yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne cā”ti āha. Nanu ca kalyāṇaputhujjanopi yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjatīti vuccatīti? Kiñcāpi vuccati, nippariyāyena pana maggaṭṭhā eva tathā vattabbā, na itare niyāmokkamanābhāvato. Tathā hi te eva “apāyesu apatamāne dhāretī”ti vuttā. Sammattaniyāmokkamanena hi apāyavinimuttisambhavo. Akkhāyatīti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, pakārattho vā. Tena “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti suttapadaṃ (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90) saṅgaṇhāti, vitthāroti vā iminā. Ettha ca ariyamaggo niyyānikatāya, nibbānaṃ tassa tadatthasiddhihetutāyāti ubhayamevettha nippariyāyena dhammoti vutto. Nibbānañhi ārammaṇapaccayabhūtaṃ labhitvā ariyamaggassa tadatthasiddhi, ariyaphalānaṃ “yasmā tāya saddhāya avūpasantāyā”tiādivacanato maggena samucchinnānaṃ kilesānaṃ paṭippassaddhipahānakiccatāya niyyānānuguṇatāya niyyānapariyosānatāya ca. Pariyattidhammassa pana niyyānadhammasamadhigamahetutāyāti iminā [M 1.0233] pariyāyena dhammabhāvo labbhati eva, svāyamattho pāṭhāruḷho evāti dassento “na kevala”ntiādimāha.

By the two phrases 'one who has attained the path' and 'one who has realized cessation', those standing in the fruit are indicated, not those standing in the path; he shows this by saying, 'and in one who is practicing as instructed.' But is it not said that even a virtuous ordinary person practices as instructed? Although it is said, without qualification it is only those standing in the path who should be spoken of thus, not others, because they have not entered the fixed course. For it is they who are described as 'he holds them back from falling into the states of woe.' For liberation from the states of woe is possible through entering the fixed course of rightness. In the word 'akkhāyati', the particle 'iti' has the sense of 'and so forth' or 'in this manner'. By this, it includes the sutta passage, 'Monks, whatever phenomena there are, conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the chief among them' (A.N. 4.34; Itiv. 90), or this is an elaboration. Herein, both the noble path, because it leads out, and Nibbāna, because it is the cause for the accomplishment of that goal, are called 'Dhamma' without qualification. For the noble path accomplishes its goal by taking Nibbāna as its object-condition; and for the noble fruits, according to the saying, 'because by that faith they are not calmed,' etc., it is through the path's function of pacifying and abandoning the defilements that have been cut off, its suitability for leading out, and its culmination in leading out. As for the Dhamma of learning, its status as Dhamma is obtained in a qualified sense, because it is a cause for attaining the liberating Dhamma. Showing that this meaning is established in the text itself, he says, 'not only,' etc.

Kāmarāgo bhavarāgoti evamādibhedo sabbopi rāgo virajjati pahīyati etenāti rāgavirāgoti maggo kathito. Ejāsaṅkhātāya taṇhāya antonijjhānalakkhaṇassa sokassa ca taduppattiyaṃ sabbaso parikkhīṇattā anejamasokanti phalaṃ kathitaṃ. Appaṭikūlanti avirodhadīpanato kenaci aviruddhaṃ, iṭṭhaṃ paṇītanti vā attho. Paguṇarūpena pavattitattā, pakaṭṭhaguṇavibhāvanato vā paguṇaṃ. Yathāha “vihiṃsasaññī paguṇaṃ na bhāsiṃ, dhammaṃ paṇītaṃ manujesu brahme”ti. Sabbadhammakkhandhā kathitāti yojanā.

Lust for sensual pleasures, lust for existence—all such kinds of lust fade away and are abandoned by means of this; thus, the path is called 'the fading away of lust.' Because craving, known as agitation, and sorrow, which is characterized by internal burning, are completely exhausted upon its arising, the fruit is called 'unagitated and sorrowless.' 'Not repulsive' means it is unopposed by anything, indicating non-opposition; or the meaning is 'desirable and excellent.' 'Proficient' because it proceeds in a proficient manner, or because it makes manifest excellent qualities. As it is said: 'Perceiving violence, I did not speak the proficient, excellent Dhamma among humans, O Brahmā.' The connection is: 'All the aggregates of the Dhamma have been spoken of.'

Diṭṭhisīlasaṅghātenāti “yāyaṃ diṭṭhi ariyā niyyānikā niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya, tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhisāmaññagato viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.324, 356; ma. ni. 1.492; 3.54) evaṃ vuttāya diṭṭhiyā, “yāni tāni sīlāni akhaṇḍāni acchiddāni asabalāni akammāsāni bhujissāni viññuppasatthāni aparāmaṭṭhāni samādhisaṃvattanikāni[V 1.0208], tathārūpehi sīlehi sīlasāmaññagato viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.324; ma. ni. 1.492; 3.54; a. ni. 6.12; pari. 274) evaṃ vuttānaṃ sīlānañca saṃhatabhāvena, diṭṭhisīlasāmaññenāti attho. Saṃhatoti ghaṭito. Ariyapuggalā hi yattha katthaci dūre ṭhitāpi attano guṇasāmaggiyā saṃhatā eva. Aṭṭha ca puggala dhammadasā teti te purisayugavasena cattāropi puggalavasena aṭṭheva ariyadhammassa paccakkhadassāvitāya dhammadasā. Tīṇi vatthūni saraṇanti gamanena tikkhattuṃ gamanena ca tīṇi saraṇagamanāni. Paṭivedesīti attano hadayagataṃ vācāya pavedesi.

“Diṭṭhisīlasaṅghātena” means by the combination of view and virtue; that is, by the commonality of view and virtue. This refers to the view thus spoken of: 'the view that is noble, leading out, that leads one who acts upon it to the complete destruction of suffering; he dwells having attained commonality in such a view' (Dī. Ni. 3.324, etc.); and the virtues thus spoken of: 'the virtues that are unbroken, unbreached, unspotted, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped, and conducive to concentration; he dwells having attained commonality in such virtues' (Dī. Ni. 3.324, etc.). “Combined” means joined. For noble individuals, even when situated far apart, are indeed combined through the harmony of their qualities. And the eight persons are seers of the Dhamma: that is, those who are four in terms of pairs of persons, are eight in terms of individual persons; they are seers of the Dhamma because they directly see the noble Dhamma. “The three objects of refuge” means the three goings for refuge, by the act of going and by going three times. “He declared” means he made known by speech what was in his heart.

Pasannakāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Act of Faith is concluded.

Saraṇagamanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Elucidation of the Discourse on Going for Refuge

Saraṇagamanassa visayapabhedaphalasaṃkilesabhedānaṃ viya kattu ca vibhāvanā tattha kosallāya hotīti “saraṇagamanesu kosallatthaṃ [M 1.0234] saraṇaṃ…pe… veditabbo”ti vuttaṃ tena vinā saraṇagamanasseva asambhavato. Kasmā panettha vodānaṃ na gahitaṃ, nanu vodānavibhāvanāpi tattha kosallāvahāti? Saccametaṃ, taṃ pana saṃkilesaggahaṇeneva atthato dīpitaṃ hotīti na gahitaṃ. Yāni hi tesaṃ saṃkilesakāraṇāni aññāṇādīni, tesaṃ sabbena sabbaṃ anuppannānaṃ anuppādanena, uppannānañca pahānena vodānaṃ hotīti. Hiṃsatthassa sara-saddassa vasenetaṃ padaṃ daṭṭhabbanti “hiṃsatīti saraṇa”nti vatvā taṃ pana hiṃsanaṃ kesaṃ, kathaṃ, kassa vāti codanaṃ sodhento “saraṇagatāna”ntiādimāha. Tattha bhayanti vaṭṭabhayaṃ. Santāsanti cittutrāsaṃ. Teneva cetasikadukkhassa gahitattā dukkhanti idha kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ. Duggatiparikilesanti duggatipariyāpannaṃ sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ. Tayidaṃ sabbaṃ parato phalakathāyaṃ āvi bhavissati. Etanti “saraṇa”nti padaṃ.

The elucidation of the agent, as well as the distinctions of the scope, divisions, results, and defilements of going for refuge, is for the sake of skillfulness therein. Therefore, it is said, 'For the sake of skillfulness in the goings for refuge, refuge… should be understood,' because without this, going for refuge itself is impossible. Why is purification not included here? Is not the elucidation of purification also conducive to skillfulness therein? That is true, but it is not included because it is indicated in meaning by the inclusion of defilements. For purification occurs through the complete non-arising of their unarisen causes—ignorance and so forth—and through the abandoning of those that have arisen. This word should be understood in accordance with the root 'sar,' which has the meaning 'to harm.' Thus, having said, 'It harms, therefore it is a refuge,' he then resolves the objection, 'That harming, of whom is it? How? And of what?' by saying, 'of those who have gone for refuge…' etc. Therein, 'fear' is the fear of the round of existence. 'Terror' is mental agitation. Since mental suffering is included by that very word, 'suffering' here is bodily suffering. 'The defilements of a bad destination' is all suffering included in a bad destination. All this will become clear later in the discourse on the result. This refers to the word 'refuge.'

Evaṃ avisesato saraṇasaddassa atthaṃ dassetvā idāni visesato dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Hite pavattamānenāti “sampannasīlā, bhikkhave, viharathā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.64, 69) atthe niyojanena. Ahitā ca nivattanenāti “pāṇātipātassa kho pāpako vipāko pāpakaṃ abhisamparāya”ntiādinā ādīnavadassanādimukhena anatthato vinivattanena. Bhayaṃ hiṃsatīti hitāhitesu appavattipavattihetukaṃ byasanaṃ appavattikaraṇena vināseti[V 1.0209]. Bhavakantārā uttāraṇena maggasaṅkhāto dhammo, itaro assāsadānena sattānaṃ bhayaṃ hiṃsatīti yojanā. Kārānanti dānavasena pūjāvasena ca upanītānaṃ sakkārānaṃ. Vipulaphalapaṭilābhakaraṇena sattānaṃ bhayaṃ hiṃsati anuttaradakkhiṇeyyabhāvatoti adhippāyo. Imināpi pariyāyenāti imināpi vibhajitvā vuttena kāraṇena.
