Having thus explained the meaning of the term 'refuge' generally, now, to explain it in detail, the phrase 'atha vā' (or) and so on is stated. 'By causing engagement in what is beneficial' means by enjoining to the purpose through such exhortations as, 'Monks, dwell perfected in virtue' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.64, 69). 'And by turning away from what is harmful' means by diverting from what is unbeneficial through the means of showing the dangers and so on, as in, 'Killing living beings has a bad result, a bad future.' 'It destroys fear' means it eliminates the calamity caused by not engaging in what is beneficial and engaging in what is harmful, by causing non-engagement in them. The connection is that the Dhamma, designated as the path, destroys the fear of beings by leading them across the wilderness of existence, and the other (the Buddha and Sangha) by giving assurance. 'Of honors' means of the acts of respect brought by way of giving and by way of veneration. The intention is that it destroys the fear of beings by causing the attainment of abundant fruit, due to being an unsurpassed recipient of offerings. 'By this method too' means by this reason, stated having been analyzed.

“Sammāsambuddho bhagavā, svākkhāto dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṅgho”ti evaṃ pavatto tattha ratanattaye pasādo tappasādo, tadeva ratanattayaṃ garu etassāti taggaru, tassa bhāvo taggarutā, tappasādo ca taggarutā ca tappasādataggarutā, tāhi. Vidhutadiṭṭhivicikicchāsammohaassaddhiyāditāya vihatakileso. “Tadeva ratanattayaṃ parāyaṇaṃ gati [M 1.0235] tāṇaṃ leṇa”nti evaṃ ākārena pavattiyā tapparāyaṇatākārapavatto cittuppādo saraṇagamanaṃ “saraṇanti gacchati etenā”ti. Taṃsamaṅgīti tena yathāvuttacittuppādena samannāgato. Evaṃ upetīti evaṃ bhajati sevati payirupāsati, evaṃ vā jānāti bujjhatīti evamattho veditabbo. Ettha ca pasādaggahaṇena lokiyasaraṇagamanamāha. Tañhi pasādappadhānaṃ, na ñāṇappadhānaṃ. Garutāgahaṇena lokuttaraṃ. Ariyā hi ratanattayaṃ guṇābhiññātāya pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garuṃ katvā passanti, tasmā tappasādena vikkhambhanavasena vihatakileso taggarutāya samucchedavasenāti yojetabbaṃ. Tapparāyaṇatā panettha taggatikatāti tāya catubbidhampi vakkhamānaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ gahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Avisesena vā pasādagarutā jotitāti pasādaggahaṇena aveccappasādassa itarassa ca gahaṇaṃ, tathā garutāgahaṇenāti ubhayenapi ubhayaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

"The Blessed One is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-expounded, the Sangha is practicing the good way"—the faith that has thus arisen in the Triple Gem is 'faith in that' (tappasāda). That very Triple Gem is weighty for this one, thus 'having that as weighty' (taggaru). The state of having that as weighty is 'weightiness in that' (taggarutā). 'Faith in that' and 'weightiness in that' together are 'faith and weightiness in that' (tappasādataggarutā). By these, one's defilements are struck down, having dispelled wrong view, doubt, delusion, lack of faith, and so forth. "That very Triple Gem is the ultimate resort, the destination, the shelter, the protection"—the arising of a mind that occurs in this manner of being devoted to that is 'going for refuge.' 'One goes for refuge by this.' 'Endowed with that' means endowed with the aforementioned arising of mind. 'Thus one approaches' means thus one resorts to, serves, attends upon; or, thus one knows and understands—this meaning should be understood. Here, by the taking up of faith, mundane going for refuge is spoken of, for that is primarily based on faith, not on knowledge. By the taking up of weightiness, the supramundane is indicated. For the noble ones, having directly known its qualities, regard the Triple Gem as weighty, like a stone parasol. Therefore, it should be connected that defilements are struck down by way of suppression through faith in that, and by way of eradication through weightiness in that. Here, 'devotion to that' is having that as one's destination; thus, it should be seen that by it, all four types of going for refuge, which will be explained, are included. Or, faith and weightiness are indicated without distinction; thus, by the taking up of faith, both unwavering faith and the other are included, and similarly by the taking up of weightiness. Thus, by both, both types of going for refuge should be connected.

Maggakkhaṇe ijjhatīti yojanā. Nibbānārammaṇaṃ hutvāti etena atthato catusaccādhigamoyeva lokuttaraṃ saraṇagamananti dasseti. Tattha hi nibbānadhammo sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena, maggadhammo bhāvanābhisamayavasena paṭivijjhiyamānoyeva saraṇagamanattaṃ sādheti, buddhaguṇā pana sāvakagocarabhūtā pariññābhisamayavasena, tathā ariyasaṅghaguṇā. Tenāha “kiccato sakalepi ratanattaye ijjhatī”ti, ijjhantañca saheva ijjhati, na lokiyaṃ viya paṭipāṭiyā asammohapaṭivedhena paṭividdhattāti adhippāyo. Ye pana vadanti “na saraṇagamanaṃ nibbānārammaṇaṃ hutvā pavattati, maggassa adhigatattā pana adhigatameva hoti ekaccānaṃ tevijjādīnaṃ lokiyavijjādayo viyā”ti, tesaṃ lokiyameva saraṇagamanaṃ siyā, na lokuttaraṃ, tañca ayuttaṃ duvidhassapi icchitabbattā. Tanti lokiyasaraṇagamanaṃ. Saddhāpaṭilābho “sammāsambuddho bhagavā”tiādinā. Saddhāmūlikāti yathāvuttasaddhāpubbaṅgamā sammādiṭṭhi buddhasubuddhataṃ dhammasudhammataṃ saṅghasuppaṭipatiñca lokiyāvabodhavaseneva [V 1.0210] sammā ñāyena dassanato. “Saddhāmūlikā sammādiṭṭhī”ti etena saddhūpanissayā yathāvuttalakkhaṇā paññā lokiyasaraṇagamananti dasseti. Tenāha “diṭṭhijukammanti vuccatī”ti “diṭṭhi eva attano paccayehi ujuṃ karīyatī”ti katvā. Diṭṭhi vā ujuṃ karīyati etenāti diṭṭhijukammaṃ, tathā pavatto cittuppādo[M 1.0236]. Evañca katvā “tapparāyaṇatākārapavatto cittuppādo”ti idañca vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. Saddhāpubbaṅgamasammādiṭṭhiggahaṇaṃ pana cittuppādassa tappadhānatāyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Saddhāpaṭilābho”ti iminā mātādīhi ussāhitadārakādīnaṃ viya ñāṇavippayuttasaraṇagamanaṃ dasseti, “sammādiṭṭhī”ti iminā ñāṇasampayuttasaraṇagamanaṃ.

The connection is: it succeeds at the moment of the path. By 'having Nibbāna as its object,' it shows that supramundane going for refuge is, in essence, the very realization of the Four Noble Truths. For there, the Dhamma of Nibbāna, being penetrated by way of realization through direct experience, and the Dhamma of the path, being penetrated by way of realization through development, alone accomplish the state of going for refuge. The qualities of the Buddha, however, being within the range of disciples, are penetrated by way of realization through full understanding, as are the qualities of the Noble Sangha. Hence it is said: 'In function, it succeeds in the entire Triple Gem.' And the intention is that when it succeeds, it succeeds simultaneously, not sequentially like the mundane, because it is penetrated by non-deluded penetration. But those who say, 'Going for refuge does not occur with Nibbāna as its object; rather, because the path is attained, it is already attained—like the mundane knowledges of some, such as the threefold knowledge,' for them, going for refuge would only be mundane, not supramundane. And that is inappropriate, because both kinds are desirable. That is mundane going for refuge. The acquisition of faith is through phrases like 'The Blessed One is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.' 'Rooted in faith' means that right view, preceded by faith as described, is to be seen as correctly discerning the Buddha's perfect enlightenment, the Dhamma's perfect exposition, and the Sangha's excellent practice, solely by way of mundane understanding. By 'right view rooted in faith,' it shows that wisdom characterized as described, dependent on faith, is mundane going for refuge. Hence it is said: 'It is called the straightening of view,' because 'view itself is made straight by its own conditions.' Or, 'view is made straight by this'—thus it is called the straightening of view, and so too the arising of the mind. And so, the phrase 'the arising of the mind in the manner of being devoted to that' is also established. The inclusion of right view preceded by faith, however, should be seen as due to that being primary for the arising of the mind. By 'the acquisition of faith,' it shows going for refuge disconnected from knowledge, like that of children and others encouraged by their mothers and others. By 'right view,' it shows going for refuge connected with knowledge.

Tayidaṃ lokiyaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ. Attā sanniyyātīyati appīyati pariccajīyati etenāti attasanniyyātanaṃ, yathāvuttaṃ diṭṭhijukammaṃ. Taṃ ratanattayaṃ parāyaṇaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ etassāti tapparāyaṇo, puggalo, cittuppādo vā, tassa bhāvo tapparāyaṇatā, yathāvuttadiṭṭhijukammameva. Saraṇanti adhippāyena sissabhāvaṃ antevāsikabhāvaṃ upagacchati etenāti sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ. Saraṇagamanādhippāyeneva paṇipatati etenāti paṇipāto. Sabbattha yathāvuttadiṭṭhijukammavaseneva attho veditabbo. Attapariccajananti saṃsāradukkhanittharaṇatthaṃ attano attabhāvassa pariccajanaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Buddhādīnaṃyevāti avadhāraṇaṃ itaresupi saraṇagamanavisesesu yathārahaṃ vattabbaṃ. Evañhi tadaññanivattanaṃ kataṃ hoti.

This is mundane going for refuge. The self is surrendered, offered, and relinquished by this—thus it is called self-surrender, which is the straightening of view as previously described. That Triple Gem is the ultimate resort, the reliance for this one—thus, one is 'one who has that as their ultimate resort' (tapparāyaṇo), whether a person or an arising of mind. The state of having that as the ultimate resort is 'devotion to that' (tapparāyaṇatā), which is precisely the straightening of view as described. By the intention of going for refuge, one undertakes the state of a disciple, the state of a pupil, by this—thus it is called undertaking discipleship. By the very intention of going for refuge, one bows down by this—thus it is called prostration. In all cases, the meaning should be understood solely by way of the straightening of view as previously described. 'Self-relinquishment' means relinquishing one's own being for the sake of crossing beyond the suffering of saṃsāra. This same principle applies to the remaining cases. The exclusive statement 'only to the Buddha and others' should be applied appropriately to other specific instances of going for refuge. For in this way, the exclusion of what is other than that is accomplished.

Evaṃ attasanniyātanādīni ekena pakārena dassetvā idāni aparehipi pakārehi dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tena pariyāyantarehipi attasanniyyātanādi katameva hoti atthassa abhinnattāti dasseti. Āḷavakādīnanti ādi-saddena sātāgirihemavatādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Nanu cete āḷavakādayo maggeneva āgatasaraṇagamanā, kathaṃ tesaṃ tapparāyaṇatāsaraṇagamanaṃ vuttanti? Maggenāgatasaraṇagamanehipi “so ahaṃ vicarissāmi gāmā gāma”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 1.246) tehi tapparāyaṇatākārassa paveditattā tathā vuttaṃ.

Having thus shown self-surrender and so forth in one way, now, to show them in other ways as well, the phrase 'moreover' and so on is introduced. By this, it shows that even by other methods, self-surrender and so forth are indeed accomplished, due to the non-difference in meaning. Regarding 'Āḷavaka and others'—by the word 'and so on,' the inclusion of Sātāgiri, Hemavata, and others should be understood. But surely, these Āḷavaka and others are ones whose going for refuge came by means of the path? How then is their going for refuge as 'devotion to that' described? Even though they were ones whose going for refuge came by the path, because they declared the manner of being devoted to that with phrases like, 'I will wander from village to village,' it is thus described.

Ñāti…pe… vasenāti ettha ñātivasena bhayavasena ācariyavasena dakkhiṇeyyavasenāti paccekaṃ “vasenā”ti padaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tattha ñātivasenāti ñātibhāvavasena. Evaṃ sesesupi. Dakkhiṇeyyapaṇipātenāti dakkhiṇeyyatāhetukena paṇipātena. Itarehīti ñātibhāvādivasappavattehi tīhi paṇipātehi. Itarehītiādinā saṅkhepato [M 1.0237] vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “tasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vandatīti paṇipātassa lakkhaṇavacanaṃ. Evarūpanti diṭṭhadhammikaṃ [V 1.0211] sandhāya vadati. Samparāyikañhi niyyānikaṃ vā anusāsanaṃ paccāsīsanto dakkhiṇeyyapaṇipātameva karotīti adhippāyo. Saraṇagamanappabhedoti saraṇagamanavibhāgo.

Regarding 'By means of kinship... etc.': here, the term 'by means of' should be connected separately with 'by means of kinship,' 'by means of fear,' 'by means of a teacher,' and 'by means of worthiness of offerings.' Therein, 'by means of kinship' means by way of being a kinsman. So too for the rest. 'By prostration due to worthiness of offerings' means by a prostration caused by the state of being worthy of offerings. 'By the others' means by the three prostrations that proceed by way of kinship and so on. To show in detail the meaning stated concisely by 'by the others,' etc., the passage beginning 'therefore,' etc., is stated. 'Venerates' is a term describing the characteristic of prostration. 'Such a form' is said with reference to the present life. For the intention is that one who hopes for instruction that is for the future life or that leads to deliverance performs only the prostration due to worthiness of offerings. 'The classification of going for refuge' means the division of going for refuge.

Ariyamaggoyeva lokuttarasaraṇagamananti āha “cattāri sāmaññaphalāni vipākaphala”nti. Sabbadukkhakkhayoti sakalassa vaṭṭadukkhassa anuppādanirodho. Etanti “cattāri ariyasaccāni, sammappaññāya passatī”ti (dha. pa. 190) evaṃ vuttaṃ ariyasaccadassanaṃ.

The noble path itself is the supramundane going for refuge, as it is said, 'The four fruits of recluseship are the fruits of fruition.' 'Cessation of all suffering' means the non-arising and cessation of all the suffering of the round of existence. This is the vision of the noble truths, as stated thus: 'One sees the four noble truths with right wisdom' (Dhp. 190).

Niccato anupagamanādivasenāti niccanti aggahaṇādivasena. Aṭṭhānanti hetupaṭikkhepo. Anavakāsoti paccayapaṭikkhepo. Ubhayenapi kāraṇameva paṭikkhipati. Yanti yena kāraṇena. Diṭṭhisampannoti maggadiṭṭhiyā sampanno sotāpanno. Kañci saṅkhāranti catubhūmakesu saṅkhatasaṅkhāresu ekasaṅkhārampi. Niccato upagaccheyyāti “nicco”ti gaṇheyya. Sukhato upagaccheyyāti “ekantasukhī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti (dī. ni. 1.76) evaṃ attadiṭṭhivasena sukhato gāhaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhivippayuttacittena pana ariyasāvako pariḷāhavūpasamanatthaṃ mattahatthiparittāsito viya cokkhabrāhmaṇo ukkārabhūmiṃ kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhato upagacchati. Attavāre kasiṇādipaññattisaṅgahaṇatthaṃ “saṅkhāra”nti avatvā “kañci dhamma”nti vuttaṃ. Imesupi vāresu catubhūmakavaseneva paricchedo veditabbo tebhūmakavaseneva vā. Yaṃ yañhi puthujjano gāhavasena gaṇhāti, tato tato ariyasāvako gāhaṃ viniveṭheti. Mātarantiādīsu janikā mātā, janako pitā, manussabhūto khīṇāsavo arahāti adhippeto. Kiṃ pana ariyasāvako aññaṃ jīvitā voropeyyāti? Etampi aṭṭhānaṃ, puthujjanabhāvassa pana mahāsāvajjabhāvadassanatthaṃ ariyasāvakassa phaladīpanatthañcevaṃ vuttaṃ. Duṭṭhacitto vadhakacittena paduṭṭhacitto. Lohitaṃ uppādeyyāti jīvamānakasarīre khuddakamakkhikāya pivanamattampi lohitaṃ uppādeyya. Saṅghaṃ bhindeyyāti samānasaṃvāsakaṃ samānasīmāyaṃ ṭhitaṃ saṅghaṃ ‘kammena uddesena voharanto anussāvanena salākaggāhenā”ti (pari. 458) evaṃ vuttehi pañcahi kāraṇehi bhindeyya[M 1.0238]. Aññaṃ satthāranti aññaṃ titthakaraṃ “ayaṃ me satthā”ti evaṃ gaṇheyyāti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti attho.

'By not approaching as permanent, etc.' means by not grasping as permanent, etc. 'It is impossible' is a rejection of the cause. 'There is no opportunity' is a rejection of the condition. By both, the reason itself is rejected. 'By which' means by which reason. 'Endowed with view' means a stream-enterer endowed with the view of the path. 'Any conditioned thing' means even a single conditioned phenomenon among the conditioned phenomena of the four planes. 'Were to approach it as permanent' means were to grasp it as 'permanent.' 'Were to approach it as pleasant': this is said with reference to grasping as pleasant by way of the view of self, as in 'the self is entirely happy and healthy after death' (DN 1.76). A noble disciple, however, with a mind dissociated from wrong view, for the sake of allaying distress, might approach some conditioned thing as pleasant, like a fastidious brahmin terrified by a mad elephant grasping a dung-heap. In the section on the self, in order to include concepts such as the kasiṇas, instead of 'conditioned thing,' the words 'any phenomenon' are stated. In these sections, too, the delimitation should be understood as being by way of the four planes, or by way of the three planes. For whatever an ordinary person grasps by way of grasping, from that very thing a noble disciple disentangles that grasping. In 'mother,' etc., the biological mother is intended, the progenitor as father, and a human being who is an arahant with taints destroyed. But would a noble disciple deprive another of life? This, too, is impossible; but this is said to show the great faultiness of the state of an ordinary person and to illustrate the fruit for a noble disciple. 'With a hostile mind' means with a mind corrupted by the intention to kill. 'Were to make blood flow' means were to make flow from a living body even as much blood as a small fly might drink. 'Were to split the Sangha' means were to split a Sangha dwelling in communion within the same boundary by the five reasons stated thus: 'by an act, by a proposal, while transacting business, by an announcement, and by the taking of voting-sticks' (Pari. 458). 'Another teacher' means another sectarian teacher; the meaning is that there exists no possibility that one would grasp such a one, thinking, 'This is my teacher.'

Na te gamissanti apāyabhūminti te buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatā tannimittaṃ apāyabhūmiṃ na gamissanti, devakāyaṃ pana paripūressantīti attho.

'They will not go to the plane of misery' means: those who have gone to the Buddha for refuge will not, on account of that, go to the plane of misery; rather, they will swell the host of gods. This is the meaning.

Dasahi [V 1.0212] ṭhānehīti dasahi kāraṇehi. Adhiggaṇhantīti adhibhavanti. Velāmasuttādivasenāpīti ettha “caturāsītisahassasaṅkhānaṃ suvaṇṇapātirūpiyapātikaṃsapātīnaṃ yathākkamaṃ rūpiyasuvaṇṇahiraññapūrānaṃ karīsassa catutthabhāvappamāṇānaṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitānaṃ caturāsītiyā hatthisahassānaṃ caturāsītiyā assasahassānaṃ caturāsītiyā rathasahassānaṃ caturāsītiyā dhenusahassānaṃ caturāsītiyā kaññāsahassānaṃ caturāsītiyā pallaṅkasahassānaṃ caturāsītiyā vatthakoṭisahassānaṃ aparimāṇassa ca khajjabhojjādibhedassa āhārassa pariccajanavasena sattamāsādhikāni satta saṃvaccharāni nirantaraṃ pavattavelāmamahādānato ekassa sotāpannassa dinnadānaṃ mahapphalataraṃ, tato sataṃ sotāpannānaṃ dinnadānato ekassa sakadāgāmissa, tato ekassa anāgāmissa, tato ekassa arahato, tato ekassa paccekabuddhassa, tato sammāsambuddhassa, tato buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa dinnadānaṃ mahapphalataraṃ, tato cātuddisaṃ saṅghaṃ uddissa vihārakaraṇaṃ, tato saraṇagamanaṃ mahapphalatara”nti imamatthaṃ dīpentassa velāmasuttassa (a. ni. 9.20) vasena. Vuttañhetaṃ “yaṃ gahapati, velāmo brāhmaṇo dānaṃ adāsi mahādānaṃ, yo ekaṃ diṭṭhisampannaṃ bhojeyya, idaṃ tato mahapphalatara”ntiādi (a. ni. 9.20). Velāmasuttādīti ādi-saddena aggappasādasuttādīnaṃ (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90) saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

'By ten reasons' means by ten causes. 'They overcome' means they overpower. Also by the Velāma Sutta and others: here, the meaning is explained by the Velāma Sutta (AN 9.20), which elucidates this matter: more fruitful than the great gift of Velāma—which was given continuously for seven years and seven months and consisted of giving away eighty-four thousand golden, silver, and bronze bowls, filled respectively with silver, gold, and bullion, each the size of a fourth of a karisa measure; eighty-four thousand elephants adorned with all ornaments; eighty-four thousand horses; eighty-four thousand chariots; eighty-four thousand cows; eighty-four thousand maidens; eighty-four thousand couches; eighty-four thousand times ten million sets of cloths; and an immeasurable quantity of various kinds of food—is a gift given to a single stream-enterer. More fruitful than that is a gift given to one hundred stream-enterers; then to a single once-returner; then to a single non-returner; then to a single arahant; then to a single paccekabuddha; then to a Sammāsambuddha. More fruitful than that is a gift given to the Sangha headed by the Buddha; more fruitful than that is building a monastery dedicated to the Sangha of the four quarters; and even more fruitful than that is going for refuge. For it is said: 'Householder, the great gift given by the brahmin Velāma—if one were to feed a single person accomplished in view, this would be far more fruitful than that,' and so on (AN 9.20). 'By the Velāma Sutta and others': by the word 'others,' the inclusion of suttas like the Aggappasāda Sutta (AN 4.34; Itivuttaka 90) should be understood.

Aññāṇaṃ vatthuttayassa guṇānaṃ ajānanaṃ tattha sammoho, “buddho nu kho, na nu kho buddho”tiādinā vicikicchā saṃsayo, micchāñāṇaṃ tassa guṇānaṃ aguṇabhāvaparikappanena viparītaggāho. Ādi-saddena anādarāgāravādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Na mahājutikanti na ujjalaṃ, aparisuddhaṃ apariyodātanti attho. Na mahāvipphāranti anuḷāraṃ. Sāvajjoti diṭṭhitaṇhādivasena sadoso. Lokiyaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ sikkhāsamādānaṃ viya [M 1.0239] aggahitakālaparicchedaṃ jīvitapariyantameva hoti, tasmā tassa khandhabhedena bhedoti āha “anavajjo kālakiriyāyā”ti. Soti anavajjo saraṇagamanabhedo. Satipi anavajjatte iṭṭhaphalopi na hotīti āha “aphalo”ti.

Ignorance is not knowing the qualities of the Triple Gem, and confusion therein. Doubt is uncertainty, with thoughts such as, 'Is he truly a Buddha, or is he not a Buddha?' Wrong knowledge is the perverse grasping of those qualities by imagining them to be non-qualities. By the word 'and so on,' lack of respect, lack of reverence, and so on are included. 'Not greatly luminous' means not radiant; the meaning is impure and uncleansed. 'Not greatly expansive' means not vast. 'Faulty' means defective by way of wrong view, craving, and so on. Worldly going for refuge, like undertaking the training rules, is without a defined time limit and lasts only until the end of life. Therefore, its breaking occurs with the breaking of the aggregates, hence the words, 'blameless at the time of death.' 'That' refers to the blameless breaking of the going for refuge. Although it is blameless, it does not yield the desired fruit—hence it is said to be 'fruitless.'

Saraṇagamanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discourse on going for refuge is concluded.

Upāsakavidhikathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Lay Follower's Way

Ko [V 1.0213] upāsakoti sarūpapucchā, tasmā kiṃlakkhaṇo upāsakoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kasmāti hetupucchā. Tena kena pavattinimittena upāsakasaddo tasmiṃ puggale niruḷhoti dasseti. Kimassa sīlanti kīdisaṃ assa upāsakassa sīlaṃ, kittakena sīlenāyaṃ sīlasampanno nāma hotīti attho. Ko ājīvoti ko assa sammāājīvo, so pana micchājīvassa parivajjanena hotīti sopi vibhajīyatīti. Kā vipattīti kā assa sīlassa, ājīvassa vā vipatti. Anantarassa hi vidhi vā paṭisedho vā. Kā sampattīti etthāpi eseva nayo.

'Who is a lay follower?' is a question about nature; therefore, this means, 'What is the characteristic of a lay follower?' 'Why?' is a question about the cause. It shows by what activating sign the term 'lay follower' becomes established for that person. 'What is his virtue?' means: what kind of virtue does this lay follower have, and with how much virtue is he called 'accomplished in virtue'? This is the meaning. 'What is his livelihood?' means: what is his right livelihood? And since that comes about by avoiding wrong livelihood, that too is analyzed. 'What is failure?' means: what is the failure of his virtue or livelihood? For of what is next there is either an injunction or a prohibition. 'What is success?' Here too, the same method applies.

Yo kocīti khattiyādīsu yo koci. Tena saraṇagamanamevettha kāraṇaṃ, na jātiādivisesoti dasseti. Upāsanatoti teneva saraṇagamanena tattha ca sakkaccakāritāya ādaragāravabahumānādiyogena payirupāsanato. Veramaṇiyoti veraṃ vuccati pāṇātipātādidussīlyaṃ, tassa maṇanato hananato vināsanato veramaṇiyo, pañca viratiyo viratippadhānattā tassa sīlassa. Tenevāha tattha tattha “paṭivirato hotī”ti.

'Whoever' means whoever among the nobles, etc. By this it is shown that taking refuge is the very reason here, not distinctions such as birth. 'An adherent' is so called from that very taking of refuge and from attending with care, through the application of devotion, reverence, and high esteem. 'Abstaining': 'enmity' (vera) is said of the immorality such as killing living beings, etc.; 'abstaining' (veramaṇī) is so called from the crushing, striking, and destroying of that enmity. The five abstinences are so called because abstinence is the principal factor of that virtue. Therefore it is said in each case, 'He abstains from it.'

Micchāvaṇijjāti na sammāvaṇijjā ayuttavaṇijjā asāruppavaṇijjā. Pahāyāti akaraṇeneva pajahitvā. Dhammenāti dhammato anapetena. Tena aññampi adhammikaṃ jīvikaṃ paṭikkhipati. Samenāti avisamena. Tena kāyavisamādiduccaritaṃ vajjetvā kāyasamādinā sucaritena jīvanaṃ dasseti. Satthavaṇijjāti āvudhabhaṇḍaṃ katvā vā kāretvā vā yathākataṃ vā paṭilabhitvā tassa vikkayo. Satthavaṇijjāti manussavikkayo[M 1.0240]. Maṃsavaṇijjāti sūnakārādayo viya migasūkarādike posetvā maṃsaṃ sampādetvā vikkayo. Majjavaṇijjāti yaṃ kiñci majjaṃ yojetvā tassa vikkayo. Visavaṇijjāti visaṃ yojetvā, visaṃ gahetvā vā tassa vikkayo. Tattha satthavaṇijjā paroparodhanimittatāya akaraṇīyā vuttā, sattavaṇijjā abhujissabhāvakaraṇato, maṃsavisavaṇijjā vadhahetuto, majjavaṇijjā pamādaṭṭhānato.

'Wrong trade' means not right trade, inappropriate trade, unsuitable trade. 'Abandoning' means by abandoning it through non-engagement. 'Righteously' means in accordance with the Dhamma, without deviating from it. By this, even other unrighteous livelihoods are rejected. 'Justly' means without injustice. By this, having avoided bodily misconduct, etc., one shows a life lived with good conduct through bodily rectitude. 'Trade in weapons' means making or having weapons made, or acquiring ready-made ones and selling them. 'Trade in beings' means the selling of human beings. 'Trade in meat' means, like butchers, raising animals such as deer and pigs, producing meat, and selling it. 'Trade in intoxicants' means preparing any intoxicant and selling it. 'Trade in poisons' means preparing poison or obtaining poison and selling it. Among these, trade in weapons is said to be unacceptable because it is a cause of harming others; trade in beings because it makes free people slaves; trade in meat and poison because they are causes of killing; and trade in intoxicants because it is a basis for heedlessness.

Tassevāti pañcaveramaṇilakkhaṇassa sīlassa ceva pañcamicchāvaṇijjālakkhaṇassa ājīvassa ca. Vipattīti bhedo pakopo ca. Yāyāti yāya paṭipattiyā. Caṇḍāloti upāsakacaṇḍālo. Malanti upāsakamalaṃ. Patikiṭṭhoti upāsakanihīno. Buddhādīsu kammakammaphalesu ca saddhāvipariyāyo assaddhiyaṃ micchādhimokkho. Yathāvuttena assaddhiyena samannāgato assaddho. Yathāvutta sīlavipatti ājīvavipattivasena dussīlo. “Iminā diṭṭhādinā [V 1.0214] idaṃ nāma maṅgalaṃ bhavissatī”ti evaṃ bālajanaparikappitakotūhalasaṅkhātena diṭṭhasutamutamaṅgalena samannāgato kotūhalamaṅgaliko. Maṅgalaṃ paccetīti diṭṭhamaṅgalādibhedaṃ maṅgalameva pattiyāyati. No kammanti kammassakataṃ no pattiyāyati. Ito bahiddhāti ito sabbaññubuddhasāsanato bahiddhā bāhirakasamaye. Dakkhiṇeyyaṃ pariyesatīti duppaṭipannaṃ dakkhiṇārahasaññī gavesati. Pubbakāraṃ karotīti dānamānanādikaṃ kusalakiriyaṃ paṭhamaṃ karoti. Ettha ca dakkhiṇeyyapariyesanapubbakāre ekaṃ katvā pañca dhammā veditabbā.

'Of that very one' refers to the virtue characterized by the five abstentions and the livelihood characterized by the five wrong trades. 'Vipatti' means breach and corruption. 'Yāyā' means by whichever practice. 'Caṇḍālo' means an outcaste lay follower. 'Malaṃ' means the stain of a lay follower. 'Patikiṭṭho' means a base lay follower. The perversion of faith in the Buddha, etc., and in kamma and its results is unbelief, a wrong conviction. One endowed with such unbelief as described is faithless. One who has the breach of virtue and livelihood as described is immoral. Thinking, 'By this seen, heard, or cognized thing, such and such will be auspicious,' one who is endowed with auspicious signs seen, heard, and cognized, which are reckoned as the curious notions concocted by foolish people, is a believer in auspicious signs. 'He trusts in auspicious signs' means he trusts only in the various kinds of auspicious signs, such as things seen; 'not in kamma' means he does not trust in the ownership of kamma. 'Outside of this' means outside this dispensation of the Omniscient Buddha, in an external doctrine. 'He seeks those worthy of offerings' means he seeks those of wrong practice, perceiving them as worthy of offerings. 'He performs a prior service' means he first performs a meritorious action such as giving and honoring. And here, by taking 'seeking those worthy of offerings' and 'performing a prior service' as one, five things are to be understood.

Vipattiyaṃ vuttavipariyāyena sampatti ñātabbā. Ayaṃ pana viseso – catunnampi parisānaṃ ratijananaṭṭhena upāsakova ratanaṃ upāsakaratanaṃ. Guṇasobhākittisaddasugandhatāhi upāsakova padumaṃ upāsakapadumaṃ. Tathā upāsakapuṇḍarīko.

Accomplishment should be understood as the opposite of what has been said regarding failure. This, however, is the distinction: a lay follower is a jewel, an 'upāsaka-jewel,' in the sense of generating delight in the four assemblies. A lay follower is a lotus, an 'upāsaka-lotus,' because of the splendor of his qualities, the sound of his fame, and his sweet fragrance. Likewise, an 'upāsaka-white lotus.'

Ādimhīti ādiatthe. Koṭiyanti pariyantakoṭiyaṃ. Vihāraggenāti ovarakakoṭṭhāsena, “imasmiṃ gabbhe vasantānaṃ idaṃ nāma panasaphalaṃ pāpuṇātī”tiādinā taṃtaṃvasanaṭṭhānakoṭṭhāsenāti attho. Ajjatanti ajjaicceva attho.

'In the beginning' means in the sense of 'beginning.' 'To the limit' means to the final limit. 'With the best of dwellings' means with a portion of an inner chamber; the meaning is with the portion of this or that dwelling place, according to the saying, 'For those dwelling in this chamber, such and such a jackfruit is obtained,' and so on. 'Today' means 'this very day.'

Pāṇehi [M 1.0241] upetanti iminā tassa saraṇagamanassa āpāṇakoṭikataṃ dassento “yāva me jīvitaṃ pavattatī”tiādinā vatvā puna jīvitena taṃ vatthuttayaṃ paṭipūjento “saraṇagamanaṃ rakkhāmī”ti uppannaṃ tassa brāhmaṇassa adhippāyaṃ vibhāvento “ahañhī”tiādimāha. Pāṇehi upetanti hi yāva me pāṇā dharanti, tāva saraṇaṃ upetaṃ, upento ca na vācāmattena, na ekavāraṃ cittuppādanamattena, atha kho pāṇe pariccajitvāpi yāvajīvaṃ upetanti evamettha attho veditabboti.

By this phrase, 'endowed with life,' he shows that his going for refuge is for life's duration. Having said, 'As long as my life lasts,' etc., and then again honoring that triple object with his life, he reveals the intention that arose in that brahmin, 'I will protect the going for refuge,' and says, 'For I,' etc. 'Endowed with life' means: for as long as my life-breaths endure, so long is the refuge undertaken. And one undertakes it not merely by words, not merely by a single arising of thought, but rather, one undertakes it for life, even at the cost of sacrificing one's life—thus the meaning here should be understood.

Upāsakavidhikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Lay Follower's Way is concluded.

Bhayabheravasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Discourse on Fear and Dread is complete.

5. Anaṅgaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Blemishless Sutta

57. Āyasmā [V 1.0215] sāriputtoti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, evamādikanti attho. Tena “bhikkhū āmantesī”tiādikaṃ sabbaṃ suttaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tenāha “anaṅgaṇasutta”nti. Tassa ko nikkhepo? Attajjhāsayo. Parehi anajjhiṭṭhoyeva hi mahāthero imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Keci panāhu “ekacce bhikkhū saṃkiliṭṭhacitte disvā tesaṃ cittasaṃkilesappahānāya ceva ekaccānaṃ āyatiṃ anuppādanāya ca ayaṃ desanā āraddhā”ti. Evaṃ sabbasuttesūti yathā ettha anaṅgaṇasutte, evaṃ ito paresūti sabbesupi suttesu anuttānaapubbapadavaṇṇanā eva karīyati. Tenāha “tasmā”tiādi. Gaṇanaparicchedoti gaṇanena paricchindanaṃ. Idañhi apparajakkhamahārajakkhatāvasena duvidhe satte paccekaṃ atthaññutānatthaññutāvasena dvidhā katvā “cattāro”ti anavasesapariyādānaṃ. Vajjīputtakādayo viya puggalavādīti na gahetabbaṃ lokasamaññānusārena atthaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ samatthānaṃ vasena desanāya āraddhattā, ayañca desanānayo satthu nissāya evāti dassento “ayañhī”tiādimāha.

57. In the phrase 'Venerable Sāriputta, etc.', the word 'etc.' (iti) has the sense of a beginning, meaning 'and so forth.' By this, it encompasses the entire sutta, starting with 'he addressed the monks.' Therefore, it is called the 'Anaṅgaṇa Sutta.' What is its basis? His own resolve. Indeed, the great elder began this teaching without being prompted by others. Some, however, say, 'Seeing certain monks with defiled minds, this teaching was begun both to abandon their mental defilements and to prevent their future arising.' 'Thus, in all suttas' means: just as here in the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta, so also in all subsequent suttas, only an explanation of words that are not obvious or are unprecedented is given. Therefore, it is said, 'For this reason,' etc. 'Delimitation by enumeration' means defining by counting. For here, having divided beings in two ways according to whether they have little dust or much dust, and each of these again in two ways according to whether they understand the meaning or do not understand the meaning, the exhaustive inclusion as 'four' is made. This should not be taken as a personalist view like that of the Vajjīputtakas and others, because the teaching was begun for the sake of those able to penetrate the meaning in accordance with worldly convention. And showing that this method of teaching is indeed dependent on the Teacher, he says, 'For this,' etc.

Sammutiparamatthadesanākathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on Conventional and Ultimate Teachings

Tattha (a. ni. ṭī. 1.1.170) sammutiyā desanā sammutidesanā, paramatthassa desanā paramatthadesanā. Tatthāti sammutiparamatthadesanāsu, na sammutiparamatthesu. Tenāha [M 1.0242] “evarūpā sammutidesanā, evarūpā paramatthadesanā”ti. Tatridaṃ sammutiparamatthānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ – yasmiṃ bhinne, buddhiyā avayavavinibbhoge vā kate na taṃsamaññā, sā ghaṭapaṭādippabhedā sammuti, tabbipariyāyato paramattho. Na hi kakkhaḷaphusanādisabhāve ayaṃ nayo labbhati, tattha rūpādidhammaṃ samūhasantānavasena pavattamānaṃ upādāya puggalavohāroti āha “puggaloti sammutidesanā”ti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Uppādavayavanto sabhāvadhammā na niccāti āha “aniccanti paramatthadesanā”ti. Esa nayo sesapadesupi. Nanu khandhadesanāpi sammutidesanāva. Khandhaṭṭho hi rāsaṭṭho, koṭṭhāsaṭṭho vāti? Saccametaṃ, ayaṃ pana khandhasamaññā phassādīsu tajjāpaññatti viya paramatthasannissayā tassa āsannatarā, puggalasamaññādayo viya na dūreti paramatthasaṅgahatā vuttā, khandhasīsena vā tadupādānā sabhāvadhammā eva gahitā. Nanu ca sabhāvadhammā sabbepi sammutimukheneva desanaṃ ārohanti, na samukhenāti sabbāpi desanā sammutidesanāva [V 1.0216] siyāti? Nayidamevaṃ desetabbadhammavibhāgena desanāvibhāgassa adhippetattā, na ca saddo kenaci pavattinimittena vinā atthaṃ pakāsetīti.

Here (A. Ni. Ṭī. 1.1.170), the teaching by way of convention is conventional teaching, and the teaching by way of the ultimate is ultimate teaching. "Here" refers to conventional and ultimate teachings, not to convention and the ultimate themselves. Therefore, it is said, "Such is conventional teaching, such is ultimate teaching." Here is the characteristic of convention and the ultimate: that which, when broken up or analyzed by the intellect into its component parts, does not retain that designation—such as pots, cloths, and the like—is convention. What is contrary to that is the ultimate. This principle does not apply to intrinsic natures such as hardness and touch. There, the term "person" is a conventional teaching, based on materiality and other phenomena occurring as a mass or continuum. The same principle applies to the remaining terms. Regarding intrinsic phenomena possessing arising and passing away, it is said, "Impermanent—this is ultimate teaching." This principle applies to the remaining terms. But is not the teaching of the aggregates also merely conventional? For the meaning of "aggregate" is either "mass" or "portion"? This is true. However, this designation of aggregates, like derived concepts such as contact, is closer to the ultimate because it is based on the ultimate, unlike designations such as "person," which are far removed; therefore, it is said to be included in the ultimate. Alternatively, under the heading of 'aggregates', it is the intrinsic phenomena themselves that are taken. But do not all intrinsic phenomena enter into a teaching only through the medium of convention, not directly? Would not all teaching then be merely conventional? No, this is not so, for the division of teachings is intended based on the division of the phenomena to be taught; and no word conveys meaning without some basis for its application.

Sammutivasena desanaṃ sutvāti “idhekacco puggalo attantapo hoti attaparitāpānuyogamanuyutto”tiādinā (ma. ni. 2.413; pu. pa. 10.25 mātikā) sammutimukhena pavattitaṃ desanaṃ sutamayañāṇuppādanavasena sutvā. Atthaṃ paṭivijjhitvāti tadanusārena catusaccasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ saha vipassanāya maggena paṭivijjhitvā. Mohaṃ pahāyāti tadekaṭṭhehi kilesehi saddhiṃ anavasesaṃ mohaṃ pajahitvā. Visesanti nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ arahattasaṅkhātañca visesaṃ. Tesanti tādisānaṃ vineyyānaṃ. Paramatthavasenāti “pañcimāni, bhikkhave, indriyānī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.472-474) paramatthadhammavasena. Sesaṃ anantaranaye vuttasadisameva. Tatthāti tassaṃ sammutivasena paramatthavasena ca desanāyaṃ. Desabhāsākusaloti nānādesabhāsāsu kusalo. Tiṇṇaṃ vedānanti nidassanamattaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ sippaganthānampīti adhippāyo sippuggahaṇañhi parato vakkhati. Sippāni vā vedantogadhe katvā “tiṇṇaṃ vedāna”nti vuttaṃ. Kathetabbabhāvena ṭhitāni, na katthaci sannihitabhāvenāti vedānampi kathetabbabhāveneva avaṭṭhānaṃ dīpento “guyhā tayī [M 1.0243] nihitā gayhatī”ti micchāvādaṃ paṭikkhipati. Nānāvidhā desabhāsā etesanti nānādesabhāsā.

Having heard the teaching by way of convention: that is, having heard, for the purpose of giving rise to knowledge based on hearing, the teaching set forth through the medium of convention, as in, "Here, a certain person is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment," etc. (MN 2.413; Pp 10.25, mātikā). Having penetrated the meaning: that is, having, in accordance with that, penetrated the meaning designated as the Four Noble Truths, together with insight and the path. Having abandoned delusion: that is, having completely abandoned delusion, together with the defilements that share its nature, without remainder. The distinction: this refers to the distinction designated as Nibbāna and Arahantship. For them: for such disciples to be trained. By way of the ultimate: that is, by way of ultimate phenomena, as in, "There are, monks, these five faculties," etc. (SN 5.472-474). The rest is just as stated in the immediately preceding method. There: in that teaching by way of convention and by way of the ultimate. Skilled in regional languages: skilled in diverse regional languages. The three Vedas: this is merely illustrative. The meaning is that the three Vedas and texts on crafts are also included, for the taking up of crafts will be mentioned later. Or, having included the crafts within the scope of the Vedas, it is said, "the three Vedas." He refutes the wrong view, "The secret hidden in the threefold lore is grasped," by showing that even the Vedas stand only as things to be spoken of, not as anything established anywhere, thus clarifying their status as mere topics for discussion. The term `nānādesabhāsā` means 'those who have various regional languages'.

Paramo uttamo attho paramattho, dhammānaṃ yathābhūtasabhāvo. Lokasaṅketamattasiddhā sammuti. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ sammutikathāya saccatātiāha “lokasammutikāraṇā”ti, lokasamaññaṃ nissāya pavattanato. Lokasamaññāya hi abhinivesena vinā ñāpanā ekaccassa sutassa sāvanā viya na musā anatidhāvitabbato tassā. Tenāha bhagavā “janapadaniruttiṃ nābhiniveseyya, samaññaṃ nātidhāveyyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.332). Dhammānanti sabhāvadhammānaṃ. Bhūtakāraṇāti yathābhūtasabhāvaṃ nissāya pavattanato. Sammutiṃ voharantassāti “puggalo satto”tiādinā lokasamaññaṃ kathentassa.

The supreme, highest meaning is the ultimate meaning (paramattha), the true nature of phenomena as they are. Convention (sammuti) is that which is established merely by worldly agreement. If this is so, how can conventional speech be true? It is said, "Because of worldly convention," for it proceeds based on worldly designation. For making things known by means of worldly designation, without clinging to it, is not false, and that designation should not be transgressed. Thus, the Blessed One said, "One should not insist on local dialect, nor should one transgress common usage" (MN 3.332). Of phenomena: of intrinsic phenomena. Because of what is real: for it proceeds based on the true nature as it is. One who uses convention: one who speaks using worldly designations such as "person," "being," and so on.

Hirottappadīpanatthanti lokapālanakicce hirottappadhamme kiccato pakāsetuṃ. Tesañhi kiccaṃ sattasantāneyeva pākaṭaṃ hotīti puggalādhiṭṭhānāya kathāya taṃ vattabbaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Yasmiñhi cittuppāde kammaṃ uppannaṃ, taṃsantāne eva tassa phalassa uppatti kammassakatā. Evañhi kataviññāṇanāso akatāgamo vā natthīti sā puggalādhiṭṭhānāya eva kathāya [V 1.0217] dīpetabbā. Tehi sattehi kātabbā puññādikiriyā paccattapurisakāropi santānavasena nipphādetabbato puggalādhiṭṭhānāya eva kathāya dīpetabbo.

To illuminate the meaning of moral shame and fear (hiri-ottappa): that is, to explain, in terms of function, the qualities of moral shame and fear in their role of protecting the world. For their function is evident only in the continuity of a being. Therefore, this must be stated in a discourse based on the individual (puggalādhiṭṭhāna). The same principle applies to the rest. In whatever mind-moment an action arises, the arising of its result in that same continuum is ownership of kamma. Thus, the fact that there is no destruction of an action done nor the arrival of a result for an action not done must be explained by a discourse based on the individual. The meritorious and other actions to be performed by those beings, and also personal effort, must be accomplished by way of the continuum, and thus this too must be explained by a discourse based on the individual.

Ānantariyadīpanatthanti cutianantaraṃ phalaṃ anantaraṃ nāma, tasmiṃ anantare niyuttāni, tannibbattanena anantarakaraṇasīlāni, anantarapayojanāni vāti ānantariyāni, mātughātādīni, tesaṃ dīpanatthaṃ. Tānipi hi santānavasena nipphādetabbato “mātaraṃ jīvitā voropetī”tiādinā (paṭṭhā. 1.1.423) puggalādhiṭṭhānāya eva kathāya dīpetabbāni, tathā “so mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.556; 3.308; ma. ni. 1.77; 2.309; 3.230; vibha. 642, 643) “so anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati ekampi jāti”ntiādinā (dī. ni. 1.244, 245; ma. ni. 1.148, 384, 431; pārā. 12) “atthi dakkhiṇā dāyakato visujjhati, no paṭiggāhakato”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.381) ca pavattā brahmavihārapubbenivāsadakkhiṇāvisuddhikathā [M 1.0244] puggalādhiṭṭhānāya eva kathāya dīpetabbā sattasantānavisayattā. “Aṭṭha purisapuggalā (saṃ. ni. 1.249), na samayavimutto puggalo”tiādinā (pu. pa. 1) ca paramatthaṃ kathentopi lokasammutiyā appahānatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ kathesi. Etena vuttāvasesāya kathāya puggalādhiṭṭhānabhāve payojanaṃ sāmaññavasena saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kāmañcetaṃ sabbaṃ apariññātavatthukānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ, pariññātavatthukānampi pana evaṃ desanā sukhāvahā hoti.

To explain the immediately effective (ānantariya) deeds: The result immediately following death is called "immediate" (anantara). Those deeds connected to that immediate result, which by producing it have the nature of causing an immediate result, or have an immediate purpose, are called ānantariya, such as matricide, etc. The purpose is to explain these. These too, because they are accomplished by way of a continuum, must be explained by a discourse based on the individual, as in "one deprives one's mother of life," etc. (Paṭṭh. 1.1.423). Similarly, the discourses on the divine abodes, recollection of past lives, and the purification of offerings—such as "with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, one dwells pervading one direction," etc. (DN 1.556; etc.), "one recollects various past lives, even a single birth," etc. (DN 1.244; etc.), and "there is an offering that is purified by the giver, not by the recipient," etc. (MN 3.381)—must be explained by a discourse based on the individual, since their domain is the continuity of a being. And even when speaking of the ultimate, as in "the eight types of individuals" (SN 1.249), and "no individual is liberated at a specific time" (Pp 1), etc., he gave a discourse on the individual in order not to abandon worldly convention. By this, it should be understood that the purpose for the remaining discourses being based on the individual is included in a general sense. And although all this is stated with reference to those for whom the subject matter is not fully understood, even for those for whom the subject matter is fully understood, such a teaching brings ease.

Mahājanoti lokiyamahājano. Na jānāti ghanavinibbhogābhāvena dhammakiccassa asallakkhaṇena. Tattha “kiṃ nāmetaṃ, kathaṃ nāmeta”nti saṃsayapakkhandatāya sammohaṃ āpajjati. Viruddhābhinivesitāya paṭisattu hoti. Jānāti ciraparicitatthā vohārakathāya. Tato eva na sammohamāpajjati, na paṭisattu hoti.

The great multitude: the worldly multitude. It does not know, due to the absence of an analysis of the compact and due to not discerning the function of phenomena. There, by rushing into doubt, thinking, "What is this? How is this?" it falls into delusion. Due to adhering to what is contradictory, it becomes hostile. One who knows through long familiarity with the meaning by means of conventional speech does not fall into delusion, nor become hostile.

Nappajahanti vohāramukhena paramatthassa dīpanato. Samaññāgahaṇavasena lokena ñāyati samaññāyati voharīyatīti lokasamaññā, tāya lokasamaññāya. Tassa tassa atthassa vibhāvane lokena nicchitaṃ, niyataṃ vā vuccati voharīyatīti lokanirutti, tassaṃ lokaniruttiyaṃ. Tathā lokena abhilapīyatīti lokasamaññatāya lokābhilāpo, tasmiṃ lokābhilāpe ṭhitāyeva appahānato. Puggalavādino viya paramatthavasena aggahetvā.

They do not abandon conventional expression, because the ultimate meaning is revealed by way of it. Because of adopting a common designation, it is known, designated, and spoken of in the world—this is worldly convention; by that worldly convention. In making distinct the meaning of this and that, what is decided or fixed by the world is called worldly definition; in that worldly definition. Thus, because it is spoken of by the world, it is a worldly designation, a worldly expression; one remains just in that worldly expression by not abandoning it. Not grasping it in terms of the ultimate meaning, as do the Personalists.

Santoti [V 1.0218] ettha santasaddo “dīghaṃ santassa yojana”ntiādīsu (dha. pa. 70) kilantabhāve āgato, “ayañca vitakko ayañca vicāro santā honti samitā”tiādīsu (vibha. 576) niruddhabhāve āgato, “adhigato kho myāyaṃ dhammo gambhīro duddaso duranubodho santo paṇīto”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.67; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337; saṃ. ni. 2.172; mahāva. 7) santañāṇagocaratāya, “upasantassa sadā satimato”tiādīsu (udā. 27) kilesavūpasame, “santo have sabbhi pavedayantī”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 15) sādhūsu, “pañcime, bhikkhave, mahācorā santo saṃvijjamānā”tiādīsu (pārā. 195) atthibhāve, idhāpi atthibhāveyeva. So ca puggalasambandhena vuttattā lokasamaññāvasenāti [M 1.0245] dassento “lokasaṅketavasena atthī”ti āha. Atthīti cetaṃ nipātapadaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ “atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.373-374; ma. ni. 1.110; 3.154; a. ni. 6.29; 10.60) viya. Saṃvijjamānāti padassa atthaṃ dassento “upalabbhamānā”ti āha. Yañhi saṃvijjati, taṃ upalabbhatīti. Aṅganti etehi taṃsamaṅgipuggalā nihīnabhāvaṃ gacchantīti aṅgaṇāni, rāgādayo. Añjati makkhetīti aṅgaṇaṃ, malādi. Añjeti tattha ṭhitaṃ ahundaratāya abhibyañjetīti aṅgaṇaṃ, vivaṭo bhūmipadeso. Dosādīnaṃ pavattiākāravisesatāya nānappakārā bahulappavattiyā tibbakilesā. Pāpakānanti lāmakānaṃ. Akusalānanti akosallasambhūtānaṃ. Icchāvacarānanti icchāvasena pavattānaṃ. Saha aṅgaṇenāti aṅgaṇanti laddhanāmena yathāvuttakilesena saha vattati.

Here, the word 'santa' is used in various contexts: in “dīghaṃ santassa yojana,” etc. (Dhammapada 70), it conveys the sense of weariness; in “ayañca vitakko ayañca vicāro santā honti samitā,” etc. (Vibhaṅga 576), it denotes cessation; in “adhigato kho myāyaṃ dhammo gambhīro duddaso duranubodho santo paṇīto,” etc. (Dīgha Nikāya 2.67; Majjhima Nikāya 1.281; 2.337; Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.172; Mahāvagga 7), it refers to being the domain of peaceful knowledge; in “upasantassa sadā satimato,” etc. (Udāna 27), it signifies the calming of defilements; in “santo have sabbhi pavedayantī,” etc. (Dhammapada 15), it describes the virtuous; in “pañcime, bhikkhave, mahācorā santo saṃvijjamānā,” etc. (Pārājika 195), it indicates existence—here too, it means existence. And since this is spoken in relation to a person, to show that it is by way of worldly convention, it is said, “existing by worldly convention.” The word 'atthi' should be understood as a particle, as in “atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā,” etc. (Dīgha Nikāya 2.373-374; Majjhima Nikāya 1.110; 3.154; Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.29; 10.60). To clarify the meaning of 'saṃvijjamānā,' it is said to mean “being found.” For what exists is found. Because persons endowed with these go to a state of degradation, they are called 'aṅgaṇāni,' meaning defilements like lust, etc. 'Añjati' means to smear, therefore 'aṅgaṇa' refers to dirt and the like. 'Añjeti' means it makes manifest what stands there because it is not hidden, therefore 'aṅgaṇa' can also mean an open space. Being of various kinds due to the specific modes of occurrence of hatred and so on, and being intense defilements due to their abundant occurrence. 'Pāpakānaṃ' means of the base. 'Akusalānaṃ' means born of unskillfulness. 'Icchāvacarānaṃ' means behaving according to desire. 'Saha aṅgaṇena' means existing together with the defilement, which has acquired the name 'aṅgaṇa,' as previously described.

Atthītipi na jānāti tādisassa yonisomanasikārassa abhāvā. Yesaṃ kilesānaṃ atthitā, tesaṃ sappaṭibhayatā visesato jānitabbāti dassetuṃ “ime kilesā nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kakkhaḷāti pharusā. Vāḷāti kururā. Na gahitabbāti na uppādetabbā. Yāthāvasarasatoti yathābhūtasabhāvato. Evañcāti “ime kilesā nāmā”tiādinā vuttappakārena. Yena vā tena vāti navakammesu vā pariyattidhutaṅgādīsu vā yena vā tena vā. Tatrāti niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ. Taṃ pana niddhāraṇaṃ saṅgaṇānaṅgaṇasamudāyatoti dassento “catūsu puggalesū”ti vatvā puna tadekadesato dassento “tesu vā dvīsu sāṅgaṇesū”ti āha. Tañhi dvayaṃ paṭhamaṃ hīnaseṭṭhabhāvena niddhārīyati paṭhamaṃ uddiṭṭhattā. Niddhāraṇañhi kvaci kutoci kenaci hotīti.

He does not know “it exists” due to the absence of such wise attention. To show that the dangerous nature of those defilements that exist should be especially understood, it is said: “These are called defilements,” etc. Herein, 'kakkhaḷā' means rough. 'Vāḷā' means cruel. 'Na gahitabbā' means they should not be produced. 'Yāthāvasarasato' means according to their actual nature. 'Evañca' refers to the manner stated by “these are called defilements,” etc. 'Yena vā tena vā' means by whatever means, whether in new works, scriptural study, ascetic practices, etc. 'Tatra' is a locative used for determination. To show that that determination is from the collection of the defiled and the undefiled, it states “among four types of persons,” and then, showing it again from a part of that, it says “or among the two defiled ones.” For that pair is first determined by way of their inferior and superior status because it is mentioned first. Determination, indeed, occurs somewhere, from something, by some means.

58. Kiñcāpi aññattha “janako hetu, pariggāhato paccayo, asādhāraṇo hetu, sādhāraṇo paccayo, sabhāgo hetu, asabhāgo paccayo, pubbakāliko hetu, sahappavatto paccayo”tiādinā [V 1.0219] hetupaccayā vibhajja vuccanti, idha pana “cattāro kho, bhikkhave, mahābhūtā hetū, cattāro mahābhūtā paccayā rūpakkhandhassa paññāpanāyā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.85) viya hetupaccayasaddā samānatthāti dassetuṃ “ubhayenapi kāraṇameva [M 1.0246] pucchatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha ubhayenāti hetupaccayavacanadvayena. Pucchati āyasmā mahāmoggallāno desanaṃ vaḍḍhetukāmo. Kiñcāpīti anujānanasambhāvanatthe nipāto. Kiṃ anujānāti? Samānepi dvinnaṃ sāṅgaṇabhāve tassā pajānanāppajānanahetukataṃ tesaṃ seṭṭhahīnataṃ. Kiṃ sambhāveti? Therassa vicittapaṭibhānatāya nānāhetūpamāhi alaṅkatvā yathāpucchitassa atthassa pākaṭakaraṇaṃ. Tenāha “nappajānātī”tiādi. Hetu ceva paccayo ca seṭṭhahīnabhāve. Tathāakkhātabbatāpi hi tesaṃ tannimittā evāti.

58. Although elsewhere cause and condition are distinguished and spoken of, such as: “the progenitor is the cause, the sustainer is the condition; the unique is the cause, the common is the condition; the similar is the cause, the dissimilar is the condition; the antecedent is the cause, the co-arisen is the condition,” etc., here, as in “Monks, the four great elements are causes, the four great elements are conditions for the manifestation of the form aggregate,” etc. (MN 3.85), the terms 'cause' and 'condition' are shown to have the same meaning. To indicate this, it is said: “He asks about the reason by both.” Herein, 'by both' means by the two terms 'cause' and 'condition.' The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna asks, wishing to expand the teaching. 'Kiñcāpi' is a particle in the sense of concession and possibility. What does it concede? The superiority and inferiority of the two, which is caused by their knowing or not knowing, even when their state of being defiled is the same. What does it make possible? The Elder’s making clear the meaning of the question as asked, adorning it with various similes of causes due to his varied and ready wit. Therefore, he said: “He does not know,” etc. He asks about both the cause and the condition for their superiority and inferiority. For the fact that they must be described in this way is indeed caused by that.

59. Tanti tesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ hīnaseṭṭhatāya kāraṇaṃ. Opammehi pākaṭataraṃ katvā dassetuṃ. Etanti sutte anantaraṃ vuccamānaṃ vīriyārambhābhāvena aṅgaṇassa appahānaṃ. Tenāha “na chandaṃ…pe… sandhāyāhā”ti. Kattukamyatāchandhanti kattukamyatāsaṅkhātaṃ aṅgaṇassa pahātukamyatāvasena uppajjanakakusaladhammacchandaṃ. Na janessatīti na uppādessati. Kusalo vāyāmo nāma chandato balavāti āha “tato balavataraṃ vāyāmaṃ na karissatī”ti, chandampi anuppādento kathaṃ tajjaṃ vāyāmaṃ karissatīti adhippāyo. Thāmagatavīriyaṃ ussoḷhībhāvappattaṃ daḷhaṃ vīriyaṃ. Sāṅgaṇaggahaṇeneva aṅgaṇānaṃ kilesavatthutāya cittassa saṃkiliṭṭhatāya saddhāya puna saṃkiliṭṭhaggahaṇaṃ savisesaṃ kiliṭṭhabhāvavibhāvananti āha “suṭṭhutaraṃ kiliṭṭhacitto”ti. Malinacittotiādīsupi “tehiyevā”ti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Ukkhalipucchanacoḷakassa viya vasāpītapilotikā viya ca dummocanīyabhāvena malaggahaṇaṃ malīnatā, pīḷanaṃ hiṃsanaṃ avipphārikatākaraṇaṃ vibādhanaṃ darathapariḷāhuppādanena paridahanaṃ upatāpanaṃ, kālanti kālanaṃ, yathāgahitassa attabhāvassa khepanaṃ āyukkhayanti attho. Karissatīti pavattessati, pāpuṇissatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathābhūto ca pāṇaṃ cajissati nāmāti āha “marissatī”ti.

59. That is the reason for the inferiority and superiority of these two persons, which is shown by making it clearer with similes. 'This' refers to the non-abandonment of defilements due to the absence of initiating energy, which is mentioned next in the sutta. Therefore, he said: “He will not arouse desire… etc.,” referring to this. 'Desire to act' means the wholesome desire that arises from the wish to abandon defilements, which is known as the desire to act. 'He will not generate it' means he will not produce it. Because wholesome effort is stronger than desire, it is said, “he will not make an effort stronger than that.” The intention is: how will one who does not even arouse desire make the effort born of it? 'Strong energy' means firm energy that has reached a state of exertion. By the very use of 'with defilements' (sāṅgaṇa)—since defilements are the basis of defilements and the mind is defiled—the further use of 'defiled' (saṃkiliṭṭha) is to illustrate a particularly defiled state; thus, it is said: “a more thoroughly defiled mind.” Similarly, in the phrases “a stained mind,” etc., they should be connected with “by those very things.” Due to the difficulty of removal, like from a mortar-wiping rag or a cloth that has absorbed grease, the grasping of a stain is 'stainedness' (malīnatā). 'Oppression' means harming; 'distress' means causing non-expansion; 'torment' means afflicting; 'burning' means producing suffering and feverish heat; 'making an end' (`kālaṃ karissati`) means the wasting away of the acquired state of existence, the exhaustion of the life-span. 'He will do' means he will bring it about; that is, he will reach it. And being such, he will indeed give up life—hence it is said: “he will die.”

Seyyathāpīti upamānidassane nipāto. Tadatthaṃ dassento “yathā nāmā”ti āha. Paṃsuādināti ādi-saddena jallādīnaṃ saṅgaho, ghaṃsanādīhīti ādi-saddena chārikāparimajjanādīnaṃ saṅgahoti. “Abhirūpāya kaññā dātabbā”tiādīsu viya antarenapi atisayatthabodhakasaddena atisayattho ñāyatīti āha “malaggahitatarāti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Paṭipucchāvacananti anumatipucchāviseso. Evaṃ [M 1.0247] kariyamānāti aparibhoga-apariyodapanarajopathanikkhipanehi kiliṭṭhabhāvaṃ āpādiyamānā. Opammaṃ sampaṭipādentoti yathūpanītaṃ upamaṃ upameyyatthena [V 1.0220] samaṃ katvā paṭipādento, saṃsandentoti attho. Sāṅgaṇo puggaloti sāṅgaṇo tasmiṃ attabhāve asujjhanakapuggalo. Āpaṇādito kulagharaṃ ānītassa malaggahitakaṃsabhājanassa tattha laddhabbāya visuddhiyā alābhato yathā anukkamena saṃkiliṭṭhatarabhāvo, evaṃ gharato nikkhantassa puggalassa pabbajjāya laddhabbāya visuddhiyā alābhato anukkamena saṃkiliṭṭhatarabhāvoti dassento “saṃkiliṭṭhakaṃsapātiyā”tiādimāha. Saṃkiliṭṭhatarabhāvo ca nāma pabbajitassa ājīvavipattivasena vā siyā ācāradiṭṭhisīlavipattīsu aññataravasena vāti taṃ sabbaṃ saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ “tassa puggalassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pācittiyavītikkamanaggahaṇena hi ekaccadiṭṭhivipattiyāpi saṅgaho hotīti. Ettha ṭhitassāti etissaṃ ājīvavipattiyaṃ ṭhitassa. Iminā nayena sesesupi yathārahaṃ vattabbaṃ. Sabbaparisasādhāraṇā mahātherassa desanā, tasmā gahapativasenapi yojetabbaṃ. Tattha ukkaṃsagatasaṃkiliṭṭhatarabhāvaṃ dassento “mātughātādiānantariyakaraṇa”nti āha. Avisodhetvāti yathā attano sīle vā diṭṭhiyā vā visuddhi hoti, evaṃ kilesamalinacittasantānaṃ avisodhetvā.

The particle 'seyyathāpi' is in the sense of indicating a simile. Explaining its meaning, he says, 'yathā nāma' (just as). By 'with dust, etc.' (`paṃsuādinā`), the inclusion of grime, etc., is meant; by 'with rubbing, etc.' (`ghaṃsanādīhi`), the inclusion of wiping with ashes, etc., is meant. Just as in phrases like 'a beautiful maiden should be given' (`abhirūpāya kaññā dātabbā`), the sense of excess is understood even without a word indicating excess, so he says, 'more defiled is meant' (`malaggahitatarāti vuttaṃ hoti`). 'Paṭipucchāvacana' is a specific kind of inquiry for consent. 'Evaṃ kariyamānā' means being brought to a state of defilement by not being used, not being cleaned, and being left exposed to dirt. 'Opammaṃ sampaṭipādento' means making the presented simile correspond with the subject of the simile, that is, comparing them. 'Sāṅgaṇo puggalo' is a person with defilements, an individual who cannot be purified in that existence. Showing that just as a defiled bronze vessel brought from a shop to a household, by not attaining the purity that should be obtained there, becomes progressively more defiled, so too a person who has gone forth from home, by not attaining the purity that should be obtained through ordination, becomes progressively more defiled, he says, 'like a defiled bronze bowl' (`saṃkiliṭṭhakaṃsapātiyā`), etc. And this state of being more defiled may arise for one who has gone forth either through a failure in livelihood, or through one of the failures in conduct, view, or virtue. To include all of that, it is said, 'of that person' (`tassa puggalassa`), etc. For by the inclusion of the transgression of a Pācittiya, the inclusion of a certain failure of view also occurs. 'Ettha ṭhitassa' means one who is established in this failure of livelihood. By this method, it should be stated for the others as is appropriate. The Elder's teaching is common to the entire assembly; therefore, it should also be applied in the case of householders. There, showing the state of being defiled to the highest degree, he says, 'the commission of an act with immediate result, such as matricide' (`mātughātādiānantariyakaraṇa`). 'Avisodhetvā' means without purifying the mental continuum stained by defilements, in such a way that there would be purity in one's own virtue or view.

Bhabbapuggaloti upanissayādisampattiyā tasmiṃ attabhāve visuddhapuggalo. Ādiṃ katvāti iminā dhovanaghaṃsanādīhi pariyodapanaṃ ādimantaṃ katvā vadati. Suddhaṭṭhānaṃ yattha vā na rajena okirīyati. Daṇḍakammaṃ katvāti “ettakā udakā, vālukā vā ānetabbā”ti daṇḍakammaṃ katvā. Ettha ṭhitassāti parisuddhe sīle ṭhitassa. Sammāvattapaṭipattisīlehi sīlavisuddhi dassitā. Vattapaṭipattiyāpi hi aṅgaṇānaṃ vikkhambhanaṃ siyā. Tathā hissā saṃkiliṭṭhakaṃsapātiyā parisuddhapariyodātabhāvo upamābhāvena vutto. Pantasenāsanavāso kilesavikkhambhanaṃ kilesānaṃ tadaṅganivāraṇaṃ. Sotāpattiphalādhigamo…pe… arahattasacchikiriyāti sattasupi ṭhānesu “parisuddhapariyodātabhāvo viyā”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Pabbajitassa hi visuddhi nāma heṭṭhimantena sīlavisuddhiyā vā siyā kammaṭṭhānānuyogavasena vivekavāsena jhānassādhigamena vā vipassanābhāvanāya vā sāmaññaphalādhigamena vāti.

'Bhabbapuggalo' is a person who is pure in that existence due to the accomplishment of supporting conditions, etc. 'Ādiṃ katvā' means that by this, he speaks of making the cleansing by washing, scrubbing, and so on, the beginning. 'Suddhaṭṭhānaṃ' is a place where one is not sprinkled with dust. 'Daṇḍakammaṃ katvā' means having imposed a penalty, saying, 'This much water or sand must be brought.' 'Ettha ṭhitassa' means one established in purified virtue. Purity of virtue is shown by means of proper observances, practices, and virtue. For by observances and practices, there may also be a suppression of defilements. Thus, the state of being completely pure and bright of that defiled bronze bowl is spoken of as a simile. 'Pantaseṇāsanavāso' is the suppression of defilements, the temporary warding off of defilements. The attainment of the fruit of stream-entry... up to the realization of arahantship—in all seven places, the phrase 'like the state of being completely pure and bright' (`parisuddhapariyodātabhāvo viyā`) should be brought in and connected. For a renunciate, purity may indeed be through purity of virtue, as stated below, or through devotion to a meditation subject, through dwelling in seclusion, through the attainment of jhāna, through the development of insight, or through the attainment of the fruits of recluseship.

Rāgaṭṭhāniyanti [M 1.0248] rāguppattihetubhūtaṃ. Visabhāgārammaṇaṃ sandhāya vadati “iṭṭhārammaṇa”nti. Tasminti iṭṭhārammaṇe. Vipannassatīti muṭṭhassati. Taṃ nimittanti subhanimittaṃ. Āvajjissatīti ayoniso āvajjissati. Sayameva aññena avomisso. Kusalavārapacchindanameva cettha anuddhaṃsanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sesanti “sāṅgaṇo saṃkiliṭṭhacitto”tiādi. Vuttanayānusārenāti paṭhamavāre vuttanayānusārena. Sabbanti mātughātādiānantariyakaraṇapariyosānaṃ sabbaṃ upamāsaṃsandanavacanaṃ.

'Rāgaṭṭhāniyaṃ' means that which has become a cause for the arising of lust. Referring to a dissimilar object, he says, 'a desirable object' (`iṭṭhārammaṇa`). 'Tasmiṃ' means in that desirable object. 'Vipannassati' means one with lost mindfulness. 'Taṃ nimittaṃ' means the sign of the beautiful. 'Āvajjissati' means he will advert to it improperly. By himself alone, not mixed with another. And here, the cutting off of the turn of the wholesome should be seen as 'not destroying' (`anuddhaṃsanaṃ`). 'Sesaṃ' means 'with defilements, with a defiled mind' (`sāṅgaṇo saṃkiliṭṭhacitto`), and so on. 'Vuttanayānusārena' means in accordance with the method stated in the first section. 'Sabbaṃ' means the entire statement of comparison, ending with the commission of an act with immediate result, such as matricide.

Ativirahābhāvatoti [V 1.0221] satisammosābhāvato, upaṭṭhitassati bhāvatoti attho. Sesanti “so arāgo”tiādi. “Dhovanaghaṃsanasaṇhachārikāparimajjanādīhī”tiādinā dutiyavārānusārena. “Ko nu kho”tiādi pucchāvasena āgataṃ, idaṃ nigamanavasenāti ayameva viseso.

'Ativirahābhāvato' means from the absence of confusion of mindfulness (`satisammosābhāvato`); the meaning is from the state of having established mindfulness (`upaṭṭhitassati bhāvato`). 'Sesaṃ' means 'he is without lust' (`so arāgo`), etc. By 'by washing, scrubbing, fine ashes, wiping, etc.' (`Dhovanaghaṃsanasaṇhachārikāparimajjanādīhī`), it is in accordance with the second section. 'Ko nu kho', etc., is presented by way of a question; this is by way of a conclusion. This alone is the distinction.

60. Aṅgaṇanti tattha tattha nāmato eva vibhāvitaṃ, na pana sabhāvato, pabhedato vāti sabhāvādito vibhāvanaṃ sandhāyāha “nānappakārato pākaṭaṃ kārāpetukāmenā”ti. Icchāya avacarānanti icchāvasena avacaraṇānaṃ. Otiṇṇānanti cittasantānaṃ anupaviṭṭhānaṃ. Te pana tattha paccayavasena nibbattattā pavattā nāma hontīti āha “pavattāna”nti. Nānappakārānanti visayabhedena pavattiākārabhedena ca nānāvidhānaṃ. Yenakāraṇena. Na kevalaṃ lābhatthikatā eva, atha kho puññavantatā sakkatagarukatā ca ettha kāraṇabhāvena gahetabbāti dassento “pakatiyāpi cā”tiādimāha. Tena lābhatthikopi na yo koci evaṃ cittaṃ uppādeti puññavā sambhāvanīyoti dasseti. Therā avajjapaṭicchādanabhayena majjhimānaṃ ārocenti, tathā majjhimā navakānaṃ, navakā pana attano navakabhāvena vighāsādādīnaṃ ārocenti “passatha tumhākaṃ therassa kamma”nti. Vighāsādādayo nāma “īdisassa santike ovādatthaṃ tumhe āgatā”ti bhikkhunīnaṃ ārocenti. Na ca maṃ bhikkhū jāneyyunti na ca vata maṃ bhikkhū jāneyyuṃ, aho vata maṃ bhikkhū na jāneyyunti yojanā. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetanti ettha kho-saddo avadhāraṇattho, pana-saddo vacanālaṅkāroti āha “atthiyevā”ti. Pubbe icchuppādavāravaṇṇanāya vuttanayena. Iti-saddo idha āsannakāraṇatthoti taṃ dassento “iminā kāraṇenā”ti āha[M 1.0249]. Idañca kopaappaccayānameva gahaṇaṃ. Tādisānanti kopaappaccayādhibhūtānanti adhippāyo.

60. 'Aṅgaṇaṃ' is explained here and there by name only, but not by its intrinsic nature or by its classification. Therefore, referring to the explanation by its intrinsic nature, etc., he says, 'by one desiring to have it made manifest in various ways' (`nānappakārato pākaṭaṃ kārāpetukāmenā`). 'Icchāya avacarānaṃ' means of those who engage by way of desire. 'Otiṇṇānaṃ' means of those that have entered into the mental continuum. But since they are produced there by way of conditions, they are called 'occurred' (`pavattā`), so he says 'pavattānaṃ'. 'Nānappakārānaṃ' means of various kinds due to the difference of object and the difference in the mode of occurrence. 'Yenakāraṇena' means for which reason. Showing that not only the desire for gain, but also being meritorious, respected, and revered should be taken as a cause here, he says, 'and also by nature' (`pakatiyāpi ca`), etc. By that, he shows that not just anyone desiring gain produces such a thought, but one who is meritorious and esteemed. The elders, for fear of concealing a fault, inform the monks of middle standing; likewise, the monks of middle standing inform the junior monks. The junior monks, however, due to their junior status, inform the eaters of scraps, etc., saying, 'Look at the deed of your elder!' The eaters of scraps, etc., inform the nuns, saying, 'You have come to such a one for an exhortation.' 'Na ca maṃ bhikkhū jāneyyuṃ': the construction is, 'Indeed, may the monks not know me! Oh, may the monks not know me!' 'Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ': here, the word 'kho' is in the sense of emphasis, and the word 'pana' is a particle for embellishing speech, so he says, 'it certainly exists' (`atthiyeva`). By the method stated previously in the explanation of the section on the arising of desire. The word 'iti' here is in the sense of the immediate cause. Showing that, he says, 'for this reason' (`iminā kāraṇena`). And this is the taking up of only anger and displeasure. 'Tādisānaṃ' means of those who are overcome by anger and displeasure; this is the intention.

Anurahoti anurūpe rahasi. Evameva hi atthaṃ dassetuṃ “vihārapaccante”tiādi vuttaṃ. Purimasadisamevāti “lābhatthiko hī”tiādinā vuttena purimena yojanānayena sadisameva.

'Anuraho' means in a suitable secluded place. Indeed, just so, to show the meaning, 'on the outskirts of the monastery' (`vihārapaccante`), etc., is said. 'Purimasadisameva' means it is exactly similar to the former method of explanation stated with 'for one who desires gain' (`lābhatthiko hi`), etc.

Codanāya paṭipuggalabhāvo, codanā ca āpattiyāti cuditakena codakassa samānabhāvo āpattiāpannatāyāti āha “samānoti sāpattiko”ti. Sappaṭipuggalenevassa codanicchāya kāraṇaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “aya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Na cāyaṃ sāpattikatāya eva samānataṃ icchati, atha kho aññathāpīti dassento “apicā”tiādimāha. Aññena vā paṭipuggalena sappaṭipuggalo. Ayañhi “sappaṭipuggalova maṃ codeyyā”ti icchati “evāhaṃ tassa paṭipuggalehi saddhiṃ ekajjhāsayo hutvā tassa upari kiñci vattuṃ kātuṃ vā labhissāmī”ti maññamāno[V 1.0222]. Imasmiṃ pana pakkhe no appaṭipuggaloti natthi etassa paṭipuggaloti appaṭipuggaloti evamattho veditabbo.

Being accused involves being a counter-person, and the accusation itself is an offense. The accused becomes equal to the accuser through having incurred an offense—hence it is said, 'samāno' (equal) means 'sāpattiko' (liable to an offense). To clarify the reason for wishing to accuse only with a counter-person, 'ayaṃ' (this), etc., was stated. And this one does not wish for equality only by being liable to an offense, but also otherwise—thus, 'apicā' (moreover), etc., was said. Alternatively, one with a counter-person is one who has another as a counter-person. For this one thinks, 'Only one with a counter-person should accuse me,' thinking, 'In this way, being of one mind with his counter-persons, I will be able to say or do something against him.' But in this case, 'no appaṭipuggalo' (not without a counter-person) means 'there is no counter-person for him,' which is 'appaṭipuggalo' (without a counter-person); this is how the meaning should be understood.

“Aho vatā”ti idaṃ padaṃ dissatīti sambandho, imassa puggalassa icchācāre ṭhitattā bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyāti vacanato “tañca kho anumatipucchāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Na hesa “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhū”tiādinā kiñci vītikkamaṃ uddissa bhagavatā pucchitabbataṃ icchati. No maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā vipassanaṃ vā antaraṃ katvāti maggabhāvanaṃ vā phalasacchikiriyaṃ vā sikhāppattavipassanānuyogaṃ vā nirodhasamāpajjanaṃ vā jhānasamāpajjanameva vā antaraṃ kāraṇaṃ katvā bhagavatā attānaṃ paṭipucchitabbaṃ no icchati. Niccaṃ aniccantiādinā anumatiggahaṇavasena pucchitabbaṃ icchati, uttānameva katvā pucchitabbaṃ icchatīti attho. Upaharante passatīti sambandho. Abhabbaṭṭhānabhikkhutāya niharissanti sāsanato.

'Aho vatā' (Alas, indeed!)—the connection is that this phrase is seen, because this person, being established in conduct according to his own will, would teach the Dhamma to the monks; thus, 'tañca kho anumatipucchāya' (and that, by asking for agreement) is said. He does not wish the Blessed One to question him by singling out any transgression, such as, 'Is it true, monk?', etc. Nor does he wish that the Blessed One should question him by making the path, or the fruit, or insight an intervening cause, that is, by interposing the cultivation of the path, or the realization of the fruit, or the practice of fully developed insight, or the attainment of cessation, or even the attainment of jhāna. Rather, he wishes to be questioned by way of seeking agreement, such as, 'Is it permanent or impermanent?', etc.—meaning, he wishes to be questioned openly. 'Upaharante passati' (seeing one who brings near)—this is the connection. Because of his state as an unfit monk, they will expel him from the Dispensation.

Taṃ sampattinti parivārasampattiñceva bhikkhūhi kariyamānaṃ sakkāragarukārasampattiñca. Gahetvā paribhuñjanti mayā saṃvibhāge kariyamāne. Sayameva paññāyatīti sayameva gantvā bhikkhūnaṃ purato attānaṃ dasseti, purato vasantaṃ pana bhikkhu purakkhatvā gacchantiyevāti adhippāyo.

That attainment refers to both the attainment of a retinue and the attainment of honor and respect being shown by the monks. They take and enjoy it when I make the distribution. 'It becomes evident by itself' means that by going himself, he shows himself before the monks. The intention is that, while he is residing in front, the monks indeed go, having placed him at the forefront.

Dakkhiṇodakanti [M 1.0250] aggato upanīyamānaṃ dakkhiṇodakaṃ. Yato eva-kāro, tato aññattha niyamo icchito. Avadhāraṇatthaṃ vā eva-kāraggahaṇanti katvā ahameva labheyyanti ahaṃ labheyyamevāti evametaṃ avadhāraṇaṃ daṭṭhabbanti adhippāyenāha “ahameva labheyyanti icchā nātimahāsāvajjā”ti, aññathā yathārutavasena avadhāraṇe gayhamāne “na aññe labheyyu”nti ayamevettha attho siyāti. Pāsādiko hotīti idaṃ tassa aggāsanādipaccāsīsanāya kāraṇadassanaṃ.

'Donation water' refers to the dedication water (dakkhiṇodaka) offered first. Since there is the particle 'eva' (alone), a restriction is intended elsewhere. Or, taking the inclusion of 'eva' for the sake of emphasis, it is with the intention that this emphasis should be understood as 'may I alone receive,' meaning 'may I indeed receive.' That is why it is said, 'The wish "may I alone receive" is not a very great fault.' Otherwise, if the emphasis is taken according to the literal meaning, the meaning here would be, 'may others not receive.' 'He is pleasing' indicates the reason for his anticipation of the foremost seat, etc.

Anumodananti maṅgalāmaṅgalesu anumodanāvasena pavattetabbadhammakathaṃ. Khaṇḍānumodananti anumodanekadesaṃ. “Pubbe anumoditapubbo anumodatū”ti avatvā therena vuttamatteyeva.

'Rejoicing' refers to the Dhamma talk that should be given in the manner of rejoicing on auspicious and inauspicious occasions. 'Partial rejoicing' means a fragment of rejoicing. It is only what was said by the elder, without his saying, 'Let one who has rejoiced before, rejoice.'

Tādisesu ṭhānesūti tādisesu pesalānaṃ bahussutānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānesu. Sabbampi ratiṃ pavattanato sabbarattikāni. Vinicchayakusalānanti anekavihitesu kaṅkhaṭṭhāniyesu kaṅkhāvinayanāya taṃ taṃ pañhānaṃ vinicchaye kusalānaṃ chekānaṃ. Tesu tesu dhammakathikesu ajjhiṭṭhesu vārena dhammaṃ kathentesu “ayaṃ byatto”ti dhammajjhesakena ajjhiṭṭhattā okāsaṃ alabhamāno.

'In such places' means in the dwelling places of those who are virtuous and learned. They are 'all-night' events because they produce delight throughout the entire night. 'Skilled in judgment' means skilled and clever in judging and deciding those various doubtful points in order to dispel doubt regarding those various questions. Among those Dhamma speakers, when they are requested or are speaking in turn, he is unable to gain an opportunity, having been invited by the one requesting the Dhamma due to the thought, 'This one is competent.'

Sakkaccañca [V 1.0223] kareyyunti bhikkhū yaṃ mama abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānañjalikammasāmīcikammādiṃ karonti. Taṃ ādareneva kareyyuṃ, yañca me parikkhārajātaṃ paṭiyādenti, tampi sundaraṃ sammadeva abhisaṅkhataṃ kareyyunti attho. Bhāriyanti pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garukātabbaṃ. Etaṃ vidhinti etaṃ “sakkareyyu”ntiādinā vuttasakkārādividhiṃ. Tenāti tena kāraṇena, bāhusaccādiguṇavisesavato eva sakkārādīnaṃ arahattāti attho. Evarūpanti īdisaṃ “piyo garū”tiādinā (a. ni. 7.37) vuttappakāraṃ. Evaṃ kareyyunti evaṃ “sakkareyyu”ntiādinā vuttappakāraṃ sakkārādiṃ kareyyuṃ. Esa nayoti yoyaṃ bhikkhuvāre vuttavidhi, eseva nayo. Ito paresu bhikkhunīvārādīsu vāresu.

'And they should do it carefully' means that whatever acts of respect the monks perform for me, such as bowing, standing up, saluting with joined palms, and proper conduct, they should do with reverence. And whatever requisites they prepare for me, they should also make them beautiful and well-prepared—this is the meaning. 'Weighty' means it should be treated with respect, like a stone umbrella. 'This method' refers to the method of honoring, etc., as stated in 'they should honor,' etc. 'Therefore' means for that reason; the meaning is that one is worthy of honor, etc., only if one possesses the special qualities of great learning and so on. 'Such-like' refers to the kind described as 'dear and respected,' etc. (Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.37). 'They should act thus' means they should perform the honoring, etc., in the manner described in 'they should honor,' etc. 'This is the method' means this very method stated in the section on monks is the same method for the subsequent sections on nuns, etc.

Ahameva lābhī assanti etthāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva avadhāraṇaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Piṇḍapātassa paṇītatā upasecanādivasenāti āha “sappitelamadhusakkharādipūritāna”nti[M 1.0251]. Mañcapīṭhādīnanti nidassanamattaṃ utusappāyānaṃ nivātānaṃ phassitatalānaṃ pihitadvārakavāḷavātapānādīnampi paṇītasenāsanabhāvato. Ādi-saddena vā tesampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sabbatthāpīti sabbesu tesu catūsupi paccayavāresu.

'May I alone be the recipient'—here too, the emphasis should be understood according to the method previously stated. The excellence of almsfood is in terms of sauces and the like, hence it is said, 'filled with ghee, oil, honey, sugar, etc.' The mention of beds and chairs is merely illustrative, since shelters suitable for the season, protected from the wind, with soft surfaces, with closed doors, windows, and vents, etc., are also excellent lodgings. Or, by the term 'etc.,' the inclusion of these should also be understood. 'In all cases' means in all four sections concerning the requisites.

61. Kāyakammaṃ disvāti idaṃ na kāyakammaṃ cakkhuviññeyyaṃ, kāyakammunā pana saha pavattaṃ oṭṭhaparipphandanaṃ bhākuṭikaraṇaṃ kāyaṅgādidassanaṃ kāyakammadassanaṃ viya hotīti katvā vuttaṃ. Vacīkammaṃ sutvāti etthāpi eseva nayo, tasmā kāyavikārajanakā dhammā “dissantī”ti vuttā, vacīvikārajanakā “sūyantī”ti. Tato eva ca te paccakkhakāle sammukhakāle dissanti nāma. Tirokkhakāle asammukhakāle sūyanti nāma. Anurūpato gahaṇaṃ anuggaho. Āraññikattanti tassa bhikkhuno dhutaguṇattānurūpato gaṇhāti. Tenāha “āraññikattaṃ anuggaṇhātī”ti. Araññe nivāso assāti āraññiko. Pantaṃ pariyantaṃ dūrataraṃ senāsanaṃ assāti pantasenāsano. Taṃ pana atthamattena dassentena “pantasenāsane vasatī”ti vuttaṃ. Bhikkhāsaṅkhātānaṃ piṇḍānaṃ pāto piṇḍāpāto, taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ uñchati gavesatīti piṇḍapātiko. Piṇḍāya patituṃ carituṃ vatametassāti vā piṇḍapāti, so eva piṇḍapātiko. Dānato avakhaṇḍanato apetaṃ apadānaṃ, saha apadānena sapadānaṃ, anavakhaṇḍanaṃ. Anugharaṃ caraṇasīlo sapadānacārī. Unnatabhāvena paṃsukūlaṃ viya paṃsukūlaṃ, paṃsu viya vā kucchitabhāvaṃ ulati gacchatīti paṃsukūlaṃ, tassa dhāraṇaṃ idha paṃsukūlaṃ, taṃ sīlamassāti paṃsukūliko.

61.
