'Seeing bodily action'—this does not mean bodily action is cognizable by the eye-consciousness, but it is said thus because the quivering of the lips, frowning, and showing of bodily gestures, etc., that occur along with bodily action are like seeing the bodily action itself. 'Hearing verbal action'—here too, the same method applies. Therefore, the states that generate bodily changes are said to be 'seen,' and those that generate verbal changes are said to be 'heard.' For that very reason, at the time of direct perception, when face to face, they are said to be 'seen.' At a time when one is out of sight, not face to face, they are said to be 'heard.' Taking something in a suitable manner is support. 'Forest-dwelling'—he takes it in accordance with that monk's quality of ascetic practices. Hence it is said, 'he supports forest-dwelling.' One whose dwelling is in the forest is a 'forest-dweller' (āraññiko). One who has a remote, bordering, or very distant lodging is a 'user of a secluded lodging' (pantasenāsano). But this is shown by its meaning alone when it is said, 'he lives in a secluded lodging.' The falling of lumps of food (piṇḍa) in the morning (pāta) is 'almsfood' (piṇḍapāta); one who gleans or seeks that almsfood is an 'alms-goer' (piṇḍapātiko). Or, one whose vow is to go about for alms is a 'piṇḍapātī,' who is the same as a 'piṇḍapātiko.' Devoid of breaking (avakhaṇḍana) is 'apadāna'; with 'apadāna' is 'sapadāna,' meaning unbroken. One whose habit is to walk from house to house without interruption is a 'sapadānacārī.' A 'paṃsukūla' is like a dust-heap (paṃsukūla) due to its piled-up nature; or, it is a 'paṃsukūla' because it goes (ulati) to a contemptible state like dust (paṃsu). Wearing that is the 'paṃsukūla' practice, and one who has that as his practice is a 'rag-robe wearer' (paṃsukūliko).

Tīhi [V 1.0224] kāraṇehi lūkhaṃ veditabbaṃ agghaphassavaṇṇaparihānito apaṃsukūlampi, ko pana vādo paṃsukūlanti adhippāyo. Thūladīghasuttakenāti thūlena olambamānena dīghasuttakena. Vaṇṇenāti ettha phassenapi parihāyatīti vattabbaṃ. Tañhi tattha kharaphassampi hotiyevāti. Kasmā pana pāḷiyaṃ āraññikādiggahaṇena cattārova dhutaguṇā vuttāti? Padhānattā, taggahaṇeneva ca ito paresampi sukhaparibhogatāya gahaṇasambhavato. Yo hi āraññiko pantasenāsano, tassa abbhokāsika-rukkhamūlika-nesajjika-yathāsanthatika-sosānikaṅgāni suparipūrāni. Yo ca piṇḍapātiko sapadānacārī ca, tassa pattapiṇḍikakhalupacchābhattikaekāsanikaṅgāni. Yo pana paṃsukūliko, tassa [M 1.0252] tecīvarikaṅgaṃ supariharamevāti. Padhānattā hi bhagavatāpi “kadāhaṃ nandaṃ passeyyaṃ, āraññaṃ paṃsukūlika”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.242; netti. 100) tattha tattha āraññikādayo eva gayhanti. Ettakāti pāḷiyaṃ āgatānaṃ paricchijja gahaṇametaṃ, na ettakā sabbepi ekassa ekaṃsato sambhavanti, nāpi ettakāyeva pāpadhammā pahātabbā. Na hi makkhapaḷāsādīnaṃ appahīnabhāvepi sabrahmacārī neva sakkaronti…pe… na pūjentīti.

It should be understood as shabby for three reasons: from the loss of value, touch, and color—even if it is not a rag-robe, what then is to be said of a rag-robe? This is the meaning. By 'thick and long threads' is meant with thick, hanging, long threads. By 'color' here, it should be said that it is diminished also in touch, for indeed, a rough touch also exists there. But why in the Pāli texts are only four ascetic qualities mentioned, such as the forest-dweller's practice? Because of their prominence, and by their inclusion, others too can be understood due to their connection with the enjoyment of ease. For one who is a forest-dweller and lives in a remote dwelling, the qualities of open-air dwelling, tree-root dwelling, sitting without lying down, using whatever seat is available, and charnel-ground dwelling are fully perfected. For one who is an alms-food eater and who practices going from house to house in order, the qualities of eating from one bowl, refusing food offered after the meal, and eating in one sitting are perfected. For one who is a rag-robe wearer, the quality of having three robes is well maintained. Because of their prominence, even the Blessed One said, 'When, O Nanda, will I see you as a forest-dweller and a rag-robe wearer?' and so on (Saṃ. Ni. 2.242; Netti. 100). There, forest-dwellers and others are specifically mentioned. This much is a limited inclusion of what has come down in the Pāli texts—it is not that all these are definitely possible for one person, nor that only these evil states must be abandoned. For if faults like hypocrisy and spite are not abandoned, fellow practitioners neither honor... nor revere them.

Tamatthanti “yassa kassacī”tiādinā vuttamatthaṃ. Upamāya pākaṭaṃ karontoti anvayato byatirekato ca udāharaṇena vibhāvento. Ahikuṇapādīnaṃ atipaṭikūlajigucchanīyatā ativiya duggandhatāya. Sā ca ahīnaṃ tikhiṇakopatāya, kukkuramanussānaṃ odanakummāsūpacayatāya sarīrassa hotīti vadanti. Imesanti ahiādīnaṃ. Vaḍḍhetvāti uparūpari khipanena racitaṃ katvā. Taṃ pana vaḍḍhitaṃ tena ca bhājanaṃ pūritaṃ hotīti āha “vaḍḍhetvā paripūretvā”ti. Janassa dassanayogyaṃ dassanīyaṃ jaññaṃ, taṃ paramaparisuddhaṃ manoharañca hotīti āha “cokkhacokkha”nti. Abhinavaniviṭṭhā mahāmātā vadhukā. Sā pana puttalābhayogyataṃ upādāya maṅgalavacanena “janī”ti vuccati, tassā niyyamānaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ janiyā haratīti jaññaṃ. Ubhayatthāti atthadvaye. Punaruttanti āmeḍitavacanamāha. Na manāpaṃ etassāti amanāpo, tassa bhāvo amanāpatā, tathāpavatto cittuppādoti āha “amanāpaṃ idanti…pe… adhivacana”nti. Buddhavesattā liṅgassa parisuddhakaṃsapātisadisakā. Kuṇaparacanaṃ viya icchāvacarehi santānassa bharitabhāvo. So pana tesaṃ appahīnatāyāti āha “icchāvacarānaṃ appahāna”nti.

The meaning is that which is stated in 'yassa kassaci' and so on. Making it clear through a simile means explaining it by way of example, both in agreement and in opposition. The extreme repulsiveness and loathsomeness of a snake's carcass and so on is due to its exceedingly foul smell. And that, they say, is due to the snake's fierce anger, and for dogs and humans, due to the accumulation of rice and gruel in the body. 'Imesaṃ' refers to the snake and so on. 'Vaḍḍhetvā' means having constructed it by piling it up layer by layer. And that which is constructed also fills the vessel, hence it is said, 'having constructed it and filled it.' 'Jaññaṃ' means that which is fit to be seen by people, lovely; that it is supremely pure and delightful, hence it is called 'cokkhacokkhaṃ.' A newly established chief consort is a bride. She, on account of her suitability for obtaining a son, is called 'janī' as an auspicious term. The gift being brought to her is called 'jaññaṃ.' 'Ubhayatthāti' refers to two meanings. 'Punaruttanti' refers to repetition. 'Na manāpaṃ etassāti' means 'displeasing to him'; the state of being displeasing is 'amanāpatā,' and a mental state that has occurred thus, hence it is said, 'this is displeasing... a designation.' Due to the Buddha's guise, the sexual organ is like a pure bronze bowl. Like a heap of corpses, the mental continuum is filled with sensual desires. And that is due to their non-abandonment, hence it is said, 'the non-abandonment of sensual desires.'

62. “Tena gāmantavihāraṃ anuggaṇhātī”ti vattabbe “āraññikatta”nti pana potthake likhitaṃ. Na hi sukkapakkhe pāḷiyaṃ āraññikaggahaṇaṃ atthi, sati ca icchāvacarappahāne gāmantavihāro ekantena na paṭikkhipitabbo, icchitabbova tādisānaṃ uttarimanussadhammapaṭicchādanato[V 1.0225]. Tathā hi vakkhati “appicchatāsamuṭṭhānehī”tiādi. Sālivarabhattaracanaṃ viya icchāvacarappahānaṃ manuññabhāvato tittihetuto ca.

62. When it should be said, 'Therefore, he approves of dwelling near a village,' the term 'forest-dwelling' is instead written in the books. Indeed, in the Sukkapakkha of the Pāli, there is no mention of forest-dwelling. And when the abandonment of sensual desires is present, dwelling near a village should not be entirely rejected—it should indeed be desired by such persons for the sake of concealing higher human qualities. For thus it will be said, 'arising from fewness of wishes,' and so on. Like the preparation of a meal of fine rice, the abandonment of sensual desires is pleasing due to its agreeable nature and because it is a cause for satisfaction.

63. Maṃ [M 1.0253] tanti ca upayogavacanaṃ paṭi-saddayogena, attho pana sampadānamevāti āha “mayhaṃ tuyha”nti ca. “Samaye”ti bhummatthe “samaya”nti upayogavacanaṃ. Gijjhakūṭapaṇḍavaisigilivebhāravepullapabbatānaṃ vasena samantato giriparikkhepena. Rājagaheti samīpatthe bhummavacananti āha “taṃ nissāya viharāmī”ti.

63. The words 'maṃ' and 'taṃ' are terms of connection used with the prefix 'paṭi', but the meaning is in fact dative; thus it is said, 'mayhaṃ' and 'tuyhaṃ'. 'Samaye' is in the locative sense; 'samayaṃ' is a term of connection. By means of the Gijjhakūṭa, Paṇḍava, Isigili, Vebhāra, and Vepulla mountains, it is surrounded on all sides by a ring of mountains. 'Rājagahe' is a locative term in the sense of proximity; thus it is said, 'I dwell depending on it'.

Purāṇayānakāraputtoti purāṇe pabbajitato pubbe yānakāraputto tathāpaññāto. Jimhanti gomuttakuṭilaṃ. Tenāha “sappagatamaggasadisa”nti. Soti paṇḍuputto. Itaroti samiti. Cintitaṭṭhānamevāti cintitacintitaṭṭhānameva tacchati, tañca kho na tassa cittānusārena, atha kho attano suttānusārena tacchanto yānakāraputto. Cittanti attano cittena mama cittaṃ jānitvā viya.

'The former son of a cart-maker' means one who was known as the son of a cart-maker before he went forth long ago. 'Jimha' means crooked like cow's urine. Thus it is said, 'like the path of a snake.' 'So' refers to Paṇḍuputta. 'Itaro' refers to Samiti. 'Only the intended spot' means he planes only the very spot he has intended; and the son of the cart-maker planes that not according to the other's mind, but rather according to his own measuring line. 'Cittaṃ' means as if knowing my mind with his own mind.

“Na saddhāya pabbajito”ti imināva kammaphalasaddhāya abhāvo nesaṃ pakāsitoti āha “assaddhāti buddhadhammasaṅghesu saddhāvirahitā”ti. Pabbajitānaṃ jīvikā attho etesanti jīvikatthā. Tenāha “iṇabhayādīhī”tiādi. Kerāṭikaṃ vuccati sāṭheyyaṃ. Saṭhānaṃ guṇavāṇijakānaṃ kammaṃ sāṭheyyanti āha “sāṭheyyañhī”tiādi. Tucchasabhāvena māno naḷo viyāti naḷo, mānasaṅkhāto uggato naḷo etesanti unnaḷā. Tenāha “uṭṭhitatucchamānā”ti. Lahukatāya vā capalā. Pharusavacanatāya kharavacanā. Tiracchānakathābahulatāya niratthakavacanapalāpino. Asaṃvutakammadvārāti idaṃ kammadvārādīnaṃ asaṃvutabhāvo uppattidvārānaṃ asaṃvutatāya eva hotīti katvā vuttaṃ. Atha vā chasu indriyesūti nimitte bhummaṃ, chasu indriyesu nimittabhūtesu asaṃvutakammadvārāti attho. Yā mattāti bhojane ayuttapariyesana-ayuttapaṭiggahaṇa-ayuttaparibhoge vajjetvā yuttapariyesana-yuttapaṭiggahaṇa-yuttaparibhogasaṅkhātā yā mattā appamattehi jānitabbā. Tenāha “yuttatā”ti. Jāgareti rattindivaṃ āvaraṇiyehi dhammehi cittaparisodhanasaṅkhāte jāgare. Tesaṃ jāgaritāya adhisīlasikkhāya gāravarahitānaṃ itarasikkhāsu patiṭṭhā eva natthīti dassento “sikkhāpadesu bahulagāravā na hontī”ti vatvā tameva gāravābhāvaṃ sarūpena vibhāvento “āpattivītikkamabahulā”ti āha.

'By 'gone forth not out of faith,' their lack of faith in kamma and its results is revealed; thus it is said, 'they are faithless, devoid of faith in the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha.' Those for whom livelihood is the purpose of having gone forth are 'jīvikatthā.' Thus it is said, 'due to fear of debt, etc.' 'Kerāṭikaṃ' is called deceit. The action of the deceitful, who trade in virtue, is 'sāṭheyya'; thus it is said, 'for deceit is...' Arrogance, being hollow by nature, is like a reed ('naḷa'); those for whom the reed called conceit has risen up are 'unnaḷā' (arrogant). Thus it is said, 'they are uplifted by hollow pride.' They are fickle ('capalā') due to lightness. They are harsh in speech ('kharavacanā') due to harsh words. They are babblers of useless words ('niratthakavacanapalāpino') due to being full of animal-talk. 'Unrestrained in the doors of action' is said because the lack of restraint in the doors of action and so on arises precisely from the lack of restraint in the doors of arising. Alternatively, 'in the six sense faculties' is a locative of cause; thus, the meaning is 'unrestrained in the doors of action' when the six sense faculties are the cause. 'The measure' refers to that measure which should be known by the heedful, which consists of proper seeking, receiving, and consuming, having avoided improper seeking, receiving, and consuming of food. Thus it is said, 'appropriateness.' 'He is wakeful' refers to wakefulness, which is the purification of the mind day and night from obstructive states. Showing that those who lack reverence for the training in higher virtue have no foundation in the other trainings due to their lack of wakefulness, it is said, 'they are not often reverent in the training rules'; and to explain this lack of reverence in its own nature, it is said, 'they are frequent in transgressions of the rules'.

Pakatiyāpi [V 1.0226][M 1.0254] siddhāya ratanattayasaddhāya kammaphalasaddhāya ca saddhā. Pivanti maññe yathā taṃ dravabhūtaṃ amataṃ laddhā. Ghasanti maññe yathā taṃ bahalapiṇḍikasudhābhojanaṃ laddhā. Attamanavācaṃ nicchārentā “sādhu sādhū”ti. Tameva pana sādhukāraṃ hadaye ṭhapetvā abbhanumodantā. Ettha ca attamanavācānicchāraṇaṃ pivanasadisaṃ katvā vuttaṃ bahiddhābhāvato, manasā abbhanumodanaṃ pana abbhantarabhāvato ghasanasadisaṃ vuttaṃ. Saṅkhādanajjhoharaṇañhi ghasananti. Rassañca ekavacanaṃ hotīti āha “rasse sati sāriputtassa upari hotī”ti. Dīghañca bahuvacanaṃ hotīti āha “dīghe sati sabrahmacārīna”nti. “Upari hotī”ti ānetvā sambandho. Ālasiyabyasanādīhīti ālasiyena vā ñātibyasanādīhi vā. “Mahānāgāti vuccantī”ti vatvā tattha kāraṇaṃ vibhāvento “tatrā”tiādimāha. Tattha “na gacchantīti nāgā, na āgacchantīti nāgā, na āguṃ karontīti nāgā”ti yo vividho vacanattho icchito, taṃ vicāretvā dassetuṃ “chandādīhī”tiādi vuttaṃ, taṃ pana ñeyyāvabodhāya vacanato appamattakāraṇaṃ.

Even by nature, faith is established in the Triple Gem and in the fruit of kamma. They drink, it seems, as if they had obtained that liquid ambrosia. They eat, it seems, as if they had obtained that thick, lump-like nectar-food. Uttering words of delight, they say, 'Excellent, excellent!' Having placed that very approval in their hearts, they rejoice. Here, the utterance of words of delight is said to be like drinking due to its external nature, while mental rejoicing is said to be like eating due to its internal nature. For chewing and ingesting is indeed called eating. And he said, 'when it is short, it is singular,' meaning 'when short, it is concerning Sāriputta.' And he said, 'when it is long, it is plural,' meaning 'when long, it is concerning all fellow practitioners.' The connection is made by bringing in 'it is concerning.' 'Ālasiyabyasanādīhi' means either due to laziness or due to misfortunes such as those concerning relatives. Having said, 'they are called great nāgas,' he explains the reason therein, beginning with 'there.' There, whatever diverse meanings are intended, such as 'they do not go, thus they are nāgas; they do not come, thus they are nāgas; they do no wrong, thus they are nāgas'—to show this, having considered them, 'due to desire, etc.,' is said. But this is a minor reason, stated for the sake of understanding what is to be known.

Sayameva āguṃ na karoti sabbathā maggena pahīnaāguttā. So kāmayogādike sabbasaṃyoge dasavidhasaṃyojanappabhedāni ca sabbabandhanāni visajja jahitvā sabbattha yakkhādīsu, sabbesu vā bhavesu kenaci saṅgena na sajjati tīhi ca vimuttīhi vimutto, tato eva iṭṭhādīsu tādibhāvappattiyā tādi, so vuttalakkhaṇena tathattā taṃsabhāvattā nāgo pavuccateti attho veditabbo. Tenāha “evamettha attho veditabbo”ti. Aññehi khīṇāsavanāgehi aggasāvakattā guṇavisesayogato pujjatarā ca pāsaṃsatarā ca. Samaṃ anumodisunti aññamaññassa subhāsitato sampaṭicchanena samappavattamodatāya samaṃ sadisaṃ abbhanumodiṃsu. Taṃ pana samanumodanaṃ “tatthā”tiādinā pāḷivaseneva dasseti.

He himself does no evil, his wrongdoing having been completely abandoned by the path. He, having cast off and abandoned all bonds—the tenfold varieties of fetters such as the yoke of sensual pleasure, and all ties—is not attached anywhere, whether to spirits or in any existence, by any clinging. Freed by the three liberations, he is thus called 'tādi' (such a one), having attained suchness in regard to desirable things and so forth. Therefore, it is to be understood that he is called 'nāga' because of suchness and having that nature as described. Thus it is said, 'Thus, the meaning should be understood here.' By other arahant nāgas, due to being the foremost disciple and possessing superior qualities, he is more revered and more praised. 'Samaṃ anumodiṃsu' (they rejoiced together) means they rejoiced equally, with shared delight, by mutually accepting each other's well-spoken words. That mutual rejoicing is shown here precisely by the Pāli phrase beginning with 'tatthā'.

Sammutiparamatthadesanākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discourse concerning conventional and ultimate truth is concluded.

Anaṅgaṇasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Illumination of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta is completed.

6. Ākaṅkheyyasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta

64. Sampannanti [V 1.0227][M 1.0255] paripuṇṇaṃ, samantato pannaṃ pattanti sampannaṃ. Tenāha “idaṃ paripuṇṇasampannaṃ nāmā”ti. Nanti “suvā”ti vuttaṃ suvagaṇaṃ. Sampannoti sammadeva panno gato upagato. Tenāha “samannāgato”ti. Sampannanti sampattiyuttaṃ. Sā panettha rasasampatti adhippetā sāmaññajotanāya visese avaṭṭhānato. Tenāha “seyyathāpi khuddamadhuṃ aneḷaka”nti, niddosanti attho. Tena vuttaṃ “idaṃ madhurasampannaṃ nāmā”ti. Sīlassa anavasesasamādānena akhaṇḍādibhāvāpattiyā ca paripuṇṇasīlā. Samādānato paṭṭhāya acchindanato sīlasamaṅgino. Samādānato hi accantavirodhidhammānuppattiyā sīlasamaṅgitā veditabbā, cetanādīnaṃ pana sīlanalakkhaṇānaṃ dhammānaṃ pavattikkhaṇe vattabbameva natthi. Visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.9) vuttā, tasmā tattha vuttanayeneva vitthārakathā veditabbāti adhippāyo.

64. 'Sampanna' means complete, fully attained, having reached everywhere. Therefore, it is said, 'This is called 'paripuṇṇasampanna' (fully complete).' The particle 'naṃ' is said to be 'suvā' (good), referring to a collection of good things. 'Sampanno' means rightly attained, gone, or reached. Therefore, it is said, 'endowed.' 'Sampanna' means connected with attainment. Here, the intended attainment is the attainment of flavor, because it illuminates the general meaning without establishing the particular. Hence, it is said, 'Just like pure, flawless honey,' meaning free from defects. Therefore, it is stated, 'This is called 'madhurasampanna' (sweetly complete).' Through the complete undertaking of virtue without omission, and by becoming unbroken and so forth, one is of complete virtue. From the moment of undertaking, by not breaking it, they are endowed with virtue. For the state of being endowed with virtue should be understood from the non-arising of qualities utterly opposed to the undertaking. However, at the moment when mental factors that characterize virtue, such as volition, are active, there is nothing further to be said. As stated in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 1.9), the detailed explanation should be understood according to the method described there—this is the intended meaning.

Khettapāripūrīti nissitapāripūriyā nissayapāripūrimāha nissitakammavipattisampattivisayattā yathā “mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī”ti. Tathā hi khettena khaṇḍapūtiādidoso vutto. Khettaṃ khaṇḍaṃ hotīti aparipūraṃ hoti sassapāripūriyā abhāvato. Tenevāha “sassaṃ na uṭṭhetī”ti. Pādamattassapi anekambaṇaphalanato mahapphalaṃ hoti. Kisalayapalālādibahutāya mahānisaṃsaṃ. Evamevanti yathā khittaṃ bījaṃ khaṇḍādicatudosavasena aparipuṇṇaṃ hoti, tadabhāvena ca paripuṇṇaṃ, evaṃ sīlaṃ khaṇḍādicatudosavasena aparipuṇṇaṃ hoti, tadabhāvena ca paripuṇṇanti, catudosatadabhāvasāmaññameva nidassananidassitabbavipattisampattīsu dasseti. Mahapphalaṃ hoti vipākaphalena. Mahānisaṃsanti vipulānisaṃsaṃ. Svāyaṃ ānisaṃso idha pāḷiyaṃ nānappakārena vitthārīyati.

The perfection of the field refers to the perfection of the support through the perfection of the dependent, because it pertains to the sphere of failure and success of the dependent's action, just as in the phrase, 'The beds are making an outcry.' Thus, by 'field', a fault such as being broken or rotten is mentioned. The field is broken—meaning it is incomplete due to the absence of a perfect crop. Hence, it is said, 'The crop does not grow.' Even a portion measuring just a foot yields great fruit, because it produces many ambaṇas of fruit. It brings great benefit because of the abundance of shoots, straw, and so on. Similarly, just as a sown seed becomes incomplete due to four faults such as being broken, and complete in their absence, so too does virtue become incomplete due to four faults such as being broken, and complete in their absence. The commonality of those four faults and their absence is shown in the failure and success of the example and the thing exemplified. It yields great fruit through the fruit of its result. It brings great benefit—meaning extensive benefit. This benefit is elaborated in various ways in this Pāli text.

Ettāvatā kirāti (a. ni. ṭī. 2.2.37; a. ni. ṭī. 3.10.71-74) kira-saddo arucisūcanattho. Tenettha ācariyavādassa attano aruccanabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Sampannasīlāti anāmaṭṭhavisesaṃ sāmaññato sīlasaṅkhepena gahitaṃ. Tañca catubbidhanti ācariyatthero “catupārisuddhisīlaṃ uddisitvā”ti āha. Tatthāti catupārisuddhisīle. Jeṭṭhakasīlanti (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 3.5.412) padhānasīlaṃ. Ubhayatthāti uddesaniddese. Idha [M 1.0256] niddese viya uddesepi pātimokkhasaṃvaro bhagavatā vutto “sampannasīlā”ti vuttattāti adhippāyo[V 1.0228]. Sīlaggahaṇañhi pāḷiyaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvaravasena āgataṃ. Tenāha “pātimokkhasaṃvaroyevā”tiādi. Tattha avadhāraṇena itaresaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ekadesena pātimokkhantogadhabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Tathā hi anolokiyolokane ājīvahetu chasikkhāpadavītikkame gilānapaccayassa apaccavekkhitaparibhoge ca āpatti vihitāti. Tīṇīti indriyasaṃvarasīlādīni. Sīlanti vuttaṭṭhānaṃ nāma atthīti sīlapariyāyena tesaṃ katthaci sutte gahitaṭṭhānaṃ nāma kiṃ atthi yathā pātimokkhasaṃvaroti ācariyassa sammukhattā apaṭikkhipantova upacārena pucchanto viya vadati. Tenāha “ananujānanto”ti. Chadvārarakkhāmattakamevāti tassa sallahukabhāvamāha cittādhiṭṭhānamattena paṭipākatikabhāvāpattito. Itaradvayepi eseva nayo. Paccayuppattimattakanti phalena hetuṃ dasseti. Uppādanahetukā hi paccayānaṃ uppatti. Idamatthanti idaṃ payojanaṃ imassa paccayassa paribhuñjaneti adhippāyo. Nippariyāyenāti iminā indriyasaṃvarādīni tīṇi padhānassa sīlassa parivāravasena pavattiyā pariyāyasīlāni nāmāti dasseti.

'Ettāvatā kira'—the word 'kira' indicates dislike. Here, it reveals the commentator's own disapproval of the teacher's view. 'Perfect in virtue' refers to virtue in general, without specifying distinctions, taken as a summary of virtue. And that it is fourfold—the elder teacher said, 'having pointed out the fourfold purity of virtue.' Here, in the fourfold purity of virtue, 'foremost virtue' refers to the principal virtue. 'In both respects'—in the summary statement and the detailed explanation. Here, in the summary statement as in the detailed explanation, the restraint of the Pātimokkha was spoken of by the Blessed One, because it is said 'perfect in virtue'—this is the meaning. For in the Pāli, the term 'virtue' is used in the sense of restraint by the Pātimokkha. Therefore, it is said, 'only the restraint of the Pātimokkha,' etc. There, by this emphasis, the inclusion of the other three is shown to be partially contained within the Pātimokkha. For an offense is laid down for looking at what is improper, for transgressing the six training rules for the sake of livelihood, and for using requisites for the sick without reflection. 'The three' refers to the virtue of restraint of the senses, etc. 'Virtue'—is there any place where these are mentioned in the texts by way of the term 'virtue', just as the restraint of the Pātimokkha is? Without directly opposing the teacher, he asks as if by way of suggestion. Hence, it is said, 'not acknowledging.' 'Merely guarding the six sense-doors'—this indicates its lightness, as it becomes natural merely through mental resolution. The same applies to the other two. 'Merely the arising of requisites'—this shows the cause by its effect. For the arising of requisites is caused by that which produces them. 'This is the purpose'—this is the benefit, the purpose for using this requisite—such is the meaning. 'Without elaboration'—by this, it is shown that the three—restraint of the senses, etc.—are called 'virtues by way of elaboration' because they function as accessories to the principal virtue.

Idāni pātimokkhasaṃvarasseva padhānabhāvaṃ byatirekato anvayato ca upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “yassā”tiādimāha. Tattha soti pātimokkhasaṃvaro. Sesānīti indriyasaṃvarādīni. Tassevāti “sampannasīlā”ti ettha yaṃ sīlaṃ vuttaṃ, tasseva. Sampannapātimokkhāti ettha pātimokkhaggahaṇena vevacanaṃ vatvā taṃ vitthāretvā…pe… ādimāha. Yathā aññathāpi “idha bhikkhu sīlavā hotī”ti (mahāni. 199) puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya uddiṭṭhaṃ sīlaṃ “pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharatī”ti (vibha. 508; mahāni. 199) niddiṭṭhaṃ.

Now, to explain the primary importance of the Pātimokkha restraint both by way of exclusion and inclusion, and by analogy, the text begins with “yassā,” etc. Herein, “so” refers to the Pātimokkha restraint. “Sesāni” refers to the restraint of the sense faculties and so forth. “Tasseva” refers to that very virtue that was spoken of in the phrase “perfect in virtue.” In “sampannapātimokkhā” (perfect in Pātimokkha), by the taking up of the term “Pātimokkha,” a synonym is stated, and expanding on that… it begins. Just as elsewhere, the virtue designated in the teaching based on the individual, “Here, a monk is virtuous” (Mahāni. 199), is explained as “he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint” (Vibha. 508; Mahāni. 199).

Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutāti yo naṃ pāti rakkhati, taṃ mokkheti moceti āpāyikādīhi dukkhehīti “pātimokkha”nti laddhanāmena sikkhāpadasīlena pihitakāyavacīdvārā. Te pana yasmā evaṃbhūtā tena samannāgatā nāma honti, tasmā vuttaṃ “pātimokkhasaṃvarena samannāgatā”ti.

“Restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha” means they are those whose bodily and verbal doors are covered by the virtue of the training precepts, which has obtained the name “Pātimokkha” because: “it frees (mokkheti) and releases (moceti) one (taṃ) who protects (pāti) and guards it from sufferings such as those of the lower realms.” And since they are of such a nature, they are said to be endowed with it. Therefore, it is said: “endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha.”

Aparo [M 1.0257] nayo (udā. aṭṭha. 31; itivu. aṭṭha. 97) – kilesānaṃ balavabhāvato, pāpakiriyāya sukarabhāvato, puññakiriyāya ca dukkarabhāvato bahukkhattuṃ apāyesu patanasīloti pātī, puthujjano. Aniccatāya vā bhavādīsu kammavegakkhitto ghaṭīyantaṃ viya anavaṭṭhānena paribbhamanato gamanasīloti pātī, maraṇavasena vā tamhi tamhi sattanikāye attabhāvassa pātanasīloti pātī, sattasantāno, cittameva vā, taṃ pātiṃ saṃsāradukkhato mokkhetīti [V 1.0229] pātimokkhaṃ. Cittassa hi vimokkhena satto vimuttoti vuccati. Vuttañhi “cittavodānā visujjhantī”ti, “anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimutta”nti (mahāva. 28) ca.

Another explanation (Udāna Commentary 31; Itivuttaka Commentary 97): Due to the strength of defilements, the ease of performing evil deeds, and the difficulty of performing meritorious deeds, the ordinary person is of a nature to fall frequently into the lower realms—hence, they are called “pātī.” Or, due to impermanence, being hurled by the force of kamma in the realms of existence and wandering without stability like a potter's wheel, one is of a nature to be ever-going—thus, they are called “pātī.” Or, by way of death, because the continuity of a being is of a nature to cause the falling of individual existence in this or that group of beings, it is called “pātī.” Or, the mind itself is a “pātī,” and that which frees this “pātī” from the suffering of saṃsāra is the Pātimokkha. For a being is said to be liberated through the liberation of the mind. As it is said: “Beings are purified by the cleansing of the mind,” and “The mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging” (Mahāva. 28).

Atha vā avijjādinā hetunā saṃsāre patati gacchati pavattatīti pātī. “Avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ sattānaṃ taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarata”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.125) hi vuttaṃ. Tassa pātino sattassa taṇhādisaṃkilesattayato mokkho etenāti pātimokkho. “Kaṇṭhekālo”tiādīnaṃ viya samāsasiddhi veditabbā.

Alternatively, because it falls, goes, and proceeds in saṃsāra due to causes such as ignorance, it is called “pātī.” For it is said: “Beings, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, run on and wander in saṃsāra” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.125). Liberation by this means from the threefold defilements of craving and so forth, for such a “falling” being, is called “Pātimokkha.” Its compound formation should be understood like that of words such as “kaṇṭhekāla.”

Atha vā pāteti vinipāteti dukkheti pāti, cittaṃ. Vuttañhi “cittena nīyati loko, cittena parikassatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.62). Tassa pātino mokkho etenāti pātimokkho. Patati vā etena apāyadukkhe saṃsāradukkhe cāti pātī, taṇhādisaṃkileso. Vuttañhi “taṇhā janeti purisaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.57), taṇhādutiyo puriso”ti (itivu. 15, 105; a. ni. 4.9) ca ādi. Tato pātito mokkhoti pātimokkho.

Or, the mind causes to fall, causes to fall utterly, and causes suffering—hence it is called “pātī.” As stated: “The world is led by the mind, dragged by the mind” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.62). Liberation by this means from that which causes falling is called “Pātimokkha.” Or, by this one falls into the suffering of the lower realms and the suffering of saṃsāra—hence it is called “pātī,” namely, the defilement of craving and so forth. As stated: “Craving gives birth to a person” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.57), and “A person has craving as their companion” (Itivuttaka 15, 105; Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.9), and so on. Liberation from that which causes falling is called “Pātimokkha.”

Atha vā patati etthāti pātī, cha ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanāni. Vuttañhi “chasu loko samuppanno, chasu kubbati santhava”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.70; su. ni. 171). Tato ajjhattikabāhirāyatanasaṅkhātato pātito mokkhoti pātimokkho. Atha vā pāto vinipāto assa atthīti pātī, saṃsāro. Tato mokkhoti pātimokkho. Atha vā sabbalokādhipatibhāvato dhammissaro bhagavā “patī”ti vuccati, muccati etenāti mokkho, patino mokkho tena paññattattāti pātimokkho[M 1.0258]. Pātimokkho eva pātimokkho. Sabbaguṇānaṃ vā mūlabhāvato uttamaṭṭhena pati ca so yathāvuttatthena mokkho cāti pātimokkho. Pātimokkho eva pātimokkho. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “pātimokkhantiādimetaṃ mukhametaṃ pamukhameta”nti (mahāva. 135) vitthāro.

Or else, because one falls into it, it is called “pātī”—namely, the six internal and external sense bases. For it is said: “The world has arisen in the six; in the six it makes its connections” (Saṃ. Ni. 1.70; Su. Ni. 171). Liberation from that “pātī,” designated as the internal and external sense bases, is called “Pātimokkha.” Or else, because it has a fall, a downfall, it is called “pātī”—namely, saṃsāra. Liberation from that is “Pātimokkha.” Or else, because he is sovereign over all the world, the Blessed One, the lord of the Dhamma, is called “Pati.” One is liberated by this, hence “mokkha.” It is the “mokkha” of the “Pati” (the Lord), because it was proclaimed by him; hence, “Pātimokkha.” Pātimokkha is simply Pātimokkha. Or else, because it is the root of all virtues, it is “pati” in the sense of “supreme,” and as previously explained, it is “mokkha”—thus, “Pātimokkha.” Pātimokkha is simply Pātimokkha. For so it is said: “The Pātimokkha—this is the beginning, this is the face, this is the principal” (Mahāva. 135), and so on in detail.

Atha vā pa-iti pakāre, atīti accantatthe nipāto, tasmā pakārehi accantaṃ mokkhetīti pātimokkho. Idañhi sīlaṃ sayaṃ tadaṅgavasena, samādhisahitaṃ paññāsahitañca vikkhambhanavasena, samucchedavasena ca accantaṃ mokkheti mocetīti pātimokkho. Pati pati mokkhoti vā pātimokkho, tamhā tamhā vītikkamadosato paccekaṃ mokkhoti attho. Pātimokkho eva pātimokkho. Mokkho vā nibbānaṃ, tassa mokkhassa patibimbabhūtoti pātimokkho[V 1.0230]. Sīlasaṃvaro hi nibbedhabhāgiyo sūriyassa aruṇuggamanaṃ viya nibbānassa udayabhūto tappaṭibhāgo viya hoti yathārahaṃ kilesanibbāpanatoti pātimokkho. Pātimokkhoyeva pātimokkho. Atha vā mokkhaṃ pati vattati mokkhābhimukhanti vā pātimokkhaṃ. Pātimokkhameva pātimokkhanti evamettha pātimokkhasaddassa attho veditabbo.

Alternatively, the prefix “pa-” indicates “in various ways,” and “ati-” is a particle signifying “utterly.” Therefore, because it utterly liberates in various ways, it is “pātimokkha.” For this virtue liberates utterly by substitution (tadaṅgavasena), by suppression (vikkhambhanavasena) when accompanied by concentration and wisdom, and by eradication (samucchedavasena); thus it is “pātimokkha.” Or, “pati pati mokkho” means “pātimokkha,” the meaning being liberation individually from each and every fault of transgression. Pātimokkha is simply Pātimokkha. Or, “mokkha” is Nibbāna, and because this is a reflection of that liberation, it is “pātimokkha.” For the restraint of virtue is conducive to penetration; like the dawn preceding the sunrise, it is a rising of Nibbāna, its counterpart, as it appropriately extinguishes defilements; therefore, it is “pātimokkha.” Pātimokkha is simply Pātimokkha. Or, because it proceeds towards liberation (mokkhaṃ pati vattati) or is facing liberation (mokkhābhimukhaṃ), it is “pātimokkha.” Pātimokkha is simply Pātimokkha. Thus, the meaning of the term “pātimokkha” should be understood in these ways.

Ācāragocarasampannāti kāyikavācasikaavītikkamasaṅkhātena ācārena ceva navesiyagocaratādisaṅkhātena gocarena ca sampannā, sampannaācāragocarāti attho. Appamattesūti atiparittakesu anāpattigamanīyesu, dukkaṭadubbhāsitamattesūti apare. Vajjesūti gārayhesu. Te pana ekantato akusalasabhāvā hontīti āha “akusaladhammesū”ti. Bhayadassinoti bhayato dassanasīlā, paramāṇumattampi vajjaṃ sineruppamāṇaṃ viya katvā bhāyanasīlā. Sammā ādiyitvāti sammadeva sakkaccaṃ sabbaso ca ādiyitvā. Sikkhāpadesūti niddhāraṇe bhummanti samudāyato avayavaniddhāraṇaṃ dassento “sikkhāpadesu taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyitvā sikkhathā”ti atthamāha. Sikkhāpadameva hi samādātabbaṃ sikkhitabbañcāti adhippāyo. Yaṃ kiñci sikkhākoṭṭhāsesūti sikkhākoṭṭhāsesu mūlapaññattianupaññatisabbatthapaññattipadesapaññattiādibhedaṃ yaṃ kiñci sikkhitabbaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ pūretabbaṃ sīlaṃ. Taṃ pana dvāravasena duvidhamevāti āha [M 1.0259] “kāyikaṃ vācasikañcā”ti. Imasmiṃ atthavikappe sikkhāpadesūti ādhāre bhummaṃ sikkhābhāgesu kassaci visuṃ aggahaṇato. Tenāha “taṃ sabba”nti.

“Endowed with good conduct and resort” (ācāragocarasampannā) means accomplished in both conduct, which is defined as non-transgression in bodily and verbal actions, and resort, which is defined as proper behavior in seeking alms, and so on. The meaning is: “accomplished in conduct and resort.” “In minor matters” (appamattesu) refers to very trivial matters that do not constitute an offense, or, according to others, to mere offenses of wrong conduct or wrong speech. “In faults” (vajjesu) refers to what is blameworthy. To clarify that these are entirely unwholesome in nature, it is said, “in unwholesome qualities” (akusaladhammesu). “Seeing danger” (bhayadassino) means having the nature of seeing danger, being habitually fearful, treating even a fault as tiny as an atom as if it were as immense as Mount Sineru. “Rightly undertaking” (sammā ādiyitvā) means undertaking properly, respectfully, and in every way. “In the training rules” (sikkhāpadesu) is a locative of determination, indicating the determination of a part from the whole. To show this, the text explains the meaning as: “Having undertaken each training rule among the training rules, you should train.” The intention is that the training rule itself is what should be undertaken and trained in. “Whatever pertains to the sections of the training” (yaṃ kiñci sikkhākoṭṭhāsesu) refers to any virtue within the various divisions of the training—such as the root regulations, supplementary regulations, universal regulations, and local regulations—that should be trained in, practiced, and fulfilled. This, however, is twofold by way of the doors, as stated: “bodily or verbal.” In this alternative interpretation, “in the training rules” (sikkhāpadesu) is a locative of basis, because no particular part is taken separately from among the divisions of the training. Therefore, it is said, “all of that.”

65. Kasmā āraddhanti (a. ni. ṭī. 3.10.71-74) desanāya kāraṇapucchā. Sīlānisaṃsadassanatthanti payojananiddeso. Ko attho kva attho kva nipātitāti? Nayidamevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sīlānisaṃsadassanatthanti hi ettha byatirekato yaṃ sīlānisaṃsassa adassanaṃ, taṃ imissā desanāya kāraṇanti kasmā āraddhanti vineyyānaṃ sīlānisaṃsassa adassanatoti atthato āpanno eva hotīti. Tenāha “sacepī”tiādi. Sīlānisaṃsadassanatthanti pana imassa atthaṃ vivarituṃ “tesa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ānisaṃsoti udayo. “Sīlavā sīlasampanno kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggalokaṃ upapajjatī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.150; 3.316; a. ni. 5.213; mahāva. 285) pana vipākaphalampi “ānisaṃso”ti vuttaṃ. Ko visesoti ko phalaviseso. Kā vaḍḍhīti ko abbhudayo. Vijjamānopi guṇo yāthāvato vibhāvito eva abhiruciṃ uppādeti, na avibhāvito, tasmā ekantato ānisaṃsakittanaṃ icchitabbamevāti dassetuṃ visakaṇṭakavāṇijo udāhaṭo.

65. 'Why do they begin?' (Kasmā āraddhanti) is a question about the reason for the teaching. 'For the purpose of showing the benefits of virtue' (sīlānisaṃsadassanatthaṃ) is an explanation of the aim. What is the meaning? Where is the meaning? Where is it placed? It should not be understood in this way. For here, 'for the purpose of showing the benefits of virtue' implies, by contrast, that the reason for this teaching is the non-seeing of the benefits of virtue; thus, the meaning 'Why do they begin?' is already included, because those to be trained do not see the benefits of virtue. Therefore, it is said, 'If even...' and so on. To elaborate on the meaning of 'for the purpose of showing the benefits of virtue,' it is stated, 'for them...' and so on. 'Benefit' (ānisaṃso) means arising. However, in passages such as, 'A virtuous one, accomplished in virtue, after the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world' (D. Ni. 2.150; 3.316; A. Ni. 5.213; Mahāva. 285), the resultant fruit (vipākaphalampi) is also called a 'benefit.' 'What is the distinction?' (Ko viseso) means 'what is the distinction in the fruit?' 'What is the growth?' (Kā vaḍḍhī) means 'what is the increase?' Even an existing quality, when properly analyzed, generates delight, but not when unanalyzed. Therefore, to show that the complete proclamation of benefits is indeed desirable, the merchant with the poisoned thorn is cited.

Tattha [V 1.0231] guḷo nāma ucchurasaṃ pacitvā cuṇṇādīhi missitvā sampiṇḍane piṇḍībhūtaṃ. Phāṇitaṃ apiṇḍitaṃ dravībhūtaṃ. Khaṇḍaṃ bhijjanakkhamaṃ. Sakkharā nāma phalikasadisā. Sakkharādīniti ādi-saddena macchaṇḍikānaṃ saṅgaho. Tasmiṃ kāle guḷādīsu visakaṇṭakavohāro apaccantadese pacuroti “paccantagāmaṃ gantvā”ti vuttaṃ. Dārake ca palāpesuṃ “visakaṇṭakaṃ mā gaṇhantū”ti.

There, 'guḷa' (jaggery) refers to sugarcane juice boiled and mixed with powders and other ingredients, then compacted into a lump. 'Phāṇita' (molasses) is the unlumped, liquid form. 'Khaṇḍa' (sugar candy) is that which is capable of being broken. 'Sakkharā' (sugar) is like crystal. The term 'sakkharādīni' (sugars, etc.) includes, by the word 'ādi' (etc.), varieties like 'macchaṇḍikā' (sugar lumps). At that time, the term 'visakaṇṭaka' (poisoned thorn) was commonly used for jaggery and similar items in outlying regions, hence it is said, 'having gone to an outlying village.' And they sent the children away, saying, 'Do not take the poisoned thorn!'

Piyoti piyāyitabbo. Piyassa nāma dassanaṃ ekantato abhinanditabbaṃ hotīti āha “viyacakkhūhi sampassitabbo”ti. Pītisamuṭṭhānapasannasommarūpapariggahañhi cakkhu “piyacakkhū”ti vuccati. Tesanti sabrahmacārīnaṃ. Manavaḍḍhanakoti pītimanassa paribrūhanato uparūpari pīticittassa uppādako. Garuṭṭhāniyoti garukaraṇassa ṭhānabhūto. Jānaṃ jānātīti ñāṇena jānitabbaṃ jānāti. Yathā vā aññe ajānantāpi jānantā viya pavattanti, na evamayaṃ, ayaṃ pana jānanto eva jānāti[M 1.0260]. Passaṃ passatīti dassanabhūtena paññācakkhunā passitabbaṃ passati, passanto eva vā passati. Evaṃ sambhāvanīyoti evaṃ viññutāya paṇḍitabhāvena sambhāvetabbo.

'Piyo' (beloved) means one who is to be loved. Seeing a beloved is entirely delightful; hence, it is said, 'he should be looked at with loving eyes' (piyacakkhūhi sampassitabbo). For the eye that grasps forms filled with joy arising from delight, serene and pleasant, is called 'loving eyes' (piyacakkhu). 'Tesaṃ' (their) refers to the fellow practitioners. 'Manavaḍḍhanako' (one who increases joy) means one who enhances the joyful mind, producing a mind of joy again and again. 'Garuṭṭhānīyo' (worthy of reverence) means one who is a basis for reverence. 'Jānaṃ jānāti' (knowing, he knows) means he knows what should be known by wisdom. Unlike others who, without knowing, may act as if they know, this one truly knows by knowing. 'Passaṃ passati' (seeing, he sees) means he sees what should be seen by the eye of wisdom, which is vision itself, or he sees while seeing. Thus, 'sambhāvanīyo' (to be esteemed) means he is to be esteemed for his intelligence and wisdom.

Sīlesvevassa paripūrakārīti sīlesu paripūrakārī eva bhaveyyāti evaṃ uttarapadāvadhāraṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evañhi iminā padena uparisikkhādvayaṃ anivattitameva hoti. Yathā pana sīlesu paripūrakārī nāma hoti, taṃ phalena dassetuṃ “ajjhatta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Vipassanādhiṭṭhānasamādhisaṃvattanikatāya hi idha sīlassa pāripūrī, na kevalaṃ akhaṇḍādibhāvamattaṃ. Tenāha “yāni kho pana tāni akhaṇḍāni…pe… samādhisaṃvattanikānī”ti. Evañca katvā upari sikkhādvayaṃ sīlassa sambhārabhāvena gahitanti sīlassevettha padhānaggahaṇaṃ siddhaṃ hoti. Tathā hi cittekaggatāsaṅkhārapariggahānaṃ sīlassānurakkhaṇabhāvaṃ vakkhati. Yaṃ pana vakkhati “sikkhattayadesanā jātā”ti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.65), taṃ itarāsampi sikkhānaṃ idha gahitatāmattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na padhānabhāvena gahitataṃ. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ sīlassa appamattakatāvacanaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ “appamattakaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, oramattaka”nti (dī. ni. 1.7). Taṃ puthujjanagocaraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tathā hi tattha na nippadesato sīlaṃ vibhattaṃ, evaṃ katvā tattha sīlamattakanti mattaggahaṇaṃ samatthitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Anūnenāti akhaṇḍādibhāvena, kassaci vā ahāpanena upapannena. Ākārenāti karaṇena sampādanena. Cittasamatheti cittasamādhāne. Yuttoti aviyutto pasuto. Yo sabbena sabbaṃ jhānabhāvanaṃ ananuyutto, so taṃ bahi nīharati nāma. Yo ārabhitvā antarā saṅkocaṃ āpajjati[V 1.0232], so taṃ vināseti nāma. Yo pana īdiso ahutvā jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, so anirākatajjhānoti dassento “bahi anīhaṭajjhāno”tiādimāha.

'He should be one who fulfills virtue' (sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī) means 'he should indeed be one who fulfills virtue.' Thus, the determination of the subsequent word should be understood. For by this word, the two higher trainings are indeed not excluded. And to illustrate with what result one is fully accomplished in virtue, the phrase 'internally' (ajjhattaṃ) and so on is stated. Here, the perfection of virtue is due to its conduciveness to concentration, which serves as the foundation for insight, not merely its unbrokenness and so forth. Hence it is said: 'Those virtues that are unbroken... leading to concentration' (yāni kho pana tāni akhaṇḍāni... samādhisaṃvattanikāni). Having established this, the two higher trainings are included here as factors contributing to virtue. Thus, the primary emphasis on virtue here is established. For it will be said that the mind's unification and the comprehension of formations serve to protect virtue. But when it is said, 'The teaching of the threefold training has arisen' (sikkhattayadesanā jātā), this refers to the mere inclusion of the other trainings here, not their primary emphasis. If so, how is the statement about virtue being 'a small matter' to be understood? For it has been said: 'This, monks, is a small matter, a trifling thing' (appamattakaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, oramattakaṃ). This is said with reference to the domain of ordinary people. For there, virtue is not analyzed in detail, and thus the word 'merely' (mattakaṃ) qualifying virtue there is justified. 'Not deficient' (anūnena) means by way of its unbrokenness and so forth, or by being complete through not losing any of its constituent qualities. 'By means' (ākārena) refers to the manner of accomplishment. 'With a composed mind' (cittasamatheti) means with a mind established in concentration. 'Diligent' (yutto) means not separate, devoted. Whoever entirely neglects the cultivation of jhāna, they cast it outside. Whoever begins but then shrinks back midway, they destroy it. But one who, not being like that, attains and dwells in jhāna—demonstrating that jhāna is not rejected—says, 'Jhāna not cast aside externally' (bahi anīhaṭajjhāno), and so on.

Aniccassa tebhūmakadhammassa, aniccanti vā anupassanā aniccānupassanā. Tathā dukkhānupassanā anattānupassanā ca. Tasseva nibbindanākārena pavattā anupassanā nibbidānupassanā. Virajjanākārena pavattā anupassanā virāgānupassanā. Nirodhassa anupassanā nirodhānupassanā. Paṭinissajjanavasena pavattā anupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanā. Suññāgāragato bhikkhu tattha laddhakāyavivekatāya samathavipassanāvasena cittavivekaṃ [M 1.0261] paribrūhento yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipattiyā lokaṃ sāsanañca attano visesādhigamaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ suññāgārañca upasobhayamāno guṇavisesādhiṭṭhānabhāvāpādanena viññūnaṃ atthato taṃ brūhento nāma hotīti vuttaṃ “brūhetā suññāgārāna”nti. Tenāha “ettha cā”tiādi. Ayameva suññāgārānubrūhanaviññuppasatthānaṃ bhājanaṃ, na senāsanapatiṭṭhāpananti dassento āha “ekabhūmakādi…pe… daṭṭhabbo”ti. Suññāgāraggahaṇena cettha araññarukkhamūlādi sabbaṃ padhānānuyogakkhamaṃ senāsanaṃ gahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) is the contemplation of the impermanent phenomena of the three realms, or simply the contemplation of impermanence. Similarly, there are the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā) and the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā). The contemplation that proceeds in the mode of disenchantment is the contemplation of disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā). The contemplation that proceeds in the mode of dispassion is the contemplation of dispassion (virāgānupassanā). The contemplation of cessation is the contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā). The contemplation that proceeds by way of relinquishment is the contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā). A monk who has gone to an empty dwelling, having obtained bodily seclusion there, cultivates mental seclusion through serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Practicing according to instruction, he adorns the world, the Dispensation, and the empty dwelling which is the basis for his own attainment of distinction. By producing the state of establishing special qualities, he truly amplifies that meaning for the wise. Thus, it is said, 'He is a cultivator of empty dwellings' (brūhetā suññāgārānaṃ). Therefore, he said, 'Here also...' and so on. Showing that this very (monk) is the receptacle of those praised by the wise for cultivating empty dwellings, and not (merely) the establishment of a dwelling place, he said, 'Onefold... etc. ... should be seen' (ekabhūmakādi... daṭṭhabbo). By the taking of 'empty dwelling' (suññāgāra) here, all suitable lodgings for striving—such as forest, roots of trees, and so on—are to be taken as included.

Taṇhāvicaritadesanāti “ajjhattikassa upādāyā”ti (vibha. 937) ādinayappavattaṃ taṇhāvicaritasuttaṃ. Taṇhāpadaṭṭhānattāti taṇhāsannissayattā. Na hi taṇhāvirahitā mānadiṭṭhipavatti atthi. Mānadiṭṭhiyo osaritvāti dassetabbatāya mānadiṭṭhiyo ogāhetvāti attho. Gahaṇatthameva hi desetabbadhammassa desanāya osaraṇaṃ. Taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiyo papañcattayaṃ sattasantānassa saṃsāre papañcanato anuppabandhanavasena vitthāraṇato. Sīlapadaṭṭhānattāti sīlādhiṭṭhānattā.

The 'teaching on the courses of craving' (Taṇhāvicaritadesanā) refers to the Taṇhāvicarita Sutta, which proceeds according to the method beginning with 'On account of the internal...' (Vibh. 937). 'Craving is the foundation' means it is dependent on craving. Indeed, there is no occurrence of conceit and views without craving. 'Having entered into conceit and views' means having plunged into conceit and views for the purpose of demonstration. Indeed, the 'entering into' the teaching of the Dhamma to be taught is precisely for the purpose of grasping it. Craving, conceit, and views are the threefold proliferation because they proliferate beings in the cycle of existence, extending as a continuous bond in the continuum of beings. 'Virtue is the foundation' means it is established in virtue.

Adhicittasikkhā vuttāti ānetvā sambandho. Vipassanāvasena suññāgāravaḍḍhaneti yojanā. Dvepi sikkhāti adhicittādhipaññāsikkhā. Saṅgahetvāti adhisīlasikkhāya saddhiṃ saṅgahetvā vuttā. Yadi evamayaṃ sikkhattayadesanā jātāti sikkhattayānisaṃsappakāsanī siyāti anuyogaṃ sandhāyāha “ettha cā”tiādi. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Indriyasaṃvaro viya pātimokkhasaṃvarassa catupārisuddhisīlassa ārakkhabhūtā cittekaggatā vipassanā ca idha gahitāti tadubhayaṃ appadhānaṃ, sīlameva pana padhānabhāvena gahitanti veditabbaṃ. Tenāha “sīlānurakkhikā evā”tiādi.

The connection is made by bringing forward the words, 'the training in the higher mind has been spoken of.' The application is: by means of insight, one increases the practice of dwelling in empty abodes. Both trainings are the training in the higher mind and the training in higher wisdom. Having been included, they are spoken of together with the training in higher virtue. Referring to the objection, 'If this is so, this teaching of the threefold training has arisen, so it would be a declaration of the benefits of the threefold training,' he says, 'And here,' etc. As to what should be said there, that has already been stated below. Just as restraint of the senses is a protection for the restraint of the Pātimokkha, the virtue of fourfold purity, so too one-pointedness of mind and insight are taken here. But both of these are secondary; it should be understood that virtue alone is taken as primary. Therefore, he says, 'They are only guardians of virtue,' etc.

Balavatarasukhanti [V 1.0233] samuppannabyādhidukkhato balavataraṃ, taṃ abhibhavituṃ samatthaṃ jhānasukhaṃ uppajjati. Balavamamattaṃ hoti, tena daḷhaattasinehena viluttahadayo kusaladhamme chaḍḍento so tathārūpesu…pe… posetā hoti. Balavamamattaṃ vā sineho na hoti “suddho saṅkhārapuñjo”ti yāthāvadassanena [M 1.0262] ahaṃkāramamaṃkārābhāvato. Dubbhikkhabhaye khudābhibhavaṃ sandhāyāha “sacepissa antāni bahi nikkhamantī”ti. Byādhibhayaṃ sandhāyāha “ussussati visussanī”ti. Ādi-saddena gahitaṃ corabhayaṃ sandhāyāha “khaṇḍākhaṇḍiko vā”ti. Ubhayassāti samathavipassanādvayassa. Ettha ca “ajjhattaṃ ceto…pe… suññāgārāna”nti imehi visesanibbedhabhāgiyabhāvāpādanena sīlaṃ rakkhituṃ samatthā eva cittekaggatāvipassanā gahitā. Yasmā parato jhānavimokkhaphalābhiññāṇaadhiṭṭhānabhāvo sīlassa uddhaṭo, tasmā tassa bhiyyopi sambhārabhūtā eva cittekaggatā vipassanā tattha tattha gahitāti veditabbā.

Stronger bliss means: a jhānic bliss arises that is stronger than the suffering from an arisen illness and is capable of overcoming it. When strong 'mine-ness' is present, with his heart plundered by strong self-love, abandoning wholesome states, he becomes a nourisher of such things... etc. Or, there is no strong 'mine-ness' or affection, due to seeing things as they truly are as 'a pure heap of formations,' and because of the absence of 'I-making' and 'mine-making.' Referring to being overcome by hunger in the face of the fear of famine, he says, 'if his intestines were to come out.' Referring to the fear of illness, he says, 'he withers, a parching.' Referring to the fear of thieves, which is included by the word 'etc.', he says, 'or hacked to pieces.' 'Of both' means of the pair of serenity and insight. And here, by these phrases, 'internally, the mind... etc... of empty dwellings,' one-pointedness of mind and insight are taken as being capable of protecting virtue by producing the state of being conducive to distinction and penetration. Since the state of being a foundation for jhāna, liberation, fruition, and direct knowledge is drawn out from virtue hereafter, therefore it should be understood that one-pointedness of mind and insight, being further requisites for it, are taken in various places.

Sīlādīti ādi-saddena yathāvuttacittekaggatāvipassanā saṅgaṇhāti, sīlassa vā mūlakāraṇabhūtaṃ sabbaṃ kammassakatañāṇañca saṅgaṇhāti kammapathasammādiṭṭhiṃ vā. Sīlañhi tadaññampi puññakiriyāvatthu teneva parisodhitaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsanti. Lābhī assanti lābhā sāya saṃvaraṇasīlaparipūraṇaṃ pāḷiyaṃ āgataṃ kimīdisaṃ bhagavā anujānātīti? Na bhagavā sabhāvena īdisaṃ anujānāti, mahākāruṇikatāya pana puggalajjhāsayena evaṃ vuttanti dassento “na cetthā”tiādimāha. Tattha ghāsesanaṃ chinnakatho na vācaṃ payuttaṃ bhaṇeti chinnakatho mūgo viya hutvā obhāsaparikathānimittaviññattipayuttaṃ ghāsesanaṃ vācaṃ na bhaṇe na katheyyāti attho. Puggalajjhāsayavasenāti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivaranto “yesañhī”tiādimāha. Raso sabhāvabhūto ānisaṃso rasānisaṃso.

'Virtue, etc.': by the word 'etc.', it includes one-pointedness of mind and insight as described; or it includes all knowledge of kamma as one's own, which is the root cause of virtue; or right view regarding the paths of kamma. For virtue, and even other bases of meritorious action purified by it, become greatly fruitful and of great benefit. The gain is the fulfillment of the virtue of restraint. Regarding the passage in the Pāli, 'They would be gainers,' the question is asked, 'What kind of gain does the Blessed One allow?' The Blessed One does not allow such a thing by its nature; but showing that it was spoken thus out of great compassion, according to the individual's disposition, he says, 'And not here,' etc. Therein, 'with talk cut off, he does not utter speech connected with the quest for food' means: having become like a mute with talk cut off, one should not speak or utter speech connected with the quest for food that is associated with allusion, talking around, making signs, and intimation. 'By the power of the individual's disposition': explaining the meaning stated briefly, he says, 'For those...' etc. The benefit of the essence is the benefit that is its inherent nature.

Paccayadānakārāti cīvarādipaccayavasena dānakārā. “Devānaṃ vā”ti vuttavacanaṃ pākaṭīkātumāha “devāpī”tiādi. “Pañcime gahapatayo ānisaṃsā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.150) anisaṃsasaddo phalapariyāyopi hotīti āha “ubhayametaṃ atthato eka”nti.

'Donors of requisites' means donors by way of requisites such as robes, etc. To make plain the statement 'or of the devas,' he says, 'devas also,' etc. In passages such as 'Householders, there are these five benefits' (Dī. Ni. 2.150), the word 'benefit' is also a synonym for 'fruit.' Therefore, he says, 'These two are one in meaning.'

Sassusasurā ca tappakkhikā ca sassusasurapakkhikā. Te ñātiyonisambandhena āvāhavivāhasambandhavasena sambandhā ñātī. Sālohitāti yonisambandhavasena. Ekalohitasambaddhāti ekena samānena lohitasambandhena sambaddhā. Peccabhāvaṃ gatāti petūpapattivasena nibbattiṃ [M 1.0263] upagatā. Te pana yasmā idha katakālakiriyā kālena katajīvitupacchedā honti, tasmā vuttaṃ “kālakatā”ti. Pasannacittoti pasannacittako. Kālakato [V 1.0234] pitā vā mātā vā petayoniṃ upapannoti adhikārato viññāyatīti vuttaṃ “mahānisaṃsameva hotī”ti, tassa tathā sīlasampannattāti adhippāyo. Ariyabhāve pana sati vattabbameva natthi. Tenāha “anekāni kappasatasahassānī”tiādi. Bahukāranti bahupakāraṃ. Upasaṅkamananti abhivādanādivasena upagamanaṃ. Payirupāsananti upaṭṭhānanti.

Mothers-in-law and fathers-in-law, and those on their side, are the 'in-laws' party.' They are relatives connected by way of the bond of marriage. 'Of the same blood' means by way of the connection of birth. 'Connected by a single bloodline' means connected by one, a common, blood connection. 'Gone to the next world' means they have attained rebirth by way of arising as a departed one. But since they have here performed the action of time, their life having been cut off by time, therefore it is said, 'deceased.' 'With a confident mind' means one who has a confident mind. It is said, 'it is of great benefit,' because it is understood from the context that a deceased father or mother has been reborn in the realm of the departed; the intention is that this is because of that person's accomplishment in virtue. But when there is the state of being a noble one, there is nothing to be said. Therefore, he says, 'for many hundreds of thousands of eons,' etc. 'Of much help' means of much assistance. 'Approaching' means going up to by way of veneration, etc. 'Attending upon' means serving.

66. Ajjhottharitāti madditā. Ukkaṇṭhāti riñcanā anabhirati ananuyogo. Sīlavā bhikkhu attano sīlakhaṇḍabhayena samāhito vipassako ca paccayaghātena aratiyā ratiyā ca sahitā abhibhavitāva hotīti āha “sīlādiguṇayuttenevā”tiādi.

66. 'Overwhelmed' means crushed. 'Discontent' means abandoning, non-delight, non-application. He says, 'only by one endowed with virtues such as virtue, etc.' to show that a virtuous bhikkhu, through fear of breaking his own virtue, and a concentrated insight meditator, is indeed an overcomer of discontent and delight associated with the destruction of requisites.

Cittutrāso bhāyatīti bhayaṃ. Ārammaṇaṃ bhāyati etasmāti bhayaṃ. Purimavārasadisattā vuttanayamevāti atidisitvāpi puna taṃ dassetuṃ “sīlādiguṇayutto hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Therassa heṭṭhā nisinnattā devatāya dārakā sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ sukhena vattituṃ asakkontā asamatthā.

Terror of the mind. One fears, thus it is fear. One fears the object on account of it, thus it is fear. Even having pointed it out as being just like the method stated in the previous section, it is said again, 'for one endowed with virtues such as virtue, etc.' in order to show it again. Because the elder was sitting below, the deity's children were unable, incapable, of standing in their own nature, of existing comfortably.

Adhikaṃ cetoti abhiceto, upacārajjhānacittaṃ. Tassa pana adhikatā pākatikakāmāvacaracittehi sundaratāya sapaṭipakkhato visuddhiyā cāti āha “abhikkantaṃ visuddhicitta”nti. Adhicittanti samādhimāha, so ca upacārasamādhi daṭṭhabbo. Vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ, samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ, apītijaṃ jhānasukhaṃ, satipārisuddhijaṃ jhānasukhanti catubbidhampi jhānasukhaṃ paṭipakkhato nikkhantataṃ upādāya “nekkhammasukha”nti vuccatīti āha “nekkhammasukhaṃ vindantī”ti. Icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpajjituṃ samatthoti iminā tesu jhānesu samāpajjanavasībhāvamāha, “nikāmalābhī”ti pana vacanato āvajjanādhiṭṭhānapaccavekkhaṇavasiyopi vuttā evāti veditabbā. Sukheneva paccanīkadhamme vikkhambhetvāti etena tesaṃ jhānasukhakhippābhiññatañca dasseti. Vipulānanti vepullaṃ pāpitānaṃ. Jhānānaṃ vipulatā nāma subhāvitabhāvena ciratarappatti, sā ca paricchedānurūpāva icchitabbbāti “vipulāna”nti vatvā “yathāparicchedeyeva vuṭṭhātuṃ samatthoti vuttaṃ hotī”ti [M 1.0264] āha. Paricchedakālañhi appatvāva vuṭṭhahanto akasiralābhī na hoti yāvadicchakaṃ pavattetuṃ asamatthattā. Idāni teyeva yathāvutte samāpajjanādivasībhāve byatirekavasena vibhāvetuṃ “ekacco hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha lābhīyeva hotīti idaṃ paṭiladdhamattassa jhānassa vasena vuttaṃ. Tathāti icchiticchitakkhaṇe. Pāribandhiketi vasībhāvassa paccanīkadhamme. Jhānādhigamassa pana paccanīkadhammā pageva vikkhambhitā, aññathā jhānādhigamo eva na siyā. Kicchena vikkhambhetīti kicchena visodheti. Kāmādīnavapaccavekkhaṇādīhi kāmacchandādīnaṃ viya [V 1.0235] aññesampi samādhipāribandhikānaṃ dūrasamussāraṇaṃ idha vikkhambhanaṃ visodhanañcāti veditabbaṃ. Nāḷikāyantanti kālamānanāḷikāyantaṃ āha.

'Adhikaṃ cetoti abhiceto' means 'a superior mind is a higher mind,' referring to the mind of access concentration. Its superiority is due to its beauty compared to ordinary sense-sphere consciousness and its purity from opponents; hence it is said, 'abhikkantaṃ visuddhicittaṃ' (an excellent, purified mind). 'Adhicittanti samādhimāha' means concentration is called the higher mind, and this should be understood as access concentration. The four kinds of jhānic happiness—the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, the rapture and happiness born of concentration, the jhānic happiness without rapture, and the jhānic happiness born of the purity of mindfulness—are called 'the happiness of renunciation' (nekkhammasukha) on account of having departed from their opposites; thus he says, 'they find the happiness of renunciation.' 'Icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpajjituṃ samatthoti' means that one is capable of attaining it at any desired moment, indicating mastery over attaining those jhānas. And by the phrase 'nikāmalābhī' (one who obtains at will), it should be understood that masteries over adverting, resolving, and reviewing are also stated. 'Sukheneva paccanīkadhamme vikkhambhetvāti' shows their quick attainment of jhānic happiness and higher knowledge by easily suppressing opposing states. 'Vipulānanti vepullaṃ pāpitānaṃ' means 'of the abundant,' that is, of those that have reached abundance. The abundance of the jhānas is long-lasting attainment through being well-developed, and that should be desired in accordance with the defined limit. Having said 'vipulānaṃ' (of the abundant), he says, 'it is said that one is capable of emerging at the exact time defined.' For one who emerges without having reached the defined time is not an effortless obtainer, being unable to sustain it for as long as desired. Now, to explain those same masteries of attainment and so on by way of contrast, it is said, 'ekacco hī' ('for some'), etc. Therein, 'lābhīyeva hoti' ('is merely an obtainer') is said with reference to a jhāna that has only just been attained. 'Tathāti' means 'thus,' that is, at any desired moment. 'Pāribandhiketi' refers to the 'paccanīkadhamme,' the opposing states to mastery. But the opposing states for the attainment of jhāna have already been suppressed; otherwise, there would be no attainment of jhāna at all. 'Kicchena vikkhambhetīti' means 'suppresses with difficulty'; 'kicchena visodheti' means 'purifies with difficulty.' It should be understood that just as one reflects on the danger of sensual pleasures to remove sensual lust, so too here, the removal to a distance of other obstacles to concentration is suppression and purification. 'Nāḷikāyantanti' refers to the 'kālamānanāḷikāyantaṃ,' the time-measuring water-clock.

Visesena rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānaṃ sabbaso vasībhāvāpāditaṃ abhiññāpādakanti adhippāyenāha “abhiññāpādake jhāne vutte”ti. Arūpajjhānampi pana adhiṭṭhānatāya pādakameva cuddasadhā cittaparidamanena vinā tadabhāvato. “Evamabhiññāpādake rūpāvacarajjhāne vutte rūpāvacaratāya kiñcāpi abhiññānaṃ lokiyavāro āgato”ti ayañhettha adhippāyo. Nanti abhiññāvāraṃ. Cattāri…pe… ariyamaggā sīlānaṃ ānisaṃso sampannasīlasseva lābhato. Pariyādiyitvāti gahetvā.

Specifically, the fourth form-realm jhāna, having been brought to complete mastery in all ways, is a basis for the higher knowledges; with this intention, he said, 'When the jhāna that is a basis for higher knowledge is spoken of.' The formless jhāna, too, is indeed a basis by way of being a foundation, for without the fourteenfold taming of the mind, that basis does not exist. 'Thus, when the form-realm jhāna that is a basis for higher knowledge is spoken of, although the mundane section on the higher knowledges has come about by way of the form-realm'—this is the intention here. 'Naṃ' refers to the section on higher knowledge. The four... etc... noble paths are the benefit of virtue, as they are obtained only by one accomplished in virtue. 'Pariyādiyitvā' means 'having taken'.

Aṅgasantatāyāti nīvaraṇādīnaṃ paccanīkadhammānaṃ sudūratarabhāvena jhānaṅgānaṃ vūpasantatāya, nibbutasabbadarathapariḷāhatāyāti attho, yato tesaṃ jhānānaṃ paṇītatarādibhāvo. Ārammaṇasantatāyāti rūpapaṭighādivigamanena saṇhasukhumādibhāvappattasantabhāvena. Yadaggena hi nesaṃ bhāvanābhisamayasabbhāvitasaṇhasukhumākārāni ārammaṇāni santāni, tadaggena jhānaṅgānaṃ santatā veditabbā. Ārammaṇasantatāya santatā lokuttaradhammārammaṇāhi paccavekkhaṇāhi dīpetabbā. Vimuttā visesena muttā. Ye hi jhānadhammā tathāpavattapubbabhāgabhāvanāhi tabbisesatāya sātisayaṃ paṭipakkhadhammehi vimuttivasena pavattanti, tato eva tathāvimuttatāya pitu aṅke vissaṭṭhaaṅgapaccaṅgo viya kumāro nirāsaṅkabhāvena ārammaṇe adhimuttā ca pavattanti, te vimokkhāti vuccanti. Tenāha “vimokkhāti paccanīkadhammehi vimuttattā ārammaṇe ca adhimuttattā”ti[M 1.0265]. Yadipi ārammaṇasamatikkamavasena pattabbāni āruppāni, na aṅgātikkamavasena, tathāpi yasmā ārammaṇe avirattassa jhānasamatikkamo na hoti, samatikkantesu ca jhānesu ārammaṇaṃ samatikkantameva hoti, tasmā ārammaṇasamatikkamaṃ avatvā “rūpāvacarajjhāne atikkamitvā”ti icceva vuttaṃ. Atikkamma rūpeti pāḷiyaṃ “sampādetabbā, passitabbā”ti vā kiñci padaṃ icchitabbaṃ, asutaparikappanena pana payojanaṃ natthīti “santāti padasambandho”ti vuttaṃ. Evañca katvā tena virāgabhāvena tesaṃ santatāti ayampi attho vibhāvito hoti. Rūpajjhānādīnaṃ viya natthi etesaṃ ārammaṇabhūtaṃ vā phalabhūtaṃ vā rūpanti arūpā. Arūpā eva āruppā. Tenāha “ārammaṇato ca vipākato ca rūpavirahitā”ti. Nāmakāyenāti sahajātanāmasamūhena.

'Through the peacefulness of the factors' means: because the hindrances and other opposing states are very far removed, through the pacification of the jhāna factors, which means all distress and feverishness are extinguished. From this comes the more refined nature of these jhānas. 'Through the peacefulness of the object' means: through the peaceful state attained by the disappearance of resistance to form, etc., and the attainment of a subtle and refined nature. For by the degree to which their objects are peaceful—having been made subtle and refined in all ways by development and realization—by that degree the peacefulness of the jhāna factors should be understood. The peacefulness through the peacefulness of the object should be illustrated by the reviewings that have supramundane phenomena as their object. 'Vimuttā' means 'especially freed.' Those jhānic states that, through such preceding development, proceed by way of being exceptionally freed from opposing states due to their distinctiveness, and because they are thus freed, proceed by being inclined towards the object without hesitation—like a child with limbs relaxed on its father's lap—are called 'liberations' (vimokkha). Hence it is said: 'They are called liberations because they are freed from opposing states and inclined towards the object.' Although the formless attainments are to be reached by transcending the object, not by transcending the factors, nevertheless, since there is no transcending of jhāna for one who is not dispassionate towards the object, and when the jhānas are transcended, the object is also transcended, therefore, instead of saying 'by transcending the object,' it is simply said, 'having transcended the form-realm jhānas.' In the Pāli, at 'having transcended form,' some word like 'should be accomplished' or 'should be seen' is to be desired, but since there is no purpose in conjecturing what is not heard, it is said, 'the connection of the word is "peaceful" (santā).' And having done so, this meaning is also clarified: their peacefulness is due to that dispassion. Unlike the form jhānas, these have no form either as object or as result; thus they are 'formless' (arūpā). The formless are indeed the formless attainments (āruppā). Hence it is said, 'devoid of form both as object and as result.' 'Nāmakāyena' means 'with the co-arisen group of mentality'.

67. Saṃyojentīti bandhanti. Kehīti āha “khandhagatī”tiādi. Asamucchinnarāgādikassa [V 1.0236] hi khandhādīnaṃ āyatiṃ khandhādīhi sambandho, samucchinnarāgādikassa pana taṃ natthi katānampi kammānaṃ asamatthabhāvāpattitoti. Rāgādīnaṃ anvayato ca saṃyojanaṭṭho siddhoti āha “khandhagati…pe… vuccantī”ti. Parikkhayenāti samucchedena sabbaso āyatiṃ anuppajjanena. Paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ anavasesato savanato pīḷanato soto, ariyamaggoti āha “sototi ca maggassetaṃ adhivacana”nti. Taṃ sotaṃ ādito panno adhigacchīti sotāpanno, aṭṭhamako. Tenāha “taṃsamaṅgīpuggalassā”ti, paṭhamamaggakkhaṇe puggalassāti adhippāyo. Idha pana panna-saddo “phalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanno”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.59) viya vattamānakālikoti āha “maggena phalassa nāmaṃ dinna”nti. Abhītakālikatte pana sarasatova nāmalābho siyā. Virūpaṃ sadukkhaṃ saupāyāsaṃ nipātetīti vinipāto, apāyadukkhe khipanako. Dhammoti sabhāvo. Tenāha “attāna”ntiādi. Kasmāti avinipātadhammatāya kāraṇaṃ pucchati. Apāyaṃ gamentīti apāyagamanīyā. Sambujjhatīti sambodhi, ariyamaggo. So pana paṭhamamaggassa adhigatattā avasiṭṭho eva adhigandhabbabhāvena icchitabboti āha “uparimaggattaya”nti.

67. 'Saṃyojenti' means 'they bind.' 'Kehi' ('By what?'), he says, 'the course of the aggregates,' and so on. For one whose lust and so on are not eradicated, there is a future connection of aggregates with aggregates; but for one whose lust and so on are eradicated, that does not exist, because even actions performed become incapable of producing results. And because the meaning of 'fetter' is established from the continuation of lust and so on, he says, 'the course of the aggregates… are called.' 'Parikkhayena' means 'by destruction,' that is, by eradication, by not arising at all in the future. Because it flows against and crushes opposing states without remainder, it is a 'stream' (soto), the noble path; thus he says, 'stream is a designation for the path.' One who has entered that stream from the beginning, who has attained it, is a 'stream-enterer' (sotāpanno), the eighth person. Hence he says, 'of the person endowed with it,' the intention being, 'of the person at the moment of the first path.' Here, however, the word 'panna' is in the present tense, as in 'one practicing for the realization of the fruit,' and so on; hence he says, 'the name of the fruit is given by means of the path.' But if it were in the past tense, the acquisition of the name would be from its own nature. Because it casts one down into what is ugly, painful, and full of despair, it is a 'place of downfall' (vinipāto), a hurler into the suffering of the plane of misery. 'Dhamma' means 'nature.' Hence he says, 'oneself,' and so on. 'Kasmā' ('Why?'): he asks for the reason for the nature of not falling into a place of downfall. Those that lead to the plane of misery are 'apāyagamanīyā.' 'Sambujjhati' ('one awakens') is 'awakening' (sambodhi), the noble path. But since the first path has been attained, only the remainder is to be desired as what is to be attained; hence he says, 'the three higher paths'.

Vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ vuttāni,na pahātabbānīti adhippāyo. Oḷārikānaṃ rāgādīnaṃ samucchindanavasena pavattamāno dutiyamaggo avasiṭṭhānaṃ tesaṃ tanubhāvāpattiyā [M 1.0266] uppanno nāma hotīti vuttaṃ “rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā”ti. Adhiccuppattiyāti kadāci karahaci uppajjanena. Pariyuṭṭhānamandatāyāti samudācāramudutāya. Abhiṇhaṃ na uppajjanti tajjassa ayonisomanasikārassa anibaddhabhāvato. Mandamandā uppajjanti vipallāsānaṃ tappaccayānañca mohamānādīnaṃ mudutarabhāvato. Bahalāva uppajjanti vatthupaṭisevanatoti adhippāyo. Tenāha “tathā hī”tiādi.

They are stated for the purpose of praising, not for the purpose of abandoning—this is the intention. The second path, operating by way of eradicating coarse lust and so on, is said to have arisen by the attenuation of the remaining ones; thus it is said, ‘by the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion’. Adhiccuppattiyā means ‘by arising occasionally’. Pariyuṭṭhānamandatāya means ‘by the mildness of their manifestation’. They do not arise frequently because the unwise attention related to them is not constant. They arise slowly because the perversions and their causes, such as delusion, conceit, etc., are milder. They arise strongly through frequent indulgence in the object—this is the intention. Hence he says, ‘Thus indeed,’ and so on.

Sakiṃ āgamanadhammoti paṭisandhivasena sakiṃyeva āgamanasabhāvo. Ekavāraṃyeva…pe… āgantvāti iminā pañcasu sakadāgāmīsu cattāro vajjetvā ekoyeva gahitoti dassento “yopi hī”tiādimāha. Tattha yvāyaṃ pañcamako sakadāgāmī “idha maggaṃ bhāvetvā devaloke nibbatto, tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā puna idhūpapajjitvā parinibbāyatī”ti vutto, tassa ekabījinā saddhiṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇanti? Ekabījissa ekā paṭisandhi, sakadāgāmissa dve paṭisandhiyoti idaṃ tesaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ. Yassa hi sotāpannassa ekaṃyeva khandhabījaṃ, na ekaṃ attabhāvaggahaṇaṃ, so ekabījīti.

Sakiṃ āgamanadhammo means ‘having the nature of returning only once through rebirth-linking’. By ‘only once… (etc.)… having come back,’ showing that among the five kinds of once-returners, four are excluded and only one is taken, he says, ‘whoever indeed…’ and so on. Here, what is the distinction between this fifth once-returner, who is described as ‘having developed the path here, is reborn in the deva-world, remains there for the duration of his lifespan, and then reappears here to attain final Nibbāna,’ and the one-seeder? The one-seeder has one rebirth-linking, the once-returner has two rebirth-linkings; this is the distinction between them. For a stream-enterer who has only one aggregate-seed, not one grasping of existence, he is called a one-seeder.

Heṭṭhāti [V 1.0237] “amahaggatabhūmiya”nti heṭṭhā sambandhanena. Heṭṭhābhāgassa hitāti heṭṭhābhāgiyā, tesaṃ. Tānīti orabbhāgiyasaṃyojanāni. Kāmāvacare nibbattatiyeva ajjhattaṃ saṃyojanattā. Tathā hesa dūratopi āvattidhammo evāti dassetuṃ gilabaḷisamacchādayo upamābhāvena vuttā. Opapātikoti iminā gabbhavāsadukkhābhāvamāha. Tattha parinibbāyīti iminā sesadukkhābhāvaṃ. Tattha parinibbānatā cassa kāmaloke khandhabījassa apunārohavasenevāti dassetuṃ “anāvattidhammo”ti vuttaṃ.

Heṭṭhā (below) is connected with ‘in the non-exalted plane’ below. Heṭṭhābhāgiyā means ‘pertaining to the lower part’, belonging to them. Tāni (those) refers to the lower fetters. He is indeed reborn in the sense-sphere because of the internal fetters. Similarly, to show that he is by nature subject to turning back even from afar, the examples of the swallowed hook, the fish, and so on are given as similes. Opapātiko means ‘of spontaneous birth’; by this, the absence of the suffering of dwelling in a womb is indicated. Tattha parinibbāyī means ‘there attains final Nibbāna’; by this, the absence of remaining suffering is indicated. And to show that his attaining final Nibbāna there in the sense-world is just by way of the aggregate-seed not sprouting again, it is said, ‘not subject to returning’.

68. Kevalāti lokiyābhiññāhi asammissā. Lokiyapañcābhiññāyopi sīlānaṃ ānisaṃso tadavinābhāvato. Tāpi dassetuṃ ākaṅkheyya ce…pe… evamādimāhāti yojanā. Āsavānaṃ anavasesappahānato arahattamaggoyeva visesato “āsavakkhayo”ti vattabbataṃ arahatīti vuttaṃ “āsavakkhaye kathite”ti, aññathā sabbāpi chaḷabhiññā āsavakkhayo evāti. Imesaṃ guṇānanti lokiyābhiññānaṃ[M 1.0267]. Yathā purisassa muṇḍitaṃ sīsaṃ sikhāvirahitattā na sobhati, evaṃ desanāya sīsabhūtāpi aggamaggakathā lokiyābhiññārahitā na sobhatīti āha “ayaṃ kathā muṇḍābhiññākathā nāma bhaveyyā”ti. Iddhivikubbanāti iddhi ca vikubbanā ca. Vikubbanaggahaṇena cettha vikubbaniddhimāha, iddhiggahaṇena tadaññaṃ sabbañca abhiññākiccaṃ. Yuttaṭṭhāneyevāti lokiyābhiññānaṃ nibbattanassa viya desanāya yuttaṭṭhāneyeva. Etena na kevalaṃ desanakkamenevāyaṃ desanā, atha kho paṭipattikkamenapīti dasseti. Visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.369) vuttā, tasmā tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbāti adhippāyo.

68. Kevalā means ‘unmixed with mundane direct knowledges’. Even the five mundane direct knowledges are a benefit of virtues due to their inseparability from them. The connection is: ‘If one wishes… (etc.)… to show these also, he says thus’. Because of the remainderless abandonment of the taints, only the path of arahantship specifically deserves to be called ‘the destruction of the taints’; hence it is said, ‘when the destruction of the taints has been spoken of,’ otherwise all six direct knowledges would be the destruction of the taints. Imesaṃ guṇānaṃ means ‘of these qualities’, i.e., of the mundane direct knowledges. Just as a man’s shaven head, lacking a topknot, does not look splendid, so too the discourse on the highest path, though it is the head of the teaching, does not shine without the mundane direct knowledges; hence he says, ‘this discourse would be called the discourse on the shaven direct knowledges’. Iddhivikubbana means ‘psychic power and transformation’. Here, by the term ‘transformation,’ transformation-psychic power is meant; by the term ‘psychic power,’ all other functions of direct knowledge are included. Yuttaṭṭhāneyeva means ‘only in the proper place for the teaching, just as for the arising of mundane direct knowledges’. By this, it is shown that this teaching is not only in the order of discourse, but also in the order of practice. They are stated in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 2.369); therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained there—this is the intention.

69. Āsavānaṃ khayāti heṭṭhimamaggena khepitāvasiṭṭhānaṃ āsavānaṃ arahattamaggena samucchindanato. Yasmā arahattamaggo na kevalaṃ āsaveyeva khepeti, atha kho avasiṭṭhe sabbakilesepi, tasmā āha “sabbakilesānaṃ khayā”ti. Lakkhaṇamattañhettha āsavaggahaṇaṃ, āsavānaṃ ārammaṇabhāvassapi anupagamanato anāsavaṃ. Yasmā pana tattha āsavānaṃ lesopi natthi, tasmā vuttaṃ “āsavavirahita”nti. Samādhi vutto cetosīsena yathā “cittaṃ paññañca bhāvaya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.23, 192; peṭako. 22; mi. pa. 2.1.9) adhippāyo. Rāgato vimuttattā avijjāya vimuttattāti idaṃ ujuvipaccanīkapaṭippassaddhidassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, na tadaññesaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ appaṭippassaddhattā. Idāni tameva samādhipaññānaṃ rāgāvijjāpaṭipakkhataṃ āgamena dassetuṃ “vuttaṃ ceta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Samathaphalanti samathassa phalaṃ lokiyasamathabhāvanāya hi vipassanāgatāya āhitaphalassa lokuttarasamathassa sarikkhakaphalo cetovimutti. Vipassanāphalanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Attanoyevāti sutamayañāṇādinā viya parapaccayataṃ [V 1.0238] nayaggāhañca muñcitvā paratoghosānugatabhāvanādhigamabhūtatāya attanoyeva paññāya paccakkhaṃ katvā sayambhuñāṇabhūtāyāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “aparappaccayena ñatvā”ti.

69. “By the destruction of the taints” means the cutting off by the path of arahantship of the taints remaining after being exhausted by the lower paths. Since the path of arahantship not only eliminates the taints but also all the remaining defilements, it is said, “by the destruction of all defilements.” Here, the mention of taints is merely illustrative, as it does not take the taints for its object; therefore it is taintless. And since there is not even a trace of taints there, it is said to be “devoid of taints.” “Concentration” is mentioned by way of the mind as chief; the meaning is as in “develop the mind and wisdom” (SN 1.23, 192; Peṭ 22; Mil 2.1.9). “Freed from lust, freed from ignorance”—this should be understood as showing a direct opposite pacification, not that other evil states are not pacified. Now, to show, by way of the scriptures, that this concentration and wisdom are opposed to lust and ignorance, it is said, “as stated,” etc. The fruit of serenity: For indeed, the liberation of mind is a fruit similar to the supramundane serenity that has yielded its fruit through the development of mundane serenity which has proceeded to insight.
