Here too, the same method applies to “the fruit of insight.” By oneself: having abandoned dependence on others and the taking up of guidance, as with knowledge derived from learning and so forth, and being of the nature of attainment arisen from development that follows the voice of another, having directly realized by one's own wisdom, which is of the nature of self-originated knowledge—this is the meaning. Hence, it is said, “knowing without dependence on others.”

Sabbampi tanti sabbampi sattarasavidhaṃ taṃ yathāvuttaṃ sīlānisaṃsaṃ. Yathā ānisaṃsavante sammadeva sampādite tadānisaṃsā dassitā eva honti tadāyattabhāvato, evaṃ ānisaṃsapadhānayogyabhāvena dassite [M 1.0268] tadānisaṃsā dassitā eva hontīti āha “sampiṇḍetvā dassento”ti. Vuttasseva atthassa punavacanaṃ nigamananti vuttaṃ “nigamanaṃ āhā”ti. Pubbeti desanārambhe. Evaṃ vuttanti “sampannasīlā”ti evamādinā ākārena vuttaṃ. Idaṃ sabbampīti idaṃ “sampannasīlā”tiādikaṃ sabbampi vacanaṃ. Etaṃ paṭiccāti etaṃ sampannasīlassa bhikkhuno yathāvuttasattarasavidhānisaṃsabhāgitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Idameva hi “iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti vacanaṃ sandhāya “sabbampi taṃ sīlānisaṃsaṃ sampiṇḍetvā dassento”ti vuttaṃ. Etthaādito chahi ānisaṃsehi parittabhūmikā sampatti gahitā, tadantaraṃ pañcahi lokiyābhiññāhi ca mahaggatabhūmikā, itarehi lokuttarabhūmikāti evaṃ catubhūmikasampadānisaṃsasīlaṃ nāmetaṃ mahantaṃ mahānubhāvaṃ, tasmā taṃsampādane sakkaccakāritā appamattena bhavitabbaṃ.

All that means all those seventeen kinds of benefits of virtue as stated before. Just as when that which possesses benefits is properly fulfilled, its benefits are indeed shown because they are dependent on it; so too, when the benefits are shown as the principal and suitable outcome, they are indeed shown—thus he says, “summarizing and presenting.” The repetition of the meaning already stated is the conclusion; thus it is said, “he speaks the conclusion.” “Previously” means at the beginning of the teaching. “Thus stated” means stated in this way beginning with “endowed with virtue.” “All this” means all this statement beginning with “endowed with virtue” and so forth. “Dependent on this” means this is said in reference to the bhikkhu endowed with virtue, who partakes of the seventeen kinds of benefits as previously described. For it is precisely with reference to this statement, “as it was said, this was said in reference to that,” that it is stated, “summarizing and presenting all those benefits of virtue.” Here, from the beginning, six benefits are taken as the attainment of the limited sphere; thereafter, five by way of mundane higher knowledges are taken as the exalted sphere, and the others as the supramundane sphere. Thus, this virtue, which is the attainment of benefits in four spheres, is indeed great and of great power. Therefore, in fulfilling it, one must act diligently and heedfully.

Ākaṅkheyyasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta is complete.

7. Vatthasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Vatthasutta

70. Chādetabbaṃ [V 1.0239] ṭhānaṃ vasati paṭicchādetīti vatthaṃ. Yaṃ samānaṃ viya na sabbaso minoti, mānassa pana samīpe, taṃ upamānaṃ. Upamīyati etāyāti upamā, upamāya bodhakavacanaṃ upamāvacanaṃ. Katthaci sutte. Atthanti upamiyatthaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ upamaṃ vatvā tadanantaraṃ atthaṃ vatvā puna upamaṃ vadanto “upamāya atthaṃ parivāretvā dassetī”ti vutto. Atthena upamaṃ parivāretvāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Idāni te cattāropi pakāre sutte āgatanayeneva dassento “seyyathāpissu, bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha dve agārāti dve paṭivissakagharā. Sadvārāti sammukhadvārā.

70. It is called 'cloth' (vatthaṃ) because it covers a place that ought to be covered and a dwelling. That which, though similar, does not entirely measure, but is near to measuring, is called a standard (upamānaṃ). That by which something is compared is called a comparison (upamā); a word that makes known a comparison is a word of comparison (upamāvacanaṃ). In some discourses, the meaning is the thing to be compared (upamiyatthaṃ). When first stating the comparison, then immediately stating the meaning, and then again stating the comparison—it is said, “He shows the meaning by surrounding it with the comparison.” Here too, the same method applies to surrounding the comparison with the meaning. Now, showing those four modes according to the way they appear in the discourse, he says, “Just as, bhikkhus,” and so on. Therein, “two houses” means two neighboring houses. “With doors” means with doors facing each other.

Svāyanti so ayaṃ evaṃ upamādassanavasenapi nānānayenapi dhammadesako bhagavā. Ekaccānaṃ veneyyānaṃ atthassa sukhāvabodho paṭhamaṃ upamādassane hetu, evaṃ paṭhamaṃ atthadassane, upamāya atthaparivāraṇe, atthena upamāparivāraṇe cā”ti imamatthaṃ dasseti “esa nayo sabbatthā”ti [M 1.0269] iminā. Dhammadhātuyāti sabbaññutaññāṇassa. Tañhi dhammadhātupariyāpannattā yathāvuttadhamme ca sabbepi ñeyyadhamme ca padahati yathāsabhāvato bujjhati bodheti cāti dhātu, dhīyanti vā dhammā etāya sabbākārato ñāyanti ñāpiyanti cāti dhammadhātu. Tassā pana suṭṭhu saccasampaṭivedhavasena laddhattā suppaṭividdhattāti, yadaggena vā ñeyyaṃ tāya suppaṭividdhaṃ, tadaggena sāpissa suppaṭividdhā evāti āha “suppaṭividdhattā”ti.

This, then, is the Blessed One, the teacher of the Dhamma, who teaches in various ways, including by way of showing similes. For some who are receptive, the reason for the easy understanding of the meaning is the showing of similes first; similarly, the showing of the meaning first, the surrounding of the meaning with similes, and the surrounding of similes with the meaning—this is shown by the phrase, “This is the method in all cases.” 'The element of the Dhamma' refers to the knowledge of omniscience. For, since it is included in the Dhamma-element, it comprehends the dhammas as previously stated and all knowable dhammas, and it understands and causes them to be understood according to their true nature; thus it is called an 'element' (dhātu). Or, because phenomena are held, known, and made known in every aspect through it, it is called the 'Dhamma-element'. Moreover, because it is obtained through the thorough penetration of the truths, it is 'well-penetrated'. Or, by whichever excellence the knowable is well-penetrated by it, by that same excellence it too is well-penetrated; thus he says, “because it is well-penetrated.”

Pakatipariyodātassa cittassa āgantukehi upakkilesehi upakkiliṭṭhabhāvadassanatthaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhavatthadassananti katvā vuttaṃ “pakatiparisuddhaṃ vattha”nti. Rajādināti ettharajo nāma reṇu. Ādi-saddena aṇutajjāridhūmādikaṃ vatthassa aparisuddhikāraṇaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Sabbaso kilissati vinassati visuddhi etenāti saṃkileso, tena saṃkilesena paṃsurajādinā saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ vaṇṇavināsanena vidūsitaṃ. Malaṃ masi. Jallikā vuccati loṇapaṭalādi chaviyā upari ṭhitaṃ sarīramalaṃ. Ādisaddena sarīrajallameva assukheḷasiṅghāṇikādikaṃ tadaññamalaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Gahitattāti pariyonandhanavasena gahitattā. Rajanti sattā tenāti raṅgaṃ, raṅgameva raṅgajātaṃ yathā kopameva kopajātaṃ. Upanāmeyyāti pakkhipeyya. Nīlakatthāyāti nīlavaṇṇatthāya. Palāsanīlādiketi ādi-saddena kāḷasāmādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Haliddikakudhaselādike pītakaraṅge. Lākhāpattaṅgarasādike [V 1.0240] lohitakaraṅge. Mahārajanaloddakandulādike mandarattaraṅge. Duṭṭhu rajitavaṇṇaṃ apabhassaraṃ. Tenāha “aparisuddhavaṇṇamevassā”ti. Īdisanti durattavaṇṇaṃ. Tasmiṃ vatthe raṅgajātaṃ sayaṃ suparisuddhaṃ samānaṃ kissa hetu kena rattavaṇṇaṃ aparisuddhaṃ hotīti raṅgajātassa niddosataṃ vadati. Tenāha “yasmā panā”tiādi.

The showing of a stained cloth is mentioned in order to demonstrate how a mind that is naturally pure becomes defiled by adventitious defilements; for this reason it is said, 'a naturally pure cloth'. 'By dust, etc.': here, 'dust' (rajo) means fine particles (reṇu). The term 'etc.' includes other causes of impurity for the cloth, such as fine soot and smoke. 'Defilement' (saṃkileso): because purity is entirely soiled, ruined, or destroyed by this. 'Defiled' (saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ): by that defilement, such as dust and dirt, it is discolored and tarnished by the destruction of its color. 'Dirt' (malaṃ) refers to soot (masi). 'Grime' (jallikā) refers to the layer of salt or other bodily impurities that accumulate on the skin. The term 'etc.' includes other bodily grime such as tears, spittle, and nasal mucus. 'Because it is taken up': because it is grasped by way of attachment. 'Dye' (raṅgaṃ): beings are colored (rajanti) by it. 'Dyed substance' (raṅgajātaṃ) is the dye itself, just as 'a state born of anger' (kopajātaṃ) is anger itself. 'Should be applied' (upanāmeyya) means 'should be put in' (pakkhipeyya). 'For blue dye' (nīlakatthāya) means 'for the sake of a blue color' (nīlavaṇṇatthāya). 'Like indigo, etc.': the term 'etc.' includes black, dark blue, and so forth. For yellow dye, like turmeric and kudhasela. For red dye, like lac and pattaṅga juice. For mandaratta dye, like mahārajana, lodda, and kandula. A badly dyed color is not radiant. Hence he says, “it would have an impure color.” 'Such' (īdisaṃ) means a badly dyed color. On such a cloth, the dye itself is very pure—for what reason, by what means, is the dyed color impure? This statement clarifies the faultlessness of the dye. Hence it is said, “but because...” and so on.

Saṃkilesapakkhaṃ dassentena asaṃkiliṭṭhameva vatthaṃ udāharitabbanti pākaṭoyamattho, saṃkiliṭṭhavatthanidassanena pana “siyā nu kho aññopi koci viseso”ti adhippāyena pucchati “kasmā panā”tiādinā. Itaro atthavisesoti dassento “vāyāmamahapphaladassanattha”ntiādimāha. Ettha ca saṃkiliṭṭhacittavisodhanavidhāne saṃkiliṭṭhavatthaṃ nidassatabbanti paṭiññā, vāyāmamahapphaladassanatthanti hetuattho. Yathā hītiādi anvayattho. Na tattha jātikāḷake viyātiādi byatirekattho. Sadisūdāharaṇaṃ pana malaggahitakaṃsapātiādi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ cittampītiādi [M 1.0270] opammatthassa upameyyaupanayanaṃ. Tattha pakatiyāti akittimena sabhāvena. Tanti cittaṃ. Sāmaññaggahaṇañcetaṃ cittabhāvāvisesato. Tenāha “sakalepī”ti. Paṇḍarameva na saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ saṃkilesehi asamannāgatabhāvato. Nanu kiriyāmayacittehi vipākasantāne visesādhānaṃ labbhati, aññathā katavināsā katabbhāgamā āpajjeyyuṃ? Kiñcāpi labbhati, tassa saṃkileso vaṭṭupanissayo, asuddhi vā na hoti, asaṃkileso vivaṭṭupanissayo, visuddhi vā na hoti eva. Upakkiliṭṭhanti panetaṃ upakkilesanārahassa cittassa vasena vuttaṃ, na vipākapabandhassa. Tenāha “pabhassaramidaṃ bhikkhave citta”nti, “paṇḍaramevā”ti ca. Tañca khoti pana sakasantatipariyāpannatāya nesaṃ kevalaṃ ekattanayavasena vuttaṃ, na vipākadhammānaṃ kilesāsamaṅgibhāvato. Atha vā upakkiliṭṭhanti iminā upakkilesahetu tattha vijjamānaṃ visesādhānamāha, na “saṃkiliṭṭhā dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 77.dukamātikā) viya taṃsamaṅgitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Visodhiyamānanti vipassanāpaññāya anukkamena sabbupakkilesehi vimociyamānaṃ. Sakkā aggamaggakkhaṇe pabhassarataraṃ kātuṃ, yato na puna upakkilissati. Evantiādi vuttassevatthassa nigamanaṃ.

It is a clear principle that to show the side of defilement, one should use an undefiled cloth as an example. However, by presenting a defiled cloth, the questioner intends to ask, 'Could there be some other special reason?' with questions like, 'But why?'. Showing that there is a special meaning, the other speaker says, 'to show the great fruit of striving,' and so on. Here, the proposition is that in the method of purifying a defiled mind, a defiled cloth is presented as an example; the reason is 'to show the great fruit of striving.' The phrase 'Just as...' and so on indicates the positive application. The phrase 'not like a congenital stain...' and so on indicates the negative application. A similar example, such as a tarnished bronze bowl, should be understood. The phrase 'Likewise, the mind...' and so on applies the meaning of the simile to its subject. There, 'by nature' means by its intrinsic, uncreated essence. 'That' refers to the mind. This is a general statement, owing to the undifferentiated nature of the mind. Hence, it is said, 'all of it.' It is pure, not defiled, because it is unassociated with defilements. Now, are not distinctions established in the resultant continuum by active consciousnesses? Otherwise, the annihilation of what was done and the arising of what was not done would result. Although such a distinction is established, its defilement is a basis for the round of existence, yet this is not an intrinsic impurity; its non-defilement is a basis for release from the round, yet this is not an intrinsic purity. However, the word 'defiled' is used here with reference to a mind that is susceptible to defilements, not to the continuum of results. Therefore, it is said, 'This mind, bhikkhus, is luminous,' and 'it is pure.' And this is said of them as being included in their own continuum, simply by way of a single continuity, not because resultant states are unassociated with defilements. Alternatively, by 'defiled' here, he indicates the distinction established there due to the cause of defilement, and it should not be understood as being endowed with it, as in 'defiled phenomena,' etc. (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 77, dual categories). 'Being purified' means being gradually freed from all defilements by insight wisdom. It can be made even more luminous at the moment of the highest path, since it will not be defiled again. 'Thus,' etc., is the conclusion of the meaning that has been stated.

Duṭṭhagatiparipūraṇavasena paṭipajjanaṃ paṭipatti. Sā eva kilesadarathapariḷāhādivasena upāyāsadukkhā, kucchitā vā gati pavatti, duggatihetūti vā duggati, duggatiyā pana paṭipattiyā gandhabbato, tassā vā nipphannabhāvato kucchito, dukkhā ca gatīti duggati. Saṃkiliṭṭhacittoti idaṃ tassā paṭipattiyā duggatibhāvadassanatthaṃ, na visesanatthaṃ. Na hi asaṃkiliṭṭhacittassa pāṇaghātādivasena pavatti. Saṃkiliṭṭhacittoti lābhāsāya sabbaso kiliṭṭhacitto[V 1.0241]. Dūteyyapahiṇagamananti dūteyyaṃ vuccati dutakammaṃ, gihīnaṃ paṇṇaṃ vā sāsanaṃ vā gahetvā tattha tattha gamanaṃ, pahiṇagamanaṃ gharāgharaṃ pesitassa khuddakagamanaṃ, dūteyyagamanaṃ pahiṇagamanañca gacchati. Vejjakammanti ananuññāte ṭhāne lābhāsāya gahaṭṭhānaṃ bhesajjaṃ karoti. Saṅghabhedakathā parato āgamissati. Veḷudānādīhīti veḷudānapattadānapupphadānādīhi micchājīvena jīvikaṃ kappeti. Sakalampīti “atthi anācāro, atthi agocaro”tiādinā vibhaṅge (vibha. 513, 514) āgataṃ sabbampi anācāraṃ agocarañca caraṇavasena paripūreti.

The practice is the undertaking that fulfills a bad destination. That very practice is painful, being afflicted by defilements, torments, and so on. Or, the course of existence is vile. Or, it is a bad destination because it is the cause of a bad destination. Alternatively, due to its connection with the practice leading to a bad destination, or because it is vile by its very nature, or because it is a painful destination, it is called a bad destination. 'With a defiled mind'—this is said to show the nature of the practice as leading to a bad destination, not to indicate a distinction. For one with an undefiled mind does not engage in actions like killing living beings. 'With a defiled mind' means a mind completely defiled by hope of gain. 'Going on errands and delivering messages'—an errand means a messenger’s task, taking letters or instructions from householders and going here and there. Delivering messages means a minor errand, going from house to house as sent. He goes on errands and delivers messages. 'Medical practice' means preparing medicine for householders in unauthorized places out of hope of gain. The topic of schism in the Saṅgha will be addressed later. 'By giving bamboo, etc.'—he makes a living by wrong livelihood through giving bamboo, leaf-containers, flowers, and so on. 'All of it'—he fulfills all improper conduct and wrong resort by engaging in them, as stated in the Vibhaṅga: 'There is misconduct, there is wrong resort,' etc.

“Nirayampi [M 1.0271] …pe… pettivisayampi gacchatī”ti vatvā tattha pettivisayagamanaṃ dassento “samaṇayakkho nāma hotī”tiādimāha.

Having said, "He goes even to hell... and to the realm of ghosts," to show his going to the realm of ghosts, he says, "He is called a demon ascetic," and so on.

Sukkapakkhe parisuddhanti sabbaso visuddhaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ. Parisuddhattā eva pariyodātaṃ, pabhassaranti attho. Surattavaṇṇamevassāti suṭṭhu rattavaṇṇameva assa. Parisuddhavaṇṇamevassāti nīlavaṇṇopissa parisuddho ca bhaveyyāti evamādiṃ sandhāyāha “kaṇhapakkhe vuttapaccanīkeneva veditabbā”ti. Raṅgajātantiādi pana tattha vuttavaseneva veditabbaṃ. Paṭipattisugatiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ paṭipattiduggatiādīsu vuttavipariyāyena veditabbaṃ. Parisuddhacittoti suddhāsayo. Dasa kusalakammapathe paripūretīti idaṃ kaṇhapakkhe “dasa akusalakammapathe paripūretī”ti vuttassa paṭipakkhadassanavasena vuttaṃ. Yathā hi tattha abhijjhābyāpādamicchādiṭṭhiggahaṇena kammapathasaṃsandananayena kammapathaṃ appattāya ca agāriyassa tathārūpāya micchāpaṭipattiyā saṅgaho icchito, evaṃ idhāpi anabhijjhāabyāpādasammādiṭṭhiggahaṇena alobhādosāmohavasena pavattā agāriyassa sammāpaṭipatti saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ, na kammapathappattāvāti. Manussamahantatanti jātirūpabhogādhipateyyādivasena manussesu mahantabhāvaṃ. Dasahi ṭhānehi aññesaṃ devānaṃ abhibhavo devamahantatā. Paṭipatti sugatiyā bhājiyamānattā “anāgāmimaggaṃ bhāvetī”ti tathā anāgāmibhāvanaṃ pāpetvā ṭhapitā. Gahitaggahaṇena sukhānubhavaṭṭhānassa adhippetattā tadabhāvato asaññibhavaṃ anādiyanto “dasasu vā brahmabhavanesū”tiādimāha.

On the bright side, 'pure' means completely pure, wholly purified, unstained. Because it is pure, it is radiant—that is the meaning. 'It should be of a very red color' means it should be of a perfectly red hue. 'It should be of a pure color' means even if it were blue, it should still be pure. Referring to this, it is said, "In the dark side, it should be understood in the opposite way." As for 'born of color,' etc., it should be understood according to what was stated there. What should be said regarding 'practice leading to a good destination,' etc., should be understood in the reverse way as explained for 'practice leading to a bad destination,' etc. 'A purified mind' means one of pure inclination. 'Fulfilling the ten wholesome courses of action'—this is stated by way of showing the contrast to what was said for the dark side: 'fulfilling the ten unwholesome courses of action.' Just as there, by taking covetousness, ill will, and wrong view, and by the method of connecting them to the courses of action, the inclusion of that kind of wrong practice of a householder is intended, even when it has not reached the course of action, so here too, by taking non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view, the wholesome practice of a householder, arising from non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, should be seen as included—not that the courses of action have been attained. 'Greatness among humans' means superiority among humans in terms of birth, form, wealth, sovereignty, and so on. 'Greatness among devas' means surpassing other devas in ten respects. Because the practice is conducive to a good destination, it is established as leading to the development of the non-returner state; thus it is said, 'one develops the path of the non-returner.' Since the intended point is a state of experiencing happiness, and due to the absence of that, he does not include the realm of non-perception, and says, 'or in the ten Brahma realms,' etc.

71. Sakabhaṇḍe chandarāgo abhijjhāyanaṭṭhena abhijjhā, abhijjhāyanāti attho. Parabhaṇḍe chandarāgo visamaṃ lubbhatīti visamalobho. Evampi abhijjhāvisamalobhānaṃ viseso hotīti dassento “atha vā”tiādimāha. Tattha attano santakaṃ taṃsadisañca yuttaṭṭhānaṃ. Yaṃ yācitaṃ, appakasirena vā sakkā laddhuṃ, taṃ pattaṭṭhānaṃ. Paradāragarudārāti ayuttaṭṭhānaṃ. Yaṃ apatthaniyaṃ, yassa [V 1.0242] vā patthanāya byasanaṃ āpajjati, taṃ appattaṭṭhānaṃ. Theroti mahāsaṅgharakkhitatthero, yena aṭṭhakathā potthakaṃ āropitā. So hi antevāsikesu sākacchantesu evamāha. Sopi imasmiṃyeva sutte vinibbhogo na labbhati cittasaṃkilesassa adhippetattā. Tenāha “yutte vā”tiādi. Ayonisomanasikāravasena [M 1.0272] uppajjanato sampatti āyatiñca dukkhasseva uppādanato na koci lobho avisamo nāma. Abhijjhāyanaṭṭhenāti yassa kassaci ārammaṇassa yuttassa ayuttassa appattassa ca abhijjāyanavasena abhipatthanāvasena ca pavattā taṇhā abhijjhāti lobhato nibbisesanti dasseti. Tenāha “ekatthametaṃ byañjanameva nāna”nti. Dūsetīti sabhāvasantaṃ asaṃkilesaṃ vināseti avisuddhaṃ karoti. Tenāha “obhāsituṃ na detī”ti. “Ime sattā ucchijjantu vinassantū”ti sattesu byāpajjanākārappavattiyā byāpādo navavidhaāghātavatthusambhavo vutto. Kodho pana saṅkhāresupi pavattanato dasavidhaāghātavatthusambhavo vutto. Ubhayampi paṭighameva, pavattanānattato bhinditvā vutto. Kujjhanavaseneva cittapariyonandhano “akkocchi maṃ avadhi ma”ntiādinā.

71. Regarding one's own possessions, desire and attachment are called covetousness (abhijjhā) in the sense of longing; the meaning is longing. Regarding others' possessions, desire and attachment are called excessive greed (visamalobha) because of being excessively greedy. To show that there is a distinction between covetousness and excessive greed, he says, 'or else,' and so on. In this context, what belongs to oneself and is similar to it is a proper object. What is requested or can be obtained with little effort is an attainable object. Another's spouse or a teacher's spouse is an improper object. What is unworthy of being desired, or whose pursuit leads to ruin, is an unattainable object. 'The elder' refers to the great elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita, by whom the commentary was compiled into a book. For when discussing with his disciples, he spoke thus. Even in this very sutta, no distinction is found because the defilement of the mind is the intended point. Hence, it is said, 'whether proper or not,' etc. Because it arises through unwise attention and produces suffering both now and in the future, no greed is truly 'non-excessive.' By the meaning of longing, it is shown that craving—whether directed toward any proper, improper, or unattainable object—which proceeds by way of desire and aspiration, is covetousness, without distinction from greed. Therefore, it is said, 'This is one in meaning, only the expression differs.' 'It defiles' means it destroys the natural purity, making it impure. Hence, it is said, 'it does not allow it to shine.' 'May these beings be destroyed, may they perish'—such malevolence directed toward beings is called ill-will, said to arise from the nine grounds of resentment. Anger, however, because it arises toward formations as well, is said to arise from the ten grounds of resentment. Both are simply aversion, but they are distinguished based on the difference in their arising. The blinding of the mind through anger is expressed as: 'He abused me, he struck me,' etc.

Suṭṭhu kataṃ karaṇaṃ sukataṃ, tassa pubbakāritālakkhaṇassa guṇassa vināsano udakapuñchaniyā viya sarīrānugataṃ udakaṃ puñchanto makkho. Tathā hi so paresaṃ guṇānaṃ makkhanaṭṭhena “makkho”ti vuccati. Idāni anagāriyassa vātiādinā saṅkhepena vuttatthaṃ vitthārena dassetuṃ “anagāriyopī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nisinnakathāparikathādivasena dhammassa kathā dhammakathānayo, ekattādidhammanīti eva vā. Pakaraṇaṃ satta pakaraṇāni, tattha kosallaṃ dhammakathānayapakaraṇakosallaṃ. Ādi-saddena vinayakkame catūsu mahānikāyesu ca kosallaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Acittīkatoti cittīkārarahito. Yathā cāyanti iminā yathāyaṃ makkho cittaṃ dūseti, evaṃ paḷāsopi cittaṃ dūseti, tasmā upakkilesoti dasseti. Aniyatā gati niyāmokkamanābhāvato. Ādi-saddena “rattaññū cirapabbajite puggale ajjhottharitvā ‘tvampi imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajito, ahampi pabbajito, tvampi sīlamatte ṭhito ahampī’ti” evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Yugaggāhagāhīti “tava vā mama vā ko viseso”ti asamampi samaṃ katvā samadhuraggāhagaṇhanako. Khīyanā usūyanā. Attano sampattiyā nigūhanaṃ tassa parehi sādhāraṇabhāvāsahanena hotīti “parehi sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ asahamānaṃ”icceva vuttaṃ. Kāraṇe hi gahite phalampi gahitameva hotīti. Aññathā attano pavedanakapuggalo kerāṭiko, “nekatikavāṇijo”tipi vadanti. Sappamukhā [M 1.0273] macchavālā ekā macchajāti āyatanamaccho. Tenāha “āyatanamaccho nāmā”tiādi. Baddhacaroti antevāsī.

A deed well done is a good deed. Hypocrisy (makkha) is the destroyer of the quality characterized by a prior deed, just as one wipes away water clinging to the body with a wiper. Indeed, one is called 'makkha' in the sense of obliterating the qualities of others. Now, to elaborate on the meaning concisely stated with 'anagāriyassa' and so on, 'anagāriyopī' and so on is stated. The method of Dhamma discussion (dhammakathānayo) is a discussion of the Dhamma by way of seated conversation, dialogue, etc., or it is the principle of unity and other Dhamma principles. The treatise (pakaraṇa) means the seven treatises; skill therein is skill in the method of Dhamma discussion and treatises. The term 'etc.' (ādi-saddena) includes skill in the Vinaya procedure and the four great Nikāyas. Acittīkato means devoid of respect. By 'just as this' (yathā cāyaṃ), it is shown that just as this makkha corrupts the mind, so too does paḷāsa (disdain) corrupt the mind, and therefore it is a defilement. Aniyatā gati (uncertain destination) means the absence of a fixed course. The term 'etc.' includes such phrases as 'having overwhelmed individuals long-known and long-ordained, saying, “You too have gone forth in this Dispensation, I too have gone forth; you stand merely in virtue, I too,”' and so on. Yugaggāhagāhī means one who takes up an equal yoke, making the unequal equal by saying, 'What difference is there between you and me?' Disparagement, envy. Concealing one's own success arises from not enduring its being shared by others; hence it is said, 'not enduring its being shared by others.' For when the cause is grasped, the fruit is also grasped. Otherwise, a person who reveals himself is a fraud; they also say, 'a deceitful merchant.' Sappamukhā macchavālā is a species of fish, an āyatanamaccho. Hence it is said, 'an āyatanamaccho by name,' and so on. Baddhacaro means a resident pupil.

Sabbaso [V 1.0243] amadditasabhāvena vā tabharitabhattasadisassa thaddhabhāvassa anonamitadaṇḍasadisatāya paggahitasiraanivātavuttikārassa ca karaṇato vā tabharita…pe… karaṇo. Taduttarikaraṇoti yaṃ yena kataṃ duccaritaṃ vā sucaritaṃ vā, taduttari, tassa dviguṇaṃ vā karaṇo. Attano maṇḍanādiatthaṃ parena kataṃ alaṅkārādiṃ. Pariyāpuṇāti vā katheti vā attano balānurūpaṃ. Kāmaṃ nikāyadvayaggahaṇādivasena pavatto sevitabbamāno eva, tathāpissa saṃkilesapakkhattā vuttaṃ “mānaṃ anissāyā”ti.

Karaṇo (the doer) means, in every way, by the nature of being unsubdued, or by the stiffness like a bowl full of rice, or by the resemblance to an unbent staff, or by the action of one who holds his head high and has an un-humble demeanor... [and so on]. Taduttarikaraṇo means doing more than, or twofold, whatever bad or good deed was done by another. Ornaments and so on made by others for one's own adornment and so on. Pariyāpuṇāti vā katheti vā means he learns or speaks according to his own ability. Though the conceit that arises by way of taking up the two Nikāyas and so on is indeed to be cultivated, nevertheless, because it belongs to the side of defilement, it is said, 'not relying on conceit.'

Uṇṇativasenāti “seyyohamasmī”tiādinā cittassa paggahaṇavasena. Pubbe kenaci attānaṃ sadisaṃ katvā pacchā tato adhikato dahanato uppajjanako atimāno. Madaggahaṇākāro jātiādiṃ paṭicca majjanākāro, sopi atthato māno eva. Pamādo tathāpavatto cittuppādo.

Uṇṇativasena means by way of the uplifting of the mind, thinking, 'I am superior,' and so on. Atimāno (excessive pride) is that which arises from having previously made oneself equal to someone, and later burning with superiority to them. Madaggahaṇākāro (the characteristic of grasping intoxication) is the characteristic of being intoxicated with regard to birth and so on; that too, in essence, is conceit. Pamādo (heedlessness) is a thought that proceeds in such a way.

Tasmā lobhamādiṃ katvā dassetīti lobhassa ādito gahaṇe kāraṇaṃ vibhāvetukāmo pucchati. Paṭhamuppattitoti tattha tattha bhave sabbapaṭhamaṃ uppajjanato. Sattānañhi yathādhigataṃ jhānādivisesaṃ ārabbha paccavekkhaṇā viya yathāladdhaṃ upapatibhavaṃ ārabbha nikanti eva. Tenāha “sabbasattāna”ntiādi. Yathāsambhavaṃ itareti itare byāpādādayo yathāpaccayaṃ uppajjanti, lobhassa viya ādito asukassa anantaraṃ asukoti vā na nesaṃ niyamo atthīti attho. Kiṃ pana ete soḷaseva cittassa upakkilesā, udāhu aññepi santīti anuyogaṃ sandhāya aññepi santīti dassento “na ca ete”tiādimāha. Yadi evaṃ kasmā ettakā eva idha vuttāti. Nayadassanavasenāti dassento āha “etena pana…pe… veditabbā”ti. Tena thinamiddhauddhaccakukkucca-vicikicchā-attukkaṃsana-paravabbhanachambhitattā- bhīrukatā-ahirikānottappa-atticchatā-pāpicchatā-mahicchatādayo saṅgahitāti veditabbaṃ.

Therefore, to explain the reason for taking greed as the beginning and showing it, he asks. Paṭhamuppattito (first arising) means because it arises as the very first in each existence. For beings, just as there is reflection concerning the distinctions of jhāna and so on according to what they have attained, so too there is delight concerning the state of rebirth they have obtained. Hence it is said, 'for all beings,' and so on. Yathāsambhavaṃ itare (the others as they arise) means that ill-will and so on arise according to conditions, and there is no fixed order for them, such as 'this after that,' as there is for greed. But are these sixteen alone the defilements of the mind, or are there others? In reference to this question, to show that there are others, he says, 'and not only these,' and so on. If so, why are only this many mentioned here? To show that it is by way of indicating the method, he says, 'but by this... it should be understood.' Thus, it should be understood that sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt, self-exaltation, disparaging others, stupefaction, cowardice, lack of shame, lack of fear of wrongdoing, excessive desire, evil desire, great desire, and so on are included.

72. Saṃkilesaṃ [M 1.0274] dassetvāti saṃkiliṭṭhavattanidassanena saṅkhepena vuttaṃ saṃkilesaṃ vibhāgena dassetvā. Vodānaṃ dassentoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Evaṃ jānitvāti “abhijjhā visamalobho ekanteneva cittassa uppakkileso”ti sabhāvato samudayato nirodhato nirodhūpāyato ca pubbabhāgapaññāya ceva heṭṭhimamaggadvayapaññāya ca jānitvā. Pajahatīti ettha accantappahānameva adhippetanti dassento “samucchedappahānavasena ariyamaggena pajahatī”ti āha. Ariyamaggenāti anāgāmimaggena. Tena hi pahānaṃ idha sabbavāresu adhippetaṃ. Kilesapaṭipāṭi idha kilesānaṃ desanākkamo. Maggapaṭipāṭipana catunnaṃ ariyamaggānaṃ desanākkamopi tāya desanāya paṭipajjanakkamopi [V 1.0244] tāya paṭipattiyā uppattikkamopi. Tattha ye ye kilesā yena yena maggena pahīyanti, maggapaṭipāṭiṃ anoloketvā tesaṃ tesaṃ kilesānaṃ tena tena maggena pahānadassanaṃ kilesapaṭipāṭi na kilesānaṃ uppattikkamo idha desanākkamo cāti dassento “abhijjhā visamalobho”tiādimāha. Yena yena pana maggena ye ye kilesā pahīyanti maggānupubbiyā, tena tena maggena tesaṃ tesaṃ kilesānaṃ pahānadassanaṃ maggapaṭipāṭiyā pahānadassananti dassento “sotāpattimaggenā”tiādimāha.

72. Saṃkilesaṃ dassetvā (having shown defilement) means having shown in detail the defilement that was briefly stated by illustrating defiled conduct. Vodānaṃ dassento (showing purification) means here too the method is the same. Evaṃ jānitvā (having known thus) means having known 'covetousness and unrighteous greed are utterly defilements of the mind' by way of their nature, origin, cessation, and the way to cessation, and by way of preliminary wisdom and the wisdom of the lower two paths. Pajahati (abandons): here, to show that complete abandonment is intended, he says, 'one abandons by the Noble Path by way of eradication.' Ariyamaggena (by the Noble Path) means by the non-returner's path. For by that path, abandonment is intended here in all instances. Kilesapaṭipāṭi (the sequence of defilements) here means the order of teaching the defilements. Maggapaṭipāṭi (the sequence of paths) means the order of teaching the four Noble Paths, the order of practicing according to that teaching, and the order of arising through that practice. There, to show that the sequence of defilements is the showing of the abandonment of those defilements by those paths by which they are abandoned, without considering the sequence of paths—and that it is not the order of arising of defilements, but the order of teaching here—he says, 'covetousness and unrighteous greed,' and so on. But to show that the showing of the abandonment of whatever defilements by whatever path, in the sequence of paths, is the showing of abandonment by the sequence of paths, he says, 'by the path of stream-entry,' and so on.

Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāneti “sa kho so, bhikkhave, bhikkhū”tiādinā āgato imasmiṃ pahānavāre. Ime kilesāti ime yathāvuttā kilesā. Sotāpattimaggavajjhā vā hontu sesamaggavajjhā vāheṭṭhā dassitamaggapaṭipāṭivasena. Tattha pana ye tatiyamaggavajjhā, tesaṃ anāgāmimaggeneva pahāne vattabbaṃ natthi, yesaṃ panettha heṭṭhimamaggavajjhānaṃ idha saṅgahe kāraṇaṃ pacchā vattukāmena aggamaggavajjhānaṃ anādiyitvā kasmā tatiyamaggavajjhānameva gahaṇaṃ katanti āha “ayamettha paveṇimaggāgato sambhavo”ti, ayaṃ imassa suttassa etasmiṃ ṭhāne ācariyapaveṇiyā kathāmaggo tato āgato atthasambhavo atthatatvanti attho. Tattha heṭṭhimamaggavajjhānaṃ idha saṅgahe kāraṇaṃ pacchā vattukāmo aggamaggavajjhānaṃ aggahaṇe yuttiṃ dassento “so cā”tiādimāha. Tenāti catutthamaggena. Sesānanti byāpādādīnaṃ[M 1.0275]. Yepīti makkhādike sandhāyāha. Taṃsamuṭṭhāpakacittānanti tesaṃ makkhādīnaṃ samuṭṭhāpakacittuppādānaṃ. Tattha makkha-paḷāsa-issā-macchariya-samuṭṭhāpakaṃ paṭighadvayacittaṃ, visesato pañcakāmaguṇalobhena saṭho māyāvī ca hoti, pañcakāmaguṇikarāgo ca anāgāmimaggeneva niravasesato pahīyati, tasmā vuttaṃ “taṃsamuṭṭhāpakacittānaṃ appahīnattā”ti. Tepi suppahīnā hontīti sambandho. Tanti paṭhamamaggeneva pahānaṃ pubbāparena na sandhiyati “yathodhi kho”ti ettha odhivacanassa maggattayavācakattā. Ratanattaye aveccappasādo nāma ariyakantasīlaṃ viya sotāpannassa aṅgāni, te ca pahānato pacchā niddiṭṭhā, tasmā idha vuttappahānaṃ vikkhambhanapahānamevāti keci vadanti. Tesaṃ icchāmattameva yathāvuttapahānasseva vasena aveccappasādānaṃ odhiso pahānassa vibhāvitattā, svāyamattho heṭṭhā yuttitopi pakāsitoyeva.

Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne means in this section on abandonment, which is introduced by the passage beginning, 'That bhikkhu, bhikkhus…' Ime kilesā means these defilements as stated. Whether they are to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry or by the remaining paths, this is according to the sequence of paths shown below. Therein, concerning those defilements to be abandoned by the third path, there is nothing to be said about their abandonment by the path of the non-returner. As for those defilements to be abandoned by the lower paths, since the author intends to state the reason for their inclusion here later, why, without taking up the defilements to be abandoned by the highest path, are only the defilements to be abandoned by the third path taken up? To this, he says, 'This here is the occurrence that has come from the traditional path.' The meaning is: in this context of this discourse, this is the method of explanation from the lineage of teachers; from that comes the origin and reality of the meaning. Therein, intending to state later the reason for including here the defilements to be abandoned by the lower paths, and showing the justification for not taking up those to be abandoned by the highest path, he says, 'And that…' and so on. Tena means by the fourth path. Sesānaṃ means of ill will and so on. Yepi is said with reference to hypocrisy and the like. Taṃsamuṭṭhāpakacittānaṃ means of the arisings of consciousness that produce that hypocrisy and the like. Therein, the two consciousnesses rooted in aversion produce hypocrisy, disdain, envy, and miserliness. And especially through greed for the five strands of sensual pleasure, one becomes deceitful and fraudulent; and craving related to the five strands of sensual pleasure is completely abandoned only by the path of the non-returner. Therefore, it is said, 'because the consciousnesses that produce them have not been abandoned.' The connection is: 'they too are well abandoned.' That abandonment by the first path does not connect with what precedes and follows, because in the phrase 'yathodhi kho,' the word 'odhi' refers to the three paths. Unshakable confidence in the Triple Gem, like the virtues dear to the Noble Ones, are factors of a stream-enterer; and since these are pointed out after the abandonment, some say that the abandonment spoken of here is only abandonment by suppression. That is merely their opinion, for it has been explained that the abandonment is in stages, by way of the aforesaid abandonment, in relation to the unshakable confidences; and this meaning has also been made clear below by way of reasoning.

74. Ekamekena padena yojetabbaṃ, yato ekamekassapi upakkilesassa sabhāvādito dassanaṃ niyyānamukhaṃ hoti, tathā ceva heṭṭhā saṃvaṇṇitaṃ. Anāgāmimaggavasena pahānaṃ vatvā pasādassa uddhaṭattā vuttaṃ “anāgāmimaggena lokuttarappasādo āgato”ti. Yadi evaṃ kasmā “lokiyo uppajjatī”ti vuttanti? “Itipi so bhagavā”tiādinayappavattassa lokiyattā. Nibbānārammaṇo [V 1.0245] eva hi lokuttaro pasādo. “Itipi so bhagavā”tiādivacanena lokiyaṃ, aveccappasādavacanena lokuttaranti lokiyalokuttaramissakaṃ pasādaṃ dassento. Avecca ratanattayaguṇe yāthāvato ñatvā pasādo aveccappasādo. So pana yasmā maggenāgatattā kenaci akampaniyo appadhaṃsiyo ca hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “acalena accutenā”ti. Tattha lokuttaro sabbaso buddhaguṇādīsu sammohaṃ viddhaṃsento tattha kiccato pavattati, itaro ārammaṇavasena te ārabbha. Taṃ vidhinti taṃ tassa uppannappakāraṃ. Anussatiṭṭhānānīti anussatikammaṭṭhānāni.

74. It should be connected with each single word, since seeing the intrinsic nature and so on of even a single imperfection becomes a means of liberation, as was explained below. Having spoken of the abandonment by way of the non-returner's path, since confidence has been taken up for discussion, it is said, 'Through the non-returner's path, supramundane confidence is attained.' If so, why is it said, 'The mundane arises'? Because of the mundane nature of the method beginning, 'Indeed, that Blessed One…' For supramundane confidence indeed has Nibbāna as its object. By the statement beginning, 'Indeed, that Blessed One…' it is mundane; by the statement of unshakable confidence it is supramundane—thus showing a confidence that is a mixture of mundane and supramundane. Unshakable confidence is the confidence that arises after having penetrated and known the qualities of the Triple Gem as they really are. And since it is attained through the path, it is unshakeable and indestructible by anyone; therefore, it is called 'unwavering and steadfast.' Therein, the supramundane operates by way of its function, completely destroying delusion regarding the Buddha’s qualities and so on, while the other operates by way of its object, taking them as its object. 'That manner' means the way in which it has arisen. 'The bases of recollection' means the meditation subjects of recollection.

75. Somanassādīti ādi-saddena ñāṇādīni saṅgaṇhāti. Corānaṃ abhiṇhaṃ sañcaraṇaṭṭhānatāya paccantaggahaṇaṃ. Paccavekkhatoti “asukasmiñca ṭhāne ime cime corā evañca evañca vināsitā”ti paccavekkhato rañño viya.

75. "With joy, etc."—by the word "etc." he includes knowledge and so forth. The border region is mentioned because it is a place frequently traversed by thieves. "He reflects"—like a king who reflects, "In such and such a place, these and those thieves were destroyed in such and such a way."

Yo [M 1.0276] yo odhi yathodhi. Yathā-saddo byāpanicchāyaṃ, kho saddo avadhāraṇeti dassento “sakasakaodhivasena cattameva hotī”tiādimāha. Tena “vanta”ntiādīsupi avadhāretabbanti dasseti. Sakasakaodhivasenāti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “dve odhī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha yaṃmaggavajjhāti yena maggena anavasesato pahātabbā. Anavasesappahānavasena hi taṃtaṃmaggavajjhānaṃ kilesānaṃ tadaññamaggavajjhehi asammissatā, aññathā ye sakasakaodhivasena uparimaggavajjhā, te heṭṭhimamaggehi pahīnāpāyagamanīyādisabhāvā eva tehi pahīyantīti pahānavasena sammissā siyuṃ. Tena teyeva pahīnā hontīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tatuttaripīti tato pahānanimittasomanassuppattito uddhampi. Paṭipakkhesu odhiso pavattikiccattā odhīti heṭṭhā tayo maggā vuccanti. Te hītiādi vuttassevatthassa vivaraṇaṃ. Imassa bhikkhunoti anāgāmiṃ sandhāyāha. Tena vuttaṃ “heṭṭhāmaggattayena catta”nti.

'Yathodhi' means according to each respective limit. Showing that the word 'yathā' is used in the sense of distributiveness and the word 'kho' is for emphasis, he says, 'it is indeed abandoned according to its respective limit,' and so on. By this, he shows that in phrases like 'vanta' and so on, it should also be understood emphatically. To explain the meaning stated briefly as 'sakasakaodhivasena,' the passage beginning 'two limits…' was started. Therein, 'to be abandoned by a particular path' means to be abandoned without remainder by that path. For it is by way of abandonment without remainder that the defilements to be abandoned by a particular path are not mixed with those to be abandoned by other paths. Otherwise, those defilements that are to be abandoned by the higher paths according to their respective limits, having the nature of leading to states of woe when abandoned, would be abandoned by those lower paths, and thus they would be mixed by way of abandonment. Therefore, 'they alone are abandoned'—this is the method here too. 'Tatuttaripi' means even beyond that, that is, beyond the arising of joy which is a sign of abandonment. Because they have the function of proceeding according to limits against their opposing factors, the three lower paths are called 'limits' (odhi). The passage beginning 'Te hi…' is an explanation of the meaning just stated. 'Of this bhikkhu'—he says this referring to the non-returner. Therefore it is said, 'abandoned by the three lower paths.'

Keci cattampi gaṇhanti, nayidamevanti dassanatthaṃ “vanta”nti vuttaṃ. Na hi yaṃ yena vantaṃ, so puna taṃ ādiyati. Tenāha “anādiyanabhāvadassanavasenā”ti. Vantampi kiñci sasantatilaggaṃ siyā, nayidamevanti dassanatthaṃ “mutta”nti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “santatito vinimocanavasenā”ti. Muttampi kiñci muttabandhanā viya phalaṃ kuhiñci tiṭṭhati, na evamidanti dassanatthaṃ “pahīna”nti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “kvaci anavaṭṭhānadassanavasenā”ti. Yathā kiñci dunnissaṭṭhaṃ puna ādāya sammadeva nissaṭṭhaṃ paṭinissaṭṭhanti vuccati, evaṃ vipassanāya nissaṭṭhaṃ ādinnasadisaṃ maggena pahīnaṃ paṭinissaṭṭhaṃ nāma hotīti dassanatthaṃ “paṭinissaṭṭha”nti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “ādinnapubbassa paṭinissaggadassanavasenā”ti. Na kāpurisena viya parammukhena nissaṭṭhaṃ[V 1.0246], atha kho abhimukheneva nissaṭṭhanti dassanatthaṃ “paṭinissaṭṭha”nti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “paṭimukhaṃ vā”tiādi. Upagantabbatoti attano hitasukhaṃ paccāsīsantena ekantena adhigantabbato. Dhāraṇatoti taṃsamaṅgīnaṃ apāyapātato sandhāraṇena. Gantho “vedo”ti vuccati “vidanti etenā”ti, vedehi ñāṇehi gato paṭipannoti vedagū. Abhijaññāti jāneyya. Vedajātāti uppannasomanassā. Ñāṇaṃ “vedo”ti vuccati “veditabbaṃ vedetī”ti. Somanassaṃ “vedo”ti vuccati ārammaṇarasaṃ vindati anubhavatīti.

Some take all four terms together. To show that it is not just this, 'vomited' is said. For what has been vomited by someone, they do not take it up again. Hence it is said, 'by way of showing the state of not taking up again.' Even something vomited might have some sesame seeds clinging to it; to show it is not like this, 'released' is said. Hence it is said, 'by way of showing the release from the continuity.' Even something released, like a fruit with its stalk broken, might remain somewhere; to show it is not like this, 'abandoned' is said. Hence it is said, 'by way of showing that it does not remain anywhere.' Just as something poorly discarded, when taken up again and properly discarded, is called 'relinquished'; so too, what is discarded by insight is like something taken up, and when abandoned by the path, it is called 'relinquished.' To show this, 'relinquished' is said. Hence it is said, 'by way of showing the relinquishment of what was previously taken up.' It is not discarded by turning away like a coward, but rather discarded by facing it directly. To show this, 'relinquished' is said. Hence it is said, 'or facing directly,' and so on. 'To be approached' means because it is certainly to be attained by one who hopes for their own welfare and happiness. 'Upholding' means by upholding those endowed with it from falling into states of woe. The text is called 'veda' because 'they know by this.' One who has gone, who has practiced, with these vedas, that is, with these knowledges, is a 'vedagū' (knower of the Veda). 'Abhijaññā' means one should know. 'Vedajātā' means those for whom joy has arisen. Knowledge is called 'veda' because 'it knows what is to be known.' Joy is called 'veda' because 'it finds and experiences the taste of the object.'

Uppannanti [M 1.0277] aveccappasādaṃ nissāya uppannaṃ. Vuttappakārameva vedanti “somanassaṃ somanassamayañāṇañcā”ti evaṃ vuttappakārameva. Atthavedanti atthe hetuphale vedaṃ. Dhammavedanti dhamme hetumhi vedaṃ. Tenāha “aveccappasādassa hetu”ntiādi. Idha dhammatthasaddā hetuphalapariyāyāti imamatthaṃ pāḷiyā eva dassetuṃ “vuttañheta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tameva atthañca dhammañcāti attho dhammoti ca vuttaṃ aveccappasādanimittaṃ yathāvuttaṃ kilesappahānañca. Atthadhammānisaṃsabhūtaṃ vedanti yathāvuttaatthadhammānisaṃsabhūtaṃ somanassamayañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ vedañca. Pāmojjanti taruṇapītiṃ āha. Paccavekkhaṇākārappavattenāti etena paccavekkhaṇā evettha anavajjasabhāvatāya dhammoti vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pīti jāyatīti parappaccayaṃ balavapītimāha. Pīṇitamanassāti passaddhiāvahehi uḷārehi pītivegehi tittacittassa. Kāyoti nāmakāyo. Vūpasantadarathoti kilesapariḷāhānaṃ dūrībhāvena suṭṭhu upasantadaratho. Paccavekkhaṇahetukaṃ cittassa samādhānaṃ idha adhippetanti āha “appitaṃ viya acalaṃ tiṭṭhatī”ti.

"Uppanna" means that which has arisen depending on unwavering confidence. They understand 'veda' in the manner already stated, as 'joy and knowledge accompanied by joy'—in just this manner already stated. "Atthaveda" means understanding the meaning in terms of cause and effect. "Dhammaveda" means understanding the Dhamma in terms of the cause. Therefore, it is said, "the cause of unwavering confidence," and so on. Here, the terms "dhamma" and "attha" are synonyms for cause and effect. To show this meaning from the Pāli itself, it is stated, "for it has been said," and so on. That very meaning and Dhamma are spoken of as 'meaning' and 'Dhamma', which are the sign of unwavering confidence and the abandoning of defilements as stated. They understand 'veda' as the benefit of meaning and Dhamma, and also as the knowledge accompanied by joy, which is the benefit of the aforesaid meaning and Dhamma. "Pāmojja" refers to nascent rapture. By "through the mode of its proceeding as reflection," it should be understood that here reflection itself, due to its faultless nature, is called 'Dhamma'. "Pīti jāyati" refers to strong rapture dependent on another condition. 'Pīṇitamanassa' means of one whose mind is satisfied by the sublime surges of rapture that bring about tranquility. "Kāya" refers to the mental body. "Vūpasantadaratha" means one whose distress is thoroughly pacified because the burning of the defilements is far removed. The stabilization of the mind caused by reflection is intended here; therefore, it is said, "it stands unwavering, as if absorbed."

76. Kāmaṃ “buddhe aveccappasādena samannāgatomhi, dhamme saṅghe aveccappasādena samannāgatomhī”ti idampi tassā paccavekkhaṇāya pavattiākārapakāsanameva, idaṃ pana visesato ratanattaye uppannasomanassādippakāsanapadaṃ. “Yathodhi kho panā”ti idampi savisesaṃ paccavekkhaṇākārappakāsanapadanti adhippāyena “idāni yathodhi…pe… pakāsetvā”ti vuttaṃ. Cattāropi pana vārā paccavekkhaṇākārappakāsanavasena ceva somanassādiānisaṃsadassanavasena ca vuttāti sakkā viññātuṃ ubhayatthāpi ubhayassa vuttattā. Yadipi ariyamaggo ekacittakkhaṇiko na puna uppajjati, paṭipakkhassa pana tena suppahīnattā taṃsamaṅgī aparihānadhammo taṃsīlādibhāveneva vuccatīti āha “tassa anāgāmimaggasampayuttaṃ sīlakkhandhaṃ dassetī”tiādi. “Evaṃdhammā te bhagavanto ahesu”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.13; ma. ni. 3.197-198; saṃ. ni. 5.378) viya idha dhamma-saddo samādhipariyāyoti āha “samādhikkhandhaṃ paññākkhandhañca dassetī”ti. Tathā hi so sampayuttadhamme ekārammaṇe avikkhipamāne [V 1.0247] avippakiṇṇe avisaṭe katvā samaṃ, sammā ca ādahanto tathā te dhāretīti ca vattabbataṃ arahatīti [M 1.0278] dhammoti ca vuccati. Anekarūpānanti anekappakārānaṃ. Antarāyo nāma appaṭiladdhassa vā alabbhanavasena, paṭiladdhassa vā parihānavasena, tadubhayampi idha natthīti dassento “maggassa vā”tiādimāha. Nevassa taṃ hoti antarāyāyāti tassa anāgāmino piṇḍapātabhojanaṃ neva hoti antarāyāya ukkaṃsagatāya paccavekkhaṇāya paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjanato. Tañcassā ukkaṃsagamanaṃ hatapaṭipakkhattāti dassento “maggena visuddhacittattā”ti āha.

76. Granted, ‘I am endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha’—this too is merely a way of showing the mode of occurrence of that reflection, but this phrase specifically shows the joy and so on that has arisen in regard to the Three Jewels. With the intention that ‘Just as, indeed...’ is also a phrase showing the mode of reflection with its specifics, it is said, ‘Now, having explained "just as, indeed..."’ Moreover, all four sections are spoken both by way of showing the mode of reflection and by way of showing the benefit of joy and so on. It can be understood that both are stated in both places because both are stated. Although the noble path is of a single mind-moment and does not arise again, since the opposition has been well abandoned by it, one who is endowed with it is said to be of a non-declining nature on account of that virtue, and so on. Therefore, it is said, 'It shows the aggregate of virtue associated with the non-returner’s path,' and so on. As in such phrases as 'Of such a nature were those Blessed Ones...' (Dī. Ni. 2.13; Ma. Ni. 3.197–198; Saṃ. Ni. 5.378), here the word 'Dhamma' is a synonym for concentration; therefore, it is said, 'It shows the aggregate of concentration and the aggregate of wisdom.' For indeed, it makes associated phenomena unified on a single object—undistracted, unscattered, and not dispersed—and because it rightly fixes them, thus it is worthy to be called and is called 'Dhamma'. 'Of various kinds' means of many types. 'An obstacle' refers either to the non-attainment of what has not been attained or to the loss of what has been attained. Showing that neither of these exists here, it is said, 'For the path...' and so on. 'Nor is that for him an obstacle' means: for the non-returner, eating almsfood is not an obstacle, because he consumes it after reviewing it with a reflection that has reached a sublime state. And showing that this sublime state of his is due to the destruction of the opposition, it is said, 'Because his mind is purified by the path.'

Etthāti etasmiṃ antarāyābhāve. Etadeva visuddhacittattameva kāraṇaṃ. Ettha ca “nevassa taṃ hoti antarāyāyā”ti iminā heṭṭhā vuttappahānaṃ anāgāmimaggenevāti siddhaṃ hoti. Anāgāmino hi sabbaso kāmarāgo pahīno hoti, rasataṇhāya abhāvato tādisapiṇḍapātaparibhogo aggamaggādhigame kathañcipi antarāyāya na hotīti. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, vattha”nti vadanto bhagavāādimhi attanā upanītavatthūpamaṃ anusandheti. Udakassa acchabhāvo paṅkasevālapaṇakādimalābhāvena pasannatāya, tabbipariyāyato bahalatāti āha “acchanti vippasanna”nti. Vaṇṇanibhāya vigatasaṃkilesatāya samujjalanaṃ pabhassaratāya vatthassa, taṃ pariyodātanti vattabbataṃ labhatīti āha “pariyodātaṃ pabhassaratāyā”ti. Ukkaṃ bandheyyāti aṅgārakapallaṃ yathā dārughaṭikaṅgārādikena na bhijjati, evaṃ tanumattikālepādinā bandheyya. Meghapaṭalato verambhavātadhārāsaṅghaṭṭanato vijjutā viya kevalaṃ vātadhārāsaṅghaṭṭanajanitā pabhā ukkāpabhā, sā pana yasmā dvinnaṃ vātadhārānaṃ vegasambhūtasaṅghaṭṭanahetukā, tasmā kāraṇavasena “vātavego ukkā”ti vuttaṃ.

Here, 'ettha' means in the absence of that hindrance. This very purity of mind is the reason. Here, with the statement 'that does not become a hindrance for him,' it is established that the abandonment mentioned below is by the non-returner's path alone. For a non-returner, all sensual desire is abandoned, and due to the absence of craving for tastes, even such consumption of almsfood does not become a hindrance in any way to the attainment of the highest path. The Blessed One, speaking the phrase 'Just as, bhikkhus, a cloth,' connects it to the simile of the cloth he himself introduced at the beginning. The clarity of water is due to its serenity, from the absence of impurities such as mud, moss, and water-plants; its opposite is turbidity. Therefore, he says 'accha' means 'very clear'. For the cloth, its radiance and brilliance, due to being free of defilements, obtains the designation 'perfectly clean'. Thus, it is said to be 'pariyodātaṃ pabhassaratāyā' (perfectly clean due to its radiance). 'Ukkaṃ bandheyyāti' means one should bind a fire-pan with a thin plaster of clay so that it does not break apart. Like lightning produced by the collision of violent wind currents from a layer of cloud, the glow of a meteor (ukkāpabhā) arises solely from the collision of wind currents. Since it is caused by the forceful collision of two wind currents, it is referred to as 'vātavego ukkā' (a wind-velocity meteor) in terms of its cause.

77. Yathānusandhivasenātiādimhi uṭṭhitadesanāya anurūpā anusandhi yathānusandhi, tassā vasena. Byatirekadassanaṃ viya hi sādhetabbassa ādimhi uṭṭhitadesanāya paṭipakkhadassanampi anurūpadesanāva sammadeva patiṭṭhāpanabhāvato, yathā taṃ āvattahārayojanāyaṃ visabhāgadhammāvattanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Yathānusandhivasena desanā āgatā”ti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārento tappasaṅgena itarepi anusandhī dassetuṃ “tayo hī”tiādimāha. Bahiddhāti bāhiresu vatthūsu. Asati paritassanāti taṇhādiṭṭhiparitassanābhāvo. Vissajjitasuttavasenāti “idha bhikkhu ekaccassā”tiādinā [M 1.0279] (ma. ni. 1.242) vissajjitasuttavasena. Yena dhammenāti sīlādivodānadhammesu akkhantiyādisaṃkilesadhammesu ca yena yena dhammena. Cha abhiññā āgatāti iminā “anurūpadhammavasena vā”ti vuttavikappaṃ dasseti, sesehi “paṭipakkhavasena vā”ti [V 1.0248] vuttavikappaṃ. Akkhantiyā hi kakacūpamovādo (ma. ni. 1.222) paṭipakkho, tathā diṭṭhiyā “netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā”ti evaṃ paṭibhāgā suññatākārena. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. “Citte saṃkiliṭṭhe duggati pāṭikaṅkhā”ti (ma. ni. 1.70) heṭṭhā kilesadesanā āgatā. Sabboti anavaseso. Sabbākārenāti ādīnavānisaṃsapaccavekkhaṇapuggaladosajānanādinā sabbappakārena.

77. In the phrase 'yathānusandhivasena' (according to the connection), the connection (anusandhi) appropriate to the teaching that arises at the beginning is called 'yathānusandhi,' and it is according to that. Just as a demonstration by way of contrast is needed for what is to be established, so too a demonstration of the opposite of the teaching that has arisen at the beginning is also a suitable teaching, because it establishes it quite rightly. This should be understood as the application of dissimilar phenomena, as in the hermeneutical method of Āvatta. To elaborate on the meaning briefly stated in 'the teaching has come according to the connection,' and to show other connections in that context, he says 'tayo hi' (for there are three), etc. 'Bahiddhā' means in external objects. 'Asati paritassanā' means the absence of agitation caused by craving and wrong view. 'By the discourse of the reply' refers to the discourse that was answered beginning with 'idha bhikkhu ekaccassa' (Here, a certain monk...) (MN 1.242). 'By whatever principle' refers to whatever principle among the purifying qualities such as virtue, etc., and the defiling qualities such as impatience, etc. 'The six direct knowledges have come' indicates the alternative mentioned as 'anurūpadhammavasena vā' (or by way of suitable qualities), while the rest indicate the alternative mentioned as 'paṭipakkhavasena vā' (or by way of opposition). For impatience, the discourse on the simile of the saw (MN 1.222) is the opposite; similarly, for views, the counterpart is the perception of emptiness in the form of 'netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā' (This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self). The same principle applies to the remaining two. The teaching on defilements below states, 'Citte saṃkiliṭṭhe duggati pāṭikaṅkhā' (When the mind is defiled, a bad destination is to be expected) (MN 1.70). 'Sabbo' means without remainder. 'Sabbākārena' means in all aspects, such as by reflecting on disadvantages and advantages, recognizing the faults in individuals, and so on.

78. “Mettā bhāvetabbā byāpādassa pahānāyā”tiādivacanato (a. ni. 9.1) mettādayo byāpādavihesāratirāgānaṃ paṭipakkhā. Yasmā “so atthī”tiādinā bhagavatā anāgāmino aggamaggādhigamanaṃ catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā kathitaṃ, tasmā taṃ dassento “idānissā”tiādimāha.

78. From such statements as 'Loving-kindness should be developed for the abandoning of ill will' (AN 9.1), loving-kindness and so on are the opposites of ill will, cruelty, discontent, and lust. Because the Blessed One, with the words 'he is,' etc., has taught the non-returner's attainment of the highest path by bringing the meditation subject of the four truths to its culmination, therefore, showing this, he said 'idānissa' (now for him), etc.

Brahmavihāradhammeti brahmavihāre ceva brahmavihārasahagatadhamme ca. Tenāha “nāmavasenā”ti. Vavatthapetvāti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Nāmantipi hi īdisesu ṭhānesu cattāro arūpino khandhā vuccanti. Iminā nayenāti etena bhūtanissitānaṃ sesupādāyadhammānaṃ sabbesampi pahātabbataṇhāvajjānaṃ tebhūmakadhammānaṃ pariggahavidhiṃ ulliṅgeti. Sabhāvato vijjamānaṃ taṃ attapaccakkhaṃ katvā ñāṇena yāthāvato paṭivijjhiyamānataṃ upādāya “atthi ida”nti yathāvavatthāpitaṃ nāmarūpaṃ. Tenevāha “ettāvatānena dukkhasaccavavatthānaṃ kataṃ hotī”ti. Sāvadhāraṇañcetaṃ vacanaṃ, lokasamaññāsiddhaṃ sattaitthipurisādi viya, ito bāhirakaparikappitaṃ pakatiādi drabyādi jīvādi kāyādi viya ca na paramatthato natthi, atthevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pajānātīti pubbabhāge tāva lakkhaṇarasādivasena ceva paṭiggahavibhāgavasena ca pakārato jānāti, aparabhāge pana pariññābhisamayavasena paṭivijjhanto jānāti. Ekantahīnā nāma akusaladhammā sampati āyatiñca dukkhamūlattā, tatthāpi visesato taṇhāti āha “dukkhassa samudayaṃ paṭivijjhanto atthi hīnanti [M 1.0280] pajānātī”ti. Attano paccayehi padhānabhāvaṃ nītattā paṇītanti iminā atthena ariyamaggova “paṇīta”nti vuccatīti āha “pahānupāyaṃ vicinanto atthi paṇītanti pajānātī”ti. “Uttamaṭṭhena ca paṇīta”nti vuccamāne nirodhasaccassapi saṅgaho siyā, tassa pana padantarena saṅgahitattā vuttanayenevettha attho veditabbo. Appamaññāmukhena vipassanābhinivesasseva katattā “brahmavihārasaññāgatassā”ti vuttaṃ. “Sabbassapi tebhūmakassa saññāgatassā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Na cettha asaṅgaho tassāpi saññāya āgatabhāvato. Lokaṃ uttaritvā samatikkamitvā nissaritvā visaṃyuttaṃ hutvā ṭhitattā vuttaṃ “uttari nissaraṇaṃ nibbāna”nti.

'Brahmavihāradhamma' means both the divine abidings and the states associated with the divine abidings. Therefore, he says 'by way of name.' 'Having determined' is to be connected by bringing them into relation. Indeed, in such contexts, the four immaterial aggregates are called 'name.' 'By this method' indicates the method of comprehending all phenomena of the three planes—those dependent on the primary elements and the remaining derivative phenomena—excluding craving which is to be abandoned. Because that which exists by its own nature has been made directly perceptible to oneself and is being penetrated as it really is by knowledge, one understands the name-and-form that has been determined thus: 'This exists.' Therefore, he says, 'To this extent, the determination of the truth of suffering has been made.' And this statement is definitive; it is not that it does not exist in an ultimate sense, like worldly conventions such as 'a being,' 'a woman,' 'a man,' etc., or like externally imagined things such as nature, substance, soul, body, etc.; it is said that it does exist. 'He understands' means that in the preliminary stage, he knows in various ways by means of characteristics, functions, etc., and by way of grasping and analysis. But later, in the subsequent stage, he knows by penetrating through full understanding and realization. Unwholesome states are entirely inferior because they are the root of suffering in the present and in the future. Among them, craving is especially inferior. Hence it is said, 'penetrating the origin of suffering, he understands that there is the inferior.' Because it has been brought to prominence by its own conditions, the noble path itself is called 'superior' in this sense. Thus it is said, 'investigating the means of abandonment, he understands that there is the superior.' If 'superior' were spoken of in the sense of 'ultimate,' the truth of cessation would also be included. However, since that is included by another term, the meaning here should be understood in the way that has been stated. Because the application of insight has been made through the divine abidings, it is said, 'one endowed with the perception associated with the divine abidings.' It could also be rightly said, 'one endowed with the perception associated with all three planes.' There is no non-inclusion here, since that too is included within perception. Because Nibbāna stands having transcended the world, having overcome it, having escaped, having become detached, it is said, 'the supreme escape is Nibbāna'.

Catūhi [V 1.0249] ākārehīti “atthi hīna”ntiādīhi catūhi pakārehi. Anvayañāṇatāya anubodhabhūtāya vipassanāpaññāya jānanattho dhammañāṇatāya paṭivedhabhūtāya maggapaññāya dassanattho sabhāvasiddhoti dassento “vipassanāpaññāya cattāri saccāni jānanato maggapaññāya passato”ti vuttaṃ. Bhayabherave vuttanayenevāti bhayabheravasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ attanā vuttaatthavacanatthapāṭhena idha pāṭhassa sadisattā atidisanto “kāmāsavāpi…pe… pajānātī”ti āha. Ettha ca yasmā “kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati…pe… avijjāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccatī”ti “khīṇā jātī”tiādīni vadatā bhagavatā catutthamaggo niddiṭṭho, tasmā yaṃ heṭṭhā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ “so ca upari catutthamaggasseva niddiṭṭhattā yujjatī”ti, taṃ suvuttamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'By four aspects' means through the four ways, such as 'there is the inferior,' etc. To show that the purpose of knowing is by insight-wisdom—which is knowledge of conformity and comprehension—and the purpose of seeing is by path-wisdom—which is knowledge of the Dhamma and penetration—is established by its own nature, it is said: 'through insight-wisdom, one knows the four truths; through path-wisdom, one sees.' 'As in the way stated in the Bhayabherava' means: because the text here is similar to the text of the explanation of the meaning stated by oneself in the commentary on the Bhayabherava Sutta, making an analogy, he says, 'from the taint of sensual desire... and so on... one understands.' Here, since the Blessed One, in saying 'the mind is freed from the taint of sensual desire... and so on... the mind is freed from the taint of ignorance,' and 'birth is destroyed,' etc., has indicated the fourth path, what was said earlier in the commentary—'and because it is shown above as the fourth path, it is fitting'—should be seen as well-stated.

Tassa codanatthāyāti tassa brāhmaṇassa bhagavā attano codanatthāya “puccha maṃ tvaṃ brāhmaṇa yadettha tayā manasābhisamīhita”nti codanāya, okāsadānatthāyāti adhippāyo. Desanāsannissayo brāhmaṇassa tathārūpo ettha ajjhāsayopi natthīti yathāvuttaanusandhittayavinimuttattā “pāṭiyekkaṃ anusandhiṃ āhā”ti vuttaṃ. Cittagatattā abbhantarena. Kilesavuṭṭhānasinānenāti kilesamalapavāhanena rāgapariḷāhādivūpasamakarena ca aṭṭhaṅgikaariyamaggasalilasinānena.

'For the purpose of prompting him' means that the Blessed One's intention was to prompt that brahmin by saying, 'Ask me, brahmin, whatever you have in mind here,' for the purpose of granting an opportunity. Since the brahmin had no such reliance on the teaching here, nor such a disposition, and because it is free from the threefold connection as previously explained, it is said, 'He spoke a single connection.' 'Internal' is due to its being a mental state. 'By the bathing that is emergence from defilements' means by the bathing in the water of the noble eightfold path, which washes away the stain of defilements and calms the fever of lust and so on.

79. Dhammasabhāmaṇḍapaṃ tāvadeva upagatattā bāhukā nadito āgataṃ viya maññamāno. Ariyaphalamaddanacuṇṇādayo telasinehassa vivecanena[M 1.0281]. Lūkhabhāvo lokaṃ, taṃ etissā atthīti lokāti sammatā. Lokkhasammataggahaṇena “tathā sā nadī loke pākaṭā”ti evaṃ pavattaṃ attano micchāgāhaṃ dīpeti. Tenāha “visuddhabhāvaṃ detīti evaṃ sammatā”ti. Pāpapavāhanena samparāyikādisampattiāvahato lokassa hitā lokyā. Lokyāti sammatāti sabbaṃ purimasadisaṃ. Tenāha “seṭṭhaṃ lokaṃ gamayatīti evaṃ sammatā”ti. Puññasammatāti pujjabhavaphalanibbattanena sattānaṃ punanena visodhanena puññāti sammatā. Tadatthadīpanatthamevāti tassā pubbe āgatadesanāya atthadīpanatthameva. Vuttassevatthassa puna dīpanaṃ kimatthiyanti āha “gāthārucikāna”nti. Cuṇṇikavacanaṃ asambhāventā tathā ca vutte atthamabujjhanakā pajjavacanaṃ sambhāventā tathā ca vutte bujjhanakā gāthārucikā. Visesatthadīpanatthanti visiṭṭhadīpanatthaṃ, purimadesanāya aññadīpanatthanti attho.

79. Having just arrived at the Dhamma assembly hall, he imagined himself as if he had come from the Bāhukā River. By the separation of the oil-like defilements with the rubbing powder of the noble fruit and so on. The state of coarseness is 'loka'; because this [river] possesses that, it is considered 'Lokā'. By grasping the conventional understanding of 'lokkha', he reveals his own wrong view that 'that river is thus renowned in the world.' Therefore, he says, 'It is considered so because it gives purity.' Because it washes away evil and brings about success in the next life, etc., and is beneficial to the world, it is 'lokyā'. 'It is considered Lokyā'—all this is similar to the preceding. Therefore, he says, 'It is considered so because it leads to the best world.' 'It is considered puñña' because by producing the fruit of a praiseworthy existence and by purifying beings again and again, it is 'puñña'. 'For the purpose of clarifying that meaning' means solely for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the teaching that came before. To the question, 'For what purpose is there a repeated clarification of the meaning already stated?' he says, 'for those fond of verses.' Those who do not appreciate prose but appreciate and understand verse when it is spoken are 'those fond of verses.' 'For the purpose of clarifying a special meaning' means for the purpose of clarifying a distinct meaning; the sense is for the purpose of clarifying something different from the previous teaching.

“Gacchati pana bhavaṃ gotamo bāhukaṃ nadiṃ sināyitu”nti (ma. ni. 1.78) heṭṭhā vuttattā [V 1.0250] bāhukanti idameva ettha tadatthadīpakaṃ. Sesāni adhikakkādivacanāni tato visiṭṭhassa atthassa bodhanato visesatthadīpakāni. Kasmā panettha bhagavatā brāhmaṇena avuttāni adhikakkādīni gahitānīti āha “yatheva hī”tiādi. Kakkanti nhānapiṇḍaṃ adhippetaṃ, nhāyitvā adhikaṃ kakkaṃ ettha gaṇhantīti adhikakkaṃ. Tenāha “nhānasambhāravasenā”tiādi. Maṇḍalavāpisaṇṭhānanti vaṭṭapokkharaṇīsaṇṭhānaṃ. Nadiyoti visuṃ nadiyo, na adhikakkādīni viya titthamattaṃ.

Because it was stated previously, 'Does the Venerable Gotama go to the Bāhukā River to bathe?' (MN 1.78), the word 'Bāhukā' itself here clarifies that meaning. The remaining words, 'Adhikakka,' etc., are clarifiers of a special meaning because they make known a meaning more specific than that. To the question, 'Why here did the Blessed One take up 'Adhikakka,' etc., which were not spoken by the brahmin?' he says, 'Just as indeed,' etc. 'Kakka' is intended to mean a bathing-lump; because after bathing they take an extra 'kakka' here, it is 'Adhikakka.' Therefore, he says, 'in terms of bathing preparations,' etc. 'Of the shape of a circular reservoir' means of the shape of a round lotus pond. 'Rivers' means separate rivers, not merely a bathing place like Adhikakka, etc.

Tīhi padehīti sundarikāpayāgabāhukāpadehi. Cattārīti adhikakkādīni cattāri. Vuttāneva hontīti lokasammatālakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇatā brāhmaṇassa adhippāyena, paramatthato pana pāpapavāhalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. Tenāha “tasmā”tiādi. Kiñci pāpasuddhiṃ na karontiyeva. Na hi naṃ sodhayeti naṃ puggalaṃ na sodhaye. Verakibbisabhāvaṃ appattā nāma kammapathabhāvaṃ appattā. Tenāha “khuddakehī”ti.

'By the three terms' refers to the terms Sundarikā, Payāga, and Bāhukā. 'Four' refers to the four beginning with Adhikakka. 'They are indeed spoken of'—the brahmin's intention is oneness of characteristic by way of worldly convention, but in an ultimate sense, it is because of the oneness of characteristic by way of washing away evil. Therefore, he says, 'Therefore,' etc. 'They do not bring about any purification from evil at all.' 'It does not purify him' means it does not purify that person. 'Not having attained the state of enmity and sin' means not having reached the state of a course of action. Hence, it is said, 'By small things.'

Paṭihanantoti ayuttabhāvadassanena taṃ diṭṭhiṃ paṭibāhanto. Tatthāyaṃ paṭibāhanavidhi yathā yaṃ kiñci udakorohanaṃ na pāpapavāhanaṃ, evaṃ [M 1.0282] yo koci nakkhattayogo pāpahetūnaṃ paṭipakkhābhāvato. Yañhi vināseti, so tassa paṭipakkho. Yathā āloko andhakārassa vijjā ca avijjāya, na evaṃ udakorohanaṃ nakkhattayogo vā pāpahetūnaṃ lobhādīnaṃ paṭipakkho, tasmā niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ “na udakorohanādi pāpapavāhana”nti. Niccaṃ phaggunīnakkhattanti suddhasīlādikassa sabbakālaṃ maṅgaladivaso evāti adhippāyo. Itaroti sīlādivasena asuddho. Niccameva uposatho ariyuposathena upavutthabhāvato. Suddhassāti parisuddhamanosamācārassa. Sucikammassāti parisuddhakāyavacīsamācārassa. Tenāha “nikkilesatāyā”tiādi. Kusalūpasañhitanti anavajjabhāvūpagataṃ. Vatasamādānanti dhutadhammasamādānādi sampannameva hoti, nāssa vipatti atthīti attho. Mama sāsaneyeva sināhi, yadi accantameva suddhiṃ icchasīti adhippāyo. Tenāha “sace”tiādi. Khematanti khemabhāvaṃ. Yathā sabbabhūtāni tapavasena khemappattāni abhayappattāni honti, evaṃ karohīti taṃ heṭṭhā dassitaṃ mettādibhāvanaṃ brāhmaṇassa saṅkhepena upadisantenassa ekaccasamādhisampadā tadavinābhāvinī paññāsampadā ca dassitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha “manodvārasuddhi dassitā”ti.

"Rejecting" means repelling that view by seeing its unsuitability. Here is the method of repulsion: just as no immersion in water is a washing away of evil, so too is no conjunction of constellations, as it is not an antidote to the causes of evil. For whatever destroys something is its antidote. Just as light is the antidote to darkness and knowledge to ignorance, immersion in water or a conjunction of constellations is not an antidote to the causes of evil, such as greed. Therefore, the conclusion must be reached here: 'Immersion in water and so on does not wash away evil.' 'Always the Phaggunī constellation' means that for one of pure virtue and so on, every day is an auspicious day—this is the intention. 'The other' refers to one who is impure in terms of virtue and so on. 'Always the Uposatha' means it is constant because one has observed the Noble Uposatha. 'Of one who is pure' refers to one whose mental conduct is thoroughly purified. 'Of one with pure deeds' refers to one whose bodily and verbal conduct are thoroughly purified. Hence it is said: 'because of being without defilements,' etc. 'Connected with the wholesome' means having attained a state of blamelessness. 'The undertaking of vows' means one is endowed with the undertaking of ascetic practices and the like; there is no failure for him—this is the meaning. 'Bathe only in my teaching, if you truly desire ultimate purity'—this is the intention. Hence it is said: 'If,' etc. 'Safety' means the state of safety. 'Just as all beings, through asceticism, attain safety and fearlessness, so should you do.' By briefly instructing the brahmin in the development of loving-kindness and so on, which was shown below, it should be understood that a certain accomplishment of concentration and the wisdom inseparable from it were shown to him. Hence it is said: 'the purity of the mind-door is shown.'

Tassa pana sampadādvayassa nissayabhūtaṃ sīlasampadaṃ dassetuṃ “sace musā na bhaṇasī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha ca yathā “sace musā na bhaṇasī”tiādinā musāvāda-pāṇātipāta-adinnādāna-paṭivirativacanena [V 1.0251] avasesakāyavacīduccaritaviratīpi vuttā eva hoti lakkhaṇahāranayena, evaṃ “saddahāno amaccharī”ti saddhādidhanasampadāniyojaneneva avasesaariyadhanasampadāniyojanampi siddhameva hotīti saddhādayo vimuttiparipācanīyadhammā brāhmaṇassa pakāsitā evāti veditabbā. Tenevāha “imāya eva paṭipattiyā kilesasuddhī”ti. Gayā sammatatarā bāhukādīhipīti adhippāyo.

To show the accomplishment of virtue, the foundation of those two accomplishments, it is said, 'If one does not speak falsely,' and so on. Here, just as by the words 'If one does not speak falsely,' and so on, which speak of abstaining from false speech, killing, and taking what is not given, the remaining abstinences from bodily and verbal misconduct are also stated by way of the method of characteristic inclusion, so too by the application of the accomplishment of the wealth of faith and so on, the application of the remaining noble wealth is also established. Therefore, it should be understood that faith and the other qualities conducive to the ripening of liberation are indeed declared to the brahmin. Hence it is said, 'By this very practice is the purification of defilements.' The intention is that Gayā is more highly regarded than the Bāhukā and so on.

80. Ekoti asahāyo, esā panassa asahāyatā ekībhāvenāti. Na hissa tāva taṇhādutiyatā vigatā. Tenevāha “na cirassevā”tiādi. Ekaggahaṇeneva kāyena vūpakaṭṭhatā vuttāti āha “vupakaṭṭho cittavivekenā”ti. Tena “divā caṅkamena nisajjāyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.423; 3.75; vibha. 519; mahāni. 161) āgataṃ jāgariyānuyogamāha. Tathābhūtassa cassa [M 1.0283] ekādasahi aggīhi āditte tayo bhave passato yathā pamādassa lesopi nāhosi, evaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ brūhento sammadeva padahati. Katthaci saṅkhāragate anapekkhacitto nibbānādhimutto eva vihāsīti dassetuṃ “appamatto”tiādi vuttaṃ. Khīṇā jātītiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

80. "Alone" means without a companion; this state of being without a companion is through solitude. For the craving that makes a second has not yet departed from him. Therefore it is said, "not long after," etc. By the very mention of 'alone,' bodily seclusion is stated, and he says, 'secluded through mental seclusion.' Therefore, he speaks of the devotion to wakefulness, as found in "walking and sitting by day," etc. For one thus abiding, seeing the three realms of existence ablaze with the eleven fires, just as there is not even a trace of negligence, so, developing the meditation subject, he rightly strives. To show that in a certain way, with a mind unconcerned with conditioned things, resolved only on Nibbāna, he dwells—hence the phrase "heedful," etc., is stated. What should be said regarding "destroyed is birth," etc., has already been stated previously. The rest is easily understood.

Vatthasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The elucidation of the subtle meaning in the commentary on the Vatthasutta is complete.

8. Sallekhasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Sallekha Sutta

81. “Cundo”ti [V 1.0252] tassa mahātherassa nāmaṃ, pūjāvasena pana mahācundoti vuccati yathā “mahāmoggallāno”ti. Attano vā cundaṃ nāma bhāgineyyattheraṃ upādāya āyasmato sāriputtattherassa bhātā ayaṃ mahāthero “mahācundo”ti paññāyittha yathā “mahāpanthako”ti. Sāyanhasamayanti bhummatthe ekaṃ upayogavacananti āha “sāyanhakāle”ti. Na hettha accanta saṃyogo sambhavatīti. Sattasaṅkhārehīti saddhivihārikaantevāsikaupāsakādisattehi ceva rūpārammaṇādisaṅkhārehi ca. Paṭinivattitvāti apasakkitvā. Nilīyananti vivecanaṃ kāyacittehi tato vivittatā. Ekībhāvoti hi kāyavivekamāha, pavivekoti cittavivekaṃ. Tato vuṭṭhitoti tato duvidhavivekato bhavaṅguppattiyā, sabrahmacārīhi samāgamena ca apeto. Abhivādāpetvāti abhivādaṃ kāretvā. Evanti yathāvuttaabhivādavasena. Paggayhāti unnāmetvā. Anupacchinnabhavamūlānaṃ tāva evaṃ abhivādo hotu, ucchinnabhavamūlānaṃ kimatthiyoti āha “etaṃ āciṇṇaṃ tathāgatāna”nti. Tena na tathāgatā samparāyikaṃyeva sattānaṃ sukhaṃ āsīsanti, atha kho diṭṭhadhammikampīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kasmā evaṃ tathāgatā abhivadantīti tattha kāraṇamāha “sukhakāmā hī”tiādi. Puthukāyāti bahū sattakāyā. Yakkhāti devā. Te hi pūjanīyatāya “yakkhā”ti vuccanti. Abhivadantīti āsīsitamevatthaṃ ñāṇakaruṇāhi abhimukhaṃ katvā vadanti.

81. "Cunda" is the name of that great elder; however, out of respect, he is called "Mahācunda," just as "Mahāmoggallāna." Alternatively, this great elder, the brother of Venerable Sāriputta, became known as "Mahācunda" with reference to his nephew, the elder named Cunda, just as "Mahāpanthaka." "Sāyanhasamayaṃ" (in the evening) is a locative expression for a single occasion, hence he says "sāyanhakāle" (at evening time). For here, a continuous connection is not possible. "Sattasaṅkhārehi" (with beings and formations) refers to beings such as co-residents, pupils, lay followers, etc., and also to formations such as visible objects, etc. "Paṭinivattitvā" (having turned back) means having retreated. "Nilīyanaṃ" (withdrawn) is seclusion, being separate from that with body and mind. For "ekībhāvo" (solitude) refers to bodily seclusion, and "paviveko" (seclusion) refers to mental seclusion. "Tato vuṭṭhito" (having emerged from that) means having departed from that twofold seclusion by the arising of the life-continuum and by meeting with fellow practitioners. "Abhivādāpetvā" (having had respects paid) means having caused respect to be paid. "Evaṃ" (thus) means in the manner of paying respects as described. "Paggayha" (held up) means having raised. For those whose roots of existence are not yet cut off, such a salutation is fitting; but what is its purpose for those whose roots of existence are cut off? Hence it is said, "this is the custom of the Tathāgatas." Therefore, it should be seen that the Tathāgatas do not merely wish for the happiness of beings in the next life, but also in this very life. Why do the Tathāgatas salute in this way? The reason is stated there: "for they desire happiness," etc. "Puthukāyā" (multitudes) means many groups of beings. "Yakkhā" (yakkhas) means deities. They are called "yakkhas" because they are worthy of worship. "Abhivadanti" (they salute) means they speak for the very purpose of blessing, facing them with knowledge and compassion.

Yāti aniyamato gahitā niyamato dassento “imā”ti āha. Imāti ca āsannapaccakkhavacananti āha “abhimukhaṃ karonto viyā”ti[M 1.0284], taṃ taṃ diṭṭhigatikaṃ cittagataṃ sammukhā viya karontoti attho. Diṭṭhiyoti purimapadalopena pāḷiyaṃ vuttanti dassento “micchādiṭṭhiyo”ti āha. Sattesu diṭṭhigatacittuppādesu uppajjamānā, sattesu vā visayabhūtesu ārabbha uppajjamānā “sattesu pātubhavantī”ti vuttā. Attavādenāti attānaṃ ārabbha pavattena vacanena. Paṭisaṃyuttāti “atthi attā”ti gāhe gāhaṇe ca visayabhāvena paṭisaṃyuttā. Diṭṭhigatikena diṭṭhiṃ gāhantehi gahaṇe gāhāpaṇe ca diṭṭhi diṭṭhivādassa visayoti tena paṭisaṃyuttā nāma hoti. “Atthi attā”ti evaṃ pavattā diṭṭhi idha attavādapaṭisaṃyuttā, na tassā visayabhūto attā. Sā ca visayabhāvato tathāpavattena vādena paṭisaṃyuttā. Lokavādappaṭisaṃyuttāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Vīsati bhavanti tato paraṃ attavādavatthuno abhāvā[V 1.0253].
