Pañcapi hi upādānakkhandhe paccekaṃ “attā”ti te ca attano nissayabhāvena gaṇhato etāsaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ sambhavo, tabbinimutto panāyaṃ visayo attaggahaṇākāro ca natthīti. Sassato attā ca loko cāti rūpādīsu aññataraṃ “attā”ti, “loko”ti vā gahetvā taṃ sassato sabbakālabhāvī nicco dhuvoti. Yathāha “rūpī attā ceva loko ca sassato cāti attānañca lokañca paññapetī”tiādi. Sassatotiādīsu paṭhamo sassatavādavasena attaggāho, dutiyo ucchedavādavasena, tatiyo ekaccasassatavādavasena, catuttho takkīvādavasena pavatto, amarāvikkhepavasena vā pavatto attaggāho. Antavāti attano paricchedatāvasena. Anantavāti aparicchedatāvasena. Antavā ca anantavā cāti tadubhayavasena, itaro takkīvādavasena pavatto attaggāho. Evaṃ pavattattā aṭṭha hontīti yojanā.

Showing those which are taken indefinitely as definite, he says 'these'. And because 'these' is a word for what is near and directly perceived, he says 'as if making it face-to-face'; the meaning is as if making that particular view-inclined state of mind present before one. Showing that 'views' is stated in the Pāli by eliding the preceding word, he says 'wrong views'. They are said to 'appear in beings' because they arise in beings when mind-states inclined to views arise, or because they arise in relation to beings as their objects. 'With self-theory' means by speech that proceeds in relation to the self. 'Connected' means connected by way of being an object in the grasping and the causing to grasp of the view 'there is a self'. When those with a tendency for views grasp a view, in the grasping and in the causing to grasp, the view is the object of the theory; thus it is called 'connected' with it. Here, the view that proceeds as 'there is a self' is what is connected with the self-theory, not the self which is its object. And it is connected with the theory that proceeds thus because it is the object. The same method applies here also to 'connected to world-theory'. There are twenty, because beyond that there is no basis for a self-theory. For these views can arise when one grasps each of the five aggregates of clinging as 'self' and as one's own support. But apart from this, there is no such object or mode of grasping a self. 'The self and the world are eternal' means that, having grasped one of form and so on as 'self' or 'world', one holds it to be eternal, existing at all times, permanent, and stable. As it is said: 'He proclaims the self and the world, saying, "The self has form and the world is eternal,"' and so on. In 'eternal', and so on, the first is the grasping of self by way of eternalism; the second, by way of annihilationism; the third, by way of partial eternalism; the fourth is a grasping of self that proceeds by way of reasoning, or that proceeds by way of equivocation. 'Finite' means by way of the self's limitation. 'Infinite' means by way of its boundlessness. 'Both finite and infinite' means by way of both of these; the other is the grasping of self that proceeds by way of reasoning. Because they proceed in this way, there are eight—this is the connection.

Ādimevāti ādimanasikārameva. Taṃ pana sarūpato dassento “vipassanāmissakapaṭhamamanasikāramevā”ti āha. Appatvāpi sotāpattimagganti iminā avadhāraṇena nivattitaṃ dasseti. Nāmarūpaparicchedato pabhuti yāva udayabbayadassanaṃ, ayaṃ idha ādimanasikāroti adhippeto paññābhāvanāya ārambhabhāvato. Udayabbayānupassanāsahitatāya cassa vipassanāmissakatā vacanaṃ. Evanti imassa atthavacanaṃ “ettakeneva upāyenā”ti[M 1.0285], yathāvuttaādimanasikārenāti attho. Etāsanti yathāvuttānaṃ attavādalokavādapaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ. Kāmañca tāsaṃ tena tadaṅgavasena pahānaṃ hotiyeva, taṃ pana nādhippetaṃ, tasmā samucchedavasena pahānaṃ paṭinissaggo ca hotīti pucchati. Sabbaso samucchinnasaṃyojanatāya anadhimānikopi samāno. “Ariyadhammo adhigato”ti māno adhimāno, so yesaṃ atthi te adhimānikā, tesaṃ udayabbayañāṇādhigamena adhimānuppatti tadavasāno ca manasikāroti adhippeto. Tena diṭṭhīnaṃ pahānaṃ na hotīti kathāpanatthaṃ ayaṃ pucchāti āha “adhimānappahānatthaṃ pucchatī”ti. “Ādimeva nu kho…pe… paṭinissaggo hotī”ti anabhisametāvī viya vadanto adhimāne ṭhito viya hotīti āha “adhimāniko viya hutvā”ti. Soti thero. Tesaṃ atthāyāti tesaṃ attano antevāsikānaṃ bhagavatā etassa micchāgāhassa vivecanatthāya. Thero kira dhammasenāpati viya saddhiṃ attano antevāsikehi bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkami.

'Initial' means the initial attention itself. To show this in its true form, he says, 'the first attention mixed with insight.' By 'even without having attained the path of stream-entry,' this emphasis shows what is excluded. From the discernment of name-and-form up to the vision of rise and fall—this is what is meant here by 'initial attention,' because it is the starting point for the development of wisdom. And the statement 'mixed with insight' is due to its association with the contemplation of rise and fall. The explanation of 'thus' is 'by just this much as the means'; the meaning is, by the initial attention as described. 'Of these' refers to the aforementioned views connected with self-doctrine and world-doctrine. And although their abandonment does indeed occur by that means through substitution of opposites, that is not what is intended here. Therefore, he asks whether their abandonment and relinquishment occur through eradication. Although he was one without overestimation, due to having completely cut off the fetters, he asks as if he has it. The conceit, 'The noble Dhamma has been attained,' is overestimation. Those who have it are 'ones with overestimation'. It is intended that for them, the arising of overestimation occurs with the attainment of the knowledge of rise and fall, and their attention ends there. To establish the point that the abandonment of views does not occur by that, this question is asked; he says, 'he asks for the sake of abandoning overestimation.' Speaking as one who has not comprehended, saying, 'Does the initial…pe…relinquishment occur?', he is as one established in overestimation. Thus, he says, 'as if being one with overestimation.' 'He' means the elder. 'For their sake' means for the sake of his own disciples, so that the Blessed One might analyze this wrong grasp. The elder, it is said, like a general of the Dhamma, approached the Blessed One together with his own disciples.

82. Yatthāti visaye bhummaṃ. Diṭṭhīnañhi ārammaṇanidassanametanti. Yasmā diṭṭhīnaṃ anusayanabhūmipi samudācaraṇaṭṭhānampi khandhā eva, tasmā āha “yattha cetā diṭṭhiyo uppajjantī tiādi pañcakkhandhe sandhāya vutta”nti. Rūpaṃ abhinivissāti “idaṃ rūpaṃ mama attā”ti [V 1.0254] diṭṭhābhinivesavasena abhinivisitvā ārabbha. Abhinivisamānā eva hi diṭṭhi naṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjati. “So attā”tiādīsu yadidaṃ cakkhādisaṅgahaṃ rūpaṃ, sahabuddhinibandhanatāya so me attā, sukhāsukhaṃ ettha lokiyatīti so loko. “Soevāhaṃ pecca paraloke bhavissāmīti tathābhāvena nicco, thirabhāvena dhuvo, sabbadābhāvitāya sassato, nibbikāratāya avipariṇāmadhammoti attho. Yadi pañcakkhandhe sandhāya vuttaṃ, kathamekavacananti āha “ārammaṇavasenā”tiādi. Nānā karīyati etenāti nānākaraṇaṃ, viseso. Jātivasenāti uppattivasena. Ye hi anibbattapubbā samānāvatthā, te uppādasaṅkhātavikārasamaṅgitāya uppajjantīti samaññaṃ labhanti. Tenāha “jātivasenā”tiādi. Punappunaṃ āsevitāti anādimati saṃsāre aparāparuppattiyā laddhāsevanā. Etena kilesānaṃ bhāvanaṭṭhena anusayatthaṃ viseseti[M 1.0286]. Thāmagatāti thāmabhāvaṃ upagatā. Etena anusaye sabhāvato dasseti. Thāmagamananti ca kāmarāgādīnaṃ anaññasādhāraṇo sabhāvo. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “thāmagato anusaye pajahatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.21). Appaṭivinītāti samucchedavinayavasena na paṭivinītā. Appahīnā hi thāmagatā kilesā anusentīti vuccanti. Etena tesaṃ kāraṇalābhe sati uppajjanārahataṃ dasseti. Samudācarantīti abhibhavanti. Etena tesaṃ vītikkamappattataṃ dasseti. Uppajjantīti pana imināva pariyuṭṭhānāvatthā dassitā.

82. 'Where' is a locative in the sense of a sphere. For this is a designation of the object of views. Since the aggregates themselves are both the ground for the latent tendencies of views and the place of their manifestation, he therefore says: 'Where these views arise,' and so on, is stated with reference to the five aggregates. 'Having adhered to form' means having adhered by way of adherence to views, thinking, 'This form is my self,' and taking it as a basis. For a view arises only when, while adhering, it takes that as its object. In 'That is the self,' and so on: that which is the collection of forms, such as the eye, is 'my self' due to its connection with co-arising cognition; that wherein pleasure and pain are experienced is 'the world'. 'I will be the same after death in the next world'—the meaning is that by being thus it is permanent, by its firmness it is stable, by its always-existing nature it is eternal, by its unalterable nature it is of an immutable dhamma. If this is stated with reference to the five aggregates, how is it in the singular? He says, 'By way of the object,' and so on. That by which one differentiates is 'differentiation', a distinction. 'By way of birth' means by way of arising. For those things that have not arisen before and are in a similar state acquire a designation when they arise, being endowed with the alteration called 'arising'. Therefore, he says, 'By way of birth,' and so on. 'Repeatedly cultivated' means that in beginningless saṃsāra, through successive rebirths, they have acquired cultivation. By this, he specifies the meaning of 'latent tendency' in the sense of the cultivation of defilements. 'Having become strong' means having attained a state of strength. By this, he shows the latent tendencies in their own nature. And 'becoming strong' is the particular nature of sensual desire and so on, not shared by others. For so it is said: 'One abandons the latent tendencies that have become strong' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.21). 'Not disciplined' means not disciplined by way of eradication. For it is the defilements that have become strong and are not abandoned that are said to 'lie latent'. By this, he shows their capability of arising when a cause is obtained. 'They manifest' means they overwhelm. By this, he shows that they have reached the state of transgression. And by this very word 'they arise', the state of obsession is shown.

Taṃ pañcakkhandhappabhedaṃ ārammaṇanti yaṃ taṃ “yattha cetā diṭṭhiyo uppajjantī”tiādinā vuttaṃ rūpupādānakkhandhādipañcakkhandhapabhedaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. Etaṃ mayhaṃ na hotīti etaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ mayhaṃ santakaṃ na hoti mama kiñcanapalibodhabhāvena gahetabbatāya abhāvato. Tenassa paramatthato taṇhāvatthubhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati tāvakālikādibhāvato. Ahampi eso na asmīti eso pañcakkhandhapabhedo ahampi na asmi, ahanti so gahetabbo na hotīti attho. Etenassa mānavatthubhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati aniccadukkhajegucchādibhāvato. Eso me attāpi na hoti attasabhāvassa tattha abhāvato mamañcassa kiñcanapalibodhabhāvena gahetabbatāya abhāvato.

That division into the five aggregates is the object. This is what was stated in 'where these views arise,' and so on, namely, that the division into the five aggregates, such as the form aggregate subject to clinging, is the object of views. 'This is not mine' means this fivefold aggregate is not my possession, because it is not to be taken as my possession or encumbrance. By this, he rejects its status as an object of craving in an ultimate sense, due to its temporary nature, and so on. 'I am not this' means this division into the five aggregates is not I; the meaning is that it should not be taken as 'I.' By this, he rejects its status as an object of conceit, due to its being impermanent, suffering, repulsive, and so on. 'This is not my self' means this is not my self because the nature of a self is absent therein, and because it is not to be taken as my possession or encumbrance.

Taṇhāva mamanti gaṇhāti etenāti taṇhāgāho. Taṃ gaṇhantoti taṃ uppādento. Tenāha “taṇhāpapañcaṃ gaṇhātī”ti. Papañceti santānaṃ vitthārento satte saṃsāre cirāyatīti papañco. Yathā vuttapabhedanti aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritapabhedaṃ. Taṇhāpapañcaṃ paṭikkhipati khandhapañcakassa taṇhāvatthukābhāvavibhāvanenāti adhippāyo. Parato padadvayepi eseva nayo. Diṭṭhekaṭṭhāti diṭṭhiyā [V 1.0255] pahānekaṭṭhā. Tena tesaṃ paṭhamamaggavajjhataṃ dasseti. Sahajekaṭṭhā pana diṭṭhiyā taṇhā eva, na māno, sā ca kho apāyagamanīyā. Yathā atthīti yena aniccadukkhāsubhānattākārena atthi, tathā passanto yathābhūtaṃ passati nāma. Tenāha “khandhapañcakañhī”tiādi. Eteneva ākārenāti ruppanādianiccādiākāreneva. Gayhamānampi appahīnavipallāsehi. Tenākārenāti “etaṃ mama”ntiādiākārena. Nevatthi yathābhūtadassanavipallāsānaṃ [M 1.0287] tadabhāvato. Suṭṭhu passantassāti yathā puna tathā na passitabbaṃ, evaṃ suṭṭhu sātisayaṃ passantassa.

Craving grasps 'mine' by this; thus it is the grasping of craving. Grasping it means producing it. Therefore, it is said, 'It grasps the proliferation of craving.' Proliferation means that which extends the continuity, causing beings to linger long in saṃsāra; thus it is proliferation. 'As previously classified' refers to the classification of the one hundred and eight modes of craving's wandering. The meaning is that it rejects the proliferation of craving by demonstrating that the five aggregates are not an object for craving. The same principle applies to the next two phrases. 'Having a single foundation with view' means having a single foundation for abandonment with view. Thus, it shows that these are to be destroyed by the first path. However, that which has a co-arisen single foundation with view is craving itself, not conceit, and it leads to the lower realms. 'As it is' means that one who sees in the way that it exists—that is, in the mode of impermanence, suffering, unattractiveness, and not-self—sees as it really is. Therefore it is said, 'the five aggregates indeed,' and so on. 'In this very way' means in the very mode of impermanence, etc., such as being afflicted. Even when grasped, it is by those whose distortions are not abandoned. 'In that way' means in the mode of 'this is mine,' and so on. It does not exist in that way, because for one who sees things as they really are, those distortions are absent. 'For one who sees thoroughly' means for one who sees so thoroughly, so exceedingly, that it is not to be seen in that way again.

Na ādimanasikāreneva diṭṭhippahānaṃ hoti, adhimānikānaṃ pana adhimānamattametaṃ dassanaṃ. Maggeneva taṃ hotīti imamatthaṃ vibhāvento “sotāpattimaggena diṭṭhippahānaṃ dassetvā”ti āha. Vibhajantoti adhimānikānaṃ jhānāni asallekhabhāvena vibhajanto. Bālaputhujjanānaṃ neva uppajjati akārakabhāvato. Na ariyasāvakānaṃ pahīnādhimānapaccayattā. Na aṭṭhānaniyojako sappāyakammaṭṭhāneyeva niyojanato.

The abandoning of wrong view does not occur by mere initial attention; for the conceited, however, this seeing is merely a matter of conceit. Explaining this meaning—that it occurs only by the Path—he said, 'Having shown the abandoning of wrong view by the path of stream-entry...' 'Analyzing' means analyzing the jhānas of the conceited as being without purification. For foolish worldlings, it does not arise because they are non-doers. For noble disciples, it does not arise because the condition for conceit has been abandoned. He is not one who directs to an unsuitable place, as he directs only to suitable meditation subjects.

Thero “yadatthaṃ saṅgho pakkosati, so attho tattha vāsīnaṃ āgatāgatānaṃ idha ijjhatī”ti taṃ udikkhanto saṅghena yāvatatiyaṃ pahitopi na gato na agāravena. Tenāha “kimeta”ntiādi. Paṇḍito hi tattha attano kiccameva karotīti aññataraṃ vuḍḍhapabbajitaṃ pāhesi. Kimetanti saṅghassa āṇāya akaraṇaṃ nāma kimetanti karaṇe ādaraṃ dīpento evamāha. Saṭṭhivassātītoti appatte pattasaññī eva saṭṭhivassātīto. Yasmā pesalā pesalehi saddhiṃ saṃsandanti samānādhimuttitāya, tasmā thero “sādhāvuso”ti vatvā hatthimāpanādiṃ sabbaṃ akāsi.

The elder, considering, 'The purpose for which the Sangha summons is fulfilled here for those who have come and are dwelling there,' did not go, even when sent for by the Sangha up to the third time; this was not out of disrespect. Therefore, he (the summoner) said, 'What is this?' and so on. Thinking, 'Indeed, a wise person there performs only his own duty,' he sent a certain senior monk. 'What is this?' means, 'What is this, this not acting upon the Sangha's command?' He spoke thus, showing earnestness in the matter. 'One who has passed sixty years' means one who has passed sixty years while perceiving attainment in what is not attained. Because the virtuous associate with the virtuous due to having the same inclination, the elder said, 'Very well, friend,' and did everything, including the measuring of the elephant.

Tādisovāti anantaraṃ vuttattherasadisova appatte pattasaññī eva saṭṭhivassātītoti attho. Padumagumbanti kamalasaṇḍaṃ. Pāsādaṃ pāvisi vissaṭṭhaṃ olokanenassa puthujjanabhāvo attanāva paññāyissatīti. Tissamahāvihāre kira therā bhikkhū tadā “sakacittaṃ pasīdatī”ti vacanaṃ pūjentā kālasseva cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ sammajjitvā ettakārammaṇameva buddhārammaṇapītiṃ uppādetvā divase divase tathā karonti. Tena vuttaṃ “tasmiñca samaye”tiādi. “Dhammadinna, idha pattacīvaraṃ ṭhapetī”ti vattāpi paṭisanthāravasena kiñci pucchitāpi nāhosi. Guṇaṃ jānātīti nimujjanādīsu vivaradānādinā guṇaṃ jānāti viya. Tumhe pana na jānittha āgantukavattassapi akaraṇato. Satthuāṇāvilaṅghinī kīdisī sā saṅghassa [V 1.0256] katikā? Katikā ca nāma sikkhāpadāvirodhena anuvattetabbā, ettakampi ajānantehi me saṃvāso natthīti ākāse abbhukkami.

'He is just like that' means he was similar to the elder mentioned immediately before, one who has passed sixty years while perceiving attainment in what is not attained. 'A lotus thicket' means a cluster of lotuses. He entered the palace, thinking, 'By his unrestrained gaze, his status as a worldling will become evident by itself.' It is said that at the Tissamahāvihāra, the elder monks at that time, honoring the saying, 'One's own mind becomes serene,' would sweep the cetiya courtyard early in the morning and, with just that as their object, would arouse joy with the Buddha as their object, doing so day after day. Therefore, it is said, 'And at that time,' and so on. Even though she said, 'Dhammadinna, place the bowl and robe here,' no one asked her anything by way of a friendly welcome. 'Knows virtue' means as if one knows virtue by giving an opening for fault-finding in matters such as immersion. 'But you did not know,' because of not performing even the duties toward a guest. 'What kind of Sangha agreement is this that transgresses the Teacher's command? An agreement, indeed, should be followed without contradicting the training rules. I will not live in communion with those who do not know even this much.' And so, she rose up into the sky.

Yaṃ [M 1.0288] tassa evamassa sallekhena viharāmīti yo “paṭhamajjhānaṃ upasampajja vihareyyā”ti vutto, tassa bhikkhuno yaṃ “paṭhamajjhānasaṅkhātaṃ paṭipattividhānaṃ kilese sallekhati, tena sallekhena ahaṃ viharāmī”ti adhimānavasena evamassa evaṃ bhaveyya ṭhānametaṃ vijjatīti evamettha sambandho veditabbo. Taṃ na yujjatīti taṃ adhimānikassa “yathāvibhaṅgaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ sallekho”ti parivitakkitaṃ na yujjati yuttaṃ na hoti. Tenāha “na hī”tiādi. Tattha sammā sabbaso ca kilese likhatīti sallekho, ariyamaggo. Tadupāyavipassanā sallekhapaṭipadā. Yaṃ pana jhānaṃ vipassanāpādakaṃ, tampi jhānaṃ pariyāyena maggapādakaṃ hotiyeva. Tenāha “avipassanāpādakattā”tiādi.

The connection here should be understood thus: for that bhikkhu of whom it is said, 'He should enter and dwell in the first jhāna,' the thought might arise out of conceit, 'I dwell by means of effacement.' He might think, 'The mode of practice designated as the first jhāna effaces the defilements; by that effacement I dwell.' This possibility exists. 'That is not proper' means that for the conceited one, the thought, 'According to the Vibhaṅga, the first jhāna is effacement,' is not proper; it is not fitting. Therefore, it is said, 'For it is not,' and so on. Here, that which rightly and completely effaces the defilements is called 'effacement' (sallekha); this is the Noble Path. The insight that is the means to it is the practice of effacement. However, a jhāna that serves as a basis for insight also indirectly serves as a basis for the path. Hence, it is said, 'Because it does not serve as a basis for insight,' and so on.

Jhānadhammavasenāti vitakkādipañcakajjhānadhammavasena. Cittuppādavasena anekavāraṃ pavattamānampi jhānaṃ ekāvajjanatāya ekavīthipariyāpannattā ekā samāpatti evāti “punappunaṃ samāpattivasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Cattāri arūpajjhānāni yathāsakaṃ ekekasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe pavattantīti āha “ārammaṇabhedābhāvato”ti. Purimakāraṇadvayavasenevāti “jhānadhammavasena, punappunaṃ samāpattivasenā”ti pubbe vuttappakārakāraṇadvayavaseneva.

'By way of jhāna factors' means by way of the five jhāna factors beginning with initial application. Although the jhāna occurs repeatedly by way of mind-arisings, because it is comprised within a single cognitive process due to a single adverting, it is just a single attainment; thus, it is said, 'by way of repeated attainment.' He said that the four formless jhānas each occur with only a single object respectively; hence, it is said, 'due to the absence of differentiation of object.' 'By way of the two former reasons' means by way of the two kinds of reasons previously stated, namely, 'by way of jhāna factors' and 'by way of repeated attainment.'

Tesaṃ arūpajjhānānaṃ kilesapariḷāhābhāvena nibbutāni aṅgāni, bhāvanāvisesavasena sukhumāni ārammaṇāni. Tasmā tānīti tesaṃ vasena tāni jhānāni santāni, tasmā “santā ete vihārā”ti vuttaṃ. Tesaṃ catunnampīti catunnampi tesaṃ arūpajjhānānaṃ.

For those formless jhānas, the factors are stilled due to the absence of the fever of the defilements, and the objects are subtle due to the excellence of the development. Therefore, 'those' (tāni): by means of them, those jhānas are peaceful (santāni); therefore, it is said, 'these are peaceful abidings.' 'Of those four' means of all four of those formless jhānas.

83. Soti adhimāniko bhikkhu, añño vā ito bāhirako tāpasaparibbājakādiko na hi sammasati. Tattha adhimāniko appatte pattasaññitāya na sammasati, itaro avisayatāya. Yatthāti yasmiṃ sallekhavatthusmiṃ, avihiṃsakatādīhi catucattālīsāya ākārehi.

83. 'He' means a conceited bhikkhu, or some other outsider such as an ascetic or wanderer, for he does not comprehend. Among them, the conceited one does not comprehend due to perceiving attainment in what is not attained; the other does not comprehend because it is not his domain. 'Wherein' means in that basis for effacement, in forty-four modes beginning with non-harming.

Aṭṭha samāpattiyo nāma kilesānaṃ vikkhambhanavasena pavattā uttaruttari santapaṇītā dhammā, na tathā lokiyā avihiṃsādayo. Tattha kathaṃ avihiṃsādayo eva sallekhabhāvena vuttā, na itarāti imamatthaṃ vibhāvento codako “kasmā panā”tiādimāha. Itaro kāmaṃ samāpattiyo [V 1.0257][M 1.0289] santapaṇītasabhāvā, vaṭṭapādakatāya pana kilesānaṃ sallekhapaṭipadā na honti, avihiṃsādayo pana vivaṭṭapādakā sallekhapaṭipadāti imamatthaṃ vibhāvento “lokuttarapādakattā”tiādimāha. Imināyeva aṭṭhasamāpattīhi avihiṃsādīnaṃ visesadīpakena suttena yathā mahapphalataraṃ hoti, taṃ pakārajātaṃ veditabbaṃ. Idañhi dakkhiṇeyyataratāya dakkhiṇāya mahapphalatarataṃ sandhāya vuttanti sambandho. Nanu tattha “sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanno”ti āgataṃ, na “saraṇagato”ti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “saraṇagamanato paṭṭhāyā”tiādi. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.379) “heṭṭhimakoṭiyā tisaraṇaṃ gato upāsakopi sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanno nāmā”ti. Yo hi vaṭṭadukkhaṃ samatikkamitukāmo pasannacitto ratanattayaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchati, tassa taṃ adhisīlādīnaṃ upanissayo hutvā anukkamena dassanamaggādhigamāya saṃvatteyyāti.

The eight attainments are states that proceed by way of suppressing the defilements, being progressively more peaceful and refined; not so are the mundane states of non-harming and so on. In this regard, explaining the meaning of how non-harming and so on are spoken of as a means of effacement, but not the others, the questioner asks, 'But why?' and so on. The other, explaining this meaning, says, 'Because they are a basis for the supramundane,' and so on: 'Though the attainments are indeed of a peaceful and refined nature, because they are a basis for the round of existence, they are not the practice of effacement for the defilements. Non-harming and so on, however, being a basis for what is contrary to the round, are the practice of effacement.' By this very sutta, which shows the distinction of non-harming and so on from the eight attainments, the manner in which it becomes more greatly fruitful should be understood. For this is stated with reference to the greater fruitfulness of an offering due to the greater worthiness of the recipient; this is the connection. With reference to the objection, 'Is it not stated there, "one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry," and not "one who has gone for refuge"?', it is said, 'starting from the going for refuge,' and so on. For this is stated in the commentary (Majjhima Nikāya Commentary 3.379): 'Even a lay follower who has gone to the three refuges, at the lowest level, is called one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.' For one who, desiring to transcend the suffering of the round of existence, goes for refuge to the Triple Gem with a confident mind, that going for refuge, having become a support for higher virtue and so on, gradually leads to the attainment of the path of vision.

Vihiṃsādivatthunti yadetaṃ vihiṃsādīnaṃ vatthuṃ vadāma, imasmiṃ vihiṃsādivatthusmiṃ. Antamicchādiṭṭhiñca micchattānaṃ ādimicchādiṭṭhiñcāti idaṃ desanākkamaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Missetvāti micchādiṭṭhibhāvasāmaññena ekajjhaṃ katvā. Tathāti iminā yathā kammapathamicchattānaṃ ante ādimhi ca vuttamicchādiṭṭhiṃ missetvā ekajjhaṃ vuttaṃ, tathā tesaṃ ante vuttasammādiṭṭhīti imamatthaṃ upasaṃharati.

'In the basis of harmfulness and so on' means: in this basis of harmfulness and so on, which we speak of. 'And the wrong view at the end, and the wrong view at the beginning of the wrongnesses'—this is said with reference to the sequence of the teaching. 'Having mixed' means having made them one through the commonality of being wrong view. 'Thus': by this, he concludes this meaning: just as the wrong view mentioned at the end and at the beginning of the wrong courses of action are mixed and spoken of as one, so too is the right view mentioned at their end.

Pāṇanti vohārato sattaṃ, paramatthato jīvitindriyaṃ. Atipātenti saraseneva patanasabhāvaṃ aticca antarā eva pātenti, atikkamma vā satthādīhi abhibhavitvā pātenti. Adinnanti parasantakaṃ. Ādiyantīti gaṇhanti. Sallekhatīti samaṃ lekhati, pajahatīti attho. Kammapathakathā esāti “atthabhañjanaka”nti vuttaṃ. Piyasuññakaraṇato pisuṇā, pisati pare satte hiṃsatīti vā pisuṇā. Pharusāti lūkhā, niṭṭhurāti attho. Niratthakanti attharahitaṃ attano paresañca hitavinimuttaṃ. Micchāti viparītā niccādivasena pavattiyā. Pāpikāti lāmikā. Ekantākusalatāya viññūhi buddhādīhi garahitā. Natthi dinnanti ādivatthukāyāti dasavatthukamicchādiṭṭhimāha. Natthikabhāvābhinivesanavasena kammapathappattiyevassā kammapathapariyāpannatā. “Rūpaṃ attā’”tiādinayappavattā attadiṭṭhi [M 1.0290] maggantarāyakarattā aniyyānikadiṭṭhi. Aniyyānikattā eva hissā micchattapariyāpannatā. Sammāti aviparītā, tato eva sobhanā sundarā, buddhādīhi pasatthattā viññuppasatthā. Sesamettha micchādiṭṭhiyaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

'Living being' (pāṇa): conventionally, a being; in the ultimate sense, the life faculty. 'They destroy life' (atipātenti): having gone beyond its natural tendency to fall, they make it fall prematurely; or, having overcome it with weapons and so on, they make it fall. 'What is not given' (adinna) means what belongs to others. 'They take' (ādiyanti) means they grasp. 'One effaces' (sallekhati): one scrapes evenly; the meaning is one abandons. This is the discourse on the course of action, so it is called 'the breaking of the meaning' (atthabhañjanaka). 'Divisive' (pisuṇā): because it makes loved ones empty of affection, or because it crushes (pisati) and harms other beings. 'Harsh' (pharusā) means rough; the meaning is cruel. 'Useless' (niratthaka) means devoid of benefit, bereft of welfare for oneself and others. 'Wrong' (micchā) means distorted, proceeding by way of (seeing) permanence, etc. 'Bad' (pāpikā) means base; being entirely unwholesome, it is censured by the wise, such as the Buddhas. 'There is nothing given,' etc.: he speaks of the wrong view with ten grounds. Its inclusion in the course of action is only by way of its reaching the course of action through adherence to a nihilistic view. The self-view that proceeds by the method 'Form is self,' etc., is a non-leading-out view because it is an obstacle to the path. Indeed, because it is non-leading-out, it is included in wrongness. 'Right' (sammā) means not distorted, and for that reason it is beautiful, excellent; it is praised by the wise, such as the Buddhas, hence praised by the intelligent. The rest here should be understood in the manner explained regarding wrong view.

Asubhādīsu [V 1.0258] subhādiākāraggahaṇato ayāthāvaaniyyānikā ayoniso uppattiyā. Akusalāti ayāthāvāaniyyānikā akusalā saṅkappā. Esa nayoti iminā “ayāthāvā aniyyānikā akusalā vācā”tiādinā tattha tattha ayāthāvādiatthaṃ atidisati. Vācāti cetanā adhippetā, tathā kammantājīvāsati ca. Yebhuyyena atītānussaraṇavasena pavattito “atītaṃ cintayato”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi loke evaṃ vadanti “yaṃ me pahūtaṃ dhanaṃ ahosi, taṃ pamādavasena pana bahuṃ khīṇa”nti. Satipatirūpakenāti “cirakatampi cirabhāsitampi saritā”ti evaṃ vuttasatuppattipatirūpakena. Uppattinti cittuppattiṃ. Tathāpavattacittuppādo hi micchāsati. Sā pana kodhavasena vā “akkocchi maṃ avadhi ma”ntiādinā (dha. pa. 3) upanayhantassa, rāgavasena vā “yānissa tāni pubbe mātugāmena saddhiṃ hasitalapitakīḷitāni anussaratī”ti (a. ni. 7.50) vuttanayena subhato anussarantassa, diṭṭhivasena vā “so kho pana me atto nicco dhuvo”tiādinā micchāabhinivisantassāti evamādinā nayena pavattatīti veditabbā.

Because of grasping the aspect of beauty and so on in the foul and so on, it is not as it really is and non-leading-out, due to its arising from unwise attention. 'Unwholesome': unwholesome thoughts are not as they really are, non-leading-out, and unwholesome. 'This is the method': by this, he applies the meaning of 'not as it really is' and so on here and there, as in 'speech that is not as it really is, non-leading-out, and unwholesome,' and so on. By 'speech,' intention is meant, and likewise for action, livelihood, and mindfulness. Because it proceeds for the most part by way of recollecting the past, it is said, 'reflecting on the past.' For in the world, people say, 'I had abundant wealth, but through negligence, much of it was lost.' 'By a counterfeit of mindfulness' means by a counterfeit of the arising of mindfulness, as stated thus: 'remembering what was done long ago and spoken long ago.' 'Arising' means the arising of the mind. For such an arising of the mind is wrong mindfulness. This, it should be understood, proceeds by way of anger in one who bears a grudge, thinking, 'He abused me, he struck me,' and so on (Dhammapada 3); or by way of lust in one who recollects as beautiful what is past, in the manner stated, 'he recalls those past laughings, talkings, and playings he had with women' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.50); or by way of view in one who wrongly adheres to the notion, 'this self of mine is permanent, stable,' and so on.

Upāyacintāvasenāti khippajālakumināduhalādiupakaraṇasaṃvidhānādīsu yutticintanādivasena pāpaṃ katvā vippaṭisāranimittaṃ, “sukataṃ mayā”ti pāmojjanimittaṃ katvā paccavekkhaṇākārena moho aññāṇaṃ. Tattha pana “asive sivā”ti vohāro viya ñāṇavohāro. Micchāsabhāvattā pana micchāñāṇaṃtveva vuccati. Ekūnavīsatibhedaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ sammā pekkhitattā sammāñāṇaṃ vuccati, itaraṃ pana jhānādipaccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ sammādiṭṭhiyāva saṅgayhati. Rūpārūpasamāpattilābhitāmattena vaṭṭato avimuttāyeva samānā “vimuttā maya”nti evaṃsaññino. Pakatipurisantarañāṇasaṅkhātāyaṃ, guṇaviyuttassa attano sakattani avaṭṭhānasaṅkhātāyaṃ, attano mahābrahmunā salokatā tassa samīpatāsaṃyujjanasaṅkhātāyaṃ [M 1.0291] vā avimuttiyaṃ vimuttisaññino. Ekantākusalatāya hīnattā pāpikā. Ayāthāvatāya viparītā. Yathāvuttenāti “avimuttāyeva samānā”ti vuttappakārena. “Mayamettha sammādiṭṭhi bhavissāmā”tiādīsu phalasammādiṭṭhiādīnipi maggasammādiṭṭhiādipakkhikānevāti adhippāyena “phalasampayuttāni…pe… veditabbā”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbepi pana phaladhamme vimuttikkhandhasaṅgahato “vimuttī”ti vuccamāne na koci virodho. Ettha sammāvimuttisaṅkhāte sallekhavatthumhi.

Delusion and ignorance, in the form of reflection, is by way of considering means—such as considering the suitability of arranging equipment like quick-nets, fish-traps, and so on—and by way of taking as a sign remorse after doing evil, or taking as a sign joy thinking, 'I have done well.' Here, however, the designation 'knowledge' is like the expression 'auspicious in what is inauspicious.' But because its nature is wrong, it is called wrong knowledge. The knowledge of reflection, of nineteen kinds, is called right knowledge because it examines rightly. Other knowledge of reflection, however, such as that concerning jhāna and so on, is included in right view itself. They are ones who perceive thus, 'We are liberated,' while they are in fact not liberated from the round, merely through having attained the form and formless attainments. They are ones who perceive liberation in non-liberation: that is, in what is designated as the knowledge of the distinction between primordial nature and spirit, or in what is designated as the non-establishment of one's own selfhood devoid of qualities, or in what is designated as one's own co-existence, proximity, and union with Mahābrahmā. 'Bad' (pāpikā), because it is inferior due to being entirely unwholesome. 'Distorted' (viparītā), because it is not as it really is. 'As stated' means in the manner stated: 'while they are in fact not liberated.' With the intention that in statements like, 'Here we shall have right view,' the right view of the fruit and so on are on the side of the right view of the path and so on, it is said, 'associated with the fruit... should be understood.' Moreover, since all states of the fruit are included in the aggregate of liberation, there is no contradiction when they are called 'liberation.' Here, in the basis for effacement designated as right liberation.

Yadi nīvaraṇavasena vuttāni, tasmā tīṇeva vuttānīti āha “abhijjhālū”tiādi. Pariyuṭṭhānappattā thinamiddhapariyuṭṭhitā. Yassa dhammassa atthitāya uddhatā nāma honti, so dhammo uddhaccanti āha “uddaccena samannāgatāti uddhatā”ti. Vicinantāti dhammoti vā adhammoti vā [V 1.0259] ādinā yaṃ kiñci sabhāvaṃ vinicchinantā. Upanāhanasīlāti parassa attano citte anubandhanasīlā. Issantīti usūyanti. Saṭhayantīti saṭhā aññathā attānaṃ aññathā pavedanakā. Te pana yasmā na yathābhūtavādino, tasmā āha “na sammā bhāsantīti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Vuttapaccanīkanayenāti “na kodhanā akkodhanā”tiādinā vuttaatthapaṭipakkhanayena.

“If they are spoken of in terms of the hindrances, then only three are mentioned,” thus it is said: “those full of greed,” and so forth. Those who have reached the state of obsession are obsessed by sloth and torpor. That state by the existence of which they are called restless is restlessness; thus it is said, “endowed with restlessness means they are restless.” “Examining” means scrutinizing any nature whatsoever, deciding whether it is Dhamma or non-Dhamma, and so forth. “Upanāhanasīlā” (given to harboring resentment) means having the habit of binding resentment in one’s own mind towards others. “Issanti” (they are envious) means they are jealous. “Saṭhayanti” (they are deceitful) means they are cunning, those who reveal themselves otherwise than they are. But because they are not speakers of the truth, it is said, “it means they do not speak rightly.” “By way of the method of stating the opposite” means in the manner of stating the meaning opposite to that stated, such as “not angry, free from anger,” and so forth.

Dukkhaṃ vaco etesu vippaṭikūlaggāhitāya vipaccanīkagāhesūti dubbacā. Te pana vacanakkhamā na hontīti āha “vattuṃ dukkhā”tiādi. Hīnācāratāya dukkhassa vā sampāpakatāya pāpakā. Asaddhammavasenāti asappurisadhammavasena. Attanā visesitabbavasena kāyaviññattiādīnaṃ kāyakammadvārādibhāvo viya assaddhiyādiasaddhammasamannāgamenaasataṃ asappurisānaṃ dhammānanti tāniyeva assaddhiyādīni asaddhammā nāma, tesaṃ vasenāha “saddhā etesaṃ natthī”ti yathā taṃ “duppaññā”ti. Suttageyyādi appaṃ sutaṃ etesanti appassutā, sutena anupapannā. Natthīti gahetabbanti iminā abhāvattho ayaṃ appa-saddo “appaḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassāna”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 10.11) viyāti dasseti. Sammāpaṭipattiyā anārambhanato kucchitā gārayhā sīdanti osīdanti saṃkilesapakkheti kusītā da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā. Akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadāya āraddhaṃ paggahitaṃ vīriyaṃ etesanti āraddhavīriyā. Anuppādanena [M 1.0292] muṭṭhā naṭṭhā sati etesanti muṭṭhassatī. Duṭṭhāti dūsitā. Duppaññā nāma dūsitabhāvo paṭipakkhena vināsitabhāvoti āha “naṭṭhapaññāti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Heṭṭhā sammādiṭṭhiggahaṇena kammassakatāpaññāya maggasammādiṭṭhiyā ca gahitattā subbacakalyāṇamittatāparivārāhi idha saddhādīhi vipassanāsambhārassa uddhaṭattā ca vuttaṃ “idha vipassanāpaññā veditabbā”ti. Tenāha “vipassanāsambhāro hī”tiādi. Yuttiṃ anapekkhitvāpi ayamattho gahetabboti dassento āha “porāṇānaṃ āṇā”ti.

Speech is difficult for them because they grasp what is contrary and hold opposing views; thus they are difficult to speak to. But they are not tolerant of words; thus it is said, “difficult to speak to,” and so forth. Because of base conduct, or because they lead to suffering, they are evil. “Through unwholesome states” means through the qualities of bad people. Just as bodily intimation and so forth are characterized by themselves as being the door of bodily action and so forth, so too, by being endowed with unwholesome states like lack of faith, these are the states of the unvirtuous, the bad people. Those very qualities, lack of faith and so forth, are called unwholesome states. By way of them, it is said, “they have no faith,” just as it is said, “they are unwise.” They have heard little of the discourses, chants, and the like—hence, they are of little learning, deficient in learning. By this it is shown that the word 'appa' has the meaning of absence, so it should be understood as 'there is not,' just as in such phrases as 'free from gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and the touch of creeping things' (AN 10.11). Because they do not engage in right practice, they are blameworthy, reprehensible; they sink, they sink down into the realm of defilement—hence, they are lazy (kusītā), by changing the ‘da’ sound to ‘ta.’ They have aroused and sustained energy for abandoning unwholesome states and acquiring wholesome states—hence, they are energetic (āraddhavīriyā). Mindfulness is lost, destroyed for them by not causing it to arise—hence, they are forgetful (muṭṭhassatī). “Corrupted” means defiled. “Unwise” (duppaññā) means the state of being corrupted, the state of being destroyed by the opponent; thus it is said, “it means their wisdom is lost.” Because below, by the inclusion of right view, both the wisdom of kamma-ownership and the right view of the path are included, and because here the requisites for insight are drawn out by faith and so forth, accompanied by good speech and good friendship, it is said, “here the wisdom of insight should be understood.” Therefore, it is said, “for it is a requisite for insight,” and so forth. Even without considering the reasoning, this meaning should be taken; showing this, it is said, “it is the instruction of the ancients.”

Lokuttaraguṇānaṃ antarāyakaranti lokuttaraguṇānaṃ adhigamassa antarāyakaraṃ. Sandiṭṭhinti saṃ attano diṭṭhiṃ, yaṃ vā taṃ vā attanā yathāgahitadiṭṭhinti attho. Sabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā parato āmasanato parāmāsī. Daḷhaggāhīti “idameva sacca”nti thiraggāhaggāhī. Paṭinissaggīti paṭinissajjanako. Kummovāti yathā kacchapo attano pādādike aṅge kenaci ghaṭṭito sabbāni aṅgāni attano kapāleyeva samodahati, na bahi nīharati, evamayampi “na sundaro tava gāho, chaḍḍehi na”nti vutto taṃ na vissajjeti. Antoyeva attano hadaye eva ṭhapetvā taṃ vadati. Kumbhīlaggāhanti saṃsumāraggāhaṃ. Gaṇhantīti yathā saṃsumārā gahitaṃ na vissajjenti, evaṃ gaṇhanti.

“The obstructer of supramundane qualities” means that which obstructs the attainment of supramundane qualities. “Sandiṭṭhi” (clearly seen) means one’s own view, or whatever view one has personally grasped—this is the meaning. “Parāmāsī” (grasping after others) means one who grasps at what is other, having transgressed its true nature. “Daḷhaggāhī” (firmly holding) means holding tightly with the thought, “This alone is true.” “Paṭinissaggī” (relinquishing) means one who relinquishes. “Kummovā” (like a tortoise) means just as a tortoise, when any of its limbs are touched, withdraws all its limbs into its own shell and does not bring them out, so too, when told, “Your grasp is not good, let it go,” this person does not release it but keeps it hidden in their own heart and speaks of it. “Kumbhīlaggāha” (crocodile’s grip) refers to the grip of a crocodile. “Gaṇhanti” (seizing) means just as crocodiles do not release what they have seized, so too they seize.

84. Evaṃ [V 1.0260] catucattālīsāya ākārehīti avihiṃsanādīhi catuadhikacattālīsappakārehi. Kasmā panettha avihiṃsā ādito vuttā? Sabbaguṇānaṃ mūlabhāvato. Avihiṃsāti hi karuṇāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, sā ca visesato sīlassa mūlakāraṇaṃ parūpaghātalakkhaṇā dussīlyā oramāpanato. Yathā hi pāṇātipāto parūpaghātalakkhaṇo, tathā paresaṃ sāpateyyāvaharaṇaṃ, sattippahāratopi dhanassāvahāro garutaroti. Tathā abrahmacariyaṃ gabbhadhāraṇādidukkhāvahanato, paradārātikkame pana vattabbameva natthi. Paresaṃ visaṃvādanabhedanamammaghaṭṭanānaṃ parūpaghātabhāvo pākaṭo eva, samphappalāpo atthaggāhāpanato anatthuppādanato, abhijjhā adinnādānādihetuto, byāpādo pāṇātipātādihetuto, micchādiṭṭhi sabbānatthahetuto [M 1.0293] parūpaghātalakkhaṇā, micchādiṭṭhi dhammikapaṭiññopi pāṇātipātādīni karoti, pare ca tattha niyojeti, kimaṅgaṃ pana itare. Vihiṃsalakkhaṇā dussīlyā oramā avihiṃsalakkhaṇā visesato sīlassa balavakāraṇaṃ. Sīlapadaṭṭhāno ca samādhi, samādhipadaṭṭhānā ca paññāti sabbaguṇānaṃ mūlabhūtā avihiṃsā. Apica uḷārajjhāsayānaṃ nisammakārīnaṃ dhīrānaṃ uttamapurisānaṃ sīlaṃ viya samādhipaññāpi paresaṃ hitasukhāvahāva sampajjantīti evampi karuṇā sabbaguṇānaṃ mūlanti sā ādito vuttā.

84. “Thus, in forty-four ways” means in forty-four modes, beginning with non-harming. But why is non-harming mentioned first here? Because it is the root of all virtues. For “non-harming” is a term for compassion, and it is especially the foundational cause of virtue, as it counteracts unwholesome conduct characterized by harming others. Just as killing living beings has the characteristic of harming others, so too does stealing others’ property—indeed, taking wealth is even more serious than striking with a weapon. Likewise, sexual misconduct brings suffering such as bearing children and so forth, but there is nothing more to say about adultery with another’s spouse. The harmful nature of deceiving others, causing division, and striking at their vulnerabilities is quite evident; and idle chatter is harmful because it prevents the grasping of what is beneficial and produces what is not beneficial. Covetousness has the characteristic of harming others as it is a cause of theft and the like; ill-will, as it is a cause of killing and the like; and wrong view, as it is a cause of all non-benefit. Even one who professes righteousness but holds wrong views commits killing and the like and encourages others in it—what need to mention the rest? The characteristic of non-harming counteracts unwholesome conduct characterized by harming, and is especially the strengthening factor of virtue. Concentration is founded on virtue, and wisdom is founded on concentration—thus, non-harming is the root of all virtues. Moreover, just as the virtue of noble, discerning, and steadfast individuals of lofty resolve brings welfare and happiness to others, so too do their concentration and wisdom. Thus, compassion is the root of all virtues, which is why it is mentioned first.

Tato paraṃ visesato “avihiṃsāsamuṭṭhānā ime dhammā”ti dassanatthaṃ kusalakammapathadhammā gahitā. Tato idaṃ guṇānaṃ mūlabhūtaṃ sīlaṃ, ettha patiṭṭhitena ime dhammā uppādetabbāti dassanatthaṃ aṭṭha sammattā gahitā. Tesaṃ visodhanāya paṭipannassa ādito evaṃ hotīti dassanatthaṃ nīvaraṇaviveko gahito, ādito nīvaraṇadvayassa aggahaṇe gahitāgahitakāraṇaṃ aṭṭhakathāya vuttameva. Kodhassa pana byāpādato bhedo vatthasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.71) vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Kodhādippahānena cettha sallekhasiddhīti dassanatthaṃ tato upakkilesavisuddhi gahitā. Sā ca subbacakalyāṇamittaappamattatāhi sijjhatīti dassanatthaṃ pakiṇṇakā gahitā. Sampannasovacassatādiguṇassa ime dhammā pāripūriṃ gacchanti, vipassanaṃ paribrūhetvā ariyamaggādhigamāya saṃvattantīti dassanatthaṃ saddhammā gahitā. Evaṃbhūtassa ayaṃ micchāgāho lokuttaraguṇādhigamassa antarāyakaro, tasmā so dūrato vajjetabbo, evaṃ yathāvuttāya sammāpaṭipattiyā ariyamaggaṃ adhigacchanto sallekhaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetīti dassanatthaṃ “sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī”tiādi vuttanti evametesaṃ catucattālīsāya sallekhākārānaṃ gahaṇapayojanaṃ anupubbī ca veditabbā. Payogato sallekhapaṭipadaṃ paṭipajjituṃ asakkontānaṃ cittuppādopi bahūpakāroti āha “cittuppādassapi bahūpakārataṃ dassetu”nti.

Then, to show specifically that “these qualities are founded on non-harming,” the wholesome paths of action are taken up. Next, to show that this virtue is the root of these qualities and that one established in it should bring these qualities into being, the eight rightnesses are taken up. To show that for one practicing for their purification, it begins thus, the seclusion from the hindrances is taken up. The reason for including or not including the two hindrances from the start is as stated in the commentary. The distinction between anger and ill-will should be understood in the way stated in the commentary on the Vatthu Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 1.71). Here, to show that effacement is accomplished through the abandoning of anger and the like, the purification from defilements is taken up. And to show that this is accomplished through being easy to admonish, good friendship, and heedfulness, the miscellaneous factors are taken up. To show that for one endowed with qualities such as being easy to admonish, these qualities reach fulfillment and, by developing insight, conduce to the attainment of the noble path, the good qualities are taken up. For such a person, this wrong grasping is an obstacle to the attainment of transcendent qualities; therefore, it should be avoided from afar. Thus, to show that by practicing rightly as stated, one attains the noble path and brings effacement to its culmination, it is said, “one who clings to one's own view,” etc. In this way, the purpose for taking up these forty-four modes of effacement and their sequence should be understood. For those unable to practice the path of effacement in terms of application, even the arising of a thought is of great benefit—thus, it is said, “to show the great benefit of the arising of a thought.”

Kusalesu [V 1.0261] dhammesūti avihiṃsādīsu yathāvuttaanavajjadhammesu. Anuvidhiyanāti cittuppādassa kāyavācāhi anuvidhānā. Tesaṃ dhammānanti avihiṃsādidhammānaṃ, tesaṃ vā cittuppādavasena pavattadhammānaṃ. Idāni [M 1.0294] yathāvuttadhammaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “kasmā panā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Saraṇagamanaṃ vācāya viññāpetuṃ asakkontassa vasena vuttaṃ “kāyena vā”ti. “Sīlaṃ kāyena samādiyatī”ti etthāpi eseva nayo. Ettha ca tathā tathā pavattasallahukakāmāvacarakusalacittuppattiṃ upādāya tathārūpakusalakāyavacīkammānaṃ bahūpakāratā vuttāti na sabhāvato cittuppādassa bahūpakārataṃ ñāyatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

“In wholesome qualities” means in the blameless qualities such as non-harming and others, as stated. “Conforming” means the conforming of body and speech to the arising of thought. “Of those qualities” refers to the qualities of non-harming and others, or those qualities that proceed by way of the arising of thought. Now, to explain the stated quality in detail, the passage beginning with “But why…” is introduced. “Or with the body” is stated with reference to one who is unable to declare the going for refuge with speech. The same method applies in “one undertakes virtue with the body.” And here, with regard to the arising of wholesome sense-sphere consciousness, which is light and occurs in various ways, the great benefit of such wholesome bodily and verbal actions is stated. Thus, it should be understood that the great benefit is not known from the intrinsic nature of the arising of thought.

85. Hitādhigamāyāti diṭṭhadhammikādihitasampattiyā, ariyamaggādhigamāya eva vā. Ariyamaggo hi ekantahitattā hito nāma. Parivajjanavasena kamanaṃ pavatti parikkamananti āha “parikkamanāya parivajjanatthāyā”ti. Sammādassanupāyasaṃvidhānena avihiṃsā paṭiyattā sammāsambuddhena. Sukhenevāti akiccheneva. Eteneva upāyenāti eteneva avihiṃsāpade vuttena vidhinā. Sabbapadānīti sesāni tecattālīsa padāni.

85. “For the attainment of welfare” means for the achievement of benefits in this very life and so forth, or for the attainment of the Noble Path. For the Noble Path, being entirely beneficial, is called “welfare.” Proceeding by way of avoidance is parikkamana; thus it is said, “for parikkamana, for the purpose of avoidance.” Non-harming was prepared by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One through the arrangement of means for right view. “Easily” means without difficulty. “By this very method” means by this very rule stated in the term “non-harming.” “All the terms” refers to the remaining forty-three terms.

86. Akusalā paṭisandhiajanakā nāma uddhaccasahagatacittuppādadhammā aññepi pavattivipākamattadāyino, dinnāya paṭisandhiyā vipākajanakā, paccayavekallena vipaccituṃ aladdhokāsā ahosikammādayo vā ajanakā. Jātivasenāti akusalajātivasena. Adhobhāgaṅgamanīyāti apāyagamanīyā. Evaṃnāmāti nāmaggahaṇena sabhāvaṃ upalakkheti sati paccayasamavāye taṃsabhāvānativattanato. Tenāha “vipākakāle aniṭṭhākantavipākattā”ti. Vuttanayeneva kusalapakkho veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso, idha paṭisandhiajanakā abhiññāsahagatadhammā, sesaṃ vuttasadisameva. Sabbe akusalāti ettha vihiṃsamekaṃ ṭhapetvā itare sabbe akusalā upamābhūtā. Vihiṃsā hi upameyyaṃ. Sabbe kusalāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Eteneva upāyenāti yathā vihiṃsānaṃ upameyyatā, tadavasesānaṃ kusalākusalānaṃ upamābhāvo vutto, iminā nayena akusalaṃ pāṇātipātādiakusalena itarena, kusalañca pāṇātipātāpaṭiviratiādikusalena itarena upametabbaṃ.

86. “Unwholesome states that do not generate rebirth-linking” are mental states accompanied by restlessness, and other phenomena that yield only resultant states during the course of existence; or those that generate results for a rebirth-linking that has already been given; or non-generating actions such as ineffective past actions which did not get an opportunity to ripen due to a lack of supporting conditions. “By nature” means by their unwholesome nature. “Destined for the lower realms” means destined for the woeful planes. “Thus named”: by the term “name,” this indicates their intrinsic nature, because when conditions are assembled, that nature is not transgressed. Therefore, it is said, “because at the time of result, the results are undesirable and unwelcome.” The wholesome side should be understood in the way already stated. Here, however, the difference is that states associated with higher knowledge are non-generating of rebirth-linking; the rest is just as stated before. “All unwholesome states”—here, having set aside harming, all the remaining unwholesome states are the simile. For harming is the subject of comparison. “All wholesome states”—here too, the same method applies. “By this very method”—just as harming is the subject of comparison, and the remaining wholesome and unwholesome states are said to be the simile, in this way an unwholesome state like killing living beings should be compared with another unwholesome state, and a wholesome state like abstaining from killing should be compared with another wholesome state.

87. Parinibbāpaneti kilesapariḷāhavūpasamane. Parito limpanaṭṭhena palipaṃ vuccati mahākaddamaṃ, taṃ pana ekantato gambhīrampi hotīti “gambhīrakaddame [M 1.0295] nimuggo”ti vuttaṃ. Palipaṃ viya [V 1.0262] palipanti pañca kāmaguṇā vuccanti, tasmā evaṃ idāni vuccamānena upamopameyyasaṃsandananayena ettha imasmiṃ ṭhāne atthayojanā veditabbā. Na hi taṃ kāraṇanti ettha kāraṇaṃ nāma hatthassa vā pādassa vā apalipannabhāvo, so pana natthi. Esa nayo upameyyepi.

87. “Complete extinguishing” is the stilling of the burning of defilements. “Mire” refers to great mud because of its characteristic of smearing all around. And that mud is also extremely deep; thus it is said, “sunk in deep mire.” The five strands of sensual pleasure are called “mire,” like mire; therefore, in this context, the connection of meaning should be understood by the method of comparing simile and subject, as is now being explained. “That is not the reason”—here, “reason” means the state of a hand or foot not being mired, but that does not exist. The same method applies to the subject of comparison.

Tattha siyā kassaci parivitakko “bhagavato desanānubhāvena bhikkhuādayo kathentī”ti. “Bhagavāyeva hi tattha uddharatī”ti vatvā upamāya tadatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “rañño”tiādi vuttaṃ. Puthujjanā tāvatiṭṭhantu, sāvakasikhāppattavisesānampi ariyānaṃ desanā satthuyeva desanāti dassetuṃ “kiñcāpī”tiādimāha. Tathā hi tehi desitasuttāni buddhavacanameva, tesaṃ desanāya laddhavisesāpi ariyā buddhaputtāyevāti.

Here, someone might have this thought: “The bhikkhus and others speak by the power of the Blessed One’s teaching.” Having said, “Indeed, the Blessed One himself raises it up,” the simile of “the king” and so on was given to clarify that meaning. Let alone ordinary people, to show that even for the noble ones who have attained distinction and reached the peak of discipleship, the teaching is the Teacher’s teaching, it is said, “Even though…” and so on. For indeed, the discourses taught by them are the word of the Buddha, and even the noble ones who have attained distinction through their teaching are truly the sons of the Buddha.

Anibbisatāyāti anibbisevanatāya. Asikkhitavinayatāyāti pañcannaṃ vinayānaṃ sādaraṃ asikkhitabhāvena. Te pana vinayā tissannaṃ sikkhānaṃ sikkhāpanena hotīti āha “tisso sikkhā sikkhāpessatī”ti. Kiṃ pana tanti? “Ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī”ti ettha vuttaṃ kiṃ pana ṭhānanti āha “apalipapalipannatta”ntiādi. Yasmā pāḷiyaṃ “so vata cundā”tiādinā sāmaññatthaṃ upamābhāvena gahetvā visesattho upameyyabhāvena vutto, tasmā tamatthaṃ “evamattho veditabbo”tiādinā sādhāraṇato vatvā puna asādhāraṇato vivaranto “kiṃ vuttaṃ hotī”tiādimāha. Parassa vihiṃsācetanaṃ nibbāpessatīti idaṃ yo avihiṃsāsaṅkhātaṃ sammāpaṭipattiṃ disvā diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjanto dhammadesanāya paro avihiṃsako hoti, tādisaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ādesanañhi tassa vacananti. Tenāha “ayaṃ yā esā vihiṃsakassā”ti. Pubbe vihiṃsakassa micchāpaṭipajjantassa. Vihiṃsāpahānāya maggaṃ bhāvayatotiādinā attano eva avihiṃsāya vihiṃsāparinibbānāya saṃvattanamāha. Tenāha “parinibbuto viyā”tiādi. Sabbapadesūti “pāṇātipātissā”tiādinā āgatesu tecattālīsāya padesu.

'Not being inclined to harass' means not engaging in harassment. 'Not being trained in discipline' means not having diligently trained in the five disciplines. And that discipline comes about through training in the three trainings; thus it is said, 'He will train in the three trainings.' But what is that line of reasoning? Regarding the statement, 'This is a possible reason,' what is the reason? He explains, 'the state of not being mired in the mire,' and so on. Because in the Pāli text, beginning with 'Indeed, Cunda,' a general meaning is taken as the simile and a specific meaning is stated as the subject of comparison, therefore, having stated that meaning generally with 'the meaning should be understood thus,' he then elaborates on the specific meaning, asking, 'What is meant?' 'He will extinguish another's intention to harm': this is said with reference to a person who, on seeing the right practice called non-harming, follows that example, and through whose teaching another becomes non-harming. For instruction is his speech. Therefore, it is said: 'This is that of the harmful one,' meaning, of one who was previously harmful and practicing wrongly. By 'cultivating the path for the abandoning of harm,' and so on, he speaks of how one's own non-harming leads to the complete extinguishing of harm. Therefore, he says, 'as if fully extinguished,' and so on. 'In all the terms' means in the forty-three terms that are given, beginning with 'of killing living beings.'

88. Evanti desitākāraparāmasanaṃ. Tassāti sallekhassa. “Atthi khvesa brāhmaṇa, pariyāyo”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 3-10) viya pariyāya-saddo kāraṇatthoti [M 1.0296] āha “sallekhakāraṇa”nti. Tesaṃ vasenāti sallekhānaṃ vasena. Mettāya upasaṃharaṇavasena hitaṃ esantena. Karuṇāya vasena anukampamānena. Pariggahetvāti parito gahetvā, paritvāti attho. Pariccāti parito itvā, samantato pharitvā icceva attho. Mā pamajjitthāti “jhāyathā”ti vuttasamathavipassanānaṃ aññāṇena, aññena vā kenaci pamādakāraṇena [V 1.0263] mā pamādaṃ āpajjittha. Niyyānikasāsane hi akattabbakaraṇampi pamādoti. Vipattikāleti sattaasappāyādivipattiyuttakāle. Yathāvuttā pañca pariyāyā aññepi sabbe sāsanaguṇā idheva saṅgahaṃ gacchantīti āha “jhāyatha, mā pamādatthāti tumhākaṃ anusāsanī”ti.

88. Evanti desitākāraparāmasanaṃ. Thus, it is a reflection on the manner taught. Tassāti sallekhassa. 'Tassa' means of austerity. ‘‘Atthi khvesa brāhmaṇa, pariyāyo’’tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 3-10) viya pariyāya-saddo kāraṇatthoti āha ‘‘sallekhakāraṇa’’nti. In phrases like "There is indeed, brahmin, a method," the word 'pariyāya' (method) has the meaning of 'cause,' hence it is said to be 'the cause of austerity.' Tesaṃ vasenāti sallekhānaṃ vasena. 'Tesaṃ vasena' means 'by means of those austerities.' Mettāya upasaṃharaṇavasena hitaṃ esantena. By means of applying loving-kindness, one seeks welfare. Karuṇāya vasena anukampamānena. By means of compassion, one shows sympathy. Pariggahetvāti parito gahetvā, paritvāti attho. 'Pariggahetvā' means 'having grasped all around,' the meaning is 'having encompassed.' Pariccāti parito itvā, samantato pharitvā icceva attho. 'Pariccā' means 'having gone all around,' the meaning is 'having pervaded all directions.' Mā pamajjitthāti ‘‘jhāyathā’’ti vuttasamathavipassanānaṃ aññāṇena, aññena vā kenaci pamādakāraṇena mā pamādaṃ āpajjittha. 'Mā pamajjittha' means 'do not be heedless' due to ignorance of the stated serenity and insight, or due to any other cause of negligence. Niyyānikasāsane hi akattabbakaraṇampi pamādoti. For in the teaching leading to liberation, even doing what should not be done is negligence. Vipattikāleti sattaasappāyādivipattiyuttakāle. 'Vipattikāle' means at the time of misfortune, such as when the seven unsuitable conditions arise. Yathāvuttā pañca pariyāyā aññepi sabbe sāsanaguṇā idheva saṅgahaṃ gacchantīti āha ‘‘jhāyatha, mā pamādatthāti tumhākaṃ anusāsanī’’ti. The five methods mentioned, as well as all other qualities of the teaching, are included here, hence it is said, "Meditate, do not be heedless—this is our instruction to you."

Sallekhasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

Sallekhasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā. The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Sallekha Sutta is concluded.

9. Sammādiṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanā

9. Sammādiṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanā. The Commentary on the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta.

89. Kathetukamyatāpucchā [V 1.0264] evāti avadhāraṇena itarā catasso pucchā nivatteti itarāsaṃ asambhavato, tattha yathāpucchitassa atthassa vissajjanato ca “ayaṃ sammādiṭṭhī”ti yāthāvato ajānantāpi puthujjanā bāhirakatāpasādayo attano samānasīle ṭhitaṃ sammādiṭṭhīti vadanti. Anussavādivasenāpīti anussavākāraparivitakkadiṭṭhinijjhānakkhantivasenapi. Yathāsamaṅgitākārassa atthassa evametanti nijjhānakkhamāpanato ekantato yāthāvaggāho hotīti āha “attapaccakkhenapī”ti, yāthāvato lakkhaṇassa paṭividdhattā attano paccakkhabhāvenāti attho. Bahunnaṃ vacanaṃ upādāyāti iminā sāsane loke ca niruḷhatāya ayaṃ āmeḍitapayogoti sāsanassa niruḷhatāya ca sampasādaṃ upādāyapi tadubhayiko āmeḍitapayogo daṭṭhabbo. Atthanti vacanatthaṃ. Lakkhaṇanti sabhāvaṃ. Upādāyāti gahetvā. Sobhanāyāti sundarāya. Pasatthāyāti pasaṃsāya. Tesu purimena dhammānaṃ yathāsabhāvāvabodhasaṅkhātaṃ sammādiṭṭhisabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tena hi sā sabbadhamme abhibhavitvā sobhati. Dutiyena sampayuttadhammesu pariṇāyikabhāvaṃ. Tena hi sā sampayuttadhamme ñāṇamaye viya taṃsamaṅginañca puggalaṃ ñāṇapiṇḍaṃ viya karoti, tassa “paṇḍito nipuṇo cheko viññū vibhāvī”tiādinā disāsu pasaṃsā pattharati.

89. Kathetukamyatāpucchā evāti avadhāraṇena itarā catasso pucchā nivatteti itarāsaṃ asambhavato, tattha yathāpucchitassa atthassa vissajjanato ca ‘‘ayaṃ sammādiṭṭhī’’ti yāthāvato ajānantāpi puthujjanā bāhirakatāpasādayo attano samānasīle ṭhitaṃ sammādiṭṭhīti vadanti. The question of the desire to speak, by its emphasis, dismisses the other four questions due to their impossibility and because the meaning is answered there as it was asked. Even ordinary people, outsiders, ascetics, and so on, not knowing it as it really is, say 'this is right view' about that which is established in their own similar virtue. Anussavādivasenāpīti anussavākāraparivitakkadiṭṭhinijjhānakkhantivasenapi. 'Anussavādivasenāpīti' means through reliance on oral tradition, reasoning about appearances, and tolerance through pondering views. Yathāsamaṅgitākārassa atthassa evametanti nijjhānakkhamāpanato ekantato yāthāvaggāho hotīti āha ‘‘attapaccakkhenapī’’ti, yāthāvato lakkhaṇassa paṭividdhattā attano paccakkhabhāvenāti attho. Because through pondering and finding it acceptable that the meaning is just so, as it is constituted, there is a definite grasp of it as it really is, it is said, 'even through personal direct experience,' meaning by the state of its being directly experienced by oneself, due to having penetrated its characteristic as it really is. Bahunnaṃ vacanaṃ upādāyāti iminā sāsane loke ca niruḷhatāya ayaṃ āmeḍitapayogoti sāsanassa niruḷhatāya ca sampasādaṃ upādāyapi tadubhayiko āmeḍitapayogo daṭṭhabbo. 'Bahunnaṃ vacanaṃ upādāya' means that due to its being established in the Teaching and in the world, this is a repetitive usage. This dual repetitive usage should be seen as based on both the established nature of the teaching and the confidence therein. Atthanti vacanatthaṃ. 'Attha' means the meaning of the word. Lakkhaṇanti sabhāvaṃ. 'Lakkhaṇa' means the intrinsic nature. Upādāyāti gahetvā. 'Upādāya' means 'having taken' or 'based on'. Sobhanāyāti sundarāya. 'Sobhanāya' means 'beautiful.' Pasatthāyāti pasaṃsāya. 'Pasatthāya' means 'praised.' Tesu purimena dhammānaṃ yathāsabhāvāvabodhasaṅkhātaṃ sammādiṭṭhisabhāvaṃ dasseti. Of these, the first shows the nature of right view, which is designated as the understanding of phenomena according to their intrinsic nature. Tena hi sā sabbadhamme abhibhavitvā sobhati. For thus it shines, having surpassed all phenomena. Dutiyena sampayuttadhammesu pariṇāyikabhāvaṃ. The second shows its role as a guide among associated phenomena. Tena hi sā sampayuttadhamme ñāṇamaye viya taṃsamaṅginañca puggalaṃ ñāṇapiṇḍaṃ viya karoti, tassa ‘‘paṇḍito nipuṇo cheko viññū vibhāvī’’tiādinā disāsu pasaṃsā pattharati. For it makes the associated phenomena as if made of knowledge, and the person endowed with it as if a mass of knowledge, and praise for that person spreads in all directions with such words as 'wise, skilled, expert, discerning, insightful.'

Kammassakatāñāṇanti [M 1.0297] kammaṃ sako etassāti kammassako, tassa bhāvo kammassakatā, tattha ñāṇaṃ “idaṃ kammaṃ sattānaṃ sakaṃ, idaṃ no saka”nti evaṃ jānanañāṇaṃ. Saccānulomikañāṇanti ariyasaccānaṃ paṭivedhassa anulomato saccānulomikaṃ ñāṇaṃ, vipassanāñāṇaṃ. No saccānulomikāyāti bāhirako saccānulomikāya sammādiṭṭhiyā no sammādiṭṭhi sabbena sabbaṃ tassa abhāvato. Tattha kāraṇamāha “attadiṭṭhiparāmāsakattā”ti. Kammassa katādiṭṭhi pana bāhirakassa attadiṭṭhiṃ anurujjhantī pavattati “atthi dinna”ntiādinayappavattito. Sāsaniko dvīhipīti sāsaniko puthujjano kammassakatāñāṇādīhi dvīhipi sammādiṭṭhi. Okkantasammattaniyāmattā “sekkho niyatāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Asekkhāya sammādiṭṭhiyā sammādiṭṭhīti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Tīsupi puggalesu sekkho idha sammādiṭṭhīti adhippetoti dassento “niyatāya niyyānikāyā”tiādimāha.

Kammassakatāñāṇanti kammaṃ sako etassāti kammassako, tassa bhāvo kammassakatā, tattha ñāṇaṃ ‘‘idaṃ kammaṃ sattānaṃ sakaṃ, idaṃ no saka’’nti evaṃ jānanañāṇaṃ. The knowledge of kamma as one's own property: 'kammaṃ sako etassa' (kamma is his own) means 'kammassako'; the state of that is 'kammassakatā'. The knowledge therein is the knowledge that understands thus: 'This kamma is the property of beings, this is not their property.' Saccānulomikañāṇanti ariyasaccānaṃ paṭivedhassa anulomato saccānulomikaṃ ñāṇaṃ, vipassanāñāṇaṃ. The knowledge that conforms with the truths: the knowledge that conforms with the penetration of the noble truths is the knowledge that conforms with the truths, which is insight-knowledge. No saccānulomikāyāti bāhirako saccānulomikāya sammādiṭṭhiyā no sammādiṭṭhi sabbena sabbaṃ tassa abhāvato. Not in conformity with the truths: an outsider's right view is not right view in conformity with the truths, because it is completely and totally absent in him. Tattha kāraṇamāha ‘‘attadiṭṭhiparāmāsakattā’’ti. The reason for this is stated: "Because of adherence to the view of self." Kammassa katādiṭṭhi pana bāhirakassa attadiṭṭhiṃ anurujjhantī pavattati ‘‘atthi dinna’’ntiādinayappavattito. But for an outsider, the view that kamma is one's own property proceeds in conformity with the view of self, due to its arising from the principle 'there is what is given,' and so on. Sāsaniko dvīhipīti sāsaniko puthujjano kammassakatāñāṇādīhi dvīhipi sammādiṭṭhi. One within the Dispensation by two factors: an ordinary person within the Dispensation possesses right view by way of two factors, namely, the knowledge of kamma as one's own property and so on. Okkantasammattaniyāmattā ‘‘sekkho niyatāyā’’ti vuttaṃ. Because of having entered the fixed course of rightness, it is said: 'A trainee by the certain.' Asekkhāya sammādiṭṭhiyā sammādiṭṭhīti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. It should be connected by supplying 'is right view' with 'by the right view of the non-trainee.' Tīsupi puggalesu sekkho idha sammādiṭṭhīti adhippetoti dassento ‘‘niyatāya niyyānikāyā’’tiādimāha. To show that among these three types of individuals, the trainee is intended here as having right view, it is said: "by the certain, the liberating," and so on.

Idāni [V 1.0265] yathāvuttamatthaṃ pāḷiyā vibhāvetuṃ “tenevāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Antadvayanti “sassataṃ, ucchedaṃ, kāmasukhaṃ, attakilamatha”nti etaṃ antadvayaṃ. Līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhanantadvayassa anupagamanaṃ atthasiddhameva. Ujubhāvenāti ujusabhāvena maggena, majjhimāya paṭipattiyāti attho. Dhamme pasādaggahaṇena satthari saṅghe ca pasādopi gahitoyeva hotīti “dhamme”icceva vutto tadavinābhāvato. Yasmā esa niyatāya sammādiṭṭhiyā samannāgato sammādiṭṭhīti adhippeto, tañca vaṭṭato niyyānaṃ vivaṭṭādhigamena hotīti āha “āgato imaṃ saddhamma”nti. Nibbānañhi santo sadā vijjamāno dhammoti katvā saddhammoti imaṃ phalehi asādhāraṇena pariyāyena vattabbataṃ labhati. Tayidamassa āgamaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayo, so ca pahānābhisamayādīhi saheva idha ijjhatīti dassento “sabbadiṭṭhigahanānī”tiādimāha. Tattha sabbadiṭṭhigahanāni vinibbeṭhento sabbakilese pajahantoti padadvayena pana pahānābhisamayamāha, jātisaṃsārā nikkhamantoti iminā pariññābhisamayaṃ. Samatikkamattho hi pariññattho. Paṭipattiṃ pariniṭṭhapentoti iminā bhāvanābhisamayanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Idāni yathāvuttamatthaṃ pāḷiyā vibhāvetuṃ ‘‘tenevāhā’’tiādi vuttaṃ. Now, to clarify the aforesaid meaning with the canonical text, what begins with "Therefore he said" was stated. Antadvayanti ‘‘sassataṃ, ucchedaṃ, kāmasukhaṃ, attakilamatha’’nti etaṃ antadvayaṃ. The two extremes are "eternalism, annihilationism, sensual pleasure, and self-mortification"—this pair of extremes. Līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhanantadvayassa anupagamanaṃ atthasiddhameva. The non-approaching of the two extremes—sloth and restlessness, and standing still and striving—is indeed the accomplishment of the goal. Ujubhāvenāti ujusabhāvena maggena, majjhimāya paṭipattiyāti attho. By uprightness means by the path that is upright in nature, that is, by the middle practice. Dhamme pasādaggahaṇena satthari saṅghe ca pasādopi gahitoyeva hotīti ‘‘dhamme’’icceva vutto tadavinābhāvato. Through the grasping of confidence in the Dhamma, confidence in the Teacher and the Sangha is also implicitly grasped; hence, it is simply stated as "in the Dhamma," due to their inseparability. Yasmā esa niyatāya sammādiṭṭhiyā samannāgato sammādiṭṭhīti adhippeto, tañca vaṭṭato niyyānaṃ vivaṭṭādhigamena hotīti āha ‘‘āgato imaṃ saddhamma’’nti. Because this one endowed with the certain right view is intended as 'one with right view,' and since that liberation from the round of existence occurs through the attainment of the unrolling, it is said: "he has come to this true Dhamma." Nibbānañhi santo sadā vijjamāno dhammoti katvā saddhammoti imaṃ phalehi asādhāraṇena pariyāyena vattabbataṃ labhati. For Nibbāna, being peaceful and ever-existent, is considered the true Dhamma; thus it obtains the designation 'true Dhamma' by this expression which is not common to the fruits. Tayidamassa āgamaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayo, so ca pahānābhisamayādīhi saheva idha ijjhatīti dassento ‘‘sabbadiṭṭhigahanānī’’tiādimāha. This coming of his is the comprehension of realization; and to show that this succeeds here together with the comprehension of abandonment and so on, he said what begins with "all thickets of views." Tattha sabbadiṭṭhigahanāni vinibbeṭhento sabbakilese pajahantoti padadvayena pana pahānābhisamayamāha, jātisaṃsārā nikkhamantoti iminā pariññābhisamayaṃ. There, by the two phrases 'unraveling all thickets of views' and 'abandoning all defilements,' he indicates the comprehension of abandonment; by 'departing from the round of births,' this indicates the comprehension of full understanding. Samatikkamattho hi pariññattho. For the meaning of transcending is the meaning of full understanding. Paṭipattiṃ pariniṭṭhapentoti iminā bhāvanābhisamayanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. By 'bringing the practice to completion,' the comprehension of development should be understood.

Kālaparicchedavacananti paricchijjatīti paricchedo, kālo eva paricchedo kālaparicchedo, yo so akusalapajānanādinā paricchinno [M 1.0298] maggavuṭṭhānakālo maggakkhaṇo, tassa vacananti attho. Tenāha “yasmiṃ kāle”ti. Akusalañcāti ca-saddo samuccayattho. Tena vakkhamānaṃ akusalamūlādiṃ samuccinoti. Dasākusalakammapathanti kutoyaṃ viseso, yāvatā aniddhāritavisesaṃ akusalaṃ gahitanti? Na sāmaññajotanāya visese avaṭṭhānato. Kiṃ vā imāya yutticintāya, yasmā paṭhamavārena uddesavasena desitassa atthassa vitthāradesanā dutiyavāro. Tenevāha “katamaṃ panāvuso”tiādi. Yasmā lokuttarā sammādiṭṭhi idha adhippetā, tasmā nirodhārammaṇāya pajānanāya maggapaññāya kiccavasena sammohato “idaṃ dukkha”nti dasaakusalakammapathaṃ paṭivijjhanto “akusalaṃ pajānātī”ti vuccatīti attho. Tassāti akusalakammapathasaṅkhātassa dukkhassa. Teneva pakārenāti “nirodhārammaṇāya pajānanāya kiccavasenā”ti vuttappakārena.

Kālaparicchedavacananti paricchijjatīti paricchedo, kālo eva paricchedo kālaparicchedo, yo so akusalapajānanādinā paricchinno maggavuṭṭhānakālo maggakkhaṇo, tassa vacananti attho. A statement defining a time: 'paricchedo' is that which is defined. 'kālaparicchedo' is the definition of time. It is that time of emerging from the path, the path-moment, which is defined by the understanding of the unwholesome and so on. This is the meaning of 'a statement of that'. Tenāha ‘‘yasmiṃ kāle’’ti. Hence it is said, 'at the time when.' Akusalañcāti ca-saddo samuccayattho. 'And the unwholesome': the word 'ca' (and) has the meaning of conjunction. Tena vakkhamānaṃ akusalamūlādiṃ samuccinoti. Through this, it conjoins what will be said, namely, the unwholesome roots and so on. Dasākusalakammapathanti kutoyaṃ viseso, yāvatā aniddhāritavisesaṃ akusalaṃ gahitanti? 'Ten unwholesome courses of action': whence this specification, inasmuch as 'unwholesome' was taken without any specified distinction? Na sāmaññajotanāya visese avaṭṭhānato. It is not for illuminating a generality, but for establishing a specification. Kiṃ vā imāya yutticintāya, yasmā paṭhamavārena uddesavasena desitassa atthassa vitthāradesanā dutiyavāro. Or what is the need for this reasoned thought? Because the second section is a detailed exposition of the meaning taught in the first section by way of a summary. Tenevāha ‘‘katamaṃ panāvuso’’tiādi. Therefore, it is said, 'But what, friends?' and so on. Yasmā lokuttarā sammādiṭṭhi idha adhippetā, tasmā nirodhārammaṇāya pajānanāya maggapaññāya kiccavasena sammohato ‘‘idaṃ dukkha’’nti dasaakusalakammapathaṃ paṭivijjhanto ‘‘akusalaṃ pajānātī’’ti vuccatīti attho. Because the supramundane right view is intended here, therefore, by the function of path-wisdom, which has cessation as its object, one penetrates the ten unwholesome courses of action from delusion as 'this is suffering,' and thus it is said that one 'understands the unwholesome.' This is the meaning. Tassāti akusalakammapathasaṅkhātassa dukkhassa. 'Of that' means of suffering, which is designated as the unwholesome courses of action. Teneva pakārenāti ‘‘nirodhārammaṇāya pajānanāya kiccavasenā’’ti vuttappakārena. 'In the same way' means in the manner stated: 'by the function of understanding with cessation as its object.'

Kusalanti etthāyaṃ vacanattho – kucchite pāpadhamme salayati calayati kampetīti kusalaṃ, kucchitena vā ākārena sayantīti kusā, pāpakā dhammā. Te kuse lunāti chindatīti kusalaṃ. Kucchitānaṃ vā sānato tanukaraṇato ñāṇaṃ kusaṃ nāma, tena lātabbaṃ gahetabbaṃ pavattetabbanti kusalaṃ. Yathā vā kuso ubhayabhāgagataṃ hatthapadesaṃ lunāti, evamidaṃ uppannānuppannavasena ubhayabhāgagataṃ saṃkilesapakkhaṃ lunāti chindati, tasmā kuso viya lunātīti [V 1.0266] kusalaṃ. Kucchitānaṃ vā sāvajjadhammānaṃ salanato saṃvaraṇato kusalaṃ. Kusaladhammavasena hi akusalā manacchaṭṭhesu dvāresu appavattiyā saṃvutā honti. Kucchite vā pāpadhamme salayati gameti apanetīti kusalaṃ. Kucchitānaṃ vā pāṇātipātādīnaṃ sānato nisānato tejanato kusā, dosalobhādayo. Sādīnavavasena cetanāya tikkhabhāvappattiyā pāṇātipātādīnaṃ mahāsāvajjatā. Te kuse lunāti chindatīti kusalaṃ. Kucchitānaṃ vā sānato antakaraṇato vināsanato kusāni, puññakiriyavasena pavattāni saddhādīni indriyāni. Tehi lātabbaṃ pavattetabbanti kusalaṃ. “Ku”iti vā bhūmi vuccati, adhiṭṭhānabhāvena taṃsadisassa attano nissayabhūtassa rūpārūpapabandhassa sampati āyatiñca anudahena vināsanato kuṃ sasantīti kusā, rāgādayo. Te viya attano [M 1.0299] nissayassa lavanato chindanato kusalaṃ. Payogasampāditā hi kusaladhammā accantameva rūpārūpadhamme appavattikaraṇena samucchindanti. Kusalassa mūlanti kusalamūlaṃ, suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanena kusalassa patiṭṭhā nidānanti attho. Akusalamūlanti etthāpi eseva nayo.

Herein, the meaning of the word 'wholesome' (kusala) is as follows: It shakes, disturbs, and agitates contemptible, evil qualities; thus it is wholesome. Or, evil states (pāpakā dhammā) are called 'kusā' because they lie (sayanti) in a contemptible manner; it cuts off and severs these 'kusā,' therefore it is wholesome. Or, knowledge is called 'kusa' because it weakens and diminishes contemptible things; by means of that knowledge, what is to be obtained, grasped, and set going is wholesome. Or, just as a blade of grass (kusa) cuts the hand that has come into contact with both its edges, so too does this cut and sever the side of defilements that has come to both sides—whether arisen or unarisen; therefore, like a blade of grass, it cuts, hence it is wholesome. Or, it is wholesome because it shakes off and restrains blameworthy states. For by means of wholesome states, unwholesome states are restrained from arising at the six sense-doors. Or, it shakes off, dispels, and removes contemptible evil qualities; thus it is wholesome. Or, greed, hatred, and the like are called 'kusā' because they sharpen, intensify, and make keen contemptible acts such as killing living beings. Due to the attainment of sharpness of volition with regard to their danger, acts like killing living beings become highly blameworthy. It cuts off and severs these 'kusā'; thus it is wholesome. Or, the faculties of faith and so forth, which have arisen through meritorious deeds, are called 'kusāni' because they destroy, put an end to, and annihilate contemptible things. By means of these, what is to be obtained and set going is wholesome. Or, 'ku' is said to be the earth (bhūmi). Lust and other defilements are called 'kusā' because they lie on the earth (`ku`), destroying the continuity of form and formless existence—which is their own support, similar to a foundation—both in the present and in the future, without burning it. Like them, this wholesome state cuts and severs its own support; thus it is wholesome. For wholesome qualities, when accomplished through effort, utterly cut off form and formless phenomena by preventing their arising. 'The root of the wholesome' (kusalamūla) means the foundation and cause of the wholesome, by establishing its well-founded nature. The same principle applies to 'the root of the unwholesome' (akusalamūla).

Akusalanti pana na kusalaṃ akusalaṃ, kusaladhammānaṃ paṭipakkhavasena akusalanti padassa attho veditabbo. Evañhi ārogyānavajjasukhavipākakosallasambhūtaṭṭhena kusalaṃ vuccatīti. Yathā yaṃ dhammajātaṃ na arogaṃ na avajjaṃ na sukhavipākaṃ na ca kosallasambhūtaṃ, taṃ akusalanti ayamattho dassito hoti. Evaṃ yaṃ na kucchitānaṃ salanasabhāvaṃ, na kusena, kusehi vā pavattetabbaṃ, na ca kuso viya lavanakaṃ, taṃ akusalaṃ nāmāti ayampi attho dassitoti veditabbo. Vatthupajānanāti dukkhādivatthuno pajānanā paṭivedho. Tathā bujjhanakapuggalānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena desanā pavattāti āha “akusalādipajānanenāpī”ti. Teneva ca saṃkhittena desanā pavattā. Bhāvanāmanasikāro pana “sabbaṃ bhikkhave abhiññeyya”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.46; paṭi. ma. 1.3) vacanato anavasesato rūpārūpadhammānaṃ pariggahavaseneva pavattati. Tenāha “desanāyevā”tiādi. Tattha manasikārapaṭivedhoti pubbabhāge pavattavipassanāmanasikāro ariyamaggapaṭivedho ca. Kassaci akopanato vitthāravaseneva vuttaṃ vipassanaṃ anuyuñjantā maggaṃ paṭivijjhantāpi vitthāranayeneva paṭivijjhantīti attho visuddhikkamassa abhāvato.

Unwholesome, however, is not wholesome; the meaning of the term 'unwholesome' should be understood as being the opposite of wholesome states. For wholesome is so called because it is by nature healthy, blameless, of pleasant result, and born of skill. Thus, whatever state is not healthy, is blameworthy, does not have a pleasant result, and is not born of skill—that is unwholesome. This is the meaning shown. Furthermore, whatever is not of the nature of shaking off contemptible things, not to be set going by 'kusa' (knowledge) or 'kusā' (faculties), nor cuts like a 'kusa' blade of grass—that is called unwholesome. This meaning, too, should be understood as shown. 'Understanding of the basis' means the penetration and understanding of the basis of suffering and so forth. Likewise, the teaching proceeds according to the disposition of the individuals who are to awaken, as it is said: 'even through the understanding of the unwholesome, etc.' For that reason, the teaching is given concisely.
