Attention directed to development, however, proceeds by way of completely comprehending all form and formless phenomena, as stated: 'Monks, all is to be fully known.' Therefore, it is said: 'Only the teaching,' etc. Therein, 'penetration through attention' refers to the attention to insight practiced in the preliminary stage and the penetration of the noble path. For some, because there is no abridgement, those who practice the insight taught in detail also penetrate the path by the detailed method; this is the meaning, because there is no separate sequence of purification.

Bhikkhūti mahāvihāre dhammasaṅgītivasena pañcanikāyamaṇḍale nisinnabhikkhū. Theroti tattha saṅghattheroti vadanti. Vatthasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayena pana mahāsaṅgharakkhitattherassa antevāsikabhikkhū [V 1.0267] sandhāya “āhaṃsū”ti vuttaṃ. Theroti pana mahāsaṅgharakkhitatthero. So hi imasmiṃ majjhimanikāye taṃ taṃ vinicchayaṃ kathesi. Rāsitoti piṇḍato, ekajjhanti attho.

'Monks' refers to the monks seated in the Mahāvihāra in the circle of the five Nikāyas for a Dhamma recitation. 'The elder' refers to the elder of the Sangha there, they say. However, according to the method stated in the commentary on the Vatthasutta, 'they said' is stated with reference to the resident pupils of the elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita. 'The elder,' moreover, is the elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita. For it was he who gave the various decisions in this Majjhima Nikāya. 'Rāsito' means 'in a lump'; the meaning is 'all together'.

Akusalakammapathavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Unwholesome Courses of Action

Akosallappavattiyāti kosallapaṭipakkhato akosallaṃ vuccati aññāṇaṃ, tato pavattanato, akosallasambhūtattāti attho. Ñāṇapaṭipakkho [M 1.0300] aññāṇaṃ mittapaṭipakkho amitto viya kusalapaṭipakkho akusalaṃ kusalena pahātabbattā, na pana kusalānaṃ pahāyatattā. Kusalameva hi payogasampāditaṃ akusalaṃ pajahati. Saha avajjehi lobhādīhi vattatīti sāvajjaṃ. Dukkho aniṭṭho catukkhandha-saṅkhāto vipāko etassāti dukkhavipākaṃ. Tattha sāvajjavacanena akusalānaṃ pavattidukkhataṃ dasseti, dukkhavipākavacanena vipākadukkhataṃ. Purimañhi pavattisambhavavasena akusalassa lakkhaṇavacanaṃ, pacchimaṃ tālantare vipākuppādanasamatthatāvasena. Tathā purimena akusalassa avisuddhasabhāvataṃ dasseti, pacchimena avisuddhavipākataṃ. Purimena akusalaṃ kusalasabhāvato nivatteti, pacchimena abyākatasabhāvato savipākattadīpakattā pacchimassa. Purimena vā avajjavantatādassanato kiccaṭṭhena rasena anatthajananarasataṃ dasseti, pacchimena sampattiatthena aniṭṭhavipākarasataṃ. Purimena ca upaṭṭhānākāraṭṭhena paccupaṭṭhānena saṃkilesapaccupaṭṭhānataṃ, pacchimena phalaṭṭhena dukkhavipākapaccupaṭṭhānataṃ. Purimena ca ayonisomanasikāraṃ akusalassa padaṭṭhānaṃ pakāseti. Tato hi taṃ sāvajjaṃ jātaṃ, pacchimena akusalassa aññesaṃ padaṭṭhānabhāvaṃ vibhāveti. Tañhi dukkhavipākassa kāraṇanti. Saṃkiliṭṭhanti saṃkilesehi samannāgataṃ, dasahi kilesavatthūhi vibādhitaṃ, upatāpitaṃ vā tehi vidūsitaṃ malīnakatañcāti attho. Idañcassa dukkhavipākatañcāti atthe idañca dukkhavipākataṃ apaccakkhatāya asaddahantānaṃ paccakkhato ādīnavadassanena saṃvejanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sādhāraṇā sabbassapi akusalassa.

Because of arising from unskillfulness: Unskillfulness is called ignorance because it is the opposite of skillfulness; it arises from that ignorance, meaning it is born of unskillfulness. Ignorance is the opposite of knowledge, just as an enemy is the opposite of a friend. Unwholesome is the opposite of wholesome because it is to be abandoned by the wholesome, not because wholesome states are abandoned. For it is the wholesome, accomplished through effort, that abandons the unwholesome. 'Blameworthy' means it occurs together with faults such as greed. 'With painful result' means its result is painful, undesirable, and designated as the four aggregates. Here, the term 'blameworthy' shows the painfulness in the arising of unwholesome states, while 'with painful result' shows the painfulness of the result. The former is a statement of the characteristic of the unwholesome based on its origin and arising, while the latter is based on its capacity to produce a result at a later time. Likewise, the former indicates the impure nature of the unwholesome, while the latter shows its impure result. The former distinguishes the unwholesome from the nature of the wholesome, while the latter distinguishes it from the indeterminate nature, since the latter reveals that it has a result. Or, the former, by showing that it is accompanied by faults, demonstrates through its function its essence of producing harm; while the latter, through its accomplishment, demonstrates its essence of leading to an undesirable result. And the former, through its mode of manifestation, presents defilement as its proximate cause; while the latter, through its result, presents a painful result as its proximate cause. And the former reveals unwise attention as the proximate cause of the unwholesome, for from that arises what is blameworthy. The latter clarifies that the unwholesome is the proximate cause for other things, for it is the cause of painful results. 'Defiled' means associated with defilements, assailed by the ten bases of defilement, or tormented, corrupted, and stained by them. This and its painful result are stated here to stir spiritual urgency in those who lack faith because it is not directly perceived, by showing the dangers directly. These are common to all that is unwholesome.

Saraseneva (dha. sa. mūlaṭī. 1) patanasabhāvassa antarā eva atīva pātanaṃ atipāto, saṇikaṃ patituṃ adatvā sīghaṃ pātananti attho. Atikkammavā satthādīhi abhibhavitvā pātanaṃ atipāto. Payogavatthumahantatādīhi mahāsāvajjatā tehi paccayehi uppajjamānāya cetanāya balavabhāvato. Ekassa hi payogassa sahasā nipphādanavasena sakiccasādhikāya bahukkhattuṃ pavattajavanehi laddhāsevanāya ca sanniṭṭhāpakacetanāya vasena payogassa mahantabhāvo. Satipi kadāci khuddake ceva mahante ca pāṇe payogassa samabhāve mahantaṃ [V 1.0268] hanantassa cetanā tibbākārā uppajjatīti vatthussa mahantabhāvo. Iti ubhayampetaṃ cetanāya [M 1.0301] balavabhāveneva hotīti. Yathāvuttapaccayapariyāyepi taṃtaṃpaccayehi cetanāya balavatāya eva mahāsāvajjabhāvo veditabbo. Payogavatthuādipaccayānañhi amahattepi hantabbassa guṇavantatāya mahāsāvajjatā, tabbipariyāyena appasāvajjatā ca vatthussa mahattāmahattesu viya daṭṭhabbā. Kilesānaṃ upakkamānaṃ dvinnañca mudutāya tibbatāya ca appasāvajjatā mahāsāvajjatāpi yojetabbā. Pāṇo pāṇasaññitā vadhakacittañca pubbabhāgiyāpi honti, upakkamo vadhakacetanāsamuṭṭhāpito. Pañca sambhārā hi pāṇātipātacetanāti sā pañcasambhāravinimuttā daṭṭhabbā. Ayañca vicāro adinnādānādīsupi yathārahaṃ vattabbo. Vijjhanapaharaṇādivasena sahatthenanibbatto sāhatthiko, āṇāpanavasena pavatto āṇattiko, ususattiyantapāsāṇādinissajjanavasena pavatto nissaggiyo, aduhalasajjanādivasena pavatto thāvaro, āthabbaṇikādīnaṃ viya mantaparijappanavasena pavatto vijjāmayo, kammavipākajiddhimayo iddhimayo dāṭhākoṭanādīni viya.

By its own nature, 'excessive falling' (atipāto) means an extreme fall even within the nature of falling; that is, a rapid fall without allowing a slow descent. Or, 'excessive falling' is falling by transgressing, by overpowering with weapons and so forth. Due to the magnitude of the means, the object, and so on, great blameworthiness arises from the strength of volition produced by those conditions. For the magnitude of the means is due to the decisive volition which accomplishes its own task by means of the sudden accomplishment of a single act, and which has gained habitual practice through repeatedly occurring impulsion-moments. Even if the means is sometimes the same for both small and large beings, the volition of one who kills a large being arises intensely—thus, the magnitude of the object. Thus, both these are due to the strength of the volition. Even in the account of conditions as stated, great blameworthiness should be understood as being due to the strength of the volition arising from those respective conditions. For even when the conditions, such as the means and the object, are not great, there is great blameworthiness due to the virtuousness of the one to be killed; and conversely, little blameworthiness should be seen, just as in the case of the greatness and smallness of the object. Little blameworthiness and great blameworthiness should also be applied according to the mildness and intensity of both the defilements and the efforts. A being, the perception of a being, and the killing intention are also preliminary factors. The effort is instigated by the killing volition. Indeed, there are five constituents for killing a living being, and the volition should be understood as distinct from these five constituents. This analysis should be applied as appropriate to taking what is not given and other offenses. Accomplished by piercing, striking, etc., with one's own hand, it is 'done with one's own hand' (sāhatthika). Carried out by command, it is 'ordered' (āṇattika). Carried out by hurling arrows, spears, stones, etc., it is 'hurled' (nissaggiya). Carried out by setting snares, etc., it is 'stationary' (thāvara). Carried out through muttering spells, like those of Atharvan practitioners, it is 'made by knowledge' (vijjāmaya). Made by psychic power (iddhimaya), which may be born from the result of kamma, like the striking of a fang, it is 'made by psychic power'.

Yadi “mama ida”nti parena pariggahitaṃ adinnaṃ, uttānaseyyakadārakasantake kathaṃ tassa pariggahasaññāya eva abhāvatoti āha “yattha paro”tiādi. Paro nāma viññū vā aviññū vā atthi tassa vatthussa sāmiko. Aviññūpi hi viññukāle yathākāmaṃ karonto adaṇḍārahoti. Mantaparijappanena parasantakaharaṇaṃ vijjāmayo, vinā mantena parasantakassa kāyavacīpayogehi parikaḍḍhanaṃ tādiseniddhivasena iddhimayo payogoti adinnādāne cha payogā sāhatthikādayo vuttā. Yathānurūpanti ettha sāhatthiko tāva pañcannampi avahārānaṃ vasena pavattati, tathā āṇattiyo nissaggiyo ca. Thāvaro theyyāvahārapasayhāvahārapaṭicchannāvahāravasena. Tathā sesāpīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

If 'what is not given' is that which is possessed by another with the thought, 'This is mine,' how can this apply in the case of the property of an infant lying on its back, since it has no perception of possession? This is explained by the phrase 'where another exists,' and so on. 'Another' refers to someone, whether perceptive or unperceptive, who is the owner of that object. For even an unperceptive person, when they become perceptive, is not liable to punishment for acting as they wish. Taking another's belongings by muttering spells is a method based on knowledge (vijjāmaya). Without spells, dragging another's belongings by means of bodily or verbal effort, through such psychic power, is a method based on psychic power (iddhimaya). Thus, in taking what is not given, six methods beginning with taking by one's own hand are stated. Regarding 'as appropriate'—here, taking by one's own hand operates in terms of all five kinds of removal, and similarly for acts by command and by hurling. A stationary device operates by way of stealthy removal, forceful removal, and concealed removal. Similarly, the remaining ones should also be understood.

Methunasamācāresūti sadārāsantosa-paradāragamanavasena duvidhesu methunasamācāresu. Ayamevahi bhedo idhādhippeto. Gottarakkhitā sagottehi rakkhitā. Dhammarakkhitā sahadhammikehi rakkhitā. Sārakkhā sasāmikā. Yassā gamane raññā daṇḍo ṭhapito, sā saparidaṇḍā. Bhariyabhāvatthaṃ dhanena kītā dhanakkītā. Chandena vasantī chandavāsinī. Bhogatthaṃ vasantī bhogavāsinī. Paṭatthaṃ vasantī paṭavāsinī. Udakapattaṃ āmasitvā gahitā odapattakinī. Cumbaṭakaṃ apanetvā gahitā [M 1.0302] obhaṭacumbaṭā. Karamarānītā dhajāhatā. Taṅkhaṇikā muhuttikā. Abhibhavitvā vītikkame micchācāro mahāsāvajjo, na tathā dvinnaṃ samānachandatāya. Abhibhavitvā vītikkamane satipi maggenamaggapaṭipattiadhivāsane purimuppannasevanābhisandhipayogābhāvato micchācāro [V 1.0269] na hoti abhibhuyyamānassāti vadanti. Sevanācitte sati payogābhāvo appamāṇaṃ yebhuyyena itthiyā sevanāpayogassa abhāvato. Tathā sati puretaraṃ sevanācittassa upaṭṭhānepi tassā micchācāro na siyā, tathā purisassapi sevanāpayogābhāveti, tasmā attano ruciyā pavattitassa vasena tayo, balakkārena pavattitassa vasena tayoti sabbepi aggahitaggahaṇena cattāro sambhārāti vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

'In sexual misconduct' means in the two kinds of sexual misconduct, namely, dissatisfaction with one's own wife and going to another's wife. Indeed, this distinction is intended here. 'Guarded by family' means protected by relatives. 'Guarded by Dhamma' means protected by fellow practitioners of the Dhamma. 'Guarded' means she has a guardian. One with whom relations are punishable by the king is 'subject to penalty.' 'Bought with wealth' means acquired through money. 'Living by consent' means staying willingly. 'Living for wealth' means staying for material gain. 'Living for clothing' means staying for garments. 'Taken by touching the water vessel' refers to one acquired by touching the water pot. 'Taken by removing the head-coil' refers to one acquired by removing the head-coil. 'Brought as a captive' means taken as a prize of war. 'For a moment' refers to a temporary union. Committing wrong conduct by overpowering is gravely blameworthy, but not so when both parties share mutual consent. Even when there is transgression by overpowering, if there is no prior arisen intention for engagement or effort on the part of the victim, it is not wrong conduct for the one being overpowered, they say. If there is an intention for engagement but no effort, it is of little account, as women generally lack the effort for engagement. Similarly, even if the intention for engagement arises beforehand, it would not be wrong conduct for her, nor for the man in the absence of the effort for engagement. Therefore, it should be understood that it is said there are three types based on one's own inclination and three based on force; thus all have four constituents by way of 'the ungrasped being grasped'.

Atthabhañjakoti kammapathavasena vuttaṃ. Kammapathakathā hesāti. Assāti visaṃvādakassa. Musā vadati etenāti cetanā musāvādo, imasmiṃ pakkhe atathākārena vatthuno viññāpanapayogo musā, taṃsamuṭṭhāpikā cetanāmusāvādoti vuttattā tato aññathā vattuṃ “aparo nayo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Attano santakaṃ adātukāmatāyātiādi musāvādasāmaññena vuttaṃ. Hasādhippāyenapi visaṃvādanapurakkhārassa musāvādo. Parassāti visaṃvādanavasena viññāpetabbassa. Soti musāvādapayogo.

The term 'destroyer of the good' is stated in terms of the path of action. This is indeed a discourse on the path of action. 'Of him' refers to the one who deceives. The phrase 'by this one speaks falsely' means that the volition is false speech. In this view, the application of making known a thing as other than it is, is falsehood; and since the volition that gives rise to it is called false speech, 'another method,' and so on, is stated to speak otherwise. The phrase 'by the desire not to give one's own property,' and so on, is stated in the general sense of false speech. Even with the intention to joke, if deception is foremost, it is false speech. 'Of another' refers to the one who is to be informed by way of deception. 'That' refers to the application of false speech.

Suññabhāvanti pītivirahitatāya rittabhāvaṃ. Pharusasaddatāya neva kaṇṇasukhā. Atthavipannatāya na hadayasukhā. Saṃkiliṭṭhacittassāti dosena, lobhena vā dūsitacittassa.

'Emptiness' means a state of voidness because of being devoid of joy. Due to harshness of sound, they are not at all pleasing to the ear. Due to being corrupt in meaning, they are not pleasing to the heart. 'Of a defiled mind' means of a mind corrupted by hatred or greed.

Ekantapharusā cetanāti etena duṭṭhacittataṃyeva vibhāveti, duṭṭhacittatā cassa amaraṇādhippāyavasena daṭṭhabbā. Sati hi maraṇādhippāye atthasiddhi, tadabhāve pāṇātipātabyāpādā siyunti. Yaṃ paṭicca pharusavācā payujjati, tassa sammukhāva sīsaṃ eti. Parammukhāpi sīsaṃ eti evāti apare. Tatthāyaṃ adhippāyo yutto siyā – sammukhā payoge agāravādīnaṃ balavabhāvato siyā cetanā balavatī, parassa ca tadatthaviññāpanaṃ, na tathā asammukhāti. Yathā ca akkosite mate āḷahane katā khamāpanā upavādantarāyaṃ nivatteti, evaṃ parammukhā payuttā pharusavācā hotiyevāti sakkā viññātuṃ. Tassāti ekantapharusacetanāya eva [M 1.0303] pharusavācābhāvassa āvibhāvatthaṃ. Mammacchedako savanapharusatāyāti adhippāyo. Cittasaṇhātāya pharusavācā na hoti kammapathā’ppattattā, kammabhāvaṃ pana na sakkā vāretuṃ. Evaṃ anvayavasena cetanāpharusatāya pharusavācaṃ sādhetvā idāni tameva byatirekavasena sādhetuṃ “vacanasaṇhatāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Esāti pharusavācā. Kammapathabhāvaṃ appattā appasāvajjā, itarā mahāsāvajjā. Tathā kilesānaṃ mudutibbatābhedehi sabbaṃ purimasadisaṃ.

'Completely harsh volition'—this reveals the state of a corrupt mind, and the corrupt mind should be understood as having a non-lethal intention. For when there is the intention for death, the purpose is achieved; in its absence, there would be killing and ill will. Regarding the one to whom harsh speech is directed, it comes to a head in their presence. Others say it comes to a head even when they are not present. Here, the intended meaning should be understood as follows: when used in person, due to the strength of disrespect and so on, the volition is stronger, and the other person clearly perceives its meaning—this is not so when not in person. Just as forgiveness made at the charnel ground after someone who was reviled has died removes the obstacle of slander, so too can it be understood that harsh speech used when the person is not present still takes effect. 'Of that' is for the purpose of revealing the absence of harsh speech from a completely harsh volition alone. The meaning is that it 'cuts the vital spots' due to its harshness to the ear. Due to gentleness of mind, it does not become harsh speech as it has not reached the path of action, but its karmic nature cannot be denied. Thus, having established harsh speech by way of positive concomitance with harshness of volition, now, to establish the same by way of negative concomitance, 'by way of gentleness of speech,' and so on, is stated. 'This' refers to harsh speech. If it has not reached the state of a path of action, it is slightly blameworthy; otherwise, it is greatly blameworthy. Similarly, regarding the distinction between mildness and intensity of defilements, everything is as stated before.

Āsevanaṃ bahulīkaraṇaṃ. Yaṃ uddissa pavattito, tena aggahite appasāvajjo, gahite mahāsāvajjo [V 1.0270] kammapathappattito. Yo koci pana samphappalāpo dvīhi sambhārehi sijjhati. Kilesānaṃ mudutibbatāvasenapi appasāvajjamahāsāvajjatā veditabbā.

Indulgence is making it abundant. When it has arisen directed towards someone, if it is not grasped by that person, it is slightly blameworthy; if grasped, it is greatly blameworthy due to reaching the path of action. Moreover, any frivolous talk is accomplished through two constituents. The state of being slightly or greatly blameworthy should also be understood according to the mildness or intensity of the defilements.

Attano pariṇāmanaṃ cittenevāti veditabbaṃ. Hitasukhaṃ byāpādayatīti yo taṃ uppādeti, tassa hitasukhaṃ vināseti. Aho vatāti iminā accantavināsacintanaṃ dīpeti. Evaṃ hissa dāruṇapavattiyā kammapathappatti. Yathābhuccagahaṇābhāvenāti yāthāvaggāhassa abhāvena aniccādisabhāvassa niccādito gahaṇena. Micchā passatīti vitathaṃ passati. Samphappalāpo viyāti iminā āsevanassa mandatāya appasāvajjataṃ, mahantatāya mahāsāvajjataṃ dasseti. Gahitākāraviparītatāti micchādiṭṭhiyā gahitākārassa viparītabhāvo. Vatthunoti tassā ayathābhūtasabhāvamāha. Tathābhāvenāti gahitākāreneva tassa diṭṭhigatikassa, tassa vā vatthuno upaṭṭhānaṃ evametaṃ, na ito aññathāti.

One should understand that the directing of oneself is by the mind alone. 'He harms well-being and happiness' means whoever produces that, destroys his well-being and happiness. 'Alas!'—this indicates the contemplation of utter destruction. Thus, by such cruel conduct, there is the attainment of the path of action. 'Due to the absence of grasping truly' means due to the absence of grasping things as they truly are, by grasping the nature of impermanence, etc., as permanence, etc. 'He sees wrongly' means he sees falsely. 'Like frivolous talk'—by this, it shows slight blameworthiness due to the weakness of indulgence, and great blameworthiness due to its intensity. 'The state of being opposite to the grasped characteristic'—this is the state of being opposite to the characteristic grasped by wrong view. 'Of the object'—this refers to its untrue nature. 'By such a nature' means the arising for one who has gone to a view, or of that object, solely by the grasped characteristic, is thus: 'This is so, not otherwise than this.'

Dhammatoti sabhāvato. Koṭṭhāsatoti phassapañcamakādīsu cittaṅgakoṭṭhāsesu yaṃ koṭṭhāsā honti, tatoti attho. Cetanādhammāti cetanāsabhāvā.

'By nature' means by inherent nature. 'By way of parts' means: from whatever parts there are among the divisions of mental factors, such as the pentad of contact and so on; that is the meaning. 'Volitional phenomena' means having the nature of volition.

Paṭipāṭiyā sattāti ettha nanu cetanā abhidhamme kammapathesu na vuttāti paṭipāṭiyā sattannaṃ kammapathabhāvo na yuttoti? Na, avacanassa aññahetukattā. Na hi tattha cetanāya akammapathattā kammapatharāsimhi avacanaṃ, kadāci pana kammapatho hoti, na sabbadāti kammapathabhāvassa aniyatattā [M 1.0304] avacanaṃ. Yadā pana kammapatho hoti, tadā kammapatharāsisaṅgaho na nivārito. Etthāha – yadi cetanāya sabbadā kammapathabhāvābhāvato aniyato kammapathabhāvoti kammapatharāsimhi avacanaṃ, nanu abhijjhādīnaṃ kammapathabhāvaṃ appattānaṃ atthitāya aniyato kammapathabhāvoti tesampi kammapatharāsimhi avacanaṃ āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati kammapathatātaṃsabhāgatāhi tesaṃ tattha vuttattā. Yadi evaṃ cetanāpi tattha vattabbā siyā? Saccametaṃ, sā pana pāṇātipātādikāti pākaṭo, tassā kammapathabhāvoti na vuttā siyā. Cetanāya hi – “cetanāhaṃ, bhikkhave, kammaṃ vadāmi (a. ni. 6.63; kathā. 539), tividhā, bhikkhave, kāyasañcetanā akusalaṃ kāyakamma”ntiādivacanato (kathā. 539) kammabhāvo pākaṭo, kammaṃyeva ca sugatiduggatīnaṃ tattha uppajjanakasukhadukkhānañca pathabhāvena pavattaṃ kammapathoti vuccatīti pākaṭo tassā kammapathabhāvo, abhijjhādīnaṃ pana cetanāsamīhanabhāvena sucaritaduccaritabhāvo cetanājanitapiṭṭhivaṭṭakabhāvena sugatiduggatitaduppajjanakasukhadukkhānaṃ pathabhāvo cāti na tathā pākaṭo kammapathabhāvoti teyeva tena sabhāvena dassetuṃ abhidhamme cetanā kammapatharāsibhāvena na vuttā[V 1.0271], atathājātiyakattā vā cetanā tehi saddhiṃ na vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mūlaṃ patvāti mūladesanaṃ patvā, mūlasabhāvesu dhammesu vuccamānesūti attho.

Regarding 'seven in sequence,' is it not the case that intention (cetanā) is not mentioned in the Abhidhamma among the paths of action (kammapatha)? Therefore, is it not unsuitable that the seven should have the nature of paths of action? No, for the absence of mention is due to another reason. It is not because intention is not a path of action that it is not mentioned in the group of paths of action; rather, it is not mentioned because its state as a path of action is inconstant—sometimes it is, and sometimes it is not. But when it is a path of action, its inclusion in the group of paths of action is not precluded. Here one might say: 'If, for intention, its state as a path of action is inconstant, leading to its omission from the group of paths of action, then since for covetousness (abhijjhā) and the like there are instances that do not attain the state of being a path of action, their state as a path of action is also inconstant; should they not also be omitted from the group of paths of action?' This does not follow, because they are mentioned there due to their participation in the nature of being a path of action. 'If so, should not intention also be mentioned there?' That is true, but it is manifest as killing living beings and so on, so its state as a path of action might not have been stated. For the nature of intention as action is manifest from such statements as, 'Monks, I say that intention is action' (A. Ni. 6.63; Kathā. 539), and 'Monks, bodily intention is threefold as unwholesome bodily action' (Kathā. 539). Moreover, it is action itself, proceeding as the path to good and bad destinies and to the happiness and suffering arising therein, that is called a 'path of action'; thus its nature as a path of action is manifest. For covetousness and the like, however, their nature as good or bad conduct by being the object of intention's striving, and their nature as the path to good and bad destinies and the happiness and suffering arising therein by being a support generated by intention, is not so manifest. Therefore, in order to show just those with that nature, intention is not mentioned in the Abhidhamma as part of the group of paths of action; or, it should be understood that intention is not mentioned together with them because it is of a different kind. 'Having reached the root' means having reached the teaching on the roots, that is, when phenomena are being spoken of in their root-nature; this is the meaning.

Adinnādānaṃ sattārammaṇanti idaṃ “pañca sikkhāpadā parittārammaṇā eva vā”ti imāya pañhapucchakapāḷiyā virujjhati. Yañhi pāṇātipātādidussīlyassa ārammaṇaṃ, tadeva taṃ veramaṇiyā ārammaṇaṃ. Vītikkamitabbavatthuto eva hi viratīti. Sattārammaṇanti vā sattasaṅkhātaṃ saṅkhārārammaṇameva upādāya vuttanti nāyaṃ virodho. Tathā hi vuttaṃ sammohavinodaniyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 714) “yāni sikkhāpadāni ettha sattārammaṇānīti vuttāni, tāni yasmā sattoti saṅkhyaṃ gataṃ saṅkhārameva ārammaṇaṃ karontī”ti. Visabhāgavatthuno “itthī, puriso”ti gahetabbato sattārammaṇoti eke. “Eko diṭṭho, dve sutā”tiādinā samphappalapane diṭṭhasutamutaviññātavasena. Tathā abhijjhāti ettha tathā-saddo “diṭṭhasutamutaviññātavasenā”ti idampi upasaṃharati, na sattasaṅkhārārammaṇataṃ eva dassanādivasena abhijjhāyanato. “Natthi sattā opapātikā”ti pavattamānāpi micchādiṭṭhi [M 1.0305] tebhūmakadhammavisayāvāti adhippāyenassā saṅkhārārammaṇatā vuttā. Kathaṃ pana micchādiṭṭhiyā sabbe tebhūmakadhammā ārammaṇaṃ hontīti? Sādhāraṇato. “Natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko”ti hi pavattamānāya atthato rūpārupāvacaradhammāpi gahitā eva hontīti.

The statement, 'Taking what is not given has beings as its object,' contradicts the Pāli passage of question and answer: 'Are the five training rules of limited object only?' For the object of immoral conduct such as killing living beings is the same as the object of abstaining from it. Indeed, abstinence is from the object that is to be transgressed. Alternatively, 'having beings as its object' is said with reference to the object of formations designated as 'beings'; thus there is no contradiction. As it is stated in the Sammohavinodanī (Vibha. Aṭṭha. 714): 'Those training rules which are said here to have beings as their object are so because they take as their object formations that are reckoned as 'beings.'' Some say it has beings as its object because a dissimilar object is grasped as 'a woman' or 'a man.' In frivolous talk, such as 'one was seen, two were heard,' it is by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. Similarly, regarding 'covetousness,' the word 'tathā' also connects this phrase, 'by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized'; this is because one covets by way of seeing, etc., not only things that have formations designated as beings for their object. Even the wrong view that arises as 'there are no spontaneously arisen beings' is said to have formations as its object with the meaning that its scope is the phenomena of the three planes. But how do all phenomena of the three planes become the object of wrong view? In a general way. For when the view arises, 'There is no fruit or result of good and bad actions,' then in meaning, the phenomena of the form and formless spheres are indeed included.

Sukhabahulatāya rājāno hasamānāpi “coraṃ ghātethā”ti vadanti, hāso pana tesaṃ aññavisayoti āha “sanniṭṭhāpaka…pe… hotī”ti.

Due to their abundance of pleasure, kings, even while laughing, say, 'Kill the thief,' but their laughter concerns a different matter. Hence it is said, 'The decisive... and so on... is.'

Kesañcīti sahajātānaṃ adinnādānādīnaṃ. Sampayuttapabhāvakaṭṭhenāti sampayutto hutvā uppādakaṭṭhena. Kesañcīti asahajātānaṃ. Upanissayapaccayaṭṭhenāti etena mūlaṭṭhena lobhassa upakārataṃ nivatteti. Suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanaṭṭho hi mūlaṭṭho, so ca hetupaccayatāavinābhāvī, tena cettha mūlamiva mūlanti gahetabbaṃ, nippariyāyato pana pubbe “kesañcī”ti vuttānaṃ sahajātānaṃ mūlabhāvo veditabbo. Ratto khotiādinā suttapadenapi pāṇātipātādīnaṃ akusalānaṃ lobhassa mūlakāraṇataṃ vibhāveti, na mūlaṭṭhenupakāratthaṃ avisesato tesaṃ hetupaccayattābhāvato.

'Of some' refers to co-arisen states such as taking what is not given, etc. 'By the quality of being associated and productive' means by having the quality of producing while being associated. 'Of some' refers to states that are not co-arisen. 'By the quality of being a decisive support condition': by this, it refutes the helpfulness of greed in the sense of a root. For the meaning of 'root' is the function of establishing a firm basis, and that is inseparable from being a root-condition. Therefore, here 'root' should be taken as 'like a root.' In the direct sense, however, the root-nature of those co-arisen states mentioned earlier by 'of some' should be understood. By the Sutta phrase 'One who is greedy...' and so on, it also clarifies that greed is the root cause of unwholesome actions such as killing living beings, not that it is helpful in the sense of a root, because for them there is no indiscriminate state of being a root-condition.

Akusalakammapathavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the unwholesome paths of action is concluded.

Kusalakammapathavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Wholesome Paths of Action

Veranti [V 1.0272] pāṇātipātādipāpadhammaṃ. So hi verahetutāya “vera”nti vuccati, taṃ maṇati “mayi idha ṭhitāya kathamāgacchasī”ti tajjentī viya nivāretīti veramaṇī. Tenāha “pajahatī”ti. “Viramaṇī”ti vattabbe niruttinayena eva-kāraṃ katvā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Vibhaṅge (vibha. 703, 704) eva niddisanavasena evaṃ vuttā. Asamādinnasīlassa sampattato yathāupaṭṭhitavītikkamitabbavatthuto virati sampattavirati, samādānavasena uppannā virati samādānavirati, samādānavasena uppannā virati samādānavirati, kilesānaṃ samucchindanavasena pavattāvirati samucchedavirati.

'Vera' refers to the evil state such as killing living beings. Because it is a cause of enmity (vera), it is called 'vera.' That which wards it off, as if threatening it, saying, 'While I am here, how can you approach?', is 'veramaṇī' (abstinence). Therefore, it is said, 'one abandons.' Although 'viramaṇī' is the correct form, it is stated as 'veramaṇī' by changing the vowel to 'e' according to etymological method. In the Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 703, 704), it is stated thus by way of simple indication. For one who has not undertaken the precepts, the abstinence from an object of transgression that has presented itself is 'abstinence by encounter' (sampattavirati). The abstinence that arises by way of undertaking the precepts is 'abstinence by undertaking' (samādānavirati). The abstinence that proceeds by way of eradicating the defilements is 'abstinence by eradication' (samucchedavirati).

Jīvamānasasassa [M 1.0306] maṃsarudhirasammissatāya allasasamaṃsaṃ. Muñci sabbattha samakaruṇatāya. Saccaṃ vatvā “etena saccavajjena mayhaṃ mātu rogo sammatū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi.

The flesh of a living being, being mixed with blood and moisture, is like raw flesh. He released it with equal compassion for all. Having spoken the truth, he made a resolution: 'By this declaration of truth, may my mother's illness be pacified.'

Mahāsappoti ajagaro. Muñcitvā agamāsi sīlatejena.

'Mahāsappa' means a python. Having released it, he departed through the power of his virtue.

Kosallaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ, kosallena, kosallato vā pavattiyā upagamanato. Kucchitasayanatoti kucchitenākārena sayanato anusayanato, pavattanato vā. “Veramaṇikusalā”ti vattabbāpi pucchānurūpaṃ vissajjananti “kusalā”ti na vuttā, “kusala”ntveva vuttā.

Skill is called knowledge; it is so called from skill, or from proceeding with skill. 'From bad lying' means from lying in a bad manner, from latent tendency, or from proceeding. Although 'skilled in abstinence' could be said, in answering according to the question, 'skilled' is not said, but only 'skill' is said.

Kāmañcettha pāḷiyaṃ viratiyova āgatā, sikkhāpadavibhaṅge (vibha. 704) pana cetanāpi āharitvā dīpitāti tadubhayampi gaṇhanto “cetanāpi vaṭṭanti viratiyopī”ti āha.

Although here in the Pāli text only abstinences are mentioned, in the Analysis of the Training Rules (Vibh. 704), intention is also brought in and explained. Therefore, taking both into account, he said, 'Both intention and abstinences are proper.'

Anabhijjhā hi mūlaṃ patvā kammapathakoṭṭhāsaṃ patvā anabhijjhāti vuttadhammo mūlato alobho kusalamūlaṃ hotīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo.

The meaning of the phenomenon called non-covetousness, which has reached the status of a root and the category of a course of action, should be understood thus: as a root, it is non-greed, a wholesome root. This same method applies to the remaining two terms as well.

Dussīlyārammaṇā tadārammaṇā jīvitindriyādiārammaṇā kathaṃ dussīlyāni pajahantīti taṃ dassetuṃ “yathā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

How do they abandon immoral conduct, when having immoral conduct as their object, having that as their object, or having the life faculty and so on as their object? To show this, the passage beginning 'But just as...' was said.

Anabhijjhā [V 1.0273] …pe… viramantassāti abhijjhaṃ pajahantassāti attho. Na hi manoduccaritato virati atthi anabhijjhādīheva tappahānasiddhito. Tesu alobhotiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ akusalamūlesu vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

'...for one who abstains' means for one who abandons covetousness. For there is no abstinence from mental misconduct, since its abandonment is accomplished precisely by non-covetousness and so on. Whatever should be said regarding non-greed and so on should be understood in the same way as was explained in the section on the unwholesome roots.

Appanāvāranti nigamanavāraṃ. Ekena nayenāti vedanādivasena arūpamukheneva anekavidhesu vipassanākammaṭṭhānesu ekena kammaṭṭhānanayena. “Ṭhapetvā abhijjhaṃ nava akusalakammapathā”ti vattabbaṃ. Dasāti vā idaṃ “kusalakammapathā”ti iminā sambandhitabbaṃ “akusalakammapathā ca dasa kusalakammapathā cā”ti. “Ṭhapetvā abhijjha”nti hi imināva akusalakammapathānaṃ navabhāvo vutto hoti. Atha vā dasāti idaṃ ubhayathāpi sambandhitabbaṃ. Abhijjhā hi pahātabbāpi sati pariññeyyataṃ nātivattatīti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “rūpataṇhā piyarūpaṃ sātarūpa”ntiādi, tasmā [M 1.0307] sā tāya pariññeyyatāya dukkhasaccepi saṅgahaṃ labhateva, pahātabbaṃ pana upādāya “ṭhapetvā abhijjha”nti vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “pariyāyena pana sabbepi kammapathā dukkhasacca”nti. Abhijjhālobhānaṃ pavattiākārasiddhabhedaṃ upādāya “ime dve dhammā”ti vuttaṃ. Suttantanayena taṇhā “samudayasacca”nti vuttāti āha “nippariyāyena samudayasacca”nti. Appavattīti appavattinimittamāha yathā “rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.314). Sappaccayatāya saṅkhatasabhāve dukkhasacce gahite appaccayatāya asaṅkhataṃ nirodhasaccaṃ paṭipakkhato āvattati, ekantasāvajje ācayagāmilakkhaṇe samudayasacce gahite sāvajjā vigamanaṃ apacayagāmilakkhaṇaṃ maggasaccaṃpaṭipakkhato āvattatīti dve āvattahāravasena veditabbānīti vuttaṃ. Tenevāha nettiyaṃ (netti. 4.niddesavāra) –

'Appanāvāra' means the concluding section. 'By one method' means, among the various subjects of insight meditation, by one method of meditation subject, by way of feeling and so on, through the approach of the formless. 'Excluding covetousness, there are nine unwholesome courses of action' should be said. Or, this 'ten' should be connected with 'wholesome courses of action,' thus: 'the ten unwholesome courses of action and the ten wholesome courses of action.' For by saying 'excluding covetousness,' the ninefold nature of the unwholesome courses of action is stated. Alternatively, this 'ten' can be connected in both ways. For covetousness, even when it is to be abandoned, does not go beyond what is to be fully understood. Thus it is said: 'Craving for form is a dear form, a delightful form,' and so on. Therefore, because it is to be fully understood, it is included even in the truth of suffering. But with regard to what is to be abandoned, it is said 'excluding covetousness.' For that reason, it is said: 'But indirectly, all courses of action are the truth of suffering.' With reference to the established distinction in the mode of occurrence of covetousness and greed, it is said: 'These two phenomena.' According to the Suttanta method, craving is called 'the truth of origin'; hence it is said: 'Directly, the truth of origin.' 'Non-occurrence' refers to the sign of non-occurrence, as in 'the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.314). When the truth of suffering, which has a conditioned nature due to having a cause, is grasped, the truth of cessation, which is unconditioned due to not having a cause, is turned to as its opposite. When the truth of origin, characterized by accumulation and being entirely faulty, is grasped, the truth of the path, characterized by the removal of what is faulty and leading to decrease, is turned to as its opposite. Thus, it is said that two truths are to be understood by way of the 'turning' method. Hence it is said in the Netti (Netti 4, Niddesavāra):

“Ekamhi padaṭṭhāne, pariyesati sesakaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ;

Āvattati paṭipakkhe, āvatto nāma so hāro”ti.

'When in one basis, one seeks the remaining basis; one turns to the opposite—that method is called 'turning'.'

Sabbākārenāti kāmarāgarūparāgādisabbappakārehi, sabbato vā apāyagamanīyādiākārato, tattha kiñcipi anavasesetvā vā. Sabbākārenevāti sabbākārato. Nīharitvāti apanetvā, samucchinditvāicceva attho. Kañci dhammaṃ anavakārīkaritvāti rūpavedanādīsu kañci ekadhammampi avinibbhogaṃ katvā, ekekato aggahetvā samūhatova gahetvāti attho. Asmīti ahamasmīti mānaggāhavasena. So pana yasmā pañcakkhandhe niravasesato gaṇhāti, tasmā vuttaṃ “samūhaggahaṇākārenā”ti. Yasmā cettha aggamaggacittaṃ vuccati, tasmā āha “diṭṭhisadisaṃ mānānusaya”nti. “Yaṃ rūpaṃ taṃ aha”ntiādinā [V 1.0274] yathā diṭṭhi rūpādiṃ “ahamasmī”ti gaṇhantī pavattati, evaṃ mānopi “seyyohamasmī”tiādināti āha “mānānusayo asmīti pavattattā diṭṭhisadiso”ti. Paricchedakaroti osānaparicchedakaro ito paraṃ dukkhassābhāvakaraṇato. Kammapathadesanāyāti kammapathamukhena pavattacatusaccadesanāya. Manasikārappaṭivedhavasenāti vipassanāmanasikāramaggappaṭivedhavasena.

'In every way' means in all ways, such as sensual desire, desire for form, and so on; or from every aspect, such as leading to states of loss; or leaving nothing whatsoever remaining. 'In every way' means from all aspects. 'Having removed' means having taken away, or rather, having eradicated—this is the meaning. 'Without making an exception of any phenomenon' means not having made any single phenomenon among form, feeling, and so on separate, not grasping them one by one, but grasping them as a group—this is the meaning. 'I am' means through the grasp of conceit that 'I am.' Since this grasps the five aggregates without remainder, it is said, 'in the manner of grasping as a group.' Because the mind of the highest path is meant here, it is said, 'the latent tendency of conceit is similar to wrong view.' Just as wrong view proceeds by grasping form and so on as 'I am,' so too conceit proceeds with 'I am superior,' and so on. Hence it is said, 'the latent tendency of conceit is similar to wrong view because it proceeds as "I am".' 'Maker of the boundary' means maker of the final boundary, because from this point on it brings about the non-existence of suffering. 'By the teaching on the course of action' means by the teaching on the Four Truths that proceeds by way of the course of action. 'By way of the penetration of attention' means by way of the penetration of the path through the attention of insight.

Kusalakammapathavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the section on the wholesome courses of action is concluded.

Āhāravāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section on Nutriment

90. Āharatīti [M 1.0308] (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.2.11) āneti, uppādeti upatthambheti cāti attho. Nibbattāti pasutā. Tato paṭṭhāya hi loke jātavohāro. Paṭisandhiggahaṇato pana paṭṭhāya yāva mātukucchito nikkhamanaṃ, tāva sambhavesino. Esa tāva gabbhaseyyakesu bhūtasambhavesivibhāgo, itaresu pana paṭhamacittādivasena vutto. Sambhava-saddo cettha gabbhaseyyakānaṃ vasena pasūtipariyāyo, itaresaṃ vasena uppattipariyāyo. Paṭhamacittapaṭhamairiyāpathakkhaṇesu hi te sambhavaṃ uppattiṃ esanti upagacchanti nāma, na tāva bhūtā uppattiyā na suppatiṭṭhitattā. Bhūtāyeva sabbaso bhavesanāya samucchinnattā. Na puna bhavissantīti avadhāraṇena nivattitamatthaṃ dasseti, “yo ca kālaghaso bhūto”tiādīsu (jā. 1.2.190) bhūta-saddassa khīṇāsavavācitā daṭṭhabbā. Vā-saddo cettha sampiṇḍanattho “agginā vā udakena vā”tiādīsu (udā. 76) viya.

90. 'Āharati' (Saṃ. Ni. Ṭīkā 2.2.11) means it brings, it produces, and it supports. 'Born' (nibbattā) means produced (pasutā). For from that point onward, the designation 'born' is used in the world. But from the taking of relinking-consciousness until emergence from the mother's womb, they are 'seekers of becoming' (sambhavesino). This, for now, is the distinction between 'become' (bhūta) and 'seeking to become' (sambhavesin) in the case of womb-born beings. For others, however, it is explained by way of the first consciousness and so on. Here, the word 'sambhava' is a synonym for birth in the case of womb-born beings, and a synonym for arising in the case of others. For at the moments of the first consciousness and the first posture, they are said to seek and attain 'sambhava' or arising, but they are not yet 'become' (bhūtā) because their arising is not well-established. Those who are truly 'become' are so because the seeking for becoming has been entirely cut off. The determination 'they will not become again' shows a meaning that has ceased. In passages like 'and one who, become, consumes time' (Jā. 1.2.190), the word 'bhūta' should be seen as denoting one whose cankers are destroyed. Here, the word 'vā' has a collective sense, as in 'by fire or by water' (Ud. 76).

Yathāsakaṃ paccayabhāvena attabhāvassa paṭṭhapanamevetthaāhārehi kātabbaanuggahoti adhippāyenāha “vacanabhedo…pe… ekoyevā”ti. Sattassa uppannadhammānanti sattassasantāne uppannadhammānaṃ. Yathā “vassasataṃ tiṭṭhatī”ti vutte anuppabandhavasena pavattatīti vuttaṃ hoti, evaṃ ṭhitiyāti anuppabandhavasena pavattiyāti attho, sā pana avicchedoti āha “avicchedāyā”ti. Anuppabandhadhammuppattiyā sattasantāno anuggahito nāma hotīti āha “anuppannānaṃ uppādāyā”ti. Etānīti ṭhitianuggahapadāni. Ubhayattha daṭṭhabbāni, na yathāsaṅkhyaṃ.

With the intention that the support to be given here by nutriments is precisely the establishment of individual existence through their respective causal function, he said: 'A difference in wording... it is just one.' 'Of the arisen phenomena of a being' means of the phenomena arisen in the continuum of a being. Just as when it is said, 'It lasts for a hundred years,' it means it proceeds by way of continuity, so 'for stability' means for proceeding by way of continuity. But that continuity is non-interruption, hence he said 'for non-interruption.' By the arising of continuous phenomena, the continuum of a being is said to be supported; hence he said, 'for the arising of the unarisen.' 'These' refers to the terms 'stability' and 'support.' They are to be understood in both cases, not respectively.

Vatthugatā [V 1.0275] ojā vatthu viya tena saddhiṃ āharitabbataṃ gacchatīti vuttaṃ “ajjhoharitabbato āhāro”ti. Nibbattitaojaṃ pana sandhāya “kabaḷīkārāhāro ojaṭṭhamakarūpāni āharatī”ti vakkhati. Oḷārikatā appojatāya, na vatthuno thūlatāya, kathinatāya vā, tasmā yasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ parittā ojā hoti, taṃ oḷārikaṃ. Sappādayo dukkhuppādakatāya oḷārikāveditabbā. Visāṇādīnaṃ tivassachaḍḍitānaṃ pūtibhūttatā mudukatāti vadanti, taracchakheḷatemikatāya pana tathābhūtānaṃ tesaṃ mudukatā. Dhammasabhāvo hesa. Sasānaṃ [M 1.0309] āhāro sukhumo taruṇatiṇasassakhādanato. Sakuṇānaṃ āhāro sukhumo tiṇabījādikhādanato. Paccantavāsīnaṃ sukhumo, tesañhi sākapaṇṇasukkhakurapadumapattampi āhāroti. Tesaṃ paranimmitavasavattīnaṃ. Sukhumotvevāti na kiñci upādāya, atha kho sukhumo icceva niṭṭhaṃ patto tato paraṃ sukhumassa abhāvato.

The nutriment inherent in the substance is said to be ‘food to be swallowed’ because it goes along with the substance, like the substance itself. But regarding the nutriment that is produced, it will be said, ‘Edible food brings about the material phenomena that have nutriment as their eighth factor.’ Coarseness is due to having little nutriment, not due to the grossness of the substance, or its hardness; therefore, whatever substance has little nutriment, that is coarse. Snakes and so on should be known as coarse because they cause the arising of suffering. They say that horns and so on, discarded for three years, become soft due to putrefaction. But the softness of those things, being moist with a hyena’s saliva, is of that kind. Such is the nature of things. The food of rabbits is subtle because they eat tender shoots of grass. The food of birds is subtle because they eat grass seeds and so on. The food of border-dwellers is subtle, for leaves of vegetables, dried boiled rice, or even lotus leaves are food for them. For those in the Paranimmitavasavatti realm, it is subtle indeed. ‘Subtle indeed’ means that it is not in relation to anything, but rather it has reached the limit of ‘subtle,’ because beyond that there is no further subtlety.

Vatthuvasena panettha āhārassa oḷārikasukhumatā vuttā, sā cassa appojamahojatāhi veditabbāti dassetuṃ “ettha cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Parissamanti khudāvasena uppannaṃ sarīrakhedaṃ. Vinodetīti vatthu tassa vinodanamattaṃ karoti. Na pana sakkoti pāletunti sarīraṃ yāpetuṃ nappahoti nissārattā. Na sakkoti parissamaṃ vinodetuṃ āmāsayassa apūraṇato.

Here, the coarseness and subtlety of food are mentioned in terms of substance; and to show that this should be understood through its slight or great quantity of nutriment, the phrase ‘and here’ and so on was stated. ‘Fatigue’ means bodily exhaustion arising from hunger. ‘Alleviates’ means the substance merely brings about its alleviation. ‘But it cannot sustain’ means it is not able to maintain the body because it is without essence. It cannot relieve fatigue because the stomach is not filled.

Chabbidhopīti iminā kassacipi phassassa anavasesitabbatamāha. Āhārassadesanākkamenevettha phassādīnaṃ dutiyāditā, na aññena kāraṇenāti āha “desanānayo evā”tiādi. Manaso sañcetanā, na sattassāti dassanatthaṃ manogahaṇaṃ yathā “cittassa ṭhiti (dha. sa. 11), cetovimutti cā”ti (ma. ni. 1.69) āha “manosañcetanāti cetanā evā”ti. Cittanti yaṃ kiñci cittaṃ, na vipākaviññāṇameva.

By ‘even of six kinds,’ it states that no contact whatsoever is omitted. That contact and the others are second, and so on, is here due only to the sequence of teaching the nutriments, and not for any other reason; thus it is said, ‘The method of teaching is just this,’ and so on. The word ‘mind’ is included to show that this is the volition of the mind, not of a being, just as in ‘the stability of mind’ (Dhs 11) and ‘liberation of mind’ (MN I 69). Thus it is said, ‘Mental volition is volition itself.’ ‘Consciousness’ means any consciousness whatsoever, not just resultant consciousness.

Pubbe “āhāranti paccaya”nti vuttattā “yadi paccayaṭṭho āhāraṭṭho”tiādinā codeti. Atha kasmā imeyeva cattāro vuttāti atha kasmā cattārova vuttā, ime eva ca vuttāti yojanā. Visesapaccayattāti etena yathā aññe paccayadhammā attano paccayuppannassa paccayāva honti, ime pana tathā ca honti aññathā cāti samānepi paccayatte atirekapaccayā honti, tasmā āhārāti vuttāti imamatthaṃ dasseti. Idāni taṃ atirekapaccayataṃ dassetuṃ “visesapaccayo hī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Visesapaccayo rūpakāyassa kabaḷīkāro āhāro upatthambhakabhāvato. Tenāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (visuddhi. 2.708; paṭṭhā. aṭṭha. paccayuddesavaṇṇanā) “rūpārūpānaṃ upatthambhakattena upakārakā cattāro āhārā āhārapaccayo”ti. Upatthambhakattañhi [V 1.0276] satipi janakatte arūpīnaṃ āhārānaṃ āhārajarūpasamuṭṭhāpakarūpāhārassa [M 1.0310] ca hoti, asati pana upatthambhakatte āhārānaṃ janakattaṃ natthīti upatthambhakattaṃ padhānaṃ. Janayamānopi hi āhāro avicchedavasena upatthambhayamāno eva janetīti upattambhakabhāvo eva āhārabhāvo. Vedanāya phasso visesapaccayo. “Phassapaccayā vedanā”ti hi vuttaṃ. “Saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”nti (udā. 1; ma. ni. 3.126) vacanato viññāṇassamanosañcetanā. “Cetanā tividhaṃ bhavaṃ janetī”ti hi vuttaṃ. “Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti pana vacanato nāmarūpassa viññāṇaṃ visesapaccayā. Na hi okkantiviññāṇābhāve nāmarūpassa attasambhavo. Yathāha “viññāṇañca hi, ānanda, mātukucchismiṃ na okkamissatha, api nu kho nāmarūpaṃ mātukucchismiṃ samuccissathā”tiādi (dī. ni. 2.115). Vuttamevatthaṃ suttena sādhetuṃ “yathāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Because it was previously said, ‘Nutriment means condition,’ one raises the objection, ‘If the meaning of food is the meaning of condition,’ and so on. ‘Then why are only these four mentioned?’ The construction is: then why are only four mentioned, and why these ones? By ‘because of being a special condition,’ this meaning is shown: just as other conditioning phenomena are merely conditions for their respective conditioned phenomena, these are so and are also otherwise. Thus, even while being the same in being a condition, they are additional conditions; therefore they are called ‘nutriments.’ Now, to show that state of being an additional condition, the passage beginning ‘For it is a special condition’ is commenced. Edible food is a special condition for the material body because of its state of being a support. Therefore it is said in the commentary (Vism 2.708; Paṭṭh-a, Paccayuddesavaṇṇanā): ‘The four nutriments are the nutriment condition because they are helpful by supporting material and immaterial phenomena.’ For the state of being a support exists even when there is the state of being a generator for the immaterial nutriments and for the material nutriment that originates nutriment-born matter. But when the state of being a support is absent, the nutriments have no state of being a generator; thus the state of being a support is primary. For even while generating, a nutriment generates only while supporting without interruption. Thus, the state of being a support is itself the state of being a nutriment. Contact is a special condition for feeling, for it is said, ‘With contact as condition, feeling.’ In accordance with ‘With formations as condition, consciousness’ (Ud 1; MN III 126), mental volition is a special condition for consciousness. For it is said, ‘Volition generates the three kinds of becoming.’ And in accordance with ‘With consciousness as condition, mentality-materiality,’ consciousness is a special condition for mentality-materiality. For in the absence of the consciousness that descends, there is no arising of mentality-materiality on its own. As it is said: ‘And if, Ānanda, consciousness were not to descend into the mother’s womb, would mentality-materiality take shape in the mother’s womb?’ and so on (DN II 115). To establish this same meaning by means of a sutta, the passage beginning ‘As it is said’ is stated.

Evaṃ yadipi paccayaṭṭho āhāraṭṭho, visesapaccayatāya pana ime eva āhārāti vuttāti taṃ nesaṃ visesapaccayataṃ avibhāgato dassetvā idāni vibhāgato dassetuṃ “ko panetthā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Mukhe ṭhapitamattoyeva asaṅkhādito, tattakenapi abbhantarassa āhārassa paccayo hoti eva. Tenāha “aṭṭha rūpāni samuṭṭhāpetī”ti. Sukhavedanāya hito sukhavedaniyo. Sabbathāpīti cakkhusamphassādivasena. Yattakā phassassa pakārabhedā, tesaṃ vasena sabbappakāropi phassāhāro. Yathārahaṃ tisso vedanā āharati, anāhārako natthi.

Thus, although the meaning of condition is the meaning of food, it is because of their being a special condition that these alone are called ‘nutriments.’ Having shown their state of being a special condition without distinction, now, to show it with distinction, the passage beginning ‘But what here?’ is commenced. As soon as it is placed in the mouth, unchewed, even by that much it becomes a condition for the internal nutriment. Therefore, it is said, ‘It originates eight kinds of material phenomena.’ It is conducive to pleasant feeling because it is beneficial for pleasant feeling. ‘In every way’ means by way of eye-contact and so on. Whatever variations of mode there are of contact, by way of them, every mode of contact is the nutriment of contact. As is appropriate, it brings the three kinds of feelings; there is no one without nutriment.

Sabbathāpīti idhāpi phassāhāre vuttanayānusārena attho veditabbo. Tisantativasenāti kāyadasakaṃ bhāvadasakaṃ vatthudasakanti tividhasantativasena. Sahajātādipaccayanayenāti sahajātādipaccayavidhinā. Paṭisandhiviññāṇañhi attanā sahajātanāmassa sahajātaaññamaññanissayavipākindriyasampayuttaatthiavigatapaccayehi paccayo hontoyeva āhārapaccayatāya taṃ āhāretī vuttaṃ, sahajātarūpesu pana vatthuno sampayuttapaccayaṃ ṭhapetvā vippayuttapaccayena, sesarūpassa aññamaññapaccayañca ṭhapetvā vuttanayenevayojanā kātabbā. Tānīti napuṃsakaniddeso anapuṃsakānampi napuṃsakehi saha vacanato.

‘In every way’: here, too, the meaning should be understood according to the method stated regarding the nutriment of contact. ‘By way of the threefold continuity’ means by way of the threefold continuity: the body-decad, the sex-decad, and the base-decad. ‘By the method of conditions such as co-nascence’ means by the principle of conditions such as co-nascence. For rebirth-consciousness, while being a condition for its co-nascent mentality by way of the conditions of co-nascence, mutuality, dependence, result, faculty, association, presence, and non-disappearance, is said to nourish it by way of the nutriment condition. However, regarding co-nascent material phenomena, the connection should be made according to the stated method by way of the disassociation condition, having set aside the association condition for the base, and having also set aside the mutuality condition for the remaining material phenomena. ‘Those’ (tāni) is a neuter designation because even non-neuter terms are spoken of together with neuter terms.

Sāsavā [M 1.0311] kusalākusalacetanāva vuttā. Visesapaccayabhāvadassanaṃ hetanti. Tenāha “avisesena panā”tiādi. Paṭisandhiviññāṇameva vuttanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Yathā tassa tassa phalassa visesato paccayatāya etesaṃ āhāraṭṭho, evaṃ avisesatopīti dassantena “avisesena panā”tiādi [V 1.0277] vuttaṃ. Tattha taṃsampayuttataṃsamuṭṭhānadhammānanti tehi phassādīhi sampayuttadhammānañceva taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpadhammānañca. Tattha sampayuttaggahaṇaṃ yathārahato daṭṭhabbaṃ, samuṭṭhānaggahaṇaṃ pana avisesato.

Tainted wholesome and unwholesome volitions themselves are stated. The reason is the showing of the state of being a special condition. Therefore, it says, ‘But without distinction,’ and so on. ‘Rebirth-consciousness itself is stated’—here too, this is the same method. To show that just as these have the meaning of nutriment by being a condition specifically for this or that fruit, so too do they have it without distinction, the passage beginning ‘But without distinction’ was stated. Therein, ‘of the phenomena associated with them and arisen from them’ means of both the phenomena associated with those things beginning with contact, and of the material phenomena arisen from them. Therein, the inclusion of ‘associated’ should be understood as is appropriate, but the inclusion of ‘arisen’ is without distinction.

Upatthambhento āhārakiccaṃ sādhetīti upatthambhentoyeva rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, ojaṭṭhamakarūpasamuṭṭhāpaneneva panassa upatthambhanakiccasiddhi. Phusantoyevāti phusanakiccaṃ karonto eva. Āyūhamānāvāti cetayamānā eva abhisandahantī eva. Vijānantamevāti upapattiparikappanavasena vijānantameva āhārakiccaṃ sādhetīti yojanā. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Āhārakiccasādhanañca tesaṃ vedanādiuppattihetutāya attabhāvassa pavattanameva.

Supporting, it fulfills the function of nutriment—thus, by merely supporting, it produces form. By the very production of matter with nutriment as the eighth factor, its function of support is accomplished. 'Touching, indeed,' means performing the function of contact. 'Accumulating, indeed,' means intending, indeed, conjoining, indeed. 'Knowing, indeed,' means that by way of conceptualizing rebirth, it fulfills the function of nutriment—this is the interpretation. The same method applies to the remaining two terms. The accomplishment of the function of nutriment for them is simply the continuation of individual existence, since it is the cause for the arising of feeling and so forth.

Kāyaṭṭhapanenāti kasmā vuttaṃ? Nanu kammajādirūpaṃ kammādināva pavattatīti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “kammajanitopī”tiādi. Upādinnarūpasantatiyā upatthambhaneneva utucittajarūpasantatīnampi upatthambhanasiddhi hotīti “dvinnaṃ rūpasantatīna”nti vuttaṃ. Upatthambhanameva sandhāya “anupālako hutvā”ti ca vuttaṃ. Rūpakāyassa ṭhitihetutā hi yāpanā anupālanā.

'Why was it said, 'by the establishing of the body'?' 'Is it not the case that kamma-born matter and so forth arise solely through kamma and so forth?'—with reference to this objection, it is said, 'Even kamma-produced...' and so on. By supporting the continuity of grasped matter, the support for the continuities of temperature-born and mind-born matter is also accomplished; hence it is said, 'of the two continuities of matter.' Referring to supporting alone, 'being a maintainer' was also said. For the cause of the stability of the material body is indeed sustaining and maintaining.

Sukhādivatthubhūtanti sukhādīnaṃ pavattiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ. Ārammaṇampi hi vasati ettha ārammaṇakaraṇavasena tadārammaṇā dhammāti vatthūti vuccati. Phusantoyevāti idaṃ phassassa phusanasabhāvattā vuttaṃ. Na hi dhammānaṃ sabhāvena vinā pavatti atthi. Vedanāpavattiyā vinā sattānaṃ sandhāvanatā natthīti āha “sukhādi…pe… hotī”ti, na cettha saññībhavakathāyaṃ asaññībhavo dassetabbo, tassāpi vā kāraṇabhūtavedanāpavattivaseneva ṭhitiyā hetuno abyāpitā. Tathā hi “manosañcetanā…pe… bhavamūlanipphādanato sattānaṃ ṭhitiyā hotī”ti vuttā, tato eva “viññāṇaṃ vijānantamevāti upapattiparikappanavasena vijānantamevā”ti vuttovāyamatthoti.

'It serves as the basis for pleasure, etc.,' means it is the ground for the arising of pleasure and so forth. For even an object is called a 'basis' because mental states that have that object as their object reside in it by way of making it an object. 'By contact alone'—this is said because contact has the nature of touching. Indeed, there is no arising of phenomena without their own intrinsic nature. Without the arising of feeling, beings would not wander on; hence it is said, 'pleasure, etc., exists.' Here, in the discussion of the state of perception, the state of non-perception should not be demonstrated, for the stability of even that state is due to the arising of feeling which is its cause; hence, the cause is not un-pervaded. Thus, it is said, 'Through mental volition... by producing the root of existence, it is for the stability of beings,' and from that, 'consciousness cognizes'—that is, 'consciousness cognizes by way of conceptualizing rebirth'—this is the meaning that has been stated.

Cattāri [M 1.0312] bhayāni daṭṭhabbāni ādīnavavibhāvanato. Nikantīti nikāmanā. Rasataṇhaṃ sandhāya vadati. Sā hi kabaḷīkāre āhāre balavatī. Teneva tattha avadhāraṇaṃ kataṃ. Bhāyati etasmāti bhayaṃ, nikantiyevabhayaṃ mahānatthahetuto. Upagamanaṃ visayindriyaviññāṇesu visayaviññāṇesu eva ca saṅgativasena pavatti, taṃ vedanādiuppattihetutāya “bhaya”nti vuttaṃ. Avadhāraṇe payojanaṃ vuttanayameva. Sesadvayepi esevanayo. Āyūhanaṃ abhisandahanaṃ, saṃvidhānantipi [V 1.0278] vadanti. Taṃ bhavūpapattihetutāya “bhaya”nti vuttaṃ. Abhinipāto tattha tattha bhave paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena nibbatti. So bhavūpapattihetukānaṃ sabbesaṃ anatthānaṃ mūlakāraṇattā “bhaya”nti vutto. Idāni nikantiādīnaṃ sappaṭibhayataṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “kiṃkāraṇā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha nikantiṃ katvāti ālayaṃ janetvā, taṇhaṃ uppādetvāti attho.

Four dangers should be seen by way of explaining the drawbacks. 'Craving' (nikanti) means intense desire. This is said with reference to craving for tastes, for it is powerful in the case of edible food. Therefore, emphasis is placed there. One is afraid of it, thus it is 'fear' (bhaya); craving itself is fear because it is the cause of great harm. 'Approach' is the occurrence by way of association in sense-objects, sense-organs, and consciousnesses, and in sense-objects and consciousnesses alone; it is called 'fear' because it is the cause for the arising of feeling, etc. The purpose of the emphasis is as previously stated. The same method applies to the remaining two. 'Accumulation' is conjoining; they also call it contrivance. It is called 'fear' because it is the cause of existence and rebirth. 'Plunging' is arising by way of taking rebirth-linking in various existences. It is called 'fear' because it is the root cause of all harms that are caused by existence and rebirth. Now, to show in detail the fearful nature of craving, etc., the passage beginning 'For what reason?' has been started. There, 'having made craving' means generating clinging, that is, arousing craving.

Phassa upagacchantāti cakkhusamphassādibhedaṃ phassaṃ pavattentā. Phassassādinoti kāyasamphassavasena phoṭṭabbasaṅkhātassa phassassa assādanasīlā. Kāyasamphassavasena hi sattānaṃ phoṭṭhabbataṇhā pavattatīti dassetuṃ phassāhārādīnavadassane phoṭṭhabbārammaṇaṃ uddhaṭaṃ “paresaṃ rakkhitagopitesū”tiādinā. Phassassādinoti vā phassāhārassādinoti attho. Sati hi phassāhāre sattānaṃ phassārammaṇe assādo, nāsatīti. Tenāha “phassassādamūlaka”ntiādi.

'They approach contact' means they set in motion the various kinds of contact such as eye-contact and so forth. 'Those who delight in contact' means those who are in the habit of delighting in contact designated as the tangible, by way of bodily contact. For craving for tangible objects arises in beings through bodily contact—to show this, in the exposition of the danger of contact as nutriment, the tangible object is highlighted with the phrase 'in others who are guarded and protected' and so forth. Or, 'those who delight in contact' means those who delight in contact as nutriment. For when there is contact as nutriment, beings find delight in the object of contact; when it is absent, they do not. Therefore, it is said: 'rooted in the delight in contact' and so forth.

Jātinimittassa bhayassa abhinipātasabhāvena gahitattā “tammūlaka”nti vuttaṃ, kammāyūhananimittanti attho.

Because the fear that is the sign of birth is taken as having the nature of plunging, it is called 'rooted in that.' The meaning is that it has the sign of the accumulation of kamma as its root.

Abhinipatatīti abhinibbattati. Paṭhamābhinibbatti hi sattānaṃ tattha tattha aṅgārakāsusadise bhave abhinipātasadisīti. Tammūlakattāti nāmarūpanibbattimūlakattā.

'It plunges into' means it is reborn. For the first rebirth of beings in existences similar to a pit of glowing embers is like plunging. 'Because it is rooted in that' means because it is rooted in the arising of name-and-form.

Tatrāti tāsu upamāsu. Bhūtamatthaṃ katvāti na parikappitamatthaṃ, atha kho bhūtaṃ bhūtapubbaṃ atthaṃ katvā. Pātheyyahatthesu gacchantesu pātheyyaṃ, gacchantaṃ viya hotīti vuttaṃ “gantvā pātheyyaṃ niṭṭhāsī”ti. Gantvāti vāgamanahetūti attho. Khuppipāsāturatāya ghanacchāyaṃ rukkhaṃ upagantuṃ asamatthā viraḷhacchāyāyaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Na dāni sakkā taṃ mayā kātuṃ [M 1.0313] atidubbalabhāvato. Parikkhalitagatitaruṇadārako khuppipāsābhibhūto ca, tasmā gacchantoyeva mato.

'Therein' (tatra) refers to those similes. 'Having made a real meaning' means not an imagined meaning, but rather having made a meaning that was real, that had happened in the past. When those with provisions in hand are going, the provisions are as if they are going; thus it is said, 'Having gone, the provisions were exhausted.' 'Having gone' means because of the act of going. Overcome by hunger and thirst, they were unable to approach a tree with dense shade, so they sat in sparse shade. 'Now, it is not possible for me to do that due to extreme weakness.' A young boy, his gait faltering and overcome by hunger and thirst, died even while going.

Sajātimaṃsatāyāti (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.2.63) samānajātimaṃsatāya, manussamaṃsatāyāti attho. Yaṃ manussamaṃsaṃ, tañhi loke jigucchanīyattā paṭikulaṃ. Tathā hi taṃ viññūhi vajjitaṃ, manussamaṃsesupi ñātimaṃsaṃ ayuttaparibhogatāya paṭikūlaṃ, tatthāpi puttamaṃsaṃ, tatthāpi piyaputtamaṃsaṃ, tatthāpi taruṇamaṃsaṃ, tatthāpi āmakamaṃsaṃ, tatthāpi agorasābhisaṅkhataṃ, tatthāpi aloṇaṃ, tatthāpi adhūpitanti evaṃ heṭṭhimato uttaruttarassa paṭikūlatarabhāvakāraṇatā [V 1.0279] daṭṭhabbā. Puttamaṃsasadisanti paṭikūlatāupaṭṭhāpanena puttamaṃsasadisaṃ katvā passati. Tattha nikantiṃ pariyādiyatīti ariyamaggena āhāre sāpekkhaṃ khepeti.

'Of the same species' flesh' (sajātimaṃsatāyāti, Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 2.2.63) means of the same kind of flesh, that is, human flesh. For human flesh is repulsive in the world because it is disgusting. Indeed, it is rejected by the wise. And even among human flesh, the flesh of relatives is repulsive because it is improper to consume. Among that, the flesh of one's child is more repulsive; among that, the flesh of a beloved child is more repulsive still; among that, the flesh of a young child is more repulsive; among that, raw flesh is more repulsive; among that, flesh prepared without fine flavors is more repulsive; among that, unsalted flesh is more repulsive; among that, unsmoked flesh is more repulsive. Thus, one should see the causality whereby each succeeding level is more repulsive than the one below it. 'Like the flesh of one's child' means, by bringing to mind its repulsiveness, one sees it as being like the flesh of one's child. 'There, he exhausts craving' means with the noble path, he destroys the desire for food.

Sā gāvīti “seyyathāpi bhikkhave gāvī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.63) evaṃ sutte vuttagāvī. Uddāletvāti uppāṭetvā. Nissāya tiṭṭhatīti paṭiccapaccayaṃ katvā pavattati. Dukkhadukkhatādivasena tiṇṇampi vedayitānaṃ dukkhabhāvaṃ sandhāyāha “vedayitadukkhassā”ti.

'That cow' refers to the cow mentioned in the sutta, as it is said, 'Just as, monks, a cow...' (Saṃ. Ni. 2.63). 'Having torn open' (uddāletvā) means having uprooted. 'It stands dependent' (nissāya tiṭṭhati) means it proceeds having made something a dependent condition. With reference to the suffering nature of all three kinds of feeling in terms of the suffering of pain, etc., it is said, 'of the suffering of what is felt.'

Sādhusammatāpi gati vipariṇāmasaṅkhāradukkhatāvasena kilesadukkhavasena ca mahāpariḷāhāyevāti vuttaṃ “mahāpariḷāhaṭṭhena tayo bhavā”ti. Yathā upakaḍḍhakā dve purisā, evaṃ kusalākusalavasena dve manosañcetanā. Yathā manosañcetanā na pavattati, tathā paṭipajjanto tattha nikantiṃ pariyādiyatīti veditabbo.

Even a destination considered good is a great torment due to the suffering of change, the suffering of conditioned formations, and the suffering of defilements; thus it was said, 'The three existences are so in the sense of great torment.' Just as two men pull, so there are two mental volitions, by way of wholesome and unwholesome. It should be understood that by practicing in such a way that mental volition does not proceed, one thereby exhausts craving in that regard.

Sattisatena hatā eva upamā sattisatahatūpamā, tassaṃ sattisatahatūpamāyaṃ. Taṃ sattisataṃ. Assa purisassa. Patitokāseti purimasattīhi patitappadese. Dukkhassa pamāṇaṃ natthi anekassa aparāparaṃ uppajjanato. Khandhajanananti khandhānaṃ aparāparuppādo, paṭhamābhinibbatti pana paṭisandhi eva. Āgucārī puriso viya paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ nānappakāradukkhuppādasannissayato, tehi ca dukkhehi upagantabbato. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ pamukhabhāvena pavattiyā “viññāṇassa dukkhuppādoti vuttā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”ti (dha. pa. 1, 2) yathā viññāṇaṃ āyatiṃ paṭisandhivasena na pavattati, evaṃ karaṇaṃ tattha nikantipariyādānaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Struck by a hundred spears—such is the simile, the simile of one struck by a hundred spears. In that simile of one struck by a hundred spears, those hundred spears belong to that man. 'It makes a place for falling' in the place struck by the first spears. There is no measure of suffering, due to its manifold and continuous arising. 'Generating the aggregates' means the continuous arising of the aggregates, but the first production is simply rebirth-linking. Like a criminal, rebirth-linking consciousness is the basis for the arising of various kinds of suffering and is to be approached by those sufferings. Due to its proceeding as the foremost among associated states, it is said, 'Consciousness is the arising of suffering.' For so it is said: 'Mind precedes all phenomena' (Dhp. 1, 2). The method for ensuring that consciousness does not proceed in the future by way of rebirth-linking should be understood therein as the complete ending of craving.

Pariññātaṃ [M 1.0314] vatthūti dukkhasaccamāha. Pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgoti pañcakāmaguṇārammaṇo rāgo. Pariññāto hotīti paricchijja jānanena samatikkanto hoti. Rasataṇhāya hi sammadeva vigatāya rūpataṇhādayopi vigatāyeva honti. Tathā ca sati kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ samucchinnameva hoti, evaṃ karaṇaṃ tattha nikantipariyādānaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pariññābhisamaye hi siddhe pahānābhisamayo siddho evāti. Pahīne ca kāmarāgasaṃyojane orambhāgiyasaṃyojanānaṃ lesopi nāvasissatīti dassento āha “natthi taṃ saṃyojana”ntiādi. Tena kabaḷīkārāhārapariññā anāgāmitaṃ pāpetīti dasseti. Sesāhārapariññā pana arahattaniṭṭhā evāti dassento “phasse bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha tisso taṇhāti kāmataṇhā rūpataṇhā arūpataṇhāti imā tisso taṇhā.

By 'the matter to be fully understood,' he speaks of the truth of suffering. 'Lust related to the five strands of sensual pleasure' is lust that has the five strands of sensual pleasure as its object. 'Is fully understood' means is transcended by knowledge that defines it. For when craving for flavors has rightly departed, craving for forms and so on have also departed. And when this is so, the fetter of sensual lust is indeed cut off; the method for this should be understood therein as the complete ending of craving. For when the breakthrough of full understanding is accomplished, the breakthrough of abandonment is also accomplished. And showing that when the fetter of sensual lust is abandoned, not even a trace of the lower fetters remains, he says, 'there is no such fetter,' and so on. By this, he shows that the full understanding of edible food leads to the state of non-returning. But showing that the full understanding of the remaining nutriments culminates in arahantship, he says, 'Monks, contact,' and so on. Therein, 'the three cravings' are craving for sensual pleasures, craving for form, and craving for the formless—these are the three cravings.

“Purimataṇhāsamudayā”ti [V 1.0280] saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “katha”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha taṇhāpaccayanibbattāti taṇhāpaccayā nibbattā. Paṭisandhikkhaṇe purimataṇhāsamudayā āhārānaṃ samudayadassaneneva pavattikkhaṇepi upādinnakaāhārasamudayo dassito hotīti taṃ anāmasitvā anupādinnakānaṃ taṇhāsamudayaṃ dassetuṃ “yasmā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idhāti imasmiṃ sutte missitvā kathitā avisesitattā. Sahajātataṇhāpaccayanibbattoti ettha sahajātaggahaṇaṃ asahajātataṇhāpaccayanibbattopi anupādinnakaāhāro labbhatīti dassanatthaṃ. So pana asahajātataṇhāpaccayanibbattatāsāmaññenapi yathāvuttaupādinnakāhārena saṃsayaṃ janeyyāti na uddhaṭo, na ca etaṃ kāraṇaṃ “rāgaṃ upanissāya domanassaṃ uppajjatī”ti vacanato, taṇhopanissayapaṭighacittasamuṭṭhānāya ca ojāya vasena anupādinnakaāhārassa labbhanato. Kathaṃ pana taṇhā ojāya upanissayapaccayo; na hi paṭṭhāne katthaci rūpassa upanissayapaccayo vutto atthīti. Nāyaṃ virodho “yasmiṃ sati yaṃ hoti, so tassa upanissayo”ti suttantanayassa adhippetattā yathāvuttatthasambhavato. Tenevāha “imissā…pe… taṇhāya nirodhenā”ti.

To explain in detail the meaning stated concisely in the phrase 'from the arising of past craving,' the section beginning with 'how' and so on is commenced. Herein, 'produced with craving as condition' means produced because of craving. Since, at the moment of rebirth-linking, by seeing the arising of nutriment from the arising of past craving, the arising of appropriated nutriment is also shown at the moment of the process, without touching upon that, the section beginning with 'but because' and so on is stated to show the arising from craving of non-appropriated nutriment. 'Here' means in this sutta, because they are spoken of mixed together, without being specified. In the phrase 'produced with co-nascent craving as condition,' the inclusion of 'co-nascent' is for the purpose of showing that non-appropriated nutriment is also obtained conditioned by non-co-nascent craving. However, that is not mentioned for fear that, due to the generality of being produced with non-co-nascent craving as condition, it might generate doubt regarding the aforementioned appropriated nutriment. Nor is this the reason, because of the statement 'depending on lust, displeasure arises,' and because non-appropriated nutriment is obtainable by way of the nutritive essence originating from a mind of aversion that has craving as its decisive support. But how is craving a decisive support condition for nutritive essence? For in the Paṭṭhāna, it is nowhere stated that there is a decisive support condition for material form. This is not a contradiction, because the Suttanta method is intended, according to which 'when this exists, that comes to be; this is its decisive support,' and because the meaning as stated is possible. Therefore, he said, 'with the cessation of this… craving…'.

Kāraṇe sabbaso niruddhe phalampi sabbaso nirujjhatīti āha “āhāranirodho paññāyatī”ti. Āhārānaṃ dukkhasaccekadesattā āhāraggahaṇaṃ [M 1.0315] dukkhasaccaggahaṇameva hotīti āha “idha cattāripi saccāni sarūpeneva vuttānī”ti. Saccadesanā dukkhādīnaṃ yāvadeva pariññeyyādibhāvasandassanatthā, tasmā jarāmaraṇādīsu pariññeyyādibhāvo asammohato sallakkhetabboti dassento “sabbattha asammuyhantena saccāni uddharitabbānī”ti āha.

When the cause has completely ceased, the result also completely ceases—thus he says, 'the cessation of nutriment is discerned.' Because nutriments are a part of the truth of suffering, the grasping of nutriment is indeed the grasping of the truth of suffering—thus he says, 'here, all four truths are stated in their own form.' The teaching of the truths is for the purpose of showing the state of suffering and so on as things to be fully understood, etc. Therefore, showing that in aging and death and so on, their state as things to be fully understood, etc., should be discerned without confusion, he says, 'the truths should be extracted everywhere by one who is not confused.'

Āhāravāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on nutriment is concluded.

Saccavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on the Truths.

91. Yena yena pariyāyena byākarotīti yena yena dukkhādijarāmaraṇādipariyāyena ariyasaccāni saṅkhepato ca vitthārato ca katheti. Dukkhanti dukkhasaccaṃ dukkhaṃ, na dukkhamattaṃ.

91. ‘In whatever way he explains’ means in whatever way, by the method of suffering, aging, death, and so on, he teaches the noble truths, both in brief and in detail. ‘Suffering’ means the noble truth of suffering, not mere suffering.

Saccavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on the truths is concluded.

Jarāmaraṇavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on Aging and Death.

92. Tesaṃ [V 1.0281] tesanti byāpanicchāvasenāyaṃ niddeso kato, tasmā yathā “gāmo gāmo ramaṇīyo”ti vutte ramaṇīyatāya tādisā sabbepi gāmā saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, evaṃ “tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ jātī”ti vutte jātisaṅkhātavikāravasena sabbepi sattā saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Tenāha “saṅkhepato anekesaṃ sattānaṃ sādhāraṇaniddeso”ti.

92. This designation, ‘of those respective beings,’ is made in the sense of distributive specification. Therefore, just as when it is said, ‘Every single village is delightful,’ all such villages are included because of their delightfulness, so too when it is said, ‘the birth of those respective beings,’ all beings are included by way of the alteration designated as birth. Therefore he said: ‘In brief, it is a general designation for many beings.’

Gatijātivasenāti (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.1.2) pañcagativasena, tatthāpi ekekāya gatiyā khattiyādibhummadevādihatthiādijātivasena ca. Nikiyyanti sattā ettha, etena vāti nikāyo, gottacaraṇādivibhāgo. Jarāya sabhāvo nāma vayohāni, tasmā jarāti vayohānisaṅkhātassa sabhāvassa niddeso, pākaṭajarāvasena niddeso khaṇḍiccādivasena gahaṇato. Jīraṇameva jīraṇatā, jīrantassa vā ākāro tā-saddena vutto. Tenāha “ayaṃ ākāraniddeso”ti. Dantādīnaṃ vasena khaṇḍaṃ jātaṃ etassāti [M 1.0316] khaṇḍito, puggalo. Tassa bhāvo khaṇḍiccaṃ. Palitaṃ etassa atthīti palito, tassa bhāvo pāliccaṃ. Vali taco etassāti valittaco, tassa bhāvo valittacatā. Ime khaṇḍiccādayo jarā. Vikārānaṃ dassanavasenāti vipattidassanavasena. Vātassāti mahato vātakkhandhassa. Khaṇḍiccādivasena gatamaggo pākaṭo, tasmā khaṇḍiccādiggahaṇaṃ jarāya kiccaniddesoti vuttanti dasseti. Na ca khaṇḍiccādīneva jarāti kalalakālato pabhuti purimarūpānaṃ jarāpattakkhaṇe uppajjamānāni pacchimarūpāni paripakkarūpānurūpāni pariṇatapariṇatāni uppajjantīti anukkamena supariṇatarūpānaṃ paripākakāle uppajjamānāni khaṇḍiccādisabhāvāni uppajjanti, tāni udakādimaggesu tiṇarukkhasaṃbhaggatādayo viya paripākagatamaggasaṅkhātesu paripakkarūpesu uppannāni “jarāya gato maggo”icceva vuttāni, na jarāti.

‘By way of destination and birth’ (Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 2.1.2) means by way of the five destinations, and within each destination, by way of birth as a khattiya, an earth-deity, an elephant, and so on. A ‘group’ (nikāya) is where beings are cast down, or that by which they are; it is a division by lineage, conduct, and so on. The intrinsic nature of aging is the decline of vitality; therefore, ‘aging’ is a designation for the intrinsic nature known as the decline of vitality; it is a designation by way of manifest aging, because it is grasped by way of broken teeth and so on. ‘Decaying’ (jīraṇatā) is the state of decay itself, or the characteristic of one who is decaying is expressed by the suffix ‘-tā.’ Therefore he says, ‘This is a designation of the characteristic.’ One whose teeth and so on have become broken (khaṇḍaṃ) is ‘one with broken teeth’ (khaṇḍito), a person. The state of that is ‘broken-toothedness’ (khaṇḍiccaṃ). One who has gray hair (palitaṃ) is ‘gray-haired’ (palito); the state of that is ‘gray-hairedness’ (pāliccaṃ). One whose skin (taco) has wrinkles (vali) is ‘wrinkle-skinned’ (valittaco); the state of that is ‘wrinkle-skinnedness’ (valittacatā). This broken-toothedness and so on is aging. ‘By way of seeing the alterations’ means by way of seeing the deterioration. ‘Of the wind’ means of a great mass of wind. The path taken by way of broken-toothedness and so on is manifest; therefore, this shows that the inclusion of broken-toothedness and so on is stated as a designation of the function of aging. And it is not that broken-toothedness and so on are themselves aging. From the time of the embryo onwards, at the moment the preceding material forms reach aging, subsequent material forms arise that are in conformity with fully ripened material forms, becoming progressively mature. Then, in sequence, at the time of the full ripening of the well-matured material forms, states having the nature of broken-toothedness and so on arise.
