These, like the state of broken grass and trees on paths of water and so on, having arisen in fully ripened material forms—which are designated as ‘the path taken by ripening’—are called ‘the path taken by aging,’ but they are not aging itself.

Pakatiyāti phalavipaccanapakatiyā, jarāya vā pāpuṇitabbaṃ phalamevapakati, tāya jarā dīpitā. Suppasannānīti suṭṭhu pasannāni. Tameva suppasannataṃ kiccato dassetuṃ “sukhumampī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tikkhavisadatā hi tesaṃ indriyānaṃ suppasannatā. Āluḷitānīti ākulāni. Avisadānīti abyattāni.

'By nature' means by the nature of the ripening of fruit, or the fruit to be attained by aging is itself the nature, and by that, aging is indicated. 'Very clear' means perfectly clear. To show that very clarity as its function, the phrase 'even the subtle' and so on is stated. Indeed, sharpness and clarity of those faculties is their being very clear. 'Disturbed' means agitated. 'Unclear' means indistinct.

Kāmaṃ rūpadhammesupi khaṇikajarā durupalakkhitā paṭicchannāva, sā pana yasmā santānavasena pavattiyā paribyattāva hotīti “pākaṭajarā”icceva vuttā. Avīci nirantarā jarā [V 1.0282] avīcijarā sati santāne sattānaṃ anuppabandhato. Tato aññesūti mandadasakādīsu pubbadasakādiparicchedato aññesu yathāvuttesu. Antarantarāti tesu eva vuttappakāresu purimadasakādito pacchimadasakādīnaṃ antarantarā. Vaṇṇavisesādīnanti vaṇṇavisesasaṇṭhānavisesasamphassavisesādīnaṃ.

Indeed, even in material phenomena, momentary aging is difficult to perceive, being concealed. However, because it is clearly evident through the continuity of its process, it is called 'manifest aging.' Uninterrupted aging is 'avīci aging,' as it is continuously connected to beings in the continuity of existence. 'As for others' means among those previously mentioned, such as the weak decades and so forth, which are different from the first decade and so on, by way of their demarcation. 'At intervals' means, among those very types previously mentioned, at intervals between earlier decades and later decades. 'Differences in appearance, etc.' refers to variations in color, shape, tactile sensation, and so on.

Vacanakavasenāti ka-kārena hi padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā vuttaṃ, tasmā cavanaṃ cutīti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ pana ekacatupañcavokārabhavesu cutiyā avisesato gahaṇanti āha “ekacatupañcakkhandhānaṃ sāmaññavacana”nti. Cavanakavasenāti vā cavanakassa puggalassa vasenāti attho. Cavanameva cavanatāti āha “bhāvavacanenā”ti. Lakkhaṇanidassananti vayasaṅkhātassa lakkhaṇassa nidassanaṃ. Cavantassa vā ākāro tā-saddena vutto [M 1.0317] “cavanatā”ti. Bhijjanaṃ bhedoti vuttaṃ “cutikkhandhānaṃ bhaṅguppattiparidīpana”nti. Yathā bhinnassa ghaṭassa kenaci pariyāyena ghanaghaṭabhāvena ṭhānaṃ natthi, evaṃ bhinnānaṃ khandhānanti cavanaṃ antarahitaṃ nāmāti āha “antaradhānanti…pe… paridīpana”nti. Yo maccūti vuccati bhedo, yañca maraṇaṃ pāṇacāgo, tadubhayaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā vuttaṃ “maccu maraṇa”nti evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Kālassa antakassa kiriyāti yā loke vuccati, sā cuti, maraṇanti attho. Cavanakālo eva vā anatikkamanīyattā visesena kāloti vuttoti tassa kiriyā atthato cutikkhandhānaṃ bhedappattiyeva. “Cuti cavanatā”tiādinā pubbe vohāramissakena niddiṭṭhaṃ.

'By way of the word `cavanaka`'—for the word is stated augmented with the letter 'ka'; therefore, it is said that `cavana` is `cuti`. However, this is generally taken without distinction as the passing away in one-, four-, or five-constituent existences, as stated: 'It is a common term for the one, four, and five aggregates.' Or, 'by way of `cavanaka`' means by way of the person who passes away. Passing away itself is `cavanatā`, as stated: 'by way of a term for a state.' 'Indication of the characteristic' means the indication of the characteristic called aging. Or the mode of one who is passing away is expressed with the suffix '-tā' as '`cavanatā`.' 'Breaking' (`bhijjanaṃ bhedo`) is stated as 'the explanation of the arising of the breaking of the aggregates at death.' Just as a broken pot cannot in any way remain a whole pot, so too with the broken aggregates—their passing away is called disappearance, as stated: 'disappearance... an explanation.' What is called `maccu` (death) is the breaking, and what is called `maraṇa` (dying) is the abandoning of life. Combining these two, it is said: '`maccu maraṇa`'—this is how the meaning should be understood here. The action of time, the end-maker, is what is called in the world `cuti` or `maraṇa`, meaning death. Or, since the time of passing away cannot be transgressed, it is specifically called 'time,' and its action is in effect the attainment of breaking of the aggregates at death. The terms '`cuti`,' '`cavanatā`,' etc., were previously explained with a mixture of conventional language.

Idāni nibbattitaparamatthanayeneva niddesoti dassetuṃ “paramatthena dīpetu”nti vuttaṃ. “Cavanakavasenā”tiādinā hi puggalavasena ca vohārādhiṭṭhānā saṃvaṇṇanā katā. Na kiñci kaḷevaraṃ nikkhipaki opapātikānaṃ cutikkhandhānaṃ antaradhānamevahoti, tato paraṃ utusamuṭṭhānarūpasantati na pavattati. “Jātisamudayā”tiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ “taṇhāsamudayā”tiādīsu vuttanayaneva sakkā viññātunti na vuttaṃ.

Now, to show that the explanation is solely by means of the ultimate meaning, it is said, 'to illuminate by the ultimate meaning.' For by the phrase 'by way of `cavanaka`,' and so on, an account has been made in terms of the person and the basis of conventional usage. No corpse is left behind; for spontaneously reborn beings, it is simply the vanishing of the aggregates at death, and after that, the continuity of materiality produced by temperature does not proceed. What should be said in the phrases 'with the arising of birth,' etc., can be understood in the same way as explained in the phrases 'with the arising of craving,' etc., and so it is not stated.

Jarāmaraṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on aging and death is concluded.

Jātivāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Birth

93. Jāyanaṭṭhenātiādi āyatanavasena yonivasena ca dvīhi dvīhi padehi sabbasatte pariyādiyitvā jātiṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Sammohavinodaniyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 191) pana “jāyamānakavasena [V 1.0283] jāti, sañjāyanavasena sañjātī”ti vuttattā tattha ekekeneva padena sabbasatte pariyādiyitvā jātiṃ dassetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sampuṇṇā jāti sañjātīti katvā “sā paripuṇṇāyatanavasena yuttā”ti vuttaṃ. Eteneva kevalaṃ jātisaddena vuttāya jātiyā aparipuṇṇāyatanatā daṭṭhabbā. Abhibyattā nibbatti abhinibbatti, pākaṭā nibbattīti attho. “Tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ…pe… abhinibbattī”ti sattavasena pavattattā vohāradesanā.

93. The phrase beginning 'in the sense of being born' is stated to show birth by encompassing all beings with two terms each, by way of the sense bases (āyatana) and by way of origin (yoni). However, in the Sammohavinodanī (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 191), because it is stated, 'Birth (jāti) is in the sense of being born, and full birth (sañjāti) in the sense of coming to be,' it should be seen that there, with each single term, birth is shown encompassing all beings. Because `sañjāti` is complete birth, it is stated, 'this is connected by way of the complete sense bases.' By this alone, the incompleteness of the sense bases should be seen in the birth stated with just the term 'jāti.' `Abhinibbatti` is manifest production; the meaning is evident production. Because the phrase 'of those various beings... production' proceeds by way of beings, it is a conventional teaching.

Tatra [M 1.0318] tatrāti ettha catuvokārabhave dvinnaṃ, ekavokārabhave dvinnaṃ, sesarūpadhātuyaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe uppajjamānānaṃ pañcannaṃ, kāmadhātuyaṃ vikalāvikalindriyavasena sattannaṃ navannaṃ dasannaṃ, puna dasannaṃ, ekādasannañca āyatanānaṃ vasena saṅgaho veditabbo. Yadipi cutikkhandhā anantarānaṃ paṭisandhikadhammānaṃ anantarādinā paccayā honti, ye pana samudayā ajanakā, te ettha upapattibhavoti adhippetā. Janako eva bhavoti adhippetoti dassento “jātiyā paccayabhūto kammabhavo veditabbo”ti āha.

'In those various existences' here refers to the inclusion by way of sense bases: two in the four-constituent existence, two in the one-constituent existence, five for those arising at the moment of rebirth-linking in the remaining form realm, and in the sense-sphere realm seven, nine, ten, again ten, and eleven, depending on whether the faculties are deficient or complete. Although the aggregates at death are a condition for the immediately subsequent rebirth-linking states by way of contiguity, etc., those causes, however, that are non-generative are here intended as existence-as-rebirth (`upapattibhava`). Showing that generative existence itself is intended, he said: 'Kammic existence (`kammabhava`) should be understood as the condition for birth.'

Jātivāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on birth is finished.

Bhavavāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Existence

94. Bhāvanabhavanaṭṭhena bhavo duvidho. Tattha kammabhavo “bhavati etasmā upapattibhavo”ti bhāvanaṭṭhena bhavo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana upapattibhavaṃ “bhavatīti bhavo”ti vatvā tassa kāraṇattā kammaṃ phalūpacārena bhavoti ayamattho vutto, ubhayatthāpi upapattibhavahetubhāvanettha kammassa kammabhavapariyāyoti dassitaṃ hoti. Sabbathāpīti bhāvanabhavanakusalākusalaupapattisampattibhavahīnapaṇītādinā sabbappakārenapi. Kāmabhavoti vuttaṃ kāmataṇhāhetukato kāmataṇhāya ārammaṇabhāvato ca. Rūpabhavūpagakammaṃ rūpabhavo, tathā arūpabhavūpagakammaṃ arūpabhavo, taṃtaṃnibbattakkhandhā rūpārūpupattibhavā, rūpārūpabhavabhāvo pana tesaṃ “kāmabhavo”ti ettha vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

94. Existence (bhava) is twofold by way of producing (bhāvana) and being (bhavana). Here, kamma-existence (kammabhava) is existence in the sense of producing, because existence-as-rebirth (upapattibhava) comes to be from it. However, in the commentary, existence-as-rebirth is described as 'existence (bhava) because it comes to be,' and since kamma is its cause, kamma is metaphorically called 'existence' in terms of its result. This shows that in both cases, kamma, being the cause of existence-as-rebirth, is designated as a synonym for kamma-existence. 'In every way' (sabbathāpi) means in all ways: by way of producing and being, skillful and unskillful, existence-as-rebirth and as attainment, inferior and superior existence, and so on. 'Sense-sphere existence' (kāmabhava) is said to be caused by sensual craving (kāmataṇhā) and to have sensual craving as its object. Kamma leading to fine-material existence is fine-material existence (rūpabhava); similarly, kamma leading to formless existence is formless existence (arūpabhava). The aggregates produced in those realms are the existence-as-rebirth of the fine-material and formless realms. But the nature of fine-material and formless existence should be understood here in the same way as 'sense-sphere existence' was explained.

Bhavavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on existence is finished.

Upādānavāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Clinging

95. Upādānanti [V 1.0284] catubbidhampi upādānaṃ. Yathā hi kāmassādavasena, bhavassādavasena vā taṃtaṃsugatibhavūpagaṃ kammaṃ karontassa kāmupādānaṃ, evaṃ ucchedādimicchābhinivesavasenāti cattāripi upādānāni yathārahaṃ tassa tassa kusalakammabhavassa upanissayavaseneva paccayā honti, akusalakammabhavassa asahajātassa anantarassa upanissayavasenapi ārammaṇavasenapi[M 1.0319]. Sahajātassa kāmupādānaṃ sahajāta-aññamañña-nissaya-sampayutta-atthi-avigata-hetu-vasena sattadhā, sesaupādānāni tattha hetupaccayabhāvaṃ pahāya maggapaccayaṃ pakkhipitvā sattadhāva paccayā honti. Anantarassa pana anantarasamanantaraanantarūpanissayanatthivigatāsevanavasena paccayā honti. Tassidampi sahajātādīti ādi-saddena saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vatthukāmaṃ upādiyati cittaṃ, puggalo vā etenāti attho. Tanti vatthukāmaṃ. Kāmetīti kāmo ca so upādiyatīti upādānañcāti yojanā. Vuttanayenāti abhidhamme vuttanayena.

95. ‘Clinging’ means the fourfold clinging. Just as for one performing kamma that leads to a particular good destination because of gratification in sensual pleasures or gratification in existence there is clinging to sensual pleasure, so too, because of adherence to wrong views such as annihilationism, the four kinds of clinging are, as appropriate, conditions for this or that wholesome kamma-existence only by way of decisive support. For unwholesome kamma-existence that is non-conascent and non-proximate, they are conditions by way of decisive support and object. For what is conascent, clinging to sensual pleasure is a condition in seven ways: by conascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root. The other types of clinging, excluding the root condition but including the path condition, also serve as conditions in seven ways. For the immediately proximate, however, they are conditions by way of immediacy, contiguity, decisive support of immediacy, absence, disappearance, and repetition. It should be understood that this too is included by the word 'etc.' in 'conascent, etc.' The mind clings to the objective basis of sensual pleasure, or the person clings by means of it; this is the meaning. 'That' refers to the objective basis of sensual pleasure. The construction is: it is 'sensual pleasure' (kāma) because one desires, and it is 'clinging' (upādāna) because one clings to it. 'In the way stated' means in the way stated in the Abhidhamma.

Sassato attāti idaṃ purimadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyamānaṃ uttaradiṭṭhiṃ nidassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā esā diṭṭhi daḷhīkaraṇavasena purimaṃ purimaṃ uttarā uttarā upādiyati, evaṃ “natthi dinna”ntiādikāpīti. Attaggahaṇaṃ pana attavādupādānanti nayidaṃ diṭṭhupādānadassananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Loko cāti attaggahaṇavinimuttagahaṇaṃ diṭṭhupādānabhūtaṃ idha purimadiṭṭhiuttaradiṭṭhivacanehi vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Sabbadiṭṭhigatassa “diṭṭhupādāna”nti etaṃ adhivacanaṃ “sabbāpi diṭṭhi diṭṭhupādāna”nti vacanato.

'The self is eternal'—this is said to indicate a subsequent view that clings to the prior view. Just as this view, by way of reinforcement, clings to one preceding view after another by means of a subsequent one, so too do views such as 'There is nothing given.' However, the grasping of a self is clinging to the doctrine of a self; it should be understood that this is not a presentation of clinging to views. And 'the world' refers to a grasping that is devoid of the grasping of a self, which constitutes clinging to views; this should be known to be stated here by the words 'prior view' and 'subsequent view.' 'Clinging to views' is a designation for the entire range of views, in accordance with the statement, 'All views are clinging to views.'

Sīlabbataṃ upādiyantīti sīlabbataṃ “suddhimaggo”ti upādiyanti. Etena micchābhinivesena. Sayaṃ vā taṃ micchābhinivesasahagataṃ. Sīlabbatasahacaraṇato sīlabbatañca taṃ daḷhaggāhabhāvato upādānañcāti sīlabbatupādānaṃ. Evaṃ suddhīti abhinivesatoti evaṃ gosīlagovatādicaraṇena saṃsārasuddhīti abhinivesabhāvato. Etena taṃ sahacaraṇato abhinivesassa taṃsaddārahataṃ dasseti.

'They cling to rules and observances' means they cling to rules and observances as 'the path to purity.' This is by means of wrong adherence. Or it is itself associated with wrong adherence. Because it accompanies rules and observances, it is 'rules and observances'; and because it is a state of firm grasping, it is 'clinging'; thus it is 'clinging to rules and observances.' 'Thus there is purity' means because of the adherence; that is, because of the adherence that 'in this way, through the practice of the cow-morality, the cow-duty, etc., there is purification from saṃsāra.' By this it shows that the adherence is fit to be designated by that word because it accompanies them.

Vadantīti “atthi me attā”tiādinā voharanti. Etena diṭṭhigatena. Attavādamattamevāti attāti vācāmattameva. Etena vācāvatthumattametaṃ, yadidaṃ bāhirakaparikappito attāti dasseti.

'They speak' means they use such expressions as 'I have a self.' This is by means of this view. 'It is merely the doctrine of a self' means it is merely the word 'self.' By this it shows that this is merely a verbal construct, that is, the self conceived by outsiders.

Taṇhā [V 1.0285] kāmupādānassāti ettha “tattha katamaṃ kāmupādānaṃ? Yo kāmesu kāmacchando kāmarāgo kāmanandī kāmataṇhā kāmasneho kāmapariḷāho kāmamucchā kāmajjhosānaṃ. Idaṃ vuccati kāmupādāna”nti vacanato taṇhādaḷhattaṃ kāmupādānaṃ. Taṇhādaḷhattanti ca purimataṇhāupanissayapaccayato daḷhabhūtā uttarataṇhā eva. Keci panāhu –

Regarding 'Craving is a condition for clinging to sensual pleasures': Here, in accordance with the passage, 'Therein, what is clinging to sensual pleasures? Whatever desire for sensual pleasures, lust for sensual pleasures, delight in sensual pleasures, craving for sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, torment by sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, obsession with sensual pleasures—this is called clinging to sensual pleasures,' the intensification of craving is clinging to sensual pleasures. And 'intensification of craving' is just the subsequent craving that has become strong because of the preceding craving as its decisive support condition. But some say:

“Appattavisayapatthanā [M 1.0320] taṇhā andhakāre corassahatthappasāraṇaṃ viya, sampattavisayaggahaṇaṃ upādānaṃ tasseva bhaṇḍaggahaṇaṃ viyā”ti. Appicchasantuṭṭhipaṭipakkhā ete dhammā pariyesanārakkhadukkhamūlāni, tasmā vuttalakkhaṇā taṇhā vuttalakkhaṇasseva upādānassa anānantarassa upanissayavasena paccayo, ārammaṇādivasenapi paccayo hotiyeva, anantarādīnaṃ pana anantarādivasena paccayo. Sabbassapi hi lobhassa taṇhāpariyāyopi kāmupādānapariyāyopi labbhatevāti. Avasesānanti diṭṭhupādānādīnaṃ. Sahajātādivasenāti sahajātānaṃ sahajātādivasena, asahajātānaṃ anantaraupanissayādivasenāti sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

'Craving is the longing for an unobtained object, like a thief stretching out his hand in the dark; clinging is the grasping of an obtained object, like the same thief seizing the goods.' These states are the opposite of having few wishes and contentment; they are the roots of the suffering of seeking and protecting. Therefore, craving with the stated characteristic is a condition for clinging with the stated characteristic, which is not immediately proximate, by way of decisive support; it is indeed also a condition by way of object, etc. But for the immediately proximate, etc., it is a condition by way of immediacy, etc. For any kind of greed can be designated as a synonym of craving and also as a synonym of clinging to sensual pleasures. 'Of the remaining' means of clinging to views, etc. 'By way of conascence, etc.' means: for conascent states, by way of conascence, etc.; for non-conascent states, by way of immediacy, decisive support, etc. All this should be understood in the way stated below.

Upādānavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on clinging is finished.

Taṇhāvāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Craving

96. “Cakkhusamphasso”tiādi phassassa mātito nāmaṃ viya puttassa vatthuto tassa nissayabhāvena uppattihetuttā, ārammaṇaṃ pana kevalaṃ uppattihetūti vuttaṃ “seṭṭhi…pe… nāma”nti. Kāmarāgabhāvenāti vatthukāmassa rajjanavasena. Rūpaṃ assādentīti rupārammaṇaṃ taṇhābhinandanāvasena abhiramamānā eva assādentī. Niccantiādinā diṭṭhābhinandanāmukhena rūpaṃ abhiramantī. Pecca na bhavissatīti bhijjitvā na hoti puna anuppajjanato. Tathā saddakaṇhādayopīti yathā rūpataṇhā kāmarāgabhāvena sassatarāgavasena ucchedarāgavasenāti ca pavattiyā tisso taṇhā, tathā saddataṇhā gandharasaphoṭṭhabbadhammataṇhāpi. Taṇhāvicaritānīti taṇhāsamudācārā, samudācāravasena pavattataṇhāti attho.

96. The words “eye-contact,” etc., are like naming a son after his mother, for the basis is the cause of its arising by way of being its support, while the object is merely a cause of its arising, as is said: “the banker's… name.” “By way of sensual lust” means by way of passion for the objects of sensual pleasure. “They delight in form” means they delight in the form-object, rejoicing in it by way of approving of it with craving. By “permanent,” etc., they rejoice in form by way of approving of it through a view. “After death, it will not be” means that having broken up, it is no more, because it does not arise again. Likewise with craving for sounds, etc. Just as craving for form proceeds in three ways—by way of sensual lust, by way of lust connected with eternalism, and by way of lust connected with annihilationism—so too do craving for sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena. “Wanderings of craving” means the expressions of craving; the meaning is craving that proceeds by way of its expression.

Ajjhattikassupādāyāti (vibha. aṭṭha. 973; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.2.2) ajjhattikaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ upādāya. Upayogatthe hi idaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Asmīti hotīti yadetaṃ ajjhattaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ [V 1.0286] upādāya taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena samūhagāhato asmīti evaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ satīti attho. Itthasmīti hotīti khattiyādīsu “idaṃpakāro aha”nti evaṃ [M 1.0321] taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena hotīti idamettha anupanidhāya gahaṇaṃ. Evamādināti ādi-saddena “evaṃsmīti, aññathāsmīti, bhavissanti, itthaṃ bhavissanti, evaṃ bhavissanti, aññathā bhavissanti, asasmīti, satasmīti, siyanti, itthaṃ siyanti, evaṃ siyanti, aññathā siyanti, apāhaṃ siyanti, apāhaṃ itthaṃ siyanti, apāhaṃ evaṃ siyanti, apāhaṃ aññathā siya”nti (vibha. 973) imesaṃ taṇhāvicaritānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tattha evaṃsmīti idaṃ samato upanidhāya gahaṇaṃ, yathā ayaṃ khattiyo, yathā ayaṃ brāhmaṇo, evaṃ ahampīti attho. Aññathāsmīti idaṃ asamaṇo upanidhāya gahaṇaṃ, yathā ayaṃ khattiyo, yathā ayaṃ brāhmaṇo, tato aññathā ahaṃ hīno vā adhiko vāti attho. Iti imāni pubbe vuttāni dveti etāni paccuppannavasena cattāri taṇhāvicaritāni. Bhavissantiādīni pana cattāri anāgatavasena vuttāni. Tesaṃ purimacatukke vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Asasmīti asatīti asaṃ. Niccassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tasmā sassato asmīti attho. Satasmīti sīdatīti sataṃ. Aniccassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tasmā asassato asmīti attho. Iti imāni dve sassatucchedavasena vuttāni. Ito parāni siyantiādīni cattāri saṃsayaparivitakkavasena vuttāni, tāni purimacatukke vuttanayena atthato veditabbāni. Apāhaṃ siyantiādīni cattāri “api nāmāhaṃ bhaveyya”nti evaṃ patthanākappanavasena vuttāni, tāni purimacatukke vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

“By clinging to the internal” (Vibha. Aṭṭha. 973; Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 2.2.2) means by clinging to the internal five aggregates. For this is a genitive in the sense of employment. “The thought ‘I am’ occurs”: when, by clinging to the internal five aggregates, one collectively grasps them by way of craving, conceit, and views, the thought ‘I am’ occurs; ‘when that exists’ is the meaning. “The thought ‘I am thus’ occurs”: among khattiyas and others, the thought ‘I am of this kind’ occurs by way of craving, conceit, and views. Here this is a grasping without comparison. “And so on”: by the word ‘and so on,’ these wanderings of craving are included: ‘I am so,’ ‘I am otherwise,’ ‘I will be,’ ‘I will be thus,’ ‘I will be so,’ ‘I will be otherwise,’ ‘I am eternal,’ ‘I am non-eternal,’ ‘I might be,’ ‘I might be thus,’ ‘I might be so,’ ‘I might be otherwise,’ ‘Would that I might not be,’ ‘Would that I might not be thus,’ ‘Would that I might not be so,’ ‘Would that I might not be otherwise’ (Vibha. 973). Among these, “I am so” is a grasping by way of comparison with an equal, meaning: “Just as this one is a khattiya, just as this one is a brahmin, so too am I.” “I am otherwise” is a grasping by way of comparison with an unequal, meaning: “Just as this one is a khattiya, just as this one is a brahmin, I am otherwise—inferior or superior.” Thus these two, together with the two previously mentioned, are four wanderings of craving concerning the present. The four beginning with “I will be” are stated concerning the future. Their meaning should be understood in the same way as the first four. “I am eternal” (asasmīti): ‘non-existent’ (asati) is ‘asaṃ’; this is a designation for the permanent, thus the meaning is ‘I am eternal.’ “I am non-eternal” (satasmīti): ‘perishing’ (sīdati) is ‘sataṃ’; this is a designation for the impermanent, thus the meaning is ‘I am non-eternal.’ Thus these two are stated by way of eternalism and annihilationism. The following four beginning with “I might be” are stated by way of doubt and speculation; their meaning should be understood in the same way as the first four. The four beginning with “Would that I might not be” are stated by way of longing and constructing, as in “Oh, would that I might be!”; their meaning should also be understood in the same way as the first four.

Ettha ca sassatucchedavasena vuttā dve diṭṭhisīsā nāma, asmi, bhavissaṃ, siyaṃ, apāhaṃ siyanti ete pana cattāro suddhasīsā eva, “itthasmī”tiādayo tayo tayoti dvādasa sīsamūlakā nāma. Evametāni dve diṭṭhisīsā, cattāro suddhasīsā, dvādasa sīsamūlakāti ajjhattikassupādāya aṭṭhārassa taṇhāvicaritāni veditabbāni.

Here, the two stated by way of eternalism and annihilationism are called the ‘view-heads’ (diṭṭhisīsā). But these four—‘I am,’ ‘I will be,’ ‘I might be,’ and ‘Would that I might not be’—are the ‘pure heads’ (suddhasīsā). The twelve, which are the three variations for each of the four heads, beginning with ‘I am thus,’ are called the ‘head-based’ ones (sīsamūlakā). Thus, these two view-heads, four pure heads, and twelve head-based ones should be understood as the eighteen wanderings of craving that arise by clinging to the internal.

Bāhirassupādāyāti bāhiraṃ khandhapañcakaṃ upādāya. Idampi hi upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Imināti iminā rupena vā…pe… viññāṇena vāti evaṃ rūpādīsu ekameva “aha”nti, itaraṃ kiñcanapalibodhabhāvena gahetvā taṇhādivasena “asmī”ti abhinivisati, “iminā”ti ayamettha viseso. Asmīti iminā khaggena vā chattena vā abhisekena vā “khattiyohamasmī”ti [M 1.0322] abhinivisati. Bāhirarūpādinissitānīti bāhirāni parasantatipariyāpannāni rūpavedanādīni nissitāni. Aṭṭhārasāti iminā “asmī”tiādinayappavattāni aṭṭhārasa, tāni pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. “Iminā”ti hi [V 1.0287] ayamevettha viseso, tasmā “dve diṭṭhisīsā”tiādinā vuttanayeneva niddhāretvā veditabbā. Ubhayaṃ pana ekajjhaṃ katvā āha “chattiṃsā”ti.

“By clinging to the external” means by clinging to the external five aggregates. This too is a genitive in the sense of employment. “By this” means “by this form… or by this consciousness.” Thus, among form, etc., one grasps just one as “I,” and having taken the rest as a source of impediment and bondage, one adheres to the thought “I am” by way of craving, etc. “By this” is the distinction here. As to “I am”: one adheres to the thought “I am a khattiya” by means of this sword, or this parasol, or this anointment. “Dependent on external form, etc.” means dependent on external form, feeling, etc., included in another's continuity. “Eighteen”: these are the eighteen that proceed in the manner of “by this I am,” etc. They should be understood in the same way as stated before. For “by this” is the only distinction here. Therefore, they should be determined and understood in the same way as stated beginning with “the two view-heads.” But having combined both, it is said “thirty-six.”

Niddesatthenāti “chayime āvuso taṇhākāyā”tiādiniddesapāḷiyā atthavacanena. Niddesavitthārāti tassa ca niddesassa aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritavasena vitthārena. Vitthārassa ca puna saṅgahatoti dvīhi ākārehi vitthāritassa aṭṭhārasataṇhāvicaritapabhedassa chaḷeva tissoyevāti ca puna saṅgahaṇato ca.

“By the meaning of the exposition” means by the statement of the meaning in the exposition text beginning, “Friends, there are these six bodies of craving.” “By the detailed exposition of the Niddesa” means by the detailed account of that exposition by way of the one hundred and eight wanderings of craving. “And by the further summary of the detailed exposition” means by the further summarizing of the divisions of the eighteen wanderings of craving—which were elaborated in two ways—as just six and just three.

Vipākavedanā adhippetā visesato attānaṃ assādetabbato. Tameva hissā assādetabbataṃ pakāsetuṃ “katha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Assādanenāti abhiratiyā. Mamāyantāti dhanāyantā. Cittakārādīnanti ādi-saddena iṭṭhavaṇṇārammaṇadāyakānaṃ saṅgaho. Sippasandassanakādīnanti ādi-saddena vejjādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Vejjā hi rasāyatanojāvasena tadupatthambhitavasena ca dhammārammaṇassa dāyakā. Svāyaṃ ādi-saddo “vīṇāvādakādī”tiādinā paccekañca yojetabbo, puttaṃ mamāyantāti puttaṃ sampiyāyantā. Putto viya cettha vedanā daṭṭhabbā, sappāyasappikhīrādīni viya vedanāya paccayabhūtāni iṭṭharūpādiārammaṇāni, dhāti viya rūpādichaḷārammaṇadāyakā cittakārādayo daṭṭhabbā.

Resultant feeling is intended, especially because it is to be savored by oneself. To explain this very quality of being savor-able, the words “how,” etc., are stated. “By savoring” means by delighting. “Cherishing” means treasuring. “Painters, etc.”: by the word “etc.” is included those who give desirable colored objects. “Those who display crafts, etc.”: by the word “etc.” is included physicians and others. For physicians, by way of elixirs and tonics and by way of the support provided by them, are givers of mind-objects. This word “etc.” should be connected individually with “lute-players, etc.” “Cherishing a son” means holding a son dear. Here, feeling should be seen as the son; desirable objects such as form, which are conditions for feeling, should be seen as like suitable ghee, milk, etc.; and painters and others, who are providers of the six sense-objects, should be seen as the wet-nurse.

Taṇhāvāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Craving is concluded.

Vedanāvāravaṇṇanā

The Elucidation of the Section on Feeling

97. Cakkhusamphassajā eva vedanā atītādibhedabhinnā rāsivasena ekajjhaṃ gahetvā eko vedanākāyo yathā vedanākkhandho, evaṃ sotasamphassajādikāti pāḷiyaṃ “chayime āvuso vedanākāyā”ti vuttanti āha “vedanākāyāti vedanāsamūhā”ti. Cakkhusamphassato jātā cakkhusamphassajā vedanā. Sā pana upādinnāpi anupādinnāpi, tadubhayassapi saṅgaṇhantena atthavaṇṇanāya katattā āha “ayaṃ tāvettha sabbasaṅgāhikakathā”ti. Idāni “vipākavidhi aya”nti upādinnayeva [M 1.0323] gaṇhanto “vipākavasenā”tiādimāha. Manodvāre manoviññāṇadhātusampayuttāti tadārammaṇamanoviññāṇadhātusampayuttā.

97. Just as feelings born from eye-contact, which are divided into past, etc., when taken together as a mass, form one body of feeling like the feeling aggregate, so too are those born from ear-contact, etc. Thus it is said in the Pāli, “Friends, there are these six bodies of feeling,” and the commentary states, “'Bodies of feeling' means collections of feeling.” Feelings born from eye-contact are eye-contact-born feelings. These may be clung-to or not clung-to. Since the commentary includes both, it states, “This is the comprehensive explanation here.” Now, taking only the clung-to as “this is the method of result,” it says “by way of result,” etc. At the mind-door, 'associated with the mind-consciousness element' means associated with the mind-consciousness element that takes that as object.

Avasesānanti [V 1.0288] sampaṭicchanādivedanānaṃ. Upanissayādīti ādi-saddena anantarādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Anantarānañhi anantarādivasena, itaresaṃ upanissayavasena phasso paccayo hoti, manodvāre pana tadārammaṇavedanānaṃ manosamphasso upanissayavasena paccayo. Advārikānanti dvārarahitānaṃ. Na hi paṭisandhiādivedanānaṃ kiñci dvāraṃ atthi. Sahajātamanosamphassasamudayāti etenassa tāsaṃ sahajātakoṭiyā paccayabhāvamāha.

By 'the remaining,' it means feelings such as receiving, etc. By 'decisive support, etc.,' it should be understood that 'etc.' includes immediately preceding, etc. For the immediately preceding consciousnesses, contact is a condition by way of the immediately preceding condition, etc.; for the others, by way of decisive support. At the mind-door, however, mind-contact is a condition by way of decisive support for those feelings that take that as their object. By 'doorless,' it means those without a door. For feelings such as rebirth-linking, there is no door. By 'arising together with co-nascent mind-contact,' it states its conditionality in the category of co-nascence for those feelings.

Vedanāvāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Section on Feeling is concluded.

Phassavāravaṇṇanā

Elucidation of the Section on Contact

98. Cakkhuṃ nissāya uppanno samphasso cakkhusamphasso. Pañcavatthukāti cakkhādipañcavatthukā cakkhādipañcavatthusannissayā. “Upādinnakakathā esā”ti bāvīsatiggahaṇaṃ, pavattikathābhāvato lokiyaggahaṇaṃ. Vipākamanasampayuttaphassāti vipākamanoviññāṇasampayuttā phassā. Paccayuppannena viya paccayenapi upādinnakeneva bhavitabbanti “channaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ āyatanāna”nti vuttaṃ.

98. Contact arisen dependent on the eye is eye-contact. By 'five-based,' it means based on the five bases beginning with the eye, dependent on the five bases beginning with the eye. The statement 'This is a discourse on what is clung-to' implies the inclusion of the twenty-two faculties; and because it is a discourse on the process of existence, it implies the inclusion of the mundane. 'Resultant contact conjoined with mind' refers to contacts associated with resultant mind-consciousness. Just as what arises from conditions must be what is clung-to, so too the condition itself must be what is clung-to; thus it is said, 'of the six sense-bases beginning with the eye.'

Phassavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Section on Contact is concluded.

Saḷāyatanavāravaṇṇanā

Elucidation of the Section on the Six Sense Bases

99. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ, tasmā yathā ettha arūpalokāpekkhāya chaṭṭhāyatanañca saḷāyatanañca saḷāyatananti ekaseso icchitabbo, evaṃ yesaṃ paccayuppanno upādinno, paccayo pana anupādinnotipi icchitabbo. Tesaṃ matena bāhirāyatanavasenapi ekaseso veditabbo “chaṭṭhāyatanañca saḷāyatanañca saḷāyatanañca saḷāyatana”nti. Visuddhimaggopi imassa āgamassa [M 1.0324] atthasaṃvaṇṇanāti āha “visuddhimagge…pe… vuttanayamevā”ti. Esa nayo aññatthāpi visuddhimaggaggahaṇe.

99. This is merely illustrative. Therefore, just as here, with respect to the formless realm, the sixth sense-base and the six sense-bases should be understood as a single remainder, so too it should be understood that for those whose conditionally produced is clung-to, the condition itself may be unclung-to. According to their view, a single remainder should also be understood by way of the external sense-bases: "the sixth sense-base and the six sense-bases, and the six sense-bases." The Visuddhimagga also comments on the meaning of this textual tradition, stating, "in the Visuddhimagga... as was stated before." This method applies elsewhere too when citing the Visuddhimagga.

Saḷāyatanavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Section on the Six Sense Bases is concluded.

Nāmarūpavāravaṇṇanā

Elucidation of the Section on Name-and-Form

100. Namanalakkhaṇanti [V 1.0289] ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ namanasabhāvaṃ tena vinā apavattanato. Ruppanaṃ sītādivirodhipaccayasannipāte visadisuppatti. Ime pana tayotiādinā sabbacittuppādasādhāraṇavaseneva taṃsaṅkhārakkhandhaggahaṇaṃ, tasmā ye yattha asādhāraṇā, tepi atthato gahitāyevāti dasseti.

100. The characteristic of bending is the nature of inclining towards an object, because without it, there is no turning towards. The characteristic of being molested is the disparate arising due to the coincidence of opposing conditions such as cold, etc. However, the inclusion in the aggregate of formations by "these three, etc.," is only in respect to what is common to all mental occurrences. Therefore, it is shown that even those which are not common are implicitly included in the meaning.

Upādiyitvāti paccaye katvā. Paccayakaraṇameva hi paccayuppannassa paccayabhūtadhammānaṃ upādiyanaṃ. Samūhasambandhe sāmivacanaṃ etanti “samūhatthe etaṃ sāmivacana”nti vuttaṃ tena vinā sambandhassa abhāvato. Tenāti tasmā. Taṃ sabbampīti taṃ bhūtupādāyapabhedaṃ sabbampi sattavīsatividhaṃ. Yassa nāmassāti catuvokārabhave nāmassa. Viññāṇampi tappariyāpannameva veditabbaṃ. Rūpassāti ekavokārabhave rūpassa. Viññāṇaṃ pana pañcavokārabhave saṅkhāraviññāṇameva. Yassa pañcavokārabhave nāmarūpassa. Tassa vasenāti sahajātassa sahajātādivasena, anantarassa anantarādivasena, itarassa upanissayādivasena tassa nāmassa yathārahaṃ tassa tassa viññāṇassa paccayabhāvo veditabbo.

'Upādiyitvā' means having made a condition. For indeed, the making of a condition is the grasping of the conditioning states for what has arisen from a condition. In the context of a collection, this is a genitive case—thus it is said, 'this is a genitive case in the sense of a collection,' because without it, there is no connection. 'Tenāti' means 'therefore.' 'Taṃ sabbampi'—all of that, the entire twenty-sevenfold division of primary and derived matter. 'Yassa nāmassāti'—in the four-aggregate existence, of name. Consciousness, too, should be understood as included within that. 'Rūpassāti'—in the one-aggregate existence, of form. But in the five-aggregate existence, consciousness is only consciousness conditioned by formations. 'Yassa pañcavokārabhave nāmarūpassa'—of name-and-form for one in the five-aggregate existence. By 'by means of that,' it means that the conditionality of that consciousness for that name, as appropriate, should be understood by way of co-nascence, etc., for the co-nascent; by way of immediately preceding, etc., for the immediately preceding; and by way of decisive support, etc., for the other.

Nāmarūpavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Section on Name-and-Form is concluded.

Viññāṇavāravaṇṇanā

The Elucidation of the Section on Consciousness

101. Tebhūmakavipākaggahaṇe kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Saṅkhāro yassa viññāṇassāti ettha aṭṭhavidhopi kāmāvacarapuññābhisaṅkhāro soḷasavidhassa kāmāvacaravipākaviññāṇassa, pañcavidhopi rūpāvacarapuññābhisaṅkhāro pañcavidhassa rūpāvacaravipākaviññāṇassa, dvādasavidhopi apuññābhisaṅkhāro sattavidhassa akusalavipākaviññāṇassa, catubbidhopi āneñjābhisaṅkāro [M 1.0325] catubbidhassa arūpāvacaravipākaviññāṇassa yathārahaṃ paṭisandhipavattīsu kammapaccayena ceva upanissayapaccayena ca paccayo hoti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.620) vuttanayena veditabbo.

101. The reason for grasping the resultants of the three planes has been stated above. Regarding 'the volitional formation that conditions consciousness,' here the eightfold wholesome volitional formation of the sense sphere conditions the sixteenfold resultant consciousness of the sense sphere; the fivefold wholesome volitional formation of the form sphere conditions the fivefold resultant consciousness of the form sphere; the twelvefold unwholesome volitional formation conditions the sevenfold unwholesome resultant consciousness; and the fourfold imperturbable volitional formation conditions the fourfold resultant consciousness of the formless sphere—each acting as a condition through kamma condition and decisive support condition in rebirth-linking and in the course of life, as appropriate. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. XVII, 293).

Viññāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Section on Consciousness is concluded.

Saṅkhāravāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Formations

102. Abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇoti [V 1.0290] abhisañcetayitasabhāvo, āyūhanalakkhaṇoti attho. Copanavasenāti kāyaviññattisaṅkhātacopanavasena. Tena pañcadvārikacetanā paṭikkhipati. Vacanabhedavasenāti vācānicchāraṇavasena. Vacīviññattisamuṭṭhāpanavasenāti attho. Yathāvuttā vīsati, nava mahaggatakusalacetanā cāti ekūnatiṃsa manosañcetanā. “Kusalānaṃ upanissayavasenā”ti vuttaṃ, ekaccānaṃ ārammaṇavasenapīti vattabbaṃ. Sahajātādivasenāti sahajāta-aññamañña-nissaya-sampayutta-atthi-avigatahetuvasena, anantarānaṃ anantarasamanantaraanantarūpanissayanatthivigatāsevanasena paccayo. Api-saddena upanissayaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

102. The characteristic of volitional formation is the nature of being intentionally willed; its meaning is the characteristic of accumulation. 'By way of impulsion' means by way of the impulsion called bodily intimation. Thereby, it excludes volition of the five sense doors. 'By way of verbal distinction' means by way of the utterance of speech; its meaning is by way of producing verbal intimation. The twenty as stated, together with the nine sublime wholesome volitions, make twenty-nine mental volitions. It is said, “by way of being a decisive support for wholesome states”; it should also be said that for some, it is by way of being an object. 'By way of conascence, etc.' means by way of the conascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root conditions; for the immediately preceding, it is a condition by way of the proximity, contiguity, proximity support, absence, disappearance, and repetition conditions. The word “api” also includes the decisive support condition.

Saṅkhāravāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Formations is concluded.

Avijjāvāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Ignorance

103. “Dukkhasacceaññāṇa”nti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “tatthā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tanti aññāṇaṃ. Satipi pahātabbatte pariññeyyattavasena antogadhaṃ. Dukkhasaccañcassāti vatthusaṅkhātaṃ sampayuttakhandhasaṅkhātañca dukkhasaccaṃ assa aññāṇassa. Taṃ hissa nissayapaccayo hoti. Tassāti dukkhasaccassa. Yāthāvalakkhaṇapaṭivedhanivāraṇenāti saṅkhataaviparītasabhāvapaṭivijjhanassa nivāraṇena. Etenassa pariññābhisamayasaṅkhātassa ariyamaggapaṭivedhassa vibandhakabhāvamāha. Ñāṇappavattiyāti “idaṃ dukkhaṃ, ettakaṃ dukkha”nti [M 1.0326] anubujjhanākārāya pubbabhāgañāṇappavattiyā. Etthāti dukkhasacce. Appadānenāti avissajjanena. Etenassā anubodhañāṇassapi vibandhakatamāha.

103. To elaborate the meaning stated briefly, namely, “ignorance of the truth of suffering,” the passage beginning with “herein” is commenced. That is ignorance. Even though it should be abandoned, it is included by way of being something to be fully understood. “And of the truth of suffering for it”: the truth of suffering, which is the basis and the associated aggregates, is for that ignorance. For that is its support condition. “Of that”: of the truth of suffering. “By obstructing the penetration of its true characteristic”: by obstructing the penetration of the unperverted conditioned nature. By this it is stated that it is an obstacle to the penetration of the Noble Path, which is called the realization of full understanding. “In the arising of knowledge”: in the arising of preliminary knowledge in the mode of understanding, “this is suffering, this much is suffering.” “Herein”: in the truth of suffering. “By not giving”: by not releasing. By this it is stated that it is an obstacle even to the knowledge of comprehension.

Tīhi kāraṇehi veditabbaṃ antogadhābhāvato. Idha sampayuttakhandhavaseneva vatthuto samudaye aññāṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ekenevāti itaraṃ kāraṇattayaṃ paṭikkhipati. Yadipi aññāṇaṃ nirodhamagge ārammaṇaṃ na karoti, kuto tadantogadhatabbatthutā, te pana jānitukāmassa tappaṭicchādanavasena anirodhamaggesu nirodhamaggaggāhahetutāvasena ca pavattamānaṃ “nirodhe paṭipadāyañca aññāṇa”nti vuccati. Tenāha “paṭicchādanato”tiādi. Tassattho vuttoyeva. Gambhīrattāti sabhāveneva gambhīrattā. Agādhaapatiṭṭhābhāvena taṃvisayassa ñāṇassa uppādetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā duddasaṃ. Purimaṃ [V 1.0291] pana saccadvayaṃ. Vañcanīyaṭṭhenāti vañcakabhāvena ayāthāvabhāvena upaṭṭhānato duddasattā gambhīraṃ, na sabhāvato, tasmā taṃvisayaṃ aññāṇaṃ uppajjati. Tatthāti tasmiṃ purimasaccadvaye aniccādisabhāvalakkhaṇassa duddasattā eva niccādivipallāsavasena pavattati aññāṇanti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ.

It should be understood by three reasons, due to its not being included. Here, ignorance regarding the origin should be seen as having the associated aggregates as its basis. By “alone,” it rejects the other three reasons. Even if ignorance does not take cessation and the path as its object, how could it be considered as having them as its internal basis? Yet, for one who desires to know them, it is called “ignorance regarding cessation and the path” because, through concealing those truths, it arises as a cause for grasping what is not the path to cessation as the path to cessation. Hence, it is said, “due to concealment,” etc. Its meaning has already been stated. “Due to profundity”: it is profound by its very nature. Because it is unfathomable and without a footing, it is hard to see, being incapable of giving rise to knowledge regarding that object. The former pair of truths, however, is profound in the sense of being deceptive—appearing falsely due to their deceptive nature, making them hard to see, not because of their intrinsic nature. Therefore, ignorance regarding that object arises. “There”: in that former pair of truths, because the characteristics of the nature of impermanence, etc., are hard to see, ignorance arises by way of the perversion of perceiving permanence, etc. This should be connected and related.

Idāni niddesavibhāgenapi avijjāya saccesu pavattivibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha dukkheti ettakena bhummaniddesena. Saṅgahatoti pariññeyyatāya dukkhena saṅgahetabbato. Tena niddhāraṇatthaṃ dasseti. Dukkhasmiñhi avijjā niddhārīyati, na aññasmiṃ. Vatthutoti ādhāratthaṃ. Dukkhasannissayā hi avijjā. Ārammaṇatoti visayatthaṃ taṃ ārabbha pavattanato. Kiccatoti byāpanatthaṃ chādanavasena taṃ byāpetvā pavattanato. Iminā nayena sesesupi attho veditabbo. Avisesatoti visesābhāvato, vuttanayena dukkhādīsu pavattiākāravisesaṃ aggahetvāti attho. Sabhāvatoti sarasalakkhaṇato. Catunnampi saccānaṃ ajānanasabhāvā hi avijjā. Kāmarāgabhavarāgā kāmāsavabhavāsavāti āha “sahajātādivasenā”ti. Nanu avijjā eva avijjāsavo, so kathaṃ avijjāya paccayoti āha “pubbuppannā”tiādi.

Now, to show the division of the arising of ignorance in relation to the truths, even by way of detailed explanation, the passage beginning with “Moreover” is stated. Here, “in suffering” is by way of this much of an exposition in the locative case. “By inclusion”: because it is to be included by suffering due to its nature as something to be fully understood. By this, the meaning of determination is shown. For ignorance is determined in relation to suffering, not in relation to anything else. “As a basis”: it is for the meaning of support. For ignorance is dependent on suffering. “As an object”: it is for the meaning of domain, since it arises in relation to that. “As a function”: it is for the meaning of pervasion, since it arises by pervading it through concealment. In this way, the meaning in the remaining cases should also be understood. “Without distinction”: due to the absence of distinction, meaning that no particular mode of arising in relation to suffering, etc., is grasped in the way stated. “By its nature”: it is by its essential characteristic. For ignorance is indeed the nature of not knowing all four truths. Regarding “sensual desire and desire for existence are the taints of sensuality and existence,” it is said, “by way of conascence, etc.” But isn’t ignorance itself the taint of ignorance? How then is it a condition for ignorance? It is said, “previously arisen,” etc.

Avijjāvāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Ignorance is concluded.

Āsavavāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Chapter on Taints

104. Āsavavāre [M 1.0327] āsava-saddattho āsavavicāro ca heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Kasmā panāyaṃ vāro vutto, nanu avijjādikāva paṭiccasamuppādadesanāti codanaṃ sandhāya “ayaṃ vāro”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Paṭiccasamuppādapadesūti paṭiccasamuppādakoṭṭhāsesu. Dvādasakoṭṭhāsā hi satthu paṭiccasamuppādadesanā. Tassāpi paccayadassanavasenāti nāyaṃ kāpilānaṃ mūlapakati viya appaccayā, atha kho sappaccayāti avijjāyapi paccayadassanavasena. Āsavasamudayenāti atītabhave āsavānaṃ samudayena etarahi avijjāya samudayo, etarahi avijjāya samudayena anāgate āsavasamudayoti evaṃ āsavāvijjānaṃ paccayapaccayuppannakabhāvena aparāparaṃ pavattamānaṃ ādikoṭiabhāveneva tannimittassa saṃsārassa ādikoṭiabhāvato anamataggatāsiddhi veditabbā.

104. In the section on taints, the meaning of the word 'taint' and the analysis of taints have already been stated above. But why was this section taught? Surely the teaching of dependent origination begins with ignorance! To address this objection, the passage beginning with “this section” is commenced. “In the parts of dependent origination” means in the divisions of dependent origination. For the Teacher's teaching of dependent origination has twelve divisions. And even for that, by way of showing its condition—it is not without a condition like the mūlaprakṛti of the Kāpilas, but rather is with a condition; thus, even for ignorance, by way of showing its condition. “By the arising of taints” means by the arising of taints in a past existence, there is the arising of ignorance now; by the arising of ignorance now, there is the arising of taints in the future. Thus, with taints and ignorance being in a state of condition and conditioned, occurring successively without a beginning or end, the establishment of its untraceable beginning should be understood from the fact that the cycle of existence, which is caused by them, also lacks a beginning and an end.

Dvattiṃsa [V 1.0292] ṭhānānīti dvattiṃsa saccappaṭivedhakāraṇāni, dvattiṃsa vā catusaccakammaṭṭhānāni. Imamhā sammādiṭṭhisuttāti yāya ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi nāma hoti, sā ariyā sammādiṭṭhi ettha vuttāti sammādiṭṭhisuttaṃ, ito sammādiṭṭhisuttato.

The thirty-two bases are the thirty-two causes for penetrating the truths, or the thirty-two subjects of meditation regarding the four truths. This is called the Discourse on Right View because the noble right view by which a noble disciple is called one with right view is spoken of herein. From this Discourse on Right View.

Catusaccapariyāyehīti catusaccādhigamakāraṇehi. Arahattapariyāyehīti “so sabbaso rāgānusayaṃ pahāyā”tiādinā arahattādhigamakāraṇehi. Tenāha “catusaṭṭhiyā kāraṇehī”ti.

“By the expositions of the Four Truths” means by the causes for realizing the Four Noble Truths. “By the expositions of Arahantship” means by the causes for attaining Arahantship, as in “having entirely abandoned the underlying tendency to lust,” etc. Therefore, it is said, “by sixty-four reasons.”

Āsavavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Taints is completed.

Sammādiṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta is completed.

10. Satipaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta

105. Jānapadinoti [V 1.0293] (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.95) janapadavanto, janapadassa vā issarā rājakumārā. Gottavasena kurū nāma. Tesaṃ nivāso yadi eko janapado, kathaṃ bahuvacananti āha “ruḷhīsaddenā”ti. Akkharacintakā hi īdisesu ṭhānesu yutte viya saliṅgavacanāni (pāṇini 1.251) icchanti, ayamettha ruḷhī yathā [M 1.0328] aññatthāpi “aṅgesu viharati, mallesu viharatī”ti ca. Tabbisesane pana janapada-sadde jāti-sadde ekavacanameva. Aṭṭhakathācariyā panāti pana-saddo visesatthajotano. Tena puthuatthavisayatāya evaṃ taṃ bahuvacananti “bahuke panā”tiādinā vakkhamānaṃ visesaṃ dīpeti. Sutvāti mandhātumahārājassa ānubhāvadassanānusārena paramparāgataṃ kathaṃ sutvā. Anusaṃyāyantenāti anuvicarantena. Etesaṃ ṭhānanti candimasūriyamukhena cātumahārājikabhavanamāha. Tenāha “tattha agamāsī”tiādi. Soti mandhātumahārājā. Tanti cātumahārājikarajjaṃ. Gahetvāti sampaṭicchitvā. Puna pucchi pariṇāyakaratanaṃ. Dovārikabhūmiyaṃ tiṭṭhanti sudhammāya devasabhāya devapurassa ca catūsu dvāresu ārakkhāya adhikatattā. Dibbarukkhasahassapaṭimaṇḍitanti idaṃ “cittalatāvana”ntiādīsupi yojetabbaṃ.

105. ‘Jānapadino’ means (as explained in Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 2.95) the people of the country, or the ruling princes of the country. By clan, they are named the Kurus. If their dwelling is one country, how is the plural form used? It is said, ‘by conventional usage.’ For grammarians accept gender and number agreements (Pāṇini 1.251) in such cases; this is a convention here, just as elsewhere in ‘he dwells among the Aṅgas’ and ‘he dwells among the Mallās.’ However, when the word ‘janapada’ (country) qualifies it as a generic term, it remains singular. The commentary teachers, however—here the word ‘pana’ (but) highlights a distinction—explain that due to the diversity of meanings, the plural is used, as in ‘but many,’ etc., to indicate a specific sense. ‘Having heard’ refers to hearing the story passed down through tradition, in accordance with seeing the majesty of King Mandhātā. ‘Following along’ means investigating. ‘Their place’ refers to the realm of the Four Great Kings, indicated by the moon and sun. Hence it is said, ‘there he went,’ etc. ‘He’ is King Mandhātā. ‘That’ is the kingdom of the Four Great Kings. ‘Having taken’ means having accepted. Again, he asked for the guide-jewel. ‘They stand at the gatekeeper’s post’ because they are appointed to guard the four gates of the Sudhammā divine assembly hall and the divine city. ‘Adorned with a thousand divine trees’—this should also be applied to phrases like ‘the Cittalatā grove,’ etc.

Pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāsīti bhassitvā pathaviyā āsanne ṭhāne aṭṭhāsi, ṭhatvā ca nacirasseva antaradhāyi tenattabhāvena rañño cakkavattissariyassa abhāvato. “Cirataraṃ kālaṃ ṭhatvā”ti apare. Devabhāvo pāturahosi devaloke pavattivipākadāyino aparāpariyāyavedanīyassa kammassa katokāsattā. Avayave siddho viseso samudāyassa visesako hotīti ekampi raṭṭhaṃ bahuvacanena voharīyati.

‘He was established on the earth’ means having fallen, he stood in a place near the ground. Having stood there, he soon disappeared in that very form, due to the absence of the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch. ‘Having stood for a longer time,’ say others. A divine existence appeared in the heavenly world, because an opportunity was made for karma, to be experienced in a subsequent existence, which gives its fruit in the course of existence. A special quality established in a part becomes a qualifier of the whole; thus, even a single kingdom is referred to in the plural.

Da-kārena atthaṃ vaṇṇayanti niruttinayena. Kammāsoti kammāsapādo vuccati uttarapadalopena yathā “rūpabhavo rūpa”nti. Kathaṃ pana so kammāsapādoti āha “tassa kirā”tiādi. Damitoti ettha kīdisaṃ damanaṃ adhippetanti āha “porisādabhāvato paṭisedhito”ti. Ime pana therāti majjhimabhāṇake vadati, te pana cūḷakammāsadammaṃ sandhāya tathā vadanti. Yakkhiniputto hi kammāsapādo alīnasattukumārakāle bodhisattena tattha damito, sutasomakāle [V 1.0294] pana bārāṇasirājā porisādabhāvapaṭisedhanena yattha damito, taṃ mahākammāsadammaṃ nāma. Puttoti vatvā atrajoti vacanaṃ orasaputtabhāvadassanatthaṃ.

They explain the meaning by the letter ‘da’ according to the method of etymology. ‘Kammāso’ is said for ‘Kammāsapādo’ by the elision of the final member of the compound, just as ‘rūpabhava’ is called ‘rūpa.’ But how then is he ‘Kammāsapāda’? He says, ‘It is said that his…,’ etc. Regarding ‘damito’ (tamed), what kind of taming is intended here? He says, ‘prevented from being a man-eater.’ ‘These elders’ refers to the Majjhimabhāṇakas (reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya), and they speak thus with reference to the Cūḷakammāsadamma. For the yakkha’s son, Kammāsapāda, was tamed there by the Bodhisatta when he was Prince Alīnasattu; but in the time of King Sutasoma of Bārāṇasī, he was tamed by preventing him from being a man-eater—that is called the Mahākammāsadamma. Having said ‘putto’ (son), the word ‘atrajo’ is stated to show his status as a legitimate (orasa) son.

Yehi āvasitapadeso kururaṭṭhanti nāmaṃ labhi, te uttarakuruto āgatā manussā tattha rakkhitaniyāmeneva pañca sīlāni rakkhiṃsu, tesaṃ diṭṭhānugatiyā [M 1.0329] pacchimā janatāti, so desadhammavasena avicchedato vattamāno kuruvattadhammoti paññāyittha, ayañca attho kurudhammajātakena (jā. 1.3.76-78) dīpetabbo. So aparabhāge yattha paṭhamaṃ saṃkiliṭṭho jāto, taṃ dassetuṃ “kururaṭṭhavāsīna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Yattha bhagavato vasanokāso koci vihāro na hoti, tattha kevalaṃ gocaragāmakittanaṃ nidānakathāya pakati, yathā taṃsakkesu viharati devadahaṃ nāma sakkānaṃ nigamoti imamatthaṃ dassento “avasanokāsato”tiādimāha.

The place where they dwelt became known as Kururaṭṭha. Those people who came from Uttarakuru maintained the five precepts there by the same principle by which they had been protected. Following their example, later generations did likewise; thus, by the custom of the region, it became known as the Kuruvattadhamma, continuing unbroken. This meaning should be illustrated by the Kurudhammajātaka (Jā. 1.3.76-78). Later, to show where it first became defiled, it is said, ‘of the inhabitants of Kururaṭṭha,’ etc. Where the Blessed One had no dwelling place such as a monastery, there the mere mention of the village for alms-gathering is the custom in the introductory story—for example, ‘he dwelt among the Sakyans in a market town of the Sakyans named Devadaha.’ To show this meaning, he says, ‘because there was no dwelling place,’ etc.

Uddesavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Outlines

106. Kasmā bhagavā imaṃ suttamabhāsīti asādhāraṇasamuṭṭhānaṃ pucchati, sādhāraṇaṃ pana pākaṭanti anāmaṭṭhaṃ, tena suttanikkhepo pucchitoti katvā itaro “kururaṭṭhavāsīna”ntiādinā aparajjhāsayoyaṃ suttanikkhepoti dasseti. Etena bāhirasamuṭṭhānaṃ vibhāvitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ajjhattikaṃ pana asādhāraṇañca mūlapariyāyasuttādiṭīkāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Kururaṭṭhaṃ kira (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.373) tadā tannivāsīnaṃ sattānaṃ yebhuyyena yonisomanasikāravantatāya pubbe ca katapuññatābalena utuādisampannameva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ “utupaccayādisampannattā”ti. Ādi-saddena bhojanādisampattiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Keci pana “pubbe kuruvattadhammānuṭṭhānavāsanāya uttarakuru viya yebhuyyena utuādisampannameva hontaṃ bhagavato kāle sātisayaṃ utusappāyādiyuttaṃ taṃ raṭṭhaṃ ahosī”ti vadanti. Cittasarīrakallatāyāti cittassa sarīrassa ca arogatāya. Anuggahitapaññābalāti laddhupakārañāṇānubhāvā, anu anu vā āciṇṇapaññātejā. Ekavīsatiyā ṭhānesūti kāyānupassanāvasena cuddasasuṭhānesu, vedanānupassanāvasena ekasmiṃ ṭhāne, tathā cittānupassanāvasena, dhammānupassanāvasena pañcasu ṭhānesūti evaṃ ekavīsatiyā ṭhānesu. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ arahatte pakkhipitvāti catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ yathā arahattaṃ pāpeti, evaṃ desanāvasena arahatte pakkhipitvā. Suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭakasuvaṇṇamañjūsāsu pakkhittāni sumanacampakādinānāpupphāni maṇiputtādisattaratanāni ca yathā bhājanasampattiyā savisesaṃ sobhanti, kiccakarāni [M 1.0330] ca honti manuññābhāvato, evaṃ sīladassanādisampattiyā bhājanavisesabhūtāya kururaṭṭhavāsiparisāya desitā [V 1.0295] ca bhagavato ayaṃ desanā bhiyyosomattāya sobhati, kiccakārī ca hotīti imamatthaṃ dasseti “yathā hi puriso”tiādinā. Etthāti kururaṭṭhe.

106. Why did the Blessed One speak this discourse? He asks about the uncommon origin; the common one, however, is evident and so not touched upon. Therefore, taking it that the placement of the discourse is being questioned, the other shows that this placement of the discourse is due to the unfailing intention of the inhabitants of Kururaṭṭha, etc. By this, it should be understood that the external origin has been explained. The internal and uncommon origin, however, should be known in the manner stated in the subcommentary on the Mūlapariyāya Sutta and others. It is said that the Kuru country, at that time, was endowed with favorable conditions, such as climate, mostly due to the inhabitants' wise attention and the power of their past merit. Therefore it is said, ‘because of being endowed with favorable climate and other conditions.’ By the word ‘etc.,’ he includes the excellence of food and other things. Some, however, say: ‘Due to the latent tendency from the past practice of the Kuruvatta Dhamma, that country, like Uttarakuru, was mostly endowed with favorable conditions such as climate, and during the time of the Blessed One, it became exceptionally endowed with a suitable climate, etc.’ ‘Due to the fitness of mind and body’ means due to the health of mind and body. ‘With the power of wisdom supported’ means having the power of knowledge that has received assistance, or the splendor of wisdom practiced again and again. ‘In twenty-one instances’ means in fourteen instances by way of the contemplation of the body, in one instance by way of the contemplation of feeling, likewise in one instance by way of the contemplation of mind, and in five instances by way of the contemplation of mental objects—thus, in twenty-one instances. ‘Having placed the meditation subject in Arahantship’ means having placed the meditation subject on the four truths in Arahantship by way of teaching, so that it leads to Arahantship. Just as various flowers like jasmine and campaka, and the seven precious gems, when placed in golden caskets and golden chests, shine with special brilliance due to the excellence of their containers, and are effective because they are pleasing, so too this teaching of the Blessed One, when taught to the assembly of the inhabitants of Kururaṭṭha, who are a special kind of container due to their endowment with virtue and insight, shines even more brilliantly and is effective. This meaning is shown by the passage, ‘Just as a person…,’ etc. ‘Here’ means in the Kuru country.

Pakatiyāti sarasato, imissā satipaṭṭhānasuttadesanāya pubbepīti adhippāyo. Anuyuttā viharanti satthu desanānusāratoti adhippāyo. Vissaṭṭhaattabhāvanāti aniccādivasena kismiñci yonisomanasikāre cittaṃ aniyojetvā rūpādiārammaṇe abhirativasena vissaṭṭhacittena bhavituṃ na vaṭṭati, pamādavihāraṃ pahāya appamattena bhavitabbanti adhippāyo.

‘Naturally’ means inherently; the intention is that this was so even before this discourse on the foundations of mindfulness. ‘They dwell devoted’ means in accordance with the Teacher's instruction—this is the intention. ‘With a scattered state of being’ means it is not proper for the mind to become scattered due to delight in objects such as forms, without directing the mind to any wise reflection such as impermanence; one should abandon heedless living and live diligently—this is the intention.

Ekāyanoti ettha ayana-saddo maggapariyāyo. Na kevalamayanameva, atha kho aññepi bahū maggapariyāyāti paduddhāraṃ karonto “maggassa hī”tiādi vatvā yadi maggapariyāyo ayana-saddo, kasmā puna maggoti vuttanti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “tasmā”tiādi. Tattha ekamaggoti eko eva maggo. Na hi nibbānagāmī maggo añño atthīti. Nanu satipaṭṭhānaṃ idha “maggo”ti adhippetaṃ, tadaññe ca bahū maggadhammā atthīti? Saccaṃ atthi, te pana satipaṭṭhānaggahaṇeneva gahitā tadavinābhāvato. Tathā hi ñāṇavīriyādayo niddese gahitā. Uddese pana satiyā eva gahaṇaṃ veneyyajjhāsayavasenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na dvedhāpathabhūtoti iminā imassa maggassa anekamaggatābhāvaṃ viya anibbānagāmibhāvābhāvañca dasseti. Ekenāti asahāyena. Asahāyatā ca duvidhā attadutiyatābhāvena vā, yā “vūpakaṭṭhakāyatā”ti vuccati, taṇhādutiyatābhāvena vā, yā “pavivittacittatā”ti vuccati. Tenāha “vūpakaṭṭhena pavivittacittenā”ti. Seṭṭhopi loke “eko”ti vuccati “yāva pare ekato karosī”tiādīsūti āha “ekassāti seṭṭhassā”ti. Yadi saṃsārato nissaraṇaṭṭho ayanaṭṭho aññesampi upanissayasampannānaṃ sādhāraṇo kathaṃ bhagavatoti āha “kiñcāpī”tiādi. Imasmiṃ khoti ettha kho-saddo avadhāraṇe, tasmā imasmiṃ yevāti attho. Desanābhedoyeva heso, yadidaṃ maggoti vā ayanoti vā. Tenāha “attho paneko”ti.

In 'Ekāyano', the word 'ayana' is a synonym for path. Not only 'ayana' itself, but there are also many other synonyms for path. While extracting the term, having said 'for the path,' etc., and addressing the objection, 'If the word 'ayana' is a synonym for path, why is 'magga' (path) mentioned again?', he says, 'therefore,' etc. Here, 'ekamagga' means the one and only path, for there is no other path leading to Nibbāna. But are not the foundations of mindfulness intended here as the 'path,' and are there not many other path-factors as well? It is true they exist, but they are included by the taking up of the foundations of mindfulness due to their inseparability. Thus, factors like wisdom and energy are included in the detailed explanation. In the summary, however, only mindfulness is taken up, which should be understood as being according to the disposition of those to be trained. 'Not being a divided path'—by this, he shows this path's lack of multiplicity, as well as the absence of its not leading to Nibbāna. 'By one' means without a companion. This state of being without a companion is twofold: either by the absence of a second person, which is called 'seclusion of body,' or by the absence of craving as a companion, which is called 'seclusion of mind.' Hence, it is said, 'with a secluded body and a secluded mind.' Even the best in the world is called 'one,' as in such sayings as, 'as long as you unify others,' etc. Therefore, it is said, 'of the one means of the best.' If the meaning of 'ayana' as the escape from saṃsāra is common to others endowed with supporting conditions, how is it of the Blessed One? He says, 'although,' etc. 'In this'—here, the word 'kho' is for emphasis; therefore, the meaning is 'in this very one.' This is merely a difference in exposition, whether it is called 'path' or 'way.' Therefore, he says, 'but the meaning is one.'

Nānāmukhabhāvanānayappavattoti [M 1.0331] kāyānupassanādimukhena tatthāpi ānāpānādimukhena bhāvanānayena pavatto. Ekāyananti ekagāminaṃ, nibbānagāminanti attho. Nibbānañhi adutiyattā seṭṭhattā ca “eka”nti vuccati. Yathāha “ekañhi saccaṃ na dutīyamatthī”ti (su. ni. 890) “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90) ca. Khayo eva antoti khayanto[V 1.0296], jātiyā khayantaṃ diṭṭhavāti jātikhayantadassī. Avibhāgena sabbepi satte hitena anukampatīti hitānukampī. Atariṃsūti tariṃsu. Pubbeti purimakā buddhā, pubbe vā atītakāle.

‘Proceeding by way of development with various approaches’ means it proceeds by way of development through the approach of contemplation of the body, etc., and even there through the approach of mindfulness of breathing, etc. ‘Ekāyana’ means going to one destination, the meaning being that it leads to Nibbāna. For Nibbāna is called ‘one’ because it is without a second and because it is supreme. As it is said: ‘There is but one truth, no second exists’ (Snp 4.11), and ‘Whatever, bhikkhus, are conditioned or unconditioned phenomena, dispassion is declared the highest among them’ (AN 4.34; Iti 90). ‘Destruction itself is the end’ is ‘khayanto’; ‘one who has seen the destruction of birth’ is ‘jātikhayantadassī’. ‘He has compassion for all beings without distinction, with their welfare in mind’ is ‘hitānukampī’. ‘Atariṃsu’ means they crossed over. ‘Pubbe’ means the previous Buddhas, or in a former time.

Tanti taṃ tesaṃ vacanaṃ, taṃ vā kiriyāvuttivācakattaṃ na yujjati. Na hi saṅkheyyappadhānatāya sattavācino eka-saddassa kiriyāvuttivācakatā atthi. “Sakimpi uddhaṃ gaccheyyā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 7.72) viya “sakiṃ ayano”ti iminā byañjanena bhavitabbaṃ. Evaṃ atthaṃ yojetvāti evaṃ padatthaṃ yojetvā. Ubhayathāpīti purimanayena pacchimanayena ca. Na yujjati idhādhippetamaggassa anekavāraṃ pavattisabbhāvato. Tenāha “kasmā”tiādi. Anekavārampi ayatīti purimanayassa, anekañcassa ayanaṃ hotīti pacchimanayassa ca paṭikkhepo.

‘That’ refers to their statement, but that capacity to express an action or course of conduct is not appropriate. Indeed, for the word 'one', which primarily denotes a being by number, the capacity to express an action or course of conduct does not exist. As in such phrases as, ‘Even once one should go upwards’ (AN 7.72), the expression should be 'a going once' (`sakiṃ ayano`). ‘Thus, having connected the meaning’ means having connected the word-meaning in this manner. ‘In both ways’ means according to the former method and the latter method. It is not appropriate here because the path intended here occurs many times. Hence, it is said, ‘Why?’ etc. ‘He goes repeatedly’ is a refutation of the former method, and ‘his going is manifold’ is a refutation of the latter method.

Imasmiṃ padeti “ekāyano ayaṃ bhikkhave maggo”ti imasmiṃ vākye, imasmiṃ vā “pubbabhāgamaggo lokuttaramaggo”ti saṃsayaṭṭhāne. Missakamaggoti lokiyena missako lokuttaramaggo. Visuddhiādīnaṃ nippariyāyahetuṃ saṅgaṇhanto ācariyatthero “missakamaggo”ti āha, itaro pariyāyahetu idhādhippetoti “pubbabhāgamaggo”ti.

‘In this passage’ refers to this statement: ‘This is the one-way path, O bhikkhus,’ or in this place of doubt: ‘Is the preliminary path the supramundane path?’ ‘The mixed path’ refers to the supramundane path mixed with the mundane. The elder teacher, encompassing the direct cause of purification and so forth, called it the ‘mixed path,’ while the other, considering the indirect cause intended here, called it the ‘preliminary path.’

Saddaṃ sutvāvāti “kālo, bhante, dhammassavanāyā”ti kālārocanasaddaṃ sutvā. Evaṃ ukkhipitvāti. Evaṃ “madhuraṃ imaṃ kuhiṃ chaḍḍemā”ti achaḍḍentā ucchubhāraṃ viya paggahetvā na vicaranti. Āluḷetīti viluḷito ākulo hotīti attho. Ekāyanamaggo vuccati pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānamaggoti. Ettāvatā idhādhippetatthe siddhe tasseva alaṅkāratthaṃ so pana yassa pubbabhāgamaggo, taṃ dassetuṃ “maggānaṭṭhaṅgiko”tiādikā [M 1.0332] gāthāpi paṭisambhidāmaggatova ānetvā ṭhapitā.

‘Having heard the sound’ means having heard the sound announcing the time: ‘It is time, venerable sir, for hearing the Dhamma.’ ‘Having lifted it thus’ means thus, like people holding a bundle of sugarcane without discarding it, saying, ‘Where shall we discard this sweet thing?’ they do not wander about. ‘Disturbed’ means agitated and confused. The one-way path is called the preliminary path of the establishment of mindfulness. Up to this point, the intended meaning here is established. However, for the sake of embellishing that very meaning, and to show of what it is the preliminary path, the verse beginning, ‘The path with eight factors,’ is also brought from the Paṭisambhidāmagga and placed here.

Nibbānagamanaṭṭhenāti nibbānaṃ gacchati adhigacchati etenāti nibbānagamanaṃ, so eva aviparītasabhāvatāya attho, tena nibbānagamanaṭṭhena, nibbānādhigamupāyatāyāti attho. Magganīyaṭṭhenāti gavesitabbatāya, “gamanīyaṭṭhenā”ti vā pāṭho, upagantabbattāti attho. Rāgādīhīti. Iminā rāgadosamohānaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ “rāgo malaṃ, doso malaṃ, moho mala”nti (vibha. 924) vacanato. “Abhijjhāvisamalobhādīhī”ti pana iminā sabbesampi upakkilesānaṃ saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ te visuṃ uddhaṭā. Sattānaṃ visuddhiyāti vuttassa atthassa ekantikataṃ [V 1.0297] dassento “tathā hī”tiādimāha. Kāmaṃ “visuddhiyā”ti sāmaññajotanā, cittavisuddhi eva panettha adhippetāti dassetuṃ “rūpamalavasena panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na kevalaṃ aṭṭhakathāvacanameva, atha kho idamettha āhaccabhāsitanti dassento “tathā hī”tiādimāha.

'By the meaning of going to Nibbāna': one goes to and attains Nibbāna by this, thus it is a 'going to Nibbāna.' That itself is the meaning due to its unperverted nature. Therefore, 'by the meaning of going to Nibbāna' means 'by being the means for attaining Nibbāna.' 'By the meaning of being sought' means by its being something to be sought; or the reading is 'by the meaning of being approached,' which means by its being something to be approached. 'By lust, etc.': by this, only lust, hatred, and delusion are included, according to the statement, 'Lust is a stain, hatred is a stain, delusion is a stain' (Vb 924). However, by the phrase 'by covetousness, unrighteous greed, etc.,' they are mentioned separately for the purpose of including all defilements. To show the definitive nature of the meaning stated as 'for the purification of beings,' he says, 'for thus indeed,' etc. Although 'for purification' is a general indication, to show that purification of mind is specifically intended here, it is said, 'but by way of the stain of form,' etc. To show that this is not merely a statement from the commentary, but that it was spoken specifically for this context, he says, 'for thus indeed,' etc.

Sā panāyaṃ cittavisuddhi sijjhamānā yasmā sokādīnaṃ anuppādāya saṃvattati, tasmā vuttaṃ “sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāyā”tiādi. Tattha socanaṃ ñātibyasanādinimittaṃ cetaso santāpo antonijjhānaṃ soko. Ñātibyasanādinimittameva sokādhikatāya “kahaṃ, ekaputtaka, kahaṃ, ekaputtakā”ti paridevavasena lapanaṃ paridevo, āyatiṃ anuppajjanaṃ idha samatikkamoti āha “pahānāyā”ti. Taṃ panassa samatikkamāvahataṃ nidassanavasena dassento “ayaṃ hī”tiādimāha.

And this purification of mind, while it is being accomplished, conduces to the non-arising of sorrow and the like; therefore, it is said, 'for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation,' and so on. Herein, sorrow (soko) is the burning of the mind, the inner anguish, caused by such things as the loss of relatives. Lamentation (paridevo) is wailing in the manner of bemoaning, due to an excess of sorrow caused by such things as the loss of relatives, with expressions like, 'Where, my only son? Where, my only son?' Here, 'overcoming' is the non-arising in the future; he says 'for abandonment' to indicate this. Then, showing by way of illustration how this brings about that overcoming, he says, 'for this,' and so on.

Tattha yaṃ pubbe taṃ visodhehīti atītesu khandhesu taṇhāsaṃkilesavisodhanaṃ vuttaṃ. Pacchāti parato. Teti tuyhaṃ. Māhūti mā ahu. Kiñcananti rāgādikiñcanaṃ. Etena anāgatesu khandhesu saṃkilesavisodhanaṃ vuttaṃ. Majjheti tadubhayavemajjhe. No ce gahessasīti na upādiyissasi ce. Etena paccuppanne khandhapabandhe upādānappavatti vuttā. Upasanto carissasīti evaṃ addhattayagatasaṃkilesavisodhane sati nibbutasabbapariḷāhatāya upasanto hutvā viharissasīti arahattanikūṭena gāthaṃ niṭṭhapesi. Tenāha “imaṃ gātha”ntiādi.

Herein, 'what was before, that purify' refers to the purification of the defilement of craving regarding the past aggregates. 'After' means in the future. 'Te' means yours. 'Māhū' means may it not be. 'Anything' refers to defilements such as lust. By this, the purification of defilements regarding the future aggregates is stated. 'In the middle' means in the space between both. 'If you grasp not' means if you do not cling. By this, the occurrence of clinging in the present continuum of aggregates is stated. 'Peaceful, you shall fare' means that when there is purification of defilements relating to the three periods of time, being peaceful through the quenching of all burning distress, you will dwell—thus, he concluded the verse with the pinnacle of arahantship. Therefore, he said, 'this verse,' etc.

Puttāti [M 1.0333] orasā, aññepi vā ye keci. Pitāti janako. Bandhavāti ñātakā. Ayañhettha attho – puttā vā pitā vā bandhavā vā antakena maccunā adhipannassa abhibhūtassa maraṇato tāṇāya na honti, tasmā natthi ñātīsu tāṇatāti. Na hi ñātīnaṃ vasena maraṇato ārakkhā atthi, tasmā paṭācāre “ubho puttā kālakatā”tiādinā (apa. therī 2.2.498) mā niratthakaṃ paridevi, dhammaṃyeva pana yāthāvato passāti adhippāyo.

'Children' means offspring, or any others whatsoever. 'Father' means the generator. 'Relatives' are kin. The meaning here is this: children, father, or relatives cannot provide refuge for one seized and overcome by the End-maker, by death. Therefore, there is no refuge in relatives. Indeed, there is no protection from death by means of relatives. Thus, regarding Paṭācārā, it is said: 'Do not lament uselessly with expressions like "Both sons have died," etc. (Ap. Therī 2.2.498), but rather see the Dhamma as it actually is'—this is the intention.

Sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitāti yathānulomaṃ pavattitāya sāmukkaṃsikāya dhammadesanāya pariyosāne sahassanayapaṭimaṇḍite sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Kathaṃ panāyaṃ satipaṭṭhānamaggavasena sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsīti āha “yasmā panā”tiādi. Na hi catusaccakammaṭṭhānakathāya vinā sāvakānaṃ ariyamaggādhigamo atthi. “Imaṃ gāthaṃ sutvā”ti pana idaṃ sokavinodanavasena pavattitāya gāthāya paṭhamaṃ sutattā vuttaṃ. Esa nayo itaragāthāyapi. Bhāvanāti [V 1.0298] paññābhāvanā. Sā hi idhādhippetā. Tasmāti yasmā rūpādīnaṃ aniccādito anupassanāpi satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā, tasmā. Tepīti santatimahāmattapaṭācārā.

'Established in the fruit of stream-entry'—at the conclusion of the progressive and uplifting Dhamma teaching, adorned with a thousand aspects, she became established in the fruit of stream-entry. But how was she established in the fruit of stream-entry by way of the path of the establishments of mindfulness? He said, 'Because...' and so on. For without the discourse on the four noble truths as a meditation subject, there is no attainment of the noble path for disciples. 'Having heard this verse'—this is said because this verse, uttered for the sake of dispelling sorrow, was heard first. The same method applies to the other verses as well. 'Development' means the development of wisdom, for that is what is meant here. Therefore—because even the contemplation of impermanence and so on in forms and so on is the development of the establishments of mindfulness, therefore. 'They too'—the great minister Santati and Paṭācārā.

Pañcasate coreti satasatacoraparivāre pañca core paṭipāṭiyā pesesi. Te araññaṃ pavisitvā theraṃ pariyesantā anukkamena therassa samīpe samāgacchiṃsu. Tenāha “te gantvā theraṃ parivāretvā nisīdiṃsū”ti. Vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvā pītipāmojjaṃ uppajjīti sambandho. Therassa hi sīlaṃ paccavekkhato suparisuddhaṃ sīlaṃ nissāya uḷāraṃ pītipāmojjaṃ uppajjamānaṃ ūruṭṭhibhedajanitaṃ dukkhavedanaṃ vikkhambhesi. Pādānīti pāde. Saññapessāmīti saññattiṃ karissāmi. Aḍḍiyāmīti jigucchāmi. Harāyāmīti lajjāmi. Vipassisanti sammasiṃ.

'Five hundred thieves'—he sent five thieves in turn, each with a retinue of a hundred thieves. Entering the forest and seeking the elder, they gradually approached him. Hence it is said, "They went, surrounded the elder, and sat down." "Having suppressed the feeling, joy and gladness arose"—this is the connection. For as the elder reflected on his perfectly purified virtue, exalted joy and gladness arose, suppressing the painful feeling caused by the breaking of his thigh bones. 'Pādāni' means 'pāde' (feet). 'I will inform' means 'I will make it known.' 'I abhor' means 'I feel disgust.' 'I am ashamed' means 'I feel shame.' 'I saw clearly' means 'I contemplated.'

Pacalāyantānanti pacalāyanaṃ niddaṃ upagatānaṃ. Vatasampannoti dhutacaraṇasampanno. Pamādanti pacalāyanaṃ sandhāyāha. Oruddhamānasoti uparuddhaadhicitto. Pañjarasminti sarīre. Sarīrañhi nhārusambandhaaṭṭhisaṅghātatāya idha “pañjara”nti vuttaṃ.

'Of those nodding off' means of those who have been overcome by drowsiness, by sleep. 'Endowed with vows' means accomplished in the practice of asceticism. 'Negligence' refers to nodding off. 'With mind restrained' means with the higher mind obstructed. 'In the cage' means in the body. For the body, being an assemblage of bones connected by sinews, is here called a 'cage.'

Pītavaṇṇāya paṭākāya pariharaṇato mallayuddhacittakatāya ca pītamallo. Tīsu rajjesūti paṇḍucoḷagoḷarajjesu. Mallā sīhaḷadīpe sakkārasammānaṃ [M 1.0334] labhantīti tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ āgamma. Taṃyeva aṅkusaṃ katvāti “rūpādayo ‘mamā’ti na gahetabbā”ti na tumhākavaggena (saṃ. ni. 3.33-34) pakāsitamatthaṃ attano cittamattahatthino aṅkusaṃ katvā. Jaṇṇukehi caṅkamati “nisinne niddāya avasaro hotī”ti. Byākaritvāti attano vīriyārambhassa saphalatāpavedanamukhena sabrahmacārīnaṃ ussāhaṃ janento aññaṃ byākaritvā. Bhāsitanti vacanaṃ. Kassa pana tanti āha “buddhaseṭṭhassa, sabbalokaggavādino”ti. Na tumhākantiādi tassa pavattiākāradassanaṃ. Tayidaṃ me saṅkhārānaṃ accantavūpasamakāraṇanti dassento “aniccā vatā”ti gāthaṃ āhari. Tena idānāhaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇe khaṇe bhaṅgasaṅkhātassa rogassa abhāvena arogo parinibbutoti dasseti.

Because he was carried around with a yellow banner and because of the depiction of a wrestling match, he was called the Yellow Wrestler. 'In the three kingdoms' means in the kingdoms of Paṇḍu, Coḷa, and Goḷa. He came to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, thinking, 'Wrestlers receive honor and respect in the island of Sri Lanka.' 'Making that very goad' means making the meaning explained in the 'Not Yours' section (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.33–34)—that 'forms and so forth should not be grasped as "mine"'—the goad for his own mind-elephant.
