He walks on his knees, thinking, 'While sitting, there is an opportunity for drowsiness.' 'Having declared' means having declared final knowledge, thereby generating enthusiasm in his fellow practitioners by announcing the fruitfulness of his own energetic effort. 'What was spoken' means the word. Whose teaching is it? He said, 'Of the foremost Buddha, the teacher of all worlds.' The phrase 'not yours' and so forth shows the manner of its application. Then, to demonstrate that this is the cause of the ultimate cessation of my formations, he uttered the verse: 'Impermanent, indeed...' Thus, he shows that he is now healthy and fully extinguished, by the absence of the disease consisting of the moment-to-moment dissolution of formations.

Assāti sakkassa. Upapattīti devūpapatti. Punapākatikāva ahosi sakkabhāveneva upapannattā. Subrahmāti evaṃ nāmo. Accharānaṃ nirayūpapattiṃ disvā tato pabhuti satataṃ pavattamānaṃ attano cittutrāsaṃ sandhāyāha “niccaṃ utrastamidaṃ citta”ntiādi. Tattha utrastanti santastaṃ bhītaṃ. Ubbigganti saṃviggaṃ. Utrastanti vā saṃviggaṃ. Ubbigganti bhayavasena saha kāyena sañcalitaṃ. Anuppannesūti anāgatesu. Kicchesūti dukkhesu. Nimittatthe bhummavacanaṃ, bhāvīdukkhapavattinimittanti [V 1.0299] attho. Uppatitesūti uppannesu kicchesūti yojanā, tadā attano parivārassa uppannadukkhanimittanti adhippāyo.

'Of him' means of Sakka. 'Rebirth' means rebirth as a deva. 'He was restored to his original state' means he was reborn again in the same state, because he was reborn as Sakka. 'Subrahma' is his name. Having seen the rebirth of the nymphs in hell, from then on, referring to the constant fear in his own mind, he said, 'This mind is always fearful,' and so on. Therein, 'fearful' (utrastaṃ) means alarmed, frightened. 'Agitated' (ubbiggaṃ) means distressed. Or, 'fearful' means distressed, and 'agitated' means shaken together with the body due to fear. 'In what has not arisen' means in future things. 'In hardships' means in sufferings. The locative case is used in the sense of a sign; the meaning is 'a sign of the occurrence of future suffering.' 'In what has arisen' should be connected with 'in hardships that have arisen'; the intention is that it is a sign of suffering that has arisen for his retinue at that time.

Bojjhāti bodhito, ariyamaggatoti attho. Aññatrāti ca padaṃ apekkhitvā nissakkavacanaṃ, tasmā bodhiṃ ṭhapetvāti attho. Esa nayo sesesupi. Tapasāti tapokammato. Tena maggādhigamassa upāyabhūtaṃ dhutaṅgasevanādisallekhapaṭipadaṃ dasseti. Indriyasaṃvarāti manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ saṃvaraṇato. Etena satisaṃvarasīsena sabbampi saṃvarasīlaṃ, lakkhaṇahāranayena vā sabbampi catupārisuddhisīlaṃ dasseti. Sabbanissaggāti sabbupadhinissajjanato sabbakilesappahānato. Kilesesu hi nissaṭṭhesu kammavaṭṭaṃ vipākavaṭṭañca nissaṭṭhameva hotīti. Sotthinti khemaṃ anupaddavataṃ.

'From enlightenment' (bojjhā) means from the noble path. And with reference to the word 'aññatra' (except), it is a word of exclusion; therefore, the meaning is 'setting aside enlightenment.' This is the method in the remaining cases as well. 'By austerity' means from the practice of austerity. By this, he shows the practice of effacement, such as the cultivation of ascetic practices, which is a means for attaining the path. 'From restraint of the senses' means from restraining the senses, with the mind as the sixth. By this, under the heading of restraint by mindfulness, he shows all restraint through virtue; or, by the method of characteristics, he shows all of the fourfold purification of virtue. 'From total relinquishment' means from relinquishing all substrates of existence, from abandoning all defilements. For when defilements are relinquished, the round of kamma and the round of results are also relinquished. 'Well-being' (sotthi) means security, freedom from adversity.

Ñāyati nicchayena kamati nibbānaṃ, taṃ vā ñāyati paṭivijjhīyati etenāti ñāyo, ariyamaggoti āha “ñāyo vuccati ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti[M 1.0335]. Taṇhāvānavirahitattāti taṇhāsaṅkhātavānavivittattā. Taṇhā hi khandhehi khandhaṃ, kammunā vā phalaṃ, sattehi vā dukkhaṃ vinati saṃsibbatīti vānanti vuccati. Tayidaṃ natthi ettha vānaṃ, na vā etasmiṃ adhigate puggalassa vānanti nibbānaṃ, asaṅkhatā dhātu. Parapaccayena vinā paccakkhakaraṇaṃ sacchikiriyāti āha “attapaccakkhatāyā”ti.

'Ñāya' (method): one certainly goes to Nibbāna by this, or it is known and penetrated by this, thus it is the 'method,' meaning the noble path. Therefore, he said, 'The ñāya is called the Noble Eightfold Path.' 'Because of being without the weaving of craving' means because of being free from the weaving known as craving. For craving weaves or sews together aggregate with aggregate, or action with result, or beings with suffering—thus it is called 'weaving' (vāna). In this, there is no weaving, or for the person who has attained this, there is no weaving—thus it is Nibbāna, the unconditioned element. Realization directly without dependence on another is called 'sacchikiriyā' (direct realization). Therefore, he said, 'due to direct experience by oneself.'

Nanu “visuddhiyā”ti cittavisuddhiyā adhippetattā visuddhiggahaṇenevettha sokasamatikkamādayopi gahitā eva honti, te puna kasmā gahitāti anuyogaṃ sandhāya “tattha kiñcāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sāsanayuttikovideti saccapaṭiccasamuppādādilakkhaṇāyaṃ dhammanītiyaṃ cheke. Taṃ taṃ atthaṃ ñāpetīti ye ye bodhaneyyapuggalā saṅkhepavitthārādivasena yathā yathā bodhetabbā, attano desanāvilāsena bhagavā te te tathā tathā bodhento taṃ tamatthaṃ ñāpeti. Taṃ taṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassentoti atthāpattiṃ agaṇento taṃ taṃ atthaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassento. Na hi sammāsambuddhā atthāpattiñāpakādisādhanīyavacanāti. Saṃvattatīti jāyati, hotīti attho. Yasmā anatikkantasokaparidevassa na kadāci cittavisuddhi atthi sokaparidevasamatikkamamukheneva cittavisuddhiyā ijjhanato, tasmā āha “sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamena hotī”ti. Yasmā pana domanassapaccayehi dukkhadhammehi puṭṭhaṃ puthujjanaṃ sokādayo abhibhavanti, pariññātesu ca tesu te na honti, tasmā vuttaṃ “sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamo dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamenā”ti. Ñāyassāti aggamaggassa tatiyamaggassa ca. Tadadhigamena hi yathākkamaṃ [V 1.0300] dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamo. Sacchikiriyābhisamayasahabhāvīpi itarābhisamayo tadavinābhāvato sacchikiriyābhisamayahetuko viya vutto “ñāyassādhigamo nibbānassa sacchikiriyāyā”ti. Phalañāṇena vā paccakkhakaraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “nibbānassa sacchikiriyāyā”ti. Sampadānavacanañcetaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Is it not that by 'purification' the purification of mind is intended, and thus by the inclusion of 'purification' the overcoming of sorrow and so forth are already included? Why then are they mentioned again? In response to this question, it is said, 'Here, although...' and so on. Sāsanayuttikovida means 'skilled in the Dispensation,' that is, expert in this exposition of the Dhamma characterized by the truths, dependent origination, and so forth. He makes known each meaning: that is, the Blessed One, by the elegance of his teaching, enlightens those individuals who are to be instructed, whether briefly or in detail, in whatever way is appropriate, thus revealing each meaning. He presents each meaning clearly, without considering implication, making it evident. For the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones do not rely on words that need to be proven by inference or other means. 'It comes to be' means it arises, it exists. Because for one who has not transcended sorrow and lamentation, there is never any purification of mind, as purification of mind is achieved precisely through the transcendence of sorrow and lamentation, therefore it is said, 'It comes to be through the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation.' Moreover, because sorrow and the like overwhelm an ordinary person afflicted by painful mental states caused by displeasure, and when these states are fully understood, they cease to exist, it is stated, 'The overcoming of sorrow and lamentation is the cessation of suffering and displeasure.' 'Of the path' refers to the supreme path and the third path. For through their attainment, the cessation of suffering and displeasure occurs in due order. The other realization, being concomitant with realization by direct experience and inseparable from it, is spoken of as if it were the cause of realization by direct experience—thus it is stated, 'the attainment of the path for the realization of Nibbāna by direct experience.' Alternatively, it may refer to the making directly perceptible through fruition-knowledge—hence the statement, 'for the realization of Nibbāna by direct experience.' This should be regarded as a dative expression.

Vaṇṇabhaṇananti pasaṃsāvacanaṃ. Tayidaṃ na idheva, atha kho aññatthāpi satthā akāsiyevāti dassento “yatheva hī”tiādimāha. Tatthaādimhi kalyāṇaṃ, ādi vā kalyāṇaṃ etassāti ādikalyāṇaṃ. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Atthasampattiyā sātthaṃ. Byañjanasampattiyā sabyañjanaṃ. Sīlādipañcadhammakkhandhapāripūrito upanetabbassa abhāvā ca kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ. Nirupakkilesato apanetabbassa abhāvā [M 1.0336] ca parisuddhaṃ. Seṭṭhacariyabhāvato sāsana brahmacariyaṃ maggabrahmacariyañca vo pakāsessāmīti ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.147) vuttanayena veditabbo. Ariyavaṃsāti ariyānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ vaṃsā paveṇiyo. Aggaññāti “aggā”ti jānitabbā sabbavaṃsehi seṭṭhabhāvato. Rattaññāti “cirarattā”ti jānitabbā. Vaṃsaññāti “buddhādīnaṃ vaṃsā”ti jānitabbā. Porāṇāti purātanā anadhunātanattā. Asaṃkiṇṇāti avikiṇṇā anapanītā. Asaṃkiṇṇapubbāti “kiṃ imehī”ti ariyehi na apanītapubbā. Na saṃkīyantīti idānipi tehi na apanīyanti. Na saṃkīyissantīti anāgatepi tehi na apanīyissanti. Appaṭikuṭṭhā…pe… viññūhīti ye loke viññū samaṇabrāhmaṇā, tehi apaccakkhatā aninditā, agarahitāti attho. Visuddhiyātiādīhīti visuddhiādidīpanehi. Padehīti vākyehi, visuddhiatthatādibhedabhinnehi vā dhammakoṭṭhāsehi.

'Praise' (vaṇṇabhaṇana) means words of commendation. Showing that this is not only here, but that the Teacher has indeed done so elsewhere too, he says, 'just as indeed,' and so on. Here, 'good in the beginning' (ādikalyāṇaṃ) means 'good at the beginning,' or 'that whose beginning is good.' The same principle applies to the remaining two phrases. It is meaningful (sātthaṃ) by virtue of the accomplishment of meaning (atthasampatti). It is well-phrased (sabyañjanaṃ) by virtue of the accomplishment of expression (byañjanasampatti). It is utterly complete (kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ) because it is fulfilled in the five aggregates of virtue, beginning with morality, and because there is nothing to be added. It is perfectly pure (parisuddhaṃ) because it is without corruption and there is nothing to be removed. Because it is the highest practice, [the Buddha says,] 'I will proclaim to you the teaching (sāsana), the holy life (brahmacariya), and the path of the holy life (maggabrahmacariya).' This is the summary here; the detailed explanation should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 1.147). 'Ariyavaṃsā' means the lineages or traditions of the noble ones, such as the Buddhas. 'Aggaññā' means it should be known as 'foremost' because it is supreme among all lineages. 'Rattaññā' means it should be known as 'long-standing.' 'Vaṃsaññā' means it should be known as 'the lineage of the Buddhas and others.' 'Porāṇā' means 'ancient,' not of the present day. 'Asaṃkiṇṇā' means 'unmixed,' not removed. 'Asaṃkiṇṇapubbā' means it has never been removed by the noble ones, as in 'What use are these?' 'Na saṃkīyanti' means even now it is not removed by them. 'Na saṃkīyissanti' means in the future too it will not be removed by them. 'Uncriticized...by the wise' (Appaṭikuṭṭhā...pe… viññūhi) means that those wise ascetics and brahmins in the world have not rejected, censured, or blamed it. 'By purity, and so on' (Visuddhiyātiādīhi) means by the expositions beginning with purity. 'By the terms' (Padehi) means by statements, or by sections of the Dhamma differentiated by distinctions such as purity, meaning, and so on.

Upaddaveti anatthe. Visuddhinti visujjhanaṃ saṃkilesappahānaṃ. Vācuggatakaraṇaṃ uggaho. Pariyāpuṇanaṃ paricayo. Atthassa hadaye ṭhapanaṃ dhāraṇaṃ. Parivattanaṃ vācanaṃ. Gandhārakoti gandhāradese uppanno. Pahontīti sakkonti aniyyānamaggāti micchāmaggā, micchattaniyatāniyatamaggāpi vā. Suvaṇṇanti kūṭasuvaṇṇampi vuccati. Paṇīti kācamaṇipi. Muttāti veḷujāpi. Pavāḷanti pallavopi vuccatīti rattajambunadādipadehi te visesitā.

'It causes harm' (upaddaveti), that is, to misfortune (anatthe). 'Purification' (visuddhi) means purifying, the abandoning of defilements. Making it come to the lips is learning. Acquiring fully is familiarity. Placing the meaning in the heart is retention. Repeating is recitation. 'Gandhāraka' means originating in the Gandhāra country. 'They are capable' (pahonti) means 'they are able' (sakkonti). 'The path of non-release' (aniyyānamaggā) means the wrong path, or the path fixed or unfixed in wrongness. The term 'gold' (suvaṇṇa) is also applied to counterfeit gold. The term 'gem' (maṇi) is also applied to a glass gem. The term 'pearl' (muttā) is also applied to a bamboo pearl. Since 'coral' (pavāḷa) is also used for 'sprout,' they are specified by terms such as 'red jambunada' and so on.

Na tato heṭṭhāti (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.5.367; dī. ni. ṭī. 2.373) idhādhippetakāyādīnaṃ vedanādisabhāvattābhāvā, kāyavedanācittavimuttassa tebhūmakadhammassa visuṃ vipallāsavatthantarabhāvena gahitattā ca heṭṭhāgahaṇesu vipallāsavatthūnaṃ aniṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, pañcamassa [V 1.0301] pana vipallāsavatthuno abhāvā “na uddha”nti āha. Ārammaṇavibhāgena hettha satipaṭṭhānavibhāgoti. Tayo satipaṭṭhānāti satipaṭṭhānasaddassa atthuddhāradassanaṃ, na idha pāḷiyaṃ vuttassa satipaṭṭhānasaddassa atthadassananti. Ādīsu hi satigocaroti ettha ādi-saddena “phassasamudayā vedanānaṃ samudayo, nāmarūpasamudayā cittassa samudayo, manasikārasamudayā dhammānaṃ samudayo”ti satipaṭṭhānāti vuttānaṃ [M 1.0337] satigocarānaṃ pakāsake suttapadese saṅgaṇhāti. Evaṃ paṭisambhidāpāḷiyampi (paṭi. ma. 3.34) avasesapāḷippadesadassanattho ādi-saddo daṭṭhabbo. Satiyā paṭṭhānanti satiyā patiṭṭhātabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Dānādīni satiyā karontassa rūpādīni kasiṇādīni ca satiyā ṭhānaṃ hontīti taṃnivāraṇatthamāha “padhānaṃ ṭhāna”nti. Pa-saddo hi idha “paṇītā dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 14 tikamātikā) viya padhānatthadīpakoti adhippāyo.

'Not below that' (Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 2.5.367; Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 2.373) is stated with reference to the undesirability of the objects of distortion among the things taken as lower, because the body and so on, which are intended here, do not have the nature of feeling and so on, and because the phenomena of the three planes, being liberated from body, feeling, and mind, are taken separately as another object of distortion. However, due to the absence of a fifth object of distortion, he said, 'not above.' Here, the division of the foundations of mindfulness is by way of the division of the objects. 'The three foundations of mindfulness' is a presentation of the extracted meaning of the word 'foundations of mindfulness,' not a presentation of the meaning of the word 'foundations of mindfulness' as stated in the Pāli text here. For in 'the sphere of mindfulness, and so on,' the word 'and so on' includes passages from the Suttas that clarify the spheres of mindfulness, which are called foundations of mindfulness, such as 'with the arising of contact, there is the arising of feelings; with the arising of name-and-form, there is the arising of mind; with the arising of attention, there is the arising of phenomena.' Similarly, in the Pāli of the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 3.34), the word 'and so on' should be seen as for the purpose of showing the remaining Pāli passages. 'Foundation of mindfulness' (satiyā paṭṭhāna) means a place where mindfulness is to be established. To prevent the view that for one who performs acts of generosity and so on with mindfulness, forms and so on, or kasinas and so on, are a basis for mindfulness, he said 'a principal basis.' The intention is that the prefix 'pa-' here, as in 'sublime phenomena,' etc. (Dhs. 14, Tikamātikā), indicates the principal meaning.

Ariyoti ariyaṃ sabbasattaseṭṭhaṃ sammāsambuddhamāha. Etthāti etasmiṃ saḷāyatanavibhaṅgasutte (ma. ni. 3.311). Suttekadesena hi suttaṃ dasseti. Tattha hi –

'Noble one' (ariya) refers to the noble one, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who is the best of all beings. 'Here' (ettha) refers to this Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta (MN 3.311). For one indicates a sutta by a portion of that sutta. There, indeed—

“Tayo satipaṭṭhānā yadariyo…pe… marahatīti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ. Idha, bhikkhave, satthā sāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ deseti anukampako hitesī anukampaṃ upādāya “idaṃ vo hitāya idaṃ vo sukhāyā’ti. Tassa sāvakā na sussūsanti, na sotaṃ odahanti, na aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapenti, vokkamma ca satthusāsanā vattanti. Tatra, bhikkhave, tathāgato na ceva anattamano hoti, na ca anattamanataṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, anavassuto ca viharati sato sampajāno. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ, yadariyo…pe… arahati.

'Three foundations of mindfulness, by which a noble one...is worthy.' This was said. And in reference to what was it said? Here, bhikkhus, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to his disciples, compassionate, seeking their welfare, out of compassion, thinking: 'This is for your welfare, this is for your happiness.' His disciples do not listen attentively, do not lend ear, do not apply their minds to full understanding, and they deviate from the Teacher’s instruction. In that case, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is neither displeased nor does he experience displeasure; he dwells without attachment, mindful and fully aware. This, bhikkhus, is the first foundation of mindfulness, by which a noble one...is worthy.

Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, satthā…pe… idaṃ vo sukhāyāti. Tassa ekacce sāvakā na sussūsanti…pe… vattanti. Ekacce sāvakā sussūsanti…pe… na ca vokkamma satthusāsanā vattanti. Tatra, bhikkhave, tathāgato na ceva anattamano hoti, na ca anattamanataṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, na ceva attamano hoti, na ca attamanataṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. Anattamanatañca attamanatañca tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjetvā upekkhato viharati sato sampajāno. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dutiyaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ…pe… arahati.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, the Teacher... 'this is for your happiness.' Some of his disciples do not listen... they behave thus. Some disciples listen... and do not behave contrary to the Teacher’s instruction. In that case, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is neither displeased nor does he experience displeasure, nor is he pleased nor does he experience pleasure. Having abandoned both displeasure and pleasure, he dwells with equanimity, mindful, and fully aware. This, bhikkhus, is called the second foundation of mindfulness... he is worthy.

Puna caparaṃ…pe… sukhāyāti. Tassa sāvakā sussūsanti…pe… vattanti. Tatra, bhikkhave, tathāgato attamano ceva hoti, attamanatañca paṭisaṃvedeti, anavassuto ca viharati [V 1.0302] sato sampajāno[M 1.0338]. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, tatiyaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ…pe… arahatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.311) –

Furthermore... 'for happiness.' His disciples listen... and conduct themselves accordingly. In this case, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is both pleased and experiences pleasure, and he dwells undefiled, mindful, and fully aware. This, bhikkhus, is called the third foundation of mindfulness... he is worthy.

Evaṃ paṭighānunayehi anavassutatā, niccaṃ upaṭṭhitassatitāya tadubhayavītivattatā “satipaṭṭhāna”nti vuttā. Buddhānaṃyeva hi niccaṃ upaṭṭhitassatitā hoti āveṇikadhammabhāvato, na paccekabuddhādīnaṃ. Pa-saddo ārambhaṃ joteti, ārambho ca pavattīti katvā āha “pavattayitabbatoti attho”ti. Satiyā karaṇabhūtāya paṭṭhānaṃ paṭṭhapetabbaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Ana-saddo hi bahulavacanena kammatthopi hotīti.

Thus, by being undefiled by aversion and attachment, by the constant presence of mindfulness, and by transcending both, it is called 'foundation of mindfulness' (satipaṭṭhāna). For indeed, the constant presence of mindfulness is unique to the Buddhas, due to its being a distinctive quality, not to the Paccekabuddhas or others. The prefix 'pa-' signifies commencement, and since commencement implies continuity, it is said, 'It should be set in motion; this is the meaning.' 'Foundation of mindfulness' (satipaṭṭhāna) is that which is to be established by mindfulness, which serves as the instrument. For the suffix '-ana' can also frequently denote the object of an action.

Tathāssa kattuatthopi labbhatīti “patiṭṭhātīti paṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha pa-saddo bhūsatthavisiṭṭhaṃ pakkhandhanaṃ dīpetīti “okkantitvā pakkhanditvā pavattatīti attho”ti āha. Puna bhāvatthaṃ sati-saddaṃ paṭṭhāna-saddañca vaṇṇento “atha vā”tiādimāha. Tena purimavikappe sati-saddo paṭṭhāna-saddo ca katthuatthoti viññāyati. Saraṇaṭṭhenāti cirakatassa cirabhāsitassa ca anussaraṇaṭṭhena. Idanti yaṃ “satiyeva satipaṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ, idaṃ idha imasmiṃ suttapadese adhippetaṃ.

Thus, its meaning as agent is also obtained—hence it is said, “It is established, thus it is an establishment.” Here, the prefix “pa-” signifies intensified engagement in the sense of plunging in—hence it is said, “Having entered and plunged in, it proceeds; this is the meaning.” Again, explaining the meaning of the terms “sati” and “paṭṭhāna” in the sense of state, he says, “Or alternatively…” By this, in the previous interpretation, the terms “sati” and “paṭṭhāna” are understood in the sense of the agent. “In the sense of recollection” means in the sense of recollecting what was done and spoken long ago. “This”—what was said as “mindfulness itself is the establishment of mindfulness”—is what is intended here in this sutta passage.

Yadi evanti yadi sati eva satipaṭṭhānaṃ, sati nāma eko dhammo, evaṃ sante kasmā “satipaṭṭhānā”ti bahuvacananti āha “satibahuttā”tiādi. Yadi bahukā etā satiyo, atha kasmā “maggo”ti ekavacananti yojanā. Maggaṭṭhenāti niyyānaṭṭhena. Niyyāniko hi maggadhammo, teneva niyyānikabhāvena ekattupagato ekantato nibbānaṃ gacchati, atthikehi ca tadatthaṃ maggīyatīti attanāva pubbe vuttaṃ paccāharati “vuttañceta”nti. Tattha catassopi cetāti kāyānupassanādivasena catubbidhāpi ca etā satiyo. Aparabhāgeti ariyamaggakkhaṇe. Kiccaṃ sādhayamānāti pubbabhāge kāyādīsu ārammaṇesu subhasaññādividhamanena visuṃ visuṃ pavattitvā maggakkhaṇe sakiṃyeva tattha catubbidhassapi vipallāsassa samucchedavasena pahānakiccaṃ sādhayamānā ārammaṇakaraṇavasena nibbānaṃ gacchanti. Catubbidhakiccasādhaneneva hettha bahuvacananiddeso. Evañca satīti maggaṭṭhena ekattaṃ upādāya “maggo”ti ekavacanena ārammaṇabhedena [M 1.0339] catubbidhataṃ upādāya “cattāro”ti ca vattabbatāya sativijjamānattā. Vacanānusandhinā “ekāyano aya”ntiādikā desanā sānusandhikāva, na ananusandhikāti adhippāyo. Vuttamevatthaṃ nidassanena paṭipādetuṃ “mārasenappamaddana”nti suttapadaṃ (saṃ. ni. 5.224) ānetvā [V 1.0303] “yathā”tiādinā nidassanaṃ saṃsandeti. Tasmātiādi nigamanaṃ.

If it is so—if mindfulness itself is the establishment of mindfulness—mindfulness is a single phenomenon. This being the case, why is it spoken of in the plural as “establishments of mindfulness”? He says, “because of the multiplicity of mindfulness,” and so on. If there are many instances of mindfulness, then why is it referred to in the singular as “the path”? The explanation is: in the sense of a path, that is, in the sense of leading out. For the path-factor is indeed that which leads out, and by that very nature of leading out, having attained oneness, it goes unerringly to Nibbāna. And because it is traversed for that purpose by those who seek it, he recalls what was previously stated by himself: “and this was said.” Here, “these four” means that these mindfulnesses are fourfold by way of the contemplation of the body, etc. “In the subsequent phase” means at the moment of the noble path. “Accomplishing the task” means that, having previously arisen separately in the preliminary phase regarding objects such as the body by dispelling perceptions of beauty and so on, at the moment of the path they accomplish the task of abandoning the fourfold distortions through their complete eradication at that very moment, and by making Nibbāna their object, they go to Nibbāna. It is precisely because of accomplishing this fourfold task that the plural is indicated here. And this being the case, because mindfulness exists which should be spoken of in the singular as “the path” on account of its unity in the sense of a path, and as “four” on account of its fourfold nature due to the distinction of objects, the teaching beginning with “this is the one way” is connected by verbal continuity; it is not disconnected. This is the intended meaning. To explain this very point by means of an illustration, he brings in the sutta passage “the crushing of Māra's army” (Saṃ. Ni. 5.224) and connects the illustration with “just as,” and so on. “Therefore,” and so on, is the conclusion.

Visesato kāyo ca vedanā ca assādassakāraṇanti tappahānatthaṃ tesu taṇhāvatthūsu oḷārikasukhumesu asubhadukkhabhāvadassanāni mandatikkhapaññehi taṇhācaritehi sukarānīti tāni tesaṃ “visuddhimaggo”ti vuttāni tathā “niccaṃ attā”ti abhinivesavatthutāya diṭṭhiyā visesakāraṇesu cittadhammesu aniccānattatādassanāni sarāgādivasena saññāphassādivasena nīvaraṇādivasena ca nātippabhedaatippabhedagatesu tesu tappahānatthaṃ mandatikkhapaññānaṃ diṭṭhicaritānaṃ sukarānīti tesaṃ tāni “visuddhimaggo”ti vuttāni. Ettha ca yathā cittadhammānampi taṇhāya vatthubhāvo sambhavati, tathā kāyavedanānampi diṭṭhiyāti satipi nesaṃ catunnampi taṇhādiṭṭhiyā vatthubhāve yo yassa sātisayapaccayo, taṃdassanatthaṃ visesaggahaṇaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tikkhapaññasamathayāniko oḷārikārammaṇaṃ pariggaṇhanto tattha aṭṭhatvā jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya vedanaṃ pariggaṇhātīti vuttaṃ. “Oḷārikārammaṇe asaṇṭhahanato”ti. Vipassanāyānikassa pana sukhume citte dhammesu ca cittaṃ pakkhandatīti cittadhammānupassanānaṃ mandatikkhapaññāvipassanāyānikānaṃ visuddhimaggatā vuttā.

Specifically, the body and feelings are a cause for savoring; for the abandoning of this, the contemplation of foulness and suffering in these gross and subtle objects of craving is easy for those of dull or sharp wisdom who are of a craving temperament. Therefore, these contemplations are called the “Path of Purification” for them. Similarly, due to being a basis for clinging to the view of “a permanent self,” the contemplation of impermanence and non-self in mental phenomena—which are the specific grounds for such views—is easy for those of dull or sharp wisdom who are of a speculative temperament, whether these phenomena are greatly or not greatly differentiated by way of lust, contact, hindrances, and so on. Thus, these contemplations are called the “Path of Purification” for them. Here, it should be understood that just as mental phenomena can serve as a basis for craving, so too can the body and feelings serve as a basis for views. Therefore, even though all four can be a basis for craving and views, a specific mention is made to show which is the predominant condition for which. It is said that one with sharp wisdom who is a tranquility-vehicle practitioner, taking a gross object, dwelling on it, attaining absorption, and emerging from it, then takes up feeling for contemplation. As for the insight-vehicle practitioner, however, the mind plunges into the subtle mind and mental phenomena, because of not being established on a gross object. Therefore, the contemplation of mind and mental phenomena is said to be the “Path of Purification” for insight-vehicle practitioners of dull or sharp wisdom.

Tesaṃ tatthāti ettha tattha-saddassa “pahānattha”nti etena yojanā. Parato tesaṃ tatthāti etthāpi esevanayo. Pañca kāmaguṇā savisesā kāye labbhantīti visesena kāyo kāmoghassa vatthu, bhavesu sukhaggahaṇavasena bhavassādo hoti bhavoghassa vedanā vatthu, santatighanagahaṇavasena visesato citte attābhiniveso hotīti diṭṭhoghassa cittaṃ vatthu, dhammesu vinibbhogassa dukkarattā dhammānaṃ dhammamattatāya duppaṭivijjhattā sammoho hotīti avijjoghassa dhammā vatthu, tasmā tesaṃ pahānatthaṃ cattārova vuttā.

In the phrase “for them, there,” the word “there” is to be connected with “for the purpose of abandoning.” As for the later phrase “for them, there,” the same method applies here too. The five strands of sensual pleasure are found in the body in a special way; thus, the body is specifically the basis of the flood of sensuality. In states of existence, through grasping at happiness, there is savoring of existence; thus, feeling is the basis of the flood of existence. Through grasping at continuity and density, there is especially an adherence to self in the mind; thus, the mind is the basis of the flood of views. In phenomena, due to the difficulty of distinguishing them and the difficulty of penetrating their nature as mere phenomena, there is delusion; thus, phenomena are the basis of the flood of ignorance. Therefore, for the purpose of abandoning these floods, the four establishments are stated.

Yadaggena [M 1.0340] ca kāyo kāmoghassa vatthu, tadaggena abhijjhākāyaganthassa vatthu, dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo anusetīti dukkhadukkhavipariṇāmadukkhasaṅkhāradukkhabhūtā vedanā visesena byāpādakāyaganthassa vatthu, citte niccaggahaṇavasena sassatassa attano sīlena suddhītiādi parāmasanaṃ hotīti sīlabbataparāmāsassa cittaṃ vatthu, nāmarūpaparicchedena bhūtaṃ bhūtato apassantassa bhavavibhavadiṭṭhisaṅkhāto idaṃsaccābhiniveso hotīti tassa dhammā vatthu, sukhavedanāssādavasena paralokanirapekkho “natthi dinna”ntiādikaṃ parāmāsaṃ uppādetīti diṭṭhupādānassa vedanā vatthu santatighanagahaṇavasena sarāgādicitte sammoho hotīti mohāgatiyā cittaṃ [V 1.0304] vatthu, dhammasabhāvānavabodhena bhayaṃ hotīti bhayāgatiyā dhammā vatthu. Ye panettha avuttā, tesaṃ vuttanayena vatthubhāvo yojetabbo. Tathā hi oghesu vuttanayā eva yogāsavesupi yojanā atthato abhinnattā. Tathā paṭhamoghatatiyacatutthaganthayojanāya vuttanayā eva kāyacittadhammānaṃ itarūpādānavatthutā yojanā, tathā kāmoghabyāpādakāyaganthayojanāya vuttanayā eva kāyavedanānaṃ chandadosāgati vatthutā yojanā vā.

Insofar as the body is the ground for the flood of sensuality, it is also the ground for the bodily fetter of covetousness. Because the underlying tendency of aversion lies latent with respect to painful feeling, that feeling—which is suffering due to pain, suffering due to change, and suffering due to conditioned formations—is specifically the ground for the bodily fetter of ill will. When, through grasping at permanence in the mind, the misapprehension arises that 'one is purified by virtue,' and so on, the mind becomes the ground for clinging to rites and rituals. For one who does not see the real as it truly is by discerning name-and-form, there arises the adherence to this as truth, which is the view of existence and non-existence; for this, phenomena are the ground. Through delight in pleasant feeling, one becomes heedless of the other world and generates misapprehensions such as 'there is no giving,' and so on; thus, feeling becomes the ground for clinging to views. Through grasping continuity as solid, delusion arises in a mind accompanied by lust and so on; thus, the mind becomes the ground for the wrong course of delusion. Through not understanding the true nature of phenomena, fear arises; thus, phenomena become the ground for the wrong course of fear. As for those not mentioned here, their status as grounds should be understood according to the method stated. For just as the method is stated for the floods, so too should the application be made for the yokes and taints, as they are not different in meaning. Similarly, just as the method is stated for the first flood and the third and fourth fetters, so too should the status of body, mind, and phenomena as grounds for the other forms of clinging be understood. Likewise, just as the method is stated for the flood of sensuality and the bodily fetter of ill will, so too should the status of body and feeling as grounds for the wrong courses of desire and aversion be understood.

“Āhārasamudayā kāyasamudayo, phassasamudayā vedanāsamudayo, (saṃ. ni. 5.408) saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti (ma. ni. 3.126; udā. 1; vibha. 225) vacanato kāyādīnaṃ samudayabhūtā kabaḷīkārāhāraphassamanosañcetanāviññāṇāhārā kāyādiparijānanena pariññātā hontīti āha “catubbidhāhārapariññattha”nti pakaraṇanayoti nettipakaraṇavasena suttantasaṃvaṇṇanānayo.

"With the arising of nutriment, the body arises; with the arising of contact, feeling arises; with formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises." Because of this statement, he says that the four nutriments—physical food, contact, mental volition, and consciousness—which are the source of the body and so on, are to be fully understood by comprehending the body and so on, for the purpose of fully understanding the four kinds of nutriment. This is the method of the treatise, that is, the method of interpreting the suttas in accordance with the Nettipakaraṇa.

Saraṇavasenāti kāyādīnaṃ kusalādidhammānañca upadhāraṇavasena. Saranti gacchanti nibbānaṃ etāyāti satīti imasmiṃ atthe ekatte ekasabhāve nibbāne samosaraṇaṃ samāgamo ekattasamosaraṇaṃ. Etadeva hi dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ekanibbānapavesahetubhūtā vā samānatā eko satipaṭṭhānassa bhāvo ekattaṃ, tattha samosaraṇaṃ [M 1.0341] taṃsabhāgatā ekattasamosaraṇaṃ. Ekanibbānapavesahetubhāvaṃ pana dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādimāha. Etasmiṃ atthe saraṇekattasamosaraṇāni saheva satipaṭṭhānekabhāvassa kāraṇatthena vuttānīti daṭṭhabbāni, purimasmiṃ visuṃ. Saraṇavasenāti vā “gamanavasenā”ti atthe sati tadeva gamanaṃ samosaraṇanti, samosaraṇe vā satisaddatthavasena avuccamāne dhāraṇatāva satīti satisaddatthantarābhāvā purimaṃ satibhāvassa kāraṇaṃ, pacchimaṃ ekabhāvassāti nibbānasamosaraṇepi sahitāneva tāni satipaṭṭhānekabhāvassa kāraṇāni vuttāni honti. Cuddasavidhena, navavidhena, soḷasavidhena, pañcavidhenāti idaṃ upari pāḷiyaṃ (ma. ni. 1.107) āgatānaṃ ānāpānapabbādīnaṃ vasena vuttaṃ, tesaṃ pana antarabhedavasena tadanugatabhedavasena ca bhāvanāya anekavidhatā labbhatiyeva. Catūsu disāsu uṭṭhānakabhaṇḍasadisatā kāyānupassanāditaṃtaṃsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanānubhāvassa daṭṭhabbā.

In the sense of recollection, that is, in the sense of bearing in mind the wholesome qualities of the body and so on. They go, they proceed to Nibbāna by this—thus, mindfulness. In this meaning, the converging, the coming together into the unity, the single essence, Nibbāna, is called "ekattasamosaraṇa" (unity-convergence). Indeed, to show this, the passage beginning with "yathā hī" is stated. Or, the sameness that serves as the cause for entering into the single Nibbāna, or the single state of the establishment of mindfulness, is called "ekattaṃ" (unity). The converging there, the participation in that nature, is called "ekattasamosaraṇa" (unity-convergence). To indicate the state of being the cause for entering into the single Nibbāna, the passage beginning with "yathā hī" is spoken. In this meaning, the terms "saraṇa," "ekatta," and "samosaraṇa" should be understood as stated together as the reasons for the oneness of the establishment of mindfulness, as distinct from the previous explanation. Alternatively, "saraṇavasenāti" can mean "by way of going," in the sense of movement. That very movement is called "samosaraṇa" (convergence). Or, if the meaning of the word "sati" (mindfulness) is not explicitly mentioned by way of the meaning of "samosaraṇa," then upholding itself is mindfulness—since there is no other meaning of the word "sati." The former is the reason for the state of mindfulness, the latter for the state of oneness. Thus, even in the convergence to Nibbāna, those are stated together as the reasons for the oneness of the establishment of mindfulness. The fourteenfold, ninefold, sixteenfold, and fivefold divisions—this is said with reference to the sections on in-and-out breathing and other practices found in the Pāli (e.g., Majjhima Nikāya 1.107). However, due to the internal divisions and the divisions following from them, the development (bhāvanā) can indeed be of many kinds. The analogy of goods prepared for setting out spread out in the four directions should be seen as illustrating the power of developing each respective establishment of mindfulness, such as contemplation of the body.

“Gocare, bhikkhave, caratha sake pettike visaye”tiādivacanato (dī. ni. 3.80; saṃ. ni. 5.372) bhikkhugocarā ete dhammā, yadidaṃ kāyānupassanādayo. Tattha yasmā kāyānupassanādipaṭipattiyā bhikkhu hoti, tasmā “kāyānupassī viharatī”tiādinā bhikkhuṃ dasseti, bhikkhumhi taṃ niyamatoti āha “paṭipattiyā bhikkhubhāvadassanato”ti. Satthu cariyānuvidhāyakattā [V 1.0305] sakalasāsanasampaṭiggāhakattā ca sabbappakārāya anusāsaniyā bhājanabhāvo.

"Monks, wander in your own ancestral domain." From statements such as this (Dī. Ni. 3.80; Saṃ. Ni. 5.372), these teachings, namely, contemplation of the body and so on, are the bhikkhus' pasture. Here, since one becomes a bhikkhu through the practice beginning with contemplation of the body, therefore, by the statement "he dwells contemplating the body," etc., the bhikkhu is shown; and it is said "by showing the state of being a bhikkhu through practice," because that is inherent in the bhikkhu. Being one who emulates the Teacher's conduct and accepts the entire dispensation, he is a vessel for every kind of instruction.

Samaṃ careyyāti kāyādivisamacariyaṃ pahāya kāyādīhi samaṃ careyya. Rāgādivūpasamena santo. Indriyadamena danto. Catumagganiyāmena niyato. Seṭṭhacaritāya brahmacārī. Kāyadaṇḍādioropanena nidhāya daṇḍaṃ. Ariyabhāve ṭhito so evarūpo bāhitapāpasamitapāpabhinnakilesatāhi brāhmaṇo samaṇo bhikkhūti veditabbo.

He should live evenly: abandoning uneven conduct of body and so forth, he should live evenly with body and so forth. Calm through the subsiding of lust and so forth. Tamed through the restraint of the senses. Restrained by the fourfold path. Living the holy life with the best conduct. Having laid down the rod by abandoning bodily punishment and so forth. Established in the noble state, such a one is to be known as a brahmin, a contemplative, a bhikkhu—one who has banished evil, quieted evil, and shattered the defilements.

“Ayañceva kāyo bahiddho ca nāmarūpa”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.373) khandhapañcakaṃ, “sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedetī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.271, 287; pārā. 11) nāmakāyo kāyoti vuccatīti tato visesanatthaṃ “kāyeti rūpakāye”ti āha.

In phrases such as 'this body and external name-and-form' (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 2.373), the five aggregates are meant, and in phrases such as 'one experiences pleasure with the body' (Ma. Ni. 1.271, 287; Pārā. 11), the mental body is called ‘body.’ Therefore, for the purpose of distinguishing from these, it was said: 'By "body" is meant the physical body.'

Asammissatoti [M 1.0342] “vedanādayopi ettha sitā ettha paṭibaddhā”ti kāye vedanādianupassanāpasaṅgepi āpanne tato asammissatoti attho. Samūhavisayatāya cassa kāya-saddassa samudāyupādānatāya ca asubhākārassa “kāye”ti ekavacanaṃ, tathā ārammaṇādivibhāgena anekabhedabhinnampi cittaṃ cittabhāvasāmaññena ekajjhaṃ gahetvā “citte”ti ekavacanaṃ, vedanā pana sukhādibhedabhinnā visuṃ visuṃ anupassitabbāti dassentena “vedanāsū”ti bahuvacanena vuttā, tatheva ca niddeso pavattito, dhammā ca paropaṇṇāsabhedā anupassitabbākārena ca anekabhedā evāti tepi bahuvacanavaseneva vuttā. Avayavīgāha-samaññātidhāvana-sārādānābhinivesanisedhanatthaṃ kāyaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgehi, tāni ca kesādīhi, kesādike ca bhūtupādāyarūpehi vinibbhujjanto “tathā na kāye”tiādimāha. Pāsādādinagarāvayavasamūhe avayavīvādinopi avayavīgāhaṃ na karonti, nagaraṃ nāma koci attho atthīti pana kesañci samaññātidhāvanaṃ siyāti itthipurisādisamaññātidhāvane nagaranidassanaṃ vuttaṃ. Aṅgapaccaṅgasamūho, kesalomādisamūho bhūtupādāyasamūho ca yathāvuttasamūhe tabbinimutto kāyopi nāma koci natthi, pageva itthiādayoti āha “kāyo vā…pe… dissatī”ti. Koci dhammoti iminā sattajīvādiṃ paṭikkhipati, avayavī pana kāyapaṭikkhepeneva paṭikkhittoti. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ kāyādisaññābhidhānānītiāha “yathāvutta…pe… karontī”ti.

"Not mixed" means that even when the occasion arises for contemplating feelings and so on in the body—since feelings and so on are based here and connected here—it is still not mixed with them. Because the word 'body' has a collection as its object and because the aspect of foulness is taken up as an aggregate, the singular 'in the body' is used. Similarly, the mind, though divided into many types by distinctions such as objects, is gathered together under the general characteristic of 'mind' and referred to in the singular as 'in the mind.' Feelings, however, being divided by distinctions such as pleasant, are to be contemplated separately; showing this, they are expressed in the plural as 'in feelings,' and the exposition proceeds accordingly. The phenomena (dhammas), too, being of more than fifty kinds and of various types according to the manner in which they are to be contemplated, are also expressed in the plural. To negate the grasping of a whole, the running after designations, the taking of an essence, and adherence, one analyzes the body into its limbs and minor limbs, those into hair and so forth, and hair and so forth into the primary elements and derived material forms, and thus it is said, 'In this way, not in the body,' etc. In the case of an aggregate of the parts of a palace or a city, even those who assert an integral whole do not grasp an integral whole. But since some might run after the designation, thinking, 'There is some entity called a city,' the example of a city is given to illustrate the running after designations like 'man' or 'woman.' An aggregate of limbs and minor limbs, an aggregate of hair, body hair, and so on, and an aggregate of primary elements and derived material forms—apart from these aggregates as described, there is no such thing as a body, let alone a woman and so on. Hence, it is said, 'A body... is not seen.' By 'any phenomenon' (koci dhammo), the notion of a being, a life-principle, and so forth is rejected. The notion of an integral whole, however, is rejected by the rejection of the body itself. If this is so, how then do the perceptions and designations of 'body' and so on arise? It is said, 'As described... they function.'

Yaṃ passati itthiṃ purisaṃ vā. Nanu cakkhunā itthipurisadassanaṃ natthīti? Saccametaṃ, “itthiṃ [V 1.0306] passāmi, purisaṃ passāmī”ti pana pavattasaññāya vasena “yaṃ passatī”ti vuttaṃ. Micchādassanena vā diṭṭhiyā yaṃ passati, na taṃ diṭṭhaṃ, taṃ rūpāyatanaṃ na hotīti attho viparītaggāhavasena micchāparikappitarūpattā. Atha vā taṃ kesādibhūtupādāyasamūhasaṅkhātaṃ diṭṭhaṃ na hoti acakkhuviññāṇaviññeyyattā, diṭṭhaṃ vā taṃ na hoti. Yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ taṃ na passatīti yaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ kesādibhūtupādāyasamūhasaṅkhātaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, taṃ paññācakkhunā bhūtato na passatīti attho. Apassaṃ bajjhateti imaṃ attabhāvaṃ yathābhūtaṃ paññācakkhunā apassanto “etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me atto”ti kilesabandhanena bajjhati.

When one sees a woman or a man. 'Is it not true that there is no seeing of a woman or a man with the eye?' 'This is true. However, the phrase “what one sees” is said based on the perception that arises, such as, “I see a woman, I see a man.”' Or, what one sees through wrong seeing, that is, wrong view, is not truly seen; the meaning is that it is not a form-base, being a form wrongly conceived due to perverted grasping. Alternatively, that aggregate designated as elements and derived material forms, such as hair and so forth, is not seen, because it is not knowable by eye-consciousness. Or, what is seen is not that. 'He does not see what is seen' means that one does not see with the eye of wisdom as it truly is the form-base that is seen as the aggregate designated as elements and derived material forms, such as hair and so forth. 'Not seeing, one is bound' means that one who does not see this individual existence as it truly is with the eye of wisdom becomes bound by the bondage of defilements, thinking, 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.'

Na [M 1.0343] aññadhammānupassīti na aññasabhāvānupassī, asubhādito aññākārānupassī na hotīti attho. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hotītiādinā tamevatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ karoti. Pathavīkāyanti kesādikoṭṭhāsapathaviṃ dhammasamūhattā “kāyo”ti vadati, lakkhaṇapathavimeva vā anekappabhedaṃ sakalasarīragataṃ pubbāpariyabhāvena ca pavattamānaṃ samūhavasena gahetvā “kāyo”ti vadati. Āpokāyantiādīsupi eseva nayo.

"Not contemplating other dhammas" means not contemplating other natures; that is, one does not contemplate in ways other than from the aspect of repulsiveness and so forth. By "What is said?" etc., he makes that very meaning clear. The earth-element body: he calls the earth element in the parts beginning with hair a "body" because it is a collection of dhammas; or, taking the characteristic earth element itself—which is of many kinds, pervades the entire body, and occurs continuously from beginning to end—as a collection, he calls it a "body." The same method applies to the water-element body and so forth.

Evaṃ gahetabbassāti “ahaṃ mama”nti evaṃ attattaniyabhāvena andhabālehi gahetabbassa. Idāni sattannaṃ anupassanākārānampi vasena kāyānupassanaṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha aniccato anupassatīti catusamuṭṭhānikakāyaṃ “anicca”nti anupassati, evaṃ passanto evaṃ cassa aniccākārampi anupassatīti vuccati. Tathābhūtassa cassa niccaggāhassa lesopi na hotīti vuttaṃ “no niccato”ti tathāhesa “niccasaññaṃ pajahatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.35) vutto. Ettha ca “aniccato eva anupassatī”ti eva-kāro luttaniddiṭṭhoti tena nivattitamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “no niccato”ti vuttaṃ. Na cettha dukkhato anupassanādinivattanamāsaṅkitabbaṃ paṭiyogīnivattanaparattā eva-kārassa, uparidesanāruḷhattā ca tāsaṃ.

Thus to be grasped: that is, to be grasped by blind fools in terms of self and what belongs to self, as "I and mine." Now, to show the contemplation of the body also by way of the seven modes of contemplation, the passage beginning "furthermore" is introduced. Herein, "one contemplates as impermanent" means one contemplates the body of fourfold origination as "impermanent." Seeing thus, it is said that one also contemplates its aspect of impermanence in this way. For one who is thus, not even a trace of the grasping of permanence remains—hence it is said, "not as permanent." For it is said thus, "one abandons the perception of permanence" (Paṭis I 197). Here, the word "only" in "one contemplates only as impermanent" is implicitly stated; therefore, to show the meaning that is excluded by it, it is said, "not as permanent." One should not suppose an exclusion of contemplating as suffering and so forth here, because the word "only" serves to exclude its opposite, and because those contemplations are included in the subsequent explanation.

Dukkhato anupassatītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – aniccassa dukkhattā tameva kāyaṃ dukkhato anupassati, dukkhassa anattattā anattato anupassati. Yasmā pana yaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā, taṃ anabhinanditabbaṃ, na tattha rajjitabbaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “nibbindati no nandati, virajjati no rajjatī”ti. So evaṃ arajjanto rāgaṃ nirodheti no samudeti, samudayaṃ na karotīti attho. Evaṃ paṭipanno ca paṭinissajjati no ādiyati. Ayañhi aniccādianupassanā tadaṅgavasena saddhiṃ kāyatannissayakhandhābhisaṅkhārehi kilesānaṃ [V 1.0307] pariccajanato, saṅkhatadosadassanena tabbiparīte nibbāne tanninnatāya pakkhandanato “pariccāgapaṭinissaggo ceva pakkhandanapaṭinissaggo cā”ti vuccati, tasmā tāya samannāgato bhikkhu vuttanayena kilese ca pariccajati, nibbāne ca pakkhandati[M 1.0344], tathābhūto ca nibbattanavasena kilese na ādiyati, nāpi adosadassitāvasena saṅkhatārammaṇaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “paṭinissajjati no ādiyatī”ti. Idānissa tāhi anupassanāhi yesaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānaṃ hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “so taṃ aniccato anupassanto niccasaññaṃ pajahatī”ti. Tattha niccasaññanti “saṅkhārā niccā”ti evaṃ pavattaviparītasaññaṃ. Diṭṭhicittavipallāsapahānamukheneva saññāvipallāsappahānanti saññāgahaṇaṃ, saññāsīsena vā tesampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nandinti sappītikataṇhaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayemeva.

In 'one contemplates as suffering,' etc., the method is the same. This, however, is the distinction: because what is impermanent is suffering, one contemplates that very body as suffering; because what is suffering is non-self, one contemplates it as non-self. Since what is impermanent, suffering, and non-self should not be delighted in, nor should one be impassioned towards it, therefore it is said: 'One becomes disenchanted and does not delight; one becomes dispassionate and is not impassioned.' Thus not being impassioned, he brings lust to cessation and does not cause it to arise; this is the meaning. And practicing thus, he relinquishes and does not take up. For this contemplation of impermanence and so forth is called 'relinquishment by way of abandonment' because, by substitution of opposites, it abandons defilements along with the formations of the aggregates that are dependent on the body, and it is called 'relinquishment by way of entering' because of seeing the faults in the conditioned and entering upon its opposite, Nibbāna, through inclination towards it. Therefore, a bhikkhu endowed with this practice abandons defilements in the manner described and enters upon Nibbāna. Being thus, he does not take up defilements by way of origination, nor does he take up a conditioned object by way of seeing it as faultless. Hence, it is said: 'He relinquishes and does not take up.' Now, to show which states are abandoned through these contemplations, it is said: 'By contemplating it as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence.' Here, 'the perception of permanence' refers to the inverted perception that arises as 'formations are permanent.' The mention of perception is by way of abandoning the distortion of perception through the abandoning of the distortions of view and thought; alternatively, it should be understood that by taking perception as the principal, those others are also included. 'Delight' refers to craving accompanied by joy. The rest is as previously explained.

Viharatīti iminā kāyānupassanāsamaṅgino iriyāpathavihāro vuttoti āha “iriyatī”ti iriyāpathaṃ pavattetīti attho. Ārammaṇakaraṇavasena abhibyāpanato “tīsu bhavesū”ti vuttaṃ, uppajjanavasena pana kilesā parittabhūmakā evāti. Yadipi kilesānaṃ pahānaṃ ātāpananti taṃ sammādiṭṭhiādīnampi attheva, ātāpa-saddo pana vīriyeyeva niruḷhoti vuttaṃ “vīriyassetaṃ nāma”nti. Atha vā paṭipakkhapahāne sampayuttadhammānaṃ abbhussahanavasena pavattamānassa vīriyassa sātisayaṃ tadātāpananti vīriyameva tathā vuccati, na aññe dhammā. Ātāpīti cāyamīkāro pasaṃsāya, atisayassa vā dīpakoti ātāpīgahaṇena sammappadhānasamaṅgitaṃ dasseti. Sammā, samantato, sāmañca pajānanto sampajāno, asammissato vavatthāne aññadhammānupassitābhāvena sammā aviparītaṃ, sabbākārapajānanena samantato, uparūpari visesāvahabhāvena pavattiyā sayaṃ pajānantoti attho. Yadi paññāya anupassati, kathaṃ satipaṭṭhānatāti āha “na hī”tiādi. Sabbatthikanti sabbattha bhavaṃ sabbattha līne uddhate ca citte icchitabbattā, sabbe vā līne uddhate ca bhāvetabbā bojjhaṅgā atthikā etāyāti sabbatthikā. Satiyā laddhūpakārāya eva paññāya ettha yathāvutte kāye kammaṭṭhāniko bhikkhu kāyānupassī viharati. Antosaṅkhepo anto olīyano, kosajjanti attho. Upāyapariggaheti ettha sīlavisodhanādi gaṇanādi uggahakosallādi ca upāyo, tabbipariyāyato anupāyo veditabbo. Yasmā ca upaṭṭhitassati yathāvuttaupāyaṃ na pariccajati, anupāyañca na upādiyati, tasmā vuttaṃ “muṭṭhassati…pe… asamattho [M 1.0345] hotī”ti. Tenāti upāyānupāyānaṃ pariggahaparivajjanesu apariccāgāpariggahesu ca asamatthabhāvena assa yogino.

By 'he dwells' is meant the dwelling in postures of one endowed with contemplation of the body; thus it is said, 'he moves,' meaning he engages in postures. It is said 'in the three realms' by way of pervading them as objects, but by way of arising, the defilements are only of the sense-sphere. Although the abandoning of defilements is called 'ardency,' that is also true of right view and so forth. However, the word 'ardency' is conventionally used for energy, as stated: 'This is a name for energy.' Alternatively, because of the surpassing effort in abandoning opposing states, the energy that arises in association with those states is called 'ardency' in a pre-eminent sense; thus, energy alone is spoken of in this way, not other states. The suffix '-ī' in 'ātāpī' (ardent) indicates praise or serves as an intensifier; by taking 'ātāpī,' it shows endowment with right exertion. 'Clearly comprehending' means knowing rightly, completely, and by oneself; rightly, without distortion, by distinguishing without admixture, by not contemplating other states; completely, by knowing all aspects; and by oneself, through the progressive arising of distinctions. If one contemplates with wisdom, how is it the establishment of mindfulness? To this it is said, 'For indeed...' 'Applicable everywhere' means that it is to be desired everywhere, whether the mind is sluggish or restless; or, because all the factors of awakening to be developed when the mind is sluggish or restless are available through it, it is called 'applicable everywhere.' It is with wisdom that has received support from mindfulness that a monk devoted to a meditation subject dwells contemplating the body as described herein. 'Internal contraction' means sinking inward; that is, laziness. 'Grasping the means'—here, the means include purification of virtue, counting, skill in learning, and so forth. What is contrary to these should be understood as 'not the means.' Because one with established mindfulness does not abandon the proper means as described, nor does he take up improper means, it is said: 'One with forgetful mindfulness... is incapable.' This incapacity of such a yogi is due to his inability to grasp and avoid the means and non-means, and to not abandon the means and not take up the non-means.

Yasmā [V 1.0308] satiyevettha satipaṭṭhānaṃ vuttā, tasmāssa sampayuttā dhammā vīriyādayo aṅganti āha “sampayogaṅgañcassa dassetvā”ti. Aṅga-saddo cettha kāraṇapariyāyo daṭṭhabbo, satiggahaṇeneva cettha samādhissati gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ tassā samādhikkhandhe saṅgahitattā. Yasmā vā satisīsenāyaṃ desanā. Na hi kevalāya satiyā kilesappahānaṃ hoti, nibbānādhigamo vā, na ca kevalā sati pavattati, tasmāssa jhānadesanāyaṃ savitakkādivacanassa viya sampayogaṅgadassanatāti aṅga-saddassa avayavapariyāyatā daṭṭhabbā. Pahānaṅganti “vivicceva kāmehī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.226; ma. ni. 1.271, 287; saṃ. ni. 2.152; a. ni. 4.123; pārā. 11) viya pahātabbaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ. Yasmā ettha lokiyamaggo adhippeto, na lokuttaramaggo, tasmā pubbabhāgiyameva vinayaṃ dassento “tadaṅgavinayena vā vikkhambhanavinayena vā”ti āha. Tesaṃ dhammānanti vedanādidhammānaṃ. Tesañhi tattha anadhippetattā “atthuddhāranayenetaṃ vutta”nti vuttaṃ.

Because mindfulness alone is spoken of here as the establishment of mindfulness, therefore it is said, 'having shown its associated factors,' referring to states such as energy. Here, the word 'factor' (aṅga) should be understood in the sense of a cause; for by grasping mindfulness, the grasping of concentration is also to be understood, since mindfulness is included in the aggregate of concentration. Or, because this teaching is headed by mindfulness. For neither the abandoning of defilements nor the attainment of Nibbāna occurs through mindfulness alone, nor does mindfulness operate alone. Therefore, just as in the teaching on jhāna the mention of initial thought and so on shows the associated factors, so here the word 'factor' should be understood in the sense of a component. 'The factor of abandoning' is to show the factor to be abandoned, as in phrases like 'quite secluded from sensual pleasures…'. Because the mundane path is intended here, not the supramundane path, therefore, showing only the preliminary discipline, it is said, 'either by abandonment by substitution or by abandonment by suppression.' 'Of those states' refers to states such as feeling. For since they are not intended there, it is said, 'this is stated by way of extracting the meaning.'

Avisesena dvīhipi nīvaraṇappahānaṃ vuttanti katvā puna ekekena vuttaṃ pahānavisesaṃ dassetuṃ “visesenā”ti āha. Atha vā “vineyya nīvaraṇānī”ti avatvā abhijjhādomanassavacanassa payojanaṃ dassento “visesenā”tiādimāha. Kāyānupassanābhāvanāya hi ujuvipaccanīkānaṃ anurodhādīnaṃ pahānaṃ dassanaṃ etassa payojananti. Kāyasampattimūlakassāti rūpa-bala-yobbanārogyādi-sarīrasampadā-nimittassa. Vuttavipariyāyato kāyavipattimūlako virodho veditabbo. Kāyabhāvanāyāti kāyānupassanābhāvanāya. Sā hi idha “kāyabhāvanā”ti adhippetā. Tenāti anurodhādippahānavacanena. Yogānubhāvo hītiādi vuttassevatthassa pākaṭakaraṇaṃ.

Having stated the abandonment of the hindrances in general for both, it is then said 'specifically' to show the specific abandonment spoken of for each. Alternatively, not having said 'having removed the hindrances,' the phrase beginning 'specifically' is stated to show the purpose of the terms 'covetousness' and 'ill-will.' For in the development of contemplation of the body, showing the abandonment of compliance and aversion, which are directly opposed, is its purpose. 'Rooted in bodily perfection' means having as its cause the sign of bodily endowments such as form, strength, youth, and health. Opposition rooted in bodily imperfection should be understood as the opposite of what was stated. 'By the development of the body' means by the development of contemplation of the body. For that is what is intended here by 'development of the body.' 'By that' refers to the statement of the abandonment of compliance and aversion. The phrase beginning 'For the power of the yogi...' clarifies the meaning of what has already been said.

Satisampajaññenāti atisampajaññaggahaṇena. Sabbatthikakammaṭṭhānanti buddhānussati mettā maraṇassati asubhabhāvanā ca. Idañhi catukkaṃ yoginā parihariyamānaṃ “sabbatthikakammaṭṭhāna”nti vuccati atisampajaññabalena avicchinnassa tassa pariharitabbattā, satiyā vā samatho vutto tassā samāddhikkhandhena saṅgahitattā.

'With mindfulness and clear comprehension' means by taking up thorough clear comprehension. 'The meditation subjects for all occasions' are the recollection of the Buddha, loving-kindness, mindfulness of death, and contemplation of the unattractive. This tetrad, when cultivated by a yogi, is called 'the meditation subjects for all occasions' because it must be cultivated uninterruptedly by the power of thorough clear comprehension, or because serenity is spoken of by means of mindfulness, since mindfulness is included in the aggregate of concentration.

Tenāti [M 1.0346] saddatthaṃ anādiyitvā bhāvatthasseva vibhajanavasena pavattena vibhaṅgapāṭhena saha. Aṭṭhakathānayoti saddatthassapi vivaraṇavasena yathārahaṃ vutto atthasaṃvaṇṇanānayo. Yathā saṃsandatīti yathā atthato adhippāyato ca avilomento aññadatthu saṃsandati sameti, evaṃ veditabbo.

'By that' means along with the Vibhaṅga text, which proceeds by way of analyzing the implied meaning without taking up the literal meaning. 'The method of the commentary' means the method of explaining the meaning, appropriately elaborating even the literal meaning. 'As it agrees' should be understood as how it agrees and harmonizes without contradicting in meaning or intention.

Vedanādīnaṃ [V 1.0309] puna vacaneti ettha nissayapaccayabhāvavasena cittadhammānaṃ vedanāsannissitattā pañcavokārabhave arūpadhammānaṃ rūpapaṭibaddhavuttito ca vedanāya kāyādianupassanāpasaṅgepi āpanne tadasammissato vavatthānadassanatthaṃ ghanavinibbhogādidassanatthañca dutiyavedanāgahaṇaṃ. Tena na vedanāyaṃ kāyānupassī, cittadhammānupassī vā, atha kho vedanānupassīyevāti vedanāsaṅkhāte vatthusmiṃ vedanānupassanākārasseva dassanena asammissato vavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Tathā “yasmiṃ samaye sukhā vedanā, na tasmiṃ samaye dukkhā adukkhamasukhā vā vedanā. Yasmiṃ vā pana samaye dukkhā adukkhamasukhā vā vedanā, na tasmiṃ samaye itarā vedanā”ti vedanābhāvasāmaññe aṭṭhatvā taṃ taṃ vedanaṃ vinibbhujitvā dassanena ghanavinibbhogo dhuvabhāvaviveko dassito hoti. Tena tāsaṃ khaṇamattāvaṭṭhānadassanena aniccatāya tato eva dukkhatāya anattatāya ca dassanaṃ vibhāvitaṃ hoti. Ghanavinibbhogādīti ādi-saddena ayampi attho veditabbo. Ayañhi vedanāyaṃ vedanānupassīyeva, na aññadhammānupassī. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā nāma bālo amaṇisabhāvepi udakabubbuḷake maṇiākārānupassī hoti, na evamayaṃ ṭhitiramaṇīyepi vedayite, pageva itarasmiṃ manuññākārānupassī, atha kho khaṇabhaṅguratāya avasavattitāya kilesāsucipaggharaṇatāya ca aniccaanattaasubhākārānupassī, vipariṇāmadukkhatāya saṅkhāradukkhatāya ca visesato dukkhānupassīyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ cittadhammesupi yathārahaṃ puna vacane payojanaṃ vattabbaṃ. “Kevalaṃ panidhā”tiādinā idha ‘ettakaṃ veditabba”nti veditabbaparicchedaṃ dasseti. Esa nayoti iminā yathā cittaṃ dhammā ca anupassitabbā, tathā tāni anupassanto “citte cittānupassī, dhammesu dhammānupassī”ti veditabboti imamatthaṃ atidisati.

Regarding the repetition of 'feelings and so forth,' the second mention of feeling is for the purpose of showing the clear definition and the breaking down of solidity, etc., even when contemplation of the body and so on might be involved. This is because mental states are dependent on feeling by way of dependent condition, and because in the five-constituent existence, formless phenomena are bound to form. Thus, one does not contemplate the body or mental states in feeling, but rather one contemplates feeling in itself. By showing only the mode of contemplating feeling in the object called 'feeling,' the unmixed distinction is shown. Similarly, it is stated: 'At the time when there is pleasant feeling, there is neither painful nor neutral feeling. And at the time when there is painful or neutral feeling, there is no other feeling.' By not standing on the general nature of feeling but discerning each particular feeling, the breaking down of solidity and the discernment of the absence of permanence are shown. Thereby, by seeing their momentary duration, the seeing of impermanence, and from that, of suffering and non-self, is clarified. By the word 'etc.' in 'breaking down of solidity, etc.,' this meaning should also be understood. For this person contemplates feeling in feeling, not other phenomena. What is meant? Just as a fool sees the form of a gem in a water bubble, which has no gem-nature, so this person does not see an attractive aspect even in a pleasant feeling, let alone in another. Rather, due to its momentary dissolution, its uncontrollability, and its oozing of the impurity of defilements, one sees the aspects of impermanence, non-self, and impurity. In particular, one contemplates suffering in terms of the suffering of change and the suffering of formations. In the same way, the purpose of the repetition should be stated appropriately for mental states and phenomena. By the phrase beginning 'But only here...,' the limit of what is to be known is shown, as in 'this much is to be known.' By 'This is the method,' the meaning is extended that just as the mind and phenomena are to be contemplated, so one contemplating them is to be known as 'one who contemplates the mind in the mind' and 'one who contemplates phenomena in phenomena.'

Yo [M 1.0347] sukhaṃ dukkhato addāti yo bhikkhu sukhavedanaṃ vipariṇāmadukkhatāya “dukkha”nti paññācakkhunā addakkhi. Dukkhamaddakkhi sallatoti dukkhavedanaṃ pīḷājananato antotudanato dunnīharaṇato ca sallanti addakkhi passi. Adukkhamasukhanti upekkhāvedanaṃ. Santanti sukhadukkhāni viya anoḷārikatāya paccayavasena vūpasantasabhāvatāya ca santaṃ. Aniccatoti hutvā abhāvato udayabbayavantato tāvakālikatoniccapaṭikkhepato ca “anicca”nti yo addakkhi. Sa ve sammaddaso bhikkhu ekaṃsena paribyattaṃ vā vedanāya sammā passanakoti attho.

‘He who sees happiness as suffering’ means that monk who, with the eye of wisdom, saw pleasant feeling as ‘suffering’ due to the suffering of change. ‘He saw suffering as a dart’ means he saw painful feeling as a dart because it generates affliction, pierces within, and is hard to remove. ‘Neither-painful-nor-pleasant’ means neutral feeling. ‘Peaceful’ means it is peaceful because, unlike pleasant and painful feelings, it is not coarse, and because its nature is calmed by way of conditions. ‘As impermanent’ means he saw it as ‘impermanent’ because it ceases to be after having been, because it possesses rise and fall, and because of its temporariness which refutes permanence. ‘Truly, that monk is one of right view’ means he is certainly one who is well-versed in and rightly perceives feeling. That is the meaning.

Dukkhātipīti saṅkhāradukkhatāya dukkhā itipi. Sabbaṃ taṃ dukkhasminti sabbaṃ taṃ vedayitaṃ dukkhasmiṃ antogadhaṃ pariyāpannaṃ vadāmi saṅkhāradukkhatānativattanato. Sukhadukkhatopi cāti [V 1.0310] sukhādīnaṃ ṭhitivipariṇāmaññāṇasukhatāya vipariṇāmaṭhitiaññāṇadukkhatāya ca vuttattā tissopi sukhato, tissopi ca dukkhato anupassitabbāti attho. Rūpādi-ārammaṇachandādi-adhipati-ñāṇādi-sahajāta- kāmāvacarādi-bhūminānattabhedānaṃ kusalākusala-taṃvipākakiriyā-nānattādibhedānañca, ādi-saddena saṅkhārikāsaṅkhārikasa-vatthukāvatthukādi-nānattabhedānañca vasenāti yojetabbaṃ. Suññatadhammassāti “dhammā hontī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 121) suññatavāre āgatasuññatasabhāvassa vasena. “Kāmañcetthā”tiādinā pubbe pahīnattā puna pahānaṃ na vattabbanti codanaṃ dasseti, maggacittakkhaṇe vā ekattha pahīnaṃ sabbattha pahīnameva hotīti visuṃ visuṃ na vattabbanti. Tattha purimāya codanāya nānāpuggalaparihāro, pacchimāya nānācittakkhaṇikaparihāro. Lokiyabhāvanāya hi kāye pahīnaṃ na vedanādīsu pahīnaṃ hoti yadipi na pavatteyya, na paṭipakkhabhāvanāya tattha sā abhijjhādomanassassa appavatti hotīti puna tappahānaṃ vattabbamevāti. Ekattha pahīnaṃ sesesupi pahīnaṃ hotīti maggasatipaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ, lokiyabhāvanāya vā sabbattha appavattimattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Pañcapi khandhā loko”ti hi vibhaṅge (vibha. 362, 364, 366, 373) catūsupi ṭhānesu vuttanti.

It is suffering because it is suffering due to the suffering of formations. I declare that all that is felt is included and encompassed within suffering, because it does not transcend the suffering of formations. And also from the perspective of pleasure and pain: because pleasure and the like are spoken of as 'pleasure' due to the knowledge of their stability and change, and as 'suffering' due to the ignorance of their change and stability, the meaning is that all three should be contemplated both as pleasure and as suffering. This should be construed in terms of the diversity of objects such as form; the dominance of desire and so on; the co-arising of knowledge and so on; the distinctions of the sense-sphere and other planes; the variety of wholesome, unwholesome, their resultant, and functional states; and by the word 'etc.,' the distinctions of prompted and unprompted, with basis and without basis, and so on, are also included. Regarding the emptiness of phenomena: this is in terms of the nature of emptiness that comes in the section on emptiness, as stated in the passage beginning, 'Phenomena exist' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 121). By the phrase beginning 'Although here,' it shows the criticism that since it was previously abandoned, its abandonment should not be stated again; or that at the moment of path-consciousness, what is abandoned in one place is abandoned everywhere, so it should not be stated separately for each. Therein, the rejoinder to the first criticism concerns different individuals; the rejoinder to the latter concerns different moments of consciousness. For by worldly development, what is abandoned in the body is not abandoned in feelings and so on, even if it does not arise. Since the non-arising of covetousness and displeasure there is not due to the development of an opposing factor, its abandonment must indeed be stated again. That what is abandoned in one place is abandoned in the rest refers to the development of the foundations of mindfulness of the path; or, with reference to worldly development, it is stated concerning the mere non-arising in all respects. For in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 362, 364, 366, 373), it is stated in all four places: 'The five aggregates are the world.'

Uddesavāravaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The explanation revealing the hidden meaning of the section on summaries is complete.

Kāyānupassanāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Contemplation of the Body

Ānāpānapabbavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on Mindfulness of Breathing

107. Bāhirakesupi [M 1.0348] ito ekadesassa sambhavato sabbappakāraggahaṇaṃ kataṃ “sabbappakārakāyānupassanānibbattakassā”ti. Tena ye ime ānāpānapabbādivasena āgatā cuddasappakārā, tadantogadhā ca ajjhattādianupassanā pakārā, tathā kāyagatāsatisutte (ma. ni. 3.154) vuttā kesādivaṇṇasaṇṭhānakasiṇārammaṇacatukkajjhānappakārā, lokiyādippakārā ca, te sabbepi anavasesato saṅgaṇhāti. Ime ca pakārā imasmiṃyeva sāsane, na ito bahiddhāti vuttaṃ “sabbappakāra…pe… paṭisedhano cā”ti. Tattha tathābhāvapaṭisedhanoti sabbappakārakāyānupassanānibbattakassa puggalassa aññasāsanassa nissayabhāvapaṭisedhano. Etena “idha, bhikkhave”ti ettha idha-saddo antogadhaevasaddatthoti dasseti[V 1.0311]. Santi hi ekapadānipi sāvadhāraṇāni yathā “vāyubhakkho”ti (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.374). Tenāha “idheva samaṇo”tiādi. Paripuṇṇasamaṇakaraṇadhammo hi so, yo sabbappakārakāyānupassanānibbattako. Parappavādāti paresaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ nānappakārā vādā titthāyatanāni.

107. Since a part of this is found even in external teachings, the inclusion of 'all aspects' is made, as in 'for one who generates the contemplation of the body in all its aspects.' By this, he includes without remainder all these: the fourteen aspects that come by way of the section on mindfulness of breathing and so on; the aspects of contemplation of the internal, etc., included therein; likewise the types of the four jhānas mentioned in the Kāyagatāsati Sutta (MN 119) with the color and shape of hair, etc., as the kasiṇa object; and the worldly and other aspects. And these aspects exist only in this Dispensation, not outside of it; thus it is said, 'of all aspects… and also the denial.' Therein, 'the denial of being so' means the denial that another teaching can be a basis for a person who generates the contemplation of the body in all its aspects. By this, it shows that in the phrase 'here, bhikkhus,' the word 'here' has the meaning of the word 'only' included within it. For there are even single words that are restrictive, such as 'wind-eater' (Dī. Nī. Ṭī. 2.374). Therefore, he said, 'Here alone is there an ascetic,' and so on. For that which makes one a complete ascetic is this very thing: being one who generates the contemplation of the body in all its aspects. 'The doctrines of others' means the various doctrines and sectarian tenets of other sectarians.

Araññādikasseva bhāvanānurūpasenāsanataṃ dassetuṃ “imassa hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Duddamo damathaṃ anupagato goṇo kūṭagoṇo. Dohanakāle yathā thanehi anavasesato khīraṃ na paggharati, evaṃ dohapaṭibandhinī kūṭadhenu. Rūpasaddādike paṭicca uppajjanakaassādo rūpārammaṇādiraso. Pubbe āciṇṇārammaṇanti pabbajjāto pubbe, anādimati vā saṃsāre paricitārammaṇaṃ.

To show that only dwelling places such as the forest are suitable for development, it is said, 'for this one,' etc. A bull that is hard to tame, that has not undergone taming, is a treacherous bull. Just as a treacherous cow does not let all the milk flow from her udders at milking time, so she is an obstacle to milking. The delight that arises in dependence on forms, sounds, and so on, is the savor of objects such as form. 'A previously frequented object' means an object familiarized before going forth, or in the beginningless cycle of existence.

Nibandheyyāti bandheyya. Satiyāti sammadeva kammaṭṭhānassa sallakkhaṇavasena pavattāya satiyā. Ārammaṇeti kammaṭṭhānārammaṇe. Daḷhanti thiraṃ, yathā satokārissa upacārappanābhedo samādhi ijjhati, tathā thāmagataṃ katvāti attho.

'He should bind' means he should tie. 'With mindfulness' means with mindfulness that proceeds by way of rightly marking the meditation subject. 'On the object' means on the meditation object. 'Firmly' means steadily. The meaning is: having made it strong, so that the concentration of the mindful practitioner, distinguished as access and absorption, is accomplished.

Visesādhigamadiṭṭhadhammasukhavihārapadaṭṭhānanti sabbesaṃ buddhānaṃ, ekaccānaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ, buddhasāvakānañca visesādhigamassa, aññena kammaṭṭhānena adhigatavisesānaṃ [M 1.0349] diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārassa ca padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ. Vatthuvijjācariyo viya bhagavā yogīnaṃ anurūpanivāsaṭṭhānupadisanato. Bhikkhu dīpisadiso araññe ekākī viharitvā paṭipakkhanimmathanena icchitatthasādhanato. Phalamuttamanti sāmaññaphalaṃ sandhāyāha. Parakkamajavayoggabhūminti bhāvanussāhajavassa yoggakaraṇabhūmibhūtaṃ.

'The proximate cause for the attainment of distinction and for a pleasant abiding in this very life' means being the proximate cause for the attainment of distinction for all Buddhas, some Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha, and for the pleasant abiding in this very life for those who have attained distinction through another meditation subject. The Blessed One is like a master of architecture in that he points out suitable dwelling places for yogis. A bhikkhu is like a leopard in that he dwells alone in the forest and accomplishes his desired goal by crushing his opponents. 'The supreme fruit' is said with reference to the fruit of recluseship. 'A ground suitable for swift striving' means being a ground that makes one fit for swift enthusiasm in development.

Assāsapassāsānaṃ vasena sikkhatoti assāsapassāsānaṃ dīgharassatāpajānana-sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedana-oḷārikoḷārikapaṭippassambhanavasena bhāvanānuyogaṃ sikkhato, tathābhūto vā hutvā tisso sikkhā pavattayato. Assāsapassāsanimitteti assāsapassāsasannissayena upaṭṭhitapaṭibhāganimitte. Assāsapassāse pariggaṇhāti rūpamukhena vipassanaṃ abhinivisanto, yo “assāsapassāsakammiko”ti vutto. Jhānaṅgāni pariggaṇhāti arūpamukhena vipassanaṃ abhinivisanto. Vatthu nāma karajakāyo cittacetasikānaṃ pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato. Añño satto vā puggalo vā natthīti visuddhadiṭṭhi “tayidaṃ dhammamattaṃ na ahetukaṃ, nāpi issarādivisamahetukaṃ, atha kho avijjādīhi eva sahetuka”nti addhattayepi kaṅkhāvitaraṇena vitiṇṇakaṅkho “yaṃ kiñci rūpa”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 1.361; ma. ni. 2.113; ma. ni. 3.86; a. ni. 4.181; paṭi. ma. 1.48) kalāpasammasanavasena [V 1.0312] tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā udayabbayānupassanādivasena vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento anukkamena maggapaṭipāṭiyā.

'He trains by means of in-breaths and out-breaths' means he trains in the application of development by way of knowing the long and short nature of the in-breaths and out-breaths, experiencing the whole body, and tranquillizing the bodily formation; or, having become thus, he develops the three trainings. 'In the sign of in-breaths and out-breaths' means in the counterpart sign that has arisen with the in-breaths and out-breaths as its support. 'He comprehends the in-breaths and out-breaths' refers to one who is intent on insight through the approach of form, who is called 'one who works with in-breaths and out-breaths.' 'He comprehends the jhāna factors' refers to one who is intent on insight through the formless approach. The 'basis' is the physical body, because it is the place for the occurrence of mind and mental factors. 'There is no other being or person'—this is the purified view. 'This is merely phenomena, not without a cause, nor from an uneven cause such as a Creator God, but it is with a cause, namely ignorance and so on.' Having crossed over doubt by overcoming doubt regarding the three periods of time, he is one who has overcome uncertainty. Applying the three characteristics by way of the comprehension of groups with phrases like 'whatever form...' (e.g., MN 28), he develops insight by way of the contemplation of arising and passing away, and so on, in due order along the path.

Parassa vā assāsapassāsakāyeti idaṃ sammasanacāravasenāyaṃ pāḷi pavattāti katvā vuttaṃ, samathavasena pana parassa assāsapassāsakāye appanānimittuppatti eva natthīti. Idaṃ ubhayaṃ na labbhatīti “ajjhattaṃ, bahiddhā”ti ca vuttaṃ idaṃ dhammadvayaghaṭitaṃ ekato ārammaṇabhāvena na labbhati.

As for 'or another's body of in-breaths and out-breaths,' this Pāli passage is stated because it proceeds by way of the range of comprehension. From the perspective of serenity, however, the arising of the absorption sign in another's body of in-breaths and out-breaths simply does not occur. Because this pair is not obtainable, it is said 'internally, externally'; this pair of phenomena, taken together, is not obtained as a single object.

Samudeti etasmāti samudayo, so eva kāraṇaṭṭhena dhammoti samudayadhammo, assāsapassāsānaṃ pavattihetukarajakāyādi. Tassa anupassanasīlo samudayadhammānupassī. Taṃ pana samudayadhammaṃ upamāmukhena dassento “yathā nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha bhastanti ruttiṃ. Gaggaranāḷinti ukkāpanāḷiṃ. Teti karajakāyādike. Yathā assāsapassāsakāyo karajakāyādisambandhī phalabhāvena, evaṃ tepi assāsapassāsakāyasambandhino hetubhāvenāti “samudayadhammā kāyasmi”nti vattabbataṃ [M 1.0350] labhantīti vuttaṃ “samudaya…pe… vuccatī”ti. Pakativācī vā dhamma-saddo “jātidhammāna”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.131; ma. ni. 3.373; paṭi. ma. 1.33) viyāti kāyassa paccayasamavāye uppajjanapakatikānupassī “samudayadhammānupassī”ti vutto. Tenāha – “karajakāyañcā”tiādi. Evañca katvā kāyasminti bhummavacanañca samatthitaṃ hoti. Vayadhammānupassīti ettha ahetukattepi vināsassa yesaṃ hetudhammānaṃ abhāve yaṃ na hoti, tadabhāvo tassa abhāvassa hotu viya voharīyatīti upacārato karajakāyādiabhāvo assāsapassāsakāyassa vayakāraṇaṃ vutto. Tenāha “yathā bhastāyā”tiādi. Ayaṃ tāvettha paṭhamavikappavasena atthavibhāvanā. Dutiyavikappavasena pana upacārena vināyeva attho veditabbo. Ajjhattabahiddhānupassanā viya bhinnavatthuvisayatāya samudayavayadhammānupassanāpi ekakāle na labbhatīti āha “kālena samudayaṃ kālena vayaṃ anupassanto”ti.

“It arises from this, thus it is the origin”; that very thing, being the cause, is the principle—the principle of arising. The bodily formation and so on is the cause for the occurrence of the in-and-out-breaths. One who is of the nature of observing this is an observer of the principle of arising. To illustrate this principle of arising with a simile, it is said, “Just as, for instance…” Here, “bellows” refers to the bellows bag. “The pipe of the furnace” means the pipe of the forge. “That” refers to the bodily formation and so on. Just as the body of in-and-out-breaths is related to the bodily formation, etc., by way of being an effect, so too are they related to the body of in-and-out-breaths by way of being a cause. Thus, they obtain the state of being sayable as “the principles of arising in the body”—this is what is meant by “arising… it is called.” Alternatively, the word “dhamma” has the sense of “nature,” as in “subject to birth” (Majjhima Nikāya 1.131; 3.373; Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.33), etc., thus one who observes the nature of the arising of the body in an assemblage of conditions is called “one who observes the principle of arising.” Therefore, it is said, “the bodily formation and so on…” And by this, the locative case “in the body” is also justified. Regarding “one who observes the principle of cessation”—here, although destruction is without a cause, the absence of that which does not exist in the absence of certain causal phenomena is spoken of figuratively as if it were the cause of its absence. Thus, by transference of meaning, the absence of the bodily formation, etc., is said to be the cause of cessation for the body of in-and-out-breaths. Therefore, it is said, “Just as from the bellows…” This, then, is the explanation of the meaning here according to the first interpretation. According to the second interpretation, however, the meaning should be understood without any transference of meaning.
