Just as the observation of the internal and external cannot be accomplished at the same time due to their having different objects, so too the observation of the principles of arising and cessation cannot be accomplished at the same time. Hence, it is said, “at one time observing arising, at another time observing cessation.”

Atthi kāyoti eva-saddo luttaniddiṭṭhoti “kāyova atthī”ti vatvā avadhāraṇena nivatthitaṃ dassento “na satto”tiādimāha. Tassattho – yo rūpādīsu sattavisattatāya paresañca sajjāpanaṭṭhena, satvaguṇayogato vā “satto”ti parehi parikappito. Tassa sattanikāyassa pūraṇato ca cavanupapajjanadhammatāya galanato ca “puggalo”ti. Thīyati saṃhaññati ettha gabbhoti “itthī”ti. Puri pure bhāge seti pavattatīti “puriso”ti. Āhito [V 1.0313] ahaṃmāno etthāti “attā”ti, attano santakabhāvena “attaniya”nti. Paro na hotīti katvā “aha”nti, mama santakanti katvā “mama”nti. Vuttappakāravinimutto aññoti katvā “kocī”ti, tassa santakabhāvena “kassacī”ti parikappetabbo koci natthi, kevalaṃ kāyo eva atthīti attattaniyasuññatameva kāyassa vibhāveti. Evanti “kāyova atthī”tiādinā vuttappakārena. Ñāṇapamāṇatthāyāti kāyānupassanāñāṇaparaṃ pamāṇaṃ pāpanatthāya. Satipamāṇatthāyāti kāyapariggāhikasatipavattaṃ satiparaṃ pamāṇaṃ pāpanatthāya. Imassa hi vuttanayena “atthi kāyo”ti aparāparuppattivasena paccupaṭṭhitā sati bhiyyoso mattāya tattha ñāṇassa satiyā ca paribrūhanāya hoti. Tenāha “satisampajaññānaṃ vaḍḍhatthāyā”ti.

Regarding “There is a body,” the word “eva” is indicated as elided; having said “only the body exists,” showing what is refuted by this emphasis, it says “not a being,” etc. The meaning is this: that which is imagined by others as a “being” due to being attached and entangled in forms, etc., and for the purpose of making others attached, or from connection with the quality of a being. It is called a “person” (`puggalo`) because it fills up [hells], and because it perishes due to its nature of passing away and being reborn. It is called “woman” (`itthī`) because the embryo is held and compacted therein. It is called “man” (`puriso`) because it lies or moves in the foremost part. It is called “self” (`attā`) because the conceit “I am” is placed therein, and “belonging to self” (`attaniya`) because it is one’s own possession. By considering it “not another,” it is called “I” (`ahaṃ`); by considering it “my possession,” it is called “mine” (`mama`). By considering it something other, distinct from the stated types, it is called “someone” (`koci`); and due to being someone's possession, it is conceived as “someone's” (`kassaci`). There is no “someone” to be imagined; only the body exists. Thus, it reveals the emptiness of self and what belongs to self in the body. “Thus” (`evaṃ`) means in the manner stated as “only the body exists,” etc. “For the sake of the measure of knowledge” (`ñāṇapamāṇatthāya`) means for the purpose of leading the knowledge of body contemplation to its further measure. “For the sake of the measure of mindfulness” (`satipamāṇatthāya`) means for the purpose of leading the established mindfulness that encompasses the body to its further measure. For, according to this stated method, the mindfulness that is present by way of the successive arising of “there is a body” serves to enhance knowledge and mindfulness there to a greater degree. Hence it is said, “for the increase of mindfulness and clear comprehension.”

Imissā [M 1.0351] bhāvanāya taṇhādiṭṭhigāhānaṃ ujupaṭipakkhattā vuttaṃ “taṇhā…pe… viharatī”ti. Tathābhūto ca loke kiñci “aha”nti vā “mama”nti vā gahetabbaṃ na passati, kuto gaṇheyya. Tenāha “na ca kiñcī”tiādi. Evampīti ettha pi-saddo heṭṭhā niddiṭṭhassa tādisassa atthassa abhāvato avuttasamuccayatthoti dassento “upari atthaṃ upādāyā”ti āha. “Eva”nti pana niddiṭṭhākārassa paccāmasanaṃ nigamanavasena katanti āha “iminā pana…pe… dassetī”ti. Pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānassa idhādhippetattā vuttaṃ “sati dukkhasacca”nti. Sā pana sati yasmiṃ attabhāve, tassa samuṭṭhāpikā taṇhā tassāpi samuṭṭhāpikā eva nāma hoti tadabhāve abhāvatoti āha “tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā”ti. Appavattīti appavattinimittaṃ, na pavattati etthāti vā appavatti. Catusaccavasenāti catusaccakammaṭṭhānavasena. Ussakkitvāti visuddhiparamparāya āruhitvā, bhāvanaṃ upari netvāti attho. Niyyānamukhanti vaṭṭadukkhato nissaraṇūpāyo.

Because this development is the direct antidote to the grasping of craving and views, it is said, “he dwells… free from craving.” And one who is thus sees nothing in the world to be grasped as “I” or “mine”—how could he grasp anything? Therefore, it is said, “and nothing whatsoever…” Regarding “Thus also” (`evampi`), here the word `pi` has the meaning of including what is unstated, because of the absence below of such a meaning as indicated; showing this, it is said, “with reference to the higher meaning.” The word “evaṃ,” however, refers back to the described manner by way of conclusion; thus it is said, “by this… he shows.” Because the preliminary stage of the foundations of mindfulness is intended here, it is said, “mindfulness is the truth of suffering.” As for that mindfulness, the craving that originates the existence in which it arises is indeed also its originator, because in the absence of that craving, there is an absence of that existence. Hence it is said, “its originator is the prior craving.” “Non-occurrence” (`appavatti`) means the sign of non-occurrence, or “it does not occur here.” “By way of the four truths” (`catusaccavasena`) means by way of the meditation subject of the four truths. “Having ascended” (`ussakkitvā`) means having ascended through the sequence of purifications; the meaning is, having brought the development upward. “The door to egress” (`niyyānamukhaṃ`) is the means of escape from the suffering of the round of existence.

Ānāpānapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on mindfulness of breathing is concluded.

Iriyāpathapabbavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Postures

108. Iriyāpathavasenāti iriyanaṃ iriyā, kiriyā, idha pana kāyikapayogo veditabbo. Iriyānaṃ patho pavattimaggoti iriyāpatho, gamanādisarīrāvatthā. Gacchanto vā hi satto kāyena kattabbakiriyaṃ kareyya ṭhito vā nisinno vā nipanno vāti. Tesaṃ vasena, iriyāpathavibhāgenāti [V 1.0314] attho. Puna caparanti puna ca aparaṃ, yathāvuttaānāpānakammaṭṭhānato bhiyyopi aññaṃ kāyānupassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ kathemi, suṇāthāti vā adhippāyo. Gacchanto vātiādi gamanādimattajānanassa gamanādigatavisesajānanassa ca sādhāraṇavacanaṃ. Tattha gamanādimattajānanaṃ idha nādhippetaṃ, gamanādigatavisesajānanaṃ pana adhippetanti taṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “tattha kāma”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Sattūpaladdhinti satto atthīti upaladdhiṃ sattaggāhaṃ na jahati na pariccajati “ahaṃ gacchāmi, mama gamana”nti gāhasabbhāvato. Tato eva attasaññaṃ “atthi attā kārako vedako”ti evaṃ pavattaṃ viparītasaññaṃ na ugghāṭeti [M 1.0352] nāpaneti apaṭipakkhabhāvato, ananabrūhanato vā. Evaṃ bhūtassa cassa kuto kammaṭṭhānādibhāvoti āha “kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā vā na hotī”ti. Imassa panātiādisukkapakkhassa vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo. Tameva hi atthaṃ vivarituṃ “idaṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ko gacchatīti gamanakiriyāya kattupucchā, sā kattubhāvavisiṭṭhaattapaṭikkhepatthā dhammamattasseva gamanasiddhidassanato. Kassa gamananti akattutāvisiṭṭhaattaggāhapaṭikkhepatthā. Kiṃkāraṇāti pana paṭikkhittakattukāya gamanakiriyāya aviparītakāraṇapucchā “gamananti attā manasā saṃyujjati, mano indriyehi, indriyāni attehī”ti evamādigamanakāraṇapaṭikkhepanato. Tenāha “tatthā”tiādi.

108. “By way of postures” (`iriyāpathavasena`): `iriyā` is movement, action (`kiriyā`); here, however, it should be understood as bodily exertion. The path (`patha`) of movements (`iriyā`), the way of occurrence, is “posture” (`iriyāpatha`), referring to the states of the body such as walking. For a being would perform the action to be done with the body while walking, or standing, or sitting, or lying down. “By means of these” means “by way of the division of postures.” “And again” (`puna caparaṃ`) means “again and something further”; the intention is: “I will speak of yet another meditation subject for body contemplation, beyond the aforementioned mindfulness of breathing meditation subject. Listen!” The phrase “whether walking, etc.” (`gacchanto vā ti ādi`) is a general statement for both the mere knowing of walking, etc., and the knowing of the specific characteristics of walking, etc. Here, the mere knowing of walking, etc., is not intended, but rather the knowing of the specific characteristics of walking, etc., is intended. To clarify this by analyzing it, it is said: “In that case, desire,” etc. “Perceiving a being” (`sattūpaladdhiṃ`) means one does not abandon or relinquish the perception that “a being exists,” the grasping of a being, due to the presence of the grasping, “I am walking, my walking.” From that, one does not uproot or remove the perverted perception of self that proceeds as “there is a self, a doer, an experiencer,” due to the absence of an antidote, or due to it not being developed. For one who is in such a state, how can there be a meditation subject or the development of the foundations of mindfulness? Thus, it is said: “There is no meditation subject or development of the foundations of mindfulness.” But as for this—the meaning of the wholesome side, etc., should be understood as the opposite of what was stated. To elaborate on this very meaning, it is said: “For this reason,” etc. Here, the question “Who walks?” (`ko gacchati`) is an inquiry about the agent of the action of walking. It is for the purpose of rejecting the notion of a self distinguished by agency, by showing that the walking is accomplished by mere phenomena. “Whose walking?” (`kassa gamanaṃ`) is for the purpose of rejecting the grasping of a self distinguished by non-agency. “By what cause?” (`kiṃkāraṇaṃ`) is a question about the true cause of the action of walking—the agent having been rejected—and is for the purpose of rejecting such causes of walking as: “The self is connected with the mind, the mind with the faculties, the faculties with the self,” etc. Therefore, it is said: “In that case,” etc.

Na koci satto vā puggalo vā gacchati dhammamattasseva gamanasiddhito tabbinimuttassa ca kassaci abhāvato. Idāni dhammamattasseva gamanasiddhiṃ dassetuṃ “cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha cittakiriyā ca sā vāyodhātuyā vipphāro vipphandanañcāti cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāro, tena. Ettha ca cittakiriyaggahaṇena anindriyabaddhavāyodhātuvipphāraṃ nivatteti, vāyodhātuvipphāraggahaṇena cetanāvacīviññattibhedaṃ cittakiriyaṃ nivatteti, ubhayena pana kāyaviññattiṃ vibhāveti. “Gacchatī”ti vatvā yathā pavattamāne kāye “gacchatī”ti vohāro hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “tasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tanti gantukāmatāvasena pavattacittaṃ. Vāyaṃ janetīti vāyodhātuadhikaṃ rūpakalāpaṃ janeti, adhikatā cettha sāmatthiyato, na pamāṇato. Gamanacittasamuṭṭhitaṃ sahajātarūpakāyassa thambhanasandhāraṇacalanānaṃ paccayabhūtena ākāravisesena pavattamānaṃ vāyodhātuṃ sandhāyāha “vāyo viññattiṃ janetī”ti. Adhippāyasahabhāvī hi vikāro viññatti, yathāvuttaadhikabhāveneva ca vāyogahaṇaṃ, na vāyodhātuyā eva janakabhāvato, aññathā viññattiyā upādāyarūpabhāvo durupapādo siyā. Purato abhinīhāro puratobhāgena kāyassa pavattanaṃ, yo “abhikkamo”ti vuccati.

No being or person goes; movement is accomplished by mere phenomena, since there is no one distinct from them. Now, to show that the accomplishment of movement is due to mere phenomena, it is said: 'By the impulse of the mind-activity and the air element,' etc. Herein, 'the impulse of the mind-activity and the air element' (cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena) refers to that which is the mind-activity and the impulse or vibration of the air element. Here, by the inclusion of 'mind-activity,' it excludes the impulse of the air element not bound to the faculties; and by the inclusion of 'the impulse of the air element,' it excludes the mind-activity that is divided into volition and verbal intimation. By both, however, it clarifies bodily intimation. Having said 'goes' (gacchati), to show how the conventional expression 'goes' arises regarding the body in motion, it is said: 'Therefore,' etc. 'That' (taṃ) refers to the mind that arises with the desire to go. 'It generates wind' means it generates a group of material qualities with a predominance of the air element. Here, predominance is in terms of capability, not quantity. Referring to the air element—which arises from the mind set on movement and which proceeds with a particular mode that is a condition for the stiffening, supporting, and moving of the co-nascent material body—he says: 'The air generates intimation.' For intimation is a modification that occurs in accordance with intention, and the inclusion of 'air' is due to the aforementioned predominance, not because the air element alone is the generator. Otherwise, the status of intimation as derived matter would be difficult to establish. 'Forward propulsion' (purato abhinīhāro) is the moving forward of the front part of the body, which is called 'advancing' (abhikkamo).

“Eseva [V 1.0315] nayo”ti atidesavasena saṅkhepato vatvā tamevatthaṃ vivarituṃ “tatrāpi hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Koṭito paṭṭhāyāti heṭṭhimakoṭito paṭṭhāya. Ussitabhāvoti ubbiddhabhāvo.

'This is the method' (eseva nayo): having stated this concisely by way of extension, to explain that very meaning, 'therein also' (tatrāpi hi), etc., was said. 'Starting from the extremity' (koṭito paṭṭhāya) means starting from the lower extremity. 'The state of being raised' (ussitabhāvo) means the state of being uplifted.

Evaṃ [M 1.0353] pajānatoti evaṃ cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva gamanādibhāvo hotīti pajānato tassa evaṃ pajānanāya nicchayagamanatthaṃ “evaṃ hotī”ti vicāraṇā vuccati loke yathābhūtaṃ ajānantehi micchābhinivesavasena, lokavohāravasena vā. Atthi panāti attano eva vīmaṃsanavasena pucchāvacanaṃ. Natthīti nicchayavasena sattassa paṭikkhepavacanaṃ. Yathā panātiādi tassevatthassa upamāya vibhāvanaṃ.

'Thus one knows' (evaṃ pajānato) means: for one who knows that the state of movement and so on occurs simply through the impulse of the mind-activity and the air element, the investigation 'thus it is' (evaṃ hoti) is spoken of for the purpose of arriving at certainty through such knowing. This is said either due to the wrong adherence of those in the world who do not know things as they truly are, or due to worldly convention. 'But is there?' (atthi pana) is a questioning phrase by way of one's own reflection. 'There is not' (natthi) is a phrase of rejection, by way of certainty, regarding a being. 'Just as,' etc. (yathā pana ti ādi) is an explanation of that same meaning by way of a simile.

Nāvā mālutavegenāti yathā acetanā nāvā vātavegena desantaraṃ yāti, yathā ca acetano tejanaṃ kaṇḍo jiyāvegena desantaraṃ yāti, tathā acetano kāyo vātāhato yathāvuttavāyunā nīto desantaraṃ yātīti evaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sace pana koci vadeyya “yathā nāvāya tejanassa ca pellakassa purisassa vasena desantaragamanaṃ, evaṃ kāyassāpī”ti, hotu, evaṃ icchitovāyamattho. Yathā hi nāvā tejanānaṃ saṃhatalakkhaṇasseva purisassa vasena gamanaṃ, na asaṃhatalakkhaṇassa, evaṃ kāyassāpīti kā no hāni, bhiyyopi dhammamattatāva patiṭṭhaṃ labhati, na purisavādo. Tenāha “yantaṃ suttavasenā”tiādi.

'A boat by the force of the wind' means: just as an insentient boat goes to another place by the force of the wind, and just as an insentient arrow shaft goes to another place by the force of the bowstring, so too the insentient body, struck by the wind, is carried to another place by the aforementioned air element. Thus, the application of the simile should be understood. However, if someone were to say, 'Just as a boat and an arrow go to another place by means of a person who impels them, so too does the body,' let it be so; this meaning is also intended. For just as a boat and an arrow move by means of a person who has the characteristic of being a composite entity, not one who lacks that characteristic, so too with the body. What loss is that to us? Indeed, the principle of mere phenomena is further established, not the doctrine of a person. Therefore, he said: 'A machine by means of strings,' etc.

Tattha payuttanti heṭṭhā vuttanayena gamanādikiriyāvasena payojitaṃ. Ṭhātīti tiṭṭhati. Etthāti imasmiṃ loke. Vinā hetupaccayeti gantukāmatācitta-taṃsamuṭṭhāna-vāyodhātu-ādihetupaccayehi vinā. Tiṭṭheti tiṭṭheyya. Vajeti vajeyya gaccheyya ko nāmāti sambandho. Paṭikkhepattho cettha kiṃ-saddoti hetupaccayavirahena ṭhānagamanapaṭikkhepamukhena sabbāyapi dhammappavattiyā paccayādhīnavuttitāvibhāvanena attasuññatā viya aniccadukkhatāpi vibhāvitāti daṭṭhabbā.

Therein, 'yoked' (payuttaṃ) means yoked by way of actions such as going, in the manner stated above. 'Stands' (ṭhāti) means it stands (tiṭṭhati). 'Here' (ettha) means in this world. 'Without cause and condition' (vinā hetupaccaye) means without causal conditions such as the mind desiring to go, the air element arising therefrom, and so on. 'Would stand' (tiṭṭhe) means it would stand (tiṭṭheyya). 'Would go' (vaje) means it would go or proceed (vajeyya gaccheyya). The connection is with 'who indeed?' (ko nāma). Here, the word 'who' (kiṃ-saddo) has the meaning of rejection. It should be understood that by rejecting standing and going in the absence of causal conditions, and thereby demonstrating that the occurrence of all phenomena is dependent on conditions, not only emptiness of self but also impermanence and suffering are revealed.

Paṇihitoti yathā yathā paccayehi pakārato nihito ṭhapito. Sabbasaṅgāhikavacananti sabbesaṃ catunnampi iriyāpathānaṃ saṅgaṇhanavacanaṃ, pubbe visuṃ visuṃ iriyāpathānaṃ vuttattā idaṃ tesaṃ ekajjhaṃ gahetvā vacananti attho. Purimanayo vā iriyāpathappadhāno vuttoti tattha kāyo appadhāno anunipphādīti idha kāyaṃ padhānaṃ appadhānañca iriyāpathaṃ anunipphādaṃ katvā dassetuṃ dutiyanayo vuttoti evampettha dvinnaṃ nayānaṃ viseso veditabbo. Ṭhitoti pavatto.

'Directed' (paṇihito) means placed or established in various ways according to the conditions. 'An inclusive statement' (sabbasaṅgāhikavacanaṃ) is a statement that includes all four postures. Since the postures were previously spoken of separately, this is a statement that takes them all together; this is the meaning. Or, in the previous method, the posture was said to be primary; there, the body was secondary and consequential. Here, to show the body as primary and the posture as secondary and consequential, the second method is stated. Thus the difference between the two methods should be understood. 'Established' (ṭhito) means occurred.

Iriyāpathapariggaṇhanampi [V 1.0316][M 1.0354] iriyāpathavato kāyasseva pariggaṇhanaṃ tassa avatthāvisesabhāvatoti vuttaṃ “iriyāpathapariggahaṇena kāye kāyānupassī viharatī”ti. Tenevettha rūpakkhandhavaseneva samudayādayo uddhaṭā. Esa nayo sesavāresupi. Ādināti ettha ādi-saddena yathā “taṇhāsamudayā kammasamudayā āhārasamudayā”ti nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rupakkhandhassa udayaṃ passatīti ime cattāro āhārā saṅgayhanti, evaṃ “avijjānirodhā rūpanirodhā”tiādayopi pañca ākārā saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

The comprehension of the postures (iriyāpathapariggaṇhana) is also the comprehension of the body that possesses the postures, since they are its particular states. Thus it is said: ‘By comprehending the postures, one dwells contemplating the body in the body’ (iriyāpathapariggahaṇena kāye kāyānupassī viharati). For that reason, arising and so on are here extracted only in terms of the aggregate of form. This is the method in the remaining sections as well. Here, by the word 'etc.' (ādi-saddena), just as by 'from the arising of craving, from the arising of kamma, from the arising of nutriment,' one who sees the characteristic of production also sees the arising of the aggregate of form, so these four nutriments are included. Similarly, by 'from the cessation of ignorance, the cessation of form,' etc., five aspects are also included. This should be understood. The rest is as already stated.

Iriyāpathapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Section on Postures is concluded.

Catusampajaññapabbavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on the Fourfold Clear Comprehension

109. Catusampajaññavasenāti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.284; saṃ. ni. 5.368; dī. ni. abhi. ṭī. 2.214) samantato pakārehi, pakaṭṭhaṃ vā savisesaṃ jānātīti sampajāno, sampajānassa bhāvo sampajaññaṃ, tathāpavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Cattāri sampajaññāni samāhaṭāni catusampajaññaṃ, tassa vasena. Abhikkamanaṃ abhikkantanti āha “abhikkantaṃ vuccati gamana”nti. Tathā paṭikkamanaṃ paṭikkantanti āha “paṭikkantaṃ vuccati nivattana”nti. Nivattananti ca nivattimattaṃ, nivattitvā pana gamanaṃ gamanameva. Abhiharantoti gamanavasena kāyaṃ upanento.

109. 'By means of the fourfold clear comprehension' (catusampajaññavasena): (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.284; Saṃ. Ni. 5.368; Dī. Ni. Abhi. Ṭī. 2.214) one who knows thoroughly in various ways, or who knows excellently and specifically, is 'one who clearly comprehends' (sampajāno). The state of one who clearly comprehends is 'clear comprehension' (sampajañña); it is knowledge that occurs thus. The four clear comprehensions brought together are the 'fourfold clear comprehension' (catusampajañña); 'by means of that' (tassa vasena). Regarding 'advancing' (abhikkamanaṃ) and 'what is advanced' (abhikkantaṃ), he said: '“What is advanced” is called going.' Similarly, regarding 'retreating' (paṭikkamanaṃ) and 'what is retreated' (paṭikkantaṃ), he said: '“What is retreated” is called turning back.' And 'turning back' (nivattanaṃ) means merely the act of turning; for after turning, going is just going. 'Bringing forward' (abhiharanto) means bringing the body forward by way of going.

Sammā pajānanaṃ sampajānaṃ, tena attanā kātabbassa karaṇasīlo sampajānakārīti āha “sampajaññena sabbakiccakārī”ti. Sampajānasaddassa sampajaññapariyāyatā pubbe vuttāyeva. Sampajaññaṃ karotevāti abhikkantādīsu asammohaṃ uppādeti eva. Sampajānassa vā kāro etassa atthīti sampajānakārī. Dhammato vaḍḍhisaṅkhātena saha atthena pavattatīti sātthakaṃ, abhikkantādi. Sātthakassa sampajānanaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ. Sappāyassa attano upakārāvahassa hitassa sampajānanaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ abhikkamādīsu bhikkhācāragocare, aññatthāpi ca pavattesu avijahite kammaṭṭhānasaṅkhāte gocare sampajaññaṃ gocarasampajaññaṃ. Abhikkamādīsu asammuyhanameva sampajaññaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ. Pariggaṇhitvāti paṭisaṅkhāya.

'Rightly knowing' is 'clear comprehension' (sampajānaṃ). One who is in the habit of acting with that is 'one who acts with clear comprehension' (sampajānakārī); hence it is said, 'one who performs all tasks with clear comprehension' (sampajaññena sabbakiccakārī). The synonymity of the word 'sampajāna' with 'sampajañña' has already been stated. 'One produces clear comprehension' means one indeed generates non-delusion in advancing and so on. Or, one is 'one who acts with clear comprehension' because one has the action of one who clearly comprehends. Because it proceeds with a purpose (attha) together with what is designated as growth (vaḍḍhi) in accordance with the Dhamma, it is 'purposeful' (sātthakaṃ), such as advancing, etc. The clear comprehension of what is purposeful is 'clear comprehension of purpose' (sātthakasampajaññaṃ). The clear comprehension of what is suitable (sappāya)—beneficial and helpful to oneself—is 'clear comprehension of suitability' (sappāyasampajaññaṃ). In advancing, etc., on the alms-round resort, and also elsewhere, the clear comprehension regarding the resort designated as the meditation subject, which has not been abandoned, is 'clear comprehension of the resort' (gocarasampajaññaṃ). In advancing, etc., the very state of not being deluded is 'clear comprehension of non-delusion' (asammohasampajaññaṃ). 'Having comprehended' (pariggaṇhitvā) means having reflected upon (paṭisaṅkhāya).

Tasminti [V 1.0317][M 1.0355] sātthakasampajaññavasena pariggahitaatthe. Attho nāma dhammato vaḍḍhīti yaṃ sātthakanti adhippetaṃ gamanaṃ, taṃ sappāyamevāti siyā kassaci āsaṅkāti tannivattanatthaṃ “cetiyadassanaṃ tāvā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Cittakammarūpakāni viyāti cittakammakatapaṭimāyo viya, yantapayogena vā vicittakammapaṭimāyo viya. Asamapekkhanaṃ gehasitaaññāṇupekkhāvasena ārammaṇassa ayoniso gahaṇaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā uppajjati upekkhā bālassa mūḷhassa puthujjanassā”tiādi (ma. ni. 3.308). Hatthiādisammaddena jīvitantarāyo, visabhāgarūpadassanādinā brahmacariyantarāyo.

Tasminti refers to the meaning grasped by means of sātthakasampajañña (purposeful clear comprehension). The meaning is growth in the Dhamma—that which is intended as beneficial. Someone might have a doubt that it is suitable, so to dispel that doubt, the phrase ‘first the viewing of a shrine’ (cetiyadassanaṃ tāva) and so on is begun. Cittakammarūpakāni viya means like images made by artistry, or like varied images made by mechanical application. Asamapekkhanaṃ (not reflecting) is the unwise grasping of an object due to the indifference of a mind attached to a house. Regarding this, it is said: ‘Having seen a form with the eye, indifference arises in a foolish, deluded ordinary person’ (cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā uppajjati upekkhā bālassa mūḷhassa puthujjanassā), and so on (MN 3.308). Through contact with elephants and so on, there is danger to life; through seeing unsuitable forms and so on, there is danger to the holy life.

Pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya bhikkhūnaṃ anuvattanakathā āciṇṇā, ananuvattanakathā pana tassā dutiyā nāma hotīti āha “dve kathā nāma na kathitapubbā”ti.

From the day of his going forth, talk of conforming was frequent among the monks. But talk of non-conforming was a secondary matter for him. Hence it is said: ‘These two topics have never been spoken of before’.

Evanti “sace panā”tiādikaṃ sabbampi vuttākāraṃ paccāmasati, na “purisassa mātugāmāsubha”ntiādikaṃ vuccamānaṃ. Yogakammassa pavattiṭṭhānatāya bhāvanāya ārammaṇaṃ kammaṭṭhānanti vuccatīti āha “kammaṭṭhānasaṅkhātaṃ gocara”nti. Uggahetvāti yathā uggahanimittaṃ uppajjati, evaṃ uggahakosallassa sampādanavasena uggahetvā. Haratīti kammaṭṭhānaṃ pavatteti, yāva piṇḍapātapaṭikkamā anuyuñjatīti attho. Na paccāharatīti āhārūpabhogato yāva divāṭṭhānupasaṅkamanā kammaṭṭhānaṃ na paṭineti.

Evam (thus) means he reflects on all the aforementioned aspects, such as ‘if, however,’ and not on what is being said, such as ‘the impurity of a woman for a man.’ Because it serves as the basis for the activity of yogic practice, the object of meditation is called kammaṭṭhāna. Hence, it is said, ‘the field known as kammaṭṭhāna.’ Uggahetvā (having grasped) means having grasped in such a way that the learning sign arises, thus accomplishing skill in grasping. Harati (he carries it) means he maintains the meditation object; that is, he continuously engages with it until returning from the alms round. Na paccāharati (he does not bring it back) means he does not bring back the meditation object from the time of consuming food until he approaches his daytime dwelling.

Sarīraparikammanti mukhadhovanādisarīrapaṭijagganaṃ. Dve tayo pallaṅketi dve tayo nisajjāvāre, dve tīṇi uṇhāsanāni. Tenāha “usumaṃ gāhāpento”ti. Kammaṭṭhānasīsenevāti kammaṭṭhānaggeneva, kammaṭṭhānaṃ padhānaṃ katvā evāti attho. Tena “pattopi acetano”tiādinā (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.109) vakkhamānaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ, yathāparihariyamānaṃ vā avijahitvāti dasseti. “Paribhogacetiyato sarīracetiyaṃ garutara”nti katvā “cetiyaṃ vanditvā”ti pubbakālakiriyāvasena vuttaṃ. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 809; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.128; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.275) “cetiyaṃ bādhayamānā bodhisākhā haritabbā”ti vuttā.

Sarīraparikamma (body maintenance) refers to bodily care, such as washing the face and so on. Dve tayo pallaṅke (two or three sittings) means two or three sitting sessions, two or three warm seats (uṇhāsanāni). Hence it is said, ‘providing warmth’ (usumaṃ gāhāpento). Kammaṭṭhānasīseneva (with the meditation subject foremost) means with the meditation subject itself, making meditation the primary focus—this is the meaning. Therefore, the phrase ‘even the bowl is inanimate’ (pattopi acetano) (MN-A 1.109) indicates the meditation subject, either being maintained or without abandoning it. Considering ‘the bodily shrine is more important than the shrine of use’ (Paribhogacetiyato sarīracetiyaṃ garutaraṃ), the phrase ‘having paid homage to the shrine’ (cetiyaṃ vanditvā) is stated in the sense of a prior action. For in the commentary (Vb-A 809; MN-A 3.128; AN-A 1.1.275), it is said, ‘A Bodhi tree branch that obstructs a shrine should be removed’ (cetiyaṃ bādhayamānā bodhisākhā haritabbā).

Janasaṅgahatthanti [M 1.0356] “mayi akathente etesaṃ ko kathessatī”ti dhammānuggahena janasaṅgahatthaṃ. Tasmāti. Yasmā “dhammakathā nāma kathetabbāyevā”ti aṭṭhakathācariyā vadanti, yasmā ca dhammakathā kammaṭṭhānavinimuttā nāma natthi, tasmā. Anumodanaṃ katvāti etthāpi “kammaṭṭhānasīsenevā”ti [V 1.0318] ānetvā sambandho. Sampattaparicchedenevāti “paricito aparicito”tiādivibhāgaṃ akatvā sampattakoṭiyāva. Bhayeti paracakkādibhaye.

Janasaṅgahatthaṃ (to gather people)—thinking, ‘If I do not speak, who will speak to them?’—is for the purpose of gathering people through the support of the Dhamma. Tasmā (therefore). Because the commentary teachers say, ‘Indeed, the Dhamma talk must be given’ (dhammakathā nāma kathetabbāyeva), and because there is no Dhamma talk that is free from meditation subjects, therefore. Anumodanaṃ katvā (having expressed appreciation), here too, the connection should be made by bringing in the phrase ‘with the meditation subject foremost’ (kammaṭṭhānasīseneva). Sampattaparicchedeneva (only to the extent of attainment)—without making distinctions such as ‘familiar or unfamiliar,’ but only up to the level of attainment. Bhaye (in fear) refers to fear such as that of foreign armies and so forth.

Kammajatejoti gahaṇiṃ sandhāyāha. Kammaṭṭhānavīthiṃ nārohati khudāparissamena kilantakāyattā samādhānābhāvato. Avasesaṭṭhāneti yāguyā aggahitaṭṭhāne. Poṅkhānupoṅkhanti kammaṭṭhānupaṭṭhānassa avicchedadassanavacanametaṃ, yathā poṅkhānupoṅkhapavattāya sarapaṭipāṭiyā avicchedo, evametassāpīti.

Kammajatejo (the fire born of kamma) is mentioned referring to the digestive fire (gahaṇi). One does not ascend the path of the meditation subject due to a weary body from hunger and fatigue, and from a lack of concentration. Avasesaṭṭhāne (in the remaining places) refers to a place where gruel is not taken. Poṅkhānupoṅkha (arrow-tip to arrow-notch) is a saying indicating the uninterrupted establishment of the meditation subject, just as there is no break in the continuous sequence of arrows proceeding one after another, so too is this.

Nikkhittadhuro bhāvanānuyoge. Vattapaṭipattiyā apūraṇena sabbavatthāni bhinditvā. “Kāme avītarāgo hoti, kāye avītarāgo, rūpe avītarāgo, yāvadatthaṃ udarāvadehakaṃ bhuñjitvā seyyasukhaṃ passasukhaṃ middhasukhaṃ anuyutto viharati, aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ paṇidhāya brahmacariyaṃ caratī”ti (dī. ni. 3.320; ma. ni. 1.186) evaṃ vutta pañcavidhacetokhilavinibandhacitto. Caritvāti pavattitvā.

Nikkhittadhuro (one who has laid down the burden) means one who has done so with regard to the application to development. By not fulfilling the duties and practices, he has broken all bases. His mind is bound by the five kinds of mental barrenness thus described: ‘He is not devoid of passion for sensual pleasures, not devoid of passion for the body, not devoid of passion for form; having eaten his fill, he lives devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of lying on his side, and the pleasure of drowsiness; he practices the holy life with an aspiration for some group of deities’ (DN 3.320; MN 1.186). Caritvā means having proceeded.

Attakāmāti attano hitasukhaṃ icchantā, dhammacchandavantoti attho. Dhammoti hi hitaṃ, tannimittakañca sukhanti. Atha vā viññūnaṃ nibbisesattā attabhāvapariyāpannattā ca attā nāma dhammo, taṃ kāmenti icchantīti attakāmā. Usabhaṃ nāma vīsati yaṭṭhiyo. Tāya saññāyāti tāya pāsāṇasaññāya, ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgatāti jānantāti adhippāyo. Soyeva nayoti “ayaṃ bhikkhū”tiādiko yo ṭhāne vutto, so eva nisajjāyapi nayo. Pacchato āgacchantānaṃ chinnabhattabhāvabhayenapi yonisomanasikāraṃ paribrūheti.

Attakāmā means those who desire their own welfare and happiness, which is to say, those with a desire for the Dhamma. For Dhamma here refers to welfare and the happiness caused by it. Alternatively, because the wise are non-different, and because it is included in personal existence, the self is called Dhamma; thus, attakāmā means those who desire it. Usabha means twenty rods. Tāya saññāya means that, by that perception of the stone, they know they have come this far—this is the intended meaning. Soyeva nayo (the same method) refers to the approach mentioned earlier, such as ‘this monk,’ etc., which was stated regarding the place, and the same method applies also in the case of sitting. It also develops wise attention for those coming from behind, due to the fear of their meal being cut off.

Bahāpadhānaṃ pūjessāmīti amhākaṃ atthāya lokanāthena cha vassāni kataṃ dukkaracariyaṃ evāhaṃ yathāsatti pūjessāmīti. Paṭipattipūjā hi [M 1.0357] satthupūjā, na āmisapūjā. Ṭhānacaṅkamanamevāti adhiṭṭhātabbairiyāpathavasena vuttaṃ, na bhojanādikālesu avassaṃ kattabbanisajjāya paṭikkhepavasena.

‘I shall honor the One of Great Striving.’ This means: ‘I shall, according to my ability, honor the arduous practice undertaken for six years by the Lord of the World for our benefit.’ Indeed, honoring through practice is the honoring of the Teacher, not honoring through material gifts. ‘Only standing and walking’—this was said with regard to the postures to be determined upon, not as a rejection of the necessary sitting during meal times and the like.

Vīthiṃ otaritvā ito cito ca anoloketvā paṭhamameva vīthiyo sallakkhetabbāti āha “vīthiyo sallakkhetvā”ti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuccati “pāsādikena abhikkantenā”ti, taṃ dassetuṃ “tattha cā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

The phrase ‘having considered the paths’ means that, having descended onto the street and without looking here and there, one should first take note of the streets. To show what is referred to by ‘with pleasing forward progress,’ the phrase ‘and there,’ etc., was stated.

Paccekabodhiṃ [V 1.0319] sacchikaroti, yadi upanissayasampanno hotīti sambandho. Evaṃ sabbattha ito paresupi. Tattha paccekabodhiyā upanissayasampadā kappānaṃ dve asaṅkhyeyyāni satasahassañca tajjaṃ puññañāṇasambharaṇaṃ, sāvakabodhiyaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ kappasatasahassañca, mahāsāvakānaṃ kappasatasahassameva, itaresaṃ atītāsu jātīsu vivaṭṭasannissayavasena nibbattitaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ kusalaṃ. Bāhiyo dārucīriyoti bahi visaye sañjātasaṃvaḍḍhatāya bāhiyo, dārucīrapariharaṇena dārucīriyoti ca samaññāto. So hi āyasmā –

He realizes individual enlightenment, if he is endowed with the supporting conditions—this is the connection. Thus, it is the same everywhere else hereafter. Therein, the perfection of supporting conditions for individual enlightenment involves accumulating merit and knowledge suitable for it for two incalculable eons and a hundred thousand eons. For the enlightenment of disciples, the chief disciples require one incalculable eon and a hundred thousand eons, while the great disciples require only a hundred thousand eons. For the others, it is the wholesome qualities conducive to penetration, developed in past lives through reliance on the unfolding of conditions. Bāhiyo Dārucīriyo (Bāhiyo of the Bark Garment)—so called because he was born and grew up in an external region (bahi), and because he was known as one who wore a garment of bark (dārucīra). Indeed, that venerable one—

“Tasmā tiha te, bāhiya, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ ‘diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṃ bhavissati, sute… mute… viññāte viññātamattaṃ bhavissatī’ti. Yato kho te, bāhiya, diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṃ bhavissati, sute… mute… viññāte viññātamattaṃ bhavissati, tato tvaṃ, bāhiya, na tena. Yato tvaṃ, bāhiya, na tena, tato tvaṃ, bāhiya, na tattha. Yato tvaṃ, bāhiya, na tattha, tato tvaṃ, bāhiya, nevidha na huraṃ na ubhayamantarena, esevanto dukkhassā”ti (udā. 10) – ettakāya desanāya arahattaṃ sacchākāsi.

“Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: ‘In the seen, there will be merely the seen; in the heard, merely the heard; in the sensed, merely the sensed; in the cognized, merely the cognized.’ When, Bāhiya, for you in the seen there will be merely the seen, in the heard merely the heard, in the sensed merely the sensed, in the cognized merely the cognized, then, Bāhiya, you will not be ‘by that.’ When, Bāhiya, you are not ‘by that,’ then, Bāhiya, you will not be ‘in that.’ When, Bāhiya, you are not ‘in that,’ then, Bāhiya, you will be neither here nor beyond nor in between the two—this itself is the end of suffering.” (Ud 1.10) — With just this much teaching, he realized arahantship.

Tanti asammuyhanaṃ. Evanti idāni vuccamānākārena veditabbaṃ. Attā abhikkamatīti iminā andhaputhujjanassa diṭṭhiggāhavasena abhikkame sammuyhanaṃ dasseti, ahaṃ abhikkamāmīti pana iminā mānaggāhavasena, tadubhayaṃ pana taṇhāya vinā na hotīti taṇhāggāhavasenapi sammuyhanaṃ dassitameva hoti. “Tathā asammuyhanto”ti vatvā taṃ asammuyhanaṃ [M 1.0358] yena ghanavinibbhogena hoti, taṃ dassento “abhikkamāmī”tiādimāha. Tattha yasmā vāyodhātuyā anugatā tejodhātu uddharaṇassa paccayo. Uddharaṇagatikā hi tejodhātūti uddharaṇe vāyodhātuyā tassā anugatabhāvo, tasmā imāsaṃ dvinnamettha sāmatthiyato adhimattatā, itarāsañca omattatāti dassento “ekeka…pe… balavatiyo”ti āha. Yasmā pana tejodhātuyā anugatā vāyodhātu atiharaṇavītiharaṇānaṃ paccayo. Tiriyagatikāya hi vāyodhātuyā atiharaṇavītiharaṇesu sātisayo byāpāroti tejodhātuyā tassā anugatabhāvo, tasmā imāsaṃ dvinnamettha sāmatthiyato adhimattatā, itarāsañca omattatāti dassento “tathā atiharaṇavītiharaṇesū”ti āha. Satipi anugamanānugantabbatāvisese tejodhātu-vāyodhātu-bhāvamattaṃ sandhāya tathā-saddaggahaṇaṃ. Tattha akkantaṭṭhānato pādassa ukkhipanaṃ uddharaṇaṃ, ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ atikkamitvā purato haraṇaṃ atiharaṇaṃ khāṇuādipariharaṇatthaṃ, patiṭṭhitapādaghaṭṭanapariharaṇatthaṃ vā passena [V 1.0320] haraṇaṃ vītiharaṇaṃ, yāva patiṭṭhitapādo, tāva āharaṇaṃ atiharaṇaṃ, tato paraṃ haraṇaṃ vītiharaṇanti ayaṃ vā etesaṃ viseso.

The absence of delusion concerning that. Thus, it should be understood in the manner now being explained. The phrase 'the self moves forward' shows delusion through the clinging to views by the blind ordinary person regarding movement. The phrase 'I move forward,' however, shows delusion through the clinging to conceit. Both of these, moreover, do not occur without craving, so delusion is also shown through the clinging to craving. Having stated 'thus, not being deluded,' he then explains that non-delusion which occurs through the dissolution of compactness by saying, 'I move forward,' and so on. Here, because the fire element is followed by the wind element, it is a condition for lifting. For the fire element is what moves in lifting, and thus the wind element's following of it in lifting. Therefore, to show the predominance of these two elements here due to their capability, and the inferiority of the others, he says, 'each... strong.' But because the wind element is followed by the fire element, it is a condition for stepping forward and stepping aside. For the wind element moves horizontally, and its excessive activity in stepping forward and stepping aside is due to the fire element's following of it. Thus, to show the predominance of these two elements here due to their capability, and the inferiority of the others, he says, 'similarly in stepping forward and stepping aside.' Although there is a distinction between that which follows and that which is to be followed, the word 'similarly' is used with reference to the mere state of the fire and wind elements. Here, lifting the foot from the place it stood is 'lifting.' Moving it forward beyond the place it stood is 'stepping forward,' either to avoid a stump, etc., or moving it sideways to avoid striking the placed foot is 'stepping aside.' Bringing it as far as the placed foot is 'stepping forward,' and moving it beyond that is 'stepping aside.' This is the distinction between them.

Yasmā pathavīdhātuyā anugatā āpodhātu vossajjanassa paccayo. Garutarasabhāvā hi āpodhātūti vossajjane pathavīdhātuyā tassā anugatabhāvo, tasmā tāsaṃ dvinnamettha sāmatthiyato adhimattatā, itarāsañca omattatāti dassento āha “vossajjane…pe… balavatiyo”ti. Yasmā pana āpodhātuyā anugatā pathavīdhātu sannikkhepanassa paccayo, patiṭṭhābhāve viya patiṭṭhāpanepi tassā sātisayakiccattā āpodhātuyā tassā anugatabhāvo, tathā ghaṭṭanakiriyāya pathavīdhātuyā vasena sannirumbhanassa sijjhanato tatthāpi pathavīdhātuyā āpodhātuanugatabhāvo, tasmā vuttaṃ “tathā sannikkhepanasannirumbhanesū”ti. Tatthāti tasmiṃ abhikkamane, tesu vā vuttesu uddharaṇādīsu chasu koṭṭhāsesu. Uddharaṇeti uddharaṇakkhaṇe. Rūpārūpadhammāti uddharaṇākārena pavattā rūpadhammā, taṃsamuṭṭhāpakā arūpadhammā ca atiharaṇaṃ na pāpuṇanti khaṇamattāvaṭṭhānato. Tattha tatthevāti yattha yattha uppannā, tattha tattheva. Na hi dhammānaṃ [M 1.0359] desantarasaṅkamanaṃ atthi. Pabbaṃ pabbantiādi uddharaṇādikoṭṭhāse sandhāya vuttaṃ, taṃ sabhāgasantativasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Atiittaro hi rūpadhammānampi pavattikkhaṇo gamanassādānaṃ devaputtānaṃ heṭṭhupariyena paṭimukhaṃ dhāvantānaṃ sirasi pāde ca baddhadhuradhārāsamāgamatopi sīghataro. Yathā tilānaṃ bhajjiyamānānaṃ paṭapaṭāyanena bhedo lakkhīyati, evaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ uppādenāti dassanatthaṃ “paṭapaṭāyantā”ti vuttaṃ. Uppannā hi ekantato bhijjantīti.

Because the water element, accompanied by the earth element, is a condition for releasing. For the water element is of a heavier nature, and thus in releasing it is accompanied by the earth element; therefore, to show that the capability of these two is predominant here, and that of the others is deficient, it is said, 'In releasing… etc., they are strong.' Moreover, because the earth element, accompanied by the water element, is a condition for settling; for due to its superior function in establishing, as in providing a foundation, it is accompanied by the water element. Similarly, because restraining is accomplished by means of the earth element in the act of striking, there too the earth element is accompanied by the water element. Therefore, it is said, 'Likewise, in settling and restraining.' Here—in that advancing, or in those six stages mentioned, such as lifting, etc. Lifting—at the moment of lifting. Material and immaterial phenomena—material phenomena occurring in the mode of lifting, and the immaterial phenomena that produce them, do not reach the stage of carrying forward because of their momentary existence. There itself—wherever they arise, right there itself. For phenomena do not travel from one place to another. 'Joint by joint,' etc., refers to the stage of lifting, etc., and should be understood as stated in terms of a similar continuity. The duration of material phenomena is exceedingly brief, swifter than the meeting of the yoke-edges bound to the heads and feet of young gods running up and down, facing each other. Just as the splitting of sesame seeds being roasted is perceived by their crackling sound, so too, to show that conditioned phenomena are known to break by their very arising, it is said 'crackling.' For what has arisen certainly breaks apart.

Saddhiṃ rūpenāti idaṃ tassa tassa cittassa nirodhena saddhiṃ nirujjhanakarūpadhammānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ, yaṃ tato sattarasamacittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppannaṃ. Aññathā yadi rūpārūpadhammā samānakkhaṇā siyuṃ, “rūpaṃ garupariṇāmaṃ dandhanirodha”ntiādivacanehi (vibha. aṭṭha. 26) virodho siyā, tathā “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmi, yaṃ evaṃ lahuparivattaṃ, yathayidaṃ citta”nti evamādipāḷiyā (a. ni. 1.48). Cittacetasikā hi sārammaṇasabhāvā yathābalaṃ attano ārammaṇapaccayabhūtamatthaṃ vibhāvento eva uppajjantīti tesaṃ taṃsabhāvanipphattianantaraṃ nirodho, rūpadhammā pana anārammaṇā pakāsetabbā, evaṃ tesaṃ pakāsetabbabhāvanivatti soḷasahi cittehi hotīti taṅkhaṇāyukatā tesaṃ icchitā, lahuviññāṇavisayasaṅgatimattapaccayatāya tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ, visayasaṅgatimattatāya ca viññāṇassa lahuparivattitā, dandhamahābhūtapaccayatāya rūpadhammānaṃ dandhaparivattitā, nānādhātuyā yathābhūtañāṇaṃ kho [V 1.0321] pana tathāgatasseva, tena ca purejātapaccayo rūpadhammova vutto, pacchājātapaccayo ca tassevāti rūpārūpadhammānaṃ samānakkhaṇatā na yujjateva, tasmā vuttanayenevettha attho veditabbo.

'With form' means that it is said with reference to the material phenomena that cease together with the cessation of each mind-moment, which arose at the arising-moment of the seventeenth mind-moment prior to that. Otherwise, if material and immaterial phenomena were simultaneous, there would be a contradiction with statements like 'form undergoes gross change and ceases slowly' (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 26), and similarly with passages like 'Monks, I do not perceive any other single phenomenon that changes as swiftly as the mind' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.48). For mind and mental factors, having an object as their nature, arise by discerning their respective objects according to their capacity, and thus their cessation follows immediately after the fulfillment of that nature. Material phenomena, however, are objectless and to be manifested. Thus, the cessation of their state of being manifested occurs with sixteen mind-moments; hence, their lifespan of that duration is intended. The three aggregates (feeling, perception, and formations) are quick to change due to depending merely on the association of consciousness with its object. Because consciousness depends merely on association with its object, it changes swiftly. Material phenomena, being dependent on the slow-changing great elements, change slowly. The knowledge of things as they truly are in their diverse elements, however, belongs only to the Tathāgata. Moreover, the pre-nascence condition is stated to be material phenomena alone, and the post-nascence condition also pertains to it. Therefore, the simultaneity of material and immaterial phenomena is not tenable. Hence, the meaning here should be understood in the way stated.

Aññaṃ uppajjate cittaṃ, aññaṃ cittaṃ nirujjhatīti yaṃ purimuppannaṃ cittaṃ, taṃ aññaṃ, taṃ pana nirujjhantaṃ aparassa anantarādipaccayabhāveneva nirujjhatīti tato laddhapaccayaṃ aññaṃ uppajjate cittaṃ. Yadi evaṃ tesaṃ antaro labbheyyāti noti āha “avīcimanusambandho”ti, yathā vīci antaro na labbhati, tadevetanti avisesavidu maññanti, evaṃ anu anu sambandho cittasantāno rūpasantāno ca nadīsotova nadiyaṃ udakappavāho viya vattati.

One mind arises, another mind ceases. The previously arisen mind is another, and that, while ceasing, does so only by being the contiguity condition, etc., for a subsequent one; thus, having obtained its condition from that, another mind arises. If so, would an interval be found between them? No. Therefore, it is said, 'uninterrupted connection.' Just as no interval is found between waves, and those who do not discern the distinction think it is the same, so too the continuity of mind and the continuity of form proceed, moment by moment, like the current of a river, like the flow of water in a river.

Abhimukhaṃ [M 1.0360] lokitaṃ ālokitanti āha “puratopekkhana”nti. Yasmā yaṃdisābhimukho gacchati tiṭṭhati nisīdati vā, tadabhimukhaṃ pekkhanaṃ ālokitaṃ, tasmā tadanugataṃ vidisālokanaṃ vilokitanti āha “vilokitaṃ nāma anudisāpekkhana”nti. Sammajjanaparibhaṇḍādikaraṇe olokitassa, ullokaharaṇādīsu ullokitassa, pacchato āgacchantaparissayassa parivajjanādīsu apalokitassa siyā sambhavoti āha “iminā vā mukhena sabbānipi tāni gahitānevā”ti.

'Looking directly ahead' (ālokita) is said to be 'looking forward.' Since looking in the direction one is facing when going, standing, or sitting is ālokita, therefore, looking in other directions, which follows from that, is called vilokita, as stated: 'Vilokita means looking in the surrounding directions.' There can be looking down (olokitassa) for sweeping and attending to belongings, looking up (ullokitassa) for lifting and carrying, and looking back (apalokitassa) for avoiding dangers approaching from behind. Therefore, it is said, 'All of these are included by this means.'

Kāyasakkhinti kāyena sacchikatavantaṃ, paccakkhakārinanti attho. So hi āyasmā vipassanākāle eva “yamevāhaṃ indriyesu aguttadvārataṃ nissāya sāsane anabhiratiādivippakāraṃ patto, tameva suṭṭhu niggaṇhissāmī”ti ussāhajāto balavahirottappo, tattha ca katādhikārattā indriyasaṃvare ukkaṃsapāramippatto, teneva naṃ satthā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ indriyesu guttadvārānaṃ yadidaṃ nando”ti (a. ni. 1.235) etadagge ṭhapesi.

'Kāyasakkhī' means one who has realized with the body, that is, one who has directly experienced. For that venerable one, at the time of insight, resolved thus: 'Whatever dissatisfaction and other unfavorable states I have experienced in the Dispensation due to unguarded sense-doors, I will thoroughly restrain that very thing.' Thus, he became energetic, strong in moral shame and fear, and due to his having made a foundation in and perfected sense restraint, he attained the highest excellence. Therefore, the Teacher declared him foremost, saying: 'Monks, among my monk disciples who guard the sense-doors, Nanda is the foremost' (A. Ni. 1.235).

Sātthakatā ca sappāyatā ca ālokitavilokitassa veditabbā. Tasmāti “kammaṭṭhānāvijahanasseva gocarasampajaññabhāvato”ti vuttamevatthaṃ hetubhāvena paccāmasati. Attano kammaṭṭhānavaseneva ālokanavilokanaṃ kātabbaṃ, khandhādikammaṭṭhānā añño upāyo na gavesitabboti adhippāyo. Ālokitādisamaññāpi yasmā dhammamattasseva pavattiviseso, tasmā tassa yāthāvato jānanaṃ asammohasampajaññanti dassetuṃ “abbhantare”tiādi vuttaṃ.

The usefulness and suitability of looking and glancing should be understood. Therefore, it refers back to that very meaning as a reason: 'because clear comprehension of the range is precisely the non-abandonment of the meditation object.' The intention is that one should look and glance only in accordance with one’s meditation object; no other method should be sought apart from meditation objects like the aggregates. Since terms like 'looking' are merely a particular mode of the activity of phenomena themselves, to show that the understanding of it as it actually is constitutes unconfused clear comprehension, the phrase 'internally' and so on is used.

“Paṭhamajavanepi [V 1.0322] …pe… na hotī”ti idaṃ pañcadvāraviññāṇavīthiyaṃ “itthī puriso”ti rajjanādīnaṃ abhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tattha hi āvajjanavoṭṭhabbanānaṃ ayoniso āvajjanavoṭṭhabbanavasena iṭṭhe itthirūpādimhi lobho, aniṭṭhe ca paṭigho uppajjati, manodvāre pana “itthī puriso”ti rajjanādi hoti, tassa pañcadvārajavanaṃ mūlaṃ, yathāvuttaṃ vā sabbaṃ bhavaṅgādi, evaṃ manodvārajavanassa mūlavasena mūlapariññā vuttā. Āgantukatāvakālikatā pana pañcadvārajavanasseva apubbabhāvavasena ittarabhāvavasena ca vuttā. Heṭṭhupariyavasena bhijjitvā patitesūti heṭṭhimassa uparimassa [M 1.0361] ca aparāparaṃ bhaṅgappattimāha. Tanti javanaṃ. Tassa na yuttanti sambandho. Āgantuko abbhāgato. Udayabbayaparicchinno tāvatako kālo etesanti tāvakālikāni.

'In the first impulsion... it does not occur'—this is said with reference to the absence of attachment and other defilements in the five-door cognitive process regarding 'a woman, a man.' For in that process, due to unwise adverting and determining, lust arises toward a pleasing form like that of a woman, and aversion arises toward a displeasing one. But in the mind-door, attachment and so on arise regarding 'a woman, a man.' The root of this is the five-door impulsion, or all the life-continuum and so on as stated. Thus, the full understanding of the root is stated by way of the root of the mind-door impulsion. The terms 'adventitious' and 'temporary' are used to denote the unprecedented nature and transient nature of the five-door impulsion. 'Having broken apart and fallen' refers to the successive dissolution of the lower and the upper. 'That' refers to the impulsion. 'It is not fitting'—this is the connection. 'Adventitious' means a visitor. 'Temporary' refers to that whose duration is limited by arising and passing away.

Etaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ. Tatthāti pañcakkhandhavasena ālokanavilokane paññāyamāne tabbinimutto ko eko āloketi, ko viloketi. Upanissayapaccayoti idaṃ suttantanayena pariyāyato vuttaṃ. Sahajātapaccayoti nidassanamattametaṃ aññamañña-sampayutta-atthiavigatādipaccayānampi labbhanato.

This is unconfused clear comprehension. Therein, when looking and glancing are discerned by way of the five aggregates, who is the one looking, who is the one glancing, apart from them? This, 'dependence condition,' is stated here according to the sutta method, by way of implication. 'Co-arising condition' is merely illustrative, since other conditions such as mutuality, association, presence, and non-disappearance are also obtainable.

Maṇisappo nāma ekā sappajātīti vadanti. Laḷananti kampananti vadanti, līḷākaraṇaṃ vā laḷanaṃ.

They say there is a species of snake called a 'jewel snake.' They say 'laḷana' means trembling, or 'laḷana' is the act of playing.

Uṇhapakatiko pariḷāhabahulo. Sīlassa vidūsanena ahitāvahattā micchājīvavasena uppannaṃ asappāyaṃ. Cīvarampi acetanantiādinā cīvarassa viya “kāyopi acetano”ti kāyassa attasuññatāvibhāvanena “abbhantare”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāvento itarītarasantosassa kāraṇaṃ dasseti. Tenāha “tasmā”tiādi. Catupañcagaṇṭhikāhatoti āhatacatupañcagaṇṭhiko, catupañcagaṇṭhikāhi vā hatasobho.

It is hot in nature, full of burning distress. Unsuitable things that have arisen by means of wrong livelihood bring harm through the corruption of virtue. By clarifying the body's emptiness of self—saying, 'the body too is insentient,' just as a robe is (as in the phrase 'the robe too is insentient,' etc.)—he explains that very meaning stated with 'internally,' etc., and thereby shows the cause for contentment with whatever one gets. Therefore, he said, 'therefore' and so on. 'Struck by four or five knots' means either having four or five knots applied, or having its beauty ruined by four or five knots.

Aṭṭhavidhopi atthoti aṭṭhavidhopi payojanaviseso. Pathavīsandhārakajalassa taṃsandhārakavāyunā viya paribhuttassa āhārassa vāyodhātunāva āsaye avaṭṭhānanti āha “vāyodhātuvaseneva tiṭṭhatī”ti. Atiharatīti yāva mukhā abhiharati. Vītiharatīti tato yāva kucchi, tāva harati. Atiharatīti vā mukhadvāraṃ atikkāmento harati. Vītiharatīti kucchigataṃ passato harati. Parivattetīti aparāparaṃ cāreti. Ettha ca āhārassa dhāraṇaparivattanasaṃcuṇṇanavisosanāni pathavīdhātusahitā eva vāyodhātu karoti, na kevalāti tāni [V 1.0323] pathavīdhātuyāpi kiccabhāvena vuttāni. Allattañca anupāletīti vāyuādīhi atisosanaṃ yathā na hoti, tathā anupāleti allaādīhi atisosanaṃ yathā na hoti, tathā anupāleti allabhāvaṃ. Tejodhātūti gahaṇīsaṅkhātā tejodhātu. Sā hi anto paviṭṭhaṃ āhāraṃ paripāceti. Añjaso hotīti āhārassa pavesanādīnaṃ maggo hoti. Ābhujatīti pariyesanajjhoharaṇajiṇṇājiṇṇatādiṃ āvajjeti, vijānātīti attho. Taṃtaṃvijānananipphādakoyeva hi [M 1.0362] payogo “sammāpayogo”ti vutto. Yena hi payogena pariyesanādi nipphajjati, so tabbisayavijānanampi nipphādeti nāma tadavinābhāvato. Atha vā sammāpayogaṃ sammāpaṭipattiṃ anvāya āgamma ābhujati samannāharati. Ābhogapubbako hi sabbopi viññāṇabyāpāroti tathā vuttaṃ.

The eightfold benefit means the eightfold specific purpose. Just as the air element supports the water that supports the earth, so too the food that has been consumed remains in its receptacle by means of the air element—hence it is said, 'It remains by means of the air element.' 'Carries over' means it brings food as far as the mouth. 'Carries through' means it transports it from there as far as the stomach. Alternatively, 'carries over' refers to carrying it past the mouth-door, while 'carries through' refers to carrying what is in the stomach to the side. 'Churns' means it circulates it back and forth. Here, the air element, in conjunction with the earth element, performs the functions of holding, churning, pulverizing, and drying the food—not by itself alone. Thus, these functions are also attributed to the earth element as part of its activity. 'And maintains moisture' means it preserves the moist state so that there is no excessive drying by wind and other factors. 'The fire element' refers to the fire element known as the 'grasper' (digestive fire). It digests the food that has entered within. 'It becomes a path' means it becomes the path for the food's entry and so forth. 'It bends' means it attends to searching, swallowing, the state of being digested or undigested, and so forth; the meaning is 'it understands.' For the very effort that produces such and such understanding is called 'right effort.' For whatever effort accomplishes searching and so forth, it also produces understanding in that domain, since the two are inseparable. Alternatively, having relied on and approached right effort, which is right practice, 'it bends,' it considers. For all cognitive activity is preceded by consideration—thus it is said.

Gamanatoti bhikkhācāravasena gocaragāmaṃ uddissa gamanato. Pariyesanatoti gocaragāme bhikkhatthaṃ āhiṇḍanato. Paribhogatoti āhārassa paribhuñjanato. Āsayatoti pittādiāsayato. Āsayati ettha ekajjhaṃ pavattamānopi kammabalavatthito hutvā mariyādavasena aññamaññaṃ asaṅkarato sayati tiṭṭhati pavattatīti āsayo, āmāsayassa upari tiṭṭhanako pittādiko. Mariyādattho hi ayamākāro. Nidheti yathābhutto āhāro nicito hutvā tiṭṭhati etthāti nidhānaṃ, āmāsayo. Tato nidhānato. Aparipakkatoti gahaṇīsaṅkhātena kammajatejena avipakkato. Paripakkatoti yathābhuttassa āhārassa vipakkabhāvato. Phalatoti nipphattito. Nissandatoti ito cito ca vissandanato. Sammakkhanatoti sabbaso makkhanato. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāya (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.294) gahetabbo.

'From going' means from going towards a village for alms by way of the alms-round. 'From searching' refers to wandering in the village for the purpose of alms. 'From consuming' means from partaking of the food. 'From the residence' refers to the residence of bile and other humors. 'Āsaya' (residence) is so called because, even though they occur together, being established by the power of kamma, they lie, stand, and proceed here without mixing with one another by way of boundaries. This is the āsaya, the bile and other humors situated above the stomach. This term has the meaning of a boundary. 'Nidhāna' (storehouse) is so called because the food, once eaten, remains accumulated here; this is the storehouse, the stomach. 'From that storehouse.' 'From being undigested' means from not being ripened by the kamma-born fire known as the 'grasper.' 'From being digested' refers to the state of the eaten food being ripened. 'From the result' means from its production. 'From secretion' refers to the flowing out from here and there. 'From being smeared' means from being completely mixed. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation should be taken from the commentary on the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā 1.294).

Aññe ca rogā kaṇṇasūlabhagandarādayo. Aṭṭhāneti manussāmanussapariggahite ayutte ṭhāne khettadevāyatanādike. Nissaṭṭhattā neva attano kassaci anissajjitattā jigucchanīyattā ca na parassa. Udakatumbatoti veḷunāḷiādiudakabhājanato. Tanti chaḍḍitaudakaṃ.

And other ailments include earaches, fistulas, and the like. 'In an unfit place' means in an unsuitable place possessed by humans or non-humans, such as a field, a shrine, and the like. Because it has been discarded, it is not one's own; and because it has not been relinquished to anyone and is repulsive, it is not another's. 'From a water vessel' means from a water container such as a bamboo tube. 'That' refers to the discarded water.

Addhānairiyāpathā cirappavattikā dīghakālikā iriyāpathā. Majjhimā bhikkhācaraṇādivasena pavattā. Cuṇṇikairiyāpathā vihāre aññatthāpi ito cito ca parivattanādivasena pavattāti vadanti. “Gateti gamane”ti pubbe abhikkamapaṭikkamaggahaṇena gamanenapi purato pacchato ca kāyassa atiharaṇaṃ vuttanti idha gamanameva gahitanti keci.

Long-journey postures are postures that are long-lasting, of a long duration. Medium postures are those that occur by way of going for alms and so on. Minor postures, they say, are those that occur by way of turning here and there within the monastery or elsewhere. Regarding 'gati means gamana (going),' some say that since the carrying of the body forward and backward was previously stated by the inclusion of 'advancing and retreating' and by 'going,' here only 'going' is taken.

Yasmā [V 1.0324][M 1.0363] mahāsīvattheravāde anantare anantare iriyāpathe pavattarūpārūpadhammānaṃ tattha tattheva nirodhadassanavasena sampajānakāritā gahitā, idañcettha sampajaññavipassanācāravasena āgataṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “tayidaṃ mahāsīvattherena vuttaṃ asammohadhuraṃ imasmiṃ satipaṭṭhānabhutte adhippeta”nti. Sāmaññaphale (dī. ni. 1.214; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.214; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.214) pana sabbampi catubbidhaṃ sampajaññaṃ labbhati yāvadeva sāmaññaphalavisesadassanaparattā tassā desanāya. Satisampayuttassevāti idaṃ yathā sampajaññakiccassa padhānatā, evaṃ satikiccassāpīti dassanatthaṃ, na satiyā sabbhāvamattadassanatthaṃ. Na hi kadāci satirahitā ñāṇappavatti atthi. Etāni padānīti sampajaññapadāni. Vibhattānevāti visuṃ vibhattāneva. Imināpi sampajaññassa viya satiyāpi padhānataṃyeva vibhāveti.

Because in the teaching of the Elder Mahāsīva, acting with clear comprehension is taken to be the seeing of the cessation of material and immaterial phenomena occurring in each successive posture, and this is arrived at through the practice of insight with clear comprehension, therefore it is said: “This duty of non-delusion, intended within this foundation of mindfulness, was spoken by the Elder Mahāsīva.” In the Sāmaññaphala Sutta (Dī. Ni. 1.214; Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.214; Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.214), however, all four kinds of clear comprehension are obtained, inasmuch as that teaching is devoted to showing the special fruits of the ascetic life. The phrase “of one associated with mindfulness” is said to show that just as the function of clear comprehension is primary, so too is the function of mindfulness—not to show merely the existence of mindfulness. For there is never any occurrence of knowledge devoid of mindfulness. “These terms” means the terms of clear comprehension. “Distinctly analyzed” means they are analyzed separately. By this, he also clarifies that mindfulness, like clear comprehension, is primary.

Aparo nayo – eko bhikkhu gacchanto aññaṃ cintento aññaṃ vitakkento gacchati, eko kammaṭṭhānaṃ avissajjetvāva gacchati, tathā eko tiṭṭhanto nisīdanto sayanto aññaṃ cintento aññaṃ vitakkento sayati, eko kammaṭṭhānaṃ avissajjetvāva sayati, etthakena pana na pākaṭaṃ hotīti caṅkamanena dīpenti. Yo hi bhikkhu caṅkamanaṃ otaritvā caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ ṭhito pariggaṇhāti “pācīnacaṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ pavattā rūpārūpadhammā pacchimacaṅkamanakoṭiṃ appatvā ettheva niruddhā, pacchimacaṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ pavattāpi pācīnacaṅkamanakoṭiṃ appatvā ettheva niruddā, caṅkamanamajjhe pavattā ubho koṭiyo appatvā ettheva niruddhā, caṅkame pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ṭhānaṃ appatvā ettheva niruddhā, ṭhāne pavattā nisajjaṃ, nisajjāya pavattā sayanaṃ appatvā etthevaniruddhā”ti, evaṃ pariggaṇhanto pariggaṇhantoyeva cittaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ otāreti, uṭṭhahanto kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāva uṭṭhahati, ayaṃ bhikkhu gatādīsu sampajānakārī nāma hoti, evampi sutte kammaṭṭhānaṃ avibhūtaṃ hoti, tasmā yo bhikkhu yāva sakkoti, tāva caṅkamitvā ṭhatvā nisīditvā sayamāno evaṃ pariggahetvā sayati “kāyo acetano, mañco acetano, kāyo na jānāti “ahaṃ mañce sayito’ti, mañco na jānāti “mayi kāyo sayito”ti, acetano kāyo acetane mañce sayito”ti, evaṃ pariggaṇhantoyeva cittaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ otāreti, pabujjhanto kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāva pabujjhati, ayaṃ sutte sampajānakārī nāma hotīti.

Another method: a monk walks thinking and pondering something else; another monk walks without letting go of the meditation subject. Likewise, one stands, sits, or lies down thinking and pondering something else; one lies down without letting go of the meditation subject. By this much, however, it is not made clear, so they explain it with walking meditation. For when a monk has entered upon a walking path and stands at the end of the path, he comprehends thus: "The material and immaterial phenomena arising at the eastern end of the walking path cease right there without reaching the western end. Those arising at the western end also cease right there without reaching the eastern end. Those arising in the middle of the walking path cease right there without reaching either end. The material and immaterial phenomena arising in walking cease right there without reaching a standing position. Those arising in standing cease right there without reaching a sitting position; those arising in sitting cease right there without reaching a lying position." Even while comprehending thus, his mind sinks into the life-continuum. When rising, he rises having taken up the meditation subject. This monk is called one who acts with clear comprehension in going, and so on. Even so, while sleeping, the meditation subject is not manifest. Therefore, a monk who, as much as he is able, after walking, standing, and sitting, lies down while comprehending thus: "The body is non-sentient, the bed is non-sentient. The body does not know, 'I am lying on the bed,' nor does the bed know, 'The body is lying on me.' A non-sentient body lies on a non-sentient bed." Even while comprehending thus, his mind sinks into the life-continuum. When awakening, he awakens having taken up the meditation subject. This one is called one who acts with clear comprehension while sleeping.

Kāyādikiriyānibbattanena [M 1.0364] tammayattā āvajjanakiriyāsamuṭṭhitattā ca javanaṃ, sabbampi vā chadvārappavattaṃ kiriyāmayapavattaṃ nāma, tasmiṃ sati jāgaritaṃ nāma hotīti pariggaṇhanto jāgarite sampajānakārī nāma. Apica rattindivaṃ cha koṭṭhāse katvā pañca koṭṭhāse jaggantopi jāgarite sampajānakārī nāma hoti. Vimuttāyatanasīsena dhammaṃ desentopi bāttiṃsatiracchānakathaṃ [V 1.0325] pahāya dasakathāvatthunissitaṃ sappāyakathaṃ kathentopi bhāsite sampajānakārī nāma. Aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu cittaruciyaṃ manasikāraṃ pavattentopi dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannopi tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī nāma. Dutiyañhi jhānaṃ vacīsaṅkhāravirahato visesato tuṇhībhāvo nāma. Rūpadhammasseva pavattiākāravisesā abhikkamādayoti vuttaṃ “rūpakkhandhasseva samudayo ca vayo ca nīharitabbo”ti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Javana (impulsive consciousness) is so called due to producing bodily and other actions, due to consisting of that, and due to arising from the action of adverting. Or, all that occurs through the six doors is called a functional process; when that is present, it is called wakefulness. One who comprehends this is called ‘one who acts with clear comprehension in wakefulness.’ Furthermore, one who divides the day and night into six portions and remains awake for five of them is also called ‘one who acts with clear comprehension in wakefulness.’ One who teaches the Dhamma under the heading of the sphere of liberation, abandoning the thirty-two kinds of worldly talk and speaking a beneficial talk based on the ten topics for discussion, is called ‘one who acts with clear comprehension in speech.’ One who directs attention according to one's mental preference towards the thirty-eight objects, or one who has attained the second jhāna, is called ‘one who acts with clear comprehension in silence.’ For the second jhāna, due to the absence of verbal formations, is specifically called silence. It was said that going forward and so on are specific modes of the occurrence of material phenomena: ‘The arising and passing away of just the form aggregate should be brought out.’ The rest is to be understood in the manner already stated.

Catusampajaññapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on fourfold clear comprehension is completed.

Paṭikūlamanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on Reflection on Repulsiveness

110. Paṭikūlamanasikāravasenāti (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.377) jigucchanīyatāya. Paṭikūlameva paṭikūlaṃ yo paṭikūlasabhāvo paṭikūlākāro, tassa manasikaraṇavasena. Antarenapi hi bhāvavācinaṃ saddaṃ bhāvattho viññāyati yathā “paṭassa sukka”nti. Yasmā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.182-183) vuttaṃ, tasmā tattha taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāyañca vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Vatthādīhi pasibbakākārena bandhitvā kataṃ āvaṭanaṃ putoḷi. Vibhūtākāroti paṇṇattiṃ samatikkamitvā asubhabhāvassa upaṭṭhitākāro. Iti-saddassa ākāratthataṃ dassento “eva”nti vatvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ sarūpato dassento “kesādipariggahaṇenā”ti āha.

110. By means of attention to the repulsive: through the quality of being disgusting. 'Repulsive' means what is repulsive, having a repulsive nature, appearing repulsive—by means of attending to that. For even without a word expressing a state, the meaning of the state is understood, as in 'the whiteness of the cloth.' Since it is stated in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. 1.182-183), therefore it should be understood according to the method explained there in its description. A bundle made by binding with cloth, etc., in the shape of a package is called a 'putoḷi.' 'Clearly appearing' means the appearance of the foulness that arises, having transcended mere concepts. Showing that the word 'iti' has the meaning of manner, he says 'thus,' and showing the reason in terms of its own nature, he states 'by the comprehension of hair, etc.'

Paṭikūlamanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on reflection on repulsiveness is completed.

Dhātumanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Contemplation of Elements

111. Dhātumanasikāravasenāti pathavīdhātuādikā catasso dhātuyo ārabbha pavattabhāvanāmanasikāravasena, catudhātuvavatthānavasenāti attho. Dhātumanasikāro dhātukammaṭṭhānaṃ catudhātuvavatthānanti hi atthato ekaṃ. Goghātakoti jīvikatthāya gunnaṃ ghātako. Antevāsikoti [M 1.0365] kammakaraṇavasena tassa samīpavāsī. Ṭhita-saddo “ṭhito vā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.263; a. ni. 5.28) ṭhānasaṅkhātairiyāpathasamaṅgitāya, ṭhā-saddassa vā gativinivattiatthatāya aññattha ṭhapetvā gamanaṃ sesairiyāpathasamaṅgitāya bodhako, idha pana yathā tathā rūpakāyassa pavattiākārabodhako adhippetoti āha “catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ yena kenaci ākārena ṭhitattā yathāṭhita”nti. Tattha ākārenāti ṭhānādinā rūpakāyassa pavattiākārena. Ṭhānādayo [V 1.0326] hi iriyāpathasaṅkhātāya kāyikakiriyāya patho pavattimaggoti “iriyāpatho”ti vuccanti. Yathāṭhitanti yathāpavattaṃ. Yathāvuttaṭṭhānamevettha “paṇidhāna”nti adhippetanti āha “yathāṭhitattā ca yathāpaṇihita”nti. Ṭhitanti vā kāyassa ṭhānasaṅkhātairiyāpathasamāyogaparidīpanaṃ. Paṇihitanti tadaññairiyāpathasamāyogaparidīpanaṃ. Ṭhitanti vā kāyasaṅkhātānaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ khaṇe sakiccavasena avaṭṭhānaparidīpanaṃ. Paṇihitanti paccayakiccavasena tehi tehi paccayehi pakārato nihitaṃ paṇihitanti evampettha attho veditabbo. Paccavekkhatīti pati pati avekkhati, ñāṇacakkhunā vinibbhujitvā visuṃ visuṃ passati.

111. 'By means of attention to the elements' means by means of the cultivation of attention that proceeds by taking as its object the four elements beginning with the earth element; that is, by means of the analysis of the four elements. Attention to the elements, the meditation subject of the elements, and the analysis of the four elements are indeed one in meaning. 'A cow butcher' means one who slaughters cows for a livelihood. 'An apprentice' means one who lives near him for the purpose of performing tasks. The word 'ṭhita' in phrases like 'whether standing' (Dī. Ni. 1.263; A. Ni. 5.28) indicates being endowed with the posture of standing. Or, because the root 'ṭhā' means the cessation of movement, it indicates being endowed with the remaining postures by setting aside 'going' elsewhere. Here, however, it is intended to indicate the manner in which the physical body exists, as stated: 'in whatever manner he is standing (yathāṭhita), due to standing in any of the four postures.' In this context, 'manner' (ākārena) refers to the manner in which the physical body exists through standing and other postures. Standing and other postures are called 'iriyāpatha' because they are the paths, the routes of occurrence for bodily actions which are postures. 'Yathāṭhita' means 'as it is occurring.' Here, 'paṇidhāna' is intended to mean precisely the position stated earlier, as he says: 'due to being as it is placed (yathāṭhita) and as it is disposed (yathāpaṇihita).' Alternatively, 'standing' (ṭhita) clarifies the engagement in the posture of standing. 'Disposed' (paṇihita) clarifies the engagement in other postures. Or, 'standing' denotes the abiding of material phenomena relating to the body, in their respective functions at each moment. 'Disposed' (paṇihita) means they are placed in various ways by their respective causes due to their causal function. Thus, the meaning should be understood here. 'He reviews' (paccavekkhati) means he examines again and again, discerning and seeing distinctly with the eye of wisdom.

Idāni vuttamevatthaṃ bhāvatthavibhāvanavasena dassetuṃ “yathā goghātakassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha posentassāti maṃsūpacayaparibrūhanāya kuṇḍakabhattakappāsaṭṭhiādīhi saṃvaḍḍhentassa. Vadhitaṃ matanti hiṃsitaṃ hutvā mataṃ. Matanti ca matamattaṃ. Tenevāha “tāvadevā”ti. Gāvīti saññā na antaradhāyati yāni aṅgapaccaṅgāni yathāsanniviṭṭhāni upādāya gāvīsamaññā matamattāyapi gāviyā, tesaṃ taṃsannivesassa avinaṭṭhattā. Vilīyanti bhijjanti vibhujjantīti bīlā bhāgā va-kārassa ba-kāraṃ, i-kārassa ī-kāraṃ katvā. Bīlasoti bīlaṃ bīlaṃ katvā. Vibhajitvāti aṭṭhisaṅghāṭato maṃsaṃ vivecetvā, tato vā vivecitamaṃsaṃ bhāgaso katvā. Tenevāha “maṃsasaññā pavattatī”ti. Pabbajitassapi apariggahitakammaṭṭhānassa. Ghanavinibbhoganti santatisamūhakiccaghanānaṃ vinibbhujanaṃ vivecanaṃ. Dhātuso paccavekkhatoti ghanavinibbhogakaraṇena dhātuṃ dhātuṃ pathavīādidhātuṃ visuṃ visuṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa. Sattasaññāti attānudiṭṭhivasena pavattā saññāti vadanti, vohāravasena pavattasattasaññāyapi [M 1.0366] tadā antaradhānaṃ yuttameva yāthāvato ghanavinibbhogassa sampādanato. Evañhi sati yathāvuttaopammatthena upameyyattho aññadatthu saṃsandati sameti. Tenevāha “dhātuvaseneva cittaṃ santiṭṭhatī”ti. Dakkhoti cheko taṃtaṃsamaññāya kusalo, yathājāte sūnasmiṃ naṅguṭṭhakhuravisāṇādivante aṭṭhimaṃsādiavayavasamudāye avibhatte gāvīsamaññā, na vibhatte, vibhatte pana aṭṭiṃmaṃsādiavayavasamaññāti jānanako. Catumahāpatho viya catuiriyāpathoti gāviyā ṭhitacatumahāpatho viya kāyassa pavattimaggabhūto catubbidho iriyāpatho. Yasmā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.306) vitthāritā, tasmā tattha taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāyañca (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.306) vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

Now, to show the meaning already stated by way of explaining the meaning of the state, the passage beginning 'just as for a cow butcher' has been said. Therein, 'of one who nourishes' means of one who fattens by nourishing with food such as bran, broken rice, cotton seeds, and so on, for the increase and growth of flesh. 'Killed, it is dead' means having been harmed, it is dead. And 'dead' means merely dead. Therefore, it is said, 'only so long.' The perception 'cow' does not disappear because the arrangement of those limbs and parts, based on which the designation 'cow' arises even for a cow that is merely dead, has not been destroyed. 'They dissolve, they break, they separate'—thus 'bīlā bhāgā' (portions), by changing the letter 'v' to 'b' and 'i' to 'ī'. 'Portion by portion' means having made it portion by portion. 'Having divided' means having separated the flesh from the skeleton, or having made the flesh separated from it into portions. Therefore, it is said, 'the perception of flesh arises.' For a renunciate who has not grasped a meditation subject, 'the breaking down of the compact' means the dismantling and analysis of the compact nature of continuity, collection, and function. 'He reviews it by way of the elements' means that by means of breaking down the compact, he reviews element by element, having separated the earth element and so on. They say that 'the perception of a being' is the perception that proceeds by way of the view of self; even the perception of a being that proceeds by way of convention then disappears, which is fitting, because the breaking down of the compact is accomplished according to reality. When this is so, the meaning of the object of comparison truly corresponds and accords with the meaning of the simile as stated. Therefore, it is said, 'the mind is established by way of the elements alone.' 'Skilled' means clever, proficient in the respective designations, knowing that in an undivided collection of parts such as bone and flesh, possessing a tail, hooves, horns, and so on, as found in the slaughterhouse, there is the designation 'cow', but not when it is divided; when divided, however, there are the designations of the parts, such as 'bone' and 'flesh'. 'The four postures are like a junction of four great roads' means that just as there is the junction of four great roads where the cow is, so the fourfold posture is the path for the body's movement. Since this is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga, it should be understood according to the method stated there and in its commentary, the Mahāṭīkā.

Dhātumanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Section on Attention to the Elements is concluded.

Navasivathikapabbavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Nine Charnel Ground Sections

112. Sivathikāya [V 1.0327] apaviddhauddhumātakādipaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ odhiso pavattānaṃ kathānaṃ tadabhidheyyānañca uddhumātakādiasubhabhāgānaṃ sivathikapabbānīti saṅgītikārehi gahitasamaññā. Tenāha “sivathikapabbehi vibhajitu”nti. Uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānāti jīvitakkhayato upari maraṇato paraṃ. Samuggatenāti uṭṭhitena. Uddhumātattāti uddhaṃ uddhaṃ dhumātattā sūnattā. Setarattehi viparibhinnaṃ vimissitaṃ nīlaṃ vinīlaṃ, purimavaṇṇavipariṇāmabhūtaṃ vā nīlaṃvinīlaṃ, vinīlameva vinīlakanti ka-kārena padavaḍḍhanamāha anatthantarato yathā “pītakaṃ lohitaka”nti (dha. sa. 616). Paṭikūlakattāti jigucchanīyattā. Kucchitaṃ vinīlaṃ vinīlakanti kucchanattho vā ayaṃ ka-kāroti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ yathā “pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.316; a. ni. 5.213; mahāva. 285). Paribhinnaṭṭhānehi kākakaṅkādīhi. Vissandamānaṃ pubbanti vissavantaṃ pubbaṃ, tahaṃ tahaṃ paggharantapubbanti attho. Tathābhāvanti vissandamānapubbabhāvaṃ.

112. The designation 'charnel ground sections' was given by the compilers of the canon to the limited discourses connected with what is cast away in a charnel ground, such as a bloated corpse, and to the foul parts, such as the bloated, which are the subject matter thereof. Therefore, it is said, 'to divide by means of the charnel ground sections.' 'After the end of life' means after the destruction of life, after death. 'Arisen' means risen up. 'Because it is bloated' means because it is swollen up, puffed up. 'Discolored' (vinīlaṃ) means blue mixed with white and red, or discolored blue, being a transformation of its former color. 'Discolored' (vinīlakaṃ) is just 'discolored' (vinīlaṃ); this is stated to be an extension of the word by the letter 'ka' without a difference in meaning, as in 'yellowish' (pītakaṃ) and 'reddish' (lohitakaṃ). 'Because it is repulsive' means because it is disgusting. Or, to show that this letter 'ka' has the meaning of contempt, it is said, 'a contemptible discolored thing is vinīlakaṃ', as in 'an evil (pāpako) report of his fame goes forth.' 'By crows, vultures, etc., from the places where it is torn apart.' 'Pus oozing' means pus flowing out; the meaning is pus trickling here and there. 'Such a state' means the state of oozing pus.

So bhikkhūti yo “passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍita”nti vutto, so bhikkhu. Upasaṃharati sadisataṃ. Ayampi khotiādi upasaṃharaṇākāradassanaṃ[M 1.0367]. Āyūti rūpajīvitindriyaṃ, arūpajīvitindriyaṃ panettha viññāṇagatikameva. Usmāti kammajatejo. Evaṃpūtikasabhāvoti evaṃ ativiya pūtikasabhāvo, na āyuādīnaṃ avigame viya mattasoti adhippāyo.
