Ediso bhavissatīti evaṃbhāvīti āha “evaṃuddhumātādibhedo bhavissatī”ti.

'That monk' refers to the monk who was addressed, 'he might see a body discarded in a charnel ground.' He applies the similarity. The passage beginning 'This body also...' shows the method of application. 'Life' is the life faculty of material form; the life faculty of immaterial form here has only the course of consciousness as its resort. 'Heat' is the fire element born of kamma. 'Of such a putrid nature' means of such an exceedingly putrid nature; the intention is that it is not so only to a moderate degree, as when life and so on have not departed. 'It will be like this' means it will come to be in such a state; thus it is said, 'it will become of the kind that is bloated and so on.'

Luñcitvā luñcitvāti uppāṭetvā uppāṭetvā. Sesāvasesamaṃsalohitayuttanti sabbaso akhāditattā tahaṃ tahaṃ sesena appāvasesena maṃsalohitena yuttaṃ. Aññena hatthaṭṭhikanti avisesena hatthaṭṭhikānaṃ vippakiṇṇatā jotitāti anavasesato tesaṃ vippakiṇṇataṃ dassento “catusaṭṭhibhedampī”tiādimāha. Terovassikānīti tirovassaṃ gatāni. Tāni pana saṃvaccharaṃ vītivattāni hontīti āha “atikkantasaṃvaccharānī”ti. Purāṇatāya ghanabhāvavigamena vicuṇṇatā idha pūtibhāvoti so yathā hoti, taṃ dassento “abbhokāse”tiādimāha. Khajjamānatādivasena dutiyasivathikapabbādīnaṃ vavatthitatthā vuttaṃ “khajjamānādīnaṃ vasena yojanā kātabbā”ti.

'Having plucked and plucked' means having torn out and torn out. 'With the last remnants of flesh and blood' means that because it was not eaten completely, it is connected here and there with the little remaining flesh and blood. 'A hand-bone in one direction...' means that the scattered nature of the hand-bones is indicated without distinction; thus, showing their scatteredness without remainder, it is said, 'even into sixty-four kinds,' and so on. 'More than a year old' means gone beyond a year. Indeed, they have passed a year, so it is said, 'having passed a year.' Here, putrefaction is the state of being crumbled due to age and the loss of compactness. Showing how that comes to be, it is said, 'in the open,' and so on. Because the meaning of the second charnel ground section and so on is established by way of being eaten, etc., it is said, 'the application should be made by way of being eaten, etc.'

Navasivathikapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Nine Charnel Ground Sections is concluded.

Imāneva [V 1.0328] dveti avadhāraṇena appanākammaṭṭhānaṃ tattha niyameti aññapabbesu tadabhāvato. Yato hi eva-kāro, tato aññattha niyameti, tena pabbadvayassa vipassanākammaṭṭhānatāpi appaṭisiddhāti daṭṭhabbā aniccādidassanato. Saṅkhāresu ādīnavavibhāvanāni sivathikapabbānīti āha “sivathikānaṃ ādīnavānupassanāvasena vuttattā”ti. Iriyāpathapabbādīnaṃ anappanāvahatā pākaṭā evāti “sesāni dvādasāpī”ti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ panettha atthato avibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

By the exclusive statement 'these two only,' the meditation subject for absorption is specified there, because of its absence in the other sections. Since there is the word 'eva' (only), it thereby excludes others; therefore, it should be seen that the status of the two sections as meditation subjects for insight is also not contradicted, due to the seeing of impermanence and so on. The charnel ground sections are explanations of the danger in formations; thus it is said, 'because they are spoken of by way of contemplation of the danger of the charnel grounds.' That the sections on the postures and so on do not lead to absorption is quite evident, thus it is said, 'the remaining twelve also.' Whatever herein is not analyzed as to its meaning is easy to understand.

Kāyānupassanāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Contemplation of the Body is concluded.

Vedanānupassanāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Contemplation of Feeling

113. Sukhaṃ vedananti ettha sukhayatīti sukhā, sampayuttadhamme kāyañca laddhassāde karotīti attho. Suṭṭhu vā khādati, khanati vā kāyikaṃ cetasikañca [M 1.0368] ābādhanti sukhā. Sukaraṃ okāsadānaṃ etissāti sukhāti apare. Vedayati ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavatīti vedanā. Vedayamānoti anubhavamāno. Kāmantiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ iriyāpathapabbe vuttameva. Sampajānassa vediyanaṃ sampajānavediyanaṃ.

113. In the phrase 'a pleasant feeling,' 'pleasant' (sukhā) is so called because it makes pleasant (sukhayati); the meaning is that it causes the associated states and the body to obtain satisfaction. Or, it is 'pleasant' because it thoroughly eats away (suṭṭhu khādati) or digs up (khanati) physical and mental affliction. Others say it is 'pleasant' (sukhā) because for it the giving of an opportunity is easy to do (sukaraṃ). 'Feeling' (vedanā) is so called because it feels (vedayati), that is, it experiences the taste of the object. 'Feeling' (vedayamāno) means experiencing. Whatever is to be said regarding 'sensual pleasure' and so on has already been said in the section on the postures. The feeling of one who is clearly comprehending is 'feeling with clear comprehension'.

“Vohāramattaṃ hotī”ti etena “sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī”ti idaṃ vohāramattanti dasseti. Vatthuārammaṇāti rūpādiārammaṇā. Rūpādiārammaṇañhi vedanāya pavattiṭṭhānatāya “vatthū”ti adhippetaṃ. Assāti bhaveyya. Dhammavinimuttassa aññassa kattu abhāvato dhammasseva kattubhāvaṃ dassento “vedanāva vedayatī”ti āha. Nitthunantoti. Balavato vedanāvegassa nirodhane ādīnavaṃ disvā tassa avasaradānavasena nitthunanto. Vīriyasamataṃ yojetvāti adhivāsanavīriyassa adhimattattā tassa hāpanavasena samādhinā samarasatāpādanena vīriyasamataṃ yojetvā. Saha paṭisambhidāhīti lokuttarapaṭisambhidāhi saha. Lokiyānampi vā sati uppattikāle tattha samatthataṃ sandhāyāha “saha paṭisambhidāhī”ti. Samasīsīti vārasamasīsī hutvā, paccavekkhaṇavārassa anantaravāre parinibbāyīti attho.

‘Vohāramattaṃ hoti’ (it is merely a convention): By this, it is shown that the statement ‘experiencing a pleasant feeling, I experience a pleasant feeling’ is merely a convention. ‘Vatthuārammaṇaṃ’ (having a physical basis as its object) means having material phenomena as its object. For a material phenomenon is intended as the ‘basis’ (vatthu) because it is the place of occurrence for feeling. ‘Assā’ti means ‘it would be.’ Since there is no other agent apart from the Dhamma, showing that the Dhamma itself is the agent, it is said: ‘The feeling itself feels.’ ‘Nitthunanto’ (groaning): Seeing the danger in suppressing the force of a strong feeling, one groans by giving it an opportunity. ‘Vīriyasamataṃ yojetvā’ (having yoked energy to balance): Because the energy of endurance is excessive, by reducing it and bringing it into balance with concentration, one yokes energy to balance. ‘Saha paṭisambhidāhi’ (together with the discriminations): Together with the supramundane discriminations. Or, with reference to the capability of mundane ones at the time of their arising, it is said: ‘together with the discriminations.’ ‘Samasīsī’ (equal-headed): Having become equal-headed in turn, the meaning is that he attains final nibbāna in the turn immediately following the turn of reviewing.

Yathā ca sukhaṃ, evaṃ dukkhanti yathā “sukhaṃ vedayatī”tiādinā sampajānavediyanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, evaṃ dukkhampi. Tattha dukkhayatīti dukkhā, sampayuttadhamme kāyañca pīḷeti vibādhatīti [V 1.0329] attho. Duṭṭhuṃ vā khādati, khanati vā kāyikaṃ cetasikañca sātanti dukkhā. Dukkaraṃ okāsadānaṃ etissāti dukkhāti apare. Arūpakammaṭṭhānanti arūpapariggahaṃ, arūpadhammamukhena vipassanābhinivesanti attho. Rūpakammaṭṭhānena pana samathābhinivesopi saṅgayhati, vipassanābhiniveso pana idhādhippetoti dassento āha. “Rūpapariggaho arūpapariggahotipi etadeva vuccatī”ti. Catudhātuvavatthānaṃ kathesīti etthāpi “yebhuyyenā”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Tadubhayanti catudhātuvavatthānassa saṅkhepavitthāradvayamāha. Saṅkhepamanasikāravasena mahāsatipaṭṭhāne, vitthāramanasikāravasena rāhulovāda- (ma. ni. 2.115-117) dhātuvibhaṅgādīsu (vibha. 174-175).

Just as with pleasure, so too with suffering—as it is said, ‘One feels pleasure,’ and so on, referring to the clear comprehension of feelings, the same applies to suffering. Here, ‘dukkhā’ (suffering) is so called because it afflicts (dukkhayati) and oppresses the associated mental and physical states—that is the meaning. Or, it badly gnaws, or digs into, both bodily and mental comfort—that is suffering. Others say it is called suffering because it is difficult to grant it an opportunity. ‘Arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ’ (formless meditation subject) refers to the comprehension of the formless, meaning a focus on insight through the perspective of formless phenomena. By means of a form-based meditation subject, however, a focus on serenity is also included, but to show that a focus on insight is intended here, it is said: ‘The comprehension of form and the comprehension of the formless—this is indeed what is meant.’ The analysis of the four elements is taught, and here too the word ‘mostly’ should be brought in and connected. ‘Tadubhayaṃ’ (both of these) refers to the twofold division of the analysis of the four elements: the concise and the detailed. The concise is by way of brief attention, as in the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness, while the detailed is by way of thorough attention, as in the Rāhulovāda (Majjhima Nikāya 2.115–117) and the Dhātuvibhaṅga (Vibhaṅga 174–175).

Yebhuyyaggahaṇena [M 1.0369] tadaññadhammavasenapi arūpakammaṭṭhānakathāya atthitā dīpitāti taṃ vibhāgena dassetuṃ “tividho hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha abhinivesoti anuppaveso, ārambhoti attho. Ārambhe eva hi ayaṃ vibhāgo, sammasanaṃ pana anavasesatova dhamme pariggahetvā vattati. Pariggahite rūpakammaṭṭhāneti idaṃ rūpamukhena vipassanābhinivesaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, arūpamukhena pana vipassanābhiniveso yebhūyyena samathayānikassa icchitabbo, so ca paṭhamaṃ jhānaṅgāni pariggahetvā tato paraṃ sesadhamme pariggaṇhāti. Paṭhamābhinipātoti sabbe cetasikā cittāyattā cittakiriyabhāvena vuccantīti phasso cittassa paṭhamābhinipāto vutto, uppannaphasso puggalo, cittacetasikarāsi vā ārammaṇena phuṭṭho phassasahajātāya vedanāya taṃsamakālameva vedeti, phasso pana obhāsassa viya padīpo vedanādīnaṃ paccayaviseso hotīti purimakālo viya vuccati, yā tassa ārammaṇābhiniropanalakkhaṇatā vuccati. Phusantoti ārammaṇassa phusanākārena. Ayañhi arūpadhammatā ekadesena anallīyamānopi rūpaṃ viya cakkhu, saddo viya ca sotaṃ cittaṃ ārammaṇañca phusanto viya saṅghaṭṭento viya ca pavattati. Tathāhesa “saṅghaṭṭanaraso”ti vuccati.

By the use of 'for the most part', it is shown that the discussion on the formless meditation subjects exists even by way of other phenomena. To explain this in detail, ‘threefold’ and so on are stated. Here, ‘abhinivesa’ means entry, that is, commencement. This classification is indeed at the commencement, but ‘sammasana’ (comprehension) operates by grasping all phenomena without remainder. ‘When the form meditation subject is grasped,’ this is said with reference to a focus on insight by way of form. However, a focus on insight by way of the formless should generally be intended by one who is a serenity-vehicle practitioner. Such a person first comprehends the factors of jhāna and then proceeds to grasp the remaining phenomena. ‘Paṭhamābhinipāto’ (first impact): Since all mental factors are dependent on the mind, they are spoken of as mental activity; thus, contact is said to be the first impact of the mind. The person in whom contact has arisen, or the mass of mind and mental factors, being touched by the object, experiences with the feeling born together with contact, at that very same time. But contact, like a lamp for light, is a specific condition for feeling and the rest. Thus, it is spoken of as if it were a prior time, which is its characteristic of directing towards the object. ‘Phusanto’ (touching) means in the manner of contacting the object. For this formless nature, though not adhering in any part, operates like the eye with form or the ear with sound—as if contacting, as if striking the mind and the object. Thus, it is said to have ‘the function of striking.’

Ārammaṇaṃ anubhavantīti issaravatāya visavitāya sāmibhāvena ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavantī. Phassādīnañhi sampayuttadhammānaṃ ārammaṇe ekadeseneva pavatti phusanādimattabhāvato, vedanāya pana iṭṭhākārasambhogādivasena pavattanato ārammaṇe nippadesato pavatti. Phusanādibhāvena hi ārammaṇaggahaṇaṃ ekadesānubhavanaṃ, vedayitābhāvena gahaṇaṃ yathākāmaṃ sabbānubhavanaṃ evasabhāvāneva tāni gahaṇānīti na vedanāya viya phassādīnampi yathāsakaṃ kiccakaraṇena sāmibhāvānubhavanaṃ codetabbaṃ. Vijānantanti paricchindanavasena visesato jānantaṃ. Viññāṇañhi minitabbavatthuṃ nāḷiyā minanto puriso viya ārammaṇaṃ paricchijja [V 1.0330] vibhāventaṃ pavattati, na saññā viya sañjānanamattaṃ hutvā. Tathā hi anena kadāci lakkhaṇattayavibhāvanāpi hoti. Imesaṃ pana phassādīnaṃ tassa tassa pākaṭabhāvo paccayavisesasiddhassa pubbābhogassa vasena veditabbā.

It experiences the object: thus, like a lord, like a master, by way of ownership, it experiences the flavor of the object. For associated phenomena such as contact, their occurrence in the object is only partial, being merely the nature of touching and so on. But for feeling, its occurrence in the object is complete, due to its occurrence as enjoying agreeable aspects and so on. Indeed, grasping an object by way of touching and so on is experiencing it partially, while grasping by way of feeling is experiencing it entirely as desired. Such is the very nature of these graspings; thus, contact and the others should not be challenged for not experiencing ownership like feeling does, each performing its respective function. It cognizes: it knows distinctly by way of delimiting. For consciousness, like a man measuring a measurable object with a measuring vessel, occurs by delimiting and distinguishing the object, not merely by perceiving, as perception does. Thus, by means of it, sometimes a clarification of the three characteristics also occurs. Now, the prominence of each of these, contact and so on, should be understood in dependence on the preceding engagement that is established by a specific condition.

Evaṃ [M 1.0370] tassa tasseva pākaṭabhāvepi “sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, abhiññeyya”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.46; paṭi. ma. 1.3) “sabbañca kho, bhikkhave, abhijāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.26) ca evamādivacanato sabbe sammasanupagā dhammā pariggahetabbāti dassento “tattha yassā”tiādimāha. Tattha phassapañcamakeyevāti avadhāraṇaṃ tadantogadhattā taggahaṇeneva gahitattā catunnaṃ arūpakkhandhānaṃ. Phassapañcamakaggahaṇañhi tassa sabbacittuppādasādhāraṇabhāvato, tattha ca phassacetanāggahaṇena sabbasaṅkhārakkhandhadhammasaṅgaho cetanāpadhānattā tesaṃ. Tathā hi suttantabhājanīye saṅkhārakkhandhavibhaṅge (vibha. 12) “cakkhusamphassajā cetanā”tiādinā cetanāva vibhattā, itare pana khandhā sarūpeneva gahitā.

Even though each of these is prominent, from such statements as 'All, bhikkhus, should be fully understood' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.46; Paṭi. Ma. 1.3) and 'All, bhikkhus, I directly know' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.26), it is shown that all phenomena amenable to comprehension should be grasped. Thus, showing this, he says 'therein, of which' and so on. Here, the specification is made specifically regarding the pentad of contact because the four immaterial aggregates are included within it, being grasped by its very inclusion. Indeed, the grasping of the pentad of contact is common to all arisings of consciousness, and in that case, the grasping of contact and volition encompasses all phenomena of the aggregate of formations because volition is predominant among them. Thus, in the analysis of the aggregate of formations in the Suttanta exposition (Vibh. 12), only volition is distinguished by phrases like 'volition born of eye-contact,' while the other aggregates are grasped by their own nature.

Vatthuṃ nissitāti ettha vatthu-saddo karajakāyavisayoti kathamidaṃ viññāyatīti āha “yaṃ sandhāya vutta”ntiādi. Kattha pana vuttaṃ? Sāmaññaphale. Soti karajakāyo. Pañcakkhandhavinimuttaṃ nāmarūpaṃ natthīti idaṃ adhikāravasena vuttaṃ. Aññathā hi khandhavinimuttampi nāmaṃ atthevāti. Avijjādihetukāti avijjātaṇhupādānādihetukā. Vipassanāpaṭipāṭiyā…pe… vicaratīti iminā balavavipassanaṃ vatvā puna tassa ussukkāpanaṃ visesādhigamanañca dassento “so”tiādimāha.

Here, in 'relying on a basis' (vatthuṃ nissita), how is it to be understood that the word 'vatthu' refers to the physical body? He says, 'With reference to what was said,' and so on. Where, then, was it said? In the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. 'So' refers to the physical body. The statement 'there is no name-and-form apart from the five aggregates' is stated by way of context. Otherwise, indeed, name would exist even apart from the aggregates. Caused by ignorance, etc.—this means caused by ignorance, craving, clinging, etc. Regarding the sequence of insight... 'he fares'—having stated strong insight by this, then showing its further stimulation and the attainment of distinction, he says, 'so,' and so on.

Idhāti imissaṃ dutiyasatipaṭṭhānadesanāyaṃ, tassā pana vedanānupassanāvasena kathetabbattā bhagavā vedanāvasena kathesi. Yathāvuttesu ca tīsu kammaṭṭhānābhinivesesu vedanāvasena kammaṭṭhānābhiniveso sukaro vedanānaṃ vibhūtabhāvatoti dassetuṃ “phassavasena hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na pākaṭaṃ hotīti idaṃ tādise puggale sandhāya vuttaṃ, yesaṃ ādito vedanāva vibhūtatarā hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Evañhi yaṃ vuttaṃ “phasso pākaṭo hoti, viññāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hotī”ti, taṃ avirodhitaṃ hoti. Vedanānaṃ uppattipākaṭatāyāti ca idaṃ sukhadukkhavedanānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Tāsañhi pavatti oḷārikā, na itarāya. Tadubhayaggahaṇamukhena vā gahetabbattā itarāyapi pavatti viññūnaṃ pākaṭā evāti “vedanāna”nti avisesaggahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yadā sukhaṃ uppajjatītiādi sukhavedanāya pākaṭabhāvavibhāvanaṃ. Neva tasmiṃ samaye dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedetīti tasmiṃ sukhavedanāsamaṅgisamaye neva dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti niruddhattā, anuppannattā ca yathākkamaṃ [M 1.0371] atītānāgatānaṃ[V 1.0331], paccuppannāya pana asambhavo vuttoyeva. Sakiccakkhaṇamattāvaṭṭhānato aniccā. Sameccasambhuyya paccayehi katattā saṅkhatā. Vatthārammaṇādipaccayaṃ paṭicca uppannattā paṭiccasamuppannā. Khayavayapalujjananirujjhanapakatitāya khayadhammā…pe… nirodhadhammāti daṭṭhabbā.

Here, in this second discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, the Blessed One spoke in terms of feeling because it was to be taught by way of the contemplation of feelings. And to show that among the three approaches to meditation mentioned, the approach by way of feelings is easier due to the manifest nature of feelings, it was said, 'through contact,' and so on. The statement, 'It is not evident,' was said with reference to such individuals for whom feelings appear more distinctly from the outset. For in this way, what was stated—'contact is evident, consciousness is evident'—is not contradicted. And the statement about the manifest arising of feelings was said with reference to pleasant and painful feelings, for their occurrence is gross, unlike the other. However, since the other feeling is also to be grasped by way of taking hold of both, its occurrence is also evident to the wise; hence, 'feelings' should be understood as a non-specific reference. 'When pleasure arises,' and so on, is a clarification of the manifest nature of pleasant feeling. 'At that time, one does not feel painful feeling' means that at the time one is endowed with pleasant feeling, one does not feel painful feeling because it has ceased or has not yet arisen, in the case of past and future feelings respectively, while the impossibility of a present one has already been stated. They are impermanent because they last only for the duration of a single functional moment. They are conditioned because they are made by causes coming together and arising together. They are dependently arisen because they arise in dependence on causes such as a base and an object. By their nature of decay, vanishing, breaking up, and ceasing, they are to be seen as subject to decay... subject to cessation.

Kilesehi āmasitabbato āmisaṃ nāma pañca kāmaguṇā, ārammaṇakaraṇavasena saha āmisehīti āmisā. Tenāha “pañcakāmaguṇāmisanissitā”ti. Ito paranti “atthi vedanā”ti evamādipāḷiṃ sandhāyāha “kāyānupassanāyaṃ vuttanayamevā”ti.

The five strands of sensual pleasure are called 'worldly things' (āmisa) because they are to be affected by the defilements. A feeling is 'worldly' (sāmisā) because it is together with worldly things (āmisehi), in the sense of taking them as its object. Therefore, it is said, 'dependent on the worldly things of the five strands of sensual pleasure.' From here onward, referring to the Pāli text beginning with 'there is feeling,' it is said, 'the method is the same as that explained in the contemplation of the body.'

Vedanānupassanāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the contemplation of feeling is concluded.

Cittānupassanāvaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Contemplation of Mind

114. Sampayogavasena (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.381) pavattamānena saha rāgenāti sarāgaṃ. Tenāha “lobhasahagata”nti. Vītarāganti. Ettha kāmaṃ sarāgapadapaṭiyoginā vītarāgavasena bhavitabbaṃ, sammasanacārassa pana idhādhippetattā tebhūmakasseva gahaṇanti “lokiyakusalābyākata”nti vatvā “idaṃ panā”tiādinā tameva adhippāyaṃ vivarati. Sesāni dve dosamūlāni, dve mohamūlānīti cattāri akusalacittāni. Tesañhi rāgena sampayogābhāvato nattheva sarāgatā, tannimittakatāya pana siyā taṃsahitatālesoti nattheva vītarāgatāpīti dukavinimuttatā evettha labbhatīti āha “neva purimapadaṃ, na pacchimapadaṃ bhajantī”ti. Yadi evaṃ padesikaṃ pajānanaṃ āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati dukantarapariyāpannattā tesaṃ. Akusalamūlesu saha moheneva vattatīti samohanti āha “vicikicchāsahagatañceva uddhaccasahagatañcā”ti. Yasmā cettha saheva mohenāti samohanti purimapadāvadhāraṇampi labbhatiyeva, tasmā vuttaṃ “yasmā panā”tiādi. Yathā pana atimūḷhatāya pāṭipuggalikanayena savisesaṃ mohavantatāya momūhacittanti vattabbato vicikicchuddhaccasahagatadvayaṃ visesato “samoha”nti vuccati, na tathā sesākusalacittānīti “vaṭṭantiyevā”ti [M 1.0372] vuttaṃ. Sampayogavasena thinamiddhena anupatitaṃ anugatanti thinamiddhānupatitaṃ pañcavidhaṃ sasaṅkhārikākusalacittaṃ saṅkuṭitacittaṃ. Saṅkuṭitacittaṃ nāma ārammaṇe saṅkocanavasena pavattanato. Paccayavisesavasena thāmajātena uddhaccena sahagataṃ pavattaṃ saṃsaṭṭhanti uddhaccasahagataṃ, aññathā [V 1.0332] sabbampi akusalacittaṃ uddhaccasahagatamevāti. Pasaṭacittaṃ nāma sātisayaṃ vikkhepavasena pavattanato.

114. 'By way of association' (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 2.381) means with lust that is occurring; thus, 'with lust' (sarāgaṃ). Therefore, it is said, 'associated with greed' (lobhasahagata). As for 'without lust' (vītarāga): here, although it should be taken as 'without lust' in opposition to the term 'with lust,' since the practice of comprehension is intended here, only what belongs to the three planes is taken. Hence, having said 'worldly wholesome and indeterminate' (lokiyakusalābyākata), he clarifies that very intention with the phrase 'But this...' (idaṃ pana), and so on. The remaining four unwholesome consciousnesses are the two rooted in aversion and the two rooted in delusion. For them, since there is no association with lust, there is no state of 'being with lust' (sarāgatā). But since they may be caused by that, there might be a slight connection with it, so there is also no state of 'being without lust' (vītarāgatā). Thus, only freedom from the pair (dukavinimuttatā) is found here, as stated: 'they partake of neither the first term nor the last term.' If so, does this result in a partial understanding? It does not, because they are included in what is between the pair. Among the unwholesome roots, because it occurs together with delusion, it is 'with delusion' (samoha), as stated: 'associated with doubt and associated with restlessness.' And since here 'with delusion' (samoha) means 'together with delusion,' the emphasis on the first term is indeed obtained; therefore, it was said, 'But since...' (yasmā pana), and so on. Just as, due to extreme delusion and, in an individual case, a special degree of delusion, it is appropriate to speak of an 'utterly deluded consciousness' (momūhacitta), so too the two consciousnesses associated with doubt and restlessness are specifically called 'with delusion' (samoha). The other unwholesome consciousnesses are not like that; hence, it is said, 'they just occur.' By way of association, 'followed and pursued by sloth and torpor' is 'accompanied by sloth and torpor' (thinamiddhānupatitaṃ). The five kinds of prompted unwholesome consciousness are 'contracted consciousness' (saṅkuṭitacittaṃ). 'Contracted consciousness' is so called because it proceeds by way of shrinking in regard to its object. Due to a specific condition, occurring together with strong restlessness, it is mixed; hence 'associated with restlessness' (uddhaccasahagataṃ). Otherwise, all unwholesome consciousness would be associated with restlessness. 'Expanded consciousness' (pasaṭacittaṃ) is so called because it proceeds by way of excessive distraction.

Kilesavikkhambhanasamatthatāya vipulaphalatāya dīghasantānatāya ca mahantabhāvaṃ gataṃ, mahantehi vā uḷāracchandādīhi gataṃ paṭipannanti mahaggataṃ. Taṃ pana rūpārūpabhūmikaṃ tato mahantassa loke abhāvato. Tenāha “rūpārūpāvacara”nti. Tassa cettha paṭiyogī parittamevāti āha “amahaggatanti kāmāvacara”nti. Attānaṃ uttarituṃ samatthehi saha uttarehīti sauttaraṃ, tappaṭipakkhena anuttaraṃ, tadubhayaṃ upādāya veditabbanti āha “sauttaranti kāmāvacara”ntiādi. Paṭipakkhavikkhambhanasamatthena samādhinā sammadeva āhitaṃ samāhitaṃ. Tenāha “yassā”tiādi. Yassāti yassa cittassa. Yathāvuttena samādhinā na samāhitanti asamāhitaṃ. Tenāha “ubhayasamādhirahita”nti. Tadaṅgavimuttiyā vimuttaṃ, kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ. Vikkhambhanavimuttiyā vimuttaṃ, mahaggatanti tadubhayaṃ sandhāyāha “tadaṅgavikkhambhanavimuttīhi vimutta”nti. Yattha tadubhayavimutti natthi, taṃ ubhayavimuttirahitanti gayhamāne lokuttaracittepi siyā āsaṅkāti tannivattanatthaṃ “samuccheda…pe… okāsova natthī”ti āha. Okāsābhāvo ca sammasanacārassa adhippetattā veditabbo. Yaṃ panettha atthato avibhattaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayamevāti.

It is called 'developed' (mahaggata) because it has gone to greatness (mahantabhāvaṃ gataṃ) through its capacity to suppress the defilements, the abundance of its fruit, and its long continuity; or because it is gone to or entered upon by great ones with lofty aspirations and so on. That, however, is of the form and formless planes, because there is nothing greater than it in the world. Therefore, it is said, 'belonging to the form and formless spheres' (rūpārūpāvacara). Here, its counterpart is limited; hence it is said, 'undeveloped' (amahaggata) refers to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). It is 'with a superior' (sauttara) because it is together with superior states capable of surpassing it. Its opposite is 'unsurpassable' (anuttara). Both should be understood by taking them up; hence it is said, 'with a superior refers to the sense-sphere,' and so on. It is 'concentrated' (samāhita) because it is well placed (sammadeva āhitaṃ) by a concentration capable of suppressing its opposite. Therefore, it is said, 'of which...' (yassā), and so on. 'Of which' means of which consciousness. That which is not concentrated by the aforesaid concentration is 'unconcentrated' (asamāhita). Hence it is said to be 'devoid of both concentrations.' 'Liberated' by momentary liberation (tadaṅgavimutti) is wholesome sense-sphere consciousness. 'Liberated' by liberation by suppression (vikkhambhanavimutti) is developed consciousness. Referring to both, it is said, 'liberated by momentary and suppression liberations.' If 'devoid of both liberations' were taken to mean that wherein both these liberations are absent, a doubt might arise regarding supramundane consciousness. To prevent this, it is said, 'For eradication... there is no opportunity.' The absence of opportunity should be understood as intended for the practitioner of comprehension. Whatever herein is not analyzed in terms of its meaning should be understood according to the method stated below.

Cittānupassanāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the contemplation of mind is concluded.

Dhammānupassanāvaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Contemplation of Phenomena

Nīvaraṇapabbavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Section on Hindrances

115. Pahātabbādidhammavibhāgadassanavasena [V 1.0333] pañcadhā dhammānupassanā niddiṭṭhāti ayamattho pāḷito eva viññāyatīti tamatthaṃ ulliṅgento “pañcavidhena [M 1.0373] dhammānupassanaṃ kathetu”nti vuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kasmā nīvaraṇādivaseneva niddiṭṭhanti? Veneyyajjhāsayato. Yesañhi veneyyānaṃ pahātabbadhammesu paṭhamaṃ nīvaraṇāni vibhāgena vattabbāni, tesaṃ vasenettha bhagavatā paṭhamaṃ nīvaraṇesu dhammānupassanā kathitā. Tathā hi kāyānupassanāpi samathapubbaṅgamā desitā, tato pariññeyyesu khandhesu āyatanesu, bhāvetabbesu bojjhaṅgesu pariññeyādivibhāgesu saccesu ca uttarā desanā desitā, tasmā cettha samathabhāvanāpi yāvadeva vipassanatthaṃ icchitā, vipassanāpadhānā vipassanābahulā ca satipaṭṭhānadesanāti tassā vipassanābhinivesavibhāgena desitabhāvaṃ vibhāvento “apicā”tiādimāha. Tattha khandhāyatanadukkhasaccavasena missakapariggahakathanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saññāsaṅkhārakkhandhapariggahampīti pi-saddena sakalapañcupādānakkhandhapariggahaṃ sampiṇḍeti itaresaṃ tadantogadhattā. “Kaṇhasukkānaṃ yugandhatā natthī”ti pajānanakāle abhāvā “abhiṇhasamudācāravasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Yathāti yenākārena. So pana “kāmacchandassa uppādo hotī”ti vuttattā kāmacchandassa kāraṇākārova, atthato kāraṇamevāti āha “yena kāraṇenā”ti. Ca-saddo vakkhamānatthasamuccayattho.

115. The contemplation of phenomena is designated in five ways by way of showing the division of phenomena beginning with those to be abandoned. This meaning is understood from the Pāli itself, so, indicating that meaning, it is said, “He teaches the contemplation of phenomena in five ways.” If so, why are they designated by way of hindrances and so on? Due to the dispositions of those to be trained. For those trainees for whom the hindrances should first be explained in detail among the phenomena to be abandoned, for their sake the Blessed One first taught the contemplation of phenomena regarding the hindrances here. Thus, the contemplation of the body was also taught with serenity as its forerunner. Then, further teachings were given regarding the aggregates and sense bases to be fully understood, the factors of enlightenment to be developed, and the truths with their divisions of what must be fully understood and so on. Therefore, here too, serenity development is desired only for the sake of insight, and the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness is primarily focused on insight and abundant in insight. To clarify its being taught by way of the aspect of devotion to insight, the text states, “Moreover…” Here, the discussion of mixed comprehension should be understood in terms of the aggregates, sense bases, and the truth of suffering. The phrase “also the comprehension of the aggregates of perception and volitional formations” indicates by the word “also” that it summarizes the comprehension of all five aggregates of clinging, because the others are included within them. Because at the time of knowing there is an absence of the 'pairing of dark and bright,' the phrase 'by way of frequent occurrence' is stated. “Yathā” means by which manner. However, since “the arising of sensual desire occurs” is said, the cause of sensual desire is just the manner of the cause; in meaning, it is just the cause, hence, it is stated, “by which reason.” The word “ca” (and) has the meaning of collecting the subsequent meanings.

Tatthāti “yathā cā”tiādinā vuttapade. Subhampīti kāmacchandopi. So hi attano gahaṇākārena “subha”nti vuccati, tenākārena pavattanakassa aññassa kāmacchandassa nimittattā “subhanimitta”nti ca. Iṭṭhaṃ, iṭṭhākārena vā gayhamānaṃ rūpādi subhārammaṇaṃ. Ākaṅkhitassa hitasukhassa anupāyabhūto manasikāro anupāyamanasikāro. Tanti ayonisomanasikāraṃ. Tatthāti nipphādetabbe ārammaṇabhūte ca duvidhepi subhanimitte. Āhāroti paccayo.

Therein: in the passage stated beginning with “yathā ca” and so on. Even the pleasant: even sensual desire. For it is called “pleasant” due to the manner of its grasping, and because it is the sign of another sensual desire that occurs by that manner, it is also called “the sign of the pleasant.” Desirable: an object such as form, etc., grasped by way of a desirable aspect, is a pleasant object. Attention that is not a means to the desired welfare and happiness is “anupāyamanasikāro” (unskillful attention). That is unwise attention. Therein: in the twofold sign of the pleasant, which is to be produced and is the object. Nutriment: the condition.

Asubhampīti asubhajjhānampi uttarapadalopena. Taṃ pana dasasu aviññāṇakāsubhesu, kesādīsu ca pavattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kesādīsu hi saññā asubhasaññāti girimānandasutte (a. ni. 10.60) vuttāti. Ettha ca catubbidhassa ayonisomanasikārassa yonisomanasikārassa [V 1.0334] ca gahaṇaṃ niravasesadassanatthaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tesu pana asubhe “subha”nti, “asubha”nti ca manasikāro idhādhippeto, tadanukūlattā vā itarepīti.

“Even the repulsive”: this also refers to repulsive meditation by ellipsis of the latter part of the compound. It should be understood as occurring in the ten inanimate repulsive objects, and in hair, etc. For in the objects beginning with hair, the perception is called “the perception of the repulsive,” as stated in the Girimānanda Sutta (A. Ni. 10.60). Here, the inclusion of the fourfold unwise attention and wise attention should be understood as having been done to show completeness without omission. Among these, attention to the repulsive as “beautiful” or as “repulsive” is what is intended here, or the others are included because they are in accordance with that.

Ekādasasu [M 1.0374] (a. ni. ṭī. 1.1.16) asubhesu paṭikūlākārassa uggaṇhanaṃ, yathā vā tattha uggahanimittaṃ uppajjati, tathā paṭipatti asubhanimittassa uggaho. Upacārappanāvahāya asubhabhāvanāya anuyuñjanaṃ asubhabhāvanānuyogo. Bhojane mattaññuno thinamiddhābhibhavābhāvā otāraṃ alabhamāno kāmacchando pahīyatīti vadanti. Bhojananissitaṃ pana āhāre paṭikūlasaññaṃ, tabbipariṇāmassa, tadādhārassa, tassa ca udariyabhūtassa asubhatādassanaṃ, kāyassa āhāraṭṭhitikatādassanañca yo sammadeva jānāti, so visesato bhojane mattaññū nāma, tassa ca kāmacchando pahīyateva. Asubhakammikatissatthero dantaṭṭhidassāvī. Abhidhammapariyāyena (dha. sa. 1159, 1503) sabbopi lobho kāmacchandanīvaraṇanti āha “arahattamaggenā”ti.

The grasping of the repulsive sign means: in the eleven repulsive objects (A. Ni. Ṭī. 1.1.16), grasping the disagreeable aspect; or, the practice in such a way that the learning sign arises there. Devotion to developing the repulsive, leading to access and absorption, is pursuing repulsive meditation. They say that sensual desire is abandoned when one cannot find an opportunity due to being moderate in food and the absence of being overcome by sloth and torpor. But one who rightly understands the perception of repulsiveness in food, its transformation, its basis, the repulsiveness of that which has become stomach-content, and the seeing of the body’s dependence on food—such a one is especially called “moderate in food,” and sensual desire is indeed abandoned for him. The Elder Asubhakammika Tissa was one who saw repulsiveness in teeth and bones. According to the Abhidhamma method (Dha. Sa. 1159, 1503), all greed is the hindrance of sensual desire; therefore, it is said to be abandoned “by the path of arahantship.”

Paṭighampi purimuppannaṃ paṭighanimittaṃ parato uppajjanakapaṭighassa kāraṇanti katvā. Mejjati hitapharaṇavasena siniyhatīti mitto, tasmiṃ mitte bhavā, mittassa vā esāti mettā, tassā mettāya.

Ill-will also, having considered the previously arisen sign of ill-will as the cause of ill-will arising later. “Mitta” means one who moistens or is affectionate by way of beneficial contact. “Mettā” is that which exists in that friend, or this belongs to a friend; of that loving-kindness.

Mettāyanassa sattesu hitapharaṇassa uppādanaṃ pavattanaṃ mettānimittassa uggaho. Odhisakaanodhisakadisāpharaṇānanti attaatipiyasahāyamajjhattaverīvasena odhisakatā, sīmāsambhede kate anodhisakatā, ekādidisāpharaṇavasena disāpharaṇatā mettāya uggahaṇe veditabbā. Vihāraracchāgāmādivasena vā odhisakadisāpharaṇaṃ, vihārādiuddesarahitaṃ puratthimādidisāvasena anodhisakadisāpharaṇanti evaṃ vā dvidhā uggahaṇaṃ sandhāya “odhisakaanodhisakadisāpharaṇāna”nti vuttaṃ. Uggaho ca yāva upacārā daṭṭhabbo, uggahitāya āsevanā bhāvanā. Tattha “sabbe sattā, pāṇā, bhūtā, puggalā, attabhāvapariyāpannā”ti etesaṃ vasena pañcavidhā, ekekasmiṃ “averā hontu, abyāpajjā, anīghā, sukhī attānaṃ pariharantū”ti catudhā pavattito vīsatividhā anodhisakapharaṇā mettā, “sabbā itthiyo, purisā, ariyā, anariyā, devā, manussā, vinipātikā”ti sattodhikaraṇavasena pavattā sattavidhā aṭṭhavīsatividhā vā, dasahi disāhi disodhikaraṇavasena pavattā dasavidhā ca, ekekāya vā disāya sattādiitthādiaverādibhedena [M 1.0375] asītādhikacatusatappabhedā ca odhibhopharaṇā veditabbā.

The generation and continuation of the spreading of welfare to beings, which is loving-kindness, is the apprehension of the sign of loving-kindness. The phrase “directed and undirected spreading in all directions” refers to the directed aspect when it is made directed by way of oneself, a very dear person, a friend, a neutral person, and a hostile being; and the undirected aspect when boundaries are dissolved. The spreading in directions, such as the east, should be understood as the apprehension of loving-kindness by way of spreading in directions. Alternatively, directed spreading in directions may be based on dwellings, streets, villages, and so forth, while undirected spreading in directions, such as the east, is without reference to specific dwellings, and so forth. Thus, the phrase “directed and undirected spreading in all directions” is stated with reference to this twofold apprehension. And the apprehension should be seen as extending up to access concentration; the repetition of what has been apprehended is development. Here, the twentyfold undirected spreading of loving-kindness, which is practiced in four ways for each of the five categories—“all beings, all living creatures, all entities, all individuals, all those included in personality”—is: “May they be free from enmity, free from ill-will, free from distress, and may they live happily.” Alternatively, it is sevenfold or twenty-eightfold when practiced by way of seven categories: “all women, all men, all noble ones, all non-noble ones, all deities, all humans, all those in states of deprivation.” And it is tenfold when practiced by way of the ten directions. For each direction, the directed spreading is understood as having four hundred and eighty distinctions, based on beings, women, and so forth, and the absence of enmity, and so forth.

Yena [V 1.0335] ayonisomanasikārena aratiādikāni uppajjanti, so aratiādīsu ayonisomanasikāro, tena. Nipphādetabbe hi idaṃ bhummaṃ. Esa nayo ito paresupi. Ukkaṇṭhitā pantasenāsanesu adhikusalesu dhammesu ca uppajjanabhāvariñcanā. Kāyavināmanāti kāyassa virūpenākārena nāmanā.

Through which unwise attention discontent and similar states arise, that unwise attention is the cause of discontent and the like. Here, the locative case has the sense of 'that which is to be produced.' This is the method here and also in the following instances. Restlessness is the arising of wavering in remote lodgings and regarding superior skillful qualities. ‘Bodily bending’ means the bending of the body into an unseemly shape.

Kusaladhammasampaṭipattiyā paṭṭhapanasabhāvatāya, tappaṭipakkhānaṃ visosanasabhāvatāya ca ārambhadhātuādito pavattavīriyanti āha “paṭhamārambhavīriya”nti. Yasmā paṭhamārambhamattassa kosajjavidhamanaṃ thāmagamanañca natthi, tasmā vuttaṃ “kosajjato nikkhantatāya tato balavatara”nti. Yasmā pana aparāparuppattiyā laddhāsevanaṃ uparūparivisesaṃ āvahantaṃ ativiya thāmagatameva hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanato tatopi balavatara”nti.

Because it has the nature of establishing wholesome qualities through proper practice and the nature of eliminating their opposites, the energy that proceeds from the element of initiative and so forth is called ‘initial application of energy.’ Since the mere initial application does not destroy laziness or attain strength, it is said, ‘It is stronger because it emerges from laziness.’ However, since repeated arising, having gained familiarity, brings about further and further distinctions and becomes exceedingly strong, it is said, ‘It is even stronger than that because of advancing to each successive stage.’

Atibhojane nimittaggāhoti atibhojane thinamiddhassa nimittaggāho, “ettake bhutte thinamiddhassa kāraṇaṃ hoti, ettake na hotī”ti thinamiddhassa kāraṇākāraṇaggāho hotīti attho. Divā sūriyālokanti divā gahitanimittaṃ sūriyālokaṃ rattiyaṃ manasikarontassapīti evamettha attho veditabbo. Dhutaṅgānaṃ vīriyanissitattā vuttaṃ “dhutaṅganissitasappāyakathāyapī”ti.

'Grasping the sign in overeating' means that in overeating there is a grasping of the sign of sloth and torpor. The meaning is that it is the grasping of the cause and non-cause of sloth and torpor, thinking, 'Eating this much is a cause for sloth and torpor; eating this much is not.' Regarding 'daylight, sunlight,' the meaning here should be understood thus: even for one who gives attention at night to the sign of sunlight grasped during the day. Because the ascetic practices are founded on energy, it is said, 'even in suitable talk connected with the ascetic practices.'

Kukkuccampi katākatānusocanavasena pavattamānaṃ cetaso avūpasamāvahatāya uddhaccena samānalakkhaṇamevāti “avūpasamo nāma avūpasantākāro, uddhaccakukkuccamevetaṃ atthato”ti vuttaṃ.

Remorse, too, arising through grieving over what was done and what was not done, brings about the mind’s lack of serenity, and thus has a characteristic similar to agitation. Therefore, it is said, ‘Lack of serenity is the state of not being serene; in meaning, this is agitation and remorse.’

Bahussutassa ganthato atthato ca suttādīni vicārentassa atthavedādipaṭilābhasabbhāvato vikkhepo na hoti, yathāvidhipaṭipattiyā yathānurūpapaṭikārappavattiyā ca katākatānusocanañca na hotīti “bāhusaccenapi…pe… uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyatī”ti āha. Yadaggena bāhusaccena uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyati, tadaggena paripucchakatāvinayapakataññutāhipi taṃ pahīyatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Buddhasevitā ca buddhasīlitaṃ āvahatīti cetaso vūpasamakarattā uddhaccakukkuccapahānakārī vuttā. Buddhattaṃ [M 1.0376] pana anapekkhitvā vinayadharā kukkuccavinodakā kalyāṇamittā vuttāti daṭṭhabbā. Vikkhepo ca bhikkhuno yebhuyyena kukkuccahetuko hotīti “kappiyākappiyaparipucchāmahulassā”tiādinā vinayanayeneva paripucchakatādayo niddiṭṭhā. Pahīne uddhaccakukkucceti niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ. Kukkuccassa domanassasahagatattā anāgāmimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo vutto.

For the learned one, who examines the suttas and other texts both in terms of their wording and their meaning, there is no distraction due to the possibility of gaining understanding of the meaning and so on. And by practicing according to the method and undertaking appropriate remedies, there is no regret over what has or has not been done. Thus, it is said, ‘Even through much learning… agitation and remorse are abandoned.’ It should be understood that to the extent that agitation and remorse are abandoned by the highest degree of learning, to that same extent they are abandoned by thorough questioning and familiarity with the Vinaya. And association with the Buddha brings about conduct like the Buddha's. Because it pacifies the mind, it is said to be a cause for the abandoning of agitation and remorse. However, it should be understood that, without reference to Buddhahood, those versed in the Vinaya are mentioned as good friends who dispel remorse. And for a monk, distraction is mostly caused by remorse. Therefore, thorough questioning and so on are pointed out according to the method of the Vinaya, as in the passage beginning ‘being much occupied with questioning about what is allowable and not allowable.’ In the phrase ‘when agitation and remorse are abandoned,’ the locative case is used in the sense of specification. Because remorse is accompanied by displeasure, its non-arising in the future is stated in relation to the path of the non-returner.

Tiṭṭhati [V 1.0336] pavattati etthāti ṭhānīyā, vicikicchāya ṭhānīyā vicikicchāṭṭhānīyā, vicikicchāya kāraṇabhūtā dhammā. Tiṭṭhatīti vā ṭhānīyā, vicikicchā ṭhānīyā etissāti vicikicchāṭṭhānīyā, atthato vicikicchā eva. Sā hi purimuppannā parato uppajjanakavicikicchāya sabhāgahetutāya asādhāraṇaṃ.

‘It stands, it proceeds here,’ thus it is a ground (ṭhānīyā). ‘The ground of doubt’ (vicikicchāṭṭhānīyā) means the states that are the cause of doubt. Or, ‘it stands,’ thus it is a ground; ‘doubt is the ground for this,’ thus it is the ground of doubt. In meaning, it is simply doubt itself. For that previously arisen doubt is a unique cause for a subsequently arising doubt, by way of being a cause of a similar nature.

Kusalākusalāti kosallasambhūtaṭṭhena kusalā, tappaṭipakkhato akusalā. Ye akusalā, te sāvajjā asevitabbā hīnā ca. Ye kusalā, te anavajjā sevitabbā paṇītā ca. Kusalāpi vā hīnehi chandādīhi āraddhā hīnā, paṇītehi paṇītā. Kaṇhāti kāḷakā, cittassa apabhassarabhāvakaraṇā. Sukkāti odātā, cittassa pabhassarabhāvakaraṇā. Kaṇhābhijātihetuto vā kaṇhā, sukkābhijātihetuto sukkā. Te eva sappaṭibhāgā. Kaṇhā hi ujuvipaccanīkatāya sukkehi sappaṭibhāgā, tathā sukkāpi itarehi. Atha vā kaṇhasukkā ca sappaṭibhāgā ca kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā. Sukhā hi vedanā dukkhāyavedanāya sappaṭibhāgā, dukkhā ca vedanā sukhāya vedanāya sappaṭibhāgāti.

‘Skillful and unskillful’: ‘skillful’ in the sense of arising from skill, ‘unskillful’ as their opposite. Those that are unskillful are blameworthy, to be avoided, and inferior. Those that are skillful are blameless, to be cultivated, and excellent. Or, even skillful things, when initiated with inferior intentions and so forth, are inferior; when initiated with excellent intentions, they are excellent. ‘Dark’ means black, making the mind lose its radiance. ‘Bright’ means white, making the mind radiant. Or, ‘dark’ refers to what arises from a dark origin, and ‘bright’ from a bright origin. These are indeed counterparts. For dark is the counterpart of bright because of direct opposition, and likewise bright is the counterpart of the other. Alternatively, the phrase 'dark-bright with counterparts' refers to dark and bright states and their counterparts. For pleasant feeling is the counterpart of painful feeling, and painful feeling is the counterpart of pleasant feeling.

Kāmaṃ bāhusaccaparipucchakatāhi aṭṭhavatthukāpi vicikicchā pahīyati, tathāpi ratanattayavicikicchāmūlikā sesavicikicchāti katvā āha “tīṇi ratanāni ārabbhā”ti. Ratanattayaguṇāvabodhe hi “satthari kaṅkhatī”ti (dha. sa. 1008, 1123, 1167, 1241, 1263, 1270; vibha. 915) ādivicikicchāya asambhavoti. Vinaye pakataññutā “sikkhāya kaṅkhatī”ti (dha. sa. 1008, 1123, 1167, 1241, 1263, 1270; vibha. 915) vuttāya vicikicchāya pahānaṃ karotīti āha “vinaye ciṇṇavasībhāvassapī”ti. Okappanīyasaddhāsaṅkhātaadhimokkhabahulassāti saddheyyavatthuno anupavisanasaddhāsaṅkhātaadhimokkhena adhimuccanabahulassa[M 1.0377]. Adhimuccanañca adhimokkhuppādanamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saddhāya vā ninnapoṇatā adhimutti adhimokkho.

Although doubt, even that with eight grounds, is abandoned through much learning and thorough questioning, still, considering that other doubts are rooted in doubt about the Triple Gem, it is said, ‘concerning the three jewels.’ For, with the understanding of the qualities of the Triple Gem, doubt such as ‘he doubts the Teacher’ (Dhs. 1008, etc.; Vibh. 915) becomes impossible. Familiarity with the Vinaya brings about the abandoning of the doubt spoken of as ‘he doubts the training’ (Dhs. 1008, etc.; Vibh. 915), hence it is said, ‘even through ingrained mastery in the Vinaya.’ ‘For one who is abundant in resolution, which is reckoned as confident faith’ means: for one who is frequently resolved by means of resolution, which is reckoned as faith that penetrates a trustworthy object. And this resolving should be understood as simply the arising of resolution. Or, the inclination and leaning by way of faith is resolution.

Subhanimittaasubhanimittādīsūti “subhanimittādīsu asubhanimittādīsū”ti ādi-saddo paccekaṃ yojetabbo. Tattha paṭhamena ādi-saddena paṭighanimittādīnaṃ saṅgaho, dutiyena mettācetovimuttiādīnaṃ. Sesamettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Regarding ‘in attractive signs, unattractive signs, and so forth,’ the word ‘and so forth’ should be connected separately to each, as in ‘in attractive signs and so forth’ and ‘in unattractive signs and so forth.’ Here, by the first ‘and so forth,’ repulsive signs and so forth are included; by the second, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness and so forth are included. What remains to be said here is as has been said before.

Nīvaraṇapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on the Hindrances is concluded.

Khandhapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on the Aggregates

116. Upādānehi [V 1.0337] ārammaṇakaraṇādivasena upādātabbā vā khandhā upādānakkhandā. Iti rūpanti ettha iti-saddo idaṃ-saddena samānatthoti adhippāyenāha “idaṃ rūpa”nti. Tayidaṃ sarūpato anavasesapariyādānaṃ hotīti āha – “ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, na ito paraṃ rūpaṃ atthī”ti. Itīti vā pakāratthe nipāto, tasmā “iti rūpa”nti iminā bhūtupādādivasena yattako rūpassa bhedo, tena saddhiṃ rūpaṃ anavasesato pariyādiyitvā dasseti. Sabhāvatoti ruppanasabhāvato cakkhādivaṇṇādisabhāvato ca. Vedanādīsupīti ettha “ayaṃ vedanā, ettakā vedanā, na ito paraṃ vedanā atthīti sabhāvato vedanaṃ pajānātī”tiādinā, sabhāvatoti ca anubhavanasabhāvato sātādisabhāvato cāti evamādinā yojetabbaṃ.

116. The aggregates are called the aggregates of clinging because they are to be clung to by means of clinging, by way of making them into objects, and so on. Here, in the phrase 'iti rūpaṃ,' the word 'iti' (thus) is used with the intention of conveying the same meaning as 'idaṃ' (this), as in 'this is form.' That this is a complete enumeration of its nature without remainder is stated thus: 'This much is form; there is no form beyond this.' Alternatively, 'iti' is a particle in the sense of manner. Therefore, by the phrase 'iti rūpaṃ,' he demonstrates form exhaustively, including all its distinctions, such as by way of the primary elements and derived form. 'By its nature' refers to both the nature of being afflicted (ruppana) and the nature of the eye, color, and so on. In the case of feeling and the rest, it should be connected thus: 'This is feeling, this much is feeling, there is no feeling beyond this—thus one understands feeling by its nature,' and 'by its nature' refers to both the nature of experiencing and the nature of being pleasant, and so on.

Khandhapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on the Aggregates is concluded.

Āyatanapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on the Sense Bases

117. Chasu ajjhattikabāhiresūti (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.384) “chasu ajjhattikesu chasu bāhiresu”ti “chasū”ti padaṃ paccekaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Kasmā panetāni ubhayāni chaḷeva vuttāni? Chaviññāṇakāyuppattidvārārammaṇavavatthānato. Cakkhuviññāṇavīthiyā [M 1.0378] pariyāpannassa hi viññāṇakāyassa cakkhāyatanameva uppattidvāraṃ, rūpāyatanameva ca ārammaṇaṃ, tathā itarāni itaresaṃ, chaṭṭhassa pana bhavaṅgamanasaṅkhāto manāyatanekadeso uppattidvāraṃ, asādhāraṇañca dhammāyatanaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. Cakkhatīti cakkhu, rūpaṃ assādeti vibhāveti cāti attho. Suṇātīti sotaṃ. Ghāyatīti ghānaṃ. Jīvitanimittatāya raso jīvitaṃ, taṃ jīvitamavhāyatīti jivhā. Kucchitānaṃ sāsavadhammānaṃ āyo uppattidesoti kāyo. Munāti ārammaṇaṃ vijānātīti mano. Rūpayati vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjamānaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetīti rūpaṃ. Sappati attano paccayehi harīyati sotaviññeyyabhāvaṃ gamīyatīti saddo. Gandhayati attano vatthuṃ sūcetīti gandho. Rasanti taṃ sattā assādentīti raso. Phusīyatīti phoṭṭhabbaṃ. Attano lakkhaṇaṃ dhārentīti dhammā. Sabbāni pana āyānaṃ tananādiatthena āyatanāni. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.510-512) taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāya (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 2.510) ca vuttanayena veditabbo.

117. Regarding the six internal and external bases (Dīgha Nikāya Ṭīkā 2.384): 'In the six internal and six external' means the word 'six' should be applied separately to each. But why are both groups said to be only six? Because of the determination of the doors and objects for the arising of the six consciousness-bodies. For the consciousness-body included in the eye-consciousness process, the eye-base is the door for its arising, and the form-base is the object; similarly for the others. As for the sixth, a portion of the mind-base, called the life-continuum mind, is the door for its arising, and the unique mental-object-base is its object. The eye is called 'cakkhu' because it sees (cakkhati), meaning it savors and distinguishes form. The ear is called 'sota' because it hears (suṇāti). The nose is called 'ghāna' because it smells (ghāyati). Taste is life, as it is a cause of life; the tongue (jivhā) is so called because it calls for (avhāyati) that life (jīvitaṃ). The body is called 'kāya' because it is the origin (āyo), the place of arising for contemptible, tainted phenomena. The mind is called 'mano' because it cognizes (munāti) an object. Form is called 'rūpa' because it reveals (rūpayati) its state, which has gone to the heart, by undergoing a change of appearance. Sound is called 'sadda' because it moves (sappati) and is carried (harīyati) by its conditions, going to the state of being cognizable by the ear. Smell is called 'gandha' because it indicates (gandhayati) its source. Taste is called 'rasa' because beings savor (rasanti) it. The tangible is called 'phoṭṭhabba' because it is touched (phusīyati). Mental objects are called 'dhammā' because they bear (dhārenti) their own characteristics. All these are called 'āyatanas' by way of the meaning of stretching out (tanana) what comes (āyānaṃ), and so on. This is a summary here. The detailed explanation should be understood according to the method described in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. 2.510-512) and its commentary (Visuddhi. Mahāṭī. 2.510).

Cakkhuñca [V 1.0338] pajānātīti ettha cakkhu nāma pasādacakkhu, na sasambhāracakkhu, nāpi dibbacakkhuādikanti āha “cakkhupasāda”nti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “yaṃ cakkhu catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādo”ti (dha. sa. 596-599). Ca-saddo vakkhamānatthasamuccayattho. Yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasenāti aviparītassa attano rasassa ceva lakkhaṇassa ca vasena, rūpesu āviñchanakiccassa ceva rūpābhighātārahabhūtapasādalakkhaṇassa ca vasenāti attho. “Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe cā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.204, 400; 3.421, 425-426; saṃ. ni. 2.43-45; 4.54-55; kathā. 465, 467) samuditāniyeva rūpāyatanāni cakkhuviññāṇuppattihetu, na visuṃ visunti imassa atthassa dassanatthaṃ “rūpe cā”ti puthuvacanaggahaṇaṃ, tāya eva ca desanāgatiyā kāmaṃ idhāpi “rūpe ca pajānātī”ti vuttaṃ, rūpabhāvasāmaññena pana sabbaṃ ekajjhaṃ gahetvā “bahiddhā catusamuṭṭhānikarūpañcā”ti ekavacanavasena attho vutto. Sarasalakkhaṇavasenāti cakkhuviññāṇassa visayabhāvakiccassa ceva cakkhupaṭihananalakkhaṇassa ca vasenāti yojetabbaṃ.

‘The eye, he understands it’—here, the eye refers to the sensitive eye, not the physical eye, nor the divine eye, etc. It is said, ‘the eye-sensitivity.’ This refers to what is stated: ‘The eye, which is sensitivity derived from the four great elements.’ The particle ‘ca’ serves to connect or accumulate the meanings to follow. By way of its true essence and characteristic—that is, by way of its own undeviating essence and characteristic, as well as by way of its function of apprehending forms and the characteristic of being a sensitive physical base capable of being impacted by forms. In passages such as ‘dependent on the eye and forms,’ etc., the form-bases collectively are the cause for the arising of eye-consciousness, not separately. To show this meaning, the plural form ‘forms’ is used. Following the same teaching method, here too it is said, ‘and forms, he understands them.’ However, considering the generality inherent in the nature of form, all are taken together and the meaning is stated in the singular as ‘external form derived from the four great elements.’ By way of its essence and characteristic—this should be connected as referring to the function of being the object of eye-consciousness and the characteristic of being subject to impact by the eye.

Ubhayaṃ paṭiccāti cakkhuṃ upanissayapaccayavasena paccayabhūtaṃ, rūpe ārammaṇādhipatiārammaṇūpanissayavasena paccayabhūte ca paṭicca. Kāmañcāyaṃ suttantasaṃvaṇṇanā[M 1.0379], nippariyāyakathā nāma abhidhammasannissitā evāti abhidhammanayeneva saṃyojanāni dassento “kāmarāga…pe… avijjāsaṃyojana”nti āha. Tattha kāmesu rāgo, kāmo ca so rāgo cāti kāmarāgo, so eva bandhanaṭṭhena saṃyojanaṃ. Ayañhi yassa saṃvijjati, taṃ puggalaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃ saṃyojeti bandhati, iti dukkhena sattaṃ, bhavādike vā bhavantarādīhi, kammunā vā vipākaṃ saṃyojeti bandhatīti saṃyojanaṃ. Evaṃ paṭighasaṃyojanādīnampi yathārahaṃ attho vattabbo. Sarasalakkhaṇavasenāti ettha pana sattassa vaṭṭato anissajjanasaṅkhātassa attano kiccassa ceva yathāvuttabandhanasaṅkhātassa lakkhaṇassa ca vasenāti yojetabbaṃ.

'Both are dependent' means the eye is a condition by way of the condition of dependence, and forms are a condition by way of object, dominant object, and object-dependence. And this suttanta commentary, called the direct exposition, is indeed supported by the Abhidhamma. Thus, showing the fetters according to the Abhidhamma method, it states: 'sensual desire... up to... the fetter of ignorance.' Herein, lust for sensual pleasures is 'sensual desire,' and that very lust is called 'sensual-desire fetter' because it is a bond. For this, when it is present in someone, it binds that person to the cycle of existence, fastening beings with suffering, or binds them to future existences, etc., or binds result with kamma—thus it is called a fetter. Similarly, the meaning of the fetter of aversion and others should be stated accordingly. By way of its essence and characteristic—here, this should be connected as referring to its own function, which is called not releasing from the round of existence, and to the characteristic of binding as previously described.

Bhavassāda-diṭṭhissāda-nivattanatthaṃ kāmassādaggahaṇaṃ. Assādayatoti abhiramantassa. Abhinandatoti sapppītikataṇhāvasena nandantassa. Padadvayenapi balavato kāmarāgassa paccayabhūtā kāmarāguppatti vuttā. Esa nayo sesesupi. Etaṃ ārammaṇanti etaṃ evaṃsukhumaṃ evaṃdubbibhāgaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. Niccaṃ dhuvanti etaṃ nidassanamattaṃ, “ucchijjissati vinassissatīti gaṇhato”ti evamādīnampi saṅgaho icchitabbo. Bhavaṃ patthentassāti “īdise sampattibhave yasmā amhākaṃ idaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ sulabhaṃ jātaṃ, tasmā āyatimpi sampattibhavo bhaveyyā”ti [V 1.0339] bhavaṃ nikāmentassa. Evarūpaṃ sakkā laddhunti yojanā. Usūyatoti usūyaṃ issaṃ uppādayato. Aññassa maccharāyatoti aññena asādhāraṇabhāvakaraṇena macchariyaṃ karoto. Sabbeheva yathāvuttehi navahi saṃyojanehi.

The delight in sensual pleasures is taken (as an example) for the purpose of abandoning the delight in existence and the delight in views. One who savors it is one who delights. One who relishes it is one who delights by way of craving accompanied by joy. Through these two terms, the arising of sensual desire, which is a condition for strong sensual desire, is stated. The same method applies to the rest. This object—so subtle, so hard to distinguish—is the object. Permanent, stable—this is merely an indication; the inclusion of things such as 'one who grasps, thinking, 'It will be cut off, it will perish,'' and so on, should also be understood as desired. For one who longs for existence, thinking, 'Because in such a fortunate existence, this desirable object has become easily attainable for us, therefore, may a fortunate existence occur in the future too,' this is the meaning. The connection is that such a thing can indeed be obtained. Being envious—this refers to one who produces envy and jealousy. Being stingy toward others—this refers to one who acts with stinginess by making something unshared with others. All these are by means of the nine fetters as previously stated.

Tañca kāraṇanti subhanimittapaṭighanimittādivibhāvaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhādirūpārammaṇañceva tajjāyonisomanasikārañcāti tassa tassa saṃyojanassa kāraṇaṃ. Avikkhambhitaasamūhatabhūmiladdhuppannataṃ sandhāya “appahīnaṭṭhena uppannassā”ti vuttaṃ. Vattamānuppannatā samudācāraggahaṇeneva gahitā. Yena kāraṇenāti yena vipassanāsamathabhāvanāsaṅkhātena kāraṇena. Tañhi tassa tadaṅgavasena ceva vikkhambhanavasena ca pahānakāraṇaṃ. Issāmacchariyānaṃ apāyagamanīyatāya paṭhamamaggavajjhatā vuttā. Yadi evaṃ “tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno hotī”ti (a. ni. 4.241) suttapadaṃ [M 1.0380] kathanti? Taṃ suttantapariyāyena vuttaṃ. Yathānulomasāsanañhi suttantadesanā, ayaṃ pana abhidhammanayena saṃvaṇṇanāti nāyaṃ doso. Oḷārikassāti thūlassa, yato abhiṇhasamuppattipariyuṭṭhānatibbatāva hoti. Aṇusahagatassāti vuttappakāraoḷārikābhāvena aṇubhāvaṃ sukhumabhāvaṃ gatassa. Uddhaccasaṃyojanassapettha anuppādo vuttoyeva yathāvuttasaṃyojanehi avinābhāvato. Sotādīnaṃ sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena pajānanā, tappaccayānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ uppādādipajānanā ca vuttanayeneva veditabbāti dassento “eseva nayo”ti atidisati.

And that cause: the distinction between the sign of the beautiful and the sign of aversion, etc., and the desirable and undesirable form-object, etc., along with the unwise attention associated with them—this is the cause for each fetter. 'It is arisen in the sense of not being abandoned' is said with reference to its arising having attained a state of not being suppressed or uprooted. The presently arisen state is understood by the very inclusion of its manifestation. 'By which cause': by the cause consisting of the development of insight and serenity. For that is the means of abandoning it both by way of substitution of opposites and by way of suppression. The states of envy and avarice are said to be overcome by the first path because they lead to states of woe. If so, how is the sutta passage 'With the destruction of three fetters, one becomes a stream-enterer' (AN 4.241) to be explained? That is stated by way of the suttanta method. For the suttanta teaching is a teaching that proceeds in sequence, whereas this is an exposition according to the Abhidhamma method—thus, there is no fault here. 'Of the gross': of what is coarse, because there is frequent arising and intense obsession. 'Associated with the subtle': gone to subtlety, to a refined state, by the absence of grossness of the kind described. Here, the non-arising of the fetter of restlessness is also stated, since it is inseparable from the fetters mentioned above. To show that the understanding of the ear, etc., by way of their intrinsic nature, essence, and characteristic, and the understanding of the arising, etc., of the fetters dependent on them, should be understood in the manner already stated, he indicates by extension: 'This is the method.'

Attano vā dhammesūti attano ajjhattikāyatanadhammesu, attano ubhayadhammesu vā. Imasmiṃ pakkhe ajjhattikāyatanapariggahaṇenāti ajjhattikāyatanapariggaṇhanamukhenāti attho, evañca anavasesato saparasantānesu āyatanānaṃ pariggaho siddho hoti. Parassa vā dhammesūti etthāpi eseva nayo. Rūpāyatanassāti aḍḍhekādasapabhedarūpasabhāvassa āyatanassa. Rūpakkhandhe vuttanayena nīharitabbāti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Sesakhandhesūti vedanāsaññāsaṅkhārakkhandhesu. Vuttanayenāti iminā atidesena rūpakkhandhe āhārasamudayāti, viññāṇakkhandhe nāmarūpasamudayāti, sesakkhandhesu phassasamudayāti imaṃ visesaṃ vibhāveti, itaraṃ pana sabbattha samānanti. Khandhapabbe viya āyatanapabbepi lokuttaranivattanaṃ pāḷiyaṃ gahitaṃ natthīti āha “lokuttaradhammā na gahetabbā”ti.

In one's own phenomena (attano vā dhammesu): in one's own internal sense-base phenomena, or in both kinds of one's own phenomena. In this case, 'by grasping the internal sense bases' means by way of grasping the internal sense bases. Thus, the complete grasping of the sense bases, including those in the continua of others, is accomplished. As for 'in another's phenomena,' the same method applies here too. The form sense base: the nature of the form sense base, which has ten and a half divisions. It should be extracted and connected in the manner stated in the form aggregate. In the remaining aggregates: in the aggregates of feeling, perception, and volitional formations. By 'in the stated manner,' this analogy distinguishes this specific point: for the form aggregate, nutriment is the arising; for the consciousness aggregate, name-and-form is the arising; and for the remaining aggregates, contact is the arising—while the rest is the same everywhere. Just as in the section on aggregates, so too in the section on sense bases, the supramundane is not included in the Pāḷi text. Hence, it is said, 'Supramundane phenomena should not be taken.'

Āyatanapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on the sense bases is concluded.

Bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on the Factors of Enlightenment

118. Bujjhanakasattassāti [V 1.0340] kilesaniddāya paṭibujjhanakasattassa, ariyasaccānaṃ vā paṭivijjhanakasattassa. Aṅgesūti kāraṇesu, avayavesu vā. Udayabbayañāṇuppādato paṭṭhāya sambodhipaṭipadāyaṃ ṭhito nāma hotīti āha “āraddhavipassakato paṭṭhāya yogāvacaroti sambodhī”ti.

118. 'Of a being who awakens' (bujjhanakasattassa) means of a being who awakens from the sleep of defilements, or of a being who penetrates the noble truths. 'In the factors' (aṅgesu) means in the causes, or in the constituents. He is said to be established on the path to full enlightenment from the arising of the knowledge of arising and passing away. Thus, it is said, '“Full enlightenment” refers to the meditator, from the one who has initiated insight onwards.'

“Satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā”ti [M 1.0381] padassa attho “vicikicchaṭṭhānīyā”ti ettha vuttanayena veditabbo. Tanti yonisomanasikāraṃ. Tatthāti satiyaṃ. Nipphādetabbe cetaṃ bhummaṃ.

The meaning of the phrase 'what is the basis for the mindfulness enlightenment factor' should be understood in the manner stated here regarding 'what is the basis for doubt.' That, indeed, is wise attention. 'There' means in mindfulness. And this is a locative case referring to that which is to be accomplished.

Sati ca sampajaññañca satisampajaññaṃ (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.385; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.5.232; a. ni. ṭī. 1.1.418). Atha vā satipadhānaṃ abhikkantādisātthakabhāvapariggaṇhanañāṇaṃ satisampajaññaṃ. Taṃ sabbattha satokāribhāvāvahattā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya hoti. Yathā paccanīkadhammānaṃ pahānaṃ anurūpadhammasevanā ca anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya hoti, evaṃ satirahitapuggalavivajjhanā, satokārīpuggalasevanā, tattha ca yuttapayuttatā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya hotīti imamatthaṃ dasseti “satisampajañña”ntiādinā.

Mindfulness and clear comprehension (satisampajañña) is mindfulness and clear comprehension. Alternatively, mindfulness and clear comprehension is the knowledge that grasps the state of having purpose, such as going forward, with mindfulness as its foundation. Because it brings about the state of acting mindfully everywhere, it is conducive to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor. Just as the abandoning of opposing qualities and the cultivation of appropriate qualities lead to the arising of unarisen wholesome states, so too avoiding individuals devoid of mindfulness, associating with individuals who act mindfully, and being suitably engaged therein, are conducive to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor. This meaning is shown by 'mindfulness and clear comprehension' and so on.

Dhammānaṃ, dhammesu vā vicayo dhammavicayo, so eva sambojjhaṅgo, tassa dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa. “Kusalākusalā dhammā”tiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāroti kusalādīsu taṃtaṃsabhāvarasalakkhaṇādikassa yāthāvato avabujjhanavasena uppanno ñāṇasampayuttacittuppādo. So hi aviparītamanasikāratāya “yonisomanasikāro”ti vutto, tadābhogatāya āvajjanāpi taggatikāva, tassa abhiṇhapavattanaṃ bahulīkāro. Bhiyyobhāvāyāti punappunabhāvāya. Vepullāyāti vipulabhāvāya. Pāripūriyāti paribrūhanāya.

The investigation of phenomena, or among phenomena, is the investigation of phenomena (dhammavicayo); that itself is an enlightenment factor, of that enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena. What should be said regarding 'wholesome and unwholesome phenomena' and so on, has already been stated below. There, 'frequent wise attention' (yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro) is the arising of a consciousness-moment associated with knowledge, through understanding as it actually is the individual nature, function, characteristics, etc., of each of the wholesome and unwholesome phenomena. That, being unperverted attention, is called 'wise attention'; the initial attending, due to its engagement with that, is also of the same nature; the repeated occurrence of that is 'frequent practice.' 'For increase' (bhiyyobhāvāya) means for repeated occurrence. 'For abundance' (vepullāya) means for an abundant state. 'For completion' (pāripūriyā) means for full development.

Paripucchakatāti pariyogāhetvā pucchakabhāvo. Ācariye payirupāsitvā pañcapi nikāye saha aṭṭhakathāya pariyogāhetvā yaṃ yaṃ tattha gaṇṭhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ, taṃ taṃ “idaṃ bhante kathaṃ, imassa ko attho”ti khandhāyatanādiatthaṃ pucchantassa dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo uppajjati. Tenāha “khandhadhātu…pe… bahulatā”ti.

'Being inquisitive' (paripucchakatā) means the state of being a questioner, having thoroughly investigated. Having attended upon a teacher and thoroughly investigated the five Nikāyas together with their commentaries, when one asks, 'Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?' regarding whatever points are knot-like there, such as the meaning of the aggregates, sense bases, and so on, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena arises. Therefore, it is said, 'the aggregates, elements… frequent practice.'

Vatthuvisadakiriyāti [V 1.0341] ettha cittacetasikānaṃ pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato sarīraṃ, tappaṭibaddhāni cīvarādīni ca idha “vatthūnī”ti adhippetāni. Tāni yathā cittassa sukhāvahāni honti, tathā karaṇaṃ tesaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “ajjhattikabāhirāna”ntiādi. Ussannadosanti vātādiussannadosaṃ. Sedamalamakkhitanti sedena ceva jallikāsaṅkhātena sarīramalena [M 1.0382] ca makkhitaṃ. Ca-saddena aññampi sarīrassa pīḷāvahaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Senāsanaṃ vāti vā-saddena pattādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Avisade sati, visayabhūte vā. Kathaṃ bhāvanamanuyuttassa tāni visayo? Antarantarā pavattanakacittuppādavasenevaṃ vuttaṃ. Te hi cittuppādā cittekaggatāya aparisuddhabhāvāya saṃvattanti. Cittacetasikesu nissayādipaccayabhūtesu. Ñāṇampīti pi-saddo sampiṇḍanattho. Tena na kevalaṃ taṃ vatthuyeva, atha kho tasmiṃ aparisuddhe ñāṇampi aparisuddhaṃ hotīti nissayāparisuddhiyā taṃnissitāparisuddhi viya visayassa aparisuddhatāya visayīnaṃ aparisuddhiṃ dasseti.

'Purification of the base' (vatthuvisadakiriyā): here, the body, being the place of occurrence for mind and mental factors, and robes and so on connected to it, are intended as 'bases.' Making them such that they are conducive to the mind's well-being is the purification of their clarity. Therefore, it is said, 'internal and external,' and so on. 'Excessive humors' (ussannadosaṃ) refers to excessive wind, etc. 'Smeared with sweat and dirt' (sedamalamakkhitaṃ) means smeared with sweat and the bodily impurity called 'jallikā.' The word 'and' (ca-saddena) also includes other bodily afflictions. 'Or lodging' (senāsanaṃ vā): the word 'or' (vā-saddena) should be understood to include bowls, etc. When it is impure, or when it has become an object. How are they objects for one devoted to meditation? It is said thus by way of the intermittent arising of consciousness-moments. For those consciousness-moments lead to the impurity of the mind's one-pointedness. In mind and mental factors, which are conditions such as support, 'and knowledge too' (ñāṇampi): the word 'too' (pi-saddo) has the meaning of inclusion. Thus, it shows that not only is that base impure, but when it is impure, knowledge also becomes impure; just as the impurity of a support leads to the impurity of what depends on it, so the impurity of the object leads to the impurity of the subject.

Samabhāvakaraṇanti kiccato anūnādhikabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Yathāpaccayaṃ saddheyyavatthusmiṃ adhimokkhakiccassa paṭutarabhāvena paññāya avisadatāya vīriyādīnañca sithilatādinā saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti. Tenāha “itarāni mandānī”ti. Tatoti tasmā saddhindriyassa balavabhāvato itaresañca mandattā. Kosajjapakkhe patituṃ adatvā sampayuttadhammānaṃ paggaṇhanaṃ anubalappadānaṃ paggaho, paggahova kiccaṃ paggahakiccaṃ. “Kātuṃ na sakkotī”ti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Ārammaṇaṃ upagantvā ṭhānaṃ, anissajjanaṃ vā upaṭṭhānaṃ. Vikkhepapaṭipakkho, yena vā sampayuttā avikkhittā honti, so avikkhepo. Rūpagataṃ viya cakkhunā yena yāthāvato visayasabhāvaṃ passati, taṃ dassanakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti balavatā saddhindriyena abhibhūtattā. Sahajātadhammesu indaṭṭhaṃ kārentānaṃ sahapavattamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ ekarasatāvaseneva atthasiddhi, na aññathā.

'Making balanced' (samabhāvakaraṇaṃ) means making them neither deficient nor excessive in function. For example, with regard to an object worthy of faith, due to the greater keenness of the function of conviction, the lack of clarity of wisdom, and the sluggishness and so on of energy and other factors, the faculty of faith becomes strong. Hence it is said, 'The others are weak.' Therefore, from the strength of the faculty of faith and the weakness of the others, exertion (paggaho), which is the strengthening and supporting of associated phenomena without yielding to the side of laziness, is the function of exertion (paggahakiccaṃ). 'Unable to perform' (kātuṃ na sakkoti) should be connected by bringing this in. Approaching and establishing the object, or not abandoning it, is presence (upaṭṭhānaṃ). It is the opposite of distraction, or that non-distraction (avikkhepo) by which associated phenomena are undistracted. That [wisdom], by which one sees the true nature of an object as it is—like the eye with a form—is unable to perform the function of seeing because it is overpowered by the strong faculty of faith. Among co-arisen phenomena, the goal is accomplished for those functioning as faculties only through the co-arising phenomena having a single taste, and not otherwise.

Tasmāti vuttamevatthaṃ kāraṇabhāvena paccāmasati. Tanti saddhindriyaṃ. Dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇenāti yassa saddheyyavatthuno uḷāratādiguṇe adhimuccanassa sātisayappavattiyā saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ jātaṃ, tassa paccayapaccayuppannatādivibhāgato yāthāvato vīmaṃsanena. Evañhi evaṃdhammatānayena sabhāvasarasato pariggayhamāne savipphāro adhimokkho na hoti “ayaṃ imesaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvo”ti parijānanavasena paññābyāpārassa sātisayattā. Dhuriyadhammesu hi yathā saddhāya balavabhāve paññāya mandabhāvo hoti, evaṃ paññāya balavabhāve saddhāya mandabhāvo hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “taṃ dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena…pe… hāpetabba”nti. Tathā [V 1.0342] amanasikārenāti yenākārena bhāvanamanuyuñjantassa saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ [M 1.0383] jātaṃ, tenākārena bhāvanāya ananuyuñjanatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Idha duvidhena saddhindriyassa balavabhāvo attano vā paccayavisesavasena kiccuttariyato vīriyādīnaṃ vā mandakiccatāya. Tattha paṭhamavikappe hāpanavidhi dassito, dutiyavikappe pana yathā manasikaroto vīriyādīnaṃ mandakiccatāya saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ jātaṃ, tathā amanasikārena, vīriyādīnaṃ paṭukiccabhāvāvahena manasikārena saddhindriyaṃ tehi samarasaṃ karontena hāpetabbaṃ. Iminā nayena sesindriyesupi hāpanavidhi veditabbo.

'Therefore' (tasmā) refers back to the meaning already stated as the reason. That (taṃ) is the faculty of faith. 'By examining the nature of phenomena' (dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena): by investigating as they really are, through distinguishing conditions and what arises conditionally, etc., that object worthy of faith in which the faculty of faith has become strong due to an especially heightened inclination towards its qualities of excellence. For when, in this way, the intrinsic nature is grasped through the method of 'such-is-the-nature,' there is no intense conviction, because the function of wisdom becomes excessive in fully comprehending, through the way of knowing definitively, 'This is the nature of these phenomena.' For in the principal phenomena, just as when faith is strong, wisdom is weak, so too when wisdom is strong, faith is weak. Hence it is said, 'That should be diminished by examining the nature of phenomena…' Similarly, 'by inattention' (amanasikārena): it is said that one should not apply oneself to meditation in the way that makes the faculty of faith strong. Here, the strength of the faculty of faith arises in two ways: either through its own particular conditions by way of superior function, or through the diminished function of energy and the others. In the first alternative, the method of diminishing has been shown. In the second alternative, just as the faculty of faith becomes strong due to the diminished function of energy and the others when one attends in a certain way, so too by inattention—that is, by attending in a way that brings about the keen function of energy and the others—one should diminish the faculty of faith by making it balanced with them. In this way, the method of diminishing should be understood for the remaining faculties as well.

Vakkalittheravatthūti so hi āyasmā saddhādhimuttāya katādhikāro satthu rūpakāyadassanapasuto eva hutvā viharanto satthārā “kiṃ te, vakkali, iminā pūtikāyena diṭṭhena, yo kho, vakkali, dhammaṃ passati, so maṃ passatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 3.87) ovaditvā kammaṭṭhāne niyojitopi taṃ ananuyuñjanto paṇāmito attānaṃ vinipātetuṃ papātaṭṭhānaṃ abhiruhi. Atha naṃ satthā yathānisinnova obhāsagissajjanena atthānaṃ dassetvā –

'The story of Venerable Vakkali' (Vakkalittheravatthu): That Venerable One, having made a resolution with faith as his dominant faculty, remained devoted to seeing the Teacher's physical form. The Teacher admonished him, saying, 'What is it to you, Vakkali, to see this putrid body? Whoever sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, sees me,' and so on (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.87). Though he was assigned a meditation subject, he did not apply himself to it and, having been dismissed, climbed a precipice to throw himself down. Then the Teacher, while remaining seated where he was, showed himself by emitting a ray of light and spoke thus:

“Pāmojjabahulo bhikkhu, pasanno buddhasāsane;

Adhigacche padaṃ santaṃ, saṅkhārūpasamaṃ sukha”nti. (dha. pa. 381);

The monk replete with joy, confident in the Buddha's Dispensation, may attain the peaceful state, the bliss of the stilling of formations.

Gāthaṃ vatvā “ehivakkalī”ti āha. So tena amateneva abhisitto haṭṭhatuṭṭho hutvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapesi, saddhāya pana balavabhāvato vipassanāvīthiṃ na otarati. Taṃ ñatvā bhagavā tassa indriyasamattapaṭipādanāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ sodhetvā adāsi. So satthārā dinnanayena vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ “vakkalittheravatthu cettha nidassana”nti.

Having recited the verse, he said, "Come, Vakkali." Then, being anointed as if with that deathless nectar, he became joyful and delighted, and he began insight meditation. However, because his faith was too strong, he did not enter the path of insight. Knowing this, the Blessed One purified his meditation subject and gave it to him for the sake of balancing his faculties. Following the method given by the Teacher, he diligently cultivated insight and attained arahantship in due course. Therefore, it is said, "Here, the story of Venerable Vakkali serves as an illustration."

Itarakiccabhedanti upaṭṭhānādikiccavisesaṃ. Passaddhādīti ādi-saddena samādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgānaṃ saṅgaho.
