Hāpetabbanti yathā saddhindriyassa balavabhāvo dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena hāyati, evaṃ vīriyindriyassa adhimattatā passaddhiādibhāvanāya hāyati samādhipakkhiyattā tassā. Tathāhi sā samādhindriyassa adhimattataṃ kosajjapātato rakkhantī vīriyādibhāvanā viya vīriyindriyassa adhimattataṃ uddhaccapātato rakkhantī ekaṃsato [M 1.0384] hāpeti. Tena vuttaṃ “passaddhādibhāvanāya hāpetabba”nti. Soṇattherassa vatthūti sukhumālasoṇattherassa [V 1.0343] vatthu. So hi āyasmā, satthu, santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā sītavane viharanto “mama sarīraṃ sukhumālaṃ, na ca sakkā sukheneva sukhaṃ adhigantuṃ, kāyaṃ kilametvāpi samaṇadhammo kātabbo”ti ṭhānacaṅkamameva adhiṭṭhāya padhānamanuyuñjanto pādatalesu phoṭesu uṭṭhitesupi vedanaṃ ajjhupekkhitvā daḷhavīriyaṃ karonto accāraddhavīriyatāya visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Satthā tattha gantvā vīṇūpamovādena ovaditvā vīriyasamatāyojanavidhiṃ dassento kammaṭṭhānaṃ sodhetvā gijjhakūṭaṃ gato. Theropi satthārā dinnanayena vīriyasamataṃ yojetvā bhāvento vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “soṇattherassa vatthu dassetabba”nti. Sesesupīti satisamādhipaññindriyesupi.

The differentiation of other functions refers to specific functions such as attending, etc. By 'tranquility, etc.', the word 'etc.' includes the enlightenment factors of concentration and equanimity. 'It should be diminished' means that just as the excessive strength of the faculty of faith diminishes through reflection on the nature of phenomena, so too does the excessive intensity of the faculty of energy diminish through the development of tranquility, etc., because the latter belongs to the side of concentration. For indeed, just as the development of energy, etc., protects the excessive intensity of the faculty of concentration from falling into sloth, so too does the development of tranquility, etc., protect the excessive intensity of the faculty of energy from falling into restlessness, and thus it certainly diminishes it. Therefore, it is said, "It should be diminished through the development of tranquility, etc." The story of Venerable Soṇa refers to the story of Venerable Soṇa the Delicate. For that venerable one, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, dwelt in the Cool Grove, thinking, "My body is delicate, and it is not possible to attain happiness easily. Even if I exhaust my body, the ascetic duty must be performed." Resolving to practice walking and standing meditation exclusively, he exerted himself diligently, enduring the pain that arose in the soles of his feet (even when blisters arose), but due to excessive energy, he could not achieve distinction. The Teacher went there and advised him with the simile of the lute, showing the method of balancing energy, purified the meditation subject, and returned to Vulture Peak. The elder, following the method given by the Teacher, balanced his energy, cultivated insight, and became established in arahantship. Therefore, it is said, "The story of Venerable Soṇa should be shown." In the remaining cases as well refers to the faculties of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

Samatanti saddhāpaññānaṃ aññamaññaṃ anūnānadhikabhāvaṃ, tathā samādhivīriyānaṃ. Yathā hi saddhāpaññānaṃ visuṃ visuṃ dhuriyadhammabhūtānaṃ kiccato aññamaññānātivattanaṃ visesato icchitabbaṃ, yato nesaṃ samadhuratāya appanā sampajjati, evaṃ samādhivīriyānaṃ kosajjuddhaccapakkhikānaṃ samarasatāya sati aññamaññūpatthambhanato sampayuttadhammānaṃ antadvayapātābhāvena sammadeva appanā ijjhatīti. Balavasaddhotiādi vuttassevatthassa byatirekamukhena samatthanaṃ. Tassattho – yo balavatiyā saddhāya samannāgato avisadañāṇo, so mudhāpasanno hoti, na aveccappasanno. Tathā hi so avatthusmiṃ pasīdati seyyathāpi titthiyasāvakā. Kerāṭikapakkhanti sāṭheyyapakkhaṃ bhajati. Saddhāhīnāya paññāya atidhāvanto “deyyavatthupariccāgena vinā cittuppādamattenapi dānamayaṃ puññaṃ hotī”tiādīni parikappeti hetupatirūpakehi vañcito, evaṃbhūto ca sukkhatakkaviluttacitto paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ nādiyati, saññattiṃ na gacchati. Tenāha “bhesajjasamuṭṭhito viya rogo atekiccho hotī”ti. Yathā cettha saddhāpaññānaṃ aññamaññaṃ samabhāvo atthāvaho, anatthāvaho visamabhāvo, evaṃ samādhivīriyānaṃ aññamaññaṃ avikkhepāvaho samabhāvo, itaro vikkhepāvaho cāti. Kosajjaṃ adhibhavati, tena appanaṃ na pāpuṇātīti adhippāyo[M 1.0385]. Uddhaccaṃ adhibhavatīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tadubhayanti saddhāpaññādvayaṃ samādhivīriyadvayañca. Samaṃ kātabbanti samarasaṃ kātabbaṃ.

Balance means that faith and wisdom are neither deficient nor excessive in relation to each other, and the same applies to concentration and energy. Just as faith and wisdom, though distinct in their functions as leading qualities, should especially not surpass each other in their respective roles—since their equilibrium leads to absorption—so too with concentration and energy. When they are harmonious, counteracting sloth and restlessness respectively, their mutual support ensures that the associated states are not vulnerable to either extreme, thus enabling proper absorption. The phrase 'one with strong faith' and so on is a confirmation of the stated meaning by way of negation. Its meaning is this: One endowed with excessive faith but lacking clear understanding becomes blindly devoted, not truly confident. Such a person places faith in unworthy things, like the disciples of heretical teachers. He follows the path of deceit. On the other hand, one who races ahead with wisdom but lacks faith speculates, thinking, "Meritorious giving arises merely from the intention to give, even without offering material things," and so on. Deceived by false reasoning, such a person, dry and barren in intellect, does not accept the words of the wise and remains unconvinced. Hence it is said, "Like a disease caused by medicine, it becomes incurable." Just as the balance between faith and wisdom brings benefit while imbalance brings harm, so too the balance between concentration and energy prevents distraction, whereas imbalance causes it. Sloth overpowers, and thus absorption is not attained—this is the meaning. Restlessness overpowers—here too, the same principle applies. 'Both' refers to the pairs of faith and wisdom, and concentration and energy. 'They should be made equal'—that is, they should be harmonized.

Samādhikammikassāti samathakammaṭṭhānikassa. Evanti evaṃ sante, saddhāya thokaṃ balavabhāve satīti attho. Saddahantoti “pathavīti manasikāramattena kathaṃ jhānuppattī”ti acintetvā “addhā sammāsambuddhena vuttavidhi ijjhissatī”ti saddahanto saddhaṃ janento. Okappentoti ārammaṇaṃ anupavisitvā viya adhimuccanavasena avakappento pakkhandanto. Ekaggatā balavatī vaṭṭati samādhippadhānattā jhānassa. Ubhinnanti samādhipaññānaṃ. Samādhikammikassa samādhino adhimattatāya [V 1.0344] paññāya adhimattatāpi icchitabbāti āha “samatāyapī”ti, samabhāvenapīti attho. Appanāti lokiyaappanā. Tathā hi “hotiyevā”ti sāsaṅkaṃ vadati. Lokuttarappanā pana tesaṃ samabhāveneva icchitā. Yathāha “samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ bhāvetī”ti (a. ni. 4.17; paṭi. ma. 2.5). Yadi visesato saddhāpaññānaṃ samādhivīriyānañca samatā icchitā, kathaṃ satīti āha “sati pana sabbattha balavatī vaṭṭatī”ti. Sabbatthāti līnuddhaccapakkhikesu pañcasu indriyesu. Uddhaccapakkhikekadese gaṇhanto “saddhāvīriyapaññāna”nti āha. Aññathā pīti ca gahetabbā siyā. Tathā hi “kosajjapakkhikena samādhinā”icceva vuttaṃ, na “passaddhisamādhiupekkhāhī”ti. Sāti sati. Sabbesu rājakammesu niyutto sabbakammiko. Tenāti tenā sabbattha icchitabbatthena kāraṇena. Āha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Sabbattha niyuttā sabbatthikā, sabbena vā līnuddhaccapakkhiyena bojjhaṅgena atthetabbā sabbatthiyā, sabbatthiyāva sabbatthikā. Cittanti kusalacittaṃ. Tassa hi sati paṭisaraṇaṃ parāyaṇaṃ appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya. Tenāha “ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā”tiādi.

'One devoted to concentration work' means one who practices serenity meditation. 'Thus' (evaṃ) means, in this case, that faith is slightly stronger. 'One who believes' (saddahanto) means one who, without pondering, "How can absorption arise merely by attending to 'earth'?" instead generates faith, believing, "Surely, the method taught by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One will succeed." 'One who trusts' (okappento) means one who, as if entering the object, resolves upon it and advances with confidence by way of determination. One-pointedness should be strong, due to concentration being predominant in jhāna. 'Of both' refers to concentration and wisdom. For one devoted to concentration work, because concentration is predominant, the predominance of wisdom should also be desired—thus it is said, "even in balance," meaning in equal measure. 'Absorption' refers to mundane absorption. Indeed, the statement "there certainly is" is made with reservation. However, supramundane absorption is desired for them only in equal measure, as it is said: "He develops serenity and insight yoked together." If special emphasis is placed on the balance of faith and wisdom, as well as concentration and energy, how is it with mindfulness? It is said: "But mindfulness should be strong and prevail everywhere." 'Everywhere' refers to the five faculties inclined toward sloth and restlessness. Taking a portion of those inclined toward restlessness, it is said: "of faith, energy, and wisdom." Otherwise, joy could also be included. For it is said: "with concentration inclined toward sloth," but not "with tranquility, concentration, and equanimity." 'That' refers to mindfulness. 'Engaged in all the king's duties' means one who performs all tasks. 'Therefore' means for that reason, because it is desired everywhere. The commentary states: 'Needed everywhere' (sabbatthikā) means engaged everywhere. Or, she is 'sought for everywhere' (sabbatthiyā) because she is to be sought for with every awakening factor pertaining to the side of sloth and restlessness; and 'sought for everywhere' is indeed 'needed everywhere' (sabbatthikā). 'The mind' refers to the wholesome mind. For it, mindfulness is the refuge, the ultimate resort—for attaining the unattained and realizing the unrealized. Therefore, it is said: "Its characteristic is guarding," and so on.

Khandhādibhede anogāḷhapaññānanti pariyattibāhusaccavasenapi khandhāyatanādīsu appatiṭṭhitabuddhīnaṃ. Bahussutasevanā hi sutamayañāṇāvahā. Taruṇavipassanāsamaṅgīpi bhāvanāmayañāṇe ṭhitattā ekaṃsato paññavā eva [M 1.0386] nāma hotīti āha “samapaññāsa…pe… puggalasevanā”ti. Ñeyyadhammassa gambhīrabhāvavasena tapparicchedakañāṇassa gambhīrabhāvaggahaṇanti āha “gambhīresu khandhādīsu pavattāya gambhīrapaññāyā”ti. Tañhi ñeyyaṃ tādisāya paññāya caritabbato gambhīrañāṇacariyaṃ, tassā vā paññāya tattha pabhedato pavatti gambhīrañāṇacariyā, tassā paccavekkhaṇāti āha “gambhīrapaññāya pabhedapaccavekkhaṇā”ti. Yathā sativepullappatto nāma arahā eva, evaṃ so eva paññāvepullappattopīti āha “arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hotī”ti. Vīriyādīsupi eseva nayo.

'Wisdom not deeply immersed in the analysis of aggregates, etc.' means those whose understanding is not firmly established regarding the aggregates, sense bases, etc., even by way of extensive textual knowledge. For associating with the very learned brings about knowledge born of study. Even one endowed with newly arisen insight, being established in knowledge born of development, is indeed certainly called 'wise'—thus it is said, "equal in wisdom... association with persons." Due to the profound nature of what is to be known, the grasp of knowledge that discerns it is also profound—thus it is said, "by profound wisdom operating in the profound aggregates, etc." For that object of knowledge should be engaged with by such wisdom, hence it is the practice of profound knowledge; or, the arising or activity of that wisdom in differentiation therein is the practice of profound knowledge; the reflection on that is what is meant by "detailed examination by profound wisdom." Just as an arahant is called one who has attained the fullness of mindfulness, so too is that one who has attained the fullness of wisdom—thus it is said, "fulfillment of development is achieved through the path of arahantship." The same principle applies to energy, etc.

“Tattaṃ ayokhilaṃ hatthe gamentī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.250, 267; a. ni. 3.36) pañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇaṃ niraye nibbattasattassa yebhuyyena sabbapaṭhamaṃ karontīti devadūtasuttādīsu tassā ādito vuttattā ca āha “pañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇato paṭṭhāyā”ti. Sakaṭavāhanādikāleti ādi-saddena tadaññaṃ manussehi tiracchānehi ca vibādhiyamānakālaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Ekaṃ buddhantaranti idaṃ aparāparaṃ petesuyeva uppajjanakasattavasena vuttaṃ, ekaccānaṃ vā [V 1.0345] petānaṃ ekaccatiracchānānaṃ viya tathā dīghāyukabhāvato. Tathā hi kāḷo nāgarājā catunnaṃ buddhānaṃ adhigatarūpadassano.

'Carrying a red-hot iron stake in the hand,' and so on—this fivefold binding punishment is generally the first inflicted on beings born in hell, as mentioned in the Devadūta Sutta and others, because it is stated from the beginning. Hence, it is said, "beginning with the fivefold binding punishment." The phrase 'at the time of cart-pulling and so on' includes, with the word 'etc.', other times when beings are oppressed by humans and animals. 'One buddha-interval'—this refers to the repeated arising of beings as hungry ghosts, or to some hungry ghosts and some animals who have such long lifespans. For example, the Nāga King Kāḷa had seen the forms of four Buddhas.

Evaṃ ānisaṃsadassāvinoti vīriyāyatto eva sabbo lokuttaro lokiyo ca visesādhigamoti evaṃ vīriye ānisaṃsadassanasīlassa. Gamanavīthinti sapubbabhāgaṃ nibbānagāminiṃ ariyamaggapaṭipadaṃ. Sā hi bhikkhuno vaṭṭanissaraṇāya gantabbā paṭipajjitabbā paṭipadāti katvā gamanavīthi nāma. Kāyadaḷhībahuloti yathā tathā kāyassa daḷhīkammapasuto. Piṇḍanti raṭṭhapiṇḍaṃ. Paccayadāyakānaṃ attani kārassa attano sammāpaṭipattiyā mahapphalabhāvassa karaṇena piṇḍassa bhikkhāya paṭipūjanā piṇḍāpacāyanaṃ.

Thus, 'seeing the benefits' means that all mundane and supramundane distinctions are attained solely by relying on energy; thus, one is accustomed to seeing the benefit in energy. The 'path of progress' is the practice of the Noble Path leading to Nibbāna, together with its preliminary parts. For it is a path that a bhikkhu must travel and practice in order to escape the round of existence; therefore, it is called the 'path of progress'. 'Firm in body' means constantly engaged in the work of strengthening the body in every way. 'Almsfood' means the alms of the country. Honoring almsfood (piṇḍāpacāyanaṃ) means venerating the almsfood by making the donors' offering to oneself bear great fruit through one's own right practice.

Nīharantoti pattatthavikato nīharanto. Taṃ saddaṃ sutvāti taṃ upāsikāya vacanaṃ paṇṇasāladvāre ṭhitova pañcābhiññatāya dibbasotena sutvā. Manussasampatti dibbasampatti ante nibbānasampattīti tisso sampattiyo[M 1.0387]. Dātuṃ sakkhissasīti “tayi katena dānamayena veyyāvaccamayena ca puññakammena khettavisesabhāvūpagamanena aparāparaṃ devamanussasampattiyo ante nibbānasampattiñca dātuṃ sakkhissasī”ti thero attānaṃ pucchati. Sitaṃ karontovāti “akiccheneva mayā vaṭṭadukkhaṃ samatikkanta”nti paccavekkhaṇāvasāne sañjātapāmojjavasena sitaṃ karonto eva.

'Taking out' means taking it out from the bowl-bag. 'Having heard that sound' means hearing the laywoman’s words with his divine ear, by means of the five higher knowledges, while standing at the door of the leaf-hut. Human attainment, divine attainment, and ultimately the attainment of Nibbāna—these are the three attainments. 'You will be able to give'—the elder asks himself, 'Will you be able to give successive human and divine attainments, and ultimately the attainment of Nibbāna, through the meritorious deeds of generosity and service done towards you, by becoming a special field of merit?' 'Smiling' means smiling at the end of his reflection, 'I have crossed over the suffering of the round with little effort,' due to the joy that arose.

Vippaṭipannanti jātidhammakuladhammādilaṅghanena asammāpaṭipannaṃ. Evaṃ yathā asammāpaṭipanno putto tāya eva asammāpaṭipattiyā kulasantānato bāhiro hutvā pitu santikā dāyajjassa na bhāgī, evaṃ kusītopi teneva kusītabhāvena asammāpaṭipanno satthu santikā laddhabbaariyadhanadāyajjassa na bhāgī. Āraddhavīriyova labhati sammāpaṭipajjanato. Uppajjati vīriyasambojjhaṅgoti yojanā. Evaṃ sabbattha.

'Gone astray' means one who has wrongly conducted himself by transgressing the laws of birth, family customs, and so on. Just as a son who has wrongly conducted himself in this way, due to that very wrong conduct, becomes an outsider to the family lineage and thus has no share in his father's inheritance, so too the lazy one, due to that very laziness and wrong conduct, has no share in the inheritance of noble wealth to be gained from the Teacher. Only one with aroused energy gains it by practicing rightly. The enlightenment factor of energy arises—this is the connection. Thus it is everywhere.

Mahāti sīlādīhi guṇehi mahanto vipulo anaññasādhāraṇo. Taṃ panassa guṇamahattaṃ dasasahassilokadhātukampanena loke pākaṭanti dassento “satthuno hī”tiādimāha.

'Great' means great, vast, and unsurpassed by others in virtues such as morality. And showing that his greatness of virtue is made evident in the world by the trembling of the ten-thousandfold world-system, he said, 'For of the Teacher,' and so on.

Yasmā satthusāsane pabbajitassa pabbajjupagamena sakyaputtiyabhāvo sampajāyati, tasmā buddhaputtabhāvaṃ dassento “asambhinnāyā”tiādimāha.

Because one who has gone forth into the Teacher's dispensation attains the state of being a Sakyan son by virtue of having undertaken the going forth, therefore, showing the state of being a son of the Buddha, he said, 'Unbroken,' and so on.

Alasānaṃ [V 1.0346] bhāvanāya nāmamattampi ajānantānaṃ kāyadaḷhībahulānaṃ yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjitvā seyyasukhādianuyuñjanakānaṃ tiracchānakathikānaṃ puggalānaṃ dūrato vajjanā kusītapuggalaparivajjanā. “Divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.423; 3.75; saṃ. ni. 4.120; a. ni. 3.16; vibha. 519; mahāni. 161) bhāvanārambhavasena āraddhavīriyānaṃ daḷhaparakkamānaṃ kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamanā āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanā. Tenāha – “kucchiṃ pūretvā”tiādi. Visuddhimagge pana jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇā sabrahmacārimahattapaccavekkhaṇāti idaṃ dvayaṃ na gahitaṃ, thinamiddhavinodanatā sammappadhānapaccavekkhaṇatāti idaṃ dvayaṃ gahitaṃ. Tattha ānisaṃsadassāvitāya eva sammappadhānapaccavekkhaṇā gahitā hoti lokiyalokuttaravisesādhigamassa vīriyāyattatādassanabhāvato. Thinamiddhavinodanaṃ [M 1.0388] tadadhimuttatāya eva gahitaṃ, vīriyuppādane yuttappayuttassa thinamiddhavinodanaṃ atthasiddhameva. Tattha thinamiddhavinodana-kusītapuggalaparivajjana-āraddhavīriyapuggalasevana-tadadhimuttatā paṭipakkhavidhamanapaccayūpasaṃhāravasena, apāyapaccavekkhaṇādayo samuttejanavasena vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādakā daṭṭhabbā.

Avoiding from afar those individuals who are lazy, who do not even know the name of development, who are addicted to bodily comfort, who eat their fill and are devoted to the pleasure of lying down, who engage in animal-like talk—this is the avoidance of lazy individuals. 'By walking and sitting throughout the day,' and so forth—associating from time to time with those who have aroused energy, those of firm exertion, by way of initiating development. This is association with energetic individuals. Therefore, it is said: 'Having filled the belly,' and so on. In the Visuddhimagga, however, the reflection on the greatness of birth and the reflection on the greatness of fellow monastics—these two are not included. The dispelling of sloth and torpor and the reflection on the right efforts—these two are included. There, the reflection on the right efforts is included precisely because it reveals the benefits, by showing that the attainment of worldly and supramundane distinctions is dependent on energy. The dispelling of sloth and torpor is included precisely because of being resolved on that; for one who is suitably engaged in arousing energy, the dispelling of sloth and torpor is indeed an accomplished fact. Here, the dispelling of sloth and torpor, the avoidance of lazy individuals, association with energetic individuals, and being resolved on that should be understood as producing the enlightenment factor of energy by way of dispelling opposing factors and providing supportive conditions; the reflection on the planes of misery and so on, by way of stimulation.

Purimuppannā pīti parato uppajjanakapītiyā kāraṇabhāvato “pītiyeva pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā”ti vuttā, tassā pana bahuso pavattiyā puthuttaṃ upādāya bahuvacananiddeso, yathā sā uppajjati, evaṃ paṭipatti, tassā uppādakamanasikāro.

The joy that arises first is said to be 'joy itself constitutes the states that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of joy' because it is the cause of the joy that arises later. However, due to its frequent occurrence and manifold nature, it is described in the plural. The practice is how it arises, and the attention is what produces it.

Buddhānussatiyā upacārasamādhiniṭṭhattā vuttaṃ “yāva upacārā”ti. Sakalasarīraṃ pharamānoti pītisamuṭṭhānehi paṇītarūpehi sakalasarīraṃ pharamāno. Dhammaguṇe anussarantassapi yāva upacārā sakalasarīraṃ pharamāno pītisambojjhaṅgo uppajjatīti. Evaṃ sesaanussatīsu pasādanīyasuttantapaccavekkhaṇāyañca yojetabbaṃ tassāpi vimuttāyatanabhāvena taggatikattā. Samāpattiyā…pe… samudācarantīti idañca upasamānussatidassanaṃ. Saṅkhārānañhi sappadesavūpasamepi nippadesavūpasame viya tathā paññāya pavattito bhāvanāmanasikāro kilesavikkhambhanasamattho hutvā upacārasamādhiṃ āvahanto tathārūpapītisomanassasamannāgato pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya hotīti. Pasādanīyesu ṭhānesu pasādasinehābhāvena thusasamahadayatā lūkhatā, sā tattha ādaragāravākaraṇena viññāyatīti āha “asakkaccakiriyāya saṃsūcitalūkhabhāve”ti.

By the recollection of the Buddha, due to its culmination in access concentration, it is said, 'up to access'. 'Pervading the entire body' means pervading the entire body with refined forms born of joy. For one who recollects the qualities of the Dhamma also, the enlightenment factor of joy arises, pervading the entire body up to access. Similarly, this should be applied to the other recollections and to the reflection on inspiring discourses, for that too is a basis of liberation and has that as its nature. 'The attainment... and so on... while engaging'—this also shows the recollection of peace. For even in the partial calming of formations, it is as if they were completely calmed; because wisdom functions in that way, the developmental attention becomes capable of suppressing defileles, bringing forth access concentration, and, being endowed with such joy and gladness, it becomes a condition for the arising of the enlightenment factor of joy. In inspiring places, the absence of reverence and affection leads to a heart like chaff, a state of coarseness. That is understood there through acting without care and respect—hence it is said, 'by careless action, the coarse state is indicated'.

Kāyacittadarathavūpasamalakkhaṇā [V 1.0347] passaddhi eva passaddhisambojjhaṅgo, tassa passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa.

Tranquility, characterized by the calming of bodily and mental distress, is itself the enlightenment factor of tranquility; of that enlightenment factor of tranquility.

Paṇītabhojanasevanatāti paṇītasappāyabhojanasevanatā. Utuiriyāpathasukhaggahaṇena sappāyautuiriyāpathaggahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tañhi tividhaṃ sappāyaṃ seviyamānaṃ kāyassa kallatāpādanavasena cittassa kallataṃ [M 1.0389] āvahantaṃ duvidhāyapi passaddhiyā kāraṇaṃ hoti. Ahetukaṃ sattesu labbhamānaṃ sukhaṃ dukkhanti ayameko anto, issarādivisamahetukanti pana ayaṃ dutiyo, ete ubho ante anupagamma yathāsakaṃ kammunā hotīti ayaṃ majjhimā paṭipatti. Majjhatto payogo yassa hoti majjhattapayogo, tassa bhāvo majjhattapayogatā. Ayañhi pahāya sāraddhakāyataṃ passaddhakāyatāya kāraṇaṃ hontī passaddhidvayaṃ āvahati, eteneva sāraddhakāyapuggalaparivajjanapassaddhakāyapuggalavasenānaṃ tadāvahanatā saṃvaṇṇitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Partaking of refined food' means partaking of suitable refined food. By 'taking comfortable seasons and postures,' the taking of suitable seasons and postures should be understood. For when this threefold suitability is partaken of, by way of producing bodily fitness it induces mental fitness, and becomes a cause for both kinds of tranquility. 'That happiness and suffering found among beings is without a cause'—this is one extreme. 'That it has an unequal cause such as a creator'—this is the second. Avoiding both these extremes, 'that it occurs according to one's own kamma'—this is the middle practice. The state of one whose application is balanced is 'balanced application'. For this, by abandoning bodily agitation and being a cause for bodily tranquility, induces both kinds of tranquility. By this very means, its capacity to induce them is described through the avoidance of individuals with agitated bodies and the association with individuals with tranquil bodies.

Yathāsamāhitākārasallakkhaṇavasena gayhamāno purimuppanno samatho eva samathanimittaṃ. Nānārammaṇe paribbhamanena vividhaṃ aggaṃ etassāti byaggo, vikkhepo. Tathā hi so anavaṭṭhānaraso bhantatāpaccupaṭṭhāno ca vutto. Ekaggatābhāvato byaggapaṭipakkhoti abyaggo, samādhi. So eva nimittanti pubbe viya vattabbaṃ. Tenāha “avikkhepaṭṭhena ca abyagganimitta”nti.

The serenity that arises first, when grasped by way of observing its characteristic mode of being well-composed, is itself the sign of serenity. Agitation (`byagga`) is distraction (`vikkhepo`); it is so called because it has various objects (`vividhaṃ aggaṃ`) as it wanders among diverse objects. For it is said to have instability as its function and bewilderment as its manifestation. Non-agitation (`abyagga`), the opposite of agitation, is concentration (`samādhi`), due to its nature of one-pointedness. That itself is the sign, as was stated before. Therefore, it is said, 'and the sign of non-agitation, in the sense of non-scattering'.

Vatthuvisadakiriyā indriyasamattapaṭipādanā ca paññāvahā vuttā, samādhānāvahāpi tā honti samādhānāvahabhāveneva paññāvahabhāvatoti vuttaṃ “vatthuvisada…pe… veditabbā”ti.

The clarification of the object and the balanced development of the faculties are said to be conducive to wisdom, and they are also conducive to concentration. It is because of being conducive to concentration that they are conducive to wisdom. Thus it is said, 'The clarification of the object... and so on... should be understood'.

Karaṇabhāvanākosallānaṃ avinābhāvato, rakkhaṇakosallassa ca tammūlakattā “nimittakusalatā nāma kasiṇanimittassa uggahaṇakusalatā”icceva vuttaṃ. Kasiṇanimittassāti ca nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Asubhanimittassādikassapi hi yassa kassaci jhānuppattinimittassa uggahaṇakosallaṃ nimittakusalatā evāti.

Due to the inseparability of skill in making and developing, and because skill in guarding is rooted in that, it is said, 'Skill in the sign means skill in grasping the kasiṇa sign'. And 'kasiṇa sign' should be seen merely as an example. For skill in grasping any sign leading to the arising of jhāna, whether the sign of foulness or any other, is indeed skill in the sign.

Atisithilavīriyatādīhīti ādi-saddena paññāpayogamandataṃ pamodavekallañca saṅgaṇhāti. Tassa paggahaṇanti tassa līnassa cittassa dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādisamuṭṭhāpanena layāpattito samuddharaṇaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

'By excessive slackness of energy, and so on'—here, the word 'and so on' includes sluggishness in the application of wisdom and lack of joy. 'The exertion of that' means the uplifting of that sluggish mind from the state of lethargy by arousing the enlightenment factor of investigation of states and so forth. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Yasmiñca [V 1.0348] kho, bhikkhave, samaye līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, kālo tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya[M 1.0390]. Taṃ kissa hetu? Līnaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, taṃ etehi dhammehi susamuṭṭhāpayaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjāletukāmo assa, so tattha sukkhāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyya, sukkhāni ca gomayāni pakkhipeyya, sukkhāni ca kaṭṭhāni pakkhipeyya, mukhavātañca dadeyya, na ca paṃsukena okireyya, bhabbo nu kho so puriso parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjāletunti? Evaṃ sante”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234).

“Monks, when the mind is sluggish, that is the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of investigation of states, the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of energy, and the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of joy. What is the reason for that? A sluggish mind, monks, is easy to arouse by these states. Just as, monks, if a man wanted to kindle a small fire, he would put dry grass on it, dry cow-dung, and dry sticks, blow on it with his mouth, and not sprinkle it with dust—would that man be able to kindle that small fire?” “Yes, that is so.” (Saṃ. Ni. 5.234)

Ettha ca yathāsakaṃ āhāravasena dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādīnaṃ bhāvanā samuṭṭhāpanāti veditabbaṃ, sā anantaraṃ vibhāvitā eva.

Here, it should be understood that the cultivation and arousing of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states and so on is by way of their respective nutriments; this has just been explained.

Accāraddhavīriyatādīhīti ādi-saddena paññāpayogabalavataṃ pamoduppilāvanañca saṅgaṇhāti. Tassa niggahaṇanti tassa uddhatacittassa samādhisambojjhaṅgādisamuṭṭhāpanena uddhatāpattito nisedhanaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā –

'By excessive energy, and so on'—here, the word 'and so on' includes forceful application of wisdom and overflowing joy. 'The restraint of that' means the restraining of that agitated mind from the fault of agitation by arousing the enlightenment factor of concentration and so on. This too was said by the Blessed One—

“Yasmiñca kho, bhikkhave, samaye uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, kālo tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo samādhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Uddhataṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, taṃ etehi dhammehi suvūpasamayaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetukāmo assa, so tattha allāni ceva tiṇāni…pe… paṃsukena ca okireyya, bhabbo nu kho so puriso mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetunti? Evaṃ bhante”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234).

"At the time, monks, when the mind is agitated, it is the time for cultivating the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity. For what reason? An agitated mind, monks, is easily calmed by these qualities. Just as, monks, if a man wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire, he would sprinkle wet grass... and dust on it—would that man be able to extinguish the great mass of fire? 'Yes, venerable sir.'" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.234)

Etthāpi yathāsakaṃ āhāravasena passaddhisambojjhaṅgādīnaṃ bhāvanā samuṭṭhāpanāti veditabbā. Tattha passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanā vuttā eva, samādhisambojjhaṅgassa vuccamānā, itarassa anantaraṃ vakkhati.

Here, too, the cultivation and arising of the enlightenment factors of tranquility and so on should be understood according to their respective nutriments. In this context, the cultivation of the enlightenment factor of tranquility has already been mentioned, that of the enlightenment factor of concentration is being discussed, and that of the other will be explained immediately after.

Paññāpayogamandatāyāti paññābyāpārassa appabhāvena. Yathā hi dānaṃ alobhappadhānaṃ, sīlaṃ adosappadhānaṃ, evaṃ bhāvanā amohappadhānā. Tattha yadā paññā na balavatī hoti, tadā bhāvanā pubbenāparaṃ visesāvahā na hoti, anabhisaṅkhato viya āhāro purisassa yogino [M 1.0391] cittassa abhiruciṃ na janeti, tena taṃ nirassādaṃ hoti, tathā bhāvanāya sammadeva avīthipaṭipattiyā [V 1.0349] upasamasukhaṃ na vindati, tenāpi cittaṃ nirassādaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “paññāpayoga…pe… nirassādaṃ hotī”ti. Tassa saṃveguppādanaṃ pasāduppādanañca tikicchananti taṃ dassento “aṭṭha saṃvegavatthūnī”tiādimāha. Tattha jātijarābyādhimaraṇāni yathārahaṃ sugatiyaṃ duggatiyañca hontīti tadaññameva pañcavidhabandhanādi-khuppipāsādi-aññamaññavibādhanādihetukaṃ apāyadukkhaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, tayidaṃ sabbaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ paccuppannabhavanissitaṃ gahitanti atīte anāgate ca kāle vaṭṭamūlakadukkhāni visuṃ gahitāni. Ye pana sattā āhārūpajīvino, tattha ca uṭṭhānaphalūpajīvino, tesaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ jīvikadukkhaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ saṃvegavatthu gahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati samaye sampahaṃsanatāti ayaṃ sampahaṃsitabbasamaye vuttanayena tena saṃvejanavasena ceva pasāduppādanavasena ca sammadeva pahaṃsanā, saṃvegajananapubbakapasāduppādanena bhāvanācittassa tosanāti attho.

Due to sluggishness in applying wisdom: because the activity of wisdom is weak. Just as generosity has non-greed as its chief quality, and virtue has non-hatred as its chief quality, so too does meditation have non-delusion as its chief quality. When wisdom is not strong, meditation does not bring about successive special attainments, just as unseasoned food does not produce delight in the mind of a yogi, thereby making it joyless. Similarly, by not properly entering the path of meditation, one does not find the bliss of peace, and thus the mind becomes joyless. Therefore, it is said, "due to sluggishness in applying wisdom... it becomes joyless." To treat this by generating urgency and serenity, the text states, "eight grounds for urgency," etc. Here, birth, aging, sickness, and death occur appropriately in good and bad destinations, but the suffering of the lower realms—caused by the fivefold bondage, hunger and thirst, mutual harm, and so on—should be seen as distinct from that. All this is taken as based on the present existence of those beings, while the sufferings rooted in the cycle of rebirth in the past and future are taken separately. But for beings who live on food, and among them those who live on the fruits of their labor, their unique suffering of livelihood is taken as the eighth ground for urgency. This is called "inspiring at the right time": that is, at the appropriate time for inspiration, it is the proper inspiration by way of generating urgency and by way of generating serenity; the meaning is the delighting of the meditative mind by first generating urgency and then generating serenity.

Sammāpaṭipattiṃ āgammāti līnuddhaccavirahena samathavīthipaṭipattiyā ca sammā avisamaṃ sammadeva bhāvanāpaṭipattiṃ āgamma. Alīnantiādīsu kosajjapakkhiyānaṃ dhammānaṃ anadhimattatāya alīnaṃ, uddhaccapakkhiyānaṃ anadhimattatāya anuddhataṃ, paññāpayogasattiyā upasamasukhādhigamena ca anirassādaṃ, tato eva ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ samathavīthipaṭipannañca. Tattha alīnatāya paggahe, anuddhatatāya niggahe, anirassādatāya sampahaṃsane na byāpāraṃ āpajjati, alīnānuddhatatāhi ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ, anirassādatāya samathavīthipaṭipannaṃ. Samappavattiyā vā alīnaṃ anuddhataṃ, samathavīthipaṭipattiyā anirassādanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati samaye ajjhupekkhanatāti ayaṃ ajjhupekkhitabbasamaye bhāvanācittassa paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu byāvaṭatāsaṅkhātaṃ paṭipakkhaṃ abhibhuyya pekkhanā vuccati.

Having arrived at right practice: by the absence of sluggishness and restlessness, and by the path of serenity practice, rightly and without deviation, having arrived at the practice of development. 'Not sluggish,' and so on: by the non-excess of states belonging to the side of laziness, it is not sluggish; by the non-excess of states belonging to the side of restlessness, it is not restless; and by the power of the application of wisdom and by the attainment of the happiness of peace, it is not joyless. Thus, it proceeds evenly toward the object and has entered upon the path of serenity. Here, due to its not being sluggish, one does not undertake the task of exertion; due to its not being restless, one does not undertake the task of restraint; due to its not being joyless, one does not undertake the task of encouragement. By its not being sluggish and not being restless, it proceeds evenly toward the object; by its not being joyless, it has entered upon the path of serenity. Alternatively, it should be seen that it is not sluggish and not restless due to its even progression, and not joyless due to its practice of the serenity path. This is called 'equanimity at the proper time': this, at the time for observing with equanimity, is called observing, having overcome the opposition which is the meditative mind's engagement in exertion, restraint, and encouragement.

Paṭipakkhavikkhambhanato vipassanāya adhiṭṭhānabhāvūpagamanato ca upacārajjhānampi samādānakiccanipphattiyā puggalassa samāhitabhāvasādhanamevāti tattha samadhurabhāvenāha “upacāraṃ vā appanaṃ vā”ti.

By the suppression of opposing states and by its attainment of the status of a foundation for insight, even access concentration, in fulfilling the task of its undertaking, is itself a means for achieving the individual's state of concentration. Therefore, by virtue of their equal standing, it says, "either access or absorption."

Upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammāti ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttānusārena veditabbaṃ.

The states associated with the enlightenment factor of equanimity: whatever needs to be said here should be understood in accordance with what was stated above.

Anurodhavirodhavippahānavasena [M 1.0392] majjhattabhāvo upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa kāraṇaṃ tasmiṃ sati sijjhanato, asati ca asijjhanato, so ca majjhattabhāvo visayavasena duvidhoti āha “sattamajjhattatā saṅkhāramajjhattatā”ti. Tadubhaye ca virujjhanaṃ passaddhisambojjhaṅgabhāvanāya eva dūrīkatanti [V 1.0350] anurujjhanasseva pahānavidhiṃ dassentena “sattamajjhattatā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatā”ti. Upekkhāya hi visesato rāgo paṭipakkho. Tathā cāha “upekkhā rāgabahulassa visuddhimaggo”ti (visuddhi. 1.269).

The state of neutrality, through the abandonment of both attraction and repulsion, is the cause for the enlightenment factor of equanimity, since it is achieved when that is present and is not achieved when it is absent. That state of neutrality is twofold by way of its object, as stated: 'neutrality toward beings and neutrality toward formations.' And opposition with regard to both of these is removed precisely by the cultivation of the enlightenment factor of tranquility; therefore, to show the method for abandoning only attachment, it is said: 'neutrality toward beings,' etc. For that reason, it is also said: 'avoiding persons who are attached to beings and formations.' For lust, in particular, is the opponent of equanimity. And so it is said: 'Equanimity is the path of purification for one who has much lust' (Visuddhimagga 1.269).

Dvīhākārehīti kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇaṃ attasuññatāpaccavekkhaṇanti imehi dvīhi kāraṇehi. Dvīhevāti avadhāraṇaṃ saṅkhyāsamānatāya. Assāmikabhāvo anattaniyatā. Sati hi attani tassa kiñcanabhāvena cīvaraṃ aññañca kiñci attaniyaṃ nāma siyā, so pana koci natthevāti adhippāyo. Anaddhaniyanti na addhānakkhamaṃ, na ciraṭṭhāyi ittaraṃ aniccanti attho. Tāvakālikanti tasseva vevacanaṃ.

By two aspects: that is, by these two reasons—reflection on ownership of kamma and reflection on the emptiness of self. 'By two only' is an emphasis limiting the number. Absence of ownership means not belonging to a self. For if there were a self, then by its being a possession, a robe or anything else could be called 'belonging to a self'; but since there is no such self at all, this is the meaning. 'Not enduring' means not capable of lasting long, not long-lasting; it is transient, impermanent—this is the meaning. 'Temporary' is a synonym for the same.

Mamāyatīti mamattaṃ karoti, “mama”nti taṇhāya pariggayha tiṭṭhati. Dhanāyantāti dhanaṃ drabyaṃ karontā.

One regards as 'mine': one makes something one's own; one stands grasping with craving, thinking 'mine.' Considering as wealth: making something into wealth, into property.

Ayaṃ satipaṭṭhānadesanā pubbabhāgamaggavasena desitāti pubbabhāgiyabojjhaṅge sandhāyāha “bojjhaṅgapariggāhikā sati dukkhasacca”nti.

This discourse on the foundations of mindfulness was taught by way of the preliminary part of the path; thus, referring to the preliminary factors of enlightenment, it is said: "Mindfulness that embraces the factors of enlightenment is the truth of suffering."

Bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the chapter on the enlightenment factors is concluded.

Catusaccapabbavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Chapter on the Four Truths

119. Yathāsabhāvatoti aviparītasabhāvato bādhanalakkhaṇato, yo yo vā sabhāvo yathāsabhāvo, tato, ruppanādikakkhaḷādisabhāvatoti attho. Janikaṃ samuṭṭhāpikanti pavattalakkhaṇassa dukkhassa janikaṃ nimittalakkhaṇassa samuṭṭhāpikaṃ. Purimataṇhanti dukkhanibbattito puretarasiddhaṃ taṇhaṃ.

119. 'According to its own nature' means according to its unperverted nature, from its characteristic of affliction. Or, whatever its nature is, from that own-nature; the meaning is from the nature of being oppressed, hardness, and so on. 'Generative, originating' means generative of suffering, which has the characteristic of occurrence, and originating that which has the characteristic of a cause. 'Former craving' means the craving that is established prior to the production of suffering.

Sasantatipariyāpannānaṃ [M 1.0393] dukkhasamudayānaṃ appavattibhāvena pariggayhamāno nirodhopi sasantatipariyāpanno viya hotīti katvā vuttaṃ “attano vā cattāri saccānī”ti. Parassa vāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tenāha bhagavā – “imasmiṃyeva byāmamatte kaḷevare sasaññimhi samanake lokañca paññapemi, lokasamudayañca paññapemi, lokanirodhañca paññapemi, lokanirodhagāminipaṭipadañca paññapemī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.107). Kathaṃ pana ādikampiko [V 1.0351] nirodhasaccāni pariggaṇhātīti? Anussavādisiddhamākāraṃ pariggaṇhāti, evañca katvā lokuttarabojjhaṅge uddissapi pariggaho na virujjhati. Yathāsambhavatoti sambhavānurūpaṃ, ṭhapetvā nirodhasaccaṃ sesasaccavasena samudayavayā veditabbāti attho.

Because cessation, being apprehended through the non-occurrence of the origins of suffering which are included in one's own continuity, is as if it too were included in one's own continuity, it is said, 'one's own four truths.' And in the case of 'another's,' this is the same method. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'In this very fathom-long body, with its perception and mind, I make known the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.107). But how does a beginner grasp the truths of cessation? One grasps the mode established by oral tradition and so on. And having done so, the grasping does not conflict even with reference to the supramundane factors of enlightenment. 'According to possibility' means in accordance with what is possible; the meaning is that, setting aside the truth of cessation, the remaining truths are to be understood by way of arising and passing away.

Catusaccapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Chapter on the Four Noble Truths is completed.

“Aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ samaṃsa”ntiādikā satta sivathikā aṭṭhikakammaṭṭhānatāya itarāsaṃ uddhumātakādīnaṃ sabhāvenevāti navannaṃ sivathikānaṃ appanākammaṭṭhānatā vuttā. Dveyevāti “ānāpānaṃ, dvattiṃsākāro”ti imāni dveyeva. Abhinivesoti vipassanābhiniveso, so pana sammasanīyadhamme pariggaho. Iriyāpathā ālokitādayo ca rūpadhammānaṃ avatthāvisesamattatāya na sammasanupagā viññattiādayo viya. Nīvaraṇabojjhaṅgā ādito na pariggahetabbāti vuttaṃ “iriyāpatha…pe… na jāyatī”ti. Kesādiapadesena tadupādānadhammā viya iriyāpathādiapadesena tadavatthā rūpadhammā pariggayhanti, nīvaraṇādimukhena ca taṃ sampayuttā taṃnissayadhammāti adhippāyena mahāsīvatthero “iriyāpathādīsupi abhiniveso jāyatī”ti āha. Atthi nu kho metiādi pana sabhāvato iriyāpathādīnaṃ ādikammikassa anicchitabhāvadassanaṃ. Apariññāpubbikā hi pariññāti.

'A skeleton with flesh,' and so on: the seven charnel ground meditations are suitable as a meditation subject on bones, while the others—the bloated corpse and so on—are so by their own nature. Thus, the suitability of the nine charnel ground meditations as absorption meditation subjects has been stated. 'Only two' means 'mindfulness of breathing and the thirty-two parts'—these two alone. Adherence refers to the adherence of insight, which is the grasping of the phenomena to be investigated. Postures, looking around, and so on, being merely particular states of material phenomena, are not suitable for investigation, unlike bodily intimation and so on. It is said that the hindrances and factors of enlightenment should not be grasped from the beginning: 'Postures... do not arise.' Just as by means of 'hair, etc.' their derived phenomena are grasped, so too by means of 'postures, etc.' the material phenomena in those states are grasped. And by way of the hindrances and so on, the associated and dependent phenomena are meant. With this intention, the great elder Mahāsīva said, 'Adherence also arises in regard to postures and so on.' But as for 'Is there in me...?' and so on, this shows the undesirable nature of postures and so on, in their intrinsic nature, for a beginner. For full understanding is preceded by non-full-understanding.

137. Kāmaṃ “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhū”tiādinā uddesaniddesesu tattha tattha bhikkhuggahaṇaṃ kataṃ, taṃ paṭipattiyā bhikkhubhāvadassanatthaṃ, desanā pana sabbasādhāraṇāti dassetuṃ “yo hi koci, bhikkhave”icceva vuttaṃ, na bhikkhuyevāti dassento “yo hi koci, bhikkhu vā”tiādimāha. Dassanamaggena ñātamariyādaṃ anatikkamitvā jānantī sikhāppattā aggamaggapaññā [M 1.0394] aññā nāma, tassa phalabhāvato aggaphalampīti āha “aññāti arahatta”nti. Appatarepi kāle sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvaṃ dassentoti yojanā.

137. Indeed, in the summaries and detailed explanations such as 'Here, monks,' the term 'monk' is used here and there to indicate the state of being a monk through practice. However, to show that the teaching is universal, it is said 'whoever, monks,' not just a monk alone. To clarify this, it is said, 'whoever, whether a monk or...' She who knows without transgressing the known standard by the path of vision, attained to the summit, is called 'aññā'—the foremost path-wisdom. Because it has the state of a fruit, it is also the foremost fruit, thus it is said, 'aññā means arahantship.' The explanation is to show the liberating nature of the teaching even in a short time.

138. Niyyātentoti nigamento.

138. 'They lead out' means bringing to a conclusion.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses

Satipaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta is completed.

Niṭṭhitā ca mūlapariyāyavaggavaṇṇanā.

And the Exposition of the Mūlapariyāya Vagga is completed.

Paṭhamo bhāgo niṭṭhito.

The first part is completed.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Majjhimanikāye

In the Majjhima Nikāya

Mūlapaṇṇāsa-ṭīkā

The Mūlapaṇṇāsa Subcommentary

(Dutiyo bhāgo)

(The Second Part)

2. Sīhanādavaggo

2. The Chapter of the Lion's Roar

1. Cūḷasīhanādasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Exposition of the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta

139. Suttadesanāvatthusaṅkhātassa [M 2.0001][V 2.0001] atthassa uppatti aṭṭhuppatti, sā tassa atthīti aṭṭhuppattikoti vuttovāyamattho. Lābhasakkārapaccayāti lābhasakkāranimittaṃ, bhagavato saṅghassa ca uppannalābhasakkārahetu, attano vā lābhasakkāruppādanahetu. Titthiyaparideviteti titthiyānaṃ “kiṃ bho samaṇoyeva gotamo samaṇo”tiādinā vippalapanimittaṃ. “Mahālābhasakkāro uppajjī”ti vatvā samantapāsādikatthaṃ tassa uppattikāraṇaṃ dassento “catuppamāṇiko hī”tiādimāha. Cattāri pamāṇāni catuppamāṇāni, catuppamāṇāni etassa atthīti catuppamāṇiko. Lokoyeva saṅgamma samāgamma vasanaṭṭhena lokasannivāso, sattakāyoti attho. Pamināti uḷāratādivisesaṃ etenāti pamāṇaṃ (a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.65) rūpaṃ rūpakāyo pamāṇaṃ etassāti rūpappamāṇo. Tato eva rūpe pasannoti rūpappasanno. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo[V 2.0002]. Ghosoti pavattathutighoso (a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.65). Lūkhanti paccayalūkhatā. Dhammoti sīlādayo guṇadhammā adhippetā.

139. The arising of the meaning designated as the occasion for the teaching of the Sutta is the 'occasion for the meaning'; because this exists for it, it is said to be 'one with an occasion for the meaning,' and this is the meaning spoken of. 'On account of gain and honour' means for the sake of gain and honour, the cause of the gain and honour that has arisen for the Blessed One and the Sangha, or the cause for producing one's own gain and honour. 'The lamentation of the sectarians' means the cause of the sectarians' prattling, such as, 'Why, friends, is the ascetic Gotama an ascetic?' Having stated, 'Great gain and honour has arisen,' he then explains the reason for its arising for the sake of universal inspiration, saying, 'For he has four measures,' etc. Four measures are 'catuppamāṇāni'; one for whom there are four measures is 'catuppamāṇiko'. The world itself, by reason of gathering, assembling, and dwelling, is an assembly of the world; the meaning is a group of beings. 'One measures distinction such as greatness, etc., by this,' thus it is a 'measure'. Form, the physical body, is the measure for him, thus he is 'one who measures by form'. Hence, one who is pleased with form is 'one who has confidence in form'. This same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Sound' refers to the sound of spreading praise. 'Coarse' means coarseness of requisites. 'Dhamma' refers to virtuous qualities such as morality and so on, which are intended.

Tesaṃ [M 2.0002] puggalānaṃ. Ārohanti uccataṃ. Sā ca kho tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle pamāṇayuttā daṭṭhabbā. Pariṇāhanti nātikisanātithūlatāvasena mitapariṇāhaṃ. Saṇṭhānanti tesaṃ tesaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ susaṇṭhitataṃ. Pāripūrinti sabbesaṃ sarīrāvayavānaṃ paripuṇṇataṃ avekallataṃ. Tattha pamāṇaṃ gahetvāti tasmiṃ rūpe rūpasampattiyaṃ pamāṇabhāvaṃ upādāya. Pasādaṃ janetīti adhimokkhaṃ uppādeti.

'Of those individuals.' 'Height' means loftiness. And that, at each particular time, should be seen as endowed with proper measure. 'Girth' means a measured girth, not being too thin or too thick. 'Shape' means the well-proportioned state of their various limbs and minor limbs. 'Completeness' means the fullness and non-deficiency of all the bodily parts. 'Taking that as the measure' means on account of its being the standard in that form, in the perfection of form. 'It generates confidence' means it produces conviction.

Paravaṇṇanāyāti “amuko ediso ca ediso cā”ti yasaguṇavacanena. Parathomanāyāti sammukhāva parassa silāghuppādanena abhitthavanena. Parapasaṃsanāyāti parammukhā parassa guṇasaṃkittanena. Paravaṇṇahārikāyāti paramparavaṇṇahārikāya paramparāya parassa kittisaddūpasaṃhārena. Tatthāti tasmiṃ thutighose.

'By praising another' means by words describing virtues, saying, 'So-and-so is like this and like that.' 'By extolling another' means by generating praise for another to their face, by directly extolling them. 'By commending another' means by speaking of another's virtues in their absence. 'By spreading another's praise' means by conveying the sound of another's fame from one to another. 'There' means in that sound of praise.

Cīvaralūkhanti thūlajiṇṇabahutunnakatādiṃ cīvarassa lūkhabhāvaṃ. Pattalūkhanti anekaganthikāhatādiṃ pattassa lūkhabhāvaṃ. Vividhaṃ vā dukkarakārikanti dhutaṅgasevanādivasena pavattaṃ nānāvidhaṃ dukkaracariyaṃ.

'Roughness of the robe' means the coarse condition of the robe, such as being thick, old, or much-patched. 'Roughness of the bowl' means the coarse condition of the bowl, such as being mended with many knots. Or, 'various difficult practices' refers to the diverse difficult conduct undertaken by way of practicing the ascetic observances and so on.

Sīlaṃ vā passitvāti sīlapāripūrivasena visuddhaṃ kāyavacīsucaritaṃ ñāṇacakkhunā passitvā. Jhānādiadhigamasiddhaṃ samādhiṃ vā. Vipassanābhiññāsaṅkhātaṃ paññaṃ vā.

Or 'having seen virtue' means having seen with the eye of wisdom the pure good conduct of body and speech by way of the fulfillment of virtue. Or concentration, which is accomplished through the attainment of jhāna and the like. Or wisdom, which is designated as insight and the higher knowledges.

Bhagavato sarīraṃ disvāti sambandho. Rūpappamāṇopi sammāsambuddheyeva pasīdati aparimitakālasamupacitapuññānubhāvanipphannāya sabbaso anavajjāya sabbākāraparipuṇṇāvayavāya rūpakāyasampattiyā samantapāsādikattā, yassā rucirabhāvo visuddhe vigatavalāhake deve puṇṇamāsiyaṃ paripuṇṇakalābhāgamaṇḍalaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ abhibhavitvā atirocati, pabhassarabhāvo saradasamayaṃ saṃvaddhitadiguṇatejakiraṇajālasamujjalaṃ sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ abhibhavati, sommakiraṇarasasamujjalabhāvehi tadubhayehi abhibhuyya vattamānaṃ ekasmiṃ khaṇe dasasahassilokadhātuṃ vijjotanasamatthaṃ mahābrahmuno pabhāsamudayaṃ abhivihacca bhāsate tapate virocati ca.

The connection is 'having seen the Blessed One's body.' Even one who judges by form becomes confident in the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One alone, because of the perfection of his physical body, which is produced by the power of merit accumulated over immeasurable time, flawless in every way, with limbs complete in all aspects, and universally inspiring. Its delightful beauty surpasses the full moon's orb with all its parts complete in a pure, cloudless sky, and shines exceedingly; its dazzling radiance surpasses the sun's orb blazing with a mass of rays whose splendor has increased twofold in the autumn season; and, existing having surpassed both of them by its shining nature of gentle, lustrous rays, it shines, glows, and radiates, in a single moment, having overcome the arising of light of the Great Brahmā, being capable of illuminating ten thousand world-systems.

Satipi [V 2.0003] aṅgapariccāgādīnaṃ dānapāramibhāve pariccāgavisesabhāvadassanatthañceva sudukkarabhāvadassanatthañca aṅgapariccāgādiggahaṇaṃ, tatthāpi ca aṅgapariccāgato visuṃ nayanapariccāgaggahaṇaṃ, pariccāgabhāvasāmaññepi rajjapariccāgato [M 2.0003] puttadārapariccāgaggahaṇañca kataṃ. Ādinā nayenāti ādi-saddena pubbayogapubbacariyādihetusampattiyā, “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.157, 255) vuttāya phalasampattiyā, “so dhammaṃ desetī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.255) vuttāya sattupakārakiriyāya ca saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Sammāsambuddheyeva pasīdati yathāvuttaguṇānaṃ anaññasādhāraṇabhāvato acchariyabbhutabhāvato ca. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

Even though the sacrifice of limbs and the like constitutes the perfection of giving, the mention of limb-sacrifice and so on is included to show the special nature of the sacrifice and its extreme difficulty. Moreover, the sacrifice of the eye is specifically mentioned as distinct from the sacrifice of limbs. Even with the generality of sacrifice, the mention of the sacrifice of children and wife is made, distinct from the sacrifice of the kingdom. The term 'by this method, etc.' (ādinā nayena) should be understood as including, by the word 'ādi,' the attainment of causes such as previous practice and past conduct, the attainment of fruition as stated in 'Thus indeed is the Blessed One,' and the activity of benefiting beings as described in 'He teaches the Dhamma.' Serene confidence arises in the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One alone, because of the unshared nature and the amazing and wondrous nature of the qualities described. This same method applies to the rest.

“Cīvaralūkhaṃ disvā”ti vatvā taṃ dassetuṃ “sace bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sāṇapaṃsukūlacīvarenāti matakaḷevaraṃ paliveṭhetvā chaḍḍitena tumbamatte kimī papphoṭetvā gahitena sāṇapaṃsukūlacīvarena. Bhāriyanti garukaṃ, dukkaranti attho. Vadhuyuvatīmajjhimitthivasena, bālayobbanapurāṇavasena vā tividhanāṭakatā. Hareṇuyūsaṃ maṇḍalakalāyaraso. “Yāpessati nāmā”ti nāma-saddaṃ ānetvā sambandho. Nāma-saddayogena hi anāgatakālassa viya payogo, yāpeti icceva attho. Appāṇakanti nirassāsaṃ nirodhitassāsapassāsaṃ.

Having stated, 'Having seen the rough robe,' the text continues with 'If the Blessed One...' and so forth to illustrate this. 'By the robe of hempen patchwork rags' means by a hempen patchwork rag-robe that had been wrapped around a corpse and discarded, and was taken after shaking off worms the size of a gourd. 'Bhāriya' means heavy; the meaning is 'difficult.' The threefold theatricality is by way of a young woman, a maiden, and a middle-aged woman, or by way of childhood, youth, and old age. 'Hareṇu juice' is the broth of maṇḍala beans. In 'yāpessati nāma,' the word 'nāma' is brought in to make the connection. For by the use of the word 'nāma,' the usage is like that of the future tense, but the meaning is simply 'he sustains.' 'Appāṇaka' means without breath, with inhalation and exhalation having ceased.

Samādhiguṇanti sādhāraṇato vuttamatthaṃ vivarati jhānādiggahaṇena. Mānadabbanimmadanena nibbisevanabhāvāpādanampi damanamevāti vuttaṃ “pāthikaputtadamanādīnī”ti. Ādi-saddena saccakāḷavakabakadamanādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Bāverunti evaṃnāmakaṃ visayaṃ. Sarasampannoti aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatena sarena samannāgato. Tena brahmassaratākaravīkabhāṇitādassanena lakkhaṇahāranayena avasesalakkhaṇapāripūriṃ viya tadavinābhāvato buddhānaṃ desanāvilāsañca vibhāveti.

He clarifies the meaning of 'the qualities of concentration,' stated in a general sense, by the inclusion of jhāna and so forth. The crushing of the substance of conceit and the bringing about of a state of non-indulgence is also called taming, as stated in 'the taming of Pāthikaputta and others.' By the word 'and so forth' is included the taming of Saccaka, Kāḷavaka, Baka, and others. 'Bāveru' refers to a region of that name. 'Endowed with a voice' means endowed with a voice possessing eight qualities. Through the display of a Brahma-like voice, resembling the sound of a karavīka bird, it manifests, by the method of inferring from characteristics, the complete fulfillment of the remaining characteristics—due to their inseparability—and also the graceful style of the Buddhas’ teachings.

Hatappabhāti buddhānubhāvena vigatatejā. Kāḷapakkhūpameti sattānaṃ byāmohandhakārābhibhavena kāḷapakkharattūpame. Sūriyeti sūriye udayitvā obhāsenteti adhippāyo.

'Hatappabhā' means their brilliance was dispelled by the Buddha's power. 'Like the dark fortnight': this is a simile for the night of the dark fortnight, because beings are overwhelmed by the darkness of delusion. 'Sūriya' means 'the sun, having risen, illuminates'—this is the intended meaning.

Siṅghāṭaketi tikoṇaracchāyaṃ. Catukketi sandhiyaṃ. Paridevantīti anutthunanavasena vippalapanti. Sokādhikakato hi vacīpalāpo paridevo. Loke uppajjamāneyeva uppannāti attano diṭṭhivādassa purātanabhāvaṃ dīpenti.

‘At a siṅghāṭaka’ means at a three-cornered intersection. ‘At a catukka’ means at a junction. ‘They lament’ means they babble by way of groaning. For verbal rambling caused by excessive sorrow is lamentation. By stating, ‘Arisen as soon as they arise in the world,’ they indicate the ancient nature of their own doctrinal view.

Sesapadesupīti [M 2.0004][V 2.0004] “idha dutiyo samaṇo”tiādīsu sesavāresupi (a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.241-242) yathā hi “vivicceva kāmehī”ti (pārā. 11; dī. ni. 1.226; saṃ. ni. 2.152; a. ni. 4.123) ettha kato niyamo “vivicca akusalehī”ti (pārā. 11; dī. ni. 1.226; saṃ. ni. 2.152; a. ni. 4.123) etthāpi katoyeva hoti sāvadhāraṇasseva atthassa icchitabbattā, evamidhāpīti. Tenāha “dutiyādayopī”tiādi. Sāmaññaphalādhigamavasena nippariyāyato samaṇabhāvoti tesaṃ vasenettha cattāro samaṇā desitāti tamatthaṃ suttantarena samatthetuṃ “tenevāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Paṭipattikkamena desanākkamena ca sakadāgāmiādīnaṃ dutiyāditā vuttāti sotāpannassa paṭhamatā avuttasiddhāti na coditā. Phalaṭṭhakasamaṇāva adhippetā samitapāpasamaṇaggahaṇato. Kasmā panettha mahāparinibbāne viya maggaṭṭhā tadatthāya paṭipannā ca na gahitāti? Veneyyajjhāsayato. Tattha hi maggādhigamatthāya vipassanāpi ito bahiddhā natthi, kuto maggaphalānīti dassentena bhagavatā “ñāyassa dhammassa padesavattī, ito bahiddhā samaṇopi natthī”ti vuttaṃ. Idha pana niṭṭhānappattameva taṃtaṃsamaṇabhāvaṃ gaṇhantena phalaṭṭhakasamaṇāva gahitā “maggaṭṭhato phalaṭṭho savisesaṃ dakkhiṇeyyo”ti. Svāyamattho dvīsu suttesu desanābhedeneva viññāyatīti.

In the remaining sections too, such as 'here is the second recluse' and so forth, in the remaining instances, just as the restriction made in 'secluded from sensual pleasures' also applies in 'secluded from unwholesome states'—because a meaning with emphasis is intended—so too is it here. Therefore, it is said, 'the second and others' and so forth. The state of being a recluse is definitively by way of attaining the fruits of recluseship. In relation to these, four recluses are taught here. To support this meaning with another sutta, it is stated, 'therefore it is said' and so forth. The second rank and so forth of the once-returner and others is stated according to the order of practice and the order of teaching; thus the first rank of the stream-enterer is implicitly understood without being stated, so it is not questioned. Only recluses established in the fruits are intended, as inferred from the mention of 'recluses who have pacified evil.' But why are those established on the path and those practicing for its sake not included here, as in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta? It is due to the disposition of those to be taught. For there, the Blessed One, showing that insight meditation for the sake of attaining the path does not exist outside this teaching—how much less the path and fruits themselves?—said: 'one who resorts to a portion of this path-like Dhamma; outside this there is no recluse.' Here, however, since only those who have reached the culmination of that particular state of recluseship are considered, only recluses established in the fruits are included, as 'one established in the fruit is especially more worthy of offerings than one established in the path.' This meaning is understood precisely from the difference in the teachings of the two suttas.

Rittāti vivittā. Tucchāti nissārā paṭipannakasārābhāvato. Pavadanti etehīti pavādā, diṭṭhigatikānaṃ nānādiṭṭhidīpakā samayāti āha “cattāro sassatavādā”tiādi. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato āgamissati. Teti yathāvuttasamaṇā. Etthāti “parappavādā”ti vutte bāhirakasamaye.

‘Rittā’ means secluded. ‘Tucchā’ means devoid of essence, because of the absence of the essence of those who have practiced. ‘They proclaim with these,’ thus they are doctrines (pavādā); they are the schools that reveal the various views of those who hold to views, as it is said: ‘the four eternalist doctrines’ and so forth. What should be said there will be explained later. ‘Those’ refers to the recluses as previously described. ‘In this context’ means, when ‘the doctrines of others’ is mentioned, it refers to the schools of outsiders.

Yanti yasmiṃ. Bhummatthe hi idaṃ paccattavacanaṃ. Ñāyo vuccati saha vipassanāya ariyamaggo. Tena hi nibbānaṃ ñāyati gammati paṭivijjhatīti. So eva nibbānasampāpakahetutāya dhammoti āha “ñāyassa dhammassā”ti.

‘Yaṃ’ means ‘in which.’ For this accusative singular is used in the sense of the locative. The Noble Path together with insight is called the path (ñāya). For by it, Nibbāna is known, reached, and penetrated. Because it is the very cause for attaining Nibbāna, it is the Dhamma; thus he said, ‘of the Dhamma which is the path.’

Tesaṃ parappavādasāsanānaṃ akhettatā khettatā ca ariyamaggassa abhāvabhāvā suparisuddhassa sīlassa suparisuddhāya samathavipassanāya abhāvato sāvato ca. Tadubhayañca durakkhātasvākkhātabhāvahetukaṃ, so ca asammāsambuddhasammāsambuddhapaveditatāyāti parājikāya [M 2.0005] satthu vipattihetutāya sāsanassa aniyyānabhāvoti dasseti.

The fact that the doctrines of others are not a field, while this one is a field, is due to the absence and presence of the Noble Path, which in turn is due to the absence and presence of perfectly purified virtue and perfectly purified serenity and insight. And both of these have as their cause the state of being poorly expounded or well-expounded. And that, in turn, is due to being proclaimed by one who is not a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One or by a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Thus, it shows that the dispensation does not lead to deliverance, because the Teacher's defeat is the cause of its failure.

Idāni [V 2.0005] yathāvuttamatthaṃ pariyāyato ca pāḷiyā ca samatthetuṃ “tenāha bhagavā”tiādinā pāḷiṃ dassetvā upamāpadesena tattha suttaṃ vibhāvento “yasmā”tiādimāha. Tattha yasmā ekaccānaṃ visesato sīhānaṃ purimaṃ pādadvayaṃ hatthakiccampi karoti, tasmā āha “surattahatthapādo”ti. Sīhassa kesā nāma kesarāyatanā khandhalomā. Gocariyahatthikulaṃ nāma pakatihatthikulaṃ, yaṃ “kālāvaka”ntipi vuccati. Ghoṭako nāma assakhaḷuṅko. Sineruparibhaṇḍe simbalirukkhehi sañchādito paññāsayojano daho simbalidaho, taṃ parivāretvā mahantaṃ simbalivanaṃ, taṃ sandhāyāha “simbalidahavane”ti. Aññatitthāvāsabhūmiyaṃ imesu samaṇesu ekacco na uppajjati, īdiso panettha vikappo natthi, sabbena sabbaṃ na uppajjantevāti dassento “ekasamaṇopī”ti āha. Ariyamaggaparikkhateti ariyamagguppattiyā abhisaṅkhate, yadā sāsanikānaṃ sammāpaṭipattiyā ariyamaggo dibbati, tadāti attho.

Now, to support the meaning as previously stated, both by way of exposition and by the Pāli text, the phrase 'therefore the Blessed One said' and so forth introduces the Pāli text, and by presenting an analogy, the commentary elucidates the sutta, beginning with 'because' and so forth. Here, because for some lions in particular, the front pair of feet also performs the function of hands, therefore it is said, 'with reddish hands and feet.' The hairs of a lion are the mane, the hairs on the shoulders. The 'Gocariya elephant family' refers to the ordinary elephant family, which is also called 'Kālāvaka.' 'Ghoṭaka' means a young horse. In the region around Sineru, a fifty-yojana lake covered with silk-cotton trees is the Simbalidaha. Surrounding it is a great silk-cotton forest; referring to that, it is said 'in the Simbalidaha forest.' To show that in the realm of the dwellings of other sectarians not even one of these recluses arises—that there is no such alternative here, that they do not arise at all—it is said, 'not even a single recluse.' 'Prepared by the Noble Path' means prepared for the arising of the Noble Path; the meaning is that when the Noble Path shines forth through the right practice of those in the dispensation, then.

Sammāti suṭṭhu. Suṭṭhu nadanaṃ nāma hetuyuttaṃ suṭṭhu katvā kathananti āha “hetunā”ti. So ca hetu aviparīto eva icchitabboti āha “nayenā”ti, ñāyenāti attho. Evaṃbhūto ca so yathādhippetatthaṃ karoti sādhetīti dassento āha “kāraṇenā”ti. Yadi tiracchānasīhassa nādo sabbatiracchānaekaccamanussāmanussanādato seṭṭhattā seṭṭhanādo, kimaṅgaṃ pana tathāgatasīhanādoti āha “sīhanādanti seṭṭhanāda”nti. Yadi tiracchānasīhanādassa seṭṭhanādatā nibbhayatāya appaṭisattutāya icchitā, tathāgatasīhanādasseva ayamattho sātisayoti āha “abhītanādaṃ appaṭināda”nti. Idānissa seṭṭhanādabhāvaṃ kāraṇena paṭipādento “imesañhī”tiādimāha. Tena “sammā”ti vuttamatthaṃ samattheti. Tattha atthitāyāti iminā sīhanādassa uttamatthataṃ dasseti. Bhūtaṭṭho hi uttamaṭṭho. Tāya eva bhūtaṭṭhatāya abhītanādatāti dassento “ime samaṇā…pe… nāma hotī”ti āha. Abhūtañhi vadato kutoci [M 2.0006] bhayaṃ vā āsaṅkā vā siyāti “idhevā”ti niyamassa aviparītataṃ dassento “amhākampi…pe… appaṭinādo nāma hotī”ti āha. Yañhi aññatthāpi atthi, taṃ idhevāti avadhāretuṃ na yuttanti.

‘Sammā’ means well. Well-roaring is speaking well, endowed with reason; hence it is said, ‘by reason’. And that reason should be understood as correct, hence it is said, ‘by method’—meaning by the right way. Such a one accomplishes the intended purpose; hence it is shown by saying, ‘by cause’. If the roar of a beastly lion is the best roar because it excels the roars of all beasts, some humans, and non-humans, how much more so the roar of the Tathāgata lion? Hence it is said, ‘the lion’s roar is the best roar’. If the best quality of a beastly lion’s roar is considered to be its fearlessness and lack of opposition, then the roar of the Tathāgata lion surpasses even this meaning; hence it is said, ‘the fearless roar, the unopposed roar’. Now, establishing its supreme roar by cause, it is said, ‘for these too…’. Thus, it supports the meaning of what was stated as ‘well’. Here, ‘because it exists’ shows the supreme reality of the lion’s roar. For the true state is the highest truth. By that very true state, it is shown as the fearless roar; hence it is said, ‘these recluses… are called…’. For one who speaks falsely, fear or suspicion may arise from anywhere; hence, to show the invariability of the rule ‘only here,’ it is said, ‘for us too… the unopposed roar is called…’. For what also exists elsewhere, it is not proper to define by saying ‘only here’.

140. Khoti avadhāraṇe. Tena vijjati evāti dasseti. Yanti karaṇatthe paccattanti āha “yena kāraṇenā”ti. Titthaṃ nāma dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo tabbinimuttassa kassaci diṭṭhivipphanditassa abhāvato. Pāragamanasaṅkhātaṃ taraṇaṃ diṭṭhigatikānaṃ (a. ni. ṭī. 2.3.62) tattha tattheva aparāparaṃ ummujjananimujjanavasena pilavananti āha “taranti uppalavantī”ti. Uppādetāti pūraṇādiko. Titthe jātāti titthiyā, yathāvuttaṃ vā diṭṭhigatasaṅkhātaṃ [V 2.0006] titthaṃ etesaṃ atthīti titthikā, titthikā eva titthiyā. Assasanti ettha, etenāti vā assāso, avassayo.

140. ‘Kho’ is used for emphasis. By this, it shows ‘it certainly exists’. ‘Yanti’ in the sense of instrumentality means ‘by which reason,’ as stated: ‘yena kāraṇena’. ‘Tittha’ means the sixty-two views, since for one who is freed from them, there is no agitation of views. The crossing over, called ‘pāragamana’, for those adhering to views (A.N.Ṭī. 2.3.62) is floundering by repeatedly rising and sinking here and there, hence it is said: ‘they cross over, they float’. ‘Uppādetā’ means one who fills or completes, and so forth. ‘Born in a ford’, hence ‘titthiyā’ (sectarians); or, as previously stated, those for whom the collection of views is called ‘tittha’ are ‘titthikā’; ‘titthikā’ are indeed ‘titthiyā’. ‘Assasanti’ means ‘they breathe’ in this, or ‘by this’; thus ‘assāso’ means relief, ‘avassayo’ means dependence.

Pakatatthaniddeso yaṃ-taṃ-saddoti tassa “bhagavatā”tiādīhi padehi samānādhikaraṇabhāvena vuttassa yena abhisambuddhabhāvena bhagavā pakato satthubhāvena adhigato supākaṭo ca, taṃ abhisambuddhabhāvaṃ saddhiṃ āgamanapaṭipadāya atthabhāvena dassento “yo so…pe… abhisambuddho”ti āha. Satipi ñāṇadassanasaddānaṃ idha paññāvevacanabhāve tena tena visesena nesaṃ savisaye visesappavattidassanatthaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. parivāra 3.1) asādhāraṇavisesavasena vijjāttayavasena vijjābhiññānāvaraṇavasena sabbaññutaññāṇamaṃsacakkhuvasena paṭivedhadesanāñāṇavasena ca te yojetvā dassento “tesaṃ tesa”ntiādimāha. Tattha āsayānusayaṃ jānatā āsayānusayañāṇena, sabbaṃ ñeyyadhammaṃ passatā sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇehi. Pubbenivāsādīhīti pubbenivāsaāsavakkhayañāṇehi. Anaññasādhāraṇapuññānubhāvanibbatto anuttarañāṇādhigamaladdhapurāvattako ca bhagavato rūpakāyo atikkammeva devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ vattatīti āha “sabbasattānaṃ…pe… passatā”ti. Paṭivedhapaññāyāti maggapaññāya. Tāya hi sabbaso ñeyyadhammesu sammohassa vidhamitattā pacchā pavattajānanaṃ tassa jānanaṃ viya vuccati.

The exposition of the natural state (pakatatthaniddeso) is as follows: That which is called "the Blessed One" and so forth, by virtue of being in the same grammatical case, is stated to be naturally evident (pakato) because the Blessed One, through his fully awakened nature (abhisambuddhabhāvena), attained the state of a teacher (satthubhāvena) and is supremely evident (supākaṭo). To show the meaning of this fully awakened nature along with the path leading to it (āgamanapaṭipadāya) as its inherent characteristic, it is said: "He who… has fully awakened…" (yo so…pe… abhisambuddho). Here, even though the terms "knowledge" (ñāṇa) and "vision" (dassana) are synonymous with wisdom (paññā), to demonstrate the distinctive manifestations of these terms in their respective domains and their specific application, they are explained through various distinctions: as unique excellences (asādhāraṇavisesa), the threefold knowledge (vijjāttaya), unobstructed knowledge and supernormal powers (vijjābhiññānāvaraṇa), omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) and the fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu), and the knowledge of penetration and teaching (paṭivedhadesanāñāṇa). Thus, explaining them by combining them, he says: "Of these…" (tesaṃ tesaṃ). Here, by the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies (āsayānusayañāṇa), one knows the inclinations and latent tendencies (āsayānusaya). By the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇa), one sees all knowable phenomena (ñeyyadhamma). With past lives and so forth (pubbenivāsādīhi), it refers to the knowledge of past lives and the destruction of the taints (pubbenivāsaāsavakkhayañāṇa). The Blessed One’s physical form (rūpakāyo), arisen from the power of unparalleled merit (anaññasādhāraṇapuññānubhāva) and obtained in previous existences through the attainment of supreme knowledge (anuttarañāṇādhigama), surpasses even the divine splendor of the gods (devānaṃ devānubhāva). Thus, it is said: "Of all beings… he sees…" (sabbasattānaṃ…pe… passatā). The wisdom of penetration (paṭivedhapaññā) refers to the wisdom of the path (maggapaññā). Because by it, delusion (sammoha) regarding all knowable phenomena (ñeyyadhamma) is completely dispelled, subsequent knowledge (pacchā pavattajānana) is called the knowing of that (tassa jānanaṃ).

Arīnanti kilesārīnaṃ, pañcavidhamārānaṃ vā sāsanapaccatthikānaṃ vā aññatitthiyānaṃ, tesaṃ hananaṃ pāṭihāriyehi abhibhavanaṃ appaṭibhānatākaraṇaṃ ajjhupekkhanaṃ [M 2.0007] vā. Kesivinayasuttañcettha (a. ni. 4.111) nidassanaṃ. Tathā ca ṭhānāṭṭhānādīni vā jānatā, yathākammupage satte passatā, savāsanānamāsavānaṃ khīṇattā arahatā, abhiññeyyādibhede dhamme abhiññeyyādito aviparītāvabodhena sammāsambuddhena. Atha vā tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇatāya jānatā, kāyakammādīnaṃ ñāṇānuparivattanena nisammakāritāya passatā, ravādīnampi (sārattha. ṭī. parivāra 3.1) abhāvasādhikāya pahānasampadāya arahatā, chandādīnaṃ ahānihetubhūtāya akkhayapaṭibhānasādhikāya sabbaññutāya sammāsambuddhena. Evaṃ dasabalaaṭṭhārasāveṇikabuddhadhammavasenapi yojanā veditabbā. Yeti caturo dhamme. Attanīti amhesu. Na rājarājamahāmattādīsu upatthambhaṃ sampassamānā, na kāyabalaṃ sampassamānāti yojanā.

"Arīnaṃ" means of the enemies—the defilements, the fivefold Māra, the enemies of the dispensation, or other sectarians; their destruction ("hananaṃ") is overcoming them with miracles, rendering them speechless, or remaining indifferent to them. The Kesivinaya Sutta (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.111) serves as an example here. Moreover, by knowing what is possible and impossible, by seeing beings according to their deeds; by being an Arahant, because the taints with their latent tendencies are destroyed; by being the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, with undistorted comprehension of phenomena in their categories, such as what should be directly known, and so forth. Alternatively, by knowing without obstruction in the three times, by seeing by examining the succession of knowledge regarding bodily actions and so forth; by being an Arahant, by the perfection of abandonment that effects the non-existence even of sounds, etc. (Sāratthappakāsinī, Parivāra 3.1); by being the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, by omniscience that is the cause of non-decline of zeal etc., and effects inexhaustible insight. Thus, the application should be understood by way of the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. "Ye" refers to the four things. "Attanīti" means "in us." The application is: "not seeing support in kings, great ministers, and so forth, nor seeing bodily strength."

Uppannapasādoti aveccappasādaṃ vadati. Vakkhati hi “cattāri sotāpannassa aṅgāni kathitānī”ti [V 2.0007] (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.140). Kāmaṃ asekkhāpi asekkhāya samasikkhatāya sahadhammikā eva, ciṇṇabrahmacariyatāya pana sahadhammaṃ carantīti na vattabbāti asekkhavāro na gahito. Sabbepeteti ete yathāvuttā bhikkhuādayo sotāpannādayo ca puthujjanā ariyā cāti sabbepi ete taṃtaṃsikkhāhi samānadhammattā sahadhammattā “sahadhammikā”ti vuccanti. Idāni nibbattitaariyadhammavaseneva sahadhammike dassento “apicā”tiādimāha. Maggadassanamhīti pariññābhisamayādivasena saccapaṭivedhena “nava maggaṅgāni, aṭṭha bojjhaṅgānī”tiādinā vivādo natthi. Ekadhammacāritāyāti samānadhammacāritāya. Na hi paṭividdhasaccānaṃ “mayā dhammo sudiṭṭho, tayā duddiṭṭho”tiādinā vivādo atthi. Diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṅghātā hi te uttamapurisā. Imināti “sahadhammikā kho panā”tiādivacanena. Tattha piyamanāpaggahaṇena sīlesu paripūrakāritāpadesena ekadesena gahitaṃ saṅghasuppaṭipattiṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā dasseti. Ye hi sampannasīlā suvisuddhadassanā, te viññūnaṃ piyā manāpāti. Ettāvatāti “atthi kho no āvuso”tiādinayappavattena ratanattayapasādajotanena akkhātā tesu tesu suttapadesesu.

"Uppannapasādo" refers to unwavering confidence. For it is said: "The four factors of a stream-enterer have been taught" (Majjhima Nikāya, Aṭṭhakathā 1.140). Even though those beyond training (asekkha) are indeed companions in the Dhamma by having the same training as those who are still training, yet because they have already completed the holy life, it cannot be said that they are 'practicing the Dhamma together' (sahadhammaṃ caranti). Therefore, the section on those beyond training is not included. "All these" (sabbepete) means all these monks and so on, stream-enterers and so on, both ordinary people and noble ones as described before — all these are called "companions in the Dhamma" because they share the same qualities and the same Dhamma by being committed to those trainings. Now, showing the companions in the Dhamma only through the arising of noble qualities, he says "moreover" (apicā) and so on. Regarding "seeing the path" (maggadassanamhi), there is no dispute about the penetration of the truths by way of full understanding, direct knowledge, etc., such as "the nine factors of the path, the eight factors of enlightenment," and so on. "Practicing the same Dhamma" (ekadhammacāritāya) means practicing in accordance with the same Dhamma. For those who have penetrated the truths, there is no dispute like, "I have clearly seen the Dhamma, but you have not." Indeed, these supreme persons are united by shared views and virtuous conduct. By this—the statement "companions in the Dhamma indeed" (sahadhammikā kho panā) and so on—he shows the complete good practice of the Saṅgha, completing what was partially taken up by the mention of 'dear and pleasing' and by the description of 'accomplishment in virtues'. For those who are accomplished in virtue and possess purified vision are dear and pleasing to the wise. "To this extent" (ettāvatā)—through the approach beginning with "Indeed, friends, we have..."—the radiance of confidence in the Triple Gem is explained in those various sutta passages.

141. Satthari pasādoti pasādaggahaṇena “bhagavatā”tiādinā vā pasādanīyā dhammā gahitā. Tena buddhasubuddhataṃ dasseti, tathā “dhamme [M 2.0008] pasādo”ti iminā dhammasudhammataṃ, itarena saṅghasuppaṭipannataṃ. Yena cittena aññattha anupalabbhamānena sāsaneyeva samaṇo ito bahiddhā natthīti ayamattho, sammadeva, patiṭṭhāpitoti veditabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ yojanā – yasmā sammāsambuddho amhākaṃ satthā, tasmā atthi kho no, āvuso, satthari pasādo, sammāsambuddhattā cassa svākhāto dhammoti atthi dhamme pasādo, tato eva ca atthi sīlesu paripūrakāritāti sahadhammikā…pe… pabbajitā cāti evamettha satthari pasādena dhamme pasādo, tena saṅghasuppaṭipattīti ayañca nayo lesenapi parappavādesu natthīti idheva samaṇo…pe… samaṇehi aññehīti.

141. “Faith in the Teacher”: by the taking up of ‘faith,’ qualities that inspire faith, such as those beginning with “the Blessed One,” are taken up. Through that, one shows the Buddha's perfect enlightenment; similarly, by “faith in the Dhamma,” the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma is shown, and by the other, the Saṅgha’s good practice.
