It should be understood that by a mind not found elsewhere, this meaning—that there is no ascetic outside this teaching—is rightly established. Here is the connection: Because the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is our Teacher, therefore, friends, we have faith in the Teacher. And because he is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-expounded by him; thus, there is faith in the Dhamma. And for that very reason, there is fulfillment of the virtues, and thus they are companions in the Dhamma... and renunciates. Thus, in this context, through faith in the Teacher, there is faith in the Dhamma, and through that, the Saṅgha’s good practice. And this method, even in a slight degree, does not exist in other doctrines; hence, ‘here alone is there an ascetic... than other ascetics.’

Paṭividdhasaccānaṃ pahīnānurodhānaṃ gehassitapemassa asambhavo evāti “idānī”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ “upajjhāyena, bhikkhave, saddhivihārikamhi puttapemaṃ upaṭṭhapetabbaṃ”tiādivacanaṃ (mahāva. 65) kathanti? Nayidaṃ gehassitapemaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, taṃsadisattā pana pemamukhena vutto mettāsneho. Na hi bhagavā bhikkhū saṃkilese niyojeti. Evarūpaṃ pemaṃ sandhāyāti pasādāvahaguṇāvahato pūraṇādīsu bhatti pasādo na hoti, pasādapatirūpakā pana lobhapavattīti daṭṭhabbā. Theroti mahāsaṅgharakkhitatthero. Yena aṭṭhakathā potthakaṃ [V 2.0008] āropitā. Ekova satthā anaññasādhāraṇaguṇattā, aññathā anacchariyattā satthulakkhaṇameva na paripūreyya. Visuṃ katvāti aññehi vivecetvā attano āveṇikaṃ katvā. “Amhākaṃ satthā”ti byāvadantānaṃ aññesaṃ satthā na hotīti atthato āpannameva hoti, tathā ca padesavattiniṃ tassa satthutaṃ paṭijānantā paripuṇṇalakkhaṇasatthutaṃ icchantānampi tato viruddhā satthubhāvapariyesanena parājitā honti. Pariyattidhammeti adhikabrahmaguṇasuttageyyādippabhedasamaye. Tattha ajasīla…pe… kukkurasīlādīsūti idaṃ yebhuyyena aññatitthiyānaṃ tādisaṃ vatasamādānasabbhāvato vuttaṃ, ādi-saddena yamaniyamacātuyāmasaṃvarādīnaṃ saṅgahoti. Adhippayāsoti adhikaṃ payasati payujjati etenāti adhippayāso, savisesaṃ adhikattabbakiriyā (a. ni. ṭī. 2.3.117). Tenāha “adhikappayogo”ti.

“Now” is said because for those who have penetrated the truths and for whom attachments have been abandoned, the existence of household-based affection is impossible. If so, how is the statement, “Monks, a preceptor should establish affection for a co-resident like that for a son” (Mahāvagga 65), to be understood? This was not spoken with reference to household-based affection, but rather, due to the similarity, it refers to loving-kindness expressed through affection. For the Blessed One does not direct monks toward defilements. Referring to such affection, it should be understood that devotion and confidence in acts of service like filling water pots do not arise from bringing about confidence and good qualities; rather, they are an activity of greed, a counterfeit of confidence. “The Elder” refers to the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita, by whom the commentary was written down in a book. The Teacher is unique, due to his qualities not shared by others; otherwise, being unsurprising, he would not fulfill the very characteristic of a Teacher. “Having made it distinct” means having separated it from others and made it his own unique quality. When they declare, “Our Teacher,” it is implied in meaning that he is not the teacher of others. And thus, those who acknowledge his teachership in a limited sense, while desiring a teacher with complete characteristics, are defeated by their search for a state of teachership contrary to that. By “the scriptural Dhamma,” it refers to the time of the divisions such as the Adhikabrahmaguṇa Sutta, Geyya, and so forth. There, “goat-practice… dog-practice,” and so forth are mostly spoken of in reference to the existence of such vow-undertakings among ascetics of other sects. The term “etc.” includes yama, niyama, the fourfold restraint, and so on. “Adhippayāso” means “that by which one strives or engages excessively”; it is a special, additional action to be done. Hence, he says, “excessive application.”

Tassa [M 2.0009] pasādassa pariyosānabhūtāti tassa satthari dhamme ca pasādassa niṭṭhānabhūtā. Niṭṭhāti mokkho. Samayavādīnañhi tasmiṃ tasmiṃ samaye tadupadesake ca pasādo yāvadeva mokkhādhigamanaṭṭho. Diṭṭhigatikā tathā tathā attano laddhivasena niṭṭhaṃ parikappenti yevāti āha “niṭṭhaṃ apaññapento nāma natthī”ti. Brāhmaṇānanti brāhmaṇavādīnaṃ. Tesaṃ ekacce brahmunā salokatā niṭṭhāti vadanti, ekacce tassa samīpatā, ekacce tena saṃyogo niṭṭhāti vadanti. Tattha ye salokatāvādino samīpatāvādino ca, te dvedhāvādino, itare advedhāvādino. Sabbepi te atthato brahmalokupapattiyaṃyeva niṭṭhāsaññino. Tattha hi nesaṃ niccābhiniveso yathā taṃ bakassa brahmuno. Tena vuttaṃ “brahmaloko niṭṭhā”ti. Brahmalokoti paṭhamajjhānabhūmi. Mahātāpasānanti vekhanasāditāpasānaṃ. Mahābrahmā viya paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ ābhassaresu eko sabbaseṭṭho natthīti “ābhassarā”ti puthuvacanaṃ. Paribbājakānanti sañcayādiparibbājakānaṃ. Anto ca mano ca etassa natthīti anantamānaso. Ājīvakānañhi sabbadābhāvato ananto, sukhadukkhādisamatikkamanato amānaso. Iminā aṭṭhahi lokadhammehi upakkiliṭṭhacittataṃ dasseti.

“The culmination of that confidence” means the final state of that confidence in the Teacher and the Dhamma. The final state is liberation. For the proponents of various doctrines, confidence in a particular doctrine and in its teacher is only for the purpose of attaining liberation. Followers of speculative views, however, conceive of a final state in various ways according to their own tenets. Therefore, it is said: “There is no one who does not declare a final state.” “Of the brahmins” refers to the proponents of brahminical doctrines. Among them, some say the final state is co-existence with Brahmā, some say it is proximity to him, and some say it is union with him. Among these, those who advocate co-existence and proximity are dualists, while the others are non-dualists. Yet all of them, in meaning, perceive rebirth in the Brahmā world as the final state. For them, there is a fixed adherence to permanence there, as was the case with Baka Brahmā. Hence, it is said: “The Brahmā world is the final state.” “The Brahmā world” refers to the plane of the first jhāna. “Of the great ascetics” refers to ascetics like Vekhanasa and others. Unlike Mahābrahmā in the first jhāna realm, among the Ābhassaras there is no single supreme one; therefore the plural ‘Ābhassarā’ is used. “Of the wanderers” refers to wanderers like Sañcaya and others. “Anantamānaso” means “he for whom there is no end (anta) and no mind (māna).” For the Ājīvikas, it is endless because of perpetual non-existence, and ‘mindless’ because of transcending pleasure, pain, and so on. This demonstrates a mind defiled by the eight worldly conditions.

Papañce yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Taṇhādiṭṭhiyova adhippetā mamaṅkāraahaṅkāravigamassa adhippetattā. Yathā pañcasu ṭhānesu ekova kileso lobho āgato, evaṃ dvīsu ṭhānesu tayo kilesā āgatā “doso moho diṭṭhī”ti. “Sadosassā”ti hi vuttaṭṭhāne paṭighaṃ akusalamūlaṃ gahitaṃ, “paṭiviruddhassā”ti virodho, “samohassā”ti moho akusalamūlaṃ, “aviddasuno”ti malyaṃ, asampajaññaṃ vā, “saupādānassā”ti “natthi dinna”ntiādinā nayena gahaṇaṃ, “papañcārāmassā”ti papañcuppattivasena.

Concerning proliferation, what is to be said has already been stated below. Craving and views are intended, since the abandonment of I-making and mine-making is intended. Just as in five instances one defilement, greed, has come up, so in two instances three defilements have come up: “hatred, delusion, and view.” For in the place where “one with hatred” is said, the unwholesome root of aversion is taken; in “one who is opposed,” opposition; in “one with delusion,” the unwholesome root of delusion; in “one who is ignorant,” dullness or lack of clear comprehension; in “one with clinging,” grasping according to the method beginning with “there is nothing given”; in “one who delights in proliferation,” it is in terms of the arising of proliferation.

Ākāratoti [V 2.0009] pavattiākārato. Padantarena rāgavisesassa vuccamānattāādito vuttaṃ sarāgavacanaṃ oḷārikaṃ rāgavisayanti āha “pañcakāmaguṇikarāgavasenā”ti. Gahaṇavasenāti daḷhaggahaṇavasena. “Anuruddhapaṭiviruddhassā”ti ekapadavasena pāḷiyaṃ āgatattā ekajjhaṃ paduddhāro kato. Tattha pana “anuruddhassā”ti subhavasenāti evamattho vattabbo. Na hi paṭivirujjhanaṃ subhavasena hoti. Papañcuppattidassanavasenāti kilesakammavipākānaṃ aparāparuppattipaccayatāya [M 2.0010] saṃsārassa papañcanaṃ papañco, tassa uppattihetubhāvadassanavasena. Taṇhā hi bhavuppattiyā visesapaccayo. Taṇhāpaccayā upādānadassanavasenāti taṇhāpaccayassa upādānassa dassanavasena, yadavatthā taṇhā upādānassa paccayo, tadavatthādassanavasena. Phalena hi hetuvisesakittanametanti. Evaṃ viddhaṃsethāti kāmarāgabhavataṇhādivasena lobhaṃ kasmā evaṃ vippakiretha. Taṇhākaraṇavasenāti taṇhāyanakaraṇavasena subhākāraggahaṇavasena. Subhanti hi ārammaṇe pavatto rāgo “subha”nti vutto.

“From the mode” means from the mode of occurrence. Because a specific kind of lust is mentioned by another term, the initially mentioned “speech with lust” refers to a gross object of lust; thus he says, “by way of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure.” “By way of grasping” means by way of firm grasping. Because “for one who is attached and opposed” comes in the Pāli as a single compound, a single analysis of the term is made. There, however, “for one who is attached” should be understood as “by way of the beautiful,” for opposition does not occur by way of the beautiful. “By way of seeing the arising of proliferation” means by way of seeing the cause of the arising of proliferation, where proliferation is the expansion of saṃsāra due to being a condition for the successive arising of defilements, kamma, and results. For craving is a specific condition for the arising of existence. “By way of seeing clinging as conditioned by craving” means by way of seeing clinging as conditioned by craving; that is, by way of seeing the state in which craving is a condition for clinging. For this is the declaration of a specific cause by means of its result. “Why would you thus destroy it?” means: why would you thus scatter greed by way of sensual lust, craving for existence, and so on? “By way of causing craving” means by way of making it an object of craving, by way of grasping the aspect of the beautiful. For lust that has arisen in regard to an object considered beautiful is called “the beautiful.”

142. Vadanti etenāti vādo, diṭṭhivādo. Diṭṭhivasena hi “sassato attā ca loko ca, asassato attā ca loko cā”ti ca diṭṭhigatikā paññapenti. Tenāha “dvemā, bhikkhave, diṭṭhiyo”ti (ma. ni. 1.142). Taṇhārahitāya diṭṭhiyā abhāvato taṇhāvaseneva ca attano sassatabhāvābhinivesoti katvā vuttaṃ “taṇhādiṭṭhivasenā”ti. Allīnāti nissitā. Upagatāti avissajjanavasena ekibhāvamiva gatā. Ajjhositāti tāya diṭṭhiyā gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpitā viya tadantogadhā. Tenāha “anupaviṭṭhā”ti. Yathā gahaṭṭhānaṃ kāmajjhosānaṃ vivādamūlaṃ, evaṃ pabbajitānaṃ diṭṭhajjhosānanti āha “vibhavadiṭṭhiyā te paṭiviruddhā”ti. Diṭṭhivirodhena hi diṭṭhigatikavirodho.

142. They speak by means of this, thus it is a doctrine, a doctrinal view. For by means of views, those who adhere to views assert such things as, 'the self and the world are eternal,' or 'the self and the world are not eternal.' Therefore, it is said: 'Bhikkhus, there are these two views.' Because there is no view free from craving, and because adherence to the notion of one's own eternal existence is solely through the power of craving, it is said: 'by means of craving and views.' 'Clung to' means dependent. 'Undertaken' means having gone as if to oneness, by way of not relinquishing. 'Engrossed' means as if swallowed by that view and completely settled, being included within it. Hence, it is said: 'entered into.' Just as for householders, engrossment in sensual pleasures is the root of disputes, so for renunciants, engrossment in views is the root. Therefore, it is said: 'they are opposed to the view of annihilation.' For through the opposition of views, there is opposition among those who adhere to views.

Khaṇikasamudayo uppādakkhaṇoti āha “diṭṭhīnaṃ nibbattī”ti. Diṭṭhinibbattiggahaṇeneva cettha yathā diṭṭhīnaṃ paṭiccasamuppannatā vibhāvitā, evaṃ diṭṭhivatthunopīti ubhayesampi aniccatā dukkhatā anattatā ca vibhāvitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yāni paṭisambhidānayena (paṭi. ma. 1.122) “paccayasamudayo aṭṭha ṭhānānī”ti vuttāni, tāni dassento “khandhāpī”tiādimāha. Tattha khandhāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ ārammaṇaṭṭhena “rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī”tiādivacanato (saṃ. ni. 3.81; 4.345). Avijjāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ upanissayādivasena paccayabhāvato. Yathāha – “assutavā, bhikkhave, puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.2, 461; saṃ. ni. 3.1, 7). Phassopi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ. Yathā cāha “tadapi phassapaccayā (dī. ni. 1.118-130), phussa phussa paṭisaṃvediyantī”ti (dī. ni. 1.144) ca[V 2.0010]. Saññāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ “saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhāti [M 2.0011] (su. ni. 880), pathaviṃ pathavito saññatvā”ti (ma. ni. 1.2) ca ādi. Vitakkopi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ “takkañca diṭṭhīsu pakappayitvā, saccaṃ musāti dvayadhammamāhū”ti (su. ni. 892; mahāni. 121) “takkī hoti vīmaṃsī”ti (dī. ni. 1.34) ca ādi. Ayonisomanasikāropi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ. Yathāha bhagavā “tasseva ayoniso manasikaroto channaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ aññatarā diṭṭhi uppajjati, atthi me attāti assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjatī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.19). Samuṭṭhāti etenāti samuṭṭhānaṃ, tassa bhāvo samuṭṭhānaṭṭho, tena. Khaṇikatthaṅgamo khaṇikanirodho. Paccayatthaṅgamo avijjādīnaṃ accantanirodho. So pana yena hoti, taṃ dassento “sotāpattimaggo”ti āha. Cattāro hi ariyamaggā yathārahaṃ tassa tassa saṅkhāragatassa accantanirodhahetu, khaṇikanirodho pana ahetuko.

The momentary arising is the moment of arising; hence, it is said, 'the arising of views.' By the very grasping of the arising of views, it should be understood that just as the dependently arisen nature of views is clarified, so too is that of the objects of views; thus, the impermanence, suffering, and non-self of both are clarified. The grounds mentioned in the Paṭisambhidāmagga as 'the arising of conditions, eight grounds' are shown by stating, 'the aggregates too,' etc. Herein, the aggregates are a basis for views by way of being an object, as in the statement, 'he regards form as self,' etc. Ignorance too is a basis for views by way of being a condition through dependence, etc. As it is said: 'The uninstructed worldling, bhikkhus, who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the noble Dhamma,' etc. Contact too is a basis for views. As it is said: 'That too is conditioned by contact,' and 'experiencing through repeated contact.' Perception too is a basis for views, for it is said: 'For perception is the source of the proliferation of concepts,' and 'having perceived earth as earth,' etc. Thought too is a basis for views, and this is said: 'Having fashioned a thought among views, they declare the twofold nature of truth and falsehood,' and 'he is a reasoner, an investigator,' etc. Unwise attention too is a basis for views. As the Blessed One said: 'For one who unwisely attends, one of the six views arises: "There is a self for me"—this view arises as true and firm,' etc. 'It originates from this,' thus it is an origin; its state is the meaning of origin; by that. Momentary passing away is momentary cessation. The passing away of the condition is the absolute cessation of ignorance, etc. That, however, by which this occurs is shown by saying, 'the path of stream-entry.' For the four noble paths, each in its own way, are the cause of the absolute cessation of this or that conditioned thing, whereas momentary cessation is without a cause.

Ānisaṃsanti udayaṃ. So pana diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikavasena duvidho. Tattha samparāyiko duggatiparikilesatāyaādīnavapakkhiko evāti itaraṃ dassento “yaṃ sandhāyā”tiādimāha. Ādīnavampi diṭṭhadhammikameva dassento “diṭṭhiggahaṇamūlakaṃ upaddava”ntiādimāha. Sotiādīnavo. Ādīnanti ādi-saddena naggiyānasanasaṅkaṭivatādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Nissarati etenāti nissaraṇanti vuccamāne dassanamaggo eva diṭṭhīnaṃ nissaraṇaṃ siyā, tassa pana atthaṅgamapariyāyena gahitattā sabbasaṅkhatanissaṭaṃ nibbānaṃ diṭṭhīhipi nissaṭanti katvā vuttaṃ “diṭṭhīnaṃ nissaraṇaṃ nāma nibbāna”nti. Iminātiādīsu vattabbaṃ anuyogavatte vuttanayameva.

'Advantage' means benefit. That, however, is twofold: in the present life and in the future life. Herein, since the future-life aspect is indeed on the side of danger due to the defilement of a bad destination, showing the other aspect, he says, 'with reference to which,' and so on. Showing the danger as also being in the present life, he says, 'the calamity rooted in grasping views,' and so on. That is the danger. As for 'danger,' by the word 'etc.' there is the inclusion of nakedness, fasting, the practice of squatting, and so on. When it is said, 'one escapes by this,' thus it is an 'escape,' the path of vision itself would be the escape from views. However, since that has been taken in the sense of 'passing away,' it is said, 'the escape from views is called Nibbāna,' on the grounds that Nibbāna, which is the escape from all conditioned things, is also the escape from views. Regarding 'By this,' and so on, what is to be said is in the same way as was stated in the section on inquiry.

143. Diṭṭhicchedanaṃ dassentoti sabbupādānapariññādassanena sabbaso diṭṭhīnaṃ samucchedavidhiṃ dassento. Vuttāyevāti –

143. 'Showing the cutting off of views' means: showing the method for the utter eradication of all views by means of the vision of the full understanding of all clinging. As was said—

“Upādānāni cattāri, tāni atthavibhāgato;

Dhammasaṅkhepavitthārā, kamato ca vibhāvaye”ti. (visuddhi. 2.645) –

"There are four kinds of clinging; classified by meaning, expounded briefly and in detail, and in order, discern them."

Gāthaṃ uddisitvā atthavibhāgādivasena vuttāyeva. Kāmaṃ ito bāhirakānaṃ “imāni upādānāni ettakāni cattāri, na ito bhiyyo”ti īdisaṃ ñāṇaṃ natthi, kevalaṃ pana keci “kāmā pahātabbā”ti vadanti, keci “natthi paro lokoti ca, micchā”ti vadanti, apare “sīlabbatena suddhīti [M 2.0012] ca, micchā”ti vadanti, attadiṭṭhiyā pana micchābhāvaṃ sabbaso na jānanti eva. Yattakaṃ pana jānanti, tassapi accantappahānaṃ na jānanti, tathāpi sabbassa pariññeyyassa [V 2.0011] pariññeyyaṃ paññapemaicceva tiṭṭhanti. Evaṃbhūtānaṃ pana nesaṃ tattha yādisī paṭipatti, taṃ dassento satthā “santi, bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha santīti saṃvijjanti. Tena tesaṃ diṭṭhigatikānaṃ vijjamānatāya avicchedataṃ dasseti. Eketi ekacce. Samaṇabrāhmaṇāti pabbajjupagamanena samaṇā, jātimattena ca brāhmaṇā. Sabbesanti anavasesānaṃ upādānānaṃ samatikkamaṃ pahānaṃ. Sammā na paññapentīti yesaṃ paññapenti, tesampi sammā pariññaṃ na paññapenti. Idāni taṃ atthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “kecī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha hotika-kuṭīcaka-bahūdaka-haṃsa-paramahaṃsa-kājaka-tidaṇḍa-monavata-seva-pārupaka-pañcamarattika- somakāraka-mugabbata-carabāka-tāpasa-niganthā-jīvaka-isi-pārāyanika-pañcātapika-kāpila- kāṇāda-saṃsāramocaka-aggibhattika-magavatika-govatika-kukkuravatika-kāmaṇḍaluka- vaggulivatika-ekasāṭaka-odakasuddhika-sarīrasantāpaka-sīlasuddhika-jhānasuddhika-catubbidha- sassatavādādayo channavuti taṇhāpāsena ḍaṃsanato, ariyadhammassa vā vibādhanato pāsaṇḍā. Vatthupaṭisevanaṃ kāmanti byāpārassa vatthuno paṭisevanasaṅkhātaṃ kāmaṃ. Theyyena sevantīti paṭihatthaādisamaññāya lokassa vacanavasena sevanti. Tīṇi kāraṇānīti “natthi dinna”ntiādinayappavattāni diṭṭhivisesabhūtāni vaṭṭakāraṇāni.

Having stated the verse, its meaning has already been explained by way of the division of meaning and so on. Indeed, those outside this dispensation have no such knowledge as: 'These clingings are fourfold; there are no more than these.' But some merely say, 'Sensual pleasures should be abandoned'; others say, 'There is no other world,' and that this is wrong; still others say, 'Purification is through rites and observances,' and that this is wrong. But they do not at all know the wrongness of the view of self. And to whatever extent they do know, they do not know its utter abandonment. Nevertheless, they stand by their claim: 'We make known what is to be fully understood of all that is to be fully understood.' To show what kind of practice such persons have, the Teacher said, 'There are, bhikkhus…' Here, 'there are' means they exist. By this he shows the uninterruptedness of the existence of those who hold such views. 'Some' means certain ones. 'Samaṇas and brahmins' means samaṇas by reason of having gone forth and brahmins by mere birth. 'Of all' means the overcoming and abandoning of all clingings without remainder. 'They do not rightly make known' means that even for those to whom they make it known, they do not rightly make known full understanding. Now, to show that meaning in detail, 'some,' etc., was said. Here, the Hotikas, Kuṭīcakas, Bahūdakas, Haṃsas, Paramahaṃsas, Kājakas, Tidaṇḍas, Monavatas, Sevas, Pārupakas, Pañcamarattikas, Somakārakas, Mugabbatas, Carabākas, Tāpasas, Nigaṇṭhas, Ājīvakas, Isis, Pārāyaṇikas, Pañcātapikas, Kāpilas, Kāṇādas, Saṃsāramocakas, Aggibhattikas, Magavatikas, Govatikas, Kukkuravatikas, Kāmaṇḍalukas, Vaggulivatikas, Ekasāṭakas, Odakasuddhikas, Sarīrasantāpakas, Sīlasuddhikas, Jhānasuddhikas, and the four kinds of eternalists, and so on—ninety-six in all—are heretics because they are bitten by the snare of craving or because they obstruct the noble Dhamma. 'Sensual pleasure' means the sensual pleasure reckoned as the partaking of an object of activity. 'They partake by stealth' means they partake in accordance with worldly parlance under the designation of 'reciprocal gift,' etc. 'Three causes' means the causes for the round of rebirths that are particular kinds of views proceeding in the manner of 'there is nothing given,' etc.

Atthasallāpikāti atthassa sallāpikā, dvinnaṃ adhippetatthasallāpavibhāvinīti adhippāyo. Dvinnañhi vacanaṃ sallāpo. Tenāha “pathavī kirā”tiādi.

`Atthasallāpikā` means one who converses about the meaning; the intention is that it clarifies the conversation about the intended meaning between two people. For the speech of two people is a conversation. Therefore it is said: 'The earth, it seems…' and so on.

Yo titthiyānaṃ attano satthari dhamme sahadhammikesu ca pasādo vutto, tassa anāyatanagatattā appasādakabhāvadassanaṃ pasādapacchedo. Tathāpavatto vādo pasādapacchedavādo vutto. Evarūpeti īdise vuttanayena kilesānaṃ anupasamasaṃvattanike. Dhammeti dhammapatirūpake. Vinayeti vinayapatirūpake. Titthiyā hi kohaññe ṭhatvā lokaṃ vañcentā dhammaṃ kathemāti “sattime kāyā akaṭā akaṭavidhā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.174) yaṃ kiñci kathetvā tathā “vinayaṃ paññapemā”ti [M 2.0013] gosīlavaggulivatādīni paññapetvā tādisaṃ sāvake sikkhāpetvā “dhammavinayo”ti kathenti, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “dhammavinaye”ti. Tenāha “ubhayenapi aniyyānikaṃ sāsanaṃ dassetī”ti. Parittampi nāma puññaṃ kātukāmaṃ maccheramalābhibhūtatāya nivārentassa antarāyaṃ tassa karoto diṭṭheva dhamme viññūhi garahitabbatā samparāye ca duggati pāṭikaṅkhā, kimaṅgaṃ pana sakalavaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇāvahe jinacakke pahāradāyino titthakarassa tadovādakarassa cāti imamatthaṃ dassento “aniyyānikasāsanamhi hī”tiādimāha. Yathā so pasādo [V 2.0012] samparāye na sammaggato attano pavattivasenāti dassento “kañci kālaṃ gantvāpi pacchā vinassati yevā”ti āha, aveccappasādo viya accantiko na hotīti attho.

The faith that heretics have in their own teacher, Dhamma, and co-religionists is spoken of. Because this is not grounded in a proper basis, seeing its uninspiring nature is the cutting off of faith. A doctrine that proceeds in such a way is called a 'faith-cutting doctrine.' 'In such' means in that which, in the way stated, is conducive to the non-pacification of the defilements. 'In the Dhamma' means in a counterfeit Dhamma. 'In the Vinaya' means in a counterfeit Vinaya. For heretics, established in hypocrisy and deceiving the world, say, 'We teach the Dhamma,' and having said whatever they please, such as, 'These seven bodies are uncreated, unmade...' (DN 1:56), and then, 'We lay down the Vinaya,' having laid down the cow-practice, the bat-practice, and so on, and having trained their disciples in such, they call it 'Dhamma-Vinaya.' It is with reference to this that 'in the Dhamma and Vinaya' was said. Therefore he says: 'He shows a teaching that is not emancipating in both ways.' For one who, being overcome by the stain of stinginess, prevents another who wishes to make even a little merit, creating an obstacle for him, there is blame from the wise in this very life and a bad destination is to be expected in the future. How much more so for the heretical teacher who strikes a blow against the Conqueror's Wheel, which leads to escape from all the suffering of the round, and for the one who gives his advice? To show this meaning, he said: 'For in a teaching that is not emancipating…' To show that such faith, because of its own nature, is not well-grounded in the future, he said: 'Even after continuing for some time, it later perishes.' The meaning is that it is not final, like confirmed confidence.

Sampajjamānā yathāvidhipaṭipattiyā tiracchānayoniṃ āvahati. Kammasarikkhakena hi vipākeneva bhavitabbaṃ. Sabbampi kāraṇabhedanti sabbampi yathāvuttaṃ titthakarānaṃ sāvakānaṃ apāyadukkhāvahaṃ micchāpaṭipattisaṅkhātaṃ kāraṇavisesaṃ. So panesa pasādo na niyyāti micchattapakkhikattā surāpītasiṅgāle pasādo viya. Suraṃ parissāvetvā chaḍḍitakasaṭaṃ surājallikaṃ. Brāhmaṇā nāma dhanaluddhāti adhippāyenāha “imaṃ vañcessāmī”ti. Kaṃsasatāti kahāpaṇasatā.

When accomplished, the practice according to their rule leads to the animal realm. For the result must be similar to the action. 'All the different causes' means all the specific causes mentioned above, reckoned as the wrong practice of the heretics' disciples, which brings the suffering of the plane of misery. But this faith does not lead out, because it sides with wrongness, like the faith in a jackal that has drunk liquor. `Surājallikaṃ` is the dregs discarded after straining liquor. With the intention, 'Brahmins are indeed greedy for wealth,' he said, 'I will deceive this one.' 'A hundred kaṃsas' means a hundred kahāpaṇas.

144. Tassāti pasādassa. Sabbopi lobho kāmupādānanteva vuccatīti āha “arahattamaggena kāmupādānassa pahānapariñña”nti. Evarūpeti īdise sabbaso kilesānaṃ upasamasaṃvattanike. Yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamānānaṃ apāyesu apatanavasena dhāraṇaṭṭhena dhamme. Sabbaso vinayanaṭṭhena vinaye. Tattha bhavadukkhanissaraṇāya saṃvattane.

144. 'Of that': of faith. Because all greed is called clinging to sensual pleasure, he said: 'the full understanding which is the abandoning of clinging to sensual pleasure by the path of arahantship.' 'In such': in that which is conducive to the complete pacification of all defilements. 'In the Dhamma': in the sense of upholding, because for those who practice as instructed it prevents them from falling into the planes of misery. 'In the Vinaya': in the sense of disciplining completely. Therein, it is conducive to the escape from the suffering of existence.

Namassamāno aṭṭhāsi dve asaṅkhyeyyāni paccekabodhipāramīnaṃ pūraṇena tattha buddhasāsane paricayena ca bhagavati pasannacittatāya ca. “Ulūkā”tyādigāthā rukkhadevatāya bhāsitā. Kāluṭṭhitanti sāyanhakāle divāvihārato uṭṭhitaṃ. Duggateso na gacchatīti duggatiṃ eso na gamissati. Morajiko murajavādako. Mahābherivādakavatthuādīnipi sitapātukaraṇaṃ ādiṃ katvā vitthāretabbāni.

He stood paying homage because of his fulfillment of the perfections for paccekabodhi for two incalculable aeons, because of his familiarity with the Buddha's dispensation, and because of his confident heart towards the Blessed One. The verse beginning 'Ulūkā...' was spoken by the tree deity. 'Risen up in time' means having risen in the evening from the day's abiding. 'He goes not to a bad state' means this one will not go to a bad destination. 'Morajiko' means a tabor-player. The stories of the great kettledrum player and others should be elaborated, beginning with the raising of the white parasol.

Paramattheti [M 2.0014] lokuttaradhamme. Kiṃ pana vattabbanti dhammepi paramatthe nimittaṃ gahetvā suṇantānaṃ. Sāmaṇeravatthūti pabbajitadivaseyeva sappena daṭṭho hutvā kālaṃ katvā devalokaṃ upapannasāmaṇeravatthu.

'In the ultimate sense': in the supramundane Dhamma. What more is to be said of those who listen, grasping the sign in the ultimate sense even from the teaching? 'The story of the novice': the story of the novice who, on the very day he went forth, was bitten by a snake, passed away, and was reborn in a devaloka.

Khīrodananti khīrena saddhiṃ sammissaṃ odanaṃ. Timbarusakanti tindukaphalaṃ. Tipusasadisā ekā vallijāti timbarusaṃ, tassa phalaṃ timbarusakanti ca vadanti. Kakkārikanti khuddakaelāḷukaṃ. Mahātipusanti ca vadanti. Vallipakkanti khuddakatipusavalliyā phalaṃ. Hatthapatāpakanti mandāmukhi. Ambakañjikanti ambilakañjikaṃ. Khaḷayāguntipi vadanti. Doṇinimmajjaninti satelaṃ tilapiññākaṃ. Vidhupananti caturassabījaniṃ[V 2.0013]. Tālavaṇṭanti tālapattehi katamaṇḍalabījaniṃ. Morahatthanti morapiñchehi kataṃ makasabījaniṃ.

`Khīrodana` means rice mixed with milk. `Timbarusaka` means the tinduka fruit. They also say that a species of creeper similar to the tipusa is called timbarusa, and its fruit is timbarusaka. `Kakkārika` means a small cucumber. They also call it `mahātipusa`. `Vallipakka` is the fruit of the small tipusa creeper. `Hatthapatāpaka` means `mandāmukhi`. `Ambakañjika` means sour gruel. They also call it `khaḷayāgu`. `Doṇinimmajjani` is sesame oil-cake with oil. `Vidhupana` is a square fan. `Tālavaṇṭa` is a round fan made from palm leaves. `Morahattha` is a fly-whisk made from peacock feathers.

Vuttanayānusārenevāti yasmā idhāpi yathāvuttaṃ sabbampi kāraṇabhedaṃ ekato katvā dassento satthā “taṃ kissa hetū”ntiādimāha, tasmā tattha aniyyānikasāsane vuttanayassa anussaraṇavasena yojetvā veditabbaṃ.

'Just in accordance with the method stated': Since here too the Teacher, having gathered together all the different causes as stated and showing them, said, 'For what reason?,' etc., therefore it should be understood by applying this to that non-emancipating teaching by way of recollecting the method stated therein.

145. Pariññanti pahānapariññaṃ. Tesaṃ paccayaṃ dassetunti upādānānaṃ pariññā nāma pahānapariññā. Tesaṃ accantanirodho adhippeto, so ca paccayanirodhena hotīti tesaṃ paccayaṃ mūlakāraṇato pabhuti dassetuṃ. Ayanti idāni vuccamāno ettha “ime cā”tiādipāṭhe “kiṃ nidānā”tiādisamāsapadānaṃ attho. Sabbapadesūti “taṇhāsamudayā”tiādīsu sabbesu padesu. Iminā eva ca sabbaggahaṇena “phassanidānā”tiādīnampi padānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Ime aññatitthiyā upādānānampi samudayaṃ na jānanti, kuto nirodhaṃ, tathāgato pana tesaṃ tappaccayapaccayānampi samudayañca atthaṅgamañca yāthāvato jānāti, tasmā – “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi aññehī”ti (ma. ni. 1.139) yathāraddhasīhanādaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dassento “ime ca, bhikkhave, cattāro upādānā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.145) nayena desanaṃ paṭiccasamuppādamukhena otārento vaṭṭaṃ dassetvā “yato ca kho”tiādinā vivaṭṭaṃ dassento arahattena desanāya kūṭaṃ gaṇhi, tamatthaṃ dassento “yasmā pana bhagavā”tiādimāha. Taṃ suviññeyyameva.

145. 'Full understanding': the full understanding that is abandonment. 'To show their condition': The full understanding of the clingings is the full understanding that is abandonment. Their final cessation is intended, and that comes about through the cessation of their condition. Thus this is said to show their condition, beginning from the root cause. 'This': this is the meaning, now being stated, of the compound words such as 'with what as source?' in the text beginning 'And these...' 'In all phrases': in all phrases such as 'from the arising of craving.' And by this word 'all,' the inclusion of phrases such as 'with contact as source' should be seen. These other heretics do not know the origin of the clingings, still less their cessation. But the Tathāgata knows as it really is the origin and the passing away of them and of the conditions for their conditions. Therefore, having brought the lion's roar he had uttered to its climax, showing that 'It is here, bhikkhus, that there is a samaṇa... empty are the doctrines of other samaṇas' (MN 11), he then brought down the teaching by way of dependent origination with the method beginning, 'And these, bhikkhus, are the four clingings...' (MN 11), thereby showing the round; and with the passage beginning, 'And when...,' he showed the rolling back of the round, and thus he took the teaching to its peak with arahantship. To show that meaning, he said, 'But since the Blessed One...' This is very easy to understand.

Cūḷasīhanādasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Exposition of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary to the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta is completed.

2. Mahāsīhanādasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary to the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta

Vesālīnagaravaṇṇanā

Description of the City of Vesālī

146. Aparāparanti [M 2.0015][V 2.0014] punappunaṃ. Visālībhūtatāyāti gāvutantaraṃ gāvutantaraṃ puthubhūtatāya. Tatrāti tassaṃ visālībhūtatāyaṃ. Chaḍḍitamatteti vissaṭṭhamatte. Ūmibhayādīhīti ūmikumbhīlaāvaṭṭasaṃsukābhayehi. Udakappavāhenāgatassapi ca usmā na vigacchati, usmā ca nāma īdisassa saviññāṇakatāya bhaveyyāti “siyā gabbho”ti cintesi. Tathā hītiādi tattha kāraṇacintā. Puññavantatāya duggandhaṃ nāhosi, sausumatāya pūtikabhāvo. Dārakānaṃ puññūpanissayato aṅguṭṭhakato cassa khīraṃ nibbatti, khīrabhattañca labhi. Carimakabhave bodhisatte kucchigate bodhisattamātu viya udaracchaviyā acchavippasannatāya nicchavi viyāti katvā āha “nicchavī ahesu”nti. Tesanti dvinnaṃ dārakānaṃ. Mātāpitaroti posakamātāpitaro. Abhisiñcitvā rājānaṃ akaṃsu rajjasampattiyā dāyakassa kammassa katattā, asambhinne eva rājakule uppannattā ca. Kumārassa puññānubhāvasañcoditā devatādhiggahitāti keci.

146. "Aparāparaṃ" means repeatedly. "Because of becoming vast" means because of becoming broad at intervals of a gāvuta. "There" means in that state of being vast. "Merely discarded" means merely thrown away. "By fears of waves, etc." means by the dangers from waves, crocodiles, whirlpools, and sharks. And though it had come by the flow of water, the heat did not depart; and thinking, "Such heat might be because it possesses consciousness," he thought, "There might be a fetus." The words "Thus," etc., refer to the consideration of the cause in that context. Due to their meritoriousness, there was no foul smell; due to the heat, there was no putrefaction. Because of the children's supporting condition of merit, milk issued from his thumb, and they obtained milk-rice. Just as in the final existence, when the Bodhisatta was in the womb, the Bodhisatta's mother's belly-skin was exceedingly clear, as if without skin (nicchavi), so it is said, "they became the Nicchavis." "Of them" means of the two children. "Mother and father" means foster parents. Having anointed him, they made him king, because a kamma productive of the attainment of kingship had been done, and because he was born in an unbroken royal family. Some say he was possessed by a deity impelled by the power of his merit.

Purassa apareti purassa aparadisāya gāvutamatte ṭhāne jīvakambavanaṃ viya sapākāramandirake. Acirapakkantoti ettha na desantarapakkamanaṃ adhippetaṃ, atha kho sāsanato apakkamananti dassento “vibbhamitvā”tiādimāha. Tenevāha “imasmā dhammavinayā”ti. Parisatīti parisāyaṃ, janasamūheti attho. Janasamūhagato pana “parisamajjhe”ti vutto. Bhāvanāmanasikārena vinā pakatiyāva manussehi nibbattetabbo dhammoti manussadhammo, manussattabhāvāvaho vā dhammo manussadhammo, anuḷāraṃ parittakusalaṃ. Yaṃ asatipi buddhuppāde vattati, yañca sandhāyāha “hīnena brahmacariyena, khattiye upapajjatī”ti. “Amhākaṃ buddho”ti buddhe mamattakārino buddhamāmakā. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo.

"Apare purassa" means to the west of the city, at a distance of about a gāvuta, in a place with an enclosure wall and a building, like Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. "Not long departed" here does not refer to leaving for another country, but rather to departing from the teaching. To indicate this, it is said, “having gone astray,” and so on. Therefore, it is said, “from this Dhamma and Vinaya.” "Parisati" means in the assembly; the meaning is in a group of people. One who has gone into a group of people is said to be “in the midst of the assembly.” A "human dhamma" is a dhamma to be produced naturally by humans without development and attention; or a "human dhamma" is a dhamma that brings about the state of being human—a non-lofty, small wholesome state. This is what exists even when no Buddha has arisen, and it is in reference to this that it is said: “With an inferior holy life, one is reborn among the khattiyas.” “Our Buddha”: those who have a sense of "mine" in regard to the Buddha are Buddha-devotees. The same method applies to the other two phrases.

Uttarimanussadhammādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Superhuman States, etc.

Alaṃ [M 2.0016] ariyāya ariyabhāvāyāti alamariyo, rūpāyatanaṃ jānāti cakkhuviññāṇaṃ viya passati cāti ñāṇadassanaṃ, dibbacakkhu. Sammasanupage ca pana dhamme lakkhaṇattayañca tathā jānāti [V 2.0015] passati cāti ñāṇadassanaṃ, vipassanā. Nibbānaṃ, cattāri vā saccāni asammohapaṭivedhato jānāti passati cāti ñāṇadassanaṃ, maggo. Phalaṃ pana nibbānavaseneva yojetabbaṃ. Paccavekkhaṇā maggādhigatassa atthassa paccakkhato jānanaṭṭhena ñāṇadassanaṃ, sabbaññutā anāvaraṇatāya samantacakkhutāya ca ñāṇadassanaṃ. Lokuttaramaggo adhippeto, tasmiñhi paṭisiddhe sabbesampi buddhaguṇānaṃ asambhavoti adhippāyo. Tenāha “tañhi so bhagavato paṭisedhetī”ti.

"Sufficient for a noble one, for the state of a noble one," thus "sufficiently noble" (alamariya). "It knows the form base and sees as with eye-consciousness": this is knowledge and vision, the divine eye. "And when one has undertaken comprehension of phenomena, one knows and sees the three characteristics in such a way": this is knowledge and vision, insight. "It knows and sees Nibbāna or the four truths by penetrating them without delusion": this is knowledge and vision, the path. The fruit, however, should be connected by way of Nibbāna. Reviewing is knowledge and vision in the sense of directly knowing the goal attained by the path. Omniscience is knowledge and vision because of its unobstruction and its being the all-seeing eye. The supramundane path is intended, for the meaning is that if that is denied, all the Buddha's qualities become impossible. Therefore it is said: "For he denies that of the Blessed One."

Sukhumaṃ dhammantaraṃ nāma jhānavipassanādikaṃ ācariyānuggahena gahitaṃ nāma natthi. Takkapariyāhatanti “iti bhavissati, evaṃ bhavissatī”ti taṃtaṃdassetabbamatthatakkanena vitakkanamattena parito āhataṃ parivattitaṃ katvā. Tenāha “takketvā”tiādi. Lokiyapaññaṃ anujānāti upanisinnaparisāya anukūladhammakathanatoti adhippāyo. Tenāha “samaṇo gotamo”tiādi. Paṭibhātīti paṭibhānaṃ, “iti vakkhāmī”ti evaṃpavattaṃ kathanacittaṃ, tato paṭibhānato jānanaṃ paṭibhānaṃ, āgamābhāvato sayameva upaṭṭhitattā sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ. Tenāha “imināssa dhammesu paccakkhabhāvaṃ paṭibāhatī”ti. Suphusitanti nibbivaraṃ. Aphusitatte hi sukhena vacīghoso na niccharati. Dantāvaraṇanti oṭṭhadvayaṃ. Jivhāpi thaddhatāya sukhena vacīghoso na niccharatīti āha “mudukā jivhā”ti. Karavīkarutamañjutāya madhuro saro. Elaṃ vuccati doso, elaṃ gaḷatīti elagaḷā, na elagaḷā anelagaḷā, niddosā, na rujjhatīti attho. Sabbametaṃ rañjanasseva kāraṇaṃ dassento vadati.

There is no such thing as a subtle inner teaching, such as jhāna and insight, grasped through the assistance of a teacher. "Hammered out by reasoning" means turned over by mere thinking, by reasoning about this or that matter to be pointed out, considering, "It will be thus, it will be so." Hence it is said, "having reasoned," etc. The meaning is that he acknowledges worldly wisdom by speaking on a suitable teaching to the assembly that has sat down. Hence it is said, "The ascetic Gotama," etc. "It occurs to him" is eloquence. The thought to speak that occurs thus, "I will say this," is eloquence. Knowing from that eloquence is eloquence. Because it is not based on a tradition and presents itself on its own, it is self-inspired eloquence. Hence it is said: "By this he obstructs his direct experience of the teachings." "Well-fitted" means without a gap. For if it is not well-fitted, the sound of speech does not issue forth smoothly. "The covering of the teeth" means the two lips. Since the sound of speech does not issue forth smoothly if the tongue is stiff, he said, "a soft tongue." The voice is sweet because of its loveliness like the cry of the karavīka bird. A fault is called ela. That which swallows a fault is elagaḷa. Not elagaḷa is anelagaḷa, flawless; the meaning is it is not obstructed. He says all this to show the cause for charming others.

Pañca dhammāti gambhīrañāṇacariyabhūtānaṃ khandhādīnaṃ uggahaṇa-savana-dhāraṇa-paricaya-yonisomanasikāre sandhāyāha. Takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyāti ettha sammā-saddo ubhayatthāpi yojetabbo “sammā takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyā”ti. Yo hi sammā dhammaṃ paṭipajjati, tasseva sammā dukkhakkhayo hoti. Yo pana vuttanayena takkaro, tassa niyyānaṃ atthato dhammasseva niyyānanti āha “so dhammo…pe… niyyāti gacchatī”ti.

"Five dhammas": he says this in reference to the grasping, hearing, retaining, practicing, and wise attention concerning the aggregates, etc., which are the domain of profound knowledge and conduct. In the phrase "of one who acts thus, for the right ending of suffering," the word "rightly" should be connected with both parts, thus: "of one who acts thus rightly, for the right ending of suffering." For one who rightly practices the Dhamma, for him alone there is the right ending of suffering. But as for one who acts thus in the way described, his liberation is in reality the liberation of the Dhamma itself. Hence he said: "That Dhamma ... leads to liberation..."

147. Kodhanoti [M 2.0017] kujjhanasīlo. Yasmā pana sunakkhatto kodhavasena kurūro pharusavacano ca, tasmā āha “kodhanoti caṇḍo pharuso cā”ti. Tasmiṃ attabhāve maggaphalānaṃ upanissayo natthīti tasmiṃ attabhāve uppajjanārahānaṃ maggaphalānaṃ upanissayo natthi. Taṃ buddhā “moghapuriso”ti vadanti yathā taṃ sudinnalāḷudāyiādike. Upanissaye satipi tasmiṃ khaṇe magge vā phale vā asati “moghapuriso”ti vadanti yathā taṃ dhaniyūpasenattherādike. Samucchinnopanissaye pana vattabbameva natthi. Yathā “makkhali moghapuriso manussakhippaṃ [V 2.0016] maññe”ti (a. ni. 1.311) tathā sunakkhattopīti āha “imassa panā”tiādi. Assāti etena. Kattari hidaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Kodhenāti kodhahetunā.

147. "Kodhano" means one with a disposition to anger. Since Sunakkhatta, due to anger, was cruel and harsh in speech, it is therefore said: "'Kodhano' means fierce and harsh." "In that existence, there is no supporting condition for the path and fruition" means that in that individual existence, there is no supporting condition for the path and fruition that could arise. The Buddhas call such a person "a vain man," as in the case of Sudinna, Lāludāyi, and others. Even when a supporting condition exists, if the path or fruition is absent at that moment, they call him "a vain man," as in the case of the Elder Dhaniya, the Elder Upasena, and others. But when the supporting condition is completely eradicated, there is nothing to be said. Just as it is said, "Makkhali is a vain man, I think, a human scrap-heap," so too is Sunakkhatta—therefore it is said, "But of this one," etc. "Assa" means "by this one." Here this is a genitive in the sense of the agent. "Kodhena" means because of anger.

Bhagavatoti sampadānavacanaṃ kuddhapadāpekkhāya. Pubbeti bhikkhukāle. Saddaṃ sotukāmoti so kira dibbacakkhunā tāvatiṃsabhavane devatānaṃ rūpaṃ passanto oṭṭhacalanaṃ passati, na pana saddaṃ suṇāti, tasmā tāsaṃ saddaṃ sotukāmo ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ “saddaṃ sotukāmo…pe… pucchī”ti. So ca atīte ekaṃ sīlavantaṃ bhikkhuṃ kaṇṇasakkhaliyaṃ paharitvā badhiramakāsi, tasmā parikammaṃ karontopi abhabbova dibbasotādhigamāya. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “upanissayo natthīti ñatvā parikammaṃ na kathesī”ti. Cintesīti attano micchāparivitakkitena ayoniso ummujjanto cintesi.

"Bhagavato" is a dative expression used in relation to the word "kuddha" (angry at). "Pubbe" means at the time he was a bhikkhu. "Desiring to hear the sound": it is said that with his divine eye he saw the forms of the devas in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and saw their lips moving, but he did not hear the sound. Therefore he desired to hear their sound. Hence it was said: "desiring to hear the sound ... he asked." And in the past he had struck a virtuous bhikkhu on the ear with a potsherd and made him deaf. Therefore, even while undertaking the preliminary work, he was incapable of attaining the divine ear. In reference to this it was said: "Knowing that he had no supporting condition, he did not teach him the preliminary work." "He thought": he thought while emerging unwisely with his own wrong thoughts.

Niyyānikattāvabodhanato abhedopacārena “desanādhammo niyyāniko”ti vutto. Niyyāno vā ariyamaggo bodhetabbo etassa atthīti niyyāniko desanādhammo. Attani atthitaṃ dasseti kiccasiddhidassanena tattha tattha pākaṭīkatattā, na paṭiññāmattena. Tathā hi yathāparādhaṃ taṃtaṃsikkhāpadapaññattiyā yathādhammaṃ veneyyajjhāsayānurūpañca aviparītadhammadesanāya devamanussehi yathābhisaṅkhatapañhānaṃ tadajjhāsayānukūlaṃ ṭhānaso vissajjanena ca bhagavato sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇacārabhāvena sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ viññūnaṃ pākaṭaṃ, tathā tattha tattha yamakapāṭihāriyakaraṇādīsu iddhividhañāṇādīnīti. Tenāha “mayhañcā”tiādi. Anveti yathāgahitasaṅketassa anugamanavasena eti [M 2.0018] jānātīti anvayo. Tenāha “anubujjhatīti attho”ti. Saṅketānugamanañcettha “yathāparādhaṃ taṃtaṃsikkhāpadapaññattiyā”tiādinā vuttanayameva. Evaṃ yojanā veditabbāti yathā sabbaññutaññāṇena yojanā katā, evaṃ “evarūpampi nāma mayhaṃ iddhividhañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ uttarimanussadhamma”ntiādinā tattha tattha yojanā veditabbā.

Because it leads to liberation and makes it known, it is called 'the teaching Dhamma is liberating' by way of figurative identification. Or, the liberating path, the noble path, is to be made known, and the teaching Dhamma has this as its content—hence it is liberating. It reveals what exists within itself through the showing of its successful function and by making it evident in various places, not merely by proclamation. For instance, by prescribing specific training rules according to offenses, by teaching the Dhamma appropriately in accordance with the dispositions of those to be trained, and by answering questions appropriately according to the intentions of devas and humans—through these, the Blessed One’s unobstructed sphere of knowledge in all things and his omniscience become evident to the wise. Likewise, in various instances, such as performing the twin miracle, his knowledge of psychic powers and so on is made clear. Therefore, it is said, 'And of me...' etc. 'He understands' (anveti) means he comes to know by way of following the accepted convention. Hence it is said, 'The meaning is "he understands."' The following of conventions here is just as explained in the passage, 'by prescribing specific training rules according to offenses...' etc. Thus, the connection should be understood. Just as the connection is made with omniscient knowledge, so too should the connection be understood in various instances, such as, 'Even such a superhuman state of mine called the knowledge of psychic power...' etc.

Uttarimanussadhammādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of Superhuman States, etc., is finished.

Dasabalañāṇavaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Knowledge of the Ten Powers

148. Yadipi ādito abhiññāttayavasena desanāya āgatattā cetopariyañāṇānantaraṃ upari tisso abhiññā vattabbā siyunti vattabbaṃ siyā, atthato pana vijjāttayaṃ yathāvuttaabhiññāttayamevāti [V 2.0017] katvā “tisso vijjā vattabbā siyu”nti vuttaṃ. Kasmā panettha “tāsu vuttāsu upari dasabalañāṇaṃ na paripūratī”ti vuttaṃ, nanu imāni ñāṇāni sesābhiññā viya attano visayassa abhijānanaṭṭhaṃ upādāya abhiññāsu vattabbāni, akampiyaṭṭhaṃ pana upatthambhanaṭṭhañca upādāya balañāṇesu yathā sammāsatiādayo indriyabalabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgesūti? Nayidamevaṃ. Tattha hi dhammānaṃ dhammakiccavisesavibhāvanaparāya desanāya vuttaṃ, idha pana satthu guṇavisesavibhāvanaparāya desanāya tathā vattuṃ na sakkā atthato anaññattā, ekaccānaṃ puthujjanānaṃ evaṃ cittaṃ uppajjeyya “kimidaṃ bhagavā heṭṭhā vuttaguṇe punapi gaṇhanto guṇādhikadassanaṃ karotī”ti. Tasmā suvuttametaṃ “upari dasabalañāṇaṃ na paripūratī”ti.

148. Although it might be said that the three higher knowledges should be mentioned after the knowledge of others' minds because they are presented in the teaching from the beginning as the threefold direct knowledge, still, since in meaning the threefold true knowledge is just the threefold direct knowledge as stated, it was said, 'the three true knowledges should be mentioned.' But why was it said here, 'When these have been stated, the knowledge of the ten powers above is not completed'? Is it not that these knowledges, like the remaining direct knowledges, should be spoken of among the direct knowledges on account of their function of directly knowing their own object, while on account of their unshakable and supporting nature, they should be spoken of among the power-knowledges—just as right mindfulness and so on are included in the faculties, powers, enlightenment factors, and path factors? This is not so. For there, it was stated in a teaching devoted to clarifying the specific functions of phenomena, but here, in a teaching devoted to clarifying the special qualities of the Teacher, it cannot be said so, as they are not different in meaning. Otherwise, a thought might arise in some worldlings thus: 'Why does the Blessed One, taking up again qualities already mentioned, make a display of superior qualities?' Therefore, it was well said: 'the knowledge of the ten powers above is not completed.'

Aññehi asādhāraṇānīti kasmā vuttaṃ (a. ni. ṭī. 3.10.21), nanu cetāni sāvakānampi ekaccānaṃ uppajjantīti? Kāmaṃ uppajjanti, yādisāni pana buddhānaṃ ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇādīni, na tādisāni tadaññesaṃ kadācipi uppajjantīti aññehi asādhāraṇānīti. Tenāha “tathāgatasseva balānī”ti. Imameva hi yathāvuttalesaṃ apekkhitvā tadabhāvato āsayānusayañāṇādīsu eva asādhāraṇaguṇasamaññā niruḷhā. Kāmaṃ ñāṇabalānaṃ ñāṇasambhāro visesapaccayo, puññasambhāropi pana nesaṃ paccayo eva[M 2.0019], ñāṇasambhārassapi vā puññasambhārabhāvato “puññussayasampattiyā āgatānī”ti vuttaṃ.

Why is it said that these are 'not shared by others' (A. Ni. Ṭī. 3.10.21), since these also arise in some disciples? Granted, they arise, but the kind of knowledge of what is possible and impossible, etc., that belongs to the Buddhas never arises in others in the same way; therefore it is said they are 'not shared by others.' For this reason he said, 'the powers belong to the Tathāgata alone.' Indeed, it is with reference to this slight trace mentioned above that the designation 'unshared quality' has become established for such knowledges as the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies, due to the absence of even that trace in others. Granted, the accumulation of knowledge is a special condition for the knowledge-powers, but the accumulation of merit is also a condition for them. Or, since the accumulation of knowledge is itself an accumulation of merit, it is said, 'they have come through the attainment of an abundance of merit.'

Pakatihatthikulanti (saṃ. ni. 2.22) giricaranadīcaravanacarādippabhedā gocariyakālāvakanāmā sabbāpi balena pākatikā hatthijāti. Dasannaṃ purisānanti thāmamajjhimānaṃ dasannaṃ purisānaṃ. Ekassa tathāgatassa kāyabalanti ānetvā sambandho. Ekassāti ca tathā heṭṭhākathāyaṃ āgatattā desanāsotena vuttaṃ. Nārāyanasaṅghātabalanti ettha nārā vuccanti rasmiyo, tā bahū nānāvidhā ito uppajjantīti nārāyanaṃ, vajiraṃ, tasmā nārāyanasaṅghātabalanti vajirasaṅghātabalanti attho. Ñāṇabalaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ āgatameva, na kāyabalaṃ viya aṭṭhakathāruḷhamevāti adhippāyo. “Saṃyuttake āgatāni tesattati ñāṇāni sattasattati ñāṇānī”ti vuttaṃ (vibha. mūlaṭī. 760), tattha pana nidānavagge sattasattati āgatāni catucattārīsañca, tesattati pana paṭisambhidāmagge (paṭi. ma. 1.73 mātikā) sutamayādīni āgatāni dissanti, na saṃyuttake. Aññānipīti etena ñāṇavatthuvibhaṅge ekakādivasena vuttāni, aññattha ca “pubbante ñāṇa”ntiādinā (dha. sa. 1076) brahmajālādīsu (dī. ni. 1.36) ca “tayidaṃ tathāgato pajānāti, imāni diṭṭhiṭṭhānāni evaṃ gahitānī”tiādinā vuttāni anekāni ñāṇappabhedāni saṅgaṇhāti. Yāthāvapaṭivedhato sayañca [V 2.0018] akampiyaṃ puggalañca taṃsamaṅgiṃ neyyesu adhibalaṃ karotīti āha “akampiyaṭṭhena upatthambhanaṭṭhena cā”ti.

'The natural elephant clan' (Saṃ. Ni. 2.22) refers to all species of elephant that are naturally strong, distinguished into types such as mountain-roaming, river-roaming, and forest-roaming, and named gocariya and kāḷāvaka. 'Of ten men' means of ten men of medium strength. The connection is made by supplying the words 'the bodily strength of one Tathāgata.' And 'of one' is said in the stream of the teaching because it is found thus in the earlier explanation. 'The compact strength of Nārāyana': here 'nārā' are called rays. Because many various ones arise from this, it is 'nārāyana,' a thunderbolt. Therefore, 'the compact strength of Nārāyana' means 'the compact strength of a thunderbolt.' Knowledge-power, however, is found in the Pāli canon itself; the meaning is that it is not, like bodily power, established only in the commentaries. It is said (Vibh-mṭ 760): 'In the Saṃyutta Nikāya there are found seventy-three knowledges and seventy-seven knowledges.' There, however, in the Nidānavagga, seventy-seven are found, and forty-four. But the seventy-three are seen to be found in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. M. 1.73, mātikā) as those based on learning, etc., not in the Saṃyutta Nikāya. By 'And other knowledges too,' he includes the many kinds of knowledge stated in the Ñāṇavatthuvibhaṅga by way of the singlefold division, etc., and elsewhere with such phrases as 'knowledge of the past' (Dhs 1367), and in the Brahmajāla Sutta, etc. (DN 1.36), with such phrases as 'This the Tathāgata understands: "These grounds for views are thus held..."' Through penetration of reality, it makes the very person endowed with it unshakable and powerful over those to be guided. Hence it is said: 'by reason of being unshakable and by reason of supporting.'

Usabhassa idanti āsabhaṃ, (a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.8) seṭṭhaṃ ṭhānaṃ. Sabbaññutapaṭijānanavasena abhimukhaṃ gacchanti, aṭṭha vā parisā upasaṅkamantīti āsabhā, pubbabuddhā. Idaṃ panāti buddhānaṃ ṭhānaṃ sabbaññutameva vadati. Tiṭṭhamānovāti avadantopi (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.2.22) tiṭṭhamānova paṭijānāti nāmāti attho. Upagacchatīti anujānāti.

'Belonging to a bull' (usabhassa idaṃ) is 'āsabhaṃ' (A. Ni. Ṭī. 2.4.8), the foremost position. They go forward by way of proclaiming omniscience, or the eight assemblies approach them, hence they are called 'āsabhā' (leaders), the former Buddhas. But this position of the Buddhas refers only to omniscience. 'Tiṭṭhamāno vā' (Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 2.2.22): the meaning is that even without speaking, just by his stance he makes the claim. 'He accepts' (upagacchati) means he assents.

Aṭṭhasu parisāsūti “abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, anekasataṃ khattiyaparisaṃ…pe… tatra vata maṃ bhayaṃ vā sārajjaṃ vā okkamissatīti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta, na samanupassāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.151) vuttāsu aṭṭhasu parisāsu. Abhītanādaṃ [M 2.0020] nadatīti parato dassitañāṇayogena dasabalohanti abhītanādaṃ nadati. Sīhanādasuttena khandhavagge (saṃ. ni. 3.78) āgatena.

'In the eight assemblies': in the eight assemblies spoken of thus: 'I recall, Sāriputta, having approached many hundred assemblies of nobles... I do not see any ground, Sāriputta, why fear or timidity should assail me there' (MN 12). 'He roars a fearless roar': Being one with the ten powers, he roars the fearless roar by means of the application of knowledge displayed to others. This is in accordance with the Sīhanāda Sutta in the Khandhavagga (SN 22.78).

“Devamanussānaṃ catucakkaṃ vattatī”ti (a. ni. 4.31) suttasesena sappurisūpassayādīnaṃ phalasampattipavatti, purimasappurisūpassayādiṃ upanissāya pacchimasappurisūpassayādīnaṃ sampattipavatti vā vuttāti ādi-saddena tattha ca cakka-saddassa gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vicakkasaṇṭhānā asani eva asanivicakkaṃ. Uracakkādīsūti ādi-saddena āṇāsamūhādīsupi cakka-saddassa pavatti veditabbā. “Saṅghabhedaṃ karissāma cakkabheda”ntiādīsu (pārā. 409; cūḷava. 343) hi āṇā “cakka”nti vuttā, “devacakkaṃ asuracakka”ntiādīsu (a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.8) samūhoti. Paṭivedhaniṭṭhattā arahattamaggañāṇaṃ paṭivedhoti “phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Tena paṭiladdhassapi desanāñāṇassa kiccanipphatti parassa bujjhanamattena hotīti “aññātakoṇḍaññassa sotāpatti…pe… phalakkhaṇe pavattaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Tato paraṃ pana yāva parinibbānā desanāñāṇappavatti tasseva pavattitassa dhammacakkassa ṭhānanti veditabbaṃ pavattitacakkassa cakkavattino cakkaratanassa ṭhānaṃ viya.

'The four wheels for devas and humans are set in motion' (AN 4.31): by the rest of the sutta is stated the occurrence of the attainment of the fruit of such things as relying on good persons, or the occurrence of the attainment of later reliance on good persons, etc., dependent on the earlier reliance on good persons, etc. By the word 'etc.' the use of the word 'cakka' in those cases too should be understood. A thunderbolt in the form of a discus is a 'thunderbolt-discus.' In 'breast-discus, etc.': by the word 'etc.' the occurrence of the word 'cakka' should be understood also for a command, a group, etc. For in such passages as 'We will create a schism in the Sangha, a breaking of the wheel' (Pārā. 409; Cv. VII), a command is called a 'wheel,' and in such passages as 'the wheel of the devas, the wheel of the asuras' (A. Ni. Ṭī. 2.4.8), it means a group. Because it is accomplished by penetration, the knowledge of the path to arahantship is called 'penetration'; it is said to arise, by name, at the moment of fruition. Therefore, the function of the teaching-knowledge, though attained by the teacher, is accomplished only through another's understanding; hence it is said, 'For Aññā Koṇḍañña, stream-entry…pe… is said to proceed, by name, at the moment of fruition.' But after that, until parinibbāna, the proceeding of the teaching-knowledge should be understood as the 'standing-place' of that very Dhamma-wheel that has been set in motion, like the standing-place of the wheel-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch whose wheel has been set in motion.

“Tiṭṭhatī”ti vuttaṃ, kiṃ bhūmiyaṃ puriso viya? Noti āha “tadāyattavuttitāyā”ti. Ṭhānanti cettha attalābho dharamānatā ca, na gatinivattīti āha “uppajjati ceva pavattati cā”ti[V 2.0019]. Yattha panetaṃ dasabalañāṇaṃ vitthāritaṃ, taṃ dassento “abhidhamme panā”tiādimāha. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

It was said, 'It stands.' Does this mean like a person on the ground? He says, 'No,' and explains: 'Because its occurrence is dependent on that.' And here 'standing' (ṭhāna) means the acquisition of its own nature and its continuance, not the cessation of movement; hence he says, 'It both arises and proceeds.' Showing where this knowledge of the ten powers is expounded in detail, he said, 'But in the Abhidhamma,' etc. This same method applies to the remaining cases too.

Samādiyantīti samādānāni, tāni pana samādiyitvā katāni hontīti āha “samādiyitvā katāna”nti. Kammameva vā kammasamādānanti etena samādānasaddassa apubbatthābhāvaṃ dasseti muttagatasadde gatasaddassa viya. Gatīti nirayādigatiyo. Upadhīti attabhāvo. Kāloti kammassa vipaccanārahakālo. Payogoti vipākuppattiyā paccayabhūtā kiriyā.

'They undertake' (samādiyanti), hence 'undertakings' (samādānāni). But since these are done after having been undertaken, he says 'of those undertaken and done.' Or, kamma itself is 'kamma-undertaking'; by this he shows that the word 'samādāna' does not have a meaning of 'before,' just like the word 'gata' in the word 'muttagata.' 'Destination' (gati) means the destinations such as hell. 'Substratum' (upadhi) means personal existence. 'Time' (kāla) is the time when the kamma is suitable for ripening. 'Endeavor' (payoga) is the activity that is a condition for the arising of the result.

Agatigāmininti nibbānagāminiṃ. Vakkhati hi “nibbānañcāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi nibbānagāmiñca maggaṃ nibbānagāminiñca paṭipada”nti (ma. ni. 1.153). Bahūsupi manussesu ekameva [M 2.0021] pāṇaṃ ghātentesu kāmaṃ sabbesaṃ cetanā tassevekassa jīvitindriyārammaṇā, taṃ pana kammaṃ tesaṃ nānākāraṃ. Tesu (vibha. aṭṭha. 811) hi eko ādarena chandajāto karoti, eko “ehi tvampi karohī”ti parehi nippīḷito karoti, eko samānacchando viya hutvā appaṭibāhamāno vicarati. Tesu eko teneva kammena niraye nibbattati, eko tiracchānayoniyaṃ, eko pettivisaye. Taṃ tathāgato āyūhanakkhaṇe eva – “iminā nīhārena āyūhitattā esa niraye nibbattissati, esa tiracchānayoniyaṃ, esa pettivisaye”ti jānāti. Niraye nibbattamānampi – “esa mahāniraye nibbattissati, esa ussadaniraye”ti jānāti. Tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattamānampi – “esa apādako bhavissati, esa dvipādako, esa catuppado, esa bahuppado”ti jānāti. Pettivisaye nibbattamānampi – “esa nijjhāmataṇhiko bhavissati, esa khuppipāsiko, esa paradattūpajīvī”ti jānāti. Tesu ca kammesu – “idaṃ kammaṃ paṭisandhimākaḍḍhissati, idaṃ aññena dinnāya paṭisandhiyā upadhivepakkaṃ bhavissatī”ti jānāti.

"Agatigāminī" means leading to Nibbāna. For it will be said: "I understand Nibbāna, Sāriputta, the path leading to Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna" (MN 1:153). Even when many people kill a single living being, though the intention of all is directed toward the same life faculty, their kamma differs in nature. Among them (Vibh-a 811), one does it with eager desire; another does it under pressure from others, who say, "Come, you too do it"; and another acts without resistance, as if sharing the same desire. Among them, one is reborn in hell because of that kamma, another in the animal realm, and another in the realm of ghosts. The Tathāgata knows at the very moment of accumulation: "Due to being accumulated in this manner, this one will be reborn in hell, this one in the animal realm, this one in the realm of ghosts." Even when they are being reborn in hell, he knows: "This one will be reborn in a great hell, this one in a subsidiary hell." When one is being reborn in the animal realm, he knows: "This one will be footless, this one two-footed, this one four-footed, this one many-footed." When one is being reborn in the realm of ghosts, he knows: "This one will be one tormented by thirst, this one will be one afflicted by hunger and thirst, this one will be one who lives on what is given by others." And regarding these kammas, he knows: "This kamma will produce rebirth-linking; this one will ripen during the course of existence after rebirth-linking has been given by another kamma."

Tathā sakalagāmavāsikesu ekato piṇḍapātaṃ dadamānesu kāmaṃ sabbesampi cetanā piṇḍapātārammaṇāva, taṃ pana kammaṃ tesaṃ nānākāraṃ. Tesu hi eko ādarena karotīti sesaṃ purimasadisaṃ, tasmā tesu keci devaloke nibbattanti, keci manussaloke, taṃ tathāgato āyūhanakkhaṇeyeva jānāti – “iminā nīhārena āyūhitattā esa manussaloke nibbattissati, esa devaloke, tatthāpi esa khattiyakule, esa brāhmaṇakule, esa vessakule, esa suddakule, esa paranimmitavasavattīsu, esa nimmānaratīsu, esa tusitesu, esa yāmesu, esa [V 2.0020] tāvatiṃsesu, esa cātumahārājikesu, esa bhummadevesū”tiādinā tattha tattha hīnapaṇītasuvaṇṇadubbaṇṇaappaparivāramahāparivāratādibhedaṃ taṃ taṃ visesaṃ āyūhanakkhaṇeyeva jānāti.

Similarly, when all the villagers together offer alms-food, though the intention of all has the alms-food as its object, their kamma is of various kinds. Among them, one gives with respect—the rest is as before. Therefore, some are reborn in the deva world, others in the human world. The Tathāgata knows at the very moment of accumulation: 'Because it was accumulated in this manner, this one will be reborn in the human world, this one in the deva world; and there, this one will be born in a khattiya family, this one in a brahmin family, this one in a vessa family, this one in a sudda family; this one among the Paranimmitavasavattī devas, this one among the Nimmānaratī devas, this one among the Tusita devas, this one among the Yāma devas, this one among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, this one among the Cātumahārājika devas, this one among the earth devas,' and so on. Thus, at the very moment of accumulation, he knows that particular distinction—the differences such as inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, having few or many attendants.

Tathā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapentesuyeva – “iminā nīhārena esa kiñci sallakkhetuṃ na sakkhissati, esa mahābhūtamattameva vavatthapessati, esa rūpapariggaheyeva ṭhassati, esa arūpapariggaheyeva, esa nāmarūpapariggaheyeva[M 2.0022], esa paccayapariggahe eva, esa lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāya eva, esa paṭhamaphaleyeva, esa dutiyaphale eva, esa tatiyaphale eva, esa arahattaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti jānāti. Kasiṇaparikammaṃ karontesupi – “imassa parikammamattameva bhavissati, esa nimittaṃ uppādessati, esa appanaṃ eva pāpuṇissati, esa jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhissatī”ti jānāti. Tenāha “imassa cetanā”tiādi.

Similarly, among those establishing insight, he knows: 'By this approach, this person will not be able to discern anything. He will only determine the great elements. He will remain merely at the comprehension of form, merely at the comprehension of the formless, merely at the comprehension of name-and-form, merely at the comprehension of conditions, or merely with insight focused on characteristics. He will attain only the first fruit, only the second fruit, or only the third fruit; or he will attain arahantship.' Among those undertaking the kasiṇa preliminary work, he knows: 'For this person it will be only preliminary work. He will produce the sign. He will attain absorption. Or, having made jhāna the basis and established insight, he will attain arahantship.' Therefore it is said: 'This intention,' etc.

Kāmanato, kāmetabbato, kāmapaṭisaṃyuttato ca kāmo dhātu kāmadhātu. Ādi-saddena byāpādadhātu-rūpadhātu-ādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Vilakkhaṇatāyāti visadisasabhāvatāya. Khandhāyatanadhātulokanti anekadhātuṃ nānādhātuṃ khandhalokaṃ āyatanalokaṃ dhātulokaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti yojanā. “Ayaṃ rūpakkhandho nāma…pe… ayaṃ viññāṇakkhandho nāma. Tesupi ekavidhena rūpakkhandho, ekādasavidhena rūpakkhandho (vibha. 33). Ekavidhena vedanākkhandho, bahuvidhena vedanākkhandho (vibha. 34-61). Ekavidhena saññākkhandho, bahuvidhena saññākkhandho (vibha. 62-91). Ekavidhena saṅkhārakkhandho, bahuvidhena saṅkhārakkhandho (vibha. 92-120). Ekavidhena viññāṇakkhandho, bahuvidhena viññāṇakkhandho”ti (vibha. 121-149) evaṃ tāva khandhalokassa, “idaṃ cakkhāyatanaṃ nāma…pe… idaṃ dhammāyatanaṃ nāma. Tattha dasāyatanā kāmāvacarā, dve cātubhūmakā”tiādinā (vibha. 156-171) āyatanalokassa, “ayaṃ cakkhudhātu nāma…pe… ayaṃ manoviññāṇadhātu nāma, tattha soḷasa dhātuyo kāmāvacarā, dve cātubhūmakā”tiādinā (vibha. 172-188) dhātulokassa anekasabhāvaṃ nānāsabhāvañca pajānāti. Na kevalaṃ upādinnakasaṅkhāralokasseva, atha kho anupādinnakasaṅkhāralokassapi – “imāya nāma dhātuyā ussannattā imassa rukkhassa khandho seto, imassa kāḷo, imassa maṭṭho, imassa sakaṇṭako, imassa bahalattaco, imassa tanuttaco, imassa pattaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivasena evarūpaṃ, imassa pupphaṃ nīlaṃ pītaṃ lohitaṃ odātaṃ sugandhaṃ duggandhaṃ, imassa phalaṃ khuddakaṃ mahantaṃ dīghaṃ rassaṃ vaṭṭaṃ susaṇṭhānaṃ dussaṇṭhānaṃ mudukaṃ pharusaṃ sugandhaṃ duggandhaṃ madhuraṃ tittakaṃ kaṭukaṃ [V 2.0021] ambilaṃ kasāvaṃ, imassa kaṇṭako tikhiṇo kuṇṭho ujuko [M 2.0023] kuṭilo tambo kāḷo odāto hotī”tiādinā pajānāti. Sabbaññubuddhādīnaṃ eva hi etaṃ balaṃ, na aññesaṃ.

From the act of desiring, from what is to be desired, and from what is connected with desire, desire as an element is the sense-sphere element. The word 'etc.' (ādi) includes the ill-will element, the form element, and so on. 'Due to having a distinct nature' (vilakkhaṇatāya) means due to having a dissimilar nature. The meaning is that one understands as it actually is the world of aggregates, the world of sense bases, and the world of elements—a world of manifold elements and diverse elements. 'This is called the aggregate of form… this is called the aggregate of consciousness. Among these, the aggregate of form is of one kind, and of eleven kinds (Vibh 33). The aggregate of feeling is of one kind, and of many kinds (Vibh 34–61). The aggregate of perception is of one kind, and of many kinds (Vibh 62–91). The aggregate of formations is of one kind, and of many kinds (Vibh 92–120). The aggregate of consciousness is of one kind, and of many kinds' (Vibh 121–149)—thus, first concerning the world of aggregates. 'This is called the eye-base... this is called the mental-object base. Herein, ten bases belong to the sense sphere, two are applicable to the four planes,' and so on (Vibh 156–171)—regarding the world of sense bases. 'This is called the eye-element... this is called the mind-consciousness-element. Herein, sixteen elements belong to the sense sphere, two are applicable to the four planes,' and so on (Vibh 172–188)—regarding the world of elements, one understands their manifold and diverse natures. Not only of the world of appropriated conditioned things, but also of the world of unappropriated conditioned things: 'Due to the abundance of such-and-such an element, the trunk of this tree is white, of this one black, of this one smooth, of this one thorny, of this one thick-barked, of this one thin-barked; the leaf of this one is of such a kind in color, shape, and so on; the flower of this one is blue, yellow, red, or white, fragrant or foul-smelling; the fruit of this one is small, large, long, short, round, well-formed or ill-formed, soft or hard, fragrant or foul-smelling, sweet, bitter, pungent, sour, or astringent; the thorn of this one is sharp, blunt, straight, crooked, copper-colored, black, or white,' and so on, one understands. For this power belongs only to the Omniscient Buddhas and the like, not to others.

Nānādhimuttikatanti nānāajjhāsayataṃ. Adhimutti nāma ajjhāsayadhātu ajjhāsayasabhāvo. So pana hīnapaṇītatāsāmaññena pāḷiyaṃ dvidhāva vuttopi hīnapaṇītādibhedena anekavidhoti āha “hīnādīhi adhimuttīhi nānādhimuttikabhāva”nti. Tattha tattha ye ye sattā yaṃyaṃadhimuttikā, te te taṃtadadhimuttike eva sevanti bhajanti payirupāsanti dhātusabhāgato. Yathā gūthādīnaṃ dhātusabhāvo eso, yaṃ gūthādīhi eva saṃsandanti samenti, evaṃ (puggalānaṃ ajjhāsayassevesa sabhāvo, yaṃ) (vibha. mūlaṭī. 813) hīnajjhāsayā dussīlādīhi eva saṃsandanti samenti, sampannasīlādayo ca sampannasīlādīheva. Taṃ nesaṃ nānādhimuttikataṃ bhagavā yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti.

The diversity of inclinations is the diversity of dispositions. Inclination means the element of disposition, the nature of disposition. Although it is spoken of in two ways in the Pāli—as inferior and superior in general—it is said to be of many kinds, such as inferior, superior, and so on, with the phrase 'the state of having diverse inclinations is due to inclinations that are inferior and so on.' There, whatever beings have whatever inclination, they associate with, follow, and attend upon those with that same inclination because of the similarity of their element. Just as the nature of elements like dung is such that they mix and unite with dung and the like, so too (the nature of individuals' dispositions is such that) those with inferior dispositions mix and unite with the immoral and so on, while those endowed with virtue mix and unite with the virtuous and so on. The Blessed One understands as it actually is this diversity of their inclinations.

Vuddhiñca hāniñcāti paccayavisesena sāmatthiyato adhikataṃ anadhikatañca. Indriyaparopariyattañāṇaniddese (vibha. 814; paṭi. ma. 1.113) “āsayaṃ jānāti anusayaṃ jānātī”ti āsayādijānanaṃ kasmā niddiṭṭhanti? Āsayajānanādinā yehi indriyehi paroparehi sattā kalyāṇapāpāsayādikā honti, tesaṃ jānanassa vibhāvanato. Evañca katvā indriyaparopariyattaāsayānusayañāṇānaṃ visuṃ asādhāraṇatā, indriyaparopariyattanānādhimuttikatāñāṇānaṃ visuṃ balatā ca siddhā hoti. Tattha āsayanti yattha sattā nivasanti, taṃ tesaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ vā yathābhūtañāṇaṃ vā āsayo. Anusayo appahīnabhāvena thāmagato kileso. Taṃ pana bhagavā sattānaṃ āsayaṃ jānanto tesaṃ tesaṃ diṭṭhigatānaṃ, vipassanāmaggañāṇānañca appavattikkhaṇepi jānāti. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ –

'Growth and decline' means what has been attained and what has not been attained, based on capability due to a distinction in conditions. In the exposition of the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of others' faculties (Vibh 814; Paṭis I 113), why is the knowing of disposition, etc., indicated by the passage 'one knows the disposition, one knows the underlying tendency'? Because this clarifies the knowing of those superior and inferior faculties by which beings come to have wholesome or unwholesome dispositions and so on. By this, the distinct, uncommon nature of the knowledges of the superiority and inferiority of faculties, of disposition, and of underlying tendency is established, and also the separate status as powers for the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of faculties and the knowledge of the diverse inclinations of beings. Here, 'disposition' (āsaya) is where beings dwell; their dwelling place—be it a speculative view or knowledge as it really is—is their disposition. 'Underlying tendency' (anusaya) is a defilement that has become strong through not being abandoned. The Blessed One, knowing the dispositions of beings, also knows their respective speculative views and the moments when the knowledges of insight and the path do not arise. For it is said:

“Kāmaṃ sevantaṃyeva bhagavā jānāti ‘ayaṃ puggalo kāmagaruko kāmāsayo kāmādhimutto’ti. Kāmaṃ sevantaññeva jānāti ‘ayaṃ puggalo nekkhammagaruko nekkhammāsayo nekkhammādhimutto’ti. Nekkhammaṃ sevantaññeva jānāti. Byāpādaṃ, abyāpādaṃ, thinamiddhaṃ, ālokasaññaṃ sevantaṃyeva [M 2.0024] jānāti ‘ayaṃ puggalo thinamiddhagaruko thinamiddhāsayo thinamiddhādhimutto’ti” (paṭi. ma. 1.113).

"Even while a person is indulging in sensual pleasures, the Blessed One knows: 'This person gives gravity to sensual pleasures, has a sensual disposition, is inclined toward sensual pleasures.' Even while a person is indulging in sensual pleasures, he knows: 'This person gives gravity to renunciation, has a renunciant disposition, is inclined toward renunciation.' Even while one is indulging in renunciation, he knows likewise. Even while one is indulging in ill will, non-ill will, sloth and torpor, or the perception of light, he knows, for instance: 'This person gives gravity to sloth and torpor, has a disposition for sloth and torpor, is inclined toward sloth and torpor'" (Paṭis I 113).

Paṭhamādīnaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānanti rūpāvacarānaṃ paṭhamādīnaṃ paccanīkajhāpanaṭṭhena ārammaṇūpanijjhānaṭṭhena ca jhānānaṃ. Catukkanayena hetaṃ vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhannaṃ vimokkhānanti ettha paṭipāṭiyā [V 2.0022] satta appitappitakkhaṇe paccanīkadhammehi vimuccanato ārammaṇe ca adhimuccanato vimokkhā nāma, aṭṭhamo pana sabbaso saññāvedayitehi vimuttattā apagamavimokkho nāma. Catukkanayapañcakanayesu paṭhamajhānasamādhi savitakkasavicāro nāma, pañcakanaye dutiyajjhānasamādhi avitakkavicāramatto, nayadvayepi upari tīsu jhānesu samādhi avitakkaavicāro, samāpattīsu paṭipāṭiyā aṭṭhannaṃ samādhītipi nāmaṃ, samāpattītipi cittekaggatāsabbhāvato, nirodhasamāpattiyā tadabhāvato na samādhīti nāmaṃ. Hānabhāgiyadhammanti appaguṇehi paṭhamajjhānādīhi vuṭṭhitassa saññāmanasikārānaṃ kāmādianupakkhandanaṃ. Visesabhāgiyadhammanti paguṇehi paṭhamajjhānādīhi vuṭṭhitassa saññāmanasikārānaṃ dutiyajjhānādipakkhandanaṃ. Iti saññāmanasikārānaṃ kāmādidutiyajjhānādipakkhandanāni hānabhāgiyavisesabhāgiyadhammāti dassitāni, tehi pana jhānānaṃ taṃsabhāvatā dhamma-saddena vuttā. Tasmāti vuttamevatthaṃ hetubhāvena paccāmasati. Vodānanti paguṇatāsaṅkhātaṃ vodānaṃ. Tañhi paṭhamajjhānādīhi vuṭṭhahitvā dutiyajjhānādiadhigamassa paccayattā “vuṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Ye (a. ni. ṭī. 3.10.21) pana “nirodhato phalasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhānanti pāḷi natthī”ti vadanti, te “nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ phalasamāpattiyā anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti imāya pāḷiyā (paṭṭhā. 1.1.417) paṭisedhetabbā. Yo samāpattilābhī samāno eva “na labhāmaha”nti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ samānaṃ eva “na kammaṭṭhāna”nti saññī hoti, so sampattiṃyeva samānaṃ “vipattī”ti paccetīti veditabbo.

The four jhānas, beginning with the first, are those of the form realm, called 'jhānas' because they burn up opposing states and because of intense mental focus on the object. This is stated according to the fourfold method. Among the eight liberations, the first seven are called 'liberations' because, in the very moment of absorption, they are freed from opposing states and because they are resolved upon their objects. The eighth, however, is called the 'liberation of departure' because it is entirely freed from perception and feeling. In the fourfold and fivefold methods, the concentration of the first jhāna is called 'with initial thought and sustained thought.' In the fivefold method, the concentration of the second jhāna is called 'without initial thought, with only sustained thought.' In both methods, the concentration in the higher three jhānas is called 'without initial thought and without sustained thought.' Regarding the attainments, the eight are also named 'concentrations' and 'attainments' because of the presence of mental unification. The attainment of cessation, however, is not named 'concentration' because it lacks that state. States inclining towards decline: for one who has emerged from the first jhāna and so on, which are of inferior quality, this is the non-inclination of perceptions and attention towards sense desire and so on. States inclining towards distinction: for one who has emerged from the first jhāna and so on, which are of superior quality, this is the inclination of perceptions and attention towards the second jhāna and so on. Thus, the inclinations of perceptions and attention towards sense desire and so on, or towards the second jhāna and so on, are shown to be states inclining towards decline and states inclining towards distinction. The nature of those jhānas as such is expressed by the word 'dhamma'. Therefore: this refers back to the meaning already stated as a reason. Purification: this refers to purification, which is termed proficiency. For it is called 'emergence' because emerging from the first jhāna and so on is a condition for the attainment of the second jhāna and so on. As for those who say, 'There is no Pāli text stating emergence from cessation into fruition attainment,' they should be refuted by this Pāli passage: 'For one emerging from cessation, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for fruition attainment by way of proximity condition.' One who, while possessing an attainment, perceives, 'I do not possess it,' or while the meditation subject is present, perceives, 'This is not a meditation subject'—such a person, though in a state of success, is convinced it is a failure. This should be understood.

149. Appananti nigamanaṃ. Na tathā daṭṭhabbanti yathā paravādinā vuttaṃ, tathā na daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sakasakakiccameva jānātīti ṭhānāṭṭhānajānanādiṃ sakaṃ sakaṃyeva kiccaṃ kātuṃ jānāti, yathāsakameva visayaṃ paṭivijjhatīti attho. Tampīti tehi dasabalañāṇehi jānitabbampi. Kammantaravipākantaramevāti [M 2.0025] kammantarassavipākantarameva jānāti, cetanācetanāsampayuttadhamme nirayādinibbānagāminipaṭipadābhūte kammanti gahetvā āha “kammaparicchedamevā”ti. Dhātunānattañca dhātunānattakāraṇañca dhātunānattakāraṇanti ekadesasarūpekaseso daṭṭhabbo.
