Tañhi ñāṇaṃ tadubhayampi jānāti, “imāya nāma dhātuyā ussannattā”tiādinā (vibha. aṭṭha. 812) tathā ceva saṃvaṇṇitaṃ. Saccaparicchedamevāti pariññābhisamayādivasena saccānaṃ paricchindanameva. Appetuṃ na sakkoti aṭṭhamanavamabalāni viya taṃsadisaṃ iddhividhañāṇaṃ viya vikubbituṃ. Etenassa balasadisatañca nivāreti. Jhānādiñāṇaṃ viya vā appetuṃ vikubbituñca. Yadipi hi “jhānādipaccavekkhaṇāñāṇaṃ sattamabala”nti tassa savitakkasavicāratā vuttā, tathāpi “jhānādīhi vinā paccavekkhaṇā natthī”ti [V 2.0023] jhānādisahagataṃ ñāṇaṃ tadantogadhaṃ katvā evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ jhānādikiccaṃ viya na sabbaṃ balakiccaṃ kātuṃ sakkotīti dassetuṃ “jhānaṃ hutvā appetuṃ na sakkoti iddhi hutvā vikubbituṃ na sakkotī”ti vuttaṃ, na pana kassaci balassa jhānaiddhibhāvatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ kiccavisesavasenapi dasabalañāṇasabbaññutaññāṇānaṃ visesaṃ dassetvā idāni vitakkattikabhūmantaravasenapi taṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Paṭipāṭiyātiādito paṭṭhāya paṭipāṭiyā.

149. 'Appana' means conclusion. It should not be seen thus: it should not be seen as stated by the opponent. Each knows its own function: it knows how to perform its own function, such as knowing what is appropriate and inappropriate; the meaning is that it penetrates its own respective domain. Even that: even that which is to be known by those ten powers of knowledge. It knows only the variety of kamma and the variety of its result: it knows only the variety of kamma and the variety of its result. Taking kamma as volition and its associated states that constitute the path leading to hell and so on, or to Nibbāna, it is said, 'only the delimitation of kamma'. The diversity of elements and the cause of the diversity of elements: the latter phrase should be understood as an 'ekadesasarūpekasesa' (a figure of speech where a part stands for the whole, representing both). For that knowledge knows both, and it is explained thus in the Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā with phrases like 'due to the predominance of such and such an element'. Only the delimitation of truths: this means only the delimitation of truths by way of full understanding, realization, and so on. It cannot enter absorption: it cannot enter absorption like the eighth and ninth powers, or transform like the similar knowledge of supernormal power. By this, its similarity to the powers is also denied. Or, like the knowledge of jhāna and so on, it cannot enter absorption or transform. For although it is said that 'the knowledge of reviewing jhāna and so on is the seventh power,' and its nature is stated to be with initial and sustained thought, still, because 'without jhāna and so on, there is no reviewing,' it should be understood that the knowledge accompanied by jhāna and so on is included within it when this is stated. Alternatively, to show that omniscient knowledge, unlike the function of jhāna and so on, cannot perform all the functions of the powers, it is said, 'it cannot enter absorption by becoming jhāna, nor transform by becoming supernormal power.' But it should be understood that no power has the nature of jhāna or supernormal power. Having thus shown the distinction between the ten powers of knowledge and omniscient knowledge based on functional differences, now, to show it based on the range of the triad of thought and the planes of existence, it is said, 'furthermore' and so on. Sequentially: from the beginning, in sequence.

Anupadavaṇṇanaṃ katvā veditabbānīti sambandho. Kilesāvaraṇaṃ niyatamicchādiṭṭhi, kilesāvaraṇassa abhāvo āsavakkhayādhigamassa ṭhānaṃ, tabbhāvo aṭṭhānaṃ, anadhigamassa pana tadubhayaṃ yathākkamaṃ aṭṭhānañca ṭhānañcāti tattha kāraṇaṃ dassento “lokiya…pe… dassanato cā”ti āha. Tattha lokiyasammādiṭṭhiyā ṭhiti āsavakkhayādhigamassa ṭhānaṃ kilesāvaraṇābhāvassa kāraṇattā. Sā hi tasmiṃ sati na hoti, asati ca hoti. Etena tassā aṭṭhitiyā tassa aṭṭhānatā vuttā eva. Nesaṃ veneyyasattānaṃ. Dhātuvemattadassanatoti kāmadhātuādīnaṃ pavattibhedadassanato. Yadaggena dhātuvemattaṃ jānāti, tadaggena cariyāvisesampi jānāti. Dhātuvemattadassanatoti vā dhammadhātuvemattadassanato. Sabbāpi hi cariyā [M 2.0026] dhammadhātupariyāpannā evāti. Payogaṃ anādiyitvāpi santatimahāmattādīnaṃ (dha. pa. 142) viya. Dibbacakkhuñāṇānubhāvato pattabbenāti ettha dibbacakkhunā parassa hadayavatthusannissayalohitavaṇṇadassanamukhena tadā pavattamānacittajānanatthaṃ parikammakaraṇaṃ nāma sāvakānaṃ, tañca kho ādikammikānaṃ, yato dibbacakkhuānubhāvato cetopariyañāṇassa pattabbatā siyā, buddhānaṃ pana yadipi āsavakkhayañāṇādhigamato pageva dibbacakkhuñāṇādhigamo, tathāpi tathā parikammakaraṇaṃ natthi vijjāttayasiddhiyā sijjhanato. Sesābhiññāttaye cetopariyañāṇaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇādhigamena pattanti ca vattabbataṃ labhatīti tathā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The connection is that these things should be understood after providing the word-by-word explanation. The hindrance of defilements is fixed wrong view. The absence of the hindrance of defilements is a condition for the attainment of the destruction of the taints; its presence is not a condition. For non-attainment, however, these two are respectively not a condition and a condition. Showing the reason for this, it is said, 'mundane... and from seeing'. In this context, the stability of mundane right view is a condition for the attainment of the destruction of the taints because it is the cause for the absence of the hindrance of defilements. For when that hindrance exists, this stability of mundane right view does not exist, and when that hindrance does not exist, this stability exists. By this, it is stated that the instability of that right view is not a condition for that attainment. This is for those beings who are trainable. 'From seeing the diversity of elements': this means from seeing the distinctions in the occurrences of the sense-sphere realm and so on. To the extent that one knows the diversity of elements, to that extent one also knows the distinctions in conduct. Alternatively, 'from seeing the diversity of elements' means from seeing the diversity of the dhamma-element. For all conduct is indeed included within the dhamma-element. Even without undertaking an effort, as in the case of Santati the great minister and others. 'Through the power of the divine eye knowledge, it is attainable': here, for disciples, there is what is called the preliminary work for knowing the mind currently occurring by means of the divine eye, through seeing the color of the blood dependent on another's heart-base. And this is for beginners, from which the attainability of the knowledge of others' minds through the power of the divine eye might come. For Buddhas, however, although the attainment of divine eye knowledge precedes the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, there is no such preliminary work, as it is accomplished by the realization of the three true knowledges. It should be understood that it is stated thus because, with regard to the remaining triad of direct knowledges, the knowledge of others' minds can be said to be attained through the attainment of divine eye knowledge.

Puna evarūpiṃ vācaṃ na vakkhāmīti cittaṃ uppādento taṃ vācaṃ pajahati nāma. Vācāya pana so attho pākaṭo hotīti “vadanto”ti vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhiṃ na gaṇhissāmīti diṭṭhiggāhapaṭikkhepo. Diṭṭhiyā anuppādanaṃ pajahanamevāti āha “pajahanto”ti. So ariyūpavādī niraye ṭhapitoyeva, nāssa nirayūpapattiyā koci vibandho ekaṃsiko ayamatthoti adhippāyo.

By generating the thought, 'I will not speak such words again,' one is said to abandon that speech. But since that meaning becomes manifest through speech, it is said 'speaking'. 'I will not grasp a view': this is the rejection of grasping at views. The non-arising of a view is itself abandonment; therefore, it says 'abandoning'. That slanderer of noble ones is as good as established in hell; there is no obstruction to his rebirth in hell. This matter is certain—this is the intended meaning.

Assāti [V 2.0024] ekaṃsikabhāvassa. Sikkhāhi sīlasamādhipaññāhi, tadatthāya vipassanāya ca vinā aññārādhanassa asambhavato “lokiyalokuttarā sīlasamādhipaññā veditabbā”ti vatvā puna āsannatare sīlādike dassento “lokuttaravaseneva vinivattetumpi vaṭṭatī”ti āha, tasmā aggamaggapariyāpannā sīlādayo veditabbā. Aggamaggaṭṭhassa hi diṭṭheva dhamme ekaṃsikā aññārādhanā, itaresaṃ anekaṃsikāti. Sampajjanaṃ sampadā, nipphattīti attho, tasmā evaṃsampadanti evaṃavirajjhanakanipphattikanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “imampi kāraṇa”ntiādi. Tattha kāraṇanti yutti. Tatrāyaṃ yuttiniddhāraṇā “nirayūpago ariyūpavādī tadādāyassa avijjamānato seyyathāpi micchādiṭṭhī”ti. Ettha ca “taṃ vācaṃ appahāyā”tiādivacanena tadādāyassa appahānena ca ariyūpavādo antarāyiko anatthāvaho ca, pahānena pana accayaṃ desetvā khamāpanena anantarāyiko atthāvaho ca yathā taṃ vuṭṭhitā desitā ca āpattīti dasseti.

'Assa' is for the state of being certain. Since the attainment of final knowledge is impossible without the trainings in virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and without insight for that purpose, it is said, 'Mundane and supramundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom should be understood.' Then, showing virtue and the others as even closer, it is stated, 'It is fitting to avert it even by means of the supramundane.' Therefore, virtue and the others comprised in the highest path should be understood. For one established in the highest path, the attainment of final knowledge is certain in this very life, but for others, it is not certain. 'Sampajjanaṃ' is 'sampadā', meaning accomplishment. Therefore, 'evaṃsampadanti' means 'thus having an accomplishment that is non-failing'. For this reason, it is said, 'this reason,' and so on. Here, 'reason' means justification. The determination of the justification is as follows: 'One who goes to hell for slandering noble ones, because of the non-existence of one who accepts that, is like one with wrong view.' Here, it shows that by the statement 'not abandoning that speech,' etc., and by not abandoning that taking up, slandering noble ones is obstructive and harmful; but by abandoning it, having confessed the transgression and obtained forgiveness, it is non-obstructive and beneficial, just as an offense that has been confessed and from which one has recovered is taught.

Dasabalañāṇavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the Ten Powers of Knowledge is finished.

Catuvesārajjañāṇavaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Knowledge of the Four Fearlessnesses

150. Byāmohabhayavasena [M 2.0027] (a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.8) saraṇapariyesanaṃ sārajjanaṃ sārado, byāmohabhayaṃ, vigato sārado etassāti visārado, tassa bhāvo vesārajjaṃ. Taṃ pana ñāṇasampadaṃ pahānasampadaṃ desanāvisesasampadaṃ khemaṃ nissāya pavattaṃ catubbidhaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. Tenāha “catūsu ṭhānesū”tiādi. Dassitadhammesūti vuttadhammesu. Vacanamattameva hi tesaṃ, na pana dassanaṃ tādisasseva dhammassa abhāvato. Bhagavatā eva vā “ime dhammā anabhisambuddhā”ti parassa vacanavasena dassitadhammesu. “Dhammapaṭisambhidā”tiādīsu (vibha. 718) viya dhamma-saddo hetupariyāyoti āha “sahadhammenāti sahetunā”ti. Hetūti ca upapattisādhanahetu veditabbo, na kārako sampāpako ca. Appamāṇanti anidassanaṃ. Nidassanañhi anvayato byatirekato pamāṇaṅgatāya “pamāṇa”nti vuccati. Nimittanti codanāya kāraṇaṃ. Tattha codako codanaṃ karotīti kāraṇaṃ, dhammo codanaṃ karoti etenāti kāraṇaṃ. Tenāha “puggalopī”tiādi. Khemanti kenaci appaṭibandhiyabhāvena anupaddutataṃ.

150. Due to fear of perplexity, seeking refuge is timidity (`sārajjanaṃ`); one who is timid (`sārado`) has this fear of perplexity. One from whom timidity has departed is fearless (`visārado`), and his state is fearlessness (`vesārajjaṃ`). This fearlessness, relying on the accomplishment of knowledge, the accomplishment of abandonment, the accomplishment of distinction in teaching, and security, proceeds as the fourfold reviewing knowledge. Hence it is said: 'In four instances,' and so on. 'Regarding the phenomena shown' means regarding the phenomena spoken of. For them, it is merely a statement, not an actual seeing, due to the absence of such a phenomenon. Or, regarding phenomena shown by way of another's statement, such as, 'These phenomena were not fully awakened to by the Blessed One.' As in passages like 'the analytical knowledge of phenomena,' the word 'dhamma' is a synonym for 'cause.' Thus it is said: 'with the dhamma, that is, with the cause.' And 'cause' should be understood as a cause that provides a reason, not as an agent or an accomplisher. 'Immeasurable' means without an example. For an example, because it serves as a measure through positive and negative concomitance, is called a 'measure.' 'Sign' means the reason for an accusation. Therein, it is a reason because an accuser makes an accusation; it is a reason because the grounds for accusation are made by means of it. Hence it is said: 'a person too,' and so on. 'Security' means being unafflicted through being unopposable by anyone.

Antarāyo [V 2.0025] etesaṃ atthi, antarāyevā yuttāti antarāyikā. Evaṃbhūtā pana te yasmā antarāyakarā nāma honti, tasmā āha “antarāyaṃ karontīti antarāyikā”ti. Asañcicca vītikkamo na tathā sāvajjoti katvā vuttaṃ “sañcicca vītikkantā”ti. Satta āpattikkhandhātiādi nidassanamattaṃ itaresampi catunnaṃ “antarāyikā”ti vuttadhammānaṃ tabbhāve byabhicārābhāvato. Idha pana methunadhammo adhippetoti idaṃ aṭṭhuppattivasena vuttaṃ ariṭṭhasikkhāpadaṃ (pāci. 417-422) viya. Yasmā taṅkhaṇampi kāmesu (a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.8) ādīnavaṃ disvā viratto (a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.8) hoti ce, visesaṃ adhigacchati, na kāmesu āsatto, tasmā vuttaṃ “methunaṃ…pe… antarāyo hotī”ti. Tattha yassa kassacīti na kevalaṃ pabbajitasseva, atha kho yassa kassaci. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “methunamanuyuttassa, mussatevāpi sāsana”nti. Tasmiṃ aniyyānikadhammeti tasmiṃ parena parikappitaaniyyānikadhammanimittaṃ. Nimittatthe hi idaṃ kammasaṃyoge bhummaṃ.

An obstacle exists for them; they are connected with an obstacle, thus they are called 'obstructive.' And since they are of such a nature as to be obstacle-makers, it is therefore said: 'They make an obstacle; thus, they are obstructive.' Because an unintentional transgression is not so blameworthy, it is stated: 'having transgressed intentionally.' The seven groups of offenses, and so on, are merely an example, since there is no deviation from that state for the other four things called 'obstructive.' Here, however, sexual intercourse is intended; this is said based on the origin of the matter, like the Ariṭṭha training rule. For if, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures even at that moment, one becomes dispassionate, one attains distinction and is not attached to sensual pleasures; therefore it is said: 'Sexual intercourse… is an obstacle.' Therein, 'for anyone' means not only for one who has gone forth, but for anyone at all. For so it is said: 'For one devoted to sexual intercourse, the teaching is forgotten.' 'In that non-liberating phenomenon' means: in that sign of a non-liberating phenomenon as conceived by another. For this locative case is used in the sense of a sign in connection with the object.

Catuvesārajjañāṇavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the Knowledge of the Four Fearlessnesses is finished.

Aṭṭhaparisavaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Eight Assemblies

151. Purisassa [M 2.0028] sūratarabhāvo nāma saṅgāme pākaṭo hoti, na gehe nisinnakāle, evaṃ vesārajjañāṇassa ānubhāvo paṇḍitaparisāsu yattha katthacīti dassento “vesārajjañāṇassa baladassanattha”nti āha. Sannipatitvā nisinnaṭṭhānanti ṭhānasīsena sannipatitakhattiyaparisameva dasseti. Eseva nayo sabbatthāti atidesena āvibhāvitamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “mārakāyikāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ sadisatthavisayattā atidesassa. Yathā hi khattiyānaṃ samūho khattiyaparisāti ayamattho labbhati, na evaṃ “māraparisā”ti ettha, mārassa parisāti pana māraparisāti ayamattho adhippeto. Tenāha “mārakāyikānaṃ…pe… na mārāna”nti. Mārakāyikānanti mārapakkhiyānaṃ. Uggaṭṭhānadassanavasenāti sārajjitabbaṭṭhānadassanavasena, evaṃ uggā khattiyā attano puññatejenāti adhippāyo. Brāhmaṇā tīsu vedesūti idaṃ itaresaṃ avisayadassanavasena vuttaṃ. Vede sajjhāyantāpi hi khattiyā vessā ca tadatthavicāraṇāya yebhuyyena asamatthā evāti. Kasmā panettha yāmādiparisā na gahitāti? Bhusaṃ kāmābhigiddhatāya yonisomanasikāravirahato. Yāmādayo hi uḷāruḷāre kāme paṭisevantā tatthābhigiddhatāya dhammassavanāya sabhāvena cittampi na uppādenti, mahābodhisattānaṃ pana buddhānañca [V 2.0026] ānubhāvena ākaḍḍhiyamānā kadāci tesaṃ payirupāsanādīni karonti tādise mahāsamaye. Teneva hi vimānavatthudesanāpi tannimittā bahulā nāhosi. Manussānaṃ vasenāyaṃ katā.

151. A man's bravery is clearly seen in battle, not while sitting at home. Similarly, to show that the power of the knowledge of fearlessness is displayed in assemblies of the wise, wherever it may be, it is said: 'to demonstrate the strength of the knowledge of fearlessness.' The phrase 'a place where they have gathered and sat down' refers specifically to an assembly of khattiyas gathered in their place of rank. The same principle applies everywhere. To clarify the meaning not made evident by this extension, the phrase 'of the Māra-kāyikas' and so on is stated, because an extension applies to a similar subject matter. For while 'khattiya assembly' is understood to mean 'a group of khattiyas,' this is not the case with 'Māra's assembly'; here, 'Māra's assembly' is intended to mean 'Māra's retinue.' Hence it is said: 'of the Māra-kāyikas… not of the Māras.' 'Of the Māra-kāyikas' means of Māra's faction. The phrase 'by seeing an eminent position' means by seeing a situation that should inspire awe. Similarly, the eminence of the khattiyas is through their own power of merit—this is the intended meaning. As for 'Brahmins versed in the three Vedas,' this is said to show what is not the domain of others. For even if khattiyas and vessas recite the Vedas, they are generally incapable of deeply investigating their meaning. Why then are assemblies like those of the Yāmas not mentioned here? Because of their extreme greed for sensual pleasures and their lack of wise attention. The Yāmas and others, indulging in progressively more sublime sensual pleasures, are so greedy for them that they do not naturally even give rise to a mind to listen to the Dhamma. Only rarely, drawn by the power of great bodhisattas and Buddhas, do they attend on them at a great occasion like this. For this very reason, the teaching on the celestial mansions was not frequently given with them as the reason. This was done with reference to human beings.

Paracakkavāḷesu ca manussānaṃ visesādhigamo natthīti pucchati “kiṃ pana bhagavā aññāni cakkavāḷānipi gacchatī”ti. Itaro yadipi tesaṃ ariyadhammādhigamo natthi, vāsanāya pana tattha gantvā dhammaṃ desetīti dassento “āmagacchatī”ti āha. Keyūraṃ nānāvidharatanaparisibbitasuvaṇṇajālavinaddhaṃ bhujābharaṇaṃ. Aṅgadaṃ nānāgandhagandhitaṃ, kevalaṃ vā suvaṇṇamayaṃ bāhuvalayaṃ. Chinnassarāti dvidhābhūtassarā (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.172) gaggarassarāti gaggarikāya viya gaggarāyamānakharassarā (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.172; a. ni. ṭī. 3.8.69). Bhāsantaranti tesaṃ bhāsaṃ (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.172; a. ni. ṭī. 3.8.69) sandhāyāha. “Vīmaṃsā [M 2.0029] uppajjatī”ti saṅkhepato vuttaṃ vivarituṃ “idaṃ vuttaṃ hotī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Since in other world-systems there is no attainment of distinction for humans, the question is asked: 'But does the Blessed One go to other world-systems as well?' The other, showing that although they have no attainment of the noble Dhamma, he still goes there and teaches the Dhamma because of his dispositions, says: 'Yes, he goes.' A keyūra is an arm ornament interwoven with a net of gold and studded with various kinds of jewels. An aṅgada is a bracelet scented with various perfumes, or simply a golden armlet. 'A broken voice' means a voice that has become twofold. 'A croaking voice' means a harsh, croaking voice like that of a water-pot. 'Speaking in another language' refers to their own language. To explain what was stated concisely as 'inquiry arises,' it is said: 'This is what is meant,' and so on.

Saṅgammāti samāgantvā. Ādito lāpo ālāpo, vacanapaṭivacanavasena samaṃ lāpo sallāpo. Sammā, samaññā vā kathā saṃkathā, saṃkathāva sākacchā.

'Having met' means having come together. Initial talk is conversation; talk together by way of speech and counter-speech is dialogue. Right talk, or talk by common agreement, is discussion; discussion itself is discourse.

Aṭṭhaparisavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Eight Assemblies is finished.

Catuyonivaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Four Modes of Birth

152. Yavanti tāya sattā amissitāpi samānajātitāya missitā viya hontīti yoni. Sā pana atthato aṇḍādiuppattiṭṭhānavisiṭṭho khandhānaṃ bhāgaso pavattivisesoti āha “khandhakoṭṭhāso yoni nāmā”ti. Aṇḍe jātāti paṭhamāya jātiyā vasena vuttaṃ, dutiyāya pana aṇḍato, aṇḍe vā bhijjamāne jātāti evamattho veditabbo. Tenāha “abhinibbhijja jāyantī”ti. Vināti etehi aṇḍādīhi bāhirapaccayehi vinā. Uppatitvā viyāti uppajjanavasena patitvā viya. Bāhirapaccayanirapekkhattāyeva vā upapatane sādhukārino upapātikā, te eva idha opapātikāti vuttā. Ādi-saddena gabbhamale nibbattamahāpadumakumārādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Nijjhāmataṇhikapetānaṃ niccaṃ dukkhāturatāya kāmasevanā natthi[V 2.0027], tasmā te gabbhaseyyakā na honti, jālavantatāya na tāsaṃ kucchiyaṃ gabbho saṇṭhāti, tasmā te opapātikāyeva saṃsedajattāyapi asambhavato. Nerayikā viyāti nidassanāpadesena tesampi opapātikattaṃ dīpeti. Avasesāti nijjhāmataṇhikanerayike ṭhapetvā avasesā vinipātikā. Yakkhānaṃ cātumahārājikatāya opapātikabhāve eva āpanne taṃ nivattetuṃ “evaṃ yakkhāpī”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi te na bhummadevā na ca vinipātikāti.

152. The term 'yoni' is used because beings, even when not actually mixed, appear to be mixed due to sharing the same kind of birth. In meaning, however, it is a particular mode of the proceeding of the aggregates in part, distinguished by the place of origin such as an egg. Hence it is said: 'A portion of the aggregates is called a womb.' 'Born in an egg' is said with reference to the first birth; but with reference to the second, it means born from the egg, or born when the egg is broken. This is the meaning to be understood. Thus it is said: 'They are born having broken forth.' 'Without' means without these external conditions such as eggs. 'As if having sprung up' means as if having alighted by way of arising. Or, precisely because they are independent of external conditions, those who are adept at arising are called 'spontaneously born' (upapātika); these same are here called 'opapātika.' By the word 'etc.,' such beings as the great Paduma princes, who are born in womb-filth, are included. For petas with scorching thirst, there is no indulgence in sensual pleasures because they are constantly afflicted by suffering; therefore, they are not womb-born. Because of their net-like constitution, a fetus does not become established in their wombs; therefore, they are only spontaneously born, since moisture-birth is also impossible for them. 'Like hell-beings' shows by way of example that they too are spontaneously born. 'The rest' means the remaining vinipātikas, having excluded the petas with scorching thirst and the hell-beings. Since yakkhas have attained the state of spontaneous birth because they belong to the realm of the Four Great Kings, to avert a certain implication, it is said, 'so too are yakkhas.' For they are neither terrestrial deities nor vinipātikas.

Catuyonivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Four Wombs is finished.

Pañcagativaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Five Destinies

153. Gantabbāti [M 2.0030] upapajjitabbā. Yathā hi kammabhavo paramatthato asatipi kārake paccayasāmaggiyā siddho taṃsamaṅginā santānalakkhaṇena sattena katoti voharīyati, tathā upapattibhavalakkhaṇā gatiyo paramatthato asatipi gamake taṃtaṃkammavasena yesaṃ tāni kammāni, tehi gantabbāti voharīyantīti. Evaṃ saddatthato gatiṃ dassetvā atthuddhāranayenapi taṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yesu nirayādibhedesu upapattibhavesu gati-saddo nirūḷho, tato aññatthāpi gatisaddappavatti atthi, taṃ ekena gati-saddena visesetvā āha “gatigatī”ti yathā “dukkhadukkhaṃ, (saṃ. ni. 4.327) rūparūpa”nti (visuddhi. 2.449) ca. Uppādāvatthāya gamanaṃ upagamananti “nibbattigatī”ti vuttā. Gatinti cittagatiṃ. Tenāha “ajjhāsayagati nāmā”ti, ajjhāsayappavattīti attho. Tadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.503) pana “gatinti nipphatti”nti attho vutto. Brahmanimantanasutte (ma. ni. 1.503) hi ayaṃ pāḷīti. Jutinti ānubhāvaṃ. Vibhavoti vināso. So hi vigamoti atthena gati. Teneva nibbānaṃ arahato gatīti (pari. 339) anupādisesanibbānaṃ arahato gati vigamo vibhavoti anekatthattā dhātūnaṃ. Dveyeva gatiyoti dveva nipphattiyoti atthoti āha “ayaṃ nipphattigati nāmā”ti.

153. 'To be gone to' means 'to be reborn into.' For just as kamma-existence, though accomplished by an assemblage of conditions, is conventionally said to be 'done' by a being who is characterized by a continuity and endowed with that kamma, even though in the ultimate sense there is no doer; so too the destinies, which are characterized by rebirth-existence, are conventionally said to be 'destinations to be gone to' by those for whom those kammas are, according to their respective kammas, even though in the ultimate sense there is no goer. Having thus shown 'destination' by its literal meaning, in order to show it also by the method of extracting the meaning, it is said 'Moreover,' etc. In rebirth-existences such as hell, the word 'gati' is established by usage. But the word 'gati' is also used elsewhere. To specify this, it is said 'gati-gati,' just as in 'dukkha-dukkha' (SN 38.14) and 'rūpa-rūpa' (Vism 14.73). Going and approaching in the state of arising is called 'the destination of generation.' 'Gati' means the mind's course. Hence it is said, 'the destination of inclination,' which means the proceeding of inclination. In its commentary (MA ii 392), however, the meaning of 'gati' is given as 'consummation.' For this is the Pāli passage in the Brahmanimantana Sutta (MN 49). 'Juti' means splendour. 'Vibhava' means destruction. For this, in the sense of departure (vigama), is a 'gati.' It is for this reason that Nibbāna is the 'gati' of an arahant. Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the Nibbāna without residue remaining is the arahant's 'gati,' departure (vigama), and destruction (vibhava). 'There are only two destinies' means there are only two consummations. Hence it is said: 'This is called the destination of consummation.'

Yassa uppajjati, taṃ brūhento eva uppajjatīti ayo, sukhaṃ. Natthi ettha ayoti nirayo. Tato eva ramitabbaṃ assādetabbaṃ tattha natthīti dassento āha “niratiatthena nirassādaṭṭhena nirayo”ti. Tiriyaṃ añcitāti devamanussādayo viya uddhaṃ dīghā ahutvā tiriyaṃ dīghābhi attho. Pakaṭṭhato sukhato ayanaṃ apagamo peccabhāvo, taṃ peccabhāvaṃ pattānaṃ visayoti [V 2.0028] petayonimeva vadati. Manaso ussannattāti satisūrabhāvabrahmacariyayogyatādiguṇavasena upacitamānasatāya ukkaṭṭhaguṇacittatāyāti atto. Ayaṃ panattho nippariyāyato jambudīpavāsīvasena veditabbo. Yathāha – “tīhi, bhikkhave, ṭhānehi jambudīpikā manussā uttarakuruke manusse adhiggaṇhanti deve ca tāvatiṃse. Katamehi tīhi? Sūrā satimanto idha brahmacariyavāso”ti (a. ni. 9.21). Tehi pana samānarūpāditāya saddhiṃ parittadīpavāsīhi itaramahādīpavāsinopi [M 2.0031] manussāteva paññāyiṃsu. Lokiyā pana “manuno apaccabhāvena manussā”ti vadanti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana paramatthadīpaniyaṃ vimānavatthusaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (vi. va. aṭṭha. 3) vuttanayena gahetabbo. Ānubhāvehīti devānubhāvasaṅkhātehi iddhivisesehi. Tattha kāmā devā kāmaguṇehi ceva iddhivisesehi ca itare iddhiviseseheva dibbanti kīḷanti jotanti, saraṇanti vā gammanti, abhitthaviyantīti vā devāti.

That which arises for one and makes one prosper is 'aya,' that is, happiness. 'Niraya' is where there is no 'aya.' Showing that there is nothing there to be delighted in or savored, he says: 'Hell (niraya) is so called because it is without delight (nirati) and without savour (nirassāda).' 'Gone across' (tiriyaṃ añcitā) means they are long sideways, not long upwards like devas and humans; this is the meaning. The state of having departed (peccabhāva) is the going away from excellent happiness; he speaks of the ghost-womb (petayoni) as the domain of those who have reached that state of having departed. 'Because of an elevated mind' (manaso ussannattā) means having a mind of superior quality, with a mind augmented by such qualities as mindfulness, heroism, and suitability for the holy life; this is the meaning. This meaning, however, should be understood without alternative as referring to the inhabitants of Jambudīpa. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, in three respects the people of Jambudīpa surpass the humans of Uttarakuru and the devas of Tāvatiṃsa. What three? They are courageous, they are mindful, and the holy life is lived here' (AN 9.20). But because they share the same form and so on with them, the inhabitants of the smaller surrounding islands and the inhabitants of the other great continents are also known as 'humans.' Worldly people, however, say: 'Humans (manussā) are so called because they are the offspring of Manu.' This is the summary here; the detailed explanation should be taken according to the method stated in the Exposition of the Vimānavatthu in the Paramatthadīpanī (Vv-a 18). 'By powers' means by the special psychic powers known as divine powers. Among them, the devas of the sense sphere sport by means of both sensual pleasures and special psychic powers, while the others sport by means of special psychic powers alone. They are called 'devas' because they sport (dibbanti), play (kīḷanti), and shine (jotanti); or because they are gone to as a refuge (saraṇa); or because they are praised (abhitthaviyanti).

Tiracchānayoniñcātiādīsūti ettha tiracchānayonipettivisayaggahaṇena khandhānaṃ eva gahaṇaṃ tesaṃ tādisassa paricchinnassa okāsassa abhāvato. Yattha vā te araññasamuddapabbatādike nibaddhavāsaṃ vasanti, tādisassa ṭhānassa vasena okāsopi gahetabbo. Nirayūpagādīhi sattehi maggitabbato maggo paṭipajjitabbā paṭipadā cāti taṃ taṃ kammameva vuttanti āha “ubhayenapī”tiādi. Yathā ca paṭipannoti iminā tassa kammassa katūpacitākāramāha. Ettha ca nirayagāmiñca maggaṃ nirayagāminiñca paṭipadanti iminā sādhāraṇato nirayasaṃvattaniyaṃ kammaṃ vatvā puna taṃ taṃ santānapatitatāya asādhāraṇataṃ dassetuṃ “yathāpaṭipanno”tiādi vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vinipatantīti vivasā, virūpaṃ vā nipatanti. Kasmā panettha pañcagatiparicchedakañāṇaṃ dassento bhagavā “nibbānañcāha”ntiādimāhāti anuyogaṃ sandhāyāha “idaṃ panā”tiādi. Na hi bhagavā attano buddhasubuddhataṃ vibhāvento sāvasesaṃ katvā desanaṃ deseti.

In the phrase 'the animal womb, etc.,' by the mention of the animal womb and the ghost domain, it is the aggregates that are referred to, because for them there is no such defined location. Or, the location may be taken as the place where they live a fixed residence, such as a forest, ocean, or mountain. Because it is to be sought by beings going to hell and so on, it is a path (magga); and because it is to be undertaken, it is a practice (paṭipadā). Thus that very kamma is spoken of. Hence he says 'by both,' etc. And by 'as one has practiced,' he indicates the mode in which that kamma has been performed and accumulated. Here, it should be understood that by saying 'the path leading to hell' and 'the practice leading to hell,' he first speaks in general of the kamma that leads to hell; then, to show its specific nature due to its falling within a particular continuity, he says 'as one has practiced,' etc. 'They fall away' (vinipatanti) means they fall helplessly, or they fall in a wretched way. With reference to the question, 'Why, when explaining the knowledge that defines the five destinies, does the Blessed One say, "and Nibbāna too," etc.?' it is said: 'But this….' For the Blessed One, when explaining his own perfect enlightenment, does not give a teaching that leaves something out.

Pañcagativaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Five Destinies is finished.

Ñāṇapavattākāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Way Knowledge Proceeds

154. Ñāṇappavattākāranti ñāṇassa pavattiākāraṃ, ñāṇassa vā pavattipakāraṃ. Ekantadukkhāti ekantena dukkhā accantadukkhā. Tā pana sabbakālaṃ dukkhā sukhālayenapi asammissāti [V 2.0029] dassento āha “niccadukkhā nirantaradukkhā”ti. Bahalāti atanukā, mahantāti attho[M 2.0032]. Tibbāti vā tikhiṇā. Kharāti kakkhaḷā. Kaṭukāti vā aniṭṭhā. Kassati khaṇīyatīti kāsu, āvāṭo. Kasīyati cīyatīti kāsu, rāsi. Phunantīti dvīhi hatthehi aṅgārāni ukkhipitvā paṭivātaṃ ophunanti, tena tesaṃ sakalasarīraṃ ḍayhati. Tenāha “paridaḍḍhagattā”ti. Purisappamāṇaṃ porisaṃ. Ekapathenevāti ekamaggabhūteneva. Anukkamanīyenāti ukkamituṃ apakkamituṃ asakkuṇeyyena.

154. 'The mode of the arising of knowledge' means the manner in which knowledge arises, or the way knowledge proceeds. 'Exclusively painful' means completely painful, extremely painful. To show that they are always painful, unmixed with even a trace of pleasure, it is said: 'constantly painful, incessantly painful.' 'Dense' means not thin, that is, 'great.' Or 'intense' means sharp. 'Harsh' means rough. Or 'bitter' means unpleasant. Because it is dug (kassati), it is a pit (kāsu); a hole. Because it is accumulated (kasīyati), it is a heap (kāsu); a mass. 'They sprinkle' means they take up embers with both hands and scatter them against the wind, whereby their entire bodies are burned. Hence it is said: 'with scorched limbs.' Porisaṃ is a man’s measure. 'By a single path' means by a single road. 'Not to be passed' means unable to go beyond or turn away from.

Nanu ca dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ paccuppannavaṇṇārammaṇaṃ, tena kathaṃ rūpantarasamaṅgiṃ niraye nibbattasattaṃ “ayaṃ so”ti jānātīti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “tattha kiñcāpī”tiādi. Yathākammūpagañāṇena “ayaṃ so”ti sallakkheti, tassa pana dibbacakkhuānubhāvena pattabbattā “dibbacakkhubalaṃ nāma etanti vuttaṃ.

But is not the knowledge of the divine eye concerned with present visible objects? How then does it know a being reborn in hell, possessing a different form, as "this is that one"? With this objection in mind, he said, "But there, although..." etc. It discerns "this is that one" through the knowledge of beings faring according to their kamma. However, since that is attainable through the power of the divine eye, it is said, "This is called the power of the divine eye."

Purimanayenevāti “gūthakūpo viya tiracchānayoni daṭṭhabbā”tiādinā aṅgārakāsupamāyaṃ vuttanayeneva. Dukkhā vedanā bahulā etāsūti dukkhabahulā. Bahalapattapalāsoti aviraḷatanuvipulapaṇṇo. Sukhaparibhogaṃ mahāpāsādaṃ dassetuṃ “dīghapāsādo”ti vuttaṃ caturassapāsādādīnaṃ khuddakattā. Uṇṇāmayaattharaṇenāti uṇṇāmayalohitaattharaṇena. Uttaraṃ uparibhāgaṃ chādetīti uttaracchado, vitānaṃ. Taṃ pana lohitavitānaṃ idhādhippetanti “rattavitānenā”ti vuttaṃ.

'In the same way as before,' that is, in the way stated in the simile of the charcoal pit, beginning with, 'one should regard the animal realm as like a cesspit.' 'Abundant in suffering' means that painful feelings are plentiful in them. 'Thick with leaves and foliage' means having dense, not sparse, broad leaves. To show the enjoyment of pleasure in a great palace, 'long palace' is said because square palaces and the like are small. 'With woolen spreads' means with red woolen spreads. 'It covers the upper part,' hence an upper covering; a canopy. But here a red canopy is intended; therefore, 'with a red canopy' is said.

Aparabhāgayojanāti pāḷiyaṃ “aparena samayenā”ti vuttassa aparabhāgassa yojanā. Sā pana ekadesena purimabhāge vutte eva suviññeyyā hotīti “yathā so”tiādimāha. Maggāruḷhamevāti maggaṃ upagatamattameva.

'Explanation of the latter portion': This is an explanation of the latter portion mentioned in the Pāli text as 'at a later time.' But that is easily understood only when the earlier portion has been stated in part; thus, he said, 'just as he,' and so on. 'Just ascended the path' means merely having approached the path.

Niyamābhāvāti “dibbacakkhunāva passatī”ti niyamassa abhāvā. “Dibbacakkhunāpi passissatī”ti idaṃ na anuttarasukhānubhavanassa dibbacakkhugocarattā vuttaṃ, anāgatassa pana tassa dibbacakkhuparibhaṇḍabhūtena anāgataṃsañāṇena dassanamevāti kāraṇūpacārena vuttaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi”cceva vuttaṃ. “Atthato pana nānā hotī”ti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “devalokasukhaṃ hī”tiādiṃ vatvā [M 2.0033] yathādassitaupamāhipi ayamattho pākaṭo evāti dassento “upamāyampī”tiādimāha. Gotrabhuñāṇuppādato paṭṭhāya nirodhaṃ passitvā uppannamaggaphalapaccavekkhaṇavasena ceva parato phalasamāpattisamāpajjanavasena ca ariyasāvako nirodhe [V 2.0030] sayito viya hoti tadapassayeneva pavattanatoti āha “nirodhasayanavaragata”nti. Tenāha “nibbānā…pe… passatī”ti.

'Absence of restriction' means the absence of a restriction such as 'he sees only with the divine eye.' 'He will also see with the divine eye'—this is not said because the experience of unsurpassed bliss is within the range of the divine eye, but rather, it is said figuratively, as it is simply the seeing of that future bliss with the knowledge of the future, which is an accessory to the divine eye. In the Pāli text, however, it is simply said, 'he understands the mind with his mind.' 'But in meaning, it is different'—to explain the meaning stated briefly, he said, 'for the bliss of the heavenly world...' and so on. To show that this meaning is clear even through the similes shown, he said, 'even in the simile,' and so on. From the arising of change-of-lineage knowledge onwards, having seen cessation, the noble disciple, by way of reviewing the path and fruit that have arisen and by way of attaining fruition attainments afterward, is as if lying down in cessation, because he proceeds with that as his support; thus, it is said, 'gone to the supreme bed of cessation.' Therefore, it is said, 'he sees Nibbāna... ' and so on.

Ñāṇapavattākāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Mode of the Arising of Knowledge is concluded.

Dukkarakārikādisuddhivaṇṇanā

Explanation of Purification by the Practice of Austerities and so on

155. Pucchānusandhiādianusandhittayato aññattā “pāṭiyekkaṃ anusandhivasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Na kevalaṃ “dukkarakārikāya suddhi hotī”ti evaṃladdhiko eva, atha kho dukkaracārīsu abhippasannoti dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Catukuṇḍikoti dvīhi pādehi hatthehīti catūhi aṅgehi kuṇḍanako āhiṇḍanako. Chamānikiṇṇanti bhūmiyaṃ khittaṃ. Bhakkhasanti āhāraṃ.

155. Because it is distinct from the threefold connection beginning with the connection of the question, it is said, 'each separately by way of connection.' Not only is one of the view that 'there is purification by the performance of austerities,' but also to show that one is pleased with those who practice austerities, it is said, 'and moreover,' and so on. 'Going on all fours' means one who crawls and wanders on four limbs, that is, with two feet and two hands. 'Scattered on the ground' means thrown on the ground. 'Food' means nourishment.

Macchariyamalādipāpadhammavigamanato mettādiguṇānubrūhanato ca brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ cariyanti brahmacariyaṃ, dānaṃ. Tathā hi taṃ bhagavatā paṇḍitapaññattaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi yathārahaṃ brahmacariyapariyāyo niddhāretvā vattabbo. Kinti kīdisaṃ. Vatanti samādinnavataṃ. Suciṇṇassāti suṭṭhu ciṇṇassa puññassa. Iddhīti ānubhāvo. Jutīti vatthābharaṇobhāsasamujjalā sarīrappabhā. Balavīriyūpapattīti kāyabalena ceva ussāhena ca samannāgamo.

Because of the removal of evil states such as the stain of miserliness and the cultivation of virtues such as loving-kindness, it is a sublime or excellent conduct, hence 'the holy life'; for example, giving. For so it has been said by the Blessed One to be declared by the wise. Thus, in other cases too, the term 'holy life' should be determined and spoken of as is appropriate. 'What?' means 'Of what kind?' 'Vow' means the vow they have undertaken. 'Of the well-practiced' means of merit well-practiced. 'Power' means potency. 'Splendor' means the bodily radiance shining with the lustre of garments and ornaments. 'Attainment of strength and energy' means being endowed with both bodily strength and effort.

Tena pāṇi kāmadadoti tena addhikānaṃ upagacchantānaṃ hatthaṃ pasāretvā asayhaseṭṭhino dānaṭṭhānadassanamayena puññena idāni mayhaṃ hattho kapparukkho viya kāmadado icchiticchitadāyī, kāmadado honto ca madhussavo iṭṭhavatthuvissajjanako jāto. Tena me brahmacariyenāti tena mama yathāvuttakāyaveyyāvaṭiyakammasaṅkhātena seṭṭhacariyena. Puññanti puññaphalaṃ. Tampi hi pujjasabhāvato, uttarapadalopena vā “evamidaṃ puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.80) “puñña”nti vuccati.

'By that hand, the giver of desires' means: by that merit gained by extending my hand to approaching travelers and by showing the giving-place of the merchant Asayha, my hand has now become like a wish-fulfilling tree, a giver of desires, granting whatever is wished for; and being a giver of desires, it has become a dispenser of desired things, flowing with honey. 'By that holy life of mine' means by that supreme conduct of mine, reckoned as the deed of bodily service, as stated. 'Merit' means the fruit of merit. For that too, because of its nature of being worthy of honor, or by the elision of the latter word, is called 'merit' in passages such as 'thus this merit increases' (Dī. Ni. 3.80).

Pañca [M 2.0034] sikkhāpadāni samāhaṭāni pañcasikkhāpadaṃ yathā “tibhavaṃ, tisakaṭa”nti ca. Brahmacariyasminti [V 2.0031] dhammadesanāya. Sā hi vineyyānaṃ brahmabhāvāvahanato brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ cariyaṃ, brahmuno vā bhagavato vācasikaṃ cariyanti “brahmacariya”nti vuccati.

The five training rules are gathered together as 'the fivefold training rule,' just as in 'the threefold existence' and 'the three carts.' 'In the holy life' means in the teaching of the Dhamma. For that, since it leads to the state of Brahma for those to be trained, is a sublime, excellent conduct, or it is the verbal conduct of Brahma or of the Blessed One; thus it is called 'the holy life'.

Sahassaṃ maccuhāyinanti sahassamattā arahattasamadhigamena maccuvisayātikkamena maccupahāyino jātā. Brahmacārī bhavissāmāti ettha yena brahmacariyena te brahmacārinoti vuccanti, taṃ brahmacariyaṃ niddhāretvā āha “methunavirati brahmacariyanti vuttā”ti.

'A thousand who have left death behind' means that a thousand, through the attainment of arahantship, by transcending the sphere of death, have become those who have left death behind. 'I will be a holy-lifer'—here, having determined that holy life by which they are called 'holy-lifers', he says: 'Abstinence from sexual intercourse is called the holy life'.

Nātikkamāmāti na aticarāma agamanīyaṭṭhānepi itaratthāpi na vītikkamāma. Tenāha “aññatra tāhi brahmacariyaṃ carāmā”ti. Amhanti amhākaṃ.

'We do not transgress' means we do not transgress even in a place one should not go, nor do we transgress elsewhere. Therefore, he says, 'Apart from them, we live the holy life.' 'Amhaṃ' means 'our'.

Attadamanavasenāti yathāpaṭiññaṃ arahantānaṃ anukaraṇākārena pavattacittadamanavasena, manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ damanenāti attho. Sikhāppattaseṭṭhacariyatāya ariyamaggo brahmacariyaṃ. Brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ carati etenāti brahmacariyaṃ, satthusāsanaṃ.

'By way of self-taming' means by way of taming the mind that proceeds in a manner that imitates the arahants according to their promise; the meaning is, by the taming of the six sense faculties with the mind as the sixth. The noble path is the holy life because it is the supreme conduct that has reached the summit. One lives a sublime, excellent life by means of it, hence 'the holy life'; the Teacher's instruction.

Ataramānānanti na taramānānaṃ desakālaṃ udikkhantānaṃ. Phalāsāva samijjhatīti sudullabhaphalepi āsā sammāpayogamanvāya samijjhati eva. Vipakkabrahmacariyosmīti visesena nipphannapaṇītajjhāsayo paripuṇṇauḷāramanoratho. So hi seṭṭhamanosamācāratāya brahmacariyapariyāyena vutto.

'Of those not hurrying' means of those who do not rush, but look for the right place and time. 'The hope for fruit indeed succeeds' means that the hope even for a fruit that is very difficult to obtain succeeds by following proper application. 'I am one whose holy life is mature' means one with a specially accomplished and refined disposition, with fulfilled and lofty aspirations. For that is spoken of by the term 'holy life' because of the supreme conduct of his mind.

Idameva suttaṃ āgataṭṭhānanti adhippāyo tepiṭake buddhavacane idameva suttapadaṃ “vīriyaṃ brahmacariya”nti āgataṭṭhānanti attho. Vīriyañhi tasmiṃ visaye uttamaṃ paramukkaṃsagataṃ tādisacariyāhetu cāti brahmacariyanti idha vuttaṃ. Caturaṅgasamannāgatanti catubbidhadukkarakiriyāya sādhakassa catubbidhassa attano pavattiākārassa vasena caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ.

The meaning is that this very discourse is the place where this statement is found in the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha's words—this very phrase, 'energy is the holy life,' is the place where it is found. For energy in that connection is supreme, most excellent, having reached the highest point, and is the cause of such conduct; hence it is called the holy life here. 'Endowed with four factors' means endowed with four factors by way of the fourfold manner of one's own activity that accomplishes the four kinds of difficult practices.

Koci chinnabhinnapaṭapilotikadharo dasantayuttassa vatthassa abhāvato nicceloti vattabbataṃ labheyyāti taṃ nivattento āha “naggo”ti. Evaṃ akāsiṃ, evampi sattapīḷā mā ahosīti adhippāyo. Yathā [M 2.0035] “abhihaṭaṃ na sādiyāmī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.155) bhikkhāpariyesane ukkaṭṭhacāritādassanaṃ, evaṃ “naehi bhaddantikādibhāvopī”ti gahetabbaṃ. Purisantaragatāyāti purisasamīpagatāya. Saṃkittīyanti etāyāti saṃkitti, gāmavāsiādīhi samudāyavasena kariyamānakiriyā. Idha pana bhattasaṃkitti adhippetāti āha “saṃkittetvā katabhattesū”ti. Dadanti [V 2.0032] tāyāti datti. Ekāhaṃ antarabhūtaṃ etassa atthīti ekāhikaṃ. Esa nayo sesapadesupi. Ekāhavārenāti ekāhikavārena. “Ekāhika”ntiādinā vuttavidhimeva paṭipāṭiyā pavattabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ puna vuttaṃ. Tenāha “iti evarūpa”ntiādi.

Someone wearing torn and tattered rags, lacking even a waistcloth, might be called unclothed. To prevent this, he says, 'naked.' The intention is, 'Thus I acted, yet may there be no affliction of beings.' Just as in 'I do not approve of what is brought,' etc. (MN 1.155), the rigorous practice in seeking alms is shown, so here 'not even adopting the state of being a “respected sir,” etc.' should be understood. 'Among men' means in the presence of a man. 'A collection' means an action done collectively by villagers, etc. Here, however, a collection for a meal is the intended meaning, hence it is said, 'at meals made after collecting.' 'That by which they give' is a gift. 'One day included in this' means lasting one day. This is the method for the remaining terms as well. 'In a one-day turn' means by a turn lasting one day. 'Lasting one day,' etc., is said again to show the continuously proceeding nature of the stated procedure. Hence it is said, 'thus of such a kind,' etc.

Erakatiṇādīni vāti erakatiṇādīni ganthitvā katanivāsanāni chavadussāni, nihīnadussānīti attho. Tantāvutānanti tantaṃ pasāretvā vītānaṃ. Pakatikaṇṭaketi salākakaṇṭake.

'Garments of eraka grass, etc.' means garments made by weaving eraka grass and so on, or shroud-cloths, that is, inferior cloths. 'Woven with threads' means woven by stretching out threads. 'Natural thorns' means thorn-stakes.

156. Nekavassagaṇasañjātanti anekavassasamūhasañjātaṃ. Nanu ca idāneva “sāyatatiyakampi udakorohanānuyogamanuyutto”ti vuttaṃ, “nekavassagaṇikaṃ rajojallaṃ kāye sannicita”nti ca, tadubhayaṃ ekasmiṃ kathaṃ sambhavatīti āha “idaṃ attano rajojallakavatasamādānakālaṃ sandhāya vadatī”ti. Eteneva “acelako homī”ti vuttaacelakapaṭiññā, “sāṇānipi dhāremī”tiādinā vuttachannakapaṭiññā, tatthāpi sāṇa-masāṇa-chavadussādi-nivattha-paṭiññā ca aviruddhāti daṭṭhabbā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle tathā tathā paṭipannattā. Teti acelakā. Saṅghātanti sabbaso ghātaṃ. Tenāha “vadha”nti. Sīlavā nāma natthi “anabhisandhikampi pāpaṃ hotī”ti evaṃ laddhikattā. Sīlaṃ adhiṭṭhāyāti idaṃ paṭikkamanakiriyaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

156. 'Accumulated over a number of years' means accumulated over a collection of many years. But was it not just said: 'He is devoted to the practice of descending into the water for a third time in the evening,' and also: 'Dust and dirt have accumulated on his body over a number of years'? How can both of these be possible for one person? He says: 'This is said with reference to the time when he undertook the vow of accumulating dust and dirt on himself.' By this same principle, the declaration 'I will be a naked ascetic,' which is the vow of a naked ascetic, and the declaration 'I will wear hemp garments,' etc., which is the vow of one who wears clothes—and there, too, the vows to wear garments of hemp, coarse hemp, shroud-cloths, and the like—should be seen as not contradictory, because he practiced in such and such a way at such and such a time. 'Those are naked ascetics.' 'Utterly' means complete destruction; therefore he says 'slaughter.' There is no such thing as a virtuous person, because of holding the view: 'Evil can be done even without intention.' 'Having undertaken the virtue' is said with reference to the act of renouncing.

Pāsaṇḍapariggahaṇatthāyāti pāsaṇḍesu asārasārabhāvavīmaṃsanatthāya. Taṃ pabbajjanti ājīvakapabbajjaṃ. Vikaṭabhojaneti vikatabhojane virūpabhojane. Tenāha “apakatibhojane”ti.

'For the purpose of taking up a sect' means for the purpose of investigating the essential and the unessential in the sects. 'That going forth' means the going forth of the Ājīvakas. 'On improper food' means on unsuitable food, on deformed food. Therefore he says 'on unnatural food'.

157. Bhiṃsanakatasminti bhāvasādhanabhāvī idaṃ padanti āha “bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ bhiṃsanakakiriyāyā”ti. “Bhiṃsanakattasmi”nti vattabbe ekassa ta-kārassa [M 2.0036] lopo daṭṭhabbo. Yebhuyyaggahaṇaṃ lomavantavasenapi yojetabbaṃ, na lomavasenāti āha “bahutarānaṃ vā”tiādi.

157. 'In the terrifying': this word is a derivative expressing a state, so he says: '`bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ` means in the act of terrifying.' When it should be `bhiṃsanakattasmiṃ`, the elision of one `ta` should be seen. The taking of the majority should also be connected with being hairy, not just with the hair; therefore he says: 'or of the greater number,' etc.

Su-sadde u-kārassa o-kāraṃ katvā pāḷiyaṃ “sotatto”ti vuttanti tadatthaṃ vivaranto “sutatto”ti āha. Suṭṭhu avatattoti vā sotatto. Sosinnoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Suddhivasanatthāyāti saṃsārasuddhigavesanatthāya.

In the Pāli, `sotatto` is stated by changing the `u` in the word `su` to an `o`. Explaining its meaning, he says `sutatto` (well-heated). Or, `sotatto` means `suṭṭhu avatatto` (thoroughly scorched). This same principle also applies to `sosinno`. 'For the sake of dwelling in purity' means for the sake of seeking purification from saṃsāra.

Vihārasminti [V 2.0033] paccatte bhummavacananti āha “vihāro eva hi ‘vihārasmi’nti vutto”ti. Teneva cāti teneva vibhattivipallāsavasena. Evaṃ atthoti ayaṃ evaṃ liṅgavipallāsavasena attho veditabbo. Dukkhappattoti ānetvā sambandho. Sabbatthāti sukhadukkhe lābhālābhādike ca. Tulitoti tulāsadiso.

`Vihārasmiṃ`: this is a locative singular, so he says: 'A dwelling (`vihāro`) itself is indeed called `vihārasmiṃ`.' And by that is meant by way of an interchange of case endings. `Evaṃ attho`: this meaning should be understood as being by way of an interchange of gender. `Dukkhappatto` is connected by supplying it. 'In all' means in pleasure and pain, gain and loss, and so on. `Tulito` means like a balance.

Dukkarakārikādisuddhivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of purification by means of austerities and so on is finished.

Āhārasuddhivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Purification by Food

158. Sujjhitunti saṃsārato sujjhituṃ.

158. 'To be purified' means to be purified from saṃsāra.

159. Āsītikapabbānīti āsītikapiṭṭhipabbāni, “kāḷapabbānī”ti vadanti. Pabbānaṃ majjhe. Unnatunnatānīti maṃse milāte dvinnaṃ sandhīnaṃ antare vātenuddhumātadhamanījālatāya unnatāni unnatānīti. Ānisadanti ānisadaṭṭhānaṃ. Nisinnaṭṭhānanti paṃsūhi, vālikāhi vā nicitaṃ nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ. Sarapoṅkhenāti sarassa poṅkhappadesena, sarapoṅkhasaññitena vā maggena. Akkantanti akkantaṭṭhānaṃ. Takkagoḷikasadisānaṃ, sarīraghaṃsanatthaṃ kata kuruvindagoḷakānaṃ vā āvaḷi vaṭṭanāhāro. Vaṃsatoti piṭṭhivaṃsato. Maṇḍaleti bhittipādānaṃ matthake ṭhapitamaṇḍalake sīsaggena patiṭṭhahanti. Na evaṃ phāsuḷiyoti yathā yathā vuttagopānasiyo papatā tiṭṭhanti, na evaṃ bodhisattassa phāsukāpi papatā ṭhitā.

159. 'Eighty joints' means the eighty joints of the backbone; they call them 'black joints.' In the middle of the joints. 'Protruding' means that when the flesh had withered, between the two joints, they were protruding because the network of veins was inflated by the wind. `Ānisadaṃ` means the place for lying down. 'The sitting place' means a sitting place piled up with dust or sand. 'With the arrow-nock' means with the nocked part of an arrow, or with a path named 'arrow-nock.' `Akkantaṃ` means the place trodden upon. `Vaṭṭanāhāra` is a string of things like balls of buttermilk, or of balls of kuruvinda stone made for rubbing the body. `Vaṃsato` means from the backbone. `Maṇḍale`: they stand on the tip of their heads on a circular base placed on top of wall-posts. `Na evaṃ phāsuḷiyo`: just as the aforesaid rafters stand collapsing, the Bodhisatta's ribs did not stand collapsing in that way.

Okkhāyikāti avakkhāyikā, heṭṭhā hutvā ninnabhāvena paññāyamānā. Evarūpāti yathāvuttarūpā, ninnatarāti attho. Yāva piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ allīnā [M 2.0037] hotīti mayhaṃ udaracchavi yāva piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ, tāva taṃ āhacca ṭhitattā allīnā hoti udariyassa parikkhayena antānañca suṭṭhumilātatāya. Bhāriyabhāriyāti garutarā. Sahaudaracchaviṃ piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ, sahapiṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ udaracchavinti yojanā. Neva nikkhamati āhārasannissayaāpodhātuyā sabbaso visukkhattā. Pūtimūlānīti lomamūlānaṃ paribrūhanake maṃse lohite ca parikkhīṇe tāni sukkhāni ṭhānato bhaṭṭhāni abhāveneva “pūtimūlānī”ti vuttāni. Tenāha “tassa panā”tiādi.

`Okkhāyikā` means sunken, appearing as a depression by being low. 'Of such a sort' means of the sort described, that is, even more sunken. 'It clung to the very backbone' means: my belly-skin clung to the backbone because, with the wasting away of the stomach and the extreme shriveling of the intestines, it was pressed against it. 'Very heavy' means heavier. The construction is: the backbone along with the belly-skin, the belly-skin along with the backbone. It does not come out because the water element dependent on nutriment has completely dried up. 'With rotten roots': when the flesh and blood that nourish the hair-roots were wasted away, those roots, being dry and having fallen from their place, are called 'with rotten roots' simply because of their absence. Therefore he said: 'But for him...' etc.

Adhigatāti idāni adhigatā. Yathā etarahi vipassanāpaññāya adhigatattāti iminā kiñcāpi [V 2.0034] mahābodhisattā paripākagatañāṇā vasībhūtajjhānābhiññā vipassanāya parikammaṃ karonti, yathā ca nesaṃ carimabhave vipassanācāro, na tathā tadāti dasseti. Etadevāti yaṃ yena vuttaṃ atthajātaṃ, etadeva ettha etasmiṃ pāṭhapadese yuttaṃ pubbenāparaṃ avirujjhanato. Itarathāti bhikkhūhi vuttappakārena ananurūpo siyā “imissā”ti vuttāya aññatte.

'Attained' means attained now. By this 'as it is now attained by insight-wisdom,' he shows that although great Bodhisattas with mature knowledge, who have mastered the jhānas and supernormal powers, undertake the preliminary work for insight, their practice of insight in their final existence was not like it was then. 'This very thing': whatever collection of meanings has been stated by whomever, that very thing is fitting here in this passage because the latter does not conflict with the former. 'Otherwise' means: it would be unsuitable in the way stated by the bhikkhus, because what is referred to as 'of this' would be something different.

Āhārasuddhivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of Purification by Food is finished.

Saṃsārasuddhiādivaṇṇanā

Exposition on Purification from Saṃsāra, etc.

160. Saṃsārenāti aparāparaṃ cavanupapajjanavasena bhavesu saṃsaraṇena. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

160. By 'saṃsāra' is meant wandering through existences by way of repeatedly dying and being reborn. Referring to this, it is said:

“Khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā, saṃsāroti pavuccatī”ti. (visuddhi. 2.619; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.95; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.60; a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.4.199; dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā; vibha. aṭṭha. 226; su. ni. aṭṭha. 2.523; udā. aṭṭha. 39; itivu. aṭṭha. 14, 58; theragā. aṭṭha. 1.67, 99; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 58; cūḷani. aṭṭha. 6; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.117; visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.127; a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.9; sārattha. ṭī. 1.1);

"The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and bases, occurring without interruption, is called saṃsāra."

Bahukanti bahukālaṃ bahukkhattuṃ. Upapajjitvāti tattha tattha bhave nibbattitvā. Āvāsenāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sattāvāse āvasanena nibbattitvā jīvanena. Khandhāyeva vuttā tesaṃyeva pavattivisesassa tena tena [M 2.0038] pariyāyena vuttattā. Bahuyāgeti ajasūkaragomāyvādike bahuvidhe mahāyaññe. Bahuaggīti vācāpeyyādivasena antamaso pākayaññādivasena ca bahukepi aggī paricaraṇena.

Much: for a long time, many times. Having arisen: having been born here and there in various existences. By dwelling: by being born and living in each and every abode of beings. Only the aggregates are spoken of, because the particular continuity of those very aggregates is spoken of in this or that way. Much sacrifice: many kinds of great sacrifices such as those involving goats, pigs, cows, and jackals. Much fire: attending to many fires by way of the Vājapeyya sacrifice and so on, even down to cooking sacrifices and the like.

161. Bāladārakopi “daharo”ti vuccatīti tato visesanatthaṃ “yuvā”ti vuttaṃ. Atikkantapaṭhamavayā sattā sabhāvena palitasirā hontīti paṭhamavaye ṭhitabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “susukāḷakeso”ti [V 2.0035] vuttaṃ. Jarājiṇṇoti jarāya jiṇṇo, na akālikena jarāya abhibhūto. Ukkaṃsagatabuddhatāya vuddho. Tenāha “vaḍḍhitvā ṭhitaaṅgapaccaṅgo”ti, ārohapariṇāhavasena vuddhirahitoti attho. Jātimahallakoti jātiyā mahallako, na bhogaparivārādīhīti attho. Addhagatoti ettha addha-saddo dīghakālavācīti āha “bahuaddhānaṃ gato”ti. Vayotiādipadalopenāyaṃ niddesoti āha “pacchimavaya”nti. Padasatampi…pe… samatthatāti padasatampi padasahassampi sotapathamāgacchantameva uggahaṇasamatthatā pariggahetuṃ samatthatā. Ayañca gatiyā byāpāroti sakkā viññātuṃ gahaṇamattabhāvato. Tadevāti padasatampi padasahassampi. Ādhāraṇaṃ apilāpanavasena hadaye dhāraṇaṃ. Upanibandhanaṃ yathā na pamuṭṭhaṃ hoti, tathā upecca aparāparaṃ nibandhanaṃ. Ayaṃ pana satiyā byāpāroti sakkā viññātuṃ. Pāḷiyañca “paramāya gatiyā ca satiyā ca dhitiyā cā”ti vuttaṃ, parato ca “evaṃ adhimattagatimanto”ti vuttaṃ. Samatthavīriyaṃ dhiti nāmāti visiṭṭhavisayaṃ dassento yathāvuttasatisamāyogaṃ tassa dīpeti. Tassāti yathāvuttagatisatidhitīhi subhadhātavacīparicitassa pariyattidhammassa āgamavasena atthadassanasamatthatā yuttivasena kāraṇadassanasamatthatā.

161. Even a young boy is called 'young' (daharo), so to specify, the word 'youth' (yuvā) is used. Since beings who have passed the first stage of life naturally have gray hair, the phrase 'with very black hair' is used to show one is in the first stage of life. 'Worn out by age' means worn out by age, not overwhelmed by untimely aging. He is mature due to having reached the peak of development. Therefore it is said: 'having grown, with limbs and members firm,' meaning he has ceased growing in height and girth. 'Elderly by birth' means elderly by lineage, not by wealth, retinue, and so on. 'Advanced in years': here the word addha signifies a long time, so it is explained as 'having traversed a long stretch of time.' This is an indication by omission of words like 'age,' so it is explained as 'the final stage of life.' 'Even a hundred verses… etc. … ability': this means the ability to grasp, the ability to comprehend, even a hundred or a thousand verses as soon as they enter the range of hearing. And this is the function of intelligence; it can be known from the mere fact of grasping. 'That same': a hundred or a thousand verses. 'Retention' means holding in the heart without letting it fade. 'Binding it closely' means approaching and binding it again and again so that it is not forgotten. This, however, is the function of mindfulness; it can be known. And in the Pāli it is said, 'with supreme intelligence, mindfulness, and fortitude,' and further on, 'thus those with superior intelligence.' 'Fortitude' is capable energy. Showing a distinguished object, he clarifies its connection with mindfulness as stated. 'His': this refers to the ability to see the meaning by way of tradition and the ability to see the cause by way of reasoning, in regard to the scriptural Dhamma that has been well-practiced with speech and is of a good disposition through the aforesaid intelligence, mindfulness, and fortitude.

Daḷhaṃ (a. ni. ṭī. 3.9.38) thiraṃ dhanu etassāti daḷhadhanvā, so eva idha “daḷhadhammā”ti vutto. Paṭisattuvidhamanatthaṃ dhanuṃ gaṇhātīti dhanuggaho, so eva usuṃ saraṃ asati khipatīti issāsoti āha “dhanuṃ gahetvā ṭhito issāso”ti. Dvisahassapalaṃ lohādibhāraṃ vahituṃ samatthaṃ dvisahassathāmaṃ. Tenāha “dvisahassathāmaṃ nāmā”tiādi. Daṇḍeti dhanudaṇḍe. Yāva kaṇḍappamāṇāti dīghato yattakaṃ kaṇḍassa pamāṇaṃ, tattake [M 2.0039] dhanudaṇḍe ukkhittamatte āropito ceva hoti jiyādaṇḍo, so ca bhāro pathavito muccati, evaṃ idaṃ “dvisahassathāmaṃ nāma dhanūti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Uggahitasippoti uggahitadhanusippo. Katahatthoti thirataraṃ lakkhesu avirajjhanasarakkhepo. Īdiso pana tattha vasībhūto katahattho nāma hotīti āha “ciṇṇavasībhāvo”ti. Kataṃ rājakulādīsu upecca asanaṃ etena so katūpāsanoti āha “rājakulādīsu dassitasippo”ti. Evaṃ katanti evaṃ antosusirakaraṇādinā sallahukaṃ kataṃ.

'Firm,' steady is the bow of this one, hence 'one with a firm bow' (daḷhadhanvā); he himself is here called 'firm in the Dhamma' (daḷhadhammā). He who takes up the bow to destroy enemies is a bow-wielder (dhanuggaho); he himself, because he shoots an arrow, is an archer (issāso). Thus it is said: 'Having taken up the bow, he stands as an archer.' A two-thousand-strength is that which is capable of bearing a load of iron and so on of two thousand palas. Therefore it is said, 'it is called a two-thousand-strength,' etc. 'Staffs': on the bow-staves. 'As far as the measure of a shaft': as long as the measure of a shaft, on a bow-staff of that size, as soon as it is lifted, the bowstring-staff is fitted and that weight is released from the ground. In this way, this should be understood as 'a bow called a two-thousand-strength.' 'Having mastered the art': having mastered the art of the bow. 'A practiced hand': one who shoots arrows very steadily without missing the targets. Such a one, having become a master in that, is called 'a practiced hand.' Thus it is said, 'one who has cultivated mastery.' 'One who has rendered service' (katūpāsano): service has been rendered by him, having approached royal families and so on. Thus it is said: 'one who has shown his skill in royal families.' 'Made thus': made light by such means as making it hollow inside.

Oloketīti udikkhati. Evaṃ santepi tesaṃ vāro paññāyatīti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ “ayaṃ paṭhamaṃ pucchati, ayaṃ dutiya”ntiādinā pucchanavāro tādisassa paññavato paññāyati sukhumassa antarassa labbhanato. Buddhānaṃ pana vāroti īdise ṭhāne buddhānaṃ desanāvāro aññesaṃ napaññāyanato buddhānaṃyeva paññāyati. Idāni tameva paññāyanataṃ yuttito dassento “vidatthicaturaṅgulachāya”ntiādimāha. Accharāsaṅghāṭamatte khaṇe aneka-koṭisahassa-cittapavattisambhavato [V 2.0036] “vidatthicaturaṅgulachāyaṃ atikkamanato puretaraṃyeva bhagavā…pe… kathetī”ti vatvā tato lahutarāpi satthu desanāpavatti atthevāti dassento “tiṭṭhantu vā tāva ete”tiādimāha. Idāni tattha kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “kasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Soḷasa padāni kathetīti etena lokiyajanassa ekapaduccāraṇakkhaṇe bhagavā aṭṭhavīsasatapadāni kathetīti dasseti. Idāni tassapi kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “kasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'He looks at' means he observes. Even so, their turn is known. The turn for questioning of those bhikkhus—'this one asks first, this one second,' and so on—is known to such a wise person because a subtle interval is obtainable. But the turn of the Buddhas: in such a situation, the teaching turn of the Buddhas is known only to the Buddhas because it is not known to others. Now, showing that very fact of its being known from reasoning, he says, 'the shadow of a span and four fingers…' etc. Because many thousands of crores of thought-moments can arise in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, having said, 'Even before the shadow of a span and four fingers is crossed, the Blessed One… speaks,' he then shows that the Teacher's teaching activity is even swifter than that, saying, 'Let these wait for now…' etc. Now, to show the reason for that, 'Why?' and so on is said. By the statement, 'He speaks sixteen words,' it is shown that in the time it takes an ordinary person to utter one word, the Blessed One speaks twenty-eight hundred words. Now, to explain the reason for that as well, 'Why?' and so on is said.

Dhammoti pāḷi. Pajjati attho etenāti padaṃ, tadattho. Atthaṃ byañjetīti byañjanaṃ, akkharaṃ. Tañhi padavākyakkharabhāvehi paricchijjamānaṃ taṃ taṃ atthaṃ byañjeti pakāseti. Tenāha “dhammapadabyañjananti pāḷiyā padabyañjanaṃ, tassa tassa atthassa byañjanakaṃ akkhara”nti. Etena aparāparehi padabyañjanehi sucirampi kālaṃ kathentassa tathāgatassa na kadāci tesaṃ pariyādānaṃ atthīti dasseti. Pañhaṃ byākaronti etenāti pañhabyākaraṇaṃ, tathāpavattapaṭibhānaṃ. Aparikkhayapaṭibhānā hi buddhā bhagavanto, yato vuttaṃ [M 2.0040] “natthi dhammadesanāya hānī”ti (dī. ni. ṭī. 3.141, 305; vibha. mūlaṭī. 1.suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā). Tenāha “iminā kiṃ dassetī”tiādi. Tathā āsannaparinibbānassapi bhagavato desanāya itarāya ca visesātāvoti paṭhamabuddhavacanampi majjhimabuddhavacanampi pacchimabuddhavacanampi sadisameva. Āsītikavassato paraṃ pañcamo āyukoṭṭhāso.

'Dhamma' means the Pāli text. 'Term' (pada) is that by which meaning is attained; that is its meaning. 'Expression' (byañjana) is that which makes the meaning clear; a syllable. For that, being delimited by its nature as terms, sentences, and syllables, makes clear and reveals this or that meaning. Therefore it is said: 'The terms and expressions of the Dhamma' means the terms and expressions of the Pāli text, the syllables that express the meaning of each. By this it is shown that even when the Tathāgata speaks for a very long time with various terms and expressions, there is never any exhaustion of them. 'Answering of questions' is that by which they answer a question; it is the spontaneous intelligence that proceeds in such a way. For the Blessed Buddhas possess inexhaustible spontaneous intelligence, as it is said: 'There is no decline in the teaching of the Dhamma.' Therefore it is said: 'What does he show by this?' and so on. Likewise, since there is no difference between the teaching of the Blessed One even when his final Nibbāna was near and his other teachings, the first utterance of the Buddha, the middle utterance, and the final utterance are all the same. After eighty years is the fifth portion of the lifespan.

162. Kāmañcettha bhagavatā nāgasamālattherassa acchariyaabbhutapavedanamukhena attano lomānaṃ haṭṭhabhāvassa paveditattā “lomahaṃsanapariyāyo”ti nāmaṃ gahitaṃ, tathāpi sabbaññutaññāṇādi-anaññasādhāraṇañāṇānubhāva-vibhāvanādivasena soḷasasamūhato sīhanādassa nadanena desanāya pavattitattā “mahāsīhanādo”tveva saṅgītikāramahātherehi nāmaṃ ṭhapitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

162. Although here the name 'Discourse on the Hairs Standing on End' was adopted because the Blessed One, by means of declaring the wonderful and marvelous qualities of the Elder Nāgasamāla, revealed that his own hairs stood on end, it should still be understood that the great elders of the council established the name 'The Great Lion's Roar' because the teaching proceeded with the roar of a lion from the sixteen bases, by way of expounding the power of the unique knowledges such as the knowledge of omniscience and so on.

Mahāsīhanādasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Exposition of the Great Lion's Roar Sutta is complete.

3. Mahādukkhakkhandhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Greater Discourse on the Mass of Suffering

163. Tato [V 2.0037] paranti tiṇṇaṃ janānaṃ upari saṅgho catuvaggakaraṇīyādikammehi paṭikammappattattā. Gāmaṃ gatoti vuccati gāmaṃ uddissa gatattā, evaṃ sāvatthiṃ pavisituṃ vihārato nikkhantā “pavisiṃsū”ti vuttā. Pariññanti pahānapariññaṃ. Sā hi samatikkamo, na itarā. Rūpavedanāsupīti “rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ, vedanānaṃ pariñña”nti etthāpi. Kāmaṃ sabbesaṃ titthiyānaṃ kāmādipariññāpaññāpanahetubhūto samayo natthi, yesaṃ pana atthi, te upādāya “sakasamayaṃ jānantā”ti vuttaṃ. “Yato yato kho bho ayaṃ bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ettāvatā kho bho kāmānaṃ pariññā hotī”ti evaṃ sarūpato paṭhamajjhānaṃ vibhāvetuṃ asakkontāpi kevalaṃ accantappahānasaññāya kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeyyuṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ vadamānā. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tādisassa āgamādhigamassābhāvato. Rūpavedanāpariññāsupi eseva nayo. Vuccethāti vucceyya. Dutiyapadepīti “anusāsaniyā vā anusāsani”nti evaṃ vuttavākyepi. Te kira bhikkhū.

163. Then, above these three persons, the Sangha is fit for rectification by acts requiring a quorum of four, and so on. It is said, 'he has gone to the village,' because he has gone with the village as his destination; similarly, those who left the monastery to enter Sāvatthī are said to have 'entered.' 'Full understanding' means the full understanding that is abandonment. For that is transcendence, not the other kind. And also in the phrase 'regarding forms and feelings,' it means 'the full understanding of forms, the full understanding of feelings.' Although there is no doctrine among all the sectarians that is a cause for proclaiming the full understanding of sensual pleasures and so on, it is said with reference to those for whom there is, 'knowing their own doctrine.' 'Whenever, friends, this bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures ... enters and dwells in the first jhāna, to that extent, friends, there is the full understanding of sensual pleasures.' Even those unable to explain the first jhāna in its own nature might proclaim the full understanding of sensual pleasures merely through the perception of complete abandonment while speaking of the first jhāna. For what reason? Because of the absence of such scriptural learning and attainment. This same method applies to the full understanding of forms and feelings. 'It should be said' means 'it might be said.' In the second phrase too—that is, in the statement, 'either by instruction or an instruction.' Those bhikkhus, it seems.

165. Na [M 2.0041] ceva sampāyissantīti na ceva sammadeva pakārehi gamessanti ñāpessanti. Tenāha “sampādetvā kathetuṃ na sakkhissantī”ti. Yasmā avisaye pañho pucchito hoti, tasmā āpajjissantīti yojanā. Sadevaketi arūpadevaggahaṇaṃ. Te hi lokiyadevehi dīghāyukatādinā ukkaṭṭhā. Samāraketi kāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ. Sabrahmaketi rūpāvacarabrahmaggahaṇaṃ. Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyāti ettha samaṇaggahaṇena pabbajite, brāhmaṇaggahaṇena jātibrāhmaṇe, puna devaggahaṇena sammutideve, manussaggahaṇena avasiṭṭhamanussakāyaṃ pariyādiyati. Lokapajāggahaṇena pana payojanaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dassitameva. Aññathā ārādhanaṃ nāma natthīti iminā kāmarūpavedanāsu assādādīnaṃ yāthāvato avabodho eva ito bāhirakānaṃ natthi, kuto pavedanāti dasseti.

165. 'They will not succeed' means they will not understand or make it known in a proper way. Therefore it is said: 'they will not be able to speak having accomplished it.' Because the question was asked about a matter outside their domain, the connection is, 'they will fall into vexation.' 'With its devas' means the inclusion of the formless devas. For they are superior to worldly devas in terms of longevity and so on. 'With Māra' means the inclusion of the sense-sphere devas. 'With Brahmā' means the inclusion of the form-sphere brahmās. In the phrase 'with its ascetics and brahmins,' 'ascetics' includes the renunciants, 'brahmins' includes brahmins by birth, 'devas' again includes conventional devas, and 'human beings' encompasses the remaining human contingent. The purpose of including 'this generation' has already been shown in the commentary. 'Otherwise, there is no such thing as satisfying them': by this it is shown that outsiders have no real understanding of the gratification, etc., in sensual pleasures, forms, and feelings; how then could they proclaim it?

166. Cittārādhananti yāthāvapavedanena paresaṃ cittassa paritosanaṃ. Bandhanaṭṭhena guṇāti kāmarāgasaṃyojanassa paccayabhāvena vatthukāmesupi bandhanaṭṭho vutto, koṭṭhāsaṭṭho vā guṇaṭṭho daṭṭhabbo. Tarayantīti taramānā yanti gacchanti. Atītādibhinnapaṭhamādivayā eva cittatā rāsibhāvena vayoguṇāti gahitāti āha “rāsaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho”ti. Cakkhuviññeyyāti vā cakkhuviññāṇataṃdvārikaviññāṇehi [V 2.0038] vijānitabbā. Sotaviññeyyātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Iṭṭhārammaṇabhūtāti sabhāveneva iṭṭhārammaṇajātikā, iṭṭhārammaṇabhāvaṃ vā pattā. Kamanīyāti kāmetabbā. Manavaḍḍhanakāti manoharā. Etena parikappanatopi iṭṭhabhāvaṃ gaṇhāti. Piyajātikāti piyāyitabbasabhāvā. Kāmūpasaṃhitāti kāmarāgena upecca sandhāniyā sambaddhā (a. ni. ṭī. 3.6.63) kātabbāti āha “ārammaṇaṃ katvā”ti.

166. 'Pleasing the mind' means satisfying the minds of others by proclaiming in accordance with reality. 'Qualities' in the sense of a bond: because it is a condition for the fetter of sensual lust, the meaning of 'bond' is stated even for sensual objects; or the meaning of 'quality' should be seen as the meaning of a 'portion.' 'They cross over' means they go quickly. The diversity of ages, such as past, etc., and initial, etc., is taken as 'qualities of age' in the sense of an aggregate; therefore it is said, 'the meaning of aggregate is the meaning of quality.' 'Cognizable by the eye' means to be known by eye-consciousness and by consciousnesses arising through that door. This same method applies to 'cognizable by the ear,' and so on. 'That have become agreeable objects' means they are by nature a kind of agreeable object, or they have attained the state of being an agreeable object. 'Lovely' means desirable. 'Pleasing to the mind' means charming. By this, it acquires the state of being agreeable even from conceptualization. 'Of a dear nature' means having a nature to be cherished. 'Connected with sensual pleasure' means they are to be approached, connected, and associated with sensual lust; therefore it is said, 'having made it an object.'

167. Saññaṃ ṭhapetvāti “imasmiṃ aṅgulikādipabbe gahite sataṃ hoti, imasmiṃ sahassa”ntiādinā saññāṇaṃ katvā gaṇanā. Acchiddagaṇanāti “ekaṃ dve”tiādinā navantavidhinā nirantaragaṇanā. Piṇḍagaṇanāti saṅkalanapaṭuppādanādinā piṇḍitvā gaṇanā. Tenāha “khettaṃ oloketvā”tiādi. Kasanaṃ kasīti kasiggahaṇena sabbo kasipaṭibaddho [M 2.0042] jīvikūpāyo gahitoti āha “kasīti kasikamma”nti. Jaṅghavaṇijjāti jaṅghasatthavasena vaṇijjaṃ āha, thalavaṇijjāti sakaṭasatthavasena. Ādi-saddena nāvāpaṇādivasena vohāraṃ. Vaṇippathoti vaṇijamaggo, dānaggahaṇavasena saṃvohāroti attho. Usūnaṃ asanakammaṃ issattaṃ, dhanusippena jīvikā, idha pana issattaṃ viyāti issattaṃ, sabbaāvudhajīvikāti āha “āvudhaṃ gahetvā upaṭṭhānakamma”nti. Porohiccāmaccakammādi rājakammaṃ. Ādi-saddena rathasippakhattavijjāsippādi-vuttāvasesaṃ mahāsippaṃ khuddakasippañca saṅgaṇhāti. Sītassa purakkhatoti sītassa purato kato. Yo hi sītakāle jīvikāhetu sītalapadesaṃ pakkhandati, so vāḷamigādīhi viya sītena paripātiyamāno tena purato kato viya hoti. Tenāha “sītena bādhiyamāno”ti. Uṇhassa purakkhatoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Saritvāti saṃsappitvā. Ghaṭṭiyamānoti hiṃsiyamāno bādhiyamāno. Ābādhanaṃ ābādho, pīḷāti attho. Kāmahetunti vā bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso yathā “visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattantī”ti (a. ni. 4.70). Tathā sesapadadvayepi. Tenevāha “kāmānameva hetū”ti. Kāmānaṃ hetūti ettha purimapadāvadhāraṇamayuttaṃ tadaññapaccayapaṭikkhepāpattito, tathā uttarapadāvadhāraṇaṃ kāmānaṃ kadāci ahetubhāvassapi sambhavato, tasmā “uppajjatiyevā”ti vuttaṃ.

167. 'Having established a perception': counting by making a sign, such as, 'when this finger-joint is taken, it is a hundred; when this one, a thousand.' 'Unbroken counting': continuous counting by the nine-ended method, such as 'one, two.' 'Lump counting': counting by summing up, by producing a total, etc. Therefore it is said, 'having surveyed the field,' etc. 'Ploughing is agriculture': by the taking up of 'agriculture,' every livelihood connected with ploughing is included; therefore it is said, 'agriculture is the work of ploughing.' 'Trade on shanks' refers to trade by means of a caravan on foot; 'trade on land' by means of a caravan of carts. By the word 'etc.,' business by means of ships, shops, and so on is included. 'The trader's path' is the way of trade; the meaning is transacting by way of giving and taking. The work of shooting arrows is archery, a livelihood by the archer's craft. But here, 'like archery' is archery, any livelihood with weapons; therefore it is said, 'service taking up a weapon.' The work of a royal chaplain, a minister, etc., is royal service. By the word 'etc.,' the remaining great and minor crafts not mentioned, such as the craft of the charioteer and the warrior's art, are included. 'Put before the cold': made to be in front of the cold. For one who, for the sake of a livelihood, plunges into a cold region in the cold season is tormented by the cold as if by a wild beast, as if he were put before it. Therefore it is said, 'being afflicted by the cold.' The same method applies to 'put before the heat.' 'Creeping' means crawling. 'Being struck' means being harmed, being afflicted. 'Affliction' is an ailment; the meaning is oppression. 'On account of sensual pleasures': this is a neuter instrumental expression, as in 'the moon and sun revolve unevenly.' The same applies to the other two phrases. Therefore it is said, 'on account of sensual pleasures themselves.' In the phrase 'the cause of sensual pleasures,' emphasizing the first word is inappropriate as it would entail the rejection of other conditions; similarly, emphasizing the latter word is inappropriate as it would allow for the possibility that sensual pleasures are sometimes without a cause. Therefore it is said, 'it arises indeed.'

Uṭṭhahatoti iminā uṭṭhānavīriyaṃ vuttanti āha “ājīvasamuṭṭhāpakavīriyenā”ti. Taṃ vīriyanti ājīvikasamuṭṭhāpakavīriyaṃ. Pubbenāparaṃ ghaṭentassāti ārambhato paṭṭhāya nirantaraṃ pavattentassa. Citte uppannabalavasokena socatīti cittasantāpena anto nijjhāyati. Kāye uppannadukkhenāti tasseva sokassa vasena kāye uppannadukkhena. Sokuddesena taṃ taṃ vippalapento vā paridevati. Uraṃ tāḷetvāti vakkhappadesaṃ paharitvā. “Mogha”ntiādi paridevanākāradassanañceva [V 2.0039] sammohāpajjanākāradassanañca. Meti vatvā puna noti puthuvacanaṃ attano ubhayathāpi voharitabbato, byāmūḷhavacanaṃ vā sokavasena.

'By one who exerts himself': by this, the energy of exertion is stated; therefore it is said, 'by the energy that originates a livelihood.' 'That energy' is the energy that originates a livelihood. 'Of one who connects the former with the latter' means of one who proceeds continuously from the start. 'He grieves with the powerful sorrow arisen in the mind' means he is inwardly consumed by mental torment. 'With the suffering arisen in the body' means with the suffering arisen in the body on account of that very sorrow. 'He laments' or babbles this and that with sorrow as his object. 'Striking his breast' means having struck the chest area. The words 'In vain,' etc., show both the mode of lamentation and the mode of falling into delusion. Having said 'my,' he again says 'our': this is a plural statement because he can be spoken of in both ways, or it is confused speech due to sorrow.
