168. Idha [M 2.0043] kāmaggahaṇena visesato vatthukāmā gahitāti kāmādiggahaṇaṃ kataṃ, nānantariyatāya pana kilesakāmopi gahito eva. Asicammanti ettha cammaggahaṇena na kevalaṃ cammamayassa, cammaparisibbitasseva vā gahaṇaṃ, atha kho sabbassapi āvudhabādhakassa gahaṇanti dassento “kheṭakaphalakādīnī”ti āha. Ādi-saddena sarādisaṅgaho. Dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvāti dhanuñceva khurappatūṇiñca sannayhitvā, dhanudaṇḍassa jiyāya tathābhāvakaraṇādipi (a. ni. ṭī. 3.5.76) dhanuno sannayhananti. Dvinnaṃ senānaṃ byūhasaṃvidhānena vā ubhatobyūḷhaṃ. Vijjotalantesūti nisitapītaphalatāya vijjotanavasena parivattamānesu.

168. Here, by the taking up of 'sensual pleasures,' sensual objects are specifically taken; thus the expression 'sensual pleasures, etc.' is used. But sensual defilements are also included, though not immediately. In 'a sword and shield,' the taking up of 'shield' does not mean only one made of hide or just one sewn with hide, but rather it means the taking up of anything that obstructs a weapon; to show this, he said, 'shields, bucklers, etc.' By the word 'etc.,' arrows and so on are included. 'Having fastened on his bow and quiver' means having fastened on both the bow and the quiver with its razor-arrows; the fastening of the bow also refers to the act of making the bow-stave so by means of the string, etc. 'Arrayed on both sides' means by the arrangement of the battle-array of the two armies. 'Flashing' means revolving in a flashing manner because their blades are sharp and polished.

Pākārasamīpātisaṅkhāratāya pākārapādā upakāriyo, yā “uddāpā”ti vuccanti. Satadantenāti anekasatadantakena, yassa tikhiṇadantāni anekasatāni mūlāni honti. Atibhāratāya dasavīsamattāpi janā ukkhipituṃ na sakkonti, yantavasena pana ukkhipitvā bandhitvā ṭhapenti. Tenāha “aṭṭhadantākārenā”tiādi. Omaddantīti oṭṭhapenti.

The supports at the foot of the wall are helpful for preparing things near the wall; these are called 'buttresses.' 'With a hundred teeth' means with many hundreds of teeth, which has many hundreds of sharp teeth as its roots. Because of its excessive weight, even ten or twenty people cannot lift it, but they lift it by means of a machine and set it in place. Therefore it is said, 'in the shape of an eight-toothed thing,' etc. 'They crush' means they press down upon.

169. Sandhimpi chindanti corikāya jīvitukāmā. Nillopanti nissesavilopaṃ, ekaṃ parittaṃ gāmaṃ parivāretvā tattha kiñcipi gayhūpagaṃ asesetvā karamaraggahaṇaṃ. Tenāha “mahāvilopa”nti. Panthaduhanakammaṃ aṭavimagge ṭhatvā addhikānaṃ vilumpanaṃ. Pahārasādhanatthaṃ (a. ni. ṭī. 2.2.1) daṇḍappahārassa sukhasiddhiatthaṃ. Kañjito nibbattaṃ kañjiyaṃ, āranālaṃ. Yaṃ “bilaṅga”ntipi vuccati, taṃ yattha siñcati, sā kañjiyaukkhalikā. Bilaṅgathālikasadisakaraṇaṃ bilaṅgathāliyaṃ. Sīsakapālaṃ uppāṭetvāti ayoguḷapavesanappamāṇaṃ chiddaṃ katvā. Saṅkhamuṇḍakammakāraṇanti saṅkhaṃ viya muṇḍakammakāraṇaṃ.

169. Desiring to live by theft, they also break into houses. 'Complete plunder' is plunder without remainder: surrounding a small village and taking all the booty, leaving nothing whatsoever that can be taken. Therefore it is said, 'great plunder.' The act of highway robbery is standing on a forest path and robbing travelers. For the purpose of accomplishing a blow, for the easy success of a blow with a stick. Kañjiyaṃ is what is produced from sour gruel; it is fermented rice-water. What is also called bilaṅga—that into which it is poured is a pot for sour gruel. The 'sour gruel bowl' is making something similar to a sour gruel bowl. 'Tearing out the skull-pan' means having made a hole the size for inserting an iron ball. The 'conch-shell tonsure' torture is the act of making the head shaven like a conch shell.

Rāhumukhakammakāraṇanti rāhumukhagata-sūriyasadisa-kammakāraṇaṃ. Jotimālikanti jotimālavantaṃ kammakāraṇaṃ. Hatthapajjotikanti hatthapajjotanakammakāraṇaṃ. Erakavattakammakāraṇanti erakavattasadise sarīrato baddhe uppāṭanakammakāraṇaṃ. Cīrakavāsikakammakāraṇanti sarīrato uppāṭitabaddhacīrakāhi nivāsāpanakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā yathā gīvato paṭṭhāya baddhe kantitvā kaṭiyameva ṭhapenti, evaṃ gopphakato paṭṭhāya [M 2.0044] kantitvā kaṭiyameva ṭhapenti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “kaṭito paṭṭhāya kantitvā gopphakesu ṭhapentī”ti vuttaṃ. Eṇeyyakakammakāraṇanti eṇīmigasadisakammakāraṇaṃ[V 2.0040]. Ayavalayāni datvāti ayavalayāni paṭimuñcitvā. Ayasūlāni koṭṭentīti kapparajaṇṇukakoṭīsu ayasūlāni pavesenti. Nti taṃ tathākatakammakāraṇaṃ sattaṃ.

The 'Rāhu's mouth' torture is an act of making one like the sun seized by Rāhu. The 'garland of light' torture is an act of torture involving a garland of light. The 'hand-torch' torture is an act of torture involving a hand-torch. The 'grass-dress' torture is an act of torture involving tearing off strips of skin from the body, like a grass dress. The 'rag-clothing' torture is an act of torture involving clothing one with rags that have been torn and fastened to the body. In performing this, they cut from the neck down, leaving it only at the waist; similarly, they cut from the ankle up, leaving it only at the waist. But in the commentary it is said: 'They cut starting from the waist and leave it at the ankles.' The 'antelope' torture is an act of torture resembling an antelope. 'Having given iron rings' means having fastened on iron rings. 'They strike with iron spikes' means they drive iron spikes into the elbow and knee joints. Thus that being is subjected to such an act of torture.

Baḷisamaṃsikanti baḷisehi maṃsuppāṭanakammakāraṇaṃ. Kahāpaṇikanti kahāpaṇamattaso chindanakammakāraṇaṃ. Koṭṭentīti chindanti. Khārāpatacchikanti tacchetvā khārāvasiñcanakammakāraṇaṃ. Palighaparivattikanti palighassa viya parivattanakammakāraṇaṃ. Ekābaddhaṃ karonti ayasūlassa koṭṭanena. Palālapīṭhakanti palālapīṭhassa viya sarīrassa saṃvellanakammakāraṇaṃ. Kāraṇikāti ghātanakārakā. Palālavaṭṭiṃ viya katvāti yathā palālapīṭhaṃ karontā palālavaṭṭiṃ katvā saṃvellanavasena naṃ (a. ni. ṭī. 2.2.1) veṭhenti, evaṃ karontīti attho. Chātakehīti bubhukkhitehi koleyyakasunakhehi. Balavanto hi te javayoggā sūrā ca honti. Kammavasena sampareti etthāti samparāyo, paraloko. Tattha bhavoti samparāyiko.

The 'flesh-hooking' torture is an act of torture involving tearing out flesh with hooks. The 'coin-cutting' torture is an act of torture involving cutting off pieces of flesh the size of a kahāpaṇa coin. 'They strike' means they cut. The 'alkaline-pickling' torture is an act of torture involving planing the skin and sprinkling it with a caustic substance. The 'turning-the-bolt' torture is an act of torture involving turning the victim around like a bolt. They make him fixed by striking with an iron stake. The 'straw-mat' torture is an act of torture involving rolling up the body like a straw mat. 'Executioners' means those who inflict the killing. 'Having made it like a coil of straw' means: just as those making a straw mat make a coil of straw and wrap it by rolling it up, so they do—this is the meaning. 'With the starving' means with hungry koleyyaka dogs. For they are strong, fit for running, and fierce. The future life (samparāya) is so called because one proceeds on (sampareti) to it by the power of kamma; it is the other world. Occurring in it is 'pertaining to the future life' (samparāyiko).

170. Chandarāgo vinīyati ceva pahīyati ca etthāti nibbānaṃ chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānañcāti. Tenāha “nibbānañhī”ti. Tattha āgammāti idaṃ yo chandarāgaṃ vineti pajahati, tassa ārammaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tīhi pariññāhīti iminā ñātatīraṇapariññāhi parijānissantīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Ko pana vādo pahānapariññāyāti dasseti? Tathabhāvāyāti parijānanakabhāvāya.

170. Lustful desire is both disciplined and abandoned in this; thus Nibbāna is the disciplining of lustful desire and the abandoning of lustful desire. Therefore he said: 'Indeed, Nibbāna…' Here, 'coming to' (āgamma): this is said with reference to the object for one who disciplines and abandons lustful desire. 'With the three kinds of full understanding': by this he shows that there is no possibility that one will fully understand by means of full understanding by knowing and full understanding by scrutinizing. What then to say of full understanding by abandonment? 'For the sake of such a state' means for the sake of the state of fully understanding.

171. Aparittenāti ahīnena. Vipulenāti mahatā. Yadi vaṇṇasampattidassanatthaṃ, vaṇṇadasakaṃ kasmā na gahitanti āha “mātugāmassa hī”tiādi. Bhojanasampadādīnaṃ alābhepīti dassanatthaṃ “duggatakule nibbattassapī”ti vuttaṃ. Thokaṃ thokaṃ vaṇṇāyatanaṃ pasīdati maṃsassa paribrūhanato thanamaṃsāni vaḍḍhanti jāyanti. Vaṇṇeti hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsento viya hotīti vaṇṇo. So eva sāmaggopabhogādinā nibhātīti nibhā. Tenāha “vaṇṇanibhāti vaṇṇoyevā”ti.

171. Aparittena means undiminished. Vipulena means great. If it is for the purpose of showing the perfection of beauty, why is the decade of beauty not taken? He said: 'Indeed, for a woman…' and so on. To show that this is so even when there is no acquisition of abundant food and so on, it was said: 'even of one born in a poor family.' Little by little the physical basis of beauty becomes bright; from the augmentation of the flesh, the flesh of the breasts increases and develops. Beauty (vaṇṇa) is so called because it is as if it reveals the state of having gone to the heart. That very thing, through harmony, enjoyment, and so on, shines forth (nibhāti); thus it is radiance (nibhā). Therefore he said: 'Beauty's radiance is just beauty.'

Bhogganti [M 2.0045] ativiya vaṅkatāya bhoggaṃ. Tādisaṃ pana sarīraṃ bhaggaṃ viya hotīti āha “bhagga”nti. Tenāha “imināpissa vaṅkabhāvameva dīpetī”ti. Dantānaṃ chinnabhinnatāya ekaccānaṃ patanena ca khaṇḍitadantaṃ. Kesānaṃ setavaṇṇatāya palitanti āha “paṇḍarakesa”nti. Kesānaṃ mattaso siyane khallāṭavohāroti bahuso siyanaṃ sandhāyāha “mahākhallāṭasīsa”nti. Vassasatikakāle [V 2.0041] uppajjanatilakāni sandhāyāha “tilakāhatagatta”nti. Tāni pana kānici setāni honti kānici kāḷānīti āha “setakāḷatilakehī”ti. Byādhikanti sañcātabyādhiṃ. Bāḷhagilānanti māraṇanti kagelaññena gilānaṃ.

Bhoggam means bent due to being extremely crooked. But since such a body is as if broken (bhagga), he said 'broken' (bhagga). Therefore he said: 'By this, too, he indicates its bent nature.' He has broken teeth (khaṇḍitadanta) because his teeth are cut and shattered and some have fallen out. Because his hair is white in color, he is grey-haired (palita); thus he said 'white-haired' (paṇḍarakesa). The term 'bald' (khallāṭa) is used when the hair is moderately thin; referring to extensive thinning, he said 'with a very bald head' (mahākhallāṭasīsa). Referring to the spots that appear at the age of a hundred years, he said 'a body afflicted with spots' (tilakāhatagatta). But since some of them are white and some are black, he said 'with white and black spots.' Byādhikam means one who has an accumulated illness. Bāḷhagilānam means sick with a terminal illness.

173. Tasmiṃ samayeti tasmiṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharaṇasamaye. Na cetetīti na abhisandahati. Byābādhanaṭṭhena byābādho, byābādhova byābajjhaṃ, natthi ettha byābajjhanti abyābajjhaṃ, dukkharahitaṃ. Tenāha “niddukkhamevā”ti.

173. 'At that time' means at the time of dwelling having entered that jhāna. 'He does not intend' means he does not form an intention. Trouble (byābādha) is so called in the sense of troubling. Trouble itself is affliction (byābajjhaṃ). 'There is no affliction here,' thus it is unafflicted (abyābajjhaṃ), which is free from suffering. Therefore he said: 'simply without suffering.'

174. Aniccādiākāroti aniccākāro dukkhākāro vipariṇāmākāro calādiākāro ca.

174. 'The characteristic of impermanence and so on' means the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristic of suffering, the characteristic of change, the characteristic of instability, and so on.

Mahādukkhakkhandhasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning, the commentary on the Great Mass of Suffering Discourse, is completed.

4. Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Shorter Discourse on the Mass of Suffering

175. Sakkesūti [V 2.0042] ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ satipaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbanti taṃ ekadesena dassento “so hī”ti āha. Tattha yena rājakumārā sakyā nāma jātā, yato tesaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānatāya janapado tathā vuccati, taṃ vattabbanti āha “sakyānaṃ pana uppatti ambaṭṭhasutte āgatāvā”ti. Kapilavatthūti vuttaṃ purimasaññāvasena.

175. Regarding 'among the Sakyans,' whatever needs to be said here should be understood in the same way as it was stated in the Commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta. Thus, showing it in part, he said: 'For he....' Here, what should be stated is that the origin of the Sakyans—how the princes came to be called Sakyans, and why their dwelling place is called a country in that way—is found in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. 'Kapilavatthu' is mentioned based on its former designation.

Nānappakārakanti “lobhadhammā”ti bahuvacanassa nimittaṃ vadati. Lobho hi tena tena avatthāvisesena pavattiākārabhedena “chando rāgotaṇhā āsatti apekkhā”tiādinā anekappabhedo, lubbhanalakkhaṇena pana “lobho”tveva vuccati. Tenāha “nānappakārakaṃ lobhaṃyevā”ti. Tathā “doso paṭigho kodho upanāho [M 2.0046] virodho”tiādinā, “muyhanaṃ asamapekkhanaṃ apaccavekkhaṇā dummejjhaṃ bālya”ntiādinā (dha. sa. 390) ca dosamohānaṃ nānappakārataṃ sandhāyāha “itaresupi dvīsu eseva nayo”ti. Pariyādiyitvāti parito sabbaso ādāya. Gahetvāti ayamettha atthoti āha “gahaṇe āgata”nti. Pariyādiyatīti parikkhīṇoti. Dī-saddañhi saddavidū khayatthaṃ vadanti.

'Of various kinds': this explains the reason for the plural in 'states of greed.' For greed, due to its specific states and different modes of occurrence, has many varieties such as 'desire, lust, craving, attachment, longing,' and so on; but by its characteristic of coveting, it is simply called 'greed.' Therefore he said: 'greed itself of various kinds.' Similarly, with reference to the diversity of hatred and delusion—with such terms as 'hatred, aversion, anger, resentment, hostility,' and 'delusion, non-consideration, non-reflection, witlessness, foolishness,' and so on (Dhs §390)—he says: 'The same principle applies to the other two as well.' 'Having overcome' (pariyādiyitvā) means having taken completely, all around. 'Having taken' (gahetvā) is the meaning here; thus it is said: 'it comes to grasping.' 'He overcomes' (pariyādiyati) means he exhausts. For philologists say the sound 'dī' has the meaning of destruction.

Ekadāti āmeḍitalopena niddesoti āha “ekekasmiṃ kāle”ti. Lobhadosamohāti paṭhamamaggena pahīnāvasesā lobhadosamohā. Niravasesā pahīyanti, aññathā dutiyamaggena kiṃ kataṃ siyāti adhippāyo. Samudācārappattaṃ pana disvā “appahīnaṃ me atthī”tipi jānāti. Evaṃ kathaṃ niravasesappahānasaññāti āha “appahīnakaṃ…pe… saññī hotī”ti. Evaṃ paṭhamamaggeneva samucchinnasaṃsayassa “ko su nāma me dhammo ajjhattaṃ appahīnoti evaṃ sandheho kathaṃ uppajjatī”ti vatvā “paṇṇattiyā akovidattā”ti kāraṇamāha. Vinayakukkuccaṃ viya hi paṇṇattiyaṃ akusalatāya ariyānampi katthaci vimatimattaṃ uppajjati yathā taṃ sabbaso appahīnasammohānanti. Attano avisaye anabhijānanaṃ paṇṇattikosallena kimettha payojanaṃ, paccavekkhaṇāmattena ayamattho sijjhatīti dassento “kiṃ tassa paccavekkhaṇā natthī”ti āha. Itaro “natthī”ti na sakkā vattunti katvā “atthī”ti vatvā tattha labbhamānavibhāgaṃ dassento “sā panā”tiādimāha. Tattha sāti [V 2.0043] paccavekkhaṇā. Sabbesanti sabbesaṃ ariyānaṃ. Yathā paripuṇṇā na hoti, na evaṃ sabbaso na hotīti āha “imāsu panā”tiādi.

'At one time' (ekadā): this is a directive with elision of reduplication, thus he says 'at each single time' (ekekasmiṃ kāle). 'Greed, hatred, and delusion': this means the greed, hatred, and delusion remaining after being abandoned by the first path. They are abandoned without remainder—otherwise, what would be accomplished by the second path? This is the intention. But on seeing a transgression occur, one knows: 'There is something unabandoned in me.' This being so, how is there a perception of abandonment without remainder? He says: 'one is percipient of what is unabandoned....' This being so, for one whose doubt has been cut off by the first path itself, how does such a doubt arise as 'What state is unabandoned in me internally?' Having said this, he states the reason: 'because of not being skilled in concepts.' For just as scruples about the Vinaya arise even for noble ones because of unskillfulness in concepts, so too some uncertainty arises in some cases for those whose delusion is not entirely abandoned. What is the use here of skill in concepts for not knowing what is beyond one's own range? To show that this matter is accomplished by mere reviewing, he says: 'Does he not have reviewing?' The other, unable to say, 'He does not,' says, 'He does,' and then, showing the distinction to be found there, says: 'But that....' Here, 'that' is reviewing. 'Of all': of all the noble ones. To show that just as it is not complete, so it is not entirely absent, he says: 'But in these....'

176. Ajjhattanti niyakajjhattaṃ adhippetanti āha “tava santāne”ti. Appahīnoti anavasesato appahīno. Duvidheti vatthukāmakilesakāme. Kilesakāmopi hi yadaggena assādīyati, tadaggena paribhuñjīyati.

176. 'Internally' (ajjhattaṃ) is intended to mean one's own internal state; thus he says 'in your continuum.' 'Unabandoned' (appahīno) means not abandoned without remainder. 'Twofold' (duvidhe): sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements. For sensual pleasure as a defilement, too, is enjoyed and indulged in to the extent that it is savored.

177. Assādīyatīti assādo, sukhaṃ. Appo appamattako assādo etesūti appassādā. Tenāha “parittasukhā”ti. Pariyesanadukkhādihetukaṃ [M 2.0047] diṭṭhadhammikaṃ tattha duccaritacaraṇena samparāyikañca dukkhamettha kāmesu bahukanti bahudukkhā. Bahupāyāsāti bahuparikkilesā. Te pana parikkilesā vakkhamānanayena bahūyevettha diṭṭhadhammikāpīti āha “diṭṭhadhammika…pe… bahū”ti. Te ca parikkilesā yasmā taṃsamaṅgino hitapaṭipattiyā antarāyakarā idha ceva paraloke ca ādīnavakāraṇañca pavattanti, tasmā vuttaṃ “diṭṭhadhammika…pe… bahū”ti. Evaṃ cepīti evaṃ “appassādā kāmā”tiādinā ākārena. Nayenāti dhammena. Kāraṇenāti yuttiyā. Suṭṭhu diṭṭhaṃ hotīti sambandho. Vipassanāpaññāyāti ariyamaggapaññāya. Sā cattāripi saccāni visesato passatīti vipassanāti adhippetā. Tenāha “heṭṭhāmaggadvayañāṇenāti attho”ti. Pītisukhanti pītisukhavantaṃ jhānadvayaṃ. Dve maggeti heṭṭhāmagge. Āvaṭṭanasīlo ābhujanasīlo na hotīti anāvaṭṭī neva hoti sabbaso appahīnakāmarāgachando. Tenāha “kasmā”tiādi. Orodhanāṭakā pajahanapaññāti ādīnavānupassanāñāṇamāha.

177. 'It is savored' (assādīyati), hence 'savor' (assādo); this means pleasure. 'Little, a small amount of savor in these,' hence 'of little savor' (appassādā). Therefore he said 'of little pleasure' (parittasukhā). Because the suffering in this very life, caused by the pain of seeking, etc., and the suffering in the next life, due to misconduct therein, is much in regard to sensual pleasures, they are 'of much suffering' (bahudukkhā). 'Of many troubles' (bahupāyāsā) means of many vexations. And since those vexations, in the way to be explained, are numerous even in this very life, he says: 'in this very life ... many.' And since those vexations are an obstacle to the practice for one's welfare and are a cause of danger both here and in the next world, it is said: 'in this very life ... many.' 'Even so' (evaṃ cepi) means in this way: 'sensual pleasures are of little savor,' etc. 'By way' (nayena) means by the Dhamma. 'By reason' (kāraṇena) means by logic. The connection is: 'it is well seen.' 'By the wisdom of insight' (vipassanāpaññāya) means by the wisdom of the noble path. It is intended as 'insight' (vipassanā) because it sees the four truths in a special way. Therefore he said: 'the meaning is by the knowledge of the two lower paths.' 'Joy and pleasure' (pītisukhaṃ) means the two jhānas that possess joy and pleasure. 'The two paths' means the lower paths. 'Not of a nature to turn back, not of a nature to bend back' means he is not a non-returner (anāvaṭṭī), as his sensual desire and lust are not entirely abandoned. Therefore he says: 'Why?,' etc. 'The wisdom that abandons what is constricting' refers to the knowledge of contemplation of danger.

179. Assādopi kathito, “appassādā”ti hi iminā yāvatako kāmesu assādo, taṃ sabbaṃ anavasesato pariggahetvā cassa parittabhāvo dassitoti ādīnavopi kathito saṅkhepeneva sesassaādīnavassa dassitattā. Taṃ kathetunti taṃ nissaraṇaṃ “ekantasukhapaṭisaṃvedī”ti iminā kathetuṃ. Imehi antehīti “pañcime, mahānāma, kāmaguṇā”tiādinā kāmaguṇadassanamukhena kāmasukhallikānuyogaṃ “ubbhaṭṭhakā honti āsanapaṭikkhittā”tiādinā attakilamathānuyogañca dassetvā imehi dvīhi antehi muttaṃ mama sāsananti, phalasamāpattipariyosānattā sāsanasampattiyā “upariphalasamāpattisīsena sakalasāsanaṃ dassetu”nti āha. Gijjhasadiso kūṭoti majjhepadalopīsamāso yathā “sākapatthivo”ti (pāṇini. 2.1.60). Dutiye panettha gijjhavantatāya gijjhā kūṭe etassāti [V 2.0044] gijjhakūṭo. Uddhaṃyeva tiṭṭhanakā nisajjāya vuṭṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya ekaṭṭhāneneva tiṭṭhanakā. Tenāha “anisinnā”ti. Nigaṇṭhassāti nāṭaputtassa. Natthi etassa parisesanti aparisesaṃ. Evaṃ saṅkhābhavacanamattamassāti āha “aparisesasaṅkhāta”nti. Niccaṭṭhena [M 2.0048] satata-saddena abhiṇhappavatti jotitā siyāti “samita”nti vuttaṃ. Tena nirantarappavattiṃ dassetīti evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

179. The savor has also been stated. For by the words 'of little savor,' whatever savor there is in sensual pleasures has been fully comprehended and its smallness shown. The danger, too, has been stated, since the remaining danger has been shown only in brief. 'To state that' means to state the escape by means of 'experiencing exclusive pleasure.' 'By these extremes': Having shown the indulgence in sensual pleasures by way of describing the five strands of sensual pleasure with 'These five, Mahānāma, are strands of sensual pleasure,' etc., and the practice of self-mortification with 'they are restless and reject seats,' etc., and having stated, 'My teaching is liberated from these two extremes,' he says this to show the entire teaching with the attainment of the higher fruitions as its head, because the accomplishment of the teaching culminates in the attainment of fruition. 'A peak like a vulture' is a compound with an elided middle term, like 'sākapattivo' (Pāṇini 2.1.60). In the second case here, because it has vultures on its peak, it is Gijjhakūṭa (Vulture's Peak). 'Those who stand upright' are those who stand in one place from the time they rise from their seat. Therefore he said 'not sitting down.' 'Of the Nigaṇṭha' means of Nāṭaputta. 'There is no remainder for him,' hence 'without remainder.' Thus it is merely a term for a state of being; thus he says 'called without remainder.' Since continuous occurrence might be indicated by the word 'satata' in the sense of 'permanent,' the word 'samitaṃ' is used. Or the meaning here should be seen thus: it shows uninterrupted occurrence.

180. Yaṃ karoti, taṃ jānātīti dukkhassa nijjaraṇakhepanaṃ nāma viññūnaṃ kiccaṃ, viññunā ca purisena katākataṃ jānitabbaṃ, tasmā tumhehi purāṇānaṃ kammānaṃ byantibhāvaṃ karontehi paṭhamaṃ tāva ettakāni purāṇāni kammānīti jānitabbāni, tato “ettakaṃ kālaṃ katena tapasā ettakāni tāni byantikatāni, idāni ettakāni kātabbānī”tiādinā ayaṃ vidhi purisena viya attanā kātabbakiccaṃ paricchinditabbanti dasseti. Tenāha “tumhehipi tathā ñātabbaṃ siyā”ti. Suddhantanti suddhakoṭṭhāsaṃ, āyatiṃ anavassavasiddhaṃ kammakkhayaṃ, tato vā dukkhakkhayanti attho. Suddhantaṃ patto atthīti pucchatīti iminā akusalānaṃ pahānaṃ, kusalānaṃ bhāvanā ca sabbena sabbaṃ nigaṇṭhasamaye natthi sabbaso visuddhibhāvanāya abhāvato, tasmā kuto dukkhakkhayassa sambhavoti dasseti.

180. He shows that 'Whatever one does, one knows it' means: the wearing away and exhaustion of suffering is the task of the wise, and a wise person should know what has been done and what has not been done. Therefore, you who are bringing past kamma to an end should first know: 'There are this many past kammas.' Then, by this method—'By austerity practiced for so long, this many have been brought to an end; now this many remain to be done,' etc.—one should determine one's own task to be done, like a person would. Therefore he said: 'You too should know thus.' 'The pure end' (suddhantaṃ) means the pure part, the destruction of kamma that is established without future inflow, or the meaning is the destruction of suffering. By asking, 'Is there anyone who has reached the pure end?', he shows that since, in the system of the Nigaṇṭhas, there is no abandoning of the unwholesome and no cultivation of the wholesome whatsoever—because there is no cultivation of complete purity at all—the destruction of suffering is impossible.

Evaṃ ajānanabhāve satīti “ahuvamheva maya”ntiādinā vuttappakārassa ajānane sati, tasmiṃ tumhehi aññāyamāneti attho. Luddāti ghorā. Te pana yasmā kāyavācāhi nihīnameva karonti, tasmā vuttaṃ “luddācārā”ti. Lohitapāṇitveva vuccati tajjākiriyācaraṇato. Māgavikakevaṭṭacoraghātakādayo māgavikādayo. Kakkhaḷakammāti pharusakammā. Te nigaṇṭhesu pabbajantīti pubbe mahādukkhasaṃvattaniyakammassa katattā hi tumhe etarahi īdisaṃ mahādukkhaṃ paccanubhavathāti dasseti.

'When there is such a state of not knowing': when there is not knowing of the kind stated in 'We were,' etc., the meaning is 'when that is not known by you.' 'Fierce' (luddā) means cruel. And since they perform only base actions with body and speech, it is said 'of fierce conduct' (luddācārā). It is called 'bloody-handed' because of performing actions that produce terror. 'Hunters, fowlers, fishermen, thieves, executioners, etc.' are 'hunters and the like.' 'Of harsh deeds' (kakkhaḷakammā) means of cruel deeds. 'They go forth among the Nigaṇṭhas': he shows that it is because you have previously done kamma conducive to great suffering that you now experience such great suffering.

Vādeti diṭṭhiyaṃ, samayeti attho. Sukhena sukhanti ettha sukhenāti paṭipattisukhena, sukhāya paṭipattiyāti attho. Sukhanti vimokkhasukhaṃ, idha loke sukhaṃ adhigacchantā kasivaṇijjādidukkhapaṭipattiyāva adhigacchanti, evaṃ mokkhasukhampīti adhippāyo. Sarīrāvayavasampattiyāpi bimbino sāroti bimbisāro. Te nigaṇṭhā…pe… sandhāya vadanti, na pana bhagavato accantasantapaṇītaṃ nibbānasukhapaṭivedanaṃ jānanti. Sahasāti ravā. Appaṭisaṅkhāti na paṭisaṅkhāya avicāretvā. Tenāha “sāhasaṃ katvā”tiādi.

He asserts a view, meaning, a tenet. 'Happiness by means of happiness': here, 'by means of happiness' means by the happiness of the practice; the meaning is, by a practice for the sake of happiness. 'Happiness' means the happiness of liberation. In this world, those who attain happiness attain it only through a painful practice such as farming and trade; similarly, the intention is that the happiness of liberation is also attained thus. Also, because of the perfection of his bodily limbs, he is Bimbisāra, meaning 'the essence of the form.' Those Nigaṇṭhas... speak with reference to this, but they do not know the Blessed One's experience of the utterly peaceful and sublime happiness of Nibbāna. 'Rashly' means with a shout. 'Without reflection' means without having reflected, without having considered. Therefore, he said, 'having acted rashly,' etc.

Aññāhi [M 2.0049][V 2.0045] vedanāhi avomissaṃ ekantaṃ sukhaṃ ekantasukhaṃ, tassa paṭisaṃvedī. Tenāha “nirantarasukhapaṭisaṃvedī”ti. Kathāpatiṭṭhāpanatthanti “ekantasukhapaṭisaṃvedī”ti evaṃ āraddhakathāya patiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ. Rājavāreti rājānaṃ uddissa āgatadesanāvāre. Sukhaṃ pucchituṃ hotīti “yadi satta rattindivāni nappahoti, kiṃ cha rattindivāni pahotī”tiādinā pucchanasukhaṃ hoti. “Ahaṃ kho”tiādinā pavatto suddhavāro suddhanissandassa phalasamāpattisukhassa vasena āgatattā. Anacchariyaṃ hoti, satta rattindivāni pahontassa ekasmiṃ rattindive kiṃ vattabbanti. Uttānatthameva vuttanayattā suviññeyyattā.

Unmixed with other feelings, exclusively happiness, is absolute happiness; one who experiences that. Therefore he said, 'experiencing uninterrupted happiness.' 'To establish the discussion' means to establish the discussion that was initiated with the words 'experiencing absolute happiness.' 'On the royal occasion' means on the occasion of a teaching delivered having the king in view. It is easy to ask about happiness: meaning, there is an ease of questioning with such words as, 'If one is not able for seven days and nights, is one able for six days and nights?' etc. The pure section beginning 'I, indeed...' proceeds thus because it has come about by way of the happiness of the attainment of fruition, which is a pure outflow. It is not wonderful: for one who is able for seven days and nights, what is to be said about one day and night? The meaning is plain because the method has been stated and it is easily understood.

Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Explanation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta is completed.

5. Anumānasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Anumāna Sutta

181. Vuttānusārenāti [V 2.0046] “kurūsu, sakkesū”ti ca ettha vuttanayānusārena, “bhaggā nāma jānapadino rājakumārā”tiādinā nayena vacanattho veditabboti attho. Vatthupariggahadivaseti nagaramāpanatthaṃ vatthuvijjācariyena nagaraṭṭhānassa pariggaṇhanadivase. Athāti pacchā. Nagare nimmiteti tattha anantarāyena nagare māpite. Tameva susumāragiraṇaṃ subhanimittaṃ katvā “susumāragiri”tvevassa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Susumārasaṇṭhānattā susumāro nāma eko giri, so tassa nagarassa samīpe, tasmā taṃ susumāragiri etassa atthīti “susumāragirī”ti vuccatīti keci. Bhesakaḷāti vuccati ghammaṇḍagacchaṃ, keci “setarukkha”nti vadanti, tesaṃ bahulatāya pana taṃ vanaṃ bhesakaḷāvananteva paññāyittha. Bheso nāma eko yakkho ayuttakārī, tassa tato gaḷitaṭṭhānatāya taṃ vanaṃ bhesagaḷāvanaṃ nāma jātanti keci. Abhayadinnaṭṭhāne jātaṃ virūḷhaṃ, saṃvaddhanti attho.

181. 'According to what has been said' means: the meaning of the word should be understood in accordance with the method stated here in 'among the Kurus, and among the Sakyans,' and by the method in 'the Bhaggas are princes of a country,' etc. 'On the day of taking possession of the site' means: on the day the city's location was surveyed by a master of site-lore for the purpose of founding the city. 'Then' means afterwards. 'When the city was built' means: when the city was founded there without obstacle. Having taken that very 'crocodile-swallowing' as a good omen, they gave it the name 'Susumāragiri' (Crocodile Hill). Some say: because it has the shape of a crocodile, there is a hill named Susumāra near that city; therefore, because that city has that Susumāragiri, it is called 'Susumāragiri.' `Bhesakaḷā` is said to be a `ghammaṇḍa` thicket; some say 'a white tree.' But because of their abundance, that wood came to be known as Bhesakaḷāvana (Bhesakaḷā Wood). Some say: a yakkha named Bhesa was an evil-doer; because that was the place he was banished from, that wood came to be named Bhesagaḷāvana. It means: grown, sprouted, and developed in a place where sanctuary was given.

Icchāpetīti yaṃ kiñci attani garahitabbaṃ vattuṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ icchaṃ uppādeti, tadatthāya tesaṃ attānaṃ vissajjetīti attho. Paṭhamaṃ dinno hitūpadeso ovādo, aparāparaṃ dinno anusāsanī. Paccuppannātītavisayo [M 2.0050] vā ovādo, anāgatavisayo anusāsanī. Otiṇṇavatthuko ovādo, itaro anusāsanī. So cāti evaṃ pavāretā so bhikkhu. Dukkhaṃ vaco etasmiṃ vippaṭikūlaggāhe vipaccanīkasāte anādare puggaleti dubbaco. Tenāha “dukkhena vattabbo”ti. Upari āgatehīti “pāpiccho hotī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.181) āgatehi soḷasahi pāpadhammehi. Pakārehi āvahaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ, tato padakkhiṇato gahaṇasīlo padakkhiṇaggāhī, na padakkhiṇaggāhī appadakkhiṇaggāhī. Vāmatoti apasabyato, vuttavipariyāyatoti adhippāyo.

'He makes them wish' means: he generates in his fellow monks a wish to say whatever is blameworthy in himself; the meaning is that for this purpose he offers himself to them. Beneficial advice given first is `ovāda`; instruction given again and again is `anusāsanī`. Or, `ovāda` has the present and past as its domain; `anusāsanī` has the future as its domain. `Ovāda` has a specific matter as its basis; the other does not. 'And that one' means: that bhikkhu who has thus invited correction. A person in whom there is speech that is difficult—one who has a contrary grasp, is hostilely disposed, and is disrespectful—is 'difficult to admonish.' Therefore he said, 'to be spoken to with difficulty.' 'By those that have come up' means: by the sixteen bad qualities that have come up beginning with 'he has evil wishes' (MN 15). That which brings about in good ways is `padakkhiṇaṃ` (dexterous); one who is disposed to grasp from that dexterous side is a `padakkhiṇaggāhī` (one who grasps things dexterously); one who is not a dexterous grasper is an `appadakkhiṇaggāhī`. 'From the left' means in an un-dexterous way; the intention is, in the opposite way to what was said.

Asantasambhāvanapatthanānanti asantehi avijjamānehi guṇehi sambhāvanassa patthanābhūtānaṃ. Paṭi-saddo paccattikapariyāyo, pharaṇaṃ vāyamanaṃ idha tathāvaṭṭhānanti āha “paṭippharatīti paṭiviruddho paccanīko hutvā tiṭṭhatī”ti. Apasādetīti khipeti tajjeti. Tathābhūto [V 2.0047] ca paraṃ ghaṭṭento nāma hotīti āha “ghaṭṭetī”ti. Paṭiāropetīti yādisena vutto, tassa paṭibhāgabhūtaṃ dosaṃ codakassa upari āropeti.

'Of aspirations for esteem for what is not real' means: of what have become aspirations for esteem on account of non-existent, unreal qualities. The prefix `paṭi-` has the sense of opposition. Here `pharaṇaṃ` is striving, persisting in that way. Thus he said: '`paṭippharati` means he stands in opposition, hostilely.' `Apasādeti` means he disparages, he threatens. And one who has become like that is one who offends another; thus he said, 'he offends.' `Paṭiāropeti` means: he imputes a corresponding fault back onto the accuser.

Paṭicaratīti (a. ni. ṭī. 2.3.68) paṭicchādanavasena carati pavattati, paṭicchādanattho eva vā carati-saddo anekatthattā dhātūnanti āha “paṭicchādetī”ti. Aññenaññanti paṭicchādanākāradassananti āha “aññena kāraṇenā”tiādi. Tattha aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ vacanaṃ vāti yaṃ codakena cuditakassa dosavibhāvanaṃ kāraṇaṃ, vacanaṃ vā vuttaṃ, tato aññeneva kāraṇena, vacanena vā paṭicchādeti. Kāraṇenāti codanāya amūlikabhāvadīpaniyā yuttiyā. Vacanenāti tadatthabodhanena. Ko āpannotiādinā codanaṃ avissajjetvā vikkhepāpajjanaṃ aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇanti dasseti, bahiddhā kathāapanāmanaṃ vissajjetvāti ayameva tesaṃ viseso. Tenāha “itthannāma”ntiādi.

`Paṭicarati` means he acts, he proceeds, by way of concealing; or, because roots have many meanings, the word `carati` just has the meaning of concealing. Thus he said, 'he conceals.' 'With another thing for another' shows the mode of concealment. Thus he said, 'with another reason,' etc. Therein, 'another reason or statement': whatever reason or statement was spoken by the accuser making plain the fault of the accused, he conceals it with a reason or statement other than that. 'With a reason' means with a rationale that shows the accusation to be groundless. 'With a statement' means with one that explains its meaning. By saying, 'Who has transgressed?' etc., without answering the accusation, he shows that resorting to distraction is 'changing the subject.' The difference between this and leading the talk astray is that in the latter case, one does so after having answered. Therefore he said, 'so-and-so,' etc.

Apadīyanti dosā etena rakkhīyanti, lūyanti, chijjantīti vā apadānaṃ, (a. ni. ṭī. 2.3.2) sattānaṃ sammā, micchā vā pavattapayogo. Tenāha “attano cariyāyā”ti.

By this, faults are taken away, protected, or cut off and severed; therefore it is `apadāna`. It is the application of beings' conduct, whether right or wrong. Therefore he said, 'by one's own conduct.'

183. Anuminitabbanti [M 2.0051] anu anu minitabbo jānitabbo. Attānaṃ anuminitabbanti ca idaṃ paccatte upayogavacanaṃ. Tenāha “anuminitabbo tuletabbo tīretabbo”ti. Attānaṃ anuminitabbanti vā attani anumānañāṇaṃ pavattetabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ nayo – appiyabhāvāvahā mayi pavattā pāpicchatā pāpicchābhāvato parasmiṃ pavattapāpicchatā viya. Esa nayo sesadhammesupi. Aparo nayo – sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyabhāvaṃ icchantena pāpicchatā pahātabbā sīlavisuddhihetubhāvato attukkaṃsanādippahānaṃ viya. Sesadhammesupi eseva nayo.

183. `Anuminitabbaṃ` means to be repeatedly inferred, to be known. And 'one should infer from oneself' is a statement of application to oneself. Therefore he said: 'to be inferred, to be weighed, to be judged.' Or, 'one should infer from oneself' means the knowledge of inference should be made to arise in oneself. Herein, this is the method: the evil desire that has arisen in me, which brings about disagreeableness, is, by its very nature as evil desire, like the evil desire that has arisen in another. This method also applies to the remaining qualities. Another method: by one who desires to be dear to his fellow monks, evil desire should be abandoned—just like the abandoning of self-exaltation and so on—because it is a cause for purity of virtue. This same method also applies to the remaining qualities.

184. Paccavekkhitabboti “na pāpiccho bhavissāmi, na pāpikānaṃ icchānaṃ vasaṃ gato”tiādinā pati pati divasassa tikkhattuṃ vā ñāṇacakkhunā avekkhitabbaṃ, ñāṇaṃ pavattetabbanti attho. Pāpicchatādīnaṃ pahānaṃ pati avekkhitabbaṃ, ayañca attho tabba-saddassa bhāvatthatāvasena veditabbo, kammatthatāvasena pana aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “attāna”nti paccatte upayogavacanaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Sikkhantenāti tissopi sikkhā sikkhantena. Tenāha “kusalesu dhammesū”ti.

184. `Paccavekkhitabbaṃ` means it should be reviewed with the eye of wisdom three times each day, thinking: 'I will not be of evil wishes, I will not have come under the sway of evil wishes,' and so on. The meaning is that knowledge should be set in motion. One should reflect upon the abandoning of evil wishes and so on. This meaning is to be understood by way of the suffix `-tabba` having the sense of 'state of being.' But in the commentary, it has been stated by taking 'oneself' as a statement of application to oneself, by way of the suffix having the sense of 'object.' 'By one who is training' means by one training in the three trainings. Therefore he said, 'in wholesome states.'

Tilakanti [V 2.0048] kāḷatilasetatilāditilakaṃ. Sabbappahānanti sabbappakārappahānaṃ. Phale āgateti phale uppanne. Nibbāne āgateti nibbānassa adhigatattā. Bhikkhupātimokkhanti “so samaṇo, sa bhikkhū”ti evaṃ vuttabhikkhūnaṃ pātimokkhaṃ, na upasampannānaṃ eva na pabbajitānaṃ evāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yasmā cidaṃ bhikkhupātimokkhaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “idaṃ divasassa tikkhattu”ntiādi. Apaccavekkhituṃ na vaṭṭati attavisuddhiyā ekantahetubhāvato.

`Tilaka` means a mark such as one made from black sesame, white sesame, etc. 'The abandoning of all' means the abandoning of all kinds. 'When the fruit has come' means when the fruit has arisen. 'When Nibbāna has come' means because Nibbāna has been attained. The `Bhikkhupātimokkha` means the Pātimokkha of the bhikkhus spoken of thus: 'that recluse, that bhikkhu.' It should be seen that this is not only for the fully ordained, nor only for the gone-forth. And because this is the Bhikkhupātimokkha, it is therefore said, 'This, three times a day,' etc. It is not proper not to review it, because it is the sole cause for one's own purification.

Anumānasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Explanation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Anumāna Sutta is completed.

6. Cetokhilasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Cetokhilasutta

185. Ceto [V 2.0049] tehi khilayati thaddhabhāvaṃ āpajjatīti cetokhilā. Tenāha “cittassa thaddhabhāvā”ti. Yasmā tehi uppannehi cittaṃ uklāpījātaṃ ṭhānaṃ viya amanuññaṃ khettaṃ viya ca khāṇukanicitaṃ amahapphalaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “kacavarabhāvā khāṇukabhāvā”ti. “Cittassā”ti ānetvā [M 2.0052] sambandhitabbaṃ. Cittaṃ bandhitvāti taṇhāpavattibhāvato kusalacārassa avasaracajanavasena cittaṃ baddhaṃ viya samorodhetvā. Tenāha “muṭṭhiyaṃ katvā viya gaṇhantī”ti. Saddatthato pana ceto virūpaṃ nibandhīyati saṃyamīyati etehīti cetaso vinibandhā yassa catubbidhaṃ sīlaṃ akhaṇḍādibhāvappattiyā suparisuddhaṃ visesabhāgiyattā appakasireneva maggaphalāvahaṃ mahāsaṅgharakkhitattherassa viya, so tādisena sīlena imasmiṃ dhammavinaye vuddhiṃ āpajjissatīti āha “sīlena vuddhi”nti. Yassa pana ariyamaggo uppajjanto virūḷhamūlo viya pādapo suppatiṭṭhito, so sāsane virūḷhiṃ āpannoti āha “maggena virūḷhi”nti. Yo sabbaso kilesanibbānappatto, so arahā sīlādidhammakkhandhapāripūriyā sativepullappatto hotīti āha “nibbānena vepulla”nti. Dutiyavikappe attho vuttanayānusārena veditabbo.

185. The mind becomes barren through them and grows rigid; thus they are called “mental barrennesses.” Hence it is said, “due to the rigidity of the mind.” For when these arise, the mind becomes like waste land, like an unpleasant field strewn with stumps, yielding little fruit. Therefore, it is said, “like rubbish, like stumps.” “Of the mind”—this should be brought in and connected. Having bound the mind: because craving is in operation, by way of not giving an opportunity for wholesome conduct, one obstructs the mind as if it were bound. Hence it is said, “as if grasping it in a fist.” But literally, the mind is variously bound and restrained by these—thus they are called “fetterings of the mind.” For one whose fourfold virtue, through attaining the state of being unbroken and so on, is perfectly pure, leading to the path and its fruits with little effort—like the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita—such a one will attain growth in this Dhamma and Discipline by means of such virtue. Thus it is said, “growth through virtue.” For one in whom the noble path arises, well-established like a deeply rooted tree, that one has attained flourishing in the Dispensation. Thus it is said, “flourishing through the path.” One who has completely attained the quenching of the defilements, an arahant, reaches fullness due to the perfection of the aggregates of virtue and other such qualities, attaining an abundance of mindfulness. Thus it is said, “abundance through Nibbāna.” The meaning in the second alternative should be understood in accordance with the method explained.

Buddhānaṃ dhammakāyo viya rūpakāyopi anaññasādhāraṇatāya anuttaraguṇādhiṭṭhānatāya ca apaccakkhakārīnaṃ saṃsayavatthu hotiyevāti “sarīre vā guṇe vā kaṅkhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha yathā mahāpurisalakkhaṇena anubyañjanādayo rūpakāyaguṇā gahitā eva honti avinābhāvatoti “dvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇappaṭimaṇḍita”micceva vuttaṃ, evaṃ anāvaraṇañāṇena sabbepi anantāparimeyyabhedā dhammakāyaguṇā gahitā eva hontīti sabbaññutaññāṇaggahaṇameva kataṃ nānantariyabhāvatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kaṅkhahīti “aho vata te guṇā na bhaveyyuṃ, bhaveyyuṃ vā”ti patthanuppādanavasena kaṅkhati. Purimo hi viparītajjhāsayo, itaro yathābhūtañāṇajjhāsayo. Vicinantoti vicayabhūtāya paññāya te vivecetukāmo tadabhāvato kicchaṃ dukkhaṃ āpajjati, kicchappatti ca tattha nicchetuṃ asamatthatāyevāti āha “vinicchetuṃ na sakkotī”ti. Vigatā cikicchāti vicikicchā. Adhimokkhaṃ na paṭilabhatīti “evameta”nti okappanavasena guṇesu vinicchayaṃ nādhigacchati. Otaritvāti ñāṇena anupavisitvā. Pasīditunti “pasannarūpadhammakāyaguṇehi bhagavā”ti pasīdituṃ. Anāvilo akālusso hotuṃ na sakkoti. “Kaṅkhatī”ti [V 2.0050] iminā dubbalā vimati vuttā, “vicikicchatī”ti iminā majjhimā, “nādhimuccatī”ti iminā balavatī, “na sampasīdatī”ti iminā tividhāyapi vimatiyā vasena uppannacittakālussiyaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

A Buddha's physical body, like his Dhamma body, becomes a basis for doubt for those who do not directly perceive it, due to its being uncommon to others and the foundation for unsurpassed qualities. Hence, it is said, “one doubts his body or his qualities.” Here, just as the qualities of the physical body—the secondary characteristics and so on—are included by the marks of a great man because they are inseparable, for which reason it is said only, “adorned with the thirty-two excellent marks”; so too, all the Dhamma-body qualities of infinite and immeasurable kinds are included by the unobstructed knowledge, for which reason only the taking up of the knowledge of omniscience is mentioned, because of their inseparability. This is how it should be understood. “He doubts” means he doubts by way of generating the wish, “Oh, if only those qualities did not exist! Or if only they did exist!” The former has a perverse disposition, the latter a disposition for knowledge of things as they are. “Investigating” means: wishing to discriminate them with the wisdom that is investigation, because of the absence of that, he falls into difficulty and suffering. And the falling into difficulty is just because of the inability to decide about it. Thus it is said, “he cannot determine.” “Doubt” (vicikicchā) is “gone is the cure” (vigatā cikicchā). “He does not gain conviction” means he does not arrive at a decision about the qualities by way of accepting, “It is so.” “Having descended” means having penetrated with knowledge. “To become confident” means to become confident thus: “The Blessed One possesses the qualities of a clear physical body and Dhamma body.” He is unable to become untroubled and unstained. By “he doubts,” weak uncertainty is stated; by “he is perplexed,” moderate; by “he does not gain conviction,” strong; and by “he does not become confident,” the mental turbidity that arises on account of this threefold uncertainty is stated. This is how it should be understood.

Ātappāyātiādito [M 2.0053] tapati santapati kileseti ātappaṃ, ārambhadhātu, tadatthāya. Anuyogāyāti yathā saṃkilesadhammānaṃ avasaro na hoti, evaṃ anu anu yuñjanaṃ anuyogo, nikkamadhātu, tadatthāya. Tenāha “punappunaṃ yogāyā”ti. Sātaccāyāti yathā uparūpari visesādhigamo hoti, tathā satatassa nirantarapavattassa anuyogassa bhāvo sātaccaṃ, parakkamadhātu, tadatthāya. Padhānāyāti santamevaṃ tividhadhātusaṃvaḍḍhitānubhāvaṃ sabbakilesaviddhaṃsanasamatthaṃ padhānasaṅkhātaṃ vīriyaṃ, tadatthāya. Ettha ca ātappāya cittaṃ na namati yathāvuttakaṅkhāvasena, pageva anuyogādiatthanti dassetuṃ cattāripi padāni gahitāni, anavasesavisesadassanatthaṃ vā. Keci pana “ātappavevacanāneva anuyogādipadānī”ti vadanti. Ettāvatā bhagavā satthari kaṅkhāya cittassa thaddhakacavarakhāṇukabhāvena akusalabhāvādiāpādanato cetokhilabhāvaṃ dasseti. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

Beginning with “for the sake of ardor”: it burns, scorches, torments the defilements—this is “ardor” (ātappa), the element of initiative; for the sake of that. “For the sake of application”: so that there is no opportunity for defiling states, repeated application is “application” (anuyoga), the element of exertion; for the sake of that. Hence it is said, “for the sake of repeated application.” “For the sake of perseverance”: so that there is attainment of successively higher distinctions, the state of continuous, uninterrupted application is “perseverance” (sātacca), the element of striving; for the sake of that. “For the sake of striving”: for the sake of energy called “striving” (padhāna), which, being enhanced in power by these three elements, is capable of destroying all defilements. Here, because of the aforesaid doubt, the mind does not incline to ardor, still less to application and the rest. To show this, or to show the distinction without remainder, all four terms are taken. Some, however, say that the terms “application” and so on are just synonyms for “ardor.” To this extent, the Blessed One shows the state of mental barrenness, because doubt in the Teacher leads to the mind’s state of being rigid, like rubbish, and like a stump, and to the production of unwholesome states and the like. The same method applies to the remaining cases.

Sikkhāggahaṇena paṭipattisaddhammassa gahitattā vuttaṃ “pariyattidhamme ca paṭivedhadhamme cā”ti. Pariyattidhamme yattha kaṅkhāya sambhavo, taṃ dassetuṃ “caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tayidaṃ nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ paramparāya paṭivedhāvahabhāvādivasenapi ekaccānaṃ tattha saṃsayuppattito. Yathā ca paṭivedhe kaṅkhā vuttā, evaṃ adhigamadhammepi pavattatīti veditabbā. Tathā hi ekacce “kasiṇādibhāvanāya jhānāni ijjhantī”ti vadanti. “Kasiṇanissando āruppāti, mettādinissando catutthabrahmavihāro”ti evamādinā kaṅkhatiyevāti. Ettha ca navalokuttaresu paññattiyaṃyeva kaṅkhāpavatti veditabbā asaṃkilesikattā lokuttaradhammānaṃ.

Since the good Dhamma of practice is included by the taking up of the training, it is said, “in the Dhamma of learning and in the Dhamma of penetration.” To show where doubt can arise in regard to the Dhamma of learning, it is said, “the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma,” and so on. This should be seen as a mere example, since for some, doubt arises there even by way of the tradition that leads to penetration and the like. And just as doubt in regard to penetration has been mentioned, so it should be understood that it also occurs in regard to the Dhamma of attainment. For some say, “The jhānas are accomplished by the development of the kasiṇas, etc.” They doubt in such ways as: “The result of the kasiṇa is the formless attainments; the result of loving-kindness, etc., is the fourth brahmavihāra.” Here, it should be understood that doubt occurs only in regard to the concepts concerning the nine supramundane states, because the supramundane dhammas are not subject to defilement.

Evarūpanti edisaṃ suppaṭipatti-ujuppaṭipatti-ñāyappaṭipatti-sāmīcippaṭipatti-saṅkhātaṃ sammāpaṭipadaṃ. Adhisīlasikkhādayo lokuttaradhammassa anudhammabhūtā veditabbā. Evañhi maggaphalasikkhāhi imāsaṃ viseso siddho hoti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “sikkhāggahaṇena paṭipattisaddhammassa gahitattā”ti. Ettha ca yathā vicikicchā vatthuttayassa sikkhāya ca guṇesu anadhimuccanaasampasīdanavasena appaṭipattibhāvato cittassa thaddhabhāvo āsappanaparisappanavasena pavattiyā kacavarakhāṇukabhāvo ca, evaṃ sabrahmacārīsu āghātacaṇḍikkādivasena [V 2.0051] cittassa thaddhabhāvo ca upahananavirujjhanādivasena [M 2.0054] kacavarakhāṇukabhāvo ca veditabbo. Ariyasaṅghavisayā vicikicchā, puggalavisayā kāci natthīti saṅghavisayāva gahitā, sāsanikavasena cāyaṃ cetokhiladesanāti sabrahmacārīvisayova kopo gahito.

“Of such a kind” means this right way of practice, known as good practice, straight practice, methodical practice, and proper practice. The trainings in the higher virtue and so forth should be understood as dhammas conforming to the supramundane Dhamma. For in this way their distinction from the trainings in the path and fruition is established. For it is said: “By the taking up of the training, the good Dhamma of practice is included.” Here, just as doubt concerning the qualities of the Triple Gem and the training—by way of not gaining conviction and not becoming confident—results in non-practice, and thereby in rigidity of mind and its state of being like rubbish and a stump because of its tendency to be unapproachable and unyielding; so too should one understand the rigidity of mind towards one's companions in the holy life—by way of resentment, fierceness, and so on—and its state of being like rubbish and a stump—by way of bearing grudges, being obstructive, and so on. Doubt is about the noble Saṅgha; there is none concerning a particular individual, so it is taken only as about the Saṅgha. And since this is a discourse on mental barrenness in the context of the Dispensation, anger is taken only in relation to one's companions in the holy life.

186. Yathā vatthukāmo, evaṃ kilesakāmopi assādanīyo evāti “kilesakāmepī”ti vuttaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā “rūpataṇhā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisatī”tiādi (dī. ni. 2.400; ma. ni. 1.133; vibha. 203). Kāmaniddese (mahāni. 1) sabbepi tebhūmakā dhammā kāmanīyaṭṭhena “kāmā”ti vuttā, balavakāmarāgavatthubhūtāyevettha kāmaggahaṇena gahitāti. Vinibaddhavatthubhāvena yathā visuṃ attano kāyo gahito, tathā paresaṃ tathārūpā rūpadhammā samūhaṭṭhenāti āha “rūpeti bahiddhārūpe”ti. Yathā hi pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo jhānādivisesādhigamassa vinibaddhāya saṃvattati, evaṃ attano kāye apekkhā bahiddhā ca sakaparikkhārañātimittādīsu apekkhāti. Keci panettha “rūpeti rūpajjhāne”tiādinā papañcenti. Tadayuttaṃ jhānādhigamavinibaddhānaṃ sīlassa ca saṃkilesabhūtānaṃ cetovinibaddhabhāvena gahitattā.

186. Just as sensual pleasures as objects are to be enjoyed, so too sensual pleasures as defilements are to be enjoyed; thus it is said, “even in sensual pleasures as defilements.” Therefore the Blessed One said: “Craving for form in the world is what is dear and agreeable; it is here that this craving arises when it arises, here that it settles when it settles,” and so on. In the Exposition of Sensual Pleasures, all phenomena of the three planes are called “sensual pleasures” in the sense of being desirable, but here, by the term “sensual pleasures,” only those that are the basis for strong sensual lust are taken. Just as one's own body is taken separately as a bound object, so the material phenomena of that kind belonging to others are taken collectively; hence it is said, “in form, that is, in external form.” For just as lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure leads to the fettering of the attainment of the special states of the jhānas and so on, so too there is concern for one's own body and, externally, concern for one's own requisites, relatives, friends, and so on. Some here elaborate, saying, “in form means in the form jhānas,” and so on. That is incorrect, because those things that are fetters to the attainment of the jhānas and are defilements of virtue have been taken under the heading of “fetterings of the mind.”

Yāvadatthanti yāva attheti abhikaṅkhati, tāva. Tenāha “yattakaṃ icchati, tattaka”nti. Nti yāvadatthaṃ udarapūraṃ bhuttaṃ. Avadehanato pūraṇato. Seyyasukhanti seyyaṃ paṭicca uppajjanakasukhaṃ. Passasukhanti passānaṃ samparivattanena uppajjanakasukhaṃ. Niddāsukhanti niddāyanena uppajjanakasukhaṃ.

“To one's satisfaction” means: as much as one needs and desires. Hence it is said, “as much as one wishes, that much.” That is, having eaten to one's satisfaction, a bellyful. By way of filling, by way of satiating. “The pleasure of lying down” is the pleasure that arises in dependence on lying down. “The pleasure of turning over” is the pleasure that arises from turning from side to side. “The pleasure of sleep” is the pleasure that arises from sleeping.

Sīlenātiādi patthanākāradassanaṃ. Vatasamādānanti dhutaṅgādivatānuṭṭhānaṃ. Tapoti vīriyārambho. So hi kilesānaṃ tapanaṭṭhena niggaṇhanaṭṭhena tapacaraṇanti vuttaṃ.

“By virtue,” etc., shows the mode of aspiration. “The undertaking of vows” means the undertaking of observances such as the ascetic practices. “Austerity” is the arousal of energy. For it is called “the practice of austerity” because it burns and restrains the defilements.

189. Chandaṃ nissāyāti chandaṃ dhuraṃ, chandaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ, chandaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā pavattivasena chandaṃ nissāya. Jeṭṭhakaṭṭhena padhānabhūtā, padhānabhāvaṃ vā pattāti padhānabhūtā. Tehi dhammehīti chandanissayena pavattasamādhinā ceva “padhānasaṅkhāro”ti vuttavīriyena ca. Upetanti sampayuttaṃ. Ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhi, nipphattiatthena paṭilābhaṭṭhena cāti attho, tassā iddhiyā pādaṃ pādakaṃ [M 2.0055] padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ. Atha vā ijjhanti tāya iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontīti iddhi, sāva uparivisesānaṃ [V 2.0052] adhiṭṭhānabhāvato pādo. Tenāha “iddhibhūtaṃ vā pādanti iddhipāda”nti. Sesesupīti vīriyiddhipādādīsupi. Assāti iddhipādassa. Attho dīpitoti dīpanatthaṃ kataṃ, tasmā visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 2.369) tassa atthavicāro gahetabbo. Iddhipādānaṃ samādhipadhānattā vuttaṃ “vikkhambhanappahānaṃ kathita”nti. Tesaṃ tesaṃ kusaladhammānaṃ anuppannānaṃ uppādanakiriyāya uppannānaṃ paribrūhanakiriyāya ussahanato ussoḷhī, thāmappattā parakkamadhātu. Sā pana catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ visesapaccayabhūtā te upādāya “pañcamī”ti vuttā, sā ca yasmā samathavipassanābhāvanāsu tattha caādimajjhapariyosānesu sādhetabbaṃ vīriyaṃ, tasmā āha “ussoḷhīti sabbattha kattabbavīriyaṃ dassetī”ti. Pubbabhāgiyasamathavipassanāsādhanaṃ pahātabbadhammavibhāgena bhinditvā āha “pañca cetokhilappahānāni pañca vinibandhappahānānī”ti. Bhabboti yutto arahati nipphattiyā. Ñāṇenāti maggañāṇena. Kilesabhedāyāti kilesānaṃ samucchindanāya. Khemassāti anupaddavassa.

189. “Relying on desire” means: relying on desire by making desire the yoke, desire the chief, and desire the forerunner. “Being primary” in the sense of being chief, or having attained the state of being primary, they are called “primary.” “By those states” refers to the concentration that arises from reliance on desire and the energy called “the volition of striving.” “Endowed with” means associated. “Spiritual power” has the sense of success, accomplishment, and attainment; of that spiritual power, the “base” is the footing, the foundation. Alternatively, “spiritual power” is that by which things succeed, prosper, and become exalted; hence, it is a “base” because it is the foundation for higher distinctions. Therefore, it is said: “A base that is a spiritual power is a base of spiritual power.” “In the remaining cases too” applies similarly to the base of spiritual power connected with energy and the others. “Of this” refers to the base of spiritual power. “The meaning has been explained” is for the purpose of clarification, so its meaning should be investigated in the commentary on the Path of Purification. Because the bases of spiritual power are distinguished by concentration, it is said: “abandonment by suppression has been stated.” “Zeal” is the exertion for generating unarisen wholesome qualities and for developing arisen ones; it is the element of effort that has attained strength. This, being a special condition for the four bases of spiritual power, is called the “fifth” in reference to them. Since energy must be applied in the development of serenity and insight—from beginning to middle to end—it is said: “'Zeal' shows the energy to be applied everywhere.” Having analyzed the means for the preliminary part of serenity and insight by a division of states to be abandoned, he says: “the five mental barrennesses to be abandoned and the five mental bondages to be abandoned.” “Capable” means fit, worthy of accomplishment. “By knowledge” refers to path knowledge. “For the breaking of defilements” means for the extirpation of the defilements. “Of the secure” means of the untroubled.

Sambhāvanattheti (sārattha. ṭī. 1.11; a. ni. ṭī. 3.7.71) “api nāmevaṃ siyā”ti vikappanattho sambhāvanattho. Evaṃ hīti evaṃ ekameva saṅkhyaṃ avatvā aparāya saṅkhyāya saddhiṃ vacanaṃ loke siliṭṭhavacanaṃ hoti yathā “dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitānī”ti. Sammā adhisayitānīti pādādīhi attanā nesaṃ kiñci upaghātaṃ akarontiyā bahivātādiparissayapariharaṇatthaṃ sammadeva upari sayitāni. Utuṃ gāhāpentiyāti tesaṃ allasinehapariyādānatthaṃ attano kāyusmāvasena utuṃ gaṇhāpentiyā. Tenāha “usmīkatānī”ti. Sammā paribhāvitānīti sammadeva sabbaso kukkuṭavāsanāya vāsitāni. Tenāha “kukkuṭagandhaṃ gāhāpitānī”ti. Ayañca kukkuṭagandhaparibhāvanā sammāadhisayanasammāparisedananipphattiyā “anunipphādī”ti (sārattha. ṭī. 1.11) daṭṭhabbā. Tehi pana saddhiṃyeva ijjhanato vuttaṃ “tividhakiriyākaraṇenā”ti. Kiñcāpi na evaṃ “aho vatime”tiādinā icchā uppajjeyya, kāraṇassa pana sampāditattā atha kho bhabbāva abhinibbhijjitunti yojanā[M 2.0056]. Kasmā bhabbāti āha “te hi yasmā tāyā”tiādi. Ettha yathā kapālassa tanutā ālokassa anto paññāyamānassa kāraṇaṃ, tathā kapālassa tanutāya nakhasikhāmukhatuṇḍakānaṃ kharatāya ca allasinehassa pariyādānaṃ kāraṇavacananti daṭṭhabbaṃ, tasmāti ālokassa anto paññāyamānato, sayañca paripākagatattā.

“In the sense of possibility” means in the sense of conjecture, as in “perhaps it might be so.” “For thus”: in the world, not stating just a single number but speaking it together with another number is elegant speech, as in “two or three drops of water.” “Properly brooded on” means: sat upon properly by her, without causing them any harm with her feet, etc., in order to ward off external dangers such as wind. “Making them absorb heat” means: making them take up heat by means of her own body's warmth in order to dry up their moisture. Hence he said, “warmed.” “Properly pervaded” means: thoroughly pervaded all over with the scent of a chicken. Hence he said, “made to take on the chicken's scent.” And this pervading with the chicken's scent should be seen as “subsequently produced” through the accomplishment of proper brooding and proper warming. But because it succeeds along with those, it is said “by the performance of a threefold action.” Although a wish might not arise thus, “Oh, if only these would…,” yet because the cause has been provided, they are indeed capable of breaking out—this is the connection. Why are they capable? He said, “For since by her…” etc. Here, it should be seen that just as the thinness of the shell is the cause for the light to be discerned inside, so the thinness of the shell and the sharpness of the tips of her claws and beak are the stated cause for the exhaustion of the moisture. “Therefore” means: because the light is discerned inside and because it has itself reached maturity.

Opammasampaṭipādananti opammatthassa upameyyena sammadeva paṭipādanaṃ. Atthenāti upameyyatthena. Yathā kukkuṭiyā aṇḍesu tividhakiriyāya karaṇaṃ kukkuṭacchāpakānaṃ aṇḍakosato [V 2.0053] nikkhamanassa mūlakāraṇaṃ, evaṃ bhikkhuno ussoḷhīpannarasāni aṅgāni avijjaṇḍakosato nikkhamanassa mūlakāraṇanti āha “tassā kukkuṭiyā…pe… samannāgatabhāvo”ti. Paṭicchādanasāmaññena avijjāya aṇḍakosasadisatāya balavavipassanāvasena avijjaṇḍakosassa tanubhāvo, vipassanāñāṇassa pariṇāmakālo vuṭṭhānagāminibhāvāpatti, tadā ca sā maggañāṇagabbhaṃ dhārentī viya hotīti āha “gabbhaggahaṇakālo”ti. Abhiññāpakkheti lokiyābhiññāpakkhe. Lokuttarābhiññā hi avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padālikāti. Gāthāya avijjaṇḍakosaṃ paharatīti desanāvilāsena vineyyasantānagataṃ avijjaṇḍakosaṃ ghaṭṭeti, yathāṭhāne ṭhātuṃ na deti.

“The adducing of the simile” means the proper presentation of the meaning of the simile to the subject of the simile. “By the meaning” means: by the meaning of the subject of the simile. Just as the hen's performance of the threefold action on the eggs is the root cause for the chicks' emergence from the eggshell, so the bhikkhu's fifteen factors of zeal are the root cause for emergence from the eggshell of ignorance. Thus he said: “of that hen… the state of being endowed.” Because of the general characteristic of covering, ignorance is similar to an eggshell. By means of powerful insight, the eggshell of ignorance becomes thin. The time of maturity for insight knowledge is the attainment of the state leading to emergence. At that time, it is as if it bears the embryo of path knowledge; thus he said: “the time of conception.” “In the section on direct knowledge” means: in the section on worldly direct knowledge. For supramundane direct knowledge splits the eggshell of ignorance. “He strikes the eggshell of ignorance with the verse” means: by the charm of the teaching, he strikes the eggshell of ignorance present in the mental continuum of the person to be trained, not allowing it to remain in its place.

Paṭisaṅkhānappahānanti tadaṅgappahānapubbakaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ. Pubbabhāgiyā iddhipādā pāḷiyaṃ gahitāti “iddhipādehi vikkhambhanappahāna”nti vuttaṃ. “Ussoḷhipannarasaṅgasamannāgato bhikkhu bhabbo abhinibbidāyā”tiādivacanato (ma. ni. 1.189) lokuttariddhipādā pana sambodhaggahaṇeneva gahitā. Magge āgateti ussoḷhīpannarasaṅgasamannāgatassa bhikkhuno vipassanaṃ ussukkāpayato magge āgate uppanne, pāḷiyaṃ vā abhinibbhidāsambodhaggahaṇehi magge āgate. Phale āgateti etthāpi vuttanayena attho veditabbo. Nibbānassa pana pāḷiyaṃ anāgatattā nissaraṇappahānaṃ na gahitaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

“Abandonment by reflection” is abandonment by suppression, which is preceded by abandonment by substitution of opposites. Since the preliminary bases of spiritual power are included in the Pāḷi, it is said, “abandonment by suppression through the bases of spiritual power.” From the statement, “A bhikkhu endowed with the fifteen factors of zeal is capable of breaking through,” etc., the supramundane bases of spiritual power, however, are included by the taking up of “full enlightenment.” “When it comes to the path” means: when the path has come and arisen for a bhikkhu endowed with the fifteen factors of zeal who is diligently cultivating insight; or, in the Pāḷi, when it comes to the path by means of “breakthrough” and “full enlightenment.” “When it comes to the fruit”: here too the meaning should be understood in the way stated. But since Nibbāna is not mentioned in the Pāḷi, abandonment by escape is not included. The rest is easy to understand.

Cetokhilasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The exposition of the concealed meaning in the commentary on the Cetokhila Sutta is completed.

7. Vanapatthapariyāyasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on Forest Tracts

190. Vanīyati [M 2.0057][V 2.0054] vivekakāmehi bhajīyati, vanute vā te attasampattiyā vasanatthāya yācanto viya hotīti vanaṃ, patiṭṭhanti ettha vivekakāmā yathādhippetavisesādhigamenāti patthaṃ, vanesu patthaṃ gahanaṭṭhāne senāsanaṃ vanapatthaṃ. Pariyāyati attano phalaṃ pariggahetvā vattatīti pariyāyo, kāraṇanti āha “vanapatthapariyāyanti vanapatthakāraṇa”nti. Vanapatthañhi taṃ upanissāya viharato upanissayakāraṇaṃ. Tenāha “vanapatthaṃ upanissāya viharatī”ti. Pariyāyati desetabbamatthaṃ patiṭṭhapetīti pariyāyo, desanā. Vanapatthaṃ ārabbha pavattā desanā vanapatthadesanā, taṃ, ubhayatthāpi vanapatthaggahaṇaṃ lakkhaṇamattaṃ gāmādīnampettha kāraṇabhāvassa, desanāya visayabhāvassa ca labbhamānattā.

190. It is called 'vana' (forest) because it is desired and resorted to by those who seek seclusion, or because it entreats them, as it were, to dwell there for its own prosperity. 'Pattha' (tract) is where those who seek seclusion establish themselves, attaining the particular distinctions they desire. 'Vanapattha' (forest tract) is a dwelling place in a dense part of the forests. 'Pariyāya' is that which proceeds by encompassing its own fruit—it is a reason. Thus he says, "'Vanapatthapariyāya' means the reason related to the forest tract." For the forest tract serves as a supporting reason for one who dwells relying on it. Therefore, it is said, "He dwells in dependence on the forest tract." 'Pariyāya' is that which establishes the meaning to be taught—it is a discourse. The discourse that arises concerning the forest tract is the 'vanapatthadesanā' (the discourse on the forest tract). In both cases, the term 'vanapattha' is merely an indication, since the state of being a reason and the state of being a subject of the discourse are attainable even by villages and so forth.

191. Nissāyāti apassāya, vivekavāsassa apassayaṃ katvāti attho. Na upaṭṭhātītiādīhi tasmiṃ vanapatthe senāsanasappāyābhāvaṃ, utupuggaladhammassavanasappāyābhāvampi vā dasseti. Jīvitasambhārāti (a. ni. ṭī. 3.9.6) jīvitappavattiyā sambhārā paccayā. Samudānetabbāti sammā ñāyena anavajjauñchācariyādinā uddhaṃ uddhaṃ ānetabbā pāpuṇitabbā. Te pana tathā samudānitā samāhaṭā nāma hontīti āha “samāharitabbā”ti. Dukkhena uppajjantīti sulabhuppādā na honti. Etena bhojanasappāyādiabhāvaṃ dasseti. Rattibhāgaṃ vā divasabhāgaṃ vāti bhummatthe upayogavacananti āha “rattikoṭṭhāse vā divasakoṭṭhāse vā”ti. Rattiṃyeva pakkamitabbaṃ samaṇadhammassa tattha anipphajjanato.

191. 'Nissāya' means relying on; that is, having made a support for dwelling in seclusion. 'They do not arise' and so on shows the lack of suitable lodgings in that forest tract, or the lack of suitable weather, persons, or hearing of the Dhamma. 'The means of life' means the requisites, the conditions for the continuation of life. 'To be procured' means they should be properly and progressively obtained by right means, such as blameless gleaning and proper conduct. Those thus procured are called 'collected'; hence he said 'to be collected.' 'They arise with difficulty' means they are not easy to obtain. By this, he shows the lack of suitable food and so on. 'During a part of the night or a part of the day' is a statement of application in the locative sense; hence he said 'in the portion of the night or in the portion of the day.' One should depart at night itself, because the ascetic's duty is not accomplished there.

192-3. Saṅkhāpīti “yadatthamahaṃ pabbajito, na metaṃ idha nipphajjati, cīvarādi pana samudāgacchati, nāhaṃ tadatthaṃ pabbajito, kiṃ me idha vāsenā”ti paṭisaṅkhāyapi. Anantaravāre saṅkhāpīti “yadatthamahaṃ pabbajito, taṃ me idha nipphajjati, cīvarādi pana na samudāgacchati, nāhaṃ tadatthaṃ pabbajito”ti paṭisaṅkhāyapīti attho. Tenāha “samaṇadhammassa nipphajjanabhāvaṃ jānitvā”ti.

192-193. 'Saṅkhāpi' means also reflecting thus: "The purpose for which I went forth is not achieved here, but robes and so on are obtained. I did not go forth for that purpose—what use is there in staying here?" In the next case, 'saṅkhāpi' means also reflecting thus: "The purpose for which I went forth is achieved here, but robes and so on are not obtained. I did not go forth for that purpose." Hence it is said, "having known the achievement of the ascetic's duty."

195-7. So [M 2.0058] puggalo anāpucchā pakkamitabbaṃ, nānubandhitabboti “so puggalo”ti padassa “nānubandhitabbo”ti iminā sambandho. Yassa yena hi sambandho, dūraṭṭhenapi so bhavati[V 2.0055]. Taṃ puggalanti “so puggalo”ti paccattavacanaṃ upayogavasena pariṇāmetvā taṃ puggalaṃ anāpucchā pakkamitabbanti attho. Atthavasena hi vibhattivipariṇāmoti. Taṃ āpucchā pakkamitabbanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Āpucchā pakkamitabbanti ca kataññutakataveditāya niyojanaṃ.

195-197. The word 'that person' (`so puggalo`) is connected with 'should not be followed' (`nānubandhitabbo`). For whatever has a connection with whatever, that connection exists even if the words are far apart. The phrase 'from that person' (`taṃ puggalaṃ`) is the nominative 'that person' (`so puggalo`) transformed into the accusative for the sake of application; the meaning is 'one should depart from that person without asking permission.' For the transformation of case is according to the meaning. The same principle applies here to 'one should depart from that person after asking permission.' And 'One should depart after asking permission' is an injunction regarding gratitude and recognition of services rendered.

198. Evarūpoti yaṃ nissāya bhikkhuno guṇehi vuddhiyeva pāṭikaṅkhā, paccayehi ca na parissamo, evarūpo daṇḍakammādīhi niggaṇhāti cepi, na pariccajitabboti dasseti “sacepī”tiādinā.

198. 'Such a one' means a person relying on whom a bhikkhu can expect only growth in virtues and no trouble with requisites. By 'even if' and so on, he shows that even if such a person reprimands one with disciplinary actions like the `daṇḍakamma`, he should not be abandoned.

Vanapatthapariyāyasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The exposition of the concealed meaning in the commentary on the Vanapatthapariyāya Sutta is completed.

8. Madhupiṇḍikasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta

199. Jātivananti [V 2.0056] sayaṃjātaṃ vanaṃ. Tenāha “aropima”nti. Paṭisallānatthāyāti ekībhāvatthāya, puthuttārammaṇato vā cittaṃ paṭinivattetvā accantasante nibbāne phalasamāpattivasena allīyāpanatthaṃ. Daṇḍo pāṇimhi assāti daṇḍapāṇi. Yathā so “daṇḍapāṇī”ti vuccati, taṃ dassetuṃ “ayañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Daṇḍavittatāyāti daṇḍe soṇḍatāya. So hi daṇḍapasuto daṇḍasippe ca sukusalo tattha pākaṭo paññāto, tasmā daṇḍaṃ gahetvāva vicarati. Jaṅghākilamathavinodanatthanti rājasabhāya ciranisajjāya uppannajaṅghāparissamassa apanayanatthaṃ. Adhiccanikkhamanoti yādicchakanikkhamano, na abhiṇhanikkhamano. Olubbhāti sannirumbhitvā ṭhito. Yathā so “olubbhā”ti vutto, taṃ dassetuṃ “gopālakadārako viyā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

199. 'Jātivana' means a self-grown forest; therefore, he said, 'unplanted.' 'For the purpose of seclusion' means for the purpose of solitude, or for turning the mind away from various objects and, by way of fruition attainment, immersing it in the ultimate peace of Nibbāna. 'A staff is in his hand' (`Daṇḍo pāṇimhi assā`) is the derivation of 'Daṇḍapāṇi.' To show how he is called 'Daṇḍapāṇi,' 'for this one...' and so on was said. 'Due to his fame with the staff' means due to his fondness for the staff. For he is devoted to the staff and highly skilled in its craft, being well-known and renowned for it. Thus, he wanders about carrying a staff. 'For dispelling weariness in the legs' means for dispelling the fatigue of the legs that arose from prolonged sitting in the royal assembly. 'An occasional departure' means a spontaneous departure, not a frequent departure. 'Leaning on' means standing while restraining himself. To show what is meant by 'leaning on,' 'like a cowherd boy...' and so on was said.

200. Vadanti etenāti vādo, diṭṭhīti āha “kiṃ vādīti, kiṃ diṭṭhiko”ti? Kimakkhāyīti kimācikkhako, kīdisadhammakatho? Acittīkārenāti anādarena. Tathāpucchane kāraṇaṃ dassento “kasmā”tiādimāha. Nassatetanti nassatu etaṃ kulaṃ.

200. A 'doctrine' (`vādo`) is that by which they speak; it means a view. Thus he said, 'What is your doctrine?' meaning, 'What is your view?' 'One who proclaims what?' means 'What does he declare? What kind of Dhamma-teacher is he?' 'Without respect' means with disregard. Showing the reason for questioning in such a way, he said, 'Why?' and so on. 'May that be destroyed' means 'May this family be destroyed.'

Atthaṃ [M 2.0059] na jānātīti atthaṃ ce ekadesena jāneyya, taṃ micchā gahetvā paṭippharitvāpi tiṭṭheyya. Tassa dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyāti tadassa atthājānanaṃ bhagavatā icchitaṃ. Viggāhikakathanti viggahakathaṃ, sārambhakathanti attho. Nanu bhagavatā saddhiṃ loke puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇā nānāvādā santīti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “tathāgato hī”tiādi. Na vivadati vivādahetukānaṃ kāmadiṭṭhijjhosānānaṃ maggeneva samugghātitattā, tadabhāvato pana loko tathāgatena vivadati. Dhammavādī yathābhūtavādī dhammavādīhi na vivadati tesaṃ vivaditukāmatāya eva abhāvato, adhammavādī pana tiṇāyapi namaññamāno tehi kiñci vivadati. Tenāha “na, bhikkhave, dhammavādī kenaci lokasmiṃ vivadatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.94). Adhammavādī pana asamucchinnavivādahetukattā vivadateva. Tathā cāha “adhammavādīva kho, bhikkhave, vivadatī”ti.

'He does not understand the meaning'—even if he were to understand a part of it, he would grasp it wrongly and persist in it. This would be for his long-lasting harm and suffering; thus, that non-understanding of the meaning by him was desired by the Blessed One. 'Viggāhikakathā' means disputatious talk; contentious speech is the meaning. In reference to the challenge, 'Is it not the case that in the world there are many ascetics and brahmins with various doctrines alongside the Blessed One?' he says, 'For the Tathāgata,' etc. He does not dispute, because the causes of dispute—such as attachment to sensual pleasures, views, and obsessions—have been uprooted by the path. Due to the absence of these, however, the world disputes with the Tathāgata. A speaker of the Dhamma is a speaker of what is real; he does not dispute with other speakers of the Dhamma, as they have no desire to dispute. But a speaker not of the Dhamma, holding them in contempt as not even worth a blade of grass, will dispute with them over something. Therefore, he said: 'Bhikkhus, a speaker of the Dhamma does not dispute with anyone in the world' (SN 3.94). But a speaker not of the Dhamma, because the causes for dispute are not eradicated, indeed disputes. And thus he said: 'Bhikkhus, it is only a speaker not of the Dhamma who disputes.'

Yathā ca panāti ettha yathā-saddo “yathā ca anuppannassa kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti, tañca [V 2.0057] pajānātī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.122) viya kāraṇatthoti āha “yena kāraṇenā”ti. Kāraṇākāro vā idha yathā-saddena vutto, so pana atthato kāraṇamevāti vuttaṃ “yena kāraṇenā”ti. “Idaṃ kathaṃ idaṃ kathaṃ”ti pavattanato kathaṃkathā, vicikicchā. Sā yassa natthi, so akathaṃkathī, taṃ akathaṃkathiṃ. Vippaṭisārakukkuccaṃ bhagavatā anāgāmimaggeneva chinnaṃ, hatthapādakukkuccaṃ aggamaggena āveṇikadhammādhigamato. Aparāparaṃ uppajjanakabhavo “bhavābhavo”ti idhādhippetoti āha “punappunabbhave”ti. Saṃvarāsaṃvaro phalāphalaṃ viya khuddakamahanto bhavo “bhavābhavo”ti vuttoti āha “hīnapaṇīte vā bhave”ti. Bhavo vuḍḍhippatto “abhavo”ti vuccati yathā “asekkhā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 11.tikamātikā). Kilesasaññāti kāmasaññādike vadati. Kilesā eva vā saññānāmena vuttā “saññā pahāya amataṃ eva pāpuṇātī”tiādīsu viya. Attano khīṇāsavabhāvaṃ dīpetīti imināva paresañca tathattāya dhammaṃ desetīti ayampi attho vibhāvitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nīharitvā kīḷāpetvāti nīharitvā ceva kīḷāpetvā ca, nīharaṇavasena vā kīḷāpetvā. Tivisākhanti tibhaṅgabhākuṭi viya nalāṭe jātattā nalāṭikaṃ.

In the phrase 'yathā ca pana,' the word 'yathā' is used in the sense of a cause, as in 'and how there is the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and he understands that' (AN 3.122); thus he says, 'by which cause.' Or, the mode of the cause is expressed here by the word 'yathā,' but in meaning it is simply the cause; thus it is said, 'by which cause.' From the occurrence of 'how is this? how is that?' comes 'how-saying' (kathaṃkathā), which is uncertainty (vicikicchā). He for whom this does not exist is one without 'how-saying' (akathaṃkathī); thus the accusative 'akathaṃkathiṃ.' Remorse and regret are cut off by the Blessed One with the path of the non-returner; scruples about hands and feet are cut off with the highest path, due to the attainment of the unique qualities. The state of repeatedly arising again and again is here intended by 'bhavābhava'; thus he says, 'in repeated existence.' Or, just as there is restraint and non-restraint, or fruit and non-fruit, so too small and great existence is called 'bhavābhava'; thus he says, 'in inferior or superior states of existence.' Existence that has reached its culmination is called 'non-existence' (abhava), as in 'the qualities of one beyond training' (Dhs. Tikamātikā 11). 'Perceptions of defilement' refers to perceptions of sensual desire and so on. Or, the defilements themselves are spoken of by the name 'perception,' as in 'having abandoned perceptions, one attains the deathless.' By this statement, 'he reveals his own state as one whose cankers are destroyed,' it should be understood that this meaning is also explained: 'he teaches the Dhamma to others so that they may become likewise.' 'Nīharitvā kīḷāpetvā' means 'having taken out and having made sport of,' or 'having made sport of by way of taking out.' 'Tivisākha' means a mark on the forehead, so called because it arises on the forehead like a three-furrowed frown.

201. Kinti [M 2.0060] nu khoti kiṃ kāraṇenāti attho. Anusandhiṃ gahetvāti pucchānusandhiṃ uṭṭhapetvā. Yatonidānanti yaṃnidānaṃ, yaṃkāraṇāti vuttaṃ hoti. Purimapade hi vibhatti alopaṃ katvā niddeso, chaajjhattikabāhirāyatanādinidānanti ayameva attho. Saṅkhāyanti saṅkhābhāvena ñāyantīti saṅkhāti āha “saṅkhāti koṭṭhāsā”ti. Kāmañcettha mānopi papañco, abhinandanasabhāve eva pana gaṇhanto “taṇhāmānadiṭṭhipapañcasampayuttā”ti āha. Tathā hi vakkhati “abhinanditabba”ntiādi. Samudācarantīti sabbaso uddhaṃ uddhaṃ pariyādāya pavattanti. Mariyādattho hi ayamākāro, tena ca yogena purisanti upayogavacanaṃ yathā “tathāgataṃ, bhikkhave, arahantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ dve vitakkā samudācarantī”ti (itivu. 38). Taṇhādayo ca yathāsakaṃ pavattiākāraṃ avilaṅghantiyo āsevanavasena uparūpari pavattanti. Tathā hi tā “papañcasaṅkhā”ti vuttā.

201. 'Kinti nu kho' means 'For what reason?' 'Taking up the connection' means raising the connection of the question. 'Yatonidānaṃ' means 'from what source,' that is to say, 'from what cause.' For in the former word, the exposition is made without eliding the case ending; the meaning is just this: 'having the six internal and external sense bases, etc., as their source.' 'They are reckoned' (saṅkhāyanti) means they are known by way of a reckoning (saṅkhā); thus he says, 'saṅkhā means classifications.'
