And although conceit is also a proliferation (papañca) here, taking it only in its aspect of delighting, he said 'associated with the proliferations of craving, conceit, and views.' For thus it will be said: 'to be delighted in,' etc. 'They assail' (samudācaranti) means they proceed by completely taking over, ever more intensely. For this prefix 'ā' has the sense of a limit, and in connection with this, 'a person' is a term in the accusative case, as in: 'Bhikkhus, two kinds of thoughts assail the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One' (Iti 38). And craving and the others, without transgressing their respective modes of operation, proceed again and again by way of cultivation. For that reason they are called 'proliferative reckonings.'

Kāraṇeti pavattipaccaye. Ekāyatanampi …pe… natthīti cakkhāyatanādi ekampi āyatanaṃ abhinanditabbaṃ abhivaditabbaṃ ajjhositabbañca natthi ce, nanu natthi eva, kasmā “natthi ce”ti vuttanti? Saccaṃ natthi, appahīnābhinandanābhivadanaajjhosānānaṃ pana puthujjanānaṃ abhinanditabbādippakārāni āyatanāni hontīti tesaṃ na sakkā natthīti vattu, pahīnābhinandanādīnaṃ pana sabbathā natthīti “natthi ce”ti vuttaṃ. Ahaṃ mamanti abhinanditabbanti [V 2.0058] diṭṭhābhinandanāya “aha”nti taṇhābhinandanāya “mama”nti rocetabbaṃ. Abhivaditabbanti abhinivisanasamuṭṭhāpanavasena vattabbaṃ. Tenāha “ahaṃ mamanti vattabba”nti. Ajjhositvāti diṭṭhi taṇhā vatthuṃ anupavisitvā gāhadvayaṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ viya katvā. Tenāha “gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā”ti. Etenāti “ettha ce natthī”tiādivacanena. Etthāti āyatanesu. Taṇhādīnaṃ avatthubhāvadassanamukhena taṇhādīnaṃyeva appavattiṃ kilesaparinibbānaṃ kathitanti. Tenāha bhagavā “esevanto”tiādi, ayameva abhinandanādīnaṃ natthibhāvakaro maggo, tappaṭippassaddhibhūtaṃ phalaṃ, taṃnissaraṇaṃ vā nibbānaṃ rāgānusayādīnaṃ anto avasānaṃ appavattīti attho. Tenāha “ayaṃ …pe… anto”ti. Sabbatthāti “esevanto paṭighānusayānaṃ”tiādīsu sabbapadesu.

'In the cause' means in the condition for its occurrence. 'If there is not even one sense base...' and so on: if there is not even one sense base, such as the eye-base, that should be delighted in, welcomed, and clung to—if there is none, then surely there is none. Why, then, is it said, 'if there is none'? It is true that for an awakened one there is none. However, for worldlings who have not abandoned delighting, welcoming, and clinging, there are sense bases of a kind to be delighted in, etc. For them, it cannot be said that there are none. But for those who have abandoned delighting, etc., they are entirely non-existent. Hence it is said, 'if there is none.' 'One should delight in “I” and “mine”' means: one should approve of 'I' through delight in view, and of 'mine' through delight in craving. 'Should be welcomed' means it should be spoken of by way of giving rise to adherence. Therefore he says: 'one should say “I” and “mine.”' 'Having clung to' means that view and craving, having entered the object, make the twofold grasp as if it were exclusive. Therefore he says: 'having swallowed and consumed it.' 'By this' means by the statement beginning, 'If here there is none.' 'Here' means in the sense bases. By way of showing the lack of a basis for craving and so on, the very non-occurrence of craving and so on is spoken of as the final quenching of the defilements. Therefore the Blessed One said, 'This is the end,' etc. This very path is what brings about the non-existence of delighting, etc.; its pacification is the fruit, and the escape from it, Nibbāna, is the end, the termination, the non-occurrence of the latent tendencies of lust and so on. This is the meaning. Therefore it is said: 'This... is the end.' 'In all cases' means in all passages such as, 'This is the end of the latent tendencies of aversion.'

Ādiyatīti [M 2.0061] pahāradānādivasena gayhati. Matthakappattaṃ kalahanti bhaṇḍanādimatte aṭṭhatvā mukhasattīhi vitudanādivasena matthakappattaṃ kalahaṃ. Yāya karotīti sambandho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Viruddhaggāhavasena nānāgāhamattaṃ, tathā viruddhavādavasena nānāvādamattaṃ. Evaṃ pavattanti garukātabbesupi gāravaṃ akatvā “tuvaṃ tuva”nti evaṃ pavattaṃ sārambhakathaṃ, yāya cetanāya yaṃ karoti, sā tuvaṃ tuvaṃ. Nissāyāti paṭicca, nissayādipaccaye katvāti attho. Kilesānaṃ uppattinimittatā tāva āyatanānaṃ hotu tabbhāve bhāvato, nirodhanimittatā pana kathaṃ. Na hettha lokuttaradhammānaṃ saṅgaho lokiyānaṃyeva adhippetattāti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “nirujjhamānāpī”tiādi. Nāmamattena nimittataṃ sandhāya vuttoti dassento “yatthuppannā, tattheva niruddhā hontī”ti vatvā tamatthaṃ suttantarena sādhento “svāyamattho”tiādimāha.

'One takes it up' means it is grasped by way of giving blows and the like. 'A quarrel that has reached its peak' means that, not being content with mere disputes and the like, it reaches the peak of quarreling by way of piercing with mouth-spears and so on. 'By which one does' is the connection. The same method applies to the remaining phrases. 'Mere diversity of views' is due to holding opposing views; similarly, 'mere diversity of speech' is due to opposing ways of speaking. Thus they proceed, not showing respect even to those who should be respected, engaging in contentious talk, a 'you-youing.' The intention by which one does this is the 'you-youing.' 'Relying on' means 'depending on'; the meaning is 'having made it a condition of dependence, etc.' Let the sense bases be the sign for the arising of the defilements, since the latter exist when the former are present; but how can they be the sign for their cessation? In reference to the objection that 'there is no inclusion of supramundane states here since only mundane states are intended,' he says, 'even while ceasing,' etc. Showing that this is said with reference to their being a sign in name only, he says, 'where they arise, there they cease,' and then, establishing this meaning with another sutta, he says, 'this is the meaning,' etc.

Tattha samudayasaccapañhenāti mahāsatipaṭṭhāne samudayasaccaniddesena. So hi “kattha uppajjamānā”tiādinā pucchāvasena pavattattā pañhoti vutto. Nanu tattha taṇhāya uppattinirodhā vuttā, na sabbakilesānanti īdisī codanā anavakāsāti dassento “yatheva cā”tiādimāha. Laddhavohāreti iminā rāgādīnaṃ appavattinimittatāya antoti samaññā nibbānassāti dasseti. Eteneva abhinandanādīnaṃ abhāvoti ca idaṃ saṃvaṇṇitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kathaṃ pana sabbasaṅkhatavinissaṭe nibbāne akusaladhammānaṃ nirodhasambhavoti āha “yañhi yattha natthi, taṃ tattha niruddhaṃ nāma hotī”ti. Yvāyaṃ appavattiyaṃ nirodhavohāro vutto, svāyamattho nirodhapañhena dīpetabbo. Na hi tattha uppajjitvā niruddhā vitakkavicārā paṭippassaddhāti vuttā, atha kho appavattā evāti.

Therein, “by the question on the truth of the origin” means by the exposition of the truth of the origin in the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness. For since it proceeds by way of a question, beginning “Where, when arising…,” it is called a “question.” To show that an objection such as, “Surely, the arising and cessation of craving are spoken of there, not of all defilements,” is baseless, he says, “And just as…,” etc. By this he shows that “end” is a designation for Nibbāna because it is the sign for the non-occurrence of lust and so on. And it should be understood that by this the absence of delighting and so on is also explained. But how is the cessation of unwholesome states possible in Nibbāna, which has wholly escaped from everything conditioned? He says: “For whatever is not present in a certain place is said to be ceased in that place.” This use of the term “cessation” for non-occurrence—this meaning is to be clarified by the question on cessation. For it is not said there that initial thought and sustained thought, having arisen, have ceased and are pacified, but rather that they are simply non-occurrent.

203. Evaṃsampadanti [V 2.0059] evaṃsampajjanakaṃ evaṃ passitabbaṃ idaṃ mama ajjhesanaṃ. Tenāha “īdisanti attho”ti. Jānaṃ jānātīti (a. ni. ṭī. 3.10.113-116) sabbaññutaññāṇena jānitabbaṃ sabbaṃ jānāti. Ukkaṭṭhaniddesena hi avisesaggahaṇena ca “jāna”nti iminā niravasesaṃ ñeyyajātaṃ pariggaṇhātīti tabbisayāya jānanakiriyāya sabbaññutaññāṇameva [M 2.0062] karaṇaṃ bhavituṃ yuttaṃ. Atha vā pakaraṇavasena “bhagavā”ti saddantarasannidhānena cāyamattho vibhāvetabbo. Passitabbameva passatīti dibbacakkhu-paññācakkhu-dhammacakkhu-buddhacakkhu-samantacakkhu-saṅkhātehi ñāṇacakkhūhi passitabbaṃ passati eva. Atha vā jānaṃ jānātīti yathā aññe savipallāsā kāmarūpapariññāvādino jānantāpi vipallāsavasena jānanti, na evaṃ bhagavā. Bhagavā pana pahīnavipallāsattā jānanto jānāti eva, diṭṭhidassanassa ca abhāvā passanto passatiyevāti attho. Dassanapariṇāyakaṭṭhenāti yathā cakkhu sattānaṃ dassanatthaṃ pariṇeti, evaṃ lokassa yāthāvadassanasādhanato dassanakiccapariṇāyakaṭṭhena cakkhubhūto, paññācakkhumayattā vā sayambhuñāṇena paññācakkhuṃ bhūto pattoti vā cakkhubhūto. Ñāṇabhūtoti etassa ca evameva attho daṭṭhabbo. Dhammā vā bodhipakkhiyā tehi uppannattā lokassa ca taduppādanato, anaññasādhāraṇaṃ vā dhammaṃ pattoti dhammabhūto. Brahmā vuccati maggo tena uppannattā lokassa ca taduppādanattā, tañca sayambhuñāṇena pattoti brahmabhūto. Catusaccadhammaṃ vadatīti vattā. Ciraṃ saccapaṭivedhaṃ pavattento vadatīti pavattā. Atthaṃ nīharitvāti dukkhādiatthaṃ tatthāpi pīḷanādiatthaṃ uddharitvā. Paramatthaṃ vā nibbānaṃ pāpayitā, amatasacchikiriyaṃ sattesu uppādento amataṃ dadātīti amatassa dātā. Bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ tadāyattabhāvato dhammassāmī.

203. “This is my request: that he be seen as thus accomplished, as endowed with such wisdom.” Therefore he says: “The meaning is ‘of such a kind.’” “Knowing, he knows” means he knows with the knowledge of omniscience everything that is to be known. For by this supreme designation and by its non-specific grasp, the word “knowing” includes the entire field of knowables without remainder. Therefore, it is proper that the instrument for the act of knowing concerning that domain should be the knowledge of omniscience itself. Alternatively, this meaning should be understood from the context and from the proximity of the other word, “the Blessed One.” “He sees only what is to be seen” means he sees with the eyes of knowledge—namely, the divine eye, the eye of wisdom, the eye of the Dhamma, the Buddha-eye, and the all-around eye—only what is to be seen. Alternatively, “knowing, he knows” means: while other proponents of the full understanding of the sense-pleasure and form spheres, though knowing, know in a distorted way, it is not so for the Blessed One. Since the Blessed One has abandoned distortion, when he knows, he truly knows; and since he is without the seeing of views, when he sees, he truly sees. This is the meaning. “He has become an eye in the sense of being a guide to vision”: just as the eye guides beings for the purpose of seeing, so he has become an eye by being a means for the world to see things as they really are, in the sense of being a guide for the task of seeing. Or, because he consists of the eye of wisdom, or because he has attained it through self-becoming knowledge, he has become the eye. The meaning of “he has become knowledge” should be understood in the same way. “He has become the Dhamma”: either because the states pertaining to enlightenment have arisen in him and he causes them to arise in the world, or because he has attained the Dhamma that is not shared by others. “He has become Brahmā”: the path is called Brahmā; because it has arisen in him and he causes it to arise in the world, and because he has attained it through self-becoming knowledge, he has become Brahmā. He is a “speaker” because he speaks the Dhamma of the Four Truths. He is a “proclaimer” because he proclaims it, setting in motion the penetration of the truths for a long time. “Having drawn out the meaning” means having extracted the meaning of suffering, etc., and within that, the meaning of oppression, etc. Or, he is the one who leads to the ultimate meaning, Nibbāna; causing the realization of the deathless to arise in beings, he gives the deathless, so he is the “giver of the deathless.” He is the “lord of the Dhamma” because the states pertaining to enlightenment are dependent on him.

204. So vā uddeso attanopi hotīti thero “yaṃ kho no”ti āha. Sabbalokasādhāraṇā hi buddhānaṃ desanāti. Idāni yehi dvārārammaṇehi purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti, tāni tāva dassento papañcasaññāsaṅkhā dassetuṃ yena saḷāyatanavibhaṅgena niddeso kato, tassa atthaṃ dassetuṃ “cakkhuñcā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha nissayabhāvenāti nissayapaccayabhāvena. Nissayapaccayo ca pasādacakkhuyeva hoti, na cuddasasambhāraṃ, catucattālīsasambhāraṃ vā sasambhāracakkhunti āha “cakkhupasādañca paṭiccā”ti. Ārammaṇabhāvenāti ārammaṇapaccayabhāvena. Ārammaṇapaccayo ca catusamuṭṭhānikarūpesu yaṃ kiñci hotīti āha “catusamuṭṭhānikarūpe ca paṭiccā”ti.

204. Or that summary also pertains to oneself; thus the Elder said, “Indeed, what for us….” For the teachings of the Buddhas are common to the entire world. Now, in order to show the proliferative perception-reckonings, he first shows the doors and objects by which they assail a person. To explain the meaning of the exposition that was made by way of the analysis of the six sense bases, the passage beginning “the eye and…” is commenced. Therein, “by way of dependence” means by way of the dependence condition. And the dependence condition is only the eye-sensitivity, not the eye with its constituents, whether of fourteen or forty-four kinds. Therefore he said, “dependent on the eye-sensitivity….” “By way of object” means by way of the object condition. And the object condition is any of the forms originated from the four causes. Therefore he said, “and dependent on forms originated from the four causes.”

Ettha cakkhu ekampi viññāṇassa paccayo hoti, rūpāyatanaṃ pana anekameva saṃhatanti [M 2.0063] imassa [V 2.0060] visesassa dassanatthaṃ nissayabhāvena “cakkhupasādañca ārammaṇabhāvena catusamuṭṭhānikarūpe cā”ti vacanabhedo kato. Kiṃ pana kāraṇaṃ cakkhu ekampi viññāṇassa paccayo hoti, rūpaṃ pana anekamevāti? Paccayabhāvavisesato. Cakkhu hi cakkhuviññāṇassa nissayapurejātaindriyavippayuttapaccayehi paccayo hontaṃ atthibhāveneva hoti tasmiṃ sati tassa bhāvato, asati abhāvato, yato taṃ atthiavigatapaccayehissa paccayo hotīti vuccati, tannissitatā cassa na ekadesena allīyanavasena icchitabbā arūpabhāvato. Atha kho garurājādīsu sissarājapurisādīnaṃ viya tappaṭibaddhavuttitāya, itare pana paccayā tena tena visesena veditabbā.

Here, the eye, though single, is a condition for consciousness, while the form-base is manifold and composite. To show this distinction, a difference in phrasing is made: “the eye-sensitivity by way of dependence and the forms with fourfold origination by way of object.” But what is the reason that the eye, though single, is a condition for consciousness, while form is manifold? It is due to the specific nature of the conditionality. For the eye, being a condition for eye-consciousness by way of the conditions of dependence, prenascence, faculty, and dissociation, is so simply by its presence—when it is present, that consciousness exists; when it is absent, it does not. Therefore it is said to be its condition by way of the presence and non-disappearance conditions. And its dependence should not be understood as clinging to a part of it, because it is non-material. Rather, it is by way of having its function bound to it, like disciples and royal men to a great king. The other conditions, however, should be understood according to their respective specific characteristics.

Sacāyaṃ paccayabhāvo na ekasmiṃ na sambhavatīti ekampi cakkhu cakkhuviññāṇassa paccayo hotīti dassetuṃ pāḷiyaṃ “cakkhuñcāvuso, paṭiccā”ti ekavacanavasena vuttaṃ. Rūpaṃ pana yadipi cakkhu viya purejātaatthi-avigatapaccayehi paccayo hoti puretaraṃ uppannaṃ hutvā vijjamānakkhaṇe eva upakārakattā tathāpi anekameva saṃhataṃ hutvā paccayo hoti ārammaṇabhāvato. Yañhi paccayadhammaṃ sabhāvabhūtaṃ, parikappitākāramattaṃ vā viññāṇaṃ vibhāventaṃ pavattati, tadaññesañca satipi paccayabhāve so tassa sārammaṇasabhāvatāya yaṃ kiñci anālambhitvā pavattituṃ asamatthassa olubbhapavattikāraṇabhāvena ālambanīyato ārammaṇaṃ nāma, tassa yasmā yathā tathā sabhāvūpaladdhi viññāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayalābho, tasmā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ rūpaṃ ārabbha pavattamānaṃ tassa sabhāvaṃ vibhāventameva pavattati. Sā cassa indriyādhīnavuttikassa ārammaṇasabhāvūpaladdhi na ekadvikalāpagatavaṇṇavasena hoti, nāpi katipayakalāpagatavaṇṇavasena, atha kho ābhogānurūpaṃ āpāthagatavaṇṇavasenāti anekameva rūpaṃ saṃhaccakāritāya viññāṇassa paccayo hotīti dassento “rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇa”nti bahuvacanavasenāha.

To show that even a single eye is a condition for eye-consciousness, it is stated in the Pāli in the singular: 'Dependent on the eye, friend…' Form, however, although like the eye it is a condition by way of the prenascence, presence, and non-disappearance conditions—having arisen earlier and being helpful at the moment of its existence—is nevertheless a condition as a manifold composite by way of being an object. For when consciousness arises distinguishing a conditioning phenomenon that has its own nature, or a mere conceived form, that phenomenon is called an ‘object’ because it must be taken as a support. This is because consciousness, by its nature of having an object, is unable to arise without taking something as a support, and this serves as the cause for its arising by way of grasping, even when other conditions are present. Since the consciousness’s obtaining of the object-condition is the perception of the object’s nature in whatever way, eye-consciousness, arising with form as its support, proceeds by distinguishing that form’s nature. And for this consciousness, whose functioning is dependent on the faculty, this perception of the object’s nature does not occur by way of the color belonging to one or two material groups, nor by way of the color belonging to a few material groups, but rather by way of the color that has come into range in accordance with its attention. Thus, to show that manifold form is a condition for consciousness through its collective action, it is said in the plural: 'and on forms, eye-consciousness arises.'

Yaṃ pana paṭṭhāne (paṭṭhā. 1.1.2 paccayaniddesa) “rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ yādisaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayo, tādisaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kīdisaṃ pana tanti[M 2.0064]? Samuditanti pākaṭoyamattho. Evañca katvā yadeke vadanti “āyatanasallakkhaṇavasena cakkhuviññāṇādayo sallakkhaṇavisayā, na drabyasallakkhaṇavasenā”ti, tampi suvuttameva hoti. Na cettha samudāyārammaṇatā āsaṅkitabbā samudāyābhogasseva abhāvato, samuditā pana vaṇṇadhammā ārammaṇapaccayā honti. Kathaṃ pana paccekaṃ asamatthā samuditā ārammaṇapaccayā honti. Na hi [V 2.0061] paccekaṃ daṭṭhuṃ asakkontā andhā samuditā passantīti? Nayidamekantikaṃ visuṃ visuṃ asamatthānampi sivikāvahanādīsu samatthatāya dassanato. Kesādīnañca yasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhitānaṃ paccekaṃ vaṇṇaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkā, tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne samuditānaṃ taṃ gahetuṃ sakkāti bhiyyopi tesaṃ saṃhaccakāritā paribyattā. Etena kiṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa paramāṇurūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ, udāhu taṃsamudāyotiādikā codanā paṭikkhittāti veditabbā. “Sotañca, āvuso, paṭiccā”tiādīsupi iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ nāmāti cakkhunissitarūpavijānanalakkhaṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ nāma uppajjati.

As to what is stated in the Paṭṭhāna (Paṭṭh. 1.1.2): 'The form base is a condition for the eye-consciousness element and for the states associated with it by way of object condition,' this is said with reference to the kind of form base that is an object condition for eye-consciousness. And what kind is that? The composite—this meaning is plain. This being so, when some say, 'Eye-consciousness and so on have as their object the specific characteristic by way of the base’s characteristic, not by way of the substance’s characteristic,' that too is well said. Here, one should not suspect that the aggregate is the object, since there is no advertence to the aggregate itself. Rather, the composite color-phenomena are the object condition. But how can things that are individually incapable become an object condition when they are composite? For surely blind people, unable to see individually, do not see when they are gathered together? This is not invariably so, for it is seen that even those who are individually incapable are capable when combined in such tasks as carrying a palanquin. Moreover, in the case of hairs and so on, in a place where their individual color cannot be grasped, in that very same place their color can be grasped when they are composite. Thus their collective action is even more evident. By this, it should be understood that objections such as, 'Is the object of eye-consciousness an atomic form or an aggregate of them?' are refuted. In such passages as, 'Dependent on the ear, friend…' the meaning should be understood in the same way. What is called 'eye-consciousness'? Eye-consciousness, which has the characteristic of cognizing a form dependent on the eye, arises.

Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgatiyāti cakkhu, rūpaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇanti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ saṅgatiyā samodhānena. Phasso nāmāti arūpadhammopi samāno ārammaṇe phusanākāreneva pavattanato phusanalakkhaṇo phasso nāma dhammo uppajjati. Sahajātādivasenāti cakkhuviññāṇasampayuttāya sahajātaaññamaññādivasena, anantarāya anantarādivasena, itarāya upanissayavasena paccayabhāvato phassapaccayā phassakāraṇā vedanā uppajjati. Anubhavanasamakālameva ārammaṇassa sañjānanaṃ hotīti “tāya vedanāya yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ vedeti, tadeva saññā sañjānātī”ti vuttaṃ. Cakkhudvārikā dhammā idhādhippetāti tadanusārena pana aparāparuppannānaṃ vedanādīnaṃ gahaṇe sati, yanti vā kāraṇavacanaṃ, yasmā ārammaṇaṃ vedeti, tasmā taṃ sañjānātīti attho. Na hi asati vedayite kadāci saññuppatti atthi. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Saññāya hi yathāsaññātaṃ vijjamānaṃ, avijjamānaṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ vitakkavasena parikappeti, yathāparikappitañca taṃ diṭṭhitaṇhāmānamaññanāhi maññamāno papañcetīti vutto. Tenevāha “pathaviṃ pathavito sañjānā”ti, “pathaviṃ pathavito [M 2.0065] saññatvā pathaviṃ maññatī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.2), “takkañca diṭṭhīsu pakappayitvā, saccaṃ musāti dvayadhammamāhū”ti (su. ni. 892; mahāni. 121) ca. Balappattapapañcavasenevāyamatthavaṇṇanā katā, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana paridubbalavasena.

‘The meeting of the three’ means: by the coming together, the conjunction, of these three—eye, form, and eye-consciousness. What is called ‘contact’? Although it is an immaterial phenomenon, because it proceeds in the manner of touching the object, the phenomenon called ‘contact,’ which has the characteristic of touching, arises. ‘By way of co-nascence, etc.’: because it is a condition for what is associated with eye-consciousness by way of co-nascence, mutuality, etc.; for the succeeding consciousness by way of contiguity, etc.; and for the other by way of decisive support, feeling arises conditioned by contact, caused by contact. Because the perceiving of the object occurs at the very same time as the experiencing of it, it is said: ‘Whatever object one feels with that feeling, that very object perception perceives.’ Here, phenomena of the eye-door are intended. Accordingly, when grasping the successively arisen feeling, etc., the word yaṃ is a term of reason, meaning: ‘Because one feels the object, therefore one perceives it.’ For perception never arises when there is no feeling. The same method applies to the other passages. For by perception one conceives by way of thought an object—existent or non-existent—as it has been perceived; and what has been conceived in such a way one is said to proliferate by way of views, craving, conceit, and imaginings. Therefore he said: ‘He perceives earth as earth; having perceived earth as earth, he conceives earth…,’ and ‘Having formed a conjecture among views, they speak of a twofold phenomenon, true and false.’ This explanation of the meaning is made by way of proliferation that has gained strength, but in the commentary it is explained by way of what is very weak.

Cakkhurūpādīhi kāraṇehīti cakkhuviññāṇaphassavedanāsaññāvitakkehi kāraṇabhūtehi. Akāraṇabhūtānampi tesaṃ atthitāya kāraṇaggahaṇaṃ. Pariññātā hi te akāraṇaṃ. Tenāha “apariññātakāraṇa”nti. Tīhipi pariññāhi apariññātavatthukaṃ. Abhibhavantīti ajjhottharanti. Sahajātā hontīti ettha “cakkhusamphassapaccayā vedanākkhandho atthi kusalo’tiādivacanato vedanāsaññā asahajātāpi gahetabbā. Yadi evanti “papañcetī”ti ettha yadi pañcadvārajavanasahajātā papañcasaṅkhā adhippetā tāsaṃ paccuppannavisayattā, kasmā atītānāgataggahaṇaṃ [V 2.0062] katanti codeti. Itaro “tathā uppajjanato”tiādinā pariharati. Tattha tathā uppajjanatoti yathā vattamānakāle, evaṃ atītakāle anāgatakāle ca cakkhudvāre papañcasaṅkhānaṃ uppajjanato atītānāgataggahaṇaṃ kataṃ, na atītesu, anāgatesu vā cakkhurūpesu cakkhudvārikānaṃ tāsaṃ uppajjanato.

‘By causes such as the eye and form’: this means by eye-consciousness, contact, feeling, perception, and thought, which have become causes. The word ‘causes’ is included because of the existence of those things that have not become causes. For when they are fully understood, they are non-causes. Hence it is said, ‘the cause not being fully understood.’ The object is not fully understood by the three kinds of full understanding. ‘They overwhelm’ means they submerge. ‘They arise together’: here, from the statement, ‘Conditioned by eye-contact, there is a wholesome feeling aggregate,’ etc., feeling and perception that are not co-nascent should also be taken. If so, one objects: ‘Regarding “he proliferates,” if the proliferations of concepts co-nascent with the five-door impulsion are intended, since their object is present, why is the past and future included?’ The other replies, saying, ‘Because they arise in that way,’ etc. Therein, ‘because they arise in that way’ means: because the proliferations of concepts arise at the eye-door in the past and future just as they do in the present time, the past and future are included; not because those proliferations at the eye-door arise from past and future eyes and forms.

Manañjāvuso, paṭiccāti ettha duvidhaṃ manaṃ kevalaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ, sāvajjanaṃ vā. Duvidhā hi kathā. Uppattidvārakathāyaṃ dvikkhattuṃ calitaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ manodvāraṃ nāma, cakkhādi viya rūpādinā yena taṃ ghaṭṭitaṃ tattha upari viññāṇuppattiyā dvārabhāvato. Paccayakathāyaṃ sāvajjanabhavaṅgaṃ, “manosamphassapaccayā atthi kusalo”tiādīsu hi sāvajjanamanosamphasso icchito, na bhavaṅgamanosamphasso asambhavato. Tattha paṭhamanayaṃ sandhāyāha “mananti bhavaṅgacitta”nti. Dhammeti tebhūmakadhammārammaṇanti iminā sabhāvadhammesu eva kilesuppattīti keci, tadayuttaṃ tadupādānāyapi paññattiyā dhammārammaṇatāya vuttattā. Idha pana tebhūmakāpi dhammā labbhantīti dassanatthaṃ “tebhūmakadhammārammaṇa”nti vuttaṃ, na paññattiyā anārammaṇattā. Evañcetaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ, aññathā akusalacittuppādā anārammaṇā nāma siyuṃ. Uppattidvārakathāyaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādi viya āvajjanampi dvārapakkhikamevāti vuttaṃ “manoviññāṇanti āvajjanaṃ vā”ti. Paccayakathāyaṃ pana āvajjanaṃ gahitanti “javanaṃ vā”ti vuttaṃ. Nayadvaye dhammānaṃ sahajātavibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “āvajjane [M 2.0066] gahite”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yuttamevāti nippariyāyato yuttameva.

Friend, regarding 'depending on the mind,' here the mind is twofold: either the bare life-continuum or adverting. The discussion is twofold. In the explanation of the arising-door, the life-continuum that has stirred twice is called the mind-door, just as the eye, etc., is struck by a form, etc., by which consciousness arises, thus serving as a door. In the explanation of conditions, mind-contact with adverting is intended, for in statements like 'with mind-contact as condition, there is the wholesome,' etc., mind-contact with adverting is intended, not mind-contact of the life-continuum, since the latter is impossible. Here, referring to the first method, it is said: '“mind” means the life-continuum consciousness.' 'Phenomena' means objects pertaining to the three realms. Some say that defilements arise only in relation to intrinsic phenomena, but this is not appropriate because it is stated that even a concept is a mental object on account of clinging to it. Here, however, to show that phenomena of the three realms are also included, it is said, 'objects pertaining to the three realms,' not because concepts are not objects. And this should be accepted thus; otherwise, the arising of unwholesome consciousnesses would be without an object. In the explanation of the arising-door, just like eye-consciousness, etc., adverting too is on the side of the door, hence it is said that 'mind-consciousness' refers to adverting. But in the explanation of conditions, since adverting is taken, it is also said to refer to 'impulsion'. To show the division of co-nascent phenomena in both methods, it is said, 'when adverting is taken,' etc. This is entirely appropriate without qualification.

So yāva na paccayapaṭivedho sambhavati, tāva paññattimukheneva sabhāvadhammā paññāyanti paccekaṃ apaññāpaneti āha “phasso nāma eko dhammo uppajjatī”ti. Evaṃ phassapaññattiṃ paññapessatīti paññapetvā tabbisayadassanaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppādessati. Imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hotīti imasmiṃ cakkhuādike paccaye sati idaṃ phassādikaṃ paccayuppannaṃ hoti. Dvādasāyatanavasenāti dvādasannaṃ āyatanānaṃ vasena āgatena paṭiccasamuppādanayavasena. Dvādasāyatanapaṭikkhepavasenāti “imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hotī”ti paccayābhāvapaccayuppannābhāvadassanakkame dvādasannaṃ āyatanānaṃ paṭikkhepavasena.

So long as the penetration of conditions does not occur, intrinsic phenomena are cognized only by way of concepts, without being designated individually. Thus he says: 'Contact is one phenomenon that arises.' In this way, having established the concept of contact, one will generate the knowledge that sees its object. 'When this exists, that comes to be' means: when this condition, such as the eye, exists, then this conditionally arisen phenomenon, such as contact, comes to be. 'By way of the twelve sense bases' means by way of the method of dependent origination that proceeds by means of the twelve sense bases. 'By way of the rejection of the twelve sense bases' means by way of the rejection of the twelve sense bases in the sequence of seeing the absence of the conditionally arisen phenomenon with the absence of the condition, as in 'When this is not, that does not come to be.'

Sāvakena pañho kathitoti ayaṃ pañho sāvakena kathito, iti iminā kāraṇena mā nikkaṅkhā ahuvattha. Atha vā saṃkhittena vuttamatthaṃ vitthārena vibhajantena etadagge ṭhapitena mahāsāvakena pañho kathitoti iminā kāraṇena etasmiṃ pañhe mā nikkaṅkhā ahuvattha, heraññike [V 2.0063] sati kahāpaṇaṃ sayaṃ nicchinantā viya ahutvā bhagavato eva santike nikkaṅkhā hotha.

'The question was spoken by a disciple': this question was spoken by a disciple; for this reason, do not be doubtful. Or, 'the question was spoken by a great disciple' who was established as the foremost in analyzing in detail a meaning stated in brief; for this reason, do not be doubtful about this question. Just as one would not, in the presence of a money-changer, examine a coin oneself, so you should become free from doubt in the presence of the Blessed One himself.

205. Ākaronti phalaṃ tāya tāya mariyādāya nibbattentīti ākārā, kāraṇāni. Pāṭiyekkakāraṇehīti channaṃ dvārānaṃ vasena visuṃ visuṃ papañcakāraṇassa niddiṭṭhattā vuttaṃ. Atha vā yadipi yattakehi dhammehi yaṃ phalaṃ nibbattati, tesaṃ samuditānaṃyeva kāraṇabhāvo sāmaggiyāva phaluppattito, tathāpi paccekaṃ tassa kāraṇamevāti katvā vuttaṃ “pāṭiyekkakāraṇehī”ti. Padehīti nāmādipadehi ceva taṃsamudāyabhūtehi vākyehi ca. Tenāha “akkharasampiṇḍanehī”ti. Akkharāniyeva hi atthesu yathāvaccaṃ padavākyabhāvena paricchijjanti. Byañjanehīti atthassa abhibyañjanato byañjanasaññitehi vaṇṇehi. Tāni pana yasmā pariyāyassa akkharaṇato “akkharānī”ti vuccanti, tasmā āha “akkharehī”ti. Ettha ca imehi ākārehi imehi padabyañjanehi papañcasamudācārassa vaṭṭassa ca vivaṭṭassa ca dassanaattho vibhattoti yojanā. Paṇḍiccenāti paññāya. “Kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, paṇḍito hoti[M 2.0067]? Yato kho bhikkhu dhātukusalo ca hotī”ti (ma. ni. 3.124) ādisuttapadavasena paṇḍitalakkhaṇaṃ dassento “catūhi vā kāraṇehī”tiādimāha. Saccapaṭivedhavasena paṇḍiccaṃ dassitanti paṭisambhidāvasena mahāpaññataṃ dassetuṃ “mahante atthe”tiādi vuttaṃ.

205. 'Modes' (ākārā) are causes (kāraṇāni) because they produce a result, bringing it to completion in this or that way. 'By individual causes': this is said because the cause of proliferation has been pointed out separately for each of the six doors. Or, although whatever result is produced by however many phenomena, their combination is the cause since the result arises from their togetherness, still, because each one is a cause, it is said 'by individual causes.' 'By words' means by words such as nouns, and by sentences which are their combinations. Therefore he says 'by the grouping of syllables.' For it is syllables themselves that are defined as words and sentences in accordance with their meanings. 'By letters' means by the sounds designated as letters (byañjana) because they manifest the meaning. But since these are called 'syllables' (akkharāni) because they are imperishable in expression, he therefore says 'by syllables.' Here the connection is this: the purpose of showing both the round of saṃsāra and the un-rounding of the process of proliferation is analyzed by means of these modes, words, and letters. 'By wisdom' means by understanding. Showing the characteristic of a wise person by way of the words of the sutta beginning, 'Venerable sir, to what extent is one called wise? When, bhikkhu, one is skilled in the elements…' (MN 113), he says, 'by four causes,' etc. Wisdom is shown by way of the penetration of the truths. To show great wisdom by way of the analytical knowledges, it is said, 'in great meanings,' etc.

Guḷapūvanti guḷe missitvā katapūvaṃ. Baddhasattuguḷakanti madhusakkharāhi piṇḍīkataṃ sattupiṇḍaṃ. Asecitabbakaṃ madhuādinā pageva tehi samayojitabbattā. Cintakajātikoti dhammacintāya cintakasabhāvo. Sabbaññutaññāṇenevassāti sabbaññutaññāṇeneva assa suttassa guṇaṃ paricchindāpetvā nāmaṃ gaṇhāpessāmi.

'A jaggery cake' means a cake made by mixing it with jaggery. 'A bound ball of barley-meal' means a lump of barley-meal made into a ball with honey and sugar. It should not be sprinkled over with honey and so on, as it must be combined with them beforehand. 'Of a reflective nature' means one whose nature is to reflect because of reflection on the Dhamma. 'By his omniscience': I will have him determine the qualities of this sutta and give it a name by means of his omniscience alone.

Madhupiṇḍikasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary to the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta is concluded.

9. Dvedhāvitakkasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Sutta on the Two Kinds of Thought

206. Dve [V 2.0064] dve bhāgeti dve dve koṭṭhāse katvā. Kāmañcettha “imaṃ ekaṃ bhāgamakāsiṃ, imaṃ dutiyabhāgamakāsi”nti vacanato sabbepi vitakkā saṃkilesavodānavibhāgena dveva bhāgā katā, aparāparuppattiyā panetesaṃ abhiṇhācāraṃ upādāya pāḷiyaṃ “dvidhā katvā”ti āmeḍitavacananti “dve dve bhāge katvā”ti āmeḍitavacanavaseneva vutto. Atha vā bhāgadvayassa sappaṭibhāgatāya tattha yaṃ yaṃ dvayampi kho ujuvipaccanīkaṃ, taṃ taṃ visuṃ visuṃ gahetukāmo bhagavā āha “dvidhā katvā vitakke vihareyya”nti. Evaṃ pana cintetvā tattha micchāvitakkānaṃ sammāvitakkānañca anavasesaṃ asaṅkarato ca gahitabhāvaṃ dassento “imaṃ ekaṃ bhāgamakāsiṃ, imaṃ dutiyabhāgamakāsi”nti avoca. Kāmapaṭisaṃyuttoti kāmarāgasaṅkhātena kāmena sampayutto, kāmena paṭibaddho vā. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – byāpajjati cittaṃ etenāti byāpādo, doso. Vihiṃsati etāya satte, vihiṃsanaṃ vā tesaṃ etanti vihiṃsā, paresaṃ viheṭhanākārena pavattassa karuṇāpaṭipakkhassa pāpadhammassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ajjhattanti ajjhattadhammārammaṇamāha. Bahiddhāti bāhiradhammārammaṇaṃ. Oḷārikoti bahalakāmarāgādipaṭisaṃyutto. Tabbipariyāyena sukhumo. Vitakko akusalapakkhikoyevāti [M 2.0068] iminā vitakkabhāvasāmaññena tatthāpi akusalabhāvasāmaññena ekabhāgakaraṇaṃ, na ekacittuppādapariyāpannatādivasenāti dasseti.

206. Having made two portions each means having made two portions each. Here, although it is said, 'I have made this one portion, I have made this the second portion,' all thoughts are made into just two portions by way of defilement and purification. However, because of their repeated occurrence one after another, the phrase 'having divided in two' in the Pāli is a repetitive expression; thus it is said 'having made two portions each' by way of the force of the repetitive expression. Alternatively, because the two portions have their counterparts, the Blessed One, wishing to take each pair separately—whatever is directly opposite—said: 'Having divided thoughts in two, one should dwell.' Having reflected thus, showing that the wrong thoughts and the right thoughts have been taken completely and without confusion, he said: 'I have made this one portion, I have made this the second portion.' Connected with sensual desire means associated with sensual desire, which is sensual craving, or bound by sensual desire. The same method applies to the rest. This, however, is the distinction: the mind is afflicted by this, thus it is ill will (byāpādo), that is, hatred (doso). One harms beings with this, or it is the harming of them, thus it is cruelty (vihiṃsā); this is a designation for the evil state that is the counterpart of compassion and proceeds by way of oppressing others. Internally refers to an object of internal phenomena. Externally refers to an object of external phenomena. Coarse means associated with thick sensual desire, etc. The opposite of that is subtle. The thought is solely on the unwholesome side: by this he shows that because of the commonality of the state of thought, and there also because of the commonality of the unwholesome state, they are made one portion, not by way of being included in a single mind-moment, etc.

Nekkhammaṃ vuccati lobhātikkantattā paṭhamajjhānaṃ, sabbākusalehi nikkhantattā sabbaṃ kusalaṃ. Idha pana kāmavitakkapaṭipakkhassa adhippetattā āha “kāmehi nissaṭo nekkhammapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko”ti. Soti nekkhammavitakko. Yāva paṭhamajjhānāti paṭhamasamannāhārato paṭṭhāya yāva paṭhamajjhānaṃ etthuppanno vitakko nekkhammavitakkoyeva. Paṭhamajjhānanti ca idaṃ tato paraṃ vitakkābhāvato vuttaṃ. Na byāpajjati cittaṃ etena, byāpādassa vā paṭipakkhoti abyāpādo, mettāpubbabhāgo mettābhāvanārambho. Na vihiṃsanti etāya, vihiṃsāya vā paṭipakkhoti avihiṃsā, karuṇāpubbabhāgo karuṇābhāvanārambho.

Renunciation: the first jhāna is called renunciation because it has transcended greed; all that is wholesome is called renunciation because it has departed from all unwholesome states. Here, however, since the counterpart of the thought of sensual desire is intended, it is said: 'The thought connected with renunciation, having departed from sensual pleasures.' That is the thought of renunciation. Up to the first jhāna: from the initial application of mind up to the first jhāna, the thought that arises in this context is solely the thought of renunciation. And 'the first jhāna' is said because beyond that there is an absence of thought. The mind is not afflicted by this, or it is the counterpart of ill will, thus it is non-ill will (abyāpādo); it is the preliminary part of loving-kindness, the beginning of the development of loving-kindness. One does not harm with this, or it is the counterpart of cruelty, thus it is non-cruelty (avihiṃsā); it is the preliminary part of compassion, the beginning of the development of compassion.

Mahābodhisattānaṃ mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhantakālato paṭṭhāya laddhāvasarā sammāsaṅkappā uparūpari savisesaṃ pavattantīti āha “chabbassāni…pe… pavattiṃsū”ti. Ñāṇassa aparipakkattā [V 2.0065] pubbavāsanāvasena satisammosato kadāci micchāvitakkalesopi hotiyevāti taṃ dassetuṃ “satisammosena…pe… tiṭṭhantī”ti āha. Yathā niccapihitepi gehe kadāci vātapāne vivaṭamatte laddhāvasaro vāto anto paviseyya, evaṃ guttindriyepi bodhisattasantāne satisammosavasena laddhāvasaro akusalavitakko uppajji, uppanno ca kusalavāraṃ pacchinditvā aṭṭhāsi, atha mahāsatto taṃmuhuttuppannameva paṭivinodetvā tesaṃ āyatiṃ anuppādāya “ime micchāvitakkā, ime sammāvitakkā”ti yāthāvato te paricchinditvā micchāvitakkānaṃ avasaraṃ adento sammāvitakke parivaḍḍhesi. Tena vuttaṃ “mayhaṃ ime”tiādi.

He said, 'For six years... they occurred,' to show that from the time of the great renunciation of the great bodhisattvas, having found their opportunity, right intentions occurred one after another in a special way. To show that because his knowledge was not yet mature and due to the force of past habitations, a stain of wrong thought would sometimes arise out of a lapse of mindfulness, he said: 'Through a lapse of mindfulness... they stand.' Just as in a house that is always shut, if a window is opened for just a moment, the wind, having found an opportunity, might enter inside, so too in the mental continuum of the bodhisattva with his faculties guarded, an unwholesome thought arose due to a lapse of mindfulness. Having arisen, it cut off the turn for the wholesome and stood fast. Then the great being, having immediately dispelled that thought which had just arisen, and in order to prevent their future arising, accurately defined them as they really are: 'These are wrong thoughts, these are right thoughts.' Not giving an opportunity to wrong thoughts, he developed the right thoughts. Therefore it was said: 'These of mine,' etc.

207. Pamādo nāma sativippavāsoti āha “appamattassāti satiyā avippavāse ṭhitassā”ti. Ātāpavīriyavantassāti kilesānaṃ niggaṇhanavīriyavato. Pesitacittassāti bhavavimokkhāya vissaṭṭhacittassa kāye ca jīvite ca nirapekkhassa. “Evaṃ paṭipākatiko jāto”ti attano attabhāvaṃ nissāya pavattaṃ somanassākāraṃ gehassitasomanassapakkhikaṃ akāsi, paññāmahantatāya sukhumadassitā.

207. Heedlessness is the absence of mindfulness; thus it is said: Of one who is heedful means of one who abides in the non-absence of mindfulness. Of one who is ardent and energetic means of one who possesses the energy for subduing the defilements. Of one with a dispatched mind means of one whose mind is sent forth for liberation from existence, who is unconcerned about body and life. 'Thus he became one with such a preparation': He made the state of joy that occurred based on his own individuality one that was on the side of joy based on the household life; this shows the subtlety of his vision due to the greatness of his wisdom.

Apariññāyaṃ [M 2.0069] ṭhitassāti na pariññāyaṃ ṭhitassa, apariggahitapariññassāti attho. Vitakko…pe… etāni tīṇi nāmāni labhatīti tādisassa uppanno micchāvitakko yathārahaṃ attabyābādhako ubhayabyābādhako ca na hotīti na vattabbo taṃ sabhāvānativattanatoti adhippāyo. Anuppannānuppādauppannaparihāninimittatāya paññaṃ nirodhetīti paññānirodhiko. Tenāha “anuppannāyā”tiādi. Natthibhāvaṃ gacchatīti paṭisaṅkhānabalena vikkhambhanappahānamāha. Nirujjhatītiādīhipi tadeva vadati. Vigatantantiādīhi pana samūlaṃ uddhaṭaṃ viya tadā appavattanakaṃ akāsinti vadati.

‘Of one who stands in non-full-understanding’ means of one who does not stand in full understanding; the meaning is, of one whose full understanding is ungrasped. It cannot be said that a wrong thought that has arisen in such a person—who obtains these three names: ‘thought,’ etc.—is not, as is proper, conducive to his own affliction and to the affliction of both; the intention is that its own nature is not to be overcome. Because it is a cause for the non-arising of the unarisen and for the decline of the arisen, it obstructs wisdom; thus it is wisdom-obstructing. Therefore he said: ‘Of the unarisen,’ etc. ‘It goes to non-existence’: this refers to abandonment by suppression through the power of reflection. By ‘It ceases,’ etc., he says the same thing. But by ‘It is destroyed,’ etc., he says that he made it non-occurrent at that time, as if it were uprooted.

208. Cittavipariṇāmabhāvo cittassa aññathattaṃ pakaticittavigamo. Anekaggatākāro vikkhepo. Tattha vitakkena cittaṃ vihaññamānaṃ viya hotīti āha “taṃ gahetvā vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ akāsī”ti. Kāruññanti paradukkhanimittaṃ cittakhedaṃ vadati. Tenevāha – “paradukkhe sati sādhūnaṃ manaṃ kampetīti karuṇā”ti (ma. ni. ṭī. 1.1; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.1). Nti karuṇāyanavasena pavattacittapakampanaṃ sandhāya “uppajjati vihiṃsāvitakko”ti āha, na sattesu vihiṃsā pavattatīti adhippāyo.

208. The state of the mind's transformation is the mind's otherness, the departure of the natural mind. Distraction is the state of non-unification. There, since the mind is as if being afflicted by thought, he said: ‘Having taken that, he made a thought of cruelty.’ ‘Compassion’: he speaks of the mental distress at the sign of others' suffering. Therefore it is said: ‘When there is suffering in others, it makes the minds of the good tremble, thus it is compassion.’ Referring to the trembling of the mind that occurs by way of compassion, he said, ‘a thought of cruelty arises’; the intention is not that cruelty is directed towards beings.

Tena tena cassākārenāti yena yena ākārena bhikkhunā anuvitakkitaṃ anuvicāritaṃ, tena [V 2.0066] tena ākārenassa cetaso nati hoti. Tenevāha “kāmavitakkādīsū”tiādi. Pahāsīti kālavipallāsena vuttanti āha “pajahatī”ti. Pahānaṃ panassa siddhameva paṭipakkhassa siddhattāti dassetuṃ “pahāsī”ti vuttaṃ yathā “asāmibhoge gāmikāādīyiṃsū”ti. Bahulamakāsīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Evamevaṃ namatīti kāmavitakkasampayogākārameva hoti, kāmavitakkasampayuttākārena vā pariṇamati. Kasanaṃ kiṭṭhaṃ, kasīti attho, tannibbattattā pana kāraṇūpacārena sassaṃ “kiṭṭha”nti vuttanti āha “sassasambādhe”ti. Cattāri bhayānīti vadhabandhajānigarahāni. Upaddavanti anatthuppādabhāvaṃ. Lāmakanti nihīnabhāvaṃ. Dhandhesūti attano khandhesu. Otāranti anuppavesaṃ kilesānaṃ. Saṃkilesato visujjhanaṃ visuddhi, sā eva vodānanti āha “vodānapakkhanti idaṃ tasseva vevacana”nti.

‘By that and that mode’: in whatever mode a bhikkhu thinks and ponders, in that mode his mind inclines. Therefore he said: ‘In regard to thoughts of sensual desire, etc.’ ‘He abandoned’: this is said with a change of tense; he says, ‘he abandons.’ To show that his abandoning is indeed accomplished because its counterpart is accomplished, ‘he abandoned’ was said, just as in ‘the villagers seized the unowned property.’ The same method applies here also to ‘he made it much.’ ‘It inclines just so’: it becomes of the nature of association with the thought of sensual desire, or it transforms into a state associated with the thought of sensual desire. Ploughing is ‘kiṭṭha,’ the meaning is agriculture. But because the crop is produced from that, by a causal metaphor the crop is called ‘kiṭṭha’; thus he said ‘in a crop-thicket.’ ‘The four fears’ are killing, bondage, loss of wealth, and blame. ‘Trouble’ means the state of the arising of harm. ‘Inferior’ means a base state. ‘In the slow things’ means in one's own aggregates. ‘Opportunity’ means the entry of the defilements. Purification from defilement is purity (visuddhi); that itself is cleansing (vodāna). Thus he said: ‘“The side of cleansing”—this is a synonym for that.’

209. Sabbakusalaṃ [M 2.0070] nekkhammaṃ sabbākusalapaṭipakkhatāya tato nissaṭattā. Nibbānameva nekkhammaṃ sabbakilesato sabbasaṅkhatato ca nissaṭattā. Kiṭṭhasambādhaṃ viya rūpādiārammaṇaṃ pamāde sati anatthuppattiṭṭhānabhāvato. Kūṭagāvo viya kūṭacittaṃ duddamabhāvato. Paṇḍitagopālako viya bodhisatto upāyakosallayogato. Catubbidhabhayaṃ viya micchāvitakkā sappaṭibhayabhāvato. Paññāya vuddhi etassa atthīti paññāvuddhiko. Vihaññati cittaṃ etenāti vighāto, cetodukkhaṃ, tappakkhiko vighātapakkhiko, na vighātapakkhikoti avighātapakkhiko. Nibbānasaṃvattaniko nibbānavaho. Ugghātīyeyyāti uddhataṃ siyā vikkhittañca bhaveyyāti attho. Saṇṭhapemīti sammadeva paṭṭhapemi. Yathā pana ṭhapitaṃ saṇṭhapitaṃ nāma hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “sannisīdāpemī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sannisīdāpemīti samādhipaṭipakkhe kilese sannisīdāpento cittaṃ gocarajjhatte sannisīdāpemi. Abyaggabhāvāpādakena ekaggaṃ karomi, yathā ārammaṇe suṭṭhu appitaṃ hoti, evaṃ sammā sammadeva ādahāmi samāhitaṃ karomi, yasmā tathāsamāhitaṃ cittaṃ suṭṭhu ārammaṇe āropitaṃ nāma hoti, na tato paripatati, tasmā vuttaṃ “suṭṭhu āropemīti attho”ti. Mā ugghātīyittāti mā haññittha, mā ūhataṃ atthāti attho.

209. All that is wholesome is renunciation because it is the counterpart of all that is unwholesome and has departed from it. Nibbāna itself is renunciation because it has departed from all defilements and all conditioned things. Like a crop-thicket, form-objects and so on are a basis for the arising of harm when there is heedlessness. Like a treacherous bull, a treacherous mind is hard to tame. Like a wise cowherd, the Bodhisatta is endowed with skill in means. Like the fourfold fear, wrong thoughts are perilous. There is growth of wisdom for this one, thus he is one with growth in wisdom. The mind is afflicted by this, thus it is distress (vighāto), mental suffering. Pertaining to that is the side of distress; not pertaining to that is the side of non-distress. Conducive to Nibbāna means leading to Nibbāna. ‘It might be stirred up’ means it might become agitated and distracted. ‘I will establish it’: I will establish it rightly. To show how what is established comes to be well established, it was said: ‘I will make it subside,’ etc. ‘I will make it subside’: making the defilements that are the counterparts of concentration subside, I make the mind subside within its object. By bringing about a state of non-agitation, I make it one-pointed; so that it is well applied to the object, I rightly and properly place it, I make it concentrated. Since a mind so concentrated is said to be well placed on the object and does not fall away from it, therefore it was said: ‘the meaning is, I place it well.’ ‘May it not be stirred up’ means may it not be struck, may it not be agitated.

210. Soyeva…pe… vuttoti iminā kiñcāpi ekaṃyeva kusalavitakkaṃ maggakkhaṇe viya tividhattasambhavato tividhanāmikaṃ katvā dassitaṃ viya hoti, na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pabandhapavattañhi upādāya ekattanayena “soyeva byāpādapaccanīkaṭṭhenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ekajātiyesu hi kusalacittesu uppanno vitakko samānākāratāya so evāti vattabbataṃ labhati yathā “sā eva tittirī, tāni eva osadhānī”ti (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.2.19). Na hi tadā mahāpurisassa asubhamettākaruṇāsannissayā te vitakkā evaṃ vuttāti.

210. ‘The same... as stated’—by this it is meant that although a single wholesome thought, as at the moment of the path, is presented as if having three names due to its threefold nature, it should not be seen in this way. For, taking its continuous occurrence into account, it is spoken of as one by way of the statement: ‘the same, in the sense of being the opposite of ill will,’ and so on. Indeed, a thought arising in wholesome states of one and the same class can be called ‘the same’ due to its similar nature, just as in ‘the same partridge, the same herbs.’ For at that time, it is not that the thoughts of the Great Being connected with the foul, loving-kindness, or compassion were said to be like that.

Samāpattiṃ [V 2.0067] nissāyāti samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā, tato vuṭṭhahitvāti attho. Vipassanāpi taruṇāti yojanā. Kāyo kilamati samathavipassanānaṃ taruṇatāya bhāvanāya pubbenāparaṃ visesassa alabbhamānattā. Tenāha “cittaṃ haññati vihaññatī”ti. Vipassanāya bahūpakārā [M 2.0071] samāpatti, tathā hi vuttaṃ – “samādhiṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvetha, samāhito yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.5; 4.99; 5.1071).

‘He relies on absorption’ means: having entered absorption and then emerged from it. And ‘insight is tender’ should be connected. The body becomes fatigued because, with serenity and insight being tender, no superior distinction is attained in the development between what came before and what came after. Therefore it is said: ‘The mind is afflicted and distressed.’ Absorption is very beneficial for insight, for it was said: ‘Bhikkhus, develop concentration; one who is concentrated knows and sees things as they really are.’

Yathā vissamaṭṭhānaṃ yodhānaṃ parissamaṃ vinodeti, tathā parissamavinodanatthaṃ phalakehi kātabbaṃ vissamaṭṭhānaṃ phalakakoṭṭhako, samāpattiyā pana vipassanā bahukāratarā samādhiparipanthakānaṃ, sabbesampi vā kilesānaṃ vimathanena dubbalabhāvāpajjanato. Tenāha “vipassanā thāmajātā samāpattimpi rakkhati, thāmajātaṃ karotī”ti. Nanu cevaṃ itarītarasannissayadoso āpajjatīti? Nayidamekantikaṃ, itarītarasannissayāpi kiccasiddhi loke labbhatīti dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Just as a resting place relieves the exhaustion of warriors, so too, a resting place made of planks—a platform—is for dispelling exhaustion. But insight is far more beneficial than absorption because, by crushing the hindrances to concentration, or all the defilements, it leads to their weakening. Therefore it is said: ‘Insight, having become strong, protects even absorption and makes it strong.’ Now, does this not involve the fault of mutual dependence? This is not absolute, for to show that the accomplishment of a task through mutual dependence can be found in the world, the phrase ‘just as’ and so on is used.

Gāmantaṃ āhaṭesūti gāmasamīpaṃ upanītesu. Etāgāvoti sati uppādanamattameva kātabbaṃ yathā gāvo rakkhitabbā, tadabhāvato. Tadāti samathavipassanānaṃ thāmajātakāle. Anupassanānaṃ lahuṃ lahuṃ uppattiṃ sandhāya “ekappahāreneva āruḷhova hotī”ti vuttaṃ, kameneva pana anupassanāpaṭipāṭiṃ ārohati.

‘Brought near the village’ means brought close to the village. Regarding ‘these cows’: just as cows are to be guarded, so only the arising of mindfulness is to be brought about, because of its absence. ‘Then’ refers to the time when serenity and insight have gained strength. With reference to the rapid and repeated arising of the contemplations, it is said: ‘He ascends as if with a single strike.’ But it is in due order that he ascends the sequence of contemplations.

215. Evaṃ bhagavā attano appamādapaṭipadaṃ, tāya ca laddhaṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ visesaṃ dassento hetusampattiyā saddhiṃ phalasampattiṃ dassetvā idāni sattūpakārasampattiṃ dassetuṃ “seyyathāpī”tiādimāhāti evaṃ ettha anusandhi veditabbā. Araññalakkhaṇayoggamattena araññaṃ. Mahāvanatāya pavanaṃ. Pavaddhañhi vanaṃ pavanaṃ. Catūhi yogehīti jighacchāpipāsābhayapaṭipattisaṅkhātayogehi. Khemaṃ anupaddavataṃ. Suvatthiṃ anupaddavaṃ āvahatīti sovatthiko. Pītiṃ kuṭṭhiṃ gameti upanetīti pītigamanīyo. Pītaṃ pānatitthaṃ gacchatīti pītagamanīyo. Sākhādīhīti kaṇṭakasākhākaṇṭakalatāvanehi. Anāsayagāmitāya udakasanniruddhopi amaggo vutto, itarāni apītigamanīyatāyapi. Ādi-saddena gahanaṃ pariggaṇhāti. Okemigaluddakassa gocare caratīti okacaro, dīpakamigo. Araññe mige disvā tehi saddhiṃ palāyeyyāti dīgharajjubandhanaṃ.

215. Thus the Blessed One, having shown his own practice of diligence and the unique distinction attained through it, and having demonstrated the attainment of the fruit along with the attainment of the causal basis, now speaks the words 'Just as,' etc., in order to show the attainment of helpfulness to beings. In this way the connection here should be understood. 'Forest' (araññaṃ) is so called merely from its suitability for the characteristic of a forest. 'Great woodland' (pavanaṃ): because it is a great forest, for a flourishing forest is called a pavana. 'By four yokes' means by the yokes described as hunger, thirst, fear, and practice. 'Safety' means freedom from danger. 'Conducive to well-being' (sovatthiko): because it brings well-being, which is freedom from danger. 'Leading to joy' (pītigamanīyo): because it leads to, brings one to, joy. 'Leading to a drinking place' (pītagamanīyo): because one goes to a drinking place for a drink. 'By branches, etc.' means by thorny branches, thorny creepers, and thorny woods. Because it is not easy to traverse, even a path blocked by water is called a non-path; others, too, are so called because they are not conducive to drinking. By the word 'etc.,' a thicket is included. Okacaro: one that roams in the feeding ground of a hunter of okemi deer; this is the dīpaka deer. 'Binding with a long rope': lest, seeing other deer in the forest, it might flee along with them.

Idha vasantīti migānaṃ āsayaṃ vadati, tato āsayato iminā maggena nikkhamanti. Ettha [V 2.0068] carantīti etasmiṃ ṭhāne gocaraṃ gaṇhanti. Ettha pivantīti [M 2.0072] etasmiṃ nipānatitthe udakaṃ pivanti. Iminā maggena pavisantīti iminā maggena nipānatitthaṃ pavisanti. Maggaṃ pidhāyāti pakatimaggaṃ pidahitvā. Na tāva kiñci karoti anavasese vanamige ghātetukāmo.

'Here they dwell'—this refers to the abode of the deer; from that abode, they depart by this path. 'Here they roam'—this means they take their pasture in this place. 'Here they drink'—this means they drink water at this watering place. 'They enter by this path'—this means they enter the watering place by this path. 'Blocking the path'—this means having blocked the usual path. Not yet doing anything, he intends to kill all the forest deer without remainder.

Avijjāya aññāṇā hutvāti avijjāya nivutattā ñāṇarahitā hutvā, nandīrāgena upanītā rūpārammaṇādīni ābandhitvā. Palobhanato okacaraṃ nandīrāgoti. Byāmohanato okacārikaṃ avijjāti katvā dasseti. Tesanti okacarokacārikānaṃ. Sākhābhaṅgenāti tādisena lūkhataragandhena sākhābhaṅgena. Manussagandhaṃ apanetvā tassa sākhābhaṅgassa gandhena. Sammattoti sammajjito byāmuñcho.

'Being ignorant due to ignorance'—this means being devoid of knowledge due to being shrouded by ignorance, and, being led on by delight and lust, clinging to forms and other objects. Delight and lust is the 'roamer' (okacaraṃ) because of enticement. Ignorance is shown to be the 'female roamer' (okacārikaṃ) because of delusion. 'Of those'—this refers to the roamer and the female roamer. 'With a broken branch'—this means with such a broken branch that has a rougher scent. Removing the human scent with the scent of that broken branch. 'Swept'—this means well-swept and cleared.

Buddhānaṃ khemamaggavicaraṇaṃ kummaggapidhānañca sabbalokasādhāraṇampi atthato veneyyapuggalāpekkhamevāti dassento “aññātakoṇḍaññādīnaṃ bhabbapuggalāna”nti āha. Ūhatoti samūhato nīhatoti āha “dvedhā chetvā pātito”ti. Nāsitāti adassanaṃ gamitāti āha “sabbena sabbaṃ samugghāṭitā”ti. Hitūpacāranti sattānaṃ hitacariyaṃ.

Showing that the Buddhas' traversing of the safe path and blocking of the wrong path, though common to the whole world, are in reality dependent on persons to be trained, he said: 'for capable persons such as Aññātakoṇḍañña.' 'Uprooted'—this means removed from the group, brought out—thus it is said: 'cut in two and thrown down.' 'Destroyed'—this means caused to disappear—thus it is said: 'completely eradicated.' 'Beneficial conduct'—this means conduct for the benefit of beings.

Dvedhāvitakkasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Exposition Clarifying the Concealed Meaning in the Commentary on the Sutta on Two Kinds of Thought is concluded.

10. Vitakkasaṇṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Sutta on the Quelling of Thoughts

216. Dasakusalakammapathavasenāti [V 2.0069] idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ vaṭṭapādakasamāpatticittassapi idha adhicittabhāvena anicchitattā. Tenāha “vipassanāpādakaaṭṭhasamāpatticitta”nti. Atha vā anuttarimanussadhammasaṅgahitameva kevalaṃ “pakaticitta”nti vattabbanti dassento “dasakusalakammapathavasena uppannaṃ cittaṃ cittamevā”ti vatvā yadettha adhicittanti adhippetaṃ, taṃ tadeva dassento “vipassanāpādakaaṭṭhasamāpatticitta”nti āha. Itarassa panettha vidhi na paṭisedhetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vipassanāya sampayuttaṃ adhicittanti keci. Anuyuttenāti anuppannassa uppādanavasena, uppannassa paribrūhanavasena anu anu yuttena. Mūlakammaṭṭhānanti pārihāriyakammaṭṭhānaṃ. Gahetvā viharantoti bhāvanaṃ anuyuñjanto. Bhāvanāya appanaṃ appattopi adhicittamanuyuttoyeva tadatthepi taṃsaddavohārato.

216. 'By way of the ten wholesome courses of action': this should be seen as a mere indication, for even the mind of an attainment that is a basis for the round of rebirth is not intended here as the higher mind. Therefore he said: 'the mind of the eight attainments that are a basis for insight.' Alternatively, to show that only what is included in the supernormal human states should be called the 'natural mind,' having said, 'the mind that has arisen by way of the ten wholesome courses of action is just mind,' he then showed what is intended here as the 'higher mind' by saying: 'the mind of the eight attainments that are a basis for insight.' It should be seen that the method here does not preclude the other. Some say the 'higher mind' is that which is associated with insight. 'By one who is devoted': by one who is devoted again and again by way of generating what has not yet arisen and augmenting what has arisen. 'The root meditation subject': the preliminary meditation subject. 'Having undertaken it, he dwells': he applies himself to the development. Even one who has not reached absorption through the development is still one devoted to the higher mind, for that term is also used with that meaning.

Yehi [M 2.0073] phalaṃ nāma yathā uppajjanaṭṭhāne pakappiyamānaṃ viya hoti, tāni nimittāni. Tenāha “kāraṇānī”ti. Kālena kālanti ettha kālenāti bhummatthe karaṇavacananti āha “samaye samaye”ti. Nanu ca…pe… nirantaraṃ manasi kātabbanti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu ca bhāvanāya vīthipaṭipannattā abbudanīharaṇavidhiṃ dassentena bhagavatā “pañca nimittāni kālena kālaṃ manasi kātabbānī”ti ayaṃ desanā āraddhāti? “Adhicittamanuyuttenā”ti vuttattā avicchedavasena bhāvanāya yuttappayutto adhicittamanuyutto nāmāti codakassa adhippāyo. Itaro bhāvanaṃ anuyuñjantassaādikammikassa kadāci bhāvanupakkilesā uppajjeyyuṃ, tato cittassa visodhanatthāya yathākālaṃ imāni nimittāni manasi kātabbānīti “kālena kāla”nti satthā avocāti dassento “pāḷiyañhī”tiādimāha. Tattha imānīti imāni pāḷiyaṃ āgatāni pañca nimittāni. Abbudanti upaddavaṃ.

Those things by which a result is, as it were, fashioned in the place of its arising, are signs. Therefore he said, 'causes.' 'From time to time': here, 'by time' is an instrumental in the sense of the locative; thus he said, 'at times, at times.' But why was it said... 'should be attended to continuously'? Was not this teaching, 'five signs are to be attended to from time to time,' begun by the Blessed One to show the method for removing a spiritual tumor for one who has entered upon the path of development? Because it was said, 'by one devoted to the higher mind,' the questioner's intention is that one called 'devoted to the higher mind' is one who is properly engaged in the development without interruption. The other replies: For a beginner who is applying himself to the development, the defilements of meditation might sometimes arise. To show that the Teacher said 'from time to time' meaning that these signs are to be attended to at the proper time for the purpose of purifying the mind from them, he said, 'For in the Pāli...' and so on. Therein, 'these' means these five signs that have come down in the Pāli. 'A tumor' means a calamity.

Chandasahagatā rāgasampayuttāti taṇhāchandasahagatā kāmarāgasampayuttā. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhaasamapekkhitesūti iṭṭhesu piyesu, aniṭṭhesu appiyesu, asamaṃ asammā pekkhitesu. Asamapekkhananti gehassitaaññāṇupekkhāvasena ārammaṇassa ayoniso gahaṇaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā upekkhā bālassa mūḷhassa puthujjanassā”tiādi (ma. ni. 3.308). Te parivitakkā. Tato nimittato aññanti tato chandūpasaṃhitādiakusalavitakkuppattikāraṇato [V 2.0070] aññaṃ navaṃ nimittaṃ. “Manasikaroto”ti hi vuttaṃ, tasmā ārammaṇaṃ, tādiso purimuppanno cittappavattiākāro vā nimittaṃ. Kusalanissitaṃ nimittanti kusalacittappavattikāraṇaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ citte ṭhapetabbaṃ, bhāvanāvasena cintetabbaṃ, cittasantāne vā saṅkamitabbaṃ. Asubhañhi asubhanimittanti. Saṅkhāresu uppanne chandūpasaṃhite vitakketi ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Evaṃ “dosūpasañhite”tiādīsu yathārahaṃ taṃ taṃ padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Yattha katthacīti “sattesu saṅkhāresū”ti yattha katthaci. Pañcadhammūpanissayoti pañcavidho dhammūpasaṃhito upanissayo.

'Accompanied by desire, connected with lust': accompanied by desire that is craving, connected with sensual lust. 'In what is liked, disliked, or regarded improperly': in what is liked, i.e., agreeable; in what is disliked, i.e., disagreeable; in what is regarded unequally, i.e., improperly. 'Improperly regarding' is the unwise grasping of an object by way of the equanimity of ignorance based on the household life. In reference to which it was said: 'Having seen a form with the eye, there is the equanimity of a foolish, deluded ordinary person,' and so on (MN 152). Those are evil thoughts. 'Another sign than that sign': another, new sign than that cause for the arising of unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, etc. For it is said, 'of one who attends'; therefore the object is the sign, or such a previously arisen mode of the mind's process is the sign. 'A sign based on the wholesome': a cause for the process of a wholesome mind is to be attended to, to be established in the mind, to be reflected upon by way of development, or to be transferred into the mental continuum. For the foul is a foul sign. When a thought connected with desire has arisen in regard to formations, this should be brought in and connected. Similarly, in such cases as 'connected with hate,' the respective word should be brought in and connected as is suitable. 'Wherever': wherever, as in 'in regard to beings or formations.' 'With five things as proximate support': a fivefold proximate support connected with the Dhamma.

Evaṃ “chandūpasañhite”tiādinā saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “imassa hatthā vā sobhanā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha “asubhato [M 2.0074] upasaṃharitabba”nti vatvā upasaṃharaṇākārassa dassanaṃ “kimhi sārattosī”ti. Chavirāgenāti chavirāgatāya kāḷasāmādivaṇṇanibhāya. Kuphaḷapūritoti pakkehi kuṇapaphalehi puṇṇo. “Kaliphalapūrito”ti vā pāṭho.

Thus, to show in detail the meaning stated in brief with the words 'connected with desire,' etc., the passage beginning 'his hands are beautiful,' etc., was started. Therein, having said, 'one should advert to it as foul,' the way of adverting is shown with 'In what are you infatuated?' 'By lust for the skin': by lust for the skin's complexion, which has the appearance of such colors as dark, brown, etc. 'Filled with foul fruit': filled with ripe corpse-fruits. Or the reading is 'filled with the fruit of strife.'

Assāmikatāvakālikabhāvavasenāti idaṃ pattaṃ anukkamena vaṇṇavikārañceva jiṇṇabhāvañca patvā chiddāvachiddaṃ bhinnaṃ vā hutvā kapālaniṭṭhaṃ bhavissati. Idaṃ cīvaraṃ anupubbena vaṇṇavikāraṃ jiṇṇatañca upagantvā pādapuñchanacoḷakaṃ hutvā yaṭṭhikoṭiyā chaḍḍanīyaṃ bhavissati. Sace pana nesaṃ sāmiko bhaveyya, na nesaṃ evaṃ vinassituṃ dadeyyāti evaṃ assāmikabhāvavasena, “anaddhaniyaṃ idaṃ tāvakālika”nti evaṃ tāvakālikabhāvavasena ca manasikaroto.

By way of its ownerless and temporary nature: This bowl, gradually undergoing discoloration and decay, becoming cracked and broken, will end up as shards. This robe, in due course undergoing discoloration and decay, will become a foot-wiping rag fit to be thrown away with the tip of a stick. But if they had an owner, he would not let them be destroyed in this way. Thus one attends by way of their ownerless nature, and by way of their temporary nature, thinking, 'This is not lasting, it is temporary.'

Āghātavinaya…pe… bhāvetabbāti – “pañcime, bhikkhave, āghātapaṭivinayā. Yattha hi bhikkhuno uppanno āghāto sabbaso paṭivinetabbo”tiādinā nayena āgatassa āghātavinayasuttassa (a. ni. 5.161) ceva kakacūpamovāda(ma. ni. 1.222-233) chavālātūpamādīnañca (itivu. 91) vasena āghātaṃ paṭivinodetvā mettā bhāvetabbā.

'The removal of resentment... should be developed': By the method that comes in the Discourse on the Removal of Resentment (AN 5.161), which begins, 'Bhikkhus, there are these five ways for the removal of resentment. Wherever resentment has arisen in a bhikkhu, it should be entirely removed,' and so on, and by way of the Advice on the Simile of the Saw (MN 21), the Simile of the Firebrand (Iti 91), etc., having dispelled resentment, loving-kindness should be developed.

Garusaṃvāsoti garuṃ upanissāya vāso. Uddesoti pariyattidhammassa uddisāpanañceva uddisanañca. Uddiṭṭhaparipucchananti yathāuggahitassa dhammassa atthaparipucchā. Pañca dhammūpanissāyāti garusaṃvāsādike pañca dhamme paṭicca. Mohadhātūti moho.

'Living with a teacher' means living in dependence on a teacher. 'Recitation' means both causing the scriptural teaching to be recited and reciting it oneself. 'Questioning what has been recited' means inquiring into the meaning of the teaching as it has been learned. 'With five things as proximate support' means depending on the five things beginning with living with a teacher. 'The element of delusion' is delusion.

Upanissitabbāti upanissayitabbā, ayameva vā pāṭho. Yattappaṭiyattoti yatto ca gāmappavesanāpucchākaraṇesu ussukkaṃ āpanno sajjito ca hotīti attho. Athassa moho pahīyatīti [V 2.0071] assa bhikkhuno evaṃ tattha yuttappayuttassa pacchā so moho vigacchati. Evampīti evaṃ uddese appamajjanenapi. Puna evampīti atthaparipucchāya kaṅkhāvinodanepi. Tesu tesu ṭhānesu attho pākaṭo hotīti suyyamānassa dhammassa tesu tesu padesu “idha sīlaṃ kathitaṃ, idha samādhi, idha paññā”ti so so attho vibhūto hoti. Idaṃ cakkhurūpālokādi [M 2.0075] imassa cakkhuviññāṇassa kāraṇaṃ, idaṃ sālibījabhūmisalilādi imassa sāliaṅkurassa kāraṇaṃ. Idaṃ na kāraṇanti tadeva cakkhurūpālokādi sotaviññāṇassa, tadeva sālibījādi kudrusakaṅkurassa na kāraṇanti ṭhānāṭṭhānavinicchaye cheko hoti.

'Should be depended upon': should be relied upon; or this is the reading. 'Ready and prepared': the meaning is that he is diligent, having undertaken the effort in making inquiries when entering a village, and is prepared. 'Then his delusion is abandoned': for that bhikkhu who is thus properly engaged in that, that delusion later departs. 'Even thus': thus, even by non-negligence in recitation. 'Again, even thus': also by dispelling doubt through inquiry into the meaning. 'The meaning becomes manifest in those various places': in the various passages of the Dhamma that is being heard, the respective meaning becomes clear, as in 'here virtue is spoken of, here concentration, here wisdom.' This—eye, form, light, etc.—is the cause of this eye-consciousness; this—rice seed, earth, water, etc.—is the cause of this rice sprout. 'This is not the cause': that same eye, form, and light, etc., are not the cause of ear-consciousness; that same rice seed, etc., is not the cause of a kodo millet sprout. Thus he becomes skilled in discriminating between possible and impossible causes.

Ārammaṇesūti kammaṭṭhānesu. Ime vitakkāti kāmavitakkādayo. Sabbe kusalā dhammā sabbākusalapaṭipakkhāti katvā “pahīyantī”ti vattabbe na sabbe sabbesaṃ ujuvipaccanīkabhūtāti “pahīyanti evā”ti sāsaṅkaṃ vadati. Tenāha “imānī”tiādi.

'In the objects': in the meditation subjects. 'These thoughts': sensual thoughts and so on. Since all wholesome states are the counterpart to all unwholesome states, when it should be said 'they are abandoned,' because not all are directly opposed to all, he speaks with reservation, 'they are indeed abandoned.' Therefore he said, 'these,' and so on.

Kusalanissitanti kusalena nissitaṃ nissayitabbaṃ. Kusalassa paccayabhūtanti tasseva vevacanaṃ, kusaluppattikāraṇaṃ yathāvuttaasubhanimittādimeva vadati. Sāraphalaketi candanamaye sāraphalake. Visamāṇinti visamākārena tattha ṭhitaṃ āṇiṃ. Haneyyāti pahareyya nikkhāmeyya.

'Based on the wholesome' means based on the wholesome, what is to be relied upon. 'Being a condition for the wholesome' is a synonym for that; it refers to the very cause for the arising of the wholesome, such as the aforesaid sign of foulness and so on. 'In a heartwood plank': in a sandalwood plank. 'An uneven peg': a peg fixed there unevenly. 'He would strike': he would strike, he would drive it out.

217. Aṭṭoti āturo, duggandhabādhatāya pīḷito. Dukkhitoti sañjātadukkho. Imināpi kāraṇenāti akosallasambhūtatāya kusalapaṭipakkhatāya gehassitarogena sarogatāya ca ete akusalā viññugarahitabbatāya jigucchanīyatāya ca sāvajjā aniṭṭhaphalatāya nirassādasaṃvattaniyatāya ca dukkhavipākāti evaṃ tena tena kāraṇena akusalādibhāvaṃ upaparikkhato.

217. 'Distressed': afflicted, oppressed by the affliction of a bad smell. 'Pained': one in whom suffering has arisen. 'By this reason too': of one who examines their nature as unwholesome, etc., for this and that reason—because of their origin in unskillfulness, their being the counterpart to the wholesome, and their being diseased with the household-life disease, these unwholesome states are blameworthy, since they are to be censured by the wise and are disgusting; and they have a painful result, since they have an undesirable fruit and lead to what is without taste.

“Āturaṃ asuciṃ pūtiṃ, passa nande samussayaṃ;

Uggharantaṃ paggharantaṃ, bālānaṃ abhinandita”nti. (apa. therī 2.4.157) –

See, Nanda, this ailing, impure, putrid body, oozing and trickling, delighted in by fools.

Evamādi kāyavicchandanīyakathādīhi vā. Ādi-saddena –

Or by such things as discourses that inspire revulsion towards the body. By the word 'etc.' is included:

“Tasseva tena pāpiyo, yo kuddhaṃ paṭikujjhati;

Kuddhaṃ appaṭikujjhanto, saṅgāmaṃ jeti dujjaya”nti. (theragā. 442) –

He who gets angry back at an angry person is thereby the worse of the two; one who does not get angry back at an angry person wins a battle hard to win.

Evamādi paṭighavūpasamanakathādikāpi saṅgaṇhāti.

Thus, it also includes discussions on the pacification of aversion and the like.

218. Na [V 2.0072] saraṇaṃ asati, ananussaraṇaṃ. Amanasikaraṇaṃ amanasikāro. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā nisīditabbanti kammaṭṭhānamanasikāreneva nisīditabbaṃ. Uggahito dhammakathāpabandhoti kammaṭṭhānassa upakāro dhammakathāpabandho. Muṭṭhipotthakoti muṭṭhippamāṇo pārihāriyapotthako. Samannānentenāti [M 2.0076] samannāharantena. Okāso na hoti āraddhassa pariyosāpetabbato. Āraddhassa antagamanaṃ anārambhovāti theravādo. Tassāti upajjhāyassa. Pabbhārasodhanaṃ kāyakammaṃ, ārabhanto eva vitakkaniggaṇhanatthaṃ saṃyuttanikāyasajjhāyanaṃ vacīkammaṃ, dassanakiccapubbakammakaraṇatthaṃ tejokasiṇaparikammanti tīṇi kammāni ācinoti. Thero tassa āsayaṃ kasiṇañca savisesaṃ jānitvā “imasmiṃ vihāre”tiādimavoca. Tenassa yathādhippāyaṃ sabbaṃ sampāditaṃ. Asatipabbaṃ nāma asatiyā vitakkaniggahaṇavibhāvanato.

218. Unmindfulness is not remembering, non-recollection. Non-attention is inattention. Having taken up a meditation subject, one should sit down attending only to that meditation subject. A memorized discourse on the Dhamma is a discourse that is helpful for the meditation subject. A fist-book is a portable book the size of a fist. 'By one who brings it to mind' means by one who collects it. There is no opportunity for anything else, as what has been undertaken must be brought to completion. The Theravāda view is that the way to complete what has been started is not to start anything else. 'His' refers to the preceptor. Cleaning the overhanging rock is a bodily action; beginning the recitation of the Saṃyutta Nikāya to suppress thoughts is a verbal action; and doing the preliminary work on the fire kasiṇa to perform the preliminary task for the act of seeing—he undertakes these three actions. The elder, knowing his disposition and the kasiṇa with its special qualities, said, 'In this monastery,' and so on. Thus everything was accomplished for him according to his intention. The section on unmindfulness is so called because it explains the suppression of thoughts arising from unmindfulness.

219. Vitakkamūlabhedaṃ pabbanti vitakkamūlassa tammūlassa ca bhedavibhāvanaṃ vitakkamūlabhedaṃ pabbaṃ. Vitakkaṃ saṅkharotīti vitakkasaṅkhāro, vitakkapaccayo subhanimittādīsupi subhādinā ayonisomanasikāro. So pana vitakkasaṅkhāro saṃtiṭṭhati etthāti vitakkasaṅkhārasaṇṭhānaṃ, asubhe subhantiādi saññāvipallāso. Tenāha “vitakkānaṃ mūlañca mūlamūlañca manasi kātabba”nti. Vitakkānaṃ mūlamūlaṃ gacchantassāti upaparikkhanavasena micchāvitakkānaṃ mūlaṃ uppattikāraṇaṃ ñāṇagatiyā gacchantassa. Yāthāvato jānantassa pubbe viya vitakkā abhiṇhaṃ nappavattantīti āha “vitakkacāro sithilo hotī”ti. Tasmiṃ sithilībhūte matthakaṃ gacchanteti vuttanayena vitakkacāro sithilabhūto, tasmiṃ vitakkānaṃ mūlagamane anukkamena thirabhāvappattiyā matthakaṃ gacchante. Vitakkā sabbaso nirujjhantīti micchāvitakkā sabbepi gacchanti na samudācaranti, bhāvanāpāripūriyā vā anavasesā pahīyanti.

219. 'The section on breaking the root of thought' is the explanation of the breaking of the root of thought and the root of that root. 'What fabricates thought' is a thought-fabrication; the condition for thought is unwise attention to the beautiful, etc., in regard to beautiful signs, etc. The settling down of thought-fabrication is where that thought-fabrication settles down; it is the distortion of perception, such as perceiving the unattractive as attractive. Therefore it is said: 'The root of thoughts and the root of the root should be attended to.' 'For one who goes to the root of the root of thoughts' means for one who, by way of investigation, goes by the path of knowledge to the root, the cause of arising, of wrong thoughts. For one who knows as it really is, thoughts do not occur as frequently as before; thus it is said: 'The course of thought becomes slack.' When it has become slack, it reaches its culmination. The course of thought has become slack in the manner described; when, in going to the root of thoughts, it gradually attains firmness and reaches its culmination, then thoughts cease entirely. This means all wrong thoughts cease and no longer arise, or through the perfection of cultivation, they are abandoned without remainder.

Kaṇṇamūle patitanti sasakassa kaṇṇasamīpe kaṇṇasakkhaliṃ paharantaṃ viya upapatitaṃ. Tassa kira sasakassa heṭṭhā mahāmūsikāhi khatamahāvāṭaṃ umaṅgasadisaṃ ahosi, tenassa pātena mahāsaddo ahosi. Palāyiṃsu “pathavī udrīyatī”ti. Mūlamūlaṃ gantvā anuvijjeyyanti “pathavī bhijjatī”ti yatthāyaṃ saso uṭṭhito, tattha gantvā tassa mūlakāraṇaṃ yaṃnūna vīmaṃseyyaṃ. Pathaviyā bhijjanaṭṭhānaṃ gate “ko jānāti, kiṃ bhavissatī”ti saso “na sakkomi sāmī”ti āha. Ādhipaccavato hi yācanaṃ saṇhamudukaṃ. Duddubhāyatīti duddubhāti saddaṃ karoti. Anuravadassanañhetaṃ. Bhaddanteti migarājassa piyasamudācāro, migarāja, bhaddaṃ te atthūti attho. Kimetanti kiṃ etaṃ, kiṃ tassa mūlakāraṇaṃ? Duddubhanti idampi tassa anuravadassanameva. Evanti yathā sasakassa mahāpathavībhedanaṃ ravanāya [V 2.0073] micchāgāhasamuṭṭhānaṃ [M 2.0077] amūlaṃ, evaṃ vitakkacāropi saññāvipallāsasamuṭṭhāno amūlo. Tenāha “vitakkāna”ntiādi.

'It fell at the base of the ear' means it fell near the hare's ear as if striking its ear-lobe. It is said that below that hare there was a large pit resembling a tunnel, which had been dug by large rats; because of its fall, a great sound arose. They fled, thinking, 'The earth is splitting apart!' 'Let me go to the very root and investigate' means: 'Let me go to the place where this hare arose, thinking, "The earth is splitting," and investigate its root cause.' When it came to going to the place where the earth was splitting, the hare said, 'Who knows what will happen? I cannot, master.' For a sovereign's request is subtle and gentle. 'It makes a "dud-dubha" sound' means it makes a thudding sound. This is perceiving it as a reverberating sound. 'Venerable sir' is an affectionate address to the king of beasts; the meaning is, 'King of beasts, may it be well with you.' 'What is this?' means: 'What is this? What is its root cause?' 'A thudding sound'—this too is perceiving it as a reverberating sound. Thus, just as the hare's notion of the great earth splitting, which arose from a wrong grasp due to the sound, was baseless, so too the course of thought, which arises from the distortion of perception, is baseless. Therefore it is said, 'Of thoughts…,' and so on.
