220. Abhidantanti abhibhavanadantaṃ, uparidantanti attho. Tenāha “uparidanta”nti. So hi itaraṃ musalaṃ viya udukkhalaṃ visesato kassaci khādanakāle abhibhuyya vattati. Kusalacittenāti balavasammāsaṅkappasampayuttena. Akusalacittanti kāmavitakkādisahitaṃ akusalacittaṃ. Abhiniggaṇhitabbanti yathā tassa āyatiṃ samudācāro na hoti, evaṃ abhibhavitvā niggahetabbaṃ, anuppattidhammatā āpādetabbāti attho. Ke ca tumhe satipi cirakālabhāvanāya evaṃ adubbalā ko cāhaṃ mama santike laddhappatiṭṭhe viya ṭhitepi idāneva appatiṭṭhe karonto iti evaṃ abhibhavitvā. Taṃ pana abhibhavanākāraṃ dassento “kāmaṃ taco cā”tiādinā caturaṅgasamannāgatavīriyapaggaṇhanamāha. Atthadīpikanti ekantato vitakkaniggaṇhanatthajotakaṃ. Upamanti “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, balavā puriso”tiādikaṃ upamaṃ.

220. 'The over-tooth' means the overcoming tooth, that is, the upper tooth. Therefore it is said, 'the upper tooth.' For it prevails over the other, like a pestle over a mortar, especially when chewing something. 'With a wholesome mind' means with a mind associated with strong right resolve. 'An unwholesome mind' means an unwholesome mind accompanied by sensual thoughts and the like. 'Should be suppressed' means it should be overpowered and restrained so that it does not arise in the future; the meaning is that the state of non-arising should be brought about for it. One should overpower it thus: 'Who are you to be so strong, even after my long cultivation, and who am I? Though you stand as if established in my presence, I will now make you unestablished.' To show this way of overpowering, he speaks of undertaking the four-factored energy with the words, 'Willingly, let the skin…' and so on. 'The Lamp of Meaning' is what exclusively illuminates the meaning of the suppression of thoughts. 'The simile' is the simile beginning, 'Suppose, bhikkhus, a strong man…'

221. Pariyādānabhājanīyanti yaṃ taṃ ādito “adhicittamanuyuttena bhikkhunā pañca nimittāni kālena kālaṃ manasi kātabbānī”ti niddiṭṭhaṃ, tattha tassa nimittassa manasikaraṇakālapariyādānassa vasena vibhajanaṃ. Nigamanaṃ vā etaṃ, yadidaṃ “yato kho, bhikkhave”tiādi. Yathāvuttassa hi atthassa puna vacanaṃ nigamananti. Tathāpaṭipannassa vā vasībhāvavisuddhidassanatthaṃ “yato kho, bhikkhave”tiādi vuttaṃ. Satthācariyoti dhanubbedācariyo. Yathā hi sasanato asatthampi satthaggahaṇeneva saṅgayhati, evaṃ dhanusippampi dhanubbedapariyāpannamevāti.

221. 'The exposition on mastery' is the classification based on the mastery of the timing for attending to a given sign, with reference to what was pointed out at the beginning: 'A bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind should from time to time attend to five signs.' Or this is the conclusion, namely, the passage beginning, 'When, bhikkhus…' For a conclusion is a restatement of the meaning already expressed. Alternatively, the passage beginning, 'When, bhikkhus…' was stated to show the purity of the state of mastery for one who has practiced accordingly. 'A teacher of the art' is a teacher of the science of archery. For just as one who is unskilled is included simply by taking up the art, so too the craft of the bow is included within the science of archery.

Pariyāyati parivitakketīti pariyāyo. Vāroti āha “vitakkavārapathesū”ti, vitakkānaṃ vārena pavattanamaggesu. Ciṇṇavasīti āsevitavasī. Paguṇavasīti subhāvitavasī. Sammāvitakkaṃyeva yathicchitaṃ tathāvitakkanato, itarassa panassa setughātoyevāti.

'A way' (pariyāya) is so called because one reflects (parivitakketi) on it. 'Sequence' (vāra): he says 'in the paths of the sequences of thoughts,' that is, in the paths along which thoughts proceed in sequence. 'Mastery through practice' (ciṇṇavasī) is mastery through habituation. 'Mastery through proficiency' (paguṇavasī) is mastery through good cultivation. This is because one can think a right thought just as one wishes, while for the other kind of thought, it is simply the destruction of its causeway.

Vitakkasaṇṭhānasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

Here ends the Elucidation of the Concealed Meaning of the Commentary on the Discourse on the Settling of Thoughts.

Niṭṭhitā ca sīhanādavaggavaṇṇanā.

The commentary on the Chapter of the Lion's Roar is completed.

3. Opammavaggo

3. The Chapter on Similes

1. Kakacūpamasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Kakacūpama Sutta

222. Moḷinti [M 2.0078][V 2.0074] kesaracanaṃ. Vehāyasanti ākāse. Ratanacaṅkoṭavarenāti ratanasilāmayavaracaṅkoṭakena sahassanetto sirasā paṭiggahi. “Suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭakavarenā”tipi (bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 23 dūrenidānakathā; jā. aṭṭha. 1.2 avidūrenidānakathā) pāṭho.

222. `Moḷi` means a hair-crest. `Vehāyasaṃ` means in the sky. `Ratanacaṅkoṭavarena` means: with a superior jeweled casket, the thousand-eyed one received it on his head. There is also a reading: 'with a superior golden casket' (see Bu.A. 23, Dūrenidānakathā; Jā.A. 1.2, Avidūrenidānakathā).

Sāti moḷi. Moḷi etassa atthīti moḷiko, moḷiko eva moḷiyo. Phaggunoti pana nāmaṃ. Saṅkhāti samaññā. Velīyati khaṇamuhuttādivasena upadisīyatīti velā, kāloti āha “tāyaṃ velāyaṃ…pe… ayaṃ kālavelā nāmā”ti. Velayati paricchedavasena tiṭṭhatīti velā, sīmā. Velayati saṃkilesapakkhaṃ cālayatīti velā, sīlaṃ. Anatikkamanaṭṭhopi cassa saṃkilesadhammanimittaṃ acalanameva. Viññupurisābhāve chapañcavācāmattaṃ ovāde pamāṇaṃ nāma. Davasahagataṃ katvāti kīḷāsahitaṃ katvā.

`Sāti` is a crest. `Moḷiko` means one who has a crest; `moḷiyo` is simply `moḷiko`. `Phagguna`, however, is a name. `Saṅkhā` means a designation. `Velā` means time, as it is indicated by moments and instants, as it is said: 'at that time... this is called that time.' `Velā` means boundary, as it stands by way of delimitation. `Velā` means virtue (sīla), as it shakes off the side of defilements. And its characteristic of non-transgression is precisely its immovability in regard to signs of defiling qualities. In the absence of wise persons, a mere five or six words is the measure of advice. `Davasahagataṃ katvā` means having made it accompanied by play.

Missībhūtoti ananulomikasaṃsaggavasena missībhūto. “Avaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī”ti saṅkhepato vuttaṃ vivarituṃ “tāpanapacanakoṭṭanādīnī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Adhikaraṇampi karotīti ettha yathā so adhikaraṇāya parisakkati, taṃdassanaṃ “imesaṃ bhikkhūna”ntiādi. Adhikaraṇaṃ ākaḍḍhatīti adhikaraṇaṃ uddissa te bhikkhū ākaḍḍhati, adhikaraṇaṃ vā tesu uppādento ākaḍḍhati. Uddesapadaṃ vāti padaso uddesamattaṃ vā. Neva piyakamyatāyāti neva attani satthuno piyabhāvakāmatāya. Na bhedādhippāyenāti na satthuno tena bhikkhunā bhedādhippāyena. Atthakāmatāyāti moḷiyaphaggunassa hitakāmatāya.

'Mixed' means being mixed due to inappropriate association. 'He speaks dispraise' is stated briefly; to elaborate, 'tormenting, roasting, pounding,' etc., is said. 'He creates a dispute'—here, the phrase 'these monks,' etc., shows how he strives for a dispute. 'He drags into a dispute' means he drags those monks into a dispute, or, producing a dispute among them, he drags them in. 'Or merely recites the passage' means merely reciting the passage word by word. 'Not out of affection' means not out of a desire for the teacher to be dear to oneself. 'Not with the intention of causing schism' means not with the intention of causing division between the teacher and that monk. 'Out of goodwill' means out of a desire for Moliya Phagguna’s welfare.

224. Avaṇṇabhāsaneti [V 2.0075] bhikkhunīnaṃ aguṇakathane. Chandādīnaṃ vatthubhāvato kāmaguṇā gehaṃ viya gehaṃ, te ca te sitā nissitāti gehassitāti vuttā. Taṇhāchandāpi tāsaṃ kattukāmatāpīti ubhayepi taṇhāchandā, paṭighachandā pana tesaṃ kattukāmatā eva. Phalikamaṇi viya pakatipabhassarassa cittasantānassa upasaṅgo viya vipariṇāmakāraṇaṃ rāgādayoti āha “rattampi cittaṃ vipariṇata”ntiādi. Hitānukampīti [M 2.0079] karuṇāya paccupaṭṭhāpanamāha. “Yassantarato na santi kopā”tiādīsu (udā. 20) viya antara-saddo cittapariyāyoti āha “dosantaroti dosacitto”ti.

224. 'Speaking dispraise' refers to speaking of the nuns’ faults. Because desire and so on are their basis, sensual pleasures are a house, like a home; and because they are dependent on and resort to them, they are called 'house-dependent.' Both craving and the desire to act on it are 'craving and desire' (taṇhāchanda); but desire associated with aversion (paṭighachanda) is only the desire to act on it. Lust and so on are a cause of transformation, like an impurity for the stream of consciousness which is naturally radiant like a crystal gem; hence it is said, 'the mind, even when passionate, is transformed,' etc. 'Compassionate for their welfare' refers to the manifestation of compassion. Just as in 'within whom there is no anger' (Udāna 20), the word 'within' (antara) is a synonym for mind; hence it is said, 'one with anger within (dosantaro) is an angry-minded one (dosacitto).'

225. Dubbacatāya ovādaṃ asampaṭicchanto citteneva paṭiviruddho aṭṭhāsi. Gaṇhiṃsu cittaṃ, hadayagāhiniṃ paṭipajjiṃsūti attho. Pūrayiṃsu ajjhāsayanti attho. Ekasmiṃ samaye paṭhamabodhiyaṃ. Ekāsanaṃ bhojanassa ekāsanabhojanaṃ, ekavelāyameva bhojanaṃ. Tañca kho pubbaṇhe evāti āha “ekaṃ purebhattabhojana”ntiādi. Sattakkhattuṃ bhuttabhojanampi imasmiṃ sutte ekāsanabhojananteva adhippetaṃ, na ekāsanikatāya ekāya eva nisajjāya bhojanaṃ. “Appaḍaṃsa…pe… samphassa”ntiādīsu viya appa-saddo abhāvatthoti āha “nirābādhataṃ, niddukkhata”nti. Padhānādivasena sallahukaṃ akicchaṃ uṭṭhānaṃ sallahukauṭṭhānaṃ. Na ekappahārenāti na ekavārena, na ekasmiṃyeva kāleti adhippāyo. Dve bhojanānīti “aparaṇhe rattiya”nti kālavasena dve bhojanāni. Pañca guṇeti appābādhādike pañca ānisaṃse. Satuppādakaraṇīyamattamevāti satuppādamattakaraṇīyameva, nivāretabbassa punappunaṃ samādapanañca nāhosi.

225. Due to stubbornness, not accepting the advice, he remained mentally opposed. They grasped his mind means they undertook a heart-captivating practice. They fulfilled their inclination means they satisfied their intent. At one time, at the first awakening. Ekāsanaṃ bhojanaṃ means eating once, at one time. And that too in the morning, hence it is said, "one meal before noon," etc. Even eating seven times is intended in this sutta as one meal, not eating in a single sitting as per the one-session practice. Just as in "free from gadflies… contact," etc., the word appa- denotes absence, hence it is said, "freedom from affliction, freedom from suffering." Sallahukauṭṭhānaṃ means a light and effortless arising. Not at one stroke means not at once, not just at one time. Two meals means two meals in terms of time: "in the afternoon and at night." Five benefits refers to the five advantages, such as being free from affliction, etc. Only enough to arouse mindfulness means only doing what is necessary to arouse mindfulness; and there was no repeated undertaking to restrain what should be restrained.

Maṇḍabhūmīti ojavantabhūmi, yattha parisiñcanena vinā sassāni kiṭṭhāni sampajjanti. Yuge yojetabbāni yoggāni, tesaṃ ācariyo yoggācariyo, tesaṃ sikkhāpanako. Gāmaṇihatthiādayopi “yoggā”ti vuccantīti āha pāḷiyaṃ “assadammasārathī”ti. Catūsu maggesu yena yena maggena icchati. Javasamagādibhedāsu gatīsu yaṃ yaṃ gatiṃ. Taṃ taṃ maggaṃ āruḷhāva otiṇṇāyeva. Neva vāretabbā rasmiviniggaṇhanena. Na vijjhitabbā patodalaṭṭhiyā. Gamanamevāti ime yuttā mama icchānurūpaṃ mandaṃ gacchanti, samaṃ gacchanti, sīghaṃ gacchantīti khuresu nimittaggahaṇaṃ paṭṭhapetvā sārathinā tesaṃ gamanameva passitabbaṃ hoti, na tattha niyojanaṃ[V 2.0076]. Tehipi bhikkhūhi. Pajahiṃsu pajahitabbaṃ. Sāladūsanāti sālarukkhavisanāsakā. Aññā ca valliyo sālarukkhe vinandhitvā ṭhitā. Bahi nīharaṇenāti sālavanato bahi chaḍḍanena. Susaṇṭhitāti saṇṭhānasampannā, mariyādaṃ [M 2.0080] bandhitvāti ālavālasampādanavasena mariyādaṃ bandhitvā. Kipillapuṭakaṃ tambakipillakapuṭakaṃ. Sukkhadaṇḍakaharaṇaṃ ālavālabbhantarā.

Maṇḍabhūmi means a fertile land, a land full of essence, where crops thrive without irrigation. Those to be yoked to a yoke are called yoggāni; their teacher is the yoggācariya, their instructor. Even elephants of a headman and so on are called yoggā, as it is said in the text: "horse-tamer, charioteer." On the four paths, by whichever path one desires. Among the various speeds like quick and even, whichever speed—having mounted that very path, they are indeed going along. They should not be restrained by pulling the reins. They should not be struck with the goad. Only the going—thus, these yoked ones go as I wish: slowly, evenly, swiftly—having established the observation of signs in the hooves, the charioteer should see only their movement, not the controlling there. By those monks too. They abandoned what should be abandoned. Sāladūsana means the destroyers of Sal trees. And other creepers that have entwined and stand on the Sal trees. By taking outside means by discarding them outside the Sal grove. Well-established means endowed with good structure; having fixed boundaries means by fixing boundaries in the way of preparing water-basins around the trees. Kipillapuṭakaṃ means the pouch of red ants. Sukkhadaṇḍakaharaṇaṃ, the removal of dry sticks, means from within the water basin.

226. Videharaṭṭhe jātasaṃvaḍḍhatāya vedehikā. Paṇḍā vuccati paññā, tāya itā gatā pavattāti paṇḍitā. Gahapatānīti gehasāminī. Soraccenāti saṃyamena. Nivātavuttīti paṇipātakārī. Nibbutāti nibbutaduccaritapariḷāhā. Uṭṭhāhikāti uṭṭhānavīriyavatī. Kibbisāti kurūrā.

226. She was born and raised in the Videha country, hence she is called Videhikā. Paṇḍā is called wisdom; one who has gone and proceeds by it is called paṇḍitā (wise). Gahapatānī means the female householder. Soraccena means with gentleness. Nivātavuttī means one who is of humble conduct. Nibbutā means one whose torment and the fever of misconduct are extinguished. Uṭṭhāhikā means energetic and persevering. Kibbisā means cruel.

227. Evaṃ akkhantiyā dosaṃ dassetvāti “guṇavanto”ti loke patthaṭakittisaddānampi akkhantinimittaṃ ayasuppattiguṇaparihāniādiṃ akkhamatāyaādīnavaṃ pakāsetvā. Vacanapatheti vacanamagge yuttakālādike. Saṇhābhāvopi hi vacanassa pavattiākāroti katvā “vacanapatho” tveva vutto. Tesaṃyeva kālādīnaṃ. Mettā etassa atthīti mettaṃ, uppannaṃ mettacittaṃ etesanti uppannamettacittā. Puna “kālena vā, bhikkhave”tiādi (pari. 362, 363) pāḷi dhammasabhāvadassanavasena pavattā “paraṃ codanāvasena vadantā nāma imehi ākārehi vadantī”ti. Adhimuñcitvāti abhirativasena tasmiṃ puggale bhāvanācittaṃ muñcitvā vissajjetvā. So puggalo ārammaṇaṃ etassāti tadārammaṇaṃ, mettacittaṃ. Yadi evaṃ padesavisayaṃ taṃ kathaṃ nippadesavisayaṃ viya hotīti codento “kathaṃ tadārammaṇaṃ sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ karotī”ti āha, itaro “pañca vacanapathe”tiādinā pariharati. Idha tadārammaṇañcāti tasseva mettacittassa ārammaṇaṃ katvāti pāḷiyaṃ vacanaseso daṭṭhabbo. Tenāha “puna tassevā”tiādi. Sabbā sattakāyasaṅkhātā pajā etassa atthīti sabbāvantoti imamatthaṃ dassento “sabbāvanta”nti āha. Vipulenāti mahājanārammaṇena. Mahantapariyāyo hi vipula-saddo, mahattañcettha bahukabhāvo. Tenāha “anekasattārammaṇenā”ti. Tañca puggalanti pañca vacanapathe gahetvā āgatapuggalaṃ. Cittassāti mettāsahagatacittassa. Ettha ca mettāsahagatena cetasā viharissāmāti sambandho. Tattha kathanti āha “tañca puggalaṃ sabbañca lokaṃ tassa cittassa ārammaṇaṃ katvā adhimuccitvā”ti.

227. 'Having thus shown the fault of impatience' means having explained the danger of the inability to endure—such as the arising of disgrace and the decline of virtues on account of impatience—even for those whose fame is spread in the world as 'virtuous'. Vacanapatha means the path of speech, such as the appropriate time and so on. And because gentleness is indeed the manner of speech's occurrence, it is called "path of speech." Of these very factors—time and so on. Mettā means loving-kindness, as it is present in this (mind); those in whom a mind of loving-kindness has arisen are called "those with an arisen mind of loving-kindness." Again, the passage beginning with "At the right time, O monks..." (Pār. 362, 363) is spoken according to the nature of the Dhamma, showing that "those who speak by way of admonishing others indeed speak in these ways." Adhimuñcitvā means having released and directed the meditative mind toward that person with delight. That person becomes the object (ārammaṇa) for it—thus, it is called "having that as its object" (tadārammaṇa), the mind of loving-kindness. If this is so, how does that limited scope become like an unlimited scope? Raising this objection, he says, "How does that object encompass the entire world?" The other explains it with the passage beginning, "the five paths of speech..." Here, "having that as its object" means making that very mind of loving-kindness the object—the remainder of the statement in the text should be understood. Hence, he says, "Again, regarding that very..." Sabbāvanta means "all-encompassing," showing this meaning that all beings, counted as groups of beings, pertain to it. Vipulena means by way of a great multitude as object. For the term "vast" (vipula) signifies a great extent, and here its greatness is a state of abundance. Thus, he says, "having numerous beings as its object." And that person refers to the individual who has been brought into the discussion by way of the five paths of speech. Of the mind means of the mind accompanied by loving-kindness. Here, the connection is: "I will dwell with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness." There, "how?" he explains: "Having resolved upon that person and the entire world as the object of that mind."

228. Tadatthadīpikanti [V 2.0077][M 2.0081] yā mettaṃ cetovimuttiṃ sammadeva bhāvetvā ṭhitassa nibbikārato kenaci vikāraṃ na āpādetabbatā, tadatthajotikaṃ. Apathavinti pathavī na hotīti apathavī. Nippathavinti sabbena sabbaṃ pathavībhāvābhāvaṃ. Tiriyaṃ pana aparicchinnāti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu cakkavāḷapabbatehi taṃ taṃ cakkavāḷaṃ paricchindati? Na, tadaññacakkavāḷapathaviyā ekābaddhabhāvato. Tiṇṇañhi cakkānaṃ antarasadise tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ lokadhātūnaṃ antareyeva pathavī natthi lokantaranirayabhāvato. Cakkavāḷapabbatantarehi sambaddhaṭṭhāne pathavī ekābaddhāva. Vivaṭṭakāle hi saṇṭhahamānāpi pathavī yathāsaṇṭhitapathaviyā ekābaddhāva saṇṭhahati. Tenāha “tiriyaṃ pana aparicchinnā”ti. Imināva gambhīrabhāvena vuttaparimāṇato paraṃ natthīti dīpitaṃ hoti.

228. Tadatthadīpikaṃ means that which illuminates its meaning: the fact that one who abides having properly developed the liberation of mind through loving-kindness cannot be made to alter by anyone, due to his unalterable state. 'Apathavī' means 'not earth,' that is, earth does not exist. 'Nippathavī' means the complete absence of earth-nature. But why is it said 'tiriyaṃ pana aparicchinnā' (unbounded horizontally)? Doesn’t Mount Cakkavāḷa define each world-system? No, because the earth of other world-systems is of an interconnected nature. Indeed, in the space resembling the interval between three wheels, in the interval between three world-systems, there is no earth, due to the existence of the Lokantarika hell. In the places connected by the intervals of the Cakkavāḷa mountains, the earth is indeed interconnected. Even when the earth is settling down during the period of re-evolution, it settles down interconnected with the earth that has already settled. Hence, it is said, 'tiriyaṃ pana aparicchinnā' (unbounded horizontally). By this very profound nature, it is indicated that there is nothing beyond the stated measure.

229. Haliddīti haliddivaṇṇaṃ adhippetanti āha “yaṃ kiñci pītakavaṇṇa”nti. Vaṇṇasaṅkhātaṃ rūpaṃ assa atthīti rūpī, na rūpīti arūpīti āha “arūpo”ti. Tenevāha “sanidassanabhāvapaṭikkhepato”ti.

229. "Haliddī" means intending the color of turmeric, hence he said, "whatever is of yellow color." That which has form, in the sense of color, is 'rūpī' (material); that which is not 'rūpī' is 'arūpī' (immaterial). Thus he said, 'arūpo' (immaterial). Therefore, he said, 'from the rejection of the nature of being visible.'

230. Pañca yojanasatānīti himavantato samuddaṃ paviṭṭhaṭṭhānavasena vuttaṃ, na anotattadahamukhato. Aññā nadiyo upādāya labbhamānaṃ gambhīrataṃ appameyyaudakatañca gahetvā “gambhīrā appameyyā”ti vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana tiṇukkāya tāpetabbattābhāvadassanaparametanti vuttaṃ “etena payogenā”tiādi.

230. "Five hundred yojanas" is said based on the point where the river enters the ocean from the Himalayas, not from the mouth of Lake Anotatta. Taking other rivers as a basis, and considering the depth that can be obtained and the immeasurable water, it is said to be 'deep and immeasurable.' In the commentary, however, it is said that this has the ultimate purpose of showing that it cannot be heated even with a grass torch, hence the phrase 'with this explanation,' etc.

231. Tūlinī viya tūlinīti āha “simbalitūlalatātūlasamānā”ti. Sassaranti evaṃpavatto saddo sassarasaddo. Anuravadassanañhetaṃ. Tathā bhabbharasaddo. Sabbametaṃ mettāvihārino cittassa dūsetuṃ asakkuṇeyyabhāvadassanaparaṃ. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – yathā mahāpathavī kenaci purisena apathaviṃ kātuṃ na sakkā, yathā ākāse kiñci rūpaṃ paṭṭhapetuṃ na sakkā, yathā gaṅgāya udakaṃ tiṇukkāya tāpetuṃ na sakkā, yathā ca biḷārabhastaṃ thaddhaṃ pharusañca samphassaṃ kātuṃ na sakkā, evamevaṃ mettāya cetovimuttiyā āsevitāya bhāvitāya bahulīkatāya pañca vacanapathe gahetvā āgatapurisena kenaci pariyāyena cittassa aññathattaṃ kātuṃ na sakkāti.

231. "Like cotton, like cotton," he says, "similar to silk-cotton or cotton from a creeper." 'Sassaranti': the sound that thus arises is the 'sassara' sound. This is meant to show reverberation. Similarly, the 'bhabbhara' sound. All this is meant to show the inability of anything to corrupt the mind of one abiding in loving-kindness. Here is the meaning in brief: just as the great earth cannot be made non-earth by anyone, just as no form can be placed in space, just as the water of the Ganges cannot be heated with a grass torch, just as a cat-skin bag cannot be made to have a stiff and rough touch, even so, for one whose liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been cultivated, developed, and practiced much, it is impossible for a person who has come, having taken hold of the five courses of speech, to alter that mind by any means.

232. Ocarakāti [M 2.0082][V 2.0078] parūpaghātavasena hīnakammakārino. Tenāha “nīcakammakārakā”ti. Anadhivāsanenāti akkhamanena. Mayhaṃ ovādakaro na hotīti paramhi anatthakārimhi cittapadosanena āghātuppādanena mama sāsane sammāpaṭipajjamāno nāma na hoti.

232. "Ocarakā" means those who are engaged in base actions by way of harming others. Therefore, it is said, "those who perform base actions." "Anadhivāsanena" means 'through not enduring,' that is, through impatience. "He is not one who follows my advice" means that one who, by corrupting the mind and generating anger towards another who causes harm, is not one who practices rightly in my dispensation.

233. Aṇunti appakaṃ tanu parittakaṃ. Thūlanti mahantaṃ oḷārikaṃ. Vacanapathassa pana adhippetattā taṃ sāvajjavibhāgena gahetabbanti āha “appasāvajjaṃ vā mahāsāvajjaṃ vā”ti. Khantiyā idaṃ bhāriyaṃ na hotīti avocuṃ “anadhi…pe… passāmā”ti. Dīgharattanti cirakālaṃ, accantamevāti attho. Accantañca hitasukhaṃ nāma aññādhigamenevāti āha “arahattena kūṭaṃ gaṇhanto”ti.

233. "Aṇu" means small, fine, or insignificant. "Thūla" means large or gross. However, since the course of speech is intended, it should be understood in terms of divisions of blameworthy acts; hence it is said, 'whether slightly blameworthy or greatly blameworthy.' They said, 'anadhi…pe… passāmā,' meaning, 'This is not a burden for patience.' 'Dīgharattaṃ' means 'for a long time,' that is, 'ultimately.' And since ultimate welfare and happiness are attained only through the attainment of final knowledge, it is said, 'seizing the peak with arahantship.'

Kakacūpamasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Kakacūpama Sutta is complete.

2. Alagaddūpamasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Alagaddūpama Sutta.

234. Bādhayiṃsūti [V 2.0079] (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.417) haniṃsu. Taṃtaṃsampattiyā vibandhanavasena sattasantānassa antare vemajjhe eti āgacchatīti antarāyo, diṭṭhadhammikādianattho, anatikkamanaṭṭhena tasmiṃ antarāye niyuttā, antarāyaṃ vā phalaṃ arahanti, antarāyassa vā karaṇasīlāti antarāyikā. Tenāha “antarāyaṃ karontīti antarāyikā”ti. Ānantariyadhammāti ānantariyasabhāvacetanādhammā. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – cutianantaraphalaṃ anantaraṃ nāma, tasmiṃ anantare niyuttā, tannibbattanena anantarakaraṇasīlā, anantarapayojanāti vā ānantarikā, te eva ānantariyāti vuttā. Kammāni eva antarāyikāti kammantarāyikā. Mokkhasseva antarāyaṃ karoti, na saggassa micchācāralakkhaṇābhāvato. Na hi bhikkhuniyā dhammarakkhitabhāvo atthi. Pākatikabhikkhunīvasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ, ariyāya pana pavattaṃ apāyasaṃvattaniyameva. Nandamāṇavako cettha nidassanaṃ. Ubhinnaṃ samānacchandatāvasena vā asaggantarāyikatā, mokkhantarāyikatā pana mokkhatthapaṭipattiyā vidūsanato, abhibhavitvā pana pavattiyaṃ [M 2.0083] saggantarāyikatāpi na sakkā nivāretunti. Ahetukadiṭṭhiakiriyadiṭṭhinatthikadiṭṭhiyova niyatabhāvaṃ pattā niyatamicchādiṭṭhidhammā. Paṭisandhidhammāti paṭisandhicittuppādamāha. Paṇḍakādiggahaṇañcettha nidassanamattaṃ sabbāyapi ahetukapaṭisandhiyā vipākantarāyikabhāvato. Yā hi ariye upavadati, sā cetanā ariyūpavādadhammā. Tato paranti khamāpanato upari. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ mahāsīhanādassa līnatthapakāsane vuttameva. Yāva bhikkhubhāvaṃ paṭijānāti pārājikaṃ āpanno. Na vuṭṭhāti sesaṃ garukāpattiṃ. Na deseti lahukāpattiṃ.

234. Bādhayiṃsu (Sārattha. Ṭī. Pācittiya 3.417) means 'they killed.' An 'antarāya' (obstacle) is so called because, by way of obstructing various attainments, it occurs in the middle of a being's continuum; it is a disadvantage in this life and the next. Those who are engaged in that obstacle in the sense that it cannot be overcome, or who deserve the result of the obstacle, or who are inclined to create obstacles—they are 'antarāyikā' (obstructors). Therefore, it is said: 'Those who create obstacles are antarāyikā.' 'Ānantariya-dhammā' means volitional states that have the nature of an immediately effective karma. Here, the meaning of the word is this: the result immediately following death is called 'anantara' (immediate). Those engaged in that immediate consequence, inclined to produce it, or having the immediate consequence as their aim are called 'ānantarika'; those same are said to be 'ānantariya.' Actions themselves are obstacles—thus, 'kammantarāyikā' (obstructive actions). It creates an obstacle only to liberation, not to heaven, because it lacks the characteristic of sexual misconduct. For a bhikkhunī does not have the status of being protected by the Dhamma. This is said with reference to an ordinary bhikkhunī; but in the case of a noble one, such an act leads only to states of deprivation. Nandamāṇavaka is the example here. Or, due to both having the same desire, it is not an obstacle to heaven; but it is an obstacle to liberation because it corrupts the practice for liberation. However, when it occurs through force, the quality of being an obstacle to heaven cannot be prevented either. The views of causelessness, inaction, and nihilism, having attained a fixed nature, are fixed wrong-view states. 'Paṭisandhi-dhammā' refers to the arising of rebirth-linking consciousness. The inclusion of paṇḍakas, etc., here is merely illustrative, since all causeless rebirth-linking is obstructive in its result. The intention that reviles the noble ones is a state of reviling the noble ones. 'Beyond that' means after asking for forgiveness. What should be said here has already been stated in the Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta. As long as he claims the status of a bhikkhu, he has incurred a pārājika offense. He does not rise from the remaining grave offenses. He does not confess the minor offenses.

Ayaṃ bhikkhu ariṭṭho. Rasena rasaṃ saṃsanditvāti anavajjena paccayaparibhuñjanarasena sāvajjaṃ kāmaguṇaparibhogarasaṃ samānetvā. Upanento viyāti bandhanaṃ upanento viya. “Ghaṭento viyā”tipi pāṭho. Upasaṃharanto viyāti sadisataṃ upasaṃharanto viya ekantasāvajje anavajjabhāvapakkhepena. Pāpakanti lāmakaṭṭhena duggatisampāpanaṭṭhena ca pāpakaṃ. Setukaraṇavasena mahāsamuddaṃ bandhantena viya. Sabbaññutaññāṇena “sāvajja”nti diṭṭhaṃ “anavajja”nti gahaṇena tena paṭivirujjhanto. Ekantato anantarāyikanti gahaṇena vesārajjañāṇaṃ paṭibāhanto. Kāmakaṇṭakehi ariyamaggasammāpaṭipatti na upakkilissatīti vadanto “ariyamagge khāṇukaṇṭakādīni [V 2.0080] pakkhipanto”ti vutto. Paṭhamapārājikasikkhāpadasaṅkhāte, “abrahmacariyaṃ pahāyā”ti (dī. ni. 1.8, 194) ādidesanāsaṅkhāte ca āṇācakke.

This monk is Ariṭṭha. "Comparing taste with taste" means equating the blameworthy taste of enjoying sensual pleasures with the blameless taste of using the requisites. "As if leading to" means as if leading to bondage. 'Ghaṭento viya' (as if joining) is also a reading. 'Upasaṃharanto viya' means as if bringing to similarity, by adding the aspect of blamelessness to what is entirely blameworthy. "Evil" means evil in the sense of being inferior and in the sense of leading to a bad destination. Like one who builds a causeway across the great ocean. He opposes the omniscient knowledge by taking what is seen by it as 'blameworthy' to be 'blameless.' By grasping things as entirely non-obstructive, he obstructs the knowledge of confidence. Saying that the Noble Path of right practice is not defiled by the thorns of sensual pleasures, he is said to be 'placing stumps and thorns on the Noble Path.' This is in regard to the wheel of command, reckoned as the first Pārājika training rule and as the instruction beginning, 'Having abandoned unchastity...' (Dī. Ni. 1.8, 194).

Pucchamānā samanuyuñjanti nāma. Pucchā hi anuyogoti. Tenādhigatāya laddhiyā anuvajjanatthaṃ paccanubhāsanena puna paṭijānāpanaṃ patiṭṭhāpanaṃ, taṃ panassa ādāya samādāpanaṃ viya hotīti āha “samanugāhanti nāmā”ti. Tassā pana laddhiyā anuyuñjitāya vuccamānampi kāraṇaṃ kāraṇapatirūpakamevāti tassa pucchanaṃ samanubhāsanaṃ. Anudahanaṭṭhena anupāyapaṭipattiyā sampati āyatiñca anudahanaṭṭhena. Mahābhitāpanaṭṭhena anavaṭṭhitasabhāvatāya. Ittarapaccupaṭṭhānaṭṭhena muhuttaramaṇīyatāya. Tāvakālikaṭṭhena parehi abhibhavanīyatāya. Sabbaṅgapaccaṅgapalibhañjanaṭṭhena chedanabhedanādiadhikaraṇabhāvena. Ugghāṭasadisatāya [M 2.0084] adhikuṭṭanaṭṭhena. Avaṇe vaṇaṃ uppādetvā anto anupavisanasabhāvatāya vinivijjhanaṭṭhena. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaanatthanimittatāya sāsaṅkasappaṭibhayaṭṭhena. Diṭṭhithāmenāti tassā diṭṭhiyā thāmagatabhāvena. Diṭṭhiparāmāsenāti diṭṭhisaṅkhātaparāmasanena. Diṭṭhiyeva hi dhammasabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā parato āmasanena parāmāso. Abhinivissāti taṇhābhinivesapubbaṅgamena diṭṭhābhinivesena “idamevettha tatha”nti abhinivisitvā. Yasmā hi abhinivesanaṃ tattha abhiniviṭṭhaṃ nāma hoti.Tasmā āha “adhiṭṭhahitvā”ti.

When questioned, they cross-examine. For questioning is indeed an inquiry. For the purpose of making him follow the view they have attained, by repeated instruction, making him reaffirm and establishing him in it—this is like taking him up and persuading him; hence it is said, 'they pursue him.' And when that view is cross-examined, even what is said as a reason is merely a semblance of a reason; therefore, their questioning is a repeated instruction. In the sense of consuming, through the practice of an unsuitable path that consumes one in the present and in the future. In the sense of great torment, due to its unstable nature. In the sense of fleeting presentation, due to its momentary attractiveness. In the sense of being temporary, due to being easily overpowered by others. In the sense of breaking all major and minor limbs, due to being a basis for cutting, breaking, and other strife. In the sense of being hammered down, by way of resembling repeated striking. In the sense of piercing, by way of creating a wound where there is none and having the nature of penetrating within. In the sense of being dangerous and fearful, because it is a cause of disadvantage in this life and the next. 'By the strength of the view' means due to that view having become entrenched. 'By the misapprehension of view' means by the grasping called view. For misapprehension is the perverse grasping of a view, having transgressed the true nature of things. 'Having adhered' means having adhered with an adherence to views preceded by an adherence to craving, thinking, 'Only this is true here.' For when there is adherence, one is said to be firmly fixed there. Therefore, it is said, 'having resolved.'

235. Natthīti vattukāmopīti attano laddhiṃ niguhetukāmatāya avajānitukāmopi. Sampaṭicchati paṭijānāti. Dve kathāti visaṃvādanakathaṃ sandhāya vadati. Abhūtakathā hi pubbe pavattā bhūtakathāya vasena dve kathāti vuccati.

235. Even when wishing to say, 'There is not,' means even when wishing to conceal his own view or wishing to disavow it. 'He accepts' means he acknowledges. 'Two speeches' means he speaks with reference to contradictory speech. For false speech, previously uttered, is called 'two speeches' in relation to the true speech.

236. Kassa kho nāmāti iminā satthā “na mama tuyhaṃ tādisassa atthāya dhammadesanā nāma bhūtapubbā”ti dasseti. Tenāha “khattiyassa vā”tiādi.

236. “For whom, indeed?”—with this the Teacher shows, “My teaching of the Dhamma has never before been for the benefit of one such as you.” Therefore, he said, “for a noble warrior,” and so forth.

Ñāṇamayā usmā etassa atthīti usmī, tathārūpehi paccayehi anusmīkato tasmiṃ attabhāve paṭivedhagabbhoapi usmīkatoti vikatabhāvato paññābījamassa imasmiṃ dhammavinaye api nu atthīti bhagavā bhikkhū pucchati. Te paṭikkhipantā vadanti ṭhānagatena duccaritena ñāṇupahatabhāvaṃ sampassantā. Nittejabhūtoti nittejaṃ bhūto tejohānippatto. Tato eva bhikkhūnampi [V 2.0081] sammukhā oloketuṃ asamatthatāya pattakkhandho adhomukho. Sahadhammikaṃ kiñci vattuṃ avisahanato appaṭibhāno. Sampattūpaganti sampattiāvahaṃ. Paṭippassambhentoti paṭisedhento.

“He has the heat of knowledge,” thus he is fiery. Being inflamed by such conditions, even the womb of penetration in that existence is inflamed. Because of his corrupted state, “Does the seed of wisdom for him in this Dhamma and Discipline even exist?”—the Blessed One asks the monks. They, rejecting this, speak, seeing that his knowledge is impaired by misconduct that has become established. “He has become without radiance” means he has become without radiance, having suffered a loss of radiance. For that very reason, being unable to look the monks in the face, he was with drooping shoulders and downcast face. Unable to say anything in accordance with the Dhamma, he was without eloquence. “Leading to attainment” means bringing about success. “He rejects” means he denies.

237. Antarāyakaraladdhiyā sabhāvavibhāvanena parisaṃ sodheti. Nissāreti nīharati avisuddhadiṭṭhitāya. Kassaci buddhānubhāvaṃ ajānantassa. Tassa hi evaṃ bhaveyya “sahasā kathita”nti. Na hi kadāci buddhānaṃ sahasā kiriyā nāma atthi. Assāti “kassacī”ti vuttabhikkhussa. Sutvāpi [M 2.0085] tuṇhībhāvaṃ āpajjeyyāti athāpi siyāti sambandho. Taṃ sabbanti “sace hī”tiādinā vuttaṃ sabbaṃ parikappanaṃ. Na karissantīti parisāya laddhiṃ sodhetīti sambandho. Laddhiṃ pakāsentoti mahāsāvajjatāvasena pakāsento. Saññāvitakkehīti subhanimittānubyañjanaggāhādivasena pavattehi saññāvitakkehi. Tenāha “kilesakāmasampayuttehī”ti. Methunasamācāranti idaṃ adhikāravasena vuttaṃ. Tadaññampi pana – “apica kho mātugāmassa ucchādanaṃ parimaddanaṃ nahāpanaṃ sambāhanaṃ sādiyatī”tiādinā (a. ni. 7.50) āgataṃ visabhāgavatthuvisayaṃ āmisaparibhogaṃ. “Aññatreva kāmehi aññatra kāmasaññāhi aññatra kāmavitakkehi samācarissatī”ti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

237. He purifies the assembly by explaining the nature of the obstructive view. He removes, he expels him because of his impure view. For someone not knowing the Buddha’s power, it might be thought, “This was spoken hastily.” For there is never any hasty action on the part of the Buddhas. “Of him” refers to the monk spoken of as “of someone.” The connection is: “Even after hearing, he might remain silent,” meaning that it could still be so. “All that” means all the speculation spoken of beginning with “if indeed,” and so forth. The connection is: “They will not do it,” meaning he purifies the view of the assembly. “Exposing the view” means revealing it by way of its great blameworthiness. “With perceptions and thoughts” means with perceptions and thoughts that proceed by way of grasping the sign of the beautiful, its secondary characteristics, and so on. Therefore, it is said, “connected with defilements and sensual desires.” “Sexual conduct”—this is said with reference to the main topic. Moreover, other things—such as what is found in the text beginning, “Furthermore, he consents to a woman anointing, massaging, bathing, or rubbing him” (AN 7.50)—pertain to the enjoyment of material things concerning an improper object. “That he would engage in it apart from sensual pleasures, apart from perceptions of sensuality, apart from thoughts of sensuality—this is not possible.”

238. Yoniso paccavekkhaṇena natthi ettha chandarāgoti nicchandarāgo, taṃ nicchandarāgaṃ. Kadāci uposathikabhāvena samādinnasīlāpi honti kadāci noti anibaddhasīlānaṃ gahaṭṭhānaṃ. Sīlasamādānabhāvato antarāyakaraṃ. Vatthukāmānaṃ sacchandarāgaparibhogañca. Apaccavekkhaṇena bhikkhūnaṃ āvaraṇakaraṃ. Paccayānaṃ sacchandarāgaparibhogañca. Ayaṃ ariṭṭho duggahitāya pariyattiyā vasena amhe ceva abbhācikkhati, attānañca khanati, bahuñca apuññaṃ pasavatīti evaṃ saññā mā hontūti duggahitāya pariyattiyā dosaṃ dassento āha. Uggaṇhantīti sajjhāyanti ceva vācuggataṃ karontā dhārenti cāti attho.

238. Through wise reflection, “there is no passionate desire here,” thus one is without passionate desire; that is “being without passionate desire.” Sometimes they have undertaken the precepts as observers of the Uposatha, sometimes not—this is for householders of unfixed virtue. It is an obstacle to the undertaking of virtue. And the enjoyment of material objects with passionate desire. Through not reflecting, it is an obstruction for monks. And the enjoyment of the requisites with passionate desire. “This Ariṭṭha, by means of a wrongly grasped teaching, both misrepresents us and destroys himself, and generates much demerit”—lest there be such a perception, he spoke, pointing out the fault of a wrongly grasped teaching. “They learn” means they both recite and, making it fluent, they bear it in mind; this is the meaning.

Suttantiādinā navappabhedampi pariyattidhammaṃ pariyādiyati. Kathaṃ suttaṃ navappabhedaṃ? Sagāthakañhi suttaṃ geyyaṃ, niggāthakaṃ suttaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ, tadubhayavinimuttañca suttaṃ udānādivisesasaññāvirahitaṃ natthi, yaṃ suttaṅgaṃ siyā, maṅgalasuttādīnañca suttaṅgasaṅgaho na siyā gāthābhāvato dhammapadādīnaṃ viya, geyyaṅgasaṅgaho vā siyā sagāthakattā sagāthāvaggassa viya, tathā ubhatovibhaṅgādīsu sagāthakappadesānanti? Vuccate –

By “Sutta,” and so forth, the ninefold division of the scriptural Dhamma is encompassed. How is the Sutta ninefold? For a sutta with verses is Geyya, and a sutta without verses is Veyyākaraṇa; and there is no sutta free from both of these and devoid of specific designations such as Udāna, which could be a Suttaṅga. And the Maṅgala Sutta and others could not be included in the Suttaṅga because they are in verse, like the Dhammapada and others; or they could be included in the Geyyaṅga because they contain verses, like the Sagāthāvagga. And what of the sections with verses in the Ubhatovibhaṅga and others? It is said:

Suttanti [V 2.0082] sāmaññavidhi, visesavidhayo pare;

Sanimittā nirūḷhattā, sahatāññena naññato. (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.nidānakathāvaṇṇanā; a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.6; sārattha. ṭī. 1.bāhiranidānakathā);

“Sutta” is the general category, the others are specific categories; with their own marks, by being established, together with another, not from another.

Sabbassapi [M 2.0086] hi buddhavacanassa suttanti ayaṃ sāmaññavidhi. Tenevāha āyasmā mahākaccāno nettiyaṃ (netti. 1.saṅgahavāra) “navavidhasuttantapariyeṭṭhī”ti. “Ettakaṃ tassa bhagavato suttāgataṃ suttapariyāpannaṃ (pāci. 655, 1242), sakavāde pañca suttasatānī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā; kathā. aṭṭha. nidānakathā) evamādi ca etassa atthassa sādhakaṃ. Tadekadesesu pana geyyādayo visesavidhayo tena tena nimittena patiṭṭhitā. Tathā hi geyyassa sagāthakattaṃ tabbhāvanimittaṃ. Lokepi hi sasilokaṃ sagāthakaṃ vā cuṇṇiyaganthaṃ “geyya”nti vadanti. Gāthāvirahe pana sati pucchaṃ katvā vissajjanabhāvo veyyākaraṇassa tabbhāvanimittaṃ. Pucchāvissajjanañhi “byākaraṇa”nti vuccati, byākaraṇameva veyyākaraṇaṃ.

For indeed, “Sutta” is the general category for all the Buddha’s word. Thus, the Venerable Mahākaccāna said in the Netti (Netti. 1. Saṅgahavāra): “The ninefold search for suttas.” “So much of the Blessed One’s teaching has come down as suttas, is included in the suttas (Pāci. 655, 1242), five hundred suttas in his own school” (Dha. Sa. Aṭṭha. Nidānakathā; Kathā. Aṭṭha. Nidānakathā), and so on—this is proof of this meaning. However, in some parts of it, specific categories like Geyya and others are established by particular marks. For example, for Geyya, the state of having verses is the mark of its being so. Indeed, in the world too, a prose work with verses or stanzas is called “Geyya.” But when verses are absent, the state of question and answer is the mark of its being Veyyākaraṇa. For question and answer is called “Byākaraṇa,” and Byākaraṇa itself is Veyyākaraṇa.

Evaṃ sante sagāthakādīnampi pucchaṃ katvā vissajjanavasena pavattānaṃ veyyākaraṇabhāvo āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati geyyādisaññānaṃ anokāsabhāvato, “gāthāvirahe satī”ti visesitattā ca. Tathā hi dhammapadādīsu kevalaṃ gāthābandhesu, sagāthakattepi somanassañāṇamayikagāthāyuttesu, “vuttañheta”nti (itivu. 1) ādivacanasambandhesu, abbhutadhammapaṭisaṃyuttesu ca suttavisesesu yathākkamaṃ gāthā-udāna-itivuttaka-abbhutadhamma-saññā patiṭṭhitā, tathā satipi gāthābandhabhāve bhagavato atītāsu jātīsu cariyānubhāvappakāsakesu jātakasaññā, satipi pañhavissajjanabhāve sagāthakatte ca kesuci suttantesu vedassa labhāpanato vedallasaññā patiṭṭhitāti evaṃ tena tena sagāthakattādinā nimittena tesu tesu suttavisesesu geyyādisaññā patiṭṭhitāti visesavidhayo suttaṅgato pare geyyādayo. Yaṃ panettha geyyaṅgādinimittarahitaṃ, taṃ suttaṅgaṃ visesasaññāparihārena sāmaññasaññāya pavattanatoti. Nanu ca sagāthakaṃ suttaṃ geyyaṃ, niggāthakaṃ suttaṃ veyyākaraṇanti suttaṅgaṃ na sambhavatīti codanā tadavatthā evāti? Na tadavatthā sodhitattā. Sodhitañhi pubbe “gāthāvirahe sati pucchāvissajjanabhāvo veyyākaraṇassa tabbhāvanimitta”nti.

This being so, does the state of being Veyyākaraṇa also apply to those with verses and so on, since they proceed by way of question and answer? It does not apply, because there is no opportunity for the designations Geyya, etc., and because it is qualified by “when there is an absence of verses.” For in the Dhammapada and similar texts, which consist solely of verse compositions; and in those with verses that are also connected with verses of joy and knowledge; and in the introductory statements connected with “[Thus] it was said” (Itivuttaka 1); and in the special suttas connected with marvelous qualities—in these, the designations Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, and Abbhutadhamma are established respectively. Similarly, even when there is a verse composition that illuminates the conduct and power of the Blessed One in past lives, the designation Jātaka is established. And even when there is question and answer and the presence of verses in certain suttas where joyful wisdom is attained, the designation Vedalla is established. Thus, by this or that mark, such as having verses, the designations Geyya, etc., are established in those particular suttas. Therefore, the specific categories, Geyya and so on, are other than the Suttaṅga. Whatever here is devoid of the marks of Geyyaṅga, etc., that is the Suttaṅga, proceeding by the general designation due to the absence of a specific designation. But is not the objection—“A sutta with verses is Geyya, and a sutta without verses is Veyyākaraṇa, so a Suttaṅga is not possible”—still in the same state? It is not in the same state, because it has been cleared up. For it was cleared up before: “When there is an absence of verses, the state of question and answer is the mark of its being Veyyākaraṇa.”

Yañca vuttaṃ “gāthābhāvato maṅgalasuttādīnaṃ suttaṅgasaṅgaho na siyā”ti (khu. pā. 5.1; su. ni. 261), taṃ na, niruḷhattā. Niruḷho hi maṅgalasuttādīnaṃ suttabhāvo. Na hi [M 2.0087] tāni dhammapadabuddhavaṃsādayo viya gāthābhāvena paññātāni, kintu suttabhāveneva. Teneva hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “suttanāmaka”nti nāmaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “sagāthakattā geyyaṅgasaṅgaho siyā”ti[V 2.0083], tadapi natthi, yasmā sahatāññena. Saha gāthāhīti hi sagāthakaṃ, sahabhāvo ca nāma atthato aññena hoti, na ca maṅgalasuttādīsu gāthāvinimutto koci suttapadeso atthi, yo “saha gāthāhī”ti vucceyya, na ca samudāyo nāma koci atthi. Yadapi vuttaṃ “ubhatovibhaṅgādīsu sagāthakappadesānaṃ geyyaṅgasaṅgaho siyā”ti, tadapi na aññato. Aññā eva hi tā gāthā jātakādipariyāpannattā, ato na tāhi ubhatovibhaṅgādīnaṃ geyyaṅgabhāvoti. Evaṃ suttādīnaṃ aṅgānaṃ aññamaññasaṅkarābhāvo veditabbo.

And as to what was said, “Because of their nature as verse, the inclusion of discourses like the Maṅgala Sutta under the Sutta component would not occur” (Khu. Pā. 5.1; Su. Ni. 261), that is not so, because of their established status. For the status of the Maṅgala Sutta and others as discourses is indeed established. They are not known by their nature as verse, like the Dhammapada or Buddhavaṃsa, but rather by their status as discourses. For that reason, in the commentary, the name “Suttanāmaka” (named a Sutta) is mentioned. As to what was said, “Because they contain verses, they could be included under the Geyya component,” that too is not the case, because it implies being together with something else. For 'sagāthaka' means 'with verses,' and the state of being together is indeed with something else in meaning. But in the Maṅgala Sutta and others, there is no portion of the discourse devoid of verses that could be called 'with verses,' nor is there any such composite. And as to what was said, “In the Ubhatovibhaṅga and others, the inclusion of verse-containing passages under the Geyya component could occur,” that too is not so, because they are from another source. For those verses are distinct, being included in the Jātaka and similar categories; therefore, they do not confer the status of Geyya upon the Ubhatovibhaṅga and others. Thus, it should be understood that there is no mutual confusion among the components, such as the Sutta and others.

Atthatthanti atthabhūtaṃ yathābhūtaṃ atthaṃ. Anatthampi keci vipallāsavasena “attho”ti gaṇhantīti “atthattha”nti visesetvā vuttaṃ. Kāraṇatthanti kāraṇabhūtaṃ atthaṃ, sīlaṃ samādhissa kāraṇaṃ, samādhi vipassanāyāti evaṃ tassa tassa kāraṇabhūtaṃ atthaṃ. Tenāha “imasmiṃ ṭhāne sīla”ntiādi. Tenetaṃ dasseti – imasmiṃ ṭhāne sīlaṃ kathitaṃ, tañca yāvadeva samādhatthaṃ, samādhi vipassanattho, vipassanā maggatthā, maggo phalattho, vaṭṭaṃ kathitaṃ yāvadeva vivaṭṭādhigamatthanti jānituṃ na sakkontīti. Evaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “attha”nti iminā bhāsitatthapayojanatthānaṃ gahitatā veditabbā. Na pariggaṇhantīti na vicārenti, nijjhānapaññākkhamā na honti, nijjhāyitvā paññāya rocetvā gahetabbā na hontīti adhippāyo. Iti evaṃ etāya pariyattiyā vādappamokkhānisaṃsā attano upari parehi āropitavādassa niggahassa mokkhapayojanā hutvā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti. Vādappamokkho vā nindāpamokkho. Yassa cāti yassa ca sīlādipūraṇena pattabbassa, maggassa vā tadadhigamena pattabbassa, phalassa vā tadadhigamena pattabbassa, anupādāvimokkhassa vā atthāya. Dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti, ñāyena pariyāpuṇantīti adhippāyo. Nānubhonti na vindanti. Tesaṃ te dhammā duggahitā upārambhamānadappamakkhapaḷāsādihetubhāvena dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti.

'The true meaning' means the actual meaning, as it really is. Since some, due to perversion, grasp what is not the meaning as 'the meaning,' it is specified as 'the true meaning.' 'The meaning as cause' means the meaning that is a cause—virtue is the cause for concentration, concentration for insight—thus, the meaning that is a cause for each respective thing. Hence it is said, 'In this place, virtue,' and so on. This shows that they are unable to know that in this place virtue is taught only for the sake of concentration; concentration for the sake of insight; insight for the sake of the path; the path for the sake of the fruit; and the round of existence is taught only for the sake of attaining the end of the round. Thus, it should be understood that in the Pāli, by the word 'meaning' (attha), both the literal meaning and the purpose are included. 'They do not grasp' means they do not investigate; they are not amenable to the wisdom of scrutiny. The meaning is that those teachings are not to be grasped by them after scrutinizing and approving with wisdom. Thus, they master the Dhamma so that this learning has the benefit of release from debate, its purpose being release from the refutation of accusations imposed upon them by others. Release from debate is release from blame. 'And for the sake of which' means for the sake of that which is to be attained by fulfilling virtue and so on, or for the sake of the path to be attained by its realization, or for the sake of the fruit to be attained by its realization, or for the sake of liberation through non-clinging. They master the Dhamma—the meaning is, they master it according to the right method. 'They do not experience' means they do not find. For them, those teachings, being poorly grasped, conduce to their long-term harm and suffering, by being a cause for finding fault, conceit, arrogance, contempt, spite, and so on.

239. Alaṃ [M 2.0088] pariyatto gado assāti alagaddo anunāsikalopaṃ da-kārāgamañca katvā. Vaṭṭadukkhakantārato nittharaṇatthāya pariyatti nittharaṇapariyatti. Bhaṇḍāgāre niyutto bhaṇḍāgāriko, bhaṇḍāgāriko viya bhaṇḍāgāriko, dhammaratanānupālako. Aññaṃ atthaṃ anapekkhitvā bhaṇḍāgārikasseva sato pariyatti bhaṇḍāgārikapariyatti. “Vaṃsānurakkhakovā”ti avadhāraṇaṃ sīhāvalokanañāyena tantidhārakova paveṇipālakovāti purimapadadvayepi yojetabbaṃ.

239. The word 'alagadda' (water snake) is formed from the phrase 'alaṃ pariyatto gado assā' by eliding the nasal and inserting the letter 'da'. The learning for the purpose of deliverance from the wilderness of the suffering of the round is 'the learning for deliverance'. One appointed to the treasury is a treasurer; like a treasurer, he is a guardian of the jewel of the Dhamma. The learning of one who is merely a treasurer, without regard for any other purpose, is 'the treasurer's learning'. The emphatic particle in 'guardian of the lineage,' by the principle of the lion's backward glance, should be applied also to the two preceding terms, thus: 'indeed a bearer of the textual tradition' and 'indeed a protector of the lineage'.

Yadi tantidhāraṇādiatthaṃ buddhavacanassa pariyāpuṇanaṃ bhaṇḍāgārikapariyatti, kasmā “khīṇāsavassā”ti visesetvā vuttaṃ, nanu ekaccassa puthujjanassapi ayaṃ nayo labbhatīti anuyogaṃ [V 2.0084] sandhāyāha “yo panā”tiādi. Attano ṭhāneti nittharaṇaṭṭhāne. Kāmaṃ puthujjano “paveṇiṃ pālessāmī”ti ajjhāsayena pariyāpuṇāti. Attano pana bhavakantārato anittiṇṇattā tassa sā pariyatti nittharaṇapariyatti eva nāma hotīti adhippāyo. Tenāha “puthujjanassā”tiādi.

If the mastering of the Buddha's word for the purpose of preserving the textual tradition is 'the treasurer's learning,' why is it specified as being 'of one whose taints are destroyed'? Surely this method is found even in the case of some ordinary persons—referring to this question, he says, 'But whoever,' and so on. 'In one's own position' means in the position of deliverance. It is true that an ordinary person masters the teachings with the intention, 'I will protect the lineage.' However, because they themselves have not crossed over the wilderness of existence, the meaning is that their learning is not in fact 'the learning for deliverance.' For this reason, he says, 'of an ordinary person,' and so on.

Nijjhānaṃ khamantīti nijjhānapaññaṃ khamanti. Tattha tattha āgate sīlādidhamme nijjhāyitvā paññāya rocetvā yāthāvato gahetabbā honti. Tenāha “idha sīla”ntiādi. Na kevalaṃ suggahitaṃ pariyattiṃ nissāya maggabhāvanāphalasacchikiriyā, paravādaniggahasakavādapatiṭṭhāpanādīnipi ijjhantīti dassetuṃ “paravāde”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tenāha “uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ sahadhammena suniggahaṃ niggahitvā”tiādi (dī. ni. 2.268). Icchiticchitaṭṭhānanti diṭṭhiviniveṭhanādivasena icchitaṃ icchitaṃ pāḷipadesaṃ. Mocetunti apanetuṃ. Ahitāya dukkhāya asaṃvattanampi tadabhāve uppajjanakahitasukhassa kāraṇameva tasmiṃ sati bhāvatoti. Suggahitaalagaddassapi hitāya sukhāya saṃvattanatā daṭṭhabbā.

'They are amenable to scrutiny' means they are amenable to the wisdom of scrutiny. The teachings on virtue and so on that are encountered in various places are to be grasped as they really are, after scrutinizing and approving of them with wisdom. Therefore, it is said, 'Here, virtue,' and so on. To show that not only are the development of the path and the realization of the fruit accomplished by relying on the well-grasped learning, but also the refutation of others' doctrines and the establishment of one's own doctrine, it is said, 'in debate with others,' and so on. Therefore, he says, 'having thoroughly refuted, in accordance with the Dhamma, a doctrine of others that has arisen,' and so on (Dī. Ni. 2.268). 'Desired, desired place' means a textual passage desired again and again for the purpose of untangling wrong views and so on. 'To release' means to remove. The very fact that it does not lead to harm and suffering is a cause for the welfare and happiness that arise in their absence, this being so because of the presence of the well-grasped teaching. It should be seen that the well-grasped snake also leads to welfare and happiness.

240. Uttaranti etenāti uttaro, sinanti bandhantīti setu, uttaro ca so setu cāti uttarasetu. Kūlaṃ paratīraṃ vahati pāpetīti kullaṃ. Kalāpaṃ katvā baddhoti veḷunaḷādīhi kalāpavasena baddho. Aṇunti idaṃ aṭṭhasamāpattiārammaṇaṃ saññojanaṃ sandhāya vadati. Thūlanti [M 2.0089] itaraṃ. Diṭṭhinti yathābhūtadassanaṃ, vipassananti attho. Evaṃ parisuddhaṃ evaṃ pariyodātanti tebhūmakesu dhammesu ñātaṃ “netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā”ti, evaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhisaṃkilesābhāvena sabbaso visuddhaṃ, parisuddhattā eva pariyodātaṃ. Na allīyethāti nikantivasena na nissayetha. Na kelāyethāti na mamāyetha. Na dhanāyethāti dhanaṃ drabyaṃ na kayirātha. Ubhayatthāti samathe vipassanāya ca.

240. 'Uttara' is so called because one crosses over (uttarati) by it; 'setu' is so called because they bind (sinanti); it is a crossing-over and a bridge, thus 'uttarasetu' (a bridge for crossing over). 'Kulla' (raft) is so called because it carries (vahati) one to the bank (kūlaṃ), the far shore. 'Bound into a bundle' means bound in the manner of a bundle with bamboo, reeds, and so on. When he says 'subtle,' he says this with reference to the fetter that has the eight attainments as its object. 'Gross' refers to the other. 'Vision' means seeing things as they truly are; the meaning is insight. 'Thus purified, thus cleansed' means, with regard to the phenomena of the three planes, it is known that 'this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'; thus, through the absence of the defilements of craving and views, it is completely pure; and because it is pure, it is cleansed. 'One should not cling' means one should not rely on it out of fondness. 'One should not treat with affection' means one should not regard it as 'mine.' 'One should not treat as wealth' means one should not make it into a treasure or possession. 'For both' means for both serenity and insight.

Asaddhammetiādīsu asataṃ hīnajjhāsayānaṃ dhammoti asaddhammo. Gāmavāsīnaṃ dhammoti gāmadhammo. Kilesānaṃ vassanasabhāvatāya vasaladhammo. Kilesehi dūsitattā thūlattā ca duṭṭhullo. Udakasuddhipariyosānatāya odakantiko. “Dhammāpi vo pahātabbā”ti imināpi ovādena bhikkhū uddissa kathentopi ariṭṭhaṃyeva niggaṇhāti.

In the passage beginning 'a bad teaching,' 'a bad teaching' (asaddhamma) is the teaching of bad people, of those with base intentions. 'A village practice' (gāmadhamma) is the practice of villagers. Because of the nature of raining down (vassana) defilements, it is 'an outcast's practice' (vasaladhamma). Because it is corrupted by defilements and is coarse, it is 'a gross offense' (duṭṭhulla). Because it ends in purification with water, it is 'ending with water' (odakantika). Even when speaking and addressing the monks with the advice, 'Teachings, too, should be abandoned by you,' he is still rebuking Ariṭṭha himself.

241. Tividhaggāhavasenāti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiggāhavasena. Yadi evaṃ “ahaṃ mamāti gaṇhātī”ti gāhadvayameva kasmā vuttanti? Nayidamevaṃ tatthāpi gāhattayasseva vuttattā. “Aha”nti [V 2.0085] hi iminā mānadiṭṭhiggāhā vuttā “ahamasmī”ti gāhasāmaññato. Diṭṭhipi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ purimuppannāya diṭṭhiyā uttaradiṭṭhiyā sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā sassatadiṭṭhiyā ca kāraṇabhāvato. Ārammaṇaṃ pañca khandhā, rūpārammaṇādīni ca. Diṭṭhiyā paccayo avijjā-phassa-saññā-vitakka-ayonisomanasikāra-pāpamittaparatoghosādiko diṭṭhiyā upanissayādipaccayo. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.124)“katamāni aṭṭha diṭṭhiṭṭhānāni avijjāpi phassopi saññāpi vitakkopi ayonisomanasikāropi pāpamittopi paratoghosopi diṭṭhiṭṭhāna”ntiādi. Rūpārammaṇāti ruppanasabhāvadhammārammaṇā. Rūpaṃ pana attāti na vattabbaṃ idha “rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.81, 345) imassa gāhassa anadhippetattā. So hi “yampi taṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhāna”ntiādinā parato vuccati. Idha pana “rūpavantaṃ attānaṃ samanupassati, attani rūpaṃ, rūpasmiṃ attāna”nti ime tayo gāhā adhippetāti keci, tadayuttaṃ. Yasmā rūpaṃ attā na hoti, attaggāhassa pana ālambanaṃ hoti, attasabhāveyeva vā rūpādidhamme ārabbha attadiṭṭhi uppajjati, na attānaṃ tassa paramatthato anupalabbhanato, tasmā rūpādiārammaṇāva attadiṭṭhīti katvā [M 2.0090] vuttaṃ, rūpaṃ pana “attā”ti na vattabbanti ayamettha attho. “Yampi taṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhāna”ntiādinā pana vipassanāpaṭivipassanā viya diṭṭhianupassanā nāma dassitā.

241. "By way of threefold grasping" means by way of grasping through craving, conceit, and views. If so, why is only the twofold grasping stated as "he grasps 'I' and 'mine'"? This is not so, for there too, the threefold grasping is indeed stated. For by "I," the graspings of conceit and view are stated, due to the general sense of grasping "I am." View too, as a ground for views, is the cause of previously arisen views, subsequently arisen views, identity view, and the eternalist view. The object is the five aggregates, form as object, etc. The condition for view is ignorance, contact, perception, thought, unwise attention, bad friends, a voice from another, etc., serving as supporting conditions for view. As stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 1.124): "What are the eight grounds for views? Ignorance, contact, perception, thought, unwise attention, bad friends, a voice from another—these are grounds for views," and so on. "Having form as object" means having phenomena that have the nature of disintegration as object. However, it should not be said here that "form is self," because the grasping "he regards form as self" is not intended here. For that is mentioned later by the phrase "that too is a ground for views." Here, however, some think that these three graspings are intended: "he regards self as possessing form, form as in self, self as in form." That is not right. Since form is not self, yet it serves as the support for the grasping of self, or because the view of self arises in relation to phenomena like form, taking them as having the nature of self—since a self is not ultimately found—therefore, it is said that the view of self has form, etc., as its object, but form should not be called "self." This is the meaning here. By the phrase "that too is a ground for views," etc., what is called the contemplation of view is shown, like insight and counter-insight.

Gandharasaphoṭṭhabbāyatanānaṃ sampattagāhindriyavisayatāya patvā gahetabbatā. Tañhi tassa attano visayaṃ paribhutvā sambandhaṃ hutvā gaṇhāti. Avasesāni sattāyatanāni viññātaṃ nāma manasā viññātabbato. Aññathā itaresampi viññātatā siyā. Pattanti adhigataṃ. Pariyesitanti gavesitaṃ. Anuvicaritanti cintitaṃ. Tenāha “manasā”ti. Ettha ca pattapariyesanānaṃ apaṭikkhepassa, visuṃ, ekajjhaṃ paṭikkhepassa ca vasena catukkoṭikaṃ dassetvā pattapariyesitehi anuvicaritassa bhedaṃ dassetuṃ “lokasmiñhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pariyesitvā pattaṃ paṭhamaṃ cetasā pacchā kāyena pattattā pattaṃ nāma. Pariyesitvā nopattaṃ pariyesitaṃ nāma kevalaṃ pariyesitabhāvato. Apariyesitvā pattañca nopattañca manasā anuvicaritabbato manasānuvicaritaṃ nāma.

The sense bases of odors, tastes, and tangibles are to be grasped by reaching them, as they are the domain of the sense faculties that grasp through contact. For a faculty grasps its own domain by pervading it and becoming connected with it. The remainder, what is cognized, is so called because it is to be cognized by the mind. Otherwise, the others too would be what is cognized. "Attained" means reached. "Sought" means searched for. "Reflected upon" means considered. Therefore, it is said, "by the mind." Here, by way of non-rejection, separate rejection, and combined rejection of what is attained and sought, a fourfold classification is shown to distinguish what is reflected upon from them. Hence, it is said, "in the world," etc. What is sought and then attained—first by the mind and later by the body—is called "attained." What is sought but not attained is called "sought," merely because it has been sought. And what is not sought, whether attained or not attained, is to be reflected upon by the mind, and is thus called 'reflected upon by the mind.'

Ayañca vikappo ākulo viyāti “atha vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pattaṭṭhenāti pattabhāvena pattatāsāmaññena. Apariyesitvā nopattaṃ manasānuvicaritaṃ nāma pattiyā pariyesanāya ca abhāvato. Sabbaṃ vā etanti “pariyesitvā pattampī”tiādinā vuttaṃ catubbidhampi. Imināti “yampi taṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ”tiādivacanena. Viññāṇārammaṇā taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiyo kathitā pārisesañāyena[V 2.0086]. Evaṃ pārisesañāyapariggahe kiṃ payojananti āha “desanāvilāsenā”tiādi. Yesaṃ vineyyānaṃ desetabbadhammassa sarūpaṃ anāmasitvā ārammaṇakicca-sampayuttadhamma-phalavisesādi-pakārantaravibhāvanena paṭivedho hoti, tesaṃ tappakārabhedehi dhammehi, yesaṃ pana yena ekeneva pakārena sarūpeneva vā vibhāvane kate paṭivedho hoti, tesaṃ taṃ vatvā dhammissarattā tadaññaṃ niravasesākāravibhāvanañca desanāvilāso. Tenāha “diṭṭhādiārammaṇavasena viññāṇaṃ dassita”nti.

And this alternative seems intricate; hence, 'or else,' etc., is said. By the meaning of 'attainment': by the state of having been attained, by the general quality of attainment. What is not attained without being sought is called 'reflected upon by the mind' because of the absence of both attainment and seeking. Or all this is the fourfold division stated by 'even what is attained after seeking,' etc. By this: by the statement 'that which is a standpoint of view,' etc. Craving, conceit, and views that have consciousness as their object are stated by the method of remainder. When it is thus grasped by the method of remainder, what is the purpose? He says: 'for the sake of the elegance of the teaching,' etc. For those trainees for whom penetration occurs not by touching upon the intrinsic nature of the Dhamma to be taught but through an explanation of its various aspects—such as the object, its function, associated states, and special fruits—the teaching is given through these different kinds of phenomena. But for those for whom penetration occurs when the explanation is made in just one way or by its intrinsic nature alone, for them, having stated that, the elegance of the teaching consists in also explaining the other aspects without remainder, due to mastery of the Dhamma. Therefore he said: 'Consciousness is shown by way of objects that are seen, etc.'

Diṭṭhiṭṭhānanti diṭṭhi eva diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Yaṃ rūpaṃ esā diṭṭhi “loko ca attā cā”ti gaṇhāti. Taṃ rūpaṃ sandhāya “so loko so attā”ti vacanaṃ vuttanti yojanā. So pecca bhavissāmīti [M 2.0091] uddhamāghātanikavādavasenāyaṃ diṭṭhīti āha “so ahaṃ paralokaṃ gantvā nicco bhavissāmī”tiādi. Dhuvoti thiro. Sassatoti sabbadābhāvī. Avipariṇāmadhammoti jarāya maraṇena ca avipariṇāmetabbasabhāvo, nibbikāroti attho. Tampi dassananti tampi tathāvuttaṃ diṭṭhidassanaṃ attānaṃ viya taṇhādiṭṭhiggāhavisesena gaṇhāti. Tenāha “etaṃ mamā”tiādi. Diṭṭhārammaṇāti diṭṭhivisayā. Kathaṃ pana diṭṭhi diṭṭhivisayā hotīti āha “vipassanāyā”tiādi. Paṭivipassanākāleti yamakato sammasanādikālaṃ sandhāyāha. Tattha akkharacintakānaṃ sadde viya, vedajjhāyīnaṃ vedasatthe viya ca diṭṭhiyaṃ diṭṭhigatikānaṃ diṭṭhiggāhappavatti daṭṭhabbā.

A standpoint for views: a view itself is a standpoint for views; this is in the way stated above. With reference to the form that this view grasps as 'the world and the self,' the statement 'that is the world, that is the self' is said. This is the construction. This view, 'I shall be after death,' is by way of a doctrine concerning the state after death, as he says: 'Having gone to the next world, I shall be eternal,' etc. Permanent means stable. Eternal means always existing. Of an unalterable nature means having a nature not to be altered by aging and death; the meaning is unchangeable. And that seeing: he grasps that seeing, which is a view so described, as if it were a self, with the specific grasping of craving and views. Therefore he says: 'This is mine,' etc. Having views as object means having views as its domain. But how is a view the domain of a view? He says: 'By way of insight,' etc. At the time of counter-insight: he says this with reference to the time of comprehension by pairs. Therein, just as for those who ponder letters sound is the object, and for those who recite the Vedas the Vedic scriptures are the object, so for those whose resort is views, the occurrence of the grasping of views should be seen as taking place in regard to views.

Samanupassatīti padassa ca tasso samanupassanā atthoti yojanā. Tena samanupassanā nāma catubbidhāti dasseti. Tattha ñāṇaṃ tāva samavisamaṃ sammā yāthāvato anupassatīti samanupassanā. Itarā pana saṃkilesavasena anu anu passantīti samanupassanā. Yadi evaṃ hotu tāva diṭṭhisamanupassanā micchādassanabhāvato, kathaṃ taṇhāmānāti? Taṇhāyapi sattānaṃ pāpakaraṇe upāyadassanavasena paññāpatirūpikā pavatti labbhateva, yāya vañcananikatisāciyogā sambhavanti. Mānopi seyyādinā dassanavaseneva tathā attānaṃ ūhatīti taṇhāmānānaṃ samanupassanāpatirūpikā pavatti labbhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Avijjamāneti “etaṃ mamā”ti evaṃ gahetabbe taṇhāvatthusmiṃ ajjhattakhandhapañcake anupalabbhamāne vinaṭṭhe. Na paritassati bhayaparittāsataṇhāparittāsānaṃ maggena samugghātitattā.

Of the word 'he contemplates,' the meaning is 'his contemplation.' This is the construction. Thereby he shows that contemplation is of four kinds. Therein, first, knowledge contemplates things rightly and in accordance with reality; this is contemplation. The others, however, contemplate again and again by way of defilement; this too is contemplation. If that is so, let the contemplation of view be accepted as such since it is wrong view, but how can this apply to craving and conceit? Even with craving, when beings devise evil means, an occurrence resembling wisdom is found, through which deceit, fraud, and crookedness arise. Conceit, too, by seeing oneself as superior and so on, infers about oneself in such a way. Thus it should be understood that an occurrence resembling contemplation is found in relation to craving and conceit. 'When it is non-existent': when the internal five aggregates, the object of craving that could be grasped as 'this is mine,' are not found, having perished. 'He is not agitated': because the agitation from fear and the agitation from craving have been uprooted by the path.

242. Catūhi kāraṇehīti “asati na paritassatī”ti vuttampi itarehi tīhi saha gahetvā vuttaṃ. Catūhi kāraṇehīti catukkoṭikasuññatākathanassa kāraṇehi. Bahiddhā asatīti bāhire [V 2.0087] vatthusmiṃ avijjamāne. Sā panassa avijjamānatā laddhavināsena vā aladdhālābhena vāti pāḷiyaṃ – “ahu vata me, taṃ vata me natthi, siyā vata me, taṃ vatāhaṃ na labhāmī”ti vuttanti tadubhayaṃ parikkhāravasena vibhajitvā tattha paritassanaṃ dassetuṃ “bahiddhā parikkhāravināse”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yānaṃ “ratho vayha”nti evamādi. Vāhanaṃ hatthiassādi.

242. 'By four reasons': what was said as 'he is not agitated when it is non-existent' is stated by taking it together with the other three. 'By four reasons' means by the reasons for the statement on the four-termed emptiness. 'When it is non-existent externally' means when an external object is non-existent. And its non-existence is due to the loss of what was obtained or the non-acquisition of what was not obtained. As it is said in the Pāli: 'Alas, I had it, but now I do not have it! Alas, may I have it, but I do not get it!' In order to show the agitation in that case by analyzing both these by way of requisites, it is said: 'at the destruction of external requisites,' etc. Therein, a vehicle is 'a chariot, a palanquin,' and so on. A mount is an elephant, a horse, and so on.

Yehi [M 2.0092] kilesehīti yehi asantapatthanādīhi kilesehi. Evaṃ bhaveyyāti evaṃ “ahu vata me”tiādinā codanādi bhaveyya. Diṭṭhiṭṭhānādhiṭṭhānapariyuṭṭhānābhinivesānusayānanti ettha aparāparaṃ pavattāsu diṭṭhīsu yā parato uppannā diṭṭhiyo, tāsaṃ purimuppannā diṭṭhiyo kāraṇaṭṭhena diṭṭhiṭṭhānāni. Adhikaraṇaṭṭhena diṭṭhādhiṭṭhānāni, pariyuṭṭhānappattiyā sabbāpi diṭṭhipariyuṭṭhānāni. “Idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”nti (ma. ni. 2.202, 427; 3.27-29; udā. 55; mahāni. 20; netti. 59) pavattiyā abhinivesā. Appahīnabhāvena santāne sayantīti anusayāti evaṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhānādīnaṃ padānaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo. Taṇhādīhi kampaniyatāya sabbasaṅkhārāva iñjitānīti sabbasaṅkhāraiñjitāni. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Upadhīyati ettha dukkhanti upadhi, khandhāva upadhi khandhūpadhi. Esa nayo sesesupi. Tadeva ca āgamma taṇhā khīyati virajjati nirujjhatīti yojanā. Ucchijjissāmi nāmassūtiādīsu nipātamattaṃ, saṃsaye vā. Tāsoti attaniyābhāvaṃ paṭicca taṇhāparittāso ceva bhayaparittāso ca. Tenāha “tāso heso”tiādi. No cassaṃ, no ca me siyāti “aha”nti kira koci no cassaṃ, “me”ti ca kiñci no siyāti. Tāsappatīkāradassanañhetaṃ.

'By which defilements': by which defilements such as longing for what is non-existent. 'Thus it would be': thus there would be complaint, etc., with 'Alas, I had it!' Regarding 'standpoints, determinations, obsessions, adherences, and underlying tendencies of views': here, among successively arising views, the earlier-arisen views are standpoints for views for the later-arisen views, in the sense of being their cause. In the sense of being a basis, they are determinations of views. Having reached the state of obsession, all are obsessions of view. In their occurrence as 'This alone is true, anything else is false,' they are adherences. Because they lie dormant in the mental continuum through not being abandoned, they are underlying tendencies. Thus the analysis of the terms 'standpoints for views,' etc., should be understood. Because they are made to tremble by craving, etc., all formations are themselves tremors; thus 'tremors of all formations.' The same method applies to the remaining two phrases. Suffering is placed upon this, thus it is a substrate; the aggregates themselves are the substrate, thus 'the substrate of the aggregates.' The same method applies to the remaining cases. And depending on that very thing, craving is destroyed, fades away, and ceases. This is the construction. In 'Shall I be annihilated? Shall I not be?' etc., the particles are mere expletives, or express doubt. Agitation: on account of the absence of what is one's own, there is both the agitation of craving and the agitation of fear. Therefore he says: 'This is that agitation,' etc. 'I might not be, and nothing might be mine': 'I,' it seems, might not be, and 'mine,' anything, might not be. This is a showing of the antidote to agitation.

243. Ettāvatāti “evaṃ vutte”tiādinā, pucchānusandhivasena pavattāya “chayimāni, bhikkhave, diṭṭhiṭṭhānānī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.241) vā. Sāpi hi ajjhattakhandhavināse paritassanakaṃ dassetvā aparitassanakaṃ dassentī pavattāti tassanakassa suññatādassanaṃ akiccasādhakampi suññatādassanamevāti imesaṃ vasena “catukkoṭikā suññatā kathitā”ti vuttaṃ. Bahiddhā parikkhāranti bāhiraṃ saviññāṇakaṃ aviññāṇakañca sattopakaraṇaṃ. Tañhi jīvitavuttiyā parikkhārakaṭṭhena “parikkhāro”ti vuttaṃ. Pariggahaṃ nāma katvāti “mama ida”nti pariggahetabbatāya pariggahitaṃ nāma katvā. Sabbopi diṭṭhiggāho “attā nicco dhuvo sassato, attā ucchijjati vinassatī”tiādinā attadiṭṭhisannissayoyevāti vuttaṃ “sakkāyadiṭṭhipamukhā dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiyo”ti. Ayāthāvaggāhinā abhinivesanapaññāpanānaṃ upatthambhabhāvato diṭṭhi eva nissayoti diṭṭhinissayo. Pariggaṇheyyāti niccādivisesayuttaṃ katvā [V 2.0088] pariggaṇheyya. Kimevaṃ pariggahetuṃ sakkuṇeyya[M 2.0093]? Sabbatthāti “taṃ, bhikkhave, attavādupādānaṃ upādiyetha, taṃ, bhikkhave, diṭṭhinissayaṃ nissayethā”ti etesupi.

243. 'To this extent': by 'when this was said,' etc., or by what was set forth in connection with the question, 'Bhikkhus, there are these six standpoints for views,' etc. (MN 22). For that teaching too proceeds by first showing agitation at the destruction of the internal aggregates and then showing non-agitation. Thus, the seeing of emptiness by one who is agitated, even if it does not accomplish the task, is still a seeing of emptiness. By means of these, it is said, 'the four-termed emptiness has been stated.' 'External requisites' means the external equipment for beings, both animate and inanimate. It is called a 'requisite' because it is an accessory for the sustenance of life. 'Having made it a possession' means having made it something that is named 'possessed' because it is to be grasped as 'this is mine.' All grasping of views—such as 'the self is permanent, stable, eternal' or 'the self is annihilated, perishes'—is entirely dependent on the view of self. Thus it is said: 'the sixty-two views headed by identity view.' Because it provides support for adherences and assertions that grasp things not in accordance with reality, a view itself is a reliance; thus 'a reliance on views.' 'He would grasp': he would grasp it having endowed it with distinctions such as permanence. How could one grasp it thus? Everywhere: even in these statements, 'Bhikkhus, one might cling to that clinging to a doctrine of self... Bhikkhus, one might rely on that reliance on views'.

244. Attani vā satīti yassa attano santakabhāvena kiñci attaniyanti vucceyya, tasmiṃ attani sati, so eva pana attā paramatthato natthīti adhippāyo. Sakkā hi vattuṃ bāhirakaparikappito attā “paramattho”ti? Siyā khandhapañcakaṃ ñeyyasabhāvattā yathā taṃ ghaṭo, yadi pana tadaññaṃ nāma kiñci abhavissa, na taṃ niyamato viparītaṃ siyāti? Na ca so paramatthato atthi pamāṇehi anupalabbhamānattā turaṅgamavisāṇaṃ viyāti. Attaniye vā parikkhāre satīti “idaṃ nāma attano santaka”nti tassa kiñcanabhāvena nicchite kismiñci vatthusmiṃ sati. Attano idanti hi attaniyanti. Ahanti satīti “ahaṃ nāmāya”nti ahaṃkāravatthubhūte paramatthato niddhāritasarūpe kismiñci sati tassa santakabhāvena mamāti kiñci gahetuṃ yuttaṃ bhaveyya. Mamāti sati “aha”nti etthāpi eseva nayo. Iti paramatthato attano anupalabbhamānattā attaniyaṃ kiñci paramatthato natthevāti sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ anattatāya anattaniyataṃ, anattaniyatāya ca anattakataṃ dasseti. Bhūtatoti bhūtatthato. Tathatoti tathasabhāvato. Thiratoti ṭhitasabhāvato nibbikārato.

244. 'When there is a self' means: when there is that self, on account of which something could be called 'belonging to a self' as its own possession; the meaning is that this very self, however, does not exist in an ultimate sense. For can it be said that an externally conceived self is 'ultimate'? It might be that the five aggregates are such, since they have a knowable nature, like a pot. But if there were anything else apart from them, would it not necessarily be the opposite? And that self does not exist in an ultimate sense, since it is not discoverable by any means of proof, like a horse's horn. 'When there are belongings' means: when there is some thing determined as 'this is my property,' by way of it being something of one's own. For 'this of a self' is what is meant by 'belonging to a self.' 'When there is "I"' means: if there were something that is the basis for the conceit 'I,' whose nature is determined in an ultimate sense, then it would be proper to grasp something as 'mine' because it is a possession of that. When there is 'mine,' the same method applies also to 'I.' Thus, since a self is not discoverable in an ultimate sense, there is ultimately nothing whatsoever that belongs to a self. This shows that because all conditioned phenomena are not-self, they do not belong to a self; and because they do not belong to a self, they are not taken as a self. 'From what is real' means according to reality. 'From what is so' means according to its true nature. 'From what is stable' means from its stable, unchanging nature.

Yasmā hutvā na hotīti yasmā pubbe asantaṃ paccayasamavāyena hutvā uppajjitvā puna bhaṅgupagamena na hoti, tasmā na niccanti aniccaṃ, adhuvanti attho. Tato eva uppādavayavattitoti uppajjanavasena nirujjhanavasena ca pavattanato. Sabhāvavigamo idha vipariṇāmo, khaṇikatā tāvakālikatā, niccasabhāvābhāvo eva niccapaṭikkhepo. Aniccadhammā hi teneva attano aniccabhāvena atthato niccataṃ paṭikkhipanti nāma. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “na niccanti anicca”nti. Uppādajarābhaṅgavasena rūpassa nirantarabādhatāti paṭipīḷanākārenassa dukkhatā. Santāpo dukkhadukkhatādivasena santāpanaṃ paridahanaṃ, tato evassa dussahatāya dukkhamatā. Tissannaṃ dukkhatānaṃ saṃsāradukkhassa ca adhiṭṭhānatāya dukkhavatthukatā. Sukhasabhāvābhāvo eva sukhapaṭikkhepo. Vipariṇāmadhammanti jarāya maraṇena ca vipariṇamanasabhāvaṃ. Yasmā idaṃ rūpaṃ paccayasamavāyena [M 2.0094] uppādaṃ, uppādānantaraṃ jaraṃ patvā avassameva bhijjati, bhinnañca bhinnameva, nāssa kassaci saṅkamoti bhavantarānupagamanasaṅkhātena saṅkamābhāvena vipariṇāmadhammataṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ “bhavasaṅkanti upagamanasabhāva”nti vuttaṃ. Pakatibhāvavijahanaṃ sabhāvavigamo nirujjhanameva. Nti aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ rūpaṃ. Imināti “no hetaṃ, bhante”ti rūpassa taṇhādiggāhānaṃ vatthubhāvapaṭikkhepena. Rūpañhi uppannaṃ ṭhitiṃ [V 2.0089] mā pāpuṇātu, ṭhitippattaṃ mā jīratu, jarappattaṃ mā bhijjatu, udayabbayehi mā kilamiyatūti na ettha kassaci vasībhāvo atthi, svāyamassa avasavattanaṭṭho anattatāsallakkhaṇassa kāraṇaṃ hotīti āha “avasavattanākārena rūpaṃ, bhante, anattāti paṭijānantī”ti. Nivāsikārakavedakaadhiṭṭhāyakavirahena tato suññatā suññaṭṭho, sāmibhūtassa kassaci abhāvo assāmikaṭṭho, yathāvuttavasavattibhāvābhāvo anissaraṭṭho, paraparikappitaattasabhāvābhāvo eva attapaṭikkhepaṭṭho.

'Because it comes to be and then is no more' means: because what did not exist before, having come to be through a combination of conditions, having arisen, is again no more by undergoing dissolution, therefore 'not permanent' means impermanent; the meaning is 'unstable.' For that very reason it is subject to arising and passing away, because it proceeds by way of arising and by way of ceasing. Here, disappearance of its nature is change; momentariness is transience; the absence of a permanent nature is itself the rejection of permanence. For impermanent things, by their very impermanent nature, indeed reject permanence in reality. For so it is said: 'Because it is not permanent, it is impermanent.' The constant affliction of form by way of arising, aging, and breaking up is its suffering nature in the sense of oppression. Torment is the burning, the consuming, by way of the suffering of pain, etc.; for that very reason, because of its unbearableness, it is the state of suffering.
