Because it is the basis for the three kinds of suffering and for the suffering of saṃsāra, it is a basis for suffering. The absence of a pleasant nature is itself the rejection of pleasure. 'Subject to change' means having the nature of changing through aging and death. Because this form arises through a combination of conditions, and after arising, having reached aging, it inevitably breaks up; and what is broken is just broken, it does not transmigrate to anyone. To make clear its nature of change through this absence of transmigration—described as not going to another existence—it is said: 'transmigration to an existence is the nature of going there.' The abandoning of its original state, the disappearance of its nature, is just cessation. Thus, form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. 'By this' means: by the rejection of form's being a basis for grasping by craving, etc., with the words 'No, venerable sir.' For with regard to form that has arisen, there is no one's mastery in the sense: 'May it not reach a static phase; having reached a static phase, may it not age; having reached aging, may it not break up; may it not be afflicted by arising and passing away.' This very state of being uncontrollable is the reason for the characteristic of not-self. Thus it is said: 'They acknowledge: "Venerable sir, form is not-self in the sense of being uncontrollable."' Through the absence of an indweller, a doer, an experiencer, and a controller, there is emptiness—this is the meaning of voidness. The absence of any owner is the meaning of ownerlessness. The absence of the state of mastery as described is the meaning of powerlessness. The absence of a self-nature conceived by others is itself the meaning of the rejection of self.

Yasmā aniccalakkhaṇena viya dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ, tadubhayena anattalakkhaṇaṃ suviññāpayaṃ, na kevalaṃ, tasmā tadubhayenettha anattalakkhaṇavibhāvanaṃ katanti dassento “bhagavā hī”tiādimāha. Tattha aniccavasenāti aniccatāvasena. Dukkhavasenāti dukkhatāvasena. Na upapajjatīti na yujjati. Tameva ayujjamānataṃ dassetuṃ “cakkhussa uppādopī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yasmā attavādī attānaṃ niccaṃ paññapeti, cakkhuṃ pana aniccaṃ, tasmā cakkhu viya attāpi anicco āpanno. Tenāha “yassa kho panā”tiādi. Tattha vetīti vigacchati nirujjhati. Iti cakkhu anattāti cakkhussa udayabbayavantatāya aniccatā, attano ca attavādinā aniccatāya anicchitattā cakkhu anattā.

He begins with 'The Blessed One indeed…' to show the following: just as the characteristic of suffering is explained by way of the characteristic of impermanence, so the characteristic of not-self is made easy to understand through both of them. And not only that, but for that reason the demonstration of the characteristic of not-self is made here through both of them. Herein, 'by way of impermanence' means by way of its impermanence. 'By way of suffering' means by way of its suffering. 'It is not tenable' means it is not logical. To show that very untenability, 'the arising of the eye, too…' etc., was said. Because a proponent of a self doctrine declares the self to be permanent, but the eye is impermanent, therefore the self, like the eye, would also be impermanent. For that reason he said, 'But for whomever…' etc. Herein, 'passes away' means it departs, it ceases. Thus, 'the eye is not-self' means: the eye is not-self because of its impermanence, since it possesses arising and passing away, and because impermanence is not wished for his self by a proponent of a self doctrine.

Kāmaṃ anattalakkhaṇasutte (saṃ. ni. 3.59; mahāva. 20) – “yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ anattā, tasmā rūpaṃ ābādhāya saṃvattatī”ti rūpassa anattatāya dukkhatā vibhāvitā viya dissati, tathāpi “yasmā rūpaṃ ābādhāya saṃvattati, tasmā anattā”ti pākaṭatāya sābādhatāya rūpassa attasārābhāvo vibhāvito, tato eva ca “na labbhati rūpe evaṃ me rūpaṃ hotu, evaṃ me rūpaṃ mā ahosī”ti rūpe kassaci anissaratā, tassa ca avasavattanākāro dassitoti āha “dukkhavasena anattataṃ [M 2.0095] dassetī”ti. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhanti yaṃ vatthu aniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ udayabbayapaṭipīḷitattā, yaṃ pana niccaṃ tadabhāvato, taṃ sukhaṃ yathā taṃ nibbānanti adhippāyo. Yaṃ tanti kāraṇaniddesovāyaṃ, yasmā rūpaṃ aniccaṃ, taṃ tasmāti attho. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattāti ettha vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Aniccanti iminā ghaṭādi viya paccayuppannattā rūpaṃ aniccanti imamatthaṃ dasseti. Imināva nayena “anattā”ti vattuṃ labbhamānepi “anattā”ti vattā nāma natthi. Evaṃ dukkhanti vadantīti etthāpi yathārahaṃ vattabbaṃ “akkhisūlādivikārappattakāle viya paccayuppannattā dukkhaṃ rūpa”ntiādinā. Duddasaṃ duppaññāpanaṃ. Tathā hi sarabhaṅgādayopi satthāro nāddasaṃsu, kuto paññāpanā. Tayidaṃ anattalakkhaṇaṃ.

Granted, in the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta it is said: 'And because, bhikkhus, form is not-self, therefore form leads to affliction,' where the suffering of form seems to be demonstrated by way of its not-self nature. Nevertheless, by the statement 'because form leads to affliction, therefore it is not-self,' the absence of a self-essence in form is demonstrated by its manifest nature of being subject to affliction. And for that very reason, by the statement 'one does not obtain in regard to form: "Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus,"' the lack of anyone's mastery over form and its uncontrollable nature are shown. Therefore he says: 'He shows the not-self nature by way of suffering.' 'What is impermanent, that is suffering' means: whatever thing is impermanent, that is suffering because it is oppressed by arising and passing away; but what is permanent, because of the absence of that, is happiness, as for instance Nibbāna—this is the meaning. 'That which... that...' is an indication of a reason; the meaning is 'because form is impermanent, therefore...'. The meaning of 'what is suffering, that is not-self' should be understood in the way stated here. By 'impermanent' he shows this meaning: 'form is impermanent because it is dependently arisen, like a pot, etc.' Although it would be possible to say 'not-self' in this same way, there is no one who actually says 'not-self' in this context. Similarly, where they say 'suffering,' it should be stated accordingly, with such words as: 'form is suffering because it is dependently arisen, like when one has reached a state of disorder such as eye-pain.' Difficult to see, difficult to make known. For even teachers like Sarabhaṅga and others did not see it; how much less could they make it known? Such is this characteristic of not-self.

Tasmātihātiādinā [V 2.0090] tiyaddhagatarūpaṃ lakkhaṇattayaṃ āropetvā vuttanti āha “etarahi aññadāpī”ti. Taṃ pana yādisaṃ tādisampi tathā vuttanti ajjhattādivisesopi vattabbo. Pi-saddena vā tassāpi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

He says 'now and at other times' to show that by the words beginning 'Therefore in this case…' it is said by ascribing the three characteristics to form belonging to the three periods of time. And whatever kind of form it is, it is also spoken of in that way; thus the distinction of internal, etc., should also be stated. Or, by the word 'pi' (also), its inclusion should be understood.

245. Ukkaṇṭhatīti nābhiramati. Aññattha “nibbidā”ti balavavipassanā vuccati, sānulomā pana saṅkhārupekkhā “vuṭṭhānagāminī”ti, sā idha kathaṃ nibbidā nāma jātāti āha “vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāya hī”tiādi. Iminā sikhāpattanibbedatāya vuṭṭhānagāminī idha nibbidānāmena vuttāti dasseti.

245. 'He is dissatisfied' means he does not delight. Elsewhere, 'disenchantment' (nibbidā) is said to be powerful insight, while equanimity towards formations that is in conformity is called 'leading to emergence.' How, then, has it come to be called 'disenchantment' here? He says, 'For by the insight leading to emergence…' etc. By this he shows that here the insight leading to emergence is called by the name 'disenchantment' because it is the disenchantment that has reached the peak.

“So anupubbena saññaggaṃ phusatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.414, 415) vatvā “saññā kho poṭṭhapāda paṭhamaṃ uppajjati, pacchā ñāṇa”nti (dī. ni. 1.416) vuttattā saññagganti vuttā lokiyāsu pahānasaññāsu sikhāpattabhāvato. Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇanti vuttā idappaccayatādassanassa matthakappattīti katvā. Tato parañhi asaṅkhatārammaṇaṃ ñāṇaṃ hoti. Tenāha – “pubbe kho susima dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ, pacchā nibbāne ñāṇa”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.70). Pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅganti vuttā maggādhigamassa paripanthabhūtasabbasaṃkilesavisuddhi padhānikassa yogino, padhānabhāvanāya vā jātaṃ aṅganti katvā. Paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhīti vuttā paramukkaṃsagatapaṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhibhāvato. Atammayatanti ettha tammayatā nāma taṇhā, kāmataṇhādīsu tāya tāya nibbattattā tammayaṃ nāma tebhūmikappavattaṃ, tassa [M 2.0096] bhāvoti katvā. Tassā taṇhāya pariyādānato vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā atammayatāti vuccati. Nissāyāti taṃ atammayataṃ paccayaṃ katvā. Āgammāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Nānattāti nānāsabhāvā bahū anekappakārā. Nānattasitāti nānārammaṇanissitā rūpādivisayā. Ekattāti ekasabhāvā. Ekattasitāti ekaṃyeva ārammaṇaṃ nissitā. Taṃ nissāyāti taṃ ekattasitaṃ upekkhaṃ paccayaṃ katvā. Etissāti etissā upekkhāya. Pahānaṃ hotīti aññāṇupekkhato pabhuti sabbaṃ upekkhaṃ pajahitvā ṭhitassa “atammayatā”ti vuttāya vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāya arūpāvacarasamāpattiupekkhāya vipassanupekkhāya ca pahānaṃ hotīti pariyādānanti vuttāti. Sabbasaṅkhāragatassa muñcitukamyatāpaṭisaṅkhānassa sikhāpattabhāvato vuṭṭhānagāminī muñcitukamyatā paṭisaṅkhānanti ca vuttā. Mudumajjhādivasena pavattiākāramattaṃ, atthato [V 2.0091] ekatthā muñcitukamyatādayo, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Dvīhi nāmehīti gotrabhu, vodānanti imehi dvīhi nāmehi.

Having said, “He gradually touches the peak of perception” (Dī. Ni. 1.414, 415), and because it is said, “Perception arises first, Poṭṭhapāda, afterwards knowledge arises” (Dī. Ni. 1.416), the worldly perceptions of abandonment are called ‘the peak of perception’ because they have reached the summit. ‘Knowledge of the stability of phenomena’ is so called because it has reached the peak of seeing specific conditionality. For after that, knowledge has the unconditioned as its object. Hence it is said: “First, Susīma, there is knowledge of the stability of phenomena, afterwards knowledge of Nibbāna” (Saṃ. Ni. 2.70). ‘The factor of striving for purity’ is so called because it is the striving of a yogin for the purification of all defilements that are obstacles to the attainment of the path, or because it is a factor born from the development of striving. ‘The purification of knowledge and vision of the path’ is so called because it is the purification of knowledge and vision of the path that has reached the highest excellence. Regarding ‘not-that-made-ness’ (atammayatā): here ‘that-made-ness’ (tammayatā) is craving. Because it is produced from this or that among sensual craving and so on, ‘that-made’ is the name for what occurs in the three planes; it is the state of that. Because of the complete abandonment of that craving, the insight leading to emergence is called ‘not-that-made-ness.’ ‘Relying on’ (nissāya) means taking that ‘not-that-made-ness’ as a condition. ‘Based on’ (āgamma) is a synonym for it. ‘Diversity’ (nānattā) means of various natures, many, and manifold. ‘Based on diversity’ (nānattasitā) means based on diverse objects like form. ‘Unity’ (ekattā) means of a single nature. ‘Based on unity’ (ekattasitā) means based on a single object. ‘Relying on that’ (taṃ nissāya) means taking that equanimity based on unity as a condition. ‘Of this’ (etissā) refers to this equanimity. ‘Abandonment occurs’ (pahānaṃ hoti): for one who stands having abandoned all equanimity, beginning from the equanimity about ignorance, the insight leading to emergence called ‘not-that-made-ness’ brings about the abandoning of the equanimity of the formless attainments and the equanimity of insight—this is called ‘complete abandonment.’ The insight leading to emergence is also called ‘the desire for release and reflection’ because it is the culmination of the reflection on the desire to be released from all conditioned phenomena. The modes of occurrence—mild, medium, etc.—are merely differences in expression; in meaning, the desire for release and so on are one, only the wording is different. ‘By two names’ (dvīhi nāmehi) refers to these two: change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) and purification (vodāna).

Virāgoti maggo, accantameva virajjati etenāti virāgo, tena. Maggena hetubhūtena. Vimuccatīti paṭippassaddhivimuttivasena vimuccati. Tenāha “phalaṃ kathita”nti.

‘Dispassion’ means the path. Because one becomes utterly dispassionate by means of it, it is called dispassion; that is, by the path as cause. ‘Is liberated’ means is liberated by way of liberation as pacification. Therefore it is said, “The fruit is spoken.”

Mahākhīṇāsavoti pasaṃsāvacanaṃ yathā “mahārājā”ti. Tathā hi taṃ pasaṃsanto satthā “ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ukkhittapaligho itipī”tiādimāhāti. Tadatthaṃ vivarituṃ “idāni tassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yathābhūtehīti yāthāvato bhūtehi. Durukkhipanaṭṭhenāti pacurajanehi ukkhipituṃ asakkuṇeyyabhāvena. Nibbānanagarappavese vibandhanena paligho viyāti palighoti vuccati. Matthakacchinno tālo pattaphalādīnaṃ anaṅgato tālāvatthu asive “sivā”ti samaññā viya. Tenāha “sīsacchinnatālo viya katā”ti. Punabbhavassa karaṇasīlo, punabbhavaṃ vā phalaṃ arahatīti ponobhaviko. Evaṃbhūto pana punabbhavaṃ deti nāmāti āha “punabbhavadāyako”ti. Punabbhavakhandhānaṃ paccayoti iminā jātisaṃsāroti phalūpacārena kāraṇaṃ vuttanti dasseti. Parikkhāti vuccati santānassa parikkhipanato. Saṃkiṇṇattāti sabbaso kiṇṇattā vināsitattā. Gabbhīrānugataṭṭhenāti gambhīraṃ anupaviṭṭhaṭṭhena. Luñcitvāti [M 2.0097] uddharitvā. Etānīti kāmarāgasaññojanādīni. Aggaḷāti vuccanti avadhāraṇaṭṭhena. Aggamaggena patito mānaddhajo etassāti patitamānaddhajo. Itarabhāroropanassa purimapadehi pakāsitattā “mānabhārasseva oropitattā pannabhāroti adhippeto”ti vuttaṃ. Mānasaṃyogeneva visaṃyuttattāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Pañcapi khandhe avisesato asmīti gahetvā pavattamāno “asmimāno”ti adhippetoti vuttaṃ “rūpe asmīti māno”tiādi.

‘A great one with taints destroyed’ is a term of praise, like ‘great king.’ For indeed, praising him, the Teacher said: “This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who has lifted the bar,” and so on. To explain its meaning, ‘now for that,’ etc., is stated. ‘As they have come to be’ means as they have actually come to be. ‘In the sense of being difficult to lift’ means because it is unable to be lifted by many people. It is called a ‘bar’ (paligha) because it is like a bar that obstructs entry into the city of Nibbāna. Like a palm tree with its top cut off, which is incapable of producing leaves, fruit, etc., just as an inauspicious palm stump might be called ‘auspicious.’ Hence he said, ‘made like a palm tree with its head cut off.’ ‘Productive of renewed existence’ (ponobhaviko) means one who has the nature of creating renewed existence, or one who deserves renewed existence as a fruit. Such a one, indeed, gives renewed existence, thus he says, ‘giver of renewed existence.’ By ‘a condition for the aggregates of renewed existence,’ it is shown that the round of births is stated as a cause by way of a figurative application to the fruit. The ‘trench’ (parikhā) is so called because it surrounds the mental continuum. ‘Being filled in’ means being completely filled in, being destroyed. ‘In the sense of having gone deep’ means in the sense of having penetrated the profound. ‘Having pulled out’ means having uprooted. ‘These’ means the fetters such as the fetter of sensual lust. ‘Bolts’ (aggaḷā) are so called in the sense of securing. ‘One whose banner of conceit has fallen’ (patitamānaddhajo) means one for whom the banner of conceit has fallen by means of the noble path. Since the laying down of other burdens has been indicated by the preceding terms, it is said: ‘He is intended as one who has laid down the burden (pannabhāro) because the burden of conceit alone has been laid down.’ ‘Because he is disjoined only from the fetter of conceit’: here too the same method applies. It is said, ‘conceit “I am” in regard to form,’ etc., because the ‘conceit “I am”’ is intended as that which proceeds by grasping the five aggregates without distinction as ‘I am.’

Nagaradvārassa parissayapaṭibāhanatthañceva sobhanatthañca ubhosu passesu esikatthambhe nikhaṇitvā ṭhapentīti āha “nagaradvāre ussāpite esikatthambhe”ti. Pākāraviddhaṃsaneneva parikkhāya bhūmisamakaraṇaṃ hotīti āha “pākāraṃ bhindanto parikkhaṃ saṃkiritvā”ti. Evantiādi upamāsaṃsandanaṃ. Santo saṃvijjamāno kāyo dhammasamūhoti sakkāyo, upādānakkhandhapañcakaṃ. Dvattiṃsa kammakāraṇā dukkhakkhandhe āgatā. Akkhirogasīsarogādayo aṭṭhanavuti rogā. Rājabhayādīni pañcavīsati mahābhayāni.

He says, ‘the pillars erected at the city gate,’ because they dig in and set up pillars on both sides of a city gate for the purpose of warding off danger and for adornment. He says, ‘breaking the wall, he fills in the trench,’ because by the demolition of the wall the trench is made level with the ground. ‘Thus,’ and so on, is the connection of the similes. The existing, present body (kāya) is a group of phenomena (dhammasamūha), thus ‘existing body’ (sakkāya); this is the five aggregates subject to clinging. Thirty-two kinds of torture have come into the mass of suffering. Ninety-eight diseases, such as eye disease, head disease, and so on. Twenty-five great fears, such as fear of kings, and so on.

246. Anadhigamanīyaviññāṇatanti [V 2.0092] “idaṃ nāma nissāya iminā nāma ākārena pavattatī”ti evaṃ duviññeyyacittataṃ. Anvesanti paccatte ekavacananti āha “anvesanto”ti. Sattopi tathāgatoti vuccati “tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.65) viya. Satto hi yatheko kammakilesehi itthattaṃ āgato, tathā aparopi āgatoti “tathāgato”ti vuccati. Uttamapuggaloti bhagavantaṃ sandhāya vadati. Khīṇāsavopīti yo koci khīṇāsavopi “tathāgato”ti adhippeto. Sopi hi yatheko catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu sūpaṭṭhitacitto satta bojjhaṅge yathābhūtaṃ bhāvetvā anuttaraṃ arahattaṃ āgato adhigato, tathā aparopi āgatoti “tathāgato”ti vuccati. Asaṃvijjamānoti paramatthato anupalabbhanīyo. Avindeyyoti na vinditabbo, duviññeyyoti attho.

246. ‘The untraceability of consciousness’ means the state of mind being difficult to cognize thus: ‘Relying on such and such, it proceeds in such and such a way.’ He says ‘seeking’ (anvesanto), using the singular for the plural ‘they seek’ (anvesanti). Even a being is called a Tathāgata, as in such passages as “a Tathāgata after death…” (Dī. Ni. 1.65). For just as one being has come (āgato) to this state through kamma and defilements, so (tathā) another has come (āgato); thus he is called a ‘Tathāgata’ (Thus-come). ‘The ultimate person’ he says referring to the Blessed One. ‘Even one with taints destroyed’: any one with taints destroyed is intended by ‘Tathāgata.’ For just as one, with mind well established in the four establishments of mindfulness, having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they have come to be, has come to, has attained, the unsurpassed state of an arahant, so another has come; thus he is called a ‘Tathāgata.’ ‘Non-existent’ means not discoverable in an ultimate sense. ‘Undiscoverable’ (avindeyya) means not to be found; the meaning is ‘difficult to cognize.’

Tathāgato satto puggaloti na paññapemi paramatthato sattasseva abhāvatoti adhippāyo. Kiṃ paññapessāmi paññattiupādānassapi dharamānakassa [M 2.0098] abhāvato. “Anuppādo khemaṃ, anuppatti khema”ntiādinā asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā pakkhandhanavasena pavattaṃ aggaphalasamāpattiatthaṃ vipassanācittaṃ vā.

The intended meaning is: I do not describe a Tathāgata as a being or a person because in an ultimate sense a being does not exist. What could I describe, since even the basis for description, while it endures, is non-existent? By such phrases as “Non-arising is security, non-occurrence is security,” it refers to the insight consciousness that proceeds by way of plunging into the unconditioned element for the purpose of attaining the highest fruit.

Tucchāti karaṇe nissakkavacananti āha “tucchakenā”ti. Vinayatīti vinayo, so eva venayiko. Tathā manti tathābhūtaṃ maṃ. Paramatthato vijjamānassa hi sattassa abhāvaṃ vadanto sattavināsapaññāpako ca nāma siyā, ahaṃ pana paramatthato avijjamānaṃ taṃ “natthī”ti vadāmi. Yathā ca loko voharati, tatheva taṃ voharāmi, tathābhūtaṃ maṃ ye samaṇabrāhmaṇā “venayiko samaṇo gotamo”ti vadantā asatā tucchā musā abhūtena abbhācikkhantīti yojanā. Appaṭisandhikassa khīṇāsavassa carimacittaṃ nirupādānato anupādāno viya jātavedo parinibbutaṃ idaṃ nāma nissitanti na paññāyatīti vadanto kimettāvatā ucchedavādī bhaveyya, nāhaṃ kadācipi atthi, nāpi koci atthīti vadāmi. Evaṃ sante kiṃ nissāya te moghapurisā sato sattassa nāma ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapetīti vadantā asatā…pe… abbhācikkhantīti ayamettha adhippāyo.

'Empty' (tucchā): this refers to the word 'with what is empty' (tucchakena) in the instrumental sense. 'He removes' (vinayati), thus 'removal' (vinayo); one who does so is an 'exterminator' (venayiko). 'Me thus' (tathā maṃ) means me who is such. For one who speaks of the absence of a being that ultimately exists would indeed be a proclaimer of the annihilation of a being, but I say that what does not ultimately exist 'does not exist.' And just as the world expresses it, so I express it. The construction is: those ascetics and brahmins who say of me, being such, 'The ascetic Gotama is an exterminator,' slander me with what is untrue, empty, false, and non-existent. When I say that the final consciousness of one without rebirth-linking, whose taints are destroyed, is extinguished like a fire without fuel because it is without sustenance, and is not described as relying on this or that, how could I, on that account, be an annihilationist? I do not ever say, 'It exists,' nor, 'Someone exists.' This being so, on what grounds do those foolish men, saying, 'He proclaims the cutting off, the destruction, the non-existence of an existing being,' slander me with what is untrue, empty, false, and non-existent? This is the meaning here.

Mahābodhimaṇḍamhīti bodhimaṇḍaggahaṇena sattasattāhamāha. Tena dhammacakkapavattanato (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 13; paṭi. ma. 2.30) pubbe vuttaṃ tantidesanaṃ vadati[V 2.0093]. Catusaccameva paññapemīti etena saccavimuttā satthudesanā natthīti dasseti. Ettha ca – “pubbe ceva etarahi ca dukkhañceva paññapemi dukkhassa ca nirodha”nti vadanto bhagavā nāhaṃ kadācipi “attā ucchijjati, vinassatī”ti vā, “attā nāma koci atthī”ti vā vadāmi. Evaṃ sante kiṃ nissāya te moghapurisā “sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapetī”ti asatā tucchena abbhācikkhantīti dasseti. Pareti amāmakā, mama ovādassa abhājanabhūtāti atthoti āha “saccāni…pe… asamatthapuggalā”ti. Adhippāyenāti iminā tesaṃ adhippāyamattaṃ, rosanavihesanāni pana tathāgatassa ākāsassa vilikhanaṃ viya na sambhavantiyevāti dasseti. Āhanati cittanti āghāto. Appatītā honti etenāti appaccayo. Cittaṃ na abhirādhayatīti anabhiraddhi. Atuṭṭhīti tuṭṭhipaṭipakkho tathāpavatto cittuppādo, kodho eva vā.

By 'the great seat of enlightenment' (Mahābodhimaṇḍamhī), he refers to the seven weeks by taking the Bodhimaṇḍa. Therefore, he speaks of the teaching previously mentioned before the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1081; Mahāva. 13; Paṭi. Ma. 2.30). By 'I proclaim only the four truths,' he shows that there is no teaching of the Teacher apart from the truths. And here, the Blessed One, saying: 'Both formerly and now, I proclaim only suffering and the cessation of suffering,' indicates that he never says, 'The self is annihilated or destroyed,' nor does he say, 'There exists some self.' If this is so, on what grounds do these misguided men falsely accuse me, saying, 'He proclaims the annihilation, destruction, and disappearance of an existing being'? 'Others' (pare) refers to those who are not my followers, who are unfit for my instruction—this is the meaning of 'those incapable of understanding the truths' (saccāni...pe... asamatthapuggalā). By 'according to (their) intention' (adhippāyena), this shows that it is only their intention; anger and resentment towards the Tathāgata are impossible, like drawing lines in the sky. 'Strikes the mind' (āhanati cittaṃ) means animosity (āghāto). 'They are displeased by this' (appatītā honti etena) means lack of conviction (appaccayo). 'The mind is not delighted' (cittaṃ na abhirādhayati) means non-contentment (anabhiraddhi). 'Displeasure' (atuṭṭhī) is the opposite of satisfaction, a state of mind thus arisen—or simply anger.

Pareti [M 2.0099] aññe ekacce. Ānandanti pamodanti etenāti ānando, pītiyā evetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sobhanamanatā somanassaṃ, cetasikasukhassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Uppilati purimāvatthāya bhijjati visesaṃ āpajjatīti uppilaṃ, tadeva uppilāvitaṃ, tassa bhāvo uppilāvitattaṃ. Yāya uppannāya kāyacittaṃ vātapūritabhattā viya uddhumāyanākārappattaṃ hoti, tassā gehassitāya odaggiyapītiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Saccāni paṭivijjhituṃ asamatthāti dukkhameva uppajjati nirujjhati ca, na añño satto nāma atthīti evaṃ jānituṃ asamatthā “attā nāma atthī”ti evaṃdiṭṭhino appahīnavipallāsā. Uttamaṃ pasādanīyaṭṭhānaṃ tathāgatampi akkosanti, kimaṅgaṃ pana bhikkhūti adhippāyo.

'Others' (pare) means some others. 'Joy' (ānando) means they rejoice, they delight in this; it is a term for rapture (pīti). 'Beautiful pleasantness' (sobhanamanatā) is gladness (somanassaṃ); it is a term for mental happiness. 'It swells' (uppilati) means the previous state is broken, it reaches a special condition; that very swelling is 'uppilaṃ', which becomes 'uppilāvitaṃ', and its state is 'uppilāvitattaṃ'. By which, once arisen, body and mind become like a wind-filled bellows, reaching a bloated state—this is a term for the exultant rapture associated with the household life (gehassitāya odaggiyapītiyā). 'Unable to penetrate the truths' means unable to know thus: 'Only suffering arises and ceases, and there is no other being'—those whose distortions are unabandoned hold the view, 'There is a self.' They even revile the Tathāgata, the supreme basis for confidence—what then of the monks? This is the meaning.

247. Anattaniyepi khandhapañcake micchāgāhavasena attaniyasaññāya pavattassa chandarāgassa pahānaṃ. Amhākaṃ neva attāti yasmā rūpavedanādiyeva attaggāhavatthu tabbinimuttassa lobhaneyyassa abhāvato. Etaṃ tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṃ na amhākaṃ rūpaṃ, na viññāṇaṃ, tasmā amhākaṃ neva attāti yojanā. Ajjhattikassa vatthuno neva attāti paṭikkhittattā bāhiravatthu attaniyabhāvena paṭikkhittaṃ hotīti āha “amhākaṃ cīvarādiparikkhāropi na hotī”ti. Khandhapañcakaṃyevāti bāhiravatthuṃ nidassanaṃ katvā khandhapañcakaṃyeva na tumhākanti pajahāpeti. Na uppāṭetvā kandaṃ viya. Na luñcitvā vā kese viyāti. Iminā rūpādīnaṃ nāmamukhena pahānaṃ icchanti. Ulliṅgitamatthaṃ chandarāgavinayena pajahāpetīti sarūpato dasseti.

247. The abandonment of the desire and lust that has arisen from the perception of 'belonging to self'—due to wrong grasping—in regard to the five aggregates, which are not one's own. Since form, feeling, etc., are merely the basis for grasping at self, and because there is no object of craving apart from that, therefore it is said, 'not our self.' The connection should be made: 'This grass, wood, branches, and leaves are not our form, nor our consciousness; therefore, they are not our self.' Because the internal basis has been rejected with 'not self,' the external basis is also rejected as 'belonging to self.' Therefore it is said: 'Even our robes and other requisites are not ours.' Having made the external basis an example, it causes one to abandon the five aggregates themselves with the thought, 'they are not yours.' Not like uprooting a bulb, nor like plucking hair. Through this, they wish to abandon form, etc., by way of name. It shows in essence that abandonment is achieved by the removal of desire and lust, which is the meaning indicated.

248. “Taṃ [V 2.0094] kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā”tiādi desanā tiparivaṭṭaṃ. Yāva imaṃ ṭhānanti “evaṃ svākkhāto”ti yāvāyaṃ pāḷipadeso. Suviññeyyabhāvena akkhātattāpi svākkhātoti āha “sukathitattā eva uttāno vivaṭo pakāsito”ti. Tiriyaṃ vidāraṇena chinnaṃ, dīghaso phālanena bhinnaṃ, tato eva tattha tattha sibbitagaṇṭhikatajiṇṇavatthaṃ pilotikā, tadabhāvato chinnapilotiko, pilotikarahitoti attho. Iriyāpatha-saṇṭhapanaavijjamānajhāna-vipassanāni chinnāya avijjamānāya paṭipattiyā sibbanagaṇṭhikaraṇasadisāni, tādisaṃ idha natthīti āha “na hettha…pe… atthī”ti. Patiṭṭhātuṃ na labhatīti pesalehi [M 2.0100] saddhiṃ saṃvāsavasenapi patiṭṭhātuṃ na labhati, visesādhigamavasena pana vattabbameva natthi.

248. 'What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent?'—this teaching, and so on, is in three cycles. 'Up to this point' (yāva imaṃ ṭhānaṃ) refers to the Pali passage 'thus well proclaimed' (evaṃ svākkhāto). Because it is proclaimed in an easily understandable way, it is also called 'well proclaimed,' as it is said: 'Well spoken, thus open, revealed, and made plain.' Torn crosswise by rending, split lengthwise by cleaving, an old cloth stitched and knotted here and there is therefore a 'rag' (pilotikā). Lacking that, it is 'chinnapilotiko,' meaning 'devoid of rags.' Postures, composure, non-existent jhāna, and insight are like stitching and knotting a cut-off, non-existent practice. Such things are not found here, hence it is said: 'There is not... there is.' 'One cannot find a footing' (patiṭṭhātuṃ na labhati) means one cannot find a footing even by dwelling with the virtuous; in terms of attaining distinction, there is nothing more to be said.

Kāraṇḍavaṃ niddhamathāti vipannasīlatāya kacavarabhūtaṃ puggalaṃ kacavaramiva nirapekkhā apanetha. Kasambuñcāpakassathāti kasaṭabhūtañca naṃ khattiyādīnaṃ majjhagataṃ sambhinnaṃ paggharitakuṭṭhaṃ caṇḍālaṃ viya apakassatha nikkaḍḍhatha. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Saṅghārāmo nāma sīlavantānaṃ kato, na dussīlānaṃ, yato etadeva. Tato palāpe vāhetha, assamaṇe samaṇamānineti yathā palāpā antosārarahitā ataṇḍulā bahi thusena vīhi viya dissanti, evaṃ pāpabhikkhū antosīlarahitāpi bahi kāsāvādiparikkhārena bhikkhū viya dissanti, tasmā “palāpā”ti vuccanti, te palāpe vāhetha odhunātha vidhamatha. Paramatthato assamaṇe vesamattena samaṇamānine evaṃ niddhamitvāna…pe… patissatāti. Tattha kappayavhoti kappetha, karothāti vuttaṃ hoti. Patissatāti pati pati satā sampajānantā suṭṭhu pajānantā. Patissatā vā sappatissā aññamaññaṃ sagāravā. Athevaṃ suddhā suddhehi saṃvāsaṃ kappentā diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena samaggā. Anukkamena paripākagatapaññatāya nipakā. Sabbassevimassa dukkhavaṭṭassa antaṃ karissatha, parinibbānaṃ pāpuṇissathāti attho.

'Cast out the Kāraṇḍava duck' (kāraṇḍavaṃ niddhamatha) means remove without concern the person who has become like refuse due to corrupted virtue. 'Drag away the impure' (kasambuñcāpakassatha) means pull away and discard that one who has become refuse, who is like an outcaste with broken, oozing leprosy among nobles and others. Why? The monastery is made for the virtuous, not the immoral—this is the reason. Then, 'winnow out the chaff' (palāpe vāhetha), meaning those who, though not true ascetics, pretend to be ascetics. Just as chaff, lacking inner substance and without grain, appears like rice covered in husk, so too do wicked monks, devoid of inner virtue, appear as monks externally through their saffron robes and other requisites. Therefore, they are called 'chaff.' Winnow them out, shake them off, and scatter them. Having thus cast out those who are not ascetics in the ultimate sense, but who merely pretend to be so by their appearance... be mindful. Here, 'arrange' (kappayavho) means to establish or do. 'Be mindful' (patissatā) means to be repeatedly aware, fully comprehending. Or, 'be mindful' means to be mutually respectful and considerate of one another. Thus, the pure, living in harmony with the pure, are united by commonality of view and virtue. Gradually, with matured wisdom, they become discerning. You will bring an end to this entire round of suffering and attain final extinguishment—this is the meaning.

Vaṭṭaṃ tesaṃ natthi paññāpanāya sabbaso samucchinnavaṭṭamūlakattā.

For them, there is no cycle for designation, since the root of the cycle has been completely cut off.

Dhammaṃ anussaranti, dhammassa vā anussaraṇasīlāti dhammānusārino. Evaṃ saddhānusārinopi veditabbā. Paṭipannassāti paṭipajjamānassa, sotāpattimaggaṭṭhopi adhippeto. Adhimattanti balavaṃ. Paññāvāhīti paññaṃ vāheti, paññā vā imaṃ puggalaṃ vahatīti paññāvāhītipi vadanti. Paññāpubbaṅgamanti paññaṃ purecārikaṃ katvā. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo paññāsaṅkhātena dhammena sarati anussaratīti dhammānusārī. Saddhāvāhīti saddhaṃ vāheti, saddhā vā [V 2.0095] imaṃ puggalaṃ vahatīti saddhāvāhītipi vadanti. Saddhāpubbaṅgamanti saddhaṃ purecārikaṃ katvā. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo saddhāya sarati anussaratīti saddhānusārī. Saddhāmattanti “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinā buddhasubuddhatāya saddahanamattaṃ. Matta-saddena aveccappasādaṃ nivatteti. Pemamattanti yathāvuttasaddhānusārena uppannaṃ tuṭṭhimattaṃ. Sinehoti keci. Evaṃ vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nisinnānanti [M 2.0101] kalāpasammasanādivasena āraddhavipassanānaṃ. Ekā saddhāti vipassanānusārena svākkhātadhammatā siddhā, tato eva ekā seṭṭhā uḷārā saddhā uppajjati. Ekaṃ pemanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Sagge ṭhapitā viya hontīti tesaṃ saddhāpemānaṃ saggasaṃvattaniyatāya abyabhicārībhāvamāha. Cūḷasotāpannoti vadanti ekadesena saccānubodhe ṭhitattā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

They recollect the Dhamma, or they are by nature inclined to recollect the Dhamma—thus they are called Dhamma-followers. In the same way, the faith-follower should be understood. 'Of one practicing' (paṭipannassa) means of one who is practicing; it also refers to one who is established on the path of stream-entry. 'Intense' (adhimattaṃ) means strong. 'Led by wisdom' (paññāvāhī) means one is carried by wisdom, or wisdom carries this person—thus they also call it 'led by wisdom.' 'With wisdom as the forerunner' (paññāpubbaṅgamaṃ) means having made wisdom the precursor. 'This is called' (ayaṃ vuccati) means this kind of person recollects and remembers through the factor called wisdom—thus this one is called a Dhamma-follower. 'Led by faith' (saddhāvāhī) means one is carried by faith, or faith carries this person—thus they also call it 'led by faith.' 'With faith as the forerunner' (saddhāpubbaṅgamaṃ) means having made faith the precursor. 'This is called' (ayaṃ vuccati) means this kind of person recollects and remembers through faith—thus this one is called a faith-follower. 'Mere faith' (saddhāmattā) means just the act of believing, simply having faith in the Buddha's perfect enlightenment, as in 'Indeed, the Blessed One is...' The word 'mere' excludes unwavering confidence. 'Mere affection' (pemamattā) means the mere satisfaction arising from faith as described above. Some say it is fondness. 'Of those who have established insight and are seated' refers to those who have begun insight practice, by way of comprehending aggregates and so on. 'One faith' (ekā saddhā) means that in accordance with insight, the well-proclaimed nature of the Dhamma is established, and from that, a single, supreme, and excellent faith arises. 'One affection' (ekaṃ pemaṃ)—here too, the same method applies. 'As if placed in heaven' speaks to the unerring nature of their faith and affection in leading to heaven. They are called 'lesser stream-enterers' because they are established in a partial realization of the truths. The rest is easily understood.

Alagaddūpamasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The clarification of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Alagaddūpama Sutta is complete.

3. Vammikasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Vammika Sutta

249. Piyavacananti [V 2.0096] piyasamudācāro. Viññujātikā hi paraṃ piyena samudācarantā “bhava”nti vā, “devānaṃ piyo”ti vā, “āyasmā”ti vā samudācaranti, tasmā sammukhā sambodhanavasena “āvuso”ti, tirokkhaṃ “āyasmā”ti ayampi samudācāro. Mahākassapauruvelakassapādayo aññepi kassapanāmakā atthīti “katarassa kassapassā”ti pucchanti. Raññāti kosalaraññā. “Sañjāniṃsū”ti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “ayaṃ panā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Assāti kumārakassapassa, “sañjāniṃsū”ti vuttasañjānanassa vā. Puññāni karontoti kappasatasahassaṃ devesu ca manussesu ca nibbattitvā dānādīni puññāni bhāvento. Osakkanteti parihāyamāne. Paṭhamanti kumārikākāle. Satthā upālittheraṃ paṭicchāpesi taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vinayakammenevassā bhikkhuniyā pabbajjāya arogabhāvaṃ.

249. “Piyavacana” means affectionate address. Indeed, people of discernment, when addressing others affectionately, use terms like “bhava,” “devānaṃ piyo,” or “āyasmā.” Therefore, “āvuso” is used for direct address, and “āyasmā” for indirect address; this too is a form of affectionate address. Since there were other Kassapas, such as Mahākassapa and Uruvelakassapa, they ask, “Which Kassapa?” “Raññā” means by the king of Kosala. To elaborate on the meaning stated briefly as “sañjāniṃsū,” the passage beginning with “ayaṃ pana” and so on was commenced. “Assāti” refers to Kumārakassapa, or to the recognition mentioned in “sañjāniṃsū.” “Puññāni karonto” means that for a hundred thousand aeons, having been reborn among gods and humans, he cultivated meritorious deeds such as generosity. “Osakkante” means while declining. “Paṭhama” refers to the time when she was a young maiden. The Teacher had the Elder Upāli settle that legal issue by means of a Vinaya act, thereby establishing the validity of that nun's ordination.

Paññattivibhāvanāti “andhavana”ntveva paññāyamānassa vibhāvanā. Olīyatīti saṅkucati saṇikaṃ vattati. Bhāṇakoti sarabhāṇako. Yaṃ atthi, taṃ gahetvāti idāni pariyesitabbaṭṭhānaṃ natthi, yathāgataṃ pana yaṃ atthi, taṃ gahetvā. Balavaguṇeti adhimattaguṇe. Kassapabhagavato kāle niruḷhasamaññāvasena vacanasantatiyā avicchedena ca imasmimpi buddhuppāde taṃ “andhavana”ntveva paññāyittha, uparūparivaḍḍhamānāya pathaviyā upari rukkhagacchādīsu sañjāyantesupīti. Sekkhapaṭipadanti sekkhabhāvāvahaṃ visuddhipaṭipattiṃ.

“Paññattivibhāvanā” means the clarification of what is designated as “Andhavana.” “Olīyati” means it shrinks or moves slowly. “Bhāṇaka” refers to a reciter. “Yaṃ atthi, taṃ gahetvā” means there is no need to seek further now; rather, one should take what is already present as it is. “Balavaguṇa” means an exceedingly great virtue. In the time of the Blessed Kassapa, due to established convention and the uninterrupted continuity of speech, it was designated as “Andhavana” even in this Buddha-dispensation, and even as trees, shrubs, and so on grew upon the earth that was rising ever higher. “Sekkhapaṭipadā” means the path of practice leading to the state of a trainee, the path of purification.

Aññatara-saddo [M 2.0102] apākaṭe viya pākaṭepi vattati eka-saddena samānatthattāti dassetuṃ “abhijānātī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhayabheravadassitampi abhikkanta-saddassa atthuddhāraṃ idha dassento evaṃ heṭṭhā tattha tattha katā atthasaṃvaṇṇanā parato tasmiṃ tasmiṃ suttapadese yathārahaṃ vattabbāti nayadassanaṃ karoti. Kañcanasannibhattacatā suvaṇṇavaṇṇaggahaṇena gahitāti adhippāyenāha “chaviya”nti. Chavigatā pana vaṇṇadhātu eva “suvaṇṇavaṇṇo”ti ettha vaṇṇaggahaṇena gahitāti apare. Vaṇṇīyati kittīyati ugghosananti vaṇṇo, thuti. Vaṇṇīyati asaṅkarato vavatthapīyatīti vaṇṇo, kulavaggo. Vaṇṇīyati phalaṃ etena yathāsabhāvato vibhāvīyatīti vaṇṇo, kāraṇaṃ. Vaṇṇanaṃ dīgharassādivasena saṇṭhahananti vaṇṇo, saṇṭhānaṃ. Vaṇṇīyati aṇumahantādivasena pamīyatīti vaṇṇo, pamāṇaṃ. Vaṇṇeti vikāramāpajjamānaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetīti [V 2.0097] vaṇṇo, rūpāyatanaṃ. Evaṃ tena tena pavattinimittena vaṇṇa-saddassa tasmiṃ tasmiṃ atthe pavatti veditabbā.

To show that the word aññatara, like eka, is used in both an unclear and a clear sense, the phrase “abhijānāti” and so on is stated. Here, even when showing the extracted meaning of the word abhikkanta as shown in the Bhayabherava Sutta, it demonstrates the method that the explanation of meaning made earlier in various places below should be stated appropriately in each respective passage of the sutta. With the intention that “skin resembling burnished gold” is understood by the grasping of “golden color,” it is said “in complexion.” Others say that the color element pertaining to the skin itself is grasped by the word “color” in the phrase “golden in color.” “Vaṇṇo” means praise, as it is glorified, celebrated, and proclaimed. “Vaṇṇo” means lineage, as it is classified and distinctly determined without confusion. “Vaṇṇo” means cause, because by it the result is clearly distinguished according to its own nature. “Vaṇṇo” means form, as it is established in terms of long, short, and other features. “Vaṇṇo” means measurement, as it is measured in terms of small, large, and other features. “Vaṇṇo” means the sense object of sight, because it manifests a heart-pleasing state as it undergoes change. Thus, the occurrence of the word “vaṇṇa” in each respective meaning should be understood according to each reason for its occurrence.

Anavasesattaṃ sakalatā kevalatā. Kevalakappāti ettha keci īsaṃ asamattā kevalā kevalakappāti vadanti, evaṃ sati anavasesattho eva kevala-saddo siyā. Anatthantarena pana kappa-saddena padavaḍḍhanaṃ katvā kevalā eva kevalakappā. Tathā vā kappanīyattā paññapetabbattā kevalakappā. Yebhuyyatā bahulabhāvo. Abyāmissatā vijātiyena asaṅkaro suddhatā. Anatirekatā taṃmattatā visesābhāvo. Kevalakappanti kevalaṃ daḷhaṃ katvāti attho. Kevalaṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ sabbasaṅkhatavivittattā. Tenāha “visaṃyogādianekattho”ti. Kevalaṃ etassa adhigataṃ atthīti kevalī, sacchikatanirodho khīṇāsavo.

“Anavasesatta” means entirety, completeness, wholeness. Here, concerning “kevalakappā,” some say it means “slightly incomplete, hence kevalakappā.” If that were so, the word 'kevala' would have to mean 'without remainder.' Alternatively, the word 'kappa' is added as a mere expletive without altering the meaning, so 'kevalakappā' is simply 'complete.' Or, it is “kevalakappā” because it is fit to be so considered and designated. “Yebhuyyatā” means prevalence, abundance. “Abyāmissatā” means unmixedness, not mixed with a different kind, purity. “Anatirekatā” means non-excessiveness, being just that much, absence of difference. “Kevalakappanti” means “making kevala firm”—this is the meaning. “Kevala” is called Nibbāna because it is entirely free from all conditioned things. Therefore, it is said, “it has many meanings beginning with disjunction.” One for whom kevala has been attained is called a “kevalī”—the one who has directly realized cessation, the one whose defilements are destroyed.

Kappa-saddo panāyaṃ saupasaggo anupasaggo cāti adhippāyena okappanīyapade labbhamānaṃ okappasaddamattaṃ nidasseti, aññathā kappa-saddassa atthuddhāre okappanīyapadaṃ anidassanameva siyā. Samaṇakappehīti vinayasiddhehi [M 2.0103] samaṇavohārehi. Niccakappanti niccakālaṃ. Paññattīti nāmaṃ. Nāmañhetaṃ tassa āyasmato, yadidaṃ kappoti. Kappitakesamassūti kattarikāya cheditakesamassu. Dvaṅgulakappoti majjhanhikavelāya vītikkantāya dvaṅgulatāvikappo. Lesoti apadeso. Anavasesaṃ pharituṃ samatthassapi obhāsassa kenaci kāraṇena ekadesapharaṇampi siyā, ayaṃ pana sabbasova pharīti dassetuṃ samantattho kappa-saddo gahitoti āha “anavasesaṃ samantato”ti.

With the intention that this word 'kappa' occurs both with and without a prefix, he points to the word 'okappa' as found in the term 'okappanīya'. Otherwise, in an extraction of the meaning of the word 'kappa', the term 'okappanīya' would not be pointed out at all. “Samaṇakappehīti” refers to monastic usages established by the Vinaya. “Niccakappanti” means perpetually. “Paññattīti” means a name. This is the name of that venerable one, namely, Kappa. “Kappitakesamassūti” means hair and beard cut with scissors. “Dvaṅgulakappoti” refers to the allowance of two finger-breadths after the midday period has passed. “Lesoti” means a pretext. Although a light capable of completely illuminating without remainder might, for some reason, only illuminate partially, here, to show that it illuminates completely in every way, the term kappa is taken in the sense of “all around,” hence it is said, “without remainder, all around.”

Samaṇasaññāsamudācārenāti “ahaṃ samaṇo”ti evaṃ uppannasaññāsamuṭṭhitena samudācārena, tannimittena vā tabbohārena. Pubbayogeti pubbayogakathāyaṃ. Papañco esāti eso tumhesu āgatesu yathāpavatto paṭisanthāro kathāsamudācāro ca amhākaṃ papañco. Ettakampi akatvā samaṇadhammameva karomāti adhippāyo.

“Samaṇasaññāsamudācārena” means with the conduct arisen from the perception “I am a monk,” or with speech on account of that. “Pubbayoge” refers to in the discourse on previous connections. “Papañco esa” means that this hospitality and conversation that has occurred upon your arrival is a proliferation for us. The intention is, “Without doing even this much, we will do only the monk’s duty.”

Ariyabhūmiṃ pattoti anāgāmiphalaṃ adhigato. Pakkusātikulaputtaṃ sandhāya vadati. Vibhajitvāti vibhāgaṃ katvā. Turitālapanavasenāti turitaṃ ālapanavasena. Tena dullabho ayaṃ samaṇo, tasmā sīghamassa pañho kathetabbo, iminā ca sīghaṃ gantvā satthā pucchitabboti turitaṃ ālapīti dasseti. “Yathā vā”tiādinā pana vacanālaṅkāravasena dvikkhattuṃ ālapati. Evamāhāti “bhikkhu bhikkhū”ti evaṃ dvikkhattuṃ avoca.

“Ariyabhūmiṃ patto” means having attained the fruit of non-returning. He is speaking with reference to the clansman Pakkusāti. “Vibhajitvā” means having analyzed. “Turitālapanavasena” means by way of quick address. This indicates that he addressed him quickly, thinking: “This recluse is rare, so the matter should be explained to him quickly, and he should go swiftly and ask the Teacher.” However, by the phrase “yathā vā” and so on, he addresses him twice for the sake of verbal embellishment. “Evamāha” means he spoke twice, saying, “Monk, monk.”

Vammikapariyāyena [V 2.0098] karajakāyaṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā dassentī devatā “ayaṃ vammiko”ti āha. Tāya pana bhāvatthassa abhāsitattā saddatthameva dassento “purato ṭhitaṃ…pe… ayanti āhā”ti avoca. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Maṇḍūkanti thalamaṇḍūkaṃ. So hi uddhumāyikāti vuccati, na udakamaṇḍūko. Tassa nivāsato vāto mā kho bādhayitthāti “uparivātato apagammā”ti vuttaṃ. Kathaṃ panāyaṃ devatā iminā nīhārena ime pañhe therassa ācikkhīti? Keci tāva āhu – yathāsutamatthaṃ upamābhāvena gahetvā attano paṭibhānena upameyyatthaṃ manasā cintetvā taṃ bhagavāva imassa ācikkhissati. Sā ca desanā atthāya hitāya sukhāya hotīti “ayaṃ vammiko”tiādinā upamāvaseneva pannarasa pañhe therassa ācikkhi. Kassapasammāsambuddhakāle kira bārāṇasiyaṃ eko seṭṭhi aḍḍho mahaddhano mahantaṃ nidhānaṃ [M 2.0104] nidahitvā palighādiākārāni kānicipi laṅgāni tattha ṭhapesi. So maraṇakāle attano sahāyassa brāhmaṇassa ārocesi – “imasmiṃ ṭhāne mayā nidhānaṃ nidahitaṃ, taṃ mama puttassa viññutaṃ pattassa dassetī”ti vatvā kālamakāsi. Brāhmaṇo sahāyakaputtassa viññutaṃ pattakāle taṃ ṭhānaṃ dassesi. So nikhanitvā sabbapacchā nāgaṃ passi, nāgo attano puttaṃ disvā “sukheneva dhanaṃ gaṇhatū”ti apagacchi. Svāyamattho tadā loke pākaṭo jāto. Ayaṃ pana devatā tadā bārāṇasiyaṃ gahapatikule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto satthari parinibbute uraṃ datvā sāsane pabbajito pañcahi sahāyakabhikkhūhi saddhiṃ samaṇadhammamakāsi. Ye sandhāya vuttaṃ “pañca bhikkhū nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā”tiādi. Tena vuttaṃ “yathāsutamatthaṃ upamābhāvena gahetvā”tiādi. Apare pana “devatā attano paṭibhānena ime pañhe evaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā therassa ācikkhī”ti vadanti. Devaputte nissakkaṃ devaputtapañhattā tassa atthassa.

The deity, having directly shown the body born of action by way of the anthill simile, said, “This is an anthill.” However, because he did not speak of the essential meaning, he merely indicated the literal meaning, saying, “Standing in front... this is it,” and so on. The same method applies to the rest. “Maṇḍūka” refers to a land frog, for it is called uddhumāyikā, not a water frog. It was said, “Having gone away from upwind,” lest the wind should trouble it from its dwelling. But how did this deity, in this manner, explain these questions to the elder? Some say: Taking the meaning as heard, by way of simile, and considering the meaning of what is being compared with his own wisdom, he thought, “The Blessed One himself will explain this to him.” And that teaching was for the sake of benefit, welfare, and happiness. Thus, through the method of similes, he explained the fifteen questions to the elder, beginning with “This is an anthill.” In the time of the Buddha Kassapa, it is said, a wealthy merchant in Varanasi buried a great treasure and placed some markers like posts and stakes there. At the time of his death, he informed his friend, a brahmin: “In this place, I have buried a treasure. Show it to my son when he comes of age.” Having said this, he died. When the merchant’s son came of age, the brahmin showed him that place. Digging there, he saw a nāga at the very end. The nāga, seeing his own son, thought, “Let him take the wealth happily,” and departed. At that time, this matter became well-known in the world. This deity, having been born in a householder’s family in Varanasi at that time, came of age and, after the Teacher’s passing, devotedly went forth into the Sāsana. With five fellow monks, he practiced the ascetic life. This is what is referred to by “five monks built a ladder,” and so on. Therefore, it was said, “Taking the meaning as heard, by way of simile,” and so on. Others say: “The deity, with his own wisdom, formulated these questions thus and explained them to the elder.” There is no doubt about that meaning, as it is a question from a devaputta.

251. Catūhi mahābhūtehi nibbattoti cātumahābhūtiko. Tenāha “catumahābhūtamayassā”ti. Vamati uggiranto viya hotīti attho. Vantakoti ucchaḍḍako. Vantussayoti upacikāhi vantassa mattikāpiṇḍassa ussayabhūto. Vantasinehasambaddhoti vantena kheḷasinehena sampiṇḍito. Asucikalimalaṃ vamatīti ettha mukhādīhi pāṇakānaṃ niggamanato pāṇake vamatīti ayampi attho labbhateva. Ariyehi vantakoti kāyabhāvasāmaññena vuttaṃ. Dukkhasaccapariññāya vā sabbassapi tebhūmakadhammajātassa pariññātattā sabbopi kāyo ariyehi chandarāgappahānena vanto eva. Taṃ sabbanti yehi tīhi aṭṭhisatehi ussito, yehi nhārūhi sambaddho, yehi maṃsehi avalitto, yena allacammena pariyonaddho, yāya chaviyā rañjito, taṃ aṭṭhiādisabbaṃ accantameva jigucchitvā virattatāyavantameva. “Yathā cā”tiādinā vattabbopamatopi vammiko viya vammikoti imamatthaṃ dasseti.

251. “Produced by the four great elements” means cātumahābhūtiko. Hence it is said, “made of the four great elements.” Vamati means 'as if ejecting'; this is the meaning. Vantako means 'discarded,' ucchaḍḍako. Vantussayo means 'a heap of a lump of earth discarded by termites.' Vantasinehasambaddho means 'compacted with the saliva of vomit.' Here, 'discharging impurities and filth' can also mean 'vomiting creatures,' since creatures emerge from the mouth and so on. 'Vomited by the noble ones' is said in a general sense regarding the body's nature. Or, because of the full understanding of the truth of suffering, since all phenomena of the three realms have been fully understood, the entire body is indeed vomited by the noble ones through the abandonment of desire and lust. All that—supported by three hundred bones, bound by sinews, smeared with flesh, wrapped in moist skin, colored by the epidermis—all that, beginning with the bones, having been utterly disgusted with it, is indeed vomited due to dispassion. The phrase 'Just as...' and so on illustrates this meaning: it is an 'anthill' because it is like an anthill.

Sambhavati [V 2.0099] etasmāti sambhavo, mātāpettiko sambhavo etassāti mātāpettikasambhavo. Tassa. Upaciyati etenāti upacayo’ odanakummāsaṃ upacayo etassāti odanakummāsūpacayo. Tassa. Adhuvasabhāvatāya [M 2.0105] aniccadhammassa, sedagūtha-pitta-semhādi-dhātukkhobha-garubhāvaduggandhānaṃ vinodanāya ucchādetabbadhammassa, parito sambāhanena parimadditabbadhammassa, khaṇe khaṇe bhijjanasabhāvatāya bhedanadhammassa, tato eva vikiraṇasabhāvatāya viddhaṃsanadhammassāti dhamma-saddo paccekaṃ yojetabbo. Tanuvilepanenāti kāyāvalepanena ucchādanavilepanena. Aṅgapaccaṅgābādhavinodanatthāyāti tādisasamuṭṭhāna-sarīravikāravigamāya. Yasmā sukkasoṇitaṃ āhāro, ucchādanaṃ parimaddanañca yathārahaṃ uppādassa, vuḍḍhiyā ca paccayo, tasmā āha “mātāpettika…pe… kathito”ti. Uccāvacabhāvoti yathārahaṃ yojetabbo – odanakummāsūpacaya-ucchādanaparimaddanaggahaṇehi uccabhāvo, vaḍḍhī. Mātāpettikasambhavaggahaṇena samudayo. Itarehi avacabhāvo, parihāni, atthaṅgamo pakāsito. Aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ saṇṭhapanampi hi vaṭṭapaccayattā vaṭṭanti.

Sambhavo means 'originates from this.' Mātāpettikasambhavo means 'its origin is from mother and father.' Of that. Upacayo means 'accumulated by this.' Odanakummāsūpacayo means 'its accumulation is rice and gruel.' Of that. The word 'dhamma' should be applied individually to: 'impermanent' due to its impermanent nature; 'to be anointed' for the removal of the heavy, foul nature and disturbance of elements like sweat, excrement, bile, and phlegm; 'to be massaged' by gentle rubbing all around; 'subject to disintegration' due to its nature of breaking moment by moment; and 'subject to dissolution' due to its nature of scattering from that very breaking. Tanuvilepanena means 'with body ointment, with anointing and smearing.' Aṅgapaccaṅgābādhavinodanatthāya means 'for the removal of such bodily disorders arising from that origin.' Since semen and blood are nutriment, and anointing and massaging are, as appropriate, causes of arising and growth, therefore it is said, 'originated from parents... as explained.' Uccāvacabhāvo (various states) should be applied as appropriate: 'high state' and 'growth' by the accumulation of rice and gruel, anointing, and massaging. 'Arising' is indicated by the origin from parents. By the others, 'low state,' 'decline,' and 'disappearance' are shown. For the stability of limbs and minor limbs also continues due to the conditions of existence.

Kodho dhūmoti ettha dhūmapariyāyena kodhassa vuttattā dhūma-saddo kodhe vattatīti vuttaṃ “dhūmo viya dhūmo”ti. Bhasmanīti bhasmaṃ. Mosavajjanti musāvādo. Dhūmo eva dhūmāyitaṃ. Icchā dhūmāyitaṃ etissāti icchādhūmāyitā, pajā. Icchādhūmāyitasaddassa taṇhāya vutti vuttanayo eva. Dhūmāyantoti vitakkasantāpena saṃtappento, vitakkentoti attho. Palipoti dukkaramahākaddamaṃ. Timūlanti tīhi mūlehi patiṭṭhitaṃ viya acalaṃ pavattanti vuttaṃ. Rajo ca dhūmo ca mayā pakāsitāti rajasabhāvakaraṇaṭṭhena “rajo”ti ca dhūmasabhāvakaraṇaṭṭhena “dhūmo”ti ca mayā pakāsitā. Pakatidhūmo viya aggissa kilesaggijālassa paññāṇabhāvato. Dhammadesanādhūmo ñāṇaggisandhīpanassa pubbaṅgamabhāvato. Ayaṃ rattiṃ dhūmāyanāti yā divā kattabbakammante uddissa rattiyaṃ anuvitakkanā, ayaṃ rattiṃ dhūmāyanā.

Here, 'anger is smoke' means that because anger is spoken of by way of the simile of smoke, the word 'smoke' applies to anger, as in 'smoke is like smoke.' Bhasmanī means 'ash.' Mosavajjaṃ means 'false speech.' Dhūmāyitaṃ is simply smoke. Icchādhūmāyitā means 'one for whom desire is smoke,' referring to beings. The usage of the word 'icchādhūmāyita' for craving is as explained. Dhūmāyanto means 'being tormented by the fever of thought,' meaning 'thinking.' Palipo means 'a difficult, vast mire.' Timūlaṃ means 'it is said to proceed unshakeably, as if established by three roots.' Rajo ca dhūmo ca mayā pakāsitā (dust and smoke have been revealed by me) means 'dust' in the sense of creating the state of dust, and 'smoke' in the sense of creating the state of smoke, have been revealed by me. Pakatidhūmo (natural smoke) is like the smoke of fire, because it indicates the blaze of the fire of defilements. Dhammadesanādhūmo (the smoke of Dhamma teaching) is because it is the precursor to the kindling of the fire of wisdom. Ayaṃ rattiṃ dhūmāyanā (this smoldering at night) refers to the excessive thinking at night regarding the tasks to be done during the day.

Sattannaṃ dhammānanti idaṃ sutte (cūḷani. mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa 28) āgatanayena vuttaṃ. Suttañca tathā ārādhanaveneyyajjhāsayavasena. Tadekaṭṭhatāya vā tadaññakilesānaṃ. Sundarapaññoti ñātatīraṇapahānapariññāya paññāya sundarapañño.

This is said regarding 'the seven qualities' according to the method found in the Sutta (Cūḷaniddesa, Mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa 28). And the Sutta is presented thus according to the disposition of those who are ready and teachable. Or by reason of its single purpose, or of other defilements. Sundarapañño means 'one whose wisdom is beautiful through wisdom consisting of knowing, investigating, and abandoning'.

Etanti [M 2.0106] “sattha”nti etaṃ adhivacanaṃ saṃkilesadhammānaṃ sasanato samucchindanato. Nti vīriyaṃ. Paññāgatikameva paññāya hitasseva adhippetattā. Lokiyāya paññāya ārambhakāle lokiyavīriyaṃ [V 2.0100] gahetabbaṃ, lokuttarāya paññāya pavattikkhaṇe lokuttaravīriyaṃ gahetabbanti yojanā. Atthadīpanāti upameyyatthadīpanī upamā.

This word 'sattha' (weapon) is a designation for defiling states because of their cutting and utter destruction. The word ending in `-nti` signifies effort. It is solely the course of wisdom, as it is intended for the benefit of wisdom itself. The connection is thus: at the time of commencing worldly wisdom, worldly effort should be undertaken; at the moment of the arising of supramundane wisdom, supramundane effort should be undertaken. `Atthadīpanā` means a simile that illuminates the meaning of the subject of the comparison.

Gāmatoti attano vasanagāmato. Manteti āthabbanamante. Te hi brāhmaṇā araññe eva vācenti “mā aññe assosu”nti. Tathā akāsīti cattāro koṭṭhāse akāsi. Evamettha vammikapañhasseva vasena upamā āgatā, sesānaṃ vasena heṭṭhā vuttanayena veditabbā.

`Gāmato` means 'from one's own dwelling village.' `Mante` means 'Atharvaṇa mantras.' For those brahmins recite them only in the forest, thinking, 'Let others not hear.' `Tathā akāsi` means 'he made four parts.' Thus, here the simile is given by way of the ant-hill question; as for the rest, it should be understood according to the method stated below.

Laṅganaṭṭhena nivāraṇaṭṭhena laṅgī, paligho. Ñāṇamukheti vipassanāñāṇavīthiyaṃ. Patatīti pavattati. Kammaṭṭhānauggahaparipucchāvasenāti catusaccakammaṭṭhānassa uggaṇhanena tassa atthaparipucchāvasena ceva vipassanāsaṅkhāta-atthavinicchaya-paripucchāvasena ca. Sabbaso ñātuṃ icchā hi paripucchā. Vipassanā ca aniccādito sabbatebhūmakadhammānaṃ ñātuṃ icchati. Evaṃ vipassanāvasena avijjāpahānamāha, uparikattabbasabbhāvato na tāva maggavasena.

`Laṅgī` means 'a bolt, a bar,' in the sense of obstructing and preventing. `Ñāṇamukhe` means 'at the opening of knowledge,' that is, in the course of insight knowledge. `Patati` means 'it proceeds.' `Kammaṭṭhānauggahaparipucchāvasena` means 'by way of learning and questioning the meditation subject,' that is, by learning the meditation subject of the four truths and by questioning its meaning, as well as by questioning the determination of meaning, which is called insight. For questioning is the desire to know completely. And insight desires to know all phenomena of the three planes, beginning with impermanence. Thus, he speaks of the abandoning of ignorance by way of insight, but not yet by way of the path, because of the existence of what is to be done further on.

Valliantare vāti vā-saddo paṃsuantare vā mattikantare vāti avuttavikappattho. Cittāvilamattakovāti cittakkhobhamattakova. Aniggahitoti paṭisaṅkhānabalena anivārito. Mukhavikulanaṃ mukhasaṅkoco. Hanusañcopanaṃ pāpeti antojappanāvatthāyaṃ. Disā vilokanaṃ pāpeti yattha bādhetabbo ṭhito, taṃdassanatthaṃ nivārakaparivāraṇatthaṃ. Daṇḍasatthābhinipātanti daṇḍasatthānaṃ parassa upari nipātanāvatthaṃ. Yena kodhena aniggahitena mātādikaṃ aghātetabbaṃ ugghātetvā “ayuttaṃ vata mayā kata”nti attānampi hanati, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “paraghātanampi attaghātanampi pāpetī”ti. Yena vā parassa haññamānassa vasena ghātakopi ghātanaṃ pāpuṇāti, tādisassa vasenāyamattho veditabbo. Kodhasāmaññena hetaṃ vuttaṃ “paraṃ ghātetvā attānaṃ ghātetī”ti. Paramussadagatoti paramukkaṃsagato. Daḷhaṃ parissayamāvahatāya kodhova kodhūpāyāso. Tenāha “balavappatto”tiādi.

The word `vā` (or) in `valliantare vā` (or between creepers) has the meaning of an unstated alternative, as in 'or between dust, or between clay.' `Cittāvilamattako` means 'merely a disturbance of the mind,' that is, merely agitation of the mind. `Aniggahito` means 'unrestrained,' that is, not prevented by the power of reflection. `Mukhavikulanaṃ` is contortion of the face. `Hanusañcopanaṃ` (clenching the jaw) leads to a state of muttering to oneself. `Disā vilokanaṃ` (looking in all directions) leads to seeing where the one to be harmed is standing, for the purpose of seeing him and for the purpose of warding off or surrounding. `Daṇḍasatthābhinipātaṃ` means the state of striking another with sticks and weapons. With reference to that unrestrained anger by which one, having struck one who should not be harmed, such as one's mother, thinks, 'Alas, what I have done is improper,' and harms oneself too, it was said: 'it leads to harming others and harming oneself.' Or, the meaning should be understood in this way: by means of which anger, because another is being harmed, the killer also meets with being killed. For this is said with regard to anger in general: 'Having harmed another, one harms oneself.' `Paramussadagato` means 'having gone to the highest point,' that is, gone to the extreme. `Kodhūpāyāso` (distress from anger) is anger itself, because it brings strong danger. Therefore, it is said, 'having reached great strength,' etc.

Dvedhāpathasamā [M 2.0107] hoti appaṭipattihetubhāvato.

It is like a forked path, because it is a cause of non-practice.

Kusaladhammo na tiṭṭhati nīvaraṇehi nivāritaparamattā. Samathapubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāvayato paṭhamaṃ samathena nīvaraṇavikkhambhanaṃ hoti, vipassanā pana tadaṅgavaseneva tāni nīharatīti vuttaṃ “vikkhambhanatadaṅgavasenā”ti.

A wholesome state does not persist because its ultimate nature is obstructed by the hindrances. For one who develops insight preceded by serenity, first there is the suppression of the hindrances by serenity, but insight removes them by way of momentary abandonment—thus it is said, 'by way of suppression and momentary abandonment'.

“Kummova [V 2.0101] aṅgāni sake kapāle”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.17) kummassa aṅgabhāvena visesato pādasīsāni eva vuccantīti āha “pañceva aṅgāni hontī”ti. Vipassanācārassa vuccamānattā adhikārato sammasanīyānameva dhammānaṃ idha gahaṇanti “sabbepi saṅkhatā dhammā”ti visesaṃ katvāva vuttaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā “pañcannetaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ adhivacana”nti.

In passages such as 'Like a turtle its limbs into its own shell' (SN 1.17), since the limbs of a turtle are its parts, its feet and head are specifically meant; thus he said, 'there are just five limbs.' Because the practice of insight is being discussed, by virtue of the context, only phenomena that are to be comprehended are to be taken here; thus, it is stated, 'all conditioned phenomena,' having made this distinction. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'This is a designation for the five aggregates subject to clinging'.

Sunanti koṭṭanti etthāti sūnā, adhikuṭṭananti āha “sūnāya uparī”ti. Asināti maṃsakantanena. Ghātiyamānāti haññamānā vibādhiyamānā. Vatthukāmānaṃ upari katvāti vatthukāmesu ṭhapetvā te accādhānaṃ katvā. Kantitāti chinditā. Koṭṭitāti bilaso vibhajitā. Chandarāgappahānanti chandarāgassa vikkhambhanappahānaṃ.

`Sūnā` is so called because they kill and pound there; `sūnāya upari` means upon a butcher's block. `Asinā` means 'with a meat-cutting knife.' `Ghātiyamānā` means 'being killed, being oppressed.' `Vatthukāmānaṃ upari katvā` means having placed them upon the objects of sensual pleasure, having made these an excessive focus. `Kantitā` means 'cut.' `Koṭṭitā` means 'divided into portions.' `Chandarāgappahānaṃ` means the abandonment of desire and lust by suppression.

Sammattāti mucchitā sammūḷhā. Nandīrāgaṃ upagamma vaṭṭaṃ vaḍḍhentīti sammūḷhattā evaādīnavaṃ apassantā nandīrāgassa ārammaṇaṃ upagantvā taṃ paribrūhenti. Nandīrāgabaddhāti nandīrāge laggattā tena baddhā. Vaṭṭe laggantīti tebhūmake vaṭṭe sajjanti. Tattha sajjattā eva dukkhaṃ patvāpi na ukkaṇṭhanti na nibbindanti. Idha anavasesappahānaṃ adhippetanti āha “catutthamaggena nandīrāgappahānaṃ kathita”nti.

`Sammattā` means 'infatuated, bewildered.' 'By approaching delight and lust, they increase the round of existence' means: being bewildered and thus not seeing the danger, they approach the object of delight and lust and augment it. 'Bound by delight and lust' means that because they are attached to delight and lust, they are bound by it. 'Clinging to the round' means they cling to the round of the three planes. Because they cling there, even when they encounter suffering, they are not troubled and do not become disenchanted. Here, abandonment without remainder is intended; thus it is said: 'The abandonment of delight and lust by the fourth path is spoken of.'

Anaṅgaṇasutte (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.63) pakāsito eva “chandādīhi na gacchantī”tiādinā. “Buddho so bhagavā”tiādi “namo karohī”ti (ma. ni. 1.249, 251) vuttanamakkārassa karaṇākāradassanaṃ. Bodhāyāti catusaccasambodhāya. Tathā damathasamathataraṇaparinibbānāni ariyamaggavasena veditabbāni. Samathaparinibbānāni pana anupādisesavasenapi yojetabbāni. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ ahosīti vipassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ ahosi. Etassa pañhassāti etassa pannarasamassa pañhassa attho. Evaṃ itaresupi vattabbaṃ vipassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ khīṇāsavaguṇehi matthakaṃ pāpento yathānusandhināva desanaṃ niṭṭhapesi, na [M 2.0108] pucchitānusandhināti adhippāyo. Nanu ca pucchāvasenāyaṃ desanā āraddhāti? Saccaṃ āraddhā, evaṃ pana “pucchāvasiko nikkhepo”ti vattabbaṃ, na “pucchānusandhivasena niṭṭhapitā”ti. Antarapucchāvasena desanāya aparivattitattā ārambhānurūpameva pana desanā niṭṭhapitā.

It is explained in the Anaṅgaṇasutta with the words, 'They do not proceed by desire, etc.' The passage beginning, 'That Blessed One is the Buddha,' shows the manner of performing the homage spoken of in the words, 'Pay homage!' 'For awakening' means for the full awakening to the four truths. Similarly, taming, serenity, crossing over, and final extinguishment should be understood by way of the noble path. But serenity and final extinguishment should also be connected by way of the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining. 'It was a meditation subject' means it was a subject for insight meditation. 'Of this question' means the meaning of this fifteenth question. The same should be said for the others. The meaning is this: bringing the insight meditation subject to its culmination with the qualities of one whose taints are destroyed, he concluded the discourse according to its own sequence, not according to the sequence of the questions. But was this discourse not begun by way of the questions? True, it was so begun, but it should be said that 'the exposition is based on the questions,' not that 'it was concluded according to the sequence of the questions.' Since the discourse was not altered by the intervening questions, it was concluded in a way that was appropriate to its beginning.

Vammikasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The explanation of the concealed meaning in the commentary on the Vammika Sutta is completed.

4. Rathavinītasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Rathavinīta Sutta

252. Mahāgovindena [V 2.0102] pariggahitatākittanaṃ tadā magadharājena pariggahitūpalakkhaṇaṃ. Tassa hi so purohito. Mahāgovindoti purātano eko magadharājāti keci. Gayhatīti gaho, rājūnaṃ gaho rājagahaṃ. Nagara-saddāpekkhāya napuṃsakaniddeso. Aññepettha pakāreti rājūhi disvā sammā patiṭṭhāpitattā tesaṃ gahaṃ gehabhūtantipi rājagahaṃ. Ārakkhasampattiādinā anatthuppattihetutāya upagatānaṃ paṭirājūnaṃ gahaṃ gahabhūtantipi rājagahaṃ, ārāmarāmaṇīyakādīhi rājate, nivāsasukhatādinā sattehi mamattavasena gayhati, pariggayhatīti vā rājagahanti evamādike pakāre. Buddhakāle ca cakkavattikāle cāti idaṃ yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ. Veḷūhi parikkhittaṃ ahosi, na pana kevalaṃ kaṭṭhakapavanameva. Rañño uyyānakāle patiṭṭhāpitaaṭṭālakavasena aṭṭālakayuttaṃ.

252. The mention of its having been founded by Mahāgovinda is a sign of its having been founded by the king of Magadha, for Mahāgovinda was his chief priest. Some say that Mahāgovinda was an ancient king of Magadha. 'It is seized' (gayhati) is a 'seizure' (gaho); the seizure by kings is Rājagaha. The neuter designation is with reference to the word 'nagara' (city). Others explain in this way: because it was well established by kings after they saw it, their 'seizure,' being their home (gehabhūtaṃ), is Rājagaha. Also, because it was a cause for the non-arising of misfortune from rival kings who approached, due to its protective features, etc., their 'seizure,' being a place of capture (gahabhūtaṃ), is Rājagaha. Or, because it shines (rājate) with parks and pleasant spots, or because it is seized (gayhati) by beings with a sense of 'mine' due to the comfort of dwelling there, or because it is fully seized (pariggayhati), it is called Rājagaha—these are the various explanations. 'At the time of a Buddha and at the time of a wheel-turning monarch'—this is said for the most part. It was surrounded by bamboos, not merely by a wooden fence. It was endowed with watchtowers because watchtowers had been established at the time of the king's park.

Jananaṃ jāti, jātiyā bhūmi jātibhūmaṃ, jāyi vā mahābodhisatto etthābhi jāti, sā eva bhūmīti jātibhūmaṃ, sā imesaṃ nivāsoti jātibhūmakāti āha “jātibhūmakāti jātibhūmivāsino”ti. Kassa panāyaṃ jātibhūmīti āha “taṃ kho panā”tiādi. Tena anaññasādhāraṇāya jātiyā adhippetattā sadevake loke supākaṭabhāvato visesanena vināpi visiṭṭhavisayova idha jāti-saddo viññāyatīti dasseti. Tenāha “sabbaññubodhisattassa jātaṭṭhānasākiyajanapado”ti. Tatthapi kapilavatthusannissayo padesoti āha “kapilavatthāhāro”ti.

'Being born' (jananaṃ) is birth (jāti); the ground (bhūmi) of birth is the 'birth-ground' (jātibhūmaṃ). Or, the Great Bodhisatta was born (jāyi) here; that very ground is the place of his noble birth (abhijāti), thus it is the 'birth-ground.' That is their dwelling place, hence they are 'of the birth-ground' (jātibhūmakā). Thus he says: '“Of the birth-ground” means dwellers in the birth-ground.' But whose birth-ground is this? He says: 'Now that…,' etc. By this he shows that because a birth not shared by others is intended, and because it is very famous in the world with its gods, here the word 'birth' is understood as referring to a distinguished subject even without a qualifier. Therefore he says: 'The Sākiyan country, the birthplace of the Omniscient Bodhisatta.' There too, it is the region connected with Kapilavatthu, so he says: 'the district of Kapilavatthu.'

Garudhammabhāvavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the State of Reverence for the Dhamma

Sākiyamaṇḍalassāti [M 2.0109] sākiyarājasamūhassa. Dasannaṃ appicchakathādīnaṃ vatthu dasakathāvatthu, appicchatādi. Tattha suppatiṭṭhitatāya tassa lābhī dasakathāvatthulābhī. Tatthāti dasakathāvatthusmiṃ.

'Of the Sākiyan circle' means of the assembly of Sākiyan rulers. The basis for the ten kinds of talk, beginning with talk on fewness of wishes, is the tenfold subject matter for talk, beginning with fewness of wishes. Because he is well established therein, he is a 'gainer' of it, a 'gainer of the tenfold subject matter for talk.' 'Therein' means in the tenfold subject matter for talk.

Garukaraṇīyatāya dhammo garu etassāti dhammagaru, tassa bhāvo dhammagarutā, tāya. “Ajjhāsayena veditabbo”ti vatvā na kevalaṃ ajjhāsayeneva, atha kho kāyavacīpayogehipi veditabboti [V 2.0103] dassento “dhammagarutāyeva hī”tiādimāha. Tiyāmarattiṃ dhammakathaṃ katvāti ettha “kumbhakārassa nivesane tiyāmarattiṃ vasanto dhammakathaṃ katvā”ti evaṃ vacanasesavasena attho veditabbo. Aññathā yathālābhavasena atthe gayhamāne tiyāmarattiṃ dhammakathā katāti āpajjati, na ca taṃ atthi. Vakkhati hi “bahudeva rattinti diyaḍḍhayāmamatta”nti. Dasabalādiguṇavisesā viya dhammagāravahetukā parahitapaṭipattipi sabbabuddhānaṃ majjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇaṃ viya sadisā evāti imassa bhagavato dhammagāravakittane “kassapopi bhagavā”tiādinā kassapabhagavato dhammagāravaṃ dasseti.

Because the Dhamma is to be revered, the Dhamma is revered (garu) by him; thus he is one who reveres the Dhamma (dhammagaru). The state of that is reverence for the Dhamma (dhammagarutā); by that reverence. Having said, 'It should be understood by inclination,' to show that it should be understood not only by inclination but also by bodily and verbal application, he says, 'Indeed, reverence for the Dhamma…,' etc. Regarding the phrase 'having given a Dhamma talk for the three watches of the night,' the meaning should be understood by supplying the rest of the sentence, thus: 'Having stayed in the potter's dwelling for the three watches of the night, he gave a Dhamma talk.' Otherwise, if the meaning is taken just as it comes, it would follow that the Dhamma talk was given for three watches, which is not the case. For it will be said: 'For a great part of the night, that is, for about one and a half watches.' Just as the special qualities such as the ten powers, so also the practice for the welfare of others, which is caused by reverence for the Dhamma, is the same among all Buddhas, like refined gold. Thus, in praising this Blessed One's reverence for the Dhamma, he shows the reverence for the Dhamma of the Blessed One Kassapa with the words, 'The Blessed One Kassapa too…,' etc.

Cārikaṃ nikkhamīti janapadacārikaṃ carituṃ nikkhami. Janapadacārikāya akāle nikkhantattā kosalarājādayo vāretuṃ ārabhiṃsu. Pavāretvā hi caraṇaṃ buddhāciṇṇaṃ. Puṇṇāya sammāpaṭipattiṃ paccāsīsanto bhagavā “kiṃ me karissasī”ti āha.

'He set out on a journey' means he set out to wander through the country. Because he departed at an unsuitable time for wandering through the country, the king of Kosala and others started to prevent him. For it is the custom of the Buddhas to wander only after having been invited. Hoping for Puṇṇa’s right practice, the Blessed One said: 'What will you do for me?'

Anahātovāti dhammasavanussukkena sāyanhe buddhāciṇṇaṃ nhānaṃ akatvāva. Attahitaparahitapaṭipattīsu ekissā dvinnañca atthitāsiddhā catubbidhatā paṭipattikatā eva nāma hotīti vuttaṃ “paṭipannako ca nāma…pe… catubbidho hotī”ti. Paṭikkhepapubbakopi hi paṭipanno atthato paṭipannattho evāti. Kāmaṃ attahitāya paṭipanno tāya sammāpaṭipattiyā sāsanaṃ sobhati, na pana sāsanaṃ vaḍḍheti appossukkabhāvato, na ca kāruṇikassa bhagavato sabbathā manorathaṃ pūreti. Tathā hi bhagavā paṭhamabodhiyaṃ ekasaṭṭhiyā ca arahantesu jātesu [M 2.0110] – “caratha, bhikkhave, bahujanahitāyā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.86-88; mahāva. 32) bhikkhū parahitapaṭipattiyaṃ niyojesi. Tena vuttaṃ “evarūpaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhagavā na pucchati, kasmā? Na mayhaṃ sāsanassa vuḍḍhipakkhe ṭhito”ti.

'Unbathed' means that out of eagerness to hear the Dhamma, he did not take the evening bath, which is the custom of the Buddhas. The fourfold nature of a practitioner is established by the presence of one or both of the practices for one's own welfare and for the welfare of others; thus it is said: 'A practitioner is… fourfold.' For even one who practices after having first rejected it is in substance a practitioner. Granted, one who practices for his own welfare adorns the Dispensation by that right practice, but he does not make the Dispensation grow, because he is not zealous, nor does he completely fulfill the wish of the compassionate Blessed One. For at the time of the first enlightenment, when sixty-one arahants had arisen, the Blessed One enjoined the bhikkhus to practice for the welfare of others, saying: 'Wander, bhikkhus, for the welfare of the many…' Therefore it is said: 'The Blessed One does not question such a bhikkhu. Why? Because he does not stand on the side of the growth of my Dispensation.'

Samudāyo appakena ūnopi anūno viya hotīti bākulattheraṃ catuttharāsito bahi katvāpi “asītimahātherā viyā”ti vuttaṃ. Asītimahātherasamaññā vā avayavepi aṭṭhasamāpattisāmaññā viya daṭṭhabbā. Īdise ṭhāne bahūnaṃ ekato kathanaṃ mahatā kaṇṭhena ca kathanaṃ satthu cittārādhanamevāti tehi bhikkhūhi tathā paṭipannanti dassento “te bhikkhū meghasaddaṃ sutvā”tiādimāha. Guṇasambhāvanāyāti vakkhamānaguṇahetukāya sambhāvanāya sambhāvito, na yena kenaci kiccasamatthatādinā.

A group, though deficient by a small number, is as if not deficient. Thus, even though the Elder Bākula was excluded from the fourth group, it was said, 'like the eighty great elders.' Or the designation 'eighty great elders' should be seen as applicable even to a part of the group, like the general term 'eight attainments' is applicable to a single attainment. In such a situation, the speaking of many as one and speaking with a great voice is solely for the purpose of pleasing the Teacher's mind. To show that those bhikkhus acted accordingly, he says: 'Those bhikkhus, having heard the sound of a cloud…,' etc. 'Out of esteem for his virtues' means he was esteemed out of an esteem based on the virtues to be described, not on account of any mere competence in duties or the like.

Garudhammabhāvavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the State of Reverence for the Dhamma is finished.

Appicchatādivaṇṇanā

Explanation of Fewness of Wishes, etc.

Appa-saddassa [V 2.0104] parittapariyāyataṃ manasi katvā āha “byañjanaṃ sāvasesaṃ viyā”ti. Tenāha “na hi tassā”tiādi. Appa-saddo panettha abhāvatthoti sakkā viññātuṃ “appābādhatañca sañjānāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.225; 2.134) viya.

Considering that the word 'appa' is a synonym for 'little,' it is said: 'The expression is as if with a remainder.' Therefore it is stated: 'For it is not so,' etc. Here, the word 'appa' can be understood in the sense of 'absence,' as in such passages as: 'And I perceive freedom from affliction,' etc. (Majjhima Nikāya 1.225; 2.134).

Atricchatā nāma (a. ni. ṭī. 1.1.63) atra atra icchāti katvā. Asantaguṇasambhāvanatāti attani avijjamānaṃ guṇānaṃ vijjamānānaṃ viya paresaṃ pakāsanā. Saddhoti maṃ jano jānātūti vattapaṭipattikārakavisesalābhīti jānātu “vattapaṭipattiāpāthakajjhāyitā”ti evamādinā. Santaguṇasambhāvanāti icchācāre ṭhatvā attani vijjamānasīladhutadhammādiguṇavibhāvanā. Tādisassa hi paṭiggahaṇe amattaññutāpi hoti.

Excessive desire (atricchatā) is so called because one desires 'here, here.' The displaying of non-existent qualities is the showing to others of qualities that do not exist in oneself as if they did exist, with the thought: 'Let people know me as a faithful person, as one who obtains special things through his observance and practice,' as in: 'one who is proficient in observance, practice, recitation, and study,' and so on. The displaying of existing qualities is, while established in willful conduct, the manifestation of the qualities of morality, ascetic practices, etc., that actually exist in oneself. For such a one, there is also immoderation in receiving.

Gaṇhantoyeva ummujji aññesaṃ ajānantānaṃyevāti adhippāyo.

The meaning is that he emerges only while taking, while others do not know.

Appicchatāpadhānaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānena catubbidhaṃ icchāpabhedaṃ dassetvā punapi puggalādhiṭṭhānena catubbidhaṃ icchāpabhedaṃ dassento “aparopi catubbidho [M 2.0111] appiccho”tiādimāha. Dāyakassa vasanti dāyakassa cittavasaṃ. Deyyadhammassa vasanti deyyadhammassa appabahubhāvaṃ. Attano thāmanti attano yāpanamattakathāmaṃ.

Having shown a fourfold division of desire based on the individual, with fewness of wishes as the main point, in order to again show a fourfold division of desire based on the individual, he says: 'And another is the fourfold person with few desires,' etc. 'According to the donor' means according to the donor's state of mind. 'According to the gift' means according to whether the gift is small or large. 'According to one's own strength' means according to one's own strength just sufficient for sustenance.

Ekabhikkhupi na aññāsi sosānikavatte sammadeva vuttittā. Abbokiṇṇanti avicchedaṃ. Dutiyo maṃ na jāneyyāti dutiyo sahāyabhūtopi yathā maṃ jānituṃ na sakkuṇeyya, tathā saṭṭhi vassāni nirantaraṃ susāne vasāmi, tasmā ahaṃ aho sosānikuttamo.
