Not even a single monk knew, because of his perfect conduct in the charnel-ground observance. 'Uninterrupted' means without a break. 'A second person would not know me' means: I have lived in the charnel ground continuously for sixty years in such a way that even a second person, a companion, would not be able to know me. Therefore, ah, I am the supreme charnel-ground-dweller!

Dhammakathāya janataṃ khobhetvāti lomahaṃsanasādhukāradānacelukkhepādivasena sannipatitaṃ itarañca “kathaṃ nu kho ayyassa santikeva dhammaṃ sossāmā”ti kolāhalavasena mahājanaṃ khobhetvā. Gatoti “ayaṃ so, tena rattiyaṃ dhammakathā katā”ti jānanabhayena pariyattiappicchatāya pariveṇaṃ gato.

'Having agitated the people with a Dhamma talk' means: having agitated the great crowd that had assembled, and others, by means of hair-raising excitement, cries of 'Sādhu!', giving of gifts, waving of robes, and so on, and by means of the uproar of those saying, 'How indeed shall we hear the Dhamma in the venerable one's presence?' 'Gone' means: he went to his monastic cell out of fear of being recognized, thinking, 'This is he; the Dhamma talk at night was given by him,' and because of his desire to be unassuming in regard to his learning.

Tayo [V 2.0105] kulaputtā viyāti pācīnavaṃsadāye samaggavāsaṃ vutthā tayo kulaputtā viya. Pahāyāti pubbabhāge tadaṅgādivasena pacchā aggamaggeneva pajahitvā.

'Like three clansmen' means: like the three clansmen who lived in harmony in the Eastern Bamboo Grove. 'Having abandoned' means: having abandoned them in the preliminary stage by such means as substitution of opposites, and afterwards by the supreme path itself.

Appicchatādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of Fewness of Wishes, etc., is finished.

Dvādasavidhasantosavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Twelvefold Contentment

Pakatidubbalādīnaṃ garucīvarādīni naphāsubhāvāvahāni sarīrakhedāvahāni ca hontīti payojanavasena naatricchatādivasena tāni parivattetvā lahukacīvaraparibhogo na santosavirodhīti āha “lahukena yāpentopi santuṭṭhova hotī”ti. Mahagghacīvaraṃ, bahūni vā cīvarāni labhitvāpi tāni vissajjetvā tadaññassa gahaṇaṃ yathāsāruppanaye ṭhitattā na santosavirodhīti āha “tesaṃ…pe… dhārentopi santuṭṭhova hotī”ti. Evaṃ sesapaccayesupi yathābalayathāsāruppasantosaniddesesu apisaddaggahaṇe adhippāyo veditabbo. Yathāsāruppasantosoyeva aggo alobhajjhāsayassa ukkaṃsanato.

For those who are naturally weak and so on, heavy robes and the like are not conducive to comfort and cause bodily fatigue. Therefore, exchanging them for lighter robes out of necessity—not out of excessive desire and so on—and using the lighter robes is not contrary to contentment. Thus it is said: 'Even while subsisting on a light one, he is content.' Even if one obtains an expensive robe or many robes, giving them up and taking others is not contrary to contentment, since this is grounded in the principle of suitability. Thus it is said: 'Even while wearing them...pe... he is content.' Similarly, in regard to the other requisites too, the intention behind the inclusion of the word 'even' in the explanations of contentment according to one's strength and contentment according to suitability should be understood. Contentment according to suitability is the highest, as it is an extolling of a non-greedy disposition.

Dvādasavidhasantosavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Twelvefold Contentment is finished.

Tividhapavivekavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Threefold Seclusion

Ekoti [M 2.0112] ekākī. Gacchatīti cuṇṇikairiyāpathavasena vuttaṃ. Caratīti vihārato bahi sañcāravasena, viharatīti divāvihārādivasena. Kāyavivekoti ca nekkhammādhimuttassa bhāvanānuyogavasena vivekaṭṭhakāyatā, na jhānavivekamattaṃ. Tenāha “nekkhammābhiratāna”nti. Parisuddhacittānanti nīvaraṇādisaṃkilesato visuddhacittānaṃ. Paramavodānappattānanti vitakkāditaṃtaṃjhānapaṭipakkhavigamena paramaṃ uttamaṃ vodānaṃ pattānaṃ. Nirupadhīnanti kilesupadhiādīnaṃ vigamena nirupadhīnaṃ.

'Alone' means solitary. 'Goes' is said with reference to the posture in a prose passage. 'Wanders' is in the sense of moving about outside the monastery; 'dwells' is in the sense of the daytime abiding, etc. 'Bodily seclusion' means the body's state of being secluded by way of application to meditation for one resolved on renunciation, not merely the seclusion of jhāna. Therefore he says: 'delighting in renunciation.' 'Of those with purified minds' means of those whose minds are purified from defilements such as the hindrances. 'Of those who have attained supreme cleansing' means of those who have attained the supreme, highest cleansing through the removal of the opposing factors of the respective jhānas, such as initial application of mind. 'Of those without acquisitions' means of those without acquisitions through the removal of the acquisitions such as the defilements.

Tividhapavivekavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Threefold Seclusion is finished.

Pañcavidhasaṃsaggavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Five Kinds of Association

Saṃsīdati [V 2.0106] etenāti saṃsaggo, rāgo. Savanahetuko, savanavasena vā pavatto saṃsaggo savanasaṃsaggo. Esa nayo sesesupi. Kāyasaṃsaggo pana kāyaparāmāso. Itthī vāti vadhū, yuvatī vā. Sandhānetunti pubbenāparaṃ ghaṭetuṃ. Sotaviññāṇavīthivasenāti idaṃ mūlabhūtaṃ savanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, tassa piṭṭhivattakamanodvārikajavanavīthīsu uppannopi rāgo savanasaṃsaggoyeva. Dassanasaṃsaggepi eseva nayo. Anitthigandhabodhisatto parehi kathiyamānavasena pavattasavanasaṃsaggassa nidassanaṃ. Tissadaharo attanā suyyamānavasena. Tattha paṭhamaṃ jātake veditabbanti itaraṃ dassento “daharo kirā”tiādimāha. Kāmarāgena viddhoti rāgasallena hadaye appito anto anuviddho.

'One sinks down because of this, thus it is association (saṃsagga)'; this means lust. Association that has hearing as its cause, or that occurs by way of hearing, is association by hearing. This is the method in the other cases as well. Bodily association, however, is bodily contact. 'Or a woman' means a daughter-in-law or a young woman. 'To connect' means to link the latter with the former. 'By way of the process of ear-consciousness': this is said referring to the basic act of hearing; even lust that arises in the subsequent mind-door cognitive series of impulsion is still association by hearing. This same method applies also to association by seeing. The Bodhisatta in the Anitthigandha Jātaka is an example of association by hearing occurring by way of what is said by others; the young Tissa, by way of what is heard by oneself. Therein, stating that the first should be known from the Jātaka, in order to show the other he says: 'The young one, it seems,' etc. 'Pierced by sensual lust' means fixed in the heart by the dart of lust, penetrated within.

Soti dassanasaṃsaggo. Evaṃ veditabboti vatthuvasena pākaṭaṃ karoti. Tasmiṃ kira gāme yebhuyyena itthiyo abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā, tasmā thero “sace antogāme na carissasī”ti āha. Kālasseva paviṭṭhattā yāguṃ adāsi, tasmā yāgumeva gahetvā gacchantaṃ “nivattatha, bhante, bhikkhaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti āhaṃsu. Yācitvāti “na mayaṃ, bhante, bhikkhaṃ dātukāmā nivattema, apica idaṃ bhante kāraṇa”nti yācitvā.

This is association by seeing. He makes it clear by way of the story that it should be understood thus. It seems that in that village the women were for the most part beautiful, lovely to see, and inspiring confidence; therefore the elder said: 'If you will not wander for alms inside the village...' Because he entered early, she gave him gruel. Therefore, as he was leaving having taken only the gruel, they said: 'Turn back, venerable sir, accept the almsfood!' 'Having requested' means: having requested, saying, 'Venerable sir, we would not have you turn back because we wish to give almsfood, but, venerable sir, this is the reason...'

Ādito [M 2.0113] lapanaṃ ālāpo, vacanapaṭivacanavasena pavatto lāpo sallāpo. Bhikkhuniyāti idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ. Yāya kāyacipi itthiyā santakaparibhogavasena uppannarāgopi sambhogasaṃsaggova.

Speaking at the outset is conversation; speech that proceeds by way of statement and reply is dialogue. 'A bhikkhunī': this is just an illustration. Lust that has arisen towards any woman whatsoever by way of using her belongings is also association by shared enjoyment.

Pañcavidhasaṃsaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Five Kinds of Association is finished.

Gāhagāhakādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Grasper, etc.

Bhikkhuno bhikkhūhi kāyaparāmāso kāyasambāhanādivasena. Kāyasaṃsagganti kāyaparāmāsasaṃsaggaṃ. Gāhagāhakoti gaṇhanakānaṃ gaṇhanakoti attho. Gāhamuttakoti ayoniso āmisehi saṅgaṇhanakehi sayaṃ muccanako. Muttagāhakoti yathāvuttasaṅgahato muttānaṃ saṅgaṇhanako. Muttamuttakoti muccanakehi sayampi muccanako. Gahaṇavasena saṅgaṇhanavasena. Upasaṅkamanti tato kiñci [V 2.0107] lokāmisaṃ paccāsīsantā, na dakkhiṇeyyavasena. Bhikkhupakkhe gahaṇavasenāti paccayalābhāya saṅgaṇhanavasenāti yojetabbaṃ. Vuttanayenāti “āmisenā”tiādinā vuttanayena.

A bhikkhu's bodily contact with other bhikkhus is by way of bodily touching, massaging, etc. 'Bodily contact' means contact by bodily touching. 'A grasper of the grasping': this means one who grasps those who grasp. 'Freed from grasping': one who frees oneself from those who improperly gather others with material things. 'A gatherer of the freed': one who gathers those who have been freed from the aforementioned entanglement. 'Freed from the freed': one who also frees oneself from those who are freeing. By way of taking; by way of gathering. They approach expecting some worldly material gain, not on account of his worthiness for offerings. In the case of a bhikkhu, 'by way of taking' should be connected with 'by way of gathering for the sake of obtaining requisites.' 'In the manner stated' means in the manner stated by the words beginning 'with a material thing,' etc.

Ṭhānanti attano ṭhānāvatthaṃ. Pāpuṇituṃ na deti uppannameva taṃ paṭisaṅkhānabalena nīharanto vikkhambheti. Tenāha “mantenā”tiādi. Yathā jīvitukāmo puriso kaṇhasappena, amittena vā saha na saṃvasati, evaṃ khaṇamattampi kilesehi saha na saṃvasatīti attho.

'Position': one's own state or condition. He does not allow it to be attained; by the power of reflection, he removes and suppresses it as soon as it has arisen. Hence it is said: 'by a mantra,' etc. Just as a person who wants to live does not dwell with a black cobra or an enemy, so he does not dwell with the defilements even for a moment; this is the meaning.

Catupārisuddhisīlaṃ lokiyaṃ lokuttarañca. Tathā samādhipi. Vipassanāya pādakā vipassanāpādakāti aṭṭhasamāpattiggahaṇena yathā lokiyasamādhi gahito, evaṃ vipassanāpādakā etesanti vipassanāpādakāti aṭṭhasamāpattiggahaṇeneva lokuttaro samādhi gahito. Yathā hi cattāri rūpajjhānāni adhiṭṭhānaṃ katvā pavatto maggasamādhi vipassanāpādako, evaṃ cattāri arūpajjhānāni adhiṭṭhānaṃ katvā pavattopi. Samāpattipariyāyo pana pubbavohārena veditabbo. Paṭipakkhasamucchedanena sammā āpajjanato vā yathā “sotāpattimaggo”ti. Evamettha sīlasamādhīnampi missakabhāvo veditabbo, na paññāya eva. Vimuttīti ariyaphalanti vuttaṃ “vimuttisampanno”ti vuttattā. Tañhi nipphādanaṭṭhena sampādetabbaṃ, na nibbānanti.

The virtue of fourfold purification is both mundane and supramundane. So too is concentration. The bases for insight are called 'vipassanāpādakā.' Just as mundane concentration is included by taking up the eight attainments, so too, since 'these are bases for insight,' supramundane concentration is also included by taking up the eight attainments. For just as the path concentration that proceeds having made the four form jhānas its foundation is a basis for insight, so too is that which proceeds having made the four formless jhānas its foundation. The way of attainment, however, should be understood according to previous convention. Or because of rightly attaining it by cutting off the opposing side, as in 'the path of stream-entry.' Thus the mixed nature of virtue and concentration here should be understood, not of wisdom alone. 'Liberation' means the noble fruit, as it is said, 'accomplished in liberation.' For that is to be accomplished in the sense of being produced, not Nibbāna.

Ettha [M 2.0114] ca appicchatāya laddhapaccayena paritussati, santuṭṭhatāya laddhā te agadhito amucchitoādīnavadassī nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati, evaṃbhūto ca katthaci alaggamānasatāya pavivekaṃ paribrūhento kenaci asaṃsaṭṭho viharati gahaṭṭhena vā pabbajitena vā. So evaṃ ajjhāsayasampanno vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā, anadhigamassa adhigamāya. Ārabhanto ca yathāsamādinnaṃ attano sīlaṃ paccavekkhati, tassa sīlassa suparisuddhataṃ nissāya uppajjati avippaṭisāro, ayamassa sīlasampadā. Tassa avippaṭisāramūlakehi pāmojjapītipassaddhisukhehi sammā brūhitaṃ cittaṃ sammadeva samādhiyati, ayamassa samādhisampadā. Tato yathābhūtaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ nibbindati, nibbindaṃ virajjati, virāgā vimuccati, ayamassa paññāsampadā. Vimuttacittatā panassa vimuttisampadā, tato vimuttito ñāṇadassananti etesaṃ dasannaṃ kathāvatthūnaṃ anupubbī veditabbā. Tassa yo dasahi kathāvatthūhi samannāgamo, ayaṃ attahitāya paṭipatti. Yā nesaṃ paresaṃ saṃkittanaṃ, ayaṃ parahitāya paṭipatti. Tāsu purimā ñāṇapubbaṅgamā ñāṇasampayuttā ca, itarā karuṇāpubbaṅgamā karuṇāsampayuttā cāti sabbaṃ ñāṇakaruṇākaṇḍaṃ vattabbaṃ.

Here, one is satisfied with the requisites obtained through fewness of wishes. Being content, when one has obtained them, one makes use of them without greed, without infatuation, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape. Being such, with a mind unattached to anything, one cultivates seclusion and dwells unentangled with anyone, whether a householder or one who has gone forth. Thus endowed with proper intention, one arouses energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized. While striving, one reflects on one's own virtue as it has been undertaken. Relying on the complete purity of that virtue, non-regret arises—this is one's accomplishment in virtue. With a mind well-developed through the joy, rapture, tranquility, and happiness that are rooted in non-regret, one's mind becomes rightly concentrated—this is one's accomplishment in concentration. Then, knowing and seeing things as they really are, one becomes disenchanted. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, one is liberated—this is one's accomplishment in wisdom. The state of a liberated mind is one's accomplishment in liberation. Then from liberation comes knowledge and vision. The sequence of these ten topics for discussion should be understood. One who is endowed with these ten topics for discussion is practicing for one's own welfare. The explanation of these to others is the practice for the welfare of others. Of these, the former is preceded by knowledge and associated with knowledge, while the latter is preceded by compassion and associated with compassion. Thus the entire section on knowledge and compassion should be stated.

Dasahi [V 2.0108] kathāvatthūhi karaṇabhūtehi bhikkhūnaṃ ovādaṃ deti, “bhikkhunā nāma atricchatādike dūrato vajjetvā sammadeva appicchena bhavitabba”ntiādinā taṃ taṃ kathāvatthuṃ bhikkhūnaṃ upadisatīti attho. Upadisanto hi tāni “tehi bhikkhū ovadatī”ti vutto. Ovadatiyeva sarūpadassanamattena. Sukhumaṃ atthaṃ parivattetvāti evampi appicchatā hoti evampīti appicchatādivasena aparāparaṃ appicchatāvuttiṃ dassetvā tattha sukhumanipuṇaṃ appicchatāsaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ jānāpetuṃ na sakkoti. Viññāpetīti yathāvuttehi visesehi viññāpeti. Kāraṇanti yena kāraṇena appicchatā ijjhati, taṃ pana “mahicchatādīsu ete dosā, appicchatāya ayamānisaṃso”tiādīnavānisaṃsadassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sammā hetunā appicchataṃ dassetīti sandassako. Gāhetunti yathā gaṇhati, tathā kātuṃ, tattha paṭṭhapetunti attho. Ussāhajananavasenāti yathā taṃ samādānaṃ niccalaṃ hoti, evaṃ ussoḷhiyā uppādanavasena sammadeva uttejetīti samuttejako. Ussāhajāteti appicchatāya jātussāhe. Vaṇṇaṃ vatvā tattha sampattiṃ āyatiñca labbhamānaguṇaṃ kittetvā sampahaṃseti sammadeva pakārehi tosetīti [M 2.0115] sampahaṃsako. Evaṃ santuṭṭhiādīsu yathārahaṃ yojanā kātabbā.

He gives advice to the bhikkhus with the ten topics for discussion as the instrument, instructing them on each topic by saying, 'A bhikkhu should indeed shun excessive desire and the like from afar and rightly be one with few wishes,' and so on; this is the meaning. For by instructing them on these, he is said to 'advise the bhikkhus with them.' He advises merely by showing its nature. Regarding 'having explained the subtle meaning': by repeatedly demonstrating the practice of having few wishes by way of 'fewness of wishes is like this, and like this,' one is not able to make known the subtle and profound meaning designated as 'fewness of wishes.' `He makes it known`: he makes it known with the distinctions mentioned above. `With reason`: the reason by which fewness of wishes is accomplished should be understood as the showing of the danger and benefit, such as: 'these are the dangers in great desire, etc.; this is the benefit in fewness of wishes.' Because he shows fewness of wishes with a proper reason, he is a `sandassaka` (one who demonstrates). `He makes them take it up`: this means to make them act so that they grasp it, to establish them in it. `By way of generating enthusiasm`: he rightly incites them so that their undertaking becomes steady; thus he is a `samuttejaka` (one who incites). `When enthusiasm has arisen`: when enthusiasm for having few wishes has arisen. Having spoken its praise—having extolled the future success and the qualities to be obtained—he gladdens them in various ways; thus he is a `sampahaṃsaka` (one who gladdens). In the same way, the application should be made to contentment and the other topics as is appropriate.

Gāhagāhakādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of Grasping, the Grasper, etc., is finished.

Pañcalābhavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Five Gains

253. Satthu sammukhā evaṃ vaṇṇo abbhuggatoti. Iminā tassa vaṇṇassa yathābhūtaguṇasamuṭṭhitataṃ dasseti. Mandamando viyāti ati viya acheko viya. Abalabalo viyāti ati viya abalo viya. Bhākuṭikabhākuṭiko viyāti ati viya dummukho viya. Anumassāti anumasitvā, dasa kathāvatthūni sarūpato visesato ca anupariggahetvāti attho. Pariggaṇhanaṃ pana nesaṃ anupavisanaṃ viya hotīti vuttaṃ “anupavisitvā”ti. Sabrahmacārīhi vaṇṇabhāsanaṃ eko lābhoti yojanā. Evaṃ sesesupi. Patthayamāno evamāha dhammagarutāyāti adhippāyo.

253. In the presence of the Teacher, such praise arose. This shows that his praise was founded on his actual qualities. ‘Like a very dull person’ means like one who is very unclever. ‘Like a very weak person’ means like one who is very weak. ‘Like one who is very sullen’ means like one with a very grim face. ‘He reflected’ means having reflected on, that is, having grasped the ten topics for discussion both in general and in detail—this is the meaning. But since grasping them is like entering into them, it is said, ‘having entered.’ The speaking of praise by his fellows in the holy life is one gain—this is the connection. So too for the rest. Aspiring, he spoke thus out of respect for the Dhamma—this is the intention.

Pañcalābhavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Five Gains is finished.

Cārikādivaṇṇanā

The Commentary on Wandering and So On

254. Abhiramanaṃ [V 2.0109] abhirataṃ, tadeva anunāsikalopaṃ akatvā vuttaṃ “abhiranta”nti. Bhāvanapuṃsakañcetaṃ. Anabhirati nāma natthi, abhiramitvā ciravihāropi natthi sammadeva pariññātavatthukattā. Sabbasahā hi buddhā bhagavanto asayhalābhino.

254. Delighting is what is meant by ‘delighted in.’ That same word is stated as ‘abhiranta’ without elision of the nasal. And this is a verbal noun in the neuter. There is no such thing as non-delight, nor is there prolonged dwelling after having delighted, because the object has been perfectly understood. For the Blessed Ones, the Buddhas, are all-enduring, obtainers of the unassailable.

Pubbe dhammagarutākittanapasaṅgena gahitaṃ aggahitañca mahākassapapaccuggamanādiṃ ekadesena dassetvā vanavāsitissasāmaṇerassa vatthuṃ vitthāretvā janapadacārikaṃ kathetuṃ “bhagavā hī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Ākāsagāmīhi saddhiṃ gantukāmo “chaḷabhiññānaṃ ārocehī”ti āha. Saṅghakammena sijjhamānāpi upasampadā satthu āṇāvaseneva sijjhanato “buddhadāyajjaṃ te dassāmī”ti vuttanti vadanti. Apare “aparipuṇṇavīsativassasseva tassa upasampadaṃ anujānanto satthā ‘buddhadāyajjaṃ te [M 2.0116] dassāmī’ti avocā”ti vadanti. Upasampādetvāti dhammasenāpatinā upajjhāyena upasampādetvā.

Previously, in connection with the praise of respect for the Dhamma, having shown in part what was taken up and not taken up—such as the going out to meet Mahākassapa—and having elaborated the story of the novice Tissa the forest-dweller, the passage beginning ‘For the Blessed One…’ was started in order to speak about the wandering through the country. Wishing to go with those who travel through the sky, he said, ‘Inform those with the six supernormal knowledges.’ Some say that although the higher ordination is accomplished by a formal act of the Saṅgha, because it is accomplished by the power of the Teacher’s command, it was said, ‘I will give you the Buddha’s inheritance.’ Others say that the Teacher, while allowing the higher ordination for one who had not yet completed twenty years, said, ‘I will give you the Buddha’s inheritance.’ ‘Having had him ordained’ means having had him ordained by the General of the Dhamma as preceptor.

Navayojanasatikaṃ majjhimadesapariyāpannameva, tato paraṃ nādhippetaṃ dandhatāvasena gamanato. Samantāti gatagataṭṭhānassa catūsu passesu. Aññenapi kāraṇenāti bhikkhūnaṃ samathavipassanātaruṇabhāvato aññenapi majjhimamaṇḍale veneyyānaṃ ñāṇaparipākādikāraṇena nikkhamati, antomaṇḍalaṃ otarati. Sattahi vātiādi “ekaṃ māsaṃ vā”tiādinā vuttānukkamena yojetabbaṃ.

The Middle Country is included within nine hundred yojanas; beyond that is not intended because of the slowness of travel. ‘All around’ means on the four sides of each place one has gone to. ‘By another reason’: he departs due to the immaturity of the monks in serenity and insight; and for another reason, such as the ripening of the knowledge-faculty of those to be trained in the middle region, he enters the inner circle. The phrase beginning ‘or by seven’ should be connected with the sequence stated in the passage beginning ‘or for one month.’

Sarīraphāsukatthāyāti ekasmiṃyeva ṭhāne nibaddhavāsena ussannadhātukassa sarīrassa virecanena phāsubhāvatthāya. Aṭṭhuppattikālābhikaṅkhanatthāyāti aggikkhandhūpamasutta (a. ni. 7.72) maghadevajātakādidesanānaṃ (jā. 1.1.9) viya dhammadesanāya aṭṭhuppattikālassa ākaṅkhanena. Surāpānasikkhāpadapaññāpane (pāci. 326) viya sikkhāpadapaññāpanatthāya. Bodhaneyyasatte aṅgulimālādike bodhanatthāya. Nibaddhavāsañca puggalaṃ uddissa cārikā nibaddhacārikā.

‘For the sake of bodily comfort’: for the sake of the comfort of a body with excessive elements due to dwelling constantly in one place, by means of purging. ‘For the sake of awaiting the time for an occasion to arise’: by awaiting the time for an occasion to arise for a Dhamma teaching, as with the teachings of the Aggikkhandhūpama Sutta (AN 7.72) and the Makhādeva Jātaka (Ja 9). ‘For the sake of laying down a training rule’: as in the laying down of the training rule on drinking intoxicants (Pāc 51). ‘For the sake of awakening beings to be enlightened’: for awakening beings such as Aṅgulimāla and others. A journey undertaken with a specific individual in mind who is a permanent resident is a ‘fixed journey.’

255. Apariggahabhāvaṃ katthaci alaggabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “yūthaṃ pahāya…pe… mattahatthī viyā”ti [V 2.0110] vuttaṃ. Asahāyakiccoti sahāyakiccarahito sīho viya. Tenassa ekavihāritaṃ tejavantatañca dasseti. Tadā pana kāyaviveko na sakkā laddhunti idamettha kāraṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Bahūhītiādi pana sabhāvadassanavasena vuttaṃ. Therassa parisā suvinītā ciṇṇagaruvāsā garuno icchānurūpameva vattati.

255. To show his state of non-possession, of not clinging anywhere, it is said: ‘Having left the herd … like a bull elephant in rut.’ ‘With no need for a companion’s help’ means like a lion, which is without need of a companion’s help. By this is shown his solitary dwelling and his majesty. But it should be seen that this is the reason here: at that time physical seclusion could not be obtained. The passage beginning ‘By many,’ however, was said by way of showing the natural state of things. The elder’s assembly was well-trained, accustomed to living in respect for their teacher, and they conducted themselves only in accordance with their teacher’s wish.

Vuttakāraṇayutte addhānagamane cārikānaṃ vohāro sāsane niruḷhoti āha “kiñcāpī”tiādi. Kenacideva nimittena kismiñci atthe pavattāya saññāya tannimittarahitepi aññasmiṃ pavatti ruḷhī nāma. Vijitamārattā saṅgāmavijayamahāyodho viya. Aññaṃ sevitvāti “mama āgatabhāvaṃ satthu ārocehī”ti ārocanatthaṃ aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ sevitvā.

He says the passage beginning ‘Although’ to show that the term ‘wandering’ (cārikā) has become the established usage in the Dispensation for a long journey connected with the aforesaid reason. Conventional usage (ruḷhī) is the name for the application of a designation, which has arisen in a certain sense due to some reason, to another sense even when that reason is absent, like calling the Buddha a ‘great warrior victorious in battle’ because he has conquered Māra. ‘Having attended on another’ means having attended on another bhikkhu for the purpose of announcing, to say: ‘Inform the Teacher that I have arrived.’

Bhagavā [M 2.0117] dhammaṃ desento taṃtaṃpuggalajjhāsayānurūpaṃ tadanucchavikameva dhammiṃ kathaṃ karotīti dassento “cūḷagosiṅgasutte”tiādimāha. Tattha sāmaggirasānisaṃsanti “kacci pana vo, anuruddhā, samaggā sammodamānā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.326) sāmaggirasānisaṃsaṃ kathesi. Āvasathānisaṃsanti “sītaṃ uṇhaṃ paṭihanatī”tiādinā (cūḷava. 295, 315) āvasathapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ. Satipaṭilābhikanti jotipālatthere lāmakaṃ ṭhānaṃ otiṇṇamatte mahābodhipallaṅke pana sabbaññutaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ patthanaṃ katvā pāramiyo pūrento āgato. Tādisassa nāma pamādavihāro na yuttoti yathā kassapo bhagavā bodhisattassa satiṃ paṭilabhituṃ dhammiṃ kathaṃ kathesi, tathā ayaṃ bhagavā tameva pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttakathaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ghaṭikārasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 2.282) kathesi. Cattāro dhammuddeseti – “upanīyati loko addhuvo, atāṇo loko anabhissaro, assako loko sabbaṃ pahāya gamanīyaṃ, ūno loko atitto taṇhādāso cā”ti (ma. ni. 2.305) ime cattāro dhammuddese kathesi. Kāmañcete dhammuddesā raṭṭhapālasutte (ma. ni. 2.304) āyasmatā raṭṭhapālattherena rañño korabyassa kathitā, te pana bhagavato eva āharitvā therena tattha kathitāti vuttaṃ “raṭṭhapālasutte”tiādi. Tathā hi vuttaṃ sutte – “atthi kho, mahārāja, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena cattāro dhammuddesā uddiṭṭhā”tiādi (ma. ni. 2.305) pānakānisaṃsakathanti “aggihuttaṃ mukhaṃ yaññā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 2.400; su. ni. 573) anumodanaṃ vatvā puna pakiṇṇakakathāvasena pānakapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ ānisaṃsakathaṃ kathesi. Ekībhāve ānisaṃsaṃ kathesi, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ bhaguṃ dhammiyā kathāya sandassesī”tiādi [V 2.0111] (ma. ni. 3.238). Anantanayanti aparimāṇadesanānayaṃ appicchatādipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammiṃ kathaṃ. Tenāha “puṇṇa, ayampi appicchakathāyevā”tiādi bahūhi pariyāyehi nānānayaṃ deseti. Kathaṃ tathā desitaṃ thero aññāsīti āha “paṭisambhidāpattassa…pe… ahosī”ti.

To show that when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, he gives a Dhamma talk that is suitable and appropriate to the disposition of each individual, he mentions the Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta and so on. There, with the passage beginning, ‘But I hope, Anuruddhas, that you are all living in concord, harmoniously’ (MN 31), he spoke on the benefit of the flavor of harmony. The benefit of a dwelling: with the passage beginning, ‘It wards off cold and heat’ (Cv VI.1.5), he spoke on the benefit connected with a dwelling. A talk for the regaining of mindfulness: when the elder Jotipāla had fallen into a low state, he made an aspiration to fully awaken to omniscience at the throne of great awakening and came along fulfilling the perfections. Because it is not proper for such a one to live in heedlessness, just as the Blessed One Kassapa gave a Dhamma talk for the Bodhisatta to regain his mindfulness, so this Blessed One gave the monks that same talk connected with a past life, the Ghaṭikāra Sutta (MN 81). He taught four summaries of the Dhamma: ‘The world is swept away, it is not permanent; the world has no shelter and no protector; the world has nothing of its own, one has to leave everything and pass on; the world is wanting, insatiate, the slave of craving’ (MN 82). And although these summaries of the Dhamma were spoken by the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla to King Koravya in the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, they were spoken by the elder there after taking them from the Blessed One, thus it is said ‘in the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta,’ etc. For so it is said in the sutta: ‘There are, great king, four summaries of the Dhamma pointed out by that Blessed One, the knowing one, the seeing one, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One…’ (MN 82). A talk on the benefit of drinks: after expressing appreciation with the passage beginning, ‘The fire-oblation is the chief of sacrifices’ (SNi 3.5), he then gave a talk on the benefits connected with drinks by way of a miscellaneous talk. He spoke on the benefit of solitude, in reference to which it is said: ‘Then the Blessed One instructed the Venerable Bhagu with a Dhamma talk…’ (AN 8.86). The endless method: a Dhamma talk connected with fewness of wishes, etc., a method of teaching with limitless applications. Therefore he says: ‘Puṇṇa, this too is a talk on fewness of wishes,’ etc. He teaches by many methods in various ways. As to how the elder understood what was taught in this way, he says: ‘Having attained the analytical knowledges … he was…’

Cārikādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on Wandering and So On is finished.

Sattavisuddhipañhavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Questions on the Seven Purifications.

256. Tato [M 2.0118] paṭṭhāyāti. Yadā jātibhūmakā bhikkhū satthu sammukhā therassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsiṃsu, tato paṭṭhāya. Sīsānulokī hutvā piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhanaṃ therena samāgame ādaravasena katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ pāṭhe “appeva nāmā”tiādi, “taramānarūpo”ti ca. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nilīna”ntiādi, taṃ akāraṇaṃ. Na hi dhammasenāpati tassa therassa nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ abhiññāñāṇena jānituṃ na sakkoti. “Kacci nu kho maṃ adisvāva gamissatī”ti ayampi cintā ādaravasenevāti yuttaṃ. Na hi satthāraṃ daṭṭhuṃ āgato sāvako api āyasmā aññātakoṇḍañño satthukappaṃ dhammasenāpatiṃ tattha vasantaṃ adisvāva gacchanako nāma atthi. Divāvihāranti sampadāne upayogavacananti āha “divāvihāratthāyā”ti.

256. From that time onward: From the time when the monks native to the birthplace praised the Elder in the presence of the Teacher. It should be understood that when meeting the Elder, he, out of respect, followed closely behind, looking back repeatedly. This is to be seen from the passage, “Perhaps,” and so on, and “appearing hurried.” However, what is mentioned in the commentary—“hidden in one place,” etc.—is without reason. For the General of the Dhamma is surely able to know the elder’s seated position through his supernormal knowledge. The thought, “Will he leave without seeing me?” also rightly arises from respect. Indeed, no disciple who comes to see the Teacher—not even the Venerable Aññāta Koṇḍañña—would ever depart without seeing the General of the Dhamma, who is like the Teacher, dwelling there. The word `divāvihāraṃ` is a dative expressing purpose; hence he says `divāvihāratthāya` (for the sake of the daytime dwelling).

257. Purimakathāyāti paṭhamālāpe. Appatiṭṭhitāyāti nappavattitāya. Pacchimakathā na jāyatīti pacchā vattabbakathāya avasaro na hoti. Satta visuddhiyo pucchi diṭṭhasaṃsandanavasena. Ñāṇadassanavisuddhi nāma ariyamaggo. Yasmā tato uttarimpi pattabbaṃ attheva, tasmā “catupārisuddhisīlādīsu ṭhitassapi brahmacariyavāso matthakaṃ na pāpuṇātī”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmāti brahmacariyavāsassa matthakaṃ appattattā. Sabbaṃ paṭikkhipīti sattamampi pañhaṃ paṭikkhipi, itaresu vattabbameva natthi.

257. In the preliminary talk means in the first conversation. “Not established” means not initiated. “No subsequent discussion arises” means there is no opportunity for a subsequent topic of conversation. He asked about the seven purifications by way of examining what he had seen. The purification of knowledge and vision is the noble path. Since there is still something further to be attained beyond that, therefore it was said, “Even for one established in the fourfold purity of virtue, etc., the holy life does not reach its culmination.” Therefore, because the culmination of the holy life was not attained. “He rejected everything” means he rejected even the seventh question; in regard to the others, there was indeed nothing to say.

Appaccayaparinibbānanti anupādisesanibbānamāha. Idāni pakārantarenapi anupādāparinibbānaṃ dassetuṃ “dvedhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha gahaṇūpādānanti daḷhaggahaṇabhūtaṃ upādānaṃ[V 2.0112]. Tenāha “kāmupādānādika”nti. Paccayūpādānanti yaṃ kiñci paccayamāha. So hi attano phalaṃ upādiyati upādānavasena gaṇhatīti upādānanti vuccati. Tenāha “paccayūpādānaṃ nāma…pe… paccayā”ti. “Anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccatī”ti vacanato (mahāva. 28, 30) arahattaphalaṃ anupādāparinibbānanti kathenti. Na ca upādānasampayuttanti upādānehi etaṃ na sahitaṃ nāpi upādānehi saha pavatti hutvā. Na ca kañci dhammaṃ upādiyatīti kassaci dhammassa ārammaṇakaraṇavasena na upādiyati[M 2.0119]. Parinibbutanteti aggamaggena kātabbakilesaparinibbānapariyosānante jātattā. Amatadhātumeva anupādāparinibbānaṃ kathenti, kathentānañca yathā tassa koci paccayo nāma natthi, evaṃ adhigatopi yathā koci paccayo nāma na hoti, tathā parinibbānaṃ apaccayaparinibbānanti dassento “ayaṃ anto”tiādimāha. Puna pucchaṃ ārabhi anupādāparinibbānaṃ sarūpato patiṭṭhāpetukāmo.

By `Appaccayaparinibbāna` he means Nibbāna without residue. Now, to show `anupādāparinibbāna` in another way, it is said, “in two ways.” Herein, `gahaṇūpādāna` means clinging that is strong grasping. Hence it is said, “such as sensual clinging, etc.” `Paccayūpādāna` means any condition whatsoever. For a condition grasps its own result, it takes hold by way of clinging, thus it is called clinging. Hence it is said, “conditional clinging is... the conditions.” From the statement, “the mind is liberated from the taints without clinging” (Mahāvagga 28, 30), they describe the fruit of Arahantship as Nibbāna without clinging. “Not associated with clinging” means this is not connected with clinging, nor does it occur together with clinging. “And does not cling to any phenomenon” means it does not grasp any phenomenon by way of making it an object. “At the final extinguishing” means because it has arisen at the end, at the conclusion of the extinguishing of defilements that is to be done by the highest path. They describe the deathless element itself as Nibbāna without clinging. And to show that this Nibbāna is unconditioned Nibbāna—in that just as there is no condition for it, so too when it is attained there is no condition whatsoever—he says, “this is the end,” and so on. Desiring to establish Nibbāna without clinging in its true nature, he began another question.

258. Sabbaparivattesūti sabbesu pañhaparivattanesu, pañhavāresūti attho. Sagahaṇadhammamevāti “etaṃ mamā”tiādinā gaṇhatīti gahaṇaṃ, saha gahaṇenāti sagahaṇaṃ, upādāniyanti attho. Vivaṭṭasannissitassa abhāvato vaṭṭameva anugatoti vaṭṭānugato. Tenāha “catupārisuddhisīlamattassapi abhāvato”ti. Yo pana catubbidhe vivaṭṭūpanissaye sīle ṭhito, sopi “aññatra imehi dhammehī”ti vattabbataṃ arahati.

258. “In all transformations” means in all instances of posing questions, that is, in the rounds of questions. By `sagahaṇadhamma` is meant a state with grasping: “grasping” (`gahaṇa`) is to grasp with the thought “this is mine,” etc.; “with grasping” (`sagahaṇa`) means together with grasping; the meaning is “subject to clinging.” `Vaṭṭānugata` means following the round of existence, because of the absence of a basis for release from it. Therefore, it is said, “because even the mere virtue of the fourfold purity is absent.” But one who is established in the four kinds of virtue that are a basis for release from the round is worthy of being described as “apart from these things.”

Sattavisuddhipañhavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Questions on the Seven Purifications is finished.

Sattarathavinītavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Relay of Seven Chariots.

259. Nissakkavacanametaṃ “yāva heṭṭhimasopānakaḷevarā”tiādīsu viya. Atthoti payojanaṃ. Cittavisuddhi hettha sīlavisuddhiṃ payojeti tassa tadatthattā. Sīlavisuddhikiccaṃ kataṃ nāma hoti samādhisaṃvattanato. Samādhisaṃvattanikā hi sīlavisuddhi nāma. Sabbapadesūti “cittavisuddhi yāvadeva diṭṭhivisuddhatthā”tiādīsu sabbapadesu, diṭṭhivisuddhiyaṃ ṭhitassa cittavisuddhakiccaṃ kataṃ nāma hotītiādinā yojetabbaṃ.

259. This is a non-elliptical expression, as in phrases such as “down to the lowest step of the staircase.” `Attha` means purpose. Here, purification of mind fulfills the purpose of purification of virtue, because the latter has the former as its purpose. The function of purification of virtue is considered fulfilled because it leads to concentration. For purification of virtue is that which leads to concentration. “In all passages” means that in all such passages as “purification of mind is only for the purpose of purification of view,” etc., the connection should be made in this way: the function of purification of mind is considered fulfilled for one established in the purification of view, and so on.

Sāvatthinagaraṃ viya sakkāyanagaraṃ atikkamitabbattā. Sāketanagaraṃ viya nibbānanagaraṃ pāpuṇitabbattā[V 2.0113]. Accāyikassa kiccassa uppādakālo viya navameneva khaṇena pattabbassa abhisamayakiccassa upādakālo. Yathā rañño sattamena rathavinītena sākete antepuradvāre oruḷhassa na tāva kiccaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ nāma hoti, saṃvidhātabbasaṃvidhānaṃ ñātimittagaṇaparivutassa surasabhojanaparibhoge niṭṭhitaṃ nāma siyā, evametaṃ ñāṇadassanavisuddhiyā kilese khepetvā tesaṃyeva paṭippassaddhipahānasādhakaariyaphalasamaṅgikāle abhisamayakiccaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ nāma hoti. Tenāha [M 2.0120] “yogino…pe… kālo daṭṭhabbo”ti. Tattha paropaṇṇāsa kusaladhammā nāma cittuppādapariyāpannā phassādayo paropaṇṇāsa anavajjadhammā. Nirodhasayaneti nibbānasayane.

Just as the city of Sāvatthī is to be surpassed, so too the city of individuality. Just as the city of Sāketā is to be reached, so too the city of Nibbāna. Like the time for the arising of an urgent task, so is the time for the arising of the task of realization, which must be attained in the ninth moment. Just as for a king who, with his seventh relay chariot, has alighted at the palace gate of Sāketā, the task is not yet considered complete, but it would be considered complete when, surrounded by a retinue of relatives and friends, he enjoys delicious food; so too, with the purification by knowledge and vision, having destroyed the defilements, the task of realization is considered complete at the time of being endowed with the noble fruition that accomplishes their subsiding and abandonment. Hence it is said: 'For the yogi... the time must be seen.' Here, the more than fifty wholesome states are the more than fifty blameless states, beginning with contact, that are included in the arising of consciousness. 'In the bed of cessation' means in the bed of Nibbāna.

“Visuddhiyo”ti vā “kathāvatthūnī”ti vā atthato ekaṃ, byañjanameva nānanti tesaṃ atthato anaññabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “itī”ti āraddhaṃ. Āyasmā puṇṇo dasa kathāvatthūni vissajjesīti satta visuddhiyo nāma vissajjantopi dasa kathāvatthūni vissajjesi tesaṃ atthato anaññattā. Eteneva dhammasenāpati sāriputtatthero satta visuddhiyo pucchanto dasa kathāvatthūni pucchīti ayampi attho vuttovāti veditabbo. Nti pañhaṃ. Kiṃ jānitvā pucchīti visuddhipariyāyena kathāvatthūni pucchāmīti kiṃ jānitvā pucchi. Dasakathāvatthulābhinaṃ theraṃ visuddhiyo pucchanto pucchitaṭṭhāneyeva pucchanena kiṃ titthakusalo vā pana hutvā visayasmiṃ pucchi, udāhu pānīyatthikamatitthehi chinnataṭehi pātento viya atitthakusalo hutvā apucchitabbaṭṭhāne avisayasmiṃ pucchīti yojanā. Iminā nayena vissajjanapakkhepi atthayojanā veditabbā. Yadatthamassa vicāraṇā āraddhā, taṃ dassentena “titthakusalo hutvā”tiādiṃ vatvā visuddhikathāvatthūnaṃ atthato anaññattepi ayaṃ viseso veditabboti dassetuṃ “yaṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tadamināti yaṃ “saṃkhittaṃ, vitthiṇṇa”nti ca vuttaṃ, taṃ iminā idāni vuccamānena nayena vidhinā veditabbaṃ.

'Purifications' or 'topics of discussion'—in meaning they are one, only the expression is different. To show that their meaning is not different, 'thus' is stated. The Venerable Puṇṇa answered the ten topics of discussion; although he answered what are called the seven purifications, he answered the ten topics of discussion because their meaning is not different. By this, it should be understood that this meaning is also stated: the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, in asking about the seven purifications, asked about the ten topics of discussion. This is the question. Knowing what did he ask? That is, knowing what did he ask, thinking, 'I am asking about the topics of discussion by way of the purifications'? When asking the elder, who had attained the ten topics of discussion, about the purifications, did he, being skilled in the fords, ask within the proper domain? Or, like one who, for the thirsty and unsatisfied, makes water fall from a broken bank, did he, being unskilled in the fords, ask in an improper place, outside the proper domain? This is the connection. In this way, the connection of the meaning should be understood on the side of the answer as well. To show the purpose for which this investigation was begun, having said, 'being skilled in the fords,' etc., and to show that this distinction should be understood even though the purifications and the topics of discussion are not different in meaning, 'For that which...' etc., is said. 'That which was said as 'in brief' and 'in detail,' that should be understood by this method and rule which is now being stated.

Ekā sīlavisuddhīti visuddhīsu visuṃ ekā sīlavisuddhi. Dasasu kathāvatthūsu cattāri kathāvatthūni hutvā āgatā appicchatādīhi vinā sīlavisuddhiyā asambhavato. Appicchakathātiādīsu kathāsīsena dasakathāvatthu gahitaṃ. Kathetabbattā vā vatthu kathāvatthūti vuttaṃ. Evañca upakārato, sabhāvato vā catunnaṃ kathāvatthūnaṃ sīlavisuddhisaṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tiṇṇaṃ kathāvatthūnaṃ cittavisuddhisaṅgahepi eseva nayo. Pañca visuddhiyoti nāmarūpaparicchedo diṭṭhivisuddhi, sappaccayanāmarūpadassanaṃ kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi, vipassanupakkilese pahāya uppannaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ [V 2.0114] maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi, udayabbayañāṇādi navavidhañāṇaṃ paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi, ariyamaggañāṇaṃ ñāṇadassanavisuddhīti imā pañca visuddhiyo.

'One is the purification of virtue' means that among the purifications, one is distinctly the purification of virtue. In the ten topics of discussion, it has come to be four topics of discussion, because the purification of virtue is impossible without fewness of wishes, etc. In 'the discussion on fewness of wishes,' etc., the ten topics of discussion are taken under the heading of 'discussion.' Or, because it is to be discussed, the subject is called a 'topic of discussion.' And thus, the inclusion of the four topics of discussion in the purification of virtue should be seen by way of assistance, or by way of its intrinsic nature. This same method applies to the inclusion of the three topics of discussion in the purification of mind. 'The five purifications' are: the discernment of mind-and-matter is the purification of view; the seeing of mind-and-matter with its conditions is the purification by overcoming doubt; the insight-knowledge that has arisen by abandoning the corruptions of insight is the purification by knowledge and vision of what is path and not-path; the ninefold knowledge beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away is the purification by knowledge and vision of the way; the knowledge of the noble path is the purification by knowledge and vision. These are the five purifications.

Sattarathavinītavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Relay of Seven Chariots is finished.

260. Sammoditunti [M 2.0121] anantaraṃ vuccamānena sammodituṃ. Aṭṭhānaparikappenāti akāraṇassa vatthuno parikappanena tadā asambhavantaṃ atthaṃ parikappetvā vacanena. Abhiṇhadassanassāti niccadassanassa, niyatadassanassāti attho.

260. 'To rejoice with' means to rejoice with what is said immediately after. 'By groundless speculation' means by speculating about a groundless matter, that is, by speaking after having speculated on a meaning that was impossible at that time. 'Of frequent seeing' means of constant seeing, that is, of regular seeing; this is the meaning.

Ukkhipīti guṇato kathitabhāvena ukkaṃseti. Therassāti āyasmato puṇṇattherassa. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne imasmiṃ kāraṇe ekapadeneva sāvakavisaye anaññasādhāraṇaguṇāvikaraṇanimittaṃ. Idāni tamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “amaccañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Apacāyamānoti pūjayanto.

'He raises up' means he extols, because his virtues have been spoken of. 'Of the Elder' means of the Venerable Elder Puṇṇa. In this instance, for this reason, a single word is the sign for making manifest qualities, uncommon and not shared by others, in the domain of a disciple. Now, to make that very meaning clearer, 'indeed, a minister,' etc., is said. 'Paying homage' means revering.

“Anumassa anumassa pucchitā”ti vuttattā vicāraṇavasenāha “kiṃ pana pañhassa pucchanaṃ bhāriyaṃ udāhu vissajjana”nti. Sahetukaṃ katvāti yuttāyuttaṃ katvā. Sakāraṇanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Pucchanampīti evaṃ sahadhammena pucchitabbamatthaṃ sayaṃ sampādetvā pucchanampi bhāriyaṃ dukkaraṃ. Vissajjanampīti sahadhammena vissajjanampi dukkaraṃ. Evañhi vissajjento viññūnaṃ cittaṃ ārādhetīti. Yathānusandhināva desanā niṭṭhitāādito saparikkhāraṃ sīlaṃ, majjhe samādhiṃ, ante vasībhāvappattaṃ paññaṃ dassetvā desanāya niṭṭhāpitattāti.

Because it is said, 'being asked about every single thing,' by way of investigation he says, 'But is the asking of the question difficult, or the answering?' 'Having made it reasoned' means having determined what is proper and improper. 'With a reason' is a synonym for that. 'Even the asking': thus, having oneself prepared the matter that should be asked in accordance with the Dhamma, even the asking is difficult, hard to do. 'And the answering': answering in accordance with the Dhamma is also difficult. For in answering thus, one gratifies the minds of the wise. The teaching was concluded in accordance with its sequence, because it was concluded by showing virtue with its requisites at the beginning, concentration in the middle, and wisdom that has attained mastery at the end.

Rathavinītasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Exposition of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Rathavinīta Sutta is complete.

5. Nivāpasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Nivāpa Sutta.

261. Nivappatīti [V 2.0115] nivāpo, nivāpaṃ vatteti, nivāpabhojanaṃ vā etassāti nevāpiko, nivāpena mige palobhetvā gaṇhanakamāgaviko. Tiṇabījānīti nivāpatiṇabījāni. Vappanti sassaṃ viya vapitabbaṭṭhena vappaṃ. “Mayaṃ viya aññe ke īdisaṃ labhissantī”ti mānamadaṃ āpajjissanti. Vissaṭṭhasatibhāvanti anussaṅkitaparisaṅkitabhāvaṃ. Tiracchānā hi vijātiyabalavatiracchānavasanaṭṭhānesu sāsaṅkā ubbiggahadayā appamattā honti visesato māgavikādimanussūpacāre, rasataṇhāya pana baddhā pamādaṃ āpajjassanti. Nivapati etthāti nivāpo, nivāpabhūmi nivāpaṭṭhānaṃ. Tenāha “nivāpaṭṭhāne”ti. “Yathākāmakaraṇīyā”ti vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “ekaṃ kirā”tiādi [M 2.0122] vuttaṃ. Tattha nīvāravanaṃ viyāti nīvārassa samūho viya. Nīvāro nāma araññe sayaṃjātavīhijāti. Meghamālā viyāti meghaghaṭā viya. Ekagghananti ekajjhaṃ viya aviraṭṭhaṃ. Pakkamantīti āsaṅkaparisaṅkā hutvā pakkamanti. Kaṇṇe cālayamānāti anāsaṅkantānaṃ pahaṭṭhākāradassanaṃ. Maṇḍalagumbanti maṇḍalakākārena ṭhitaṃ gumbaṃ.

261. 'One scatters bait' (nivappati), thus it is 'bait' (nivāpo). One who carries on the baiting (nivāpaṃ vatteti), or for whom there is the food of bait (nivāpabhojanaṃ), is a 'baiter' (nevāpiko), that is, a hunter who catches deer by luring them with bait. 'Grass seeds' means bait-grass seeds. 'They sow' (vappanti); 'what is sown' (vappaṃ) is so called because it is to be sown like a crop. 'Who else like us will obtain such a thing?'—thus they will fall into pride and conceit. 'A state of lapsed mindfulness' means a state of being without suspicion and apprehension. For animals, in places inhabited by stronger animals of other species, are suspicious, agitated at heart, and heedful, especially in the vicinity of humans such as hunters; but bound by craving for taste, they will fall into heedlessness. 'One scatters bait here' (nivapati ettha), thus it is a 'feeding ground' (nivāpo), a bait-land, a bait-place. Hence it is said, 'at the feeding ground.' To explain the meaning of what was said as 'to be dealt with as one wishes,' 'reportedly, one...' etc., is said. Therein, 'like a forest of wild rice' means like a clump of wild rice. 'Wild rice' (nīvāro) is a species of self-grown grain in the forest. 'Like a garland of clouds' means like a mass of clouds. 'As a single solid mass' means like being all together, not separated. 'They depart' means they depart having become suspicious and apprehensive. 'Wagging their ears' is the showing of a delighted appearance by those who are not suspicious. 'A circular thicket' means a thicket standing in a circular shape.

262. Kappetvāti upamābhāvena parikappetvā. Mige attano vase vattāpanaṃ vasībhāvo. So eva ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhi, pabhāvanaṭṭhena ānubhāvo.

262. 'Having contrived' means having conceived it by way of a simile. 'Mastery' is the bringing of deer under one's own control. That very thing, in the sense of success, is spiritual power (iddhi); in the sense of dominance, it is might (ānubhāvo).

263. Bhayena bhogatoti bhayena saha sabhayaṃ nivāpaparibhogato. Balavīriyanti kāyabalañca uṭṭhānavīriyañca. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana balameva vīriyaṃ. Balanti ca sarīrabalaṃ, tañca atthato manasikāramaggehi aparāparaṃ sañcaraṇakavātoti vuttaṃ “aparāparaṃ sañcaraṇavāyodhātū”ti.

263. 'From enjoying with fear' means from enjoying the bait fearfully, together with fear. 'Strength and energy' means bodily strength and rousing energy. In the commentary, however, strength itself is energy. And 'strength' is bodily strength, and that, in meaning, is the wind that moves to and fro through the paths of attention; thus it is said, 'the wind element that moves to and fro'.

264. Sikkhitakerāṭikāti paricitasāṭheyyā, vañcakāti attho. Iddhimanto viya ānubhāvavanto viya. Pacurajanehi parabhūtā jātāti parajanā, mahābhūtā. Tenāha “yakkhā”ti. Samantā sappadesanti samantato padesavantaṃ vipulokāsasannivāsaṭṭhānaṃ. Tassa pana sappadesatā mahāokāsatāyāti vuttaṃ “mahantaṃ okāsa”nti.

264. ‘Sikkhitakerāṭikā’ means well-trained in deceit (paricitasāṭheyyā); the meaning is ‘vañcakā’ (deceivers). They are like those possessing supernormal power (iddhimanto viya), like those possessing influence (ānubhāvavanto viya). ‘Pacurajanehi parabhūtā jātā’ means they are dominated by many people, and are therefore ‘parajanā’ (other people), or ‘mahābhūtā’ (great beings). Therefore, it is said, ‘yakkhā’ (demons). ‘Samantā sappadesaṃ’ means a location entirely possessing a region (samantato padesavantaṃ), a spacious habitation area (vipulokāsasannivāsaṭṭhānaṃ). The extent of its possessing a region is its great spaciousness, as stated, ‘a great space’ (mahantaṃ okāsaṃ).

265. Ghaṭṭessantīti “sabhayasamuṭṭhāna”nti saññādānavasena cittaṃ cetessanti, tāsessantīti [V 2.0116] attho. Pariccajissantīti nibbisissanti. Mahallakoti jātiyā mahallako jiṇṇo. Dubbaloti byādhivasena, pakatiyā vā balavirahito.

265. ‘Ghaṭṭessanti’ means they will agitate the mind by way of causing fear, by giving rise to the perception of ‘arising with fear’ (sabhayasamuṭṭhānaṃ); the meaning is ‘they will frighten’ (tāsessanti). ‘Pariccajissanti’ means they will become disgusted (nibbisissanti). ‘Mahallako’ means old in age (jātiyā mahallako), aged (jiṇṇo). ‘Dubbalo’ means weak because of illness (byādhivasena), or naturally lacking strength (pakatiyā vā balavirahito).

267. Nivāpasadisatāya nivāpoti vā. Lokapariyāpannaṃ hutvā kilesehi āmasitabbatāya lokāmisānīti vā. Vaṭṭe āmisabhūtattā vaṭṭāmisabhūtānaṃ. Vasaṃ vattetīti kāmaguṇehi kāmaguṇe giddhe satte tasseva gedhassa vasena attano vase vattetīti. Tenāha –

267. Or because it is like a feeding ground (nivāpasadisatāya), it is called ‘nivāpa’ (feeding ground). Or ‘lokāmisāni’ (worldly bait) because, having become subject to the world (lokapariyāpannaṃ hutvā), it is to be touched by defilements (kilesehi āmasitabbatāya). ‘To those who are the bait of the round’ (vaṭṭāmisabhūtānaṃ) because they have the nature of bait in the round of existence (vaṭṭe āmisabhūtattā). ‘It turns (beings) under its power’ (vasaṃ vatteti) means that by sensual qualities, it turns under its own power beings who are greedy for sensual qualities, by the power of that same greed. Therefore, it was said:

“Antalikkhacaro [M 2.0123] pāso, yvāyaṃ carati mānaso;

Tena taṃ bādhayissāmi, na me samaṇa mokkhasī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.151; mahāva. 33);

‘The snare that moves in the sky—this mental snare that roams about—with that I will harass you; you shall not escape me, ascetic!’ (Saṃ. Ni. 1.151; Mahāva. 33).

Ayanti paṭhamamigajātūpamā. Vānapatthassa satova papañcaparadattikādisaputtadāranikkhamanaṃ sandhāyāha “saputtabhariyapabbajjāyā”ti.

This is the first simile, that of the deer. Referring to the going forth (nikkhamanaṃ) of a forest-dweller (vānapatthassa) from proliferation (papañca), dependence on others' gifts (paradattikā), and so on, together with his children and spouse (saputtadāra), he says, ‘by the going forth with children and wife’ (saputtabhariyapabbajjāya).

268. Kāmato cittassa vimutti idha cetovimuttīti adhippetāti āha “cetovimutti nāma…pe… uppannaajjhāsayo”ti. Kāme vissajjetvā puna tattha nimuggatāya dutiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇā dutiyamigajātūpamā vuttā.

268. Here, the liberation of the mind from sensual desires (kāmato cittassa vimutti) is intended as mental liberation (cetovimutti). Thus, it is said: ‘Mental liberation is… an inclination that has arisen’ (cetovimutti nāma…pe… uppannaajjhāsayo). Because the second group of ascetics and brahmins, having cast off sensual desires, plunge back into them, the second simile of the deer is stated.

269. Tatiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇā yathāpariccatte kāme pariccajitvā evaṃ ṭhitā, na dutiyā viya tattha nimuggāti adhippāyena “kiṃ pana te akaṃsū”ti pucchati. Itare kāmaṃ ujukaṃ kāmaguṇesu na nimuggā, pariyāyena pana nimuggā diṭṭhijālena ca ajjhotthaṭāti dassento “gāmanigamajanapadarājadhāniyo”tiādimāha. Diṭṭhijālampi taṇhājālānugatamevāti āha “mārassa pāpimato diṭṭhijālena parikkhipitvā”ti.

269. With the intention that the third group of ascetics and brahmins, having renounced sensual desires as they should be renounced, remain steadfast and do not plunge back into them like the second group, the question is asked: ‘But what did they do?’ Showing that others, though not directly plunged into sensual pleasures, are indirectly plunged and covered over by a net of views, he says, ‘villages, towns, districts, and royal cities,’ etc. The net of views is also accompanied by the net of craving, as stated: ‘enveloped by the Evil One’s net of views’ (mārassa pāpimato diṭṭhijālena parikkhipitvā).

271. Khandhakilesābhisaṅkhāramārā vā idha māraggahaṇena gahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Akkhīni bhindi daṭṭhuṃ asamatthabhāvāpādanena. Tenāha “vipassanāpādakajjhāna”ntiādi. Kiñcāpi māro yaṃ kiñci jhānaṃ samāpannassapi bhikkhuno cittaṃ imaṃ nāma ārammaṇaṃ nissāya vattatīti na jānāti, idhādhippetassa pana bhikkhuno vasena “vipassanāpādakajjhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Teneva pariyāyenāti “na mārassa akkhīni bhindī”ti evamādinā yathāvuttapariyāyena. Adassanaṃ gatoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Cakkhussa padaṃ patiṭṭhāti ca idha ārammaṇaṃ adhippetaṃ taṃ pariggayha [V 2.0117] pavattanatoti āha “appatiṭṭhaṃ nirārammaṇa”nti. Soti māro. Disvāti dassanahetu. Yasmā maggena catusaccadassanahetu āsavā na parikkhīṇā. Phalakkhaṇe hi te khīṇāti vuccantīti.

271. Here, ‘Māra’ should be understood as referring to the Māras of the aggregates, defilements, and formations (khandhakilesābhisaṅkhāramārā). ‘Blinded the eyes’ (akkhīni bhindi) means rendering them incapable of seeing (daṭṭhuṃ asamatthabhāvāpādanena). Hence it is said: ‘the jhāna that supports insight’ (vipassanāpādakajjhānaṃ), etc. Although Māra does not know upon what object the mind of any monk absorbed in jhāna dwells, here it is said ‘the jhāna that supports insight’ (vipassanāpādakajjhānaṃ) in reference to the intended monk. By that very reasoning (teneva pariyāyena), it is said, ‘he did not blind Māra’s eyes’ (na mārassa akkhīni bhindī), etc., as explained by the aforementioned reasoning. ‘Gone beyond sight’ (adassanaṃ gato)—here too, the same principle applies. And ‘the eye’s foundation’ (cakkhussa padaṃ patiṭṭhāti) here refers to the object (ārammaṇaṃ adhippetā), meaning its functioning by grasping that object; hence it is said, ‘unestablished, without an object’ (appatiṭṭhaṃ nirārammaṇaṃ). ‘He’ (so) is Māra. ‘Having seen’ (disvā) means because of seeing (dassanahetu). Because the taints are not fully destroyed by the path, which is the cause of seeing the four truths—they are said to be destroyed only at the moment of fruition.

Loketi sattaloke saṅkhāraloke ca. Sattavisattabhāvenāti laggabhāvena ceva savisesaṃ āsattabhāvena ca. Atha vātiādinā niddesanayavasena (mahāni. 3, cūḷani. mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa 22, 23; cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 124) visattikāpadaṃ niddisati. Visatāti vitthaṭā [M 2.0124] rūpādīsu tebhūmakadhammesu byāpanavasena visaṭāti purimavacanameva takārassa ṭakāraṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Visālāti vipulā. Visakkatīti parisakkati sahati. Ratto hi rāgavatthunā pādena tāliyamānopi sahati. Osakkanaṃ, vipphandanaṃ vā visakkanantipi vadanti. Visaṃharatīti yathā tathā kāmesu ānisaṃsaṃ dassentī vividhehi ākārehi nekkhammābhimukhappavattito cittaṃ saṃharati saṅkhipati, visaṃ vā dukkhaṃ, taṃ harati upanetīti attho. Visaṃvādikāti aniccādiṃ niccādito gaṇhāpentī visaṃvādikā hoti. Dukkhanibbattakassa kammassa hetubhāvato visamūlā, visaṃ vā dukkhadukkhādibhūtā vedanā mūlaṃ etissāti visamūlā. Dukkhasamudayattā visaṃ phalaṃ etissāti visaphalā. Taṇhāya rūpādikassa dukkhasseva paribhogo hoti, na amatassāti sā “visaparibhogā”ti vuttā. Sabbattha niruttivasena saddasiddhi veditabbā. Yo panettha padhāno attho, taṃ dassetuṃ puna “visālā vā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nittiṇṇo uttiṇṇoti upasaggavasena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Niravasesato vā tiṇṇo nittiṇṇo. Tena tena maggena uddhamuddhaṃ tiṇṇo uttiṇṇo. Yaṃ panettha atthato avibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

‘Loka’ refers to the world of beings (sattaloke) and the world of formations (saṅkhāraloke). ‘Sattavisattabhāvena’ means by way of being attached (laggabhāvena) and also specially attached (savisesaṃ āsattabhāvena). Or, by way of explanation (niddesanayavasena), beginning with ‘atha vā’ (or else), it indicates the term ‘visattikā’ (Mahāni. 3, Cūḷani. Mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa 22, 23; Cūḷani. Khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 124). ‘Visatā’ means spread out (vitthaṭā), pervading (byāpanavasena) in the three realms of phenomena such as form (rūpādīsu tebhūmakadhammesu); ‘visaṭā’ is simply the previous word stated by changing the ‘t’ to ‘ṭ’. ‘Visālā’ means vast (vipulā). ‘Visakkati’ means it strives (parisakkati) and endures (sahati). For one who is lustful endures even being struck by the foot on account of the object of lust. Some also say ‘visakkanaṃ’ means retreating (osakkanaṃ) or trembling (vipphandanaṃ). ‘Visaṃharati’ means that, in various ways, showing the advantages of sensual pleasures, it draws back (saṃharati), contracts (saṅkhipati), the mind inclined toward renunciation (nekkhammābhimukhappavattito); or it brings suffering (dukkhaṃ) like poison (visaṃ)—this is the meaning. ‘Visaṃvādikā’ means it makes one grasp the impermanent as permanent, etc., thus it is deceptive (visaṃvādikā hoti). Because it is the root of suffering-producing kamma, it is called ‘visamūlā’ (having poison as its root); or because suffering and pain (dukkhadukkhādibhūtā vedanā) are its root, it is called ‘visamūlā’. Because it is the origin of suffering (dukkhasamudayattā), its fruit is suffering (visaṃ phalaṃ etissā), hence ‘visaphalā’ (having poison as its fruit). Craving enjoys only the suffering of forms, etc., not the deathless, thus it is called ‘visaparibhogā’ (enjoying poison). Everywhere, the establishment of the word should be understood by way of etymology. But here, to show the main meaning, it is further said, ‘or else vast’ (visālā vā pana), etc. ‘Nittiṇṇo’ (crossed over) and ‘uttiṇṇo’ (crossed over) are words expanded by prefixes (upasaggavasena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ). Or, ‘nittiṇṇo’ means completely crossed over (niravasesato vā tiṇṇo). ‘Uttiṇṇo’ means crossed over upward and upward by various paths (tena tena maggena uddhamuddhaṃ tiṇṇo). What is not distinctly explained here should be easily understood.

Nivāpasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Exposition of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Nivāpa Sutta is complete.

6. Pāsarāsisuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Pāsarāsi Sutta

272. Sādhumayanti [V 2.0118] ettha sādhu-saddo āyācanattho, na “sādhāvuso”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 182) viya abhinandanādiatthoti āha “āyācantā”ti. Tenāha pāḷiyaṃ “labheyyāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na sakkonti, kasmā? Buddhā hi garū honti, paramagarū uttamaṃ gāravaṭṭhānaṃ, na yathā tathā upasaṅkamanīyā. Tenāha “ekacāriko sīho”tiādi.

272. Here, in 'sādhumayanti,' the word 'sādhu' has the meaning of requesting, not the meaning of approval, etc., as in 'sādhāvuso' and so forth (Saṃ. Ni. 1.246; Su. Ni. 182). Therefore, he says 'requesting.' Hence, in the Pāli text, it is said, 'may we obtain,' and so on. Why are they not able? For Buddhas are revered, supremely revered, the highest object of reverence, not to be approached in just any way. Hence it is said, 'the lion walks alone,' and so on.

“Pākaṭakiriyāyā”ti saṅkhepena vuttaṃ vivarituṃ “yaṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhagavā sabbakālaṃ kimevamakāsīti? Na sabbakālamevamakāsi. Yadā pana akāsi, taṃ dassetuṃ “bhagavā paṭhamabodhiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Manussattabhāveti iminā purisattabhāvaṃ ulliṅgeti. Dhanapariccāgo kato nāma natthi bhagavato dharamānakāleti adhippāyo.

To elaborate on ‘Pākaṭakiriyāyā,’ which was stated concisely, the words ‘yaṃ hī,’ etc., are said. Did the Blessed One always act in this way? He did not always act thus. But when he did act thus, to show that, 'the Blessed One at the time of his first enlightenment' and so on is said. 'Manussattabhāveti'—by this, the state of being a human is indicated. The meaning is that there was no relinquishment of wealth by the Blessed One while the Blessed One was living.

Mālākacavaranti [M 2.0125] milātamālākacavaraṃ. Rajojallaṃ na upalimpati acchatarachavibhāvato. Vuttañhetaṃ “sukhumattā chaviyā kāye rajojallaṃ na limpatī”ti. Yadi evaṃ kasmā bhagavā nahāyatīti āha “utuggahaṇattha”nti.

'Mālākacavara' means a withered garland of flowers. Dust and dirt do not cling to him because of the extreme purity of his skin. For it is said, 'Due to the fineness of the skin, dust and dirt do not cling to the body.' If that is so, why does the Blessed One bathe? It is said, 'For the sake of the season.'

Vihāroti jetavanavihāro. Vīsatiusabhaṃ gāvutassa catuttho bhāgoti vadanti. Kadācīti kasmiñci buddhuppāde. Acalamevāti aparivattameva anaññabhāvato, mañcānaṃ pana appamahantatāhi pādānaṃ patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānassa hānivaḍḍhiyo hontiyeva.

'Vihāra' means the Jetavana Monastery. They say it is twenty usabhas, a quarter of a gāvuta. 'Kadāci' means during some Buddha-appearance. 'Truly immovable' means unchanging, not altering its nature; however, due to the slight variations in the size of the couches, there can indeed be decreases or increases in the placement of the legs.

Yantanāḷikāhi paripuṇṇasuvaṇṇarasadhārāhi. Nhānavattanti “pabbajitena nāma evaṃ nhāyitabba”nti nahānacārittaṃ dassetvā. Yasmā bhagavato sarīraṃ sudhantacāmīkarasamānavaṇṇaṃ suparisodhitapavāḷarucirakaracaraṇāvaraṃ suvisuddhanīlaratanāvaḷisadisakesatanuruhaṃ, tasmā tahaṃ tahaṃ vinissatajātihiṅgulakarasūpasobhitaṃ upari mahaggharatanāvaḷisañchāditaṃ jaṅgamamiva kanakagirisikharaṃ virocittha. Tasmiñca samaye dasabalassa sarīrato nikkhamitvā chabbaṇṇarasmiyo samantato asītihatthappamāṇe padese ādhāvantī vidhāvantī ratanāvaḷiratanadāma-ratanacuṇṇa-vippakiṇṇaṃ viya, pasāritaratanacittakañcanapaṭṭamiva, āsiñcamānalākhārasadhārā-citamiva[V 2.0119], ukkāsatanipātasamākulamiva, nirantaraṃ vippakiṇṇa-kaṇikāra-kiṅkiṇika-pupphamiva, vāyuvegasamuddhata-cinapiṭṭhacuṇṇa-rañjitamiva, indadhanu-vijjulatā-vitānasanthatamiva, gaganatalaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ pavanañca sammā pharanti. Tena vuttaṃ “vaṇṇabhūmi nāmesā”tiādi. Atthanti upameyyatthaṃ. Upamāyoti “īdiso ca hotī”ti yathārahaṃ tadanucchavikā upamā. Kāraṇānīti upamupameyyasambandhavibhāvanāni kāraṇāni. Pūretvāti vaṇṇanaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā. Thāmo veditabbo “atitthe pakkhando”ti avattabbattā.

With pipes filled with streams of liquid gold. 'Nhānavatta' means having shown the bathing custom, saying, 'One who has gone forth should bathe in this way.' Because the Blessed One’s body was the color of refined gold, with excellent hands and feet well-polished and radiant like coral, and with hair and body-hair like a string of pure blue sapphires, it shone brilliantly, adorned here and there with the emanating sheen of natural vermilion, covered above with priceless jeweled garlands—like a moving golden mountain peak. And at that time, six-colored rays, emanating from the body of the Ten-Powered One, spread across an area of eighty cubits in all directions, racing and darting about, as if scattering jeweled garlands, strings of jewels, and powdered gems; as if an unfurled golden tapestry embroidered with jewels; as if adorned with streams of liquid lac poured down; as if a dense fall of shooting stars; as if an endless shower of kaṇikāra and kiṅkiṇika flowers were scattered; as if colored with powdered cinnabar stirred up by the force of the wind; as if a canopy woven with rainbows and lightning—they thoroughly pervaded the sky, that place, and the forest. Thus it is said, 'This is called the realm of beauty,' and so on. 'Attha' means the object of comparison. 'Upamā' means 'such is the case,' a simile appropriate and fitting to that. 'Kāraṇāni' means the reasons that elaborate the connection between the simile and the object of comparison. 'Pūretvā' means having completed the description in full. The strength should be understood, for 'plunging in where there is no ford' is unspeakable.

273. Kaṇṇikāti sarīragatabindukatāni maṇḍalāni. Parikkhārabhaṇḍanti uttarāsaṅgaṃ saṅghāṭiñca sandhāya vadati. Kiṃ panāyaṃ nayo buddhānampi sarīre hotīti? Na hoti, vattadassanatthaṃ panetaṃ katanti dassetuṃ “buddhānaṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Gamanavasena kāyassābhinīharaṇaṃ gamanābhihāro. Yathādhippāyāvattanaṃ adhippāyakopanaṃ.

273. 'Kaṇṇikā' refers to circular marks on the body that are like drops. 'Parikkhārabhaṇḍa' refers to the upper robe and the double robe. But does this principle apply to the bodies of the Buddhas as well? It does not. However, to show that this is done to indicate a convention, 'but for the Buddhas' and so on is said. The directing of the body by way of movement is 'gamanābhihāro'. The turning back according to one's intention is 'adhippāyakopana'.

Aññatarāya pāramiyāti nekkhammapāramiyā. Vīriyapāramiyāti apare. Mahābhinikkhamanassāti mahantassa carimabhave abhinikkhamanassa. Tañhi mahantaṃ [M 2.0126] bhogakkhandhaṃ mahantañca ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ mahantañca cakkavattisiriṃ pajahitvā sadevakassa lokassa samārakassa ca acinteyyāparimeyyabhedassa mahato atthāya hitāya sukhāya pavattattā mahanīyatāya ca mahantaṃ abhinikkhamananti vuccati.

'By one perfection' means the perfection of renunciation. Others say it means the perfection of energy. 'Of the Great Renunciation' means of the great renunciation in his final existence. For that is called the Great Renunciation because, having abandoned a great mass of wealth, a great circle of relatives, and the great glory of a universal monarch, it proceeded for the great welfare, benefit, and happiness of the world with its gods and Māra, which is immeasurable and inconceivable in its aspects; and also because of its supreme nobility, it is called a great renunciation.

Purimoti “katamāya nu kathāya sannisinnā bhavathā”ti evaṃ vuttaattho. Kā ca pana voti ettha ca-saddo byatireke. Tena yathāpucchitāya kathāya vakkhamānaṃ vippakatabhāvaṃ joteti. Pana-saddo vacanālaṅkāre. Yāya hi kathāya te bhikkhū sannisinnā, sā eva antarākathābhūtā vippakatā visesena puna pucchīyati. Aññāti antarā-saddassa atthamāha. Aññattho hi ayaṃ antarā-saddo “bhūmantaraṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā) samayantara”ntiādīsu viya, antarāti vā vemajjheti attho. Dasakathāvatthunissitāti “kiṃ sīlaṃ nāma, kathañca pūretabbaṃ, kāni cassa saṃkilesavodānānī”tiādinā appicchādinissitā sīlādinissitā ca kathā. Ariyoti niddoso. Atha vā atthakāmehi araṇīyoti ariyo, ariyānaṃ ayanti vā ariyoti. Bhāvanāmanasikāravasena tuṇhī bhavanti, na ekaccabāhirakapabbajitā viya mūgabbatasamādānena. Dutiyajjhānampi ariyo tuṇhībhāvo vacīsaṅkhārapahānato. Mūlakammaṭṭhānanti pārihāriya kammaṭṭhānampi. Jhānanti dutiyajjhānaṃ.

'Purimo' means the meaning stated thus: 'What discussion were you seated together for?' In 'Kā ca pana vo,' the word 'ca' is used in the sense of exclusion. Thus, it highlights the unfinished state of the discussion that was being spoken about when asked. The word 'pana' is an ornament to speech. For the discussion those monks were seated together for—that very interim discussion, being unfinished, is specifically asked about again. 'Aññā' explains the meaning of the word 'antarā.' For this word 'antarā' has another meaning, such as 'between lands' (as in Dhammasaṅgaṇī Aṭṭhakathā, Nidānakathā) or 'between times,' and so on; or it means 'in the middle.' 'Dependent on the ten topics of discussion' refers to discussions rooted in fewness of desires, etc., and rooted in virtue, etc., such as 'What is virtue? How should it be fulfilled? What are its corruptions and purifications?' and so on. 'Ariyo' means faultless. Or, 'ariyo' means worthy of being resorted to by those who desire benefit; or 'ariyo' means belonging to the noble ones. They become silent through meditation and mental attention, not like some external wanderers who adopt a vow of silence. The second jhāna is also noble silence because it abandons verbal formations. 'Mūlakammaṭṭhāna' refers even to the portable meditation subject. 'Jhāna' here means the second jhāna.

274. “Sannipatitānaṃ [V 2.0120] vo, bhikkhave, dvaya”nti (ma. ni. 1.273; udā. 12, 28, 29) aṭṭhuppattivasena desanā pavattāti tassā uparidesanāya sambandhaṃ dassetuṃ “dvemā, bhikkhave, pariyesanāti ko anusandhī”ti anusandhiṃ pucchati. Ayaṃ tumhākaṃ pariyesanāti yā mahābhinikkhamanapaṭibaddhā dhammī kathā, sā tumhākaṃ dhammapariyesanā dhammavicāraṇā ariyapariyesanā nāma. Apāyamagganti anatthāvahaṃ maggaṃ. Uddesānukkamaṃ bhinditvāti uddesānupubbiṃ laṅghitvā. Dhamma-saddo “amosadhammaṃ nibbāna”ntiādīsu viya pakatipariyāyo. Jāyanasabhāvoti jāyanapakatikoti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

274. To show the connection between the teaching that arose from the occasion of 'Monks, for you who have gathered, there are two things to be done...' (MN 1.273; Ud. 12, 28, 29) and the subsequent teaching, he asks about the connection: 'Regarding "Monks, there are these two pursuits," what is the connection?' This pursuit of yours—that is, the Dhamma talk connected with the Great Renunciation—is your Dhamma pursuit, your Dhamma investigation, called the noble pursuit. 'The path to loss' means the path leading to harm. 'Breaking the sequence of enunciation' means skipping over the order of enunciation. The word 'Dhamma' here is a synonym for 'nature,' as in phrases like 'the unfailing nature, Nibbāna,' and so on. 'Jāyanasabhāva' means 'having the nature of arising.' The same principle applies to the remaining terms.

Sabbatthāti yathā “puttabhariya”nti dvandasamāsavasena ekattaṃ, esa nayo sabbattha “dāsidāsa”ntiādīsu sabbapadesu. Parato vikāraṃ anāpajjitvā [M 2.0127] sabbadā jātarūpameva hotīti jātarūpaṃ, suvaṇṇaṃ. Dhavalasabhāvatāya rañjīyatīti rajataṃ, rūpiyaṃ. Idha pana suvaṇṇaṃ ṭhapetvā yaṃ kiñci upabhogaparibhogārahaṃ rajataṃteva gahitaṃ. Upadhīyati ettha dukkhanti upadhayo. Cutīsaṅkhātaṃ maraṇanti ekabhavapariyāpannaṃ khandhanirodhasaṅkhātaṃ maraṇamāha. Khaṇikanirodho pana khaṇe khaṇe. Tenāha “sattānaṃ viyā”ti. Saṃkilissatīti dūsavisena viya attānaṃ dūsissati. Tenāha bhagavā – “pañcime, bhikkhave, jātarūpassa upakkilesā ayo loha”ntiādi (a. ni. 5.23). Malaṃ gahetvāti yehi sahayogato malinaṃ hoti, tesaṃ malinabhāvapaccayānaṃ vasena malaṃ gahetvā. Jīraṇato jarādhammavāre jātarūpaṃ gahitanti yojanā. Ye pana jātidhammavārepi jātarūpaṃ na paṭhanti, tesaṃ itaresaṃ viya jīraṇadhammavāre sarūpato anāgatampi upadhiggahaṇena gahitamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pariggahe ṭhitānaṃ pana vasena vuccamāne apākaṭānampi jātijarāmaraṇānaṃ vasena yojanā labbhateva. Jātarūpasīsena cettha sabbassapi anindriyabaddhassa gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, puttabhariyādiggahaṇena viya mittāmaccādiggahaṇaṃ.

'Everywhere' means that just as in a dual compound like 'puttabhariya' (son and wife), unity is expressed, this method applies everywhere, such as in 'dāsidāsa' (slave-men and slave-women) and all other similar terms. Without undergoing alteration from outside, it always remains in its original form—thus, it is called 'jātarūpa' (gold), which is suvaṇṇa (gold). Because it has a bright or white nature, it is called 'rajata' (silver), which is rūpiya (silver). Here, however, excluding gold, whatever is suitable for use and consumption is taken as 'rajata'. 'Upadhayo' (substrata) means that suffering is based on them. Death, known as ceasing, refers to the death consisting of the cessation of aggregates within a single existence. Momentary cessation, however, occurs at every moment. Therefore, he said, 'as with beings.' 'Saṃkilissati' (becomes defiled) means it defiles itself, like a potent poison. Thus the Blessed One said: 'Monks, these five are the impurities of gold: iron, copper...' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.23). 'Taking the impurity' means taking on impurity by way of those factors which, through association, cause it to be impure. The connection is that 'jātarūpa' is taken in the context of aging, due to its decay. For those who do not recite 'jātarūpa' even in the context of birth, it should be understood that, as with the others, even though it has not appeared in its own form, it is included by the grasping of substrata. However, when speaking in terms of those situated within possession, a connection can indeed be made even with unmanifest birth, aging, and death. Here, under the heading 'jātarūpa' (gold), the inclusion of everything inanimate should be understood, just as the inclusion of friends, ministers, and so on is understood by the inclusion of 'puttabhariya' (son and wife).

275. Ariyehi pariyesanā, ariyānaṃ pariyesanāti vā ariyapariyesanāti samāsadvayaṃ dasseti “ayaṃ, bhikkhave”tiādinā.

275. He shows the two compound formations for 'ariyapariyesanā'—'a search by the noble ones' or 'a search of the noble ones'—with the passage beginning, 'This, O monks,' and so on.

276. Mūlato paṭṭhāyāti yaṃ mahābhinikkhamanassa mūlabhāvesuādīnavadassanaṃ, tato paṭṭhāya. Yasmā te bhikkhū tattha mahābhinikkhamanakathāya sannisinnā, sā ca nesaṃ antarākathā vippakatā, tasmā bhagavā tesaṃ mūlato paṭṭhāya mahābhinikkhamanakathaṃ kathetuṃ ārabhi. Ahampi pubbeti visesavacanaṃ aparipakkañāṇena sayaṃ carimabhave tīsu pāsādesu tividhanāṭakaparivārassa dibbasampattisadisāya mahāsampattiyā anubhavanaṃ, abhinikkhamitvā padhānapadahanavasena [V 2.0121] attakilamathānuyogañca sandhāyāha. Anariyapariyesanaṃ pariyesinti etthāpi eseva nayo. Pañcavaggiyāpīti yathāsakaṃ gihibhogaṃ anuyuttā taṃ pahāya pabbajitvā attakilamathānuyoge ṭhitā satthu dhammacakkapavattanadesanāya (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 13; paṭi. ma. 2.30) tampi pahāya ariyapariyesanaṃ pariyesiṃsūti.

276. "From the root" means: from the seeing of danger in the fundamental aspects of the Great Renunciation, starting from there. Because those bhikkhus were gathered there for a discussion on the Great Renunciation, and their discussion was interrupted, the Blessed One began to relate the discourse on the Great Renunciation from its very beginning. "I too, formerly"—this is a specific statement, referring to his own experience in his final existence, with knowledge not yet matured, of enjoying great prosperity comparable to divine fortune in the three palaces, surrounded by three kinds of theatrical troupes, and then, having renounced, engaging in the practice of exertion and self-mortification. Here too, the same method applies to "seeking the ignoble search." The group of five also, having each been devoted to household enjoyments, abandoned that, went forth, and engaged in self-mortification; but then, upon the Teacher's discourse on setting in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma, they abandoned that too and sought the noble search.

277. Kāmaṃ [M 2.0128] dahara-saddo “daharaṃ kumāraṃ mandaṃ uttānaseyyaka”nti (ma. ni. 1.496) ettha bāladārake āgato, “bhadrena yobbanena samannāgato”ti pana vakkhamānattā yuvāvatthā idha dahara-saddena vuttāti āha “taruṇova samāno”ti. Paṭhamavayena ekūnatiṃsavayattā. Jātiyā hi yāva tettiṃsavayā paṭhamavayo. Anādaratthe sāmivacanaṃ yathā “devadattassa rudantassa pabbajī”ti. Kāmaṃ assumuccanaṃ rodanaṃ, taṃ assumukhānanti iminā pakāsitaṃ, taṃ pana vatvā “rudantāna”nti vacanaṃ balavasokasamuṭṭhānaṃ ārodanavatthuṃ pakāsetīti āha “kanditvā rodamānāna”nti. Kiṃ kusalanti gavesamānoti kinti sabbaso avajjarahitaṃ ekanta niyyānikaṃ pariyesamāno. Varapadanti vaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇatthikehi ekantena varaṇīyaṭṭhena varaṃ, pajjitabbaṭṭhena padaṃ. Tuṅgasarīratāya dīgho, piṅgalacakkhutāya piṅgaloti dīghapiṅgalo. Dhammoti vinayo, samayoti attho. Sutvāva uggaṇhinti tena vuccamānassa savanamatteneva uggaṇhiṃ vācuggataṃ akāsiṃ.

277. Although the word "dahara" (young) is used for a young child in the phrase "a young, foolish infant lying on his back," since it will be said, "endowed with fortunate youth," here the word "dahara" refers to the stage of youth. Hence it is said, "being youthful." "In the first stage of life," being twenty-nine years of age. For, from birth up to the thirty-third year is the first stage of life. The genitive case is used in the sense of disregard, as in "he went forth while Devadatta was weeping." Although the shedding of tears is weeping, and that is expressed by "with tearful faces," having said that, the word "weeping" reveals the object of lamentation arising from strong sorrow; hence it is said, "wailing and weeping." Searching for "What is skillful?" means searching for what is entirely blameless and exclusively leading to release. "The excellent state": "excellent" because it is to be chosen exclusively by those who seek release from the suffering of the cycle; "state" because it is to be attained. "Tall and golden-eyed": tall due to his towering body, golden-eyed due to his tawny eyes; hence "Tall and Golden-eyed." "Dhamma" means discipline; "samaya" means meaning. "Having heard, I learned": merely by hearing what was being said by him, I learned it, I mastered it verbally.

Paṭilapanamattakenāti puna lapanamattakena. Jānātīti ñāṇo, ñāṇoti vādo ñāṇavādo, taṃ ñāṇavādaṃ. “Vadāmī”ti āgatattā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “jānāmī”ti uttamapurisavasena attho vutto. Aññepi bahūti aññepi bahū mama tathābhāvaṃ jānantā “ayaṃ imaṃ dhammaṃ jānātī”ti, “akampanīyatāya thiro”ti vā evaṃ vadanti.
