Lābhīti aññāsīti dhammassa uddisanena mahāpaññatāya “ayaṃ attanā gatamaggaṃ pavedeti, na anussutiko”ti aññāsi. Assāti bodhisattassa. Etadahosīti etaṃ “na kho āḷāro kālāmo”tiādi manasi ahosi, cintesīti attho.

"Paṭilapanamattakenāti" means: merely by re-speaking. "Jānātīti ñāṇo, ñāṇoti vādo ñāṇavādo, taṃ ñāṇavādaṃ": He knows, therefore he is a knower; a statement about a knower is a knower-statement; that knower-statement. Because "I speak" appears, in the commentary the meaning is given in the first person as "I know." "Aññepi bahūti": many others also, knowing my state to be such, say thus: "This one knows this Dhamma," or "He is firm due to being unshakable." "Lābhīti aññāsīti": through the exposition of the Dhamma and because of his great wisdom, he (Āḷāra Kālāma) knew: "This one declares the path he has trodden himself, not one based on oral tradition." "Assāti" means: of the Bodhisatta. "Etadahosīti": this, "Not so, Āḷāra Kālāma," etc., occurred to his mind; he thought, that is the meaning.

Heṭṭhimasamāpattīhi vinā uparimasamāpattīnaṃ sampādanassa asambhavato “satta samāpattiyo maṃ jānāpesī”ti āha. Payogaṃ kareyyanti bhāvanaṃ anuyuñjeyyanti attho. Evamāhāti evaṃ “ahaṃ, āvuso”tiādimāha, sattannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ adhigamaṃ paccaññāsīti attho.

Because the higher meditative attainments cannot be accomplished without the lower ones, he said, "He made me know the seven attainments." "Payogaṃ kareyyanti" means: he should apply himself to cultivation. "Evamāhāti": he spoke thus, saying, "I, friend," etc., meaning he acknowledged the attainment of the seven meditative states.

Anusūyakoti anissukī. Tena mahāpurise pasādaṃ pavedesi. Bodhisattassa tā samāpattiyo [V 2.0122] nibbattetvā ṭhitassa purimajātiparicayena ñāṇassa ca mahantatāya tāsaṃ gati ca abhisamparāyo ca upaṭṭhāsi[M 2.0129]. Tena “vaṭṭapariyāpannā evetā”ti nicchayo udapādi. Tenāha “nāyaṃ dhammo nibbidāyā”tiādi. Ekaccānaṃ virāgabhāvanāsamatikkamāvahopi neva tesampi accantāya samatikkamāvaho, sayañca vaṭṭapariyāpannoyeva, tasmā neva vaṭṭe nibbindanatthāya, yadaggena na nibbidāya, tadaggena na virajjanatthāya, rāgādīnaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ na nirujjhanatthāya, na upasamatthāya, tasmā taṃ abhiññeyyadhammaṃ na abhijānanatthāya…pe… saṃvattatīti yojanā.

"Anusūyakoti" means: not envious. Thereby he showed his confidence in the great being. For the Bodhisatta, who had produced and was abiding in those meditative attainments, their destination and future life became manifest due to his familiarity from previous births and the greatness of his knowledge. Because of that, the conviction arose in him, "These are indeed included in the cycle of rebirth." Therefore, he said, "This Dhamma is not for disenchantment," etc. Although for some it brings about the overcoming of the development of dispassion, it does not bring about their complete overcoming, and it is itself included in the cycle. Therefore, it is not for the purpose of becoming disenchanted with the cycle; insofar as it is not for disenchantment, it is not for the purpose of dispassion, not for the purpose of the cessation of evil states such as lust, not for the purpose of their appeasement. Therefore, it does not lead to the direct knowing of that Dhamma which is to be directly known... and so on. This is the construction of the meaning.

Yāvadeva ākiñcaññāyatanupapattiyāti sattasu samāpattīsu ukkaṭṭhaṃ gahetvā vadati. Uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya acutidhammaṃ pariyesituṃ yuttattā tañca anatikkantajātidhammamevāti mahāsatto pajahatīti āha “yañca ṭhānaṃ pāpetī”tiādi. Tato paṭṭhāyāti yadā samāpattidhammassa gatiñca abhisamparāyañca abbhaññāsi, tato paṭṭhāya. Makkhikāvasenāti bhojanassa makkhikāmissatāvasena. Manaṃ na uppādeti bhuñjitunti adhippāyo. Mahantena ussāhenāti idaṃ katipāhaṃ tattha bhāvanānuyogamattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na aññesaṃ viya kasiṇaparikammādikaraṇaṃ. Na hi antimabhavikabodhisattānaṃ samāpattinibbattane bhāriyaṃ nāma. Analaṅkaritvāti anu anu alaṃkatvā punappunaṃ “iminā na kiñci payojana”nti katvā.

"Just for the sake of rebirth in the base of nothingness": he speaks, taking the highest among the seven attainments. Because it is fitting to rise up and strive to seek the deathless state, and because that attainment itself does not transcend the nature of birth, the great being abandons it; hence it is said: "and whatever state he attains," etc. "From that point onward" means: from when he fully understood the destination and future life of the state of attainment, from that point onward. "Like a fly" means: in the manner of a fly mixed with food. The intention is: "He does not generate a mind to partake of it." "With great effort": this is said referring to being engaged in meditation there for only a few days, not like others who perform preliminary work such as kasina preparation. For bodhisattas in their final existence, there is indeed no great difficulty in producing the attainments. "Analaṅkaritvāti" means: not being satisfied with it again and again, repeatedly thinking, "There is no use in this."

278. Vācāya uggahitamattovāti ettha pubbe vuttanayānusārena attho veditabbo.

278. "Vācāya uggahitamattovāti": here, the meaning should be understood according to the method previously stated.

279. Mahāvelā viya mahāvelā, vipulavālikapuñjatāya mahanto velātaṭo viyāti attho. Tenāha “mahāvālikarāsīti attho”ti. Uru maru sikatā vālukā vaṇṇu vālikāti ime saddā samānatthā, byañjanameva nānaṃ.

279. "Mahāvelā viya mahāvelā": like a great sandbank, a great sandbank; the meaning is like a great shore due to a vast heap of sand. Therefore, it is said, "the meaning is a great heap of sand." The words uru, maru, sikatā, vālukā, vaṇṇu, and vālikā—these words have the same meaning; only the expression differs.

Senā nigacchi nivisi etthāti senānigamo, senāya niviṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ. Senānigāmoti pana ayaṃ samaññā aparakālikā. Gocaragāmanidassanañcetaṃ. Uparisuttasminti mahāsaccakasutte. Idha pana bodhipallaṅko adhippeto ariyapariyesanāya vuccamānattā.

The army went and settled here, hence Senānigamo, a military town; it is the place where the army settled. However, this designation 'Senānigamo' is of a later time. This is also an indication of a village for alms-resort. In the sutta above, the Mahāsaccaka Sutta. Here, however, the throne of awakening is intended, as it is spoken of in connection with the noble search.

280. “Ñāṇadassana”nti [M 2.0130] ca ekajjhaṃ gahitapadadvayavisayavisesassa anāmaṭṭhattā “me”ti ca gahitattā anavasesañeyyāvabodhanasamatthameva ñāṇavisesaṃ bodheti, na ñāṇamattaṃ, na dassanamattanti āha “sabbadhammadassanasamatthañca me sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ udapādī”ti. Akuppatāyāti vimokkhantatāya sabbaso paṭipakkhadhammehi asaṅkhobhanīyatāya. Tenāha “rāgādīhi [V 2.0123] na kuppatī”ti. Ārammaṇasantatāyapi tadārammaṇānaṃ atthi viseso yathā taṃ “āneñjavihāre”ti āha “akuppārammaṇatāya cā”ti. Paccavekkhaṇañāṇampīti na kevalaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇameva, atha kho yathādhigate paṭivedhasaddhamme ekūnavīsatividhapaccavekkhaṇañāṇampi.

280. The phrase "knowledge and vision," because the specific object of these two terms taken together is not mentioned, and because the word "my" is included, indicates a special knowledge capable of understanding all knowable things without remainder—not mere knowledge, and not mere vision. Thus it is said: "The all-knowing knowledge arose in me, capable of seeing all phenomena." "By immovability" means: by the finality of liberation, by being completely unshakable by all opposing states. Therefore, it is said: "It is not shaken by lust and so forth." Even regarding the continuity of the object, there is a distinction among its objects, as in "in the imperturbable dwelling"; hence it is said, "and because its object is imperturbable." "Reviewing knowledge as well" means: not only the all-knowing knowledge, but also the nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge concerning the true Dhamma that has been penetrated as it is.

281. Paṭividdhoti (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.64; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.172; sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.7) sayambhuñāṇena “idaṃ dukkha”ntiādinā paṭimukhaṃ nibbijjhanavasena patto, yathābhūtaṃ avabuddhoti attho. Gambhīroti mahāsamuddo viya makasatuṇḍasūciyā aññatra samupacitaparipakkañāṇasambhārehi aññesaṃ ñāṇena alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭho. Tenāha “uttānabhāvapaṭikkhepavacanameta”nti. Yo alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭho, so ogāhitumasakkuṇeyyatāya sarūpato ca passituṃ na sakkāti āha “gambhīrattāva duddaso”ti. Dukkhena daṭṭhabboti kicchena kenacideva daṭṭhabbo. Yaṃ pana daṭṭhumeva na sakkā, tassa ogāhetvā anu anu bujjhane kathā eva natthīti āha “duddasattāva duranubodho”ti. Dukkhena avabujjhitabbo avabodhassa dukkarabhāvato. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne – “taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho dukkarataraṃ vā durabhisambhavataraṃ vā”ti suttapadaṃ (saṃ. ni. 5.1115) vattabbaṃ. Santārammaṇatāya vā santo. Nibbutasabbapariḷāhatāya nibbuto. Padhānabhāvaṃ nītoti vā paṇīto. Atittikaraṭṭhena atappako sādurasabhojanaṃ viya. Ettha ca nirodhasaccaṃ santaṃ ārammaṇanti santārammaṇaṃ, maggasaccaṃ santaṃ santārammaṇañcāti santārammaṇaṃ. Anupasantasabhāvānaṃ kilesānaṃ saṅkhārānañca abhāvato nibbutasabbapariḷāhatāya santapaṇītabhāveneva ca asecanakatāya atappakatā daṭṭhabbā. Tenāha “idaṃ dvayaṃ lokuttarameva sandhāya vutta”nti. Uttamañāṇavisayattā na takkena avacaritabbo, tato eva nipuṇañāṇagocaratāya ca saṇho. Sukhumasabhāvattā ca nipuṇo, bālānaṃ avisayattā [M 2.0131] paṇḍitehi eva veditabboti paṇḍitavedanīyo. Ālīyanti abhiramitabbaṭṭhena sevīyantīti ālayā, pañca kāmaguṇā. Ālayanti allīyantī abhiramaṇavasena sevantīti ālayā, taṇhāvicaritāni. Ramantīti ratiṃ vindanti kīḷanti laḷanti. Ālayaratāti ālayaniratā.

281. ‘Paṭividdho’ means having attained by way of direct penetration with self-arisen knowledge, as in ‘this is suffering,’ etc.; the meaning is, understood as it truly is. ‘Gambhīro’ (profound) is like the great ocean, whose foundation is unattainable by the knowledge of others—except for those with an accumulation of ripened wisdom—just as the ocean floor is unattainable by a mosquito’s proboscis. Therefore, it is said, ‘This is a statement rejecting superficiality.’ That which has an unattainable foundation cannot be plunged into, and its nature cannot be seen; thus, it is said, ‘due to its profundity, it is hard to see.’ ‘To be seen with difficulty’ means it is to be seen by someone only with great effort. As for that which cannot be seen at all, there is no question of plunging into it and awakening to it little by little; thus, it is said, ‘due to its being hard to see, it is hard to comprehend.’ It is to be comprehended with difficulty because comprehension is difficult to accomplish. In this context, the sutta passage should be cited: ‘What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more difficult to do or more difficult to fully accomplish?’ (SN 56.31). Or, ‘santo’ (peaceful) because it has a peaceful object. ‘Nibbuto’ (extinguished) because all feverishness is extinguished. Or, ‘paṇīto’ (sublime) because it has been brought to a state of excellence. ‘Atappako’ (unsating) in the sense of not causing satiety, like a delicious meal. Here, the truth of cessation is a peaceful object, thus ‘santārammaṇaṃ’ (having a peaceful object). The truth of the path is peaceful and has a peaceful object, thus ‘santārammaṇaṃ’. The quality of being unsating should be understood from the absence of unpacified defilements and formations, from the extinguishing of all feverishness, and from its nature of being peaceful, sublime, and delicious. Therefore, it is said, ‘These two are spoken of with reference only to the supramundane.’ It is not to be fathomed by logic, as it is the domain of supreme knowledge; for that very reason, and because it is the sphere of subtle knowledge, it is ‘saṇho’ (subtle). And because of its subtle nature, it is ‘nipuṇo’ (refined); as it is not the domain of fools, it is to be known only by the wise, thus ‘paṇḍitavedanīyo’ (to be known by the wise). ‘Ālayā’ (attachments) are the five strands of sensual pleasure, because they are resorted to in the sense of being delighted in. ‘Ālayā’ (attachments) are the wanderings of craving, because they cling, that is, they are resorted to by way of delighting. ‘Ramanti’ (they delight) means they find pleasure, they play, they revel. ‘Ālayaratā’ means devoted to attachments.

Ṭhānaṃ sandhāyāti ṭhāna-saddaṃ sandhāya. Atthato pana ṭhānanti ca paṭiccasamuppādo eva adhippeto. Tiṭṭhati phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti ṭhānaṃ, saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccayabhūtā avijjādayo. Imesaṃ saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccayāti idappaccayā, avijjādayova. Idappaccayā eva idappaccayatā yathā “devo eva devatā”ti, idappaccayānaṃ vā avijjādīnaṃ attano phalaṃ pati paccayabhāvo [V 2.0124] uppādanasamatthatā idappaccayatā. Tena samatthapaccayalakkhaṇo paṭiccasamuppādo dassito hoti. Paṭicca samuppajjati phalaṃ etasmāti paṭiccasamuppādo. Padadvayenapi dhammānaṃ paccayaṭṭho eva vibhāvito. Tenāha “saṅkhārādipaccayānaṃ etaṃ adhivacana”nti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 2.572-573) vuttanayena veditabbo.

‘Referring to ṭhāna’ means referring to the word ‘ṭhāna.’ In meaning, however, ‘ṭhāna’ is intended to mean dependent origination itself. It is called ‘ṭhāna’ because the effect stands (tiṭṭhati), its existence being dependent on that—namely, ignorance and the other factors that are conditions for formations and so on. The conditions for these formations and so on are ‘these conditions’ (idappaccayā), that is, ignorance and the rest. ‘These conditions’ itself is ‘conditionality’ (idappaccayatā), just as ‘a deva is indeed devatā (divinity).’ Or, ‘conditionality’ is the state of being a condition for its own effect, the capacity to produce, on the part of ‘these conditions,’ namely ignorance and the rest. Thus, dependent origination is shown to have the characteristic of a competent condition. ‘Dependent origination’ (paṭiccasamuppādo) is that from which an effect arises in dependence. Through both terms, the meaning of phenomena as conditions is clarified. Therefore, it is said: ‘This is a designation for the conditions beginning with formations.’ This is the summary here; the detailed explanation should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary to the Visuddhimagga.

Sabbasaṅkhārasamathotiādi sabbanti sabbasaṅkhārasamathādisaddābhidheyyaṃ sabbaṃ atthato nibbānameva. Idāni tassa nibbānabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “yasmā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nti nibbānaṃ. Āgammāti paṭicca ariyamaggassa ārammaṇapaccayabhāvahetu. Sammantīti appaṭisandhikūpasamavasena sammanti. Tathā santā savisesaṃ upasantā nāma hontīti āha “vūpasammantī”ti. Etena “sabbe saṅkhārā sammanti etthāti sabbasaṅkhārasamatho, nibbāna”nti dasseti. Sabbasaṅkhatavisaṃyutte ca nibbāne sabbasaṅkhāravūpasamapariyāyo heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Paṭinissaṭṭhāti samucchedavasena pariccattā honti. Sabbā taṇhāti aṭṭhasatappabhedā sabbāpi taṇhā. Sabbe kilesarāgāti kāmarāgarūparāgādibhedā sabbepi kilesabhūtā rāgā, sabbepi vā kilesā idha “kilesarāgā”ti veditabbā, na lobhavisesā eva cittassa vipariṇatabhāvāpādanato[M 2.0132]. Yathāha “rattampi cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ, duṭṭhampi cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ, mūḷhampi cittaṃ vipariṇata”nti (pārā. 271). Virajjantīti palujjanti.

‘The cessation of all formations,’ and so on—here, ‘all’ refers to everything denoted by terms like ‘the cessation of all formations’; in essence, it is Nibbāna itself. Now, to reveal its nature as Nibbāna, it is said, ‘Because indeed…’ and so on. Nibbāna. ‘Āgamma’ (in dependence on) means ‘having depended on,’ because it is the object-condition for the Noble Path. ‘Sammanti’ (they cease) means they cease by way of the pacification that involves no further relinking. Being thus, they become pacified in a special way, hence he says, ‘vūpasammanti’ (they are fully pacified). By this, it is shown: ‘All formations cease here—this is the cessation of all formations, Nibbāna.’ Regarding Nibbāna, which is disconnected from all conditioned phenomena, the expression ‘the full pacification of all formations’ should be understood in the manner explained below. This same method applies to the remaining phrases. ‘Paṭinissaṭṭhā’ (relinquished) means they are abandoned by way of eradication. ‘Sabbā taṇhā’ (all craving) means all craving in its 108 kinds. ‘Sabbe kilesarāgā’ (all defilements of lust) means all lusts which are defilements, such as sensual lust and lust for form; or all defilements should be understood here as ‘defilements of lust,’ not merely specific forms of greed, because they cause a distorted state of mind. As it is said: ‘A mind affected by lust is distorted; a mind affected by hate is distorted; a mind affected by delusion is distorted’ (Pārā. 271). ‘Virajjanti’ (they fade away) means they are destroyed.

Ciranisajjācirabhāsanehi piṭṭhiāgilāyanatālugalasosādivasena kāyakilamatho ceva kāyavihesā ca veditabbā. Sā ca kho desanāya atthaṃ ajānantānaṃ vasena vuttā, jānantānaṃ pana desanāya kāyaparissamopi satthu aparissamova. Tenāha bhagavā – “na ca maṃ dhammādhikaraṇaṃ vihesesī”ti (udā. 10). Tenevāha “yā ajānantānaṃ desanā nāma, so mama kilamatho assā”ti. Ubhayanti cittakilamatho ceva cittavihesā cāti ubhayampetaṃ buddhānaṃ natthi bodhimūleyeva samucchinnattā.

Through prolonged sitting and prolonged speaking, bodily fatigue and bodily distress should be understood by way of back-ache, drying of the palate and throat, and so on. And that was spoken with regard to those who do not understand the meaning of the teaching; for those who understand, however, even bodily exertion from teaching is no exertion for the Teacher. Therefore, the Blessed One said: ‘And no matter concerning the Dhamma wearied me’ (Ud 1.10). For that reason, he said: ‘That which is called teaching for those who do not understand, that would be my fatigue.’ Both—mental fatigue and mental distress—these two do not exist for the Buddhas, because they were utterly cut off at the very root of enlightenment.

Anubrūhanaṃ sampiṇḍanaṃ. Soti “apissū”ti nipāto. Manti paṭi-saddayogena sāmiatthe upayogavacananti āha “mamā”ti. Vuddhippattā vā acchariyā anacchariyā. Vuddhiatthopi hi a-kāro hoti yathā “asekkhā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 11.tikamātikā). Kappānaṃ satasahassaṃ cattāri ca asaṅkhyeyyāni sadevakassa lokassa dhammasaṃvibhāgakaraṇatthameva pāramiyo pūretvā [V 2.0125] idāni adhigatadhammarajjassa tattha appossukkatāpattidīpanatā, gāthātthassa acchariyatā, tassa vuddhippatti cāti veditabbaṃ. Atthadvārena hi gāthānaṃ anacchariyatā. Gocarā ahesunti upaṭṭhahesuṃ. Upaṭṭhānañca vitakketabbatāti āha “parivitakkayitabbataṃ pāpuṇiṃsū”ti.

Augmenting, summarizing. ‘So’ is the particle ‘apissu’ (indeed). ‘Maṃ’ is a usage in the sense of ownership in connection with the word ‘paṭi-’ (as in paṭibhāti maṃ, ‘it occurs to me’), hence he says ‘mama’ (my). Or, ‘anacchariyā’ means ‘marvelous,’ having attained growth. For the prefix ‘a-’ can also have the meaning of growth, as in ‘asekkhā dhammā’ (qualities beyond training). It should be understood thus: for one who, having fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand eons for the sole purpose of distributing the Dhamma to the world with its gods, has now attained the kingdom of the Dhamma—the showing of his lack of eagerness in that regard, the marvelousness of the meaning of the verses, and its attainment of growth. For through the door of meaning, the verses are un-marvelous. ‘Gocarā ahesuṃ’ means they arose. And arising is something to be reflected upon; hence it is said, ‘They reached a state fit to be reflected upon.’

Yadi sukhāpaṭipadāva, kathaṃ kicchatāti āha “pāramīpūraṇakāle panā”tiādi. Evamādīni duppariccajāni dentassa. Ha-iti vā “byatta”nti etasmiṃ atthe nipāto. Ekaṃsattheti keci. Ha byattaṃ, ekaṃsena vā alaṃ nippayojanaṃ evaṃ kicchena adhigatassa dhammassa desitanti yojanā. Halanti vā “ala”nti iminā samānatthaṃ padaṃ “halanti vadāmī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.65; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.172) viya. Rāgadosapariphuṭṭhehīti phuṭṭhavisena viya sappena rāgena dosena ca samphuṭṭhehi abhibhūtehi. Rāgadosānugatehīti rāgena ca dosena ca anubandhehi.

If it is an easy practice, why is it said to be arduous? He says: ‘But at the time of fulfilling the perfections…’ and so on, while giving such things that are difficult to relinquish. Or, ‘ha’ is a particle in the sense of ‘manifest.’ Some say it is in the sense of ‘certainly.’ The connection is: ‘Ha’ (manifestly), or ‘certainly enough,’ it is useless to teach the Dhamma attained with such difficulty. Or ‘halaṃ’ is a word with the same meaning as ‘alaṃ’ (enough), as in ‘halaṃ vadāmī’ (I say enough) and similar instances. ‘Rāgadosapariphuṭṭhehi’ means by those who are suffused with and overcome by lust and hatred, like a snake suffused with its poison. ‘Rāgadosānugatehi’ means by those who are pursued by lust and hatred.

Kāmarāgarattā [M 2.0133] bhavarāgarattā ca nīvaraṇehi nivutatāya, diṭṭhirāgarattā viparītābhinivesena. Na dakkhantīti yāthāvato dhammaṃ na paṭivijjhissanti. Evaṃ gāhāpetunti “anicca”ntiādinā sabhāvena yāthāvato dhammaṃ jānāpetuṃ. Rāgadosaparetatāpi nesaṃ sammūḷhabhāvenevāti āha “tamokhandhena āvuṭā”ti.

Attached to sensual lust and attached to existence-lust, being covered by the hindrances; and attached to the lust for views due to perverted clinging. 'They do not see' means they will not penetrate the Dhamma as it actually is. Thus, to make them grasp—that is, to make them understand the Dhamma as it actually is through its intrinsic nature, such as 'impermanent' and so on. Their being overcome by lust and hatred is also due to their state of delusion; hence, he said: 'Covered by a mass of darkness.'

282. Dhammadesanāya appossukkatāpattiyā kāraṇaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “kasmā panā”tiādinā sayameva codanaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tattha aññātavesenāti imassa bhagavato sāvakabhāvūpagamanena aññātarūpena. Tāpasavesenāti keci. So pana arahattādhigameneva vigaccheyya. Tividhaṃ kāraṇaṃ appossukkatāpattiyā paṭipakkhassa balavabhāvo, dhammassa gambhīratā, tattha ca sātisayaṃ gāravanti, ta dassetuṃ “tassa hī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. (Tattha paṭipakkhā nāma rāgādayo kilesā sammāpaṭipattiyā antarāyakarattā. Tesaṃ balavabhāvato ciraparibhāvanāya sattasantānato dubbisodhiyatāya te satte mattahatthino viya dubbalapurisaṃ adhibhavitvā ajjhottharitvā anayabyasanaṃ āpādentā anekasatayojanāyāmavitthāraṃ sunicitaṃ ghanasannivesaṃ kaṇṭakaduggampi adhisenti. Dūrappabhedaducchejjatāhi dubbisodhiyataṃ pana dassetuṃ “athassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ca anto amaṭṭhatāya kañjiyapuṇṇā lābu. Cirapārivāsikatāya takkabharitā cāṭi. Snehatintadubbalabhāvena vasāpītapilotikā. Telamissitatāya añjanamakkhitahattho dubbisodhanīyā vuttā, hīnūpamā cetā rūpapabandhabhāvato acirakālikattā ca malīnatāya, kilesasaṃkileso eva pana dubbisodhanīyataro anādikālikattā [V 2.0126] anusayitattā ca. Tenāha “atisaṃkiliṭṭhā”ti. Yathā ca dubbisodhanīyataratāya, evaṃ gambhīraduddasaduranubodhānampi vuttaupamā hīnūpamāva).

282. To clarify the reason for his disinclination to teach the Dhamma, he himself raises the objection, “But why?” and so on. Here, “in an unknown guise” refers to his approaching in a form that is known because he has become a disciple of the Blessed One. Some say it means “in the guise of an ascetic,” but that would have disappeared with the attainment of arahantship. The threefold reason for this disinclination is the strength of the opposition, the profundity of the Dhamma, and his extraordinary reverence for it. To illustrate this, the passage beginning with “For him…” is introduced. (Here, the opposition refers to defilements like lust, which obstruct right practice. Due to their strength, their long familiarity within the mental continuum of beings, and the difficulty of purifying them, they overwhelm a weak person like a mad elephant, leading him to ruin. They settle upon even a dense, thorny thicket spanning hundreds of leagues, firmly established and with a solid mass. To show how hard they are to purify because they are difficult to penetrate and cut through, the passage beginning with “And for him…” is stated. Here, a gourd filled with sour gruel is hard to clean because its inside is unpolished; a pot full of buttermilk, because it has been standing for a long time; a rag that has absorbed grease, because it is weakened by being soaked in oil; a hand smeared with ointment, because it is mixed with oil—these are said to be hard to clean. These are inferior similes because of their material nature and short duration of impurity. But the stain of the defilements is even harder to purify because it is beginningless and lies latent. Hence it is said, “exceedingly defiled.” And just as these similes are inferior in regard to the difficulty of cleansing, so too are they inferior in regard to the Dhamma’s profundity, difficulty of perception, and difficulty of comprehension.)

Paṭipakkhavigamanena gambhīropi dhammo supākaṭo bhaveyya. Paṭipakkhavigamanaṃ pana sammāpaṭipattipaṭibaddhaṃ, sā saddhammassavanādhīnā. Taṃ satthari dhamme ca pasādāyattaṃ, so garuṭṭhāniyānaṃ ajjhesanahetukoti panāḷikāya sattānaṃ dhammasampaṭipattiyā brahmayācanānimittanti taṃ dassento “apicā”tiādimāha.

By the removal of the opposing factors, even the profound Dhamma can become very clear. The removal of the opposing factors, however, is connected with right practice, and that practice depends on hearing the good Dhamma. That, in turn, depends on confidence in the Teacher and the Dhamma, and that confidence is caused by requesting instruction from one worthy of respect. Thus, showing that, in the manner of a conduit, the request by Brahmā is the cause for beings’ attainment of the Dhamma, he says, “Moreover…” and so on.

Upakkilesabhūtaṃ [M 2.0134] appaṃ rāgādirajaṃ etassāti apparajaṃ, apparajaṃ akkhi paññācakkhu yesaṃ te taṃsabhāvāti katvā apparajakkhajātikāti ayamattho vibhāvito “paññāmaye”tiādinā. Appaṃ rāgādirajaṃ yesaṃ taṃsabhāvā apparajakkhajātikāti evampi saddattho sambhavati. Dānādidasapuññakiriyavatthūni saraṇagamanaparahitapariṇāmanehi saddhiṃ (dvādasa hontīti) “dvādasapuññakiriyavasenā”ti vuttaṃ.

“Little dust” (`apparajaṃ`) means that there is little dust of lust and other defilements (`upakkilesa`) in a person. “Of a nature with little dust in their eyes” (`apparajakkhajātikā`) means that their eye—the eye of wisdom—has little dust; because they are of such a nature, they are called this. This meaning is clarified by the phrase “in the wisdom…” and so on. Alternatively, this literal meaning is also possible: they are of a nature with little dust in their eyes because there is little dust of lust and so on in them. The ten grounds for meritorious action beginning with giving, together with going for refuge and dedicating merit for the welfare of others (making twelve), are referred to as “by way of the twelve meritorious actions.”

Rāgādimalena samalehi pūraṇādīhi chahi satthārehi satthupaṭiññehi kabbaracanāvasena cintākaviādibhāve ṭhatvā takkapariyāhataṃ vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ cintito. Te kira buddhakolāhalānussavena sañjātakutūhalaṃ lokaṃ vañcetvā kohaññe ṭhatvā sabbaññutaṃ paṭijānantā yaṃ kiñci adhammaṃyeva dhammoti dīpesuṃ. Tenāha “te hi puretaraṃ uppajjitvā”tiādi. Apāpuretanti etaṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsanantaradhānato pabhuti pihitaṃ nibbānanagarassa mahādvāraṃ ariyamaggaṃ saddhammadesanāhatthena apāpura vivara.

The six self-proclaimed teachers beginning with Pūraṇa, stained with the filth of lust and so on, stood in the state of speculative poets and the like, composing verses and thinking their own original thoughts, which were based on reasoning and followed by investigation. It seems that, having heard the “Buddha-uproar,” they deceived the world in which curiosity had arisen, and standing in hypocrisy, they claimed omniscience and taught as Dhamma whatever was not Dhamma. Hence he says, “For they arose earlier…,” and so on. “Open up”: this means, with the hand of the teaching of the good Dhamma, open, uncover, the great gate to the city of Nibbāna—the noble path—which has been closed since the disappearance of the Dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa.

Selapabbato ucco hoti thiro ca, na paṃsupabbato missakapabbato cāti āha “sele yathā pabbatamuddhanī”ti. Dhammamayaṃ pāsādanti lokuttaradhammamāha. So hi sabbaso pasādāvaho, sabbadhamme atikkamma abbhuggataṭṭhena pāsādasadiso ca. Paññāpariyāyo vā idha dhamma-saddo. Sā hi abbhuggataṭṭhena “pāsādo”ti abhidhamme (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 16) niddiṭṭhā. Tathā cāha –

A rocky mountain is high and firm, not like a mountain of dust or a composite mountain; hence it is said, “as on a rocky mountain peak.” “The palace made of Dhamma” refers to the supramundane Dhamma. For it is altogether inspiring, and it is like a palace in that it has risen up, surpassing all things. Or else the word “Dhamma” here is a term for wisdom, for wisdom is designated as a “palace” in the Abhidhamma (Dhs-A 16) because it has risen up. And so it is said:

“Paññāpāsādamāruyha, asoko sokiniṃ pajaṃ;

Pabbataṭṭhova bhūmaṭṭhe, dhīro bāle avekkhatī”ti. (dha. pa. 28);

“Having ascended the palace of wisdom, the sorrowless one looks upon the sorrowing people. As one standing on a mountain looks upon those on the ground, so the wise one looks upon the fools.”

Uṭṭhehīti [V 2.0127] vā dhammadesanāya appossukkatāsaṅkhātasaṅkocāpattito kilāsubhāvato uṭṭhaha.

“Arise”: or, arise from the state of weariness, from falling into the state of contraction known as a lack of enthusiasm for teaching the Dhamma.

283. Garuṭṭhāniyaṃ payirupāsitvā garutaraṃ payojanaṃ uddissa abhipatthanā ajjhesanā, sāpi atthato yācanāva hotīti āha “ajjhesananti yācana”nti. Padesavisayaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ ahutvā buddhānaṃyeva [M 2.0135] āveṇikabhāvato idaṃ ñāṇadvayaṃ “buddhacakkhū”ti vuccatīti āha “imesañhi dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ buddhacakkhūti nāma”nti. Tiṇṇaṃ maggañāṇānanti heṭṭhimānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ maggañāṇānaṃ “dhammacakkhū”ti nāmaṃ catusaccadhammadassanamattabhāvato. Yato tāni ñāṇāni vijjūpamabhāvena vuttāni, aggamaggañāṇaṃ pana ñāṇakiccassa sikhāppattiyā na dassanamattaṃ hotīti “dhammacakkhū”ti na vuccati, tato taṃ vajirūpamabhāvena vuttaṃ. Vuttanayenāti “apparajakkhā”ti ettha vuttanayena. Yasmā mandakilesā “apparajakkhā”ti vuttā, tasmā bahalakilesā “mahārajakkhā”ti veditabbā. Paṭipakkhavidhamanasamatthatāya tikkhāni sūrāni visadāni, vuttavipariyāyena mudūni. Saddhādayo ākārāti saddahanādippakāre vadati. Sundarāti kalyāṇā. Sammohavinodaniyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 814) pana “yesaṃ āsayādayo koṭṭhāsā sundarā, te svākārā, viparītā dvākārā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ imāya atthavaṇṇanāya aññadatthu saṃsandati sametīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kāraṇaṃ nāma paccayākāro, saccāni vā.

283. An `ajjhesanā` is an aspiration and request made after attending upon one worthy of respect, aiming at a higher purpose. Since this is in meaning a request (`yācanā`), he says, “‘Ajjhesanā’ means a request.” Since there is no knowledge and vision with a limited scope, and because this pair of knowledges is unique to the Buddhas, it is called the “Buddha-eye.” Hence he says, “The name of these two knowledges is ‘Buddha-eye.’” “Of the three path knowledges”: the name of the lower three path knowledges is “Dhamma-eye” because they are a mere seeing of the Dhamma of the Four Truths. Since those knowledges are spoken of as being like lightning, while the knowledge of the highest path, having reached the peak of the function of knowledge, is not a mere seeing, it is not called the “Dhamma-eye”; therefore it is spoken of as being like a diamond. “In the stated manner”: in the manner stated here regarding “those with little dust.” Since those with few defilements are called “those with little dust,” those with thick defilements should be known as “those with much dust.” The faculties are sharp, keen, and clear because they can demolish the opposition; by the reverse of what was stated, they are dull. “Aspects such as faith”: he speaks of the modes such as believing. “Beautiful”: auspicious. But in the Sammohavinodanī it is said: “Those whose parts, such as their disposition, are beautiful are ‘of good form’ (`svākārā`); the opposite are ‘of bad form’ (`dvākārā`).” It should be seen that this certainly corresponds and agrees with this explanation of the meaning. “Cause” (`kāraṇa`) means the mode of condition, or the Truths.

Ayaṃ panettha pāḷīti ettha apparajakkhādipadānaṃ atthavibhāvane ayaṃ tassatthassa vibhāvanī pāḷi. Saddhādīnaṃ vimuttiparipācakadhammānaṃ balavabhāvo tappaṭipakkhānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ dubbalabhāveneva hoti, tesañca balavabhāvo saddhādīnaṃ dubbalabhāvenāti vimuttiparipācakadhammānaṃ atthitānatthitāvasena apparajakkhamahārajakkhatādayo pāḷiyaṃ vibhajitvā dassitā. Khandhādayo eva lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena loko. Sampattibhavabhūto loko sampattibhavaloko, sugatisaṅkhāto upapattibhavo. Sampatti sambhavati etenāti sampattisambhavaloko. Sugatisaṃvattaniyo kammabhavo. Duggati saṅkhātaupapattibhavaduggati saṃvattaniyakammabhavā vipattibhavalokavipattisambhavalokā.

“This here is the Pāḷi”: in this explanation of the meaning of terms such as “with little dust,” this is the Pāḷi text that clarifies that meaning. The strength of the qualities that ripen one for liberation, such as faith, comes from the weakness of the opposing evil states; and the strength of those evil states comes from the weakness of faith and the other qualities. Thus, the states of having little dust, having much dust, and so on, are shown by analyzing them in the Pāḷi according to the presence or absence of the qualities that ripen one for liberation. The aggregates and so on are “the world” (loko) because they are subject to breaking up and decaying (lujjana-palujjana). The world that is an existence of attainment (sampattibhava) is the “world of attainment-existence” (sampattibhavaloko), that is, existence in rebirth reckoned as a good destination. That by which attainment comes to be is the “world of the arising of attainment” (sampattisambhavaloko), that is, the kamma-existence that leads to a good destination. Existence in rebirth reckoned as a bad destination and the kamma-existence that leads to a bad destination are, respectively, the “world of misfortune-existence” and the “world of the arising of misfortune.”

Puna ekakadukādivasena lokaṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “eko loko”tiādi vuttaṃ. Āhārādayo viya hi āhāraṭṭhitikā saṅkhārā lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti. Ettha eko loko sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikāti yāyaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānāya kathāya sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ paccayāyattavutti, tāya sabbe saṅkhārā ekova loko ekavidho pakārantarassa abhāvato. Dve lokātiādīsupi iminā [M 2.0136] nayena attho veditabbo. Nāmaggahaṇena cettha nibbānassa aggahaṇaṃ tassa alokasabhāvattā. Nanu ca āhāraṭṭhitikāti ettha paccayāyattavuttitāya maggaphalānampi lokatā [V 2.0128] āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati pariññeyyānaṃ dukkhasaccadhammānaṃ idha “loko”ti adhippetattā. Atha vā na lujjati na palujjatīti yo gahito tathā na hoti, so lokoti taṃ-gahaṇarahitānaṃ lokuttarānaṃ natthi lokatā. Upādānānaṃ ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā upādānakkhandhā. Dasāyatanānīti dasa rūpāyatanāni. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

Again, to show the world divided by way of ones, twos, etc., the passage beginning “One world…” is stated. For formations, being sustained by nutriment, are 'world' in the sense of breaking up and decaying. Here, by the statement based on the person, “One world: all beings are sustained by nutriment,” all formations have a conditionally arisen occurrence. By this, all formations are just one world, of one kind, as there is no other mode. The meaning should be understood in this way also for “two worlds,” and so on. And here, by the inclusion of “name,” Nibbāna is not included, because its nature is not-world. But is it not the case that, by being sustained by nutriment, the path and fruition would also be “world” due to their conditionally arisen occurrence? This does not follow, because here “world” is intended to mean the phenomena of the truth of suffering, which are to be fully understood. Or else, “world” is that which, though grasped as “it does not break up, it does not decay,” is not so. Thus for the supramundane things, which are devoid of that grasping, there is no state of being a world. The aggregates that are the objects of clinging are the clinging-aggregates. “The ten bases” means the ten material bases. The rest here is easy to understand.

Vivaṭṭajjhāsayassa adhippetattā tassa ca sabbaṃ tebhūmakakammaṃ garahitabbaṃ vajjitabbañca hutvā upaṭṭhātīti vuttaṃ “sabbe abhisaṅkhārā vajjaṃ, sabbe bhavagāmikammā vajja”nti. Apparajakkhamahārajakkhādīsu pañcasu dukesu ekekasmiṃ dasa dasa katvā “paññāsāya ākārehi imāni pañcindriyāni jānātī”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā anvayato byatirekato ca saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ paropariyattaṃ jānātīti katvā tathā vuttaṃ. Ettha ca apparajakkhādibhabbādivasena āvajjentassa bhagavato te sattā puñjapuñjāva hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, na ekekā.

Because his disposition is for what is not the round of existence, and because all kamma pertaining to the three planes of existence presents itself to him as something to be censured and avoided, it is said: 'All formations are faulty; all kamma leading to becoming is faulty.' In the five dyads—beginning with those with little dust and those with much dust—by taking ten aspects for each, it is said: 'He knows these five faculties in fifty ways.' Or alternatively, it is stated thus because he knows the superiority and inferiority of the faculties such as faith by way of positive and negative correlation. And here, when the Blessed One adverts to beings according to their classification, beginning with those with little dust, those beings appear to him in clusters, not individually.

Uppalāni ettha santīti uppalinī, gacchopi jalāsayopi, idha pana jalāsayo adhippetoti āha “uppalavane”ti. Yāni udakassa anto nimuggāneva hutvā pusanti vaḍḍhanti, tāni antonimuggaposīni. Dīpitānīti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pakāsitāni, idheva vā “aññānipī”tiādinā bhāsitāni.

'There are water lilies here,' thus it is an uppalinī. This can mean either a thicket or a reservoir of water, but here a reservoir of water is intended; hence the text says 'in a pond of water lilies.' Those that are nourished and grow while remaining submerged in the water are 'nourished while submerged.' 'Explained' means they are clarified in the commentary, or they are stated right here by the words 'and others too,' etc.

Ugghaṭitaññūti ugghaṭitaṃ nāma ñāṇugghaṭanaṃ, ñāṇe ugghaṭitamatte eva jānātīti attho. Vipañcitaṃ vitthāritameva atthaṃ jānātīti vipañcitaññū. Uddesādīhi netabboti neyyo. Saha udāhaṭavelāyāti udāhāre udāhaṭamatteyeva. Dhammābhisamayoti catusaccadhammassa ñāṇena saddhiṃ abhisamayo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādinā nayena saṃkhittena mātikāya ṭhapiyamānāya desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhituṃ samattho puggalo “ugghaṭitaññū”ti vuccati. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ saṃkhittena mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā vitthārena atthe [M 2.0137] vibhajiyamāne arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ samattho puggalo “vipañcitaññū”ti vuccati. Uddesatoti uddesahetu, uddisantassa, uddisāpentassa vāti attho. Paripucchatoti atthaṃ paripucchantassa. Anupubbena dhammābhisamayo hotīti anukkamena arahattappatti hoti. Na tāya jātiyā dhammābhisamayo hotīti tena attabhāvena maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā antamaso jhānaṃ vā vipassanaṃ vā nibbattetuṃ na sakkoti. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo padaparamoti ayaṃ puggalo byañjanapadameva paramaṃ assāti padaparamoti vuccati.

One who understands upon a concise statement (ugghaṭitaññū): 'Concise statement' means the opening up for knowledge; the meaning is that he understands as soon as the knowledge is opened up. One who understands upon elaboration (vipañcitaññū): he understands the meaning only when it is elaborated in detail. One who is guidable (neyyo): he is to be led by means of headings, etc. At the very moment of utterance: just as soon as it is uttered. Breakthrough to the Dhamma: the breakthrough, along with knowledge, to the Dhamma of the Four Truths. This is said: a person who is capable of attaining arahantship by directing his knowledge in accordance with the teaching when a summary heading (mātikā) is laid down concisely in the way of 'the four establishments of mindfulness,' etc., is called an 'ugghaṭitaññū.' This is said: a person who is capable of reaching arahantship when a summary heading is laid down concisely and the meaning is analyzed in detail is called a 'vipañcitaññū.' By means of a heading: on account of a heading, for one who states it or has it stated. By means of questioning: for one who questions about the meaning. The breakthrough to the Dhamma occurs gradually: the attainment of arahantship occurs sequentially. In that life there is no breakthrough to the Dhamma: in that existence he is unable to generate the path or the fruit, or even jhāna or insight. This person is called one for whom the letter is the limit (padaparama): this person is called a padaparama because for him the mere letter or word is the ultimate.

Kammāvaraṇenāti [V 2.0129] (vibha. aṭṭha. 826) pañcavidhena ānantariyakammena. Vipākāvaraṇenāti ahetukapaṭisandhiyā. Yasmā pana duhetukānampi ariyamaggapaṭivedho natthi, tasmā duhetukā paṭisandhipi “vipākāvaraṇamevā”ti veditabbā. Kilesāvaraṇenāti niyatamicchādiṭṭhiyā. Assaddhāti buddhādīsu saddhārahitā. Acchandikāti kattukamyatākusalacchandarahitā. Uttarakurukā manussā acchandikaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhā. Duppaññāti bhavaṅgapaññāya parihīnā. Bhavaṅgapaññāya pana paripuṇṇāyapi yassa bhavaṅgaṃ lokuttarassa paccayo na hoti, sopi duppañño eva nāma. Abhabbā niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattanti kusalesu dhammesu sammattaniyāmasaṅkhātaṃ maggaṃ okkamituṃ adhigantuṃ abhabbā. Na kammāvaraṇenātiādīni vuttavipariyāyena veditabbāni.

'By the obstruction of kamma' means by the five kinds of kamma with immediate result. 'By the obstruction of result' means by rootless rebirth-linking. But since there is no penetration of the noble path even for those with two roots, two-rooted rebirth-linking, too, should be understood as 'an obstruction of result.' 'By the obstruction of defilement' means by fixed wrong view. 'Faithless' means destitute of faith in the Buddha and so forth. 'Without desire' means destitute of wholesome desire consisting in the wish to act. The humans of Uttarakuru are said to have entered a state of being without desire. 'Devoid of wisdom' means deficient in the wisdom of the life-continuum. But even if one's wisdom of the life-continuum is complete, if one's life-continuum is not a condition for the supramundane, one is still called 'devoid of wisdom.' 'Incapable of entering the fixed course in wholesome states' means they are incapable of entering, that is, of attaining the path, which is designated as the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states. The phrases beginning 'not by the obstruction of kamma' should be understood in the opposite way to what has been stated.

Nibbānassa dvāraṃ pavisanamaggo. Vivaritvā ṭhapito mahākaruṇūpanissayena sayambhuñāṇena adhigatattā. Saddhaṃ pamuñcantūti attano saddhaṃ pavesentu, saddahanākāraṃ upaṭṭhapentūti attho. Sukhena akicchena pavattanīyatāya suppavattitaṃ. Na bhāsiṃ na bhāsissāmīti cintesiṃ.

The door to Nibbāna is the path of entry. It was opened and established because it was attained by self-become knowledge with great compassion as its decisive support. 'Let them release their faith' means let them send forth their own faith, let them establish the mode of confidence—this is the meaning. Well set in motion because it can be kept going with ease, without trouble. 'I did not speak, nor will I speak'—thus I thought.

284. Dhammaṃ desessāmīti evaṃ pavattitadhammadesanāpaṭisaṃyuttassa vitakkassa sattamasattāhato paraṃ aṭṭhamasattāheyeva uppannattā vuttaṃ “aṭṭhame sattāhe”ti. Na itarasattāhāni viya paṭiniyatakiccalakkhitassa aṭṭhamasattāhassa nāma pavattitassa sabbhāvā.

284. The thought connected with teaching the Dhamma, 'I will teach the Dhamma,' arose in the eighth week after the seventh week; hence it is said, 'in the eighth week.' For there was in fact an eighth week, so-named, which was marked by a specific task, unlike the other weeks.

Vivaṭanti [M 2.0138] devatāviggahena vivaṭaaṅgapaccaṅganiddāya janānaṃ pākaṭaṃ vippakāranti attho. “Buddhattaṃ anadhigantvā na paccāgamissāmī”ti uppannavitakkātisayahetukena pathavīparivattanacetiyaṃ nāma dassetvā. Sākiyakoliyamallarajjavasena tīṇi rajjāni. Rukkhamūleti nigrodhamūle. Vatvā pakkāmi, pakkamantiyā cassā mahāsatto ākāraṃ dassesi suvaṇṇathālaggahaṇāya, sā “tumhākaṃ taṃ pariccattamevā”ti pakkāmi.

'Opened' means that because the deities withdrew, the limbs and minor limbs of the sleeping people became exposed and dishevelled. Having shown the 'Earth-Turning Shrine,' so-called because of the excellence of the thought that arose, 'I will not return without attaining Buddhahood.' Three kingdoms: the kingdoms of the Sākiyas, Koliyas, and Mallas. 'At the foot of the tree' means at the foot of the banyan tree. Having spoken, she departed. As she was departing, the Great Being made a gesture for her to take the golden bowl, but she departed, saying, 'It has already been relinquished by you.'

Divāvihāraṃ katvāti nānāsamāpattiyo samāpajjanena divāvihāraṃ viharitvā. “Kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca, aṭṭhi ca avasissatu, upasussatu sarīre maṃsalohita”ntiādinā sutte (ma. ni. 2.184; saṃ. ni. 2.237; a. ni. 2.5; 8.13; mahāni. 17, 196) āgatanayena caturaṅgavīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā.

Having spent the day abiding: having spent the day abiding by entering into various meditative attainments. Having resolved upon the four-factored energy in the way that comes in the sutta beginning: 'Willingly, let only skin, sinews, and bones remain, and let the flesh and blood in my body dry up' (MN 70; SN 12.22; AN 2.5; etc.).

Navayojananti ubbedhato vuttaṃ, puthulato dvādasayojanā, dīghato yāva cakkavāḷā āyatāti [V 2.0130] vadanti. Ajjhottharanto upasaṅkamitvā – “uṭṭhehi so, siddhattha, ahaṃ imassa pallaṅkassa anucchaviko”ti vatvā tattha sakkhiṃ otārento attano parisaṃ niddisi. Ekappahāreneva – “ayameva anucchaviko, ayameva anucchaviko”ti kolāhalamakāsi, taṃ sutvā mahāsatto…pe… hatthaṃ pasāreti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

'Nine yojanas': this is said of its height; in width it is twelve yojanas, and in length, they say, it extends as far as the world-sphere. Approaching and overwhelming him, Māra said, 'Arise, Siddhattha! I am the one worthy of this seat!' and saying so, calling on his witness there, he pointed to his own retinue. With a single shout his retinue made an uproar, 'He is the worthy one! He is the worthy one!' Hearing this, the Great Being ... stretched out his hand. In reference to which it was said:

“Acetanāyaṃ pathavī, aviññāya sukhaṃ dukhaṃ;

Sāpi dānabalā mayhaṃ, sattakkhattuṃ pakampathā”ti. (cariyā. 1.124);

'This earth is without consciousness, uncomprehending of pleasure and pain; yet even she, by the power of my giving, trembled seven times.' (Cp 1.124)

Pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ visodhetvāti ānetvā sambandho sīhāvalokanañāyena. Vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ sammasitvāti catusaccamanasikāraṃ sandhāyāha. Imassa pallaṅkassa atthāyāti pallaṅkasīsena adhigatavisesaṃ dasseti. Tattha hi sikhāppattavimuttisukhaṃ avijahanto antarantarā ca paṭiccasamuppādaṅgaṃ manasikaronto ekapallaṅkena nisīdi. Ekaccānanti yā adhigatamaggā sacchikatanirodhā ekadesena ca buddhaguṇe jānanti, tā ṭhapetvā tadaññesaṃ devatānaṃ. Aññepi buddhattakarāti visākhāpuṇṇamato paṭṭhāya rattindivaṃ evaṃ niccasamāhitabhāvahetukānaṃ buddhaguṇānaṃ upari aññepi [M 2.0139] buddhattasādhakā, “ayaṃ buddho”ti buddhabhāvassa paresaṃ vibhāvanā dhammā kiṃ nu kho atthīti yojanā.

The connection with 'having purified the knowledge of recollecting past abodes' is brought in by the method of the lion's backward glance. 'Having reviewed the round and its unravelling'—this is said in reference to the attention to the Four Truths. 'For the sake of this seat'—this shows the special attainment achieved at the head of the seat. For there he sat on that one seat without abandoning the bliss of liberation attained at the peak, while in between repeatedly giving attention to the factors of dependent origination. 'Of some': this refers to deities other than those who have attained the path, have realized cessation, and know in part the Buddha's qualities. The connection is: 'Are there any other qualities that make one a Buddha?'—that is, apart from the Buddha-qualities due to his state of constant concentration day and night since the Visākhā full moon, are there other qualities that accomplish Buddhahood, qualities that reveal his state as a Buddha to others with the thought, 'This is a Buddha'?

Animisehīti dhammapītivipphāravasena pasādavikasitaniccalatāya nimesarahitehi. Ratanacaṅkameti devatāhi māpite ratanamayacaṅkame. Ratanabhūtānaṃ sattannaṃ pakaraṇānaṃ tattha ca anantanayassa dhammaratanassa sammasanena taṃ ṭhānaṃ ratanagharacetiyaṃ nāma jātantipi vadanti. Evanti vakkhamānākārena. Chabbaṇṇānaṃ rasmīnaṃ dantehi nikkhamanato chaddantanāgakulaṃ viyāti nidassanaṃ vuttaṃ.

'With unblinking eyes' means with eyes devoid of blinking because of their unwavering state, opened in confidence due to the suffusion of joy in the Dhamma. 'The Jewelled Walk' means on the jewelled cloister created by the deities. They also say that place became known as the 'Jewel House Shrine' because of the reviewing there of the seven treatises, which are like jewels, and of the Dhamma-jewel with its infinite methods. 'Thus' means in the manner that will be described. The illustration 'like the clan of Chaddanta elephants' is stated because of the six-coloured rays issuing from his teeth.

Heṭṭhā lohapāsādappamāṇoti navabhūmakassa sabbapaṭhamassa lohapāsādassa heṭṭhā lohapāsādappamāṇo. Khandhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 5) pana tattha “bhaṇḍāgāragabbhappamāṇa”nti vuttaṃ.

'The size of the Brazen Palace below' means the size of the area below the very first nine-storied Brazen Palace. But in the Commentary to the Khandhakas, it is said there to be 'the size of the treasury chamber.'

Paccaggheti abhinave. Paccekaṃ mahagghatāya paccaggheti keci, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Na hi buddhā bhagavanto mahagghaṃ paṭiggaṇhanti paribhuñjanti vā. Piṇḍapātanti ettha manthañca madhupiṇḍikañca [V 2.0131] sandhāya vadati. Ayaṃ vitakkoti – “kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya”nti ayaṃ parivitakko.

'Fresh' (paccaggha) means new. Some say it means 'fresh' because of being individually of great value, but that is not good. For the Blessed Ones, the Buddhas, do not accept or use things of great value. 'Almsfood': here this refers to the barley-gruel and the honey-ball. 'This thought': this is the reflection, 'To whom, now, should I teach the Dhamma first?'

Paṇḍiccenāti samāpattipaṭilābhasaṃsiddhena adhigamabāhusaccasaṅkhātena paṇḍitabhāvena. Veyyattiyenāti samāpattipaṭilābhapaccayena pārihāriyapaññāsaṅkhātena byattabhāvena. Medhāvīti tihetukapaṭisandhipaññāsaṅkhātāya taṃtaṃitikattabbatāpaññāsaṅkhātāya ca medhāya samannāgatoti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Mahājāniyoti mahāparihāniko. Āgamanapādāpi natthīti idaṃ paṭhamaṃ vattabbaṃ, athāhaṃ tattha gaccheyyaṃ, gantvā desiyamānaṃ dhammampissa sotuṃ sotapasādopi natthīti yojanā. Kiṃ pana bhagavatā attano buddhānubhāvena te dhammaṃ ñāpetuṃ na sakkāti? Āma, na sakkā. Na hi parato ghosaṃ antarena sāvakānaṃ dhammābhisamayo sambhavati, aññathā itarapaccayarahitassapi dhammābhisamayena bhavitabbaṃ, na ca taṃ atthi. Vuttañhetaṃ – “dveme, bhikkhave, paccayā sammādiṭṭhiyā uppādāya parato ca ghoso ajjhattañca yonisomanasikāro”ti (a. ni. 2.127). Pāḷiyaṃ rāmasseva samāpattilābhitā āgatā, na udakassa, taṃ tassa bodhisattena samāgatakālavasena vuttaṃ[M 2.0140]. So hi pubbepi tattha yuttappayutto viharanto mahāpurisena khippaññeva samāpattīnaṃ nibbattitabhāvaṃ sutvā saṃvegajāto mahāsatte tato nibbijja pakkante ghaṭento vāyamanto nacirasseva aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattesi. Tena vuttaṃ “nevasaññānāsaññāyatane nibbattoti addasā”ti. Ete aṭṭha brāhmaṇāti sambandho. Chaḷaṅgavāti chaḷaṅgaviduno. Mantanti mantapadaṃ. “Nijjhāyitvā”ti vacanaseso, mantetvāti attho. Viyākariṃsūti kathesuṃ.

By sagacity (paṇḍiccena): by the state of being a sage which is accomplished through the attainment of meditative absorptions and is designated as extensive learning through attainment. By skillfulness (veyyattiyena): by the state of competence designated as the wisdom of practical management, which is a condition for attaining meditative absorptions. Wise (medhāvī): possessing the wisdom designated as that of a three-rooted rebirth-linking and the wisdom concerning what should be done in each particular case; this is how the meaning should be understood here. One of great knowledge (mahājāniyo): one prone to great decline. There is not even a basis for going (āgamanapādāpi natthi): this should be stated first, and the connection is: 'I have no means of going there; and even if I were to go, there would be no faculty of hearing to hear the Dhamma being taught.' But could the Blessed One not make them know the Dhamma by his own Buddha-power? Yes, he could not. For without the voice of another, the breakthrough to the Dhamma is not possible for disciples; otherwise, a breakthrough to the Dhamma would have to occur even for one devoid of other conditions, but this is not so. For it is said: 'Bhikkhus, there are two conditions for the arising of right view: the voice of another and wise attention within' (AN 2.127). In the Pāli, it is Rāma's attainment of the absorption that is mentioned, not Udaka's; this was said by the Bodhisatta in connection with the time he met him. For even earlier, while dwelling there diligently, upon hearing from the Great Being how he had quickly generated the absorptions, he became stirred with urgency. After the Great Being, becoming disenchanted, had departed from there, he strove and exerted himself and before long generated the eight absorptions. Therefore it is said: 'He saw that he had generated the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' These eight brahmins: this is the connection. One who knows the six limbs (chaḷaṅgavā): one who knows the six limbs. The sacred text (mantam): the words of the sacred text. 'Having reflected' (nijjhāyitvā): this is the rest of the sentence; it means 'having recited.' They declared (viyākariṃsu): they spoke.

Yathāmantapadanti lakkhaṇamantasaṅkhātavedavacanānurūpaṃ. Gatāti paṭipannā. “Dveva gatiyo bhavanti anaññā”ti (dī. ni. 2.33; 3.199-200; ma. ni. 2.384, 398) vuttaniyāmena nicchinituṃ asakkontā brāhmaṇā vuttameva paṭipajjiṃsu, na mahāpurisassa buddhabhāvappattiṃ paccāsīsiṃsu. Ime pana koṇḍaññādayo pañca “ekaṃsato buddho bhavissatī”ti jātanicchayattā mantapadaṃ atikkantā. Puṇṇapattanti tuṭṭhidānaṃ. Nibbitakkāti nibbikappā, na dvedhā takkā.

In accordance with the words of the sacred text (yathāmantapadam): in conformity with the words of the Veda, designated as the sacred text on characteristics. Destinations (gatā): they followed. Unable to determine with certainty according to the principle stated, 'There are only two destinations, no other' (DN 2.33; 3.199–200; MN 2.384, 398), the brahmins simply followed what was said and did not expect the Great Being to attain Buddhahood. But these five, beginning with Koṇḍañña, having reached the firm conclusion that 'He will definitely become a Buddha,' went beyond the words of the sacred text. A full bowl (puṇṇapattam): a gift of satisfaction. Without thought (nibbitakkā): without uncertainty; not of two minds.

Vappakāleti vapanakāle. Vapanatthaṃ bījāni nīharaṇantena tattha aggaṃ gahetvā dānaṃ bījaggadānaṃ nāma. Lāyanaggādīsupi eseva nayo. Dhaññaphalassa nātipariṇatakāle puthukakāle. Lāyaneti sassalāyane. Yathā lūnaṃ hatthakaṃ katvā veṇivasena bandhanaṃ veṇikaraṇaṃ. Veṇiyo pana purisabhāravasena [V 2.0132] bandhanaṃ kalāpo. Khale kalāpānaṃ ṭhapanadivase aggaṃ gahetvā dānaṃ khalaggaṃ. Madditvā vīhīnaṃ rāsikaraṇadivase aggaṃ gahetvā dānaṃ bhaṇḍaggaṃ. Koṭṭhāgāre dhaññassa pakkhipanadivase dānaṃ koṭṭhaggaṃ. Uddharitvāti khalato dhaññassa uddharitvā. Navannaṃ aggadānānaṃ dinnattāti idaṃ tassa rattaññūnaṃ aggabhāvatthāya katābhinīhārānurūpaṃ pavattitasāvakapāramiyā ciṇṇante pavattitattā vuttaṃ. Tiṇṇampi hi bodhisattānaṃ taṃtaṃpāramiyā sikhāppattakāle pavattitaṃ puññaṃ apuññaṃ vā garutaravipākameva hoti, dhammassa ca sabbapaṭhamaṃ sacchikiriyāya vinā kathaṃ rattaññūnaṃ aggabhāvasiddhīti. Bahukārā kho ime pañcavaggiyāti idaṃ pana upakārānussaraṇamattakameva paricayavasena āḷārudakānussaraṇaṃ viya.

At the time of sowing: at sowing time. Taking the first portion of the seeds brought for sowing and giving it is called the gift of the first portion of the seeds. The same principle applies to the first portion of the reaping and so on. When the grain-fruit is not yet fully ripe, at the time of making flattened rice. At the reaping: at the reaping of the crop. Just as what is reaped is made into a handful and tied with a strip of bamboo, this is called making a sheaf. But a bundle tied according to a man's load is a large sheaf. On the day of placing the large sheaves on the threshing floor, taking the first portion and giving it is the first portion from the threshing floor. After threshing, on the day of making a heap of the paddy, taking the first portion and giving it is the first portion of the goods. On the day of putting the grain into the granary, the gift is the first portion from the granary. Having lifted up: having lifted the grain from the threshing floor. Because the gifts of the first portion of the new grain were given: this was said because it occurred at the culmination of his practice of the disciple's perfections, undertaken in conformity with the aspiration he had made to be preeminent among those of long standing. For all three types of Bodhisattas, at the time of reaching the peak of their respective perfections, any merit or demerit performed has a very weighty result. And without first directly realizing the Dhamma, how could the attainment of preeminence among those of long standing be accomplished? 'These ascetics of the group of five were of great help': this, however, is merely a recollection of their assistance out of familiarity, like the recollection of Āḷāra and Udaka.

285. Vivareti majjhe. Tenāha “tigāvutantare ṭhāne”ti. Ayojiyamāne upayogavacanaṃ na pāpuṇāti sāmivacanassa pasaṅge antarā-saddayogena [M 2.0141] upayogavacanassa icchitattā. Tenāha “antarāsaddena pana yuttattā upayogavacanaṃ kata”nti.

285. It explains: in the middle. Therefore he said, 'in a place within three gāvutas.' In a context for the genitive case, if it is not used, the locative case is not obtained; but the locative case is desired in connection with the word antarā. Therefore he said, 'but because it is connected with the word antarā, the locative case has been used.'

Sabbaṃ tebhūmakadhammaṃ abhibhavitvā pariññābhisamayavasena atikkamitvā. Catubhūmakadhammaṃ anavasesaṃ ñeyyaṃ sabbaso ñeyyāvaraṇassa pahīnattā sabbaññutaññāṇena avediṃ. Rajjanadussanamuyhanādinā kilesena. Appahātabbampi kusalābyākataṃ tappaṭibaddhakilesamathanena pahīnattā na hotīti āha “sabbaṃ tebhūmakadhammaṃ jahitvā ṭhito”ti. Ārammaṇatoti ārammaṇakaraṇavasena.

Having overcome all phenomena of the three planes, having transcended them by way of full understanding and breakthrough. I have known without remainder all knowable phenomena of the four planes with the knowledge of omniscience, because the obstruction to the knowable has been completely abandoned. By the defilement of lusting, hating, and becoming deluded, etc. Even what is not to be abandoned—the wholesome and the indeterminate—does not exist, because it is abandoned by the crushing of the defilements connected with it; therefore he said, 'having abandoned all phenomena of the three planes, he stands.' As object: by way of taking it as an object.

Kiñcāpi lokiyadhammānampi yādiso lokanāthassa adhigamo, na tādiso adhigamo parūpadeso atthi, lokuttaradhamme panassa lesopi natthīti āha “lokuttaradhamme mayhaṃ ācariyo nāma natthī”ti. Paṭibhāgapuggaloti sīlādīhi guṇehi paṭinidhibhūto puggalo. Sahetunāti sahadhammena sapāṭihīrakatāya. Nayenāti abhijānanatādividhinā. Cattāri saccānīti idaṃ tabbinimuttassa ñeyyassa abhāvato vuttaṃ. Sayaṃ buddhoti sayameva sayambhuñāṇena buddho. Vigatapariḷāhatāya sītibhūto. Tato eva nibbuto. Āhañchanti āhanissāmi. Veneyyānaṃ amatādhigamāya ugghosanādiṃ katvā satthu dhammadesanā amatadundubhīti vuttā.

Although even in regard to worldly states, the attainment of the Lord of the World is such that there is no such attainment based on another's instruction, in regard to the supramundane Dhamma there is not even a trace of this. Thus he said, 'In regard to the supramundane Dhamma, I have no teacher.' A comparable person is a person who is a substitute in terms of qualities such as virtue. With cause: with the Dhamma, with the performance of miracles. By the method: by the way of direct knowledge, etc. The four truths: this is said because there is nothing knowable apart from them. Self-awakened: awakened by his own self-arisen knowledge. He has become cool, because his distress has departed. For that very reason, he is extinguished. 'I shall beat': I shall strike. The Teacher's teaching of the Dhamma is called the drum of the Deathless because he makes proclamations and so on for those to be trained to attain the Deathless.

Anantañāṇo jitakilesoti anantajino. Evampi nāma bhaveyyāti evaṃvidhe nāma rūparatane īdisena ñāṇena bhavitabbanti adhippāyo. Ayaṃ hissa pabbajjāya paccayo jāto, katādhikāro cesa. Tathā hi bhagavā tena samāgamatthaṃ padasāva taṃ maggaṃ paṭipajji.

His knowledge is endless and he has conquered the defilements, thus he is the Endless Conqueror. 'Could it be so?': the intention is that in such a jewel of a physical form, there should be such knowledge. This became the reason for his going forth, and he was one who had made his aspiration. For the Blessed One undertook that journey on foot in order to meet him.

Koṭṭhāsasampannāti [V 2.0133] aṅgapaccaṅgasaṅkhātaavayavasampannā. Aṭṭīyatīti aṭṭo hoti, domanassaṃ āpajjatīti attho.

Endowed with portions means endowed with the parts designated as limbs and appendages. He is troubled means he is afflicted, he experiences displeasure; this is the meaning.

Avihaṃ upapannāseti avihesu nibbattā. Vimuttāti aggaphalavimuttiyā vimuttā. Te hitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, dibbayogaṃ upajjhagunti te upakā dayo mānusaṃ attabhāvaṃ jahitvā orambhāgiyasaṃyojanappahānena avihesu nibbattamattāva aggamaggādhigamena dibbayogaṃ uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanaṃ samatikkamiṃsu.

They have arisen in Aviha: they were reborn in the Aviha realm. Liberated: liberated by the liberation of the highest fruit. Having abandoned the human body, they went beyond the divine yoke: those such as Upaka, having abandoned the human state of existence, just by being reborn in the Aviha realm through the abandoning of the lower fetters, transcended the divine yoke—the higher fetters—by attaining the highest path.

286. Saṇṭhapesunti [M 2.0142] “neva abhivādetabbo”tiādinā (mahāva. 12) saṇṭhaṃ kiriyākāraṃ akaṃsu. Tenāha “katikaṃ akaṃsū”ti. Padhānatoti pubbe anuṭṭhitadukkaracaraṇato. Pabhāvitanti vācāsamuṭṭhānaṃ, vacīnicchāraṇanti attho. “Ayaṃ na kiñci visesaṃ adhigamissatī”ti anukkaṇṭhanatthaṃ. “Mayaṃ yattha katthaci gamissāmā”ti mā vitakkayittha. Obhāsoti vipassanobhāso. Nimittanti kammaṭṭhānanimittaṃ. Ekapadenevāti ekavacaneneva. “Anena pubbepi na kiñci micchā vuttapubba”nti satiṃ labhitvā. Yathābhūtavādīti uppannagāravā.

286. They established: they made a formal agreement beginning, 'He should not be greeted,' etc. (Mv I.12), thus establishing a course of action. Therefore it is said, 'They made an agreement.' From striving: because of the difficult practice previously undertaken. Influenced: the arising of speech, meaning the utterance of words. 'This one will not attain any distinction': this was for the purpose of not being concerned. 'We will go wherever': do not think thus. Radiance: the radiance of insight. Sign: the sign of the meditation subject. With a single word: with a single utterance. Having gained the recollection, 'Never before has anything false been spoken by him.' As one who speaks what is true: because respect had arisen.

Antovihāreyeva ahosi daharakumāro viya tehi bhikkhūhi pariharito. Maleti saṃkilese. Gāmato bhikkhūhi nīhaṭaṃ upanītaṃ bhattaṃ etassāti nīhaṭabhatto, tena nīhaṭabhattena bhagavatā. Ettakaṃ kathāmagganti – “dvemā, bhikkhave, pariyesanā”ti ārabhitvā yāva – “natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti padaṃ, ettakaṃ desanāmaggaṃ. Kāmañcettha – “tumhepi mamañceva pañcavaggiyānañca maggaṃ ārūḷhā, ariyapariyesanā tumhākaṃ pariyesanā”ti aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ. Tena pana – “so kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, attanā jātidhammo samāno…pe… asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ ajjhagamanti, atha kho, bhikkhave, pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū mayā evaṃ ovadiyamānā…pe… anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ ajjhagamaṃsu…pe… natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti imasseva suttapadassa attho vibhāvitoti katvā vuttaṃ “bhagavā yaṃ pubbe avaca tumhepi mamañceva pañcavaggiyānañca maggaṃ āruḷhā, ariyapariyesanā tumhākaṃ pariyesanāti. Imaṃ ekameva anusandhiṃ dassento āharī”ti.

He was indeed cared for by those monks within the monastery as if he were a young boy. 'Mala' means defilement. The food brought forth and offered by the monks from the village was for him; thus, he was 'Nīhaṭabhatta' (one for whom food is brought forth), and the Blessed One was that Nīhaṭabhatta. This much is the path of discourse: beginning with 'Monks, there are these two quests,' up to the phrase 'There is now no more rebirth'—this much is the path of the teaching. And here, the commentary's statement is: 'You too have ascended the path of both myself and the group of five monks; your quest is the noble quest.' But by this—'I, monks, though myself subject to birth… attained the undefiled, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. Then, monks, the group of five monks, being thus instructed by me… attained the supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna… There is now no more rebirth'—the meaning of this very Sutta passage has been elucidated. Therefore, it is said: 'The Blessed One, showing just this one connection, brought forth what he had previously said: "You too have ascended the path of both myself and the group of five monks; your quest is the noble quest."'

287. Anagāriyānampīti pabbajitānampi. Pañcakāmaguṇavasena anariyapariyesanā hoti gadhitādibhāvena paribhuñjanato. Micchājīvavasenapi anariyapariyesanā hotīti tato visesanatthaṃ [V 2.0134] “pañcakāmaguṇavasenā”ti vuttaṃ sacchandarāgaparibhogassa adhippetattā. Idāni catūsu paccayesu kāmaguṇe niddhāretuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Paribhogarasoti paribhogapaccayapītisomanassaṃ. Ayaṃ pana rasasamānatāvasena gahaṇaṃ upādāya [M 2.0143] “raso”ti vutto, na sabhāvato. Sabhāvena gahaṇaṃ upādāya pītisomanassaṃ dhammārammaṇaṃ siyā, na rasārammaṇaṃ. Appaccavekkhaṇaparibhogoti paccavekkhaṇarahito paribhogo, idamatthitaṃ anissāya gadhitādibhāvena paribhogoti attho. Gadhitāti taṇhāya baddhā. Mucchitāti mucchaṃ mohaṃ pamādaṃ āpannā. Ajjhogāḷhāti adhiogāḷhā, taṃ taṃ ārammaṇaṃ anupavisitvā ṭhitā. Ādīnavaṃ apassantāti sacchandarāgaparibhoge dosaṃ ajānantā. Apaccavekkhitaparibhogahetuādīnavaṃ nissarati atikkamati etenāti nissaraṇaṃ, paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ.

287. 'Even for the homeless' means for those who have gone forth. The ignoble quest occurs through the five strands of sensual pleasure due to indulging in them with greed and so forth. The ignoble quest also occurs through wrong livelihood; therefore, to distinguish it, it is said 'through the five strands of sensual pleasure,' as the intention is enjoyment driven by desire and lust. Now, to determine sensual pleasure among the four requisites, 'therein' and so forth is said. 'The delight of enjoyment' means the joy and gladness conditioned by enjoyment. This is called 'delight' (raso) by way of similarity to taste, not by its intrinsic nature. Intrinsically, joy and gladness would have a mental object as their basis, not a taste object. 'Enjoyment without reflection' means enjoyment devoid of reflection; the meaning is indulging without relying on its true purpose, with greed and so forth. 'Greedy' means bound by craving. 'Infatuated' means having fallen into infatuation, delusion, and heedlessness. 'Immersed' means deeply immersed, having entered and settled into that particular object. 'Not seeing the danger' means not knowing the fault in enjoyment driven by desire and lust. 'The escape' (nissaraṇa) is the knowledge of reflection, by which one escapes and transcends the danger arising from unreflective enjoyment.

Pāsarāsinti pāsasamudāyaṃ. Luddako hi pāsaṃ oḍḍento na ekaṃyeva, na ca ekasmiṃyeva ṭhāne oḍḍeti, atha kho taṃtaṃmigānaṃ āgamanamaggaṃ sallakkhetvā tattha tattha oḍḍento bahūyeva oḍḍeti, tasmā te cittena ekato gahetvā “pāsarāsī”ti vuttaṃ. Vāgurassa vā pāsapadesānaṃ bahubhāvato “pāsarāsī”ti vuttaṃ.

'A heap of snares' means a collection of snares. For a hunter, when setting snares, does not set just one, nor in just one place. Instead, observing the paths where various animals come, he sets many snares here and there. Therefore, mentally gathering them together, it is called a 'heap of snares.' Or, because the snare-places of a net are numerous, it is called a 'heap of snares.'

Pāsarāsisuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Pāsarāsi Sutta is concluded.

7. Cūḷahatthipadopamasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Shorter Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant's Footprint

288. Setaparivāroti [V 2.0135] setapaṭicchado, setavaṇṇālaṅkāroti attho. Pubbe pana “setālaṅkārā”ti assālaṅkāro gahito, idha cakkapañjarakubbarādirathāvayavesu kātabbālaṅkāro. Evaṃ vuttenāti evaṃ “setāya suda”ntiādinā pakārena saṃyuttamahāvagge (saṃ. ni. 5.4) vuttena. Nātimahā yuddhamaṇḍale sañcārasukhatthaṃ. Yodho sārathīti dvinnaṃ, paharaṇadāyakena saddhiṃ tiṇṇaṃ vā.

288. 'With a white retinue' means with a white covering, that is, adorned with white coloring. Previously, 'white ornaments' was taken to mean horse ornaments, but here it means ornaments to be made on chariot parts like wheels, frames, poles, and so forth. 'Thus spoken' means thus spoken in the manner beginning with 'with a white chariot, indeed,' as stated in the Mahāvagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya (SN 45.4). 'Not too large' is for ease of movement on the battlefield. 'The warrior and the charioteer' refers to two, or three including the weapon-giver.

Nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karoti nagarasobhanatthaṃ. Idaṃ kira tassa brāhmaṇassa jāṇussoṇiṭṭhānantaraṃ jātisiddhaṃ paramparāgataṃ cārittaṃ. Tenāha “ito ettakehi divasehī”tiādi. Cārittavasena nagaravāsinopi tathā tathā paṭipajjanti. Puññavādimaṅgalakathane niyuttā māṅgalikā. Suvatthipattanāya sovatthikā. Ādi-saddena vandīādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Yasasirisampattiyāti yasasampattiyā sirisampattiyā ca, parivārasampattiyā ceva vibhavasobhāsampattiyā cāti attho.

He circumambulates the city for the city's beautification. This, indeed, was the customary practice of that brahmin in the position of Jāṇussoṇi, established by birth and handed down through tradition. Therefore, he said, 'from this many days hence,' and so forth. Following this custom, the city-dwellers also act accordingly. Those engaged in auspicious speech, declaring merit, are 'māṅgalikā'. Those for the attainment of well-being are 'sovatthikā'. The term 'and so forth' (ādi) includes bards (vandī) and others. 'By the attainment of fame and splendor' means by the attainment of fame and the attainment of splendor, and by the attainment of a retinue and the attainment of the splendor of wealth—this is the meaning.

Nagarābhimukho [M 2.0144] pāyāsi attano bhikkhācāravelāya. Paṇḍito maññeti ettha maññeti idaṃ “maññatī”ti iminā samānatthaṃ nipātapadaṃ. Tassa iti-saddaṃ ānetvā atthaṃ dassento “paṇḍitoti maññatī”ti āha. Anumatipucchāvasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “udāhu no”ti. “Taṃ kiṃ maññati bhavaṃ vacchāyano samaṇassa gotamassa paññāveyyattiya”nti hi vuttamevatthaṃ puna gaṇhanto “paṇḍito maññe”ti āha. Tasmā vuttaṃ “bhavaṃ vacchāyano, samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ paṇḍitoti maññati, udāhu no”ti, yathā te khameyya, tathā naṃ kathehīti adhippāyo.

He set out toward the city at his own time for the alms round. In 'Paṇḍito maññeti', 'maññeti' here is a particle having the same meaning as 'maññati' (he thinks). To show its meaning by bringing in the word 'iti', it is stated as 'paṇḍito iti maññati' (he thinks, 'He is wise'). This was said in the manner of a question seeking agreement. Therefore, he said, 'or not?' For, taking up again the meaning of what was said—'What does the venerable Vacchāyana think of the ascetic Gotama’s manifestation of wisdom?'—he said, 'I think he is wise.' Therefore, it was said: 'Venerable Vacchāyana, do you think the ascetic Gotama is wise, or not?' The intention is, 'Speak of him as is acceptable to you.'

Ahaṃ ko nāma, mama avisayo esoti dasseti. Ko cāti hetunissakke paccattavacananti āha “kuto cā”ti. Tathā cāha “kena kāraṇena jānissāmī”ti, yena kāraṇena samaṇassa gotamassa paññāveyyattiyaṃ jāneyyaṃ, taṃ kāraṇaṃ mayi natthīti adhippāyo. Buddhoyeva bhaveyya, abuddhassa sabbathā buddhañāṇānubhāvaṃ jānituṃ na sakkāti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “appamattakaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, oramattakaṃ sīlamattakaṃ, yena puthujjano tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ vadamāno vadeyya (dī. ni. 1.7), atthi, bhikkhave, aññeva dhammā gambhīrā duddasā duranubodhā [V 2.0136] …pe… yehi tathāgatassa yathābhuccaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamāno vadeyyā”ti (dī. ni. 1.28) ca. Etthāti “sopi nūnassa tādisovā”ti etasmiṃ pade. Pasattha pasatthoti pasatthehi attano guṇeheva so pasattho, na tassa kittinā, pasaṃsāsabhāveneva pāsaṃsoti attho. Tenāha “sabbaguṇāna”ntiādi. Maṇiratananti cakkavattino maṇiratanaṃ. Sadevake loke pāsaṃsānampi pāsaṃsoti dassetuṃ “pasatthehi vā”ti dutiyavikappo gahito.

He shows, 'Who am I? This is beyond my scope.' 'And from where?'—this is said to indicate the reason with a personal statement. Similarly, he says, 'By what means would I know?'—meaning that the means by which one might understand the ascetic Gotama’s manifestation of wisdom do not exist in me. Only a Buddha could know a Buddha; for a non-Buddha, it is entirely impossible to comprehend the power of a Buddha’s knowledge. For it has been said: 'Monks, it is a trifling matter, a minor matter, a mere matter of virtue, by which an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata… There are, monks, other qualities profound, hard to see, hard to understand… by which one speaking rightly might truly praise the Tathāgata.' 'Here' refers to the phrase 'he too must surely be just like that.' 'The praised one is praised' means: he is praised for his own praiseworthy qualities, not because of his reputation; the meaning is that he is praiseworthy by his very nature of being praiseworthy. Hence it is said, 'of all virtues,' etc. 'Jewel gem' means the jewel gem of a wheel-turning monarch. To show that even among those praised in the world with its gods, he is praiseworthy, the second alternative 'or by the praiseworthy' is taken.

Araṇīyato attho, so eva vasatīti vasoti atthavaso, tassa tassa payogassa ānisaṃsabhūtaṃ phalanti āha “atthavasanti atthānisaṃsa”nti. Attho vā vuttalakkhaṇo vaso etassāti atthavaso, kāraṇaṃ. Nāgavanavāsikoti hatthināgānaṃ vicaraṇavane tesaṃ gahaṇatthaṃ vasanako. Anuggahitasippoti asikkhitahatthisippo āyatavitthatassa padamattassa dassanena “mahā vata, bho nāgo”ti niṭṭhāgamanato. Parato pana bhagavatā vuttaṭṭhāne. Uggahitasippo puriso nāgavanikoti āgato āyatavitthatassa [M 2.0145] padassa uccassa ca nisevitassa byabhicārabhāvaṃ ñatvā tattakena niṭṭhaṃ agantvā mahāhatthiṃ disvāva niṭṭhāgamanato. Ñāṇaṃ pajjati etthāti ñāṇapadāni, khattiyapaṇḍitādīnaṃ dhammavinaye vinītattā vinayehi adhigatajjhānādīni. Tāni hi tathāgatagandhahatthino desanāñāṇena akkantaṭṭhānāni. Cattārīti pana vineyyānaṃ idha khattiyapaṇḍitādivasena catubbidhānaṃyeva gahitattā.

The meaning (attho) is to be attained. Because that very thing dwells (vasati), it is 'vaso'; thus 'atthavaso'. He says that this is the fruit which is the benefit of each particular application, meaning 'atthānisaṃsa' (the benefit of the meaning). Or, 'atthavaso' is that which has the stated meaning as its basis (vaso); this is the reason. 'Dweller in an elephant forest' means one who dwells in the forest where elephant-nāgas roam for the purpose of capturing them. 'Untrained in the skill' means an untrained elephant-handler, who, upon seeing merely a long and wide footprint, concludes, 'Indeed, sirs, this is a great elephant!' But in a later passage, where it is spoken by the Blessed One, a trained elephant-handler comes, and knowing the absence of deviation in a footprint that is long, wide, high, and well-trodden, does not conclude upon seeing only that much, but only upon seeing the great elephant itself. 'Footprints of knowledge' (ñāṇapadāni) are so called because 'knowledge arises here'; these are the attainments of jhāna and so forth, gained through the disciplines by those like wise Khattiyas, who are disciplined in the Dhamma and Vinaya. For these are indeed the places frequented by the teaching-knowledge of the Tathāgata, the scent-elephant. 'Four' (cattāri) is mentioned because here only four kinds of trainable persons are taken up, namely wise Khattiyas and so forth.

289. Puggalesu paññāya ca nipuṇatā paṇḍitasamaññā nipuṇatthassa dassanasamatthatāvasenevāti āha “sukhumaatthantarapaṭivijjhanasamatthe”ti. Kata-saddo idha nipphannapariyāyo. Pare pavadanti ettha, etenāti parappavādo, parasamayo. Parehi pavadanaṃ parappavādo, viggāhikakathāya paravādamaddanaṃ. Tadubhayampi ekato katvā pāḷiyaṃ vuttanti āha “viññātaparappavāde ceva parehi saddhiṃ katavādaparicaye cā”ti, parasamayesu paravādamaddanesu ca nipphanneti attho. Vālavedhirūpeti vālavedhipatirūpe. Tenāha “vālavedhidhanuggahasadise”ti. Vālanti anekadhā bhinnassa vālassa aṃsusaṅkhātaṃ vālaṃ. Bhindantā viyāti ghaṭādiṃ saviggahaṃ muggarādinā bhindantā viya, diṭṭhigatāni ekaṃsato bhindantāti adhippāyo. “Atthaṃ guyhaṃ paṭicchannaṃ katvā pucchissāmā”ti saṅkhataṃ padapañhaṃ pucchantīti dassetuṃ “dupadampī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vadanti etenāti vādo, doso. Pucchīyatīti pañho, attho. Pucchati etenāti pañho, saddo. Tadubhayaṃ ekato gahetvā āha “evarūpe pañhe”tiādi. “Evaṃ puccheyya, evaṃ vissajjeyyā”ti [V 2.0137] ca pucchāvissajjanānaṃ sikhāvagamanaṃ dasseti. Seyyoti uttamo, paramo lābhoti adhippāyo.

289. Among individuals, skillfulness in wisdom is designated as 'paṇḍita' (wise) on account of the capacity to see subtle meanings; therefore, it is said, 'capable of penetrating subtle distinctions of meaning.' Here, the word 'kata' has the sense of 'accomplished.' 'Parappavāda' is so called because others proclaim by means of it; it means the doctrine of others, another system. 'Parappavāda' also means a proclamation by others, or the crushing of another's view through disputatious talk. Combining both, it is said in the Pāli, 'in understanding the doctrines of others and in familiarity with debate conducted with them,' meaning one is accomplished in others' systems and in crushing others' views. 'Vālavedhirūpeti' (like a hair-splitter) means 'resembling a hair-splitter.' Therefore, it is said, 'like an archer who splits hairs.' 'Vāla' refers to a hair, specifically a filament of a hair that has been split in many ways. 'As if splitting' means like one splitting a pot or similar physical object with a hammer; the intention is 'decisively splitting wrong views.' To show that they ask a contrived verbal question, thinking, 'Having concealed the meaning and made it hidden, we will ask,' it is said, 'even a two-word question,' and so on. That by which one speaks is a 'vāda' (assertion); this means a fault (dosa). That which is asked is a 'pañha' (question); this means the meaning. That by which one asks is a 'pañha' (question); this means the word. Taking both together, it is said, 'in such questions,' and so on. 'One should ask thus, one should reply thus'—this shows the pinnacle of understanding of questioning and answering. 'Seyyo' means 'supreme,' the highest gain; this is the intention.

Evaṃ attano vādavidhamanabhayenapi pare bhagavantaṃ pañhaṃ pucchituṃ na visahantīti vatvā idāni vādavidhamanena vināpi na visahanti evāti dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi āraddhaṃ.
