Cittaṃ pasīdati pare attano attabhāvampi vissatthaṃ niyyādetukāmā honti odhisakamettāpharaṇasadisattā tassa mettāyanassa. Dassanasampannāti daṭṭhabbatāya sampannā dassanānuttariyabhāvato, ativiya dassanīyāti attho.

Thus, having stated that others are unable to question the Blessed One even out of fear of the destruction of their own arguments, now, to show that they are unable even without the destruction of their arguments, the passage beginning with 'apicā' (moreover) is introduced. Their minds become serene, and others, being trustful, are willing to offer up even their own being, because his loving-kindness is like the pervasion of boundless loving-kindness. 'Dassanasampanna' (endowed with vision) means 'perfected in being worthy of seeing' because of the unsurpassed nature of his vision; the meaning is that he is exceedingly lovely to behold.

Saraṇagamanavasena [M 2.0146] sāvakāti lokiyasaraṇagamanena sāvakā, lokuttarasaraṇagamanena pana sāvakattaṃ parato āgamissati, tañca pabbajitavasena vuccati, idha gahaṭṭhavasena, ubhayatthāpi saraṇagamanena sāvakattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Te hi paralokavajjabhayadassāvino kulaputtā, ācārakulaputtāpi tādisā bhavanti. Thokenāti iminā “manaṃ anassāmā”ti padassatthaṃ vadati.

By way of going for refuge, they are disciples. They are disciples through worldly going for refuge, but discipleship through supramundane going for refuge will come later. That is said in terms of the ordained life, but here, in terms of the householder life. In both cases, discipleship is to be understood by way of going for refuge. For those sons of good family see the danger of what is blameworthy in the other world, and sons of good conduct also become like that. 'Thokena' (by a little) explains the meaning of the phrase 'we will not be disobedient'.

290. Udāharīyati ubbegapītivasenāti, tathā vā udāharaṇaṃ udānaṃ. Tenāha “udāhāraṃ udāharī”ti. Assa dhammassāti assa paṭipattisaddhammapubbakassa paṭivedhasaddhammassa. Soti hatthipadopamo hatthipadopamabhāvena vuccamāno dhammo. Ettāvatāti ettakena paribbājakena vuttakathāmaggamattena. Kāmaṃ tena vuttakathāmaggenapi hatthipadopamabhāvena vuccamāno dhammo paripuṇṇova arahattaṃ pāpetvā paveditattā, so ca kho saṅkhepato, na vitthāratoti āha “na ettāvatā vitthārena paripūro hotī”ti. Yadi yathā vitthārena hatthipadopamo paripūro hoti, tathā desanā āraddhā, atha kasmā kusaloti na vuttoti codanā.

290. It is uttered on account of uplifting joy; or, similarly, an utterance is an 'udāna' (inspired utterance). Therefore, it is said, 'udāhāraṃ udāharī' (he uttered an inspired utterance). 'Of this Dhamma' means of this good Dhamma of penetration which is preceded by the good Dhamma of practice. 'That' refers to the Dhamma spoken of as the simile of the elephant's footprint. 'Thus far' means merely by that path of discourse spoken by the wanderer. Although the Dhamma spoken of as the simile of the elephant's footprint is indeed complete even with that path of discourse—since it was proclaimed in a way that leads to arahantship—yet that is in brief, not in detail. Therefore, it is said, 'it is not fully complete in detail with just this.' The objection is: if the teaching was begun in detail, just as the simile of the elephant's footprint is complete in detail, then why was 'kusalo' (skillful) not said?

291. Āyāmatopīti pi-saddena ubbedhenapi rassāti dasseti. Nīcakāyā hi tā honti. Uccāti uccakā. Nisevanaṃ, nisevati etthāti vā nisevitaṃ. Nisevanañcettha kaṇḍuyitavinodanatthaṃ ghaṃsanaṃ. Tenāha “khandhappadese ghaṃsitaṭṭhāna”nti. Uccāti anīcā, ubbedhavantiyoti attho. Kāḷārikāti viraḷadantā, visaṅgatadantāti attho. Tenāha “dantāna”ntiādi. Kaḷāratāyāti viraḷatāya. Ārañjitānīti rañjitāni, vilikhitānīti attho. Kaṇerutāyāti kuṭumalasaṇṭhānatāya. Ayaṃ vāti ettha vā-saddo saṃsayitanicchayattho yathā aññatthāpi “ayaṃ vā imesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sabbabālo sabbamūḷho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.181).

291. 'Āyāmatopi' (even in length)—the particle 'pi' indicates that they are short even in height. For they are of low stature. 'Uccā' means tall. 'Nisevanaṃ' is a place of resort, or that wherein one resorts. Here, 'nisevana' means rubbing for the purpose of relieving an itch. Therefore, it is said, 'a place rubbed on the shoulder region.' 'Uccā' means 'not low,' that is, 'possessing height.' 'Kāḷārikā' means 'having sparse teeth,' that is, 'having disconnected teeth.' Therefore, it is said, 'of the teeth,' and so on. 'Kaḷāratāya' means 'due to sparseness.' 'Ārañjitāni' means 'colored,' that is, 'scratched.' 'Kaṇerutāya' means 'due to having a bud-like shape.' 'Ayaṃ vā'—here, the word 'vā' has the sense of making a determination about something that was in doubt, just as elsewhere, such as in 'This one, indeed, among these ascetics and brahmins, is the most foolish, the most stupid...' (Dī. Ni. 1.181).

Nāgavanaṃ [V 2.0138] viyāti mahāhatthino vāmanikādīnañca padadassanaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ nāgavanaṃ viya. Ādito paṭṭhāya yāva nīvaraṇappahānā dhammadesanā tathāgatassa [M 2.0147] bāhiraparibbājakādīnañca padadassanabhāvato. Ādito paṭṭhāyāti ca “taṃ suṇāhī”ti padato paṭṭhāya. Kusalo nāgavaniko viya yogāvacaro pariyesanavasena pamāṇaggahaṇato. Matthake ṭhatvāti imassa suttassa pariyosāne ṭhatvā. Imasmimpi ṭhāneti “evameva kho brāhmaṇā”tiādinā upameyyassa atthassa upaññāsanaṭṭhānepi.

'Nāgavanaṃ viya' (like an elephant forest) means 'like an elephant forest which is a place for seeing the footprints of great elephants and of female elephants such as the Vāmanikā. From the beginning up to the abandonment of the hindrances, the Tathāgata's teaching of the Dhamma is so because it is a place for seeing the footprints of outside wanderers and others. 'From the beginning' means starting from the word 'taṃ suṇāhī' (listen to this). 'Like a skilled elephant-tracker' refers to the meditator, on account of taking the measure by way of investigation. 'Standing at the head' means standing at the conclusion of this discourse. 'In this place too' means even in the place where the meaning of the object of comparison is presented, with the words 'evameva kho, brāhmaṇa' (just so, brahmin), and so on.

Svāyanti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.190) idha-saddamattaṃ gaṇhāti, na yathāvisesitabbaṃ idha-saddaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati “katthaci padapūraṇamattamevā”ti. Lokaṃ upādāya vuccati loka-saddena samānādhikaraṇabhāvena vuttattā. Sesapadadvaye pana saddantarasannidhānamattena taṃ taṃ upādāya vuttatā daṭṭhabbā. Okāsanti kañci padesaṃ indasālaguhāya adhippetattā. Padapūraṇamattameva okāsāpadisanassapi asambhavato.

'Svāyaṃ' (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.190) takes merely the word 'idha', not the word 'idha' as something to be qualified. For it will be said, 'Sometimes it is merely an expletive.' It is said 'with reference to the world' because it is spoken in apposition with the word 'loka'. However, in the case of the remaining two phrases, it should be understood that they are spoken with reference to this or that simply due to their proximity to another word. 'Okāsa' means a certain place, because the Indasāla Cave is intended. For it is impossible for even the designation of a place to be a mere expletive.

Tathāgata-saddādīnaṃ atthaviseso mūlapariyāyaṭṭhakathā(ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.12) visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāsu vutto eva. Tathāgatassa sattanikāyantogadhatāya “idha pana sattaloko adhippeto”ti vatvā tatthāyaṃ yasmiṃ sattanikāye, yasmiñca okāse uppajjati, taṃ dassetuṃ “sattaloke uppajjamānopi cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha imasmiṃyeva cakkavāḷeti imissā eva lokadhātuyā. “Aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā dve arahanto sammāsambuddho apubbaṃ acarimaṃ uppajjeyyu”nti (dī. ni. 3.161; ma. ni. 3.129; a. ni. 1.278; netti. 57; mi. pa. 5.1.1) ettha jātikhettabhūtā dasasahassilokadhātu “ekissā lokadhātuyā”ti vuttā. Idha pana imaṃyeva lokadhātuṃ sandhāya “imasmiṃyeva cakkavāḷe”ti vuttaṃ. Tisso hi saṅgītiyo āruḷhe tepiṭake buddhavacane visayakhettaṃ āṇākhettaṃ jātikhettanti tividhe khette ṭhapetvā imaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ aññasmiṃ cakkavāḷe buddhā uppajjantīti suttaṃ natthi, na uppajjantīti pana atthi. Kathaṃ? “Na me ācariyo atthi, sadiso me na vijjati (ma. ni. 1.285; 2.341; mahāva. 11; kathā. 405; mi. pa. 4.5.11), ekomhi sammāsambuddho”ti (ma. ni. 1.285; 2.341; kathā. 405; mahāva. 11) evamādīni imissā lokadhātuyā ṭhatvā vadantena bhagavatā – “kiṃ panāvuso, sāriputta, atthetarahi [M 2.0148] añño samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā bhagavatā samasamo sambodhiyanti evaṃ puṭṭhāhaṃ, bhante, noti vadeyya”nti vatvā tassa kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ – “aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso, yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā dve arahanto sammāsambuddhā”ti [V 2.0139] imaṃ suttaṃ dassentena dhammasenāpatinā ca buddhānaṃ uppattiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ imaṃ lokadhātuṃ ṭhapetvā aññattha anuppatti vuttā hotīti.

The distinction in the meaning of terms like 'Tathāgata,' and so on, has been explained in the commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Sutta (Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.12) and in the expositions on the Visuddhimagga. Because the Tathāgata is included within the seven abodes of beings, it is said, 'Here, the world of beings is intended.' To indicate in which abode of beings and in which realm he arises, it is stated, 'even when arising in the world of beings,' and so on. Here, 'in this very world-system' refers to this very universe. 'It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen, that in one world-system two Arahant Fully Enlightened Ones arise simultaneously, neither before nor after the other' (Dī. Ni. 3.161; Ma. Ni. 3.129; A. Ni. 1.278; Netti. 57; Mi. Pa. 5.1.1). Here, the ten-thousandfold world-system, which serves as the place of birth, is referred to as 'one world-system.' In this context, however, it is specifically this world-system that is intended by the phrase 'in this very world-system.' In the Tipiṭaka as established by the three councils, setting aside the three kinds of spheres—the sphere of influence, the sphere of authority, and the sphere of birth—there is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise in another world-system apart from this world-system, while there is a sutta stating they do not arise. How so? The Blessed One, while dwelling in this very world-system, made statements such as: 'I have no teacher; none equal to me exists (Ma. Ni. 1.285; 2.341; Mahāva. 11; Kathā. 405; Mi. Pa. 4.5.11). I am the sole Fully Enlightened One' (Ma. Ni. 1.285; 2.341; Kathā. 405; Mahāva. 11). And the General of the Dhamma, to show the reason why he would reply, 'No, venerable sir,' if asked, 'But, friend Sāriputta, is there now another ascetic or brahmin equal to the Blessed One in supreme enlightenment?', cited the sutta: 'It is impossible, it cannot happen, that in one world-system two Arahant Fully Enlightened Ones arise.' By these means, it is stated that, apart from this world-system, which is the place of the Buddhas' arising, they do not arise elsewhere.

Sujātāyātiādinā vuttesu catūsu vikappesu paṭhamo vikappo buddhabhāvāya āsannatarapaṭipattidassanavasena vutto. Āsannatarāya hi paṭipattiyaṃ ṭhito “uppajjatī”ti vuccati uppādassa ekantikattā, pageva paṭipattiyā matthake ṭhito. Dutiyo buddhabhāvāvahapabbajjato paṭṭhāya āsannapaṭipattidassanavasena, tatiyo buddhakaradhammapāripūrito paṭṭhāya buddhabhāvāya paṭipattidassanavasena. Na hi mahāsattānaṃ tusitabhavūpapattito paṭṭhāya bodhisambhārasambharaṇaṃ nāma atthi. Catuttho buddhakaradhammasamārambhato paṭṭhāya. Bodhiyā niyatabhāvāpattito pabhuti hi viññūhi “buddho uppajjatī”ti vattuṃ sakkā uppādassa ekantikattā, yathā pana “tiṭṭhanti pabbatā, sandanti nadiyo”ti tiṭṭhanasandanakiriyānaṃ avicchedamupādāya vattamānapayogo, evaṃ uppādatthāya paṭipajjanakiriyāya avicchedamupādāya catūsu vikappesu “uppajjati nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbapaṭhamaṃ uppannabhāvanti sabbehi upari vuccamānehi visesehi paṭhamaṃ tathāgatassa uppannatāsaṅkhātaṃ atthitāvisesaṃ.

In the four alternatives mentioned beginning with 'By Sujātā,' the first alternative is stated to show the very near path to Buddhahood. For one established on a very near path, it is said, 'he arises,' because of the certainty of his arising—how much more so for one at the summit of the path. The second alternative shows the near path starting from the going forth that leads to Buddhahood. The third alternative shows the path to Buddhahood starting from the fulfillment of the qualities that make a Buddha. Indeed, for great beings, there is no accumulation of the requisites of enlightenment starting from their rebirth in the Tusita realm. The fourth alternative starts from the undertaking of the qualities that make a Buddha. From the attainment of a state fixed for enlightenment onward, it is possible for the wise to say, 'a Buddha arises,' because of the certainty of his arising. Just as the present tense is used with reference to the uninterrupted actions of 'mountains stand' and 'rivers flow,' so too, with reference to the uninterrupted action of proceeding toward arising, in these four alternatives it is said, 'he is said to arise.' 'The state of having arisen first of all' means the special state of existence reckoned as the Tathāgata's having arisen, which is first before all the distinctions to be mentioned hereafter.

So bhagavāti (a. ni. ṭī. 2.3.64) yo “tathāgato araha”ntiādinā kittitaguṇo, so bhagavā. Imaṃ lokanti nayidaṃ mahājanassa sammukhāmattaṃ lokaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, atha kho anavasesaṃ pariyādāyāti dassetuṃ “sadevaka”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tenāha “idāni vattabbaṃ nidassetī”ti. Pajātattāti yathāsakaṃ kammakilesehi nibbattattā. Pañcakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ pārisesañāyena itaresaṃ padantarehi saṅgahitattā. Sadevakanti ca avayavena viggaho samudāyo samāsattho. Chaṭṭhakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ paccāsattiñāyena. Tattha hi so jāto tannivāsī ca. Brahmakāyikādibrahmaggahaṇanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Paccatthikapaccāmittasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇanti [M 2.0149] nidassanamattametaṃ apaccatthikānaṃ asamitābāhitapāpānañca samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sassamaṇabrāhmaṇivacanena gahitattā. Kāmaṃ “sadevaka”ntiādivisesanānaṃ vasena sattavisayo loka-saddoti viññāyati tulyayogavisayattā tesaṃ, “salomako sapakkhako”tiādīsu pana atulyayogepi ayaṃ samāso labbhatīti byabhicāradassanato pajāgahaṇanti āha “pajāvacanena sattalokaggahaṇa”nti.

'That Blessed One' (A. Ni. Ṭī. 2.3.64) means: he whose qualities are praised with such words as 'the Tathāgata, the Arahant,' he is the Blessed One. 'This world' is not said referring merely to the world in the presence of the multitude; rather, to show that it encompasses it without remainder, 'with its devas,' etc., is said. Therefore he says: 'Now what is to be said is shown.' 'Because it is a generation' means because it is generated by one's own kamma and defilements. The inclusion of the five sense-sphere devas is by the principle of what is left over, as the others are included by the other terms. The compound 'with its devas' is analyzed by its parts, but its meaning is a collective. The inclusion of the sixth sense-sphere deva is by the principle of proximity, for he was born there and is a resident there. This same method applies to the inclusion of the brahmās, such as the Brahmakāyika devas. The inclusion of hostile and inimical ascetics and brahmins is merely an illustration, for non-hostile ascetics and brahmins whose evil is not allayed and warded off are also included by the expression 'with its ascetics and brahmins.' Although it is understood that the word 'loka' refers to the world of beings on account of such qualifiers as 'with its devas'—because their connection is of the same kind—since in cases like 'with its fur and feathers' this compound is found even when the connection is not of the same kind, a deviation is seen. Therefore, he says 'the inclusion of "pajā"' and states: 'by the word "pajā" the world of beings is included.'

Arūpino [V 2.0140] sattā attano āneñjavihārena viharantā “dibbantīti devā”ti imaṃ nibbacanaṃ labhantīti āha “sadevakaggahaṇena arūpāvacaradevaloko gahito”ti. Tenevāha “ākāsānañcāyatanūpagānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyata”nti (a. ni. 3.117). Samārakaggahaṇena chakāmāvacaradevaloko gahito tassa savisesaṃ mārassa vase vattanato. Rūpī brahmaloko gahito arūpībrahmalokassa visuṃ gahitattā. Catuparisavasenāti khattiyādicatuparisavasena. Itarā pana catasso parisā samārakādiggahaṇena gahitā evāti. Avasesasabbasattaloko nāgagaruḷādibhedo.

The formless beings, dwelling in their own imperturbable abodes, obtain the etymology 'they are devas because they sport,' hence it is said: 'By the inclusion of "with its devas," the formless-sphere deva world is included.' For that reason it is said: 'for companionship with the devas who have reached the base of infinite space' (AN 3.117). By the inclusion of 'with Māra,' the six sense-sphere deva worlds are included, because they exist especially under Māra's control. The form-sphere brahmā world is included, because the formless brahmā world is included separately. 'By way of the four assemblies' means by way of the four assemblies beginning with the nobles. But the other four assemblies are included by the inclusion of 'with Māra,' and so on. The remaining world of all beings is of various kinds, such as nāgas and garuḷas.

Ettāvatā bhāgaso lokaṃ gahetvā yojanaṃ dassetvā idāni tena tena visesena abhāgasova lokaṃ gahetvā yojanaṃ dassetuṃ “apicetthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ukkaṭṭhaparicchedatoti ukkaṃsagabhivijānanena. Pañcasu hi gatīsu devalokova seṭṭho. Tatthāpi arūpino “dūrasamussāritakilesadukkhatāya, santapaṇītaāneñjavihārasamaṅgitāya, ativiya dīghāyukatāyā”ti evamādīhi visesehi ativiya itarehi ukkaṭṭhā. Brahmā mahānubhāvotiādiṃ dasasahassiyaṃ mahābrahmuno vasena vadati. “Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedato”ti hi vuttaṃ. Anuttaranti seṭṭhaṃ navalokuttaraṃ. Bhāvānukkamo bhāvavasena paresaṃ ajjhāsayavasena “sadevaka”ntiādīnaṃ padānaṃ anukkamo. Tīhākārehīti devamārabrahmasahitatāsaṅkhātehi tīhi pakārehi. Tīsu padesūti “sadevaka”ntiādīsu tīsu padesu. Tena tenākārenāti sadevakattādinā tena tena pakārena. Tedhātukameva pariyādinnanti porāṇā panāhūti yojanā.

Having thus taken the world by parts and shown the connection, now, to take the world without division by its specific features and show the connection, the passage beginning 'Moreover, here' is stated. Herein, 'by the distinction of superiority' means by the ascertainment of excellence. For among the five destinations, the deva world is the best. Even there, the formless beings are extremely superior to the others because of such special features as their having kept defilements and suffering far away, their being endowed with a peaceful, sublime, and imperturbable dwelling, and their having an extremely long lifespan. He speaks of 'Brahmā of great power,' etc., with reference to the Mahābrahmā of the ten-thousand-fold world system, for it is said, 'by the distinction of superiority.' 'Unsurpassed' means the best, that is, the nine supramundane states. The sequence of states is the sequence of the terms 'with its devas,' etc., according to the state and according to the disposition of others. 'By three modes' means by the three ways reckoned as being together with devas, Māra, and Brahmā. 'In three terms' means in the three terms 'with its devas,' etc. 'By each mode' means by each characteristic, such as being with the devas. The ancients, however, say: 'The three realms alone are encompassed'—this is the connection.

Abhiññāti [M 2.0150] ya-kāralopenāyaṃ niddeso, abhijānitvāti ayamettha atthoti āha “abhiññāya, adhikena ñāṇena ñatvā”ti. Anumānādipaṭikkhepoti anumānaupamānaatthāpattiādipaṭikkhepo ekappamāṇattā. Sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇācāratāya hi sabbapaccakkhā buddhā bhagavanto. Anuttaraṃ vivekasukhanti phalasamāpattisukhaṃ. Tena vītimissāpi kadāci bhagavato dhammadesanā hotīti āha “hitvāpī”ti. Bhagavā hi dhammaṃ desento yasmiṃ khaṇe parisā sādhukāraṃ vā deti, yathāsutaṃ vā dhammaṃ paccavekkhati, taṃ khaṇaṃ pubbabhāgena paricchinditvā phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, yathāparicchedañca samāpattito vuṭṭhāya ṭhitaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya dhammaṃ deseti.

'By direct knowledge' (abhiññā) is a directive with the elision of the letter 'y'; 'having directly known' (abhijānitvā) is the meaning here, hence it is said: 'by direct knowledge, having known with superior knowledge.' 'The rejection of inference, etc.' means the rejection of inference, comparison, presumption, and the like, because for them there is only one means of proof. For the Blessed Ones, the Buddhas, have unobstructed knowledge and conduct in all things, as they directly perceive everything. 'The unsurpassed bliss of seclusion' is the bliss of the attainment of fruition. Therefore the Blessed One's teaching of the Dhamma is sometimes interspersed with this, hence it is said, 'even having left it.' For when the Blessed One is teaching the Dhamma, at a moment when the assembly expresses its approval or reflects on the Dhamma as heard, he delimits that moment with the preliminary part, enters the attainment of fruition, and having emerged from the attainment according to the delimitation, he teaches the Dhamma starting from the point where he had stopped.

Desakāyattena āṇādividhinā atisajjanaṃ pabodhanaṃ desanāti sā pariyattidhammavasena veditabbāti āha “desanāya tāva catuppadikāyapi gāthāyā”tiādi. Sāsitabbapuggalagatena yathāparādhādisāsitabbabhāvena [V 2.0141] anusāsanaṃ tadaṅgavinayādivasena vinayanaṃ sāsananti taṃ paṭipattidhammavasena veditabbanti āha “sīlasamādhivipassanā”tiādi. Kusalānanti maggakusalānaṃ, kusalānanti vā anavajjānaṃ. Tena phaladhammānampi saṅgaho siddho hoti. Ādibhāvo sīladiṭṭhīnaṃ tammūlakattā uttarimanussadhammānaṃ. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ atthe kathāvadhisaddappabandho gāthāvasena suttavasena ca vavatthito pariyattidhammo, yo idheva “desanā”ti vutto. Tassa pana attho visesena sīlādi evāti āha “bhagavā hi dhammaṃ desento…pe… nibbānaṃ dassetī”ti. Tattha sīlaṃ dassetvāti sīlaggahaṇena sasambhāraṃ sīlaṃ gahitaṃ. Tathā maggaggahaṇena sasambhāro maggoti tadubhayena anavasesato pariyattiatthaṃ pariyādiyati. Tenāti sīlādidassanena. Atthavasena hi idha desanāya ādikalyāṇādibhāvo adhippeto. Kathikasaṇṭhitīti kathikassa saṇṭhānaṃ kathanavasena samavaṭṭhānaṃ.

Instruction and awakening by way of command, etc., dependent on the teacher, is 'teaching' (desanā). It should be understood as the Dhamma of learning (pariyatti), hence it is said: 'By teaching, first, even a four-lined verse,' etc. Admonition and discipline—by way of momentary discipline, etc.—related to the person to be instructed according to his faults and other things to be instructed about, is 'instruction' (sāsana). It should be understood as the Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti), hence it is said: 'virtue, concentration, and insight,' etc. 'Of wholesome states' means of the wholesome states of the path, or 'wholesome' means blameless. By this, the inclusion of resultant states (phaladhammā) is established. The 'beginning' consists of virtue and view, because the higher human qualities are rooted in them. The composition of words in the form of verses and suttas concerning this or that subject matter is the established Dhamma of learning, which is here called 'teaching.' But its meaning is specifically virtue, etc., hence it is said: 'For the Blessed One, when teaching the Dhamma ... he shows Nibbāna.' Therein, 'having shown virtue' means that by the inclusion of virtue, virtue with its requisites is included. Similarly, by the inclusion of the path, the path with its requisites is included. By both, the meaning of the Dhamma of learning is encompassed without remainder. 'By this' means by showing virtue, etc. For here, the quality of being good in the beginning, etc., of the teaching is intended in terms of its meaning. 'The speaker's arrangement' means the speaker's disposition, his stance by way of speaking.

Na so sātthaṃ deseti niyyānatthavirahato tassā desanāya. Ekabyañjanādiyuttā vāti sithilādibhedesu byañjanesu ekappakāreneva, dvippakāreneva vā byañjanena yuttā vā damiḷabhāsā viya. Sabbattha niroṭṭhaṃ katvā vattabbatāya sabbaniroṭṭhabyañjanā vā kirātabhāsā viya. Sabbattheva vissajjanīyayuttatāya [M 2.0151] sabbavissaṭṭhabyañjanā vā yavanabhāsā viya. Sabbattheva sānusāratāya sabbaniggahitabyañjanā vā pārasikādimilakkhabhāsā viya. Sabbāpesā ekadesabyañjanavaseneva pavattiyā aparipuṇṇabyañjanāti katvā “abyañjanā”ti vuttā. Amakkhetvāti apalicchetvā avināsetvā, ahāpetvāti vā attho.

He does not teach what is meaningful, because his teaching is devoid of the meaning of release. Or it is connected with a single consonant, etc., meaning that among the consonants with distinctions such as lax, it is connected with consonants of only one type or two types, like the Tamil language. Or, because it must be spoken everywhere without using the lips, it has only non-labial consonants, like the Kirāta language. Or, because it is everywhere connected with the visarga, it has only consonants with visarga, like the Yavana language. Or, because it is everywhere with the anusvāra, it has only consonants with the niggahīta, like the language of the Persians and other barbarians. All these are called 'without clear phrasing' (abyañjanā) on the grounds that they are incomplete in phrasing, proceeding by way of only a portion of the phrasing. 'Without smearing' (amakkhetvā) means without cutting off, without destroying, or the meaning is 'without omitting'.

Bhagavā yamatthaṃ ñāpetuṃ ekagāthampi ekavākyampi deseti, tamatthaṃ tāya desanāya sabbaso paripuṇṇameva katvā deseti, evaṃ sabbatthāti āha “ekadesanāpi aparipuṇṇā natthī”ti. Ullumpanasabhāvasaṇṭhitenāti saṃkilesapakkhato vaṭṭadukkhato ca uddharaṇasabhāvāvaṭṭhitena cittena. Tasmāti yasmā sikkhāttayasaṅgahaṃ sakalaṃ sāsanaṃ idha “brahmacariya”nti adhippetaṃ, tasmā. Brahmacariyanti iminā samānādhikaraṇāni sabbapadāni yojetvā atthaṃ dassento “so dhammaṃ deseti…pe… pakāsetīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo”ti āha.

The Blessed One, in order to make known a meaning, teaches even a single verse or a single sentence; and having made that meaning entirely complete through that teaching, he teaches it. Thus, in every way, it is said: “Not even a single teaching is incomplete.” “Established in the nature of uplifting” means with a mind established in the nature of lifting one up from the side of defilements and from the round of suffering. “Therefore”—because here the entire Dispensation, which comprises the threefold training, is intended by “the holy life,” therefore. “The holy life”—by connecting all the words in apposition with this and showing the meaning, he says: “He teaches the Dhamma… he clarifies it—thus the meaning here should be understood.”

Dūrasamussāritamānasseva sāsane sammāpaṭipatti sambhavati, na māna jātikassāti āha “nihatamānattā”ti. Ussannattāti bahulabhāvato. Bhogārogyādivatthukā madā suppaheyyā honti nimittassa anavaṭṭhānato’ na tathā kulavijjāmadāti khattiyabrāhmaṇakulīnānaṃ pabbajitānampi jātivijjā nissāya mānajappanaṃ duppajahanti āha “yebhuyyena hi…pe… mānaṃ karontī”ti[V 2.0142]. Vijātitāyāti nihīnajātitāya. Patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkontīti suvisuddhiṃ katvā sīlaṃ rakkhituṃ na sakkonti. Sīlavasena hi sāsane patiṭṭhāti. Patiṭṭhātunti vā saccapaṭivedhena lokuttarāya patiṭṭhāya patiṭṭhātuṃ. Yebhuyyena hi upanissayasampannā sujātā eva honti, na dujjātā.

“Right practice in the Dispensation is possible only for one whose conceit has been far removed, not for one who is conceited by nature,” thus it is said, “because of having destroyed conceit.” “Because of abundance” means because of prevalence. The intoxications of pride based on such things as wealth and health are easy to abandon because their basis is unstable, but not so the intoxication with clan and knowledge. Even for those gone forth from noble warrior and brahmin families, the conceited talk based on birth and knowledge is difficult to abandon. Thus it is said: “for the most part… they are conceited.” “Because of being of a different birth” means because of being of inferior birth. “They are unable to establish themselves” means they are unable to protect their virtue after having made it perfectly pure. For it is by means of virtue that one is established in the Dispensation. Or, “to establish themselves” means to be established with the supramundane establishment through the penetration of the truths. For the most part, those endowed with a supporting condition are well-born, not ill-born.

Parisuddhanti rāgādīnaṃ accantameva pahānadīpanato nirupakkilesatāya sabbaso visuddhaṃ. Saddhaṃ paṭilabhatīti pothujjanikasaddhāvasena saddahati. Viññujātikānañhi dhammasampattigahaṇapubbikā saddhāsiddhi dhammapamāṇadhammappasannabhāvato. Jāyampatikā vasantīti kāmaṃ “jāyampatikā”ti vutte gharasāmikagharasāminivasena dvinnaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ viññāyati. Yassa pana [M 2.0152] purisassa anekā pajāpatiyo honti, tattha kiṃ vattabbaṃ? Ekāyapi tāya vāso sambādhoti dassanatthaṃ “dve”ti vuttaṃ. Rāgādinā sakiñcanaṭṭhena, khettavatthuādinā sapalibodhaṭṭhena. Rāgarajādīnaṃ āgamanapathatāpi uppajjanaṭṭhānatā evāti dvepi vaṇṇanā ekatthā, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Alagganaṭṭhenāti asajjanaṭṭhena appaṭibaddhabhāvena. Evaṃ akusalakusalappavattīnaṃ ṭhānabhāvena gharāvāsapabbajjānaṃ sambādhabbhokāsataṃ dassetvā idāni kusalappavattiyā eva aṭṭhānaṭhānabhāvena tesaṃ taṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

“Perfectly pure”: because it shows the utter abandonment of lust and so on, it is entirely pure through its freedom from defilements. “He acquires faith”: this means he has faith in the manner of a worldling’s faith. For those of a wise nature, the accomplishment of faith is preceded by the grasping of the Dhamma-asset, because they take the Dhamma as their standard and are pleased with the Dhamma. “A couple living together”: although “a couple” is stated, it is understood that two people are taken, the master and mistress of the house. But what is to be said when a man has many wives? To show that living even with one is cramped, “two” is mentioned. Because of lust and so on, it is “with impediments”; because of fields, property, and so on, it is “with obstacles.” The state of being a path for the approach of the dust of lust and so on is just the state of being a place for their arising; thus both explanations have one meaning, only the phrasing is different. “By way of not clinging” means by way of not attaching, by the state of not being bound. Having thus shown the cramped nature of the household life and the open nature of the homeless life by way of their being a basis for the occurrence of unwholesome and wholesome states, now, to show this for them by way of being an unsuitable and a suitable basis for the occurrence of wholesome states alone, “furthermore,” etc., is said.

Saṅkhepakathāti visuṃ visuṃ paduddhāraṃ akatvā saṅkhepato atthavaṇṇanā. Ekampi divasanti ekadivasamattampi. Akhaṇḍaṃ katvāti dukkaṭamattassapi anāpajjanena akhaṇḍitaṃ katvā. Kilesamalena amalīnanti taṇhāsaṃkilesādivasena asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ katvā. Paridahitvāti nivāsetvā ceva pārupitvā ca. Agāravāso agāraṃ uttarapadalopena, tassa vaḍḍhiāvahaṃ agārassa hitaṃ. Bhogakkhandhoti bhogarāsi bhogasamudāyo. Ābandhanaṭṭhenāti “putto nattā”tiādinā pemavasena saparicchedaṃ sambandhanaṭṭhena. “Amhākamete”ti ñāyantīti ñātī. Pitāmahapituputtādivasena parivattanaṭṭhena parivaṭṭo.

“A brief explanation”: an explanation of the meaning in brief, without extracting each word separately. “Even for a single day”: even for the measure of a single day. “Having made it unbroken”: having made it unbroken by not committing even an offense of wrong-doing. “Unsoiled by the stain of defilement”: having made it undefiled by way of craving, defilements, and so on. “Having put on”: having worn the lower robe and draped the upper robe. “A house” (agāra) is from “household life” (agāravāsa) by elision of the final word; it brings increase to the house (agārassa vaḍḍhiāvahaṃ), it is for the welfare of the house (agārassa hitaṃ). “A mass of wealth”: a heap of wealth, an accumulation of wealth. “In the sense of binding”: in the sense of connecting with delimitation by way of affection, as in “son,” “grandson,” etc. “Relatives” (ñāti): they are known (ñāyanti) as “these are ours.” “Retinue” (parivaṭṭo): in the sense of revolving (parivattana) by way of grandfather, father, son, and so on.

292. Sāmaññavācīpi sikkhā-saddo sājīva-saddasannidhānato upari vuccamānavisesāpekkhāya ca visesaniviṭṭhova hotīti vuttaṃ “yā bhikkhūnaṃ adhisīlasaṅkhātā sikkhā”ti. Sikkhitabbaṭṭhena sikkhā. Saha ājīvanti etthāti sājīvo. Sikkhanabhāvenāti sikkhāya sājīve ca sikkhanabhāvena. Sikkhaṃ paripūrentoti sīlasaṃvaraṃ paripūrento. Sājīvañca avītikkamantoti – “nāmakāyo padakāyo niruttikāyo byañjanakāyo”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 39) vuttasikkhāpadaṃ bhagavato vacanaṃ avītikkamanto hutvāti attho. Idameva [V 2.0143] ca dvayaṃ “sikkhana”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha sājīvānatikkamo sikkhāpāripūriyā paccayo. Tato hi yāva maggā sikkhāpāripūrī hotīti.

292. Although the word “training” (sikkhā) has a general meaning, because of its proximity to the word “livelihood” (sājīva) and with respect to the special qualities mentioned further on, it is established in a specific sense. Thus it is said: “the training for bhikkhus designated as the higher virtue.” “Training” (sikkhā) is so called in the sense that it should be trained in (sikkhitabba). “With which one lives” (saha ājīvanti) is “livelihood” (sājīva). “By the nature of training”: by the nature of training in the training and in the livelihood. “Fulfilling the training”: fulfilling the restraint of virtue. “And not transgressing the livelihood”: this means not transgressing the word of the Blessed One, the training rule spoken of as “the collection of nouns, the collection of verbs, the collection of expressions, the collection of letters.” This very pair is called “the training.” Therein, not transgressing the livelihood is a condition for the fulfillment of the training. For from that, the fulfillment of the training proceeds up to the path.

Pajahitvāti samādānavasena pariccajitvā. Pahīnakālato paṭṭhāya…pe… viratovāti etena pahānassa viratiyā ca samānakālataṃ dasseti[M 2.0153]. Yadi evaṃ “pahāyā”ti kathaṃ purimakālaniddesoti? Tathā gahetabbataṃ upādāya. Dhammānañhi paccayapaccayuppannabhāve apekkhite sahajātānampi paccayapaccayuppannabhāvena gahaṇaṃ purimapacchimabhāveneva hotīti gahaṇapavattiākāravasena paccayabhūtesu hirottappañāṇādīsu pahānakiriyāya purimakālavohāro, paccayuppannāsu ca viratīsu viramaṇakiriyāya aparakālavohāro ca hotīti “pahāya paṭivirato hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Pahāyāti vā samādānakālavasena vuttaṃ, pacchā vītikkamitabbavatthusamāyogavasena paṭiviratoti. Pahāyāti vā –

“Having abandoned” means having relinquished by way of undertaking. “From the time of abandoning onwards… he abstains”—this indicates the simultaneity of abandonment and abstention. If so, how is “having abandoned” a designation of prior time? On account of its having to be understood in that way. For when the condition-and-conditionally-arisen nature of phenomena is considered, even co-arisen phenomena are apprehended as prior and subsequent. This is due to the mode of the process of apprehension: with respect to the conditions, such as shame, fear of wrongdoing, and wisdom, the act of abandoning is spoken of as prior in time; and with respect to the abstentions, which are conditionally arisen, the act of abstaining is spoken of as subsequent in time. Hence it is said, “having abandoned, he abstains.” Alternatively, “having abandoned” is said with reference to the time of undertaking, and afterwards “he abstains” with reference to the encountering of a transgressive object. Or, “having abandoned”:

“Nihantvāna tamokhandhaṃ, uditoyaṃ divākaro;

Vaṇṇapabhāya bhāseti, obhāsetvā samuggato”ti ca. (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 2.578) –

“Having struck down the mass of darkness, this sun has risen; it shines with color and radiance, having illuminated as it ascended.”

Evamādīsu viya samānakālavasena veditabbo. Atha vā pāṇo atipātīyati etenāti pāṇātipāto, pāṇaghātahetubhūto ahirikānottappadosamohavihiṃ sādiko cetanāpadhāno saṃkilesadhammo, taṃ samādānavasena pahāya. Tato…pe… viratova hotīti avadhāraṇena tassā viratiyā kālādivasena apariyantataṃ dasseti. Yathā hi aññe samādinnaviratikāpi anavaṭṭhitacittatāya lābhajīvikādihetu samādānaṃ bhindanteva, na evamayaṃ. Ayaṃ pana pahīnakālato paṭṭhāya orato viratoti. Adinnādānaṃ pahāyātiādīsupi iminā nayena attho veditabbo.

It should be understood as referring to the same time, as in these and other examples. Or else: “destruction of life” (pāṇātipāta) is so called because life (pāṇa) is destroyed (atipātīyati) by it; it is a defiled state that is the cause of killing life, is characterized by lack of shame, lack of fear of wrongdoing, hatred, delusion, and violence, and has volition as its chief component. This one abandons by way of undertaking. Then… “he abstains”—by this emphasis it shows the unlimitedness of that abstinence in terms of time and so on. For while others who have undertaken abstinence might break their undertaking because of instability of mind for the sake of gain, livelihood, and so on, this is not so for this one. This one, rather, abstains continuously from the time of abandonment onwards. The meaning of “having abandoned taking what is not given,” and so on, should be understood in the same way.

Daṇḍanaṃ daṇḍanipātanaṃ daṇḍo. Muggarādipaharaṇavisesopi idha paharaṇavisesoti adhippeto. Tenāha “ṭhapetvā daṇḍaṃ sabbampi avasesaṃ upakaraṇa”nti. Daṇḍanasaṅkhātassa paraviheṭhanassa parivajjitabhāvadīpanatthaṃ daṇḍasatthānaṃ nikkhepavacananti āha “parūpaghātatthāyā”tiādi. Vihiṃsanabhāvatoti vibādhanabhāvato. Lajjīti ettha vuttalajjāya ottappampi vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi pāpajigucchanapāputtāsarahitaṃ, pāpabhayaṃ vā alajjanaṃ atthi. Yassa vā dhammagarutāya dhammassa ca attādhīnattā attādhipatibhūtā lajjākiccakārī, tassa [V 2.0144] lokādhipatibhūtaṃ ottappaṃ kiccakaranti vattabbameva natthīti “lajjī”icceva vuttaṃ. Dayaṃ mettacittataṃ āpannoti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu [M 2.0154] dayā-saddo “adayāpanno”tiādīsu karuṇāya vattatīti? Saccametaṃ, ayaṃ pana dayā-saddo anurakkhaṇatthaṃ antonītaṃ katvā pavattamāno mettāya ca karuṇāya ca pavattatīti idha mettāya pavattamāno vutto. Mijjati siniyhatīti mettā, sā etassa atthīti mettaṃ, mettaṃ cittaṃ etassa atthīti mettacitto, tassa bhāvo mettacittatā, mettāicceva attho.

“A rod” (daṇḍo) is a striking (daṇḍana), the inflicting of a blow (daṇḍanipātana). A specific kind of weapon such as a club is intended here as a specific kind of striking instrument. Hence it is said: “setting aside the rod, all the remaining equipment.” The words about laying down the rod and weapon are stated to show that one has avoided harming others, which is designated as punishment. Thus it is said: “for the purpose of harming others,” etc. “From the state of harming” means from the state of vexing. “Conscientious” (lajjī): here, when shame (lajjā) is mentioned, it should be understood that moral dread (ottappa) is also mentioned. For there is no moral dread without disgust at evil, nor shame without fear of evil. Or, for one for whom shame, which is dominated by the self, performs its function because of reverence for the Dhamma and because the Dhamma is dependent on oneself, there is no need to state that moral dread, which is dominated by the world, performs its function; thus only “conscientious” is stated. Why is it said, “He is endowed with kindness (dayā), possessed of a mind of loving-kindness (mettacitta)”? Does not the word “kindness” in such phrases as “without kindness” refer to compassion (karuṇā)? That is true. However, this word “kindness,” occurring with the internalized meaning of protection, applies to both loving-kindness and compassion. Here it is said with reference to loving-kindness. “Loving-kindness” (mettā) is so called because one is affectionate (mijjati, siniyhati). He has this, thus he has loving-kindness (mettaṃ); his mind has this, thus he has a mind of loving-kindness (mettacitto); the state of this is loving-mindedness (mettacittatā). The meaning is simply loving-kindness.

Sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampīti etena tassā viratiyā sattavasena apariyantataṃ dasseti. Pāṇabhūteti pāṇajāte. Anukampakoti karuṇāyanako. Yasmā pana mettā karuṇāya visesapaccayo hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “tāya eva dayāpannatāyā”ti. Evaṃ yehi dhammehi pāṇātipātā virati sampajjati, tehi lajjāmettākaruṇādhammehi samaṅgibhāvo dassito, saddhiṃ piṭṭhivaṭṭakadhammehīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etthāha – kasmā “pāṇātipātaṃ pahāyā”ti ekavacananiddeso kato, nanu niravasesānaṃ pāṇānaṃ atipātato virati idhādhippetā? Tathā hi vuttaṃ “sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī viharatī”ti. Teneva hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sabbe pāṇabhūte hitena anukampako”ti puthuvacananiddesoti? Saccametaṃ, pāṇabhāvasāmaññavasena panettha pāḷiyaṃ ādito ekavacananiddeso kato, sabbasaddasannidhānena puthuttaṃ viññāyamānamevāti sāmaññaniddesaṃ akatvā bhedavacanicchāvasena dassetuṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ bahuvacanavasena attho vutto. Kiñca bhiyyo – sāmaññato saṃvarasamādānaṃ, tabbisesato saṃvarabhedoti imassa visesassa dassanatthaṃ ayaṃ vacanabhedo katoti veditabbaṃ. Viharatīti vuttappakāro hutvā ekasmiṃ iriyāpathe uppannaṃ dukkhaṃ aññena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā attabhāvaṃ harati pavattetīti attho. Tenāha “iriyati pāletī”ti.

By 'compassionate for the welfare of all living beings,' he shows the unlimitedness of that abstinence in terms of beings. 'Living beings' means those born as beings. 'Compassionate' means one who acts with compassion. Since loving-kindness is a special condition for compassion, it is therefore said, 'by that very possession of kindness.' Thus, it is shown that he is endowed with the qualities through which abstinence from killing living beings is accomplished—shame, loving-kindness, and compassion—along with their supporting qualities. Here it may be asked: Why is the singular expression 'having abandoned the destruction of life' used? Is not the abstinence from killing all living beings without exception intended here? For it is said, 'he dwells compassionate for the welfare of all living beings.' And for that reason, in the commentary, the explanation is given in the plural: 'compassionate for all living beings with their welfare.' This is true. But in the Pāli text, the singular expression is used from the beginning based on the general characteristic of a 'living being,' while plurality is understood from the proximity of the word 'all.' Thus, without making a general statement, the commentary states the meaning in the plural with the wish to express a distinction. Furthermore, this variation in wording should be understood as made to show this distinction: the undertaking of restraint is general, but the divisions of restraint are particular. 'He dwells' means: having become as described, he cuts off the suffering that has arisen in one posture by means of another posture and maintains his personal existence. Hence, it is said, 'he moves about, he maintains.'

Na kevalaṃ kāyavacīpayogavasena ādānameva, atha kho ākaṅkhapissa pariccattavatthuvisayāvāti dassetuṃ “cittenapī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Theneti theyyaṃ karotīti theno, coro. Sucibhūtenāti ettha sucibhāvo adhikārato saddantarasannidhānato ca theyyasaṃkilesaviramaṇanti āha “athenattāyeva sucibhūtenā”ti. Kāmañcettha “lajjī [M 2.0155] dayāpanno”tiādi na vuttaṃ, adhikāravasena pana atthato vā vuttamevāti veditabbaṃ. Yathā hi lajjādayo pāṇātipātapahānassa visesapaccayo, evaṃ adinnādānapahānassapīti, tasmā sāpi pāḷi ānetvā vattabbā. Esa nayo ito paresupi. Atha vā sucibhūtenāti etena hirottappādīhi [V 2.0145] samannāgamo, ahirikādīnañca pahānaṃ vuttamevāti “lajjī”tiādi na vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

To show that taking occurs not only by way of bodily and verbal action, but that one can desire, even with the mind, an object that has been relinquished by another, it is said 'even by mind,' etc. 'A thief' (thena) is one who commits theft (theyyaṃ); a robber (cora). 'With a self become pure': here purity, on account of the context and the proximity of other words, means abstaining from the defilement of theft. Thus he says: 'by being not a thief, one has a self become pure.' Although 'conscientious, endowed with kindness,' etc., is not stated here, it should be understood as stated in meaning on account of the context. For just as shame and so on are special conditions for abandoning the destruction of life, so too are they for abandoning taking what is not given; therefore that Pāli passage should be brought in and stated. This is the method in the subsequent cases as well. Alternatively, by 'with a self become pure,' the possession of moral shame and fear of wrongdoing and the abandoning of shamelessness and so on are stated; thus 'conscientious,' etc., is not stated.

Aseṭṭhacariyanti aseṭṭhānaṃ cariyaṃ, aseṭṭhaṃ vā cariyaṃ. Mithunānaṃ vuttākārena sadisabhūtānaṃ ayanti mithuno, yathāvutto durācāro. Ārācārī methunāti etena – “idha brāhmaṇa, ekacco…pe… na heva kho mātugāmena saddhiṃ dvayaṃdvayasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, apica kho mātugāmassa ucchādanaparimaddananhāpanasambāhanaṃ sādiyati, so tadassādeti, taṃ nikāmeti, tena ca vittiṃ āpajjatī”tiādinā (a. ni. 7.50) vuttā sattavidhamethunasaṃyogāpi paṭivirati dassitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Ignoble conduct' means the conduct of the ignoble, or ignoble conduct. 'Sexual intercourse' (mithuna) is the 'going' (ayana) of those who have become similar—that is, couples (mithunānaṃ)—in the way described; it is the aforementioned misconduct. That he fares remotely from sexual intercourse is shown by this: 'Here, brahmin, a certain person... does not engage in the twofold act with a woman, but he enjoys being anointed, massaged, bathed, and kneaded by a woman. He savors that, desires that, and attains satisfaction through that.' Thus, it should be understood that abstinence from the seven kinds of sexual union is shown.

Saccena saccanti purimena vacīsaccena pacchimaṃ vacīsaccaṃ sandahati asaccena anantarikattā. Tenāha “yo hī”tiādi. Haliddirāgo viya na thirakato hotīti ettha kathāya anavaṭṭhitabhāvena haliddirāgasadisatā veditabbā, na puggalassa. Pāsāṇalekhā viyāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Saddhā ayati pavattati etthāti saddhāyo, saddhāyo eva saddhāyiko yathā “venayiko”ti (ma. ni. 1.246; a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 8), saddhāya vā ayitabbo saddhāyiko, saddheyyoti attho. Vattabbataṃ āpajjativisaṃvādanatoti adhippāyo.

'Truth to truth' means he connects a later verbal truth with a former verbal truth, as there is no untruth in between. Hence it is said: 'For one who...,' etc. 'Like turmeric dye that is not made fast': here the similarity to turmeric dye should be understood in terms of the instability of the speech, not of the person. 'Like a line on a rock': here too the same method applies. 'One who inspires faith' (saddhāyo): faith (saddhā) goes (ayati) and proceeds (pavattati) in him, thus he is saddhāyo. Saddhāyo is the same as saddhāyiko, as in venayiko (one devoted to the Vinaya). Or, saddhāyiko means one who should be followed with faith (saddhāya), that is, trustworthy (saddheyyo). The intention is that he becomes reliable because he does not deceive.

Anuppadātāti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.9; a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.198) anubalappadātā, anuvattanavasena vā padātā. Kassa pana anuvattanaṃ padānañcāti? “Sahitāna”nti vuttattā sandhānassāti viññāyati. Tenāha “sandhānānuppadātā”ti. Yasmā pana anuvattanavasena sandhānassa padānaṃ ādhānaṃ, rakkhaṇaṃ vā daḷhīkaraṇaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “dve jane samagge disvā”tiādi. Āramanti etthāti ārāmo, ramitabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Yasmā pana ā-kārena vināpi ayamattho labbhati, tasmā vuttaṃ “samaggarāmotipi pāḷi, ayamevettha attho”ti.

'A promoter' (anuppadātā) means one who gives supporting strength, or one who gives by way of following up. But whose following up and giving? Since it is said 'of those who are united,' it is understood to be of concord. Hence he says, 'a promoter of concord.' For the giving to concord by way of following up is a foundation, a protection, or a strengthening. Therefore it is said: 'Having seen two people in concord,' etc. 'A delight' (ārāmo) is where they delight; a place for delighting. Since this meaning is obtained even without the prefix ā-, it is said: 'Samaggarāmo is also a Pāli reading; this is the meaning here.'

Etthāti [M 2.0156] –

Herein—

“Nelaṅgo setapacchādo, ekāro vattatī ratho;

Anīghaṃ passa āyantaṃ, chinnasotaṃ abandhana”nti. (saṃ. ni. 4.347; udā. 65; peṭako. 25;dī. ni. ṭī. 1.9) –

"Stainless, with a white canopy,

The single-spoked chariot rolls on;

See it coming, untroubled,

With stream cut off, unbound."

Imissā [V 2.0146] gāthāya. Sīlañhettha “nelaṅga”nti vuttaṃ. Tenevāha – citto gahapati, “nelaṅganti kho, bhante, sīlānametaṃ adhivacana”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.347; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.9). Sukumārāti apharusatāya mudukā. Purassa esāti ettha pura-saddo tannivāsīvācako daṭṭhabbo “gāmo āgato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.9) viya. Tenevāha “nagaravāsīna”nti. Manaṃ appāyati vaḍḍhetīti manāpā. Tena vuttaṃ “cittavuddhikarā”ti.

Of this verse. Herein, virtue is called 'faultless' (nelaṅga). Therefore Citta the householder said: 'Venerable sir, "faultless" is a designation for the virtues.' 'Delicate' (sukumārā) means soft because of its lack of harshness. Here, in 'of the city' (purassa esā), the word 'city' (pura) should be seen as denoting its inhabitants, as in 'the village has come,' etc. Therefore he says 'of the city-dwellers.' 'Agreeable' (manāpā) means it makes the mind (manaṃ) grow, it increases it. Hence it is said, 'causing the mind to grow.'

Kālavādītiādi samphappalāpāpaṭiviratassa paṭipattidassanaṃ. Atthasaṃhitāpi hi vācā ayuttakālapayogena atthāvahā na siyāti anatthaviññāpanavācaṃ anulometi, tasmā samphappalāpaṃ pajahantena akālavāditā pariharitabbāti vuttaṃ “kālavādī”ti. Kāle vadantenapi ubhayānatthasādhanato abhūtaṃ parivajjetabbanti āha “bhūtavādī”ti. Bhūtañca vadantena yaṃ idhaloka-paraloka-hitasampādakaṃ, tadeva vattabbanti dassetuṃ “atthavādī”ti vuttaṃ. Atthaṃ vadantenapi lokiyadhammasannissitameva avatvā lokuttaradhammasannissitaṃ katvā vattabbanti dassanatthaṃ “dhammavādī”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā ca attho lokuttaradhammasannissito hoti, taṃdassanatthaṃ “vinayavādī”ti vuttaṃ. Pañcannañhi saṃvaravinayānaṃ, pañcannañca pahānavinayānaṃ vasena vuccamāno attho nibbānādhigamahetubhāvato lokuttaradhammasannissito hotīti. Evaṃ guṇavisesayuttova attho vuccamāno desanākosalle sati sobhati, kiccakaro ca hoti, na aññathāti dassetuṃ “nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā”ti vuttaṃ. Idāni taṃ desanākosallaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “kālenā”tiādimāha. Pucchādivasena hi otiṇṇavācāvatthusmiṃ ekaṃsādibyākaraṇavibhāgaṃ sallakkhetvā ṭhapanāhetuudāharaṇaṃ saṃsandanādiṃ taṃtaṃkālānurūpaṃ vibhāventiyā parimitaparicchinnarūpāya vipulatara-gambhīrodāra-paramattha-vitthārasaṅgāhikāya kathāya ñāṇabalānurūpaṃ pare yāthāvato dhamme patiṭṭhāpento “desanākusalo”ti vuccatīti evamettha atthayojanā veditabbā.

'One who speaks at the right time,' etc., shows the practice of one who abstains from frivolous talk. For even speech connected with the good, if used at the wrong time, would not be beneficial; it would conform to speech that makes known what is not the good. Therefore, one who is abandoning frivolous talk should avoid speaking at the wrong time; hence 'one who speaks at the right time' is said. Even when speaking at the right time, one should avoid what is not true, since it accomplishes harm for both parties; hence 'one who speaks what is true' is said. And when speaking what is true, one should speak only what brings about welfare in this world and the next; to show this, 'one who speaks on the good' is said. Even when speaking on the good, one should not speak relying only on worldly states, but should speak having established it on the supramundane Dhamma; to show this, 'one who speaks on the Dhamma' is said. And to show how the meaning is connected with the supramundane Dhamma, 'one who speaks on the discipline' is said. For when the meaning is spoken by way of the five disciplines of restraint and the five disciplines of abandoning, it is connected with the supramundane Dhamma because it is a cause for the attainment of Nibbāna. To show that only when the meaning is spoken endowed with such special qualities does it shine, if there is skill in teaching, and it is effective, but not otherwise, it is said: 'he speaks speech that is a treasure.' Now, to clarify that skill in teaching, 'at the right time,' etc., is said. For one is called 'skilled in teaching' who—when a topic of speech has been introduced by way of a question or the like—discerns the divisions of categorical and analytical answers, etc.; who analyzes the reason for setting aside a question, the example, the comparison, etc., appropriate to the particular occasion; and who, by means of speech that is measured and defined yet which comprehends the vast, profound, sublime, and ultimate meaning, establishes others in the Dhamma as it really is, in accordance with their knowledge and strength. This is how the construction of the meaning should be understood here.

293. Evaṃ [M 2.0157] paṭipāṭiyā satta mūlasikkhāpadāni vibhāvetvā satipi abhijjhādipahānaindriyasaṃvarasatisampajaññajāgariyānuyogādike uttaradesanāyaṃ vibhāvetuṃ taṃ pariharitvā ācārasīlasseva vibhajanavasena pāḷi pavattāti tadatthaṃ vivarituṃ “bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha bījānaṃ gāmo samūho bījagāmo. Bhūtānaṃ jātānaṃ nibbattānaṃ rukkhagacchalatādīnaṃ samūho bhūtagāmo. Nanu ca rukkhādayo cittarahitatāya na jīvā, cittarahitatā ca paripphandābhāvato chinne viruhanato visadisajātikabhāvato catuyoniapariyāpannato ca veditabbā, vuḍḍhi pana pavāḷasilālavaṇānampi vijjatīti na tesaṃ jīvabhāve [V 2.0147] kāraṇaṃ, visayaggahaṇañca nesaṃ parikappanāmattaṃ supanaṃ viya ciñcādenaṃ, tathā dohaḷādayo, tattha kasmā bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā paṭivirati icchitāti? Samaṇasāruppato tannivāsisattānurakkhaṇato ca. Tenevāha – “jīvasaññino hi moghapurisa manussā rukkhasmi”ntiādi (pāci. 89).

293. Having thus explained the seven root training rules in sequence, and setting aside the higher teachings to be explained on abandoning covetousness and so forth, restraint of the senses, mindfulness, clear comprehension, wakefulness, and similar practices, the text proceeds to elaborate on conduct and virtue by way of classification. To clarify this, the passage beginning with 'abstaining from injuring seed-group and plant-group' is stated. Here, 'seed-group' (bījagāma) refers to a collection of seeds. 'Plant-group' (bhūtagāma) refers to a collection of living, grown, and produced things such as trees, shrubs, and creepers. Now, one might argue that trees and the like are not living beings because they lack consciousness, and their lack of consciousness can be understood from the absence of responsive movement, from their growing when cut, from their being of a dissimilar nature, and from their exclusion from the four modes of birth. Moreover, growth is also seen in non-living things like coral, salt, and rocks—so that is not a reason for considering them alive. And their perception of objects is merely conceptual, like a dream or the touch-sensitivity of a sensitive plant, and so too with cravings and the like. Why, then, is abstaining from injuring seed-group and plant-group desired? It is because it befits an ascetic and protects the beings that dwell therein. For this reason, it is said: 'Foolish men, perceiving life in trees...' (Pāc. 89) and so on.

Mūlameva bījaṃ mūlabījaṃ, mūlabījaṃ etassātipi mūlabījaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Phaḷubījanti pabbabījaṃ. Paccayantarasamavāye sadisaphaluppattiyā visesakāraṇabhāvato viruhaṇasamatthe sāraphale niruḷho bījasaddo tadatthasaṃsiddhiyā mūlādīsupi kesuci pavattatīti mūlādito nivattanatthaṃ ekena bīja-saddena visesetvā vuttaṃ “bījabīja”nti “rūparūpaṃ (visuddhi. 2.449), dukkhadukkha”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.327; 5.165; netti. 11) ca yathā. Kasmā panettha bījagāmabhūtagāmaṃ uddharitvā bījagāmo eva niddiṭṭhoti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, nanu avocumha – “mūlameva bījaṃ mūlabījaṃ, mūlabījaṃ etassātipi mūlabīja”nti. Tattha purimena bījagāmo niddiṭṭho, dutiyena bhūtagāmo, duvidhopesa mūlabījañca mūlabījañca mūlabījanti sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesanayena vā uddiṭṭhoti veditabbo. Tenevāha “pañcavidhassā”tiādi. Nīlatiṇarukkhādikassāti allatiṇassa ceva allarukkhādikassa ca. Ādi-saddena osadhigacchalatādīnaṃ saṅgaho.

The root itself is the seed, hence, root-seed; that which has a root as its seed is also root-seed. The same method applies to the rest. Node-seed (phaḷubīja) means joint-seed (pabbabīja). The word 'seed' is established in the sense of an essential fruit capable of sprouting, being a specific cause for the production of a similar fruit through the combination of other conditions. For the accomplishment of that meaning, it is also applied by some to roots, etc. To prevent it from being restricted to roots and so on, it is specified with the single word 'seed' and called 'seed-seed,' just as in 'form-form' (Visuddhimagga 2.449) and 'suffering-suffering' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.327; 5.165; Netti 11). Why here, after setting forth both the seed-group and the plant-group, is only the seed-group specified? This should not be seen in that way. Did we not say: 'The root itself is the seed, hence, root-seed; that which has a root as its seed is also root-seed'? Therein, the first specifies the seed-group, the second, the plant-group. These two—the root-seed and that which has a root as its seed—are to be understood as designated as 'root-seed' either by a general designation or by the method of one remaining. Therefore, it is said, 'of five kinds,' etc. 'Of green grass, trees, etc.' means of both fresh grass and fresh trees, etc. The term 'etc.' includes medicinal herbs, shrubs, creepers, and so on.

Ekaṃ bhattaṃ ekabhattaṃ, taṃ assa atthīti ekabhattiko. So pana rattibhojanenapi siyāti tannivattanatthaṃ āha “rattūparato”ti. Evampi aparaṇhabhojīpi siyā ekabhattikoti tannivattanatthaṃ “virato vikālabhojanā”ti [M 2.0158] vuttaṃ. Aruṇuggamanakālato paṭṭhāya yāva majjhanhikā ayaṃ buddhādīnaṃ ariyānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇo bhojanassa kālo nāma, tadañño vikālo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana dutiyapadena rattibhojanassa paṭikkhittattā “atikkante majjhanhike yāva sūriyatthaṅgamanā bhojanaṃ vikālabhojanaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ.

One meal, a single meal; he has that, therefore he is a one-meal eater. But he might also partake of night meals; to prevent that, it is said, "abstaining from night meals." Even so, he might still partake of afternoon meals as a one-meal eater; to prevent that, it is said, "abstaining from untimely food." From the time of dawn until midday, this is the time for eating, customary and constantly practiced by noble ones such as the Buddha; any other time is untimely. In the commentary, however, since night meals are prohibited by the second term, it is said: "Eating after midday until sunset is called untimely eating."

“Sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”ntiādinayappavattaṃ (dī. ni. 2.90; dha. pa. 183; netti. 30, 50, 116, 124) bhagavato sāsanaṃ accantarāguppattiyā naccādidassanaṃ na anulometīti āha “sāsanassa ananulomattā”ti. Attanā payojiyamānaṃ, parehi payojāpiyamānañca naccaṃ naccabhāvasāmaññena pāḷiyaṃ ekeneva nacca-saddena gahitaṃ, tathā gītavādita-saddena cāti āha “naccananaccāpanādivasenā”ti. Ādi-saddena gāyanagāyāpanavādanavādāpanāni saṅgayhanti. Dassanena cettha savanampi saṅgahitaṃ virūpekasesanayena[V 2.0148]. Yathāsakaṃ visayassa ālocanasabhāvatāya vā pañcannaṃ viññāṇānaṃ savanakiriyāyapi dassanasaṅkhepasabbhāvato “dassanā”icceva vuttaṃ. Tenāha “pañcahi viññāṇehi na kañci dhammaṃ paṭivijānāti aññatra abhinipātamattā”ti. Avisūkabhūtassa gītassa savanaṃ kadāci vaṭṭatīti āha “visūkabhūtā dassanā”ti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ paramatthajotikāyaṃ khuddakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (khu. pā. aṭṭha. 2.pacchimapañcasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ gītaṃ vaṭṭati, gītūpasaṃhito dhammo na vaṭṭatī”ti. Yaṃ kiñcīti ganthitaṃ vā aganthitaṃ vā yaṃ kiñci pupphaṃ. Gandhajātanti gandhajātikaṃ. Tassapi “yaṃ kiñcī”ti vacanato pisitassa apisitassapi yassa kassaci vilepanādi na vaṭṭatīti dasseti.

"Not doing any evil," and so on—the teaching of the Blessed One, which unfolds in this way, does not conform to the arising of intense passion through seeing dances and the like. Therefore, it is said, "because it is contrary to the teaching." Dancing, whether performed by oneself or caused to be performed by others, is referred to in the Pāli texts by the single term "dance." Similarly, singing and playing music are also denoted by their respective terms. The word "and so on" includes singing, causing others to sing, playing instruments, and causing others to play instruments. Here, hearing is also included under seeing, by the method of one remaining of dissimilar things. Due to the nature of perception being the same for each sense object, even the act of hearing is briefly referred to as "seeing." Hence, it is said, "With the five senses, one does not discern any phenomenon except a mere impingement." Listening to songs that are not a distracting spectacle is sometimes allowed. Therefore, it is said, "seeing that is a distracting spectacle." As stated in the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha: "Singing connected with the Dhamma is permissible, but the Dhamma connected with singing is not permissible." "Whatever"—whether strung or unstrung—any flower. "Of the fragrant kind"—that which possesses fragrance. From the phrase "whatever," it is also shown that no unguents, whether ground or unground, are permissible for anyone.

Uccāti ucca-saddena samānatthaṃ ekaṃ saddantaraṃ. Seti etthāti sayanaṃ. Uccāsayanaṃ mahāsayanañca samaṇasārupparahitaṃ adhippetanti āha “pamāṇātikkantaṃ akappiyattharaṇa”nti. Āsanañcettha sayaneneva saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yasmā pana ādhāre paṭikkhitte tadādhārā kiriyā paṭikkhittāva hoti, tasmā “uccāsayanamahāsayanā”icceva vuttaṃ, atthato [M 2.0159] pana tadupabhogabhūtanisajjānipajjanehi virati dassitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā uccāsayanamahāsayanañca uccāsayanamahāsayanañca uccāsayanamahāsayananti etasmiṃ atthe ekasesena ayaṃ niddeso kato yathā “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”nti (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1; udā. 1), āsanakiriyāpubbakattā vā sayanakiriyāya sayanaggahaṇena āsanampi gahitanti veditabbaṃ.

"Uccāti" is another word synonymous with "ucca." "One lies down here, therefore it is a bed (sayana)." "Uccāsayanaṃ" and "mahāsayanaṃ" are understood to denote luxurious and grand beds, unsuitable for ascetics; therefore, it is said, "beyond the proper measure, an unallowable bedding." Here, seating should also be understood as included with bedding. Since, however, when the base is prohibited, the action dependent on it is also prohibited, therefore "uccāsayanamahāsayanaṃ" is stated; in meaning, however, restraint from sitting and lying down, which are actions related to its use, is shown. Alternatively, "uccāsayanamahāsayanañca" and "uccāsayanamahāsayanañca" are joined as "uccāsayanamahāsayanaṃ" by way of ekasesa, in this meaning, just as in "name-and-form conditions the six sense bases" (Majjhima Nikāya 3.126; Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.1; Udāna 1). Or, because the act of sitting precedes the act of lying down, by the mention of "bed" the act of sitting is also included. This should be understood.

Dārumāsakoti ye vohāraṃ gacchantīti iti-saddena evaṃpakāre dasseti. Aññehi gāhāpane upanikkhittasādiyane ca paṭiggahaṇattho labbhatīti āha “neva naṃ uggaṇhāti, na uggaṇhāpeti, na upanikkhittaṃ sādiyatī”ti. Atha vā tividhaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ kāyena vācāya manasāti. Tattha kāyena paṭiggahaṇaṃ uggaṇhanaṃ, vācāya paṭiggahaṇaṃ uggahāpanaṃ, manasā paṭiggahaṇaṃ sādiyananti tividhampi paṭiggahaṇaṃ ekajjhaṃ gahetvā “paṭiggahaṇā”ti vuttanti āha “neva naṃ uggaṇhātī”tiādi. Esa nayo āmakadhaññapaṭiggahaṇātiādīsupi. Nīvārādiupadhaññassa sāliādimūladhaññantogadhattā vuttaṃ “sattavidhassā”ti. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañca vasāni bhesajjāni acchavasaṃ macchavasaṃ susukāvasaṃ sukaravasaṃ gadrabhavasa”nti (mahāva. 262) vuttattā idaṃ odissa anuññātaṃ nāma, tassa pana “kāle paṭiggahita”nti (mahāva. 262) vuttattā paṭiggahaṇaṃ vaṭṭati. Sati paccayeti āha “aññatra odissa anuññātā”ti.

The word 'iti' indicates such kinds of wooden tokens as are commonly used. The meaning of acceptance is obtained by causing others to take it and by consenting to what is deposited. Therefore, it is said, 'He neither takes it himself, nor causes it to be taken, nor consents to what is deposited.' Alternatively, acceptance is threefold: by body, speech, and mind. Here, acceptance by the body is taking, acceptance by speech is causing to be taken, and acceptance by mind is consenting. Thus, having combined all three kinds of acceptance into one, it is said 'from acceptance,' as in 'He neither takes it himself,' etc. The same principle applies to receiving raw grain, etc. Because secondary grains such as wild rice, etc., are included within primary grains such as cultivated rice, it is said 'of seven kinds.' 'I allow, monks, five kinds of fats as medicine: bear fat, fish fat, porpoise fat, hog fat, and donkey fat' (Mahāvagga 262). Therefore, this is said to be specifically permitted; but since it is said of that, 'received at the proper time' (Mahāvagga 262), its acceptance is allowable. When there is a reason, it is said, 'except what is specifically permitted.'

Sarūpena [V 2.0149] vañcanaṃ rūpakūṭaṃ, patirūpena vañcanāti attho. Aṅgena attano sarīrāvayavena vañcanaṃ aṅgakūṭaṃ. Gahaṇavasena vañcanaṃ gahaṇakūṭaṃ. Paṭicchannaṃ katvā vañcanaṃ paṭicchannakūṭaṃ. Akkamatīti nippīḷeti, pubbabhāge akkamatīti sambandho.

Deception by appearance is called form-fraud; the meaning is deception by resemblance. Deception by means of one's own body parts is called limb-fraud. Deception by taking hold is called seizure-fraud. Deception done by covering up is called hidden-fraud. "Akkamati" means to oppress; the connection is that it oppresses the earlier part of the measure.

Hadayanti nāḷiādīnaṃ mānabhājanānaṃ abbhantaraṃ. Tilādīnaṃ nāḷiādīhi minanakāle ussāpitasikhāyeva sikhā. Sikhābhedo tassāhāpanaṃ.

The interior (hadaya) is the inner part of measuring vessels like the nāḷi. When measuring grains like sesame with nāḷi measures, the peak is just the raised peak. The breaking of the peak is its removal or leveling.

Kecīti [M 2.0160] sārasamāsācariyā, uttaravihāravāsino ca. Vadhoti muṭṭhipahārakasātāḷanādīhi vihesanaṃ, vibādhananti attho. Viheṭhanatthopi hi vadha-saddo dissati “attānaṃvadhitvā vadhitvā rodatī”tiādīsu (pāci. 879, 881). Yathā hi apariggahabhāvasāmaññe satipi pabbajitehi appaṭiggahitabbavatthuvibhāgasandassanatthaṃ itthikumāridāsidāsādayo vibhāgena vuttā. Evaṃ parassa haraṇabhāvato adinnādānabhāvasāmaññe satipi tulākūṭādayo adinnādānavisesabhāvadassanatthaṃ vibhāgena vuttā, na evaṃ pāṇātipātapariyāyassa vadhassa puna gahaṇe payojanaṃ atthi, tattha sayaṃkāro, idha paraṃkāroti ca na sakkā vattuṃ “kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā chappayogā”ti vacanato. Tasmā yathāvutto evettha attho yutto. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “vadhoti māraṇa”nti vuttaṃ, tampi pothanameva sandhāyāti ca sakkā viññātuṃ māraṇa-saddassapi vihiṃsane dissanato.

Some, that is, the teachers who summarize the essence, and the residents of the Uttaravihāra. 'Assault' (vadha) means harassing by means of fist-blows, whipping, etc.; the meaning is oppressing. Indeed, the word 'vadha' is also seen in the sense of harassing, as in such passages as 'having struck himself again and again, he weeps' (Pāc. 879, 881). For just as, although the general principle of non-possession applies, distinctions such as women, girls, male slaves, and female slaves are specified to show the things that should not be accepted by the ordained; and just as, although the general principle of taking what is not given applies to taking what belongs to others, distinctions like false balances are specified to illustrate particular forms of taking what is not given; in the same way, there is no purpose in taking up 'assault' again as a synonym for the destruction of life. Nor can it be said that in the former case it is an action by oneself and here it is an action by another, because of the statement: 'Volition, which originates action through body and speech, has six applications.' Therefore, the meaning as stated above is proper here. In the Commentary, however, it is said: ''Assault' is killing,' but this can be understood as referring to striking, since the word 'killing' is also seen in the sense of injuring.

294. Cīvarapiṇḍapātānaṃ yathākkamaṃ kāyakucchipariharaṇamattajotanāyaṃ avisesato aṭṭhannaṃ parikkhārānaṃ antare tappayojanatā sambhavatīti dassento “te sabbepī”tiādimāha. Etepīti navaparikkhārikādayopi appicchāva santuṭṭhāva. Na hi tatthakena mahicchatā, asantuṭṭhitā vā hotīti.

294. To show that, for the purpose of merely indicating the maintenance of the body and belly, in due order beginning with robes and almsfood, their usefulness is found without distinction among the eight requisites, he says, 'all these too,' etc. 'These too' means: even those with the nine requisites, etc., are of few wishes and are content. For by that much one is not of great wishes or discontented.

Catūsu disāsu sukhaṃ viharati, tato eva sukhavihāraṭṭhānabhūtā catasso disā assa santīti vā cātuddiso. Tattha cāyaṃ satte vā saṅkhāre vā bhayena na paṭihaññatīti appaṭigho. Dvādasavidhassa santosassa vasena santussanako santussamāno. Itarītarenāti uccāvacena. Parissayānaṃ bāhirānaṃ sīhabyagghādīnaṃ, abbhantarānañca kāmacchandādīnaṃ kāyacittupaddavānaṃ abhibhavanato parissayānaṃ sahitā. Thaddhabhāvakarabhayābhāvena acchambhī. Eko asahāyo. Tato eva khaggamigasiṅgasadisatāya khaggavisāṇakappo careyyāti attho.

He dwells happily in the four directions; or, because the four directions are for him a place of happy dwelling, he is 'one of the four directions' (cātuddiso). In this, he is not struck down by fear on account of beings or formations; thus he is 'unobstructed' (appaṭigho). By way of the twelve kinds of contentment, he is one who is content, being contented. 'With this or that' means with high and low. Because he overcomes external dangers such as lions and tigers, and internal afflictions of body and mind such as sensual desire, he is one who endures dangers. Because of the absence of fear that causes stiffness, he is 'unawed' (acchambhī). He is 'alone,' without a companion. Because of this, being similar to the horn of a rhinoceros, the meaning is 'he should wander alone.'

Chinnapakkho[V 2.0150], asañjātapakkho vā sakuṇo gantuṃ na sakkotīti “pakkhī sakuṇo”ti pakkhi-saddena visesetvā sakuṇo pāḷiyaṃ vuttoti [M 2.0161] āha “pakkhayutto sakuṇo”ti. Yassa sannidhikāraparibhogo kiñci ṭhapetabbaṃ sāpekkhāya ṭhapanañca natthi, tādiso ayaṃ bhikkhūti dassento “ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho”tiādimāha. Ariyanti apenti tato dosā, tehi vā ārakāti ariyoti āha “ariyenāti niddosenā”ti. Ajjhattanti attani. Niddosasukhanti nirāmisasukhaṃ kilesavajjarahitattā.

Because a bird with broken wings or with undeveloped wings cannot fly, the word 'bird' (sakuṇo) is specified in the Pāli by the word 'pakkhī' as 'a winged bird'; thus he says, 'a bird endowed with wings.' To show that 'such is this bhikkhu, for whom there is no enjoyment involving storing things, nor any setting aside with the expectation that something should be kept,' he says, 'Here, this is the brief meaning,' etc. Faults go away from him, or he is far from them, thus he is noble (ariya); hence he says, ''By the noble' means by the faultless.' 'Internal' means in oneself. 'Faultless happiness' means unworldly happiness, because it is devoid of the fault of defilements.

295. Yathāvutte sīlasaṃvare patiṭṭhitasseva indriyasaṃvaro icchitabbo tadadhiṭṭhānato, tassa ca paripālakabhāvatoti vuttaṃ “so iminā ariyena sīlakkhandhena samannāgato bhikkhū”ti. Sesapadesūti “na nimittaggāhī hotī”tiādīsu padesu. Yasmā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.15) vuttaṃ, tasmā tassa līnatthappakāsiniyaṃ saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.15) vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Rūpādīsu nimittādiggāhaparivajjanalakkhaṇattā indriyasaṃvarassa kilesehi anavasittasukhatā avikiṇṇasukhatā cassa vuttā.

295. For one established in the aforesaid restraint in virtue, restraint of the faculties is to be wished for, since it is founded upon that and because it is its protector. Thus it is said: 'that bhikkhu, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue…' 'In the remaining passages' means in such passages as 'he is not a grasper of signs.' Since this is stated in the Visuddhimagga (Vism I, 15), it should be understood by the method stated in its commentary, the Līnatthappakāsinī (Vism-mhṭ I, 15). Because restraint of the faculties is characterized by avoiding the grasping of signs, etc., in regard to forms, etc., for him there is said to be happiness not inundated by defilements and unscattered happiness.

296. Paccayasampattinti paccayapāripūriṃ. Ime cattāroti sīlasaṃvaro santoso indriyasaṃvaro satisampajaññanti ime cattāro araññavāsassa sambhārā. Tiracchānagatehi vattabbataṃ āpajjati isisiṅgassa pituādayo viya. Vanacarakehīti vanacarakamātugāmehi. Bheravasaddaṃ sāventi, tāvatā apalāyantānaṃ hatthehi sīsaṃ…pe… karonti. Paṇṇattivītikkamasaṅkhātaṃ kāḷakaṃ vā. Micchāvitakkasaṅkhātaṃ tilakaṃ vā. Tanti pītiṃ vibhūtabhāvena upaṭṭhānato khayato sammasanto.

296. 'Accomplishment in requisites' means the fulfillment of requisites. 'These four' means: these four are the provisions for forest dwelling: restraint in virtue, contentment, restraint of the faculties, and mindfulness and clear comprehension. He becomes subject to being reproached by animals, like the father of Isisiṅga and others. 'By forest-wanderers' means by female forest-wanderers. They make them hear a terrifying sound; of those who do not flee at that, they strike their heads with their hands... and so on. Or the black mark called the transgression of a designation. Or the mole called wrong thought. Contemplating that rapture from its manifest arising to its decay.

Vivittanti janavivittaṃ. Tenāha “suñña”nti. Sā ca vivittatā nissaddabhāvena lakkhitabbāti āha “appasaddaṃ appanigghosa”nti. Āvasathabhūtaṃ senāsanaṃ viharitabbaṭṭhena vihārasenāsanaṃ. Masārakādi mañcapīṭhaṃ tattha attharitabbaṃ bhisiupadhānañca mañcapīṭhasambandhito mañcapīṭhasenāsanaṃ. Cimilikādi bhūmiyaṃ santharitabbatāya santhatasenāsanaṃ. Rukkhamūlādi paṭikkamitabbaṭṭhānaṃ caṅkamanādīnaṃ okāsabhāvato okāsasenāsanaṃ.

'Secluded' means secluded from people. Therefore he says, 'empty.' And that seclusion is to be characterized by soundlessness; thus he says, 'with little sound, with little noise.' A lodging that is a dwelling place is a 'dwelling-lodging' in the sense that it is to be dwelled in. A bed and chair such as a masāraka, and a mattress and pillow to be spread on it, is a 'bed-and-chair-lodging' because of its connection with a bed and chair. A ground-covering such as a cimilikā is a 'spread-lodging' because it is to be spread on the ground. The foot of a tree, etc., is a 'space-lodging' because it is a place for returning to and provides space for walking meditation and so on.

“Anucchavikaṃ [V 2.0151] dassento”ti vatvā tameva anucchavikabhāvaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “tattha hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Acchannanti iṭṭhakachadanādinā antamaso rukkhasākhāhipi na channaṃ.

Having said, 'Showing what is suitable,' in order to explain that very suitability, the words 'For there...' etc., were stated. 'Uncovered' means not covered by roofing tiles and so on, not even by the branches of a tree.

Bhattassa [M 2.0162] pacchatoti bhattabhuñjanassa pacchato. Ūrubaddhāsananti ūrūnaṃ adhobandhanavasena nisajjaṃ. Heṭṭhimakāyassa anujukaṭṭhapanaṃ nisajjāvacaneneva bodhitanti. Ujuṃ kāyanti ettha kāya-saddo uparimakāyavisayoti āha “uparimaṃ sarīraṃ ujukaṃ ṭhapetvā”ti. Taṃ pana ujukaṭṭhapanaṃ sarūpato payojanato ca dassetuṃ “aṭṭhārasā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na paṇamantīti na oṇamanti. Na paripatatīti na vigacchati, vīthiṃ na vilaṅgheti. Tato eva pubbenāparaṃ visesappattiyā kammaṭṭhānaṃ vuddhiṃ phātiṃ upagacchati. Mukhasamīpeti mukhassa samīpe nāsikagge vā uttaroṭṭhe vā. Idha pari-saddo abhi-saddena samānatthoti āha “kammaṭṭhānābhimukha”nti, bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇato nivāretvā kammaṭṭhānaṃyeva purakkhatvāti attho. Parīti pariggahaṭṭho “pariṇāyikā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 16) viya. Niyyānaṭṭho paṭipakkhato niggamanaṭṭho, tasmā pariggahitaniyyānasatinti sabbathā gahitāsammosaṃ pariccattasammosaṃ satiṃ katvā, paramaṃ satinepakkaṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti attho.

'After the meal' means after eating the meal. 'The cross-legged posture' means sitting by way of binding the thighs below. The straightening of the lower body is understood just by the word 'sitting.' 'An upright body': here the word 'body' refers to the upper body; thus he says, 'having set the upper body straight.' To show that setting upright in its nature and purpose, 'eighteen,' etc., was said. 'They do not bend' means they do not incline. 'It does not fall away' means it does not depart, it does not transgress its course. Thereby, through the attainment of one distinction after another, the meditation subject goes to growth and expansion. 'Near the mouth' means near the mouth, at the tip of the nose or on the upper lip. Here the prefix 'pari-' has the same meaning as the prefix 'abhi-'; thus he says, 'facing the meditation subject,' the meaning being that, having prevented the mind from going to external, diverse objects, one places only the meditation subject to the fore. 'Pari-' has the sense of grasping, as in 'pariṇāyikā,' etc. (Dhs. §16). 'Niyyāna' has the sense of escape, of departing from the opposite. Therefore, 'mindfulness with escape grasped' means having established mindfulness that has in every way grasped non-confusion and abandoned confusion, that is, having established supreme mindfulness and vigilance.

Vikkhambhanavasenāti ettha vikkhambhanaṃ anuppādanaṃ appavattanaṃ na paṭipakkhena suppahīnatā. Pahīnattāti ca pahīnasadisataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ jhānassa anadhigatatā. Tathāpi nayidaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ viya sabhāvato vigatābhijjhaṃ, atha kho bhāvanāvasena. Tenāha “na cakkhuviññāṇasadisenā”ti. Eseva nayoti yathā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ sabhāvena vigatābhijjhaṃ abyāpannañca, na bhāvanāya vikkhambhitattā, na evamidaṃ. Idaṃ pana cittaṃ bhāvanāya parisodhitattā abyāpannaṃ vigatathinamiddhaṃ anuddhataṃ nibbicikicchañcāti attho. Idaṃ ubhayanti satisampajaññamāha.

'By way of suppression': here suppression means non-arising, non-occurrence, not a complete abandoning by its opposite. And 'by means of abandonment' is said with reference to a state similar to abandonment, due to the non-attainment of jhāna. Still, this is not devoid of covetousness by nature, like eye-consciousness, but rather by way of cultivation. Therefore he says, 'not like eye-consciousness.' This is the method: just as eye-consciousness is by nature devoid of covetousness and non-ill will, not because it has been suppressed by cultivation, so this is not. But this mind, because it has been purified by cultivation, is without ill will, devoid of sloth and torpor, not restless, and without doubt; this is the meaning. 'This twofold' refers to mindfulness and clear comprehension.

297. Ucchinditvā pātentīti ettha ucchindanaṃ pātanañca tāsaṃ paññānaṃ anuppannānaṃ uppajjituṃ appadānameva. Iti mahaggatānuttarapaññānaṃ ekaccāya ca parittapaññāya anuppattihetubhūtā nīvaraṇā dhammā itarāya ca samatthataṃ vihanantiyevāti paññāya dubbalīkaraṇā vuttā. Idampi paṭhamajjhānaṃ veneyyasantāne patiṭṭhāpiyamānaṃ ñāṇaṃ pajjati etthāti ñāṇapadaṃ. Ñāṇaṃ vaḷañjeti etthāti ñāṇavaḷañjaṃ.

297. 'Having cut off, they make them fall': here, cutting off and making fall is simply the non-giving of an opportunity to arise for those kinds of wisdom that have not yet arisen. Thus the hindrances are called 'weakeners of wisdom' because they are the cause for the non-arising of lofty and supramundane wisdom and of some limited wisdom, and because they destroy the competence of other wisdom. This first jhāna, too, is a 'basis for knowledge' (ñāṇapadaṃ) because knowledge, being established in the mental continuum of a disciple, proceeds in it. It is a 'track for knowledge' (ñāṇavaḷañjaṃ) because one uses knowledge in it.

299. Na [V 2.0152] tāva niṭṭhaṃ gato bāhirakānaṃ ñāṇena akkantaṭṭhānānipi siyunti. Yadi evaṃ anaññasādhāraṇe maggañāṇapade kathaṃ na niṭṭhaṅgatoti āha [M 2.0163] “maggakkhaṇepī”tiādi. Tīsu ratanesu niṭṭhaṃ gato hotīti buddhasubuddhataṃ dhammasudhammataṃ saṅghasuppaṭipattitañca ārabbha ñāṇena niṭṭhaṃ nicchayaṃ upagato hoti.
