Kāmañcettha paṭhamamaggeneva sabbaso vicikicchāya pahīnattā sabbassapi ariyasāvakassa kaṅkhā vā vimati vā natthi, tattha pana yathā paññāvepullappattassa arahato savisaye ñāṇaṃ savisesaṃ ogāhati, na tathā anāgāmiādīnanti ratanattaye sātisayaṃ ñāṇanicchayagamanaṃ sandhāya “aggamaggavasena tatthaniṭṭhāgamanaṃ vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ panettha avibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

299. The outsiders have not yet reached finality, since there can also be positions they have grasped with their knowledge. If so, how is it not finalized in the unique domain of path-knowledge? It is said, "even at the moment of the path," etc. One is finalized in the Three Jewels—that is, one reaches finality and certainty through knowledge concerning the perfect Buddhahood of the Buddha, the perfect nature of the Dhamma, and the perfect practice of the Sangha. Although here, with all doubt abandoned by the first path itself, there is no uncertainty or hesitation for any noble disciple, still, just as the knowledge of an arahant who has attained fullness of wisdom penetrates distinctly in its own domain, it is not so for non-returners and others. Therefore, regarding the surpassing attainment of certainty through knowledge in the Three Jewels, it is said that "the reaching of finality is spoken of there by way of the supreme path." And what is unexplained here is indeed easily understood.

Cūḷahatthipadopamasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta is concluded.

8. Mahāhatthipadopamasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Greater Discourse on the Elephant Footprint Simile

300. Jaṅgalānanti [V 2.0153] ettha yo nipicchalena amuduko nirudakatāya thaddhalūkhabhūmippadeso, so “jaṅgalo”ti vuccati. Tabbahulatāya pana idha sabbo bhūmippadeso jaṅgalo, tasmiṃ jaṅgale jātā, bhavāti vā jaṅgalā, tesaṃ jaṅgalānaṃ. Evañhi nadīcarānampi hatthīnaṃ saṅgaho kato hoti. Samodhātabbānaṃ viya hi samodhāyakānampi jaṅgalaggahaṇena gahetabbato. Pathavītalacārīnanti iminā jalacārino na nivatteti adissamānapādattā. Pāṇānanti sādhāraṇavacanampi “padajātānī”ti saddantarasannidhānena visesaniviṭṭhameva hotīti āha “sapādakapāṇāna”nti. “Muttagata”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.119; a. ni. 9.11) gata-saddo anatthantaro viya, jāta-saddo anatthantaroti āha “padajātānīti padānī”ti. Samodhānanti samavarodhaṃ, antogamaṃ vā. Mahantattenāti vipulabhāvena.

300. "Jaṅgalānaṃ": here, a patch of ground that is not slimy, not soft, without water, hard and rough is called "jaṅgala." However, here, all patches of ground are considered "jaṅgala" due to their abundance. Those born in such a "jaṅgala," or existing in it, are called "jaṅgalā," hence "jaṅgalānaṃ." Thus, even river-dwelling elephants are included. For just as those to be included, so too those that include are to be taken by the term "jaṅgala." "Pathavītalacārīnaṃ": this does not exclude water-dwellers, because their feet are not seen. "Pāṇānaṃ": though a general term, it becomes specific due to the proximity of the word "padajātāni," hence he says "sapādakapāṇānaṃ" (of living beings with feet). In expressions such as "muttagata," the word "gata" has no separate meaning; similarly, the word "jāta" has no separate meaning, therefore he says "padajātāni means padāni (footprints)." "Samodhānaṃ": means inclusion, or entering within. "Mahantattena": means due to largeness.

Kusalā dhammāti anavajjasukhavipākā dhammā, na anavajjamattadhammā. Kusalattike āgatanayena hi idha kusalā dhammā gahetabbā, na bāhitikasutte āgatanayena. Catubbidho saṅgahoti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu ekavidhovettha saṅgaho adhippetoti? Na, atthaṃ aggahetvā aniddhāritatthassa saddasseva gahitattā. Saṅgaha-saddo tāva attano atthavasena [M 2.0164] catubbidhoti ayañhettha attho. Atthopi vā aniddhāritaviseso sāmaññena gahetabbataṃ patto “saṅgahaṃ gacchatī”ti ettha saṅgaha-saddena vacanīyataṃ gatoti na koci doso, niddhārite visese tassa ekavidhatā siyā, na tato pubbeti. Sajātisaṅgahoti samānajātiyā, samānajātikānaṃ vā saṅgaho. Dhātukathāvaṇṇanāyaṃ pana “jātisaṅgaho”icceva vuttaṃ, taṃ jāti-saddassa sāpekkhasaddattā jātiyā saṅgahoti vutte attano jātiyāti viññāyati sambandhārahassa aññassa avuttattāti katvā vuttaṃ. Idha pana rūpakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 594) viya pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “sajātisaṅgaho”icceva vuttaṃ. Sañjāyanti etthāti sañjāti, sañjātiyā saṅgaho sañjātisaṅgaho, sañjātidesavasena saṅgahoti attho. “Sabbe rathikā”ti vutte sabbe rathayodhā rathena yujjhanakiriyāya ekasaṅgahoti. “Sabbe dhanuggahā”ti vutte sabbe issāsā dhanunā vijjhanakiriyāya ekasaṅgahoti āha “evaṃ kiriyavasena saṅgaho”ti. Rūpakkhandhena saṅgahitanti rūpakkhandhena ekasaṅgahaṃ rūpakkhandhoteva gaṇitaṃ, gahaṇaṃ gatanti attho.

"Wholesome phenomena" are those that have blameless and happy results, not merely blameless phenomena. Here, wholesome phenomena should be understood according to the method presented in the Kusalattika, not as in the Bāhitika Sutta. Why is it said that the grouping is fourfold? Is not the intended grouping here only onefold? No, because without grasping the meaning, only the word itself has been taken, its meaning being undetermined. The term "grouping" (saṅgaha), indeed, is fourfold in its own meaning, and this is the meaning here. Alternatively, since the meaning, with its particularity undetermined, having attained the state of being taken generally, has come to be expressed by the term "grouping" in the phrase "it goes to grouping," there is no fault. When a particular is determined, its oneness may apply, but not before that. "Same-kind grouping" (sajātisaṅgaha) means grouping with those of the same kind or the grouping of those of the same kind. In the Dhātukathā commentary, however, it is simply called "kind-grouping" (jātisaṅgaha). This is because the term "kind" (jāti) is a relative term; when it is said "grouping by kind," it is understood as "grouping by one’s own kind," since no other suitable relation is stated. But here, as in the Rūpakaṇḍa commentary, it is stated clearly as "same-kind grouping" to make it evident. "Sañjāti" means "they arise together in this"; thus, "sañjātisaṅgaho" means grouping by shared arising, that is, grouping by way of shared origin. When it is said, "All are charioteers," it means all chariot warriors are a single grouping by the action of fighting with chariots. When it is said, "All are archers," it means all bowmen are a single grouping by the action of shooting with bows. Thus, it is said, "Thus is grouping by action." "Grouped by the aggregate of form" means counted as a single grouping with the aggregate of form, as the aggregate of form itself; it has undergone being taken as such.

Diyaḍḍhameva [V 2.0154] saccaṃ bhajati maggasaccadukkhasaccekadesabhāvato. Saccekadesantogadhampi saccantogadhameva hotīti āha “saccānaṃ antogadhattā”ti. Idāni tamatthaṃ sāsanato ca lokato ca upamaṃ āha ritvā dīpetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sādhikamidaṃ, bhikkhave, diyaḍḍhasikkhāpadasatanti idaṃ yasmiṃ kāle taṃ suttaṃ desitaṃ, tadā paññattasikkhāpadavasena vuttaṃ, tato paraṃ pana sādhikāni dvesatāni sikkhāpadānīti. Sikkhānaṃ antogadhattā adhisīlasikkhāya. Ettha ca “sīlaṃ sikkhantopi tisso sikkhā sikkhatī”ti visamoyaṃ upaññāso. Tattha hi yo pahātabbaṃ pajahati, saṃvaritabbato saṃvaraṃ āpajjati, ayamassa adhisīlasikkhā. Yo tattha cetaso avikkhepo, ayamassa adhicittasikkhā. Yā tattha vīmaṃsā, ayamassa adhipaññāsikkhā. Iti so kulaputto sarūpato labbhamānā eva tisso sikkhā sikkhatīti dīpito, na sikkhānaṃ antogadhatāmattena. Tenāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “yo tathābhūtassa saṃvaro, ayamettha adhisīlasikkhā, yo tathābhūtassa [M 2.0165] samādhi, ayamettha adhicittasikkhā, yā tathābhūtassa paññā, ayaṃ adhipaññāsikkhā. Imā tisso sikkhā tasmiṃ ārammaṇe tāya satiyā tena manasikārena sikkhati āsevati bhāveti bahulīkarotī”ti. Idha pana saccānaṃ antogadhattā sacca-saddābhidheyyatāmattena catūsu saccesu gaṇanantogadhā hontīti? Na, tatthāpi hi nippariyāyato adhisīlasikkhāva labbhati, itarā pariyāyatoti katvā “sikkhānaṃ antogadhattā”ti vuttaṃ.

One and a half truths indeed partake of truth, being a part of the truth of the path and the truth of suffering. Even though it is included within a part of a truth, it is still included within truth itself—hence it is said, 'because of being included in the truths.' Now, in order to reveal that meaning, having drawn an analogy from both the teaching and the world, it is said, 'Just as…' and so on. Here, 'This, bhikkhus, is more than one hundred and fifty training rules' refers to the time when that sutta was taught, meaning the rules laid down at that time. But thereafter, there were more than two hundred training rules. Because of being included within the trainings, it pertains to the higher training in virtue. Here, the statement 'even while training in virtue, one trains in the three trainings' is an inappropriate presentation. For in that case, one who abandons what should be abandoned and attains restraint from what should be restrained—this is their higher training in virtue. The non-distraction of mind in that—this is their higher training in concentration. The investigation in that—this is their higher training in wisdom. Thus, that person of good family trains in the three trainings as they are obtained in their own nature—this is explained, not merely by the inclusion in the trainings themselves. Therefore, the commentary states: 'The restraint of one who is of such a nature—this here is the higher training in virtue. The concentration of one who is of such a nature—this here is the higher training in concentration. The wisdom of one who is of such a nature—this is the higher training in wisdom. These three trainings are cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced by that person through that mindfulness and that mental attention on that object.' Here, however, is it because of being included in the truths that they are included in the enumeration of the four truths merely by being designated by the word 'truth'? No, for even there, only the higher training in virtue is obtained in a definitive sense, while the others are obtained in an indirect sense—hence it is said, 'because of being included within the trainings.'

Catūsu ariyasaccesu saṅgahaṃ gacchantīti ca tato amuccitvā tasseva antogadhataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Evañca katvā “yathā ca ekassa hatthipadassā”tiādinā dassitā hatthipadopamā samatthitā daṭṭhabbā. Ekasmimpi dvīsupi tīsupi saccesu gaṇanaṃ gatā dhammāti idaṃ na kusalattikavaseneva veditabbaṃ, atha kho tikadukesu yathārahaṃ labbhamānapadavasena veditabbaṃ. Tattha ekasmiṃ sacce gaṇanaṃ gato dhammo asaṅkhatadhammo daṭṭhabbo, dvīsu saccesu gaṇanaṃ gatā kusalā dhammā, tathā akusalā dhammā, abyākatā ca dhammā, tīsu saccesu gaṇanaṃ gatā saṅkhatā dhammā, evaṃ aññesampi tikadukapadānaṃ vasena ayamattho yathārahaṃ vibhajitvā vattabbo. Tenāha “ekasmimpi…pe… gatāva hontī”ti. Ekadeso hi samudāyantogadhattā viseso viya sāmaññena samūhena saṅgahaṃ labhati. Tenāha “saccānaṃ antogadhattā”ti. Desanānukkamoti ariyasaccāni uddisitvā dukkhasaccaniddesavasena pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ vibhajanaṃ. Tattha ca rūpakkhandhaniddesavasenaādito ajjhattikāya pathavīdhātuyā vibhajananti. Ayaṃ imissā desanāya anukkamo.

And that they are included in the four noble truths is said with reference to their inclusion within them, from which they are not separate. Having done so, the simile of the elephant’s footprint, as shown by 'just as in the case of a single elephant’s footprint…,' should be understood as fully established. That phenomena are counted in one, two, or three truths should not be understood merely in terms of the wholesome triad, but rather according to how the terms are appropriately found in the triads and dyads. Here, the phenomenon counted in one truth should be seen as the unconditioned phenomenon. In two truths, the phenomena counted are wholesome phenomena, as well as unwholesome phenomena and indeterminate phenomena. In three truths, the phenomena counted are conditioned phenomena. In this way, this meaning should be analyzed and stated appropriately for other triads and dyads. Hence it is said, 'even in one… they are included.' For a part, being included within the whole, obtains inclusion by the general group, like a particular instance. Therefore, it is said, 'due to being included in the truths.' The sequence of the teaching is this: after stating the noble truths, the analysis of the five aggregates of clinging proceeds by way of the exposition of the truth of suffering. And therein, starting with the exposition of the form aggregate, is the analysis of the internal earth element. This is the sequence of this teaching.

301. Taṃ [V 2.0155] panetaṃ upamāhi vibhāvetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sujātanti sundaraṃ, susaṇṭhitaṃ supariṇatañcāti adhippāyo. Pesiyoti vilīve. Mudubhāvato kucchibhāgaṃ ādāya. Itare ca cattāro koṭṭhāseti pañcadhā bhinnakoṭṭhāsesu itare ca cattāro koṭṭhāse. Itare ca tayo koṭṭhāsetiādito catudhā bhinnakoṭṭhāsesu itare ca tayo koṭṭhāse.

301. To clarify this with similes, it is said, 'Just as…,' and so on. Here, 'well-born' means beautiful, well-formed, and well-matured; this is the intention. 'A piece of flesh' means in a dissolved state. Taking the belly portion on account of its softness. 'And the other four sections' means the other four sections among the five divided sections. 'And the other three sections' means the other three sections among the initially four divided sections.

Rājaputtūpamāyāti rañño jeṭṭhaputtaupamāya. Nti piḷandhanaṃ. Ure vāyāmajanitaariyajātiyā oraso. Mukhato jātoti mukhato niggatadhammadesanāya [M 2.0166] jāto, buddhānaṃ vā dhammakāyassa mukhabhūtaariyadhammato jāto. Tato eva dhammajo dhammanimmito. Satthu dhammadāyādasseva gahitattā dhammadāyādo. Tenāha “no āmisadāyādo”ti. Nti “bhagavato putto”tiādivacanaṃ. Mahāpaññatādiguṇehi sātisayaṃ anupubbabhāve ṭhitattā sammā yathābhūtaṃ vadamāno vattuṃ sakkonto vadeyya.

By 'the simile of a king's son' is meant the simile of a king's eldest son. The particle 'ti' is an embellishment. 'Legitimate' (oraso, lit., 'born from the breast') means by the noble birth generated through effort. 'Born from the mouth' means born from the Dhamma teaching that emerged from the mouth, or born from the noble Dhamma which is the mouthpiece of the Buddhas' Dhamma body. For that very reason, one is Dhamma-born, Dhamma-created. Because of being taken as the Teacher's heir of the Dhamma, one is a 'Dhamma-heir.' Therefore, it is said, 'not an heir of material things.' The word 'iti' refers to such statements as 'the Blessed One's son.' Due to being established in a surpassing, gradual state through qualities such as great wisdom, speaking rightly as it truly is, being able to speak, one would speak.

Akutobhayaṃ nibbānaṃ nibbānagāminiñca. Rāgarajādīnaṃ vigamena vigatarajaṃ dhammaṃ desentaṃ sugataṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ parosahassaṃ payirupāsatīti yojanā.

Nibbāna is the fearless state, and the path leads to Nibbāna. More than a thousand bhikkhus were attending upon the Sugata, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who was teaching the Dhamma that is free from dust through the removal of the dust of passion and so on. This is the syntactical connection.

“Sevetha bhajathā”ti vatvā tattha kāraṇamāha “paṇḍitā bhikkhū anuggāhakā”ti. Paṇḍitāpi samānā na appassutā, atha kho ovādānusāsanīhi anuggāhakāti purimā upamā therasseva vasena udāhaṭā, dutiyā pana bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassapi vasena udāhaṭā.

Having said, 'One should associate with, one should attend upon,' he states the reason for it: 'Wise bhikkhus are helpful.' Though they are wise, they are not of little learning; rather, they are helpful with advice and instruction. The first simile was cited in connection with the elder alone, while the second was cited in connection with the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

302. Ajjhattikāti sattasantānapariyāpannā. Ajjhattaṃ paccattanti padadvayenapi taṃtaṃpāṭipuggalikadhammā vuccantīti āha “ubhayampetaṃ niyakādhivacanamevā”ti. Sasantatipariyāpannatāya pana attāti gahetabbabhāvūpagamanavasena attānaṃ adhikicca uddissa pavattaṃ ajjhattaṃ, taṃtaṃsattasantānapariyāpannatāya paccattaṃ. Tenāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (visuddhi. 1.307) “attani pavattattā ajjhattaṃ, attānaṃ paṭicca paṭicca pavattattā paccatta”nti. Kakkhaḷanti kathinaṃ. Yasmā taṃ thaddhabhāvena sahajātānaṃ patiṭṭhā hoti, tasmā “thaddha”nti vuttaṃ. Kharigatanti kharasabhāvesu gataṃ tappariyāpannaṃ, kharasabhāvamevāti attho. Yasmā pana kharasabhāvaṃ pharusākārena upaṭṭhānato pharusākāraṃ hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “pharusa”nti. Upādinnaṃ nāma sarīraṭṭhakaṃ. Tattha yaṃ kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ nippariyāyato “upādinna”nti vuccati, itaraṃ anupādinnaṃ. Tadubhayampi idha taṇhādīhi ādinnagahitaparāmaṭṭhavasena upādinnamevāti dassetuṃ “sarīraṭṭhakañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ādinnanti abhiniviṭṭhaṃ. Mamanti gahitaṃ. Ahanti parāmaṭṭhaṃ[V 2.0156]. Dhātukammaṭṭhānikassāti catudhātuvavatthānavasena dhātukammaṭṭhānaṃ pariharantassa. Etthāti [M 2.0167] etasmiṃ dhātukammaṭṭhāne. Tīsu koṭṭhāsesūti tippakāresu koṭṭhāsesu. Na hi te tayo cattāro koṭṭhāsā.

302. 'Internal' means included within a being’s continuum. By the two terms 'internal' (ajjhattaṃ) and 'personal' (paccattaṃ) are meant the phenomena pertaining to each particular individual; thus he says: 'Both these are just designations for what is one’s own.' It is called 'internal' (ajjhattaṃ) because, being included in one’s own continuum and by way of approaching the state of what is to be grasped as 'self,' it occurs with reference to the self. It is called 'personal' (paccattaṃ) because it is included in the continuum of this or that being. Therefore it is said in the commentary (Vism. I 307): 'Because it occurs in the self (attani), it is “internal”; because it occurs in dependence on the self (attānaṃ paṭicca), it is “personal.”' 'Hard' means stiff. Because, due to its stiffness, it is a foundation for co-arisen phenomena, it is called 'stiff.' 'Gone to roughness' (kharigata) means gone to a rough nature, included in it; the meaning is that it is simply of a rough nature. And because a rough nature, from its appearing in a harsh manner, has a harsh appearance, it is called 'harsh' (pharusa). 'Clung-to' (upādinna) refers to the corporeal octad. Therein, what is produced by kamma is called 'clung-to' in the primary sense; the other is 'not-clung-to.' To show that here both are 'clung-to' in the sense of being seized, grasped, and misapprehended by craving and so on, it is said: 'for the corporeal octad…,' etc. Here, 'seized' (ādinna) means adhered to. 'Mine' (mama) means grasped. 'I' (ahaṃ) means misapprehended (parāmaṭṭha). 'Of one who practices the meditation subject of the elements' means of one who cultivates the meditation subject on the elements by way of analyzing the four elements. 'In this' means in this meditation subject on the elements. 'In the three parts' means in the three kinds of parts. For those are not three or four parts.

Vuttappakārāti “kesā lomā”tiādinā vuttappakārā. Nānāsabhāvatoti satipi kakkhaḷabhāvasāmaññe sasambhāravibhattito pana kesādisaṅghātagatanānāsabhāvato. Ālayoti apekkhā. Nikantīti nikāmanā. Patthanāti taṇhāpatthanā. Pariyuṭṭhānanti taṇhāpariyuṭṭhānaṃ. Gahaṇanti kāmupādānaṃ. Parāmāsoti parato āmasanā micchābhiniveso. Na balavā ālayādi. Yadi evaṃ kasmā vibhaṅge bāhirāpi pathavīdhātu vitthāreneva vibhattāti? Yathādhammadesanattā tattha vitthāreneva desanā pavattā, yathānulomadesanattā panettha vuttanayena desanā saṃkhittā.

‘Of the stated kind’ means of the kind stated beginning with ‘hair of the head, body hair,’ etc. ‘Of diverse nature’: this refers to the diversity found in the collection of things such as hair of the head, a diversity based on the division of their constituents, even though there is a common characteristic of hardness. ‘Attachment’ (ālayo) means yearning (apekkhā). ‘Liking’ (nikanti) means desiring (nikāmanā). ‘Aspiration’ (patthanā) means the aspiration of craving. ‘Obsession’ (pariyuṭṭhāna) means the obsession of craving. ‘Grasping’ (gahaṇa) means the clinging to sensual pleasures. ‘Misapprehension’ (parāmāso) means wrong adherence, a handling from a wrong angle. Attachment, etc., are not strong. If so, why in the Vibhaṅga is the external earth element also analyzed in detail? Because the teaching there is an exposition according to the phenomena, it proceeds in detail; but here, because the teaching is an exposition that follows a certain line, the teaching is concise in the way stated.

Yojetvā dassetīti ekajjhaṃ katvā dasseti. Sāti ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu. Sukhapariggaho hoti “na me so attā”ti. Siddhe hi anattalakkhaṇe dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ aniccalakkhaṇañca siddhameva hoti saṅkhatadhammesu tadavinābhāvatoti. Visūkāyatīti visūkaṃ virūpakiriyaṃ pavatteti. Sā pana atthato vipphandanamevāti āha “vipphandatī”ti. Assāti ajjhattikāya pathavīdhātuyā. Acetanābhāvo pākaṭo hoti dhātumattatāya dassanato. Taṃ ubhayampīti taṃ pathavīdhātudvayampi.

‘Having connected, he shows’ means having brought them together, he shows. ‘That’ is the internal earth element. There is an easy grasp of the thought, ‘This is not my self.’ For when the characteristic of not-self is established in conditioned phenomena, the characteristics of suffering and impermanence are also established, since they are inseparable from it. ‘It writhes’ means it engages in distorted action. But in meaning this is just throbbing; thus he says, ‘it throbs.’ ‘Of it’ means of the internal earth element. Its lack of consciousness becomes clear through seeing it as a mere element. ‘Both of them’ means the pair of earth elements.

Tato visesatarenāti tato bāhiramahāpathavito visesavantatarena, lahutarenāti attho. Kuppatīti luppati. Vilīyamānāti pakatiudake loṇaṃ viya vilayaṃ gacchantī. Udakānugatāti udakaṃ anugatā udakagatikā. Tenāha “udakameva hotī”ti. Abhāvo eva abhāvatā, na bhavatīti vā abhāvo, tathāsabhāvo dhammo. Tassa bhāvo abhāvatā. Vayo vināso dhammo sabhāvo etassāti vayadhammo, tassa bhāvo vayadhammatā, atthato khayo eva. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Tenāha “sabbehipi imehi padehi aniccalakkhaṇameva vutta”nti. Viddhaṃsanabhāvassa pana paveditabbattā kāmaṃ aniccalakkhaṇameva vuttaṃ sarūpato, itarānipi atthato vuttānevāti dassento āha “yaṃ panā”tiādi.

‘More excellently than that’ means more excellently, that is, more lightly, than the external great earth. ‘It is agitated’ means it is destroyed. ‘Dissolving’: like salt dissolving in ordinary water. ‘Gone along with water’: it has followed the water, has the same course as water. Hence it is said, ‘It becomes just water.’ The state of non-existence (abhāvatā) is simply non-existence. Or, ‘it does not exist’ is non-existence, a phenomenon of such a nature; the state of this is the state of non-existence. A phenomenon of a vanishing nature (vayadhammo) is one whose nature is vanishing, destruction; the state of this is the state of having a vanishing nature (vayadhammatā), which in meaning is simply destruction. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Therefore, it is said: ‘By all these terms, only the characteristic of impermanence is expressed.’ However, since the state of dissolution is to be made known, to show that although only the characteristic of impermanence is explicitly stated, the others are also stated in meaning, he says, ‘But what…,’ and so on.

Mattaṃ [M 2.0168] khaṇamattaṃ tiṭṭhatīti mattaṭṭho, appamattaṭṭho mattaṭṭhako, atiittarakhaṇikoti attho. Tenāha “parittaṭṭhitikassā”ti. Ṭhitiparittatāyāti ekacittapavattimattatāṭhānalakkhaṇassa itarabhāvena[V 2.0157]. Ekassa cittassa pavattikkhaṇamatteneva hi sattānaṃ paramatthato jīvanakkhaṇo paricchinno. Tenāha “ayaṃ hī”tiādi.

‘It stands for a measure, a mere moment,’ thus it is of ‘measured standing’ (mattaṭṭho). `Mattaṭṭhaka` means of little standing (`appamattaṭṭho`); the meaning is ‘exceedingly momentary.’ Therefore he says: ‘of one with a brief duration.’ By ‘the brevity of its duration’ is meant its having the characteristic of lasting only for the occurrence of a single thought, being different from a long duration. For in the ultimate sense, the life-moment of beings is delimited by just the occurrence-moment of a single thought. Therefore he says, ‘For this…,’ etc.

Jīvitanti jīvitindriyaṃ. Sukhadukkhāti sukhadukkhā vedanā. Upekkhāpi hi sukhadukkhāsveva antogadhā iṭṭhāniṭṭhabhāvato. Attabhāvoti jīvitavedanāviññāṇāni ṭhapetvā avasiṭṭhadhammā vuttā. Kevalāti attaniccabhāvena avomissā. Ekacittasamāyuttāti ekena cittena sahitā ekacittakkhaṇikā. Lahuso vattate khaṇoti tāya eva ekakkhaṇikatāya lahuko atiittaro jīvitādīnaṃ khaṇo vattati vītivattatīti attho. Idanti gāthāvacanaṃ.

‘Life’ means the life faculty. ‘Pleasure and pain’ means pleasant and painful feelings. For equanimity too is included under pleasure and pain on account of being desirable and undesirable. ‘Individual existence’ refers to the remaining phenomena, setting aside life, feeling, and consciousness. ‘Mere’ means unmixed with a self or with permanence. ‘Conjoined with a single thought’ means associated with one thought, lasting for a single thought-moment. ‘The moment passes swiftly’: the meaning is that because of that very momentariness, the exceedingly brief moment of life and so on passes swiftly, that is, it passes away. ‘This’ refers to the words of the verse.

Yasmā sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ aparāparasañcaraṇaṃ labhamānameva pavattati, na alabhamānaṃ, tasmā assāsapassāsūpanibaddhaṃ. Tathā mahābhūtānaṃ samavuttitaṃ labhamānameva pavattati. Pathavīdhātuyā hi āpodhātuādīnaṃ vā aññatarapakopena balasampannopi puriso patthaddhakāyo vā, atisārādivasena kilinnapūtikāyo vā, mahāḍāhapareto vā, sañchijjamānasandhibandhano vā hutvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇāti. Kabaḷīkārāhārānaṃ yuttakāle labhantasseva jīvitaṃ pavattati, alabhantassa parikkhayaṃ gacchati, viññāṇe pavattamāneyeva ca jīvitaṃ pavattati, na tasmiṃ appavattamāne. Jīvitanti ettha iti-saddena iriyāpathūpanibaddhatāsītuṇhūpanibaddhatādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Catunnañhi iriyāpathānaṃ samavuttitaṃ labhamānameva jīvitaṃ pavattati, aññatarassa pana adhimattatāya āyusaṅkhārā upacchijjanti, sītuṇhānampi samavuttitaṃ labhamānameva pavattati, atisītena pana atiuṇhena vā abhibhūtassa vipajjatīti.

Because the life of beings continues only when it obtains the successive occurrence of in-breaths and out-breaths, and not when it does not obtain them, it is therefore bound up with the in-breaths and out-breaths. Similarly, it continues only when it obtains the equilibrium of the great elements. For when there is a derangement of the earth element, or the water element and the others, or of any one of them, even a strong man—having a stiffened body, or a wet and putrid body because of dysentery and the like, or being overcome by a great fever, or having his ligaments severed—reaches the destruction of life. Life continues only for one who obtains edible food at the proper time; for one who does not obtain it, it perishes. And life continues only when consciousness is occurring, not when it is not occurring. Here, by the word ‘etc.’ (implied after ‘life’), there is the inclusion of being bound up with the postures, bound up with cold and heat, and so on. For life continues only when it obtains the equilibrium of the four postures; but when one of them becomes excessive, the life-formations are cut off. Life also continues only when it obtains the equilibrium of cold and heat; for one who is overcome by extreme cold or extreme heat perishes.

Taṇhupādinnassāti iminā hi paccayuppannatākittanena sarasapabhaṅgutaṃyeva vibhāveti. Dukkhānupassanāya taṇhāggāhassa aniccānupassanāya mānaggāhassa anattānupassanāya diṭṭhiggāhassa ujuvipaccanīkabhāvato ekaṃseneva tīhi anupassanāhi gāhāpi vigacchantīti āha “noteva hotī”ti. Ekaṃyeva āgataṃ bāhirāya pathavīdhātuyā antaradhānadassanapavattajotanāya.

‘Of what is clung to by craving’: by this statement of its conditioned nature, he clarifies the fragility of what is delightful. Because contemplation of suffering is directly opposed to the grasp of craving, contemplation of impermanence to the grasp of conceit, and contemplation of not-self to the grasp of views, the grasps are definitely removed by these three contemplations; thus he says, ‘it is not so.’ This one point alone is mentioned for the purpose of illuminating what arises from seeing the disappearance of the external earth element.

Pariggahanti [M 2.0169] dhātupariggahaṇaṃ. Paṭṭhapentoti ārabhanto desento. Sotadvāre balaṃ dassetīti yojanā. Kammaṭṭhānikassa baladassanāpadesena kammaṭṭhānassa ānubhāvaṃ dasseti. Vācāya ghaṭṭanameva vuttaṃ sotadvāre baladassanabhāvato. Balanti ca bāhirāya viya ajjhattikāyapi pathavīdhātuyā acetanābhāvadassanena [V 2.0158] rukkhassa viya akkosantepi paharantepi nibbikāratā. Sampativattamānuppannabhāvenāti tadā paccuppannabhāvena. Samudācāruppannabhāvenāti āpāthagate tasmiṃ aniṭṭhe saddārammaṇe ārammaṇakaraṇasaṅkhātauppattivasena sotadvāre javanavedanā dukkhāti vacanato. Tathā hi “upanissayavasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Vedanādayopīti “vedanā aniccā”ti ettha vuttavedanā ceva saññādayo ca. Te hi phassena samānabhūmikā na pubbe vuttavedanā. Dhātusaṅkhātameva ārammaṇanti yathāpariggahitaṃ pathavīdhātusaṅkhātameva visayaṃ. Pakkhandatīti vipassanācittaṃ aniccantipi dukkhantipi anattātipi sammasanavasena anupavisati. Etena bahiddhāvikkhepābhāvamāha, pasīdatīti pana iminā kammaṭṭhānassa vīthipaṭipannataṃ. Santiṭṭhatīti iminā uparūpari visesāvahabhāvena avatthānaṃ paṭipakkhābhibhavena niccalabhāvato. Vimuccatīti iminā taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiggāhato visesena muccanaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana samuṭṭhānavasena attho vutto “adhimokkhaṃ labhatī”ti. Sotadvāramhi ārammaṇe āpāthagateti idaṃ mūlapariññāya mūladassanaṃ. Sotadvārehi āvajjanavoṭṭhabbanānaṃ ayoniso āvajjayato voṭṭhabbanavasena iṭṭhe ārammaṇe lobho, aniṭṭhe ca paṭigho uppajjati, manodvāre pana “itthī, puriso”ti rajjanādi hoti, tassa pañcadvārajavanaṃ mūlaṃ, sabbaṃ vā bhavaṅgādi. Evaṃ manodvārajavanassa mūlavasena pariññā. Āgantukatāvakālikapariññā pana pañcadvārajavanasseva apubbabhāvavasena itarabhāvavasena ca veditabbā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana satipaṭṭhānasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ vutto eva.

‘They grasp’ means the grasping of the elements. ‘They establish’ means commencing, teaching. The connection is: ‘It shows strength at the ear-door.’ By the pretext of showing strength to one with a meditation subject, it shows the power of the meditation subject. Only the impact of speech is stated, since strength is shown at the ear-door. And ‘strength’ is imperturbability even when one is abused or struck, like a tree, by seeing the non-sentient nature of the internal as well as the external earth element. ‘By the state of having arisen in the present’ means by the state of being present at that time. ‘By the state of arising as an occurrence’ means: because of the statement, ‘The feeling of the impulsion at the ear-door is painful,’ by way of the arising designated as the taking of an object when that undesirable sound-object has come into range. For thus it is said, ‘by way of dependence.’ ‘Feeling and so on’ refers to the feeling stated in ‘feeling is impermanent,’ as well as perception and so on. For these are on the same plane as contact, not the feeling previously mentioned. ‘The object is just what is designated as element’ means the domain is just what is designated as the earth element as it has been grasped. ‘It leaps forward’ means the insight-mind enters by way of comprehending as impermanent, as suffering, and as non-self. By this it states the absence of external distraction; but by this, ‘it becomes serene,’ it states that the meditation subject has entered the path. By this, ‘it stands firm,’ is meant its remaining, which brings further and further special qualities, because of its immovable nature due to having overcome opposing factors. By this, ‘it is liberated,’ is meant special release from the grasp of craving, conceit, and views. In the commentary, however, the meaning is explained by way of origination as: ‘obtains resolution.’ ‘When the object has come into range at the ear-door’: this is the seeing of the root for the full understanding of the root. At the ear-doors, for one who adverts and determines unwisely, greed arises for a desirable object and aversion for an undesirable one; but at the mind-door, lust, etc., occurs towards ‘woman,’ ‘man.’ The root of that is the five-door impulsion, or all of it, beginning with the life-continuum. Thus, there is full understanding by way of the root of the mind-door impulsion. But the full understanding of what is adventitious and temporary should be known only in the case of the five-door impulsion, by way of its unprecedented nature and its different nature. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation is given in the Exposition of the Foundations of Mindfulness.

Yāthāvato dhātūnaṃ pariggaṇhanavasena katapariggahassapi anādikālabhāvanāvasena ayoniso āvajjanaṃ sacepi uppajjati. Voṭṭhabbanaṃ patvāti voṭṭhabbanakiccataṃ patvā. Ekaṃ dve vāre āsevanaṃ labhitvā, na āsevanapaccayaṃ. Na hi upekkhāsahagatāhetukacittaṃ āsevanapaccayabhūtaṃ atthi. Yadi siyā, paṭṭhāne kusalattike paṭiccavārādīsu [M 2.0170] “na maggapaccayā āsevane dve, āsevanapaccayā na magge dve”ti ca vattabbaṃ siyā, “na maggapaccayā āsevane ekaṃ (paṭṭhā. 1.1.221), āsevanapaccayā na magge eka”nti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.152) ca pana vuttaṃ. Ekaṃ dve vāreti ettha ca ekaggahaṇaṃ vacanasiliṭṭhatāya vasena vuttaṃ. Na hi dutiye moghavāre ekavārameva voṭṭhabbanaṃ pavattati. Dvikkhattuṃ vā tassa pavattiṃ sandhāya ekavāraggahaṇaṃ, tikkhattuṃ pavattiṃ sandhāya dvevāraggahaṇaṃ. Tattha dutiyaṃ tatiyañca pavattamānaṃ laddhāsevanaṃ viya hoti. Yasmā pana “voṭṭhabbanaṃ patvā ekaṃ dve vāreāsevanaṃ labhitvā cittaṃ bhavaṅgameva otaratī”ti idaṃ dutiyamoghavāravasena vuttaṃ bhaveyya. So ca ārammaṇadubbalatāya eva hotīti abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ niyamito. Idha pana tikkhānupassanānubhāvena akusaluppattiyā asambhavavasena ayonisova āvajjato ayoniso vavatthānaṃ [V 2.0159] siyā, na yoniso, tasmiñca pavatte mahati atimahati vā ārammaṇe javanaṃ na uppajjeyyāti ayamattho vicāretvā gahetabbo.

Even for one who has grasped the elements as they really are, if unwise adverting arises due to a habit from beginningless time, having reached determining—that is, having fulfilled the function of determining—and having obtained repetition once or twice, it is not by way of repetition condition. For there is no rootless consciousness accompanied by equanimity that is a repetition condition. If there were, in the Paṭṭhāna, in the wholesome triad, in the section on conditional relations, etc., it would have to be stated: ‘Two are not by path condition in the context of repetition, and two are by repetition condition not in the context of the path.’ But instead it is said: ‘One is not by path condition in the context of repetition (Paṭṭh. 1.1.221), and one is by repetition condition not in the context of the path’ (Paṭṭh. 1.1.152). And here, the taking of ‘once or twice’ is stated for the sake of elegance of speech. For in the second futile moment, determining does not occur more than once. The taking of ‘once’ refers to its occurrence twice, and the taking of ‘twice’ refers to its occurrence thrice. In that case, the second and third occurrences are as if they have obtained repetition. However, since it might be said, ‘Having reached determining and obtained repetition once or twice, the mind subsides into the life-continuum,’ this would be stated by way of the second futile moment. And that this occurs only because of the weakness of the object is determined in the Abhidhamma commentary. Here, however, by the power of sharp insight, because of the impossibility of the arising of the unwholesome, for one adverting unwisely there might be unwise determination, not wise determination. And when that occurs, impulsion would not arise toward a great or very great object—this meaning should be investigated and understood.

Etasseva vā satipi duvidhatāparikappane so ca yadi anulome vedanāttike paṭiccavārādīsu “āsevanapaccayā na magge dve, na maggapaccayā āsevane dve”ti ca vuttaṃ siyā, (labbheyya), na ca vuttaṃ. Yadi pana voṭṭhabbanampi āsevanapaccayo siyā, kusalākusalānampi siyā. Na hi āsevanapaccayaṃ laddhuṃ yuttassa āsevanapaccayatāpi dhammo āsevanapaccayo hotīti avutto atthi, voṭṭhabbanassa pana kusalākusalānaṃ āsevanapaccayabhāvo avutto – “kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca kusalo dhammo uppajjati nāsevanapaccayā. Akusalaṃ…pe… nāsevanapaccayā”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.93-94) vacanato paṭikkhitto ca. Athāpi siyā asamānavedanānaṃ vaseneva vuttanti ca, evamapi yathā – “āvajjanā kusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ akusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.417) vuttaṃ, evaṃ “āsevanapaccayena paccayo”tipi vattabbaṃ siyā. Taṃ jātibhedā na vuttanti ce? Bhūmibhinnassa kāmāvacarassa rūpāvacarādīnaṃ āsevanapaccayabhāvo viya jātibhinnassapi bhaveyyāti vattabbo eva siyā, abhinnajātikassa ca vasena yathā – “āvajjanā sahetukānaṃ khandhānaṃ anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti [M 2.0171] vuttaṃ, evaṃ “āsevanapaccayena paccayo”tipi vattabbaṃ siyā, na ca vuttaṃ. Tasmā vedanāttikepi “āsevanapaccayā na magge ekaṃ, na maggapaccayā āsevane eka”nti evaṃ gaṇanāya niddhāriyamānāya voṭṭhabbanassa āsevanapaccayattassa abhāvā ayaṃ moghavāro upaparikkhitvā gahetabbo.

Or, even if there is this twofold conjecture, if in the positive method, in the feeling triad, in the section on conditional relations, etc., it were said: ‘Two are by repetition condition, not in the path group; and two are not by path condition, in the repetition group,’ it could be accepted, but it is not said. However, if determination were also a repetition condition, it would be so for wholesome and unwholesome states as well. For there is no unstated principle that a state fit to receive the repetition condition is itself a repetition condition. But the status of determination as a repetition condition for wholesome and unwholesome states is unstated—and it is rejected by the statement: ‘A wholesome state arises in dependence on a wholesome state not by way of repetition condition. An unwholesome… not by way of repetition condition’ (Paṭṭh. 1.1.93-94). And if it should be said that this is stated only with reference to dissimilar feelings, even so, just as it is said, ‘Adverting is a condition for wholesome aggregates and for unwholesome aggregates by way of contiguity condition’ (Paṭṭh. 1.1.417), so too it should have been said, ‘by way of repetition condition.’ If it is asked, ‘Was it not said because of the difference in kind?’ the rejoinder would be: ‘Just as there is the state of repetition condition for the sense-sphere consciousness in relation to the form-sphere, etc., which are different in plane, so too it could be for what is different in kind.’ And with reference to those of the same kind, just as it is said, ‘Adverting is a condition for aggregates with roots by way of contiguity condition,’ so too it should have been said, ‘by way of repetition condition,’ but it is not said. Therefore, since in the feeling triad too, when the count is determined as, ‘One is by repetition condition, not in the path group; and one is not by path condition, in the repetition group,’ because of the absence of determination’s being a repetition condition, this futile moment should be examined and understood.

Voṭṭhabbanaṃ pana vīthivipākasantatiyā āvaṭṭanato āvajjanā, tato visadisassa javanassa karaṇato manasikāroti ca vattabbataṃ labheyya, evañca katvā paṭṭhāne “voṭṭhabbanaṃ kusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ anantarapaccayena paccayo”tiādi na vuttaṃ, “āvajjanā”icceva (paṭṭhā. 1.1.417) vuttaṃ, tampi voṭṭhabbanato paraṃ catunnaṃ pañcannaṃ vā javanānaṃ ārammaṇapurejātaṃ bhavituṃ asakkontaṃ rūpādiṃ ārabbha pavattamānaṃ voṭṭhabbanaṃ javanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Javanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvāti ca javanassa uppajjanaṭṭhāne dvikkhattuṃ pavattitvāti attho, na javanabhāvenāti. Āsevanaṃ labhitvāti cettha āsevanaṃ viya āsevananti vuttovāyamattho. Vipphārikattā cassa dvikkhattuṃ vā tikkhattuṃ vā pavattiyeva cettha āsevanasadisatā. Vipphārikatāya hi viññattisamuṭṭhāpakatā cassa vuccati. Vipphārikampi javanaṃ viya anekakkhattuṃ appavattiyā asuppatiṭṭhitatāya ca na nippariyāyato āsevanabhāvena [V 2.0160] vattatīti na imassa āsevanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana phalacittesu maggapariyāyo viya pariyāyavasena vuttaṃ.

However, determination, because it turns the process-resultant continuity, might be called ‘adverting’; and because it produces a dissimilar impulsion, it might also be called ‘attention.’ For this reason, in the Paṭṭhāna it is not said, ‘Determination is a condition for the wholesome aggregates by way of contiguity condition,’ and so on, but only ‘Adverting’ is said (Paṭṭh. 1.1.417). Moreover, that determination, arising in relation to a form-object, etc., that is unable to be a prenascent object-condition for the four or five impulsions that follow it, stands in the place of impulsion and then sinks into the life-continuum. ‘To stand in the place of impulsion’ means to occur twice in the place where impulsion arises, not that it has the nature of impulsion. And here, as to ‘having obtained repetition,’ the intended meaning is that it is like repetition. Its similarity to repetition here lies in its very occurrence two or three times due to its pervasiveness. For because of its pervasiveness, it is also said to be the producer of bodily and verbal intimation. Although pervasive, because it does not occur many times like impulsion and is not well-established, it does not function as repetition in the primary sense; thus this was not said with the meaning of actual repetition. In the commentary, however, it is said in a figurative sense, like the figurative use of ‘path’ for the fruition consciousnesses.

Ayanti “sacepī”tiādinā vutto ekavārampi rāgādīnaṃ anuppādanavasena vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto yogāvacaro. Koṭippattoti matthakaṃ patto. Paṭipakkhehi anabhibhūtattā visadavipassanāñāṇatāya tikkhavipassako. Ārammaṇaṃ pariggahitameva hoti “evaṃ me javanaṃ javita”nti sārammaṇassa javanassa hutvā abhāvavavatthāpanassa kammaṭṭhānabhāvato, tathā āvajjanavasena vā taṃ ārammaṇaṃ vissajjetvā tāvadeva mūlakammaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ ārammaṇaṃ pariggahitameva hoti. Dutiyassa pana vasenāti “aparassa rāgādivasena ekavāraṃ javanaṃ javatī”tiādinā vuttassa nātitikkhavipassakassa vasena “tassa dhātārammaṇameva cittaṃ pakkhandatī”tiādinā imasmiṃ sutte āgatattā. “Tamenaṃ upadhipahānāya paṭipannaṃ upadhipaṭinissaggāya kadāci karahaci satisammosā upadhipaṭisaṃyuttā sarasaṅkappā samudācaranti. Dandho udāyi satuppādo, atha kho [M 2.0172] naṃ khippameva pajahati vinodeti byantīkaroti anabhāvaṃ gametī”ti laṭukikopame. Tassa hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sotāpannādayo tāva pajahantu, puthujjano kathaṃ pajahatī”ti codanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā “āraddhavipassako hi satisammosena sahasā kilese uppanne ‘mādisassa nāma bhikkhuno kileso uppanno’ti saṃvegaṃ katvā vīriyaṃ paggayha vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā maggena kilese samugghāteti, iti so pajahati nāmā”ti attho vutto. Tena vuttaṃ – “tassa dhātārammaṇameva cittaṃ pakkhandatītiādinā imasmiṃ sutte āgatattā”tiādi. Indriyabhāvane ca majjhimassa vasena ayamattho veditabbo.

Ayanti: This refers to the meditator spoken of in the passage beginning, “sacepi,” who is doing the work of insight by way of not producing lust and other defilements even once. Koṭippatto: This means having reached the peak, the summit. Because of being unovercome by opposing forces and possessing clear insight-knowledge, one is a sharp meditator. The object is indeed apprehended, as in the thought, “Thus my impulsion has occurred,” because the meditation subject consists in establishing the non-existence of the impulsion after it has occurred with its object. Alternatively, having dismissed that object by way of adverting, the original meditation subject, the fundamental object of meditation, is immediately apprehended. For the second case, that is, for the one who is not a very sharp meditator, spoken of in the passage beginning, “aparassa rāgādivasena ekavāraṃ javanaṃ javatī,” it is said in this discourse: “His mind rushes toward the object consisting of elements,” and so on. As in the Laṭukikopama Sutta: “When one is practicing for the abandonment of attachments, for the relinquishment of attachments, occasionally, due to a lapse in mindfulness, thoughts connected with attachments arise. Slow, Udāyi, is the arising of mindfulness, but one quickly abandons it, dispels it, eliminates it, and brings it to naught.” In its commentary, after posing the objection, “Let the stream-enterers and others abandon them, but how does an ordinary person abandon them?” it is explained: “When defilements suddenly arise in a meditator who has initiated insight due to a lapse in mindfulness, he, stirred by urgency, reflects, ‘A defilement has arisen in a monk such as I!’ He then arouses effort, develops insight, and eradicates the defilements with the path. Thus, it is said, he abandons them.” Therefore, it is said: “His mind rushes toward the object consisting of elements,” and so on, as is found in this discourse. And in the context of the cultivation of the faculties, this meaning should be understood as pertaining to the one of moderate sharpness.

Pariggahavasenāti dhātupariggahavasena. Mammacchedanādivasena pavattaakkosanādiṃ aniṭṭhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ patvā sotadvāre kilamati puggalo, tathā pothanapaharaṇādikaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ patvā kāyadvāre kilamati.

By way of apprehension, that is, by way of apprehension of the elements. A person becomes weary at the ear-door upon encountering an undesirable object, such as reviling that cuts to the quick; similarly, one becomes weary at the body-door upon encountering an undesirable object such as slapping, striking, and the like.

Samudācarantīti sabbaso uddhaṃ ācaranti. Tayidaṃ amanāpehi samudācaraṇaṃ nāma pothanapaharaṇādivasena upakkamanamevāti āha “upakkamantī”ti, bādhantīti attho. Tathāsabhāvoti yathā pāṇippahārādīhi ghaṭṭitamatto vikāraṃ āpajjati, tathāsabhāvo. “Ubhatodaṇḍakena cepi, bhikkhave, kakacenā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.232) ovādadānaṃ nāma anaññasādhāraṇaṃ buddhānaṃyeva āveṇikanti āha “vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatāti anussarantopi…pe… kakacūpamovādaṃ anussarantopī”ti vuttaṃ. Tassapi pariyattidhammabhāvatoti keci[V 2.0161]. Yaṃ pana kakacokantakesupi manussesu appadussanaṃ nibbikāraṃ, taṃ satthusāsanaṃ anussarantopi sammāpaṭipattilakkhaṇaṃ dhammaṃ anussaratiyevāti evaṃ vā ettha attho veditabbo. Bhikkhuno guṇanti ariyadhammādhigamanasiddhaṃ guṇamāha. So ca sabbesampi ariyānaṃ guṇoti taṃ anussarantopi saṅghaṃ anussarati evāti vuttaṃ.

‘They assail’ means they behave completely overbearingly. This assailing by disagreeable ones is indeed an attack by way of striking, hitting, and so on—hence it is said, ‘they attack,’ meaning ‘they harass.’ ‘Of such a nature’ means: just as one undergoes a change as soon as one is struck by a blow from the hand and so on, so is this of such a nature. The giving of the admonition in the passage beginning, “Even if, monks, with a two-edged saw…” (MN 1.232) is unique, an exclusive quality of the Buddhas; hence it is said, “Recollecting too what was spoken by the Blessed One… recollecting the admonition of the Simile of the Saw…” Some say this too pertains to the nature of the Dhamma that is learned. But when, even among people who are like the thorns of a saw, one remains unresentful and undisturbed, that—recollecting the Teacher’s instruction—is indeed recollecting the Dhamma, which is characterized by right practice. This is how the meaning here should be understood. ‘A monk’s virtue’ refers to the virtue accomplished through the attainment of the noble Dhamma. And since that virtue belongs to all the noble ones, recollecting it is also recollecting the Sangha; so it is said.

Vipassanupekkhā adhippetā, tasmā upekkhā kusalanissitā na saṇṭhātīti vipassanāvasena sabbasmimpi saṅkhāragate ajjhupekkhanaṃ na labhatīti attho. Chaḷaṅgupekkhāti chaḷaṅgupekkhā viya chaḷaṅgupekkhā iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu nibbikāratāsāmaññena[M 2.0173]. Tenāha “sā panesā”tiādi. Chaḷaṅgupekkhāṭhāne ṭhapeti “lābhā vata me, suladdhaṃ vata me”tiādinā attamanataṃ āpajjanto.

Equanimity of insight is intended. Therefore, ‘equanimity based on the wholesome does not persist’ means that one does not, by way of insight, attain indifference toward all conditioned things. ‘Six-factored equanimity’ means equanimity that is like the six-factored equanimity, due to the common characteristic of being undisturbed towards the agreeable and disagreeable. Hence it is said, “But this,” and so on. One who experiences joy with thoughts such as, “A gain for me, indeed! A good gain for me, indeed!” places this in the position of the six-factored equanimity.

303. Āpogatanti ābandhanavasena āpo, tadeva āposabhāvaṃ gatattā āpogataṃ, sabhāveneva āpobhāvaṃ vā pattanti attho. Yasmā pana so āpobhāvasaṅkhāto allayūsabhāvo sasambhārapathavīsasambhāraudakādigate sabbasmimpi āpasmiṃ vijjati, tasmā vuttaṃ “sabbaāpesu gataṃ allayūsabhāvalakkhaṇa”nti, dravabhāvalakkhaṇanti attho. “Pakuppatī”ti pākatikapakopaṃ sandhāyāha “oghavasena vaḍḍhatī”ti. Tenāha “ayamassa pākatiko pakopo”ti. Itaraṃ pana dassetuṃ “āposaṃvaṭṭakāle panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ogacchantīti ettha ogamananti pariyādānaṃ adhippetaṃ, na adhogamanamattanti āha “uddhane…pe… pāpuṇantī”ti.

303. ‘Āpogata’ means: it is the water element (āpo) by way of its binding nature; and because it has gone to the state of the water element, it is ‘āpogata.’ The meaning is that it has reached the state of the water element by its own intrinsic nature. Moreover, since that nature of cohesive moisture, known as the state of the water element, is found in all water element—that which is in the earth element with its components, in water with its components, and so on—it is therefore said: “gone into all water elements, characterized by the nature of cohesive moisture,” meaning, characterized by the nature of fluidity. ‘Is agitated’ (pakuppati) is said with reference to its natural agitation: ‘it increases like a flood.’ Hence it is said: “This is its natural agitation.” To show the other case, it is said: “But at the time of the cosmic contraction by water…” and so on. Here, by ‘they go down’ (ogacchanti), complete consumption is intended, not merely descending. Thus it is said: “…up to… they reach…”

304. Sabbatejesu gatanti indhanādivasena anekabhedesu sabbesu tejokoṭṭhāsesu gataṃ pavattaṃ. Yathā pīti eva pītigataṃ, evaṃ tejo eva tejogataṃ, tejanavasena pavattimattanti attho. Evaṃ āpogataṃ, vāyogatañca veditabbanti āha “purime”tiādi. Ekāhikajarādibhāvenāti ekāhikādijarābhedena. Usumajātoti usmābhibhūto. Jīratīti jiṇṇo hoti. Tejodhātuvasena labbhamānā imasmiṃ kāye jarāpavatti pākaṭajarāvasena veditabbāti dassetuṃ “indriyavekallatta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Valipalitādibhāvanti valitapalitabhāvaṃ, aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ sithilabhāvañca. Kuppitenāti khubhitena. Satakkhattuṃ tāpetvā tāpetvā sītūdake pakkhipitvā uddhaṭasappi satadhotasappīti vadanti. Sarīre pakatiusumaṃ atikkamitvā uṇhabhāvo santāpo, sarīrassa dahanavasena pavatto mahādāho paridāhoti ayameva tesaṃ viseso. Asitanti suttaṃ. Khāyitanti khāditaṃ. Sāyitanti assāditaṃ. Sammā paripākaṃ gacchatīti samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā vasena vuttaṃ. Asammāparipākopi visamapākiniyā gahaṇiyā [V 2.0162] vasena veditabbo. Rasādibhāvenāti rasarudhiramaṃsamedanhāruaṭṭhiaṭṭhimiñjasukkabhāvena. Vivekanti puthubhāvaṃ aññamaññaṃ visadisabhāvaṃ. Asitādibhedassa [M 2.0174] āhārassa pariṇāme raso hoti, taṃ paṭicca rasadhātu uppajjatīti attho. Evaṃ rasassa pariṇāme “rudhira”ntiādinā sabbaṃ netabbaṃ.

304. In all fires, it goes—meaning it occurs in all portions of the fire element, of various kinds by way of fuel and so on. Just as joy is joy-gone, so fire is fire-gone, occurring merely by way of the fire element—this is the meaning. Similarly, water-gone and air-gone should be understood, as stated in 'the former' and so on. By the nature of one-day decay, etc.—meaning through the various stages of decay, such as one-day decay. Overcome by heat—meaning overpowered by heat. It decays—meaning it becomes worn out. To show that the process of decay found in this body by way of the fire element should be understood as manifest decay, 'the impairment of the faculties' and so on is stated. The state of wrinkles and gray hair—meaning the condition of wrinkles and gray hair, as well as the looseness of the major and minor limbs. Stirred—meaning agitated. They say that ghee, having been heated a hundred times, immersed in cold water, and then taken out, is called hundred-times-washed ghee. In the body, the state of heat that surpasses the natural warmth is a burning sensation; the great burning that occurs by way of the body's consuming is a scorching heat—this is their distinction. Eaten—meaning swallowed. Chewed—meaning masticated. Savored—meaning tasted. It reaches proper digestion—this is said with reference to the evenly digesting stomach. Improper digestion should also be understood with reference to the unevenly digesting stomach. By the nature of nutritive essence, etc.—meaning through the states of nutritive essence, blood, flesh, fat, sinews, bones, bone marrow, and semen. Separation—meaning distinctness, the dissimilarity from one another. Through the transformation of food of the kinds eaten, etc., nutritive essence arises. Dependent on that, the nutritive essence element arises—this is the meaning. Similarly, through the transformation of nutritive essence, 'blood' and so on should all be inferred.

Haritantanti haritameva, anta-saddena padavaḍḍhanaṃ kataṃ yathā “vanantaṃ suttanta”nti. Cammanillekhanaṃ cammaṃ likhitvā chaḍḍitakasaṭaṃ.

Haritantaṃ means simply green; the word 'anta' is used as a word-extender, as in 'vanantaṃ' and 'suttantaṃ'. Cammanillekhanaṃ is the refuse discarded after scraping leather.

305. Uggārahikkārādīti ettha ādi-saddena uddekakhīpanādipavattakavātānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Uccārapassāvādīti ādi-saddena pittasemhalasikādinīharaṇavātassa ceva usumavātassa ca saṅgaho veditabbo. Yadipi kucchi-saddo udarapariyāyo, koṭṭha-saddena pana abbhantarassa vuccamānattā tadavasiṭṭho udarapadeso idha kucchi-saddena vuccatīti āha “kucchisayā vātāti antānaṃ bahivātā”ti. Samiñjanapasāraṇādīnīti ādi-saddena ālokanavilokanauddharaṇādikā sabbā kāyikakiriyā saṅgahitā. Avasavati udakaṃ etasmāti ossavanaṃ, chadananto. Idhāti imasmiṃ ṭhāne.

305. In Uggārahikkārādi, the term 'ādi' (etc.) should be understood to include winds that cause retching, sneezing, and similar actions. In Uccārapassāvādi, the term 'ādi' here refers to the winds that expel bile, phlegm, lymph, etc., as well as the heat-producing wind. Although the term 'kucchi' generally refers to the abdomen, since 'koṭṭha' denotes the inner cavity, the remaining part of the abdominal region is here referred to by the term 'kucchi.' Thus, it is said: 'The winds dwelling in the kucchi are the winds outside the intestines.' In Samiñjanapasāraṇādīni, the term 'ādi' includes all bodily actions such as looking, glancing around, lifting up, etc. Ossavanaṃ is so called because water flows down from it; it is the eaves of a roof. Idhā means in this place.

306. Nissattabhāvanti anattakataṃ. Yathādassitā hi catasso dhātuyo anattaniyaṃ kevalaṃ dhātumattā nissattanijjīvāti imamatthaṃ dasseti. Parivāritoti parivāritabhāvena ṭhito parivuto. Tenāha “etānī”tiādi, kaṭṭhādīni sannivesavisesavasena ṭhapitānīti adhippāyo. Aññathā agārasamaññāya bhāvato. Tenāha “kaṭṭhādīsu panā”tiādi. Yadatthaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “seyyathāpi, āvuso”tiādi āraddhaṃ, tamatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “yathā kaṭṭhādīnī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

306. The state of being without a being means being rendered as not-self. This shows the meaning that the four elements, as demonstrated, do not belong to a self; they are merely elements, without a being, without life. Surrounded means standing in a state of being surrounded, encompassed. Hence it is said, 'these,' etc., the intention being that things like wood are placed in a specific arrangement. Otherwise, there would be the state of being a 'house' by designation. Therefore, it is stated, 'but in wood, etc.' To clarify and show the meaning for which the Pāli passage beginning 'Just as, friends...' was started, it is said, 'just as wood, etc.'

Kāmaṃ heṭṭhā “mattaṭṭhakassa kāyassā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.302) avibhāgena ekadesena ca upādārūpampi kathitaṃ, tathā vedanādayo khandhabhāvena pariggahetvā na kathitā, tathā taṇhāpi samudayasaccabhāvena. Itarāni pana saccāni sabbena sabbaṃ na kathitāni. Tenevāha “heṭṭhā…pe… na kathitānī”ti. Cakkhupasāde niruddheti cakkhupasāde vinaṭṭhe. Upahateti pubbakimiādīhi upaddute. Palibuddheti pubbādiuppattiyā vinā paṭicchādite. Tajjoti tassānurūpo, cakkhuviññāṇuppattiyā anurūpoti attho. Cakkhussa [M 2.0175] rūpārammaṇe āpāthagate uppajjanamanasikāro hadayasannissayopi cakkhumhi sati hoti, asati na hotīti [V 2.0163] katvā “cakkhuṃ paṭicca uppajjanamanasikāro”ti vutto. Bhavaṅgāvaṭṭanaṃ tassa yathā ārammaṇapaccaye, evaṃ pasādapaccayepi hotīti vuttaṃ “cakkhuñca rūpe ca paṭiccā”ti. Nti cakkhudvāre kiriyamanodhātucittaṃ. Aññavihitassāti aññārammaṇapasutassa. Tadanurūpassāti tesaṃ cakkhurūpatadābhogānaṃ anurūpassa.

To be sure, below, in the passage beginning 'of the body consisting of a measure of bones' (MN 1.302), derived materiality is also mentioned without distinction and as a single part. Similarly, feeling and the other aggregates are not discussed, as they are included by way of being aggregates, and craving, too, is not discussed, as it is included by way of the truth of the origin. But the other truths are not discussed at all. Therefore it is said: 'below …pe… not discussed.' When the eye-sensitivity has ceased means when the eye-sensitivity has been destroyed. Afflicted means afflicted by pus, worms, and so on. Obstructed means covered without the arising of pus and so on. Arisen from that means corresponding to it, that is, corresponding to the arising of eye-consciousness. The attention that arises when a form-object has come into the range of the eye is dependent on the heart-base; it occurs when the eye is present but not when it is absent. Thus it is called 'attention that arises dependent on the eye.' The turning of the life-continuum occurs for it dependent on the object-condition and also on the sensitivity-condition; thus it is said, 'dependent on the eye and on forms.' This refers to the functional mind-element consciousness at the eye-door. Of one dwelling otherwise means of one intent on another object. Suitable for that means suitable for those, namely, the eye, the form, and the advertence to it.

Cattāri saccāni dasseti sarūpato atthāpattito cāti adhippāyo. Tappakāro bhūto, tappakāraṃ vā patto tathābhūto, tassa, yathā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ uppajjati, tādisassa paccayākārasamavetassāti attho. Tisamuṭṭhānarūpanti utukammāhārasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ. Idañca satipi tadā bhavaṅgāvaṭṭanacittasamuṭṭhānarūpe kevalaṃ cakkhuviññāṇasamuṭṭhitarūpassa abhāvamattaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ. Saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti nagaraṃ viya rajje rūpakkhandhe saṅgahetabbataṃ gahetabbataṃ gacchati. “Tathābhūtassā”ti vuttattā vedanādayo cakkhuviññāṇasampayuttāva, viññāṇampi cakkhuviññāṇameva. Saṅkhārāti cetanāva vuttā cetanāpadhānattā saṅkhārakkhandhassāti adhippāyo. Tattha pana phassajīvitindriyamanasikāracittaṭṭhitiyopi saṅkhārakkhandhadhammāva. Ekato saṅgaho “pañcakkhandhā”ti ekato gaṇanā. Samāgamoti yathāsakaṃ paccayavasena samodhānaṃ. Samavāyoti aññamaññassa paccayabhāvena samavetatāya samuditabhāvo.

The intention is that he shows the Four Truths both in their own nature and by implication. Of such a nature means become of that nature, or having reached that nature. The meaning is: of that which is of such a kind, endowed with the conditional structure, just as eye-consciousness arises. Form with a triple origin means form originated from temperature, kamma, and nutriment. And this is said having taken it as merely the absence of form originated from eye-consciousness, even though at that time there is form originated from the consciousness of the life-continuum turning to an object. It comes to be included: just as a city is included in a kingdom, so it comes to be included, to be taken up, in the aggregate of materiality. Because it is said, 'of such a nature,' feeling and the other states are associated with eye-consciousness, and consciousness itself is just eye-consciousness. Formations refers to volition alone, the intention being that volition is the principal factor of the aggregate of formations. Here, however, contact, the life faculty, attention, and the stability of consciousness are also phenomena of the aggregate of formations. A collective inclusion is the single reckoning as 'the five aggregates.' Coming together is the convergence in accordance with their respective conditions. Concomitance is the state of being combined through their co-presence by way of being a condition for one another.

Paccayuppannadhammo paṭicca samuppajjati etasmāti paṭiccasamuppādo, paccayākāro. Paccayadhamme passantopi paccayuppannadhamme passati, te passantopi paccayadhamme passatīti vuttaṃ “yo paṭiccasamuppāda”ntiādi. Chandakaraṇavasenāti taṇhāyanavasena. Ālayakaraṇavasenāti apekkhākaraṇavasena. Anunayakaraṇavasenāti anurajjanavasena. Ajjhogāhitvāti ārammaṇaṃ anupavisitvā viya gilitvā viya niṭṭhapetvā viya daḷhaggahaṇavasena. Chandarāgo vinayati pahīyati etthāti chandarāgavinayo chandarāgapahānañcāti vuccati nibbānaṃ. Āharitvāti pāḷiyaṃ sarūpato anāgatampi atthato ānetvā saṅgaṇhanavasena gahetabbaṃ. Āharaṇavidhiṃ pana dassento “yā imesū”tiādimāha. Imesu tīsu ṭhānesūti yathāvuttesu sukhadukkhādīsu tīsu abhisamayaṭṭhānesu. Diṭṭhīti pariññābhisamayādivasena pavattā sammādiṭṭhi yāthāvadassanaṃ. Evaṃ saṅkappādayopi [M 2.0176] yathārahaṃ veditabbā. Bhāvanāpaṭivedhoti bhāvanāvasena paṭivedho, na ārammaṇakaraṇamattena. Ayaṃ maggoti ayaṃ catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ paṭivijjhanavasena pavatto aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Ettāvatāpīti evaṃ ekasmiṃ cakkhudvāre vatthu pariggahamukhenapi catusaccakammaṭṭhānassa matthakaṃ pāpanena bahuṃ vipulaṃ paripuṇṇameva bhagavato sāsanaṃ kataṃ anuṭṭhitaṃ hoti.

A conditionally arisen phenomenon dependently arises from this; thus it is dependent origination, the conditional structure. One who sees the conditioning phenomena also sees the conditionally arisen phenomena; one who sees these also sees the conditioning phenomena. Thus it is said: 'One who sees dependent origination…' and so on. By way of making desire means by way of craving. By way of making attachment means by way of longing. By way of making compliance means by way of delighting in. Having plunged into means by way of a firm grasp, as if having entered the object, as if having swallowed it, as if having settled it. Desire and lust is disciplined, is abandoned, herein; thus Nibbāna is called the disciplining of desire and lust and the abandoning of desire and lust. Having brought: it should be taken by way of adducing and including by its meaning even what has not come in its own form in the Pāḷi text. To show the method of adducing, he says, 'which in these,' and so on. In these three instances means in the three instances of breakthrough concerning pleasure, pain, etc., as stated. View is right view, the seeing of things as they really are, which proceeds by way of the breakthrough of full understanding, etc. Similarly, intention and the rest should be understood as appropriate. Penetration through development is penetration by way of development, not merely by making it an object. This path is the Noble Eightfold Path that proceeds by way of penetrating the four noble truths. By this much: thus, by bringing the meditation subject of the four truths to its culmination even by way of grasping the basis at a single sense door, the eye-door, the Blessed One’s teaching comes to be accomplished and fulfilled as something great, extensive, and complete.

Uppajjitvā [V 2.0164] niruddhameva bhavaṅgacittaṃ āvajjanacittassa paccayo bhavatīti vuttaṃ “taṃ niruddhampī”ti. Mandathāmagatamevāti mahatiyā niddāya abhibhūtassa vasena vuttaṃ, kapimiddhaparetassa pana bhavaṅgacittaṃ kadāci āvajjanassa paccayo bhaveyyāti. Bhavaṅgasamayenevāti bhavaṅgasseva pavattanasamayena paguṇajjhānapaguṇakammaṭṭhānapaguṇaganthesu tesaṃ paguṇabhāveneva ābhogena vināpi manasikāro pavattati. Tathā hi paguṇaṃ ganthaṃ paguṇabhāveneva nirantaraṃ viya ajjhayamāne aññavihitatāya “ettako gantho gato, ettako avasiṭṭho”ti sallakkhaṇā na hoti. Catusamuṭṭhānampīti sabbaṃ catusamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ, na pubbe viya tisamuṭṭhānamevāti adhippāyo. Pubbaṅgamattā oḷārikattā ca phassacetanāva saṅkhārakkhandhoti gahitā, na aññesaṃ abhāvā. Ekadesameva sammasantoti yathāuddiṭṭhaṃ atthaṃ heṭṭhā anavasesato aniddisitvā ekadesameva niddisanavasena desanāya āmasanto. Imasmiṃ ṭhāneti yathāuddiṭṭhassa atthassa “ajjhattikañceva, āvuso, cakkhu”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 1.306) chadvāravasena niddisanaṭṭhāne. Heṭṭhā parihīnadesananti – “yaṃ upādārūpaṃ cattāro arūpino khandhā upari tīṇi ariyasaccānī”ti niddesavasena parihīnaṃ atthajātaṃ sabbaṃ. Taṃtaṃdvāravasenāti cakkhudvārādikaṃ taṃtaṃdvāravasena. Catusaccavasena āraddhā desanā catusacceneva pariyosāpitāti āha “yathānusandhināva suttantaṃ niṭṭhapesī”ti.

The life-continuum consciousness that has just arisen and ceased becomes a condition for the adverting consciousness; thus it is said, 'that which has ceased…' Affected by sluggishness: this is said with reference to one who is overcome by deep sleep; but for one afflicted by 'monkey-sleep,' the life-continuum consciousness would only sometimes be a condition for adverting. At the very time of the life-continuum means at the time of the occurrence of the life-continuum itself. For those proficient in jhāna, proficient in a meditation subject, or proficient in the texts, attention proceeds even without advertence, simply because of their proficiency. For example, when one is reciting a familiar text continuously, as if without a break, because of being proficient, there is no marking, 'So much of the text has passed, so much remains,' due to being engaged otherwise. Of fourfold origin: the intention is that all materiality is of fourfold origin, not just of triple origin as before. Contact and volition alone are taken as the aggregate of formations because they are primary and coarse, not because the others are absent. Touching upon only a part means touching upon the teaching by way of indicating only a part, without indicating exhaustively below the meaning as it was stated. In this place means in the place where the meaning of what was stated is indicated by way of the six doors, with the words 'The internal eye, friends…' (MN 1.306), etc. The teaching below is deficient: the entire body of meaning that was omitted by way of the explanation: 'derived materiality, the four immaterial aggregates, and the three noble truths above.' By way of the respective doors means by way of the respective doors, the eye-door, etc. The discourse that was begun in terms of the four truths is concluded in terms of the four truths; thus he said: 'He concluded the sutta in accordance with its own connection.'

Mahāhatthipadopamasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

Here ends the Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Greater Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant's Footprint.

9. Mahāsāropamasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Great Simile of the Heartwood Sutta

307. Nacirapakkanteti [M 2.0177][V 2.0165] na ciraṃ pakkante, pakkantassa sato na cirasseva. Saliṅgenevāti muṇḍiyakāsāyaggahaṇādinā attano purimaliṅgeneva. Pāṭiyekke jāteti vipannācāradiṭṭhitāya pakāsanīyakammakaraṇato paraṃ aññatitthiyasadise visuṃ bhūte. Kulaputtoti jātimattena kulaputto. Asambhinnāyāti sambhedarahitāya, jātisaṅkaravirahitāyāti atto. Jātisīsena idha jātivatthukaṃ dukkhaṃ vuttanti āha “otiṇṇoti yassa jāti anto anupaviṭṭhā”ti. Jāto hi satto jātakālato paṭṭhāya jātinimittena dukkhena anto anupaviṭṭho viya vibādhīyati. Jarāyātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Cattāro paccayā labbhantīti lābhā, catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ labbhamānānaṃ sukatabhāvo suṭṭhu abhisaṅkhatabhāvo. Vaṇṇabhaṇananti guṇakittanaṃ. Apaññātāti sambhāvanāvasena na paññātā. Lābhādinibbattiyābhāvadassanañhetaṃ. Tenāha “ghāsacchādanamattampi na labhantī”ti. Appesakkhāti appānubhāvā. Sā pana appesakkhatā adhipateyyasampattiyā ca parivārasampattiyā ca abhāvena pākaṭā hoti. Tattha parivārasampattiyā abhāvaṃ dassento “appaparivārā”ti āha.

307. (Nacirapakkante): Not long after he has departed means not long after departing; for one who has departed, it is not long. (Saliṅgeneva): With his own former sign means with his previous sign, such as taking up the shaven head, ochre robes, and so on. (Pāṭiyekke jāte): Having become separate means having become distinct, like those of other sects, after performing an act of proclamation due to corrupt conduct and wrong view. (Kulaputto): A clansman means a clansman merely by birth. (Asambhinnāya): Unmixed means free from mixture, that is, free from the mingling of birth. (Jātisīsena): By the heading of birth. Here, suffering based on birth is meant. Thus he says: ‘overcome’ means one whom birth has entered into. For a being, from the time of birth, is oppressed as if entered into by the suffering caused by birth. This is the method in regard to aging and so on too. (Lābhā): Gains means the four requisites are obtained. (Sukatābhisaṅkhatā): This means the state of being well-made and the state of being thoroughly prepared of the four requisites that are obtained. (Vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ): The speaking of praise is the extolling of qualities. (Apaññātā): Not known means not known by way of esteem. This is to show the absence of the arising of gain, etc. For this reason he says: ‘they do not obtain even a mere sufficiency of food and clothing.’ (Appesakkhā): Of little influence means of little power. That state of being of little influence becomes manifest through the absence of the accomplishment of sovereignty and the accomplishment of a retinue. There, showing the absence of the accomplishment of a retinue, he says: ‘with a small retinue.’

Sārenapi keci ajānanena aññālābhena vā asārabhūtampi kattabbaṃ karontīti tato visesanatthaṃ “sārena sārakaraṇīya”nti vuttanti taṃ dassento “akkhacakkayuganaṅgalādika”nti āha. Brahmacariyassāti sikkhāttayasaṅgahassa sāsanabrahmacariyassa. Mahārukkhassa maggaphalasārassa ñāṇadassanapheggukassa samādhitacassa sīlapapaṭikassa cañcalasabhāvā saṃsappacārīti ca cattāro paccayā sākhāpalāsaṃ nāma. Tenevāti lābhasakkārasilokanibbattaneneva. Sāro me pattoti imasmiṃ sāsane adhigantabbasāro nāma iminā lābhādinibbattanena anuppattoti vosānaṃ niṭṭhitakiccaṃ āpanno.

Because some, even with heartwood, through ignorance or for other gain, do a task meant for non-heartwood, in order to distinguish from that, it is said: ‘with heartwood, what is to be done with heartwood.’ To show this, he says: ‘an axle, wheel, yoke, plough, etc.’ (Brahmacariyassa): Of the holy life refers to the holy life of the dispensation, which comprises the threefold training. Of the great tree—whose heartwood is the path and fruit, whose softwood is knowledge and vision, whose inner bark is concentration, and whose outer bark is virtue—the four requisites are called the branches and foliage, which are restless in nature and move about. (Teneva): By that very means means by the very production of gain, honor, and renown. (Sāro me patto): I have attained the heartwood means: ‘The heartwood to be realized in this dispensation has been attained by this production of gain, etc.’; he has reached the conclusion, finished the task.

310. Ñāṇadassananti ñāṇabhūtaṃ dassanaṃ visayassa sacchikaraṇavasena pavattaṃ abhiññāñāṇaṃ. Sukhumaṃ rūpanti devādīnaṃ, aññampi vā sukhumasabhāvaṃ rūpaṃ. Tenāha “antamaso…pe… viharantī”ti, dibbacakkhu hi idha ukkaṭṭhaniddesena “ñāṇadassana”nti gahitaṃ.

310. (Ñāṇadassanaṃ): Knowledge and vision means vision that is knowledge, the knowledge of the higher powers, which occurs by way of directly realizing its object. (Sukhumaṃ rūpaṃ): Subtle form means the form of deities and so on, or any other form of a subtle nature. For this reason he says: ‘even down to… they dwell.’ For here the divine eye is taken as ‘knowledge and vision’ by way of a supreme designation.

311. Asamayavimokkhaṃ [M 2.0178][V 2.0166] ārādhetīti ettha adhippetaṃ asamayavimokkhaṃ pāḷiyā eva dassetuṃ “katamo asamayavimokkho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhannañhi samāpajjanasamayopi atthi asamayopi, maggavimokkhena pana vimuccanassa samayo vā asamayo vā natthi. Yassa saddhā balavatī, vipassanā ca āraddhā, tassa gacchantassa tiṭṭhantassa nisīdantassa bhuñjantassa ca maggaphalapaṭivedho nāma na hotīti na vattabbaṃ, iti maggavimokkhena vimuccantassa samayo vā asamayo vā natthīti so asamayavimokkho. Tenāha “lokiyasamāpattiyo hī”tiādi.

311. Regarding ‘he attains the timeless liberation,’ in order to show the timeless liberation intended here from the Pāli canon itself, the words ‘What is the timeless liberation?’ etc., were spoken. For the eight attainments, there is a time and a non-time for attaining them, but for liberation by the path there is no time or non-time for being liberated. It should not be said that for one whose faith is strong and whose insight has been initiated, there is no penetration to the path and fruit while walking, standing, sitting, or eating. Thus, for one being liberated by the path-liberation, there is no time or non-time; this is the timeless liberation. For this reason he says: ‘For the mundane attainments…’ etc.

Na kuppati, na nassatīti akuppā, kadācipi aparihānasabhāvā. Sabbasaṃkilesehi paṭippassaddhivasena cetaso vimuttīti cetovimutti. Tenāha “arahattaphalavimuttī”ti. Ayamattho payojanaṃ etassāti etadatthaṃ, sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ, tassa esā paramakoṭi. Yathāraddhassa sāropamena phalena desanā niṭṭhāpitāti āha “yathānusandhināva desanaṃ niṭṭhapesī”ti. Yaṃ panettha atthato avibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

It is not shaken, it does not perish, thus it is unshakable (akuppā), its nature being never to decline. The liberation of mind (cetovimutti) is the mind’s liberation by way of the pacification of all defilements. For this reason he says, ‘the liberation by the fruit of arahantship.’ This is the purpose, this is the benefit of it—that is, of the holy life in the dispensation; this is its supreme culmination. Because the discourse is concluded with a fruit comparable to heartwood in relation to what was undertaken, he says, ‘he concluded the teaching in accordance with its sequence.’ Whatever here is not explained in terms of its meaning is easy to understand.

Mahāsāropamasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Great Simile of the Heartwood Sutta is completed.

10. Cūḷasāropamasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Shorter Simile of the Heartwood Sutta

312. Piṅgaladhātukoti [V 2.0167] piṅgalasabhāvo piṅgalacchaviko, piṅgalakkhoti vā attho. Pabbajitasamūhasaṅkhāto saṅgho, na sīlādiguṇehi saṅgahitabbabhāvena. Saṅgho etesaṃ atthi parivārabhūtoti saṅghino. Svevāti so eva pabbajitasamūhasaṅkhāto. Ācārasikkhāpanavasenāti attanā parikappitaacelavatādiācārasikkhāpanavasena. Paññātāti yathāsakaṃ samādinnavatavasena ceva viññātaladdhivasena ca paññātā. Laddhikarāti tassā micchādiṭṭhiyā uppādakā. Bahujanassāti puthujanassa. Tassa pana āgamasampadāpi nāma natthi, kuto adhigamoti ekaṃsato andhaputhujjano evāti āha “assutavato andhabālaputhujjanassā”ti. Na hi viññū appasādanīye pasīdanti. Maṅgalesu kātabbadāsakiccakaro dāso maṅgaladāso.

312. (Piṅgaladhātuko): ‘Of a tawny nature’ means of a tawny nature, of a tawny complexion, or the meaning is ‘tawny-eyed.’ The Sangha is designated as the group of renunciants, not in the sense of being comprised of qualities such as virtue. The Sangha is their retinue, thus they are ‘possessors of a Sangha’ (saṅghino). (Sveva): ‘Just that’ refers to that very group of renunciants. (Ācārasikkhāpanavasena): ‘By way of teaching conduct’ means by way of teaching the conduct they have themselves devised, such as the vow of nakedness, etc. (Paññātā): ‘Known’ means known both according to their own adopted vows and according to their recognized attainments. (Laddhikārā): ‘Originators’ are the originators of that wrong view. (Bahujanassa): ‘Of the many people’ means of the worldling. But he has no accomplishment in the scriptures, so how could there be realization? Thus he is entirely a blind worldling. Hence it is said: ‘of an uninstructed, blind, foolish worldling.’ For the wise do not find inspiration in what is uninspiring. A slave who does the work of a slave that is to be done on festive occasions is a maṅgaladāso.

Tantāvutānanti [M 2.0179] tante pasāretvā vītānaṃ. Gaṇṭhanakilesoti saṃsāre bandhanakileso. Evaṃ vāditāyāti evaṃ paṭiññatāya, evaṃ diṭṭhitāya vā. Niyyānikāti niyyānagatisappāṭihīrakā anupārambhabhūtattāti adhippāyo. No ce niyyānikāti ānetvā yojanā. Tesaṃ sabbaññupaṭiññāya abhūtattā tassā abhūtabhāvakathanena tassa brāhmaṇassa na kāci atthasiddhīti āha “nesaṃ aniyyānikabhāvakathanena atthābhāvato”ti.

(Tantāvutānaṃ): ‘Like a spread-out canopy’ means a canopy made by stretching out threads. (Gaṇṭhanakileso): ‘The defilement that ties’ is the defilement that binds in saṃsāra. (Evaṃ vāditāya): ‘Because it is so asserted’ means because it is so professed, or because it is so viewed. (Niyyānikā): ‘Leading to release’ means leading to deliverance, being a sure path, because it is not subject to censure; this is the intention. ‘If it does not lead to release’ is the connection to be supplied. Since their claim to omniscience was false, by stating its falsity, no purpose was accomplished for that brahmin. Hence it is said: ‘because by stating that their teaching does not lead to release, there is no purpose.’

318. Nihīnalokāmise līno ajjhāsayo etassa, na pana nibbāneti. Līnajjhāsayo. Sāsanaṃ sithilaṃ katvā gaṇhāti sikkhāya na tibbagāravattā.

318. His disposition is attached to the base bait of the world; it does not, however, lead to extinguishment. He has a sluggish disposition. He takes up the teaching loosely because he does not have a strong reverence for the training.

323. Heṭṭhāti anantarātītasutte mahāsāropame. Paṭhamajjhānādidhammā vipassanāpādakāti vipassanāya padaṭṭhānabhūtā. Idhāti imasmiṃ cūḷasāropame āgatā. Nirodhapādakāti anāgāmino, arahanto vā nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjituṃ samatthā. Tasmāti nirodhapādakattā. Paṭhamajjhānādidhammā ñāṇadassanato uttaritarāti veditabbā.

323. (Heṭṭhā): ‘Below’ means in the immediately preceding sutta, the Mahāsāropama. (Vipassanāpādakā): ‘A basis for insight’ means the states beginning with the first jhāna are the proximate cause for insight. (Idha): ‘Here’ means what has come in this Cūḷasāropama. (Nirodhapādakā): ‘A basis for cessation’ means non-returners or arahants are capable of attaining the attainment of cessation. (Tasmā): ‘Therefore,’ because they are a basis for cessation, the states beginning with the first jhāna should be understood as higher than knowledge and vision.

Cūḷasāropamasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Shorter Simile of the Heartwood Sutta is completed.

Niṭṭhitā ca opammavaggavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Chapter of Similes is concluded.

4. Mahāyamakavaggo

4. The Great Chapter on the Pairs

1. Cūḷagosiṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Shorter Gosiṅga Sutta

325. Ñātīnaṃ [V 2.0168][M 2.0180] (a. ni. ṭī. 3.6.19) nivāsaṭṭhānabhūto gāmo ñātiko, so eva nātiko. So kira gāmo yesaṃ santako, tesaṃ pubbapurisena attano ñātīnaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvena nivesito, tena “nātiko”ti paññāyittha. Atha pacchā tattha dvīhi dāyādehi dvidhā vibhajitvā paribhutto. Tenāha “dvinnaṃ cūḷapitimahāpitiputtānaṃ dve gāmā”ti. Giñjakā vuccanti iṭṭhakā, giñjakāhiyeva kato āvasatho giñjakāvasatho. Tasmiṃ kira padese mattikā sakkharamarumbavālikādīhi asammissā akaṭhinā saṇhā sukhumā, tāya katāni kulālabhājanānipi silāmayāni viya daḷhāni, tasmā te upāsakā tāya mattikāya dīghaputhulaiṭṭhakā kāretvā tāhi ṭhapetvā dvārabāhavātapānakavāṭatulāyo sesaṃ sabbaṃ dabbasambhārena vinā iṭṭhakāhi eva pāsādaṃ kāresuṃ.
