Tenāha “iṭṭhakāhevā”tiādi.

325. The village that was the dwelling place of relatives (ñātīnaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānabhūto gāmo) is Ñātika; that itself is Nātika. It is said that this village, which belonged to them, was established by their ancestor for the common use of his relatives; hence, it became known as “Nātika.” Later, it was divided in two and enjoyed by two heirs. Hence it is said: “two villages for the two sons of Cūḷapiti and Mahāpiti.” “Giñjakā” are called bricks; a residence made of bricks is a “giñjakāvasatha.” It is said that in that region the clay was unmixed with gravel, pebbles, sand, and the like—it was soft, fine, and smooth. Vessels made from it were as strong as if made of stone. Therefore, those lay followers had long and thick bricks made from that clay and, using them, had a mansion built entirely of bricks, without any other building materials, except for the doorposts, window frames, door panels, and beams. Hence it is said: “only of bricks,” etc.

Gosiṅgasālavanadāyanti gosiṅgasālavananti laddhanāmaṃ rakkhitaṃ araññaṃ. Jeṭṭhakarukkhassāti vanappatibhūtassa sālarukkhassa. Sāmaggirasanti samaggabhāvādiguṇaṃ vivekasukhaṃ. Uparipaṇṇāsake upakkilesasutte (ma. ni. 3.237-238) puthujjanakālo kathito, idha cūḷagosiṅgasutte khīṇāsavakālo kathito. Katakiccāpi hi te mahātherā attano diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraṃ paresaṃ diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjanañca sampassantā paramañca vivekaṃ anubrūhantā sāmaggirasaṃ anubhavamānā tattha viharanti. Tadāti tasmiṃ upakkilesasuttadesanākāle. Teti anuruddhappamukhā kulaputtā. Laddhassādāti vipassanāya vīthipaṭipattiyā adhigatassādā. Vipassanā hi pubbenāparaṃ visesaṃ āvahantī pavattamānā sātisayaṃ pītisomanassaṃ āvahati. Tenāha bhagavā –

(Gosiṅgasālavanadāyaṃ): ‘The Gosiṅga Sāla-tree Wood’ means a protected wilderness that has received the name “Gosiṅga Sāla-tree Wood.” (Jeṭṭhakarukkhassa): ‘Of the eldest tree’ means of the sāla tree that is the lord of the forest. (Sāmaggirasaṃ): ‘The delight of harmony’ means the bliss of seclusion and the quality of being in concord, etc. In the Upakkilesa Sutta in the Uparipaṇṇāsaka, the time of the worldlings is described, while here in the Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta the time of those whose taints are destroyed is described. For although those great elders had done what had to be done, they dwelled there experiencing the delight of harmony, cultivating supreme seclusion, while seeing their own happy dwelling in this very life and the following of their example by others. (Tadā): ‘That time’ means at the time of the discourse on the Upakkilesa Sutta. (Te): ‘They’ means the clansmen headed by Anuruddha. (Laddhassādā): ‘Having obtained the taste’ means those who have attained the taste by the path of practice of insight. For insight, as it proceeds, bringing a special quality from what precedes to what follows, brings exceptional joy and gladness. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Yato yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhati pītipāmojjaṃ, amataṃ taṃ vijānata”nti. (dha. pa. 374);

“Whenever one comprehends the rise and fall of the aggregates, one obtains joy and delight; that is the deathless for those who know.”

Laddhapatiṭṭhā [V 2.0169][M 2.0181] maggaphalādhigamanena. Sati hi maggaphalādhigame sāsane patiṭṭhā laddhā nāma hoti, no aññathā.

‘A footing is gained’ (Laddhapatiṭṭhā) is through the attainment of the path and its fruit. For when there is attainment of the path and its fruit, a footing in the Dispensation is said to be gained, not otherwise.

Kāmaṃ sāriputtamoggallānāpi mahāsāvakapariyāpannāva, aggasāvakabhāvena pana nesaṃ visesadassanatthaṃ “dhammasenāpatimahāmoggallānattheresu vā”ti visuṃ gahaṇaṃ. Satipi hi sāmaññayoge visesavanto visuṃ gayhanti yathā “brāhmaṇā āgatā, vāsiṭṭhopi āgato”ti. Tesu pana visuṃ gahitesupi “asītimahāsāvakesū”ti asītiggahaṇaṃ appakaṃ ūnamadhikaṃ vā gaṇanupagaṃ na hotīti. Antamasoti idaṃ dhammabhaṇḍāgārikassa upaṭṭhākabhāvena āsannacāritāya vuttaṃ. Anīkāti hatthānīkā, hatthānīkato hatthisamūhatoti attho. Kāḷasīho yebhuyyena yūthacaroti katvā vuttaṃ “yūthā nissaṭo kāḷasīho viyā”ti. Kesarī pana ekacarova. Vātacchinno valāhako viyāti vātacchinno pabbatakūṭappamāṇo valāhakacchedo viya. Tesaṃ paggaṇhanatoti yathā nāma jighacchitassa bhojane, pipāsitassa pānīye, sītena phuṭṭhassa uṇhe, uṇhena phuṭṭhassa sīte, dukkhitassa sukhe abhiruci uppajjati, evamevaṃ bhagavato kosambake bhikkhū aññamaññaṃ vivādāpanne disvā apare samaggāvāsaṃ vasante āvajjitassa ime tayo kulaputtā āpāthaṃ āgamiṃsu, atha ne paggaṇhitukāmo upasaṅkami, evāyaṃ paṭipattianukkamena kosambakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vinayanupāyo hotīti. Tenāha “tesaṃ paggaṇhanato”ti. Eteneva pacchimajanataṃ anukampanatoti idampi kāraṇaṃ ekadesena saṃvaṇṇitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ukkaṃsitvāti yathābhūtehi guṇehi sampahaṃsanena visesetvā visiṭṭhe katvā pasaṃsāvasena cetaṃ āmeḍitavacanaṃ.

Although Sāriputta and Moggallāna are indeed included among the great disciples, their separate mention as '...or the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna' is for the purpose of showing their distinction. For even when there is a common connection, those who are distinguished are mentioned separately, as in: 'The brahmins have come, and Vāsiṭṭha too has come.' But even when they are mentioned separately, the mention of 'the eighty great disciples' is so that the count is not included in the reckoning as too little or too much. Even: this is said on account of his close association as the attendant of the Treasurer of the Dhamma. Anīka: this means an elephant corps; the meaning is, from a group of elephants. The black lion is generally a herd-animal; on account of this it is said 'like a black lion that has left its herd.' But the maned lion is solitary. 'Like a cloud torn by the wind': this means like a piece of cloud the size of a mountain peak torn by the wind. On account of supporting them: just as a desire arises in a hungry person for food, in a thirsty person for water, in one afflicted by cold for heat, in one afflicted by heat for cold, in a suffering person for happiness, just so, when the Blessed One saw the bhikkhus at Kosambī fallen into dispute with one another while others were dwelling in harmony, these three clansmen came into his range of attention. Then, wishing to support them, he approached. In this way, this becomes a method of discipline for the Kosambī bhikkhus by way of this course of practice. Hence it is said: 'on account of supporting them.' By this very means, on account of compassion for future generations: this reason too should be seen as partially explained. Having extolled: this means having made them distinguished by praising them with their real qualities; this is a repeated word by way of praise.

Taṃ araññaṃ rakkhati vanasāminā āṇatto. Rakkhitagopitaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ, na mahāvanādi viya apariggahitaṃ. Sīlādippabhedāya attatthāya paṭipannā attakāmā, na apariccattasinehāti āha “attano hitaṃ kāmayamānā”ti. Tenāha “yo hī”tiādi. Bhindeyyāti vināseyya.

He guards that wilderness, having been appointed by the lord of the forest. It is a guarded and protected woodland, not un-owned like a great forest. Desiring their own good are those who have undertaken the practice for their own welfare, which is distinguished by virtue, etc. They are not those with unabandoned affection; thus he says, 'desiring their own welfare.' Therefore it is said: 'For he who,' etc. Would break: this means would destroy.

Dubbalamanussāti paññāya dubbalā aviddasuno manussā. Tānīti abhijātiādīsu uppannapāṭihāriyāni. Cīvaragabbhena paṭicchādetvāti cīvarasaṅkhāte ovarake nigūhitvā viya. Na hi cīvarapārupanamattena buddhānubhāvo paṭicchanno hoti. “Mā sudha kocimaṃ buddhānubhāvaṃ aññāsī”ti pana [M 2.0182] tathārūpena iddhābhisaṅkhārena taṃ chādetvā gato bhagavā tathā vutto. Tenāha “aññātakavesena agamāsī”ti.

Feeble men: this means men who are feeble in wisdom, unlearned. These: this means the miracles that arose in connection with his noble birth, etc. Having concealed it with the robe-chamber: this means as if having hidden it in an inner chamber called a 'robe-chamber.' For the Buddha’s power is not concealed merely by the wearing of a robe. But the Blessed One is spoken of thus because, thinking, 'Let no one at all recognize this Buddha-power,' he departed having concealed it with such a volitional formation of psychic power. Hence it is said: 'he went in an unknown guise.'

Abhikkamathāti [V 2.0170] padaṃ abhimukhabhāvena vidhimukhena vadatīti āha “ito āgacchathā”ti. Buddhānaṃ kāyo nāma suvisuddhajātimaṇi viya sobhano, kiñci malaṃ apanetabbaṃ natthi, kimatthaṃ bhagavā pāde pakkhālesīti āha “buddhāna”ntiādi.

The word 'approach' is spoken as a command with a sense of facing towards; thus he says, 'Come here.' The body of the Buddhas is beautiful like a perfectly pure, high-quality gem. There is no stain to be removed. Why did the Blessed One wash his feet? It is said: 'For the Buddhas,' etc.

326. Anuruddhāti vā ekasesanayena vuttaṃ virūpekasesassapi icchitabbattā, evañca katvā bahuvacananiddesopi samatthito hoti. Iriyāpatho khamatīti sarīrassa lahuṭṭhānatāya catubbidhopi iriyāpatho sukhappavattiko. Jīvitaṃ yāpetīti yāpanālakkhaṇaṃ jīvitaṃ imaṃ sarīrayantaṃ yāpeti sukhena pavatteti. Uḷuṅkayāguṃ vā kaṭacchubhikkhaṃ vāti idaṃ makaravuttiyā missakabhattena yāpanaṃ vattanti katvā vuttaṃ. Tenāha “bhikkhācāravattaṃ pucchatī”ti.

326. 'Anuruddhā' is said by way of the method of ellipsis, since an ellipsis of dissimilar items is also intended; and having done so, the plural designation is also justified. The posture is tolerable: this means that, due to the lightness of the body, all four postures proceed with ease. He maintains his life: this means he maintains, he makes proceed with ease, this bodily mechanism, the life which has the characteristic of maintenance. 'Gruel from a ladle or almsfood from a spoon': this is said because they speak of subsisting on mixed food in the 'crocodile’s manner.' Therefore, it is said: 'He asks about the practice of the alms-round.'

Aññamaññaṃ saṃsandatīti satipi ubhayesaṃ kalāpānaṃ paramatthato bhede pacurajanehi duviññeyyanānattaṃ khīrodakasammoditaṃ accantameva saṃsaṭṭhaṃ viya hutvā tiṭṭhati. Tenāha “visuṃ na hoti, ekattaṃ viya upetī”ti. Piyabhāvadīpanāni cakkhūni piyacakkhūni. Piyāyati, piyāyitabboti vā piyoti. Samaggavāsassa yaṃ ekantakāraṇaṃ, taṃ pucchanto bhagavā “yathā kathaṃ panā”tiādimāhāti “kathanti kāraṇapucchā”ti vuttaṃ. Yo nesaṃ mettāsahitānaṃyeva kammādīnaṃ aññamaññasmiṃ paccupaṭṭhānākāro, taṃ sandhāya “katha”nti pucchā. Tathā hi parato “evaṃ kho mayaṃ, bhante”tiādinā therehi vissajjanaṃ kathitaṃ.

They accord with one another: even though there is a difference between the two groups in the ultimate sense, the diversity, which is hard to be discerned by ordinary people, stands as if it were utterly mixed like milk and water blended together. Hence it is said: 'it is not separate, it seems to attain oneness.' Eyes that show a state of affection are affectionate eyes. Dear means one who is dear or one who should be held dear. The Blessed One, asking about the sole cause of their harmonious living, said, 'But how then...?' Thus it is said, 'how' is a question about the cause. The question 'how' refers to the mode of mutual presence of their actions, etc., which are accompanied by loving-kindness. For further on the explanation by the elders is stated, beginning with: 'Thus, venerable sir....'

Mittaṃ etassa atthīti mettaṃ, kāyakammaṃ. Āvīti pakāsaṃ. Rahoti appakāsaṃ. Yañhi uddissa mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ paccupaṭṭhapeti, taṃ tassa sammukhā ce, pakāsaṃ hoti, parammukhā ce, appakāsaṃ. Tenāha “āvi ceva raho cāti sammukhā ceva parammukhā cā”ti. Itarānīti parammukhā kāyavacīkammāni. “Tatthā”tiādinā saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “yaṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sammajjanādivasena paṭijaggitabbayuttaṃ ṭhānaṃ vā. Tathevāti yathā sammukhā kate mettākāyakamme vuttaṃ, tatheva[M 2.0183]. “Kacci khamanīya”nti evamādikā kathā sammodanīyakathā. Yathā parehi saddhiṃ attano chiddaṃ na hoti, tathā paṭisanthāravasena pavattā kathā paṭisanthārakathā. “Aho tadā therena mayhaṃ dinno ovādo, dinnā anusāsanī”ti evaṃ kālantare saritabbayuttā, chasāraṇīyapaṭisaṃyuttā vā kathā sāraṇīyakathā. Suttapadaṃ nikkhipitvā tassa atthaniddesavasena sīlādidhammapaṭisaṃyuttā kathā dhammīkathā. Sarena suttassa uccāraṇaṃ sarabhaññaṃ. Pañhassa ñātuṃ icchitassa atthassa pucchanaṃ pañhapucchanaṃ. Tassa yathāpucchitassaādisanaṃ [V 2.0171] pañhavissajjanaṃ. Evaṃ samannāharatoti evaṃ manasikaroto, evaṃ mettaṃ upasaṃharatoti attho.

He has a friend (mittaṃ), thus it is loving-kindness (mettaṃ); this is bodily action. Openly means manifestly. Secretly means not manifestly. For when one establishes loving-kindness in bodily action with someone in mind, if it is face-to-face, it is manifest; if it is behind their back, it is not manifest. Hence it is said: 'Openly and secretly,' that is, 'both face-to-face and behind one's back.' The others refers to bodily and verbal actions done behind one's back. By 'In that regard,' etc., what was stated concisely is elaborated upon by what is said beginning with 'For when…' Or a place that should be looked after by way of sweeping, etc. Similarly means: just as it is said concerning loving-kindness in bodily action done face-to-face, so it is here. Talk such as, 'I hope you are keeping well?' is congenial talk. Talk that proceeds by way of a friendly welcome, so that there is no rift between oneself and others, is hospitable talk. Talk that should be recalled at a later time, such as, 'Ah, at that time the elder gave me advice and instruction,' or talk connected with the six qualities of cordiality, is memorable talk. Having laid down a phrase from the sutta, talk connected with the Dhamma, such as on virtue, etc., by way of explaining its meaning, is Dhamma talk. The recitation of a sutta with a melodious voice is chanting. The asking of a question about a meaning one wishes to know is questioning. The answering of that question as it was asked is replying to the question. Thus bringing it to mind means thus attending, thus directing loving-kindness; this is the meaning.

Ekato kātuṃ na sakkā, tasmā nānā. Hitaṭṭhenāti attano viya aññamaññassa hitabhāvena. Nirantaraṭṭhenāti antarābhāvena bhedābhāvena. Aviggahaṭṭhenāti avirodhabhāvena. Samaggaṭṭhenāti sahitabhāvena. Paribhaṇḍaṃ katvāti bahalatanumattikālepehi limpetvā. Cīvaraṃ vā dhovantīti attano cīvaraṃ vā dhovanti. Paribhaṇḍaṃ vāti attano paṇṇasālāya paribhaṇḍaṃ vā karonti.

It cannot be done by one alone; therefore, it is diverse. For the sake of benefit means in the sense of being beneficial to one another as to oneself. By way of uninterruptedness means by way of the absence of an interval, the absence of a division. By way of non-conflict means by way of the absence of opposition. By way of harmony means by way of being united. Having done the finishing work means having plastered it with thick or thin layers of clay. Or washing a robe means they wash their own robe. Or doing finishing work means they do the finishing work on their own leaf-hut.

327. Paṭiviruddhā evāti etthāpi “yebhuyyenā”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Tesaṃ appamādalakkhaṇanti tesaṃ appamajjanasabhāvaṃ. Kacci pana vo anuruddhā samaggāti etthāpi voti nipātamattaṃ, paccattavacanaṃ vā, kacci tumheti evamattho veditabbo. Samuggapātinti samuggapuṭasadisaṃ pātiṃ.

327. 'Opposed indeed': here too, the word 'for the most part' should be brought in and connected. 'Their characteristic of heedfulness' means their nature of non-negligence. 'But are you, Anuruddhas, harmonious?': here too, 'vo' is merely a particle, or it is a second person pronoun, so the meaning should be understood as 'but are you?' 'A bowl with a lid' means a bowl resembling a casket.

Paṇṇasālāyaṃ anto bahi ca sammajjanena sodhitaṅgaṇatā vattapaṭipatti. Paṭivisamattamevāti attano yāpanapaṭivisamattameva. Osāpetvāti pakkhipitvā. Pamāṇamevāti attano yāpanapamāṇameva. Vuttanayena jahitvāti pāḷiyaṃ vuttanayena jahitvā.

The practice of the observance is the state of having a courtyard cleaned by sweeping both inside and outside the leaf-hut. 'Only a portion' means only a portion for one's own sustenance. 'Having stored it away' means having put it in. 'Only the measure' means only the measure for one's own sustenance. 'Having abandoned in the way stated' means having abandoned according to the way stated in the Pāli text.

Hatthena hatthaṃ saṃsibbantāti attano hatthena itarassa hatthaṃ daḷhaggahaṇavasena bandhantā. Vilaṅgheti desantaraṃ pāpeti etenāti vilaṅghako, hattho. Hattho eva vilaṅghako hatthavilaṅghako, tena hatthavilaṅghakena.

'Clasping hand with hand' means binding the other's hand with one's own hand by way of a firm grasp. 'Vilaṅghaka' is that by which one makes something cross over to another place; this is the hand. The hand itself is the 'vilaṅghaka,' hence 'hatthavilaṅghaka' (hand-crosser); by means of that hand-crosser.

Taṃ akhaṇḍaṃ katvāti taṃ tīsupi divasesu dhammassavanaṃ pavattanavasena akhaṇḍikaṃ katvā. Etanti “pañcāhikaṃ kho panā”tiādivacanaṃ. Pañcame pañcame [M 2.0184] ahani bhavatīti pañcāhikaṃ. Bhagavatā pucchitena anuruddhattherena. Pamādaṭṭhānesuyevāti aññesaṃ pamādaṭṭhānesuyeva. “Pamādaṭṭhānesuyevā”ti vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “aññesañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Papañcakaraṇaṭṭhānānīti kathāpapañcassa karaṇaṭṭhānāni vissaṭṭhakathāpavattanena kammaṭṭhāne pamajjanaṭṭhānāni. Tatthāpi “mayaṃ, bhante, kammaṭṭhānaviruddhaṃ na paṭipajjāmā”ti sikhāppattaṃ attano appamādalakkhaṇaṃ thero dasseti. Ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ muñcitvāti pana idaṃ tadā vihārasamāpattīnaṃ vaḷañjābhāvena vuttaṃ.

'Having made it unbroken' means having made the hearing of the Dhamma on all three days uninterrupted by causing it to proceed. 'This' refers to the statement beginning, 'But for five days…' 'Pañcāhikaṃ' means occurring on every fifth day. This was said by the Venerable Anuruddha when asked by the Blessed One. 'Only in the grounds for negligence' means only in what are grounds for negligence for others. To make the meaning of what was said as 'Only in the grounds for negligence' clearer, what is said beginning 'For others…' was stated. 'Grounds for making proliferation' means grounds for the proliferation of talk; grounds for neglecting the meditation subject by engaging in unrestrained conversation. Therein, the elder shows his own characteristic of heedfulness that has reached its peak, saying: 'Venerable sir, we do not practice what is contrary to the meditation subject.' 'Having relinquished such a state': this was said because at that time there was no use of the meditative attainments.

328. Jhānassa [V 2.0172] adhippetattā “alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso”icceva vuttaṃ. Attano sammāpaṭipannatāya satthu cittārādhanatthaṃ tassa ca visesādhigamassa satthu paccakkhabhāvato thero “kiñhi no siyā, bhante”ti āha. Yāvadevāti yattakaṃ kālaṃ ekaṃ divasabhāgaṃ vā sakalarattiṃ vā yāva satta vā divase.

328. Because jhāna is intended, it is said thus: 'a superior state of noble knowledge and vision is enough.' Because of his own proper practice, for the sake of pleasing the Teacher's mind, and because that attainment of a superior state was directly perceived by the Teacher, the elder said: 'Indeed, venerable sir, what would not be ours?' 'For as long as' means for whatever period of time: for part of a day, or a whole night, or for up to seven days.

329. Samatikkamāyāti sammadeva atikkamanāya. Sati hi upari visesādhigame heṭṭhimajjhānaṃ samatikkantaṃ nāma hoti paṭippassaddhi ca. Tenāha “paṭippassaddhiyā”ti. Ñāṇadassanavisesoti kāraṇūpacārena vuttoti veditabbo. Vedayitasukhatoti vedanāsahitajjhānasukhato vā phalasukhato vā. Avedayitasukhanti nibbānasukhaṃ viya vedanārahitaṃ sukhaṃ. Avedayitasukhanti ca nidassanamattametaṃ, taṃ pana aphassaṃ asaññaṃ acetananti sabbacittacetasikarahitameva. Tato ca satipi rūpadhammappavattiyaṃ tassa acetanattā sabbaso saṅkhāradukkhavirahitatāya santatarā paṇītatarā ca nirodhasamāpattīti vuccate. Tenāha “avedayitasukhaṃ santataraṃ paṇītataraṃ hotī”ti. Tena vuttaṃ “imamhā cā”tiādi.

329. 'For transcending' means for rightly transcending. For when there is the attainment of a superior state above, the lower jhāna is transcended and there is also pacification. Hence it is said, 'for pacification.' 'A superior state of knowledge and vision' should be understood as spoken figuratively, by way of cause. 'From the bliss that is felt' means from the bliss of jhāna accompanied by feeling or from the bliss of fruition. 'The bliss that is not felt' is bliss devoid of feeling, like the bliss of Nibbāna. 'The bliss that is not felt' is a mere designation; it is without contact, without perception, without volition, that is, utterly devoid of all mind and mental factors. And then, although there is a continuation of material phenomena, because it is non-volitional and completely free from the suffering of formations, the attainment of cessation is called more peaceful and more sublime. Hence it is said: 'The bliss that is not felt is more peaceful and more sublime.' Therefore it is stated, 'from this too,' etc.

330. Sāmaggirasānisaṃsameva nesaṃ bhagavā kathesi ajjhāsayānukūlattā tassa. Anusāvetvāti anupagamanavasena sammadeva ārocetvā. “Anusaṃsāvetvā”ti vā pāṭho, so evattho. Tato paṭinivattitvāti etarahi bhagavato ekavihāre ajjhāsayoti satthu manaṃ gaṇhantā “idheva tiṭṭhathā”ti vissajjitaṭṭhānato nivattitvā[M 2.0185]. Pabbajjādīnīti ādi-saddena upasampadā-visuddhi-dhutakammaṭṭhānānuyoga-jhānavimokkha-samāpatti-ñāṇadassana-maggabhāvanā-phalasacchikiriyādike saṅgaṇhāti. Adhigantvāpīti pi-saddena yathādhigatānampi. Attano guṇakathāya aṭṭiyamānāti bhagavantaṃ nissāya adhigantvāpi dhammādhikaraṇaṃ satthuvihesābhāvadīpane bhagavato pākaṭaguṇānaṃ kathāya aṭṭiyamānāpīti yojanā. Devatāti taṃtaṃsamāpattilābhiniyo devatā. Mukhaṃ me sajjanti mukhaṃ me kathane samatthaṃ, kathane yogyanti attho.

330. The Blessed One spoke to them only on the benefits of the taste of harmony because this was suitable to their inclination. 'Having announced' means having rightly informed them by way of not approaching. Or the reading is 'anusaṃsāvetvā'; the meaning is the same. 'Then having turned back' means: having grasped the Teacher's mind that 'Now the Blessed One's inclination is for dwelling alone,' they turned back from the place where they had been dismissed with the words, 'Stay right here.' 'Going forth, etc.': by the word 'etc.' it includes higher ordination, purification, ascetic practices, application to meditation subjects, jhāna, liberation, attainments, knowledge and vision, development of the path, realization of the fruit, and so on. 'Even having attained': the word 'pi' (even) also includes 'of what had been attained.' The construction is: even though they were distressed by talk of their own virtues, which they had attained in dependence on the Blessed One, and even though they were distressed by talk of the Blessed One's manifest virtues when explaining, in the context of the Dhamma, the absence of trouble for the Teacher. 'Deities' means the deities who were attainers of those respective attainments. 'My mouth is ready' means my mouth is capable of speaking, suitable for speaking.

331. Evaṃ āgatoti evaṃ āṭānāṭiyasutte āgato. Paliveṭhenteti codente. Maccharāyantīti attano guṇānaṃ bhagavatopi ārocanaṃ asahamānā maccharāyantīti so cintetīti katvā vuttaṃ.

331. 'Thus it comes' means thus it comes in the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta. 'Surrounding' means reproving. 'Being possessive': this was said because he thought: 'They are being possessive, being unable to bear the announcement of their own qualities even to the Blessed One.'

01 Tesaṃ [V 2.0173] lābhāti tesaṃ vajjirājūnaṃ vajjiraṭṭhavāsīnañca manussattaṃ, patirūpadesavāsādiko, bhagavato tiṇṇañca kulaputtānaṃ dassanavandanadānadhammassavanādayo lābhā. Suladdhā lābhāti yojanā. Pasannacittaṃ anussareyyāti taṃ kulañhetaṃ sīlādiguṇe cittaṃ pasādetvā anussareyya. Vuttaṃ tesaṃ “anussaraṇampāhaṃ, bhikkhave, tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahūpakāraṃ vadāmī”ti (itivu. 104; saṃ. ni. 5.184).

'Theirs is a gain' refers to the gains of those Vajjian kings and the inhabitants of the Vajjian country—human existence, dwelling in a suitable region, etc.—and the gains for the three clansmen, such as seeing and venerating the Blessed One, giving, and hearing the Dhamma. The construction is: 'A gain well gained.' 'Should recollect with a confident mind' means that this clan, having generated confidence in their qualities such as virtue, should recollect them. It is said of them: 'Recollection of those bhikkhus, I say, bhikkhus, is of great benefit.'

Cūḷagosiṅgasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Concealed Meaning in the Commentary on the Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta is concluded.

2. Mahāgosiṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Mahāgosiṅga Sutta.

332. Kocidevāti [V 2.0174] gosiṅgasālavanasāmantato niviṭṭhesu yo koci gāmo gocaragāmo bhavissati, tasmā anibaddhabhāvato gocaragāmo na gahito, vasanaṭṭhānameva paridīpitaṃ, tato eva araññanidānakaṃ nāmetaṃ. Sabbatthāti devaloke manussaloke ca. Thirakārakehīti sāsane thirabhāvakārakehi. Savanante jātattāti catusaccagabbhassa dhammassavanassa pariyosāne ariyāya jātiyā jātattā. Yathā paṭivedhabāhusaccaṃ ijjhati, tathā dhammassa savanato sāvakā[M 2.0186]. Sūriyo viya bhāsuraguṇaraṃsitāya mohandhakāravidhamanato. Cando viya ramaṇīyamanoharasītalaguṇatāya kilesapariḷāhavūpasamato. Sāgaro viya gambhīrathiravipulānekaguṇatāya ṭhitadhammasabhāvato. Guṇamahantatāya therassa abhiññātatā, guṇamahantatā ca suttesu āgatanayeneva ñātabbāti taṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “na kevala”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Sīhanādasuttanti majjhimanikāye āgataṃ mahāsīhanādasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 1.146). Therapañhasuttanti suttanipāte aṭṭhakavagge āgataṃ sāriputtasuttaṃ (su. ni. 961-981). Therasīhanādasuttanti imassa ca therassa janapadacārikāya satthu sammukhā sīhanādasuttaṃ. Abhinikkhamananti therasseva mahatā ñātiparivaṭṭena mahatā ca bhogaparivaṭṭena saha gharāvāsapariccāgo abhinikkhamanaṃ. Esa nayo ito paresupi. Yadidanti nipāto, yo ayanti attho.

332. 'Kocidevāti' refers to any village near the Gosiṅga Sāla forest that may serve as a village for alms-gathering. Since it was not specifically designated, the alms-resort village is not mentioned; only the dwelling place is indicated, hence it is called 'having its source in the wilderness.' 'Everywhere' means in both the deva world and the human world. 'By those who make firm' refers to those who establish stability in the Dispensation. 'Born at the end of hearing' means being born with the noble birth at the conclusion of hearing the Dhamma, which is the womb of the Four Noble Truths. Just as proficiency in penetration and extensive learning is achieved, so too are they disciples through hearing the Dhamma. Like the sun, by the radiance of his virtuous qualities, he dispels the darkness of delusion. Like the moon, by his pleasing, charming, and cool qualities, he pacifies the fever of defilements. Like the ocean, by his depth, stability, vastness, and multitude of qualities, he is established in the true nature of the Dhamma. The elder's renown is due to the greatness of his qualities, and this greatness of qualities is to be understood by the method found in the suttas. Therefore, to show this in detail, it is said, 'Not only...' etc. 'The Lion's Roar Sutta' refers to the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta found in the Majjhima Nikāya. 'The Elder's Question Sutta' refers to the Sāriputta Sutta in the Aṭṭhakavagga of the Sutta Nipāta. 'The Elder's Lion's Roar Sutta' refers to the Lion's Roar Sutta proclaimed by this elder in the Teacher's presence during his travels through the countryside. 'Going forth' refers to the elder's renunciation of household life along with a great retinue of relatives and a great circle of wealth. This is the method for the others as well. 'Yadidaṃ' is a particle meaning 'that is'.

Mahāpaññe bhikkhū gahetvāti āyasmato kira sāriputtattherassa parivārabhikkhūpi mahāpaññā eva ahesuṃ. Dhātuso hi sattā saṃsandanti. Sayaṃ iddhimātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ panattho dhātusaṃyuttena (saṃ. ni. 2.99) dīpetabbo – gijjhakūṭapabbate gilānaseyyāya nisinno bhagavā ārakkhatthāya parivāretvā vasantesu sāriputtamoggallānādīsu ekamekaṃ attano parisāya saddhiṃ caṅkamantaṃ voloketvā bhikkhū āmantesi – “passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, sāriputtaṃ sambahulehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ caṅkamantanti. Evaṃ, bhante. Sabbe kho ete, bhikkhave, bhikkhū mahāpaññā”ti sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

“Having taken monks of great wisdom”: Indeed, the attendant monks of the Venerable Elder Sāriputta were also of great wisdom. For beings converge according to their element. The same principle applies in cases like “himself possessing psychic power.” This meaning, however, should be illustrated by the Connected Discourses on Elements (SN 14.15): While the Blessed One was lying on his sick-bed at the Vulture Peak, surrounded for protection by Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and other monks, he observed each of them walking up and down with their own retinue. He then addressed the monks: “Do you see, monks, Sāriputta walking up and down with a large number of monks?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “All these monks, monks, are of great wisdom.” The entire passage should be elaborated.

Vananteti upavanante. Meghavaṇṇāyāti nīlābhāya. Samuddakucchito uggacchantassa viya upaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Cakkavāḷapabbatamatthakasamīpe ābhāpharaṇavasena pavattiyā “pācīnacakkavāḷapabbatamatthake”ti vuttaṃ, na cakkavāḷapabbatamatthake candamaṇḍalassa vicaraṇato. Tathā [V 2.0175] sati lokantarikanirayesupi candimasūriyānaṃ ābhā phareyya. Ubbedhavasena hi cakkavāḷapabbatassa vemajjhato candimasūriyā vicaranti. Sālakusumapabhānaṃ atirattatāya vuttaṃ “lākhārasena siñcamānaṃ viyā”ti. Upagāyamānā viyāti payirupāsanavasena upecca gāyamānā viya[M 2.0187]. Kāya nu kho ajja ratiyāti ajja jhānasamāpattiratiyā eva nu kho, udāhu dhammasākacchāratiyā dhammadesanāratiyāti cintesi.

“At the edge of the forest” means at the edge of the grove. “Like the color of a cloud” refers to a blue hue. “As if rising from the ocean’s depths” is said with reference to its rising appearance. “At the summit of the eastern mountain range” is said because the light spreads near the peak of the Cakkavāḷa mountain, not because the moon’s disk moves over the Cakkavāḷa mountain. If that were so, the light of the moon and sun would also fill the Lokantarika hells. For the moon and sun move at mid-height of the Cakkavāḷa mountain. “Like pouring molten lac” is said due to the extreme redness of the Sāl tree blossoms. “As if singing” means approaching and singing in homage. “In what joy today?” he wondered—is it in the joy of meditative absorption, or in the joy of Dhamma discussion and Dhamma teaching?

Dve candamaṇḍalāni viya paramasobhaggappattāya kantiyā. Dve sūriyamaṇḍalāni viya ativiya suvisuddhasamujjalāya guṇavibhūtiyā. Dve chaddantanāgarājāno viya mahānubhāvatāya. Dve sīhā viya tejussadatāya. Dve byagghā viya anolīnavuttitāya. Sabbapāliphullamevāti sabbameva samantato vikasitaṃ.

“Like two moon-disks” describes their supreme beauty and loveliness. “Like two sun-disks” signifies their exceedingly pure and very bright glory of virtue. “Like two Chaddanta elephant kings” denotes their great power. “Like two lions” reflects their majestic energy. “Like two tigers” suggests their unshrinking conduct. “All in full bloom” means absolutely everything around is fully blossomed.

333. Kathā upacarati pavattati etthāti kathāupacāro, savanūpacāro padeso, taṃ kathāupacāraṃ. Ramaṇīyameva rāmaṇeyyakaṃ. Ujjaṅgaleti lūkhapadese kaṭhinapadese. Dosehi itā apagatāti dosinā ta-kārassa na-kāraṃ katvā. Dibbā maññe gandhāti devaloke gandhā viya. Divi bhavāti dibbā. Dve therāti sāriputtattheraānandattherā. Ānandatthero tāva mamāyatu akhīṇāsavabhāvato, sāriputtatthero kathanti? Na idaṃ mamāyanaṃ gehassitapemavasena, atha kho guṇabhattivasenāti nāyaṃ doso.

333. “Where conversation approaches and proceeds” is the place of conversation, a place within earshot. “Delightful indeed” is rāmaṇeyyakaṃ. “Ujjaṅgale” means in a rough place, in a hard place. “Dosinā” (moonlit): The commentary explains this as “gone away from faults” (dosehi itā), with the ‘t’ of a hypothetical dositā having been changed to ‘n’. “Divine scents, it seems” are like the fragrances in the heavenly world. “Divine” means existing in heaven. “The two elders” are the Elders Sāriputta and Ānanda. Elder Ānanda might still have possessiveness since he was not yet one whose taints were destroyed. But what about the Elder Sāriputta? This possessiveness is not based on affection connected with the household life, but on devotion to virtues—thus, this is not a fault.

Anumatiyā pucchā anumatipucchā, anumatiggahaṇatthaṃ pucchanaṃ. Tattha yasmā adhammikampi vuddhassa anumatiṃ itaro paṭikkhipituṃ na labhati, tena sā anujānitabbāva hoti, tasmā saṅghakhuddakato paṭṭhāya anumati pucchitabbā. Tenāha “anumatipucchā nāmesā”tiādi. Khuddakato paṭṭhāyāti kaṇiṭṭhato paṭṭhāya. Paṭibhāti upaṭṭhātīti paṭibhānaṃ, yathādhippeto attho, taṃ paṭibhānaṃ. Sikhāppattā vepullappattā na bhavissati padesañāṇe ṭhitehi bhāsitattā. Sikhāppattā vepullappattā bhavissati sabbaññutaññāṇena saṃsanditattā. Vuttamevatthaṃ upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha paccatthikā aṭṭiyanti dukkhāyanti etenāti aṭṭo, vinicchitabbavohāro. Gāmabhojakanti yasmiṃ gāme so uppanno, taṃ gāmabhojakaṃ. Janapadabhojakanti yasmiṃ janapade so uppanno, taṃ janapadabhojakaṃ. Mahāvinicchayaamaccanti yasmiṃ rajje so janapado, tassa rājadhāniyaṃ mahāvinicchayaamaccaṃ. Senāpatinti yassa rañño so amacco, tassa senāpatiṃ. Tathā uparājanti[M 2.0188]. Idaṃ panettha pakaticārittavasena vuttaṃ upameyyatthānurūpatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aparāparaṃ na sañcarati vinicchayanārahena vinicchitabhāvato.

A question about permission is a permission-question; it is a question for the purpose of receiving permission. Herein, since another cannot refuse the permission of an elder even if it is improper, it must be granted. Therefore, permission should be asked starting from the most junior in the Sangha. Hence it is said, “This is called the permission question,” and so on. “Starting from the most junior” means beginning with the youngest. “Paṭibhānaṃ” (inspiration) is what occurs to one, that is, the intended meaning. It will not reach the peak and full development because it is spoken by those established in partial knowledge. It will reach the peak and full development because it is connected with the knowledge of omniscience. To clarify the meaning that has been stated by way of a simile, the words “Just as…” and so on were stated. “Aṭṭo” (a legal case) is that by which opponents are troubled and pained; it is a matter to be decided. “Gāmabhojaka” means the headman of the village in which the case arose. “Janapadabhojaka” means the governor of the province in which the case arose. “Mahāvinicchayaamacca” means the chief justice in the capital of the kingdom where that province is located. “Senāpati” means the commander-in-chief of the king whom that minister serves. Similarly, the viceroy. Here, this is said according to the natural course of things, as is appropriate to the subject of the simile. It does not proceed from one to another because it has been decided by one who is competent to decide.

Pakaṭṭhānaṃ [V 2.0176] (a. ni. ṭī. 2.4.22) ukkaṭṭhānaṃ sīlādiatthānaṃ bodhanato, sabhāvaniruttivasena buddhādīhi bhāsitattā ca pakaṭṭhānaṃ vacanappabandhānaṃ āḷīti pāḷi, pariyattidhammo. Purimassa atthassa pacchimena atthena anusandhānaṃ anusandhi. Atthamukhena pana pāḷipadesānampi anusandhi hotiyeva, so ca pubbāparānusandhi-pucchānusandhi-ajjhāsayānusandhi-yathānusandhivasena catubbidho. Taṃtaṃdesanānaṃ pana pubbāparasaṃsandanaṃ pubbāparaṃ. Pāḷivasena anusandhivasena pubbāparavasenāti paccekaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Uggahitanti byañjanaso atthaso ca uddhaṃ uddhaṃ gahitaṃ, pariyāpuṇanavasena ceva paripucchāvasena ca hadayena gahitanti attho. Vaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇatthikehi sotabbato sutaṃ, pariyattidhammo, taṃ dhāretīti sutadharo. Yo hi sutadharo, sutaṃ tasmiṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ hoti suppatiṭṭhitaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “sutassa ādhārabhūto”ti. Tenāha “yassa hī”tiādi. Ekapadaṃ ekakkharampi avinaṭṭhaṃ hutvā sannicīyatīti sannicayo, sutaṃ sannicayo etasminti sutasannicayo. Ajjhosāyāti anupavisitvā. Tiṭṭhatīti na mussati.

Pāḷi: The term pāḷi is explained as a line (āḷi) of excellent (pakaṭṭha) compositions of words, because it makes known excellent things such as virtue, and because it was spoken by the Buddhas and others with natural expression; it means the scriptural doctrine. The connection (anusandhi) is the linking of a former meaning with a later meaning. Moreover, a connection of Pāḷi passages also occurs by way of the meaning, and this is fourfold: sequential connection, question-based connection, intention-based connection, and connection as appropriate. The linking of the various teachings should be connected individually: through the Pāḷi, through connection, or through sequence. “Uggahitaṃ” means what has been progressively learned, both in terms of wording and meaning, through mastery and inquiry, grasped by the heart. “Sutaṃ” is what is to be heard by those seeking liberation from the suffering of the round; it is the scriptural doctrine. One who retains it is called a “sutadhara.” For in one who is a sutadhara, what has been heard is well-established; thus, it is said, “He is a repository for what has been heard.” Hence it is stated, “For whom…” and so on. An accumulation (sannicayo) is when even a single word or a single syllable is accumulated without being lost; he in whom there is an accumulation of what has been heard is a “sutasannicayo.” “Ajjhosāya” means having settled upon. “Tiṭṭhati” means it does not disappear.

Ṭhitā paguṇāti paguṇā vācuggatā. Niccalitanti aparivattitaṃ. Saṃsanditvāti aññehi saṃsanditvā. Samanuggāhitvāti paripucchāvasena atthaṃ ogāhetvā. Pabandhassa vibandhābhāvato gaṅgāsotasadisaṃ, “bhavaṅgasotasadisa”nti vā pāṭho, akittimaṃ sukhappavattīti attho. Suttekadesassa suttassa ca vacasā paricayo idha nādhippeto, vaggādivasena pana adhippetoti āha “suttadasaka…pe… sajjhāyitā”ti, “dasa suttāni gatāni, dasa vaggāgatā”tiādinā sallakkhetvā vācāya sajjhāyitāti attho. Manasā anu anu pekkhitā bhāgaso nijjhāyitā cintitā manasānupekkhitā. Rūpagataṃ viya paññāyatīti rūpagataṃ viya cakkhussa vibhūtaṃ hutvā paññāyati. Suppaṭividdhāti nijjaṭaṃ niggumbaṃ katvā suṭṭhu yāthāvato paṭividdhā.

Established and familiar: Familiar, learned by heart. “Unshaken”: Unchanged. “Having compared”: Having compared with others. “Having thoroughly grasped”: Having penetrated the meaning by way of inquiry. Like the stream of the Ganges, because of the absence of any impediment to the flow—or the reading is “like the stream of the life-continuum”—the meaning is that its flow is effortless and pleasant. Here, verbal familiarity with a part of a sutta or a whole sutta is not intended, but it is intended by way of sections, etc. Hence it is said, “a decade of suttas… chanted.” The meaning is that having noted, “Ten suttas have passed, ten sections have passed,” etc., one chants it verbally. “Mentally scrutinized”: Repeatedly examined with the mind, reflected upon part by part, considered. It appears as if it has assumed a physical form; that is, it appears having become manifest to the eye. “Well penetrated”: Having disentangled it and cleared it of undergrowth, it is well penetrated in accordance with reality.

Pajjati attho ñāyati etenāti padaṃ, tadeva atthaṃ byañjetīti byañjananti āha “padameva atthassa byañjanato padabyañjana”nti. Akkharapāripūriyā padabyañjanassa [M 2.0189] parimaṇḍalatā, sā pana pāripūrī evaṃ veditabbāti āha “dasavidhabyañjanabuddhiyo aparihāpetvā”ti. Aññaṃ upārambhakaranti yathānikkhittasuttato aññaṃ tassa ananulomakaṃ suttaṃ āharati. Tadatthaṃ otāretīti tassa āhaṭasuttasseva atthaṃ vicāreti. Tassa kathā aparimaṇḍalā nāma hoti atthassa aparipuṇṇabhāvato. Yathānikkhittassa suttassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanāvaseneva suttantarampi ānento bahi ekapadampi na gacchati nāma. Amakkhentoti avināsento. Taṃ taṃ atthaṃ suṭṭhu vavatthitaṃ katvā dassento tulikāya paricchindanto viya. Gambhīrataramatthaṃ [V 2.0177] gamento gambhīramātikāya udakaṃ pesento viya. Uttānamātikāya hi mariyādaṃ ottharitvā udakaṃ aññathā gaccheyya. Ekaṃyeva padaṃ anekehi pariyāyehi punappunaṃ saṃvaṇṇento padaṃ koṭṭento sindhavājānīyo viya. So hi vaggitāya gatiyā pade padaṃ koṭṭento gacchati. Kathāmaggena tassa kathā parimaṇḍalā nāma hoti dhammato atthato anusandhito pubbāparato ācariyuggahatoti sabbaso paripuṇṇabhāvato.

Meaning is attained, is known, by this; thus it is a 'pada' (word). It expresses that very meaning; thus it is a 'byañjana' (expression). Hence it is said: 'The word itself, by expressing the meaning, is a word-expression.' The roundness of the word-expression comes from the completeness of the letters. And that completeness should be understood thus, as he said: 'without abandoning the tenfold understanding of expressions.' 'Finding fault with another' means that one brings up another discourse that is not in conformity with the discourse as laid down. 'He brings down its meaning' means that he investigates the meaning of only that discourse that was brought up. His talk is called 'unrounded' because of the incompleteness of the meaning. When explaining the meaning of the discourse as laid down, even when bringing in another discourse, he does not go outside by even a single word. 'Not smearing' means not destroying. Showing each and every meaning after having well established it is like demarcating with a painter's brush. Leading to a deeper meaning is like sending water through a deep channel. For with a shallow channel, having overstepped the boundary, the water would go elsewhere. Explaining one and the same word again and again in many ways is like a Sindh thoroughbred striking hoof on hoof. For it goes with a bounding gait, striking hoof on hoof. His talk is called 'rounded' by way of the path of discourse because it is entirely complete in every way: in regard to the Dhamma, the meaning, the connection, the sequence, and what has been received from the teacher.

Anuppabandhehīti vissaṭṭhehi āsajjamānehi. Nātisīghaṃ nātisaṇikaṃ nirantaraṃ ekarasañca katvā parisāya ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ dhammaṃ kathento vissaṭṭhāya kathāya katheti nāma, na aññathāti dassento “yo bhikkhū”tiādimāha. Araṇiṃ manthento viya, uṇhakhādanīyaṃ khādanto viyāti sīghaṃ sīghaṃ kathanassa udāharaṇaṃ, gahitaṃ gahitamevātiādi laṅghetvā kathanassa. Purāṇapaṇṇantaresu hi paripātiyamānagodhā kadāci dissati, evamekaccassa atthavaṇṇanā katthaci na dissati. Ohāyāti ṭhapetvā. Yopītiādinā ekarūpena kathāya akathanaṃ dasseti. Petaggi nijjhāmataṇhikapetassa mukhato niccharaṇakaaggi. Vitthāyatīti appaṭitānatamāpajjati. Kenaci rogena dukkhaṃ patto viya nitthunanto. Kandanto viyāti ukkuṭṭhiṃ karonto viya. Appabandhā nāma hoti sukhena appavattabhāvato. Ācariyehi dinnanaye ṭhitoti ācariyuggahaṃ amuñcanto, yathā ca ācariyā taṃ taṃ suttaṃ saṃvaṇṇesuṃ, teneva nayena saṃvaṇṇentoti attho. Acchinnadhāraṃ katvāti “nātisīghaṃ nātisaṇika”ntiādinā heṭṭhā vuttanayena avicchinnaṃ kathāpabandhaṃ katvā. Anusayasamugghātāyāti iminā tassā kathāya arahattapariyosānataṃ dasseti[M 2.0190]. Evarūpenāti nayidaṃ ekavacanaṃ tattakavasena gahetabbaṃ, atha kho lakkhaṇe pavattanti dassento “tathārūpeneva bhikkhusatena bhikkhusahassena vā”ti vuttaṃ. Pallaṅkenāti pallaṅkapadesena, pallaṅkāsanantenāti attho. Iminā nayenāti vārantarasādhāraṇaṃ atthaṃ atidisati, asādhāraṇaṃ pana vakkhatevāti.

'Uninterruptedly' means clearly and without getting stuck. When one speaks the Dhamma not too fast and not too slow, continuously and with a single flavour, in a way suitable to the assembly's disposition, one is said to speak with clear speech, not otherwise; showing this, he said: 'Whatever monk…' and so on. 'Like one drilling a fire-stick' or 'like one eating hot food' are examples of speaking very quickly; 'what is grasped is just grasped,' etc., is an example of speaking while skipping over things. For in old palm-leaf manuscripts a lizard that has fallen in between is sometimes seen; so too, for some, the explanation of the meaning is not seen somewhere. 'Having left behind' means having set aside. By 'And whoever…' etc., he shows the not speaking of the talk in a uniform way. The fire of a 'peta' is the fire issuing from the mouth of a 'peta' consumed by thirst. 'It spreads out' means it becomes unsupported. Groaning like one who has met with suffering from some disease. 'Like one wailing' means like one making an outcry. It is called 'unconnected' because it does not proceed easily. 'Standing in the method given by the teachers' means not abandoning what has been received from the teachers; the meaning is that just as the teachers explained this or that sutta, in that very same way one should explain it. 'Having made it an unbroken stream' means having made the flow of the talk uninterrupted in the way stated above with 'not too fast, not too slow,' etc. 'For the uprooting of the underlying tendencies': by this he shows that that talk culminates in arahantship. 'Of such a kind': this singular is not to be taken as just that much, but rather, showing that it proceeds in terms of a characteristic, it is said 'by a hundred or a thousand monks of such a kind.' 'With the cross-legged posture' means in the region of the cross-legged posture; the meaning is 'ending with the cross-legged seat.' 'By this method': he extends this to the meaning common to other occasions, but the uncommon meaning will be stated.

334. Āramati etenāti ārāmo.

334. One delights in this, thus it is a park.

335. Dhuvasevananti niyatasevitaṃ. Pāsādapariveṇeti pāsādaṅgaṇe. Nābhiyā patiṭṭhitānanti nābhiyā bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhitānaṃ. Arantarānīti aravivarāni taṃtaṃarānaṃ vemajjhaṭṭhānāni.

335. 'Constantly frequented' means regularly frequented. 'In the palace precinct' means in the palace courtyard. 'Established at the hub' means of those established on the ground at the hub. 'The interstices of the spokes' means the openings of the spokes, the places in the very middle of those spokes.

336. Samādinnaaraññadhutaṅgo āraññiko, na araññavāsamattena.

336. A forest-dweller is one who has undertaken the forest-dweller's ascetic practice, not one merely by reason of living in the forest.

337. Na [V 2.0178] osādentīti na avasādenti, na avasādanāpekkhā aññamaññaṃ pañhaṃ pucchantīti attho. Pavattinīti paguṇā.

337. 'They do not cause to sink' means they do not disparage; the meaning is that they do not ask questions of one another with the expectation of disparaging. 'Fluent' means skilled.

338. Lokuttarā vihārasamāpatti nāma therassa arahattaphalasamāpattiyo, pariyāyato pana nirodhasamāpattipi veditabbā.

338. The supramundane abiding in attainment refers to the elder's attainments of the fruit of arahantship; however, alternatively, it should also be understood as the attainment of cessation.

339. Sādhukāro ānandattherassa dinno. Tenāha bhagavā “yathā taṃ ānandova sammā byākaramāno byākareyyā”tiādi. Sammāti suṭṭhu, yathāajjhāsayanti adhippāyo. Yena hi yaṃ yathācittaṃ kathitaṃ, taṃ sammā kathitaṃ nāma hoti. Sampattavasena hi yathākārī tathāvādī sobhati. Tenāha “attano anucchavikamevā”tiādi. Bahussuto bhikkhu tattha tattha sutte sīlādīnaṃ āgataṭṭhāne tesaṃ suviditattā yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāno tāni paripūretīti āha “sīlassa āgataṭṭhāne”tiādi. Maggādipasavanāya vipassanāgabbhaṃ gaṇhāpetvā paripākaṃ gametvāti attho.

339. The expression of approval was given to the Elder Ānanda. For that reason the Blessed One said: 'Just as Ānanda, explaining correctly, would explain,' and so on. 'Correctly' means well; the intention is 'according to his disposition.' For whatever is spoken by someone in accordance with his mind is called 'correctly spoken.' For by way of success, one who acts as he speaks shines. For that reason he said: 'only what is suitable for oneself,' and so on. A learned monk, because he is well-acquainted with those places in the suttas where morality and other virtues are mentioned, fulfills them by practicing as instructed. Thus it is said: 'in the place where morality is mentioned,' and so on. The meaning is: having made him grasp the 'embryo of insight' for the purpose of generating the path, etc., and having brought it to maturity.

340. “Eseva nayo”ti atidesavasena saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivaranto “āyasmā hi revato”tiādimāha.

340. 'This is the very method': elaborating on the meaning stated concisely by way of extension, he said: 'For the Venerable Revata…' and so on.

342. Aparepi [M 2.0191] nānappakāre kileseti aparepi nānappakāre dosamohādikilese. Dhunitvāti vidhametvā.

342. 'And other various defilements' means other various defilements such as hatred, delusion, and so on. 'Having shaken off' means having dispelled.

343. Āyasmā mahāmoggallāno evaṃ byākāsīti sambandho. Sakalampi cakkhuviññāṇavīthigataṃ cittaṃ cakkhuviññāṇanti aggahetvā cakkhusannissitameva pana viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tadanantaraṃ sampaṭicchanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ santīraṇantiādinā saṇhaṃ sukhumaṃ atiittarakhaṇavantaṃ cittantaraṃ cittanānattaṃ. Khandhādīnañca nānattasaṅkhātaṃ khandhantarādi. Pathavīkasiṇe paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā tatheva tatiyaṃ jhānantiādinā ārammaṇaṃ anukkamitvā jhānasseva ekantarikabhāvena ukkamanaṃ jhānokkantikaṃ nāma. Pathavīkasiṇe paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā puna tadeva tejokasiṇetiādinā jhānaṃ anukkamitvā ārammaṇasseva ekantarikabhāvena ukkamanaṃ ārammaṇokkantikaṃ nāma. “Paṭhamajjhānaṃ pañcaṅgika”ntiādinā yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ duvaṅgikanti jhānaṅgamattasseva vavatthāpanaṃ aṅgavavatthānaṃ. “Idaṃ pathavīkasiṇaṃ…pe… idaṃ odātakasiṇa”nti ārammaṇamattasseva vavatthāpanaṃ ārammaṇavavatthānaṃ. Pathavīkasiṇe paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā tattheva itaresampi samāpajjanaṃ [V 2.0179] aṅgasaṅkanti. Pathavīkasiṇe paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā tadeva āpokasiṇeti evaṃ sabbakasiṇesu ekasseva jhānassa samāpajjanaṃ ārammaṇasaṅkanti. Ekatovaḍḍhanaṃ ubhatovaḍḍhananti idaṃ khandhādidesanāyaṃ labbhati. Abhidhammabhājanīye hi vedanākkhandhaṃ bhājento bhagavā tike gahetvā dukesu pakkhipi, duke gahetvā tikesu pakkhipi, idaṃ ekatovaḍḍhanaṃ. Tike ca duke ca ubhatovaḍḍhananīhārena kathesi, idaṃ ubhatovaḍḍhanaṃ. Evaṃ sesakhandhesu dhātāyatanādīsu ca yathārahaṃ vibhaṅgappakaraṇe (vibha. 32-33; 155-156, 183-184) abhidhammabhājanīye āgatanayena veditabbaṃ. Tenāha “ābhidhammikadhammakathikasseva pākaṭa”nti. Khandhādīsu sabhāvadhammesu tīsu lakkhaṇesu paññattiyaṃ samayantaresu ca kosallābhāvato ayaṃ sakavādo ayaṃ paravādoti na jānāti. Tato eva sakavādaṃ…pe… dhammantaraṃ visaṃvādeti. Khandhādīsu pana kusalatāya ābhidhammiko sakavādaṃ…pe… na visaṃvādeti.

343. The connection is: 'The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna explained thus.' Not taking the entire cognitive process that has entered the course of eye-consciousness to be eye-consciousness, but rather that the consciousness dependent on the eye is eye-consciousness, immediately after that is reception, immediately after that is investigation, and so on—this succession of subtle, refined, extremely momentary states of consciousness is the diversity of consciousness. And what is known as the diversity of the aggregates, etc., is the distinction of aggregates, etc. Having attained the first jhāna on the earth kasiṇa and then likewise the third jhāna, and so on, by skipping over a jhāna in an alternating manner is called 'jhāna-skipping.' Having attained the first jhāna on the earth kasiṇa and then again that same jhāna on the fire kasiṇa, and so on, by maintaining the jhāna and skipping over an object in an alternating manner is called 'object-skipping.' 'The first jhāna is five-factored,' and so on, up to 'the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is two-factored'—the determination of just the jhāna-factors is 'factor-determination.' 'This is the earth kasiṇa… this is the white kasiṇa'—the determination of just the object is 'object-determination.' Having attained the first jhāna on the earth kasiṇa and then attaining the other jhānas on that same object is 'factor-transition.' Having attained the first jhāna on the earth kasiṇa and then that same jhāna on the water kasiṇa, and so on—attaining one and the same jhāna on all the kasiṇas is 'object-transition.' 'Single-sided increase' and 'double-sided increase'—this is found in the exposition of the aggregates, etc. For in the Abhidhamma Analysis, when analyzing the feeling aggregate, the Blessed One took triads and placed them in dyads, and took dyads and placed them in triads; this is 'single-sided increase.' He spoke by the method of increasing both triads and dyads; this is 'double-sided increase.' So too it should be understood as applicable to the remaining aggregates, elements, bases, etc., according to the method that has come down in the Book of Analysis in the Abhidhamma Analysis. Therefore it is said: 'It is clear only to a Dhamma-speaker who is an expert in Abhidhamma.' Because of a lack of skill in the three characteristics concerning intrinsic-nature phenomena in the aggregates, etc., in concepts, and in other systems, one does not know: 'This is my own teaching, this is another's teaching.' For that very reason one contradicts one's own teaching… and another teaching. But because of skill in the aggregates, etc., the expert in Abhidhamma does not contradict his own teaching.

344. Cittaṃ [M 2.0192] attano vase vattetuṃ sakkoti paṭisaṅkhānabhāvanābalehi pariggaṇhanasamatthattā. Idāni tamatthaṃ byatirekato anvayato ca vibhāvetuṃ “duppañño hī”tiādimāha. Tattha sabbānassāti sabbāni assa. Visevitavipphanditānīti kilesavisūkāyikāni ceva duccaritavipphanditāni ca. Bhañjitvāti madditvā. Bahīti kammaṭṭhānato bahi puthuttārammaṇe.

344. One is able to make the mind proceed under one's own control because of the ability to grasp it by the powers of reflection and cultivation. Now, to make that meaning clear by way of negative and positive concomitance, he said: 'For one of weak wisdom…' and so on. Therein, 'sabbānassā' means 'sabbāni assa' (all his). 'Scattered throbbings' means both the exhibitions of the defilements and the throbbings of misconduct. 'Having broken' means having crushed. 'Outside' means outside the meditation subject, on a variety of objects.

345. Pariyāyenāti ettha pariyāya-saddo “atthi khvesa, brāhmaṇa, pariyāyo”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 3-9) viya kāraṇatthoti āha “sobhanakāraṇaṃ atthī”ti. Yadi bhagavā – “idha, sāriputta, bhikkhu pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto”tiādinā attano mahābodhipallaṅkaṃ sandhāyāha, evaṃ sante sammāsambuddheheva saṅghārāmo sobhetabbo, na aññehīti āpannanti āha “apica pacchimaṃ janata”ntiādi. Nibbānatthāya paṭipattisāraṃ etassāti paṭipattisāro, taṃ paṭipattisāraṃ. Nippariyāyenevāti kenaci pariyāyena lesena vinā mukhyena nayeneva. Yo “arahattaṃ appatvā na vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti daḷhasamādānaṃ katvā nisinno taṃ adhigantvāva uṭṭhahati. Evarūpena idaṃ gosiṅgasālavanaṃ sobhati, sāsane sabbārambhānaṃ tadatthattāti attho. Āsavakkhayāvahaṃ paṭipattiṃ ārabhitvā āsavakkhayeneva desanāya pariyosāpitattā yathānusandhināva desanaṃ niṭṭhapesīti.

345. “By means of a way”: here, the term “way” is used in the sense of a reason, as in passages like, “There is indeed, brahmin, a way” (AN 8.11; Pārā. 3–9), hence it is said, “There is a beautiful reason.” If the Blessed One had said, “Here, Sāriputta, a monk returns from his almsround after the meal,” etc., referring to his own great Bodhi-seat, then it would follow that only a Perfectly Enlightened One could beautify a monastery, not others—which would be a faulty conclusion; hence it is said, “Moreover, for future generations,” etc. The compound `paṭipattisāro` means 'one whose essence of practice is for the sake of Nibbāna'; it refers to that very essence of practice. “Without any indirect way”: without any indirect way or pretext, but directly by the principal method. Whoever sits down with the firm resolve, “I will not rise until I attain arahantship,” rises only after achieving it. In this way, this Gosiṅga sāla-wood forest is beautified, because in the Dispensation, all endeavors are for that purpose. Having undertaken the practice leading to the destruction of the taints, he concluded the teaching with the destruction of the taints itself, thus completing the discourse according to the natural sequence.

Mahāgosiṅgasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The exposition revealing the concealed meaning of the commentary on the Mahāgosiṅga Sutta is concluded.

3. Mahāgopālakasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Greater Discourse on the Cowherd

346. Tatthāti [V 2.0180] gopālakasutte. Tisso kathāti (a. ni. ṭī. 3.11.17) tisso aṭṭhakathā, tividhā suttassa atthavaṇṇanāti attho. Ekekaṃ padaṃ nāḷaṃ mūlaṃ etissāti evaṃsaññitā ekanāḷikā, ekekaṃ vā padaṃ nāḷaṃ atthaniggamanamaggo etissāti ekanāḷikā. Tenāha “ekekapadassa atthakathana”nti. Cattāro aṃsā bhāgā atthasallakkhaṇūpāyā etissāti caturassā. Tenāha “catukkaṃ bandhitvā kathana”nti. Niyamato nisinnassa āraddhassa [M 2.0193] vatto saṃvatto etissā atthīti nisinnavattikā, yathāraddhassa atthassa visuṃ visuṃ pariyosāpikāti attho. Tenāha “paṇḍitaṃ gopālakaṃ dassetvā”tiādi. Ekekapadassāti piṇḍatthadassanavasena bahunnaṃ padānaṃ ekajjhaṃ atthaṃ akathetvā ekamekassa padassa atthavaṇṇanā. Ayaṃ sabbattheva labbhati. Catukkaṃ bandhitvāti kaṇhapakkhe upamūpameyyadvayaṃ, tathā sukkapakkheti idaṃ catukkaṃ yojetvā. Ayaṃ īdisesu eva suttesu labbhati. Pariyosānagamananti keci tāva āhu – “kaṇhapakkhe upamaṃ dassetvā upamā ca nāma yāvadeva upameyyasampaṭidānatthāti upameyyatthaṃ āharitvā saṃkilesapakkhaniddeso ca vodānapakkhavibhāvanatthāyāti sukkapakkhampi upamūpameyyavibhāgena āharitvā suttatthassa pariyosāpana”nti. Kaṇhapakkhe upameyyaṃ dassetvā pariyosānagamanādīsupi eseva nayo. Apare pana “kaṇhapakkhe sukkapakkhe ca taṃtaṃupamūpameyyatthānaṃ visuṃ visuṃ pariyosāpetvāva kathanaṃ pariyosānagamana”nti vadanti. Ayanti nisinnavattikā. Idhāti imasmiṃ gopālakasutte. Sabbācariyānaṃ āciṇṇāti sabbehipi pubbācariyehi ācaritā saṃvaṇṇitā, tathā ceva pāḷi pavattāti.

346. “Therein” refers to the Gopālaka Sutta. “Three discussions” (as mentioned in the Subcommentary to the Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.11.17) means three types of commentary, a threefold explanation of the meaning of the discourse. “Ekanāḷikā” is so called because each word is like a single reed or root. Alternatively, it is called “ekanāḷikā” because it follows a single path of extracting the meaning of each word. Hence it is said, “explaining the meaning of each word.” “Caturassā” means it has four parts—methods for discerning the meaning. Hence it is said, “tying together and explaining in fourfold divisions.” “Nisinnavattikā” means it has a fixed sequence for one who is seated and engaged, systematically bringing each intended meaning to a conclusion. Hence it is said, “having shown the wise cowherd,” etc. “Explaining each word” means not explaining the meaning of many words together in a group, but elaborating on the meaning of each word individually. This method is universally applicable. “Tying together in fourfold divisions” refers to pairing the dark side with its simile and counterpart, and similarly the bright side. This fourfold arrangement is found in such discourses. Regarding “bringing to a conclusion,” some say: “First, presenting the simile on the dark side, for similes serve only to illustrate their counterparts, then extracting the meaning of the counterpart to explain the section on defilement; and since the exposition of the side of defilement is for the purpose of clarifying the side of purification, one also brings in the bright side with its division into simile and counterpart, thus bringing the meaning of the discourse to its conclusion.” The same method applies when presenting the counterpart on the dark side and bringing the discussion to its conclusion. Others, however, say: “Bringing to a conclusion is to explain the meanings of the respective similes and counterparts on both the dark and bright sides by bringing each to its own separate conclusion.” This is “nisinnavattikā.” “Here” means in this Gopālaka Sutta. “Practiced by all teachers” means it has been followed and praised by all previous teachers, and thus the Pāli text has been transmitted.

Aṅgīyanti avayavabhāvena ñāyantīti aṅgāni, bhāgā. Tāni panettha yasmā sāvajjasabhāvāni, tasmā āha “aṅgehīti aguṇakoṭṭhāsehī”ti. Gomaṇḍalanti gosamūhaṃ. Pariharitunti rakkhituṃ. Taṃ pana pariharaṇaṃ pariggahetvā vicaraṇanti āha “pariggahetvā vicaritu”nti. Vaḍḍhinti gunnaṃ bahubhāvaṃ bahugorasatāsaṅkhātaṃ parivuddhiṃ. “Ettakamida”nti rūpīyatīti rūpaṃ, parimānaparicchedopi sarīrarūpampīti āha “gaṇanato vā vaṇṇato vā”ti. Na pariyesati vinaṭṭhabhāvasseva ajānanato. Nīlāti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho. Tena setasabalādivaṇṇaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

‘They are limbs’ (aṅgāni): because they are known as components, they are parts (bhāgā). Since they are here of a blameworthy nature, it is therefore said: ‘with limbs, meaning with portions devoid of virtue.’ ‘A herd of cattle’ means a group of cows. ‘To protect’ means to guard. But that protection is to take charge and move about; hence it is said, ‘having taken charge, to move about.’ ‘Growth’ means an abundance of cattle, an increase reckoned as a great quantity of dairy products. Because it is given form as ‘this much,’ it is form (rūpaṃ); it is also the measure and delimitation, and bodily form. Hence it is said: ‘by counting or by color.’ One does not search for it because of not knowing that it is lost. ‘Blue’: here the word ‘iti’ has the sense of ‘etc.’ Thus it includes colors such as white, dappled, and so on.

Dhanusattisūlādīti [V 2.0181] ettha issāsācariyānaṃ gāvīsu kataṃ dhanulakkhaṇaṃ. Kumārabhattigaṇānaṃ gāvīsu kataṃ sattilakkhaṇaṃ. Issarabhattigaṇānaṃ gāvīsu kataṃ sūlalakkhaṇanti yojanā. Ādi-saddena rāmavāsudevagaṇādīnaṃ gāvīsu kataṃ pharasucakkādilakkhaṇaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

Here, regarding ‘the bow, spear, and so forth,’ the connection is as follows: the bow-mark was made on the cows of the archery teachers; the spear-mark was made on the cows of the group devoted to the princes; the stake-mark was made on the cows of the group devoted to the lords. By the word ‘so forth,’ the axe-mark, discus-mark, etc., made on the cows of the groups of Rāma, Vāsudeva, and others are included.

Nīlamakkhikāti piṅgalamakkhikā, khuddamakkhikā eva vā. Saṭati rujati etāyāti sāṭikā, saṃvaddhā sāṭikāti āsāṭikā. Tenāha “vaḍḍhantī”tiādi.

‘A blue fly’: a tawny fly, or just a small fly. ‘A maggot’ (sāṭikā): it is so called because it clings (saṭati) and afflicts (rujati). ‘A large maggot’ (āsāṭikā) is a developed maggot. Hence it is said: ‘growing,’ etc.

Vākenāti [M 2.0194] vākapattena. Cīrakenāti pilotikena. Antovasseti vassakālassa abbhantare. Niggāhanti susumārādiggāharahitaṃ. Pītanti pānīyassa pītabhāvaṃ. Sīhabyagghādiparissayena sāsaṅko sappaṭibhayo.

‘With a bark garment’ means with a bark-cloth. ‘With rags’ means with a piece of torn cloth. ‘During the rains’ means within the rainy season. ‘A safe place’ means one free from crocodiles and other seizers. ‘Drinkable’ refers to the drinkable state of the water. ‘Through danger from lions, tigers, etc.,’ he is anxious and fearful.

Pañca ahāni bhūtāni etassāti pañcāhito, so eva vāroti pañcāhikavāro. Evaṃ sattāhikavāroti veditabbo. Ciṇṇaṭṭhānanti caritaṭṭhānaṃ gocaraggahitaṭṭhānaṃ.

‘Five days have passed for him,’ thus, he is called ‘five-day-bound,’ which is the five-day period. Similarly, the seven-day period should be understood. ‘A frequented place’ means a place of habitual movement, a grazing ground.

Pituṭṭhānanti pitarā kātabbaṭṭhānaṃ, pitarā kātabbakaraṇanti attho. Yathāruciṃ gahetvā gacchantīti gunnaṃ rucianurūpaṃ gocarabhūmiyaṃ vā nadipāraṃ vā gahetvā gacchanti. Gobhattanti kappāsaṭṭhikādimissaṃ gobhuñjitabbaṃ bhattaṃ, bhattaggahaṇeneva yāgupi gahitā.

‘The father’s position’ means the position to be taken by a father, that is, doing what a father should do. ‘Taking as they please and going’ means they take the cattle to the grazing ground or to the other side of the river according to the cattle’s liking and go. ‘Cow-fodder’ means the food to be eaten by the cows, a mixture of cotton seeds and the like. By mentioning ‘food,’ even gruel is included.

347. “Dvīhākārehī”ti vuttaṃ ākāradvayaṃ dassetuṃ “gaṇanato vā samuṭṭhānato vā”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ pāḷiyaṃ āgatāti “upacayo santatī”ti jātiṃ dvidhā bhinditvā hadayavatthuṃ aggahetvā “dasa āyatanāni pañcadasa sukhumarūpānī”ti evaṃ rūpakaṇḍapāḷiyaṃ (dha. sa. 651-655) āgatā. Pañcavīsati rūpakoṭṭhāsāti salakkhaṇato aññamaññasaṅkarābhāvato rūpabhāgā. Rūpakoṭṭhāsāti vā visuṃ visuṃ appavattitvā kalāpabhāveneva pavattanato rūpakalāpā. Koṭṭhāsāti ca aṃsā, avayavāti attho. Koṭṭhanti vā sarīraṃ, tassa aṃsā kesādayo koṭṭhāsāti aññepi avayavā koṭṭhāsā viya koṭṭhāsā. Seyyathāpīti upamāsaṃsandanaṃ. Tattha rūpaṃ pariggahetvāti yathāvuttaṃ rūpaṃ salakkhaṇato ñāṇena pariggaṇhitvā. Arūpaṃ vavatthapetvāti taṃ rūpaṃ nissāya ārammaṇañca katvā pavattamāne vedanādike cattāro khandhe “arūpa”nti vavatthapetvā. Rūpārūpaṃ pariggahetvāti puna tattha yaṃ ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ, taṃ rūpaṃ, tadaññaṃ arūpaṃ, ubhayavinimuttaṃ kiñci natthi attā vā attaniyaṃ vāti evaṃ rūpārūpaṃ pariggahetvā. Tadubhayañca avijjādinā paccayena sappaccayanti paccayaṃ sallakkhetvā aniccādilakkhaṇaṃ [V 2.0182] āropetvā yo kalāpasammasanādikkamena kammaṭṭhānaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetuṃ na sakkoti, so na vaḍḍhatīti yojanā.

347. ‘By two modes’: this was said to show the two modes, namely: ‘either by enumeration or by origin.’ Thus it comes in the Pāli text: ‘accumulation, continuity’—dividing production into two, not including the heart-base, and stating ‘ten bases, fifteen subtle material phenomena’; thus it comes in the Pāli of the Section on Materiality (Dhs 651–655). ‘The twenty-five portions of materiality’: they are divisions of materiality because, owing to their individual characteristics, there is no mutual confusion. Or, ‘portions of materiality’ are material groups (rūpakalāpā) because they do not arise separately but only as a group. And ‘portions’ (koṭṭhāsā) means parts (aṃsā), components (avayavā). Or, the body is a ‘storehouse’ (koṭṭha), and its parts (aṃsā)—hair of the head, etc.—are ‘portions’ (koṭṭhāsā); just so, other components are like portions, thus ‘portions.’ ‘Just as’: this is for the purpose of comparison. Therein, ‘having comprehended materiality’ means having comprehended the aforesaid materiality by means of knowledge of its individual characteristic. ‘Having determined the immaterial’ means having determined the four aggregates beginning with feeling, which arise dependent on that materiality and taking it as object, as ‘immaterial.’ ‘Having comprehended the material and immaterial’ means, again, having comprehended the material and immaterial thus: whatever has the characteristic of being afflicted is material; what is other than that is immaterial; there is nothing—no self or what belongs to a self—that is liberated from both. And having discerned that ‘both of these are conditioned by ignorance and other conditions,’ and having superimposed the characteristics of impermanence, etc., one who is unable to bring the meditation subject to its culmination by the method beginning with the comprehension of groups does not grow. This is the connection.

Ettakaṃ [M 2.0195] rūpaṃ ekasamuṭṭhānanti cakkhāyatanaṃ, sotaghānajivhākāyāyatanaṃ itthindriyaṃ purisindriyaṃ jīvitindriyanti aṭṭhavidhaṃ kammavasena, kāyaviññatti vacīviññattīti idaṃ dvayaṃ cittavasenāti ettakaṃ rūpaṃ ekasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Saddāyatanamekaṃ utucittavasena dvisamuṭṭhānaṃ. Rūpassa lahutā mudutā kammaññatāti ettakaṃ rūpaṃ utucittāhāravasena tisamuṭṭhānaṃ. Rūpagandharasaphoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ ākāsadhātu āpodhātu kabaḷīkāro āhāroti ettakaṃ rūpaṃ utucittāhārakammavasena catusamuṭṭhānaṃ. Upacayo santati jaratā rūpassa aniccatāti ettakaṃ rūpaṃ na kutoci samuṭṭhātīti na jānāti. Samuṭṭhānato rūpaṃ ajānantotiādīsu vattabbaṃ “gaṇanato rūpaṃ ajānanto”tiādesu vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

He does not know that the following materiality has a single origin: the eight kinds born of kamma—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body bases, the femininity and masculinity faculties, and the life faculty; and the two kinds born of consciousness—bodily intimation and verbal intimation. He does not know that the sound base alone has a twofold origin, being born of temperature and consciousness. He does not know that the following materiality has a threefold origin, being born of temperature, consciousness, and nutriment: the lightness, softness, and wieldiness of materiality. He does not know that the following materiality has a fourfold origin, being born of temperature, consciousness, nutriment, and kamma: the visible form, odor, taste, and tangible bases, the space element, the water element, and physical nutriment. He does not know that the following materiality does not arise from any source: the accumulation, continuity, decay, and impermanence of materiality. What should be said about such cases as ‘not knowing materiality by its origin’ should be understood in the way stated for the cases such as ‘not knowing materiality by enumeration.’

Kammalakkhaṇoti attanā kataṃ duccaritakammaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti kammalakkhaṇo, bālo. Vuttañhetaṃ – “tīṇimāni, bhikkhave, bālassa bālalakkhaṇāni. Katamāni tīṇi? Duccintitacintī hoti, dubbhāsitabhāsī, dukkaṭakammakārī. Imāni kho…pe… lakkhaṇānī”ti (a. ni. 3.2; netti. 116). Attanā kataṃ sucaritakammaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti kammalakkhaṇo, paṇḍito. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “tīṇimāni, bhikkhave, paṇḍitassa paṇḍitalakkhaṇāni. Katamāni tīṇi? Sucintitacintī hoti, subhāsitabhāsī, sukatakammakārī. Imāni kho…pe… paṇḍitalakkhaṇānī”ti (ma. ni. 3.253; a. ni. 3.3; netti. 116). Tenāha “kusalākusalaṃ kammaṃ paṇḍitamālalakkhaṇa”nti. Bāle vajjetvā paṇḍite na sevatīti yaṃ bālapuggale vajjetvā paṇḍitasevanaṃ atthakāmena kātabbaṃ, taṃ na karoti. Tathābhūtassa ayamādīnavoti dassetuṃ puna “bāle vajjetvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yaṃ bhagavatā “idaṃ vo kappatī”ti anuññātaṃ, tadanulomañce, taṃ kappiyaṃ. Yaṃ “idaṃ vo na kappatī”ti paṭikkhittaṃ, tadanulomañce, taṃ akappiyaṃ. Yaṃ kosallasambhūtaṃ, taṃ kusalaṃ, tappaṭipakkhaṃ akusalaṃ. Tadeva sāvajjaṃ, kusalaṃ anavajjaṃ. Āpattito ādito dve āpattikkhandhā garukaṃ, tadaññaṃ lahukaṃ. Dhammato mahāsāvajjaṃ garukaṃ, appasāvajjaṃ lahukaṃ. Sappaṭikāraṃ satekiccaṃ, appaṭikāraṃ atekicchaṃ. Dhammatānugataṃ kāraṇaṃ, itaraṃ akāraṇaṃ. Taṃ ajānantoti kappiyākappiyaṃ garukalahukaṃ satekicchātekicchaṃ ajānanto suvisuddhaṃ katvā sīlaṃ rakkhituṃ na sakkoti, kusalākusalaṃ sāvajjānavajjaṃ kāraṇākāraṇaṃ ajānanto khandhādīsu [M 2.0196][V 2.0183] akusalatāya rūpārūpapariggahampi kātuṃ na sakkoti, kuto tassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vaḍḍhanā. Tenāha “kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vaḍḍhetuṃ na sakkotī”ti.

One with the characteristic of his kamma: for a fool, his characteristic is the bad conduct he has done himself. For it is said: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of a fool. What three? He thinks bad thoughts, speaks bad speech, and does bad deeds. These, bhikkhus, are the … characteristics of a fool.’ For a wise person, his characteristic is the good conduct he has done himself. And this too is said: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of a wise person. What three? He thinks good thoughts, speaks good speech, and does good deeds. These, bhikkhus, are the … characteristics of a wise person.’ Therefore it is said: ‘Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is the characteristic of the wise and the fool.’ He does not avoid fools and associate with the wise: he does not do what should be done by one who desires his own welfare, namely, avoiding foolish persons and associating with the wise. To show the danger for one who is like this, it is said again, ‘avoiding fools,’ etc. Here, what the Blessed One has permitted by saying, ‘This is allowable for you,’ if it is in accordance with that, it is allowable. What he has rejected by saying, ‘This is not allowable for you,’ if it is in accordance with that, it is unallowable. What arises from skillfulness is wholesome; its opposite is unwholesome. The latter is blameworthy; the wholesome is blameless. From the perspective of offenses, the first two classes of offenses are grave; the others are light. From the perspective of the Dhamma, what is very blameworthy is grave; what is slightly blameworthy is light. What has a remedy is remediable; what has no remedy is irremediable. What is in accordance with the nature of things is a reason; the other is not a reason. Not knowing this—not knowing what is allowable and unallowable, grave and light, remediable and irremediable—he is unable to guard his virtue by making it perfectly pure. Not knowing what is wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, a reason and not a reason, he is unable even to undertake the comprehension of form and the formless with respect to the aggregates because of his unskillfulness. How then could he take up a meditation subject and develop it? Therefore it is said: ‘He is unable to take up a meditation subject and develop it.’

Govaṇasadise attabhāve uppajjitvā tattha dukkhuppattihetuto micchāvitakkā āsāṭikā viyāti āsāṭikāti āha “akusalavitakkaṃ āsāṭikaṃ ahāretvā”ti.

Because, having arisen in an existence similar to a cow's, wrong thoughts are a cause for the arising of suffering therein, they are like gadflies’ eggs. Thus he said ‘gadflies’ eggs,’ in reference to the phrase ‘not having removed the unwholesome thoughts that are like gadflies’ eggs.’

“Gaṇḍoti kho, bhikkhave, pañcannetaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ adhivacana”nti vacanato (a. ni. 8.56) chahi vaṇamukhehi vissandamānayūso gaṇḍo viya pilotikakhaṇḍena chahi dvārehi vissandamānakilesāsuci attabhāvavaṇo satisaṃvarena pidahitabbo, ayaṃ pana evaṃ na karotīti āha “yathā so gopālako vaṇaṃ na paṭicchādeti, evaṃ saṃvaraṃ na sampādetī”ti.

In accordance with the saying, ‘“A boil,” bhikkhus, is a designation for these five aggregates subject to clinging’ (AN 8.56), the wound of one’s individual existence—from which the impurity of defilements oozes through the six doors, like a boil with pus oozing from six openings—should be covered with mindfulness-restraint as with a piece of cloth. But this one does not do so; thus it is said: ‘Just as that cowherd does not cover the wound, so he does not accomplish restraint.’

Yathā dhūmo indhanaṃ nissāya uppajjamāno saṇho sukhumo taṃ taṃ vivaraṃ anupavissa byāpento sattānaṃ ḍaṃsamakasādiparissayaṃ vinodeti, aggijālasamuṭṭhānassa pubbaṅgamo hoti, evaṃ dhammadesanāñāṇassa indhanabhūtaṃ rūpārūpadhammajātaṃ nissāya uppajjamānā saṇhā sukhumā taṃ taṃ khandhantaraṃ āyatanantarañca anupavissa byāpeti, sattānaṃ micchāvitakkādiparissayaṃ vinodeti, ñāṇaggijālasamuṭṭhānassa pubbaṅgamoti dhūmo viyāti dhūmoti āha “gopālako dhūmaṃ viya dhammadesanādhūmaṃ na karotī”ti. Attano santikaṃ upagantvā nisinnassa kātabbā tadanucchavikā dhammakathā upanisinnakathā. Katassa dānādipuññassa anumodanakathā anumodanā. Tatoti dhammakathādīnaṃ akaraṇato. “Bahussuto guṇavā”ti na jānantīti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu attano jānāpanatthaṃ dhammakathādi na kātabbamevāti? Saccaṃ, na kātabbameva, suddhāsayena pana dhamme kathite tassa guṇajānanataṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā –

Just as smoke, arising dependent on fuel, fine and subtle, enters and pervades every crack and crevice, dispelling the troubles of beings such as gadflies and mosquitoes, and is the forerunner for the arising of a blaze of fire; so too the knowledge of the Dhamma teaching, arising dependent on the fuel of the mass of material and immaterial phenomena, fine and subtle, enters and pervades the various aggregates and sense bases, dispelling the troubles of beings such as wrong thoughts, and is the forerunner for the arising of the blaze of knowledge. Because it is like smoke, it is called smoke. Thus he said: ‘Just as the cowherd does not make smoke, so he does not make the smoke of the Dhamma teaching.’ The appropriate Dhamma talk to be given to one who has approached and sat down nearby is a ‘talk for one sitting near.’ A talk of appreciation for merit made, such as giving, is an ‘appreciation.’ From that: from not giving Dhamma talks and so on. Why was it said, ‘They do not know he is learned and virtuous’? Is it not the case that one should not give Dhamma talks and so on for the purpose of making oneself known? True, one should not do so. But this was said in reference to his virtues becoming known when the Dhamma is taught with a pure intention. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“Nābhāsamānaṃ jānanti, missaṃ bālehi paṇḍitaṃ;

Bhāsaye jotaye dhammaṃ, paggaṇhe isinaṃ dhaja”nti. (saṃ. ni. 2.241);

“They do not know one who does not speak, a wise man mingled with the fools. One should speak and illuminate the Dhamma; one should raise the seers’ banner.”

Taranti etthāti titthaṃ, nadītaḷākādīnaṃ nahānādiatthaṃ otaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. Yathā pana taṃ udakena otiṇṇasattānaṃ sarīramalaṃ pavāheti, parissamaṃ vinodeti, visuddhiṃ uppādeti, evaṃ bahussutā attano samīpaṃ otiṇṇasattānaṃ [M 2.0197] dhammūdakena cittamalaṃ pavāhenti, parissamaṃ vinodenti, visuddhiṃ uppādenti, tasmā te titthaṃ viyāti titthaṃ. Tenāha “titthabhūte bahussutabhikkhū”ti. Byañjanaṃ kathaṃ ropetabbanti, bhante, idaṃ byañjanaṃ ayaṃ saddo kathaṃ imasmiṃ atthe [V 2.0184] ropetabbo, kena pakārena imassa atthassa vācako jāto. “Nirūpetabba”nti vā pāṭho, nirūpetabbaṃ ayaṃ sabhāvanirutti kathamettha niruḷhāti adhippāyo. Imassa bhāsitassa ko atthoti saddatthaṃ pucchati. Imasmiṃ ṭhāneti imasmiṃ pāḷipadese. Pāḷi kiṃ vadetīti bhāvatthaṃ pucchati. Attho kiṃ dīpetīti bhāvatthaṃ vā saṅketatthaṃ vā. Na paripucchatīti vimaticchedanapucchāvasena sabbaso pucchaṃ na karoti. Na paripañhatīti pari pari attano ñātuṃ icchaṃ na ācikkhati na vibhāveti. Tenāha “na jānāpetī”ti. Teti bahussutabhikkhū. Vivaraṇaṃ nāma atthassa vibhajitvā kathananti āha “bhājetvā na dassentī”ti. Anuttānīkatanti ñāṇena apākaṭīkataṃ guyhaṃ paṭicchannaṃ. Na uttānīkarontīti sinerumūlakaṃ vālikaṃ uddharanto viya pathavīsandhārodakaṃ vivaritvā dassento viya ca uttānaṃ na karonti. Evaṃ yassa dhammassa vasena bahussutā “tittha”nti vuttā pariyāyato, idāni tameva dhammaṃ nippariyāyato titthanti dassetuṃ “yathā cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dhammo hi taranti etena nibbānaṃ nāma taḷākanti “tittha”nti vuccati. Tenāha bhagavā sumedhabhūto –

‘They cross here,’ thus it is a ford (tittha): a place in rivers, lakes, and so on, for descending for the purpose of bathing, etc. Just as water washes away the bodily impurities of beings who have entered it, removes their fatigue, and produces purity, so the learned bhikkhus, with the water of the Dhamma, wash away the mental impurities of beings who have approached them, remove their fatigue, and produce purity. Therefore they are like a ford, thus they are a ‘ford.’ Hence it is said, ‘the learned bhikkhus who are fords.’ ‘Venerable sir, how should the phrasing be construed?’ means: ‘How should this phrasing, this word, be applied to this meaning? In what way has it come to designate this meaning?’ Or the reading is ‘should be determined.’ The intention is: how has this natural designation become established here? ‘What is the meaning of this utterance?’—thus he asks for the literal meaning. ‘In this passage’ means in this portion of the Pāli text. ‘What does the Pāli say?’—thus he asks for the contextual meaning. ‘What does the meaning illuminate?’—thus he asks for the contextual meaning or the implied meaning. He does not question thoroughly: he does not ask any questions at all in order to cut off doubt. He does not inquire all around: he does not state or make clear his wish to know all around. Therefore it is said, ‘he does not make it known.’ They: the learned bhikkhus. An explanation is a statement that analyzes the meaning. Thus it is said: ‘They do not show it by analyzing it.’ Not made plain: not made manifest by knowledge; secret, concealed. They do not make it plain: just as one removing sand at the foot of Sineru does not make the underground water plain by opening up and showing the earth’s stratum of water, so they do not make it plain.
