Thus, that Dhamma by means of which the learned are figuratively called a ‘ford’—to show that this very Dhamma is non-figuratively a ford, it is said, ‘And just as…,’ etc. For the Dhamma is that by which they cross to the lake named Nibbāna; thus it is called a ‘ford.’ Therefore the Blessed One, having become one of supreme wisdom, said:

“Evaṃ kilesamaladhovaṃ, vijjante amatantaḷe;

Na gavesati taṃ taḷākaṃ, na doso amatantaḷe”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.14);

“When the deathless pool exists for washing off the stain of defilements, he does not search for that pool; the fault is not in the deathless pool.”

Dhammasseva nibbānassotaraṇatitthabhūtassa otaraṇapakāraṃ ajānanto “dhammatitthaṃ na jānātī”ti vutto.

Not knowing the way to enter the Dhamma itself, which is the ford for crossing over to Nibbāna, he is said ‘not to know the ford of the Dhamma.’

Pītāpītanti gogaṇe pītaṃ apītañca gorūpaṃ na jānāti na vindati. Avindanto hi na labhatīti vutto. “Ānisaṃsaṃ na vindatī”ti vatvā tassa avindanākāraṃ dassento “dhammassavanaggaṃ gantvā”tiādimāha.

Those that have drunk and those that have not: in a herd of cattle, he does not know or find the cattle that have drunk and those that have not drunk. For one who does not find is said ‘not to obtain.’ Having said, ‘He does not find the benefit,’ to show the manner of his not finding it, he said, ‘Having gone to the pinnacle of hearing the Dhamma…,’ etc.

Ayaṃ lokuttaroti padaṃ sandhāyāha “ariya”nti. Paccāsattiñāyena anantaravidhippaṭisedho vā, ariya-saddo vā niddosapariyāyo daṭṭhabbo. Aṭṭhaṅgikanti ca visuṃ ekajjhañca aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ upādāya gahetabbaṃ, aṭṭhaṅgatā [M 2.0198] bāhullato ca. Evañca katvā sattaṅgassapi ariyamaggassa saṅgaho siddho hoti.

Referring to this term ‘supramundane,’ he says ‘noble.’ Or the exclusion of the immediately following method should be seen by the principle of proximity; or the word ‘noble’ should be seen as a synonym for ‘faultless.’ And ‘eightfold’ should be taken by comprising the eightfoldness both separately and collectively, and its eightfoldness is due to its prevalence. By doing so, the inclusion of the seven-factored noble path is also established.

Cattāro satipaṭṭhānetiādīsu avisesena satipaṭṭhānā vuttā. Tattha kāyavedanācittadhammārammaṇā [V 2.0185] satipaṭṭhānā lokiyā, tattha sammohaviddhaṃsanavasena pavattā nibbānārammaṇā lokuttarāti evaṃ ime lokiyā, ime lokuttarāti yathābhūtaṃ na pajānāti.

In ‘the four foundations of mindfulness,’ etc., the foundations of mindfulness are spoken of without distinction. Among them, the foundations of mindfulness that have the body, feelings, mind, and dhammas as their object are mundane, while those that have Nibbāna as their object and proceed by way of demolishing delusion are supramundane. Thus he does not understand as it really is which of these are mundane and which are supramundane.

Anavasesaṃ duhatīti paṭiggahaṇe mattaṃ ajānanto kismiñci dāyake saddhāhāniyā kismiñci paccayahāniyā anavasesaṃ duhati. Vācāya abhihāro vācābhihāro. Paccayānaṃ abhihāro paccayābhihāro.

He milks without remainder: not knowing the proper measure in accepting, he milks without remainder, causing a loss of faith in some donors and a loss of requisites from others. An offering by way of speech is a ‘verbal offering.’ An offering of requisites is a ‘requisites-offering.’

Ime amhesu garucittīkāraṃ na karontīti iminā navakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammasampaṭipattiyā abhāvaṃ dasseti ācariyupajjhāyesu pitupemassa anupaṭṭhāpanato. Tena ca sikkhāgāravatābhāvadīpanena saṅgahassa abhājanabhāvaṃ, tena therānaṃ tesu anuggahābhāvaṃ. Na hi sīlādiguṇehi sāsane thirabhāvappattā ananuggahetabbe sabrahmacārī anuggaṇhanti, niratthakaṃ vā anuggahaṃ karonti. Tenāha “navake bhikkhū”ti. Dhammakathābandhanti paveṇiāgataṃ pakiṇṇakadhammakathāmaggaṃ. Saccasattapaṭisandhipaccayākārapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ suññatādīpanaṃ guyhaganthaṃ. Vuttavipallāsavasenāti “na rūpaññū”tiādīsu vuttassa paṭisedhassa paṭikkhepavasena aggahaṇavasena. Yojetvāti “rūpaññū hotīti gaṇanāto vā vaṇṇato vā rūpaṃ jānātī”tiādinā, “tassa gogaṇopi na parihāyati, pañcagorasaparibhogatopi na paribāhiro hotī”tiādinā ca atthaṃ yojetvā. Veditabboti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ padese yathārahaṃ attho veditabbo.

By the words, 'They do not show reverence to us,' this indicates the lack of proper Dhamma practice in the new bhikkhus due to their not establishing a fatherly affection for their teachers and preceptors. And by this, by showing their lack of respect for the training, it shows their unworthiness for inclusion, and thereby the elders' lack of support for them. For those who have attained stability in the Dispensation through such virtues as morality do not support their fellow monastics who are unworthy of support, nor do they give meaningless support. Therefore he said, 'the new bhikkhus.' The bond of Dhamma-talk is the traditional path of miscellaneous Dhamma-talk. The secret text elucidating emptiness, connected with the seven truths, rebirth-linking, and the mode of conditions. Due to the perversion of what is said: in statements like 'he does not know form,' this means by way of rejecting the stated negation, that is, through non-acceptance. Having construed: by construing the meaning with phrases like 'he knows form means he knows form by counting or by appearance,' and 'his herd of cattle does not diminish, nor is he excluded from the enjoyment of the five products of the cow.' It should be understood: the meaning should be understood as is appropriate in each particular passage.

Mahāgopālakasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Mahāgopālaka Sutta is completed.

4. Cūḷagopālakasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Cūḷagopālaka Sutta

350. Celukkāhīti [V 2.0186] celamayāhi ukkāhi. Ukkabhūtāni celāni etthāti ukkacelā, nagaraṃ. Sabbā gaṅgā pākaṭā hutvā paññāyatīti pakaticakkhussa [M 2.0199] pākaṭā hutvā upaṭṭhāti, dibbacakkhussa pana samantacakkhussa vā yattha katthaci nisinnassapi bhagavato pākaṭā hutvā paññāyateva. Sotthīti anupaddavo. Vaḍḍhīti aparihāni. Ārogyanti arogatā ābādhābhāvo.

350. ‘With cloth torches’ (celukkāhi): this means with torches made of cloth. The city is called Ukkacelā because cloths there serve as torches. The entire Ganges becomes manifest and is perceived: it becomes manifest and appears to the ordinary eye, but to the divine eye or the all-seeing eye of the Blessed One, it becomes manifest and is perceived even when he is sitting anywhere at all. ‘Safely’ (sotthi): this means without misfortune. ‘Prosperity’ (vaḍḍhi): this means non-decline. ‘Health’ (ārogya): this means good health, the absence of illness.

Magadho janapado nivāso etassāti māgadho, māgadhova māgadhiko. Paññāya nāma duṭṭhubhāvo natthi ekantānavajjatāya, tasmā du-saddo abhāvavācī “dussīlo”tiādīsu viya, jāti-saddo ca sabhāvatthoti āha “nippaññasabhāvo”ti. -Saddo ārambhatthoti āha “patāresīti tāretuṃ ārabhī”ti paratīraṃ gāvīnaṃ appattattā. Suvidehānanti sundaravidehānaṃ. Videharaṭṭhaṃ kira bhūmibhāgadassanasampattiyā ca vanarāmaṇeyyakādinā ca sundaraṃ. Āmaṇḍalikaṃ karitvāti āvatte patitā temaṇḍalākārena paribbhamitvā. Katipayāpi gāviyo asesetvā nadīsotena vūḷhattā vuttaṃ “avaḍḍhiṃ vināsaṃ pāpuṇiṃsū”ti. Katipayāsupi hi avasiṭṭhāsu gāvīsu anukkamenapi siyā gogaṇassa vaḍḍhīti. Vissamaṭṭhānanti parissamavinodanaṭṭhānaṃ. Titthā bhaṭṭhāti gahetuṃ asamatthatāya titthaṃ appattā. Arogo nāma nāhosīti lomamattampi asesetvā sabbā gāviyo nadīsote vinaṭṭhāti attho.

One for whom the country of Magadha is his residence is a Magadhan (māgadho); māgadhiko is just māgadho. Because wisdom is by nature faultless, being entirely blameless, the prefix du- signifies absence, as in dussīlo (immoral), and the word jāti signifies intrinsic nature; therefore he said, ‘one whose nature is devoid of wisdom’ (nippaññasabhāvo). ‘He began to make them cross’ (patāresi means tāretuṃ ārabhi), because the cows did not reach the far bank. ‘Of the Suvidehas’ (suvidehānaṃ): of the beautiful Videhas. The country of Videha, it is said, is beautiful because of the perfection of its scenic landscape and the delightfulness of its forests. ‘Having made a circle’ (āmaṇḍalikaṃ karitvā): having fallen into a whirlpool, they whirled around in a threefold circle. Because some cows were swept away without remainder by the river’s current, it is said, ‘they met with non-increase and destruction.’ For even if only a few cows had remained, the herd might have gradually increased. ‘A place of rest’ (vissamaṭṭhānaṃ): a place for dispelling fatigue. ‘Missed the ford’ (titthā bhaṭṭhā): they did not reach the ford because they were unable to get a footing. ‘Not a single one was safe’ (arogo nāma nāhosi): the meaning is that all the cows perished in the river’s current without even a hair remaining.

Yesu khandhāyatanadhātūsu idha lokasamaññā, te ajānantā “akusalā imassa lokassā”ti vuttāti āha “idhaloke khandhadhātāyatanesu akusalā achekā”ti. Ayameva nayo “akusalā parassa lokassā”ti etthāpīti āha “paralokepi eseva nayo”ti. Māro ettha dhīyatīti māradheyyaṃ. Māroti cettha kilesamāro veditabbo. Khandhābhisaṅkhārā hi tassa pavattanabhāvena gahitā, maccumāro visuṃ gahito eva, kilesamāravaseneva ca devaputtamārassa kāmabhave ādhipaccanti. Tesanti ye idhalokādīsu achekā, tesaṃ. Te pana ukkaṭṭhaniddesena dassento āha “iminā cha satthāro dassitā”ti.

Because they do not know those aggregates, sense bases, and elements that are designated as ‘this world,’ they are called ‘unskillful in this world.’ Thus he said: ‘unskillful and inexpert in this world in regard to the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.’ This same method applies also to ‘unskillful in the other world.’ Thus he said: ‘In the other world, too, this is the same method.’ ‘Māra’s domain’ (māradheyyaṃ): Māra is established here. Here, Māra should be understood as Māra as the defilements. For the aggregates and formations are taken as the sphere of his operation. Māra as death is taken separately. And it is only by way of Māra as the defilements that Māra as a devaputta holds dominion in the sense-sphere existence. ‘Of them’ (tesaṃ): of those who are inexpert in this world and so on. But showing them by way of an eminent designation, he said: ‘By this, the six teachers are shown.’

351. Balavagāvoti balavante gorūpe. Te pana dammataṃ upagatagoṇā ceva dhenuyo cāti āha [V 2.0187] “dantagoṇe ceva dhenuyo cā”ti[M 2.0200]. Avijātagāvoti na vijātagāviyo. Vacchaketi khuddakavacche. Appattho hi ayaṃ ka-saddo. Tenāha “taruṇavacchake”ti. Kisābalaketi dubbale.

351. ‘Strong cattle’ (balavagāvo): strong bovine creatures. These are bulls that have been tamed and cows. Thus he said: ‘tamed bulls and cows.’ ‘Cows that have not given birth’ (avijātagāvo): cows that have not calved. ‘Calves’ (vacchake): small calves. The suffix -ka here has a diminutive sense. Therefore he said, ‘young calves.’ ‘Weak and feeble’ (kisābalake): weak ones.

352. Mārassa taṇhāsotaṃ chetvāti khandhamārasambandhītaṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ sotaṃ samucchinditvā. Tayo koṭṭhāse khepetvā ṭhitāti anāgāmino sandhāyāha. Sabbavāresūti sakadāgāmisotāpannaaṭṭhamakavāresu. Tattha pana yathākkamaṃ catumaggavajjhānaṃ kilesānaṃ dve koṭṭhāse khepetvā ṭhitā, ekakoṭṭhāsaṃ khepetvā ṭhitā, paṭhamaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ khepentoti vattabbaṃ. Dhammaṃ anussaranti, dhammassa vā anussaraṇasīlāti dhammānusārino. Dhammoti cettha paññā adhippetā. Saddhaṃ anussaranti, saddhāya vā anussaraṇasīlāti saddhānusārino.

352. ‘Having cut Māra’s stream of craving’: having cut off the stream called craving, which is connected with Māra as the aggregates. ‘Those who stand having exhausted three portions’: this is said with reference to non-returners. ‘In all cases’: in the cases of the once-returner, the stream-enterer, and the eighth person. There, however, it should be said respectively: ‘those who stand having exhausted two portions of the defilements to be abandoned by the four paths’; ‘those who stand having exhausted one portion’; and ‘those who are exhausting the first portion.’ ‘Dhamma-followers’ (dhammānusārino): they follow along with the Dhamma, or they are disposed to follow along with the Dhamma. Here, by ‘Dhamma’ wisdom is intended. ‘Faith-followers’ (saddhānusārino): they follow along with faith, or they are disposed to follow along with faith.

Jānatāti ettha jānanakiriyāvisayassa avisesitattā adhikāravasena anavasesañeyyavisesā adhippetāti āha “sabbadhamme jānantenā”ti. Antosāravirahato abbhuggataṭṭhena ca naḷo viyāti naḷo, mānoti āha “vigatamānanaḷaṃ kata”nti. Khemaṃ patthethāti ettha catūhi yogehi anupaddavattā “khema”nti arahattaṃ adhippetaṃ. Patthanā ca chandapatthanā, na taṇhāpatthanāti āha “kattukamyatāchandena arahattaṃ patthethā”ti. Pattāyeva nāma tassa pattiyā na koci antarāyo. Sotthinā pāragamanaṃ uddissa desanaṃ ārabhitvā khemappattiyā desanāya pariyosāpitattā yathānusandhināva desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesīti.

‘By one who knows’: here, since the object of the act of knowing has not been specified, by the power of the context all knowable things without remainder are intended. Thus he said: ‘by one who knows all things.’ Like a reed (naḷo viya): A reed (naḷo) is so called because it is devoid of inner substance and has risen up. This is pride (māno). Thus he said: ‘made into a reed devoid of pride.’ ‘You should aspire for security’: here, by ‘security’ (khemaṃ) arahantship is intended, because it is security from the four yokes. And the aspiration is an aspiration of wholesome desire, not an aspiration of craving. Thus he said: ‘you should aspire for arahantship with the wholesome desire to attain it.’ His attainment is indeed attained; there is no obstacle to his attainment. Having begun the discourse with the aim of a safe crossing to the far shore, and having concluded the discourse with the attainment of security, he thus brought the discourse to its conclusion in accordance with its own sequence.

Cūḷagopālakasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Cūḷagopālaka Sutta is completed.

5. Cūḷasaccakasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Cūḷasaccaka Sutta

353. Haṃsavaṭṭakacchannenāti [V 2.0188] haṃsavaṭṭakapaṭicchannena, haṃsamaṇḍalākārenāti attho.

353. Haṃsavaṭṭakacchannena: this means covered with a haṃsavaṭṭaka; the meaning is ‘in the shape of a circle of geese.’

Vadanti etenāti vādo, maggo. Kiṃ vadanti? Uttaraṃ. Vādānaṃ satāni vādasatāni. “Nigaṇṭho pañcavādasatāni, nigaṇṭhī pañcavādasatānī”ti evaṃ nigaṇṭho [M 2.0201] ca nigaṇṭhī ca pañca pañca vādasatāni uggahetvā vicarantā. Kiriyato te pucchiṃsu, liṅgato pana nigaṇṭhabhāvo ñāto. Tenāha “ahaṃ vādaṃ āropessāmī”ti.

‘A doctrine’ (vādo) is that by which they speak (vadanti etena); it is a path (maggo). What do they speak of? What is higher. Vādasatāni means hundreds of doctrines. ‘The Nigaṇṭha has five hundred doctrines, the Nigaṇṭhī has five hundred doctrines’—thus both the male Nigaṇṭha and the female Nigaṇṭhī wander about having mastered five hundred doctrines each. They asked about their practice, but their status as Nigaṇṭhas was known from their characteristic mark. Therefore he said: ‘I will initiate a debate.’

Jagganto sammajjanādivasena. Divātaranti atidivaṃ. “Kassa pucchā, kassa vissajjanaṃ hotū”ti paribbājikāhi vutte thero āha “pucchā nāma amhākaṃ pattā”ti. Pucchā vādānaṃ pubbapakkho, yasmā tumhe vādapasutā vādābhiratā dhajaṃ paggayha vicaratha, tasmā vādānaṃ pubbapakkho amhākaṃ patto, evaṃ santepi tumhākaṃ mātugāmabhāvato pubbapakkhaṃ demāti āha “tumhe pana mātugāmā nāma paṭhamaṃ pucchathā”ti. Tā paribbājikā ekekā aḍḍhateyyasatavādamaggaṃ pucchantiyo vādasahassaṃ pucchiṃsu. Yathā nisitassa khaggassa kumudanāḷacchedane kimatthi bhāriyaṃ, evaṃ paṭisambhidāppattassa sāvakesu paññavantānaṃ aggabhāve ṭhitassa dhammasenāpatino puthujjanaparikappitapañhavissajjane kimatthi bhāriyaṃ. Tenāha “thero khaggenā”tiādi. Tattha nijjaṭaṃ niggaṇṭhiṃ katvāti yathā tā puna tattha jaṭaṃ gaṇṭhiṃ kātuṃ na visahanti, tathā vijaṭetvā kathesi. Ayaṃ thero caturaṅgasamannāgate andhakāre sahassavaṭṭikaṃ dīpento viya aññesaṃ avisaye andhakārabhūte pañhe pucchitamatteyeva vissajjesīti therassa paññāveyyattiyaṃ disvā sayañca antimabhavikatāya kohaññe ṭhātuṃ asakkontiyo “ettakameva, bhante, mayaṃ jānāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Therassa visayanti therassa paññāvisayaṃ.

‘Being vigilant’ (jagganto) means by way of sweeping and so on. Divātaraṃ means too early in the day. When the female wanderers said, ‘Whose is the question, whose is the answer?’ the elder replied, ‘The question has fallen to us.’ The question is the opening statement of a debate. Since you are intent on debate, delight in debate, and wander about having raised your banner, the opening statement of the debate has fallen to us. Nevertheless, because you are women, we give you the opening statement. Thus he said: ‘But you, being women, may ask first.’ Those female wanderers, each asking about the path of two hundred and fifty doctrines, asked a thousand questions about doctrines. Just as for a sharpened sword there is no difficulty in cutting a water lily stalk, so for the General of the Dhamma—who has attained the analytical knowledges and stands as the foremost of the wise among the disciples—what difficulty is there in answering questions concocted by worldlings? Hence it is said: ‘The elder with a sword,’ and so on. Therein, having made it untangled and unknotted means that he spoke having so disentangled it that they were unable to make a tangle or a knot in it again. This elder, like one lighting a thousand-wick lamp in the fourfold darkness, answered the questions—which were obscure and in a domain beyond others—as soon as they were asked. Seeing the elder’s sagacity, and being themselves in their final existence and thus unable to stand on deceit, they said: ‘This much only, venerable sir, do we know.’ The elder’s scope means the elder’s scope of wisdom.

Neva antaṃ na koṭiṃ addasaṃsūti ekanti vattabbassa bahubhāvato tassā pucchāya attho evamanto evamavasānakoṭīti na passiṃsu na jāniṃsu. Thero tāsaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ olokento pabbajjāruciṃ disvā āha “idāni kiṃ karissathā”ti? Uttaritarapaññoti vādamaggaparicayena medhāvitāya ca yādisā tāsaṃ paññā, tato uttaritarapañño.

They saw neither an end nor a limit: this means that because of the multiplicity of what could be said in a single instance, they did not see, did not know, that the meaning of that question had such an end, such a final limit. The elder, observing their disposition and seeing their inclination for the going forth, said: 'What will you do now?' Of superior wisdom: this means that whatever wisdom they had through their familiarity with the path of debate and their intelligence, he possessed a wisdom superior to that.

Kathāmaggoti [V 2.0189] vādamaggo. Tasmā tehi tehi parappavādādīhi bhassaṃ vādamaggaṃ pakārehi vadetīti bhassappavādako. Paṇḍitavādoti ahaṃ paṇḍito nipuṇo bahussutoti evaṃvādī. Yaṃ yaṃ nakkhattācārena ādisatīti nakkhattagatiyā kālañāṇena “asukadivase candaggāho bhavissati, sūriyaggāho bhavissatī”tiādinā yaṃ yaṃ ādesaṃ bhaṇati. Sādhuladdhiko ñāṇasampattiyā sundaro. Āropitoti paṭiññāhetunidassanādidosaṃ [M 2.0202] upari āropito vādo svāropito. Dosapadaṃ āropentena vādinā paravādimhi abhibhuyya tassa dhātukkhobhopi siyā, cittavikkhepena yena doso tena saṅkappito sampavedhitoti. Thūṇanti sarīraṃ khobhitanti katvā. Thūṇanti hi lohitapittasemhānaṃ adhivacanaṃ sabbaṅgasarīradhāraṇato. Apica thūṇapado nāma atthi kathāmaggo vādamaggaṃ gaṇhantānaṃ. Saccako pana kohaññe ṭhatvā attano vādappabhedavasena pare vimhāpento “thūṇaṃ cepāha”ntiādimāha. Sāvakānaṃ vinayaṃ nāma sikkhāpadaṃ, tañca dhammadesanā hotīti esā eva cassa anusāsanīti vinayanādimukhena sammāsambuddhassa mataṃ sāsanaṃ pucchanto saccako “kathaṃ pana, bho, assajī”tiādimāha. Athassa thero “lakkhaṇattayakathā nāma anaññasādhāraṇā buddhāveṇikā dhammadesanā, tatra ca mayā aniccakathāya samuṭṭhāpitāya taṃ asahanto saccako tucchamānena paṭapaṭāyanto kurumāno licchavī gahetvā bhagavato santikaṃ āgamissati, athassa bhagavā vādaṃ madditvā aniccanti patiṭṭhapento dhammaṃ kathessati, tadā bhavissati vijahitavādo sammāpaṭipattiyā patiṭṭhito”ti cintetvā aniccānattalakkhaṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ bhagavato anusāsanaṃ dassento “evaṃ, bho, aggivessanā”tiādimāha.

Path of speech means the path of debate. Therefore, because he speaks on the path of debate in various ways, refuting the doctrines of others, he is a bhassappavādako (a speaker of refutations). Paṇḍitavādo means one who speaks thus: 'I am wise, skilled, and very learned.' Whatever he predicts by the practice of astrology means whatever prediction he makes by knowledge of time through the movement of the stars, such as: 'On such-and-such a day there will be a lunar eclipse, there will be a solar eclipse.' Sādhuladdhika means handsome because of his accomplishment in knowledge. Āropito (propounded): a thesis is well-propounded (svāropito) when faults concerning the proposition, reason, example, and so on, are placed upon the opponent. When a debater imposes a point of fault, having overpowered the other debater, there can even be a disturbance of his bodily elements; he is agitated and thoroughly shaken by mental distraction due to that fault. Thūṇaṃ (a pillar): this is said because it shakes the body. For thūṇa is a designation for blood, bile, and phlegm, because they support the entire body with all its limbs. Moreover, for those who take up the path of debate, there is a path of discussion called the 'pillar-point.' But Saccaka, standing on deceit and bewildering others by means of his own types of debate, said: 'If I were a pillar,' and so on. The discipline for disciples is the training rules, and that is a teaching of the Dhamma, and this is his instruction—thus Saccaka, asking about the teaching, the doctrine of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, by way of discipline and so on, said: 'But how is it, good Assaji?' and so on. Then the elder, thinking: 'The talk on the three characteristics is a Dhamma teaching unique to the Buddhas, not shared with others. And when I raise the talk on impermanence, Saccaka, unable to bear it, sputtering with empty pride and making a commotion, will take the Licchavis and go to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, having crushed his thesis and establishing the teaching on impermanence, will teach the Dhamma. Then he will have abandoned his wrong view and will be established in right practice,' showed the Blessed One’s instruction connected with the characteristics of impermanence and not-self, saying: 'Thus it is, Aggivessana,' and so on.

Kasmā panettha dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ aggahitanti āha “thero panā”tiādi. “Upārambhassa okāso hotī”ti saṅkhepato vuttaṃ vivarituṃ “maggaphalānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pariyāyenāti saṅkhāradukkhatāpariyāyena. Ayanti saccako. Nayidaṃ tumhākaṃ sāsanaṃ nāmāti yattha tumhe avaṭṭhitā, idaṃ tumhākaṃ sabbaññusāsanaṃ nāma na hoti dukkhato anissaraṇattā, atha kho mahāāghātanaṃ nāmetaṃ, mahādukkhaniddiṭṭhattā pana nirayussado nāma ussadanirayo nāma, tasmā natti nāma tumhākaṃ sukhāsā. Uṭṭhāyuṭṭhāyāti ussukkaṃ katvā, dukkhameva jīrāpentā sabbaso dukkhameva anubhavantā, āhiṇḍatha vicarathāti. Sabbamidaṃ tassa micchāparikappitameva. Kasmā? Dukkhasaccūpasañhitāyeva hettha nippariyāyakathā nāma. Tassa hi pariññatthaṃ bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati. Maggaphalāni saṅkhārabhāvena “yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkha”nti pariyāyato dukkhaṃ, na nippariyāyato. Tenāha “tasmā”tiādi. Sotuṃ ayuttaṃ micchāvādattāti adhippāyo.

Why was the characteristic of suffering not taken up here? It is said: 'But the elder,' and so on. To explain what was stated concisely as 'There is an opportunity for reproach,' the words 'the paths and fruits,' and so on, were said. Therein, 'by way of' means by way of the suffering due to formations. This one means Saccaka. 'This in which you are established is not what is called the teaching of the All-Knower, because it is no escape from suffering. Rather, it is a great slaughterhouse. And since great suffering is pointed out, it is a nirayussada, that is, an Ussada hell. Therefore you have no hope of happiness. Rising up again and again means making an effort, wearing yourselves out with suffering, experiencing nothing but suffering, you wander and roam.' All this is just his wrong speculation. Why? Because here the direct teaching is connected with the truth of suffering. For it is for the full understanding of that that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. The paths and fruits, in as much as they are formations, are suffering indirectly, according to the principle 'whatever is impermanent, that is suffering,' not directly. Therefore it is said, 'Therefore,' and so on. The intention is: 'It is unfit to be heard because it is wrong view.'

354. Saha [V 2.0190][M 2.0203] atthānusāsanaṃ agāranti sandhāgāraṃ, rājakulānaṃ santhāpanaagārantipi sandhāgāraṃ, tasmiṃ santhāgāreti attho. Ekasmiṃ kāle tādise kāle rājakiccānaṃ santhānamettha vicārentīti sandhāgāraṃ, tasmiṃ santhāgāretipi attho. Patiṭṭhitanti “aniccaṃ anattā”ti ca paṭiññātaṃ. Idāneva piṭṭhiṃ parivattentoti bhagavato nalāṭaṃ anoloketvā vimukhabhāvaṃ āpajjanto. Surāghareti surāsampādakagehe. Piṭṭhakilañjanti piṭṭhaṭhapanakiḷañjaṃ. Vālanti caṅgavāraṃ. Sāṇasāṭakakaraṇatthanti sāṇasāṭakaṃ karonti etenāti sāṇasāṭakakaraṇaṃ, suttaṃ, tadatthaṃ. Sāṇavākā etesu santīti sāṇavākā, sāṇadaṇḍā. Te gahetvā sāṇānaṃ dhovanasadisaṃ kīḷitajātaṃ yathā “uddālapupphabhañjikā, sāṇabhañjikā”ti ca. Kiṃ so bhavamānoti kīdiso hutvā so bhavamāno, kiṃ honto loke aggapuggalassa sammāsambuddhassa vādāropanaṃ nāma tato uttaritarasūraguṇo eva yakkhādibhāvena so bhavamāno abhisambhuṇeyya. Ayaṃ pana appānubhāvatāya pisācarūpo kiṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ niddāyanto ajja pabujjhitvā evaṃ vadatīti adhippāyo. Tenāha “kiṃ yakkho”tiādi.

354. Santhāgāra (assembly hall) means a house (agāra) with (saha) instruction on the meaning (attha-anusāsanaṃ). An assembly hall is also the establishing-house (santhāpana-agāraṃ) of royal families; the meaning is, in that assembly hall. At a certain time, at such a time, they deliberate here on the arrangement of royal duties, therefore it is an assembly hall; the meaning is, in that assembly hall. Established means 'impermanent' and 'not-self' were asserted. Now turning his back means turning away, not looking at the Blessed One's forehead. In the liquor house means in the house where liquor is prepared. Flour mat means a mat for placing flour on. Vāla means a basket. For making a hempen cloth means for the purpose of thread, which is the instrument for making a hempen cloth. Sāṇavākā means 'hemp bark is in these,' thus sāṇavākā; that is, hemp stalks. Taking these, they play a game similar to the washing of hemp, such as 'the breaking of uddāla flowers' and 'the breaking of hemp.' What is this fellow becoming? What kind of being is he, what is he becoming, that he could challenge the supreme person in the world, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, to a debate? Only one with heroic qualities superior to that, such as a yakkha or the like, could accomplish this. But this one, of little power, like a goblin—has he been sleeping all this time and just woken up today to speak thus? This is the intention. Therefore it is said: 'What, a yakkha?' and so on.

355. Mahāmajjhanhikasamayeti mahati majjhanhikakāle, gaganamajjhe sūriyagatavelāya. Divāpadhānikā padhānānuyuñjakā. Vattaṃ dassetvāti pacchābhattaṃ divāvihārūpagamanato pubbe kātabbavattaṃ dassetvā paṭipajjitvā. Bhagavantaṃ dassentoti bhagavati gāravabahumānaṃ vibhāvento ubho hatthe kamalamakulākāre katvā ukkhippa bhagavantaṃ dassento.

355. At the time of high noon means at the great time of midday, at the time when the sun has reached the middle of the sky. Divāpadhānikā means those devoted to striving during the day. Having shown the duty means having shown and undertaken the duty to be done after the meal before going to the day's abiding. Indicating the Blessed One means displaying reverence and great respect toward the Blessed One, raising both hands in the shape of a lotus bud and indicating the Blessed One.

Taṃ sandhāyāti taṃ aparicchinnagaṇanaṃ sandhāya evaṃ “mahatiyā licchaviparisāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Kiṃ sīsena bhūmiṃ paharanteneva vandanā katā hoti? Kerāṭikāti saṭhā. Mocentāti bhikkhādānato mocentā. Avakkhittamattikāpiṇḍo viyāti heṭṭhākhittamattikāpiṇḍo viya. Yattha katthacīti attano anurūpaṃ vacanaṃ asallapento yattha katthaci.

Referring to that: referring to that innumerable crowd, it was thus said: 'with a great assembly of Licchavis.' Is homage done merely by striking one's head on the ground? Kerāṭikā means fraudulent. Freeing means freeing from the giving of alms. Like a lump of clay thrown down means like a lump of clay cast downwards. Anywhere at all means not conversing with speech befitting oneself, anywhere at all.

356. Dissati [M 2.0204] “idaṃ imassa phala”nti apadissati etenāti deso, kāraṇaṃ, tadeva tassa pavattiṭṭhānatāya okāsoti āha “kañcideva desanti kañci okāsaṃ kiñci kāraṇa”nti. Okāso ṭhānanti ca kāraṇaṃ vuccati “aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.161; ma. ni. 3.128-131; a. ni. 1.268-295; vibha. 809). Yadākaṅkhasīti na vadanti anavasesadhammavisayattā paṭiññāya. Tumhanti tumhākaṃ. Yakkha…pe… paribbājakānanti ettha “pucchāvuso, yadākaṅkhasī”tiādīni (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. āḷavakasutta) pucchāvacanāni yathākkamaṃ yojetabbāni.

356. By this it is pointed out, 'This is the fruit of this'; thus it is a deso, a reason. That very thing, being the basis for its occurrence, is an occasion (okāso); thus he says: 'some desa means some occasion, some reason.' An occasion and a basis are also called a reason, as in such passages as: 'This is impossible, there is no occasion' (Dīgha Nikāya 3.161; Majjhima Nikāya 3.128–131; Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.268–295; Vibhaṅga 809). They do not say, 'Whenever you wish,' because the promise has the entire Dhamma as its scope without remainder. Tumhaṃ means 'your.' Here, in regard to 'the yakkha…pe… the wanderers,' the words of invitation to ask, such as 'Ask, friend, whenever you wish' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.246; Sutta Nipāta, Āḷavakasutta), should be connected in due order.

Ñatvā [V 2.0191] sayaṃ lokamimaṃ parañcāti idaṃ mahāsatto nirayaṃ saggañca tesaṃ paccakkhato dassetvā āha.

Having himself known this world and the other: the great being said this after having shown them hell and heaven directly.

Taggha te ahamakkhissaṃ, yathāpi kusalo tathāti yathā pakārena sukusalo sabbaññū jānāti katheti, tathā ahaṃ kathessāmi. Tassa pana kāraṇaṃ akāraṇañca avijānanto rājānaṃ karotu vā mā vā, ahaṃ pana te akkhissāmīti āha “rājā ca kho…pe… na vā”ti.

'Indeed, I will explain to you, just as one who is skilled': this means, just as a very skilled person, an omniscient one, knows and speaks, so will I speak. But whether the king, not knowing its reason and non-reason, acts or does not, I will still explain to you. Thus he says: 'whether the king…pe… or not.'

Kathitaniyāmeneva kathentoti teparivaṭṭakathāya dukkhalakkhaṇampesa kathessati, idha pana aññathā sāvakena assajinā kathitaṃ, aññathā samaṇena gotamenāti vacanokāsapariharaṇatthaṃ dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ anāmasitvā therena kathitaniyāmeneva aniccānattalakkhaṇameva kathentena bhagavatā – “rūpaṃ anattā yāva viññāṇaṃ anattā”ti vutte saccako taṃ asampaṭicchanto upamāya atthañāpane upamāpamāṇaṃ yathā “go viya gavayo”ti attānaṃ upameyyaṃ katvā upamāpamāṇena patiṭṭhāpetukāmo āha “upamā maṃ, bho gotama, paṭibhātī”ti, upamaṃ te karissāmi, upamāyapidhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānantīti adhippāyo. Bhagavā upamāsatena, aññena vāpi pamāṇena tava attā patiṭṭhāpetuṃ na labbhā attano viya pamāṇassapi anupalabbhanatoti āha “paṭibhātu taṃ aggivessanā”ti. Yathā hi attā nāma koci paramatthato na upalabbhati ekaṃsena anupaladdhito, evassa ñāpakapuggalaṃ pamāṇampi na upalabbhati. Tenāha “āhara taṃ [M 2.0205] upamaṃ vissattho”ti, na tena tava attavādo patiṭṭhaṃ labhatīti adhippāyo.

'Speaking in the very way it was spoken': this means he will speak of the characteristic of suffering with the talk of the three rounds. But here, in order to avoid the opportunity for saying, 'It was spoken of in one way by the disciple Assaji, and in another way by the ascetic Gotama,' the Blessed One, without touching upon the characteristic of suffering, speaking in the very way it had been spoken by the elder, spoke only of the characteristics of impermanence and non-self. When it was said by the Blessed One, 'Form is non-self… down to… consciousness is non-self,' Saccaka, not accepting it, wishing to establish his view by means of a simile and a standard of comparison in order to make the meaning known through a simile—just as one might say 'a gayal is like a cow'—making himself the thing to be compared, said: 'A simile occurs to me, venerable Gotama.' The intention is: 'I will give you a simile, for by a simile some intelligent people understand the meaning of what is said.' The Blessed One said, 'Let it occur to you, Aggivessana,' because your self cannot be established by a hundred similes or by any other standard, since, like the self itself, a standard for it is also not found. For just as no self whatsoever is found in an ultimate sense, being absolutely unobtainable, so too a person who could make it known and a standard for it are not found. Therefore he said, 'Bring forth that simile confidently,' the intention being: 'Your doctrine of self will not gain a footing by means of it.'

Yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ kāyikaṃ vā puññāpuññaṃ purisapuggale upalabbhati, tena viññāyati rūpattāyaṃ purisapuggalo, tathā yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ sukhadukkhapaṭisaṃvedanaṃ purisapuggale upalabbhati, yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ nīlādisañjānanaṃ, yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ rajjanadussanādi, yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ ārammaṇapaṭivijānanaṃ purisapuggale upalabbhati, tena viññāyati viññāṇattāyaṃ purisapuggaloti. Evaṃ rūpādilakkhaṇo attā tattha tattha kāye kalyāṇapāpakānaṃ kammānaṃ vipākaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, evañcetaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ, aññathā kammaphalasambandho na yujjeyyāti imamatthaṃ dassento “iminā kiṃ dīpetī”tiādimāha. Tattha teti sattā. Patiṭṭhāyāti nissāya. “Rūpattāyaṃ purisapuggalo”tiādinā rūpādidhamme “attā”ti vatvā puna “rūpe patiṭṭhāyā”tiādiṃ vadanto ayaṃ nigaṇṭho attano vādaṃ bhindati patiṭṭhānassa, patiṭṭhāyakassa ca abhedadīpanato. Rūpādayo [V 2.0192] vedanādisabhāvā attā tannissayena puññādikiriyāsamupaladdhito idha yaṃ nissāya puññādikiriyā samupalabbhati, te rūpādayo sattasaññitā attasabhāvā diṭṭhā yathā taṃ devatādīsu, ye pana sattasaññitā tato aññe asattasabhāvā diṭṭhā yathā taṃ kaṭṭhakaliṅgarādīsūti evaṃ sādhetabbaṃ atthaṃ sahetuṃ katvā dassento nigaṇṭho nidassanaṃ ānesīti āha “ativiya sakāraṇaṃ katvā upamaṃ āharī”ti. Tassa pana “balakaraṇīyā”ti vuttapurisappayogā viya bījagāmabhūtagāmāpi sajīvā evāti laddhīti te sadisūdāharaṇabhāvena vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sace pana ye jīvassa ādhāraṇabhāvena sahitena pavattetabbabhāvena sallakkhetabbā, te sajīvāti icchitā, na kevalena pavattetabbabhāvena. Evaṃ sati “balakaraṇīyā kammantā”ti vadantena visadisūdāharaṇabhāvena upanītanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Whatever bodily merit or demerit is found in an individual person, by that it is known that this individual person is of the nature of form. Similarly, whatever experience of pleasure and pain is found in an individual person, whatever perception of blue and so on is found, whatever liking, aversion, and so on is found, whatever discrimination of an object is found in an individual person, by that it is known that this individual person is of the nature of consciousness. Thus a self characterized by form and so on experiences in the body here and there the result, pleasure and pain, of good and bad kamma. And this should be accepted thus; otherwise the connection between kamma and its fruit would not be tenable. Showing this meaning, he said, 'What does he clarify by this?' and so on. Therein, te means beings. Patiṭṭhāya means having depended. Having said by 'this individual person is of the nature of form,' etc., that the phenomena of form, etc., are 'self,' and then again saying 'having depended on form,' etc., this Nigaṇṭha breaks his own thesis by showing the non-difference between the basis and that which depends on the basis. The Nigaṇṭha brought a demonstration, showing with reason the point to be established thus: 'Form, etc., which have the nature of feeling, etc., are the self. Since meritorious actions and so on are found in dependence on them, here those things—form, etc.—in dependence on which meritorious actions and so on are found, are seen as having the nature of self and are designated as "beings," as in the case of devas and so on. But those designated as "beings" that are other than these are seen as having a non-sentient nature, as in the case of sticks, clods, and so on.' Thus it is said: 'He brought a simile, making it very well-reasoned.' It should be understood that for him, according to his tenet, just as the effort of a person is spoken of as 'work to be done with strength,' so too seed-kinds and plant-kinds are living; thus they are mentioned as a similar example. But if it is held that only those things are living which are to be marked by their functioning in conjunction with their role as a support for life, and not by their mere functioning, then it should be understood that by saying 'work to be done with strength,' a dissimilar example has been adduced.

Samattho nāma natthi attavādabhañjanassa anattatāpatiṭṭhāpanassa ca sugatāveṇikattā. Yaṃ panetarahi sāsanikā yathāsatti tadubhayaṃ karonti, taṃ buddhehi dinnanaye ṭhatvā tesaṃ desanānusārato. Nivattetvāti [M 2.0206] nīharitvā, visuṃ katvāti attho. Sakalaṃ vesālinti sabbavesālivāsinaṃ janaṃ nissayūpacārena nissitaṃ vadati yathā “gāmo āgato”ti. Saṃvaṭṭitvāti sampiṇḍitvā, ekajjhaṃ gahetvāti attho.

There is no one capable of refuting the doctrine of self and establishing the truth of non-self, as this is unique to a Sugata. But that the adherents of the teaching nowadays do both to the best of their ability is by standing in the method given by the Buddhas, in accordance with their teaching. 'Having turned back' means having led out, that is, having made separate. 'The whole of Vesālī' refers to all the people dwelling in Vesālī; it is a statement of the container for the contained by way of metonymy, as when one says, 'The village has come.' 'Having rolled up' means having lumped together, that is, having taken as one.

357. Patiṭṭhapetvāti yathā taṃ vādaṃ na avajānāti, evaṃ paṭiññaṃ kāretvāti attho. Ghāti-saddo hiṃsanattho, tato ca saddavidū arahatthaṃ tāya-saddaṃ uppādetvā ghātetāyanti rūpasiddhiṃ icchantīti āha “ghātāraha”nti. Jāpetāyantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Vattituñca marahatīti ma-kāro padasandhikaro. Visesetvā dīpetīti “vattati”icceva avatvā “vattituñca marahatī”ti dutiyena padena bhagavatā vuttaṃ visesetvā dīpeti.

357. 'Having established' means having made him make a promise in such a way that he does not despise that thesis. The word ghāti has the meaning of harming. From that, grammarians, wishing to form the word ghātetāya, derive the suffix -tāya in the sense of 'worthy of,' and thus it is said ghātāraha (worthy of being harmed). This same method applies also in jāpetāya and so on. In 'vattituñca marahatī,' the 'm' is for euphonic conjunction. 'He clarifies the distinction': this means that instead of just saying 'vattati,' the Blessed One clarifies the distinction by means of the second phrase, 'vattituñca marahatī' (and is fit to speak).

Pāsādikaṃ abhirūpanti abhimatarūpasampannaṃ sabbāvayavaṃ. Tato eva susajjitaṃ sabbakālaṃ suṭṭhu sajjitākārameva. Evaṃvidhanti yādisaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, taṃ dasseti “dubbaṇṇa”ntiādinā. Imasmiṃ ṭhāneti “vattati te tasmiṃ rūpe vaso”ti etasmiṃ kāraṇaggahaṇe. Kāraṇañhetaṃ bhagavatā gahitaṃ “vattati…pe… mā ahosī”ti. Tenetaṃ dasseti rūpaṃ anattā avasavattanato, yañhi vase na vattati, taṃ anattakameva diṭṭhaṃ yathā taṃ sampatti. Vādanti dosaṃ niggahaṃ āropessati. Sattadhā muddhā phalatīti sahadhammikasākacchāhi tathāgate, pucchante abyākaraṇena vihesāya kayiramānattā tatiye vāre dhammatāvasena vihesakassa sattadhā muddhā phalati yathā taṃ sabbaññupaṭiññāya bhagavato sammukhabhāvūpagamane. Vajirapāṇi [V 2.0193] pana kasmā ṭhito hotīti? Bhagavā viya anukampamāno mahantaṃ bhayānakaṃ rūpaṃ māpetvā tāsetvā imaṃ diṭṭhiṃ vissajjāpemīti tassa purato ākāse vajiraṃ āharanto tiṭṭhati, na muddhaṃ phāletukāmo. Na hi bhagavato purato kassaci anattho nāma hoti. Yasmā pana bhagavā ekaṃsato sahadhammikameva pañhaṃ pucchati, tasmā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “pucchite”icceva vuttaṃ.

'Inspiring confidence and very beautiful' means endowed with a pleasing form, complete in all limbs. For that very reason it is well-adorned, always having a very well-adorned appearance. 'Of such a kind': he shows what kind is meant by 'ill-favored,' and so on. 'In this case' means in this grasping of a reason: 'Does your control extend over that form?' And this reason was taken up by the Blessed One: 'Would your control extend…pe… may it not be so.' By this he shows that form is non-self because it is not subject to control. For whatever is not subject to control is seen to be non-self, like one's property. 'He will find fault' means he will impute a fault, a refutation. 'The head splits into seven pieces': When harassment is committed by not answering a question put by the Tathāgata in a discussion in accordance with the Dhamma, on the third occasion the harasser's head splits into seven pieces by the power of the Dhamma, as when one approaches the presence of the Blessed One who has made the claim to omniscience. But why does Vajirapāṇi stand there? Feeling compassion like the Blessed One, he stands in the sky in front of him holding a vajra, having created a great terrifying form to frighten him, thinking, 'I will make him abandon this view'; he is not intent on splitting his head. For in the presence of the Blessed One no one comes to any harm. But since the Blessed One asks a question that is exclusively in accordance with the Dhamma, it is said in the commentary simply 'when asked.'

Ādittanti dippamānaṃ. Akkhināsādīnīti ādi-saddena eḷakasīsasadisakesamassuādīnaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. “Diṭṭhivissajjāpanattha”nti vatvā nayidaṃ yadicchāvasena [M 2.0207] āgamanaṃ, atha kho ādito mahābrahmānaṃ purato katvā attanā katapaṭiññāvasenāti dassento “apicā”tiādimāha. Nti vajirapāṇiṃ. Taṃ saccakassa paṭiññāya parivattanakāraṇaṃ. Aññepi nu khotiādi saccakassa vīmaṃsakabhāvadassanaṃ. Avīmaṃsakena hi taṃ disvā mahāyakkhoti vadeyya, tenassa asāruppaṃ siyā, ayaṃ pana aññesaṃ abhītabhāvaṃ upadhāretvā “addhāme yakkhaṃ na passanti, tasmā mayhameva bhayaṃ uppanna”nti tīretvā yuttappattavasena paṭipajji.

'Aflame' means blazing. 'Eyes, nose, etc.': by the word 'etc.' he includes hair like a goat's head, a beard, and so on. Having said, 'For the purpose of making him abandon the view,' he says 'Moreover,' etc., to show that this coming was not at random but was by reason of the promise he himself had made from the start, having put Mahābrahmā at the head. (This refers to Vajirapāṇi.) That is the reason for the reversal of Saccaka's promise. 'Are there others too?' etc., shows Saccaka's investigative nature. For a non-investigative person, on seeing it, would say, 'It is a great yakkha,' which would be unsuitable for him. But this one, having observed the fearlessness of the others, concluded, 'Surely they do not see the yakkha; therefore fear has arisen only in me,' and so he proceeded in a suitable manner.

358. Upadhāretvāti byākātabbamatthaṃ sallakkhetvā. Eseva nayoti saṅkhāraviññāṇesupi saññāya viya nayoti attho. Vuttavipariyāyenāti “akusalā dukkhā vedanā mā ahosi, akusalā domanassasampayuttā saññā mā ahosī”tiādinā nayena attho veditabbo. Sappadaṭṭhavisanti sabbasattānaṃ sappadaṭṭhaṭṭhāne sarīrapadese patitaṃ visaṃ. Allīnoti saṃsiliṭṭho. Upagatoti na apagato. Ajjhositoti gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā ṭhito. Parito jāneyyāti samantato sabbaso kiñcipi asesetvā jāneyya. Parikkhepetvāti āyatiṃ anuppattidhammatāpādanavasena sabbaso khepetvā. Tathābhūto cassa khayavayaṃ upaneti nāmāti āha “khayaṃ vayaṃ anuppādaṃ upanetvā”ti.

358. ‘Having considered’ means having discerned the meaning to be explained. ‘This is the same method’ means that the method is the same for formations and consciousness as it is for perception; this is the meaning. ‘By the opposite of what was stated’ means the meaning should be understood in this way: ‘May unwholesome painful feeling not be; may unwholesome perception associated with displeasure not be,’ and so on. ‘The venom of a snakebite’ is the venom that has fallen on a bodily part, in the place of a snakebite, of any being. ‘Adhered’ means clung. ‘Approached’ means not departed. ‘Consumed’ means having swallowed and finished it. ‘Should know thoroughly’ means one should know completely, in every way, leaving nothing whatsoever remaining. ‘Having exhausted’ means having entirely exhausted it by way of bringing about its nature of non-arising in the future. Being such, it leads to its destruction and passing away; this is what is meant by the words, ‘having brought it to destruction, passing away, and non-arising.’

359. Attano vādassa asārabhāvato, yathāparikappitassa vā sārassa abhāvato antosāravirahito ritto. Vippakāranti diṭṭhiyā sīlācārassa ca vasena virūpataṃ sāparādhataṃ sāvajjataṃ tesaṃ upari āropetvā. Sinnapattoti tanukapatto. Viphāritanti viphāḷitaṃ.

359. Empty, because his own doctrine is without substance, or because the substance he had imagined is absent; thus he is devoid of inner substance, hollow. ‘Misrepresentation’ means imputing deformity, guilt, and fault to them on account of their views and conduct. ‘A rotten leaf’ means a thin leaf. ‘Split asunder’ means burst open.

Asārakarukkhaparicitoti palāsādiasārarukkhakoṭṭane kataparicayo. Thaddhabhāvanti vipakkabhāvaṃ, tikkhabhāvanti attho. Natthīti sadā natthīti na vattabbaṃ. Parisatīti catuparisamajjhe[V 2.0194]. Tathā hi “gaṇṭhikaṃ paṭimuñcitvā paṭicchannasarīrā”ti vuttaṃ. Yantāruḷhassa viyāti byākaraṇatthaṃ vāyamayantaṃ āruḷhassa viya.

‘One accustomed to worthless trees’ means one who is practiced in cutting worthless trees such as the palāsa and so on. ‘Stiffness’ means a state of opposition, that is, sharpness. ‘It does not exist’: it should not be said that it always does not exist. ‘In the assembly’ means in the midst of the fourfold assembly. For it is said: ‘Having untied the knot, with their bodies covered.’ ‘Like one mounted on a machine’ means like one who has mounted a contraption and is striving to provide an explanation.

360. Diṭṭhivisūkānīti [M 2.0208] diṭṭhikiñcakāni. Diṭṭhisañcaritānīti diṭṭhitāḷanāni. Diṭṭhivipphanditānīti diṭṭhiiñjitāni. Tesaṃ adhippāyaṃ ñatvāti tesaṃ licchavikumārānaṃ iñjiteneva ajjhāsayaṃ jānitvā. Tenāha “ime”tiādi.

360. ‘Contortions of view’ means the splinters of view. ‘Wanderings of view’ means the fluctuations of view. ‘Quiverings of view’ means the stirrings of view. ‘Having known their intention’ means having known the disposition of those Licchavi youths by their very gestures. Therefore he said: ‘These,’ and so on.

361. Yasmiṃ adhigate puggalo satthusāsane visārado hoti parehi asaṃhāriyo, taṃ ñāṇaṃ visāradassa bhāvoti katvā vesārajjanti āha “vesārajjappattoti ñāṇappatto”ti. Tato evamassa na paro paccetabbo etassa atthīti aparappaccayo. Na paro pattiyo saddahātabbo etassa atthīti aparappattiyo. Kāmaṃ saccako sekkhabhūmi asekkhabhūmīti idaṃ sāsanavohāraṃ na jānāti. Passatīti pana dassanakiriyāya vippakatabhāvassa vuttattā “na ettāvatā bhikkhukiccaṃ pariyosita”nti aññāsi, tasmā puna “kittāvatā panā”ti pucchaṃ ārabhi. Tena vuttaṃ “passatīti vuttattā”tiādi.

361. When this is attained, a person becomes confident in the Teacher’s dispensation and unshakeable by others. Because that knowledge is the state of one who is confident, it is called ‘confidence.’ Thus it says: ‘attained to confidence’ means ‘attained to knowledge.’ Hence he is ‘not dependent on another’ because for him there is no other to be relied upon. He is ‘not trusting in another’ because for him there is no other to be trusted. Granted, Saccaka does not know this terminology of the teaching—‘the trainee’s stage’ and ‘the adept’s stage’—but since it was said, ‘he sees,’ and since the incompleteness of the act of seeing was stated, he understood: ‘The monk’s task is not finished to this extent.’ Therefore he began to ask further, ‘But to what extent…?’ Hence it was said: ‘Because it was said, “he sees,”’ and so on.

Yathābhūtaṃ passatīti dassanaṃ, visiṭṭhaṭṭhena anuttariyaṃ, dassanameva anuttariyanti dassanānuttariyaṃ, dassanesu vā anuttariyaṃ dassanānuttariyaṃ. Lokiyapaññāti cettha vipassanāpaññā veditabbā. Sā hi sabbalokiyapaññāhi visiṭṭhaṭṭhena “anuttarā”ti vuttā. Lokiyapaṭipadānuttariyesupi eseva nayo. Idāni nippariyāyatova tividhampi anuttariyaṃ dassetuṃ “suddhalokuttaramevā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Satipi sabbesampi lokuttaradhammānaṃ anuttarabhāve ukkaṭṭhaniddesena aggamaggapaññā tato uttaritarassa abhāvato dassanānuttariyaṃ. Tenāha “arahattamaggasammādiṭṭhī”ti. Sesāni maggaṅgānīti sesāni arahattamaggaṅgāni. Tāni hi matthakappattāni nibbānagāminī paṭipadāti. Aggaphalavimuttīti aggamaggassa phalavimutti arahattaphalaṃ. Khīṇāsavassāti sabbaso khīyamānāsavassa. Nibbānadassananti aggamaggasammādiṭṭhiyā sacchikiriyābhisamayamāha. Tattha maggaṅgānīti aṭṭha maggaṅgāni. Catusaccantogadhattā sabbassa ñeyyadhammassa “cattāri saccāni buddho”ti vuttaṃ. Saccānugatasammohaviddhaṃsaneneva hi bhagavato sabbaso ñeyyāvaraṇappahānaṃ. Nibbisevanoti niruddhakilesavisevano.

‘Seeing as it really is’ is seeing. Because it is excellent, it is unsurpassed. Seeing itself is unsurpassed, thus ‘unsurpassed seeing.’ Or, among seeings it is the unsurpassed, thus ‘unsurpassed seeing.’ Herein, by ‘mundane wisdom’ insight wisdom is to be understood. For it is called ‘unsurpassed’ because it is more excellent than all mundane wisdoms. This same method applies to the unsurpassed mundane path. Now, to show the threefold unsurpassed directly, it is said, ‘purely supramundane,’ and so on. Although all supramundane states are unsurpassed, by way of a supreme designation the wisdom of the highest path is the ‘unsurpassed seeing’ because there is nothing further beyond it. Therefore it says, ‘the right view of the path of arahantship.’ ‘The remaining path factors’ means the remaining factors of the path of arahantship. For these, having reached the peak, are the path leading to Nibbāna. ‘The supreme fruit-liberation’ is the fruit-liberation of the supreme path, the fruit of arahantship. ‘Of one whose taints are destroyed’ means of one whose taints are utterly destroyed. ‘The vision of Nibbāna’ refers to the realization and direct experience by means of the right view of the supreme path. Therein, ‘path factors’ means the eight path factors. Because the entire domain of the knowable is included in the four truths, it is said, ‘The Buddha [knows] the four truths.’ For it is precisely by destroying the delusion concerning the truths that the Blessed One has completely abandoned the obstruction to the knowable. ‘Without indulgence’ means one for whom indulgence in the defilements has ceased.

362. Dhaṃsīti anuddhaṃsanasīlā. Anupahatanti avikkhittaṃ. Sakalanti anūnaṃ. Kāyaṅganti [V 2.0195] kāyameva aṅganti vadanti, kāyasaṅkhātaṃ aṅgaṃ sīsādiavayavanti [M 2.0209] attho. Tathā “hotu, sādhū”ti evamidaṃ vācāya avayavo vācaṅganti.

362. ‘Not aggressive’ means not having a destructive nature. ‘Unimpaired’ means undistracted. ‘Complete’ means without deficiency. ‘Body-part’: they say the body itself is a part; the meaning is that a part designated as ‘body’ is a limb such as the head and other limbs. Similarly, ‘so be it,’ ‘good,’ and so on are parts of speech, thus ‘speech-part.’

363. Āharantīti abhiharanti. Puññanti puññaphalasaṅkhāto ānubhāvo. Puññaphalampi hi uttarapadalopena “puñña”nti vuccati – “kusalānaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammānaṃ samādānahetu evamidaṃ puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.80). Tenāha “āyatiṃ vipākakkhandhā”ti. Puññamahīti mahati puññaphalavibhūti setacchattamakuṭacāmarādi. Tena vuttaṃ “vipākakkhandhānaṃyeva parivāro”ti. Licchavīhi pesitena khādanīyabhojanīyena samaṇo gotamo sasāvakasaṅgho mayā parivisito, tasmā licchavīnameva taṃ puññaṃ hotīti. Tenāha “taṃ dāyakānaṃ sukhāya hotū”ti. Yasmā pana bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca saccakena dānaṃ dinnaṃ, na licchavīhi, tasmā bhagavā saccakassa satiṃ parivattento “yaṃ kho”tiādimāha. Tena vuttaṃ “iti bhagavā”tiādi. Nigaṇṭhassa matena vināyevāti saccakassa cittena vinā eva tassa dakkhiṇaṃ khettagataṃ katvā dasseti. Tenāha “attano dinnaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ…pe… niyyātesī”ti.

363. ‘They bring’ means they offer. ‘Merit’ means the power designated as the fruit of merit. For the fruit of merit is also called ‘merit’ by eliding the last word, as in: ‘Bhikkhus, on account of undertaking wholesome qualities, this merit thus increases,’ and so on (DN 33). Therefore it is said: ‘the future aggregates of result.’ ‘The greatness of merit’ means the great splendor of the fruit of merit, such as a white parasol, a crown, a yak-tail fan, and so on. Therefore it is said: ‘it is just an accessory of the aggregates of result.’ Saccaka thinks: ‘The ascetic Gotama and his community of disciples were served by me with food and delicacies sent by the Licchavis, so that merit belongs to the Licchavis.’ Hence, he says: ‘May that be for the happiness of the donors.’ However, because the gift was given by Saccaka to the Blessed One and the community of bhikkhus, not by the Licchavis, the Blessed One, redirecting Saccaka's mindfulness, says, ‘Whatever…,’ and so on. Therefore it is said: ‘Thus the Blessed One…,’ etc. ‘Even without the Nigaṇṭha's consent’ means that even without Saccaka's intention, he shows that his offering has reached a worthy field. Hence, it is said: ‘his own given offering… he dedicated.’

Cūḷasaccakasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Cūḷasaccaka Sutta is completed.

6. Mahāsaccakasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Mahāsaccaka Sutta

364. Ekaṃ [V 2.0196] samayaṃ bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharatīti iminā tadā bhagavato vesāliyaṃ nivāsaparicchinno pubbaṇhādibhedo sabbo samayo sādhāraṇato gahito, tathā tena kho pana samayenāti ca iminā. Pubbaṇhasamayanti pana iminā tabbiseso, yo bhikkhācāratthāya paccavekkhaṇakālo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “tīhi padehi ekova samayo vutto”ti vuttaṃ visesassa sāmaññantogadhattā. Mukhadhovanassa pubbakālakiriyābhāvasāmaññato vuttaṃ “mukhaṃ dhovitvā”ti. Mukhaṃ dhovitvā eva hi vāsadhuro ce, velaṃ sallakkhetvā yathāciṇṇaṃ bhāvanānuyogaṃ, ganthadhuro ce, ganthaparicaye katipaye nisajjavāre anuyuñjitvā pattacīvaraṃ ādāya vitakkamāḷaṃ upagacchati.

364. By this phrase, 'At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī,' the entire period of the Blessed One’s residence in Vesālī is generally taken, including its divisions such as the morning; and similarly by this phrase, 'at that particular time.' But by this phrase, 'the morning time,' a specific part of it is taken, which is the time for reviewing for the sake of the alms-round. In the commentary, however, it is said: 'The same time is indicated by three phrases,' because the specific is included within the general. The phrase 'having washed his face' is stated generally, referring to the common act of washing the face as a preliminary activity. For having washed his face, if he was one who bore the yoke of residence, after observing the time, he would engage in his customary practice of meditation; if he was one who bore the yoke of study, after applying himself for some seated periods to the study of the texts, he would take his bowl and robe and approach the Vitakkamāḷa.

Kāraṇaṃ [M 2.0210] yuttaṃ, anucchavikanti attho. Pubbe yathācintitaṃ pañhaṃ apucchitvā aññaṃ pucchanto maggaṃ ṭhapetvā ummaggato parivattento viya hotīti āha “passena tāva pariharanto”ti.

'A suitable reason' means 'appropriate.' By asking another question without having first asked the question he had previously considered, he is like one who sets aside the path and turns onto a wrong path. Hence it is said: 'first turning aside.'

365. Ūrukkhambhopi nāma bhavissatīti ettha nāma-saddo vimhayatthoti katvā vuttaṃ “vimhayatthavasenā”tiādi. “Andho nāma pabbataṃ abhiruhissatī”tiādīsu viya vimhayavācīsaddayogena hi “bhavissatī”ti anāgatavacanaṃ. Kāyanvayanti kāyānugataṃ. “Ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.379; ma. ni. 1.112; ma. ni. 3.154) kāyassa asubhāniccāditāya anupassanā kāyabhāvanāti āha “kāyabhāvanāti pana vipassanā vuccatī”ti. Anāgatarūpanti abhīte atthe anāgatasaddāropanaṃ anāgatappayogo na sameti. Atthopīti “ūrukkhambhopi nāma bhavissatī”ti vuttaatthopi na sameti. Ayanti attakilamathānuyogo. Tesanti nigaṇṭhānaṃ.

365. 'Even a thigh-post might become...': here the word 'nāma' is for the purpose of astonishment, thus it is said 'by way of astonishment,' and so on. For, as in such statements as 'A blind man, indeed, might climb a mountain,' the future tense 'bhavissati' is used in conjunction with a word expressing astonishment. 'Following the body' means 'connected with the body.' By means of such phrases as 'This body, too, is of such a nature, has such a constitution, and has not gone beyond it,' the contemplation of the body's impurity, impermanence, and so on, is the development of the body. Thus it is said: 'But "development of the body" is called insight.' 'Future form': the application of the word 'future' to a past matter is not a fitting use of 'future.' The meaning too, that is, the meaning stated in 'Even a thigh-post might become,' does not fit. 'This' refers to the devotion to self-mortification. 'Of them' refers to the Nigaṇṭhas.

366. Attano adhippetakāyabhāvanaṃ vitthārento vitthārato dassento ye taṃ anuyuttā, te nāmagottato vibhāvento “nando vaccho”tiādimāha. Kiliṭṭhatapānanti kāyassa kilesanatapānaṃ puggalānaṃ. Jātamedanti medabhāvāpattivasena uppannamedaṃ. Purimaṃ pahāyāti kālaparicchedena anāhāraappāhāratādivasena kāyassa apacinanaṃ khedanaṃ pariccajitvā. Kāyabhāvanā [V 2.0197] pana na paññāyatīti niyamaṃ paramatthato kāyabhāvanāpi tava ñāṇena na ñāyati, sesatopi na dissati.

366. Elaborating on his own intended development of the body, showing it in detail, and distinguishing by name and clan those devoted to it, he said: 'Nanda, Vaccha,' and so on. 'Of defiled austerity' means the defiling austerity of the body of persons. 'Having produced fat' means the fat that arose by way of reaching a state of fatness. 'Having abandoned the former' means having given up the wasting away and tormenting of the body by way of periods of fasting, eating little, and so on. 'But development of the body is not discerned': as a rule, in the ultimate sense, the development of the body is not known by your knowledge, nor is it seen in other respects.

367. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāneti “kāyabhāvanampi kho tvaṃ, aggivessana, na aññāsi, kuto pana tvaṃ cittabhāvanaṃ jānissasī”ti imasmiṃ ṭhāne. Tathā “yo tvaṃ evaṃ oḷārikaṃ dubbalaṃ kāyabhāvanaṃ na jānāsi, so tvaṃ kuto santasukhumaṃ cittabhāvanaṃ jānissasī”ti etasmiṃ atthavaṇṇanāṭhāne. Abuddhavacanaṃ nāmetaṃ padanti kāyabhāvanāsaññitavipassanāto cittabhāvanā santā, vipassanā pana pādakajjhānato oḷārikā ceva dubbalā cāti ayañca etassa padassa attho. “Abuddhavacanaṃ nāmetaṃ vacanaṃ [M 2.0211] siyā”ti vatvā thero pakkamituṃ ārabhati. Atha naṃ mahāsīvatthero “vipassanā nāmesā na ādito subrūhitā balavatī tikkhā visadā hoti, tasmā taruṇavasenāyamattho veditabbo”ti dassento “dissati, bhikkhave”ti suttapadaṃ (saṃ. ni. 2.62) āhari. Tattha ādānanti paṭisandhi. Nikkhepananti cuti. Oḷārikanti arūpadhammehi duṭṭhullabhāvattā oḷārikaṃ. Kāyanti catusantatirūpasamūhabhūtaṃ kāyaṃ. Oḷārikanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, oḷārikākārenāti attho. Teneva vuttaṃ “ādānampi nikkhepanampī”ti.

367. In this context, that is, in the context of the passage: 'But you, Aggivessana, do not even know the development of the body; how then will you know the development of the mind?' And similarly, in this place of meaning-explanation: 'You who do not know such a gross and weak development of the body, how will you know the peaceful and subtle development of the mind?' 'This is not the word of the Buddha'—this phrase means that mental development is peaceful in comparison to insight, which is designated as bodily development; but insight is gross and weak in comparison to the basic jhāna. This is the meaning of this phrase. Having said, 'This word might not be the word of the Buddha,' the elder began to depart. Then the great elder Mahāsīva, showing that 'This insight is not from the beginning well-cultivated, strong, sharp, and clear; therefore this meaning should be understood as referring to its youthful stage,' adduced the sutta passage: 'It is seen, bhikkhus...' (SN 12.62). Therein, 'taking up' means rebirth-linking. 'Laying down' means decease. 'Gross' means gross because of its coarseness in comparison with immaterial phenomena. 'Body' means the body that is the collection of the four continuities of material form. 'Gross' is a neuter designation indicating manner, meaning 'in a gross manner.' For that reason it is said, 'both taking up and laying down.'

368. Sukhasārāgena samannāgatoti sukhavedanāya balavatararāgena samaṅgībhūto. Paṭṭhāne paṭisiddhā avacaneneva. Tasmāti sukhe ṭhite eva dukkhassānuppajjanato. Evaṃ vuttanti “sukhāya vedanāya nirodhā uppajjati dukkhā vedanā”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ, na anantarāva uppajjanato. Khepetvāti kusalāni khepetvā. Gaṇhitvā attano eva okāsaṃ gahetvā. Ubhatopakkhaṃ hutvāti “kadāci sukhavedanā, kadāci dukkhavedanā”ti pakkhadvayavasenapi vedanā cittassa pariyādāya hoti yathākkamaṃ abhāvitakāyassa abhāvitacittassa.

368. 'Endowed with strong lust for pleasure' means being endowed with a very strong lust for pleasant feeling. It is prohibited in the Paṭṭhāna simply by not being mentioned. 'Therefore' means because suffering does not arise when pleasure is present. 'Thus it is said': it is said thus, 'With the cessation of pleasant feeling, painful feeling arises,' but not because it arises immediately after. 'Having exhausted' means having exhausted wholesome qualities. 'Having seized' means having seized its own opportunity. 'Having become twofold': by way of the two sides, 'sometimes pleasant feeling, sometimes painful feeling,' feeling overwhelms the mind of one with an undeveloped body and an undeveloped mind, respectively.

369. Vipassanā ca sukhassa paccanīkāti sukkhavipassakassaādikammikassa mahābhūtapariggahādikāle bahi cittacāraṃ nisedhetvā kammaṭṭhāne eva satiṃ saṃharantassa aladdhassādaṃ kāyasukhaṃ na vindati, sambādhe vaje sanniruddho gogaṇo viya vihaññati vipphandati, accāsannahetukañca sarīre dukkhaṃ uppajjateva. Tena vuttaṃ “dukkhassa āsannā”ti. Tenāha “vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā”tiādi. Addhāne gacchante gacchanteti mahābhūtapariggahādivasena kāle gacchante. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sarīrapadese. Dukkhaṃ dūrāpagataṃ hoti samāpattibalena vikkhambhitattā appanābhāvato. Anappakaṃ vipulaṃ. Sukhanti jhānasukhaṃ[V 2.0198]. Okkamatīti jhānasamuṭṭhānapaṇītarūpavasena rūpakāyaṃ anupavisati, nāmakāyokkamane vattabbameva natthi. Kāyapassaddhikammikassapi sammasanabhāvanā paṭṭhapetvā nisinnassa kassaci āditova kāyakilamathacittupaghātāpi sambhavanti, samādhissa pana apaccanīkattā siniddhabhāvato ca [M 2.0212] na sukkhavipassanā viya sukhassa vipaccanīko, anukkamena ca dukkhaṃ vikkhambhetīti āha “yathā samādhī”ti. Yathā samādhi, vipassanāya panetaṃ natthīti āha “na ca tathā vipassanā”ti. Tena vuttanti yasmā vipassanā sukhassa paccanīkā, sā ca kāyabhāvanā, tena vuttaṃ “uppannāpi sukhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, bhāvitattā kāyassā”ti. Tathā yasmā samādhi dukkhassa paccanīko, so ca cittabhāvanā, tena vuttaṃ “uppannāpi dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, bhāvitattā cittassā”ti yojanā.

369. And insight is antagonistic to pleasure. For a beginner practicing dry insight, having prevented the mind from wandering outside and concentrating mindfulness only on the meditation subject, not having obtained the taste, he does not find bodily pleasure. Like a herd of cattle confined in a narrow pen, he is vexed and struggles. And because the cause is very near, suffering certainly arises in the body. For that reason it is said, 'near to suffering.' Therefore he said, 'having established insight,' and so on. As time passes—that is, as time is spent by way of comprehending the great elements, etc.—here and there, that is, in this or that part of the body, suffering is far removed, being suppressed by the power of attainment due to the state of absorption. The pleasure is not insignificant but extensive. 'Pleasure' means jhāna-pleasure. 'It descends' means that by way of the refined material form arisen from jhāna, it enters the material body; there is nothing to be said about its descending into the mental body. Even for one practicing with bodily tranquility, for someone sitting after having established the development of comprehension, from the very beginning bodily weariness and mental affliction can occur. But concentration, being non-antagonistic and smooth by nature, is not antagonistic to pleasure as dry insight is; and it gradually suppresses suffering. Hence it is said, 'as with concentration.' As with concentration, but this is not so for insight; hence it is said, 'but not so with insight.' Therefore it is said: because insight is antagonistic to pleasure, and that is the development of the body, for that reason it is said, 'Even when a pleasant feeling has arisen, it does not remain overwhelming the mind, because of the developed state of the body.' Similarly, because concentration is antagonistic to suffering, and that is the development of the mind, for that reason it is said, 'Even when a painful feeling has arisen, it does not remain overwhelming the mind, because of the developed state of the mind.' This is the connection.

370. Guṇe ghaṭṭetvāti apadesena vinā samīpameva netvā. Taṃ vata mama cittaṃ uppannā sukhā vedanā pariyādāya ṭhassatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti yojanā.

370. 'Having brought into contact with the qualities' means having brought it very near without any pretext. The connection is: 'There is no possibility that an arisen pleasant feeling will remain overwhelming my mind.'

371. Kiṃ na bhavissati, sukhāpi dukkhāpi vedanā yathāpaccayaṃ uppajjatevāti attho. Tamatthanti sukhadukkhavedanānaṃ uppattiyā attano cittassa anabhibhavanīyatāsaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ. Tattha tāva pāsarāsisutte bodhipallaṅke nisajjā “tattheva nisīdi”nti vuttā. Idha mahāsaccakasutte dukkarakārikāya dukkaracaraṇe nisajjā “tattheva nisīdi”nti vuttā.

371. 'What will not be?': the meaning is that both pleasant and painful feelings will certainly arise in accordance with conditions. 'That purpose' means the purpose described as the invincibility of one's own mind in the face of the arising of pleasant and painful feelings. There, in the Pāsarāsi Sutta, the sitting on the seat of awakening is spoken of as 'he sat right there.' Here, in the Mahāsaccaka Sutta, the sitting during the practice of austerities is spoken of as 'he sat right there.'

374. Chandakaraṇavasenāti taṇhāyanavasenāti attho. Sinehakaraṇavasenāti sinehanavasena. Mucchākaraṇavasenāti mohanavasena pamādāpādanena. Vipāsākaraṇavasenāti pātukamyatāvasena. Anudahanavasenāti rāgagginā anudahanavasena. Lokuttaramaggavevacanameva vaṭṭanissaraṇassa adhippetattā.

374. 'By way of causing desire' means by way of craving. 'By way of causing affection' means by way of affection. 'By way of causing infatuation' means by way of delusion, by causing negligence. 'By way of causing thirst' means by way of longing. 'By way of burning' means by way of burning with the fire of lust. It is a synonym for the supramundane path, because escape from the round of existence is intended.

Allaggahaṇena kilesānaṃ asamucchinnabhāvaṃ dasseti, sasnehaggahaṇena avikkhambhitabhāvaṃ, udake pakkhittabhāvaggahaṇena samudācārāvatthaṃ, udumbarakaṭṭhaggahaṇena attabhāvassa asārakattaṃ. Imināva nayenāti “allaṃ udumbarakaṭṭha”ntiādinā vuttanayena. Saputtabhariyapabbajjāyāti puttabhariyehi saddhiṃ kataparibbājakapabbajjāvasena veditabbā. Kuṭīcakabahūdakahaṃsa-paramahaṃsādibhedā brāhmaṇapabbajjā.

By the taking up of 'wet,' it shows the uneradicated state of the defilements; by the taking up of 'sappy,' their unsuppressed state; by the taking up of 'being thrown into water,' their state of active manifestation; by the taking up of 'udumbara wood,' the corelessness of personal existence. 'By this same method' means by the method stated in 'a wet, sappy udumbara stick,' and so on. 'The going forth with wife and children' should be understood by way of the going forth as a wanderer made together with wife and children. The brahmin going-forth has divisions such as Kuṭīcaka, Bahūdaka, Haṃsa, and Paramahaṃsa.

376. Kutopi [M 2.0213][V 2.0199] imassa āposineho natthīti koḷāpaṃ. Tenāha “chinnasinehaṃ nirāpa”nti. Koḷanti vā sukkhakaliṅgaraṃ vuccati, koḷaṃ koḷabhāvaṃ āpannanti koḷāpaṃ. Paṭipannassa upakkamamahattanissitatā pakatiyā kilesehi anabhibhūtatāya. Atintatā paṭipakkhabhāvanāya. Tathā hi sukkhakoḷāpabhāvo, ārakā udakā thale nikkhittabhāvo ca nidassito. Opakkamikāhīti kilesaatiniggaṇhanupakkamappabhavāhi. Vedanāhīti paṭipattivedanāhi. Dukkhā paṭipadā hi idhādhippetā.

376. There is no moisture for this from any source, thus it is koḷāpaṃ. Hence it is said, 'with moisture cut off, without moisture.' Or koḷa is called a dry log; having attained the state of a dry log, it is koḷāpaṃ. For one who has undertaken the practice, because of reliance on great effort, he is by nature not overcome by the defilements. Atintatā (unmoistened) is through the development of opposing factors. Thus, the state of being a dry log and the state of being placed on dry land far from water are shown. Opakkamikāhi means arising from the effort of intensely suppressing the defilements. Vedanāhi means by the feelings of the practice. For here the painful practice is intended.

377. Kiṃ pana na samattho, yato evaṃ parehi cintitumpi asakkuṇeyyaṃ dukkaracariyaṃ chabbassāni akāsīti adhippāyo. Katvāpi akatvāpi samatthova kāraṇassa nipphannattā. “Yathāpi sabbesampi kho bodhisattānaṃ carimabhave antamaso sattāhamattampi dhammatāvasena dukkaracariyā hotiyeva, evaṃ bhagavā samattho dukkaracariyaṃ kātuṃ, evañca naṃ akāsi, na pana tāya buddho jāto, atha kho majjhimāya eva paṭipattiyā”ti tassā byatirekamukhena sadevakassa lokassa bodhāya amaggabhāvadīpanatthaṃ, imassa pana bhagavato kammavipākavasena chabbassāni dukkaracariyā ahosi. Vuttañhetaṃ –

377. What, was he not capable? The intention is: since he undertook for six years a difficult practice that others could not even conceive of. Whether he had done it or not, he was capable because the cause had been accomplished. 'Just as for all Bodhisattas in their final existence, as a matter of nature, there is a difficult practice for at least seven days, so the Blessed One was capable of undertaking the difficult practice, and he did so. But he did not become a Buddha by means of it; rather, it was by the middle practice.' This was to show, by way of contrast, that it was not the path to enlightenment for the world with its gods. For this Blessed One, however, the six years of difficult practice occurred as a result of kamma. For it has been said:

“Avacāhaṃ jotipālo, kassapaṃ sugataṃ tadā;

Kuto nu bodhi muṇḍassa, bodhi paramadullabhā.

Then I, Jotipāla, said to Kassapa, the Well-Farer: 'Whence can there be enlightenment for a shaveling? Enlightenment is supremely difficult to obtain.'

Tena kammavipākena, acariṃ dukkaraṃ bahuṃ;

Chabbassānuruvelāyaṃ, tato bodhimapāpuṇiṃ.

By the result of that kamma, I practiced many austerities for six years at Uruvelā; after that I attained enlightenment.

Nāhaṃ etena maggena, pāpuṇiṃ bodhimuttamaṃ;

Kumaggena gavesissaṃ, pubbakammena vārito”ti.

Not by this path did I attain supreme enlightenment; I sought by a wrong path, obstructed by former kamma.

Dukkaracariyāya bodhāya amaggabhāvadassanatthaṃ dukkaracariyaṃ akāsīti keci. Atha vā lokanāthassa attano parakkamasampattidassanatthāya dukkaracariyā. Paṇītādhimuttiyā hi paramukkaṃsagatabhāvato abhinīhārānurūpaṃ sambodhiyaṃ tibbachandatāya sikhāppattiyā tadatthaṃ īdisampi nāma dukkaracariyaṃ akāsīti loke attano vīriyānubhāvaṃ vibhāvetuṃ – “so ca me pacchā pītisomanassāvaho bhavissatī”ti lokanātho dukkaracariyaṃ [M 2.0214] akāsi. Tenāha “sadevakassa lokassā”tiādi. Tattha vīriyanimmathanaguṇoti vīriyassa saṃvaḍḍhanasampādanaguṇo. Yathāvuttamatthaṃ [V 2.0200] upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “pāsāde”tiādi vuttaṃ. Saṅgāme dve tayo sampahāreti dvikkhattuṃ tikkhattuṃ vā parasenāya pahārapayoge. Padhānavīriyanti sammappadhānehi āsevanavīriyaṃ, sabbaṃ vā pubbabhāgavīriyaṃ.

Some say he undertook the difficult practice in order to show that it is not the path to enlightenment. Or, the difficult practice was for the Lord of the World to show the perfection of his own striving. For because his refined resolution had reached the highest excellence, and because his intense desire for enlightenment, which was in conformity with his aspiration, had reached its peak, he undertook such a difficult practice for that purpose, in order to display in the world the power of his own energy—thinking, 'And this will later be a source of joy and gladness for me'—the Lord of the World undertook the difficult practice. Hence he said, 'for the world with its gods,' and so on. Here, 'the quality of churning out energy' means the quality of augmenting and accomplishing energy. To illustrate the aforesaid meaning by a simile, 'in a palace,' and so on, was said. 'In battle, he delivers two or three blows' means in the application of striking the enemy army two or three times. 'The energy of striving' means the energy of cultivation connected with the right strivings, or all the preliminary energy.

Abhidantanti abhibhavanadantaṃ, uparidantanti attho. Tenāha “uparidanta”nti. So hi itaraṃ musalaṃ viya udukkhalaṃ visesato kassaci khādanakāle abhibhuyya vattati. Kusalacittenāti balavasammāsaṅkappayuttena kusalacittena. Akusalacittanti kāmavitakkādisahitaṃ akusalacittaṃ. Akusalacittassa pavattituṃ appadānaṃ niggaho. Taṃtaṃpaṭikkhepavasena vinodanaṃ abhinippīḷanaṃ. Vīriyatāpena vikkhambhanaṃ abhisantāpanaṃ. Sadarathoti sapariḷāho. Padhānenāti padahanena, kāyassa kilamathuppādakena vīriyenāti attho. Viddhassāti tudassa. Satoti samānassa.

'The upper tooth' (abhidanta) means the tooth that overcomes; the meaning is the upper tooth. Hence it is said, 'the upper tooth.' For it prevails over the other like a pestle over a mortar, especially when one is chewing something. 'With a wholesome mind' means with a wholesome mind connected with strong right thought. 'Unwholesome mind' means an unwholesome mind accompanied by sensual thought and so on. 'Suppression' is not giving an opportunity for an unwholesome mind to arise. 'Dispelling' and 'crushing' are by way of rejecting them one by one. 'Suppressing by suspension' and 'scorching' are by the heat of energy. 'With distress' means with anguish. 'Through striving' means by exertion, that is, by the energy that produces bodily fatigue. Viddhassa means of one who is pierced. Sato means of one who is present.

378. Sīsaveṭhananti sīsaṃ rajjuyā bandhitvā daṇḍakena parivattakaveṭhanaṃ. Arahanto nāma evarūpā hontīti iminā yathāyaṃ, evaṃ visaññībhūtāpi hutvā viharantīti dasseti. Tenāha “matakasadisā”ti, vedanāppattā viya hontīti attho. Supinappaṭiggahaṇato paṭṭhāyāti paṭisandhiggahaṇe setavāraṇasupinaṃ passitvā brāhmaṇehi byākatakālato paṭṭhāya.

378. 'Head-binding' means binding the head with a rope and twisting it with a stick. By this, 'Arahants are of such a nature,' it shows that just as this one, they dwell even having become unconscious. Hence it is said, 'like the dead'; the meaning is that they are as if assailed by feeling. 'From the reception of the dream' means from the time it was interpreted by the brahmins, after he saw the dream of the white elephant at the moment of rebirth-linking.

379. Dhammasarīrassa arogabhāvena sādhūti marisaniyoti māriso, piyāyanavacanametaṃ. Tenāha “sampiyāyamānā”tiādi. Ajajjitanti evaṃ abhuñjitaṃ bhakārassa jakārādesaṃ katvā. Tenāha “abhojana”nti. Evaṃ mā karitthāti “lomakūpehi ajjhohāressāma anuppavesessāmā”ti yathā tumhehi vuttaṃ, evaṃ mā karittha. Kasmā? Yāpessāmahanti ahañca yāvadatthaṃ āhāramattaṃ bhuñjanto yathā yāpessāmi, evaṃ āhāraṃ paṭisevissāmi.

379. Because of the health of his Dhamma-body, they said, 'Good, friend!' Mārisa is a term of endearment. Hence it is said, 'being shown affection,' and so on. Ajajjitaṃ means 'uneaten' (abhuñjitaṃ), with the letter 'j' substituted for 'bh.' Hence it is said, 'non-eating.' 'Do not do so' means: 'Do not do as you have said, "We will feed you through the pores of your skin, we will make it enter."' Why? 'I will sustain myself' means: 'I will sustain myself by consuming just as much food as is needed; in that way I will make use of food.'

380-81. Etāva paramanti ettakaṃ paramaṃ, na ito paraṃ opakkamikadukkhavedanāvediyanaṃ atthīti attho. Rañño gahetabbanaṅgalato aññāni sandhāya [M 2.0215] “ekena ūna”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ suvaṇṇaparikkhataṃ, itarāni rajataparikkhatāni. Tenāha “amaccā ekenūnaaṭṭhasatarajatanaṅgalānī”ti. Āḷārudakasamāgame laddhajjhānāni vaṭṭapādakāni, ānāpānasamādhi pana kāyagatāsatipariyāpannattā sabbesañca bodhisattānaṃ vipassanāpādakattā “bodhāya maggo”ti vutto. Bujjhanatthāyāti catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ, sabbasseva vā ñeyyadhammassa abhisambujjhanāya[V 2.0201]. Satiyā anussaraṇakaviññāṇaṃ satānusāriviññāṇaṃ. Kassā pana satiyāti taṃ dassetuṃ “nayida”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

380-81. 'This much is the utmost' means this is the maximum; there is no experiencing of painful feeling produced by effort beyond this. With reference to the plows other than the one to be taken by the king, it is said, 'one less.' That one was adorned with gold, the others with silver. Hence it is said, 'the ministers had one less than one hundred and eight silver plows.' The jhānas obtained in the encounter with Āḷāra and Udaka are a basis for the round of rebirths, but mindfulness of breathing, because it is included in mindfulness directed to the body and is a basis for insight for all Bodhisattas, is called 'the path to enlightenment.' 'For the sake of awakening' means for the full understanding of the four noble truths, or of all knowable phenomena. Consciousness that follows upon mindfulness is recollection-consciousness. But whose mindfulness? To show this, 'not this,' and so on, was said.

382. Paccupaṭṭhitāti taṃtaṃvattakaraṇavasena patiupaṭṭhitā upaṭṭhāyakā. Tenāha “paṇṇasālā”tiādi. Paccayabāhullikoti paccayānaṃ bāhullāya paṭipanno. Āvattoti pubbe paccayagedhappahānāya paṭipanno, idāni tato paṭinivatto. Tenāha “rasagiddho…pe… āvatto”ti. Dhammaniyāmenāti dhammatāya. Tameva dhammataṃ dassetuṃ “bodhisattassā”tiādimāha. Bārāṇasimeva tatthāpi ca sabbabuddhānaṃ avijahitadhammacakkapavattanaṭṭhānameva agamaṃsu. Pañcavaggiyā kira visākhamāsassa addhamāsiyaṃ gatā. Tenāha “tesu gatesu aḍḍhamāsaṃ kāyavivekaṃ labhitvā”ti.

382. 'Were in attendance' means attendants were present to perform their various duties. Hence it is said, 'the leaf-hut,' and so on. 'Given to abundance of requisites' means one who is devoted to an abundance of requisites. 'Reverted' means that formerly he was devoted to abandoning greed for requisites, but now he has turned back from that. Hence it is said, 'greedy for tastes... reverted.' 'By the fixed course of the Dhamma' means by nature. To show that very nature, he said, 'of the Bodhisatta,' and so on. They went right to Bārāṇasī, for that is the place, never abandoned by any of the Buddhas, for setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. The group of five, it seems, left during the half-month of Visākha. Hence it is said, 'after they had gone, having obtained physical seclusion for half a month.'

387. “Addhābhoto gotamassa sāvakācittabhāvanānuyogamanuyuttā viharanti, no kāyabhāvana”nti imaṃ sandhāyāha “ekaṃ pañhaṃ pucchi”nti.
