Imaṃ dhammadesananti “abhijānāmi kho panāha”ntiādikaṃ dhammadesanaṃ. Asallīno taṇhādiṭṭhikilesānaṃ samucchinnattā tehi sabbaso na litto. Anupalittoti tasseva vevacanaṃ taṇhānandiyā abhāvena. Gocarajjhattamevāti gocarajjhattasaññite phalasamāpattiyā ārammaṇe, nibbāneti attho. Yaṃ sandhāya pāḷiyaṃ “purimasmiṃ samādhinimitte”ti vuttaṃ sannisīdāpemīti phalasamāpattisamādhinā accantasamādānavasena cittaṃ sammadeva nisīdāpemi. Pubbābhogenāti samāpajjanato pubbe pavattaābhogena. Paricchinditvāti samāpajjanakkhaṇaṃ paricchinditvā. Tenāha “sādhukāra…pe… avicchinneyevā”ti. Evamassa paricchinnakālasamāpajjanaṃ yathāparicchinnakālaṃ vuṭṭhānañca buddhānaṃ na bhāriyaṃ vasībhāvassa tathāsuppaguṇabhāvatoti dassento āha “buddhānaṃ hī”tiādi. Dhammasampaṭiggāhakānaṃ assāsavāre vā. Tadā hi desiyamānaṃ dhammaṃ upadhāretuṃ na [M 2.0216] sakkonti, tasmā tasmiṃ khaṇe desitadesanā niratthakā siyā. Na hi buddhānaṃ niratthakā kiriyā atthi.

387. 'Surely the disciples of the honorable Gotama dwell devoted to the development of the mind, not the development of the body.' With reference to this, it is said, 'he asked one question.' This Dhamma teaching is the one beginning, 'But I recall...' and so on. 'Unsluggish': because the defilements of craving and views have been eradicated, he is not stained by them at all. 'Unstained' is a synonym for this, due to the absence of craving and delight. 'Within its own pasture' means in the object of the attainment of fruition, designated 'its own pasture'; the meaning is Nibbāna. It is with reference to this that it is said in the Pāli text, 'on the former sign of concentration.' 'I make it settle down' means I make the mind settle down properly by means of the concentration of the attainment of fruition, by way of extreme stabilization. 'By a previous advertence' means by the advertence that occurred before entering the attainment. 'Having determined' means having determined the moment of entering the attainment. Hence it is said, 'with applause... without interruption.' To show that for the Buddhas, entering the attainment for a determined period and emerging at the determined time is not difficult because their state of mastery is so well-practiced, he says, 'For the Buddhas...' and so on. Or during the in-breath of the recipients of the Dhamma. For at that time they are unable to pay attention to the Dhamma being taught; therefore a teaching delivered at that moment would be useless. For the Buddhas have no useless actions.

Okappanīyametanti “tassā eva kathāyā”tiādinā vuttaṃ ativiya acchariyagataṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ sutvā īdisī paṭipatti sammāsambuddhasseva hotīti upavādavasena vadati, na sabhāvena. Tenāha “satthari pasādamattampi na uppanna”nti. Kāyadarathoti paccayavisesavasena rūpakāyassa parissamākāro. Upādinnaketi indriyabaddhe. Anupādinnaketi anindriyabaddhe. Vikasanti sūriyarasmisamphassena. Tadabhāvena makulāni honti. Kesañci tintinikādirukkhānaṃ[V 2.0202]. Patilīyanti nissayarūpadhammaavipphārikatāya. Arūpadhammatāya pañcaviññāṇānañceva kiriyāmayaviññāṇānañca appavattisaññitā avipphārikatā hoti, yattha niddāsamaññā. Tenāha “darathavasena bhavaṅgasotañca idha niddāti adhippeta”nti. Tattha darathavasenāti darathavaseneva, na thinamiddhavasenāti avadhāraṇaṃ avadhāraṇaphalañca niddhāretabbaṃ. Taṃ sandhāyāti kāyassa darathasaṅkhātasarīragilānahetukaṃ niddaṃ sandhāya. Sarīragilānañca bhagavato natthīti na sakkā vattuṃ “piṭṭhi me āgilāyatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.300; ma. ni. 2.22; cūḷava. 345) vacanato. Sammohavihārasminti paccatte etaṃ bhummavacananti āha “sammohavihāroti vadantī”ti, sammohavihārasmiṃ vā pariyāpannaṃ etaṃ vadanti, yadidaṃ divā niddokkamananti yojanā.

This is trustworthy: as stated in 'that very speech,' etc. Having heard an extremely marvelous account of the origin, he speaks by way of disparagement, saying such a practice belongs only to a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, not by its own nature. Therefore it is said: 'Not even a trace of confidence arose in him toward the Teacher.' 'Bodily fatigue': this is the state of exhaustion of the physical body due to a specific condition. 'Appropriated': connected with the faculties. 'Unappropriated': not connected with the faculties. They 'bloom' through contact with the sun's rays. In its absence, they become buds, as with certain trees like the tintiṇikā. They 'retreat' due to the non-manifestation of the phenomena of the physical basis. Because they are non-material phenomena, the non-manifestation of the five sense consciousnesses and the functional consciousnesses, which is designated as non-occurrence, is what is meant by 'sleep.' Therefore it is said: 'Here, the stream of the life-continuum, on account of fatigue, is intended by “sleep.”' Therein, 'on account of fatigue' means solely on account of fatigue, not on account of sloth and torpor; this emphasis and the result of the emphasis should be determined. Referring to that: referring to the sleep caused by the bodily illness called 'bodily fatigue.' And it cannot be said that the Blessed One had no bodily illness, for it is said: 'My back is aching.' 'In an abiding of delusion': this is a locative with a personal reference, thus he says: 'they call it an “abiding of delusion.”' Or, they say this is included in an abiding of delusion, that is, sleeping during the day; this is the connection.

389. Upanītehīti dosamaggaṃ nindāpathaṃ upanītehi. Abhinanditvāti sampiyāyitvā. Tenāha “cittena sampaṭicchanto”ti. Anumoditvāti “sādhu sādhū”ti desanāya thomanavasena anumoditvā. Tenāha “vācāyapi pasaṃsanto”ti. Sampatte kāleti pabbajjāyogge kāle anuppatte.

389. “By those who have brought”: by those brought to the path of fault, the way of blame. “Having delighted in”: having cherished it. Therefore it is said: “accepting with the mind.” “Having rejoiced”: having rejoiced, saying “Good, good!” by way of extolling the teaching. Therefore it is said: “also praising with speech.” “When the time arrived”: when the time suitable for going forth has arrived.

Gaṇaṃ vinodetvāti gaṇaṃ apanetvā gaṇapalibodhaṃ chinditvā. Papañcanti avasesakilesaṃ. “Puññavā rājapūjito”ti vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “tasmiñhi kāle”tiādi vuttaṃ. Chandavāsaharaṇena uposathakammaṃ karonto.

“Having dispelled the group”: having removed the group, having cut off the obstruction of the group. “Proliferation”: the remaining defilements. To explain the meaning stated as “The meritorious one, honored by the king,” it is said, “At that time,” etc. Performing the Uposatha act by bringing the consent of the absent.

Sakalaṃ [M 2.0217] rattiṃ buddhaguṇānaṃyeva kathitattā therassa ñāṇaṃ desanāvibhavañca vibhāvento āha “ettakāva, bhante, buddhaguṇā”ti. Imāya, bhante, tumhākaṃ dhammakathāya anavasesato buddhaguṇā kathitā viya jāyanti, evaṃ santepi anantāparimeyyāva te, kiṃ ito parepi vijjantevāti theraṃ tattha sīhanādaṃ nadāpetukāmo āha “udāhu aññepi atthī”tiādi. Rajjassa padesikattā, yathāvuttasubhāsitassa ca anagghattā vuttaṃ “ayaṃ me duggatapaṇṇākāro”ti. Tiyojanasatikanti idaṃ parikkhepavasena vuttaṃ, tañca kho manussānaṃ paribhogavasenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Because the qualities of the Buddha had been spoken of for the entire night, revealing the elder's knowledge and power of exposition, he said: “Venerable sir, are the Buddha's qualities only so many?” He said this wishing to make the elder utter a lion's roar on that point, thinking: “By this Dhamma talk of yours, venerable sir, it seems as if the qualities of the Buddha have been spoken of without remainder. Even so, they are infinite and immeasurable. Do any more exist beyond this?” Thus he asked: “Or are there others too?” and so on. Because the kingdom was a small region and the well-spoken statement was priceless, it was said: “This is my poor person's gift of vegetables.” “Three hundred leagues”: this is said by way of circumference, and it should be understood in terms of human utilization.

Mahāsaccakasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Greater Discourse to Saccaka is concluded.

7. Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhayasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Shorter Discourse on the Destruction of Craving

390. Tatrāti [V 2.0203] tasmiṃ pubbārāmamigāramātupāsādānaṃ atthavibhāvane ayaṃ idāni vuccamānā anupubbī kathā. Maṇīnanti ettha padumarāgamaṇīnaṃ adhippetattā āha “aññehi cā”ti. Tena indanīlādimaṇīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Nīlapītalohitodātamañjiṭṭhapabhassarakabaravaṇṇavasena sattavaṇṇehi.

390. “There”: in the explanation of the meaning of the Eastern Park, Migāramātā's Mansion, this is the sequential discourse that is now being spoken. “Of jewels”: here, because rubies are intended, it says “and by others.” By this, the inclusion of gems such as sapphires is to be understood. By way of seven colors: blue, yellow, red, white, madder, radiant, and variegated.

Taṇhā sabbaso khīyanti etthāti taṇhāsaṅkhayo (a. ni. ṭī. 3.7.61), tasmiṃ. Taṇhāsaṅkhayeti ca visaye idaṃ bhummanti āha “taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā”ti. Vimuttacittatāyāti sabbasaṃkilesehi vimuttacittatāya. Aparabhāgapaṭipadā nāma ariyasaccābhisamayo, sā sāsanacārigocarā paccattaṃ veditabbatoti āha “pubbabhāgappaṭipadaṃ saṃkhittena desethāti pucchatī”ti. Akuppadhammatāya khayavayasaṅkhātaṃ antaṃ atītāti accantā, so eva aparihānasabhāvattā accantā niṭṭhā etassāti accantaniṭṭho. Tenāha “ekantaniṭṭho satataniṭṭhoti attho”ti. Na hi paṭividdhassa lokuttaradhammassa dassanaṃ kuppanaṃ nāma atthi. Accantameva catūhi yogehi khemo etassa atthīti accantayogakkhemī. Maggabrahmacariyassa vusitattā, tassa ca aparihānasabhāvattā accantaṃ brahmacārīti [M 2.0218] accantabrahmacārī. Tenāha “niccabrahmacārīti attho”ti. Pariyosānanti brahmacariyassa pariyosānaṃ.

Craving is completely destroyed herein; hence, this is 'the destruction of craving'; in that. The phrase 'in the destruction of craving' is a locative of sphere; thus it is said, 'having made that the object.' 'By liberation of mind' means by the mind's freedom from all defilements. The subsequent practice is the breakthrough to the noble truths; since this is to be personally realized and falls within the domain of the Dispensation's practice, it is said that he asks: 'Explain the preliminary practice briefly.' Because of its unshakeable nature, it has passed beyond the end designated as destruction and dissolution; hence, it is 'ultimate.' For him, that very thing, due to its non-declining nature, is the ultimate consummation; hence, he is 'one of ultimate consummation.' Therefore, it is said, the meaning is 'one of absolute consummation, one of perpetual consummation.' Indeed, there is no wavering in the vision of the supramundane Dhamma once it has been penetrated. He has ultimate security from the four bonds; hence, he is 'one of ultimate security from the bonds.' Because the holy life of the path has been lived, and because of its non-declining nature, he is ultimately a liver of the holy life; hence, he is 'one who ultimately lives the holy life.' Therefore, it is said, the meaning is 'one who perpetually lives the holy life.' 'The consummation' means the consummation of the holy life.

Vegāyatīti turitāyati. Sallakkhesīti cintesi, attanā yathā sutāya satthu desanāya anussaraṇavasena upadhāresi. Anuggaṇhitvāvāti atthavinicchayavasena anuggahetvā eva. Chasu dvāresu niyuttāti chadvārikā, tehi.

“It quickens” means it hastens. “He observed” means he reflected, he considered; he bore it in mind by way of recollecting for himself the Teacher's teaching as he has heard it. “Having grasped it” means having grasped it precisely by way of determining the meaning. “Pertaining to the six doors” means engaged at the six doors; by them.

Pañcakkhandhāti pañcupādānakkhandhā. Sakkāyasabbañhi sandhāya idha “sabbe dhammā”ti vuttaṃ vipassanāvisayassa adhippetattā, tasmā āyatanadhātuyopi taggatikā eva daṭṭhabbā. Tenāha bhagavā “nālaṃ abhinivesāyā”ti. Na yuttā abhinivesāya “etaṃ mama, eso me attā”ti ajjhosānāya. “Alameva nibbindituṃ alaṃ virajjitu”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.272; saṃ. ni. 2.124-125, 128, 134, 143) viya alaṃ-saddo yuttatthopi hotīti āha “na yuttā”ti. Sampajjantīti bhavanti. Yadipi “tatiyā, catutthī”ti idaṃ visuddhidvayaṃ [V 2.0204] abhiññāpaññā, tassā pana sappaccayanāmarūpadassanabhāvato, sati ca paccayapariggahe sappaccayattā (nāmarūpassa aniccatā, aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ, dukkhañca anattāti atthato) lakkhaṇattayaṃ supākaṭameva hotīti āha “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti ñātapariññāya abhijānātī”ti. Tatheva tīraṇapariññāyāti iminā aniccādibhāvena nālaṃ abhinivesāyāti nāmarūpassa upasaṃharati, na abhiññāpaññānaṃ sambhāradhammānaṃ. Purimāya hi atthato āpannalakkhaṇattayaṃ gaṇhāti salakkhaṇasallakkhaṇaparattā tassā, dutiyāya sarūpato tassā lakkhaṇattayāropanavasena sammasanabhāvato. Ekacittakkhaṇikatāya abhinipātamattatāya ca appamattakampi. Rūpapariggahassa oḷārikabhāvato arūpapariggahaṃ dasseti. Dassento ca vedanāya āsannabhāvato, visesato sukhasārāgitāya, bhavassādagadhitamānasatāya ca sakkassa vedanāvasena nibbattetvā dasseti.

“The five aggregates” means the five aggregates subject to clinging. For here “all phenomena” is said with reference to the whole of identity, because the object of insight is intended. Therefore, the bases and elements too should be seen as having the same destination. Thus, the Blessed One said, “They are not fit for adherence.” It is not proper for adherence, for grasping as “This is mine, this is my self.” In statements like “It is enough to become disenchanted, enough to become dispassionate,” the word “enough” also has the meaning of “proper,” hence it is said, “not proper.” “They are accomplished” means they come to be. And as for “the third, the fourth,” this refers to the twofold purification, direct knowledge and wisdom. Because this involves seeing name-and-form with its conditions, and because when its conditions are grasped, the three characteristics—impermanence, suffering, and nonself—become very clear, it is said: “He directly knows by the full understanding of the known as impermanent, suffering, and nonself.” Similarly, by the full understanding by judgment, he concludes from this state of impermanence and so on that name-and-form is not fit for adherence—but this does not apply to the constituent phenomena of direct knowledge and wisdom. For the first grasps the three characteristics that are implicitly present in meaning, since it is concerned with discerning its own characteristic; the second grasps them in their own nature, since it involves contemplation by superimposing the three characteristics. Even a little bit is significant, because of its momentary nature, lasting for a single mind-moment, and because it is a mere falling upon the object. Due to the gross nature of grasping form, it shows the grasping of the formless. And while showing this, because of the proximity to feeling, and especially due to lust for the essence of pleasure and the mind's greed for the delight in existence, he explains it by generating it in terms of feeling for Sakka.

Uppādavayaṭṭhenāti udayabbayasabhāvena uppajjitvā nirujjhanena. Aniccāti addhu vā. Aniccalakkhaṇaṃ aniccatā udayavayatā. Tasmāti yasmā pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ khayato vayato dassanañāṇaṃ aniccānupassanā, taṃsamaṅgī ca puggalo aniccānupassī[M 2.0219], tasmā. Khayavirāgoti khayasaṅkhāto virāgo saṅkhārānaṃ palujjanā. Yaṃ āgamma sabbaso saṅkhārehi virajjanā hoti, taṃ nibbānaṃ accantavirāgo. Nirodhānupassimhipīti nirodhānupassipadepi. “Eseva nayo”ti abhidisitvā taṃ ekadesena vivaranto “nirodhopi hi…pe… duvidhoyevā”ti āha. Sabbāsavasaṃvare vuttavossaggova idha “paṭinissaggo”ti vuttoti dassento “paṭinissaggo vuccati vossaggo”tiādimāha. Pariccāgavossaggo vipassanā. Pakkhandanavasena appanato pakkhandanavossaggo maggo aññassa tadabhāvato. Soti maggo. Ārammaṇatoti kiccasādhanavasena ārammaṇakaraṇato. Evañhi maggato aññesaṃ nibbānārammaṇānaṃ pakkhandanavossaggābhāvo siddho hoti. Pariccajanena pakkhandanena cāti dvīhipi vā kāraṇehi. Sabbesaṃ khandhānaṃ vossajjanaṃ tappaṭibaddhasaṃkilesappahānena daṭṭhabbaṃ. Cittaṃ pakkhandatīti maggasampayuttaṃ cittaṃ sandhāyāha. Ubhayampetaṃ vossajjanaṃ. Tadubhayasamaṅgīti vipassanāsamaṅgī maggasamaṅgī ca. “Aniccānupassanāya niccasaññaṃ pajahatī”tiādivacanato (paṭi. ma. 1.52) yathā vipassanāya kilesānaṃ pariccāgapaṭinissaggo labbhati, evaṃ āyatiṃ tehi kilesehi uppādetabbakhandhānampi pariccāgapaṭinissaggo vattabbo, pakkhandanapaṭinissaggo pana magge labbhamānāya ekantakāraṇabhūtāya vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāya vasena veditabbo, magge pana tadubhayampi ñāyāgatameva nippariyāyatova labbhamānattā. Tenāha “tadubhayasamaṅgī puggalo”tiādi.

“By the meaning of arising and passing away” means by the nature of arising and dissolving, by arising and ceasing. “Impermanent” means not lasting. The characteristic of impermanence is impermanence, arising and passing away. “Therefore” means: since the knowledge of seeing the decay and passing away of the five aggregates is the contemplation of impermanence, and the person endowed with it is one who contemplates impermanence, therefore. “Dispassion through decay” means this is dispassion designated as decay, the crumbling of formations. That on account of which there is complete dispassion towards all formations is Nibbāna, the ultimate dispassion. “Even in the contemplation of cessation” means also in the term ‘contemplation of cessation.’ Having indicated, “This is the method,” he explains it in part, saying: “For cessation, too … is twofold.” Showing that the relinquishment (vossagga) mentioned in the context of the restraint of all taints is here called “abandonment” (paṭinissagga), he says: “Abandonment is called relinquishment,” and so on. The relinquishment by giving up is insight. The relinquishment by plunging in is the path, because of its applying itself by way of plunging in, and because of the absence of this in anything else. That is the path. “As an object” means because of making it an object by way of accomplishing its function. For in this way it is established that, apart from the path, there is no relinquishment by plunging in for other things that have Nibbāna as their object. “By giving up and by plunging in” means or by both these reasons. The relinquishing of all the aggregates should be seen as the abandoning of the defilements connected with them. “The mind plunges in”: he says this referring to the mind associated with the path. Both these are relinquishment. “One endowed with both” means endowed with both insight and the path. From the statement, “Through the contemplation of impermanence, one abandons the perception of permanence,” etc., just as through insight the abandonment by giving up defilements is obtained, so too the abandonment by giving up the aggregates that would be produced by those defilements in the future is to be understood. The abandonment by plunging in, however, is to be understood by way of the insight leading to emergence, which is obtained in the path and is the exclusive cause. But in the path, both are obtained by right method, being obtained directly. Therefore, he said: “The person endowed with both,” etc.

Pucchantassa [V 2.0205] ajjhāsayavasena “na kiñci loke upādiyatī”ti ettha kāmupādānavasena upādiyanaṃ paṭikkhipīyatīti āha “taṇhāvasena na upādiyatī”ti. Taṇhāvasena vā asati upādiyane diṭṭhivasena upādiyanaṃ anavakāsamevāti “taṇhāvasena”icceva vuttaṃ. Na parāmasatīti nādiyati, diṭṭhiparāmāsavasena vā “nicca”ntiādinā na parāmasati. Saṃkhitteneva khippaṃ kathesīti tassa ajjhāsayavasena papañcaṃ akatvā kathesi.

In accordance with the questioner’s intention, when it is said, “He does not cling to anything in the world,” here clinging by way of the clinging to sensual pleasures is rejected. Thus he says, “He does not cling by way of craving.” Or, when there is no clinging by way of craving, clinging by way of views has no opportunity to arise, hence it is just said, “by way of craving.” “He does not grasp” means he does not take up, or he does not misapprehend by way of the misapprehension of views, with such ideas as “permanent,” etc. “He spoke briefly and quickly” means in accordance with that one’s intention, he spoke without elaborating.

391. Abhisamāgantvāti abhimukhañāṇena ñeyyaṃ samāgantvā yāthāvato viditvā. Tenāha “jānitvā”ti. Yathāparisaviññāpakattāti yathāparisaṃ [M 2.0220] dhammasampaṭiggāhikāya mahatiyā, appakāya vā parisāya anurūpameva viññāpanato. Pariyantaṃ na niccharatīti na pavattati. Mā niratthakā agamāsīti idaṃ dhammatāvasena vuttaṃ, na satthu ajjhāsayavasena. Ekañhetaṃ satthu vacīghosassa aṭṭhasu aṅgesu, yadidaṃ parisapariyantatā. Chiddavivarokāsoti chiddabhūto, vivarabhūto vā okāsopi natthi, bhagavato saddāsavanakāraṇaṃ vuttameva. Tasmāti yathāvuttakāraṇato.

391. “Having fully understood” means having come upon the knowable with direct knowledge and having known it as it really is. Hence he said, “having known.” “Because of making things understood according to the assembly” means because of making things understood in a way that is suitable for the assembly that is receptive to the Dhamma, whether it is large or small. “It does not go beyond the limit” means it does not proceed beyond. “May you not have come in vain”: this is said according to the nature of things, not according to the Teacher’s intention. For this is one of the eight qualities of the Teacher’s voice, namely, that it is limited to the assembly. “A gap, an opening, an opportunity” means there is no such gap or opening; the reason for hearing the Blessed One’s voice has already been stated. “Therefore” means for the reason stated.

Pañca aṅgāni etassāti pañcaṅgaṃ, pañcaṅgaṃ eva pañcaṅgikaṃ. Mahatīādi vīṇāvisesopi ātatamevāti “cammapariyonaddhesū”ti visesitaṃ. Ekatalaṃ kumbhathūṇadaddarādi. Cammapariyonaddhaṃ hutvā tantibaddhaṃ ātatavitataṃ. Tenāha “tantibaddhapaṇavādī”ti. Gomukhīādīnampi ettheva saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Vaṃsādīti ādi-saddena saṅkhasiṅgādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Sammādīti sammatāḷakaṃsatāḷasilāsalākatāḷādi. Tattha sammatāḷaṃ nāma daṇḍamayatāḷaṃ. Kaṃsatāḷaṃ lohamayaṃ. Silāya ayopattena ca vādanatāḷaṃ silāsalākatāḷaṃ. Samappitoti sammā appito upeto. Tenāha “upagato”ti. Upaṭṭhānavasena pañcahi tūriyasatehi upeto. Evaṃbhūto ca yasmā tehi upaṭṭhito samannāgato nāma hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “samaṅgībhūtoti tasseva vevacana”nti. Paricāretīti parito cāreti. Kāni pana cāreti, kathaṃ vā cāretīti āha “sampattiṃ…pe… cāretī”ti. Tattha tato tatoti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ vādite tattha tattha ca vādakajane. Apanetvāti vādakajane nisedhetvā. Tenāha “nissaddāni kārāpetvā”ti. Devacārikaṃ gacchatiyeva devatānaṃ manussānañca anukampāya. Svāyamattho vimānavatthūhi (vi. va. 1) dīpetabbo.

It has five parts (pañca aṅgāni etassa): hence it is five-limbed (pañcaṅgaṃ). Five-limbed (pañcaṅgaṃ) is the same as fivefold (pañcaṅgikaṃ). Since even a special kind of lute (vīṇā) such as the mahatī is a stringed instrument (ātata), it is specified by ‘in those covered with leather.’ One-sided (ekatalaṃ) are the kumbhathūṇa, daddara, and so on. Being covered with hide and bound with strings, it is a stringed-and-percussion instrument (ātatavitataṃ). Hence he said, ‘the paṇava drum bound with strings, and so on.’ The inclusion of the gomukhī horn and so on should be seen here as well. Flutes, etc. (vaṃsādi): by the word ‘etc.’ (ādi), conch-trumpets, horns, and so on are included. Cymbals, etc. (sammādi): the sammatāḷa, kaṃsatāḷa, silāsalākatāḷa, and so on. Among these, the sammatāḷa is a wooden clapper; the kaṃsatāḷa is made of bronze; the silāsalākatāḷa is a clapper for striking a stone with an iron plate. Endowed with (samappito): well furnished, possessed of. Hence he said, ‘attended by.’ He is attended by five hundred musical instruments by way of service. And since one who is like this is served and attended by them, he is called ‘endowed.’ Therefore it is said: ‘Furnished with (samaṅgībhūto) is a synonym for that very word.’ He enjoys himself (paricāreti): he moves about all around. But what does he cause to move about, or how does he cause it to move about? He says: ‘His fortune … he causes to move about.’ Therein, from this and that: with regard to each instrument being played and each musician. Having dismissed: having forbidden the musicians. Hence he said, ‘having had them made silent.’ He indeed goes on a tour among the devas out of compassion for devas and humans. This meaning should be illustrated by means of the Vimanavatthu (Vv 1).

392. Appeva sakena karaṇīyenāti mārisa, moggallāna, mayaṃ sakena karaṇīyena appeva bahukiccāpi na homa. Apica devānaṃyevāti apica kho pana devānaṃyeva tāvatiṃsānaṃ karaṇīyena [V 2.0206] visesato [M 2.0221] bahukiccāti atthayojanā. Bhummaṭṭhakadevatānampi keci aṭṭā sakkena vinicchitabbā hontīti āha “pathavito paṭṭhāyā”ti. Niyamentoti avadhārento. Taṃ pana karaṇīyaṃ sarūpato dassetuṃ “devānaṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tāsanti devadhītudevaputtapādaparicārikānaṃ. Maṇḍanapasādhanakārikāti maṇḍanapasādhanasaṃvidhāyikā. Aṭṭakaraṇaṃ natthi saṃsayasseva abhāvato.

392. ‘Perhaps because of our own duties’: Friend Moggallāna, perhaps because of our own duties we are not very busy, though we have many duties. ‘Moreover, for the devas’: the construction of the meaning is: ‘Moreover, we are especially busy with the duties of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.’ Since some cases of the earth-dwelling devas have to be decided by Sakka, he says, ‘starting from the earth.’ Determining (niyamento): defining. To show that duty in its own nature, it is said: ‘For of the devas…,’ and so on. Of them (tāsaṃ): of the celestial nymphs, sons of the devas, and foot-attendants. Makers of ornaments and decorations: those who arrange the ornaments and decorations. There is no legal case because there is no doubt at all.

Yanti savanuggahaṇādivasena suparicitampi yaṃ atthajātaṃ. Na dissati, paññācakkhuno sabbaso na paṭibhātīti attho. Kecīti sārasamāsācariyā. Somanassasaṃveganti somanassasamuṭṭhānaṃ saṃvegaṃ, na cittasantāsaṃ.

That which is not seen (yanti na dissati): that collection of meanings which, though one is well-acquainted with it by way of hearing, grasping, etc., is not seen; the meaning is, it does not appear at all to the eye of wisdom. Some: the teachers who compose summaries of the essence. Joyful sense of urgency: a sense of urgency (saṃvega) that arises from joy, not mental terror.

Samupabyūḷhoti yujjhanavasena sahapatito samogāḷho. Evaṃbhūto ca yasmā samūhavasena sampiṇḍito hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “sannipatito rāsibhūto”ti. Anantare attabhāveti idaṃ dutiyaṃ sakkattabhāvaṃ tato anantarātītena sakkattabhāvena sakkattabhāvasāmaññato ekamiva katvā gahaṇavasena vuttaṃ, aññathā “tatiye attabhāve”ti vattabbaṃ siyā. Maghattabhāvo hi ito tatiyoti. Atha vā yasmiṃ attabhāve so devāsurasaṅgāmo ahosi, tassa anantarattā maghattabhāvassa vuttaṃ “anantare attabhāve”ti. Sattānaṃ hitesitāya mātāpituupaṭṭhānādinā cariyāhi bodhisattacariyā viyassa cariyā ahosi. Satta vatapadānīti satta vatakoṭṭhāse.

Samupabyūḷha means completely immersed, fallen together, deeply submerged due to the nature of the battle. Being thus, and because he is massed together as a group, it is said, "gathered into a heap." "In the immediately subsequent existence"—this refers to the second state of Sakka. It is spoken of as if it were one with the immediately preceding Sakka-state due to the commonality of being a Sakka-state; otherwise, it should be said, 'in the third existence,' for the state of Magha is the third from this. Alternatively, "in the immediately subsequent existence" is said referring to the Magha-state, because of its being immediately after the existence in which that battle between gods and demons took place. His conduct, such as attending to parents, was for the welfare of beings, like the conduct of a Bodhisatta. "The seven practices" means the seven sections of vows.

Mahāpānanti mahantaṃ surāpānaṃ. Gaṇḍapānanti gaṇḍasurāpānaṃ, adhimattapānanti attho. Pariharamānāti parivārentā. Vedikāpādāti sinerussa pariyante vedikāparikkhepā. Pañcasu ṭhānesūti pañcasu paribhaṇḍaṭṭhānesu nāgasenādīhi ārakkhaṃ ṭhapesi.

Great drinking means drinking a large amount of liquor. Gaṇḍapāna means drinking liquor in a great amount; the meaning is excessive drinking. Pariharamāna means attending on. Vedikāpāda refers to the railing enclosure around the edge of Mount Sineru. In five places means he placed guards like Nāgasena and others in five places where requisites were collected.

393. Rāmaṇeyyakanti ramaṇīyabhāvaṃ. Masāragallatthambheti kabaramaṇimaye thambhe. Suvaṇṇādimaye ghaṭaketi “rajatatthambhesu suvaṇṇamaye, suvaṇṇatthambhesu rajatamaye”tiādinā suvaṇṇādimaye ghaṭake vāḷarūpakāni ca. Pabāḷhaṃ mattoti pamatto. Tenāha “ativiya matto”ti. Nāṭakaparivārenāti accharāparivārena.

393. Rāmaṇeyyaka means the state of being delightful. Masāragallatthambhe means on pillars made of variegated gems. Suvaṇṇādimaye ghaṭake means vessels made of gold and so forth, and figures of wild animals, as in ‘golden ones on silver pillars, and silver ones on golden pillars,’ and so on. Pabāḷhaṃ matto means heedless. Hence it is said, “exceedingly intoxicated.” Nāṭakaparivārena means with a retinue of celestial nymphs.

Acchariyabbhutanti [M 2.0222] padadvayenapi vimhayanākārova vutto, tasmā sañjātaṃ acchariyabbhutaṃ vimhayanākāro etesanti sañjātaacchariyaabbhutā, tathā pavattacittuppādā. Acchariyabbhutahetukā sañjātā [V 2.0207] tuṭṭhi etesanti sañjātatuṭṭhino. Saṃvigganti sañjātasaṃvegaṃ. Svāyaṃ saṃvego yasmā purimāvatthāya cittassa calanaṃ hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “calita”nti.

Acchariyabbhuta is expressed by two words, thus indicating a state of astonishment. Therefore, 'sañjātaacchariyaabbhutā' means those in whom wonder and amazement have arisen, and similarly, those in whom such thoughts have arisen. 'Sañjātatuṭṭhino' means those in whom joy has arisen due to the cause of wonder. 'Saṃvigga' means agitation has arisen. Because this agitation is a movement of the mind away from a former state, therefore it is said to be 'calita'.

394. Tamaṃ vinoditanti pāṭihāriyadassanena “aho therassa iddhānubhāvo”ti sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ sañjātabahumāno, īdisaṃ nāma sāsanaṃ labhitvāpi mayaṃ niratthakena bhogamadena sammattā bhavāmāti yoniso manasikāruppādanena sammohatamaṃ vinoditaṃ vidhamitaṃ. Eteti mahāthero sakko cāti te dvepi samānabrahmacariyatāya sabrahmacārino.

394. 'Tamaṃ vinoditaṃ' means the darkness of delusion was dispelled, banished. This was done by witnessing the miracle and thinking, 'Ah, the elder’s psychic power!', whereby great respect for the proper practice arose; and by generating wise attention, thinking, 'Even though we have obtained such a teaching, we are intoxicated by the meaningless pride of possessions!' 'Ete' refers to the great elder and Sakka; those two, due to their shared holy life, are companions in the holy life.

395. Paññātānanti pākaṭānaṃ cātumahārāja-suyāma-santusita-paranimmitavasavattimahābrahmānaṃ aññataro, na yesaṃ kesañcīti adhippāyo. Āraddhadhammavaseneva pariyosāpitattā yathānusandhināva niṭṭhapesi.

395. 'Paññātānaṃ' refers to one of the well-known Four Great Kings, Suyāma, Santusita, Paranimmitavasavatti, and Mahābrahma; the intention is, not just anyone. Since the discourse was concluded by means of the Dhamma that was begun, he concluded it in accordance with the connection.

Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhayasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The exposition clarifying the hidden meaning of the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhayasutta is complete.

8. Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhayasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta.

396. Laddhimattanti [V 2.0208] micchāgāhamattaṃ, na diṭṭhābhiniveso. Sassatadiṭṭhīti niccābhiniveso. Soti ariṭṭho bhikkhu. Kathetvā samodhānentanti yojanā. Samodhānentanti ca nigamentanti attho. Tattha tatthevāti tesu tesu eva bhavesu nirujjhanti, na bhavantaraṃ saṅkamanti. Viññāṇaṃ pana abhinnasabhāvaṃ anaññanti adhippāyo. Idhalokatoti imasmā attabhāvā. Paralokanti parabhavasaññitaṃ attabhāvaṃ. Sandhāvatīti niccatāya kenaci asambaddhaṃ viya gacchati. Tena idhalokato paralokagamanamāha. Saṃsaratīti iminā paralokato idhāgamanaṃ. Sandhāvatīti vā bhavantarasaṅkamanamāha. Saṃsaratīti tattha tattha aparāparasañcaraṇaṃ.

396. 'Laddhimatta' means merely a wrong grasp, not an entrenched view. 'Sassatadiṭṭhi' is an entrenched belief in permanence. 'So' refers to the monk Ariṭṭha. 'Kathetvā samodhānenta' means explaining and connecting. 'Samodhānenta' and 'nigamenta' have the same meaning. 'Tattha tattheva' means they cease in those very existences; they do not transmigrate to another existence. Consciousness, however, is of an unbroken nature and not different; this is the intention. 'Idhalokato' refers to from this present existence. 'Paralokaṃ' refers to the existence regarded as the next life. 'Sandhāvati' means it runs on, as if unconnected, due to its supposed permanence; by this, the going from this world to the next is stated. 'Saṃsarati' means the coming back here from the next life. Alternatively, 'sandhāvati' refers to the transition between existences, and 'saṃsarati' refers to the repeated wandering from one place to another.

“Paccaye [M 2.0223] sati bhavatī”tiādinā viññāṇassa anvayato byatirekato ca paṭiccasamuppannabhāvaṃ dassento sassatabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Buddhena akathitaṃ kathesīti iminā “yaṃ abhāsitaṃ alapitaṃ tathāgatena, taṃ bhāsitaṃ lapitaṃ tathāgatenāti dīpetī”ti (cūḷava. 352, 353) imasmiṃ bhedakaravatthusmiṃ sandissatīti dasseti. Jinacakke pahāraṃ detīti “tadevidaṃ viññāṇaṃ…pe… anañña”nti niccataṃ paṭijānanto – “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā (dha. pa. 277), rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, anicca”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.93-94) ca ādinayappavatte satthu dhammacakke khīlaṃ uppādento pahāraṃ deti. Sabbaññutaññāṇena aniccanti diṭṭhaṃ paveditañca viññāṇaṃ niccanti paṭijānanto vesārajjañāṇaṃ paṭibāhati. Sotukāmaṃ jananti ariyadhammādhigamassa ekantaupāyabhūtaṃ vipassanāmaggaṃ sotukāmaṃ janaṃ niccaggāhapaggaṇhanena visaṃvādeti. Tato eva ariyapathe ariyadhammavīthiyaṃ tassā paṭikkhipanena tiriyaṃ nipatitvā.

"When there is a condition, it comes to be"—thus, by showing the dependent origination of consciousness through both presence and absence, he rejects the notion of permanence. By saying, "What was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata, you declare as spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata," he shows that this resembles the divisive matters mentioned in the Cūḷavagga (352, 353). He strikes a blow against the wheel of the Conqueror—by asserting the permanence of consciousness, saying, "This very consciousness… is not other," he drives a wedge into the Teacher’s Dhamma-wheel, which was set in motion with such teachings as, "All conditioned things are impermanent" (Dhammapada 277), and "Form, monks, is impermanent" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.93-94). By asserting that consciousness is permanent, which was seen and proclaimed as impermanent through the knowledge of omniscience, he obstructs the knowledge of confidence. He deceives those eager to hear by promoting the grasping of permanence, when the path of insight—the sole means for attaining the noble Dhamma—is what they are eager to hear. Thus, by rejecting that path, he falls across the noble path, the highway of the noble Dhamma.

398. Viññāṇasīsena attanā gahitaṃ attānaṃ vibhāvento “yvāyaṃ, bhante”tiādimāha. Tattha vado vedeyyotiādayo sassatadiṭṭhiyā eva abhinivesākārā. Vadatīti vado, vacīkammassa kārakoti attho. Iminā hi kārakabhāvupāyikasattānaṃ hitasukhāvabodhanasamatthataṃ attano dasseti. Vediyova vedeyyo, jānāti anubhavati cāti attho. Īdisānañhi padānaṃ bahulā kattusādhanataṃ saddavidū maññanti. Vedayatīti taṃ taṃ anubhavitabbaṃ anubhavati. Tahiṃ tahinti tesu tesu bhavayonigatiṭhitisattāvāsasattanikāyesu.

398. Explaining the self that he himself has grasped, with consciousness as its head, he says, "This one, venerable sir," and so on. Herein, "speaker" and "feeler" are expressions of adherence to the eternalist view. "Speaker" means one who speaks, the agent of verbal action. By this, he demonstrates his own ability to make beings, who are connected with the means of the state of being an agent, aware of their welfare and happiness. "Feeler" means one who feels, that is, one who knows and experiences. Indeed, those skilled in grammar consider such words to frequently be formed in the agent sense. "He feels" means he experiences that which is to be experienced. "Therein, therein" refers to those various realms of existence, wombs, destinations, stations, abodes of beings, and groups of beings.

399. Taṃ [V 2.0209] vādaṃ paggayha ṭhitattā sātissa chinnapaccayatā aviruḷhadhammatā ca veditabbā. Heṭṭhāti alagaddasuttasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.236-237) sandhāyāha. Parato heṭṭhāti vuttaṭṭhānepi eseva nayo. Pāṭiyekko anusandhīti tīhipi anusandhīhi avomisso visuṃyeveko anusandhi. Nanu cāyampi sātissa ajjhāsayavasena pavattitattā ajjhāsayānusandhiyevāti? Na, niyyānamukhena appavattattā. Niyyānañhi purakkhatvā pucchādivasena pavattā itarā desanāpucchānusandhiādayo. Idha tadabhāvato [M 2.0224] vuttaṃ “pāṭiyekko anusandhī”ti. Parisāya laddhiṃ sodhentoti yādisī sātissa laddhi, tadabhāvadassanavasena parisāya laddhiṃ sodhento, parisāya laddhisodhaneneva sāti gaṇato nissārito nāma jāto.

399. Because Sāti stood upholding that view, it should be understood that his conditions were severed and his Dhamma was undeveloped. The phrase "below" refers to the commentary on the Alagaddūpama Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 2.236-237). This same method applies also in the place mentioned further on as "below". "A separate connection" means a single connection that is quite distinct, unmixed with the three other connections. But is this not also a connection of intention, since it proceeds according to Sāti’s inclination? No, because it does not proceed by way of deliverance. For the others, such as the teaching-question connection, proceed by way of questions and so forth, having placed deliverance at the forefront. Here, due to the absence of that, it is called "a separate connection." "Purifying the assembly’s view" means: by showing the non-existence of what Sāti believes, he purifies the assembly’s view. Just by this purification of the assembly’s view, Sāti becomes, as it were, expelled from the community.

400. Yaṃ yadevāti idaṃ yadipi avisesato paccayadhammaggahaṇaṃ, “viññāṇantveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchatī”ti pana vuttattā taṃtaṃviññāṇassa samaññānimittapaccayajātaṃ gahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ – “cakkhuviññāṇantveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchatī”tiādi. Atha vā taṃtaṃdvāraniyataṃ itarampi sabbaṃ tassa tassa viññāṇassa paccayajātaṃ idha “yaṃ yadevā”ti gahitaṃ, tattha pana yaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ, tena samaññāti “cakkhuviññāṇantvevā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dvārasaṅkantiyā abhāvanti viññāṇassa dvārantarasaṅkamanassa abhāvaṃ. Svāyaṃ oḷārikanayena mandabuddhīnaṃ sukhāvabodhanatthaṃ nayadassanavasena vutto. Na hi kadāci paccuppannaṃ viññāṇaṃ vigacchantaṃ anantaraviññāṇaṃ saṅkamati anantarādipaccayālābhe tassa anuppajjanato.

400. Although this phrase "whatever" is an indiscriminate grasping of conditional phenomena, since it is said, "it is reckoned simply as consciousness," it should be understood that the collection of conditions, signs, and designations for each respective consciousness is grasped. Therefore, it is stated in the Pāli text: "It is reckoned simply as eye-consciousness," and so on. Alternatively, every other collection of conditions for each respective consciousness, determined by its respective door, is here grasped by "whatever." But there, that which is specific is designated by that name; thus it is said, "simply as eye-consciousness," and so on. "The absence of transition between doors" means the absence of consciousness's transition to another door. This is stated by way of showing a method, according to a gross method, for the easy understanding of those with dull intellect. For a present consciousness, while ceasing, never transits to a subsequent consciousness, because without obtaining the immediate and other conditions, that subsequent consciousness does not arise.

Evamevāti yathā aggi upādānaṃ paṭicca jalanto anupādāno tattheva nibbāyati, na katthaci saṅkamati, evameva. “Paccayavekallena tattheva nirujjhatī”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, na hettha anuppādanirodho icchito tādisassa nirodhassa idha anadhippetattā, atha kho khaṇanirodho, so ca sābhāvikattā na paccayavekallahetuko? Saccametaṃ, taṃtaṃdvārikassa pana viññāṇassa dvārantaraṃ asaṅkamitvā tattha tattheva nirujjhanaṃ idhādhippetaṃ. Yesañca paccayānaṃ vasena dvārantarikaviññāṇena bhavitabbaṃ, tesaṃ tadabhāvato paccayavekallaggahaṇaṃ, tasmā paccayavekallena na sotādīni saṅkamitvā sotaviññāṇantiādi saṅkhyaṃ gacchatīti yojanā. Etena yaṃ viññāṇaṃ cakkhurūpādipaccayasāmaggiyā vasena cakkhuviññāṇasaṅkhyaṃ gacchati, tattha tattheva nirujjhati tāvakālikabhāvato, tassa pana sotasaddādipaccayābhāvato kuto sotaviññāṇādisamaññā, evamappavattito tassa kuto saṅkamoti dassitaṃ hoti. Viññāṇappavatteti viññāṇappavattiyaṃ. Dvārasaṅkantimattanti dvārantarasaṅkamanamattampi na vadāmi tattha tattheva [V 2.0210] bhijjanato paccayassa uppādavantato sati ca uppāde avassaṃbhāvī nirodhoti hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccatā dīpitā hotīti.

Just so: just as a fire, burning dependent on fuel, is extinguished right there when there is no fuel and does not go anywhere, so too is it. Why is it said, "It ceases right there due to a lack of conditions"? Cessation without further arising is not intended here, for such a cessation is not the meaning here; rather, it is momentary cessation, and that, being natural, is not caused by a lack of conditions. This is true. However, what is intended here is that the consciousness at a particular door ceases right there without transiting to another door. And because those conditions by which a consciousness at another door would arise are absent, the term "lack of conditions" is used. Therefore, the construction is: due to a lack of conditions, it does not transit to the ear, etc., and get the designation "ear-consciousness," etc. By this it is shown: that consciousness which, through the convergence of conditions such as the eye and a form, gets the designation "eye-consciousness," ceases right there because of its momentary nature. Since the conditions for it, such as the ear and a sound, are absent, how could it get the designation "ear-consciousness," etc.? Since it does not arise thus, how could it transit? This is what is shown. "In the process of consciousness" means in the continuity of consciousness. As for "mere transition between doors": I do not speak even of a mere transition to another door, because it breaks up right there. Since a condition has an arising, and when there is arising, cessation is inevitable, impermanence is thereby shown through the meaning of non-existence.

401. “Paṭiccasamuppannaṃ [M 2.0225] viññāṇaṃ vuttaṃ mayā, aññatra paccayā natthi viññāṇassa sambhavo”ti pāḷiyā anvayato ca byatirekato ca viññāṇassa saṅkhatatāva dassitāti āha “sappaccayabhāvaṃ dassetvā”ti. Hetupaccayehi jātaṃ nibbattaṃ “bhūta”nti idhādhippetaṃ, taṃ atthato pañcakkhandhā tabbinimuttassa sappaccayassa abhāvato, yañca khandhapañcakaṃ attano tesañca bhikkhūnaṃ, taṃ “bhūtamida”nti bhagavā avocāti āha “idaṃ khandhapañcaka”nti. Attano phalaṃ āharatīti āhāro, paccayo. Sambhavati etasmāti sambhavo, āhāro sambhavo etassāti āhārasambhavaṃ. Tenāha “paccayasambhava”nti. Tassa paccayassa nirodhāti yena avijjādinā paccayena khandhapañcakaṃ sambhavati, tassa paccayassa anuppādanirodhā. Khaṇanirodho pana kāraṇanirapekkho.

401. "Consciousness arisen dependently has been spoken of by me; apart from a condition, there is no origination of consciousness." By this Pāli passage, the conditioned nature of consciousness is shown through both presence and absence. Hence it is said, "by showing its nature of having conditions." That which is born, produced by causes and conditions, is here meant by "bhūta" (that which has come to be). In meaning, this is the five aggregates, because apart from them there is no entity that has conditions. And that which is the five aggregates—both his own and those of the monks—the Blessed One called "this has come to be." Hence it is said, "this fivefold aggregate." That which brings its own fruit is an "āhāra" (nutriment), a condition. "It arises from this" (sambhavati etasmā) is an origin (sambhavo). "Nutriment is its origin" (āhāro sambhavo etassa) is "arisen from nutriment" (āhārasambhavaṃ). Therefore, it is said, "arisen from a condition." "From the cessation of that condition" means from the cessation through non-arising of that condition, such as ignorance, by which the fivefold aggregate arises. Momentary cessation, however, is independent of a cause.

Nossūti saṃsayajotano nipātoti āha “bhūtaṃ nu kho idaṃ, na nu kho bhūta”nti. Bhūtamidaṃ nossūti ca iminā khandhapañcakameva nu kho idaṃ, udāhu attattaniyanti evaṃjātiko saṃsayanākāro gahito. Tadāhārasambhavaṃ nossūti pana iminā sahetukaṃ nu kho idaṃ bhūtaṃ, udāhu ahetukanti yathā ahetukabhāvāpanno saṃsayanākāro gahito, evaṃ visamahetukabhāvāpannopi saṃsayanākāro gahitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Visamahetunopi paramatthato bhūtassa ahetukabhāvato. Visamahetuvādopi parehi parikappitamattatāya sabhāvaniyatiyadicchādivādehi samānayogakkhamoti. Nirodhadhammaṃ nossūti iminā yathā aniccaṃ nu kho idaṃ bhūtaṃ, udāhu niccanti aniccataṃ paṭicca saṃsayanākāro gahito, evaṃ dukkhaṃ nu kho, udāhu na dukkhaṃ, anattā nu kho, udāhu na anattātipi saṃsayanākāro gahitoyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ aniccassa dukkhabhāvādiavassaṃbhāvato, nicce ca tadubhayābhāvato. Yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇatoti aviparītasarasato salakkhaṇato ca, kiccato ceva sabhāvato cāti attho. Vipassanāya adhiṭṭhānabhūtāpi paññā vipassanā evāti vuttaṃ “vipassanāpaññāyā”ti. Sarasatoti ca sabhāvato. Salakkhaṇatoti sāmaññalakkhaṇato. Tenāha “vipassanāpaññāya sammā passantassā”ti. Vuttanayenevāti “yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇato”ti vuttanayeneva. Ye yeti tassaṃ parisāyaṃ ye ye bhikkhū. Sallakkhesunti sammadeva upadhāresuṃ.

'Nossū' is a particle indicating doubt; hence it is said: 'Is this indeed real, or is it not real?' And by 'Is this real, or is it not so?' a form of doubt is taken, such as: 'Is this merely the five aggregates, or is it a self or something belonging to a self?' But by 'It arises from nutriment, or is it not so?' a form of doubt is taken, such as: 'Is this real thing with a cause, or is it without a cause?' Just as a form of doubt is taken regarding its being causeless, so too should it be seen as a form of doubt regarding its having an inappropriate cause. For an inappropriate cause, from the ultimate perspective, is causeless for that which has come into being. And the doctrine of inappropriate causes, being merely conceived by others, is comparable to doctrines of inherent nature, fate, or chance in terms of logical consistency. By 'It is subject to cessation, or is it not so?' just as a form of doubt is taken concerning impermanence—'Is this real thing impermanent, or is it permanent?'—so too should it be seen that a form of doubt is taken: 'Is this suffering, or is it not suffering? Is this non-self, or is it not non-self?'—because that which is impermanent necessarily entails suffering and so on, and that which is permanent entails the absence of both. 'According to its true essence and characteristic' means according to its undistorted essence and its characteristic, that is, both in function and intrinsic nature. Even the wisdom that is the foundation of insight is insight itself; thus it is said 'with insight wisdom' (vipassanāpaññāya). 'According to its essence' means according to its intrinsic nature. 'According to its characteristic' means according to its general characteristic. Therefore, it is said: 'for one who sees rightly with insight wisdom.' 'In the same way as stated' means in the way stated by 'according to its true essence and characteristic.' 'Whoever' means those monks, whoever they were, in that assembly. 'They discerned' means they considered rightly.

Tehīti [M 2.0226][V 2.0211] tehi bhikkhūhi. Tatthāti tissaṃ vipassanāpaññāyaṃ. Nittaṇhabhāvanti taṇhābhāvaṃ “etaṃ mama”nti taṇhāggāhassa pahīnataṃ. Etenapi bhagavā “ahaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammesupi taṇhāpahānameva vaṇṇemi, sāti pana moghapuriso attabhāvepi taṇhāsaṃvaddhaniṃ viparītadiṭṭhiṃ paggayha tiṭṭhatī”ti sātiṃ niggaṇhāti. Sabhāvadassanenāti dhammānaṃ aviparītasabhāvadassanena. Paccayadassanenāti kāraṇadassanena anavasesato hetuno paccayassa ca dassanena. Allīyethāti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena nissayetha. Tenāha “taṇhādiṭṭhīhī”ti. Kelāyethāti pariharaṇakeḷiyā parihareyyātha. Tenāha “kīḷamānā vihareyyāthā”ti. Dhanaṃ viya icchantāti dhanaṃ viya drabyaṃ viya icchaṃ taṇhaṃ janentā. Tenāha “gedhaṃ āpajjeyyāthā”ti. Mamattaṃ uppādeyyāthāti “mamamida”nti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena abhinivesaṃ janeyyātha. Nikantivasenapi gahaṇatthāya no desito, tassa vā saṇhasukhumassa vipassanādhammassa gahaṇaṃ nāma nikantiyā eva siyā, na oḷārikataṇhāyāti vuttaṃ “nikantivasenā”ti.

'By them' means by those monks. 'Therein' means in that threefold insight wisdom. 'Absence of craving' means the absence of craving, the abandonment of the grasping of craving by thinking 'this is mine.' By this too, the Blessed One rebukes Sāti, saying: 'Monks, I praise the abandonment of craving even regarding phenomena, but this foolish man Sāti clings to a wrong view that nourishes craving even regarding his individual existence.' 'By seeing the true nature' means by seeing the undistorted intrinsic nature of phenomena. 'By seeing conditions' means by seeing the cause, that is, by seeing completely, without remainder, both the root cause and the condition. 'One should not cling' means one should not depend on it by way of craving and views. Hence it is said, 'through craving and views.' 'One should not delight' means you should avoid it with the play of avoidance. Hence it is said, 'you would dwell playing.' 'Like desiring wealth' means generating craving as if desiring wealth or property. Hence it is said, 'you would fall into greed.' 'One should not generate possessiveness' means you should not generate attachment by way of craving and views, thinking 'this is mine.' It is not taught for the sake of grasping even through desire; or, the grasping of that subtle and refined Dhamma of insight could only be through desire, not through coarse craving. Thus it is said, 'through desire.'

402. Paṭicca etasmā phalaṃ etīti paccayo, sabbo kāraṇavisesoti āha “khandhānaṃ paccayaṃ dassento”ti. Yāva avijjā hi sabbo nesaṃ kāraṇaviseso idha dassito. Puna ādito paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānā, antato paṭṭhāya yāva ādīti anulomato paṭilomato ca vaṭṭavivaṭṭadassanavasena nānānayehi paṭiccasamuppādo dassito, niccaggāhassa nimittabhūto kilesopi idha natthīti dīpeti. Tampi vuttatthamevāti tampi “ime ca, bhikkhave, cattāro āhārā”tiādi yāva “taṇhāpabhavā”ti pāḷipadaṃ, tāva vuttatthameva sammādiṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.89). Sesaṃ paṭiccasamuppādakathābhāvato visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.570) vitthāritāvāti imināva saṅgahitaṃ.

402. 'Because on account of this, a result comes into being,' it is a condition; every specific cause is meant. Thus he said, 'showing the condition for the aggregates.' For as far back as ignorance, every specific cause for them is shown here. Again, from the beginning up to the end, and from the end back to the beginning—that is, in forward and reverse order—dependent origination is shown through various methods by way of showing the cycle and its reversal. This also reveals that there is not even a defilement here that could be a basis for grasping at permanence. 'That too is merely what has already been stated' means that the Pāli passage from 'these four nutriments, monks' up to 'originating from craving,' is merely what has already been stated in the commentary on the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 1.89). The remainder, because it is an account of dependent origination, is included by this reference to what is elaborated in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhimagga 2.570).

404. Imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hotītiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ paramatthadīpaniyaṃ udānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (udā. aṭṭha. 1) vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

404. Whatever is to be said concerning 'when this exists, that comes to be,' and so on, should be understood in the same way as it is explained in the Paramatthadīpanī, the commentary on the Udāna (Udāna Aṭṭhakathā 1).

407. Paṭidhāvanāti paṭisaraṇaṃ, pubbe attano āgataṃ atītaṃ addhānaṃ uddissa taṇhādiṭṭhivasena paṭigamananti attho. Nanu vicikicchāvasena pāḷiyaṃ [M 2.0227] paṭidhāvanā āgatāti? Saccaṃ āgatā, sā pana taṇhādiṭṭhihetukāti “taṇhādiṭṭhivasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ yathādhigate ñāṇadassane.

407. 'Running back' (paṭidhāvanā) means recourse; the meaning is the act of returning by way of craving and wrong view, with reference to the past time that one has previously come upon. But has not 'running back' appeared in the Pāli text in connection with doubt? Truly, it has appeared, but that doubt is caused by craving and wrong view; hence it was said 'by way of craving and wrong view.' 'Therein' (tattha) means in that knowledge and vision as it has been attained.

Niccalabhāvanti [V 2.0212] suppatiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ, titthiyavādavātehi akampiyabhāvañca. Garūti garuguṇayutto. Bhāriko pāsāṇacchattasadiso. Akāmā anuvattitabboti saddhāmattakeneva anuvattanamāha, na aveccappasādena. Kiccanti satthukiccaṃ. Brāhmaṇānanti jātimantabrāhmaṇānaṃ. Vatasamādānānīti magavatādivatasamādānāni. Diṭṭhikutūhalānīti taṃtaṃdiṭṭhiggāhavasena “idaṃ saccaṃ, idaṃ sacca”ntiādinā gahetabbakutūhalāni. Evaṃ nissaṭṭhānīti yathā mayā tumhākaṃ ovādo dinno, evaṃ nissaṭṭhāni vatādīni taṃ atikkamitvā kiṃ gaṇheyyātha. Sayaṃ ñāṇena ñātanti paraneyyataṃ muñcitvā attano eva ñāṇena yāthāvato ñātaṃ. Evaṃbhūtañca sayaṃ paccakkhato diṭṭhaṃ nāma hotīti āha “sayaṃ paññācakkhunā diṭṭha”nti. Sayaṃ vibhāvitanti tehi bhikkhūhi tassa atthassa paccattaṃ vibhūtabhāvaṃ āpāditaṃ. Upanītāti upakkamena dhammadesanānusārena nītā. Mayāti kattari karaṇavacanaṃ. Dhammenāti kāraṇena. Etaṃ vacananti etaṃ “sandiṭṭhiko”tiādivacanaṃ.

'Immovability' (niccalabhāva) means the state of being well-established, and the state of being unshaken by the winds of sectarian doctrines. 'Weighty' (garu) means endowed with weighty qualities. 'Burdensome' (bhārika) is like a stone umbrella. 'To be followed unwillingly' (akāmā anuvattitabbo) speaks of following with mere faith, not with experiential confidence. 'Duty' (kicca) refers to the teacher's duty. 'Of brahmins' (brāhmaṇānaṃ) refers to brahmins by birth. 'Undertakings of observances' (vatasamādānāni) means undertakings of observances such as the Maghavata and so on. 'Curiosities about views' (diṭṭhikutūhalāni) refers to the curiosities to be grasped by way of clinging to this or that view, thinking 'this is true, this is true,' and so on. 'Thus discarded' (evaṃ nissaṭṭhāni) means: just as advice has been given to you by me, so these observances and so on have been discarded; having gone beyond that, what would you grasp? 'Known by oneself through knowledge' (sayaṃ ñāṇena ñātaṃ) means known truly by one's own knowledge, having abandoned being led by others. And such a thing is called 'seen for oneself directly'; hence it is said 'seen by oneself with the eye of wisdom.' 'Made manifest by oneself' (sayaṃ vibhāvitaṃ) means that the meaning was brought to a state of personal manifestation by those monks. 'Led to' (upanītā) means led by the approach in accordance with the teaching of the Dhamma. 'By me' (mayā) is the instrumental case used for the agent. 'By the Dhamma' (dhammena) means by reason. 'This statement' (etaṃ vacanaṃ) refers to the statement beginning 'visible here and now' (sandiṭṭhiko).

408. Taṃ sammohaṭṭhānaṃ assa lokassa. Samodhānenāti samāgamena. Gabbhati attabhāvabhāvena vattatīti gabbho, kalalādiavattho dhammapabandho, tannissitattā pana sattasantāno “gabbho”ti vutto yathā “mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī”ti. Tannissayabhāvato mātukucchi “gabbho”ti veditabbo, gabbho viyāti vā. Yathā hi nivāsaṭṭhānatāya sattānaṃ ovarako “gabbho”ti vuccati, evaṃ gabbhaseyyakānaṃ yāva abhijāti nivāsaṭṭhānatāya mātukucchi “gabbho”ti vuttoti.

408. That would be a cause of delusion for the world. 'By combination' (samodhānena) means by coming together. 'Womb' or 'embryo' (gabbho) is so called because it proceeds (`gabbhati`) by way of individual existence; it is a continuum of phenomena in the state beginning with the kalala. And because the continuity of a being is dependent on that, it is called 'gabbha,' just as in the expression 'the beds are shouting.' The mother's womb should be understood as 'gabbha' because it is the basis for that, or because it is like a womb. For just as an inner chamber is called a 'gabbha' because it is a dwelling place for beings, so the mother's womb is called 'gabbha' because it is the dwelling place for those who lie in the womb up until their birth.

Yamekarattinti yassaṃ ekarattiyaṃ. Bhummatthe hi idaṃ upayogavacanaṃ, accantasaṃyoge vā. Paṭhamanti sabbapaṭhamaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe. Gabbheti mātukucchiyaṃ. Māṇavoti satto. Yebhuyyena sattā rattiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhantīti [M 2.0228] rattiggahaṇaṃ. Abbhuṭṭhitovāti uṭṭhitaabbho viya, abhimukhabhāvena vā uṭṭhito eva maraṇassāti adhippāyo. So yātīti so māṇavo yāti paṭhamakkhaṇato paṭṭhāya gacchateva. Sa gacchaṃ na nivattatīti so evaṃ gacchanto khaṇamattampi na nivattati, aññadatthu maraṇameva upagacchatīti gāthāya attho.

By 'yamekarattiṃ' is meant 'on that single night.' For this is a term of application in the locative sense, or in the sense of complete connection. By 'paṭhamaṃ' is meant the very first, at the moment of rebirth-linking. By 'gabbha' is meant in the mother's womb. By 'māṇavo' is meant a being. The mention of night is because most beings take rebirth-linking at night. By 'abbhuṭṭhito' is meant like a rising cloud, or it has risen facing death—this is the meaning. By 'so yāti' is meant that young being goes from the first moment onward. By 'sa gacchaṃ na nivattati' is meant that as he goes thus, he does not turn back even for a moment; indeed, he approaches only death—this is the meaning of the verse.

Utusamayaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na lokasamaññātarajassa lagganadivasamattaṃ. Idāni vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “mātugāmassa kira yasmi”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ gabbhāsaye. Saṇṭhahitvāti nibbattitvā. Bhijjitvāti aggahitagabbhā eva bhinnā hutvā. Ayañhi tassā sabhāvo. Vatthu suddhaṃ hotīti paggharitalohitattā anāmayattā ca gabbhāsayo suddho hoti. Suddhavatthuttā [V 2.0213] tato paraṃ katipayadivasāni khettameva hoti gabbhasaṇṭhahanassa parittassa lohitalesassa vijjamānattā. Sambhavassa pana kathaṃ sabbhāvoti āha “tasmiṃ samaye”tiādi. Itthisantānepi sukkadhātu labbhateva. Tenāha “aṅgaparāmasanenapi dārako nibbattatiyevā”ti. Yathā pārikāya nābhiparāmasanena sāmassa bodhisattassa, diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya nābhiparāmasanena maṇḍabyassa nibbatti. Gandhabboti gandhanato uppajjanagatiyā nimittupaṭṭhāpanena sūcanato gandhoti laddhanāmena bhavagāmikammunā abbati pavattatīti gandhabbo, tattha uppajjanakasatto. Tenāha “tatrūpagasatto”ti. Kammayantayantitoti tatrūpapattiāvahena kammasaṅkhātena pellanakayantena tathattāya pellito upanīto. Mahantena jīvitasaṃsayenāti vijāyanaparikkilesena “jīvissāmi kho, na nu kho jīvissāmi ahaṃ vā, putto vā me”ti evaṃ pavattena jīvitasaṃsayena vipulena garutarena saṃsayena. Taṃ ṭhānanti thanappadesamāha. Kīḷanti tenāti kīḷanaṃ, kīḷanameva kīḷanakaṃ.

It was said with reference to the season, not merely the worldly reckoning of days of menstruation. Now, to make the meaning clearer, it is said: 'For a woman, indeed, in which...' and so on. By 'tattha' is meant in that womb. By 'saṇṭhahitvā' is meant having arisen. By 'bhijjitvā' is meant having broken, the embryo itself not having been grasped. For this is its nature. By 'vatthu suddhaṃ hoti' is meant that the womb becomes pure due to the flowing out of blood and being free from disease. Because the basis is pure, thereafter for a few days it is merely a field, as only a small amount of blood remains for the settling of the embryo. But how is the existence of an arising to be understood? It is said: 'At that time,' and so on. Even in the female lineage, the sperm element is certainly obtained. Therefore, it is said: 'Even by the touching of a limb, a child is indeed born.' Just as by the touching of Pārikā’s navel, the Bodhisatta Sāma was born, and by the touching of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s navel, Maṇḍabya was born. By 'gandhabba' is meant a being to be born there. The term is explained as one who goes and indicates his impending birth by presenting a sign of his destiny; by this sign, called 'gandha', and propelled by kamma leading to becoming, he goes and proceeds. Therefore, it is said: 'a being approaching that place.' By 'kammayantayantito' is meant propelled and led to that state by the pushing mechanism called kamma, which brings about rebirth there. By 'mahantena jīvitasaṃsayena' is meant with great uncertainty of life, that is, with the distress of childbirth, thinking: 'Shall I live? Or shall I not live? Will it be me or my child?'—thus with great and heavy uncertainty of life. By 'taṃ ṭhānaṃ' is meant the breast region. By 'kīḷanti tena' is meant play; play itself is a plaything.

409. Sārajjatīti sārattacitto hoti. Byāpajjatīti byāpannacitto hoti. Kāye kesādidvattiṃsāsucisamudāye taṃsabhāvārammaṇā sati kāyasati. Anupaṭṭhapetvāti anuppādetvā, yathāsabhāvato kāyaṃ anupadhāretvāti attho. Parittacetasoti kilesehi [M 2.0229] parito khaṇḍitacitto. Tenāha “akusalacitto”ti. Ete akusaladhammā. Nirujjhantīti nirodhaṃ pattā honti. Taṇhāvasena abhinandatīti sappītikataṇhāvasena abhimukhaṃ hutvā nandati. Abhivadatīti taṇhāvasena taṃ taṃ ārammaṇaṃ abhinivissa vadati. Ajjhosāyāti anaññasādhāraṇaṃ viya ārammaṇaṃ taṇhāvasena anupavisitvā. Tenāha “gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā”ti. Dukkhaṃ kathaṃ abhinandatīti ettha dukkhahetukaṃ abhinandanto dukkhaṃ abhinandati nāmāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana yāvatā yassa dukkhe diṭṭhitaṇhā abhinandanā appahīnā, tāvatāyaṃ dukkhaṃ abhinandati nāmāti dassetuṃ “ahaṃ dukkhito mama dukkhanti gaṇhanto abhinandati nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Tena gāhadvayahetukā tattha abhinandanāti dasseti. Puna ekavāranti punapi ekavāraṃ. Phalahetusandhihetuphalasandhivasena dvisandhī. “Gabbhassāvakkanti hotī”tiādinā atthato sarūpato ca etarahi phalasaṅkhepassa. Sarūpeneva ca itaradvayassa desitattā āha “tisaṅkhepa”nti.

409. By 'sārajjati' is meant one has an attached mind. By 'byāpajjati' is meant one has a hostile mind. Mindfulness of the body is mindfulness having as its object the inherent nature of the body, the aggregate of the thirty-two impure parts beginning with head hair. By 'anupaṭṭhapetvā' is meant not generating, that is, not contemplating the body as it truly is. By 'parittacetaso' is meant a mind limited and fragmented by defilements. Hence it is said, 'akusalacitto' (unwholesome-minded). These are unwholesome states. By 'nirujjhanti' is meant they reach cessation. By 'taṇhāvasena abhinandati' is meant one delights by facing the object with craving accompanied by pleasure. By 'abhivadati' is meant speaking with craving, clinging to that object with craving. By 'ajjhosāya' is meant entering into an object as if uniquely possessed by craving. Hence it is said, 'having swallowed and completely settled upon it.' As to 'how does one delight in suffering?': here it should be seen that one who delights in what causes suffering is said to delight in suffering. In the commentary, however, to show that as long as craving and wrong view regarding suffering are not abandoned, one is said to delight in suffering, it is stated, 'holding onto "I am suffering, my suffering," one delights in it.' This shows the delighting there is caused by a twofold grasping. By 'puna ekavāraṃ' is meant once again. There are two connections: the fruit-to-cause connection and the cause-to-fruit connection. By 'gabbhassāvakkanti hoti' and so on, the summary of the result is now given in terms of meaning and form. And since the other two are taught by their form alone, it is said, 'tisaṅkhepa' (a threefold summary).

410-414. Samathayānikassa bhikkhuno vedanāmukhena saṅkhepeneva yāva arahattā kammaṭṭhānaṃ idha kathitanti āha “saṃkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttiṃ dhārethā”ti. “Imaṃ taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti”nti ca bhagavā yathādesitaṃ desanaṃ avocāti vuttaṃ “imaṃ…pe… vimuttidesana”nti[V 2.0214]. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ desanā vimuttīti āha “desanā hi…pe… vimuttīti vuttā”ti. Yassā taṇhāya vasena sāti bhikkhu sassataggāhamahāsaṅghāṭapaṭimukko, sā sabbabuddhānaṃ desanā hatthāvalambamānepi durugghāṭiyā jātāti āha “mahātaṇhājālataṇhāsaṅghāṭapaṭimukka”nti. Mahātaṇhājāleti mahante taṇhājaṭe. Taṇhāsaṅghāṭeti taṇhāya saṅghāṭe. Tathābhūto ca tassa abbhantare kato nāma hotīti āha “anupaviṭṭho antogadho”ti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

410-414. For a monk devoted to serenity, the meditation subject is taught here in brief, by way of feeling, up to arahantship. Hence it is said, 'briefly, one should maintain liberation through the destruction of craving.' By 'imaṃ taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttiṃ' is meant that the Blessed One spoke the teaching as it was taught—thus it is said, 'this...teaching of liberation.' If so, how is the teaching liberation? It is said, 'the teaching, indeed,...is called liberation.' On account of that craving, the monk Sāti was bound by the great cloak of the grasp of eternalism. That craving becomes difficult to unfasten even when supported by the teaching of all Buddhas. Hence it is said, 'bound by the great net and cloak of craving.' By 'mahātaṇhājāla' is meant the great tangle of craving. By 'taṇhāsaṅghāṭa' is meant the cloak of craving. And one who is thus is said to be 'anupaviṭṭho antogadho' (entered and deeply immersed within). The rest is easily understood.

Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhayasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The exposition of the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, revealing the hidden meaning, is complete.

9. Mahāassapurasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Mahāassapura Sutta.

415. Jānapadinoti [V 2.0215] janapadavanto, janapadassa vā issarā rājakumārā gottavasena aṅgā nāma. Tesaṃ nivāso yadi eko janapado[M 2.0230], kathaṃ bahuvacananti āha “ruḷhīsaddenā”ti. Akkharacintakā hi īdisesu ṭhānesu yutte viya saliṅgavacanāni (pāṇini 1.2.51) icchanti. Ayamettha ruḷhī yathā “kurūsu viharati, mallesu viharatī”ti ca. Tabbisesane pana janapadasadde jātisadde ekavacanameva. Tenāha “aṅgesu janapade”ti. Assā vuccanti pāsāṇāni, tāni sundarāni tattha santīti “assapura”nti so nigamo vuttoti kecī. Apare pana ājānīyo asso rañño tattha gahaṇaṃ upagatoti “assapura”nti vuttoti vadanti. Kiṃ tehi, nāmametaṃ tassa nigamassa. Yasmā pana tattha bhagavato nibaddhavasanaṭṭhānaṃ kiñci nāhosi, tasmā “taṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā viharati”cceva vuttaṃ. Tathā hi pāḷiyaṃ “assapuraṃ nāma aṅgānaṃ nigamo”ti gocaragāmakittanameva kataṃ.

415. 'Jānapadino' means 'possessing a country,' or 'the rulers of a country,' the royal princes known as Aṅgas by lineage. If their dwelling is a single country, how is it in the plural? It is said, 'by conventional usage.' Indeed, grammarians in such cases prefer forms that agree in gender and number (Pāṇini 1.2.51), as appropriate. Here, this is the conventional usage, as in 'he dwells among the Kurus, he dwells among the Mallās.' However, when specifying, the word 'janapada' (country), when used as a class name, is in the singular. Hence it is said, 'in the Aṅgas' country.' 'Assā' are called stones, and since beautiful ones are found there, some say the town is called 'Assapura.' Others, however, say that a noble horse belonging to the king was taken there, hence it is called 'Assapura.' What does it matter? That is the name of that town. But since the Blessed One had no fixed dwelling place there, it is simply said, 'making that his alms-resort village, he dwelt.' Indeed, in the Pāli, it is only stated, 'a town of the Aṅgas named Assapura,' merely indicating it as an alms-resort village.

Evarūpena sīlenātiādīsu sīlaggahaṇena vārittasīlamāha. Tena sammāvācākammantājīve dasseti. Ācāraggahaṇena cārittasīlaṃ. Tena parisuddhaṃ kāyavacīsamācāraṃ. Paṭipattiggahaṇena samathavipassanāmaggaphalasaṅgahaṃ sammāpaṭipattiṃ. Lajjinoti iminā yathāvuttasīlācāramūlakāraṇaṃ. Pesalāti iminā pārisuddhiṃ. Uḷāraguṇāti iminā paṭipattiyā pāripūriṃ. Bhikkhusaṅghasseva vaṇṇaṃ kathentīti idaṃ tesaṃ upāsakānaṃ yebhuyyena bhikkhūnaṃ guṇakittanapasutatāya vuttaṃ. Te pana saddhammepi sammāsambuddhepi abhippasannā eva. Tenāha “buddhamāmakā dhammamāmakā”ti. Vatthuttaye hi ekasmiṃ abhippasannā itaradvaye abhippasannā eva tadavinābhāvato. Piṇḍapātāpacāyaneti lakkhaṇavacanametaṃ yathā “kākehi sappi rakkhitabba”nti, tasmā paccayapaṭipūjaneti vuttaṃ hoti. Paccayadāyakānañhi kārassa attano sammāpaṭipattiyā mahapphalabhāvassa karaṇaṃ idha “piṇḍapātāpacāyana”nti adhippetaṃ.

In phrases such as 'with such virtue,' the term 'virtue' refers to virtue as restraint (vārittasīla). Through this, it shows right speech, right action, and right livelihood. By the term 'conduct' (ācāra), it refers to virtue as practice (cārittasīla). Through this, purified bodily and verbal conduct is indicated. By the term 'practice' (paṭipatti), it encompasses right practice, which includes serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), and the fruit (phala). 'Conscientious' (lajjī) refers to the root cause of virtue and conduct as previously described. 'Gentle' (pesala) indicates purity. 'Possessing lofty qualities' (uḷāraguṇa) signifies the fulfillment of practice. 'Praising the Saṅgha of monks'—this is said because these lay devotees are generally inclined to extol the virtues of the monks. Yet, they are also deeply devoted to the true Dhamma and the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Therefore, it is said, 'regarding the Buddha as their own, regarding the Dhamma as their own.' For in the threefold basis, being devoted to one implies devotion to the other two due to their inseparability. 'Honoring almsfood' (piṇḍapātāpacāyana) is a characteristic expression, just as it is said, 'ghee should be protected by crows.' Hence, it means reverential service to requisites. For the donors of requisites, the act of making their own right practice highly fruitful is what is intended here by 'honoring almsfood.'

Samaṇakaraṇāti samaṇabhāvakarā, samaṇabhāvassa kārakāti attho. Te pana ekantato attano santāne uppāditā vaḍḍhitā ca hontīti āha “samādāya paripūritā”ti. Samaṇaggahaṇañcettha samaṇavasena, na sāmaññamattenāti āha “samitapāpasamaṇa”nti. Brāhmaṇakaraṇāti etthāpi vuttanayenevattho veditabbo. Byañjanato eva cāyaṃ bhedo, yadidaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇāti[V 2.0216], na atthato. Samaṇena kattabbadhammāti [M 2.0231] samaṇadhamme ṭhitena sampādetabbadhammā. Yo hi heṭṭhimasikkhāsaṅkhātasamaṇabhāve suppatiṭṭhito, tena ye uparisikkhāsaṅkhātasamaṇabhāvā sampādetabbā, tesaṃ vaseneva vuttasamaṇena kattabbadhammā vuttāti. Tathā hi tesaṃ samaṇabhāvāvahataṃ sandhāyāha “tepi ca samaṇakaraṇā hontiyevā”ti. Idha panāti mahāassapure. Hirottappādivasena desanā vitthāritāti hirottappa-parisuddhakāyavacīmanosamācārājīvaindriyasaṃvara-bhojanemattaññuta- jāgariyānuyogasatisampajañña-jhānavijjāvasena samaṇakaraṇadhammadesanā vitthārato desitā, na tikanipāte viya saṅkhepato. Phalaggahaṇeneva vipākaphalaṃ gahitaṃ, taṃ pana ukkaṭṭhaniddesena catubbidhaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ānisaṃsaggahaṇena piyamanāpatādiudrayo. Tasseva atthoti tasseva avañcāpadasseva atthaniddeso. “Yassā hī”tiādinā byatirekavasena atthaṃ vadati. Ettakena ṭhānenāti ettakena pāḷipadesena. Hirottappādīnaṃ upari pāḷiyaṃ vuccamānānaṃ samaṇakaraṇadhammānaṃ. Vaṇṇaṃ kathesīti guṇaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ abhāsi. Satipaṭṭhāne vuttanayenāti “apica vaṇṇabhaṇanameta”ntiādinā satipaṭṭhānavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.373; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.106) vuttanayena.

'Samaṇakaraṇā' means 'that which makes one a samaṇa,' or 'the doer of the state of being a samaṇa.' They are entirely produced and developed in one's own continuity; hence it is said, 'undertaken and fulfilled.' Here, the term 'samaṇa' refers specifically to one who is a samaṇa by virtue, not merely by general designation; hence it is stated as 'a samaṇa who has pacified evil.' Similarly, 'brāhmaṇakaraṇā' should be understood in the same way as explained. The distinction here is only in terms of wording, namely 'samaṇa' and 'brāhmaṇa,' not in meaning. 'Duties to be performed by a samaṇa' refers to the duties to be accomplished by one established in the qualities of a samaṇa. For one who is well-established in the state of a samaṇa, which is the lower training, must accomplish the higher states of a samaṇa, which are the higher training; it is in terms of these that the duties to be performed by a samaṇa are spoken of. Therefore, referring to their capacity to bring about the state of a samaṇa, it is said, 'they too are indeed makers of samaṇas.' 'Here' refers to Mahā-assapura. The teaching on the qualities that make one a samaṇa is expounded in detail—by way of moral shame and moral dread, pure bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, right livelihood, sense restraint, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, mindfulness and clear comprehension, jhāna, and knowledge—not concisely as in the Tikanipāta. By the term 'fruit,' the resultant fruit is understood, which, in the highest explanation, should be seen as the fourfold fruit of asceticism. By the term 'benefits,' the arising of advantages such as being dear and agreeable is meant. This is the explanation of the meaning of that very term, 'avañcāpada.' With 'For whom...' and so on, it states the meaning by way of contrast. 'By this much' means by this much of the Pāli passage. This refers to the qualities that make one a samaṇa, which are spoken of further on in the Pāli text, beginning with moral shame and moral dread. 'He spoke praise' means he proclaimed their virtue and benefits. 'In the manner stated in the Satipaṭṭhāna' refers to the way explained in the commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna with the words, 'Moreover, this is a statement of praise,' and so on.

416. Yaṃ hirīyatīti yena dhammena hetubhūtena vā jigucchati. Karaṇe hetaṃ paccattavacanaṃ. Yanti vā liṅgavipallāsena vutto, dhammoti attho. Hirīyitabbenāti upayogatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, hirīyitabbayuttakaṃ kāyaduccaritādinti attho. Ottappitabbenāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Ajjhattaṃ niyakajjhattaṃ jātiādi samuṭṭhānaṃ etissāti ajjhattasamuṭṭhānā hirī, bahiddhā attato bahibhūto parasatto samuṭṭhānaṃ etissāti bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ. Attādhipatito āgatā attādhipateyyā, attānaṃ adhipatiṃ katvā pavattā. Lajjāsabhāvasaṇṭhitāti pāpajigucchanasabhāvaṭṭhāyinī. Sappatissavalakkhaṇattā garunā kismiñci vutte gāravavasena patissavanaṃ patissavo, saha patissavenāti sappatissavaṃ, patissavabhūtaṃ taṃsabhāvañca yaṃ kiñci gāravaṃ. Jātiādimahattatāpaccavekkhaṇena uppajjamānā ca hirī tattha gāravavasena pavattatīti sappatissavalakkhaṇāti vuccati. Bhayasabhāvasaṇṭhitanti pāpato bhāyanasabhāvaṭṭhāyī, vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvilakkhaṇattā [M 2.0232] vajjaṃ bhāyati taṃ bhayato passatīti vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvī, evaṃsabhāvaṃ ottappaṃ. Ajjhattasamuṭṭhānāditā ca hirottappānaṃ tattha tattha pākaṭabhāveneva vuccati, na paresaṃ kadāci aññamaññavippayogā. Na hi lajjanaṃ nibbhayaṃ, pāpabhayaṃ vā alajjanaṃ hotīti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1.balarāsivaṇṇanā) vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Lokamariyādassa pālanato lokapāladhammā nāma. Sukkāti [V 2.0217] odātā pabhassarabhāvakārakā, sukkābhijātihetutāya vā sukkā. Sambhedanti ācāramariyādāsaṅkaraṃ. Devabhāvāvahā dhammāti devadhammā.

416. 'That which one is ashamed of' (yaṃ hirīyati) means that by which, or by which dhamma as a cause, one feels disgust. This is an instrumental case used for the agent. Alternatively, 'yaṃ' is used due to a change of gender, meaning 'dhamma' (phenomenon). 'Hirīyitabbenāti' is in the instrumental case to indicate application—meaning what should be ashamed of, such as bodily misconduct. 'Ottappitabbena' follows the same principle. 'Ajjhatta' refers to one's own internal origin, such as birth, etc., hence 'ajjhattasamuṭṭhānā hirī' (moral shame arising internally). 'Bahiddhā' means external, pertaining to another being external to oneself, hence 'bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ' (moral dread arising externally). 'Attādhipateyyā' means arising from self-sovereignty; it proceeds by taking oneself as the authority. 'Lajjāsabhāvasaṇṭhitā' means established in the nature of shame, abiding in the quality of disgust towards evil. 'Sappatissavalakkhaṇattā' refers to the characteristic of being reverential—when something is said by a respected person, the respectful response is reverence. 'Sappatissava' means accompanied by reverence, embodying respect, and whatever respect that is. Moral shame (hirī) arises from reflecting on the greatness of birth, etc., and thus functions with reverence—hence it is called 'sappatissavalakkhaṇā' (marked by reverence). 'Bhayasabhāvasaṇṭhita' means established in the nature of fear—abiding in the nature of fearing evil. 'Vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvilakkhaṇattā' means one fears wrongdoing and perceives it as dangerous—thus, moral dread (ottappa) has this nature. The internal and external origins of moral shame and moral dread are mentioned here to clarify their manifestations, not to imply they are always separate, since they are never mutually separated. For shame is never without fear, nor is fear of wrongdoing without shame. This is a summary here; the detailed explanation should be understood as given in the Aṭṭhasālinī (Dhammasaṅgaṇī Commentary). 'Lokapāladhammā' (world-guarding principles) are so called because they protect the world's conventions. 'Sukkā' means 'pure,' being bright and illuminating, or pure because it is the cause of pure rebirths. 'Sambheda' means 'confusion'—the mixing of moral boundaries. 'Devabhāvāvahā dhammā' means 'principles leading to a divine state,' hence 'divine principles' (devadhammā).

Sukkadhammasamāhitāti yathāvuttasukkadhammasamaṅgino. Santoti vūpasantadosā. Sappurisāti santajanā. Saparahitasādhakā hi sādhavo.

'Sukkadhammasamāhitā' means 'endowed with pure qualities,' i.e., possessing the pure qualities as described. 'Santa' means 'peaceful,' i.e., those whose defilements are pacified. 'Sappurisa' means 'good people,' i.e., peaceful people. For the virtuous (sādhu) are those who accomplish the welfare of themselves and others.

Avayavavinimuttassa samudāyassa abhāvato, avayavena ca samudāyassa apadisitabbato ovādūpasampadāvahaovādekadeso ovādūpasampadāti. Idhāti imasmiṃ assapure. Ete hirottappadhammā. Samaṇadhammā nāmāti dassitā mūlabhūtasamaṇabhāvakarā dhammāti katvā. Tathā hi tesaṃ ādito gahaṇaṃ.

Since there is no collection separate from its parts, and since the collection must be designated by its parts, a portion of advice that brings about acceptance of the guidance is called 'ovādūpasampadā' (acceptance of guidance). 'Here' refers to this Assapura. These are the qualities of moral shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa). They are shown to be 'samaṇadhammā' (duties of an ascetic), taking them as the fundamental qualities that create the state of being an ascetic. For thus is their initial taking up.

Yassa adhigamena nippariyāyato samaṇā nāma honti, so ariyamaggo “samaṇassa kammaṃ paṭipadā”ti katvā sāmaññaṃ, tassa pana phalabhāvato, ārammaṇakaraṇavasena araṇīyato phalanibbānāni sāmaññattho. Rāgaṃ khepetīti rāgakkhayo, ariyamaggo. Rāgo khīyati etthāti rāgakkhayo, nibbānaṃ. Phalaṃ pana kāraṇūpacārena rāgakkhayo daṭṭhabbo. Dosakkhayo mohakkhayoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Sāmaññabhūto attho sāmaññattho, maggo, sāmaññassa atthoti sāmaññattho, phalanti āha “maggampi phalampi ekato katvā sāmaññattho kathito”ti. Tayidaṃ ukkaṭṭhaniddesena vuttaṃ. Sīlādipubbabhāgapaṭipadāpi hi idha “sāmaññattho”ti gahitā. Tenevāha “sati uttarikaraṇīye”ti. Paṭivedayāmīti punappunaṃ ñāpemi.

Through the attainment of which (path) one is truly called a samaṇa, that Noble Path, by being 'the practice of a samaṇa,' is thus 'sāmañña' (asceticism). And from the perspective of its fruition, due to being an object and a cause worthy of veneration, the fruits and Nibbāna are the meaning of sāmañña. 'He destroys lust' (rāgaṃ khepeti)—thus, 'rāgakkhaya' (the destruction of lust) is the Noble Path. 'Lust is destroyed here' (rāgo khīyati ettha)—thus, 'rāgakkhaya' is Nibbāna.
