The fruit, however, should be seen as 'rāgakkhaya' by way of causal imputation. The destruction of hatred (dosakkhaya) and the destruction of delusion (mohakkhaya)—here too, the same method applies. 'Sāmaññattho' (the meaning of sāmañña) is the meaning that constitutes sāmañña, i.e., the path. 'Sāmaññattho' is the meaning of sāmañña, i.e., the fruit. Thus, it is said: 'Having combined both the path and the fruit, the meaning of sāmañña is explained.' This is stated by way of an elevated explanation. For here, even the preliminary practice of virtue (sīla), etc., is included as 'sāmaññattho' (the meaning of sāmañña). Therefore, it is said: 'when there is a further task to be done.' 'Paṭivedayāmi' means 'I make known repeatedly.'

417. Kammapathavasenevāti akusalakammapathabhāveneva, tato tādisampi akusalakammaṃ bhikkhussa kātuṃ na yuttanti duṭṭhullabhāveneva tato [M 2.0233] oramatīti adhippāyo. Sikkhāpadabaddhenāti sikkhāpadapaññāpanena. Pānīyaghaṭe vā patte vā kākānaṃ hatthaṃ vā daṇḍaṃ vā leḍḍuṃ vāti sabbamidaṃ nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yattha katthaci hi ṭhitānaṃ aññesampi pāṇīnaṃ uṭṭhāpanādi sabbaṃ aniṭṭhakaraṇaṃ idha aparisuddhakāyasamācārabhāveneva saṅgahitanti. Uttānoti uddhamuddhaṃ tanotīti uttāno. Evaṃbhūto ca kenaci anuppādabhūmiyaṃ sañjātasālakalyāṇīkhandho viya uparūpari uggatuggato pākaṭo ca hotīti āha “uggato pākaṭo”ti. Anāvaṭoti anivuto. Tenāha “asañchanno”ti, nacchādetabboti attho. Ekasadiso visuddhabhāvena. Antarantare chiddarahito pubbenāparaṃ sammāpaṭipattiyā sandhānena. Saṃvuto kāyikassa saṃvarassa anupakkilesato. Tenāha “kilesānaṃ dvāraṃ pidahanenā”ti.

417. “By way of the path of action” means by way of unwholesome paths of action; therefore, such unwholesome action is not fitting for a monk to commit because of its grossness, and thus he refrains from it—this is the intended meaning. “Bound by the training rule” means by the establishment of the training rule. “In a water pot or a bowl, or at crows with a hand, a stick, or a clod”—all this should be seen merely as an example. For any disturbance or harm caused to other beings, wherever they may be, such as causing them to get up, is included here under the aspect of impure bodily conduct. “Manifest” means stretching upwards. And one who is thus, like a beautiful sal tree trunk born on fertile ground, becomes prominent and evident, rising higher and higher—hence it is said, “risen and evident.” “Uncovered” means not concealed. Therefore it is said, “uncovered,” meaning it should not be concealed. “Uniform” means by way of purity. “Without gaps” means free from breaks, seamlessly connected by proper practice from beginning to end. “Restrained” refers to the non-defilement of bodily restraint. Hence it is said, “by closing the door to defilements.”

418. Ettha [V 2.0218] yathā lahukataraṃ kākuṭṭhāpanādikāyakammaṃ kāyasamācārassa aparisuddhabhāvāvahaṃ sallekhavikopanato, micchāvitakkanamattañca manosamācārassa, evaṃ yaṃ kiñci aniyyānakathākathanamattaṃ vacīsamācārassa aparisuddhabhāvāvahaṃ sallekhavikopanato, na hasādhippāyena musākathananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Hasādhippāyena hi musākathanaṃ sikkhāpadabaddheneva paṭikkhittanti.

418. Here, just as a lighter bodily action, such as causing a crow to fly up, leads to impurity of bodily conduct because it undermines self-effacement, and merely wrong thoughts lead to impurity of mental conduct, so too any mere talk that is not conducive to release leads to impurity of verbal conduct because it undermines self-effacement. It should be understood that this does not refer to lying with the intention of jesting, for lying with the intention of jesting is prohibited by the training rule itself.

420. Ājīvopi ekacco kammapathavasena vārito labbhati. So pana atioḷāriko kāyavacīsamācāravāresu vuttanayo evāti na gahitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ye pana “tādiso bhikkhūnaṃ ayogyato na gahito”ti vadanti, taṃ micchā tathā sati kāyavacīsamācāravārepi tassa aggahetabbabhāvāpattito. “Khādatha pivathā”ti pucchā attano khāditukāmatādīpanena, pariyāyakathābhāvato panesā sallekhavikopanā jātā.

420. A certain livelihood is also found to be prohibited by way of the path of action. But that is too coarse, being of the type described in the sections on bodily and verbal conduct; therefore, it should be understood as not being included here. But those who say, 'Such a livelihood is not included because it is unsuitable for monks,' are wrong, because, if that were so, it would follow that it should not be included in the section on bodily and verbal conduct either. The question, “Eat? Drink?” by revealing one’s own desire to eat, etc., and since it is a roundabout way of speaking, becomes a cause for undermining self-effacement.

422. Anesanaṃ pahāya dhammena samena paccaye pariyesanto pariyesanamattaññū nāma. Dāyakassa deyyadhammassa attano ca pamāṇaññutāpaṭiggaṇhanto paṭiggahaṇamattaññū nāma. Yoniso paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjanto paribhogamattaññū nāma.

422. One who, having abandoned improper seeking, searches for requisites righteously and equitably is called “one who knows moderation in seeking.” One who receives, knowing the measure of the donor, of the offering, and of oneself, is called “one who knows moderation in receiving.” One who consumes after wisely reflecting is called “one who knows moderation in using.”

423. Ekasmiṃ [M 2.0234] koṭṭhāseti majjhimayāmasaññite ekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse. “Vāmena passena sentī”ti evaṃ vuttā. Dakkhiṇapassena sayāno nāma natthi dakkhiṇahatthassa sarīraggahaṇādipayogakkhamato. Purisavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ.

423. “In one section” means in the one section called the middle watch. “They lie on the left side”—thus it was said. There is no mention of lying on the right side because the right hand is capable of being used for grasping the body and so on. And this is said with reference to a man.

Tejussadattāti iminā sīhassa abhīrukabhāvaṃ dasseti. Bhīrukā hi sesamigā attano āsayaṃ pavisitvā santāsapubbakaṃ yathā tathā sayanti, sīho pana abhīrukabhāvato satokārī bhikkhu viya satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāva sayati. Tenāha “dve purimapāde”tiādi. Seti abyāvaṭabhāvena pavattati etthāti seyyā, catutthajjhānameva seyyā. Kiṃ pana taṃ catutthajjhānanti? Ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ. Tattha hi ṭhatvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā bhagavā anukkamena aggamaggaṃ adhigato tathāgato jātoti keci, tayidaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ nāma na seyyā. Apare pana “catutthajjhānasamanantarā bhagavā parinibbāyī”ti vuttapadaṃ gahetvā “lokiyacatutthajjhānasamāpatti tathāgataseyyā”ti vadanti, tathā sati parinibbānakālikā tathāgataseyyāti āpajjati, na ca bhagavā catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjanabahulo vihāsi, aggaphalajhānaṃ panettha “catutthajjhāna”nti adhippetaṃ. Tattha yathā sattānaṃ niddupagamanalakkhaṇā seyyā [V 2.0219] bhavaṅgacittavāravasena hoti, tañca tesaṃ paṭhamajātisamanvayaṃ yebhuyyavuttikaṃ, evaṃ bhagavato ariyajātisamanvayaṃ yebhuyyavuttikaṃ aggaphalabhūtaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ “tathāgataseyyā”ti veditabbaṃ. Sīhaseyyāti seṭṭhaseyyāti āha “uttamaseyyā”ti.

By ‘Tejussadattā’ (because of its abundance of fierceness), the lion’s fearlessness is shown. For other timid animals enter their lairs and sleep haphazardly, preceded by terror; but the lion, being fearless, sleeps having established mindfulness, like a mindful monk. Hence it is said, “with the two front paws,” etc. “He sleeps” (seti) means he abides without being engaged; thus it is called “sleep” (seyyā). The fourth jhāna itself is “sleep.” But what is that fourth jhāna? The fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing. Some say that having abided therein and developed insight, the Blessed One gradually attained the supreme path and became the Tathāgata—but this basis is not “sleep.” Others, taking the statement that “the Blessed One attained final nibbāna immediately after the fourth jhāna,” say that “the mundane fourth jhāna absorption is the sleep of the Tathāgata.” If that were so, it would follow that the Tathāgata’s sleep occurs at the time of final nibbāna; but the Blessed One did not frequently abide in the fourth jhāna. Here, the jhāna of the highest fruition is intended by “fourth jhāna.” Just as for beings, sleep, which is characterized by falling asleep, occurs by way of the process of the life-continuum consciousness, and that is generally connected with their first birth, so too for the Blessed One, the fourth jhāna which is the highest fruition, generally connected with the noble birth, should be understood as “the sleep of the Tathāgata.” “Lion’s sleep” means the best sleep; thus it is said, “the supreme sleep.”

426. Vigatantānīti iṇamūlāni. Tesanti iṇamūlānaṃ. Pariyantoti avaseso.

426. `Vigatantāni` means the roots of debt. `Tesaṃ` means of the roots of debt. `Pariyanto` means remainder.

Pavattinivāraṇena catuiriyāpathaṃ chindanto. Ābādhatīti pīḷeti. Dukkhitoti sañjātadukkho. Appaṃ balaṃ balamattā. Appattho hi ayaṃ mattā-saddo “mattāsukhapariccāgā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 290) viya, balavattho pana mattā-saddo anatthantaro. Sesanti “tassa hi bandhanā muttomhīti āvajjayato tadubhayaṃ hotī”tiādinā vattabbaṃ sandhāyāha. Sabbapadesūti vuttāvasiṭṭhesu sabbapadesu. Yenakāmaṃ yathāruci gacchatīti yenakāmaṃgamoti [M 2.0235] anunāsikalopaṃ akatvā niddeso. Bhujo attano yathāsukhaviniyogo isso icchitabbo etthāti bhujisso, sāmiko. So pana aparasantakatāya “attano santako”ti vutto. Dullabhaāpatāya kaṃ tārenti etthāti kantāroti āha “nirudakaṃ dīghamagga”nti.

Cutting off the four postures by restraining activity. `Ābādhati` means it oppresses. `Dukkhito` means one in whom suffering has arisen. `Balamattā` means a little strength. For here the word 'mattā' has the meaning of 'a little,' as in such phrases as 'by giving up a little happiness' (Dhp. 290); but the word 'mattā' with the meaning of strength has a different meaning. `Sesam` (the remainder): he says this with reference to what should be stated, beginning with, 'For one reflecting, “I am freed from that bondage,” both arise,' and so on. `Sabbapadesu` means in all the remaining places mentioned. `Yenakāmaṃgamo` means 'one who goes as he wishes'; this is a statement made without eliding the nasal. `Bhujisso`: one who is free (`bhujo`), a master (`sāmiko`), for whom his own disposal as he wishes is to be desired. But because he is not the property of another, he is called 'his own master.' `Kantāro`: a place where one crosses water (`kaṃ`) with difficulty; he says this means 'a long road without water.'

Vināsetīti khādanadubbiniyojanādīhi yathā iṇamūlaṃ kiñci na hoti, tathā karoti. Yamhi rāgavatthumhi. So puggalo. Tena rāgavatthunā, puriso ce itthiyā, itthī ce purisena. Iṇaṃ viya kāmacchando daṭṭhabbo pīḷāsamānato.

`Vināseti` means he acts in such a way that, through consuming, misuse, and so on, no root of debt whatsoever remains. `Yamhi rāgavatthumhi` refers to the object of lust. `So` refers to the person. `Tena rāgavatthunā` means by that object of lust—if a man, by a woman; if a woman, by a man. Sensual desire should be seen as a debt, because of the similarity in oppression.

Na vindatīti na jānāti. Upaddavethāti sukhavihārassa upaddavaṃ karotha, vibādhethāti attho. Rogo viya byāpādo daṭṭhabbo sukhabhañjanasamānato.

`Na vindati` means does not know. `Upaddavetha` means 'cause trouble for a pleasant abiding,' the meaning being 'obstruct.' Ill-will should be seen as a disease, because of the similarity in destroying happiness.

Nānāvidhahetūpāyālaṅkatatāya khandhāyatanadhātupaṭiccasamuppādādidhammanītivicittatāya ca vicittanaye. Dhammassavaneti dhammakathāyaṃ. Kathā hi sotabbaṭṭhena “savana”nti vuttā. Evamettha sīlaṃ vibhattaṃ, evaṃ jhānābhiññā, evaṃ vipassanāmaggaphalānīti neva tassa dhammassavanassa ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ jānāti. Uṭṭhiteti niṭṭhite. Aho kāraṇanti tattha tattha paṭiññānurūpena nikkhittasādhanavasena gahitakāraṇaṃ. Aho upamāti tasseva kāraṇassa patiṭṭhāpanavasena anvayato byatirekato ca patiṭṭhaṃ udāharaṇādi. Bandhanāgāraṃ viya thinamiddhaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ dukkhato niyyānassa vibandhanato.

In `vicittanaye` (in the varied method): because of being adorned with various causes and means, and because of the variety of the principles of Dhamma such as the aggregates, sense bases, elements, dependent origination, and so on. `Dhammassavane` means in the exposition of the Dhamma. For a talk is called 'hearing' in the sense that it is to be heard. 'Thus, here virtue is analyzed, so too the jhānas and higher knowledges, and insight, path, and fruition'—yet he does not know the beginning, middle, or end of that Dhamma hearing. `Uṭṭhite` means when it is finished. `Aho kāraṇaṃ` means the reason grasped by way of the proof put forward in accordance with the proposition in each case. `Aho upamā` means the example, etc., established for the purpose of confirming that very reason, through positive and negative concomitance. Sloth and torpor should be seen as a prison, because it obstructs the escape from suffering.

Yasmā [V 2.0220] kukkuccanīvaraṇaṃ uddhaccarahitaṃ natthi, yasmā vā uddhaccakukkuccaṃ samānakiccāhārapaṭipakkhaṃ, tasmā kukkuccassa visayaṃ dassento “vinaye apakataññunā”tiādimāha. Yathā hi uddhaccaṃ sattassa avūpasamakaraṃ, tathā kukkuccampi. Yathāpi uddhaccassa ñātivitakkādi āhāro, tathā kukkuccassapi. Yathā ca uddhaccassa samatho paṭipakkho, tathā kukkuccassapīti. Dāsabyaṃ viya uddhaccakukkuccaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ aseribhāvāpādanato.

Because the hindrance of worry is not without restlessness, or because restlessness and worry have similar functions, nourishment, and opposition, therefore, to show the sphere of worry, he said, “by one who has done wrong in the discipline,” and so on. For just as restlessness does not lead to the calming of a being, so too does worry. Just as thoughts about relatives and the like are nourishment for restlessness, so are they for worry. And just as serenity is the counterpart to restlessness, so it is for worry. Restlessness and worry should be seen as slavery, since they lead to a state of non-freedom.

Soḷasavatthukā vicikicchā aṭṭhavatthukaṃ vicikicchaṃ anupaviṭṭhāti āha “aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu vicikicchā”ti. Vicikicchantoti saṃsayanto. Adhimuccitvāti [M 2.0236] pattiyāyetvā. Gaṇhitunti saddheyyavatthuṃ pariggahetuṃ. Abhimukhaṃ sappanaṃ āsappanaṃ, parito sappanaṃ parisappanaṃ. Padadvayenapi cittassa anicchanākārameva vadati. Khemantagāmimaggaṃ na pariyogāhati etenāti apariyogāhanaṃ, ussaṅkitaparisaṅkitabhāvena chambhitaṃ hoti cittaṃ yassa dhammassa vasena, so dhammo chambhitattanti vicikicchanākāramāha. Tenāha “cittassa uppādayamānā”ti. Kantāraddhānamaggo viyāti sāsaṅkakantāraddhānamaggo viya daṭṭhabbā appaṭipattihetubhāvato.

He said, “doubt in eight places,” because the sixteen-based doubt is included within the eight-based doubt. ‘Doubting’ means being uncertain. ‘Having decided’ means having come to a conviction. ‘To grasp’ means to take hold of a matter for faith. `Āsappanaṃ` is approaching towards; `parisappanaṃ` is approaching all around. By these two terms as well, he speaks only of the mind's state of indecision. It is ‘non-penetration’ because one does not penetrate the path leading to the safe land by means of it. The state of rigidity is the characteristic of doubt: that quality by which the mind becomes rigid due to being suspicious and apprehensive. Therefore, he said, “arousing in the mind.” It should be seen as like a dangerous wilderness path, because it is a cause of non-practice.

Natthi ettha iṇanti aṇaṇo, tassa bhāvo āṇaṇyaṃ, kassaci iṇassa adhāraṇaṃ. Samiddhakammantoti nipphannajīvikappayogo. Paribundhati uparodhetīti ra-kārassa la-kāraṃ katvā palibodho, aserivihāro, tassa mūlaṃ kāraṇanti palibodhamūlaṃ. Cha dhamme bhāvetvāti asubhanimittaggāhādike cha dhamme uppādetvā vaḍḍhetvā. Cha dhamme bhāvetvāti ca mettānimittaggāhādayo ca tattha tattha cha dhammāti vuttāti veditabbo. Pajahatīti vikkhambhanavasena pajahati. Tenāha “ācārapaṇṇattiādīni sikkhāpiyamāno”tiādi. Paravatthumhīti visabhāgavatthusmiṃ, paravisaye vā. Paravisayā hete bhikkhuno, yadidaṃ pañca kāmaguṇā. Āṇaṇyamiva kāmacchandappahānaṃ āha piyavatthuabhāvāvahato.

‘There is no debt here,’ thus ‘debtless.’ The state of that is ‘debtlessness,’ the non-incurring of anyone's debt. ‘Prosperous in undertakings’ means the application of a perfected livelihood. ‘It obstructs, it hinders’; changing the letter ‘r’ to ‘l’ gives `palibodha`, hindrance, a state of non-freedom. Its root or cause is the ‘root of hindrance.’ ‘Having developed the six things’ means having produced and increased the six things, such as apprehending the sign of foulness. And ‘having developed the six things’ should be understood as the six things spoken of in their respective contexts, such as apprehending the sign of loving-kindness. ‘Abandons’ means one abandons by way of suppression. Therefore, he said, “being trained in the regulations of conduct, etc.” ‘In another’s object’ means in a dissimilar object, or in another’s domain. For these are another’s domain for a monk, that is, the five strands of sensual pleasure. He speaks of the abandoning of sensual desire as being like debtlessness because it brings about the absence of dear objects.

Ācāravipattipaṭibāhakāni sikkhāpadāni ācārapaṇṇattiādīni. Ārogyamiva byāpādappahānaṃ āha kāyacittānaṃ phāsubhāvāvahato.

The training rules that prevent failure in conduct are the regulations of conduct and so on. He speaks of the abandoning of ill will as being like health because it brings about a state of ease for body and mind.

Bandhanā mokkhamiva thinamiddhappahānaṃ āha cittassa niggahitabhāvāvahato.

He speaks of the abandoning of sloth and torpor as being like release from bondage because it brings about the mind's unconstrained state.

Bhujissaṃ viya uddhaccakukkuccappahānaṃ āha cittassa seribhāvāvahato.

He speaks of the abandoning of restlessness and worry as being like a freed person because it brings about the mind's freedom.

Tiṇaṃ [V 2.0221] viyāti tiṇamiva katvā. Agaṇetvāti acintetvā. Khemantabhūmiṃ viya vicikicchāpahānaṃ āha anussaṅkitāparisaṅkitabhāvena sammāpaṭipattihetubhāvato.

‘Like grass’ means having treated it as grass. ‘Not reckoning’ means not considering. He speaks of the abandoning of doubt as being like a land of security because, through being without suspicion or apprehension, it is a cause of right practice.

427. Kirīyati (a. ni. ṭī. 3.5.28-29) gabbhāsaye khipīyatīti karo, sambhavo, karato jātoti karajo, mātāpettikasambhavoti attho. Mātuyā hi sarīrasaṇṭhāpanavasena [M 2.0237] karato jātoti karajoti apare. Ubhayathāpi karajakāyanti catusantatirūpamāha. Temetīti tintaṃ karoti. Ko panettha tintabhāvoti āha “snehetī”ti, pītisnehena pīṇanaṃ karotīti attho. Tenāha “sabbattha pavattapītisukhaṃ karotī”ti. Pītisamuṭṭhānapaṇītarūpehi sakalassa karajakāyassa pariphuṭatāya cettha taṃsamuṭṭhāpakapītisukhānaṃ sabbattha pavatti jotitā. Parisandetītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Tatthāpi hi “samantato sandeti temeti sneheti, sabbattha pavattapītisukhaṃ karotī”tiādinā yathārahaṃ attho veditabbo. Paripūretīti vāyunā bhastaṃ viya imaṃ karajakāyaṃ pītisukhena pūreti. Samantato phusatīti imaṃ karajakāyaṃ pītisukhena phusati. Sabbāvatoti a-kārassa ā-kāro kato, sabbāvayavavatoti atthoti āha “sabbakoṭṭhāsavato”ti, maṃsādisabbābhāgavatoti attho. Aphuṭaṃ nāma na hoti pītisukhasamuṭṭhānehi rūpehi sabbatthakameva byāpitattā. Kātuñceva yojetuñca cheko sannetuṃ paṭibaloti yojanā. Nhānīyacuṇṇānaṃ parimaddanavasena piṇḍaṃ karontena hatthena bhājanaṃ nippīḷetabbaṃ hotīti āha “sannentassa bhijjatī”ti. Anugatāti anupaviṭṭhā. Parigatāti parito samantato tintā. Tintabhāveneva samaṃ antaraṃ bāhirañca etissāti santarabāhirā. Sabbatthakamevāti sabbattheva. Na ca pagghariṇī pamāṇayuttasseva udakassa sittattā. Ettha ca nhānīyapiṇḍaṃ viya karajakāyo, taṃ temetvā sampiṇḍitapamāṇayuttaudakaṃ viya paṭhamajjhānasukhaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

427. ‘It is scattered,’ that is, ‘it is cast’ in the womb, thus `karo`, an origin. ‘Born from what originates’ is `karaja`; the meaning is ‘originating from mother and father.’ Others say it is `karaja` because it is born from what originates, by way of the establishing of the body from the mother. In both ways, by ‘the body born of action’ (`karajakāya`), he speaks of the materiality of the four continuities. ‘It moistens’ means it makes moist. What here is the state of being moist? He says, “it suffuses with affection,” meaning it nourishes with the affection of joy. Therefore, he said, “it produces joy and happiness that pervade everywhere.” Here, because the entire body born of action is pervaded by the sublime materiality arisen from joy, the pervasion everywhere of the joy and happiness that produce it is thereby indicated. This same method applies to “it flows around,” and so on. There too the meaning should be understood as appropriate, as in “it flows all around, it moistens, it suffuses with affection, it produces joy and happiness that pervade everywhere.” ‘It fills’ means it fills this body born of action with joy and happiness, like a bellows with wind. ‘It touches all around’ means it touches this body born of action with joy and happiness. In `sabbāvato`, the ‘a’ has been made into ‘ā’; the meaning is ‘possessing all limbs,’ thus he says, “possessing all its parts,” meaning possessing all its portions, such as flesh. Nothing remains unpervaded, because it is pervaded everywhere by the materiality arisen from joy and happiness. The connection is: ‘one skilled in making and joining is able to knead.’ He says, “for one who is kneading, it breaks apart,” because when making a ball by kneading bath powder, the vessel should be squeezed by hand. ‘Permeated’ means entered into. ‘Pervaded’ means moistened all around. ‘With its inside and outside together’ means its interior and exterior are together with the state of being moist. ‘Everywhere’ means in every place. And it is not dripping, because it has been sprinkled with a suitable measure of water. Here, the body born of action should be seen as the ball of bath powder, and the happiness of the first jhāna should be seen as the suitably measured water that moistens and binds it.

428. Heṭṭhā ubbhijjitvā uggacchanaudakoti rahadassa adhothūladhārāvasena ubbhijja uṭṭhahanaudako. Antoyeva ubbhijjanaudakoti rahadassa abbhantareyeva thūladhārā ahutvā uṭṭhitaudakasirāmukhehi ubbhijjanako. Āgamanamaggoti nadītaḷākakandarasaraādito āgamanamaggo.

428. ‘Water springing up from below’ means water emerging and rising from the bottom of a lake in thick jets. ‘Water springing up from within’ means water springing up inside the lake itself from the openings of water veins, without becoming thick jets. ‘Path of arrival’ means the path of arrival from rivers, lakes, mountain crevices, ponds, and so on.

429. Uppalagacchāni ettha santīti uppalinī (a. ni. ṭī. 3.5.28-29), vāri. Ayamettha vinicchayo, tathā hi loke rattakkhiko “puṇḍarīkakkho”ti vuccati. Keci pana [V 2.0222] “rattaṃ padumaṃ, setaṃ puṇḍarīka”nti vadanti. Uppalādīni viya karajakāyo, udakaṃ [M 2.0238] viya tatiyajjhānasukhanti ayampi attho “purimanayenā”ti atideseneva vibhāvitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

429. ‘Uppalinī’ means ‘where there are clumps of blue lotuses,’ or ‘water.’ This is the determination here; for in the world, one with red eyes is called ‘white-lotus-eyed.’ Some, however, say, “The red is the lotus, the white is the white lotus.” This meaning too—that the body born of action is like blue lotuses and so on, and the happiness of the third jhāna is like water—should be understood as having been explained by extension from the ‘previous method.’

430. Nirupakkilesaṭṭhenāti rajojallādinā anupakkiliṭṭhatāya amalīnabhāvena. Amalīnampi kiñci vatthu pabhassarasabhāvaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ “pabhassaraṭṭhenā”ti. Utupharaṇanti uṇhautupharaṇaṃ. Sabbatthakameva jhānasukhena phuṭṭho karajakāyo yathā utunā phuṭṭhavatthasadisoti āha “vatthaṃ viya karajakāyo”ti. Tasmāti “vatthaṃ viyā”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ hetubhāvena paccāmasati, karajakāyassa vatthasadisattā catutthajjhānasukhassa ca utupharaṇasadisattāti attho. Santasabhāvattā ñāṇuttarattā cettha upekkhāpi sukhe saṅgahitāti catutthajjhānepi sukhaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. “Parisuddhena pariyodātena pharitvā nisinno hotī”ti vacanato catutthajjhānacittassa vatthasadisatā vuttā. Catutthajjhānasamuṭṭhānarūpehi bhikkhuno kāyassa phuṭabhāvaṃ sandhāya “taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ utupharaṇaṃ viyā”ti vuttaṃ. Purisassa kāyo viya bhikkhuno karajakāyoti ayaṃ panattho pākaṭoti na gahito, gahito eva vā “yathā hi katthaci…pe… kāyo phuṭo hotī”ti vuttattā.

430. "By the meaning of being free from defilements" means by being untainted by dust, grime, and so on, and by being stainless in nature. Since anything stainless is of a radiant nature, it is stated as "by the meaning of radiance." "Spreading of warmth" means the diffusion of heat. He says, "the physical body is like a cloth," because the physical body, entirely pervaded by jhāna happiness, is like a cloth pervaded by warmth. Therefore, it refers back to the meaning stated by "like a cloth," and so on, as a reason; the meaning is that the physical body is similar to a cloth, and the bliss of the fourth jhāna is similar to the spreading of warmth. Due to its peaceful nature and supreme quality of knowledge, equanimity is also included in bliss here, so the term "bliss" is used even in the fourth jhāna. From the statement, "He sits pervading it with a purified and cleansed mind," the similarity of the fourth jhāna consciousness to a cloth is stated. Regarding the body of the monk being pervaded by the form produced by the fourth jhāna, it is said, "The form produced by it is like the spreading of warmth." This meaning, that the monk's physical body is like a man's body, is obvious and therefore not taken here, or rather, it is taken as stated: "Just as in some cases... the body is pervaded."

431. Pubbenivāsañāṇaupamāyanti pubbenivāsañāṇassa dassitaupamāyaṃ. Taṃdivasaṃkatakiriyāgahaṇaṃ pākatikasattassapi yebhuyyena pākaṭā hotīti dassanatthaṃ. Taṃdivasagatagāmattayaggahaṇeneva mahābhinīhārehi aññesampi pubbenivāsañāṇalābhīnaṃ tīsu bhavesu katā kiriyā yebhuyyena pākaṭā hotīti dīpitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

431. "By the simile of the knowledge of past lives" means by the simile shown for the knowledge of past lives. The grasping of deeds done on that day is generally evident even for an ordinary being—this is stated for the purpose of illustration. It should be seen that by grasping the three villages reached on that day alone, it is shown that for others who have attained the knowledge of past lives through great aspirations, the deeds done in the three existences are generally evident.

432. Sammukhadvārāti aññamaññassa abhimukhadvārā. Aparāparaṃ sañcaranteti taṃtaṃkiccavasena ito cito ca sañcarante. Ito pana gehā…pe… pavisanavasenapīti idaṃ cutūpapātañāṇassa visayadassanavasena vuttaṃ. Dvinnaṃ gehānaṃ antare ṭhatvāti dvinnaṃ gehadvārānaṃ sammukhaṭṭhānabhūte antaravīthiyaṃ vemajjhe ṭhatvā. Tesu hi ekassa ce pācīnamukhadvāraṃ itarassa pacchimamukhaṃ, tassa sammukhaṃ ubhinnaṃ antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhitassa dakkhiṇāmukhassa, uttarāmukhassa vā cakkhumato purisassa tattha pavisanakanikkhamanakapurisā yathā sukheneva [M 2.0239] pākaṭā honti, evaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇasamaṅgino cavanakaupapajjanakapurisā. Yathā pana tassa purisassa aññeneva khaṇena pavisantassa dassanaṃ, aññena nikkhamantassa dassanaṃ, evaṃ imassapi aññeneva khaṇena cavamānassa dassanaṃ, aññena upapajjamānassa dassananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ñāṇassa pākaṭāti ānetvā sambandho. Tassāti ñāṇassa.

432. "Face to face doorways" means doorways directly facing each other. "Moving back and forth" refers to those who move here and there according to their various tasks. Here, "from the house... entering..." is stated with reference to showing the range of the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. "Standing between two houses" means standing in the middle of the street, in the space between, directly facing the doorways of two houses. For if one has an eastern-facing door and the other a western-facing door, a person with sight standing in the street between them, facing south or north, can easily see people entering and leaving; similarly, for a person endowed with the divine eye knowledge, beings passing away and being reborn are manifest. Just as that person sees someone entering at one moment and someone leaving at another, so too it should be understood that this one sees a being passing away at one moment and a being being reborn at another. The connection is made by supplying the words "manifest to the knowledge." "Its" refers to the knowledge.

433. Pabbatasikharaṃ [V 2.0223] yebhuyyena saṃkhittaṃ saṅkucitaṃ hotīti idha pabbatamatthakaṃ “pabbatasaṅkhepo”ti vuttaṃ, pabbatapariyāpanno vā padeso pabbatasaṅkhepo. Anāviloti akālusso. Sā cassa anāvilatā kaddamābhāvena hotīti āha “nikkaddamo”ti. Ṭhitāsupi nisinnāsupi gāvīsu. Vijjamānāsūti labbhamānāsu. Itarā ṭhitāpi nisinnāpi carantīti vuccanti sahacaraṇañāyena. Tiṭṭhantameva, na kadācipi carantaṃ. Dvayanti sippisammukaṃ macchagumbanti imaṃ ubhayaṃ tiṭṭhantanti vuttaṃ, carantampīti adhippāyo. Kiṃ vā imāya sahacariyāya, yathālābhaggahaṇaṃ panettha daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sakkharakathalassa hi vasena “tiṭṭhanta”nti, sippisambukassa macchagumbassa ca vasena “tiṭṭhantampi, carantampī”ti yojanā kātabbā.

433. A mountain peak is mostly compact and contracted, thus here the summit of the mountain is called "the mountain's compactness," or a region belonging to the mountain is the mountain's compactness. "Unclouded" means not murky. Its uncloudedness is due to the absence of mud, hence it is said, "free from mud." Among the cows, whether standing or sitting. "Existing" means obtainable. The others, whether standing or sitting, are said to be moving, by the principle of association. "Staying still" means never moving at all. "Both" refers to the oyster and conch and the school of fish—these two are said to be "staying still," but the intention is to include those that also move. Alternatively, what is the point of this association? Taking according to availability should be understood here. Indeed, with regard to gravel and pebbles, "staying still" applies; and with regard to the oyster, conch, and the school of fish, the connection should be made as "staying still and also moving."

434. Bhikkhūti bhinnakilesoti bhikkhu. So hi paramatthato samaṇotināmako. Tattha ariyamaggena sabbaso pāpānaṃ samitāvīti samaṇo. Tenāha “samitapāpattā”ti. Seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmā vuccati sammāsambuddho, tato āgatoti brahmā, ariyamaggo, taṃ asammohapaṭivedhavasena aññāsīti brāhmaṇo. Taṃsamaṅgitāya hissa pāpānaṃ bāhitabhāvo. Tenāha “bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇo”ti. Aṭṭhaṅgikena ariyamaggajalena nhātavā niddhotakilesoti nhātako. Gatattāti pahānābhisamayavasena paṭividdhattā. Tenāha “viditattā”ti. Nissutattāti samucchedappahānavasena santānato sabbaso nihatattā. Tenāha “apahatattā”ti, mariyādavasena kilesānaṃ hiṃsitattā ariyamaggehi odhiso sabbaso kilesānaṃ samucchinnattāti attho. Tenāha “hatattā”ti. Ārakattāti suppahīnatāya vippakaṭṭhabhāvato. Tenāha “dūrībhūtattā”ti. Ubhayampi ubhayattha yojetabbaṃ – kilesānaṃ ārakattā [M 2.0240] hatattā dūrībhūtattā ca ariyo, tathā arahanti. Yaṃ panettha atthato na vibhattaṃ, taṃ uttānatthattā suviññeyyameva.

434. A bhikkhu is so called because he has broken the defilements (bhinnakilesa). Indeed, in the ultimate sense, he is called an ascetic (samaṇa). Here, because he has entirely pacified evil through the noble path, he is a samaṇa. Thus it is said, "because of having pacified evil (samitapāpattā)." The Supreme Being, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, is called 'Brahmā' in the sense of being the best; that which comes from him, the noble path, is Brahmā. One who has known it through non-deluded penetration is a 'brāhmaṇa.' Because of being endowed with that, his evil is expelled. Thus it is said, "because of having expelled evil (bāhitapāpattā), he is a brāhmaṇa." One who has bathed in the water of the noble eightfold path, having washed away the defilements, is a 'nhātaka' (one who has bathed). "Because of having gone (gatattā)" means because of having penetrated through abandonment and realization; therefore, it is said, "because of having known (viditattā)." "Because of having gone out (nissutattā)" means because of being altogether annihilated from his continuum by means of eradication and abandonment. Thus it is said, "because of having driven out (apahatattā)"; the meaning is that by the standard of the noble paths, the defilements have been destroyed, and by those same noble paths, the defilements have been completely uprooted without remainder. Thus it is said, "because of having destroyed (hatattā)." "Because of being far (ārakattā)" means because of being completely separated due to being well-abandoned; therefore, it is said, "because of having become distant (dūrībhūtattā)." Both terms should be applied in both cases: because of being far from defilements, having destroyed them, and being distant, one is an Ariya; similarly, one is an Arahant. As for what has not been explained in detail here, its meaning is plain and easily understood.

Mahāassapurasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Exposition Clarifying the Concealed Meaning in the Commentary on the Mahāassapura Sutta is concluded.

10. Cūḷaassapurasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Cūḷaassapura Sutta

435. Purimasadisamevāti [V 2.0224] “assapuravāsīnaṃ bhikkhusaṅghe gāravabahumānaṃ nipaccakārañca disvā bhikkhū piṇḍapātāpacāyane niyojento idaṃ suttaṃ abhāsī”ti purimasutte mahāassapure (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.415) vuttasadisameva. Samaṇānaṃ anucchavikāti samaṇānaṃ samaṇabhāvassa anucchavikā patirūpā. Samaṇānaṃ anulomappaṭipadāti samaṇānaṃ sāmaññasaṅkhātassa ariyamaggassa anukūlappaṭipadā.

435. "Just like the previous one" means it is just as was stated in the previous sutta at Mahāassapura (MN.A.II, 415): "Having seen the great respect, reverence, and deference of the inhabitants of Assapura towards the Saṅgha of monks, and instructing the monks on venerating the alms-food, he spoke this discourse." "Suitable for ascetics" means suitable and proper for the state of an ascetic. "A practice in conformity with ascetics" means a practice that is conducive to the noble path, which is known as the ascetic life.

436. Ete dhammāti ete pāḷiyaṃ āgatā abhijjhābyāpādādayo pāpadhammā. Uppajjamānāti uppajjamānā eva, pageva santāne bhāvitā. Malineti malavante kiliṭṭhe. Malaggahiteti gahitamale sañjātamale. Samaṇamalāti samaṇānaṃ samaṇabhāvassa malā. Dussantīti vipajjanti vinassanti. Samaṇadosāti samaṇānaṃ samaṇabhāvadūsanā. Kasaṭeti asāre. Nirojeti nitteje. Ayato sukhato apetāti apāyā, nirayādayo, taṃ phalaṃ arahanti, taṃ payojanaṃ vā etesanti āpāyikā. Ṭhānāni abhijjhādayo. Tenāha “apāye”tiādi. Kāraṇabhāvena duggatipariyāpannāya vedanāya hitānīti duggativedaniyāni. Tena vuttaṃ “duggatiyaṃ vipākavedanāya paccayāna”nti. Tikhiṇaṃ ayanti vekantakasadisaṃ sāraayaṃ. Ayenāti ayoghaṃsakena. Koñcasakuṇānaṃ kira kucchiyaṃ nivutthaṃ yaṃ kiñci kharaṃ tikhiṇañca hoti. Tathā hi tesaṃ vaccaṃ aṭṭhimpi pāsāṇampi vilīyāpeti. Tena vuttaṃ “koñcasakuṇe khādāpentī”ti. Taṃ kira ayacuṇṇaṃ aggināpi kicchena dayhati, bhesajjabalena pana sukhena dayheyya. Tena vuttaṃ “susikkhitā ca naṃ ayakārā bahuhatthakammamūlaṃ labhitvā karontī”tiādi. Atitikhiṇaṃ hoti, aññataraṃ ayobandhanaṃ pheggudaṇḍaṃ viya sukheneva chindanti. Sasabiḷāracammehi [M 2.0241] saṅghaṭitaṭṭhena saṅghāṭīti vuccati āvudhaparicchadoti āha “saṅghāṭiyāti kosiyā”ti. Pariyonaddhanti parito onaddhaṃ chāditaṃ. Samantato veṭhitanti sabbaso pihitaṃ.

436. “These states” refers to the evil states such as covetousness and ill-will that have come down in the Pāli texts. “Arising” means they arise indeed, how much more so when developed in the continuum. “Stained” means defiled, tainted. “Seized by stains” means taken by stains, born of stains. “The stains of ascetics” are the defilements of ascetics, the blemishes of their asceticism. “They are corrupted” means they perish, they are destroyed. “The faults of ascetics” are the corruptions of their ascetic state. “Harsh” means worthless. “Without splendour” means without energy. Apāya means 'deprived of happiness,' referring to states of misery such as hell and so forth. Those who deserve that fruit or for whom that is the purpose are called āpāyikā (leading to misery). The bases are covetousness and so on. Therefore it is said, “in a state of misery,” etc. By reason of being causes, they are conducive to feeling that pertains to a bad destination—hence “productive of painful results”. Therefore it is said, “causes for the resultant feeling in a bad destination.” “Sharp iron” means like a vekantaka thorn, the best iron. “With iron” means with an iron hammer. It is said that in the belly of the heron bird, whatever is harsh and sharp is digested. Indeed, their excrement can even dissolve bones and stones. Therefore it is said, “feeding it to the heron birds.” That iron powder, it is said, is difficult to burn even with fire, but with the power of medicine, it can be burned easily. Therefore it is said, “well-trained ironworkers, having obtained much material for handiwork, make it,” etc. It becomes excessively sharp, and they easily cut a certain iron band with it as if it were a stick of worthless wood. Because it is joined together with skins of rabbits and cats, it is called a saṅghāṭī; it is said to be a weapon-covering, hence it is said, “saṅghāṭī means a sheath.” “Covered” means completely wrapped, concealed. “Enveloped all around” means entirely covered.

437. Rajoti āgantukarajo. Jallanti sarīre uṭṭhānakaloṇādimalaṃ. Rajojallañca vatasamādānavasena anapanītaṃ etassa atthīti rajojalliko, tassa. Tenāha “rajojalladhārino”ti. Udakaṃ orohantassātiādīnamattho mahāsīhanādasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttoyeva. Sabbametantiādīsu sabbasopi vatasamādānavasenāti adhippāyo. Yasmā sabbametaṃ bāhirasamayavaseneva [V 2.0225] kathitaṃ, tasmā saṅghāṭikassāti pilotikakhaṇḍehi saṅghaṭitattā “saṅghāṭī”ti laddhanāmavatthadhārinoti attho. Tathā hi pāḷiyaṃ “saṅghāṭikassa”icceva vuttaṃ, na “bhikkhuno”ti. Tenāha “imasmiṃ hī”tiādi. Kasmā panettha bhagavatā saṅghāṭikattādīniyeva vatasamādānāni paṭikkhittānīti? Nayadassanametaṃ aññesampi pañcātapamūgavatādīnaṃ tappaṭikkhepeneva pasiddhito. Apare pana bhaṇanti – “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saṅghāṭikassa saṅghāṭidhāraṇamattena sāmaññaṃ vadāmī”ti vutte tattha nisinno koci titthantaraladdhiko acelakattaṃ nu kho kathanti cintesi, apare rajojallakattaṃ nu kho kathanti, evaṃ taṃ taṃ cintentānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena bhagavā imāneva vatasamādānāni idha paṭikkhipīti. Saṅghāṭikanti nivāsanapārupanavasena saṅghāṭivantaṃ. Tenāha “saṅghāṭikaṃ vattha”ntiādi. Attano ruciyā mittādayo saṅghāṭikaṃ kareyyuṃ, pacchā viññutaṃ pattakāle saṅghāṭikatte samādapeyyuṃ.

437. Dust is adventitious dust. Filth is the dirt that arises in the body, such as sweat and grime. Because dust and filth are not removed due to undertaking a certain practice, he possesses this; hence he is called a 'dust-and-filth-wearer'. The meaning of “descending into water,” and so forth, has already been stated in the commentary on the Great Lion's Roar Sutta. In “all this,” and so on, the intention is that all these are due to undertaking a certain practice. Because all this was spoken of only in terms of external doctrines, therefore, “of one with a patchwork robe,” the meaning is, of one wearing a cloth that has obtained the name “patchwork robe” because it is assembled from pieces of cloth. For in the Pāli it is said just, “of one with a patchwork robe,” not “of a bhikkhu.” Hence he said, “in this case” and so on. But why did the Blessed One reject here undertaking the practices of the patchwork robe and so on? This is a demonstration of the method, since the rejection of others as well, such as those who undertake the five-fire austerity and the vow of silence, is clear through this very rejection. Others, however, say: When it was said, “Monks, I do not declare asceticism merely because of wearing a patchwork robe,” someone sitting there, who had obtained a doctrine from another sect, thought, “Is he speaking of nakedness?” Others thought, “Is he speaking of dust-and-filth-wearing?” Thus, according to the inclinations of those considering this and that, the Blessed One rejected these very practices here. “Patchwork-robed,” means one possessing a patchwork robe as an under and upper garment. Hence it is said, “a patchwork robe,” and so on. Friends and others might make a patchwork robe according to their own liking, and later, when the time comes for understanding, they might encourage one to adopt the patchwork-robe practice.

438. Attānaṃ visujjhantaṃ passati abhijjhādīnaṃ samudācārābhāvato. Maggena asamucchinnattā visuddhoti pana na vattabbo. Pāmojjanti taruṇapītimāha. Tassa hi attano sammāpaṭipattiyā kilesānaṃ vikkhambhitattā cittassa visuddhataṃ passantassa pāmojjaṃ jāyati, taṃ tuṭṭhākāraṃ. Tenāha “tuṭṭhākāro”ti. Pītīti passaddhiāvahā balavapīti. Nāmakāyo passambhatīti iminā ubhayampi passaddhiṃ vadati. Vediyatīti anubhavati vindati. Idāni tena nīvaraṇehi cittassa visodhanattaṃ laddhanti āha [M 2.0242] “appanāppattaṃ viya hotī”ti. Aññattha uṭṭhitā aññaṃ ṭhānaṃ upagatāti ettakena upamābhāvena uccanīcatāsāmaññena heṭṭhā asaddhammānaṃ paṭipakkhavasena desanāya pariyosāpitattā vuttaṃ “yathānusandhinā”ti. Mahāsīhanādasutte maggo pokkharaṇiyā upamito “seyyathāpi, sāriputta, pokkharaṇī”tiādiṃ (ma. ni. 1.154) ārabhitvā upamāsaṃsandane “tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno, tathā ca iriyati, tañca maggaṃ samāruḷho, yathā āsavānaṃ khayā”ti (ma. ni. 1.154) vuttattā. Yathā hi puratthimādidisāhi āgatā purisā taṃ pokkharaṇiṃ āgamma visuddharūpakāyā vigatapariḷāhā ca honti, evaṃ khattiyādikulato āgatā tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammavinayaṃ sāsanaṃ āgamma visuddhanāmakāyā vigatakilesapariḷāhā ca honti. Tasmā sabbakilesānaṃ samitattā paramatthasamaṇo hotīti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

438. One sees oneself purified by the non-occurrence of unwholesome states such as covetousness. However, one cannot be said to be purified because they have not yet been cut off by the path. “Joy” means initial delight. For when one sees the purity of mind due to the suppression of defilements through one's own right practice, joy arises—this is a state of satisfaction. Hence it is said, “a state of satisfaction.” “Rapture” means strong joy that brings tranquility. “The mental body becomes tranquil”—this indicates both kinds of tranquility. “Experiences” means one feels and attains. Now, because the mind has been cleansed of the hindrances, it is said, “it is as if having attained absorption.” “Having arisen elsewhere, having gone to another place”—this much is said by way of analogy, through a general similarity of high and low. Since the teaching concludes by way of opposition to the lower states, it is said, “in accordance with the connection.” In the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, the path is compared to a lotus pond: “Just as, Sāriputta, a lotus pond...” and so on (MN I 154). In connecting the analogy, it is said: “this person practices in such a way, conducts themselves thus, and has embarked on the path in such a way that it leads to the destruction of the taints” (MN I 154). For just as men coming from the east or other directions, upon reaching that lotus pond, become purified in body and free from fever, so too do those coming from khattiya and other clans, upon embracing the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, become purified in mental body and free from the fever of defilements. Therefore, because all defilements have been pacified, one is an ascetic in the ultimate sense. The rest is easily comprehensible.

Cūḷaassapurasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The clarification of the hidden meaning in the Commentary on the Cūḷaassapura Sutta is concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca mahāyamakavaggavaṇṇanā.

And the commentary on the Great Chapter of Pairs is concluded.

5. Cūḷayamakavaggo

5. The Minor Chapter of Pairs

1. Sāleyyakasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sāleyyaka Sutta

439. Mahājanakāye [M 2.0243][V 2.0226] sannipatiteti keci “pahaṃsanavidhiṃ dassetvā rājakumāraṃ hāsessāmā”ti, keci “taṃ kīḷanaṃ passissāmā”ti evaṃ mahājanasamūhe sannipatite. Devanaṭanti dibbagandhabbaṃ. Kusalaṃ kusalanti vacanaṃ upādāyāti “kacci kusalaṃ? Āma kusala”nti vacanapaṭivacanavasena pavattakusalavāditāya te manussā ādito kusalāti samaññaṃ labhiṃsu. Tesaṃ kusalānaṃ issarāti rājakumārā kosalā. Kosale jātā. Tesaṃ nivāsoti sabbaṃ pubbe vuttanayameva. Tenāha “so padeso kosalāti vuccatī”ti.

439. When a great crowd had assembled: some thinking, “We will make the prince laugh by showing the method of causing laughter,” and others, “We will watch that performance”—thus a great multitude assembled. Divine dancer means a divine gandhabba. Taking up the expression ‘well, well’: that is, due to their habit of speaking of what is well, saying in conversation and reply, “Is it well? Yes, it is well,” those people from the beginning gained the designation ‘Kusala.’ The lords of those Kusala people were the princes, the Kosalans. They were born in Kosala. Their dwelling—all this is in the way previously stated. Therefore it is said, “That region is called Kosala.”

Cārikaṃ caramānoti sāmaññavacanampi “mahatā…pe… tadavasarī”ti vacanato visesaṃ niviṭṭhamevāti āha “aturitacārikaṃ caramāno”ti. Mahatāti guṇamahattenapi saṅkhyāmahattenapi mahatā. Tasmiñhi bhikkhusamūhe keci adhisīlasikkhāvasena sīlasampannā, tathā keci sīlasamādhisampannā, keci sīlasamādhipaññāsampannāti guṇamahattenapi so bhikkhusamūho mahāti. Taṃ anāmasitvā saṅkhyāmahattameva dassento “sataṃ vā”tiādimāha. Aññagāmapaṭibaddhajīvikāvasena samosaranti etthāti samosaraṇaṃ, gāmo nivāsagāmo. Nti sālaṃ brāhmaṇagāmaṃ. Vihāroti bhagavato viharaṇaṭṭhānaṃ. Etthāti etasmiṃ sāleyyakasutte. Aniyamitoti asukasmiṃ ārāme pabbate rukkhamūle vāti na niyamito, sarūpaggahaṇavasena na niyamitvā vutto. Tasmāti aniyamitattā. Atthāpattisiddhamatthaṃ parikappanavasena dassento “vanasaṇḍo bhavissatī”ti āha, addhā bhaveyyāti attho.

Although 'wandering on tour' is a general expression, because of the phrase 'with a great... and so on... he arrived there,' a specific meaning is indeed intended; hence, it is said, 'wandering on an unhurried tour.' 'Great' refers to greatness both in virtue and in number. For in that assembly of monks, some are accomplished in the higher training in virtue, some are accomplished in virtue and concentration, and some are accomplished in virtue, concentration, and wisdom—thus, that assembly of monks is also great in terms of virtue. Without touching upon that, showing only the greatness in number, it says, 'a hundred or...' and so on. 'An assembly' is where they assemble for the sake of a livelihood connected with another village; 'village' is a residential village. Sālā is the brahmin village. 'Dwelling' is the Blessed One's dwelling place. 'Here' refers to this Sāleyyaka Sutta. 'Not specified' means it is not specified whether it was in a certain monastery, on a mountain, or at the foot of a tree—it is stated without specification, by way of taking its general form. Therefore, because it was not specified, showing the meaning established by implication by way of conjecture, it is said, 'It must have been a forest grove,' which means, 'it surely would have been.'

Upalabhiṃsūti (sārattha. ṭī. 1.1.verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.255; a. ni. ṭī. 2.3.64) savanavasena upalabhiṃsūti imamatthaṃ dassento “sotadvāra…pe… jāniṃsū”ti āha. Avadhāraṇaphalattā sabbampi vākyaṃ antogadhāvadhāraṇanti āha “padapūraṇamatte vā [V 2.0227] nipāto”ti. Avadhāraṇattheti pana iminā iṭṭhatthāvadhāraṇatthaṃ kho-saddaggahaṇanti dasseti. “Assosu”nti [M 2.0244] padaṃ kho-sadde gahite tena phullitamaṇḍitavibhūsitaṃ viya hontaṃ pūritaṃ nāma hoti, tena ca purimapacchimapadāni saṃsiliṭṭhāni honti, na tasmiṃ aggahiteti āha “padapūraṇena byañjanasiliṭṭhatāmattamevā”ti. Matta-saddo visesanivattiattho. Tenassa anatthantaradīpanataṃ dasseti, eva-saddena pana byañjanasiliṭṭhatāya ekantikataṃ. Sālāyaṃ jātā saṃvaḍḍhakā sāleyyakā yathā “katteyyakā ubbheyyakā”ti.

'They obtained' (Sāratthaṭīkā 1.1.Verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā; Dīghanikāyaṭīkā 1.255; Aṅguttaranikāyaṭīkā 2.3.64). To show this meaning, 'they obtained by way of hearing,' it is said: 'through the ear-door... and so on... they knew.' Because the result is emphasis, the entire sentence contains an implicit emphasis; thus it is said: 'or the particle is merely for filling in the word.' But by 'in the sense of emphasis,' this indicates the inclusion of the word 'kho' for the sake of emphasizing the desired meaning. When the word 'kho' is included, the word 'they heard' becomes filled, as if blossomed, adorned, and embellished, and thus the preceding and following words are well-connected. If it is not included, it is said: 'by filling in the word, there is merely euphony of consonants.' The word 'merely' serves to exclude a specification. Thus, it shows that this does not illuminate another meaning, and by the word 'eva,' the euphony of consonants is made certain. Those born and raised in Sālā are the Sāleyyakā, just as there are the 'Katteyyakā' and 'Ubbheyyakā.'

Samitapāpattāti accantaṃ anavasesato savāsanaṃ samitapāpattā. Evañhi bāhirakavītarāgasekkhāsekkhapāpasamanato bhagavato pāpasamanaṃ visesitaṃ hoti. Anekatthattā nipātānaṃ idha anussavattho adhippetoti āha “khalūti anussavanatthe nipāto”ti. Ālapanamattanti piyālāpavacanaṃ. Piyasamudāhārā hete “bho”ti vā “āvuso”ti vā “devānaṃpiyā”ti vā. Gottavasenāti ettha taṃ tāyatīti gottaṃ. Gotamoti hi pavattamānaṃ abhidhānaṃ buddhiñca ekaṃsikavisayatāya tāyati rakkhatīti gotamagottaṃ. Yathā hi buddhi ārammaṇabhūtena atthena vinā na vattati, evaṃ abhidhānaṃ abhidheyyabhūtena, tasmā so tāni tāyati rakkhatīti vuccati. So pana atthato aññakulaparamparāsādhāraṇaṃ tassa kulassa ādipurisasamudāgataṃ taṃkulapariyāpannasādhāraṇaṃ sāmaññarūpanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Uccākulaparidīpanaṃ uditoditavipulakhattiyakulavibhāvanato. Sabbakhattiyānañhi ādibhūtamahāsammatamahārājato paṭṭhāya asambhinnaṃ uḷāratamaṃ sakyarājakulaṃ. Kenaci pārijuññenāti ñātipārijuññabhogapārijuññādinā kenacipi pārijuññena parihāniyā anabhibhūto anajjhotthaṭo. Tathā hi kadācipi tassa kulassa tādisapārijuññābhāvo, abhinikkhamanakāle ca tato samiddhatamabhāvo loke pākaṭo paññātoti. Sakyakulā pabbajitoti idaṃ vacanaṃ bhagavato saddhāpabbajitabhāvadīpanaṃ vuttaṃ mahantaṃ ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ mahantañca bhogakkhandhaṃ pahāya pabbajitabhāvadīpanato. Ettha ca samaṇoti iminā parikkhakajanehi bhagavato bahumatabhāvo dassito samitapāpatādīpanato, gotamoti iminā lokiyajanehi uḷāratamakulīnatādīpanato.

'Because evil has been stilled' (`Samitapāpattā`) means because evil has been stilled completely, without remainder, together with its latent tendencies. In this way, the Blessed One's pacification of evil is distinguished from that of outsiders, those free from lust, trainees, and those beyond training. Because particles have many meanings, here the meaning of 'report' is intended, thus it is said: '`khalu` is a particle in the sense of report.' 'Merely a term of address' refers to affectionate speech. For these are affectionate expressions, such as 'bho,' 'āvuso,' or 'devānaṃpiyā.' 'By clan' (`Gottavasena`): here, `gotta` is derived from that which protects (`tāyati`). For the name 'Gotama' protects and guards the current designation and the intellect by being their exclusive object. Just as the intellect does not operate without an object, so a designation does not operate without what is designated; therefore, it is said to protect and guard them. In meaning, it should be understood as a generic term for that lineage, originating from the ancestral founder and common to all members included in that clan. 'Illumination of a high clan' highlights the exalted lineage, demonstrating the risen, exalted, and vast Khattiya clan. For among all Khattiyas, the Sakyan royal lineage stands unbroken and most sublime, beginning from the great King Mahāsammata, the first of all. 'By any deficiency' means not overcome or subjugated by any deficiency or decline whatsoever, such as of relatives or wealth. Indeed, such a deficiency never occurred in his clan, and at the time of his renunciation, his supreme prosperity was manifest and renowned in the world. 'Gone forth from the Sakyan clan' signifies the Blessed One’s renunciation in faith, demonstrating that he went forth having abandoned a great retinue of relatives and a vast mass of wealth. Here, 'ascetic' (`samaṇa`) shows the high regard the Blessed One commands among discerning people, by indicating his stilling of evil, while 'Gotama' demonstrates his supreme nobility among worldly people, by indicating his most sublime lineage.

Abbhuggatoti ettha abhi-saddo itthambhūtākhyāne, taṃyogato pana “bhavantaṃ gotama”nti upayogavacanaṃ sāmiatthepi samānaṃ itthambhūtayogadīpanato [M 2.0245] “itthambhūtākhyānatthe”ti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “tassa kho pana bhoto gotamassāti attho”ti. Kalyāṇoti bhaddako. Sā cassa kalyāṇatā uḷāravisayatāyāti āha “kalyāṇaguṇasamannāgato”ti. Taṃvisayatā hettha samannāgamo. Seṭṭhoti etthāpi eseva nayo yathā “bhagavāti vacanaṃ seṭṭha”nti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā; visuddhi. 1.142; udā. aṭṭha. 1; itivu. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā; mahāni. aṭṭha. 50). “Bhagavā [V 2.0228] araha”ntiādinā guṇānaṃ saṃkittanato saṃsaddanato ca kittisaddo vaṇṇoti āha “kittiyevā”ti. Kittipariyāyopi hi sadda-saddo yathā taṃ “uḷārasaddā isayo guṇavanto tapassino”ti. Thutighosoti abhitthavudāhāro. Ajjhottharitvāti paṭipakkhābhāvena anaññasādhāraṇatāya ca abhibhavitvā.

Regarding `abbhuggato`, here the prefix `abhi-` is in the sense of describing a specific quality. Due to its connection with this, the expression 'the venerable Gotama'—although an accusative expression used in the genitive sense of 'of the master'—is said to be 'in the sense of describing a specific quality' because it reveals this connection. Therefore, it is said, 'the meaning is "of that venerable Gotama".' `Kalyāṇo` means auspicious. And that auspiciousness of his is due to his sublime scope; thus it is said: 'endowed with auspicious qualities.' Here, 'endowment' signifies the possession of that scope. Regarding `seṭṭho` (best), the same method applies, as in 'the word "Bhagavā" is best' (Pārājika-aṭṭhakathā 1.Verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā; Visuddhimagga 1.142; Udāna-aṭṭhakathā 1; Itivuttaka-aṭṭhakathā, Nidānavaṇṇanā; Mahāniddesa-aṭṭhakathā 50). Because the virtues, such as 'The Blessed One, the Arahant,' are proclaimed and sounded forth, the word `kitti` means praise; hence, it is said, 'indeed, `kitti`.' For the word `sadda` (sound) is also a synonym for `kitti` (report), as in, 'the sages, virtuous and ascetic, have a sublime report.' `Thutighoso` means an utterance of praise. `Ajjhottharitvā` means having overcome, due to the absence of an opponent and because of being unique.

So bhagavāti yo so samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūretvā sabbakilese bhañjitvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho devānaṃ atidevo sakkānaṃ atisakko brahmānaṃ atibrahmā lokanātho bhāgyavantatādīhi kāraṇehi bhagavāti laddhanāmo, so bhagavā. “Bhagavā”ti hi idaṃ satthu nāmakittanaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “bhagavāti netaṃ nāmaṃ mātarā kata”ntiādi (mahāni. 149, 198, 210; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 2). Parato pana “bhagavā”ti guṇakittanameva. Evaṃ “araha”ntiādīhi padehi ye sadevake loke ativiya paññātā buddhaguṇā, te nānappakārato vibhāvitāti dassetuṃ paccekaṃ itipi-saddo yojetabboti āha “itipi arahaṃ, itipi samāsambuddho…pe… itipi bhagavā”ti. “Itipetaṃ bhūtaṃ, itipetaṃ taccha”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.6) viya hi idha iti-saddo āsannapaccakkhakāraṇattho, pi-saddo sampiṇḍanattho tena tesaṃ guṇānaṃ bahubhāvadīpanato. Tāni guṇasallakkhaṇakāraṇāni saddhāsampannānaṃ viññujātikānaṃ paccakkhāni evāti dassento “iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇenāti vuttaṃ hotī”tiādi. Tato visuddhimaggato. Tesanti “araha”ntiādīnaṃ. Vitthāro atthaniddeso gahetabbo. Tato eva taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.130) vutto “ārakāti arahaṃ suvidūrabhāvato, ārakāti arahaṃ āsannabhāvato, rahitabbassa abhāvato, sayañca arahitabbato, natthi [M 2.0246] etassa rahogamanaṃ gatīsu paccājāti, pāsaṃsabhāvato vā araha”ntiādinā “araha”ntiādīnaṃ padānaṃ attho vitthārato veditabbo.

That Blessed One is he who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, shattered all defilements, and fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. He is the supreme god beyond gods, the supreme Sakka beyond Sakkas, the supreme Brahmā beyond Brahmās, the lord of the world; and for reasons such as being fortunate, he has received the name 'Blessed One'. Indeed, 'Blessed One' is a proclamation of the Teacher's name. For so it is said: 'This name “Blessed One” was not given by his mother,' and so on (Mahāni. 149, 198, 210; Cūḷani. Ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 2). Furthermore, 'Blessed One' is solely a proclamation of qualities. Thus, to show that the qualities of the Buddha—which are exceedingly well-known in the world with its gods—are revealed in various ways through terms such as 'Arahant,' the particle 'itipi' should be applied to each one, as was said: 'Thus he is an Arahant, thus he is a Perfectly Enlightened One… thus he is the Blessed One.' Here, as in phrases like 'Thus this is real, thus this is true' (Dī. Ni. 1.6), the particle 'iti' has the meaning of making something immediately present, while the particle 'pi' has the meaning of aggregation, thereby indicating the abundance of those qualities. To show that these reasons for recognizing his qualities are evident to the faithful and discerning, it is said: 'This means it is said for this and that reason,' and so on. This is from the Visuddhimagga. The detailed explanation of the meaning of these terms, 'Arahant' and so on, should be understood from there. Therefore, in its commentary (Visuddhi. Mahāṭī. 1.130), it is said that the meaning of terms such as 'Arahant' should be understood in detail as follows: 'He is an Arahant because he is far (ārakā) due to being very distant [from defilements]; an Arahant because he is near (āsanna) [to the faithful]; because of the absence of what is to be done in secret; because he himself is worthy of offerings; because for him there is no secret-going among the realms of existence; or an Arahant because of his praiseworthy nature,' and so on.

Bhavanti cettha (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.130; sārattha. ṭī. 1.verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā) –

And herein are these verses (Visuddhi. Mahāṭī. 1.130; Sārattha. Ṭī. 1. Verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā):

“Sammā nappaṭipajjanti, ye nihīnāsayā narā;

Ārakā tehi bhagavā, dūre tenārahaṃ mato.

“Those people with base intentions who do not practice rightly—the Blessed One is far from them; for that reason, he is considered a distant Arahant.”

Ye sammā paṭipajjanti, suppaṇītādhimuttikā;

Bhagavā tehi āsanno, tenāpi arahaṃ jino.

“Those with excellent resolve who practice rightly—the Blessed One is near to them; for that reason also, the Conqueror is an Arahant.”

Pāpadhammā [V 2.0229] rahā nāma, sādhūhi rahitabbato;

Tesaṃ suṭṭhu pahīnattā, bhagavā arahaṃ mato.

“Evil qualities are called 'secret' because they are to be shunned by the good; because the Blessed One has utterly abandoned them, he is considered an Arahant.”

Ye sacchikatasaddhammā, ariyā suddhagocarā;

Na tehi rahito hoti, nātho tenārahaṃ mato.

“The Guide is never separated from those noble ones who have realized the true Dhamma and whose domain is pure; therefore, he is considered an Arahant.”

Raho vā gamanaṃ yassa, saṃsāre natthi sabbaso;

Pahīnajātimaraṇo, arahaṃ sugato mato.

“He for whom there is no secret going in saṃsāra whatsoever, who has abandoned birth and death—that Sugata is considered an Arahant.”

Guṇehi sadiso natthi, yasmā loke sadevake;

Tasmā pāsaṃsiyattāpi, arahaṃ dvipaduttamo.

“Since in the world with its devas there is none equal to him in virtues, therefore, also because he is worthy of praise, the supreme among bipeds is an Arahant.”

Ārakā mandabuddhīnaṃ, āsannā ca vijānataṃ;

Rahānaṃ suppahīnattā, vidūnamaraheyyato;

Bhavesu ca rahābhāvā, pāsaṃsā arahaṃ jino”ti.

“Far from the dull-witted, and near to the discerning; because of the utter abandonment of secret evils, and because of being worthy of offerings from the wise; and because of the absence of secret evils in states of existence, the Victorious One, the Arahant, is praiseworthy.”

Sundaranti bhaddakaṃ. Tañca passantassa hitasukhāvahabhāvena veditabbanti āha “atthāvahaṃ sukhāvaha”nti. Tattha atthāvahanti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthasañhitahitāvahaṃ. Sukhāvahanti tappariyāpannatividhasukhāvahaṃ. Tathārūpānanti tādisānaṃ. Yādisehi pana guṇehi bhagavā samannāgato, tehi catuppamāṇikassa lokassa sabbathāpi accantāya pasādanīyoti dassetuṃ “anekehipī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yathābhūta…pe… arahatanti iminā dhammappamāṇānaṃ lūkhappamāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ bhagavato pasādāvahatamāha, itarena itaresaṃ. Dassanamattampi sādhu [M 2.0247] hotīti ettha kosiyasakuṇassa vatthu kathetabbaṃ. Ekaṃ padampi sotuṃ labhissāma, sādhutaraṃyeva bhavissatīti ettha maṇḍūkadevaputtavatthu kathetabbaṃ.

‘Sundara’ means auspicious. And it should be understood as bringing benefit and happiness to one who sees it; thus it is said, 'bringing benefit, bringing happiness.' Herein, 'bringing benefit' means bringing welfare connected with the good of this life, the good of the life to come, and the ultimate good. 'Bringing happiness' means bringing the threefold happiness associated with that. 'Of such a kind' refers to such beings. Moreover, to show that the Blessed One, endowed with such qualities, is in every way and utterly inspiring of faith for the world that judges by four measures, it is said, 'with many,' etc. Herein, by the words 'as it truly is... up to arahant,' it is declared how the Blessed One is supremely inspiring of faith for beings of Dhamma-measure and coarse-measure; by the other, for others. 'Even a mere glimpse is good'—here the story of the Kosiyā bird should be told. 'If we get to hear even a single word, it will be even more excellent'—here the story of the Maṇḍūka devaputta should be told.

Iminā nayena agārikapucchā āgatāti idaṃ yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ. Yebhuyyena hi agārikā evaṃ pucchanti. Anagārikapucchāyapi eseva nayo. Yathā na sakkonti…pe… vissajjentoti iminā satthu tesaṃ brāhmaṇagahapatikānaṃ niggaṇhanavidhiṃ dasseti. Tesañhi saṃkhittarucitāya saṅkhepadesanā, tāya atthaṃ ajānantā vitthāradesanaṃ āyācanti, sā ca nesaṃ saṃkhittarucitā paṇḍitamānitāya, so ca māno yathādesitassa atthassa ajānante appatiṭṭho hoti[V 2.0230], iti bhagavā tesaṃ mānaniggahavidhiṃ cintetvā saṅkhepeneva pañhaṃ vissajjesi, na sabbaso desanāya asallakkhaṇatthaṃ. Tenāha “paṇḍitamānikā hī”tiādi. Yasmā maṃ tumhe yācatha, saṃkhittena vuttamatthaṃ na jānitthāti adhippāyo.

When it is said, 'By this method, the householder’s question arose,' this is stated generally. For it is mostly householders who ask in this way. The same method applies to the questions of non-householders as well. By the words, 'As they are unable… to answer,' the Teacher shows the method of reproving those brahmins and householders. For them, because of their delight in brevity, the teaching is concise. Not understanding the meaning from that concise teaching, they request a detailed explanation. And that delight of theirs in brevity is due to their conceit of being wise, but that conceit is unestablished in those who do not understand the meaning as it was taught. Thus, the Blessed One, considering the method for subduing their pride, answered the question concisely—not so completely as to make the meaning of the teaching indiscernible. Therefore, he said: “For they are conceited to be wise…” and so on. The intention is: “Since you ask me, you did not understand the meaning of what was spoken concisely.”

440. “Ekavidhena ñāṇavatthu”ntiādīsu (vibha. 751) viya koṭṭhāsattho vidha-saddo, so ca vibhattivacanavipallāsaṃ katvā paccatte karaṇavacanavasena “tividha”nti vutto. Attho pana karaṇaputhuvacanavasena daṭṭhabboti āha “tividhanti tīhi koṭṭhāsehī”ti. Pakārattho vā vidha-saddo, pakāratthattāyeva labbhamānaṃ adhammacariyāvisamacariyābhāvasāmaññaṃ, kāyadvārikabhāvasāmaññaṃ vā upādāya ekattaṃ netvā “tividha”nti vuttaṃ. Pakārabhede pana apekkhite “tividhā”icceva vuttaṃ hoti. Kāyenāti ettha kāyoti copanakāyo adhippeto, so ca adhammacariyāya dvārabhūto tena vinā tassā appavattanato. Kāyenāti ca hetumhi karaṇavacanaṃ. Kiñcāpi hi adhammacariyāsaṅkhātacetanāsamuṭṭhānā sā viññatti, na ca sā paṭṭhāne āgatesu catuvīsatiyā paccayesu ekenapi paccayena cetanāya paccayo hoti, tassā pana tathāpavattamānāya kāyakammasaññitāya cetanāya pavatti hotīti tena dvārena lakkhitabbabhāvato tassā kāraṇaṃ viya ca sabbohāramattaṃ hoti. Kāyadvārenāti vā kāyena dvārabhūtena kāyadvārabhūtenāti taṃ itthambhūtalakkhaṇe karaṇavacanaṃ. Adhammaṃ carati etāyāti adhammacariyā, [M 2.0248] tathāpavattā cetanā. Adhammoti pana taṃsamuṭṭhāno payogo daṭṭhabbo. Dhammato anapetāti dhammā, na dhammāti adhammā, adhammā ca sā cariyā cāti adhammacariyā. Paccanīkasamanaṭṭhena samaṃ, samānaṃ sadisaṃ yuttanti vā samaṃ, sucaritaṃ. Samato vigataṃ, viruddhaṃ vā tassāti visamaṃ, duccaritaṃ. Sā eva visamā cariyāti visamacariyā. Sabbesu kaṇhasukkapadesūti “catubbidhaṃ vācāya adhammacariyāvisamacariyā hotī”tiādinā uddesaniddesavasena āgatesu sabbesu kaṇhapadesu – “tividhaṃ kho gahapatayo kāyena dhammacariyāsamacariyā hotī”tiādinā uddesaniddesavasena āgatesu sabbesu sukkapadesu ca.

440. In phrases like 'Ekavidhena ñāṇavatthu' (Vibhaṅga 751), the word 'vidha' has the meaning of 'section' (koṭṭhāsa), and here, by changing the inflection and number, it is used in the instrumental sense to express particularity; hence, 'tividha' (threefold) is stated. But the meaning should be understood by way of a plurality of instruments; therefore, it is said, 'tividha means by three sections.' Alternatively, the word 'vidha' signifies 'mode' or 'aspect,' and because of its meaning as 'mode,' the generality of the state of unrighteous conduct and misconduct, or the generality of existence through the door of the body, which is obtained, is brought to unity, and thus 'tividha' (threefold) is said. However, when distinctions of modes are considered, it is said as 'tividhā' (threefold). 'By body' (kāyena) here refers to the causative body (copanakāyo), which is the door for unrighteous conduct, as without it, it cannot arise. And 'kāyena' is the instrumental case in the sense of cause. Although the intimation (viññatti) called unrighteous conduct arises from volition (cetanā), it is not a condition (paccayo) for that volition by any of the twenty-four conditions in the Paṭṭhāna. However, because the activity of the volition known as bodily action occurs in that way, and because it is to be characterized by that door, it is like a cause and is merely a conventional term. Or, 'by the bodily door' (kāyadvārena) means 'by means of the body as a door,' where the instrumental case indicates the characteristic of being of such a nature. 'Unrighteous conduct' (adhammacariyā) is that by which one conducts oneself unrighteously; it is volition that has so arisen. 'Unrighteousness' (adhamma) should be seen as the application arising from it. That which does not depart from righteousness is 'righteous' (dhamma); what is not righteous is 'unrighteous' (adhamma); and that conduct which is unrighteous is 'unrighteous conduct' (adhammacariyā). 'Samaṃ' means subduing what is hostile; or 'samaṃ' means 'the same,' 'similar,' 'suitable,' which is good conduct (sucaritaṃ). That which has departed from 'sama,' or is opposed to it, is 'uneven' (visamaṃ), which is misconduct (duccaritaṃ). That very uneven conduct is 'misconduct' (visamacariyā). 'In all dark and bright sections' refers to all the unwholesome sections that come in the order of statement and analysis, such as 'fourfold unrighteous conduct and misconduct by speech,' etc., and all the wholesome sections that come in the order of statement and analysis, such as 'threefold righteous and even conduct by body,' etc.

Rodeti kurūrakammantatāya parapaṭibaddhe satte assūni mocetīti ruddo, so eva luddo ra-kārassa la-kāraṃ katvā. Kakkhaḷoti luddo. Dāruṇoti pharuso. Sāhasikoti sāhassakārī. Sacepi na lippanti. Tathāvidho paresaṃ ghātanasīlo lohitapāṇītveva vuccati yathā dānasīlo paresaṃ dānatthaṃ adhotahatthopi “payatapāṇī”tveva vuccati. Paharaṇaṃ pahāradānamattaṃ hataṃ, pavuddhaṃ paharaṇaṃ parassa māraṇaṃ pahatanti dassento “hate”tiādimāha. Tattha niviṭṭhoti abhiniviṭṭho pasuto.

He makes beings attached to others weep on account of his cruel actions, causing them to shed tears; thus, he is called 'rudda.' That same 'rudda' becomes 'ludda' by changing the 'r' to an 'l'. 'Kakkhaḷa' means 'ludda' (cruel). 'Dāruṇa' means harsh. 'Sāhasika' means one who acts rashly. Even if his hands are not stained, such a person whose nature is to kill others is called 'lohitapāṇī' (bloody-handed), just as a generous person, even with unwashed hands for the purpose of giving to others, is called 'payatapāṇī' (with hands outstretched). 'Striking' (paharaṇaṃ) is merely giving a blow. To show that 'struck' (hataṃ) and 'advanced striking' (pavuddhaṃ paharaṇaṃ) mean striking to kill another, he says 'hate,' and so on. Therein, 'niviṭṭha' means firmly attached, intent.

Yassa [V 2.0231] vasena “parassā”ti sāminiddeso, taṃ sāpateyyaṃ. Yañhi sāmaññato gahitaṃ, taṃ teneva sāminiddesena pakāsitanti āha “parassa santaka”nti. Parassaparavittūpakaraṇanti vā ekamevetaṃ samāsapadaṃ, yaṃ kiñci parasantakaṃ visesato parassa vittūpakaraṇaṃ vāti attho. Tehi parehīti yesaṃ santakaṃ, tehi. Yassa vasena puriso “theno”ti vuccati, taṃ theyyanti āha “avaharaṇacittassetaṃ adhivacana”nti. Theyyasaṅkhātena, na vissāsatāvakālikādivasenāti attho.

That on account of which there is the designation of ownership, 'another's,' is property. For what is taken in a general sense is made clear by that very designation of ownership; hence, it is said, 'belonging to another.' Alternatively, 'another's property and belongings' is a single compound word, meaning whatever belongs to another, specifically another's wealth or belongings. 'By those others' means by those to whom it belongs. That on account of which a person is called a 'thief' is theft; it is said, 'this is a designation for the mind of stealing.' The meaning is: by what is reckoned as theft, not by way of taking in trust, borrowing for a time, and so on.

Mate vāti vā-saddo avuttavikappattho. Tena pabbajitādibhāvaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Etenupāyenāti yaṃ mātari matāya, naṭṭhāya vā pitā rakkhati, sā piturakkhitā. Yaṃ ubhosu asantesu bhātā rakkhati, sā [M 2.0249] bhāturakkhitāti evamādiṃ sandhāyāha. Sabhāgakulānīti āvāhakiriyāya sabhāgāni kulāni. Dassukavidhiṃ vā uddissa ṭhapitadaṇḍārājādīhi. Sammādiṭṭhisutte (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.89) “asaddhammādhippāyena kāyadvārappavattā agamanīyaṭṭhānavītikkamacetanā”ti evaṃ vuttamicchācāralakkhaṇavasena.

In the phrase 'mate vā' (or when the mother is dead), the word 'vā' has the meaning of an unstated alternative. Thereby, it includes the state of one who has gone forth, and so on. 'By this method' means: when the mother is dead or has disappeared, the father protects her; she is one protected by her father (piturakkhitā). When both are absent, the brother protects her; she is one protected by her brother (bhāturakkhitā). It is said with reference to this and other such cases. 'Families of similar standing' (sabhāgakulāni) means families of similar standing for the act of marriage. Or, by kings and others who have established punishments with reference to the rules for robbers. This is by way of the characteristic of sexual misconduct stated thus in the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya Commentary 1.89): 'The volition of transgressing an improper place, arising through the bodily door with an unrighteous intention.'

Hatthapādādihetūti hatthapādādibhedanahetu. Dhanahetūti dhanassa lābhahetu jānihetu ca. Lābhoti ghāsacchādanāni labbhatīti lābho. Kiñcikkhanti kiñcimattakaṃ āmisajātaṃ. Tenāha “yaṃ vā”tiādi. Jānantoyevāti musābhāvaṃ tassa vatthuno atthi, taṃ jānanto eva.

'Because of hands, feet, etc.' means the reason for the cutting off of hands, feet, etc. 'Because of wealth' means a cause for the gain of wealth and a cause for loss. 'Gain' is so called because food and clothing are obtained. 'A little something' means any small amount of material goods. Therefore, it is said, 'or whatever,' and so on. 'Knowing indeed' means: knowing that the state of that matter is false.

Aṇḍakāti vuccati rukkhe aṇḍasadisā gaṇṭhiyo. Yathā thaddhā visamā dubbinītā ca honti, evamevaṃ khuṃsanavambhanavasena pavattavācāpi hi “aṇḍakā”ti vuttā. Tenāha “yathā sadose rukkhe”tiādi. Kakkasāti pharusā eva, so panassā kakkasabhāvo byāpādanimittatāya tato pūtikāti. Tenāha “yathā nāmā”tiādi. Kaṭukāti aniṭṭhā. Amanāpāti na manavaḍḍhanī, tato eva dosajananī, cittasandosuppattikārikā. Mammesūti ghaṭṭanena dukkhuppattito mammasadisesu jātiādīsu. Lagganakārīti evaṃ vadantassa evaṃ vadāmīti atthādhippāyena lagganakārī, na byañjanavasena. Kodhassa āsannā tassa kāraṇabhāvato. Sadosavācāyāti attano samuṭṭhāpakadosassa vasena sadosavācāya vevacanāni.

'Lumps' (aṇḍakā) refers to the egg-like knots on a tree. Just as they are hard, uneven, and unruly, so too, speech proceeding from belittling and disparaging is called 'lumpy.' Hence it is said, 'just as on a defective tree,' and so on. 'Harsh' (kakkasā) means rough. That harshness is foul because it is a cause of ill-will. Therefore it is said, 'just as by name,' and so on. 'Bitter' (kaṭukā) means undesirable. 'Unpleasing' (amanāpā) means not delighting the mind, and for that reason, it generates aversion and causes mental affliction. 'At the vital spots' (mammesu) refers to matters like birth, which are like vital spots because pain arises when they are struck. 'Causing clinging' (lagganakārī) means causing clinging by way of the intended meaning, 'To one who speaks thus, I will speak thus,' not by way of the letter. 'Near to anger' because it is a cause of it. These are synonyms for 'faulty speech' (sadosavācā), so called on account of the fault that originates it.

Akālenāti ayuttakālena. Akāraṇanissitanti nipphalaṃ. Phalañhi kāraṇanissitaṃ nāma tadavinābhāvato. Akāraṇanissitaṃ nipphalaṃ, samphanti attho. Asabhāvavattāti ayāthāvavādī. Asaṃvaravinayapaṭisaṃyuttassāti saṃvaravinayarahitassa, attano suṇantassa ca na saṃvaravinayāvahassa vattā. Hadayamañjūsāyaṃ nidhetunti ahitasaṃhitattā cittaṃ anuppavisetvā nidhetuṃ[V 2.0232]. Ayuttakāleti dhammaṃ kathentena yo attho yasmiṃ kāle vattabbo, tato pubbe pacchā tassa akālo, tasmiṃ ayuttakāle vattā hoti. Anapadesanti bhagavatā asukasutte evaṃ vuttanti suttāpadesavirahitaṃ. Aparicchedanti paricchedarahitaṃ[M 2.0250]. Yathā pana vācā paricchedarahitā hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “suttaṃ vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Upalabbhanti anuyogaṃ. Bāhirakathaṃyevāti yaṃ suttaṃ, jātakaṃ vā nikkhittaṃ, tassa sarīrabhūtaṃ kathaṃ anāmasitvā tato bahibhūtaṃyeva kathaṃ. Sampajjitvāti viruḷhaṃ āpajjitvā. Paveṇijātakāvāti anujātapārohamūlāniyeva tiṭṭhanti. Āharitvāti nikkhittasuttato aññampi anuyogaupamāvatthuvasena tadanupayoginaṃ āharitvā. Jānāpetunti etadatthamidaṃ vuttanti jānāpetuṃ yo sakkoti. Tassa kathetunti tassa tathārūpassa dhammakathikassa bahumpi kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Na atthanissitanti attano paresañca na hitāvahaṃ.

‘At an inappropriate time’ means at an unsuitable time. ‘Not based on a cause’ means fruitless. For a result is called dependent on a cause because it cannot occur without it. ‘Not based on a cause’ is fruitless; it means frivolous talk. ‘Speaking falsely’ means speaking untruthfully. ‘Unconnected with restraint and discipline’ means lacking restraint and discipline, and speaking in a way that does not bring restraint and discipline to oneself or to the listener. ‘To bury in the heart’s casket’ means, because it is connected with what is unbeneficial, to conceal it without allowing it to enter the mind. ‘At an inappropriate time’ refers to when a Dhamma speaker should speak about a certain meaning at a certain time, but instead speaks before or after that—this is speaking at an unsuitable time. ‘Without reference’ means devoid of scriptural reference, such as not citing, ‘The Blessed One has said thus in such-and-such a sutta.’ ‘Unbounded’ means lacking boundaries. To illustrate how speech can be unbounded, it is said, ‘a sutta or…’ ‘To pursue’ means to investigate. ‘Merely external talk’ refers to not touching upon the essential body of a sutta or Jātaka that has been set forth, but only engaging with talk that is external to it. ‘Having grown’ means having become prevalent. ‘The lineage of Jātakas’ means only the roots of subsequent offshoots remain. ‘Having brought’ means bringing in something else unsuitable for it from the sutta that was set forth, by way of investigation, simile, and subject matter. ‘To make known’ means one who is able to explain, ‘This was said for this purpose.’ ‘For him to speak’ means it is proper for such a Dhamma speaker to speak much. ‘Not grounded in benefit’ means it does not bring welfare to oneself or others.

Abhijjhāyanaṃ yebhuyyena parasantakassa dassanavasena hotīti “abhijjhāya oloketā hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Abhijjhāyanto vā abhijjhāyitaṃ vatthuṃ yattha katthaci ṭhitampi paccakkhato passanto viya abhijjhāyatīti vuttaṃ “abhijjhāya oloketā hotī”ti. Kammapathabhedo na hoti, kevalaṃ lobhamattova hoti pariṇāmanavasena appavattattā. Yathā pana kammapathabhedo hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “yadā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pariṇāmetīti attano santakabhāvena pariggayha nāmeti.

The act of coveting mostly arises from seeing another’s possessions, hence it is said, ‘one is one who looks with covetousness.’ Or, one who covets, even if the object of covetousness is situated elsewhere, covets as if seeing it directly; thus it is said, ‘one is one who looks with covetousness.’ There is no breach of the path of action; it is merely greed, because it does not proceed to the point of appropriation. However, to show how a breach of the path of action occurs, it is said, ‘but when,’ etc. ‘Appropriates’ means to claim it by grasping it as one's own possession.

Vipannacittoti byāpādena vipattiṃ āpāditacitto. Tenāha “pūtibhūtacitto”ti. Byāpādo hi visaṃ viya lohitassa cittaṃ pūtibhāvaṃ janeti. Dosena duṭṭhacittasaṅkappoti visena viya sappiādikopena dūsitacittasaṅkappo. Ghātīyantūti hanīyantu. Vadhaṃ pāpuṇantūti maraṇaṃ pāpuṇantu. Mā vā ahesunti sabbena sabbaṃ na hontu. Tenāha “kiñcipi mā ahesu”nti, anavasesavināsaṃ pāpuṇantūti attho. Haññantūti ādicintanenevāti ekantato vināsacintāya eva.

‘Corrupted mind’ means a mind that has been brought to corruption through ill will. Hence it is said, ‘with a mind become rotten.’ For ill will produces a state of rottenness in the mind, just as poison does in the blood. ‘Evil-minded thoughts due to hatred’ means thoughts corrupted by hatred, like ghee and such spoiled by poison. ‘May they be slain’ means may they be killed. ‘May they come to destruction’ means may they meet death. ‘May they not be’ means may they utterly cease to exist. Hence it is said, ‘may they be nothing at all,’ meaning may they reach complete annihilation. ‘May they perish’ means by merely such thinking, that is, solely through thoughts of destruction.

Micchādiṭṭhikoti ayoniso uppannadiṭṭhiko. So ca ekantato kusalapaṭipakkhadiṭṭhikoti āha “akusaladassano”ti. Vipallatthadassanoti dhammatāya vipariyāsaggāhī. Natthi dinnanti deyyadhammasīsena dānaṃ vuttanti āha “dinnassa phalābhāvaṃ sandhāya vadatī”ti. Dinnaṃ pana annādivatthuṃ kathaṃ paṭikkhipati. Esa nayo “yiṭṭhaṃ huta”nti etthāpi. Mahāyāgoti sabbasādhāraṇaṃ mahādānaṃ. Paheṇakasakkāroti pāhunakānaṃ kattabbasakkāro. Phalanti ānisaṃsaphalañca nissandaphalañca. Vipākoti sadisaṃ [M 2.0251] phalaṃ. Paraloke ṭhitassa ayaṃ loko natthīti paraloke ṭhitassa kammunā laddhabbo ayaṃ loko na hoti. Idhaloke ṭhitassapi paraloko natthīti idhaloke ṭhitassa kammunā laddhabbo paraloko na hoti. Tattha kāraṇamāha “sabbe tattha tattheva ucchijjantī”ti[V 2.0233]. Ime sattā yattha yattha bhavayonigatiādīsu ṭhitā tattha tattheva ucchijjanti nirudayavināsavasena vinassanti. Phalābhāvavasenāti mātāpitūsu sammāpaṭipattimicchāpaṭipattīnaṃ phalassa abhāvavasena “natthi mātā, natthi pitā”ti vadati, na mātāpitūnaṃ, nāpi tesu sammāpaṭipattimicchāpaṭipattīnaṃ abhāvavasena tesaṃ lokapaccakkhattā.
