Bubbuḷakassa viya imesaṃ sattānaṃ uppādo nāma kevalova, na cavitvā āgamanapubbakoti dassanatthaṃ “natthi sattā opapātikā”ti vuttanti āha “cavitvā upapajjanakasattā nāma natthīti vadatī”ti. Samaṇena nāma yāthāvato jānantena kassaci kiñci akathetvā saññatena bhavitabbaṃ, aññathā ahopurisikā nāma siyā, kiṃ paro parassa karissati, tathā attano sampādanassa kassaci avasaro eva natthi tattha tattheva ucchijjanatoti āha “ye imañca…pe… pavedentī”ti. Ettāvatāti “natthi dinna”ntiādinā byapadesena. Dasavatthukāti paṭikkhipitabbāni dasa vatthūni etissāti dasavatthukā.

‘A holder of wrong view’ means one whose view has arisen from unwise consideration. And he is entirely opposed to wholesome views, hence it is said, ‘one who sees the unwholesome.’ ‘Distorted perception’ means grasping things with a reversal of their true nature. Regarding ‘There is nothing given,’ since giving is spoken of with the gift-worthy object as its head, he says this with reference to the absence of a result from what is given. But how does he reject what is given, such as food and other things? The same principle applies to ‘sacrifice’ and ‘offering’ here. ‘Great sacrifice’ refers to a grand offering common to all. ‘Honoring guests’ means the honoring to be done to visitors. ‘Fruit’ refers both to the fruit of benefit and the fruit of consequence. ‘Result’ means a corresponding fruit. ‘For one established in the next world, this world does not exist’—meaning that for one established in the next world, this world cannot be obtained through kamma. ‘For one established in this world, the next world does not exist’—meaning that for one established in this world, the next world cannot be obtained through kamma. There, the reason is stated: ‘All beings are cut off right there and there.’ These beings, wherever they are situated in the realms of existence, such as birth, womb, and destiny, are cut off right there and there, perishing by way of non-arising destruction. ‘Due to the absence of results’—because of the absence of results from right or wrong conduct toward parents, he says, ‘There is no mother, no father,’ not because of the absence of mothers and fathers themselves, nor because of the absence of right or wrong conduct toward them, since they are directly seen in the world. To illustrate that the arising of these beings is merely like that of a bubble, not preceded by coming from somewhere after passing away, it is said, ‘There are no spontaneously born beings,’ meaning, ‘He says there are no beings who are reborn after passing away.’ To explain the view that ‘those who declare this world and the next…,’ the reasoning is as follows: since beings are cut off right there and then, what can one person do for another? There is no opportunity for one's own attainment. A recluse, knowing things as they are, should be restrained and not teach anything to anyone; otherwise, it would be mere conceit. ‘To this extent’—by the expression beginning with ‘There is nothing given,’ etc. ‘Tenfold’—because it has ten things that are rejected, it is called tenfold.

441. Anabhijjhādayo heṭṭhā atthato pakāsitattā uttānatthāyeva.

441. Since non-covetousness and so on have been explained in meaning previously, their meaning is clear.

442. Saha byayati gacchatīti sahabyo, sahavattanako, tassa bhāvo sahabyatā, sahapavattīti āha “sahabhāvaṃ upagaccheyya”nti. Brahmānaṃ kāyo samūhoti brahmakāyo, tappariyāpannatāya tattha gatāti brahmakāyikā. Kāmaṃ cetāya sabbassapi brahmanikāyassa samaññāya bhavitabbaṃ, “ābhāna”ntiādinā pana dutiyajjhānabhūmikādīnaṃ upari gahitattā gobalībaddañāyena tadavasesānaṃ ayaṃ samaññāti āha “brahmakāyikānaṃ devānanti paṭhamajjhānabhūmidevāna”nti. Ābhā nāma visuṃ devā natthi, parittābhādīnaṃyeva pana ābhāvantatāsāmaññena ekajjhaṃ gahetvā pavattaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ, yadidaṃ “ābhā”ti yathā “brahmapārisajjabrahmapurohitamahābrahmānaṃ [M 2.0252] brahmakāyikā”ti. Parittābhānantiādi panāti ādi-saddena appamāṇābhānaṃ devānaṃ ābhassarānaṃ devānanti imaṃ pāḷiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Ekato aggahetvāti ābhāti vā, ekattakāyanānattasaññāti vā ekato aggahetvā. Tesaṃyevāti ābhāti vuttadevānaṃyeva. Bhedato gahaṇanti kāraṇassa hīnādibhedabhinnatādassanavasena parittābhādiggahaṇaṃ. Iti bhagavā āsavakkhayaṃ dassetvāti evaṃ bhagavā dhammacariyaṃ, samacariyaṃ, vaṭṭanissitaṃ sugatigāmipaṭipadaṃ, vivaṭṭanissitaṃ āsavakkhayagāmipaṭipadaṃ katvā tibhavabhañjanato āsavakkhayaṃ dassetvā arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhapesi.

442. ‘One who goes along with’ is a companion (sahabyo), one who shares in activity (sahavattanako); the state of being a companion is companionship (sahabyatā), that is, co-existence, as it is said, ‘He would enter into companionship (sahabhāvaṃ upagaccheyya).’ The assembly of Brahmās is the Brahmā-body (brahmakāyo); those who belong to that category and are found there are called Brahmā-body deities (brahmakāyikā). Although this designation should apply to the entire Brahmā host, since ‘the Ābhā deities’ and so forth are mentioned, which refers to those above the second jhāna realm and so on, by the maxim of the ox and the bull this designation applies to those remaining. Thus it is said, ‘the Brahmā-body deities, meaning the deities of the first jhāna realm.’ There are no separate deities called ‘Ābhā.’ Rather, this term is a designation collectively applied to the ‘limited radiance’ (parittābhā) deities and others, due to their common possession of radiance; just as ‘Brahmā-body deities’ is used for Brahmā’s attendants, Brahmā’s ministers, and the Great Brahmā. The phrase ‘limited radiance and so on’ includes, by the word ‘and so on,’ this Pali expression encompassing the ‘immeasurable radiance’ (appamāṇābhā) deities and the ‘radiant’ (ābhassarā) deities. ‘Without taking them together’—whether as ‘radiance’ or as ‘the perception of diversity in a single body’—without taking them together. ‘Of those very ones’ means precisely those deities mentioned as ‘radiance.’ ‘The distinction in grasping’ refers to the grasping of limited radiance and so on by way of showing that the cause is differentiated by inferior and superior distinctions. Thus, the Blessed One—having taught the righteous conduct, the balanced conduct, the path dependent on the round of existence leading to a good destination, and the path independent of the round of existence leading to the destruction of the taints—thereby showed the destruction of the taints by shattering the three levels of existence, and concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship.

Idha ṭhatvāti imasmiṃ dhammacariyāsamacariyāya niddese ṭhatvā. Devalokā samānetabbāti chabbīsatipi [V 2.0234] devalokā samodhānetabbā. Vīsati brahmalokāti taṃtaṃbhavapariyāpannanikāyavasena vīsati brahmalokā, vīsati brahmanikāyāti attho. Dasakusalakammapathehīti yathārahaṃ dasakusalakammapathehi kammūpanissayapaccayabhūtehi kevalaṃ upanissayabhūtehi ca nibbatti dassitā.

‘Here standing’ means standing firm in this exposition of the practice of Dhamma and virtuous conduct. ‘The heavenly worlds should be included’ means all twenty-six heavenly worlds should be gathered together. ‘Twenty Brahma worlds’ refers to the twenty Brahma worlds according to the classification of existence, that is, twenty Brahma realms. ‘By the ten wholesome courses of action’ means that rebirth is shown to arise appropriately through the ten wholesome courses of action, which serve as kamma-related support conditions and also merely as support conditions.

Tiṇṇaṃ sucaritānanti tiṇṇaṃ kāmāvacarasucaritānaṃ. Kāmāvacaraggahaṇañcettha manosucaritāpekkhāya. Vipākenevāti iminā vipākuppādeneva nibbatti hoti, na upanissayatāmattenāti dasseti. “Upanissayavasenā”ti vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “dasa kusalakammapathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dutiyādīni bhāvetvātiādīsupi “sīle patiṭṭhāyā”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Kasmā panettha “upanissayavasenā”ti vuttaṃ, nanu paṭisambhidāmagge (paṭi. ma. 1.41) – “paṭhamena jhānena nīvaraṇānaṃ pahānaṃ sīlaṃ, veramaṇi sīlaṃ, cetanā sīlaṃ, saṃvaro sīlaṃ, avītikkamo sīla”ntiādinā sabbesupi jhānesu sīlaṃ uddhaṭanti tassa vasena uparidevalokānampi vipākena nibbatti vattabbāti? Na, tassa pariññāya desanattā, pariññāya desanatā cassa “yattha ca pahāna”ntiādinā visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyañca (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 2.837, 839) pakāsitā eva. Tathā hi idhāpi “dasa kusalakammapathā hi sīla”ntiādinā sīlassa rūpārūpabhavānaṃ upanissayatā vibhāvitā, na nibbattakatāya. Kasmā panettha bhāvanālakkhaṇāya dhammacariyāya bhavavisese vibhajiyamāne asaññabhavo na gahitoti āha “asaññabhavo [M 2.0253] pana…pe… na niddiṭṭho”ti. Bāhirakā hi ayathābhūtadassitāya asaññabhavaṃ bhavavippamokkhaṃ maññamānā tadupagajjhānaṃ bhāvetvā asaññesu nibbattanti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ brahmajālaṭṭhakathāyaṃ taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāyañca (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.68-73; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.68-73) vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

“Of the three good conducts” refers to the three good conducts of the sense-sphere. The inclusion of the sense-sphere here is with reference to mental good conduct. “By the result alone”: this shows that rebirth occurs solely through the arising of that result, not merely by way of dependence. To explain the meaning of “by way of dependence,” it is said: “For the ten wholesome courses of action are virtue,” etc. In such phrases as “having developed the second, etc.,” the phrase “established in virtue” should be brought in and connected. But why is it said here “by way of dependence”? Is it not stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 1.41): “By the first jhāna, the abandoning of hindrances is virtue; abstinence is virtue; intention is virtue; guarding is virtue; non-transgression is virtue,” etc., and since virtue is mentioned in all the jhānas, should it not be said that rebirth in higher divine realms is also possible through the result by that means? No, because it is taught for the sake of full understanding. And that it is taught for full understanding is indeed made clear in the commentary on the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. Mahāṭī. 2.837, 839) with the phrase “where there is abandoning,” etc. Similarly, here too, by stating “for the ten wholesome courses of action are virtue,” etc., the role of virtue as a support condition for the realms of form and formlessness is made clear, not its role as a direct producer. But why, when the practice of Dhamma characterized by development is being analyzed in relation to specific existences, is the non-percipient existence not included? He said: “The non-percipient existence, however… is not mentioned.” For outsiders, due to their wrong view, mistakenly believing the non-percipient existence to be liberation from existence, develop the jhāna leading to it and are reborn among the non-percipient beings. This is the summary here. As for what should be further explained, it should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta and its sub-commentary (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.68-73; Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.68-73).

Sāleyyakasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Sāleyyaka Sutta is concluded.

2. Verañjakasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Verañjaka Sutta

444. Verañjavāsinoti [V 2.0235] verañjagāmavāsino. Keci pana “vividharaṭṭhavāsino verañjakā”ti etamatthaṃ vadanti, tesaṃ matena “verajjakā”ti pāḷiyā bhavitabbanti. Aniyamitakiccenāti “iminā nāmā”ti evaṃ na niyamitena kiccena. Ayaṃ visesoti ayaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānadhammādhiṭṭhānakato imesu dvīsu suttesu desanāya viseso, attho pana desanānayo ca majjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇaṃ viya avisiṭṭhoti dasseti. Kasmā pana bhagavā katthaci puggalādhiṭṭhānadesanaṃ deseti, katthaci dhammādhiṭṭhānanti? Desanāvilāsato veneyyajjhāsayato ca. Desanāvilāsappattā hi buddhā bhagavanto, te yathāruci katthaci puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ katvā, katthaci dhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ katvā dhammaṃ desenti. Ye pana veneyyā sāsanakkamaṃ anotiṇṇā, tesaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānadesanaṃ desenti. Ye otiṇṇā, tesaṃ dhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Sammutisaccavisayā puggalādhiṭṭhānā, itarā paramatthasaccavisayā. Purimā karuṇānukūlā, itarā paññānukūlā. Saddhānusārigottānaṃ vā purimā. Te hi puggalappamāṇā, pacchimā dhammānusārīnaṃ. Saddhācaritatāya vā lokādhipatīnaṃ vasena puggalādhiṭṭhānā, paññācaritatāya dhammādhipatīnaṃ vasena dhammādhiṭṭhānā. Purimā ca neyyatthā, pacchimā nītatthā. Iti bhagavā taṃ taṃ visesaṃ avekkhitvā tattha tattha duvidhaṃ desanaṃ desetīti veditabbaṃ.

444. “Verañjavāsino” means those who dwell in the village of Verañja. Some, however, say that “Verañjakā” refers to those who dwell in various districts, and according to their view, the Pāli reading should be “Verajjakā.” “Aniyamitakiccenāti” means a duty not fixed as “by this name.” “This distinction” refers to the difference in the teaching in these two suttas based on the standpoint of individuals and the standpoint of the Dhamma. It shows that the meaning and the method of teaching are, however, not distinct, like gold that is not split in the middle. But why does the Blessed One sometimes teach based on the standpoint of individuals and sometimes based on the standpoint of the Dhamma? It is due to the skill in teaching and the inclinations of those to be trained. For the Blessed Buddhas, having attained skill in teaching, expound the Dhamma as they please, sometimes based on the standpoint of individuals and sometimes based on the standpoint of the Dhamma. To those trainees who have not yet entered the path of the teaching, they teach based on the standpoint of individuals. To those who have entered, they teach based on the standpoint of the Dhamma. The teaching based on individuals pertains to conventional truth, while the other pertains to ultimate truth. The former is favorable to compassion, the latter to wisdom. Or, the former is for those of the faith-follower lineage, for they take persons as their measure; the latter is for those of the Dhamma-follower lineage. Or, on account of a faith-disposition, the teaching based on individuals is for those for whom the world is predominant; on account of a wisdom-disposition, the teaching based on the Dhamma is for those for whom the Dhamma is predominant. The former is of provisional meaning, the latter of definitive meaning. Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One, considering each particular distinction, teaches these two kinds of teachings here and there accordingly.

Verañjakasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Verañjaka Sutta is concluded.

3. Mahāvedallasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Mahāvedalla Sutta

449. Garubhāvo [M 2.0254][V 2.0236] gāravaṃ, pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garukaraṇīyatā. Saha gāravenāti sagāravo, garunā kismiñci vutte gāravavasena patissavanaṃ patissavo, saha patissavena sappatissavo, patissavabhūtaṃ taṃsabhāgañca yaṃ kiñci garukaraṇaṃ. Sagārave sappatissavacanaṃ sagāravasappatissavacanaṃ. Garukaraṇaṃ vā gāravo, sagāravassa sappatissavacanaṃ sagāravasappatissavacanaṃ. Etena sabhāveneva sagāravassa tathāpavattaṃ vacananti dasseti. Aññattha du-saddo garahatthopi hoti “dukkhaṃ dupputto”tiādīsu viya, idha pana so na sambhavati kucchitāya paññāya abhāvatoti āha “paññāya duṭṭhaṃ nāma natthī”ti. “Dussīlo”tiādīsu viya abhāvattho du-saddoti vuttaṃ “appañño nippaññoti attho”ti. Kittakenāti kena parimāṇena. Taṃ pana parimāṇaṃ yasmā parimeyyassa atthassa paricchindanaṃ hoti, nu-saddo ca pucchāya jotako, tasmā “kittāvatā nu khoti kāraṇaparicchedapucchā”ti vatvā “kittakena nu kho evaṃ vuccatīti attho”ti āha. “Kāraṇaparicchedapucchā”ti iminā “kittāvatā”ti sāmaññato pucchābhāvo dassito, na visesato, tassa pucchāvisesabhāvañāpanatthaṃ mahāniddese āgatā sabbāva pucchā atthuddhāranayena dasseti “pucchā ca nāmā”tiādinā. Adiṭṭhaṃ jotīyati etāyāti adiṭṭhajotanā, pucchā. Diṭṭhasaṃsandanā sākacchāvasena vinicchayakaraṇaṃ. Vimati chijjati etāyāti vimaticchedanā. Anumatiyā pucchā anumatipucchā. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave”tiādipucchāya hi “kiṃ tumhākaṃ anumatī”ti anumati pucchitā hoti. Kathetuṃ kamyatāya pucchā kathetukamyatāpucchā.

449. The state of being weighty is respect; it is the quality of being worthy of reverence, like a stone umbrella. “With respect” means respectful. When something is said by a venerable one, the response out of respect is compliance; one who is compliant is one who possesses compliance; and whatever act of reverence is of the nature of compliance and shares in it. The speech of one who is respectful and compliant is respectful and compliant speech. Or, reverence is respect; the speech of one who is respectful and compliant is respectful and compliant speech. By this, it is shown that the speech of a respectful person proceeds accordingly by its very nature. Elsewhere, the prefix “du-” can imply blame, as in “suffering, a bad son” (dukkhaṃ dupputto) and similar cases. But here, it does not apply because there is no corrupt wisdom. Hence, it is said: “There is nothing called corrupt wisdom.” As in cases like “immoral” (dussīlo), the prefix “du-” conveys absence. Thus, it is said: “It means lacking wisdom, devoid of wisdom.” “By how much?” means by what measure. Since that measure is the determination of the meaning to be measured, and the particle “nu” indicates a question, therefore, having said “‘To what extent, then?’ is a question about determining the reason,” it is said: “The meaning is, ‘By how much is it said thus?’” By “a question about determining the reason,” the general nature of the question in “to what extent” is shown, not its specifics. To clarify the particular nature of that question, all questions appearing in the Mahāniddesa are explained by extracting their meanings, starting with, “What indeed is a question?” What is unseen is illuminated by this; thus, “illumination of the unseen” is a question. “Comparison of what is seen” is decision-making by way of discussion. Doubt is cut off by this; thus, “cutting off of doubt.” A question seeking approval is an approval-seeking question. For in questions like, “What do you think, monks?” approval is sought by asking, “What is your approval?” A question arising from the desire to speak is a desire-to-speak question.

Lakkhaṇanti ñātuṃ icchito yo koci sabhāvo. Aññātanti yena kenaci ñāṇena aññātabhāvaṃ āha. Adiṭṭhanti dassanabhūtena paccakkhaṃ viya adiṭṭhataṃ. Atulitanti “ettakaṃ ida”nti tulanabhūtena atulitataṃ. Atīritanti tīraṇabhūtena akatañāṇakiriyāsamāpanataṃ. Avibhūtanti ñāṇassa apākaṭabhāvaṃ. Avibhāvitanti ñāṇena apākaṭīkatabhāvaṃ. Idha diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā adhippetā, na adiṭṭhajotanā vimaticchedanā cāti.

“Characteristic” means any nature that one wishes to know. “Unknown” means the state of being unknown by any kind of knowledge. “Unseen” means the state of not being seen by what constitutes vision, that is, by direct perception. “Unmeasured” means the state of not being measured by what constitutes measuring, as in “this much.” “Uninvestigated” means the state of the action of investigative knowledge not being brought to completion. “Unmanifest” means the state of not being evident to knowledge. “Unclarified” means the state of not being made manifest by knowledge. Here, a question comparing what has been seen is intended, not one illuminating what has not been seen nor one cutting off doubt.

Kathamayaṃ [M 2.0255] attho viññāyatīti āha “thero hī”tiādi. Sayaṃ vinicchinantoti sayameva tesaṃ pañhānaṃ atthaṃ visesena nicchinanto. Idaṃ suttanti idaṃ pañcavīsatipañhapaṭimaṇḍitasuttaṃ, na [V 2.0237] yaṃ kiñci anavaseseneva matthakaṃ pāpesīti. “Sayameva pañhaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā sayaṃ vinicchinanto”ti ettha catukkoṭikaṃ bhavatīti dassento “ekacco hī”tiādimāha. Pañhaṃ samuṭṭhāpetuṃyeva sakkotīti pucchanavidhiṃyeva jānāti. Na nicchetunti nicchetuṃ na sakkoti, vissajjanavidhiṃ na jānātīti attho. Visesaṭṭhānanti aññehi asadisaṭṭhānaṃ. Therena sadisoti therena sadiso sāvako natthi.

"How is this meaning understood?" He said, "For the elder indeed," and so on. "Deciding by oneself" means that he himself distinctly determines the meaning of those questions. "This discourse" means this sutta adorned with twenty-five questions; it is not just any discourse, for he brought it to its culmination without remainder. Showing that here, in "having raised the question himself, he decides it himself," there is a fourfold possibility, he said, "For some indeed," and so on. "Only capable of raising the question" means he knows only the method of questioning. "He cannot decide" means he is incapable of deciding, that is, he does not know the method of answering. "A place of distinction" means a place dissimilar to others. "Equal to the elder" means there is no disciple equal to the elder.

Saṃsanditvāti saṃyojetvā samānaṃ katvā, yathā tattha sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pavattaṃ, tathā taṃ avilometvāti attho. Līḷāyantoti līḷaṃ karonto. Dhammakathikatāya aggabhāvappattiyā tattha appaṭihatañāṇatāya buddhalīḷāya viya catunnaṃ parisānaṃ gamanaṃ gaṇhanto dhammakathaṃ katheti.

"Having connected together" means having joined and made equal, meaning that just as omniscient knowledge functions there, so too without deviating from that. "Acting with grace" means making a graceful gesture. Due to achieving the foremost state in teaching the Dhamma, and due to unobstructed knowledge therein, like the Buddha's graceful manner, he delivers the Dhamma discourse while perceiving the disposition of the four assemblies.

Ito vā etto vā anukkamitvāti uggahitakathāmaggato yattha katthaci īsakampi anukkamitvā uggahitaniyāmenevāti attho. Tenāha “yaṭṭhikoṭi”ntiādi. Ekapadikanti ekapadanikkhepamattaṃ. Daṇḍakasetunti ekadaṇḍakamayaṃ setuṃ. Heṭṭhā ca upari ca suttapadānaṃ āharaṇena tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ heṭṭhupariyaṃ karonto. Jātassarasadisañca gāthaṃ, suttapadaṃ vā nikkhipitvā tattha nānāupamākāraṇāni āharanto tāni ca tehi suttapadehi bodhento samuṭṭhāpento “jātassare pañcavaṇṇāni kusumāni phullāpento viya sinerumatthake vaṭṭisahassaṃ jālento viyā”ti vutto.

"Proceeding in order from here or there" means proceeding according to the grasped rule, without deviating even a little from the grasped course of the teaching at any point. Hence he said, "like the tip of a staff," etc. "A single step" means merely the placing of a single word. "A bridge of a single staff" means a bridge made of a single staff. By bringing together the lines of the suttas from below and above, he makes the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha’s word, connected below and above. And having laid down a verse or a line of a sutta, and then bringing forth various similes and reasons, explaining and establishing them with those lines of the sutta, he is said to be "like one making five-colored flowers bloom on the Jātassara lake, or like one lighting a thousand lamps on the summit of Mount Sineru."

Ekapaduddhāreti ekasmiṃ paduddhāraṇakkhaṇe. Padavasena saṭṭhi padasatasahassāni gāthāvasena pannarasa gāthāsahassāni. Ākaḍḍhitvā gaṇhanto viyāti paccekaṃ pupphāni anocinitvā vallimeva ākaḍḍhitvā ekajjhaṃ pupphāni katvā gaṇhanto viya. Tenāha “ekappahārenevā”ti. Gatimantānanti atisayāya ñāṇagatiyā yuttānaṃ. Dhitimantānanti dhāraṇabalena yuttānaṃ.

"In a single utterance of a word" means in a single moment of quoting a word. By way of words, sixty hundred thousand words; by way of verses, fifteen thousand verses. Like one who, not picking the individual flowers, pulls the entire vine and gathers the flowers all together. Therefore, it is said, "with a single strike." Gatimantānaṃ means those endowed with surpassing quickness of knowledge. Dhitimantānaṃ means those endowed with the power of retention.

Anantanayussadanti [M 2.0256] paccayuppannabhāsitatthanibbānavipākakiriyādivasena anantapabhede visaye pavattiyā anantanayehi ussannaṃ upacitaṃ. Caturoghanittharaṇatthikānaṃ titthe ṭhapitanāvā viyāti yojanā. Sahassayuttaājaññarathoti vejayantarathaṃ sandhāya vadati.

Anantanayussada means flourishing and accumulated in infinite ways, due to its occurrence in an infinite variety of objects such as conditions, the arisen, the meaning of what is spoken, Nibbāna, result, and action. The connection is that it is like a boat placed at a landing-place for those who desire to cross the four floods. "A chariot yoked to a thousand thoroughbreds" refers to the Vejayanta chariot.

Yasmā pucchāyaṃ byāpanicchānayena “duppañño duppañño”ti āmeḍitavasena vuttaṃ, tasmā dhammasenāpati pucchitamatthaṃ vissajjento pucchāsabhāgena “nappajānāti nappajānātī”ti āmeḍitavasenevāha. Tattha iti-saddo kāraṇatthoti dassento “yasmā nappajānāti, tasmā duppaññoti [V 2.0238] vuccatī”ti āha. Idaṃ dukkhanti idaṃ upādānakkhandhapañcakaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ. Tañca kho ruppanaṃ vediyanaṃ sañjānanaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ vijānananti saṅkhepato ettakaṃ. Ito uddhaṃ kiñci dhammajātaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ nāma natthīti yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇato pavattikkamato ceva pīḷanasaṅkhatasantāpavipariṇāmalakkhaṇato ca yathābhūtaṃ ariyamaggapaññāya nappajānāti. Avasesapaccayasamāgame udayati uppajjati, svāyaṃ samudayo saṃsārapavattibhāvenāti āha “pavattidukkhapabhāvikā”ti, dukkhasaccassa uppādikāti attho. Yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇatoti yathābhūtaṃ anupacchedakaraṇarasato ceva sampiṇḍananidānasaṃyogapalibodhalakkhaṇato ca.

Because in the question the phrase "a person of poor wisdom, a person of poor wisdom" was stated by way of repetition for the sake of emphasis, therefore the General of the Dhamma, when answering the question, spoke in a corresponding manner, by way of repetition, with the phrase "does not understand, does not understand." Here, showing that the word 'iti' has the sense of 'because,' he said, "Because one does not understand, therefore one is called a person of poor wisdom." "This is suffering" means this fivefold aggregate of clinging is the noble truth of suffering. And that, in brief, is this much: being afflicted, feeling, perceiving, forming, and cognizing. Beyond this, there is no phenomenon whatsoever called the noble truth of suffering. He does not understand as it really is with the wisdom of the noble path, either from its intrinsic nature and mode of occurrence, or from its characteristic of oppression, being conditioned, torment, and change. When the remaining conditions converge, it arises, it is produced; this is the origin, by way of the continuation of saṃsāra. Thus, it is said, "productive of the suffering of continued existence," meaning it is the producer of the truth of suffering. "From its intrinsic nature" means as it really is, from its function of causing non-cessation and from its characteristic of being accumulation, a source, a bond, and an impediment.

Idaṃ nāma ṭhānaṃ patvāti idaṃ nāma appavattikāraṇaṃ āgamma. Nirujjhatīti anuppādanirodhavasena nirujjhati, tenāha “ubhinnaṃ appavattī”ti. Yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇatoti yathābhūtaṃ accutirasato ceva nissaraṇavivekāsaṅkhatāmatalakkhaṇato ca. Ayaṃ paṭipadāti ayaṃ sammādiṭṭhiādikā samodhānalakkhaṇā paṭipajjati etāyāti paṭipadā. Dukkhanirodhaṃ gacchatīti dukkhanirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena gacchati ārabbha pavattati. Yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇatoti yathābhūtaṃ kilesappahānakaraṇasarasato ceva niyyānahetudassanādhipateyyalakkhaṇato ca nappajānāti. Anantaravāreti dutiyavāre. Imināva nayenāti “idaṃ dukkhaṃ, ettakaṃ dukkha”ntiādinā paṭhamavāre vuttanayena. Tattha hi duppaññaniddesattā pajānanapaṭikkhepavasena desanā āgatā, idha paññavantaniddesattā pajānanavasenāti ayameva viseso. Etthāti dutiyavāre.

"Having arrived at this state" means having come to this cause of non-occurrence. "It ceases" means it ceases by way of cessation through non-arising; hence he said, "the non-occurrence of both." "From its intrinsic nature" means as it really is, from its function of being unshakeable and from its characteristic of being an escape, seclusion, the unconditioned, the deathless. "This is the path": this, beginning with right view, is characterized by unification; one proceeds by this, hence it is the path. "It goes to the cessation of suffering" means it proceeds, having been undertaken, towards the cessation of suffering, Nibbāna, by way of realization and direct experience. "From its intrinsic nature" means he does not understand as it really is, from its function of causing the abandoning of defilements and from its characteristic of being deliverance, a cause, vision, and sovereignty. "In the immediately following section" means in the second section. "By this very method" means by the method stated in the first section, beginning with "this is suffering, this much is suffering." For there, because it is the exposition concerning a person of poor wisdom, the teaching came by way of rejecting understanding; here, because it is the exposition concerning a person of wisdom, it comes by way of understanding—this is the only difference. "Here" means in the second section.

Savanatoti [M 2.0257] kammaṭṭhānassa savanato uggaṇhāti. Ganthasavanamukhena hi tadatthassa uggahaṇaṃ. Ṭhapetvā taṇhantiādi tassa uggahaṇākāranidassanaṃ. Abhinivisatīti vipassanābhinivesavasena abhinivisati vipassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ paṭṭhapeti. No vivaṭṭeti vivaṭṭe abhiniveso na hoti avisayattā. Ayanti catusaccakammaṭṭhāniko.

"By hearing" means he grasps the meditation subject by hearing it. For the grasping of its meaning is through the hearing of texts. The phrase "having set aside craving" and so on is an illustration of the manner of grasping it. "He applies himself" means he applies himself by way of inclination towards insight; he establishes the insight meditation subject. "He does not turn away" means there is no inclination towards turning away because it is not the object. "This one" refers to one who takes the four noble truths as a meditation subject.

Pañcakkhandhāti pañcupādānakkhandhā. Khandhavasena vipassanābhinivesassa cakkhādivasena vedanādivasena ca satipi anekavidhatte sukaraṃ suviññeyyanti catudhātumukhena taṃ dassetuṃ “dhātukammaṭṭhānavasena otaritvā”ti āha. Rūpanti vavatthapetīti ruppanaṭṭhena rūpanti asaṅkarato paricchindati. Tadārammaṇāti taṃ rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattanakā. Nāmanti vedanādicatukkaṃ namanaṭṭhena nāmanti vavatthāpeti. Yamakatālakkhandhaṃ bhindanto viya yamakaṃ bhinditvā “arūpaṃ, rūpañcā”ti dveva ime dhammā, na ettha koci attā vā attaniyaṃ vāti nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapeti paricchindati [V 2.0239] pariggaṇhāti. Ettāvatā diṭṭhivisuddhi dassitā. Taṃ panetaṃ nāmarūpaṃ na ahetukaṃ. Yasmā sabbaṃ sabbattha sabbadā ca natthi, tasmā sahetukaṃ. Kīdisena hetunā? Na issarādivisamahetunā. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 2.447) vuttanayena gahetabbaṃ. Sahetukattā eva sapaccayaṃ. Avijjādayoti avijjātaṇhupādānakammāhārādayo. Evanti “taṃ paneta”ntiādinā vuttappakārena avijjādike paccaye ceva rūpavedanādike paccayuppannadhamme ca vavatthapetvā paricchinditvā pariggahetvā. Vuttañhetaṃ “avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo, taṇhāsamudayā rūpasamudayo”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.50). Ettāvatā kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiṃ dasseti.

The five aggregates means the five aggregates of clinging. Although the application of insight is manifold—by way of aggregates, by way of the eye and so on, and by way of feelings and so on—it is easy and well-understood. Therefore, to show it by way of the four elements, it is said, 'having descended by way of the element meditation subject.' He defines 'form' as 'form' in the sense of affliction, thus distinguishing it without confusion. Tadārammaṇa means those things that proceed by taking that form as their object. He defines 'name' as the quartet beginning with feeling, explaining it as 'name' in the sense of bending. Just as one splitting a double-headed palm fruit splits it into two, so too, breaking the pair apart, he defines, distinguishes, and comprehends name-and-form, saying, 'these are just two phenomena: the formless and form; here there is no self or what belongs to a self.' By this much, the purification of view is demonstrated. But this name-and-form is not without cause. Since it is not the case that everything exists everywhere and at all times, it is with cause. By what kind of cause? Not by an unequal cause such as a creator god. What should be said here is to be understood in the way stated in the commentary on the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā 2.447). Because it has a cause, it also has a condition. Avijjādayo means ignorance, craving, clinging, kamma, nutriment, and so on. Evaṃ means defining, distinguishing, and comprehending both the conditions beginning with ignorance and the conditionally arisen phenomena such as form, feeling, and so on, in the manner stated beginning with 'But this name-and-form...' For it is said: 'With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form; with the arising of craving, there is the arising of form' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.50). By this much, the purification by overcoming doubt is demonstrated.

Hutvāti hetupaccayasamavāye uppajjitvā. Abhāvaṭṭhenāti tadanantarameva vinassanaṭṭhena. Aniccāti aniccā addhuvā. Aniccalakkhaṇaṃ āropetīti tesu pañcasu khandhesu aniccatāsaṅkhātaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ niropeti. Tatoti aniccalakkhaṇāropanato paraṃ, tato vā aniccabhāvato. Udayabbayappaṭipīḷanākārenāti uppādanirodhehi pati pati abhikkhaṇaṃ pīḷanākārena hetunā dukkhā aniṭṭhā, dukkhamā vā. Avasavattanākārenāti kassaci vasena avasavattanākārena. Anattāti na sayaṃ attā, nāpi nesaṃ koci attā atthīti anattāti. Tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvāti [M 2.0258] evaṃ aniccassa dukkhabhāvato, dukkhassa ca anattabhāvato khandhapañcake tividhampi sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā. Sammasantoti udayabbayañāṇuppattiyā uppanne vipassanupakkilese pahāya maggāmaggaṃ vavatthapetvā udayabbayañāṇādivipassanāpaṭipāṭiyā saṅkhāre sammasanto gotrabhuñāṇānantaraṃ lokuttaramaggaṃ pāpuṇāti.

Hutvā means having arisen through the confluence of causes and conditions. Abhāvaṭṭhena means in the sense of non-existence, that is, in the sense of destruction immediately thereafter. Anicca means impermanent, unstable. It imposes the characteristic of impermanence—that is, it establishes the general characteristic known as impermanence in these five aggregates. Tato means after imposing the characteristic of impermanence, or from the state of impermanence itself. In the manner of being afflicted by rise and fall—that is, being painful, undesirable, or suffering due to being constantly afflicted by arising and ceasing. In the manner of being unempowered—that is, in the manner of not being subject to anyone's will. Anattā means it is not a self, nor is there any self that is theirs—thus, it is not-self. Having imposed the three characteristics—thus, because what is impermanent is suffering, and what is suffering is not-self, having imposed the threefold general characteristic on the five aggregates. Sammasanto means having abandoned the imperfections of insight that arise with the arising of knowledge of rise and fall, having distinguished the path from what is not the path, and fully contemplating the formations through the sequence of insight knowledges beginning with the knowledge of rise and fall, one attains the supramundane path immediately after the lineage-change knowledge.

Ekapaṭivedhenāti ekeneva ñāṇena paṭivijjhanena. Paṭivedho paṭighātābhāvena visaye nissaṅgacārasaṅkhātaṃ nibbijjhanaṃ. Abhisamayo avirajjhitvā adhigamanasaṅkhāto avabodho. “Idaṃ dukkhaṃ, ettaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito bhiyyo”ti paricchinditvā yāthāvato jānanameva vuttanayena paṭivedhoti pariññāpaṭivedho, idañca yathā ñāṇe pavatte pacchā dukkhassa sarūpādiparicchede sammoho na hoti, tathā pavattiṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ, na pana maggañāṇassa “idaṃ dukkha”ntiādinā pavattanato. Tenāha “tasmiñcassa khaṇe”tiādi. Pahīnassa puna apahātabbatāya pakaṭṭhaṃ hānaṃ cajanaṃ samucchindanaṃ pahānaṃ, pahānameva vuttanayena paṭivedhoti pahānapaṭivedho. Ayampi yena kilesena appahīyamānena maggabhāvanāya na bhavitabbaṃ, asati ca maggabhāvanāya yo uppajjeyya, tassa padaghātaṃ karontassa anuppattidhammataṃ āpādentassa ñāṇassa tathāpavattiyā paṭighātābhāvena [V 2.0240] nissaṅgacāraṃ upādāya evaṃ vutto. Sacchikiriyā paccakkhakaraṇaṃ anussavākāraparivitakkādike muñcitvāva sarūpato ārammaṇakaraṇaṃ “idaṃ ta”nti yāthāvasabhāvato gahaṇaṃ, sā eva vuttanayena paṭivedhoti sacchikiriyāpaṭivedho. Ayampi yassa āvaraṇassa asamucchindanato ñāṇaṃ nirodhaṃ ālambituṃ na sakkoti, tassa samucchindanato taṃ sarūpato vibhāvitameva pavattatīti evaṃ vutto.

Ekapaṭivedhena means by penetrating with a single knowledge. Paṭivedha is the penetration characterized by unattached conduct in the object, due to the absence of obstruction. Abhisamaya is the understanding characterized by attainment without deviation. The knowledge of 'This is suffering, this much is suffering, there is no more than this,' by defining it and knowing it as it truly is, is called pariññāpaṭivedha (penetration by full understanding) in the manner stated. This is said by taking into account the progression of knowledge in such a way that there is no confusion later regarding the definition of the nature of suffering and so on, and not by the path-knowledge functioning with 'This is suffering' and so on. Hence it is said, 'At that moment...' and so on. Pahāna is the excellent abandoning, relinquishing, and uprooting, such that what is abandoned need not be abandoned again. This abandoning itself is called pahānapaṭivedha (penetration by abandoning) in the manner stated. This too is stated thus, based on the knowledge's unattached conduct due to the absence of obstruction, as it strikes at the foundation of the defilement that, if not abandoned, would prevent the development of the path, and which, if the path were absent, would arise, thereby bringing it to the state of non-arising. Sacchikiriyā is direct realization, the making manifest, the taking of the object in its true nature as 'this is that,' freeing oneself from hearsay, conceptual proliferation, and so on. This itself is called sacchikiriyāpaṭivedha (penetration by realization) in the manner stated. This too is said in this way because when knowledge cannot take cessation as its object due to an uneradicated hindrance, upon its eradication, it proceeds as clearly manifested in its own nature.

Bhāvanā uppādanā vaḍḍhanā ca. Tattha paṭhamamagge uppādanaṭṭhena bhāvanā, dutiyādīsu vaḍḍhanaṭṭhena, ubhayatthāpi vā ubhayaṃ veditabbaṃ. Paṭhamamaggopi hi yathārahaṃ vuṭṭhānagāminiyaṃ pavattaṃ parijānanādiṃ vaḍḍhento pavattoti tatthāpi vaḍḍhanaṭṭhena bhāvanāti sakkā viññātuṃ. Dutiyādīsupi appahīnakilesappahānato puggalantarasādhanato ca uppādanaṭṭhena bhāvanā, sā eva vuttanayena paṭivedhoti bhāvanāpaṭivedho. Ayampi yathā ñāṇe pavatte pacchā maggadhammānaṃ sarūpaparicchede sammoho na hoti, tathā [M 2.0259] pavattiṃ gahetvā vutto. Tiṭṭhantu tāva yathādhigatā maggadhammā, yathāpavattesu phalesupi ayaṃ yathādhigatasaccadhammesu viya vigatasammohova hoti sekkhopi samāno. Tena vuttaṃ – “diṭṭhadhammo pattadhammo viditadhammo pariyogāḷhadhammo”ti (mahāva. 27). Yathā cassa dhammā tāsaṃ jotitā yathādhigatasaccadhammāvalambiniyo maggavīthito parato maggaphalapahīnāvasiṭṭhakilesanibbānānaṃ paccavekkhaṇā pavattanti. Dukkhasaccadhammā hi sakkāyadiṭṭhiādayo. Ayañca atthavaṇṇanā pariññābhisamayenātiādīsupi vibhāvetabbā. Kiccatoti asammohato. Nirodhaṃ ārammaṇatoti ettha “ārammaṇatopī”ti pi-saddo luttaniddiṭṭho daṭṭhabbo nirodhepi asammohapaṭivedhassa labbhanato. Etassāti catusaccakammaṭṭhānikassa puggalassa.

Development is both arising and growth. Here, in the first path, development is in the sense of arising; in the second and subsequent paths, it is in the sense of growth. Alternatively, both aspects should be understood in both cases. For even the first path, while proceeding appropriately, increases the full understanding and so forth that occurs in the insight leading to emergence, so even there, development can be understood in the sense of growth. Similarly, in the second and subsequent paths, development is in the sense of arising due to the abandoning of unabandoned defilements and the accomplishment of further stages for the individual. That very development, as explained, is the penetration of development. This too is stated by taking the progression of knowledge in such a way that later there is no delusion regarding the discernment of the nature of path-factors. For now, let the path-factors as attained remain. Just as in the case of the truth-dharmas as realized, so too in the arisen fruits, he, though a trainee, becomes free from delusion. Hence it is said: “One who has seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and fathomed the Dhamma” (Mahāvagga 27). And his states are illuminated by them; and after the path-process, reflections proceed, relying on the truth-dharmas as realized, concerning the path, the fruit, the abandoned defilements, the remaining defilements, and Nibbāna. For the phenomena of the truth of suffering are identity-view and so forth. This exposition should also be elucidated in terms of full understanding, realization, and so forth. The function is non-delusion. Regarding “taking cessation as the object”—here, the word “pi” (also) should be understood as elided, because non-deluded penetration is attainable also regarding cessation. “Of this” refers to the individual engaged in the meditation on the four truths.

Paññavāti niddiṭṭho nippariyāyato paññavantatāya idha adhippetattā. Pāḷitoti dhammato. Atthatoti aṭṭhakathāto. Anusandhitoti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sutte taṃtaṃanusandhito. Pubbāparatoti pubbenāparassa saṃsandanato. Saṅgītikkamena cettha pubbāparatā veditabbā. Taṃtaṃdesanāyameva vā pubbabhāgena aparabhāgassa saṃsandanato. Viññāṇacaritoti vijānanacarito vīmaṃsanacarito tepiṭake buddhavacane vicāraṇācāravepullato. Paññavāti na vattabbo maggenāgatāya paññāya abhāvato. Ajja ajjeva arahattanti ittaraṃ atikhippamevāti adhippāyo. Paññavāpakkhaṃ bhajati sekkhapariyāyasabbhāvato. Sutte pana paṭivedhova kathito saccābhisamayavasena āgatattā.

“Wise” is specified here directly, because the state of being wise is intended, without circumlocution. “Pāli” means according to the Dhamma. “Meaning” means according to the commentary. “Connection” refers to the respective connections in those respective suttas. “Sequence” refers to the connection of what comes before with what comes after. Here, the sequence should be understood by the order of the recitations. Or, it is due to the connection of the latter part with the former part in each respective teaching. “Intellectual temperament” refers to a knowing temperament, an investigating temperament, due to the abundance of the conduct of inquiry into the Buddha’s words in the Tipiṭaka. “Wise” should not be said in this case, because the wisdom that comes with the path is absent. “Today, just today, arahantship”—the meaning is that it is exceedingly swift. He resorts to the side of wisdom due to the presence of the state of a trainee. But in the sutta, penetration itself is spoken of because it comes by way of the realization of the truths.

Esāti anantare vutto ariyapuggalo. Kammakārakacittanti bhāvanākammassa pavattanakacittaṃ[V 2.0241]. Sukhavedanampi vijānātīti ko vediyati, kassa vedanā, kiṃkāraṇā vedanā, sopi kassaci abhāvaggahaṇamukhena sukhaṃ vedanaṃ sabhāvato samudayato atthaṅgamato assādato ādīnavato ca yathābhūtaṃ paricchindanto pariggaṇhanto sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vijānāti nāma. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Yasmā “satipaṭṭhāne”ti iminā satipaṭṭhānakathaṃ upalakkheti. Tāya hi tadattho veditabbo, tasmā taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāyampi (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.380) vuttanayena tassattho veditabbo[M 2.0260]. Kāmañcetaṃ viññāṇaṃ vedanāto aññampi ārammaṇaṃ vijānāti, anantaravāre pana rūpamukhena vipassanābhinivesassa dassitattā idha arūpamukhena dassetuṃ “sukhantipi vijānātī”tiādinā niddiṭṭhaṃ, pucchantassa vā ajjhāsayavasena.

“This” refers to the noble person spoken of immediately before. “The mind that performs the action” refers to the mind that initiates the task of meditation. Regarding “It knows pleasant feeling too”—who feels, whose feeling is it, what is the cause of the feeling? By way of apprehending the absence of any owner, discerning and comprehending the pleasant feeling as it really is—with its intrinsic nature, its arising, its passing away, its gratification, and its drawbacks—he is said to know the pleasant feeling. The same method applies to the remaining two phrases. Because by “in the foundations of mindfulness” the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness is indicated, its meaning should be understood through that. Therefore, its meaning should also be understood in line with the method stated in its commentary (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 2.380). Although this consciousness also cognizes an object other than feeling, since the application of insight by way of form has been shown in the preceding passage, here, to show it by way of the formless, it is stated as “it knows pleasure too,” and so forth, or according to the inclination of the questioner.

Saṃsaṭṭhāti sampayuttā. Tenāha “ekuppādādilakkhaṇena saṃyogaṭṭhenā”ti. Visaṃsaṭṭhāti vippayuttā. Bhinditvāti aññabhūmikassa aññabhūmidassaneneva vināsetvā, saṃbhinditvā vā. Saṃsaṭṭhabhāvaṃ pucchatīti taṃcittuppādapariyāpannānaṃ pañcaviññāṇānaṃ saṃsaṭṭhabhāvaṃ pucchati. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ pucchāya avasaro visaṃsaṭṭhabhāvāsaṅkāya eva abhāvato? Na, cittuppādantaragatānaṃ maggapaññāmaggaviññāṇānaṃ vipassanāpaññāvipassanāviññāṇānañca vomissakasaṃsaṭṭhabhāvassa labbhamānattā. Vinivaṭṭetvāti aññamaññato vivecetvā. Nānākaraṇaṃ dassetuṃ na sakkāti idaṃ kevalaṃ saṃsaṭṭhabhāvameva sandhāya vuttaṃ, na sabhāvabhedaṃ, sabhāvabhedato pana nānākaraṇaṃ nesaṃ pākaṭameva. Tenāha “ārammaṇato vā vatthuto vā uppādato vā nirodhato vā”ti. Idāni tameva sabhāvabhedaṃ visayabhedena suṭṭhu pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “tesaṃ tesaṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Visayoti pavattiṭṭhānaṃ issariyabhūmi, yena cittapaññānaṃ tattha tattha pubbaṅgamatā vuccati.

“Connected” means associated. Hence it is said, “by the characteristic of arising together, etc., in the sense of connection.” “Disconnected” means dissociated. “Having broken apart” means having destroyed by merely seeing another plane as another plane, or having shattered it. “He asks about the state of being connected”—thus, he inquires about the connected state of the five consciousnesses included within that mind-arising. If so, how is there an opportunity for the question, given the very absence of any suspicion of a disconnected state? No, because a mixed state of connection is found for path-wisdom and path-consciousness, and for insight-wisdom and insight-consciousness, which are included in other mind-arisings. “Having turned away” means having separated from one another. “It is not possible to show the distinction”—this is said solely with reference to the state of connection, not to the distinction in their intrinsic nature. However, from the standpoint of their intrinsic nature, their distinction is indeed evident. Hence it is said, “by way of object, basis, arising, or cessation.” Now, to clearly demonstrate that very distinction in their intrinsic nature through the difference in their domains, it is said, “But for each of these…” “Domain” means the sphere of activity, the domain of mastery, by which the leadership of consciousness and wisdom is spoken of in each respective case.

Kāmañca vipassanāpi paññāvaseneva kiccakārī, maggopi viññāṇasahitova, na kevalo, yathā pana lokiyadhammesu cittaṃ padhānaṃ tatthassa dhorayhabhāvena pavattisabbhāvato. Tathā hi taṃ “chadvārādhipati rājā”ti (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.181) vuccati, evaṃ lokuttaradhammesu paññā padhānā paṭipakkhavidhamanassa visesato tadadhīnattā. Tathā hi maggadhamme sammādiṭṭhi eva paṭhamaṃ gahitā. Ayañca nesaṃ visayavasena pavattibhedo, tathā ca paññāpanavidhi na kevalaṃ thereheva dassito, apica kho bhagavatāpi dassitoti vibhāvento “sammāsambuddhopī”tiādimāha. Yattha paññā na labbhati, tattha cittavasena pucchane vattabbameva natthi yathā “kiṃcitto tvaṃ bhikkhū”tiādīsu (pārā. 132-135). Yattha pana paññā labbhati, tatthāpi cittavasena jotanā hoti yathā – “ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapeti sannisādeti ekodiṃ karoti samādahati (saṃ. ni. 4.332), yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ [M 2.0261][V 2.0242] cittaṃ uppannaṃ hotī”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1). Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana lokiyadhammesu cittavasena, lokuttaradhammesu paññāvasena codanaṃ byatirekamukhena dassetuṃ “katamā te bhikkhu paññā adhigatā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yebhuyyavasena cetaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi katthaci lokiyadhammā paññāsīsenapi niddisīyanti – “paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhino kāmasahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti hānabhāginī paññā”tiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 1.1). Saññāsīsenapi – “uddhumātakasaññāti vā sesarūpārūpasaññāti vā ime dhammā ekatthā, udāhu nānatthā”tiādīsu (pārā. aṭṭha. 45.padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā). Tathā lokuttaradhammāpi katthaci cittasīsena niddisīyanti – “yasmiṃ samaye lokuttaraṃ cittaṃ bhāvetī”ti (dha. sa. 277), tathā phassādisīsenapi – “yasmiṃ samaye lokuttaraṃ phassaṃ bhāveti, vedanaṃ saññaṃ cetanaṃ bhāvetī”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 277).

It is true that insight performs its function by means of wisdom, and the path, too, is accompanied by consciousness, not alone. Just as in worldly phenomena the mind is chief—due to its being the bearer of the burden and the existence of its operation—so too in supramundane phenomena wisdom is chief, because the destruction of opposing factors is especially dependent on it. Thus, it is said: “The mind is the king, the lord of the six doors” (Dhammapada Aṭṭhakathā 2.181). For in the path factors, right view is taken up first. This is the distinction in their operation based on their respective domains. And this method of designation was not only shown by the elders but also by the Blessed One, as he, elucidating, said: “even the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One…” and so on. Where wisdom is not found, there is nothing to be said in a question based on the mind, as in: “What is your state of mind, monk?” (Pārājika 132-135). But where wisdom is found, there is also clarification by way of the mind, as in: “One steadies the mind internally, settles it, unifies it, and concentrates it” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.332), and “At the time when a wholesome sense-sphere mind has arisen…” (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1). In the commentary, however, to show the contrast, the prompting concerning worldly phenomena is by way of the mind, while that concerning supramundane phenomena is by way of wisdom, as in: “What wisdom have you attained, monk?” This should be understood as being stated by way of preponderance. For sometimes, worldly phenomena are also indicated with wisdom as the heading, as in: “For one who has attained the first jhāna, perceptions and thoughts connected with sensuality arise; this is wisdom that partakes of decline” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.1). And with perception as the heading: “Are the perception of a bloated corpse or the remaining perceptions of form and formlessness one in meaning, or different in meaning?” (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 45, Padabhājanīya-vaṇṇanā). Likewise, supramundane phenomena are also sometimes indicated with the mind as the heading, as in: “At the time when one develops a supramundane mind…” (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 277), and also with contact, etc., as the heading: “At the time when one develops supramundane contact, feeling, perception, volition…” (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 277).

Catūsu sotāpattiyaṅgesūti sappurisasevanā, saddhammassavanaṃ, yonisomanasikāro, dhammānudhammapaṭipattīti imesu catūsu sotāpattimaggassa kāraṇesu. Kāmaṃ cetesu satiādayopi dhammā icchitabbāva tehi vinā tesaṃ asambhavato, tathāpi cettha saddhā visesato kiccakārīti veditabbā. Saddo eva hi sappurise payirupāsati, saddhammaṃ suṇāti, yoniso ca manasi karoti, ariyamaggassa ca anudhammaṃ paṭipajjati, tasmā vuttaṃ “ettha saddhindriyaṃ daṭṭhabba”nti. Iminā nayena sesindriyesupi attho daṭṭhabbo. Catūsu sammappadhānesūti catubbidhasammappadhānabhāvanāya. Catūsu satipaṭṭhānesūtiādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca sotāpattiyaṅgesu saddhā viya sammappadhānabhāvanāya vīriyaṃ viya ca satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāya – “satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassa”nti (dī. ni. 2.373; ma. ni. 1.106; saṃ. ni. 5.384, 407) vacanato pubbabhāge kiccato sati adhikā icchitabbā. Evaṃ samādhikammikassa samādhi, “ariyasaccabhāvanā paññābhāvanā”ti katvā tattha paññā pubbabhāge adhikā icchitabbāti pākaṭoyamattho, adhigamakkhaṇe pana samādhipaññānaṃ viya sabbesampi indriyānaṃ saddhādīnaṃ samarasatāva icchitabbā. Tathā hi “ettha saddhindriya”ntiādinā tattha tattha etthaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Evanti yaṃ ṭhānaṃ, taṃ indriyasamattādiṃ paccāmasati. Savisayasmiṃyevāti attano attano visaye [M 2.0262] eva. Lokiyalokuttarā dhammā kathitāti lokiyadhammā lokuttaradhammā ca tena tena pavattivisesena kathitā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – saddhāpañcamesu indriyesu saha pavattamānesu tattha tattha visaye saddhādīnaṃ kiccādhikatāya tassa tasseva daṭṭhabbatā vuttā, na sabbesaṃ. Evaṃ aññepi lokiyalokuttarā dhammā yathāsakaṃ visaye pavattivisesavasena bodhitāti.

In the four factors of stream-entry—associating with good people, listening to the true Dhamma, wise reflection, and practicing the Dhamma in conformity with the Dhamma—these four are the causes for the path of stream-entry. Although other states such as mindfulness are also desirable here, since without them these factors cannot arise, still, in this context, faith is to be understood as being especially active. For it is one with faith who associates with good people, listens to the true Dhamma, reflects wisely, and practices the Dhamma in conformity with the Dhamma. Therefore, it is said, "Here, the faculty of faith should be seen." In the same way, the meaning should be understood for the remaining faculties. In the four right strivings: by the cultivation of the fourfold right striving. The same method applies to the four foundations of mindfulness and so on. Here, just as faith is predominant among the factors of stream-entry, and energy is predominant in the cultivation of right striving, so too in the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness—as stated, "Being mindful, one subdues covetousness and displeasure in the world"—mindfulness is especially desirable in the preliminary stage on account of its function. Similarly, for one practicing concentration, concentration is especially desirable; and since "the development of the noble truths is the development of wisdom," wisdom is especially desirable there in the preliminary stage. This meaning is clear. At the moment of attainment, however, just as with concentration and wisdom, an equal balance of all the faculties, faith and the others, is desirable. For this reason, the taking up of 'here' in each case is done by way of "Here, the faculty of faith," and so on. 'Thus' refers back to that state, the balance of the faculties and so on. 'In their own respective spheres' means in each one's own domain. Worldly and supramundane phenomena are discussed: worldly and supramundane phenomena are explained according to their specific modes of operation. This is what is meant: when the five faculties, beginning with faith, are occurring together, the fact that each one should be seen as predominant in its respective domain is stated because of the predominance of the function of faith and the others, not of all of them. In the same way, other worldly and supramundane phenomena are to be understood according to their respective spheres and specific modes of operation.

Idāni [V 2.0243] saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ tattha tattha atirekakiccataṃ upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatridaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ rājapañcamā sahāyā viya vimuttiparipācakāni pañcindriyāni. Nesaṃ kīḷanatthaṃ ekajjhaṃ vīthiotaraṇaṃ viya indriyānaṃ ekajjhaṃ vipassanāvīthiotaraṇaṃ. Sahāyesu paṭhamādīnaṃ yathāsakageheva vicāraṇā viya saddhādīnaṃ sotāpattiaṅgādīni patvā pubbaṅgamatā. Sahāyesu itaresaṃ tattha tattha tuṇhībhāvo viya sesindriyānaṃ tattha tattha tadanvayatā. Tassa pubbaṅgamabhūtassa indriyassa kiccānugatatā. Na hi tadā tesaṃ sasambhārapathavīādīsu āpādīnaṃ viya kiccaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, saddhādīnaṃyeva pana kiccaṃ vibhūtaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati puretaraṃ tathāpaccayehi cittasantānassa abhisaṅkhatattā. Ettha ca vipassanākammikassa bhāvanā visesato paññuttarāti dassanatthaṃ rājānaṃ nidassanaṃ katvā paññindriyaṃ vuttaṃ. Itītiādi yathādhigatassa atthassa nigamanaṃ.

Now, to illustrate by a simile the predominant function of the faculties of faith and others in various contexts, the passage beginning "Just as..." is stated. Here is the application of the simile: the five faculties that bring liberation to maturity are like a king with his four companions. Their descending together into a street for the purpose of play is like the faculties' descending together into the path of insight. Among the companions, the consultation of the first and others in their own respective homes is like faith and the others taking the lead, having reached the factors of stream-entry and so on. The silence of the other companions in various situations is like the conformity of the remaining faculties in those contexts. There is a following of the function of the faculty that has taken the lead. For at that time, the function of the others is not evident, like that of water and so on on the earth with its constituents. But the function of faith and the others is clearly manifest, standing out beforehand because the mind-stream has been conditioned by such causes. And here, to show that the development of one practicing insight is especially led by wisdom, the faculty of wisdom is mentioned, with the king as the example. The passage beginning "Thus..." is the conclusion of the meaning as it has been understood.

Maggaviññāṇampīti ariyamaggasahagataṃ apacayagāmiviññāṇampi. Tatheva taṃ vijānātīti saccadhammaṃ “idaṃ dukkha”ntiādinā nayeneva vijānāti ekacittuppādapariyāpannattā maggānukūlattā ca. Yaṃ vijānātīti ettha vijānanapajānanāni vipassanācittuppādapariyāpannāni adhippetāni, na “yaṃ pajānātī”ti ettha viya maggacittuppādapariyāpannāti āha “yaṃ saṅkhāragata”ntiādi. Tathevāti “anicca”ntiādinā nayena. Ekacittuppādapariyāpannattā vipassanābhāvato ca samānapaccayehi saha pavattikatā ekuppādatā, tato eva ekajjhaṃ saheva nirujjhanaṃ ekanirodhatā, ekaṃyeva vatthuṃ nissāya pavatti ekavatthukatā, ekaṃyeva ārammaṇaṃ ārabbha pavatti ekārammaṇatā. Hetumhi cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Tena ekuppādāditāya saṃsaṭṭhabhāvaṃ sādheti. Anavasesapariyādānañcetaṃ, ito tīhipi sampayuttalakkhaṇaṃ hotiyeva.

Even path-consciousness: even the consciousness associated with the noble path that leads to the cessation of accumulation. 'It understands it in the same way' means it understands the true nature of things in the manner of 'This is suffering,' etc., because it is included within a single thought-moment and is conducive to the path. Here, by 'what it knows' are meant the acts of knowing and fully understanding included within an insight thought-moment, not, as is the case with 'what it fully understands,' those included within a path thought-moment. Thus, it is said, 'what is conditioned,' etc. 'In the same way' means in the manner of 'impermanent,' etc. Because it is included within a single thought-moment and, due to the development of insight, occurs together with similar conditions, its co-arising is a single arising; for that very reason, its ceasing all at once together is a single cessation; its occurring dependent on a single basis is a single-basisness; its occurring with a single object is a single-objectness. And this is an instrumental expression in the sense of cause. By this, it establishes the state of being conjoined through its single arising, etc. And this is a complete inclusion; from this, the three characteristics of association are indeed present.

Maggapaññaṃ [M 2.0263] sandhāya vuttaṃ, sā hi ekantato bhāvetabbā, na pariññeyyā, paññāya pana bhāvetabbatāya taṃsampayuttadhammāpi taggatikāva hontīti āha “taṃsampayuttaṃ panā”tiādi. Kiñcāpi vipassanāpaññāya bhāvanāvasena pavattanato taṃsampayuttaviññāṇampi tatheva pavattati, tassa pana pariññeyyabhāvānativattanato pariññeyyatā vuttā. Tenevāha – “yampi taṃ dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ, tampi khayadhammaṃ vayadhammaṃ virāgadhammaṃ nirodhadhamma”nti.

This is said with reference to path-wisdom, for that must be exclusively developed, not fully comprehended. However, because wisdom is to be developed, the states associated with it also share that same nature. Hence it is said, "And those associated states, etc." Although the consciousness associated with insight-wisdom also proceeds in the same way, because it proceeds by way of development, its nature of being something to be fully comprehended is stated because it does not transcend the state of being something to be fully comprehended. Therefore it is said: "And that knowledge of the stability of phenomena is also subject to decay, subject to vanishing, subject to dispassion, subject to cessation."

450. Evaṃ santepīti vedanāti evaṃ sāmaññaggahaṇe satipi. Tebhūmikasammasanacāravedanāvāti bhūmittayapariyāpannā, tato eva sammasanañāṇassa gocarabhūtā vedanā eva adhippetā sabrahmacārīnaṃ upakārāvahabhāvena desanāya āraddhattā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “caturoghanittharaṇatthikāna”ntiādi[V 2.0244]. Esa nayo paññāyapi. Idha sukhādisaddā tadārammaṇavisayāti imamatthaṃ suttena sādhetuṃ “rūpañca hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ekantadukkhanti ekanteneva aniṭṭhaṃ, tato eva dukkhamatāya dukkhaṃ. Ārammaṇakaraṇavasena dukkhavedanāya anupatitaṃ, otiṇṇañcāti dukkhānupatitaṃ, dukkhāvakkantaṃ. Sukhena anavakkantaṃ abhavissāti yojanā. Nayidanti ettha idanti nipātamattaṃ. Sārajjeyyunti sārāgaṃ uppādeyyuṃ. Sukhanti sabhāvato ca iṭṭhaṃ. Sārāgā saṃyujjantīti bahalarāgahetu yathārahaṃ dasahipi saṃyojanehi saṃyujjanti. Saṃyogā saṃkilissantīti tathā saṃyuttatāya taṇhāsaṃkilesādivasena saṃkilissanti, vibādhīyanti upatāpīyanti cāti attho. Ārammaṇanti iṭṭhaṃ, aniṭṭhaṃ, majjhattañca ārammaṇaṃ yathākkamaṃ sukhaṃ, dukkhaṃ, adukkhamasukhanti kathitaṃ. Evaṃ avisesena pañcapi khandhe sukhādiārammaṇabhāvena dassetvā idāni vedanā eva sukhādiārammaṇabhāvena dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pākatikapacurajanavasenāyaṃ kathitāti katvā “purimaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā”ti vuttaṃ. Visesalābhī pana anāgatampi sukhaṃ vedanaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoteva. Vuttametaṃ satipaṭṭhānavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.380; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.79). Vedanāya hi ārammaṇaṃ vediyantiyā taṃsamaṅgīpuggalo vedetīti vohāramattaṃ hoti.

450. Even so, etc. (regarding feeling): even when there is such a general apprehension. The feeling that is the range of contemplation pertaining to the three realms: that is, feeling included within the three realms, and thus only the feeling that is the object of contemplation-knowledge is intended here, because the teaching was undertaken for the sake of bringing benefit to fellow practitioners. As it is said, "for those intent on crossing the four floods," and so on. The same method applies to wisdom as well. Here, the terms pleasant, etc., refer to their respective objects; to establish this meaning, the sutta states, "form, etc." Absolutely painful—entirely undesirable, hence painful by its nature as suffering. What is fallen into suffering, invaded by suffering, is that which is associated with painful feeling by way of making it an object, that which has descended into it. The construction is: it would not have been invaded by pleasure. Here, `idaṃ` is merely a particle. They would become lustful—they would generate lust. Pleasant—by nature desirable. Lustful, they become bound—due to abundant lust, they become bound by the ten fetters as appropriate. Being bound, they become defiled—thus, being bound, they become defiled by way of craving, defilements, etc., meaning they are afflicted and tormented. Object—desirable, undesirable, and neutral objects are respectively called pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Having thus shown the five aggregates in general as objects of pleasure, etc., now to show feeling itself as the object of pleasure, etc., it is said, "furthermore," etc. This is spoken by way of ordinary, numerous people, hence it is said, "making a past pleasant feeling the object." But one who gains distinction can also make a future pleasant feeling the object. This is stated in the commentary on the foundations of mindfulness (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.380; Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.79). For when feeling is the object, the person who shares in it feels it—this is merely a conventional expression.

Sabbasaññāyāti sabbāyapi catubhūmikasaññāya. Sabbatthakasaññāyāti sabbasmiṃ cittuppāde pavattanakasaññāya. Vatthe vāti vā-saddena vaṇṇadhātuṃ saṅgaṇhāti[M 2.0264]. Pāpentoti bhāvanaṃ upacāraṃ vā appanaṃ vā upanento. Uppajjanakasaññāpīti “nīlaṃ rūpaṃ, rūpārammaṇaṃ nīla”nti uppajjanakasaññāpi.

All perceptions: this refers to all perceptions, even those associated with the four planes of existence. The perception of being everywhere: this refers to the perception that occurs in every instance of consciousness. In the object, or: by the word 'or', it includes the color element. Leads to: this means bringing about development, or access concentration, or absorption. Even the perception of arising: this refers to perceptions like 'blue form, the object of form is blue,' which are perceptions of arising.

Asabbasaṅgāhikattāti sabbesaṃ vedanāsaññāviññāṇānaṃ asaṅgahitattā. Takkagatanti suttakantanakatakkamhi, suttavattanakatakkamhi vā veṭhanavasena ṭhitaṃ. Parivaṭṭakādigatanti suttaveṭhanaparivaṭṭakādigataṃ. Vissaṭṭhattāva na gahitā, yadaggena paññā viññāṇena saddhiṃ sampayogaṃ labhāpitā, tadaggena vedanāsaññāhipi sampayogaṃ labhāpitā evāti. Tadeva sañjānāti saṃsaṭṭhabhāvato.

Not being included with all: meaning because of not being gathered with all feelings, perceptions, and consciousnesses. Like a spindle: meaning standing in the manner of a wrapping on a spindle for spinning thread or on a spindle for winding thread. Like something belonging to a spool, etc.: meaning like something belonging to a thread-winding spool, etc. Because it is released, it is not grasped; for by whatever point wisdom is made to associate with consciousness, by that very point feelings and perceptions are also made to associate. It cognizes that very thing because of the state of being intermingled.

Sañjānāti vijānātīti ettha “pajānātī”ti padaṃ ānetvā vattabbaṃ pajānanavasenapi visesassa vakkhamānattā. Jānātīti ayaṃ saddo ca laddatoyevettha aviseso, atthato pana visesato icchitabbo. Anekatthattā hi dhātūnaṃ tena ākhyātapadena nāmapadena ca vuttamatthaṃ upasaggapadaṃ jotakabhāvena viseseti, na vācakabhāvena. Tenāha “tassapi jānanatthe viseso veditabbo”ti[V 2.0245]. Etena saññāviññāṇapaññāpadāni antogadhajānanatthe yathāsakaṃ visiṭṭhavisaye ca niṭṭhānīti dasseti. Tenevāha “saññā hī”tiādi. Sañjānanamattamevāti ettha matta-saddena visesanivattiatthena vijānanapajānanākāre nivatteti, eva-saddena kadācipi imissā te visesā natthevāti avadhāreti. Tenevāha “aniccaṃ dukkha”ntiādi. Tattha viññāṇakiccampi kātuṃ asakkontī saññā kuto paññākiccaṃ kareyyāti “lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ pāpetuṃ na sakkoti”cceva vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “maggapātubhāva”nti.

"He perceives, he discerns"—here, the word "comprehends" should be introduced and stated, because the distinction will be explained in terms of comprehension. The word "knows" is indeed found here without distinction, but in meaning, a distinction should be intended. For since roots have multiple meanings, a prefix specifies the meaning expressed by that verb or noun in a clarifying, not a denotative, role. Therefore it is said: "The distinction in its knowing meaning should also be understood." By this it is shown that the terms 'perception,' 'consciousness,' and 'wisdom,' while included within the general meaning of knowing, culminate in their respective distinct domains. Hence it is said: 'For perception,' and so on. 'Merely perceiving only'—here, the word 'merely' (matta) negates the modes of discerning and comprehending by conveying the sense of limitation, and the word 'only' (eva) emphasizes that these distinctions never exist in it. Hence it is said: 'impermanent, suffering,' and so on. There, since perception is incapable of performing even the function of consciousness, how could it perform the function of wisdom? Thus it is said: 'It cannot lead to the penetration of characteristics,' but it is not said: 'It cannot manifest the path.'

Ārammaṇe pavattamānaṃ viññāṇaṃ na saññā viya nīlapītādimattasañjānanavasena pavattati, atha kho tattha aññampi tādisaṃ visesaṃ jānantameva pavattatīti āha “viññāṇa”ntiādi. Kathaṃ pana viññāṇaṃ lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ pāpetīti? Paññāya dassitamaggena. Lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāya hi anekavāraṃ lakkhaṇāni paṭivijjhitvā pavattamānāya paguṇabhāvato paricayavasena ñāṇavippayuttacittenapi vipassanā sambhavati, yathā taṃ paguṇassa ganthassa ajjhayane tattha tattha gatāpi vārā [M 2.0265] na upadhārīyanti. “Lakkhaṇapaṭivedha”nti ca lakkhaṇānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇamattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na paṭivijjhanaṃ. Ussakkitvāti udayabbayañāṇādiñāṇapaṭipāṭiyā ārabhitvā. Maggapātubhāvaṃ pāpetuṃ na sakkoti asambodhasabhāvattā. Ārammaṇampi sañjānāti avabujjhanavaseneva, na sañjānanamattena. Tathā lakkhaṇapaṭivedhampi pāpeti, na vijānanamattena, attano pana aññāsādhāraṇena ānubhāvena ussakkitvā maggapātubhāvampi pāpeti.

Consciousness, when occurring in an object, does not function like perception, which operates merely by recognizing blue, yellow, and so on. Rather, it functions by knowing some other such distinction in that very object. Thus it is said: 'Consciousness,' and so on. But how does consciousness lead to the penetration of characteristics? Through the path shown by wisdom. For insight, when it occurs, having repeatedly penetrated the characteristics through insight focused on characteristics as objects, becomes familiar through repeated practice. Even with a mind dissociated from knowledge, insight can arise, just as in the case of one who has mastered a text, the passages gone over are not consciously noted at every point during recitation. 'Penetration of characteristics' is said with reference merely to making the characteristics the object, not to their actual penetration. 'Ussakkitvā' (having striven) means having begun with the sequence of knowledges such as the knowledge of arising and passing away. It cannot bring about the manifestation of the path due to its nature of not being fully awakened. It also perceives the object only in the manner of understanding, not merely by perception. Similarly, it leads to the penetration of characteristics, not merely by discerning, but by striving through its own unique power, which is not shared by others, and thus brings about the manifestation of the path.

Idāni yathāvuttamatthaṃ upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ajātabuddhīti asañjātabyavahārabuddhi. Upabhogaparibhoganti upabhogaparibhogārahaṃ, upabhogaparibhogavatthūnaṃ paṭilābhayogganti attho. Kūṭoti kahāpaṇapatirūpako tambakaṃsādimayo. Chekoti mahāsāro. Karatoti aḍḍhasāro. Saṇhoti mudujātiko samasāro. Iti-saddo ādiattho. Tena pādasāraparopādasāraaḍḍhasārādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Jānanto ca pana naṃ rūpaṃ disvāpi…pe… asukācariyena katotipi jānāti tathā heraññikaganthassa suggahitattā. Evamevantiādi upamāsaṃsandanaṃ. Saññāvibhāgaṃ akatvā piṇḍavaseneva ārammaṇassa gahaṇato dārakassa kahāpaṇadassanasadisā vuttā. Tathā hi sā yathāupaṭṭhitavisayapadaṭṭhānā vuccati. Viññāṇaṃ ārammaṇe ekaccavisesaggahaṇasamatthabhāvato gāmikapurisakahāpaṇadassanasadisaṃ vuttaṃ. Paññā pana ārammaṇe anavasesāvabodhato heraññikakahāpaṇadassanasadisā vuttā. Nesanti saññāviññāṇapaññānaṃ[V 2.0246]. Visesoti sabhāvaviseso. Duppaṭivijjho pakatipaññāya. Imināva nesaṃ accantasukhumataṃ dasseti.

Now, to clarify the meaning as previously stated, it is said: 'Just as,' and so on, by way of simile. Here, 'ajātabuddhī' means a mind with undeveloped practical discernment. 'Upabhogaparibhoganti' means 'worthy of enjoyment and use'; the meaning is 'suitable for acquiring objects of enjoyment and use'. 'Kūṭo' means a counterfeit coin made of copper, bronze, etc. 'Cheko' means of great substance. 'Karato' means of half substance. 'Saṇho' means of soft nature, of uniform substance. The word 'iti' has the meaning of 'etcetera'. By this, the inclusion of those of quarter substance, more than quarter substance, half substance, and so on, is to be understood. 'Jānanto ca pana naṃ rūpaṃ disvāpi…pe… asukācariyena katotipi jānāti tathā heraññikaganthassa suggahitattā' means that even upon seeing its appearance, one knows it was made by a certain craftsman, because the goldsmith's treatise has been thoroughly mastered. 'Evamevanti' and so on, is the connection of the simile. Without making a distinction, perception is said to be like a child seeing a coin, due to its grasping the object as a whole. For it is said to have the immediately presented object as its proximate cause. Consciousness is said to be like a villager seeing a coin, due to its ability to grasp certain distinctions in the object. Wisdom, however, is said to be like a goldsmith examining a coin, due to its comprehension of the object without residue. 'Nesaṃ' (of these) refers to perception, consciousness, and wisdom. 'Viseso' (distinction) means a distinction in their nature. 'Duppaṭivijjho' (difficult to penetrate) means difficult to penetrate with ordinary wisdom. By this, their extreme subtlety is shown.

Ekārammaṇe pavattamānānanti ekasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe pavattamānānaṃ. Tena abhinnavisayābhinnakālatādassanena avinibbhogavuttitaṃ vibhāvento duppaṭivijjhataṃyeva ulliṅgeti. Vavatthānanti asaṅkarato ṭhapanaṃ. Ayaṃ phasso…pe… idaṃ cittanti nidassanamattametaṃ. Iti-saddo vā ādiattho. Tena sesadhammānampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Idanti arūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ vavatthānakaraṇaṃ. Tatoti yaṃ vuttaṃ tilatelādiuddharaṇaṃ, tato. Yadi dukkarataraṃ, kathaṃ tanti āha “bhagavā panā”tiādi.

'Ekārammaṇe pavattamānānaṃ' (occurring on a single object) means 'occurring on one and the same object'. By showing their inseparability and non-distinction in object and time, he highlights their difficulty of penetration. 'Vavatthānaṃ' (distinction) means establishing without confusion. 'Ayaṃ phasso…pe… idaṃ cittaṃ' (this is contact…this is consciousness) is merely an indication. Or the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'etcetera'. By this, the inclusion of the remaining phenomena should also be understood. 'Idaṃ' (this) refers to the distinguishing of formless phenomena. 'Tato' (from that) refers to what was said about extracting oil from sesame seeds, etc. If it is so very difficult, how then? He said: 'But the Blessed One,' and so on.

451. Nissaṭenāti [M 2.0266] nikkhantena ataṃsambandhena. Pariccattenāti pariccattasadisena paccayabhāvānupagamanena paccayuppannasambandhābhāvato. Nissakkavacanaṃ apādānadīpanato. Karaṇavacanaṃ kattuatthadīpanato. Kāmāvacaramanoviññāṇaṃ na niyamato “idaṃ nāma pañcadvārikāsambandhā”ti sakkā vattuṃ, rūpāvacaraviññāṇaṃ pana na tathāti, tasseva pañcahi indriyehi nissaṭatā vuttāti āha “rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānacittenā”ti. Catutthajjhānaggahaṇaṃ tasseva arūpāvacarassa padaṭṭhānabhāvato. Parisuddhenāti visesato asaṃkilesikattāva. Tañhi vigatūpakkilesatāya visesato parisuddhaṃ. Tenāha “nirupakkilesenā”ti. Jānitabbaṃ neyyaṃ, saparasantānesu idaṃ atisayaṃ jānitabbato bujjhitabbaṃ bodhetabbaṃ vāti attho. Neyyanti vā attano santāne netabbaṃ pavattetabbanti attho. Tenāha “nibbattetuṃ sakkā hoti. Ettha ṭhitassa hi sā ijjhatī”ti. Pāṭiyekkanti visuṃ visuṃ, anupadadhammavasenāti attho. Abhinivesābhāvatoti vipassanābhinivesassa asambhavato. Kalāpato nayatoti kalāpasammasanasaṅkhātato nayavipassanato. Bhikkhunoti sāvakassa. Sāvakasseva hi tatra anupadadhammavipassanā na sambhavati, na satthu. Tenāha “tasmā”tiādi. Vissajjesīti tappaṭibaddhachandarāgappahānena pajahati.

451. 'Nissaṭena' (detached) means departed, without connection to that. 'Pariccattena' (relinquished) means like something relinquished, due to not taking on the state of a condition and thus being without a relationship to what is conditionally arisen. 'Nissakkavacanaṃ' (the word for 'detached') indicates the source. 'Karaṇavacanaṃ' (the instrumental case) indicates the meaning of the agent. Sense-sphere mind-consciousness cannot be definitively said: 'This is related to the five sense-doors,' but form-sphere consciousness is not so; therefore, its detachment from the five faculties is stated. Thus it is said: 'with the fourth-jhāna form-sphere consciousness.' The mention of the fourth jhāna is because it serves as the proximate cause for the formless sphere. 'Parisuddhena' (pure) means especially pure due to being unpolluted. For it is especially pure because it is free from defilements. Hence it is said: 'free from defilements.' It should be known as 'neyyaṃ' (what is to be known); the meaning is that it is to be known, awakened, or enlightened especially in one's own and others' continuities. Alternatively, 'neyyaṃ' means it should be led forth or established in one's own continuity. Hence it is said: 'It can be produced. For one established in this, it succeeds.' 'Pāṭiyekkaṃ' (individually) means 'separately, separately,' the meaning is 'in terms of successive phenomena'. 'Abhinivesābhāvato' (due to the absence of adherence) means due to the impossibility of adherence to insight. 'Kalāpato nayato' (by the method of aggregates) means by the method of insight known as the comprehension of aggregates. 'Bhikkhuno' (for a bhikkhu) refers to a disciple. For it is only for the disciple that insight into successive phenomena is not possible there, not for the Teacher. Hence it is said: 'Therefore,' and so on. 'Vissajjesi' (he relinquished) means he abandons by giving up the desire and lust connected to it.

Hatthagatattāti hatthagatasadisattā, āsannattāti attho. Yadā hi lokanātho bodhimūle aparājitapallaṅke nisinno – “kicchaṃ vatāyaṃ loko āpanno”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.57; saṃ. ni. 2.4, 10) paṭiccasamuppādamukhena vipassanābhinivesaṃ katvā adhigantabbasabbaññutaññāṇānurūpaṃ chattiṃsakoṭisahassamukhena mahāvajirañāṇaṃ nāma mahābodhisattasammasanaṃ pavattento anekākārasamāpattidhammasammasane anupadameva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanadhammepi [V 2.0247] aparāparaṃ sammasi. Tenāha “bhagavā panā”tiādi. Paropaññāsāti dvepaññāsaṃ. Kāmañcettha keci dhammā vedanādayo phassapañcamakādīsu vuttāpi jhānakoṭṭhāsādīsupi saṅgahitā, taṃtaṃpaccayabhāvavisiṭṭhena pana atthavisesena dhammantarāni viya hontīti evaṃ vuttaṃ. Tathā hi lokuttaracittuppādesu navindriyatā vuccati. Aṅguddhārenāti tattha labbhamānajhānaṅgabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgānaṃ uddharaṇena. Aṅga-saddo [M 2.0267] vā koṭṭhāsapariyāyo, tasmā aṅguddhārenāti phassapañcamakādikoṭṭhāsānaṃ samuddharaṇena. Yāvatā saññāsamāpattiyoti yattakā saññāsahagatā jhānasamāpattiyo, tāhi vuṭṭhāya adhigandhabbattā tāvatikā veneyyānaṃ aññāpaṭivedho arahattasamadhigamo.

'Hatthagatattā' (because it is in hand) means 'like being in hand'; the meaning is 'because it is near'. For when the Lord of the World was seated on the unconquered seat at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having directed insight through the doorway of dependent origination, beginning with 'Alas, this world has fallen into difficulty' (Dī. Ni. 2.57; Saṃ. Ni. 2.4, 10), and setting in motion the great diamond knowledge called the great bodhisatta-comprehension, which corresponds to the omniscient knowledge to be attained through thirty-six thousand koṭis of doorways, he comprehended in immediate succession, among the many kinds of meditative attainments, even the phenomena of the neither-perception-nor-non-perception attainment, again and again. Hence it is said: 'But the Blessed One,' and so on. 'Paropaññāsa' (over fifty) means fifty-two. Although some phenomena here, such as feelings, etc., are mentioned among the fivefold contact, etc., and are also included in the sections on jhāna, etc., yet due to the distinct nature of their conditional relationships, they become as if they were different phenomena. Thus it is said. Indeed, in the arising of supramundane consciousness, nine faculties are spoken of. 'Aṅguddhārena' (by extracting the factors) means by extracting the jhāna factors, enlightenment factors, and path factors obtainable there. Or the word 'aṅga' is a synonym for 'section'; therefore, 'aṅguddhārena' means by collecting the sections such as the fivefold contact, etc. 'Yāvatā saññāsamāpattiyo' (as far as the attainments of perception) means as many jhāna attainments as are accompanied by perception.
