"Drink the gruel" means one should be dismissed, the intention being that they are incapable of a Dhamma discussion.

463. Puññābhisaṅkhārādīsūti ādi-saddena kāyasañcetanādi lakkhaṇe kāyasaṅkhārādikepi saṅgaṇhāti, na apuññāneñjābhisaṅkhāre eva. Kāyapaṭibaddhattā kāyena saṅkharīyati, na kāyasamuṭṭhānattā. Cittasamuṭṭhānā hi te dhammāti. Nibbattīyatīti ca idaṃ kāye sati sabbhāvaṃ[V 2.0262], asati ca abhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Vācanti vacīghosaṃ. Saṅkharotīti janeti. Tenāha “nibbattetī”ti. Na hi taṃ vitakkavicārarahitacittaṃ vacīghosaṃ nibbattetuṃ sakkoti. Cittapaṭibaddhattāti etena cittassa nissayādipaccayabhāvo cittasaṅkhārasaṅkharaṇanti dasseti. Aññamaññamissāti atthato bhinnāpi kāyasaṅkhārādivacanavacanīyabhāvena aññamaññamissitā abhinnā viya, tato eva āluḷitā saṃkiṇṇā avibhūtā apākaṭā duddīpanā duviññāpayā. Ādānaggahaṇamuñcanacopanānīti yassa kassaci kāyena ādātabbassa ādānasaṅkhātaṃ gahaṇaṃ, vissajjanasaṅkhātaṃ muñcanaṃ, yathātathācalanasaṅkhātaṃ copananti imāni pāpetvā sādhetvā uppannā. Kāyato pavattā saṅkhārā, kāyena saṅkharīyantīti ca kāyasaṅkhārātveva vuccanti. Hanusaṃcopananti hanusañcalanaṃ. Vacībhedanti vācānicchāraṇaṃ. Vācaṃ saṅkharontīti katvā idha vacīsaṅkhārātveva vuccanti.

463. In "meritorious formations, etc.," the word "etc." also includes bodily formations and so on, which have the characteristic of bodily volition and so on; it does not refer only to demeritorious and imperturbable formations. Because it is connected to the body, it is formed by the body, not because it originates from the body, for these phenomena are mind-originated. And "is produced" is said with reference to its existence when the body is present and its non-existence when it is not. "Speech" means vocal sound. "Forms" means generates; hence, it is said, "produces." For a mind devoid of initial and sustained thought cannot produce vocal sound. "Because it is connected to the mind"—by this it is shown that the mind's being a support condition and so on is the forming of mental formations. "Mutually mixed" means that although distinct in meaning, bodily formations and so on, by way of being the word and the thing meant, are mutually mixed as if they were not distinct; for that very reason they are agitated, confused, indistinct, not manifest, difficult to illuminate, and difficult to make understood. "Taking, seizing, releasing, and moving" means the seizing called 'taking,' the releasing called 'letting go,' and the moving called 'moving as is appropriate' of whatever is to be taken by the body—these arise having been brought about and accomplished. Formations that proceed from the body and are formed by the body are called "bodily formations." "Jaw movement" means the motion of the jaw. "Uttering speech" means the emission of speech. Because they form speech, they are here called "verbal formations."

464. Samāpajjissanti [M 2.0284] padaṃ nirodhassa āsannānāgatabhāvavisayaṃ āsannaṃ vajjetvā dūrassa gahaṇe payojanābhāvato. Nirodhapādakassa nevasaññānāsaññāyatanacittassa ca gahaṇato paṭṭhāya nirodhaṃ samāpajjati nāmāti adhippāyena “padadvayena nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattikālo kathito”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā cittaṃ bhāvitaṃ hotīti ettha addhānaparicchedacittaggahaṇaṃ itaresaṃ nānantariyabhāvato. Na hi baladvayañāṇasamādhicariyānaṃ vasībhāvāpādanacittehi vinā addhānaparicchedacittaṃ acittakabhāvāya hoti.

464. The word "will attain" refers to the near future state of cessation, since there is no purpose in taking what is distant while excluding what is near. It is with the intention that one is said to "attain cessation" starting from the taking up of the mind of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is the foundation for cessation, that it is said, "By the two words, the time of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is described." Similarly, in "the mind is so developed," here the mind that determines the duration is taken, because the others are not immediately preceding. For without the minds that bring about mastery in the two powers—the practice of knowledge and concentration—the mind that determines the duration does not lead to the mindless state.

Sesasaṅkhārehīti kāyasaṅkhāracittasaṅkhārehi. Dutiyajjhāneyeva nirujjhati anuppattinirodhena. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Vuṭṭhahissanti padaṃ vuṭṭhahanassa āsannānāgatabhāvavisayaṃ āsannaṃ vajjetvā dūrassa gahaṇe payojanābhāvato. Nirodhato vuṭṭhānassa ca cittuppādena paricchinnattā tato oramevāti āha “padadvayena antonirodhakālo kathito”ti. Tathā cittaṃ bhāvitaṃ hotīti yathā yathāparicchinnakālameva acittakabhāvo, tato paraṃ sacittakabhāvo hoti, tathā nirodhassa parikammacittaṃ uppāditaṃ hoti.

"By the remaining formations" means by the bodily and mental formations. In the second jhāna itself, it ceases with a cessation of non-arising. This same principle applies in the other cases as well. The word "will emerge" refers to the near future state of emerging, since there is no purpose in taking what is distant while excluding what is near. And because emergence from cessation is defined by the arising of a mind, it refers only to the time prior to that; thus it is said, "By the two words, the time within cessation is described." "The mind is so developed" means that the preparatory mind for cessation is produced in such a way that the mindless state lasts for a precisely defined time, after which the state with a mind occurs.

Paṭisaṅkhāti paṭisaṅkhāya idameva kātabbaṃ jānitvā appavattimattaṃ. Samāpajjantīti acittakabhāvaṃ sampadeva āpajjanti. Atha kasmā sattāhameva samāpajjantīti? Yathākālaparicchedakaraṇato, tañca yebhuyyena āhārūpajīvīnaṃ sattānaṃ upādinnakapavattassa ekadivasaṃ bhuttāhārassa sattāhameva yāpanato.

"Reflecting" means, having reflected and known that just this is to be done, it is mere non-occurrence. "They attain" means they truly attain the mindless state. But why do they attain it for only seven days? Because of the determination of a time limit; and this is because, for most beings who subsist on food, the sustenance for the continuity of the appropriated body from a single day's meal lasts for seven days.

Sabbā [V 2.0263] phalasamāpatti assāsapassāse na samuṭṭhāpetīti idaṃ natthīti āha “samuṭṭhāpetī”ti. Yā pana na samuṭṭhāpeti, taṃ dassento “imassa pana…pe… na samuṭṭhāpetī”ti āha. Tattha imassāti idha pāḷiyaṃ vuttanirodhasamāpajjanabhikkhuno. Tassa pana phalasamāpatti catutthajjhānikāvāti niyamo natthīti āha “kiṃ vā etenā”tiādi. Abbohārikāti sukhumattabhāvappattiyā “atthī”ti voharituṃ asakkuṇeyyāti keci. Nirodhassa pana pādakabhūtāya catutthajjhānādisamādhicariyāya vasena acatutthajjhānikāpi nirodhānantaraphalasamāpatti assāsapassāse [M 2.0285] na samuṭṭhāpetīti abhāvato eva te abbohārikā vuttā. Evañca katvā sañjīvattheravatthumhi ānītasamāpattiphalanidassanampi suṭṭhu upapajjati. Tenāha “bhavaṅgasamayenevetaṃ kathita”nti. Kiriyamayapavattavaḷañjanakāleti ettha kiriyamayapavattaṃ kāyavacīviññattivipphāro, tassa vaḷañjanakāle pavattanasamaye. Vācaṃ abhisaṅkhātuṃ na sakkonti aviññattijanakattā tesaṃ vitakkavicārānaṃ.

All fruition attainments do not produce in-and-out breathing—this is refuted by saying, 'they do produce.' But as to what does not produce it, this is shown by saying, 'However, for this… it does not produce.' Herein, 'for this' refers to the monk mentioned in the Pāli who is attaining cessation. However, there is no fixed rule that his fruition attainment must be of the fourth jhāna, hence it is said, 'What of that?' and so on. Some say it is 'inexpressible' because, having attained a subtle state, one is unable to express it as 'it exists.' But since, by means of the practice of concentration such as the fourth jhāna which is the basis for the attainment of cessation, even the fruition attainment immediately following cessation, which is not of the fourth jhāna, does not produce in-and-out breathing, for this very reason they are called 'inexpressible.' And this being the case, the illustration of the fruition of attainment brought about in the story of the Elder Sañjīva is also very fitting. Therefore, it is said, 'This was spoken of in terms of the life-continuum.' As for the phrase 'at the time of the employment of functional activity,' here 'functional activity' is the manifestation of bodily and verbal intimation; 'at the time of its employment' means at the time of its occurrence. They are unable to form speech because their thought and examination do not generate intimation.

Saguṇenāti sarasena, sabhāvenāti attho. Suññatā nāma phalasamāpatti rāgādīhi suññattā. Tathā rāganimittādīnaṃ abhāvā animittā, rāgapaṇidhiādīnaṃ abhāvā appaṇihitāti āha “animittaappaṇihitesupi eseva nayo”ti. Animittaṃ appaṇihitañca nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannaphalasamāpattiyaṃ phasso animitto phasso appaṇihito phasso nāmāti imamatthaṃ “eseva nayo”ti iminā atidisati.

'With its quality' means with its essence; the meaning is, by its own nature. The fruition attainment is named 'emptiness' because it is empty of lust and so on. Similarly, because of the absence of the sign of lust and so on, it is 'signless'; and because of the absence of the aspiration for lust and so on, it is 'undirected'—thus it is said, 'The same principle applies also to the signless and the undirected.' In the fruition attainment that has arisen having taken the signless and undirected Nibbāna as its object, contact is called 'signless contact' and 'undirected contact'—this meaning is indicated by the phrase 'this is the same principle.'

Attasuññatādassanato anattānupassanā suññatā, niccanimittugghāṭanato aniccānupassanā animittā, sukhappaṇidhipaṭikkhepato dukkhānupassanā appaṇihitāti āha – “suññatā…pe… vipassanāpi vuccatī”ti. Aniccato vuṭṭhātīti saṅkhārānaṃ aniccākāraggāhiniyā vuṭṭhānagāminiyā parato ekatovuṭṭhānaubhatovuṭṭhānehi nimittapavattato vuṭṭhāti. Aniccato pariggahetvāti ca idaṃ “na ekantikaṃ evampi hotī”ti katvā vuttaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Appaṇihitavipassanāya maggotiādinā, suññatavipassanāya maggotiādinā ca yojanaṃ sandhāyāha “eseva nayo”ti. Vikappo āpajjeyya āgamanassa vavatthānassa abhāvena avavatthānakarattā. Evañhi tayo phassā phusantīti evaṃ saguṇato ārammaṇato ca nāmalābhe suññatādināmakā tayo phassā phusantīti aniyamavacanaṃ. Sameti yujjati ekasseva phassassa nāmattayayogato.

'From seeing the emptiness of self, the contemplation of not-self is emptiness. From uprooting the sign of permanence, the contemplation of impermanence is signless. From rejecting the aspiration for happiness, the contemplation of suffering is undirected'—thus it is said: ‘Emptiness… and so on… insight is also called.’ 'One emerges from impermanence' means that by means of the insight leading to emergence, which grasps the impermanent aspect of formations, one emerges from the occurrence of the sign, whether by emerging from one or emerging from both. And 'having comprehended it as impermanent'—this is stated considering, ‘It is not exclusively so.’ The same principle applies to the rest. Referring to the connection with 'the path of undirected insight,' and so on, and with 'the path of emptiness insight,' and so on, it is said, ‘This is the same principle.’ A doubt might arise, since it would be indeterminate due to the absence of a determination of its source. For thus, the statement 'three contacts make contact' is an indefinite statement, as the three contacts named emptiness and so on acquire their names from their qualities and objects. It is reconciled—it is fitting, due to a single contact being connected with three names.

Sabbasaṅkhatavivittatāya [V 2.0264] nibbānaṃ viveko nāma upadhivivekoti katvā. Ninnatā tappaṭipakkhavimukhassa tadabhimukhatā. Poṇatā onamanaṃ, pabbhāratā tato vissaṭṭhabhāvo.

Nibbāna is called seclusion due to its complete detachment from all conditioned things, meaning seclusion from the substrata of existence. Inclination (ninnatā) is the turning away from what opposes it and the facing towards it. Inclination (poṇatā) is bending, and sloping (pabbhāratā) is the state of being released from that.

465. Cakkhādito rūpādīsu pavattarūpakāyato uppajjanato pañcadvārikaṃ sukhaṃ kāyikaṃ nāma, manodvārikaṃ cetophassajātāya cetasikaṃ [M 2.0286] nāma. Sabhāvaniddeso sukhayatīti katvā. Madhurabhāvadīpakanti iṭṭhabhāvajotanaṃ. Vedayitabhāvadīpakanti vedakabhāvavibhāvakaṃ. Vedanā eva hi paramatthato ārammaṇaṃ vedeti, ārammaṇaṃ pana veditabbanti. Dukkhanti sabhāvaniddesotievamādiatthavacanaṃ sandhāyāha “eseva nayo”ti. Ṭhitisukhāti ṭhitiyā dharamānatāya sukhā, na ṭhitikkhaṇamattena. Tenāha “atthibhāvo sukha”nti. Vipariṇāmadukkhāti vipariṇamanena vigamanena dukkhā, na nirodhakkhaṇena. Tenāha “natthibhāvo dukkha”nti. Apariññātavatthukānañhi sukhavedanuparamo dukkhato upaṭṭhāti. Svāyamattho piyavippayogena dīpetabbo. Ṭhitidukkhā vipariṇāmasukhāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tenāha “atthibhāvo dukkhaṃ, natthibhāvo sukha”nti. Dukkhavedanuparamo hi sattānaṃ sukhato upaṭṭhāti. Evañhi vadanti – “tassa rogassa vūpasamena aho sukhaṃ jāta”nti. Jānanabhāvoti yāthāvasabhāvato avabujjhanaṃ. Adukkhamasukhañhi vedanaṃ jānantassa sukhaṃ hoti tassa sukhumabhāvato, yathā tadaññe dhamme salakkhaṇato sāmaññalakkhaṇato ca sammadeva avabodho paramaṃ sukhaṃ. Tenevāha –

465. Pleasure at the five doors, arising from the physical body which is engaged with forms and so on through the eye and so on, is called 'bodily'; that at the mind door, born of mental contact, is called 'mental.' The exposition of its intrinsic nature is because it brings happiness. 'Illuminating sweetness' means making manifest the agreeable nature. 'Illuminating the state of being felt' means clarifying the nature of experiencing. For in the ultimate sense, it is feeling that experiences the object, while the object is what is to be experienced. As for suffering, referring to the statement 'this is the exposition of its intrinsic nature' and so on, it is said, 'The same principle applies.' 'Happiness in stability' means happiness due to its duration, not merely by the moment of its presence. Therefore it is said, 'Existence is happiness.' 'Suffering in change' means suffering due to alteration and disappearance, not by the moment of its cessation. Therefore it is said, 'Non-existence is suffering.' For those who have not fully understood the underlying reality, the cessation of pleasant feeling appears as suffering. This meaning should be illustrated by separation from the beloved. 'Suffering in stability and happiness in change'—here too, the same principle applies. Therefore it is said, 'Existence is suffering, non-existence is happiness.' For beings, the cessation of painful feeling appears as happiness. Thus they say, 'With the calming of that illness, oh, what happiness has arisen!' 'The state of knowing' means understanding according to its actual nature. For one who knows neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, there is happiness due to its subtlety, just as the right comprehension of other phenomena by their specific and general characteristics is the highest happiness. Therefore it is said—

“Yato yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhatī pītipāmojjaṃ, amataṃ taṃ vijānata”nti. (dha. pa. 374);

"Whenever one discerns the rise and fall of the aggregates, one obtains joy and delight. That is the deathless for the discerning."

Ajānanabhāvoti ettha vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo. Dukkhañhi sammohavihāroti. Aparo nayo jānanabhāvoti jānanassa ñāṇassa sabbhāvo. Ñāṇasampayuttā hi ñāṇopanissayā ca adukkhamasukhā vedanā sukhā iṭṭhākārā. Yathāha “iṭṭhā ceva iṭṭhaphalā cā”ti. Ajānanabhāvo dukkhanti ettha vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo.

As for 'the state of not knowing,' here the meaning should be understood in the opposite sense of what was said. For abiding in delusion is indeed suffering. Another explanation: 'the state of knowing' is the very existence of knowing, of wisdom. For neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings that are associated with wisdom and have wisdom as their support are pleasant and of a desirable nature. As it is said: 'They are desirable and bear desirable fruit.' As for 'the state of not knowing is suffering,' here the meaning should be understood in the opposite sense of what was said.

Katamo anusayo anusetīti kāmarāgānusayādīsu sattasu anusayesu katamo anusayo anusayavasena pavattati? Appahīnabhāvena hi santāne anusayantīti anusayā, anurūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ labhitvā uppajjantīti attho. Etena kāraṇalābhe sati uppajjanārahatā nesaṃ dassitā. Appahīnā hi kilesā kāraṇalābhe sati uppajjanti. Tenāha “appahīnaṭṭhena sayito viya hotī”ti. Te ca nippariyāyato [M 2.0287] anāgatā kilesā daṭṭhabbā, atītā paccuppannā [V 2.0265] ca taṃsabhāvattā tathā vuccanti. Na hi dhammānaṃ kālabhedena sabhāvabhedo atthi. Yadi appahīnaṭṭho anusayaṭṭho, nanu sabbepi kilesā appahīnā anusayā bhaveyyunti? Na mayaṃ appahīnatāmattena anusayaṭṭhaṃ vadāma, atha kho pana appahīnaṭṭhena thāmagatā kilesā anusayā. Idaṃ thāmagamanañca rāgādīnameva āveṇiko sabhāvo daṭṭhabbo, yato abhidhamme – “thāmagataṃ anusayaṃ pajahatī”ti vuttaṃ. Soti rāgānusayo. Appahīnoti appahīnabhāvamukhena anusayanaṭṭhamāha. So ca apariññātakkhandhavatthuto, pariññātesu patiṭṭhaṃ na labhati. Tenāha “na sabbāya sukhāya vedanāya so appahīno”ti. Ārammaṇavasena cāyaṃ anusayaṭṭho adhippeto. Tenāha “na sabbaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ ārabbha uppajjatīti attho”ti.

'Which latent tendency lies dormant?' means: among the seven latent tendencies, such as the latent tendency of sensual lust, which latent tendency operates by way of a latent tendency? They are called 'latent tendencies' because they lie dormant in the continuum due to not being abandoned; the meaning is that they arise when they obtain a suitable cause. By this, their potential to arise when a cause is obtained is shown. For unabandoned defilements arise when a cause is obtained. Therefore, it is said: 'It lies as if dormant in the sense of not being abandoned.' And these should be understood as future defilements in the strict sense, while past and present ones are called so because of having that same nature. For there is no difference in the intrinsic nature of phenomena based on temporal divisions. If the state of not being abandoned is the meaning of a latent tendency, would not all unabandoned defilements be latent tendencies? We do not say that the mere state of not being abandoned is the meaning of a latent tendency, but rather that defilements which have become strong due to not being abandoned are latent tendencies. And this becoming strong should be seen as the exclusive nature of lust and the like, since in the Abhidhamma it is said: 'One abandons the firmly established latent tendency.' That is, the latent tendency of lust. 'Not abandoned' states the meaning of lying dormant through the mode of not being abandoned. And that is due to the aggregates as basis not being fully understood; it does not find a footing in what has been fully understood. Therefore, it is said: 'It is not abandoned in relation to all pleasant feeling.' And this meaning of a latent tendency is intended in terms of the object. Hence, it is said, the meaning is: 'It does not arise in relation to all pleasant feeling.'

Vatthuvasenapi pana anusayaṭṭho veditabbo, yo “bhūmiladdha”nti vuccati. Tena hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (visuddhi. 2.834) vuttaṃ –

Moreover, the meaning of an underlying tendency should also be understood by way of the basis, which is called 'ground-obtained.' Therefore, it is said in the commentary (Visuddhimagga 2.834):

“Bhūmīti vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā tebhūmakā pañcakkhandhā. Bhūmiladdhaṃ nāma tesu khandhesu uppattirahaṃ kilesajātaṃ. Tena hi sā bhūmiladdhā nāma hoti, tasmā bhūmiladdhanti vuccati, sā ca kho na ārammaṇavasena. Ārammaṇavasena hi sabbepi atītānāgate pariññātepi ca khīṇāsavānaṃ khandhe ārabbha kilesā uppajjanti mahākaccānauppalavaṇṇādīnaṃ khandhe ārabbha soreyyaseṭṭhinandamāṇavakādīnaṃ viya. Yadi ca taṃ bhūmiladdhaṃ nāma siyā, tassa appaheyyato na koci bhavamūlaṃ pajaheyya, vatthuvasena pana bhūmiladdhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yattha yattha hi vipassanāya apariññātā khandhā uppajjanti, tattha tattha uppādato pabhuti tesu vaṭṭamūlaṃ kilesajātaṃ anuseti. Taṃ appahīnaṭṭhena bhūmiladdhanti veditabba”ntiādi.

“‘Ground’ refers to the five aggregates of the three realms, which serve as the object of insight. ‘Ground-obtained’ means the class of defilements fit to arise in those aggregates. For that reason, it is called ‘ground-obtained’; thus it is called ‘ground-obtained,’ but this is not in terms of the object. For in terms of the object, defilements arise in relation to all past and future aggregates, and even the fully understood aggregates of arahants, just as they arose in relation to the aggregates of Mahākaccāna, Uppalavaṇṇā, and others for Soreyya the merchant, Nanda the youth, and others. If that were called ‘ground-obtained,’ then no one would abandon the root of existence due to its unabandonability. Rather, ‘ground-obtained’ should be understood by way of the basis. For wherever aggregates not fully understood by insight arise, from the moment of their arising, the class of defilements, which is the root of the round of existence, lies latent in them. That should be understood as ‘ground-obtained’ in the sense of not being abandoned,” and so on.

Esa nayo sabbatthāti iminā “na sabbāya dukkhāya vedanāya so appahīno, na sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ ārabbha uppajjatī”tiādiṃ atidisati. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. “Yo anusayo yattha anuseti[M 2.0288], so pahīyamāno tattha pahīno nāma hotī”ti tattha tattha pahānapucchā, taṃ sandhāyāha “kiṃ pahātabbanti ayaṃ pahānapucchā nāmā”ti.

By 'This is the method in all cases,' he extends the principle to such statements as: 'It is not unabandoned with respect to every painful feeling, nor does it arise in relation to every painful feeling,' and so on. Here, what should be said is to be understood in the same way as has been stated. 'Whatever underlying tendency lies latent, wherever it lies latent, when it is being abandoned, it is called “abandoned” there'—this is the question of abandonment in each case. Referring to this, he says: '“What is to be abandoned?”—this is called the question of abandonment.'

Ekeneva byākaraṇenāti “idhāvuso, visākha, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.374) ekeneva vissajjanena. Dve pucchāti anusayapucchā pahānapucchāti dvepi pucchā vissajjesi. “Rāgaṃ tena pajahatī”ti idamekaṃ vissajjanaṃ, “na tattha rāgānusayo anusetī”ti idamekaṃ vissajjanaṃ, pucchānukkamañcettha anādiyitvā pahānakkamena vissajjanā pavattā[V 2.0266]. “Dve pucchā vissajjesī”ti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “idhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tathāvikkhambhitameva katvāti iminā yo rāgaṃ vikkhambhetvā puna uppajjituṃ appadānato tathāvikkhambhitameva katvā maggena samugghāteti, tassa vasena “rāgaṃ tena pajahati, na tattha rāgānusayo anusetī”ti vattabbanti dasseti. Kāmoghādīhi catūhi oghehi saṃsārabhavogheneva vā vegasā vuyhamānesu sattesu taṃ uttaritvā pattabbaṃ, tassa pana gādhabhāvato patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā – “tiṇṇo pāraṅgato thale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇo”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.238; itivu. 69; pu. pa. 187).

'By a single explanation' means by one answer, namely: 'Here, friend Visākha, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures...' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.374). 'Two questions' means the question about the underlying tendency and the question about abandonment; he answered both questions. 'He abandons lust by that'—this is one answer. 'No underlying tendency of lust lies latent there'—this is another answer. Here, not following the order of the questions, the answer proceeded according to the order of abandonment. To elaborate on the meaning stated concisely as 'he answered two questions,' 'Here...' and so on was said. Therein, by 'having suppressed it just so,' he shows that for one who, having suppressed lust and prevented it from arising again by not giving it an occasion, then eradicates it by the path, it should be said: 'He abandons lust by that; no underlying tendency of lust lies latent there.' While beings are being swept away swiftly by the four floods beginning with the flood of sensual desire, or by the flood of existence in saṃsāra, that which is to be attained by crossing over serves as a support, for it is a firm footing. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Having crossed over, gone to the far shore, the brahmin stands on high ground' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.238; Itivuttaka 69; Puggalapaññatti 187).

Suññatādibhedena anekabhedattā pāḷiyaṃ “anuttaresū”ti bahuvacananiddesoti “anuttarā vimokkhā”ti vatvā puna tesaṃ sabbesampi arahattabhāvasāmaññena “arahatte”ti vuttaṃ. Visaye cetaṃ bhummaṃ. Patthanaṃ paṭṭhapentassāti “aho vatāhaṃ arahattaṃ labheyya”nti patthanaṃ upaṭṭhapentassa, patthentassāti attho. Paṭṭhapentassāti cettha hetumhi antasaddo. Kathaṃ pana arahattavisayā patthanā uppajjatīti? Na kāci arahattaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā patthanā uppajjati anadhigatattā avisayabhāvato. Parikappitarūpaṃ pana taṃ uddissa patthanā uppajjati. “Uppajjati pihāpaccayā”ti vuttaṃ paramparapaccayataṃ sandhāya, ujukaṃ pana paccayabhāvo natthīti vuttaṃ “na patthanāya paṭṭhapanamūlakaṃ uppajjatī”ti. Idaṃ pana sevitabbaṃ domanassaṃ akusalappahānassa kusalābhivuḍḍhiyā ca nimittabhāvato. Tenāha bhagavā – “domanassampāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi sevitabbampi asevitabbampī”ti (dī. ni. 2.359-362). Tīhi māsehi sampajjanakā temāsikā[M 2.0289]. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Imasmiṃ vāreti imasmiṃ pavāraṇavāre. Visuddhipavāraṇanti “parisuddho aha”nti evaṃ pavattaṃ visuddhipavāraṇaṃ. Arahantānameva hesa pavāraṇā.

Because there are many distinctions, such as emptiness, in the Pāḷi it is explained in the plural as 'anuttaresu.' After stating 'anuttarā vimokkhā,' it is further said 'arahatte' because all of them share the commonality of the state of arahantship. This is a locative of sphere. 'For one who establishes an aspiration' means for one who sets forth the wish, 'Oh, may I attain arahantship!'—this is the meaning. Here, in 'paṭṭhapentassa,' the suffix '-anta' indicates the reason. But how does an aspiration directed toward arahantship arise? No aspiration arises by taking arahantship as its object, because it has not yet been attained and thus lies beyond one's scope. Rather, the aspiration arises directed towards a conceptualized form of it. It is said that 'it arises due to longing,' referring to an indirect chain of conditions, but there is no direct causal connection—hence, it is said, 'it does not arise rooted in the establishment of an aspiration.' This grief, however, should be cultivated because it serves as a cause for abandoning the unwholesome and for the growth of the wholesome. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'O lord of the devas, I declare grief to be twofold—that which should be cultivated and that which should not' (Dīghanikāya 2.359-362). 'Temāsikā' are those who are clearly comprehending for three months. The same method applies to the remaining two terms. 'In this vāra' refers to this Pavāraṇā occasion. 'Visuddhipavāraṇa' means the purity-invitation that proceeds thus: 'I am purified.' Indeed, this is the Pavāraṇā only of the arahants.

Na kadāci pahātabbassa pahāyakatā atthīti dassento “na domanassena vā”tiādiṃ vatvā pariyāyenetaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ vibhāvento “ayaṃ panā”tiādimāha. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato vitthārena āgamissati. Paṭipadaṃ gahetvā patthanaṃ katvā patthanaṃ ṭhapetvā. Paṭisañcikkhatīti ovādavasena attānaṃ samuttejento katheti. Sīlena hīnaṭṭhānanti aññehi arahattāya paṭipajjantehi sīlena hīnaṭṭhānaṃ kiṃ tuyhaṃ atthīti adhippāyo. Suparisuddhanti akhaṇḍādibhāvato sudhotajātimaṇi viya suṭṭhu parisuddhaṃ. Supaggahitanti kadācipi saṅkocābhāvato vīriyaṃ suṭṭhu paggahitaṃ. Paññāti vipassanāpaññā paṭipakkhehi anadhibhūtatāya akuṇṭhā tikkhavisadā saṅkhārānaṃ sammasane sūrā hutvā vahati pavattati. Pariyāyenāti tassa domanassassa [V 2.0267] arahattupanissayatāpariyāyena. Ārammaṇavasena anusayanaṃ idhādhippetanti āha “na taṃ ārabbha uppajjatī”ti. Anuppajjanamettha pahānaṃ nāmāti vuttaṃ “pahīnova tattha paṭighānusayoti attho”ti. Tatiyajjhānena vikkhambhetabbā avijjā, sā eva ariyamaggena samucchindīyatīti “avijjānusayaṃ vikkhambhetvā”tiādi vuttaṃ, anusayasadisatāya vā. “Rāgānusayaṃ vikkhambhetvā”ti etthāpi eseva nayo. Catutthajjhāne nānuseti nāma tattha kātabbakiccākaraṇato.

To show that that which is to be abandoned never has the quality of abandoning, he says, 'not by sorrow,' etc. This is stated indirectly, and explaining it, he says, 'But here,' etc. What should be said on this point will be explained in detail later. Having taken up the practice, having made the aspiration, having established the aspiration. 'He reflects' means he speaks while rousing himself by way of self-admonition. 'A state inferior in virtue'—the meaning is: 'What state inferior in virtue do you have, when others are practicing for arahantship?' 'Perfectly purified'—thoroughly purified like a well-washed, genuine jewel, being unbroken, etc. 'Well exerted'—energy is thoroughly exerted, because there is never any slackening. 'Wisdom'—insight wisdom, unhindered by opposing factors, is unblunted, sharp, clear, and valiant in comprehending formations; it proceeds and continues. 'By a roundabout way'—by way of that sorrow's being an indirect supporting condition for arahantship. That an underlying tendency by way of object is intended here is what he says by 'it does not arise regarding that.' That non-arising here is called abandonment is the meaning of 'the underlying tendency of aversion is indeed abandoned there.' Ignorance is to be suppressed by the third jhāna, and it is that very ignorance that is eradicated by the noble path; thus it is said, 'having suppressed the underlying tendency of ignorance,' etc., or because of its similarity to an underlying tendency. 'Having suppressed the underlying tendency of lust'—here too, the same method applies. 'It does not lie latent in the fourth jhāna' means because there is no task to be done there.

466. Tasmāti paccanīkattā sabhāvato kiccato paccayato cāti adhippāyo. Visabhāgapaṭibhāgo kathito “kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā dhammā”tiādīsu viya. Andhakārāti andhakārasadisā appakā sabhāvato. Avibhūtā apākaṭā anoḷārikabhāvato. Tato eva duddīpanā duviññāpanā. Tādisāvāti upekkhāsadisāva. Yathā upekkhā sukhadukkhāni viya na oḷārikā, evaṃ avijjā rāgadosā viya na oḷārikā. Atha kho andhakārā avibhūtā duddīpanā duviññāpanāti attho. Sabhāgapaṭibhāgo kathito “paṇidhi paṭighoso”tiādīsu viya. Yattakesu ṭhānesūti dukkhādīsu yattakesu ṭhānesu, yattha vā ñeyyaṭṭhānesu. Visabhāgapaṭibhāgoti andhakārassa [M 2.0290] viya āloko vighātakapaṭibhāgo. Vijjāti maggañāṇaṃ adhippetaṃ, vimuttīti phalanti āha “ubhopete dhammā anāsavā”ti. Anāsavaṭṭhenātiādīsu paṇītaṭṭhenātipi vattabbaṃ. Sopi hi vimuttinibbānānaṃ sādhāraṇo, vimuttiyā asaṅkhataṭṭhena nibbānassa visabhāgatāpi labbhateva. Pañhaṃ atikkamitvā gatosi, apucchitabbaṃ pucchantoti adhippāyo. Pañhānaṃ paricchedapamāṇaṃ gahetuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne aṭṭhatvā tato paraṃ pucchanto nāsakkhi pañhānaṃ pariyantaṃ gahetuṃ. Appaṭibhāgadhammassāti nippariyāyato sabhāgapaṭibhāgena appaṭibhāgadhammassa. Anāgatādipariyāyena nibbānassa sabhāgapaṭibhāgo vutto, visabhāge ca attheva saṅkhatadhammā, tasmā nippariyāyato kiñci sabhāgapaṭibhāgaṃ sandhāya pucchatīti katvā “accayāsī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Asaṅkhatassa hi appatiṭṭhassa ekantaniccassa sato nibbānassa kuto nippariyāyena sabhāgassa sambhavo. Tenāha “nibbānaṃ nāmeta”ntiādi.

466. Therefore, because it is opposed, the meaning is by way of nature, function, and condition. The dissimilar counterpart is spoken of, as in 'states that are counterparts of the dark and the bright,' etc. 'Darkness' means similar to darkness, slight in nature. Unmanifest, unclear, not coarse—therefore, hard to illuminate and hard to understand. Such indeed—just like equanimity. Just as equanimity is not coarse like pleasure and pain, so ignorance is not coarse like lust and hatred. Rather, 'darkness is unmanifest, hard to illuminate, and hard to understand'—this is the meaning. The similar counterpart is spoken of, as in 'aspiration and resonance,' etc. In whatever instances of suffering, etc., or in whatever knowable things. The dissimilar counterpart is like light, which is the destructive counterpart of darkness. 'Knowledge' means the knowledge of the path; 'liberation' means the fruit—thus it is said, 'both these states are taintless.' By way of being taintless—it should also be said by way of being sublime. For that too is common to liberation and Nibbāna, and even through the unconditioned nature of liberation, Nibbāna’s dissimilarity can be established. He has gone beyond the question, asking what should not be asked—this is the meaning. Having stayed in the proper place to grasp the extent and measure of the questions, then asking further, he could not grasp the limit of the questions. Of a state without a counterpart means, in a literal sense, of a state without a similar counterpart. The similar counterpart of Nibbāna is stated in terms of the future, etc., and in the dissimilar there certainly are conditioned states. Therefore, asking literally with reference to some similar counterpart, it is said, 'he overreached,' etc. For how could there be any literal similar counterpart of Nibbāna, which is unconditioned, unestablished, and exclusively eternal? Therefore, it is said, 'Nibbāna is called,' etc.

Viraddhoti ettha sabhāgapaṭibhāgaṃ pucchissāmīti nicchayābhāvato pucchitamatthaṃ virajjhitvāva pucchi, na ajānitvāti attho. Etena heṭṭhā sabbapucchā diṭṭhasaṃsandananayena jānitvāva pavattāti dīpitaṃ hoti. Therī pana taṃ taṃ pucchitamatthaṃ sabhāvato vibhāventī satthu desanāñāṇaṃ anugantvāva vissajjesi. Nibbānogadhanti nibbānaṃ ogāhitvā ṭhitaṃ nibbānantogadhaṃ. Tenāha “nibbānabbhantaraṃ nibbānaṃ anupaviṭṭha”nti. Assāti brahmacariyassa.

Missed—here, because there was no resolve to ask about a similar counterpart, he asked having deviated from the intended meaning of the question, not out of ignorance—this is the meaning. By this, it is shown that all previous questions proceeded after knowing by the method of direct connection. But the elder nun, analyzing the matter that was asked about according to its nature, following the Teacher’s knowledge of the teaching, gave the answer. Immersed in Nibbāna—meaning, having plunged into Nibbāna, abiding within Nibbāna, deeply immersed in Nibbāna. Therefore, it is said, 'within Nibbāna, having entered Nibbāna.' 'Assa' means of the holy life.

467. Paṇḍiccena [V 2.0268] samannāgatāti ettha vuttapaṇḍiccaṃ dassetuṃ “dhātukusalā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tenevāha – “kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, paṇḍito hoti? Yato kho, ānanda, bhikkhu dhātukusalo ca hoti, āyatanakusalo ca paṭiccasamuppādakusalo ca ṭhānāṭṭhānakusalo ca. Ettāvatā nu kho, ānanda, bhikkhu paṇḍito hotī”ti (ma. ni. 3.124). Paññāmahattaṃ nāma theriyā asekkhappaṭisambhidappattāya paṭisambhidāyo pūretvā ṭhitatāti taṃ dassetuṃ “mahante atthe”tiādi vuttaṃ. Rājayuttehīti rañño kamme niyuttapurisehi. Āhaccavacanenāti satthārā karaṇādīni āhanitvā pavattitavacanena. Yadettha atthato na vibhattaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā suviññeyyameva.

467. 'Endowed with wisdom'—here, to illustrate the mentioned wisdom, the phrase 'skilled in the elements,' etc., is stated. Therefore, it is said: 'To what extent, venerable sir, is one a wise person? When, Ānanda, a monk is skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and impossible, to that extent, Ānanda, a monk is a wise person' (Majjhima Nikāya 3.124). 'Greatness of wisdom' means the elder nun's state of having fulfilled the discriminations, as one who has attained the discriminations of a non-learner. To illustrate this, the phrase 'in great meanings,' etc., is stated. 'By royal servants' means by persons appointed to the king's work. 'By the compelling word' means by the word spoken by the Teacher, having hit upon the causes, etc. Whatever here is not distinct in meaning is easily understood due to the method stated previously.

Cūḷavedallasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The explanation of the hidden meaning of the commentary on the Cūḷavedalla Sutta is complete.

5. Cūḷadhammasamādānasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Cūḷadhammasamādāna Sutta

468. Dhammoti [M 2.0291][V 2.0269] gahitagahaṇānīti dhammo vā hotu itaro vā, dhammoti paggahitaggāhappavattā cariyāva. Āyūhanakkhaṇeti tassa dhammoti gahitassa pavattanakkhaṇe. Sukhanti akicchaṃ. Tenāha “sukara”nti. Dukkhavipākanti aniṭṭhaphalavipaccanaṃ.

468. The phrase 'dhammoti gahitagahaṇānīti' (meaning 'the grasping of what is grasped as Dhamma') signifies that whether it is the Dhamma or something else, 'Dhamma' refers to the conduct that is firmly grasped and undertaken. 'Āyūhanakkhaṇeti' means the moment of undertaking that grasped Dhamma. 'Sukhanti' means without difficulty. Hence it is said 'sukara' (easy). 'Dukkhavipākanti' means the ripening of undesirable results.

469. Yathā cakkhādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ yathāsakaṃ visayaggahaṇaṃ sabhāvasiddhaṃ, evaṃ manasopi. Te ca visayā iṭṭhākārato gahaṇe na koci doso, purisattabhāve na ca te dosaṃ pavattentīti ayaṃ tesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ laddhīti āha “vatthukāmesupi kilesakāmesupi doso natthī”ti, assādetvā visayaparibhoge natthi ādīnavo, tappaccayā na koci antarāyoti adhippāyo. Pātabyataṃ āpajjantīti paribhuñjanakataṃ upagacchanti. Paribhogattho hi ayaṃ pā-saddo kattusādhano ca tabya-saddo, yathāruci paribhuñjantīti attho. Kilesakāmopi assādiyamāno vatthukāmantogadhoyeva, kilesakāmavasena pana nesaṃ assādetabbatāti āha “vatthukāmesu kilesakāmena pātabyata”nti. Kilesakāmenāti karaṇatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Pātabyataṃ paribhuñjitabbatanti etthāpi kattuvaseneva attho veditabbo. Moḷiṃ katvāti veṇibandhavasena moḷiṃ katvā. Tāpasaparibbājikāhīti tāpasapabbajjūpagatāhi. Pariññaṃ paññapentīti idaṃ “pahānamāhaṃsū”ti padasseva vevacananti “pahānaṃ samatikkamaṃ paññapentī”ti vuttaṃ. Tena kāmā nāmete aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammāti yāthāvato parijānanaṃ idha “pahāna”nti adhippetaṃ, na vinābhāvamattanti dasseti. Māluvāsipāṭikāti māluvāvidalaṃ māluvāphale poṭṭalikā. Santāsaṃ āpajjeyyāti sāle adhivatthadevatāya pavattiṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ. Tadā hi tassā evaṃ hoti. Koviḷārapattasadisehīti mahākoviḷārapattasaṇṭhānehi. Saṇṭhānavasena hetaṃ vuttaṃ, māluvāpattā pana koviḷārapattehi mahantatarāni ceva ghanatarāni ca honti. Vipulabahughanagarupattatāya mahantaṃ bhāraṃ janetvā. Sāti māluvālatā. Oghananti heṭṭhato olambanahetubhūtaṃ ghanabhāvaṃ.

469. Just as the five faculties—beginning with the eye—each grasp their respective objects by their inherent nature, so too does the mind. And when those objects are grasped in a pleasing form, there is no fault in the grasping itself, nor do they cause any fault in the human condition. This is the view held by those ascetics and brahmins, as stated: 'There is no fault in the objects of desire or in the defilements of desire.' There is no danger in enjoying and indulging in sense objects, and thus no obstacle arises from them—this is the intended meaning. 'They are liable to indulgence' means they become objects of consumption. For here, the root 'pā-' (in 'pātabyataṃ') signifies consumption, and the suffix '-tabya' is used in an agentive sense, meaning 'they consume as they please.' Even when defiled desires are enjoyed, they remain included within the objects of desire. But because they are liable to be enjoyed through defiled desires, it is said: 'They are liable to indulgence through defiled desires in the objects of desire.' Here, 'kilesakāmena' is an instrumental case indicating the means. 'Pātabyataṃ' means 'liable to be consumed,' and here too, the meaning should be understood from the agent's perspective. 'Having made a topknot' means forming a topknot by braiding the hair. 'By female ascetics and wanderers' refers to those who have taken up the life of asceticism or wandering. 'They declare full understanding' is synonymous with the phrase 'they speak of abandonment.' Thus, it is said: 'They declare abandonment and transcendence.' Here, 'abandonment' refers to the complete understanding of desires as they truly are—impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—not merely their absence. 'The Māluvā pod' refers to the split pod or fruit of the Māluvā creeper. 'They might cause alarm' is said with reference to the deity dwelling in the Sāl tree, for at that time, the deity would think thus. 'Like the leaves of the Koviḷāra tree' refers to the shape of large Koviḷāra leaves. This is said in terms of appearance, for Māluvā leaves are larger and thicker than Koviḷāra leaves. Due to their vast, numerous, dense, and heavy leaves, they create a great burden. 'Sā' refers to the Māluvā creeper. 'Oghana' refers to the dense mass hanging below, serving as the cause of hanging down.

Andhavanasubhagavanaggahaṇaṃ [M 2.0292] tesaṃ abhilakkhitabhāvato. Nāḷikerādīsu tiṇajātīsu. Khādanupalakkhaṇaṃ upacikānaṃ uṭṭhahanaggahaṇanti āha “uṭṭhaheyyu”nti. Keḷiṃ karontī viyāti vilambananadī [V 2.0270] viya keḷiṃ karontī. Idāni ahaṃ taṃ ajjhottharinti pamodamānā viya ito cito ca vipphandamānā vilambantī. Samphassopi sukho mudutaluṇakomalabhāvato. Dassanampi sukhaṃ ghanabahalapattasaṃhatatāya. Somanassajātāti pubbe anussavavasena bhavanavināsabhayā santāsaṃ āpajji, idāni tassā sampattidassanena palobhitā somanassajātā ahosi.

The mention of Andhavana and Subhagavana is due to their being distinctive. Among coconut trees and the like, in grassy areas. It is said that 'uṭṭhaheyyu' refers to the emergence of termites, characterized by their gnawing. As if playing, like a meandering river playing. As if rejoicing, 'Now I shall overwhelm it,' she, struggling here and there, lingered. Even the touch is pleasant due to its soft, tender, and delicate nature. The sight is also pleasant because of the dense, thick, and compact nature of the leaves. 'Born of joy' means that previously, due to the fear of the destruction of her abode from hearsay, she was seized by terror, but now, seeing its abundance, she became born of joy.

Viṭabhiṃ kareyyāti ātānavitānavasena jaṭentī jālaṃ kareyya. Tathābhūtā ca ghanapattasañchannatāya chattasadisī hotīti āha “chattākārena tiṭṭheyyā”ti. Sakalaṃ rukkhanti upari sabbasākhāpasākhaṃ sabbarukkhaṃ. Bhassamānāti paliveṭhanavaseneva otaramānā. Yāva mūlā otiṇṇasākhāhīti māluvā bhārena onamitvā rukkhassa yāva mūlā otiṇṇasākhāhi puna abhiruhamānā. Sabbasākhāti heṭṭhā majjhe upari cāti sabbāpi sākhāyo paliveṭhentī. Saṃsibbitvā jālasantānakaniyāmena jaṭetvā. Evaṃ aparāparaṃ saṃsibbanena ajjhottharantī. Sabbasākhā heṭṭhā katvā sayaṃ upari ṭhatvā mahābhārabhāvena vāte vā vāyante deve vā vassante padāleyya. Sākhaṭṭhakavimānanti sākhāpaṭibaddhaṃ vimānaṃ. Yasmā idha satthārā “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave”tiādinā bhūtapubbameva vatthu upamābhāvena āhaṭaṃ, tasmā “idaṃ pana vimāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

'She would make a canopy' means: intertwining by way of spreading out and across, she would make a net. And being thus, due to being covered with dense leaves, she is like a canopy; thus it is said, 'she would stand in the form of a canopy.' 'The entire tree' means: above, all its branches and twigs, the whole tree. 'Falling down' means: descending by way of wrapping around. 'With branches descended to the root' means: the Māluvā creeper, having bent down with its weight, climbs up again with branches that have descended to the root of the tree. 'All branches' means: below, in the middle, and above, she entwines all the branches. Having bound them together, having woven them in the manner of a continuous net. Thus, by repeatedly binding, she overspreads it. Having placed all the branches below, standing herself above, due to the great weight, when the wind blows or the god rains, she would break it. 'The mansion supported by branches' means: a mansion attached to the branches. Since here the Teacher, with 'Just as, monks,' etc., brought forth a past event as an analogy, therefore, 'this mansion,' etc., was said.

471. Bahalarāgasabhāvoti paccavekkhaṇāhi nīharituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya balavā hutvā abhibhavanarāgadhātuko. Rāgajanti rāganimittajātaṃ. Diṭṭhe diṭṭhe ārammaṇeti diṭṭhe diṭṭhe visabhāgārammaṇe. Nimittaṃ gaṇhātīti kilesuppattiyā kāraṇabhūtaṃ anubyañjanaso nimittaṃ gaṇhāti, sikkhāgāravena pana kilesehi nissitaṃ maggaṃ na paṭipajjati, tato eva ācariyupajjhāyehi āṇattaṃ daṇḍakammaṃ karoteva. Tenāha “na tveva vītikkamaṃ karotī”ti. Hatthaparāmāsādīnīti – “ehi tāva tayā vuttaṃ mayā vuttañca amutra gantvā vīmaṃsissāmā”tiādinā hatthaggahaṇādīni karonto, na karuṇāmettānidānavasena. Mohajātikoti bahalamohasabhāvo.

471. 'Of a strongly lustful nature' means: having the element of lust that overpowers, having become strong due to the inability to remove it through reflection. 'Born of lust' means: born of the sign of lust. 'In each seen object' means: in each seen, dissimilar object. 'One grasps the sign' means: one grasps the sign along with its secondary characteristics, which is the cause for the arising of defilements; but out of respect for the training, one does not follow the path associated with defilements, and for that very reason, one carries out the disciplinary action commanded by one's teachers and preceptors. Therefore, it is said, 'one does not, however, transgress.' 'By touching hands, etc.' means: doing things like grasping the hand, etc., with such words as, 'Come, let us go there and investigate what you have said and what I have said,' not on the basis of compassion and loving-kindness. 'Of a deluded nature' means: of a strongly deluded nature.

472. Kammaniyāmenāti [M 2.0293] purimajātisiddhena lobhussadatādiniyamitena kammaniyāmena. Idāni taṃ lobhussadatādiṃ vibhāgena dassetuṃ “yassa hī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha kammāyūhanakkhaṇeti kammakaraṇavelāya. Lobho balavāti tajjāya sāmaggiyā sāmatthiyato lobho adhiko [V 2.0271] hoti. Alobho mandoti tappaṭipakkho alobho dubbalo hoti. Kathaṃ panete lobhālobhā aññamaññaṃ ujuvipaccanīkabhūtā ekakkhaṇe pavattanti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ “ekakkhaṇe pavattantī”ti, nikantikkhaṇaṃ pana āyūhanakkhaṇameva katvā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Esa nayo sesesu. Pariyādātunti abhibhavituṃ na sakkoti. Yo hi “evaṃsundaraṃ evaṃvipulaṃ evaṃmahagghañca na sakkā parassa dātu”ntiādinā amuttacāgatādivasena pavattāya cetanāya sampayutto alobho sammadeva lobhaṃ pariyādātuṃ na sakkoti. Dosamohānaṃ anuppattiyaṃ tādisapaccayalābheneva adosāmohā balavanto. Tasmāti lobhādosāmohānaṃ balavabhāvato alobhadosamohānañca dubbalabhāvatoti vuttameva kāraṇaṃ paccāmasati. Soti taṃsamaṅgī. Tena kammenāti tena lobhādiupanissayavatā kusalakammunā. Sukhasīloti sakhilo. Tamevatthaṃ akkodhanoti pariyāyena vadati.

472. 'By the order of kamma' means: by the order of kamma established in previous births, determined by the prominence of greed and so forth. Now, to show that prominence of greed and so forth in detail, the passage beginning with 'For whom...' is introduced. Therein, 'the moment of accumulating kamma' means: at the time of performing the kamma. 'Greed is strong' means: due to the capacity of the totality of conditions that produce it, greed is dominant. 'Non-greed is weak' means: non-greed, its opposite, is feeble. But how can these, greed and non-greed, which are direct opposites of each other, occur in a single moment? This should not be understood as 'they occur in a single moment'; rather, it is said thus by taking the decisive moment as the moment of accumulation itself. This method applies to the rest. 'Cannot overcome' means: it is unable to overpower. For the non-greed associated with the volition that arises from the inability to relinquish, etc., thinking, 'Such a beautiful, abundant, and costly thing cannot be given to another,' is truly unable to overcome greed. When hatred and delusion do not arise, it is precisely by obtaining such conditions that non-hatred and non-delusion are strong. 'Therefore' means: he recalls the very reason stated, namely, because of the strength of greed, hatred, and delusion, and because of the weakness of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. 'He' means: one endowed with that. 'By that kamma' means: by that wholesome kamma which has greed and the like as a strong support. 'Pleasant in conduct' means: gentle. He expresses that same meaning with the synonym 'free from anger'.

Mandā alobhādosā lobhadose pariyādātuṃ na sakkonti, amoho pana balavā mohaṃ pariyādātuṃ sakkotīti evaṃ yathārahaṃ paṭhamavāre vuttanayeneva atidesattho veditabbo. Purimanayenevāti pubbe vuttanayānusārena. Duṭṭhoti kodhano. Dandhoti mandamañño. Sukhasīlakoti sukhasīlo.

The extended meaning should be understood appropriately according to the method stated in the first case, thus: 'Weak non-greed and non-hatred cannot overcome greed and hatred, but strong non-delusion can overcome delusion.' 'By the previous method' means: in accordance with the method stated before. 'Duṭṭho' means: one who is angry. 'Dandho' means: one who is slow-witted. 'Sukhasīlako' means: one who is pleasant in conduct.

Ettha ca lobhavasena, dosamoha-lobhadosa-lobhamoha-dosamoha-lobhadosamohavasenāti tayo ekakā, tayo dukā, eko tikoti lobhādiussadavasena akusalapakkhe eva satta vārā, tathā kusalapakkhe alobhādiussadavasenāti cuddasa vārā labbhanti. Tattha alobhadosamohā, alobhādosamohā, alobhadosāmohā balavantoti āgatehi kusalapakkhe tatiyadutiyapaṭhamavārehi dosussadamohussadadosamohussadavārā gahitā eva honti. Tathā [M 2.0294] akusalapakkhe lobhādosāmohā, lobhadosāmohā, lobhādosamohā balavantoti āgatehi tatiyadutiyapaṭhamavārehi adosussadaamohussadaadosāmohussadavārā gahitā evāti akusalakusalapakkhesu tayo tayo vāre antogadhe katvā aṭṭheva vārā dassitā. Ye pana ubhayasammissatāvasena lobhālobhussadavārādayo apare ekūnapaññāsa vārā kāmaṃ dassetabbā, tesaṃ asambhavato eva na dassitā. Na hi “ekasmiṃ santāne antarena avatthantaraṃ lobho ca balavā alobho cā”tiādi yujjati. Paṭipakkhavasena vāpi etesaṃ balavadubbalabhāvo sahajātadhammavasena [V 2.0272] vā. Tattha lobhassa tāva paṭipakkhavasena anabhibhūtatāya balavabhāvo, tathā dosamohānaṃ adosāmohehi. Alobhādīnaṃ pana lobhādianabhibhavanato. Sabbesañca samānajātiyasamadhibhuyya pavattivasena sahajātadhammato balavabhāvo. Tena vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.472) – “lobho balavā, alobho mando. Adosāmohā balavanto, dosamohā mandā”tiādi, so ca nesaṃ mandabalavabhāvo purimūpanissayato tathā āsayassa paribhāvitatāya veditabbo. Tenevāha “kammaniyāmenā”ti. Sesaṃ vuttanayattā suviññeyyamevāti.

And here, by way of greed; hatred; delusion; greed-hatred; greed-delusion; hatred-delusion; and greed-hatred-delusion—three singles, three pairs, one triad—thus, on the unwholesome side, there are seven cases based on the prominence of greed and so forth. Similarly, on the wholesome side, based on the prominence of non-greed and so forth, fourteen cases are obtained. Therein, on the wholesome side, by the third, second, and first cases which are 'non-greed, hatred, and delusion are strong,' 'non-greed, non-hatred, and delusion are strong,' and 'non-greed, hatred, and non-delusion are strong,' the cases of prominence of hatred, prominence of delusion, and prominence of hatred-delusion are indeed included. Likewise, on the unwholesome side, by the third, second, and first cases which are 'greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are strong,' 'greed, hatred, and non-delusion are strong,' and 'greed, non-hatred, and delusion are strong,' the cases of prominence of non-hatred, prominence of non-delusion, and prominence of non-hatred-non-delusion are indeed included. Thus, by including three cases each in the unwholesome and wholesome sides, only eight cases are shown. But those other forty-nine cases, such as the case of the prominence of both greed and non-greed, due to being mixed, could be shown if desired; however, because they are impossible, they are not shown. For it is not logical that 'in one continuum, without an intervening different state, both greed and non-greed are strong,' and so on. Alternatively, their strength and weakness is either by way of opposition or by way of co-nascent phenomena. Therein, greed's strength is due to not being overcome by way of opposition; similarly for hatred and delusion by non-hatred and non-delusion. The weakness of non-greed and the others, however, is from not overpowering greed and the others. And for all of them, their strength is from co-nascent phenomena by way of occurring having overcome those of the same class. Therefore, it is said in the commentary (Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 2.472): 'Greed is strong, non-greed is weak. Non-hatred and non-delusion are strong, hatred and delusion are weak,' and so on. And their weakness and strength should be understood as being from prior supporting conditions and from the cultivation of their disposition. For that reason, he said, 'by the order of kamma.' The rest is easily understood because it follows the method already stated.

Cūḷadhammasamādānasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Cūḷadhammasamādānasutta is complete.

6. Mahādhammasamādānasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Great Discourse on Undertakings

473. Evaṃ [V 2.0273] idāni vuccamānākāro kāmo kāmanaṃ icchā etesanti evaṃkāmā. Evaṃ chando chandanaṃ rocanaṃ ajjhāsayo etesanti evaṃchandā. Abhimukhaṃ, abhinivissa vā pakārehi eti upagacchatīti adhippāyo, laddhi. Sā hi laddhabbavatthuṃ abhimukhaṃ “evameta”nti abhinivisantī tena tena pakārena upagacchati, hatthagataṃ katvā tiṭṭhati na vissajjeti. Evaṃ vuccamānākāro adhippāyo etesanti evaṃadhippāyā. Bhagavā mūlaṃ kāraṇaṃ etesaṃ yāthāvato adhigamāyāti bhagavaṃmūlakā. Tenāha “bhagavantañhi nissāya mayaṃ ime dhamme ājānāma paṭivijjhāmā”ti. Amhākaṃ dhammāti [M 2.0295] tehi attanā adhigantabbatāya vuttaṃ. Sevitabbānañhi yāthāvato adhigamañāṇāni adhigacchanakasambandhīni, tāni ca sammāsambuddhamūlakāni anaññavisayattā. Tenāha “pubbe kassapasambuddhenā”tiādi. Bhagavā netā tesanti bhagavaṃnettikā. Netāti sevitabbadhamme vineyyasantānaṃ pāpetā. Vinetāti asevitabbadhamme vineyyasantānato apanetā. Tadaṅgavinayādivasena vā vinetā. Anunetāti ime dhammā sevitabbā, ime na sevitabbāti ubhayasampāpanāpanayanatthaṃ paññapetā. Tenāha “yathāsabhāvato”tiādi.

473. Thus, the form now being spoken of is desire (kāma), longing (kāmana), and wish (icchā); they have these, thus they are 'those with such desires.' Thus, inclination (chanda), delight (chandana, rocana), and disposition (ajjhāsaya); they have these, thus they are 'those with such inclinations.' It goes towards (eti) or approaches (upagacchati) an object, or adheres to it (abhinivissa) in various ways (pakārehi)—this is an intention (adhippāya), a view (laddhi). For that view, approaching the object to be grasped, facing it and adhering to it as 'thus it is,' approaches it in various ways; having taken it in hand, it stands fast and does not let go. Thus, the form being spoken of is intention; they have this, thus they are 'those with such intentions.' The Blessed One is the root (mūla), the cause (kāraṇa), for their true realization; thus, they are 'rooted in the Blessed One' (bhagavaṃmūlakā). Therefore, it is said: 'For, relying on the Blessed One, we understand and penetrate these teachings.' 'Our teachings' is said by them with reference to what is to be realized by themselves. For the knowledges of the true realization of what should be cultivated are connected with the one who realizes them, and these are rooted in the Perfectly Enlightened One, as they have no other sphere. Therefore, it is said: 'Previously by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa,' and so on. The Blessed One is their leader (netā); thus, they are 'led by the Blessed One' (bhagavaṃnettikā). 'Leader' means he who leads those to be trained to the teachings that are to be cultivated. 'Discipliner' (vinetā) means he who removes from those to be trained the teachings that are not to be cultivated. Or, he is a discipliner by means of substitution, and so on. 'He who prescribes' (anunetā) means he who declares, for the purpose of both causing attainment and removal, 'These teachings should be cultivated; these should not be cultivated.' Therefore, it is said: 'According to their true nature,' and so on.

Paṭisaranti etthāti paṭisaraṇaṃ, bhagavā paṭisaraṇaṃ etesanti bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Paṭisarati sabhāvasampaṭivedhavasena paccekamupagacchatīti vā paṭisaraṇaṃ, bhagavā paṭisaraṇaṃ etesanti bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Paṭivedhavasenāti paṭivijjhitabbatāvasena. Asatipi mukhe atthato evaṃ vadanto viya hotīti āha “phasso āgacchati, ahaṃ bhagavā kiṃ nāmo”ti. Paṭibhātūti ettha paṭi-saddāpekkhāya “bhagavanta”nti upayogavacanaṃ, attho pana sāmivacanavaseneva veditabboti dassento āha “bhagavato”ti paṭibhātūti ca bhagavato bhāgo hotu. Bhagavato hi esa bhāgo, yadidaṃ dhammassa desanā, amhākaṃ pana bhāgo savananti adhippāyo. Keci pana paṭibhātūti padissatūti atthaṃ vadanti, ñāṇena dissatu, desīyatūti vā attho. Upaṭṭhātūti ca ñāṇassa paccupaṭṭhātu.

One resorts to this, thus it is a 'resort' (paṭisaraṇa). The Blessed One is their resort, thus they are 'those who have the Blessed One as a resort.' Or, 'resort' means one approaches individually by way of penetrating the true nature. The Blessed One is their resort, thus they are 'those who have the Blessed One as a resort.' 'By way of penetration' means by way of what is to be penetrated. Even if not spoken aloud, in meaning it is as if one were speaking thus, he says: 'Contact arises. What am I called, O Blessed One?' Regarding 'Let it be clear to you' (paṭibhātu), here, with reference to the prefix 'paṭi,' the accusative 'bhagavantaṃ' is used, but the meaning should be understood in the sense of the genitive. To show this, he says 'bhagavato paṭibhātu,' meaning 'let it be the Blessed One's portion.' For this is the Blessed One's portion, namely, the teaching of the Dhamma, while our portion is listening—this is the intention. Some, however, say the meaning of 'let it be clear' is 'let it be evident'; or the meaning is 'let it be seen by knowledge,' or 'let it be taught.' And 'let it be present' means let it be present to knowledge.

474. Nissayitabbeti [V 2.0274] attano santāne uppādanavasena apassayitabbe. Tatiyacatutthadhammasamādānāni hi apassāya sattānaṃ etarahi āyatiñca sampattiyo abhivaḍḍhanti. Bhajitabbeti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Sevitabbeti vā sappurisupassayasaddhammassavanayonisomanasikāre sandhāyāha. Bhajitabbeti tappaccaye dānādipuññadhamme.

474. One should depend on it: meaning, one should rely on it in the sense of generating it in one's own mental continuum. For through reliance on the third and fourth undertakings of the Dhamma, the accomplishments of beings increase both in the present and in the future. One should associate with it: this is a synonym for the former. Or, one should cultivate it: this is said with reference to associating with good persons, hearing the true Dhamma, and wise attention. One should associate with it: this refers to the meritorious qualities, such as giving, which are conditioned by that.

475. Uppaṭipāṭiākārenāti paṭhamaṃ saṃkilesadhamme dassetvā pacchā vodānadhammadassanaṃ satthu desanāpaṭipāṭi, yathā – “vāmaṃ muñca, dakkhiṇaṃ gaṇhā”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 498; visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.14), tathā uppaṭipāṭipakārena, sā ca kho purimesu dvīsu dhammasamādānesu[M 2.0296], pacchimesu pana paṭipāṭiyāva mātikā paṭṭhapitā. Yathādhammarasenevāti pahātabbapahāyakadhammānaṃ yathāsabhāveneva. Sabhāvo hi yāthāvato rasitabbato jānitabbato “raso”ti vuccati. Paṭhamaṃ pahātabbadhamme dassetvā tadanantaraṃ “ime dhammā etehi pahīyantī”ti pahāyakadhammadassanaṃ desanānupubbī. Gahaṇaṃ ādiyanaṃ attano santāne uppādanaṃ.

475. In a reverse order: The Teacher’s sequence of teaching is to first show the defiling qualities and then the purifying qualities, as in, 'Release the left, take the right.' It is in such a reverse manner, and this applies to the first two undertakings of the Dhamma, whereas for the latter ones, the matrix is established in the natural sequence. According to the essence of the Dhamma: meaning, according to the true nature of the qualities to be abandoned and the qualities that abandon them. For the true nature, because it is to be tasted and known as it really is, is called 'essence' (rasa). The teaching sequence is to first show the qualities to be abandoned and immediately after that to show the qualities that abandon, with the words: 'These qualities are abandoned by these.' Taking up means adopting, generating them in one’s own continuum.

478. Vadhadaṇḍādīhi bhītassa upasaṅkamane, micchā caritvā tathā apagamane ca pubbāparacetanānaṃ vasena micchācāro dukkhavedano hoti, tathā issānindādīhi upaddutassa aparacetanāvasena, evaṃ abhijjhāmicchādiṭṭhīsupi yathārahaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tissannampi cetanānanti pubbāparasanniṭṭhāpakacetanānaṃ. Adinnādānaṃ musāvādo pisuṇavācā samphappalāpoti imesaṃ catunnaṃ sanniṭṭhāpakacetanānaṃ sukhasampayuttā vā upekkhāsampayuttā vāti ayaṃ nayo idha adhikatattā na uddhaṭo. Domanassameva cettha dukkhanti idaṃ pubbabhāgāparabhāgacetanāpi cettha āsannā domanassasahagatā eva hontīti katvā vuttaṃ. Anāsannā pana sandhāya “pariyeṭṭhiṃ vā āpajjantassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Teneva micchācārābhijjhāmicchādiṭṭhīnaṃ pubbabhāgāparabhāgacetanā āsannā sanniṭṭhāpakacetanāgatikāvāti dassitaṃ hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pariyeṭṭhinti micchācārādīsu vītikkamitabbavatthumālāgandhādipariyesanaṃ. Pāṇātipātādīsu māretabbavatthuāvudhādipariyesanaṃ āpajjantassa. Akicchenapi tesaṃ pariyesanaṃ sambhavatīti “vaṭṭatiyevā”ti sāsaṅkaṃ vadati.

478. For one who is afraid to approach due to fear of execution, punishment, and so on, or for one who, having engaged in misconduct, then withdraws, wrong conduct is experienced as painful on account of the prior and subsequent intentions. Similarly, for one afflicted by envy, blame, and so on, it is on account of the subsequent intention. Likewise, this should be understood as appropriate in the cases of covetousness and wrong view. Of the three kinds of intention: this means the prior, subsequent, and accomplishing intentions. For taking what is not given, false speech, divisive speech, and idle chatter, the principle of whether the accomplishing intentions are associated with pleasure or with equanimity is not taken up here, as it is additional. Here, 'grief itself is suffering' is said because the proximate prior-stage and subsequent-stage intentions are accompanied by grief. But referring to the non-proximate ones, it is said, 'or when one undertakes a search,' and so on. Thus, it should be understood that it is shown that the proximate prior-stage and subsequent-stage intentions of wrong conduct, covetousness, and wrong view have the nature of the accomplishing intention. 'Searching' means, in the case of wrong conduct and so on, the searching for the object to be transgressed, such as garlands and perfumes. In the case of taking life and so on, it means undertaking the search for the object to be killed, weapons, etc. Because their search is possible even without difficulty, he speaks with reservation, 'it is indeed possible.'

479. Sukhavedanā hontīti sukhavedanāpi hontīti adhippāyo. Tāsaṃ cetanānaṃ asukhavedanatāpi labbhatīti “sukhavedanāpi hontiyevā”ti sāsaṅkavacanaṃ. Somanassameva cettha sukhanti idaṃ pubbabhāgāparabhāgacetanāpi somanassasahagatā eva hontīti katvā vuttaṃ. Tañca kho [V 2.0275] micchācāravajjānaṃ channaṃ vasena. Micchācārassa pana pubbāparabhāgassa vasena “kāyikaṃ sukhampi vaṭṭatiyevāti sāsaṅkavacanaṃ.

479. 'They are of pleasant feeling' means they are also of pleasant feeling. Because those intentions can also be of unpleasant feeling, there is the statement with reservation: 'they are indeed also of pleasant feeling.' Here, 'gladness itself is pleasure' is said because the prior-stage and subsequent-stage intentions are also accompanied by gladness. And that is in respect of the six actions, excluding wrong conduct. But in the case of wrong conduct, with respect to its prior and subsequent stages, there is the statement with reservation: 'bodily pleasure is indeed also possible.'

480. Dosajapariḷāhavasenassa siyā kāyikampi dukkhanti adhippāyena “so gaṇhantopi dukkhito”ti vuttaṃ. Cetodukkhameva vā sandhāya tassa aparāparuppattidassanatthaṃ “dukkhito domanassito”ti vuttaṃ.

480. Due to the burning born of hatred, there may also be bodily suffering; with this intention it is said, 'even when taking, he is afflicted.' Alternatively, referring only to mental suffering, to show its successive arising, it is said, 'afflicted and grieved.'

481. Dasasupi [M 2.0297] padesūti dasasupi koṭṭhāsesu, vākyesu vā. Upekkhāsampayuttatāpi sambhavatīti “sukhasampayuttā hontiyevā”ti idha sāsaṅkavacanaṃ. Pāṇātipātā paṭiviratassa kāyopi siyā vigatadarathapariḷāhoti pāṇātipātāveramaṇiādipaccayā kāyikapaṭisaṃvedanāpi sambhavatīti sahāpi sukhenāti ettha kāyiyasukhampi vaṭṭatiyeva.

481. 'In all ten instances' means in all ten portions, or sentences. Because association with equanimity is also possible, there is here the statement with reservation: 'they are indeed associated with pleasure.' For one who abstains from taking life, the body may also be without fever and burning. Because a bodily feeling conditioned by abstinence from taking life and so on is also possible, here in the phrase 'together with pleasure,' bodily pleasure is indeed also applicable.

482. Tittakālābūti upabhuttassa ummādādipāpanena kucchitatittakaraso alābu. Na ruccissati aniṭṭharasatāya aniṭṭhaphalatāya ca.

482. A 'bitter gourd' is a gourd with a vile, bitter taste which, when consumed, causes madness and other such things. It will not be liked, due to its disagreeable taste and its disagreeable result.

483. Rasaṃ detīti rasaṃ dasseti vibhāveti.

483. “Gives taste” means it reveals and makes taste distinct.

484. Pūtimuttanti pūtisabhāvamuttaṃ. Taruṇanti dhārāvasena nipatantaṃ hutvā uṇhaṃ. Tenassa uparimuttatamāha. Muttañhi passāvamaggato muccamānaṃ kāyusmāvasena uṇhaṃ hoti.

484. 'Putrid urine' means urine that is putrid by nature. 'Fresh' means it is warm as it falls in a stream. Therefore, he speaks of it as 'most recently passed.' For urine, when being released from the urinary passage, is warm on account of the body's heat.

485. Yaṃ bhagandarasaṃsaṭṭhaṃ lohitaṃ pakkhandatīti bhagandarabyādhisahitāya lohitapakkhandatāya vasena yaṃ lohitaṃ vissavati. Pittasaṃsaṭṭhaṃ lohitaṃ pakkhandatīti ānetvā sambandho.

485. 'Blood mixed with a fistula flows' means that blood flows out by way of a discharge of blood accompanied by the disease of a fistula. The phrase 'Blood mixed with bile flows' is to be connected in the same way.

486. Ubbiddheti dūre. Abbhamahikādiupakkilesavigamena hi ākāsaṃ uttuṅgaṃ viya dūraṃ viya ca khāyati. Tenāha “dūrībhūte”ti. Tamaṃyeva tamagataṃ “gūthagataṃ muttagata”nti (ma. ni. 2.119; a. ni. 9.11) yathā. Bhāsate ca tapate ca virocate ca idaṃ catutthaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ vibhajantena kusalakammapathassa vibhajitvā dassitattā.

486. `Ubbiddha` means far. For with the removal of defilements such as clouds and mist, the sky appears as if towering and distant. Therefore, it is said, 'become distant.' This is like 'darkness itself has gone to darkness,' as in 'gone to excrement, gone to urine' (MN 2.119; AN 9.11). And 'it shines, glows, and radiates'—this fourth undertaking of the Dhamma is so described because the path of wholesome action has been shown by analyzing it.

Saṅgararukkho [V 2.0276] kandamādasapova. Sarabhaññavasenāti atthaṃ avibhajitvā padaso sarabhaññavasena. Osārentassāti uccārentassa. Saddeti osāraṇasadde. Adhigatavisesaṃ anārocetukāmā devatā tattheva antaradhāyi. Taṃ divasanti satthārā desitadivase. Iti attano visesādhigamanimittatāya ayaṃ devatā imaṃ suttaṃ piyāyati. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

The Saṅgara tree is like a tree with sap from its root. 'By way of melodious recitation' means without analyzing the meaning, word by word, by way of melodious recitation. 'Of one who intones' means of one who utters. 'Sound' means the sound of intoning. The deity, not wishing to announce her special attainment, disappeared right there. 'That day' means on the day it was taught by the Teacher. Thus, because it was a sign of her own special attainment, this deity holds this sutta dear. The rest is clear.

Mahādhammasamādānasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The clarification of the hidden meaning in the Commentary on the Great Discourse on Undertakings is complete.

7. Vīmaṃsakasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Investigator's Discourse

487. Atthavīmaṃsakoti [M 2.0298][V 2.0277] attatthaparatthādiatthavijānanako. Saṅkhāravīmaṃsakoti saṅkhatadhamme salakkhaṇato sāmaññalakkhaṇato vā āyatanādivibhāgato ca vīmaṃsako. Satthuvīmaṃsakoti “satthā nāma guṇato ediso ediso cā”ti satthu upaparikkhako. Vīmaṃsakoti vicārako. Yaṃ cetaso sarāgādivibhāgato paricchindanaṃ, taṃ cetopariyāyo. Tenāha “cittapariccheda”nti. Yasmā cetopariyāyañāṇalābhī – “idaṃ cittaṃ ito paraṃ pavattaṃ idamito para”nti parassa cittuppattiṃ pajānāti, tasmā vuttaṃ “cetopariyāyanti cittavāra”nti. Vāratthepi hi pariyāya-saddo hoti – “kassa nu kho, ānanda, pariyāyo ajja bhikkhuniyo ovaditu”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.398). Cittacārantipi pāṭho, cittapavattinti attho. Evaṃ vijānanatthāyāti idāni vuccamānākārena vīmaṃsanatthāya.

487. 'An examiner of meaning' means one who knows meanings, such as one's own welfare and the welfare of others. 'An examiner of formations' means one who examines conditioned phenomena according to their specific characteristics or general characteristics, and according to classifications such as the sense bases. 'An examiner of the Teacher' means one who investigates the Teacher, thinking, 'The Teacher is endowed with such and such qualities.' 'Examiner' means an investigator. That which is the delimitation of the mind according to its divisions, such as with lust, is the penetration of minds. Hence, it is said, 'the delimitation of the mind.' Because one who has obtained the knowledge of the penetration of minds knows the arising of another’s mind, thinking, 'This mind has proceeded from this, this from that,' therefore it is said, 'penetration of minds means the course of the mind.' For the word 'pariyāya' also occurs in the sense of 'turn,' as in, 'Whose turn is it today, Ānanda, to advise the bhikkhunīs?' and so on (MN 3.398). There is also the reading 'cittacāra,' meaning 'the occurrence of the mind.' 'For the purpose of knowing thus' means for the purpose of examining in the manner now being described.

488. Kalyāṇamittūpanissayanti kalyāṇamittasaṅkhātaṃ brahmacariyavāsassa balavasannissayaṃ. Upaḍḍhaṃ attano ānubhāvenāti iminā puggalena sampādiyamānassa brahmacariyassa upaḍḍhabhāgamattaṃ attano vimuttiparipācakadhammānubhāvena sijjhati. Upaḍḍhaṃ kalyāṇamittānubhāvenāti itaro pana upaḍḍhabhāgo yaṃ nissāya brahmacariyaṃ vussati, tassa kalyāṇamittassa upadesānubhāvena hoti, sijjhatīti attho. Lokasiddho eva ayamattho. Lokiyā hi –

488. 'Strong dependence on good friends' means the strong support for the living of the holy life, which is known as 'good friends.' 'Half by one’s own power' means that half of the holy life being accomplished by this individual is achieved by the power of one's own qualities that ripen liberation. 'Half by the power of good friends' means that the other half of the holy life, which is lived in dependence on that good friend, is achieved by the power of that good friend’s instruction; this is the meaning. This meaning is indeed established in the world. For worldly people say:

“Pādo siddho ācariyā, pādo hissānubhāvato;

Taṃvijjāsevakā pādo, pādo kālena paccatī”ti. –

"One quarter is accomplished by the teacher, one quarter by one’s own power, one quarter by fellow practitioners of that knowledge, and one quarter matures in time."

Vadanti. Attano dhammatāyāti attano sabhāvena, ñāṇenāti attho. Kalyāṇamittatāti kalyāṇo bhadro sundaro mitto etassāti kalyāṇamitto, tassa bhāvo kalyāṇamittatā, kalyāṇamittavantatā. Sīlādiguṇasampannehi kalyāṇapuggaleheva ayanaṃ pavatti kalyāṇasahāyatā. Tesu eva cittena ceva kāyena ca ninnapoṇapabbhārabhāvena pavatti kalyāṇasampavaṅkatā. Māhevanti evaṃ mā āha, “upaḍḍhaṃ brahmacariyassā”ti mā kathehīti attho. Tadamināti ettha nti nipātamattaṃ [M 2.0299] da-kāro padasandhikaro i-kārassa a-kāraṃ katvā niddeso. Imināpīti idāni vuccamānenapīti [V 2.0278] attho. Pariyāyenāti kāraṇena. Idāni taṃ kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “mamaṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

They say. 'According to one's own nature' means by one's own inherent nature; the meaning is 'by knowledge.' Good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā) is defined thus: one who has a good, excellent, beautiful friend is a 'good friend'; the state of being such is 'good friendship,' the quality of having good friends. Association with good persons endowed with qualities such as virtue is 'good companionship' (kalyāṇasahāyatā). Association with them with mind and body inclined, devoted, and leaning toward them is 'good association' (kalyāṇasampavaṅkatā). 'Do not say so' means 'do not speak thus; do not say, "Half of the holy life."' Regarding 'tadaminā': here, 'ti' is a mere particle, the letter 'd' is for conjunction, and the explanation is given by changing 'i' to 'a'. 'Even by this' means 'even by what is now being said.' 'By this method' means 'for this reason.' Now, to show that reason, it was said, 'For it is because of me...' and so on.

Yathā cettha, aññesupi suttesu kalyāṇamittupanissayameva visesoti dassento “bhikkhūnaṃ bāhiraṅgasampattiṃ kathentopī”tiādimāha. Tattha vimuttiparipācaniyadhammeti vimuttiyā arahattassa paripācakadhamme. Paccayeti gilānapaccayabhesajje. Mahājaccoti mahākulīno.

And just as here, also in other suttas, to show that strong dependence on good friends is indeed the distinguishing factor, it is said, 'Even when speaking of the external accomplishments of the monks,' and so on. Therein, 'the qualities that ripen liberation' refers to the factors that mature liberation, that is, arahantship. 'Requisites' refers to medicines and requisites for the sick. 'Of great birth' means of a great family.

Kāyiko samācāroti abhikkamapaṭikkamādiko satisampajaññaparikkhato pākatiko ca. Vīmaṃsakassa upaparikkhakassa. Cakkhuviññeyyo nāma cakkhudvārānusārena viññātabbattā. Sotaviññeyyoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Saṃkiliṭṭhāti rāgādisaṃkilesadhammehi vibādhitā, upatāpitā vidūsitā malīnā cāti attho. Te pana tehi samannāgatā hontīti āha “kilesasampayuttā”ti. Yadi na cakkhusotaviññeyyā, pāḷiyaṃ kathaṃ tathā vuttāti āha “yathā panā”tiādi. Kāyavacīsamācārāpi saṃkiliṭṭhāyeva nāma saṃkiliṭṭhacittasamuṭṭhānato. Bhavati hi taṃhetukepi tadupacāro yathā “semho guḷo”ti. “Mā me idaṃ asāruppaṃ paro aññāsī”ti pana paṭicchannatāya na na upalabbhanti. “Na kho mayaṃ, bhante, bhagavato kiñci garahāmā”ti vatvā garahitabbābhāvaṃ dassento “bhagavā hī”tiādimāha. Abhāvitamaggassa hi garahitabbatā nāma siyā, na bhāvitamaggassa. Esa uttaro māṇavo “buddhampi garahitvā pakkamissāmī”ti katvā anubandhi. Evaṃ cintesi mahābhinikkhamanadivase attano vacane aṭṭhitattā. Kiñci vajjaṃ apassanto māro evamāha –

'Bodily conduct' refers to going forward and returning, and so on, which is surrounded by mindfulness and clear comprehension, and is natural. It is for the investigator, the examiner. 'Known by the eye' means it is knowable in accordance with the eye-door. 'Known by the ear' follows the same method here. 'Defiled' means oppressed, afflicted, corrupted, and stained by defiling states such as lust; this is the meaning. And they are endowed with those defilements, hence it is said, 'associated with defilements.' If they are not knowable by the eye or ear, how are they stated thus in the Pāli text? He says, 'But as follows,' and so on. Bodily and verbal conduct, too, are indeed called defiled because they arise from a defiled mind. For there is such a figurative usage for something based on its cause, as in 'phlegm-causing sugar.' But with the thought, 'May another not know this unseemly behavior of mine,' due to concealment, they are not perceived. Saying, 'Indeed, venerable sir, we do not blame the Blessed One for anything,' he shows there is nothing blameworthy by stating, 'for the Blessed One,' and so on. For one whose path is undeveloped, there might indeed be something blameworthy, but not for one whose path is developed. This young man Uttara, thinking, 'I will criticize even the Buddha and then leave,' followed him. Thus he thought, because on the day of the Great Renunciation, he did not stand firm in his own words. Seeing no fault whatsoever, Māra said thus—

“Satta vassāni bhagavantaṃ, anubandhiṃ padāpadaṃ;

Otāraṃ nādhigacchissaṃ, sambuddhassa satīmato”ti. (su. ni. 448);

"For seven years I followed the Blessed One, step by step; yet I could not find a flaw in the mindful Awakened One."

Kāle kaṇhā, kāle sukkāti yathāsamādinnaṃ sammāpaṭipattiṃ parisuddhaṃ katvā pavattetuṃ asakkontassa kadāci kaṇhā aparisuddhā kāyasamācārādayo, kadāci sukkā parisuddhāti evaṃ antarantarā byāmissavasena [M 2.0300] vomissakā. Nikkilesāti nirupakkilesā anupakkiliṭṭhā.

'At times dark, at times bright' means that for one who is unable to maintain the rightly undertaken practice in purity, there is sometimes dark, impure bodily conduct and the like, and sometimes bright, pure conduct; thus, from time to time, they are intermingled and mixed.

Anavajjaṃ vajjarahitattā. Dīgharattanti accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ. Samāpannoti sammā āpanno samaṅgībhūto. Tenāha “samannāgato”ti. Attanā katassa asāruppassa paṭicchādanatthaṃ āraññako [V 2.0279] viya hutvā. Tassa parihāranti uḷārehi pūjāsakkārehi manussehi tassa parihariyamānataṃ. Atidappitoti evaṃ manussānaṃ sambhāvanāya ativiya datto gabbito.

'Blameless' because it is devoid of fault. 'For a long time' is a usage in the sense of continuous connection. 'Attained' means rightly attained, endowed with. Therefore, it is said, 'endowed.' Like a forest-dweller, in order to conceal the unseemly behavior done by oneself. 'His being honored' means his being looked after by people with generous offerings and honors. 'Overly conceited' means being excessively arrogant and proud due to the esteem of people.

Na ittarasamāpannoti jānāti. Kasmā? Sīlaṃ nāma dīghena addhunā jānitabbaṃ, na ittarena. Idāni anekajātisamudācāravasena tathāgato imaṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ dīgharattaṃ samāpanno, tañcassa ativiya acchariyanti dassetuṃ “anacchariyaṃ ceta”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

He knows: 'This is not an attainment for a short while.' Why? For virtue is to be known over a long period, not a short one. Now, by way of conduct accumulated over many births, the Tathāgata has for a long time been endowed with this wholesome quality, and to show that this is exceedingly marvelous, it was said: 'And this is no wonder,' and so on.

Araññagāmaketi araññapadese ekasmiṃ khuddakagāme. Tattha nesaṃ divase divase piṇḍāya caraṇassa avicchinnataṃ dassetuṃ “piṇḍāya carantī”ti vuttaṃ. Pivantīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Dullabhaloṇo hoti samuddassa dūratāya.

"In a remote village" means in a small village in a remote area. To show the unbroken continuity of their going for alms day by day, it is said, "they go for alms." The same principle applies to "they drink." Salt was scarce due to its distance from the sea.

Tadā kira videharaṭṭhe soḷasa gāmasahassāni mahantāneva. Tenāha – “hitvā gāmasahassāni, paripuṇṇāni soḷasā”ti. Idāni kasmā “sannidhiṃ dāni kubbasī”ti maṃ ghaṭṭethāti vatthukāmo taṃ anāvikatvā “loṇa…pe… na karothā”ti āha. Gandhāro tassādhippāyaṃ vibhāvetukāmo “kiṃ mayā kataṃ vedehīsī”ti āha.

At that time, indeed, in the Videha country, there were sixteen thousand great villages. Therefore, it is said: "Having abandoned sixteen thousand fully prosperous villages." Now, wishing to state the matter, why do you harass me, saying, "Now you make an accumulation?" Without revealing that, he said, "Salt... do not do it." Gandhāra, wishing to reveal his purpose, said, "What have I done to you, Videhan?"

Itaro attano adhippāyaṃ vibhāvento “hitvā”ti gāthamāha. Itaro “dhammaṃ bhaṇāmī”ti gāthanti evaṃ sabbāpi nesaṃ vacanapaṭivacanagāthā. Tattha pasāsasīti ghaṭṭento viya anusāsasi.
