Na pāpamupalimpati cittappakopābhāvato. Mahatthiyanti mahāatthasaṃhitaṃ. No ce assa sakā buddhītiādi vedehaisino – “ācariyo mama hitesitāya ṭhatvā dhammaṃ eva bhaṇatī”ti yoniso ummujjanākāradassanaṃ. Tenāha “evañca pana vatvā”tiādi.

The other, revealing his own intention, spoke the verse beginning with "hitvā." The other spoke the verse "I speak the Dhamma." Thus, all their statements and replies are verses. There, "pasāsasi" means you instruct as if striking. "No evil defiles" because of the absence of mental agitation. "Mahatthiyaṃ" means connected with great purpose. "If he did not have his own wisdom," and so on, is the Videha sage's way of properly understanding, thinking, "The teacher, standing for my welfare, speaks only the Dhamma." Therefore, it is said, "And having said thus," and so on.

“Ñattā”ti loke ñāyati vissutoti ñāto, ñātassa bhāvo ñattaṃ. Ajjhāpannoti upagato. Ñatta-ggahaṇena patthaṭayasatā vibhāvitāti [M 2.0301] āha “yasañca parivārasampatti”nti. Kinti kiṃpayojanaṃ, ko ettha dosoti adhippāyo.

"Famous": he is known and renowned in the world; thus, he is known. The state of being known is fame. "Approached" means he has drawn near. By the mentioning of fame, widespread renown is clarified; therefore, it is said, "glory and the attainment of a retinue." "What?" means "what is the purpose, what is the fault here?"

Tattha tattha vijjhantoti yasamadena parivāramadena ca matto hutvā gāmepi vihārepi janavivittepi saṅghamajjhepi aññe bhikkhū ghaṭṭento “mayhaṃ nāma pādā itaresaṃ pādaphusanaṭṭhānaṃ phusantī”ti aphusitukāmatāya aggapādena bhūmiṃ phusanto viya carati. Onamatīti nivātavuttitāya avanamati anuddhato atthaddho hoti. Akiñcanabhāvanti “pabbajitena nāma akiñcanañāṇena [V 2.0280] samapariggahena bhavitabba”nti akiñcanajjhāsayaṃ paṭiavekkhitvā. Lābhepi tādī, alābhepi tādīti yathā alābhakāle lābhassa laddhakālepi tathevāti tādī ekasadiso. Yase satipi mahāparivārakālepi.

"Here and there he pierces" means that, intoxicated with fame and a retinue, whether in a village, a monastery, a solitary place, or amidst the Saṅgha, he jostles other monks thinking, "My feet touch the places where others' feet touch," and thus walks as if touching the ground only with the tip of his foot, out of a desire not to touch. "He bows down" means he is humble in conduct; he is not haughty, not stiff. Regarding the state of having nothing, he reflects on the disposition of having nothing, thinking, "A renunciant should have the knowledge of having nothing and be of equal possessions." "The same in gain, the same in loss" means that just as he is in a time of no-gain, so too is he when gain is obtained; thus he is the same, of one kind. This is so even when there is fame, even at a time of a great retinue.

Abhayo hutvā uparatoti nibbhayo hutvā bhayassa abhāveneva oramitabbato uparato bhayahetūnaṃ pahīnattā. Tañca kho na katipayakālaṃ, atha kho accantameva uparatoti accantūparato. Atha kho bhāyitabbavatthuṃ avekkhitvā tato bhayena uparato. Kilesā eva bhāyitabbato kilesabhayaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Satta sekkhāti satta sekkhāpi bhayūparatā, pageva puthujjanoti adhippāyo.

"Being fearless, he has ceased" means that, being fearless, he has desisted due to the very absence of fear, as the causes of fear have been abandoned. And this is not for a limited time; rather, he has ceased completely, thus he is "utterly ceased." Furthermore, having considered the object of fear, he has ceased from fear of it. Since the defilements themselves are to be feared, this is the fear of defilements. This same principle applies in the other cases. "The seven trainees": the meaning is that even the seven trainees have ceased from fear, to say nothing of an ordinary person.

Thaṇḍilapīṭhakanti thaṇḍilamañcasadisaṃ pīṭhakanti attho. Nissāyāti apassāya taṃ apassāyaṃ katvā. Dvinnaṃ majjhe thaṇḍilapīṭhakā dvāre ṭhatvā olokentassa nevāsikabhikkhussa na paññāyi. Asaññatanīhārenāti na saññatākārena. “Maṃ bhāyanto heṭṭhāmañcaṃ paviṭṭho bhavissatī”ti heṭṭhāmañcaṃ oloketvā. Ukkāsi “bahi gacchanto akkositvā mā apuññaṃ pasavī”ti. Adhivāsetunti tādisaṃ iddhānabhāvaṃ disvāpi paṭapaṭāyanto attano kodhaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto.

"Thaṇḍilapīṭhaka" means a seat similar to a ground-couch. "Nissāya" means leaning against it, having made it a support. The resident monk, standing in the doorway and looking between the two benches, was not seen. "Asaññatanīhārena" means not in a restrained manner. Thinking, "Fearing me, he must have entered under the bed," he looked under the bed. He coughed, thinking, "Lest, in going outside, he should curse me and generate demerit." Being unable to endure, even after seeing such a display of psychic power, he was grumbling and unable to control his own anger.

Khayenevāti rāgassa accantakkhayeneva vītarāgattā. Na paṭisaṅkhāya vāretvāti na paṭisaṅkhānabalena rāgapariyuṭṭhānaṃ nivāretvā vītarāgattā. Evaṃ vuttappakārena. Kāyasamācārādīnaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhānaṃ vītikkamiyānañca abhāvaṃ ācārassa vodānaṃ cirakālasamāciṇṇatāya ñātassa sahitabhāvepi anupakkiliṭṭhatāya abhayūparatabhāvasamannesanāya ākarīyati ñāpetuṃ icchito attho pakārato ñāpīyati etehīti ākārā, [M 2.0302] upapattisādhanakāraṇāni. Tāni pana yasmā attano yathānumatassa atthassa ñāpakabhāvena vavatthīyanti, tasmā tāni tesaṃ mūlakāraṇabhūtāni anumānañāṇāni ca dassento bhagavā – “ke panāyasmato ākārā ke anvayā”ti avocāti imamatthaṃ vibhāvento “ākārāti kāraṇāni, anvayāti anubuddhiyo”ti āha. Yathā hi loke diṭṭhena dhūmena adiṭṭhaṃ aggiṃ anveti anumānato jānāti, evaṃ vīmaṃsako bhikkhu – “bhagavā ekekavihāresu suppaṭipannesu duppaṭipannesu ca yathā ekasadisatādassanena abhayūparatataṃ anveti anumānato jānāti, suppaṭipannaduppaṭipannapuggalesu anussādanānapasādanappattāya satthu aviparītadhammadesanatāya sammāsambuddhataṃ saṅghasuppaṭipattiñca anveti anumānato jānāti, evaṃ jānanto ca abhayūparato tathāgato sabbadhi vītarāgattā, yo [V 2.0281] yattha vītarāgo, na so tannimittaṃ kiñci bhayaṃ passati seyyathāpi brahmā kāmabhavanimittaṃ, tathā sammāsambuddho bhagavā aviparītadhammadesanattā, svākhāto dhammo ekantaniyyānikattā, suppaṭipanno saṅgho aveccappasannattā”ti vatthuttayaṃ guṇato yāthāvato jānāti.

"Through destruction alone" means through the complete destruction of lust alone, due to being free from lust. "Not having restrained through reflection" means not having prevented the arising of lust by the power of reflection, due to being free from lust. Thus, in the manner described. The absence of defiled transgressions of bodily conduct and so on, the purity of conduct known through long practice, remaining undefiled even when in association with others—this is for the investigation of the state of being fearless and ceased. The desired meaning is made known in various ways by these; hence they are called "ākārā" (reasons), which are the causes for establishing the proof. Since these are determined by their nature of making known the meaning as one has inferred it, the Blessed One, showing that they are the root causes of those inferential knowledges, said, "What, then, venerable sir, are the reasons, what are the inferences?" Explaining this meaning, it is said, "'Ākārā' are causes, 'anvayā' are subsequent understandings." Just as in the world, from seen smoke one infers an unseen fire and knows it through inference, so too a discerning monk infers and knows through inference that the Blessed One is fearless and has ceased by observing his impartiality towards both the well-practiced and the ill-practiced in various dwellings; he infers and knows through inference the perfect enlightenment of the Teacher from his non-perverted teaching of the Dhamma, which applies to well-practiced and ill-practiced individuals through encouragement and criticism, and also the good practice of the Saṅgha. Knowing thus, he knows the three bases in reality according to their qualities: "The Tathāgata is fearless and has ceased, being free from lust everywhere; for whoever is free from lust in any regard sees no fear from that cause, just as a Brahmā sees no fear from the cause of the sensual realm of existence. Likewise, the Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One because his teaching of the Dhamma is not perverted; the Dhamma is well-proclaimed because it leads exclusively to deliverance; the Saṅgha is of good practice because it inspires unwavering confidence."

Gaṇabandhanenāti “mama saddhivihārikā mama antevāsikā”ti evaṃ gaṇe apekkhāsaṅkhātena bandhanena baddhā payuttā. Tāya tāya paṭipattiyāti “sugatā duggatā”ti vuttāya suppaṭipattiyā duppaṭipattiyā ca. Ussādanāti guṇavasena ukkaṃsanā. Apasādanāti hīḷanā. Ubhayattha gehassitavasenāti iminā sammāpaṭipattiyā paresaṃ uyyojanatthaṃ – “paṇḍito, bhikkhave, mahākaccāno”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.205; 3.285, 322) guṇato ukkaṃsanampi āyatiṃ saṃvarāya yathāparādhaṃ garahaṇampi na nivāreti.

"By the bond of a group" means being bound and yoked by the bond of attachment to a group, such as the thought, "These are my fellow residents, my pupils." "By this and that conduct" means by good conduct and bad conduct, which are described as "well-gone" and "ill-gone." "Ussādanā" means extolling based on virtues. "Apasādanā" means criticizing. Regarding "in both cases due to attachment": this shows that extolling based on virtues for the purpose of urging others towards right conduct—such as saying, "Wise, monks, is Mahākaccāna," etc.—does not preclude future restraint, nor does blaming according to the offense.

489. Vīmaṃsakassapi adhippāyo vīmaṃsanavasena pavatto. Mūlavīmaṃsako hetuvāditāya. Gaṇṭhivīmaṃsakassa anussutibhāvato vuttaṃ “parasseva kathāya niṭṭhaṅgato”ti. Tenāha bhagavā – “parassa cetopariyāyaṃ ajānantenā”ti. Tathāgatova paṭipucchitabboti iminā pubbe sādhāraṇato vuttaṃ anumānaṃ ukkaṃsaṃ pāpetvā vadati. Ukkaṃsagatañhetaṃ anumānaṃ, yadidaṃ sabbaññuvacanaṃ avisaṃvādaṃ sāmaññato aputhujjanagocarassa [M 2.0303] atthassa anumānato. Tividho hi attho, koci paccakkhasiddho, yo rūpādidhammānaṃ paccattavedaniyo aniddisitabbākāro. Koci anumānasiddho, yo ghaṭādīsu pasiddhena paccayāyattabhāvena sādhiyamāno saddādīnaṃ aniccatādiākāro. Koci okappanasiddho, yo pacurajanassa accantamadiṭṭho saddhāvisayo paralokanibbānādi. Tattha yassa satthuno vacanaṃ paccakkhasiddhe anumānasiddhe ca atthe na visaṃvādeti aviparītappavattiyā, tassa vacanena saddheyyatthasiddhi, saddheyyarūpā eva ca yebhuyyena satthuguṇā accantasambhavato.

489. For the examiner, the intention proceeds by way of examination. The root examiner argues from his causal reasoning. For the knot examiner, it is said, ‘he has come to a conclusion through another’s speech,’ due to it being hearsay. Therefore, the Blessed One said: ‘By one who does not know the course of another’s mind.’ By this statement, ‘The Tathāgata himself should be questioned,’ he speaks, having elevated the previously mentioned general inference to the highest level. This inference is indeed exalted, namely, that the word of the Omniscient One is non-contradictory, from the inference of a meaning that is generally beyond the scope of an ordinary person. For meaning is threefold: some is established by direct experience, which is the indescribable nature of phenomena such as form, to be experienced personally. Some is established by inference, which is the nature of impermanence and so on in sounds and other things, being proven through the well-known state of dependence on causes, as in the case of a pot and the like. Some is established by conviction, which is an object of faith utterly unseen by most people, such as the next world, Nibbāna, and so on. In this regard, when a teacher’s word does not contradict meanings established by direct experience and by inference, due to his non-erroneous conduct, then by his word there is the establishment of a meaning to be believed; and indeed, the qualities of the Teacher are for the most part of a nature to be believed, due to their being ultimately possible.

Esa mayhaṃ pathoti yvāyaṃ ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlasaṅkhāto mayhaṃ oramattako guṇo, esa aparacittaviduno vīmaṃsakassa bhikkhuno mama jānanapatho jānanamaggo. Esa gocaroti eso ettako eva tassa mayi gocaro, na ito paraṃ. Tathā hi brahmajālepi (dī. ni. 1.7) bhagavatā ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlameva niddiṭṭhaṃ. Etāpāthoti ettakāpātho. Yo sīle patiṭṭhito “etaṃ mamā”ti, “imināhaṃ sīlena devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā”ti taṇhāya parāmasanto, tassa [V 2.0282] visesabhāgiyatāya, nibbedhabhāgiyatāya vā akāraṇena taṇhaṃ anativattanato so tammayo nāma. Tenāha “na tammayo na sataṇho”tiādi.

‘This is my path’ means: this minor quality of mine, designated as the virtue ending with livelihood as the eighth, this is the path for knowing me, the way of knowing for an examining monk who knows another’s mind. ‘This is the pasture’ means: this much is his pasture in regard to me, not beyond this. For indeed, in the Brahmajāla Sutta, the Blessed One has pointed out only the virtue ending with livelihood as the eighth. ‘Etāpātha’ means a path of this extent. One who is established in virtue and clings to it with craving, thinking, ‘This is mine,’ and ‘By this virtue I will become a god or some other deity,’ is called ‘identified with that’ because he does not transcend craving, and because that virtue is not a cause for a share in distinction or a share in penetration. Therefore, it is said: ‘Not identified with that, not with craving,’ and so on.

Sutassa uparūpari visesāvahabhāvena uttaruttarañceva tassa ca visesassa anukkamena paṇītatarabhāvato paṇītatarañca katvā deseti. Savipakkhanti pahātabbapahāyakabhāvena sappaṭipakkhaṃ. Kaṇhaṃ paṭibāhitvā sukkanti idaṃ dhammajātaṃ kaṇhaṃ nāma, imassa pahāyakaṃ idaṃ sukkaṃ nāmāti evaṃ kaṇhaṃ paṭibāhitvā sukkaṃ. Sukkaṃ paṭibāhitvā kaṇhanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Idha pana “iminā pahātabba”nti vattabbaṃ. Saussāhanti sabyāpāraṃ. Kiriyamayacittānañhi anupacchinnāvijjātaṇhāmānādike santāne sabyāpāratā saussāhatā, savipākadhammatāti attho. Tasmiṃ desite dhammeti tasmiṃ satthārā desite lokiyalokuttaradhamme. Ekaccaṃ ekadesabhūtaṃ maggaphalanibbānasaṅkhātaṃ paṭivedhadhammaṃ abhiññāya abhivisiṭṭhāya maggapaññāya jānitvā. Paṭivedhadhammena maggena. Desanādhammeti desanāruḷhe pubbabhāgiye bodhipakkhiyadhamme niṭṭhaṃ gacchati – “addhā imāya [M 2.0304] paṭipadāya jarāmaraṇato muccissāmī”ti. Pubbe pothujjanikasaddhāyapi pasanno, tato bhiyyosomattāya aviparītadhammadesano sammāsambuddho so bhagavāti satthari pasīdati. Niyyānikattāti vaṭṭadukkhato eva tato niyyānāvahattā. Vaṅkādīti ādi-saddena aññaṃ asāmīcipariyāyaṃ sabbaṃ dosaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

He teaches by making what has been heard successively higher and more refined, due to its bringing about distinction upon distinction, and due to that distinction becoming progressively more sublime in sequence. ‘With its counterpart’ means with its opposite, in the sense of what is to be abandoned and what abandons it. ‘Having rejected the dark, the bright’ means: this class of things is called dark; this, which abandons it, is called bright. Thus, having rejected the dark, the bright. In ‘having rejected the bright, the dark,’ the method is the same, but here it should be stated, ‘to be abandoned by this.’ ‘With effort’ means with activity. For, in the case of functional consciousnesses, in the continuum where ignorance, craving, conceit, and so on are uninterrupted, activity is effort; the meaning is the state of having a result. ‘In that Dhamma which was taught’ means in that mundane and supramundane Dhamma taught by the Teacher. ‘Having directly known a certain part,’ that is, having known with the distinguished wisdom of the path a certain portion, the Dhamma of penetration, designated as path, fruit, and Nibbāna. ‘By the Dhamma of penetration’ means by the path. ‘In the Dhamma of the teaching’ means he comes to a conclusion regarding the preliminary wings to awakening that have come into the teaching, thinking: ‘Surely, by this practice, I will be freed from aging and death.’ Though previously confident with an ordinary person’s faith, he now gains confidence in the Teacher to a greater degree, thinking, ‘That Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One, a teacher of the non-perverted Dhamma.’ ‘Because it is emancipating’ means because it leads out from the suffering of the cycle. ‘Crookedness, etc.’: by the word ‘etc.’, every other fault, the improper course of conduct, is included.

490. Imehi satthuvīmaṃsanakāraṇehīti “parisuddhakāyasamācāratādīhi ceva uttaruttaripaṇītapaṇītaaviparītadhammadesanāhi cā”ti imehi yathāvuttehi satthuupaparikkhanakāraṇehi. Akkharasampiṇḍanapadehīti tesaṃyeva kāraṇānaṃ sambodhanehi akkharasamudāyalakkhaṇehi padehi. Idha vuttehi akkharehīti imasmiṃ sutte vuttehi yathāvuttassa atthassa abhibyañjanato byañjanasaññitehi akkharehi. Okappanāti saddheyyavatthuṃ okkantitvā pasīdanato okappanalakkhaṇā. Saddhāya mūlaṃ nāmāti aveccappasādabhūtāya saddhāya mūlaṃ nāma kāraṇanti saddahanassa kāraṇaṃ parisuddhakāyasamācārādikaṃ. Thirā paṭipakkhasamucchedena suppatiṭṭhitattā. Harituṃ na sakkāti apanetuṃ asakkuṇeyyā. Itaresu samaṇabrāhmaṇadevesu vattabbameva natthīti āha “samitapāpasamaṇena vā”tiādi.

490. ‘By these reasons for examining the Teacher’ means by these aforesaid reasons for scrutinizing the Teacher, that is, ‘by purity of bodily conduct and so forth, and by the teachings of the Dhamma that are successively sublime and non-perverted.’ ‘By terms that are groupings of syllables’ means by the terms which are designations of those very reasons and are characterized by a collection of syllables. ‘By the syllables stated here’ means by the syllables mentioned in this sutta, which are designated as expressions because they manifest the aforesaid meaning. ‘Conviction’ is characterized by conviction because one becomes confident after having settled upon a believable object. ‘The root of faith’ means the cause of faith that has become verified confidence; the cause of belief is purity of bodily conduct and so forth. ‘Firm’ because it is well-established through the eradication of its opposite. ‘Cannot be carried away’ means one would be unable to remove it. Regarding other ascetics, brahmins, and devas, there is nothing to be said, thus he said, ‘by an ascetic who has stilled evil,’ and so on.

“Buddhānaṃ [V 2.0283] kesañci sāvakānañca vibādhanatthaṃ māro upagacchatī”ti sutapubbattā “ayaṃ māro āgato”ti cintesi. Ānubhāvasampannena ariyasāvakena pucchitattā musāvādaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhi. Eteti yathāvutte samitapāpasamaṇādayo ṭhapetvā. Sabhāvasamannesanāti yāthāvasamannesanā aviparītavīmaṃsā. Sabhāvenevāti sabbhāveneva yathābhūtaguṇato eva. Suṭṭhu sammadeva. Samannesitoti upaparikkhito. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

Because he had previously heard, ‘Māra approaches to obstruct some Buddhas and their disciples,’ he thought, ‘This Māra has come.’ Being questioned by a noble disciple endowed with spiritual power, he was unable to speak a falsehood. ‘These’ means excluding the aforesaid ascetics who have stilled evil and so forth. ‘Investigation into the intrinsic nature’ means investigation according to reality, a non-perverted examination. ‘By its intrinsic nature’ means by its true nature, from its quality as it really is. ‘Thoroughly and rightly.’ ‘Investigated’ means scrutinized. The rest is easily understood.

Vīmaṃsakasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The explanation of the Vīmaṃsaka Sutta, which reveals its recondite meaning, is concluded.

8. Kosambiyasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Kosambiya Sutta

491. Tasmāti [V 2.0284] yasmā kosambarukkhavatī, tasmā nagaraṃ kosambītisaṅkhamagamāsi. Kusambassa vā isino nivāsabhūmi kosambī, tassāvidūre bhavattā nagaraṃ kosambī.

491. ‘Therefore’ means: because it possessed Kosamba trees, the city came to be known as Kosambī. Or, Kosambī was the dwelling place of the sage Kusamba; because the city was not far from it, it was called Kosambī.

Ghositaseṭṭhinā [M 2.0305] kārite ārāmeti ettha ko ghositaseṭṭhi, kathañcānena ārāmo kāritoti antolīnāya codanāya vissajjane samudāgamato paṭṭhāya ghositaseṭṭhiṃ dassetuṃ “addilaraṭṭhaṃ nāma ahosī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Kedāraparicchinnanti tattha tattha kedārabhūmiyā paricchinnaṃ. Gacchantoti kedārapāḷiyā gacchanto. Pahūtapāyasanti pahūtataraṃ pāyasaṃ, taṃ pana garu siniddhaṃ antarāmagge appāhāratāya mandagahaṇiko samāno jīrāpetuṃ nāsakkhi. Tenāha “jīrāpetuṃ asakkonto”tiādi. Yasavati rūpavati kulaghare nibbatti. Ghositaseṭṭhi nāma jātoti evamettha saṅkhepeneva ghositaseṭṭhivatthuṃ katheti, vitthāro pana dhammapadavatthumhi (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.sāmāvatīvatthu) vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Regarding ‘in the park built by the merchant Ghosita’: in the answer to the implicit question, “Who is Ghosita the merchant, and how was the park built by him?” the passage beginning, “There was a country named Addila,” was started in order to show the merchant Ghosita from his origin. ‘Bounded by fields’ means bounded here and there by paddy field land. ‘Going’ means going along the embankment of a paddy field. ‘Abundant milk-rice’ means very abundant milk-rice. But since it was heavy and rich, and he had little food on the way, he had slow digestion and was unable to digest it. Therefore, it is said, ‘Unable to digest,’ and so on. She was born in a good family, famous and beautiful. ‘Ghosita the merchant was born’: thus here the story of the merchant Ghosita is told only in brief; the detailed account, however, should be understood in the way it is told in the story in the Dhammapada Commentary (the story of Sāmāvatī).

Upasaṃkappanavasenāti upasaṅkappananiyāmena. Āhāraparikkhīṇakāyassāti āhāranimittaparikkhīṇakāyassa, āhārakkhayena parikkhīṇakāyassāti attho. Suññāgāreti janavivitte phāsukaṭṭhāne.

‘By way of applying’ means by the method of applying. ‘For one whose body is exhausted by food’ means for one whose body is exhausted with regard to the sign of food; the meaning is, for one whose body is depleted by the exhaustion of food. ‘In an empty dwelling’ means in a comfortable place secluded from people.

Kalahassa pubbabhāgo bhaṇḍanaṃ nāmāti kalahassa hetubhūtā paribhāsā taṃsadisī ca aniṭṭhakiriyā bhaṇḍanaṃ nāma. Hatthaparāmāsādivasenāti kujjhitvā aññamaññassa hatthe gahetvā parāmasanaaccantabandhanādivasena. “Ayaṃ dhammo”tiādinā viruddhavādabhūtaṃ āpannāti vivādāpannā. Tenāha “viruddhabhūta”ntiādi. Mukhasannissitatāya vācā idha “mukha”nti adhippetāti āha “mukhasattīhīti vācāsattīhī”ti. Saññattinti saññāpanaṃ “ayaṃ dhammo, ayaṃ vinayo”ti saññāpetabbataṃ. Nijjhattinti yāthāvato tassa nijjhānaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “saññattivevacanameveta”nti vuttaṃ.

Kalahassa pubbabhāgo bhaṇḍanaṃ nāma (the preceding part of a quarrel is called 'bhaṇḍanaṃ') means the abusive language and similar disagreeable actions that are the cause of a quarrel are called 'bhaṇḍanaṃ'. Hatthaparāmāsādivasena (by means of touching with the hand, and so forth) means by seizing each other's hands in anger, touching, excessive binding, and so forth. By 'This is the Dhamma,' and so forth, they have fallen into a state of conflicting arguments (viruddhavādabhūtaṃ āpannā), that is, they are engaged in dispute (vivādāpannā). Therefore it was said, 'of a conflicting nature,' and so forth. Because speech is associated with the mouth, here 'mouth' is intended (adhippetaṃ); hence it is said, 'by the spears of the mouth (mukhasattīhi),' meaning 'by the spears of speech (vācāsattīhi).' Saññatti means making known, that which is to be made known: 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya.' Nijjhatti means the thorough understanding of it as it is. In the commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, it is said, 'This is merely a synonym for saññatti.'

Sace hoti desessāmīti subbacatāya sikkhākāmatāya ca āpattiṃ passi. Natthi te āpattīti [V 2.0285] anāpattipakkhopi ettha sambhavatīti adhippāyenāha. Sā panāpatti eva. Tenāha – “tassā āpattiyā anāpattidiṭṭhi ahosī”ti.

If it is so, thinking, 'I will confess,' he sees an offense due to his docility and desire for training. 'There is no offense for you'—this is said with the intention that here the side of non-offense is also possible. But it is indeed an offense. Therefore, it is said: 'Regarding that offense, he had the view of non-offense.'

492. Kalahabhaṇḍanavasenāti kalahabhaṇḍanassa nimittavasena. Yathānusandhināva gatanti kalahabhaṇḍanānaṃ sāraṇīyadhammapaṭipakkhattā tadupasamāvahā [M 2.0306] heṭṭhādesanāya anurūpāva uparidesanāti yathānusandhināva uparisuttadesanā pavattā. Saritabbayuttāti anussaraṇārahā. Sabrahmacārīnanti sahadhammikānaṃ. Piyaṃ piyāyitabbaṃ karontīti piyakaraṇā. Garuṃ garuṭṭhāniyaṃ karontīti garukaraṇā. Saṅgahaṇatthāyāti saṅgahavatthuvisesabhāvato sabrahmacārīnaṃ saṅgaṇhanāya saṃvattantīti sambandho. Avivādanatthāyāti saṅgahavatthubhāvato eva na vivādanāya. Sati ca avivādanahetubhūtasaṅgāhaṇatte tesaṃ vasena sabrahmacārīnaṃ samaggabhāvo bhedābhāvo siddhoyevāti āha “sāmaggiyā”tiādi. Mijjati siniyhati etāyāti mettā, mittabhāvo, mettā etassa atthīti mettaṃ, kāyakammaṃ. Taṃ pana yasmā mettāsahagatacittasamuṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “mettacittena kattabbaṃ kāyakamma”nti. Imāni mettakāyakammādīni bhikkhūnaṃ vasena āgatāni pāṭhe bhikkhūhi paccupaṭṭhapetabbatāvacanato. Bhikkhuggahaṇeneva cettha sesasahadhammikānampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Bhikkhuno sabbampi anavajjakāyakammaṃ ābhisamācārikakammantogadhamevāti āha – “mettacittena…pe… kāyakammaṃ nāmā”ti. Vattavasena pavattiyamānā cetiyabodhīnaṃ vandanā mettāsadisīti katvā tadatthāya gamanaṃ mettaṃ kāyakammanti vuttaṃ. Ādi-saddena cetiyabodhibhikkhūsu vuttāvasesaapacāyanādiṃ mettāvasena pavattaṃ kāyikaṃ kiriyaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

492. Kalahabhaṇḍanavasena (on account of quarrels and disputes) means on account of the causes of quarrels and disputes. Yathānusandhināva gataṃ (following the connection) means that since quarrels and disputes are opposed to the qualities conducive to friendliness, the subsequent discourse, which is conducive to their subsiding, follows appropriately after the previous teaching, being in accordance with the connection. Saritabbayutta (fit to be remembered) means deserving to be remembered. Sabrahmacārīnaṃ (of fellow practitioners) means of those who share the same Dhamma. Piyaṃ piyāyitabbaṃ karontīti piyakaraṇā (making for endearment) means behaving in a way that fosters affection. Garuṃ garuṭṭhāniyaṃ karontīti garukaraṇā (making for respect) means behaving in a way that fosters reverence. Saṅgahaṇatthāya (for the sake of inclusion) means that, due to their nature as special grounds for fostering harmony, they lead to the unification of fellow practitioners—this is the connection. Avivādanatthāya (for the sake of non-dispute) means that, due to their nature as grounds for fostering harmony, they prevent disputes. And when there is harmony that is the cause of non-dispute, the unity and absence of division among fellow practitioners are certainly achieved through these qualities; thus it is said: 'for the sake of unity (sāmaggiyā),' and so forth. Mettā is so called because through it one is softened (mijjati) and feels affection (siniyhati); it is the state of a friend. A bodily action is called mettaṃ because it possesses mettā. Because it arises from a mind imbued with loving-kindness, it is said: 'Bodily action should be done with a loving mind.' These loving bodily actions, and so forth, are mentioned in the text in relation to monks because it is said that monks should establish them. However, by the mention of monks, it should be understood that other fellow practitioners are also included. For a monk, all blameless bodily actions are included within the scope of proper conduct. Hence it is said: 'Bodily action done with a loving mind... is called such (kāyakammaṃ nāmā).' Actions performed as a duty, such as paying homage to shrines (cetiya) and Bodhi trees, are considered akin to loving-kindness. Therefore, going for such purposes is called 'loving bodily action.' By the term 'and so forth' (ādi-saddena), it includes other respectful actions toward shrines, Bodhi trees, and monks, as well as any physical acts performed with loving-kindness.

Tepiṭakampi buddhavacanaṃ kathiyamānanti adhippāyo. Tīṇi sucaritāni kāyavacīmanosucaritāni. Cintananti iminā evaṃ cintanamattampi mettaṃ manokammaṃ, pageva vidhipaṭipannā bhāvanāti dasseti.

The intention is that the Tipiṭaka, too, is spoken of as the word of the Buddha. The three good conducts are good conduct of body, speech, and mind. By 'thinking' (cintanaṃ), it shows that even mere thinking in this way is a mental act of loving-kindness, how much more so systematic meditation practice.

Sahāyabhāvūpagamanaṃ tesaṃ purato. Tesu karontesuyeva hi sahāyabhāvūpagamanaṃ sammukhā kāyakammaṃ nāma hoti. Kevalaṃ “devo”ti avatvā guṇehi thirabhāvajotanaṃ devattheroti vacanaṃ paggayha vacanaṃ. Mamattabodhanaṃ vacanaṃ mamāyanavacanaṃ. Ekantatirokkhakassa manokammassa sammukhatā nāma viññattisamuṭṭhāpanavaseneva hoti, tañca kho loke kāyakammanti pākaṭaṃ paññātaṃ hatthavikārādiṃ anāmasitvā eva [M 2.0307] dassento “nayanāni ummīletvā”ti āha. Tathā hi vacībhedavasena pavatti na gahitā.

The act of approaching them as friends was before them. For, even while they were doing so, the act of approaching as friends right in front of them is called a bodily action. Not merely saying 'deva,' the word 'devatthera' is an uplifting speech that illuminates the firmness of his qualities. A speech expressing 'mineness' is a word of possessiveness. The presence of a mental action, which is entirely concealed, is manifested only through the arising of communication; and showing this, without referring to things like hand gestures which are widely known in the world as 'bodily action,' he said, 'having opened the eyes.' For in that way, an occurrence by means of a verbal distinction is not taken.

Laddhapaccayā [V 2.0286] labbhantīti lābhā, parisuddhāgamanā paccayā. Na sammā gayhamānāpi na dhammaladdhā nāma na hontīti tappaṭisedhanatthaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “dhammaladdhā”ti vuttaṃ. Deyyaṃ dakkhiṇeyyañca appaṭivibhattaṃ katvā bhuñjatīti appaṭivibhattabhogī. Tenāha “dve paṭivibhattāni nāmā”tiādi. Cittena vibhajananti etena – “cittuppādamattenapi vibhajanaṃ paṭivibhattaṃ nāma, pageva payogato”ti dasseti.

Gains (lābhā) are so called because they are obtained when the conditions for them are obtained; these are conditions of pure acquisition. To negate the idea that gains are lawfully obtained even when not properly acquired, the Pāli text states 'lawfully obtained' (dhammaladdhā). One who enjoys without having divided what is suitable for giving and what is suitable for offerings is called 'one who enjoys without division' (appaṭivibhattabhogī). Therefore it is said, 'There are two divisions (dve paṭivibhattāni),' and so forth. By 'dividing with the mind' (cittena vibhajanaṃ), it shows that 'even dividing with a mere thought is called dividing; how much more so, dividing through action.'

Paṭiggaṇhantova…pe… passatīti iminā āgamanato paṭṭhāya sādhāraṇabuddhiṃ upaṭṭhāpeti. Evaṃ hissa sādhāraṇabhogitā sukarā, sāraṇīyadhammo cassa supūro hoti. Vattanti sāraṇīyadhammapūraṇavattaṃ.

Paṭiggaṇhantova…pe… passatīti (even while receiving... seeing)—by this, he establishes an awareness of commonality from the time of arrival. For in this way, his sharing of requisites is easy, and his qualities conducive to friendliness are well fulfilled. Vattaṃ (practice) means the practice of fulfilling the qualities conducive to friendliness.

Dātabbanti avassaṃ dātabbaṃ. Attano palibodhavasena sapalibodhasseva pūretuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā odissakadānampissa na sabbattha vāritanti dassetuṃ “tena panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Adātumpīti pi-saddena dussīlassapi atthikassa sati sambhave dātabbanti dasseti. Dānañhi nāma kassaci na nivāritaṃ.

Dātabbanti (what should be given) means it must certainly be given. To show that specific giving is not always prohibited for him, since one with personal obstacles might not be able to fulfill a commitment entirely because of those obstacles, it is said, 'but in that case (tena pana),' and so forth. Adātumpīti (even not giving)—the particle 'pi' indicates that even to an immoral person, if he is needy and there is a possibility, it should be given. For giving is not forbidden to anyone.

Mahāgirigāmo nāma nāgadīpapasse eko gāmo. Sāraṇīyadhammo me, bhante, pūrito…pe… pattagataṃ na khīyatīti āha tesaṃ kukkuccavinodanatthaṃ. Taṃ sutvā tepi therā “sāraṇīyadhammapūrako aya”nti abbhaññaṃsu. Daharakāle eva kiresa sāraṇīyadhammapūrako ahosi, tassā ca paṭipattiyā avañjhabhāvavibhāvanatthaṃ “ete mayhaṃ pāpuṇissantī”ti āha.

Mahāgirigāma is a village near Nāgadīpa. 'My qualities conducive to friendliness, venerable sir, are fulfilled... the contents in the bowl do not diminish,' he said in order to dispel their unease. Having heard that, those elders acknowledged, 'This one is a fulfiller of qualities conducive to friendliness.' Even in his youth, it seems, he was a fulfiller of qualities conducive to friendliness, and to demonstrate the unfailing nature of his practice, he said, 'These will come to me.'

Ahaṃ sāraṇīyadhammapūrikā, mama pattapariyāpannenapi sabbāpimā bhikkhuniyo yāpessantīti āha “mā tumhe tesaṃ gatabhāvaṃ cintayitthā”ti.

Thinking, 'I am a fulfiller of qualities conducive to friendliness; even with what is contained in my bowl, all these nuns will be able to maintain themselves,' she said, 'Do not you all worry about their plight.'

Sattasu āpattikkhandhesu ādimhi vā ante vā, vemajjheti ca idaṃ uddesāgatapāḷivasena vuttaṃ. Na hi añño koci āpattikkhandhānaṃ anukkamo atthi. Pariyante chinnasāṭako viyāti vatthante, dasante vā chinnavatthaṃ viya. Khaṇḍanti khaṇḍavantaṃ, khaṇḍitaṃ vā. Chiddanti etthāpi eseva nayo[M 2.0308]. Visabhāgavaṇṇena upaḍḍhaṃ, tatiyabhāgaṃ vā sambhinnavaṇṇaṃ sabalaṃ, visabhāgavaṇṇeheva pana bindūhi antarantarā vimissaṃ kammāsaṃ, ayaṃ imesaṃ viseso. Taṇhādāsabyato mocanavacaneneva tesaṃ sīlānaṃ vivaṭṭupanissayatamāha. Bhujissabhāvakaraṇatoti iminā bhujissakarāni bhujissānīti uttarapadalopenāyaṃ niddesoti dasseti. Aviññūnaṃ appamāṇatāya [V 2.0287] “viññuppasatthānī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṇhādiṭṭhīhi aparāmaṭṭhattāti – “imināhaṃ sīlena devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā”ti taṇhāparāmāsena – “imināhaṃ sīlena devo hutvā tattha nicco dhuvo sassato bhavissāmī”ti diṭṭhiparāmāsena ca aparāmaṭṭhattā. Parāmaṭṭhunti codetuṃ. Sīlaṃ nāma avippaṭisārādipārampariyena yāvadeva samādhisampādanatthanti āha “samādhisaṃvattakānī”ti. Samānabhāvo sāmaññaṃ, paripuṇṇacatupārisuddhibhāvena majjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇassa viya bhedābhāvato sīlena sāmaññaṃ sīlasāmaññaṃ, taṃ gato upagatoti sīlasāmaññagato. Tenāha “samānabhāvūpagatasīlo”ti.

Regarding the seven classes of offenses, 'at the beginning, at the end, or in the middle' is stated according to the Pāli text that has come down by recitation. For there is no other sequence for the classes of offenses. 'At the edge, like a torn robe' means at the border or at the end, like a torn cloth. 'Fragmented' (khaṇḍa) means having fragments, or broken. For 'flawed' (chidda), the principle is the same. 'Mottled' (sabala) means that half or a third part is of a mixed color, with a dissimilar color. 'Variegated' (kammāsa) means interspersed with spots of dissimilar colors; this is the distinction between them. By the statement of 'liberation from the slavery of craving,' he indicates that those virtues are supportive of turning away from the cycle of rebirth. By 'making one a free man,' he shows that this is a description by way of elision of the latter word, as in bhujissakarāni becoming bhujissāni. Because the ignorant are no measure, it is said, 'praised by the wise.' 'Not adhered to by craving and views' means not adhered to by the craving-adherence, 'By this virtue, I will become a god or some other god,' nor by the view-adherence, 'By this virtue, having become a god, I will be eternal, permanent, and everlasting there.' 'Adhered to' is stated in order to challenge this. Virtue is said to be 'conducive to concentration' because, through the sequence beginning with non-remorse, it is for the sole purpose of accomplishing concentration. 'Sameness' (sāmañña) is an equal state. Just as there is no break in the middle of refined gold due to its state of complete fourfold purity, so there is sameness in virtue; this is virtue-sameness (sīlasāmañña). One who has gone to, has reached that, is 'one who has attained virtue-sameness.' Therefore, he says, 'one whose virtue has attained a state of sameness.'

Yāyaṃ diṭṭhīti yā ayaṃ diṭṭhi mayhañceva tumhākañca paccakkhabhūtā. Catusaccadassanaṭṭhena diṭṭhi, “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā, sabbe dhammā anattā”ti, “sammāsambuddho bhagavā, svākhāto bhagavatā dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṅgho”ti ca diṭṭhiyā sāmaññaṃ samānadiṭṭhibhāvaṃ. Aggaṃ itaresaṃ sāraṇīyadhammānaṃ padhānabhāvato. Etasmiṃ sati sukhasiddhito tesaṃ saṅgāhikaṃ, tato eva tesaṃ saṅghāṭanikaṃ gopānasiyo aparipatante katvā saṅgaṇhāti dhāretīti saṅgāhikaṃ. Saṅghāṭanti aggabhāvena saṅghāṭabhāvaṃ. Saṅghāṭanaṃ etesaṃ atthīti saṅghāṭanikaṃ, saṅghāṭaniyanti vā pāṭho, saṅghāṭane niyuttanti vā saṅghāṭanikaṃ, ka-kārassa ya-kāraṃ katvā saṅghāṭaniyaṃ. Sāmaññato eva gahitattā napuṃsakaniddeso.

'This view' means this view which is directly evident to both me and you. 'View' (diṭṭhi) is in the sense of seeing the Four Noble Truths. 'Sameness of view' (diṭṭhiyā sāmaññaṃ) means the state of having a common view (samānadiṭṭhibhāvaṃ), such as 'All conditioned formations are impermanent, all conditioned formations are suffering, all things are not-self,' and 'The Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened one, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Saṅgha is practicing the good way.' It is 'supreme' (aggaṃ) among the other qualities of concord because it is primary. When this is present, because happiness is accomplished, it is 'unifying' (saṅgāhikaṃ) for them. From that itself, it is what 'binds them together' (saṅghāṭanikaṃ). Like rafters, by preventing them from falling apart, it holds them together and supports them; thus it is 'unifying' (saṅgāhikaṃ). 'Binding' (saṅghāṭa) means the state of binding, due to being foremost. 'That which binds' (saṅghāṭanikaṃ) is so called because it possesses binding. Or the reading is saṅghāṭaniyaṃ. Or, because it is employed in binding, it is saṅghāṭanikaṃ; by changing the letter 'ka' to 'ya', it becomes saṅghāṭaniyaṃ. The neuter designation is used because it is taken in a general sense.

493. Paṭhamamaggasammādiṭṭhipi evaṃsabhāvā, aññamaggasammādiṭṭhīsu vattabbameva natthīti āha “yāyaṃ sotāpattimaggadiṭṭhī”ti. Ettāvatāpīti ettakenapi rāgādīsu ekekena pariyuṭṭhitacittatāyapi pariyuṭṭhitacittoyeva nāma hoti, pageva dvīhi, bahūhi vā pariyuṭṭhitacittatāya. Sabbatthāti sabbesu aṭṭhasupi vāresu. Suṭṭhu ṭhapitanti yathā maggabhāvanā upari saccābhisambodho hoti, evaṃ sammā ṭhapitaṃ. Tenāha “saccānaṃ bodhāyā”ti. Taṃ ñāṇanti [M 2.0309] “natthi kho me taṃ pariyuṭṭhāna”ntiādinā pavattaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. Ariyānaṃ hotīti ariyānameva hoti. Tesañhi ekadesatopi pahīnaṃ vattabbataṃ arahati. Tenāha “na puthujjanāna”nti. Ariyanti vuttaṃ “ariyesu jāta”nti katvā. Lokuttarahetukatāya lokuttaranti vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “yesaṃ panā”tiādi. Tathā hissa puthujjanehi asādhāraṇatā. Tenāha “puthujjanānaṃ pana abhāvato”ti. Sabbavāresūti sabbesu itaresu chasu vāresu.

493. The right view of the first path is of such a nature; regarding the right view in the other paths, there is nothing more to be said. Hence he says, 'this right view of the stream-entry path.' 'Even to this extent' means that even when the mind is overwhelmed by just one of these, such as lust, it is still called 'a mind that is overwhelmed,' how much more so when it is overwhelmed by two or many. 'In all cases' means in all eight instances. 'Well-established' means rightly established, in such a way that after the development of the path there is the full awakening to the truths. Therefore, he says, 'for the awakening to the truths.' 'That knowledge' is the reviewing knowledge that proceeds with, 'For me, that obsession is no more,' and so on. 'It belongs to the noble ones' means it belongs only to the noble ones. For in their case, what is abandoned even in part is worthy of being mentioned. Therefore, he says, 'not for worldlings.' 'Noble' is said because it is 'born among the noble ones.' It is called 'supramundane' because its cause is supramundane. For that reason, he says, 'But for those,' and so on. For in this way, it is not shared by worldlings. Therefore, he says, 'but due to its absence for worldlings.' 'In all instances' means in all the remaining six instances.

494. Paccattanti pāṭiyekkaṃ attani mama citteyeva. Tenāha “attano citte”ti. “Paccattaṃ [V 2.0288] attano citte nibbutiṃ kilesavūpasamaṃ labhāmī”ti imamatthaṃ “eseva nayo”ti iminā atidisati.

494. 'Personally' (paccattaṃ) means individually, within oneself, in my own mind. Therefore, he says, 'in one's own mind.' The meaning, 'Personally, in my own mind, I obtain extinguishment, the calming of defilements,' is referred to by the phrase, 'this is the method.'

495. Tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyāti idaṃ “yathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā samannāgato”ti imassa atthassa paccāmasananti āha “tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyāti evarūpāya sotāpattimaggadiṭṭhiyā”ti.

495. 'With such a view'—this is a restatement of the meaning of 'endowed with a view of such a kind.' Therefore, he says, 'with such a view means with a view of this kind, namely, the right view of the stream-entry path.'

496. Sabhāvenāti niyatapañcasikkhāpadatādisabhāvena. Saṅghakammavasenāti mānattacariyādisaṅghakammavasena. Daharoti bālo. Kumāroti dārako. Yasmā daharo “kumāro”ti ca “yuvā”ti ca vuccati, tasmā mandoti vuttaṃ. Mandindriyatāya hi mando. Tenāha “cakkhusotādīnaṃ mandatāyā”ti. Evampi yuvāvatthāpi keci mandindriyā hontīti tannivattanatthaṃ “uttānaseyyako”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi uttānaseyyako, kathamassa aṅgārakkamananti? Yathā tathā aṅgārassa phusanaṃ idha “akkamana”nti adhippetanti āha “ito cito cā”tiādi. Manussānanti mahallakamanussānaṃ. Na sīghaṃ hattho jhāyati kathinahatthatāya. Khippaṃ paṭisaṃharati mudutaluṇasarīratāya. Adhivāseti kiñci payojanaṃ apekkhitvā.

496. 'By nature' means by the inherent nature of being fixed in the five training rules, and so on. 'By way of a formal act of the Saṅgha' means by way of a formal act of the Saṅgha, such as the mānatta penance. 'Young' (daharo) means a child. 'Boy' (kumāro) means a child. Because a young one is called 'boy' and 'youth,' therefore 'dull' (mando) is said. For one is dull due to dullness of faculties. Therefore, he says, 'due to the dullness of the eye, ear, and so on.' Even so, some in a state of youth may have dull faculties; to preclude this, 'lying on his back' is said. If he is lying on his back, how can there be treading on embers for him? Any touching of the embers is here intended as 'treading'; therefore he says, 'from here and there,' and so on. 'Of humans' means of adult humans. The hand does not burn quickly due to its toughness. He withdraws it swiftly due to the softness and tenderness of his body. 'He endures,' expecting some purpose.

497. Uccāvacānīti mahantāni ceva khuddakāni ca. Tatthevāti sudhākammādimhiyeva. Kasāvapacanaṃ sudhādisaṅkharaṇatthaṃ, udakānayanaṃ dhovanādiatthaṃ, haliddivaṇṇadhātulepanatthaṃ kucchakaraṇaṃ. Bahalapatthanoti daḷhachando. Vacchakanti nibbattadhenupagavacchaṃ. Apacinātīti apavindati, āloketīti [M 2.0310] attho. Tenāha “apaloketī”ti. Tanninno hotīti adhisīlasikkhādininnova hoti uccāvacānampi kiṃkaraṇīyānaṃ cārittasīlassa pūraṇavaseneva karaṇato, yonisomanasikāravaseneva ca tesaṃ paṭipajjanato. Therassa santike aṭṭhāsi yonisomanasikārābhāvato “taṃ taṃ samullapissāmī”ti.

497. 'High and low' means both large and small. 'Therein' means in plastering work and so on. 'Cooking astringent substances' is for preparing plaster and the like; 'fetching water' is for washing and so on; 'making a brush' is for applying turmeric-colored mineral pigment. 'Strong in longing' means firm in intention. 'A calf' means a calf that has approached a cow that has given birth. 'He discerns' (apacināti) means he finds, that is, he observes. Therefore, he says, 'he observes' (apaloketi). 'He is inclined towards that' means he is inclined towards the training in higher virtue and so on, because he performs even the various high and low duties that need to be done solely for the sake of fulfilling the virtue of conduct, and because he undertakes them with wise attention. He stood near the elder, and due to a lack of wise attention, thought, 'I will chatter about this and that.'

498. Balaṃ eva balatāti āha “balena samannāgato”ti. Atthikabhāvaṃ katvāti tena dhammena savisesaṃ atthikabhāvaṃ uppādetvā. Sakalacittenāti desanāyaādimhi majjhe pariyosāneti sabbattheva pavattatāya sakalena anavasesena cittena.

498. As 'strength-ness' (balatā) is simply strength, he says, 'endowed with strength.' 'Having made a state of neediness' means having generated a special state of neediness for that Dhamma. 'With the whole mind' means with the entire, complete mind, because it is engaged everywhere—at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end of the teaching.

500. Sabhāvoti ariyasāvakassa puthujjanehi asādhāraṇatāya āveṇiko sabhāvo. Suṭṭhu samannesitoti sammadeva upaparikkhito. Sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāyāti sotāpattiphalassa sacchikaraṇena, sacchikatabhāvenāti attho. Tenāha “sotāpattiphalasacchikatañāṇenā”ti. Paṭhamamaggaphalassa [V 2.0289] paccavekkhaṇañāṇavisesā hete pavattiākārabhinnā. Tenevāha “sattahi mahāpaccavekkhaṇañāṇehī”ti. Ayaṃ tāva ācariyānaṃ samānakathāti “idamassa paṭhamaṃ ñāṇa”ntiādinā vuttāni paccavekkhaṇañāṇāni, na maggañāṇānīti evaṃ pavattā paramparāgatā pubbācariyānaṃ samānā sādhāraṇā imissā pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathā atthavaṇṇanā. Tattha kāraṇamāha “lokuttaramaggo hi bahucittakkhaṇiko nāma natthī”ti. Yadi so bahucittakkhaṇiko siyā nānābhisamayo, tathā sati saṃyojanattayādīnaṃ ekadesappahānaṃ pāpuṇātīti ariyamaggassa anantaraphalattā ekadesasotāpannatādibhāvo āpajjati, phalānaṃ vā anekabhāvo, sabbametaṃ ayuttanti tasmā ekacittakkhaṇikova ariyamaggo.

500. “Sabhāvo” means the inherent nature of a noble disciple, which is unique and not shared with ordinary people. “Suṭṭhu samannesito” means well-investigated. “Sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya” means by the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; that is, by the state of having realized it. Therefore, it is said, “by the knowledge that has realized the fruit of stream-entry.” These are particular knowledges of reviewing the first path and its fruit, differing in their modes of occurrence. Therefore it is said, “by the seven great reviewing knowledges.” This is the consistent explanation of the teachers: the reviewing knowledges stated as “this is his first knowledge” and so on, are not the path knowledges. Thus, this traditional explanation of the Pāli is the common and consistent commentary of the ancient teachers. Therein, the reason is stated: “For the supramundane path does not occur for multiple thought-moments.” If it were to occur for multiple thought-moments, there would be diverse realizations; and in that case, a partial abandonment of the three fetters and so on would result. Because the noble path has an immediate fruit, a state of partial stream-entry and so on would occur, or the fruits would be multiple. All of this is incorrect. Therefore, the noble path occurs in only a single thought-moment.

Yaṃ pana suttapadaṃ nissāya vitaṇḍavādī ariyamaggassa ekacittakkhaṇikataṃ paṭikkhipati, taṃ dassento “satta vassānīti hi vacanato”ti āha. Kilesā pana lahu…pe… chijjantīti vadantena hi khippaṃ tāva kilesappahānaṃ, dandhapavattikā maggabhāvanāti paṭiññātaṃ hoti. Tattha sace maggassa bhāvanāya āraddhamattāya kilesā pahīyanti, sesā maggabhāvanā niratthakā siyā, atha pacchā kilesappahānaṃ, kilesā pana lahu [M 2.0311] chijjantīti idaṃ micchā, “sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāyā”ti vakkhatīti. Tato suttapaṭijānanato. Maggaṃ abhāvetvāti ariyamaggaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā abhāvetvā. Attharasaṃ viditvāti suttassa aviparīto attho eva attharaso, taṃ yāthāvato ñatvā. Evaṃ vitaṇḍavādivādaṃ bhinditvā vuttamevatthaṃ nigametuṃ “imāni satta ñāṇānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

Regarding the passage in the sutta based on which the contentious speaker rejects the single-thought-moment nature of the noble path, to illustrate this, he says, “Because of the statement ‘seven years’.” By one who says, “Defilements… are quickly cut off,” it is asserted that the abandonment of defilements is rapid, and the cultivation of the path is slow. Here, if defilements are abandoned merely upon beginning the cultivation of the path, the remaining cultivation of the path would be pointless. But if the abandonment of defilements happens later, then the statement “defilements are quickly cut off” is false, since it will be said, “for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.” This follows from acknowledging the sutta. “Not having developed the path” means not having developed the noble path to its fulfillment. “Having understood the essence of the meaning” means having known the undistorted meaning of the sutta, which is the essence of the meaning, as it actually is. Having thus refuted the contentious argument, to conclude the meaning that was stated, it is said, “These seven knowledges,” and so on. The rest is easily understood.

Kosambiyasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā samattā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Kosambiya Sutta is complete.

9. Brahmanimantanikasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Brahmanimantanika Sutta

501. “Sassato [V 2.0290] attā ca loko cā”ti (dī. ni. 1.30) evaṃ pavattā diṭṭhi sassatadiṭṭhi (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.175). Saha kāyenāti saha tena brahmattabhāvena. Brahmaṭṭhānanti attano brahmavatthuṃ. “Aniccaṃ nicca”nti vadati aniccatāya attano apaññāyamānattā. Thiranti daḷhaṃ, vināsābhāvato sārabhūtanti attho. Uppādavipariṇāmābhāvato sadā vijjamānaṃ. Kevalanti paripuṇṇaṃ. Tenāha “akhaṇḍa”nti. Kevalanti vā jātiādīhi amissaṃ, virahitanti adhippāyo. Uppādādīnaṃ abhāvato eva acavanadhammaṃ. Koci jāyanako vā…pe… upapajjanako vā natthi niccabhāvato. Ṭhānena saddhiṃ tannivāsīnaṃ niccabhāvañhi so paṭijānāti. Tisso jhānabhūmiyoti dutiyatatiyacatutthajjhānabhūmiyo. Catutthajjhānabhūmivisesā hi asaññasuddhāvāsāruppabhavā. Paṭibāhatīti santaṃyeva samānaṃ ajānantova natthīti paṭikkhipati. Avijjāya gatoti avijjāya saha gato pavatto. Sahayoge hi idaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Tenāha “samannāgato”ti. Aññāṇīti avidvā. Paññācakkhuvirahato andho bhūto, andhabhāvaṃ vā pattoti andhībhūto.

501. “The self and the world are eternal”—a view that has thus arisen is the eternalist view. “Together with the body” means together with that state of being a Brahmā. “The Brahmā-place” means one's own Brahmā-basis. He says “impermanent as permanent” because its own impermanence is not discerned. “Firm” means solid; the meaning is, being the essence due to the absence of destruction. It exists always because of the absence of arising and changing. “Complete” means whole. Hence it is said “unbroken.” Or “complete” means unmixed with birth and so forth; the intention is “devoid of.” It is of a nature not to pass away precisely because of the absence of arising and so on. There is no one who is born or reborn, due to its eternal nature. For he professes the eternal nature of the dwellers there along with the place. “The three jhāna-planes” refers to the second, third, and fourth jhāna-planes. For the special planes of the fourth jhāna are the non-percipient beings, the Pure Abodes, and the formless realms. “He denies” means, while it does exist, not knowing it, he rejects it, saying, “it is not.” “Gone by ignorance” means gone along with, or proceeded with, ignorance. This is an instrumental case in the sense of association. Hence it is said “endowed.” “Ignorant” means unwise. “Become blind” means, due to being devoid of the eye of wisdom, he has become blind, or has attained a state of blindness.

502. Tadā bhagavato subhagavane viharaṇassa avicchinnataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “subhagavane viharatīti ñatvā”ti. Tattha pana tadāssa bhagavato adassanaṃ sandhāyāha “kattha nu kho gatoti olokento”ti. Brahmalokaṃ gacchantaṃ disvāti iminā katipayacittavāravasena tadā bhagavato [M 2.0312] brahmalokagamanaṃ jātaṃ, na ekacittakkhaṇenāti dasseti. Na cettha kāyagatiyā cittapariṇāmanaṃ adhippetaṃ – “seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyyā”tiādivacanato (ma. ni. 1.501). Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Vichandanti chandavigamaṃ. Apasāditoti diṭṭhiyā gāhassa viparivattanena santajjito. “Metamāsado”ti vacanena upatthambho hutvā.

502. With reference to the uninterrupted residence of the Blessed One in Subhagavana at that time, it was said, “Knowing that he dwells in Subhagavana.” But with reference to the Blessed One’s being unseen at that time, it was said, “Looking around, wondering, ‘Where has he gone?’” By this phrase, “Seeing him going to the Brahmā-world,” it is shown that the Blessed One’s journey to the Brahmā-world occurred over several turns of thought-processes, not in a single thought-moment. Here, a transformation of mind by means of bodily movement is not intended—as stated in the passage, “Just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm…” Whatever should be said here has already been stated below. “Vichanda” means the disappearance of desire. “Repulsed” means being intimidated by the reversal of the grip of wrong view. The statement, “Do not approach me,” served as a support.

Anvāvisitvāti āvisanavasena tassa attabhāvaṃ adhibhavitvā. Tathā abhibhavato hi tassa sarīraṃ paviṭṭho viya hotīti vuttaṃ “sarīraṃ pavisitvā”ti. Yañhi sattaṃ devayakkhanāgādayo āvisanti, tassa pākatikakiriyamayaṃ cittappavattiṃ nivāretvā attano iddhānubhāvena yaṃ icchitaṃ hasitalapitādi, taṃ tena kārāpenti, kārentā ca āviṭṭhapuggalassa cittavasena [V 2.0291] kārenti. “Attanovā”ti na vattabbametaṃ acinteyyattā kammajassa iddhānubhāvassāti keci. Apare pana yathā tadā cakkhuviññāṇādipavatti āviṭṭhapuggalasseva, evaṃ kiriyamayacittapavattipi tasseva, āvesakānubhāvena pana sāmaññatā parivattati. Tathā hi mahānubhāvaṃ puggalaṃ te āvisituṃ na sakkonti, tikicchāvuṭṭhāpane pana chavasarīraṃ anupavisitvā satantaṃ karoti vijjānubhāvena. Korakhattiyādīnaṃ pana chavasarīrassa uṭṭhānaṃ vacīnicchāraṇañca kevalaṃ buddhānubhāvena. Acinteyyā hi buddhānaṃ buddhānubhāvāti. Abhibhavitvā ṭhitoti sakalalokaṃ attano ānubhāvena abhibhavitvā ṭhito. Jeṭṭhakoti padhāno, tādisaṃ vā ānubhāvasampannattā uttamo. Passatīti daso. Visesavacanicchāya abhāvato anavasesavisayo daso-saddoti āha “sabbaṃ passatī”ti. Sabbajananti laddhanāmaṃ sabbasattakāyaṃ. Vase vatteti, seṭṭhattā nimmāpakattā ca attano vase vatteti. Lokassa īsanasīlatāya issaro. Sattānaṃ kammassa kārakabhāvena kattā. Thāvarajaṅgamavibhāgaṃ sakalaṃ lokaṃ nimmānetīti nimmātā.

“Having possessed” means having overpowered his individual existence by means of entering. For when one overpowers thus, it is as if one has entered the body; hence the phrase “having entered the body.” When beings such as devas, yakkhas, or nāgas possess someone, they prevent the natural activity of that person’s mind and, by their own psychic power, make them perform whatever they wish—laughing, speaking, etc.—and while causing such actions, they cause them through the mind of the possessed person. Some hold that “of one’s own” cannot be said here due to the incomprehensibility of the psychic power born of kamma. Others, however, say that just as at that time the activity of eye-consciousness and so on belongs to the possessed person, so too does the activity of functional consciousness belong to them, but its normal state is altered by the power of the possessor. For they cannot possess a being of great power; but in healing, one can enter a corpse and make it conscious by the power of spells. However, the rising of the corpse of Korakkhattiya and others, as well as the utterance of speech, is solely due to the power of the Buddha. The powers of the Buddhas are indeed inconceivable. “Standing having overpowered” means standing having overpowered the entire world by his power. “Foremost” means chief, or supreme because he is endowed with such power. Because he sees (passati), he is a seer (dasa). Due to the absence of a term indicating distinction, the word “dasa” has an object without remainder; hence it is said, “he sees all.” “All people” is a name given to the entire mass of beings. “He wields power over them”; because he is supreme and the creator, he wields power over them. Due to his nature of ruling the world, he is the lord. As the agent of beings’ kamma, he is the maker. He creates the entire world, divided into the stationary and the moving, hence he is the creator.

Guṇavisesena loke pāsaṃsattā seṭṭho. Tādiso ca ukkaṭṭhatamo hotīti āha “uttamo”ti. Sattānaṃ nimmānaṃ tathā tathā sajanaṃ visajanaṃ viya hotīti āha “tvaṃ khattiyo”tiādi. Jhānādīsu attano citte ca ciṇṇavasittā vasī. Bhūtānanti nibbattānaṃ. Bhavaṃ abhijātaṃ [M 2.0313] arahantīti bhabyā, sambhavesino, tesaṃ bhabyānaṃ. Tenāha “aṇḍajajalābujā sattā”tiādi.

One is best in the world because of being praised for a special quality. Such a one is the most excellent; hence, it is said, “the highest.” The creation of beings is like assigning and dismissing them in various ways—hence, it is said, “You are a noble,” and so on. One is a master because of having practiced and achieved mastery in one’s own mind in things like jhāna. “Bhūtāni” means those who have arisen. “Bhabyā” refers to those worthy of a noble becoming, those seeking existence. Hence, it is said, “beings born from eggs, from wombs,” and so forth.

Pathavīādayo niccā dhuvā sassatā. Ye tesaṃ “aniccā”tiādinā garahakā jigucchā sattā, te ayathābhūtavāditāya matakāle apāyaniṭṭhā ahesuṃ. Ye pana pathavīādīnaṃ “niccā dhuvā”tiādinā pasaṃsakā, te yathābhūtavāditāya brahmakāyūpagā ahesunti māro pāpimā anvayato byatirekato ca pathavīādimukhena saṅkhārānaṃ pariññāpaññāpane ādīnavaṃ vibhāveti tato vivecetukāmo. Tenāha “pathavīgarahakā”tiādi. Ettha ca māro pathavīādidhātumahābhūtaggahaṇena manussalokaṃ, bhūtaggahaṇena cātumahārājike, devaggahaṇena avasesakāmadevalokaṃ, pajāpatiggahaṇena attano ṭhānaṃ, brahmaggahaṇena brahmakāyike gaṇhi. Ābhassarādayo pana avisayatāya eva anena aggahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Taṇhādiṭṭhivasenāti taṇhābhinandanāya diṭṭhābhinandanāya ca vasena. “Etaṃ mama, eso me attā”ti abhinandino abhinandakā, abhinandanasīlā vā. Brahmuno ovāde ṭhitānaṃ iddhānubhāvaṃ dassetīti tesaṃ tattha sannipatitabrahmānaṃ iddhānubhāvaṃ tassa mahābrahmuno ovāde ṭhitattā nibbattaṃ katvā dasseti. Yasenāti [V 2.0292] ānubhāvena. Siriyāti sobhāya. Maṃ brahmaparisaṃ upanesīti yādisā brahmaparisā issariyādisampattiyā, tattha maṃ uyyojesi. Mahājanassa māraṇatoti mahājanassa vivaṭṭūpanissayaguṇavināsanena ānubhāvena māraṇato. Ayasanti yasapaṭipakkhaṃ akittikammānubhāvañcāti attho.

The earth and other elements are permanent, stable, eternal. Those beings who, with words like “impermanent,” criticize and despise them, speak falsely and at death fall into states of woe. But those who praise the earth and other elements with words like “permanent” and “stable,” speak truthfully and are reborn in the Brahma-world. Thus, Māra the Evil One, through the earth and other elements, reveals the dangers in fully understanding the formations by way of inclusion and exclusion, wishing to divert them from it. Therefore, it is said, “those who criticize the earth,” etc. Here, Māra grasps the human world through the elements like earth, the realm of the Four Great Kings through the term “beings,” the remaining sensual heavens through the term “gods,” his own abode through the term “Pajāpati,” and the Brahma-world through the term “Brahma.” The Ābhassara and other realms, however, are not included here, as they are beyond his sphere. By means of craving and views—that is, through delight in craving and delight in views. “This is mine, this is my self”—those who delight, who are prone to delight, or whose nature is to delight. He displays the psychic power of those standing firm in Brahma’s instruction—that is, having produced the psychic power of those Brahmās assembled there due to their adherence to the Great Brahma’s instruction, he displays it. By fame—that is, by power. By splendor—that is, by radiance. He led me to his Brahma assembly—that is, he appointed me to a Brahma assembly such as his, endowed with sovereignty and other attainments. The killing of the multitude—that is, killing by the power that destroys the virtues of the great multitude, which are the supporting condition for their progress. Disgrace—that is, the opposite of fame, and the result of deeds causing ill-repute. This is the meaning.

503. Kasiṇaṃ āyunti vassasataṃ sandhāya vadati. Upanissāya setīti upasayo, upasayova opasāyiko yathā “venayiko”ti (ma. ni. 1.246; a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 8) āha “samīpasayo”ti. Sayaggahaṇañcettha nidassanamattanti dassetuṃ “maṃ gacchanta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Anekatthattā dhātūnaṃ vattanattho daṭṭhabbo. Mama vatthusmiṃ sayanakoti mayhaṃ ṭhāne visaye vattanako. Bāhitvāti nīcaṃ katvā, abhibhavitvā vā. Jajjharikāgumbatoti ettha jajjharikā nāma pathaviṃ pattharitvā jātā ekā gacchajāti.

503. He says 'the entire lifespan' with reference to a hundred years. 'Upasayo' is so called because one lies down (seti) relying upon (upanissāya) it; 'opasāyiko' is derived from this, just as 'venayiko' is. He says 'samīpasayo' (lying near). Here, the use of the term 'sayana' (lying) is merely illustrative, as is shown by phrases like 'maṃ gacchanta' (going to me). Because roots have multiple meanings, the sense of acting or existing should be understood. 'Mama vatthusmiṃ sayanako' means one who acts or exists in my place or domain. 'Bāhitvā' means lowering or overpowering. Regarding 'jajjharikāgumbato,' here 'jajjharikā' is a type of creeping plant that spreads over the ground.

Imināti [M 2.0314] “sace kho tvaṃ bhikkhū”tiādivacanena. Esa brahmā. Upalāpetīti saṅgaṇhāti. Apasādetīti niggaṇhāti. Sesapadehīti vatthusāyiko yathākāmakaraṇīyo bāhiteyyoti imehi padehi. Mayhaṃ ārakkhaṃ gaṇhissasīti mama ārakkhako bhavissasi. Lakuṇḍakataranti nīcataraṃ nihīnavuttisarīraṃ.

By this—with the statement beginning “sace kho tvaṃ bhikkhū.” This is Brahmā. “Upalāpeti” means to conciliate, to win over. “Apasādeti” means to reject, to subdue. By “the remaining expressions” (sesapadehi)—by these expressions: “vatthusāyiko,” “yathākāmakaraṇīyo,” “bāhiteyyo,” meaning one who resides on the property, one who can be treated as one pleases, and one who is to be kept out. “Mayhaṃ ārakkhaṃ gaṇhissasi” means you will become my guardian. “Lakuṇḍakataranti” means having a lower, more degraded body and way of life.

Phusitumpi samatthaṃ kiñci na passati, pageva ñāṇavibhavanti adhippāyo. Nipphattinti nipphajjanaṃ, phalanti attho. Tañhi kāraṇavasena gantabbato adhigantabbato gatīti vuccati. Ānubhāvanti pabhāvaṃ. So hi jotanaṭṭhena virocanaṭṭhena jutīti vuccati. Mahatā ānubhāvena paresaṃ abhibhavanato mahesoti akkhāyatīti mahesakkho. Tayidaṃ abhibhavanaṃ kittisampattiyā parivārasampattiyā cāti āha “mahāyaso mahāparivāro”ti.

He sees nothing that he is even capable of touching, let alone the splendor of knowledge—this is the meaning. “Nipphatti” means accomplishment, the fruit. Because it is to be reached or attained by way of its cause, it is called “gati” (destination). “Ānubhāva” means power. It is called “juti” (radiance) in the sense of shining and illuminating. Because he overpowers others with great power, he is called “mahesakkho” (one of great influence). This overpowering comes from the accomplishment of fame and the accomplishment of a retinue, as stated: “mahāyaso mahāparivāro” (of great fame and great following).

Pariharantīti sineruṃ dakkhiṇato katvā parivattanti. Disāti bhummatthe etaṃ paccattavacananti āha “disāsu virocamānā”ti. Attano jutiyā dibbamānāya vā. Tehīti candimasūriyehi. Tattakena pamāṇenāti yattake candimasūriyehi obhāsiyamāno lokadhātusaṅkhāto eko loko, tattakena pamāṇena. Idaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ buddhānaṃ uppattiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ padhānaṃ, tasmā yebhuyyena etthupapannā devatā aññesu cakkavāḷesu devatā abhibhuyya vattanti. Tathā hi brahmā sahampati dasasahassabrahmaparivāro bhagavato santikaṃ upagañchi. Tenāha “ettha cakkavāḷasahasse tuyhaṃ vaso vattatī”ti. Idāni “ettha te vattate vaso”ti vuttaṃ vase vattanaṃ sarūpato [V 2.0293] dassetuṃ “paroparañca jānāsī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha paṭhamagāthāyaṃ vuttaṃ ettha-saddaṃ ānetvā attho veditabboti dassento “ettha cakkavāḷasahasse”ti āha. Uccanīceti jātikularūpabhogaparivārādivasena uḷāre ca anuḷāre ca. Ayaṃ iddho ayaṃ pakatimanussoti iminā “sarūpato evassa sattānaṃ paroparajānanaṃ, na samudāgamato”ti dasseti. Yaṃ pana vakkhati “sattānaṃ āgatiṃ gatinti, taṃ kāmaloke sattānaṃ ādānanikkhepajānanamattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na kammavipākajānanaṃ. Yadi hi samudāgamato jāneyya, attanopi jāneyya, na cassa taṃ atthīti, tathā āha “itthambhāvoti [M 2.0315] idaṃ cakkavāḷa”ntiādi. Rāgayogato rāgo etassa atthīti vā rāgo, virajjanasīlo virāgī, taṃ rāgavirāginaṃ. Sahassibrahmā nāma tvaṃ cūḷaniyā eva lokadhātuyā jānanato. Tayāti nissakke karaṇavacanaṃ. Catuhatthāyāti anekahatthena sāṇipākārena kātabbapaṭappamāṇaṃ dīghato catuhatthāya, vitthārato dvihatthāya pilotikāya kātuṃ vāyamanto viya gopphake udake nimujjitukāmo viya ca pamāṇaṃ ajānanto vihaññatīti niggaṇhāti.

They circle around Sineru, keeping it to their right. 'Disā' (direction): this is a nominative used in the sense of the locative, as it is said, “shining in the directions.” By their own radiance, or by divine radiance. “Tehi” (by them)—that is, by the moon and sun. “Tattakena pamāṇena” (by that measure)—the extent to which a single world-system is illuminated by the moon and sun, that is the measure. This world-sphere is the supreme and foremost birthplace of the Buddhas, which is why the deities mostly born here surpass the deities in other world-spheres. For instance, Brahmā Sahampati, with a retinue of ten thousand Brahmās, approached the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said, “Here, in a thousand world-spheres, your dominion prevails.” Now, to show the nature of this dominion, it is said, “you know others, inferior and superior,” and so on. Here, the meaning should be understood by bringing in the word “here” from the first verse, as it is said, “here in a thousand world-spheres.” “Uccanīce” (high and low)—in terms of birth, family, form, wealth, retinue, and so on, whether grand or humble. “This one is powerful, this one is an ordinary person”—by this, it is shown that his knowledge of other beings, inferior and superior, is of their nature, not from direct encounter. As for what is said, “the coming and going of beings,” this refers merely to knowing the taking up and laying down of beings in the sensual realm, not to knowing the results of kamma. If he knew by direct encounter, he would know his own as well, but that is not the case. Therefore, it is said, “such is the nature of this world-sphere,” and so on. One is 'rāgī' (lustful) because of connection with lust, or because lust exists for him. One whose nature is to be dispassionate is 'virāgī.' This refers to the lustful and the dispassionate. You are called 'Sahassibrahmā' (Thousandfold Brahmā) because you know only this minor world-system. 'Tayā' (by you)—this is an instrumental case in a non-agentive sense. 'Catuhatthāya' (four hands long)—he rebukes him for struggling without knowing the proper measure, like one trying to make something the size of a screen with a small rag four hands long and two hands wide, or like one wanting to sink in ankle-deep water.

504. Taṃ kāyanti tadeva nikāyaṃ. Jānitabbaṭṭhānaṃ patvāpīti anaññasādhāraṇā mayhaṃ sīlādayo guṇavisesā tāva tiṭṭhantu, īdisaṃ lokiyaṃ parittakaṃ jānitabbaṭṭhānampi patvā. Ayaṃ imesaṃ atisayena nīcoti nīceyyo, tassa bhāvo nīceyyanti āha “tayā nīcatarabhāvo pana mayhaṃ kuto”ti.

504. “Taṃ kāyaṃ” (that body) means that very collection. “Jānitabbaṭṭhānaṃ patvāpi” (even having reached the state of what should be known): The meaning is: Let my unique special qualities, such as morality, which are not shared by others, stand for now; even having attained this insignificant, worldly state of what should be known. “Nīceyyo” means one who is exceedingly low among these; the state of being so is “nīceyya.” Then he asks, “But how could there be for me a state lower than you?”

Heṭṭhūpapattikoti uparūparito cavitvā heṭṭhā laddhūpapattiko. Evaṃ saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “anuppanne buddhuppāde”ti āha. Heṭṭhūpapattikaṃ katvāti heṭṭhūpapattikaṃ patthanaṃ katvā. Yathā kenaci bahūsu ānantariyesu katesu yaṃ tattha garutaraṃ balavaṃ, tadeva paṭisandhiṃ deti, itarāni pana tassa anubalappadāyakāni honti, na paṭisandhidāyakāni, evaṃ catūsu rūpajjhānesu bhāvitesu yaṃ tattha garutaraṃ chandapaṇidhiadhimokkhādivasena sābhisaṅkhārañca, tadeva ca paṭisandhiṃ deti, itarāni pana aladdhokāsatāya tassa anubalappadāyakāni honti, na paṭisandhidāyakāni, tannibbattitajjhāneneva āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti hotīti āha “tatiyajjhānaṃ paṇītaṃ bhāvetvā”ti. Tatthāti subhakiṇhabrahmaloke. Puna tatthāti ābhassarabrahmaloke. Paṭhamakāleti tasmiṃ bhave paṭhamasmiṃ kāle. Ubhayanti atītaṃ attano nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ, tattha nibbattiyā hetubhūtaṃ attano katakammanti ubhayaṃ. Pamussitvā kālassa ciratarabhāvato. Vītināmeti paṭipajjantīti ca tadā tassā kiriyāya pavattikkhaṇaṃ upādāya pavattamānapayogo.

“Heṭṭhūpapattiko” (one who is reborn below) means having passed away from higher realms and obtained rebirth in lower ones. Thus, to explain in detail the meaning stated briefly, he said, “before the arising of a Buddha.” “Heṭṭhūpapattikaṃ katvā” (having made rebirth below) means having made the aspiration for rebirth below. Just as when many immediately retributive actions have been performed by someone, the heaviest and most powerful among them determines rebirth, while the others only provide supporting strength to it without being the cause of rebirth—similarly, among the four form jhānas developed, whichever is heaviest due to desire, determination, resolution, etc., and is volitional, that alone determines rebirth. The others, because they do not get an opportunity, only provide supporting strength to it without being the cause of rebirth. Future rebirth arises from that jhāna alone—hence it is said, “having developed the third jhāna as excellent.” “Tattha” (there) refers to the Subhakiṇha Brahma-world. “Puna tattha” (again there) refers to the Ābhassara Brahma-world. “Paṭhamakāle” (at the first time) means in the first moment of that existence. “Ubhayaṃ” (both) refers to the past—one’s own place of birth and one's own deeds that were the cause of rebirth there. “Pamussitvā” (having forgotten) due to the very long passage of time. The expressions “vītināmeti” (passes time) and “paṭipajjanti” (they proceed) are present tense usages referring to the very moment that action occurred.

Apāyesīti [V 2.0294] pāyesi. Pipāsiteti tasite. Ghammanīti ghammakāle. Sampareteti ghammapariḷāhena pipāsāya abhibhūte. Nti pānīyadānaṃ. Vatasīlavattanti samādānavasena vatabhūtaṃ cārittasīlabhāvena samāciṇṇattā [M 2.0316] sīlavattaṃ. Suttappabuddhova anussarāmīti supitvā pabuddhamatto viya supinaṃ tava pubbanivutthaṃ mama pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇena anussarāmi, sabbaññutaññāṇena viya paccakkhato passāmīti attho.

“Apāyesi” means he gave water to drink. “Pipāsita” means thirsty. “Ghammani” means in the hot season. “Sampareta” means overcome by the scorching heat and thirst. This refers to the gift of water. “Vatasīlavattaṃ”: “Vata” (vow) because it is undertaken as an observance; “sīlavatta” (virtuous conduct) because it is constantly practiced as virtuous conduct. “Suttappabuddhova anussarāmi” (like one awakened from sleep, I remember) means: just as one who has just awakened from sleep remembers a dream, so I remember your former life with my knowledge of past lives, as if seeing directly with the knowledge of omniscience—this is the meaning.

Karamareti vilumpitvā ānīte. Kammasajjanti yuddhasajjaṃ, āvudhādāyininti attho.

“Karamareti” means those brought by plunder. “Kammasajjaṃ” (equipped for action) means ready for war; the meaning is taking up weapons.

Eṇīkūlasminti eṇīmigabāhullena “eṇīkūla”nti saṅkhaṃ gate gaṅgāya tīrappadese. Gayhaka nīyamānanti gayhavasena karamarabhāvena corehi attano ṭhānaṃ nīyamānaṃ.

“Eṇīkūlasmiṃ” means on the bank of the Ganges in the region known as “Eṇīkūla” because of the abundance of Eṇī deer. “Gayhaka nīyamānaṃ” (being led away as a captive) means being taken to their own place by thieves as a captive and as plunder.

Āvāhavivāhavasena mittasanthavaṃ katvā. “Evaṃ amhesu kīḷantesu gaṅgeyyako nāgo kupito”ti mayi saññampi na karontīti. Susukāranti susūti pavattaṃ bheravanāganissāsaṃ.

Having established friendships through marriage alliances. “Evaṃ amhesu kīḷantesu gaṅgeyyako nāgo kupito” (while we were playing like this, the Nāga Gaṅgeyyaka became angry), yet they paid no attention to me. “Susukāra” means the terrifying exhalation of the Nāga, occurring as a hissing sound.

Gahītanāvanti viheṭhetukāmatāya gatinivāraṇavasena gahitaṃ niggahitaṃ nāvaṃ. Luddenāti kurūrena. Manussakappāti nāvāgatānaṃ manussānaṃ viheṭhetukāmatāya.

“Gahītanāvaṃ” (a seized boat) means a boat taken and held back with the intention to harm, by way of obstructing its passage. “Luddena” means by the cruel one. “Manussakappā” (with intention toward humans) means with the intention to harm the humans in the boat.

Baddhacaroti paṭibaddhacariyo. Tenāha “antevāsiko”ti. Taṃ nissāyevāti raññā upaṭṭhiyamānopi rājānaṃ pahāya taṃ kappaṃ antevāsiṃ nissāyeva.

“Baddhacaro” (bound in conduct) means one whose conduct is restricted. Hence it is said, “antevāsiko” (a pupil). “Taṃ nissāyeva” (depending on him alone) means even though attended upon by the king, abandoning the king, he depends on that worthy pupil alone.

Sambuddhimantaṃ vatinaṃ amaññīti ayaṃ sammadeva buddhimā vatasampannoti amaññi sambhāvesi ca.

“Sambuddhimantaṃ vatinaṃ amaññīti” means he thought, “This one is truly wise and endowed with observances,” and he esteemed him.

Nānattabhāvesūti nānā visuṃ visuṃ attabhāvesu.

“Nānattabhāvesu” (in various states of existence) means in diverse, separate, individual embodiments.

Addhāti ekaṃsena. Mametamāyunti mayhaṃ etaṃ yathāvuttaṃ tattha tattha bhave pavattaṃ āyuṃ. Na kevalaṃ mama āyumeva, atha kho aññampi sabbaññeyyaṃ jānāsi, na tuyhaṃ aviditaṃ nāma atthi. Tathā hi buddho sammāsambuddho tuvaṃ. No ce kathamayamattho ñāto? Tathā hi sammāsambuddhattā eva te ayaṃ jalito jotamāno ānubhāvo obhāsayaṃ sabbampi brahmalokaṃ obhāsento dibbamāno tiṭṭhatīti satthu asamasamataṃ pavedesi.

“Addhā” means certainly. “Mametamāyuṃ” (this is my lifespan) means this lifespan of mine that has occurred in various existences, as stated. Not only my lifespan, but you also know all that is to be known; there is nothing unknown to you. For truly, you are the Buddha, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. If not, how could this matter be known? Thus, because you are the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, this radiant, shining power of yours illuminates the entire Brahma world, standing resplendent—thus he proclaimed the Teacher’s incomparable state.

Pathavattenāti [M 2.0317][V 2.0295] pathavīattena. Tenāha “pathavīsabhāvenā”ti. Ettha ca yasmā – “sabbasaṅkhārasamathoti”ādinā (mahāva. 7; dī. ni. 2.64, 67; ma. ni. 1.281; saṃ. ni. 1.172) sādhāraṇato, “yattha neva pathavī”ti asādhāraṇato ca pathaviyā asabhāvena nibbānassa gahetabbatā atthi, taṃ nivattetvā pathaviyā anaññasādhāraṇaṃ sabhāvaṃ gahetuṃ “pathaviyā pathavattenā”ti vuttaṃ. Nāpahosinti na pāpuṇiṃ. Idha pathaviyā pāpuṇanaṃ nāma “etaṃ mamā”tiādinā gahaṇanti āha “taṇhādiṭṭhimānaggāhehi na gaṇhi”nti.

“Pathavattena” (by earthness) means by the earth-nature. Hence it is said, “by the earth-nature.” Here, because Nibbāna can be understood as the non-nature of earth—both generally, as in “the stilling of all formations,” and specifically, as in “where there is no earth”—to avert that interpretation and instead to grasp the unique nature of earth not common to anything else, it is said, “by the earthness of earth.” “Nāpahosiṃ” (I was not able) means I did not attain. Here, attainment of earth means grasping through “this is mine,” etc. Hence it is said, “he did not grasp with the grasps of craving, views, and pride.”

Vāditāyāti vādasīlatāya. Sabbanti akkharaṃ niddisitvāti “sabbaṃ kho ahaṃ brahme”tiādinā bhagavatā vuttaṃ sabba-saddaṃ – “sace kho te mārisa sabbassa sabbattena ananubhūta”nti paccanubhāsanavasena niddisitvā. Akkhare dosaṃ gaṇhantoti bhagavatā sakkāyasabbaṃ sandhāya sabba-sadde gahite sabbasabbavasena tadatthaparivattanena sabba-saddavacanīyatāsāmaññena ca dosaṃ gaṇhanto. Tenāha “satthā panā”tiādi. Tattha yadi sabbaṃ ananubhūtaṃ “natthi sabba”nti loke anavasesaṃ pucchati. Sace sabbassa sabbattena anavasesasabhāvena ananubhūtaṃ appattaṃ, taṃ gaganakusumaṃ viya kiñci na siyā. Athassa ananubhūtaṃ atthīti assa sabbattena ananubhūtaṃ yadi atthi, “sabba”nti idaṃ vacanaṃ micchā, sabbaṃ nāma taṃ na hotīti adhippāyo. Tenāha “mā heva te rittakamevā”tiādi.

“Vāditāyāti” means by the habit of arguing. “Sabbaṃ”: having pointed out the word 'all' as spoken by the Blessed One in the phrase 'sabbaṃ kho ahaṃ brahme' and so on, by way of repeating it back, as in 'if, sir, all is unexperienced by you in its allness.' “Akkhare dosaṃ gaṇhanto”: when the Blessed One used the word 'all' referring to the 'all' of personal identity (sakkāya), he found fault by transforming its meaning to the 'all' of everything, due to the commonality of what can be denoted by the word 'all'. Therefore, it is said: 'But the Teacher,' and so on. Here, if 'all' is unexperienced, he asks about everything in the world without remainder, 'Does 'all' not exist?' If the entirety of all, in its complete nature, is unexperienced and unattained, it would be like a flower in the sky—it would be nothing. But if there is something unexperienced by him, then if something of the entirety is unexperienced, the statement 'all' is false—meaning that it is not truly 'all'. Therefore, it is said: 'Let it not be empty for you,' and so on.

Ahaṃ sabbañca vakkhāmi, ananubhūtañca vakkhāmīti ahaṃ “sabba”nti ca vakkhāmi, “ananubhūta”nti ca vakkhāmi, ettha ko dosoti adhippāyo. Kāraṇaṃ āharantoti sabbassa sabbattena ananubhūtassa atthibhāve kāraṇaṃ niddisanto. Vijānitabbanti maggaphalapaccavekkhaṇañāṇehi visesato sabbasaṅkhatavisiṭṭhatāya jānitabbaṃ. Anidassananti idaṃ nibbānassa sanidassanaduke dutiyapadasahitatādassananti adhippāyena “cakkhuviññāṇassa āpāthaṃ anupagamanato anidassanaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbasaṅkhatavidhuratāya vā natthi etassa nidassananti anidassanaṃ. Natthi etassa antoti anantaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “tayida”ntiādi.

“Ahaṃ sabbañca vakkhāmi, ananubhūtañca vakkhāmi”: the intention is, 'I will speak of “all,” and I will speak of “the unexperienced.” What fault is there in this?' “Kāraṇaṃ āharanto”: pointing out the reason for the existence of the unexperienced in its allness. “Vijānitabbaṃ”: it should be distinctly known by the knowledges of reviewing the path and fruition, because of its distinction from all conditioned things. “Anidassanaṃ”: this is called 'without indication' because it does not come into the range of eye-consciousness; this is to show its inclusion with the second term in the pair 'with indication' concerning Nibbāna. Or, because it is devoid of all conditioned things, there is no indication of it—thus, it is 'without indication'. There is no end of it—thus, it is 'endless'. Therefore, it is said: 'this indeed,' and so on.

Bhūtānīti paccayasambhūtāni. Asambhūtanti paccayehi asambhūtaṃ, nibbānanti attho. Apabhassarabhāvahetūnaṃ sabbaso abhāvā sabbato [M 2.0318] pabhāti sabbatopabhaṃ. Tenāha “nibbānato hī”tiādi. Tathā hi vuttaṃ – “tamo tattha na vijjatī”ti. (Netti. 104) pabhūtamevāti pakaṭṭhabhāvena ukkaṭṭhabhāvena vijjamānameva. Arūpībhāvena adesikattā sabbato pabhavati vijjatīti sabbatopabhaṃ. Tenāha “puratthimadisādīsū”tiādi. Pavisanti etthāti pavisaṃ, tadeva [V 2.0296] sa-kārassa bha-kāraṃ, vi-kārassa ca lopaṃ katvā vuttaṃ “pabha”nti. Tenāha “titthassa nāma”nti.
